( Tim Shallice and Elizabeth Warrington , 1970) had a two-item span and normal long-term learning: a double dissociation that supports separate stores. Yet neither store proved unitary, and mere repetition does little for LTM. Exam trap The stage model has three stores; working memory is NOT one of them (RML 2025), and information must pass through short-term (sometimes "short-term (working)") memory to reach LTM. RML 2024 keys "McCray and Hunter" ( J. W. McCrary and W. S. Hunter , 1953) for first observing the primacy-recency effect, although Ebbinghaus noted it in 1885. Better recall of the last items is recency, not the Flynn effect (rising IQ scores) or halo effect (a rating bias). As order effects in a psychophysics experiment, primacy and recency are controlled by counterbalancing (Section 1.3). Working memory Multiply 24 by 7 in your head and you must hold numbers, calculate and store a partial result at once. Alan Baddeley and Graham Hitch (1974) therefore recast STM as working memory , a limited-capacity system for holding and manipulating information during reasoning and comprehension. Using the dual-task method, they found that people holding six digits still reasoned accurately, so STM must have several parts (Figure 1.9). Central executive attentional controller Visuospatial sketchpad visual cache and inner scribe Episodic buffer (added in 2000) binds information into episodes Phonological loop phonological store and articulatory control process Long-term memory visual semantics episodic long-term memory language Figure 1.9 Baddeley's working memory model (Baddeley and Hitch, 1974; episodic buffer added by Baddeley, 2000). The central executive directs attention but stores nothing; the three subsidiary systems hold information and exchange it with long-term memory. The phonological loop stores and rehearses auditory-verbal information: a phonological store (inner ear) holds speech sounds for about two seconds, and an articulatory control process (inner voice) refreshes them. Similar-sounding items are confused, spans are larger for short words (the word-length effect), and articulatory suppression (saying "the, the, the") abolishes the word-length effect. The visuospatial sketchpad holds visual and spatial information, such as a mentally rotated object; Robert Logie (1995) split it into a visual cache and an inner scribe. The central executive , an attentional controller that stores nothing, focuses, divides and switches attention and inhibits unwanted responses. Random number generation loads it, and dorsolateral prefrontal damage causes a dysexecutive syndrome. In the Stroop task ( John Ridley Stroop , 1935), naming the ink colour of RED printed in blue is slow because automatic reading competes with controlled colour naming, an interference in selective attention (Section 1.5). The episodic buffer , added by Baddeley in 2000, holds about four chunks and binds information from the loop, the sketchpad and LTM into single, coherent episodes. STM is storage alone (forward span); working memory is storage plus processing, tested by complex span and by backward digit span. Exam trap Random number generation loads the central executive (RML 2022); repeating a word loads the loop, a spatial configuration the sketchpad, irrelevant speech the phonological store. A "visual executive loop" (Amity 2023) does not exist, and the Stroop effect is selective attention, not memory. Levels of processing Fergus Craik and Robert Lockhart (1972) argued that memory is a by-product of how deeply information is processed. Their levels of processing run from shallow structural processing (is the word in capitals?) through phonemic processing (does it rhyme with WEIGHT?) to deep semantic processing (does it fit the sentence?), and deeper processing leaves more durable traces, as Craik and Endel Tulving (1975) confirmed. Maintenance rehearsal, mere repetition, adds little to LTM; elaborative rehearsal, linking an item to meaning, builds it. Words judged for "Does this describe you?" are recalled about twice as well as words judged for meaning: the self-reference effect ( T. B. Rogers , Nicholas Kuiper and W. S. Kirker , 1977). Words you generate also beat words you merely read (the generation effect). Critics called depth circular, since it is defined by the memory it explains, and Donald Morris , John Bransford and Jeffery Franks (1977) found that rhyme processing wins on a rhyming test: memory depends on the match between study and test (transfer-appropriate processing). Exam trap The self-reference effect is Rogers, Kuiper and Kirker's (keyed "Rogers and Kuiper", RML 2024), not Craik and Lockhart's, Allan Paivio 's (dual coding theory, 1971: verbal plus imagery codes) or Michael Posner 's (attention). It means better recall of self-related information (IHBAS 2020), not self-concept, self-schema or self-awareness (Personality chapter). The systems of long-term memory Clive Wearing kept skills and facts but lost his past, so long-term memory is not one store. In 1972 Endel Tulving (1927 to 2023) separated episodic memory , personal events with their what, where and when (your first day of college), from semantic memory , the network of facts and concepts that make up our knowledge of the world, also called generic memory. Episodic recall carries autonoetic consciousness, a sense of travelling back in time; semantic memory carries only noetic knowing. Knowing how (riding a bicycle) is procedural memory . Tulving's patient K.C. kept his general knowledge but lost every episode of his life. Explicit memory involves conscious recollection, tested by recall and recognition; implicit memory is an influence of past experience on behaviour, feelings or thought without conscious recollection ( Peter Graf and Daniel Schacter , 1985), roughly Larry Squire 's declarative and nondeclarative memory. Declarative memory needs the hippocampus; nondeclarative memory covers procedural skills (striatum), priming, classical conditioning (amygdala, cerebellum) and habituation. In priming , earlier exposure eases processing of the same item (repetition priming) or a related one: BUTTER is recognised faster after BREAD (semantic priming; David Meyer and Roger Schvaneveldt , 1971), even with a masked, unseen prime, so semantic priming is a tool for studying subliminal perception. Exam trap Implicit memory does NOT involve conscious recollection (RML 2020); it "affects performance without conscious awareness" (RML 2025), and limited capacity describes STM. Procedural memory is one kind of implicit memory. Autobiographical memory holds the specific episodes of one's own life; older adults recall a surplus from ages 10 to 30, the reminiscence bump ( David Rubin and colleagues, 1986). Prospective memory , remembering to act in future (a tablet at 8 p.m.), contrasts with retrospective memory. Roger Brown and James Kulik (1977) named the flashbulb memory , a vivid memory of the circumstances in which one learned of a shocking event, and credited it to a "Now Print!" mechanism. Key study: Neisser and Harsch, the Challenger disaster (1992) The morning after the Challenger shuttle exploded in January 1986, Ulric Neisser and Nicole Harsch had students write down how they heard the news. Two and a half years later, a quarter of 44 were wrong on every major detail, yet confident. After 11 September 2001, Jennifer Talarico and David Rubin (2003) found that flashbulb and everyday memories lost consistency equally, but flashbulb memories stayed more vivid and more confidently believed. Flashbulb memories are thus special in vividness and confidence, not accuracy, and arise from emotional arousal at encoding plus rehearsal. Eidetic imagery , a visual image that lingers half a minute or more, occurs in a few children and rarely in adults. Metamemory ( John Flavell , 1971), knowledge and control of one's own memory, is part of metacognition and includes the feeling of knowing, a sense that one could recognise an answer one cannot recall. In the tip-of-the-tongue state , which Roger Brown and David McNeill (1966) produced with definitions of rare words (sextant), people knew the first letter and syllable count: the word was stored but not retrievable. Exam trap A vivid recollection of an important event is a flashbulb memory (RML 2025), not an engram, hindsight bias (the "knew it all along" distortion of memory) or equipotentiality. Its confidence stays very high as accuracy falls (NIMHANS 2026 recall), and arousal plus rehearsal explains it, not Now Print!, lack of interference or eidetic imagery. Tip-of-the-tongue is a retrieval failure (RML 2024), not storage, repression or aphasia (Wernicke's or Broca's, where language itself is damaged). Planning, monitoring and controlling memory is metacognition (IHBAS 2020), not attention, inhibition or a knowledge base. Networks, schemas and reconstruction In the hierarchical network of Allan Collins and Ross Quillian (1969), concepts are nodes (ANIMAL, BIRD, CANARY) and, by cognitive economy, each property is stored once at the highest node it fits, so "A canary has skin" takes longer to verify than "A canary can sing". In the spreading activation model of Collins and Elizabeth Loftus in 1975, activation spreads to related concepts and primes them. In connectionism , or parallel distributed processing ( David Rumelhart , James McClelland and colleagues, 1986), a concept is a pattern of simultaneous activation across many interconnected units, and knowledge lies in the connection weights. A proposition is the smallest unit of knowledge that can be true or false. Exam trap "A network of interconnected nodes" (IHBAS 2024) keys the connectionist model, although Collins and Quillian's network also has nodes; "associative" and "linkage" describe any network rather than name a model. Parallel distributed processing means associative networks and simultaneous activation (IHBAS 2025), not serial processing. A schema is organised knowledge, built from experience, that guides perception and memory; the schema approach studies how such knowledge is used to understand behaviour. A script, a schema for a routine (the restaurant script of Roger Schank and Robert Abelson , 1977: enter, order, eat, pay, leave), belongs to generic memory. The schema idea came from Frederic Charles Bartlett (1886 to 1969). In Remembering (1932), English students retelling the Native American tale "The War of the Ghosts" shortened it and emphasised a few details (levelling and sharpening, in Gordon Allport and Leo Postman 's later terms), explained away puzzling events (rationalisation) and turned canoes into boats. Remembering is an "effort after meaning": reconstructive memory rebuilds the past from fragments and schemas. Asked how fast filmed cars were going when they "smashed" rather than "hit" each other, students gave higher speeds and a week later more often recalled broken glass that was never shown (32 against 14 per cent; Elizabeth Loftus and John Palmer , 1974). This is the misinformation effect : memory distorted by leading questions or misleading later information. Whole false events can be implanted (being lost in a shopping mall as a child), and people who study bed, rest, tired and dream recall the absent "sleep" (the Deese-Roediger-McDermott paradigm). In source monitoring ( Marcia Johnson and colleagues, 1993) we attribute a memory to its origin from its contextual details; reality monitoring, perceived versus imagined, is one kind. Source errors cause source amnesia (a fact remembered without its source), cryptomnesia (another's idea recalled as one's own) and false eyewitness identifications. Déjà vu is the illusion of recognition, jamais vu its reverse, and pseudologia fantastica pathological lying. In the recovered memory controversy Loftus warned that suggestive therapy can implant false memories of abuse, though real abuse can also be forgotten and recalled. Exam trap Failing to recall the relevant elements of an autobiographical experience is a source-monitoring deficit (RML 2022); "personal-" and "social-monitoring" are invented. Defence lawyers fear source errors (Amity 2023), not forgetting or poor eyesight; confidence does not mean accuracy. Schema theory is Bartlett's, not Wundt's, Titchener's or Watson's, and his rationalisation is not the defence mechanism. Scripts come from generic memory (RML 2025). Retrieval and forgetting Much forgetting is a failure to find what is still stored: given category names as cues, people recall far more words (Endel Tulving and Zena Pearlstone , 1966). By the encoding specificity principle (Tulving and Donald Thomson , 1973), a cue works to the extent that it was encoded with the memory; recognition beats recall because the test supplies the item. In context-dependent memory the physical setting must match: divers recalled words best where they had learned them, underwater or on the beach ( Duncan Godden and Alan Baddeley, 1975). In state-dependent memory the internal state must match: material learned while drunk is recalled better when drunk again ( Donald Goodwin and colleagues, 1969). Gordon Bower (1981) added mood-dependent memory and mood-congruent memory, the easier recall of material matching one's current mood. Exam trap Rahul, who expects to do better in his usual classroom (IHBAS 2024), shows encoding specificity, keyed because context-dependent memory is not offered; "the principle of congruity" is a distractor. Offered both (JEMAS 2025), choose context-dependent for surroundings and state-dependent for internal states. Alcohol-induced amnesia is state-dependent memory (RML 2022). Forgetting is useful: it clears out unneeded detail and reduces interference, and the more is retained, the less is forgotten. First, decay theory , credited to Edward Lee Thorndike 's (1874 to 1949) law of disuse, says unused traces fade with time. But John Jenkins and Karl Dallenbach (1924) found that after eight hours of sleep students recalled over half of their nonsense syllables, and after eight waking hours about a tenth: events, not time, caused the loss. Table 1.15 lists other named effects on retention. Interference theory blames other memories. In proactive interference earlier learning disrupts newer learning; in retroactive interference newer learning disrupts older memories (PRO: old disrupts new; RETRO: new disrupts old). Dialling your old phone number instead of the new one is proactive, as is earlier psychology intruding on a later sociology test; losing the old number to the new one is retroactive. After lists A-B and then A-C, recalling A-B measures retroactive and recalling A-C proactive interference. Arthur Melton and J. M. Irwin (1940) blamed response competition and unlearning. Exam trap RML 2024 keys an English speaker applying English grammar to Spanish as "retroactive". The key is wrong: old disrupts new, so it is proactive. "Interference from new information" (IHBAS 2024) is retroactive. Decay theory is keyed to Thorndike (RML 2024), not Ebbinghaus, Tulving or Melton and Irwin. In retrieval failure, or cue-dependent forgetting (Tulving, 1974), the trace survives but the cues do not match. Retrieval can even cause forgetting: practising some items of a category (FRUIT-orange) makes the unpractised ones (FRUIT-banana) harder to recall than items of unpractised categories ( Michael Anderson , Robert Bjork and Elizabeth Bjork , 1994), through inhibition of competitors. Sigmund Freud (1856 to 1939) proposed motivated forgetting through repression , the unconscious exclusion of threatening memories from awareness; suppression is conscious, and evidence for repression is weak. Last, consolidation ( Georg Elias Müller and Alfons Pilzecker , 1900) can fail: a head injury or electroconvulsive therapy erases recent memories, and by Ribot's law ( Théodule Ribot , 1881) the new perishes before the old. Exam trap Retrieval-induced forgetting (RML 2020) is keyed "practised information remembered better than unpractised", but its defining half is that related unpractised items suffer. Repression is unconscious, suppression conscious (RML 2025); motivated forgetting covers both, and inhibition weakens competitors. In anterograde amnesia new memories cannot be formed after an injury; in retrograde amnesia memories from before it are lost, usually sparing the remote past. Of the other "a-" disorders, aphasia (with alexia and acalculia) affects language, apraxia skilled movement and agnosia recognition; dementia is a progressive decline in memory, judgement and abstraction. In 1953 the neurosurgeon William Beecher Scoville removed both medial temporal lobes, with most of the hippocampus and amygdala, from Henry Gustav Molaison (1926 to 2008), known as H.M., to relieve his epilepsy. Scoville and Brenda Milner reported in 1957 a profound anterograde amnesia: he reread magazines with fresh interest and never learned his new address. Yet his intelligence, digit span and childhood memories were intact, and over three days he improved at tracing a star in a mirror while denying that he had ever done it. Exam trap H.M.'s main deficit was anterograde amnesia for declarative memory (Real PYQ 2024); procedural, short-term and old memories were spared. Both medial temporal lobes were removed, not frontal, parietal or occipital cortex. The hippocampus is the structure damaged in anterograde amnesia and critical for consolidation (JEMAS 2025, RML 2024, RML 2023), not the hypothalamus, pituitary, cortex, amygdala (emotional memory), prefrontal cortex (working memory) or cerebellum (motor learning). Korsakoff's syndrome (Korsakoff's psychosis; Sergei Korsakoff , late 1880s) results mainly from thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency in chronic alcoholism, often after Wernicke's encephalopathy ( Carl Wernicke , 1881: confusion, ataxia, nystagmus); together they form the Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, which damages the mammillary bodies and mediodorsal (dorsomedial) thalamus. It brings dense anterograde amnesia, extensive retrograde amnesia and confabulation , sincere false stories that fill memory gaps, unlike malingering (deliberate faking), delirium (acute, fluctuating consciousness) or confusion. Alzheimer's disease, by contrast, first erodes recent episodic memory, and Huntington's and Parkinson's diseases impair procedural learning. Exam trap Memory deficits, confabulation and nystagmus in a chronic drinker (Real PYQ 2024) is Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, not Alzheimer's, vascular or frontotemporal dementia. The alcohol-related illness with profound retrograde amnesia (RML 2024) is Korsakoff's psychosis; the vitamin is B1, not B12, D or folate. Infantile amnesia, the lack of memories from the first three or four years, reflects an immature hippocampus and the lack of language. Transient global amnesia is a sudden anterograde amnesia lasting hours. Dissociative amnesia, a loss of personal memories with no medical cause (generalised when it covers the whole life), belongs to the Psychiatric Disorders chapter. Richard Semon (1904) called the physical memory trace the engram . Karl Spencer Lashley (1890 to 1958) cut away rats' cortex after maze learning and found that memory loss depended on how much was removed (mass action), not where, with areas substituting for one another (equipotentiality): memories are distributed across the cortex ("In search of the engram", 1950). Donald Olding Hebb (1904 to 1985) proposed in 1949 that neurons active together strengthen their links, and Timothy Bliss and Terje Lømo (1973) found such long-term potentiation (LTP), a lasting strengthening of hippocampal synapses after high-frequency stimulation and the leading cellular candidate for memory. The hippocampus consolidates new memories into the neocortex, partly during sleep, so remote memories survive its damage. Improving memory A mnemonic adds organisation, meaning or imagery. The method of loci, credited to Simonides of Ceos , places vivid images along a familiar route; the peg-word system links items to rhyming number pegs (one is a bun); the keyword method (Richard Atkinson, 1975) links a foreign word to a sound-alike image (Spanish "pato", duck: a duck in a pot). An acronym is a word of first letters (VIBGYOR); an acrostic is a sentence of first letters ("Every Good Boy Deserves Fruit"). SQ3R ( Francis P. Robinson , 1946) is Survey, Question, Read, Recite, Review; PQRST is Preview, Question, Read, Self-recitation, Test. Testing and spacing beat rereading, overlearning gives diminishing returns, and sleep consolidates. Exam trap A first-letter sentence is an acrostic, not an acronym, peg-word or keyword. Seeing the chai stall is not thinking; working out whether you can afford a second cup is. Banished by Watson, thought returned with the cognitive revolution (Section 1.2): cognitive psychology studies the structuralists' topics (consciousness, imagery, thought) by objective measures. Elements, Imagery and Types of Thought Thought uses five elements: images , concepts , symbols , propositions (the smallest units of knowledge that can be true or false) and language . Roger Newland Shepard and Jacqueline Metzler (1971) found that the time to judge two rotated block figures identical rose linearly with the angle between them, as if the image were turned at a steady speed: mental rotation . Stephen Michael Kosslyn 's image-scanning studies (1978) suggested that images depict space, against Zenon Walter Pylyshyn 's view (1973) that knowledge is stored as propositions. Allan Paivio 's dual-coding theory (1971) gives pictures and concrete words both a verbal and an imagery code, so they are remembered better than abstract words. Table 1.16 lists types of thinking. Autistic thinking is fantasy, not autism. Loosening of associations, circumstantiality and word salad are disorders of the form of thought (Psychiatric Disorders chapter). Concepts: Rules and Prototypes A concept is a mental category of things sharing properties, formed through observation, discrimination, generalisation and abstraction. The classical view defines it by necessary and sufficient features, which suits artificial concepts set by a rule: conjunctive (all attributes: a voter is a citizen, adult and enrolled), disjunctive (any one: "out" in cricket) or relational ("taller than"). Jerome Seymour Bruner , Jacqueline Goodnow and George Austin (1956) found that people learn them by testing hypotheses, by scanning or focusing ; conservative focusing , changing one attribute at a time, works best, and focus gambling changes several. Natural concepts are fuzzier. Ludwig Wittgenstein (1953) saw that games share only a family resemblance , and Eleanor Rosch showed in the 1970s that typicality is graded: "a robin is a bird" is verified faster than "a penguin is a bird". We classify by similarity to a prototype , the abstract, averaged best example, and learn the basic level (chair, not furniture) first; exemplar theory stores many instances instead. How concepts are networked in memory is told in Section 1.7. Exam trap Artificial concepts by hypothesis testing = Bruner , not Rosch (natural concepts), Clark Leonard Hull (gradual associative abstraction, 1920) or Watson. A prototype is abstract and averaged , not a template (exact copy), a feature (a part) or a geon (a simple solid). Problem Solving: Strategies and Obstacles A problem is a gap between an initial state and a goal state, well defined (a sudoku) or ill defined ("choose a career"). Allen Newell and Herbert Alexander Simon ( Human Problem Solving , 1972; the General Problem Solver) treated solving as search through a problem space of states linked by operators (legal moves). An algorithm guarantees the solution but may be slow (trying every padlock code); a heuristic is a quick rule of thumb with no guarantee. Means-end analysis sets subgoals that reduce the biggest difference from the goal (to reach Bengaluru, first reach the station); working backward starts from the goal; hill climbing always takes the step that gets closest, so it stalls when a backward step is needed; analogy reuses an earlier solution, though people rarely notice one unprompted ( Mary Gick and Keith Holyoak 's radiation problem, 1980); trial and error is the most primitive. Stage models range from Dewey (1910) to Sternberg's problem-solving cycle. The Gestaltists stressed insight , a sudden restructuring of the problem: Wolfgang Köhler 's chimpanzee Sultan suddenly joined two sticks to reach a banana (1917), and Norman Maier 's nine-dot problem (1930) defeats people until they let the lines leave the square. Janet Metcalfe and David Wiebe (1987) found "warmth" ratings flat until just before an insight solution, but rising steadily on algebra. Incubation , setting a problem aside, often helps. Experience can also block a solution. Key study: Duncker's candle problem (1945) Karl Duncker asked people to fix a candle to a wall with matches and a box of drawing pins. Few thought of pinning up the emptied box as a shelf, but many more did when the box came empty. Knowing an object's usual use (top-down processing) blinded them to its other uses: functional fixedness . Functional fixedness has a strategic cousin, mental set (Einstellung): in Abraham Luchins 's water jars (1942), people drilled on B minus A minus 2C kept using it when A minus C was far simpler. Confirmation bias and irrelevant information also obstruct. Exam trap A heuristic is "a general rule that is usually right": efficient, not guaranteed , not more accurate than an algorithm. Functional fixedness concerns objects (a matchbox seen only as a container, not a platform) and reflects overactive top-down processing; mental set concerns strategies . As fixedness is a special case of set, one paper keyed mental set "the most basic and common obstacle"; fixation is the umbrella word, "mental barrier" no term, trial and error a strategy. In a mental status examination, insight is awareness of illness, graded 1 to 6; intellectual insight is grade 5. Reasoning: Deduction and Induction Deductive reasoning moves from general premises to a conclusion that must be true if they are ("All Mysuru autos must use the meter; this is one; so it must"). Inductive reasoning moves from specific observations to a probable generalisation that the next case may overturn ("every auto I took overcharged, so all do"). An argument is valid if its conclusion follows from its form, sound if its premises are also true. Charles Sanders Peirce (1839 to 1914) called inference to the best explanation, as in diagnosis, abductive reasoning . In research, deduction tests theory against data (quantitative work), induction builds theory from data (qualitative work), and the hypothetico-deductive method of Karl Raimund Popper (1902 to 1994) is the full cycle of hypothesis, deduced prediction and test. Exam trap "Starts with a theory and tests it with observations" = deductive . "Gathers data, looks for patterns, then generates a theory", "specific observations to broader generalisations", "theory development" and "qualitative research" = inductive . Keys prefer "deductive reasoning" to "hypothetico-deductive method" and rest deductive validity on the soundness of the initial theory . Heuristics was keyed as NOT reflecting induction; probabilistic conclusions, decision making and concept formation do. In syllogisms (two premises, one conclusion), belief bias makes people accept invalid arguments with believable conclusions, and the atmosphere effect (Robert Woodworth and Saul Sells, 1935) lets a "some" or "no" premise suggest a matching conclusion. For "if p, then q", modus ponens (p, so q) and modus tollens (not q, so not p) are valid; affirming the consequent (q, so p) and denying the antecedent (not p, so not q) are fallacies. In Peter Cathcart Wason 's selection task (1966), under one person in ten turns the right cards (Figure 1.10), yet a permission rule ("if drinking beer, must be over 19") makes the same logic easy. Rule: If a card has a vowel on one side, it has an even number on the other. The two cards with heavy outlines (E and 7) are the only ones that could reveal a counterexample. The popular choice of the 4 card tests for confirmation, which can never prove a general rule. Philip Nicholas Johnson-Laird (1983) argued that we reason with mental models of possible situations, not formal rules. In Wason's 2-4-6 task (1960), people guessed "rising by two" and tested only fitting sequences (the rule was any increasing numbers): confirmation bias , seeking and favouring evidence for what one already believes. Exam trap Confirmation bias was keyed as "closely related to" representativeness , a debatable key (recognition is least related). Acting on an expectation until it comes true is a self-fulfilling prophecy , not confirmation bias, the base-rate fallacy or "motivational reaction" (no term). Piaget's formal operations bring hypothetico-deductive (a capacity, not a stage), counterfactual and metacognitive reasoning; dialectical reasoning, integrating contradictions, is postformal (Developmental Psychology chapter). Judgement and Decision Making Normative models say how a rational agent should decide, maximising expected utility; descriptive models say how people actually decide. Simon's bounded rationality holds that information, mental capacity and time limit choice, so people practise satisficing , taking the first good-enough option (Nobel Prize, 1978). Gerd Gigerenzer (born 1947) adds that fast and frugal heuristics, such as the recognition heuristic (choosing the option you recognise), are often ecologically rational. Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman (Kahneman's Nobel Prize, 2002) catalogued the heuristics of judgement and their biases (Table 1.17). Representativeness invites base-rate neglect : a description that "sounds like" an engineer is judged an engineer whether engineers are 30 or 70 in 100. Most people judged Linda, a socially concerned philosophy graduate, likelier to be "a feminist bank teller" than "a bank teller", although a conjunction cannot be likelier than its parts: the conjunction fallacy . Prospect theory (1979) explains this framing effect , the same choice decided differently when worded as gains or as losses: outcomes are gains or losses from a reference point, and losses loom about twice as large as equal gains ( loss aversion ), which also drives the endowment effect (overvaluing what we own), status quo bias (preferring no change) and the sunk-cost fallacy (persisting because of past investment). Hindsight bias , the "I knew it all along" effect ( Baruch Fischhoff , 1975), and overconfidence (confidence exceeding accuracy) distort self-knowledge. Representativeness errs when people ignore base rates and focus solely on similarity ; the other options describe availability, anchoring and confirmation bias. Overrating how well we would have predicted events = hindsight , not the just-world hypothesis or "decisiveness". Creativity Creativity is producing work that is both novel and appropriate. Joy Paul Guilford , whose 1950 American Psychological Association address launched its study, equated it with divergent production, scored by fluency (number of ideas), flexibility (number of categories), originality (statistical rarity) and elaboration (detail). Graham Wallas ( The Art of Thought , 1926) described four stages: preparation (defining and working on the problem), incubation (setting it aside while work continues outside awareness), illumination (the sudden insight) and verification (testing and refining it). Exam trap Order: preparation, incubation, illumination, verification ("Please Incubate Ideas Very carefully"). Sensitivity, fluency, flexibility and originality are Guilford's abilities; analytical, creative and practical are Sternberg's intelligences; "problem-finding, brainstorming, selection, implementation" is not Wallas. Creativity is measured by the Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking ( Ellis Paul Torrance , 1966) and Sarnoff Mednick 's Remote Associates Test (1962): which word links cottage, Swiss and cake? (Cheese.) Edward de Bono 's lateral thinking (1967) challenges assumptions; Alex Faickney Osborn 's brainstorming ( Applied Imagination , 1953) defers judgement and seeks quantity. By the threshold hypothesis, creativity and IQ correlate only up to an IQ of about 120. In Robert Jeffrey Sternberg and Todd Lubart's investment theory (1991), creative people "buy low and sell high". The creative personality is open to experience, independent and tolerant of ambiguity. The Structure of Language Language combines arbitrary symbols by rules into unlimited messages. Charles Francis Hockett (1960) listed its design features, notably semanticity (meaning), arbitrariness (nothing in "dog" is doglike), displacement (talking about what is absent), generativity (endless new sentences) and duality of patterning (meaningless sounds build meaningful units). The phoneme is the smallest unit of sound that distinguishes words (/p/ and /b/ in pat and bat) and has no meaning; the morpheme is the smallest unit of meaning, free (cat) or bound (-s), so "cats" has two. Syntax governs how words combine, semantics is meaning, pragmatics is use in social context ("Can you pass the salt?" is a request) and prosody is rhythm and intonation. Noam Chomsky 's transformational grammar ( Syntactic Structures , 1957; Aspects , 1965) separates surface structure , the words as spoken, from deep structure , who did what to whom: "Visiting relatives can be boring" has one surface and two deep structures. Competence is tacit knowledge of the rules, performance their imperfect use. Exam trap Smallest unit of meaning = morpheme ; basic unit of sound = phoneme ; a syllable is a unit of pronunciation, a consonant one kind of phoneme. Emotional prosody depends on right-hemisphere regions homotopic to the language areas , not Broca's area, motor cortex or occipital lobe. Recursive thought ("I think that you think...") is perspective taking, not reversibility (Piaget's mental undoing of an action), referential style (below) or reconstruction (rebuilding a memory). Acquiring Language Burrhus Frederic Skinner 's Verbal Behavior (1957) explained language by reinforcement of verbal operants such as the mand (a request) and the tact (naming). Chomsky's 1959 review replied that children produce sentences they never heard, make errors no adult models ("I goed") and are rarely corrected for grammar. He proposed an innate language acquisition device (LAD) holding a universal grammar , argued from the poverty of the stimulus : children's input is too sparse to explain the grammar they reach. Bruner's language acquisition support system (LASS, 1983) stresses adult scaffolding and child-directed speech (motherese): higher and wider pitch, slower rate, more pauses, shorter utterances. Dan Isaac Slobin 's language-making capacity (1985) is a set of cognitive and perceptual operating principles specialised for language. Eric Heinz Lenneberg (1967) proposed a critical period from about two to puberty, now usually called a sensitive period; Genie, isolated until 13, learned words but never grammar. Infants coo at about 2 months and babble at about 6; at about 12 months a single word, a holophrase , does a sentence's work; at 18 to 24 months comes what Roger Brown (1925 to 1997) called telegraphic speech , two words without function words ("more milk"); and at 2 to 3 years overregularisation ("two foots"). Children overextend words ("dog" for every animal), underextend them ("dog" only for their own) and learn new words from one exposure (fast mapping); Katherine Nelson (1973) found some children's first words mostly object names, a referential style. Language is most often compromised in autism spectrum disorder. Exam trap Chomsky's innate capacity is the LAD (an inborn processor activated by verbal input, holding universal grammar, the rules common to all languages), not the phonological loop (working memory), the zone of proximal development (Vygotsky) or a schema; LASS = Bruner , LMC = Slobin . Irreversible deficits after early deprivation support sensitive periods , not semantics or syntax (levels of language) or nativism (the broader theory that language is innate). Language and Thought Benjamin Lee Whorf (1897 to 1941), a student of Edward Sapir (1884 to 1939), argued that language shapes thought. The strong version, linguistic determinism, has failed: Brent Berlin and Paul Kay (1969) found colour terms entering languages in a near-universal order, and Rosch found that the Dani, with two colour terms, remember focal colours as English speakers do. The weak version, linguistic relativity (language influences thought), survives: Hindi kinship terms ( chacha , mama , phupha ) make speakers track which side an uncle is on. Steven Pinker (1994) holds that we think in "mentalese". For Jean Piaget (1896 to 1980), thought comes first and language expresses it; preschoolers' egocentric speech simply fades. For Lev Semyonovich Vygotsky ( Thinking and Speech , 1934), thought and speech have separate roots that merge at about two, after which thought becomes verbal; social speech becomes self-guiding private speech and then inner speech . He traced concepts from heaps through complexes to true concepts in adolescence, tied to society's tasks, social institutions and self-reflection. Exam trap Vygotsky: thought depends on language; Piaget: language depends on thought. "One studied early, the other later language" is wrong: both studied the same years. Private speech guides behaviour and is internalised ; it is not regression, imitation, disorder or fading egocentrism. Gender plays no part in Vygotsky's account. "Language and thought involve..." expects simultaneous processes; "independent" fits only their early roots. Linguistic relativity = Whorf , not Chomsky, Piaget or Pinker. Bilingualism is the use of two languages, and a polyglot speaks many (a linguist studies language scientifically); bilingual children reach milestones on time. Apes such as Washoe, Nim Chimpsky and Kanzi learn meaningful symbols but little grammar. Speech perception is categorical (/ba/ switches abruptly to /pa/ as voice onset time rises) and audiovisual: in the McGurk effect, a heard "ba" dubbed onto lips saying "ga" is heard as "da". Reading builds most directly on spoken language, above all awareness of its sounds, not on theory of mind, imagination or mental representation. Aphasia is an acquired disorder of language from brain damage, not of intelligence, memory or abstract thinking (Broca's aphasia impairs production, Wernicke's comprehension: Physiological Psychology chapter). Answers: (1) functional fixedness, (2) induction, (3) incubation, (4) morpheme, (5) telegraphic, (6) inner. 1.9 Intelligence: Theories, Measurement, Heredity and Environment Medium yield · 63 Qs Everyone thinks they recognise intelligence, yet psychologists still argue over what it is, whether it is one thing or many, and how much of it a test can capture. Defining Intelligence Alfred Binet (1857 to 1911) put judgement at the centre: "to judge well, to comprehend well, to reason well." Edwin Garrigues Boring (1886 to 1968) retorted in 1923 that intelligence is "what the tests test", an operational definition (one framed by its measuring procedure). David Wechsler (1896 to 1981) gave the most quoted definition (1944): "the aggregate or global capacity of the individual to act purposefully, to think rationally and to deal effectively with his environment", aggregate because it comprises many abilities, global because they work as one. Robert Jeffrey Sternberg (born 1949), who re-polled the experts with Douglas Detterman in 1986, stresses adapting to, selecting and shaping real-world environments. Achievement tests look back at what a specific course taught (a board examination); aptitude tests look ahead to the capacity to learn a specific skill with training (the Differential Aptitude Tests), so they anchor guidance; intelligence tests predict learning in general. Among lay (implicit) theories, Carol Susan Dweck (born 1946) contrasted an entity theory, or fixed mindset, with an incremental theory, or growth mindset ( Mindset , 2006), the belief that effort develops intelligence. Fixed-mindset children avoid challenges; children praised for effort, not cleverness, persist after failure. Exam trap The WAIS is an intelligence test, not an aptitude, achievement or attitude (evaluative stance) test. RML 2022 keyed the aptitude test as "the heart of the guidance programme", over the case study (a life history), the interview and the cumulative record (a running school file); textbooks give the phrase to counselling, so choose it if offered. From Galton to Binet: The First Tests and the IQ Francis Galton (1822 to 1911), author of Hereditary Genius (1869) and father of differential psychology, measured reaction time and sensory acuity in his London anthropometric laboratory (1884). James McKeen Cattell (1860 to 1944) coined the term mental test (1890) for a similar battery, which failed to predict college grades (Clark Wissler, 1901). Asked by the French ministry to pick out children needing special schooling, Binet and the physician Théodore Simon (1873 to 1961) measured judgement and reasoning instead, keeping items that older children passed more often than younger ones. Their 1905 scale had 30 items of rising difficulty; the 1908 revision grouped them by age, a child's mental age being the age level of the items passed; the 1911 revision reached adults. ( Jean Piaget standardised tests in Simon's laboratory around 1920 but did not build the first test.) Henry Herbert Goddard (1866 to 1957) translated the scale into English in 1908. In 1912 William Stern (1871 to 1938) divided mental age by chronological age, coining the intelligence quotient (IQ) ; Lewis Madison Terman (1877 to 1956) multiplied it by 100 in his 1916 Stanford-Binet . So the ratio IQ = (MA ÷ CA) × 100: a 10-year-old with a mental age of 8 scores 80. In 1917 Robert Mearns Yerkes (1876 to 1956) led the first group tests, for army recruits: the verbal Army Alpha and, for the illiterate, the pictorial Army Beta. Exam trap Stern coined IQ; Terman popularised it. Inverting the ratio (10 ÷ 8 × 100 = 125) is the usual slip: a mental age below chronological age always gives an IQ below 100. James McKeen Cattell coined "mental test"; Raymond Cattell, unrelated, gave us fluid and crystallised intelligence and the 16PF personality questionnaire. Deviation IQ and What a Score Means The ratio IQ fails for adults: mental age stops growing in the late teens, so an ordinary 40-year-old with a mental age of 16 would score (16 ÷ 40) × 100 = 40. The Wechsler-Bellevue scale (1939) dropped mental age and compared each person with norms from a large representative sample of the same age. In this deviation IQ (the "standard IQ"; loosely, the actual score relative to the expected mean score for one's age) every age group has a mean of 100 and a standard deviation (SD), the typical distance of scores from the mean, of 15: IQ = 100 + 15 z ( z : distance from the mean in SDs). Because IQs are roughly normally distributed, any IQ converts to a percentile, the percentage of people scoring below it (Figure 1.11): 100 is the 50th percentile and 85, one SD below, the 16th. Stanford-Binet deviation IQs used an SD of 16 from 1960 until the fifth edition (2003), so there an IQ of 136 gives z = 36 ÷ 16 = 2.25, about the 98.7th percentile. WAIS-IV bands: 130 or above very superior, 90 to 109 average, 80 to 89 low average, 70 to 79 borderline ("very low" in newer editions), 69 or below extremely low. Exam trap The original Stanford-Binet used the ratio IQ. The deviation IQ is not "only for adults", not built from unstandardised raw scores, and no less reliable than the ratio IQ, whose meaning shifts with age. The Wechsler Scales, the SB5 and Other Tests Wechsler, at New York's Bellevue Hospital, set out to fix the Stanford-Binet's faults: little appeal for adults, too much word manipulation, too much weight on speed and reliance on mental age. His tests add non-verbal performance subtests and give a profile as well as a total. The family is the WAIS (1955; WAIS-IV 2008, ages 16 to 90), the WISC (1949; WISC-V 2014, 6 years to 16 years 11 months) and the WPPSI (from 2 years 6 months). In the WAIS-IV, four index scores (Table 1.18) replaced the Verbal and Performance IQs and combine into the Full Scale IQ (FSIQ), with an optional General Ability Index; the WISC-V and WAIS-5 (2024) have five. Letter-Number Sequencing, keyed as core in the WAIS-IV but not the WISC-V, is strictly supplemental in one and secondary in the other; it is still the best answer, as the other options are core in both. The Stanford-Binet Fifth Edition (SB5; Gale Roid, 2003; ages 2 to 85 and over; mean 100, SD 15) measures five factors drawn from Carroll's model ( below ) and Alan Baddeley's working memory: Fluid Reasoning, Knowledge, Quantitative Reasoning, Visual-Spatial Processing and Working Memory, each verbal and non-verbal. The Kaufman Brief Intelligence Test (KBIT-2) has a Verbal (crystallised) and a Nonverbal (fluid) scale. For infants, the Bayley Scales (cognitive, language and motor development up to 42 months) yield a developmental quotient (DQ); the McCarthy Scales cover about 2½ to 8½ years. The WAIS-IV FSIQ is highly reliable (about .98). Content validity asks whether items sample the domain, concurrent validity whether scores agree with a criterion measured at the same time (an established test given alongside), predictive validity whether they forecast a later one, and construct validity whether the test behaves as theory predicts. IQ correlates about .5 with school grades and job performance (Frank Schmidt and John Hunter, 1998). The WAIS documents intellectual disability or decline, as for a disability allowance; children's special educational needs call for the WISC. Culture-Fair and Indian Tests Because vocabulary and information depend on schooling, psychologists sought a culture-free test; that proved impossible, so a culture-fair test instead minimises language, reading and specific knowledge. The classic is Raven's Progressive Matrices (Standard form 1938) by Spearman's student John Carlyle Raven (1902 to 1970): each of its 60 progressively harder items is a pattern with a piece missing, solved by inferring the rule. It is the classic test of fluid intelligence and the best single marker of g, widely used with Indian norms. Raymond Cattell's figure-only Culture Fair Intelligence Test works the same way. In India, V. V. Kamat 's Binet-Kamat Test (1930s) adapted the Stanford-Binet and is heavily verbal; Arthur J. Malin 's Intelligence Scale for Indian Children (MISIC, 1969) adapts the WISC and is half verbal; C. M. Bhatia 's Battery of Performance Tests of Intelligence (1955) has five performance subtests (Kohs block design, Alexander's pass-along, pattern drawing, immediate memory, picture construction), needs no reading and has rural and urban norms; normed on 11- to 16-year-olds, it is also used with illiterate adults. So for an illiterate rural 10-year-old, where the WISC-IV and SB5 rest on schooling and foreign norms, Bhatia's Battery best minimises cultural and educational bias. Exam trap Raven's measures fluid intelligence: prefer it to crystallised, verbal, social or even "general intelligence". It is culture-fair, not culture-free. The Battery is C. M. Bhatia's, not that of Girishwar Misra, Durganand Sinha or J. B. P. Sinha (cultural, indigenous and organisational psychologists). Factor Theories: From g to CHC Factor analysis asks how few underlying factors explain a table of correlations among tests. Its inventor, Charles Edward Spearman (1863 to 1945), found in 1904 that schoolchildren's marks and sensory scores all correlated positively, the positive manifold , and explained it by a general factor (g) common to every test plus a specific factor (s) peculiar to each: the two-factor theory . Louis Leon Thurstone (1887 to 1955) found seven primary mental abilities (1938): verbal comprehension, word fluency, number, space, associative memory, perceptual speed and reasoning. Because these correlate, g returned at the top of hierarchies such as Philip Ewart Vernon 's (1950) and John Bissell Carroll 's three strata (1993); Kevin McGrew merged Carroll's model with Cattell and Horn's into the CHC theory behind most modern tests (Table 1.19). Joy Paul Guilford (1897 to 1987) went the other way. His structure of intellect (1967) crosses five operations (cognition, memory, divergent production, convergent production, evaluation), four contents (figural, symbolic, semantic, behavioural) and six products, giving 5 × 4 × 6 = 120 abilities, later 150 and then 180. Raymond Bernard Cattell (1905 to 1998), later with John Leonard Horn (1928 to 2006), split g in two (1963). Fluid intelligence (Gf) is the ability to reason and solve novel problems independently of acquired knowledge; measured by matrices, it peaks in the early twenties and then declines. Crystallised intelligence (Gc) is the repertoire of information, cognitive skills and strategies acquired through education and experience; measured by vocabulary and information, it holds or rises into the sixties. In Cattell's investment theory, Gf invested in learning crystallises as Gc; Horn later extended the list to about nine broad abilities. Table 1.19 Other factor theories and the hierarchies. "Ability to deal with new problems" is Gf; block design, matrix reasoning and coding do not measure Gc, and processing speed and working memory are correlates, not definitions, of it. Gardner, Sternberg, PASS and Emotional Intelligence Howard Gardner (born 1943) built his theory from brain damage and prodigies, not factor analysis. Frames of Mind (1983) proposed seven relatively independent multiple intelligences : linguistic, logical-mathematical, spatial, musical, bodily-kinaesthetic, interpersonal and intrapersonal; naturalist was added in 1999 and existential only considered. Critics note that most correlate with one another and with g. Sternberg's triarchic theory ( Beyond IQ , 1985) has three parts. The componential or analytical part is the mental machinery: metacomponents that plan and monitor, performance components that execute, and knowledge-acquisition components that learn. The experiential or creative part copes with novelty and automatises the familiar. The contextual or practical part adapts to the environment, shapes it or selects a better one: a clerk who learns her office's unwritten rules adapts, one who changes a pointless procedure shapes, one who leaves for a better job selects. In the late 1990s this grew into successful intelligence , the ability to achieve success in life by one's own standards and within one's culture through a balance of analytical, creative and practical abilities; it rests partly on tacit knowledge, the unspoken know-how a setting demands. Exam trap Componential = analytical, experiential (not "experimental", and not Dweck's "incremental") = creative, contextual = practical. "Verbal, performance, full scale" is Wechsler; "fluid, crystallised" is Cattell; "linguistic, logical-mathematical, spatial" is Gardner. The PASS model of the Odisha-born Jagannath Prasad Das (born 1931), Jack A. Naglieri and John R. Kirby (1994), built on Alexander Romanovich Luria 's (1902 to 1977) functional units of the brain, has four processes: Planning, Attention, Simultaneous (parts into a whole) and Successive (serial order), measured by the Cognitive Assessment System. Stephen J. Ceci 's bioecological view (1990) ties each cognitive potential to its context. Edward Lee Thorndike 's (1874 to 1949) social intelligence (1920), the ability to understand and manage people, foreshadowed emotional intelligence , defined by Peter Salovey and John D. Mayer (1990) as the ability to monitor and use one's own and others' emotions; their four-branch ability model (perceiving, using, understanding and managing emotions) is measured by the MSCEIT. Daniel Goleman (born 1946) popularised a mixed model (1995): knowing one's emotions, managing them, motivating oneself, recognising others' emotions and handling relationships (relabelled in 1998 as self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy and social skills). Reuven Bar-On 's EQ-i (emotional quotient, 1997) and trait EI are self-report versions; Danah Zohar proposed spiritual intelligence (2000). Exam trap Salovey and Mayer coined emotional intelligence; Goleman popularised it. His 1998 labels rename the same five parts, so match the question's wording, and if both lists appear choose the original 1995 one ("knowing one's emotions" to "handling relationships"). "IQ, EQ, SQ, CQ" is no one's model of EI. Heredity, Environment and the Brain Higher IQ goes with faster reaction and inspection times, larger working memory, slightly larger brains and, in Richard Haier's 1988 study, lower brain glucose use (neural efficiency); intelligence is polygenic. Family studies compare relatives of differing closeness, adoption studies compare children with their biological and adoptive parents, and twin studies compare monozygotic (MZ) twins, who share virtually all genes, with dizygotic (DZ) twins, who share half, most powerfully when reared apart. In Thomas J. Bouchard Jr. and Matt McGue's 1981 review, MZ twins correlated .86 on IQ when reared together and .72 when reared apart (about .70 in Bouchard's Minnesota Study of Twins Reared Apart, from 1979), DZ twins .60. Heritability is the proportion of variation in a trait, within one population at one time, associated with genetic variation; it says nothing about one individual. It rises with age, and Eric Turkheimer (2003) found it near .10 in the poorest families, a gene-environment interaction. Richard Lewontin 's seeds (1970) show why it cannot explain group gaps: varied seed differs genetically within each tray, yet the gap between a rich-soil and a poor-soil tray is wholly environmental. In Irving Gottesman 's reaction range (1963), genes set limits and environment decides where within them a person lands. Iodine, nutrition and schooling raise IQ; early intervention (Head Start, 1965; the Milwaukee Project; the Abecedarian Project, 1972, from infancy) brings IQ gains that often fade but lasting school and life benefits. James Robert Flynn (1934 to 2020) showed in 1984 that average scores rose about 3 points a decade, the Flynn effect , too fast for genes. Neither Arthur Robert Jensen (1923 to 2012), who argued in 1969 that group IQ gaps are partly genetic, nor The Bell Curve ( Richard J. Herrnstein and Charles Murray , 1994) has direct support, and Claude Steele and Joshua Aronson (1995) showed that stereotype threat , fear of confirming a group stereotype, depresses scores. Exam trap Individual differences come from many genetic and environmental factors together, not from genes, environment or income alone. Linkage studies, which track DNA markers through families, are neither twin nor adoption designs. Each of psychology's answers below grew from the failures of the last. What motivation is In psychology, motivation (Latin movere , to move) is the set of processes that start, direct, energise and sustain behaviour. Take thirst. A need is a state of deficiency (the body lacks water, felt or not). A drive is the aroused, tense state the need produces, which energises behaviour. A motive is any internal state directing behaviour towards a goal, usually a learned one such as achievement. An incentive is an external object that attracts or repels; the goal is the end state pursued. The motivational cycle runs need, drive, instrumental behaviour, goal, relief, until the need returns. The primary motives (biological, unlearned, mostly homeostatic) include hunger, thirst, sleep, pain avoidance, sex and the maternal drive; the secondary motives (psychosocial, learned), such as achievement, affiliation, power and gregariousness, grow from experience. Henry Murray's viscerogenic (bodily) and psychogenic (mental) needs draw the same line. Doing something for its own sake is intrinsic motivation ; doing it for a separable outcome such as marks or praise is extrinsic motivation . A toddler who struggles to open a box she knows is empty is intrinsically motivated: no bodily imbalance (homeostasis), payoff (extrinsic) or learned social motive (secondary) is involved. Malingering (feigning for an external reward) and factitious disorder (feigning without one) differ on this line. Exam trap Gregariousness is a social motive , though McDougall called it an instinct ("psychological" and "personal" motives are not standard classes). Among the perspectives (Section 1.2), inner forces beyond individual control are psychodynamic ; free will and an innate tendency to grow to one's maximum potential are humanistic (Maslow, Rogers). Instinct theories An instinct is a complex, unlearned, stereotyped pattern of behaviour shared by a whole species. William James (1842 to 1910) held in 1890 that humans have more instincts than animals, not fewer. William McDougall (1871 to 1938), in An Introduction to Social Psychology (1908), made instincts, each paired with an emotion (flight with fear, pugnacity with anger), the prime movers of all behaviour; he later listed eighteen. His hormic psychology (Greek horme , urge) holds that behaviour is purposive. Sigmund Freud (1856 to 1939) divided the instincts ( Trieb ) in 1920 into the life instincts (Eros), whose energy is the libido , and the death instinct (Thanatos), which, turned outwards, appears as aggression and war. Investing psychic energy in an object is cathexis ; the id is the reservoir of the instincts. The ethologists Konrad Lorenz and Nikolaas Tinbergen (Nobel Prize 1973) described fixed action patterns released by a sign stimulus : a male stickleback attacks anything with a red belly. Yet as an account of human motives, instinct theory had already collapsed by the late 1920s: naming is not explaining (a "gregarious instinct" is circular), the lists ran into thousands, and Zing-Yang Kuo (1930) found that kittens reared with rats seldom killed them. Exam trap The instinct theory of motivation is McDougall's , not James's, Freud's or Maslow's. Freud's "innate forces" are instincts , not needs (Maslow, Murray), drives (Hull) or the id (their reservoir). War and violence express the death instinct . Drives, arousal and incentives Drive theory grew from physiology. Walter Bradford Cannon (1871 to 1945) named homeostasis (1926; The Wisdom of the Body , 1932), the body's thermostat-like correction around a set point, building on the milieu intérieur of Claude Bernard (1813 to 1878). On it Clark Leonard Hull (1884 to 1952) built drive-reduction theory (1943): a need creates a drive, a state of tension, and any response that reduces the drive is reinforced. In Hull's equation ( S E R = S H R × D × K × V), K is incentive motivation (reward size) and V stimulus-intensity dynamism (stronger stimuli evoke the learned response more readily). Primary drives arise from tissue needs; secondary drives , such as learned fear, are acquired. Exam trap "Greater stimulus intensity, greater probability of the learned response" is stimulus-intensity dynamism , not incentive motivation, response amplitude (vigour) or reaction threshold (the minimum for any response). A deviation from homeostasis creates a drive , not equilibrium (the restored state), regulation (the correction) or dissonance (Festinger). Drive theory is about reducing physiological needs . Yet Harry Frederick Harlow 's (1905 to 1981) monkeys took apart puzzles that hid no food (1950), rats worked for non-nutritive saccharin, and students paid to lie in sensory-deprivation cubicles (1954) quit within days. Donald Olding Hebb 's (1904 to 1985) optimal arousal theory (1955) says organisms seek a moderate level of arousal. In 1908 Robert Mearns Yerkes and John Dillingham Dodson had found that mice learned a brightness discrimination fastest under intermediate shock, and the harder the discrimination, the weaker the best shock. The Yerkes-Dodson law , as later taught (Figure 1.12), makes performance an inverted-U function of arousal or anxiety, with a lower optimum for complex tasks than for simple ones. Simple or well-learned task Complex or new task best for simple task best for complex task high low Performance low high Arousal or anxiety too little: drowsy, careless too much: tense, disorganised Figure 1.12 The Yerkes-Dodson law. Performance is an inverted-U function of arousal, and the peak for a complex or new task (dashed) lies at a lower arousal level than the peak for a simple or well-learned task (solid). Robert Zajonc (1965) explained social facilitation the same way: an audience raises arousal, which strengthens the dominant response, helping easy, well-learned tasks and impairing novel or difficult ones. People differ too: Marvin Zuckerman 's (1928 to 2018) sensation seeking is the urge for varied, novel, intense experience despite risk. Exam trap Yerkes-Dodson is an inverted-U relationship between performance and anxiety: more precise than "curvilinear", and never linear or M-shaped. A complex task is done best at moderate arousal, with a lower optimum , not at very high arousal or at a level independent of difficulty. Drives push; incentives pull. The incentive theory holds that behaviour is driven mainly by external rewards: Otto Tinklepaugh 's monkeys (1928) refused lettuce after seeing a banana hidden. The expectancy-value theory multiplies the expectancy of success by the value of the outcome, so either at zero kills motivation. Its roots are the learned expectancies of Edward Chace Tolman (1886 to 1959) and the social learning theory of Julian Bernard Rotter (1954), in which behaviour depends on expectancy and reinforcement value; organisational texts give the social learning name to the framework built on expectancy, demand and incentive, which combines the cognitive framework (Tolman's expectancies) with the behaviouristic one (reinforcement); "supportive" is not a framework but a model of organisational behaviour (autocratic, custodial, supportive, collegial). Richard Lester Solomon and John Corbit's opponent-process theory (1974) explains acquired motives such as addiction: an opposite after-reaction grows with repetition, bringing tolerance and withdrawal. Maslow's hierarchy and other lists of needs Abraham Harold Maslow (1908 to 1970), with Carl Rogers a founder of humanistic psychology (Section 1.2), set out in 1943 ("A Theory of Human Motivation") and 1954 ( Motivation and Personality ) a hierarchy of needs (Figure 1.13): physiological, safety, belongingness and love (social), esteem, and self-actualisation, becoming all that one can be. By prepotency , unmet lower needs are strongest and must be largely satisfied before higher ones take charge: a starving man dreams of food, not fame. Physiological and safety needs are thus the lower needs . The four lower levels are deficiency needs (D-needs), which stop motivating once met; self-actualisation is a growth or being (B) need, which strengthens as it is satisfied. The four lower levels are deficiency (D) needs; self-actualisation is a growth or being (B) need. Lower needs are prepotent: when unmet they dominate behaviour, and they must be largely met before higher needs take charge. Exam trap Bottom to top: physiological, safety, belongingness, esteem, self-actualisation . "Which is NOT a level?" Ego (Freud). Physiological and safety needs are lower needs : "greatest potency" is half-true (they are prepotent), and "transformational" is a leadership term. The hierarchical theory is A. H. Maslow's , not McClelland's, Atkinson's or Mowrer's. RML 2025 keyed physiological as the need mostly met before esteem; the level immediately below esteem is belongingness (social belonging) , so choose that when offered. Self-actualisers, by Maslow's estimate 1 per cent of people or fewer, show metamotivation towards metaneeds or B-values such as truth, beauty and justice; frustrated, these breed metapathologies such as cynicism and apathy. They report peak experiences , moments of ecstatic awe. Maslow later added cognitive and aesthetic needs and, beyond self-actualisation, self-transcendence . The term self-actualisation was coined by Kurt Goldstein (1878 to 1965) in 1939. Critics fault Maslow's hand-picked sample, weak evidence for the ranking and Western bias. Exam trap "Striving for fulfilment of one's potential" is self-actualisation , not self-concept, ideal self (Rogers) or self-efficacy (Bandura). Self-actualisers show metamotivation , not D-motivation; "E-" and "F-motivation" are invented. Clayton Paul Alderfer 's ERG theory (1969) shrinks the ladder to existence, relatedness and growth, lets several needs act at once and adds frustration-regression : blocked at a higher need, a person falls back on a lower one (Table 1.21). Viktor Frankl's will to meaning belongs to logotherapy (Section 1.2), not REBT, existential-humanistic therapy or ACT. Murray, McClelland and achievement Henry Alexander Murray (1893 to 1988), in Explorations in Personality (1938), listed about twenty psychogenic needs, among them n Achievement, n Affiliation (companionship), n Dominance (control of others) and n Exhibition (being seen and heard). A press is an environmental force that helps or hinders a need. Christiana Morgan and Murray's Thematic Apperception Test (TAT, 1935) reads needs and presses from stories told about ambiguous pictures (Assessment chapter). Exam trap Murray's need-press theory underlies the TAT , a projective test whose stories reveal unconscious needs, conflicts and motives; not the Rorschach, Jung's word association test or sentence completion, and not a test of IQ or memory. David Clarence McClelland (1917 to 1998) scored TAT stories for the need for achievement (nAch, 1953), a learned desire to meet standards of excellence, and later for power (nPow) and affiliation (nAff). High scorers prefer moderate risk, personal responsibility and quick feedback; businessmen he trained in Kakinada, Andhra Pradesh, in the 1960s went on to start more businesses. John William Atkinson (1923 to 2003) explained why in 1957: the tendency to approach success = motive to succeed × probability of success (Ps) × incentive (1 − Ps), and Ps × (1 − Ps) is 0.25 at Ps = 0.5 but only 0.09 at 0.1 or 0.9, so success-oriented people choose intermediate tasks, while those ruled by the motive to avoid failure pick very easy or very hard ones. Matina Souretis Horner (1972) proposed a fear of success in women, later read as cultural stereotyping. Explanations matter too. Rotter's locus of control (1966) is internal when people credit their own effort, external when they credit luck or others (not low self-efficacy or Adler's inferiority complex). Bernard Weiner (born 1935) classified the causes of success and failure by locus , stability and controllability : ability is internal, stable and uncontrollable; effort internal, unstable and controllable. "I am useless at maths" breeds hopelessness; "I did not practise enough" breeds effort. Intrinsic motivation and the self Daniel Ellis Berlyne (1960) traced curiosity to novelty, complexity and incongruity, and Robert White (1959) united Harlow's manipulation drive, exploration and play as effectance motivation , the urge to deal effectively with the environment. That competence motive has two modern heirs. The first is self-efficacy , introduced by Albert Bandura (1925 to 2021) in 1977: the belief that one can carry out the actions a particular task needs. It governs which tasks people attempt, how hard they try and how long they persist, and it grows mainly from mastery experiences, then from watching others, persuasion and bodily states. It is the core of his social cognitive theory (1986), built on triadic reciprocal causation : person, behaviour and environment influence one another. (Observational learning belongs to Section 1.6.) Exam trap The reciprocal causation model belongs to social cognitive theory , not drive reduction or constructivism (learners building their own knowledge, after Piaget and Vygotsky), and that theory highlights self-efficacy , not external rewards only, biological drives or goal difficulty. "Two-factor theories" are Herzberg's (work), Mowrer's (avoidance), Schachter and Singer's (emotion) and Spearman's (intelligence). Key study: Lepper, Greene and Nisbett's magic markers (1973) Mark Lepper , David Greene and Richard Nisbett let nursery-school children who liked drawing with magic markers draw for an expected certificate, an unexpected one, or nothing. One to two weeks later, the expected-award children spent about half as much free time drawing as the others; surprise awards did no harm. Criticism. Verbal or informative rewards do not undermine interest either, so the effect is narrower than often claimed. This overjustification effect occurs because the reward moves the reason for an enjoyed activity outside the person. Edward L. Deci and Richard M. Ryan built such findings into the second heir, self-determination theory (SDT, 1985), with three innate needs: autonomy , competence and relatedness . Its cognitive evaluation theory explains the magic markers: rewards felt as controlling lower intrinsic motivation, while informational ones, such as unexpected praise, raise it. Motivation runs from amotivation through increasingly internalised extrinsic regulation to intrinsic motivation, driven by internal reward and growth. Exam trap SDT's needs are autonomy, competence and relatedness , not affiliation or achievement (McClelland), independence, superiority or excellence. Its motivation driven by internal reward and growth is intrinsic ; amotivation is its absence, external regulation the least autonomous form. Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi (1934 to 2021) called intrinsic motivation at its most absorbing flow (1975, 1990): action and awareness merge and time vanishes when challenge and skill are balanced (too hard brings anxiety, too easy boredom). It is not Maslow's peak experience, Rogers's fully functioning person or Frankl's will to meaning. Finally, Leon Festinger 's (1957) cognitive dissonance , the tension of acting against one's beliefs (Arvind, who finds smoking disgusting, smokes at a party), motivates its reduction by a change of attitude or behaviour; effort justification is one form of that reduction, not the state (Social Psychology chapter). Conflict and frustration The blocking of goal-directed behaviour by obstacles, personal limits or conflicting motives is frustration . Pressure is the demand to perform or conform: Ramesh, made to work hard, fast and a lot in a call centre, is under pressure, not blocked (frustration), torn (conflict) or facing unpredictability. Kurt Lewin (1890 to 1947) described the conflicts in 1935. Approach-approach (two attractive goals) is easiest to resolve; avoidance-avoidance (two evils) produces vacillation and attempts to leave the field; in an approach-avoidance conflict one goal both attracts and repels; and double approach-avoidance , several such goals, is the commonest in real life. Neal Elgar Miller 's (1909 to 2002) gradients (1944) explain the vacillation: both tendencies strengthen near the goal, but avoidance is steeper, so the person hovers where they cross. Frustration may lead to aggression , direct or displaced; regression , as in Roger Barker, Tamara Dembo and Lewin's children (1941), who played like toddlers once attractive toys were screened off; fixation , as in Norman Maier 's (1949) rats, which kept jumping one way after the problem became soluble; withdrawal; or defence mechanisms (Personality chapter). The frustration-aggression hypothesis of John Dollard , Leonard Doob, Miller, Orval Hobart Mowrer and Robert Sears (1939) held that frustration always leads to aggression; Leonard Berkowitz (1989) recast it in terms of negative affect. Exam trap An after-the-fact, socially acceptable reason for behaviour really driven by other motives is rationalisation ; re-channelling sexual or aggressive impulses into valued outlets is sublimation ; a safer target is displacement ; attributing one's own impulse to others is projection ; turning it into its exaggerated opposite is reaction formation ; pushing a threatening thought out of awareness is repression ; refusing to acknowledge an unpleasant reality is denial ; compensation pushed to excess is overcompensation (the full list: Personality chapter). Hunger, thirst and sex In 1912 Walter Cannon and A. L. Washburn showed that stomach contractions coincide with hunger pangs, yet people without stomachs still feel hunger. Glucostatic (blood sugar) and lipostatic (body fat) set-point theories followed; John Pinel and Steven Barnes argue instead that we eat mainly for anticipated pleasure, with weight drifting to a settling point . In 1940 Albert Hetherington and Stephen Ranson found that lesions of the ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH) made rats overeat and grow obese; in 1951 the Indian physiologist Bal Krishan Anand and John Brobeck found that lesions of the lateral hypothalamus (LH) caused aphagia (no eating) and adipsia (no drinking). Eliot Stellar's dual-centre theory (1954) made the LH the feeding centre and the VMH the satiety centre. Since revised (VMH lesions raise insulin; other nuclei matter), it now shares the stage with leptin from fat, insulin from the pancreas and ghrelin from the empty stomach. Exam trap Satiety centre: VMH , lesion gives hyperphagia and obesity. Feeding centre: LH , lesion gives aphagia and weight loss ( L ateral, L ose). "Ventromedial hippocampus" and "lateral thalamus" are invented; the cerebrum and basal ganglia are not hunger centres. The hypothalamus as a whole is the master homeostatic regulator (hunger, thirst, temperature; its suprachiasmatic nucleus is the circadian clock), not the cerebellum (movement) or pineal gland (melatonin). Stanley Schachter 's externality hypothesis (1968 to 1971) held that obese people respond more to external food cues, such as the clock, than to internal ones (eating disorders: Psychiatric Disorders chapter). Thirst is osmotic (salty body fluid draws water from cells) or hypovolaemic (blood volume falls, signalled through angiotensin II). Alfred Charles Kinsey surveyed the sexual behaviour of men (1948) and women (1953); William Howell Masters and Virginia Eshelman Johnson (1966) observed a four-phase sexual response cycle of excitement, plateau, orgasm and resolution; Helen Singer Kaplan (1979) put desire first (desire, excitement, orgasm). Hormones such as testosterone matter less in human sexuality than in other mammals. In Carl Warden's obstruction box (1931) the maternal drive outran thirst and hunger; pain avoidance (aroused by tissue damage) and sleep (Section 1.5) complete the primary motives. Exam trap Masters and Johnson: excitement, plateau, orgasm, resolution . Sequences that insert desire (Kaplan), start with plateau or end in "refractory" (the male recovery period) are scrambles. The reports on sexual behaviour are Kinsey's , not Freud's, Anna Freud's or Horney's. Motivation at work, school and clinic Frederick Herzberg (1923 to 2000) asked about two hundred engineers and accountants when they had felt exceptionally good or bad at work. His two-factor theory (1959) separates motivators (Table 1.22), in the work itself, which create satisfaction, from hygiene factors , in its context, which cause dissatisfaction when poor but, when improved, merely remove it. If Priya, a sales executive, has E = 0.8, I = 0.9 and V = 0.7, her force is about 0.50; if her firm is known not to pay bonuses, I drops to 0.2 and her force to about 0.11. John Stacy Adams 's equity theory (1963) says people compare their ratio of outcomes to inputs with others' and act to remove inequity. In the goal-setting theory of Edwin Locke and Gary Latham (from 1968), specific, difficult but attainable goals, with commitment and feedback, beat vague "do your best" goals. Exam trap Hygiene factors prevent dissatisfaction but do not by themselves motivate (they are not self-actualisation needs, nor for high achievers only); job satisfaction depends on work motivation and job environment , not "or" or "only". Vroom's outcomes must be valuable ; guaranteed rewards, effort unrelated to performance and unimportant rewards kill motivation. Goals should be specific and challenging , with feedback, not vague, easy or value-free. In school, informational feedback, praise for effort and attribution retraining (Carol Dweck, 1975) sustain effort. In the clinic, motivational interviewing (William Richard Miller and Stephen Rollnick, 1991) treats resistance to change as ambivalence, an approach-avoidance conflict, and draws out the client's own reasons to change.
