Answers: (1) need, drive, (2) lower, (3) belongingness and love, (4) press, (5) relatedness, (6) hygiene. 1.11 Emotion and Stress Medium yield · 74 Qs Your heart pounds as the question paper is handed out. Is that pounding the fear itself, or something your mind has still to interpret? This section takes emotion apart, then turns to stress and coping. What an emotion is An emotion is a brief, whole-person response to an event that matters to you, with three components: physiological arousal (a pounding heart, sweating palms), expressive behaviour (face, voice, posture, action) and conscious experience ("I am afraid"). The theories that follow quarrel mainly about the order of these three. A feeling is the subjective part of an emotion. An emotion lasts seconds to minutes and has an object (you are angry at someone); a mood lasts hours or days, is weaker and often has no object. Affect is the umbrella term for your present good or bad feeling state and, clinically, its observable expression, rated for quality, range and reactivity; persistence is what defines mood. Temperament is the inborn style of emotional reactivity (Alexander Thomas and Stella Chess's easy, difficult and slow-to-warm-up types are in the Developmental chapter). Are there basic emotions, innate and universal, each with its own face? Paul Ekman (born 1934) and Wallace V. Friesen found six with universally recognised expressions: happiness, sadness, fear, anger, surprise and disgust, with contempt added in 1986. Silvan Tomkins (1962) listed nine innate affects; Carroll Izard 's differential emotions theory (1977) listed ten, including shame and guilt; and Robert Plutchik 's wheel (1980) set eight primaries opposite one another (joy and sadness, trust and disgust, fear and anger, surprise and anticipation), with neighbours blending into dyads such as love (joy plus trust). Dimensional models place emotions in a space instead: Wundt's three-dimensional theory of feeling (Section 1.1) and the circumplex of James Russell (1980), a circle of valence (pleasant to unpleasant) by arousal. Exam trap Jealousy, shame, guilt, pride and love are not among Ekman's six. Shame and guilt are Izard's, trust and anticipation Plutchik's. "Our current mood and feelings" is affect , not mood. Body first or label first Common sense says you see a bear, feel afraid, and therefore tremble. William James (1842 to 1910) in 1884 and the Danish physician Carl Georg Lange (1834 to 1900) in 1885 reversed the order. The James-Lange theory holds that the stimulus first triggers bodily changes and that the emotion is our perception of them: "we feel sorry because we cry, angry because we strike, afraid because we tremble." The textbook sequence is stimulus, arousal, awareness ("interpretation") of the arousal, then emotion (Figure 1.14, top row), where the "interpretation" is just the brain noticing what the body is doing. Walter Bradford Cannon (1871 to 1945) objected in 1927 that emotion survives when the viscera are cut off from the brain; that the same visceral changes accompany fear, anger, fever and exercise; that the viscera are too insensitive and slow for quick, fine distinctions; and that injected adrenaline produces symptoms without real emotion. In the Cannon-Bard theory , developed with Philip Bard (1898 to 1977), the thalamus signals the cortex and the body at once, so feeling and arousal occur simultaneously and independently (second row). If arousal is so similar across emotions, what tells fear from joy? In 1962 Stanley Schachter and Jerome Singer answered with the two-factor theory : emotion is physiological arousal, which sets its intensity, plus a cognitive label drawn from the situation, which names it. Key study: Schachter and Singer's adrenaline experiment (1962) Students given adrenaline (epinephrine), described as a vitamin, were told its true effects, told nothing or misinformed; a placebo group got saline. Each then waited with a stooge acting euphoric or angry. The aroused but uninformed caught the stooge's mood most; the informed, who could blame the injection, least. Criticism. The effects were small, and in replications unexplained arousal simply felt anxious. A label can be wrong. In misattribution of arousal people mistake the source of their arousal: in 1974 Donald Dutton and Arthur Aron found that men approached by an attractive woman on the swaying Capilano suspension bridge telephoned her far more often than men on a low, solid bridge. Fear had been read as attraction. Dolf Zillmann 's excitation transfer theory (1970s) adds that leftover arousal from one event intensifies the next emotion. Exam trap Match theory to sequence. Common sense: emotion, then body (the view James rejected). James-Lange: body first, then emotion. Cannon-Bard: emotion and visceral reaction simultaneous , via the thalamus. Schachter-Singer: cognition plus arousal , and the only one that explains misattribution. No classic theory makes the somatic nervous system the seat of emotion, and "emotions are learned through reinforcement" is behaviourism. Appraisal, faces and opposing processes Richard S. Lazarus (1922 to 2002) put thought first. In his cognitive appraisal (cognitive-mediational) theory, primary appraisal asks "Does this matter to me?" (harm-loss, threat or challenge), secondary appraisal asks "What can I do about it?", and reappraisal revises both (Figure 1.14, bottom row). Robert Zajonc (1923 to 2008) argued for affective primacy ("preferences need no inferences", 1980; debated with Lazarus in 1984): by the mere exposure effect, repeated exposure raises liking even for shapes seen too briefly to be recognised, so affect can come first. The facial feedback hypothesis , rooted in Tomkins's work, says that our own expressions modulate our feelings; in the pen study of Fritz Strack , Leonard Martin and Sabine Stepper (1988), holding a pen in the teeth, which forces a smile, made cartoons seem funnier, an effect now judged real but small. Charles Darwin 's The Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals (1872) founded the evolutionary view of expressions as inherited adaptations. Richard Solomon 's opponent-process theory (1974) holds that every strong emotion triggers a slow, opposite after-reaction that grows with repetition: a drug's high fades while withdrawal deepens. The emotional brain and body The body's side of emotion is run by the autonomic nervous system. Its sympathetic division prepares for fight or flight: it dilates the pupils, speeds the heart and breathing, dries the mouth, halts digestion and releases adrenaline from the adrenal medulla, and its sweating lowers skin resistance (the galvanic skin response). The parasympathetic division ("rest and digest") reverses each effect, constricting the pupils. Heartbeat and breathing themselves are paced by the medulla of the hindbrain; the hypothalamus only orchestrates them. Bard's cats, with the cortex removed, showed sham rage , an undirected hissing fury that vanished only when the hypothalamus was removed too: the hypothalamus organises rage and the cortex restrains it. In 1937 James Papez (1883 to 1958) proposed an emotional loop, the Papez circuit : hippocampus, fornix, mammillary bodies, anterior thalamus, cingulate gyrus, entorhinal cortex and back to the hippocampus. Paul MacLean (1913 to 2007) added the amygdala and other structures in 1952 and named the whole the limbic system , the classic "seat of emotion", which regulates emotion, motivation and memory (Table 1.23). Its key member is the amygdala , deep in each temporal lobe. When Heinrich Klüver and Paul Bucy removed both anterior temporal lobes of rhesus monkeys (1937, 1939), wild animals became tame. Klüver-Bucy syndrome is placidity (loss of fear, even of snakes), psychic blindness or visual agnosia, hyperorality, hyperphagia and hypersexuality; human cases often add aphasia and amnesia, because nearby temporal cortex is damaged too. The amygdala detects threat, drives fear conditioning and gives emotional events their extra memorability, an advantage that disappears when noradrenaline is blocked with propranolol (Cahill and McGaugh, 1994). Joseph LeDoux (born 1949) found a fast, crude low road from the thalamus straight to the amygdala and a slower, detailed high road through the cortex. Such subcortical routes probably explain affective blindsight, the recognition of emotional faces shown in a cortically blind field. The prefrontal cortex regulates emotion ( Phineas Gage 's rod injury of 1848; Antonio Damasio 's somatic markers, 1994). Damage to its control of the brainstem, after stroke, multiple sclerosis, ALS or brain injury, can cause pseudobulbar affect : sudden, involuntary laughing or crying out of proportion to the actual mood, which is not depression. The polygraph records arousal, not lies, so frightened innocent suspects can fail it; David T. Expression and four emotions The Fore of Papua New Guinea, who had seen no films or magazines, matched Ekman and Friesen's faces to stories far above chance (1971), confusing only fear with surprise. Cultures differ instead in display rules , learned norms for when an emotion may be shown. The Facial Action Coding System (1978) codes faces as muscle action units, and a genuine Duchenne smile engages the muscles around the eyes. Posture, gesture and voice carry emotion too. Women are, on average, more facially expressive, largely through socialisation. Fear answers a present danger; anxiety is diffuse and future-oriented; a phobia is a persistent, irrational fear of a specific object or situation. The catharsis hypothesis, that venting anger drains it, fails: hitting a punching bag while thinking of an insulter increased aggression ( Brad Bushman , 2002). Disgust guards against contamination ( Paul Rozin and April Fallon , 1987). Ed Diener (1946 to 2021) defined subjective well-being (1984) by three components: life satisfaction (cognitive), frequent positive affect and infrequent negative affect. Good fortune fades: by Harry Helson 's adaptation-level theory (1964) and the hedonic treadmill of Philip Brickman and Donald Campbell (1971), lottery winners are no happier than others a year or so later, and relative deprivation ( Samuel Stouffer , 1949) makes us judge ourselves against others. Barbara Fredrickson 's broaden-and-build theory (1998) says positive emotions widen thought and build lasting resources. Savoring ( Fred Bryant and Joseph Veroff , 2007) is enhancing and prolonging the enjoyment of positive experiences. Exam trap Diener: life satisfaction, not physical, spiritual or social wellness. Fredrickson: broaden-and-build; flow is Csikszentmihalyi, cognitive distortions Beck, psychodynamic theory Freud. Savoring is not avoiding negatives, relaxing or reflecting on trauma. How emotions develop and are regulated Katharine Banham Bridges (1932) saw the newborn's general excitement split first into distress and delight , and only then into anger, fear, elation and the rest. Primary emotions are present by about six months. The self-conscious emotions (embarrassment, pride, shame, guilt) need a sense of self, so they appear after 12 months, from about 18 months. Edward Tronick 's still-face procedure (1978), in which a mother suddenly freezes her face, shows that even young infants expect emotional give-and-take. In the process model of James Gross (1998), emotion regulation has five families of strategies, in the order an emotion unfolds: situation selection, situation modification, attentional deployment (distraction, rumination), cognitive change, chiefly cognitive reappraisal ("my racing heart is my body getting ready"), and response modulation, which includes expressive suppression. Alexithymia ( Peter Sifneos , 1973) is difficulty identifying and describing one's own feelings, not anhedonia (loss of pleasure). Daniel Goleman 's emotional intelligence (1995; Section 1.9) has five domains: knowing one's emotions, managing them, motivating oneself, recognising others' emotions and handling relationships (later relabelled self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy and social skills); empathy has emotional, cognitive and empathic-concern components. Exam trap Reappraisal is cognitive change ; suppression is response modulation. First infant emotions: distress and delight (Bridges); fear, rage and love are Watson's. Goleman: if the 1995 list (knowing and managing one's emotions, motivating oneself, recognising others' emotions, handling relationships) and the later self-awareness relabelling both appear, choose the 1995 wording. Stress and the body's emergency systems Stress has been defined as a stimulus (the stressor), as a response (Selye's "nonspecific response of the body to any demand") and as a transaction in which demands are appraised as exceeding one's resources. Cannon's fight-or-flight response (1915) is the fast route: within seconds the sympathetic nerves act and the adrenal medulla releases adrenaline. What if the emergency never ends? Hans Selye (1907 to 1982) found that every noxious agent he gave rats, from tissue extracts to cold, produced the same triad: enlarged adrenal glands, shrunken immune tissue and stomach ulcers. In 1936 he proposed the general adaptation syndrome ( The Stress of Life , 1956), with three stages in fixed order. In the alarm reaction the body mobilises, as in fight or flight. In the stage of resistance cortisol stays high and the body adapts, at a cost. In the stage of exhaustion adaptive capacity runs out and diseases of adaptation such as ulcers and hypertension appear. He later (1974) separated eustress , beneficial stress, from distress. Resistance runs on the slower hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis (HPA axis): the hypothalamus releases corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH), the anterior pituitary adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), and the adrenal cortex cortisol, which feeds back on the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary to switch the system off. Shelley E. Taylor (2000) added tend-and-befriend: females especially meet stress by protecting offspring and seeking allies, a pattern linked to oxytocin. Exam trap Alarm, resistance, exhaustion. Illness is not a stage, and the stages are Selye's, not life events theory, the health belief model or protection motivation theory. The adrenal glands are the stress glands; the pituitary only releases ACTH, and the posterior pituitary is not in the HPA axis. Insulin (pancreas), thyroxine (thyroid) and melatonin (pineal) are distractors. Sources of stress and the transactional model Thomas Holmes and Richard Rahe 's Social Readjustment Rating Scale (1967) scores 43 life events in life change units, from death of a spouse (100) through marriage (50) to minor violations of the law (11); because change itself is the stressor, even holidays count. Allen Kanner , Lazarus and colleagues (1981) showed that daily hassles , the irritations of everyday life, predict symptoms better than major events, while uplifts, the small pleasures that offset them, matter less. An acute stressor is brief (a pop quiz); a chronic one lasts (HIV disease, cancer, marital discord); a cataclysmic one, such as a flood or war, strikes many people at once. Frustration and conflict are covered under motivation (Section 1.10). At work, organisational stressors are task, role and interpersonal demands, structure and leadership, as distinct from environmental (political uncertainty) and individual (family, money) factors. Role conflict (incompatible expectations) and Robert Karasek 's high-demand, low-control jobs (1979) can end in burnout ( Herbert Freudenberger , 1974), which Christina Maslach 's inventory (1981) measures as exhaustion, depersonalisation and reduced accomplishment. In Lazarus and Susan Folkman 's transactional model of stress (1984), stress is a person-environment relationship appraised as taxing or exceeding one's resources: primary appraisal judges harm-loss, threat or challenge, secondary appraisal judges the resources for coping, and coping and reappraisal follow. In one exam hall, Ananya appraises the paper as a threat and her preparation as thin, and shakes; Kiran sees a challenge, trusts his practice, and feels keyed up but focused. The diathesis-stress model ( Paul Meehl , 1962; Joseph Zubin and Bonnie Spring , 1977) explains why stress makes one person ill and spares another: a disorder appears when a pre-existing vulnerability, often biological, is triggered by stress; usually neither is enough alone. Exam trap The SRRS measures life events , not hassles, physiological reactions or cognitive change. Secondary appraisal is the resources question; "coping resource assessment" is not the model's term. Diathesis-stress is not "genes only", "environment only", "unconscious conflicts only", "learned experiences alone" or supernatural; humanistic, sociocultural and cognitive models blame blocked growth, social forces and faulty thinking. Coping, personality and health Problem-focused coping acts on the stressor (a revision plan); emotion-focused coping acts on the feelings (reappraisal, support, acceptance, but also denial). The best choice fits controllability: plan while the exam can still be prepared for, reappraise once the result is out. Approach coping beats avoidance in the long run. Defence mechanisms (Personality chapter) differ in being unconscious: repression involuntarily blocks painful feelings (suppression is deliberate); displacement redirects anger to a safer target (anger at a husband shouted at a child); sublimation channels it into a valued outlet (kickboxing); projection attributes one's own feelings to others; isolation of affect strips the feeling from an idea (a gruesome fantasy told calmly), whereas denial rejects the reality; rationalisation offers a plausible excuse; and reaction formation turns a feeling into its opposite. Social support protects both directly and as a buffer when stress is high ( Sheldon Cohen and Thomas Wills , 1985). Robert S. Weiss (1973) separated emotional isolation , lacking a deep attachment to one specific person, from social isolation, lacking a circle of friends. Suzanne Kobasa 's hardiness (1979) is commitment, control and challenge; Aaron Antonovsky 's sense of coherence (1979) is comprehensibility, manageability and meaningfulness; resilience is bouncing back from adversity. Dispositional optimism ( Michael Scheier and Charles Carver , 1985), a general expectancy of good outcomes, aids coping and recovery. Martin Seligman and Steven Maier (1967) found that dogs given inescapable shock stopped trying to escape, learned helplessness (Section 1.6), which Seligman later reversed into learned optimism. In 1959 the cardiologists Meyer Friedman and Ray Rosenman described the Type A behaviour pattern : competitive striving, time urgency and hostility. In their Western Collaborative Group Study, Type A men developed coronary heart disease about twice as often as relaxed Type B men; later work found hostility to be the toxic component. A cancer-prone Type C, unassertive and suppressing negative emotion, has weak support. Johan Denollet 's Type D personality (mid-1990s) is negative affectivity plus social inhibition, and predicts a poor outlook in heart disease. George Engel 's biopsychosocial model (1977) explains illness through biological, psychological and social factors together. Psychoneuroimmunology began when Robert Ader and Nicholas Cohen (1975) conditioned immune suppression in rats by pairing saccharin with an immunosuppressive drug; chronic stress suppresses immunity and slows healing. Three models predict health behaviour: the health belief model ( Irwin Rosenstock and colleagues, 1950s: perceived susceptibility, severity, benefits, barriers and cues to action), Ronald Rogers 's protection motivation theory (1975: threat appraisal and coping appraisal) and Icek Ajzen 's theory of planned behaviour (1985: attitude, subjective norm and perceived behavioural control, close to Albert Bandura's self-efficacy, belief in one's capability to act). Stress management (Clinical chapter) includes Edmund Jacobson 's progressive muscle relaxation (1929), tensing and releasing muscle groups in turn; Herbert Benson 's relaxation response (1975); biofeedback, learning to control a bodily signal displayed on a monitor; meditation, as in Jon Kabat-Zinn 's mindfulness-based stress reduction (1979); regular aerobic exercise; and cognitive restructuring, replacing distorted thoughts with realistic ones, which Donald Meichenbaum combined with coping skills in stress inoculation training (1970s). Exam trap Type A is competitiveness, impatience and hostility; options with "non-competitiveness" are wrong, and introversion or extraversion is no risk factor. Offered both Type A and hostility, RML 2024 keyed Type A; for the toxic component , answer hostility. Type D is not hostility, optimism or perfectionism. Learned helplessness is Seligman and Maier, not Beck, Sullivan or Kahneman. Biopsychosocial means social, not cultural. Emotional isolation is not incompetence or low self-esteem. The Case of Max Friedrich's Key, Revisited Go back to the winter of 1879 and the student pressing his key. You can now take his act apart with the whole chapter. The stimulus had to cross a threshold (Section 1.3) and be organised into an object (Section 1.4); apperception was attention bringing it into focus (Section 1.5); practice shortened the times, which is learning (Section 1.6); the instruction was held in memory (Section 1.7); choosing when to press was a small decision (Section 1.8); observers differed in speed, one root of the study of individual differences and intelligence (Section 1.9); and the readiness and strain of waiting were motivation and emotion (Sections 1.10 and 1.11). Friedrich's numbers are forgotten, but his question, how long a mental act takes and what it is made of, runs through every section of this chapter. Chapter summary 1.1 Psychology as a Science: Roots, Founders and the First Schools. Psychology, once the study of the soul, is now the scientific study of behaviour and covert mental processes. Its long past lies in philosophy (Plato's nativism, Aristotle's laws of association, Descartes' dualism, Locke's tabula rasa , the associationists, Leibniz and Herbart on apperception, Kant) and in physiology (Muller, Helmholtz, localisation), with Darwin and Galton adding function and individual differences. Fechner's psychophysics (1860) and Donders' chronometry measured the mind. Wundt founded the first laboratory at Leipzig in 1879 and taught voluntarism through controlled introspection. Titchener 's structuralism sought the elements of consciousness; James 's functionalism asked what the mind is for, and Witmer opened the first clinic (1896). 1.2 Schools and Systems, the Cognitive Revolution and Indian Psychology. From about 1900 to 1960 psychology was a preparadigmatic field of rival schools. Watson founded behaviourism in 1913; Tolman, Hull, Guthrie and Skinner refined it. Gestalt psychology (Wertheimer's phi phenomenon, 1912; Kohler; Koffka) held that the whole differs from the sum of its parts, and Lewin defined the life space. Psychoanalysis was the first force, humanism (Maslow, Rogers) the third and transpersonal psychology the fourth, beside existential psychology and Seligman's positive psychology. The cognitive revolution (1956 onwards) restored the mind. Sengupta and Bose pioneered modern psychology at Calcutta; Indian psychology rests on Samkhya's purusha, prakriti and three gunas, Patanjali's eight limbs, the four states and the five koshas. 1.3 Sensation and Psychophysics. Sensation is the detection and transduction of physical energy; perception is its interpretation, so illusions distort perception. Muller's specific nerve energies and the all-or-none law explain how quality and intensity are coded, and every sense but smell relays through the thalamus. Fechner's psychophysics (1860) defines the absolute threshold as 50 percent detection and the JND as the smallest detectable change; Weber's law, Fechner's logarithmic law and Stevens' power law link stimulus to sensation, and signal detection theory separates sensitivity (d′) from response bias. Rods serve scotopic vision and foveal cones colour and acuity; colour is trichromatic then opponent; pitch is coded by place and timing; gate control explains pain. 1.4 Perception: Organising and Interpreting the World. Perception is the selection, organisation and interpretation of sensory signals. Constructivist theories (Helmholtz's unconscious inference, Gregory's hypotheses, the Bayesian union of priors and evidence) treat it as top-down inference; Gibson's direct, ecological theory, with its affordances, is the classic bottom-up account, and Neisser's perceptual cycle joins the two. The Gestalt laws, crowned by Prägnanz, organise the field into figure, ground and groups. Depth comes from two binocular cues (retinal disparity, convergence) and many monocular ones; the visual cliff (Gibson and Walk, 1960) showed depth perception by crawling age. Constancies keep objects stable, while illusions such as the Müller-Lyer reveal misapplied size scaling and differ from hallucinations and delusions. 1.5 Attention and Consciousness. Attention selects the little that reaches awareness; its span, studied by Jevons (1871) and with the tachistoscope, is about six to eight items. Cherry's dichotic listening (1953) led to Broadbent's early filter (1958), Treisman's attenuation model (1964) and late selection (Deutsch and Deutsch, 1963). In the Stroop effect (1935) automatic reading defeats selective attention, and vigilance declines over a watch (Mackworth). James described a stream of consciousness, Freud conscious, preconscious and unconscious levels. The suprachiasmatic nucleus times sleep, whose NREM and REM stages cycle every 90 minutes, four to six times a night. Dreams are explained by Freud, Jung and activation-synthesis; hypnosis rests on suggestibility. 1.6 Learning: Conditioning, Cognition and Observation. Learning is a relatively permanent change in behaviour, or its potential, resulting from experience (Kimble). In classical conditioning (Pavlov) a neutral stimulus paired with a UCS becomes a CS; extinction, spontaneous recovery, generalisation and discrimination follow. Watson's Little Albert showed conditioned fear, and Jones and Wolpe reversed it through counterconditioning and systematic desensitisation (reciprocal inhibition). Rescorla, Kamin and Garcia showed that conditioning depends on prediction and preparedness. In operant conditioning (Thorndike's law of effect, Skinner) consequences change behaviour: reinforcement increases it, punishment decreases it, and schedules shape its pattern, variable ratio most strongly. Tolman's latent learning, Köhler's insight and Bandura's observational learning showed much learning without direct reinforcement. 1.7 Memory: Encoding, Storage, Retrieval and Forgetting. Memory is studied as encoding , storage and retrieval ; Ebbinghaus (1885) measured forgetting with nonsense syllables and savings. Atkinson and Shiffrin's multi-store model (1968) separates sensory, short-term (seven plus or minus two chunks, mainly acoustic) and long-term memory, and Baddeley and Hitch (1974) recast short-term memory as working memory : central executive, phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad and, from 2000, the episodic buffer. Depth of processing, Tulving's episodic and semantic memory, implicit memory, schemas and Bartlett's reconstruction, encoding specificity, decay, interference and repression explain remembering and forgetting, while H.M., Korsakoff's syndrome and Lashley's search for the engram reveal its biology. 1.8 Thinking, Problem Solving, Reasoning, Decision Making and Language. Thinking manipulates internal representations: images (Shepard and Metzler's mental rotation; Paivio's dual coding), concepts (Bruner's hypothesis testing for artificial concepts, Rosch's prototypes for natural ones) and propositions. Problems yield to algorithms, heuristics or Gestalt insight, and are blocked by functional fixedness (Duncker, 1945) and mental set (Luchins, 1942). Deduction runs from theory to data, induction from data to theory. Simon's bounded rationality and satisficing, and Tversky and Kahneman's heuristics and prospect theory, describe real decisions. Creativity is divergent production passing through Wallas's four stages. Language is built from phonemes and morphemes; Chomsky's LAD, the critical period, Whorf's linguistic relativity and Vygotsky's inner speech complete the picture. 1.9 Intelligence: Theories, Measurement, Heredity and Environment. Intelligence has been defined as judgement (Binet), what the tests test (Boring) and Wechsler's aggregate or global capacity (1944). Binet and Simon's 1905 scale introduced mental age; Stern coined the IQ (1912), Terman's Stanford-Binet (1916) made the ratio IQ famous, and Wechsler's deviation IQ (mean 100, SD 15) replaced it. The WAIS-IV has four indices; Raven's matrices test fluid intelligence, and Bhatia's Battery suits illiterate Indian children. Spearman's g, Thurstone's primary abilities, Guilford's cube, Cattell's fluid and crystallised intelligence, Gardner's multiple intelligences and Sternberg's triarchic theory offer rival structures. Heritability is a population statistic, and intellectual disability requires adaptive deficits as well as low IQ. 1.10 Motivation. Motivation energises and directs behaviour: a need produces a drive that pushes, while incentives pull. McDougall's instincts gave way to Hull's drive reduction (1943), which could not explain curiosity; Hebb proposed optimal arousal, and the Yerkes-Dodson law (1908) makes performance an inverted U of arousal with a lower optimum for complex tasks. Maslow's hierarchy of needs runs physiological, safety, belongingness, esteem, self-actualisation; Alderfer reduced it to ERG. Murray's needs and press underlie the TAT; McClelland studied achievement, power and affiliation. Self-efficacy, self-determination theory and flow explain intrinsic motivation. Lewin classified conflicts; the VMH is the satiety centre, the LH the feeding centre; Herzberg, Vroom and Locke explain work. 1.11 Emotion and Stress. An emotion joins arousal, expression and conscious experience; a mood is longer and diffuse, and affect is the current feeling state. Ekman named six universal basic emotions. James-Lange puts bodily change before feeling, Cannon-Bard makes them simultaneous via the thalamus, Schachter and Singer add a cognitive label (explaining misattribution), and Lazarus puts appraisal first. The limbic system , above all the amygdala , organises fear. Stress runs through Selye's alarm, resistance and exhaustion and the HPA axis; life events, hassles and appraisal shape it, and coping, support, hardiness and Type A or D personality link it to illness. Type D personality, biopsychosocial model, Psychoneuroimmunology From the past papers Functionalism, an early school of thought in psychology, was most closely associated with which psychologist? (IHBAS 2024) (a) Edward Titchener (b) John Watson (c) William James (d) G. Stanley Hall Answer: (c) William James. James's Principles of Psychology (1890) inspired the functionalist question of what the mind is for, and Dewey and Angell made it a formal school at Chicago. Titchener founded the rival structuralism, Watson founded behaviourism, and Hall, though functionalist in spirit, is examined for institutions such as the first American research laboratory (1883) and the APA (1892). The first person to use the term clinical psychology in print was (RML 2020) (a) Erik Erikson (b) Sigmund Freud (c) Lightner Witmer (d) Cattell Answer: (c) Lightner Witmer. Witmer opened the first psychological clinic at the University of Pennsylvania in 1896 and used the term in print in his journal The Psychological Clinic (1907). Erikson is known for the psychosocial stages, Freud for psychoanalysis, and James McKeen Cattell for coining "mental test". Match List I with List II LIST I (Psychologist) LIST 2 (Theory) A. Later Social Learning (IHBAS 2024) (a) A-1, B-2, C-3, D-4 (b) A-3, B-1, C-4, D-2 (c) A-2, B-1, C-3, D-4 (d) A-3, B-2, C-4, D-1 Answer: (b) A-3, B-1, C-4, D-2. Dollard and Miller recast Freud in Hull's terms in 1950 (early social learning); Skinner's system is radical behaviourism; Bandura and Walters gave the later social learning theory (1963); Maslow is self-actualisation. Option (d) tempts only if you forget that Skinner, not Maslow, is the radical behaviourist. Which is the correct order of the last four of Patanjali's eight limbs? (NIMHANS 2026 recall) (a) Dharana, pratyahara, dhyana, samadhi (b) Pratyahara, dharana, dhyana, samadhi (c) Pratyahara, dhyana, dharana, samadhi (d) Dhyana, dharana, pratyahara, samadhi Answer: (b) Pratyahara, dharana, dhyana, samadhi. The senses are first withdrawn inward (pratyahara), the mind is then fixed on one point (dharana), the fixing becomes an unbroken flow (dhyana) and finally absorption (samadhi). Each wrong option swaps two of these steps. Which statement is INCORRECT? (Amity 2023) (a) Cones are most prevalent in the central retina (b) Cones are sensitive to moderate to high levels of light (c) Cones provide only monochromatic information (d) Cones provide excellent acuity Answer: (c) Cones provide only monochromatic information. Cones, with three pigments, give colour vision; it is the rods, with one pigment (rhodopsin), that give colourless scotopic vision. The other three statements are true: cones are packed in the fovea, work in moderate to bright light and give excellent acuity. In signal detection theory, the ability to distinguish a stimulus from background noise is: (IHBAS 2025) (a) Sensitivity (d′) (b) Criterion (β) (c) ROC curve (d) JND Answer: (a) Sensitivity (d′). d′ is the separation between the noise and signal-plus-noise distributions and does not depend on the observer's willingness to say "yes". The criterion (β) is that willingness (response bias), the ROC curve plots hit rate against false alarm rate, and the JND belongs to classical psychophysics. Among monocular cues for depth perception is (JEMAS 2025) (a) Convergence (b) Retinal disparity (c) Assimilation (d) Interposition Answer: (d) Interposition. An object that partly hides another is seen as nearer, and one eye is enough to see it. Convergence and retinal disparity are the only two binocular cues, and assimilation is not a depth cue at all (it is Piaget's term). Illusions are (JEMAS 2025) (a) misinterpretation of stimuli arising from an external object (b) real perceptual object perceived in a distorted way (c) vivid mental images (d) perception without an adequate external stimulus Answer: (a) Misinterpretation of stimuli arising from an external object. In an illusion a real stimulus is misread. Option (b) is a sensory distortion such as micropsia, (c) is imagery, and (d) is the definition of a hallucination. The Stroop effect demonstrates interference in (JEMAS 2025) (a) Long-term memory retrieval (b) Working memory (c) Selective attention (d) Procedural memory Answer: (c) Selective attention. Automatic word reading cannot be filtered out while naming the ink colour, so the task shows a failure of selective attention. The memory options are distractors; no stored memory is being retrieved or rehearsed. According to Freud, the ___ mind includes accessible memories, which can be recalled at will (RML 2020) (a) Conscious (b) Preconscious (c) Unconscious (d) Psychic determinism Answer: (b) Preconscious. The conscious holds only what is in awareness now, and the unconscious cannot be recalled at will; psychic determinism is a principle (no mental event is accidental), not a level of mind. Systematic desensitization technique is based upon the idea of: (IHBAS 2025) (a) Reciprocal inhibition (b) Law of effect (c) Habituation (d) Adaptation to stress Answer: (a) Reciprocal inhibition. Wolpe paired each step of an anxiety hierarchy with relaxation, a response incompatible with anxiety, so the anxiety bond weakens. The law of effect is Thorndike's operant principle, habituation underlies exposure and response prevention, and adaptation to stress belongs to stress theory. Among the following schedules of reinforcement, which typically produces the highest rate of response and is most resistant to extinction? (Real PYQ 2024) (a) Fixed Ratio (b) Variable Ratio (c) Fixed Interval (d) Variable Interval Answer: (b) Variable Ratio. Ratio schedules reward fast responding, and unpredictability removes any reason to pause and makes it hard to tell that reinforcement has stopped, as with slot machines. Fixed ratio shows a pause after each reinforcer, fixed interval a scallop and variable interval only a moderate, steady rate. The famous patient H.M. (Henry Molaison) underwent surgical removal of the medial temporal lobes, including the hippocampus, to treat severe epilepsy. While he retained most of his intellectual abilities and working memory, his primary and most profound deficit was in: (Real PYQ 2024) (a) Procedural memory (b) Semantic memory (c) Anterograde amnesia (d) Retrograde amnesia Answer: (c) Anterograde amnesia. After the 1953 operation H.M. could not form new declarative memories, although his intelligence, digit span and childhood memories survived. Procedural memory was spared (he learned mirror tracing), old semantic knowledge was intact, and his retrograde amnesia covered only the years before surgery. Which of the following terms refers to difficulty recalling information due to interference from new information? (IHBAS 2024) (a) Retroactive interference (b) Proactive interference (c) Decay theory (d) Retrieval failure Answer: (a) Retroactive interference. New learning reaching back to disrupt older memories is retroactive (RETRO: new disrupts old); proactive interference is the reverse, old disrupting new. Decay blames the passage of time and retrieval failure a mismatch of cues, not competition from new learning. In which method does the researcher gather data, look for patterns, and then generate a theory or hypothesis? (RML 2023) (a) Deductive reasoning (b) Hypothetico-deductive method (c) Inductive reasoning (d) Abductive reasoning Answer: (c) Inductive reasoning. Induction runs from specific observations to a probable generalisation, so data come first and theory last, as in most qualitative research. Deduction and the hypothetico-deductive method run the other way, from a theory to a tested prediction; abduction infers the best explanation of a surprising fact. What is the primary difference between Piaget and Vygotsky's theories of language development? (RML 2021) (a) Piaget argued thought depends on language while Vygotsky argued language depends on thought (b) Vygotsky argued thought depends on language while Piaget argued language depends on thought (c) Vygotsky was concerned with early language development while Piaget was concerned with later language development. (d) None of the above Answer: (b). For Piaget, language expresses concepts already built through action; for Vygotsky, thought and speech merge at about two, after which thought becomes verbal and depends on language. Option (a) swaps the names, and (c) is false because both studied the same preschool years. The term IQ was invented by (JEMAS 2025) (a) Lewis Termon (sic) (b) Gordon Allport (c) William Stern (d) John Watson Answer: (c) William Stern. Stern proposed the intelligence quotient, mental age divided by chronological age, in 1912. Terman is the tempting wrong answer: he multiplied the quotient by 100 and popularised it in the 1916 Stanford-Binet, but did not coin it; Allport (traits) and Watson (behaviourism) never worked on the IQ. A 10-year-old child from a rural area, with no formal schooling, is brought for an intellectual assessment due to academic struggles. The child is illiterate and has had minimal exposure to formal testing materials. Which of the following tests would be the MOST appropriate to use to minimize cultural and educational bias? (Real PYQ 2024) (a) Bhatia's Battery of Performance Tests of Intelligence (b) Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children (WISC-IV) (c) Stanford-Binet Intelligence Scale (5th ed.) (d) Malin's Intelligence Scale for Indian Children (MISIC) Answer: (a) Bhatia's Battery of Performance Tests of Intelligence. Its five performance subtests need no reading, and it has Indian rural norms. The WISC-IV and SB5 rest on school-built verbal knowledge and foreign norms; MISIC is the tempting Indian option, but half of it is verbal, adapted from the WISC. The ‘satiety centre’ of the brain is located in the: (RML 2024) (a) Lateral hypothalamus (b) Ventromedial hippocampus (c) Lateral thalamus (d) Ventromedial hypothalamus Answer: (d) Ventromedial hypothalamus. Bilateral VMH lesions make rats overeat and grow obese (Hetherington and Ranson, 1940), so Stellar's dual-centre theory (1954) called the VMH the satiety centre. The lateral hypothalamus is the opposite, the feeding centre, whose destruction causes aphagia (Anand and Brobeck, 1951); "ventromedial hippocampus" and "lateral thalamus" are invented by changing one word. According to Herzberg's Two-Factor Theory, which of the following factors are considered motivators that lead to job satisfaction? (RML 2023) (a) Salary and benefits (b) Job security and work conditions (c) Recognition and opportunities for advancement (d) Company policies and interpersonal relationships Answer: (c) Recognition and opportunities for advancement. Herzberg's motivators lie in the content of the work: achievement, recognition, the work itself, responsibility, advancement and growth. Salary, benefits, job security, working conditions, company policies and relationships are hygiene factors, which prevent dissatisfaction when good but do not by themselves motivate. The seat of emotion is to be found in _________________. (RML 2024) (a) Reticular formation (b) Hind brain (c) Limbic system (d) Forebrain Answer: (c) Limbic system. MacLean's limbic system (1952), built on Papez's circuit and including the amygdala, is the classic seat of emotion. The reticular formation governs arousal and wakefulness, the hindbrain paces heartbeat and breathing, and "forebrain" is too broad, although the limbic system lies within it. 'Psychological disorders develop when a biological predisposition is set off by a stressful situation', is proposed by (JEMAS 2025) (a) Humanistics existential models. (b) Socio-cultural model. (c) Diathesis-stress model. (d) Cognitive model. Answer: (c) Diathesis-stress model. A pre-existing vulnerability (diathesis) set off by a stressful trigger is the model's definition (Meehl, 1962; Zubin and Spring, 1977). Humanistic-existential models blame blocked growth, sociocultural models social forces and cognitive models faulty thinking; none is defined by predisposition plus stress. High-yield sheet The facts this chapter's questions ask most, most-asked first. Last read before the exam. Systematic desensitisation (Joseph Wolpe, Psychotherapy by Reciprocal Inhibition , 1958) rests on reciprocal inhibition : relaxation, a response incompatible with anxiety, is paired step by step with a graded anxiety hierarchy. asked 17 times Working memory (Alan Baddeley and Graham Hitch, 1974) has four components: the central executive (an attentional controller that stores nothing, loaded by random number generation), the phonological loop (auditory-verbal information), the visuospatial sketchpad (visual and spatial information, including mental rotation) and the episodic buffer, added in 2000, which binds information into coherent episodes. asked 11 times The token economy is operant conditioning with tokens as secondary reinforcers, developed by Teodoro Ayllon and Nathan Azrin ( The Token Economy , 1968); it is the listed therapy not derived from classical conditioning. asked 10 times Abraham Maslow 's hierarchy of needs (1943, 1954), bottom to top: physiological, safety, belongingness and love (social), esteem, self-actualisation. Physiological and safety needs are the lower needs; ego is not a level. asked 10 times Korsakoff's syndrome follows thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency in chronic alcoholism, often after Wernicke's encephalopathy (confusion, ataxia, nystagmus); it damages the mammillary bodies and mediodorsal thalamus and causes dense anterograde amnesia, extensive retrograde amnesia and confabulation, sincere false stories that fill memory gaps. asked 8 times The empty chair technique belongs to Gestalt therapy (Fritz Perls, with Laura Perls and Paul Goodman), an experiential here-and-now therapy that is not the Gestalt psychology of Wertheimer, Kohler and Koffka. asked 7 times Variable ratio reinforcement gives the highest, steadiest rate and the greatest resistance to extinction; fixed ratio gives high rates with a post-reinforcement pause, fixed interval the scallop, variable interval moderate steady rates, and continuous reinforcement the fastest learning and fastest extinction. asked 7 times Extinction is the fading of a conditioned response when the CS is repeatedly presented without the UCS, or of an operant response that is no longer reinforced; a parent who ignores tantrums is using extinction, not operant escape. asked 7 times Reinforcement always increases behaviour and punishment decreases it; positive adds and negative removes a stimulus, so switching off a shock is negative reinforcement , while time-out and response cost are negative punishment . asked 7 times H.M. (Henry Molaison) had both medial temporal lobes, including the hippocampus and amygdala, removed by William Beecher Scoville in 1953; Scoville and Brenda Milner (1957) reported a profound anterograde amnesia for declarative memory, with normal short-term memory, limited retrograde amnesia and spared procedural learning (mirror tracing). asked 7 times Raymond Cattell (with John Horn) split g into fluid intelligence (Gf), reasoning with novel problems independently of acquired knowledge and measured best by Raven's Progressive Matrices, and crystallised intelligence (Gc), the repertoire of information, cognitive skills and strategies, measured by vocabulary and information. asked 7 times The limbic system is the classic "seat of emotion": Paul MacLean named it in 1952, enlarging James Papez's 1937 circuit, and it regulates emotion, motivation and memory; hunger and thirst belong to the hypothalamus. asked 7 times The amygdala is the structure for fear and aggression: it detects threat, drives fear conditioning and gives emotional events their extra memorability, while the hippocampus stores the facts. asked 7 times The hippocampus is the structure damaged in anterograde amnesia and is critical for consolidating new declarative memories; it is not the store of remote memories. asked 6 times Narendra Nath Sengupta set up India's first psychology laboratory (1915) and first Department of Psychology (1916) at the University of Calcutta and is the father of modern psychology in India; keys naming Bose or Uma Chaudhuri for the first laboratory are wrong. asked 5 times Humanistic psychology (Maslow, Rogers) is the third force , after psychoanalysis (first) and behaviourism (second); transpersonal psychology is the fourth force. asked 5 times The Stroop effect (John Ridley Stroop, 1935): naming the ink colour of a conflicting colour word (RED printed in green) is slowed because automatic word reading interferes; it shows a limit of selective attention (interference in reaction time), not a memory effect. asked 5 times Proactive interference : earlier learning disrupts newer learning (dialling your old phone number); retroactive interference : newer learning disrupts older memories. RML 2024 keys English grammar intruding on newly learned Spanish as retroactive, but it is proactive. asked 5 times Inductive reasoning moves from specific observations to probable generalisations (gather data, find patterns, build theory: the logic of theory development and qualitative research); deductive reasoning starts from a theory and tests its predictions against observations. asked 5 times Graham Wallas ( The Art of Thought , 1926): preparation, incubation, illumination, verification; incubation (setting the problem aside) is second and illumination (the insight) third. asked 5 times Functional fixedness (Karl Duncker's candle problem, 1945) is seeing an object only in its usual use; mental set (Abraham Luchins's water jars, 1942) is reusing a strategy that worked before, and was keyed as the most basic and common obstacle to problem solving. asked 5 times Henry Murray 's need-press theory (1938) underlies the Thematic Apperception Test (Morgan and Murray, 1935), a projective test whose stories reveal the teller's needs, conflicts and motives. asked 5 times Wilhelm Wundt opened the first psychology laboratory at Leipzig in 1879 (not Vienna, Paris or Cambridge); Galton's London laboratory (1884) was anthropometric. asked 4 times Patanjali's eight limbs , in order: yama, niyama, asana, pranayama, pratyahara (withdrawal of the senses), dharana (concentration on one point), dhyana (unbroken meditation), samadhi (absorption); karma and jnana are not limbs. asked 4 times Tamas is the guna of inertia, lethargy, darkness, dullness and ignorance; a person who has stopped eating and cannot get herself to act shows tamas alone. asked 4 times Every sense except smell relays through the thalamus on its way to the cortex (vision via the lateral geniculate nucleus, hearing via the medial geniculate nucleus); the olfactory nerve (cranial nerve I) bypasses it. asked 4 times The suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) of the hypothalamus is the master circadian pacemaker, entrained by light through the retinohypothalamic tract; SCN lesions abolish circadian rhythms, not total sleep. asked 4 times REM (paradoxical) sleep : a desynchronised, fast, low-voltage EEG like waking, rapid eye movements, atonia of the core muscles, genital arousal and vivid dreams; EEG synchrony and delta waves belong to N3, spindles and K-complexes to N2. asked 4 times Carl Jung split the unconscious into a personal (individual) unconscious and the collective unconscious , an inherited layer of archetypes shared by all humanity, which he explained by the similar brain structure of all human races. asked 4 times William Stern coined the intelligence quotient in 1912;
