A4 PDF of the whole book, colour (821 pages) A4 PDF, black and white (821 pages) Chapter 1 Psychology as a Science: Roots, Founders and the First Schools In this chapter 1.1 What Is Psychology? : define psychology as it has been defined across history, state its four goals, separate basic from applied work and name the main fields, including the one that studies animals. 1.2 Philosophical Roots: A Long Past : trace nativism, rationalism, empiricism and associationism from Plato to Kant, and lay out the classic positions on the mind-body problem. 1.3 Physiological and Biological Roots : explain how nerve physiology, brain localisation, Darwin's evolution and Galton's study of individual differences prepared the ground for a laboratory science. 1.4 Measuring the Mind: Psychophysics and Mental Chronometry : show how Weber, Fechner, Donders and Ebbinghaus proved that mental events could be measured. 1.5 Wilhelm Wundt and the Founding of Experimental Psychology : describe Wundt's laboratory, his voluntarism, his theory of feeling, his method and his folk psychology, and name his famous students. 1.6 Structuralism and Its European Rivals : explain Titchener's structuralism, its method and its errors, and the challenges from Wurzburg, Brentano, Stumpf and G. E. Muller. 1.7 Functionalism and the American Pioneers : explain why functionalism arose, what James, Dewey, Angell, Carr and Woodworth contributed, and who built American psychology's institutions. 1.8 Reading the History: Zeitgeist, Great Persons and "Fathers" : compare the two ways of explaining history, master the "father of" and "first" questions, and trace the arrival of psychology in India. Weightage. 46 of the 819 questions mapped in this book (5.6%) test this chapter, 12 of them from real past papers. 1 of its 8 sections is High yield. Leipzig, in the winter of 1879. In a small room of an old university building known as the Konvikt, a doctoral student named Max Friedrich sits in front of a clockwork timer called a Hipp chronoscope, a machine built to measure intervals in thousandths of a second. A stimulus is presented; Friedrich presses a telegraph key. Then the procedure is changed: now he must press the key not the instant he senses the stimulus, but only once he has clearly grasped what it is. The second kind of reaction takes longer, and the extra time, Friedrich and his supervisor reasoned, is the time the mind needs to apperceive , to bring an impression into the clear focus of attention. Trial after trial, the numbers go into a notebook. His supervisor was a 47-year-old professor of philosophy, Wilhelm Wundt. When Wundt had arrived in Leipzig four years earlier, the university had given him this room to store the apparatus he used in lecture demonstrations. By the winter of 1879 it had become something new: a place where students carried out original experiments on the mind and published them as research. Friedrich's study of the duration of apperception became the first dissertation to come out of that room, and historians who later combed the Leipzig archives dated the start of the work to the last weeks of 1879. Here is the puzzle that should bother you. Almost nothing in that room was new. The chronoscope had been built for physicists and astronomers. The idea of measuring the time taken by mental acts came from a Dutch physiologist. The word apperception came from a German philosopher who had died in 1716. And at Harvard, in 1875, the same year Wundt got his room, an American named William James had also been given space for psychological apparatus. So why does every textbook in the world, and nearly every entrance paper in India, treat Leipzig in 1879 as the moment psychology was born? The answer to that question is the subject of this chapter. To find it you need to know where the parts in that room came from: the philosophers who argued for two thousand years about where knowledge comes from, the physiologists who timed nerves and mapped brains, the naturalists who put human beings back among the animals, and the physicists who dared to measure sensation. Then you need to see what Wundt and his students built from those parts, and what the next generation, in Germany and in America, did with it. Remember Max Friedrich pressing his key; we will come back to him at the end of the chapter. 1.1 What Is Psychology? Medium yield · 5 Qs Ask ten people at a chai stall what psychology is and you will hear ten answers: reading minds, treating madness, understanding why people do what they do. Ask ten textbooks and you will get fewer answers, but you will notice something odd: the textbooks of 1890, 1920 and today do not agree with one another either. The definition of psychology has changed several times, and each change tells you which school was in charge. Entrance papers love these definitions, so we start with them. From soul to behaviour: a definition that kept changing The word itself is Greek: psyche (breath, soul) and logos (study or reasoned account). Literally, then, psychology began as "the study of the soul". The Greek philosophers did not use the word as the name of a subject; it first appears in Latin book titles of the sixteenth century (the German scholar Rudolf Goclenius used it in 1590), and the philosopher Christian Wolff (1679 to 1754) made it standard with two books, Psychologia empirica (1732) and Psychologia rationalis (1734). For the Greeks and the medieval scholars, the soul was the principle of life and reason; Aristotle (384 to 322 BCE) wrote the first systematic treatise on it, De Anima ( On the Soul ), which is why some older Indian textbooks call him the "father of psychology". From the seventeenth century, philosophers spoke less of the soul and more of the mind : its ideas, its reasoning, its sensations. When psychology became a laboratory science in the nineteenth century, the definition narrowed again. For Wundt and his student Titchener, psychology was the science of conscious experience , studied by trained observers looking inward. William James, in 1890, opened his great textbook with the sentence "Psychology is the Science of Mental Life, both of its phenomena and of their conditions." Then came the revolt. In 1905 and again in 1908 the British psychologist William McDougall (1871 to 1938) defined psychology as the positive science of the conduct or behaviour of living creatures, and in 1913 John B. Watson declared that psychology should drop consciousness altogether and study only behaviour , by which he meant anything an organism does that can be observed and measured from outside. (Watson and behaviourism are the subject of Chapter 2.) The new definition spread through the textbooks. Robert Sessions Woodworth (1869 to 1962), whom you will meet again in Section 1.7, defined psychology as the scientific study of the activities of the individual in relation to the environment. The definition you will most often find credited in Indian textbooks, "psychology is the scientific study of behaviour", is attributed to the American textbook writer Norman L. Munn . Watson's definition won battles but lost the war. By the 1960s psychologists were again studying memory, imagery and thinking, and today's standard definition reunites the two halves: psychology is the scientific study of behaviour and mental processes . Each phrase in that definition is doing work. Behaviour is overt: speaking, walking, blushing, pressing a key. By contrast, mental processes are internal and covert: perceiving, remembering, thinking, dreaming, feeling. You cannot see a student remembering the year of Wundt's laboratory, but you can infer it from what he writes. And scientific means that claims are tested against systematic, public observation that someone else could repeat, not against authority or intuition. An old classroom quip sums up the whole story: first psychology lost its soul, then it lost its mind, then it lost consciousness, and now it has behaviour, of a sort. Table 1.1 puts the sequence in order. Table 1.1 How psychology has been defined. Period Psychology is the study of Associated with Ancient Greece the soul (psyche) Plato, Aristotle ( De Anima ) 17th to 19th century the mind Descartes, Locke, the associationists 1879 to about 1910 conscious experience; "mental life" Wundt, Titchener; James (1890) 1905 to 1913 onward conduct, behaviour McDougall (1905, 1908); Watson (1913) Textbook definitions activities of the individual in relation to the environment; the scientific study of behaviour Woodworth; N. L. Munn Today behaviour and mental processes most modern textbooks Exam trap "In the definition of psychology, mental processes mean ..." The answer is internal, covert processes . "Outward behaviour" and "overt actions and reactions" describe the other half of the definition, and "only animal behaviour" describes neither. A related bank question asks who "first proposed and established psychology as the scientific study of behaviour" and keys N. L. Munn , because Indian textbooks quote that definition from Munn. Historically McDougall (1905, 1908) and Watson (1913) came first; if Watson appears as an option alongside Munn, read the stem closely: "established" behaviourism points to Watson, "the definition" points to Munn. Do not confuse William James (science of mental life) with any behaviour definition. The four goals: describe, explain, predict, control Every science tries to do four things with the events it studies, and psychology is no exception. Take one example and push it through all four: a student who "blanks out" in the examination hall at Mysuru even though he knew the material the night before. Describe. First we must say exactly what happens, and to whom: racing heart, sweaty palms, a mind that will not retrieve answers, perhaps in the first ten minutes only. Careful description separates this from simple lack of preparation. Explain. Next we ask why. Perhaps very high arousal and catastrophic thoughts ("If I fail, everything is over") compete with retrieval for limited attention. An explanation is a cause that can be tested. Predict. A good explanation lets us forecast who will blank out and when: students with high scores on a test-anxiety scale, under time pressure, on high-stakes papers. Control (many textbooks now say influence or change ). Finally we use the knowledge to change the outcome: practice under timed conditions, relaxation training, rehearsing realistic self-statements. This goal is where clinical psychology lives. Some textbooks add a fifth goal, improving the quality of life, but the four above are the classic list. Watson put prediction and control at the very centre of his definition, a point we will return to in Chapter 2. Basic and applied research Psychologists who study a problem only to understand it are doing basic research ; those who study it to solve a practical problem are doing applied research . When Hermann Ebbinghaus memorised lists of meaningless syllables in the 1880s to discover how quickly memories fade, he was doing basic research; when Lightner Witmer opened a clinic in 1896 to help a boy who could not learn to spell, he was doing applied work. The line is not a wall: Witmer's clinic drew on the basic science of the laboratory, and applied problems constantly raise new basic questions. You will see in Section 1.7 that the split between "pure" and "applied" psychology was one of the main arguments between the first two schools. The fields of psychology Modern psychology is a family of specialities. You will study several of them in other books of this series, so here we need only a map (Table 1.2). Two of them deserve a sentence more, because entrance papers test the boundary between them. Put simply, clinical psychology is the assessment, diagnosis and treatment of psychological disorders and distress; its practitioners work with conditions ranging from anxiety to schizophrenia, in hospitals, clinics and private practice. counselling psychology overlaps heavily but has traditionally focused on people in the normal range who face adjustment problems: career choice, relationships, study difficulties, life transitions. In India, the Rehabilitation Council of India licenses clinical psychologists, not counsellors, to work with psychiatric disorders, which is one reason your interviewers will care whether you understand the difference. The branch that studies the behaviour of animals is comparative psychology : it compares species, often in the laboratory, to understand how behaviour and learning evolved and what is common to humans and other animals. Its biological cousin, ethology , studies animal behaviour in natural settings and is associated with the zoologists Konrad Lorenz and Nikolaas Tinbergen. You will see in Section 1.3 that comparative psychology grew directly out of Darwin's work. Three more names in Table 1.2 are easily confused. The first, evolutionary psychology , explains present-day behaviour and mental mechanisms as adaptations shaped by natural selection, that is, as part of our genetic inheritance from ancestors who faced recurring problems of survival and reproduction. The second, behaviour genetics , asks a narrower question: how much of the variation among people in a trait is due to differences in their genes, studied mainly through twins, families and adoption. The third, differential psychology , is the study of individual differences in abilities and personality; the German psychologist William Stern (1871 to 1938) named it in 1900, but its founder in practice was Francis Galton (Section 1.3). Table 1.2 The main fields of psychology. Field What it studies Clinical Assessment, diagnosis and treatment of psychological disorders Counselling Adjustment problems of people in the normal range: career, relationships, transitions Health How behaviour, stress and beliefs affect physical illness and recovery Developmental Change across the lifespan, from conception to old age Social How people think about, influence and relate to one another Industrial-organisational Behaviour at work: selection, training, motivation, leadership, organisations Educational and school Learning and teaching; children's learning problems in schools Forensic Psychology applied to law: testimony, criminal behaviour, competence Comparative Animal behaviour, compared across species Neuropsychology Brain-behaviour relations, often through people with brain damage Abnormal The nature and causes of psychological disorders (psychopathology) Experimental Basic processes (sensation, learning, memory) studied by experiment Differential Individual differences in ability and personality Evolutionary Behaviour and mind as products of natural selection Exam trap "Which branch focuses on the study of animal behaviour?" is comparative psychology . Abnormal psychology studies disorders; differential psychology studies individual differences among people; social psychology studies people in relation to others. "What does clinical psychology primarily focus on?" is the assessment and treatment of mental illness ; industrial applications and organisational management belong to industrial-organisational psychology, and behavioural changes in animals to comparative psychology. The bank question asking which branch studies "behaviour in relation to genetic inheritance" keys evolutionary psychology ; if behaviour genetics is ever offered as an option, prefer it for questions about heritability. With a definition and a map in hand, we can ask how this discipline came to exist at all. The German memory researcher Hermann Ebbinghaus put the answer in one famous sentence in 1908: "Psychology has a long past, but only a short history." The long past is two thousand years of philosophy and a century of physiology; the short history begins in rooms like Wundt's. Figure 1.1 lays out the short history; the next three sections trace the long past that made it possible. Roots: 1850 to 1890 Schools and institutions: 1892 to 1925 1850 Helmholtz times the nerve impulse; Fechner's insight (22 October) 1859 Darwin, On the Origin of Species 1860 Fechner, Elements of Psychophysics 1861 Broca: speech area (patient Tan) 1869 Galton, Hereditary Genius 1873/74 Wundt, Principles of Physiological Psychology 1879 Wundt's Leipzig laboratory: research begins 1883 Hall: first US research laboratory (Johns Hopkins) 1885 Ebbinghaus, On Memory 1890 James, Principles of Psychology; Cattell coins "mental test" 1892 APA founded at Clark; Hall first president 1894 Washburn: first woman PhD in psychology 1896 Witmer's clinic (Pennsylvania); Dewey's reflex arc paper 1898 Titchener names structuralism 1905 Calkins: first woman APA president 1906 Angell, The Province of Functional Psychology 1913 Watson's behaviourist manifesto 1915/16 Calcutta: first Indian laboratory and department 1922 Bose founds the Indian Psychoanalytic Society 1925 Indian Psychological Association founded Figure 1.1 The short history of psychology at a glance. Notice how the roots (left) cluster in German physiology and British biology, and how quickly the institutions (right) followed once Wundt's laboratory opened in 1879. 1.2 Philosophical Roots: A Long Past Medium yield · 5 Qs Long before anyone measured a reaction time, philosophers had asked the three questions that still organise much of psychology. Where does knowledge come from? How are ideas connected to one another? And how is the mind related to the body? Psychology inherited all three, and the answers given between ancient Athens and eighteenth-century Germany are examined every year in Indian entrance papers. Let us define the main positions first, then meet the people who held them. On the first question, there are two classic answers. The first, nativism , holds that some knowledge, ideas or abilities are inborn, present before any experience. The second, empiricism , holds that all knowledge comes from experience, delivered through the senses. A third term, rationalism , is often paired with nativism: it holds that reason, not the senses, is the chief source of knowledge, and that the senses can deceive. Keep the two contrasts apart. Nativism versus empiricism is a question about origins (inborn or learned?). Rationalism versus empiricism is a question about the route to knowledge (reasoning or sensing?). In practice the rationalists were usually nativists, and the empiricists were nearly always anti-nativists, which is why exam setters sometimes treat the pairs as one. Plato and Aristotle Plato (about 427 to 347 BCE) was a nativist and a rationalist. In his dialogue Meno , Socrates draws a theorem of geometry out of an uneducated slave boy simply by asking him questions, and concludes that the boy was not learning but recollecting knowledge his soul already possessed. For Plato, the senses show us only shifting copies of the true, unchanging Forms; real knowledge comes from reason turning inward. He also divided the soul into three parts (reason, spirit and appetite), an early model of conflict within the mind that you may hear echoed when you study Freud. Plato's student Aristotle disagreed. In De Anima he treated the soul not as a separate thing trapped in the body but as the form or function of a living body, the way seeing is the function of an eye. And he was an empiricist: the mind at birth, he wrote, is like a writing tablet on which nothing has yet been written, and knowledge begins with the senses. (Hold on to that tablet; John Locke will pick it up two thousand years later.) Aristotle also gave psychology its first theory of how one idea leads to another. In his short work On Memory and Recollection he observed that when we try to recall something we start from a thing that is similar to it, contrary to it, or was contiguous with it (close to it in time or place). These are the laws of association : similarity , contrast and contiguity , to which later writers added frequency (ideas experienced together often are linked more strongly). Try it on yourself. Hear the name "Sachin" and "Tendulkar" follows by contiguity, because you have always met the two words together; "Virat Kohli" may follow by similarity (another great Indian batsman); and the thought of the slowest batsman you ever watched may follow by contrast. Exam trap Aristotle is the empiricist of the pair and Plato the nativist ; students often reverse them because Aristotle is called the "father of psychology" (for De Anima ) and they assume he must have founded everything. Aristotle's three laws are similarity, contrast, contiguity . David Hume's three laws (below) are resemblance, contiguity in time or place, and cause and effect . If a question lists "contrast", it is Aristotle; if it lists "cause and effect", it is Hume. Rene Descartes: the body as a machine As a young man early in the seventeenth century, Rene Descartes (1596 to 1650) walked in the royal gardens at Saint-Germain-en-Laye, near Paris, where hydraulic statues moved, played music and even sprayed water at visitors who stepped on hidden plates in the path. The statues seemed alive, yet they were only pipes, water and valves. Descartes drew a bold conclusion: perhaps the living body is the same kind of machine. Nerves could be tubes, and "animal spirits", a fine fluid stored in the brain's cavities, could flow through them to inflate the muscles. Using this model, Descartes gave the first clear description of the reflex : an automatic, unlearned response to a stimulus that needs no mind at all. Put your hand near a fire, he said, and the heat moves particles in the skin, which tug on a thread inside the nerve, which opens a tiny valve in the brain, which releases animal spirits that flow back down to the arm muscles and pull the hand away. The details were wrong, but the idea that much behaviour is mechanical stimulus and response would run, through the Russian physiologists, all the way to behaviourism. The body, then, is a machine, and animals, which Descartes believed had no souls, are nothing but machines (automata). But the human being has something more: a mind, a thinking thing that has no size or location and cannot be doubted. "I think, therefore I am" (in French, je pense, donc je suis ), he wrote in his Discourse on Method (1637). This is dualism : mind and body are two different kinds of substance, the thinking substance and the extended (physical) substance. And because the two plainly affect each other (a pinprick causes pain; a decision moves an arm), Descartes was an interactionist. He placed the meeting point in the pineal gland , a small structure deep in the brain, chosen because, unlike most brain structures, it is single rather than paired and sits near the centre of the brain. His last book, The Passions of the Soul (1649), described how bodily events stir the emotions through this gland. Descartes was also a rationalist and a nativist. He held that certain innate ideas are not learned from experience but are built into the mind: the ideas of God, of the self, of infinity, and the axioms of geometry. You will see why this matters when we reach Kant and, in Chapter 2, the Gestalt psychologists. Remember Descartes left psychology four legacies: (1) mechanism and the reflex, which led through reflex physiology to Pavlov and behaviourism; (2) innate ideas , which led through Kant to the nativism of the Gestalt school; (3) dualism , which created the modern mind-body problem; and (4) rationalism , against which the British empiricists reacted. A practice question asks what Descartes' dualism "influenced" and keys behaviourism and Gestalt psychology on exactly this reasoning. "Empiricism and rationalism" is the wrong pairing because Descartes was himself a founder of modern rationalism, and empiricism was the reaction against him. The British empiricists: Hobbes, Locke, Berkeley and Hume Across the English Channel a very different tradition grew up, one that insisted the mind contains nothing that did not come in through the senses. Thomas Hobbes (1588 to 1679), best known for his political book Leviathan (1651), was its blunt forerunner. Hobbes was committed to materialism , the view that only matter exists; he held that sensations are motions in the body caused by motions outside it, and that thinking is a "train of thoughts" in which one motion follows another in the order in which they were first experienced. He also argued that human action is driven by the pursuit of pleasure and the avoidance of pain. Many historians call him the founder of British empiricism. The philosopher who made empiricism a full theory of mind was John Locke (1632 to 1704). Locke tells us that his great book began when a group of five or six friends met in his rooms to discuss a philosophical problem and got nowhere; it struck him that before arguing about what we know, they ought to examine what the human understanding is capable of knowing. Nearly twenty years later he published An Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1690). Its central claim is that the mind at birth is "white paper, void of all characters", the idea usually summed up by the Latin tabula rasa (blank or scraped tablet). There are no innate ideas. Every idea comes from one of two sources: sensation (experience of the outside world) or reflection (the mind's experience of its own operations, such as thinking and doubting). Locke divided ideas into simple ideas , which cannot be broken down further (the redness, sweetness and roundness of an apple), and complex ideas , which the mind builds by combining simple ones (the idea "apple" itself). This is the beginning of the "mental chemistry" that runs through the rest of this chapter: complex mental life built from simple elements. He also distinguished two kinds of qualities in objects. The primary qualities (solidity, extension or size, shape, motion and number) exist in the object itself, and our ideas of them resemble the object. The secondary qualities (colour, sound, taste, smell and warmth) exist only as powers to produce sensations in a perceiver. Locke's own demonstration is worth doing. Put one hand in hot water and the other in cold water for a minute; then plunge both into a bowl of lukewarm water. The same water feels cold to the first hand and warm to the second. Since the water cannot be both hot and cold, warmth must be in the perceiver, not in the water. Its size and shape, by contrast, feel the same to both hands. Finally, in the fourth edition of the Essay (1700) Locke added a chapter titled "Of the Association of Ideas", giving psychology the phrase. Interestingly, he used association mainly to explain irrational connections: ideas joined by chance or custom (a room where something terrible happened becomes unbearable) that produce prejudice and what he did not hesitate to call a kind of madness. Indian context In 1688 the Irish scientist William Molyneux wrote to Locke with a puzzle: if a man born blind, who had learned to tell a cube from a sphere by touch, were suddenly given sight, could he tell which was which by looking alone? Locke, a good empiricist, said no: the link between seen and felt shape must be learned. For three centuries "Molyneux's problem" could not be tested. Then, in a study published in 2011, Richard Held, Pawan Sinha and colleagues working with Project Prakash in India tested children who had been blind from birth with treatable cataracts. Immediately after surgery the children could see the shapes clearly but could not pick out by sight the shape they had just felt; within days, the link appeared. Locke's answer was largely right, and the learning was fast. George Berkeley (1685 to 1753), an Irish bishop, pushed Locke's argument to a startling end. If colour and warmth exist only in the perceiver, why not size and shape too? All we ever know are our own perceptions. To exist, for any object, is to be perceived: in Latin, esse est percipi . This position is called subjective idealism or mentalism. Berkeley also made a lasting contribution to the psychology of perception. In An Essay Towards a New Theory of Vision (1709) he argued that we are not born able to see distance; we learn it, by associating visual cues (such as the feeling of the eyes converging on a near object, or blur) with the experience of reaching and walking. This is the first empiricist theory of depth perception, and the nativist reply to it is one of the threads of Chapter 4. David Hume (1711 to 1776), a Scot, published A Treatise of Human Nature in 1739 and 1740. He divided the contents of the mind into impressions (vivid, immediate experiences) and ideas (faint copies of impressions, as when you remember a taste). Ideas are joined, he said, by three laws of association: resemblance, contiguity in time or place, and cause and effect. He thought of association as a kind of gentle mental force, the mind's equivalent of Newton's gravity. Then he turned the analysis on causation itself and found that we never see one event make another happen; we see only that the two have always been joined (constant conjunction), and the mind forms the habit of expecting one after the other. Even the self, Hume said, is nothing but "a bundle or collection of different perceptions". Hume's scepticism woke the German philosopher Immanuel Kant, as we shall see. Associationism: Hartley, the two Mills and Bain Out of British empiricism grew a doctrine with a name of its own. Its name, associationism , refers to the view that complex mental life, including memory, thought and emotion, is built up by linking simple elements (sensations and ideas) according to a few laws, above all contiguity and frequency. Four writers turned it into a system. David Hartley (1705 to 1757), a physician, published Observations on Man in 1749. He was the first to give association a physiological basis: sensations are vibrations in the nerves and brain, and they leave behind miniature vibrations, which he called vibratiuncles , that are ideas. When two vibrations occur together often, they become linked, so that one later sets off the other. Contiguity, strengthened by repetition, was for Hartley the master law, and he distinguished simultaneous from successive associations. Historians usually credit him with founding associationism as a formal doctrine. James Mill (1773 to 1836) took the doctrine to its most mechanical extreme in Analysis of the Phenomena of the Human Mind (1829). For him a complex idea is nothing more than the sum of the simple ideas that compose it: the idea of a house is the ideas of bricks, mortar, windows and so on, added together, and the idea of "everything" is all the other ideas at once. This view is called mental mechanics . His son, John Stuart Mill (1806 to 1873), saw the flaw. In A System of Logic (1843) he argued that ideas can fuse into a whole with properties that none of the parts possessed, just as hydrogen and oxygen combine into water, which is like neither gas. His favourite example was Newton's colour disc: paint the colours of the spectrum on a wheel and spin it, and you see white, which is not experienced as "seven colours added". This is mental chemistry . Think of masala chai. James Mill would say your idea of its taste is tea plus milk plus ginger plus cardamom plus sugar; John Stuart Mill would say the taste of good chai is a new whole that is in none of the ingredients. The younger Mill's idea anticipates both Wundt's creative synthesis (Section 1.5) and the Gestalt slogan that the whole is different from the sum of its parts (Chapter 2). The last of the associationists, the Scot Alexander Bain (1818 to 1903), brought the tradition to the edge of modern psychology. His The Senses and the Intellect (1855) and The Emotions and the Will (1859) were the standard British textbooks of psychology for half a century, and they tied every mental process to what was then known of the nervous system. Bain described how a random ("spontaneous") movement that happens to bring pleasure is retained and repeated, a trial-and-error account of learning that anticipates Thorndike. In 1876 he founded Mind , the first journal devoted to psychology and philosophy. Exam trap Mental mechanics belongs to the father, James Mill; mental chemistry to the son, John Stuart Mill. Do not mix up James Mill with William James, or John Stuart Mill with John Locke. "Tabula rasa" is Locke , not Plato (nativist), Descartes (innate ideas) or Kant (innate categories). If asked the source of knowledge "as per empiricists", the answer is sensory experience ; "logical reasoning" and "contemplation" are the rationalists' routes. The continental rationalists: Leibniz, Herbart and Kant While the British were building the mind out of sensations, philosophers in Germany insisted that the mind is active, organised and partly unconscious. Their ideas reached Wundt directly, so we need them in some detail. Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz (1646 to 1716), co-inventor of the calculus, pictured reality as made of countless monads : simple, indivisible, active units of force, each of which mirrors the whole universe from its own point of view. Monads do not act on one another (they are "windowless"); they are kept in step by a harmony that God arranged in advance. Applied to mind and body, this "pre-established harmony" is a form of parallelism, which we will meet below. More important for psychology was Leibniz's theory of consciousness. He argued that we receive many perceptions too weak to notice individually, which he called petites perceptions (small perceptions). Standing on a beach, you hear the roar of the sea, yet that roar is made of the sounds of thousands of single waves, none of which you could hear on its own. When enough small perceptions add up, they cross into clear awareness, a step Leibniz called apperception . Consciousness is therefore a matter of degree, not all or none, and much mental activity goes on below awareness. Against Locke he wrote, in his New Essays on Human Understanding , that there is nothing in the intellect that was not first in the senses, "except the intellect itself". Johann Friedrich Herbart (1776 to 1841), who succeeded to Kant's chair at Konigsberg, turned Leibniz's ideas into a kind of mental mechanics with mathematics. Ideas, he said, have strength, and they compete: incompatible ideas push each other down. An idea that is pushed down does not vanish; it sinks below a boundary he called the threshold of consciousness (a limen), where it remains active and strives to return. Fechner would borrow the idea of a threshold for psychophysics, and Freud's repressed ideas that push to return to awareness have a family resemblance to it. The ideas currently in consciousness form an organised body that Herbart called the apperceptive mass . A new idea is understood, or apperceived, only by being taken up into this mass of existing ideas; an idea that finds nothing related to attach to is not grasped at all. Herbart was also a great educational theorist, and the classroom lesson follows directly: teach new material by linking it to what the child already knows. (His followers later turned this into the "formal steps" of lesson planning, which teacher-training colleges in India still teach.) You have experienced this yourself: the term "apperception" is far easier to learn now, attached to Leibniz's sea and Herbart's competing ideas, than it would be as an isolated word in a list. Herbart said psychology could be empirical and mathematical, but he did not believe it could be experimental, and he kept it separate from physiology. Within forty years both claims would be overturned in Leipzig. Exam trap An IHBAS 2025 question asks what the "apperceptive mass" constitutes and keys pure perception and pre-existing ideas , meaning a new perception taken up into the store of ideas already in the mind. The term is Herbart's ; Wundt took over and reworked the idea of apperception, which is why the question names him. The distractors each belong to someone else: "a compound of elemental processes bound by association" is the associationist (and structuralist) picture of the mind; "sensation and pure perception" leaves out the existing ideas that are the whole point; "sensation plus unconscious inference" is Helmholtz's theory of perception (Section 1.3). Apperception as a word was coined by Leibniz. The most influential German philosopher of all, Immanuel Kant (1724 to 1804), answered Hume in his Critique of Pure Reason (1781). Hume had shown that experience alone can never give us necessary connections such as causality. Kant replied that the mind does not wait passively for experience to write on it; it imposes its own built-in forms on whatever the senses deliver. Space and time are the forms through which we must perceive anything, and categories such as causality, unity and substance are the frames through which we must think about it. We never know things as they are in themselves, only as our minds organise them. This is nativism of a sophisticated kind, and it passed through the perceptual nativists of the nineteenth century into Gestalt psychology. Kant also issued a challenge. Psychology, he argued, could never be a true natural science, because mental events cannot be measured, cannot be put to experiment, and are distorted by the very act of observing them. The history in the rest of this chapter can be read as a series of replies to Kant: Herbart made psychology mathematical, Fechner made it measurable, and Wundt made it experimental. The answers given over the next three centuries form a small set of positions that every psychology student must be able to name (Figure 1.2). The first, interactionism , is Descartes' own answer: mind and body are different substances that causally affect each other. Its weakness is the one Descartes never solved, namely how something with no physical properties can push on something physical. Some of his followers, notably Nicolas Malebranche, proposed occasionalism : mind and body never act on each other, and God produces the bodily event on each occasion of the mental one, and the reverse. The second, psychophysical parallelism , holds that mental events and bodily events run side by side, perfectly correlated, but neither causes the other. Leibniz's picture was two clocks that keep identical time because they were set together at the start, not because one drives the other. Parallelism was attractive to the first experimental psychologists because it let them correlate mental events with physiological ones without worrying about causation; Wundt and Titchener both held versions of it. The third, epiphenomenalism , holds that bodily (brain) events cause mental events, but mental events cause nothing; consciousness is a by-product. Its best-known advocate, the English biologist Thomas Henry Huxley (1825 to 1895), compared consciousness to the whistle of a steam engine: it accompanies the work of the engine but does nothing to drive it. Finally, monism denies that there are two substances at all. Materialist monism (Hobbes) says only matter exists and mind is a process of the body. Idealist monism (Berkeley) says only minds and their perceptions exist. And double-aspect theory , associated with the Dutch philosopher Baruch Spinoza (1632 to 1677), says there is one underlying reality that shows itself in two ways: seen from the inside it is mind, seen from the outside it is body, as the same curved line is concave from one side and convex from the other. Fechner, the founder of psychophysics, held a view close to this one. A word on the philosophy of science Questions about the mind sit inside larger philosophical questions about what exists and how we can know it, and a few terms from the philosophy of science turn up in psychology papers. The term ontology (from the Greek for "being") names the branch of philosophy that deals with existence: what kinds of things are real? Is the mind a thing, a process, or an illusion? By contrast, epistemology deals with knowledge: how do we know what we know, and what counts as good evidence? The nativist-empiricist debate above is an epistemological debate. In the nineteenth century the French philosopher Auguste Comte (1798 to 1857) founded positivism , the view that genuine knowledge comes only from observable, verifiable facts, and that speculation about unobservable causes should be abandoned. Comte rejected introspection on the ground that the mind cannot observe itself, any more than the eye can see itself, an objection you will meet again when Wundt's method comes under fire. Post-positivism , associated with the twentieth-century philosopher Karl Popper, accepts that all scientific knowledge is fallible and provisional, so that theories are tested by trying to refute them rather than by piling up confirmations. Scientific realism holds that the unobservable entities described by our best theories (electrons, genes, perhaps memory traces) really exist. Of these terms, only ontology is defined by the question of existence. Philosophy, then, handed psychology its questions and some brilliant guesses. What it could not supply was a way to settle the arguments. For that, psychology had to borrow the methods of a different parent: experimental physiology. 1.3 Physiological and Biological Roots Lower yield · 1 Q By the middle of the nineteenth century, physiologists in Germany, France and Britain were doing something philosophers never had: cutting, stimulating, timing and measuring living nervous systems. Their findings did two things for the future psychology. They showed that the machinery of mind could be studied by experiment, and they gave Wundt, who trained as a physiologist, his methods and his confidence. Nerves carry the message The first great discovery was about the wiring. In 1811 the Scottish anatomist Charles Bell (1774 to 1842) described, in a privately printed pamphlet, evidence that the nerve roots entering the spinal cord at the front and at the back have different functions. In 1822 the French physiologist Francois Magendie (1783 to 1855) showed it decisively in experiments on young animals. The result is the Bell-Magendie law : the dorsal (back) roots of the spinal nerves carry sensory information in, and the ventral (front) roots carry motor commands out. The nervous system, in other words, has separate input and output channels, an anatomical basis for the distinction between sensation and movement, and ultimately for the stimulus-response unit. (The two men's quarrel over who deserved credit is a classic example of simultaneous discovery, which we discuss in Section 1.8.) The most influential physiologist of the age was Johannes Muller (1801 to 1858) of Berlin, whose Handbook of Human Physiology (published in parts from 1833 to 1840) summarised the field for a generation. Muller's best-known idea is the doctrine of specific nerve energies : the quality of a sensation depends not on the stimulus but on which nerve is stimulated. The optic nerve, however it is excited, produces only sensations of light; the auditory nerve only sound. You can test this now: close your eyes and press gently on the outer corner of one eyelid. You will see a patch of light, though no light has entered your eye; pressure on the optic pathway is "read" as light. A blow to the head makes a boxer "see stars" for the same reason. Muller's idea meant that we never perceive the world directly, only the state of our own nerves, a physiological version of the philosophers' point that experience is not the same as the object (the modern form of the idea, "labelled lines", is covered in Chapter 3). Muller's students included Hermann von Helmholtz and Emil du Bois-Reymond, and Wundt himself spent a semester in his Berlin laboratory. Muller believed that the speed of the nerve impulse was so great that it might never be measured. His student proved him wrong within a decade. Key study: Helmholtz times the nerve impulse (1850) Question. Is the nerve impulse effectively instantaneous, like light, or does it take measurable time? Method. Hermann von Helmholtz (1821 to 1894) used a frog's nerve with the muscle still attached. He stimulated the nerve first at a point far from the muscle and then at a point near it, and timed the delay before the muscle twitched. Result. Stimulation farther from the muscle produced a later twitch, and dividing the difference in distance by the difference in time gave a speed of only about 27 metres per second, roughly the speed of a car on a highway. Conclusion. Nervous activity is a physical process that takes time. If nerve conduction takes time, so may perceiving and deciding, and those times can be measured. Caveat. When Helmholtz tried to measure reaction times in human beings, the results varied so much from trial to trial and person to person that he gave up, an early hint of the individual differences that Galton and Cattell would later study. Helmholtz was perhaps the greatest scientist of the century, and three more of his ideas reach psychology. First, his theory of unconscious inference : perception is not a simple copy of sensation but a conclusion the mind draws, quickly and without awareness, from sensory data and past experience. When you see a distant elephant as huge though its image on your retina is tiny, you are "inferring" its size from its distance. This made Helmholtz an empiricist about perception, and it is the ancestor of modern ideas of perception as hypothesis-testing (Chapter 4). Second, building on a suggestion made by the English physician Thomas Young (1773 to 1829) in 1802, Helmholtz developed the trichromatic theory of colour vision, the Young-Helmholtz theory, which holds that colour vision depends on three types of receptor, most sensitive to different parts of the spectrum. Third, he proposed a resonance (place) theory of hearing. All three are developed in Chapters 3 and 4. For this chapter, remember that Wundt worked as Helmholtz's assistant at Heidelberg for several years. Exam trap "Helmholtz gave the trichromatic theory of colour vision" is the keyed answer to the bank question about him. The distractors are carefully chosen. The just noticeable difference belongs to Weber and Fechner (Section 1.4); the law of effect to Thorndike (Chapter 6). "Proposed the concept of the unconscious" is a trap because Helmholtz did propose unconscious inference , but the concept of the unconscious mind in the psychodynamic sense belongs to Freud (and its philosophical roots to Leibniz and Herbart). Mapping functions onto the brain If the nerves are wires, is the brain a single organ that does everything everywhere, or a collection of specialised parts? The modern answer, localisation of function , emerged through a strange mixture of quackery and careful science. The quackery came first. The Viennese physician Franz Joseph Gall (1758 to 1828) was a skilled brain anatomist, but he is remembered for a bolder claim: that the brain is made up of separate organs for separate mental faculties (such as acquisitiveness, combativeness or love of offspring), that a well-developed faculty means a larger organ, and that a larger organ pushes out the skull above it. By feeling the bumps on a person's head, therefore, one could read his character. Gall's collaborator Johann Gaspar Spurzheim (1776 to 1832) popularised the system under the name phrenology and carried it across Europe and America, where "phrenological parlours" read heads for a fee. Phrenology was wrong in its method (skull shape does not reflect the brain beneath, and Gall chose his evidence selectively), but it was right in its central assumption that different parts of the brain do different things. Phrenology's first scientific critic was the French physiologist Pierre Flourens (1794 to 1867). In the 1820s he used the method of ablation (also called extirpation): surgically removing a part of the brain of an animal, usually a pigeon or rabbit, and observing what behaviour was lost. He found real localisation at the level of large structures: damage to the cerebellum disrupted the coordination of movement, damage to the medulla stopped breathing and heartbeat, and removal of the cerebral hemispheres abolished perception and voluntary action. But within the cerebral hemispheres he found no faculties in particular places: the effects of damage seemed to depend on how much tissue was removed, and the cortex seemed to act as a whole. Flourens' ablation method became standard in physiological psychology, and his view of the cortex as acting as a whole was revived a century later by Karl Lashley (covered in the Physiological Psychology book). Localisation within the cortex was finally demonstrated through language. In 1861 the French surgeon Paul Broca (1824 to 1880) examined a patient named Leborgne, known in the hospital as "Tan" because that was nearly the only syllable he could say. Tan understood much of what was said to him but could not produce speech. When he died, Broca's autopsy found damage in the left frontal lobe, in a region now called Broca's area, and by 1865 Broca had concluded that "we speak with the left hemisphere". In 1874 the 26-year-old German neurologist Carl Wernicke (1848 to 1905) described the opposite pattern: patients with damage to the left temporal lobe who spoke fluently but meaninglessly and could not understand speech. Broca's aphasia is effortful, non-fluent speech with relatively preserved comprehension; Wernicke's aphasia is fluent speech with poor comprehension. (The aphasias, including the transcortical and conduction forms, are covered in the Physiological Psychology book.) Meanwhile, in 1870, the German physicians Gustav Fritsch (1838 to 1927) and Eduard Hitzig (1838 to 1907) applied weak electric currents to the exposed cortex of dogs and found a strip of the frontal lobe where stimulation produced movements of specific body parts on the opposite side of the body: the motor cortex. Electrical stimulation now joined ablation and clinical autopsy as a method of mapping the brain. Table 1.4 brings the localisation story together. Table 1.4 The localisation pioneers. It had a plausible theory, confident practitioners, satisfied customers and an apparently huge body of supporting cases, yet it was false, because its evidence was gathered selectively and never put to a fair test. Every assessment tool you will learn to use, from an intelligence test to a projective test, must earn its place by evidence of reliability and validity (the Assessment book), not by the confidence of the person using it. Charles Darwin: the human animal Physiology showed that the mind had machinery. Biology showed where the machinery came from. When Charles Darwin (1809 to 1882) published On the Origin of Species in 1859, he proposed that species change over generations through natural selection : individuals vary, some variations help their owners survive and reproduce, and those variations become more common in later generations. In The Descent of Man (1871) he applied the theory to human beings, and in The Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals (1872) he argued that facial expressions of emotion are inherited and universal, shared with other animals because they once served adaptive purposes (baring the teeth in anger is a remnant of preparing to bite). He even published a diary of his infant son's development (1877), one of the first "baby biographies". Darwin gave psychology three gifts, and each grew into a branch of the discipline. Continuity between species. If humans evolved from other animals, then animal minds differ from ours in degree, not kind, and studying animals can tell us about ourselves. This is the foundation of comparative psychology and of all later animal research on learning. Function. If a trait exists because it helped survival, then the right question to ask about any mental process is what it is for . This question is the heart of functionalism (Section 1.7), and through functionalism, of today's evolutionary psychology. Variation. Natural selection works on differences between individuals, so those differences are worth measuring. This idea was taken up by Darwin's own half-cousin. Francis Galton and the measurement of individual differences Francis Galton (1822 to 1911) shared a grandfather, the physician-poet Erasmus Darwin, with Charles Darwin. Independently wealthy, he never held a university post, and he could not see anything without wanting to count it: he once tried to make a "beauty map" of Britain by secretly tallying attractive and unattractive women he passed in different towns. After reading the Origin , he devoted himself to human variation, and in doing so he founded the study of individual differences . His first major book, Hereditary Genius (1869), traced the families of eminent judges, statesmen, scientists and others, and found that eminence ran in families far more than chance would predict. Galton concluded that ability is inherited. The flaw is obvious to you now: eminent families also pass on wealth, education and connections, so his data could not separate heredity from environment. Galton saw the problem himself and, in 1875, proposed studying twins to separate the effects of "nature and nurture" (a phrase he popularised). He was the first to use twin studies for this purpose. Key study: Galton's anthropometric laboratory (1884) Question. How much do people differ in basic physical and mental capacities? Method. At the International Health Exhibition in London in 1884, Galton set up an anthropometric laboratory where, for threepence, visitors were measured on height, weight, arm span, breathing capacity, strength of grip, swiftness of a blow, keenness of sight and hearing, colour discrimination, reaction time and the highest pitch they could hear (tested with a whistle he designed). More than 9,000 people passed through. Reasoning. Following the empiricist logic that all knowledge enters through the senses, Galton assumed that people with sharper senses and quicker reactions would be more intelligent. Result. He obtained the first large body of data on human individual differences, and to analyse it he had to invent new statistics. Criticism. The assumption linking sensory keenness to intelligence turned out to be wrong, as Cattell's followers discovered (Section 1.7); intelligence testing had to wait for Binet's very different approach (Chapter 9). The statistics may be Galton's greatest legacy. Studying the heights of parents and children (and, earlier, the sizes of sweet-pea seeds), he noticed that very tall parents tend to have children who are tall but less extreme than themselves, a phenomenon now called regression to the mean (1886). From this he developed the idea of correlation , a measure of how closely two variables vary together (1888); his younger colleague Karl Pearson (1857 to 1936) later produced the formula for the correlation coefficient that you will use in the Research Methodology book. Galton also pioneered the questionnaire (asking people to describe the vividness of their mental image of that morning's breakfast table), and in 1879 he devised the word association test: he read a word and noted the first association it called up, and was startled to find how many of his own associations reached back to childhood and revealed thoughts he would rather not publish. Carl Jung later developed word association into a clinical technique (the Personality book). There is a darker side. In 1883 Galton coined the word eugenics for the programme of improving the human stock by encouraging the "fit" to have more children and discouraging the "unfit". Eugenics was later used to justify forced sterilisation and, in Nazi Germany, mass murder. Galton's statistics are permanent tools of psychology; his eugenics is a permanent warning. Animal minds: from anecdote to Morgan's canon Darwin's idea of continuity invited a new question: how intelligent are animals? Darwin's young friend George John Romanes (1848 to 1894) set out to answer it, and his Animal Intelligence (1882) is usually treated as the first book of comparative psychology. Romanes gathered stories, from naturalists, pet owners and newspaper readers, of animals doing clever things: a cat that opened a door latch, a dog that seemed to plan. This anecdotal method had two weaknesses. Anecdotes are selected (no one writes in to report a dog doing something stupid), and they invite anthropomorphism , reading human thoughts and feelings into animal behaviour. The correction came from the British psychologist Conwy Lloyd Morgan (1852 to 1936). Morgan's own fox terrier, Tony, learned to open the garden gate by lifting the latch with his head. A visitor who saw only the finished act would have credited Tony with understanding how latches work, but Morgan had watched the learning: it came slowly, through many chance successes while Tony poked his head through the railings. In An Introduction to Comparative Psychology (1894) Morgan stated the rule now called Morgan's canon : "In no case may we interpret an action as the outcome of the exercise of a higher psychical faculty, if it can be interpreted as the outcome of the exercise of one which stands lower in the psychological scale." It is a principle of parsimony : prefer the simplest explanation that fits the facts. Key study: Clever Hans (1904 to 1907) The claim. In Berlin, a retired schoolteacher, Wilhelm von Osten, exhibited a horse called Hans that seemed to add, subtract and answer questions by tapping its hoof. A commission that included the psychologist Carl Stumpf found no trickery in 1904. Method. Stumpf's student Oskar Pfungst then tested Hans systematically, varying whether the questioner knew the answer and whether Hans could see the questioner. Result. Hans answered correctly only when the questioner knew the answer and was visible. Without meaning to, questioners tensed as the taps began and relaxed slightly, or raised their heads, when the right number was reached, and Hans had learned to stop at that cue. Conclusion (published 1907). The horse was clever, but at reading people, not at arithmetic: a perfect illustration of Morgan's canon. The "Clever Hans effect" is why modern experiments use observers who do not know which condition a participant is in. Comparative psychology soon moved from anecdote into the laboratory. Edward Thorndike's puzzle-box studies of cats (1898, Chapter 6) and Margaret Floy Washburn's textbook The Animal Mind (1908, Section 1.7) carried it into the twentieth century, and Watson would build behaviourism on it. Clinical link Morgan's canon is good clinical sense. A child who will not read aloud in class may have a reading disability, poor eyesight, anxiety or a hearing problem before we conclude that he is "defiant" or "lazy". Test the simpler, lower-level explanations first. You will see in Section 1.7 that the first patient at the world's first psychological clinic turned out to have exactly such a simple problem.
