Reading old history with care One last lesson concerns the reader rather than the past. It is tempting to judge old ideas by what we know now: to laugh at phrenology, to dismiss introspection as naive, to treat Wundt as a dull cataloguer of sensations. In 1965 the historian George Stocking made the standard name for this habit familiar to historians of the behavioural sciences: presentism , interpreting and judging the past by the standards and concerns of the present. Its opposite, historicism , tries to understand past thinkers on their own terms: what questions they were asking, what evidence they had, what their contemporaries believed. Presentism is not always wrong (we do want to know which old ideas turned out to be true), but a purely presentist history becomes a story of heroes and fools, and it gets the facts wrong. Phrenology, judged historically, was a serious theory that got localisation right and method wrong; introspection was abandoned because it could not settle disputes, not because its users were foolish. The fate of Wundt's reputation is the classic case. For much of the twentieth century American students met Wundt mainly through Titchener, who translated him, presented his own structuralism as the faithful continuation of Wundt's programme, and was far more of an elementist than Wundt ever was. Few Americans read the ten volumes of the Volkerpsychologie , and the most influential history of the period was written by Boring, who had taken his doctorate under Titchener at Cornell. The result was a Wundt who was narrow, mechanical and introspective in Titchener's style. Only in the 1970s did historians who went back to Wundt's own German texts, among them Arthur Blumenthal in "A Reappraisal of Wilhelm Wundt" (1975), recover the Wundt you met in Section 1.5: a voluntarist who stressed attention, will and creative synthesis, who limited introspection to short, controlled judgements, and who wrote a whole second psychology of culture. Translation was part of the problem, which is why the German terms in Table 1.10 are worth knowing exactly. Examiners like to put them side by side as options. The case of Max Friedrich's key, revisited Go back to the winter of 1879 and look again at the doctoral student pressing his telegraph key. You can now name the ancestry of almost everything in that room. The clockwork chronoscope belonged to the physicists, and the very idea that observers differ in how long they take to respond had been forced on the astronomers by the personal equation. The logic of the experiment, comparing a simple reaction with one that requires an extra mental act and subtracting the times, was Donders' subtraction method of 1868. The mental act being timed, apperception, had been named by Leibniz and given its psychological meaning by Herbart. The belief that a mental process could be measured at all was Fechner's answer to Kant, and the assumption that each mental event has a bodily partner running alongside it was the psychophysical parallelism that Wundt inherited from Leibniz. Even the plan of asking a trained observer to report under controlled, repeatable conditions was laid down in Wundt's four rules of experimental introspection. So what was new? Not the parts but the purpose. For the first time, a student was doing original research on the mind, in a room set aside for it, under a professor who had announced a new science and would soon give it a journal, a textbook tradition and a stream of students. That is the whole answer to the puzzle the chapter began with, and it needs both theories of history from Section 1.8: the Zeitgeist had put every part on the bench, and one determined person assembled them into an institution. Friedrich's own measurements are long forgotten, and the hope of timing apperception by simple subtraction did not survive the problem of pure insertion described in Section 1.4. But the room outlived its first experiment. Within a generation its graduates had carried it to Wurzburg, Cornell, Columbia, Pennsylvania and Harvard. In Philadelphia in 1896 one of them, Lightner Witmer, brought the same patient, measuring attitude to a boy who could not spell, and in 1915 a student of another, Munsterberg, carried the laboratory to Calcutta. The clinical psychology you are preparing to study is a direct descendant of that winter in Leipzig. Chapter summary 1.1 What Is Psychology? The word comes from the Greek psyche (soul) and logos (study); Christian Wolff made it standard in the 1730s, and Aristotle's De Anima was the first treatise on the soul. The definition has changed with each school: the soul, then the mind, then conscious experience (Wundt and Titchener; James's "science of mental life", 1890), then behaviour (McDougall, 1905 and 1908; Watson, 1913; Woodworth; the definition Indian textbooks credit to N. L. Munn). Today psychology is the scientific study of behaviour, which is overt, and mental processes, which are internal and covert. Its four goals are to describe, explain, predict and control (or influence). Basic research seeks understanding for its own sake; applied research solves practical problems. Clinical psychology assesses and treats psychological disorders, while counselling psychology serves people in the normal range with adjustment problems. Comparative psychology studies animal behaviour across species, ethology studies it in natural settings, evolutionary psychology explains behaviour as the product of natural selection, behaviour genetics asks how much variation is due to genes, and differential psychology studies individual differences. 1.2 Philosophical Roots: A Long Past. Nativism holds that some knowledge is inborn and empiricism that all knowledge comes from experience; rationalism makes reason the chief route to knowledge. Plato was a nativist and rationalist who saw learning as recollection; Aristotle was an empiricist who gave the first laws of association (similarity, contrast, contiguity). Descartes treated the body as a machine, described the reflex, held innate ideas and proposed dualism with interaction through the pineal gland. The British empiricists followed: Hobbes the materialist; Locke with the tabula rasa, sensation and reflection, simple and complex ideas, and primary and secondary qualities; Berkeley with esse est percipi and a learned theory of depth; Hume with impressions, ideas and the laws of resemblance, contiguity and cause and effect. The associationists Hartley, James Mill (mental mechanics), John Stuart Mill (mental chemistry) and Bain built the mind out of linked elements. On the continent, Leibniz proposed monads, petites perceptions and apperception, Herbart the threshold of consciousness and the apperceptive mass, and Kant innate categories and the claim that psychology could never be a science. The mind-body positions are interactionism, psychophysical parallelism, epiphenomenalism (Huxley), materialist and idealist monism, and Spinoza's double-aspect theory. Ontology concerns existence and epistemology knowledge; Comte's positivism rejected introspection. 1.3 Physiological and Biological Roots. The Bell-Magendie law (1811, 1822) separated sensory dorsal roots from motor ventral roots. Johannes Muller's doctrine of specific nerve energies held that the quality of a sensation depends on the nerve stimulated. Helmholtz measured the speed of the nerve impulse in 1850 (about 27 metres per second) and proposed unconscious inference and the trichromatic theory. Localisation of function came through Gall and Spurzheim's phrenology (right idea, wrong method), Flourens' ablation studies, Broca's patient Tan (1861), Wernicke's sensory aphasia (1874) and Fritsch and Hitzig's electrical mapping of the motor cortex (1870). Darwin's natural selection (1859) and his book on emotional expression (1872) gave psychology continuity between species, the question of function and an interest in variation. His half-cousin Galton founded the study of individual differences with Hereditary Genius (1869), twin studies, the anthropometric laboratory (1884), regression, correlation, word association and the questionnaire, and coined eugenics (1883). Romanes' anecdotal method invited anthropomorphism, which Lloyd Morgan's canon of parsimony (1894) corrected, as Pfungst's study of Clever Hans (1907) showed. 1.4 Measuring the Mind: Psychophysics and Mental Chronometry. Weber found that the just noticeable difference is a constant proportion of the standard stimulus (Weber's law). Fechner, after his insight of 22 October 1850, proposed that sensation grows with the logarithm of stimulus intensity (S = k log I), published Elements of Psychophysics in 1860, gave the three classical psychophysical methods and is the founder of psychophysics; Boring argued that 1860 could even be taken as psychology's founding date. The astronomers' personal equation revealed individual differences in reaction time. Donders' subtraction method (1868) compared simple, go/no-go and choice reactions to time the stages of identification and choice, founding mental chronometry, though it assumes "pure insertion" of stages. Ebbinghaus extended measurement to memory with nonsense syllables, the savings method and the forgetting curve ( On Memory , 1885). 1.5 Wilhelm Wundt and the Founding of Experimental Psychology. Wundt (1832 to 1920), trained in medicine and physiology and once Helmholtz's assistant, published Principles of Physiological Psychology (1873 to 1874), moved to Leipzig in 1875, began laboratory research in 1879 and founded Philosophische Studien in 1881. Psychology for Wundt studied immediate experience, analysed into sensations and simple feelings. His system was voluntarism: the mind actively organises experience through attention and will, apperception brings contents into the focus of consciousness, and creative synthesis produces wholes with new properties. His tridimensional theory of feeling (1896) described feelings as pleasure-displeasure, tension-relaxation and excitement-depression. His method was controlled internal perception ( innere Wahrnehmung ), not armchair self-observation ( Selbstbeobachtung ), governed by four rules. Higher mental processes he studied through language, myth and custom in the ten-volume Volkerpsychologie (1900 to 1920). His students included Hall, Cattell, Munsterberg, Kulpe, Titchener, Witmer, Kraepelin, Spearman and, briefly, Bekhterev. 1.6 Structuralism and Its European Rivals. Titchener carried a stricter version of Wundt's programme to Cornell and named it structuralism (1898). He sought the elements of consciousness (sensations, images and affections) and their attributes (quality, intensity, duration, clearness, extensity), kept only the pleasant-unpleasant dimension of feeling, and trained observers to avoid the stimulus error. Meaning came from context, and perception was a complex of sensory and imaginal processes. Kulpe's Wurzburg school found imageless thought and showed how the Aufgabe, the determining tendency and set (Einstellung) direct thinking; the resulting controversy exposed the unreliability of introspection. Brentano's act psychology (1874) studied mental acts and their intentionality, Stumpf studied tone and trained the Gestalt founders, and G. E. Muller extended psychophysics and memory research at Gottingen. Structuralism declined because introspection could not settle disputes, observation altered experience, elementism missed wholes, its subject matter was narrow and it refused application; cognitive psychology later revived its topics. 1.7 Functionalism and the American Pioneers. Functionalism studied the mind as it functions in adapting the organism to its environment, drawing on Darwin, pragmatism and American practicality. James's Principles of Psychology (1890) described the stream of consciousness, habit, the material, social and spiritual selves and the pure ego, and the James-Lange theory of emotion. Dewey's reflex arc paper (1896) founded the Chicago school, Angell's "Province of Functional Psychology" (1906) defined it and Carr's adaptive act matured it. At Columbia, Cattell coined "mental test" (1890), Woodworth gave the S-O-R formula and dynamic psychology, and Thorndike began the study of animal learning. Hall took the first American doctorate (1878), opened the first American research laboratory (1883), founded the American Journal of Psychology (1887) and the APA (1892), and described adolescence as storm and stress. Witmer opened the first psychological clinic (1896) and named clinical psychology; Munsterberg founded forensic and industrial psychology. Calkins became the first woman APA president (1905), Washburn the first woman PhD in psychology (1894), and Hollingworth disproved claims about women's inferiority. Functionalism dissolved into the mainstream and led to behaviourism, applied psychology and evolutionary psychology. 1.8 Reading the History: Zeitgeist, Great Persons and "Fathers". The great-person (personalistic) theory, stated by Carlyle in 1841, explains history through exceptional individuals; the Zeitgeist (naturalistic) theory, championed by Boring, explains it through the spirit of the times, citing multiple discoveries (Bell and Magendie, Darwin and Wallace, James and Lange), premature discoveries such as Mendel's, and contextual forces such as economic opportunity, war and prejudice. Psychology began in Germany because of its research universities, its broad idea of Wissenschaft and its experimental physiology; it began with Wundt because he, unlike the precursors, declared the science, gave it a laboratory, a journal and students; and 1879 marks the start of original student research. "Father" can mean founder, namer, chief influence or first in a country, so the qualifier in the question decides. In India, Seal drew up a syllabus in 1905, Sengupta set up the first laboratory (1915) and the first department (1916) at Calcutta and is the founder of modern psychology in India, Bose earned the first Indian doctorate (1921) and founded the Indian Psychoanalytic Society (1922), Mysore's department began in 1924 under Gopalaswamy, and the Indian Psychological Association followed in 1925. Which branch of psychology focuses on the study of animal behavior? (RML 2025) (a) Social psychology (b) Abnormal psychology (c) Comparative psychology (d) Differential psychology Answer: (c) Comparative psychology. It compares behaviour and learning across species, a branch that grew out of Darwin's idea of continuity and Romanes' Animal Intelligence (1882). Social psychology studies people in relation to one another, abnormal psychology studies disorders, and differential psychology studies individual differences among people. What does clinical psychology primarily focus on? (IHBAS 2024) (a) Industrial applications (b) Assessment and treatment of mental illness (c) Behavioural changes in animals (d) Organizational management Answer: (b) Assessment and treatment of mental illness. Clinical psychology, named by Lightner Witmer, assesses, diagnoses and treats psychological disorders. Industrial applications and organisational management belong to industrial-organisational psychology, and behavioural change in animals to comparative psychology. In the nature versus nurture debate, which early philosopher argued that the mind was a "tabula rasa" or blank slate at birth? (IHBAS 2024) (a) Plato (b) Rene Descartes (c) John Locke (d) Immanuel Kant Answer: (c) John Locke. In his Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1690) Locke described the mind at birth as "white paper", with every idea coming from sensation or reflection. Plato thought learning was recollection of inborn knowledge, Descartes believed in innate ideas, and Kant held that the mind imposes innate forms and categories on experience; all three are on the nativist side. ____ is a source of knowledge as per Empiricists. (Panwar Systems & Theories bank) (a) Logical reasoning (b) Theories (c) Sensory experiences (d) Contemplations Answer: (c) Sensory experiences. Empiricism holds that all knowledge comes from experience delivered through the senses. Logical reasoning and contemplation are the rationalists' routes to knowledge (Plato, Descartes, Leibniz), and theories are products of knowledge rather than its source. According to Wundt 'apperceptive mass' constitutes ___________ . (IHBAS 2025) (a) Compound of elemental processes bound by association (b) Sensation and pure perception (c) Pure perception and preexisting ideas (d) Sensation plus unconscious inference Answer: (c) Pure perception and preexisting ideas. The apperceptive mass is the organised body of ideas already in the mind, into which a new perception is taken up and understood; the term is Herbart's, and Wundt reworked the idea of apperception. Option (a) is the associationist and structuralist picture of the mind, option (b) leaves out the existing ideas that are the whole point, and option (d) is Helmholtz's theory of perception. Herman von Helmholtz (1821-94): (Panwar Systems & Theories bank) (a) He was a proponent of the just noticeable difference (b) He gave the trichromatic theory of colour vision (c) He proposed the concept of the unconscious (d) He gave the law of effect Answer: (b) He gave the trichromatic theory of colour vision. Building on Thomas Young's suggestion of 1802, Helmholtz developed the Young-Helmholtz theory of three receptor types. The just noticeable difference is Weber's and Fechner's, the law of effect is Thorndike's, and although Helmholtz proposed unconscious inference in perception, the concept of the unconscious mind belongs to Freud and, before him, to Leibniz and Herbart. What do Hermann Ebbinghaus, Francis Galton and Sigmund Freud share in common? (RML 2020) (a) Each of them worked independently and were pioneers in the field of psychology (b) Each of them founded a formal psychology laboratory (c) Each of them developed novel observational methods to study how the mind works (d) (a) and (c) Answer: (d) (a) and (c). All three worked largely alone and were pioneers, and all three invented methods: Ebbinghaus nonsense syllables and the savings method, Galton the questionnaire, word association and correlation, Freud free association. The RML 2020 key printed (a), but since (c) is also true, (d) is the more defensible answer and is the one the Panwar bank keys. Option (b) is false because Freud never founded a laboratory. Who established the first laboratory for experimental study of psychology? (Panwar Systems & Theories bank) (a) Galton (b) Weber (c) Wundt (d) Jung Answer: (c) Wundt. Wundt's Leipzig laboratory began research in 1879, the conventional founding date of psychology as an independent science. Galton's laboratory (London, 1884) was anthropometric, a centre for measuring individual differences; Weber was a physiologist who founded no psychology laboratory; Jung developed word association as a clinical tool in Zurich. Who gave the concept of 'Folk psychology'? (RML 2024) (a) Wilhelm Maximilian Wundt (b) Sigmund Freud (c) Ivan Pavlov (d) Wilhelm Roentgen Answer: (a) Wilhelm Maximilian Wundt. His ten-volume Volkerpsychologie (1900 to 1920) studied the higher mental processes through language, myth and custom. Freud founded psychoanalysis and Pavlov discovered classical conditioning; Roentgen was the physicist who discovered X-rays, there only because he shares Wundt's first name. Charles Spearman is to Factor Analysis as Wilhelm Wundt is to: (Real PYQ 2024) (a) Psychoanalysis (b) Introspection (c) Functionalism (d) Humanism Answer: (b) Introspection. The analogy pairs each pioneer with his signature method: Spearman (himself a Leipzig doctorate) invented factor analysis, and Wundt made controlled introspection the method of the first laboratory. Psychoanalysis is Freud's, functionalism is associated with James, and humanism with Maslow and Rogers. Who among the following has defined perception as a complex of sensory and imaginal events? (IHBAS 2024) (a) Kimbel (b) Titchener (c) Bruner (d) Schafer Answer: (b) Titchener. For the structuralist Titchener, a perception is built from sensations supplied by the object plus images supplied by past experience, which is also the heart of his context theory of meaning. Bruner and Schafer belong to the "New Look" research of the 1940s, which showed that needs and values shape perception (Chapter 4), and Kimble is known for work on learning; none of them held the structuralist definition. The current approach to psychology most closely aligned with the structuralists in its interest in topics like consciousness, mental imagery and thought process is: (Panwar Systems & Theories bank) (a) Neuroscience (b) Cognitive psychology (c) Behaviourism (d) Functionalism Answer: (b) Cognitive psychology. It studies the structuralists' topics, consciousness, imagery and thought, with reaction times, error patterns and brain imaging instead of trained introspection. Neuroscience studies the brain rather than the contents of experience, behaviourism banished consciousness altogether, and functionalism asked what the mind is for rather than what it is made of. Functionalism, an early school of thought in psychology, was most closely associated with which psychologist? (IHBAS 2024) (a) Edward Titchener (b) John Watson (c) William James (d) G. Stanley Hall Answer: (c) William James. James's Principles of Psychology (1890) inspired the functionalist attitude, and Dewey and Angell turned it into a school at Chicago. Titchener founded the rival structuralism, Watson founded behaviourism, and Hall, though functionalist in spirit, is examined for institutions (the APA, the first American research laboratory) and for adolescence. Functionalism is how people work, play, and adapt to their surroundings. This viewpoint was given by: (Amity 2023) (a) William James (b) William Wundt (c) Charles Darwin (d) John B. Watson Answer: (a) William James. The functionalist question of how the mind helps us adapt is James's. "William Wundt" is Wilhelm Wundt misnamed, the voluntarist of Leipzig; Darwin inspired functionalism but belonged to no psychological school; Watson founded behaviourism. The aim of Functionalism was to study ______ as it functions in adapting the ______ to its environment. (Panwar Systems & Theories bank) (a) Organism, Mind (b) Mind, Organism (c) Thinking, Organism (d) Attention, Individual Answer: (b) Mind, Organism. The functionalists studied the mind as an instrument that adapts the whole living organism to its environment, the Darwinian question of what consciousness is for. Option (a) reverses the order, and options (c) and (d) narrow the subject to single processes, which is not how the school defined itself. The term "stream of consciousness", referring to the flow of thoughts in the human mind, was coined by which psychologist? (IHBAS 2024) (a) Carl Jung (b) Wilhelm Wundt (c) William James (d) B.F. Skinner Answer: (c) William James. In the Principles (1890) James argued that consciousness "is nothing jointed; it flows", against the structuralists' picture of separate elements. Jung is known for analytical psychology and the collective unconscious, Wundt analysed consciousness into elements, and Skinner, a radical behaviourist, did not study consciousness at all. The first person to use the term clinical psychology in print was (RML 2020) (a) Erik Erikson (b) Sigmund Freud (c) Lightner Witmer (d) Cattell Answer: (c) Lightner Witmer. Witmer opened the first psychological clinic in 1896, proposed the new field that year, and used the term in print in the first issue of his journal The Psychological Clinic (1907). Erikson is known for the psychosocial stages, Freud for psychoanalysis, and Cattell for coining "mental test". American Psychological Association (APA) was founded in: (Panwar Systems & Theories bank) (a) 1892 (b) 1893 (c) 1896 (d) 1897 Answer: (a) 1892. The APA was founded at Clark University in July 1892, with G. Stanley Hall as its first president. 1896 is the tempting distractor because it is the year of Witmer's clinic and Dewey's reflex arc paper. Who among the following was the first female president of the American Psychological Association (APA)? (Panwar Systems & Theories bank) (a) Margaret Floy Washburn (b) Leta Stetter Hollingworth (c) Karen Horney (d) Mary Calkins Answer: (d) Mary Calkins. Mary Whiton Calkins became APA president in 1905. Washburn was the first woman to earn a PhD in psychology (1894) and the second woman president (1921); Hollingworth is known for the psychology of women and of gifted children; Karen Horney was a psychoanalyst who was never APA president. Who is often referred to as the "Founder of Modern Psychology in India"? (Panwar Systems & Theories bank) (a) Girindra Shekhar Bose (b) Narendra Nath Sen Gupta (c) Amitosh Mukherjee (d) M.V. Gopalswamy Answer: (b) Narendra Nath Sen Gupta. Trained under Munsterberg at Harvard, Sengupta set up India's first laboratory of experimental psychology (1915) and its first department of psychology (1916) at Calcutta. Bose is the father of psychoanalysis in India (1922), Gopalaswamy began the Mysore department (1924), and "Amitosh Mukherjee" is not a founder of Indian psychology (perhaps a garbling of Sir Ashutosh Mookerjee, the vice-chancellor who backed the Calcutta department, an administrator rather than a psychologist). Which of the following Indian psychologists played a key role in establishing the first psychology laboratory in India? (Panwar Systems & Theories bank) (a) Anand C. Paranjpe (b) Uma Chaudhuri (c) Sudhir Kakar (d) G. Misra Answer: (b) Uma Chaudhuri, as keyed; historically, none of the four. The first laboratory was N. N. Sengupta's, at Calcutta in 1915, and he is not among the options. Uma Chaudhuri of Calcutta is known for the Indian modification of the Thematic Apperception Test (1960), and she is the name the key expects; Paranjpe, Kakar and Misra are later leaders of indigenous Indian psychology (Section 2.8). If Sengupta is ever offered, choose him. High-yield sheet The facts this chapter's questions ask most, most-asked first. Last read before the exam. In 1913 a twenty-six-year-old German psychologist named Wolfgang Kohler sailed to Tenerife, in the Canary Islands, to take charge of a small research station that the Prussian Academy of Sciences kept there for the study of chimpanzees. He expected a short posting. Then the First World War broke out, the sea lanes closed, and he stayed until 1920. For six years he had little to do but watch apes think. His most gifted subject was a chimpanzee called Sultan. One day Kohler placed a banana outside the bars of Sultan's cage, beyond reach. Inside the cage lay two hollow bamboo sticks, one thin enough to slide into the other, but each too short to reach the fruit on its own. Sultan tried one stick, then the other. He pushed one stick out with the second, so that the first touched the banana, but he could not draw it in. After more than an hour Kohler gave up and left a keeper to watch. Sultan sat on a box, idly playing with the two sticks. By chance he found himself holding them in a line, and he pushed the thin one into the end of the thick one. According to Kohler's record, he jumped up at once, ran to the bars and raked in the banana with his new long stick. When the sticks came apart, he joined them again without hesitation. What had happened inside Sultan? Kohler was sure he knew: the ape had suddenly seen the situation in a new way, the two sticks reorganised in his perception into one tool. But in the very year Kohler reached Tenerife, a young American at Johns Hopkins University, John B. Watson, was telling psychologists that "inside" questions of this kind had no place in a science at all; all that could be studied was what the animal did. In Vienna, Sigmund Freud would have asked a different question again: what hidden wish does the behaviour serve? Forty years later, a cognitive psychologist would describe Sultan as an information-processing system searching a "problem space", and today a researcher trained in the Indian tradition might ask about the state of attention in which the solution arrived. Same ape, same sticks, five different stories. That is what this chapter is about. Between about 1900 and 1960 psychology was divided into rival schools , each with its own idea of what psychology should study, how it should study it, and what a human being is. You will meet each school in turn, see why it arose, what it discovered, and why it declined or was absorbed. Remember Sultan; you will meet him again at the end of the chapter. 2.1 Schools, Systems and Paradigms Lower yield · 3 Qs Chapter 1 ended with the first two schools of scientific psychology, structuralism and functionalism. This chapter picks up the story where they left it. Before we meet the newcomers, though, it helps to be clear about what a "school" actually is, because the word is used loosely, and the vocabulary of the field matters as much as its content. What makes a school of thought A school of thought is a group of psychologists who share a common set of assumptions about what psychology should study (its subject matter), how it should study it (its method), and what kind of explanation counts. A school usually has a recognisable founder or leader, a statement of its programme (often called its manifesto), a university or laboratory that serves as its home, a journal in which its members publish, a stream of students who carry its ideas into other institutions, and, just as important, a rival school against which it defines itself. Behaviourism, for example, had Watson as its founder, his 1913 paper as its manifesto, and structuralism's introspection as its enemy. Two classic books gave the age of schools its shape. Robert Sessions Woodworth (1869 to 1962) of Columbia University surveyed the rivals in Contemporary Schools of Psychology (1931), and Edna Heidbreder (1890 to 1985) described Seven Psychologies (1933). Notice their dates. The schools flourished roughly between the 1890s and the 1950s; after that, as you will see in Section 2.7, psychology gradually traded rival schools for overlapping "perspectives". Two related words are worth separating. A system of psychology is an organised and internally consistent body of assumptions, methods and theory that tries to cover the whole field; a theory is narrower, an explanation of one set of facts (a theory of forgetting, a theory of colour vision). Courses called "Systems and Theories" study both: the great systems, and the theories they produced. Kuhn's paradigms and a preparadigmatic science Why did psychology split into warring schools when physics and chemistry did not? A helpful answer comes from a physicist turned historian, Thomas Samuel Kuhn (1922 to 1996). In The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962), Kuhn argued that a mature science works within a paradigm : a shared framework of assumptions, problems, methods and model solutions that all workers in the field accept. Under a paradigm, scientists do what Kuhn called normal science : puzzle-solving within the accepted framework. Over time, results accumulate that the paradigm cannot explain (anomalies). When they pile up, the field enters a crisis; a new framework appears; and if it wins, the result is a scientific revolution, or paradigm shift . Newton's physics giving way to Einstein's is Kuhn's model case. A field that has no single accepted paradigm, but several competing schools, each with its own problems and methods, is in Kuhn's term a preparadigmatic science . Kuhn himself noticed this in the social sciences. In the preface to his book he recalled a year spent among social scientists and how struck he was by the number and extent of their open disagreements about what the legitimate problems and methods even were. The age of schools in psychology fits that description well: a structuralist and a behaviourist did not merely disagree about results, they disagreed about what counted as data. Whether psychology has since acquired a paradigm (or whether the cognitive revolution was a true Kuhnian revolution) is still debated, and we return to the question at the end of Section 2.7. The four forces You will often read that psychology has had three or four "forces". The numbering comes from the humanistic psychologists of the 1960s, above all Abraham Maslow, who called their own movement the third force to set it against the two forces that, in their view, dominated mid-century psychology. Table 2.1 sets out the sequence. Notice that the numbers describe a sequence of influence in the eyes of the humanists, not strict dates of birth: psychoanalysis (from the 1890s) is the first force and behaviourism (1913) the second. Table 2.1 The forces in psychology. Force School Key figures Picture of the person First Psychoanalysis Freud and his successors Driven by unconscious conflict and early childhood Second Behaviourism Watson, Skinner Shaped by the environment through conditioning Third Humanistic psychology Maslow, Rogers Free, growth-seeking, capable of self-actualisation Fourth Transpersonal psychology Maslow, Sutich, Grof Capable of experiences that go beyond the individual self Figure 2.1 lays the schools out in time, so that you can see which ones overlapped and which ones replaced each other. Keep it in mind as you read; each bar is the subject of one part of this chapter. Structuralism (1879) Functionalism (1890s) Psychoanalysis, the first force (1890s) Gestalt (1912) Behaviourism (1913) Neobehaviourism Humanistic (third force) Cognitive (1956) Transpersonal (1969) Positive psychology (1998) Indian Psychology movement (2002) 1880 1900 1920 1940 1960 1980 2000 Figure 2.1 The schools of psychology in time. Each bar runs from a school's founding event to the point where it stopped being a dominant, separate school (bars reaching the right edge are still active traditions). Notice how Gestalt and behaviourism were born a year apart, and how the cognitive and humanistic movements grew up side by side in the 1950s. Exam trap "Which is the fourth force?" The answer is transpersonal psychology . In counselling textbooks, however, Paul Pedersen (1991) called multiculturalism the "fourth force" in counselling. If both appear in the options, read the stem: "in psychology" points to transpersonal; "in counselling" may point to multiculturalism. "Experiential" psychology is not one of the numbered forces. 2.2 Behaviourism: From Watson's Manifesto to Skinner Medium yield · 9 Qs In 1913, structuralism (Wundt and Titchener) and functionalism (James, Dewey and Angell) were still arguing about consciousness: what its elements were, or what it was for. Both relied on introspection, the trained observation of one's own experience. A young professor at Johns Hopkins decided that the whole argument was a mistake. Psychology, he said, should stop studying consciousness altogether. To understand how anyone could say such a thing in 1913, and be applauded for it, you need to see the ground that had been prepared. The ground prepared: animal psychology and Russian objective psychology The first preparation came from the study of animals. After Charles Darwin (1809 to 1882) argued for continuity between humans and other species, animal minds became a serious topic. George John Romanes (1848 to 1894) collected stories of clever animals (his anecdotal method), and Conwy Lloyd Morgan (1852 to 1936) answered with his canon of 1894: never interpret an action as the result of a higher mental faculty if it can be explained by a lower one (both are covered in Chapter 1). Jacques Loeb (1859 to 1924), a physiologist who taught Watson at Chicago, went further and explained animal movement as tropisms , forced, mechanical orientations toward or away from light, gravity and chemicals, with no mind required. And Edward Lee Thorndike (1874 to 1949), in his 1898 dissertation Animal Intelligence , put hungry cats in puzzle boxes and showed that they escaped not by reasoning but by gradual trial and error, stamped in by satisfying consequences: his law of effect (Chapter 6). If animal behaviour could be studied so precisely without asking what the animal was conscious of, why not human behaviour too? The second preparation came from Russia, where a tradition of objective psychology had grown out of physiology. Ivan Mikhailovich Sechenov (1829 to 1905), in Reflexes of the Brain (1863), argued that all acts of conscious and unconscious life are reflexes in their origin. Ivan Petrovich Pavlov (1849 to 1936), who won the 1904 Nobel Prize for his work on digestion, discovered around the turn of the century that his dogs began to salivate to signals that preceded food; he called these conditioned reflexes and spent the rest of his life studying them (Chapter 6). Vladimir Mikhailovich Bekhterev (1857 to 1927) studied what he called association reflexes, conditioning motor responses such as withdrawing a limb from an electric shock, and named his whole approach reflexology ; his Objective Psychology appeared between 1907 and 1912. Bekhterev's motor conditioning, more than Pavlov's salivation, gave Watson a method he could use on people. The third preparation was home-grown. American functionalism had already pulled psychology toward practical questions (education, testing, industry) and toward the study of what organisms do to adapt. Behaviourism, in a sense, was functionalism with the mind removed. Watson's manifesto (1913) John Broadus Watson (1878 to 1958) grew up poor in South Carolina, earned his doctorate at the University of Chicago in 1903 with a study of learning in rats, and moved to Johns Hopkins in 1908. He had never been comfortable with introspection; he later admitted that he hated serving as a subject in introspective experiments and preferred animals, which could not be asked what they were experiencing. Early in 1913 he gave a lecture at Columbia University, published that March in Psychological Review as "Psychology as the Behaviorist Views It". It is the founding document of behaviourism , the school that defines psychology as the science of observable behaviour. Key study: "Psychology as the Behaviorist Views It" (1913) Watson's paper opens with a sentence every student of the history of psychology should know almost by heart: psychology as the behaviourist views it "is a purely objective experimental branch of natural science. Its theoretical goal is the prediction and control of behavior. Introspection forms no essential part of its methods." He added that the behaviourist "recognizes no dividing line between man and brute". The paper made four claims. (1) Subject matter : behaviour, not consciousness. (2) Method : objective observation, never introspection. (3) Goal : prediction and control, which made psychology useful to education, business and medicine. (4) Continuity : the same principles apply to humans and animals. In later books Watson phrased the goal precisely: given the stimulus, to predict the response, and given the response, to identify the stimulus that produced it. Watson was elected President of the American Psychological Association in 1915, only two years later; the manifesto had found an audience ready for it. What methods did Watson allow? Four: observation, with or without instruments; testing (he liked tests as samples of behaviour, not as measures of mental capacities); the verbal report method, in which speech is treated as behaviour, so that what a person says counts as data but is not taken as a window on consciousness; and, from 1915, the conditioned reflex method borrowed from Pavlov and Bekhterev. Watson's programme: thinking, emotion and the "twelve infants" A science of behaviour has to say something about the things introspectionists cared about, such as thought and feeling. Watson had an answer for each, and his answers show you the spirit of the school. Thinking as subvocal speech. Watson argued that thinking is nothing but talking to oneself so quietly that the movements cannot be seen: thought is subvocal speech , small movements of the tongue and larynx (he called them laryngeal habits). This view is called peripheralism , because it locates mental life in the peripheral muscles rather than in central brain processes. It led Watson to divide behaviour into explicit (overt) responses that anyone can see, and implicit (covert) responses such as subvocal speech, which cannot be seen by an observer but can, in principle, be measured with instruments. This is exactly the sense in which modern textbooks say covert behaviour is measurable but not directly observable, and why the "mental processes" in today's definition of psychology (the scientific study of behaviour and mental processes) are internal, covert processes. Was Watson right about thought? A dramatic test came in 1947, when Scott Smith and his colleagues at the University of Utah gave Smith himself a dose of curare large enough to paralyse every skeletal muscle, keeping him alive on a respirator. If thinking were movement of the speech muscles, Smith should have been unable to think. He reported afterwards that he had remained fully aware, had understood what was said to him and could remember it. Peripheralism did not survive. Emotion. Watson held that infants show just three unlearned emotional reactions: fear (to loud noises and sudden loss of support), rage (to hampering of movement) and love (to stroking and gentle handling). Every other emotion, he argued, is built from these three by conditioning. Environmentalism. Watson's most quoted words appeared in his popular book Behaviorism (1925). "Give me a dozen healthy infants, well-formed, and my own specified world to bring them up in and I'll guarantee to take any one at random and train him to become any type of specialist I might select: doctor, lawyer, artist, merchant-chief and, yes, even beggar-man and thief, regardless of his talents, penchants, tendencies, abilities, vocations, and race of his ancestors." This is environmentalism in its purest form: the belief that behaviour is shaped almost entirely by experience rather than heredity. What is usually left out is the next sentence, in which Watson conceded that he was "going beyond my facts", adding that so had the advocates of the contrary view, and they had been doing it for thousands of years. Consistent with this, Watson first accepted, and then by the mid-1920s rejected, the idea of human instincts. Little Albert. To show that emotions are conditioned, Watson and his graduate student Rosalie Rayner (1898 to 1935) conditioned fear in an eleven-month-old infant, "Albert B.", in 1920, pairing a white rat with a loud noise made by striking a steel bar behind his head. Albert came to fear the rat, and the fear generalised to a rabbit, a dog, a fur coat and a Santa Claus mask. The study, its method and its ethical problems are told in full in Chapter 6. The same year, Watson's affair with Rayner became public; he was forced to resign from Johns Hopkins, married Rayner, and spent the rest of his working life in advertising at the J. Walter Thompson agency. His academic career had lasted barely twenty years, but the school he named outlived him by decades. Exam trap Who defined psychology as the science of behaviour? Watson (1913) made behaviour the subject matter of psychology, so for "founder of behaviourism" and "Watson defined psychology as the science of ..." the answers are behaviourism and behaviour (not soul, mind or consciousness: the soul was the subject matter of the ancient philosophers, the mind that of later philosophers, and consciousness that of Wundt and Titchener). One Panwar item, however, keys N. L. Munn as the first to establish psychology as "the scientific study of behaviour": Norman Leslie Munn's widely used textbooks popularised that wording. If Watson is an option, prefer Watson; if the options are Munn, Woodworth and Wundt, the key is Munn. Woodworth is remembered for the S-O-R formula and a quip often credited to him: psychology first lost its soul, then its mind, then consciousness. Rationalism is a philosophical position (Descartes), not a school Watson founded. Functionalism belongs to James, Dewey and Angell; structuralism to Titchener. Three meanings of "behaviourism" As the school matured, it became clear that "behaviourism" could mean three different things, and the three are easily confused. The difference lies in what each says about the mind. Table 2.2 Three kinds of behaviourism. Kind What it says about mental events Typical figures Metaphysical (eliminative) Minds and conscious states do not exist as anything other than behaviour Watson in his most extreme statements Methodological Mental events may exist, but they are private and cannot be studied scientifically; only public behaviour counts as data Watson in practice; most neobehaviourists Radical Private events (thoughts, feelings) are real and are themselves behaviour, obeying the same laws; but they are not the causes of overt behaviour Skinner, who adopted the term in 1945 (Mary Whiton Calkins had first used it, for Watson's view, in 1921) The word "radical" in radical behaviourism does not mean "extreme". Skinner meant it in its root sense: thoroughgoing, going to the roots. Ironically, radical behaviourism is the only one of the three that lets thoughts and feelings into the science; methodological behaviourism simply sets them aside. Neobehaviourism: logical positivism and operationism Watson's crusading behaviourism dominated American psychology from about 1913 to 1930. Historians of psychology usually describe what followed as a second stage, neobehaviourism (about 1930 to 1960), and a third, sociobehaviourism or social learning theory (about 1960 onward). The neobehaviourists, Tolman, Hull, Guthrie and Skinner, kept Watson's demand for objectivity but wanted to make behaviourism more rigorous and more theoretical. They drew on two ideas from the philosophy of science. The first was logical positivism , the philosophy of the Vienna Circle of the 1920s, which held that a statement is meaningful only if it can be verified by observation (or is true by definition). Talk of unobservable "minds" was therefore not false but meaningless unless it could be tied to observables. The second was operationism , proposed by the American physicist Percy Williams Bridgman (1882 to 1961) in The Logic of Modern Physics (1927): a scientific concept means nothing more than the set of operations used to measure it. The psychologist S. S. Stevens brought the idea into psychology in 1935. The legacy is the operational definition that every research methods course still teaches: "hunger" in a rat experiment is defined as "twenty-three hours without food", and "intelligence" as "the score on this test". Edward Chace Tolman's purposive behaviourism. Edward Chace Tolman (1886 to 1959) of the University of California at Berkeley was the behaviourist who let cognition in by the back door. He called his system purposive behaviourism and set it out in Purposive Behavior in Animals and Men (1932), a book he dedicated, with typical humour, to the white rat. Tolman insisted on studying molar behaviour , whole goal-directed acts such as a rat running a maze or a person going home, rather than Watson's molecular behaviour , the individual muscle twitches and glandular secretions that make up an act. Molar behaviour, Tolman observed, "reeks of purpose": a rat that finds its usual route blocked takes another, so what it has learned is not a chain of movements but where the food is. To explain this without returning to introspection, Tolman introduced the intervening variable in the mid-1930s: an unobserved process inferred between the observable stimulus and the observable response and defined operationally by the conditions that produce it. Hunger, expectancy and demand are intervening variables. On one side sit the independent variables (environmental stimuli, hours of deprivation, heredity, previous training, age); on the other, behaviour; in between, the processes that link them. In effect, Watson's S-R formula became S-O-R, the formula Woodworth had used to insert the organism between stimulus and response. Tolman's most famous intervening variable was the cognitive map , a mental representation of the layout of the environment, which he described in "Cognitive Maps in Rats and Men" (1948). The best evidence for it was latent learning , learning that occurs without reinforcement and stays hidden until there is a reason to show it. In the classic experiment of Tolman and Charles Honzik (1930), rats that explored a maze for ten days without food made many errors; once food appeared in the goal box on day 11, their errors fell by the very next day to the level of rats rewarded from the beginning. They had been learning the maze all along (the full study is in Chapter 6). For Tolman, rats learn what leads to what (expectancies), not stimulus-response habits. Clark Leonard Hull's hypothetico-deductive system. If Tolman was the playful neobehaviourist, Clark Leonard Hull (1884 to 1952) of Yale University was the system-builder. Hull admired Newton's Principia and wanted a psychology built the same way, by the hypothetico-deductive method : state a small set of postulates, deduce precise testable predictions (theorems) from them, test the predictions experimentally, and revise the postulates when they fail. His Principles of Behavior (1943) made him for two decades the most cited psychologist in the world. At the centre of Hull's theory is drive reduction . A biological need (for food, water, relief from pain) produces a drive (D), an aroused state that energises behaviour; any response that reduces the drive is reinforced. Reinforced repetitions build habit strength , written S H R , the strength of the learned bond between a stimulus and a response, which grows with the number of reinforced trials. Habit alone does not produce behaviour; it must be energised by drive. Hull's 1943 formula for reaction potential , the tendency to make the response, was therefore multiplicative: S E R = S H R × D The multiplication matters: if either habit or drive is zero, there is no behaviour, however strong the other. A well-trained but completely satiated rat does not run the maze. Later versions added incentive motivation (K, the size of the reward) and stimulus intensity (V), and subtracted inhibition (fatigue-like reactive inhibition and conditioned inhibition). Hull's students, especially Kenneth Spence, Neal Elgar Miller and O. Hobart Mowrer, carried his ideas into many fields. One famous offshoot was John Dollard and Neal Miller's Personality and Psychotherapy (1950), which translated Freud's ideas into Hull's vocabulary of drive, cue, response and reinforcement; it is usually called the early social learning theory, as distinct from the later social learning theory of Albert Bandura and Richard Walters (1963). Edwin Ray Guthrie's contiguity theory. Edwin Ray Guthrie (1886 to 1959) of the University of Washington offered the simplest theory of all, in The Psychology of Learning (1935). His one law was contiguity : a combination of stimuli that has accompanied a movement will, on its recurrence, tend to be followed by that movement. Reinforcement is not needed; what matters is only that stimulus and movement occur together. Learning is one-trial learning : a stimulus-movement association reaches full strength on its first pairing. Why, then, does practice help? Because a skill is made of many movements, each attached to many stimuli, and practice attaches the act to more and more of the situations in which it must occur. Guthrie also gave practical advice on breaking habits (the threshold, fatigue and incompatible-response methods, Chapter 6). Burrhus Frederic Skinner's radical behaviourism. Burrhus Frederic Skinner (1904 to 1990) of Harvard became the most famous psychologist of the twentieth century; a 2002 survey ranking the most eminent psychologists placed him first, ahead of Piaget and Freud. Skinner distinguished respondent behaviour, elicited by a preceding stimulus as in Pavlov's experiments, from operant behaviour, emitted by the organism and controlled by its consequences. His tools (the operant chamber or "Skinner box", the cumulative recorder) and findings (reinforcement schedules, shaping) are covered in Chapter 6. Here what matters is his system. Skinner was a radical behaviourist (Table 2.2) and also an anti-theorist. In a 1950 paper he asked whether theories of learning were necessary at all and answered no: psychology should describe functional relations between environmental events and behaviour, without inventing intervening variables, drives or cognitive maps. This is why Skinner's approach is sometimes called descriptive behaviourism, or the "empty organism" approach (a description Skinner disliked, since he never denied that the organism has insides; he denied that inner events explain anything). His major books are worth knowing by title and year: The Behavior of Organisms (1938); Walden Two (1948), a novel about a utopian community run on reinforcement principles; Science and Human Behavior (1953); Verbal Behavior (1957), which treated language as operant behaviour shaped by a verbal community; and Beyond Freedom and Dignity (1971), which argued that the idea of an autonomous, free person is a pre-scientific fiction we can no longer afford. Zing-Yang Kuo, the behaviourist who abolished instinct. The most extreme environmentalist of all was a Chinese psychologist trained at Berkeley, Zing-Yang Kuo (1898 to 1970). In "Giving Up Instincts in Psychology" (1921) he argued that the concept of instinct explains nothing. He backed the claim with an elegant experiment (1930): kittens reared alone, kittens reared watching their mothers kill rats, and kittens reared together with rats. Most of the kittens that watched their mothers became rat-killers, while only a small minority of those raised alongside rats ever killed one, and some seemed to treat rats as companions. "Rat-killing instinct," Kuo concluded, depends on rearing. Table 2.3 sets the main behaviourists side by side. Table 2.3 The behaviourists compared. Criticism, decline and legacy By the 1950s behaviourism had won American psychology, and it was beginning to lose. The criticisms came from several directions at once. It could not explain language: Noam Chomsky's 1959 review of Skinner's Verbal Behavior , discussed in Section 2.6, argued that children produce sentences they have never heard and never been reinforced for. It ignored biology: two of Skinner's own former students, Keller and Marian Breland, reported in 1961 that the animals they trained for commercial shows kept "misbehaving", drifting back toward instinctive food-getting actions (instinctive drift), and John Garcia showed that rats learn some associations far more easily than others (Chapter 6). Its central concepts strained against its own evidence: Tolman's rats seemed to carry maps in their heads, and Kohler's apes seemed to reason. And it seemed to many to leave out exactly what makes us human: purpose, meaning and freedom. The humanists (Section 2.5) attacked from that side, the cognitive psychologists (Section 2.6) from the other. Yet behaviourism did not so much die as dissolve into the rest of psychology. Its demand for objective, operationally defined, replicable measurement became simply the way psychology is done. Its laws of learning remain the core of Chapter 6. And it gave clinical psychology one of its most effective toolkits. Clinical link Behaviour therapy applies learning principles to psychological problems. Mary Cover Jones (1896 to 1987) removed a small boy's fear of rabbits in 1924 by gradually bringing a rabbit closer while he ate. Joseph Wolpe (1915 to 1997), in Psychotherapy by Reciprocal Inhibition (1958), developed systematic desensitisation : relaxation, which is incompatible with anxiety, is paired with an imagined hierarchy of feared situations. (The method is Wolpe's, not Skinner's, Watson's or Pavlov's.) Skinner's operant principles produced token economies and applied behaviour analysis, now widely used with children with autism. The therapies themselves are taught in the Clinical book. 2.3 Gestalt Psychology and Kurt Lewin High yield · 16 Qs Behaviourism rebelled against structuralism by throwing out consciousness. A second rebellion, in Germany, began a year earlier and took the opposite route: it kept consciousness but threw out the idea that consciousness is built from elements. Where Titchener had analysed experience into sensations, images and feelings, and Watson analysed behaviour into reflexes, the Gestalt psychologists argued that both had made the same mistake. They had taken the whole apart and assumed that the parts were more real than the whole. Wertheimer and the phi phenomenon (1912) Max Wertheimer (1880 to 1943) was born in Prague and trained under Oswald Kulpe at Wurzburg. As the story is usually told, in the summer of 1910 he was travelling by train to a holiday in the Rhineland when an idea about seen motion struck him so forcefully that he got off at Frankfurt, bought a toy stroboscope (a device that creates the impression of movement from a series of still pictures), and began experimenting in his hotel room. Historians suspect the story has been polished over the years, but what followed is well documented. At the Psychological Institute in Frankfurt, Wertheimer used a tachistoscope (an instrument that flashes visual displays for precisely controlled intervals) to study apparent motion. His two main observers were younger psychologists, Wolfgang Kohler and Kurt Koffka. The three of them became the founders of Gestalt psychology, and Wertheimer's 1912 paper on the experimental study of seen motion is the school's founding document. The experiment was simple. Two lines were flashed one after the other in slightly different positions. When the interval between them was very short (around 30 milliseconds), observers saw two lines at once; when it was long (around 200 milliseconds), they saw one line and then the other. But at intervals in between (around 60 milliseconds), they saw a single line move from one position to the other. Wertheimer called this apparent movement the phi phenomenon . (He distinguished "pure phi", a sense of motion without any moving object, from the smooth movement of the object itself, later called beta movement; the details belong to Chapter 4.) Why did such a small effect launch a school? Because the motion was not in either stimulus. Each line, analysed on its own, was stationary. An elementist, adding up two static sensations, could never arrive at movement. The perceived motion was a property of the whole pattern of stimulation in time, and it was as real in experience as anything else. If something as basic as seen motion could not be built from elements, perhaps nothing in perception could. The idea was not entirely new. In 1890 the Austrian philosopher Christian von Ehrenfels (1859 to 1932), whose lectures Wertheimer had attended in Prague, had described form qualities (Gestaltqualitaten): a melody played in a different key consists of entirely different notes, yet we hear the same melody. The melody, then, is something more than its notes. Ehrenfels, however, treated the form quality as an extra element added to the sensations. Wertheimer's radical step was to reverse the order: the whole comes first, and the parts get their character from their place in it. The German word Gestalt means form, shape or configuration, an organised whole. Kohler: insight, transposition and isomorphism Wolfgang Kohler (1887 to 1967), born in Reval (now Tallinn in Estonia), took his doctorate in Berlin under Carl Stumpf and was the school's scientist and chief spokesman. You have already met him on Tenerife (1913 to 1920). His observations there, published in German in 1917 and in English as The Mentality of Apes (1925), challenged Thorndike's trial-and-error account of animal problem-solving. Thorndike's cats, Kohler argued, had been put in puzzle boxes whose mechanisms they could not see; of course they fumbled. Give an animal a problem whose elements are all in view, and it may solve it by insight : a sudden reorganisation of the perceptual field so that the relations needed for a solution are seen. Sultan's two sticks, and the boxes his companions stacked to reach fruit hung from the roof, were Kohler's showpieces. Insightful solutions, he noted, appear suddenly, are carried out smoothly once found, are retained, and transfer readily to similar problems. Insight learning as a type of learning is treated in Chapter 6. Key study: Kohler's chickens and transposition (1918) The question. When an animal learns to choose one of two stimuli, does it learn the absolute properties of the stimulus (this particular shade of grey) or a relation between stimuli (the darker of the two)? The method. Kohler trained hens to peck grain from the darker of two grey papers; grain on the lighter one was out of bounds. Then he gave them a test pair: the old "correct" darker grey, now beside an even darker new grey. The result. Most of the time the hens pecked at the new, darker grey, the one they had never been rewarded on, and ignored the shade that had been reinforced. Kohler found the same with chimpanzees. The conclusion. The animals had learned a relation ("the darker one"), not an absolute stimulus. Kohler called this transposition , by analogy with a melody transposed to a new key. It was a direct challenge to the stimulus-response view that a specific stimulus becomes bonded to a response. The criticism: Kenneth Spence (1937) later showed that a stimulus-response account combining generalisation gradients of excitation and inhibition could predict transposition too, and that transposition breaks down when the test pair is far from the training pair. Kohler's most ambitious idea was physiological. In Die physischen Gestalten ("Physical Gestalten", 1920) he proposed isomorphism : the organisation of experience corresponds in structure (not in literal copy) to the organisation of electrical field processes in the brain. A perceived circle does not mean a circle drawn on the cortex, but a pattern of brain activity with the same relational order. The theory was tested in the 1950s. Karl Lashley and his colleagues laid strips of gold foil across the visual cortex of monkeys (1951), and Roger Sperry inserted mica plates and tantalum wires into the cortex of cats (1955), to short-circuit or block any such electrical fields. Perception was essentially unaffected. The field version of isomorphism did not survive, although the broader idea that experience and brain activity share a structure lives on in cognitive neuroscience. Kohler became director of the Psychological Institute at the University of Berlin in 1922, the most prestigious post in German psychology. When the Nazis began dismissing Jewish professors in 1933, he published a newspaper article in their defence, one of the last openly critical pieces to appear in Germany, and resisted the regime's interference with his institute until he resigned and emigrated in 1935. He spent the rest of his career at Swarthmore College in Pennsylvania and was President of the American Psychological Association in 1959. Koffka: development and the behavioural environment Kurt Koffka (1886 to 1941) was the school's great communicator. His Growth of the Mind (German 1921, English 1924) applied Gestalt ideas to child development, arguing that infants perceive organised wholes from the beginning rather than assembling them from sensations. In 1922 he introduced Gestalt psychology to American readers in an article in the Psychological Bulletin titled "Perception: An introduction to the Gestalt-theorie". The article was so influential that for years Americans assumed Gestalt psychology was only about perception, which the founders found frustrating. Koffka moved to Smith College in Massachusetts in 1927, and his Principles of Gestalt Psychology (1935) is the school's most systematic textbook. Koffka's most memorable lesson is a German legend he retold in the Principles . On a winter evening, in a driving snowstorm, a man on horseback rode across a wide, wind-swept plain and arrived at last at an inn. The innkeeper, astonished, asked where he had come from. The rider pointed back across the plain. "Do you know," said the innkeeper, "that you have ridden across Lake Constance?" The rider dropped dead at his feet. In what environment, Koffka asks, did the rider's behaviour take place? In the geographical environment , the physical world, he crossed thin ice over deep water. But he behaved as if he were crossing solid ground, because his behavioural environment , the world as perceived, was a frozen plain. Behaviour, Koffka argued, is governed by the behavioural environment. It is one of the cleanest arguments in psychology for studying the world as the person experiences it. The three founders, together with the neurologist Kurt Goldstein and the psychiatrist Hans Gruhle, launched the school's journal, Psychologische Forschung ("Psychological Research"), in 1921. The central ideas of Gestalt psychology The whole is different from the sum of its parts. This is the school's slogan, and it is usually quoted as "the whole is greater than the sum of its parts". Koffka himself thought "greater" was the wrong word: in the Principles he wrote that it is more correct to say the whole is something else than the sum of its parts, because summing is a meaningless procedure, whereas the whole-part relationship is meaningful. A square drawn with four lines is not "more" than four lines; it is a different kind of thing, with properties (squareness, closedness, an inside) that none of the lines possesses. Textbooks use both versions for the Gestalt principle. Field theory. The Gestalt psychologists borrowed the concept of a field from nineteenth-century physics, where Faraday and Maxwell had shown that electrical and magnetic events are properties of a whole field of forces rather than of isolated particles. Field theory in psychology holds that perception, thought and behaviour are determined by the whole field of interacting forces present at the moment, not by isolated stimuli. Iron filings around a magnet do not each "decide" where to go; the field organises them. Organisation and Pragnanz. Because experience is organised into wholes, the Gestalt psychologists set out the laws by which the organisation happens. Wertheimer's 1923 paper on the laws of perceptual organisation described proximity, similarity, closure, good continuation and common fate, all governed by an overarching law of Pragnanz : perceptual organisation will always be as "good" (simple, regular, symmetrical, stable) as the conditions allow. Figure-ground organisation, first analysed by the Danish psychologist Edgar Rubin (1886 to 1951) in 1915, was adopted as a cornerstone: the figure is seen as a thing, nearer, with a clear contour and shape, usually smaller and more memorable, whereas the ground seems shapeless, diffuse, farther away and to continue behind the figure. The laws themselves, with demonstrations, are taught in Chapter 4. Productive thinking. Wertheimer's last book, Productive Thinking (published in 1945, two years after his death), brought Gestalt ideas to problem-solving and education. He distinguished reproductive thinking , the blind application of a memorised method, from productive thinking , in which the thinker grasps the structure of the problem and sees why a solution works. His favourite example came from a school classroom. Children taught the formula for the area of a parallelogram (base times height) by rote could apply it to the textbook figure but were helpless when the figure was turned on its side. A child who saw that the triangle "sticking out" at one end could be moved to fill the gap at the other, turning the parallelogram into a rectangle, understood the formula and could never be fooled by a rotation. Wertheimer also interviewed Albert Einstein at length about how the theory of relativity had been discovered. Karl Duncker's work on functional fixedness (1945) continued this line (Chapter 8). Notice the method row. The Gestalt psychologists did not use Titchener's trained introspection, which taught observers to report sensations and to avoid the "stimulus error" of naming the object. They wanted exactly what Titchener forbade: a description of experience as it naturally presents itself to an untrained observer, a book as a book and not as patches of colour. This descriptive approach is called phenomenological, and it links Gestalt psychology to the phenomenology of Husserl (Section 2.5). Exam trap Founders. The Gestalt trio is Wertheimer (founder), Kohler and Koffka. Watson, William James and Pavlov are favourite distractors. Lewin is Gestalt-influenced but is not one of the founders. Most important school for perception? Gestalt psychology. "The whole is greater than the sum of its parts and the parts are related to each other and to the whole" in a management or organisational stem refers to systems theory , associated with Ludwig von Bertalanffy's general systems theory, not to Gestalt psychology, motivation theory, contingency theory or Fayol's administrative theory. The Bender Visual Motor Gestalt Test (Lauretta Bender, 1938) borrowed its designs from Wertheimer's 1923 figures, but it is a test of visual-motor integration (Assessment book), not a Gestalt theory. Kurt Lewin: field theory applied to the person The Gestalt founders worked mainly on perception and thinking. It was a younger colleague at the Berlin Institute, Kurt Lewin (1890 to 1947), who carried field theory into motivation, personality and, finally, social life. Lewin's starting point was that behaviour at any moment is a function of the whole psychological situation. He expressed it in a formula that appears in his Principles of Topological Psychology (1936): B = f(P, E) Behaviour (B) is a function (f) of the person (P) and the environment (E). The person and the environment are not independent: they form one interdependent field, which Lewin called the life space (LSp), the totality of facts that determine a person's behaviour at a given moment. So the formula is often written B = f(LSp). The life space contains the person and the psychological environment, the environment as it exists for that person (Koffka's behavioural environment again), not the physical world as a geographer would map it. A rule a student has never heard of is not in her life space; an exam she fears is, even though it is a week away. To describe the life space, Lewin borrowed from a branch of mathematics called topology, which deals with regions, boundaries and connections rather than distances and sizes; hence topological psychology . The life space is divided into regions (activities, goals, groups) separated by boundaries, some of which act as barriers. Movement from one region to another, in thought or action, is called locomotion. Because topology alone cannot express direction and strength, Lewin added two dynamic concepts. A valence is the attracting (positive) or repelling (negative) quality a region has for the person; a vector is a force acting on the person, with a direction and a strength, toward or away from a region. Lewin later added hodological space (from the Greek hodos , path), a geometry of paths that represents the routes, including detours, by which a person can reach a goal. Figure 2.2 puts these terms together. The person and the psychological environment together make up the life space. The goal has positive valence and exerts a force (vector) on the person; a barrier blocks the direct route, so the person must find a detour path; a region of negative valence pushes the person away. Notice that everything in the diagram is the situation as the person sees it. Tension systems and the Zeigarnik effect. Lewin proposed that an intention to reach a goal sets up a tension system within the person, which is discharged only when the goal is reached. One prediction follows directly: unfinished tasks should leave tension behind them and so stay active in the mind. According to a story told by his students, Lewin noticed this one evening at a Berlin restaurant, where a waiter remembered every detail of the unpaid orders but could not recall what had been ordered at a table that had already settled its bill. His student Bluma Zeigarnik (1900 to 1988) tested the idea in 1927. Participants were given a series of simple tasks, half of which were interrupted before completion. Afterwards they recalled the interrupted tasks nearly twice as often as the completed ones. Better memory for interrupted than for completed tasks is the Zeigarnik effect . A second student, Maria Ovsiankina (1898 to 1993), showed in 1928 that people given the chance spontaneously go back to interrupted tasks and finish them, the Ovsiankina effect . Remember the pair this way: Zeigarnik, people remember unfinished tasks; Ovsiankina, people resume them. Contemporaneity. A further principle of Lewin's field theory is that only the present field can influence present behaviour. The past matters only to the extent that it has left traces in the life space now; the future, only as present expectations. This principle of contemporaneity is the most direct "here-and-now" idea in Gestalt-derived psychology. Lewin also analysed conflict as a balance of valences (approach-approach, avoidance-avoidance and approach-avoidance, Chapter 10). Group dynamics and action research. Lewin, who was Jewish, left Germany in 1933, worked briefly at Cornell University and then at the Iowa Child Welfare Research Station, and in 1945 founded the Research Center for Group Dynamics at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. There he turned field theory to groups, which he saw as dynamic wholes whose properties are not the sum of their members'. He coined the term group dynamics . With Ronald Lippitt and Ralph White (1939) he compared boys' clubs run under autocratic, democratic and laissez-faire leadership (Social book). He also founded action research , research carried out in partnership with the people affected by a social problem, in a repeating cycle of planning, acting, observing the results and reflecting, then planning again. A summer workshop he led in 1946 gave rise to the T-group (training group) and the National Training Laboratories. His three-stage model of change (unfreezing, moving, refreezing) is still taught in management courses. Lewin is widely called the father of modern social psychology, and his motto summarises his career: "There is nothing so practical as a good theory." Exam trap Life space = the person plus the psychological environment (not society and group, not person and group, not environment and group). Lewin founded action research, group dynamics and modern experimental social psychology; he did not found psychoanalysis (Freud), psychophysics (Fechner) or functionalism (James, Dewey, Angell). Zeigarnik = recall of interrupted tasks; Ovsiankina = resumption of interrupted tasks. Topological = regions and boundaries; hodological = paths. Emigration, legacy, and a different "Gestalt" With the rise of the Nazis, all four leading figures, Wertheimer (1933, to the New School for Social Research in New York), Koffka (already at Smith from 1927), Kohler (1935) and Lewin (1933), ended up in the United States. There they met a psychology dominated by behaviourism, taught at small colleges rather than major research universities, and wrote in a second language. Gestalt psychology never became a dominant American school. Its influence, however, was enormous and lasting. Its account of perceptual organisation is still taught almost unchanged. Its insistence on insight and understanding prepared the ground for cognitive psychology (Section 2.6). And through Lewin, his students (Leon Festinger among them) and Gestalt-minded social psychologists such as Fritz Heider and Solomon Asch, it shaped modern social psychology. One thing Gestalt psychology did not produce is Gestalt therapy. Gestalt therapy was developed in the 1940s and 1950s by Frederick Salomon Perls (Fritz Perls, 1893 to 1970), a German-born psychoanalyst, with his wife Laura Perls and the writer Paul Goodman; the book Gestalt Therapy (1951) was written by Perls, Ralph Hefferline and Goodman. It is an experiential, humanistic therapy that emphasises awareness in the here and now, personal responsibility, and the completion of "unfinished business" (a phrase that echoes Zeigarnik's interrupted tasks). Its best-known technique is the empty chair , in which the client speaks to an imagined person, or a disowned part of the self, placed in an empty chair, and then changes seats to answer. Perls had worked with the holistic neurologist Kurt Goldstein, and he borrowed the word Gestalt and a general holism, but little else. The Gestalt-trained psychologist Mary Henle published a careful comparison in 1978 and concluded that the connection between the two is largely one of name. The therapy itself is taught in the Clinical book. Exam trap Gestalt psychology (Wertheimer, Kohler, Koffka) is not Gestalt therapy (Perls). The empty chair technique belongs to Gestalt therapy, not to psychoanalysis, CBT or person-centred therapy. Questions sometimes blur the two.
