Answers: (1) preparadigmatic, (2) peripheralism, (3) love, (4) radical, (5) operationism, (6) latent, map, (7) drive, (8) phi, (9) transposition, (10) psychological. 2.4 Psychoanalysis as a School: The First Force Medium yield · 6 Qs Behaviourism and Gestalt psychology were both born in university laboratories, as quarrels with structuralism about how to study normal minds. Psychoanalysis came from somewhere else entirely: the consulting room of a Viennese doctor treating patients whose symptoms made no medical sense. It never really belonged to academic psychology, yet it changed the way the whole twentieth century thought about the mind. This section tells its history as a school; Freud's theory of personality (the stages, defences and dynamics) is taught in full in the Personality book. From neurology to hysteria: Charcot, Bernheim and Breuer Sigmund Freud (1856 to 1939) did not set out to be a psychologist. He qualified in medicine at the University of Vienna in 1881 after years of research in the physiological laboratory of Ernst Brucke, a leader of the mechanistic school of German physiology, where he studied the nerve cells of fish and other animals under the microscope. Unable to support a family on a researcher's pay, he went into private practice in 1886 as a neurologist , a specialist in diseases of the nerves. Many of the patients who came to him suffered from hysteria , a condition (today classed among the conversion and dissociative disorders) in which people developed paralyses, blindness, loss of feeling or fits with no detectable damage to the nervous system. Three encounters shaped what Freud did with these patients. From October 1885 to February 1886 he studied in Paris with Jean-Martin Charcot (1825 to 1893), the most famous neurologist in Europe, who showed at the Salpetriere hospital that hysterical symptoms could be produced and removed under hypnosis. That meant the symptoms had a psychological, not an anatomical, cause. Charcot's pupil Pierre Janet (1859 to 1947) went on to explain hysteria as dissociation , a splitting off of some mental functions from the rest of consciousness into what he called the subconscious; his ideas ran parallel to Freud's, and the two later disputed priority. In 1889 Freud visited Hippolyte Bernheim (1840 to 1919) at Nancy, the rival French school, which taught that hypnosis was simply heightened suggestibility; Freud was struck by evidence that patients could later recall what had happened under hypnosis when pressed, which suggested that forgotten memories were not lost but kept out of awareness. The third and decisive influence was a senior Viennese physician and friend, Josef Breuer (1842 to 1925). Between 1880 and 1882 Breuer had treated a gifted young woman, known in the literature as Anna O. (her real name was Bertha Pappenheim), who suffered paralysis, disturbances of vision and speech, and periods of altered consciousness. Breuer found that when, under light hypnosis, she talked about the circumstances in which a symptom had first appeared, and expressed the feelings she had held back at the time, the symptom eased. Anna O. called the treatment "the talking cure" and "chimney sweeping". Breuer called it the cathartic method , from the Greek catharsis , purging: emotion that had been "strangulated" was released. Breuer and Freud published Studies on Hysteria in 1895, and that book is usually taken as the beginning of psychoanalysis. (Anna O. was Breuer's patient, not Freud's; she later became a pioneering social worker and campaigner for women's rights.) Freud soon gave up hypnosis, partly because not all patients could be hypnotised. He replaced it first with a "pressure technique" (pressing on the patient's forehead and insisting that a memory would come) and then with free association , in which the patient lies on a couch and reports everything that comes to mind, however trivial, embarrassing or illogical. The places where associations stall, he argued, mark resistance, the mind's defence against painful material. By 1896 he was calling his method psychoanalysis. The Interpretation of Dreams and the growth of a movement In the late 1890s, after the death of his father, Freud undertook a systematic self-analysis, much of it through his own dreams. The result was The Interpretation of Dreams , which appeared in November 1899 but was dated 1900 by its publisher, a fitting debut for the new century. In it Freud argued that every dream is the disguised fulfilment of a wish, and he called the interpretation of dreams "the royal road to a knowledge of the unconscious" (dream theory is in Chapter 5). It sold only a few hundred copies in its first years. Yet a circle gathered. From 1902 a small group met at Freud's apartment on Wednesday evenings; in 1908 it became the Vienna Psychoanalytic Society, and in 1910 the International Psychoanalytical Association was founded, with Carl Jung as its first president. International recognition came in 1909, when G. Stanley Hall invited Freud to lecture at Clark University in Worcester, Massachusetts, as part of the university's twentieth-anniversary celebrations. Freud travelled with Jung and Sandor Ferenczi, gave five lectures in German, and received an honorary doctorate, his first academic honour. William James, by then old and ill, came to hear him. The Clark lectures are the usual marker for the arrival of psychoanalysis in America. Two models of the mind The topographic model. In The Interpretation of Dreams (1900) Freud described the mind as having three regions, a topographic model (topography means the mapping of places). The conscious contains what we are aware of at this moment. The preconscious contains material that is not in awareness now but can easily be recalled, such as your phone number or what you ate this morning. The unconscious contains wishes, memories and impulses that are actively kept out of awareness because they are unacceptable, and that can reach consciousness only in disguised form, in dreams, slips of the tongue and symptoms. The popular image of the mind as an iceberg, mostly below the waterline, illustrates this model, though the image is not Freud's own. The structural model. In The Ego and the Id (1923) Freud added a second map, the structural model , which describes three agencies rather than three regions. The id is the oldest and most primitive part of the personality, present at birth and entirely unconscious; it is the source of instinctual energy and operates on the pleasure principle, demanding immediate gratification and caring nothing for logic, time or morality (impulsive, irrational, pleasure-seeking: these words always point to the id). The ego develops to deal with reality; it operates on the reality principle, delays gratification, and uses realistic thought (secondary process) to find safe ways of meeting the id's demands. The superego is the internalised voice of parents and society, made up of the conscience and the ego-ideal. The ego, caught between the id, the superego and the outside world, protects itself against the anxiety these conflicts produce by means of defence mechanisms such as repression. The two models are not rivals: the ego and superego are partly conscious and partly unconscious, while the id is wholly unconscious. Exam trap Freud began his career as a neurologist , not as a psychiatrist, philosopher or (obviously) a psychoanalyst. Father of psychoanalysis : Freud, not Bernheim (Nancy school of hypnosis), not Adler (individual psychology), not Jung (analytical psychology). Psychosocial theory is Erikson's; psychoanalytic theory is Freud's. Gratification, irrational, impulsive = id. Freud's three anxieties are realistic, neurotic (fear that id impulses will break through and be punished) and moral; "innate anxiety" is not a technical term in any of these theories; Horney's basic anxiety and the existentialists' existential anxiety are different concepts (see Table 2.5 and Section 2.5). Dissenters and neo-Freudians Freud demanded loyalty to the core of his theory, above all to the sexual basis of neurosis, and some of his ablest followers broke away. Alfred Adler left in 1911 and Carl Jung in 1913 to 1914; each founded his own school. A later generation, often called the neo-Freudians , kept the idea of unconscious dynamics but shifted the emphasis from biological instincts to social relationships, culture and the ego. Strictly, Adler and Jung are "dissenters" and Horney, Fromm and Sullivan the neo-Freudians proper, while Anna Freud and Erikson are ego psychologists and Klein the founder of the object relations school; introductory textbooks usually group them all together. Its home was the clinic, not the university; its data were case histories, dreams and free associations, not experiments; and its aim was to relieve suffering as well as to understand it. Its central claims, that much of mental life is unconscious, that childhood experience shapes the adult, and that symptoms have meaning, entered everyday thought so completely that we hardly notice them. It is the first force in psychology (Table 2.1), and the broader psychodynamic perspective descended from it still explains behaviour, and many mental disorders, in terms of unconscious urges and the hidden struggle over their expression. Its critics were just as important to the history of the field. The philosopher Karl Popper (1902 to 1994) argued that psychoanalysis was unscientific because it was unfalsifiable: any behaviour at all could be explained after the event, so no observation could ever count against it. Behaviourists dismissed its concepts as untestable, and later the humanists complained that it built a whole picture of human nature from the study of sick people. Modern psychodynamic research has answered some of these charges with controlled studies, but the debate shaped how all the later schools defined themselves. Clinical link Short-term psychodynamic psychotherapy, which focuses on recurring relationship patterns, the transference and avoided feelings, has a growing body of controlled evidence for depression and some anxiety and personality problems. When an interviewer asks you which psychotherapy "school" you find most convincing, remember that modern practice borrows across schools; see eclecticism in Section 2.7. 2.5 The Third Force and Beyond: Humanistic, Existential, Transpersonal and Positive Psychology High yield · 16 Qs By the 1950s, a student of psychology in America could choose between two great pictures of human nature. Psychoanalysis showed a creature driven by blind instincts and scarred by childhood. Behaviourism showed a creature shaped, like a laboratory rat, by its schedule of rewards. Both pictures were deterministic, and to a growing number of psychologists both seemed to leave out what mattered most: the capacity to choose, to grow, to create, to love, to look for meaning. The movement that grew out of this dissatisfaction called itself the third force. The birth of humanistic psychology Abraham Harold Maslow (1908 to 1970) began his career as an enthusiastic behaviourist. He took his doctorate at the University of Wisconsin in 1934, studying dominance and sexual behaviour in monkeys, and as a young man he believed Watson's behaviourism could solve the world's problems. Two experiences changed his mind: the Second World War, and the birth of his first child. He later said that holding his baby made him feel small and not really in control, and that anyone who had a baby could not be a behaviourist. Maslow decided to study not sick people, as Freud had done, nor rats, but the healthiest, most fulfilled people he could find. His hierarchy of needs (1943) and his concept of self-actualisation , the fulfilment of one's unique potential, are taught in Chapter 10. His books Motivation and Personality (1954) and Toward a Psychology of Being (1962) became the movement's texts, and it was Maslow who named it the third force. Carl Ransom Rogers (1902 to 1987) came to the same place by a different road, through counselling. In Counseling and Psychotherapy (1942) and Client-Centered Therapy (1951) he argued that every person has an actualising tendency , an innate drive to grow and develop, which flourishes when others offer unconditional positive regard, empathy and genuineness, and is blocked when love is given only on "conditions of worth". His theory is phenomenological: what matters is the person's own perceived world, the phenomenal field. (Rogers's theory belongs to the Personality book and his therapy to the Clinical book.) Two other founders deserve a place. Charlotte Buhler (1893 to 1974), a Viennese developmental psychologist who studied the course of whole human lives through biographies, brought a European lifespan perspective and was an early president of the movement's association. Rollo May (1909 to 1994) brought existential philosophy into American psychology, as you will see below. The movement acquired the trappings of a school quickly. In 1961 Maslow and Anthony Sutich (1907 to 1976) launched the Journal of Humanistic Psychology , and the Association for Humanistic Psychology was formed in the early 1960s (sources differ on the exact year, usually giving 1961 or 1962). In November 1964 a small invitational conference at Old Saybrook, Connecticut, brought together Maslow, Rogers, May, Buhler, Gordon Allport, Henry Murray, George Kelly and others; the Old Saybrook conference is usually treated as the formal birth of humanistic psychology as a movement. In 1971 the American Psychological Association created a Division of Humanistic Psychology. What did the humanists believe? James Bugental (1915 to 2008), the Association's first president, summarised it in five postulates in 1964: Human beings, as human, supersede the sum of their parts; they cannot be reduced to components. Human beings have their existence in a uniquely human context, which is relational: we live among other people. Human beings are aware, and are aware of being aware; awareness is part of what it is to be human. Human beings have choice, and with choice comes responsibility. Human beings are intentional: they seek meaning, value and creativity, and aim at goals. Put simply, humanistic psychology emphasises free will, conscious experience, the whole person, the innate tendency to grow, and the reaching of maximum potential. Its method is phenomenological: understand people from inside their own experience. Its view of psychological disorder follows. Disturbance arises when growth is blocked, when people deny their real feelings to win approval and their self-concept becomes incongruent with their experience. Healing comes from relationships that offer acceptance, respect for the client and belief in the person's potential, not from reinforcement contingencies (a behavioural idea) or the uncovering of unconscious conflict (a psychoanalytic one). Phenomenology Several schools in this chapter call their method "phenomenological", so the word needs a clear definition. Phenomenology is the philosophical method founded by Edmund Husserl (1859 to 1938) for describing experience exactly as it presents itself, before any theory about its causes is applied. Husserl's call was "back to the things themselves". His central technique was bracketing (Greek epoche ): deliberately suspending one's assumptions about the external reality and causes of an experience, in order to describe the experience itself. He took from his teacher Franz Brentano the idea of intentionality , that consciousness is always consciousness of something. Phenomenology fed three streams in psychology: the Gestalt psychologists' description of naive experience (through Carl Stumpf, who also taught Husserl), the existential psychologists, and the humanists' focus on the subjective world of the client. Today interpretative phenomenological analysis is a respected qualitative research method (Research Methodology book). Existential psychology Humanistic psychology was optimistic: people naturally grow toward fulfilment. Existential psychology , its close relative, is more sober. It begins from the "givens" of human existence that no one escapes, death, freedom, isolation and the absence of any ready-made meaning, and asks how people live authentically in the face of them. Its roots are in European philosophy. Soren Kierkegaard (1813 to 1855), the Danish thinker usually called the father of existentialism, analysed anxiety in The Concept of Anxiety (1844) as the "dizziness of freedom" that comes with having to choose. Martin Heidegger (1889 to 1976), in Being and Time (1927), described human existence as Dasein , literally "being there": the human being is not a mind looking at a separate world but is always already being-in-the-world , thrown into a situation not of its choosing and living toward its own death. Jean-Paul Sartre (1905 to 1980) declared that for human beings "existence precedes essence": we are not born with a fixed nature but must continually create ourselves through our choices, so that we are "condemned to be free", and to deny that freedom is bad faith. The statement that "each person must continually recreate himself; the meaning of life is never fixed but constantly changes" is pure existentialism. Two Swiss psychiatrists turned Heidegger's philosophy into a clinical method. Ludwig Binswanger (1881 to 1966) founded Daseinsanalysis (existential analysis), which tries to understand a patient's "world-design". He described three simultaneous modes of being-in-the-world: the Umwelt (the biological and physical world around us), the Mitwelt (the world with others) and the Eigenwelt (one's own world, the relationship with oneself). The existential therapist Emmy van Deurzen later added a fourth, the Uberwelt , the spiritual world of values and beliefs. Medard Boss (1903 to 1990), who worked closely with Heidegger himself, developed Daseinsanalysis further. The most widely read existential psychiatrist is Viktor Emil Frankl (1905 to 1997) of Vienna. Frankl survived Theresienstadt, Auschwitz and Dachau's subcamps; his wife, parents and brother died in the camps. In Man's Search for Meaning (German 1946, English 1959) he described how prisoners who held on to a reason to live, a task to finish or a person to return to, were better able to endure. He founded logotherapy (from the Greek logos , meaning), often called the "third Viennese school of psychotherapy" after Freud's psychoanalysis and Adler's individual psychology. Where Freud saw a will to pleasure and Adler a will to power, Frankl saw the will to meaning as the primary human motive. When it is frustrated, people fall into an existential vacuum , a sense of emptiness and boredom; when the frustration produces symptoms, Frankl called the result noogenic neurosis (from the Greek noos , mind or spirit), a neurosis arising not from psychological conflict or biology but from the spiritual dimension, from problems of meaning. Meaning, Frankl taught, can be found in three ways: by creating a work or doing a deed (creative values), by experiencing something or loving someone (experiential values), and by the attitude we take toward unavoidable suffering (attitudinal values). His techniques include paradoxical intention and dereflection (Clinical book). Rollo May brought European existentialism to American readers in Existence (1958), edited with Ernest Angel and Henri Ellenberger. In The Meaning of Anxiety (1950) he distinguished normal anxiety , which is proportionate to the threat, does not require repression and can be used constructively, from neurotic anxiety , which is disproportionate and involves repression. Existential anxiety, the anxiety of facing death, freedom and meaninglessness, is normal in this sense. Finally, the American psychiatrist Irvin David Yalom (born 1931), in Existential Psychotherapy (1980), organised the field around four "ultimate concerns": death, freedom (with its responsibility), existential isolation, and meaninglessness. The fourth world, Uberwelt , is van Deurzen's addition, not Heidegger's. Transpersonal psychology: the fourth force Toward the end of his life Maslow came to believe that humanistic psychology itself was a transitional stage. In the preface to the second edition of Toward a Psychology of Being (1968) he wrote of a still "higher" fourth psychology, transpersonal, centred in the cosmos rather than in human needs and interests. His studies of self-actualising people had shown him that many reported peak experiences , moments of awe, unity and self-transcendence. In 1969 Maslow and Sutich founded the Journal of Transpersonal Psychology . Transpersonal psychology , the fourth force , studies experiences in which the sense of identity extends beyond (trans) the individual person: mystical and peak experiences, meditation and altered states of consciousness, spiritual development and self-transcendence. Its leading figures include the psychiatrist Stanislav Grof (born 1931), who studied non-ordinary states of consciousness, Charles Tart (born 1937), who wrote on states of consciousness, Ken Wilber (born 1949), whose spectrum of consciousness and integral theory tried to unite Western psychology with Eastern traditions, and, earlier, the Italian psychiatrist Roberto Assagioli (1888 to 1974), founder of psychosynthesis. Frankl, with his stress on self-transcendence, is often claimed as a forerunner. Because so much transpersonal psychology draws on yoga, Vedanta and Buddhism, it forms a natural bridge to Indian psychology in Sections 2.8 and 2.9. Positive psychology The last movement in this family is the youngest. The phrase "positive psychology" first appeared as the title of the final chapter of Maslow's Motivation and Personality (1954), but it remained a passing label. The field as it exists today was launched by Martin Elias Peter Seligman (born 1942), the psychologist who had made his name with research on learned helplessness and depression (Chapter 6). Elected President of the American Psychological Association for 1998, he used his presidency to argue that psychology had become a science of repairing damage and had forgotten its other two missions: making the lives of ordinary people more fulfilling, and nurturing talent. Seligman later told how the idea crystallised. He was weeding his garden with his five-year-old daughter Nikki, who was throwing weeds into the air and dancing. He shouted at her. She walked away, came back, and told him that from her third birthday to her fifth she had been a whiner, that on turning five she had decided to stop, that it was the hardest thing she had ever done, and that if she could stop whining, he could stop being such a grouch. Raising Nikki, Seligman realised, was not about correcting her whining but about recognising and nurturing the strength she had just shown. Psychology, he concluded, should do the same. In January 2000 Seligman and Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi (1934 to 2021) edited a special issue of the American Psychologist that announced positive psychology : the scientific study of positive experiences, positive individual traits and the institutions that enable them (its "three pillars"). Csikszentmihalyi was already known for his research on flow , the absorbing state of complete engagement in an activity whose challenge matches one's skill. Other landmarks followed. Character Strengths and Virtues (2004), by Christopher Peterson and Seligman, classified 24 character strengths under six virtues as a kind of "manual of the sanities" to set beside the diagnostic manuals. In Flourish (2011) Seligman proposed the PERMA model of well-being: Positive emotion, Engagement, Relationships, Meaning and Accomplishment (detail in the Motivation and Emotion chapters). Several research programmes are now considered part of positive psychology. C. R. Snyder's hope theory describes hope as the combination of agency (the will to reach a goal) and pathways (the ways to reach it); promoting hope is a typical positive psychology intervention. Fred Bryant and Joseph Veroff (2007) studied savouring , the capacity to attend to, appreciate and deliberately enhance the enjoyment of positive experiences, past, present or anticipated; savouring is to good events what coping is to bad ones. Barbara Fredrickson's broaden-and-build theory holds that positive emotions broaden attention and thinking and build lasting personal resources, and Ed Diener's research on subjective well-being measures happiness as high life satisfaction, frequent positive feeling and infrequent negative feeling. Positive psychology interventions, such as writing down three good things each day, using one's signature strengths in a new way, or delivering a gratitude letter, have been tested in randomised trials. How does positive psychology relate to humanism? Seligman was at pains to distance his field from what he saw as the unscientific, self-help side of humanistic psychology; positive psychology is meant to be empirical. Humanistic psychologists replied, with some justice, that positive psychology had rediscovered their themes and given them new names. Most textbooks now treat humanistic psychology as its forerunner. Exam trap Founder of positive psychology : Seligman (with Csikszentmihalyi). Maslow coined the phrase in 1954 but did not found the field. Howard Gardner is multiple intelligences; Steven Pinker is language and evolutionary psychology; Bandura is self-efficacy and social cognitive theory. Savouring = enhancing the enjoyment of positive experiences (not avoiding negative ones, not relaxation, not reflecting on trauma). The primary focus of positive psychology interventions is building strengths such as hope, not behaviour therapy, psychoanalysis or DBT. Criticisms of the third force Humanistic psychology has been criticised on four main grounds. First, its concepts (self-actualisation, growth, authenticity) are vague and hard to test; Maslow's description of self-actualisers rested on a small, hand-picked sample of people he admired. Second, its optimism can seem naive in the face of real human destructiveness, a criticism made from inside the movement by Rollo May. Third, it is individualistic: by concentrating so heavily on the individual's inner world, the humanistic and phenomenological approaches miss the wider social, cultural and economic contexts that shape experience and identity, and they reflect a Western, individualist ideal of the self. Fourth, some critics argued that its celebration of self-fulfilment encouraged self-absorption. Positive psychology tried to answer the first criticism with data; cross-cultural and Indian psychologists, as you will see, have pressed the third. Scan Your Brain Fill in the blanks. A second group of critics attacked it for leaving out the mind, and this second attack proved decisive in the laboratories. Between the late 1940s and the late 1960s, the study of memory, attention, language, thinking and perception, all of which behaviourism had pushed to the edges, returned to the centre of experimental psychology. The change was so rapid and so complete that it is usually called the cognitive revolution . Why did it happen when it did? Why behaviourism waned Several pressures converged, and it helps to keep them separate. Anomalies inside behaviourism. You have already met two: Tolman's rats that learned maps without reward, and Kohler's apes that solved problems by insight. A third came from Karl Spencer Lashley (1890 to 1958), once Watson's own student. At the Hixon Symposium on "Cerebral Mechanisms in Behavior" in 1948 (published in 1951), Lashley gave a paper on "The Problem of Serial Order in Behavior". A pianist playing a fast passage, or a person speaking a sentence, produces movements far too quickly for each one to be triggered by sensory feedback from the one before, as a chain of stimulus-response links would require. The sequence must be planned in advance, centrally, and organised hierarchically. In other words, behaviour requires internal plans. The war and its machines. The Second World War posed problems that behaviourism could not answer: how radar operators could stay alert through long watches, how pilots could cope with too many dials and messages at once, how to design controls that people would not misread. Psychologists working on these problems, such as Donald Broadbent in Britain, found themselves talking about attention, capacity and the flow of information through a person. Information, feedback and computers. In 1948 the engineer Claude Elwood Shannon (1916 to 2001) published a mathematical theory of communication that measured information in units called bits, and the mathematician Norbert Wiener (1894 to 1964) published Cybernetics , the science of control and feedback in animals and machines. A machine with a goal and a feedback loop (a thermostat, a guided missile) behaves purposefully, and nobody thinks it is mystical to say so. Then came the stored-program digital computer, and in 1950 Alan Mathison Turing (1912 to 1954) asked whether machines could think. Computers made internal states respectable. A computer's behaviour cannot be understood without reference to its program and its memory, which nobody can see. If a machine could be described in terms of stored symbols and rules for manipulating them, why not a person? Language. The final blow came from linguistics, as you will see shortly. Seen through Kuhn's eyes (Section 2.1), these were anomalies piling up until the old framework entered a crisis. 1956 and after If the revolution has a birthday, it is in 1956. From 10 to 12 September of that year, a Symposium on Information Theory was held at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. George Armitage Miller (1920 to 2012), one of the participants, later dated the birth of cognitive science to its second day, 11 September 1956. On that day Allen Newell (1927 to 1992) and Herbert Alexander Simon (1916 to 2001) described the Logic Theorist , a computer program (written with Cliff Shaw) that proved theorems from Whitehead and Russell's Principia Mathematica , the first program to model human problem-solving. Noam Chomsky (born 1928), a young linguist, presented a paper on formal models of language. And Miller himself spoke about the limits of short-term memory, the subject of his famous 1956 paper "The Magical Number Seven, Plus or Minus Two", which showed that people can hold about seven items (between five and nine) in immediate memory, and that the limit can be stretched by grouping items into larger meaningful units, or chunks (Chapter 7). The same year saw the Dartmouth summer research project at which John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, Claude Shannon and others launched the field of artificial intelligence (McCarthy had coined the term in the 1955 proposal for the meeting), and the publication of A Study of Thinking by Jerome Seymour Bruner (1915 to 2016), Jacqueline Goodnow and George Austin, which analysed the strategies people use to discover concepts (Chapter 8). In 1957 Chomsky published Syntactic Structures , and in 1958 Donald Eric Broadbent (1926 to 1993) published Perception and Communication , which presented the filter model of attention (Chapter 5). Broadbent's book is regarded as the first major theory cast explicitly in information-processing terms: information flows through a series of stages of limited capacity, drawn as a box-and-arrow flow chart. Key study: Chomsky's review of Verbal Behavior (1959) The background. In Verbal Behavior (1957), Skinner had argued that language is operant behaviour like any other: children learn to speak because the verbal community reinforces some sounds and not others, and adult speech is controlled by stimuli and reinforcement histories. The argument. In a long review in the journal Language (1959), Chomsky argued that this could not work. Children acquire the grammar of their language rapidly, at about the same age everywhere, from speech that is fragmentary and full of errors (later called the poverty of the stimulus). They constantly produce and understand sentences they have never heard, so these sentences cannot have been reinforced. Their errors, such as "I goed" or "two mouses", are not imitations of anything adults say; they are over-applications of rules. And when Skinner's terms (stimulus, response, reinforcement) are stretched to cover language, Chomsky argued, they lose their precise laboratory meaning and become a vague paraphrase of ordinary talk. The conclusion. Language is rule-governed, creative and generative, and human beings must come equipped with an innate capacity for acquiring it (Chapter 8). The criticism. Behaviour analysts, notably Kenneth MacCorquodale (1970), replied that Chomsky had misunderstood Skinner's position. Skinner never answered publicly. Whatever its fairness, the review was read as a manifesto for the new cognitive psychology, and it made Chomsky, a linguist rather than a psychologist, one of the movement's heroes. The pieces came together quickly. In 1960 Miller, Eugene Galanter and Karl Pribram published Plans and the Structure of Behavior , which replaced the reflex arc with the TOTE unit (Test, Operate, Test, Exit), a feedback loop in which an organism compares its current state with a goal, acts, and tests again. The same year, Bruner and Miller founded the Center for Cognitive Studies at Harvard. Then, in 1967, Ulric Neisser (1928 to 2012) published Cognitive Psychology , the first textbook of the new field, which gave it its name. Neisser defined cognition as "all the processes by which the sensory input is transformed, reduced, elaborated, stored, recovered, and used". He is called the father of cognitive psychology , the study of internal mental processes such as perception, attention, memory, language, problem-solving and reasoning. (Characteristically, Neisser later criticised his own field: in Cognition and Reality , 1976, he argued that laboratory cognitive psychology had lost touch with how people use their minds in real life, its ecological validity.) The approach rests on four assumptions. Mental processes can be broken into a sequence of stages. Each stage has a limited capacity. Processing takes time, so the time a task takes (the reaction time) reveals what stages it involves, an idea that revived Donders's mental chronometry from the nineteenth century (Chapter 1). And mental processes can be described as operations on internal representations (symbols and rules), at the level of the "software", without first knowing the "hardware" of the brain. A worked example shows how the approach thinks. A fast bowler releases a cricket ball at 140 kilometres an hour, and the batsman has about half a second before it reaches him. In information-processing terms: light from the ball is registered by the eyes (sensory input); attention selects the ball from the crowd, the bowler's arm and the sightscreen (selection); the line and length of the delivery are recognised by matching them against patterns stored from thousands of earlier deliveries (pattern recognition, drawing on long-term memory); a shot is selected and its motor program retrieved (decision and response selection); and the bat moves (output). Each stage takes time, and an expert's advantage lies partly in doing some stages faster and partly in anticipating the ball before it is bowled, from cues in the bowler's run-up, which is top-down processing (Chapter 4). Forerunners: Bartlett and Piaget The cognitive revolution was a revolution mainly in America. In Europe, the study of the mind had never stopped, and two European psychologists in particular are treated as forerunners. Frederic Charles Bartlett (1886 to 1969) of Cambridge, in Remembering (1932), asked English students to read and later recall a Native American folk tale, "The War of the Ghosts". Their recall grew shorter, lost its unfamiliar supernatural details and was rationalised into the shape of an English story. Bartlett concluded that remembering is reconstruction guided by a schema , an organised mental structure of knowledge built from past experience (Chapter 7). Jean Piaget (1896 to 1980) of Geneva spent half a century, from the 1920s on, studying how children's thinking develops. He called his field genetic epistemology, the study of the origins and growth of knowledge, and described how children build schemas and adapt them through assimilation (fitting new experience into existing schemas) and accommodation (changing schemas to fit new experience). Piaget studied thinking directly at a time when American psychology refused to, which is why he is often named a pioneer of cognitive psychology; in the 2002 survey of eminent psychologists he ranked second only to Skinner. His stage theory is taught in the Developmental book. Other forerunners include the Gestalt psychologists (insight and productive thinking), Tolman (cognitive maps), the Wurzburg school (thought without images, Chapter 1) and the Russian psychologist Lev Semyonovich Vygotsky (1896 to 1934), who studied the relation between thought and language. Exam trap The first major information-processing theory was Broadbent's (1958), not Treisman's (her attenuation work began around 1960), not Chomsky's (1957 was Syntactic Structures , a work of linguistics), and certainly not Watson's (1920 was Little Albert). Father of cognitive psychology : Neisser (1967), though Miller and Bruner were central figures. Pioneer contributor to cognitive psychology in an Amity item with options Piaget, Kohler, Chomsky and Kohlberg: the key is Piaget , who studied thinking from the 1920s; Chomsky was a linguist whose 1959 review fuelled the revolution; Kohler belongs to Gestalt; Kohlberg studied moral development. Chomsky's review was of Verbal Behavior (1957) and appeared in 1959. Cognitive science and cognitive neuroscience Cognitive psychology soon joined a larger enterprise. Cognitive science is the interdisciplinary study of mind and intelligence, bringing together psychology, artificial intelligence and computer science, linguistics, philosophy, neuroscience and anthropology; it acquired its own journal and, in 1979, a Cognitive Science Society. For its first twenty years cognitive psychology mostly ignored the brain, in keeping with the "software" assumption. That changed in the late 1970s, when, as Michael Gazzaniga (born 1939) tells it, he and George Miller coined the term cognitive neuroscience in the back of a New York taxi. Cognitive neuroscience studies how mental processes are carried out by the brain, combining the experimental tasks of cognitive psychology with methods for measuring brain activity: the study of patients with brain damage, electrical recording (EEG and event-related potentials), positron emission tomography (PET) from the 1980s, functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) from the 1990s, and transcranial magnetic stimulation. Its methods are taught in the Physiological book. Connectionism and parallel distributed processing The serial, box-and-arrow model had a problem. Brains are made of billions of slow neurons, each firing at most a few hundred times a second, yet people recognise a face in a fraction of a second. A strictly serial process with such slow parts could not be that fast. The answer, many researchers argued, was that the brain does many things at once. Connectionism models the mind as a network of many simple, neuron-like processing units joined by connections of varying strength (weights). Each unit adds up the activation it receives and passes activation on; many units are active at the same time (parallel processing); and a piece of knowledge is stored not in one place but as a pattern of weights spread across the whole network (distributed representation). The landmark was the two-volume Parallel Distributed Processing (1986) by David Everett Rumelhart (1942 to 2011), James Lloyd McClelland (born 1948) and the PDP Research Group, which gave the approach its other name, parallel distributed processing (PDP). Figure 2.3(b) shows a simple network. Networks learn by adjusting their weights. One idea goes back to Donald Hebb (1949), who proposed that a connection between two neurons strengthens when they are active together; another, the back-propagation rule popularised in 1986 by Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton and Ronald Williams, adjusts weights in proportion to the network's errors. Connectionist models have several brain-like properties. They degrade gracefully: damage a few units and performance worsens a little rather than failing completely. They are content-addressable: a partial cue can retrieve a whole memory. And they generalise: Rumelhart and McClelland's 1986 model of the English past tense learned regular and irregular verbs from examples, with no rules written in, and even went through a stage of over-regularising ("goed") as children do. Connectionism has deep roots, in Warren McCulloch and Walter Pitts's model neurons (1943) and Frank Rosenblatt's perceptron (1958), and today's deep-learning systems are its descendants. Cognition enters behaviour therapy The cognitive revolution did not stop at the laboratory door. Albert Bandura (1925 to 2021), whose Bobo doll studies you will meet in Chapter 6, moved social learning theory steadily toward cognition. In 1977 he introduced the concept of self-efficacy , a person's belief in his or her capacity to carry out the actions needed to deal with a particular situation, as a unifying explanation of how people change. Expectations, not reinforcements alone, drive behaviour. His mature system is social cognitive theory (1986). At the same time, Albert Ellis (1913 to 2007) developed rational therapy, later renamed rational emotive behaviour therapy, from 1955, and Aaron Temkin Beck (1921 to 2021) developed cognitive therapy for depression in the 1960s, both based on the idea that maladaptive thoughts produce distress. The merger of these ideas with behaviour therapy produced cognitive-behavioural therapy (CBT), the therapy that focuses on changing maladaptive thought patterns. Clinical link Psychotherapy has gone through three "waves" that mirror this chapter's history: behaviour therapy (the legacy of behaviourism), cognitive therapy and CBT (the legacy of the cognitive revolution), and a third wave of acceptance and mindfulness-based therapies, including acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT), dialectical behaviour therapy (DBT) and mindfulness-based cognitive therapy (MBCT), which draw explicitly on Buddhist ideas (Section 2.9). Psychoanalysis is not one of the waves of CBT. Each therapy is taught in the Clinical book. 2.7 Psychology Today: Perspectives, Eclecticism and the Enduring Issues Medium yield · 6 Qs By the 1970s the age of schools was over. Few psychologists now call themselves behaviourists or Gestaltists; instead they speak of perspectives , ways of approaching a question that coexist and complement one another. The difference is real. A school claimed to be the right way to do psychology; a perspective claims only to be a useful angle on a problem that other perspectives also illuminate. The biological perspective , also called the neurobiological perspective, holds that behaviour is ultimately governed by the brain and nervous system. The evolutionary perspective asks what adaptive problem a behaviour helped our ancestors solve; it was developed into evolutionary psychology by researchers such as David Buss, Leda Cosmides and John Tooby. The sociocultural perspective , inspired in part by Vygotsky, studies how culture and social context shape thought and behaviour. The biopsychosocial model was proposed by the American psychiatrist George Libman Engel (1913 to 1999) in a 1977 paper in Science , as an alternative to the purely biomedical model of illness: any illness, physical or mental, must be understood as the product of biological, psychological and social factors acting together. It is now the standard framework of clinical psychology and psychiatry. You will also see "developmental" listed as a perspective in some textbooks, meaning the study of how people change as they mature across the lifespan; strictly, developmental psychology is a field of study that uses all the other perspectives. Within the sociocultural approach, three terms are easily confused. Cross-cultural psychology compares psychological processes across different cultures, usually with the same measures, to find out which are universal and which vary (the work of Harry Triandis, John Berry and Geert Hofstede is typical). Cultural psychology studies, often from within a single culture, how culture and mind "make each other up", treating culture as part of the mind rather than as a variable acting on it. Indigenous psychology builds psychological concepts and theories from within a culture's own traditions instead of importing them; Durganand Sinha's call to indigenise psychology in India, which you will meet in Section 2.8, is an example. Exam trap "Who studies how psychological processes may differ among people of different cultures?" The textbook answer is cross-cultural psychologists . One Panwar item keys social psychologists , presumably because culture is part of the social context; if both appear, cross-cultural psychology is the more precise answer. "Behaviour is governed by the brain and nervous system" = neurobiological (not psychophysical, which is Fechner's study of stimulus-sensation relations, and not neo-behaviouristic). "Unconscious processes and early childhood" = psychodynamic . "Stimulus-response associations through conditioning" = behavioural . "Internal mental processes" = cognitive . "Free will and personal growth" = humanistic . Eclecticism If every perspective captures part of the truth, why choose one? Eclecticism is the practice of selecting concepts, methods or techniques from different schools according to what best fits the problem in hand. Frederick Thorne argued for an eclectic approach to counselling around 1950, and Arnold Lazarus later distinguished technical eclecticism , using techniques from any school without necessarily accepting its theory (his multimodal therapy is the best-known example), from theoretical integration , which tries to combine the theories themselves. A third route looks for the common factors , such as the therapeutic relationship and the instillation of hope, that make different therapies work. Surveys repeatedly find that eclectic or integrative is the most common orientation among practising clinicians. The danger, critics point out, is a shapeless mixture with no principle for choosing. The enduring issues Schools come and go, but the questions that divided them do not. The historian of psychology Robert Irving Watson (1909 to 1980) argued in a 1967 paper, "Psychology: A Prescriptive Science", that since psychology lacks a single paradigm, its history is better organised by prescriptions : contrasting attitudes, held more or less strongly by different psychologists at different times, about what psychology should be and do. He listed eighteen pairs, among them conscious versus unconscious mentalism, determinism versus indeterminism, empiricism versus rationalism, mechanism versus vitalism, molecularism versus molarism, monism versus dualism, nomotheticism versus idiographicism, and peripheralism versus centralism. At the end of Section 2.5 you saw one consequence. Critics charged that even humanistic psychology, for all its talk of the whole person, reflected a Western, individualist ideal of the self. Yet the questions psychology asks (what the mind is, why we suffer, how attention can be trained, what the self really is) were being asked in India more than two thousand years before Wundt opened his laboratory in Leipzig. The Bhagavad Gita is the most famous example. It opens with a warrior, Arjuna, standing in his chariot between two armies. Facing his own teachers and cousins across the field, he tells his charioteer Krishna that his limbs are failing, his mouth is dry, his body trembles and his hair stands on end, that his bow is slipping from his hand and his mind is reeling. He sits down and refuses to fight, because every course open to him seems wrong. The rest of the poem is a dialogue in which Krishna helps him understand his own mind and find his way back to action. A modern reader can hardly miss that it has the shape of a counselling session with a man paralysed by anxiety and moral conflict. This section and the next tell two connected stories. The first is how modern, Western-style psychology came to India in the early twentieth century, and how Indian psychologists gradually moved from copying it to questioning it. The second is what the classical Indian systems actually say about the mind. We begin by separating two phrases that sound almost the same. Psychology in India and Indian psychology Psychology in India means the discipline as it is taught and practised in Indian universities, hospitals and clinics. For most of its first century it was Western psychology carried on in India: laboratories on the Leipzig model, theories from Europe and America, and tests translated or adapted for Indian use. Most of this book is psychology in that sense. Indian psychology , in the sense used by the movement that took shape around the year 2000, is something else: an approach to psychology rooted in the ideas and practices of the classical Indian traditions (the Upanishads, Samkhya, Yoga, Vedanta, Buddhism and Jainism, the Bhagavad Gita and Ayurveda), joined in later centuries by Indian Sufism and, in the twentieth century, by Sri Aurobindo. It is not the psychology of Indians either; a study of how Indian students cope with examination stress belongs to cross-cultural or cultural psychology (Section 2.7). Its advocates stress that, like the psychology that came out of Germany, it is meant to be universal. Its claims about attention, the self and suffering are claims about human beings anywhere, which happen to have been worked out in India. What makes the approach distinctive? Its leading scholars usually point to five features. It is consciousness-centred. Consciousness is treated as fundamental rather than as a by-product of the brain, and a sharp line is drawn between consciousness itself, the silent witness, and the mind's changing contents and instruments (thoughts, feelings, memories), which are treated as part of nature. It is holistic. Body, mind and spirit are treated as one system, and so are the person, the family and the community; health is a state of balance among them. It is transformative. The aim is not only to describe the mind but to change it, toward freedom from suffering and the realisation of one's true nature (called moksha , kaivalya or nirvana in different systems). Disciplines such as yoga and meditation are its laboratory techniques. It values disciplined first-person methods. Where Western psychology after Watson distrusted introspection, the Indian traditions developed elaborate methods for training and refining it, and they treat the reports of a trained observer as evidence. It is relational and value-laden. The self is understood in relation to others and to dharma , the order of duties that sustains social and moral life, so ethics is part of psychology rather than outside it. Table 2.10 sets these features against mainstream Western psychology. Remember that the contrast is one of emphasis, not a wall. Behaviourists also wanted to change behaviour, humanists also cared about values, and over the last forty years Western psychology has borrowed meditation and mindfulness from India on a large scale (Section 2.9). Not by rejecting modern treatment. Its practitioners combine traditional practices (yoga postures and breathing, meditation, a regulated daily routine and diet, reflection on the values of texts such as the Gita ) with modern psychotherapy and, where needed, medication, and they aim at the well-being of the whole person rather than the removal of a symptom alone. The Ayurvedic and yogic ideas behind this approach are taught in Section 2.9. Exam trap The primary focus of Indian psychology is the integration of Indian philosophical and contemplative traditions with psychological concepts and methods. It is not the exclusive application of Western theories (that is psychology in India at its most imitative), not the study of folklore and mythology, and not meditation without a psychological context. How it differs from Western psychology : it emphasises holistic and spiritual approaches, including family and community, rather than the isolated individual; it does not rely only on ancient texts without modern relevance, and it is Indian (not Western) psychology that stresses spirituality. Atman is the true self, eternal consciousness; not the physical body, not Jung's collective unconscious and not a passing state of mind. The pioneers: how modern psychology came to India The story of psychology in India begins in Calcutta, then the capital of British India and home of its leading university. In 1905, on the initiative of the philosopher Brajendranath Seal (1864 to 1938), the University of Calcutta introduced experimental psychology as a subject within its philosophy curriculum. Seal, a scholar of both Western science and Indian philosophy, wanted Indian students to learn the new laboratory psychology. The university's vice-chancellor, the mathematician and lawyer Asutosh Mookerjee (1864 to 1924), backed him. What was missing was someone trained to run a laboratory. That person was Narendra Nath Sengupta (1889 to 1944; the name is also written Sen Gupta). Sengupta had studied at Harvard under Hugo Munsterberg, who had himself taken his doctorate with Wundt at Leipzig, so there is a direct line of teachers running from Wundt's laboratory to Calcutta. In 1915 Sengupta set up the first psychology laboratory in India at the University of Calcutta, modelled on the German laboratories, and in 1916 the university created a separate Department of Psychology (often called the Department of Experimental Psychology), the first in the country, with Sengupta in charge. With the sociologist Radhakamal Mukerjee he wrote Introduction to Social Psychology: Mind in Society (1928), one of the first social psychology textbooks written by Indian authors, and he later moved to Lucknow University. For his laboratory, his department and the students he trained, Sengupta is called the father, or founder, of modern psychology in India. Among the first generation of Calcutta psychologists was a physician who would take the subject in a completely different direction. Girindrasekhar Bose (1887 to 1953; also written Girindra Shekhar Bose) had qualified in medicine and become fascinated by the mind through his own medical practice. His thesis on the concept of repression, published in 1921 as Concept of Repression , earned him what is usually described as the first doctorate in psychology awarded by an Indian university (some Indian study notes give 1916 or 1922 for this degree; 1921, the year of the thesis, is the date most histories give). He sent a copy to Freud, and the two corresponded for the next sixteen years or so. In 1922 Bose founded the Indian Psychoanalytical Society in Calcutta, one of the earliest psychoanalytic societies outside Europe and North America, and in 1947 he launched its journal, Samiksha . When Sengupta left Calcutta, Bose succeeded him as head of the psychology department. He is the father of psychoanalysis in India. Bose did not simply import Freud. His best-known idea, the theory of opposite wishes , holds that every wish comes paired with its opposite: the wish to beat goes with the wish to be beaten, the wish to be male with the wish to be female, the wish to see with the wish to be seen. One member of each pair is expressed in consciousness and behaviour while the other is repressed, and the two can change places. For Bose it was this play of opposites, rather than a fixed Oedipus complex, that lay at the centre of mental life, and he reported that the Oedipal conflict did not hold the same central place in his Indian patients as in Freud's Viennese ones. Freud read his work with interest but was not persuaded. Bose's ideas show an Indian thinker reworking psychoanalysis through his own culture's preoccupation with the reconciliation of opposites, an early example of what would later be called indigenisation. Institutions followed the pioneers. In 1923 the Indian Science Congress opened a section for psychology and educational science. In 1925 Sengupta founded the Indian Psychological Association , and in 1926 the association's Indian Journal of Psychology , the first Indian psychology journal, began publication. From imitation to indigenisation For its first fifty years, psychology in India was largely imitative. Indian psychologists, many trained in Britain or America, repeated Western experiments on Indian participants and used Western tests in translation. Did the results mean what they meant in London or Chicago? Increasingly, the answer seemed to be no. The psychologist who did most to name the problem and chart a way out was Durganand Sinha (1922 to 1998) of the University of Allahabad. In Psychology in a Third World Country: The Indian Experience (1986) he described psychology in India as passing through four broad phases: a period before independence in which the Western academic and experimental tradition was transplanted largely unchanged; a period of rapid expansion after independence, still mostly imitative; a problem-oriented phase from about the 1970s, in which psychologists turned to India's own pressing problems (poverty, deprivation, rural development, social change); and finally a phase of indigenisation , the effort to make psychology's concepts, theories and methods fit the culture in which they are used. Indigenous psychologists distinguish two routes, a pair of terms usually credited to the Filipino psychologist Virgilio Enriquez and used by Sinha in his later writing. Indigenisation from without takes a Western concept or tool and modifies it to suit local conditions. Indigenisation from within builds concepts, theories and methods from the culture itself, from its traditions, texts, languages and everyday life. Test adaptation is the clearest example of indigenisation from without. The pictures of the Thematic Apperception Test (TAT), drawn in the United States, showed American faces, clothes and settings, and Indian respondents told thin, guarded stories about them. Uma Chowdhury (the name is also spelled Chaudhuri) of Calcutta redrew the cards with Indian figures and scenes, producing an Indian modification of the TAT around 1960 (the tests themselves are covered in the Assessment book). Two contributions from organisational psychology show indigenisation moving further, toward concepts grown from Indian conditions. Jai B. P. Sinha , studying Indian organisations in the 1970s, found that neither the authoritarian leadership common in Indian offices nor the participative style recommended by American research worked best. In The Nurturant Task Leader (1980) he proposed the nurturant-task leader : a leader who combines a strong task orientation (clear goals, discipline, insistence on hard work) with nurturance (warmth, personal care and guidance, interest in the subordinate's growth), and who makes that nurturance depend on the subordinate's work. The style fits a culture that values hierarchy and personal relationships, and Sinha saw it as a stage through which a work group could move toward fuller participation as subordinates matured (leadership styles in general are covered in the Social book). Udai Pareek (1925 to 2010) of the Indian Institute of Management, Ahmedabad, was a founder of human resource development in Indian organisations; he developed the concepts and scales of role stress (he identified ten organisational role stressors, among them role overload, role ambiguity and role stagnation) and role efficacy , and, with G. Trivedi, a widely used socio-economic status scale for rural India (1964). Psychoanalysis, too, was reworked from within. Sudhir Kakar (born 1938), a psychoanalyst influenced by Erik Erikson, wrote The Inner World: A Psycho-analytic Study of Childhood and Society in India (1978), which traced how the Indian family, with its long and intense early bond between mother and son and its many caretakers in the joint family, shapes an identity more relational than the Western ideal of the autonomous individual. In Shamans, Mystics and Doctors (1982) he studied India's traditional healers as psychotherapists in their own right. Kakar is the leading figure of a cultural psychoanalysis of India, the field Bose began. Exam trap Two Sinhas. The Indian Psychology movement Indigenisation asked psychology to fit Indian conditions. By the 1990s a growing number of psychologists wanted something bolder: to take the Indian traditions themselves seriously as sources of psychological theory and method, on an equal footing with the Western schools. The turning point came in 2002, when a national conference on yoga and Indian approaches to psychology, held in Pondicherry (now Puducherry), closed with a statement signed by the psychologists present, the Pondicherry Manifesto of Indian Psychology . The manifesto argued that Indian psychologists had too long confined themselves to replicating Western research, that the Indian traditions contain a rich and systematic understanding of consciousness and the self, together with methods for exploring and transforming them, and that this knowledge should be developed into a modern psychology useful anywhere in the world. Notice that Figure 2.1 marks 2002 as the start of the Indian Psychology movement. Several people carried the movement forward. Matthijs Cornelissen , a Dutch-born physician and psychologist long resident at the Sri Aurobindo Ashram, was one of its prime movers and founded the Indian Psychology Institute in Pondicherry, which runs courses and workshops grounded largely in Sri Aurobindo's integral psychology. Koneru Ramakrishna Rao (born 1932), a philosopher and parapsychologist and a former vice-chancellor of Andhra University, became its most prolific theorist; with Anand C. Paranjpe of Simon Fraser University in Canada, author of Self and Identity in Modern Psychology and Indian Thought (1998), and Ajit K. Dalal of the University of Allahabad, he edited the Handbook of Indian Psychology (2008), the movement's first comprehensive reference work, and with Paranjpe he later wrote Psychology in the Indian Tradition (2016). Cornelissen, Girishwar Misra and Suneet Varma , both of the University of Delhi, edited the two-volume Foundations of Indian Psychology (2011), one volume on theories and concepts and one on practical applications. Misra is also one of the most influential scholars of cultural and indigenous psychology in India. The movement has its critics. Some worry that it romanticises the past, that it blurs the line between religion and science, or that claims about pure consciousness cannot be tested. Its defenders answer that the first-person methods of yoga and Buddhism can be made as disciplined as any laboratory technique, that many traditional claims (about meditation, breathing and attention, for example) are now being tested experimentally, and that Western psychology's own assumptions are no less culture-bound for being familiar. The debate is a live one, and you will find both sides in Indian journals today. Exam trap Who led the early-2000s Indian Psychology movement and founded the Indian Psychology Institute?
