The case of Sultan's sticks, revisited Go back to Tenerife, to the chimpanzee sitting on his box and idly playing with two bamboo sticks until, suddenly, he fitted one into the other and raked in the banana. You can now tell all five of the stories the opening promised. A strict behaviourist would refuse to say anything about what went on inside Sultan; she would describe the solution as a response that was emitted and then reinforced, and would want to know his history of reinforcement with sticks. Kohler, the Gestalt psychologist, saw insight: a sudden restructuring of the perceptual field, two separate sticks reorganised into one tool, a solution that appeared all at once, was carried out smoothly and was repeated without hesitation. A psychoanalyst would look past the problem to the motive it served. A cognitive psychologist would model Sultan as an information-processing system searching a problem space, holding the goal in working memory and testing operators against it. And a psychologist trained in the Indian tradition would notice what Kohler himself recorded but did not dwell on: the answer came not while Sultan was straining at the bars but after he had given up and sat quietly, when the restless, rajasic effort had subsided, much as many human solvers report that a solution arrives when they stop forcing it (incubation, Chapter 8). The schools did not merely tell different stories; they tested one another. In 1945 Herbert Birch found that young chimpanzees with no previous experience of playing with sticks rarely solved a similar problem, but that after a few days of free play with sticks they did. Insight, it turned out, draws on a learning history, which is exactly what a behaviourist would have predicted, while the sudden reorganisation of that learning is exactly what a Gestalt psychologist would have predicted. That is the lesson of this chapter. Each school saw something real, overreached, and was corrected by its rivals; and psychology today, with its overlapping perspectives, its information-processing models, its third-wave therapies drawn from Buddhist mindfulness and its renewed interest in India's own traditions, is the sum of those corrections. Sultan's two sticks, joined end to end, are not a bad image of it. Chapter summary 2.1 Schools, Systems and Paradigms. A school of thought is a group sharing assumptions about psychology's subject matter, method and explanation, usually with a founder, a manifesto, a home, a journal, students and a rival; Woodworth's Contemporary Schools of Psychology (1931) and Heidbreder's Seven Psychologies (1933) surveyed them. A system is an organised body of assumptions covering the whole field; a theory explains one set of facts. Kuhn's The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962) described paradigms, normal science, anomalies, crises and paradigm shifts; a field with competing schools and no shared paradigm is a preparadigmatic science, which fits psychology's age of schools. The humanists numbered the forces: psychoanalysis first, behaviourism second, humanistic psychology third and transpersonal psychology fourth (multiculturalism is Pedersen's "fourth force" in counselling). 2.2 Behaviourism: From Watson's Manifesto to Skinner. Behaviourism was prepared by animal psychology (Darwin, Romanes, Morgan's canon, Loeb's tropisms, Thorndike's puzzle boxes of 1898), by Russian objective psychology (Sechenov, Pavlov and Bekhterev's reflexology) and by functionalism. Watson's 1913 manifesto made psychology "a purely objective experimental branch of natural science" aiming at prediction and control without introspection. He treated thought as subvocal speech (peripheralism), proposed three innate emotions (fear, rage, love), conditioned Little Albert with Rayner (1920) and made the extreme environmentalist "twelve infants" claim (1925). Behaviourism may be metaphysical, methodological or radical. The neobehaviourists drew on logical positivism and Bridgman's operationism (1927): Tolman's purposive behaviourism (molar behaviour, intervening variables, cognitive maps, latent learning), Hull's hypothetico-deductive system (drive reduction, habit strength, reaction potential = habit strength × drive), Guthrie's contiguity and one-trial learning, and Skinner's radical, anti-theoretical behaviourism ( Walden Two , Verbal Behavior 1957, Beyond Freedom and Dignity 1971). Kuo abolished instinct. Dollard and Miller (1950) gave early social learning theory, Bandura and Walters (1963) the later one. Behaviourism declined under attack from Chomsky, the Brelands and Garcia but left operational definition and behaviour therapy (Jones 1924, Wolpe 1958). 2.3 Gestalt Psychology and Kurt Lewin. Wertheimer's 1912 paper on the phi phenomenon (apparent movement, with Kohler and Koffka as observers) founded Gestalt psychology, building on Ehrenfels's form qualities. Kohler's apes on Tenerife (1913 to 1920; The Mentality of Apes , 1917 and 1925) showed insight; his hens showed transposition; his theory of isomorphism was tested and rejected in its field form. Koffka's Growth of the Mind , his 1922 article and his Principles of Gestalt Psychology (1935) spread the school, and his Lake Constance story separated the geographical from the behavioural environment. The whole is different from (popularly, greater than) the sum of its parts; field theory, Pragnanz, figure-ground (Rubin, 1915) and productive thinking (Wertheimer, 1945) followed. Lewin's B = f(P, E) located behaviour in the life space (the person and the psychological environment), described with topological and hodological concepts, valences and vectors; his students found the Zeigarnik (recall) and Ovsiankina (resumption) effects; he founded group dynamics and action research. Gestalt therapy (Perls, empty chair) is not Gestalt psychology. 2.4 Psychoanalysis as a School: The First Force. Freud began as a neurologist. Charcot's demonstrations of hysteria under hypnosis (Paris, 1885 to 1886), Janet's dissociation, Bernheim's suggestion (Nancy, 1889) and above all Breuer's treatment of Anna O. (the "talking cure", the cathartic method; Studies on Hysteria , 1895) led Freud to free association and psychoanalysis. The Interpretation of Dreams (1900) called dreams the royal road to the unconscious, and the Clark University lectures (1909) brought psychoanalysis to America. The topographic model divides the mind into conscious, preconscious and unconscious; the structural model (1923) into id, ego and superego. Adler and Jung dissented; Horney, Fromm and Sullivan (the neo-Freudians), Anna Freud and Erikson (ego psychology) and Klein (object relations) followed. Popper criticised psychoanalysis as unfalsifiable. 2.5 The Third Force and Beyond. Maslow (self-actualisation) and Rogers (the actualising tendency, conditions of worth), with Buhler and May, founded humanistic psychology, the third force, which emphasises free will, growth, the whole person and phenomenological understanding; landmarks were the Journal of Humanistic Psychology (1961), the Association for Humanistic Psychology (1961 or 1962), Bugental's five postulates and the Old Saybrook conference (1964). Phenomenology (Husserl) brackets assumptions to describe experience. Existential psychology (Kierkegaard, Heidegger's Dasein, Sartre, Binswanger's Umwelt, Mitwelt and Eigenwelt, Boss, Frankl's logotherapy, will to meaning and noogenic neurosis, May, Yalom's four ultimate concerns) confronts death, freedom, isolation and meaninglessness. Transpersonal psychology (Maslow and Sutich, 1969; Grof, Tart, Wilber, Assagioli) is the fourth force. Positive psychology was launched by Seligman (APA president for 1998) with Csikszentmihalyi (flow) in 2000, and includes PERMA, character strengths, hope and savouring. Humanistic and phenomenological approaches are criticised as vague and as missing social and cultural context. 2.6 The Cognitive Revolution. Behaviourism waned under anomalies (Tolman, Kohler, Lashley's 1948 paper on serial order), wartime problems of attention, information theory (Shannon), cybernetics (Wiener), the computer (Turing, 1950) and linguistics. In 1956 came the MIT symposium (Newell and Simon's Logic Theorist, Chomsky, Miller's magical number seven plus or minus two), the Dartmouth project on artificial intelligence and Bruner's A Study of Thinking ; Broadbent's Perception and Communication (1958) was the first major information-processing theory; Chomsky's 1959 review of Verbal Behavior became a manifesto; and Neisser's Cognitive Psychology (1967) named the field. The information-processing approach treats the mind as a series of limited-capacity stages operating on representations. Bartlett (schema) and Piaget were forerunners. Cognitive science and cognitive neuroscience followed, and connectionism (Rumelhart and McClelland's Parallel Distributed Processing , 1986) modelled knowledge as weights in parallel networks. Bandura's self-efficacy (1977), Ellis and Beck brought cognition into therapy, producing CBT and later its mindfulness-based third wave. 2.7 Psychology Today: Perspectives, Eclecticism and the Enduring Issues. Schools gave way to overlapping perspectives: biological (neurobiological), evolutionary, psychodynamic, behavioural, cognitive, humanistic, sociocultural and Engel's biopsychosocial model (1977); developmental psychology is a field that uses them all. Cross-cultural psychology compares cultures, cultural psychology studies how culture and mind make each other up, and indigenous psychology builds theory from within a culture. Eclecticism selects from several schools (Lazarus's technical eclecticism versus theoretical integration, and common factors). The enduring issues, which Robert I. Watson (1967) called prescriptions, include mind-body, nature-nurture, free will-determinism, mechanism-vitalism, molar-molecular, nomothetic-idiographic (Windelband, Allport), objectivism-subjectivism and empiricism-rationalism; whether psychology has a Kuhnian paradigm is still debated. 2.8 Indian Psychology I: The Movement, Its Pioneers and Samkhya's Map of the Mind. Psychology in India is the discipline as practised in India; Indian psychology is an approach rooted in classical Indian thought, consciousness-centred, holistic, transformative, relational and open to disciplined first-person methods. Experimental psychology entered the Calcutta curriculum in 1905 (Seal); Sengupta founded the first laboratory (1915) and department (1916) and the Indian Psychological Association (1925), whose Indian Journal of Psychology began in 1926; Bose, father of Indian psychoanalysis, founded the Indian Psychoanalytical Society (1922) and proposed the theory of opposite wishes; Gopalaswamy began psychology at Mysore (1924). Durganand Sinha led indigenisation (from without and from within); Uma Chowdhury adapted the TAT; J. B. P. Sinha proposed the nurturant-task leader (1980); Pareek studied role stress; Kakar applied psychoanalysis to Indian childhood. The Pondicherry Manifesto (2002), Cornelissen's Indian Psychology Institute, the Handbook of Indian Psychology (Rao, Paranjpe and Dalal, 2008) and Foundations of Indian Psychology (Cornelissen, Misra and Varma, 2011) launched the Indian Psychology movement. The darshanas are astika or nastika by their acceptance of the Vedas. Samkhya (Kapila; Ishvarakrishna's Samkhya Karika ) is a dualism of passive, conscious purusha and active, unconscious prakriti, which evolves into buddhi, ahamkara, manas, the ten organs, the subtle and the gross elements (25 tattvas); liberation (kaivalya) comes from discriminating the seer from the seen. Prakriti is made of three gunas: sattva (clarity, harmony), rajas (activity, passion, restlessness) and tamas (inertia, dullness, ignorance), elaborated in the Gita . The antahkarana comprises manas (sensory mind), ahamkara (I-maker), buddhi (intellect) and, in Vedanta, chitta (memory). 2.9 Indian Psychology II: Yoga, the Self and the Paths of Transformation. Patanjali's Yoga Sutras define yoga as chitta-vritti-nirodha, aiming at kaivalya; they list five vrittis (pramana, viparyaya, vikalpa, nidra, smriti), two means (abhyasa and vairagya), five kleshas (avidya, asmita, raga, dvesha, abhinivesha) and the eight limbs: yama, niyama, asana, pranayama, pratyahara, dharana, dhyana and samadhi, the first five outer and the last three inner. The Gita offers the paths of action, knowledge, devotion and meditation, with nishkama karma, action without attachment to its fruits. The Upanishads identify the atman with Brahman; Shankara's Advaita Vedanta treats the world as maya. The Mandukya Upanishad describes waking (jagrat), dreaming (svapna), deep sleep (sushupti) and turiya, the fourth; the Taittiriya describes five sheaths (annamaya, pranamaya, manomaya, vijnanamaya, anandamaya), grouped into gross, subtle (linga) and causal bodies. Buddhism teaches the Four Noble Truths, the Noble Eightfold Path, anatta and the five skandhas, systematised in the Abhidhamma, with samatha, vipassana and mindfulness (sati) as practices that now underlie MBSR, MBCT, DBT and ACT. Sufi psychology describes seven stages of the nafs and the goal of fana. Sri Aurobindo's integral psychology places the psychic being at the centre of the person. Ayurveda describes three doshas (vata, pitta, kapha), treats rajas and tamas as doshas of the mind and includes Charaka's sattvavajaya psychotherapy. Karma (with samskaras and three kinds of karma) and dharma (svadharma, the purusharthas, the ashramas and dharma-sankata) shape how Indians explain their lives. doshas, karma, dharma, purusharthas, dharma-sankata From the past papers Match List I (psychologist) with List II (theory): A. Dollard and Miller, B. Skinner, C. Bandura and Walters, D. Maslow; 1. Radical behaviorism, 2. Self-actualization, 3. Early social learning, 4. Later social learning. (IHBAS 2024) (a) A-1, B-2, C-3, D-4 (b) A-3, B-1, C-4, D-2 (c) A-2, B-1, C-3, D-4 (d) A-3, B-2, C-4, D-1 Answer: (b) A-3, B-1, C-4, D-2. Dollard and Miller translated Freud into Hull's terms in 1950 (early social learning); Skinner's system is radical behaviourism; Bandura and Walters gave the later social learning theory (1963); Maslow is self-actualisation. Option (d) is tempting only if you forget that Skinner, not Maslow, is the radical behaviourist. Psychology studies both overt and covert behaviour. Covert behaviour is: (IHBAS 2020) (a) Observable and measurable (b) Measurable but not observable (c) Only measurable (d) Only observable Answer: (b) Measurable but not observable. Covert (implicit) behaviour, such as Watson's subvocal speech, cannot be seen by an observer but can be measured with instruments. Overt behaviour is both observable and measurable, so (a) describes the wrong kind; (c) says much the same as (b) but less precisely, and (d) is the reverse of the truth. Latent learning was demonstrated by: (IHBAS 2025) (a) Tolman (b) Bandura (c) Skinner (d) Kohler Answer: (a) Tolman. Tolman and Honzik (1930) showed that unrewarded rats learned a maze and revealed it at once when food appeared, evidence for a cognitive map. Bandura is observational learning, Skinner operant conditioning and Kohler insight. Gestalt psychology emphasizes: (IHBAS 2025) (a) Reinforcement and punishment (b) Neurotransmitter balance (c) Cognitive distortions (d) The whole is greater than the sum of its parts Answer: (d) The whole is greater than the sum of its parts. This is the school's slogan (Koffka preferred "different from"). Reinforcement and punishment are behaviourist, neurotransmitters biological, and cognitive distortions belong to Beck's cognitive therapy. In Lewin's topological system, emphasis was placed on the study of 'life space,' which includes: (Amity 2023) (a) Person and psychological environment (b) Society and group (c) Person and group (d) Environment and group Answer: (a) Person and psychological environment. The life space is the person plus the environment as it exists for that person, hence B = f(P, E). Groups were a later application of field theory (group dynamics), not part of the definition of the life space. Kurt Lewin is widely titled the father of modern social psychology. Which OTHER field is he also credited with founding? (Amity recall) (a) Psychoanalysis (b) Action research (c) Psychophysics (d) Functionalism Answer: (b) Action research. Lewin founded action research, the cycle of planning, acting, observing and reflecting with the people affected. Psychoanalysis is Freud's, psychophysics Fechner's and functionalism belongs to James, Dewey and Angell. Which therapy focuses on "empty chair technique"? (IHBAS 2025) (a) CBT (b) Gestalt therapy (c) Psychoanalysis (d) DBT Answer: (b) Gestalt therapy. The empty chair is Fritz Perls's technique for dialogue with an absent person or a disowned part of the self. Note that Gestalt therapy is Perls's, not the Gestalt psychology of Wertheimer, Kohler and Koffka; CBT, psychoanalysis and DBT do not use the technique as a signature. Which perspective in psychology emphasizes unconscious processes and early childhood experiences? (RML 2025) (a) Behavioral (b) Psychodynamic (c) Humanistic (d) Cognitive Answer: (b) Psychodynamic. The psychodynamic perspective, descended from Freud, explains behaviour by unconscious conflict and early experience. Behavioural stresses conditioning, humanistic free will and growth, and cognitive internal mental processes. Noogenic anxiety is described under: (IHBAS 2020) (a) Humanistic school (b) Gestalt school (c) Existential school (d) Psychodynamic school Answer: (c) Existential school. Frankl's noogenic neurosis (and anxiety) arises from frustrated meaning, the spiritual dimension, which places it in existential psychology. The humanistic school is a close neighbour, but the concept is Frankl's, not Maslow's or Rogers's. The concept of "Dasein," which refers to human existence as "being-in-the-world," is primarily associated with which school of psychology? (Real PYQ 2025) (a) Behavioral psychology (b) Existential psychology (c) Cognitive psychology (d) Psychoanalytic psychology Answer: (b) Existential psychology. Dasein is Heidegger's term ( Being and Time , 1927), made clinical by Binswanger and Boss in Daseinsanalysis. None of the other schools uses it. Viktor Frankl's concept of the "will to meaning," the fundamental motivational force in humans to find purpose in life, is central to which therapeutic school? (Real PYQ 2024) (a) Rational Emotive Behavior Therapy (REBT) (b) Logotherapy (c) Existential-Humanistic Therapy (d) Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) Answer: (b) Logotherapy. Frankl's own school, the "third Viennese school", rests on the will to meaning. Existential-humanistic therapy is the broad family it belongs to, so (c) is the tempting but less specific answer; REBT is Ellis's and ACT is Hayes's. Savoring is a concept in Positive Psychology that involves: (IHBAS 2024) (a) Avoiding negative experiences (b) Enhancing the enjoyment of positive experiences (c) Minimizing stress through relaxation (d) Reflecting on past traumas Answer: (b) Enhancing the enjoyment of positive experiences. Bryant and Veroff defined savouring as attending to, appreciating and intensifying positive experiences, past, present or anticipated; it is to good events what coping is to bad ones. The other options describe avoidance, relaxation and trauma work. Who is a pioneer contributor to Cognitive Psychology? (Amity 2023) (a) Jean Piaget (b) Kohler (c) Chomsky (d) Kohlberg Answer: (a) Jean Piaget. Piaget studied the growth of thinking from the 1920s, long before the cognitive revolution, and is treated as a forerunner of cognitive psychology. Chomsky was a linguist whose 1959 review fuelled the revolution, Kohler a Gestalt psychologist and Kohlberg a theorist of moral development. "Third-wave CBT" includes all EXCEPT: (IHBAS 2025) (a) Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (b) Dialectical Behavior Therapy (c) Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy (d) Psychoanalysis Answer: (d) Psychoanalysis. The third wave comprises acceptance and mindfulness-based therapies such as ACT, DBT and MBCT, many drawing on Buddhist practice. Psychoanalysis is the first force and is not a wave of CBT at all. In Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT), the "core mindfulness" skills are primarily derived from which tradition? (Real PYQ 2025) (a) Stoicism (b) Zen Buddhism (c) Psychoanalysis (d) Existentialism Answer: (b) Zen Buddhism. Marsha Linehan drew DBT's mindfulness skills from Zen practice and balanced them against cognitive-behavioural change strategies. Stoicism influenced Ellis's REBT; psychoanalysis and existentialism are unrelated to DBT's mindfulness module. What is the primary focus of Indian psychology? (RML 2025) (a) The application of Western psychological theories exclusively (b) The promotion of meditation without psychological context (c) The study of Indian folklore and mythology (d) The integration of Indian philosophical traditions with psychological concepts Answer: (d) The integration of Indian philosophical traditions with psychological concepts. Indian psychology draws its concepts and methods from Samkhya, Yoga, Vedanta, Buddhism and related traditions. Option (a) describes imitative psychology in India, and Indian psychology is neither mythology nor meditation stripped of theory. Who is regarded as the pioneer of psychology in India, establishing the first Indian psychological laboratory? (IHBAS 2024) (a) G. S. Rathi (b) S. K. Mangal (c) Girindrashekhar Bose (d) A. K. Singh Answer as keyed: (c) Girindrashekhar Bose. Strictly, the first laboratory was set up by N. N. Sengupta at Calcutta in 1915, and Sengupta is not among the options. Bose, Sengupta's Calcutta colleague and the father of Indian psychoanalysis, is the only pioneer listed; Mangal and A. K. Singh are textbook authors. Who is considered the father of Indian psychology? (RML 2025) (a) Narendra Nath Sen Gupta (b) Sudhir Kakar (c) Giriswar Misra (d) G. R. S. Rao Answer as keyed: (d) G. R. S. Rao. The key appears to intend a leader of the Indian Psychology movement, most plausibly K. Ramakrishna Rao, co-editor of the Handbook of Indian Psychology (2008). If the question meant modern scientific psychology in India, the answer would be (a) Sengupta; Kakar is a psychoanalyst and Misra a contemporary scholar of indigenous psychology. The concept of the three gunas comes mainly from which school of Indian philosophy, alongside the Bhagavad Gita? (NIMHANS 2026 recall) (a) Nyaya (b) Charvaka (c) Samkhya (d) Mimamsa Answer: (c) Samkhya. Samkhya's prakriti is composed of sattva, rajas and tamas, and the Gita builds its psychology of personality on them. Nyaya is the school of logic, Charvaka materialism, and Mimamsa the school of Vedic ritual and duty. In Samkhya dualism, the principle of pure consciousness, the passive witness, is Purusha. The three gunas belong to its counterpart, which is: (Amity recall) (a) Atman (b) Prakriti (c) Brahman (d) Ahamkara Answer: (b) Prakriti. Prakriti, primordial matter, is made of the three gunas. Atman and Brahman are Vedantic terms for the self and ultimate reality, and ahamkara is one of prakriti's products, not its counterpart. Bavisha lost her job. Since then she is stressed, has stopped eating properly and cannot get herself to do anything. According to yogic philosophy, the main issue she is dealing with is: (NIMHANS 2026 recall) (a) Yama alone (b) Tamas alone (c) Both yama and tamas (d) Rajas alone Answer: (b) Tamas alone. Withdrawal, loss of appetite and inability to act are the signature of tamas, the guna of inertia and dullness. Yama is the first limb of yoga (ethical restraints), not a mental state, so (a) and (c) fail; rajas would show as restless over-activity. In Indian psychology, the 'inner instrument' (antahkarana) classically has four functions. Which one is the EGO or 'I-maker'? (Amity recall) (a) Manas (b) Buddhi (c) Ahamkara (d) Chitta Answer: (c) Ahamkara. Ahamkara refers experience to a separate "I". Manas is the sensory mind that doubts and deliberates, buddhi the intellect that decides, and chitta the store of memory impressions. According to Patanjali's Yoga Sutras, the primary goal of yoga is: (JEMAS 2025) (a) Physical fitness (b) Control of the mind (citta vritti nirodha) and liberation (kaivalya) (c) Cognitive enhancement (d) Emotional regulation only Answer: (b) Control of the mind and liberation. Sutra 1.2 defines yoga as the stilling of the mind's fluctuations, and its aim is kaivalya, consciousness resting in itself. Fitness, sharper cognition and calmer emotions may be by-products, but none is the goal. Which is the correct order of the last four of Patanjali's eight limbs? (NIMHANS 2026 recall) (a) Dharana, pratyahara, dhyana, samadhi (b) Pratyahara, dharana, dhyana, samadhi (c) Pratyahara, dhyana, dharana, samadhi (d) Dhyana, dharana, pratyahara, samadhi Answer: (b) Pratyahara, dharana, dhyana, samadhi. The senses must first be withdrawn (pratyahara) before attention can be fixed (dharana), the fixed attention becomes an unbroken flow (dhyana) and the flow becomes absorption (samadhi). The other options swap concentration and meditation or put withdrawal after concentration. In the Pancha Kosha model, the five sheaths of the self run from gross to subtle. The OUTERMOST sheath, the physical body sustained by food, is: (Amity recall) (a) Annamaya kosha (b) Pranamaya kosha (c) Manomaya kosha (d) Anandamaya kosha Answer: (a) Annamaya kosha. Anna means food, and the food sheath is the gross body. Pranamaya is the vital sheath of breath, manomaya the mental sheath of perception and emotion, and anandamaya the innermost bliss sheath. The empty chair technique belongs to Gestalt therapy , developed by Fritz Perls with Laura Perls and Paul Goodman ( Gestalt Therapy , 1951), which stresses here-and-now awareness; it is not the Gestalt psychology of Wertheimer, Kohler and Koffka. asked 7 times Patanjali's eight limbs (sutra 2.29), in order: yama, niyama, asana, pranayama, pratyahara (withdrawal of the senses), dharana (concentration on one point), dhyana (unbroken flow of meditation), samadhi (absorption). Karma and jnana are not limbs. asked 4 times Tamas is the guna of inertia, lethargy, darkness, dullness and ignorance; a person who has stopped eating properly, withdrawn and cannot get herself to act shows tamas alone. asked 4 times Narendra Nath Sengupta set up India's first psychology laboratory (1915) and first Department of Psychology (1916) at the University of Calcutta, and is the father of modern psychology in India. Keys naming Bose or Uma Chaudhuri for the first laboratory are wrong. asked 5 times Sigmund Freud founded psychoanalysis, the first force; the psychodynamic perspective explains behaviour, and many disorders, by unconscious urges and conflict and by early childhood experience. asked 4 times Indian psychology integrates Indian philosophical and contemplative traditions with psychological concepts; it is holistic and spiritual, includes family and community, and treats mental health by combining traditional practices with modern therapy. asked 3 times Humanistic psychology (Maslow, Rogers) is the third force , after psychoanalysis (first) and behaviourism (second); transpersonal psychology is the fourth force. asked 5 times Humanistic psychology emphasises free will, personal growth , an innate tendency to grow and reaching one's full potential; disorder comes from blocked growth, not from reinforcement or unconscious conflict. asked 4 times The three gunas are sattva, rajas and tamas, the strands of prakriti (not of purusha); the doctrine comes mainly from Samkhya , with the Bhagavad Gita . Ahimsa, vata and prakriti are not gunas. asked 4 times John B. Watson founded behaviourism with "Psychology as the Behaviorist Views It" (1913): psychology is the science of observable behaviour, its goal prediction and control (given the stimulus, predict the response), learned through stimulus-response conditioning. asked 4 times Viktor Frankl founded logotherapy on the will to meaning ; frustrated meaning produces an existential vacuum and noogenic neurosis, ideas of the existential school. asked 3 times Positive psychology was founded by Martin Seligman (APA president for 1998; American Psychologist special issue with Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi, 2000); its interventions build strengths such as hope, and savouring means enhancing the enjoyment of positive experiences. asked 3 times Gestalt psychology : the whole is different from (popularly, greater than) the sum of its parts. asked 3 times In Samkhya (Kapila), purusha is pure, passive, unchanging consciousness, and prakriti is active, ever-changing primordial matter, made of the three gunas and evolving into the five great elements. asked 3 times The five koshas ( Taittiriya Upanishad ), outer to inner: annamaya (food body, outermost), pranamaya (vital), manomaya (mind and senses: perception), vijnanamaya (intellect), anandamaya (bliss). The subtle body (linga sharira) is the three middle sheaths. asked 3 times Existential psychology confronts death, freedom, isolation and meaninglessness, holds that meaning is never fixed and must be continually created, and uses Heidegger's Dasein (being-in-the-world, 1927); uncovering unconscious desires is a psychoanalytic aim. asked 3 times Kurt Lewin : B = f(P, E); the life space is the person plus the psychological environment; he founded action research and group dynamics and is the father of modern social psychology. asked 2 times Edward Chace Tolman proposed the cognitive map ("Cognitive Maps in Rats and Men", 1948) and demonstrated latent learning (Tolman and Honzik, 1930). asked 2 times Ahamkara is the I-maker (ego) of the antahkarana; manas is the sensory mind, buddhi the intellect, chitta the memory store. The Gita 's three elements of mind are manas, buddhi and ahamkara. asked 2 times Max Wertheimer founded Gestalt psychology with his 1912 paper on the phi phenomenon, with Kohler and Koffka; Gestalt is the school that contributed most to the study of perception. asked 2 times Cognitive psychology studies internal mental processes (attention, memory, problem solving) with the mind-as-information-processor metaphor; Ulric Neisser's Cognitive Psychology (1967) named it. asked 2 times Covert behaviour (thoughts, subvocal speech) is measurable but not directly observable; the "mental processes" in the definition of psychology are internal, covert processes. asked 2 times Sattva = harmony, balance, clarity; rajas = restlessness, passion, desire and over-activity. asked 2 times Girindrasekhar Bose founded the Indian Psychoanalytical Society (Calcutta, 1922), is the father of psychoanalysis in India, and proposed the theory of opposite wishes. asked 2 times The Indian Psychology movement : Matthijs Cornelissen led it and founded the Indian Psychology Institute (Pondicherry); the Handbook of Indian Psychology (Rao, Paranjpe and Dalal) appeared in 2008; the Pondicherry Manifesto dates from 2002. asked 2 times Patanjali's goal of yoga is chitta-vritti-nirodha, the stilling of the mind's fluctuations (sutra 1.2), leading to liberation (kaivalya). asked once Atman is the true self, eternal pure consciousness, not the body, a passing state of mind or a collective unconscious. asked once Jean Piaget , who studied the growth of thinking from the 1920s (genetic epistemology), is a pioneer contributor to cognitive psychology. asked once Early social learning theory is Dollard and Miller (1950); later social learning theory is Bandura and Walters (1963); radical behaviourism is Skinner's; self-actualisation is Maslow's. asked once The developmental perspective studies how people change as they mature across the lifespan. asked once

distinguish sensation from perception and explain transduction, sensory coding and sensory adaptation. 3.2 Thresholds: how weak a stimulus, how small a difference : define the absolute threshold and the difference threshold (JND) and explain why both are defined as 50 percent points. 3.3 The psychophysical laws: Weber, Fechner and Stevens : state, apply and criticise Weber's law, Fechner's law and Stevens' power law. 3.4 The classical psychophysical methods : describe the methods of limits, constant stimuli and adjustment, their errors and controls, and modern staircase methods. 3.5 Signal detection theory : separate sensitivity (d′) from the response criterion, read a 2 by 2 outcome table and an ROC curve, and apply the theory to real decisions. 3.6 Vision I: light, the eye and the two receptor systems : trace light through the eye and contrast rods with cones, dark adaptation, the Purkinje shift, acuity and lateral inhibition. 3.7 Vision II: colour : explain colour mixing, the trichromatic and opponent-process theories, their dual-process resolution and the forms of colour blindness. 3.8 Hearing : relate the dimensions of sound to pitch, loudness and timbre, follow sound through the ear, and compare the theories of pitch, sound localisation and the types of hearing loss. 3.9 The chemical senses: taste and smell : describe the five basic tastes, papillae and taste buds, the olfactory system, pheromones and flavour. 3.10 The skin senses and pain : describe touch, pressure and temperature, and explain pain through gate control theory, endorphins and phantom limbs. 3.11 The body senses: kinesthesis and balance : distinguish kinesthesis from the vestibular sense and the roles of the semicircular canals and otolith organs. 3.12 Senses in concert and senses deprived : explain sensory interaction, synaesthesia and the effects of sensory deprivation. Weightage. 44 of the 819 questions mapped in this book (5.4%) test this chapter, 16 of them from real past papers. 1 of its 12 sections is High yield. On the morning of 22 October 1850, a forty-nine-year-old former professor of physics lay in bed in Leipzig and worked out how to measure the mind. His name was Gustav Theodor Fechner, and for most of the previous decade he had been too ill to work at all. In the late 1830s Fechner had been studying afterimages, the ghostly colours that linger in your vision after you stare at a bright light, and he had used his own eyes as the instrument, gazing at the sun through coloured glass. The experiments damaged his eyes. A long breakdown followed: he could not bear light, could hardly eat, and could not read. He gave up his chair of physics and spent about three years withdrawn from the world, much of the time in darkened rooms. When he recovered, Fechner turned to an old philosophical puzzle: how are mind and body related? The great philosopher Immanuel Kant had argued that psychology could never become a true natural science, because mental events cannot be measured, and without measurement there is no mathematics and no science. Fechner's insight that October morning was a way around Kant. You cannot hold a ruler against a sensation. But you can measure the physical stimulus that produces it, and you can find out how much that stimulus must change before a person notices any difference at all. If every just-noticeable step in sensation is treated as one unit, sensation can be counted, and the relation between the physical world and the mental world can be written as an equation. Fechner spent the next decade testing the idea, lifting weights, comparing lights and judging distances, thousands of judgements at a time. He found that his Leipzig colleague Ernst Heinrich Weber had already discovered the key regularity, and he generously named it Weber's law. In 1860 Fechner published Elemente der Psychophysik ( Elements of Psychophysics ), and with it founded a new science. Nineteen years before Wilhelm Wundt opened his laboratory, Fechner had shown that the mind could be measured. Psychophysicists still celebrate 22 October as Fechner Day. This chapter explores the territory Fechner opened. It asks how the sense organs turn energy into experience, how weak a stimulus can be before you miss it, how small a change you can notice, and why a "threshold" turns out to be a decision as much as a sensation. It then walks through each sense in turn: vision, hearing, taste, smell, touch, temperature, pain, body position and balance. Keep Fechner's damaged eyes in mind. At the end of the chapter you will see that the afterimages that injured him are now well understood, and that his famous law has been both honoured and revised. 3.1 Sensation and perception: from energy to experience Medium yield · 10 Qs Look up from this page for a moment. You see a room full of objects, each with a colour, a shape and a place. You probably hear something too: a fan, traffic, a voice in the next room. It all seems effortless and immediate, as if the world simply pours into your head. It does not. What actually reaches you is a shower of physical energy (photons striking the back of your eyes, pressure waves in the air, molecules drifting into your nose), and everything you experience is built by your nervous system out of that raw material. This section introduces the first steps of that construction. Sensation versus perception Psychologists traditionally divide the process into two stages. sensation is the process by which sense organs detect physical energy from the environment and convert it into neural signals. perception is the process by which the brain organises and interprets those signals so that they become meaningful objects and events. Think of a batsman at the crease. Light reflected from the ball forms an image on his retinas, and receptors there fire: that is sensation. Recognising, in a fraction of a second, that the ball is a googly spinning the other way: that is perception. The boundary between the two is not sharp, and many modern researchers treat them as one continuous process. But the distinction is useful, and examiners like it, because it tells you where an error happens. Consider an optical illusion such as the Muller-Lyer figure, in which two lines of identical length look unequal because one carries outward-pointing fins and the other inward-pointing fins. Your receptors register the two lines accurately; the image of each line on your retina really is the same length. The error arises later, when the brain interprets the lines in the light of the fins. Optical illusions are therefore distortions of perception, not of sensation (Chapter 4 explains why the brain makes such errors). The idea that experience can be broken into sensory building blocks has a long history. The structuralists, led in America by Edward Bradford Titchener (1867 to 1927), treated sensations as the elements of consciousness and hoped to catalogue them the way chemists catalogue elements, a "periodic table" of the elements of sensation; Titchener counted more than 44,000 distinguishable sensation qualities, most of them visual or auditory. For Titchener, a perception was a complex of sensory and imaginal elements: sensations, plus the images that past experience attaches to them, with meaning supplied by this context (Chapter 1 tells the full story of structuralism). A modern descendant of this idea treats perception as inference. Hermann von Helmholtz (1821 to 1894), whose work runs through this chapter, argued in the 1860s that perception involves unconscious inference: the brain draws conclusions about the world from incomplete sensory evidence, using past experience. Today this view is formalised in the Bayesian approach to perception , named after the eighteenth-century mathematician Thomas Bayes. According to it, every perceptual experience combines two ingredients: prior beliefs (what you already expect to be out there, learned from experience) and sensory evidence (what the receptors are reporting now). When the evidence is clear, it dominates; when it is weak or ambiguous, the prior carries more weight. Walking down a dimly lit lane at night, you may "see" a dog lying by a gate when it is really a sack of cement, because dogs by gates are common (a strong prior) and the light is poor (weak evidence). Genes, culture and emotional states can all shape a person's priors, but the Bayesian formula itself has just those two inputs: prior beliefs and sensory evidence. Exam trap "Optical illusions result from distortion in ..." The answer is perception , not sensation: the receptors register the stimulus correctly, and the error is in interpretation. "Translation" and "adaptation" are bait. Likewise, "according to the Bayesian approach, perception is influenced by ..." has the answer prior beliefs and sensory evidence ; options naming only genes, culture or emotions describe things that can shape priors, not the approach itself. Receptors and transduction Every sense begins with a receptor , a specialised cell (or the specialised ending of a neuron) that responds to one particular form of energy. The receptor's job is transduction : the conversion of physical energy into the electrical and chemical language of the nervous system. Light, sound and molecules cannot travel along nerves; only neural signals can. So in the eye, light changes the shape of a pigment molecule, which changes the receptor's electrical state; in the ear, the bending of tiny hairs opens ion channels; in the nose, an odour molecule binds to a receptor protein. Each is a different trick for the same task. Table 3.1 groups the receptors by the energy they transduce. Table 3.1 Receptors classified by the energy they transduce. Receptor class Energy detected Examples Sense Photoreceptors Light (electromagnetic) Rods and cones of the retina Vision Mechanoreceptors Mechanical bending, pressure, stretch Hair cells of the cochlea and vestibular organs; skin corpuscles; muscle spindles Hearing, balance, touch, kinesthesis Chemoreceptors Dissolved or airborne molecules Taste receptor cells; olfactory receptor neurons Taste, smell Thermoreceptors Temperature change Warm and cold free nerve endings Temperature Nociceptors Actual or threatened tissue damage Free nerve endings in skin, muscle and organs Pain Receptors can also be classified by where their information comes from. The British physiologist Charles Scott Sherrington (1857 to 1952), in The Integrative Action of the Nervous System (1906), distinguished exteroceptors , which report on the outside world (eyes, ears, skin), interoceptors , which report on the internal organs (a full bladder, a churning stomach), and proprioceptors , which report on the position and movement of the body itself (Section 3.11). Once a receptor has transduced its stimulus, the signal travels toward the central nervous system along afferent (sensory, incoming) nerve fibres. Commands travel outward to muscles and glands along efferent (motor, outgoing) fibres. The simplest complete loop, from receptor through afferent fibre to the spinal cord and back out along an efferent fibre to a muscle, is the reflex arc: the knee jerk is the textbook example. (The philosopher-psychologist John Dewey famously criticised the reflex arc as a model of behaviour in 1896; Chapter 1 explains why.) Sensory coding: specific nerve energies and labelled lines Here is a puzzle that troubled nineteenth-century physiologists. Every sensory nerve carries the same kind of signal: brief electrical impulses called action potentials. An impulse from the eye looks exactly like an impulse from the ear. So how does the brain know whether a message means "red" or "middle C" or "sour"? The German physiologist Johannes Peter Muller (1801 to 1858) gave the classic answer in his Handbook of Human Physiology (1833 to 1840). His doctrine of specific nerve energies states that the quality of a sensation depends on which nerve is stimulated, not on what stimulates it. Each sensory nerve, however it is excited, produces its own characteristic sensation. You can test this yourself. Close your eyes and press very gently on the outer corner of one eyelid: you will see a spot of light (a phosphene), although no light has entered the eye. The pressure excited the optic nerve's receptors, and the optic nerve can only "speak" light. A hard blow to the back of the head makes people "see stars" for the same reason. Muller drew a startling conclusion: we are never directly aware of objects in the world, only of the activity of our own nerves. Helmholtz, Muller's student, later extended the idea within a single sense, proposing that different fibres in the eye and ear carry different colours and pitches (an idea you will meet again in his theories of colour and hearing). Modern neuroscience keeps the core of Muller's insight under the name labelled-line coding : the quality of a sensation is signalled by which neurons are active, because each pathway is wired to a particular brain region, as if each line carried a label. Activity in the visual pathway to the occipital lobe is experienced as sight; activity in the auditory pathway to the temporal lobe is experienced as sound. Within a sense, however, quality is often coded by the pattern of activity across many receptor types rather than by single labelled lines. This across-fibre pattern coding is especially important in taste and smell, where each receptor type responds to many chemicals and a particular flavour or odour corresponds to a particular profile of activity across the whole population. What about intensity? A dim light and a bright light, a whisper and a shout, must also be told apart. Here a basic fact of neurophysiology matters. An action potential obeys the all-or-none law: once a neuron's threshold is reached, the impulse fires at full, constant size and travels along the axon without shrinking, and a stronger stimulus does not produce a bigger impulse. A stimulus too weak to reach threshold produces no action potential at all, not a "miniature" one (only small graded changes in voltage that fade away). Intensity therefore cannot be coded by the size of impulses. It is coded instead by rate coding (stronger stimuli make each neuron fire more often) and by recruitment (stronger stimuli activate more neurons, including less sensitive ones). Note one curiosity: signals can also be carried by a decrease in activity. The rods and cones of your retina are most active in darkness, and light actually reduces their activity (Pinel and Barnes's textbook makes this point with some relish). A final piece of wiring is worth knowing for general psychology. Before reaching the cerebral cortex, almost every sensory pathway relays through the thalamus, the brain's sensory switching station: vision through its lateral geniculate nucleus, hearing through its medial geniculate nucleus, and touch, pain and taste through its ventral posterior nuclei. Smell is the exception: olfactory signals run from the olfactory bulb straight to the olfactory cortex and the amygdala without a thalamic relay on the way (Section 3.9). The details belong to the Physiological Psychology book. Explaining experience and behaviour through the workings of the brain and nervous system in this way is the neurobiological (biological) approach to psychology, whose main premise is that behaviour is governed by the brain and nervous system. It differs from the psychophysical approach that fills most of this chapter, which studies the lawful relation between physical stimuli and the sensations they produce without needing to know what the neurons are doing (Chapter 2 compares the approaches). Exam trap The doctrine of specific nerve energies belongs to Johannes Muller , not Helmholtz (Helmholtz extended it) and not Fechner. "The principal sensory relay to the cortex for every sense except smell" is the thalamus ; the hypothalamus regulates drives such as hunger and temperature, the medulla controls breathing and heart rate, the corpus callosum connects the two hemispheres, the basal ganglia help to control movement, and the hippocampus serves memory. The lateral geniculate nucleus is visual; the medial geniculate nucleus is auditory ("M for music"). Sensory adaptation When you put on a wristwatch in the morning you feel it on your skin. Ten minutes later you do not, although it is still pressing on exactly the same spot. When you walk into a home where a garland of Mysuru jasmine hangs by the door, the scent is striking; the family who have been sitting there all evening hardly notice it. This is sensory adaptation : a decline in sensitivity (and in receptor response) to a stimulus that remains constant. Adaptation is built into the receptors and the early stages of each sensory pathway, and it is automatic. The English philosopher John Locke (1632 to 1704) described a neat demonstration in 1690. Put one hand in a bowl of hot water and the other in a bowl of cold water for a minute, then plunge both into a bowl of lukewarm water. The same lukewarm water feels cool to the first hand and warm to the second. Each hand has adapted to its starting temperature, so each judges the new water relative to that adapted level. Why should the senses be designed to fade out unchanging stimulation? Because change is what usually matters. A constant stimulus (the pressure of your clothes, the hum of a refrigerator) rarely carries new information, whereas a change (a touch on the shoulder, a sudden silence) may signal something important. Adaptation frees the senses to respond to change. Vision is the dramatic case: if an image is held perfectly still on the retina, it fades from view within seconds, and your eyes avoid this only by moving constantly (Section 3.6). Exam trap Do not confuse sensory adaptation with habituation . Adaptation is a reduced response of the sensory system itself to a constant stimulus. Habituation is a learned decrease in behavioural response to a stimulus that is repeated and proves unimportant (you stop jumping at the ticking clock), and it can be reversed instantly if the stimulus changes (dishabituation). Habituation is the simplest form of learning and is covered in Chapter 6. Adaptation to light and dark is called visual adaptation , not "visual accommodation" (accommodation is the focusing of the lens, Section 3.6). 3.2 Thresholds: how weak a stimulus, how small a difference Lower yield · 2 Qs Fechner's new science, psychophysics , is the study of the quantitative relationship between the physical properties of stimuli and the sensations they produce. It asks two basic kinds of question. The first is about detection: what is the weakest stimulus a person can detect? The second is about discrimination: what is the smallest change in a stimulus a person can notice? The answers are called thresholds. The absolute threshold The absolute threshold is the minimum intensity of a stimulus that a person can detect. The older term for a threshold is limen (Latin for "threshold"), which survives in two words you should know. A stimulus below the absolute threshold is subliminal (below the limen); one above it is supraliminal . At first sight the absolute threshold sounds like a simple switch: below a certain intensity you detect nothing, above it you always detect the stimulus. Experiments show that no such switch exists. If you present a faint tone many times at each of several intensities, there is no single intensity at which "never heard" suddenly becomes "always heard". Instead, the percentage of "yes, I heard it" responses climbs gradually, tracing an S-shaped curve called the psychometric function (Figure 3.1). Why the gradual climb? Because the nervous system is never silent. Neurons fire spontaneously, attention wanders, receptors vary slightly from moment to moment, and even the stimulus itself fluctuates (a very dim light delivers a variable number of light particles from one flash to the next). So the same faint tone is sometimes detected and sometimes missed. Psychophysicists therefore define the absolute threshold statistically: it is the stimulus intensity that is detected on 50 percent of the trials on which it is presented. Not 100 percent, and not "the first time it is noticed", but half the time. 0 25 50 75 100 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9 Stimulus intensity (arbitrary units) Percentage of yes responses 50 percent yes = absolute threshold Real observer (ogive) Fixed threshold (step) Observed data Figure 3.1 The psychometric function for detection. Eugene Galanter (1962) gave a set of everyday approximations that appear in almost every introductory text (Table 3.2). They are rough, but they make the point that our senses, at their best, are astonishingly sensitive. Table 3.2 Approximate absolute thresholds for five senses (after Galanter, 1962). Sense Approximate absolute threshold Vision A candle flame seen from about 48 km (30 miles) on a dark, clear night Hearing The tick of a watch from about 6 metres (20 feet) under very quiet conditions Taste One teaspoon of sugar dissolved in about 7.5 litres (two gallons) of water Smell One drop of perfume diffused through a six-room apartment Touch The wing of a bee falling on your cheek from a height of 1 centimetre Key study: How few particles of light can you see? (Hecht, Shlaer and Pirenne, 1942) Question. Light comes in tiny packets called quanta (photons). What is the smallest number of quanta a fully dark-adapted human can detect? Method. Selig Hecht , Simon Shlaer and Maurice Pirenne, working in New York, flashed a very brief spot of blue-green light (wavelength 510 nanometres, close to the peak sensitivity of the rods) onto a rod-rich region of the retina about 20 degrees from the centre of gaze. Observers, including the authors themselves, sat in darkness and reported whether they had seen each flash. Result. At threshold, the flash delivered only about 54 to 148 quanta to the front of the eye. After allowing for light lost in the eye's media and for light that passed through the retina unabsorbed, they calculated that only about 5 to 14 quanta were actually absorbed by rods. Spread across hundreds of rods, this meant that no single rod could have absorbed more than one quantum. Conclusion. A single rod responds to a single quantum of light, and the coincidence of a handful of such events produces the experience of seeing. The human eye at threshold works close to the limit set by physics. Why it matters here. Because the number of quanta in a dim flash fluctuates randomly from flash to flash, some of the variability in "seeing" a threshold flash lies in the light itself. The threshold is probabilistic by its very nature. The difference threshold and the JND Detection is only half of psychophysics. Much of the time we need to tell whether something has changed: whether the dal needs more salt, whether the music has been turned up, whether one mango is heavier than another. The difference threshold (or difference limen) is the smallest difference between two stimuli that a person can detect 50 percent of the time. The amount of change at that threshold is called the just noticeable difference (JND). The terms are effectively interchangeable in examinations: the difference threshold is the JND. Difference thresholds are measured by comparing a fixed standard stimulus with a variable comparison stimulus . If you hold a 100-gram standard weight in one hand and a series of comparison weights in the other, you might find that you can tell 102 grams from 100 grams half the time; the JND at that standard is then 2 grams. Along the way you will find a comparison value that feels exactly equal to the standard; this is the point of subjective equality (PSE), and it need not coincide with the true physical equality point. (A systematic gap between the PSE and the standard is called a constant error.) Ernst Heinrich Weber measured one especially elegant kind of difference threshold on the skin. Touch the skin with the two points of a pair of compasses. If the points are far apart, you feel two touches; bring them closer and, at some separation, the two touches merge into one. The smallest separation at which two points are felt as two is the two-point threshold . Weber found that it varies enormously across the body, from about 2 millimetres on the fingertips and lips to several centimetres on the back and thigh (Section 3.10 explains why). It was while measuring such thresholds, and the JNDs for lifted weights, that Weber noticed the regularity that bears his name. Exam trap "The minimum level of a stimulus that can be detected" is the absolute threshold ; "the smallest change that can be detected" is the difference threshold (JND). "Sensory adaptation point" and "perceptual boundary" are invented distractors, and so is "signal detection of response". A question defining "the point at which a stimulus is strong enough to trigger a response only 50 percent of the time" wants threshold ; response bias is a signal detection term for a person's readiness to say "yes" (Section 3.5), and the phi phenomenon is the illusion of movement produced by lights flashing in sequence, described by Max Wertheimer in 1912 (Chapter 4). 3.3 The psychophysical laws: Weber, Fechner and Stevens Lower yield · 3 Qs Thresholds tell us where sensation begins and how finely it can be graded. The next question is more ambitious: is there a general law relating the size of a stimulus to the size of the sensation it produces? Three answers have been proposed, by Weber, Fechner and Stevens. Each was a real advance, each captures something true, and each fails somewhere. Learn them as a sequence, because each one grew out of the one before. Weber's law: the JND is a constant fraction Ernst Heinrich Weber (1795 to 1878) was a professor of anatomy and physiology at Leipzig. In studies of touch and the muscle sense published in 1834 ( De Tactu ) and 1846, he asked people to compare lifted weights. He noticed, among other things, that discrimination was finer when people actively lifted the weights than when the weights simply rested on a passive hand. His enduring discovery, however, was this: the JND is not a fixed amount. With a light standard weight, a small extra amount is noticed; with a heavy standard, a much larger amount is needed. What stays constant is the ratio of the JND to the standard. In symbols, Weber's law is ΔI / I = k where I is the intensity of the standard stimulus, ΔI (read "delta I") is the increase needed to produce a just noticeable difference, and k is a constant for that sensory dimension, called the Weber fraction (or Weber's constant). A small Weber fraction means fine discrimination; a large one means coarse discrimination. A worked example shows how the law works. Suppose the Weber fraction for lifted weights is about 0.02 (one-fiftieth). Then with a 500-gram standard, the JND is 0.02 × 500 = 10 grams: you will just notice the difference between 500 and 510 grams. With a 5-kilogram standard, the JND is 0.02 × 5,000 = 100 grams. Ten grams added to the heavier load would go completely unnoticed. Or take your morning chai. If a cup sweetened with two teaspoons of sugar needs roughly an extra half teaspoon before anyone notices it is sweeter, then a cup with four teaspoons needs roughly an extra whole teaspoon. The absolute amount needed doubles; the proportion stays the same. The everyday consequences are everywhere. A single candle transforms a dark room but is invisible in sunlight. A shopkeeper knows that a fifty-rupee discount feels generous on a two-hundred-rupee item and trivial on a fifty-thousand-rupee phone. In each case what we notice is proportional change, not absolute change. Table 3.3 gives approximate Weber fractions for several dimensions. Dimension Approximate Weber fraction Change needed on a standard of 100 units Pitch (frequency of a middle tone) About 0.003 (about 1/333) About 0.3 Electric shock About 0.01 About 1 Heaviness of lifted weights About 0.02 (1/50) About 2 Brightness of light About 0.02 to 0.08 About 2 to 8 Loudness (sound intensity) About 0.05 to 0.1 About 5 to 10 Pressure on the skin About 0.14 (1/7) About 14 Taste (salt) and smell About 0.08 to 0.3 About 8 to 30 Where does Weber's law fail? It holds well across the middle range of intensities for most senses, but it breaks down at the extremes. Near the absolute threshold, the Weber fraction rises sharply: when a stimulus is barely detectable, a proportionally much larger change is needed before any difference is noticed. It can also drift at very high intensities, and for pure tones the fraction for loudness declines slowly as intensity increases, a small but systematic departure known as the "near miss" to Weber's law. Weber's law is best regarded as an excellent approximation over the range in which we usually live. Fechner's law: sensation grows with the logarithm of the stimulus Gustav Theodor Fechner (1801 to 1887) took Weber's finding and built it into a law of sensation itself. Weber's law tells you how big a JND is; it says nothing about how strong a sensation is. Fechner's bridge was a single bold assumption: every JND represents the same increase in sensation, no matter where on the scale it occurs . The step from 100 to 102 grams and the step from 1,000 to 1,020 grams are both one JND, so, Fechner assumed, both add one equal unit to the felt heaviness. With that assumption, the strength of any sensation can be measured simply by counting how many JNDs it lies above the absolute threshold. Now combine this with Weber's law. Start at the threshold and climb one JND at a time. Because each JND is a constant fraction of the current intensity, the physical intensities at successive JNDs form a geometric series (each one multiplied by the same factor), while the sensation steps form an arithmetic series (1, 2, 3, 4 units). A quantity that rises arithmetically while another rises geometrically is a logarithm. The result is Fechner's law : S = k log I where S is the magnitude of the sensation, I is the physical intensity (strictly, measured in multiples of the threshold intensity) and k is a constant that depends on the sense. Because it rests on Weber's law, it is often called the Weber-Fechner law. A worked example makes the logarithm concrete. Picture a dark room on Diwali night. Light one diya and the room is transformed. Light a second and the room gets noticeably brighter. To get the same sized step again, Fechner's law says you will need not three diyas but four; then eight; then sixteen; then thirty-two. Each doubling of the physical light adds roughly one equal step of brightness. By the time sixty-four diyas are burning, adding one more makes no visible difference at all. Scales of this kind are familiar from science and engineering: the astronomers' magnitude scale for the brightness of stars (much older than Fechner) and the decibel scale for sound (introduced by telephone engineers in the 1920s; Section 3.8) are both logarithmic, and both fit how our senses actually grade intensity. Fechner's achievement went beyond the equation. In the Elemente of 1860 he coined the word psychophysics, set out the experimental methods for measuring thresholds (Section 3.4), and distinguished "outer psychophysics" (the relation between the stimulus and sensation, which he could study) from "inner psychophysics" (the relation between brain activity and sensation, which he could not). For founding the field he is called the father of psychophysics, and his work showed the young science of psychology that mental events could be measured. One reader who took that lesson to heart was Hermann Ebbinghaus (1850 to 1909), who came across a second-hand copy of the Elemente and set out to measure memory with the same rigour (Chapter 7). Fechner's method of scaling sensation is called indirect scaling , because it measures sensation indirectly, through discrimination (counting JNDs), rather than by asking people how strong a sensation feels. Where does Fechner's law fail? Its weak point is its founding assumption. There is no direct evidence that all JNDs are subjectively equal, and when people are asked to judge sensory magnitudes directly, their judgements often do not follow a logarithmic curve. For some dimensions, such as electric shock, sensation grows faster than intensity, which no logarithmic law can describe. That is where Stevens enters the story. Stevens' power law: ask people directly Stanley Smith Stevens (1906 to 1973) of Harvard University argued that there was no need to count JNDs: people can judge the magnitude of their sensations directly, and their judgements are lawful. His main method, magnitude estimation , works like this. The experimenter presents a standard stimulus (called the modulus) and assigns it a number, say 10. The observer is then given other stimuli and asked to assign each a number proportional to how intense it seems: a light that looks twice as bright as the standard gets 20; one that looks half as bright gets 5. Across hundreds of studies, Stevens found that the results for every continuum he tested were described by a power function. In 1957 he set out what is now called Stevens' power law : S = k I n where S is the judged magnitude of the sensation, I is the physical intensity, k is a scaling constant and the exponent n is characteristic of each sensory continuum. Taking logarithms of both sides gives log S = log k + n log I : plotted on log-log axes, every power function becomes a straight line whose slope is the exponent. That is how exponents are measured in practice. The exponent tells you how sensation grows. When n is less than 1, sensation grows more slowly than intensity, a pattern called response compression : brightness has an exponent of about 0.33, so to double the apparent brightness of a light you must increase its physical intensity about eightfold (because 2 raised to the power 1/0.33 is 8). When n equals 1, sensation grows in proportion to intensity, as it does for the apparent length of a line. When n is greater than 1, sensation grows faster than intensity, a pattern called response expansion : electric shock has an exponent of about 3.5, so doubling the current makes the shock feel roughly eleven times as intense (2 raised to the power 3.5 is about 11). Continuum Exponent (n) Type of growth Brightness (large target, dark-adapted eye) 0.33 Compression Smell (coffee odour) 0.55 Compression Loudness (3,000 Hz tone, measured as sound pressure) 0.67 Compression Apparent length of a line 1.0 Proportional Taste (sugar) 1.3 Expansion Heaviness of lifted weights 1.45 Expansion Electric shock (through the fingers) 3.5 Expansion Why should the senses differ like this? A plausible functional answer is that compression lets the eye and ear handle an enormous range of physical intensities (the brightest light we can tolerate is billions of times more intense than the dimmest we can see) within a manageable range of experience, whereas expansion makes potentially harmful stimuli, such as electric current, feel alarming quickly. Stevens strengthened his case with cross-modality matching . Instead of using numbers, observers match the intensity of one sense to another: for example, they squeeze a hand grip until the effort feels as strong as a sound is loud. If both senses follow power laws with known exponents, the power law predicts the exponent of the matching function (it should equal the ratio of the two exponents), and the matches came out close to the predictions. This showed that the power law was not merely an artefact of how people use numbers. Stevens was a productive figure in other ways too: in 1946 he proposed the four scales of measurement (nominal, ordinal, interval and ratio) taught in the Research Methodology book, and in 1936 he defined the sone, a unit of loudness. Where does Stevens' law fail? Magnitude estimates are affected by the range of stimuli presented, by the choice of modulus, by the order of presentation and by individual habits with numbers, so exponents vary from study to study. Some critics argue that magnitude estimation measures how people map sensations onto numbers rather than sensation itself. Even so, the power law describes direct magnitude judgements far better than Fechner's logarithm, and in 1961 Stevens titled a famous paper "To honor Fechner and repeal his law". The two laws are best seen as answers to different questions: Fechner's law describes discriminability (how many just noticeable steps lie between two stimuli), while Stevens' law describes apparent magnitude (how big a sensation seems). Fechner's Elemente described three procedures, and with small changes they are still in use in every vision clinic, hearing clinic and perception laboratory in the world. Each involves a trade-off between speed and accuracy, and each is vulnerable to particular errors. Understanding those errors, and how they are controlled, is as important for examinations as knowing the procedures. A few terms first. In threshold work the experimenter presents stimuli in a series , which may be ascending (starting well below threshold and increasing step by step) or descending (starting well above threshold and decreasing). The point in a series at which the observer's response changes (from "no" to "yes", or the reverse) is the transition point . When two stimuli are compared, the observer may also show a time-order error : a systematic tendency to judge the second of two equal stimuli as different from the first, simply because it comes second. A similar space error arises when a stimulus is judged differently because it appears on the left rather than the right. Errors of this kind are controlled by counterbalancing : arranging the order (or position) of conditions so that each occurs equally often in each place, so that the errors cancel out. The method of limits In the method of limits (Fechner called it the method of just noticeable differences; it is also called the method of minimal changes), the experimenter changes the stimulus in small steps, in alternating ascending and descending series, and records where the observer's response changes. To find the absolute threshold for a faint tone, for example, a descending series starts with a clearly audible tone and lowers it step by step until the observer first says "no"; an ascending series starts with an inaudible tone and raises it until the observer first says "yes". The threshold for each series is taken as the midpoint between the last two responses, and the overall threshold is the average across all series. Table 3.6 shows a worked example. Table 3.6 A worked example of the method of limits for the absolute threshold of a tone (intensity in arbitrary steps). The overall threshold is the mean transition point, 4.0. Notice that ascending transitions are higher than descending ones, the signature of the error of habituation. Series Direction and start Responses Transition point 1 Descending from 9 "Yes" from 9 down to 4, "no" at 3 3.5 2 Ascending from 1 "No" from 1 up to 4, "yes" at 5 4.5 3 Descending from 8 "Yes" from 8 down to 4, "no" at 3 3.5 4 Ascending from 2 "No" from 2 up to 4, "yes" at 5 4.5 The method of limits is quick and intuitive, but it suffers from two opposite errors, both caused by the predictable order of the stimuli. In the error of habituation (also called the error of perseveration), the observer falls into the habit of giving the same response and keeps giving it after the true threshold has been crossed: continuing to say "no" too long in an ascending series (so the ascending threshold comes out too high) and continuing to say "yes" too long in a descending series (so the descending threshold comes out too low). In the error of anticipation (or expectation), the observer, knowing that a change is coming, switches response too early: saying "yes" prematurely in an ascending series and "no" prematurely in a descending series. The two errors push the transition points in opposite directions. The cure is counterbalancing. Ascending and descending series are alternated in equal numbers, so that whatever error inflates the ascending thresholds is balanced by the corresponding error in the descending ones, and the starting point of each series is varied so that the observer cannot simply count steps to the expected change. The same logic applies to other order effects in psychophysical experiments, such as primacy and recency effects: they are controlled by counterbalancing the order of presentation. The method of limits can also measure difference thresholds. The observer compares each comparison stimulus with the standard and responds "greater", "equal" or "less". The range of comparison values judged "equal" is called the interval of uncertainty; its midpoint gives the point of subjective equality, and half its width gives the difference threshold. The method of constant stimuli The method of constant stimuli (Fechner's method of right and wrong cases, also called the frequency method) removes the predictable order altogether. The experimenter first chooses a small set of fixed ("constant") stimulus values, usually five to nine, spaced so that the weakest is almost never detected and the strongest almost always is. Each value is then presented many times, often fifty or a hundred times, in a random order. The proportion of "yes" responses is calculated for each value and plotted against stimulus intensity to give the psychometric function (Figure 3.1). The absolute threshold is the intensity that corresponds to 50 percent detection, read off (interpolated from) the curve. For difference thresholds, each comparison is paired with the standard and the observer says whether it is "heavier" or "lighter" (or "louder", "brighter" and so on). The comparison value judged "heavier" 50 percent of the time is the point of subjective equality. The difference threshold is conventionally taken as half the distance between the 75 percent and 25 percent points. Because the stimuli arrive in random order, the observer cannot anticipate a change or settle into a habit, so the errors of habituation and anticipation disappear. The method of constant stimuli is therefore regarded as the most accurate and reliable of the classical methods. Its cost is time: many trials are needed, and many are spent on stimuli far from threshold, which tell the experimenter little. It also requires pilot work to choose a sensible set of values. The method of adjustment In the method of adjustment (Fechner's method of average error, also called the method of reproduction), the observer controls the stimulus. To measure an absolute threshold, the observer turns a knob until a tone is just audible; to measure a point of subjective equality, the observer adjusts a comparison line until it looks equal in length to a standard. The procedure is repeated many times. The average setting gives the threshold or the point of subjective equality, and the variability of the settings (their average deviation or standard deviation, the "average error" that gives the method its name) is an index of the difference threshold: the more finely a person can discriminate, the more tightly the settings cluster. The method of adjustment is fast and engaging, and it is the natural way to measure the size of an illusion: observers adjust a plain line until it matches the apparent length of the Muller-Lyer line, and the difference between the setting and the true length (the constant error) measures how strong the illusion is. Its weakness is precision. The stimulus changes continuously under the observer's own control, so motor skill, impatience and the observer's beliefs can all creep into the settings, and the experimenter loses control over exactly which stimuli are presented.
