Method Other names Procedure Strengths Weaknesses Limits Method of just noticeable differences; minimal changes Stimulus changed in small steps in alternating ascending and descending series Quick, simple Errors of habituation and anticipation; needs counterbalancing Constant stimuli Method of right and wrong cases; frequency method Fixed set of values, each presented many times in random order Most accurate; no order errors; gives full psychometric function Slow; many wasted trials Adjustment Method of average error; reproduction Observer adjusts the stimulus until it is just detectable or matches the standard Fastest; ideal for measuring PSE and illusions Least precise; observer controls the stimulus Staircases and forced choice: the modern refinements Modern laboratories and clinics mostly use adaptive procedures that combine the speed of the method of limits with the efficiency of concentrating trials near threshold. In a staircase method , the stimulus is made weaker after every "yes" (or correct) response and stronger after every "no" (or incorrect) response. The intensity therefore climbs and descends around the threshold like a person walking up and down a staircase, and the threshold is estimated as the average of the reversal points, the intensities at which the direction changed. The method was popularised in psychophysics by Tom Cornsweet in 1962. Refinements change the rule to target a particular percentage: in the widely used "two-down, one-up" staircase, the stimulus is made harder only after two correct responses in a row, which makes the staircase settle at about 71 percent correct. To stop observers from guessing the rule, experimenters often interleave two staircases, one starting high and one low, at random. A close cousin is the tracking method that Georg von Bekesy (1899 to 1972) built into an audiometer in 1947. The listener holds down a button whenever the tone is audible; while the button is pressed the intensity falls, and when it is released the intensity rises. The result is a zigzag trace that hugs the listener's threshold as the frequency sweeps from low to high, an audiogram drawn by the listener's own responses. Many modern procedures also replace "yes or no" with a forced-choice procedure . In two-alternative forced choice, the stimulus appears in one of two intervals (or locations) and the observer must say which, even when guessing. Chance performance is 50 percent, so the threshold is usually set at the 75 percent correct point, halfway between chance and perfection. The great advantage of forced choice is that it removes the observer's willingness to say "yes" from the measurement. A cautious person and a bold person can no longer differ simply because one says "yes" more readily. That problem, the contamination of thresholds by the observer's decision style, is exactly what signal detection theory was invented to solve. Clinical link Every routine sensory assessment is a psychophysical experiment. Pure-tone audiometry finds the absolute threshold for tones of different frequencies, usually with an ascending method of limits or a staircase. An eye chart measures a visual threshold for detail. Automated perimetry, used to detect glaucoma, maps detection thresholds across the visual field. When a clinical psychologist tests a patient's two-point threshold or pain threshold as part of a neuropsychological examination, the same principles (50 percent points, counterbalanced series, attention to response bias) decide whether the result can be trusted. Exam trap Match the names: method of limits = method of just noticeable differences = minimal changes; method of constant stimuli = method of right and wrong cases = frequency method; method of adjustment = method of average error = reproduction. In the method of limits, the error of habituation means continuing the previous response too long, and the error of anticipation means changing the response too early. Both, along with primacy, recency and time-order effects, are controlled by counterbalancing (alternating ascending and descending series), not by "randomisation", "pairing" or a "double-blind technique". Randomisation is the cure in a different method: constant stimuli. 3.5 Signal detection theory Medium yield · 4 Qs During the Second World War, radar operators sat for hours in front of screens watching for the faint blip that meant an enemy aircraft. The screen was never clean. It sparkled with "noise": random flecks produced by the equipment and the atmosphere. A real aircraft at long range produced a blip barely stronger than the noise. Every few seconds the operator had to make a decision under uncertainty: is that an aircraft or just noise? Say "aircraft" too readily and fighters are scrambled for nothing; say it too reluctantly and the bombers arrive unannounced. Two operators with equally good eyes could perform very differently because they set different standards for raising the alarm. The classical idea of a threshold had no room for this. It assumed that a stimulus is either above the threshold (and detected) or below it (and missed), with the observer passively reporting the result. Yet experimenters had long noticed awkward facts. If they slipped "catch trials" into a detection experiment (trials on which no stimulus was presented), some observers said "yes" anyway. Observers who were paid for each detection reported more stimuli, and their measured thresholds fell, although their eyes and ears had not changed. A threshold, it seemed, measured not only what an observer could sense but also how willing the observer was to say so. The origins of the theory signal detection theory (SDT) began in engineering. In the early 1950s, W. Wesley Peterson, Theodore G. Birdsall and W. C. Fox at the University of Michigan developed a mathematical "theory of signal detectability" for radar and radio receivers, published in 1954. In the same year Wilson P. Tanner Jr. and John A. Swets applied it to human observers in a paper titled "A decision-making theory of visual detection". The definitive statement for psychology came in the 1966 book Signal Detection Theory and Psychophysics by David M. Green and John A. Swets. The central claim is simple and powerful: performance in any detection task depends on two independent things, the observer's sensitivity and the observer's decision criterion , and the two can be measured separately. Noise, signals and the four outcomes SDT starts by admitting that the observer's internal state is never quiet. noise , in SDT, is all the random background activity that is present whether or not a signal occurs: static on a screen, hum in a room, and above all the spontaneous firing of the observer's own neurons. On every trial the observer experiences some amount of internal "evidence" for a signal. On trials with no signal, this evidence comes from noise alone, and it varies from trial to trial, forming the noise distribution . On trials with a signal, the signal adds to the noise, so the evidence tends to be larger, forming the signal-plus-noise distribution . The two distributions overlap (Figure 3.3a). Some noise-alone trials produce more evidence than some signal trials, and the observer, who experiences only the evidence, cannot tell which kind of trial produced it. So the observer must adopt a rule: if the evidence on this trial exceeds a certain level, say "yes, a signal was present"; otherwise say "no". That cut-off level is the criterion . Every trial then ends in one of four outcomes, set out in Table 3.8. A hit is saying "yes" when a signal is present. A miss is saying "no" when a signal is present. A false alarm is saying "yes" when only noise is present. A correct rejection is saying "no" when only noise is present. Table 3.8 The four outcomes of a detection trial. The hit rate and the false alarm rate together contain all the information, because misses = 1 minus the hit rate and correct rejections = 1 minus the false alarm rate. The hit rate is the proportion of signal trials on which the observer said "yes"; the false alarm rate is the proportion of noise trials on which the observer said "yes". Notice what a hit rate alone cannot tell you. A smoke alarm that rings constantly has a perfect hit rate: it never misses a fire. It is also useless, because its false alarm rate is perfect too. Any honest measure of detection must look at hits and false alarms together. Sensitivity: d′ The first quantity SDT measures is sensitivity , the ability to distinguish a signal from noise. It is indexed by d prime (written d′), the distance between the means of the noise and signal-plus-noise distributions, expressed in standard deviation units. When the two distributions lie far apart, signal trials almost always produce more evidence than noise trials, and detection is easy (large d′). When they overlap completely, the observer cannot do better than guess (d′ = 0). Sensitivity depends on the strength of the signal, on the amount of noise and on the acuity of the observer's sensory system. Crucially, it does not depend on how willing the observer is to say "yes". In practice d′ is calculated from the hit rate (H) and the false alarm rate (F) by converting each into a z score from the standard normal table: d′ = z (H) minus z (F). You do not need to compute it in the examination, but you must understand what makes it large or small. If the hit rate equals the false alarm rate, the observer is saying "yes" just as often when nothing is there as when something is, and d′ is zero. The further the hit rate rises above the false alarm rate, the larger d′ becomes, so sensitivity is highest when hits clearly outnumber false alarms. (Some Indian exam notes write this loosely as "d = hits minus false alarms"; the direction is right, but the real formula subtracts the z scores of the two rates, not the raw counts.) If false alarms exceed hits, the observer is doing worse than chance, which signals confusion or a misunderstanding of the task. The criterion: liberal and conservative observers The second quantity is the observer's response bias , the location of the criterion. It is expressed either as β (beta), the ratio of the heights of the signal and noise distributions at the criterion, or as c , the distance of the criterion from the point midway between the two distributions. An observer whose criterion is low, who says "yes" on rather weak evidence, has a liberal criterion (also called lax or risky): such an observer earns many hits but also many false alarms ( β below 1; c negative). An observer whose criterion is high, who says "yes" only when the evidence is strong, has a conservative criterion (strict or cautious): few false alarms, but more misses ( β above 1; c positive). A neutral observer places the criterion where the two distributions cross ( β = 1; c = 0). What sets the criterion? Two kinds of factor, neither of them sensory. The first is expectation: if signals are common, it pays to say "yes" more readily; if they are rare, it pays to be cautious. The second is the payoff matrix, the rewards for hits and correct rejections and the costs of misses and false alarms. A smoke detector is deliberately set to a very liberal criterion because a miss (an undetected fire) is catastrophic while a false alarm (burnt toast) is merely annoying. A court of law, by contrast, demands proof "beyond reasonable doubt", a very conservative criterion, because society judges convicting an innocent person (a false alarm) to be worse than acquitting a guilty one (a miss). SDT shows that an ideal observer should shift the criterion in exactly these ways, and real observers do. Worked example: three radiologists, one sensitivity Each of four radiologists reads the same 200 mammograms, half showing a tumour. Dr A detects 84 percent of the tumours (H = 0.84) and wrongly flags 16 percent of the healthy scans (F = 0.16): d′ is about 2.0, and the criterion is neutral ( c = 0). Dr B, recently criticised for missing a tumour, now flags anything suspicious: H = 0.93, F = 0.31. Her d′ is still about 2.0; only her criterion has moved, to a liberal position ( c about −0.5). Dr C, worried about unnecessary biopsies, flags only clear cases: H = 0.69, F = 0.07. Again d′ is about 2.0, with a conservative criterion ( c about +0.5). Dr D has a hit rate of 0.84, just like Dr A, but a false alarm rate of 0.50. His d′ is only about 1.0. He is genuinely less able to tell tumours from healthy tissue. Comparing hit rates alone would rank Dr B best and Dr C worst, and would rate Dr D as good as Dr A. SDT shows that A, B and C are equally skilled and differ only in caution, while D is the weakest reader. (Figure 3.3b plots A, B and C on the same ROC curve.) The ROC curve If you change an observer's criterion (by changing the payoffs or the proportion of signal trials, or by asking for confidence ratings) while keeping the signal the same, the hit rate and false alarm rate move together. Plotting hit rate against false alarm rate for each criterion produces a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve, named after its origin in radar engineering (Figure 3.3b). Each curve is an isosensitivity curve: every point on it has the same d′ and differs only in bias. A conservative observer sits near the lower left; a liberal observer sits near the upper right. If the observer has no sensitivity at all, the curve is the diagonal, where hits equal false alarms. The greater the sensitivity, the more the curve bows towards the upper left corner, where hits are high and false alarms low. The area under the ROC curve is therefore a convenient bias-free index of accuracy, ranging from 0.5 (chance) to 1.0 (perfect discrimination). ROC curves also settled the theoretical argument. A strict "high threshold" theory, in which a stimulus is either detected or not and the observer simply guesses on undetected trials, predicts ROC curves that are straight lines. Real data almost always produce smoothly bowed curves of the kind SDT predicts. This is the main reason signal detection theory replaced the idea of a fixed sensory threshold: detection is a continuous process of weighing evidence, and the 50 percent "threshold" of classical psychophysics turns out to mix two quantities, sensitivity and bias, that SDT can separate. Key study: Are fingerprint experts really better? (Thompson and colleagues, 2014) Question. When a fingerprint examiner declares a "match", is that because experts discriminate better than novices, or simply because they are more willing to say "match"? Method. Matthew Thompson and colleagues gave experienced examiners and untrained novices genuine pairs of crime-scene prints, some matching and some only similar. Result. Both groups correctly said "match" on roughly 70 percent of truly matching pairs, so their hit rates were nearly identical. The difference lay in false alarms: novices said "match" to similar but non-matching pairs on 57 percent of trials, experts on fewer than 2 percent. Conclusion. Converted to SDT terms, the experts' d′ was far higher (roughly 2.7 against roughly 0.4 for novices), and the experts were also more conservative. A hit rate alone would have shown no difference; the false alarm rate revealed everything. Why it matters. The same analysis applies to eyewitness line-ups, lie detection and medical screening: never judge a detector by its hits without its false alarms. Signal detection in the real world Once you have the idea, you will see signal detection problems everywhere. An airport baggage screener looks for a rare weapon among thousands of harmless bags; because real threats are so rare, screeners drift towards a conservative criterion, which is why security agencies insert fake threat images to keep them alert (vigilance and its decline over long watches are discussed in Chapter 5). A polygraph examiner who calls almost everyone "deceptive" will catch nearly every liar but will brand many innocent people as liars, and the polygraph's modest sensitivity is the core of the scientific case against relying on it. In recognition memory, deciding whether a face or word is "old" or "new" has exactly the same structure, and memory researchers measure d′ and bias in the same way (Chapter 7). And whenever a claim is made that people respond to "subliminal" stimuli, the first SDT question is whether the stimuli were truly undetectable (d′ of zero) or merely below a cautious observer's criterion (Chapter 4 covers subliminal perception). Clinical link Every screening test you will use as a clinical psychologist, from a depression questionnaire to a dementia screen, is a signal detector with a criterion: its cut-off score. Lowering the cut-off catches more true cases (higher hit rate) at the price of more false positives; raising it does the reverse. In diagnostic language the hit rate is called the test's sensitivity , and one minus the false alarm rate is its specificity , and test developers choose cut-offs by drawing exactly the ROC curves described here. The choice is not purely statistical: it depends on the payoffs, such as the cost of missing a suicidal patient versus the cost of an unnecessary referral. Exam trap The ability to distinguish a signal from background noise is sensitivity (d′) ; the willingness to say "yes" is the criterion (β or c) , also called response bias; the ROC curve is the plot that displays both; the JND belongs to classical psychophysics, not SDT. The parameter that SDT added to classical threshold theory is the response criterion . Beware a second meaning of "sensitivity": in diagnostic testing it means the hit rate alone, which is not the same as d′. SDT is attributed to Green and Swets (1966, the classic book), Tanner and Swets (1954, first psychological application) and, in Indian notes, to the engineers Peterson and Birdsall; any of these can appear as the keyed answer. Exam trap: "receiver operant characteristics" IHBAS 2025 asked what "receiver-operant characteristics" refer to "in communication studies" and keyed the answer as factors in the audience influencing persuasion . In the communication (persuasion) framework, the "receiver" is the audience, and receiver characteristics (intelligence, self-esteem, involvement, initial attitude) are audience factors that moderate persuasion (Social Psychology book). Do not confuse this with the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve of signal detection theory, which plots hit rate against false alarm rate as the criterion changes. The option "physiological thresholds of auditory perception" is bait for students who half-remember the SDT term; it describes neither concept. Scan Your Brain Fill in the blanks. We begin with the stimulus itself, follow light through the eye to the receptors, and then examine the remarkable fact that each human eye contains two quite different visual systems, one for daylight and one for the dark. Light Light is electromagnetic radiation, the same kind of energy as radio waves, X-rays and microwaves. Like all such radiation it travels as waves (and, as physicists insist, as particles called photons) at about 300,000 kilometres per second. What distinguishes light from other electromagnetic radiation is only its wavelength. The human eye responds to wavelengths between about 380 and 760 nanometres (a nanometre is a billionth of a metre); this narrow band is the visible spectrum . Some textbooks round it to 400 to 700 nanometres, but 380 to 760 is the standard examination answer. There is nothing physically special about this band: it is simply the range our photopigments absorb. Just below it lies ultraviolet radiation, which bees can see; just above it lies infrared, which rattlesnakes and other pit vipers can sense, letting them detect warm-blooded prey in what is darkness to us. For any wave travelling at a fixed speed, wavelength and frequency are inversely related: speed equals frequency multiplied by wavelength, so the shorter the wavelength, the higher the frequency. Violet light (around 400 nanometres) therefore has a shorter wavelength and a higher frequency than red light (around 700 nanometres). The same inverse relation holds for sound. Three physical properties of light map onto three psychological dimensions of visual experience. Wavelength is experienced mainly as hue , the quality we name with colour words: short wavelengths look violet and blue, middle wavelengths green and yellow, long wavelengths orange and red. Intensity (the amount of light energy, the height or amplitude of the wave) is experienced mainly as brightness . Purity (the extent to which light consists of a single wavelength rather than a mixture) is experienced as saturation , the vividness of a colour: a pure red is highly saturated, while red diluted with white light looks pink, a less saturated version of the same hue. It first passes through the cornea , the transparent, curved front surface of the eye, which does most of the focusing (roughly two-thirds of the eye's bending power). It then crosses a watery fluid (the aqueous humour) and passes through the pupil , the opening in the centre of the coloured iris . The iris is a ring of muscle that changes the size of the pupil: it constricts the pupil in bright light and dilates it in dim light. This involves a trade-off. A small pupil gives a sharper image with a greater depth of focus; a large pupil lets in more light but sacrifices sharpness. The eye favours acuity when light is plentiful and sensitivity when it is scarce. Behind the pupil lies the lens , which fine-tunes the focus. Its shape is adjusted by the ciliary muscles: when you look at something near, the lens becomes thicker and rounder, bending light more strongly; when you look at something distant, it is pulled flatter. This process of changing the shape of the lens to bring images into focus is called accommodation . With age the lens stiffens and loses the ability to round up, which is why most people need reading glasses in their forties (presbyopia). Other common focusing errors arise from the shape of the eyeball: in short-sightedness (myopia) the eyeball is too long and distant objects focus in front of the retina; in long-sightedness (hyperopia) it is too short and near objects focus behind it. A clouded lens is a cataract, which remains the leading cause of blindness in India and is corrected by replacing the lens surgically. Light then crosses the jelly-like vitreous humour and arrives at the retina , the thin sheet of neural tissue lining the back of the eye, where transduction takes place. The retina is built, oddly, inside out. The receptors (rods and cones) lie at the very back, against the pigment layer, so light must pass through the other retinal layers before reaching them. The receptors connect to bipolar cells , which connect to retinal ganglion cells , whose axons run across the inner surface of the retina and gather together to leave the eye as the optic nerve (cranial nerve II). Two further cell types, horizontal cells and amacrine cells , carry signals sideways across the retina, allowing neighbouring regions to influence each other; you will see why that matters when we reach lateral inhibition. Two regions of the retina have special names. Near the centre of the retina, in a small yellowish area called the macula, is a tiny pit, the fovea , where the overlying layers are pushed aside so that light falls directly on the receptors. The fovea contains only cones, packed tightly together, and it gives us our sharpest, most detailed, colour vision; when you look straight at something, you are turning your eyes so that its image falls on the fovea. A few millimetres towards the nose lies the optic disc , where the ganglion cell axons leave the eye and blood vessels enter. Because the optic disc has no receptors at all, it creates a blind spot in each eye's field of vision. (The farthest forward edge of the retina, where it ends near the ciliary body, is the ora serrata, named for its serrated outline; it has no special role in detailed vision.) You can find your blind spot. Draw a small cross and, about 8 centimetres to its right, a dot the size of a pea. Close your left eye, stare steadily at the cross with your right eye and move the page slowly towards and away from your face. At about 25 to 30 centimetres the dot vanishes, because its image has fallen on the optic disc. Yet you never notice a hole in your vision, even with one eye closed. The brain fills the gap with whatever surrounds it, a process called completion or filling in: draw a line passing through the dot's position, and when the dot disappears the line appears unbroken. Rods and cones: two visual systems in one eye The human retina contains two kinds of photoreceptor, named for their shapes. The rods number roughly 120 million per eye; the cones number only about 6 to 7 million (estimates vary). Their distribution is strikingly different: the fovea contains cones and no rods at all, while the density of rods peaks about 20 degrees away from the fovea and rods dominate the periphery. This is why, on a dark night, you can often see a faint star more clearly by looking slightly to one side of it than by looking straight at it. In the nineteenth century, researchers noticed that animals active only by day tend to have cone-rich retinas while nocturnal animals have rod-rich ones. From this observation came the duplexity theory of vision: rods and cones mediate two different kinds of vision. photopic vision is cone-mediated vision in good light; it provides high acuity and colour. scotopic vision is rod-mediated vision in dim light; it is extremely sensitive but lacks both detail and colour. (Twilight vision, with both systems contributing, is called mesopic.) At night, everything looks grey because only the rods are working, and rods cannot distinguish wavelengths. Why should one system be sensitive and the other sharp? Part of the answer is chemistry and part is wiring. The rods contain a single photopigment, rhodopsin (sometimes called visual purple), which is so sensitive that a rod can respond to a single quantum of light, as Hecht and his colleagues showed. The cones contain three different photopigments, each most sensitive to a different range of wavelengths, which is the basis of colour vision (Section 3.7). The wiring difference is convergence. In rod pathways, the outputs of many rods (often hundreds) converge on a single ganglion cell, so the weak signals from many rods add together and a dim light becomes detectable; but the brain cannot tell which of those many rods was stimulated, so detail is lost. In the fovea, by contrast, each cone may have something close to a private line to the brain, so detail is preserved, but each cone needs more light to drive its pathway. Sensitivity is bought at the price of acuity, and acuity at the price of sensitivity. Table 3.10 summarises the contrast. Table 3.10 Rods and cones compared. The false statement in "which statement about cones is incorrect?" is that cones provide only monochromatic information: it is the rods that give colourless vision. The retina and the iris are structures, not receptor types. Visual adaptation: from sunlight to darkness Walk from a sunny street into a dark cinema and for a minute you can hardly see the seats. Gradually the room "brightens" until you can see the faces of people around you. Nothing in the cinema has changed; your eyes have. dark adaptation is the gradual increase in the eye's sensitivity to light of low intensity that occurs in darkness. The reverse process, light adaptation , is the rapid decrease in sensitivity that occurs when you move into bright light; it takes from a few seconds to about a minute, which is why sunlight dazzles you only briefly. Together these are called visual adaptation, the process of adjusting to different intensities of light. If you measure a person's absolute threshold for light at intervals after entering complete darkness, you obtain the classic dark adaptation curve (Figure 3.4). It has two distinct branches. For the first 7 to 10 minutes, the threshold falls quickly and then levels off: this is the cone branch, as the cones recover their sensitivity. Then there is a kink, the rod-cone break , after which the threshold falls again, slowly, for another 20 minutes or so: this is the rod branch, as the far more sensitive rods take over. After about 30 minutes in the dark the eye is many thousands of times more sensitive than it was in daylight. The main mechanism is chemical. Light "bleaches" rhodopsin, splitting it into its components, and in darkness the pigment slowly regenerates; until it does, the rods cannot respond. This has a neat practical use. Wearing red goggles, or working under dim red light, lets the cones see well enough to read and work while the rods, which barely respond to red, dark-adapt in the meantime. Military pilots waiting to fly night missions, astronomers and darkroom workers have all used this trick, and so did radiologists in the days when X-ray images were viewed on dim fluoroscope screens. Indian context Rhodopsin is built from a protein (opsin) and retinal, a molecule made from vitamin A. When vitamin A is scarce, rhodopsin cannot be regenerated fast enough and dark adaptation fails: the person develops night blindness (nyctalopia), often the first sign of deficiency. Vitamin A deficiency was long a major cause of preventable childhood blindness in India, which is why young Indian children receive periodic high-dose vitamin A supplementation through the public health system. The Purkinje shift Rods and cones are not equally sensitive to all wavelengths. Under photopic (daylight) conditions the visual system is most sensitive to light of about 555 to 560 nanometres, in the yellow-green; under scotopic (night) conditions its peak sensitivity shifts to about 500 nanometres, in the blue-green, the wavelength rhodopsin absorbs best. This shift has a visible consequence that was first described in 1825 by the Czech physiologist Jan Evangelista Purkyne (1787 to 1869), usually spelled Purkinje in English. Walking in his garden at dusk, Purkinje noticed that his red and yellow flowers, which had looked brighter than his blue ones in daylight, became darker than the blue ones as night fell. The Purkinje shift (or Purkinje effect) is this change in relative brightness as illumination falls: long-wavelength colours (reds) lose brightness sooner, and short-wavelength colours (blues and greens) look relatively brighter, as vision passes from cones to rods. It is one reason a red object, a red cricket ball included, becomes hard to pick out as daylight fades. Visual acuity and eye movements visual acuity is the ability to see fine detail. It is usually measured with the letter chart devised by the Dutch ophthalmologist Herman Snellen (1834 to 1908) in 1862. Normal acuity is recorded as 6/6 (or 20/20 in feet): at 6 metres you can read what a person with standard vision reads at 6 metres. A score of 6/12 means you need to be at 6 metres to read what a standard eye reads from 12 metres away. Acuity is highest at the fovea, falls steeply in the periphery (because of the distribution of cones and the convergence of rods) and drops in dim light. The visual system also has a temporal limit: a light flickering faster than a certain rate (the critical flicker fusion frequency, typically around 50 to 60 flashes per second in bright light) is seen as steady, which is why a film made of separate frames looks continuous. Your eyes are never still. When you read or scan a scene, they jump from point to point in rapid movements called saccades (several per second), separated by brief pauses called fixations, during which information is taken in. They also follow moving objects smoothly (smooth pursuit) and turn inwards or outwards for near and far targets (vergence). Even during a fixation, when you try to hold your gaze perfectly still, the eyes make tiny involuntary movements: a fine tremor, slow drifts and small rapid flicks called microsaccades. These tiny movements are not a defect. In the early 1950s, researchers devised ways of producing a stabilised retinal image , an image that moves with the eye and therefore stays fixed on the same receptors (one method mounted a tiny projector on a contact lens). Within a few seconds the image faded and disappeared, sometimes returning in fragments. Visual neurons respond mainly to change, so an unchanging image adapts out of existence. A milder version, Troxler fading (described in 1804), can be seen by fixating steadily on a point while a faint blurry patch sits in your peripheral vision: the patch fades. The constant small movements of the eyes keep the image shifting across the receptors and so prevent sensory adaptation from erasing the visual world. Saccades and microsaccades, in other words, ensure constant perception. Exam trap "Tiny rapid movements of the eyes ensure ..." Answer: saccades (strictly, microsaccades) ensure constant perception . A fixation is the pause between saccades, not a movement. Eye movements prevent sensory adaptation; they do not ensure it. Do not confuse accommodation (the lens changing shape to focus, Section 3.6), adaptation (sensitivity changing with light level) and Piaget's assimilation and accommodation (cognitive development, Developmental book). Getting adjusted to different intensities of light is visual adaptation . Lateral inhibition and Mach bands Look at a set of grey stripes arranged in steps from light to dark, each stripe a perfectly uniform grey. Most people see each stripe as slightly lighter along the edge next to its darker neighbour and slightly darker along the edge next to its lighter neighbour, so the stripes seem gently scalloped. These illusory light and dark bands at edges are called Mach bands , after the Austrian physicist and philosopher Ernst Mach (1838 to 1916), who described them in 1865. The explanation is lateral inhibition : the tendency of active neurons in a sensory network to suppress the activity of their neighbours. In the retina, horizontal and amacrine cells carry inhibitory signals sideways, so each receptor's output is reduced in proportion to the activity of the receptors around it. Now consider a border between a light region and a dark one. A cell just on the light side of the border has some dark neighbours, so it receives less inhibition than cells deeper in the light region, and it signals "brighter": a light band. A cell just on the dark side has some light neighbours, so it receives more inhibition than cells deeper in the dark region, and it signals "darker": a dark band. The net effect is to exaggerate contrast at edges. Lateral inhibition was demonstrated directly by Haldan Keffer Hartline (1903 to 1983) and Floyd Ratliff in the eye of the horseshoe crab ( Limulus ), whose large receptors could be recorded one at a time; Hartline shared the 1967 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with Ragnar Granit and George Wald for work on the physiology and chemistry of vision. Edge enhancement is useful. The boundaries of objects are where the information is, and a system that sharpens edges helps us see where one object ends and another begins. The same mechanism contributes to simultaneous contrast, in which a grey patch looks lighter on a black background than on a white one. (The Hermann grid, in which grey smudges appear at the intersections of white lines between black squares, was long explained the same way, although recent research suggests the full story is more complicated.) Exam trap Mach bands are explained by lateral inhibition in the retina, which enhances edge perception (it does not dull edges, lower overall brightness or enhance colour). The opponent-process theory explains colour phenomena such as afterimages, not brightness bands; the rod-cone dichotomy explains differences between day and night vision; temporal summation is the adding together of weak signals over time. 3.7 Vision II: colour Lower yield · 1 Q In 1666 a young Isaac Newton darkened his room, let a thin beam of sunlight through a hole in the shutter, and passed it through a glass prism. The white light spread into a band of colours from red to violet. Passed through a second prism, the colours could be recombined into white. White light, Newton concluded, is a mixture of all the colours. But he added a remark that sounds as if it were written by a psychologist: "For the Rays to speak properly are not coloured." Light has wavelengths; colour is something the nervous system creates. This section asks how. Mixing colours: additive and subtractive Two very different kinds of colour mixing are easily confused. additive colour mixing is the mixing of lights. When two lights shine on the same spot, the wavelengths they contain are added together, and the result reaches the eye as a combination. Red light plus green light gives yellow; green plus blue gives cyan; red plus blue gives magenta; red, green and blue together give white. Your phone screen and a television work this way: each pixel contains tiny red, green and blue elements, and every colour on the screen is an additive mixture of the three. subtractive colour mixing is the mixing of paints, inks and dyes. A pigment looks coloured because it absorbs (subtracts) some wavelengths and reflects the rest. Mixing two pigments means that each absorbs its share, so the mixture reflects only the wavelengths that both pigments reflect. Blue paint reflects mostly blue and some green; yellow paint reflects mostly yellow and some green; mixed together they absorb everything except green, which is what you see. Mix enough pigments and almost everything is absorbed, producing a muddy dark brown or black, as anyone who has seen the colours at the end of a Holi celebration will know. Printers use cyan, magenta and yellow inks (plus black) for this reason. The rule to remember: lights add towards white; pigments subtract towards black. Some pairs of colours are special. complementary colours are pairs of hues that, when mixed as lights in the right proportions, produce white or grey: blue and yellow, red and green (strictly, red and a bluish green). On a colour circle, complementary colours sit opposite each other. They will turn out to be the key to one of the two great theories of colour vision. The trichromatic theory In 1802 the English physician and physicist Thomas Young (1773 to 1829) proposed that the eye does not need a separate receptor for every hue. Three kinds of receptor, each responding to a different part of the spectrum, would be enough, with each colour signalled by the ratio of activity across the three. Hermann von Helmholtz developed and refined the idea in 1852, and it has been known ever since as the Young-Helmholtz trichromatic theory (also called the component theory). The main evidence came from colour-matching experiments. An observer sees a test light of a particular colour and adjusts the intensities of three "primary" lights until their mixture looks identical to it. With three suitably chosen primaries, any colour can be matched; with only two, many cannot. Three is the magic number because there are three kinds of receptor. One striking consequence is the existence of metamers : lights with physically different mixtures of wavelengths that look exactly the same colour, because they produce the same ratio of activity across the three receptor types. Your phone's yellow (a mixture of red and green light) and the yellow of a sodium street lamp (a single wavelength) are metamers. The physiological proof came more than 160 years after Young. In 1964 two research groups, one of them led by George Wald (1906 to 1997), measured the light absorbed by the pigment inside single cones and found exactly three types. Today they are called short-wavelength (S) cones, peaking at about 420 nanometres (violet-blue); medium-wavelength (M) cones, peaking at about 530 nanometres (green); and long-wavelength (L) cones, peaking at about 560 nanometres (yellow-green, but they respond further into the red than the others). Each type responds to a broad range of wavelengths; what signals colour is the ratio between them. Humans share this trichromatic system with the apes and Old World monkeys; most other mammals, including dogs, have only two cone types. The opponent-process theory The trichromatic theory explains colour matching beautifully, but several everyday facts fit it poorly. Stare at a red patch for half a minute, then look at a white wall: you see a green patch. Why green, of all colours? Nobody ever sees a reddish green or a bluish yellow, although reddish blue (purple) and greenish yellow are easy to imagine. Yellow looks like a pure, unmixed colour, not like a blend of red and green. And people with colour blindness tend to confuse colours in pairs: red with green, or blue with yellow. The German physiologist Ewald Hering (1834 to 1918) built these observations into the opponent-process theory , published in 1878. Hering proposed three opponent systems, each signalling one of a pair of opposed sensations by changing its activity in one direction or the other: a red versus green system, a blue versus yellow system and a black versus white (brightness) system. Because the two members of a pair are signalled by opposite activity in the same system, they cannot be experienced together at the same place; hence there is no reddish green. The theory gives an elegant account of the negative afterimage , the image in complementary colours that appears after prolonged staring at a coloured stimulus. Staring at red fatigues the red side of the red versus green system. When you then look at a white surface, which stimulates both sides equally, the rested green side dominates, and you see green. Staring at blue produces a yellow afterimage; staring at white produces a black one. You can see this with a flag: stare for thirty seconds at a version of the Indian tricolour painted in blue (top), black (middle) and magenta (bottom), the complements of saffron, white and green, then look at a white wall, and the familiar saffron, white and green appear. (A brief, intense flash, such as a camera flash, can instead leave a positive afterimage, a short-lived image in the original colours, caused by receptors continuing to fire for a moment after the light is gone.) Opponent cells were eventually found. In the 1950s Gunnar Svaetichin recorded opponent responses from cells in the fish retina, and in the 1960s Russell De Valois and his colleagues found cells in the lateral geniculate nucleus of monkeys that were excited by red and inhibited by green (or the reverse), and others that were excited by blue and inhibited by yellow. In 1957 Leo Hurvich and Dorothea Jameson had already shown that Hering's ideas could be made quantitative and could predict colour-matching data. The dual-process resolution For decades, supporters of the two theories argued as though only one could be right. Both were right, about different stages of the visual system. According to the dual-process theory (sometimes called the zone theory), colour is coded in two stages. At the first stage, in the receptors, the three cone types work exactly as Young and Helmholtz proposed. At the second stage, in the retinal ganglion cells and the lateral geniculate nucleus, the cone signals are combined into opponent channels exactly as Hering proposed: the difference between L and M cone signals forms a red versus green channel; the difference between S cone signals and the sum of L and M forms a blue versus yellow channel; and the sum of L and M signals forms a brightness channel (Figure 3.5). Stage 1 is trichromatic: three cone types with different peak sensitivities. Stage 2 is opponent: ganglion cells and the lateral geniculate nucleus combine cone signals, adding some and subtracting others, into red versus green, blue versus yellow and black versus white channels. Colour matching reflects Stage 1; afterimages and the pairing of colour confusions reflect Stage 2. Two further theories are worth knowing by name. The American logician and psychologist Christine Ladd-Franklin (1847 to 1930) proposed an evolutionary theory of colour vision in 1892: vision began as achromatic (black and white), later divided into blue and yellow, and later still yellow divided into red and green. Her theory neatly predicted that the most recently evolved distinction, red versus green, would be the most fragile, which is exactly the commonest form of colour blindness. And the inventor Edwin Land (1909 to 1991), founder of the Polaroid company, proposed the retinex theory to explain colour constancy, our tendency to see an object's colour as stable under very different lighting (Chapter 4 discusses the constancies). Colour blindness was long called Daltonism in his honour. Dalton asked that his eyes be examined after his death; one was preserved, and in 1995 DNA analysis of the tissue showed that he had lacked the M (green-sensitive) cone pigment. "Colour blindness" is a misleading name, because very few colour-blind people see no colour at all. The accurate term is colour vision deficiency , and it comes in three degrees (Table 3.12). In anomalous trichromacy , the mildest and most common form, all three cone types are present but one has a shifted sensitivity, so certain colours are matched differently from normal. In dichromacy , one cone type is missing altogether and the person matches all colours with two primaries. The three forms are named with Greek numbers in the order long, medium, short: protanopia ("first", missing L cones: reds look dim and are confused with greens), deuteranopia ("second", missing M cones: reds and greens confused, Dalton's condition) and tritanopia ("third", missing S cones: blues and yellows confused). In monochromacy , the rarest form, the person has at most one functioning cone type. Rod monochromats (achromatopsia) have no working cones at all; they see only shades of grey, have poor acuity and are dazzled by daylight, exactly as you would predict for someone who must rely on rods alone. The most widely used screening test is the set of plates designed by the Japanese ophthalmologist Shinobu Ishihara (1879 to 1963) and published in 1917. Each Ishihara plate shows a circle of coloured dots in which a number is formed by dots of one hue against a background of another; a person with normal colour vision reads the number easily, while a person with a red-green deficiency sees a different number or none. The standard Ishihara plates screen for red-green defects and do not detect tritan defects. Finer diagnosis uses arrangement tests such as the Farnsworth-Munsell 100 Hue test and the anomaloscope, in which the viewer adjusts a mixture of red and green light to match a yellow light; how much red or green the person needs reveals the type and degree of deficiency. In India, colour perception standards are part of the medical examination for jobs such as railway driver, pilot and many posts in the armed forces. He did not propose the JND (Weber and Fechner), the unconscious mind (that is Freud's concept; Helmholtz's unconscious inference concerns perception) or the law of effect (Thorndike). Hearing works in the dark, around corners and through walls, and it carries spoken language, which is why losing it is so isolating. As with vision, we begin with the physical stimulus, follow it through the ear to the receptors, and then ask how the brain extracts pitch, loudness and direction from what the receptors report. Sound: the stimulus Sound is a wave of pressure travelling through a medium such as air or water. When a tabla player strikes the drumhead, the skin moves rapidly out and in. Each outward movement pushes the neighbouring air molecules together, creating a region of slightly higher pressure (a compression); each inward movement leaves a region of slightly lower pressure (a rarefaction). These alternating compressions and rarefactions travel outward at about 340 metres per second in air, and more than four times faster in water, although each air molecule only jostles back and forth in place. Because sound needs molecules to carry it, there is no sound in a vacuum: the roaring explosions of a space film are a cinematic fiction. Sound waves have three physical properties, and they map onto three psychological dimensions of hearing (Table 3.9 set them beside their visual counterparts; Figure 3.6 draws them). The frequency of a sound is the number of complete cycles of compression and rarefaction passing a point each second. It is measured in hertz (Hz), after the German physicist Heinrich Hertz: one hertz is one cycle per second. Frequency is experienced mainly as pitch , how high or low a sound seems: the deep thud of a dhol has a low frequency, the shriek of a whistle a high one. As with light, frequency and wavelength are inversely related, so a 100 Hz hum has a wavelength of about 3.4 metres and a 10,000 Hz hiss a wavelength of about 3.4 centimetres, a difference that will matter when we come to locating sounds. The amplitude (intensity) of a sound is the size of its pressure changes, the height of the wave, and it is experienced mainly as loudness . The complexity of a sound is its mixture of frequencies, and it is experienced as timbre (pronounced "tam-ber"), the tone quality that lets you tell one sound source from another. Timbre needs a word of explanation. A tuning fork produces a pure tone , a sound of a single frequency whose pressure changes trace a smooth sine wave. Almost every other sound is complex. When a veena player plucks a string, the string vibrates as a whole at its fundamental frequency , which largely sets the pitch, and at the same time in halves, thirds, quarters and so on, producing harmonics (overtones) at two, three, four and more times the fundamental. Early in the nineteenth century the French mathematician Joseph Fourier showed that any complex wave can be described as a sum of simple sine waves, and the ear, as you will see, performs something close to this analysis mechanically. A veena, a flute and a human voice sounding the same note share a fundamental but differ in their mixtures of harmonics, which is why you can tell them apart with your eyes closed. Timbre also depends on how a sound begins and fades: play a recording of a piano backwards and it no longer sounds like a piano. Pitch is not simply frequency in disguise. A complex tone made of 200, 300 and 400 Hz components is heard with the pitch of 100 Hz, although it contains no energy at 100 Hz at all, because 100 Hz is the fundamental the three components share. This missing fundamental effect is why a man's voice still sounds like a man's voice over a telephone line that cuts out almost everything below about 300 Hz. Pitch also shifts a little with loudness, and loudness depends on frequency: a 50 Hz tone must be far more intense than a 3,000 Hz tone to sound equally loud. Pitch and loudness are psychological dimensions, measured with the psychophysical methods of Section 3.4; frequency and amplitude are physical ones, measured with instruments. Stevens built ratio scales for both: the mel for pitch and the sone for loudness. Each trace shows air pressure rising and falling over time. More cycles per second (higher frequency) is heard as higher pitch; taller waves (greater amplitude) as louder sound; adding harmonics to the same fundamental changes the timbre but not the pitch. The healthy young human ear responds to frequencies from about 20 Hz to about 20,000 Hz. It is most sensitive between about 2,000 and 5,000 Hz, the range that carries many of the consonants of speech, and least sensitive at the extremes. Frequencies below 20 Hz (infrasound) are felt as vibration rather than heard; elephants use them to call to one another over several kilometres. Frequencies above 20,000 Hz (ultrasound) are silent to us but audible to dogs (up to about 45,000 Hz) and to bats (well above 100,000 Hz). Francis Galton (1822 to 1911), the Victorian polymath who founded the study of individual differences, invented a high-pitched whistle in 1876 to test the upper limit of hearing in people and animals; it is the ancestor of the "silent" dog whistle. The upper limit falls steadily with age, and by middle age many people hear little above about 12,000 to 14,000 Hz. Loudness and the decibel The range of intensities the ear can handle is staggering. The most intense sound you can tolerate carries roughly a million million (10 12 ) times the energy of the faintest sound you can detect. A scale running from 1 to a million million is useless in daily practice, so acousticians use a logarithmic scale, the same kind of scale that Fechner's law says our senses themselves use (Section 3.3). The unit is the decibel (dB), one-tenth of a bel, a unit named after Alexander Graham Bell, the inventor of the telephone. Zero decibels is set at a reference pressure close to a young listener's absolute threshold for a 1,000 Hz tone. It does not mean "no sound": very sensitive ears can detect sounds slightly below 0 dB. On the decibel scale, every increase of 10 dB is a tenfold increase in sound intensity (energy). A 20 dB sound is therefore 100 times as intense as a threshold sound, a 60 dB conversation a million times as intense, and a 120 dB rock concert a million million times as intense. (Strictly, the familiar scale of sound pressure level is defined by pressure, which grows tenfold for every 20 dB; the conclusions are the same.) Perceived loudness grows far more slowly than intensity. As a rough rule, every 10 dB increase makes a sound seem about twice as loud, which is Stevens' power law at work: tenfold more energy raised to an exponent of about 0.3 (equivalent to the exponent of 0.67 for sound pressure in Table 3.4) is roughly a doubling. Decibels measure the physical stimulus; the psychological unit of loudness is the sone and of pitch the mel. Frequency and wavelength are inversely related for sound as for light. The ear: outer, middle and inner The ear is a chain of energy converters (Figure 3.7). The outer ear collects airborne sound; the middle ear turns it into the vibration of three tiny bones; the inner ear turns that into waves in fluid and, finally, into neural signals. The outer ear. The visible flap of skin and cartilage is the pinna (or auricle). Its folds funnel sound into the auditory canal and subtly alter the high frequencies of a sound according to the direction it comes from, which helps you tell whether a sound is above or below you, in front or behind. The auditory canal, about 2.5 centimetres long, resonates like an organ pipe and boosts frequencies around 2,000 to 5,000 Hz, one reason our sensitivity peaks there. At its inner end is the tympanic membrane (eardrum), a thin, cone-shaped membrane that vibrates in step with the pressure changes that strike it. The middle ear. Behind the eardrum lies a small air-filled cavity containing the three ossicles , the smallest bones in the body: the malleus (hammer), attached to the eardrum; the incus (anvil); and the stapes (stirrup), whose footplate fits into the oval window , a membrane-covered opening into the inner ear. Why bother with bones? Because the inner ear is filled with fluid, and fluid is far harder to set in motion than air. If airborne sound struck the fluid directly, almost all of its energy (about 99.9 percent) would bounce off, which is why people underwater can barely hear someone shouting from the poolside. The middle ear solves this problem in two ways. The eardrum is about 17 to 20 times larger in area than the oval window, so the force collected over the large drum is concentrated onto the small window, and the ossicles act as a lever. Together these raise the pressure about twentyfold. Two tiny muscles in the middle ear (the tensor tympani and the stapedius) also contract reflexively to loud sounds, stiffening the chain and damping the vibration; this acoustic reflex takes a few tens of milliseconds, too slow to protect the ear from a sudden firecracker blast. Finally, the Eustachian (auditory) tube connects the middle ear to the throat and keeps the air pressure equal on both sides of the eardrum. Your ears "pop" when it opens during a flight or a fast drive down a ghat road. In young children the tube is short and nearly horizontal, which is one reason middle-ear infections are so common in childhood. The inner ear. The cochlea (from the Greek kokhlos , land snail) is a coiled, fluid-filled tube about the size of a pea, making about two and a half to two and three-quarter turns and roughly 35 millimetres long if uncoiled. It is divided along its length into three chambers. The partition that forms the floor of the middle chamber is the basilar membrane , a flexible strip that is narrow and stiff at the base of the cochlea (near the oval window) and several times wider and floppier at the apex (the tip of the coil). Resting on the basilar membrane is the organ of Corti , the receptor organ of hearing, named after the Italian anatomist Alfonso Corti, who described it in 1851. It contains the hair cells , the auditory receptors, each topped by a tuft of tiny stiff hairs (stereocilia), with a second membrane, the tectorial membrane, lying over them. When the stapes pushes the oval window inward, the fluid of the cochlea is displaced and a wave runs along the basilar membrane; the pressure is finally released at a second, flexible window lower down, the round window, which bulges outward. The human cochlea has about 3,500 inner hair cells , in a single row, and about 12,000 outer hair cells , in three rows. The inner hair cells are the true sensory receptors: about 95 percent of the roughly 30,000 fibres of the auditory nerve carry their signals. The outer hair cells act as an amplifier. They lengthen and shorten in time with the sound, pumping energy into the basilar membrane's vibration and sharpening its response to particular frequencies. In doing so they produce faint sounds of their own that travel back out through the middle ear. These otoacoustic emissions can be picked up by a tiny microphone placed in the ear canal, and recording them is now a quick, painless way to screen the hearing of newborn babies, who cannot answer "yes, I heard it". From the cochlea, signals travel along the auditory nerve, the cochlear branch of the vestibulocochlear nerve (cranial nerve VIII), to the cochlear nuclei of the brainstem. From there the pathway runs to the superior olives on both sides, the first place where signals from the two ears meet, then through the inferior colliculi of the midbrain to the medial geniculate nucleus of the thalamus, and finally to the primary auditory cortex in the temporal lobe. Every stage is laid out in order of frequency, like the keys of a piano, an arrangement called tonotopic organisation . Because each ear sends signals to both hemispheres, damage to the auditory cortex on one side does not make the opposite ear deaf. (The Physiological Psychology book traces this pathway in detail.) Air pressure waves (outer ear) become vibrations of the eardrum and the three ossicles (middle ear), then pressure waves in the fluid of the cochlea that bend the hair cells of the organ of Corti (inner ear). Only at the hair cells is sound transduced into neural signals. From vibration to nerve impulse: the hair cells Transduction in the ear is purely mechanical, and it is among the fastest in any sense. As the basilar membrane moves up and down, the hair cells riding on it are pushed against the overlying tectorial membrane, and their stereocilia bend. The stereocilia on each hair cell stand in rows of increasing height, and the tip of each is joined to its taller neighbour by a fine filament called a tip link. Bending the bundle towards its tallest stereocilia stretches the tip links, which pull open mechanically gated ion channels. Positively charged ions, mainly potassium from the unusually potassium-rich fluid (endolymph) bathing the top of the hair cell, flow in, and the cell depolarises. Depolarisation makes the hair cell release the neurotransmitter glutamate onto the auditory nerve fibres beneath it, and they fire. Bending the bundle the other way closes the channels and the cell hyperpolarises. At low frequencies, therefore, the hair cell's voltage rises and falls in step with the sound wave itself. Because no chemical cascade intervenes between movement and channel opening, the whole process takes only microseconds. Notice how different this is from the other senses you have met. In the rods and cones, light triggers a chemical cascade that closes sodium channels, so photoreceptors hyperpolarise to light (Section 3.1 noted that they are most active in the dark). In taste and smell, transduction begins when a molecule binds to a receptor (Section 3.9). Hair cells are also fragile. Intense noise can snap tip links and tear stereocilia, and in mammals, unlike birds, lost hair cells do not grow back, which is why noise-induced hearing loss is permanent. Exam trap Cochlear hair cells transduce sound by the direct mechanical bending of their stereocilia , which opens cation channels; potassium flows in and the cell depolarises. "Closure of sodium channels" is a garbled version of what happens in photoreceptors, not hair cells; "depolarisation by GABA release" is wrong twice over (GABA is the brain's main inhibitory transmitter, and hair cells release glutamate); "chemical signalling" describes taste and smell. The correct order of structures from the outside in is pinna, auditory canal, tympanic membrane, ossicles (malleus, incus, stapes), oval window, cochlea, organ of Corti (hair cells), auditory nerve. Any option that puts the oval window before the ossicles, or the cochlea before the eardrum, is wrong. How we hear pitch: place, frequency and volleys The ear must code two things about every sound: how loud it is and how high it is. Loudness is the easier problem. Louder sounds make the basilar membrane vibrate more vigorously, the hair cells bend further, auditory nerve fibres fire faster (rate coding, Section 3.1), and more fibres are recruited, including less sensitive ones. Pitch is harder, and the attempt to explain it produced one of the longest-running debates in sensory psychology. There are two basic ideas: that pitch is signalled by where on the basilar membrane the hair cells are most stimulated, and that it is signalled by when , the timing of the nerve impulses. Place theory. Helmholtz, whom you met as a champion of the trichromatic theory, proposed the first version in 1863 in On the Sensations of Tone . He thought of the basilar membrane as a set of transverse fibres of graded length, like the strings of a piano or a harp, each resonating to one particular frequency: short fibres near the base for high tones and long fibres near the apex for low tones. A tone would set its own fibre vibrating, the hair cells at that place would fire, and pitch would be signalled by place, an application of Muller's specific nerve energies within a single sense. This place theory (in Helmholtz's form, the resonance or "harp" theory) had a problem: the basilar membrane is not a row of separate, tensed strings but a continuous strip, and its fibres cannot vibrate independently. The decisive evidence came from Georg von Bekesy, the Hungarian physicist whose tracking audiometer you met in Section 3.4. Working first in the laboratory of the Hungarian telephone service in Budapest and later at Harvard, he showed that the basilar membrane responds to a tone not by resonating at one spot but with a travelling wave , and that the place where the wave peaks depends on frequency. For this work he received the 1961 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Key study: Bekesy watches the travelling wave (1920s to 1950s; Nobel Prize 1961) Question. What does the basilar membrane actually do when a tone enters the ear? Method. Bekesy opened the cochleas of human cadavers and of animals, made the delicate membrane visible under a microscope, and illuminated it with a flickering (stroboscopic) light that "froze" its rapid motion. He also built enlarged mechanical models of the cochlea. Result. A tone sets up a wave that travels along the membrane from the base towards the apex, like a ripple running along a shaken rope. The wave grows to a peak at one place and then dies away rapidly. High frequencies peak near the narrow, stiff base; low frequencies travel further and peak near the wide, floppy apex (Figure 3.8). Conclusion. Frequency is mapped onto place along the membrane: Helmholtz's conclusion was right, although his mechanism was wrong. Criticism. Bekesy's peaks were broad, too broad to explain how finely we can discriminate pitch, partly because he worked with dead tissue and very loud sounds. Measurements in living cochleas, beginning in the 1970s, revealed much sharper peaks, produced by the outer hair cells acting as the cochlear amplifier. Place coding is now firmly established. The cochlea is tonotopically organised, and so is every later stage of the auditory pathway. The most striking practical proof is the cochlear implant (described at the end of this section), which works by placing electrodes at different points along the cochlea: stimulating near the base produces a high-pitched sensation and stimulating further towards the apex a lower one. Place theory explains high frequencies especially well. Its weaknesses lie at the bottom of the range. Low-frequency tones, below a few hundred hertz, set much of the membrane near the apex moving with a broad, poorly defined peak, so place alone cannot explain how precisely we tell one low tone from another. And place cannot explain the missing fundamental: a tone made of 200, 300 and 400 Hz has no energy at the 100 Hz place, yet we hear a 100 Hz pitch. Frequency theory. In 1886 the British physiologist William Rutherford (1839 to 1899) proposed a radically different idea. He compared the ear to the newly invented telephone, whose diaphragm vibrates as a whole and sends an electrical signal down the wire at the same frequency as the sound. In the ear, he suggested, the whole basilar membrane vibrates in step with the sound, and the auditory nerve fires at the same frequency: a 200 Hz tone produces 200 impulses a second, and the brain reads pitch from the rate of firing. This frequency theory (also called the telephone theory, or the temporal theory) explains low pitches well, and the missing fundamental poses no problem for it, because a complex tone with components at 200, 300 and 400 Hz still repeats its overall pattern 100 times a second. Its fatal weakness is the refractory period. After firing, a neuron needs about a millisecond before it can fire again, so no single neuron can fire much more than about 1,000 times a second, yet we hear pitches up to 20,000 Hz. Frequency theory alone cannot explain pitch above about 1,000 Hz. The volley principle. In 1930 two Princeton psychologists, Ernest Glen Wever (1902 to 1991) and Charles William Bray (born 1904), recorded the electrical activity of the auditory nerve of a cat while sounds were played to it. When they amplified the signal through a loudspeaker in another room, they could understand speech spoken into the cat's ear. (Much of this "Wever-Bray effect" was later traced to the cochlear microphonic, the electrical response of the hair cells themselves.) To explain how the nerve could follow frequencies beyond the limit of any single fibre, Wever and Bray proposed the volley principle , developed in Wever's book Theory of Hearing (1949). Imagine a squad of soldiers ordered to keep up a fire of 3,000 shots a minute when each soldier can fire only 1,000 times a minute: they fire in rotation. In the same way, groups of auditory nerve fibres fire in staggered volleys. Each fibre fires only on some cycles of the sound wave, but always at the same phase of the wave (a property now called phase locking), and because different fibres take different cycles, the group as a whole fires on every cycle. Volleying lets timing information follow frequencies up to about 4,000 to 5,000 Hz, above which phase locking breaks down. The modern resolution. As with colour vision, both camps were partly right. Today's view, sometimes called the duplex or place-frequency theory, holds that the auditory system uses both codes. For low frequencies, below about 1,000 Hz, the timing of impulses follows the sound wave and carries pitch (frequency theory); from about 1,000 to about 4,000 or 5,000 Hz, volleys of timed firing and place work together; above about 5,000 Hz, where timing fails, pitch is signalled by place alone. The exact boundaries differ from textbook to textbook, but the pattern does not: frequency (temporal) coding for low pitches, place coding for high pitches. Table 3.14 summarises the theories.
