In the early 1950s Eugene Aserinsky (1921 to 1998) was a graduate student in physiology at the University of Chicago, nearly thirty years old, short of money and living with his wife and young son in a converted army barracks. His supervisor, Nathaniel Kleitman (1895 to 1999), was the most senior sleep researcher in the world, and he had given Aserinsky a modest job: watch the eyes of sleepers and see what they do. Most scientists of the day thought that sleep was simply the brain switching off, a long quiet night of nothing, so the project did not look promising. Aserinsky found an old, temperamental recording machine in a basement, repaired it as best he could and began taping electrodes around the eyes of anyone who would sleep in his laboratory. One of his first volunteers was his eight-year-old son, Armond. As the boy slept, the pens of the machine scratched out slow, lazy lines, exactly as expected. Then, deep into the night, the pens began to jerk sharply from side to side, the tracing of eyes darting about as if the sleeper were wide awake and watching something. Aserinsky assumed that his old machine had failed again. But the boy was asleep, and the jerking pens came back, in bursts, at regular intervals through the night. They came back in adult volunteers too. Aserinsky then did the obvious thing that nobody had done before: he woke people up during these bursts of eye movement and asked them what had been going on in their minds. Most of them described vivid, story-like dreams. Woken at other times, they usually reported nothing much. In 1953, Aserinsky and Kleitman published their discovery in the journal Science : sleep contains recurring periods of rapid eye movement, and these periods are when we dream. That short paper did something larger than add a fact to physiology. It showed that consciousness does not simply switch on in the morning and off at night. The mind changes state, many times a night, and each state has its own brain activity and its own kind of experience. This chapter is about those states. It begins with attention, the process that decides which tiny part of the world reaches awareness at all, and then moves to consciousness itself, the body's daily clocks, sleep, dreams, hypnosis, meditation and the changes that drugs produce. Keep Armond's dancing eyes in mind; you will meet them again in Section 5.7. 5.1 Attention: what it is, how it behaves and what captures it Lower yield · 1 Q Sit for a moment in a busy chai stall near the Mysuru bus stand. Buses roar past, the stove hisses, two men argue about cricket, a radio plays a film song, your tea is too hot, your shoe pinches and a crow is calling from the roof. All of this reaches your sense organs at once, yet at any instant you are clearly aware of only a small part of it. If your friend starts telling you about tomorrow's exam, the cricket argument fades into a murmur. Then someone at the next table says your name, and suddenly you are listening to them instead. The process that is doing this choosing is attention. Defining attention The most quoted definition comes from William James (1842 to 1910), the American philosopher-psychologist, in his Principles of Psychology of 1890: "Everyone knows what attention is. It is the taking possession by the mind, in clear and vivid form, of one out of what seem several simultaneously possible objects or trains of thought. Focalization, concentration, of consciousness are of its essence. It implies withdrawal from some things in order to deal effectively with others." Notice the two halves of that definition. Attention is a process of selection (one object out of several) and of concentration (that object is held clearly and vividly while others are withdrawn from). Modern textbooks say much the same thing in plainer words: attention is the process by which we select some information from the vast amount available to the senses and to memory, and concentrate mental resources on it. Why do we need such a process at all? Because the brain's capacity to process information fully is limited. You can register a great deal at the level of the sense organs, but you cannot analyse it all for meaning, remember it all or act on it all. Attention is the gatekeeper between the flood of sensation and the narrow channel of awareness, which is why Indian exam notes often summarise the sequence as sensation, then attention, then perception. (Sensation and perception have their own chapters, Chapters 3 and 4.) Psychologists have classified attention in several ways. A classic classification, set out by Edward Bradford Titchener (1867 to 1927), separates involuntary attention (his "primary" attention), which is pulled by the stimulus without effort (a sudden bang), from voluntary attention (his "secondary" attention), which you direct deliberately and with effort (forcing yourself to read a dull chapter), and adds a third, habitual attention (his "derived primary" attention), which began as voluntary but has become effortless through long practice and interest (the cricket fan who notices a score flashing on a distant shop television without trying). A clinical classification, proposed by McKay Moore Sohlberg and Catherine Mateer in 1987 for rehabilitating brain-injured patients, describes five levels: focused attention (responding to a single stimulus at all), sustained attention (keeping that response going over time), selective attention (holding focus in the presence of distractors), alternating attention (switching back and forth between tasks) and divided attention (responding to two tasks at the same moment). You will meet each of these again in this chapter. The characteristics of attention Classical general psychology describes attention by five characteristics. Each is a simple observation about how attention behaves, and each is a favourite source of exam questions. Selectivity. Attention picks out a few stimuli and neglects the rest. The mother asleep through traffic noise but awake at her baby's faintest whimper shows selectivity at work even during sleep. Shifting. Attention moves from one object to another, often several times a second, as when your eyes and mind move between the teacher, the blackboard and your notes. Shifting can be voluntary or forced by a new stimulus. Span. Attention can take in only a limited number of items in a single glance. This limit is called the span of attention, and it is examined in detail below. Fluctuation. Even when you try to keep attention on one unchanging stimulus, its clarity waxes and wanes. This is different from shifting: in fluctuation the object stays the same but your hold on it rises and falls. Division. Under some conditions attention can be shared between two activities at once, such as walking and talking. How far it can be divided, and why it often cannot, is the subject of Section 5.4. The span of attention The span of attention (also called the span of apprehension) is the number of separate objects that can be clearly perceived in a single brief exposure, too short for the eyes to move or for counting. The question is old. The Scottish philosopher Sir William Hamilton (1788 to 1856) remarked in his lectures that if you throw a handful of marbles on the floor, you will find it difficult to see more than six, or seven at most, at one view without confusion. Key study: Jevons and the beans (1871) The English economist and logician William Stanley Jevons (1835 to 1882) turned Hamilton's remark into an experiment, with himself as the only participant. He threw random handfuls of black beans into a shallow box, glanced at them for an instant, called out an estimate of how many there were, and then counted them. Over about a thousand trials he was never wrong with three or four beans; errors began at five, and his accuracy fell steadily as the number rose. He published the result in Nature in 1871. Later laboratory work used the tachistoscope , an apparatus that flashes a display for a fraction of a second, and arrived at the figure that general psychology textbooks still give: for unrelated items, the adult span of attention is about six to eight, usually summarised as "about seven". For perfectly accurate, effortless enumeration the limit is lower, about four; this rapid, error-free judgement of small numbers was named subitising by E. L. Kaufman and colleagues in 1949. The span of attention explains a lot of everyday design. An Indian vehicle registration number is not printed as one long string such as KA09AB1234. It is broken into short groups (a two-letter state code, a two-digit district code, a letter series and a number of no more than four digits), so that a witness to an accident can take in each group at a glance. The same reason lies behind short telephone groupings and four-digit PINs. The closely related limit on how much we can hold in mind for a few seconds, George Miller's "magical number seven, plus or minus two" of 1956, belongs to short-term memory and is taught in Chapter 7. Exam trap When a question asks why number plates carry only about four digits with a few letters, the answer is span of attention , not selective, divided or sustained attention. Do not confuse the span of attention (how many items can be apprehended in one glance; Jevons, tachistoscope studies) with the memory span of Miller (how many items can be held and repeated back). The numbers are similar; the processes are not. Fluctuation of attention Hold a watch at the distance where its ticking is just audible and listen carefully. You will notice that the ticking seems to fade out and come back, although the watch has not changed. The classical laboratory demonstration of this fluctuation of attention used the Masson disc , a white disc carrying a broken line of small grey segments that, when the disc is spun, forms faint grey rings at the threshold of visibility. A person who fixes the disc steadily reports that the faint rings appear and disappear, again and again. Ambiguous figures, such as Rubin's vase-faces figure (see Chapter 4), show something similar: attention cannot be held on one organisation for long and keeps flipping between them. Part of the fluctuation has peripheral causes (small eye movements and the adaptation of receptors), and part is central. The broader lesson is that attention is never static. It needs constant renewal, and when a task gives it nothing new, it drifts. That drift, as you will see in Section 5.5, is where daydreams come from. The determinants of attention What decides which stimulus wins? The determinants of attention are traditionally divided into two groups. External determinants (also called objective factors) are properties of the stimulus itself, and they explain why advertisers do what they do. Internal determinants (subjective factors) are properties of the person: motives, interests, expectations and attitudes. Table 5.1 sets them out. Table 5.1 The determinants of attention. Determinant What it means Everyday example Intensity Stronger stimuli capture attention more than weaker ones A loud horn; a bright floodlight Size Larger stimuli are noticed before smaller ones A full-page newspaper advertisement Contrast A stimulus that differs from its background stands out One person in white at a wedding of bright silks Change A sudden change, including sudden silence, is noticed The fan stopping during a power cut Movement Moving stimuli capture attention over still ones Blinking and scrolling shop signs Novelty New or unusual stimuli attract attention A camel walking down a Bengaluru road Repetition A repeated stimulus is more likely to be noticed (up to a point) A jingle repeated in every IPL break Motives Needs direct attention toward what satisfies them A hungry person notices every food stall Interests We attend to what we care about A cricket fan spots a score from across a room Mental set Readiness to perceive a particular stimulus A runner waiting for the starter's gun Attitudes and emotions Beliefs and feelings bias what we notice An anxious student notices every frown Two of these deserve a further word. Mental set is a temporary readiness to perceive or respond in a particular way, created by instructions, expectation or recent experience. A student waiting for exam results online sees her roll number leap out of a long list because she is set for it. Repetition, meanwhile, cuts both ways. A stimulus repeated a few times gains attention, but a stimulus repeated endlessly without change loses it, because the nervous system habituates to it. This is why advertisers keep changing the details of a campaign while keeping the brand the same, and why external and internal determinants usually work together: the size and colour of the hoarding get your eyes there, and your hunger or interest decides whether you stay. Exam trap Learn which list each determinant belongs to. Intensity, size, contrast, change, movement, novelty, repetition, colour and position are external (objective). Motives, interests, mental set, attitudes, emotions and habit are internal (subjective). "Fluctuation" and "span" are not determinants at all; they are characteristics of attention. Also keep shifting (attention moves to a different object) apart from fluctuation (attention to the same object waxes and wanes). 5.2 Selective listening: filters, attenuators and late selection Medium yield · 5 Qs The chai stall showed you a puzzle. You can follow your friend's voice through a wall of noise, and yet your name, spoken by a stranger, still gets through. How can the mind be ignoring the other voices and also listening to them? This puzzle drove the first great theoretical debate of cognitive psychology, and it was fought with headphones. The cocktail party problem and dichotic listening The British engineer Colin Cherry (1914 to 1979), working on problems of communication, named the puzzle in 1953. He called it the cocktail party problem : how do we manage to follow one conversation when many people are talking at once? The everyday experience of hearing your own name across a crowded room, even though you were not listening to that conversation, is called the cocktail party phenomenon (or cocktail party effect). Key study: Cherry's shadowing experiments (1953) Cherry invented the method that dominated attention research for twenty years. In dichotic listening , a person wears headphones and a different message is played to each ear. To make sure they really attend to one ear, they must repeat the attended message aloud, word for word, as it arrives, a technique called shadowing . Afterwards they are asked what they noticed in the other, unattended ear. The results were striking. People could report almost nothing about the content of the unattended message. They did not notice when it switched from English to German, or when the speech was played backwards. But they almost always noticed physical changes: a switch from a male to a female voice, or a pure tone in place of speech. Cherry concluded that the unattended message is processed only for its physical features, not for meaning. A few years later the British psychologist Neville Moray added two findings that pulled in opposite directions. First, in 1959 he showed that a short list of words repeated 35 times in the unattended ear left no trace in memory: people did not recognise the words afterwards. That supported Cherry. Second, about a third of his participants noticed when an instruction in the unattended ear was preceded by their own name. Your name, it seems, can break through a channel you are not listening to. This is the laboratory version of the cocktail party phenomenon, and any theory of attention has to explain both halves of Moray's result. Broadbent's filter model (1958): early selection The first theory came from Donald Eric Broadbent (1926 to 1993), a British psychologist who had served in the Royal Air Force and studied the problems of pilots and air traffic controllers swamped with radio messages. In his book Perception and Communication (1958) he proposed the filter model of attention. This was the first major theory to treat the mind explicitly as an information-processing system, a sequence of stages through which information flows, like messages through a telephone exchange, and it is often described as the starting point of the information-processing approach in cognitive psychology. Broadbent's model has three parts (see the top row of Figure 5.1). All incoming messages first enter a sensory buffer , a brief store that holds them for a second or two. Next comes a selective filter , which lets through only one message, chosen on the basis of a physical characteristic such as which ear it arrives at, the pitch of the voice or its loudness. Everything else is blocked. Finally, the selected message passes into a limited-capacity channel where it is analysed for meaning and can enter awareness and memory. Because the filter works on physical features before any analysis of meaning, Broadbent's is the classic early selection model, and because the filter passes one channel and blocks the other completely, like a railway switch, it is sometimes called an all-or-none or "switch" model. The filter is also the first bottleneck in attention theory: a narrow point in the system through which only a little information can pass at once. Broadbent supported his model with the split-span experiment (1954). Three pairs of digits were played simultaneously, one digit of each pair to each ear (for example 7 to the left ear and 2 to the right, then 4 and 9, then 3 and 6). People found it much easier to recall the digits ear by ear (743, then 296) than pair by pair (72, 49, 36). Broadbent's explanation was that the filter is set to one ear at a time; recalling by ear means switching the filter only once, while recalling by pairs means switching it back and forth. The model fitted Cherry's findings well, but it could not survive long. If the unattended message is blocked before meaning is analysed, how could Moray's participants hear their own names? And there was more trouble. Jeffrey Gray and A. A. I. Wedderburn (1960) played "Dear 7 Jane" to one ear and "9 Aunt 6" to the other; people reported "Dear Aunt Jane", grouping by meaning across the ears, not by ear as the filter predicts. Anne Marie Treisman (1935 to 2018) found in 1960 that when the story being shadowed suddenly switched to the other ear, people often followed the story into the "wrong" ear for a word or two before catching themselves: meaning in the unattended ear was guiding them. And in 1972 Robert Corteen and B. Wood conditioned people to expect a mild electric shock when they heard certain city names; later, when those names (and even other city names never paired with shock) were played in the unattended ear, the participants showed a galvanic skin response, although they could not report hearing the words. Something in the unattended channel was being analysed for meaning. Broadbent (1958): early selection Two messages Sensory buffer Filter (all-or-none) Meaning analysis Response Unattended message is blocked at the filter, before its meaning is analysed Treisman (1964): attenuation Two messages Sensory buffer Attenuator (turns down) Dictionary units Response Unattended message passes weakly; low-threshold words (your name) still fire Deutsch and Deutsch (1963): late selection Two messages Sensory buffer Full analysis of both Selection (late) Response Both messages are analysed for meaning; selection happens just before response Figure 5.1 Three answers to "where is the bottleneck?". Broadbent places a complete block early, Treisman turns the unattended message down instead of off, and Deutsch and Deutsch let everything be analysed for meaning and select only at the response. Treisman's attenuation model (1964) Treisman's answer, set out fully in 1964, kept Broadbent's idea of an early stage that works on physical features but changed what that stage does. In her attenuation model , the filter is not a switch but a volume control, an attenuator . The attended message passes at full strength; unattended messages are not blocked but turned down, so that a weakened version still travels on to the next stage (middle row of Figure 5.1). The next stage is a mental dictionary of dictionary units , one for each word you know, and each unit has its own threshold , the amount of activation it needs before it fires and the word reaches awareness. Thresholds are not equal. Words that are personally important (your own name, "fire", "help") have permanently low thresholds, so even an attenuated signal is enough to fire them. Words that are made probable by the context of the attended message have their thresholds temporarily lowered too, which is why Treisman's participants followed the story into the wrong ear: the next word of the story was expected, so its unit fired even from the weakened channel. Treisman also proposed that analysis runs through a hierarchy, from physical cues to syllable patterns to individual words to grammar and meaning, and that when capacity runs short, the later stages of analysis are simply not carried out for the unattended message. The attenuation model explains everything that troubled Broadbent: Moray's own-name effect, Gray and Wedderburn's grouping by meaning, Corteen and Wood's skin responses and Treisman's own ear-switching. That is why it is the standard answer when a question asks which model best explains the cocktail party phenomenon. It is also why Treisman's theory is called a filter-attenuation theory: it is a modified filter theory, still early selection in spirit, but leaky. Exam trap "Filter-attenuation theory" is Treisman , not Broadbent (pure filter), Johnston or Heinz (multimode theory). The attenuation model is dated 1964 (her ear-switching experiment was 1960). Some Indian notes give 1980 for the attenuation model; 1980 is the year of a different Treisman theory, feature integration theory (Treisman and Gelade), taught in Section 5.3. If a question asks which model "better explains the cocktail party effect", the answer is the attenuator model; Broadbent's switch model cannot explain why your name gets through. Late selection: Deutsch and Deutsch (1963) and Norman (1968) At the opposite extreme, J. Anthony Deutsch and Diana Deutsch argued in 1963 that there is no early filter at all. In their late selection model, every incoming message is fully analysed, including for meaning, automatically and without capacity limits. The bottleneck comes only at the end, when the system must decide which analysed message to respond to, remember or become aware of (bottom row of Figure 5.1). Selection is based on importance : the most pertinent message wins the response. On this view you do understand the cricket argument at the next table; you simply do not respond to it, and you will not remember it, unless it becomes more important than your friend's voice. Donald Arthur Norman (born 1935) refined the late-selection view in 1968. He proposed that what gets selected depends on two things added together: the strength of the sensory input (how loud and clear it is) and its pertinence (how relevant it is to current goals and expectations). A faint word that is highly pertinent can beat a loud word that is irrelevant. Norman's idea gives a late-selection account of the own-name effect: your name is so pertinent that it is selected even though the voice saying it is faint. So which is right, early or late? The evidence pointed both ways. Treisman and Riley (1969) found that people detected target words far more often in the shadowed message than in the unattended one, which is awkward for a theory in which both are fully analysed. Yet the skin-response and own-name findings show some analysis of meaning in the unattended channel. The debate was eventually resolved not by declaring a winner but by asking a better question: when does selection happen early, and when late? Flexible selection: Johnston and Heinz (1978) and Lavie's perceptual load theory William A. Johnston and Steven P. Heinz proposed in 1978 that the bottleneck has no fixed position. In their multimode theory (flexible multimode model), selection can occur at any of three stages: at the stage of sensory representation (early, on physical features), at the stage of semantic representation (late, on meaning), or after both have been built and are entering consciousness. The listener chooses the mode, but there is a price: the later the selection, the more mental effort and capacity it consumes. Johnston and Heinz showed that when two messages differed physically (one male voice, one female), people selected early and had capacity left for a secondary task; when the messages could be told apart only by meaning, selection had to be late and secondary-task performance suffered. Attention is, in their phrase, flexible but costly. The most influential modern resolution is the perceptual load theory of Nilli Lavie , developed in the mid-1990s (with Yehoshua Tsal in 1994, and in her own paper of 1995). Lavie argued that perception has limited capacity and that it runs automatically until that capacity is full. When the main task carries a high perceptual load (many items, hard discriminations), it uses up all the capacity, so nothing is left over for distractors and they are not processed at all: selection looks early. When the main task is easy ( low perceptual load ), spare capacity spills over automatically onto the distractors, which are then processed and can interfere: selection looks late. The early-late debate, on this view, was a debate about task difficulty. A practical prediction follows: if you want to stop being distracted, a harder, more absorbing task helps more than willpower does. (Lavie added that a high load on working memory, a cognitive load, has the opposite effect and makes distraction worse, because it weakens the control needed to ignore distractors.) Deutsch and Deutsch's late selection ( 1963 ) came before Treisman's full attenuation model ( 1964 ), although textbooks usually teach Treisman first. Broadbent ( 1958 ) is the answer to "the first major theoretical effort in information-processing psychology". And "bottleneck" in an attention question refers to the narrow stage in processing; it is not a name for the cocktail party phenomenon (the "bottleneck effect" in biology is something else entirely, a sharp fall in a population's genetic variety). 5.3 Visual attention: spotlights, binding and blindness to the obvious Lower yield · 1 Q The early debate was conducted with the ears, but vision is our dominant sense, and from the 1970s most attention research moved to the eyes. The questions changed shape. What is visual attention like : a beam that sweeps across the scene, or something more flexible? What is it for , beyond picking one thing out? And how much of the visual world do we actually see when we are not attending to it? The answer to the last question turned out to be: far less than you think. The spotlight and the zoom lens You can attend to something without looking straight at it. Fix your eyes on this word, and without moving them, notice the margin of the page. Moving attention with the eyes is overt attention ; moving attention while the eyes stay still is covert attention . Michael I. Posner (born 1936), whose experiments are described below, likened covert attention to a spotlight : a beam of limited width that illuminates one region of space, so that whatever falls inside it is processed faster and better, and that can be moved from place to place independently of the eyes. William James had anticipated the idea in 1890 when he described consciousness as having a bright focus , surrounded by a dimmer margin or fringe . A real spotlight has a fixed beam. Charles Eriksen and James St James argued in 1986 that visual attention is more like a zoom lens : you can widen the attended area to take in a whole scene or narrow it to a single letter, but there is a trade-off. The wider the area, the lower the resolution; the same amount of processing power is spread more thinly. A batsman watching the bowler's hand narrows his zoom lens to a tiny patch of space; a fielder at deep midwicket keeps it wide to watch the whole ground. Later work found that under some conditions attention can even be split between two separate locations, like two spotlights, so both metaphors are best treated as approximations of a flexible system. Posner's cueing task: endogenous and exogenous attention Key study: Posner's spatial cueing paradigm (1980) Posner asked people to keep their eyes on a central point and press a key as soon as a light appeared in a box to the left or right. Before the light, a cue appeared. Sometimes it was a central cue, an arrow at fixation pointing left or right; sometimes it was a peripheral cue, a brief brightening of one of the boxes. Most cues were valid (the target appeared where the cue indicated), some were invalid (the target appeared on the other side) and on some trials a neutral cue gave no information. Responses were fastest after valid cues, slowest after invalid cues and in between after neutral cues. Because the eyes never moved, the benefit and the cost could only mean that attention itself had moved, covertly, to the cued location. The two kinds of cue revealed two systems. An arrow at fixation must be interpreted and used deliberately; this is endogenous attention (also called voluntary, goal-directed or top-down attention), controlled by the person's intentions. It takes a few hundred milliseconds to deploy and, crucially, people ignore central arrows if they learn the arrows are usually wrong. A flash in the periphery grabs attention whether you want it to or not; this is exogenous attention (reflexive, stimulus-driven or bottom-up), and it is fast and automatic, pulling attention even when the flash predicts nothing. You use endogenous attention when you search a crowded railway platform for your friend's red bag; exogenous attention takes over when a pigeon suddenly flaps up beside you. Later imaging work by Maurizio Corbetta and Gordon Shulman (2002) mapped these onto a dorsal fronto-parietal network for goal-directed attention and a right-hemisphere ventral network that acts as a "circuit breaker", redirecting attention to unexpected events. Posner himself, with Steven Petersen in 1990, went on to describe three attention networks: alerting (getting ready), orienting (moving attention to a location) and executive control (resolving conflict). The peripheral flash has one more surprise. If the target appears very soon after an uninformative flash (within about a quarter of a second), responses at the flashed location are faster. If it appears later than about 300 milliseconds, responses at that location become slower than elsewhere. Attention, having been pulled to the spot and found nothing, is now biased against going back. Posner and Yoav Cohen described this inhibition of return in 1984. Its likely function is to make visual search efficient: once you have checked a location, you are discouraged from wasting time checking it again, rather like a person searching a house who does not reopen a cupboard she has just looked in. Feature integration theory (Treisman and Gelade, 1980) Look at a ripe red tomato. Its redness is analysed by colour-sensitive neurons, its roundness by shape-sensitive neurons, its position by yet other circuits, in different parts of the visual brain. Yet you see one red, round object in one place, not a floating redness next to a floating roundness. How are the separate features put back together? This is the binding problem , and Anne Treisman's second great theory, developed with Garry Gelade in 1980, proposed that attention is the solution. Feature integration theory divides visual processing into two stages. In the first, preattentive stage , simple features (colour, orientation, size, curvature, motion) are registered automatically, in parallel, across the whole visual field, each in its own feature map. No attention is needed and no effort is felt. In the second, focused attention stage , attention is directed to one location at a time and acts as a kind of glue: it combines the features found at that location into a single object. Because the glue can be applied to only one location at a time, this stage is serial. The theory makes a clear prediction about visual search, tested by Treisman and Gelade. Suppose you must find a target among distractors. In feature search the target differs from every distractor by a single feature: a red letter among green letters, a vertical line among horizontals. The target is found at the preattentive stage and seems to leap out of the display, a phenomenon called pop-out , and search time hardly changes whether there are 5 distractors or 30. In conjunction search the target is defined only by a combination of features, say a green T among green X's and brown T's. No single feature map can find it; attention must visit items one by one, binding features at each, so search time rises in a straight line with the number of items. Figure 5.2 shows the pattern. Treisman and Gelade also found that when the target was absent, the conjunction slope was about twice as steep as when it was present, exactly what a serial, self-terminating search predicts: on average you find a present target halfway through, but you must check every item to be sure it is absent. 400 800 1200 1 5 15 30 Number of items in the display Search time (ms) Conjunction search (serial: about 29 ms per item) Feature search (parallel pop-out: nearly flat) Figure 5.2 Feature versus conjunction search (target-present trials, approximate values in the pattern reported by Treisman and Gelade, 1980). A target defined by one feature pops out, so search time stays almost flat as the display grows; a target defined by a conjunction of features needs serial attention to each item, so search time climbs steadily. If attention is the glue, then features that are not attended should sometimes be glued wrongly. They are. Treisman and Hilary Schmidt (1982) flashed displays of coloured letters very briefly while people's attention was occupied by a second task. Participants often reported seeing, with confidence, combinations that were not there, such as a red X when the display contained a red T and a green X. These illusory conjunctions are strong evidence that features are registered separately and combined only with attention. Patients with damage to both parietal lobes (Balint's syndrome), who have severe difficulty directing spatial attention, produce illusory conjunctions even with long, leisurely displays. Later research qualified the theory (Jeremy Wolfe's guided search model showed that feature information can guide the serial stage, so many conjunction searches are faster than pure serial search), but the distinction between parallel feature detection and attention-dependent binding remains one of the most important ideas in the field. Exam trap Anne Treisman gave us two theories: the attenuation model of auditory selection (1964) and feature integration theory of visual binding (1980, with Gelade). Questions mixing them up are common. In feature integration theory, the preattentive stage is automatic and parallel (features), the focused attention stage is serial and binds features into objects; pop-out belongs to feature search, linear search slopes to conjunction search, and illusory conjunctions are the error that occurs when attention is unavailable. Blind to the obvious: inattentional blindness and change blindness Most people believe that they see everything in front of their eyes and that anything unusual would immediately catch their attention. Two families of experiments show that this belief is false. Key study: the invisible gorilla (Simons and Chabris, 1999) Daniel J. Simons and Christopher F. Chabris , then at Harvard University, filmed two teams of students, one in white shirts and one in black, passing basketballs among themselves. Viewers were asked to count the passes made by the white team, a task that demands close attention. Partway through the clip a woman in a full gorilla suit walks into the middle of the players, turns to the camera, thumps her chest and walks off; she is in full view for several seconds. Around half of the viewers did not see her at all, and many refused to believe she had been there until the clip was replayed. When viewers counted the black team's passes instead, far more of them (83 per cent) noticed the black gorilla, because her colour now matched what they were attending to. The gorilla study is the best-known demonstration of inattentional blindness : the failure to notice a fully visible but unexpected object or event because attention is engaged elsewhere. The term was introduced by Arien Mack and Irvin Rock , whose 1998 book reported that many people failed to see an unexpected shape flashed near the point they were fixating while they judged which arm of a cross was longer. The lesson is that seeing is not just a matter of light reaching the retina; without attention, an object may never reach awareness at all. Change blindness is a related but different failure: the failure to notice that something in a scene has changed , even a large change, when the change happens during a brief interruption such as an eye movement, a blink, a cut in a film or a flicker. Ronald Rensink, Kevin O'Regan and James Clark (1997) showed that people can stare for many seconds at two alternating photographs, separated by a brief blank, without spotting that a large object (a jet engine on an aeroplane, for example) appears in one and not the other; this is the flicker paradigm . In a famous field version by Simons and Daniel Levin (1998), an experimenter stopped pedestrians on a university campus to ask for directions; while they talked, two workmen carried a door between them, and behind the door the experimenter was replaced by a different person in different clothes. About half the pedestrians carried on giving directions to the new person without noticing the switch. Continuity errors in films, which audiences almost never spot, are everyday change blindness. Keep the two apart. In inattentional blindness, an unexpected object is present and is not seen at all. In change blindness, the person may well see both versions of the scene but fails to notice the difference between them, because noticing a change requires attending to the changed item and comparing it across time. Neither should be confused with perceptual constancy , the tendency to see objects as having stable size, shape and colour although their image on the retina changes (taught in Chapter 4); constancy is a success of perception, not a failure of attention. Exam trap "Failing to notice significant changes in the environment, even obvious ones" is change blindness (Rensink and colleagues; the Simons and Levin door study). Failing to see an unexpected object that is in plain view while busy with another task is inattentional blindness (Mack and Rock; the gorilla). If the question stresses change , choose change blindness; if it stresses an unexpected object , choose inattentional blindness. The attentional blink Attention is limited not only in space but in time. In 1992 Jane Raymond, Kimron Shapiro and Karen Arnell used rapid serial visual presentation : letters flashed one after another in the same place at about ten per second. Participants had to identify a first target (say, a white letter among black ones) and then report whether a second target (say, the letter X) appeared later in the stream. If the second target came within roughly 200 to 500 milliseconds after the first, it was very often missed; before and after that window it was seen well. This brief "blindness" after a target is called the attentional blink . The usual explanation is that attention is still busy consolidating the first target into memory when the second arrives, so the second decays before it can be processed. (Curiously, a second target that comes immediately after the first, with no item between, is often spared, apparently because it slips into the same attentional episode.) Divided attention asks the reverse question: how far can we do two things at once? You can walk and talk, and an experienced driver can drive and hold a conversation. But a learner driver cannot, and nobody can hold two conversations at the same time. Why do some pairs of tasks combine easily and others not at all? Three answers have been proposed: that we have one limited pool of capacity, that we have several pools, and that practice makes some processes stop needing capacity at all. Kahneman's capacity model (1973) In his book Attention and Effort (1973), Daniel Kahneman (1934 to 2024), later a Nobel laureate in economics, replaced the bottleneck with a different picture. Attention, he proposed, is a single, limited pool of mental effort, or capacity , that can be shared out among activities. This is the capacity model (also called resource or central capacity theory). Two tasks can be performed together as long as their combined demand does not exceed the capacity available; when it does, performance on one or both suffers. The amount of capacity is not fixed: it rises and falls with arousal, so that a drowsy person has less to share out and a moderately alert one has more. How the capacity is divided depends on an allocation policy , which is shaped by four influences: enduring dispositions (built-in tendencies to attend to novel or moving stimuli, or to one's own name), momentary intentions (what you are trying to do right now), the evaluation of demands (the system's judgement of how much each task needs) and the current level of arousal. Kahneman measured effort through the size of the pupil, which widens as a mental task becomes harder. The capacity model explained why difficult tasks interfere more than easy ones, and why practice, which makes tasks easier, makes them easier to combine. But it had a weakness: it predicts that two equally difficult tasks should interfere equally with a third, and they do not. What matters is how similar they are. Multiple resource theory and dual-task interference The study of what happens when people perform two tasks together is called the dual-task paradigm , and its main finding is that interference depends heavily on similarity. In a striking demonstration, Alan Allport, Barbara Antonis and Patricia Reynolds (1972) found that skilled pianists could sight-read music while shadowing speech with little loss on either task, although shadowing two spoken messages would have been impossible. Christopher Wickens captured this in his multiple resource theory (1984, refined in later work). Instead of a single pool, Wickens proposed several separate pools of resources, defined along a few dimensions: the stage of processing (perceptual and cognitive processing versus responding), the modality of input (visual versus auditory), the code of processing (spatial versus verbal) and, within vision, focal versus peripheral (ambient) vision. Two tasks that draw on different pools can be time-shared well; two tasks that compete for the same pool interfere. Driving (visual, spatial, manual) combines reasonably well with listening to the radio (auditory, verbal), and badly with reading a text message (visual, verbal, manual). Practice also changes what can be combined. In a famous study, Elizabeth Spelke, William Hirst and Ulric Neisser (1976) trained two students for several months to read short stories while writing down words dictated to them. At first their reading speed and comprehension collapsed; after weeks of practice they read as fast and understood as well as when reading alone, while writing to dictation. Practice had apparently turned one of the tasks into something that no longer needed much capacity. Multitasking and the phone in the car What people call multitasking is, for most tasks, rapid switching between them. Every switch has a switch cost : responses are slower and more error-prone just after a switch than when the same task is repeated, as Robert Rogers and Stephen Monsell showed in 1995. The real-world consequences are serious. David Strayer and William Johnston (2001) had people perform a simulated driving task while talking on a mobile phone; they missed nearly twice as many red lights and braked more slowly than when driving alone, and a hands-free phone was no better than a hand-held one. Listening to the radio or a recorded book did not have this effect. The problem is the conversation, not the hands. Later work by Strayer's group found that drivers talking on phones were impaired about as much as drivers at the legal limit for alcohol, and that they looked straight at roadside objects and then failed to remember them: inattentional blindness at the wheel. A two-wheeler rider in Bengaluru with a phone wedged inside his helmet is not doing two things well; he is doing two things badly. Automatic versus controlled processing Spelke's students point to the third answer. Some mental processes demand attention and effort; others run off by themselves. In 1975 Michael Posner and Charles Snyder proposed three criteria for an automatic process : it occurs without intention, it occurs without conscious awareness, and it does not interfere with other ongoing mental activity. Two years later Richard M. Shiffrin and Walter Schneider (1977) made the distinction the basis of a major theory. Controlled processes are slow, serial, effortful, limited by capacity, open to awareness and flexible: you can change them at once when the situation changes. Automatic processes are fast, run in parallel, need little or no capacity, are hard to stop once triggered and are inflexible. Table 5.3 lists the contrasts. Key study: Shiffrin and Schneider's search experiments (1977) Participants memorised a set of up to four characters and then searched rapidly presented displays for any of them. In the consistent mapping condition, targets and distractors never swapped roles (for example, targets were always consonants and distractors always digits). In the varied mapping condition, the same characters served as targets on some trials and distractors on others. With consistent mapping, search speed hardly depended on how many items had to be compared: search had become automatic and parallel. With varied mapping, every extra item added time: search was controlled and serial. When participants were trained for 2,100 trials with one set of letters as targets and another as distractors, search became automatic; when the roles were then reversed, it took nearly 1,000 trials before performance recovered even to its starting level. Automatic processes, once learned, are fast but stubborn. Table 5.3 Automatic versus controlled processing (Posner and Snyder, 1975; Shiffrin and Schneider, 1977). Patricia Devine (1989) applied it to prejudice: because cultural stereotypes are learned by everyone in a society, they are activated automatically in high- and low-prejudiced people alike when a member of the group is encountered; what distinguishes low-prejudiced people is that they use controlled processing to override the activated stereotype and replace it with their own egalitarian beliefs. (The social psychology of prejudice is taught in the Social Psychology book.) And the stubbornness of automatic processes produces the most famous interference effect in psychology. The Stroop effect (1935) Key study: Stroop's colour-word experiments (1935) John Ridley Stroop (1897 to 1973), an American psychologist, published "Studies of interference in serial verbal reactions" in 1935, based on his doctoral research at George Peabody College. In one experiment, people simply read aloud colour words printed in conflicting ink colours (the word RED printed in green ink) and were barely slower than when reading the same words printed in black. In another, they had to name the ink colour of such words, saying "green" to RED printed in green, and here performance collapsed: naming the ink colours of 100 conflicting words took about 74 per cent longer than naming the colours of plain coloured patches, and errors rose. A third experiment showed that days of practice reduced the interference but did not abolish it. Stroop himself soon left experimental work to teach the Bible, never knowing that his dissertation would become one of the most cited studies in psychology. The Stroop effect is the slowing of colour naming (and the rise in errors) when the word and the ink colour conflict. Notice its asymmetry. Words interfere strongly with naming colours, but colours hardly interfere with reading words. Why? The most widely accepted explanation is in terms of automaticity. For a literate adult, reading is so overlearned that it is automatic: you cannot look at a familiar word and not read it. Naming an ink colour, by contrast, is a controlled process that needs attention. When the two conflict, the automatically produced word ("red") competes with the deliberately produced colour name ("green") at the stage of choosing a response, and resolving that conflict takes time. A related account, the relative speed of processing explanation, says that words are simply processed faster than colours, so the word's name arrives at the response stage first and must be suppressed. Later connectionist models (Jonathan Cohen, Kevin Dunbar and James McClelland, 1990) recast both ideas in terms of the strength of the pathways involved: the word-reading pathway, trained by years of practice, is stronger. What, then, does the Stroop effect demonstrate? Above all, a limit on selective attention : we cannot completely filter out a stimulus dimension whose processing is automatic, even when we are told to ignore it and it hurts our performance to attend to it. Within a single stimulus, one attribute (the word) dominates the other (the ink colour) in controlling the response. It is also a measure of interference in reaction time due to conflicting information, and of the ability to inhibit a dominant response, which is why the Stroop task is one of the standard tests of the inhibition component of executive function and why it is used clinically to assess frontal lobe and attention problems. The emotional Stroop task applies the same logic: people name the ink colour of emotional and neutral words, and anxious individuals are slower with words related to their worries (a person with a spider phobia slows down on "web" and "hairy"), revealing an attentional bias toward threat. Exam trap The Stroop effect is an attention phenomenon: specifically, a failure of selective attention caused by interference from automatic word reading. It is not primarily about long-term memory retrieval, working memory, procedural memory, perception or language development, which are the usual distractors, and it does not show improved recall for related items or better accuracy under divided attention. One past paper (RML 2024) asks what the Stroop effect is "an account of" and keys stimulus dominance : one dimension of the stimulus (the printed word) dominates the other (its ink colour). "Semantic dominance" is the tempting wrong option because the intruding word is meaningful, but the keyed term describes one attribute of the stimulus overpowering another; "instructional" and "conceptual" dominance are not terms used for this effect. Vigilance and sustained attention Some jobs require attention not to many things at once but to one thing for a very long time, while waiting for something rare to happen. Air traffic controllers watching radar screens, radar operators, airport baggage screeners, lifeguards and nurses monitoring intensive-care displays all depend on sustained attention , the ability to keep attention on a task over a prolonged period; when the events to be detected are infrequent and unpredictable, it is usually called vigilance . Key study: the Mackworth clock (1948) During the Second World War, the Royal Air Force noticed that radar operators hunting for enemy submarines missed more signals as their watches went on. Norman Mackworth built a laboratory model of the problem. A pointer moved around a blank clock face in small regular jumps; occasionally, and unpredictably, it made a double jump, and the observer had to press a key whenever this happened. Over a two-hour watch, detection fell sharply, with the largest drop within the first half hour; a short break or a telephone message restored it. Mackworth had demonstrated the vigilance decrement : the decline in detection over time on a monotonous monitoring task. Two kinds of explanation have been offered for the decrement. One is that boring, understimulating tasks lower arousal, so the observer becomes less alert. The other, now more favoured, is that vigilance is hard mental work that steadily depletes attentional resources; people rate vigilance tasks as surprisingly effortful and stressful. Signal detection analysis (Chapter 3) adds that part of the decrement is a shift in criterion: tired observers become more cautious about saying "yes, there it is". Clinically, sustained attention is measured with the Continuous Performance Test (respond to a rare target letter in a long stream), and it is one of the first functions to suffer from sleep loss, as you will see in Section 5.8. Brain recordings provide another window: when a rare target appears among frequent non-targets (the oddball task), the brain produces a positive event-related potential about 300 milliseconds later, the P300, which indexes the allocation of attention to the target and is reduced in conditions such as schizophrenia and Alzheimer's disease. Exam trap Air traffic controllers and radar readers are the textbook example of sustained attention (vigilance) , not selective attention (choosing one input among several), divided attention (two tasks at once) or "perceptual attention" (not a standard category). The classic experiment is Mackworth's clock test (1948). Clinical link Disorders of attention are among the commonest problems a clinical psychologist assesses. In attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity begin in childhood (the disorder itself is covered in the Disorders book). In hemispatial neglect , usually after damage to the right parietal lobe, patients ignore the left side of space: they eat from only the right half of the plate, shave half the face and bisect a horizontal line far to the right, although their vision is intact. Delirium is defined by an acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention and awareness, and that attentional disturbance, together with its acute onset, fluctuating course and usually identifiable (often reversible) medical cause, is the most reliable feature separating it from dementia, which begins insidiously and progresses slowly, with attention relatively preserved early. Attention is measured with tests such as the Continuous Performance Test, the Test of Everyday Attention, the Stroop and the Trail Making Test (taught in the Psychological Assessment book). 5.5 Consciousness: definitions, levels and the brain High yield · 18 Qs Everything in the last four sections was about how information gets selected. But selected for what? The usual answer is: for awareness. The gorilla that was not attended to was not experienced; the word that broke through the attenuator was. Attention is, very often, the gateway to consciousness. It is time to ask what lies on the other side of the gate. What consciousness is Consciousness is one of those words that everyone understands until asked to define it. A workable definition, used in most introductory texts, is that consciousness is our awareness of ourselves and of our environment: of our sensations, perceptions, thoughts, feelings and memories at any given moment. It helps to separate two meanings. The first is consciousness as a level or state of wakefulness, running from coma through drowsiness to alert wakefulness; this is what a doctor checks at a road accident. The second is consciousness as content : what, in particular, you are aware of right now. The two can come apart. A patient in a vegetative state opens the eyes and has sleep-wake cycles (wakefulness is present) but shows no sign of awareness, whereas a patient with locked-in syndrome , after damage to the brainstem, is fully aware but almost completely paralysed, able to communicate only with eye movements. The level of consciousness is measured clinically with the Glasgow Coma Scale , published by the neurosurgeons Graham Teasdale and Bryan Jennett in 1974. It scores three responses: eye opening (1 to 4), verbal response (1 to 5) and motor response (1 to 6), giving a total from 3 (deep coma) to 15 (fully alert). A score of 8 or less is generally taken to mean coma. The scale measures consciousness, not attention, memory or intelligence, and it is used every day in emergency rooms across India. William James and the stream of consciousness The founders of experimental psychology tried to study consciousness by breaking it into elements. Wilhelm Wundt and Edward Titchener trained observers to introspect, to report the sensations, images and feelings that made up an experience, much as a chemist breaks a compound into its elements. Titchener described introspection as a highly specialised form of self-observation, and his structuralism set out to describe the components of consciousness, their combinations and their connections (Chapter 1). William James thought this was a mistake. Consciousness, he wrote in 1890, "does not appear to itself chopped up in bits ... It is nothing jointed; it flows. A 'river' or a 'stream' are the metaphors by which it is most naturally described. In talking of it hereafter, let us call it the stream of thought, of consciousness, or of subjective life." The phrase stream of consciousness has belonged to James ever since, and it later gave its name to a style of novel-writing that imitates the flow of thought. James listed five characteristics of this stream. Every thought is part of a personal consciousness: it belongs to someone. Within each person, consciousness is always changing : no state, once gone, can recur exactly. It is sensibly continuous : even after sleep, you know that your thoughts this morning belong to the same self as last night's. It deals with objects independent of itself : thought is always about something. And it is selective : it is interested in some parts of its objects to the exclusion of others, which is James's link between consciousness and attention. One feature of the stream of consciousness has received particularly intense research attention: daydreaming , the spontaneous drift of thought away from the task and the surroundings toward fantasies, memories and plans. From the 1960s the American psychologist Jerome L. Singer (1924 to 2010) showed that daydreaming is not a sign of laziness or disorder but a normal, almost universal part of mental life, and that it can serve planning, creativity and self-reflection. More recently, Matthew Killingsworth and Daniel Gilbert (2010) used a smartphone app to interrupt thousands of people at random moments; minds were wandering in nearly half of the samples, and people were less happy when their minds wandered than when they were focused, whatever they were doing. Brain imaging has linked mind wandering to the default mode network , a set of midline brain regions that become more active when we are not engaged in an external task. Exam trap "Stream of consciousness" was coined by William James ( Principles of Psychology , 1890), not by Jung, Wundt or Skinner. Wundt studied the elements of consciousness by introspection; James opposed this with the image of a flowing stream, which is why he is linked with functionalism. The feature of the stream that has received the most research attention is daydreaming , not gender differences, brain-wave patterns or eye movements. Levels of consciousness: Freud's iceberg and the modern unconscious James described the stream as it appears to the person having it. Sigmund Freud (1856 to 1939) insisted that most of mental life never appears in the stream at all. In The Interpretation of Dreams (1900) he set out what is now called his topographic model of the mind, which divides it into three regions, usually drawn as an iceberg (Figure 5.3). The conscious is whatever you are aware of at this moment, a small tip above the water. The preconscious holds material that is not in awareness right now but can be recalled at will without difficulty: your mobile number, what you ate yesterday, the name of your school. The unconscious , by far the largest region, holds wishes, impulses and memories that are actively kept out of awareness by repression because they would cause anxiety; they cannot be recalled at will and are known only indirectly, through dreams, slips of the tongue, symptoms and the free associations of the analytic patient. Freud's principle of psychic determinism held that nothing in mental life is accidental: even a slip of the tongue (a parapraxis , popularly a "Freudian slip") is caused by unconscious motives. In 1923 Freud added a second, structural model of id, ego and superego (the id, wholly unconscious, works on the pleasure principle; the ego works on the reality principle; the superego is the internalised conscience); that model, and psychoanalysis as a theory of personality, belong to the Personality book. The picture of behaviour driven by unconscious inner forces that lie largely beyond the person's control, and shaped by early childhood experience, is the heart of the psychodynamic perspective (Chapter 2). waterline Preconscious Unconscious (the largest part) Conscious what you are aware of right now (the sentence you are reading) Preconscious out of awareness, recallable at will (your mobile number, a friend's name) Unconscious kept out of awareness by repression; known only indirectly, through dreams, slips of the tongue and symptoms Figure 5.3 Freud's topographic model drawn as an iceberg. Only the tip is conscious; the preconscious lies just below the surface and can be brought up at will; the much larger unconscious is held down by repression and shows itself only indirectly. Freud's specific claims about repression and the Oedipus complex have fared poorly in research, but the general idea that much mental activity goes on outside awareness has fared very well; it is the part of his thought that modern research most clearly supports. Modern psychologists, however, usually distinguish the dynamic, motivated unconscious of Freud from two other things. The nonconscious refers to processes that are never accessible to awareness at all, however hard you try: the regulation of blood pressure and body temperature, or the early stages of visual processing that compute depth from the two eyes. The cognitive unconscious , a term popularised by John Kihlstrom in 1987, refers to the mental processes that operate outside awareness but are not repressed, simply automatic. You met examples in Section 5.2 (Corteen and Wood's skin responses to unattended words) and Section 5.4 (automatic reading in the Stroop task). Others include priming and implicit memory (Chapter 7), and three findings deserve special mention: Blindsight. Lawrence Weiskrantz (1926 to 2018) studied patients with damage to the primary visual cortex who insist that they see nothing in part of the visual field, yet, when forced to guess, point to objects there and discriminate their orientation far better than chance. Visual information is processed and used without being consciously seen. The "low road" to fear. Joseph LeDoux showed that a fast pathway from the thalamus to the amygdala, bypassing the cortex, allows rapid, crude detection of threat and the start of a defensive response before the threat is consciously recognised (Chapter 11). Implicit attitudes. The Implicit Association Test (Anthony Greenwald and colleagues, 1998) measures how quickly people pair concepts (for example, social groups with good or bad words) and is used to reveal automatic, often unacknowledged stereotyping (taught in the Social Psychology book). Exam trap Accessible memories that can be recalled at will are preconscious , not unconscious. The unconscious cannot be reached at will; that is its defining feature. Psychic determinism is Freud's principle that all mental events are caused, not a level of consciousness. "Subconscious" is a popular word that Freud did not use as a technical term; in exam options prefer conscious, preconscious and unconscious. The model of three levels is the topographic model (1900); id, ego and superego form the later structural model (1923). Consciousness and the brain, and the hard problem Where does consciousness come from in the brain? The first clue about the level of consciousness came in 1949, when Giuseppe Moruzzi and Horace Magoun found that electrically stimulating the reticular formation in the brainstem of a sleeping or anaesthetised cat immediately changed its EEG to the pattern of alert wakefulness. The reticular activating system , a network running from the brainstem through the thalamus to the cortex, maintains arousal; damage to it produces coma. The contents of consciousness, in contrast, seem to depend on widespread, coordinated activity across the cortex and thalamus. Francis Crick and Christof Koch made the search for the neural correlates of consciousness , the minimal brain activity sufficient for a specific conscious experience, a respectable scientific programme from 1990, and Bernard Baars's global workspace theory (1988) proposed that information becomes conscious when it is "broadcast" widely across the brain, so that many specialised systems can use it at once, rather like an actor stepping into the spotlight on a stage watched by a large audience. (The split-brain studies of Roger Sperry and Michael Gazzaniga, which bear on the unity of consciousness, are taught in the Physiological Psychology book.) Even a complete map of these correlates would leave one question open. In 1995 the Australian philosopher David Chalmers (born 1966) distinguished the "easy problems" of consciousness, explaining how the brain discriminates stimuli, integrates information, focuses attention and reports on its states, from the hard problem of consciousness : why any of this processing is accompanied by subjective experience at all. Why does the activity of neurons responding to a certain wavelength feel like the redness of a tomato, instead of going on "in the dark"? The easy problems are hard in practice but are problems of mechanism; the hard problem asks why mechanism should produce experience, and there is no agreed answer. Altered states of consciousness Your ordinary waking consciousness is not the only state your mind can be in. An altered state of consciousness (ASC) is a temporary, qualitative change in the overall pattern of mental functioning, such that the person feels that consciousness is radically different from its ordinary state. The definition is associated with the American psychologist Charles Tart (born 1937), whose edited book Altered States of Consciousness (1969) made the term standard; the psychiatrist Arnold Ludwig (1966) listed the features such states tend to share, including disturbed thinking, a changed sense of time, loss of control, changes in emotional expression and body image, perceptual distortion, a sense that experiences are deeply meaningful or indescribable, and increased suggestibility. Some altered states occur naturally every day (sleep and dreaming); others are induced psychologically (hypnosis, meditation, sensory deprivation, rhythmic drumming or chanting) or physiologically (fever, lack of oxygen, fasting and psychoactive drugs). The rest of this chapter examines the most important of them, beginning with the one you enter every night. But sleep is governed by a clock, so we start with the clock. Indian context Indian philosophy analysed states of consciousness long before Western psychology. The Mandukya Upanishad describes four states. In jagrat (waking) consciousness is directed outward to the physical world; in svapna (dreaming) it is directed inward to subtle images; in sushupti (deep, dreamless sleep) there is neither object nor desire, only an undifferentiated rest (the self in this state is called prajna ). The fourth state, turiya (literally "the fourth"), is not a further condition alongside the others but pure consciousness itself, the silent witness present in all three and identified with the Atman , the true self or soul, understood as eternal, unchanging consciousness (as distinct from the perishable body and the passing states of mind). Vedanta texts often speak of avastha-traya , "the three states", with turiya as what lies beyond them. Indian psychology, whose primary focus is the integration of these Indian philosophical traditions with psychological concepts, is taught in Chapter 2. 5.6 Biological rhythms: the body's clocks Lower yield · 4 Qs If you have ever travelled overnight by train from Mysuru to Delhi and back, you know that the body has opinions about time. You feel sleepy at certain hours whatever you are doing, and alert at others. These opinions come from biological rhythms, regular cyclical changes in physiology and behaviour, and the most important of them is set by a tiny clock deep in the brain. Circadian rhythms A circadian rhythm is a biological cycle of about 24 hours (from the Latin circa diem , "about a day"; the term was coined by the chronobiologist Franz Halberg in 1959). The sleep-wake cycle is the obvious example, but almost every bodily process has one. Body temperature falls through the night and is lowest in the early morning hours, which is why night-shift workers feel coldest and most error-prone around four or five in the morning; it rises through the day. The stress hormone cortisol peaks shortly after waking. The hormone melatonin rises in the evening and is highest in the middle of the night. Are these rhythms just responses to the day outside, or does the body keep time by itself? The test is to remove every time cue. Volunteers have lived for weeks in caves and underground bunkers with no daylight, no clocks and no news, eating and sleeping whenever they wished. Their rhythms persisted, but drifted: under constant conditions human rhythms run with a period slightly longer than 24 hours (about 24.2 hours in careful modern studies), so that each "day" they went to bed a little later. A rhythm that runs on in the absence of time cues is called free-running , and its persistence proves that there is an internal clock. Under normal conditions the clock is reset every day by environmental cues called zeitgebers (German, "time givers"). Light is by far the most powerful; meals, exercise and social activity are weaker zeitgebers. The process of being kept in step with the 24-hour day is called entrainment . The suprachiasmatic nucleus and melatonin The master clock is the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), a pair of small clusters of neurons in the hypothalamus, sitting just above the optic chiasm (hence "supra-chiasmatic"). The evidence that it is the clock is unusually complete. When the SCN is destroyed in rats and hamsters, circadian rhythms of sleep, activity, eating and drinking disappear: the animals sleep about the same total amount, but at random times of day and night. SCN neurons removed from the brain and kept alive in a dish continue to fire in a 24-hour rhythm. And when Martin Ralph and colleagues (1990) transplanted the SCN from hamsters with a mutant short-period clock into normal hamsters whose own SCN had been destroyed, the recipients took on the donor's rhythm. The clock itself is molecular: in each SCN cell, "clock genes" switch each other on and off in a feedback loop that takes about a day to complete, a discovery recognised by the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2017. How does light reach the clock? Not through the ordinary visual pathway. A special class of retinal ganglion cells containing the photopigment melanopsin responds to overall brightness and sends signals directly to the SCN along the retinohypothalamic tract . (Some blind people whose rods and cones are destroyed still have entrained rhythms because these cells survive.) The SCN, in turn, controls the pineal gland , which secretes melatonin in darkness; light suppresses it. Melatonin, sometimes called the hormone of darkness, signals "night" to the rest of the body and promotes sleepiness, and melatonin taken at bedtime in the new location can help reset the clock after long flights. Exam trap The SCN is the master circadian pacemaker , entrained by light through the retinohypothalamic tract; SCN lesions disrupt circadian rhythms , not total sleep amount. Do not confuse it with neighbouring hypothalamic regions that are popular distractors: the lateral and ventromedial hypothalamus (hunger and satiety, Chapter 10), the preoptic area (temperature regulation and, in its ventrolateral part, sleep onset; Section 5.7), the paraventricular nucleus (stress hormones), the hypothalamic control of anterior pituitary hormones, and the mammillary bodies (memory). Memory consolidation belongs to the hippocampus, language to Broca's and Wernicke's areas, and long-term memory is not "stored" in the SCN. Jet lag, shift work, larks and owls The clock works well as long as life keeps to a regular schedule. Problems arise when the zeitgebers change suddenly ( jet lag , after flying across time zones) or when work forces us to be awake at the wrong phase of the clock ( shift work ). Both produce sleep disturbance, fatigue, poor concentration and digestive upset, because the internal clock and the external day are out of step, and because different bodily rhythms re-adjust at different speeds. Flying east is harder than flying west. Flying east from London to Bengaluru shortens your day, so you must fall asleep and wake earlier than your clock wants (a phase advance ); flying west lengthens it (a phase delay ), and since the free-running clock naturally runs a little longer than 24 hours, delaying it is easier. Full adjustment takes roughly a day for each time zone crossed. For the same reason, rotating shifts are easier to tolerate when they move forward, from morning to evening to night, than backward; Charles Czeisler and colleagues showed in 1982 that switching a group of industrial workers to forward rotation improved their health and productivity. People also differ in the phase of their clocks. "Larks" (morning types) wake early and peak early; "owls" (evening types) are sluggish in the morning and alert at night. These differences, called chronotypes, are partly genetic, and they shift with age: adolescents drift strongly toward owl-ness, which is why a 7 a.m. coaching class is a biological ordeal for many sixteen-year-olds, while older adults drift back toward larkishness. Sleepiness, finally, is not set by the clock alone. The Swiss researcher Alexander Borbély proposed in 1982 the influential two-process model of sleep regulation. Process S (sleep pressure) is homeostatic: it builds up the longer you are awake (partly through the accumulation of the chemical adenosine in the brain) and dissipates during sleep. Process C is the circadian rhythm from the SCN, which promotes wakefulness during the biological day. You fall asleep easily when sleep pressure is high and the circadian alerting signal is low. Caffeine works by blocking adenosine receptors, hiding sleep pressure for a few hours without removing it. Ultradian and infradian rhythms Not all rhythms are daily. Ultradian rhythms are cycles shorter than a day, repeating more than once in 24 hours. The best known is the roughly 90-minute cycle of sleep stages that you will meet in the next section; Kleitman suggested that a similar 90-minute basic rest-activity cycle continues through the day as well, as fluctuations in alertness, and pulses of many hormones follow ultradian rhythms. Infradian rhythms are cycles longer than a day: the human menstrual cycle of about 28 days is the classic example. Cycles of about a year, called circannual rhythms, include hibernation, bird migration and, in humans, seasonal affective disorder , a form of depression that recurs in the dark months of winter and can be treated with bright-light therapy. For most of history that third was a blank: you closed your eyes, and some hours later you opened them. Sleep could not be studied because the sleeper could not report on it. What changed this was a machine that could listen to the brain. Listening to the sleeping brain: the EEG In 1929 the German psychiatrist Hans Berger (1873 to 1941) published the first recordings of electrical activity from the human scalp, the electroencephalogram (EEG). The EEG picks up the summed activity of millions of cortical neurons. When those neurons fire in an unsynchronised way, each doing its own work, their activity largely cancels out and the EEG shows small, fast waves; when large numbers fire together in rhythm, the waves become large and slow. Waves are described by their frequency (cycles per second, or hertz, Hz) and their amplitude (height, which reflects voltage). The first rhythm Berger described, a regular wave of about 10 Hz seen when a person rests with eyes closed, is still sometimes called the Berger rhythm; we now call it alpha. A modern sleep laboratory records three measures together, a procedure called polysomnography : the EEG, the electrooculogram (EOG), which records eye movements from electrodes beside the eyes, and the electromyogram (EMG), which records muscle tension, usually from under the chin.
