As sleep deepens, the waves become slower and larger; in REM sleep the EEG returns to a fast, low-voltage, waking-like pattern. The discovery of REM sleep Now return to Eugene Aserinsky and the jerking pens. What Aserinsky and Kleitman reported in 1953 was that the bursts of rapid eye movement coincided with periods of low-voltage, fast EEG, like that of a waking person, and that people woken from these periods usually reported dreams. Their student William Charles Dement (1928 to 2020), then a medical student and later the founder of the world's first sleep disorders clinic at Stanford, joined the work, and in 1957 Dement and Kleitman described the full pattern: the stages of sleep follow one another in a regular cycle of about 90 minutes, repeated through the night, with a period of rapid-eye-movement sleep at the end of each cycle. In their studies, about 80 per cent of awakenings from REM periods produced vivid, story-like dream reports, compared with only a small fraction of awakenings from other stages. In 1959 the French researcher Michel Jouvet (1925 to 2017) found that in cats this state is accompanied by a complete loss of muscle tone and called it paradoxical sleep , because the brain looks awake while the body is more deeply relaxed than at any other time. Sleep researchers therefore divide sleep into two basic kinds. REM sleep (rapid eye movement sleep) is the paradoxical stage. NREM sleep (non-REM sleep) is everything else, and it is subdivided into stages by its EEG. The standard scoring manual of Allan Rechtschaffen and Anthony Kales (1968) recognised four NREM stages, numbered 1 to 4, with stages 3 and 4 together called slow-wave sleep. In 2007 the American Academy of Sleep Medicine merged stages 3 and 4 into a single stage, so that modern texts (including Pinel) describe three NREM stages, N1 , N2 and N3 , plus REM (sometimes labelled R). Many exam questions still use the older numbering, so you must know both. A night's journey through the stages Picture a student going to bed after a long day of revision. As she lies with her eyes closed and relaxes, her EEG shows regular alpha waves. Then, over a few minutes, she passes through the stages of sleep. Stage N1 is the brief transition from waking to sleep, lasting only a few minutes. Alpha waves give way to slower, irregular theta waves of low amplitude, and the eyes may roll slowly. She is easy to wake, and if woken she may insist she was not asleep. This is the stage of the hypnic jerk , the sudden muscle twitch that sometimes jolts us awake with a feeling of falling, and of dreamlike hypnagogic images (Section 5.9). N1 makes up only about 5 per cent of a night's sleep. Stage N2 is light but definite sleep. The EEG is mostly theta, punctuated by two signature waveforms: sleep spindles , short waxing and waning bursts of 11 to 15 Hz waves, and K-complexes , single large sharp waves, a large negative (upward) deflection followed at once by a large positive (downward) one, which often appear when a sound occurs during sleep. Heart rate and breathing slow, body temperature falls and the eyes are still. N2 is the most common stage, about half of an adult's total sleep. Stage N3 is deep sleep. The EEG is dominated by delta waves, the largest and slowest of all, which is why N3 is called slow-wave sleep (SWS). In the older system, stage 3 had 20 to 50 per cent delta and stage 4 more than 50 per cent; together they formed slow-wave sleep. This is the hardest stage to wake from: a person roused from N3 is groggy and confused for several minutes. Breathing and heart rate are slow and regular, the release of growth hormone is at its daily peak, and the brain uses less energy than at any other time. N3 is also when sleepwalking and sleep terrors occur. After N3 the sleeper climbs back up through N2, and then, about 70 to 90 minutes after falling asleep, something remarkable happens. The EEG becomes fast, low-voltage and desynchronised, much like that of an alert, waking person, with bursts of rapid eye movements under the closed lids. This is REM sleep. Its features are a list of paradoxes (Table 5.6 sets them against those of NREM sleep): The brain is highly active: its oxygen use and blood flow in many regions rise to waking levels, and the EEG shows beta and theta waves with characteristic sawtooth waves. The eyes dart rapidly from side to side in bursts. The large skeletal muscles of the body core are almost completely paralysed, a state called REM atonia , produced by brainstem circuits that actively inhibit motor neurons in the spinal cord, although small muscles of the fingers and face may twitch. Heart rate, blood pressure and breathing become irregular, and there is genital arousal (penile erection or clitoral engorgement) in nearly every REM period, whatever the content of the dream; even infants show it. Most vivid, emotional, story-like dreams occur in REM sleep. Despite the waking-like EEG, a person in REM sleep is hard to wake by meaningless sounds, although meaningful ones (their own name, a baby's cry) can wake them easily. The 90-minute cycle and its changes across the night One sequence of NREM stages followed by a REM period is a sleep cycle . Each cycle lasts about 90 minutes (anywhere from about 70 to 110 minutes), so a typical adult night of seven to eight hours contains four to six cycles . But the cycles are not identical, and the way they change is a favourite exam point (Figure 5.5). Early in the night, cycles contain long periods of N3 and very short REM periods; the first REM period may last only about 10 minutes. As the night goes on, N3 shrinks and often disappears altogether in the last cycles, while REM periods lengthen to half an hour or more. Slow-wave sleep is concentrated in the first third of the night; REM sleep in the last third. This is why you are most likely to be woken from a dream by your morning alarm, and why sleepwalking and sleep terrors (N3 events) happen within a few hours of falling asleep. Brief awakenings, usually forgotten by morning, are normal. The standard answer is four to six (about 90 minutes each over seven to eight hours), and that is the keyed answer when it is offered (RML 2024). Some sources give "four to five" or "about five", and one past paper (RML 2022) keys 4 to 7 because 4 to 6 was not among its options; choose the option that contains four to six and excludes the extremes (2 to 4 is too few, 8 to 12 too many). Also remember the direction of change: N3 decreases and REM increases across the night, not the reverse. Sleep across the lifespan Sleep changes dramatically with age, as Howard Roffwarg and his colleagues Joseph Muzio and William Dement showed in a classic paper in 1966 (Figure 5.6). A newborn baby sleeps about 16 hours a day, and about half of that is REM sleep; newborns also often enter REM directly at sleep onset. Total sleep and the proportion of REM fall steeply through infancy and childhood. By adolescence REM makes up about 20 to 25 per cent of sleep, and it stays near that level through adulthood, declining slightly in old age. Roffwarg proposed that the huge amount of REM sleep in infancy provides internally generated stimulation that helps the developing brain mature, an idea known as the ontogenetic hypothesis. In older adults total sleep falls to about six hours, slow-wave sleep shrinks greatly (in many elderly people N3 almost disappears), sleep becomes lighter and more broken by awakenings, and its timing shifts earlier in the evening. 0 4 8 12 16 Hours of sleep per day 50% REM Newborn 16 h 25% REM Age 2 13 h 20% REM Age 10 9.5 h 22% REM Age 20 7.75 h 19% REM Age 50 6.75 h 15% REM Age 75 6 h NREM sleep REM sleep Figure 5.6 Total daily sleep and REM sleep across the lifespan (approximate values redrawn after Roffwarg, Muzio and Dement, 1966). Both total sleep and the share of REM fall steeply in early life; REM is half of a newborn's sleep but about a fifth of an adult's. What switches sleep on and off You read in Section 5.5 that the reticular activating system keeps the cortex awake. Sleep is not simply this system running down. It is actively switched on. A group of inhibitory neurons in the ventrolateral preoptic area (VLPO) of the hypothalamus, which use the transmitter GABA, become active at sleep onset and shut down the arousal systems of the brainstem and hypothalamus; the arousal systems, in turn, inhibit the VLPO. Because each side suppresses the other, the brain flips quickly between sleep and wakefulness, like a light switch, instead of drifting between them; Clifford Saper and his colleagues called this the "flip-flop switch". The switch is stabilised by orexin (also called hypocretin), a peptide made by neurons in the lateral hypothalamus that keeps the system firmly in the waking position; its loss causes narcolepsy (Section 5.8). REM sleep is generated in the brainstem, particularly the pons. "REM-on" neurons in a region called the sublaterodorsal nucleus trigger REM sleep and, through circuits in the medulla, the atonia that goes with it; "REM-off" neurons in the ventrolateral periaqueductal grey hold REM in check. During REM, waves of activity called PGO waves (ponto-geniculo-occipital) travel from the pons through the visual thalamus to the occipital cortex, a fact that will matter when we come to theories of dreaming. Exam trap Slow-wave (NREM) sleep begins when neurons in the ventrolateral preoptic area become active. The suprachiasmatic nucleus is the circadian clock (it decides when sleep is likely, not how it is switched on). The sublaterodorsal nucleus is a REM-on region, and the ventrolateral periaqueductal grey is a REM-off region; both concern REM, not slow-wave sleep. 5.8 Why we sleep, what deprivation does and when sleep goes wrong Medium yield · 4 Qs Sleep is costly. An animal asleep is not eating, mating or watching for predators. Yet every mammal and bird that has been studied sleeps, and even fruit flies and roundworms have sleep-like states. Something so universal and so risky must do something important. But what? Theories of why we sleep Pinel groups the answers into two kinds. Recuperation theories (also called restorative theories), associated with the British psychiatrist Ian Oswald among others, hold that being awake disrupts the body's internal balance in some way and that sleep is needed to restore it: to replenish energy, repair tissue, clear waste products and restore the brain. There is real evidence for restoration. Growth hormone is released mainly during slow-wave sleep. Slow-wave sleep increases after unusually tiring days and after sleep loss. And in 2013 Lulu Xie, Maiken Nedergaard and colleagues showed in mice that the spaces between brain cells widen during sleep, allowing cerebrospinal fluid to flush out waste products, including the protein beta-amyloid that accumulates in Alzheimer's disease, a cleaning system called the glymphatic system. Adaptation theories (Pinel's term; also called adaptive, evolutionary or circadian theories), associated with Wilse Webb and Ray Meddis in the 1970s, hold that sleep is less a response to the wear of waking than a behaviour that evolution timed to keep animals still and safe during the part of the day when activity would be useless or dangerous, and to conserve energy. They explain well why different species sleep such different amounts. Large grazing animals, which must eat for most of the day and cannot hide from predators, sleep only a few hours; animals that are safe in burrows or at the top of the food chain, and that can meet their needs quickly, sleep much longer. They also explain why sleep is so tightly tied to the circadian clock. A third family of theories stresses memory consolidation . As far back as 1924, John Jenkins and Karl Dallenbach found that people forgot less of what they had learned if they slept after learning than if they stayed awake (Chapter 7). Modern research suggests that slow-wave sleep helps to consolidate factual, declarative memories, partly by "replaying" the day's patterns of hippocampal activity, while REM sleep helps to consolidate procedural skills and emotional memories; Avi Karni and colleagues (1994) found that improvement on a visual skill overnight disappeared when participants were deprived of REM sleep. Giulio Tononi and Chiara Cirelli have added that sleep may prune back the synaptic strengthening of the day, keeping the brain efficient. These theories are not rivals so much as parts of one answer: sleep probably does several jobs, and its timing has been fitted to each species' way of life. Sleep deprivation Key study: Randy Gardner's 264 hours (1964) In the winter of 1963 to 1964, Randy Gardner, a 17-year-old high-school student in San Diego, set out to break the world record for staying awake as a school science project, kept awake by two friends. William Dement heard about it and joined them. Gardner stayed awake for 264 hours, eleven days. He grew irritable, his speech became slurred, his memory and concentration lapsed, and he had brief perceptual distortions, but he never became psychotic; near the end he held a press conference and conducted himself well. Afterwards he slept for about 14 hours and then returned to his normal schedule. He did not need to recover all the lost sleep, a typical finding. Laboratory studies give a more systematic picture. Even moderate sleep loss produces three consistent effects: increased sleepiness, more negative mood and, above all, poor performance on tasks of sustained attention , the dull vigilance tasks of Section 5.4. Sleep-deprived people suffer microsleeps , episodes of a few seconds in which the eyelids droop, the EEG shows sleep and the person stops responding, even while sitting or standing; at the wheel of a car on a highway, a microsleep can be fatal. Chronic partial deprivation is also harmful: Hans Van Dongen and colleagues (2003) found that people restricted to six hours a night for two weeks performed as badly on attention tests as people kept awake for one or two whole nights, yet they rated themselves as only slightly sleepy. Total deprivation for weeks is lethal in rats (Allan Rechtschaffen's studies in the 1980s), and a rare inherited human prion disease that destroys the thalamus and abolishes sleep, fatal familial insomnia, is invariably fatal. Interpreting human deprivation studies requires caution, however, because sleep loss is so often confounded with stress. REM deprivation and REM rebound In 1960 Dement woke volunteers every time they entered REM sleep, night after night, and woke a control group equally often during NREM sleep. Two things happened. First, the REM-deprived volunteers tried to enter REM more and more often each night, so that they had to be woken ever more frequently. Second, when they were finally allowed to sleep undisturbed, they spent much more time than usual in REM sleep. This compensatory increase is called REM rebound . Dement at first thought REM deprivation also caused anxiety and irritability, but later studies did not confirm serious psychological harm; people taking antidepressants that suppress REM sleep for months show no obvious ill effects. REM rebound is clinically familiar too: alcohol and many sleeping pills suppress REM, and when they are stopped, REM rebounds with intense, often disturbing dreams, which can tempt the person to go back to the drug. Sleep disorders: an overview Sleep disorders fall into a few broad groups: insomnia (difficulty falling asleep or staying asleep, or unrefreshing sleep), hypersomnia (excessive sleepiness), breathing-related disorders and the parasomnias , abnormal behaviours or experiences that occur during sleep or the transitions into and out of it. Table 5.7 gives a brief overview; diagnostic criteria and treatment are taught in the Psychiatric Disorders book. Table 5.7 The main sleep disorders in brief. Disorder Key features Stage or mechanism Insomnia Trouble falling or staying asleep; the commonest sleep complaint; sleeping pills can cause tolerance and rebound insomnia Often linked to stress, anxiety, depression and poor sleep habits Narcolepsy Irresistible daytime sleep attacks, cataplexy, sleep paralysis, hypnagogic hallucinations REM intrudes into waking; loss of orexin (hypocretin) neurons Obstructive sleep apnoea Breathing stops repeatedly as the airway collapses; loud snoring, gasping, daytime sleepiness Airway obstruction; commoner with obesity; central apnoea is a failure of the brain's drive to breathe Sleepwalking (somnambulism) Sitting up, walking or doing complex acts while asleep; hard to wake; no memory next day NREM parasomnia from N3, early in the night; commoner in children Sleep terrors (night terrors) Sudden scream, intense fear and racing heart; inconsolable; little or no dream recall NREM parasomnia from N3, early in the night Nightmares Frightening dreams that wake the sleeper, who is quickly alert and recalls the dream vividly REM sleep, later in the night REM sleep behaviour disorder Acting out dreams, often violently (punching, kicking); mostly older men Loss of normal REM atonia; often precedes Parkinson's disease Restless legs syndrome Uncomfortable sensations in the legs and an urge to move them, worse at rest and in the evening A sensorimotor disorder that delays sleep onset A few of these deserve a closer look. Narcolepsy , named by the French physician Jean-Baptiste-Édouard Gélineau in 1880, is a disorder of hypersomnia in which elements of REM sleep intrude into waking life. Its sufferers fall asleep at inappropriate moments, in the middle of a conversation or a meal, and when they do they often go straight into REM sleep. The most dramatic symptom is cataplexy , a sudden loss of muscle tone during full wakefulness, usually triggered by strong emotion such as laughter or anger: the knees buckle or the person collapses, fully conscious, for a minute or two. It is, in effect, REM atonia switched on while awake. Sleep paralysis (the inability to move for a few moments just as one falls asleep or wakes up) and hypnagogic hallucinations complete the classic picture, although both also occur occasionally in healthy people. The discovery in 1999 and 2000 that narcoleptic dogs carry a mutation in the orexin receptor gene and that human patients have lost most of their orexin-producing neurons explained the disorder. Sleep apnoea often masquerades as insomnia or as daytime fatigue: the sleeper wakes briefly dozens or hundreds of times a night to restart breathing, usually without remembering it. REM sleep behaviour disorder , first described by Carlos Schenck, Mark Mahowald and colleagues in 1986, is the mirror image of cataplexy: the atonia that should accompany REM sleep fails, so the sleeper acts out the dream, sometimes injuring a bed partner. And the contrast between sleep terrors and nightmares is a classic exam point: the first comes from deep NREM sleep early in the night with little recall, the second from REM sleep late in the night with vivid recall. Exam trap Somnambulism means sitting, walking or performing complex behaviour while asleep. Extreme fear, agitation and screaming while asleep describes sleep terrors ; acting out dreams (including nightmares) describes REM sleep behaviour disorder ; uncomfortable sensations in the legs causing movement and lost sleep describe restless legs syndrome . Sleepwalking and sleep terrors arise from N3 (slow-wave) sleep, not REM: a person in REM sleep is paralysed and cannot walk. Sleep talking (somniloquy) can occur in any stage. Clinical link The first-line treatment for chronic insomnia is not a sleeping pill but cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I), which outperforms medication in the long run. Its techniques are examined by name. Stimulus control (Richard Bootzin, 1972) re-associates the bed with sleep: go to bed only when sleepy, use the bed only for sleep, get up if not asleep within about 20 minutes, and rise at the same time every day. Sleep restriction (Arthur Spielman) limits the time in bed to the time actually slept, building sleep pressure, and then extends it gradually. Paradoxical intention , a technique from Viktor Frankl's logotherapy, asks the patient to lie in bed in the dark and try as hard as possible to stay awake ; this removes the performance anxiety of "trying to sleep", which is what keeps many insomniacs awake. Dereflection , Frankl's other technique, is different: it redirects attention away from oneself and the symptom toward other meaningful goals. A man told to try to stay awake is receiving paradoxical intention. 5.9 Dreams Medium yield · 8 Qs Every culture has wondered about dreams. In the ancient world they were messages from gods or ancestors; in the Indian epics they foretell victory and disaster; in twentieth-century Vienna they became the key to the unconscious. Sleep research has answered some old questions and sharpened others. Before we look at the theories, let us be clear about what dreams are actually like. What dreams are like A dream is a sequence of images, feelings and thoughts experienced during sleep, usually as a story in which the dreamer takes part. Vivid, emotional, narrative dreams are most common in REM sleep, but mental activity also occurs in NREM sleep, mostly as shorter, more thought-like fragments; late in the night, NREM dreams can be as story-like as REM dreams. Everyone dreams every night, including people who insist they never do: "non-dreamers" have normal amounts of REM sleep and report dreams when woken from it. Early laboratory work tested common beliefs about dreams. Do dreams flash by in an instant? No: in 1957 Dement and Kleitman woke people either 5 or 15 minutes after a REM period began and asked which it had been, judging only from the length of their dream; they were correct in 92 of 111 cases, so dreams unfold in roughly real time. Can outside stimuli enter dreams? Yes: when Dement and Edward Wolpert (1958) sprayed water on sleepers in REM sleep and woke them a few seconds later, the water had been worked into the dream in 14 of 33 cases (a leaking roof, a sudden downpour on a stage). What do people dream about? Calvin Hall, who collected tens of thousands of dream reports, and Robert Van de Castle (1966), who devised a coding system for them, found that most dreams are surprisingly ordinary: familiar settings and people, everyday activities and the dreamer's current concerns. Negative emotions such as anxiety and fear are more common than positive ones, and being chased, falling and failing an exam are among the commonest themes worldwide. Fragments of the previous day's events, which Freud called the day residue , appear often. Why should a brain produce such experiences at all? The theories fall into a few families. Freud: dreams as disguised wishes Freud's The Interpretation of Dreams appeared in November 1899, but the publisher dated it 1900 to mark the new century, and 1900 is the date to remember. Freud called the interpretation of dreams "the royal road to a knowledge of the unconscious activities of the mind". His central claim was that every dream is a wish fulfilment : the disguised fulfilment of a repressed wish, often sexual or aggressive and often dating from childhood. During sleep the ego's guard is lowered, and these wishes press toward expression. If they appeared undisguised, the dreamer would be so disturbed that he would wake, so an internal censor disguises them. In this sense, Freud said, dreams are the guardians of sleep. Freud therefore distinguished two levels of every dream. The manifest content is the dream as the dreamer remembers and reports it: the story, the people, the places. The latent content is its hidden meaning, the unconscious wishes and thoughts that gave rise to it. The mental process that turns latent content into manifest content is the dream work , and it uses four main mechanisms: Condensation : several latent ideas are compressed into a single image. A person in a dream who has your teacher's face, your father's voice and your uncle's walk condenses feelings about all three. Displacement : the emotional significance of an important but threatening object is shifted onto a trivial, harmless one. Anger at a parent may appear as anger at a stray dog. Symbolisation (Freud's "considerations of representability"): abstract thoughts are turned into concrete, mostly visual images and symbols, so that a wish to be free of an obligation might appear as a flight from a locked room. Secondary revision (secondary elaboration): on waking and in recall, the mind tidies the confused material into a more coherent, logical-seeming story, hiding the latent meaning further. To interpret a dream, the analyst asks the patient to free associate to each element of the manifest content, retracing the dream work backwards toward the latent thoughts. The theory has been enormously influential in culture and in psychotherapy, but its scientific standing is weak. There is no convincing evidence that dreams systematically disguise wishes; many dreams (the repeated nightmares of trauma survivors, for example) are hard to see as wishes at all, as Freud himself came to accept in 1920; and the brain science on which he built the theory is now obsolete. What has survived is the broader idea that dreams draw on our emotional concerns. Exam trap The Interpretation of Dreams : 1900 (printed in November 1899 but dated 1900). Manifest content is what is remembered; latent content is the hidden meaning. The four mechanisms of the dream work are condensation, displacement, symbolisation (representation) and secondary revision; "sublimation" and "projection" are defence mechanisms, not dream-work mechanisms, and "day residue" is the raw material, not a mechanism. "Royal road to the unconscious" refers to dreams, not to free association or slips of the tongue. Jung: dreams as messages from the psyche Carl Gustav Jung (1875 to 1961), once Freud's closest colleague, broke with him in 1913 partly over dreams. For Jung a dream is not a disguise but a natural, spontaneous self-portrait of the psyche, speaking in the language of symbols. Its chief function is compensatory : it balances a one-sided conscious attitude, so that a man who is outwardly all confidence may dream of being lost and helpless. Dreams can also be prospective , anticipating future development. Here Jung's disagreement with Freud over the unconscious matters. Jung held that the unconscious exists on two levels: a personal (individual) unconscious of the person's own forgotten and repressed experiences, and beneath it the collective unconscious , the inherited layer of the psyche shared by all humanity, which he accounted for in evolutionary terms, through the similar brain structure inherited by all human races. Some dreams draw on the collective unconscious and present universal images, the archetypes (such as the persona, the social mask; the shadow, the disowned dark side; the anima, the feminine side of a man; the animus, the masculine side of a woman; and the wise old man), which Jung found repeated in myths and religions across cultures. Early in his career, at the Burghölzli clinic in Zurich, Jung had also developed the word association test , in which hesitations and odd replies to stimulus words reveal unconscious emotional complexes. Instead of free association, Jung used amplification , enriching a dream symbol by comparing it with parallel images from myth, folklore and religion. (Jung's theory of personality is taught in the Personality book.) Activation-synthesis: dreams from the brainstem The discovery of REM sleep made a purely physiological theory possible. In 1977 the Harvard psychiatrists J. Allan Hobson (1933 to 2021) and Robert McCarley proposed the activation-synthesis hypothesis . During REM sleep, circuits in the pons fire spontaneously and send waves of activation (the PGO waves of Section 5.7) up to the forebrain, stimulating visual, motor and emotional areas more or less at random. That is the activation . The cortex, which is built to make sense of input, does its best with this chaotic barrage and weaves it into a story, drawing on the dreamer's memories and concerns. That is the synthesis . Think of how you see faces and animals in drifting clouds: the clouds are random, but your brain imposes a meaning on them. The hypothesis explains several features of dreams neatly. Dreams are intensely visual because the visual system is activated. They are bizarre, with sudden scene shifts, because the input is random. We dream of running yet being unable to move because motor areas are activated while the body is paralysed. And dreams are quickly forgotten because the brain chemicals that support memory formation (noradrenaline and serotonin) are almost absent in REM sleep. On this view dreams are not disguised messages; any meaning is added by the synthesising brain, although that meaning can still reflect the dreamer's personality. The hypothesis has been criticised: the neuropsychologist Mark Solms showed that patients with certain forebrain lesions stop dreaming although their REM sleep is intact, so dreaming depends on the forebrain, not just the pons, and dreaming also occurs outside REM. Hobson himself later revised the theory, and in 2009 proposed that dreaming is a kind of "protoconsciousness", a virtual-reality rehearsal that helps develop and maintain waking consciousness. Information-processing, memory and threat-simulation theories Information-processing theories see dreaming as a by-product or part of the brain's overnight handling of the day's experiences. In one early, provocative version, Francis Crick (1916 to 2004) and Graeme Mitchison (1983) proposed "reverse learning": REM sleep weakens unwanted, parasitic connections formed during the day, so that, in their phrase, we dream in order to forget. More influential today are memory-consolidation views, which link dreams to the role of sleep in strengthening and integrating memories (Section 5.8): new learning is replayed and connected with older memories, and dream content reflects fragments of this process. When Robert Stickgold and colleagues (2000) had people play the computer game Tetris for hours, many saw falling blocks as they drifted off to sleep, including amnesic patients who could not remember having played. Rosalind Cartwright, studying people going through divorce, argued that dreams also help regulate mood, working through emotional problems overnight. The neurocognitive or continuity view of William Domhoff holds that dreams express our waking concerns and conceptions, using the same cognitive systems that we use when awake; dreams develop gradually in childhood as these systems mature. The Finnish psychologist Antti Revonsuo took an evolutionary approach in his threat-simulation theory (2000). Dreams, he argued, evolved as a virtual training ground in which our ancestors rehearsed responses to threats (being chased, attacked, injured or rejected) safely during sleep, making them better at handling such threats when awake. In support, threatening events are greatly over-represented in dreams relative to waking life, and children who have lived through real danger dream of threats more often. Critics note that many dreams contain no threat, and that the rehearsal would be useless if it is forgotten by morning. Table 5.8 brings the theories of dreaming together. Theory Proposer and year Central idea Wish fulfilment Freud, 1900 Dreams are disguised fulfilments of repressed wishes; manifest content hides latent content Compensation and archetypes Jung Dreams are undisguised symbolic messages that balance conscious attitudes and may show archetypes Activation-synthesis Hobson and McCarley, 1977 The cortex synthesises a story from random brainstem activation during REM sleep Reverse learning Crick and Mitchison, 1983 REM sleep erases unwanted connections; we dream in order to forget Information processing and memory consolidation Stickgold and others Dreams reflect the overnight processing and consolidation of recent experience Continuity (neurocognitive) Hall; Domhoff Dreams express waking concerns using waking cognitive systems Threat simulation Revonsuo, 2000 Dreams evolved to rehearse responses to threats Lucid dreams Sometimes a dreamer realises, within the dream, that he is dreaming, and may even take control of what happens next, choosing to fly or to turn and face a pursuer. This is a lucid dream , a term coined by the Dutch psychiatrist Frederik van Eeden in 1913. For a long time scientists doubted that such dreams were real rather than reports made up after waking. The doubt was settled by an ingenious method. Keith Hearne in Britain in the 1970s, and Stephen LaBerge at Stanford in the early 1980s, asked lucid dreamers to make a pre-arranged pattern of eye movements (left, right, left, right) as soon as they became lucid. Because the eye muscles are not paralysed in REM sleep, the signals appeared clearly on the EOG, in the middle of unmistakable REM sleep. Many people have at least one lucid dream in their lives, and a few have them regularly; lucid dreaming techniques have been tried as a treatment for recurring nightmares. Hypnagogic and hypnopompic imagery The borders of sleep have experiences of their own. Hypnagogic imagery occurs while falling asleep (in N1): flashes of light, geometric patterns, faces, landscapes, snatches of speech or music, or the sensation of falling that may end in a hypnic jerk. The Tetris images described above are hypnagogic. Hypnopompic imagery is similar imagery experienced while waking up, sometimes so vivid that a person sees a figure standing by the bed for a moment after opening the eyes. (The terms are credited to the French scholar Alfred Maury and the British writer Frederic Myers respectively.) Such images are common and normal, and they are distinguished from the hallucinations of psychosis by occurring only at the edges of sleep. When they combine with sleep paralysis, the experience can be terrifying, typically a sense of an evil presence pressing on the chest; many cultures interpret it as an attack by a spirit or ghost. Frequent, intense episodes, together with daytime sleep attacks, should raise the question of narcolepsy. Exam trap Hypnagogic = falling asleep (think "going" to sleep); hypnopompic = waking up. The activation-synthesis hypothesis is Hobson and McCarley (1977) , not Freud or Crick; threat simulation is Revonsuo (2000) ; "we dream in order to forget" is Crick and Mitchison's reverse learning. Lucid dreaming was verified by pre-arranged eye-movement signals during REM sleep (LaBerge), because the eyes are the one set of muscles free to move. Scan Your Brain Fill in the blanks. On stage, the hypnotist swings a watch, the volunteers' eyes close, and moments later grown adults are clucking like hens. Is this a special state of consciousness, or are the volunteers simply playing along? Psychologists have argued about that question for two centuries, and the argument is a good model of how science sorts real effects from wishful thinking. Hypnosis is best defined as a social interaction in which one person, the hypnotist, offers suggestions for changes in perception, feeling, memory or behaviour, and the other person, the participant, experiences those changes as real and as happening by themselves, without deliberate effort. It usually begins with an induction : the participant is asked to focus attention (on the hypnotist's voice or a point on the wall), to relax and to let go of critical evaluation. The essential ingredient, the crux of the whole phenomenon, is suggestibility : a heightened readiness to accept and respond to suggestions. A suggestion is a communication that invites an automatic, non-volitional response, such as "your arm is becoming lighter and is rising by itself". Notice what is not required: neither sleep nor a special swinging watch, and not even a formal induction, since suggestible people respond to many suggestions without one. Exam trap The main crux of hypnosis is suggestibility . The "analytical mind" and "logical mind" are what hypnosis is said to quieten, not what it rests on. Hypnosis is not sleep: the EEG of a hypnotised person is a waking EEG, and people under hypnosis can hear, respond and, in general, refuse. From animal magnetism to the Nancy school: a short history The story begins with the Viennese physician Franz Anton Mesmer (1734 to 1815). From the mid-1770s, Mesmer claimed that health depended on the free flow of an invisible universal fluid through the body, which he called animal magnetism , and that a physician could redirect it to cure disease. In Paris from 1778 he treated fashionable patients in groups around a tub (the baquet ) filled with "magnetised" water and iron rods; many fell into convulsive "crises" and declared themselves cured. In 1784 King Louis XVI appointed a royal commission, which included the American scientist Benjamin Franklin and the chemist Antoine Lavoisier. In some of the first blind experiments in history, they showed that people reacted dramatically to objects they merely believed had been magnetised, and not at all to objects secretly magnetised. The commission concluded that the effects were real but were caused by imagination, not by any fluid. Mesmer was discredited, but "mesmerism" lived on. In the same year one of his followers, the Marquis de Puységur, found that some patients entered not a convulsive crisis but a calm, sleep-like trance in which they spoke and obeyed instructions and afterwards remembered nothing; he called it artificial somnambulism . The name we use came from the Scottish surgeon James Braid (1795 to 1860), practising in Manchester. After watching a travelling mesmerist's demonstration in 1841, Braid concluded that there was no magnetic fluid; the trance was a physiological and psychological effect of prolonged, fixed attention, which he produced by having patients stare at a bright object held above their eyes. He called the state "neuro-hypnotism" (nervous sleep), from Hypnos, the Greek god of sleep, and the shortened form hypnotism (hypnosis) stuck; his book Neurypnology appeared in 1843. Braid later realised that the state was not sleep at all and tried to rename it "monoideism", concentration on a single idea, but it was too late to change the name. Indian context Some of the most remarkable early uses of mesmerism took place in Bengal. James Esdaile (1808 to 1859), a Scottish surgeon with the East India Company at Hooghly, began in 1845 to operate on patients in a mesmeric trance, before chemical anaesthesia had reached India. Over the next few years he reported hundreds of operations, including amputations and the removal of large tumours, performed with little apparent pain and with a lower death rate than usual; the government gave him a small mesmeric hospital in Calcutta, and he described his work in Mesmerism in India (1846). Once ether and chloroform became available, mesmeric surgery quickly disappeared, but Esdaile's reports remain an early documented case of hypnotic analgesia. In the second half of the nineteenth century, hypnosis became the centre of a famous French controversy. At the Salpêtrière hospital in Paris, the great neurologist Jean-Martin Charcot (1825 to 1893) studied hypnosis in his patients with hysteria and concluded that hypnotisability was itself a sign of a diseased nervous system, a pathological state that passed through fixed stages and was found mainly in hysterics. His prestige made hypnosis respectable for scientific study. Against him stood the Nancy school : the country doctor Ambroise-Auguste Liébeault (1823 to 1904), who had treated poor patients with hypnosis for years, and the professor of medicine Hippolyte Bernheim (1840 to 1919), who joined him. They argued that hypnosis is a normal phenomenon, that most healthy people can be hypnotised, and that it works entirely through suggestion. The Nancy view won the argument, and it is essentially the modern view. The young Sigmund Freud learned from both sides: he studied with Charcot in Paris in 1885 to 1886 and visited Bernheim at Nancy in 1889. With the Viennese physician Josef Breuer (1842 to 1925), he used hypnosis to help patients with hysteria recall and emotionally discharge forgotten traumatic experiences, the "cathartic method" first developed with Breuer's patient Anna O. Breuer and Freud reported their ideas on the psychical mechanism of hysterical phenomena in 1893 and in Studies on Hysteria in 1895. Freud soon abandoned hypnosis, because many patients could not be hypnotised and the improvements often did not last, and replaced it with free association , in which the patient, relaxing on a couch, reports whatever comes to mind without censoring it; this became the technique on which psychoanalysis was built. A generation later, the American learning theorist Clark Hull's Hypnosis and Suggestibility (1933) brought hypnosis into the experimental laboratory. Exam trap Mesmer : animal magnetism (1770s and 1780s), not the word hypnosis. Braid : coined hypnotism (1840s; Neurypnology , 1843). Charcot : hypnosis as pathology linked to hysteria (Salpêtrière, Paris). Liébeault and Bernheim : the Nancy school, hypnosis as normal suggestion. Freud and Breuer : the mechanism of hysteria (1893) and Studies on Hysteria (1895); Freud, not Bernheim, is the father of psychoanalysis, and free association replaced hypnosis. Who can be hypnotised? Hypnotic susceptibility People differ greatly in how readily they respond to hypnotic suggestions, a trait called hypnotic susceptibility (or hypnotisability). It is measured by standardised scales in which a standard induction is followed by a graded series of suggestions, from easy to hard, and the person's score is the number passed. The best known are the Stanford Hypnotic Susceptibility Scales , devised by André Weitzenhoffer and Ernest Ropiequet Hilgard (1904 to 2001) at Stanford University (Forms A and B in 1959, Form C in 1962), each with 12 items. An easy item is that an outstretched arm becomes heavy and drops; harder items include hallucinating a buzzing fly, posthypnotic amnesia and failing to see an object that is in plain view. The Harvard Group Scale (Ronald Shor and Emily Orne, 1962) adapts the test for groups. Scores form a roughly bell-shaped distribution: perhaps 10 to 15 per cent of people are highly hypnotisable, a similar proportion respond to almost nothing, and most fall in between. Susceptibility is remarkably stable; in one study it correlated about 0.7 with the same person's score 25 years later. It is not related to gullibility, weakness of will or most personality traits, but it is related to absorption , the tendency to become deeply immersed in imaginative experiences such as a novel, a film or a daydream (Auke Tellegen and Gilbert Atkinson, 1974). What hypnosis can and cannot do Separating the real effects of hypnosis from the myths is one of the most practically useful things a psychologist can do (Table 5.9). Table 5.9 What hypnosis can and cannot do. Hypnosis can Hypnosis cannot Reduce pain substantially (hypnotic analgesia), used in surgery, dentistry, childbirth and burns care Give superhuman strength or endurance; motivated people who are not hypnotised can match the feats Produce posthypnotic suggestions, which are carried out on a cue after hypnosis has ended Reliably recover accurate memories; it increases false recall and confidence together Produce posthypnotic amnesia, which is reversed by a pre-arranged cue Truly regress adults to childhood ways of thinking, or to "past lives" Alter perception, including positive and negative hallucinations in highly hypnotisable people Reliably force people to act against their deeply held values Help as an addition to therapy for pain, irritable bowel syndrome, habit control and anxiety Work equally on everyone; responsiveness depends on susceptibility Hypnotic analgesia is the most robust effect: in highly hypnotisable people it can rival morphine, and in the 1990s Pierre Rainville and colleagues showed that suggestions changing how unpleasant a painful stimulus felt changed activity in the anterior cingulate cortex, a brain region involved in the emotional side of pain. A posthypnotic suggestion is an instruction given during hypnosis to be carried out later, after hypnosis has ended, in response to a cue: a participant told that she will open a window when the experimenter touches his tie may do so, and then explain, quite sincerely, that the room felt stuffy. Posthypnotic amnesia , forgetting what happened during hypnosis until a cue is given, is instructive because the memories return intact when the cue is given; they were stored all along, and only retrieval was blocked. The memory myths are the most dangerous. Under hypnosis people do report more "memories", but the extra items are as likely to be false as true, and, crucially, hypnosis makes people more confident in everything they recall, a problem called memory hardening. Jean-Roch Laurence and Campbell Perry (1983) suggested to hypnotised people that they had been woken by loud noises on a particular night the previous week; about half later "remembered" the noises, and some insisted on them even after being told of the suggestion. For this reason, many courts treat hypnotically refreshed testimony with great caution or refuse it altogether, and "recovered memories" of abuse produced under hypnosis cannot be trusted without independent evidence. Hypnotic age regression does not make adults think like children; it makes them act as they believe children act. Theories of hypnosis: a special state or a social role? The theoretical debate is between those who think hypnosis involves a special division of consciousness and those who think it is ordinary social and cognitive behaviour. Ernest Hilgard's neodissociation theory , set out in his book Divided Consciousness (1977), revived an idea of the French psychiatrist Pierre Janet. Hilgard proposed that the mind contains several subsystems of control, normally coordinated by a central executive. Hypnotic suggestion splits consciousness into separate streams: one part of the mind carries out the suggestion and has experiences that are walled off from the other, which remains unaware of them. The evidence that made the theory famous came by accident. During a classroom demonstration of hypnotic deafness, a blind student showed no response to loud sounds. A member of the class asked whether "some part" of him might be hearing, so Hilgard quietly told the student that if some part of him could hear, his index finger should rise. It rose. Hilgard called this concealed, aware part of the mind the hidden observer . In later experiments using the cold pressor test, in which a hand is held in ice water, hypnotised participants given analgesia suggestions reported very little pain aloud, while their hidden observer, reporting through automatic writing or key presses, reported pain almost as high as in the normal waking state. The pain was registered, Hilgard concluded, but kept out of the main stream of awareness by an amnesia-like barrier. The social-cognitive theory of hypnosis (also called sociocognitive or role theory) denies that any special state is needed. Its roots lie in Theodore Sarbin's role theory of the 1950s: hypnotised people are enacting the role of "hypnotised subject" as their culture understands it, not faking but absorbed in the role, as an actor can be absorbed in a part. Theodore Xenophon Barber (1927 to 2005) showed in the 1960s that ordinary participants given "task-motivating" instructions (to try their hardest to imagine and experience what is suggested) responded to suggestions almost as well as hypnotised participants. Nicholas Spanos (1942 to 1994) argued that hypnotic responses are goal-directed actions shaped by expectations and by how the situation is interpreted; in a direct challenge to Hilgard, he showed that the hidden observer reported more pain or less pain depending on what participants had been told the hidden observer would experience, suggesting that the hidden observer was itself a product of suggestion. Irving Kirsch added that the expectation of responding is itself a powerful cause of responding. Martin Orne, for his part, used the "real-simulator" design, comparing hypnotised participants with people instructed to fake hypnosis, and found subtle differences, such as "trance logic", the untroubled acceptance of logical contradictions (seeing a hallucinated person and the real person at the same time). Today the two camps have moved closer. Almost everyone agrees that hypnosis is not sleep, that it is not a magical surrender of will, and that expectation and suggestion drive it. But brain imaging shows that, in highly hypnotisable people, suggestion produces real changes in brain activity: Stephen Kosslyn and colleagues (2000) found that the suggestion to see colour in a grey pattern activated colour-processing regions, and Amir Raz, Michael Posner and colleagues (2002) found that a posthypnotic suggestion that words were meaningless symbols greatly reduced the Stroop effect, an effect that, as you saw in Section 5.4, people cannot normally switch off. Table 5.10 summarises the two positions. Table 5.10 Two views of hypnosis. Question Neodissociation (Hilgard) Social-cognitive (Sarbin, Barber, Spanos) Is hypnosis a special state? Yes: a division of consciousness No: ordinary processes of expectation and role enactment Key evidence The hidden observer; cold pressor analgesia Task-motivated controls perform as well; hidden observer reports follow instructions Why responses feel involuntary The executive is unaware of the split-off control Participants interpret their own goal-directed actions as happening by themselves Clinical link Hypnosis has respectable clinical uses, mostly as an addition to other treatment: for chronic and procedural pain, irritable bowel syndrome, smoking and weight control, and anxiety; adding hypnotic techniques to cognitive behavioural therapy has been found to improve outcomes. The idea of dissociation, central to Hilgard's theory, also links hypnosis to the dissociative disorders, such as dissociative identity disorder, which requires two or more distinct personality states with recurrent gaps in memory (covered in the Disorders book). And the history of hypnosis is a reminder of the difference between symptoms produced unconsciously, as in conversion disorder, and symptoms faked deliberately for gain, as in malingering. 5.11 Meditation, sensory deprivation and psychoactive drugs Lower yield · 3 Qs Hypnosis showed that a few words from another person can change experience. The last altered states in this chapter are produced in other ways: by deliberately training one's own attention, by taking stimulation away, and by putting chemicals into the brain. Meditation Meditation is a family of practices that train attention and awareness, usually with the aim of calming the mind and bringing mental processes under greater voluntary control. The many techniques of the world's traditions fall into two broad kinds, which differ in what they do with attention. In concentrative meditation (now often called focused-attention meditation), attention is fixed on a single object: the breath, a repeated word or sound (a mantra ), a candle flame, an image or a prayer. Whenever the mind wanders, as it constantly will, the meditator notices this and gently brings attention back. The best-known modern form is transcendental meditation (TM), introduced by Maharishi Mahesh Yogi (1918 to 2008) in India in the mid-1950s and spread worldwide from 1958, especially after the Beatles stayed at his ashram in Rishikesh in 1968. In TM the meditator sits comfortably and silently repeats a personal mantra for about 20 minutes, twice a day. In mindfulness meditation (also called opening-up or open-monitoring meditation), attention is not narrowed but widened: the meditator observes whatever arises, thoughts, feelings, bodily sensations and sounds, with calm, non-judging awareness, noticing each and letting it pass without holding on to it or pushing it away. Its roots are in Buddhist vipassana ("insight") practice. Concentrative meditation is like narrowing the zoom lens of Section 5.3 to a single point; mindfulness is like opening it wide while keeping it steady. What does meditation do? In 1970 Robert Keith Wallace reported that during TM, oxygen consumption, heart rate and breathing rate fell, skin resistance rose (a sign of relaxation) and alpha waves increased. The Harvard cardiologist Herbert Benson (1935 to 2022) then showed that the same changes, which he called the relaxation response (1975), could be produced by any similar technique (sitting quietly, relaxing the muscles and repeating a neutral word) and were not unique to TM. A sceptical review by David Holmes (1984) went further, concluding that meditation reduced physiological arousal no more than simply resting with the eyes closed. Later and better-controlled work has been kinder. Jon Kabat-Zinn (born 1944) developed mindfulness-based stress reduction (MBSR) in 1979 for patients with chronic pain and stress, and Zindel Segal, Mark Williams and John Teasdale combined mindfulness with cognitive therapy in mindfulness-based cognitive therapy (MBCT, 2002), which substantially reduces relapse in people who have had three or more episodes of depression. Imaging studies have reported structural and functional brain changes in long-term meditators, for example greater cortical thickness in attention-related regions (Sara Lazar and colleagues, 2005). Meditation research also teaches an important lesson about evidence. Suppose researchers survey 10,000 randomly selected adults in ten countries and find that people who meditate regularly report less stress than people who rarely or never meditate. Can we conclude that meditation lowers stress? Not necessarily. Random selection makes the sample representative, and a large sample makes the estimate precise, but neither makes the study an experiment. Without random assignment of people to meditate or not, the finding is correlational: perhaps calmer people find it easier to keep up a meditation habit, or perhaps a third factor, such as a healthier lifestyle or more free time, produces both. Only an experiment can show that meditation causes the reduction (the logic is taught in the Research Methodology book). Indian context Meditation is among India's oldest contributions to psychology. In Patanjali's Yoga Sutras , the eight limbs of yoga ( ashtanga ) move from ethical restraints and observances ( yama , niyama ), posture ( asana ) and breath control ( pranayama ) to withdrawal of the senses from their objects ( pratyahara ), concentration ( dharana ), meditation ( dhyana ) and absorption ( samadhi ). Dharana and dhyana are close to what psychologists call concentrative meditation, while Buddhist vipassana is the source of mindfulness practice. Sufism describes its process of psycho-spiritual transformation as a comparable journey, from our mundane surface awareness to the depths and heights of self-consciousness, using practices such as dhikr , the rhythmic repetition of divine names. (Indian psychology is taught in Chapter 2.) Sensory deprivation Meditation reduces the variety of what we attend to. What happens if the world's input is taken away almost entirely? In the early 1950s, in Donald Hebb's laboratory at McGill University in Montreal, William Bexton, Woodburn Heron and Thomas Scott (1954) tried to find out. Key study: the McGill sensory deprivation experiments (1954) Male students were paid 20 dollars a day, generous money at the time, to do nothing at all. Each lay on a comfortable bed in a lit cubicle for as long as he could bear, wearing translucent goggles that let in diffuse light but no patterns, cotton gloves and long cardboard cuffs that limited touch, with his head on a U-shaped foam pillow and the steady hum of an air conditioner masking other sounds. He came out only to eat and use the toilet. Although the money was good, most volunteers quit within two or three days. They found it hard to think clearly or concentrate, did worse on simple cognitive tests, became irritable and restless, and many experienced hallucinations, beginning with dots and geometric patterns and developing into whole scenes; Heron later described one volunteer who saw a procession of squirrels with sacks over their shoulders marching across a snowfield. They also became more easily persuaded by recorded talks about the supernatural. The McGill studies, sometimes described as research into the "pathology of boredom", showed that the waking brain needs a steady flow of varied stimulation to function normally, an idea that fed into arousal theories of motivation (Chapter 10). Later researchers softened the picture. The neuroscientist John Lilly developed the flotation tank, in which a person floats in skin-temperature salt water in darkness and silence, and the psychologist Peter Suedfeld showed that short sessions of sensory deprivation , which he called the restricted environmental stimulation technique (REST), are often experienced as deeply relaxing and can help people stop smoking. The clinical relevance is real: hallucinations are common in people with severe visual loss (the Charles Bonnet syndrome), and the monotony of an intensive care unit contributes to confusion in some patients. Psychoactive drugs The most common way people deliberately alter consciousness is chemical: the morning coffee, the evening drink, the cigarette, the cup of bhang at Holi. A psychoactive drug is a chemical substance that changes perception, mood, thought or consciousness by acting on the nervous system, mostly at synapses: some mimic a neurotransmitter, some block its receptors, and some change how much of it is released or how quickly it is removed. (The synaptic mechanisms are taught in the Physiological Psychology book.) Three terms describe what happens with repeated use. Tolerance is the decreasing effect of the same dose with repeated use, so that larger doses are needed to get the original effect; tolerance to one drug often brings tolerance to similar drugs (cross-tolerance, as between alcohol and benzodiazepines). Dependence is a state in which the person needs the drug to function normally. Physical dependence means that the body has adapted to the drug's presence, so that stopping it produces withdrawal; psychological dependence is a compulsive craving to use the drug for its emotional effects. Withdrawal is the set of unpleasant symptoms that follows stopping a drug on which one is physically dependent, and the symptoms are usually the opposite of the drug's effects: anxiety and tremor after alcohol, fatigue and depression after stimulants, and pain, diarrhoea and gooseflesh after opiates. Table 5.11 summarises the main classes. Table 5.11 The main classes of psychoactive drugs. Class Examples Main effects Notes Depressants Alcohol; barbiturates; benzodiazepines (Valium, Xanax, Rohypnol, Halcion) Slow nervous system activity; relaxation, disinhibition, sedation, sleep Enhance GABA; dangerous in combination; suppress REM sleep Stimulants Caffeine, nicotine, amphetamines, cocaine, MDMA (ecstasy) Increase arousal, alertness and energy; euphoria; reduced appetite Cocaine blocks dopamine reuptake; a "crash" follows Opiates (opioids) Opium, morphine, heroin, codeine, fentanyl Pain relief, euphoria, drowsiness, constricted pupils Mimic endorphins; overdose stops breathing; strong dependence Hallucinogens (psychedelics) LSD, psilocybin, mescaline Distorted perception, hallucinations, altered sense of self and time Mostly act on serotonin receptors; "bad trips" and flashbacks Cannabis Marijuana, ganja, charas, bhang (THC) Relaxation, mild euphoria, altered time sense, impaired memory and coordination Mixed effects; raises psychosis risk in vulnerable users Depressants slow the activity of the nervous system. Alcohol, the most widely used, acts largely by enhancing the inhibitory transmitter GABA; at low doses it disinhibits (which is why it can look like a stimulant), at higher doses it impairs judgement, coordination and memory, and at very high doses it can be fatal. Claude Steele and Robert Josephs (1990) described its effect on thought as alcohol myopia : alcohol narrows attention to the most salient cues of the moment, so that a drunk person responds to immediate provocations and forgets distant consequences. The barbiturates (such as phenobarbital and amobarbital) were once widely prescribed as sedatives and sleeping pills, but the margin between an effective and a fatal dose is narrow, and they have largely been replaced by the benzodiazepines , a class that includes diazepam (sold as Valium), alprazolam (Xanax), flunitrazepam (Rohypnol) and triazolam (Halcion). Benzodiazepines are used to reduce anxiety (as anxiolytics), to sedate and to induce sleep (as hypnotics); they are much safer than barbiturates on their own but still cause tolerance and dependence, and they are dangerous when combined with alcohol. Stimulants increase nervous system activity. Caffeine works by blocking adenosine receptors (Section 5.6); nicotine acts on acetylcholine receptors; amphetamines increase the release of dopamine and noradrenaline; cocaine blocks their reuptake, prolonging their action, and is followed by a "crash" of fatigue and low mood. MDMA (ecstasy) is a stimulant with mild hallucinogenic effects that releases large amounts of serotonin. Opiates , derived from the opium poppy (morphine, codeine and heroin) and their synthetic relatives (opioids such as fentanyl), relieve pain and produce euphoria because they mimic the brain's own opioids, the endorphins and enkephalins, at opiate receptors; they produce strong physical dependence, and overdose kills by stopping breathing. Hallucinogens (psychedelics) distort perception and thought. The best known, LSD (lysergic acid diethylamide), was first synthesised by the Swiss chemist Albert Hofmann (1906 to 2008), who discovered its extraordinary effects by accident in 1943; psilocybin (from certain mushrooms) and mescaline (from the peyote cactus) have similar effects, largely through serotonin receptors. Cannabis (marijuana, and in India ganja, charas and bhang) is usually placed in a class of its own because its effects are mixed: its active ingredient, THC (tetrahydrocannabinol), acts on the brain's cannabinoid receptors to produce relaxation and mild euphoria, heightened sensory experience, a slowed sense of time, increased appetite and impaired short-term memory and coordination; at high doses it can produce hallucinations, and heavy use in adolescence raises the risk of psychosis in vulnerable people. Exam trap Valium, Xanax, Rohypnol and Halcion are all benzodiazepines . They are also sedatives and hypnotics in function, which makes those options tempting, but the question asks for the drug class they share, and "sedative" and "hypnotic" describe uses that barbiturates and other drugs share too. They are not barbiturates ; examples of barbiturates are phenobarbital, amobarbital (sodium amytal) and secobarbital. Alcohol is a depressant, not a stimulant, despite its early disinhibiting effect; MDMA is usually classed as a stimulant with hallucinogenic properties. Clinical link Tolerance, withdrawal and craving are the building blocks of substance use disorders, which are among the commonest problems in Indian psychiatric practice (alcohol above all, then cannabis, opioids and tobacco); the diagnostic criteria and treatments are covered in the Psychiatric Disorders book. Two facts from this chapter recur in the clinic: benzodiazepines and alcohol suppress REM sleep, so stopping them brings vivid dreams and broken sleep that tempt relapse, and long-term sleeping-pill use can itself cause insomnia, a reason that CBT-I is preferred. The case of Armond's dancing eyes, revisited Think back to the night in Chicago when the pens of Eugene Aserinsky's old machine began to jerk while his son slept. You can now say exactly what he was seeing. About 70 to 90 minutes after falling asleep, Armond had passed down through N1, N2 and the delta waves of N3, climbed back up, and entered his first period of REM sleep: a desynchronised, waking-like EEG, bursts of rapid eye movements, the large muscles of his body held in atonia by circuits in his brainstem, and, very probably, a dream. Through the rest of the night the pattern returned every 90 minutes or so, four to six times, the REM periods growing longer toward morning. At his age, about a fifth to a quarter of his sleep was REM; as a newborn it had been half. The discovery that Aserinsky first suspected was a machine fault also changed how psychologists think about consciousness. Sleep is not the absence of mind but a sequence of states, switched on by the brain's own circuits and timed by a clock in the hypothalamus. Waking consciousness, too, turned out to be far smaller and more selective than it feels: a narrow stream chosen by attention from a flood of input, while much of the mind's work goes on unseen. Hypnosis, meditation, sensory deprivation and drugs show how far that stream can be bent. Aserinsky's real contribution, in the end, was to wake people up and ask them what they had been experiencing, which is the question this whole chapter has been asking. Chapter summary 5.1 Attention: what it is, how it behaves and what captures it. William James (1890) defined attention as the mind taking possession of one of several possible objects, with focalisation and concentration as its essence. Attention may be involuntary, voluntary or habitual, and Sohlberg and Mateer's clinical model distinguishes focused, sustained, selective, alternating and divided attention. Its characteristics are selectivity, shifting, a limited span, fluctuation and limited division. The span of attention, studied by Jevons (1871) with beans and later with the tachistoscope, is about six to eight unrelated items (about four for errorless subitising), which is why number plates use short groups. Fluctuation is shown by the Masson disc. Attention is determined by external factors (intensity, size, contrast, change, movement, novelty, repetition) and internal factors (motives, interests, mental set, attitudes). 5.2 Selective listening: filters, attenuators and late selection. Cherry (1953) named the cocktail party problem and used dichotic listening with shadowing; listeners noticed physical but not semantic changes in the unattended ear, although Moray (1959) found that about a third heard their own names. Broadbent's filter model (1958), the first information-processing theory, placed an all-or-none filter early. Treisman's attenuation model (1964) turned unattended messages down rather than off, with dictionary units of varying thresholds, and best explains the cocktail party phenomenon. Deutsch and Deutsch (1963) and Norman (1968) placed selection late. Johnston and Heinz (1978) made selection flexible but costly, and Lavie's perceptual load theory showed that high load produces early selection and low load late selection. 5.3 Visual attention: spotlights, binding and blindness to the obvious. Covert visual attention behaves like a spotlight or a zoom lens (Eriksen and St James, 1986). Posner's cueing task (1980) separated endogenous (voluntary, central cues) from exogenous (automatic, peripheral cues) attention and revealed inhibition of return. Treisman and Gelade's feature integration theory (1980) proposed a parallel preattentive stage for features and a serial focused-attention stage that binds them, explaining pop-out, linear conjunction search slopes and illusory conjunctions. Inattentional blindness (Mack and Rock; Simons and Chabris's gorilla, 1999), change blindness (Rensink and colleagues; Simons and Levin) and the attentional blink (Raymond and colleagues, 1992) show how much goes unseen without attention. 5.4 Divided attention, automaticity, the Stroop effect and vigilance. Kahneman's capacity model (1973) treats attention as a single pool of effort allocated by policy; Wickens's multiple resource theory explains why similar tasks interfere more than different ones. Phone use impairs driving even when hands-free. Posner and Snyder (1975) and Shiffrin and Schneider (1977) distinguished fast, parallel, effortless, inflexible automatic processes from slow, serial, effortful, flexible controlled ones. The Stroop effect (1935) shows that automatic word reading interferes with colour naming, a failure of selective attention and a measure of inhibition. Vigilance, or sustained attention, declines over time (Mackworth's clock, 1948), as in radar and air traffic control work. ADHD, neglect and delirium are clinical disorders of attention. 5.5 Consciousness: definitions, levels and the brain. Consciousness is awareness of ourselves and our environment, with a level (measured by the Glasgow Coma Scale) and a content. James (1890) described a personal, changing, continuous, object-directed and selective stream of consciousness, whose most studied feature is daydreaming. Freud's topographic model divides the mind into conscious, preconscious (recallable at will) and unconscious (repressed) levels; modern psychology adds the nonconscious and the cognitive unconscious, supported by blindsight, fast threat processing and implicit attitudes. The reticular activating system maintains arousal; Chalmers's hard problem asks why processing is experienced at all. Altered states of consciousness (Tart, Ludwig) include sleep, hypnosis, meditation and drug states; the Mandukya Upanishad describes waking, dreaming, deep sleep and turiya. 5.6 Biological rhythms: the body's clocks. Circadian rhythms of about 24 hours free-run at about 24.2 hours without time cues and are entrained by zeitgebers, chiefly light. The suprachiasmatic nucleus of the hypothalamus is the master clock, receiving light through the retinohypothalamic tract and controlling melatonin release from the pineal gland. Jet lag is worse flying east (phase advance), and shift rotations work better forward. Borbély's two-process model combines homeostatic sleep pressure with the circadian signal. Ultradian rhythms (such as the 90-minute sleep cycle) are shorter than a day; infradian rhythms (such as the menstrual cycle) are longer. 5.7 The stages of sleep. Polysomnography records EEG, EOG and EMG. Beta marks alert waking, alpha relaxed waking with eyes closed, theta N1, spindles and K-complexes N2, and delta N3 (slow-wave sleep; stages 3 and 4 in the older system). REM sleep, discovered by Aserinsky and Kleitman (1953) and called paradoxical by Jouvet, combines a desynchronised EEG, rapid eye movements, atonia, autonomic variability, genital arousal and vivid dreams. Cycles of about 90 minutes repeat four to six times a night, with N3 early and REM late. REM forms half of a newborn's sleep and about a fifth of an adult's (Roffwarg and colleagues, 1966). The VLPO switches sleep on; orexin stabilises waking; the pons generates REM. 5.8 Why we sleep, what deprivation does and when sleep goes wrong. Recuperation theories stress restoration and waste clearance, adaptive theories stress safety and energy conservation, and other theories stress memory consolidation. Sleep deprivation (Randy Gardner's 264 hours) mainly impairs mood and sustained attention and produces microsleeps; REM deprivation produces REM rebound. Sleep disorders include insomnia, narcolepsy with cataplexy, sleep apnoea, NREM parasomnias (sleepwalking and sleep terrors, from N3), REM parasomnias (nightmares and REM sleep behaviour disorder) and restless legs syndrome. CBT-I uses stimulus control, sleep restriction and paradoxical intention. 5.9 Dreams. Dreams are most vivid in REM sleep, unfold in roughly real time, incorporate outside stimuli and usually reflect everyday concerns. Freud (1900) saw dreams as disguised wish fulfilments in which the dream work (condensation, displacement, symbolisation, secondary revision) turns latent into manifest content; Jung saw them as compensatory symbolic messages that can carry archetypes. Hobson and McCarley's activation-synthesis hypothesis (1977) explains dreams as the cortex's synthesis of random brainstem activation; information-processing, memory-consolidation and continuity theories link dreams to the handling of experience; Revonsuo's threat-simulation theory (2000) gives them an evolutionary function. Lucid dreams were verified with eye signals; hypnagogic imagery occurs falling asleep and hypnopompic imagery waking up. 5.10 Hypnosis. Hypnosis is a social interaction based on suggestibility. Its history runs from Mesmer's animal magnetism and the 1784 commission through Braid, who coined hypnotism, Charcot's view of it as pathology, the Nancy school's view of it as normal suggestion, and Freud and Breuer's cathartic method. Susceptibility, measured by the Stanford scales, is stable and linked to absorption. Hypnosis can relieve pain and produce posthypnotic suggestions and reversible amnesia, but it cannot give superhuman strength or reliably recover memories. Hilgard's neodissociation theory and hidden observer contrast with the social-cognitive theories of Sarbin, Barber and Spanos. 5.11 Meditation, sensory deprivation and psychoactive drugs. Concentrative meditation (including TM) focuses attention on one object; mindfulness meditation opens it to whatever arises. Meditation produces Benson's relaxation response, and MBSR and MBCT have clinical value, though correlational surveys cannot prove that meditation causes benefits. The McGill sensory deprivation studies (1954) produced impaired thinking and hallucinations, while brief REST can relax. Psychoactive drugs (depressants including alcohol and benzodiazepines, stimulants, opiates, hallucinogens and cannabis) alter consciousness through synaptic actions and produce tolerance, dependence and withdrawal.
