In 1913 a young German psychologist named Wolfgang Köhler (1887 to 1967) sailed to Tenerife, in the Canary Islands, to run a small research station of the Prussian Academy of Sciences. The station kept a colony of chimpanzees, and Köhler, one of the three founders of Gestalt psychology, wanted to answer a question that had been nagging him: could an ape solve a problem by understanding it, or only by blundering about until it stumbled on the answer? The First World War broke out the following year and kept him on the island far longer than he had planned, until 1920. The war's loss was psychology's gain. The brightest of Köhler's chimpanzees was a male called Sultan. In one test a banana lay on the ground outside the bars of Sultan's enclosure, too far to reach by hand. Inside lay two hollow bamboo sticks, neither long enough on its own to reach the fruit. Sultan tried one stick, then the other. He pushed one stick out with the other until its tip touched the banana, but he could not draw the fruit in. Eventually he seemed to give up and sat playing idly with the sticks. Then, according to the record Köhler published, he happened to hold the two sticks in a line, pushed the thinner one into the hollow end of the thicker, jumped up, ran to the bars and raked in the banana with his new, longer tool. When the test was repeated he made the double stick at once, without fumbling. Other chimpanzees stacked boxes to reach fruit hung from the roof, or fetched a stick from another room to use as a rake. To Köhler, these solutions did not look like the slow, accidental trial and error that Edward Thorndike had described in cats escaping from puzzle boxes in 1898. They appeared suddenly, as a whole, and once found they were kept. Köhler called this Einsicht , insight, and described the work in a 1917 book that appeared in English in 1925 as The Mentality of Apes . What was going on inside Sultan's head in the moment before he jumped up? Did he "see" a picture of the joined sticks? Did he have a concept of a tool? Was he reasoning? And here is the question that will follow us to the end of this chapter: Sultan had no words, so was he thinking at all? Remember Sultan; you will meet him again at the end of the chapter. 8.1 What Is Thinking? Lower yield · 3 Qs Ask ten people what thinking is and most of the answers will go round in a circle ("thinking is when you think about things"). Psychologists define thinking (or thought) as the mental manipulation of internal representations of information to form new representations: to understand something, solve a problem, reason, decide or create. The key word is manipulation . Seeing the chai stall in front of you is not thinking, and neither is simply remembering what a cup cost yesterday. Working out whether you can afford a second cup and still catch the bus is. Thinking takes what perception and memory supply and transforms it. A broader word you will meet constantly is cognition : all the mental processes by which we acquire, store, transform and use knowledge, from attention and perception through memory to language and thought. Thinking is the part of cognition that does the transforming. Attention, perception and memory have their own chapters (4 to 7); this chapter is about what the mind does with what they deliver. How Thought Came Back Into Psychology If you want a science of thought you need some way to observe it, and for the first half of the twentieth century psychology could not agree on one. The structuralists, led in America by Edward Bradford Titchener (1867 to 1927), held that every thought is built from sensations, images and feelings, and that trained introspection could reveal them. In the first decade of the 1900s a group of researchers at the University of Würzburg, led by Oswald Külpe (1862 to 1915), gave trained observers simple tasks (find a word that is a superordinate of "bird", for example) and asked them to describe what passed through their minds. To everyone's surprise the observers often reported thoughts with no image or sensation in them at all. This became known as imageless thought . The Würzburg group also noticed that the task itself (the Aufgabe ) steered thinking without being consciously present; Narziss Ach called this guiding influence the determining tendency . Titchener's observers at Cornell, doing the same kind of introspection, insisted that they always found images. Who was right? There was no way to tell, because introspective reports cannot be checked by anyone else. That deadlock was one reason John Broadus Watson (1878 to 1958) threw introspection out of psychology in 1913. For Watson thinking was nothing more than implicit, subvocal speech: tiny movements of the larynx and tongue (you will see in Section 8.9 how that idea was tested and failed). Thought came back with the cognitive revolution of the 1950s and 1960s. Noam Chomsky (born 1928) attacked the behaviourist account of language; Allen Newell (1927 to 1992) and Herbert Alexander Simon (1916 to 2001) built computer programs that solved problems; Jerome Seymour Bruner (1915 to 2016) and his colleagues published A Study of Thinking (1956); and in 1967 Ulric Neisser (1928 to 2012) wrote the textbook Cognitive Psychology , which gave the new field its name. Notice the irony. Cognitive psychology returned to the very topics the structuralists had cared about (consciousness, mental imagery, thought) but measured them objectively, with reaction times and error rates, instead of trusting introspective reports. (The history of the schools is told in Chapter 2.) Exam trap Which modern approach is closest to structuralism? Cognitive psychology, because it studies the structuralists' topics (consciousness, imagery, thought processes), not behaviourism (which banned them), not functionalism (which asked what the mind is for ) and not neuroscience (which studies the nervous system that underlies all behaviour rather than continuing the structuralists' programme). Who pioneered cognitive psychology? Neisser named the field (1967) and is often called its father; Chomsky, Newell and Simon, Bruner and George Miller drove the revolution. Jean Piaget, who studied how children's thinking develops, is keyed as "a pioneer contributor to cognitive psychology" in one recent paper. Köhler was a forerunner (Gestalt work on insight). Lawrence Kohlberg is the name to reject: he is examined for moral development. The Elements of Thought What is thought made of? Textbooks list five building blocks. To see them at work, imagine you are deciding how to get to an exam hall across Mysuru early on a Monday morning. Images. You "see" the route in your mind's eye: the crowded junction, the bus stop beside the temple. A mental image is a quasi-perceptual representation of something not present to the senses, and images can be auditory or tactile as well as visual. Concepts. You think about "buses", "auto-rickshaws" and "traffic jams". A concept is a mental category that groups things sharing common properties (Section 8.2 is devoted to them). Symbols and signs. The ₹ sign on the fare chart and the number 201 on the bus are symbols: they stand for something purely by convention. A sign, in the older textbook usage, has a natural or causal link to what it signals: dark clouds are a sign of rain, smoke a sign of fire. Propositions. "The eight o'clock bus is usually late." A proposition is the smallest unit of knowledge that can be judged true or false; it asserts a relation between concepts. Language. Finally you tell yourself, in words, "Take the auto." Language is the most powerful symbol system we have, because a finite set of words and rules can express an unlimited number of propositions. Older textbooks sometimes add a sixth element, implicit muscular activity, which reflects Watson's motor theory of thought. Most modern accounts drop it. Mental Imagery: Are There Pictures in the Head? When you imagine the route to the exam hall, is there really something like a picture in your head, or does it only feel that way? Psychologists define mental imagery as the mental representation of a stimulus that is not physically present, experienced as if one were perceiving it. For decades the question of what images "are" seemed unanswerable, for exactly the reasons that sank the imageless-thought debate. Then, in 1971, an experiment showed that images could be measured with a stopwatch. Key study: Shepard and Metzler's mental rotation (1971) The question. When you judge whether two objects in different orientations are the same, do you turn one of them in your mind? The method. Roger Newland Shepard (1929 to 2022) and Jacqueline Metzler showed eight adults pairs of line drawings of three-dimensional objects, each built from ten cubes joined face to face. The second object was rotated by 0 to 180 degrees relative to the first, either in the picture plane or in depth, and was either the same object or its mirror image. Participants pressed "same" or "different" as fast as they could. The result. The time needed to say "same" increased in a straight line with the angle between the two objects, by roughly one second for every 60 degrees (Figure 8.1), and rotation in depth took no longer than rotation in the picture plane. The conclusion. People appear to rotate an analogue representation through intermediate positions, much as one would turn a real object; Shepard called this mental rotation . The criticism. A straight line shows that the process is gradual and continuous, but it does not prove that the representation is literally a picture. 0 1 2 3 4 5 0 60 120 180 Angle of rotation between the two objects (degrees) Time to answer "same" (s) Each extra 60 degrees adds about one second Figure 8.1 The mental rotation function, idealised from Shepard and Metzler (1971). Notice that the line is straight: the further the object must be turned, the longer the judgement takes, just as if a real object were being rotated at a steady speed. Stephen Michael Kosslyn (born 1948) extended the stopwatch approach. In one experiment (Kosslyn, Ball and Reiser, 1978) participants memorised a map of a fictional island with seven landmarks (a hut, a tree, a rock, a well, a lake, a patch of sand and a patch of grass). Later, with eyes closed, they imagined a black speck travelling from one landmark to another. The time taken rose in a straight line with the real distance on the map, as if they were scanning across a picture. In another study, people asked to imagine a rabbit beside an elephant took longer to "see" whether the rabbit had whiskers than people who imagined the same rabbit beside a fly: next to the elephant, the imagined rabbit was small and its details hard to inspect. Kosslyn concluded that images are depictive representations that preserve spatial layout, size and distance. Not everyone was convinced. In 1973 Zenon Walter Pylyshyn (1937 to 2022) launched what became known as the imagery debate . According to his propositional theory , the experience of an image is an epiphenomenon, a by-product that does no work; underneath, knowledge is stored as abstract, language-like propositions ("the hut is north of the lake"). Why, then, does scanning time follow distance? Pylyshyn's answer was tacit knowledge : participants know how long it takes to look across a real map and, consciously or not, they reproduce that timing when asked to "scan" an image. The debate was eventually settled largely by the brain. Imagining an object activates early visual cortex, including the primary visual cortex, and does so in a spatially organised way. Brain damage that disturbs vision tends to disturb imagery in parallel. In a famous demonstration, Edoardo Bisiach and Claudio Luzzatti (1978) asked patients with left-sided neglect after right-hemisphere damage to imagine standing on the cathedral steps in Milan's Piazza del Duomo and describe what they "saw". They listed buildings on the right of the square only. Asked to imagine standing at the opposite end, they now listed the buildings they had left out, and omitted the ones they had just named. A purely propositional store has no left or right side to neglect. Yet images are not simply photographs either: Deborah Chambers and Daniel Reisberg (1985) found that people who formed an image of the ambiguous duck-rabbit figure could not "flip" it in imagery, although they flipped it at once when they drew their image on paper. The modern consensus is that images are depictive, but they come with their interpretation attached. Another Canadian psychologist, Allan Paivio (1925 to 2016), asked a related question about memory. His dual-coding theory (1971) proposes two separate but interconnected systems for representing information: a verbal system for words and a nonverbal or imagery system for pictures and objects. Concrete words such as "elephant" can be coded in both systems, whereas abstract words such as "justice" are coded mainly in the verbal one. Two codes give two routes to retrieval, which explains why concrete words are remembered better than abstract ones (the concreteness effect ) and pictures better than words (the picture superiority effect ). Imagery mnemonics such as the method of loci exploit the same advantage (Chapter 7). Exam trap "According to dual-coding theory, which information is more easily remembered?" The answer is visual (pictorial, imageable) information, because it can be coded twice. Verbal, auditory and abstract "semantic" material usually gets only the verbal code. Dual coding belongs to Paivio (1971) ; do not confuse it with Craik and Lockhart's levels of processing (1972) or with Baddeley and Hitch's working memory model (1974). And keep the two imagery theorists straight: Kosslyn = depictive images (scanning the island); Pylyshyn = propositions and tacit knowledge. Types of Thinking Not all thinking is alike. Some of it is aimed at a goal and checked against reality; some drifts. Some narrows down to one answer; some fans out. The distinctions below recur in every entrance paper, usually as "match the type with its description" or "who coined the term" items. Table 8.1 gathers them. The most basic contrast is between directed and undirected thinking. Directed (or realistic) thinking is controlled by a goal and constrained by logic and reality: planning a journey, solving a sum, writing an answer. Undirected or associative thinking lets one idea call up the next by association, with no goal steering it; daydreaming in a warm afternoon lecture is the everyday example, and Freud's free association is its clinical use. At the far end of undirected thinking lies what the Swiss psychiatrist Eugen Bleuler (1857 to 1939) called autistic thinking in his 1911 monograph on dementia praecox, the book that made his new terms "schizophrenia" and "autism" famous. Autistic thinking is thinking governed by wishes and needs rather than by reality: fantasy in which you top the merit list, receive the award and silence your critics. Because the word "autistic" invited confusion, Bleuler later offered the alternative dereistic thinking (thinking "away from reality"). Jean Piaget borrowed Bleuler's term and placed the young child's egocentric thought halfway between autistic thought and mature directed thought, a point you will meet again in Section 8.9. The American psychometrician Joy Paul Guilford (1897 to 1987) contributed the most famous pair. In convergent thinking , thought narrows down to the single best or correct answer, as when you solve a multiple-choice question or a crossword clue. In divergent thinking , it fans out to generate many possible answers, as when you list all the uses you can think of for a brick. Divergent thinking is the core of Guilford's account of creativity and of most creativity tests (Section 8.6). By critical thinking psychologists mean the careful evaluation of claims, arguments and evidence before accepting them; the philosopher Robert Ennis's widely used definition is "reasonable reflective thinking focused on deciding what to believe or do". Checking who wrote a health message forwarded on a family WhatsApp group, and on what evidence, is critical thinking. Creative thinking , by contrast, produces ideas or products that are both new and useful. Critical thinking evaluates; creative thinking generates. Good problem solvers alternate between them. The term reflective thinking belongs to the American philosopher and educator John Dewey (1859 to 1952). In How We Think (1910) he defined it as the active, persistent and careful consideration of a belief in the light of the grounds that support it, and described it as beginning with a felt difficulty and moving through defining the problem, suggesting solutions, reasoning out their implications and testing them. (Those five steps are also one of the earliest models of problem solving; see Section 8.3.) Finally, the Gestalt psychologist Max Wertheimer (1880 to 1943), in Productive Thinking (published in 1945, after his death), distinguished productive thinking , which restructures a problem and so produces genuine understanding, from reproductive thinking , which merely reapplies a learned method. A child who sees that a parallelogram can be turned into a rectangle by cutting off a triangle at one end and moving it to the other end has thought productively; a child who simply plugs numbers into a memorised formula has thought reproductively. Clinical link In the mental status examination, disturbances of thinking are classically sorted under four headings. The stream of thought (its speed and flow: pressure of thought, poverty of thought, thought block); the form of thought, meaning how ideas are linked (loosening of associations or derailment, tangentiality, circumstantiality, flight of ideas, "knight's move" thinking, word salad, neologisms), the formal thought disorder characteristic of schizophrenia, of which word salad is the most severe form; the content of thought (delusions, overvalued ideas, preoccupations); and the possession of thought, the sense that one's thoughts are one's own (obsessions, and thought insertion, withdrawal and broadcasting). A patient whose answer wanders through needless detail but finally reaches the point shows circumstantiality , a disorder of form; one who drifts off and never returns shows tangentiality . The disorders themselves are covered in the Psychiatric Disorders book. 8.2 Concepts Medium yield · 4 Qs Imagine a world without concepts. Every dog you met would be a brand-new creature: you would not know whether it might bite, whether it eats grass, or whether it can be stroked. A concept is a mental representation of a category, a class of objects, events, ideas or people that share common properties. Concepts give us two enormous savings. They provide cognitive economy , because we can store what we know about dogs once rather than separately for every dog; and they support inference , because once you classify a new animal as a dog you can predict a great deal about it that you have not observed. Most of the elements of thought described in Section 8.1 depend on concepts. How Concepts Are Formed The term concept formation refers to the process by which we learn to group things into categories and to attach the right properties to each. Many textbooks, especially in India, describe it as passing through a series of steps. Follow a two-year-old learning the concept "dog". Observation. The child meets many particular instances: the neighbour's dog, the street dog near the gate, a dog in a picture book. Discrimination. The child notices differences: dogs bark and cows do not; dogs are smaller than cows; cats have a different face. Generalisation. The child notices what the instances have in common (four legs, fur, a tail, barking) and extends the label to new animals that share these features. Abstraction. The child pulls out the common features and represents them apart from any particular dog, so that "dog" now means the shared pattern, not Tommy next door. Many books add a final step of naming or labelling, because attaching a word to the abstraction makes the concept stable and shareable. The steps overlap in real life, and mistakes along the way are informative: the toddler who calls every four-legged animal "dog" has generalised too widely (an overextension; see Section 8.8). The first laboratory study of concept learning was carried out by Clark Leonard Hull (1884 to 1952), better known for his learning theory (Chapter 6). In 1920 Hull taught participants nonsense names for Chinese characters. Characters that shared a particular radical (a component stroke pattern) all received the same name, although the radical was embedded in otherwise different characters. Participants gradually came to name new characters correctly, often without being able to say what the common element was. Hull concluded that a concept is learned by the gradual, reinforced abstraction of a common element, an associative, step-by-step view. The Classical View and Artificial Concepts The oldest account of concepts goes back to Aristotle. According to the classical view (also called the defining-attribute view), every concept is defined by a set of defining features that are individually necessary and jointly sufficient. "Triangle" is a closed figure with three straight sides: anything with all three features is a triangle, and anything lacking one of them is not. "Bachelor" is an unmarried adult male. On this view membership is all-or-none, the boundaries are sharp, and every member is as good a member as any other. The classical view fits well-defined, rule-based categories, and these are exactly the categories that dominated early laboratory work. An artificial concept (or formal concept) is one defined by an explicit rule, typically invented by an experimenter, such as "all cards with two red borders". The rules can be combined in three logical ways: A conjunctive concept requires the joint presence of two or more attributes ("red and square"). An eligible voter in India is a conjunctive concept: an Indian citizen and aged eighteen or over and on the electoral roll. A disjunctive concept requires one attribute or another, or both ("red or square"). "Out" in cricket is beautifully disjunctive: bowled, or caught, or leg before wicket, or run out, or stumped, and so on. Two dismissals can share no feature at all and still both be "out". A relational concept is defined by a relationship between attributes rather than by the attributes themselves: "taller than", "between", "uncle" (a brother of one's parent), or "a card with more figures than borders". People find conjunctive concepts easiest and disjunctive ones hardest, partly because we expect members of a category to share something. Key study: Bruner, Goodnow and Austin's A Study of Thinking (1956) The question. When people learn an artificial concept, do they gradually strengthen associations (as Hull thought), or do they actively form and test hypotheses? The method. Jerome Bruner, Jacqueline Goodnow and George Austin used an array of 81 cards that varied on four attributes, each with three values: the shape of the figures (cross, circle or square), their colour (red, green or black), the number of figures (one, two or three) and the number of borders (one, two or three). The experimenter had a concept in mind, such as "red circles". In the selection paradigm the participant chose cards one at a time and was told whether each was a positive instance; in the reception paradigm the experimenter chose the cards. The result. Participants did not behave like associative machines. They formed hypotheses about the rule and used recognisable strategies to test them (Table 8.2). The conclusion. Concept attainment is an active process of hypothesis testing. This is the "hypothesis-testing model of concept formation". The criticism. The concepts were artificial and rule-defined; the real concepts of everyday life, as Eleanor Rosch was to show, are not like that. Exam trap "The researcher whose theory explains how we form artificial concepts by developing hypotheses" is Jerome Bruner (with Goodnow and Austin, 1956). Eleanor Rosch is the name for natural concepts and prototypes. Clark Hull (1920) did study concept learning, but as gradual associative abstraction of a common element, not hypothesis testing. John Watson has nothing to do with concepts. Also remember: in cricket, "out" is disjunctive (any one of several conditions), a voter is conjunctive (all conditions), "uncle" is relational . Natural Concepts and Prototype Theory Try to give a classical definition of "game". The philosopher Ludwig Wittgenstein (1889 to 1951) tried, in his posthumous Philosophical Investigations (1953), and failed. Cricket has teams and a winner; solitaire has no team; ring-a-ring-a-roses has no winner; chess involves skill, snakes and ladders only luck. There is no single feature that all games share. Instead, Wittgenstein said, games are related by a network of overlapping similarities, the way members of a family resemble one another: one has the father's nose and the mother's eyes, another the mother's eyes and the grandmother's chin, yet no single feature runs through them all. He called this family resemblance . Eleanor Rosch (born 1938) turned Wittgenstein's insight into experimental psychology in the 1970s. A natural concept is a category that people form through ordinary experience with the world (bird, fruit, furniture, vehicle), as opposed to an artificial concept defined by an experimenter's rule. Rosch showed that natural concepts have three properties that the classical view cannot explain. First, members differ in how typical they are. Asked to rate how good an example of "bird" each animal is, people agree that a robin or a sparrow is an excellent example, a hen a poorer one and a penguin a poor one. Second, typicality has measurable consequences. In a sentence verification task, people say "true" faster to "A robin is a bird" than to "A penguin is a bird", although both are equally true; this is the typicality effect . Typical members are also named first when people list category members, and children learn them first. Third, the boundaries of natural concepts are fuzzy. Michael McCloskey and Sam Glucksberg (1978) found that people disagreed about whether a stroke is a disease or a tomato a fruit, and many even changed their own answers when asked again a few weeks later. Rosch's explanation is prototype theory . A prototype is the best, most typical representative of a category: an abstract average or central tendency of the members we have encountered, not any particular one of them. Rosch and Carolyn Mervis (1975) showed that an item's typicality depends on its family resemblance score, the number of features it shares with other members of the category. A new object is classified by comparing it with the prototype; the more similar it is, the faster and more confidently it is accepted. Rosch made a second discovery about how categories are arranged vertically. Rosch and colleagues (1976) distinguished three levels: the superordinate level (furniture, animal), the basic level (chair, dog) and the subordinate level (kitchen chair, Labrador). The basic level is psychologically privileged. It is the most general level at which members share a common shape and are used with similar movements, it is the level children learn first, and it is the level people use to name things: shown pictures of objects, Rosch's participants used basic-level names 1,595 times, subordinate names 14 times and a superordinate name just once. The basic level gives the best trade-off between being informative and being distinctive. Figure 8.2 shows both of Rosch's discoveries side by side. (Experts shift downwards: a birdwatcher says "Indian robin" where you say "bird".) Exam trap "An idealised representative object of a category" is a prototype , and a prototype is abstract and averaged : it need not be any real member you have met. Do not confuse it with three terms from pattern recognition (Chapter 4): a template is an exact stored copy that input must match; features are the elementary parts (lines, angles) that feature-analysis theories detect; geons are the 36 or so simple three-dimensional shapes in Irving Biederman's recognition-by-components theory (1987). Family resemblance began with Wittgenstein (1953) and was tested by Rosch and Mervis (1975). Exemplar Theory Prototype theory has a weakness. If all you keep is an average, how do you know that birds vary a great deal in size, or that a small, plain brown bird may still be a sparrow? An alternative, exemplar theory , developed by Douglas Medin and Marguerite Schaffer (1978) and later Robert Nosofsky, proposes that we store many specific remembered instances ( exemplars ) of each category, and classify a new item by comparing it with all of them. A new animal is called a dog if it resembles the dogs you remember more than it resembles the cats you remember. Typicality effects still appear, because typical items resemble many stored exemplars; but the theory also explains why we know about a category's variability and its unusual members. Most researchers now think we use both kinds of representation: prototypes when categories are large and well learned, exemplars when they are small or newly learned. A third approach, the theory or knowledge-based view, adds that concepts are embedded in our wider explanatory knowledge: you know that a whale is a mammal not because it looks like other mammals (it looks like a fish) but because of what you know about how it breathes and bears its young. The first influential model of how, the hierarchical network model of Allan Collins and Ross Quillian (1969), pictured knowledge as a semantic network : concepts are nodes , and labelled links connect them ("canary IS A bird", "bird HAS wings"). To save space (cognitive economy), each property is stored only once, at the highest level to which it applies: "has skin" at the animal node, "can fly" at the bird node, "can sing" at the canary node. The model predicts that verifying a sentence takes longer the more links must be travelled, and so it does: "A canary can sing" is verified faster than "A canary can fly", which is faster than "A canary has skin". But the model could not explain the typicality effect, or why "A pig is an animal" is verified faster than "A pig is a mammal" (Rips, Shoben and Smith, 1973), which the hierarchy says should be the other way round. Collins and Elizabeth Loftus (1975) replaced the rigid hierarchy with a spreading activation model. Links now vary in strength, short for closely related concepts and long for distant ones, and activating one node spreads activation outward to its neighbours. This explains semantic priming : you recognise "nurse" faster just after reading "doctor" than after reading "bread" (Meyer and Schvaneveldt, 1971). A different kind of network arrived in 1986 with Parallel Distributed Processing by David Rumelhart, James McClelland and the PDP Research Group. In connectionism , knowledge is not stored in individual nodes that each stand for a concept. A concept is a pattern of activation distributed across many simple, neuron-like units, and all knowledge lies in the strengths (weights) of the connections between units, which change gradually with experience. Connectionist networks learn from examples, generalise to new ones, and degrade gracefully when damaged rather than losing whole facts, which makes them attractive models of the brain. Organised knowledge structures for familiar situations are also called schemas , and schemas for routine event sequences (going to a restaurant, attending a wedding) are called scripts (Schank and Abelson, 1977); their role in memory is discussed in Chapter 7. Exam trap "Which model proposes that memory is organised in a network of interconnected nodes?" A recent paper keyed connectionist model . That works, because connectionist (PDP) models are networks of interconnected units. But be careful: Collins and Quillian's semantic network model is also literally a network of nodes, so an option reading "semantic network model" would be equally defensible. When "network model" and "connectionist model" both appear, follow the key (connectionist), and remember the difference: semantic networks have one node per concept (localist); connectionist networks spread each concept over many units (distributed). "Associative model" is the older umbrella idea from Aristotle and the British associationists; "linkage model" is not a standard term. Scan Your Brain Fill in the blanks. The answers are below; cover them first. The Würzburg school reported that some thoughts contain no image; this finding is called thought. Shepard and Metzler found that the time to judge two objects as the same increased with the angle between them. Pylyshyn argued that images are epiphenomenal and that knowledge is stored as abstract . According to Paivio's theory, concrete words are remembered well because they have both a verbal and an imagery code. Bleuler's term for wish-fulfilling thinking that ignores reality is thinking. A concept such as "out" in cricket, satisfied by any one of several conditions, is a concept. In Bruner's study, choosing a positive card and changing one attribute at a time is called . Wittgenstein's idea that members of a category share overlapping features but no single common one is called . Rosch's "chair", as opposed to "furniture" or "kitchen chair", belongs to the level. Theories in which a category is represented by many stored instances are called theories. Answers: (1) imageless, (2) linearly, (3) propositions, (4) dual-coding, (5) autistic (or dereistic), (6) disjunctive, (7) conservative focusing, (8) family resemblance, (9) basic, (10) exemplar. 8.3 Problem Solving Medium yield · 9 Qs Sultan had a problem, and so do you most days. A problem exists whenever you are in one state (the initial state ), want to be in another (the goal state ), and the route from one to the other is not obvious. Problem solving is thinking directed at getting from the first to the second. Psychologists have studied it in two very different traditions: the Gestalt tradition of Köhler and Duncker, which asked how a problem is suddenly seen in a new way, and the information-processing tradition of Newell and Simon, which asked how a problem is searched . You need both. Kinds of Problems A well-defined problem has a clearly specified initial state, a clear goal and a clear set of allowable moves: an algebra equation, a sudoku, the Tower of Hanoi. An ill-defined problem leaves one or more of these vague: "write a good answer on attachment theory", "choose a career", "help this client feel less hopeless". Most of the problems of real life, and nearly all clinical problems, are ill-defined, and much of the work of solving them lies in defining them. Researchers also distinguish knowledge-lean problems, which can be solved with the information given, from knowledge-rich problems, which need expertise; and insight problems, solved by a sudden change of view, from non-insight (analytic) problems, solved step by step. The Problem Space In 1956 Allen Newell and Herbert Simon, working with the programmer Cliff Shaw, unveiled the Logic Theorist , a computer program that proved theorems from Whitehead and Russell's Principia Mathematica . They followed it in the late 1950s with the General Problem Solver (GPS), designed to solve any well-defined problem, and set out the full theory in their 1972 book Human Problem Solving . Their method was to have people think aloud while solving puzzles, record every utterance (a verbal protocol ), and check whether the program went through the same steps. Their central idea was the problem space : an abstract description of all the possible states a problem can be in. It contains the initial state, the goal state, the operators (the legal moves that change one state into another), all the intermediate states those moves can produce, and the constraints on which moves are allowed. Solving a problem means searching this space for a path from the initial state to the goal. Take the Tower of Hanoi: three discs of decreasing size sit on the left of three pegs; the goal is to move them all to the right peg, moving one disc at a time and never placing a larger disc on a smaller. The shortest solution takes seven moves (in general, 2 n minus 1 moves for n discs). For three discs you could map the whole space on a sheet of paper; for a game such as chess, the number of possible paths is astronomically large. Because short-term memory is small and we can do only one thing at a time, Newell and Simon argued, people cannot search such spaces exhaustively. They must take shortcuts. Algorithms Versus Heuristics An algorithm is a step-by-step procedure that is guaranteed to produce the solution if it is followed correctly. Long division is an algorithm. So is trying every combination of a three-digit padlock: there are only 1,000 combinations, and if you try them all, one will open the lock. Algorithms are certain but often slow, and for many problems they are impossibly slow. A heuristic is a rule of thumb: a mental shortcut that usually leads to a solution quickly but does not guarantee one. The word comes from the same Greek root as "eureka" (to find), and the mathematician George Pólya popularised it in How to Solve It (1945). Suppose you must unscramble MSTAE into an English word. An algorithm would test all 120 possible orderings. A heuristic says: put consonant clusters that often begin English words at the front, and try familiar endings. "ST" looks promising, and STEAM (or MATES, MEATS, TAMES) appears within seconds. The price of speed is that a heuristic can mislead; you will see in Section 8.5 that the same trade-off runs through judgement and decision making. Exam trap "A rule of thumb that allows an efficient search for the solution of a problem" is a heuristic , not an algorithm. The defining contrast: an algorithm guarantees a solution; a heuristic is efficient but not guaranteed , "a general rule that is usually right". Wrong options to reject: "a heuristic always produces a solution" (that is an algorithm), "a heuristic is more accurate than an algorithm" (it is less certain, not more accurate), "heuristics can only be used by computers", "heuristics always produce errors". Education and learning are not problem-solving methods at all. Heuristic Strategies Newell and Simon regarded means-end analysis as the most important heuristic of all, and it was the engine of GPS. It has three steps: note the most important difference between the current state and the goal state; set a subgoal of reducing that difference; and select an operator that achieves the subgoal. Then repeat. Suppose you are in Mysuru and need a certificate attested at an office in Bengaluru by Friday. The biggest difference is distance, so the subgoal is "get to Bengaluru"; the operator is a train. A new difference appears (you are at home, not at the station), creating a sub-subgoal ("get to the station") with its own operator (an auto). Breaking a problem into such subgoals is the heart of the method. The strategy of working backward starts from the goal and works back towards the initial state. It is useful when the goal is clearly specified and there are many possible paths forward from the start. Try this: water lilies on a pond double the area they cover every day, and the pond is completely covered on day 30. On which day was it half covered? Working forward is hopeless; working backward gives the answer at once: day 29. Planning a revision timetable from the exam date backwards is the same strategy. The heuristic of hill climbing is simpler than means-end analysis: at each step you choose the move that takes you closest to the goal state, judged by some simple measure of progress. It is like trying to reach the top of a hill in thick fog by always stepping uphill. It works when progress is steady, but it fails whenever reaching the goal requires a move that takes you temporarily further away, because hill climbing looks only one step ahead and never plans. The classic demonstration is the Hobbits and Orcs problem (a version of the missionaries and cannibals puzzle): three hobbits and three orcs must cross a river in a boat that holds two, and the orcs must never outnumber the hobbits on either bank. At one point the only legal move is to bring two creatures back across the river, apparently undoing progress, and that is precisely where solvers stall (Thomas, 1974). Climbers call the trap a false summit; problem solvers call it a local maximum . Solving by analogy means using the solution of an earlier, similar problem to solve a new one. It is powerful when people notice the analogy, and the striking finding is how rarely they do. Key study: Gick and Holyoak's radiation problem (1980) The problem. Karl Duncker had posed it in 1945. A patient has an inoperable stomach tumour. A ray strong enough to destroy the tumour will also destroy the healthy tissue it passes through; a ray weak enough to spare the tissue will not destroy the tumour. What can the doctor do? The method. Mary Gick and Keith Holyoak first had participants memorise a story about a general who wished to capture a fortress. Every road to the fortress was mined so that a large force would set off the mines, but small groups could pass safely; the general divided his army and had the groups converge on the fortress at the same moment. Then participants attempted the radiation problem. The result. Only about 10 per cent solved the radiation problem without the story. Of those who had memorised the story, about 40 per cent used it spontaneously, but about 80 per cent solved the problem once told that the story might help. (The answer: aim several weak rays at the tumour from different directions so that they converge on it.) The conclusion. People can transfer a solution across problems that share structural similarity (the underlying principle of convergence), but they often fail to notice an analogy when the surface features (armies versus rays) differ. In a later study, Mark Keane (1987) used a story that was superficially similar to the problem (a surgeon using rays on a cancer), and 88 per cent of participants recalled it spontaneously. The most primitive strategy of all is trial and error : trying responses more or less at random and keeping whatever works. Edward Lee Thorndike 's cats in their puzzle boxes (1898) escaped this way, their escape times falling gradually over many trials (Chapter 6). Trial and error works when the possible moves are few and mistakes are cheap; it is hopeless for problems with large problem spaces. Table 8.4 summarises the strategies. Table 8.4 Problem-solving strategies. Strategy What you do Example Weakness Algorithm Follow a procedure that guarantees the answer Trying all 1,000 padlock codes Slow; impossible in large spaces Means-end analysis Reduce the biggest difference by setting subgoals Mysuru to Bengaluru by subgoals Demands memory for subgoals Working backward Start from the goal and reason back Water lilies, day 29 Needs a well-specified goal Hill climbing Take whichever move gets closest to the goal Always stepping uphill in fog Stuck when a backward move is needed Analogy Reuse the solution of a similar earlier problem Fortress story to radiation problem Analogies often go unnoticed Trial and error Try responses until one works Thorndike's cats Inefficient in large spaces Exam trap Match the description to the heuristic. "Choosing the option that moves you closer to the goal state" is hill climbing . "Breaking the problem into smaller parts" is subgoaling, the core of means-end analysis . "Employing the solution of a similar earlier problem" is analogy . "Trying different solutions until one works" is trial and error . Hill climbing differs from means-end analysis in having no subgoals: it looks only one step ahead. Insight and Incubation The Gestalt psychologists did not think that problems were solved by search. For Köhler, Wertheimer, Karl Duncker (1903 to 1940) and Norman Maier (1900 to 1977), many problems are solved by insight : a sudden restructuring of the way the problem is represented, so that its elements are seen in a new relationship and the solution becomes obvious, often with an "aha" experience. Köhler listed the marks of insightful solutions in his apes: the transition from helplessness to solution is sudden and complete; the solution, once found, is performed smoothly; it is retained; and it transfers to similar problems. Compare Thorndike's cats, whose times fell gradually and erratically over dozens of trials. Try the nine-dot problem in Figure 8.3 before you read on: join all nine dots with four straight lines without lifting your pen or retracing a line. Norman Maier used it in research in 1930, and most people fail. They assume, without being told, that the lines must stay inside the square the dots form. The solution requires going outside it. Yet even when people are told explicitly that they may go outside the square, only a minority succeed, which tells us that restructuring the problem is necessary but not sufficient: after the insight, there is still a search to do. (a) The puzzle, with the imagined boundary dashed 1 2 3 4 (b) The solution leaves the square Figure 8.3 The nine-dot problem. Most people fail because they impose a boundary that the instructions never mention; lines 1 and 2 must run beyond the square formed by the dots. Insight here means relaxing a self-imposed constraint. Maier's other famous task, the two-string problem (1931), showed that insight can be nudged without awareness. Two strings hang from the ceiling, too far apart to hold both at once, and the task is to tie them together. The solution is to tie a heavy object, such as a pair of pliers, to one string and set it swinging like a pendulum, then catch it while holding the other. When Maier, walking past, casually brushed one string so that it swung, many participants solved the problem shortly afterwards, and most of them denied having noticed his hint. Key study: Metcalfe and Wiebe's warmth ratings (1987) The question. Is insight really sudden, or does it only feel sudden? The method. Janet Metcalfe and David Wiebe gave people insight problems and ordinary analytic problems (such as algebra), and at short, regular intervals asked them to rate how "warm" they felt, that is, how close to the solution. The result. On analytic problems warmth rose gradually and steadily, as you would expect from step-by-step search. On insight problems warmth stayed low and flat until just before the solution, then jumped. The conclusion. Insight problems are solved by a qualitatively different, sudden process, as the Gestaltists had claimed, and people cannot sense their approach to an insight solution. The criticism. Feelings of warmth are self-reports; some later researchers argue for a "business as usual" view in which insight uses ordinary memory and search processes that simply happen to end abruptly. Köhler's own conclusions also met a challenge. Herbert Birch (1945) found that young chimpanzees with no previous experience of handling sticks rarely solved stick problems; after a few days of playing with sticks, they solved them readily. Insight, it seems, builds on past experience rather than replacing it. What should you do when you are stuck? Often, the best advice is to stop. Researchers call the period during which a problem is set aside incubation ; after it, the solution sometimes arrives with surprisingly little effort. The term comes from Graham Wallas's stages of creative thought (Section 8.6). Why might a break help? Perhaps the mind continues to work on the problem unconsciously; perhaps fatigue lifts; but the best-supported explanation is that a break lets you forget a misleading approach that had been blocking you (the forgetting fixation hypothesis of Steven Smith and Steven Blankenship). A meta-analysis by Ut Na Sio and Thomas Ormerod (2009) concluded that incubation effects are real but modest, and largest for creative problems that have many possible solutions. Exam trap Two meanings of "insight". In problem solving, insight (Köhler, Gestalt) is the sudden restructuring of a problem. In the mental status examination, insight means the patient's awareness that he or she is ill, graded on a six-point scale: complete denial (grade 1); slight awareness of being ill and needing help, while denying it at the same time (grade 2); awareness of being ill but blaming others or external or physical causes (grade 3); awareness that the illness is due to something unknown in oneself (grade 4); intellectual insight , admitting illness and its psychological roots without applying the knowledge to change behaviour ( grade 5 ); and true emotional insight, which does lead to change (grade 6). Read the stem to see which meaning is meant. Obstacles to Problem Solving If problem solving were only a matter of search and insight, more of us would be good at it. The Gestaltists were especially interested in how past experience, usually our best friend, can get in the way. The first obstacle, functional fixedness , is the tendency to think of an object only in terms of its usual function, which blinds us to other uses that would solve a problem. Karl Duncker's candle problem , published in his monograph On Problem Solving (English translation 1945), is the classic demonstration. Participants received a candle, a book of matches and a box of drawing pins, and were asked to fix the candle to the wall so that it would burn without dripping wax onto the table. Most tried to pin the candle directly to the wall or to stick it on with melted wax. The solution is to empty the box, pin it to the wall as a shelf, and stand the candle in it. Far more people solved the problem when the box was presented empty, with the pins beside it, because an empty box does not look so much like a container. Functional fixedness is a case of top-down processing working too well: what we know about an object's typical use dominates what we perceive about its actual properties. Curiously, it seems to be learned. Tim German and Margaret Defeyter (2000) found that five-year-olds, who have not yet learned to think of objects in terms of their designed function, showed no functional fixedness on a version of the task, whereas six- and seven-year-olds did. A mental set is the broader tendency to approach a problem in a way that has worked before, even when a better or simpler method is available. Its classic demonstration is the water-jar experiment of Abraham Luchins (1942), whose German term for the phenomenon, Einstellung ("setting" or "attitude"), gives it its other name, the Einstellung effect. Work through Table 8.5. You have three jars of given capacities and an unlimited water supply, and you must measure out exactly the required amount. Table 8.5 Water-jar problems of the kind Luchins used (capacities in litres). Problem Jar A Jar B Jar C Obtain exactly Set problem (one of five) 21 127 3 100 Critical problem 23 49 3 20 Extinction problem 28 76 3 25 The set problem is solved by filling B, pouring off enough to fill A once, and then pouring off enough to fill C twice: B minus A minus 2C (127 minus 21 minus 6 is 100). After five problems that all yield to the same formula, people meet the critical problem. B minus A minus 2C still works (49 minus 23 minus 6 is 20), but so does a far simpler method: A minus C (23 minus 3). Most participants who had practised the formula used the long method and never noticed the short one. On the extinction problem the formula no longer works (76 minus 28 minus 6 is 42), and only A minus C does. In one report, 95 per cent of people without the training solved it, against only 36 per cent of those who had acquired the set. Even chess masters show the effect, overlooking a short winning line because a familiar long one comes to mind first. The other obstacles are easier to describe. Confirmation bias , the tendency to seek evidence that supports our current hypothesis rather than evidence that could refute it, keeps us on a wrong track (it is examined with Wason's experiments in Section 8.4). Irrelevant information distracts: "Your drawer holds black and brown socks in the ratio 4 to 5; how many must you pull out in the dark to be sure of a matching pair?" The ratio is irrelevant; the answer is three. Fixation , the Gestaltists' general word for being stuck on an inappropriate representation, covers both functional fixedness and mental set; and anxiety, fatigue and time pressure all narrow the search. Exam trap Functional fixedness is about objects (the box seen only as a container); mental set is about strategies (the formula that worked before). Functional fixedness is usually described as a special case of mental set, which is why one recent paper keyed mental set as "the most basic and common obstacle to problem solving". Names: candle problem = Duncker (1945) ; water jars and Einstellung = Luchins (1942) ; nine-dot and two-string problems = Maier . "Mental barrier" is not a technical term, and trial and error is a strategy, not an obstacle. Seeing a matchbox only as a container, not as a platform, is functional fixedness. Stages of Problem Solving and the Expert Advantage Several writers have broken problem solving into stages. Dewey (1910), as you saw, described a felt difficulty, its definition, suggested solutions, reasoning about them and testing. Pólya's How to Solve It (1945) offered four steps for mathematics students: understand the problem, devise a plan, carry out the plan, and look back to check. Robert Jeffrey Sternberg (born 1949) describes a problem-solving cycle of seven steps: identify the problem, define and represent it, formulate a strategy, organise the information, allocate resources (time, effort, money), monitor progress, and evaluate the solution. It is a cycle because evaluation often reveals a new problem. Whatever the labels, every scheme moves from understanding the problem, through generating and choosing a strategy, to carrying it out and checking the result. Why are experts better problem solvers? Not, it turns out, because they have better general reasoning. William Chase and Herbert Simon (1973), building on the Dutch psychologist Adriaan de Groot, showed chess positions for five seconds and asked players to reconstruct them. Masters reproduced real game positions far more accurately than novices, but when the pieces were placed at random, their advantage disappeared. Experts store thousands of meaningful patterns, or chunks , and see a board as a few familiar configurations rather than as twenty-odd separate pieces. Similarly, Michelene Chi and her colleagues (1981) found that physics experts sorted problems by their underlying principle (conservation of energy, say), whereas novices sorted them by surface features (problems with inclined planes, problems with springs). Experts spend longer representing a problem before starting, and then often work forward from what they know, whereas novices plunge in and work backward from the unknown. Clinical link Thomas D'Zurilla and Marvin Goldfried (1971) turned research on problem solving into a therapy. Problem-solving therapy teaches clients a structured sequence: a positive problem orientation, defining and formulating the problem, generating many alternative solutions without judging them, deciding among them, and implementing and verifying the chosen solution. It is used for depression, for people at risk of self-harm (who often show narrow, rigid problem solving under stress), and in primary care. Notice how much of it is the research of this section put to work: defining ill-defined problems, brainstorming to escape mental set, and evaluating outcomes. 8.4 Reasoning High yield · 9 Qs Reasoning is the process of drawing conclusions from premises or evidence. It overlaps with problem solving (you often reason your way to a solution) but its focus is on the inference : what follows from what? Philosophers have studied the rules of correct reasoning since Aristotle. Psychologists ask a different question: how do people actually reason, and why do they so often go wrong? Deduction, Induction and Abduction The first kind, deductive reasoning , moves from general premises to a specific conclusion that must be true if the premises are true. It is sometimes called top-down reasoning. "All autos in Mysuru must charge by the meter. This is a Mysuru auto. Therefore this auto must charge by the meter." The second kind, inductive reasoning , moves from specific observations to a general conclusion that is probable but never certain; it is bottom-up. "Every auto I have taken in Mysuru has asked for more than the meter. Therefore Mysuru autos overcharge." The next auto may prove you wrong. Deductive conclusions go no further than the premises; inductive conclusions go beyond them, which is both their power and their risk. Two terms keep deduction honest. An argument is valid when its conclusion follows necessarily from its premises because of its logical form, whatever the content. An argument is sound when it is valid and its premises are true. "All psychologists are vegetarians; Sihan is a psychologist; therefore Sihan is a vegetarian" is perfectly valid but unsound, because the first premise is false. So the truth of a deductive conclusion is only as good as the truth of the premises (or theory) it starts from. The American philosopher Charles Sanders Peirce (1839 to 1914) described a third kind of inference, abductive reasoning : inference to the best explanation. A surprising fact is observed; if some hypothesis were true, the fact would follow naturally; therefore there is reason to suspect the hypothesis is true. Diagnosis is abductive. A clinician sees early waking, weight loss, slowed speech and hopelessness, and infers the disorder that best explains them, while remaining ready to revise the conclusion. Science combines all three. In the hypothetico-deductive method , associated with the philosopher Karl Raimund Popper (1902 to 1994), a researcher derives a hypothesis from a theory, deduces a prediction that could be observed, and tests it. If the prediction fails, the hypothesis is refuted; if it succeeds, the hypothesis survives, but it is not proved, because another hypothesis might have made the same prediction. (You will see in a moment that this asymmetry is simply modus tollens versus affirming the consequent.) In research methods, a deductive approach starts from theory and tests it against data, as most quantitative research does; an inductive approach starts from data, looks for patterns and builds theory, as most qualitative research does (grounded theory is the purest example). Exam trap Recent papers ask the research-methods face of reasoning. "Starts with a theory and tests it with observations" = deductive reasoning . "Gathers data, looks for patterns, then generates a theory" or "moves from specific observations to broader generalisations" = inductive reasoning , which is the reasoning of theory development and of qualitative research . Abductive = best explanation. The hypothetico-deductive method is the full cycle of hypothesis, deduced prediction and test; when both "deductive reasoning" and "hypothetico-deductive method" appear, the keys have chosen the plain label. One paper asked what the "validity of conclusions" in deduction depends on, keying the soundness of the initial theory . Strictly, logical validity depends on form alone, and soundness on true premises; the item uses "validity" loosely to mean "trustworthiness", so choose the soundness option. Syllogisms, Belief Bias and the Atmosphere Effect A syllogism is an argument with two premises and a conclusion, introduced by Aristotle. In a categorical syllogism each statement uses one of four quantifiers: all, no, some, or some ... not. "All B are C; all A are B; therefore all A are C" is valid. "All A are B; all C are B; therefore all A are C" is not: all cats are mammals and all dogs are mammals, but it does not follow that all cats are dogs. People make many errors on syllogisms, and the errors are systematic. The most famous is belief bias : the tendency to accept invalid conclusions that are believable and to reject valid conclusions that are unbelievable. Consider: "All roses are flowers. Some flowers fade quickly. Therefore some roses fade quickly." Most people accept it because the conclusion is plausible, yet it is invalid: the flowers that fade quickly might all be marigolds. Now consider: "All mammals can fly. Elephants are mammals. Therefore elephants can fly." The conclusion is absurd, but the argument is perfectly valid. Jonathan Evans , Julie Barston and Paul Pollard (1983) showed that belief and logic both influence judgements and interact: belief has its biggest effect on invalid arguments, where believable conclusions are accepted far more often than unbelievable ones. An older account of syllogistic error is the atmosphere effect , proposed by Robert Woodworth and Saul Sells in 1935. The "mood" of the premises creates an atmosphere that biases the conclusion people accept: if either premise is particular ("some"), people favour a particular conclusion; if either premise is negative ("no"), they favour a negative one. So "Some A are B; some B are C; therefore some A are C" feels right, although it is invalid. Loren and Jean Chapman (1959) offered a rival explanation, illicit conversion : people treat "All A are B" as if it also meant "All B are A". Exam trap Belief bias (reasoning: judging an argument by the believability of its conclusion) is easy to confuse with three social biases that share the word: correspondence bias or the fundamental attribution error (explaining others' behaviour by their dispositions), self-serving bias (credit for success, blame situations for failure), and confirmation bias (seeking supporting evidence). Atmosphere effect = Woodworth and Sells (1935) . Conditional Reasoning and the Wason Selection Task Much everyday reasoning uses conditional statements of the form "if p, then q". The "if" part (p) is the antecedent ; the "then" part (q) is the consequent . Given such a rule and one further fact, four kinds of argument are possible, and only two are valid. Table 8.6 uses a cricket example: "If it rains, the match is cancelled." Table 8.6 The four forms of conditional argument. Form Pattern Cricket example Valid? Modus ponens (affirming the antecedent) If p then q; p; so q It rained, so the match was cancelled Valid Modus tollens (denying the consequent) If p then q; not q; so not p The match was not cancelled, so it did not rain Valid Affirming the consequent If p then q; q; so p The match was cancelled, so it rained Invalid (a bad pitch could cancel it) Denying the antecedent If p then q; not p; so not q It did not rain, so the match was not cancelled Invalid (same reason) The valid inference called modus ponens ("the mode that affirms") is made correctly by nearly everyone. Its partner, modus tollens ("the mode that denies"), is equally valid but is made far less often; people hesitate to reason from the absence of the consequent. Meanwhile many people accept the two fallacies, affirming the consequent and denying the antecedent , as if they were valid. One reason is that everyday language often uses "if" to mean "if and only if": when a parent says "If you finish your homework, you can watch television", the child rightly infers that no homework means no television. Logic does not allow that inference; conversation usually does. Key study: The Wason selection task (1966) The task. The British psychologist Peter Cathcart Wason (1924 to 2003) showed people four cards, each with a letter on one side and a number on the other (Figure 8.4), and a rule: "If a card has a vowel on one side, then it has an even number on the other side." Which cards must you turn over to find out whether the rule is true? Decide before reading on. The result. Most people choose E alone, or E and 4. Typically fewer than one person in ten gives the correct answer: E and 7. E must be turned because an odd number behind it would break the rule (this is modus ponens). The 7 must be turned because a vowel behind it would break the rule (modus tollens). The 4 is irrelevant: the rule says nothing about what must be behind an even number, so whatever is there cannot falsify the rule (choosing it is affirming the consequent). The conclusion. People look for cards that could confirm the rule, or simply cards that match the items named in it (Jonathan Evans's matching bias ), rather than cards that could falsify it. Rule: If a card has a vowel on one side, it has an even number on the other. E K 4 7 TURN LEAVE LEAVE TURN could hide an odd rule silent on K cannot falsify could hide a vowel Figure 8.4 The abstract Wason selection task. The two cards with heavy outlines (E and 7) are the only ones that could reveal a counterexample. The popular choice of the 4 card tests for confirmation, which can never prove a general rule. The story took a twist when the same logical task was given meaningful content. Richard Griggs and James Cox (1982) told participants to imagine they were police officers checking the rule "If a person is drinking beer, then the person must be over 19 years of age". The four cards read "drinking beer", "drinking cola", "16 years of age" and "22 years of age". About three-quarters now chose correctly ("drinking beer" and "16 years"), although the logic was identical to the vowels and numbers. Why? Patricia Cheng and Keith Holyoak (1985) proposed that people reason with pragmatic reasoning schemas , rules of thumb for familiar situations such as permissions and obligations ("if you want to do X, you must satisfy Y"). The evolutionary psychologist Leda Cosmides (1989) went further: she argued that natural selection equipped us with a specialised cheater-detection mechanism for social contracts ("if you take the benefit, you must pay the cost"), and that the task becomes easy whenever it is framed as catching someone who has cheated. Rules about what people must or may do (deontic rules) are reliably easier than rules about what is the case (indicative rules), though researchers still argue about why. Mental Models If people do not reason with formal logic, how do they reason? The most influential answer comes from the British psychologist Philip Nicholas Johnson-Laird (born 1936), whose book Mental Models appeared in 1983. A mental model is an internal representation of a possible state of affairs described by the premises, built to resemble the situation rather than the sentences. Given "The cup is to the right of the plate; the spoon is to the left of the plate", you build one model (spoon, plate, cup) and read the conclusion off it: the cup is to the right of the spoon. Reasoning, on this view, has three steps: construct a model of the premises, draw a tentative conclusion from it, and search for an alternative model in which the premises are true but the conclusion false. If you find none, the conclusion is valid. The theory predicts, correctly, that problems are harder the more models they require, and that people often stop after the first model, which produces errors when other models exist. The rival mental logic approach holds that people do have inference rules in their heads, such as modus ponens, but lack others, such as modus tollens, which must be derived in several steps. Inductive Reasoning and Hypothesis Testing Most of the reasoning that keeps us alive is inductive: generalising from experience, reasoning from one case to a similar one (analogy), and inferring causes from patterns of events. The Scottish philosopher David Hume pointed out in the eighteenth century that induction can never be logically guaranteed. Europeans observed thousands of swans, every one of them white, and concluded that all swans are white; then, in 1697, Dutch explorers found black swans in Western Australia. Concept formation (Section 8.2) is inductive, and so is everyday judgement under uncertainty (Section 8.5). Key study: Wason's 2-4-6 task (1960) The method. Wason told participants that the sequence 2-4-6 fits a rule he had in mind, and asked them to discover the rule by proposing sequences of their own; after each, he said whether it fitted. They were to announce the rule only when sure. The result. Most people formed a hypothesis such as "numbers increasing by two" and tested it with sequences like 8-10-12 and 20-22-24, all of which fitted. Confident, they announced their rule, and were told it was wrong. Only about one in five announced the correct rule the first time. The rule was simply "any three increasing numbers". The conclusion. People test hypotheses by seeking instances that would confirm them, never trying a sequence such as 1-2-3 or 6-4-2 that could have shown their hypothesis to be wrong. Later writers called this confirmation bias; Wason himself, a few years later, spoke of a "verification bias". The criticism. Joshua Klayman and Young-Won Ha (1987) pointed out that testing instances that fit your hypothesis (a positive test strategy ) is not irrational in itself; it fails on the 2-4-6 task because the true rule is much broader than the hypothesis people start with. The term confirmation bias , now firmly attached to Wason's experiments, refers to the tendency to search for, interpret, favour and remember information in ways that confirm what we already believe, and to neglect evidence that could disconfirm it. It is one of the most robust findings in psychology, and it matters wherever people test beliefs: in science, in courtrooms, in diagnosis and in prejudice. A self-fulfilling prophecy (Robert Merton, 1948) is a different thing. Confirmation bias changes how we see the evidence; a self-fulfilling prophecy changes the world , because our expectation alters our behaviour, which in turn makes the expected event more likely (a teacher's low expectations lead to less attention and so to poorer results). The social face of these ideas is covered in the Social Psychology book. Exam trap "Which does NOT reflect inductive reasoning: probabilistic conclusions, heuristics, decision making, concept formation?" The key is heuristics . Inductive conclusions are probabilistic, concept formation is induction from instances, and decision making under uncertainty rests on inductive judgements of likelihood; a heuristic is a shortcut strategy rather than a form of inference. The item is debatable (heuristics generate probabilistic judgements), but follow the key. "Confirmation bias is closely related to which heuristic?" One paper keyed representativeness , reasoning that both involve judging by fit to a preconceived model. No standard textbook ties confirmation bias to one particular heuristic; it is a bias in hypothesis testing (Wason's tasks). Use the key if the item recurs. The recognition heuristic (Gerd Gigerenzer's group) means choosing the option you recognise, and is the least related. Finally, "acting in line with one's own expectation so that the expected event becomes more likely" is a self-fulfilling prophecy , not confirmation bias (which distorts only how evidence is read), not the base-rate fallacy (Section 8.5) and not "motivational reaction", which is not a technical term. Reasoning Across the Lifespan: a Pointer Reasoning develops. In Jean Piaget's theory (taught fully in the Developmental Psychology book), the concrete operational child of about 7 to 11 years can reason logically about concrete, present objects: she understands conservation, reversibility (mentally undoing an action) and transitive inference (if Asha is taller than Bina and Bina taller than Chitra, Asha is taller than Chitra). From about 11 or 12, in the formal operational stage, the adolescent can reason about the abstract and the possible. Formal operations include hypothetico-deductive reasoning (forming hypotheses and testing them systematically, as in Piaget and Inhelder's pendulum problem), propositional reasoning about statements rather than objects, counterfactual reasoning about states of affairs contrary to fact, and a new capacity for thinking about thinking, which Piaget described as "operations on operations" and which we would now call metacognition. Some theorists argue that adult thought goes beyond formal operations. What they call dialectical thinking , described by Klaus Riegel (1973) and Michael Basseches (1984), is the ability to hold contradictory perspectives together, to see truth as relative to context and changing over time, and to integrate opposing ideas into a new synthesis. It is the hallmark of postformal thought, not of formal operations. Exam trap "Formal operational reasoning involves all EXCEPT: hypothetical, counterfactual, dialectical, metacognitive." The answer is dialectical (postformal; Riegel, Basseches). Hypothetico-deductive reasoning is a capacity that emerges in the formal operational stage; it is not itself one of Piaget's four stages, and a concrete operational child "struggles with" it. Reversibility, transitive inference, conservation and reduced egocentrism are concrete operational achievements. Earlier milestones make tempting distractors: object permanence (knowing that hidden objects still exist) and deferred imitation (copying a model after a delay) belong to the sensorimotor stage (birth to about 2), and symbolic or pretend play to the preoperational stage (about 2 to 7), whose child still lacks conservation , the understanding that quantity stays the same when only appearance changes (water poured into a taller, thinner glass is not "more"). The four stages themselves are sensorimotor, preoperational, concrete operational and formal operational; "reversibility of formal operations" is a scrambled option, since reversibility is concrete operational.
