Take the auto or wait for the bus? Accept the first seat you are offered in counselling or hold out for a better college? Two related processes are at work in such choices. Judgement is estimating how likely something is, usually from incomplete information ("How likely is it that this topic will be asked?"). Decision making is choosing among options, and it usually depends on judgements. For most of the twentieth century economists assumed that people make both rationally. Psychologists discovered otherwise, and in 2002 one of them won the Nobel Prize in Economics for showing it. How We Should Decide: Normative Models It helps to separate three kinds of model. A normative model says how an ideal, fully rational agent should decide, using the rules of logic and probability. A descriptive model says how people actually decide. A prescriptive model offers practical advice for bringing real decisions closer to the normative ideal. Most of this section is about the gap between the first two. The central normative idea is expected value : multiply each possible outcome by its probability and add the results. A lottery ticket costs ₹100 and gives a 1 in 1,000 chance of winning ₹50,000. Its expected value is ₹50,000 divided by 1,000, which is ₹50, so on average you lose ₹50 on every ticket. In 1738 the Swiss mathematician Daniel Bernoulli pointed out that people value outcomes not by their money value but by their utility (subjective worth), and that utility shows diminishing returns: an extra ₹1,000 means far more to a student than to a millionaire. John von Neumann and Oskar Morgenstern (1944) formalised expected utility theory : a rational decision maker, whose preferences are consistent (if she prefers A to B and B to C, she must prefer A to C), always chooses the option with the highest expected utility. When options differ on several attributes, a fully rational chooser uses a compensatory strategy: weigh every attribute of every option, so that a weakness on one attribute can be compensated by a strength on another. Choosing a paying-guest room in Mysuru, you would score each room on rent, distance from college, food and safety, multiply by how much each attribute matters to you, and total the scores. Real people, faced with many options, more often use non-compensatory shortcuts. In elimination by aspects , described by Amos Tversky in 1972, you pick the most important attribute, eliminate every option that falls below your cut-off on it ("nothing over ₹8,000 a month"), move to the next attribute, and continue until one option is left. A room that is perfect in every other way is gone the moment it fails the first test. Bounded Rationality and Satisficing The first serious challenge to the rational model came from Herbert Simon, the same Simon who, with Newell, modelled problem solving. In a series of papers from 1955 and in his 1957 book Models of Man , Simon argued that real decision makers have bounded rationality : their rationality is limited by the information available to them, by the limited capacity of their minds to process it, and by the time available to decide. A person who tried to compute the expected utility of every possible option before buying a mobile phone would still be comparing specifications when the phone became obsolete. Instead, said Simon, people practise satisficing , a word he coined in 1956 by blending "satisfy" and "suffice". Satisficing means setting an aspiration level (good enough on the features that matter), examining options one at a time, and choosing the first that meets it. You decide that any phone under ₹20,000 with a good camera and a day's battery will do, and you buy the first one that qualifies. Satisficing does not find the best option, but it finds a good one at a sensible cost. Simon received the Nobel Prize in Economics in 1978, largely for this work. The German psychologist Gerd Gigerenzer (born 1947) has developed Simon's idea in a more optimistic direction. Gigerenzer argues that the mind holds an "adaptive toolbox" of fast and frugal heuristics that use little information and yet perform well in the environments they evolved for. In the recognition heuristic , if you recognise one of two options and not the other, you infer that the recognised one scores higher. Daniel Goldstein and Gigerenzer (2002) asked American students which of two German cities was larger. When the students recognised only one city of a pair, they chose it about 90 per cent of the time. Strikingly, the same students did slightly better on German cities, many of which they had barely heard of, than on American cities, where they usually recognised both names and had to rely on what they knew: a "less-is-more" effect. For Gigerenzer, heuristics are not mere sources of error but tools that are ecologically rational . Exam trap Bounded rationality and satisficing belong to Herbert Simon (1950s; Nobel 1978), not to Kahneman or Tversky, whose names go with heuristics and biases and prospect theory. Howard Gardner is the multiple-intelligences theorist (Chapter 9). Elimination by aspects is Tversky (1972) ; the recognition heuristic and fast and frugal heuristics are Gigerenzer . Heuristics and Biases In 1969 two Israeli psychologists at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, Amos Tversky (1937 to 1996) and Daniel Kahneman (1934 to 2024), began a collaboration that would change the study of judgement. Their method was disarmingly simple: they posed short problems to ordinary people and to experts, and catalogued the systematic ways in which the answers departed from the rules of probability. In a famous 1974 paper in Science , "Judgment under uncertainty: Heuristics and biases", they argued that people judge probability using a small number of heuristics. These usually serve us well, but they lead to predictable errors, called biases . Tversky died in 1996; when the Nobel Prize recognised the work in 2002, it went to Kahneman alone, because the prize is not awarded after death. The availability heuristic (Tversky and Kahneman, 1973) is judging the frequency or probability of an event by how easily examples come to mind. Answer quickly: are there more English words that begin with the letter K, or more words that have K as their third letter? Most people say more begin with K, because words are easy to retrieve by their first letter (kitchen, king, kind) and hard to retrieve by their third (ask, make, like). In fact there are about twice as many with K in third position. Availability usually works because frequent events really are easier to recall, but anything that makes an event memorable distorts it: dramatic, vivid or recent events. After a widely reported train accident, people overestimate the danger of train travel; deaths from plane crashes and terrorism are overestimated, and deaths from diabetes and asthma underestimated. Norbert Schwarz and his colleagues (1991) showed that it is the ease of recall, not the number of examples, that matters: people asked to list twelve occasions on which they had been assertive (a hard task) later rated themselves as less assertive than people asked to list only six. The representativeness heuristic (Kahneman and Tversky, 1972) is judging the probability that something belongs to a category by how much it resembles the typical member of that category. The trouble is that resemblance ignores other information that matters for probability, above all base rates. The most important casualty is base-rate neglect : the failure to take account of how common something is in the population. Kahneman and Tversky (1973) described "Jack", a 45-year-old man who is conservative, careful and ambitious, shows no interest in politics and enjoys carpentry and mathematical puzzles. Participants were told that Jack's description had been drawn at random from 100 descriptions, either 70 engineers and 30 lawyers or 30 engineers and 70 lawyers. Both groups judged it about 90 per cent likely that Jack was an engineer: the description sounded like an engineer, and the base rate made almost no difference. Now try the taxi-cab problem yourself. A cab was involved in a hit-and-run at night. In the city, 85 per cent of cabs are Green and 15 per cent are Blue. A witness says the cab was Blue, and tests show that she identifies colours correctly 80 per cent of the time under those conditions. What is the probability that the cab was Blue? Most people answer 80 per cent. Work it through with 100 accidents instead of percentages. Fifteen involve Blue cabs, and the witness correctly calls 12 of them Blue. Eighty-five involve Green cabs, and she wrongly calls 17 of them Blue. So she says "Blue" 29 times, and is right 12 times: the probability is 12 out of 29, about 41 per cent. The low base rate of Blue cabs pulls the answer far below the witness's accuracy. Key study: Linda the bank teller (Tversky and Kahneman, 1983) The problem. "Linda is 31 years old, single, outspoken and very bright. She majored in philosophy. As a student, she was deeply concerned with issues of discrimination and social justice, and also participated in anti-nuclear demonstrations." Which is more probable: (a) Linda is a bank teller, or (b) Linda is a bank teller and is active in the feminist movement? The result. In one version about 85 per cent of participants chose (b). Why it is wrong. The probability of two things both being true can never exceed the probability of either one alone: every feminist bank teller is a bank teller, so (a) must be at least as likely as (b). Choosing (b) is the conjunction fallacy . The explanation. The description is representative of a feminist, so the conjunction "feels" more probable. The criticism. Some participants may read (a) as "a bank teller who is not a feminist", and the error shrinks when the problem is posed in frequencies ("Of 100 women like Linda, how many..."), as Gigerenzer has emphasised. But the fallacy survives careful rewording. Representativeness also explains the gambler's fallacy : the belief that after a run of one outcome, the opposite outcome is "due". On 18 August 1913, at the casino in Monte Carlo, the roulette ball fell on black 26 times in a row, and gamblers lost fortunes betting on red in the belief that red had become ever more likely. But a roulette wheel has no memory; each spin is independent. People expect even a short sequence to look like a "representative" random sequence, with reds and blacks well mixed. The same expectation produces insensitivity to sample size . A large hospital delivers about 45 babies a day and a small one about 15. Over a year, which hospital records more days on which over 60 per cent of babies born are boys? Most people say the two are about the same; in fact the small hospital will, because small samples stray further from the population average. The third heuristic is anchoring and adjustment : estimating a quantity by starting from an initial value (the anchor) and adjusting from it, usually too little. In Tversky and Kahneman's demonstration (1974), a wheel of fortune, apparently random but rigged, stopped at either 10 or 65 in front of participants, who were then asked what percentage of African countries were members of the United Nations. Median estimates were 25 per cent after seeing 10 and 45 per cent after seeing 65: an obviously irrelevant number dragged the estimates. In another study, people given five seconds to estimate 8 × 7 × 6 × 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 gave a median answer of 2,250; those shown 1 × 2 × 3 × 4 × 5 × 6 × 7 × 8 gave 512. Both anchored on the first few products and adjusted too little; the true answer is 40,320. The struck-out "MRP" above a sale price in a shop window is an anchor. Base-rate neglect, the gambler's fallacy and insensitivity to sample size are all representativeness errors. Framing, Prospect Theory and Loss Aversion According to expected utility theory, the way a choice is described should not matter if the outcomes are the same. Tversky and Kahneman showed that it matters a great deal. The framing effect is the finding that logically equivalent descriptions of a choice lead to different decisions. Key study: The Asian disease problem (Tversky and Kahneman, 1981) The method. Participants were told that the United States was preparing for an unusual disease expected to kill 600 people, and that two programmes had been proposed. One group chose between: Programme A, "200 people will be saved", and Programme B, "a one-third probability that 600 people will be saved and a two-thirds probability that no one will be saved". A second group chose between: Programme C, "400 people will die", and Programme D, "a one-third probability that nobody will die and a two-thirds probability that 600 people will die". The result. In the first (gain) frame, 72 per cent chose the certain option A. In the second (loss) frame, 78 per cent chose the risky option D. Yet A and C are identical (200 live, 400 die), and so are B and D. The conclusion. When outcomes are framed as gains, people are risk averse; when the same outcomes are framed as losses, people become risk seeking. Rational choice cannot explain this; prospect theory can. Kahneman and Tversky set out prospect theory in 1979 as a descriptive theory of decisions under risk. It has three key ideas. First, people evaluate outcomes as gains or losses relative to a reference point , usually the current state or an expectation, not in terms of final wealth. A salary of ₹50,000 feels like a gain if you expected ₹40,000 and like a loss if you expected ₹60,000. Second, the value function shows diminishing sensitivity in both directions (Figure 8.5): the difference between gaining ₹100 and ₹200 feels larger than the difference between gaining ₹1,100 and ₹1,200. The curve is therefore concave for gains, which makes people risk averse for gains (a sure ₹500 beats a 50 per cent chance of ₹1,000), and convex for losses, which makes them risk seeking for losses (a 50 per cent chance of losing ₹1,000 beats a sure loss of ₹500). Third, the curve is steeper for losses than for gains. This is loss aversion : losing ₹1,000 hurts roughly twice as much as winning ₹1,000 pleases, so most people refuse a fifty-fifty bet unless they stand to win about twice what they might lose. Prospect theory adds that people overweight small probabilities, which helps explain why the same person buys both a lottery ticket and an insurance policy. Compare the two thin vertical lines: a loss of 50 lowers felt value about twice as much as a gain of 50 raises it. That asymmetry is loss aversion. Loss aversion explains a family of everyday biases. The endowment effect , named by the economist Richard Thaler in 1980, is the tendency to value something more simply because we own it. In a classic experiment (Kahneman, Knetsch and Thaler, 1990), students who were given a university coffee mug demanded roughly twice as much to sell it as other students were willing to pay to buy one. Giving up the mug is coded as a loss, and losses loom large. Status quo bias (William Samuelson and Richard Zeckhauser, 1988) is the preference for keeping things as they are, because any change involves losing something. Defaults exploit it: in countries where citizens are organ donors unless they opt out, far more people are donors than in countries where they must opt in. The sunk-cost fallacy is continuing to invest in a course of action because of what has already been spent on it, although past costs cannot be recovered and should not affect a decision about the future. Hal Arkes and Catherine Blumer (1985) sold season tickets for a university theatre at full price or at a discount, assigned at random. Those who had paid full price attended more plays in the first half of the season, although the money was equally gone in both cases. Staying in a film you dislike because the ticket cost ₹300, or continuing a failing project "because we have already put two years into it", are the same error, captured by the phrase "throwing good money after bad". Overconfidence and Hindsight We are also poor judges of our own knowledge. Overconfidence is the tendency for confidence to exceed accuracy. In calibration studies, people answer general-knowledge questions and rate how sure they are; when they say they are 100 per cent certain, they are wrong far more often than that would allow. A close relative is the planning fallacy (Kahneman and Tversky, 1979): we underestimate how long our own tasks will take, even when we know that similar tasks took longer in the past. (Check your revision timetable.) Then there is hindsight bias , the "I knew it all along" effect: the tendency, once an outcome is known, to believe that it was more predictable than it really was. Baruch Fischhoff (born 1946) called it "creeping determinism". Before President Richard Nixon's visits to China and the Soviet Union in 1972, Fischhoff and Ruth Beyth (1975) asked people to estimate the probabilities of various possible outcomes. After the visits, the same people were asked to recall their estimates. They remembered having given higher probabilities to the events that had actually happened, and lower ones to those that had not. Hindsight bias makes the past look inevitable, which is why it is so hard to learn from it. Exam trap "The tendency to assume we would have been better at predicting actual events than is really true" is the hindsight effect (Fischhoff, 1975). The just-world hypothesis (Melvin Lerner) is the belief that people get what they deserve, a social psychology concept. "Decisiveness" is not a bias. Confirmation bias concerns testing beliefs, not misremembering predictions. And keep the decision terms straight: sunk cost = past investment; endowment = ownership; status quo = preference for no change; all three are driven by loss aversion. Two Systems of Thought Try this. A cricket bat and a ball cost ₹1,100 in total. The bat costs ₹1,000 more than the ball. How much does the ball cost? The answer that leaps to mind is ₹100, and it is wrong: if the ball cost ₹100, the bat would cost ₹1,100, and together they would cost ₹1,200. The ball costs ₹50. This is an Indian version of the "bat-and-ball" item from Shane Frederick's Cognitive Reflection Test (2005), and it neatly separates two kinds of thinking. According to dual-process theory , judgement and reasoning involve two different kinds of processing. Keith Stanovich and Richard West (2000) gave them the neutral labels that Kahneman later made famous in Thinking, Fast and Slow (2011). System 1 is fast, automatic, effortless, associative and intuitive; it generates impressions and is the home of the heuristics. System 2 is slow, deliberate, effortful and rule-based; it is limited by working memory and can check, and sometimes override, the answers System 1 proposes. "₹100" is System 1's answer; ₹50 is what System 2 finds if you let it work. Belief bias in syllogisms (Section 8.4) is the same conflict: System 1 judges the believability of the conclusion, System 2 its logic. The "systems" are best thought of as modes of processing, not separate places in the brain. Feeling plays a larger part in decisions than the rational model admits. Paul Slovic's affect heuristic describes judging risks and benefits by how we feel about something: a technology we like seems low in risk and high in benefit. The neurologist Antonio Damasio's somatic marker hypothesis (1994) proposes that bodily signals of emotion, learned from past outcomes, steer choices; patients with damage to the ventromedial prefrontal cortex, who can reason perfectly well about a decision, nonetheless make disastrous real-life choices. (Emotion is the subject of Chapter 11.) Decisions made by groups bring further distortions, such as groupthink (Irving Janis, 1972), in which a cohesive group's desire for agreement overrides realistic appraisal and leads to poor decisions; these are covered in the Social Psychology book. Clinical link In the client. Aaron Beck's cognitive distortions are clinical relatives of the biases in this section. Catastrophising is expecting that the worst will happen; all-or-nothing (dichotomous) thinking sees experiences as wholly good or wholly bad; selective abstraction (the mental filter) focuses on negative details and ignores positive ones; personalisation takes events too personally; overgeneralisation draws sweeping conclusions from one event. In the clinician. Clinicians anchor on a first impression, judge by availability after a memorable case, and neglect base rates. If a screening test detects 90 per cent of cases of a disorder that affects 1 per cent of people, and wrongly flags 10 per cent of healthy people, then of 1,000 people screened, 9 true cases and 99 healthy people test positive: only about 8 per cent of positives have the disorder. Loren and Jean Chapman (1967) found that clinicians "saw" correlations between Draw-a-Person signs (such as large eyes) and symptoms (such as suspiciousness) that were not in the data, an illusory correlation . Paul Meehl's Clinical Versus Statistical Prediction (1954) showed that simple actuarial formulas usually predict at least as well as clinical judgement. 8.6 Creativity Medium yield · 5 Qs What do a new raga improvisation, a vaccine designed in record time and a child's drawing of a purple elephant playing the tabla have in common? Each is creative. Most researchers now define creativity as the ability to produce work that is both novel (original, unexpected) and appropriate (useful, or fitted to the constraints of the task), a definition associated with Robert Sternberg and Todd Lubart. Both halves matter. Novelty without appropriateness is merely odd: a random string of words is original but not creative. Appropriateness without novelty is merely competent. Creativity can be studied from four directions, which Mel Rhodes (1961) called the four Ps : the creative person (traits and abilities), the creative process (the stages of thought), the creative press (the environment that supports or stifles it) and the creative product (what is made, and how it is judged). Creativity also varies in scale. "Big-C" creativity is eminent, field-changing work (Srinivasa Ramanujan's mathematics, Rabindranath Tagore's poetry); "little-c" creativity is everyday originality (a new recipe, a clever way to rearrange a small room). James Kaufman and Ronald Beghetto (2009) added mini-c , the personally meaningful insights of learning, and Pro-c , professional-level creativity, to make a Four C model . Guilford and Divergent Thinking The scientific study of creativity is usually dated to September 1950, when J. P. Guilford gave his presidential address to the American Psychological Association. Guilford complained that creativity had been shamefully neglected: of some 121,000 titles indexed in Psychological Abstracts over the previous 23 years, only 186 bore definitely on creativity, fewer than two in every thousand. In his Structure of Intellect model (Chapter 9), Guilford distinguished convergent production , the generation of the one correct answer, from divergent production , the generation of many varied answers, and identified creativity largely with divergent production. He broke divergent thinking into four abilities, which are still the standard scoring categories of creativity tests: The first is fluency : the sheer number of relevant ideas produced. The second is flexibility : the number of different categories the ideas fall into, that is, the ease of shifting from one kind of idea to another. The third is originality : the statistical unusualness of the ideas, how rarely other people give them. The fourth is elaboration : the amount of detail used to develop and embellish an idea. Guilford also listed sensitivity to problems (noticing that something needs doing) and redefinition (seeing familiar things in new ways) among the creative abilities. Here is how scoring works. Asked to list uses for a brick in two minutes, Ravi writes: build a wall, build a house, build a temple, a doorstop, a paperweight, a pestle for crushing masala, a marker for the stumps in street cricket. His fluency is 7. The ideas fall into four categories (construction, weight, kitchen tool, sport), so his flexibility is 4. If, in a large group, only Ravi thought of the masala and the stumps, those two earn originality credit. Had he written "a doorstop wrapped in an old sari so it will not scratch the floor", he would earn elaboration credit as well. The Creative Process: Wallas's Four Stages The most famous account of the creative process came from Graham Wallas (1858 to 1932), an English political scientist and one of the founders of the London School of Economics. In The Art of Thought (1926), drawing on the self-reports of the physicist Hermann von Helmholtz and the mathematician Henri Poincaré, he proposed four stages (Table 8.8). Table 8.8 Wallas's four stages of the creative process (1926). Order Stage What happens Conscious? 1 Preparation The problem is defined, information gathered and solutions attempted, often without success Yes, effortful 2 Incubation The problem is set aside; work on it continues, if at all, outside awareness No 3 Illumination The solution appears suddenly, the "aha" moment of insight Sudden entry into awareness 4 Verification The idea is tested, worked out and refined Yes, effortful Poincaré's account of discovering a class of mathematical functions (which he called Fuchsian functions) fits the stages almost perfectly. After days of fruitless work (preparation), he left on a geological excursion and stopped thinking about mathematics (incubation). "At the moment when I put my foot on the step" of a bus, he wrote, the idea came to him, with complete certainty (illumination). Back home, he verified the result at leisure (verification). Wallas also described a fleeting moment just before illumination, a dim feeling that a solution is on its way, which he called intimation ; some textbooks count it as a fifth stage. Notice that Wallas's model and the Gestalt research of Section 8.3 describe the same phenomena from two angles: incubation and illumination are what problem-solving researchers call incubation and insight. Exam trap The order is preparation, incubation, illumination, verification (a memory hook: " P lease I ncubate I deas V ery carefully"). Second stage = incubation; third = illumination ("achieving insight"); "leaving the problem while considering other things" = incubation; "testing or carrying out the solution" = verification; "formulating the problem and making initial attempts" = preparation. Some books add intimation between incubation and illumination, which is why you may read of "five stages". Do not confuse the stages with Guilford's abilities (fluency, flexibility, originality, elaboration, sensitivity) or with Sternberg's analytical, creative and practical intelligences. A sequence such as "problem-finding, brainstorming, selection, implementation" resembles the later applied creative problem-solving schemes that grew out of Osborn's brainstorming work, not Wallas. Measuring Creativity The most widely used creativity test is the Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking (TTCT), published by Ellis Paul Torrance (1915 to 2003) in 1966. The TTCT has a verbal form, with activities such as Ask-and-Guess (asking questions about a picture and guessing its causes and consequences), Product Improvement (making a toy more fun to play with), Unusual Uses and Just Suppose (imagining the consequences of an improbable event), and a figural form, with Picture Construction, Picture Completion and Repeated Figures (turning many identical circles or parallel lines into different pictures). Responses are scored on Guilford's dimensions of fluency, flexibility, originality and elaboration; later editions of the figural test also score abstractness of titles and resistance to premature closure. Torrance followed some of his child participants for decades, and their test scores predicted later creative achievement modestly but genuinely. Sarnoff Mednick (1928 to 2015) approached creativity through association. In his associative theory (1962), creativity is the forming of new combinations of remote associative elements that are useful. People differ in their associative hierarchies . An uncreative person has a steep hierarchy: one or two strong, conventional associations to a word ("table" calls up "chair", then little else). A creative person has a flat hierarchy: many weaker associations, including remote ones, are almost equally available. Mednick's Remote Associates Test (RAT) presents three words and asks for a fourth word linked to all three. What links cottage, Swiss and cake? (Cheese.) Cream, skate and water? (Ice.) Note the irony: although the RAT measures remote association, each item has only one correct answer, so it also demands convergent thinking. Michael Wallach and Nathan Kogan (1965) showed that the conditions of testing matter. When divergent-thinking tasks were presented to children as relaxed, untimed games rather than as tests, the creativity scores hung together and were largely independent of intelligence scores. Instead of a test, some researchers judge products directly. In Teresa Amabile's consensual assessment technique , experts in a domain rate the creativity of products (poems, collages, designs) independently, and their agreement is usually high: creativity, like beauty, is recognised reliably by those who know the field. Enhancing Creativity: Lateral Thinking and Brainstorming The Maltese physician and writer Edward de Bono (1933 to 2021) introduced the term lateral thinking in The Use of Lateral Thinking (1967). Ordinary vertical thinking, he said, is logical and sequential: it digs the same hole deeper. Lateral thinking deliberately moves sideways to dig a hole somewhere else, by challenging assumptions, reversing the problem, using a random word as a starting point, or making a deliberately provocative statement (which he marked with the made-up word "po") to jolt thinking out of its usual tracks. In Six Thinking Hats (1985) he proposed that a group take one perspective at a time: white for facts, red for feelings, black for caution, yellow for benefits, green for new ideas and blue for managing the thinking process. Brainstorming was developed by the advertising executive Alex Faickney Osborn (1888 to 1966) at his agency from 1939 and popularised in his book Applied Imagination (1953). Its four rules are: defer judgement (no criticism during idea generation); go for quantity, because quantity breeds quality; welcome wild ideas; and combine and improve on others' ideas. The rules are sound, but the group format is not. Many studies have compared interacting brainstorming groups with nominal groups , the same number of individuals working alone whose ideas are pooled afterwards. The nominal groups usually produce more ideas, and better ones. Michael Diehl and Wolfgang Stroebe (1987) identified the main culprit as production blocking : in a group only one person can speak at a time, so others forget or suppress ideas while they wait. Evaluation apprehension and social loafing add to the loss. Writing ideas down silently first ("brainwriting") or brainstorming electronically recovers much of it. Creativity and Intelligence Are creative people simply intelligent people? The usual answer is the threshold hypothesis , associated with Guilford, Torrance and others. Below an IQ of about 120, creativity and intelligence are positively correlated: you need a certain level of intelligence to be creative. Above that threshold the correlation largely disappears, and other factors (personality, motivation, knowledge, environment) decide who is creative. Intelligence, in short, is necessary but not sufficient for creativity. Jacob Getzels and Philip Jackson (1962) compared adolescents at a Chicago school who scored very high on creativity tests but not on IQ tests with others who scored very high on IQ but not on creativity. Both groups did equally well in school achievement, but teachers preferred the high-IQ students; the high-creative students showed more humour, more unconventional goals and more playful, imaginative stories. A 2005 meta-analysis by Kyung Hee Kim put the overall correlation between creativity and intelligence scores at only about 0.17. Creativity and intelligence overlap, but they are not the same thing (theories of intelligence are the subject of Chapter 9). Theories of Creativity Several traditions have offered explanations of creativity. For Freud, creative work is a sublimation of instinctual energy into socially valued activity, and the psychoanalyst Ernst Kris spoke of creativity as "regression in the service of the ego", a controlled dipping into primary-process thought. The humanists saw creativity as an expression of growth: Abraham Maslow distinguished the rare "special-talent" creativity of the genius from the "self-actualising" creativity open to anyone, and Carl Rogers argued that psychological safety and freedom foster it. Mednick's associative theory you have already met. Three modern theories are most examined. The investment theory of creativity was proposed by Robert Sternberg and Todd Lubart (1991) and developed in their book Defying the Crowd (1995). Creative people, they argued, are like good investors: they "buy low", pursuing ideas that are unknown or out of favour but have growth potential, and they "sell high", moving on once the idea has become accepted and valuable. Doing this requires a confluence of six resources: intellectual abilities (the synthetic ability to see problems in new ways, the analytic ability to judge which ideas are worth pursuing, and the practical ability to persuade others of their value), knowledge (enough to know the field, but not so much that it entrenches you), a legislative thinking style (a preference for creating one's own rules and ways of doing things), personality (tolerance of ambiguity, willingness to take sensible risks, perseverance), intrinsic motivation, and a supportive environment. Teresa Amabile (born 1950) proposed a componential model (1983) with three components: domain-relevant skills (knowledge and technique in the field), creativity-relevant processes (a cognitive style that breaks set, tolerates ambiguity and persists), and intrinsic task motivation . Her "intrinsic motivation principle" holds that people are most creative when they work for the interest and challenge of the task itself. In one study (1985), creative-writing students who had first ranked extrinsic reasons for writing (money, recognition) wrote less creative poems than those who had first ranked intrinsic reasons (enjoyment, self-expression). Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi (1934 to 2021) proposed a systems model (1988) in which creativity is not inside a person at all but emerges from the interaction of three parts: the individual , who produces a variation; the domain , the body of symbolic knowledge (mathematics, Carnatic music) in which the variation is made; and the field , the gatekeepers (editors, critics, examiners) who decide whether it enters the domain. In the 1950s and 1960s, researchers at the Institute of Personality Assessment and Research at Berkeley, including Frank Barron and Donald MacKinnon, invited eminent writers, scientists and architects for intensive weekends of assessment. MacKinnon's (1962) study of architects, judged creative or less creative by their peers, became the classic. The most creative architects were independent in judgement, self-confident and open to their own feelings and to new experience; they preferred complexity (on Barron's art-preference tests they liked complex, asymmetrical figures that less creative people disliked), had wide interests and high aesthetic sensitivity, and showed a notable openness to traits stereotyped as feminine. Later work confirms the picture. In Gregory Feist's (1998) meta-analysis, openness to experience was the personality trait most consistently linked to creativity in both artists and scientists, along with autonomy, drive and confidence; tolerance of ambiguity and willingness to take risks complete the profile. Clinical link Is there a link between creativity and mental illness? Nancy Andreasen (1987) interviewed writers at the University of Iowa Writers' Workshop and found far higher lifetime rates of mood disorder, particularly bipolar disorder, than in matched controls, and Kay Redfield Jamison's Touched with Fire (1993) documented the same pattern in the lives of eminent poets and artists. The samples were small and selective, and the link, where it exists, seems strongest for milder mood elevation and for first-degree relatives rather than for severe illness. How is that possible? Language is so familiar that we rarely notice how strange it is. A language is a system of arbitrary symbols (spoken words or manual signs) that are combined according to rules, allowing the members of a community to communicate an unlimited number of messages. Many animals communicate; as you will see in Section 8.9, whether any other animal has language is a much harder question. To answer it we first need to know what makes language language. The Defining Properties of Language In 1960 the American linguist Charles Francis Hockett (1916 to 2000) listed thirteen design features that together distinguish human language from animal communication systems. The thirteen are: the vocal-auditory channel, broadcast transmission and directional reception, rapid fading, interchangeability (anyone who can hear a message can also send it), total feedback (speakers hear themselves), specialisation, semanticity, arbitrariness, discreteness, displacement, productivity, cultural (traditional) transmission and duality of patterning. With Stuart Altmann he later added prevarication (the ability to lie), reflexiveness (using language to talk about language) and learnability. Five of the features carry most of the weight, and they are the ones you are examined on. Semanticity. Linguistic symbols carry meaning: they refer to objects, events, actions and ideas. Arbitrariness. There is no natural connection between the form of a word and what it means. The same animal is "dog" in English, kutta in Hindi and nayi in Kannada, and nothing about any of these sounds is doglike. The Swiss linguist Ferdinand de Saussure (1857 to 1913) made this "arbitrariness of the sign" the first principle of modern linguistics (1916). Onomatopoeic words such as "buzz" are the rare exceptions. Displacement. Language allows displacement , communication about things that are not here and now: yesterday's lecture, next month's results, a city you have never visited, a unicorn that never existed. Generativity (Hockett's productivity ): a finite set of words and rules can generate an infinite number of new sentences, which listeners understand at once although they have never heard them. Duality of patterning. Language is organised on two levels. Meaningless sounds (phonemes) combine into meaningful units (morphemes and words), and these combine into sentences. The same three sounds /k/, /æ/ and /t/ make "cat", "act" and "tack". A related property, recursion , allows a phrase to be embedded inside another phrase of the same kind, without limit: "the girl who met the boy who lost the pen that his father bought". Marc Hauser, Noam Chomsky and Tecumseh Fitch (2002) proposed that recursion is the one feature of language that is uniquely human. The same embedding applied to minds gives recursive thought ("I think that you think that I am bluffing"), a form of perspective taking that develops in late childhood and is covered in the Developmental Psychology book. Do not confuse it with Piaget's reversibility (mentally undoing an action, Section 8.4), with Katherine Nelson's referential style of early word learning (Section 8.8), or with reconstruction , the rebuilding of a memory at recall (Chapter 7). Indian context The scientific study of language structure has a long Indian history. Around the fourth century BCE (the dates are uncertain), the grammarian Pāṇini composed the Aṣṭādhyāyī , a grammar of Sanskrit in nearly 4,000 compact rules (sūtras) that generate the correct forms of words from roots and affixes. Modern linguists regard it as the earliest generative grammar, a set of finite rules that produces all and only the correct forms. Some nine centuries later, the philosopher Bhartṛhari, in the Vākyapadīya , argued that meaning is grasped as an indivisible whole ( sphoṭa ) rather than sound by sound, and that "there is no cognition in the world that does not follow language": an Indian position on the language and thought question of Section 8.9. The Units of Language Language is a hierarchy of units, each built from the one below (Table 8.10). At the bottom is the phoneme , the smallest unit of sound that can distinguish one word from another in a particular language. The /p/ in "pat" and the /b/ in "bat" are different phonemes because swapping them changes the word. A phoneme has no meaning of its own: /p/ means nothing. English has about 40 to 45 phonemes, depending on the dialect, and the world's languages range from about a dozen to more than a hundred. Languages also differ in which sound differences count. In Hindi the unaspirated /k/ of kal (yesterday or tomorrow) and the aspirated /kh/ of khal (a villain) are different phonemes; in English the same two sounds occur (in "skin" and "kin") but never distinguish words, so English speakers barely hear the difference. The study of a language's sound system is phonology . Phonemes combine into the morpheme , the smallest unit of language that carries meaning. "Cat" is one morpheme; "cats" is two (cat plus the plural -s); "unhappiness" is three (un + happy + ness). A free morpheme can stand alone as a word (happy, cat, run). A bound morpheme cannot (un-, -ness, -s, -ed). Bound morphemes are either inflectional , adding grammatical information without changing the word's class (the plural -s, the past tense -ed, -ing), or derivational , creating a new word, often of a new class (happy becomes happiness; teach becomes teacher). The study of word structure is morphology . Notice that a syllable (ba-na-na) is a unit of pronunciation organised around a vowel: it is neither the smallest unit of sound nor the smallest unit of meaning. Words are combined into phrases and sentences according to syntax , the rules of sentence structure. "The dog bit the man" and "The man bit the dog" contain the same words; only syntax tells you who needs the injection. English is a subject-verb-object language; Hindi and Kannada put the verb last (subject-object-verb: Ram ne seb khaaya , "Ram the apple ate"). Grammar is the umbrella term for a language's phonological, morphological and syntactic rules. The study of meaning is semantics : the meaning of words, and how word meanings combine into the meaning of sentences. The study of how language is used in social context is pragmatics : how speakers convey, and listeners infer, more than the literal words say. "Can you pass the salt?" is literally a question about ability, but everyone understands it as a request. The philosopher H. Paul Grice (1975) argued that conversation rests on a cooperative principle expressed in four maxims: give as much information as needed and no more (quantity), say what you believe true (quality), be relevant (relation), and be clear (manner). Finally, prosody is the melody of speech: its rhythm, stress and intonation. "You're coming?" and "You're coming." differ only in prosody. Prosody also carries emotion (the warmth, sarcasm or anger in a voice), and this emotional prosody depends chiefly on regions of the right hemisphere that mirror the left hemisphere's language areas; damage there produces aprosodia , flat or uninterpretable emotional tone (Elliott Ross, 1981). Level Definition Example Phoneme (phonology) Smallest unit of sound that distinguishes words; no meaning of its own /p/ versus /b/ in pat and bat Morpheme (morphology) Smallest unit that carries meaning; free or bound un + happy + ness (three) Word (lexicon) Free-standing unit made of one or more morphemes teacher Syntax Rules for combining words into phrases and sentences Dog bites man versus man bites dog Semantics Meaning of words and sentences Knowing that a bachelor is unmarried Pragmatics Use of language in social context "Can you pass the salt?" as a request Prosody Rhythm, stress and intonation of speech "You're coming?" versus "You're coming." Exam trap "The smallest unit of meaning " is the morpheme . "The basic units of sound used in a spoken language" are phonemes . Syllables and consonants are not the answer to either: a consonant is just one kind of phoneme, and a syllable is a unit of pronunciation. Keep the other levels apart by their definitions: rules for combining words into sentences = syntax ; meaning = semantics ; culturally appropriate use in context = pragmatics ; intonation and emotional tone = prosody , processed mainly by the right hemisphere regions homotopic to the left-hemisphere language areas (not by Broca's area). Chomsky's Transformational Grammar In 1957 a 28-year-old linguist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Noam Chomsky, published a short book, Syntactic Structures , that changed both linguistics and psychology. He began with a sentence that has since become famous: "Colorless green ideas sleep furiously." It is meaningless, yet every English speaker recognises it as grammatical, while "Furiously sleep ideas green colorless" is not. So our knowledge of grammar cannot be knowledge of meaning, and it cannot be knowledge of which words usually follow which, because none of these words normally follow one another. It must be knowledge of abstract rules. Chomsky proposed a generative grammar : a finite set of rules that can generate all, and only, the grammatical sentences of a language. Phrase-structure rules describe how a sentence breaks into its constituents: a sentence (S) consists of a noun phrase (NP) and a verb phrase (VP); a noun phrase can consist of a determiner and a noun ("the dog"); a verb phrase can consist of a verb and a noun phrase ("chased the cat"). Transformational rules then convert one structure into another, turning an active sentence into a passive one or a statement into a question. In Aspects of the Theory of Syntax (1965), Chomsky distinguished two levels of structure. The surface structure is the actual form of the sentence as it is spoken or written: the words in their order. The deep structure is the underlying, abstract structure that represents the basic grammatical relations, who did what to whom. Transformations map deep structure onto surface structure. Two kinds of example show why both levels are needed: One deep structure can appear as different surface structures. "The dog chased the cat" and "The cat was chased by the dog" look different but say the same thing. One surface structure can come from different deep structures. "Visiting relatives can be boring" means either that it is boring to visit relatives or that relatives who visit are boring. "The shooting of the hunters was terrible" is ambiguous in the same way: were the hunters shooting badly, or being shot? Chomsky also distinguished competence , a speaker's tacit, unconscious knowledge of the rules of the language, from performance , the actual use of language in real situations, which is marred by slips of the tongue, false starts, hesitations and the limits of memory. (The distinction echoes Saussure's earlier contrast between langue , the language system, and parole , actual speech.) Linguistics, for Chomsky, is the study of competence. In later work, Chomsky replaced deep and surface structure with a theory of universal principles and parameters (1981) and then the Minimalist Program (1995), but the 1957 and 1965 ideas are the ones psychology absorbed, and the ones you will be asked about. Exam trap 1957 = Syntactic Structures (transformational generative grammar); 1959 = Chomsky's review of Skinner's Verbal Behavior ; 1965 = Aspects of the Theory of Syntax (deep and surface structure, competence and performance, the language acquisition device). Ambiguous sentences such as "Visiting relatives can be boring" illustrate one surface structure with two deep structures ; active and passive pairs illustrate one deep structure with two surface structures . Competence is knowledge; performance is use. 8.8 Acquiring Language Medium yield · 8 Qs By the age of five, without a single grammar lesson, a typical child has a vocabulary of thousands of words and commands most of the grammar of her language, including rules that her parents could not state if asked. She does this whether her language is Kannada, Tamil, English or Mandarin, and whether her parents are professors or labourers. How? Three families of theory compete to explain it. Learning Theory: Skinner's Verbal Behavior For Burrhus Frederic Skinner (1904 to 1990), language was behaviour like any other, acquired through reinforcement, shaping and imitation. In Verbal Behavior (1957) he classified "verbal operants" by their controlling conditions. A mand is a demand or request reinforced by what it asks for (the child says "milk" and gets milk). A tact names something in the environment and is reinforced socially ("car!", "Yes, that's a car!"). An echoic repeats what has just been heard. An intraverbal responds to someone else's words without repeating them ("How are you?" "Fine."). Textual behaviour is reading aloud, and transcription is writing down what is heard (taking dictation). An autoclitic modifies the speaker's own verbal behaviour ("I think...", "I'm not sure, but..."). Learning theory explains some things well: children learn the particular language, words and accent they hear, and they learn frequent words earlier. In 1959 Chomsky published a review of Verbal Behavior in the journal Language that is often said to have ended behaviourism's claim on language. His arguments were these. Children constantly produce sentences they have never heard and therefore cannot have imitated or been reinforced for. Their characteristic errors ("I goed", "two mouses") are not imitations of anything adults say; they show that the child has extracted a rule and is over-applying it. Parents rarely correct grammar anyway: Roger Brown and Camille Hanlon (1970) found that parents responded to the truth of what children said, not its form, approving "Mama isn't boy, he a girl" because it was true. And children everywhere acquire language too fast and too uniformly for trial-and-error learning to explain. The Nativist Theory: Chomsky's Language Acquisition Device Chomsky's alternative was that children are born with an innate, biologically based capacity for language, which he called the language acquisition device (LAD). The LAD contains a universal grammar : a set of principles and categories common to all human languages (every language has nouns and verbs, consonants and vowels, ways of negating and of asking questions). Exposure to a particular language does not teach the child grammar from scratch; it sets the values of a small number of parameters , like switches. English puts the verb before its object; Hindi and Kannada put it after; a child hearing either language needs only to set the switch. The central argument for nativism is the poverty of the stimulus : the speech children hear is fragmentary, full of errors and false starts, and contains almost no information about which sentences are not allowed, yet every normal child arrives at the same intricate grammar. The input, Chomsky argued, is too poor to explain the output, so much of the knowledge must be innate. Further evidence came from the regular, universal sequence of milestones (Table 8.12), from deaf children who, brought together without an adult model, create a full sign language of their own (as happened in Nicaragua from the late 1970s), and from the critical period discussed below. Steven Pinker (born 1954) popularised the nativist case in The Language Instinct (1994). Critics reply that the LAD is a label rather than an explanation, that nativism ignores the rich social interaction in which language is learned, and that the input is richer than Chomsky supposed. Jenny Saffran, Richard Aslin and Elissa Newport (1996) played eight-month-old infants a continuous stream of nonsense syllables for just two minutes. The infants learned which syllables tended to follow one another, and so where the "word" boundaries lay: powerful statistical learning that needs no innate grammar. Interactionist Theories Interactionist theories accept that children bring special capacities to the task but insist that social interaction does essential work. Jerome Bruner, in Child's Talk (1983), answered Chomsky's LAD with a language acquisition support system (LASS): the structured help that adults provide. Bruner emphasised formats , routine, predictable games such as peekaboo and picture-book reading ("What's that?" "A cow!" "Yes, it's a cow!"), within which the child can work out what words refer to. The adult's support is a form of scaffolding , a term introduced by David Wood, Bruner and Gail Ross in 1976 for help that is adjusted to the child's level and withdrawn as competence grows. Part of the support system is the special way adults talk to infants, known as motherese , baby talk or, more neutrally, child-directed speech (infant-directed speech). Compared with speech between adults, it has a higher overall pitch and a wider, exaggerated range of pitch (a sing-song melody), a slower rate, shorter and simpler utterances (a lower mean length of utterance), more repetition, more questions, clearer pronunciation, more frequent and longer pauses, and a focus on the here and now. Infants prefer to listen to it, and its exaggerated contours help them pick out words and phrase boundaries. But it is not strictly necessary: in some cultures adults talk relatively little to infants, and their children still learn to speak. The developmental psycholinguist Dan Isaac Slobin (born 1939), comparing acquisition across dozens of languages, proposed that children bring a language-making capacity (LMC) to the task (1985). Unlike the LAD, the LMC is not innate knowledge of grammar. It is a set of cognitive and perceptual abilities, which Slobin called operating principles , that are highly specialised for learning language: for example, "pay attention to the ends of words" (where many languages put their grammatical endings) and "avoid exceptions" (which produces overregularisation). Motherese has a shorter mean length of utterance, higher pitch, wider pitch range, slower rate and more pauses than adult-to-adult speech. Is There a Critical Period for Language? In Biological Foundations of Language (1967), Eric Heinz Lenneberg (1921 to 1975) argued that language must be acquired during a critical period , a biologically fixed window of development (roughly from the age of two to puberty, in his account) during which the brain is especially receptive to linguistic input and after which full acquisition becomes impossible. He linked the end of the window to the completion of brain maturation and lateralisation. Today most researchers prefer the softer term sensitive period : a window during which learning is easiest and most complete, although some learning is still possible afterwards. The most famous, and saddest, evidence came from a girl known as Genie. In November 1970, social workers in Los Angeles found a 13-year-old girl who had been kept by her father in near-total isolation, strapped to a potty chair or confined in a crib, from about the age of 20 months. She had heard almost no language and could not speak. Over the following years, studied in detail by the linguist Susan Curtiss (1977), Genie learned many words and could communicate, but her grammar never developed. Her utterances remained telegraphic ("Applesauce buy store"), with little use of function words or word-order rules. The case supports a sensitive period for grammar in particular, but it is not clean: Genie was also severely abused and malnourished, and nobody knows whether she was developmentally normal to begin with. Key study: Johnson and Newport's immigrants (1989) The question. Does the age at which you start learning a second language limit how well you finally learn it? The method. Jacqueline Johnson and Elissa Newport tested Korean and Chinese immigrants to the United States who had all lived there for years, but who had arrived at ages ranging from 3 to 39. Participants judged whether each of 276 spoken English sentences was grammatical. The result. Those who had arrived between 3 and 7 performed like native speakers. Performance fell steadily with each later age of arrival up to puberty; those who arrived as adults scored lower and varied widely, unrelated to their age at arrival. The conclusion. There is a maturational sensitive period for acquiring grammar that closes gradually through childhood. The criticism. Age of arrival is confounded with amount and kind of exposure, schooling and motivation. Exam trap "Infants who have no exposure to language show severely limited language development that is not reversible" supports sensitive (critical) periods of development . Semantics and syntax are levels of language, not developmental principles; nativism is the broader theory that language is innate, and the item asks for the term the evidence supports most directly. Critical period for language = Lenneberg (1967) ; Genie studied by Susan Curtiss . Milestones of Language Development Language begins before the first word. Newborns already prefer their mother's voice to a stranger's (Anthony DeCasper and William Fifer, 1980), having heard it in the womb. Young infants can discriminate the speech sounds of all the world's languages, but their perception narrows to their own language during the first year. Janet Werker and Richard Tees (1984) found that English-learning infants of 6 to 8 months could distinguish two Hindi consonants (a retroflex "ta" and a dental "ta") that English does not use, but by 10 to 12 months most could not; Hindi-learning infants kept the distinction. Infants become specialists in the sounds that matter around them. Production follows its own timetable (Table 8.12). At about two months infants begin cooing , producing vowel-like sounds ("ooo", "aah"), often in response to a smiling face. At about six months babbling begins: consonant-vowel combinations, soon repeated in strings ("ba-ba-ba", "da-da-da"). Babbling is at first universal, and early babbling sounds similar whatever language the child hears; but it gradually drifts towards the sounds of the home language. Deaf infants' vocal babbling is delayed and reduced, and deaf infants exposed to sign language "babble" with their hands, producing rhythmic, syllable-like hand movements (Laura-Ann Petitto and Paula Marentette, 1991). Babbling, it seems, is the practice of language's sound units in whatever medium the child meets. The first recognisable words appear around the first birthday, often for people, animals, food and toys that move or can be acted on. In the one-word stage a single word can do the work of a whole sentence: "Milk!" may mean "I want milk", "The milk spilled" or "That is milk". Such a word is called a holophrase . Katherine Nelson (1973) noticed two styles among children at this stage: referential children's first fifty words were mostly names for objects, while expressive children used more social formulas ("stop it", "thank you", "I want it"). Vocabulary grows slowly at first and then, around 18 months and about 50 words, accelerates sharply: the vocabulary spurt or naming explosion. Early word meanings rarely match adult ones. In overextension a child applies a word too broadly: "dog" for every four-legged animal, "papa" for every man. In underextension the child applies it too narrowly: "dog" only for the family dog, "car" only for cars seen moving in the street. And children learn words astonishingly fast. Susan Carey and Elsa Bartlett (1978) casually asked preschoolers to "bring me the chromium tray, not the red one", where the tray was olive green. A week later, some of the children still had a partial idea of what "chromium" meant, after a single exposure. This ability to form a quick first hypothesis about a word's meaning from one encounter is called fast mapping . Between 18 and 24 months children begin to combine two words. Roger Brown (1925 to 1997) called this telegraphic speech , because, like a telegram, it keeps the content words (nouns, verbs, adjectives) and leaves out function words and grammatical endings: "Mummy go", "more milk", "allgone ball", "Daddy shoe". These short utterances already express a small set of meaning relations: agent and action, action and object, possession, location, recurrence and disappearance. Brown, in A First Language (1973), followed three children (Adam, Eve and Sarah) and measured progress by the mean length of utterance (MLU) in morphemes, which predicts grammatical development better than age. Grammatical morphemes then appear in a remarkably regular order, beginning with -ing and the plural -s. From about two to three years, children's grammar shows its most revealing error. Having learned rules such as "add -ed for the past" and "add -s for the plural", children apply them to irregular words they had previously used correctly: "I goed", "two foots", "the mouses". This overregularisation means that performance gets worse before it gets better (a U-shaped pattern), and it is strong evidence that children are learning rules, not imitating. Jean Berko (1958) showed the same thing with her "wug test". She showed children a picture of a small imaginary creature: "This is a wug. Now there is another one. There are two of them. There are two ...?" Preschoolers happily answered "wugs", applying a rule to a word they had never heard. Between three and five, sentences lengthen and become complex, with questions, negatives and embedded clauses; pragmatic skills grow too (four-year-olds simplify their speech when talking to two-year-olds), and in the school years children develop metalinguistic awareness , the ability to think about language itself, which shows up in their delight in puns and riddles. Referential versus expressive styles are Katherine Nelson's (1973), and "referential style" is a language-development term, not a perspective-taking one. Clinical link Language delay is often the first thing that brings a child to a clinic. Widely used red flags include no babbling or pointing by 12 months, no single words by 16 months, no spontaneous two-word phrases by 24 months, and any loss of language or social skills at any age. Hearing should always be checked first. Of the neurodevelopmental conditions, language and communication are most consistently compromised in autism spectrum disorder , where delayed speech is often accompanied by echolalia, pronoun reversal ("you want juice" meaning "I want juice") and, even in fluent speakers, impaired pragmatics. Developmental language disorder, by contrast, affects language with relatively intact social communication. In attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder language difficulties are common but are not a defining feature; specific learning disability is defined by difficulty with academic skills (reading, writing, arithmetic) rather than by delayed speech; and childhood dissociative conditions do not characteristically arrest language development. (The disorders are covered in the Psychiatric Disorders book.) 8.9 Language, Thought and Communication Medium yield · 8 Qs We can now return to the question Sultan raised at the start of this chapter. What is the relationship between language and thought? Does the language you speak shape the way you think? Can you think without language at all? Does Language Shape Thought? The Sapir-Whorf Hypothesis Benjamin Lee Whorf (1897 to 1941) was a fire-prevention inspector for an insurance company in Connecticut and, in his spare time, a student of linguistics under the anthropologist-linguist Edward Sapir (1884 to 1939). In his work he noticed that workers who were careful around drums labelled "gasoline" smoked carelessly near drums labelled "empty", although the "empty" drums were full of explosive vapour. The word, it seemed, had shaped the behaviour. Whorf went on to argue, from his study of the Hopi language of Arizona, that the Hopi conceive of time quite differently from speakers of European languages because their grammar treats it differently. His essays, collected after his death as Language, Thought, and Reality (1956), gave his name and Sapir's to the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis . The hypothesis comes in two strengths. The strong version, linguistic determinism , holds that language determines thought: we can think only in the categories our language provides, and speakers of very different languages live in different mental worlds. The weak version, linguistic relativity , holds that language influences thought: the habits of a language make some distinctions easier to notice, remember or express, without making others unthinkable. The strong version has not survived. Later fieldwork found that Hopi has plenty of ways of talking about time. The often-repeated claim that "Eskimo" languages have dozens or hundreds of words for snow turned out to be an exaggeration that grew with each retelling. And the most systematic test, on colour, pointed the other way. Brent Berlin and Paul Kay (1969), in Basic Color Terms , examined 98 languages and found that they have between two and eleven basic colour terms, added in a nearly universal order: a language with only two terms has words for dark and light (black and white); a language with three adds red; then come green and yellow; then blue; then brown; and finally purple, pink, orange and grey. Colour vocabularies, in other words, are constrained by universal features of perception. Eleanor Rosch, publishing as Eleanor Rosch Heider (1972), then studied the Dani of New Guinea, whose language has only two basic colour terms ( mili for dark, cool colours and mola for light, warm ones). The Dani remembered the "focal" colours (the best red, the best green) better than non-focal ones, and learned names for them more easily, just as English speakers do. Lacking a word for a colour did not stop them perceiving and remembering it. The weak version, however, has strong support. Russian has two basic words for what English calls blue: goluboy (light blue) and siniy (dark blue). Jonathan Winawer and his colleagues (2007) found that Russian speakers discriminated two blues faster when the shades fell on opposite sides of the goluboy-siniy boundary than when they fell on the same side; English speakers showed no such effect. Speakers of languages that describe space in absolute terms (north, south) rather than relative ones (left, right) keep track of compass directions with remarkable accuracy. You can see the same thing in kinship terms. A Hindi speaker must choose between chacha (father's younger brother), tau (father's elder brother), mama (mother's brother), mausa and phupha , where English offers only "uncle", so Hindi speakers habitually attend to which side of the family a relative belongs to. English speakers can understand the distinction perfectly well; they simply do not have to make it every time they speak. That is linguistic relativity in its defensible, weak form. Steven Pinker (1994) argues against even this much emphasis on language: we think, he says, in a language-independent "mentalese", which is why translation is possible and why babies and animals can think without words. Exam trap The linguistic relativity hypothesis is associated with Benjamin Lee Whorf (and his teacher Edward Sapir). Chomsky (universal grammar), Piaget (thought before language) and Pinker (mentalese, The Language Instinct ) are all wrong answers, and Pinker is a critic. Strong version = determinism; weak version = relativity (the one with support). Berlin and Kay's colour universals and Heider's Dani study count against the strong version. Piaget Versus Vygotsky Recall Watson's claim from Section 8.1 that thinking is merely subvocal speech. It was put to a dramatic test in 1947, when the anaesthetist Scott Smith had himself injected with curare, the drug that paralyses all the skeletal muscles, including those of the larynx and tongue (his breathing was maintained artificially). Afterwards he reported that he had remained fully conscious throughout, had understood what was said around him and had been able to think clearly. Thinking does not require movements of the speech muscles. But that does not settle how language and thought are related, and on this the two great developmental theorists disagreed. For Jean Piaget (1896 to 1980), thought comes first. Children build concepts through action on the world, and language is a way of expressing understanding that is already there; a child says "allgone" only after understanding that objects persist and can disappear. In The Language and Thought of the Child (1923) Piaget described egocentric speech : speech that is not adapted to a listener, such as the "collective monologue" of a group of preschoolers, each talking about his own activity without responding to the others. For Piaget, egocentric speech reflected the egocentrism of young children's thought, a stage between Bleuler's autistic thought and socialised, directed thought, and it simply faded away, around the age of seven, as thought became socialised. Lev Semyonovich Vygotsky (1896 to 1934), the Russian founder of sociocultural theory, read Piaget closely and disagreed. In Thinking and Speech (1934; translated as Thought and Language in 1962), he argued that thought and speech have different genetic roots. There is pre-linguistic thought , the practical intelligence of infants and of Köhler's chimpanzees; and there is pre-intellectual speech , the crying, babbling and first words of the infant, used socially and emotionally but not yet as a tool of thought. At around two years of age the two lines meet: the child, in the words Vygotsky quoted, "discovers that each thing has its name", asks constantly for names, and from then on thought becomes verbal and speech becomes rational. Speech, for Vygotsky, begins as social communication with others. Children then turn it on themselves as private speech (Piaget's egocentric speech) to plan and guide their own actions, and it gradually "goes underground" to become inner speech , silent verbal thought that is abbreviated, condensed and dense with personal meaning. So private speech does not simply disappear: it is internalised. Vygotsky supported this with an ingenious experiment. When he introduced obstacles into children's activities (for example, taking away the coloured pencil a child needed for a drawing), the amount of egocentric speech nearly doubled, because the children used it to work out what to do. Later research, notably by Laura Berk, confirms that children use more private speech on harder tasks and that those who do so tend to perform better. Vygotsky summarised development in four stages of speech and thought: a primitive or natural stage of pre-intellectual speech and pre-verbal thought; a naive psychology stage in which the child uses grammatical forms such as "because" before grasping the logical relations they express; an external sign stage of egocentric speech and external aids such as counting on fingers; and an ingrowth stage in which these operations are internalised as inner speech and mental calculation. Vygotsky also studied how true concepts develop. With his colleague Leonid Sakharov he gave children blocks of different colours, shapes, heights and sizes, each marked underneath with one of four nonsense words ( lag , bik , mur , cev ) that stood for combinations of height and size. Young children grouped the blocks into unorganised heaps ; older children formed complexes , groupings based on shifting, concrete links, including pseudoconcepts that look like real concepts but rest on visible similarity; only in adolescence do true concepts appear, based on abstract, systematic features. Vygotsky linked this achievement to the new tasks that society sets adolescents, to their participation in social institutions such as school and work, and to the growth of self-reflection, the ability to step back and reflect on one's acting self. He distinguished everyday (spontaneous) concepts, picked up in daily life, from scientific concepts, learned systematically through instruction; the two meet and enrich each other in the zone of proximal development, the gap between what a learner can do alone and what she can do with guidance (Developmental Psychology book).
