Options that swap the names, or that say one studied early and the other later language, are wrong. Private speech, for Vygotsky, guides and regulates behaviour and is internalised as inner speech ; it is not a regression to autistic thinking, mere imitation, a sign of disorder, or egocentrism that fades only with schooling. In Vygotsky's account of adolescent conceptual thinking, societal tasks, social institutions and self-reflection all matter; gender differences play no part. One recent paper asked whether a person's language and thought involve simultaneous, independent, shared or alternate processes, with "simultaneous" as the expected answer: in mature verbal thought, language and thought run together and interdependently. "Independent" describes only their separate early roots, and "shared" is the most defensible alternative if the key is disputed. Bilingualism Most people in the world, and most people in India, speak more than one language. Bilingualism is the ability to use two languages; a person fluent in many languages is a polyglot or multilingual (a linguist, by contrast, studies language scientifically, whether or not she speaks many, and an orator is simply a skilled public speaker). In simultaneous bilingualism, a child learns two languages from birth, as two first languages; in sequential bilingualism, a second language is added after the first is established. Uriel Weinreich (1953) distinguished compound bilinguals, who learned both languages in the same context and attach two labels to a single set of meanings, from coordinate bilinguals, who learned them in separate contexts and have partly separate meaning systems (and subordinate bilinguals, who reach the second language through the first). Wallace Lambert distinguished additive bilingualism, in which a second language is added while the first remains valued and maintained, from subtractive bilingualism, in which the second language gradually replaces the first, as often happens to minority languages. Early studies claimed that bilingualism harmed children's intelligence, but they compared poor immigrant children with middle-class monolinguals and tested them in their weaker language. When Elizabeth Peal and Wallace Lambert (1962) compared balanced French-English bilingual children in Montreal with monolinguals matched for social class, the bilinguals did better on both verbal and non-verbal tests. Since then Ellen Bialystok and others have reported that bilinguals show greater metalinguistic awareness and, in some studies, better executive control, presumably from constantly managing two languages; some studies even report a later onset of dementia symptoms. These advantages are now debated, and several large studies find small or no executive benefits. The costs are better established and modest: bilingual children reach the main milestones of language development on the usual timetable, but bilinguals tend to have a smaller vocabulary in each language and to retrieve words slightly more slowly. Code-switching , moving between languages within a conversation ("Kal exam hai, so I'm going to sleep early"), follows grammatical rules and is a sign of competence, not confusion. Indian context India is one of the most multilingual societies on earth, with 22 languages listed in the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution and hundreds of mother tongues. Multilingualism is the ordinary condition: a Mysuru student may speak Kannada at home, English in class, Hindi with friends from the north and some Tamil or Telugu with neighbours. The three-language formula , adopted in the National Policy on Education of 1968, asks schools to teach the regional language, Hindi and English (with another modern Indian language in Hindi-speaking states). For a clinician, this means assessing and treating clients in their dominant language whenever possible, since emotional memories are often encoded in the language in which they were lived. Can Animals Learn Language? Animals certainly communicate. The Austrian zoologist Karl von Frisch, who shared a Nobel Prize in 1973, showed that a honeybee's "waggle dance" tells its hivemates the direction and distance of a food source: a genuine case of displacement, but the system is fixed, cannot express anything new, and is not learned. Vervet monkeys give different alarm calls for leopards, eagles and snakes, and other vervets respond appropriately (running up trees, looking up, or standing up and scanning the ground) even to recordings of the calls (Robert Seyfarth, Dorothy Cheney and Peter Marler, 1980): semanticity, but no combination of calls into new messages. Could an ape do better if taught? Early attempts to teach chimpanzees to speak failed; Vicki, raised as a child by Keith and Catherine Hayes in the late 1940s, learned to say only about four words (mama, papa, cup and up), because the ape vocal tract cannot produce human speech. So researchers turned to other media. From 1966 Beatrix Gardner and Allen Gardner taught the chimpanzee Washoe American Sign Language; she learned about 130 signs and combined them, famously signing "water bird" on seeing a swan. David Premack taught a chimpanzee called Sarah to use plastic tokens on a magnetic board, and Duane Rumbaugh taught Lana to press symbols (lexigrams) on a computer keyboard. Then came the sceptics. Herbert Terrace raised a chimpanzee with the pointed name Nim Chimpsky and taught him sign language. When Terrace and his colleagues analysed hours of videotape (1979), they found that most of Nim's signs were prompted by his teachers or were partial imitations of signs the teacher had just made; his utterances did not grow longer in a rule-governed way, and his longest, sixteen signs long, was "Give orange me give eat orange me eat orange give me eat orange give me you". Terrace's answer to the question in the title of his paper, "Can an ape create a sentence?", was no. The most impressive evidence came later from Sue Savage-Rumbaugh 's bonobo Kanzi, who learned lexigrams spontaneously as an infant by watching researchers try to train his adoptive mother, and who could carry out novel spoken requests ("put the soap on the apple") at a level roughly comparable to a child of two to two and a half. The current verdict is that apes can learn symbols with meaning (semanticity, arbitrariness, some displacement), but show little productive grammar and no clear recursion. On Hockett's list, generativity remains the human signature. Speech Perception Listen to someone speaking a language you do not know and you will notice something important: you cannot tell where one word ends and the next begins. The speech signal is continuous; the gaps we "hear" between words in our own language are mostly supplied by our knowledge (the segmentation problem ). Worse, each phoneme is pronounced differently depending on the sounds around it ( coarticulation ), so there is no fixed acoustic pattern for, say, /d/. How do we perceive speech at all? Part of the answer is categorical perception : the tendency to perceive a continuously varying stimulus as falling into discrete categories, with sharp boundaries between them and poor discrimination within them. Alvin Liberman (1917 to 2000) and his colleagues at the Haskins Laboratories (1957) created synthetic syllables that changed in equal acoustic steps from one consonant to another. Consider the difference between /ba/ and /pa/. Both are made by opening the lips; they differ in voice onset time (VOT), the delay between the release of the lips and the start of vocal-cord vibration, which is short for /ba/ and longer for /pa/. When VOT is varied smoothly, listeners do not hear a gradual change. They hear /ba/, /ba/, /ba/, and then, at a boundary of about 25 milliseconds in English, an abrupt switch to /pa/ (Figure 8.6). Two sounds 20 milliseconds apart are easy to tell apart if they straddle the boundary and almost impossible if they fall on the same side. Peter Eimas and his colleagues (1971) found the same boundary in infants only one and four months old, which at first suggested a special inborn mechanism for speech; but chinchillas show it too, so it may reflect general properties of mammalian hearing that languages have exploited. 0 50 100 0 10 20 30 40 50 60 Voice onset time (milliseconds) Per cent identified heard as /ba/ (dashed) boundary heard as /pa/ (solid) Figure 8.6 Categorical perception of speech. As voice onset time increases in equal steps, listeners' labels do not change gradually: they switch from /ba/ to /pa/ abruptly near 25 milliseconds. Idealised curves of the kind first reported by Liberman and colleagues. Speech perception also uses the eyes. In the McGurk effect , described by Harry McGurk and John MacDonald (1976), the sound of a person saying "ba" is dubbed onto a video of the same person's lips saying "ga". Viewers hear "da", a compromise between what they hear and what they see; when they close their eyes, they hear "ba" again. The illusion persists even when you know exactly how it works, which shows how automatically sight and sound are combined. Knowledge and context fill in gaps too. In the phonemic restoration effect , Richard Warren (1970) replaced the first /s/ in "legislatures" in a recorded sentence with a cough. Listeners "heard" the missing /s/ and could not say where the cough had occurred. Remarkably, a word heard later in the sentence can determine which sound is restored: "the *eel was on the axle" is heard as "wheel", "the *eel was on the orange" as "peel". Speech perception is as much top-down as bottom-up, a point you met for vision in Chapter 4. Reading and Aphasia: Pointers Reading is a recent cultural invention, a few thousand years old, built on top of spoken language. Before children can learn to read in an alphabetic script, they must already have spoken vocabulary and grammar, and above all phonological awareness : the knowledge that spoken words are made of smaller sounds (syllables, rhymes and phonemes) that can be manipulated. Phonological awareness in the preschool years is one of the best predictors of later reading. So the cognitive skill that learning to read builds on most directly is spoken language, not theory of mind (the understanding that other people have beliefs and desires of their own), imagination, or the general capacity for mental representation. In the alphasyllabic scripts of India, such as Kannada and Devanagari, the basic written unit is the akshara (roughly a consonant with its vowel), and awareness of syllables and aksharas plays the same role. Skilled reading, according to Max Coltheart's dual-route model , uses two routes: a lexical route that recognises familiar words as wholes (essential for irregular words such as "yacht" and "colonel") and a non-lexical route that converts letters to sounds by rule (essential for new words and nonwords such as "blint"). Damage to the lexical route produces surface dyslexia (irregular words are "regularised", so "pint" is read to rhyme with "mint"); damage to the non-lexical route produces phonological dyslexia (familiar words can be read, but nonwords cannot). Developmental dyslexia and specific learning disorders are covered in the Psychiatric Disorders book. Finally, language can be lost. An acquired disturbance of language caused by brain damage, typically to the left hemisphere after a stroke, is called aphasia . It is a disorder of language specifically, not of intelligence, memory, abstract thinking or the muscles of speech (weakness of the speech muscles is dysarthria ). In 1861 the French physician Paul Broca (1824 to 1880) described a patient, Louis Victor Leborgne, nicknamed "Tan" because it was almost the only syllable he could say; at autopsy Broca found damage in the left inferior frontal gyrus, now called Broca's area. In 1874 the German neurologist Carl Wernicke (1848 to 1905) described a different syndrome after damage to the posterior part of the left superior temporal gyrus, now Wernicke's area. The two classic aphasias, and the brain's language network, are treated fully in the Physiological Psychology book; the essentials are in the box below. Clinical link Broca's aphasia (expressive, non-fluent): effortful, halting, agrammatic speech much like telegraphic speech, with relatively preserved comprehension and impaired repetition; patients are usually aware of their difficulty and frustrated by it. Broca's area is involved in speech production . Wernicke's aphasia (receptive, fluent): fluent, well-articulated speech with normal prosody but empty of meaning, full of word substitutions (paraphasias) and invented words (neologisms), with poor comprehension and repetition; patients are often unaware of their errors. Conduction aphasia : fluent speech and good comprehension but strikingly poor repetition, after damage to the arcuate fasciculus linking the two areas. Global aphasia affects everything. Damage to the corresponding right-hemisphere regions spares grammar but disturbs emotional prosody, humour, metaphor and the flow of conversation. Three neighbours are not aphasias of speech: damage to the left angular gyrus disturbs reading and writing (alexia with agraphia); pure alexia (alexia without agraphia), in which the patient can write but cannot read, follows left occipital damage; and inability to recognise faces is prosopagnosia , a disorder of visual recognition. The case of Sultan and the two sticks, revisited Go back to Tenerife, to the moment before Sultan jumped up. You can now describe what happened in several vocabularies. In Newell and Simon's terms, the banana problem was well defined (a clear initial state, a clear goal), but Sultan's problem space lacked the one operator that would solve it: joining two sticks into one. Hill climbing could never have found it. Pushing one stick out with the other brought a tip closer to the banana without bringing the banana any closer to Sultan, a local maximum from which no small step led further. In Gestalt terms he solved the problem by insight: the two short sticks were suddenly seen as parts of one long one, and the solution appeared all at once, was performed smoothly and was kept, exactly the marks of insight that Köhler listed. His idle play with the sticks even resembles Wallas's incubation followed by illumination, and Metcalfe and Wiebe's warmth ratings suggest that, had he been able to tell us, he would have felt no nearer the answer a moment before he found it. Herbert Birch's work adds the caution: Sultan had handled sticks before, and insight grows out of experience rather than replacing it. Was he thinking without words? Everything in this chapter says yes. Of the five elements of thought he plainly had images and concepts (a concept of "stick" flexible enough to include a stick made of two sticks), though not conventional symbols, propositions or language. The curare experiment showed that human thought does not need the muscles of speech, and Vygotsky placed Köhler's chimpanzees at the very start of his account of thought and language, as the clearest case of pre-linguistic thought: practical intelligence that has not yet met speech. What Sultan lacked is what the last three sections of the chapter describe, a generative symbol system that can refer to things not present. Washoe, Nim and Kanzi showed that apes can learn symbols that mean something, but not a grammar that produces endless new sentences. In children, Vygotsky argued, the two lines meet at about the age of two, and from then on thought becomes verbal: we can reason about what is absent, test hypotheses we have never acted out, and tell someone else how we solved a problem. Sultan could do the first thing this chapter describes. He could not do the last: he had no way to tell another chimpanzee how he had done it. Chapter summary 8.1 What Is Thinking? Thinking is the mental manipulation of internal representations to form new ones, the part of cognition that transforms what perception and memory supply. The Würzburg school of Oswald Külpe reported imageless thought, against Titchener's view that every thought contains images; Watson (1913) reduced thinking to subvocal speech; and the cognitive revolution (Chomsky, Newell and Simon, Bruner, and Neisser's Cognitive Psychology of 1967) brought thought back with objective measures. The elements of thought are images, concepts, symbols and signs, propositions and language. Shepard and Metzler (1971) found that the time to compare rotated objects rises linearly with the angle (mental rotation), and Kosslyn's island-scanning studies suggested depictive images; Pylyshyn's propositional theory (1973) explained such results by tacit knowledge, but imagery's use of visual cortex and the imaginal neglect of Bisiach and Luzzatti's patients favour depictive images. Paivio's dual-coding theory (1971) explains why pictures and concrete words are remembered best. Thinking may be directed or undirected, autistic or dereistic (Bleuler, 1911), convergent or divergent (Guilford), critical, creative, reflective (Dewey, 1910), and productive or reproductive (Wertheimer, 1945). 8.2 Concepts. A concept is a mental representation of a category; concepts give cognitive economy and support inference. Concept formation is described as observation, discrimination, generalisation and abstraction, often followed by naming; Hull (1920) treated it as gradual associative abstraction. The classical view defines a concept by necessary and sufficient features and fits artificial concepts, which may be conjunctive (this and that), disjunctive (this or that) or relational. Bruner, Goodnow and Austin (1956) showed that people attain artificial concepts by testing hypotheses, with conservative focusing the most efficient strategy, alongside focus gambling and simultaneous and successive scanning. Natural concepts, as Eleanor Rosch showed, have typicality gradients, fuzzy boundaries and Wittgenstein's family resemblance; prototype theory represents them by an abstract, averaged best example, and the basic level (chair, dog) is learned and named first. Exemplar theory (Medin and Schaffer, 1978) stores many instances instead. Concepts are linked in semantic networks (Collins and Quillian, 1969; spreading activation, Collins and Loftus, 1975) or, in connectionism (Rumelhart and McClelland, 1986), distributed across many interconnected units. 8.3 Problem Solving. A problem is a gap between an initial state and a goal state; problems may be well defined or ill defined. Newell and Simon (General Problem Solver; Human Problem Solving , 1972) described solving as search through a problem space of states and operators. An algorithm guarantees a solution; a heuristic is an efficient rule of thumb that does not. The main heuristics are means-end analysis (reducing differences by subgoals), working backward, hill climbing (which fails at a local maximum, as in the hobbits and orcs problem) and analogy, which people use readily when told to but rarely notice spontaneously (Gick and Holyoak, 1980); trial and error is the most primitive strategy (Thorndike, 1898). Gestalt psychologists stressed insight, a sudden restructuring of the problem (Köhler's apes, Maier's nine-dot and two-string problems), and Metcalfe and Wiebe's warmth ratings (1987) confirmed that insight solutions arrive suddenly; incubation helps, probably by letting a misleading approach be forgotten. The obstacles are functional fixedness (Duncker's candle problem, 1945), mental set or Einstellung (Luchins's water jars, 1942), confirmation bias and irrelevant information. Stage models run from Dewey and Pólya to Sternberg's problem-solving cycle, and experts excel because they store meaningful chunks and represent problems by deep principles (Chase and Simon, 1973; Chi, 1981). 8.4 Reasoning. Deductive reasoning moves from general premises to a conclusion that must be true if the premises are; an argument is valid by its form and sound if its premises are also true. Inductive reasoning moves from specific observations to probable generalisations and is the logic of theory development and qualitative research, while abductive reasoning (Peirce) is inference to the best explanation; Popper's hypothetico-deductive method combines them. In syllogisms people show belief bias (Evans, Barston and Pollard, 1983) and the atmosphere effect (Woodworth and Sells, 1935). Of the four conditional arguments, modus ponens and modus tollens are valid, while affirming the consequent and denying the antecedent are fallacies. In Wason's selection task (1966) few people choose the correct cards (E and 7), but performance improves with familiar permission rules (Griggs and Cox, 1982), explained by pragmatic reasoning schemas (Cheng and Holyoak, 1985) or cheater detection (Cosmides, 1989). Johnson-Laird's mental models theory (1983) holds that we reason by building and checking models of possible situations. Wason's 2-4-6 task (1960) revealed confirmation bias. In Piaget's theory, hypothetico-deductive, counterfactual and metacognitive reasoning emerge with formal operations; dialectical thinking is postformal. 8.5 Judgement and Decision Making. Normative models (expected value; expected utility, von Neumann and Morgenstern, 1944) say how a rational agent should decide; descriptive models say how people actually decide. Simon's bounded rationality holds that information, mental capacity and time limit choice, so people satisfice rather than optimise; Tversky's elimination by aspects (1972) is a non-compensatory shortcut, and Gigerenzer's fast and frugal heuristics, such as the recognition heuristic, can be ecologically rational. Tversky and Kahneman (1974) described the availability heuristic (the K-words), the representativeness heuristic, which produces base-rate neglect, the conjunction fallacy (Linda, 1983), the gambler's fallacy and insensitivity to sample size, and anchoring and adjustment. The framing effect (the Asian disease problem, 1981) shows risk aversion for gains and risk seeking for losses, explained by prospect theory (1979): outcomes are judged from a reference point, sensitivity diminishes, and losses loom about twice as large as gains (loss aversion), which also underlies the endowment effect, status quo bias and the sunk-cost fallacy. Overconfidence, the planning fallacy and Fischhoff's hindsight bias (1975) distort judgements of our own knowledge. Dual-process theory contrasts fast, intuitive System 1 with slow, deliberate System 2, and Beck's cognitive distortions are the clinical cousins of these biases. 8.6 Creativity. Creativity is the production of work that is both novel and appropriate, studied through Rhodes's four Ps (person, process, press, product) and at levels from mini-c to Big-C. Guilford's 1950 address launched the field; he identified creativity with divergent production and scored it by fluency, flexibility, originality and elaboration. Wallas (1926) described four stages: preparation, incubation, illumination and verification, with intimation sometimes added. Creativity is measured by the Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking (1966), Mednick's Remote Associates Test (1962), which rests on his associative theory, and Amabile's consensual assessment technique. De Bono's lateral thinking (1967) and Osborn's brainstorming (rules: defer judgement, go for quantity, welcome wild ideas, combine) aim to enhance it, although nominal groups outperform interacting ones because of production blocking. The threshold hypothesis holds that intelligence is necessary but not sufficient for creativity: the two are correlated below an IQ of about 120 but hardly at all above it, and overall the correlation is weak (about 0.17 in Kim's 2005 meta-analysis); Getzels and Jackson (1962) found high-creative and high-IQ adolescents equally successful at school. Sternberg and Lubart's investment theory (buy low, sell high; six converging resources), Amabile's componential model with its intrinsic motivation principle, and Csikszentmihalyi's systems model (individual, domain and field) are the main modern theories. Creative people are above all open to experience, independent, tolerant of ambiguity and willing to take risks. 8.7 The Structure of Language. A language is a system of arbitrary symbols combined by rules to produce unlimited messages. Hockett (1960) listed design features, of which semanticity, arbitrariness, displacement, generativity (productivity) and duality of patterning are the most examined; recursion may be uniquely human. The units of language form a hierarchy: phonemes (smallest units of sound that distinguish words), morphemes (smallest units of meaning, free or bound, inflectional or derivational), words, syntax (rules of sentence structure), semantics (meaning), pragmatics (use in social context, including Grice's maxims) and prosody (rhythm, stress and intonation, with emotional prosody served by right-hemisphere regions). Chomsky's Syntactic Structures (1957) proposed a transformational generative grammar of phrase-structure and transformational rules, and Aspects of the Theory of Syntax (1965) distinguished surface structure from deep structure (ambiguous sentences have one surface structure and two deep structures) and competence (tacit knowledge) from performance (actual use). 8.8 Acquiring Language. Skinner's Verbal Behavior (1957) explained language by reinforcement of verbal operants (mand, tact, echoic, intraverbal, textual, transcription, autoclitic). Chomsky's 1959 review replied that children produce novel sentences, make rule-based errors and are rarely corrected for grammar, and proposed an innate language acquisition device containing universal grammar, defended by the poverty of the stimulus; Pinker popularised nativism, while statistical learning (Saffran, Aslin and Newport, 1996) shows the input is richer than Chomsky supposed. Interactionists stress social support: Bruner's language acquisition support system (formats and scaffolding) and child-directed speech, with its higher, wider pitch, slower rate, more pauses and shorter utterances; Slobin's language-making capacity is a set of language-tuned cognitive and perceptual operating principles. Lenneberg (1967) proposed a critical period from about two to puberty, supported, imperfectly, by Genie and by Johnson and Newport's immigrants (1989). The milestones are cooing (about 2 months), babbling (about 6 months), holophrases (about 12 months), the vocabulary spurt with fast mapping (about 18 months), telegraphic speech (18 to 24 months), overregularisation (2 to 3 years), and complex sentences and metalinguistic awareness after that, with overextension and underextension along the way. Language is most consistently compromised in autism spectrum disorder. 8.9 Language, Thought and Communication. The Sapir-Whorf hypothesis has a strong version, linguistic determinism, which has failed (Hopi time, Berlin and Kay's colour universals of 1969, Heider's Dani study of 1972), and a weak version, linguistic relativity, which is supported (Russian blues, absolute spatial languages, kinship terms); Pinker argues that we think in a language-independent mentalese. The curare experiment (1947) refuted Watson's motor theory. Piaget held that thought comes first and egocentric speech simply fades; Vygotsky held that thought and speech have separate roots that merge at about two, after which private speech guides behaviour and is internalised as inner speech; he also traced concepts from heaps through complexes to true concepts in adolescence. Bilingualism may be simultaneous or sequential, compound, coordinate or subordinate (Weinreich), additive or subtractive (Lambert); balanced bilinguals can show advantages (Peal and Lambert, 1962), though executive benefits are debated. Bees and vervet monkeys communicate, and apes (Washoe, Sarah, Lana, Nim, Kanzi) learn meaningful symbols but little productive grammar. Speech perception is categorical (Liberman, 1957; voice onset time), audiovisual (the McGurk effect, 1976) and partly top-down (phonemic restoration). Reading builds on spoken language and phonological awareness (dual-route model), and aphasia is an acquired language disorder: Broca's (production) and Wernicke's (comprehension), treated fully in the Physiological Psychology book. (Amity 2023) (a) Jean Piaget (b) Kohler (c) Chomsky (d) Kohlberg Answer: (a) Jean Piaget (the keyed answer). Piaget's studies of how children's thinking develops, begun in the 1920s, were among the first systematic accounts of mental structures and processes, decades before the cognitive revolution. According to the dual-coding theory of memory, which type of information is more easily remembered? (RML 2023) (a) Verbal information (b) Visual information (c) Auditory information (d) Semantic information Answer: (b) Visual information. In Paivio's theory (1971), pictures and concrete, imageable material are coded both in the imagery system and in the verbal system, giving two routes to retrieval (the picture superiority and concreteness effects). Verbal and auditory material, and abstract meaning, usually receive only the verbal code. "Semantic" tempts students who confuse dual coding with Craik and Lockhart's levels of processing. The researcher who formulated the theory which explains how we form artificial concepts rather than natural concepts by developing a hypothesis is: (IHBAS 2020) (a) Clark Hull (b) Eleanor Rosch (c) Jerome Bruner (d) John Watson Answer: (c) Jerome Bruner. With Goodnow and Austin (1956), Bruner showed that people learning artificial, rule-defined concepts form and test hypotheses, using strategies such as conservative focusing. Rosch is the name for natural concepts and prototypes; Hull (1920) treated concept learning as gradual associative abstraction of a common element, not hypothesis testing; Watson did no work on concepts. Which model proposes that memory is organized in a network of interconnected nodes? (IHBAS 2024) (a) Associative model (b) Connectionist model (c) Network model (d) Linkage model Answer: (b) Connectionist model (the keyed answer). Connectionist, or parallel distributed processing, models (Rumelhart and McClelland, 1986) represent knowledge as patterns of activation across a network of interconnected units whose connection weights store what has been learned. "Network model" is the strongest distractor, because Collins and Quillian's semantic network is also a network of nodes, but follow the key. "Associative model" is the older, general idea of linked ideas, and "linkage model" is not a standard term. A rule-of-thumb that allows for an efficient search for the selection of a problem is termed as (RML 2024) (a) Algorithm (b) Education (c) Learning (d) Heuristic Answer: (d) Heuristic. ("Selection" in the stem is a slip for "solution".) A heuristic is an efficient shortcut that usually works but does not guarantee success. An algorithm is the opposite case, a step-by-step procedure that guarantees a solution but may be slow; education and learning are not problem-solving strategies at all. The tendency to think of the use of objects only in terms of their habitual use is known as: (RML 2024) (a) Mental barrier (b) Functional fixedness (c) Einstellung (d) Trial and error Answer: (b) Functional fixedness , demonstrated by Duncker's candle problem (1945), in which the box is seen only as a container. Einstellung (mental set) is the related fixation on a previously successful strategy (Luchins's water jars), not on an object's use; "mental barrier" is not a technical term; trial and error is a problem-solving strategy, not an obstacle. Which is the most basic and common obstacle to problem solving? (Amity 2023) (a) Confirmation bias (b) Mental set (c) Functional fixedness (d) Fixation Answer: (b) Mental set , the tendency to keep using an approach that worked before. Functional fixedness is usually treated as a special case of mental set, applied to objects, so it is narrower. Fixation is the Gestaltists' umbrella word for being stuck rather than a specific obstacle, and confirmation bias concerns how hypotheses are tested rather than how a problem is approached. In which method does the researcher start with a theory and then test it with observations? (RML 2023) (a) Inductive reasoning (b) Deductive reasoning (c) Abductive reasoning (d) Hypothetico-deductive method Answer: (b) Deductive reasoning , which runs from the general (a theory) to the specific (a prediction tested against observations). Inductive reasoning runs the other way, from data to theory; abductive reasoning infers the best explanation of a surprising observation. The hypothetico-deductive method also begins with theory, but it is the whole cycle of hypothesis, deduced prediction and test, and the key chooses the plain label. In deductive reasoning, the validity of conclusions depends on the: (RML 2023) (a) Breadth of observations (b) Depth of data collected (c) Soundness of the initial theory (d) Use of statistical analysis Answer: (c) Soundness of the initial theory. A deductive conclusion is only as trustworthy as the premises it starts from: a valid argument from a false premise can reach a false conclusion. (Strictly, logicians say validity depends on form and soundness on true premises, so the item uses "validity" loosely.) Breadth of observations and depth of data are concerns of inductive, data-first research, and statistics is a tool, not the basis of deduction. Which of the following does NOT reflect inductive reasoning? (RML 2024) (a) Probabilistic conclusions (b) Heuristics (c) Decision making (d) Process involved in concept formation Answer: (b) Heuristics (the keyed answer). Inductive conclusions are probabilistic by nature; concept formation abstracts general categories from specific instances; decision making under uncertainty rests on inductive estimates of likelihood. A heuristic is a shortcut strategy rather than a form of inference, although it can produce inductive judgements, which is why the item is debatable. Formal operational reasoning involves all the following EXCEPT: (RML 2022) (a) hypothetical reasoning (b) counterfactual reasoning (c) dialectical reasoning (d) metacognitive reasoning Answer: (c) Dialectical reasoning. Holding contradictory perspectives together and integrating them is postformal thought (Riegel, 1973; Basseches, 1984), beyond Piaget's final stage. Hypothetical (hypothetico-deductive), counterfactual and metacognitive reasoning ("operations on operations") are exactly what emerges in the formal operational stage from about 11 or 12. Who is known for his work on the concept of bounded rationality, which suggests that decision-making is often constrained by factors such as limited information and cognitive resources? (RML 2023) (a) Herbert Simon (b) Daniel Kahneman (c) Amos Tversky (d) Howard Gardner Answer: (a) Herbert Simon , who also coined "satisficing" (1956) and won the Nobel Prize in Economics in 1978. Kahneman and Tversky tempt because they too showed that people depart from rational choice, but their contributions are heuristics and biases and prospect theory; Gardner is the theorist of multiple intelligences. The representativeness heuristic can lead to errors when: (RML 2023) (a) Individuals ignore base rates and focus solely on similarity (b) Individuals rely on readily available information (c) Individuals fail to consider alternative explanations (d) Individuals adjust their judgements based on initial estimates Answer: (a). Representativeness judges probability by resemblance to the typical case, and its classic failure is base-rate neglect, as with Jack the "engineer" and the taxi-cab problem. Option (b) describes the availability heuristic, (c) confirmation bias and (d) anchoring and adjustment. Confirmation bias is closely related to which heuristics? (RML 2023) (a) Availability heuristic (b) Representativeness heuristic (c) Anchoring and adjustment heuristic (d) Recognition heuristic Answer: (b) Representativeness heuristic (the keyed answer). The key reasons that both involve judging by fit to a preconceived model: evidence that "looks like" what we expect is accepted. No standard textbook ties confirmation bias to one heuristic (it is a bias in hypothesis testing, Wason, 1960), so treat this as a recall of the key. Availability concerns ease of retrieval and anchoring an initial value; the recognition heuristic (Gigerenzer) simply favours the option one recognises and is the least related. The tendency to assume that we would have been better at predicting actual events than is really true is termed as: (RML 2024) (a) Hindsight effect (b) Just world hypothesis (c) Decisiveness (d) Confirmation Answer: (a) Hindsight effect , the "I knew it all along" bias shown by Fischhoff and Beyth (1975) with predictions about Nixon's 1972 visits. The just-world hypothesis (Melvin Lerner) is the belief that people get what they deserve; decisiveness is not a bias; confirmation bias concerns how we seek and read evidence for a belief, not how we misremember our own predictions. The correct sequence of the four stages of creative thinking, as proposed by Graham Wallas, is: (Real PYQ 2024) (a) Preparation, Illumination, Incubation, Verification (b) Incubation, Preparation, Verification, Illumination (c) Preparation, Incubation, Illumination, Verification (d) Illumination, Preparation, Verification, Incubation Answer: (c) , from The Art of Thought (1926). The other options scramble the logic of the sequence: incubation (setting the problem aside) has to follow the effortful work of preparation and comes before the sudden illumination it prepares, and verification must come last because there has to be an idea to test. Which is the smallest unit of meaning in speech perception? (RML 2024) (a) Syllables (b) Consonant (c) Phonemes (d) Morphemes Answer: (d) Morphemes , such as the two in "cat-s". Phonemes are the smallest units of sound that distinguish words, but they carry no meaning of their own; a consonant is just one kind of phoneme; a syllable is a unit of pronunciation built around a vowel. The brain region most critically involved in processing the prosody or emotional tone of speech (speech intonation) is typically: (Real PYQ 2024) (a) Left inferior frontal gyrus (Broca's area) (b) Right hemisphere regions homotopic to language areas (c) Primary motor cortex (d) Occipital lobe Answer: (b). Emotional prosody depends chiefly on right-hemisphere regions that mirror the left hemisphere's language areas, and damage there produces aprosodia (Ross, 1981). Broca's area serves speech production and grammar rather than emotional tone; the primary motor cortex moves the speech muscles without interpreting anything; the occipital lobe is visual. Adults typically talk to babies in a special way. This has been defined as 'Motherese', 'baby talk register' or 'adult-child speech'. Identify one characteristic of this type of adult-child speech. (RML 2021) (a) The mean length of utterance is shorter in adult-child speech than it is in adult-adult speech. (b) Adults speak much more quickly to babies than they do to other adults. (c) Adults pause more frequently when they talk to other adults than they do when they talk to babies. (d) Adult-child speech has a lower pitch and a narrower range of pitch. Answer: (a). Child-directed speech uses shorter, simpler utterances. Each other option reverses a real feature: adults speak more slowly to babies, pause more often with babies than with adults, and use a higher pitch with a wider range. When infants and very young children live in environments where they have no exposure to or experience with language, their language development is severely limited. These limitations are not reversible. This supports which of the following terms? (RML 2021) (a) Sensitive periods of development (b) Semantics (c) Syntax (d) Nativism Answer: (a) Sensitive periods of development. Irreversible deficits after early deprivation (Genie; Lenneberg, 1967) are the defining evidence for a sensitive or critical period. Semantics and syntax are levels of language, not developmental principles; nativism is the broader claim that the capacity for language is innate, which such evidence fits but does not name directly. Who emphasised the linguistic relativity hypothesis? (Amity 2023) (a) Noam Chomsky (b) Jean Piaget (c) Steven Pinker (d) B.L. Whorf Answer: (d) B. L. Whorf , Sapir's student, who argued from the Hopi language that language shapes habitual thought. Chomsky stresses the universal grammar common to all languages, the opposite emphasis; Piaget held that thought precedes and shapes language; Pinker is an outspoken critic of Whorf who argues that we think in "mentalese". What is the primary difference between Piaget and Vygotsky's theories of language development? (RML 2021) (a) Piaget argued thought depends on language while Vygotsky argued language depends on thought (b) Vygotsky argued thought depends on language while Piaget argued language depends on thought (c) Vygotsky was concerned with early language development while Piaget was concerned with later language development. (d) None of the above Answer: (b). For Piaget, language expresses concepts already formed through action; for Vygotsky, thought and speech merge at about two, after which thought becomes verbal and depends on language. Option (a) swaps the names, and (c) is false, because both studied the same preschool years (Piaget's egocentric speech and Vygotsky's private speech are the same phenomenon, interpreted differently). In Vygotsky's writings, conceptual thinking is linked to all the following EXCEPT: (RML 2022) (a) the distinction between the acting 'I' and the reflecting 'I' (b) the problems and developmental tasks that society creates for adolescents (c) participation in particular societal institutions (d) gender differences Answer: (d) Gender differences. Vygotsky linked the emergence of true concepts in adolescence to the tasks society sets adolescents, to their participation in social institutions such as school and work, and to self-reflection, the ability to step back from the acting self. Gender plays no part in his account. A person's language and thought involve (JEMAS 2025) (a) Simultaneous processes. (b) Independent processes. (c) Shared processes. (d) Alternate process. Answer: (a) Simultaneous processes (the expected answer; the official key is not available). In mature verbal thought, language and thought run together and depend on each other, as Vygotsky described once their two lines merge at about two. "Independent" describes only their separate early roots (pre-linguistic thought and pre-intellectual speech); "shared" is the most defensible alternative if the key is disputed; "alternate", meaning that they take turns, describes no theory. Aphasia is the disturbance in: (IHBAS 2020) (a) Language function due to organic disease (b) Intellectual functioning (c) Abstract thinking (d) Memory Answer: (a). Aphasia is an acquired disorder of language caused by brain damage, classically to Broca's area (non-fluent aphasia) or Wernicke's area (fluent aphasia) in the left hemisphere. Intelligence, abstract thinking and memory can all be intact; a general loss of intellectual functioning suggests intellectual disability or dementia, and a loss of memory suggests amnesia. Inductive reasoning moves from specific observations to broader, probable generalisations: gather data, find patterns, build theory. It is the reasoning of theory development and of qualitative research. asked 4 times Graham Wallas , The Art of Thought (1926): preparation, incubation, illumination, verification. Incubation (setting the problem aside) is second; illumination (the sudden insight) is third; intimation is sometimes added before illumination. asked 5 times Vygotsky versus Piaget: Vygotsky held that thought depends on language (the two lines merge at about age two, after which they work together); Piaget held that language depends on thought. For Vygotsky, private speech guides behaviour and is internalised as inner speech. asked 4 times Functional fixedness is seeing an object only in terms of its usual function (Karl Duncker's candle problem, 1945: the box seen only as a container). It is about objects, mental set is about strategies, and it reflects top-down processing working too well. asked 4 times A heuristic is a rule of thumb that allows an efficient search and is usually right but does not guarantee a solution; an algorithm guarantees a solution but may be slow. asked 3 times Deductive reasoning starts from a theory or general premises and tests specific predictions against observations; a deductive conclusion is only as trustworthy as the soundness of its premises (the initial theory). asked twice Noam Chomsky's language acquisition device is an innate, biologically based capacity containing universal grammar, argued from the poverty of the stimulus; not the phonological loop, the zone of proximal development or a schema. asked 3 times The morpheme is the smallest unit of meaning (cat + s is two); the phoneme is the smallest unit of sound that distinguishes words and has no meaning of its own. asked twice Cognitive psychology is the modern approach closest to structuralism, because it studies consciousness, imagery and thought; Ulric Neisser named it (1967), and one paper keyed Jean Piaget as its pioneer contributor (not Kohlberg). asked twice Mental set (Einstellung) is the habit of reusing a strategy that worked before, shown by Abraham Luchins's water jars (1942); keyed as the most basic and common obstacle to problem solving. asked twice Confirmation bias is seeking, interpreting and remembering evidence that confirms one's existing belief (Wason's 2-4-6 task, 1960); A4 PDF of the whole book, colour (821 pages) A4 PDF, black and white (821 pages) Chapter 9 Intelligence: Theories, Measurement, Heredity and Environment In this chapter 9.1 What is intelligence? : compare the major definitions of intelligence and distinguish intelligence from aptitude and achievement. 9.2 From Galton to Binet: the birth of mental testing : trace the history of testing from Galton's anthropometric laboratory to the Stanford-Binet and the Army Alpha and Beta. 9.3 The IQ and the modern tests : calculate ratio and deviation IQs, describe the Wechsler, Stanford-Binet, culture-fair and Indian tests, and judge what IQ scores predict. 9.4 The structure of intelligence: factor theories : explain how factor analysis produced Spearman's g, Thurstone's primary abilities, Guilford's cube, fluid and crystallised intelligence and the CHC model. 9.5 Broader views: multiple, triarchic, PASS and emotional intelligence : describe the process and multiple-intelligence theories and weigh the evidence for each. 9.6 Intelligence, speed and the brain : summarise the information-processing and biological correlates of measured intelligence. 9.7 Heredity and environment : define heritability correctly and interpret twin, adoption and intervention studies, the Flynn effect and the debate over group differences. 9.8 The extremes: intellectual disability and giftedness : classify intellectual disability, explain the role of adaptive behaviour, and describe giftedness and savant syndrome. Weightage. 63 of the 819 questions mapped in this book (7.7%) test this chapter, 22 of them from real past papers. 1 of its 8 sections is High yield. In 1904 the French Ministry of Public Instruction had a problem that any Indian school inspector would recognise. The education laws of the early 1880s had made primary schooling free and compulsory, so every child in Paris now sat in a classroom, and some of them could not keep up. Which of these children were slow because they lacked the capacity to learn at the ordinary pace, and which were simply badly taught, mischievous, often absent or disliked by their teachers? Teachers' opinions were no help: the same child could be called "backward" by one teacher and "lazy" by the next. The ministry set up a commission to study the education of what it called "abnormal" children, and one of its members was a 47-year-old psychologist named Alfred Binet. Binet had spent years watching children think, including his own two young daughters, and he had become convinced that the measures then in fashion (reaction times, the sharpness of hearing, the size of the head) told you almost nothing about a child's mind. Intelligence, he argued, shows itself in judgement: in understanding a question, keeping a goal in mind and noticing your own mistakes. So, with a young physician named Théodore Simon, he did something disarmingly simple. They collected dozens of small tasks, tried them on children in Paris schools and institutions, and kept the ones that older children passed more often than younger children. The result, published in 1905, was a ladder of 30 tasks. At the bottom, a child had only to follow a lighted match with the eyes; near the top, the child had to explain how two abstract words differed or build a sentence around three given words. How far up the ladder a child climbed, compared with other children of the same age, was the measure. Binet was proud of the scale and wary of it. It was, he insisted, a practical tool for picking out children who needed special help, not a ruler that measured some fixed quantity inside the head. He prescribed "mental orthopaedics", classroom exercises in attention and self-control, to help slow children improve, and in 1909 he protested against "the brutal pessimism" of those who claimed that a person's intelligence is a fixed quantity that cannot be increased. Binet died in 1911. Within a decade his ladder had crossed the Atlantic and been turned into something he had warned against. In the United States it was used to label newly arrived immigrants as "feeble-minded", to rank well over a million army recruits, and to argue that intelligence is simply inherited and that whole nations were born less able. Remember Binet's two claims: that intelligence is complex and a test can only sample it, and that it can be raised. By the end of this chapter you will be able to judge, with a century of evidence in hand, how right he was. 9.1 What Is Intelligence? Lower yield · 3 Qs Everyone uses the word, and everyone believes they recognise intelligence when they see it: the classmate who solves a puzzle in seconds, the grandmother who keeps the household accounts in her head, the cricket captain who reads a match two overs ahead of everyone else. Yet when psychologists have tried to pin the word down, they have disagreed for more than a century. It is worth starting with the disagreements, because they shape every theory and every test in this chapter, and because examiners love to ask who said what. Definitions from Binet to the Experts Alfred Binet (1857 to 1911) put judgement at the centre: "to judge well, to comprehend well, to reason well, these are the essential activities of intelligence." He also called it good sense, practical sense, initiative and the faculty of adapting oneself to circumstances, and in 1909 he compressed it into four words: comprehension, invention, direction (holding a goal in mind) and censorship (criticising one's own attempts). Binet's view is sometimes classified as a unifactor theory , the idea that intelligence is one general, undivided capacity, because his scale produced a single overall level; the label is also attached to Lewis Terman and William Stern, whom you will meet in Section 9.2. In 1921 the Journal of Educational Psychology asked more than a dozen leading American psychologists to define intelligence. The replies varied revealingly. Lewis Madison Terman said it was the ability to carry on abstract thinking. Edward Lee Thorndike called it "the power of good responses from the point of view of truth or fact." Others stressed the capacity to learn or to adapt to relatively new situations. Two years later, exasperated, the Harvard historian of psychology Edwin Garrigues Boring (1886 to 1968) wrote that intelligence is "what the tests test." He was making a serious point about method. Until psychologists agree on a theory, the only definition anyone can check is an operational definition , one that defines a concept by the procedure used to measure it. The definition most often quoted in Indian examinations is that of David Wechsler (1896 to 1981): intelligence is "the aggregate or global capacity of the individual to act purposefully, to think rationally and to deal effectively with his environment." It is usually dated 1944, from the third edition of his book The Measurement of Adult Intelligence ; almost the same words appear in the 1939 first edition, so you may see either year. Notice the two key words. Aggregate means that intelligence is made of many distinct abilities; global means that they work together as a whole. That double view, many parts but one whole, is exactly how his tests are built: separate subtests whose scores are summed into one full-scale score. Sixty-five years after the 1921 symposium, Robert Jeffrey Sternberg and Douglas Detterman repeated the exercise, putting the same question to about two dozen experts and publishing the replies as What Is Intelligence? (1986). The overlap with 1921 was considerable: higher-level abstract reasoning, problem solving and the capacity to learn appeared in both. But the 1986 experts gave more weight to metacognition (knowing about, and controlling, one's own thinking) and to the culture that decides which abilities count as intelligent. Sternberg's own definition makes the cultural point explicit: intelligence is mental activity directed toward purposive adaptation to, and selection and shaping of, real-world environments relevant to one's life. Hold on to the three verbs adapt, select and shape; they return as the "contextual" part of his triarchic theory in Section 9.5. Finally, after the storm over the book The Bell Curve (Section 9.7), Linda Gottfredson drafted a statement signed by 52 researchers and published in December 1994. Its definition is the working definition most researchers use today: "a very general mental capability that, among other things, involves the ability to reason, plan, solve problems, think abstractly, comprehend complex ideas, learn quickly and learn from experience." It is, the statement added, "not merely book learning, a narrow academic skill, or test-taking smarts." What do these definitions share? Three themes recur: the capacity to learn from experience, the capacity to reason abstractly, and the capacity to adapt to the environment. Where they part company is on two questions. Is intelligence one thing or many? And how much of it can a test capture? Those two disagreements organise the rest of this chapter. Table 9.1 collects the definitions you are most likely to be asked about. Table 9.1 Classic definitions of intelligence. Who When Intelligence is ... Alfred Binet 1905 to 1911 Judgement, good sense, adapting to circumstances; comprehension, invention, direction, censorship Lewis Terman 1921 The ability to carry on abstract thinking Edward Thorndike 1921 The power of good responses from the point of view of truth or fact Edwin Boring 1923 What the tests test (an operational definition) David Wechsler 1944 (1939) The aggregate or global capacity to act purposefully, think rationally and deal effectively with the environment Robert Sternberg 1985 Mental activity directed toward adapting to, selecting and shaping real-world environments Linda Gottfredson and 51 cosignatories 1994 A very general mental capability to reason, plan, solve problems, think abstractly, learn quickly and learn from experience Intelligence, Aptitude and Achievement Three words are often used loosely, and examiners exploit the looseness. Achievement is what a person has already learned through a specific course of instruction; an achievement test, such as a Class 10 board examination in mathematics, looks backwards at the effects of known teaching. An aptitude is a capacity to acquire, with training, some specific knowledge or skill. Walter Van Dyke Bingham (1880 to 1952) defined it in 1937 as a condition or set of characteristics regarded as symptomatic of a person's ability to acquire, with training, some knowledge, skill or set of responses, such as the ability to speak a language or produce music. An aptitude test therefore looks forwards: it predicts how well someone will learn to fly, to type or to study engineering before the training begins. The classic battery is the Differential Aptitude Tests of George Bennett, Harold Seashore and Alexander Wesman (1947). Because they predict how well a student will do in different courses and careers, aptitude tests are central tools of educational and vocational guidance. Intelligence tests sit between the two. They sample broad abilities that schooling influences but does not directly teach, and they predict learning and problem solving in general rather than in one field. The boundary is fuzzy (a vocabulary subtest is partly an achievement measure), so the difference is best understood as one of breadth and purpose, as Table 9.2 shows. Table 9.2 Achievement, aptitude and intelligence tests compared. Type of test What it measures Time orientation Example Achievement Effects of a specific, known course of learning Past School board examination; reading attainment test Aptitude Potential to learn a specific skill with training Future, specific Differential Aptitude Tests; clerical or mechanical aptitude tests Intelligence Broad reasoning and learning ability Future, general Wechsler scales; Stanford-Binet; Raven's matrices Exam trap The Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale (WAIS) is an intelligence test, not an aptitude, achievement or attitude test. An attitude test measures a person's evaluative stance towards an object (the Social book). One paper (RML 2022) keyed the aptitude test as "the heart of the guidance programme". The standard phrase in guidance textbooks is that counselling is the heart of the guidance programme, so if counselling is offered, choose it; when counselling is not among the options, as in that paper, the aptitude test is the expected answer, because guidance decisions about courses and careers rest on it. The other usual options are guidance tools of a different kind: the case study is an intensive study of one person's history and circumstances, the interview is a face-to-face conversation to gather information and build rapport, and the cumulative record is a running file of a student's marks, test results, health and activities kept across the school years. Implicit Theories: What Ordinary People and Cultures Believe The definitions above are explicit theories , formal theories built by psychologists and tested against data. Ordinary people carry implicit theories of intelligence , beliefs about what intelligence is that guide how they judge themselves and others. In 1981 Sternberg and his colleagues simply asked people in a railway station, a supermarket and a college library to list the behaviours of an intelligent person. Three clusters emerged: practical problem-solving ability (reasons logically, sees all sides of a problem), verbal ability (speaks clearly, reads widely) and social competence (accepts others for what they are, admits mistakes). Laypeople, in other words, already included the social and practical abilities that the psychometric tests left out. Implicit theories also differ in a way that changes behaviour. Carol Susan Dweck (born 1946) distinguished an entity theory of intelligence, the belief that intelligence is a fixed quantity you either have or lack, from an incremental theory , the belief that it can be developed through effort and good strategies. In her popular book Mindset (2006) these became the fixed mindset and the growth mindset . Children who hold an entity theory tend to avoid challenges and give up after failure, because failure seems to reveal a permanent lack; children with an incremental theory treat failure as information and persist. Praise can push a child towards one theory or the other. In a well-known series of experiments with American fifth-graders, Claudia Mueller and Dweck (1998) praised some children for being clever ("you must be smart at this") and others for working hard; after a later failure, the children praised for ability chose easier tasks, enjoyed the work less and performed worse than those praised for effort. The mindset research therefore recommends praising effort and strategy, not innate ability. Large school studies of brief mindset interventions have found real but small average effects on grades, with larger effects for low-achieving students, so the idea is useful but not magic. Indian context The Indian-born psychologist J. P. Das (Section 9.5) has pointed out that the closest Indian word, buddhi , is broader than the Western test-based idea. It includes discrimination between right and wrong, self-knowledge, determination and feeling, not only speed and accuracy of reasoning. Studies of everyday Indian conceptions likewise give a large place to social competence, responsibility and wisdom. This is one reason a test built on one culture's implicit theory can misjudge people from another. Exam trap "Incremental" belongs to Dweck's entity versus incremental theories, not to Sternberg's triarchic theory, whose three parts are componential, experiential and contextual. Options such as "incremental" and "experimental" in a Sternberg question are bait. A "growth mindset" is the belief that intelligence is malleable and can be developed through effort. 9.2 From Galton to Binet: The Birth of Mental Testing Medium yield · 5 Qs Binet's 1905 scale is usually called the first intelligence test, and it was. But it was a reaction against an earlier attempt that had failed, and you cannot understand why Binet succeeded without knowing why his predecessors did not. Francis Galton and the Anthropometric Laboratory Francis Galton (1822 to 1911), a half-cousin of Charles Darwin, was fascinated by the fact that eminent men seemed to come from a small number of families. In Hereditary Genius (1869) he traced the family trees of judges, statesmen, scientists and poets and concluded that "natural ability" was inherited. (The obvious objection, that eminent families also pass on wealth, schooling and connections, did not trouble him much.) In 1874 he popularised the phrase "nature and nurture", in 1875 he proposed comparing twins as a way of separating the two, and in 1883 he coined the word eugenics for the programme of improving the human stock by selective breeding, an idea that later did great harm. How was natural ability to be measured? Galton followed the empiricist logic that all knowledge enters through the senses, so the people with the keenest senses and quickest reactions should be the most intelligent. At the International Health Exhibition in London in 1884 he opened an anthropometric laboratory (anthropometry is the measurement of the human body) where, for a small fee, about 9,000 visitors had their head size, grip strength, reaction time, visual acuity and highest audible pitch measured. To analyse such data he developed the ideas of regression and correlation, later put into mathematical form by his protégé Karl Pearson. For this work Galton is often called the father of differential psychology , the study of individual differences, and of psychometrics. He had, however, measured the wrong things. James McKeen Cattell and the "Mental Test" The American James McKeen Cattell (1860 to 1944) took his doctorate under Wilhelm Wundt in Leipzig and then worked with Galton in England. In an 1890 paper in the journal Mind , "Mental Tests and Measurements", he coined the term mental test and proposed a battery of ten: grip pressure, rate of hand movement, two-point touch threshold, the pressure needed to cause pain, the smallest noticeable difference in weight, reaction time to sound, time to name colours, bisection of a 50-centimetre line, judgement of a ten-second interval, and the number of letters remembered after one hearing. At Columbia University he tested entering students every year. The test of these tests came in 1901. Cattell's own student Clark Wissler correlated the scores of Columbia students with their college grades and with one another. The correlations with grades were close to zero, and the tests barely correlated with each other. If reaction time and pitch discrimination were measures of one underlying intelligence, they should have hung together and predicted academic success; they did neither. The sensory approach collapsed, leaving the field open for someone who would measure higher mental processes directly. Binet and Simon: Measuring Judgement That someone was Binet, working with the physician Théodore Simon (1873 to 1961; a few sources give 1872). Their approach differed from Galton's in two decisive ways. First, they measured complex functions (comprehension, reasoning, memory, judgement) rather than simple sensations. Second, they chose items empirically: a task stayed in the scale only if older children passed it more often than younger children, so success on the scale tracked mental development. Key study: The Binet-Simon scales (1905, 1908, 1911) Question. Could an objective test pick out schoolchildren who needed special education, without relying on teachers' impressions? Method. In 1905 Binet and Simon published 30 items arranged in order of increasing difficulty, from following a lighted match with the eyes to defining abstract words. In the 1908 revision they grouped the items by the age at which most normal children passed them (ages 3 to 13). A child's mental age was the age level of the items the child could pass (Binet's own term was "mental level"). A 7-year-old who passed the items typical of 9-year-olds had a mental age of 9. The 1911 revision, published the year Binet died, extended the scale into the adult range. Result. For the first time a single, standardised procedure could rank children's intellectual development. Conclusion and criticism. Binet regarded the score as a practical sample of performance, not a measure of fixed inborn capacity, and he warned against using it to label children for life. Those warnings were largely ignored once the test reached America. There is a footnote to this story that examiners enjoy. Around 1920 a young Swiss biologist named Jean Piaget worked in Simon's laboratory in Paris, standardising reasoning tests on Parisian children. He became less interested in whether the children got the answers right than in the systematic ways they got them wrong, and that curiosity grew into his theory of cognitive development (the Developmental book). So Piaget came out of the Binet tradition, but he did not create the first intelligence test. Across the Atlantic: Goddard, Stern and Terman Henry Herbert Goddard (1866 to 1957), research director of the Vineland Training School for "feeble-minded" children in New Jersey, translated the Binet-Simon scale into English in 1908. He grouped people with intellectual disability into idiots (the most severe), imbeciles, and a new category he named in 1910: the moron , from a Greek word for foolish, for people with mental ages of roughly 8 to 12. His book The Kallikak Family (1912) claimed to trace "feeble-mindedness" down two branches of one family, and from 1913 his team tested immigrants arriving at Ellis Island in New York, classifying many as feeble-minded on the strength of a translated test given through interpreters to frightened, exhausted travellers. These terms are now purely historical, but they appear as options in exam questions. Meanwhile, in Germany, William Stern (1871 to 1938) saw a problem with mental age. A child who is two years behind at age 4 is much more retarded in development than one who is two years behind at age 14. In 1912 he proposed dividing mental age by chronological age to give a "mental quotient", in German the Intelligenzquotient . Stern therefore coined the term and the ratio of the intelligence quotient (IQ) . It was Lewis Madison Terman (1877 to 1956) of Stanford University who made the IQ famous. His 1916 American revision of the Binet-Simon scale, the Stanford-Binet Intelligence Scale , multiplied Stern's quotient by 100 to remove the decimal and reported the result as the IQ: IQ = (mental age ÷ chronological age) × 100 This is the ratio IQ . Work two cases through. A 10-year-old with a mental age of 8 has an IQ of (8 ÷ 10) × 100 = 80. A 10-year-old with a mental age of 12 has an IQ of 120. A child performing exactly at age level always scores 100, whatever the age, which is what made the number so appealing. Terman's Stanford-Binet became the standard American test for decades, and Terman, unlike Binet, believed it measured an inherited capacity. Testing Goes to War: Army Alpha and Army Beta When the United States entered the First World War in 1917, Robert Mearns Yerkes (1876 to 1956), then president of the American Psychological Association (and the same Yerkes as the Yerkes-Dodson law of Chapter 10), led a committee, with Terman and Goddard among its members, that built the first large-scale group intelligence tests. The Army Alpha was a written, verbal test for recruits who could read English. The Army Beta was a non-verbal, pictorial test, given by demonstration and mime, for recruits who were illiterate or did not speak English. About 1.75 million men were tested. Group testing had arrived: one examiner could now test hundreds of people at once. The aftermath is a lesson in the misuse of data. In A Study of American Intelligence (1923) the psychologist Carl Brigham used the army results to rank immigrant groups, with northern Europeans on top, ignoring the obvious fact that recent immigrants scored lower the fewer years they had lived in the United States, that is, the less English and American schooling they had. Such arguments were cited in the debates that led to the restrictive Immigration Act of 1924. Brigham publicly retracted his conclusions in 1930. Table 9.3 gathers the milestones of this history, together with the later tests you will meet in Section 9.3. Clinical link The Ellis Island and army episodes are the origin of three rules every clinical psychologist follows: test a person in a language and format they understand, interpret the score against norms from a comparable population, and never treat a single score as a verdict on a person's worth or future. In India, with its many languages and very unequal schooling, these rules decide which test you choose (Section 9.3). Table 9.3 Milestones in the measurement of intelligence. Year Who Milestone 1869 Francis Galton Hereditary Genius : ability runs in families 1884 Francis Galton Anthropometric laboratory, London: sensory and motor measures 1890 James McKeen Cattell Coins "mental test" 1901 Clark Wissler Cattell's tests fail to predict college grades 1904 Charles Spearman General factor g (Section 9.4) 1905 Alfred Binet and Théodore Simon First intelligence scale: 30 items; revised 1908 (mental age) and 1911 1908 Henry Goddard English translation of the Binet-Simon scale 1912 William Stern Intelligence quotient: mental age divided by chronological age 1916 Lewis Terman Stanford-Binet; IQ multiplied by 100 1917 Robert Yerkes Army Alpha (verbal) and Army Beta (non-verbal) group tests 1938 John Raven Standard Progressive Matrices 1939 David Wechsler Wechsler-Bellevue scale; deviation IQ 1955 David Wechsler Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale (WAIS) 2003 Gale Roid Stanford-Binet, fifth edition (SB5) 2008 Pearson WAIS-IV, with four index scores Exam trap Stern versus Terman. William Stern coined "intelligence quotient" (1912); Terman multiplied it by 100 and popularised it in the Stanford-Binet (1916). "Who invented the term IQ?" is Stern. Two Cattells. James McKeen Cattell coined "mental test" (1890); Raymond Bernard Cattell, unrelated and a generation later, gave us fluid and crystallised intelligence, the Culture Fair Intelligence Test and the 16PF. Galton versus Binet. Galton founded the study of individual differences and ran the first mental-measurement laboratory; Binet (with Simon) built the first practical intelligence test. Alpha versus Beta. Alpha is for the literate (verbal); Beta is for the illiterate (non-verbal). 9.3 The IQ and the Modern Tests High yield · 32 Qs The ratio IQ had a fatal flaw, and the way it was fixed gave us the IQ we use today. To see the flaw, push an adult through the formula. From Ratio IQ to Deviation IQ Mental age grows quickly in childhood, slows in adolescence and stops growing in the mid to late teens. Chronological age keeps climbing. Take a perfectly ordinary 40-year-old whose mental age, like that of most adults, levelled off at about 16: the ratio formula gives (16 ÷ 40) × 100 = 40, a score that would label an average adult as severely impaired. Terman patched the problem by treating every adult as if he or she were about 16 years old, but the patch hid a second flaw. Even in childhood, the spread of ratio IQs differs from age to age, so an IQ of 115 might put a 6-year-old in a different position relative to his age-mates than a 12-year-old with the same number. A score that means different things at different ages is a poor score. David Wechsler's solution, introduced with the Wechsler-Bellevue Intelligence Scale in 1939, was to abandon mental age altogether. A person's raw score is compared with the scores of a large, representative sample of people of the same age (the norms ), and the IQ simply reports how far above or below the average of that age group the person falls. This is the deviation IQ ; because it is a standard score, some books call it the "standard IQ". The mean of every age group is set at 100 and the standard deviation (SD) , the typical distance of scores from the mean, is set at 15. In formula form, if z is the number of standard deviations a person scores above or below the age-group mean (a z score ): deviation IQ = 100 + 15 z A 40-year-old who scores exactly at the mean of 40-year-olds gets 100; one who scores one standard deviation above them gets 115. The meaning of 115 is now the same at every age: better than about 84 per cent of one's age-mates. Study guides sometimes describe Wechsler's method as "the actual score divided by the expected mean score for the person's age"; that is a loose way of saying the same thing, that the person is compared with the expected performance of his or her own age group, and if you meet that wording as an option, it is the one intended. Other standard scores work the same way with different numbers: the T score used by many personality and neuropsychological tests has a mean of 50 and an SD of 10, and the Wechsler subtest scaled scores have a mean of 10 and an SD of 3. A percentile rank is different again; it is not a standard score but simply the percentage of the norm group scoring below a person. Because IQ scores are approximately normally distributed, the familiar properties of the normal curve let you translate any IQ into a percentile, the percentage of people scoring below it. Now an older Stanford-Binet style question: on a test with a mean of 100 and an SD of 16, a person scores 136. Then z = (136 − 100) ÷ 16 = 2.25, and the normal-curve table gives about 0.987 of the area below z = 2.25, so about 98.7 per cent of people score lower. The SD matters. The Stanford-Binet adopted the deviation IQ in its 1960 revision (Form L-M) with an SD of 16, kept 16 in the fourth edition (1986), and moved to 15, in line with the Wechsler scales, only in the fifth edition (2003). Always check which SD a question gives you. Exam trap Ratio IQ = (MA ÷ CA) × 100, from Stern (1912) and Terman (1916); the original Stanford-Binet used it. Deviation IQ is a standard score with mean 100 and SD 15, comparing a person with same-age peers; Wechsler introduced it in 1939, and modern tests (including the SB5) use it. The deviation IQ is not "only for adults", it does not use raw scores without standardisation, and the ratio IQ is not the more reliable of the two (its meaning shifts from age to age, which is why it was abandoned). The old Stanford-Binet SD was 16, not 15. The Wechsler Scales Wechsler, a Romanian-born American who had tested army recruits in 1918, was chief psychologist at Bellevue Psychiatric Hospital in New York when he built his first scale. He set out to correct several faults he saw in the Stanford-Binet: it was designed for children, so its items had little appeal for adults; it leaned heavily on verbal, word-manipulation tasks; it placed too much weight on speed; and it rested on the concept of mental age, which made no sense for adults. His answer had four features that still define the Wechsler tests. They are point scales rather than age scales : items are grouped by type into subtests, and points are earned within each subtest, rather than items being grouped by the age at which they are passed, as in Binet's ladder. They combine verbal subtests with non-verbal performance tests (block designs, picture puzzles) that require little or no language. They yield subtest and part scores as well as a total, so a clinician can see a profile of strengths and weaknesses. And they use the deviation IQ. The family has grown with every generation (Table 9.4). Until the 2000s each test produced a Verbal IQ , a Performance IQ and a Full Scale IQ (FSIQ) . The newer editions replaced the verbal-performance split with index scores built on factor-analytic research (Section 9.4). Table 9.4 The Wechsler family of intelligence scales.
