Watch the invented baits: "ventromedial hippocampus " and "lateral thalamus " do not exist as hunger centres. The cerebrum and basal ganglia are not hunger centres either. The hypothalamus as a whole is the body's master homeostatic regulator (hunger, thirst, temperature, circadian rhythm via the SCN, and control of the pituitary); the cerebellum coordinates movement and the pineal gland secretes melatonin. One paper (Amity 2023) keyed "regulation of emotions" as the function of the limbic system rather than "both emotions and hunger and thirst"; classical textbooks treat the hypothalamus (hunger, thirst) as closely linked to the limbic system, so read the options carefully, but expect "emotion" as the limbic answer. Hunger and satiety signals The body tells the brain about its energy state through chemical messengers. In 1950 a spontaneous mutation in a mouse colony at the Jackson Laboratory in Maine produced ob/ob mice , which eat excessively and weigh up to three times as much as normal mice. In 1994 Jeffrey Friedman and his colleagues identified the missing product of the ob gene: a hormone released by fat cells, which they named leptin (from the Greek leptos , thin). Leptin signals the size of the body's fat stores to the hypothalamus and, in normal animals, reduces eating; injecting it into ob/ob mice made them eat less and lose weight. Hopes that leptin would cure human obesity faded, however, because most obese people already have high leptin levels and seem to be resistant to it. The pancreatic hormone insulin plays a similar long-term signalling role. In the short term, ghrelin , a hormone released mainly by the empty stomach (identified in 1999), rises before meals and promotes hunger, while gut peptides such as cholecystokinin (CCK), released from the intestine as food arrives, promote satiety (Gibbs, Young and Smith showed in 1973 that injecting CCK reduced meal size in rats). Satiety also depends on variety. In sensory-specific satiety , the pleasure of a particular food falls as you eat it, while the pleasure of other foods is barely affected; this is why there is always room for dessert, and why rats offered a varied "cafeteria diet" of tasty foods eat far more and grow obese. External cues, dieting and eating disorders If eating were controlled only by internal signals, the clock on the wall would not matter. Stanley Schachter (1922 to 1997) of Columbia University suspected that it does matter, and that it matters more for some people. His externality hypothesis (1968 to 1971) proposed that obese people are unusually responsive to external food cues (the sight, smell and taste of food, the time of day) and relatively insensitive to internal cues of hunger and fullness. In one study by Schachter and Larry Gross (1968), participants worked in a room with a rigged clock; obese participants ate more crackers when the clock showed that it was past dinner time than when it showed an earlier hour, while normal-weight participants were little affected. Obese participants also ate more when more food was visible and ate less when the food took effort to get. Later research, summarised by Judith Rodin in 1981, showed that responsiveness to external cues is found at all body weights and does not on its own explain obesity, but the idea that environmental cues drive eating survives in the positive-incentive view. Peter Herman and Janet Polivy added the concept of restrained eating : chronic dieters who control their intake by willpower rather than by internal cues. In a classic 1975 study by Herman and Deborah Mack, restrained eaters who were first required to drink a milkshake then ate more ice cream in a "taste test" than restrained eaters who had not, as if, once the diet was "broken", there was no reason to hold back. Obesity (a body mass index of 30 or above), anorexia nervosa (restriction of intake leading to significantly low weight, with an intense fear of gaining weight) and bulimia nervosa (recurrent binge eating with compensatory behaviours such as vomiting) are disorders of this motivational system; their diagnosis and treatment are covered in the Psychiatric Disorders book. Thirst Water makes up more than half of body weight, and two different kinds of loss produce thirst. The first, osmotic thirst , arises when the fluid outside the cells becomes too salty (after a salty meal, or when water is lost through sweating). Water then moves out of the cells by osmosis, and the cells shrink. Specialised neurons called osmoreceptors , in a region at the front of the hypothalamus (the organum vasculosum of the lamina terminalis), detect the change and trigger both thirst and the release of vasopressin (antidiuretic hormone) from the posterior pituitary, which makes the kidneys conserve water. The second, hypovolaemic thirst , arises when the volume of blood and other extracellular fluid falls, as after bleeding, diarrhoea or vomiting, even if its saltiness is unchanged. Receptors in the heart and large blood vessels detect the drop in pressure, and the kidneys release renin, which leads to the formation of angiotensin II ; angiotensin acts on the brain (the subfornical organ) to produce thirst and also an appetite for salt, which is needed to restore volume. Drinking usually stops long before the water has been absorbed, because signals from the mouth, stomach and intestines meter the intake. Cannon had proposed that thirst is simply a dry mouth, but wetting the mouth does not abolish thirst for long, and the theory failed for much the same reason as his stomach theory of hunger. Sexual motivation Sex is classed as a primary motive, yet it differs from hunger and thirst in a fundamental way: no tissue is depleted when it is unsatisfied, and no individual dies for lack of it. It serves the survival of the species rather than of the individual, and in human beings it is shaped heavily by learning, culture and relationships. Scientific study of human sexual behaviour began with surveys. Alfred Charles Kinsey (1894 to 1956), a zoologist at Indiana University who had spent years classifying gall wasps, turned the same taxonomic zeal on human sexuality. Kinsey and his colleagues interviewed thousands of Americans and published Sexual Behavior in the Human Male (1948) and Sexual Behavior in the Human Female (1953), together known as the Kinsey reports . They shocked the public by showing that practices officially condemned, such as premarital and extramarital sex and homosexual experience, were far commoner than anyone had admitted. Kinsey described sexual orientation not as two boxes but as a continuum, the Kinsey scale, from 0 (exclusively heterosexual) to 6 (exclusively homosexual). His samples were volunteers rather than random samples, a weakness critics stressed. Where Kinsey asked people what they did, William Howell Masters (1915 to 2001), a gynaecologist, and Virginia Eshelman Johnson (1925 to 2013) observed it directly. In their laboratory in St. Louis they recorded the physiological responses of several hundred volunteers (382 women and 312 men) during thousands of sexual response cycles and reported the results in Human Sexual Response (1966). They described a four-phase sexual response cycle : excitement (rising arousal, with engorgement of the genitals with blood, erection and vaginal lubrication), plateau (arousal levels off at a high level), orgasm (rhythmic muscular contractions and intense pleasure) and resolution (the body gradually returns to its unaroused state). Men enter a refractory period after orgasm during which another orgasm is not possible, while many women can have multiple orgasms if stimulation continues. Their second book, Human Sexual Inadequacy (1970), launched modern sex therapy. The New York sex therapist Helen Singer Kaplan (1929 to 1995) noticed that many of her patients' problems began before excitement, with a lack of interest in sex. In Disorders of Sexual Desire (1979) she proposed a three-phase (triphasic) model: desire, excitement, orgasm . Adding desire as the first phase is the key difference between Kaplan and Masters and Johnson, and diagnostic systems later organised sexual dysfunctions by phase. Rosemary Basson later (2000) proposed a circular model of female sexual response in which desire often follows, rather than precedes, arousal and intimacy. Hormones matter, but less in humans than in other mammals. In many female mammals sexual receptivity is confined to the oestrous period around ovulation, when oestrogen is high. Testosterone supports sexual desire in both men and women, and castration in adulthood reduces but does not always abolish it. Hormones have organisational effects before birth, shaping the developing brain and body, and activational effects from puberty onwards, switching behaviour on (the Physiological book develops this). Exam trap Masters and Johnson: Excitement, Plateau, Orgasm, Resolution (EPOR, four phases, 1966). Kaplan: Desire, Excitement, Orgasm (three phases, 1979). Options that put desire into a Masters and Johnson sequence, or put plateau before excitement, or end with "refractory" instead of resolution, are scrambles. The reports on the sexual behaviour of men (1948) and women (1953) are Kinsey's , not Freud's, Anna Freud's or Karen Horney's. Maternal drive, pain avoidance and other biological motives How strong are the biological drives, compared with each other? In the 1920s and 1930s Carl Warden and his colleagues at Columbia University built the Columbia obstruction box : a rat was placed in a start compartment separated from a goal (food, water, a mate, its pups, or a novel area) by an electrified grid, and the experimenters counted how many times in a fixed period the rat would cross the grid to reach the goal. In Warden's results ( Animal Motivation , 1931) the maternal drive produced the most crossings, followed by thirst, hunger, sex and exploration: a mother rat would cross the shock grid to reach her pups more often than a hungry rat would to reach food. Maternal behaviour in rats is primed by the hormones of pregnancy and birth, such as oestrogen, prolactin and oxytocin, but it is not purely hormonal: virgin female rats left with pups for several days begin to build nests and retrieve the pups. In primates, Harlow's later studies of contact comfort showed how much the infant's own motive for attachment matters (the Developmental book covers attachment). Pain avoidance is a powerful primary motive that, unlike hunger, has no cycle: it is aroused by tissue damage and lasts as long as the damage does. Its importance is clearest in its absence: people born with congenital insensitivity to pain suffer repeated injuries, burns and joint damage, and often die young. The need to keep body temperature, oxygen supply and elimination in balance are further primary motives, usually satisfied so automatically that they become noticeable only when blocked. Sleep behaves like a drive too, building up with time awake and discharged by sleeping; its stages, rhythms and theories are covered in Chapter 5. 10.10 Motivation in Practice: Work, School and Clinic High yield · 7 Qs Motivation theories are tested hardest outside the laboratory: in offices and factories, in classrooms and in consulting rooms. This section applies the chapter's ideas to those three settings, and introduces the work-motivation theories that entrance papers ask about every year. Motivation at work In the late 1950s Frederick Herzberg (1923 to 2000) and his colleagues Bernard Mausner and Barbara Snyderman interviewed about two hundred engineers and accountants in the Pittsburgh area using the critical incident technique : each person described a time he had felt exceptionally good about his job and a time he had felt exceptionally bad, and what had caused it. The results, published in The Motivation to Work (1959), surprised them. The things that made people feel good were not simply the opposite of the things that made them feel bad. Herzberg's two-factor theory (also called motivator-hygiene theory) proposed two separate sets of factors, shown in Table 10.13. Table 10.13 Herzberg's two factors. Motivators (satisfiers): job content Hygiene factors (dissatisfiers): job context Achievement Company policy and administration Recognition Supervision The work itself Relationships with supervisor and peers Responsibility Working conditions Advancement Salary Growth Status and job security Herzberg's motivators are intrinsic to the work itself, and their presence produces satisfaction and genuine motivation. His hygiene factors are features of the job environment, and their absence or poor quality produces dissatisfaction; but improving them merely removes dissatisfaction, without producing positive motivation. The word "hygiene" was chosen deliberately: like clean water, good hygiene prevents disease but does not make you healthy. The opposite of satisfaction, in this theory, is not dissatisfaction but "no satisfaction", and the opposite of dissatisfaction is "no dissatisfaction". The practical recommendation is job enrichment : building responsibility, achievement and growth into jobs, rather than relying on pay and perks. Critics point out that the critical-incident method invites self-serving answers (people credit good events to their own achievement and blame bad ones on the company), and that pay can motivate as well as satisfy. Still, Herzberg's lesson that job satisfaction depends on both the content of the work and its environment is the answer examiners expect. Exam trap Herzberg's motivators are recognition, achievement, advancement, responsibility, growth and the work itself. Salary , benefits, job security, working conditions, company policies and interpersonal relationships are hygiene factors , which prevent dissatisfaction but do not by themselves motivate . "Job satisfaction depends on" work motivation and job environment (both, not either, and not disposition alone). Hygiene factors are not Maslow's self-actualisation needs; if anything they correspond to Maslow's lower needs, and the motivators to his higher needs. Herzberg asked what motivates; the next theories ask how motivation works. Victor Harold Vroom (born 1932), in Work and Motivation (1964), applied expectancy-value logic to the workplace in his expectancy theory , often called VIE theory. Motivational force depends on three beliefs. Expectancy (E) is the belief that effort will lead to successful performance ("if I work harder, I will meet my target"). Instrumentality (I) is the belief that performance will lead to outcomes ("if I meet my target, I will get the bonus"). Valence (V) is the value of those outcomes to the person ("I want the bonus"). The three multiply: Motivational force = E × I × V. Work it through for Priya, a sales executive in Bengaluru. If she is fairly sure that extra calls will meet her target (E = 0.8), confident that the target brings a bonus (I = 0.9) and keen on the bonus (V = 0.7), her motivation is 0.8 × 0.9 × 0.7, about 0.50. If her company has a history of not paying promised bonuses, instrumentality drops to 0.2 and her motivation falls to about 0.11, even though nothing about her effort or ability has changed. Motivation is highest when effort leads to performance, performance leads to rewards, and the rewards are valued. John Stacy Adams 's equity theory (1963, 1965) adds a social comparison. People compare the ratio of their outcomes (pay, recognition, promotion) to their inputs (effort, skill, experience, time) with the same ratio for a comparison person. When the ratios are equal, they feel equity. When their own ratio is lower (underpayment inequity) they feel angry and resentful; when it is higher (overpayment inequity) they feel guilty, although people tolerate this more easily. Inequity motivates its own reduction: a person may change his inputs (work less), seek higher outcomes (ask for a raise), distort his perceptions ("he deserves more; he has a harder job"), change the comparison person, or leave. If Ravi learns that Suresh, who joined at the same time and does the same work, earns more, equity theory predicts that Ravi's effort will fall, whatever his absolute salary. The most strongly supported work-motivation theory is goal-setting theory , developed over several decades by Edwin Locke (born 1938) and Gary Latham (born 1945), beginning with Locke's 1968 paper and summarised in their book A Theory of Goal Setting and Task Performance (1990). Its central finding is that specific, difficult (but attainable) goals lead to higher performance than easy goals, vague goals, or the exhortation to "do your best". Goals work through four mechanisms: they direct attention, mobilise effort, increase persistence and encourage the search for strategies. They work best under four conditions: when the person is committed to the goal, when there is feedback on progress, when the person has the ability, and when the task is not so complex that a demanding outcome goal causes panic (for complex new tasks, learning goals work better). Organisational writers later popularised "SMART" goals; the acronym is a management mnemonic, not Locke and Latham's theory. Two further ideas complete the picture. In The Human Side of Enterprise (1960), Douglas McGregor contrasted Theory X managers, who assume that workers dislike work and must be controlled, with Theory Y managers, who assume that workers seek responsibility and are self-motivated; the assumptions tend to be self-fulfilling. And J. Richard Hackman and Greg Oldham's job characteristics model (1976) identified five core features of motivating jobs: skill variety, task identity, task significance, autonomy and feedback. Exam trap Expectancy theory is Vroom (1964) ; motivation is highest when effort leads to performance, performance leads to outcomes, and the outcomes are valuable (not uncertain, difficult or negative). If rewards are guaranteed regardless of performance, instrumentality collapses and so does motivation. Goal-setting theory is Locke and Latham : goals should be specific and challenging , with feedback; vague, easy or feedback-free goals are the wrong options. Equity theory is Adams ; the two-factor theory of work is Herzberg ; ERG is Alderfer. Motivation in education Almost every idea in this chapter has a classroom application. The overjustification research warns against tangible rewards for activities students already enjoy, while cognitive evaluation theory suggests that feedback which informs ("your answer shows clear reasoning") supports intrinsic motivation and feedback which controls ("you must score above 80") undermines it. Attribution theory explains why students who attribute failure to low ability give up while those who attribute it to effort persist; in 1975 Carol Dweck showed that "helpless" children could be retrained to attribute failure to insufficient effort, after which they persisted longer. Dweck's later work distinguished students who hold an entity (fixed) theory of intelligence from those who hold an incremental (growth) theory, and showed that praising effort and strategy rather than ability encourages the latter. Achievement goal research contrasts mastery goals (to learn and improve) with performance goals (to look competent compared with others); mastery goals tend to produce deeper learning and more persistence after failure. Self-efficacy, built through mastery experiences such as graded practice papers, predicts both effort and results, and expectancy-value theory explains why a student works hardest at subjects he both expects to master and values. Finally, the Yerkes-Dodson law reminds teachers and students that a moderate level of exam arousal helps, while high anxiety harms performance, especially on difficult questions. Motivation in the clinic Disturbances of motivation run through psychopathology. Anhedonia , the loss of interest or pleasure, is a core symptom of depression, and avolition , a reduction in self-initiated purposeful activity, is a negative symptom of schizophrenia (both are covered in the Psychiatric Disorders book). Addiction can be understood through opponent processes and incentive sensitisation (Section 10.4), and treatments such as contingency management deliberately use extrinsic reinforcers (vouchers for drug-free urine samples) to compete with the drug. Behavioural activation treats depression by scheduling rewarding activities, on the reasoning that action can come before motivation and rebuild it. The best-known clinical method built directly on motivation is motivational interviewing (MI), developed by the American psychologist William Richard Miller (born 1947) in the early 1980s and set out with the British psychologist Stephen Rollnick in Motivational Interviewing (1991). MI is a collaborative, client-centred style of conversation for strengthening a person's own motivation to change. It assumes that people with problems such as harmful drinking are usually not "in denial" but ambivalent : they are caught in an approach-avoidance conflict about change, exactly as in Section 10.8. Confrontation tends to push them to defend the status quo. Instead, the counsellor expresses empathy, helps the client see the discrepancy between current behaviour and deeper goals and values, avoids arguing (originally phrased as "rolling with resistance"), supports self-efficacy, and listens for and reinforces the client's own change talk . Its core skills are summarised as OARS: open questions, affirmations, reflective listening and summaries. MI is often combined with James Prochaska and Carlo DiClemente's transtheoretical model of the stages of change: precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action and maintenance. The detailed technique belongs to the Clinical book; the motivational insight belongs here: people change most readily when change serves their own values, when they believe they can do it, and when they feel autonomous rather than controlled. The case of Harlow's puzzle-solving monkeys, revisited Go back to the rhesus monkey in Madison, pulling the pin, lifting the hook and swinging open a hasp with nothing behind it. In 1950 the most powerful theory in American psychology could not say what need was being reduced. You can now give several answers, and each comes from a different part of this chapter. The monkey was showing one of the general motives of Section 10.1, a manipulation drive that is inborn yet repairs no tissue deficit. A caged monkey with nothing to do is under-aroused, and optimal arousal theory predicts that it will seek stimulation, just as the students in Hebb's sensory-deprivation cubicles at McGill could not bear to go without it. Berlyne would point to the collative properties of the puzzle (its novelty, its complexity, the uncertainty about how it comes apart); Robert White would point to the satisfaction of having an effect on the world; Deci and Ryan would call it the need for competence. In the simplest language of all, the monkey was intrinsically motivated: the reward was the activity itself, exactly as it is for the toddler who opens an empty box or for you, finishing a crossword that nobody will ever check. Harlow's odd side observation, that bringing food into the test tended to disrupt the monkeys' smooth performance, has a modern echo too. Two decades later Edward Deci's paid puzzle solvers and Lepper, Greene and Nisbett's rewarded preschool artists showed that an expected external reward can crowd out an internal interest, and cognitive evaluation theory explained why: a reward that feels controlling shifts the perceived cause of the behaviour from inside the person to outside. One more thread runs from that laboratory. Harlow's doctoral student Abraham Maslow left Wisconsin convinced that motivation had to be studied at its highest as well as its lowest levels, and he went on to build the hierarchy of needs. So the small wooden board in Madison stands at a crossroads of the whole chapter. It marked the limits of instinct and drive-reduction theory, and it pointed the way to curiosity, competence, growth and the self. Chapter summary 10.1 What Motivation Is. Motivation (from the Latin movere , to move) is the set of processes that activate behaviour, direct it, set its intensity and keep it going; it is never seen directly but inferred as an intervening variable. A need is a physiological deficiency, a drive is the aroused psychological state the need produces, a motive is the broader and often learned state that directs behaviour towards a goal, an incentive is an external object that attracts or repels, and a goal is the end state pursued. Put in order, they form the motivational cycle: need, drive, instrumental behaviour, goal, relief. Primary motives (biological, unlearned and mostly homeostatic, such as hunger and thirst) are contrasted with secondary motives (psychosocial and learned, such as achievement, affiliation and gregariousness), with general motives such as curiosity and manipulation in between; Murray's viscerogenic and psychogenic needs draw the same line, and Allport's functional autonomy (1937) explains how a learned motive can outlive its origin. Intrinsic motivation is doing something for its own sake; extrinsic motivation is doing it for a separable outcome. The main families of theory are instinct and psychodynamic, drive and arousal, incentive and expectancy, humanistic, and cognitive. 10.2 Instinct Theories. An instinct is a complex, unlearned, species-specific and stereotyped pattern of behaviour. William James (1890) argued that human beings have more instincts than animals, not fewer. William McDougall (1908) made instincts, each with a cognitive, affective and conative aspect and each paired with a primary emotion, the prime movers of all behaviour in his purposive, hormic psychology, and later listed eighteen propensities. Freud's instincts ( Trieb ) have a source, aim, impetus and object; in 1920 he divided them into the life instincts (Eros, whose energy is the libido) and the death instinct (Thanatos, seen in war and aggression), with the id as their reservoir and cathexis as the investment of their energy. The ethologists Lorenz, Tinbergen and von Frisch (Nobel Prize 1973) described fixed action patterns released by sign stimuli. Instinct theory declined because naming a behaviour does not explain it, because the lists grew to absurd lengths (L. L. Bernard, 1924), and because culture and rearing (Kuo, 1930) shaped behaviour that was supposed to be inborn. 10.3 Drives, Homeostasis and Arousal. Claude Bernard described the constant milieu intérieur, and Walter Cannon named the body's self-correcting balance homeostasis (1926; The Wisdom of the Body , 1932), a negative-feedback system defending a set point. Woodworth introduced the word drive (1918), and Clark Hull's drive-reduction theory (1943) held that a need creates a drive and that any response which reduces the drive is reinforced; in his equation S E R = S H R × D × K × V, drive energises but habit directs. Secondary drives are learned, as Neal Miller's fearful rats (1948) and Mowrer's two-factor theory of avoidance (1947) showed. Drive reduction could not explain Harlow's puzzle solvers, Butler's window-watching monkeys, Sheffield and Roby's saccharin-running rats or the misery of sensory deprivation, which led to Hebb's optimal arousal theory (1955). The Yerkes-Dodson law (1908) describes an inverted-U relation between arousal and performance, with a lower optimum for complex tasks; Zajonc's drive theory of social facilitation (1965) applies the same logic to audiences; and Zuckerman's sensation seeking shows that people differ in the level of arousal they seek. 10.4 The Pull of the Goal: Incentives, Expectancies and Opponent Processes. Incentive theory holds that behaviour is pulled by external rewards rather than pushed by internal tension; Tinklepaugh's monkeys (1928) refused lettuce when they expected banana, and Crespi's contrast effects (1942) forced Hull to add incentive motivation (K) to his equation. Berridge and Robinson separated wanting from liking in their incentive-sensitisation theory of addiction (1993). Expectancy-value theories, from Tolman, Lewin's valences and Rotter's formula (1954) to Atkinson, Vroom and Eccles, make motivation the product of the expectancy that an action will succeed and the value of its outcome, so that motivation vanishes if either is zero. Solomon and Corbit's opponent-process theory of acquired motivation (1974) proposes that every strong emotional state (the a-process) triggers a sluggish opposing b-process that grows stronger with repetition, which explains tolerance, withdrawal and the exhilaration of the veteran parachutist; it must not be confused with Hering's opponent-process theory of colour vision. 10.5 Hierarchies of Need: Maslow, Alderfer and Other Lists. Humanistic psychology, the third force, emphasises free will and an innate tendency to grow. Abraham Maslow (1943, 1954) ordered human needs from physiological through safety, belongingness and love, and esteem to self-actualisation, with the principle of prepotency: unmet lower needs dominate and must be largely satisfied before higher needs take charge. The four lower levels are deficiency (D) needs; self-actualisation is a growth or being (B) need. Self-actualisers show metamotivation towards metaneeds (B-values) whose frustration produces metapathologies, they report peak experiences, and Maslow later added cognitive and aesthetic needs and self-transcendence. Goldstein coined the term self-actualisation. The theory has been criticised for its hand-picked sample, weak evidence for the ordering (Wahba and Bridwell, 1976), counter-examples and cultural bias. Alderfer's ERG theory (1969) reduces the levels to existence, relatedness and growth, lets several needs operate at once and adds frustration-regression. Other lists include those of Murray, Fromm, McClelland, Deci and Ryan, Glasser (whose five needs include power or achievement) and Frankl, whose will to meaning is the basis of logotherapy. 10.6 Psychosocial Motives and Achievement. Henry Murray's Explorations in Personality (1938) described about twenty psychogenic needs, manifest and latent, and the press of the environment (alpha press as it is, beta press as perceived) that helps or hinders them; the Thematic Apperception Test of Morgan and Murray (1935) was built to measure them. David McClelland scored TAT stories for the need for achievement (nAch), whose holders prefer moderate risk, personal responsibility and quick feedback, and added the needs for power and affiliation, all three learned; his Kakinada training studies tested whether nAch can be taught. John Atkinson's theory (1957) makes the tendency to approach success equal to Ms × Ps × (1 − Ps), which peaks at intermediate difficulty, so success-oriented people prefer moderate tasks while failure-avoidant people choose very easy or very hard ones. Matina Horner proposed a fear of success in women (1968, 1972), later reinterpreted as a reflection of cultural stereotypes. Building on Heider's attributions and Rotter's locus of control (1966), Bernard Weiner classified the causes of success and failure by locus, stability and controllability, and showed how each dimension shapes emotion and expectancy. 10.7 Intrinsic Motivation, Competence and the Self. Harlow's manipulation drive, Butler's visual exploration and Berlyne's curiosity (1960), aroused by the collative variables of novelty, complexity, surprise and incongruity, showed that organisms seek stimulation and knowledge for their own sake. Robert White (1959) unified these findings as effectance or competence motivation. Albert Bandura's self-efficacy (1977), a task-specific belief in one's capability built mainly through mastery experiences, is the motivational core of his social cognitive theory and its triadic reciprocal causation. Deci's Soma puzzles (1971) and Lepper, Greene and Nisbett's magic markers (1973) demonstrated the overjustification effect, in which expected tangible rewards undermine intrinsic interest. Deci and Ryan's self-determination theory (1985) proposes three innate needs, autonomy, competence and relatedness; its cognitive evaluation theory separates the controlling from the informational aspect of rewards, and its continuum runs from amotivation through external, introjected, identified and integrated regulation to intrinsic motivation. Csikszentmihalyi's flow is total absorption when challenge and skill are balanced, and Festinger's cognitive dissonance (1957) is a drive-like tension that motivates people to make their beliefs and actions consistent. 10.8 Conflict and Frustration. Frustration is the blocking of goal-directed behaviour, arising from environmental obstacles, personal limitations or conflict between motives; it differs from pressure, the demand to perform or conform, and from change. Kurt Lewin (1935) described approach-approach conflicts (the easiest to resolve), avoidance-avoidance conflicts (vacillation and attempts to leave the field) and approach-avoidance conflicts (ambivalence), and later writers added the double approach-avoidance conflict typical of real-life decisions. Neal Miller's gradients (1944, 1959) showed that both approach and avoidance strengthen near the goal but that avoidance is steeper, so the organism vacillates where the lines cross; Dollard and Miller's clinical rule is to reduce fear before increasing desire. Classic reactions to frustration are aggression (direct or displaced, as in scapegoating), regression (Barker, Dembo and Lewin, 1941), fixation (Maier, 1949), withdrawal and apathy, and defence mechanisms. The frustration-aggression hypothesis of Dollard, Doob, Miller, Mowrer and Sears (1939) was softened by Miller (1941) and reformulated by Berkowitz (1989) in terms of negative affect and aggressive cues. 10.9 Biological Motives: Hunger, Thirst, Sex and Others. Cannon and Washburn's swallowed balloon (1912) linked hunger pangs to stomach contractions, but people without stomachs still feel hunger. Glucostatic and lipostatic set-point theories gave way, in Pinel's account, to a positive-incentive view with a settling point for body weight. In the classic dual-centre theory (Stellar, 1954), lesions of the ventromedial hypothalamus, the satiety centre, cause hyperphagia and obesity (Hetherington and Ranson, 1940), and lesions of the lateral hypothalamus, the feeding centre, cause aphagia and adipsia (Anand and Brobeck, 1951); modern work has revised both claims and emphasises insulin, the paraventricular and arcuate nuclei, and signals such as leptin, ghrelin and cholecystokinin. Schachter's externality hypothesis and Herman's restrained eating show the power of external cues. Thirst is osmotic (cell dehydration detected by osmoreceptors) or hypovolaemic (loss of blood volume, signalled through angiotensin II). Kinsey's reports (1948, 1953) surveyed sexual behaviour, Masters and Johnson (1966) described excitement, plateau, orgasm and resolution, and Kaplan (1979) added desire. In Warden's obstruction box the maternal drive was the strongest; pain avoidance, temperature regulation and sleep complete the list of primary motives. 10.10 Motivation in Practice: Work, School and Clinic. Herzberg's two-factor theory (1959) separates motivators intrinsic to the work (achievement, recognition, the work itself, responsibility, advancement, growth), which create satisfaction, from hygiene factors in the job environment (policy, supervision, relationships, conditions, salary, security), which only prevent dissatisfaction; job satisfaction depends on both. Vroom's expectancy theory (1964) makes motivational force the product of expectancy, instrumentality and valence; Adams' equity theory explains reactions to unfair outcome-to-input ratios; and Locke and Latham's goal-setting theory shows that specific, challenging goals with commitment and feedback raise performance. McGregor's Theory X and Theory Y and Hackman and Oldham's job characteristics model complete the work picture. In schools, informational feedback, attribution retraining (Dweck, 1975), incremental beliefs about ability, mastery goals, self-efficacy and moderate arousal all support learning. In the clinic, anhedonia, avolition and addiction are disturbances of motivation, and William R. Miller and Stephen Rollnick's motivational interviewing (1991) resolves ambivalence by evoking the client's own reasons for change, often alongside Prochaska and DiClemente's stages of change. She knows there is nothing in the box. This is an example of: (RML 2024) (a) Intrinsic motivation (b) Homeostasis (c) Extrinsic motivation (d) Secondary motivation Answer: (a) Intrinsic motivation. The box is empty, so the only reward is the activity of opening it, which is what doing something for its own sake means (compare Harlow's puzzle-solving monkeys). Homeostasis would need a bodily imbalance to correct, extrinsic motivation needs a separable payoff such as a sweet or praise, and secondary motivation refers to learned social motives such as achievement or approval, none of which is being served here. The phenomenon of "gregariousness" has a: (RML 2022) (a) Social motive (b) Biological motive (c) Psychological motive (d) Personal motive Answer: (a) Social motive. Gregariousness, the tendency to seek the company of others, is classed with affiliation among the social (secondary or psychosocial) motives. "Biological" tempts only because McDougall listed gregariousness among his instincts; "psychological motive" and "personal motive" are not standard class names in the classification of motives. Which model asserts that inner forces largely beyond individual control drive human behavior? (RML 2025) (a) Cognitive model (b) Behavioral model (c) Humanistic model (d) Psychodynamic model Answer: (d) Psychodynamic model. Freud's model places the causes of behaviour in unconscious instincts and conflicts that the person neither sees nor controls. The cognitive model locates the causes in conscious thoughts and beliefs, the behavioural model in conditioning and reinforcement from the environment, and the humanistic model in free will and personal growth, which is the opposite of control by hidden forces. According to Freud, human beings are motivated by powerful 'innate forces' which are known as: (Amity 2023) (a) Needs (b) Drives (c) Instincts (d) Id Answer: (c) Instincts. Freud's word Trieb is conventionally translated "instinct", and he grouped the instincts into the life instincts (Eros) and the death instinct. "Needs" is the vocabulary of Maslow and Murray; "drives" is Hull's term (and a fair literal translation of Trieb , but not the classical answer); the id is the reservoir that holds the instincts, not the forces themselves. Deviations from homeostasis can create an internal state of biological and psychological tension. What is the best term for this state? (RML 2021) (a) Regulation (b) Drive (c) Dissonance (d) Equilibrium Answer: (b) Drive. In Hull's theory a departure from homeostasis is a need, and the aroused, tense state it produces is a drive, which energises behaviour until the need is reduced. Equilibrium is the balanced state that homeostasis restores, the opposite of tension; regulation is the corrective process (negative feedback), not the tension itself; dissonance is Festinger's tension between inconsistent cognitions, not a bodily deviation. The Yerkes-Dodson law states that between performance and anxiety, there is: (RML 2024) (a) Inverted-U shaped relationship (b) Curvilinear relationship (c) Linear relationship (d) M-shaped relationship Answer: (a) Inverted-U shaped relationship. Performance rises with arousal up to a moderate level and then falls, and the peak comes at a lower level of arousal for complex tasks (Figure 10.2). "Curvilinear" is true but less specific, so the precise inverted U wins; a linear relationship would mean that more anxiety always helps or always hurts; no two-peaked (M-shaped) version of the law exists. According to Zajonc's drive theory of social facilitation, the presence of others raises arousal, which strengthens the dominant response. This means an audience will MOST improve performance on a task that is: (Amity recall) (a) Novel and difficult (b) Easy and well-learned (c) Creative and open-ended (d) Performed for the first time Answer: (b) Easy and well-learned. On an easy or well-practised task the dominant (most probable) response is the correct one, so the extra arousal from an audience strengthens it and performance improves. On novel, difficult or first-time tasks the dominant response is more often an error, and on creative, open-ended tasks it is the obvious, stereotyped idea, so an audience tends to impair performance there. In Incentive Theory, motivation is primarily driven by: (RML 2025) (a) Intrinsic satisfaction (b) External rewards (c) Biological drives (d) Self-efficacy beliefs Answer: (b) External rewards. Incentive theory says behaviour is pulled by external goals, as Tinklepaugh's lettuce-refusing monkeys and Crespi's contrast effects showed. Intrinsic satisfaction is the core of self-determination theory, biological drives push from within in Hull's theory, and self-efficacy beliefs belong to Bandura's social cognitive theory. The same paper asked what drive theory explains motivation as a process to do: reduce physiological needs , not seek external rewards (incentive theory), set long-term goals (goal-setting theory) or increase social connections (affiliation). Which stage is characterised by realising your full potential according to Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs? (RML 2021) (a) Safety Needs (b) Social Needs (c) Esteem Needs (d) Self-Actualisation Needs Answer: (d) Self-Actualisation Needs. Self-actualisation, the top of the hierarchy, is the need to become everything one is capable of becoming. Safety needs concern security and order, social needs concern belonging and love, and esteem needs concern respect and achievement; all three are deficiency needs that must be largely met before self-actualisation takes charge. According to Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs, which need must be mostly fulfilled before an individual seeks esteem needs? (RML 2025) (a) Self-actualization needs (b) Physiological needs (c) Social belonging needs (d) Safety needs Answer: (c) Social belonging needs. The printed key gives (b). The level immediately below esteem is belongingness and love, so it is the need that must be mostly fulfilled just before esteem needs take over. Physiological and safety needs must be met as well, but they come earlier in the sequence and so are not the best answer to "before esteem"; self-actualisation lies above esteem and cannot be its precondition (see the Exam trap in Section 10.5). In Reality Therapy, developed by William Glasser, which of the following is considered one of the five basic genetic needs? (Real PYQ 2025) (a) Self-actualization (b) Power or Achievement (c) Collective Unconscious (d) Unconditional positive regard Answer: (b) Power or Achievement. Glasser's five basic needs are survival, love and belonging, power (achievement and recognition), freedom and fun. Self-actualisation is the top of Maslow's hierarchy, the collective unconscious is Jung's inherited layer of the psyche, and unconditional positive regard is one of Rogers's therapeutic conditions; none of them is a Glasser need. Viktor Frankl's concept of the "will to meaning," the fundamental motivational force in humans to find purpose in life, is central to which therapeutic school? (Real PYQ 2024) (a) Rational Emotive Behavior Therapy (REBT) (b) Logotherapy (c) Existential-Humanistic Therapy (d) Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) Answer: (b) Logotherapy. Frankl held that the primary human motive is the will to meaning, in contrast to Freud's will to pleasure and Adler's will to power, and built logotherapy on it. Existential-humanistic therapy (Rollo May, James Bugental) shares the concern with meaning but is not Frankl's school; REBT (Albert Ellis) disputes irrational beliefs, and ACT (Steven Hayes) trains acceptance and values-based action. McClelland's theory of needs proposes three acquired needs that drive behaviour. They are the needs for: (Amity recall) (a) Achievement, affiliation, and power (b) Safety, esteem, and self-actualization (c) Existence, relatedness, and growth (d) Autonomy, competence, and relatedness Answer: (a) Achievement, affiliation, and power. McClelland scored achievement, affiliation and power imagery in TAT stories and insisted that these needs are learned. Option (b) lists three of Maslow's levels, (c) is Alderfer's ERG theory, and (d) gives the three innate needs of Deci and Ryan's self-determination theory. Which of the following is NOT one of the three fundamental psychological needs according to Self-Determination Theory? (RML 2025) (a) Autonomy (b) Competence (c) Affiliation (d) Relatedness Answer: (c) Affiliation. The three innate needs of self-determination theory are autonomy, competence and relatedness. Affiliation looks like relatedness, which is why it is the bait, but it is McClelland's learned need (nAff), not an SDT need. The same paper asked which SDT motivation is driven by internal rewards and personal growth: intrinsic motivation , not extrinsic motivation, not amotivation (the absence of motivation) and not external regulation (the least autonomous form of extrinsic motivation). Reciprocal causation model has been described under: (IHBAS 2020) (a) Social cognitive theory (b) Two-factor theory (c) Drive reduction theory (d) Constructivist theory Answer: (a) Social cognitive theory. Bandura's social cognitive theory (1986) rests on triadic reciprocal causation, in which personal factors, behaviour and environment influence one another. "Two-factor theory" names several other theories (Herzberg, Mowrer, Schachter and Singer, Spearman); drive-reduction theory is Hull's one-way chain from need to drive to behaviour; constructivist theory (Piaget, Vygotsky, Bruner) is a theory of learning in which learners actively build their own knowledge, not a causal model of motivation. Social Cognitive Theory highlights the importance of which factor in motivation? (RML 2025) (a) External rewards only (b) Biological drives (c) Self-efficacy (d) Goal difficulty Answer: (c) Self-efficacy. In Bandura's theory, belief in one's capability to carry out a task decides which tasks people attempt, how hard they try and how long they persist. External rewards do matter in the theory, but not "only"; biological drives belong to Hull; goal difficulty is the central variable of Locke and Latham's goal-setting theory. Who introduced the concept of "flow" in psychology? (RML 2023) (a) Carl Rogers (b) Abraham Maslow (c) Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi (d) Viktor Frankl Answer: (c) Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi. Csikszentmihalyi described flow (1975, 1990), the absorbed, autotelic state that arises when challenge and skill are in balance. Maslow's peak experiences are brief, ecstatic moments in self-actualisers, Rogers described the fully functioning person, and Frankl the will to meaning. Arvind is a college student who has strong negative feelings about smoking cigarettes. His grandfather died of lung cancer and he believes smoking is disgusting. One night at a party, Arvind's friends all go outside for a cigarette and he decides to smoke as well. What will he most likely experience as a result? (RML 2021) (a) Justification of efforts (b) Increased drive to smoke (c) Cognitive Dissonance (d) Drive Reduction Answer: (c) Cognitive Dissonance. Acting against a strongly held belief creates the tension Festinger (1957) called cognitive dissonance, which Arvind will be motivated to reduce, perhaps by telling himself that one cigarette at a party does not count. Justification of effort is a particular kind of dissonance reduction after suffering for a goal, drive reduction is Hull's account of satisfying a bodily need, and nothing in the story suggests an increased drive to smoke. If Ramesh works in a call centre, and has to work very hard, do a lot of work, and that too at a fast rate, he experiences: (RML 2020) (a) Conflict (b) Frustration (c) Unpredictability (d) Pressure Answer: (d) Pressure. Pressure is the demand to perform at a high level, quickly and well (or to conform to others' expectations). Frustration would mean that a goal is blocked, conflict that incompatible motives pull him in different directions, and unpredictability that he cannot foresee what will happen; Ramesh's problem is simply the demand itself. The 'satiety centre' of the brain is located in the: (RML 2024) (a) Lateral hypothalamus (b) Ventromedial hippocampus (c) Lateral thalamus (d) Ventromedial hypothalamus Answer: (d) Ventromedial hypothalamus. Bilateral VMH lesions produce hyperphagia and obesity (Hetherington and Ranson, 1940), so Stellar's dual-centre theory (1954) called the VMH the satiety centre. The lateral hypothalamus is the opposite, the feeding centre, whose destruction causes aphagia (Anand and Brobeck, 1951); "ventromedial hippocampus" and "lateral thalamus" are invented by changing one word. JEMAS 2025 asked the same question with the cerebrum and the basal ganglia as baits; neither is a hunger centre. Masters and Johnson's sexual response cycle is distinct from Kaplan's model. Which of the following correctly reflects Masters and Johnson's sequence? (IHBAS 2025) (a) Excitement → Plateau → Orgasm → Resolution (b) Plateau → Excitement → Orgasm → Resolution (c) Excitement → Desire → Plateau → Orgasm → Refractory (d) Desire → Arousal → Plateau → Orgasm → Resolution Answer: (a) Excitement → Plateau → Orgasm → Resolution. Masters and Johnson (1966) observed four phases in that order. Option (b) reverses excitement and plateau; options (c) and (d) insert desire, which is Helen Singer Kaplan's addition (desire, excitement, orgasm, 1979), and (c) also ends with "refractory", which is the male recovery period after orgasm, not a phase of the cycle. According to Herzberg's Two-Factor Theory, which of the following factors are considered motivators that lead to job satisfaction? (RML 2023) (a) Salary and benefits (b) Job security and work conditions (c) Recognition and opportunities for advancement (d) Company policies and interpersonal relationships Answer: (c) Recognition and opportunities for advancement. Herzberg's motivators belong to the content of the work: achievement, recognition, the work itself, responsibility, advancement and growth. Salary, benefits, job security, working conditions, company policies and interpersonal relationships are all hygiene factors: when they are poor they cause dissatisfaction, but improving them only removes the dissatisfaction without creating motivation. Job satisfaction depends on (JEMAS 2025) (a) work motivation or job environment. (b) only work motivation. (c) personal disposition only. (d) work motivation and job environment. Answer: (d) work motivation and job environment. Herzberg's research showed that satisfaction comes from the content of the work (motivators) while dissatisfaction comes from its context (hygiene factors), so the two together determine how a person feels about the job. "Or" and "only" make a single source sufficient, and personal disposition plays a part but is not the only determinant. In Expectancy Theory, motivation is highest when an individual believes: (1) effort leads to performance, (2) performance leads to outcomes, and (3) outcomes are: (RML 2025) (a) Uncertain (b) Valuable (c) Difficult (d) Negative Answer: (b) Valuable. Vroom's motivational force is expectancy × instrumentality × valence, and the third term, valence, is the value of the outcome to the person. Uncertain outcomes lower instrumentality, "difficult" describes the task rather than the outcome, and a negative valence repels. A second item in the same paper turned the idea round: motivation is highest when effort leads to performance and performance to desired rewards, not when rewards are guaranteed regardless of performance (instrumentality collapses), when effort is unrelated to performance (expectancy is zero) or when rewards are unimportant (valence is zero). In Goal-Setting Theory, what characteristic makes a goal most effective at motivating behavior? (RML 2025) (a) Being vague and flexible (b) Being specific and challenging (c) Being easy to accomplish (d) Avoiding feedback Answer: (b) Being specific and challenging. Locke and Latham found that specific, difficult but attainable goals, accepted by the person and accompanied by feedback, produce higher performance than vague "do your best" goals or easy goals. Avoiding feedback is wrong because feedback is one of the conditions that makes goals work. A parallel item in the same paper offered "unrelated to personal values" as a bait; a goal the person does not value wins little commitment, and commitment is another of the theory's conditions. High-yield sheet The facts this chapter's questions ask most, most-asked first. Last read before the exam. Abraham Maslow is the author of the hierarchical theory of motivation ("A Theory of Human Motivation", 1943; Motivation and Personality , 1954). Bottom to top: physiological, safety, belongingness and love (social), esteem, self-actualisation. "Ego" is not a level; it is Freud's. asked 5 times Henry Murray 's need-press theory ( Explorations in Personality , 1938) underlies the Thematic Apperception Test (Christiana Morgan and Murray, 1935): a projective test in which stories about ambiguous pictures reveal the teller's needs, conflicts and motives. asked 5 times The ventromedial hypothalamus is the classic satiety centre: lesions cause hyperphagia and obesity (Hetherington and Ranson, 1940). The lateral hypothalamus is the feeding centre: lesions cause aphagia, adipsia and weight loss (Anand and Brobeck, 1951). asked 4 times Sigmund Freud : the innate forces that motivate us are instincts ; war and violence express the death instinct , libido is the energy of the life instincts, the id is the reservoir of unorganised instinctual drives, and cathexis is the investment of psychic energy in an object. asked 4 times Frederick Herzberg 's two-factor theory (1959): motivators (achievement, recognition, the work itself, responsibility, advancement, growth) create satisfaction; hygiene factors (salary, security, conditions, policy, supervision, relationships) only prevent dissatisfaction. Job satisfaction depends on work motivation and job environment. asked 3 times Self-actualisation , the striving to realise one's full potential, is the top of Maslow's hierarchy; the term was coined by Kurt Goldstein (1939) and made famous by Maslow. asked 4 times Humanistic psychology , the third force of Abraham Maslow and Carl Rogers, emphasises free will, personal growth and an innate tendency to grow and reach one's maximum potential. asked 4 times Self-determination theory (Edward Deci and Richard Ryan, 1985) names three innate needs: autonomy, competence and relatedness (not affiliation). Intrinsic motivation, driven by internal reward and growth, is its most self-determined form. asked 3 times The Yerkes-Dodson law (Robert Yerkes and John Dodson, 1908): an inverted-U relation between arousal or anxiety and performance, with a lower optimum for complex or difficult tasks. asked 3 times Victor Vroom 's expectancy (VIE) theory (1964): motivational force = expectancy × instrumentality × valence, highest when effort leads to performance, performance leads to rewards, and the rewards are valued. asked 2 times Edwin Locke and Gary Latham 's goal-setting theory: specific, challenging (but attainable) goals, with commitment and feedback, raise performance more than vague or easy goals. asked 2 times A deviation from homeostasis creates a drive , a state of tension; Clark Hull 's drive-reduction theory (1943) explains motivation as reducing physiological needs. asked 2 times Albert Bandura 's social cognitive theory (1986) makes self-efficacy (1977) the key motivational factor and rests on triadic reciprocal causation of person, behaviour and environment. asked 2 times Rationalisation is an after-the-fact, socially acceptable reason for behaviour that was really driven by other (unacceptable or unconscious) motives. asked 3 times Leon Festinger 's cognitive dissonance (1957): acting against one's beliefs, like Arvind smoking at the party, creates tension that motivates a change of attitude or behaviour to reduce it. asked 2 times Viktor Frankl 's will to meaning, the primary human motive, is the basis of logotherapy. asked 2 times Masters and Johnson (1966): excitement, plateau, orgasm, resolution; Helen Singer Kaplan (1979) put desire first. The reports on male (1948) and female (1953) sexual behaviour are Alfred Kinsey 's. asked 2 times The hypothalamus is the master homeostatic regulator (hunger, thirst, temperature, control of the pituitary); its suprachiasmatic nucleus is the circadian clock. asked 2 times In Maslow's hierarchy the need immediately below esteem is belongingness and love (social belonging); RML 2025 printed "physiological" as the key. asked once Gregariousness , seeking the company of others, is a social (secondary, psychosocial) motive. asked once A toddler who works to open a box she knows is empty shows intrinsic motivation : the activity is its own reward. asked once Incentive theory : behaviour is pulled by external rewards, not pushed by internal drives. asked once Flow , total absorption when challenge and skill are balanced, was introduced by Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi . asked once Pressure is the demand to perform (work hard, fast and a lot, like Ramesh in the call centre) or to conform; it differs from frustration, conflict and change. asked once David McClelland 's three learned needs: achievement, affiliation and power. asked once William Glasser 's five basic needs: survival, love and belonging, power (achievement), freedom and fun. asked once Robert Zajonc 's drive theory of social facilitation (1965): an audience raises arousal and strengthens the dominant response, so it most improves easy, well-learned tasks. asked once The psychodynamic model holds that inner forces largely beyond individual control drive behaviour. asked once William McDougall ( An Introduction to Social Psychology , 1908) developed the instinct theory of motivation (hormic psychology). asked once In Hull's equation, stimulus-intensity dynamism (V) means a stronger stimulus makes the learned response more likely; incentive motivation (K) is reward size. asked once
