Hippocampus Declarative memory and context of fear Bechara and colleagues (1995) Cingulate cortex Part of Papez's circuit; emotional attention and pain distress Papez (1937) Prefrontal cortex Regulation of emotion, decisions, social conduct Phineas Gage (1848); Damasio (1994) Lie detection: the polygraph and the guilty knowledge test If lying makes people anxious, and anxiety shows in the body, then measuring the body should reveal lies. That is the logic of the polygraph (literally "many writings"), commonly called the lie detector, which records several measures of autonomic arousal at once: heart rate, blood pressure, breathing and skin conductance. The usual procedure is the control question technique . The examiner compares the suspect's responses to relevant questions ("Did you take the money from the office?") with responses to control questions designed to make almost anyone slightly uncomfortable ("Before the age of 25, did you ever take something that did not belong to you?"). A bigger response to the relevant questions is taken as a sign of deception. The problem is that the polygraph detects arousal, not lies. An innocent suspect accused of a crime is likely to react strongly to the relevant question simply out of fear of being disbelieved, so innocent people are often wrongly judged deceptive. Guilty people can learn countermeasures, such as biting the tongue or pressing the toes to the floor during control questions, which raise their arousal and mask the difference. Reviews of real criminal cases estimate the accuracy of the control question technique at not much better than chance, and a major review by the US National Research Council in 2003 concluded that polygraph testing is too inaccurate to be relied on for security screening. A better method changes the question. The guilty knowledge test (also called the concealed information test) does not try to catch a lie. Instead it presents details of the crime that only the guilty person would know, mixed with equally plausible false details, and looks for a consistent response to the true ones. In the classic study by David T. Lykken (1959), volunteers carried out a mock theft of a purse from an office. They were then asked, for example, "Where did we find the purse? In the washroom? In a locker? Hanging on a coat rack?" Using skin conductance alone, 88 percent of the mock criminals were correctly identified, and none of the innocent participants was judged guilty. Innocent people react to all the alternatives alike, because to them all are equally meaningless. Indian context Indian investigators have used polygraph tests, narco-analysis (questioning under a sedative drug) and brain-based tests such as the brain electrical activation profile. In Selvi v. State of Karnataka (2010), the Supreme Court of India held that administering these tests to a person without consent violates the right against self-incrimination under Article 20(3) of the Constitution and personal liberty under Article 21. They may be given only with the person's consent, and even then the results themselves are not admissible as evidence, although facts later discovered with their help may be. The judgement drew directly on the scientific doubts about such tests summarised above. Exam trap The limbic system is the classic "seat of emotion" , so when the options are "limbic system" versus one of its parts (hippocampus, thalamus, hypothalamus), choose the limbic system for a general question about emotional behaviour. Reject the reticular formation (arousal, wakefulness and attention), the pituitary (the "master" endocrine gland), the cerebellum (coordination and balance) and the corpus callosum (connects the hemispheres). Technically the limbic system is part of the forebrain, but "forebrain" is too broad to be the keyed answer. Amygdala, not hippocampus , for fear, aggression, threat detection, fear conditioning and the emotional enhancement of memory. The hippocampus stores the facts; the amygdala adds the emotional boost. The suprachiasmatic nucleus is the circadian clock, not an emotion structure. Lesion effects that are easy to swap. Bilateral amygdala (temporal lobe) removal produces Klüver-Bucy tameness, hyperorality and hypersexuality, not fear. Intense rage, attack posture and raised hair come from removing the cortex (sham rage) or stimulating the hypothalamus. Overeating and obesity come from damage to the ventromedial hypothalamus (Chapter 10). Severe anterograde amnesia "as in H.M." comes from the hippocampus and medial temporal lobe (Chapter 7). Cerebellar damage disturbs balance and coordination, and caudate nucleus (basal ganglia) damage disturbs movement and habit learning; neither produces Klüver-Bucy syndrome. A Klüver-Bucy option that includes "hyperalertness" or "avolition and alogia" is wrong: placidity, not alertness, and the "A" symptoms are schizophrenia's. Sympathetic arousal dilates the pupils. In an "odd one out" list of sympathetic effects (raised heart rate, lowered skin resistance, faster breathing, pupil constriction), the odd one is pupil constriction, which is parasympathetic. Heartbeat and breathing are paced by the hindbrain (medulla) ; the hypothalamus regulates them indirectly. If the question asks which division "modulates" involuntary heartbeat and respiration and offers hindbrain, that is the keyed answer. Papez circuit order: hippocampus, fornix, mammillary bodies, (mammillothalamic tract), anterior thalamus, cingulate gyrus, entorhinal cortex, back to hippocampus. The amygdala is not in Papez's original loop (some textbooks, Pinel and Barnes among them, draw it with the neighbouring structures); MacLean added it to the limbic system. Limbic system versus hypothalamus. When a question asks for the function of the limbic system, the keyed answer is the regulation of emotion (with motivation and memory as runners-up). Hunger, thirst and temperature are the classic functions of the hypothalamus, so an option such as "both emotion and hunger and thirst" was not keyed (Amity 2023), even though MacLean counted the hypothalamus as part of the limbic system. 11.5 Expressing and reading emotion Lower yield · not asked yet Darwin claimed in 1872 that emotional expressions are inherited and universal. For most of the twentieth century, however, the dominant view in the social sciences was the opposite. Anthropologists such as Margaret Mead and Ray Birdwhistell, the founder of kinesics (the study of body movement as communication), argued that expressions are learned like a language and vary from culture to culture. A smile in one society, they suggested, might signal something quite different in another. Who was right? Are facial expressions universal? The universality hypothesis states that certain basic emotions are expressed by the same facial movements, and recognised from them, in all human cultures. Ekman's first test, published with E. Richard Sorenson and Friesen in 1969, showed photographs of posed expressions to people in the United States, Brazil, Japan, New Guinea and Borneo, and found strong agreement about which emotion each face showed, especially among the literate groups. But literate people might simply have learned Western expressions from films and magazines. The decisive test needed people who had not. Key study: Ekman and Friesen among the Fore of New Guinea (1971) Question. Would people with almost no contact with outsiders recognise the same facial expressions as Westerners? Method. In the late 1960s Ekman and Friesen worked with the South Fore, a preliterate people in the highlands of Papua New Guinea who had seen no films or magazines and had little contact with Westerners. Through a translator, a participant heard a short story ("her friends have come, and she is happy"; "her child has died, and she feels very sad"; "she is angry and about to fight") and then chose which of three photographed faces fitted the story. In a second part of the study, Fore people were asked to show the face they would make in each story; their expressions were video-recorded and later shown to American students. Results. The Fore chose the expected face far above chance for happiness, sadness, anger, disgust and surprise. The one consistent confusion was between fear and surprise, which the Fore often mixed up. American students also recognised the Fore's posed expressions. Conclusion. At least six expressions are universal, as Darwin had argued. Criticisms. The forced-choice format can exaggerate agreement, the photographs were posed and exaggerated, and translation may have helped. More recent fieldwork in other isolated societies (for example, Carlos Crivelli and colleagues' 2016 study in the Trobriand Islands, where a wide-eyed "gasping" face was read as a threat rather than as fear) suggests that agreement is weaker than once believed. Further support for an inborn basis comes from people who could never have learned expressions by watching. Children born blind smile, cry and frown much like sighted children. In a neat natural experiment, David Matsumoto and Bob Willingham (2009) compared the faces of judo athletes at the moment of winning or losing a medal: congenitally blind athletes at the 2004 Paralympic Games produced the same expressions as sighted athletes at the 2004 Olympic Games. Display rules and cultural differences If expressions are universal, why do people from different cultures so often seem to express emotion differently? Ekman and Friesen's answer was display rules : culturally learned norms about which emotions may be shown, by whom, to whom and when. Display rules can lead people to intensify an expression (looking delighted with a gift you do not like), de-intensify it (looking only mildly pleased when you have beaten a friend), neutralise it (keeping a poker face) or mask it with a different expression (smiling to hide anger). At an Indian wedding, the bride's tears at her bidaai are expected and appropriate; at a funeral, laughter must be hidden; and many young people learn to mask anger in front of elders. The classic demonstration was Friesen's study of 1972. Japanese and American students watched unpleasant film clips of surgery and accidents while their faces were secretly recorded. When they watched alone, both groups showed very similar expressions of disgust and distress. When a higher-status experimenter sat with them, the Japanese students more often masked their negative expressions with polite smiles. The underlying expression was universal; its public display was governed by culture. The sociologist Arlie Hochschild extended the idea to work in The Managed Heart (1983): flight attendants, receptionists and call-centre staff must follow workplace display rules, smiling whatever they feel, and this "emotional labour" is a known contributor to burnout (Section 11.9). Culture also shapes how expressions are read. A meta-analysis by Hillary Elfenbein and Nalini Ambady (2002) found that emotions are recognised across cultures well above chance, but more accurately within one's own culture, an in-group advantage rather like understanding your own regional accent best. Rachael Jack and colleagues (2012) showed that East Asian observers rely more on the eyes, and Western observers more on the mouth, when reading faces; tellingly, a Japanese-style emoticon puts the emotion in the eyes (^_^) whereas the Western one puts it in the mouth :). Cultures also differ in which emotions they value . Jeanne Tsai has shown that North Americans tend to prize high-arousal positive states such as excitement, whereas East Asians tend to prize low-arousal positive states such as calm, a difference visible even in the smiles shown in children's storybooks. Measuring the face: FACS, the Duchenne smile and microexpressions To study expressions precisely, Ekman and Friesen published the Facial Action Coding System (FACS) in 1978. FACS describes any facial movement as a combination of numbered action units , each corresponding to the action of one or more facial muscles; for example, action unit 12 is the lip corner puller (zygomaticus major) and action unit 6 is the cheek raiser (the outer part of orbicularis oculi). Trained coders can describe any expression, real or faked, in these anatomical terms, without guessing at the emotion behind it. FACS is used in research on depression, pain, deception, infant development and animation. FACS made it possible to settle an old question: how can you tell a real smile from a polite one? In 1862 the French neurologist Guillaume-Benjamin-Amand Duchenne de Boulogne (1806 to 1875) stimulated the facial muscles of volunteers electrically and photographed the results. He noticed that a smile of genuine enjoyment involves two muscles: the zygomaticus major, which pulls the lip corners up, and the orbicularis oculi, which encircles the eye, raising the cheeks and producing "crow's feet" wrinkles at the outer corners. The zygomaticus is easy to control voluntarily; the outer part of the orbicularis oculi is not. A genuine smile, which Ekman named the Duchenne smile , therefore involves the eyes; a polite or forced smile (sometimes called a social smile) involves only the mouth. Look at the eyes of anyone posing for a photograph. When people try to hide an emotion, the true feeling may leak out in a microexpression , a full facial expression that flashes across the face for only a fraction of a second (roughly between a twenty-fifth and a fifth of a second) before it is suppressed. Microexpressions were first described by Ernest Haggard and Kenneth Isaacs in 1966 and popularised by Ekman's work on deception. A caution is in order, however. When people are tested on whether they can tell liars from truth-tellers, accuracy is disappointing: a large review by Charles Bond and Bella DePaulo (2006) found an average of about 54 percent, barely above the 50 percent expected by guessing, and professionals such as police officers do little better. Beyond the face: body, voice and gesture Faces are not the whole story. Posture, gesture, gaze, touch and the tone of the voice (prosody) all carry emotion. Pride, for example, has a recognisable display involving the whole body: a small smile, the head tilted slightly back, an expanded chest and the arms raised or the hands on the hips; Jessica Tracy and Matsumoto found the same display in congenitally blind athletes after victories. Indeed, when emotions are very intense, the body can be more informative than the face. Hillel Aviezer and colleagues (2012) showed people photographs of professional tennis players at the moment of winning or losing a crucial point. From the faces alone, viewers could not reliably tell winners from losers; from the bodies, they could. Some body language is culture-specific: a sideways head-wobble that signals agreement in much of South India can confuse a visitor who reads it as "no". Exam trap The "7-38-55 rule" is a misquotation. Albert Mehrabian's experiments (1967, 1971) found that when a speaker's words, tone of voice and facial expression conflict about feelings or attitudes (saying "I like you" in a hostile tone, for example), listeners rely more on the face (55 percent) and tone (38 percent) than on the words (7 percent). Mehrabian himself warned that this applies only to such inconsistent messages about feelings, not to communication in general. Gender differences in emotion Do women and men differ in emotion? The answer depends on which component you measure. On expression , the differences are reliable: women are, on average, more facially expressive and smile more than men. On recognition , women are on average more accurate at decoding nonverbal cues, a difference documented in Judith Hall's review of 1978 and many later studies. On experience and physiology , the differences are much smaller and less consistent; Ann Kring and Albert Gordon (1998), for instance, found that women were more expressive while watching emotional films but did not report experiencing more emotion than men. Most researchers attribute the expressive differences largely to socialisation and display rules ("boys don't cry"; girls should not show anger) layered on top of a shared emotional system, and they note that the stereotype of the "emotional woman" exaggerates differences that are modest and vary by emotion; anger, for example, is not more often expressed by women. Exam trap Ekman's universality research used the Fore of Papua New Guinea , not the Trobriand Islanders (Crivelli's later challenge) and not Mead's Samoans. The usual confusion in the Fore data was fear with surprise. Display rules govern showing emotions; they do not change the emotion felt. The Duchenne smile is identified by the eye muscle (orbicularis oculi); the zygomaticus alone gives a social smile. FACS codes muscle action units , not emotions. Scan Your Brain Fill in the blanks. The answers are below; cover them first. The division of the autonomic nervous system that dilates the pupils and dries the mouth is the division. The violent but undirected rage of a cat whose cortex has been removed is called rage. The loop of hippocampus, fornix, mammillary bodies, anterior thalamus and cingulate gyrus is the circuit. Paul MacLean coined the term system in 1952. Tameness, hyperorality, hypersexuality and psychic blindness after bilateral temporal lobe removal make up syndrome. LeDoux's direct pathway from the sensory thalamus to the amygdala is called the road. Damasio's idea that bodily "gut feelings" guide decisions is the marker hypothesis. The lie-detection method that tests for knowledge only the culprit would have is the knowledge test. Culturally learned norms about when emotions may be shown are called rules. A genuine smile that involves the orbicularis oculi muscle around the eyes is a smile. Answers: (1) sympathetic, (2) sham, (3) Papez, (4) limbic, (5) Klüver-Bucy, (6) low, (7) somatic, (8) guilty, (9) display, (10) Duchenne. 11.6 Four emotions up close Lower yield · 3 Qs General theories are only half of the story of emotion. Each emotion also has its own causes, functions and disorders. Four have attracted the most research and the most exam questions: fear, anger, happiness and disgust. Fear and anxiety Fear is the emotional response to a present, identifiable danger: the dog that is snarling at you now. It is intense, rises quickly, prepares the body for fight or flight, and fades when the danger passes. Anxiety is a more diffuse, future-oriented state of apprehension about possible threats: the worry, muscle tension and vigilance of the night before an exam. When anxiety has no particular object at all, it is described as free-floating . A useful distinction for the clinic, made by Charles Spielberger in his State-Trait Anxiety Inventory (1970), separates state anxiety (how anxious you are at this moment) from trait anxiety (a stable tendency to respond to many situations with anxiety). Both fear and anxiety are adaptive in moderate doses: they keep us away from cliffs and make us prepare for examinations. They become clinical problems when they are out of proportion to the real danger, persistent and disabling. A phobia is a persistent, irrational fear of a specific object or situation that leads to avoidance; generalised anxiety disorder involves continued, uncontrollable apprehension about many unspecified things; and panic disorder involves sudden surges of intense fear and a "fear of fear" (these disorders are covered in the Disorders book). Why are phobias of snakes, heights and spiders so much more common than phobias of electric sockets or cars, which are far more dangerous today? Martin Seligman's idea of preparedness (Chapter 6) proposes that evolution has prepared us to learn fears of the dangers our ancestors faced, and Arne Öhman's research shows that such fear-relevant stimuli are detected and conditioned especially quickly, partly through LeDoux's low road. The link between arousal and performance, the inverted U of the Yerkes-Dodson law, is discussed in Chapter 10. Anger, aggression and the myth of catharsis Three terms need separating. Anger is an emotion, a feeling of displeasure and antagonism, usually in response to a perceived wrong. Aggression is behaviour intended to harm someone. Hostility is an attitude, a lasting, cynical mistrust of and ill will towards others. You can be angry without being aggressive, and aggressive without being angry (a hired thug). The distinction matters later in this chapter, because it is hostility, rather than anger or the broader Type A pattern, that has turned out to be most dangerous for the heart. What should an angry person do with the anger? A long tradition says: let it out. The idea of catharsis goes back to Aristotle, who wrote that tragedy purges the audience of pity and fear; Sigmund Freud and Josef Breuer used a "cathartic method" in which patients relived and discharged buried feelings; and the ethologist Konrad Lorenz compared aggressive energy to water building up behind a dam. The catharsis hypothesis holds that expressing anger or aggression in a safe way, by hitting a pillow, shouting, playing violent games or watching violence, drains it and so reduces later aggression. It is one of the most popular ideas in pop psychology, and one of the most thoroughly disconfirmed. Key study: does venting feed the flame? (Bushman, 2002) Method. Brad Bushman first made participants angry: each wrote an essay and received a harsh evaluation from a supposed fellow student ("This is one of the worst essays I have read!"). Participants were then assigned to one of three groups. The rumination group hit a punching bag while thinking about the person who had insulted them (a photograph of the "evaluator" was shown). The distraction group hit the punching bag while thinking about becoming physically fit (a photograph of an athlete was shown). The control group simply sat quietly for two minutes. All then had the chance to blast the evaluator with unpleasant noise. Results. The rumination group was the angriest and the most aggressive; the control group, who did nothing, was the least angry and least aggressive; the distraction group fell in between. Conclusion. Venting while thinking about the provocation fed anger rather than draining it. Doing nothing at all worked better than "letting it out". Why does catharsis fail? Venting keeps the provocation in mind (rumination), rehearses aggressive responses so that they become more available, and keeps arousal high, which, as excitation transfer predicts, can be added to the next provocation. What does work is reducing arousal (relaxation, slow breathing, a time-out), reappraising the provocation (perhaps the other person was under pressure), distraction, humour, and assertive rather than aggressive communication. The theories of aggression themselves, including the frustration-aggression hypothesis, are covered in Chapter 10 and in the Social book. Happiness and subjective well-being For most of its history psychology studied misery far more than happiness. That changed in the 1980s, largely through the work of Ed Diener (1946 to 2021), whose landmark review of 1984 defined subjective well-being (SWB), the scientific term for what people call happiness. Diener's tripartite model says that subjective well-being has three components: a cognitive one, life satisfaction , a person's overall judgement of how his or her life is going; and two affective ones, the frequent presence of positive affect and the relative absence of negative affect . A happy person, in this sense, judges life to be satisfying and experiences frequent pleasant and infrequent unpleasant emotions. Diener and his colleagues measured the cognitive component with the five-item Satisfaction With Life Scale (1985). What makes people happy? Research has produced some surprises. Close relationships are among the strongest correlates of happiness; income matters a good deal when it lifts people out of poverty but much less once basic needs are met. One reason for the weak effect of good fortune is adaptation. According to the adaptation-level theory of Harry Helson (1898 to 1977), set out in 1964, we judge every new experience against a neutral point set by our recent experience, and that neutral point moves as experience changes. Philip Brickman and Donald Campbell (1971) applied the idea to happiness and called the result the hedonic treadmill : as our circumstances improve, our expectations rise to match, so that we keep running without getting any happier. In a famous study, Brickman, Dan Coates and Ronnie Janoff-Bulman (1978) found that lottery winners were not significantly happier than a comparison group a year or so later and took less pleasure in everyday events, while people paralysed in accidents were less happy than the comparison group but not nearly as unhappy as most people would predict. Later research has softened the treadmill: some events, such as long unemployment, widowhood or severe disability, can lower well-being for years, and people differ in how fully they adapt. A second reason is comparison. Relative deprivation is the feeling that one is worse off than the people one compares oneself with, whatever one's absolute position. The term comes from the wartime research of Samuel Stouffer and colleagues, published as The American Soldier (1949): military policemen, who had poor chances of promotion, were more satisfied with their promotion prospects than men in the Army Air Corps, who were promoted far more often, because the airmen compared themselves with the many colleagues who had been promoted faster. If you receive a ten percent salary rise at your Mysuru office, you are pleased, until you discover that your colleague received fifteen. Comparison even works backwards in time and possibility: Victoria Medvec, Scott Madey and Thomas Gilovich (1995) found that Olympic bronze medallists looked happier than silver medallists, because silver medallists compare themselves with the gold they just missed, whereas bronze medallists compare themselves with finishing without any medal. What are positive emotions for ? Negative emotions have obvious survival value: fear narrows attention and prepares escape. Barbara Fredrickson proposed in 1998, and developed in 2001, the broaden-and-build theory of positive emotions. Its first claim (the broaden part) is that positive emotions such as joy, interest, contentment and love widen our momentary "thought-action repertoire": they make attention and thinking broader, more flexible and more creative, and make us more open to people and ideas. Its second claim (the build part) is that, over time, these broadened moments build lasting personal resources, physical (health), intellectual (knowledge), social (friendships) and psychological (resilience, optimism), which help us cope with later adversity. Fredrickson and Robert Levenson (1998) also found an undo effect : after a fear-inducing film, participants who then watched a film evoking contentment or amusement recovered their resting heart rate and blood pressure faster than those who watched a neutral or sad film. (A later claim that flourishing requires a precise ratio of about three positive emotions to every negative one turned out to rest on faulty mathematics, and that part of the work was formally withdrawn.) Positive psychology, the movement launched by Martin Seligman in 1998, also studies how people make the most of good experiences. Savoring , a concept developed by Fred Bryant and Joseph Veroff (their book appeared in 2007), is the capacity to attend to, appreciate and enhance positive experiences. It is the mirror image of coping: coping manages bad experiences, savoring amplifies good ones. We can savour the past (reminiscing), the present (savouring the moment) and the future (anticipation). Bryant and Veroff described savouring processes such as basking (in praise or pride), thanksgiving (gratitude), marvelling (awe) and luxuriating (physical pleasure), and strategies such as sharing the experience with others, building memories, sharpening the senses and absorbing oneself fully. Lingering over the first sip of filter coffee on a cold morning, rather than gulping it while scrolling your phone, is savouring. Disgust Disgust is the emotion of rejection: in the words of Paul Rozin and April Fallon (1987), revulsion at the prospect of taking an offensive object into the body. Its facial expression, a wrinkled nose, raised upper lip and sometimes a protruding tongue, is literally the face of spitting something out, exactly as Darwin's principle of serviceable habits predicts, and its function is to protect us from contamination and disease. Disgust obeys what Rozin calls the laws of "sympathetic magic". By the law of contagion , anything that has touched a disgusting thing becomes disgusting itself: most people refuse a glass of juice into which a completely sterilised cockroach has been dipped. By the law of similarity , things that look like disgusting things are treated as disgusting: people avoid chocolate fudge shaped like dog faeces even though they know exactly what it is. Disgust develops late. Toddlers will put almost anything in their mouths, and a full adult sense of disgust appears only during the school years, learned largely from the reactions of others. Over development, disgust spreads outward from core disgust (spoiled food, body products, vermin) to animal-reminder disgust (death, wounds and anything that reminds us we are animals), interpersonal disgust (contact with strangers or the "unclean") and finally moral disgust at cheating or cruelty. Brain imaging shows that both feeling disgust and seeing disgust on another person's face activate the anterior insula. Clinically, heightened disgust sensitivity plays a part in contamination-type obsessive-compulsive disorder and in blood-injection-injury phobia. Exam trap Diener's tripartite model of subjective well-being is life satisfaction (cognitive) plus high positive affect plus low negative affect. Options that replace life satisfaction with "physical wellness", "spiritual wellness" or "social wellness" are distractors. Do not confuse it with Seligman's PERMA model (positive emotion, engagement, relationships, meaning, accomplishment) or Carol Ryff's six-part model of psychological well-being. Barbara Fredrickson = broaden-and-build (and the undo effect). Flow theory is Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi's; cognitive distortions are Aaron Beck's (and David Burns's popular list); psychodynamic theory is Freud's. Savoring (Bryant and Veroff) means enhancing and prolonging the enjoyment of positive experiences. It is not "avoiding negative experiences", "minimising stress through relaxation" or "reflecting on past traumas". Hedonic treadmill is Brickman and Campbell (1971), building on Helson's adaptation-level theory (1964). Relative deprivation began with Stouffer's The American Soldier (1949). The catharsis hypothesis predicts that venting reduces aggression; the evidence shows it usually increases it. 11.7 Emotional development and regulation Medium yield · 6 Qs Emotions are not fully formed at birth, and they do not run their course untouched once they begin. This section looks at how emotions emerge in infancy, and at how people of every age manage the emotions they have. How emotions develop John B. Watson, as you saw in Table 11.2, believed that newborns have only three innate emotional reactions: fear (to loud noises and loss of support), rage (to restriction of movement) and love (to stroking and cuddling). A more careful observational account came from the psychologist Katharine M. Banham Bridges , who, from observations of infants in Montreal, in 1932 described emotional development as a process of differentiation , like a branching tree. At birth, she reported, the infant shows only a diffuse general excitement . Within the first three months this splits into two broad states, distress and delight . Distress then branches into anger, disgust and fear in the following months, and delight into elation and affection; by about two years the child shows a wide range of emotions, including jealousy and joy. Modern research, using methods such as Izard's coding of infant faces, finds that differentiation happens faster than Bridges thought. By about six months infants show most of the primary emotions : joy, interest, surprise, sadness, anger, disgust and fear. The social smile , a smile directed at a human face, appears at about six to eight weeks, and wariness of strangers (stranger anxiety) at around six to eight months. A second group, the self-conscious emotions (embarrassment, pride, shame, guilt and envy), requires something more: a sense of oneself as a separate person who can be evaluated. Michael Lewis and Jeanne Brooks-Gunn (1979) showed that infants first recognise themselves in a mirror (touching a spot of rouge secretly placed on their own nose) between about 15 and 24 months, and the self-conscious emotions appear only after this, from about 18 months onwards; pride, shame and guilt, which require knowing the rules by which one is judged, become clear between about two and three years. Self-conscious emotions therefore appear well after 12 months. Infants also learn to use other people's emotions as information. In social referencing , a child faced with an uncertain situation looks to a caregiver's face to decide how to feel and act. In a classic study by James Sorce, Joseph Campos and colleagues (1985), one-year-olds crawled towards a "visual cliff" (a glass-covered drop) of uncertain depth while their mothers, on the far side, posed either a happy or a fearful face. About three-quarters of the infants crossed when the mother looked happy; none crossed when she looked afraid. Infants also expect emotional responsiveness from caregivers. In Edward Tronick's "still-face" procedure (first described in 1978), a mother interacts normally with her infant and then suddenly holds her face still and unresponsive; within moments the infant tries harder and harder to re-engage her, then becomes distressed and turns away. Even very young infants actively expect emotional give-and-take. (Temperament, attachment and the rest of emotional development are covered in the Developmental book.) Emotion regulation: Gross's process model From the first months, caregivers help infants manage their emotions by soothing, distracting and feeding them; gradually children take over the job themselves. Emotion regulation refers to the processes by which we influence which emotions we have, when we have them, and how we experience and express them. The most influential framework is the process model of emotion regulation of James J. Gross (1998). Gross pointed out that an emotion unfolds over time: we enter a situation, attend to some aspect of it, appraise its meaning, and then respond. We can intervene at each of these points, which gives five families of strategies (Figure 11.4). Consider a student on the night before an entrance examination. Situation selection : choosing which situations to enter. The student decides not to join the anxious group chat where everyone is comparing marks on mock tests. Situation modification : changing the situation one is in. When a friend keeps quizzing her on topics she has not revised, she asks him to stop. Attentional deployment : directing attention within the situation. She distracts herself with a walk, or concentrates on the topics she knows well. Rumination, dwelling on the feeling and its causes, is also a form of attentional deployment, an unhelpful one. Cognitive change : changing how one appraises the situation. The central strategy here is cognitive reappraisal : "This exam is a chance to show what I have learned, and there are other colleges if it goes badly"; or "My racing heart is my body getting ready to perform." Response modulation : acting on the emotional response once it has arisen. Examples are slow breathing, exercise, drinking, and expressive suppression , keeping a calm face while feeling panic inside. The first four families act before the emotional response is fully formed, so Gross called them antecedent-focused ; the fifth acts on the response after it has formed, so it is response-focused . The emotion unfolds from left to right Situation Attention Appraisal Response 1. Situation selection 2. Situation modification 3. Attentional deployment 4. Cognitive change 5. Response modulation Antecedent-focused strategies (1 to 4) Response-focused Figure 11.4 Gross's process model of emotion regulation (1998). An emotion unfolds from situation to attention to appraisal to response, and each of the five families of strategies acts at a different point. Reappraisal belongs to cognitive change (4); suppression belongs to response modulation (5). Are all strategies equally good? Gross's research compared the two most studied ones, reappraisal and suppression. In experiments by Gross and Robert Levenson in the 1990s, participants watched a disgusting film; those told to suppress their expressions showed less disgust on their faces but felt just as disgusted, and their sympathetic arousal actually increased . Suppression is effortful: later studies found that it also impairs memory for what happened during the suppression and makes conversation partners feel less connected. Reappraisal, by contrast, reduces both the feeling and the expression at little cost. Using the Emotion Regulation Questionnaire, Gross and Oliver John (2003) found that habitual reappraisers report more positive emotion, closer relationships and greater well-being, and habitual suppressors the reverse. Reappraisal can even improve performance under pressure: Jeremy Jamieson and colleagues (2010) told some students preparing for a graduate admission test that feeling anxious and aroused could help them perform; those students scored higher on the mathematics section than students given no such message. Clinical link Difficulties in emotion regulation run through many disorders: depression (rumination), anxiety disorders (avoidance, a form of situation selection taken too far), substance use (response modulation with a drug) and borderline personality disorder. Dialectical behaviour therapy, developed by Marsha Linehan, teaches four skills modules, mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation and interpersonal effectiveness, and cognitive behaviour therapy is in large part systematic training in reappraisal (Clinical book). Alexithymia: no words for feelings Some people find it hard to know what they are feeling at all. The psychiatrist Peter E. Sifneos (1920 to 2008) coined the term alexithymia in 1973, from the Greek a (lack), lexis (word) and thymos (emotion): literally, "no words for emotions". He had noticed that many of his patients with psychosomatic illnesses could describe their physical symptoms in detail but could not describe their feelings. Alexithymia is a personality trait rather than a diagnosis, and it has four features: difficulty identifying feelings and telling them apart from bodily sensations ("I feel sick" rather than "I feel anxious"); difficulty describing feelings to others; an externally oriented, concrete style of thinking focused on practical details rather than inner experience; and a limited fantasy life. It is usually measured with the Toronto Alexithymia Scale (TAS-20), and it is more common in people with psychosomatic complaints, depression, eating disorders, substance use, post-traumatic stress and autism spectrum conditions. For the therapist, it means that "How did that make you feel?" may draw a blank, and that helping the client label emotions is often the first task. Emotional intelligence If people differ in recognising and managing emotions, perhaps this is a kind of intelligence. Peter Salovey and John Mayer introduced the scientific concept of emotional intelligence in 1990, and Daniel Goleman's best-selling Emotional Intelligence (1995) made it famous. Goleman's popular model has five domains: knowing one's own emotions (self-awareness), managing one's emotions, motivating oneself, recognising emotions in others (empathy), and handling relationships; later he relabelled them self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy and social skills. Goleman's empathy domain deserves a closer look, because empathy is itself a part of emotion. Social psychologists such as Robert Baron and Nyla Branscombe describe it as having three distinct components. Emotional empathy is sharing the feelings of another person, feeling distressed when a friend is distressed. The cognitive component , sometimes called empathic accuracy or perspective taking, is perceiving accurately what another person is thinking and feeling. Empathic concern is feeling concern and compassion for the other person's welfare, the component most closely tied to helping (Social book). A clinician needs all three: accuracy to understand the client, concern to want to help, and enough control over emotional empathy not to be swamped by the client's distress. The ability model of Mayer and Salovey, the trait models, their measurement and the debate over whether emotional intelligence is really an intelligence are covered in Chapter 9. Exam trap Gross's five families, in order: situation selection, situation modification, attentional deployment, cognitive change, response modulation. Reappraisal is cognitive change , not response modulation; suppression is response modulation . Distraction and rumination are attentional deployment. Expressive suppression (Gross) is not Freud's suppression or repression. In Gross's sense it is hiding the outward expression of a feeling. In defence-mechanism language, repression is the unconscious, involuntary banishing of a thought or feeling from awareness, while suppression is the conscious, deliberate pushing of it out of mind. First emotions in infancy. In Bridges's (1932) scheme, the first differentiation of general excitement is into distress and delight . Watson's three innate emotions were fear, rage and love. Self-conscious emotions (embarrassment, pride, shame, guilt) appear after 12 months, from about 18 months, because they need self-recognition. Alexithymia (Sifneos, 1973) is difficulty identifying and describing one's own feelings; it is not the absence of emotion, and it is not anhedonia (the inability to feel pleasure, a symptom of depression). Goleman's five domains come in two wordings. The 1995 book lists knowing one's emotions, managing emotions, motivating oneself, recognising emotions in others and handling relationships; the later relabelling is self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy and social skills. A practice mock keyed the 1995 wording, so prefer it when both appear. Empathy's three components are emotional empathy, a cognitive component (empathic accuracy) and empathic concern; "behavioural aspect" and "positivity" are not among them. Brickman and Campbell's term for adapting to good fortune so that happiness returns to its old level is the hedonic . Feeling worse off than the people you compare yourself with is called relative . Fredrickson's theory that positive emotions widen thinking and build resources is the theory. Looking to a caregiver's face to decide how to react to an uncertain situation is social . Answers: (1) anxiety, (2) catharsis, (3) negative, (4) treadmill, (5) deprivation, (6) broaden-and-build, (7) referencing, (8) cognitive, (9) alexithymia. 11.8 Stress and the body's emergency systems Medium yield · 6 Qs Think back to the men on the Capilano bridge. For the minute or two it took to cross, their hearts pounded, their palms sweated and their blood carried a surge of adrenaline. Then they reached the far side and it was over. Now imagine a bridge that never ends: a threat or a demand that goes on for weeks, months or years. That is the territory of stress. Everything you have learned about the bodily side of emotion, the sympathetic nervous system, the hypothalamus and the amygdala, is also the machinery of stress. What changes is time. A system built for emergencies lasting minutes is asked to run for months, and the price is paid in health. What is stress? Three ways to define it The word is used so loosely ("I'm so stressed about Monday") that psychologists have had to decide what it should mean. Three answers have been given, and each one is tied to a research tradition you will meet in this chapter. The stimulus definition treats stress as something out in the environment: a demand or event that puts pressure on a person, as a load puts pressure on a bridge. A death in the family, an examination or a flood is the stress, and the research question is how much of it a person has faced. To avoid confusion, the event itself is now called a stressor : any event or circumstance that threatens, challenges or harms a person's well-being and so calls for adjustment. Holmes and Rahe's counting of life events (Section 11.9) is the classic stimulus approach. The response definition treats stress as what happens inside the person: the physiological and psychological reaction to a stressor. Hans Selye, whom you are about to meet, defined stress as "the nonspecific response of the body to any demand made upon it." Cannon's and Selye's work on the body's emergency reactions is the classic response approach, and some writers borrow the engineer's word strain for this reaction. The transactional definition , associated with Richard Lazarus, says that stress lies neither in the event alone nor in the response alone but in the relationship between person and environment. A situation becomes stressful when a person appraises its demands as taxing or exceeding his or her resources. The same viva voce examination is a crushing threat to one candidate and an exciting challenge to another. This is the definition most psychologists use today, and Section 11.9 develops it. Putting the three together, stress can be defined as the process by which we perceive and respond to events, called stressors, that we appraise as threatening or challenging. Stressors can be physical (cold, injury, infection, noise) or psychological (an insult, a deadline, a loss). One of the boldest claims of early stress research was that the body responds to both kinds in much the same way. Cannon: fight or flight and homeostasis Walter Cannon, whose attack on the James-Lange theory you met in Section 11.2, began his career at Harvard watching digestion with the newly discovered X-rays. He noticed that the rhythmic movements of a cat's stomach stopped dead whenever the animal was frightened or enraged. Over the following years he traced the reason. In Bodily Changes in Pain, Hunger, Fear and Rage (1915) he described how pain, fear and rage activate the sympathetic nervous system and the adrenal glands, which together prepare the animal for violent action. He called this the fight-or-flight response : an immediate, coordinated mobilisation of the body either to attack a threat or to escape from it. The heart beats faster and harder, blood pressure rises, breathing quickens and the airways widen, blood is diverted from the skin and gut to the skeletal muscles and brain, the liver releases glucose for fuel, the pupils dilate, digestion stops, and the blood clots more readily, which limits bleeding from a wound. Every item is a preparation for running or fighting (compare Table 11.5). The machinery behind this response is now called the sympathetic-adrenal-medullary axis (SAM axis). The hypothalamus activates the sympathetic nervous system. Sympathetic nerves act directly on the organs within a second or two, and they also stimulate the adrenal medulla , the inner core of the adrenal glands that sit on top of each kidney, to release adrenaline (epinephrine) and noradrenaline (norepinephrine) into the bloodstream. Because these hormones circulate, they spread and prolong the sympathetic effects throughout the body. The SAM axis is fast: it acts in seconds. Cannon also gave physiology one of its central ideas. He coined the term homeostasis in 1926 and popularised it in The Wisdom of the Body (1932): the tendency of the body to keep its internal environment, such as temperature, blood sugar and the balance of salt and water, stable within narrow limits (the motivational side of homeostasis, drive reduction, is in Chapter 10). Fight or flight is a temporary, deliberate departure from resting balance in the service of survival; when the emergency passes, the parasympathetic division restores it. Cannon even argued, in a famous essay on "voodoo death" (1942), that a person convinced of having been fatally cursed could die from a prolonged, unrelieved emergency reaction. Modern researchers add a third option that often comes before fighting or fleeing: freezing , the motionless watchfulness of a deer caught in headlights, organised by the periaqueductal grey of the midbrain (Section 11.4). Hence the modern phrase "fight, flight or freeze". Selye's general adaptation syndrome Cannon studied the emergency. The scientist who asked what happens when the emergency does not end was an endocrinologist working in Montreal, and he came to the question by accident. Key study: Selye's rats and "a syndrome produced by diverse nocuous agents" (1936) Question. In the mid-1930s Hans Selye (1907 to 1982), a young Vienna-born researcher at McGill University, was hunting for a new sex hormone. Method. He injected rats with extracts of ovary and placenta and examined their organs. Result. The rats showed a striking triad of changes: the adrenal cortex was enlarged; the thymus, spleen and lymph nodes had shrunk; and the lining of the stomach and intestine was covered in bleeding ulcers. Selye was thrilled, until he found that extracts of other organs produced the same triad, and so did a plain toxic chemical, formalin. His hormone had vanished. Then came the insight: perhaps he had found not a hormone but the body's general response to any damaging agent. He exposed rats to cold, heat, surgical injury, forced exercise and restraint, and the same triad appeared every time. Conclusion. In a short letter to Nature in 1936, "A syndrome produced by diverse nocuous agents," Selye proposed that the body reacts to all such agents with one nonspecific pattern. He later named it the general adaptation syndrome and brought it to a wide audience in The Stress of Life (1956). Criticism. The stressors were physical and often extreme, and the subjects were rats; whether psychological stressors in people work the same way had still to be shown. The general adaptation syndrome (GAS) is Selye's description of how the body responds to prolonged stress, in three stages that always occur in the same order: alarm, resistance, exhaustion (Figure 11.5). Stage 1. In the alarm reaction the body first recognises the stressor and mobilises against it. Selye described a brief shock phase in which resistance actually dips below normal (body temperature and blood pressure may fall), followed by a countershock phase in which the sympathetic system and the adrenal glands spring into action. The alarm reaction is, in effect, Cannon's fight-or-flight response. An overwhelming stressor can kill during this stage. Stage 2. In the stage of resistance , if the stressor continues, the body settles into sustained adaptation. Stress hormones, especially cortisol, stay high; resistance to this stressor rises above normal, and outwardly the person seems to be coping. But resources are being spent all the time, and resistance to other , new stressors falls. Selye's rats that had adapted to cold, for example, became unusually vulnerable to other stressors. Stage 3. In the stage of exhaustion , if the stress goes on long enough, the body's capacity to adapt, which Selye pictured as a limited store of "adaptation energy", is used up. Resistance collapses, signs of the alarm reaction return, and the organism becomes vulnerable to what Selye called diseases of adaptation : high blood pressure, heart disease, ulcers, kidney disease, arthritis and lowered resistance to infection. In the extreme, the outcome is death. In the alarm reaction, resistance first dips below normal (shock) and then rises (countershock). During resistance it stays above normal while the body adapts. If the stressor continues, resistance collapses in exhaustion and diseases of adaptation appear. The thick curve shows resistance; the labelled horizontal line marks the normal resting level. Selye also insisted that stress is not always bad. In Stress Without Distress (1974) he distinguished eustress (from the Greek eu , good), stress that is pleasant, motivating or beneficial, from distress , stress that is unpleasant and harmful. A wedding, a promotion, a hard-fought cricket match or a well-prepared examination can all be eustress; a bereavement or a long illness is distress. Whether a stressor is experienced as eustress depends on its intensity, on how long it lasts and, above all, on how it is appraised. Eustress is not the absence of stress; it is the optimal amount, the moderate arousal that the Yerkes-Dodson principle (Chapter 10) says helps performance. Pinel and Barnes note a biological echo: brief stressors actually strengthen some parts of the immune system (Section 11.10). How well has the theory lasted? Its central claims, that psychological and physical stressors can trigger the same bodily response and that long-lasting stress can make us ill, have stood. Three of its details have not. First, the response is less nonspecific than Selye thought. The American physiologist John W. Mason showed in the early 1970s that different stressors produce different patterns of hormones, and that when the psychological upset is removed (monkeys deprived of food but given flavoured, non-nutritive pellets, so that they were not upset by the deprivation), the usual hormonal stress response largely fails to appear. Emotional appraisal, in other words, is a key ingredient, which is exactly Lazarus's point. Second, Selye largely ignored the sympathetic nervous system; modern accounts give the SAM axis and the HPA axis equal billing. Third, exhaustion is now thought to come less from running out of hormones than from the damage done by prolonged exposure to them, as the next subsection explains. The HPA axis: the slower stress system The body's second stress system, the one whose effects Selye saw in his rats' enlarged adrenal glands, is the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis (HPA axis). It works in three hormonal steps. First, the paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus releases corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH, also called corticotropin-releasing factor). Second, CRH travels a short distance through a private blood supply to the anterior pituitary gland, which responds by releasing adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) into the general circulation. Third, ACTH reaches the adrenal cortex , the outer layer of the adrenal glands, and stimulates it to secrete glucocorticoids , the steroid hormones that help regulate glucose metabolism. The main glucocorticoid in humans is cortisol (in rats it is corticosterone). The level of circulating glucocorticoids is the most commonly used physiological measure of stress. The HPA axis is slower than the SAM axis: cortisol levels peak roughly 20 to 40 minutes after a stressor begins, and its effects last for hours. Cortisol raises blood sugar by making glucose from protein and fat, which fuels sustained effort; it damps down inflammation and immune activity; and it slows digestion, growth and reproduction, which can wait until the crisis is over. It also feeds back on the brain. Cortisol acts on receptors in the hypothalamus and the anterior pituitary (and the hippocampus) to switch off further release of CRH and ACTH, a negative feedback loop that works like a thermostat. In many patients with severe (melancholic) depression this feedback is weakened: given dexamethasone, a synthetic glucocorticoid that normally suppresses the body's own cortisol, their cortisol stays high (the dexamethasone suppression test is discussed in the Disorders book). The trouble is that the HPA axis was built for the zebra's problem, not ours. The neuroscientist Robert Sapolsky made the point in the title of his book Why Zebras Don't Get Ulcers (1994): a zebra's stress is acute, a desperate sprint from a lion that is over in minutes, one way or the other. Human beings switch on the same response for loans, traffic, deadlines and family quarrels, and leave it switched on. Prolonged high cortisol suppresses immune function, raises blood pressure and blood sugar, encourages fat storage around the abdomen and damages the hippocampus, which is packed with glucocorticoid receptors: chronic stress reduces dendritic branching and the birth of new neurons there and impairs hippocampus-dependent memory. Peter Sterling and Joseph Eyer (1988) called the body's active adjustment to demands allostasis ("stability through change"), and Bruce S. McEwen (1938 to 2020) named its cost allostatic load : the cumulative wear and tear on the body produced by repeated or chronic activation of the stress systems. Allostatic load is the modern replacement for Selye's stage of exhaustion. Table 11.7 sets the two stress systems side by side. Table 11.7 The body's two stress systems.
