The case of the Capilano bridge, revisited Go back to the men swaying above the Capilano River in 1974, and you can now say a great deal about what was happening to them. As each man stepped onto the bridge, his low road from thalamus to amygdala flagged the drop as dangerous before he had thought about it, and his sympathetic nervous system and adrenal medulla, Cannon's fight-or-flight machinery, set his heart pounding and his palms sweating. James would have said that his fear simply was the feeling of those changes; Cannon would have said that feeling and arousal rose together. Then a smiling woman appeared with a questionnaire. Here Schachter and Singer's two-factor theory does the work: a man aroused for one reason found a second, attractive explanation standing in front of him, and some of the arousal was labelled as attraction. Dutton and Aron did not rest on one field study, which had an obvious weakness (perhaps the men who choose a frightening bridge are simply bolder). In a laboratory experiment reported in the same paper, men who expected to receive strong electric shocks found a female confederate more attractive than men who expected only mild ones. The misattribution of arousal, and Zillmann's excitation transfer, have been part of emotion theory ever since. The bridge also illustrates the second half of the chapter. The crossing was an acute stressor, a few minutes of alarm reaction followed by recovery, and for many of the men it was probably eustress, the kind of thrill that tourists pay to experience. Whether a man felt threat or challenge depended on his appraisal and on his secondary appraisal of whether he could cope with the sway, exactly as Lazarus and Folkman would predict. Solomon's opponent-process theory would add that the relief on reaching solid ground was the b-process, and that a man who crossed every day would come to feel less fear and more exhilaration. And if the bridge had been a permanent condition of life, with no far side to reach, the HPA axis, allostatic load and the stage of exhaustion would have taken over from the brief, harmless surge that made a stranger's telephone number so appealing. Chapter summary 11.1 What is an emotion? An emotion is a brief, whole-person response to a significant event, with three components: physiological arousal, expressive behaviour and conscious experience (modern theorists add appraisal and action tendency). A feeling is the subjective component; a mood is longer, weaker and often objectless; affect is the umbrella term for good or bad states and, clinically, the observable expression of emotion (rated for quality, range and reactivity in the mental status examination); temperament is the inborn style of emotional reactivity. Basic-emotion lists include Watson's three (fear, rage, love), Tomkins's nine affects (1962), Izard's ten (differential emotions theory), Ekman's six (happiness, sadness, fear, anger, surprise, disgust; contempt added in 1986), Plutchik's eight primaries arranged as opposites on a wheel with dyads such as love and awe (1980) and Panksepp's seven brain systems. Dimensional models include Wundt's tridimensional theory, Russell's circumplex of valence by arousal (1980) and Barrett's theory of constructed emotion. 11.2 The classic theories: from the body to the label. The James-Lange theory (1884, 1885) says that bodily changes come first and that the feeling of them is the emotion ("we feel afraid because we tremble"). Cannon (1927) objected that emotion survives separation of viscera from brain, that visceral changes are similar across emotions, insensitive and slow, and that artificial arousal (Marañón's adrenaline injections) produces bodily symptoms and at most an "as if" emotion; the Cannon-Bard theory holds that the thalamus triggers feeling and arousal simultaneously and independently. Schachter and Singer's two-factor theory (1962) says that emotion requires arousal plus a cognitive label; in their adrenaline experiment, aroused participants without an explanation caught the euphoria or anger of a stooge. Misattribution of arousal (Dutton and Aron's bridge, 1974; Valins's false heartbeats) and Zillmann's excitation transfer follow from the theory. 11.3 Appraisal, feedback, evolution and opposing processes. Arnold (1960) introduced appraisal, and Lazarus built the cognitive appraisal (cognitive-mediational) theory: primary appraisal asks whether an event matters and whether it is harm, threat or challenge, secondary appraisal asks what can be done, and reappraisal revises both; the subincision film study showed that changing appraisals changes arousal. Zajonc argued for affective primacy from the mere exposure effect (1980, 1984), and Lazarus replied that appraisal can be automatic. The facial feedback hypothesis (Tomkins, Izard; Strack, Martin and Stepper's pen study, 1988) holds that expressions modulate feelings, although the effect is small. Darwin (1872) explained expressions by serviceable habits, antithesis and direct nervous action and founded the evolutionary view. Solomon and Corbit's opponent-process theory (1974) explains tolerance, withdrawal and acquired pleasures through a slow, strengthening b-process. 11.4 The emotional brain and body. The sympathetic division of the autonomic nervous system arouses (dilating the pupils, lowering skin resistance) and the parasympathetic division calms; the medulla of the hindbrain paces heartbeat and breathing, and the hypothalamus orchestrates. Bard's decorticate cats showed sham rage, organised by the hypothalamus; Hess elicited attack by hypothalamic stimulation. Papez (1937) proposed a circuit from hippocampus through fornix, mammillary bodies, anterior thalamus and cingulate gyrus; MacLean named the limbic system (1952), the classic "seat of emotion", and the triune brain. Bilateral temporal lobe removal produces Klüver-Bucy syndrome (tameness, psychic blindness, hyperorality, hypersexuality); the amygdala detects threat, supports fear conditioning and enhances emotional memory. LeDoux described a fast low road and a slower high road to the amygdala; affective blindsight shows emotional processing without awareness. Damasio's somatic marker hypothesis gives the ventromedial prefrontal cortex a role in decisions. The polygraph detects arousal, not lies; the guilty knowledge test (Lykken, 1959) is more accurate. 11.5 Expressing and reading emotion. Ekman and Friesen's studies of the Fore of New Guinea supported the universality of six facial expressions, with fear and surprise most often confused; blind athletes produce the same expressions as sighted ones. Display rules, cultural norms for showing emotion, explain cultural differences (Friesen's Japanese and American students, 1972), and emotional labour at work contributes to burnout. Recognition shows an in-group advantage. FACS (1978) codes expressions as muscle action units; the Duchenne smile involves the orbicularis oculi around the eyes; microexpressions may betray concealed feelings, but people detect lies at little better than chance. Body posture can be more informative than the face at high intensity. Women are on average more facially expressive and better at decoding nonverbal cues, differences attributed mainly to socialisation. 11.6 Four emotions up close. Fear is a response to present danger; anxiety is diffuse and future-oriented, and Spielberger separated state from trait anxiety. Anger is an emotion, aggression a behaviour and hostility an attitude; the catharsis hypothesis fails, because venting while ruminating increases aggression (Bushman, 2002). Diener's subjective well-being has three components: life satisfaction, positive affect and low negative affect. Helson's adaptation-level theory and Brickman and Campbell's hedonic treadmill explain why good fortune fades (lottery winners), and relative deprivation (Stouffer, 1949) explains why comparisons matter. Fredrickson's broaden-and-build theory says positive emotions widen thought and build resources, and savoring (Bryant and Veroff) prolongs positive experience. Disgust, studied by Rozin, protects against contamination and follows the laws of contagion and similarity. 11.7 Emotional development and regulation. Bridges (1932) described differentiation from general excitement into distress and delight and then into specific emotions; primary emotions appear in the first six months, while self-conscious emotions such as embarrassment, pride, shame and guilt appear after 12 months, once self-recognition develops. Infants use social referencing (the visual cliff) and expect emotional reciprocity (Tronick's still face). Gross's process model (1998) lists five families of regulation strategies: situation selection, situation modification, attentional deployment, cognitive change (including reappraisal) and response modulation (including suppression); reappraisal is generally healthier than suppression. Alexithymia (Sifneos, 1973) is difficulty identifying and describing one's feelings. Goleman's five domains of emotional intelligence are pointed to Chapter 9. 11.8 Stress and the body's emergency systems. Stress has been defined as a stimulus (the stressor), as a response (Selye: the nonspecific response of the body to any demand) and, most usefully, as a transaction in which demands are appraised as exceeding resources. Cannon described the fight-or-flight response (1915), run by the fast sympathetic-adrenal-medullary axis with adrenaline and noradrenaline, and coined homeostasis. Selye's general adaptation syndrome (1936; The Stress of Life , 1956) has three stages: alarm, resistance and exhaustion, the last bringing diseases of adaptation; he also distinguished eustress from distress (1974). The slower HPA axis runs from hypothalamic CRH to anterior pituitary ACTH to cortisol from the adrenal cortex, with negative feedback; chronic activation produces allostatic load (McEwen). Taylor's tend-and-befriend (2000) describes an affiliative stress response, especially in females, involving oxytocin. 11.9 Sources of stress and the transactional model. Holmes and Rahe's Social Readjustment Rating Scale (1967) scores 43 life events in life change units (death of a spouse 100, marriage 50), counting positive as well as negative change, but it ignores appraisal and predicts illness only weakly; India has its own Presumptive Stressful Life Events Scale. Daily hassles (Kanner, Coyne, Schaefer and Lazarus, 1981) predict symptoms better than major events; uplifts matter less. Stressors may be acute or chronic, and cataclysmic, personal or background (Lazarus and Cohen, 1977). Frustration, conflict (Lewin's types and Miller's gradients), pressure and change are further sources. Work stress arises from environmental, organisational (task and role demands) and individual factors; role conflict, role ambiguity and Karasek's high-demand, low-control jobs are especially harmful, and chronic work stress can lead to burnout (Freudenberger, 1974; Maslach's three dimensions). Control and predictability reduce the damage of stressors (Weiss's rats). Lazarus and Folkman's transactional model (1984) explains stress through primary appraisal, secondary appraisal, coping and reappraisal, and the diathesis-stress model explains disorder as vulnerability triggered by stress. 11.10 Coping, personality and health. Coping is the changing effort to manage demands appraised as taxing. Problem-focused coping acts on the stressor and emotion-focused coping on the feelings; people use both, and the best strategy fits the controllability of the situation. Approach coping wins in the long run over avoidance coping; defence mechanisms are unconscious, coping is conscious. Social support (emotional, instrumental, informational and appraisal) protects health directly and by buffering stress; Weiss separated emotional from social isolation. Hardiness (Kobasa, 1979: commitment, control, challenge), dispositional optimism (Scheier and Carver), optimistic explanatory style and learned optimism (Seligman, building on learned helplessness), resilience (Werner's Kauai study) and Antonovsky's sense of coherence (comprehensibility, manageability, meaningfulness) protect against stress. Friedman and Rosenman's Type A pattern (competitiveness, time urgency, hostility) predicted heart disease in the Western Collaborative Group Study, but hostility is the toxic component; Type B is relaxed, Type C (cancer-prone) has weak support, and Denollet's Type D combines negative affectivity with social inhibition. Engel's biopsychosocial model (1977) frames health psychology; Ader and Cohen's conditioned immunosuppression (1975) founded psychoneuroimmunology, and chronic stress suppresses immunity and slows healing, while acute stress can boost innate immunity. Health behaviour is predicted by the health belief model, protection motivation theory and the theory of planned behaviour. Stress management uses progressive muscle relaxation (Jacobson), the relaxation response (Benson), biofeedback, meditation and mindfulness (Kabat-Zinn), exercise, cognitive restructuring and stress inoculation training (Meichenbaum). universality hypothesis, uplifts, valence From the past papers Which of the following is NOT one of the six universally recognized basic emotions described by Ekman? (RML 2025) (a) Anger (b) Fear (c) Jealousy (d) Disgust Answer: (c) Jealousy. Ekman's six are happiness, sadness, fear, anger, surprise and disgust (contempt was added in 1986). Jealousy is a complex social emotion, a blend of fear, anger and sadness about losing a relationship to a rival, and has no universal facial expression. Our current mood and feelings are best described by the term: (RML 2024) (a) Emotion (b) Mood (c) Affect (d) Feeling Answer: (c) Affect. Affect is the umbrella term for one's present feeling state and, clinically, its moment-to-moment expression. A mood is a sustained, pervasive state lasting hours or days; an emotion is a brief response to a specific event; a feeling is only the subjective part of an emotion. According to the James-Lange theory of emotion, what is the correct order of events? (RML 2025) (a) Event → Emotion → Interpretation → Arousal (b) Event → Arousal → Emotion (c) Event → Arousal → Interpretation → Emotion (d) Interpretation → Arousal → Emotion Answer: (c) Event, arousal, interpretation, emotion. In James-Lange the body reacts first and the felt emotion is the awareness (the "interpretation") of the bodily change. Option (b) is not false but leaves out that step, so the fuller textbook sequence (c) is keyed. Options (a) and (d) put emotion or interpretation before arousal, which reverses the theory. Schachter and Singer's theory of emotion differs from the theories of James-Lange and Cannon-Bard. How does it differ? (RML 2020) (a) It includes development and arousal (b) It includes the limbic system (c) It includes cognition and arousal (d) It has never been criticised Answer: (c) It includes cognition and arousal. The two-factor theory requires both physiological arousal and a cognitive label taken from the situation. It says nothing about development or the limbic system, and it has been criticised heavily, notably by the failed replications of Marshall and Zimbardo and of Maslach (1979). Which theory of emotion explains the phenomenon of misattribution of arousal (for example, feeling romantic attraction when actually scared)? (RML 2025) (a) James-Lange theory (b) Two-factor theory (c) Cannon-Bard theory (d) Facial feedback hypothesis Answer: (b) Two-factor theory. If emotion is arousal plus a label, the label can be wrong, as on the Capilano bridge. James-Lange and Cannon-Bard have no labelling step, and the facial feedback hypothesis concerns the effect of one's own expressions on feelings. According to experts on socioemotional development like Campos (2009) and Kagan (2010), self-conscious emotions appear at which age? (RML 2022) (a) 6 to 9 months (b) Before 9 months (c) After 12 months (d) 3 months Answer: (c) After 12 months. Embarrassment, pride, shame and guilt require a sense of self, which appears with mirror self-recognition at about 15 to 24 months; these emotions emerge from about 18 months. The earlier ages fit the primary emotions, which are present by about six months. The first emotions expressed by infants are: (IHBAS 2020) (a) Pain and anger (b) Rage and fear (c) Fear and euphoria (d) Delight and distress Answer: (d) Delight and distress. In Bridges's differentiation scheme (1932) the newborn's general excitement splits first into distress and delight, and only later into anger, fear, elation and the rest. Rage and fear (with love) are Watson's three innate emotions, a different and older claim. In James Gross's process model of emotion regulation, cognitive reappraisal belongs to which family of strategies? (Recall set) (a) Response modulation (b) Cognitive change (c) Situation selection (d) Attentional deployment Answer: (b) Cognitive change. Reappraisal changes the meaning of the situation before the emotional response is fully formed. Response modulation includes expressive suppression; situation selection is choosing which situations to enter; attentional deployment includes distraction and rumination. Savoring is a concept in Positive Psychology that involves: (IHBAS 2024) (a) Avoiding negative experiences (b) Enhancing the enjoyment of positive experiences (c) Minimizing stress through relaxation (d) Reflecting on past traumas Answer: (b) Enhancing the enjoyment of positive experiences. Bryant and Veroff defined savoring as attending to, appreciating and prolonging good experiences, past, present or future. Avoiding bad experiences and relaxing away stress are forms of coping, not savoring, and dwelling on trauma is rumination. Barbara Fredrickson is known for her work on: (IHBAS 2024) (a) Cognitive distortions (b) Flow theory (c) Broaden-and-build theory (d) Psychodynamic theory Answer: (c) Broaden-and-build theory. Fredrickson proposed that positive emotions broaden thought-action repertoires and build lasting resources. Flow is Csikszentmihalyi's, cognitive distortions are Beck's (and Burns's), and psychodynamic theory is Freud's. Choose the odd one out regarding the pattern of sympathetic activation during emotion: (Amity 2023) (a) Increased heart rate (b) Pupil constriction (c) Lowered skin resistance (d) Increased breathing rate Answer: (b) Pupil constriction. Sympathetic arousal dilates the pupils; constriction is parasympathetic. Faster heart rate and breathing, and lowered skin resistance from sweating (the galvanic skin response), are all sympathetic effects. Non-voluntary coping responses like heart-beat, respiration are modulated by: (JEMAS 2025) (a) Hypothalamus (b) Cerebellum (c) Hind brain (d) Amygdala Answer: (c) Hind brain. The cardiovascular and respiratory centres lie in the medulla oblongata, part of the hindbrain. The hypothalamus orchestrates them only indirectly, the amygdala triggers fear responses through the hypothalamus and brainstem, and the cerebellum coordinates movement. The seat of emotion is to be found in: (RML 2024) (a) Reticular formation (b) Hind brain (c) Limbic system (d) Forebrain Answer: (c) Limbic system. MacLean's limbic system (1952), including the amygdala, hypothalamus, hippocampus and cingulate gyrus, is the classic seat of emotion. The reticular formation governs arousal and wakefulness, the hindbrain vital functions, and "forebrain" is too broad an answer, although the limbic system lies within it. Which cluster of symptoms is seen in Klüver-Bucy syndrome? (JEMAS 2025) (a) Agnosia, aphasia, hyperorality, hyperphagia, hypersexuality (b) Agnosia, avolition, alogia, asexuality (c) Hypersexuality, altered emotional response, hyperorality, hyperalertness (d) Hypersexuality, hypo-sensitivity, delayed reaction Answer: (a). Bilateral temporal lobe (amygdala) damage produces psychic blindness (agnosia), hyperorality, hyperphagia and hypersexuality, and in humans often aphasia because the nearby temporal cortex is damaged. Option (c) is tempting, but the monkeys became placid, not hyperalert; avolition and alogia are negative symptoms of schizophrenia, and "asexuality" is the opposite of what happens. 'Psychological disorders develop when a biological predisposition is set off by a stressful situation', is proposed by: (JEMAS 2025) (a) Humanistic existential models (b) Socio-cultural model (c) Diathesis-stress model (d) Cognitive model Answer: (c) Diathesis-stress model. A diathesis (vulnerability) plus a stressful trigger is the definition of the model (Meehl, 1962; Zubin and Spring, 1977). Humanistic-existential models stress blocked growth and meaning, sociocultural models social forces, and cognitive models maladaptive thinking; none of them is defined by predisposition plus stress. In order, starting from the first stage, what are the stages of the general adaptation syndrome? (RML 2024) (a) Resistance, alarm, exhaustion (b) Alarm, resistance, exhaustion (c) Resistance, illness, alarm (d) Alarm, exhaustion, illness Answer: (b) Alarm, resistance, exhaustion. Selye's body first mobilises (alarm), then adapts (resistance), then, if stress continues, runs down (exhaustion). Illness is a consequence of exhaustion, not a stage, and resistance cannot come before the alarm that triggers it. Which endocrine gland is primarily responsible for controlling the body's stress response and stress-related metabolic changes? (Real PYQ 2025) (a) Thyroid gland (b) Adrenal glands (c) Pituitary gland (d) Pancreas Answer: (b) Adrenal glands. The adrenal medulla releases adrenaline and noradrenaline (SAM axis) and the adrenal cortex releases cortisol (HPA axis). The pituitary releases ACTH but is not itself the stress gland; the thyroid sets metabolic rate and the pancreas controls blood sugar through insulin and glucagon. Which of the following would be considered an acute stressor? (RML 2024) (a) A pop quiz (b) HIV disease (c) Marital discord (d) Colon cancer Answer: (a) A pop quiz. An acute stressor is brief, with a clear beginning and end. HIV disease, cancer and a troubled marriage last for months or years with no clear end, so they are chronic stressors. Social Readjustment Rating Scale of Holmes and Rahe focuses upon: (IHBAS 2025) (a) Life events (b) Physiological reactions (c) Cognitive changes (d) Daily hassles Answer: (a) Life events. The SRRS (1967) scores 43 major life changes in life change units, from death of a spouse (100) to minor violations of the law (11). Daily hassles were measured by Kanner and colleagues (1981); physiological reactions belong to Selye's tradition and cognitive appraisal to Lazarus's. According to the Transactional Model of Stress, which term refers to the individual's assessment of whether they have the resources to cope with a stressor? (IHBAS 2024) (a) Initial threat evaluation (b) Secondary appraisal (c) Coping resource assessment (d) Situational capacity evaluation Answer: (b) Secondary appraisal. In Lazarus and Folkman's model (1984), primary appraisal judges whether an event is relevant and whether it is harm, threat or challenge; secondary appraisal judges the options and resources for coping. The other three phrases sound plausible but are not terms of the model. Which factor is an organizational stressor leading to job related stress? (IHBAS 2024) (a) Family and economic problems (b) Political uncertainty (c) Task and role demands (d) Number of dependents in family Answer: (c) Task and role demands. Organisational stressors arise within the job: task demands, role demands (role conflict, ambiguity, overload), interpersonal demands, structure and leadership. Family and economic problems and the number of dependants are individual factors; political uncertainty is an environmental factor. Type A behavior pattern is characterized by: (IHBAS 2020) (a) Non-competitiveness, impatience and hostility (b) Impatience, non-competitiveness, and aggression (c) Competitiveness, impatience and hostility (d) Hostility, lack of aggression and competitiveness Answer: (c) Competitiveness, impatience and hostility. Friedman and Rosenman's Type A combines competitive achievement striving, time urgency (impatience) and hostility. Every other option contains a "non-" or "lack of" that contradicts the pattern. Which of the following factor is most directly linked to a higher risk for coronary heart disease? (RML 2024) (a) Type A personality (b) Type B personality (c) Hostility (d) Self-efficacy Answer (as keyed): (a) Type A personality. Type A was the classic coronary-prone pattern of the Western Collaborative Group Study, and it is the keyed answer. Be aware, though, that later research identifies hostility, one component of Type A, as the part that carries most of the risk, so a stem asking for the "toxic component" of Type A should be answered with hostility. Type B is the low-risk pattern, and self-efficacy is a protective belief. The "D-type" personality, identified as a risk factor for poor prognosis in cardiovascular disease, is characterized by: (Real PYQ 2024) (a) Hostility and competitiveness (b) The joint tendency to experience negative emotions and to inhibit self-expression in social situations (social inhibition) (c) An optimistic and resilient outlook on life (d) Perfectionism and rigidity Answer: (b). Denollet's Type D (distressed) personality is negative affectivity combined with social inhibition. Hostility and competitiveness describe Type A; optimism and resilience are protective factors; perfectionism and rigidity belong to obsessive-compulsive personality descriptions. Learned helplessness phenomenon is offered by: (JEMAS 2025) (a) Aaron T. Beck (b) Martin Seligman and Steven F. Maier (c) Harry Stack Sullivan (d) Daniel Kahneman Answer: (b) Martin Seligman and Steven F. Maier. Their dogs (1967), given inescapable shocks, later failed to escape avoidable ones; the idea became a model of depression and, through explanatory style, of learned optimism. Beck is known for cognitive therapy, Sullivan for the interpersonal theory of psychiatry and Kahneman for judgement heuristics and prospect theory. High-yield sheet The facts this chapter's questions ask most, most-asked first. Last read before the exam. The limbic system is the classic "seat of emotion": Paul MacLean named it in 1952, enlarging James Papez's 1937 circuit, and it regulates emotion, motivation and memory. Hunger and thirst are the hypothalamus; arousal is the reticular formation; coordination is the cerebellum. asked 7 times The amygdala is the structure for fear and aggression: threat detection, fear conditioning (LeDoux's low and high roads) and the emotional enhancement of memory (Cahill and McGaugh, 1994). The hippocampus stores the facts; the amygdala adds the emotional boost. asked 7 times The diathesis-stress model : a disorder appears when a pre-existing vulnerability (diathesis, often biological) is set off by a stressful situation (Meehl, 1962; Zubin and Spring, 1977). Not genes alone, environment alone or unconscious conflict alone. asked 4 times Klüver-Bucy syndrome (Heinrich Klüver and Paul Bucy, 1937 and 1939): bilateral removal of the anterior temporal lobes (amygdala) in monkeys produces tameness and loss of fear, hyperorality, hypersexuality, psychic blindness (visual agnosia) and hyperphagia. asked 4 times James-Lange theory (William James, 1884; Carl Lange, 1885): event, bodily arousal, awareness ("interpretation") of the arousal, emotion; "we feel afraid because we tremble". Feeling and arousal at the same time, via the thalamus, is Cannon-Bard (1927). asked 4 times Type A behaviour pattern (Meyer Friedman and Ray Rosenman, 1959): competitiveness, time urgency (impatience) and hostility; it predicted coronary heart disease (about twice the risk) in the Western Collaborative Group Study. Hostility is the toxic component; Type B is the low-risk pattern. asked 3 times Repression is the involuntary blocking of painful feelings from awareness (suppression is deliberate); isolation of affect keeps the idea but strips its feeling (a gruesome fantasy told calmly); projection attributes one's own unacceptable feelings to someone else. asked 3 times The adrenal glands are the stress glands. HPA axis: hypothalamus (CRH), anterior pituitary (ACTH), adrenal cortex (cortisol), with cortisol's negative feedback on the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary; the adrenal medulla releases adrenaline and noradrenaline (SAM axis). asked 4 times Displacement redirects a feeling onto a safer target (angry with her husband, a woman shouts at her child); sublimation channels it into a socially valued activity (anger into a kickboxing class). asked 3 times Schachter and Singer's two-factor theory (1962): emotion is physiological arousal plus a cognitive label, so it adds cognition to arousal, and it explains misattribution of arousal (Dutton and Aron's Capilano bridge, 1974). asked twice Selye's general adaptation syndrome (1936; The Stress of Life , 1956): alarm, resistance, exhaustion, always in that order. Illness is not a stage, and the GAS is not life events theory or the health belief model. asked twice Sympathetic arousal dilates the pupils, speeds heart rate and breathing and lowers skin resistance; pupil constriction is parasympathetic. Heartbeat and breathing are paced by the medulla of the hindbrain . asked twice Infant emotions : in Bridges's scheme (1932) general excitement differentiates first into distress and delight ; self-conscious emotions (embarrassment, pride, shame, guilt) appear after 12 months, from about 18 months, once mirror self-recognition develops. asked twice Type D personality (Johan Denollet, mid-1990s; Lancet 1996): negative affectivity plus social inhibition, a predictor of poor prognosis in coronary heart disease. asked twice Affect is the current feeling state and its observable expression, rated for quality, range and reactivity; mood is the sustained, pervasive state, defined by its persistence. asked twice Papez circuit (1937): hippocampus, fornix, mammillary bodies, anterior thalamus, cingulate gyrus, entorhinal cortex, back to the hippocampus. asked twice Pseudobulbar affect : sudden, brief, involuntary outbursts of laughing or crying out of proportion to the actual mood, after stroke, multiple sclerosis, ALS or brain injury; it is not depression. asked twice Ekman's six universal emotions: happiness, sadness, fear, anger, surprise and disgust (contempt added in 1986). Jealousy, shame and guilt are not on the list. asked once Gross's process model (1998): situation selection, situation modification, attentional deployment, cognitive change (reappraisal) and response modulation (suppression). asked once Lazarus and Folkman's transactional model (1984): primary appraisal asks whether an event matters (harm, threat or challenge); secondary appraisal asks whether I have the resources to cope. asked once Holmes and Rahe's Social Readjustment Rating Scale (1967) measures life events: 43 changes in life change units, death of a spouse 100, marriage 50. Daily hassles are Kanner, Coyne, Schaefer and Lazarus (1981). asked once Acute versus chronic stressors : a pop quiz is acute; HIV disease, cancer and marital discord are chronic. asked once Organisational stressors are task and role demands (and interpersonal demands, structure, leadership); family and economic problems are individual factors, political uncertainty an environmental one. asked once Biopsychosocial model (George Engel, 1977): biological, psychological and social factors, not "cultural" in place of social. asked once Barbara Fredrickson : the broaden-and-build theory of positive emotions (1998, 2001) and the undo effect. Flow is Csikszentmihalyi's. asked once Savoring (Fred Bryant and Joseph Veroff): attending to, enhancing and prolonging the enjoyment of positive experiences. asked once Emotional isolation (Robert Weiss, 1973) is the lack of a deep attachment to one specific person; lacking a circle of friends is social isolation. asked once Learned helplessness : Martin Seligman and Steven Maier (1967), dogs given inescapable shock; not Beck, Sullivan or Kahneman. asked once Theory of planned behaviour (Icek Ajzen): attitude, subjective norm and perceived behavioural control (keyed as "self-efficacy") shape intention. asked once Diener's tripartite model of subjective well-being: life satisfaction (cognitive), positive affect and low negative affect. asked once

title: Master Guide for Clinical Psychology — Amit Panwar
text: Master Guide for Clinical Psychology — Amit Panwar A cheat-map of exactly what the MPhil / MA Clinical Psychology entrances test, lifted straight from Amit Panwar's Master Guide for Clinical Psychology and folded in clean. Four parts: the exam pattern analysis (what CIP, IHBAS, RML and NIMHANS hammer every year, plus the questions that actually repeat), an A–Z terminology glossary , 24 named therapies with founder + key concepts + techniques, and 25 landmark experiments with who/when/where/what. Read it once for the map, then drill the glossary and experiments cold. Source Amit Panwar, Master Guide for Clinical Psychology (Power Within Psychology). Transcribed verbatim; only obvious scan slips were cleaned. Marketing/contact pages dropped. Two of the experiments (Harry Harlow's monkeys, the Darley "Good Samaritan / bystander" pair) appear twice in the original numbering — both kept as the guide lists them. In this guide Exam pattern analysis & repeated questions Why revising UGC-NET JRF papers pays off A–Z terminology glossary 24 important therapies (founder · concepts · techniques) 25 landmark experiments (who · year · where · what) 1. Exam pattern analysis: what actually gets tested Admission into CIP Ranchi, IHBAS, RML and NIMHANS (for MA/MPhil, PGDCP/PDCP, PsyD and PhD Clinical Psychology) is competitive, but the entrances recur in shape. The structure across institutes is similar: MCQs dominate , covering theoretical concepts, psychological tools, research methods, psychotherapies and clinical diagnosis. 1.1 Sections that show up Area What they ask General Psychology Classical theories — Sigmund Freud, Carl Jung, Alfred Adler, B. F. Skinner, Albert Bandura; cognition, memory, sensation, perception, learning. Clinical Psychology Disorders, diagnosis, defense mechanisms, therapeutic approaches. Psychological Testing & Assessment Intelligence (Binet, Wechsler, Bhatia Battery, Performance tests), personality, projective tests; test construction. Psychotherapy & Counselling CBT, DBT, psychodynamic, client-centred; applied / case-based. Research Methods & Statistics Design, hypothesis testing, ANOVA, chi-square, correlation, factor analysis. Developmental Psychology Lifespan, stage theories, attachment. Biopsychology Brain anatomy and its link to psychological function. 1.2 Commonly asked topics, with real stems A. General & Clinical Psychology. Foundational theories of Sigmund Freud, Carl Jung, Alfred Adler, B. F. Skinner, Bandura come up constantly. "Psychoanalytic theory about human personality was proposed by?" (CIP) "Insight learning is studied by?" (CIP) B. Psychometric Testing & Intelligence. Binet, Wechsler, Bhatia Battery / Performance tests — components and Indian-context applications. "The prototype of the modern intelligence test was developed by?" (CIP) "Bhatia Battery of Performance Test includes which test?" (CET) Key tip Go deep on test theory and application; drill test-construction concepts ( reliability, validity ) — they're commonly tested. C. Research Methodology & Statistics. Design, hypothesis testing, and stats. Know ANOVA, chi-square, correlation, factor analysis cold. "Degrees of freedom in a chi-square 3×4 table?" (CIP) "What is Cronbach's Alpha used for?" (RML) D. Clinical Diagnosis & Disorders. DSM-5 criteria, especially schizophrenia, OCD, PTSD, depression; defense mechanisms; therapy approaches. "Which defense mechanism is most common in Borderline Personality Disorder?" (RINPAS) "Which therapy focuses on changing negative thought patterns?" — CBT (CIP) E. Neuropsychology & Biopsychology. Brain structures — hippocampus, amygdala, thalamus, hypothalamus — and their functions. "Which structure allows communication between the hemispheres?" (RINPAS) "What is the role of the hippocampus in memory?" (NIMHANS) F. Therapies & Treatment Approaches. CBT, DBT, psychodynamic, client-centred — and applying them. "Functional Analysis is considered under which therapy?" (RINPAS) 1.3 Repeated questions across exams (use this to sharpen the mocks) Many items recur near-verbatim across papers. These are the highest-value drills. Theme Repeated stem Seen in Psychological theories "What are the basic types of defense mechanisms according to Freud?" (Id/Ego/Superego, displacement, repression) IHBAS, CIP, RML MPhil Psychometric tests "Which intelligence test includes the Pattern Drawing Test?" CET, RML Neuropsychology "Damage to the hippocampus affects?" RINPAS, NIMHANS, IHBAS Clinical disorders "Which disorder is characterised by repetitive intrusive thoughts?" (OCD) IHBAS, NIMHANS Defense + BPD "Which defense mechanism is most commonly associated with borderline personality disorder?" IHBAS, CIP, NIMHANS (first via UGC-NET) 1.4 Strategy for cracking the MPhil entrances Focus on core areas: master psychoanalytic, behavioural and cognitive theories; DSM-5 categories, criteria and treatments for common disorders; brain anatomy tied to cognition and memory. Practise previous-year papers: they expose recurring themes and question patterns — drill MCQs on the Bhatia Battery, CBT techniques and brain functions. Master psychometrics & research: intelligence tests, methodology and statistical tools are tested heavily; command of them is a real edge. Stay current: DSM-5 revisions and emerging trends in psychotherapy and neuropsychology. Time management: front-load high-yield topics (research methods, clinical disorders, brain functions); revise and take timed mocks to build speed and accuracy. 2. Why revising UGC-NET JRF papers pays off One of the strongest levers for these entrances: revise UGC-NET JRF papers. The overlap with MPhil Clinical Psychology entrances is large and well-documented. High overlap of topics & questions. Clinical and abnormal psychology (schizophrenia, OCD, personality disorders and their DSM-5 criteria), psychoanalytic theory and research methodology all recur in both. "What are the key diagnostic criteria for schizophrenia?" turns up across UGC-NET, GATE and MPhil papers. Theorist items — e.g. "Which theorist proposed the collective unconscious?" — appear in MPhil exams after first showing in UGC-NET JRF. Strong focus on research methods & statistics. ANOVA, t-tests, chi-square, validity and reliability are repeated. "Degrees of freedom in a chi-square 3×4 table?" appears across UGC-NET and GATE with slight variations in MPhil papers. Psychometric & intelligence tests. WAIS, Binet, and the Bhatia Battery are frequent. "Bhatia Battery of Performance Test includes which test?" has appeared across CIP Ranchi, UGC-NET and GATE — high repetition. Direct repeats in MPhil exams. Items on cognitive distortions, memory systems and CBT techniques carry over from UGC-NET into IHBAS, CIP and NIMHANS papers (e.g. shortlisting rounds). High-utility shared topics. Neuropsychology (hippocampus, amygdala, neurotransmitters; serotonin in depression), cognitive psychology and clinical diagnostics overlap heavily across UGC-NET JRF, GATE and MPhil. Bottom line UGC-NET JRF papers cover the same foundational topics and carry repeated questions and terminology. Folding them into your practice strengthens concepts, drills the repeats, and lifts your odds across the board. 3. A–Z terminology glossary Quick definitions for the key terms the guide flags. Searchable — type any term in the library search and this entry surfaces. A Agraphia The partial or complete inability to write, usually caused by brain damage. Aphasia Partial or complete loss of the ability to speak or comprehend language, typically caused by brain injury or neurological conditions. Aphonia The inability to produce vocal sounds due to damage to the larynx or related structures. Apraxia A disorder where an individual struggles to produce normal movement or speech despite intact muscles and comprehension. Anorexia Nervosa An eating disorder marked by an intense fear of gaining weight and a distorted body image, leading to extreme restriction of food intake. Amygdala A structure in the brain's limbic system involved in emotion regulation, particularly fear and aggression. Anterograde Amnesia The inability to form new memories following brain damage, with preserved recall of past events. Attachment Theory Developed by John Bowlby; explains how early relationships with caregivers shape emotional bonds, with types such as secure, anxious and avoidant. Attention Span The length of time an individual can concentrate on a task without becoming distracted. Autosome Any chromosome that is not a sex chromosome, carrying genetic information unrelated to sex determination. B Behavioural Theories Theories such as classical and operant conditioning that explain learning through associations, reinforcements and punishments (Ivan Pavlov, B. F. Skinner). Borderline Personality Disorder A disorder of unstable moods, relationships and behaviour, often marked by impulsive actions and intense fears of abandonment. Broca's Area A frontal-lobe region responsible for speech production; damage results in Broca's aphasia. Brute Force A problem-solving strategy that tries all possible solutions until the correct one is found. C Catharsis The release of pent-up emotions and psychological tension through expression, resulting in emotional relief. Chi-Square Test A statistical test used to examine the association between two categorical variables. Chunking A memory strategy where information is grouped into larger, meaningful units, making it easier to recall. Classical Conditioning Learning where a neutral stimulus becomes associated with a meaningful one, eliciting a conditioned response (Ivan Pavlov). Client-Centred Therapy A humanistic approach by Carl Rogers emphasising unconditional positive regard, empathy and client autonomy. Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) A widely used therapy focused on altering negative thought patterns and behaviours to treat psychological disorders. Cognitive Dissonance The discomfort of holding conflicting beliefs or behaviours, motivating people to reduce the inconsistency (Leon Festinger). Cognitive Distortions Irrational thought patterns (all-or-nothing thinking, catastrophising) that lead to emotional distress (CBT framework). Cognitive Psychology The study of mental processes like memory, problem-solving, perception and decision-making. Conformity The tendency to change behaviour or beliefs to align with group norms, often under social pressure. D Defense Mechanisms Unconscious strategies that protect the ego — e.g. repression, displacement, projection (Sigmund Freud). Degrees of Freedom (df) The number of values free to vary when calculating a statistic. Dialectical Behaviour Therapy (DBT) An offshoot of CBT by Marsha Linehan, aimed at borderline personality disorder via mindfulness and emotion regulation. Displacement A defense mechanism where negative emotions are redirected from the original source to a less threatening target. Down's Syndrome (Trisomy 21) A congenital condition caused by an extra copy of chromosome 21, leading to developmental and intellectual delays. E EEG (Electroencephalogram) A method for recording electrical activity in the brain using electrodes on the scalp. Extinction In classical conditioning, the weakening and disappearance of a conditioned response when the CS is no longer paired with the US. Eclectic Therapy An approach combining elements from different therapeutic techniques to best meet the client's needs. Empiricism The belief that knowledge comes primarily from sensory experience and observable evidence. Epigenetics The study of how environmental factors influence gene expression without changing the DNA sequence. Ethnocentrism Viewing one's own culture as superior and judging other cultures by its standards. F Factor Analysis A statistical method to identify underlying relationships between variables, often used in psychometrics. Flashbulb Memory Vivid, detailed memories of significant, emotionally charged events, often resistant to decay. G Gate Control Theory A theory of pain perception: a neural "gate" in the spinal cord modulates pain by controlling signal flow to the brain. Gene A unit of heredity composed of DNA carrying genetic information that influences traits and characteristics. Genotype The genetic makeup of an individual, including dominant and recessive genes. Groupthink A phenomenon where group members prioritise consensus over critical thinking, leading to poor decisions. H Halo Effect A general impression of a person (positive or negative) influencing judgements about their other, unrelated traits. Hallucinations Sensory perceptions occurring without external stimuli, common in psychotic disorders such as schizophrenia. Hippocampus A brain structure crucial for forming new memories, particularly long-term memory processing. House-Tree-Person Test A projective test in which individuals draw a house, tree and person to assess personality traits. Hypothesis A testable prediction made by researchers, usually formed before an experiment. I Illusion A misperception or distortion of a sensory experience where perception does not match reality. Implicit Memory Memory that influences behaviour unconsciously, without intentional retrieval (e.g. procedural memory, riding a bike). Insight Learning A problem-solving process where understanding arises suddenly (Wolfgang Köhler's chimpanzee experiments). Insight-Oriented Therapy Psychotherapy aimed at helping clients gain awareness of unconscious thoughts, emotions and behaviours. Internal Locus of Control The belief that one controls one's own life events and outcomes, vs. external factors like luck or fate. J Just Noticeable Difference (JND) The smallest change in sensory stimulation a person can detect 50% of the time. Just-World Hypothesis A bias where people believe the world is fair, assuming individuals get what they deserve even in misfortune. K Klüver-Bucy Syndrome A disorder from temporal-lobe and amygdala damage, causing hypersexuality, visual agnosia and reduced fear responses. Klinefelter Syndrome (XXY) A genetic condition in males caused by an extra X chromosome, leading to developmental delays and specific physical traits. L Lateralisation of Brain Function Certain mental processes are specialised to the left or right hemisphere (e.g. language is typically left-hemisphere). Learned Helplessness Feeling unable to control or change a situation after repeated failure, leading to passivity and depression. Limbic System Brain structures regulating emotion, memory and motivation — includes hippocampus, amygdala and hypothalamus. Linguistic Relativity Hypothesis (Sapir-Whorf) Language influences thought and perception; speakers of different languages may experience the world differently. M Memory Systems The categorisation of memory into short-term, long-term and working memory, with subtypes like episodic and semantic. Null Hypothesis A statistical hypothesis stating there is no effect or difference; the baseline assumption in hypothesis testing. N Narcolepsy A sleep disorder of excessive daytime sleepiness and sudden sleep attacks, often with muscle weakness (cataplexy). Neurotransmitters Chemical messengers across synapses — e.g. serotonin (mood), dopamine (reward), GABA (inhibitory). Neuroplasticity The brain's ability to reorganise and form new neural connections, especially after injury or during learning. Nomothetic Approach Seeking general laws that apply to all individuals (vs. the idiographic focus on the unique individual). Nurture Assumption The hypothesis that development is largely shaped by environment (nurture) rather than genetics (nature). O Object Permanence Understanding that objects continue to exist when unseen — Jean Piaget's sensorimotor stage. Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD) Intrusive thoughts (obsessions) and repetitive behaviours (compulsions) performed to reduce anxiety. Operant Conditioning B. F. Skinner's theory of how behaviour is shaped by consequences, through reinforcement and punishment. Overgeneralisation A cognitive distortion: applying a single event or experience to an entire range of situations. P Phenotype The observable traits of an individual, influenced by both genetics and environment. Premack Principle In operant conditioning, high-probability behaviours reinforce low-probability ones ("games after homework"). Priming Exposure to one stimulus influences the response to a later stimulus, often outside conscious awareness. Projection A defense mechanism: attributing one's own unacceptable thoughts or motives to another person. Prosocial Behaviour Voluntary behaviour aimed at helping others, motivated by empathy or social norms. Psychoanalysis Sigmund Freud's approach exploring unconscious thoughts and desires via free association and dream analysis. R Reinforcement In operant conditioning, increasing a behaviour by adding a positive outcome (positive) or removing an aversive stimulus (negative). Reciprocal Determinism Albert Bandura's view that behaviour, environment and cognition all influence one another bidirectionally. Regression to the Mean Extreme data points tend to move closer to the average on subsequent measurements. Regression Analysis A statistical method to predict the relationship between a dependent variable and one or more independent variables. Reliability The consistency of a test or measure in producing stable, repeatable results (e.g. test-retest reliability). Retrograde Amnesia The inability to recall memories formed before the onset of amnesia. S Scaffolding In Lev Vygotsky's theory, support from more knowledgeable others that helps a learner reach a higher level of understanding. Schemas Mental frameworks used to organise and interpret information, shaping perception and memory. Schizophrenia A severe disorder with hallucinations, delusions, disorganised speech and impaired functioning. Short-Term Memory (STM) Temporary storage lasting ~15–30 seconds, with limited capacity. Social Learning Theory Albert Bandura's view that learning occurs through observation, imitation and modelling, with reinforcement and punishment. Somatoform Disorders Disorders with physical symptoms lacking a medical cause — e.g. conversion disorder, hypochondriasis. Standardisation Establishing uniform procedures for administering and scoring tests to ensure consistency across situations. Stereotypes Oversimplified, generalised beliefs about groups of people, often based on race, gender or ethnicity. Stroop Test Naming the ink colour of a word, hardest when the word names a different colour (e.g. "red" printed in blue). T Temperament Biologically based tendencies to feel or act a certain way, present from early childhood; the foundation of personality. Transference In psychotherapy, clients projecting feelings and attitudes from past relationships onto the therapist. Transactional Analysis Eric Berne's theory examining interactions (transactions) based on Parent, Adult and Child ego states. T-Test A test comparing the means of two groups to see whether the difference is statistically significant. Turner Syndrome (XO) A condition in females from partial or complete absence of one X chromosome, with delayed development and infertility. U Unconditional Positive Regard Carl Rogers' term for a therapist's non-judgemental acceptance and support of a client, regardless of what they say or do. Unconscious Motivation Desires, urges or thoughts that influence behaviour but exist outside conscious awareness (Freudian). Universal Emotions Per Paul Ekman, basic emotions such as happiness, sadness, anger and fear are recognised and expressed similarly across all human cultures. V Validity The degree to which a test measures what it is supposed to. Types: construct, criterion and content validity. Variable Ratio Schedule A reinforcement schedule rewarding behaviour after an unpredictable number of responses, giving high response rates (e.g. gambling). Visual Agnosia A disorder where a person can see but cannot recognise or interpret visual information, due to brain damage. W Working Memory Short-term memory that actively holds and manipulates information; crucial for reasoning, learning and comprehension. Wernicke's Area A region involved in language comprehension; damage causes Wernicke's aphasia (fluent but nonsensical speech). X Xenophobia An irrational fear or dislike of people from other countries or cultures. X-Linked Disorders Genetic disorders from mutations on the X chromosome, often affecting males more severely (e.g. colour blindness, haemophilia). Y Yerkes-Dodson Law Performance improves with arousal up to a point, after which further arousal hinders performance. Youth Bulge A demographic phenomenon where a large share of a population is young, often linked to social instability. Z Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD) Lev Vygotsky's gap between what a learner can do alone and what they can achieve with guidance or collaboration. Zeigarnik Effect The tendency to remember uncompleted or interrupted tasks better than completed ones — tension aids memory. 4. 24 important therapies Founder · key concepts · techniques for each. NIMHANS/MET love "Therapy X was founded by?" and "Technique Y belongs to which therapy?" — drill both directions. Therapy Founder Key concepts Techniques 1. Animal-Assisted Therapy (AAT) No single founder (various psychologists & animal therapists) Uses animals (dogs, horses) to improve emotional well-being, enhance cognition and reduce stress; used for PTSD, anxiety, depression. Structured interaction with animals to build rapport and reduce anxiety. 2. Attachment Therapy Based on John Bowlby's attachment theory Building and repairing attachment bonds, often in children with trauma, neglect or inconsistent caregiving. Activities to build trust and strengthen the caregiver–child relationship. 3. Bibliotherapy No specific individual (used as an adjunct) Reading material that relates to the person's struggle to support healing and growth. Reading and discussing books, poetry or essays that give insight. 4. Cognitive Analytic Therapy (CAT) Anthony Ryle (1980s) Integrates cognitive and analytic approaches to understand problematic patterns of thinking, feeling and relating. Mapping behaviour patterns, identifying maladaptive thinking, reformulation letters to build insight. 5. Coherence Therapy Bruce Ecker & Laurel Hulley Symptoms arise from learned emotional responses; therapy uncovers and resolves them. Emotional uncovering, experiential work, creating moments of change. 6. Dance Movement Therapy (DMT) Marian Chace and other dance therapists (1940s) Movement as a form of expression to enhance emotional, cognitive and physical well-being. Movement exploration, body mirroring, expressive dance. 7. Developmental Needs Meeting Strategy (DNMS) Shirley Jean Schmidt Unmet childhood developmental needs drive adult emotional and psychological issues. Healing attachment wounds by meeting unmet developmental needs. 8. Dramatherapy Influenced by Jacob L. Moreno & Peter Slade Drama and theatre techniques to facilitate emotional expression, self-awareness and conflict resolution. Role-play, improvisation, storytelling, guided imagery. 9. EMDR (Eye Movement Desensitisation & Reprocessing) Francine Shapiro (1987) Treats trauma by processing distressing memories and reducing their impact; client recalls trauma while focusing on bilateral stimuli. Eye movements, bilateral tapping, cognitive restructuring of traumatic memories. 10. Functional Analytic Psychotherapy (FAP) Robert Kohlenberg & Mavis Tsai Uses the therapeutic relationship to change problematic interpersonal behaviours as they emerge in session. Reinforcing adaptive behaviour in the relationship, in-vivo exposure, emotional validation. 11. Hypnotherapy Modern form attributed to Milton Erickson (roots in Franz Mesmer, 18th c.) Hypnosis to create focused attention, heightened suggestibility and deep relaxation; used for phobias, addictions, chronic pain. Trance induction, suggestion therapy. 12. Integral Therapy Ken Wilber Integral theory integrating multiple perspectives — internal/external, individual/collective — into a holistic whole. Working across four quadrants to create a holistic approach to therapy and development. 13. Intensive Short-Term Dynamic Psychotherapy (ISTDP) Habib Davanloo Active therapy to overcome resistance and access repressed emotions; tackles deep-rooted problems in a short time. Emotionally focused interventions, unlocking the unconscious, working through defenses. 14. Logotherapy Viktor Frankl Existential therapy centred on finding meaning in life, even amid suffering; humans are driven by a "will to meaning." Socratic dialogue, dereflection, paradoxical intention. 15. Metacognitive Therapy Adrian Wells Modifies dysfunctional metacognitive beliefs that maintain anxiety and depression. Detachment from thought processes, attention training, challenging metacognitive beliefs. 16. Multimodal Therapy (MMT) Arnold Lazarus Evaluates seven dimensions of personality — the BASIC ID: Behaviour, Affect, Sensation, Imagery, Cognition, Interpersonal relationships, Drugs/biology. Tailored interventions for each modality based on the person's specific needs. 17. Narrative Therapy Michael White & David Epston Sees people as separate from their problems; clients "re-author" their lives with empowering narratives. Externalising problems, identifying unique outcomes, re-authoring personal stories. 18. Play Therapy Virginia Axline & Carl Rogers (influences) Play as a medium for children to express emotions, resolve conflicts and process difficult experiences. Sand tray, role-playing, art-based activities, storytelling. 19. Positive Psychotherapy Nossrat Peseschkian Emphasises inherent capacities for growth and healing; focuses on strengths rather than pathology. Balancing techniques, active goal-setting, identifying personal strengths. 20. Rational Living Therapy (RLT) Aldo R. Pucci A cognitive-behavioural approach building on REBT to replace irrational beliefs with more logical ones. Cognitive restructuring, disputing irrational beliefs, a rational-living plan. 21. Reality Therapy William Glasser Based on choice theory: clients take control of their lives by making better choices; emphasises personal responsibility and the present. Action planning, focusing on current behaviour, exploring new choices. 22. Sexual Identity Therapy No single founder Addresses sexual orientation, identity and gender identity in a supportive, affirming way. Exploratory discussion, psychoeducation, supportive counselling. 23. Solution-Focused Brief Therapy (SFBT) Steve de Shazer & Insoo Kim Berg Short-term, goal-oriented; finds solutions in the present rather than dwelling on past problems. Miracle question, scaling questions, identifying exceptions. 24. Structural Family Therapy Salvador Minuchin Looks at family hierarchies, boundaries and subsystems and how they shape individual behaviour and mental health. Joining, restructuring family interactions, boundary setting. 5. 25 landmark experiments The classic studies, with who ran them, when, where and what they showed. The entrances ask these as "Experiment X was conducted by?" and "Which study demonstrated effect Y?". Experiment Conducted by Year Where What it showed 1. Hawthorne Studies Elton Mayo 1924–1932 Western Electric, Hawthorne Works, Chicago Productivity rose when workers knew they were observed — the Hawthorne effect . 2. Little Albert Experiment John B. Watson & Rosalie Rayner 1920 Johns Hopkins University A baby was classically conditioned to fear a white rat; fear generalised to similar stimuli. Now a landmark in research ethics. 3. Halo Effect Experiment Edward Thorndike 1920 Case Western University A positive impression of one quality (e.g. attractiveness) led people to overestimate other qualities. 4. The Monster Study Wendell Johnson 1939 University of Iowa Attempted to induce stuttering in orphan children through negative speech therapy — one of the most unethical studies in psychology. 5. Robbers Cave Experiment Muzafer Sherif 1954 Robbers Cave State Park, Oklahoma Intergroup conflict arises between groups and is resolved through superordinate goals . 6. Asch Conformity Experiment Solomon Asch 1951 Swarthmore College Participants conformed to clearly wrong answers given by a group — the power of social pressure. 7. Cognitive Dissonance Experiment Leon Festinger 1957 Stanford University Discomfort when behaviour conflicts with belief; participants justified their behaviour by changing their beliefs. 8. Harlow's Monkey Experiment Harry Harlow 1961 University of Wisconsin-Madison Infant monkeys preferred a cloth "mother" (comfort) over a wire one (food) — contact comfort drives attachment. 9. Fantz Looking Chamber Experiment Robert Fantz 1961 Case Western Reserve University Infants preferred looking at human faces over patterns — innate visual preferences. 10. Bobo Doll Experiment Albert Bandura 1961 Stanford University Children who watched an adult act aggressively toward a doll imitated it — observational / social learning. 11. Milgram Obedience Experiment Stanley Milgram 1961 Yale University Participants administered what they believed were painful shocks when told to by an authority — obedience over morality. 12. Schachter & Singer Experiment on Emotion Stanley Schachter & Jerome Singer 1962 Columbia University Supported the two-factor theory of emotion (arousal + cognitive labelling); participants misattributed arousal based on others' behaviour. 13. Ainsworth Strange Situation Mary Ainsworth 1969 Johns Hopkins University Assessed infant attachment via reaction to a caregiver's absence/return; three styles — secure, insecure-avoidant, insecure-resistant. 14. Split-Brain Experiment Roger Sperry 1968 California Institute of Technology Studied severed-corpus-callosum patients; showed the two hemispheres have specialised functions (Nobel Prize). 15. The Good Samaritan Experiment John Darley & C. Daniel Batson 1973 Princeton University Situational factors (being in a hurry) drove helping more than values — even among theology students. 16. Stanford Prison Experiment Philip Zimbardo 1971 Stanford University A simulated prison showed the extreme psychological effects of perceived power; guards turned abusive, prisoners traumatised — ended early. 17. Marshmallow Test Walter Mischel 1972 Stanford University A longitudinal study of delayed gratification in children; those who waited for a larger reward had better later outcomes. 18. Bystander Effect (Good Samaritan study) John Darley & Bibb Latané 1968 Columbia University People are less likely to help in distress when others are present — responsibility is diffused. 19. Ross's False Consensus Effect Study Lee Ross 1977 Stanford University People overestimate how much others share their beliefs, attitudes and behaviours — the false consensus effect . 20. Selective Attention (The Invisible Gorilla) Daniel Simons & Christopher Chabris 1999 Harvard University Counting basketball passes, many viewers missed a gorilla walking through — inattentional blindness . 21. Car Crash Experiment Elizabeth Loftus & John Palmer 1974 University of California, Irvine The misinformation effect : question wording ("smashed" vs "hit") altered recalled speed of the cars. 22. A Class Divided Jane Elliott 1968 Riceville, Iowa After MLK's assassination, Elliott split her class by eye colour, treating one group as superior then reversing it — showing prejudice is arbitrary and damaging. 23. Learned Helplessness Experiment Martin Seligman 1967 University of Pennsylvania Dogs given unavoidable shocks stopped trying to escape even when they could — learned helplessness , a model for depression. 24. Surrogate Mother Experiment (Harlow's monkeys) Harry Harlow 1961 University of Wisconsin-Madison Monkeys offered a wire mother (food) and a cloth mother (comfort) chose comfort — contact comfort over feeding. 25. Visual Cliff Experiment Eleanor Gibson & Richard Walk 1960 Cornell University Infants placed on a glass surface over an apparent drop avoided the "cliff" — depth perception develops early.

title: Biopsychology (Pinel & Barnes), in full depth
text: Biopsychology (Pinel & Barnes), in full depth The whole of Pinel's Biopsychology , all eighteen chapters, rewritten as real explanatory prose instead of bullet fragments. Every concept is built from scratch in full sentences, every mechanism is walked through step by step, the experiment or the patient behind each claim is named, the theorist is named wherever there is one, and worked examples are given where a concept only clicks once you push a number or a case through it. Read a chapter cold and you should finish it understanding the concept, not merely recognising the words. How to read this The chapter order is Pinel's own, so it doubles as a map of the book. Chapters 1 to 5 are the foundations (what the field is, where the machinery came from, how it is built, how it signals, how we study it). Chapters 6 to 8 are sensation and movement. Chapters 9 to 11 are plasticity and memory. Chapters 12 to 15 are the motivated behaviours. Chapters 16 to 18 are the higher functions and the clinic. Nothing in a later chapter assumes you skipped an earlier one, but Chapters 3 and 4 are the load-bearing ones: if the action potential and the synapse are solid, everything downstream reads easily. The artwork is the book's own. Every numbered figure in Biopsychology is here, all 310 of them, plus all nine numbered tables, cropped straight out of the source and dropped at the paragraph that explains it rather than collected at the end of a chapter. Nothing has been redrawn or summarised. If you open a chapter and a picture you remember from the book is not there, it is a bug: screenshot it and it gets fixed. The eighteen chapters Biopsychology as a neuroscience Evolution, genetics and experience Anatomy of the nervous system Neural conduction and synaptic transmission The research methods of biopsychology The visual system Mechanisms of perception: hearing, touch, smell, taste and attention The sensorimotor system Development of the nervous system Brain damage and neuroplasticity Learning, memory and amnesia Hunger, eating and health Hormones and sex Sleep, dreaming and circadian rhythms Drug use, addiction and the brain's reward circuits Lateralisation, language and the split brain Biopsychology of emotion, stress and health Biopsychology of psychiatric disorders How the eighteen chapters fit together 1. Biopsychology as a neuroscience Biopsychology is the scientific study of the biology of behaviour. That one-line definition hides the thing that makes the field distinctive, so it is worth unpacking slowly. Neuroscience as a whole is the study of the nervous system, and it is enormous: it includes people who study how a single ion channel folds, people who model networks mathematically, and people who develop drugs. Biopsychology is the branch of neuroscience that keeps behaviour at the centre of the question. A biopsychologist does not ask "what does this structure do" in the abstract; the question is always "what does this structure do to what the organism thinks, feels, or does". Pinel's phrase for the discipline's contribution is that biopsychologists bring to neuroscience a knowledge of behaviour and of the methods of behavioural research, which the other neurosciences do not supply on their own. You can know everything about a receptor and still have no idea what an animal will do, because behaviour has its own laws and its own measurement problems. The name was not always this. Earlier labels included psychobiology, behavioural biology and behavioural neuroscience, and you will still meet all of them. Pinel prefers biopsychology precisely because the word order carries the argument: bio is the adjective and psychology is the noun, so the discipline is a kind of psychology that uses biology, not a kind of biology that happens to notice behaviour. The founding text: Hebb, 1949 Biopsychology has a reasonably clean origin date. In 1949 Donald O. Hebb published The Organization of Behavior , and this is generally taken as the first comprehensive theory of how complex psychological phenomena (perception, emotion, thought, memory) could be produced by ordinary activity in the brain. Why that mattered is easy to miss now that it is obvious. Before Hebb, the widespread assumption among psychologists was that complex mental events were simply too complex to be traceable to neural activity, so the honest thing was to study behaviour and leave the brain alone. Hebb's move was to show that you could actually specify a mechanism. The human brain: Appearances can be deceiving! Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 1.1 His mechanism was the Hebb synapse , usually compressed into the slogan "cells that fire together wire together". Stated properly: if a presynaptic neuron repeatedly participates in firing a postsynaptic neuron, some growth process or metabolic change occurs at that synapse so that the presynaptic neuron's later ability to fire the postsynaptic one is increased. Chain those strengthened synapses together and you get a cell assembly , a set of neurons that has been wired into a functional unit by experience and can now be re-activated as a whole by any part of it. Chain assemblies in sequence and you get a phase sequence , which is Hebb's account of a train of thought. Notice the structure of the argument: a single local, plausible, physical rule, applied repeatedly, yields something that looks psychological. That is the template for essentially every biopsychological explanation that follows in this book. Hebb built his theory from a genuinely mixed evidence base, and this is the second thing he established as normal practice: experiments on laboratory animals, clinical case studies of human patients, and logical argument all counted. He did not privilege one. High-yield Hebb (1949), The Organization of Behavior = the founding of biopsychology as a discipline, and the first real theory of how psychological phenomena arise from brain activity. Hebbian learning: co-active neurons strengthen their synapse. Cell assembly (a wired-together group) then phase sequence (a chain of assemblies, i.e. a thought). Nobel prizes specifically related to the nervous system or behavior. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Table 1.1 Human subjects and animal subjects Biopsychology studies both humans and non-human animals, and each has real advantages, so the choice is a research-design decision rather than a matter of taste. Human participants have three obvious advantages. They follow instructions, which means you can run a task instead of waiting for a behaviour to occur spontaneously. They report subjective experience, which is the only direct access anyone has to conscious content. And they are cheaper: no purpose-built housing, no colony maintenance. There is a fourth advantage that is easy to overlook: they have a human brain, and if the question is about a specifically human capacity such as syntax, only a human brain will do. Animal subjects have a different and equally real set of advantages. Their nervous systems are simpler, so the effect you are looking for is not buried under the extra machinery. The comparative approach becomes available: studying the same system across species lets you separate the general biological principle from the local human quirk, and it is usually only across species that you can see what a structure is for . It is possible to run genuinely invasive experiments, meaning lesions, direct stimulation, single-cell recording, and selective breeding, which are the only methods that establish causation cleanly. And practically, you can control genetics, rearing, and history in ways that are simply not possible with people. The six divisions of biopsychology Pinel divides the field six ways. The division is by method and subject , not by topic, which is the single most common thing students get wrong here. Two people can both be studying memory and belong to different divisions. The six divisions of biopsychology, and how they overlap. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 1.4 Division The defining question Method and subjects Physiological psychology What neural mechanism produces this behaviour? Direct manipulation of the brain: lesions, electrical stimulation, surgery. Almost always laboratory animals. Pure research. Psychopharmacology How do drugs change behaviour and the brain? Manipulation by drug rather than by scalpel. Animals and humans. Strongly applied: it is where therapeutic drugs come from. Neuropsychology What are the psychological effects of brain damage? Human patients with existing brain damage. Case studies plus standardised test batteries. Never experimental brain damage. The most applied division. Psychophysiology How does physiological activity relate to behaviour in intact people? Non-invasive recording from the surface of healthy human volunteers: EEG, heart rate, blood pressure, skin conductance, pupil diameter, EMG, EOG. Cognitive neuroscience What is the neural basis of cognition? Predominantly functional brain imaging (fMRI, PET) in healthy humans performing cognitive tasks. Highly collaborative and interdisciplinary. Comparative psychology How and why did this behaviour evolve? Comparison across species , including ethology (behaviour in the wild) and evolutionary/behavioural genetics. Visual tracking of a pendulum by a healthy control participant (top) and three participants with schizophrenia. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 1.5 Functional brain imaging is the major method of cognitive neuroscience. This image—taken from the top of the head with the participant lying on her back—reveals the locations of high levels of neural activity at one level of the brain as th… Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 1.6 Trap Three of these six names are routinely confused, and papers exploit it. Physiological psychology = invasive manipulation, animals, pure research. Psychophysiology = non-invasive measurement, healthy humans, no manipulation of the brain at all. Neuropsychology = pre-existing brain damage in human patients. The give-away words in a question stem are "lesioned rats" (physiological), "skin conductance in volunteers" (psychophysiology), and "patient with left temporal damage" (neuropsychology). The six major divisions of biopsychology with examples of how they have approached the study of memory. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Table 1.2 Converging operations: why one method is never enough Every method in the list above is flawed, and each is flawed in its own particular direction. Lesion studies establish that a structure is necessary but tell you nothing about what it contributes when intact, and a lesion inevitably damages fibres that are merely passing through. Imaging shows correlated activity but cannot show that the activity is doing any work. Human case studies are rich but uncontrolled, since the damage was not assigned to the patient by a researcher. Animal experiments are controlled but raise the question of whether the finding generalises. The field's response is the strategy Pinel calls converging operations : attack a single problem with several methods whose weaknesses do not overlap, and trust the conclusion only where they agree. The classic worked example is Korsakoff's syndrome . Human case studies of chronic alcoholics showed a devastating amnesia, which invited the conclusion that alcohol is the cause. But converging evidence changed the answer. Some patients with the syndrome had no history of alcohol at all, but did have severe malnutrition. Alcoholics eat badly and alcohol interferes with the absorption of thiamine (vitamin B 1 ). Giving thiamine to Korsakoff patients halted progression, and thiamine-deprived animals developed comparable brain damage without alcohol. The conclusion that survives all the methods is that Korsakoff's syndrome is caused by thiamine deficiency , with alcohol as the usual route to that deficiency and an additional independent toxin in its own right. No single method could have got there. Scientific inference: how you study something you cannot see The brain's workings are not directly observable, so biopsychology relies on scientific inference : you measure something you can observe, and reason back to the invisible mechanism that must have produced it. This is not a weakness peculiar to the field. It is what physics does with subatomic particles. What matters is that the inference is disciplined. President Calvin Coolidge and Mrs. Grace Coolidge. Many students think the Coolidge effect is named after a biopsychologist named Coolidge. In fact, it is named after President Calvin Coolidge, of whom the following story is told. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 1.2 The textbook illustration is the perception of movement during eye movement. Your eyes are constantly making rapid saccades , so the image of the world sweeps across your retina many times a second, yet the world does not appear to jump. Two competing inferences are available. Either the brain tracks the eye's position by monitoring feedback from the eye muscles, or it uses the motor command it has just issued to the eye muscles, that is, it knows where it told the eye to go. You cannot see which. But you can design an observation that separates them. If the eye is prevented from moving while the command to move is still issued, a feedback account predicts the world will look stationary (no movement occurred, no feedback), whereas a command-based account predicts the world should appear to jump (a command was issued, so a compensation is applied that nothing cancels). The world does appear to move. The inference is therefore that the visual system compensates using the outgoing motor signal , a copy of the command, rather than sensory feedback from the muscles. Note the form: an unobservable mechanism, two rival accounts, and one observable consequence on which they disagree.
