That gap is the central tension of the field, taken up in section 1.10. 1.6 Where clinical psychologists work Internationally, clinical psychologists work in general hospitals (psychiatry, and increasingly neurology, paediatrics, oncology and pain services); psychiatric hospitals ; outpatient clinics and community mental health services ; private practice ; universities and medical colleges ; schools , usually as consultants alongside school psychologists and counsellors; forensic and correctional settings , assessing fitness to stand trial, mental state at the time of an offence, risk of violence and child custody; rehabilitation centres for brain injury, substance dependence and developmental disabilities; and industry , through employee assistance and occupational health programmes. In India the pattern is shaped by the public health system and by the scarcity of trained clinical psychologists. In the public sector the largest group works in general hospital psychiatry units , the psychiatry departments of medical college and district hospitals, alongside psychiatrists, psychiatric social workers and psychiatric nurses. The national and regional institutes are both treatment and training centres. The National Institute of Mental Health and Neurosciences (NIMHANS) in Bengaluru is the country's leading institution, with a department of clinical psychology running child and adolescent, neuropsychology, family and addiction services and training students through a competitive entrance examination. The Central Institute of Psychiatry at Ranchi, founded in 1918, is one of the country's oldest psychiatric institutions and a long-standing training centre. Others include the Institute of Human Behaviour and Allied Sciences in Delhi and the Lokopriya Gopinath Bordoloi Regional Institute of Mental Health in Tezpur. At community level, the District Mental Health Programme , launched in 1996 under the National Mental Health Programme of 1982 and built on a pilot in Bellary district of Karnataka, aims to bring care to each district through a team that includes a psychiatrist, a clinical psychologist, a psychiatric social worker and a psychiatric nurse; many of these posts have been hard to fill. The national tele-mental-health service, Tele-MANAS, launched in 2022, is a newer public setting. Indian clinical psychologists also work in private practice, increasingly online; in special schools, rehabilitation and de-addiction centres; in community mental health organisations; in courts and child welfare; and in corporate wellness. They contribute to the assessments through which intellectual disability and specific learning disability are formally certified. 1.7 How clinical psychology differs from its neighbouring professions Several professions work in the same territory, often with the same patient. They differ in training, in the questions they are equipped to answer, in the methods they may use, and in how they are regulated. Psychiatry. A psychiatrist is a medical doctor: in India, a Bachelor of Medicine and Bachelor of Surgery followed by a postgraduate qualification in psychiatry such as the Doctor of Medicine. As physicians, psychiatrists can prescribe medication, order investigations, admit patients and give physical treatments such as electroconvulsive therapy (Ugo Cerletti and Lucio Bini, 1938). The clinical psychologist holds a psychology degree, does not prescribe, and specialises in psychological assessment, psychological treatment and research. The two overlap, since some psychiatrists practise psychotherapy and every clinical psychologist must understand diagnosis and medication, but the core of one is medicine and of the other psychology. In a good team they are colleagues with different tools. Counselling psychology. Its roots lie in the vocational guidance movement, usually traced to Frank Parsons, who opened a vocation bureau in Boston in 1908 and whose Choosing a Vocation appeared in 1909, and in student counselling. It was later shaped by Carl Rogers, whose 1942 book Counseling and Psychotherapy gave it a humanistic emphasis on the relationship and the client's capacity for growth. Historically counselling psychologists worked with the normal range of adjustment (careers, life transitions, relationship strain), emphasised strengths and prevention, and worked in settings such as university counselling centres, while clinical psychologists worked more with severe disorder, in hospitals, using formal testing. In the United States the difference has narrowed greatly, and both are licensed as psychologists. In India the difference is also legal: counselling psychology is taught through master's degrees but is not a category the Rehabilitation Council registers. School psychology. School psychologists assess children with learning and behavioural difficulties, plan special educational provision and consult with teachers and parents. In the United States they usually hold a specialist-level or doctoral degree. In India school psychology has not developed as a separate licensed profession; schools usually employ counsellors, and children with suspected learning disabilities are commonly assessed by clinical psychologists in hospitals and clinics. Health psychology. Health psychology applies psychology to physical health: why people smoke or skip medication, how stress affects the body, how people cope with chronic illness and pain. It rests on the biopsychosocial model proposed by the physician George Engel in 1977; the American Psychological Association created its health psychology division in 1978, with Joseph Matarazzo a leading figure in defining the field. Many health psychologists are researchers; the clinical branch overlaps with clinical psychology in medical settings. Psychiatric social work. In India the established qualification has been a Master of Social Work followed by a two-year Master of Philosophy in Psychiatric Social Work, and the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 defines psychiatric social workers by that qualification and provides for their registration as mental health professionals. Their focus is the person in their social world: family work, social and economic circumstances, community resources and welfare entitlements, discharge planning and rehabilitation. They are not trained in psychological testing. Psychiatric nursing. Psychiatric nurses are trained nurses specialised in mental health, in India through qualifications such as a Master of Science in Psychiatric Nursing, registered through the nursing councils. They provide round-the-clock ward care, monitor patients, administer prescribed medication, manage risk, provide psychoeducation and increasingly work in the community. Psychotherapists and counsellors without licensing. In many countries, India included, "psychotherapist" and "counsellor" have not been protected titles, so people with anything from a short certificate to a master's degree may offer therapy, and clients have little way to judge competence and no regulator to complain to. This differs from planned task sharing , in which community health workers are trained to deliver a specific structured treatment under supervision, an approach tested in careful trials, including in India. The problem is unregulated practice, not non-psychologists helping. India's National Commission for Allied and Healthcare Professions Act of 2021 brought psychologists other than clinical psychologists, and various counsellors, into a new regulatory framework, but its machinery has been slow to take shape, so check the current position before relying on it. Profession Basic training Central focus Prescribes? Regulation in India Clinical psychologist Formerly master's in psychology plus two-year clinical MPhil; now the Council-regulated two-year master's. Abroad, usually a doctorate. Psychological assessment, treatment and research across all severities and ages No (only in a few American states, after extra training) Rehabilitation Council of India, Central Rehabilitation Register Psychiatrist Medical degree plus postgraduate psychiatry Diagnosis and medical treatment of mental disorders Yes National Medical Commission and state medical councils Counselling psychologist Master's in counselling psychology; abroad, often a doctorate Normal-range adjustment, careers, transitions, strengths No Not a Rehabilitation Council category School psychologist Abroad, specialist or doctoral degree Learning and behaviour in schools No Not a distinct Indian profession Health psychologist Postgraduate health psychology Health behaviour, coping with physical illness, prevention No No separate register Psychiatric social worker Master of Social Work plus MPhil in Psychiatric Social Work Family, social circumstances, community resources, rehabilitation No Defined by qualification in the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 Psychiatric nurse Nursing degree plus psychiatric nursing specialisation Ward and community nursing care, administering medication No (administers only) Nursing councils Unlicensed therapist or counsellor Anything from a certificate to a master's Varies No Title historically unprotected Trap. Psychiatrist versus psychologist: the psychiatrist has a medical degree and can prescribe; the clinical psychologist has a psychology degree, does not prescribe in India, and is the specialist in psychological testing. Clinical versus counselling psychologist: historically the range of clients (severe disorder versus normal-range adjustment) and the roots (testing and hospitals versus vocational guidance); in India also a legal difference, since only the clinical psychologist is registered by the Rehabilitation Council. 1.8 The prescription privileges debate "Prescription privileges" means limited legal authority for psychologists, after substantial extra training, to prescribe psychiatric medication. In the United States the movement gained momentum through a Department of Defense demonstration project in the 1990s that trained a small number of military psychologists to prescribe. New Mexico became the first state to grant such authority in 2002, followed by Louisiana in 2004 and later a handful of others, including Illinois, Iowa and Idaho. The extra training typically involves a postdoctoral master's degree in clinical psychopharmacology, supervised practice and an examination, and prescribing is usually done in collaboration with the patient's physician. The American Psychological Association has supported the movement. The case for it rests on access and integration : rural areas have too few psychiatrists, one clinician who understands both the psychology and the medication might offer more coherent care, and other non-physicians such as nurse practitioners already prescribe. The case against comes from two directions. Medical organisations argue that psychiatric drugs act on the whole body, interact with other medicines and are given to patients whose physical illnesses may themselves cause psychological symptoms, so safe prescribing needs a full medical education. Some psychologists object that the profession would lose its identity as the discipline of psychological treatment, drift into the medical model it has long criticised, and become more exposed to the pharmaceutical industry. In India the debate is not live: prescribing is restricted to registered medical practitioners, and clinical psychologists work alongside psychiatrists who prescribe. 1.9 Clinical psychology as a profession in India The Rehabilitation Council of India and its Act The body that regulates the training and registration of clinical psychologists in India is the Rehabilitation Council of India (RCI) . Set up in 1986 as a registered society, it became a statutory body through the Rehabilitation Council of India Act, 1992 , amended in 2000 to broaden its role, and functions under the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment through the Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities. It regulates the training of rehabilitation professionals, recognises institutions and courses, standardises syllabi, maintains the register of qualified professionals, and promotes research and continuing education. Students are often puzzled that clinical psychologists fall under a disability council rather than a health council. The reason is historical: the Council registers the range of professionals who work with persons with disabilities, such as special educators, audiologists and speech therapists, and psychologists were included because psychological assessment and intervention are central to identifying and rehabilitating intellectual disability, learning disability, mental illness and other disabilities. The consequence is clear: in India it is the Council's recognition that makes a clinical psychology qualification a professional one. The Central Rehabilitation Register and why registration matters A person who completes a Council-recognised course may be entered on the Central Rehabilitation Register and receives a registration number. Under the Act, only a professional with a recognised qualification who is enrolled on the register may practise as a rehabilitation professional, hold such a post in government or publicly run institutions, sign certificates the law requires from such a professional, or give expert evidence in court in that field, and contravening these provisions is an offence. Registration must be renewed periodically, with renewal tied to the Council's continuing rehabilitation education programmes. In practice, registration is what allows appointment to government hospital posts, makes a psychologist's report acceptable in official processes such as disability certification, and lets the public check whether someone calling themselves a clinical psychologist is qualified. The Mental Healthcare Act 2017 India's main mental health law points to the same gate. The Mental Healthcare Act 2017 defines a clinical psychologist by reference to a clinical psychology qualification recognised by the Rehabilitation Council, or a master's in psychology followed by a two-year full-time Master of Philosophy in Clinical Psychology (or in Medical and Social Psychology) with supervised clinical training, approved by the Council. It then provides for clinical psychologists, psychiatric social workers and mental health nurses to be registered by the State Mental Health Authority to work as "mental health professionals", the category, alongside psychiatrists, to which the Act's provisions refer. The training routes For decades the route was long and narrow: a three-year bachelor's degree, a two-year master's in psychology, then a competitive entrance examination for a handful of seats on a two-year, full-time Master of Philosophy (MPhil) in Clinical Psychology at a Council-approved centre such as NIMHANS, the Central Institute of Psychiatry, the Institute of Human Behaviour and Allied Sciences or a medical college psychiatry department. It combined theory papers with intensive supervised clinical work and a dissertation, and led to registration. That route is being replaced. The National Education Policy 2020 recommended discontinuing the MPhil, and the University Grants Commission's regulations of 2022 stopped universities from offering it. The Council responded with a professional two-year RCI-regulated Master of Arts (or Master of Science) in Clinical Psychology , which from the 2025 to 2026 academic year serves as the licensing route at the major centres; NIMHANS calls its version the Master's in Clinical Psychology. Under the Council's programme document, entry rests on a four-year bachelor's degree in psychology, with alternative routes for students from the older three-year system; there are six papers over two years, with roughly half the marks from practical work, case records and a research thesis; trainees must complete minimum numbers of supervised case histories, interviews and psychodiagnostic and neuropsychological assessments, and supervised hours in psychotherapy and behaviour therapy; and selection is prescribed as entrance test and interview weighted 70 percent and 30 percent, though institutions have adopted this at different speeds. Only the second leads to registration. The degree's name proves nothing; what matters is whether that programme at that campus is on the Rehabilitation Council's list of approved institutions. 1.10 Science and practice: the central tension Researchers study groups under controlled conditions and report what happens on average. Practitioners face one person, now, with several problems at once, a family with its own views, and circumstances no study sampled. Researchers are tempted to see practitioners as relying on intuition; practitioners are tempted to see research as irrelevant. Much of the history of clinical psychology is the history of attempts to bring the two together. Two episodes show why science matters to practice. In 1952 Hans Eysenck argued that about two thirds of neurotic patients improved within two years with or without psychotherapy, so there was no convincing evidence that therapy helped. Decades of research followed, and in 1977 Mary Lee Smith and Gene Glass combined hundreds of outcome studies using the then new technique of meta-analysis and concluded that psychotherapy was, on average, clearly more effective than no treatment: the question was settled by evidence, not by therapists' conviction. In 1954 Paul Meehl's Clinical versus Statistical Prediction reviewed studies in which simple statistical rules predicted outcomes as well as or better than experienced clinicians using the same information. His point was not that clinicians are useless but that judgement is fallible, prone to seeing what one expects and to overconfidence, and should be checked against structured methods. The modern expression of the scientific side is evidence-based practice . David Sackett and colleagues described evidence-based medicine in 1996 as the conscientious and judicious use of the best current evidence in decisions about individual patients. In psychology, a Society of Clinical Psychology task force in the mid-1990s, whose work is associated with Dianne Chambless, drew up criteria and lists of empirically supported treatments, and in 2006 an American Psychological Association task force defined evidence-based practice in psychology as "the integration of the best available research with clinical expertise in the context of patient characteristics, culture, and preferences". All three parts matter. Critics note that trial patients are often selected for a single clear diagnosis while real patients rarely have one, that short manual-based treatments are easier to test and so dominate the lists, and that factors common to all therapies, such as the therapeutic relationship, may matter more than specific techniques. A useful bridge was proposed by George Stricker and Steven Trierweiler in 1995: the clinician as a local clinical scientist , who brings the scientific attitude, not only the published findings, to each case, treating hunches as hypotheses, gathering information in the session to test them, considering alternative explanations, watching for their own biases, and attending to features of the client and culture that no general study captured. Case. A 19-year-old student has stopped attending college. The psychologist's first hunch is depression, but she holds it as one hypothesis among several: depression, social anxiety about a new English-medium college after schooling in Tamil, a substance problem, or bullying. She gives brief depression and social anxiety questionnaires and asks him to record when he avoids college and what he is thinking. He attends happily when unlikely to be asked to speak, and avoids exactly the classes with presentations. Her hypothesis shifts to social anxiety linked to language, the plan changes, and she keeps measuring to check she was right. This is why a foundations course starts here: the identity sets the standard by which everything later is judged, tests by reliability and validity, therapies by evidence of what works for whom, conduct by ethics and registration. The same standard applies to positive psychology. Martin Seligman, during his 1998 presidency of the American Psychological Association and in a 2000 special issue of the American Psychologist edited with Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi, argued that after the Second World War, with funding flowing through the Veterans Administration and the new National Institute of Mental Health into treating illness, psychology had become largely a science of repairing damage and had neglected building strengths. The growth clause in the Division 12 definition was always there; positive psychology asked the field to act on it, and later chapters show that some of its own famous claims did not survive scrutiny, which is why the scientific standard must apply there too. Key. Being a scientist-practitioner does not mean every clinician runs studies. It means every clinician thinks like a scientist about their own practice: choosing treatments by evidence, measuring outcomes, treating formulations as hypotheses, checking judgement against structured tools, and fitting the evidence to the particular person and culture. 1.11 A day in the life: the roles made concrete Case. Ananya (a composite, not a real person) is a clinical psychologist registered with the Rehabilitation Council, seven years into work in the psychiatry department of a government medical college hospital in a mid-sized Indian city. This is an ordinary Tuesday. At 8.30, in the case conference, the team discusses a 24-year-old man admitted with a first episode of psychosis. The psychiatrist has started medication; Ananya will assess his cognitive functioning once he settles, and proposes psychoeducation for his parents, who believe the illness is black magic. At 9.30 she assesses an 8-year-old boy referred by his school for poor marks, interviewing his parents, observing him, and giving an intelligence test standardised on Indian children, an adaptive behaviour measure, and reading, writing and arithmetic tests. She keeps several explanations open: intellectual disability, a specific learning disorder, trouble at home, an undetected hearing or vision problem, or studying in English when the family speaks Kannada. His intelligence is average and his reading far below it; her report recommends assessment for specific learning disorder, remedial teaching and examination accommodations. At 11.30 a 32-year-old software engineer comes for her sixth session of cognitive behaviour therapy for panic disorder. Her weekly questionnaire and panic diary show attacks falling from daily to twice a week. They practise bringing on the feared bodily sensations so she learns they are not dangerous, and plan a family session because her mother-in-law calls the problem weakness. At 1.00 a physician asks whether a 70-year-old man who wants to stop dialysis is depressed and able to decide. Ananya assesses his mood and cognition, hears his reasons, and advises the physician, who keeps responsibility for the decision. At 2.00 she supervises two master's trainees and discusses a 15-year-old client who has disclosed self-harm and asked that her parents not be told. At 3.00 she enters outcome data from the department's group programme for alcohol dependence; at 4.00 a departmental meeting covers rosters and next week's District Mental Health Programme outreach camp. Read the day against the six activities. The conference and the boy's evaluation are assessment , aimed at understanding. The dialysis question is consultation and also prediction : is this wish the product of a treatable depression? The panic session and family work are intervention , aimed at alleviating discomfort. The trainees' session is supervision , its ethical weight visible in the self-harm dilemma; the outcome data are research ; the rosters and camp are administration . In one day she has met maladjustment (the boy failing at school), disability (psychosis, a possible learning disorder) and discomfort (panic). The scientist-practitioner identity runs through it: rival hypotheses about the boy, tested rather than assumed; weekly measurement of panic; a treatment chosen for its research support; an evaluation of her own department's programme. So does culture: the language of schooling, beliefs about black magic, a family's reading of panic as weakness. And registration matters, because her report will feed into disability certification and school accommodations, and her government post requires it. A private practitioner would do the same six things in a different balance, with far more psychotherapy. Recap. Clinical psychology, as the American Psychological Association's Society of Clinical Psychology defines it, integrates science, theory and practice to understand, predict and alleviate maladjustment, disability and discomfort, and to promote adaptation, adjustment and personal development across all aspects of functioning, the life span, cultures and socioeconomic levels. Lightner Witmer founded the field with his University of Pennsylvania clinic in 1896 and named it in 1907, using "clinical" for a method of studying one individual in order to help them. The profession is distinguished by science and practice integrated in one person, the individual case approach, expertise in measurement, breadth and cultural awareness. Its members assess, treat, research, teach and supervise, consult and administer, in hospitals, national institutes, district programmes, private practice, courts and rehabilitation centres. They differ from psychiatrists (medical training, prescribing), counselling psychologists (vocational roots, normal-range adjustment) and the other neighbouring professions in training, focus and regulation, and prescription privileges exist only in a few American states. In India the Rehabilitation Council of India regulates the profession under its 1992 Act through the Central Rehabilitation Register, the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 defines clinical psychologists by Council-recognised training, and the MPhil route is giving way to the Council-regulated two-year master's. Beneath everything lies the tension between science and practice, which the scientist-practitioner model, evidence-based practice and the local clinical scientist each try to resolve. Critically examine the definition given by the Society of Clinical Psychology (Division 12 of the American Psychological Association), explaining each component with examples. Discuss the contribution of Lightner Witmer. What did he mean by "clinical", and how far does the modern profession remain faithful to his idea? Using a day in the life of a clinical psychologist, show how assessment, intervention, research, teaching and supervision, consultation and administration fit together in practice. 2 How clinical psychology came to be Clinical psychology is a young profession built on very old questions. People have always tried to explain why someone hears voices, sinks into despair or cannot learn to read. Over the centuries the explanations changed, and each new explanation brought a new kind of helper: the priest, the physician, the asylum keeper, the psychiatrist and, only in the last hundred and thirty years, the clinical psychologist. This chapter tells that story as a chain of causes, in which each stage grew out of problems the previous stage could not solve. It moves from supernatural and humoral ideas of madness, through the asylums and the moral treatment (Philippe Pinel and William Tuke) reformers, to psychiatry's classification of disorders; then to the laboratory psychology that supplied the first testing tools, Lightner Witmer's first clinic, Sigmund Freud, the two world wars, the training conferences, Hans Eysenck's attack on psychotherapy and the evidence-based era. It closes with the growth of the profession in India, the system in which you will train. Examiners use this material to test whether you understand why the profession looks the way it does, not only whether you can recite dates. 2.1 Before psychology: spirits, humours and the body The oldest explanation of disturbed behaviour is supernatural. If a person suddenly behaved in ways the community could not understand, the most available explanation was that an outside force had entered them: a demon, an offended god, an angry ancestor or a curse. The logic is consistent: if a spirit is the cause, the cure is to remove or placate it, so treatment took the form of prayer, sacrifice, exorcism and sometimes punishment of the body the spirit occupied. Textbooks often mention trephination , the Stone Age practice of cutting a hole in the skull, as an attempt to release evil spirits. Treat that claim with caution: some trephined skulls show healing, so people survived the operation, but there is no record of why it was done, and many historians think it more often treated head injuries or headaches. The decisive break came in classical Greece with Hippocrates (usually dated around 460 to 370 BCE) and the writings associated with his name. The Hippocratic physicians held that mental disturbance has natural causes, located thought and madness in the brain, and argued that epilepsy, "the sacred disease", was no more divine than any other illness. Their explanation was the theory of the four humours : blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile. Health was a balance of these fluids and illness an excess or deficiency of one. Too much black bile produced melancholia (literally "black bile"), a state of sadness and fear; other described states included mania and phrenitis , an acute delirium with fever. Treatment followed from the theory: diet, rest, bathing and removal of the excess humour by bleeding or purging. The theory was wrong in its details but right in its method: mental disturbance belongs to nature, can be classified by observation, and should be treated by physicians rather than priests. The Greek physician Galen , practising in Rome in the second century CE, extended this into four enduring temperaments : sanguine (cheerful, blood), phlegmatic (calm, phlegm), choleric (irritable, yellow bile) and melancholic (gloomy, black bile). Because his works were taught for over a thousand years in Europe and the Islamic world, Galenic medicine framed thinking about body and mind until the scientific revolution. Indian medicine offered a parallel: Ayurveda explains health as a balance of three doshas (vata, pitta and kapha), and the Charaka Samhita describes unmada , severe mental disturbance, while a separate branch dealt with spirit possession. Natural and supernatural explanations lived side by side, as they still do in Indian families who visit a temple or dargah before, or alongside, a psychiatrist. Trap. Do not write that the ancient world was purely superstitious and that science began only in Europe after 1800. Natural explanations of madness are over two thousand years old in Greek and Indian medicine. What was new in the nineteenth century was the experimental method and the institutions that made systematic study possible. 2.2 Asylums and the moral treatment reform In medieval and early modern Europe supernatural explanation revived. The Malleus Maleficarum ("The Hammer of Witches", 1480s) was a manual for identifying witches, and some historians argue that many people executed as witches were mentally ill, though others think this is exaggerated. A few physicians protested; the Dutch physician Johann Weyer argued in 1563 that many accused witches were ill and needed medical care. From the sixteenth to the eighteenth centuries, cities increasingly confined the mad in asylums , the best known being London's Bethlem Hospital, whose nickname "Bedlam" became a word for chaos. The motive was social, not therapeutic: growing towns wanted beggars and the insane off the streets. Chains, beatings, bleeding and overcrowding were common, and some asylums let paying visitors watch the inmates. The belief underneath was that a person who had lost reason was closer to an animal, to be restrained rather than understood. Late eighteenth-century Enlightenment ideas of human dignity collided with this reality, producing moral treatment . "Moral" here meant psychological or emotional, as opposed to physical. The reformers held that the insane were ordinary people disturbed by stress, grief or a disordered life, who could recover if treated with respect in a calm environment with useful work and a relationship of trust. Who gave us this. Philippe Pinel (1745 to 1826), a French physician, became physician at the Bicêtre hospital in Paris in 1793, during the Revolution, and later at the Salpêtrière. He is famous for removing the patients' chains, and his 1801 treatise on mental alienation argued for careful observation and humane, psychological treatment. The heroic picture of Pinel striking off the chains needs correcting. Much of the practical reform came from Jean-Baptiste Pussin , the ward's governor, who had first come to Bicêtre as a patient himself (for a physical illness) and had already begun replacing chains with gentler restraint. Pinel learned from him and credited him; the single-hero legend was polished later. Who gave us this. William Tuke (1732 to 1822), an English Quaker merchant, opened the York Retreat in 1796 after a Quaker woman died in the local York Asylum, where her friends had been refused visits. The Retreat offered a country house, gardens, work, shared meals and kindness, without chains. In the United States the great campaigner was Dorothea Dix (1802 to 1887), a Massachusetts schoolteacher. Teaching Sunday school in a jail in 1841, she found mentally ill women held in unheated cells with criminals. She surveyed the state's jails and almshouses and in 1843 presented a memorial to the Massachusetts legislature describing people confined "in cages, closets, cellars, stalls, pens". For four decades she lobbied state after state and helped found or enlarge dozens of state hospitals. Moral treatment worked best in small institutions where a superintendent knew every patient. The state hospitals Dix fought for filled far beyond capacity with chronic patients, the elderly, people with syphilis of the brain and poor immigrants. Staff could no longer know their patients, recovery rates fell, and by the late 1800s the asylum was once again mainly custodial. That failure pushed psychiatry towards biology and classification, and left open the question of how to give effective psychological help to many people. Why it matters. Chaining is not only history. In 2001 a fire at a faith-healing shrine at Erwadi in Tamil Nadu killed many mentally ill people who were chained and could not escape. The debates of Pinel's and Dix's time about dignity and restraint are the debates that shaped India's Mental Healthcare Act of 2017. 2.3 Psychiatry organises itself: Kraepelin and classification By the nineteenth century asylum doctors had become a medical specialty, psychiatry. Their problem was that asylum patients looked bewilderingly varied and there was no agreed way to sort them, so doctors could not predict recovery, compare results or search for causes. A scientific success encouraged a biological approach: general paresis, a common asylum illness with grandiose delusions and progressive dementia, was shown to be caused by syphilis infecting the brain. If one madness had a physical cause, perhaps all did. Who gave us this. Emil Kraepelin (1856 to 1926), a German psychiatrist who had trained in Wilhelm Wundt's laboratory, published a textbook of psychiatry in 1883 and revised it through many editions. In the sixth edition (1899) he separated dementia praecox from manic-depressive insanity . Kraepelin kept detailed records of large numbers of patients and followed them over years. His insight was that symptoms at one moment can mislead; what distinguishes disorders is their course and outcome . Dementia praecox began young and deteriorated without full recovery; manic-depressive insanity came in episodes with recovery between them. That division, between what we now call schizophrenia and the mood disorders, remains the backbone of classification. Eugen Bleuler renamed dementia praecox "schizophrenia" in 1911, arguing it did not always end in dementia and that its core was a splitting of mental functions, not a split personality. The official systems grew from Kraepelin's approach: the International Classification of Diseases added mental disorders in its sixth revision (1948), the American Psychiatric Association published the first Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM) in 1952, and the symptom-based editions from 1980 onward are called "neo-Kraepelinian". Key. By 1900 two traditions were ready: psychiatry, which classified disorders and ran the institutions, and a new scientific psychology that could measure individual minds. Clinical psychology was born where they met. Kraepelin was not a clinical psychologist; his gift to the field was the classification it would later assess and treat within. 2.4 Scientific psychology supplies the tools Clinical psychology needed psychology to exist first as a science separate from philosophy. Three lines of nineteenth-century work fed it: Wilhelm Wundt's laboratory, which made psychology experimental; Francis Galton's and Cattell's study of individual differences, which made measuring persons possible; and Alfred Binet's intelligence test, which gave the first clinical psychologists their main tool. Who gave us this. Wilhelm Wundt (1832 to 1920) founded the first laboratory of experimental psychology at the University of Leipzig in 1879, the conventional birth date of psychology as an independent science. Wundt studied conscious experience through trained introspection under controlled conditions, measuring reaction times with instruments. He sought general laws of the mind and had little interest in individual differences or practical application. His importance for clinical work is that he showed mental processes could be measured, and that he trained the students who carried the method outward, including Emil Kraepelin, James McKeen Cattell and Lightner Witmer. Francis Galton (1822 to 1911), an English scientist and half-cousin of Charles Darwin, asked the opposite question: how and why do people differ? Inspired by evolution, which depends on variation, he published Hereditary Genius in 1869 and opened an anthropometric laboratory in London in 1884, where the public paid to have reaction time, grip strength and sensory sharpness measured. To analyse the data he developed the ideas of correlation and regression that every psychology student now uses. He also coined the word eugenics and urged that the "unfit" be discouraged from having children, an idea that later fed forced sterilisation laws and Nazi policy. Testing's history is bound up with that ideology, which is why clinicians are trained to ask what a score will be used for. James McKeen Cattell (1860 to 1944) took his doctorate under Wundt and then worked with Galton. In an 1890 article he coined the term mental test for a battery of simple measures: grip strength, reaction time, sensitivity to pain, memory for letters and judgement of time. The hope that these revealed mental efficiency failed. In 1901 Clark Wissler, a student at Columbia, found that the tests hardly correlated with college grades. Simple sensory measures did not capture complex thinking, which cleared the way for a different kind of test. Who gave us this. Alfred Binet (1857 to 1911) and Théodore Simon (1872 to 1961) published the Binet-Simon scale in Paris in 1905, the first practical intelligence test, revised in 1908 and 1911. The scale answered a practical problem. France had made schooling compulsory, and the education ministry wanted a fair way to identify children needing special education, rather than relying on teachers' impressions. Binet argued that intelligence shows itself in judgement, comprehension, reasoning and memory, and must be tested directly. With Simon he arranged thirty tasks in order of difficulty. The 1908 revision grouped tasks by the age at which typical children passed them, giving the idea of mental level , later mental age : a seven-year-old passing only five-year-old tasks was two years behind. Binet insisted the score described present performance, not a fixed inborn quantity, and that low scorers could be helped by teaching. Both warnings were largely ignored in America. Henry Goddard translated the scale for the Vineland Training School in New Jersey, but the influential American version came from Lewis Terman (1877 to 1956) of Stanford University, who published the Stanford-Binet Intelligence Scale in 1916. Terman revised the items, standardised them on American children and adopted the intelligence quotient (IQ) proposed by the German psychologist William Stern : mental age divided by chronological age, multiplied by 100. A ten-year-old with a mental age of twelve has an IQ of 120. Giving the Stanford-Binet became the core job of the early clinical psychologist. Trap. Alfred Binet did not invent the IQ; Stern proposed it and Lewis Terman popularised it. Cattell coined "mental test", but his sensory and motor tests failed to predict school success. Keep the three names apart. 2.5 Lightner Witmer and the first psychological clinic Who gave us this. Lightner Witmer (1867 to 1956) earned his doctorate under Wilhelm Wundt and succeeded Cattell at the University of Pennsylvania, where in 1896 he opened the first psychological clinic . He coined the term clinical psychology and in 1907 founded the journal The Psychological Clinic . He is regarded as the founder of the field. The clinic began with one referral. A schoolteacher attending Witmer's classes brought him a boy who was a "chronic bad speller" and asked whether psychology, the science of the mind, could help. Witmer examined the boy's vision, memory and reading habits and designed remedial teaching. Other children followed, mostly with learning, speech or behaviour problems. Later that year he urged the American Psychological Association (founded 1892) to use psychology this way; most academics, who thought applied work beneath pure science, were unenthusiastic. By "clinical" Witmer did not mean medical. He borrowed the word to name a method : the intensive study of one individual by observation and experiment, with the aim of producing change. His clinic set lasting patterns. Assessment came first and relied on measurement rather than speculation. Assessment was tied to intervention, so diagnosis served a plan of help. Physicians, social workers and teachers worked as a team. The clinic also trained students and generated research. Do not overstate his influence. Witmer worked mainly with children and educational problems, took little interest in adult mental illness and was hostile to psychoanalysis. The post-war profession, focused on adult psychopathology and psychotherapy, owed more to Sigmund Freud and the wars. Other early developments broadened the field: William Healy opened a clinic for a Chicago juvenile court in 1909, beginning the child guidance movement, and Clifford Beers 's 1908 autobiography A Mind That Found Itself , describing his abuse in mental hospitals, launched the mental hygiene movement. Trap. The founder of clinical psychology is Lightner Witmer (1896), not Wilhelm Wundt (who founded experimental psychology in 1879), Sigmund Freud (psychoanalysis) or Emil Kraepelin (psychiatric classification). 2.6 Sigmund Freud and the psychoanalytic influence While Lightner Witmer tested children in Philadelphia, a Viennese neurologist was building a different approach. Sigmund Freud (1856 to 1939) studied in Paris in 1885 and 1886 with Jean-Martin Charcot , who showed that the paralyses of "hysteria" could be produced and removed by hypnosis, that is, by psychological means. In Vienna the physician Josef Breuer had found that his patient "Anna O" gained relief by talking about the emotional events tied to her symptoms, the "talking cure". Breuer and Freud published Studies on Hysteria in 1895. Freud replaced hypnosis with free association , asking patients to say whatever came to mind, and published The Interpretation of Dreams (dated 1900). Psychoanalysis held that much of mental life is unconscious , that symptoms are disguised expressions of conflicts rooted in childhood, and that the mind protects itself with defence mechanisms such as repression. The analyst listened to associations and dreams, noted the patient's resistance , and interpreted the transference , the reliving of feelings about past figures in the relationship with the analyst. Freud's 1909 lectures at Clark University in Massachusetts, at the invitation of G. Stanley Hall, spread these ideas across America. Freud shaped clinical psychology in four ways. He established psychotherapy, a structured conversation with a trained listener, as a legitimate treatment when most care was custody or physical methods. He defended "lay analysis" by non-physicians, though American institutes long restricted training to doctors until psychologists won a lawsuit in the 1980s. He shifted attention from asylum psychosis to the everyday anxieties and depressions of people in the community, the population later served in outpatient practice. And he inspired projective tests , which assume ambiguous material reveals unconscious processes: Hermann Rorschach 's inkblots (1921) and the Thematic Apperception Test of Henry Murray and Christiana Morgan (1935). The criticisms were serious too: the theory was hard to test, since almost any outcome could be explained afterwards; its evidence came from Freud's interpretations of few patients; and its long treatment was unavailable to most people. Those criticisms set up Hans Eysenck's challenge (section 2.9). Why it matters. Nearly every later therapy defined itself against Sigmund Freud: behaviour therapy rejected the unconscious, client-centred therapy rejected the expert interpreter, and cognitive therapy was founded by a psychoanalytically trained psychiatrist who lost faith in the theory. Yet the importance of the relationship, early experience and defences remains part of ordinary clinical thinking. 2.7 The world wars: from testers to therapists When the United States entered the First World War in 1917, the army had to sort well over a million recruits for training, officer selection or rejection. Robert Yerkes (1876 to 1956), then president of the American Psychological Association, led a committee, including Lewis Terman and Henry Goddard, that produced the first mass group tests , because the hour-long individual Stanford-Binet was useless at that scale. Army Alpha was a written, verbal test for recruits who could read English, with arithmetic, analogies, number series and general information. Army Beta was a non-verbal test for those who could not read or did not speak English, given by demonstration and using pictures, mazes and block counting. The programme made testing famous but left a shameful legacy: the tests were loaded with American cultural knowledge, and low scores among some immigrant groups were used in the early 1920s to argue for racial differences and restrictive immigration laws. The lesson that scores reflect language, schooling and culture matters to anyone using Western tests in India. Between the wars testing spread into schools, courts and child guidance clinics, but the clinical psychologist remained essentially a tester , usually of children, handing results to psychiatrists who controlled diagnosis and treatment. The Second World War changed this because it created a need psychiatry could not meet. Many recruits were rejected on psychiatric grounds and many more broke down in combat; psychologists recruited to select soldiers found themselves interviewing, running groups and treating them, and proved they could do it. After the war millions of veterans returned, many with psychiatric problems, and the hospitals of the Veterans Administration , the federal agency for former service members, were overwhelmed. From 1946 it funded doctoral training in clinical psychology, paying students to train in its hospitals, and became the largest employer of clinical psychologists. The National Mental Health Act of 1946 led to the National Institute of Mental Health in 1949, which funded research and training grants. This money created demand, redefined the job as work with adults with serious problems, and made treatment part of it. It also raised a question: which universities trained adequately? The Veterans Administration asked the American Psychological Association to find out, which led to accreditation and to the Boulder Conference. Key. The First World War made psychologists testers on a national scale (Army Alpha and Army Beta, Robert Yerkes). The Second World War and its aftermath made them therapists, because need outran the supply of psychiatrists and the Veterans Administration and National Institute of Mental Health paid for training. Trap. Alpha was verbal, for literate English speakers; Beta was non-verbal, for the illiterate and non-English speaking. And both belong to the First World War (1917 to 1918), not the Second. 2.8 How to train a clinical psychologist: Boulder, Vail and the clinical scientists The recurring question in training is how to balance the scientist who produces knowledge and the practitioner who helps individuals. Three answers have been given, each when the previous one seemed inadequate. Who gave us this. David Shakow (1901 to 1981), who had trained interns for years at Worcester State Hospital in Massachusetts, chaired the American Psychological Association committee whose 1947 report (the Shakow Report) proposed doctoral training combining research and clinical work. The Boulder Conference of 1949 adopted its principles. In 1949 psychologists from universities and clinics met for two weeks at Boulder, Colorado, and endorsed the scientist-practitioner model . Clinical psychologists would be trained in university psychology departments for the Doctor of Philosophy (PhD), combining general psychology and research methods with supervised assessment and therapy, a year-long internship and an original dissertation. Practice would raise questions for research, and research would guide practice. Critics soon noted that most graduates went into practice and did little research, and that the supply of graduates could not meet demand. Those frustrations produced the Doctor of Psychology (PsyD). The University of Illinois began the first PsyD programme in 1968 under Donald Peterson , and in 1973 a national conference at Vail, Colorado, endorsed the practitioner-scholar model . Its graduates are primarily practitioners who understand and use research rather than produce it, much as a physician understands pharmacology without developing drugs. Training emphasises assessment and therapy, and the doctoral project may be a case study or programme evaluation. Critics point to large classes, high fees and weaker research grounding in some professional schools. The third model answered the opposite worry, that practice had drifted from science. In 1991 Richard McFall of Indiana University published "A Manifesto for a Science of Clinical Psychology", holding that only scientific clinical psychology is legitimate and that services should be offered only when evidence supports them. In the mid-1990s research-intensive programmes formed the Academy of Psychological Clinical Science . The clinical scientist model keeps the PhD and treats practice as the application of tested science. Boulder pairs with the PhD and the scientist-practitioner; Vail with the PsyD and the practitioner-scholar. The first PsyD (1968) came before Vail (1973), which endorsed a change already under way. Indian training, with supervised hospital practice plus a dissertation, is closest to Boulder. 2.9 Eysenck's challenge and the turn to evidence By 1950 psychotherapy was central to clinical psychology, yet nobody had shown convincingly that it worked. Hans Eysenck (1916 to 1997), a German-born psychologist at the Institute of Psychiatry in London, exploited that gap. In his 1952 paper "The effects of psychotherapy: An evaluation" he compared reported improvement among neurotic patients given psychoanalysis or eclectic therapy with two baselines: discharge rates from state hospitals giving custodial care, and improvement among insurance claimants treated by general practitioners. He concluded that about two thirds of neurotic patients improve within roughly two years whether treated or not, which he called spontaneous remission , and that therapy, especially psychoanalysis, did no better. Critics showed that the studies defined improvement differently, that his baseline groups were not comparable with therapy patients, and that reanalyses put spontaneous remission lower than he claimed. But the challenge was healthy: Eysenck was not proving therapy useless, only denying anyone the right to claim it worked without proper tests. Researchers responded with controlled outcome studies, and then with a new way to combine them. In 1977 Mary Lee Smith and Gene Glass , who had coined the term meta-analysis the year before, pooled 375 controlled studies. They expressed each result as an effect size , the difference between treated and control groups in standard deviation units. The average was about 0.68, meaning the average treated person ended better off than about 75 percent of untreated people. Eysenck called it "an exercise in mega-silliness", arguing that pooling good and bad studies averages rubbish, but the method survived by weighting studies for quality. Smith and Glass also found only small differences between therapies, feeding the continuing debate over whether therapies work through specific techniques or common factors such as the relationship and hope. Key. Eysenck (1952): no proof therapy beats spontaneous remission. Smith and Glass (1977): 375 studies, average effect size about 0.68, clear benefit. The profession moved from "we see it works" to "we believe it when controlled evidence shows it". 2.10 Later waves and the modern era New therapies arose from the 1950s, each partly a reaction to the last. Behaviour therapy applied learning principles to clinical problems; Joseph Wolpe 's 1958 Psychotherapy by Reciprocal Inhibition introduced systematic desensitisation for phobias, and Hans Eysenck's group championed the approach. It was brief, focused and testable, exactly what Eysenck had demanded. The humanistic "third force" rejected both psychoanalysis and behaviourism (John B. Watson, 1913): Carl Rogers (1902 to 1987) developed client-centred therapy ( Client-Centered Therapy , 1951), in which the therapist offers genuineness, unconditional positive regard and empathy rather than interpretation. Rogers, a psychologist, also strengthened psychologists' claim to do therapy and was among the first to record and study sessions. The cognitive revolution followed: Albert Ellis developed rational therapy in the 1950s, and Aaron Beck built cognitive therapy around automatic negative thoughts ( Cognitive Therapy of Depression , 1979). These merged into cognitive behaviour therapy (CBT), the most tested psychotherapy. In 1998 Martin Seligman used his presidency of the American Psychological Association to launch positive psychology, the second half of your course. Four developments define the recent era. Evidence-based practice , the heir of the Eysenck debate, began with mid-1990s lists of empirically supported treatments; in 2005 the American Psychological Association defined it as integrating the best research with clinical expertise in the context of the patient's characteristics, culture and preferences. Managed care , the American insurance system that controls costs by limiting sessions and demanding proof of progress, pushed clinicians towards brief, measurable treatment. Prescription privileges for specially trained psychologists began in New Mexico in 2002 and Louisiana in 2004, with a few other states following; supporters cite the shortage of psychiatrists, opponents cite safety. Indian psychologists do not prescribe. Telehealth grew rapidly during the COVID-19 pandemic from 2020, and India launched the Tele-MANAS helpline in 2022; it widens access but raises questions of privacy, crisis management and remote test validity. 2.11 Clinical psychology in India Indian clinical psychology grew inside psychiatric hospitals under colonial and then national government, which explains why training is hospital-based and why a rehabilitation council regulates it. Colonial asylums, largely custodial, were governed from 1912 by the Indian Lunacy Act. Academic psychology began at the University of Calcutta , which opened India's first psychology department in 1916 under Narendra Nath Sengupta , trained at Harvard, so the discipline began, as in Germany, with laboratory work. Who gave us this. Girindrasekhar Bose (1887 to 1953), a Calcutta physician, developed psychoanalytic ideas partly independently of Sigmund Freud, corresponded with him, earned Calcutta's first doctorate in psychology with a thesis on repression, and in 1922 founded the Indian Psychoanalytical Society . Bose was among Asia's earliest psychotherapists. He proposed a theory of opposite wishes , in which every wish is paired with its opposite and symptoms reflect their balance, and he questioned whether the Oedipus complex fitted Indian families in Freud's form. The Central Institute of Psychiatry at Ranchi was founded in 1918 as the Ranchi European Lunatic Asylum, for European patients only, and soon renamed the Ranchi European Mental Hospital. Its superintendent Owen Berkeley-Hill , a psychoanalytically trained British psychiatrist and member of Bose's Society, introduced occupational therapy and more open, humane care. After independence it opened to all Indians and was later renamed. In 1954 the Government of India established the All India Institute of Mental Health in Bangalore to train the professionals the new nation lacked. It began a two-year Diploma in Medical and Social Psychology , among the earliest professional trainings for Indian clinical psychologists; the name shows psychologists were trained to work beside psychiatrists, attending to the social context of illness. In 1974 the institute merged with the old mental hospital to form NIMHANS , the National Institute of Mental Health and Neuro Sciences. The diploma grew into the two-year Master of Philosophy (M.Phil) in clinical psychology, combining assessment, therapy, supervised hospital work and a dissertation, which spread to Ranchi and other centres. Regulation came through the Rehabilitation Council of India , made a statutory body by the Rehabilitation Council of India Act of 1992 . Because mental illness and intellectual disability are disabilities, clinical psychologists fall within its scope: it approves programmes and keeps the Central Rehabilitation Register, and practising as a clinical psychologist without registration is an offence. The Mental Healthcare Act of 2017 defines a clinical psychologist by a qualification from a council-approved institution. After the National Education Policy of 2020 discontinued the M.Phil, the council moved training to a two-year regulated master's programme in clinical psychology. Trap. Bose, not Sengupta, founded the Indian Psychoanalytical Society. NIMHANS (1974) grew out of the All India Institute of Mental Health (1954). Indian clinical psychologists are registered with the Rehabilitation Council of India, not a medical council. 2.12 The whole story on one page: a timeline Date Event Around 400 BCE Hippocratic humoral theory 1793 and 1796 Pinel at Bicêtre; Tuke's York Retreat 1843 Dix's memorial to the Massachusetts legislature 1879 Wundt's Leipzig laboratory 1890 Cattell coins "mental test" 1896 Lightner Witmer's clinic, University of Pennsylvania 1899 Kraepelin separates dementia praecox from manic-depressive insanity 1905 Binet-Simon scale 1907 The Psychological Clinic founded 1916 Stanford-Binet; Calcutta psychology department 1917 to 1918 Army Alpha and Army Beta 1918 Ranchi European Lunatic Asylum 1922 Indian Psychoanalytical Society 1946 to 1949 Veterans Administration training; National Institute of Mental Health 1949 Boulder Conference 1952 Hans Eysenck's critique; first DSM 1954 All India Institute of Mental Health, Bangalore 1973 Vail Conference 1974 NIMHANS formed 1977 Smith and Glass meta-analysis 1991 McFall's manifesto 1992 Rehabilitation Council of India Act 2002 and 2004 Prescription privileges: New Mexico, Louisiana 2017 Mental Healthcare Act Recap.
