Using a clinical example, show how cultural factors and the five Ps shape understanding and treatment. 5 The clinical interview and the mental status examination Before any test is given, any diagnosis written or any therapy begun, a clinician sits with a person and talks. That disciplined talk, the clinical interview, is the most used assessment method in clinical psychology and psychiatry, and the mental status examination is the part of it that records, in a precise shared vocabulary, how the person's mind is working at the moment of meeting. This chapter teaches both from the ground up, from interviewing skills and structured instruments to the Indian case history format and every heading of the mental status examination. Every viva and clinical posting will ask you to take a history and write a mental status examination, and the interview is where assessment most often goes wrong. The chapter ends with a worked mini-interview and a written summary. 5.1 What a clinical interview is, and why it dominates assessment A clinical interview is a planned, purposeful conversation between a trained professional and a person seeking help (or someone who knows that person well), held to understand the person's difficulties, gather what is needed for diagnosis and formulation, decide on care, and begin a working relationship. It is planned , because the clinician enters with goals and an outline; purposeful , because every question has a reason; a conversation , because the relationship is itself being built; and clinical , because it runs under professional rules of consent, confidentiality and responsibility. The clinical textbooks (Pomerantz; Trull and Phares) explain why it is the most used tool. It needs no equipment and works anywhere. It is flexible, so the clinician can follow an unexpected lead at once. It alone gathers history, observes behaviour live and builds the relationship simultaneously. And it frames every other method: tests are chosen, interpreted and explained through interviews. A clinician can practise without a particular test; none practises without interviewing. Interview versus conversation A conversation has no set goal, while an interview is directed towards specific information and decisions. In conversation disclosure is mutual; in an interview the roles are asymmetric, and the clinician does not answer the client's disclosures with personal ones. Politeness steers conversation away from painful topics; the interviewer deliberately and tactfully asks about suicide, sexuality, substance use and family conflict. The interviewer, unlike a friend, is responsible for structure, time, safety and the information, and attends as much to how things are said as to what. Who gave us this. Harry Stack Sullivan, the American psychiatrist, set out the modern view in The Psychiatric Interview (published in 1954, after his death). He called the interviewer a participant observer : someone whose own manner shapes what the patient says, and who must therefore observe the interaction, including his own part in it, as data. Trap. Rapport is not friendship, and the interview is not "just talking". It is an assessment instrument with its own reliability and validity (section 5.10). A warm interview that misses a suicide plan has failed. 5.2 Kinds of interview by purpose One meeting often serves several purposes, but naming them tells the clinician what must be achieved. The intake interview (admission interview in hospitals) is the first formal contact with a service. It asks why the person has come and why now, how urgent the problem is, and whether this is the right service. It screens for risk, explains services and confidentiality, and ends with a disposition: accept, refer or admit. In India it also settles the legal basis of admission under the Mental Healthcare Act 2017, which distinguishes an independent admission (the person consents) from a supported admission (the person needs very high support in decision-making and specified risk conditions are met). The case history interview builds a chronological account of the person's life and illness from the patient and informants, often over several sessions (section 5.8). The diagnostic interview asks whether the person meets criteria for disorders in DSM-5-TR or ICD-11, working systematically through symptoms, duration, impairment and exclusions such as substance use; structured instruments (section 5.5) belong here. The mental status examination interview records present functioning, observed and tested in the room: the history is longitudinal , the story over time; the mental status examination is cross-sectional , a snapshot of now (section 5.9). The crisis interview is taken up in section 5.3. The termination or exit interview closes therapy or a hospital stay. It reviews goals and progress, consolidates learning, names early warning signs of relapse, arranges follow-up and makes room for the feelings endings bring; at discharge it also covers medication and whom to call in an emergency. 5.3 The crisis interview and suicide risk assessment A crisis is a time-limited state in which a stressful event, such as a suicide attempt, bereavement or assault, overwhelms a person's usual coping. The crisis interview is therefore short, centred on the here and now, and directive. The clinician makes the setting safe for both parties, establishes calm contact, defines the precipitating problem concretely, assesses risk to self, to others and from others (such as domestic violence), identifies strengths and supporters, agrees a specific plan for the next hours and days, and arranges follow-up. The full history waits. Suicide risk assessment Every interview includes suicide risk, and the first rule is to ask directly . Research has consistently found that asking does not plant the idea or increase suicidal thinking; many people are relieved to be asked. Questions move from general to specific. Hopelessness comes first: "Have you felt life is not worth living?" Passive death wishes follow: "Have you wished you could sleep and not wake up?" Active ideation is then asked: "Have you thought of ending your life?" Plan and intent are explored: "Have you thought how, when and where? How likely is it that you would act?" Means and preparation are checked: "Is there pesticide or medicine at home? Have you written a note or given things away?" Past attempts are reviewed, including how the person was found and how he or she felt about surviving. Risk factors include a previous attempt (the strongest single predictor), depression, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia and substance use, hopelessness (which Aaron Beck and colleagues showed predicts eventual suicide better than depression severity), recent loss, chronic painful illness, isolation, family history of suicide, impulsivity and access to lethal means, including stored pesticide in rural India. Protective factors include children, religious objections and family support. The outcome is a reasoned level of risk and a matching plan: safety planning, removal of means, involving family, closer follow-up or admission. Trap. No scale can predict whether a particular individual will die by suicide; the event is rare enough that even good predictors throw up many false alarms. Assessment guides management, it does not forecast. A denial of intent does not cancel a high-risk picture. Why it matters. Section 115 of the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 presumes, unless proved otherwise, that a person who attempts suicide was under severe stress and shall not be tried and punished under Section 309 of the Indian Penal Code, and directs the government to provide care and rehabilitation. The clinician's stance after an attempt is care, not reporting a crime. 5.4 Interviewing children, adolescents, couples, families, and through interpreters Children are brought by adults, so there are always several informants: child, parents and often teachers. They often disagree usefully: parents tend to report visible behaviour such as defiance better, children their own fears and sadness. The interviewer uses short, concrete questions in the child's words, time anchors a child can use ("before or after Diwali?"), shorter sessions, and for young children play and drawing. Confidentiality is explained simply, with its key limit: if someone is hurting the child, the clinician will tell someone who can keep the child safe. Adolescents are often brought unwillingly and are alert to adults "taking the parents' side". See them alone for part of the session, say plainly what will and will not be shared with parents, and stay non-judgemental. A widely taught framework is HEADSS: home, education, activities, drugs, sexuality, and suicide and depression. In India, board examination and coaching pressure, phones and relationships deserve direct questions. Couples and families seen together (a conjoint interview) make the relationship pattern the focus: who speaks first, who speaks for whom, who stays silent, which alliances appear. The clinician stays neutral, gives everyone a voice, sets ground rules and turns blame into description. Circular questions ("When your father gets angry, what does your mother do?") reveal patterns rather than accusations, and a genogram maps three generations. Screening for domestic violence is always done with each partner alone. Through interpreters : a trained interpreter is better than a relative, and a child must never interpret for a parent. Brief the interpreter to translate everything literally, including disorganised speech; speak to the patient directly, in short units; debrief afterwards. Interpreters may make thought-disordered speech sound coherent, so formal thought disorder is judged cautiously across languages. 5.5 Structured, semi-structured and unstructured interviews In the unstructured interview the clinician chooses the questions, wording and order. It offers flexibility, freedom to follow leads and easy rapport, but poor reliability: two clinicians may cover different ground and disagree. The United States and United Kingdom Diagnostic Project (1972) showed this: New York psychiatrists diagnosed schizophrenia far more readily than London ones, a gap that largely vanished under a standard interview and definitions. Robert Spitzer and colleagues in the 1970s named two sources of disagreement: information variance (clinicians obtain different information) and criterion variance (they apply different rules to the same information). Structured interviews reduce the first; the operational criteria of DSM-III (1980) reduce the second. In the fully structured interview every question is scripted word for word in fixed order, with fixed response options and scoring, so trained lay interviewers can give it in population surveys. The Diagnostic Interview Schedule, built for the Epidemiologic Catchment Area study in the United States, and the World Health Organization's Composite International Diagnostic Interview are examples. They are highly reliable but rigid, and blind to what they do not ask. The semi-structured interview fixes the ground and core questions but lets the clinician rephrase, probe and judge whether a symptom is truly present, trading a little reliability for much clinical sense. It opens with an open-ended overview, then works through diagnostic modules, each question printed beside the criterion it tests; the interviewer rates the criterion, not merely the answer, and skips out of a module once an essential criterion is absent. Clinician, Research and personality disorders versions exist. The Anxiety and Related Disorders Interview Schedule for DSM-5 (ADIS-5) , by Timothy Brown and David Barlow, is semi-structured and centred on anxiety, obsessive-compulsive and trauma-related disorders, with mood sections and screening for other conditions. Its hallmark is dimensional rating: a Clinician's Severity Rating from 0 to 8 for each diagnosis, with 4 conventionally the threshold of clinical significance. The Mini International Neuropsychiatric Interview (MINI) , by David Sheehan, Yves Lecrubier and colleagues (1998), is a short structured interview for DSM and ICD diagnoses. Each module opens with screening questions; a "no" skips the module, and most items are yes or no. Often completed in about a quarter of an hour, it suits drug trials and busy clinics, at the cost of depth. The Schedules for Clinical Assessment in Neuropsychiatry (SCAN) were developed under the World Health Organization around the tenth edition of the Present State Examination, originally devised by the British psychiatrist John Wing. The clinician questions flexibly, then rates each experience against precise definitions in a glossary, an approach designed for cross-cultural use. The Kiddie Schedule for Affective Disorders and Schizophrenia (K-SADS) , the child version of the adult Schedule for Affective Disorders and Schizophrenia, was originated by Joaquim Puig-Antich and colleagues; its widely used Present and Lifetime version was published in 1997 by Joan Kaufman, Boris Birmaher and colleagues for ages 6 to 18. Parent and child are interviewed separately and the clinician reconciles the accounts into summary ratings, opening diagnostic supplements only where screening is positive. Trap. The SCID is called "structured" but is semi-structured, because its ratings rest on clinical judgement. The fully structured, lay-administered instruments are the Diagnostic Interview Schedule and the Composite International Diagnostic Interview; the MINI is described by its authors as structured. 5.6 Core interviewing skills Rapport is a working relationship of trust in which the client feels safe to say difficult things. Carl Rogers argued in 1957 that therapist empathy, unconditional positive regard and congruence (genuineness) are necessary conditions for change; they are the raw material of rapport. Attending is the base of the "microskills" hierarchy that Allen Ivey began teaching in 1968: posture, eye contact, a calm voice and verbal tracking (staying with the client's topic). Gerard Egan, in The Skilled Helper (1975), summarised physical attending as SOLER: face the client squarely, open posture, lean slightly forward, eye contact, relaxed; in India sustained gaze with elders or across genders may need softening. Active listening means hearing content, feeling and meaning, and showing it. An open question invites an extended answer ("What has been troubling you?"); a closed question asks for a fact or a yes or no ("Did you sleep last night?"). Open questions give rich, self-directed accounts; closed ones pin down details and help with rambling or crisis-stricken clients. The funnel moves from open to closed within each area. Facilitation keeps the client talking without steering: nodding, "go on", repeating a key word. Paraphrasing restates content in fewer words ("So the fights began after your brother's marriage"). Reflection of feeling names the emotion beneath the words ("You felt humiliated"). Clarification makes a vague statement concrete ("When you say tension, what happens?"); in Indian clinics "tension", "weakness" and "gas" must always be clarified. Confrontation is not aggression but the tentative pointing out of a discrepancy ("You say home is fine, yet your husband no longer speaks to you"). Interpretation offers a hypothesis linking patterns beyond what the client said; it comes from the psychodynamic tradition and rarely belongs in a first interview. Summarising draws together a longer stretch, at transitions and the end, inviting correction. Silence gives time to think and feel, though a long pause may also signal thought block or depressive slowing. Empathy is understanding the client's experience from within his or her frame of reference and communicating it; it differs from sympathy , feeling sorry from outside ("I can see how frightening that was" versus "Poor you"). What to avoid Leading questions ("You've been depressed, haven't you?") invite agreement from anxious or deferential clients. "Why" questions ("Why did you drink again?") sound accusatory; "What was happening before you drank?" gets the same information without blame. Premature advice and reassurance ("Just think positively") closes exploration and signals that distress is not being taken seriously. Jargon ("Any anhedonia?") confuses; "Do you still enjoy things?" works. Double questions , interruptions, judgemental remarks and heavy note-taking also damage the interview. 5.7 The phases of an interview and its setting The setting is private, quiet and uninterrupted, with chairs at an angle rather than across a desk; where violence is possible, neither person's exit is blocked. Notes are brief and explained ("I'll jot down a few points"), stopped during emotional disclosures, and written up soon after with verbatim samples of key statements. The opening sets the frame: greeting, introducing oneself and one's role, the purpose and time available, and a confidentiality statement , that what is said stays within the treating team, with limits for serious risk of harm to self or others, child abuse and legal orders. The Mental Healthcare Act 2017 lists confidentiality among the rights of persons with mental illness. The clinician then opens broadly: "What brings you here today?" The body explores the problem, history and mental status, funnelling from open to closed and signposting transitions ("Now I'd like to ask about your family"). The closing is announced ahead ("We have ten minutes left") and includes a summary, "Is there anything important I haven't asked?", next steps and a safety check. 5.8 Case history taking Indian training follows a fixed sequence, and the order itself prevents omissions. The record opens with the informants , their relationship to the patient, and whether their information is reliable (consistent, credible) and adequate (enough for a picture). Identifying data cover name, age, sex, education, occupation, income, marital status, religion, language, urban or rural domicile and socioeconomic status. Chief complaints are listed in the patient's and informant's own words, chronologically, each with its duration ("Suspiciousness towards neighbours, five months"). History of present illness records onset (abrupt, acute or insidious), precipitants, course (continuous, episodic, fluctuating), progress (improving, static, deteriorating), each symptom's effect on functioning, sleep, appetite and weight, treatment tried (including faith healers), and relevant negatives such as no head injury or substance use. Past history covers earlier psychiatric episodes and their outcome, and medical illnesses, head injuries and seizures. Family history is drawn as a three-generation genogram: consanguinity, family type (nuclear, joint, extended), mental illness, suicide and substance use in relatives, and dynamics such as authority, communication and attitude to the patient's illness. Personal history follows the life course: pregnancy, birth and milestones; childhood problems such as bed-wetting, tantrums or school refusal; schooling, performance and reason for stopping; jobs, changes and satisfaction; menstrual history for women; sexual knowledge, orientation, experiences and worries; marital history (arranged or chosen, adjustment, children, in-law conflict); and substance use, with age at first use, pattern, quantity, last use, tolerance and withdrawal. Premorbid personality describes the person before the illness, mainly from informants: attitudes to self, others and work, social relationships, moral and religious standards, predominant mood, leisure, fantasy life, habits and reaction to stress. The write-up then adds examination findings, diagnosis, formulation and a management plan. Trap. Premorbid personality is not a personality disorder, and must not be described from the present state. A withdrawn patient with schizophrenia may have been outgoing before; revealing that change is the section's purpose. 5.9 The mental status examination The mental status examination is a systematic description of observable behaviour and reported inner experience at the time of the interview. It rests on the descriptive phenomenology of Karl Jaspers, whose General Psychopathology (1913) taught that an experience must first be described exactly as the patient lives it, before its cause is guessed. It combines observation with questioning and testing, written in plain terms with verbatim samples. Appearance, behaviour, psychomotor activity and attitude General appearance and behaviour are observed from the first moment: build, apparent versus stated age, grooming, dress for season and occasion, scars (including self-harm marks), expression, eye contact and ease of rapport. Self-neglect suggests depression, schizophrenia or dementia; flamboyant dress suggests mania; muttering, smiling to oneself or turning towards an empty corner is hallucinatory behaviour . Psychomotor activity may be increased ( agitation , to be distinguished from akathisia , the drug-induced restlessness of antipsychotics) or decreased ( retardation in depression; stupor , a conscious but mute, immobile state). Abnormal movements include tremor, tics and tardive dyskinesia. Catatonic signs include posturing, waxy flexibility (a limb stays where the examiner places it, tested by gently moving it), negativism, echopraxia, mannerisms (odd flourishes on purposeful acts) and stereotypies (purposeless repeated movements). Attitude towards the examiner is recorded as cooperative, guarded, suspicious, hostile, over-familiar or indifferent. Speech Speech is described for rate, volume, tone, quantity, reaction time, spontaneity, relevance and coherence. Pressure of speech (rapid, loud, hard to interrupt) is typical of mania; poverty of speech (little speech) and poverty of content (enough words, little information) occur in schizophrenia. Dysarthria is faulty articulation; dysphasia is a disorder of language itself, such as word-finding difficulty, and points to brain disease. Mood and affect Mood is the sustained emotional state the person reports; affect is the observable, moment-to-moment expression of emotion: mood is the climate, affect the weather. Mood is asked ("How have you been feeling in your spirits?"), recorded in the patient's words and rated (euthymic, depressed, elated, irritable, anxious). Affect is described for range (full, restricted, blunted, flat), reactivity, intensity, stability, appropriateness to content, congruence with mood and communicability. Flat or inappropriate affect (laughing while describing a death) suggests schizophrenia; labile affect, shifting rapidly, occurs in mania and organic states. Thought: stream, form, content, possession Stream is the speed and flow of thinking. In flight of ideas (mania) speech leaps between topics with traceable links such as rhymes ( clang associations ) and distractions; in retardation (depression) thoughts are slow and few; thought block is a sudden stop with the mind going blank (schizophrenia); perseveration , repeating an idea beyond relevance, suggests organic disease. Form is logical organisation, and its disturbance is formal thought disorder : loosening of associations (ideas slide with no understandable link), tangentiality (never reaching the point), circumstantiality (excessive detail, but the point is reached), neologisms and word salad . It is judged from a recorded sample of free talk. Content covers preoccupations, worthlessness, guilt, suicidal and homicidal ideas, phobias, overvalued ideas and delusions. A delusion is a false belief, firmly held, not correctable by evidence or reasoning, and not explained by the person's culture or religion. Types include persecutory, referential (neutral events carry special meaning), grandiose, guilt, nihilistic, somatic, jealous and erotomanic. An overvalued idea is an understandable, emotionally charged belief that dominates life without a delusion's fixity. Delusions are elicited gently ("Do you feel anyone is against you?"), their conviction tested ("Could there be another explanation?"), and checked against the informant and the culture. Possession concerns whether thoughts feel like one's own. An obsession is a recurrent, intrusive, unwanted thought, image or impulse recognised as one's own and resisted, often linked to a compulsion performed to relieve anxiety. In thought alienation thoughts feel alien: insertion (put in by an outside agency), withdrawal (taken out) and broadcasting (spreading so others know them), which Kurt Schneider counted among the first-rank symptoms of schizophrenia. Trap. An obsession is "my own thought, which I do not want"; thought insertion is "not my thought, someone put it there". Confusing them confuses obsessive-compulsive disorder with schizophrenia. Textbooks also differ on whether flight of ideas belongs under stream or form. Perception A hallucination is a perception without an external stimulus, experienced as real, located outside and not under voluntary control; an illusion is a misperception of a real stimulus, such as a rope taken for a snake in dim light. Auditory hallucinations, commonest in schizophrenia, may address the patient (second person) or discuss him (third person), comment on his actions, argue, echo his thoughts, or give commands, which raise risk. Visual hallucinations suggest delirium or alcohol withdrawal; tactile ones, such as insects crawling under the skin, occur in withdrawal and stimulant use; olfactory and gustatory ones suggest temporal lobe disease. Hypnagogic and hypnopompic hallucinations, on falling asleep and waking, are normal. Depersonalisation and derealisation (self or world feeling unreal) are recorded here. Questions are normalised ("Some people under stress hear voices when no one is there; has that happened?"), and any voice is characterised by number, content, location and response. Cognitive functions Consciousness ranges from alert through drowsy and clouded to stupor and coma; impairment or fluctuation suggests delirium. Orientation is tested for time, place and person; in organic states time is lost first and personal identity last, and with unschooled patients time may be judged by season or festival. Attention (directing the mind) and concentration (sustaining it) are tested by serial sevens from 100, serial threes for those with less schooling, days or months backwards, and digit span. Memory is tested at three spans: immediate (digit span forward, normally about seven digits, or repeating three words), recent (recalling the three words after five minutes; the last day's events, checked with the informant) and remote (verifiable personal and public events). Recent memory usually fails before remote memory in dementia, and confabulation fills gaps in Korsakoff syndrome. Intelligence is estimated from general knowledge suited to the background, simple arithmetic and vocabulary, compared with education. Abstract thinking is tested with similarities ("How are an orange and a banana alike?"), differences ("a lie and a mistake") and proverbs ("Empty vessels make the most noise"; or the Hindi "Ek machhli saare talaab ko ganda kar deti hai", one fish dirties the whole pond). Concrete answers suggest organic disease, intellectual disability or schizophrenia, but also limited schooling; bizarre answers suggest thought disorder. Judgement and insight Judgement is the capacity to assess a situation and act appropriately. Personal judgement is the realism of one's own plans; social judgement is behaviour in social situations, observed and reported; test judgement uses hypothetical situations ("What would you do if you found a stamped, addressed envelope on the road?"). Test judgement is the weakest guide, since a correct textbook answer can coexist with disastrous real conduct. Insight is awareness of being ill, of the illness's nature and of the need for treatment, graded on the six-point scale of the Kaplan and Sadock tradition used in Indian training. Grade Description 1 Complete denial of illness. 2 Slight awareness of being sick and needing help, while denying it at the same time. 3 Awareness of being sick, but blaming others, external factors or physical causes. 4 Awareness that the illness is caused by something unknown in oneself. 5 Intellectual insight: admitting illness due to one's own irrational feelings, without applying this to future behaviour. 6 True emotional insight: emotional awareness of one's motives and feelings, leading to real change. Grades 1 to 3 in psychosis 5.10 Reliability, validity, bias and culture As an instrument, the interview is judged for reliability : whether two interviewers agree about the same person ( inter-rater ) and whether conclusions hold across occasions ( test-retest ), with diagnostic agreement usually expressed by the chance-corrected kappa statistic. Validity asks whether it measures what it claims to; self-report is distorted by memory, insight, social desirability and denial, so informants and records are safeguards. Two clinicians can agree and both be wrong: reliability does not guarantee validity. The halo effect , named by Edward Thorndike in 1920, is the spread of one salient impression to unrelated judgements: a well-dressed, articulate patient may be judged less ill or less at risk than he is. Confirmatory bias is seeking and remembering evidence for an early hypothesis while overlooking evidence against it; a clinician who decides in five minutes that it is "just stress" may never ask about voices. Related errors are anchoring on first information, premature closure, and diagnostic overshadowing , attributing new symptoms to an existing diagnosis. Remedies are structured coverage, a deliberate differential diagnosis, seeking disconfirming evidence, and supervision. Cultural factors in India Family presence : patients usually come accompanied and relatives answer for them; this gives collateral history and support, but suicidal ideas, substance use, sexual concerns and ill-treatment may stay hidden, so the patient is also seen alone as routine. Language : distress is often voiced through idioms and bodily complaints ("tension", weakness, burning in the head, the Punjabi "sinking heart"); Dhat syndrome, distress over supposed semen loss, was named by N. N. Wig in 1960. Record the patient's words and clarify rather than translating straight into psychiatric terms. Stigma : fear of the "mental" label and its effect on marriage and family standing delays help-seeking, sends many first to faith healers, and leads to minimising; framing questions around sleep, stress and functioning helps. Gender : women may not speak freely before husbands or in-laws, or discuss menstrual, sexual or marital matters with a male clinician, and domestic violence may surface only in private; offer a chaperone or same-gender clinician. Men may hide distress behind physical complaints or anger. Beliefs and hierarchy : possession, black magic and the evil eye are shared cultural explanations, not delusions unless they exceed what the person's community believes; the DSM-5 Cultural Formulation Interview (16 questions) explores the person's own explanation. Schooling strongly affects serial sevens and proverbs. 5.11 A worked mini-interview and mental status summary Case. Mr S, 26, a science graduate and data-entry operator living in a joint family in a Karnataka town, is brought by his father and brother with five months of withdrawal to his room, reduced talk, suspiciousness towards neighbours, muttering and smiling to himself, poor sleep, and six weeks off work. Onset was insidious, course continuous and worsening; the father is a reliable, adequate informant. Seeing him alone, the clinician introduces herself as a trainee clinical psychologist, explains that what he says stays within the team unless someone's safety is at risk, in which case she will tell him first, and says they have forty minutes ( opening and confidentiality statement ). He says, "I don't know why they brought me. I'm not mad." She replies, "It sounds as though coming here wasn't your idea, and you're worried what people might think" ( reflection of feeling ). "Everyone on our street is already talking." "Talking?" ( facilitation ). "About me. When I pass, they cough." "Could you tell me about that from when it began?" ( open question ). He describes a quarrel over a water tank five months ago, after which neighbours cough as a signal whenever he passes and have "joined with the office people" to get him dismissed. She paraphrases this back and he agrees. "How sure are you, out of a hundred?" "A hundred." "Could there be another reason people cough?" "No, it's too regular." She does not argue; she has established fixity. Then a normalised closed question : "When you're alone, do you hear people talking when no one is there?" After a long pause: "At night. Two men, outside the wall. One says 'he's finished', the other laughs." No commands. A gentle confrontation : "You said work was fine, but your father says you haven't gone for six weeks?" "They're all in it." "That sounds frightening and exhausting" ( empathy ). Then directly : "Have you thought life isn't worth living, or of ending it?" "Sometimes it would be easier to be dead, but I won't do anything; my mother would suffer." No plan or past attempt. Asked what is happening to him: "Nothing is wrong with my mind; the neighbours are the problem. Maybe I need a sleeping tablet." She summarises , asks what she has missed, and arranges for him to meet the team psychiatrist ( closing ), without debating the delusion. Written mental status summary Appearance and behaviour: young man of stated age, thin, poorly groomed, seasonally dressed; poor, intermittent eye contact; rapport established with difficulty; seen muttering and glancing at the window while waiting. Psychomotor activity: mildly decreased; no catatonic signs. Attitude: guarded, later cooperative. Speech: relevant, coherent, low volume, reduced quantity, increased reaction time. Mood: "fed up and tired"; objectively anxious. Affect: anxious, restricted, reactive, appropriate and congruent. Thought: normal stream, no formal thought disorder; persecutory delusion of a neighbour and colleague conspiracy; delusion of reference (coughing as signals); passive death wishes without plan or intent; no obsessions or thought alienation. Perception: third-person auditory hallucinations, two male voices from outside at night, commenting on him; no commands. Cognition: alert, oriented in all three spheres; serial sevens to 65 with one error; six digits forward; three of three words recalled at five minutes; remote memory intact; intelligence clinically average; concrete proverb interpretation ("An empty pot makes more sound"), significant for a graduate. Judgement: personal and social impaired (stopped work on delusional grounds); test intact. Insight: grade 2, denies illness but accepts help for sleep. This is a psychotic disorder of five months without prominent mood disturbance. Under ICD-11, one month of such symptoms allows a diagnosis of schizophrenia; under DSM-5-TR, with under six months of total disturbance, it would currently be schizophreniform disorder. Delusional disorder is less likely given the hallucinations, and substance and medical causes must still be excluded. Recap. The clinical interview is a planned, purposeful, professional conversation and the most used assessment method. Interviews differ by purpose and are adapted for children, adolescents, families and interpreted sessions. Unstructured interviews maximise flexibility and rapport, fully structured ones maximise reliability, and semi-structured instruments such as the SCID-5, ADIS-5, SCAN and K-SADS balance the two, with the MINI as a brief structured option. Skilled interviewing rests on rapport, attending, the open-to-closed funnel and the listening skills, and avoids leading and "why" questions, premature advice and jargon. The case history gives the longitudinal story under fixed headings; the mental status examination, grounded in Karl Jaspers' phenomenology, gives the cross-sectional picture from appearance to insight. Interviews must be checked for reliability, validity, the halo effect and confirmatory bias, and adapted to Indian realities of family presence, language, stigma and gender. Suicide risk is always asked about directly, to guide management rather than to predict. Why is it the most widely used assessment method in clinical psychology? Discuss the reliability and validity of the clinical interview, the biases that affect it, and the cultural factors that shape interviewing in India. 6 Psychological assessment: tests, observation, judgement and the report Almost every decision a clinical psychologist makes rests on assessment. Before anyone is offered therapy, certified as having an intellectual disability, or told whether their forgetfulness is an early dementia, somebody has to gather information, understand the person and tell whoever will act on it. In Indian hospitals much of a clinical psychologist's week goes into exactly this: intelligence testing for disability certificates, personality testing on psychiatry wards and neuropsychological testing after head injury. This chapter builds that work from the ground up, from psychometrics through the main families of instruments and clinical judgement to the report, the ethics of testing and a worked case: ground both clinical textbooks on your list (Pomerantz; Trull and Phares) cover at length. 6.1 Assessment versus testing, and what assessment is for A psychological test is a standardised procedure for obtaining a sample of behaviour and describing it with scores or categories. It observes only a small, carefully chosen slice of behaviour (answers to forty vocabulary questions, say) and infers something larger. Psychological assessment is the broader process of gathering and integrating information from many sources to answer a question about a person and support a decision. Its sources include interview, history, observation, reports from family or teachers, records and, usually, tests. The test produces a number; the clinician produces the meaning. Good assessment is multi-method and multi-informant , because every method has blind spots; agreement across methods builds confidence, and disagreement is information to explain. Assessment serves several purposes. Screening is a brief first pass over many people to find those who need fuller evaluation, such as a short depression questionnaire given to every primary care patient. Diagnosis classifies a person's difficulties using the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM) or the International Classification of Diseases (ICD), including ruling out alternatives. Treatment planning decides which problems to target first, which strengths to build on and what may get in the way. Outcome evaluation repeats measurement during and after treatment to show whether the person is actually improving. Research uses instruments to select participants and measure variables. Forensic questions come from the legal system: fitness to stand trial, mental state at the time of an offence, risk of violence, custody or compensation. Indian practice adds disability certification, which brings concessions in education and employment. The organiser of every assessment is the referral question : what the referrer actually needs to know, and what decision rides on it. Referrals often arrive vague ("psychometry please", "IQ and personality"). A psychiatrist who writes "personality assessment" may really be asking, "Is this patient's odd thinking psychotic or a personality style, because I must decide whether to start an antipsychotic?" The clinician turns such requests into answerable questions, often by phoning the referrer, and those questions dictate which tests are chosen and what the report must say. Key. Tests are tools; assessment is the clinician's reasoning, using those tools and much else, to answer a specific referral question. No test score on its own is a diagnosis, and running the same "psychometry" battery on every client, whatever the question, is testing, not assessing. 6.2 Psychometric foundations: standardisation, norms and reliability Standardisation means a test is given, scored and interpreted the same way every time. The manual fixes instructions, item order, time limits, permitted prompts and scoring, so that score differences reflect differences between people, not between sessions. A raw score (34 items correct) means nothing until compared with a relevant group, the normative sample . Raw scores are converted into derived scores: percentile ranks (the percentage of the norm group scoring below the person), z scores (mean 0, standard deviation 1), T scores (mean 50, standard deviation 10) and deviation IQ (mean 100, standard deviation 15). Such tests are norm-referenced ; a criterion-referenced test instead compares performance with a fixed standard of mastery. Norms are only as good as their sample, which should be large, recent and representative. This is why Indian norms matter . An American-normed test may contain unfamiliar content and, above all, ignores education, which strongly affects scores and varies enormously across India; a rural adult with five years of schooling judged against American norms may look impaired when he is not. Translation is not adaptation: items must be checked for cultural meaning and fresh norms collected. Norms also age. Intelligence test scores rose across the twentieth century (the Flynn effect , documented in many countries by James Flynn), so a test with old norms compares today's client with a lower-scoring population and overestimates ability, a real issue with Indian adaptations normed decades ago. Reliability is consistency of measurement. Classical test theory treats every observed score as a true score plus random error; reliability, a coefficient from 0 to 1, indexes how little error there is, and each type detects a different source of error. Type How it is estimated Error it detects Test-retest Same test given twice, some interval apart; scores correlated. Fluctuation over time. Suits stable traits, not passing states. Parallel forms Two equivalent versions with different items; scores correlated. The particular items chosen; also avoids practice effects. Split-half One test split into halves (often odd versus even items); halves correlated, then corrected upward with the Spearman-Brown formula because each half is shorter. Inconsistency of content within one sitting. Internal consistency Average interrelation of all items, usually coefficient alpha, introduced by Lee Cronbach in 1951. Whether the items measure the same thing. Inter-rater Two trained raters score the same responses independently; agreement indexed by correlation, kappa or the intraclass correlation. The scorer. Essential for projective tests, observation and interviews. By a common rule of thumb, coefficients in the 0.70s suffice for group research, but decisions about an individual call for about 0.90 or above. 6.3 Validity, measurement error and the accuracy of decisions Validity is the degree to which evidence supports a particular interpretation and use of scores. It belongs to an interpretation, not to a test in the abstract: a reading test can be valid for finding poor readers and invalid as a measure of intelligence in a child with dyslexia. Content validity asks whether the items adequately sample the domain, as judged by experts; a depression scale asking only about sadness, ignoring sleep, appetite and hopelessness, has poor content validity. It differs from face validity , merely whether the test looks relevant to the test-taker. Criterion validity asks whether scores relate to an outside criterion. If the criterion is measured at about the same time, this is concurrent validity (a new depression questionnaire against clinicians' diagnoses that week); if it lies in the future, it is predictive validity (entrance scores predicting first-year marks). Construct validity concerns theoretical attributes that cannot be observed directly, such as anxiety or extraversion. Lee Cronbach and Paul Meehl argued in 1955 that it is established by deriving predictions from the theory of the construct (a "nomological network") and checking whether scores behave as predicted. Two kinds of evidence are central: convergent validity , high correlation with other measures of the same construct, and discriminant validity , low correlation with measures of different constructs. Donald Campbell and Donald Fiske formalised this in 1959 in the multitrait-multimethod matrix: an anxiety questionnaire should correlate more with an interview rating of anxiety than with a questionnaire on another trait, even though that shares its method. Key. Reliability sets a ceiling on validity: a test cannot correlate with anything more strongly than it correlates with itself. An unreliable test cannot be valid, but a reliable test can still be invalid. The standard error of measurement The standard error of measurement sizes the margin of error around a score: the test's standard deviation multiplied by the square root of (1 minus the reliability). For an intelligence test with standard deviation 15 and reliability 0.91, one minus 0.91 is 0.09, whose square root is 0.3, so the standard error is 4.5 points. About 95 percent of the time the true score lies within roughly two standard errors, about 9 points, of the observed score. A child scoring 72 therefore has a true score most plausibly between about 63 and 81, a band that straddles the region used for intellectual disability. So current diagnostic guidance allows for measurement error and weighs adaptive functioning rather than treating 70 as a sharp line. Sensitivity, specificity and base rates Sensitivity is the proportion of people with a condition whom the test correctly identifies; specificity is the proportion without it whom the test correctly clears. Moving a cut-off trades one for the other. But the clinician's real question is: given this positive result, how likely is the condition? That is the positive predictive value , and it depends heavily on the base rate , how common the condition is among the people tested. Paul Meehl and Albert Rosen showed in 1955 that ignoring base rates makes even good tests mislead. 1,000 people; sensitivity and specificity both 90 percent Base rate 2 percent (community) Base rate 30 percent (specialist clinic) People with the condition 20 300 True positives 18 270 False positives (10 percent of those without it) 98 of 980 70 of 700 Chance a positive result is correct 18 of 116, about 16 percent 270 of 340, about 79 percent When a condition is rare, most positives are false alarms, so screening must be followed by full assessment. Trap. "90 percent sensitivity" does not mean a positive result is 90 percent likely to be correct; that depends on the base rate. 6.4 Intelligence assessment In 1905 Alfred Binet and Théodore Simon, asked by French authorities to identify children needing special schooling, published graded tasks arranged by the age at which typical children pass them, giving a mental age . In 1912 William Stern proposed dividing mental age by chronological age, and Lewis Terman's 1916 Stanford revision, the Stanford-Binet , multiplied that ratio by 100 to give the intelligence quotient (IQ). This ratio IQ failed for adults, whose mental age stops rising while their chronological age does not. Modern tests use the deviation IQ (David Wechsler), comparing a person with others of the same age on a scale with mean 100 and standard deviation 15: about two thirds of people score between 85 and 115, and roughly 2 percent below 70. The Stanford-Binet fifth edition (2003) measures five factors (fluid reasoning, knowledge, quantitative reasoning, visual-spatial processing and working memory), each through verbal and nonverbal tasks. The Wechsler scales David Wechsler, at Bellevue Hospital in New York, found the Binet too verbal and child-centred for adults; his Wechsler-Bellevue scale (1939) introduced verbal and performance scores alongside a full-scale score, and the adult deviation IQ. It led to the Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children (WISC, 1949) and the Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale (WAIS, 1955), each built from short subtests such as vocabulary, block design and digit span. Recent editions replaced the verbal and performance split with factor-based index scores : four in the adult fourth edition (2008), five in the children's fifth edition (2014). The adult indexes are Verbal Comprehension (verbal reasoning), Perceptual Reasoning (analysing visual designs and solving novel problems), Working Memory and Processing Speed; the children's edition splits Perceptual Reasoning into Visual Spatial and Fluid Reasoning. Interpretation moves from the most reliable, most general score downward: Full Scale IQ, then index differences larger than chance, and only cautiously single subtests; reading pathology into subtest "scatter" has proved unreliable. Raven's Progressive Matrices John C. Raven published the Progressive Matrices in 1938. Each item is a pattern with a piece missing, and items grow progressively harder; there are Standard, Coloured (for young children, older adults and people with intellectual disability) and Advanced forms. Needing no speech or reading, it is used across languages as a measure of general reasoning, but it is "culture-reduced", not "culture-free": familiarity with abstract printed puzzles, a product of schooling, still matters. Indian tests and adaptations The Binet-Kamat Test , V. V. Kamat's adaptation of the Stanford-Binet for Indian children, was among the earliest. Bhatia's Battery of Performance Tests of Intelligence (C. M. Bhatia, 1955) was built for Indian conditions and low literacy, with five subtests: Koh's Block Design, Alexander's Passalong, Pattern Drawing, Immediate Memory for digits, and Picture Construction. Malin's Intelligence Scale for Indian Children (Arthur J. Malin, 1969) adapts the Wechsler children's scale, yields verbal, performance and full-scale quotients, and remains common in child guidance clinics. The Vineland Social Maturity Scale (Edgar Doll, 1935; adapted for India by Malin) is not an intelligence test: it is an interview with a carer about everyday competence in self-help, locomotion, communication, occupation, socialisation and self-direction, giving a social age and social quotient. It matters because intellectual disability requires adaptive as well as intellectual deficits. All these norms are old and regional, and a report should say so. Interpreting IQ and its limits An IQ summarises performance on particular tasks, at one time, against one norm group. It predicts school achievement reasonably well but is affected by schooling, language, motivation, anxiety and fatigue, and it does not capture creativity, practical wisdom or adaptive functioning. Report it as a range with a descriptive category, never as a fixed, innate quantity: two tests normed decades apart can give one child noticeably different IQs. 6.5 Objective personality assessment "Objective" describes the format, structured items and mechanical scoring, not objective truth. Inventories are built by rational construction (items theory says should tap a trait), empirical criterion keying (keeping whatever items separate groups) or factor analysis (letting item intercorrelations reveal the dimensions). The Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory The Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory (MMPI) was published in 1943 by the psychologist Starke Hathaway and the psychiatrist J. Charnley McKinley at the University of Minnesota. Its innovation was empirical criterion keying . They gave a large pool of statements to diagnosed psychiatric patients and to "Minnesota normals" (largely visitors to the University hospitals). An item went onto, say, the depression scale if depressed patients answered it differently from normals, whatever its content, so some items seem unrelated to their scale. The scales rest on how patients actually respond, but they overlap heavily and reflect 1930s diagnostic groups. Its second great contribution was the validity scales , which check how the person approached the test. Cannot Say counts omitted items. The L (Lie) scale detects naive attempts to look virtuous ("I have never told a lie"). The F (Infrequency) scale contains items rarely endorsed by normal people; high scores suggest random responding, exaggeration or very severe disturbance. The K (Correction) scale detects subtler defensiveness, and a fraction of it is added to several clinical scales. Later editions added scales for inconsistent and yea-saying responding. Scale Name Scale Name 1 Hypochondriasis 6 Paranoia 2 Depression 7 Psychasthenia 3 Hysteria 8 Schizophrenia 4 Psychopathic Deviate 9 Hypomania 5 Masculinity-Femininity 0 Social Introversion Scores are T scores; on the second edition, 65 or above is clinically significant. Because the names are dated, clinicians use numbers and interpret code types , the two or three highest scales: a "2-7" profile suggests an anxious, depressed, self-critical person; a "4-9" profile impulsive, rule-breaking behaviour. The MMPI-2 (1989, 567 items) restandardised the test on a new American sample. The MMPI-2-Restructured Form (2008) introduced Restructured Clinical scales that strip out a common "demoralisation" factor which had inflated the old scales together, and the MMPI-3 (2020) updated norms and scales again. The Millon, the NEO, the Sixteen Personality Factor and the Eysenck questionnaires Theodore Millon's Millon Clinical Multiaxial Inventory (1977) was built from his own theory of personality and aligned with the DSM personality disorders, with further scales for clinical syndromes. It uses base rate scores calibrated to each disorder's expected prevalence among patients and, being normed on patients, overstates pathology if given to community members. The NEO Personality Inventory of Paul Costa and Robert McCrae (revised edition 1992, 240 items) measures normal personality on the five-factor model : Neuroticism, Extraversion, Openness to experience, Agreeableness and Conscientiousness, each divided into six facets. The model grew from the lexical hypothesis , that important personality differences become encoded as words in ordinary language. It has few checks on test-taking attitude. Raymond Cattell factor-analysed trait words and ratings to produce the Sixteen Personality Factor Questionnaire (1949), measuring sixteen primary "source traits" such as warmth, dominance and emotional stability, which combine into global factors such as extraversion and anxiety. Hans Eysenck argued instead for a few broad, biologically based dimensions. The Eysenck Personality Questionnaire (1975), written with Sybil Eysenck, measures Extraversion, Neuroticism and Psychoticism, plus a Lie scale. Trap. Eysenck's Psychoticism scale measures tough-mindedness, hostility and impulsivity, not psychosis, and MMPI scale 8 does not diagnose schizophrenia. Interpret scales by their items and research, not their labels. 6.6 Projective personality assessment The projective hypothesis holds that when people make sense of an ambiguous stimulus with no right answer, they must organise it using their own needs, conflicts and ways of perceiving, and so reveal them. Lawrence Frank named these "projective methods" in 1939, drawing on psychoanalytic ideas about unconscious processes. Many now call them performance-based measures. The Rorschach Inkblot Test The Swiss psychiatrist Hermann Rorschach published ten inkblots in Psychodiagnostik (1921): five black and grey, two with red, three multicoloured. In the response phase the person says what each blot might be; in the inquiry the examiner asks where each percept was seen and what made it look that way. Responses are coded for location (whole blot, common detail, unusual detail, white space), determinants (form, colour, shading, movement), content , form quality (how well the percept fits the blot's shape) and popular responses. Rival scoring systems made research incomparable until John Exner merged them into the Comprehensive System (1974), with standard administration, coding, norms and indices (for disordered thinking, depression and suicide risk, for example). Concerns about its norms and weaker variables led Gregory Meyer and colleagues to publish the Rorschach Performance Assessment System (2011), which keeps the best-supported variables, uses international reference data, and standardises response numbers (the examiner prompts for two or three per card and stops at four). The Thematic Apperception Test Christiana Morgan and Henry Murray introduced the Thematic Apperception Test in 1935 at the Harvard Psychological Clinic. Its cards show ambiguous scenes, plus one blank card, and the person tells a story for each: what is happening, what led up to it, what the characters feel, and how it ends. Murray read stories through his theory of needs (inner motives such as achievement or affiliation) and press (environmental forces), usually through the "hero" the storyteller identifies with. Clinicians typically use eight to twelve cards and interpret qualitatively, which limits reliability. Uma Chowdhury produced Indian adaptations of it and of the Children's Apperception Test (Leopold Bellak and Sonya Sorel Bellak, 1949). Sentence completion and drawings Sentence completion tests offer stems ("My mother...", "I feel guilty when...") for the person to complete; the Rotter Incomplete Sentences Blank (Julian Rotter, 1950) has forty stems and an adjustment score. Drawing tests ask for a person, a house and tree, or the family. Karen Machover (1949) turned the Draw-a-Person into a personality test, reading features such as large eyes as signs of suspiciousness. Drawings help rapport with children, but sign-by-sign interpretation has the weakest research support of any projective method. The scientific debate Scott Lilienfeld, James Wood and Howard Garb's review in 2000 crystallised the criticisms: inconsistent administration and scoring, weak inter-rater reliability for some methods, norms that made ordinary people look disturbed, poor validity for many specific signs, and little incremental validity (added accuracy beyond interviews and questionnaires). Defenders countered that properly coded Rorschach variables are reliable, and a 2013 meta-analysis by Joni Mihura and colleagues supported a middle position: variables tied to perceptual accuracy and disordered thinking were well supported, many others were not. The defensible summary, important because these tests remain standard in Indian training and hospitals, is that projective tests are not all equal and systematically scored variables beat impressionistic reading. 6.7 Behavioural assessment Behavioural assessment grew from behaviour therapy in the 1960s. Traditional tests treat a response as a sign of an underlying trait; behavioural assessment treats behaviour as a sample of what the person does in particular situations. It is situational, repeated over time and tied directly to treatment. Frederick Kanfer and George Saslow (1965) proposed such behavioural analysis as an alternative to diagnostic labels, since it points straight at what to change. A functional analysis identifies what causes and maintains a behaviour. The ABC model records Antecedents (setting, people and demands just before), the Behaviour defined observably, and its Consequences (what follows and may reinforce it). Problem behaviours usually serve a function: gaining attention, escaping a demand, obtaining something tangible, or sensory stimulation. Treatment targets the function. Case. An eight-year-old boy with autism bangs his head when a worksheet is presented (antecedent), and the teacher then removes it to comfort him (consequence): the behaviour serves escape. He is taught to ask for a break, worksheets are shortened, and head-banging no longer removes them. A child seeking attention by the same behaviour would need a different plan. Naturalistic observation watches behaviour where it occurs (classroom, home, ward). Analogue observation recreates the situation in the clinic: a role play, or a behavioural avoidance test in which a person with a phobia approaches the feared object step by step. Target behaviours are defined operationally, and recording may be by frequency , duration , latency , interval recording (noting whether the behaviour occurred in each short interval) or time sampling . Observers are trained and their agreement checked, because they drift from definitions over time. In self-monitoring clients record their own behaviour, thoughts or feelings as they occur, such as cigarettes smoked or the thought records of cognitive behaviour therapy; smartphone ecological momentary assessment prompts recordings several times a day. Rating scales and checklists gather structured reports. The best known in child work is the Child Behavior Checklist from the system developed by Thomas Achenbach: parents rate over a hundred problem behaviours (teacher and adolescent forms exist), and scores form syndrome scales grouped as internalising (anxiety, depression, withdrawal, somatic complaints) and externalising (aggression, rule-breaking). Informants often disagree, which shows whether a problem is confined to one setting. Reactivity is the change in behaviour caused by observing it: children behave better with a stranger in the classroom, smokers smoke less while counting. It is reduced by unobtrusive observation and habituation, and in therapy it can even help, since self-monitoring alone often improves behaviour. 6.8 Neuropsychological assessment and cognitive screening Neuropsychological assessment measures cognitive functions to understand how brain damage or dysfunction affects behaviour. It is requested after head injury or stroke, when dementia is suspected, and around brain surgery. It samples attention, processing speed, memory, language, visuospatial skills and executive functions (planning, flexibility, inhibition, working memory) against age- and education-appropriate norms. Fixed batteries give everyone the same comprehensive set. The Halstead-Reitan Neuropsychological Battery , begun by Ward Halstead and developed by Ralph Reitan, includes the Category Test, Tactual Performance Test, Seashore Rhythm Test, Speech-Sounds Perception Test, Finger Tapping Test and Trail Making Test, summarised in an Impairment Index. The Luria-Nebraska Neuropsychological Battery standardised the qualitative bedside examination of the Russian neuropsychologist Alexander Luria into scored scales. Flexible approaches instead choose tests to fit the referral question. In India, the NIMHANS Neuropsychological Battery , developed at the National Institute of Mental Health and Neurosciences, Bengaluru, by Shobini Rao and colleagues, provides norms by age, education and sex, with a separate children's battery, using tests such as digit vigilance, verbal fluency, the Wisconsin Card Sorting Test, the Tower of London and verbal learning tests. The Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE), published by Marshal Folstein, Susan Folstein and Paul McHugh in 1975, is a ten-minute bedside screen scored out of 30: orientation, registration and recall of three words, attention and calculation (serial sevens), language tasks and copying intersecting pentagons. A score below about 24 has often been used to suggest impairment, but scores depend heavily on education, and the test misses mild and executive impairment, for which the Montreal Cognitive Assessment is often preferred. Trap. A low MMSE score in someone with four years of schooling, or in delirium or severe depression, does not establish dementia, and a normal score does not rule out mild or frontal impairment. A screen is not a diagnosis. 6.9 Clinical judgement: clinical versus statistical prediction, and clinicians' biases Data must be combined into a judgement, such as whether a patient will relapse. In clinical prediction the clinician combines the information in their head. In statistical or actuarial prediction it is fed into an explicit rule, a formula or table derived from past cases, which works the same way every time. The distinction concerns how data are combined, not what data are used; a clinician's interview rating can be an input to a formula. Who gave us this. Paul Meehl, in Clinical versus Statistical Prediction (1954), reviewed about twenty studies and found the mechanical method as accurate or more accurate in nearly all. A meta-analysis of 136 studies by William Grove and colleagues in 2000 found mechanical prediction equal or superior in the large majority of comparisons and clearly worse in only a small minority. Formulas win because they apply the same weights every time, are never tired or swayed by vivid details, and derive their weights from real outcomes; clinicians rarely get systematic feedback, so experience does not correct their errors. Meehl allowed a "broken leg" exception: a formula may predict a man goes to the cinema every Tuesday, but if he has just broken his leg you should override it. The danger is seeing broken legs everywhere. Clinicians remain essential for deciding what to measure, gathering good data and handling rare circumstances. In risk assessment, structured professional judgement is a middle path: tools such as the Historical Clinical Risk Management-20 (HCR-20) make the clinician rate a fixed list of evidence-based risk factors before judging. Bias How it appears in assessment Remedy Confirmation bias (Peter Wason, 1960) Forming an early hypothesis and then noticing only information that fits it. List alternatives; seek evidence that would disconfirm the favoured one. Availability heuristic (Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman, 1973) Judging a diagnosis likely because a memorable similar case comes easily to mind. Check base rates, not memorable examples. Overconfidence Confidence exceeding accuracy, often growing with experience while accuracy does not. Seek outcome feedback; state uncertainty; use actuarial aids. Illusory correlation (Loren Chapman, 1967) Seeing a link between a test sign and a trait that is not really there. Rely on research evidence, not clinical lore. Barnum effect Accepting vague statements true of almost everyone as a personal description. Ask of each report sentence whether it fits most people. Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman described the availability heuristic in 1973. Loren Chapman and Jean Chapman showed in 1967 that students shown drawings randomly paired with symptoms "discovered" the same links clinicians believed in (large eyes with suspiciousness) although the pairings contained none. Bertram Forer (1949) found students rated one identical, horoscope-style "personal" description as highly accurate; Meehl later named this the "Barnum effect", after the showman P. T. Barnum. Bias can be narrowed, never removed, by structured instruments, base rates, deliberately considering alternatives, actuarial tools, written reasoning and consultation. 6.10 Integrating the data, writing the report, and the ethics of testing Integration builds one coherent account from all sources instead of reporting tests one by one. The clinician looks for convergence (low mood in the interview, on the MMPI depression scale and in a parent's report), explains discrepancies (a client who denies anxiety on a questionnaire but trembles throughout testing), sets findings in the context of history and culture, and weighs each source by its reliability and validity, producing a formulation that answers the referral question. A standard report runs through identifying information; the reason for referral; procedures used; background history; behavioural observations, including effort and how far results can be trusted; results and interpretation, integrated by domain or question with scores as ranges; and a summary answering the referral question, with diagnostic impressions and specific, feasible recommendations. Write for the referral source. A teacher needs to know what to do in class, not what a Perceptual Reasoning Index is; a psychiatrist needs a clear diagnostic answer; a court needs conclusions tied to the legal question with their limits stated. Avoid jargon or explain it at once, describe behaviour concretely, include strengths, state uncertainty honestly, and avoid Barnum statements. The client, too, deserves feedback in plain language, checked for understanding. Stephen Finn's Therapeutic Assessment goes further, making clients collaborators who pose their own questions, so that assessment itself becomes therapeutic. Competence. Use only tests you are trained in; publishers restrict complex instruments to qualified users. In India the Rehabilitation Council of India registers clinical psychologists, whom the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 recognises as mental health professionals. Informed consent. The client or guardian should understand the purpose, who will see the results and the limits of confidentiality, which matter most in forensic, employment and school referrals. Test security. Items, manuals and scoring keys must not be circulated or coached, since a test whose answers are known measures nothing. Cultural fairness. Tests must suit the person's language, education and culture; results for people unlike the normative sample need cautious interpretation and a stated limitation. Responsible use. Avoid obsolete tests and norms, and never adopt computer-generated interpretations uncritically. 6.11 A case from referral question to report Case. Arjun, nine, in class 4 of an English-medium school in Pune, is referred by his teacher: "Slow learner. Please test IQ." His family speaks Marathi at home. Clarifying the question. A call reveals the teacher's real question: why is a lively boy who follows class discussion failing English and written work, and does he need a special school? The working questions become: is his intellect average or below; if average, is there a specific learning, attention or emotional problem; and what help does he need? Hypotheses include intellectual disability, specific learning disorder, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, anxiety, sensory problems and simple lack of English exposure. Test selection. A paediatric check excludes vision and hearing problems. After interviewing parents and teacher, the psychologist selects Malin's Intelligence Scale for Indian Children (Indian norms, though old), the Vineland Social Maturity Scale, standardised reading, spelling and arithmetic tests, the Child Behavior Checklist (parent and teacher forms), interval-recorded observation in an English and a mathematics period, and a sentence completion form read aloud. Results. Arjun tried hard, so scores can be trusted. His full-scale quotient was 101 (verbal 97, performance 106), average allowing for measurement error, as was his social quotient. He read at about a class 2 level, slowly, stumbling over sounding out words; his Marathi reading was also behind, which argues against mere lack of English exposure. Arithmetic was at class level except for word problems he could not read. Parent ratings were normal apart from worry about school; the teacher rated borderline attention problems. He was off-task in about half the observed intervals in English but about one tenth in mathematics, and asked to sharpen his pencil or visit the toilet whenever reading aloud was due, which let him escape it. He completed one stem: "I feel stupid when... I read in front of everyone." Report summary. "Arjun is a friendly, hard-working boy of average intelligence. He does not have an intellectual disability and does not need a special school. His difficulties are specific to reading and spelling in both English and Marathi and fit a specific learning disorder with impairment in reading. His inattention appears mainly when he must read and seems to be avoidance of a humiliating task rather than a general attention disorder; review this once his reading improves. We recommend structured, phonics-based remedial teaching; examination accommodations such as extra time and having questions read to him; not asking him to read aloud before the class for now; praise for effort; and review in one year. He may be eligible for certification as having a specific learning disability." Recap. Assessment answers a referral question by many methods, of which testing is one; its purposes run from screening and diagnosis to treatment planning, outcome evaluation, research and forensic work. A score means something only if the test is standardised, reliable, valid for the purpose and normed on relevant, recent samples (a real issue in India); every score carries a standard error, and a positive result's value depends on the base rate. Intelligence is assessed with the Wechsler scales, the Stanford-Binet, Raven's matrices and Indian tests such as Bhatia's battery and Malin's scale. Personality is assessed with objective inventories such as the MMPI and the NEO and with projective methods such as the Rorschach, whose support is variable-specific. Behavioural assessment rests on functional analysis and observation; neuropsychological assessment on batteries such as the Halstead-Reitan and the NIMHANS battery, with the MMSE only a screen. Statistical prediction usually matches or beats clinical judgement, which is prone to predictable biases. Findings end in a clear report for the referral source, governed by rules on competence, consent, test security and cultural fairness.
