Questions this chapter lets you answer: Distinguish assessment from testing, describe the purposes of clinical assessment, and explain why the referral question should organise every assessment. Define reliability and validity and their main types, and explain with worked examples how the standard error of measurement, sensitivity, specificity and base rates affect decisions about individuals. Trace intelligence testing from Binet to the current Wechsler scales, describe the main Indian tests, and evaluate the uses and limits of IQ. Describe the construction, validity scales and clinical scales of the MMPI and its revisions, and compare it with other objective inventories. Explain the projective hypothesis, describe the Rorschach and the Thematic Apperception Test, and evaluate the scientific debate about them. Discuss clinical versus statistical prediction and the biases in clinical judgement, and explain how to reduce them when integrating data and writing a report. 7 Psychotherapy: what it is, the main approaches, and whether it works Chapter 3 set out the theories behind the main models of clinical psychology. This chapter walks into the consulting room: what psychotherapy is, who comes and what they expect, how a course of therapy runs, and what a therapist of each school actually does. It then asks the question every viva asks: does any of this work, how do we know, and does it matter which therapy a person receives? Psychotherapy is the clinical psychologist's core skill, and the outcome debate is among the most examined areas in the clinical textbooks. The chapter closes with one client followed through a full course of cognitive behaviour therapy. 7.1 What psychotherapy is, and how a course of therapy runs No definition satisfies every school, but a working one covers them all: psychotherapy is a planned, collaborative relationship in which a trained professional uses psychological methods, grounded in a theory of how problems arise and how people change, to help a person reduce distress and change troubling patterns of feeling, thinking, behaving or relating. "Trained professional" separates therapy from a wise elder's help; therapy is not "just talking". "Psychological methods" means conversation, the relationship and structured practice rather than medicines. "Grounded in a theory" means a rationale explains the problem and justifies the procedure. "Collaborative" makes the client an active partner. All of it sits inside an ethical frame of consent, confidentiality and boundaries. Counselling overlaps heavily; by convention it is shorter and aimed at adjustment problems in people functioning reasonably well. People come with depression, anxiety, trauma, marital conflict, grief or a sense of being stuck; some are sent by a parent, college or court and may not believe they have a problem. All bring expectations. Role expectations concern what each party will do: many first-time clients expect a doctor who questions and then prescribes advice, and are puzzled when asked to explore feelings or keep a diary. Outcome expectations concern whether therapy will help, and duration expectations how long it will take. Badly mismatched expectations predict dropout, so many therapists begin with role induction : a plain explanation of how therapy works and what the client's part is. Most courses of therapy pass through four phases. Assessment. The first one to three sessions gather the problem, its history, background, strengths and any risk to self or others, often with standardised questionnaires. Consent is taken and the limits of confidentiality explained. Assessment ends in a case formulation : a working hypothesis about how the problem developed and what keeps it going. Goal setting. Good goals are specific and observable ("attend classes three days a week"), not vague ("feel better"). The working phase. Techniques are applied and most change happens; setbacks and strains in the relationship are expected. Termination. A planned ending reviews what changed and how, prepares for future difficulties (relapse prevention), and gives room to feelings about ending, sometimes followed by spaced "booster" sessions. Sessions usually last 45 to 50 minutes, often weekly, within a stable frame of time, place, fees and boundaries. A psychodynamic session is deliberately unstructured so the client's material can emerge. A cognitive behavioural session is structured; the sequence taught by Judith Beck runs: mood check, bridge from the last session, agenda set together, homework review, agenda items, new homework, and a closing summary with the client's feedback. Homework means tasks carried out between sessions: recording thoughts, practising relaxation, facing a feared situation. The logic is arithmetic: one hour a week with the therapist against more than a hundred waking hours without. Reviews find that therapies using homework tend to do better, and clients who complete more improve more. Undone homework is treated as information (too hard, badly explained, blocked by a belief such as "nothing will help"), not defiance. 7.2 Common factors and the therapeutic alliance Therapies with incompatible theories all seem to help. A psychoanalyst explains depression through loss and anger turned inward, a behaviourist through lost reinforcement, a cognitive therapist through negative thinking. If all succeed, perhaps what heals is what they share. This is the common factors argument. Rosenzweig and the Dodo bird verdict Saul Rosenzweig made the argument in a short 1936 paper. The success of different methods, he suggested, owed more to "implicit common factors" than to their theories: the therapist's personality, the release of feeling, and above all a consistent, believable way of understanding one's difficulties, whose coherence mattered more than its literal truth. He borrowed a line from Lewis Carroll's Alice's Adventures in Wonderland , where after a chaotic race the Dodo declares: "Everybody has won, and all must have prizes." In 1975 Lester Luborsky and colleagues reviewed comparative studies, found few differences in outcome, and put the Dodo's line in their title; the label "Dodo bird verdict" (genuine therapies produce roughly equal benefit) dates from that review. Trap. Rosenzweig introduced the Dodo analogy in 1936; Luborsky and colleagues popularised the "Dodo bird verdict" in 1975. The verdict concerns average comparisons between competently delivered therapies, not every therapy for every problem: for obsessive-compulsive disorder and specific phobias, exposure-based methods appear to have a specific advantage, and the verdict remains contested. Jerome Frank and the shared features of healing The psychiatrist Jerome Frank , in Persuasion and Healing (1961), compared psychotherapy with religious healing, shamanism and placebo. People seek help, he argued, less for particular symptoms than because they are demoralised : helpless, hopeless and unable to cope. Every healing tradition combats demoralisation through four shared features: (1) an emotionally charged, confiding relationship with a helper; (2) a healing setting that marks the helper as a source of help; (3) a rationale or "myth" that plausibly explains the sufferer's problems; and (4) a ritual or procedure based on that rationale, requiring the active participation of both and believed by both to restore health. "Myth" did not mean falsehood; the explanation heals because it is shared and believed. Wampold's contextual model Bruce Wampold , in The Great Psychotherapy Debate (2001), set two models against each other. In the medical model , therapy works like a drug: a specific ingredient corrects a specific deficit. In the contextual model , therapy is a social healing practice: once a bond forms, benefit flows through the real relationship , a genuine connection that heals in itself; through expectations , as the client accepts an explanation and believes the treatment will work; and through specific ingredients , which matter because they lead the client to take health-promoting actions such as facing fears. Wampold reads small differences between therapies and larger ones between therapists as favouring the contextual model; critics say he underweights conditions where specific procedures clearly matter. Client, therapist and expectancy factors Client factors include severity, chronicity, motivation, social support and readiness to change. Therapist factors matter too: some therapists consistently outperform colleagues delivering the same manual. Expectancy and hope probably explain much of the rapid improvement that often precedes any technique. Michael Lambert offered a widely reproduced estimate in 1992 of each factor's contribution; it came from his reading of the literature, not a statistical analysis, and must be quoted as an estimate. Source of improvement Lambert's estimate What it includes Extratherapeutic (client and life) factors About 40 percent Client strengths, support, chance events, spontaneous recovery Common factors About 30 percent Empathy, warmth, acceptance, the alliance Expectancy (placebo) About 15 percent Hope and belief in the treatment Specific techniques About 15 percent Procedures unique to a school The therapeutic alliance The most studied common factor is the therapeutic alliance . The idea began in psychoanalysis, but in 1979 Edward Bordin gave it a form any school could use, with three components: Goals: agreement on what the therapy aims to change. Tasks: agreement on the activities through which change will happen (exploring childhood, keeping thought records, exposure) and a shared sense that they are relevant. Bond: the emotional tie of trust, liking and respect. This made the alliance measurable, and large meta-analyses consistently find a moderate correlation between alliance and outcome, roughly 0.25 to 0.30, across therapies. Being a correlation, it could partly reflect early improvement strengthening the alliance, though the link largely survives when prior change is controlled. Research on ruptures , strains shown through withdrawal (going quiet, agreeing too readily) or confrontation (complaining), suggests that ruptures openly repaired can strengthen the alliance. 7.3 Psychodynamic therapy in practice Psychodynamic therapy descends from Sigmund Freud 's psychoanalysis: unconscious conflicts and early relationship patterns are helped to surface in the room. Classical analysis meant four or five couch sessions a week for years; modern psychodynamic therapy is usually weekly and face to face. Free association is the "fundamental rule": the client says whatever comes to mind without censoring it as trivial or embarrassing. Interpretation , the main intervention, offers a hypothesis about hidden meaning, built up gradually. The therapist first clarifies ("You've mentioned your manager three times today"), then confronts an avoidance ("Each time you reach how angry you were, you change the subject"), then interprets ("Perhaps anger at someone in authority feels dangerous, as it did with your father"). Good interpretations are timely, tentative and close to what the client can almost see. Transference is the client's unconscious transfer onto the therapist of feelings belonging to earlier figures: a client harshly criticised as a child may be sure the therapist is silently judging him. Because the pattern appears live, it can be examined as it happens. Countertransference is the therapist's emotional reaction to the client. Freud saw it as an obstacle; in 1950 Paula Heimann argued it is also an instrument, since what the therapist feels (boredom, protectiveness, irritation) may reveal how the client affects others. Resistance is any way the client unknowingly opposes painful material: lateness, forgotten sessions, silence, intellectualising, or a sudden "everything is fine". It is explored, not fought, because what is avoided usually matters. Working through , from Freud's 1914 paper "Remembering, Repeating and Working-Through", is the slow revisiting of an insight across many situations until it changes how the person feels and acts. One insight does not cure. Brief psychodynamic therapy limits the number of sessions, agrees a single focus such as one core conflict, makes the therapist more active, and selects clients who can form a relationship quickly and tolerate strong feeling. David Malan 's "triangle of conflict" (hidden feeling, the anxiety it arouses, the defence against it) and "triangle of person" (the pattern with the therapist, current others and past figures) remain standard teaching tools. James Mann 's time-limited psychotherapy uses exactly twelve sessions and makes the approaching ending part of the work. 7.4 Client-centred therapy in practice Carl Rogers developed client-centred (later person-centred) therapy from the 1940s. His 1957 paper "The necessary and sufficient conditions of therapeutic personality change" claimed that if six conditions hold over time, constructive change follows, and nothing else is needed: Two persons are in psychological contact. The client is in a state of incongruence , vulnerable or anxious. The therapist is congruent (genuine) in the relationship. The therapist experiences unconditional positive regard for the client. The therapist experiences empathic understanding of the client's internal frame of reference and tries to communicate it. The client perceives, at least minimally, that empathy and regard. Diagnosis, interpretation, advice and technique are all absent; the relationship is the treatment. The visible activity is reflection : restating the client's meaning, especially the feeling behind it, so the client can hear it and go further. It is not parroting; late in life Rogers disliked "reflection of feelings" as a mechanical label and preferred to call it testing his understanding. Case. Client: My parents keep asking when I'll get a proper job. I just nod. Then I go to my room and can't do anything. Therapist: You nod along, and afterwards there's a heaviness, as if the energy has drained out. Client: Yes. I feel I've failed them. But also... I'm angry. It's my life. Therapist: Two feelings side by side: guilt at letting them down, and anger that the decision isn't left to you. The therapist does not reassure, advise or interpret the parents' motives, and never runs ahead of what the client feels. Feeling understood rather than judged, he reaches the anger he had kept out of awareness: incongruence beginning to resolve. Research partly supports Rogers: meta-analyses find therapist empathy moderately related to outcome across therapies, and genuineness and positive regard more modestly so. But "necessary and sufficient" has not held in its strong form: for some disorders structured methods outperform the relationship alone. The core conditions are powerful facilitative factors, not a complete treatment. 7.5 Behaviour therapy techniques Behaviour therapy applies learning principles directly to problem behaviour, working on what can be observed and measured now and testing its methods experimentally. Relaxation training. Edmund Jacobson 's progressive muscle relaxation has the client tense and release muscle groups in turn, learning to notice and let go of tension. With slow breathing, it is used for stress and generalised anxiety and as a building block of desensitisation. Systematic desensitisation. Joseph Wolpe described it in Psychotherapy by Reciprocal Inhibition (1958): since a person cannot be deeply relaxed and anxious at once, relaxation can gradually replace anxiety. The client learns relaxation; builds an anxiety hierarchy of feared scenes rated on a 0 to 100 scale of subjective units of distress ; then, while relaxed, imagines the lowest scene, stopping if anxiety rises, and moves up only when a scene can be held calmly. Exposure and flooding. Later research showed the active ingredient to be chiefly exposure : prolonged, repeated contact with the feared stimulus without escape, graded or intense, imagined or in real life ( in vivo ). Flooding places the client at once in the most feared situation until anxiety falls; it can work fast but is distressing and needs full consent. The older explanation is habituation , fear declining with sustained contact; newer inhibitory-learning accounts hold that the person learns something new ("the disaster did not happen") that competes with the old fear. Exposure and response prevention , the main behavioural treatment for obsessive-compulsive disorder, was pioneered by Victor Meyer in 1966 and developed extensively by Edna Foa . The client touches a "contaminated" doorknob and then does not wash. Compulsions relieve anxiety briefly, which is exactly what keeps the obsession alive; blocking them teaches that anxiety subsides and the feared outcome does not occur. Contingency management and token economies. Contingency management systematically reinforces wanted behaviour; in substance use treatment, clients earn vouchers for drug-free urine tests. A token economy applies this to a whole ward: Teodoro Ayllon and Nathan Azrin described one at Anna State Hospital, Illinois, in 1968, where long-stay patients earned tokens for self-care and ward tasks, exchangeable for privileges. Behaviour improved, but gains often faded when tokens stopped, and critics questioned making basic comforts conditional. Behavioural activation draws on Peter Lewinsohn 's view that depression is maintained by low positive reinforcement: withdrawal reduces reward, deepening low mood and further withdrawal. The client monitors activity and mood, sees the link, and schedules activities that bring pleasure or mastery. A 1996 component study found activation alone did about as well as full cognitive therapy, establishing it as a treatment in its own right. Social skills training teaches interpersonal behaviour (starting a conversation, making a request, refusing) through instruction, modelling, role-play, feedback and homework, in schizophrenia, social anxiety and developmental conditions. Trap. Systematic desensitisation is graded, uses relaxation and is usually imaginal; flooding is ungraded, uses no relaxation and starts at the top of the hierarchy. Exposure and response prevention adds a second element: blocking the compulsion. 7.6 Cognitive therapy and cognitive behaviour therapy techniques Cognitive therapies, developed by Aaron Beck from the 1960s and Albert Ellis from 1955, rest on the principle that interpretations of events shape feelings and actions. Cognitive behaviour therapy (CBT) combines these methods with behavioural ones. Beck called the stance collaborative empiricism : therapist and client test the client's beliefs together, like scientists. Identifying automatic thoughts. These are quick evaluations that arise in a situation and feel simply true: "They think I'm stupid", "I'll never cope". Beneath them lie intermediate beliefs (rules such as "If I'm not perfect, I'm a failure") and core beliefs ("I am worthless"). The classic cue, at a moment of mood change, is "What was going through your mind just then?" Clients learn to spot thinking errors: all-or-nothing thinking, catastrophising, mind reading, overgeneralisation, personalisation and "should" statements. Thought records are written forms with columns for the situation, emotion and intensity, the automatic thought and belief in it, evidence for, evidence against, a balanced alternative, and a re-rating of emotion. The aim is accurate, not positive, thinking; the balanced thought must be believable. Socratic questioning replaces telling with asking: "What is the evidence for and against?", "Is there another explanation?", "What would you tell a friend?", "What is the worst, best and most realistic outcome?". This is guided discovery : a conclusion the client reaches is more convincing than one handed over. The downward arrow asks repeatedly "If that were true, what would it mean about you?" to reach the core belief. Behavioural experiments test beliefs by action. The client states a prediction ("If I speak in the seminar, people will laugh"), rates belief in it, tries it and records what happened. Experiments often drop safety behaviours , small precautions (avoiding eye contact, rehearsing every sentence) that stop the person learning the feared outcome would not have happened anyway. Disputing irrational beliefs. Ellis's rational emotive behaviour therapy uses the ABC model : an activating event (A) does not itself cause the emotional and behavioural consequences (C); the beliefs (B) about it do. Disturbance comes from rigid demands ("I must succeed") and their offshoots: awfulising, low frustration tolerance ("I can't stand it") and global self-rating ("I am a failure"). Therapy adds D, disputing , and E, an effective new belief. Disputes are empirical ("Where is the evidence you must succeed?"), logical ("Does wanting it mean you must have it?") and pragmatic ("Where does this belief get you?"). Ellis was famously forceful and set "shame-attacking" homework. Trap. Aaron Beck treats beliefs as hypotheses tested collaboratively through questions and experiments; Ellis vigorously disputes irrational "musts". Beck speaks of automatic thoughts and schemas, Ellis of irrational beliefs and the ABC model. 7.7 The third wave: acceptance, mindfulness and dialectics In 2004 Steven Hayes described a "third wave" of behavioural and cognitive therapy. The first wave changed behaviour; the second changed the content of thoughts; the third changes the person's relationship to thoughts and feelings through acceptance, mindfulness, values and dialectics. Acceptance and commitment therapy Acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT), developed by Hayes and colleagues, holds that suffering is magnified by experiential avoidance , the struggle to escape unwanted inner experiences, and cognitive fusion , taking thoughts as literal truths. It builds psychological flexibility through six processes: acceptance, cognitive defusion (seeing thoughts as thoughts), contact with the present moment, self-as-context (a stable observing self), values, and committed action. Techniques include prefacing a thought with "I'm having the thought that..." and the "passengers on the bus" metaphor, where thoughts are noisy passengers who can shout without taking the wheel. A cognitive therapist asks "Is this thought true?"; this therapist asks "Does holding on to it help you live the life you value?" Dialectical behaviour therapy Marsha Linehan developed dialectical behaviour therapy (DBT) for chronically suicidal women with borderline personality disorder, publishing her manuals in 1993. Pure change-oriented therapy left these clients feeling invalidated; pure acceptance left dangerous behaviour unchanged. The dialectic holds both: "You are doing the best you can, and you need to do better." Her biosocial theory sees the disorder as biological emotional vulnerability meeting an invalidating environment. Treatment has four modes: individual therapy, a skills group, telephone coaching and a therapists' consultation team. The group teaches mindfulness , distress tolerance , emotion regulation and interpersonal effectiveness . Individual work targets life-threatening behaviour first, then therapy-interfering behaviour, then behaviour damaging quality of life, using a daily diary card and chain analysis , a step-by-step reconstruction of the events, thoughts and feelings leading to a problem behaviour. Mindfulness-based cognitive therapy Zindel Segal, Mark Williams and John Teasdale set out mindfulness-based cognitive therapy in a 2002 book, combining Jon Kabat-Zinn 's mindfulness-based stress reduction with cognitive therapy as an eight-week group course with daily practice (body scan, sitting meditation, a "three-minute breathing space"). It targets relapse in people recovered from recurrent depression, in whom a small dip in mood can reactivate old negative thinking and spiral into a new episode. Mindfulness teaches decentring , seeing thoughts as passing mental events, and a shift from a driven "doing" mode to an accepting "being" mode. Trials found it reduced relapse in people with three or more previous episodes, but not clearly in those with fewer. Trap. Mindfulness-based cognitive therapy prevents relapse in people currently well after recurrent depression; it is not a first-line treatment for acute severe depression. Acceptance and commitment therapy does not dispute thoughts; it changes how the person relates to them. 7.8 Group, family and couples therapy Group therapy treats several clients, often six to ten, with one or two therapists, from structured skills groups to interpersonal process groups where members' relationships with each other are the material. Irvin Yalom , in The Theory and Practice of Group Psychotherapy (first edition 1970), named the therapeutic factors through which groups help. Yalom's therapeutic factor What it means Instillation of hope Seeing others improve shows change is possible. Universality Discovering others share one's "unique" shame. Imparting information Teaching and advice from therapist or members. Altruism Helping others raises self-worth. Corrective recapitulation of the primary family group Old family patterns re-emerge and are reworked. Development of socialising techniques Learning social skills through feedback. Imitative behaviour Modelling oneself on the therapist or members. Interpersonal learning Learning how one affects others; trying new ways of relating. Group cohesiveness Belonging and acceptance; the group's alliance. Catharsis Expressing strong feeling, joined to understanding. Existential factors Facing responsibility, mortality and the limits of others. Family therapy treats the family as a system: a symptom in the "identified patient" is part of patterns in the whole, and causation is circular rather than linear. Salvador Minuchin 's structural family therapy reshapes boundaries and hierarchy, for example between an enmeshed parent and adolescent; Murray Bowen stressed differentiation of self and mapped generations in a genogram. The strongest evidence concerns schizophrenia: high expressed emotion in relatives (critical comments, hostility, emotional over-involvement) predicts relapse, and family psychoeducation that lowers it reduces relapse. Couples therapy treats the relationship itself: behavioural couples therapy trains communication and problem-solving, while emotionally focused therapy works on attachment needs beneath cycles of blame and withdrawal. 7.9 Does it work? From Eysenck to meta-analysis "Does therapy work?" hides two questions. Efficacy asks whether a treatment works under ideal research conditions: selected clients with one diagnosis, trained therapists following a manual, random allocation. Effectiveness asks whether it works in ordinary practice, with clients who have several problems and therapists of varied skill. Efficacy studies maximise internal validity (confidence the treatment caused the change); effectiveness studies maximise external validity (generalisability). The main efficacy design is the randomised controlled trial : random assignment to the treatment or a comparison (waiting list, treatment as usual, a psychological placebo, or another therapy) spreads unknown differences evenly, so an outcome difference can be attributed to treatment. Assessors can be blind to group, but therapist and client cannot. On the effectiveness side, Martin Seligman 's 1995 analysis of a Consumer Reports survey found readers reported substantial benefit, more with longer treatment, though it relied on retrospective self-report without a control group. Eysenck's 1952 challenge In 1952 Hans Eysenck published "The effects of psychotherapy: an evaluation". Pooling existing reports, he set improvement rates for neurotic patients treated by psychoanalysis (about 44 percent) and eclectic therapy (about 64 percent) against state hospital discharges and insurance disability claimants seen by general practitioners, of whom about 72 percent, roughly two-thirds, improved within two years. He concluded that psychotherapy had not been shown to beat spontaneous remission . Critics, notably Allen Bergin , showed the comparison to be flawed: the baseline groups differed in diagnosis and severity, improvement criteria varied, and psychoanalytic patients who left early were counted as failures. Reanalyses gave far lower spontaneous remission rates. Still, the paper forced the field to test its claims. Smith and Glass: meta-analysis and effect size In 1977 Mary Lee Smith and Gene Glass applied meta-analysis to 375 controlled studies: instead of counting wins and losses, each result is converted into a common metric, the effect size , and averaged. They found an average of about 0.68, with small differences between types of therapy; an expanded 1980 analysis of 475 studies found about 0.85. Eysenck called the 1977 study "an exercise in mega-silliness" for mixing good and poor studies; this "garbage in, garbage out" objection made later meta-analyses weigh study quality, but the central finding has held. The effect size here, Cohen's d after Jacob Cohen , is the difference between treated and control averages divided by the standard deviation (the typical spread of scores): how many standard deviations apart the groups sit. Cohen's rough benchmarks are 0.2 small, 0.5 medium and 0.8 large. An effect of 0.68 means the average treated person is better off than about 75 percent of untreated people; 0.85 raises this to about 80 percent. Case. Untreated clients average 30 on an anxiety scale with a standard deviation of 10; treated clients average 23. The difference of 7, divided by 10, gives an effect size of 0.7: the average treated client scores better than roughly three-quarters of untreated clients. This does not mean 75 percent of clients improved; it locates the average treated person within the untreated distribution. The dose-effect relationship In 1986 Kenneth Howard and colleagues pooled earlier outcome data and plotted percentage improved against sessions attended. The curve rose steeply, then flattened: roughly half of clients had improved measurably by about eight sessions and roughly three-quarters by about 26. This negatively accelerating curve is the dose-effect relationship ; acute distress responded faster than long-standing personality problems. Howard's group later proposed a phase model (1993): remoralisation (restored hope, often within a few sessions), then remediation (symptom relief), then rehabilitation (changing long-standing patterns). Trap. Efficacy is ideal-conditions evidence; effectiveness is real-world evidence. An effect size is not a percentage of people helped. Hans Eysenck claimed improvement did not exceed spontaneous remission, not that therapy harmed. 7.10 Empirically supported treatments, harm and dropout Which therapies work for which problems? In 1995 a task force of the American Psychological Association's clinical psychology division, chaired by Dianne Chambless , listed "empirically validated" treatments, later renamed empirically supported treatments , with criteria refined in later papers. A well-established treatment needed at least two good between-group experiments, by different research teams, showing it superior to placebo or another treatment, or equivalent to an established one; or a large series of well-designed single-case experiments; with a treatment manual and a clearly described sample. A probably efficacious treatment needed, for example, two experiments showing superiority to a waiting list, or strong experiments from only one team. The lists shaped training and guidelines and were dominated by cognitive behavioural treatments. Critics said they favoured short, manualised therapies easy to trial, treated diagnosis as the unit of treatment, and ignored relationship and therapist. The American Psychological Association's 2006 policy on evidence-based practice in psychology broadened the frame: best available research integrated with clinical expertise, in the context of the client's characteristics, culture and preferences. Deterioration and harm. Bergin named the deterioration effect in the 1960s, noticing that some treated clients got worse. Commonly cited estimates associated with Lambert put deterioration at roughly 5 to 10 percent of adult clients. Harm comes from poor therapy (ruptured alliance, boundary violations, missed risk) or harmful treatments. Scott Lilienfeld (2007) listed potentially harmful therapies, including "Scared Straight" programmes for young offenders (linked to more, not less, offending), critical incident stress debriefing straight after trauma, and "recovered memory" techniques that can create false memories. Routine outcome monitoring, with a brief measure every session and alerts when a client is not on track, has been shown to reduce deterioration. Dropout means leaving before goals are reached, usually without a planned ending. Estimates depend on definition: a widely cited 1993 meta-analysis found about 47 percent; a larger 2012 meta-analysis with stricter definitions found about 20 percent. Younger clients, clients with personality disorders and those seen by trainees drop out more; clear explanation, agreed goals and early attention to expectations reduce it. Some dropouts simply feel better already, as the dose-effect curve predicts. 7.11 Psychotherapy in India Textbook psychotherapy grew up in Europe and North America and assumes an individualistic client, comfortable confiding in a stranger and aiming at autonomy. Family involvement. In India the family is usually inside the treatment: relatives bring the client, attend the first interview, hold important history and share decisions about treatment, marriage and work. An early example is Vidya Sagar 's work at the Amritsar Mental Hospital in the 1950s, where families stayed with patients in tents on the hospital grounds and joined in their care. Family involvement brings resources (support, help with homework, a wider view) and confidentiality dilemmas, especially with young adults. Directive expectations. Many Indian clients expect an authority who diagnoses and advises, and a purely non-directive stance can seem evasive. The psychiatrist J. S. Neki , in a 1973 paper, proposed the guru-chela relationship as a therapeutic paradigm. Western therapy, he argued, treats dependence as something to resolve quickly in pursuit of autonomy, whereas Indian tradition accepts and values dependence on a guide. The guru is warm but authoritative, guides actively, and leads the disciple through trust towards eventual self-realisation. Neki suggested Indian therapists use a more directive, dependent early relationship as a route to growth rather than resisting it. Cultural adaptation changes delivery while keeping the active ingredients: the client's language and idioms of distress (many describe psychological suffering through the body, as "tension", weakness or pain); family involvement in formulation and homework; stories and philosophical ideas the client already values; respect for spiritual or karmic explanations alongside a psychological one; and shorter courses where travel and cost demand it. Given the shortage of professionals, task-sharing has grown: in the Healthy Activity Program in Goa, developed by Vikram Patel and colleagues, lay counsellors delivered brief behavioural activation-based treatment for depression that outperformed enhanced usual care in a randomised controlled trial. Yoga and meditation are indigenous to the subcontinent, and mindfulness itself comes from Buddhist meditation. Indian centres, notably the National Institute of Mental Health and Neurosciences in Bengaluru, have researched yoga as an add-on to standard treatment for conditions including depression and schizophrenia. Clinicians integrate breathing, relaxation and meditation as complements to evidence-based care, not replacements. The Mental Healthcare Act 2017 recognises clinical psychologists with qualifications recognised by the Rehabilitation Council of India as mental health professionals. 7.12 A case: one client across a course of cognitive behaviour therapy This composite case shows the chapter's pieces working together over fourteen sessions. Sessions 1 and 2: assessment, formulation and goals Karan, 23, is brought by his mother three months after failing, for the second time, to win a postgraduate seat. He sleeps until noon, has stopped studying and seeing friends, and feels worthless. He admits passing thoughts that his family "would be better off" without him; the therapist asks directly, finds no plan or intent, and agrees a safety plan. His score of 19 on the nine-item Patient Health Questionnaire indicates moderately severe depression. The therapist explains confidentiality and how the therapy works, and, with Karan's consent, invites his mother in for the last ten minutes. In session 2 they build a formulation: praise in childhood came mainly for marks, and Karan formed the rule "If I don't succeed, I'm worthless" over a core belief "I am a failure". The rejection activated it; low mood led to withdrawal, withdrawal to no achievement, which seemed to prove the belief. Goals: study three hours a day, five days a week; meet a friend weekly; bring his score below 10. Homework: an hourly activity and mood diary. Sessions 3 and 4: behavioural activation The diary shows mood lowest when lying in bed scrolling his phone and highest on an evening walk and when a cousin visited. They schedule a morning walk, one hour of study and one call to a friend, building up gradually; his mother agrees to notice effort rather than mention the exam. By session 4 his score is 15: early remoralisation. Sessions 5 to 7: automatic thoughts and Socratic questioning Sitting down to study, Karan catches the thought "What's the point, I'll fail again", believed at 90 percent. On a thought record he lists evidence for (two failures) and against (he missed the cut-off narrowly, his score rose between attempts, he cleared another entrance). Asked what he would tell a friend, he says bad luck plus a study plan that needed changing. His balanced thought, "I've fallen short twice by small margins, which says my preparation needs changing, not that I'm incapable", cuts belief in the original to 50 percent. He names his errors: all-or-nothing thinking and fortune-telling. By session 7 his score is 11. Sessions 8 to 10: experiments, the core belief and a rupture Karan predicts that friends told about the second failure will look down on him (belief 80 percent). He tells two; one describes his own failed attempt and they form a study group. Belief falls to 20 percent. In session 9 he says the forms "feel like school"; the therapist acknowledges this and switches to spoken thought records, repairing the rupture. The downward arrow reaches "I am a failure", and Karan notices he would never apply that label to his cousin for the same result. Sessions 11 to 14: relapse prevention and ending Sessions move to fortnightly. Karan writes a plan of what helped, his warning signs (sleeping late, skipping walks, "what's the point" thoughts) and what he will do if they return; his mother joins part of session 13 to learn the signs. At session 14 his score is 6, he studies daily, meets friends and has registered for the next entrance. Boosters are set for one and three months. Common factors (alliance, hope, a believable rationale, family support) and specific techniques (activation, thought records, Socratic questioning, experiments) worked together, as the contextual and phase models predict. Recap. Psychotherapy is a planned, collaborative, theory-based relationship that moves through assessment, goal setting, a working phase and termination, with homework carrying change into daily life. The common factors tradition, from Rosenzweig's Dodo through Frank and Wampold, locates much of therapy's power in what all therapies share, above all Bordin's alliance of goals, tasks and bond. Each school still has distinctive practices: interpretation of transference and resistance, Carl Rogers' core conditions, exposure and reinforcement, thought records and experiments, and third-wave acceptance and mindfulness. Groups add Irvin Yalom's therapeutic factors; family work treats the system. Eysenck's 1952 challenge was answered by Smith and Glass's 1977 meta-analysis, and Howard's dose-effect curve showed most improvement arriving early. Therapy can also harm, and clients drop out. In India, family involvement, directive expectations and Neki's guru-chela model shape delivery.
