Using concepts from this chapter, design and justify an intervention plan for a burned-out mental health trainee, including its limits. 14 Optimism, hope, resilience and growth after adversity Clinical psychology grew up studying what goes wrong. This chapter asks an equally clinical question: when life delivers a blow, why do some people keep going, some fall and recover, some stay down, and some report being changed for the better? The answers come from separate research traditions: what you expect (optimism), how you explain what happened (learned helplessness and explanatory style), how you think about goals (hope), adaptation despite serious risk (resilience), protective orientations (hardiness (Suzanne Kobasa, 1979) and sense of coherence) and positive change after trauma (post-traumatic growth), all held together by Richard Lazarus and Susan Folkman's model of coping. These ideas matter clinically because they are measurable, predict real outcomes and in several cases can be taught; the controversies around them are taught here too, because examiners expect them. The positive psychology texts (Baumgardner and Crothers; the Oxford Handbook of Positive Psychology) cover this ground in detail, and the clinical textbooks (Pomerantz; Trull and Phares) draw on it when they discuss stress, coping and health. 14.1 Dispositional optimism: expecting good outcomes Dispositional optimism is a relatively stable tendency to expect that good things, rather than bad things, will happen in one's life. The key word is generalised : confidence about one driving test is a specific expectancy, whereas dispositional optimism is a default expectation, carried across the domains of life, that the future will on the whole turn out well. Dispositional pessimism is the generalised expectation of bad outcomes. Who gave us this. Michael Scheier and Charles Carver introduced dispositional optimism in 1985, in a paper in the journal Health Psychology that also presented the Life Orientation Test. In 1994 Scheier, Carver and a colleague published the Life Orientation Test Revised (LOT-R), the form used in most research today. The idea came from Scheier and Carver's self-regulation model of behaviour , in which people pursue goals and keep comparing where they are with where they want to be. When an obstacle appears, the person asks, at least briefly, whether success is still likely. If yes, effort continues or increases; if no, effort is withdrawn and the goal may be abandoned. Dispositional optimism is that expectancy lifted to the level of a trait: facing almost any obstacle, the optimist assumes things will work out and keeps engaging, while the pessimist disengages sooner. Measuring optimism The original Life Orientation Test had twelve items, four of them unscored fillers that disguise its purpose. Because its scores overlapped heavily with neuroticism and anxiety, critics worried that "optimism" was merely the absence of negative emotion, so the 1994 revision removed items that were about coping rather than expectancy. The revised test has ten items: three optimistic (for example "In uncertain times, I usually expect the best"), three pessimistic and reverse scored (for example "If something can go wrong for me, it will") and four fillers, each rated from 0 (strongly disagree) to 4 (strongly agree), giving a total of 0 to 24. Optimism measured this way still predicted outcomes after neuroticism and anxiety were controlled. Optimism, coping and health Optimism works largely through coping. Optimists tend to use approach coping : planning, seeking information, acting on problems that can be solved, reframing positively and accepting what cannot be changed. Pessimists lean towards avoidant coping : denial, wishful thinking, giving up, and escape through alcohol or other substances. In Carver's studies of women treated for early breast cancer, optimism predicted less distress over the following year, largely through acceptance and positive reframing. The best known health study concerns recovery after coronary artery bypass surgery . Scheier and colleagues (1989) measured optimism in men before bypass surgery. Optimists reached recovery milestones such as sitting up and walking sooner, returned to normal activities sooner after discharge and reported better quality of life months later; a later study by the same group found optimists less likely to be rehospitalised. Meta-analytic reviews support a modest but reliable link between optimism and physical health, working through behaviour, coping and possibly physiology. Trap. Optimism is not denial. Research by Lisa Aspinwall and colleagues found that optimists pay closer attention to health-risk information relevant to them, because they expect acting on it to help. The optimist says "this is serious, and I can do something about it"; the person in denial says "this is not happening". 14.2 Defensive pessimism and the limits of optimism Defensive pessimism , described by Julie Norem and colleagues in the 1980s, is a strategy in which a person anxious about a performance deliberately sets low expectations, despite usually having done well, and then mentally rehearses everything that could go wrong. A student before a viva says, "I will forget everything, they will ask about statistics, my voice will shake", and then prepares for each disaster. The low expectation cushions a possible failure, and the rehearsal turns anxiety into preparation. Norem contrasted it with strategic optimism , in which less anxious people set high expectations and avoid dwelling on the event. Defensive pessimists perform worse when prevented from using their strategy, for example when cheered up or distracted beforehand, while strategic optimists perform worse when forced to dwell on what could go wrong. Norem set out the argument in The Positive Power of Negative Thinking (2001). Trap. The dispositional pessimist expects bad outcomes and withdraws effort; the defensive pessimist expects bad outcomes as a tactic and then works harder. Optimism can also mislead. Neil Weinstein (1980) showed that most people rate their own chances of illness, accidents or divorce as lower than the average person's, which cannot be true of everyone; this unrealistic optimism can lead people to skip precautions such as wearing a helmet. Martin Seligman therefore argued for flexible optimism : optimistic thinking where the aim is to persist or recover morale, and pessimistic caution where being wrong would be catastrophic, as when a pilot decides whether ice on the wings needs removing. 14.3 Learned helplessness: from the laboratory to depression In the mid-1960s at the University of Pennsylvania, Martin Seligman and Steven Maier, then graduate students, noticed that dogs that had earlier received shocks they could do nothing about later failed to learn a simple escape response, and designed an experiment to find out why. Who gave us this. Martin Seligman and Steven Maier published the core learned helplessness experiments in 1967. The reformulated, attributional theory came from Lyn Abramson, Seligman and John Teasdale in 1978. The triadic design used three groups. The first received shocks it could stop by pressing a panel with its head. The second was "yoked" to the first: each dog received exactly the same shocks at the same times, but nothing it did mattered, because the shock stopped only when its partner pressed the panel. The third received no shocks. Because groups one and two received physically identical shocks, any difference between them must come from control, not from pain. Next day all the dogs were placed in a shuttle box , where a signal was followed by shock through the floor and the dog could escape by jumping a low barrier. The escapable-shock and no-shock dogs quickly learned to jump. Most yoked dogs lay down, whined and passively took the shock. Seligman and Steven Maier concluded that these dogs had learned that outcomes were independent of their responses, and that this expectation transferred to the new situation: learned helplessness . Three deficits were described: motivational (failure to try), cognitive (difficulty learning that a response works even after it succeeds) and emotional (fear followed by passivity). Dogs given earlier experience of escapable shock were protected, which was called immunisation , and helpless dogs recovered after being dragged across the barrier repeatedly until they moved on their own. Why the theory had to change In the 1970s the effect was reproduced in people using inescapable noise or unsolvable problems, and Seligman proposed learned helplessness as a model of depression. But human responses varied in how widely helplessness spread, whether self-esteem fell and how long it lasted. There was also a paradox: depressed people blame themselves intensely, yet the theory said they believed they had no control. The reformulated model of Abramson, Seligman and Teasdale (1978) solved this by adding attribution: after an uncontrollable bad event people ask why it happened, and the kind of answer shapes what follows. Dimension The two poles What it determines Example for failing an examination Internal versus external Caused by me, or by circumstances and others Whether self-esteem drops "I am stupid" versus "The paper was unusually hard" Stable versus unstable A lasting cause, or a temporary one How long helplessness lasts "I will never be good at this" versus "I was ill that week" Global versus specific Affects many areas of life, or only this one How widely helplessness spreads "I fail at everything" versus "I am weak in statistics" People who explain bad events with internal, stable and global causes should be most at risk of depression when bad events occur. This is a diathesis-stress model: the attributional tendency is the vulnerability, and it produces depression only together with negative events. In 1989 Abramson and colleagues extended it into the hopelessness theory of depression , in which stable, global attributions lead to hopelessness (the expectation that good outcomes will not come and nothing can be done), which then causes a subtype of depression. 14.4 Explanatory style, learned optimism and the 2016 reversal Seligman and Christopher Peterson called a person's habitual way of explaining events explanatory style . A pessimistic explanatory style explains bad events as internal, stable and global and good events as external, unstable and specific ("I got lucky this once"); an optimistic explanatory style reverses both patterns. In Learned Optimism (1990), Martin Seligman translated the dimensions into the "three Ps". Permanence is stability: does the cause last ("always", "never") or pass ("lately")? Pervasiveness is globality: does it spread across life ("all teachers are unfair") or stay in its box ("this teacher is unfair")? Personalisation is internality: do I blame myself, or see the full set of causes? The healthy alternative to personalisation is not blaming others but taking appropriate responsibility without condemning one's whole self. The standard measure is the Attributional Style Questionnaire , published in 1982 by Peterson, Seligman and colleagues. It presents twelve hypothetical events, six good and six bad, half about achievement and half about relationships. The respondent imagines each happening, writes down its one major cause and rates that cause on seven-point scales for internality, stability and globality; scores are combined separately for bad and good events. Peterson also developed the Content Analysis of Verbatim Explanations , which scores explanatory style from letters, diaries or interviews; applied to essays by young Harvard graduates, it showed that a pessimistic style predicted poorer health from middle age (Peterson, Seligman and colleagues, 1988). Learned optimism If explanatory style is learned, it can be relearned. Seligman adapted Albert Ellis's ABC model into an ABCDE sequence. A is the adversity; B is the automatic belief about why it happened; C is the consequence, the feelings and actions that flow from the belief rather than from the adversity itself; D is disputation, arguing with the belief as if an outside critic had said it (what is the evidence, what are the alternatives, what are the real implications, is the belief useful?); E is energisation, the lift in mood and energy that follows. This is cognitive restructuring as used in cognitive behaviour therapy (CBT), aimed at permanence, pervasiveness and personalisation. Seligman's group applied it in the Penn Resiliency Program for schoolchildren, whose preventive effects later reviews found real but small. Learned helplessness at fifty: the reversal In 2016 Maier and Seligman published "Learned helplessness at fifty: Insights from neuroscience" in Psychological Review, drawing on Maier's decades of work on the brain circuits involved. Passivity in the face of prolonged aversive events turned out to be the default, unlearned response , driven by strong activation of serotonin neurons in a brainstem region, the dorsal raphe nucleus. What animals learn, when shock is escapable, is control : detecting that a response ends the shock engages the medial prefrontal cortex, which inhibits the dorsal raphe and switches off the default passivity. That learned expectation of control then protects the animal in later stress, which is the real basis of immunisation. Key. The 1967 theory said helplessness is learned. The 2016 revision says passivity is the default response to prolonged bad events, and control is what is learned. Clinically, the aim shifts to building expectations of control, which connects directly to hope and self-efficacy (Albert Bandura, 1977). 14.5 Hope theory: goals, pathways and agency In everyday speech hope can be a passive wish ("I hope it doesn't rain"). C. R. Snyder gave the word a precise cognitive meaning: hope is the perceived capacity to produce routes to desired goals, together with the motivation to use those routes. Who gave us this. C. R. (Rick) Snyder, a clinical psychologist at the University of Kansas, set out hope theory and the Adult Hope Scale with colleagues in 1991, in a paper that summed up the theory as "the will and the ways". He later co-edited the Oxford Handbook of Positive Psychology. Goals are the anchor: any valued target, from finishing a thesis to walking again after injury. Hope matters most for goals of intermediate probability; if success is certain hope is unnecessary, and if truly impossible it cannot operate. Pathways thinking ("waypower") is the perceived ability to generate workable routes to goals, and another route when one is blocked: "there is a way to do this; if that fails, I can try this." Agency thinking ("willpower") is the perceived capacity to start moving along a pathway and keep going: "I can do this; I will not give up." The components are additive and iterative : pathways without agency produce plans never carried out, agency without pathways produces energy with nowhere to go, and each feeds the other during goal pursuit. Barriers are central; high-hope people treat them as problems to route around, while low-hope people read them as signs the goal is out of reach. Emotions are by-products of perceived progress: perceived success produces positive emotion, perceived failure negative emotion, and both feed back into later hope. Snyder proposed that hope is learned in childhood through consistent, responsive caregiving. The Adult Hope Scale has twelve items: four pathways items (for example "I can think of many ways to get out of a jam"), four agency items (for example "I energetically pursue my goals") and four fillers, rated in its common form on an eight-point scale from definitely false to definitely true. Shorter state and children's versions also exist. Higher hope has been associated with better academic and athletic performance, better adjustment to illness and injury, and greater well-being. Hope, optimism and self-efficacy compared Self-efficacy , from Albert Bandura (1977), is the belief that one can carry out a specific behaviour, usually in one domain; optimism expects good outcomes without saying how. Snyder argued that agency resembles self-efficacy but is broader, while pathways has no counterpart in either. The three correlate, but each predicts well-being partly independently. Construct Who and when The question it answers Focus Typical measure Dispositional optimism Michael Scheier and Charles Carver, 1985 Will things generally turn out well for me? Outcomes; silent on how they come about Life Orientation Test Revised Optimistic explanatory style Abramson, Martin Seligman and Teasdale, 1978; Peterson and Seligman Why did that happen? Causal explanations of past events Attributional Style Questionnaire Self-efficacy Albert Bandura, 1977 Can I perform this particular behaviour? Personal capability in one domain Domain-specific self-efficacy scales Hope C. R. Snyder, 1991 Can I find ways to my goals, and will I use them? Goals plus pathways plus agency Adult Hope Scale Hope in therapy Snyder argued that hope is a common factor across psychotherapies: people arrive demoralised, and effective therapies of every school restore morale. Hope therapy , developed by Snyder and colleagues, has four overlapping parts. Hope finding uncovers existing hope through stories of past goals the client achieved. Hope bonding builds a collaborative alliance that itself supplies agency. Hope enhancing teaches the client to set clear, personally chosen goals, break them into small steps, generate several pathways with plans for likely obstacles, and use agency self-talk. Hope reminding helps the client use these skills independently. Trap. Snyder's hope is cognitive and active, not a feeling or wish. A person who "hopes" for a good result but sees no route and has no drive to act is, in Snyder's terms, low in hope. 14.6 Resilience: what it is and how it was discovered Resilience is positive adaptation in the context of significant adversity or risk. Both conditions are required: a genuine threat (poverty, abuse, disaster, serious loss or injury) and adaptation that is good by age-appropriate standards. A comfortable child who does well is not resilient; he or she has simply not been tested. Is resilience a trait , a process or an outcome ? Most developmental researchers treat it as a dynamic process: an interaction over time between the person and his or her relationships and environment, which can differ across domains (doing well academically while struggling emotionally) and across life. Suniya Luthar and colleagues (2000) urged language that treats resilience as a process, because talk of children who "have" resilience invites blaming those who do not cope and ignores their environment. The pioneers Norman Garmezy, struck that many children of mothers with schizophrenia developed well, shifted attention from what causes disorder to what allows competence; his Project Competence at the University of Minnesota trained Ann Masten. Emmy Werner's Kauai Longitudinal Study followed all 698 children born in 1955 on the Hawaiian island of Kauai from before birth into middle adulthood. About one third were high risk, facing several adversities by age two, such as birth complications, chronic poverty, family discord or parental mental illness. Most of these children had serious learning, behaviour or mental health problems by adolescence, but roughly one in three grew into competent, confident and caring young adults. Werner's books Vulnerable but Invincible (1982) and Overcoming the Odds (1992) described what set them apart: an infant temperament that drew positive responses from caregivers; at least one stable, caring adult, often a grandparent, older sibling, aunt or teacher rather than a parent; competence in some skill; and often faith or a sense of purpose. Many who struggled as adolescents recovered later through "second chances" such as further education or a stable marriage. Michael Rutter , the British child psychiatrist, showed in his Isle of Wight studies that single family adversities (such as severe marital discord, low social status, overcrowding, paternal criminality, maternal psychiatric disorder and placement in care) each carried little extra risk alone, but that risk rose sharply, more than additively, when several occurred together. In his 1987 paper on protective mechanisms he argued for studying mechanisms rather than lists of factors, and defined a true protective factor as one whose effect appears specifically under risk. He also described steeling effects : successfully handling manageable stress can strengthen a person against later stress, much as a vaccine does. "Ordinary magic" Ann Masten's 2001 article in the American Psychologist, "Ordinary magic: Resilience processes in development", drew these findings together. Earlier writers had called such children "invulnerable", implying rare, extraordinary qualities. Masten argued that resilience is common and arises from the normal functioning of basic human adaptive systems . The same short list keeps appearing: close relationships with competent, caring adults; thinking and problem-solving skills; the ability to regulate emotion and behaviour; a positive self-view and motivation to master the environment; and effective schools, communities and cultural or religious supports. Resilience fails when these systems are damaged, as when a child loses a caregiver, or overwhelmed by extreme, prolonged adversity. Key. Resilience is ordinary, not heroic: it comes from ordinary systems working under pressure, so the way to promote it is to protect and restore those systems. 14.7 Risk, protection and adult trajectories after loss and trauma A risk factor raises the probability of a poor outcome; cumulative risk means the number of risks often matters more than any single one. A promotive factor helps at all levels of risk, while a protective factor , strictly, reduces the effect of risk and so matters most when risk is high. Level Common risk factors Common protective factors Individual Difficult temperament, chronic illness or disability, poor emotion regulation, earlier trauma Easy temperament, problem-solving skill, self-regulation, self-efficacy, hope, humour, faith or purpose Family Poverty, parental conflict or violence, parental mental illness or substance misuse, abuse or neglect, loss of a parent At least one warm, consistent caregiver; warmth with structure; supportive siblings and extended family; stable routines Community Violence, discrimination, poor schools and services, disaster, displacement Caring teachers and mentors, good schools, safe neighbourhoods, religious and community organisations, accessible services George Bonanno's trajectories In a 2004 article in the American Psychologist on loss, trauma and human resilience, George Bonanno challenged two assumptions: that anyone who does not show intense distress after a loss is in denial and will suffer "delayed grief", and that resilience after such events is rare. From longitudinal data on bereaved spouses, disaster survivors and others, Bonanno and colleagues described four trajectories. Resilience is stable healthy functioning with at most brief disturbance; in his studies it was usually the most common trajectory, often describing a majority. Recovery is clearly elevated symptoms for months, then a gradual return towards earlier functioning, often over one to two years. Chronic dysfunction is high distress beginning soon after the event and lasting years, as in prolonged grief, persistent post-traumatic stress or depression. Delayed reactions are initial coping followed by rising symptoms; Bonanno found this uncommon, contrary to the older belief in delayed grief. Bonanno argued that there are many routes to resilience, including hardiness and positive emotion, and later emphasised flexibility , using different coping strategies as situations demand. Trap. The claim that resilience is the commonest response has been challenged. Frank Infurna and Suniya Luthar (2016) showed that the statistical method behind many trajectory studies (growth mixture modelling) rests on assumptions that can inflate the resilient group; with those assumptions relaxed, resilience after spousal loss, divorce and unemployment looked considerably less common. The safe answer: resilience is common, but its prevalence depends on the event, the outcome measured and the method. 14.8 Hardiness and sense of coherence Hardiness Suzanne Kobasa (who later published as Suzanne Ouellette) introduced hardiness in 1979 in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. Studying executives at a large American utility company during heavy organisational change, she compared those who reported many stressful events yet stayed healthy with those who fell ill. The healthy group differed in three attitudes, the three Cs . Commitment is the tendency to involve oneself fully in what one is doing and find it worthwhile, rather than feeling alienated. Control is the belief that one can influence events through one's own efforts, rather than feeling powerless. Challenge is the belief that change, not stability, is normal and offers opportunities for growth rather than mainly threats. Her colleague Salvatore Maddi described hardiness as existential courage that turns stressful circumstances into opportunities, and developed hardiness training . Critics noted that the first study measured illness and hardiness at the same time, so illness might have lowered hardiness rather than the reverse; that early scales overlapped with low neuroticism; and that challenge was usually the weakest component. Sense of coherence and salutogenesis Aaron Antonovsky, an American-born medical sociologist working in Israel, turned the medical question around. Medicine is pathogenic in orientation, asking what causes disease. Antonovsky proposed a salutogenic orientation (from the Latin salus , health, and Greek genesis , origin): why do people stay well despite constant stressors? His question was sharpened by a study of women in Israel that included concentration camp survivors, a substantial minority of whom were in good health despite their experiences. Who gave us this. Aaron Antonovsky set out salutogenesis in Health, Stress, and Coping (1979) and developed the sense of coherence and its measurement in Unraveling the Mystery of Health (1987). Antonovsky placed everyone on a health ease/dis-ease continuum rather than dividing people into healthy and sick. His metaphor: medicine stands downstream pulling drowning people out, whereas the salutogenic question is how to make people better swimmers in a river everyone is in. His answer was the sense of coherence , a pervasive, enduring though dynamic feeling of confidence with three components. Comprehensibility (cognitive) is the sense that one's inner and outer world is ordered, predictable and explicable rather than chaotic. Manageability (instrumental) is the sense that resources, one's own or those of trusted others, are available to meet the demands one faces. Meaningfulness (motivational) is the sense that life's demands are worth investing energy in, challenges rather than burdens; Antonovsky considered it the most important of the three. A strong sense of coherence grows from generalised resistance resources : characteristics of the person, group or environment that help with a wide variety of stressors, such as material security, knowledge, a firm identity, social support, cultural stability and faith. They build it through life experiences that are consistent, balanced between overload and underload, and allow a say in decisions. It is measured by the Orientation to Life Questionnaire , in a 29-item and a widely used 13-item version; higher scores are linked to better perceived health and quality of life. Critics note that scores correlate so strongly with low anxiety and depression that the scale may not measure anything distinct, and that the three components rarely separate in factor analysis. Trap. Do not muddle Suzanne Kobasa's commitment, control and challenge with Aaron Antonovsky's comprehensibility, manageability and meaningfulness. Hardiness came from personality psychology studying stressed executives; sense of coherence from medical sociology asking why people stay healthy. Meaningfulness resembles commitment and manageability resembles control, but comprehensibility and challenge have no exact counterparts. 14.9 Coping as the frame: appraisal, proactive coping and benefit finding In Stress, Appraisal, and Coping (1984), Richard Lazarus and Susan Folkman proposed a transactional model : stress lies in the relationship between person and environment, arising when a person appraises demands as taxing or exceeding his or her resources. Primary appraisal asks whether the event matters, and how: irrelevant, benign, or stressful, with stressful appraisals divided into harm or loss, threat, and challenge. Secondary appraisal asks what can be done, taking stock of resources and options. Coping is the changing cognitive and behavioural effort to manage those demands, and reappraisal updates the picture as events unfold. Problem-focused coping acts on the problem; emotion-focused coping manages the distress. Neither is inherently better: problem-focused coping tends to help when the situation is controllable and emotion-focused when it is not. Folkman later added meaning-focused coping , using values and goals to sustain well-being in situations that cannot be solved, through positive reappraisal, revising goals and finding benefit. Optimism, hope and sense of coherence strengthen secondary appraisal, hardiness's challenge shapes primary appraisal, and explanatory style is a habitual reappraisal after the event. Proactive coping , described by Lisa Aspinwall and Shelley Taylor (1997), is effort made in advance of a potentially stressful event to prevent it or change its form: building resources such as money, skills and relationships, recognising early warning signs, appraising them, making preliminary efforts and using feedback, as a student does who keeps up with reading all term. Benefit finding is perceiving positive consequences of an adverse experience, such as closer relationships or changed priorities. Researchers distinguish it from benefit reminding , deliberately recalling those benefits as a coping strategy. A 2006 meta-analysis found benefit finding associated with less depression and more positive well-being, but also with more intrusive thoughts about the event, suggesting it is part of an active, sometimes painful process of working through. Benefit finding overlaps heavily with post-traumatic growth. 14.10 Post-traumatic growth Post-traumatic growth is positive psychological change experienced as a result of the struggle with highly challenging life crises. The change goes beyond the person's previous level in some respect, and it comes from the struggle with the aftermath, not from the trauma itself. Who gave us this. Richard Tedeschi and Lawrence Calhoun, at the University of North Carolina at Charlotte, introduced the term in the mid-1990s and published the Post-Traumatic Growth Inventory (PTGI) in the Journal of Traumatic Stress in 1996. The inventory has 21 items, each rated from 0 (I did not experience this change as a result of my crisis) to 5 (I experienced this change to a very great degree). Factor analysis produced five domains; a later expanded version broadened the spiritual domain, criticised as too narrowly religious, to spiritual and existential change. Domain Items What it captures How it might sound Relating to others 7 Closer relationships, compassion, willingness to express emotion and accept help "I found out who really cares, and I let people in now." New possibilities 5 New interests, a new path, openness to opportunities not previously considered "I would never have become a counsellor otherwise." Personal strength 4 Feeling stronger and more self-reliant than one had realised "If I survived that, I can handle this." Spiritual change 2 Deeper spiritual understanding or stronger faith "My faith became my own rather than a habit." Appreciation of life 3 Changed priorities, valuing each day and small things "I no longer take an ordinary morning for granted." How growth happens Tedeschi and Calhoun describe trauma as a "seismic" event that shakes core beliefs, for example that the world is fair, predictable and meaningful and that the self is worthy. At first the person experiences intrusive rumination , unwanted thoughts and images of the event. Over time, especially with support and chances to talk, this can give way to deliberate rumination , a reflective effort to make sense of what happened and rebuild beliefs; growth emerges from the rebuilding and is woven into a revised life story. Growth and distress coexist : people often report growth while still grieving or symptomatic. Tedeschi and Calhoun advised clinicians to act as expert companions , noticing growth when the client raises it rather than pushing it. Resilience means functioning stays relatively stable; recovery means it drops and returns; growth means that in some domain it ends up higher than before. Highly resilient people may report less growth, because an event that does not shake their beliefs leaves less to rebuild. Real growth or illusion? The main criticism concerns self-report . The inventory asks people to judge how much they have changed, which requires remembering accurately what they were like before; people are poor at such comparisons and tend to underrate their past selves, which makes the present look like growth. Patricia Frazier and colleagues (2009) measured students before and after a traumatic event and found that self-reported growth was only weakly related to actual measured change in the same qualities, and that perceived growth went with more distress, not less. The scale also offers no option for negative change, and cultural "silver lining" scripts may encourage growth reports. Andreas Maercker and Tanja Zoellner proposed a Janus-face model , after the two-faced Roman god: one face is constructive, self-transcending growth linked to better long-term adjustment; the other is illusory, self-deceptive growth that mainly soothes distress in the short term. Key. Reported growth is meaningful to survivors, but a high inventory score is not proof of actual change. Never make growth an expectation; a client who reports none is not failing. 14.11 The Indian context Most of this research was done in North America and Western Europe. In India the family , often extended or joint, is usually the first and largest source of support after adversity: relatives take turns at the hospital bedside, pool money for treatment and share caregiving. The same system can also strain, through expectations, conflict over decisions, or stigma that leads families to hide mental illness. Community supports , including neighbours, self-help groups, colleagues and religious institutions such as temples, mosques, churches and gurudwaras, provide material help and belonging. Help-seeking often passes through elders and religious or traditional healers before reaching mental health services, so a clinician works with these networks rather than around them. Cultural meanings of adversity must be discussed in careful, general terms, because beliefs vary widely across individuals, communities and religions. Many Indian traditions hold, broadly, that actions have consequences that unfold over long periods ( karma ), and ideas of fate are common. Such beliefs can work either way. For some they support acceptance, reduce bitterness towards others and make suffering comprehensible and meaningful, echoing Aaron Antonovsky's comprehensibility and meaningfulness and Susan Folkman's meaning-focused coping. For others they feed self-blame, much like an internal, stable attribution, or a fatalistic passivity resembling helplessness. The Bhagavad Gita's teaching of acting without attachment to the fruits of action is often read as full effort combined with acceptance that outcomes are not wholly in one's control, which resembles high agency with acceptance. The clinician's task is to explore what the belief means to this person, not to assume. Finally, the standard scales in this chapter were developed in Western samples, so adapted versions must be validated for the group assessed. Access matters too: the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 recognises a right to mental health care, and the national tele-mental health service, Tele-MANAS, reaches people far from specialist clinics. 14.12 Case: a road accident survivor across the first year Case. Arjun, a 27-year-old software tester in Pune, was riding his motorcycle home on a highway at night when a truck swerved into his lane. After two operations on open fractures of his right leg, surgeons performed a below-knee amputation. He lives with his parents; his elder brother lives nearby. Month one. In hospital he had nightmares and flashbacks of headlights, startled at loud noises and said, "My life is finished. I ruin everything I touch. I will never work properly again." His grandmother told visitors it must be his karma, which made him feel the accident was his fault. His mother and brother took turns at his bedside, and colleagues collected money for treatment. Months two to four. During prosthetic fitting he was low, avoided road travel and refused to discuss the accident. A psychologist at the rehabilitation centre screened him for post-traumatic stress and depression; both were in the clinical range, and he began trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy. Months five to eight. He set a goal with his therapist: walking into his office unaided by the first anniversary. They broke it into steps (standing with the prosthesis, walking the corridor, stairs, car journeys with his brother) and planned alternatives for setbacks such as stump pain. Disputing his early explanations, he began to say, "A truck driver swerved; my recovery is slow, not impossible; I am good at my job and my leg does not change that." His brother helped him file a claim before the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal, easing financial worry. Months nine to twelve. He returned to work part time, joined a peer group of amputees and began talking to college students about helmets and highway safety. At one year he said, "I still hate highways and my leg hurts in the cold. But I am closer to my brother than ever, I notice small things, and I know I can handle hard things. Whatever the reason it happened, my duty now is to act well." Trajectory. Arjun fits Bonanno's recovery trajectory, not resilience: symptoms were clearly elevated for months, then declined. Early screening mattered, because persisting symptoms would have signalled the chronic trajectory. Explanatory style. His month-one statements are textbook pessimism: permanent ("never"), pervasive ("everything I touch") and personal ("I ruin"), with the karma comment feeding personalisation. His later statements show disputation at work (an external cause, an unstable explanation for slow progress, a bounded view of the loss), which is Seligman's ABCDE within cognitive behavioural therapy. Hope. Rehabilitation was hope theory applied: a valued goal of intermediate probability, pathways built from small steps and plans for barriers, and agency growing with each success. Resilience and sense of coherence. Protection came from every level: individual (skills), family (mother and brother, the adult version of Werner's caring adults) and community (colleagues, the rehabilitation centre, the peer group, the compensation system). Therapy and medical explanation raised comprehensibility , family and financial support raised manageability , and the safety talks gave his suffering meaningfulness . Growth. His one-year statements map onto four domains: relating to others, new possibilities, personal strength and appreciation of life. The growth coexists with pain and fear, and because his reports are retrospective, the behavioural evidence (returning to work, volunteering) matters. His reworking of the karma belief, from self-blame to present duty, shows a cultural meaning becoming a resource once explored rather than dismissed. Recap. Dispositional optimism, from Michael Scheier and Charles Carver, is a generalised expectation of good outcomes, measured by the Life Orientation Test Revised, that works mainly through approach coping and predicts outcomes such as recovery after bypass surgery, while Julie Norem's defensive pessimism shows that low expectations can serve anxious people well. Learned helplessness began with Martin Seligman and Steven Maier's dogs, was reformulated in attributional terms by Lyn Abramson, Seligman and John Teasdale, gave rise to explanatory style (permanence, pervasiveness, personalisation) and learned optimism, and was reversed in 2016 when Maier and Seligman concluded that passivity is the default and control is learned. C. R. Snyder's hope theory defines hope as goals pursued through pathways and agency thinking, distinct from optimism and self-efficacy, and it underpins hope therapy. Resilience is positive adaptation despite significant adversity, an ordinary process (Ann Masten's "ordinary magic") built from protective factors at individual, family and community levels, grounded in Emmy Werner's Kauai study and Michael Rutter's work, with George Bonanno's trajectories describing adult responses, though how common resilience is remains debated. Hardiness (commitment, control, challenge) and Aaron Antonovsky's sense of coherence (comprehensibility, manageability, meaningfulness) are protective orientations, and Richard Lazarus and Susan Folkman's appraisal model, proactive coping and benefit finding frame them all. Post-traumatic growth, measured in five domains by Richard Tedeschi and Lawrence Calhoun's inventory, differs from resilience and recovery, coexists with distress and may be partly illusory because it rests on retrospective self-report. In India, family, community and cultural meanings such as karma can protect or burden, and the clinician explores them, as the road accident case shows. Describe its five domains and how it is thought to occur, distinguish it from resilience and recovery, and evaluate the criticism that reported growth may be illusory. 15 Love, relationships, meaning and spirituality Earlier chapters looked at well-being mostly from the inside. This chapter turns outward and upward. Outward, because the most consistent finding in the science of well-being is that people flourish in the company of others. Upward, because people also ask why their lives matter, and many answer through meaning, religion or a personal spirituality. The positive psychology texts (Baumgardner and Crothers; the Oxford Handbook) give these topics whole chapters, and the clinical textbooks (Pomerantz; Trull and Phares) return to them in couple therapy, grief work and culturally sensitive practice. Two worked cases close the chapter. 15.1 The need to belong: why relationships sit at the centre of well-being In 1995 Roy Baumeister and Mark Leary argued in the journal Psychological Bulletin that the need to belong is a fundamental human motivation. They set criteria that any fundamental need should meet: it should operate in nearly all people and cultures, arise readily under ordinary conditions, shape emotion and thought, and harm health and adjustment when frustrated. The desire for close bonds meets all of them. People form attachments quickly, even with strangers thrown together by chance; they resist ending bonds, even bad ones; and loss of belonging through rejection, divorce, death or exile produces anxiety, depression and loneliness. Their key point is that the need has two parts. People need frequent, pleasant interactions with a few others, and those interactions must occur within a stable, lasting framework of mutual concern , a relationship expected to continue in which each cares about the other's welfare. Neither part alone is enough: a salesperson who chats warmly with hundreds of customers has contact without a bond, and a husband working abroad for years has a bond with little contact. Positive psychology evidence points the same way. In 2002 Ed Diener and Martin Seligman published "Very happy people". They screened 222 university students on several happiness measures and compared the happiest tenth with average and unhappy students. The very happy group did not have more objectively good events. What set them apart was social: they spent less time alone, and all of them had good close relationships, as rated by themselves and by their friends. Good relationships looked necessary but not sufficient for very high happiness: every very happy person had them, but having them did not guarantee it. Trap. "Very happy people" is correlational and used American undergraduates. It shows that close relationships go with very high happiness; it does not prove relationships cause it, since happy people also attract friends. Write "necessary but not sufficient" and name the design limits. 15.2 Social support, health and loneliness Social support means the resources other people provide, or that we believe they would provide, when we need them. It may be emotional (care, reassurance), instrumental (practical help such as money or meals), informational (advice) or appraisal (feedback that helps a person evaluate their situation). Perceived support is the belief that help would be there; received support is help actually given. Perceived support is the more reliable predictor of well-being, because being helped can also make a person feel incompetent or indebted. In 1985 Sheldon Cohen and Thomas Wills set out two models of how support protects. The main effect model says that being embedded in relationships benefits people at all times, through regular positive experience, identity and pressure towards healthy habits. The stress-buffering model says support matters most under high stress, because it makes stressors look less threatening and helps people cope. Both have evidence. The health consequences are large: in 2010 Julianne Holt-Lunstad, Timothy Smith and Bradley Layton pooled 148 studies and found that people with stronger social relationships had roughly a 50 percent greater likelihood of survival over the periods studied, an effect comparable to well-known risks such as smoking. The pathways are behavioural, physiological and psychological. Loneliness is not the same as being alone. John Cacioppo, whose book with William Patrick, Loneliness , appeared in 2008, defined it as perceived social isolation : the painful sense that one's relationships are fewer or less satisfying than one wants. One can be lonely in a large joint family. Cacioppo offered an evolutionary account: as hunger signals the need for food, loneliness signals that bonds are threatened and pushes the person to repair them. But the signal also makes the lonely person watchful for rejection, so they read ambiguous behaviour as hostile, withdraw, and confirm their fears. This is why the most effective loneliness interventions target the lonely person's social thinking, not just their opportunities for contact. Key. Belonging needs frequent pleasant contact inside a stable bond of mutual concern. Perceived support predicts well-being better than received support. Loneliness is perceived, not objective, isolation, and it sustains itself through hypervigilance to rejection. 15.3 Love: Sternberg's triangle, Lee's styles, passionate and companionate love Sternberg's triangular theory In 1986 Robert Sternberg proposed in Psychological Review that love has three components, pictured as the corners of a triangle. Intimacy is the emotional component: closeness, warmth, trust and feeling understood. Passion is the motivational component: romantic and physical attraction and the drive towards union. Commitment is the cognitive component: in the short term the decision that one loves the person, in the long term the decision to maintain that love. Each can be present or absent, giving eight kinds of love. Kind of love Intimacy Passion Commitment What it looks like Nonlove No No No Casual daily dealings with acquaintances. Liking Yes No No Warm friendship without desire or long-term pledge. Infatuated love No Yes No "Love at first sight" for someone barely known. Empty love No No Yes A marriage kept from duty after warmth and desire have gone; in some arranged marriages, the starting point from which intimacy grows. Romantic love Yes Yes No A close, passionate affair with no decision about the future. Companionate love Yes No Yes A long marriage or deep friendship in which passion has faded. Fatuous love No Yes Yes A whirlwind engagement: commitment built on passion without intimacy. Consummate love Yes Yes Yes The complete form, which Sternberg said is easier to reach than to keep. The components change over time: passion rises fast and then tends to decline, intimacy grows gradually, and commitment builds as the relationship proves itself. Sternberg argued that satisfaction depends partly on how well the partners' triangles match. Research supports the distinction, though in real couples the components overlap more than the triangle suggests. John Alan Lee's love styles The Canadian sociologist John Alan Lee, in Colours of Love (1973), described styles of loving, compared to colours on a wheel. The primary styles are eros (passionate love centred on strong attraction), ludus (game-playing, uncommitted love) and storge (friendship-based love that grows slowly). Mixtures give the secondary styles pragma (practical love that chooses a partner who fits set criteria), mania (possessive, jealous, dependent love) and agape (selfless, giving love). They are best seen as attitudes to love that can shift across relationships, not fixed types. Passionate and companionate love Elaine Hatfield drew the most widely taught distinction. Passionate love is an intense longing for union with another, with physiological arousal, intrusive thoughts about the beloved and idealisation. Companionate love is the calmer affection, trust and tenderness felt towards someone with whom one's life is deeply intertwined. Hatfield explained passion with a two-factor account: passionate love arises when a person is physiologically aroused and labels the arousal as love. The famous support is Donald Dutton and Arthur Aron's 1974 study, in which men met by an attractive interviewer on a high, swaying suspension bridge showed more attraction to her than men on a low, stable bridge, apparently misattributing fear arousal to attraction. Trap. Sternberg's "companionate love" is intimacy plus commitment, one of eight combinations. Hatfield's "companionate love" is one of only two broad kinds. The ideas are similar, but the theories differ and must be credited separately. 15.4 Adult attachment: love as an attachment process John Bowlby proposed that infants have an attachment system that keeps them close to a caregiver, and Mary Ainsworth's Strange Situation identified secure, anxious-ambivalent and avoidant infant patterns. In 1987 Cindy Hazan and Phillip Shaver proposed that adult romantic love is itself an attachment process run by the same system. Through a newspaper "love quiz", they asked readers which of three short paragraphs, written to mirror Ainsworth's patterns, best described them in close relationships. A little over half chose the secure description, and the rest split between avoidant and anxious. Style Core belief Typical behaviour in relationships Secure I am worthy of love; others are generally reliable. Comfortable with closeness and dependence; trusts; raises conflict openly; seeks and gives support. Anxious I may not be lovable enough; others may leave me. Wants more closeness than the partner offers; fears abandonment; jealous; reads small signs as rejection; seeks constant reassurance. Avoidant Depending on others is risky or unnecessary. Uncomfortable with closeness; prizes independence; suppresses emotion; withdraws under stress; offers little support to a distressed partner. Later work refined this. Kim Bartholomew and Leonard Horowitz (1991) crossed a positive or negative model of self with a positive or negative model of others to give four styles: secure, preoccupied, dismissing-avoidant and fearful-avoidant, the last wanting closeness yet fearing it. Shaver and colleagues then showed in 1998 that attachment is best measured on two continuous dimensions , anxiety (fear of rejection) and avoidance (discomfort with closeness), through the Experiences in Close Relationships questionnaire; a secure person is low on both. Under threat, anxious people hyperactivate the attachment system (clinging, protesting, monitoring the partner), while avoidant people deactivate it (suppressing needs, keeping distance). Pair the two and a pursue-withdraw cycle often follows: the more one seeks reassurance, the more the other retreats, confirming both partners' fears. Why it matters. Much modern couple therapy treats conflict as protest about attachment security. Styles are moderately stable but not destiny: a reliable relationship or therapy can build "earned security". 15.5 What makes relationships last: John Gottman's research John Gottman, working with Robert Levenson from the 1980s and later in his University of Washington laboratory, studied couples by observation rather than questionnaire alone. Couples discussed a disagreement while being videotaped; faces, words and tone were coded moment by moment, physiological signals such as heart rate were recorded, and the couples were followed for years. The four horsemen Four patterns predicted divorce so strongly that Gottman named them, after the biblical image, the four horsemen of the apocalypse . Horseman What it is Example Antidote Criticism Attacking the partner's character instead of complaining about a behaviour. "You never think of anyone but yourself." Gentle start-up: state the situation, your feeling and a request. Contempt Speaking from superiority: sarcasm, mockery, eye-rolling, insults. "Of course the great genius forgot again." Build a culture of appreciation; express fondness and respect. Defensiveness Counter-attacking or playing the innocent victim, which blames the partner. "It's not my fault, you're the one who..." Take responsibility for even part of the problem. Stonewalling Withdrawing: going silent, looking away, leaving. Staring at the phone while the partner speaks. Self-soothing: a break of at least twenty minutes, then return. Gottman identified contempt as the single strongest predictor of divorce, because it communicates disgust. Stonewalling is tied to flooding , diffuse physiological arousal in which a person cannot take in what the partner says and so shuts down. He also stressed repair attempts that stop negativity escalating and turning towards a partner's small bids for connection. The five to one ratio Gottman's most quoted finding, summarised in What Predicts Divorce? (1994), is that in stable couples, during conflict discussions , positive behaviours (interest, humour, affection, validation) outnumbered negative ones (criticism, anger, contempt, defensiveness) by about five to one ; in couples heading for divorce the ratio was near one to one. Good couples still fight; what matters is the balance. Trap. Do not confuse Gottman's five to one with Marcial Losada's "positivity ratio" of about 2.9 to 1, which Nicholas Brown, Alan Sokal and Harris Friedman showed in 2013 to rest on invalid mathematics. Gottman's figure is an observed average in stable couples during conflict, not a law or a magic threshold. Publicised claims that Gottman "predicts divorce with over 90 percent accuracy" also need caution: they came from fitting models to couples whose outcomes were already known, which inflates accuracy. 15.6 Capitalisation, minding, and marriage in the Indian context Capitalisation and active-constructive responding Most relationship research asks how partners handle bad events. Shelly Gable asked what happens when things go right. Christopher Langston had used capitalisation in 1994 for telling others about a positive event, which boosts positive feeling beyond the event itself. Gable, Harry Reis, Emily Impett and Evan Asher (2004) showed that the benefit depends on the listener's response, which can be active or passive and constructive or destructive. Constructive Destructive Active Active-constructive: enthusiastic, engaged. "That's wonderful! How did they tell you?" Active-destructive: deflating. "That means longer hours; can you manage?" Passive Passive-constructive: quiet approval. "That's nice," while reading on. Passive-destructive: ignoring or turning to oneself. "Guess what happened to me today." Only active-constructive responding was reliably linked with greater satisfaction, intimacy, trust and daily positive feeling. Surprisingly, passive-constructive responding, which sounds supportive, behaved much like the destructive responses, because it signals that the listener does not really care. The mechanism is perceived responsiveness : the sense that the partner understands, values and cares for the self. Minding the relationship John Harvey and Julia Omarzu (1997) proposed that relationships are maintained by minding , which Baumgardner and Crothers present as the "mindful relationship". It has five components: knowing and being known through continued self-disclosure and attentive listening; relationship-enhancing attributions , explaining a partner's good behaviour by their character and bad behaviour by passing circumstances; acceptance and respect for what is learnt; reciprocity , so both partners do the minding; and continuity over the life of the relationship, not just in courtship. Arranged and love marriage in India Students often ask whether arranged marriages are happier than love marriages. Only careful, general statements are supportable. The categories blur: many Indian marriages are "semi-arranged", with families introducing and the couple choosing. Comparisons suffer from selection, since those who take each route differ in background and expectations, so differences in satisfaction cannot be credited to the type of marriage. No consistent, large difference has been shown, and the popular claim that "love grows in arranged marriages" rests on small, old studies. In Sternberg's language, arranged marriages may start with commitment and build intimacy, while love marriages start with passion and intimacy and must build commitment. A clinician should also remember that consent, coercion, dowry and family involvement in conflict affect well-being in ways satisfaction ratings miss. 15.7 Prosocial behaviour, altruism and kindness Prosocial behaviour is any action intended to benefit another: helping, sharing, donating, comforting, volunteering. Altruism describes the motive: helping whose ultimate goal is the other's welfare rather than one's own. The same act, such as giving blood, can be altruistic or egoistic depending on why it is done. Kindness , one of the character strengths in the Values in Action (VIA) classification, is the enduring tendency to do good deeds for others. Is any helping truly selfless? Robert Cialdini's negative-state relief model said no: we help to relieve our own sadness at another's suffering. Daniel Batson proposed the empathy-altruism hypothesis : when we feel empathic concern for a person in need (sympathy, compassion and tenderness focused on them), we become motivated to relieve their suffering for their sake; without it, we help mainly for egoistic reasons such as avoiding guilt. His key test was the ease-of-escape design . In a 1981 study, participants watched a young woman, "Elaine", apparently receiving electric shocks and could offer to take her place. Low-empathy participants helped when escape was hard but mostly left when leaving was easy, as egoism predicts; high-empathy participants helped even when they could easily walk away, as altruism predicts. Cialdini replied that empathy creates a sense of "oneness", so helping the other partly helps an expanded self. Batson's work remains the standard evidence that altruism is possible. Helping also benefits the helper. Elizabeth Dunn, Lara Aknin and Michael Norton reported in Science in 2008 that spending more on others went with greater happiness and, experimentally, that people given five or twenty dollars and told to spend it on others that day ended up happier than those told to spend it on themselves. The amount did not matter; the use did. Larger replication efforts suggest the effect is real but smaller than first reported. Key. Prosocial describes the act; altruism describes the motive. Batson's hypothesis says empathic concern produces genuinely other-oriented motivation, tested with the ease-of-escape design. Prosocial spending raises the giver's happiness, though modestly. 15.8 Forgiveness What forgiveness is and is not Definitions vary, but researchers agree on what forgiveness is not . It is not pardoning (a legal release from punishment), condoning (treating the offence as acceptable), excusing (deciding the person was not responsible), or forgetting the hurt. Nor is it reconciliation , the restoration of a relationship, which needs both people and renewed trust. A woman can forgive an abusive former partner and wisely never reconcile with him. Forgiveness is an inner change in the victim; reconciliation is an interpersonal event. McCullough's motivational view Michael McCullough, with Everett Worthington and colleagues (1997), defined forgiveness as a set of prosocial changes in motivation towards a transgressor. After a hurt, people are naturally motivated to avoid the offender and to seek revenge ; forgiving means these motives decline and benevolence grows. McCullough's Transgression-Related Interpersonal Motivations Inventory measures these motives, making forgiveness measurable. Worthington's REACH model Everett Worthington, whose own mother was murdered, developed a five-step intervention that spells REACH. Recall the hurt as objectively as possible. Empathise with the offender, trying to understand the pressures behind the act, which is not excusing it. Give the altruistic gift of forgiveness, often by remembering times one was forgiven oneself. Commit publicly to forgive. Hold on to forgiveness when anger returns, knowing that recurring hurt does not mean the forgiveness was false. Worthington also separates decisional forgiveness (deciding to treat the offender without revenge) from emotional forgiveness (the slower replacement of negative feelings with empathy and compassion). Enright's process model Robert Enright defines forgiveness as a willed giving up of resentment towards someone who acted unjustly, with an effort to offer them compassion they may not deserve. His process model groups about twenty units into four phases. In the uncovering phase the person faces the injury and the anger and shame it caused. In the decision phase they see that current strategies are failing and consider forgiveness. In the work phase they reframe the offender in wider context, build empathy and accept the pain. In the deepening phase they find meaning in the suffering and release from resentment. Forgiveness and health Charlotte vanOyen Witvliet and colleagues (2001) had participants imagine a real offender in unforgiving ways (rehearsing the hurt, holding a grudge) and in forgiving ways. Unforgiving imagery raised heart rate and blood pressure. Forgiveness goes with less depression and anxiety and better self-rated health. There is a dark side: James McNulty's studies of newlyweds found that when a partner often behaved badly, a spouse's tendency to forgive predicted that the bad behaviour continued. Forgiveness should never be pressed on someone still in an unsafe relationship. Trap. Forgiveness does not require reconciliation. Forgiveness is an inner change in the victim's motives and feelings; reconciliation restores the relationship and requires trustworthiness from the offender. 15.9 Meaning in life Viktor Frankl and logotherapy Viktor Frankl, a Viennese psychiatrist, survived Nazi concentration camps including Auschwitz, where members of his family died. Man's Search for Meaning , first published in German in 1946, draws a lesson from camp life: prisoners who kept a sense that something still awaited them, a loved one or an unfinished task, endured better. Frankl quoted Nietzsche's idea that one who has a why to live can bear almost any how, and argued that even when everything else is taken, a person keeps the freedom to choose their attitude to their circumstances. From this came logotherapy (from the Greek logos , meaning), called the "third Viennese school of psychotherapy" after Sigmund Freud's psychoanalysis and Alfred Adler's individual psychology. Where Freud stressed a will to pleasure and Adler a will to power, Frankl held that the primary human motive is a will to meaning . When it is frustrated, people fall into an existential vacuum of boredom and emptiness, which can produce noogenic neurosis , distress arising from the existential dimension. Meaning, for Frankl, is discovered rather than invented, through three avenues : Creative values: meaning found by creating a work or doing a deed, what we give to the world. Experiential values: meaning found by experiencing beauty, truth or nature, or by encountering another person in love, what we receive from the world. Attitudinal values: meaning found in the stand we take towards unavoidable suffering, the deepest source when the other two are closed. Logotherapy's techniques include paradoxical intention (asking an anxious patient to wish for what they fear, breaking the cycle of anticipatory anxiety) and dereflection (turning attention from excessive self-observation towards people and tasks). Steger's Meaning in Life Questionnaire Michael Steger and colleagues (2006) built the most used modern measure, the Meaning in Life Questionnaire : ten items on a seven-point scale forming two five-item subscales. Presence of meaning is how far a person feels their life is meaningful; search for meaning is how actively they are looking for it. The two are largely independent: one can have meaning and still search. Presence is consistently linked with higher life satisfaction and lower depression. Search tends to go with lower well-being in American samples, but Steger and colleagues found search and presence positively related in Japan, so what searching signifies depends on culture. Meaning-making after loss Crystal Park, building on work with Susan Folkman (1997) and reviewing the field in 2010, gives the standard meaning-making model . Each person holds global meaning : broad beliefs (for example, that the world is fair), goals and a sense of purpose. A stressful event receives a situational meaning , an appraisal of what this event means. Distress comes from the discrepancy between the two. Meaning-making reduces it either by changing the appraisal to fit existing beliefs (assimilation: "it was God's plan") or by changing global beliefs to accommodate the event (accommodation: "the world is not always fair, but people can still be good"). The meanings made include acceptance, revised goals and growth. Park stresses that searching helps only when meaning is found; prolonged, unsuccessful searching goes with more distress. Meaning versus happiness Roy Baumeister, Kathleen Vohs, Jennifer Aaker and Emily Garbinsky (2013) surveyed about four hundred American adults and found that happiness and meaningfulness overlap substantially but have different correlates. Happiness went with satisfied needs and wants, health, enough money, being a "taker" and a focus on the present. Meaningfulness went with linking past, present and future, being a "giver", expressing oneself and, strikingly, more stress and worry. Raising children is the classic example. 15.10 Religion and spirituality Religion usually means an organised, institutional system of beliefs, practices, rituals and community concerned with the sacred. Spirituality usually means a personal search for connection with the sacred or transcendent, inside or outside a religion. Kenneth Pargament defined spirituality as "a search for the sacred", where the sacred includes the divine and anything that takes on sacred qualities by association, such as a marriage or a calling. The two overlap heavily, but some people are "spiritual but not religious". Intrinsic and extrinsic orientation Gordon Allport, with J. Michael Ross in their 1967 Religious Orientation Scale, distinguished two ways of being religious. An intrinsic orientation treats religion as a master motive, internalised and lived in every area of life. An extrinsic orientation uses religion as a means to other ends, such as status, security or community. In Allport's summary, the extrinsic person uses religion while the intrinsic person lives it. It also resolved a puzzle about prejudice among churchgoers: prejudice went with the extrinsic orientation, not the intrinsic. Intrinsic religiousness is also more consistently linked with well-being. Religious coping Pargament's The Psychology of Religion and Coping (1997), and the short measure he developed with colleagues (the Brief RCOPE, 1998), showed that religion can help or harm coping depending on how it is used. Positive religious coping Negative religious coping (religious struggle) Benevolent reappraisal: seeing the stressor as part of a loving plan or a chance to grow. Punishing God reappraisal: "God is punishing me for my sins." Collaborative coping: working with God to solve the problem. Passive deferral: waiting for God to fix it without personal effort. Seeking spiritual support, connection and comfort. Spiritual discontent: feeling abandoned by or angry with God. Seeking help from clergy or the religious community. Interpersonal religious discontent: conflict with the community or its leaders. Positive religious coping goes with better adjustment and growth; negative coping goes with depression, anxiety and poorer health. In a study by Pargament and colleagues (2001), religious struggle among medically ill older patients predicted a higher risk of dying over a two-year follow-up. Religion, spirituality and well-being Across many studies, religiousness and spirituality show a modest positive association with life satisfaction and a modest negative association with depression, substance misuse and mortality. Three explanations dominate. Social support : religious communities give belonging and practical help. Meaning : religion offers a framework for understanding suffering and a sense of purpose, Park's global meaning in action. Health behaviour : many traditions discourage smoking, alcohol and risky conduct. Ed Diener, Louis Tay and David Myers (2011) added a qualification: the link is stronger in nations with difficult living conditions and weaker in wealthy, secure nations, where non-religious people find support and meaning elsewhere. Trap. The link is correlational and modest. Healthier people can attend services more (reverse causation), and religion can also bring guilt and struggle. Write "religion is associated with well-being, mainly through social support, meaning and health behaviour", never "religion makes people happy". Indian concepts of well-being Indian traditions offer rich, if not always empirically tested, ideas about well-being. The Upanishads distinguish ananda , a bliss rooted in realising one's true self, from passing pleasure ( sukha ). The Bhagavad Gita teaches nishkama karma , action without attachment to its fruits, and describes the sthitaprajna , a person of steady wisdom who stays even-minded in gain and loss. Buddhist traditions describe loving-kindness ( maitri ) and compassion ( karuna ), which inspired modern compassion practices, and seva (selfless service) connects to the prosocial research above. These ideas matter clinically because Indian clients often make sense of suffering through karma, dharma or divine will, and culturally sensitive therapy works with those meanings rather than dismissing them. 15.11 Humility, compassion and self-compassion Humility was long confused with low self-esteem. June Price Tangney (2000) argued that true humility involves an accurate assessment of one's abilities (neither inflated nor falsely low), the ability to acknowledge mistakes and limits, openness to new ideas, keeping achievements in perspective , a low focus on the self , and appreciation of the worth of all people and things. Compassion is the feeling that arises on witnessing suffering, joined to a motivation to help. Paul Gilbert, founder of compassion-focused therapy, defines it as sensitivity to suffering in self and others with a commitment to try to relieve and prevent it. It differs from empathy (sharing or understanding another's feeling) and sympathy (feeling sorry for someone). Feeling another's pain as one's own, called empathic distress, tends to produce withdrawal and burnout, whereas compassion sustains helping. Gilbert's therapy strengthens a soothing emotion system to balance the threat and drive systems in people high in shame and self-criticism. Kristin Neff (2003) brought self-compassion into psychology from Buddhist thought: treating oneself, in failure or suffering, with the kindness one would show a good friend. It has three components, each with an opposite, measured by her twenty-six-item Self-Compassion Scale. Component Meaning Its opposite Self-kindness Being warm and understanding towards oneself when failing or feeling inadequate. Self-judgement: harsh self-criticism. Common humanity Seeing suffering and imperfection as part of shared human experience. Isolation: feeling alone in one's failure. Mindfulness Holding painful thoughts and feelings in balanced awareness, neither suppressing nor exaggerating them. Over-identification: being swept away by the emotion. Self-compassion is not self-esteem . Self-esteem rests on evaluating oneself positively, often by comparison, so it rises and falls with success and can slide into narcissism; self-compassion needs no comparison and is available precisely when one fails. Nor is it self-pity or self-indulgence. Juliana Breines and Serena Chen (2012) found that students encouraged to be self-compassionate after failing a hard test studied longer for a retest than those given a self-esteem boost, so self-compassion supports motivation rather than complacency. It is strongly inversely associated with depression and anxiety, though critics argue that the scale's negatively worded items partly measure distress itself, which may inflate that association. 15.12 Two cases worked through Case. Ananya (31) and Rohit (33), married five years after a family-introduced but mutually chosen match, come to a counselling centre in Pune saying "we fight about everything". Asked to discuss a planned visit by Rohit's parents, Ananya says, "You always side with your family; you have no spine." Rohit replies, "You make everything a drama," then looks at his phone while Ananya rolls her eyes. The therapist names Gottman's horsemen: criticism, defensiveness, stonewalling and contempt (the eye-roll). Rohit reports a racing heart, a sign of flooding, so she teaches the antidotes: a gentle start-up ("I felt left out of the decision; can we plan it together?"), taking responsibility for part of the problem, and a twenty-minute break when flooded. When Ananya mentioned being chosen to lead a project, Rohit said "That's nice" and returned to the television, a passive-constructive response that Gable's research shows works much like a destructive one. For homework both practise active-constructive responding: asking questions, showing enthusiasm and helping the other relive good news. An attachment lens adds depth: Ananya's anxiety about coming second to Rohit's family and his avoidant retreat form a pursue-withdraw cycle. After eight sessions they escalate less and have agreed how visits will be planned. Case. Mr Suresh Iyer (58), a retired bank officer in Chennai, lost his wife of thirty years to a sudden heart attack. Four months later he sleeps poorly, has stopped going to the temple and says, "She never harmed anyone. We prayed every day. What was the point?" In Park's model, his global meaning (a just world in which devotion is protected) collides with the situational meaning (a sudden, undeserved death). His words also show negative religious coping, a sense of abandonment by God. On the Meaning in Life Questionnaire he scores very low on presence and high on search. The psychologist does not push a silver lining, and screens for depression and prolonged grief disorder (a diagnosis in both DSM-5-TR and ICD-11), since meaning work does not replace treatment. Early sessions help him make sense of the loss and voice his anger at God without judgement. Gradually he accommodates his beliefs: "Perhaps prayer is not a guarantee. It was what held us together." He returns to the temple for comfort and community rather than explanation, a shift to positive religious coping. Frankl's avenues then shape a future: creatively, a scholarship in his wife's name at her school; experientially, closeness with his daughter and grandchildren; attitudinally, carrying his grief as a sign of how much the marriage meant. A year later he calls his life not happy in the old way but meaningful again, Baumeister's distinction made concrete. Recap. Baumeister and Leary showed that belonging is a fundamental need for frequent pleasant contact within a stable bond, and Ed Diener and Martin Seligman found good relationships necessary but not sufficient for very high happiness; social support protects health, and loneliness is perceived isolation. Love has been mapped as Sternberg's triangle of intimacy, passion and commitment, as Lee's six styles and as Hatfield's passionate and companionate love, while Cindy Hazan and Phillip Shaver showed that adult romance runs on the attachment system. Gottman identified criticism, contempt, defensiveness and stonewalling as predictors of breakdown and found stable couples keep about five positive behaviours for each negative one during conflict, and Gable showed that active-constructive responses to good news build intimacy. C. Daniel Batson argued for genuine altruism, Dunn showed that giving raises the giver's happiness, and forgiveness, distinct from reconciliation, is taught through REACH and Enright's four phases. Meaning, from Frankl's will to meaning to Steger's presence and search and Park's meaning-making after loss, is related to but distinct from happiness, and religion, especially intrinsic faith and positive coping, is modestly associated with well-being through support, meaning and health behaviour. Humility, compassion and Neff's self-compassion complete the picture of a person connected to others, to purpose and to themselves.
