PNS (Schwann) regenerates better than CNS. 13. Learning, memory & amnesia The landmark case. Patient H.M. had both medial temporal lobes (including the hippocampus) removed in 1953 to stop seizures. He could no longer form new long-term explicit memories (severe anterograde amnesia ) yet kept old memories, normal IQ, and could still learn new motor skills (mirror drawing) without remembering having practised. This proved (1) the hippocampus is needed to form new declarative memories but is not the storehouse, and (2) declarative and procedural memory are separate systems. The taxonomy of memory Type Subtype Brain region Declarative (explicit) Episodic (events) Hippocampus + medial temporal lobe Semantic (facts) Temporal neocortex Non-declarative (implicit) Procedural (skills, habits) Striatum / basal ganglia Classical conditioning (motor) Cerebellum Emotional conditioning Amygdala Patient K.C. (Tulving) lost episodic memory but kept semantic knowledge, dissociating the two. Clive Wearing (herpes encephalitis) had a ~7–30 second span yet could still play piano (spared procedural/musical). Long-term potentiation (LTP): the molecular cascade LTP = a long-lasting strengthening of a synapse after high-frequency stimulation, the leading cellular model of learning, first shown in the hippocampus ( Bliss & Lømo, 1973 ). The cascade: Baseline: glutamate is released onto the postsynaptic spine; AMPA receptors open (Na⁺ in, depolarising), but NMDA receptors, though glutamate-bound, are plugged by Mg²⁺ at resting potential, so nothing flows through them. Strong / paired stimulation: the postsynaptic membrane depolarises enough to electrostatically expel the Mg²⁺ plug. The NMDA channel is now open with glutamate and voltage present, so Ca²⁺ flows in . Ca²⁺ activates CaMKII , which phosphorylates AMPA receptors (more conductance) and inserts new AMPA receptors into the spine. Next glutamate release at the same spine → bigger AMPA response = the synapse is potentiated . With sustained activity, gene transcription ( CREB ) + protein synthesis (Arc, BDNF) makes it last hours to days = late-phase LTP . This is the molecular face of Donald Hebb's rule: "neurons that fire together wire together." Block NMDA (APV, ketamine) → no LTP → no spatial learning (Morris water maze). The opposite process is LTD . The engram (physical memory trace) was named by Richard Semon and hunted by Karl Lashley. Amnesias Anterograde = cannot form new memories after the event (H.M.). Retrograde = lost memories from before the event. Ribot's law: recent memories are more vulnerable than remote ones. Korsakoff's syndrome = thiamine (B1) deficiency , usually from chronic alcoholism; damages the mammillary bodies + dorsomedial thalamus . Hallmark: dense anterograde amnesia + confabulation . The acute precursor is Wernicke's encephalopathy (confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia); together = Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome . Trap H.M. = bilateral medial temporal/hippocampus → anterograde amnesia, intact procedural learning; the hippocampus forms declarative memory but is not the permanent store. Korsakoff = thiamine , mammillary bodies + thalamus, confabulation . LTP needs NMDA ; AMPA carries the fast current. 14. Hunger, eating & health The classic theory and its limits. The old dual-centre hypothalamic hypothesis said the lateral hypothalamus (LH) is the "hunger/go" centre and the ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH) is the "satiety/stop" centre. Lesion evidence: VMH lesion → hyperphagia + obesity ; LH lesion → aphagia . True but oversimplified — eating is a network governed by many peptides. The modern arcuate-nucleus loop Neurons Co-release What they do POMC / CART neurons α-MSH (a POMC product) + CART Promote satiety — project to the paraventricular nucleus, activate MC4R → ↓ food intake NPY / AgRP neurons NPY + AgRP + GABA Promote hunger — same target; AgRP blocks MC4R, NPY excites feeding directly; also inhibit POMC neurons The peripheral signals Signal Source Effect Leptin Adipose (fat) tissue, proportional to fat stores ↓ appetite (long-term adiposity signal); excites POMC, inhibits NPY/AgRP, acts via the arcuate nucleus Insulin Pancreas (β-cells), post-meal ↑ satiety; glucose uptake (same direction as leptin) Ghrelin Empty stomach (X/A cells) ↑ appetite — excites NPY/AgRP; rises before meals, falls after PYY 3-36 Gut L-cells, post-meal ↓ appetite — inhibits NPY CCK Gut/duodenum I-cells, fat/protein meal ↑ short-term satiety via vagus → NTS → meal termination Arcuate POMC + NPY/AgRP project to the paraventricular nucleus (PVN) and the lateral hypothalamus (LH) , whose orexin neurons link feeding to arousal (an animal must wake to eat). MC4R mutations are the commonest monogenic cause of human obesity. Two frameworks & eating disorders Set-point theory: the body defends a fixed weight like a thermostat. Explains homeostasis but not why we overeat or why obesity rises. Positive-incentive theory (favoured): we eat largely for the anticipated pleasure of food (its incentive value), shaped by taste, learning and availability. (A related refinement is settling point : weight settles where opposing forces balance.) Obesity: evolved drive to store energy meets cheap palatable food; leptin resistance in many cases. Anorexia nervosa (restriction, low weight, body-image disturbance; high mortality) and bulimia nervosa (binge-purge). Trap VMH = satiety (lesion → obese); LH = feeding (lesion → aphagia). Leptin from fat lowers appetite; ghrelin from the stomach raises it (do not swap). Leptin is high in obese people (leptin resistance), not deficient. Positive-incentive over pure set-point. 15. Hormones, sex & the HPA axis The endocrine system is the body's slow, broadcast signalling system: glands release hormones into the blood to act on distant targets, commanded by the brain through the hypothalamus → pituitary link. Steroid hormones are lipid-soluble (intracellular receptors, gene transcription); peptide hormones are water-soluble (surface receptors). ADH = water reabsorption. The HPG axis & sexual differentiation The hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal (HPG) axis: hypothalamus → GnRH → pituitary → FSH/LH → gonads → sex steroids. (GnRH is pulsatile; the female pattern is cyclic, the male tonic.) Genetic sex is set at fertilisation (XX/XY). The SRY gene on the Y triggers the gonads to become testes; without it they become ovaries. Testes secrete testosterone (masculinises Wolffian ducts) and anti-Müllerian hormone (regresses female ducts). The default body plan is female unless androgens intervene. Natural experiments: androgen insensitivity (AIS) — XY with non-functional androgen receptors → female phenotype; congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) — fetal androgen excess masculinises an XX individual; 5-alpha-reductase deficiency ("guevedoces") — apparent females masculinising at puberty. SRY → testes; default is female. Aromatisation: in rodents testosterone masculinises the male brain by being converted to estradiol within the brain (aromatase); female fetuses are protected from circulating maternal estradiol by alpha-fetoprotein. Male = mPOA; female = VMH; maternal/pair-bonds = oxytocin/vasopressin. The HPA axis & stress endocrinology The HPA axis appears under four hats: biopsych "draw the axis", abnormal psych "HPA in MDD/PTSD/Cushing's", stress/health psych "Selye + allostatic load", and assessment "dexamethasone suppression test". A stressor (physical, psychological, immune) is sensed; the amygdala flags threat, prefrontal/hippocampus appraises context. The paraventricular nucleus (PVN) of the hypothalamus releases CRH (41-amino-acid peptide) + AVP into the hypophyseal portal blood. Anterior-pituitary corticotrophs release ACTH (cleaved from POMC, alongside β-endorphin + MSH) into systemic blood. The adrenal cortex, zona fasciculata releases cortisol (+ small DHEA). Cortisol acts everywhere (gluconeogenesis, immunosuppression, sodium retention) and feeds back to shut off CRH + ACTH. Adrenal-cortex layers (outside in): G lomerulosa (aldosterone), F asciculata (cortisol), R eticularis (androgens) — "GFR, salt-sugar-sex". The medulla makes adrenaline/NE via the fast SAM axis (seconds), whereas the HPA is the slower sustained arm (minutes). Cortisol actions & rhythm Metabolic: ↑ gluconeogenesis, glycogenolysis, lipolysis, proteolysis (catabolic; raises blood glucose). Immune: anti-inflammatory, ↓ lymphocytes, neutrophilia. CV: maintains vascular tone, permissive for catecholamines. CNS: alertness; chronic excess → hippocampal atrophy, memory deficits, mood change. GI: ↑ gastric acid (ulcers). Bone: ↑ resorption → osteoporosis. Diurnal rhythm: peak ~30 min after waking (the cortisol awakening response ), trough ~midnight, tied to the SCN. Disrupted in shift work, depression, insomnia, jet lag. Two receptors, two feedback loops Receptor Affinity Where Role MR (mineralocorticoid) High Hippocampus & some PVN Tonic, basal cortisol regulation; saturated at low cortisol levels GR (glucocorticoid) Low Hippocampus, PFC, amygdala, hypothalamus, pituitary, everywhere Stress-level feedback shutoff; recruited when cortisol is high The hippocampus is the brain's main inhibitor of the HPA axis via GR. Sustained high cortisol → dendritic atrophy in CA3, suppressed neurogenesis in the dentate gyrus, eventual volume loss → less feedback → more cortisol → more damage (the Sapolsky loop; ↓ BDNF underpins the neurotrophic hypothesis of depression ). The amygdala by contrast tends to hypertrophy/hyperreact. HPA in disorders MDD: hyperactive HPA (one of the most replicated findings), elevated baseline cortisol, blunted/flattened rhythm, enlarged adrenals, impaired GR feedback. Dexamethasone suppression test (DST): 1 mg dexamethasone at night → in health, morning cortisol is suppressed; in ~50% of melancholic/psychotic depression there is non-suppression (sensitivity ~40–50%, specificity ~80–90%; the Carroll DST — suggestive, not diagnostic). SSRIs + CBT normalise the axis over weeks. PTSD (paradox): often low basal cortisol with enhanced negative feedback (super-suppression on low-dose DST) and high CSF CRH — hypersensitive GRs. Contrast with MDD (hypercortisol + failed feedback). Cushing's disease = pituitary ACTH-secreting adenoma; Cushing's syndrome = any cause of hypercortisolism (often iatrogenic steroids). Central obesity, moon face, buffalo hump, purple striae, hypertension, hyperglycaemia, thin skin; depression in 50–80%. Addison's = primary adrenal insufficiency (↓ cortisol + aldosterone): fatigue, weight loss, hyperpigmentation (high ACTH → MSH), apathy/depression. Also: HPA hyperactivity in first-episode schizophrenia and anorexia nervosa; childhood maltreatment → durable HPA dysregulation via GR-promoter methylation (Meaney). Stress theory Cannon (1915) coined "fight or flight" (the acute SAM response) and "homeostasis". Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome (GAS): alarm → resistance → exhaustion ; he coined "stress" (the response) and "stressor" (the trigger). McEwen updated this with allostasis (stability through change), allostatic load (wear-and-tear of chronic adaptation) and allostatic overload (load becomes pathology). Richard Lazarus & Susan Folkman added cognitive appraisal (primary: is it threatening? secondary: can I cope?) and the problem-focused vs emotion-focused coping distinction. Measuring the axis: salivary cortisol (diurnal rhythm/CAR), 24-h urinary free cortisol (Cushing's screen), midnight serum cortisol, the DST (low-dose 1 mg screen; high-dose 8 mg distinguishes pituitary from ectopic ACTH), the CRH stimulation test, and the Trier Social Stress Test (TSST) . High-yield PVN → CRH → (anterior pituitary) ACTH → (adrenal cortex) cortisol → negative feedback at hypothalamus + pituitary via MR (high-affinity, tonic) and GR (low-affinity, stress). Chronic stress shrinks the hippocampus → feedback fails → cortisol stays high. MDD = hyper-cortisol + failed suppression; PTSD = hypo-cortisol + super-suppression. "Stress" = Hans Selye, "fight or flight"/"homeostasis" = Cannon, "allostatic load" = McEwen, "appraisal" = Lazarus & Susan Folkman. 16. Sleep, dreaming & circadian rhythms Sleep splits into NREM (3 stages) and REM . NREM REM Brain activity Slows progressively Fast, almost like awake Muscle tone Normal, relaxed Atonia (paralysed) Eye movements Slow or absent Rapid bursts Dreaming Rare, thought-like Vivid, narrative Heart rate / BP / breathing Low, stable, regular Variable, elevated, irregular Thermoregulation Works Fails (poikilothermic) Memory role Declarative consolidation (esp. NREM 3) Procedural + emotional consolidation The four stages (read off the EEG) NREM 1 (~5%) — theta waves (4–8 Hz) , very light, easily woken; hypnagogic images, hypnic jerks. NREM 2 (~45–55%, most of the night) — theta + sleep spindles (12–14 Hz bursts) + K-complexes ; spindles come from the thalamus and gate sensory input. The sign of being "truly asleep". NREM 3 (~15–20%) — delta waves (0.5–4 Hz, high amplitude) , deep slow-wave sleep, hard to rouse (sleep inertia). Growth hormone released; immune repair. Parasomnias (sleepwalking, sleep terrors, enuresis) arise here, common in children. Dominates the first half of the night. REM (~20–25%) — mixed-frequency, low-amplitude EEG resembling waking ("paradoxical"), rapid eye movements, muscle atonia , vivid narrative dreams, autonomic instability, genital tumescence. REM episodes lengthen across the night (first ~10 min, last 45+ min) and dominate the second half . NOT delta-dominant. The cycle = ~90 minutes, 4–6 cycles per 8 hours; if sleep is cut short you lose REM disproportionately. Across the lifespan: newborns sleep 16–18 h with ~50% REM and enter sleep via REM (adults via NREM 1); REM% and total sleep fall with age, and the elderly have less N3, more awakenings, and a phase advance. Neural control — the flip-flop switch Sleep-promoting: the ventrolateral preoptic nucleus (VLPO) of the anterior hypothalamus releases GABA + galanin to inhibit every wake-promoter. Adenosine builds with wakefulness to drive sleep pressure (caffeine blocks adenosine receptors). Wake-promoting (ARAS): pontine cholinergic (PPT/LDT → thalamus), locus coeruleus (NE), dorsal raphe (5-HT), tuberomammillary nucleus (histamine — why old H1 antihistamines sedate), all supervised by lateral-hypothalamus orexin/hypocretin neurons that bias the switch toward "wake". Flip-flop: VLPO and the wake nuclei mutually inhibit each other, making the system bistable (sharp transitions, unstable intermediate states). Lose orexin → the switch flips erratically → daytime sleep attacks + fragmented night sleep = narcolepsy. REM-ON/REM-OFF: REM is driven by cholinergic REM-on cells (PPT/LDT) while aminergic REM-off cells (NE locus coeruleus, 5-HT raphe) fall silent. PGO waves herald REM onset. REM atonia: descending glycine + GABA inhibition from the sublaterodorsal nucleus (subLDT) → medial medulla (magnocellular/gigantocellular nucleus) → spinal motor neurons paralyses skeletal muscle (sparing diaphragm + eye muscles). Lesion this (Jouvet's cats) → "REM without atonia". The human analogue is REM sleep behaviour disorder , which strongly predicts Parkinson's / Lewy body dementia within 10–15 years. Circadian: the master clock is the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) (~24.2 h free-running period), entrained ("set") by light via the retinohypothalamic tract (from intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells, a zeitgeber ); the SCN drives the pineal to release melatonin in darkness. Borbély's two-process model: homeostatic sleep debt (Process S) × circadian rhythm (Process C). Sleep, memory & deprivation Declarative memory consolidates in NREM (slow-wave; hippocampal replay during delta); procedural in REM + stage-2 spindles ; emotional in REM . After REM deprivation there is REM rebound . Sleep deprivation paradoxically lifts depression short-term (↑ BDNF, ↓ REM intrusion). Spindles + K-complexes → NREM 2. Delta / slow-wave / "deep sleep" → NREM 3. Paradoxical sleep = REM. Parasomnias (sleepwalking, night terrors, enuresis) → NREM 3 , not REM. The transmitter that peaks in REM is ACh ; NE, 5-HT and histamine all drop . SCN = the clock (light via retinohypothalamic tract); melatonin from the pineal. Narcolepsy = orexin loss; cataplexy is pathognomonic. 17. Reward, drugs of abuse & addiction The mesolimbic reward circuit, end-to-end The VTA (ventral tegmental area, midbrain) is the origin of mesolimbic dopamine neurons. They project up the medial forebrain bundle (MFB) — the bundle James Olds & Peter Milner (1954) stimulated to produce self-stimulation. The main target is the nucleus accumbens (NAc) in the ventral striatum. From NAc, output goes to the ventral pallidum , then back via mediodorsal thalamus → prefrontal cortex , which sends glutamatergic feedback; the amygdala & hippocampus add affective + contextual signal. Dopamine signals reward prediction error (Schultz), not "pleasure": it fires when an outcome is better than expected, is silent when expected, dips when worse. "Wanting" (incentive salience, mesolimbic DA) is dissociable from "liking" (the hedonic hotspot, opioid + cannabinoid signalling in NAc shell + ventral pallidum). Addiction is mostly wanting without liking — the addict craves long after the drug stops being fun (Robinson & Berridge's incentive-sensitisation theory). Behavioural assays: intracranial self-stimulation (MFB/VTA give the highest lever-press rates), conditioned place preference , and drug self-administration . Core concepts Tolerance = needing more drug for the same effect (dose-response shifts right; receptor downregulation). Withdrawal = aversive symptoms when the drug stops, often the mirror image of its effects (opponent process: NAc DA below baseline, amygdala stress system activated). Together = physical dependence . Sensitisation = the reverse of tolerance: increased response with repetition (the incentive/"wanting" component). Conditioned (Siegel) tolerance: tolerance is partly learned and cued by the setting, so a usual dose in a novel environment can become an overdose. ΔFosB is a transcription factor accumulating with chronic use, a molecular switch for addiction. Drugs of abuse — mechanism by class The unifying claim: every drug of abuse, by some route, raises dopamine in the NAc . Cocaine blocks DAT; amphetamine reverses it (+ empties vesicles via VMAT2). Alcohol is "GABA-A positive modulator + NMDA antagonist + endogenous-opioid release" — which is why naltrexone cuts craving. Tolerance and sensitisation are opposites ; "wanting" (DA) ≠ "liking" (opioid). Disulfiram blocks aldehyde dehydrogenase; acamprosate stabilises NMDA glutamate; varenicline is a partial α4β2 agonist. 18. Lateralisation, language & the split brain Most functions are bilateral, but some are lateralised . In ~90% of people (including most left-handers) language sits in the left hemisphere; the right is biased toward spatial processing, faces, music and emotional prosody. The split-brain studies (Sperry & Gazzaniga) Cutting the corpus callosum (commissurotomy, to stop severe epilepsy) leaves two hemispheres that cannot talk to each other. Because each visual field projects to the opposite hemisphere, an object flashed to the left visual field → right hemisphere cannot be named (language is on the left), yet the left hand (right hemisphere) can pick it out by touch. The left hemisphere ("the interpreter," Michael Gazzaniga) confabulates explanations. Sperry won the Nobel (1981). Dichotic listening (Kimura): different sounds to each ear; the right-ear advantage for words reflects left-hemisphere dominance. The Wada test (sodium amobarbital into one carotid) clinically establishes the language-dominant hemisphere before surgery. The aphasias Aphasia Lesion Fluency Comprehension Repetition Broca's (expressive) Left inferior frontal (Broca's area; patient "Tan") Non-fluent, effortful Intact Impaired Wernicke's (receptive) Left superior temporal (Wernicke's area) Fluent but meaningless Impaired Impaired Conduction Arcuate fasciculus Fluent Intact Impaired (the hallmark) Global Large left perisylvian Non-fluent Impaired Impaired Transcortical Around (sparing) the language zones Varies Varies Intact (preserved) Trap Broca = non-fluent but comprehends ("broken" speech); Wernicke = fluent but does not comprehend (word salad). Conduction aphasia = intact fluency and comprehension but poor repetition (arcuate fasciculus); transcortical aphasias spare repetition. In split-brain patients the right hemisphere can't name but can point/select with the left hand. 19. Emotion, stress & health The neural circuitry of emotion Papez circuit (the early emotion loop): hippocampus → fornix → mammillary bodies → anterior thalamus → cingulate → entorhinal → back to hippocampus. Paul MacLean extended this into the limbic system . Amygdala = the hub of fear and threat detection. Its lateral nucleus is the input gate (sensory input from thalamus + cortex), the basal/accessory basal nuclei integrate cortical context, and the central nucleus (CeA) is the output gate → hypothalamus (autonomic), PAG (freezing, analgesia), brainstem (startle), basal forebrain (vigilance). Joseph LeDoux's two roads to fear: a fast crude low road (thalamus → lateral amygdala) and a slower precise high road (thalamus → cortex → lateral amygdala). The lateral amygdala stores the CS-US association via LTP at its glutamate synapses. Klüver-Bucy syndrome (bilateral amygdala / anterior-temporal lesion, e.g. after HSV encephalitis or lobectomy): hyperorality (mouthing objects), hypersexuality, placidity/tameness, visual agnosia, hypermetamorphosis. Theories of emotion Theory Claim One-liner James-Lange Body response comes first ; emotion is the perception of it "We feel afraid because we tremble" Cannon-Bard Bodily arousal and emotion occur simultaneously (thalamic theory); supported by "sham rage" in decorticate animals Body + feeling fire together Schachter-Singer Two-factor: arousal + a cognitive label Arousal + interpretation = emotion Lazarus Cognitive appraisal precedes and causes emotion Think first, then feel Related ideas: display rules (cultural rules for showing emotion), the facial-feedback hypothesis (expression feeds back to intensify feeling), the Yerkes-Dodson inverted-U (optimal arousal is lower for complex tasks, higher for simple/well-learned ones), and the polygraph/GSR (detects autonomic arousal, not lying per se). McGaugh showed emotional arousal (basolateral amygdala + stress hormones) strengthens memory consolidation. High-yield James-Lange = body → emotion. Cannon-Bard = body & emotion at once. Schachter-Singer = arousal + label. Lazarus = appraisal first. Amygdala = fear (lateral = input, central = output); bilateral lesion = Klüver-Bucy. (Stress, HPA axis, Selye GAS and allostatic load are covered in full under §15.) 20. Biopsychology of psychiatric disorders Learn each disorder by its leading biological hypothesis plus the drug that follows from it. The diathesis-stress model frames disorders as biological vulnerability × environmental stress. Schizophrenia Dopamine hypothesis (original): too much DA. Evidence: D2-blocking drugs work; amphetamine (raises DA) mimics a paranoid psychosis. Updated: mesolimbic hyperdopaminergia → positive symptoms (hallucinations, delusions); mesocortical hypodopaminergia → negative/cognitive symptoms (avolition, flat affect). Glutamate / NMDA-hypofunction hypothesis: PCP / ketamine produce the full spectrum (positive + negative + cognitive), whereas DA-only drugs produce only positive symptoms. Structural: ventricular enlargement, reduced cortical grey matter (PFC + temporal), reduced hippocampal volume. Drugs: typicals (haloperidol, chlorpromazine) = pure D2 blockade → EPS / tardive dyskinesia. Atypicals (clozapine, risperidone, olanzapine) = D2 + 5-HT2A blockade → fewer EPS, more metabolic effects. Clozapine = the only one shown to help treatment-resistant cases and reduce suicide; needs WBC monitoring (agranulocytosis). Depression Monoamine hypothesis: deficit of 5-HT & NE (TCAs raise both, SSRIs raise 5-HT, MAOIs raise everything). Limitation: monoamines rise in hours but mood lifts in weeks. Neuroplasticity / BDNF hypothesis: loss of hippocampal volume + low BDNF; effective antidepressants raise BDNF and promote neurogenesis over weeks (fits the time course). HPA hypothesis: hypercortisolism + DST non-suppression in melancholic depression (see §15). Drugs: SSRI (first line), SNRI (venlafaxine, duloxetine), atypicals (bupropion = NDRI; mirtazapine = α2 + 5-HT2/3 antagonist), TCA, MAOI (tyramine diet). Ketamine/esketamine (NMDA antagonist) gives a rapid effect, reframing the field as glutamate-dependent. Somatic options: ECT, rTMS, DBS, VNS. Bipolar, anxiety & addiction Bipolar: strong polygenic loading. Lithium = first-line mood stabiliser (mechanism via inositol monophosphatase + GSK-3β inhibition; also reduces suicide in bipolar specifically). Antidepressant monotherapy can flip a patient into mania. Anxiety: amygdala-centred fear circuit with weaker prefrontal regulation. GABA-A modulation (benzos) gives fast relief; 5-HT (SSRI/SNRI) is first-line maintenance for panic, GAD, OCD, PTSD, social anxiety. OCD = cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical loop overactivity (caudate hyperactivity on PET, normalising with high-dose SSRI / CBT). Addiction: hijack of mesolimbic DA (see §17) with tolerance + sensitisation + opponent-process withdrawal; long-term cue-induced craving driven by amygdala + PFC + hippocampus. Trap Schizophrenia positive symptoms = excess mesolimbic dopamine (treated by D2 antagonists ; they can worsen the mesocortical-hypo negative symptoms) + NMDA hypofunction; depression = too little 5-HT/NE (plus BDNF + HPA). Typicals → EPS/tardive dyskinesia; clozapine → agranulocytosis. Lithium = bipolar, not depression alone; lithium and clozapine each reduce suicide in their disorder. 21. Clinical neuropsychology: syndromes & batteries NIMHANS weights this heavily: named clinical syndromes, the lesion behind each, and the assessment batteries by name. Lesion syndromes (high-yield) Lesion Syndrome Broca's area (L inferior frontal) Non-fluent aphasia, comprehension intact Wernicke's area (L superior temporal) Fluent but meaningless speech, poor comprehension Arcuate fasciculus Conduction aphasia (poor repetition) Bilateral hippocampus / medial temporal Anterograde amnesia (H.M.) Mammillary bodies + dorsomedial thalamus (thiamine) Wernicke-Korsakoff: confabulation, amnesia Right inferior parietal Left hemispatial neglect + anosognosia Left parietal (angular gyrus) Gerstmann's syndrome: agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia, left-right disorientation Bilateral amygdala / anterior temporal Klüver-Bucy: hyperoral, hypersexual, placid, visual agnosia Substantia nigra Parkinson's: bradykinesia, rigidity, resting tremor Caudate / putamen Huntington's: chorea, dementia Subthalamic nucleus Hemiballismus (violent flinging of one side) Cerebellum Ataxia, dysmetria, intention tremor, dysdiadochokinesia Frontal lobe (orbitofrontal) Disinhibition, personality change (Phineas Gage) Fusiform face area (ventral occipitotemporal) Prosopagnosia (cannot recognise familiar faces) Named clinical syndromes Syndrome Defining feature Locus Prosopagnosia Cannot recognise faces (objects ok) Fusiform face area (bilateral/right occipitotemporal) Capgras delusion Belief a loved one is replaced by an identical impostor Face recognition intact but emotional/limbic response lost Hemispatial neglect Ignores one side of space (usually left) Right parietal Gerstmann's syndrome Agraphia + acalculia + finger agnosia + L-R disorientation (the tetrad) Left angular gyrus Anosognosia Denial / unawareness of one's own deficit Right parietal often Wernicke-Korsakoff Wernicke (confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia) → Korsakoff (amnesia + confabulation) Thiamine deficiency; mammillary bodies + thalamus The three "A"s Family Definition Examples Agnosia Failure to recognise despite intact basic sensation Visual object agnosia, prosopagnosia, associative vs apperceptive, astereognosis Apraxia Inability to perform learned skilled movements despite intact strength/comprehension Ideomotor, ideational, constructional, dressing (often left parietal) Aphasia Impaired language (production/comprehension) Broca, Wernicke, conduction, global, transcortical Assessment batteries Battery What it is Halstead-Reitan Fixed, comprehensive quantitative battery (Category Test, Tactual Performance, Trail Making, etc.); yields an impairment index Luria-Nebraska Standardised battery based on Alexander Luria's qualitative approach (motor, rhythm, tactile, language, memory scales) NIMHANS Neuropsychological Battery India-developed, normed for the Indian population; attention, executive function, memory, language, visuospatial domains Bender-Gestalt Copying geometric designs; screens visuomotor integration / organic impairment Wisconsin Card Sorting Test (WCST) Frontal/executive set-shifting; perseveration = frontal damage Wechsler Memory Scale Standardised memory assessment Trap Agnosia = can't recognise; apraxia = can't perform a learned movement; aphasia = can't language; anosognosia = denial of deficit. Capgras = "replaced by impostor"; prosopagnosia = "can't recognise the face at all". Right parietal → left neglect + anosognosia; left angular gyrus → Gerstmann. Halstead-Reitan = fixed quantitative; Luria-Nebraska = standardised Luria qualitative; Bender-Gestalt = visuomotor screen; perseveration on WCST = frontal lobe. 22. Genetic, chromosomal & metabolic disorders Examiners ask "which disorder is associated with which gene / chromosome / enzyme / behaviour". For each, know (1) the genetic mechanism, (2) one physical/biochemical sign, (3) one behavioural/cognitive sign. Disorder Mechanism One-line ID IQ / behaviour Down syndrome Trisomy 21 (95% maternal non-disjunction; 5% translocation/mosaic) Flat face, epicanthal folds, single palmar crease, hypotonia, Brushfield spots IQ 30-70; sociable; early-onset Alzheimer's after 40 (extra APP gene). Most common chromosomal cause of ID Edwards Trisomy 18 Clenched fists, overlapping fingers, rocker-bottom feet Severe ID; <10% survive 1 year Patau Trisomy 13 Cleft lip/palate, polydactyly, holoprosencephaly Severe ID; <10% survive 1 year Klinefelter 47,XXY Tall, gynecomastia, small testes, infertility Verbal < performance IQ; shy, immature; testosterone replacement Turner 45,X0 (only viable monosomy) Short stature, webbed neck, shield chest, amenorrhoea, streak ovaries Normal verbal IQ, visuospatial deficit ; social difficulty XYY 47,XYY Tall males, normal phenotype Mild ID/impulsivity; "criminal chromosome" myth disproved Triple X 47,XXX Tall females, normal phenotype Mild language delay, normal IQ Fragile X CGG repeat on FMR1, X-linked (>200 repeats silences FMRP) Long face, large ears, macroorchidism (post-puberty) Most common inherited ID; hand-flapping, ~30% ASD; premutation → FXTAS Williams Microdeletion 7q11.23 (elastin gene) Elfin face, supravalvular aortic stenosis, hypercalcaemia Mild-mod ID; hypersocial "cocktail party" speech, musical affinity Prader-Willi Paternal 15q11-13 deletion (or maternal UPD) Infant hypotonia, later hyperphagia, obesity, small hands/feet Mild ID, compulsive eating, skin-picking, temper outbursts Angelman Maternal 15q11-13 deletion (UBE3A) Ataxic gait, microcephaly, seizures Severe ID, no speech, inappropriate laughter , "happy puppet" Cri-du-chat 5p deletion (5p−) High-pitched cat-like cry, microcephaly, hypertelorism Severe ID, motor + language delay DiGeorge / VCFS 22q11.2 deletion (most common microdeletion) CATCH-22: Cardiac, Abnormal facies, Thymic hypoplasia, Cleft palate, Hypocalcaemia Mild ID; highest known single risk for schizophrenia (~25×) Rett MECP2, X-linked dominant (only girls survive) Normal 6-18 mo then head-growth deceleration Loss of purposeful hand use → stereotyped hand-wringing ; removed from DSM-5 PDD section Huntington's CAG repeat on chr 4 (HTT), autosomal dominant, anticipation Chorea, caudate atrophy Onset 30-50; subcortical dementia ; depression + high suicide Wilson's ATP7B, autosomal recessive (copper) Kayser-Fleischer rings , hepatic + neuro signs, parkinsonism Personality change, psychosis; reversible with chelation (penicillamine/zinc) PKU PAH deficiency, autosomal recessive (chr 12) Musty/mousy odour , fair skin/hair, eczema Severe ID if untreated; preventable by Phe-free diet (Guthrie test screen) Tay-Sachs Hexosaminidase A deficiency, AR (Ashkenazi, HEXA chr 15) Cherry-red macula , exaggerated startle Regression by 6 mo, death by 3-5 yr; no treatment Lesch-Nyhan HGPRT deficiency, X-linked recessive (purines) Hyperuricaemia, gout Compulsive self-mutilation (lip/finger biting), aggression, choreoathetosis Galactosaemia GALT deficiency, AR Jaundice, cataracts, hepatomegaly after milk ID if untreated; lactose-free diet Maple syrup urine BCKD deficiency, AR (leucine/isoleucine/valine) Sweet-smelling urine, neonatal lethargy Seizures, ID, coma if untreated Hurler / Hunter MPS (α-L-iduronidase / iduronate-2-sulfatase) Coarse facies, hepatosplenomegaly; Hurler corneal clouding, Hunter clear cornea Progressive ID; Hunter = X-linked, Hurler = AR Neurofibromatosis 1 NF1 gene, chr 17, autosomal dominant ≥6 café-au-lait spots, neurofibromas, Lisch nodules Learning disability ~50%, ADHD overlap Tuberous sclerosis TSC1 (9q) / TSC2 (16p), autosomal dominant Ash-leaf macules, facial angiofibromas, cortical tubers, seizures ID + autism in ~50%; high epilepsy Fetal alcohol syndrome Prenatal alcohol exposure Short palpebral fissures, smooth philtrum, thin upper lip, microcephaly Growth retardation, ADHD, learning disability; most common preventable cause of ID Congenital hypothyroidism (cretinism) Iodine deficiency / thyroid dysgenesis Coarse features, large tongue, umbilical hernia, hypotonia Severe ID + short stature if untreated; preventable by neonatal screen + thyroxine High-yield Imprinting: P aternal = P rader -Willi, M aternal = Angel m an — same 15q11-13 locus, opposite parent of origin, opposite phenotype. Trinucleotide-repeat (anticipation): Huntington (CAG), Fragile X (CGG), Friedreich (GAA), myotonic (CTG). X-linked recessive: Lesch-Nyhan, Hunter, DMD, haemophilia. Maternal PKU: a mother off-diet in pregnancy damages even a heterozygote fetus (Phe crosses the placenta). Trap "Most common chromosomal cause of ID" = Down ; "most common inherited cause" = Fragile X . Single palmar crease + flat face + early Alzheimer's = Down. Cat-like cry = Cri-du-chat. Elfin face + hypersocial = Williams. Happy puppet + laughter = Angelman. Self-mutilation + gout in a boy = Lesch-Nyhan. Musty urine + fair child = PKU. Cherry-red macula + Ashkenazi = Tay-Sachs. KF rings = Wilson's. 22q11.2 = CATCH-22 + highest schizophrenia risk. 23. Landmark studies, walked through Stems love the who-did-what swap. Learn the procedure, not just the headline. David Hubel & Torsten Wiesel (1959+) — recorded single V1 cells in cats/monkeys: feature detectors (simple = orientation + position; complex = orientation regardless of position + motion; hypercomplex = adds length), ocular-dominance + orientation columns, and a visual critical period (monocular-deprivation amblyopia). Nobel 1981. Trap: "feature detector" ≠ "grandmother cell". James Olds & Peter Milner (1954) — rats lever-pressed thousands of times/hour for electrical self-stimulation of the septal area / medial forebrain bundle = intracranial self-stimulation reward (ICSS), later mapped to mesolimbic DA (VTA → NAc). (Not memory — that is the other Milner, Brenda.) William Scoville & (Brenda) Milner (1957) — patient H.M. : bilateral medial-temporal removal → dense anterograde amnesia , intact IQ + working memory + procedural learning ( mirror-drawing , Milner's demonstration). The most-cited memory case. Roger Sperry & Michael Gazzaniga (1960s) — split-brain: right hemisphere can't name an LVF object but the left hand can select it; left hemisphere = "the interpreter". Sperry Nobel 1981. Karl Lashley (1929) — maze-lesion search for the engram yielded mass action (deficit ∝ amount of cortex destroyed) + equipotentiality . Hebb (1949, his student) countered with cell assemblies ("fire together, wire together"); LTP (Bliss & Lømo 1973) later vindicated him. Wilder Penfield (1930s–50s) — awake cortical stimulation mapped the motor (precentral) + sensory (postcentral) homunculi ; the disproportion reflects innervation density, not body size. Phineas Gage (1848) — tamping iron through the orbitofrontal / ventromedial PFC → personality change, disinhibition, intact basic cognition (Antonio Damasio's somatic-marker reconstruction). K.C. (Endel Tulving) & Clive Wearing — episodic loss with spared semantic (K.C.); encephalitis amnesic with ~7-second span but spared music/procedural (Clive Wearing). O'Keefe (1971) & the Morris water maze — hippocampal place cells = the cognitive map; the Mosers found entorhinal grid cells (shared 2014 Nobel). The water maze is the standard hippocampal spatial-memory test. Eric Kandel — Aplysia gill-withdrawal: habituation (less transmitter) vs sensitisation (more, via serotonin → cAMP); long-term memory needs protein synthesis + CREB . Nobel 2000. McGaugh & Joseph LeDoux — basolateral amygdala + stress hormones strengthen emotional-memory consolidation; LeDoux's two roads (low: thalamus→amygdala; high: thalamus→cortex→amygdala). Cannon-Bard, Papez & Paul MacLean — Cannon-Bard thalamic theory (simultaneous body + emotion; "sham rage" in decorticate animals); Papez circuit; MacLean's limbic-system concept. Bell-Magendie, Broca, Brown-Séquard — dorsal roots sensory, ventral roots motor (Bell-Magendie); Broca = left-frontal production (patient "Tan"), Wernicke = left-temporal comprehension; Brown-Séquard = ipsilateral touch/motor loss + contralateral pain/temp loss. Bouchard — Minnesota Study of Twins Reared Apart → high heritability estimates; heritability is a population statistic. 24. Extended concept bank The remaining named terms an MCQ can pull, grouped by home topic. Each is the kind of one-line fact a distractor is built from. Neuroanatomy & cells Nissl substance = rough ER in the soma (Nissl stain reveals cell bodies). Neuron doctrine = Cajal's principle that the neuron is the discrete unit (beat Golgi's reticular theory). Gyri/sulci/fissures = ridges/grooves/deep grooves. Commissures: corpus callosum (largest), anterior commissure, massa intermedia. Tract/nerve = axon bundle in CNS/PNS; nucleus/ganglion = cell-body cluster in CNS/PNS. White = myelinated axons, grey = cell bodies. Reticular formation = brainstem arousal/tone network (houses the ARAS). Area postrema = medullary vomiting centre (a circumventricular organ lacking a BBB). Blood-brain barrier = tight endothelial junctions + astrocyte end-feet. Conduction & synapses Nernst / equilibrium potential = the voltage at which an ion's electrical + chemical gradients balance (K⁺ ≈ −90 mV). Neuromodulator = transmitter that tunes many neurons diffusely. Gap junction = electrical synapse. Retrograde messengers = NO + endocannabinoids . Acetylcholinesterase degrades ACh (inhibitors used in Alzheimer's, myasthenia, nerve agents); MAO + COMT degrade monoamines. Senses & sensorimotor Rhodopsin = rod photopigment. Duplexity theory , Purkinje shift , centre-surround , magno/parvo , scotoma/blindsight , tonotopy , conductive vs sensorineural deafness, vestibular canals/otoliths, cutaneous receptors, A-delta vs C fibres, PAG , phantom limb (Ramachandran's mirror box). Muscle spindle vs GTO , alpha/gamma motor neurons, monosynaptic stretch reflex, reciprocal innervation, central pattern generators, Betz cells, mirror neurons, direct/indirect basal-ganglia pathways. Development, plasticity, hunger, hormones Neural crest, radial glia, growth cone + chemoaffinity (Roger Sperry), neurotrophins (NGF/BDNF), apoptosis vs necrosis, LTD, kindling, excitotoxicity, diaschisis, constraint-induced therapy, neurogenesis sites (dentate gyrus + SVZ). Arcuate NPY/AgRP vs POMC/CART, set point vs settling point, sham eating / VMH finickiness, cephalic phase, steroid vs peptide hormones, releasing vs tropic hormones, pulsatile/cyclic GnRH, aromatisation, AIS, CAH, 5-α-reductase deficiency, sexually dimorphic nucleus (SDN). Sleep, addiction, emotion, psychiatric PGO waves, adenosine, Borbély's two-process model, zeitgeber, free-running rhythm, recuperation vs adaptation theories, fatal familial insomnia, incentive-sensitisation, conditioned (Siegel) tolerance, ΔFosB, sham rage/decortication, polygraph/GSR, display rules/facial feedback, allostatic load. Diathesis-stress, glutamate/NMDA-hypofunction, mesolimbic vs mesocortical DA, typical vs atypical antipsychotics, BDNF/neurotrophic hypothesis, HPA/DST, ketamine/esketamine, ECT/rTMS/DBS/VNS, tardive dyskinesia/EPS, SERT & the OCD cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical loop. 25. Fast glossary (A–Z) Last-mile recall: every nameable term, structure, transmitter, syndrome and theorist on this page reduced to a single line (with who/where). Cover the right column and self-test. Term One-line definition (and who/where) Acetylcholine NMJ + parasympathetic + memory transmitter; low in Alzheimer's; cleared by acetylcholinesterase. Action potential All-or-none spike: Na⁺ in (depolarise) → K⁺ out (repolarise); intensity coded by frequency. Adenosine Sleep-pressure molecule; caffeine is its antagonist. Agnosia Failure to recognise despite intact sensation (e.g. prosopagnosia). Amygdala Fear/threat hub + emotional-memory modulator; bilateral lesion → Klüver-Bucy. Anosognosia Denial/unawareness of one's own deficit (often right parietal). Aphasia Impaired language: Broca (non-fluent), Wernicke (fluent, no comprehension), conduction (bad repetition). Aplysia Sea slug Eric Kandel used to show habituation/sensitisation at the synapse. Apraxia Loss of skilled learned movement despite intact strength. Arcuate nucleus Hypothalamic appetite hub (NPY/AgRP "eat" vs POMC/CART "stop") where leptin and ghrelin act. ARAS Brainstem reticular activating system maintaining arousal/wakefulness. Aromatisation hypothesis Testosterone converted to estradiol in the brain masculinises it (rodents). Basal ganglia Caudate/putamen/GP/STN/SN; movement selection & force; Parkinson's, Huntington's. Bell-Magendie law Dorsal spinal roots sensory, ventral roots motor. Bregma Skull landmark used as origin for stereotaxic coordinates. Brown-Séquard Cord hemisection: ipsilateral touch/motor loss + contralateral pain/temp loss. Cannon-Bard Bodily arousal and emotion occur simultaneously (thalamic). Capgras delusion Belief a loved one is an identical impostor (emotional response lost). CCK Duodenal short-term satiety signal (meal termination). Cerebellum Coordination, timing, motor learning; lesion → ataxia, intention tremor, dysmetria. Cortisol Adrenal-cortex (zona fasciculata) stress hormone; endpoint of the HPA axis. CREB Transcription factor required for long-term (protein-synthesis-dependent) memory (Kandel). Critical period Window when experience must occur for normal wiring (David Hubel & Wiesel amblyopia). DCML Fine touch/proprioception; crosses in the medulla. Dopamine hypothesis Schizophrenia positive symptoms from excess mesolimbic DA (D2 antagonists treat them). Dorsal/ventral streams Dorsal "where/how" (parietal); ventral "what" (temporal). Engram The physical memory trace (term: Semon; searched by Karl Lashley). Epigenetics Experience switches genes on/off without changing sequence (methylation silences). Equipotentiality Within an area any part can substitute for another (Lashley). Feature detector Cortical cell tuned to a stimulus property (Hubel & Torsten Wiesel). fMRI (BOLD) Functional imaging of blood-oxygen change; good spatial, poorer temporal. GABA Main inhibitory transmitter; GABA-A target of benzos, alcohol, barbiturates. Gate control Non-painful input closes a dorsal-horn gate on pain (Melzack & Wall). GAS Hans Selye's alarm → resistance → exhaustion stress response. Gerstmann's Left angular gyrus tetrad: agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia, L-R disorientation. Ghrelin Stomach "hunger hormone"; raises appetite. Glutamate Main excitatory transmitter; NMDA/AMPA; LTP + excitotoxicity. Donald Hebb's rule Co-active neurons strengthen their connection ("fire together wire together"). Heritability Proportion of population variance due to genetic variance (not a personal %). Hippocampus Forms new declarative memories + spatial maps; H.M.'s loss → anterograde amnesia. HPA axis Hypothalamus (CRH) → pituitary (ACTH) → adrenal cortex (cortisol); the slow stress arm. Incentive-sensitisation Addiction sensitises "wanting" (DA) apart from "liking" (Robinson & Berridge). Ionotropic vs metabotropic Ligand-gated channel (fast) vs G-protein-coupled receptor (slow, lasting). James-Lange Emotion is the perception of bodily response (body first). Klüver-Bucy Bilateral amygdala/temporal lesion: hyperorality, hypersexuality, placidity, visual agnosia. Korsakoff's Thiamine deficiency; mammillary bodies + thalamus; amnesia + confabulation. Joseph LeDoux's two roads Fast subcortical "low road" vs slow cortical "high road" to the amygdala. Leptin Fat-derived hormone lowering appetite (long-term adiposity signal); high in obesity. LGN / MGN Thalamic relays for vision (LGN → V1) and hearing (MGN → Heschl's gyrus). Lithium First-line mood stabiliser; reduces suicide in bipolar (GSK-3β / inositol). LTP / LTD NMDA-dependent synaptic strengthening (Ca²⁺ → CaMKII → AMPA insertion) vs weakening. Mass action Memory deficit proportional to total cortex destroyed (Lashley). Melatonin Pineal hormone of darkness; driven by the SCN. Meninges Dura → arachnoid → pia; CSF in the subarachnoid space. Mirror neurons Fire both during and while observing an action (Giacomo Rizzolatti, F5). Monoamine hypothesis Depression = deficit of 5-HT/NE (basis of SSRIs). Morris water maze Hidden-platform test of hippocampal spatial memory. NMDA receptor Glutamate coincidence detector; Mg²⁺-blocked at rest; Ca²⁺ entry triggers LTP. Narcolepsy Sleep attacks + cataplexy from loss of orexin/hypocretin. Nodes of Ranvier Gaps where the AP regenerates (saltatory conduction). Olds & Milner Intracranial self-stimulation reward (septal area / MFB). Oligodendrocyte / Schwann CNS myeliner (many axons) vs PNS myeliner (one segment; aids regeneration). Opponent-process Colour coded in red-green/blue-yellow/black-white pairs after the retina (Ewald Hering). Orexin / hypocretin Lateral-hypothalamus peptide stabilising wakefulness; loss → narcolepsy. Organising vs activating Early permanent hormonal structuring vs later reversible behavioural switching. Oxytocin / ADH Made in hypothalamus, released by posterior pituitary (bonding/milk; water reabsorption). PAG Midbrain hub of descending opioid pain control. Papez circuit Hippocampus → fornix → mammillary → anterior thalamus → cingulate emotion loop. Parkinson's Substantia-nigra DA loss + Lewy bodies; resting tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia. Wilder Penfield Awake cortical stimulation → motor/sensory homunculus. Place theory Pitch coded by peak location on basilar membrane; best for high frequencies (von Békésy). Prosopagnosia Inability to recognise familiar faces (fusiform face area). Pyramidal tract Voluntary fine movement; decussates at the medullary pyramids. Raphe nuclei Brainstem source of serotonin. Refractory period Absolute (no spike possible, Na⁺ inactivated) vs relative (needs stronger stimulus). REM sleep Low-voltage "paradoxical" EEG + atonia + vivid dreams (not delta); ACh peaks. Resting potential ~−70 mV from leaky K⁺ channels (pump maintains the gradient). Saltatory conduction AP "jumps" between Nodes of Ranvier in myelinated axons. SCN Hypothalamic master circadian clock entrained by light. Schachter-Singer Two-factor emotion: arousal + a cognitive label. Serotonin Mood/sleep/appetite transmitter (from tryptophan); raphe; low → depression/OCD. Split brain Callosotomy patients; right hemisphere can't name (Roger Sperry & Michael Gazzaniga). SRY gene Y-chromosome trigger for testis formation; default body plan female. Stereotaxic surgery Reaching a deep target by 3-D coordinates from bregma. Substantia nigra Midbrain DA source; degenerates in Parkinson's. Tardive dyskinesia Involuntary movements from chronic D2 blockade. Thalamus Sensory relay for all senses except smell. TMS Non-invasive magnetic "virtual lesion"; also a depression treatment. Tolerance vs sensitisation Decreased vs increased response with repeated drug use (opposites). Trichromatic theory Colour from three cone types at the receptor level (Young-Helmholtz). Endel Tulving Episodic vs semantic memory distinction (patient K.C.). VTA → NAc Mesolimbic dopamine reward pathway hijacked by addictive drugs. VMH / LH Ventromedial = satiety (lesion → obesity); lateral = feeding (lesion → aphagia). VLPO Ventrolateral preoptic nucleus; GABAergic sleep "off switch". Wada test Carotid amobarbital to find the language-dominant hemisphere before surgery. Wernicke's area / aphasia Left superior temporal; fluent but meaningless speech, poor comprehension. Wernicke-Korsakoff Thiamine deficiency: Wernicke (confusion/ataxia/ophthalmoplegia) → Korsakoff (amnesia + confabulation). WCST Frontal/executive set-shifting; perseveration = frontal damage. Yerkes-Dodson Inverted-U arousal-performance law; optimum lower for complex tasks. Zeitgeber External time-cue (chiefly light) that entrains the circadian clock.

title: Cognitive Psychology — the whole domain, explained cold
text: Cognitive Psychology — the whole domain, explained cold Built from Eysenck & Keane, Cognitive Psychology: A Student's Handbook , the book you listed for cognitive. This is the full-depth version : for every named model you get what it claims, who proposed it, the key experiment (what was done and what was found), and the contrast with its rival in a red trap box. Tables stay as quick-reference, but read the prose around them first. Cognition spans perception, attention, memory, knowledge, language and thinking, so this single page walks the book chapter by chapter. Rebuilt to full depth 2026-05-29. Effects Phenomena Theories Theorists Social Psych Cognitive Lookalikes How cognitive is tested. (1) Name the model from its claim ("we store info in three stores" = multi-store). (2) Pin the model to its author (working memory = Alan Baddeley & Graham Hitch). (3) Tell rival models apart — that's where the distractor lives: Gregory vs Gibson, early vs late selection, episodic vs semantic, prototype vs exemplar, Broca vs Wernicke. Learn each in its contrast pair, and learn the one experiment that decides between them. Jump to: 1. Approaches 2. Visual perception 3. Object & face recognition 4. Attention 5. STM & working memory 6. Long-term memory 7. Forgetting & everyday memory 8. Concepts & knowledge 9. Language 10. Problem solving & expertise 11. Judgement & decision making 12. Reasoning ★ At-a-glance compare ★ MCQ traps ★ Key studies ★ Glossary ★ Self-test 1. Approaches to human cognition Eysenck & Keane open by saying cognitive psychology is not one method but four converging approaches , each with its own logic and limits. The point of knowing all four is that an exam stem will describe a technique and ask which approach it belongs to. Experimental cognitive psychology What it claims: you can infer the hidden stages of mental processing in healthy people by measuring behaviour under controlled conditions — chiefly reaction time (RT) and accuracy/error rate . It is the oldest strand and the historical core of the field. If a manipulation slows people down, that stage must require processing. Key logic: the subtraction/additive-factors idea — compare two tasks differing in one operation, and the RT difference estimates that operation's duration. Limit: behaviour alone is ambiguous about the underlying architecture (many models predict the same RT), and lab tasks may lack ecological validity. Cognitive neuropsychology + modularity What it claims: studying brain-damaged patients reveals the normal architecture of cognition, because damage can knock out one ability while sparing another. The bedrock assumption is modularity (Fodor): the mind contains specialised, domain-specific, informationally encapsulated modules that can be independently impaired. Key logic — the double dissociation : patient A is impaired on task X but fine on Y, while patient B is fine on X but impaired on Y. That pattern is strong evidence the two tasks rely on separate systems (one alone could be explained by task difficulty). Example: H.M. (studied by William Scoville and Brenda Milner, 1957) lost the ability to form new long-term memories yet had normal short-term span; other patients (e.g. K.F.) show the reverse — together a double dissociation of STM and LTM. Limit: damage is rarely clean, the brain reorganises, and single cases generalise poorly. Cognitive neuroscience methods What it claims: by measuring the living brain we can locate where and time when cognition happens. The methods trade off spatial against temporal resolution, and the exam loves to ask which method gives which. Method Measures Strength fMRI Blood-oxygen (BOLD) — indirect metabolic signal Excellent spatial resolution (mm), poor temporal (seconds); shows where . PET Radioactive tracer, blood flow/metabolism Good spatial, very poor temporal; needs injected tracer. EEG / ERP Scalp electrical activity; ERP = signal averaged to an event Excellent temporal resolution (ms), poor spatial; shows when . TMS Magnetic pulse that briefly disrupts a region Creates a "virtual lesion" → tests if a region is necessary (causal, not just correlational). Spatial vs temporal mnemonic: fMRI/PET = WHERE (great space, poor time). EEG/ERP = WHEN (great time, poor space). TMS = whether it's NECESSARY (causal). fMRI and EEG are merely correlational; only TMS and lesions establish that a region is causally required. Computational cognitive science & connectionism (PDP) What it claims: if a theory is precise enough, you can implement it as a running computer program; a model that actually reproduces human performance (including human errors ) is a strong test of the theory. The dominant style is connectionism / parallel distributed processing (PDP) : networks of simple, neuron-like units connected by weighted links, where knowledge is distributed across the pattern of weights rather than stored in one location, and learning happens by gradually adjusting weights (e.g. back-propagation). NIMHANS tests harder — connectionism. Be ready for the contrast with classical "symbolic" models. Symbolic (e.g. Allen Newell & Herbert Simon's physical-symbol-system) manipulates discrete rules and symbols, processing serially. Connectionist/PDP uses distributed sub-symbolic representations and parallel processing; its hallmarks are graceful degradation (partial damage = partial loss, not total crash), generalisation, and learning from examples. NIMHANS may ask which framework explains prototype effects or developmental error patterns (e.g. the U-shaped curve in learning the past tense) — that's connectionism. Bottom-up vs top-down; serial vs parallel Two cross-cutting distinctions run through the whole book. Bottom-up (data-driven) processing starts from the stimulus and works up. Top-down (concept-driven) processing brings expectations, context and stored knowledge to bear. Information processing (the frame Donald Broadbent founded) treats the mind as stages from input → encoding → storage → retrieval → output. Within that frame, processing can be serial (one stage at a time, in sequence) or parallel (several at once). Almost every debate below is really "how much top-down vs bottom-up?" and "serial or parallel?" Recap — approaches. Experimental = RT/accuracy in healthy people. Neuropsychology = patients + double dissociation + modularity. Neuroscience = fMRI/PET (where) · EEG-ERP (when) · TMS (necessary). Computational = running models; PDP = distributed, parallel, learns weights, degrades gracefully. Cutting across all: bottom-up vs top-down, serial vs parallel. 2. Visual perception The central question: how much does perception build on the stimulus alone, and how much does it require inference from stored knowledge? The two classic answers are Gregory's and Gibson's, and they are the single most tested pair in perception. Gregory — constructivist / indirect theory (top-down) What it claims: the retinal image is impoverished and ambiguous, so perception is an active construction — the brain forms and tests perceptual hypotheses , the "best guess" about what is out there, using stored knowledge and context. Perception is therefore largely top-down and indirect. Key evidence: visual illusions are Gregory's strongest card. The hollow-mask illusion (a concave face is seen as convex because we "know" faces are convex) and the Müller-Lyer illusion show perception departing from the stimulus toward what the brain expects. He also pointed to degraded conditions (poor light) where guessing is clearly needed. Gibson — direct / ecological theory (bottom-up) What it claims: in the real world the optic array is information-rich, not impoverished. As we move, the optic flow and invariants (texture gradients, horizon ratio) specify layout directly , so no inference or hypothesis is needed — perception is bottom-up and "direct." His signature concept is the affordance : objects directly offer their possibilities for action (a chair affords sitting, a handle affords grasping). Key evidence: pilots and animals navigate using optic flow; texture gradients give depth without "thinking." Limit: Gibson struggles to explain illusions (why would the array mislead us?) and downplays the role of stored knowledge. Gregory vs Gibson: Gregory = indirect/constructivist, top-down, perception is a hypothesis (best for illusions and poor viewing conditions). Gibson = direct/ecological, bottom-up, the info is already in the optic array (best for rich, moving real-world viewing). Stem says "inference / hypothesis / illusion" → Gregory. Stem says "affordance / optic array / optic flow / invariant" → Gibson. Modern view: both are partly right — perception is mostly direct but uses top-down processing when input is degraded. Marr — computational theory of vision What it claims: vision is information-processing that builds the scene in stages of increasingly rich representation , mostly bottom-up. The three stages: Primal sketch — 2-D, captures edges, bars, blobs and intensity changes from the raw image. 2½-D sketch — depth and orientation of surfaces from the viewer's vantage point (still egocentric). 3-D model — an object-centred representation, independent of viewpoint, suitable for recognition. David Marr also famously argued any information-processing system must be understood at three levels : the computational (what problem is solved and why), the algorithmic (what representations and steps), and the implementational/hardware (how it is physically realised). Gestalt grouping laws Who: Max Wertheimer, Kurt Koffka, Wolfgang Köhler. What it claims: the perceptual system organises elements into wholes by innate principles, so that "the whole is other than the sum of its parts." The grouping laws: proximity (near things group), similarity (alike things group), closure (we complete gaps), continuity / good continuation (we follow smooth lines), common fate (things moving together group), and the overarching law of Prägnanz (we perceive the simplest, most stable, "best" organisation possible). Limit: the laws are descriptive, not explanatory, and were mostly demonstrated with 2-D figures. Depth cues and constancies Binocular cues need two eyes: retinal (binocular) disparity (the slight difference between the two retinal images, the basis of stereopsis) and convergence (the inward turn of the eyes for near objects). Monocular / pictorial cues need only one eye and work in pictures: linear perspective, interposition (overlap), texture gradient, relative size, height in the visual field, aerial perspective, light and shadow , plus the motion-based motion parallax . Perceptual constancies keep the world stable despite a changing retinal image: size, shape, colour and brightness/lightness constancy. Milner & Goodale — two visual streams What it claims: the visual cortex splits into two functionally distinct pathways. The ventral stream ("what" / vision-for-perception) runs to the temporal lobe and supports conscious recognition and identification. The dorsal stream ("where / how" / vision-for-action) runs to the parietal lobe and guides visually controlled action online. Key evidence — patient DF: DF had ventral-stream damage (visual-form agnosia from carbon-monoxide poisoning). She could not report the orientation of a slot, yet she could post a card through it accurately — her action system "knew" what her perception system could not. The mirror-image patient (optic ataxia, dorsal damage) can describe an object but mis-reaches for it. That is a double dissociation of perception and action. Ventral vs dorsal: Ventral = "What" (temporal lobe, conscious recognition; DF's damaged stream). Dorsal = "Where/How" (parietal lobe, guiding action; optic-ataxia patients). DF can act on what she cannot consciously perceive — remember "post the card she can't describe." Recap — perception. Gregory (top-down, hypotheses, illusions) vs Gibson (bottom-up, affordances, optic array). David Marr builds primal → 2½-D → 3-D, analysed at computational/algorithmic/implementational levels. Gestalt = proximity, similarity, closure, continuity, common fate, Prägnanz. Depth = binocular (disparity, convergence) + monocular/pictorial. Milner & Goodale: ventral "what" vs dorsal "where/how", patient DF dissociates them. 3. Object & face recognition How do we go from a 2-D retinal pattern to "that's a cup" or "that's my brother" despite changes in size, angle and lighting? The chapter runs from crude template matching to Irving Biederman's geons, then to a dedicated face model. Template theory What it claims: recognition is matching the input to a stored whole-pattern template ; the best match wins. Fatal flaw: it needs a separate template for every size, orientation, font and partial view of every object — combinatorially impossible. Normalisation (rescaling/rotating before matching) only partly rescues it. This failure motivated feature theories. Feature theory — Pandemonium (Selfridge) What it claims: recognition proceeds by detecting component features rather than whole templates. Selfridge's Pandemonium model is the classic metaphor: layers of "demons" — image demons register the raw input, feature demons shout when their feature is present, cognitive demons shout louder the more of their features are detected, and a decision demon picks the loudest. Support: we confuse letters that share features (E↔F), and visual search is harder among similar-featured distractors. Limit: ignores context and the spatial relations between features (a face is not just two eyes + a nose in any arrangement). Biederman — recognition-by-components (geons) What it claims: objects are recognised by decomposing them into a small alphabet of basic 3-D volumetric primitives called geons (geometric ions — cylinders, cones, blocks, wedges; about 36 of them). Because geons are defined by non-accidental properties (features like straight vs curved edges that stay constant across most viewpoints), recognition is largely view-invariant : as long as the key geons and their arrangement are visible, you recognise the object from many angles. Builds on David Marr & Keith Nishihara's object-centred (viewpoint-independent) representation idea. Support: objects become hard to recognise precisely when degradation hides geon junctions; recognition survives degradation that spares them. Limit: recognition is not perfectly view-invariant (some views are reliably faster), and it explains category-level ("a chair") far better than specific-instance (" my chair") recognition. Bruce & Young — model of face recognition What it claims: face recognition runs through a sequence of stages with separable routes. Faces first undergo structural encoding (building a description of the face). For familiar faces this feeds Face Recognition Units (FRUs) — one per known face, signalling "this face is familiar." An activated FRU triggers the Person Identity Node (PIN) , which stores semantic/biographical info (their job, where you know them from). Only after the PIN can you retrieve the name , via a separate name-generation store. Key prediction and evidence: because the name comes last and through its own route, you can feel a face is familiar and recall facts about the person yet be unable to retrieve the name — but you never get the reverse (a name without familiarity). Diary studies of everyday recognition errors confirm exactly this asymmetry. Expression analysis and lip-reading run in parallel separate routes, which is why some patients lose identity recognition but still read emotion, or vice versa. Prosopagnosia & the FFA What it claims/observes: prosopagnosia is a selective inability to recognise faces despite largely intact object recognition and intact vision — patients may identify people only by voice, gait or a distinctive feature. It is associated with damage to the fusiform face area (FFA) in the ventral temporal cortex, a region that responds preferentially to faces. The double dissociation between prosopagnosia (faces lost, objects spared) and object agnosia (objects lost, faces relatively spared) supports the idea that face processing is at least partly special / domain-specific . Apperceptive vs associative agnosia (Lissauer) What it claims: visual agnosia is failure to recognise objects despite adequate vision, and Lissauer split it in two by where the breakdown is. Apperceptive agnosia = the percept itself cannot be formed; the patient cannot copy or match a drawing. Associative agnosia = the percept is built fine (the patient can copy the drawing accurately) but it cannot be linked to stored meaning, so they still cannot name it or say what it is for. Apperceptive vs associative agnosia: apperceptive can't copy the drawing (perception is broken); associative can copy it faithfully but still can't say what it is (perception intact, meaning lost). The copying test is the dividing line. Lissauer = "perception lost" vs "meaning lost." Recap — recognition. Template (rigid, fails on variation) → feature/Pandemonium (Oliver Selfridge's demons, ignores relations) → Irving Biederman's geons (view-invariant volumetric parts, builds on David Marr & Keith Nishihara). Faces: Bruce & Young structural encoding → FRU → PIN → name (name is last, hence familiarity-without-name but never the reverse). Prosopagnosia/FFA = faces lost specifically. Agnosia: apperceptive (can't copy) vs associative (can copy, can't name). 4. Attention Attention is "selection under limited capacity." The historic debate is where in processing the bottleneck sits — early (before meaning) or late (at response). The tool that built the debate is dichotic listening : different messages to each ear, and the listener "shadows" (repeats aloud) one. Broadbent — filter (early-selection) theory What it claims: there is a single limited-capacity channel preceded by a filter that selects one input on the basis of physical features (which ear, pitch) before meaning is analysed. The unattended channel is blocked. Key evidence: in dichotic split-span studies, people recalled by ear rather than chronological order, fitting channel-by-channel selection. The finding that broke it: listeners often noticed their own name on the unattended ear (Neville Moray's cocktail-party result) and could switch ears to follow meaning — impossible if the filter blocks meaning entirely. Treisman — attenuation theory What it claims: the filter does not block the unattended channel, it turns it down (attenuates) . Attenuated input is still analysed, but only items with low thresholds — your name, danger words, contextually expected words — get through. This is the cocktail-party account: most background talk is filtered, but salient input breaks through. Status: early selection but leaky ; explains the own-name effect that sinks strict Broadbent while keeping selection early. Deutsch & Norman — late-selection theory What it claims: all inputs are fully processed for meaning, and selection happens late — at the response/awareness stage — based on relevance. Deutsch & Deutsch proposed it; Norman refined it (selection by pertinence). Tension: full semantic analysis of everything is metabolically expensive, and most evidence favours an early-but-flexible bottleneck (Anne Treisman), so late selection is generally seen as too strong. Kahneman — capacity / resource theory What it claims: instead of a fixed structural bottleneck, attention is a limited pool of mental effort/resources flexibly allocated. Two tasks interfere when their combined demand exceeds the pool; effort rises with arousal and task difficulty (indexed by pupil dilation). This explains dual-task performance: easy tasks combine, hard ones compete. Refinement (Allport, Wickens): there may be multiple resource pools (e.g. separate verbal and spatial), so two tasks interfere more if they draw on the same pool. Posner spotlight + cueing; Eriksen zoom-lens What it claims: visual attention is like a movable spotlight that can be directed independently of the eyes (covert attention). Michael Posner's cueing paradigm: a cue points to a location, then a target appears either at the cued (valid) or another (invalid) location. Finding: RTs are faster after valid cues and slower after invalid ones (a "cost" for re-orienting) — direct evidence attention can move covertly to a location and speed processing there. Eriksen's zoom-lens adds that the spotlight's size is adjustable: it can be a narrow high-resolution beam or a wide low-resolution one, trading area for processing power. Treisman — Feature Integration Theory (FIT) What it claims: individual features (colour, orientation, size) are registered in parallel, pre-attentively , across the whole field on separate "feature maps." Focused attention is then the "glue" that binds features at a location into a single object. Key evidence: (1) Pop-out vs serial search — a target defined by a single feature (a red bar among green) "pops out" with search time flat regardless of set size (parallel), whereas a target defined by a conjunction of features (a red vertical among red horizontals and green verticals) requires slow item-by-item search rising with set size (serial). (2) Illusory conjunctions — when attention is overloaded or divided, people wrongly recombine features across objects (report a "red X" when shown a red O and a green X), proving features are coded separately before binding. Inattentional & change blindness Inattentional blindness (Simons & Chabris): when attention is engaged elsewhere (counting basketball passes), people fail to see a salient unexpected event — the person in the gorilla suit walking through. Change blindness (Rensink): with a brief disruption (a flicker or "mudsplash") between two scenes, people fail to notice large changes to the scene. Both show that without attention there is strikingly little conscious perception, and that we do not hold a rich detailed picture of the world in mind. Automatic vs controlled processing (Shiffrin & Schneider) + Stroop What it claims: with practice, controlled processing (slow, serial, effortful, capacity-limited, flexible) becomes automatic (fast, parallel, effortless, capacity-free, hard to suppress). Evidence: Schneider & Richard Shiffrin's consistent-mapping search becomes automatic and set-size-independent with practice, whereas varied-mapping search stays controlled. The Stroop effect is the showcase of unavoidable automaticity: naming the ink colour of a colour word ("RED" printed in blue) is slowed because reading the word is automatic and intrudes on the controlled colour-naming task. Early vs late selection: Broadbent filters before meaning and blocks the rest (early, all-or-none). Treisman attenuates rather than blocks, so salient meaning leaks through (early but leaky). Deutsch-Norman processes everything for meaning and selects at response (late). The own-name / cocktail-party finding kills strict Donald Broadbent and best fits Anne Treisman. Spotlight vs zoom-lens vs FIT: Michael Posner's spotlight = attention moves to a location (cueing costs/benefits). Eriksen's zoom-lens = the spotlight changes size (area vs resolution trade-off). Treisman's FIT = attention binds features into objects (pop-out vs serial search, illusory conjunctions). Don't mix the "where" of attention (spotlight) with the "binding" job (FIT). Recap — attention. Bottleneck debate: Donald Broadbent (early, blocks) → Anne Treisman (early, attenuates, own-name leaks) → Deutsch-Norman (late, by pertinence) → Daniel Kahneman (capacity/effort, no fixed bottleneck). Space: Posner spotlight (cueing), Eriksen zoom-lens. Binding: Treisman's FIT (parallel feature maps + attention as glue; pop-out vs serial; illusory conjunctions). Limits of attention: inattentional (gorilla) and change blindness. Practice: controlled → automatic; Stroop = automatic reading intruding. 5. Short-term & working memory The chapter moves from the structural "three boxes" model to Alan Baddeley & Graham Hitch's active, multi-component working memory, and ends with the levels-of-processing (Fergus Craik and Robert Lockhart, 1972) critique. Atkinson & Shiffrin — multi-store (modal) model What it claims: memory is three structural stores in series — sensory register → short-term store (STS) → long-term store (LTS) — linked by control processes. Attention moves info from sensory to STM; rehearsal maintains it in STM and transfers it to LTM. STM is limited in capacity and duration; LTM is effectively unlimited and permanent. Key evidence — the serial-position curve: in free recall, the first items ( primacy ) and last items ( recency ) are recalled best. Primacy reflects extra rehearsal into LTM; recency reflects items still in STM. Crucially they dissociate: a delay with a distractor task wipes out recency (STM emptied) but leaves primacy intact; a faster presentation rate hurts primacy (less rehearsal) but not recency. Two variables, two ends → two stores. Patient evidence (H.M.: good STM, no new LTM; K.F.: poor STM, normal LTM) gives the double dissociation. Limit: treats STM as a single passive store and rehearsal as the only route to LTM — both wrong. Sperling — iconic memory (and echoic) What it claims: there is a brief, high-capacity sensory store for vision ( iconic memory ). The experiment: George Sperling flashed a 3×4 grid of letters for 50 ms. In whole report people recalled only ~4–5 letters. In partial report , a tone (high/medium/low) cued which row to report after the display vanished; people then reported almost any cued row in full. Since they could report whichever row was cued, all ~9–12 letters were briefly available — capacity is large. As the cue was delayed, performance fell to whole-report levels by ~1 second, showing iconic memory decays in about ½ second . The auditory equivalent, echoic memory , lasts longer (~2–4 s). Miller — magic number 7 ± 2 & chunking What it claims: immediate (short-term) memory span is about 7 ± 2 items . The key insight is that the limit is set by the number of chunks , not raw items: by recoding ("HBOFBICIA" → "HBO FBI CIA") you pack more information into the same number of slots, so chunking expands effective capacity. (Later work, e.g. Cowan, argues the true limit is closer to ~4 chunks once rehearsal is controlled.) Baddeley & Hitch — working memory model What it claims: STM is not one passive store but an active multi-component system that holds and manipulates information. Components: Central executive — attentional controller; allocates resources, switches and coordinates tasks. Limited capacity, modality-free; the least specified part. Phonological loop — verbal/acoustic store with two parts: the phonological store ("inner ear," holds speech-based info for ~2 s) and the articulatory rehearsal process ("inner voice," refreshes it by subvocal rehearsal). Visuospatial sketchpad — holds and manipulates visual and spatial information ("inner eye"). Episodic buffer (added 2000) — limited store that binds information from the loop, sketchpad and LTM into a single multimodal episode, and is the interface to long-term memory. Evidence for the phonological loop: (1) Word-length effect — memory span is worse for longer words because they take longer to rehearse (the loop holds about 2 s of speech). (2) Phonological-similarity effect — lists of similar-sounding letters (B, P, T, V) are recalled worse than dissimilar ones, showing the store is acoustic/phonological. (3) Articulatory suppression — repeating "the, the, the" ties up the rehearsal process and abolishes both the word-length effect and (for visually presented items) the phonological-similarity effect. Evidence for separate subsystems: people can do a verbal task and a visuospatial task at the same time with little interference, but two verbal (or two spatial) tasks compete — the dual-task logic that demands two specialised stores. Craik & Lockhart — levels of processing What it claims: retention depends not on which "store" or how long you rehearse, but on the depth of processing at encoding. Shallow processing of physical features (is it capital letters?) or sound (does it rhyme?) gives poor memory; deep, semantic processing (does it fit this sentence? what does it mean?) gives strong memory. Memory is a by-product of how you processed the item. Evidence: Fergus Craik & Endel Tulving's orienting-task studies — deeper (semantic) judgements produced far better later recognition than shallow ones, even though semantic processing felt no "harder." Distinguishes maintenance rehearsal (mere repetition, little benefit) from elaborative rehearsal (linking to meaning, big benefit). Limit: "depth" is hard to define independently of the memory it predicts (circularity). Multi-store vs working memory: Atkinson-Shiffrin's STM is a single passive store ; Baddeley-Hitch splits it into active components doing different jobs. The decisive evidence is dual-task: verbal + visuospatial can run together (different subsystems) but two verbal tasks collide (same subsystem) — impossible for a single STM box. Iconic (Sperling) vs working memory: iconic memory is a pre-attentive sensory store, very large, lasts ~½ s, decays automatically. STM/WM is post-attentive, ~7 chunks (or ~4), lasts ~15–30 s without rehearsal, and (in WM) manipulates info. Don't call the partial-report store "short-term memory." Recap — STM/WM. Atkinson-Shiffrin: sensory → STM → LTM, supported by the serial-position curve (recency = STM, primacy = LTM, and they dissociate). George Sperling's partial report: iconic memory is large but ~½ s. Miller: 7±2 chunks, expandable by chunking. Baddeley-Hitch WM: central executive + phonological loop (word-length, phonological-similarity, articulatory suppression) + visuospatial sketchpad + episodic buffer. Craik & Robert Lockhart: depth of processing beats rehearsal time; elaborative > maintenance. 6. Long-term memory LTM is not one thing. The chapter carves it into systems (declarative vs procedural; episodic vs semantic), explains how retrieval depends on cues, and grounds the divisions in amnesia.
