Cohen & Squire — declarative vs procedural (non-declarative) What it claims: the deepest split is between declarative memory (explicit, conscious, "knowing that " — facts and events, depends on the medial temporal lobe/hippocampus) and procedural / non-declarative memory (implicit, "knowing how " — skills, conditioning, priming, depends on other systems like the basal ganglia and cerebellum). Evidence: amnesics like H.M. cannot form new declarative memories yet can learn new motor skills (mirror-drawing) and show priming — improving across days while denying they ever did the task. That dissociation proves the two are separate systems. Tulving — episodic vs semantic What it claims: within declarative memory, episodic memory stores personally experienced events tied to a time and place ("my last birthday"), accompanied by mental "time travel" and conscious recollection. Semantic memory stores general facts and knowledge stripped of their learning context ("Paris is the capital of France"). Evidence: in some amnesics episodic memory is devastated while semantic knowledge is relatively preserved (and developmental amnesics can acquire semantic facts despite poor episodic memory) — a dissociation supporting two systems. Tulving & Thomson — encoding specificity What it claims: retrieval succeeds to the extent that cues present at recall match the cues encoded at the time of learning — memory is about the match between encoding and retrieval, not the strength of the trace alone. This is the umbrella for: context-dependent memory (Godden & Alan Baddeley's divers recalled word lists best when tested in the same environment — land or underwater — as they learned them) and state-dependent memory (recall is better when your internal state, e.g. mood or sobriety, matches learning). It also explains why recognition can sometimes fail where recall succeeds (recognition failure of recallable words). Ebbinghaus — the forgetting curve What it did: Hermann Ebbinghaus tested himself on lists of nonsense syllables (to control for prior meaning) and measured the savings method (how much faster relearning is than original learning). Finding: the forgetting curve — forgetting is steep at first then levels off (most loss happens soon after learning, then the rate slows). He also documented the spacing benefit of distributed practice. Bartlett — reconstructive memory & schemas What it claims: remembering is not replay but reconstruction guided by schemas (organised prior knowledge). The study — "War of the Ghosts": Frederic Bartlett had English participants read an unfamiliar Native American folk tale, then recall it repeatedly over time. Recall became shorter, more coherent, and distorted toward the participants' own cultural expectations — unfamiliar/supernatural elements were dropped or "rationalised" (e.g. "canoe" became "boat"). This showed memory actively reshapes material to fit existing schemas. Caveat the exam may probe: Bartlett's methods were loosely controlled, but the reconstructive principle is well established and underlies Elizabeth Loftus's later eyewitness work. Consolidation What it claims: a new memory is initially fragile and becomes stable over time through consolidation ; disruption (e.g. a head injury, ECT) shortly after learning erases the unconsolidated trace, which is why retrograde amnesia is typically worse for recent memories (Ribot's gradient). The hippocampus binds the memory at first; over time (systems consolidation) the memory becomes increasingly independent of the hippocampus and reliant on the neocortex. Sleep aids consolidation. Patient H.M. (Scoville & Milner) What happened: to treat severe epilepsy, surgeon William Scoville removed H.M.'s medial temporal lobes bilaterally , including most of the hippocampus . The result: dense anterograde amnesia — he could not form new long-term declarative memories — with intact short-term memory (normal digit span), intact procedural learning (he improved at mirror-drawing across days while denying he had ever done it), and largely preserved older memories. Why it matters: H.M. is the founding case that (1) STM and LTM are separate systems, (2) the hippocampus is critical for forming new declarative memories but not for STM or for retrieving old ones, and (3) declarative and procedural memory are dissociable. Episodic vs semantic: if the fact is tied to when/where you learned it (an event with mental time-travel), it's episodic; if it's free-floating general knowledge, it's semantic. Amnesics often lose episodic while semantic survives. Anterograde vs retrograde amnesia: antero = can't form new memories after the injury (H.M.); retro = lost memories from before the injury. Mnemonic: antero = "ahead/forward in time"; retro = "back in time." H.M.'s defining deficit is anterograde. Recap — LTM. Declarative (knowing that, hippocampal) vs procedural (knowing how) — dissociated in H.M. Within declarative: episodic (events, time/place) vs semantic (facts), Endel Tulving. Retrieval = encoding-specificity match (context/state-dependent; Godden & Baddeley divers). Ebbinghaus: nonsense syllables, savings, steep-then-flat forgetting curve. Frederic Bartlett: reconstructive, schema-driven, War of the Ghosts. Consolidation stabilises traces (hippocampus → neocortex). H.M. (Scoville & Milner): bilateral hippocampal loss → anterograde amnesia, intact STM and skills. 7. Forgetting & everyday memory Why memories fail, and how memory works outside the lab. The exam wants the named mechanisms and Elizabeth Loftus's eyewitness findings. Decay vs interference Decay theory: the memory trace simply fades with time if not used — a passive process. Hard to test cleanly because time always lets other activity in. Interference theory (better supported for LTM): forgetting is caused by competition between memories. Proactive interference = old learning disrupts new (your old phone number intrudes on the new one). Retroactive interference = new learning disrupts old (learning French makes you lose Spanish). Mnemonic: PRO = prior interferes forward ; RETRO = recent reaches back . Cue-dependent forgetting & TOT What it claims (Endel Tulving): often the trace is intact but the right retrieval cue is missing — "availability vs accessibility." Provide the cue and the memory returns, which is why recognition often beats free recall. The tip-of-the-tongue (TOT; Roger Brown and David McNeill, 1966) state is the vivid case: you can report the first letter, number of syllables and similar-sounding words, proving the memory is there but not fully accessible. Repression / motivated forgetting What it claims (Sigmund Freud): threatening or anxiety-laden memories are actively pushed out of conscious awareness. Highly controversial and hard to demonstrate experimentally; mentioned for completeness and because it underlies the "recovered memory" debate. Loftus — misinformation, leading questions, weapon focus What it claims: memory is reconstructive and post-event information can rewrite it . The car-crash study (Elizabeth Loftus & John Palmer): participants watched a film of a car accident, then were asked how fast the cars were going when they " smashed / collided / bumped / hit / contacted " each other. The single verb changed the speed estimate — "smashed" produced the highest estimates — and a week later those given "smashed" were more likely to falsely "remember" broken glass that was never in the film. The misinformation effect: misleading post-event details get incorporated into the memory. Weapon focus: when a weapon is present, attention narrows onto it, worsening memory for other details such as the culprit's face. Together these undermine eyewitness reliability. Brown & Kulik — flashbulb memory What it claims: shocking, emotionally significant public events create vivid, detailed, confidently held memories of the moment one heard the news — as if a "flashbulb" captured the scene. The catch the exam wants: flashbulb memories feel highly accurate and are held with great confidence, but research (e.g. on people's memories of disasters) shows they decay and distort like ordinary memories — confidence is not accuracy. Prospective memory What it claims: prospective memory is remembering to perform an intended action in the future (take the pill, post the letter), as opposed to retrospective memory (recalling past information). It splits into event-based (do it when a cue occurs — "give Mum the message when you see her") and time-based (do it at a time — "call at 3pm"); time-based is harder because there is no external cue, so it relies more on self-initiated monitoring. Proactive vs retroactive interference: PROactive — prior (old) learning interferes with new. RETROactive — recent (new) learning interferes with old, reaching back . Direction of the arrow is the trick. NIMHANS tests harder — prospective memory. Expect the event- vs time-based split, the claim that time-based is harder (no external cue, needs self-initiated retrieval), and that prospective memory has a "remember to remember" component absent from retrospective memory. May be linked clinically to frontal-lobe/executive function and to everyday-memory failures in patients. Recap — forgetting. Decay (passive fading, weakly supported) vs interference (proactive = old→new, retroactive = new→old). Cue-dependent/TOT = it's there but inaccessible (Endel Tulving). Repression = Sigmund Freud, controversial. Elizabeth Loftus: misinformation, leading-verb car-crash study (broken glass), weapon focus. Roger Brown & James Kulik flashbulb = vivid + confident but not actually accurate. Prospective memory: event- vs time-based, time-based harder. 8. Concepts & knowledge representation How are categories ("bird," "furniture") stored? The progression: rigid definitions fail, so we move to prototypes, then exemplars, and to network theories of how concepts connect. Defining-attribute (classical) view What it claims: a concept is defined by a set of necessary and sufficient features — anything with all of them is a member, anything missing one is not, and all members are equal. Why it fails: most natural categories have fuzzy boundaries and no clean defining set (Wittgenstein's "game"), and people reliably rate some members as more typical than others (a robin is a "better" bird than a penguin) — which a defining-feature view cannot allow, since membership is all-or-none. Rosch — prototype theory What it claims: categories are organised around a prototype — an abstract best/average example summarising the central tendency of the category. Membership is graded by similarity to the prototype , which directly explains typicality effects (typical members are categorised faster and named first). Eleanor Rosch also identified the basic level (e.g. "dog") as the most informative, fastest-named, first-learned level — more useful than the superordinate ("animal") or subordinate ("collie"). Evidence: typicality predicts verification speed, production frequency and learning order. Medin & Schaffer — exemplar theory What it claims: we do not abstract a single prototype; instead we store many specific exemplars (remembered instances) and categorise a new item by its similarity to those stored instances. Advantage over prototypes: exemplar models retain information about variability and atypical members, and account for context and frequency effects that a single averaged prototype loses. Collins & Quillian — hierarchical semantic network What it claims: concepts are nodes in a hierarchy (canary → bird → animal) and properties are stored at the highest level they apply to — cognitive economy ("has skin" stored once at "animal," not repeated at every animal). Prediction & evidence: sentence-verification time should increase with the distance travelled in the hierarchy — "A canary can sing" (0 levels) is verified faster than "A canary can fly" (1 level) faster than "A canary has skin" (2 levels). Reaction times broadly confirmed this. Problems: the typicality effect ("A robin is a bird" verified faster than "A penguin is a bird," same distance) and familiarity effects break the strict-distance prediction. Collins & Loftus — spreading activation What it claims: revised the network to drop the strict hierarchy: concepts are linked by semantic relatedness , with shorter/stronger links between more related concepts. Activating one concept causes activation to spread along links to related concepts, pre-activating them. Evidence — semantic priming: people verify "nurse" faster after seeing the related word "doctor" than after an unrelated word, because "doctor" pre-activated "nurse." This handles typicality and relatedness effects the rigid hierarchy could not. Schema & script (Bartlett; Schank & Abelson) What it claims: larger bodies of knowledge are organised as schemas (structured packets of expectations about objects/situations) that guide comprehension, inference and memory. A script (Schank & Abelson) is a schema for a stereotyped event sequence — the restaurant script (enter → seated → order → eat → pay → leave). Evidence: people falsely "recall" script-consistent actions that were never stated (you infer they paid the bill), and read script-typical sentences faster — showing scripts fill gaps with default inferences. Prototype vs exemplar: prototype = one abstracted average per category, judged by similarity to the ideal. Exemplar = many stored individual instances , judged by similarity to remembered cases. "Compare to the ideal bird" = prototype (Eleanor Rosch); "compare to all the actual birds I've seen" = exemplar (Medin & Schaffer). Allan Collins & Ross Quillian vs Collins & Elizabeth Loftus: Quillian = strict hierarchy + cognitive economy, predicts verification time by distance (and is broken by typicality). Loftus = spreading activation over a relatedness web, predicts semantic priming . Same first author "Collins," very different models. Recap — knowledge. Classical defining-attribute view fails (fuzzy boundaries, typicality). Eleanor Rosch: prototypes + typicality + basic level. Medin & Schaffer: exemplars (stored instances, keep variability). Networks: Allan Collins & Ross Quillian hierarchy + cognitive economy + verification-by-distance; Collins & Loftus spreading activation + semantic priming. Schemas/scripts (Schank & Abelson restaurant script) fill gaps with default inferences. 9. Language Language covers acquisition, comprehension (parsing, reading, listening), production, and the brain basis. Each subtopic has a signature model and a signature finding. Sapir-Whorf — linguistic relativity What it claims: the language you speak shapes the way you think. Strong form (linguistic determinism): language determines thought and limits what you can conceive — widely rejected (people think about concepts they have no single word for). Weak form (linguistic relativity): language influences habitual thought and perception — has some support (e.g. colour-term boundaries can shift colour discrimination; grammatical gender nudges object descriptions). Chomsky vs Skinner — language acquisition What it claims: against B. F. Skinner's behaviourist account (language learned by imitation and reinforcement), Noam Chomsky argued grammar is too complex and acquired too fast, on too little/imperfect input, to be learned by reinforcement — the "poverty of the stimulus." He proposed an innate Language Acquisition Device (LAD) embodying a Universal Grammar common to all languages. He distinguished surface structure (the actual words/syntax of a sentence) from deep structure (its underlying meaning), linked by transformational rules — which is why one surface form can be ambiguous (two deep structures) and two different surface forms can share a meaning. Frazier — garden-path model (parsing) What it claims: syntactic parsing is initially syntax-first and serial : we commit to one structure using simple principles such as minimal attachment (build the simplest tree, fewest nodes) and late closure (attach new words to the current phrase). When that first parse turns out wrong we have to reanalyse — the "garden path." Classic sentence: "The horse raced past the barn fell" — we read "raced" as the main verb and stumble at "fell," which forces reinterpretation ("the horse [that was] raced past the barn fell"). Reading-time spikes at the disambiguating word are the evidence. Coltheart — dual-route model of reading What it claims: reading aloud uses two routes from print to sound. The lexical (direct) route looks the whole word up in the mental lexicon — needed for irregular words ("yacht," "pint") that don't follow rules. The non-lexical / grapheme-phoneme (sub-lexical) route applies spelling-to-sound rules — needed for novel words and non-words ("glorp"). The clinching dissociation in acquired dyslexia: surface dyslexia = lexical route damaged, so irregular words are "regularised" (read "pint" to rhyme with "mint") but non-words are fine. Phonological dyslexia = grapheme-phoneme route damaged, so familiar words are read but non-words cannot be sounded out. The double dissociation maps cleanly onto the two routes. Levelt — speech production What it claims: producing speech runs through ordered stages: conceptualisation (deciding the message) → formulation (selecting words — lemma /meaning then lexeme /sound — and building syntax) → articulation (motor output), with a self-monitoring loop. Evidence — speech errors: systematic slips reveal the stages — Spoonerisms ("dear old queen" → "queer old dean") show sound-level exchange at formulation, while word-substitution and "freudian slip" errors implicate the lemma-selection stage. The tip-of-the-tongue (Roger Brown and David McNeill, 1966) state shows lemma retrieved but lexeme (sound) not yet available. McGurk effect & cohort model (perception) Harry McGurk & John MacDonald: speech perception is multimodal — seeing lips say "ga" while hearing "ba" makes you perceive "da," a fusion of the two. Vision overrides audition, proving we integrate seen and heard speech automatically. Marslen-Wilson's cohort model: on hearing a word's onset, all words consistent with it are activated (the "cohort"); as more sound arrives, candidates are eliminated until one remains at the uniqueness point . Context can further narrow the cohort, which is why we recognise spoken words remarkably early. Aphasias — Broca, Wernicke, conduction Broca's aphasia (Paul Broca): non-fluent , effortful, halting, agrammatic speech (function words dropped), with comprehension relatively spared. Lesion: left frontal lobe (Broca's area). Wernicke's aphasia (Carl Wernicke): fluent but empty, meaningless " word salad " with neologisms and paraphasias, and poor comprehension ; patients often unaware of the deficit. Lesion: left posterior temporal lobe (Wernicke's area). Conduction aphasia: fluent speech and good comprehension but a striking inability to repeat , from damage to the arcuate fasciculus connecting the two areas. Broca vs Wernicke: Broca = Broken speech — can't produce fluently but understands (frontal). Wernicke = fluent nonsense — speaks easily but can't comprehend (temporal). Conduction = can't repeat (arcuate fasciculus). Mnemonic: Broca/Broken/front; Wernicke/Word-salad/back. Surface vs phonological dyslexia: surface = lexical route gone → trips on irregular words (regularises "pint"), non-words OK. Phonological = grapheme-phoneme route gone → trips on non-words , real words OK. Map each dyslexia to the route it lost. Recap — language. Sapir-Whorf: strong (determinism) rejected, weak (relativity) some support. Chomsky LAD/Universal Grammar + deep/surface structure vs B. F. Skinner's reinforcement. Frazier garden-path: syntax-first, minimal attachment, "horse raced past the barn fell." Coltheart dual-route: lexical (irregular words, surface dyslexia) vs grapheme-phoneme (non-words, phonological dyslexia). Levelt: conceptualise → formulate → articulate, speech errors reveal stages. McGurk = multimodal; Marslen-Wilson cohort = onset activates many, narrows to uniqueness point. Aphasias: Broca (frontal, non-fluent), Wernicke (temporal, fluent nonsense), conduction (arcuate, can't repeat). 10. Problem solving & expertise Two traditions meet here: the Gestalt focus on insight and the obstacles to it, and the information-processing focus on search through a problem space (Allen Newell & Herbert Simon), plus what makes experts expert. Gestalt insight & restructuring (Köhler, Sultan) What it claims: some problems are solved not by gradual search but by a sudden restructuring of how the problem is represented — the " aha " of insight . Evidence: Wolfgang Köhler's chimpanzee Sultan suddenly stacked boxes / joined two sticks to reach a banana after apparent contemplation, rather than by trial-and-error, suggesting a perceptual reorganisation of the situation. Duncker — functional fixedness What it claims: a barrier to insight is functional fixedness — the tendency to see an object only in terms of its usual function. The candle problem: given a candle, a box of tacks and matches, people struggle to mount the candle on the wall because they see the box as a container , not as a potential shelf ; the solution is to empty the box, tack it to the wall, and stand the candle on it. People solve it faster when the box is presented empty (its "container" function de-emphasised). Luchins — mental set (Einstellung) What it claims: a mental set (Einstellung) is the tendency to keep using a previously successful strategy even when a simpler one is available. The water-jar task: after solving several problems with the same multi-step formula, participants kept applying it to later problems that had a far simpler solution, and some failed problems solvable only the simple way. Prior success entrenches a rigid approach. Newell & Simon — means-ends analysis, problem space, GPS What it claims: problem solving is search through a problem space — the set of all states (start, goal, intermediate) and the operators that move between them. Because the space is huge, we use heuristics , chiefly means-ends analysis : note the difference between the current state and the goal, find an operator that reduces it, and if that operator can't be applied yet, set a subgoal to enable it. Implemented in their General Problem Solver (GPS) program. Evidence: verbal protocols ("think-aloud") on the Tower of Hanoi and similar well-defined puzzles matched the means-ends, subgoal-setting account. Well- vs ill-defined problems Well-defined problems have a clearly specified start state, goal state and operators (chess, Tower of Hanoi) — ideal for the problem-space approach. Ill-defined problems lack one or more of these ("write a good essay," "be happy"); most real-world problems are ill-defined, which is a limit on the laboratory puzzle tradition. Expertise & chunking (de Groot; Chase & Simon) What it claims: expert advantage is knowledge-based , not raw memory. The chess studies: de Groot found masters and novices searched similar numbers of moves, but masters perceived the board in better-organised units. Chase & Simon then showed that, briefly shown a real game position, masters recall the pieces far better than novices — but only for meaningful positions . For random arrangements the master's advantage vanishes. Conclusion: experts don't have bigger memories; they encode the board as a few familiar chunks (and templates), which only helps when the configuration is meaningful. Gick & Holyoak — analogical transfer What it claims: we can solve a new problem by mapping the solution from a structurally similar one ( analogical transfer ). The radiation–fortress study: participants who had read the fortress story (a general splits his army to converge on a fort from many roads) were far more likely to solve Karl Duncker's radiation problem (use multiple weak rays converging on a tumour) — but usually only when hinted to use the story. The key finding: spontaneous transfer is poor because people are misled by surface similarity and miss the deeper structural analogy; an explicit cue, or seeing multiple analogues, helps them abstract the shared schema. Functional fixedness vs mental set: functional fixedness (Karl Duncker) = stuck on an object's usual use (the box is "just a box"). Mental set / Einstellung (Luchins) = stuck on a procedure that used to work (keep using the long water-jar formula). Object vs method. Recap — problem solving. Gestalt insight/restructuring (Köhler's Sultan). Blocks to insight: Duncker functional fixedness (candle/box), Luchins mental set (water-jar). Allen Newell & Herbert Simon: problem space + operators, means-ends analysis + subgoals, GPS, Tower of Hanoi. Well- vs ill-defined problems. Expertise = chunks not memory (de Groot; Chase & Simon — masters beat novices only on real, not random, boards). Gick & Holyoak: analogical transfer is poor without a hint because surface beats structure (radiation/fortress). 11. Judgement & decision making Amos Tversky & Daniel Kahneman showed that people don't compute probabilities normatively; they use fast heuristics that usually work but produce systematic biases . Then prospect theory and dual-process theory explain choice under risk and the two "minds" behind it. The three heuristics (Tversky & Kahneman) Availability: judge how likely/frequent something is by how easily examples come to mind . Because vivid, recent or dramatic events come to mind easily, people overestimate plane crashes, shark attacks and homicide relative to commoner but duller risks. Representativeness: judge probability by how much something resembles the stereotype/prototype of the category, ignoring base rates and sample size. Anchoring & adjustment: an initial value (the anchor) biases the final estimate because adjustment from it is insufficient — e.g. estimates of a product (8×7×…×1 vs 1×2×…×8) differed by starting point, and arbitrary numbers (a spun wheel) shifted estimates of unrelated quantities. Base-rate neglect (the Tom W. / lawyer-engineer problem) What it shows: when given a personality sketch that sounds like an engineer, people judge "Tom W. is an engineer" as likely regardless of the stated base rate (whether the sample was 70 engineers/30 lawyers or the reverse). The representativeness of the description swamps the prior probability — a failure to combine evidence with base rates (Bayesian reasoning). Conjunction fallacy (the Linda problem) What it shows: given a sketch of Linda as a socially-conscious philosophy graduate, people judge " Linda is a bank teller and active in the feminist movement " as more probable than "Linda is a bank teller." That is logically impossible — a conjunction can never be more probable than one of its constituents. The cause is representativeness: the feminist-teller story resembles Linda better, and resemblance overrides probability. Prospect theory (Kahneman & Tversky) What it claims: people evaluate outcomes not as final wealth but as gains and losses relative to a reference point . The value function is S-shaped: concave for gains (risk-averse), convex for losses (risk-seeking to avoid a sure loss), and steeper for losses than gains — this is loss aversion ("losses loom larger than gains," roughly twice as much). Probabilities are also weighted non-linearly (small probabilities overweighted). This explains why the same objective outcome is chosen or rejected depending on framing. Framing effect (the Asian disease problem) What it shows: the identical choice flips with wording. When a disease programme is framed in terms of lives saved ("200 of 600 will be saved"), people choose the sure option (risk-averse for gains); when the same outcome is framed as deaths ("400 of 600 will die"), people choose the gamble (risk-seeking for losses). A direct demonstration of prospect theory's reference-dependence and loss aversion. Simon — bounded rationality & satisficing What it claims: real decision-makers have limited information, time and computational capacity, so they cannot optimise; they exercise bounded rationality and satisfice — search only until an option that is "good enough" (meets an aspiration level) is found, then stop, rather than evaluating every alternative for the optimum. Dual-process theory (System 1 / System 2) What it claims: two modes of thought. System 1 is fast, automatic, effortless, intuitive, parallel and emotional — the source of heuristics. System 2 is slow, controlled, effortful, analytic and rule-based, and can override System 1 when engaged. Many biases (Linda, base-rate neglect) arise because System 1's intuitive answer is accepted without System 2 checking it. Availability vs representativeness: availability = judging by how easily examples come to mind (overrate plane crashes, recent news). Representativeness = judging by how much it resembles the stereotype (Linda, Tom W.). The conjunction fallacy (Linda) and base-rate neglect (Tom W.) both stem from representativeness , not availability. Recap — judgement. Heuristics: availability (ease of recall), representativeness (resemblance → base-rate neglect Tom W. and conjunction fallacy Linda), anchoring & adjustment. Prospect theory: gains/losses from a reference point, S-shaped value function, loss aversion. Framing (Asian disease) flips choice between save/die wording. Simon: bounded rationality, satisficing (good enough). Dual-process: System 1 fast/intuitive vs System 2 slow/analytic. 12. Reasoning Reasoning splits into deductive (drawing certain conclusions from premises) and inductive (generalising probably from cases). The recurring theme is that content and context , not pure logic, drive human reasoning — and that we are biased toward confirming and toward believable conclusions. Deductive vs inductive Deductive reasoning moves from general premises to a logically certain conclusion (syllogisms, conditionals); if the premises are true and the form valid, the conclusion must be true. Inductive reasoning moves from specific observations to a probable generalisation; the conclusion can be well-supported but never guaranteed (the basis of science and everyday prediction). Wason — the selection task What it shows: given four cards showing, say, A, K, 4, 7 and the rule " if a card has a vowel on one side, it has an even number on the other ," people must say which cards to turn to test the rule. The logically correct answer is the vowel (A) and the odd number (7) — i.e. P and not-Q (turn the case that could falsify the rule). Most people fail the abstract version, typically picking A and 4 (a matching/confirmation bias). Content effect: with a familiar, deontic rule — "if you drink alcohol you must be over 18," cards "beer, coke, 22, 16" — performance leaps, because we readily check the beer-drinker and the 16-year-old. Concrete, real-world (especially permission) content unlocks correct logic. Wason — the 2-4-6 task & confirmation bias What it shows: told that "2, 4, 6" fits a rule the experimenter has in mind, participants must discover the rule by proposing their own number-triples and getting yes/no feedback. The actual rule is broad (" any three ascending numbers "), but people fixate on a narrow hypothesis (e.g. "even numbers ascending by 2") and test only triples that confirm it (8-10-12) rather than ones that could falsify it. This confirmation bias — seeking supporting rather than disconfirming evidence — leaves them announcing the wrong rule with confidence. Evans — belief bias What it shows: in syllogistic reasoning, people judge an argument's validity by whether they believe the conclusion rather than whether it logically follows. They accept invalid syllogisms with believable conclusions ("Some addictive things are not cigarettes" type errors) and reject valid ones with unbelievable conclusions . Belief in the conclusion overrides logical structure — a key piece of evidence that everyday reasoning is not formal logic. Johnson-Laird — mental models theory What it claims: we reason not by applying formal logical rules but by constructing mental models of the situations the premises describe, then reading off conclusions and (ideally) searching for counterexample models. Key prediction: reasoning errors and difficulty increase with the number of models a problem requires — problems needing only one model are easy; those needing several are error-prone because people fail to construct all of them (and tend to consider just one). Explains why some valid inferences are far harder than others of the same logical "type." Atmosphere effect; pragmatic reasoning schemas Atmosphere effect (Robert Woodworth & Saul Sells): in syllogisms, the "mood" of the premises biases the conclusion accepted — if premises contain "some," people favour a "some" conclusion; if they contain a negative, they favour a negative conclusion — regardless of validity. Pragmatic reasoning schemas (Cheng & Holyoak): rather than pure logic or mere familiarity, we reason using abstract but content-bound schemas such as permission ("to do X you must satisfy Y") and obligation . This neatly explains the selection-task content effect: the drinking-age version triggers the permission schema and so yields correct "P and not-Q" checking even though it is not a familiar everyday memory. Peter Wason's two tasks: the selection task (4 cards, P/not-Q) tests conditional/deductive logic and is solved by familiar/permission content. The 2-4-6 task tests hypothesis testing and exposes confirmation bias . Both are Wason — don't conflate them. Belief bias vs atmosphere effect: belief bias = judging by whether you believe the conclusion (Evans). Atmosphere effect = being swayed by the quantifiers/mood of the premises (some/all/no — Robert Woodworth & Saul Sells). Conclusion-believability vs premise-mood. Recap — reasoning. Deductive (certain) vs inductive (probable). Wason selection task: P and not-Q is correct, abstract fails, familiar/permission content succeeds. Wason 2-4-6: confirmation bias (seek confirming, not falsifying, triples). Evans belief bias: validity judged by conclusion believability. Johnson-Laird mental models: difficulty ↑ with number of models. Atmosphere effect (premise mood) and Cheng & Holyoak pragmatic schemas (permission/obligation explain the content effect). NIMHANS tests harder — embodied cognition. Beyond the classical "mind as computer" view, embodied (grounded) cognition holds that cognition is shaped by the body and its sensorimotor systems: abstract concepts are partly grounded in bodily/perceptual experience (understanding "grasp an idea" recruits motor representations), and thought is "for" action. Contrast it with the amodal, symbol-manipulation assumption of classical cognitivism. NIMHANS may pair this with the extended/situated-cognition idea that cognition uses the body and environment as part of the processing system. NIMHANS tests harder — metacognition. Metacognition = "thinking about thinking": knowledge and regulation of one's own cognitive processes (Flavell). It splits into metacognitive knowledge (what you know about your memory/strategies), monitoring (judgements of learning, feeling-of-knowing, the tip-of-the-tongue (Roger Brown and David McNeill, 1966) state as a metamemory signal) and control (deciding how long to study, when to stop). Expect links to study strategies, to frontal-lobe function, and to clinical insight (e.g. impaired metacognition in some disorders). ★ At-a-glance compare table The whole page compressed to one scan-able grid: each row is a model, its author, and its single most testable claim or finding. Know what was done and what was found . Patient H.M. (Scoville & Milner) Bilateral medial-temporal resection (incl. hippocampus) to treat epilepsy → dense anterograde amnesia, intact STM (normal digit span), intact procedural learning (mirror-drawing improves while he denies practising), older memories largely spared. Shows: STM ≠ LTM; hippocampus needed to form new declarative memories; declarative ≠ procedural. Sperling — partial report 3×4 letter grid flashed 50 ms. Whole report ≈ 4–5 letters; a post-display tone cueing one row → near-perfect for that row, so ~all 9–12 were briefly available. Delaying the cue collapses performance by ~1 s. Shows: iconic memory is high-capacity but decays in ~½ s. Dichotic listening (Cherry, Broadbent, Moray) Different messages to each ear; shadow one. Listeners notice physical changes (a tone, a switch to a different voice) on the unattended ear but little of its content — yet they detect their own name (cocktail-party effect). Shows: selection is early but leaky → supports Treisman over strict Donald Broadbent. Posner — spatial cueing A cue points to a location; target appears at the cued (valid) or another (invalid) spot. Valid cues speed RT, invalid cues slow it (a cost). Shows: attention can move covertly to a location, independent of the eyes (the spotlight). Loftus & Palmer — car crash Watch an accident film; the verb in "how fast when they ___?" (smashed/hit/contacted) raises or lowers the speed estimate; a week later "smashed" subjects falsely recall broken glass. Shows: misinformation/leading questions reshape memory — reconstructive, fallible eyewitness memory. Wason — selection task 4 cards + a conditional rule; correct answer is P and not-Q (the falsifying cards). Abstract version mostly failed (people pick P and Q); a familiar deontic version (drinking-age) is solved easily. Shows: reasoning depends on content/context, not pure logic (→ pragmatic schemas). Chase & Simon — chess expertise Briefly shown a board, masters recall piece positions far better than novices — but only for real game positions , not random ones. Shows: expertise is organised knowledge (chunks), not superior raw memory. Bartlett — War of the Ghosts English participants repeatedly recall an unfamiliar Native American tale; recall shortens and distorts toward their own cultural schemas (unfamiliar elements dropped/rationalised). Shows: memory is reconstructive and schema-driven. ★ Fast glossary (A–Z) Affordance — Gibson: an object's directly perceived possibilities for action. Anchoring — initial value biases an estimate (Amos Tversky & Daniel Kahneman). Anterograde amnesia — can't form new memories after injury (H.M.). Articulatory suppression — blocking rehearsal ("the the the"); abolishes word-length effect. Attenuation — Anne Treisman: unattended channel turned down, not off. Availability heuristic — judge frequency by ease of recall. Base-rate neglect — ignoring priors (Tom W.). Belief bias — judging validity by conclusion believability (Evans). Bottom-up — data/stimulus-driven processing. Bounded rationality — Simon: satisfice, not optimise. Change blindness — missing changes across a disruption (Rensink). Chunking — grouping items to expand STM (Miller). Cognitive economy — store a property once at the highest node (Allan Collins & Ross Quillian). Cohort model — Marslen-Wilson: onset activates candidates, narrow to uniqueness point. Confirmation bias — seeking confirming, not falsifying, evidence (2-4-6 task). Conjunction fallacy — A&B judged more probable than A (Linda). Connectionism / PDP — distributed, parallel networks that learn weights. Consolidation — stabilising of a new memory over time. Constructivist perception — Gregory: top-down, hypothesis-driven. Context-dependent memory — recall better when environment matches encoding (divers). Controlled processing — slow, serial, effortful (vs automatic). Declarative memory — explicit "knowing that" (facts/events). Deep structure — Noam Chomsky: underlying meaning of a sentence. Direct perception — Gibson: bottom-up, optic array. Double dissociation — opposite sparing in two patients → two systems. Echoic memory (named by Ulric Neisser, 1967) — auditory sensory store (~2–4 s). Encoding specificity — recall best when cues match encoding (Endel Tulving & Thomson). Episodic buffer — Alan Baddeley: multimodal binding store + LTM link. Episodic memory — events tied to time/place (Tulving). ERP — event-related potential; great temporal resolution. Exemplar theory — categorise by stored instances (Medin & Schaffer). FFA — fusiform face area; damage → prosopagnosia. Feature Integration Theory — Treisman: attention binds features into objects. Flashbulb memory — vivid, confident, not actually accurate (Roger Brown & James Kulik). Forgetting curve — steep then flat loss (Ebbinghaus). Framing effect (Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman, 1981) — wording (save vs die) flips choice (Asian disease). Functional fixedness — fixed on usual use of an object (Karl Duncker, candle). Garden-path — initial parse must be revised (Frazier). Geons — Biederman's ~36 volumetric primitives. Gestalt laws — proximity, similarity, closure, continuity, common fate, Prägnanz. Heuristic — fast, usually-good mental shortcut. Iconic memory — visual sensory store (~½ s; George Sperling). Illusory conjunction — wrongly combining features without attention. Inattentional blindness — missing the unexpected (gorilla; Simons & Chabris). Insight — sudden restructuring "aha" (Gestalt/Köhler). Interference — proactive (old→new) / retroactive (new→old). LAD — language acquisition device; innate grammar (Chomsky). Late selection — meaning fully processed, select at response (Deutsch-Norman). Levels of processing — depth, not duration, drives memory (Craik & Robert Lockhart). Lexical route — whole-word reading; lost in surface dyslexia. Loss aversion — losses loom larger than gains (prospect theory). Means-ends analysis — reduce gap to goal via subgoals (Allen Newell & Herbert Simon). Mental models — reason by simulating possibilities (Johnson-Laird). Mental set / Einstellung — over-applying an old strategy (Luchins). Metacognition — thinking about one's own thinking (Flavell). Minimal attachment — build the simplest parse tree (Frazier). Misinformation effect — post-event info rewrites memory (Elizabeth Loftus). Modularity — separable, domain-specific cognitive modules (Fodor). Multi-store model — sensory → STM → LTM (Richard Atkinson & Richard Shiffrin). Phonological loop — verbal store + rehearsal (inner ear/voice). Phonological similarity effect — similar-sounding lists recalled worse. PIN — person identity node (Bruce & Young). Pop-out — single-feature target found in parallel (flat search slope). Pragmatic reasoning schema — permission/obligation rules (Cheng & Holyoak). Primacy / recency — best recall of first (LTM) / last (STM) items. Procedural memory — implicit "knowing how" (skills). Prospect theory — reference-dependent, loss-averse value (Kahneman & Tversky). Prospective memory — remembering to act later (event- vs time-based). Prosopagnosia — selective face-recognition loss. Prototype — abstracted best example of a category (Eleanor Rosch). Recognition-by-components — object recognition via geons (Irving Biederman). Representativeness — judge by resemblance to stereotype. Retrograde amnesia — loss of memories from before injury. Satisficing — choosing "good enough" (Simon). Savings method — relearning speed-up measures retention (Ebbinghaus). Schema / script — organised knowledge / event sequence (Frederic Bartlett; Schank & Abelson). Serial-position curve — primacy + recency in free recall. Spreading activation — activation flows along a relatedness web (Collins & Loftus). Spotlight / zoom-lens — movable, resizable focus of attention (Michael Posner; Eriksen). Stroop effect — automatic word-reading intrudes on colour naming. Surface structure — actual words/syntax of a sentence (Chomsky). System 1 / 2 — fast intuitive vs slow analytic thinking. Template theory — match input to whole stored pattern (fails on variation). TMS — transient "virtual lesion"; tests necessity. Top-down — concept/expectation-driven processing. TOT — tip-of-the-tongue; accessible-but-not-retrieved. Two visual streams — ventral "what" / dorsal "where-how" (Milner & Goodale). Universal Grammar — innate grammatical principles (Chomsky). Weapon focus — a weapon narrows attention, worsening other recall. Word-length effect — longer words → smaller span (phonological loop). Working memory — active multi-component STM (Baddeley & Graham Hitch). ★ Self-test (active recall) Cover the rest of the page and answer aloud. If you can't, reread that section. 1. Approaches What logic lets neuropsychology claim two abilities are separate systems? Which method tells you when (not where) something happens? Which establishes that a region is necessary ? Name two hallmarks of PDP. 2. Perception How does Gregory explain illusions and how does that differ from Gibson? Name David Marr's three stages in order. What did patient DF show about the two visual streams? 3. Recognition Why does template theory fail? What are geons and why do they give view-invariance? Put the Bruce & Young stages in order — and why can you have familiarity without a name but never a name without familiarity? 4. Attention What dichotic-listening finding sinks strict Donald Broadbent and fits Anne Treisman? In FIT, what are illusory conjunctions evidence of? What's the difference between pop-out and serial search? 5. STM & WM What does the serial-position curve show, and how do you dissociate its two ends? Name the three classic phonological-loop effects. What does articulatory suppression abolish? 6. LTM Distinguish episodic from semantic, and declarative from procedural. State encoding specificity (Endel Tulving and Donald Thomson, 1973) in one line. What exactly did H.M. lose and retain? 7. Forgetting Proactive vs retroactive interference — which direction is which? What did the Elizabeth Loftus & John Palmer verb manipulation show? Why is time-based prospective memory harder? 8. Knowledge Prototype vs exemplar in one line each. What does sentence-verification time predict in Allan Collins & Ross Quillian, and what breaks that prediction? What is semantic priming evidence for? 9. Language Strong vs weak Sapir-Whorf — which survives? Map surface vs phonological dyslexia onto Coltheart's two routes. Broca vs Wernicke: fluency, comprehension, lesion site for each? 10. Problem solving Functional fixedness (Karl Duncker, 1945) vs mental set — give the classic task for each. What is means-ends analysis? Why do chess masters beat novices only on real boards? 11. Judgement Which heuristic drives the Linda and Tom W. problems? State loss aversion and the shape of the value function. What flips choice in the Asian disease problem? 12. Reasoning What's the correct answer to the abstract selection task, and what makes people get it right? What bias does the 2-4-6 task expose? State the core prediction of mental-models theory. That's the cognitive syllabus at full depth, Eysenck & Keane in book order. Method: read the prose to learn each model's claim + key study, use the tables to self-quiz (cover author / cover claim), drill every red trap box as a pair, and finish on the self-test. The type sweeps: Effects , Phenomena , Theories , Theorists , Lookalikes . Sihan MET 2026 + NIMHANS prep · /notes/cognitive/ · from Eysenck & Keane, Cognitive Psychology: A Student's Handbook · rebuilt to full depth 2026-05-29

title: Developmental Psychology
text: Developmental Psychology The lifespan story of how mind, behaviour, and relationships unfold, told through the theorists MET 2026 and NIMHANS love to test: Jean Piaget and Vygotsky on cognition, Bronfenbrenner on context, Erik Erikson, Sigmund Freud, Marcia on identity and psychosocial growth, Lawrence Kohlberg and Gilligan on morality, John Bowlby, Mary Ainsworth, Main, Harlow on attachment, Baumrind on parenting, Alexander Thomas and Stella Chess plus Mary Rothbart and John Bates and Kagan on temperament, plus prenatal development, language, adolescence, and aging. Read top to bottom once, then revise off the tables and the red Trap boxes. In this book Foundational principles Prenatal development and teratogens Piaget: cognitive development Vygotsky: sociocultural theory Bronfenbrenner: ecological systems / bioecological model Erikson: psychosocial stages Marcia: identity statuses Freud: psychosexual stages Kohlberg and Gilligan: moral development Attachment: Bowlby, Ainsworth, Main, Harlow Baumrind: parenting styles Temperament: Thomas & Chess, Rothbart & Bates, Kagan Language development Adolescence Aging and late adulthood Theorist hooks (one line each) Top MCQ traps and 30-second recall 1. Foundational Principles Principle Meaning Example Cephalocaudal Head to toe Head control before walking Proximodistal Center to periphery Trunk control before fine finger movement Continuity vs Discontinuity Gradual growth vs stage jumps Vocab growth (continuous) vs Piaget stages (discontinuous) Nature vs Nurture Genes vs environment; modern view = interactionist Twin studies, behavioral genetics Critical period Rigid window; miss it and the capacity is lost Lorenz imprinting in geese Sensitive period Flexible window; learning easier but still possible later L1 acquisition, depth perception Stability vs Change Do traits persist or shift across life? Temperament (mostly stable), IQ (some plasticity) Active vs Passive child Does the child shape their own development? Bidirectionality (Urie Bronfenbrenner, Bell) Trap Critical = rigid biological window (lost if missed). Sensitive = optimal but flexible. Konrad Lorenz's imprinting = critical. Language learning = sensitive (you can still learn L2 at 30, just harder). 2. Prenatal Development and Teratogens Three prenatal stages Stage Duration Key event Germinal 0-2 weeks Zygote to blastocyst to implantation Embryonic 2-8 weeks Organogenesis; most vulnerable to teratogens Fetal 8 weeks to birth Growth and refinement; viability ~24 weeks Teratogens (high-yield) Alcohol — Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder (FASD); FAS = facial anomalies, growth restriction, CNS damage. Most common preventable cause of intellectual disability. Tobacco — low birth weight, prematurity. Thalidomide — limb malformations (1950s-60s, classic teratogen exam case). Rubella — heart, eye, ear defects in 1st trimester. Lead, mercury — CNS damage. Zika — microcephaly. Trap The embryonic period (weeks 2-8) is most vulnerable, not the fetal period. Organs are forming. By the fetal period, organs already exist and growth is the main task. 3. Piaget: Cognitive Development The 4 stages Stage Age Achievements Limits Sensorimotor 0-2 Object permanence (~8mo), goal-directed action, deferred imitation (end) No symbolic thought early on Preoperational 2-7 Symbolic thought, language, pretend play Egocentrism, animism, centration, no conservation Concrete Operational 7-11 Conservation, reversibility, classification, seriation, decentration Tied to concrete reality; abstract is shaky Formal Operational 11+ Abstract, hypothetico-deductive, propositional logic Adolescent egocentrism (imaginary audience, personal fable) Sensorimotor: the 6 substages Reflexive schemes (0-1mo) Primary circular reactions (1-4mo, on own body) Secondary circular reactions (4-8mo, on objects) Coordination of secondary schemes (8-12mo, intentional, object permanence , A-not-B error) Tertiary circular reactions (12-18mo, experimentation) Mental representation (18-24mo, deferred imitation, symbolic thought) Key concepts Schema — mental framework for understanding the world. Assimilation — fitting new info into an existing schema (a horse = a "doggie"). Accommodation — modifying the schema for new info ("ok, that's a horse, not a doggie"). Equilibration — the drive to balance assimilation and accommodation; the engine of cognitive change. Egocentrism — preoperational; can't take another's perspective. Three Mountains task. Animism — preoperational; attributing life to objects. Centration — focus on one feature at a time; blocks conservation. Conservation — quantity stays the same despite a change in form (number, mass, volume). Order: number then mass then liquid then length then area then weight then volume (last, ~11). Trap Object permanence (sensorimotor, ~8mo) is NOT conservation (concrete operational, ~7yr). Different stages, different concepts. Also: "egocentrism" in dev psych is a cognitive limit, not narcissism or a personality trait. Critiques of Piaget Underestimated infants (modern habituation studies show object permanence earlier). Stages less discrete than he claimed ( horizontal décalage = uneven performance within a stage). Underplayed culture (Lev Vygotsky's main attack). Not everyone reaches formal operational, especially for unfamiliar content. 4. Vygotsky: Sociocultural Theory ZPD (Zone of Proximal Development) — the gap between what a child can do alone vs with help from a more knowledgeable other (MKO). Scaffolding — temporary, tailored support, withdrawn as competence grows. This is Jerome Bruner's term , applied to Lev Vygotsky's framework. Private speech — kids talk to themselves while problem-solving. It becomes inner speech and guides cognition. Jean Piaget called this "egocentric speech" and dismissed it; Vygotsky said it is central. Tools of thought — language is the master tool, internalized from social interaction. Higher mental functions are socially mediated . Cultural specificity — cognitive development depends on the cultural tools available (counting systems, writing, schooling). Trap "Scaffolding" is Jerome Bruner , not Vygotsky. Vygotsky's own terms are ZPD and MKO. High-yield Jean Piaget vs Vygotsky in one line: Piaget = child as a lone scientist (development drives learning). Lev Vygotsky = child as an apprentice (learning drives development, mediated by culture). 5. Bronfenbrenner: Ecological Systems / Bioecological Model Core idea Urie Bronfenbrenner (1917-2005), Russian-born American developmental psychologist. Development is shaped by ongoing interaction between the person and a set of nested environmental systems . Originally Ecological Systems Theory , from "The Ecology of Human Development" (1979). Later renamed the Bioecological Model (1994, refined 2005) to give biology more weight and add the PPCT mechanism. Co-founded the Head Start program (1965) in the US, an applied use of the theory. High-yield One-line answer: Development = person × proximal processes × nested context × time. The 5 systems (innermost to outermost) 5.1 Microsystem Immediate settings with direct face-to-face contact ; the most direct effect on development. Examples: family, school, peer group, neighbourhood, daycare, workplace (for adults). Influence is bidirectional : the child shapes the environment, and the environment shapes the child. 5.2 Mesosystem Interactions between two or more microsystems . Not a setting itself; a system of microsystems . Examples: parent-teacher communication, family-peer overlap, home-daycare and home-school links. Strong, supportive mesosystem links predict better developmental outcomes. 5.3 Exosystem Settings the child does not directly participate in , but which still affect them via the microsystem. Examples: parent's workplace, school board decisions, mass media, parent's social network, local government policy. 5.4 Macrosystem The overarching cultural blueprint , the "cultural envelope" around all the other systems. Examples: ideologies, customs, laws, religion, SES, cultural values, the economic system, war/peace. Does not refer to a specific setting; refers to the cultural patterning that shapes all settings. 5.5 Chronosystem The time dimension . Added later, after the original 4 systems. Three flavours of "time" effects: Life transitions : normative (school entry, puberty) and non-normative (parents' divorce, death of a parent). Historical events the person lives through (pandemic, war, recession). Sociohistorical conditions of the cohort (cohort effects, the sociohistorical era). Quick-reference table System What it is Examples Microsystem Direct, face-to-face settings; bidirectional Family, school, peers, daycare Mesosystem Interactions between microsystems (a system of microsystems, not a setting itself) Parent-teacher meeting, home-school link, family-peer overlap Exosystem Settings the child is not in but which still affect them Parent's workplace, school board, mass media, parent's social network Macrosystem Cultural blueprint, the "envelope" around all other systems Ideologies, customs, laws, religion, SES, cultural values Chronosystem Time dimension; added later (originally 4 systems) Divorce, parental death, pandemic, sociohistorical era PPCT Model (1994 refinement, often asked) Urie Bronfenbrenner refined the theory into the Bioecological Model using the PPCT mechanism. This is the engine of the modern version. Process — proximal processes The engine of development , the most important driver. Regular, reciprocal interactions over extended time between the person and the people, objects, and symbols in the immediate environment. Examples: parent-child play, reading together, sustained peer activity, learning a skill from a mentor. Must be regular and over long stretches of time to count as proximal processes, not one-off events. Person — individual traits Three sub-types: Sub-type Definition Examples Demand characteristics Visible traits that pull responses from others Age, gender, skin colour, physical appearance Resource characteristics Skills, abilities, experiences Intelligence, prior knowledge, social skills Force characteristics Temperament, motivation, persistence Curiosity, drive, distractibility, regulation Context — the 5 nested systems Micro / Meso / Exo / Macro / Chrono, as covered above. Time Micro-time : continuity vs interruption within an activity (e.g. an uninterrupted reading session). Meso-time : consistency of activities across days and weeks. Macro-time : the chronosystem level, sociohistorical change across the lifespan. High-yield exam pointers Originally 4 systems ; the chronosystem was added later. Bidirectionality is a key examiner trigger word, especially in microsystem questions. Two phases of theory: Ecological Systems Theory (1979) then Bioecological Model (1994) with PPCT. Proximal processes are the engine , not the context. Context only modifies how proximal processes operate. The mesosystem is not a setting ; it is a system of relationships between settings. Compare and contrast (very high-yield) Theorist Focus Mechanism Jean Piaget Cognitive stages, internal Schemas, assimilation, accommodation Lev Vygotsky Sociocultural ZPD, scaffolding (Jerome Bruner), more knowledgeable other Urie Bronfenbrenner Ecological / multi-layered context Person × Process × Context × Time Erik Erikson Psychosocial stages 8 crises across the lifespan Albert Bandura Social learning Observation, modeling, self-efficacy High-yield If the stem mentions nested environments, cultural context, a parent's workplace affecting the child, or indirect influence, the answer is Urie Bronfenbrenner . Applications Child welfare policy — interventions at multiple system levels (family + school + community). Inclusive education — coordinating microsystems (home, school, peers). Public health — tobacco control, vaccination uptake (macro + exo levels). Family therapy — recognising that the family microsystem sits inside larger systems. Head Start program (Bronfenbrenner co-founded) — early childhood intervention targeting micro + meso systems. Critique Hard to operationalise and test empirically; too many simultaneous variables. Originally underplayed biology (fixed in the bioecological revision via the "Person" component). Criticised for being descriptive more than predictive ; doesn't say which system dominates when. Cultural specificity is unclear; the macrosystem treats "culture" as a single bucket. Trap Exosystem does NOT mean no influence. The child isn't in it, but it shapes them through their microsystem (e.g. dad loses his job, stress rises at home, the child's development is affected). Trap Mass media affecting a child = exosystem , not macrosystem. Media is a setting, not a cultural blueprint. By contrast, "culture, religion, ideology, SES" = macrosystem ; "parent's workplace" = exosystem ; "sibling fight at home" = microsystem ; "parent-teacher meeting" = mesosystem . Trap The chronosystem was added later . Older textbooks list only 4 systems. If a question says "Bronfenbrenner originally proposed 5 systems," that is false. PPCT belongs to the Bioecological Model (1994) , not the original 1979 theory. 6. Erikson: 8 Psychosocial Stages Age Conflict Virtue (if resolved) Bad outcome 0-1.5 Trust vs Mistrust Hope Suspicion, withdrawal 1.5-3 Autonomy vs Shame/Doubt Will Compulsive self-doubt 3-6 Initiative vs Guilt Purpose Inhibition 6-12 Industry vs Inferiority Competence Inertia, low self-worth 12-18 Identity vs Role Confusion Fidelity Identity crisis 18-40 Intimacy vs Isolation Love Loneliness 40-65 Generativity vs Stagnation Care Self-absorption 65+ Integrity vs Despair Wisdom Regret, fear of death Mnemonic " T rust A utonomy I nitiative I ndustry I dentity I ntimacy G enerativity I ntegrity" — TAIIIIGI roughly tracks the stages. 7. Marcia: Identity Statuses (Erikson stage 5 expansion) Status Crisis explored? Commitment made? Description Diffusion No No Drifting, uncommitted Foreclosure No Yes Commitment without exploration (handed down by parents) Moratorium Yes (in progress) No Active exploration, no commitment yet Achievement Yes (resolved) Yes Explored and committed 8. Freud: Psychosexual Stages Age Stage Erogenous zone / theme Fixation traits 0-1 Oral Mouth, feeding Smoking, overeating, dependency 1-3 Anal Bowel control Anal-retentive (orderly, stingy) or anal-expulsive (messy) 3-6 Phallic Genitals; Oedipus / Electra; superego forms Vanity, recklessness 6-12 Latency Sexual urges dormant, same-sex friendships, school focus (no fixation classically) 12+ Genital Mature sexuality, healthy adult relationships (if all prior resolved) 9. Kohlberg and Gilligan: Moral Development Level Stage Driver Preconventional (self-interest) 1. Punishment-obedience Avoid punishment 2. Instrumental exchange Self-benefit, "what's in it for me" Conventional (social rules) 3. Good boy / good girl Approval of others 4. Law and order Maintain social order, duty Postconventional (abstract principles) 5. Social contract Laws as agreed contracts, can be changed 6. Universal ethical principles Internal moral compass, e.g. justice, dignity Methodology = the Heinz dilemma (steal the drug to save your wife?). The stage is the reasoning , not the choice itself. Trap Carol Gilligan's critique : Lawrence Kohlberg's stages reflect a male "justice" orientation ; women often reason via an "ethics of care" (relationships, responsibility). Gilligan added a parallel orientation; she did not replace Kohlberg. 10. Attachment: Bowlby, Ainsworth, Main, Harlow Bowlby's 4 phases Age Phase Behavior 0-6 wk Pre-attachment Indiscriminate signals (cry, smile) 6 wk-8 mo Attachment-in-the-making Prefers familiar caregivers, no clear protest at separation yet 8 mo-18 mo Clear-cut attachment Separation anxiety and stranger anxiety peak; secure base behavior 18-24 mo+ Reciprocal relationships Internal working model; goal-corrected partnership Ainsworth's Strange Situation: 4 styles Style Separation behavior Reunion behavior Caregiver pattern Secure (B, ~60%) Distressed Easily comforted, returns to play Sensitive, responsive Avoidant (A, ~20%) Little distress Avoids/ignores caregiver Rejecting, unresponsive Resistant / Ambivalent (C, ~10%) Very distressed Seeks and resists contact, can't be soothed Inconsistent Disorganized (D) Confused, freezing, contradictory Approach and avoid, dazed Frightening / abusive / unresolved trauma Trap Disorganized (D) was added by Main and Solomon , not Ainsworth. Ainsworth's original 3 = A/B/C. Adult attachment (Main, AAI) Secure-Autonomous (corresponds to B) Dismissing (corresponds to A) Preoccupied (corresponds to C) Unresolved / disorganized (corresponds to D) Foundational attachment experiments Harry Harlow — wire vs cloth mother monkeys. Contact comfort beats food. Demolished the pure drive-reduction view of attachment. Konrad Lorenz — imprinting in geese, the classic critical period example. Bowlby's WHO Report (1951) — the "maternal deprivation hypothesis"; institutional rearing harms development. Influenced post-WWII childcare policy. 11. Baumrind: Parenting Styles High demand Low demand High warmth Authoritative (best outcomes) Permissive / Indulgent Low warmth Authoritarian Neglectful / Uninvolved Authoritative — high warmth + high demand, clear limits, explanations. Best child outcomes (competence, self-regulation, school). Authoritarian — high demand, low warmth, "because I said so." Linked to lower self-esteem, more anxiety. Permissive — high warmth, few demands. Linked to impulsivity, lower achievement. Neglectful — low on both (added by Maccoby and Martin as the 4th style). Worst outcomes. Trap Authoritative is NOT authoritarian. Authoritative = warm + firm (good). Authoritarian = cold + harsh (bad). The words look similar; the outcomes are opposite. 12. Temperament: Thomas & Chess, Rothbart & Bates, Kagan Thomas and Chess: the three temperament types Easy (~40%) — regular routines, positive mood, adapts to change. Difficult (~10%) — irregular, intense reactions, slow to adapt. Slow-to-warm-up (~15%) — low activity, mild reactions, gradual to adapt. The remaining ~35% don't fit cleanly into one category. High-yield Goodness of fit (Alexander Thomas and Stella Chess): the match between a child's temperament and environmental demands predicts adjustment, not temperament alone. Outcome depends on temperament × environment. Rothbart and Bates: the structural model (3 dimensions) Mary Rothbart and John Bates reframed temperament as constitutionally based individual differences in reactivity and self-regulation . Their structural model reduces to exactly three broad dimensions . Learn the list as a closed set, because the classic exam item ("which is NOT included") is answered by spotting the intruder. # Dimension What it captures 1 Surgency / extraversion Positive affect, high activity level, approach, sociability, impulsivity 2 Negative affectivity Fear, frustration/anger, sadness, discomfort, low soothability 3 Effortful control Voluntarily focusing and shifting attention and inhibiting a dominant response; the self-regulatory core, tied to executive attention Effortful control is the piece unique to Rothbart's account: it is the top-down, self-regulatory system that lets the child override a reactive tendency, and it develops with executive attention across the preschool years. Kagan: behavioral inhibition (set apart) Jerome Kagan owns behavioral inhibition — the tendency toward wariness, withdrawal, and physiological arousal when facing the unfamiliar (novel people, objects, situations). Kagan studied inhibited vs uninhibited children and linked inhibition to amygdala reactivity. It overlaps conceptually with fear inside Mary Rothbart's negative affectivity, but it is not one of the three named Rothbart-and-Bates dimensions. That mismatch is exactly what the "inhibition to the unfamiliar" trap tests. Trap "Inhibition to the unfamiliar" / behavioral inhibition looks like it should belong on the Rothbart-and-Bates list, but it is Jerome Kagan's construct. The three Rothbart-and-Bates dimensions are only surgency, negative affectivity, and effortful control . Anything else offered (extraversion is fine — it is surgency; but "inhibition to the unfamiliar" is the intruder) is the answer to a "which is NOT included" item. Match each construct to its theorist Surgency, negative affectivity, effortful control → Mary Rothbart & John Bates. Behavioral inhibition / inhibition to the unfamiliar → Jerome Kagan. Easy / difficult / slow-to-warm-up types + goodness of fit → Alexander Thomas & Stella Chess. 13. Language Development Age Milestone 0-2 mo Crying, reflexive sounds 2-4 mo Cooing (vowels) 6 mo Babbling (consonants + vowels, "bababa") 10-14 mo First word; holophrastic speech (one word = whole thought) 18-24 mo Two-word / telegraphic speech ("more milk") 2-3 yr Vocab burst, simple sentences, overregularization ("goed", "foots") 3-5 yr Complex grammar, ~2000 words by age 5 Theories of language acquisition Theorist School Mechanism B. F. Skinner Behaviorist Operant conditioning, imitation, reinforcement Noam Chomsky Nativist LAD , Universal Grammar, the poverty of stimulus argument Vygotsky / Bruner Social-interactionist Language emerges from social interaction; LASS (Jerome Bruner) Jean Piaget Cognitive Thought before language; language reflects cognition Trap Overregularization ("goed", "mouses") is a sign of rule learning , not regression. The child has learned the past-tense rule and is over-applying it. 14. Adolescence Puberty — primary (gonads) and secondary (hair, voice) sex characteristics. Girls typically mature 1-2 years earlier than boys. Adolescent egocentrism (Elkind) — the imaginary audience (everyone is watching me) and the personal fable (I am unique and immune to harm). Identity — the central task (Erikson stage 5); Marcia's 4 statuses. Risk-taking — the limbic system matures before the prefrontal cortex (the dual systems model). Storm and stress (G. Stanley Hall) — an older view; modern data show most adolescents are not in chronic conflict. 15. Aging and Late Adulthood Primary aging — biological (sensory decline, slower processing). Secondary aging — disease and lifestyle (preventable). Crystallized intelligence — preserved or improves with age (vocab, knowledge). Fluid intelligence — declines (processing speed, novel problem-solving). The Cattell-Horn-Carroll model. Socioemotional selectivity theory (Carstensen) — older adults prioritize emotionally meaningful goals as their time horizon shrinks. Kübler-Ross 5 stages of dying — denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance. Often misunderstood as universal/linear; she did not claim that. 16. Theorist Hooks (one line each) Theorist Hook Jean Piaget 4 cognitive stages, schemas, equilibration Lev Vygotsky ZPD, MKO, sociocultural, language as tool Jerome Bruner Scaffolding, modes of representation (enactive/iconic/symbolic), LASS Erik Erikson 8 psychosocial conflicts across life Sigmund Freud 5 psychosexual stages, id/ego/superego John Bowlby Attachment as a biological survival system, IWM Mary Ainsworth Strange Situation, A/B/C styles Main and Solomon Disorganized (D) Harry Harlow Wire vs cloth mother, contact comfort beats food Konrad Lorenz Imprinting, critical period Lawrence Kohlberg 3 levels, 6 stages of moral reasoning, Heinz dilemma Carol Gilligan Ethics of care, gendered critique Diana Baumrind Parenting styles (3, then 4 with Maccoby and Martin) Albert Bandura Social learning, observation, Bobo doll, self-efficacy Urie Bronfenbrenner Ecological systems, PPCT, micro/meso/exo/macro/chrono Thomas and Chess Temperament types (easy/difficult/slow-to-warm-up), goodness of fit Rothbart and Bates Structural model: 3 dimensions (surgency, negative affectivity, effortful control) Jerome Kagan Behavioral inhibition / inhibition to the unfamiliar (inhibited vs uninhibited) James Marcia 4 identity statuses Gesell Maturation, normative milestones Hall Adolescence as "storm and stress" B. F. Skinner Operant theory of language Noam Chomsky LAD, Universal Grammar 17. Top MCQ Traps and 30-Second Recall Object permanence (sensorimotor) is NOT conservation (concrete operational). Critical period (rigid, biological) vs sensitive period (flexible). Authoritative is NOT authoritarian. One word apart, opposite outcomes. Disorganized attachment was Main and Solomon, not Mary Ainsworth. "Scaffolding" is Jerome Bruner's term, applied to Vygotsky's ZPD. Bronfenbrenner exosystem = child not in it, but still affected (parent's workplace). Bronfenbrenner mesosystem = link between microsystems, not a setting itself. Chronosystem was added later; originally 4 systems. PPCT = Bioecological Model (1994), not the original 1979 theory. Carol Gilligan added "ethics of care"; she did not replace Lawrence Kohlberg. Overregularization ("goed") is rule-learning, not regression. The embryonic period (weeks 2-8) is most teratogen-vulnerable, not the fetal period. FAS / FASD = the most common preventable cause of intellectual disability. Egocentrism (Jean Piaget) = a cognitive limit, not a personality trait. Goodness of fit (Alexander Thomas and Stella Chess) — the outcome depends on the temperament × environment match. High-yield 30-second recall: Jean Piaget (4 cognitive stages, equilibration), Lev Vygotsky (ZPD, MKO, sociocultural), Urie Bronfenbrenner (5 nested systems + PPCT, exosystem trap), Erik Erikson (8 psychosocial conflicts), Bowlby/Ainsworth/Main (4 attachment styles B/A/C/D), Diana Baumrind (4 parenting styles, authoritative is best), Lawrence Kohlberg (3 levels × 2 stages, Carol Gilligan adds care), Alexander Thomas and Stella Chess (temperament + goodness of fit), Noam Chomsky vs Skinner on language. Critical vs sensitive period. Conservation is not object permanence.

title: Abnormal Psychology & Classification
text: Abnormal Psychology & Classification The complete abnormal-psychology and diagnostic-classification chapter for MET 2026 / NIMHANS M.Phil entrance: what counts as abnormal, the models and approaches, the ICD and DSM systems end to end (history, F-codes, ICD-10 vs ICD-11, ICD vs DSM), the mental status exam, and every disorder family with its diagnostic thresholds, durations, differentiators, mnemonics, and exam traps. One entry per concept, every unique detail kept. Read once for coverage, then revise off the tables and the red Trap boxes. In this book Defining abnormality (the 4 Ds) Historical models & conceptions Approaches to psychopathology The ICD: WHO's classification (full breakdown) DSM vs ICD & the DSM-5 structure Mental status examination (MSE) Neurodevelopmental disorders Schizophrenia & other psychotic disorders Mood disorders (bipolar & depressive) Anxiety disorders OCD & related disorders Trauma- & stressor-related disorders Dissociative disorders Somatic symptom & related disorders Feeding & eating disorders Sleep-wake disorders Substance-related & addictive disorders Personality disorders Suicide risk assessment Treatments & therapy quick-map Master MCQ trap list 30-second recall script 1. Defining abnormality (the 4 Ds) Deviance — statistical or social norm violation. Distress — subjective suffering. Dysfunction — impairs daily life / role functioning. Danger — risk to self or others. Trap Deviance alone is not abnormal. A genius IQ is statistically deviant but not pathological. You always need at least distress or dysfunction alongside it. High-yield Some textbooks list a 5th D, Duration , used for chronicity criteria (the recurring duration thresholds like ≥ 6 months, ≥ 2 years, etc. that define many disorders below). 2. Historical models & conceptions Era Model Key name(s) Prehistoric / Ancient Supernatural (demons, possession) Trephination Greek / Roman Biological, four humors Hippocrates, Galen Middle Ages Demonological return, witch trials Malleus Maleficarum (1487) Renaissance Asylum reform begins Pinel (Bicêtre, "moral treatment"), Tuke (York Retreat) 19th c. Biological, classification Emil Kraepelin ( dementia praecox ), Eugen Bleuler (renamed schizophrenia , 4 As) Early 20th c. Psychological Sigmund Freud (psychoanalysis), John B. Watson (behaviorism) Mid 20th c. Cognitive-behavioral Aaron Beck (depression / CBT), Albert Ellis (REBT) 1980s+ Biopsychosocial integration Engel (1977) Trap Emil Kraepelin coined dementia praecox (emphasising early onset and a deteriorating course). Eugen Bleuler renamed it schizophrenia ("split mind", referring to fragmented thought, not split personality). Do not confuse with DID. 3. Approaches to psychopathology Approach Cause Treatment Biological Genes, neurotransmitters, brain Meds, ECT, psychosurgery Psychodynamic Unconscious conflict, early experience Psychoanalysis, free association, transference Behavioral Maladaptive learning Conditioning, exposure, reinforcement Cognitive Distorted thoughts, schemas CBT, cognitive restructuring (Aaron Beck), REBT (Albert Ellis) Humanistic Blocked self-actualization Person-centered (Carl Rogers), Gestalt (Fritz Perls) Sociocultural Family, culture, stigma, oppression Family therapy, community psychology Biopsychosocial All three interact ( Engel, 1977 ) Integrative Diathesis-stress Predisposition × stressor Reduce both load 4. The ICD: WHO's classification (full breakdown) Definition The ICD (International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems) is the WHO's global classification of all diseases, not just mental ones. Mental disorders occupy a single chapter of it. DSM (American Psychiatric Association) covers mental disorders only. So: ICD = whole-body, global, free, used for official health statistics; DSM = mental-only, US, paywalled, research-heavy. NIMHANS / India officially codes on ICD . 4.1 What ICD is & who owns it Question Answer Full name International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems Publisher WHO (World Health Organization). DSM is APA, the contrast examiners love. Scope All diseases and health conditions, every body system. Mental & behavioural disorders are just one chapter . Purpose Global standard for mortality & morbidity statistics , billing, epidemiology. Official tool for cause-of-death and disease reporting worldwide. Cost Free , multilingual. DSM is copyrighted and sold by APA. Used where ~194 WHO member states, including India . DSM dominates US clinical research. 4.2 Version history (the dates they ask) Version Year Note ICD-6 1949 First edition to include a section on mental disorders. Common MCQ. ICD-8 1965 ICD-9 1975 US used a clinical modification, ICD-9-CM , for decades. ICD-10 1990 endorsed, 1992 in use Still tested. Mental disorders = Chapter V (F-codes) . Alphanumeric coding introduced here. ICD-11 Adopted 2019, in force 1 Jan 2022 Fully digital "foundation" architecture. Mental disorders = Chapter 06 . High-yield Lock the three dates: ICD-6 (1949) = first mental-disorder section · ICD-10 (1992) = F-codes · ICD-11 (in force 2022) = current. 4.3 Where mental disorders live ICD-10 ICD-11 Chapter Chapter V Chapter 06 Title Mental and Behavioural Disorders Mental, Behavioural or Neurodevelopmental Disorders Code prefix F (F00–F99) Alphanumeric 6 -codes (e.g. 6A20 for schizophrenia) Companion text "Blue Book" (Clinical Descriptions & Diagnostic Guidelines) + "Green Book" (research criteria) CDDR (Clinical Descriptions and Diagnostic Requirements) High-yield Why "F"? No mnemonic meaning, it is simply the letter assigned to the mental-disorders chapter (Chapter V) in ICD-10's alphanumeric scheme.
