Extended concept bank (the rest of the book, chapter by chapter) The chapters above are the spine. This bank picks up the remaining named terms theorist by theorist — the full defence-mechanism list, every Jungian archetype, Alfred Adler's safeguarding tendencies, Karen Horney's ten neurotic needs, Erik Erikson's virtues, Maslow's B-values, George Kelly's eleven corollaries, and so on — so each has a home you can slot it into. Every entry is the kind of one-line fact an MCQ distractor is built from. Freud — the full defence-mechanism list (catalogued by Anna Freud) Defence One line Repression The master defence: unconscious blocking of threatening material. (Conscious version = suppression , the only mature/conscious one.) Denial Refuse to accept an external reality. Projection Attribute your own unacceptable impulse to someone else. Displacement Redirect an impulse onto a safer substitute target . Sublimation Channel the impulse into a socially valued activity (the healthiest classical defence). Reaction formation Act as the opposite of the true impulse. Rationalisation Invent a logical-sounding excuse for the real reason. Regression Retreat to an earlier developmental stage under stress. Intellectualisation Strip the emotion out, deal only with abstract facts. Identification Take on the qualities of an admired/feared other (incl. identification with the aggressor). Introjection Absorb another's values/qualities wholesale into the self. Undoing A ritual act to magically "cancel" a bad thought/deed. Isolation of affect Keep the memory, sever the feeling. Splitting See self/others as all-good or all-bad (borderline; Klein/Kernberg). Projective identification Project a part of the self into another and induce them to act it out (Melanie Klein). Compensation Make up for a weakness by excelling elsewhere (more Adlerian). Fantasy / daydreaming Gratify frustrated wishes imaginatively (immature). Acting out / somatisation Discharge conflict through action / bodily symptoms (immature). Mature set (George Vaillant) Sublimation, humour , altruism , suppression , anticipation . NIMHANS — Vaillant's maturity hierarchy. Psychotic (denial of external reality, delusional projection, distortion) → immature (projection, acting out, passive aggression, fantasy, splitting, somatisation) → neurotic (repression, displacement, reaction formation, intellectualisation, rationalisation, undoing) → mature (sublimation, humour, altruism, suppression, anticipation). Repression = unconscious/neurotic; suppression = conscious/mature. Jung — the full archetype list Archetype What it is Persona The public mask, the role we present to society. Shadow The dark, animal, denied side; the source of creativity as well as vice. Anima The feminine side within a man. Animus The masculine side within a woman. Self The unifying, central archetype of wholeness; goal of individuation, symbolised by the mandala . Great Mother Archetype of nurturance and fertility (and devouring). Wise Old Man Archetype of meaning, wisdom, the spirit/sage. Hero The figure who conquers evil; champion of the ego against the unconscious. Trickster / others Plus rebirth, child, maiden, etc. — Jung held archetypes are innumerable. Other Jung terms to own: complexes (emotionally charged clusters in the personal unconscious, e.g. a mother complex), the two attitudes (introversion / extraversion), the four functions (thinking, feeling = rational; sensing, intuiting = irrational), individuation (lifelong integration into the self), and the transcendent function (uniting opposites). Adler — birth order & safeguarding tendencies Position Typical Adlerian portrait First-born "Dethroned" by the next child; often conservative, responsible, power-oriented, may feel insecure. Second / middle Competitive, ambitious (runs to catch the pacemaker ahead); often the best-adjusted. Youngest Pampered baby of the family; can be highly motivated to outdo all, or dependent and avoidant. Only child Never dethroned; precocious, may be pampered, rivalrous with adults rather than peers. Safeguarding tendencies (Alfred Adler's neurotic protections of self-esteem, a forerunner of defence mechanisms): excuses ("yes, but…" / "if only…"), aggression (depreciation, accusation, self-accusation), and distancing / withdrawal (moving backward, standing still, hesitating, constructing obstacles). Plus the core terms: inferiority feelings → compensation → (if it fails) inferiority complex or over-compensating superiority complex ; style of life ; creative power of the self ; fictional finalism ; social interest (Gemeinschaftsgefühl) ; the three life tasks (work, friendship/society, love). Horney — the ten neurotic needs & three trends The three trends (toward / against / away) are distilled from ten neurotic needs : (1) affection & approval, (2) a dominant partner to run one's life, (3) narrow limits to life (undemanding), (4) power, (5) exploitation of others, (6) prestige/social recognition, (7) personal admiration, (8) personal achievement/ambition, (9) self-sufficiency & independence, (10) perfection & unassailability. Trend Needs it groups Type Moving toward people (compliance) Affection, a dominant partner, narrow limits (1–3) Self-effacing / compliant Moving against people (aggression) Power, exploitation, prestige, admiration, achievement (4–8) Expansive / aggressive Moving away from people (detachment) Self-sufficiency, perfection (9–10) Resigned / detached Plus: basic anxiety (isolated and helpless in a hostile world) vs basic hostility ; the idealised (self-)image and the "tyranny of the should" ; real self vs idealised self; rejection of penis envy in favour of cultural power-envy and men's "womb envy" . Erikson — the eight stages with virtues (and Marcia's statuses) Stage (age) Crisis Basic virtue / strength Maladaptation Infancy (0–1) Trust vs mistrust Hope Withdrawal Early childhood (1–3) Autonomy vs shame/doubt Will Compulsion Play age (3–5) Initiative vs guilt Purpose Inhibition School age (6–11) Industry vs inferiority Competence Inertia Adolescence (12–18) Identity vs role confusion Fidelity Repudiation Young adulthood Intimacy vs isolation Love Exclusivity Middle adulthood Generativity vs stagnation Care Rejectivity Old age Ego integrity vs despair Wisdom Disdain James Marcia's four identity statuses (crisis/exploration × commitment): diffusion (neither), foreclosure (commitment, no exploration), moratorium (exploring, no commitment yet), achievement (commitment after exploration). Erik Erikson coined "identity crisis" ; key term epigenetic principle . Allport — the trait taxonomy & the proprium Level / term What it is Cardinal trait So dominant it pervades a whole life (rare; a "Scrooge"). Central traits The 5–10 core descriptors of a person (the reference-letter words). Secondary dispositions Situation-specific preferences, shown only sometimes. Common vs individual traits Shared/comparable across people vs unique to the person (he favoured the latter, personal dispositions ). Proprium Gordon Allport's word for the self/ego, developing through ~7 aspects (bodily self → self-identity → self-esteem → self-extension → self-image → rational coping → propriate striving ). Functional autonomy A motive becomes independent of its origin (perseverative vs propriate functional autonomy). Idiographic / morphogenic Study of the unique individual (Allport's preferred approach; he rejected factor analysis). Maslow — the full hierarchy, B-values & the self-actualiser Hierarchy (bottom → top): physiological → safety → belongingness/love → esteem → self-actualisation ; later additions split the upper region into cognitive (know/understand) and aesthetic needs below self-actualisation, and self-transcendence above it. Lower four = deficiency (D-)needs ; the top = being (B-)needs / growth needs . Characteristics of self-actualisers: accurate perception of reality; acceptance of self/others/nature; spontaneity & naturalness; problem-centred (not self-centred); need for privacy & autonomy; freshness of appreciation; peak experiences ; Gemeinschaftsgefühl (social interest); deep but few interpersonal relationships; democratic character; ethical discrimination of means/ends; philosophical humour; creativeness; resistance to enculturation. B-values (the "meta-needs" pursued at the top): truth, goodness, beauty, unity/wholeness, aliveness, uniqueness, perfection, justice, order, simplicity, richness, effortlessness, playfulness, self-sufficiency, meaningfulness. The Jonah complex = fear of one's own greatness; metapathology = the malaise from frustrated B-values; measured by the POI (Shostrom) . Rogers — the fully functioning person Core machinery: the actualising tendency (and the organism's organismic valuing process ); the self / self-concept ; real self vs ideal self → congruence vs incongruence ; conditions of worth imposed by conditional positive regard; the cure = unconditional positive regard (UPR) ; the therapist's three core conditions = empathy, congruence/genuineness, UPR. The fully functioning person (Carl Rogers' ideal of growth) shows: (1) openness to experience (no defensiveness), (2) existential living (fully in the present moment), (3) organismic trusting (trusting one's own judgement), (4) experiential freedom (sense of free choice and responsibility), and (5) creativity . Kelly — the fundamental postulate & eleven corollaries Fundamental postulate: "a person's processes are psychologically channelised by the ways in which they anticipate events." The eleven corollaries : Corollary One line Construction We anticipate events by construing their replications (we read recurring themes). Individuality People differ in how they construe the same event. Organisation Each person organises constructs into a hierarchy (some superordinate to others). Dichotomy Constructs are bipolar (kind–cruel). Choice We pick the pole of a construct that promises the most extension/definition of our system. Range Each construct applies only to a limited range of events (its range of convenience). Experience We revise constructs as we successively construe events. Modulation How much a system can change is limited by the permeability of its constructs. Fragmentation We can hold sub-systems that are mutually inconsistent. Commonality People who construe experience similarly are psychologically similar. Sociality To relate to someone you must construe their construction processes (role-taking). Plus Kelly's cognitive re-definitions of emotion: anxiety (events lie outside one's constructs), threat (awareness of imminent comprehensive change), fear (imminent incidental change), guilt (acting against one's core role construct), hostility (forcing reality to validate a failed construct). Assessment: Rep Test / rep grid , self-characterisation sketch , fixed-role therapy ; philosophy = constructive alternativism . Skinner & Bandura — the learning machinery Term Whose / what Operant vs respondent B. F. Skinner: operant (emitted, shaped by consequences) vs respondent/classical (elicited reflex). Positive/negative reinforcement Add pleasant / remove aversive — both increase behaviour. Positive/negative punishment Add aversive / remove pleasant — both decrease behaviour (Skinner thought punishment unreliable). Schedules Fixed/variable × ratio/interval; variable-ratio = highest, most extinction-resistant responding (the slot machine). Shaping Reinforcing successive approximations. Extinction / superstition Stop reinforcing → behaviour fades; accidental reinforcement → "superstitious" pigeon behaviour. Functional analysis (A-B-C) Antecedent → Behaviour → Consequence (Skinner's "assessment"). Observational learning Albert Bandura: attention → retention → production → motivation; vicarious reinforcement . Reciprocal determinism Behaviour ↔ personal/cognitive factors ↔ environment, a three-way loop. Self-efficacy (4 sources) Mastery (strongest) → vicarious → verbal persuasion → physiological/emotional state. Self-regulation / self-system Internal standards + self-judgement; later moral disengagement , collective efficacy . Trait, facet & temperament terms Term Whose / what Surface vs source trait Cattell: visible cluster vs underlying causal factor (16 source traits → 16PF). Erg / sentiment / attitude Cattell's dynamic traits: ergs (innate drives), sentiments (learned), attitudes. Fluid vs crystallised intelligence Cattell: raw reasoning vs accumulated knowledge. PEN Hans Eysenck: Psychoticism, Extraversion, Neuroticism (EPI → EPQ); biological, arousal-based. Big Five / OCEAN Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, Neuroticism (Goldberg coined "Big Five"; NEO-PI-R (Paul Costa and Robert McCrae)). HEXACO Ashton & Lee: 6 factors, adds Honesty-Humility (low H = the dark triad). BIS / BAS Gray's Reinforcement Sensitivity: BIS (punishment → anxiety), BAS (reward → impulsivity). Locus of control / I-E Scale Julian Rotter (internal vs external; from expectancy × reinforcement value). Sensation seeking / SSS Zuckerman: thrill-and-adventure, experience, disinhibition, boredom susceptibility. Learned helplessness / optimism Martin Seligman; explanatory style = internal–external × stable–unstable × global–specific. Flow Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi: challenge matches skill → absorbed engagement. EAS temperament Buss & Plomin: Emotionality, Activity, Sociability. Inhibited / uninhibited Jerome Kagan's infant temperament (precursor of introversion). Easy / difficult / slow-to-warm-up Alexander Thomas & Stella Chess's temperament types; goodness of fit . Fast glossary (one line each, A–Z) Last-mile recall: every nameable personality term/theorist on this page reduced to a single line and its author, alphabetical so you can self-test by covering the right column. If a name fires but the definition doesn't, that is the gap to drill. Term One-line definition (and who) Actualising tendency Innate drive of every organism to maintain and enhance itself (Carl Rogers). Anal stage 1–3 yrs, toilet training; fixation → retentive (orderly/stingy) or expulsive (messy) (Freud). Anima / animus The inner feminine in a man / masculine in a woman (Carl Jung). Archetype Universal inherited image in the collective unconscious (Jung). Attachment / Strange Situation Innate secure-base bond (John Bowlby); measured by the Strange Situation (Mary Ainsworth). Basic anxiety Feeling isolated and helpless in a hostile world (Karen Horney). Birth order First-born dethroned, middle competitive, youngest pampered, only precocious (Alfred Adler). Bobo doll Children imitate observed aggression; learning ≠ performance (Albert Bandura). Cardinal / central / secondary Gordon Allport's three trait levels (dominant / core / situational). Castration anxiety / penis envy Phallic-stage fears of boy / girl in the Oedipus/Electra complex (Freud). Collective unconscious Inherited layer shared by all humanity, holds archetypes (Jung, NOT Freud). Compensation Overcoming felt inferiority by developing strengths (Adler). Conditions of worth "I'll value you only if…"; the root of incongruence (Rogers). Congruence Close match of real self and ideal self (well-being) (Rogers). Constructive alternativism There is always another way to construe any event (Kelly). Creative power of the self We actively shape our own personality, not passive products (Adler). Defence mechanisms Unconscious ego distortions reducing anxiety; catalogued by Anna Freud. Displacement Redirect an impulse onto a safer target (Freud). Epigenetic principle An inborn plan unfolds the stages in fixed order (Erik Erikson). Eros / Thanatos Life instinct (libido) / death instinct (aggression) (Freud). Expectancy × reinforcement value Behaviour potential in social-learning theory (Julian Rotter). Factor analysis Statistic that finds the few dimensions behind many trait ratings (Raymond Cattell; Hans Eysenck). Fictional finalism We live "as if" toward future fictional goals (Adler). Fixation Libido stuck at a psychosexual stage from over/under-gratification (Freud). Five-Factor Model (OCEAN) Five universal trait dimensions; NEO-PI-R (Paul Costa & Robert McCrae; Goldberg "Big Five"). Flow Absorbed state when challenge matches skill (Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi). Free association Say whatever comes, censorship off, to reach the unconscious (Freud). Fully functioning person Open, present-living, organism-trusting, free, creative (Rogers). Functional analysis (A-B-C) Antecedent → Behaviour → Consequence (B. F. Skinner). Functional autonomy A motive becomes independent of its origin (Allport). Good-enough mother / transitional object Adequate (not perfect) mothering; the security blanket (Donald Winnicott). Humours / temperaments Sanguine, choleric, melancholic, phlegmatic (Hippocrates/Galen). Id / ego / superego Pleasure principle / reality principle / internalised morality (Freud). Idealised self / tyranny of the should The impossible self-image we tyrannise ourselves toward (Horney). Identity statuses Diffusion, foreclosure, moratorium, achievement (James Marcia, operationalising Erikson). Identity vs role confusion The adolescent crisis; virtue = fidelity (Erikson). Idiographic / morphogenic Study of the unique individual (Allport) vs nomothetic general laws. Individual psychology Adler's school: striving for superiority, social interest. Individuation Lifelong integration of all parts into the self (Jung). Inferiority / superiority complex Paralysing self-doubt / over-compensation for it (Adler). Internal working model "Are others reliable, am I worthy?" template from early care (Bowlby). Introversion / extraversion Energy turned inward vs outward (coined by Jung). Jonah complex Fear of one's own greatness that blocks self-actualisation (Abraham Maslow). Latent vs manifest content The hidden wish vs the remembered dream (Freud). Learned helplessness → optimism Uncontrollable shock kills effort; flips via explanatory style (Martin Seligman). Lexical hypothesis If a trait matters, language coins a word; ~18,000 words (Allport & Henry Odbert). Libido Sexual life-energy (Freud); de-sexualised general psychic energy (Jung). Locus of control / I-E Scale Outcomes from self (internal) vs fate/others (external) (Rotter). Logotherapy / will to meaning Meaning is the primary motive; existential vacuum if frustrated (Viktor Frankl). Man-the-scientist Each person forms, tests and revises personal constructs (Kelly). Mandala Symbol of the self / wholeness (Jung). Mature defences Sublimation, humour, altruism, suppression, anticipation (George Vaillant). Minnesota twins / heritability Traits ~40–60% heritable; shared environment adds little (Bouchard). Need for achievement (nAch) Motive scored from TAT stories (David McClelland; Murray's needs). Needs & press / personology / TAT Inner needs meet environmental press (Murray & Morgan). Neurotic trends Moving toward / against / away from people (Horney). Oedipus / Electra complex Phallic-stage desire for opposite-sex parent, rivalry with same-sex (Freud). Operant conditioning Behaviour shaped by its consequences (Skinner). Organismic valuing process The gut sense of what is right for the organism (Rogers). Peak experience Moment of ecstasy and wholeness in self-actualisers (Maslow). PEN Psychoticism, Extraversion, Neuroticism; biological (Eysenck). Persona / shadow / self Mask / dark denied side / unifying centre — archetypes (Jung). Personal constructs / Rep Grid Bipolar templates; elicited by the Role Construct Repertory Test (Kelly). Personal vs collective unconscious Your own repressed material vs the inherited human layer (Jung). Positions (paranoid-schizoid / depressive) Early modes of relating to objects, not stages (Melanie Klein). Possible / proprium Proprium = Allport's self, developing through ~7 aspects to propriate striving. Projection Attribute your own impulse to another (Freud). Projective identification Project a part of self into another and induce them to enact it (Klein). Psychosexual stages Oral, anal, phallic, latency, genital (Freud). Q-sort Sort cards for real vs ideal self; correlation = congruence (Rogers; Stephenson's tool). Reaction formation Behave as the opposite of the true impulse (Freud). Reciprocal determinism Behaviour, person and environment shape each other (Bandura). Reinforcement schedules Variable-ratio gives the most extinction-resistant responding (Skinner). Repression vs suppression Unconscious blocking (neurotic) vs deliberate set-aside (mature, conscious) (Freud; Vaillant). Safeguarding tendencies Excuses, aggression, distancing that protect self-esteem (Adler). Self-actualisation Top need; realising one's full potential (Maslow). Self-efficacy Belief one can perform a specific task; strongest source = mastery (Bandura). Self psychology / mirroring Cohesive self, selfobjects, narcissism from failed mirroring (Heinz Kohut). Sensation seeking / SSS Need for varied, novel, intense experience (Zuckerman). Separation-individuation Symbiosis → rapprochement → object constancy (Margaret Mahler). Shaping Reinforcing successive approximations to a target behaviour (Skinner). Social interest (Gemeinschaftsgefühl) Innate feeling of kinship with humanity; mark of health (Adler). Somatotypes Endomorph / mesomorph / ectomorph body-temperament types (Sheldon). Source vs surface trait Deep causal factor vs visible cluster; 16 source traits (Cattell). Splitting All-good / all-bad views of self and others (Klein; Otto Kernberg, borderline). Striving for superiority The one dynamic force: striving toward completion/perfection (Adler). Style of life The unique goal-pursuing pattern formed by ~age 5 (Adler). Sublimation Channel an impulse into a socially valued activity; healthiest classical defence (Freud). Topographic model Conscious / preconscious / unconscious (the iceberg) (Freud). Triguna Sattva (balance), Rajas (activity), Tamas (inertia); VPI (Indian / Samkhya). Tridosha Vata / Pitta / Kapha mind-body constitution (Ayurveda). Type A / B / C / D Hostile-urgent → CHD / relaxed / cancer-prone / distressed (Friedman & Rosenman; Denollet). Ultimate concerns Death, freedom, isolation, meaninglessness (Irvin Yalom). Unconditional positive regard Acceptance with no conditions of worth; the cure (Rogers). Interactionism; ~40–60% (Bouchard's Minnesota twins). Supplements (object relations, existential, type, Indian) Match: good-enough mother, separation-individuation, mirroring/self, borderline organisation/TFP, positions. Donald Winnicott, Margaret Mahler, Heinz Kohut, Otto Kernberg, Melanie Klein. John Bowlby vs Mary Ainsworth, who gave the theory and who the Strange Situation? Bowlby = theory (secure base, internal working model); Ainsworth = Strange Situation + the three styles (Main added disorganised). What did Harry Harlow's monkeys prefer, and what does it prove? The cloth (comfort) over the wire (feeding) mother; attachment is about contact comfort, not food. Viktor Frankl, May, Irvin Yalom, own each by a phrase. Logotherapy/will to meaning; the daimonic/meaning of anxiety; four ultimate concerns (death, freedom, isolation, meaninglessness). Triguna's three gunas and the test that measures them? Sattva (balance), Rajas (activity), Tamas (inertia); the Vedic Personality Inventory (VPI). Sheldon vs Ernst Kretschmer? Sheldon = somatotypes (endo/meso/ecto); Kretschmer = body build linked to psychosis type. Recap — self-test. If you can answer these cold, you own the spine, the named layer and the rival-theory discriminations. Re-test the misses, then run "All the MCQ traps" and the A–Z glossary once more the night before. That sequence (recall → trap discrimination → glossary sweep) is the highest-yield last-mile routine for this domain. Companion pages: the compact version is in the general-psych notes (§10) ; the one-line testable list is in the textbook's Rapid Recall ; the personality tests in depth (MMPI/16PF/NEO/projectives, scoring) are on the tests deep-dive . title: Social & General Psychology
text: Social & General Psychology One consolidated revision chapter for the whole domain: the foundational ("general") psychology of perception, attention, memory, learning, emotion, motivation, intelligence, cognition, personality, development, consciousness and stress, and the full social-psychology arc from research methods through social cognition, attribution, the self, attitudes, prejudice, attraction, influence, prosocial behaviour, aggression and groups, closing with the landmark experiments walked through and a fast A–Z glossary. Anchored to Baron & Branscombe's Social Psychology and standard general-psychology texts; every named effect, theorist, date, table, mnemonic and MCQ trap from both source sets is preserved. The dominant question type NIMHANS and MET test is which name goes with which effect , so the lookalike pairs are flagged throughout in trap boxes. Read it like a textbook, then drill the traps and glossary. In this book Psychology as a science: methods & perspectives Sensation & perception Attention Memory Learning Cognition: thinking, language & social cognition Emotion Motivation Intelligence Personality Developmental psychology Consciousness & sleep Stress, coping & health Social perception & attribution The self Attitudes & persuasion Stereotyping, prejudice & discrimination Attraction, relationships & love Social influence: conformity, compliance, obedience Prosocial behaviour (helping) Aggression Groups & individuals Landmark studies, walked through Schools & history of psychology The MCQ traps, collected Fast glossary (A–Z) 1. Psychology as a science: methods & perspectives What the field claims. Social psychology is the scientific study of how the thoughts, feelings and behaviour of individuals are influenced by the actual, imagined or implied presence of others (Gordon Allport's classic definition). The key word is scientific : it settles questions by study, not intuition. The governing insight, repeated throughout, is the power of the situation : ordinary people help, conform, obey and aggress far more because of where they are and who is around than because of fixed traits. That theme, situation over disposition, returns in obedience (Stanley Milgram), bystander apathy (Bibb Latané & John Darley) and attribution (the fundamental attribution error is precisely our failure to see it). The role of theory. A theory is an integrated set of principles that explains and predicts observed events. Good science runs a loop: a theory generates a falsifiable hypothesis ; a study tests it; results refine or refute it. A theory is never "proven", only supported or disconfirmed. The core research methods Method What you do Strength / limit Experimental Manipulate one factor (the independent variable, IV ), hold all else constant, measure the effect on the dependent variable, DV . Use random assignment to conditions. The only method that establishes cause and effect . Limit: artificiality, low external validity if over-controlled. Correlational Measure two or more variables as they naturally occur and see if they covary (correlation coefficient, −1 to +1). Good for real-world variables you cannot ethically manipulate. Limit: correlation ≠ causation (direction problem + third-variable problem). Survey Ask a representative sample questions to describe a population's attitudes/behaviour. Cheap, broad. Limit: sampling bias, wording effects, social-desirability responding. Systematic / naturalistic observation Watch and record behaviour as it occurs without intervening (e.g. counting jaywalkers). High realism. Limit: no control, observer effects, no causal claim. High-yield The IV is the cause you dial (the knob), the DV the effect you read off (the dial). Random assignment is what lets you claim the knob, not pre-existing differences between people, moved the dial; correlational work has no knob, so it cannot tell you which dial drives. A mediator is the mechanism between cause and effect, explaining why (frustration → anger → aggression: anger mediates). A moderator changes the strength or direction of a relationship, telling you when / for whom it holds (heat raises aggression more for provoked people). A meta-analysis statistically combines many studies to estimate the true effect size. Ethics, deception and replication Because the true purpose can change behaviour, social psychology often uses deception (a cover story), permitted only under strict safeguards: informed consent , the right to withdraw, minimising harm, and a thorough debriefing that reveals the true purpose and removes any after-effects. An Institutional Review Board / ethics committee must approve the study first. The field also takes its replication crisis seriously: a finding is trusted only when independent labs replicate it, which is why classics (Stanley Milgram, marshmallow studies) are now discussed alongside their replications and failures. The four perspectives Baron uses Perspective Core claim Cognitive To explain social behaviour, study how people think : notice, store, recall, interpret. The dominant modern lens (schemas, heuristics, attribution live here). Evolutionary Some tendencies (mate choice, helping kin, fear of strangers) were shaped by natural selection for survival/reproduction. Social neuroscience Links social behaviour to brain and biology (fMRI, hormones): amygdala in out-group fear, oxytocin in trust. Cultural / multicultural Many findings hold differently across cultures; must test whether an effect is universal or culture-bound (individualist vs collectivist). High-yield The researcher is also a thinker prone to the very biases the field studies, so methods (random assignment, double-blind procedures, pre-registration, replication) exist partly to fence out the researcher's expectancy bias / experimenter effects. NIMHANS asks methods crisply: name the only method that proves causation (experimental), say why correlation cannot (third-variable + directionality), and distinguish mediator (the why ) from moderator (the when/for whom ); also the purpose of debriefing after deception and what an ethics board protects. Lock: Gordon Allport's definition = "actual, imagined or implied presence of others"; IV = manipulated, DV = measured; a theory is supported or disconfirmed, never proven; four perspectives = cognitive · evolutionary · social neuroscience · cultural. 2. Sensation & perception Sensation is detecting raw stimulus energy at the receptors; perception is the brain organising and interpreting it. Transduction converts stimulus energy into neural signals. Psychophysics (thresholds) Concept Meaning Absolute threshold Smallest intensity detectable 50% of the time Difference threshold (JND) Smallest detectable change between two stimuli (50% of the time) Weber's law The JND is a constant proportion of the stimulus, not a fixed amount Fechner's law Sensation grows with the logarithm of stimulus intensity Stevens' power law Sensation is a power function of intensity (often fits better than Fechner) Subliminal / priming Stimuli below the absolute threshold can still prime responses Signal detection theory Detection is a decision under uncertainty, not a fixed threshold. Four outcomes: hit , miss , false alarm , correct rejection . d-prime (d′) measures true sensitivity; beta is the response criterion (willingness to say "yes"). Motivation and expectation shift beta, not sensitivity. Theories of perception High-yield The two camps: Gibson's direct / bottom-up theory (the stimulus itself carries enough information; perception is data-driven) versus Gregory's constructivist / top-down theory (perception is an active hypothesis built from prior knowledge and inference). Most modern views combine both. Gestalt organisation, depth & constancy "The whole is greater than the sum of its parts." Gestalt laws: proximity, similarity, closure, continuity (good continuation), common fate, figure-ground, prägnanz (simplicity). Founders: Max Wertheimer, Kurt Koffka, Wolfgang Köhler . Binocular depth cues: retinal disparity, convergence. Monocular cues: relative size, interposition, linear perspective, texture gradient, motion parallax, aerial perspective. Perceptual constancies: size, shape, colour, brightness, the object looks stable despite a changing retinal image. Feature integration theory (Anne Treisman): a preattentive stage detects individual features in parallel, then focused attention binds them into a whole object; failed binding produces illusory conjunctions . Pattern recognition & perceptual set Template, prototype and feature-detection theories of recognition; Irving Biederman's recognition-by-components (geons) builds objects from basic 3D primitives. Perceptual set / expectancy: context, motivation, culture and prior knowledge bias what we perceive (top-down). Illusions: Müller-Lyer, Ponzo, Ames room, moon illusion, Kanizsa triangle (illusory contours), the McGurk effect (vision alters what we hear). Illusions reveal the brain's interpretive shortcuts. 3. Attention Attention is the selective allocation of limited processing capacity. The big debate: where in the stream does selection happen (early vs late), and how much capacity is there (bottleneck vs flexible resources)? Bottleneck / filter models (where does selection happen?) Model Claim Donald Broadbent (1958, early selection) A single filter blocks unattended input early , by physical features (pitch, location), before meaning. Based on Colin Cherry's dichotic-listening / shadowing work. Anne Treisman (1964, attenuation) The filter attenuates (turns down) rather than fully blocks; high-priority words with low thresholds (your name, "fire") still break through. Deutsch & Deutsch / Norman (late selection) All input is fully processed for meaning; selection happens late , at the response/awareness stage. Johnston & Heinz (multimode) Selection is flexible, early or late depending on task demands, but later selection costs more capacity. Capacity / resource models (how much is there?) Model Claim Daniel Kahneman (1973, single capacity) One limited pool of effort allocated across tasks; arousal changes the pool size; an allocation policy decides where it goes. Wickens (multiple resources) Several separate pools (visual vs auditory, verbal vs spatial); two tasks interfere most when they draw on the same pool (why you can drive and listen but not read and listen). Norman & Bobrow Data-limited (poor stimulus quality) vs resource-limited (available attention) performance. Lavie (perceptual load theory) High load → early selection (no spare capacity, distractors filtered); low load → spare capacity spills onto distractors (late). Reconciles the early/late debate. Spatial / visual attention & control Spotlight model (Michael Posner): attention is a movable spotlight enhancing processing wherever it points. Zoom-lens (Eriksen): it widens or narrows, trading area for resolution. Posner cueing paradigm: a valid cue speeds detection, an invalid one slows it. Endogenous (voluntary, goal-driven, central cue) vs exogenous (reflexive, stimulus-driven, peripheral cue) orienting; phases: disengage → move → engage. Feature integration theory (Anne Treisman): preattentive parallel feature registration, then focused attention binds features; feature search ("pop-out") is parallel and fast, conjunction search is serial; failed binding = illusory conjunctions. Guided search (Wolfe) refines FIT: top-down knowledge guides attention to likely targets. Automatic vs controlled (Schneider & Richard Shiffrin): automatic is fast, parallel, effortless, hard to suppress (Stroop happens because reading is automatic); controlled is slow, serial, effortful, flexible; practice automatises a skill. Supervisory Attentional System (Norman & Shallice): routine action runs on automatic schemas via contention scheduling; the SAS (frontal) intervenes only for novel/risky situations; failures → action slips / capture errors. Types: selective (one source), divided (across tasks), sustained (vigilance), alternating/switching (toggle, with a switch cost). Key phenomena Cocktail-party effect (Cherry): follow one voice yet still detect your own name in an ignored stream. Stroop effect: naming the ink colour of a colour-word is slowed because reading is automatic. Inattentional blindness (Simons & Chabris invisible-gorilla) and change blindness : without attention, even large changes go unnoticed. Attentional blink: in rapid serial visual presentation a second target is missed ~200–500 ms after the first. Vigilance decrement (Mackworth's clock test): sustained-attention performance declines over time, faster when signals are rare. Psychological refractory period: a second response is delayed when two stimuli arrive close together (evidence for a central bottleneck). Spatial neglect: right-parietal damage leaves patients ignoring the left side of space (a clinical breakdown of spatial attention). Trap The cocktail-party effect (hearing your name in an unattended conversation) supports late /attenuation selection, NOT Broadbent's early filter, the most common attention MCQ. Broadbent = early/physical; Anne Treisman = attenuation; Deutsch-Norman = late/meaning; Lavie = depends on load. Feature search pops out (parallel); conjunction search is serial. 4. Memory Multi-store model (Atkinson-Shiffrin) Sensory memory → short-term/working memory → long-term memory, with attention and rehearsal as the gates. Store Capacity / duration Sensory: iconic (visual) Large; ~0.25–1 s (George Sperling's partial-report) Sensory: echoic (auditory) ~2–4 s Short-term memory 7 ± 2 items (Miller), ~15–30 s; chunking expands it Long-term memory Effectively unlimited, durable Working memory (Baddeley & Hitch) Four parts: central executive (control), phonological loop (verbal/acoustic), visuospatial sketchpad (visual/spatial), and the episodic buffer (added 2000, integrates information across systems). Types of long-term memory Explicit / declarative (conscious): episodic (events) and semantic (facts, meanings). Implicit / non-declarative (unconscious): procedural (skills), priming, classical conditioning. Processes, forgetting & distortion Encoding → storage → retrieval. Levels of processing (Fergus Craik & Robert Lockhart): deep semantic encoding beats shallow. Forgetting: decay; interference (proactive = old disrupts new; retroactive = new disrupts old); cue-dependent / retrieval failure; encoding failure. Ebbinghaus forgetting curve: rapid early loss then levelling; spacing and overlearning slow it. Serial position effect: primacy (LTM) + recency (STM); a delay wipes recency, not primacy. Reconstructive memory: Frederic Bartlett (schemas distort recall, "War of the Ghosts"); Elizabeth Loftus (misinformation effect, leading questions reshape memory). Amnesia: anterograde (cannot form new memories, e.g. H.M.) vs retrograde (cannot recall old). Korsakoff = thiamine deficiency + confabulation. Retrieval, cues & enhancement Encoding specificity (Endel Tulving): retrieval is best when recall cues match encoding cues. Context-dependent (same place) and state-dependent (same mood/physiological state) memory; mood-congruent recall. Recall vs recognition vs relearning (savings) as measures of retention; recognition is usually easier than recall. Flashbulb memories: vivid, confident memories of shocking events, felt accurate but still prone to distortion. Tip-of-the-tongue = retrieval failure with partial access. Spacing and testing effects: spaced practice and active retrieval beat massed re-reading. Consolidation: the hippocampus binds new memories; sleep aids consolidation; reconsolidation makes reactivated memories briefly editable. 5. Learning Classical conditioning (Pavlov) A neutral stimulus paired with an unconditioned stimulus (UCS) becomes a conditioned stimulus (CS) eliciting a conditioned response (CR). Phases: acquisition, extinction, spontaneous recovery, generalisation, discrimination, higher-order conditioning. Watson's Little Albert = conditioned fear. Garcia effect = taste aversion learned in one trial over a long delay (biological preparedness). Operant conditioning (Thorndike, Skinner) Thorndike's law of effect : responses followed by satisfaction are stamped in. B. F. Skinner formalised it. Add (positive) Remove (negative) Increase behaviour (reinforcement) Positive reinforcement (give a reward) Negative reinforcement (remove an aversive) Decrease behaviour (punishment) Positive punishment (add an aversive) Negative punishment (remove a reward) High-yield Schedules of reinforcement: Fixed Ratio, Variable Ratio, Fixed Interval, Variable Interval. Variable Ratio gives the highest, steadiest rate and the most resistance to extinction (gambling). Ratio beats interval; variable beats fixed. Shaping = reinforcing successive approximations. Premack principle = a high-frequency behaviour reinforces a low-frequency one ("eat your vegetables, then dessert"). Cognitive & observational learning Edward Tolman: latent learning + cognitive maps (rats learned the maze without reinforcement). Wolfgang Köhler: insight learning (chimps solved problems suddenly, the "aha"). Albert Bandura: observational learning / modelling (Bobo doll); steps = attention, retention, reproduction, motivation. Martin Seligman: learned helplessness; biological constraints (preparedness) limit what can be conditioned. High-yield Rescorla-Wagner model: conditioning depends on surprise / prediction error , not mere pairing; the CS must reliably predict the UCS. Explains blocking (a new cue learns nothing if an existing cue already predicts the UCS) and the contingency (not just contiguity) requirement, Robert Rescorla showed the CS must signal information. More terms: stimulus generalisation vs discrimination ; spontaneous recovery of an extinguished CR; overshadowing (a salient cue overshadows a weak one); latent inhibition (a pre-exposed stimulus is harder to condition). Operant: escape vs avoidance learning, discriminative stimulus (signals when a response pays off), extinction burst , and the partial-reinforcement extinction effect (intermittently reinforced behaviour resists extinction). 6. Cognition: thinking, language & social cognition Thinking, problem-solving & decision making Concepts & categories: classical (defining features) vs prototype vs exemplar theories; we categorise by comparison to a best example (prototype); basic-level categories (Eleanor Rosch). Problem solving: algorithms (guaranteed, slow) vs heuristics (fast rules of thumb); strategies = means-end analysis, working backward, analogy; insight vs incremental search; incubation. Barriers: fixation, mental set, functional fixedness. Decision making: System 1 (fast, intuitive) vs System 2 (slow, deliberate). Reasoning: deductive (general → specific, logically certain) vs inductive (specific → general, probabilistic); confirmation bias and belief bias distort it. Mental imagery: Shepard & Metzler's mental rotation, imagery is analog and spatial. Metacognition: thinking about and monitoring one's own thinking. Language Structure: phonemes → morphemes → syntax → semantics → pragmatics. Stages: cooing, babbling, one-word (~12 mo), telegraphic (~24 mo). Noam Chomsky: language acquisition device + universal grammar (nativist). B. F. Skinner: language learned by reinforcement (behaviourist), demolished by Chomsky's review. Benjamin Lee Whorf: linguistic relativity (language shapes thought). Critical/sensitive period (Eric Lenneberg); the case of Genie. Social cognition: how we think about the social world The problem. The social world throws more information at us than we can fully process, so the mind takes shortcuts. We are "cognitive misers" , spending mental effort sparingly, defaulting to fast, cheap strategies that are usually good enough but sometimes badly wrong. Underlying everything is the dual-process view (System 1 vs System 2): automatic processing is fast, effortless, unconscious, emotional; controlled processing is slow, effortful, deliberate, logical. This same automatic/controlled split reappears in persuasion (peripheral vs central route) and prejudice (implicit vs explicit attitudes). Heuristics and the schemas they run on Term Who What it is Heuristics (availability, representativeness, anchoring & adjustment) Tversky & Daniel Kahneman Mental shortcuts: judge by ease of recall (availability) / resemblance to a prototype (representativeness) / clinging to a first value then adjusting too little (anchoring). Schema Frederic Bartlett (social use: Fiske & Taylor) Mental framework guiding what we notice, encode and recall about people/situations. Priming — A recently activated schema shapes the next interpretation, even unconsciously. High-yield Availability: you fear plane crashes more than car crashes because crashes make the news and spring to mind easily. Representativeness: told someone is quiet and loves poetry you guess "librarian" over "salesperson" because they fit the prototype, ignoring that salespeople vastly outnumber librarians (base-rate neglect). Anchoring: the first value you hear drags your estimate toward it. A schema is the bigger structure these run on; priming switches a schema on so it colours what comes next. Schemas bias three things, attention , encoding (usually schema-consistent info, though wildly inconsistent info also grabs attention) and retrieval , and they show the perseverance effect (beliefs survive even after the evidence that created them is discredited; first impressions are sticky). The biases of social thought Term Who What it is Self-fulfilling prophecy Robert Merton An expectation makes itself come true by changing behaviour (basis of the Pygmalion / Rosenthal effect). Counterfactual thinking Kahneman & Amos Tversky Imagining "what might have been"; near-misses sting most (the bronze medallist is happier than the silver). Optimistic / unrealistic-optimism bias Neil Weinstein We think bad things are less likely to happen to us than to others. Negativity bias — Negative info weighs more heavily than equally strong positive info. Planning fallacy Kahneman & Tversky We chronically underestimate how long our own tasks will take. Magical thinking — Assumptions defying causality (laws of contagion / similarity; won't eat fudge shaped like dog faeces). Thought suppression & rebound effect Daniel Wegner Trying not to think of something (the "white bear") makes it intrude more; the monitoring process keeps it primed. Overconfidence barrier — More confidence in our judgements than their accuracy warrants. Base-rate fallacy Kahneman & Tversky Ignoring underlying category frequency for vivid case information (engine behind representativeness errors). Conjunction fallacy ("Linda" problem) Tversky & Kahneman Judging a conjunction ("feminist bank teller") as likelier than its component ("bank teller"), logically impossible. False consensus effect Ross et al. Overestimating how many others share our opinions, traits and choices. False uniqueness effect — Underestimating how common our desirable abilities are. Hindsight bias Baruch Fischhoff "I knew it all along", once an outcome is known we see it as inevitable. Framing effect Tversky & Kahneman The same option chosen/rejected by gain ("90% survive") vs loss ("10% die") wording. Confirmation bias — Seeking and weighting belief-consistent evidence, ignoring disconfirming evidence (keeps schemas alive). Illusion of control Ellen Langer Overestimating personal control over chance outcomes (blowing on dice, picking lottery numbers). Gambler's fallacy / hot-hand — Misreading independent random events as due to "even out" or as streaky. Bias blind spot Emily Pronin Seeing bias in others far more readily than in oneself. Sunk-cost fallacy / loss aversion / prospect theory Kahneman & Tversky Honouring past investment; losses loom larger than equivalent gains; choices framed around a reference point. Affect and cognition cut both ways. Mood shapes thought (positive mood broadens thinking, increases heuristic use; we recall mood-congruent material) and thought shapes mood (appraisal of an event determines how you feel). A good mood makes you a lazier, more shortcut-prone thinker. Trap Two near-twins: availability = judged by how easily examples come to mind (recent, vivid, emotional); representativeness = judged by how well it matches a prototype (neglects base rates). "Easy to recall / vivid" → availability; "fits the stereotype/category" → representativeness. All the heuristics-and-biases items trace to Amos Tversky & Daniel Kahneman. High-yield NIMHANS / clinical map. Wegner's rebound effect is the model behind why "just stop thinking about it" fails in OCD, PTSD intrusions and insomnia, and why acceptance-based therapies (ACT, mindfulness) outperform suppression; pair it with the perseverance effect, which explains why a discredited self-belief ("I'm a failure") persists in depression. Negativity bias + counterfactual thinking underlie depressive rumination ("if only I had…"); depressive realism / pessimistic explanatory style is the opposite of optimistic bias; magical thinking is a named symptom in OCD and schizotypal personality. Cognitive therapy is essentially retraining these automatic biases. 7. Emotion Theory Sequence James-Lange Stimulus → body arousal → you label the emotion ("I tremble, therefore I am afraid") Cannon-Bard Stimulus → arousal AND emotion at the same time (thalamus routes both) Schachter-Singer (two-factor) Arousal + a cognitive label = emotion; same arousal, different label, different emotion Lazarus (appraisal) Cognitive appraisal comes first, then emotion Robert Zajonc Some emotional reactions occur before/without cognition ("preferences need no inferences") Facial-feedback hypothesis (Tomkins; Paul Ekman) Facial expressions feed back and intensify/trigger the felt emotion Ekman: six basic universal emotions (happiness, sadness, anger, fear, surprise, disgust). Components of emotion: physiological arousal, expressive behaviour, conscious experience. Yerkes-Dodson law: performance peaks at moderate arousal (inverted U); harder tasks peak at lower arousal. Robert Plutchik's wheel: eight primary emotions in opposing pairs blending into secondary emotions (joy + trust = love). Dimensional models: Russell's circumplex maps emotion on valence (pleasant–unpleasant) × arousal (high–low). Joseph LeDoux's two roads to fear: a fast "low road" (thalamus → amygdala) for quick reaction, a slow "high road" (via cortex) for accurate appraisal. Cognitive appraisal (Lazarus): primary appraisal (is it relevant/threatening?) then secondary (can I cope?). Display rules: culturally learned norms for when/how to show emotion; basic expressions universal, display rules vary. Emotional intelligence (Peter Salovey & John Mayer; popularised by Daniel Goleman): perceiving, using, understanding, regulating emotion. Trap James-Lange = body first; Cannon-Bard = simultaneous; Schachter-Singer = body + label. This ordering is the single most common emotion-theory exam item. 8. Motivation Instinct theory: behaviour driven by innate biological programs. Drive-reduction (Clark Hull): a need creates a drive; behaviour reduces it to restore homeostasis. Arousal theory: we seek an optimal level of arousal (links to Yerkes-Dodson). Incentive theory: external rewards pull behaviour. Abraham Maslow's hierarchy: physiological → safety → love/belonging → esteem → self-actualisation (later: cognitive, aesthetic, transcendence). Intrinsic vs extrinsic: intrinsic = for its own sake; extrinsic = for a reward. The overjustification effect : paying for an already-enjoyed activity can reduce intrinsic motivation. Self-determination theory (Edward Deci & Richard Ryan): autonomy, competence, relatedness. David McClelland: needs for achievement, affiliation, power (measured via the TAT). ERG theory (Alderfer): Maslow condensed to Existence, Relatedness, Growth; allows frustration-regression. Expectancy theory (Victor Vroom): motivation = expectancy × instrumentality × valence. Goal-setting theory (Locke & Latham): specific, challenging, accepted goals drive performance. Approach-avoidance conflict (Kurt Lewin): approach-approach, avoidance-avoidance, approach-avoidance conflicts. Specific drives: hunger (lateral hypothalamus starts eating, ventromedial stops it; set-point/leptin); arousal/sensation-seeking; achievement motivation (need for achievement vs fear of failure). 9. Intelligence Theorist Model Spearman (1904) Two-factor: general intelligence g + specific s ; invented factor analysis Thurstone (1938) 7 Primary Mental Abilities (no single g) Cattell & Horn Fluid intelligence (Gf, reasoning) vs crystallised (Gc, learned knowledge) J. P. Guilford Structure of Intellect (up to 180 cells); convergent vs divergent thinking Howard Gardner (1983) Multiple intelligences (8): linguistic, logical-mathematical, spatial, musical, bodily-kinaesthetic, interpersonal, intrapersonal, naturalist Robert Sternberg Triarchic: analytical, creative, practical (successful intelligence) Vernon / Carroll (CHC) Hierarchical three-stratum (g → broad → narrow); the dominant modern model Tests: Wechsler (WAIS/WISC, deviation IQ, SD 15), Stanford-Binet (SD 16, SB-5 uses 15), Raven's Progressive Matrices (culture-reduced g). Ratio IQ = (mental age / chronological age) × 100. Flynn effect = rising IQ scores across generations. Heritability estimates are population statistics, not individual destiny. Francis Galton (first to study individual differences, hereditary genius), Binet & Simon (first practical test, mental age), Lewis Terman (Stanford-Binet, longitudinal study of gifted "Termites"). Emotional intelligence (Goleman) broadens the construct beyond academic g. Extremes: intellectual disability (DSM bands; adaptive functioning matters, not just IQ), giftedness, savant syndrome . Heritability & environment: twin/adoption studies; the Flynn effect and stereotype-threat findings show environment matters; reliability/validity and cultural bias are key test-construction concerns. 10. Personality Psychodynamic (Freud) Structure: id (pleasure principle), ego (reality principle), superego (morality/conscience). Topographic: conscious, preconscious, unconscious (the iceberg). Psychosexual stages: oral → anal → phallic (Oedipus/Electra) → latency → genital; fixation shapes the adult personality. Defence mechanisms: repression, denial, projection, displacement, reaction formation, rationalisation, sublimation, regression (Anna Freud catalogued these). Neo-Freudians Carl Jung: collective unconscious, archetypes, introversion/extraversion. Alfred Adler: inferiority complex, striving for superiority, birth order. Karen Horney: basic anxiety, womb envy (countered Sigmund Freud). Erik Erikson: psychosocial stages (see Development). Trait theories Theorist Model Gordon Allport Cardinal, central, secondary traits Raymond Cattell 16 Personality Factors (16PF), via factor analysis Hans Eysenck Three dimensions: extraversion, neuroticism, psychoticism (PEN) Costa & Robert McCrae Big Five / OCEAN: Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, Neuroticism Humanistic & social-cognitive Carl Rogers: self-concept, congruence (real vs ideal self), unconditional positive regard, the fully functioning person. Abraham Maslow: self-actualisation (see Motivation). Albert Bandura: reciprocal determinism (behaviour ↔ person ↔ environment), self-efficacy. Julian Rotter: locus of control (internal vs external). High-yield Assessment: projective tests (Rorschach inkblots, TAT) tap the unconscious; objective inventories (MMPI, 16PF, NEO-PI) are self-report and standardised. 11. Developmental psychology Theorist Stages / idea Jean Piaget (cognitive) Sensorimotor (0–2, object permanence) → preoperational (2–7, egocentrism, no conservation) → concrete operational (7–11, conservation) → formal operational (11+, abstract). Schemas, assimilation, accommodation. Erik Erikson (psychosocial) 8 crisis stages: trust v mistrust → autonomy v shame → initiative v guilt → industry v inferiority → identity v role confusion → intimacy v isolation → generativity v stagnation → integrity v despair. Lawrence Kohlberg (moral) Preconventional (punishment/reward) → conventional (social approval, law and order) → postconventional (social contract, universal ethics). Lev Vygotsky (sociocultural) Zone of proximal development, scaffolding, the social origin of thought (more-knowledgeable other). Sigmund Freud (psychosexual) See Personality. Attachment (John Bowlby; Ainsworth's Strange Situation): secure, insecure-avoidant, insecure-resistant/ambivalent, and disorganised (Main & Solomon). Harry Harlow = contact comfort. Temperament (Alexander Thomas & Stella Chess): easy, difficult, slow-to-warm-up. Nature vs nurture & epigenetics; maturation vs learning; continuous vs stage (discontinuous) views; critical vs sensitive periods. Theory of mind (false-belief / Sally-Anne task, ~4 yrs); Vygotsky vs Piaget on private speech and the social origin of thought. Parenting styles (Diana Baumrind): authoritative, authoritarian, permissive, neglectful. Lifespan: Paul Baltes' lifespan perspective; Kübler-Ross stages of grief; emerging adulthood (Arnett); fluid decline vs crystallised stability in ageing. Moral development: Carol Gilligan's ethic-of-care critique of Kohlberg; Piaget's heteronomous → autonomous morality. Trap Conservation (quantity stays the same despite shape change) appears in concrete operational , not preoperational. Object permanence is the sensorimotor milestone. 12. Consciousness & sleep Sleep stages: NREM 1 (theta, hypnagogic) → NREM 2 (sleep spindles, K-complexes) → NREM 3 (delta, deep/slow-wave) → REM (paradoxical: brain active, body paralysed, dreaming); ~90-minute cycles, REM lengthens toward morning. Circadian rhythm: ~24-hour cycle, governed by the suprachiasmatic nucleus; melatonin from the pineal gland. Dream theories: Sigmund Freud (wish fulfilment, manifest vs latent content); activation-synthesis (Hobson & McCarley, brain makes sense of random REM activity); information-processing/consolidation. Sleep disorders: insomnia, narcolepsy, sleep apnoea, night terrors (NREM) vs nightmares (REM), somnambulism. Altered states: hypnosis, meditation, psychoactive drugs (depressants, stimulants, hallucinogens, opioids) altering consciousness via neurotransmitters. Theories of hypnosis: Hilgard's neodissociation ("hidden observer") vs the social-cognitive/role-enactment view. Functions of sleep: restoration, energy conservation, memory consolidation; sleep deprivation effects. Drug concepts: tolerance, dependence, withdrawal, the reward pathway (dopamine, nucleus accumbens). Consciousness debates: the "hard problem"; the cognitive unconscious; global workspace theory. 13. Stress, coping & health Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome: alarm → resistance → exhaustion. Richard Lazarus & Susan Folkman: primary appraisal (is it a threat?) then secondary appraisal (can I cope?). Problem-focused coping (change the stressor) vs emotion-focused coping (manage the feeling). Physiology: the HPA axis and sympathetic "fight-or-flight" (Cannon); cortisol as the chronic-stress hormone. Type A (competitive, hostile, time-urgent) vs Type B; hostility links to heart disease. Buffers: social support, perceived control, optimism, hardiness (Suzanne Kobasa: commitment, control, challenge). Stressors: Holmes & Rahe Social Readjustment Rating Scale (life-change units); daily hassles vs uplifts (Lazarus); acute vs chronic stress. Tend-and-befriend (Taylor): an alternative to fight-or-flight, oxytocin-linked, more often described in women. Health: psychoneuroimmunology (stress suppresses immunity); the biopsychosocial model; learned optimism (Martin Seligman). 14. Social perception & attribution The problem. To navigate other people we must answer two questions: what are they feeling now (read from nonverbal cues) and why did they do that (attribution). Social perception is how we form impressions and infer causes from limited information. Nonverbal communication Before a word is spoken we read nonverbal channels : facial expressions (Paul Ekman's six basic emotions are largely universal), eye contact (gaze), body language and posture, touch , and paralanguage (tone, pace, pauses). These leak information the person may not mean to send, which is why we often trust the nonverbal over the verbal. Baron's cues to deception : microexpressions (fleeting true feelings flashing before they are masked), interchannel discrepancies (the face says one thing, the hands or voice another), and changes in eye contact and linguistic style. Despite all this, people detect lies barely above chance, because liars control the easy channels and we over-trust the face. Nonverbal "leakage" (Ekman & Friesen): true feelings escape through the channels we control least (legs, feet, voice pitch) while we manage the face. Attribution: explaining behaviour Theory / term Who What it is Attribution theory Fritz Heider We explain behaviour as internal (disposition) or external (situation); the person as "naïve psychologist." Correspondent inference theory Jones & Davis We infer a trait from acts that are freely chosen, unexpected and low in social desirability. Covariation model Harold Kelley Attribution uses consensus, consistency & distinctiveness; high all three → situation/stimulus; low consensus + low distinctiveness + high consistency → the person. Plus the discounting principle (downweight a cause if other plausible causes are present) and the augmenting principle (upweight a cause that produced an act despite obstacles). High-yield Walk Kelley's three Cs. Your friend laughs at a comedian. Consensus: does everyone laugh? Distinctiveness: does she laugh only at this comedian? Consistency: does she laugh every time? High on all three → it's the comedian (external); low consensus + low distinctiveness + high consistency → it's her (internal). Fritz Heider gave the basic internal/external split; Edward E. Jones & Keith Davis asked when an act reveals a true trait; Kelley added the data-driven rule. The two-step attribution model (Gilbert): we first automatically make a dispositional inference, then effortfully correct for the situation, and the correction fails when we are busy or tired, which is why the FAE is so robust. The attributional biases Term Who What it is Fundamental attribution error (correspondence bias) coined by Lee Ross Over-blaming others' character, under-weighting their situation. Actor–observer effect Jones & Richard Nisbett My acts = situation; your acts = your character. Self-serving bias — My success = me; my failure = bad luck/situation. (Better-than-average effect: most rate themselves above average, a statistical impossibility en masse.) Just-world hypothesis Melvin Lerner Belief that people get what they deserve → blaming the victim. Defensive attribution — Blaming a victim more as consequences worsen and as we resemble the victim less, to feel safe ("it couldn't happen to me"). Ultimate attribution error Thomas Pettigrew The FAE applied to groups : an out-group member's bad act is blamed on disposition, their good act explained away as luck/exception. The cognitive cement of prejudice. Facial-feedback hypothesis Tomkins; Paul Ekman Your facial expression feeds back to intensify/trigger the felt emotion. Thin slices Ambady & Robert Rosenthal Surprisingly accurate judgements from very brief (seconds) exposure to behaviour. Impression formation & management Solomon Asch showed first impressions form fast and that some traits are central (swapping "warm" for "cold" transforms the whole impression, while "polite/blunt" barely moves it). The primacy effect means early information weighs most. Baron contrasts Asch's configural / gestalt view (traits fuse into a whole) with Norman Anderson's information-integration / averaging model (we mentally average the weighted values of each trait). We also lean on an implicit personality theory (a lay assumption about which traits go together, "warm people are also generous"), which is how one central trait drags the rest, and on the halo effect (Edward Thorndike: one global positive impression bleeds into ratings of unrelated traits). On the flip side, impression management (self-presentation) is our effort to control the impression others form of us, a theme Erving Goffman framed dramaturgically (life as theatre, front-stage vs back-stage); tactics include self-promotion (look competent), ingratiation (flattery, agreement) and self-deprecation . Trap The attribution swap: FAE (Ross) = judging others (blame the person, ignore their situation); actor–observer (Edward E. Jones & Richard Nisbett) = the gap between explaining your own acts (situation) vs others' acts (character); self-serving = explaining your own outcomes (credit success, dodge blame for failure). Read whose behaviour and whose outcome the stem is about. Separately, Solomon Asch (configural, central traits reorganise the whole) vs Anderson (averaging the weighted trait values). High-yield NIMHANS / clinical map. Depression's negative (pessimistic) attributional style (internal, stable, global for failures) is the mirror image of the self-serving bias, which depressed people lose . The just-world belief explains victim-blaming in trauma work. The FAE is exactly why we pathologise individuals while underrating their situations, the bias clinical formulation tries to correct. Attribution models in order: Fritz Heider (naïve psychologist, internal/external) → Edward E. Jones & Keith Davis (correspondent inference) → Harold Kelley (covariation three Cs). 15. The self The problem. The self is both the thinker and the thing thought about. How do we build a self-concept (content, "who am I"), set our self-esteem (evaluation, "how do I feel about who I am"), and protect that esteem? The recurring finding is that the self is fundamentally social : we know ourselves largely by comparison to, and reflection in, others. Building the self-concept (content side) Term Who What it is Looking-glass self Charles Cooley We build the self-concept from how we imagine we appear to others; the self as a social reflection. The "I" and the "me" William James / G.H. Mead The self as both knower/actor ("I") and object known/evaluated ("me"). Self-reference effect Rogers et al. Information processed in relation to the self is remembered better; the self is a powerful memory organiser. Self-schema Hazel Markus Cognitive generalisations about the self that organise and guide processing of self-relevant information. Possible selves Markus & Nurius Images of what we might become (hoped-for, feared, expected) that motivate and guide behaviour. Self-complexity Patricia Linville Many distinct self-aspects buffer mood swings; a simple self lets one bad domain flood the whole self. Self-concept clarity Jennifer Campbell How clearly, confidently and consistently self-beliefs are defined; low clarity links to low self-esteem. Sociometer theory Mark Leary Self-esteem is an internal gauge of social acceptance/belonging; it drops when we feel rejected. Objective self-awareness theory Duval & Wicklund Focusing attention on the self (a mirror, a camera) makes us compare to standards and feel the gap. Self-regulation & ego depletion Roy Baumeister Self-control draws on a limited resource that fatigues with use (the "strength model"; note replication debate). Measuring and protecting the self Theory / term Who What it is Social comparison theory Leon Festinger We evaluate ourselves by comparison to others (upward = motivating but deflating; downward = self-enhancing). Self-perception theory Daryl Bem When attitudes are weak/ambiguous, we infer them by observing our own behaviour ("I'm eating salad, I guess I like salad"). Self-discrepancy theory E. Tory Higgins Actual vs ideal self → dejection (sadness); actual vs ought self → agitation (anxiety, guilt). Self-monitoring Mark Snyder High self-monitors tailor behaviour to the situation; low ones act from inner attitudes. Self-efficacy Albert Bandura Belief in your capacity to carry out the actions a specific task needs. Self-handicapping Berglas & Jones Setting up an excuse in advance (not studying, drinking before a test) to protect self-esteem from possible failure. Self-verification William Swann We seek feedback confirming our existing self-view, even when negative. Self-affirmation theory Claude Steele Affirming a valued part of the self (in another domain) buffers threats to self-integrity. Spotlight effect Thomas Gilovich Overestimating how much others notice and judge us (the stain on your shirt). BIRGing / CORFing Robert Cialdini Basking in reflected glory ("we won") vs cutting off reflected failure (distancing from losers). Terror management theory Greenberg, Pyszczynski & Solomon Awareness of mortality drives us to defend our cultural worldview and bolster self-esteem. The self across cultures (high-yield NIMHANS contrast) Hazel Markus & Shinobu Kitayama drew the field's biggest cultural distinction: the independent self-construal (individualist/Western, the self defined by internal traits, separate, self-promoting) versus the interdependent self-construal (collectivist cultures including India, the self defined by relationships, roles and group harmony). This explains cultural differences in the FAE (weaker in collectivist cultures), self-serving bias, self-enhancement (lower in East Asian samples) and conformity. India is the textbook collectivist/interdependent case. Trap Two self-discrepancy directions (Higgins): falling short of your ideal self (hopes, what you want to be) → dejection (sad). Falling short of your ought self (duties, what you should be) → agitation (anxious). Ideal→sad, ought→anxious. And dissonance vs self-perception: Festinger involves arousal and a strong prior attitude; Bem (this section) involves no arousal, just calm inference from a weak attitude. High-yield NIMHANS / clinical map. Self-efficacy (Bandura) and self-esteem are workhorses of CBT. Self-discrepancy theory (Higgins) models depression (ideal-self gap) vs anxiety (ought-self gap). Self-verification (Swann) explains why people with low self-esteem resist positive feedback and stay in confirming (even abusive) relationships, a real treatment obstacle. Terror management connects to existential anxiety. Most of these terms are esteem-protecting manoeuvres rather than neutral descriptions; the cooler cognitive exceptions are social comparison (Festinger) and self-perception (Bem). 16. Attitudes & persuasion The problem. An attitude is an evaluation of an object along a like–dislike dimension. The classic ABC structure has three components: A ffective (feelings), B ehavioural (action tendencies), C ognitive (beliefs). The two big questions: do attitudes predict behaviour? and how do you change them? Where attitudes come from, and the implicit/explicit split Attitudes form mostly via low-level learning: classical conditioning (an object paired with positive/negative stimuli, including subliminal conditioning and mere exposure ), instrumental conditioning (attitudes earning approval are reinforced), and observational learning / social comparison (adopting the attitudes of models and reference groups). Twin studies show a partly heritable component. Term What it is Explicit attitudes Conscious, reportable, controllable evaluations. Implicit attitudes Automatic, often unconscious evaluations, measured by the Implicit Association Test (IAT) via reaction times; can diverge from what we say, and predict spontaneous behaviour. Functions of attitudes (Daniel Katz): knowledge (organise the world), utilitarian/instrumental (gain reward, avoid punishment), ego-defensive (protect self-esteem), and value-expressive (state who we are). Changing an attitude requires addressing its function (the same surface attitude may be ego-defensive in one person and value-expressive in another). The attitude–behaviour link For decades the embarrassing answer was "barely". The famous demonstration is the LaPiere study : a researcher toured 1930s America with a Chinese couple and was served almost everywhere, yet most of those same establishments later said by mail they would refuse Chinese guests. The resolution came from Martin Fishbein & Icek Ajzen : attitudes predict behaviour best through intentions , shaped by attitudes plus subjective norms plus (in the planned-behaviour update) perceived behavioural control. Attitudes also predict better when strong, specific, accessible and based on direct experience. Persuasion: how attitudes change Theory / term Who What it is Yale attitude-change approach Carl Hovland Who says what to whom: source (credibility, attractiveness), message and audience factors. Elaboration Likelihood Model (ELM) Petty & John Cacioppo Persuasion via the central route (thoughtful scrutiny of arguments, when motivated & able) vs the peripheral route (surface cues: attractiveness, length, expert badge). Heuristic-Systematic Model (HSM) Shelly Chaiken Same dual-route idea: systematic (effortful argument analysis) vs heuristic ("experts are right"). Theory of reasoned action / planned behaviour Fishbein & Icek Ajzen Intention (from attitudes + subjective norms + perceived behavioural control) predicts behaviour. Inoculation theory William McGuire A weak counter-argument first "vaccinates" an attitude against later strong attacks. Psychological reactance Jack Brehm Threaten a freedom → people want the forbidden thing more (boomerang effect). Sleeper effect Carl Hovland A low-credibility message has little impact at first but gains force over time as the source is forgotten but the content remembered. Fear appeals — Fear persuades best at moderate levels and only with a clear, doable way to avoid the threat; too much fear triggers denial. Forewarning — Warning people that a persuasion attempt is coming lets them marshal counter-arguments and resist. Need for cognition Cacioppo & Petty A trait, the enjoyment of effortful thinking; high-NFC people are persuaded via the central route, low-NFC via the peripheral. Mere-thought / attitude polarisation Abraham Tesser Merely thinking about an attitude object, without new information, makes the attitude more extreme. Bogus pipeline Jones & Sigall A fake lie-detector that makes people report their true (often less socially desirable) attitudes; a methods trick for measuring real prejudice. LaPiere study Richard LaPiere The classic attitude–behaviour gap: stated prejudice did not match actual service to a Chinese couple. High-yield The dual route, intuitively. When you care and can concentrate (buying a house) you take the central route, weighing real arguments, and the attitude is durable. When you do not care or are distracted (a soft-drink jingle) you take the peripheral route, swayed by who is pretty or how many points were listed, and the attitude is flimsy. ELM (Richard Petty & John Cacioppo) and HSM (Chaiken) are the same insight: central = systematic, peripheral = heuristic, the automatic/controlled split applied to persuasion. Katz's four functions and the sleeper effect are clean single-best-answer items; fear appeals (moderate + efficacy) underpin health-communication design. Cognitive dissonance & consistency theories The most-tested idea in the chapter. When two cognitions clash, or behaviour contradicts an attitude, we feel an unpleasant tension ( dissonance ) and are driven to reduce it, usually by changing the attitude to fit the behaviour . Theory / term Who What it is Cognitive dissonance Leon Festinger Tension from clashing cognitions drives attitude change to reduce it. Insufficient justification / induced compliance Festinger & Carlsmith The $1 group changed their attitude more than the $20 group (less external reward = more dissonance = more internal attitude change). Effort justification Aronson & Mills The harder/more embarrassing the initiation, the more we value the group we joined. Balance theory Fritz Heider We seek consistency among liking relationships (P-O-X triangles; an imbalanced triangle pressures change). Hypocrisy paradigm Aronson et al. Make people publicly advocate a behaviour (e.g. condom use), then remind them of past failures to do it → dissonance drives real behaviour change. Free-choice dissonance Jack Brehm After a hard choice between close options, we boost the chosen and derogate the rejected option ("spreading of alternatives"). High-yield Why $1 beat $20. Participants did a boring task then were paid to tell the next person it was fun. Those paid $20 had a big external reason to lie ("I did it for the money"), so no dissonance, attitude unchanged. Those paid $1 had no good external reason, so the only way to resolve "I said it was fun but I had no reason to lie" was to decide it actually was fun. Less reward, more attitude change. Same logic in effort justification. NIMHANS / clinical: effort justification is one reason expensive/effortful therapy can be valued more (and underlies hazing/cult commitment); reactance (Brehm) explains why heavy-handed advice backfires and is the rationale for motivational interviewing; dissonance is harnessed in attitude-change health interventions. Trap Dissonance vs self-perception: both predict attitude follows behaviour. Leon Festinger (dissonance) = there is arousal/discomfort , applies when the attitude was strong/clear and the behaviour contradicts it. Bem (self-perception) = no arousal , you simply infer the attitude by watching yourself, applies when the attitude was weak or unclear . The deciding clue is whether the stem mentions tension/discomfort (Festinger) or a calm inference (Bem). 17. Stereotyping, prejudice & discrimination The three words kept straight. A stereotype is the cognitive component (a belief about a group's traits). Prejudice is the affective component (a negative feeling toward a group). Discrimination is the behavioural component (unequal treatment). They are the ABC of intergroup bias. Sources of prejudice Theory / term Who What it is Social identity theory Tajfel & Turner Part of our self-esteem comes from group membership → we favour the in-group and derogate the out-group. Minimal group paradigm Henri Tajfel Even arbitrary, meaningless group splits (coin toss, dot-estimation, Klee vs Kandinsky) produce in-group favouritism. Realistic conflict theory Muzafer Sherif Competition over scarce resources breeds intergroup hostility (Robbers Cave); superordinate (shared) goals reduce it. Authoritarian personality Theodor Adorno A rigid, conventional, submissive-to-authority personality (F-scale) prone to prejudice. Right-wing authoritarianism (RWA) Bob Altemeyer Better-validated successor to Adorno: submission to authority + conventionalism + aggression toward sanctioned targets. Social dominance orientation (SDO) Sidanius & Pratto A preference for group-based hierarchy and inequality; predicts prejudice independently of RWA. System justification theory John Jost People are motivated to defend and rationalise the existing social order, even when it disadvantages their own group. Self-image threat & prejudice Fein & Spencer People derogate out-group members more after their own self-esteem is threatened, and doing so restores it. Scapegoat theory (frustration–aggression roots) Frustration is displaced onto a weaker out-group blamed for problems. Integrated Threat Theory (realistic vs symbolic threat) Stephan & Stephan Prejudice is fed by perceived realistic threats (resources, safety) and symbolic threats (values, worldview), plus intergroup anxiety and negative stereotypes. High-yield Identity vs competition vs personality, three engines.
