Social identity (Henri Tajfel & John Turner): bias arises just from categorising people into us/them, no real conflict needed (minimal-group studies prove arbitrary groups suffice). Realistic conflict (Muzafer Sherif): bias arises from real competition over resources, and Robbers Cave showed shared goals dissolve it. Authoritarian personality (Adorno): bias sits inside a personality type . NIMHANS loves to swap these three. Indian-context applications (caste, religion, language as in-group/out-group lines) fit social identity and realistic conflict. The cognitive machinery of stereotypes Term Who What it is Illusory correlation Hamilton & Gifford Perceiving a link between minority-group membership and rare (negative) behaviour that is not really there. Out-group homogeneity effect — "They're all alike"; we see less variability in out-groups than in our own group. Stereotype threat Steele & Aronson Fear of confirming a negative stereotype about your group depresses your performance on the stereotyped task. Stereotype content model Susan Fiske Groups judged on warmth × competence → four emotions: admiration (warm+competent), envy (cold+competent), pity (warm+incompetent), contempt (cold+incompetent). Subtyping — Filing stereotype-disconfirming individuals into a special "exception" subtype, protecting the overall stereotype. Shifting standards Monica Biernat Judging members of different groups against different, group-based yardsticks ("good… for a woman"). The modern, subtle forms (and the cost to targets) Term Who What it is Modern / subtle (aversive) racism — People who endorse equality still hold automatic negative reactions and discriminate when they can attribute it to something else; bias is implicit, not openly avowed. Hostile vs benevolent sexism Glick & Fiske Two-part "ambivalent sexism": hostile (women seeking power are a threat) plus benevolent (women are wonderful but fragile and need protection). Benevolent sounds positive but still keeps women subordinate. Tokenism — A trivial positive act toward an out-group member used as an excuse to then discriminate; also the strain on a lone "token". Glass ceiling — An invisible barrier keeping qualified members of devalued groups out of top positions. Reducing prejudice Theory / term Who What it is Contact hypothesis Gordon Allport Contact reduces prejudice only if four conditions hold: equal status, common goals, intergroup cooperation, institutional support. Jigsaw classroom Elliot Aronson Cooperative learning where each pupil holds one essential piece of the lesson → forces interdependence, cuts prejudice. A practical application of the contact hypothesis. Common in-group identity model (recategorisation) Gaertner & Dovidio Get rival groups to recategorise "us vs them" into a single inclusive "we" → former out-group members now get in-group warmth. Trap Stereotype threat vs self-fulfilling prophecy: stereotype threat (Steele & Aronson) = the target's own anxiety about confirming the stereotype hurts their performance; self-fulfilling prophecy (Merton) = the perceiver's expectation changes how they treat the target, eliciting the expected behaviour. One is driven from inside the target, the other from the outside perceiver. Hostile vs benevolent sexism (Glick & Fiske): the "nice"-sounding one (cherish and protect) is benevolent, still subordinating. Note Steele appears twice across the syllabus: stereotype threat here and self-affirmation in §15. 18. Attraction, relationships & love The problem. Why do we like and love some people and not others, and what holds relationships together? The chapter moves from the cold predictors of initial attraction to theories of love and then to the economic models of why relationships last or end. Predictors of initial attraction Theory / term Who What it is Propinquity (proximity) effect Leon Festinger, Schachter & Back The closer people live or sit, the more likely they form friendships (the Westgate housing study). Mere-exposure effect Robert Zajonc Repeated exposure to a stimulus, by itself, increases liking for it. Similarity–attraction Donn Byrne We like those with similar attitudes (not "opposites attract"); the "law of attraction". Reward / reinforcement-affect model Byrne & Clore We like people associated with rewards, even when they merely happened to be present when something good occurred. Gain–loss theory of attraction Aronson & Linder We are most attracted to someone whose liking for us increases over time (a gain) and most stung when it decreases (a loss). Matching hypothesis Walster & Berscheid We tend to pair with partners of roughly our own level of physical attractiveness. "What is beautiful is good" Dion, Berscheid & Walster The physical-attractiveness stereotype: we assume good-looking people also have better personalities. Evolutionary mate preferences David Buss Across cultures, men weight youth and attractiveness (fertility cues), women status and resources (provisioning); evolved reproductive strategies (parental investment). Reciprocity of liking — We like those who like us; learning someone likes you boosts your liking for them. Need to belong Baumeister & Leary A fundamental motive to form and maintain lasting positive relationships; its frustration harms health and well-being. High-yield Why proximity and exposure come first. You cannot like someone you never encounter, so propinquity (Leon Festinger's housing study: friendships clustered by who lived nearest stairs and mailboxes) sets the pool; mere exposure (Zajonc) does its quiet work, familiarity breeds liking; only then do similarity (Byrne, the real rule, not "opposites attract") and looks filter further. Critique to keep: the evolutionary mate-preference account (Buss) is heavily tested but also heavily criticised, social-role theory (Eagly & Wood) argues the same sex differences fall out of women's restricted access to resources and power, not genes. Know both sides; NIMHANS likes "which explanation." Theories of love Theory / term Who What it is Triangular theory of love Robert Sternberg Intimacy + passion + commitment combine into 7 types: liking (intimacy only), infatuation (passion only), empty (commitment only), romantic (intimacy+passion), companionate (intimacy+commitment), fatuous (passion+commitment), and consummate (all three). Passionate vs companionate love Hatfield & Berscheid Intense arousal and longing (passionate) vs deep affection, trust and care that lasts (companionate). Two-factor theory of love (misattribution of arousal) Dutton & Aron Arousal from a scary suspension bridge gets relabelled as romantic attraction to the person met there. Adult attachment styles Hazan & Shaver Secure / anxious-ambivalent / avoidant styles carried from infant attachment into romantic love. Four-category attachment model Bartholomew & Horowitz Model-of-self × model-of-other gives secure, preoccupied, dismissing-avoidant and fearful-avoidant styles. Why relationships last or end Theory / term Who What it is Social exchange theory Thibaut & Harold Kelley Relationships weighed as rewards minus costs, against a comparison level (CL) and the comparison level for alternatives (CL-alt). Equity theory Walster / Adams We are happiest when our ratio of inputs to outcomes matches the partner's (over- and under-benefit both cause distress). Investment model Caryl Rusbult Commitment = satisfaction + investment size − quality of alternatives. Accommodation: committed partners inhibit retaliation and respond constructively. Communal vs exchange relationships Clark & Mills Communal partners give based on the other's needs without scorekeeping; exchange partners track reciprocity. Social penetration / self-disclosure Altman & Taylor Relationships deepen as self-disclosure grows in breadth and depth ; reciprocal disclosure builds intimacy. Phases of dissolution Steve Duck Break-ups move through stages: intrapsychic → dyadic → social → grave-dressing (constructing the break-up story). High-yield The two-factor love trick. Dutton & Aron's bridge study is misattribution of arousal in action: men who crossed a high, swaying bridge (arousal from fear) were more attracted to the woman who met them there than men on a safe bridge. Arousal + a label (Schachter–Singer's two-factor theory) = the felt emotion. Baron also covers the dark side: loneliness (the painful gap between desired and actual relationships, a health risk), jealousy (evolutionary sex differences: men fear sexual infidelity, women emotional), and social allergens (a partner's small repeated annoyances accumulating into disgust). NIMHANS / clinical: adult attachment (Cindy Hazan & Phillip Shaver) bridges to Bowlby/Ainsworth; the investment model (Rusbult) is the standard frame for why people stay in unsatisfying or abusive relationships (high investment + low alternatives = high commitment despite low satisfaction). Trap The "who studied liking" cluster: Byrne = similarity · Robert Zajonc = mere exposure · Festinger = propinquity · Robert Sternberg = triangular love · Caryl Rusbult = investment model · Dutton & Aron = misattributed arousal (the bridge). These names rotate as each other's distractors; fix one hook per name. 19. Social influence: conformity, compliance, obedience The three levels. Conformity = changing to match a group with no direct request. Compliance = changing in response to a direct request (the sales techniques). Obedience = changing in response to a direct order from an authority. The levels rise from implicit group pressure to explicit command. Conformity & obedience Term Who What it is Conformity Solomon Asch Going along with a unanimous group's obviously wrong answer (line-judging task); ~33% conformity per trial. Norm formation Muzafer Sherif Used the autokinetic illusion (a still dot of light appears to move) to show groups converge on a shared norm. Informational vs normative influence Deutsch & Gerard We conform to be right (informational, especially when uncertain) vs to be liked/accepted (normative). Obedience to authority Stanley Milgram 65% of ordinary people delivered "lethal" 450V shocks when an authority calmly ordered them to continue. Minority influence / conversion Serge Moscovici A consistent minority can shift the majority via genuine private conversion (often delayed, internalised) rather than mere public compliance. Idiosyncrasy credits Edwin Hollander Conforming early earns "credits" a member can later spend on dissent or innovation without rejection. Social impact theory Bibb Latané Influence on a target = a function of the strength , immediacy and number of sources present. What raises or lowers Asch conformity, and kinds of norms. Conformity rises with group size (up to ~3–4, then plateaus) and unanimity , and collapses the moment one ally/dissenter breaks ranks. Baron separates two kinds of social norm (a Cialdini distinction): Term Who What it is Descriptive norms Robert Cialdini et al. What most people actually do ("everyone litters here"). Tell people what is, and they copy it. Injunctive norms Cialdini et al. What most people approve/disapprove of ("littering is wrong"). More durable for changing behaviour. Mindlessness / the "because" effect Ellen Langer A request with any reason ("...because I have to make copies") gains compliance even when the reason is empty. Symbolic social influence — We are influenced by others even when merely imagined or represented (a mental image of a parent's reaction shapes behaviour). High-yield Muzafer Sherif vs Solomon Asch, the two faces of conformity. Sherif used an ambiguous task (how far did the dot move? nobody knows), so people genuinely looked to others, this is informational influence producing real, internalised norm change. Asch used an unambiguous task (which line is longer? obvious), so people who caved did so to avoid standing out, this is normative influence, often just public compliance. Deutsch & Gerard named the two motives. Compliance techniques Term Who What it is Six principles of influence Robert Cialdini Reciprocity, commitment/consistency, social proof, authority, liking, scarcity. Foot-in-the-door Freedman & Fraser Agreement to a small request first → a bigger one later gets agreed to (via commitment/consistency). Door-in-the-face Robert Cialdini A big request refused first → the smaller real request now looks reasonable (reciprocal concession). Lowballing Robert Cialdini Get a commitment at a good price, then raise the cost; people stick to the deal anyway. That's-not-all technique Jerry Burger Add a bonus or drop the price before the person decides → boosts compliance. Pique technique — An unusual request ("can you spare 37 cents?") disrupts automatic refusal and raises compliance by making people think. Disrupt-then-reframe Davis & Knowles A confusing twist followed by a reframe ("it's 300 pennies… that's a bargain!") boosts compliance. Norm of reciprocity Alvin Gouldner We feel obliged to return favours (the engine behind door-in-the-face and free samples). Agentic vs autonomous state Stanley Milgram People shift from acting on their own values (autonomous) to seeing themselves as an authority's tool, not responsible (agentic state), the mechanism of obedience. Trap Foot-in-the-door vs door-in-the-face: FITD = small → big (Jonathan Freedman & Scott Fraser, via consistency); DITF = big → small (Robert Cialdini, via reciprocal concession). Lowballing = get the yes, then change the deal. That's-not-all = sweeten the offer before the yes. Examiners love swapping the direction. High-yield NIMHANS. Milgram and Asch are perennial: lock the headline numbers (Milgram ~65% to maximum voltage; Asch ~33% conformity per trial, ~75% conformed at least once) and the situational factors that reduce obedience (authority less close/legitimate, peers who rebel, victim more present). Minority influence (Moscovici) via consistency is the standard contrast to majority conformity. Clinically, these explain compliance pressures in institutions and the value of even one dissenting ally. 20. Prosocial behaviour (helping) The problem. Why do we help, when do we fail to, and is helping ever truly selfless? The chapter splits into situational work (the bystander effect: why help fails) and motivational work (egoism vs altruism: why we help at all). When help fails: the bystander effect Term Who What it is Bystander effect & 5-step decision model Latané & John Darley More witnesses → less help. Five steps: notice → interpret as emergency → take responsibility → know how to help → decide to act. (Sparked by the Kitty Genovese case.) Diffusion of responsibility Darley & Bibb Latané "Someone else will do it"; responsibility spreads thin in a crowd (fails step 3). Pluralistic ignorance — Everyone stays calm because no one else looks worried, so no one reads it as an emergency (fails step 2). High-yield Why a crowd freezes you. The five-step model is a chain, and the crowd snaps it at two links. At step 2 (interpret) you look around, see calm faces, and conclude it must not be an emergency, that is pluralistic ignorance . At step 3 (take responsibility) , with many present, each assumes someone else will act, that is diffusion of responsibility . More witnesses make both failures more likely, so paradoxically you are less likely to be helped in a big crowd. Expect a scene with a "which step failed" stem. Why we help: egoism vs altruism Term Who What it is Empathy–altruism hypothesis C. Daniel Batson Feeling empathy for the victim produces genuinely selfless helping, aimed at their welfare, not our own relief. Negative-state relief model Robert Cialdini We help to relieve our own bad mood; helping is ultimately egoistic. Arousal: cost–reward model Piliavin et al. A bystander's unpleasant arousal at seeing distress motivates help; we help when costs of helping are low and costs of not helping are high. Empathic joy hypothesis Smith et al. We help partly for the pleasure of having a positive impact; we want feedback that our help worked. Kin selection / reciprocal altruism Hamilton; Trivers Evolutionary: help relatives (shared genes, kin selection) or those likely to return the favour (reciprocal altruism). Norm of social responsibility — A social norm that we should help those who depend on us, regardless of return. Prosocial / altruistic personality — A cluster (empathy, just-world belief, social responsibility, internal locus, low egocentrism) predicting consistent helping. Volunteerism & the functional approach Clary & Snyder Sustained helping is driven by the personal functions it serves (values, understanding, career, social, esteem, protective). Threat-to-self-esteem / reactions to receiving help Nadler & Fisher Receiving aid can feel demeaning and imply inferiority, so recipients sometimes refuse or resent help, especially from a similar other. What boosts helping: similarity to the victim, seeing a helpful model , feeling gratitude , being in a good mood (the "feel-good, do-good" effect ; guilt also raises helping), and the victim being not responsible for their plight. Helping drops with a hurry (the Good Samaritan study, John Darley & Batson: seminary students late for a talk stepped over a slumped man), diffuse responsibility, and ambiguity. Overjustification (over-rewarding helping can undermine the intrinsic motive); defensive helping (helping an out-group condescendingly to maintain the in-group's status). Trap Why we help, egoism vs altruism: C. Daniel Batson (empathy–altruism) = there is true altruism, born of empathy and aimed at the other's welfare. Robert Cialdini (negative-state relief) and Piliavin (arousal:cost-reward) = we ultimately help to fix our own discomfort, so helping is egoistic. That contrast (selfless vs self-serving motive) is the question. 21. Aggression The first distinction. Aggression is behaviour intended to harm another who does not want to be harmed. Types: hostile aggression (driven by anger, the goal is to hurt, often impulsive) vs instrumental aggression (a cold means to another end, money, status), plus relational aggression (harming through gossip, exclusion, reputation). The chapter traces an arc: from a simple drive theory (frustration always causes aggression), through its cognitive reformulation (frustration only readies aggression, cues pull the trigger), to social learning and integrative models. Theory / term Who What it is Frustration–aggression hypothesis John Dollard, Doob, Miller et al. Original strong form: frustration (a blocked goal) always breeds aggression, and aggression always traces to frustration. Reformulated frustration–aggression Leonard Berkowitz Frustration creates only a readiness (negative affect); aggression follows when aggressive cues are present. Weapons effect Berkowitz & LePage The mere presence of a weapon increases aggression, because the weapon is an aggressive cue. Cognitive-neoassociation Leonard Berkowitz Aversive events (heat, pain, frustration) trigger negative affect that automatically primes a network of anger and fight/flight responses. Social learning of aggression Albert Bandura Aggression is learned by observing and imitating models (the Bobo doll studies). General Aggression Model (GAM) Anderson & Bushman Integrative: person + situation inputs → internal state (arousal, affect, cognition) → appraisal → aggressive (or not) act. Excitation-transfer theory Dolf Zillmann Left-over physiological arousal from one source (exercise, a prior fright) intensifies aggression in a later, unrelated provoking situation. Catharsis hypothesis (Freud / Lorenz roots) The idea that venting "drains" aggression. Largely unsupported ; venting tends to raise later aggression. High-yield The arc in one breath. John Dollard et al. said frustration → aggression, full stop, too rigid. Leonard Berkowitz rescued it: frustration only builds a charge of negative affect ( readiness ); whether it discharges depends on aggressive cues , hence the weapons effect (a gun on the table makes you more aggressive). Bandura's Bobo doll added that we also just copy aggressive models. And the popular belief in catharsis is a myth : venting fuels rather than drains aggression, a high-yield "which is false" item. Social & cultural causes, and reduction Term Who What it is Media violence & desensitisation Anderson, Bushman Repeated violent media raises aggressive thoughts, affect and behaviour and blunts emotional response to real violence; primes aggressive scripts. Culture of honour Nisbett & Cohen In cultures (e.g. the US South) where reputation must be defended, insults trigger far more aggression; aggression is culturally shaped. Heat hypothesis Anderson Higher temperatures reliably increase aggression and violent-crime rates. Alcohol myopia Steele & Josephs Alcohol narrows attention to immediate provoking cues and impairs inhibition, disinhibiting aggression. Hostile attribution bias Kenneth Dodge Aggressive individuals over-read others' ambiguous acts as hostile, then retaliate; central to aggressive children and conduct problems. Displaced & triggered displaced aggression — Aggression aimed at a safer target than the real provoker; a minor provocation from that target then triggers an outsized response. Narcissism / threatened egotism Baumeister & Bushman Inflated, unstable high self-esteem (narcissism), not low self-esteem, predicts aggression when the ego is threatened. Confluence model of sexual aggression Malamuth Sexual coercion arises from the confluence of hostile masculinity and impersonal-sex orientation; violent pornography raises acceptance of aggression toward women. Bullying Dan Olweus Repeated aggression against a less powerful target; involves bullies, victims and bystanders. Reducing aggression. Catharsis does not work. What does: punishment only if prompt, certain and proportionate (or it backfires); incompatible responses (humour, empathy, mild non-aggressive feelings that can't co-exist with anger); apology and mitigating information ; cognitive interventions and exposure to non-aggressive models ; and self-regulation training. Frustration (Freud/Lorenz also gave the older instinct view of aggression). Trap Two Berkowitz ideas kept apart: reformulated frustration–aggression (frustration → readiness, cue → act) and cognitive-neoassociation (aversive events prime an anger network) are both his. Do not confuse excitation-transfer (Zillmann) , where arousal carries over from a prior unrelated event, with the weapons effect, where an external cue triggers aggression. And the catharsis hypothesis is largely disproven , examiners frame it as the false option. High-yield NIMHANS. Determinants of aggression as a list: biological (low serotonin, high testosterone, amygdala/prefrontal function, alcohol disinhibition) and situational/social (heat, provocation, crowding, frustration, media/violent models, culture of honour). The catharsis myth and the weapons effect are classic single-best-answer traps. Dodge's hostile attribution bias is core to the clinical model of conduct disorder and is itself a clean attribution-error item. 22. Groups & individuals The problem. What does the mere presence of, or membership in, a group do to the individual, to effort, self-restraint and decision quality? The chapter pairs opposing effects (presence can boost or sap effort; groups can decide better or worse), and the deciding variable is usually whether you are individually identifiable. A group's structure has four ingredients: roles (expected behaviours for a position), status (rank), norms (shared rules), and cohesiveness (the forces binding members). Presence of others: facilitation vs loafing Term Who What it is Social facilitation Norman Triplett; Robert Zajonc An audience or co-actor boosts performance on easy/well-learned tasks but hurts hard/novel ones (Zajonc: arousal strengthens the dominant response). Evaluation apprehension Nickolas Cottrell It is the fear of being judged , not mere physical presence, that creates the facilitation arousal. Social loafing Bibb Latané, Williams & Harkins People exert less effort in a group when individual output cannot be identified (Ringelmann rope-pull roots). Ringelmann effect Max Ringelmann Per-person pull on a rope falls as the group grows, from coordination loss + reduced effort (historical root of loafing). Process loss vs process gain Ivan Steiner Group output usually falls short of the sum of members' potential because of coordination and motivation losses. Brainstorming productivity loss — Real interacting groups generate fewer ideas than the same number working alone (nominal groups win), due to production blocking and evaluation apprehension. Transactive memory Daniel Wegner Groups develop a shared who-knows-what system, so members offload knowledge and recall more together. Deindividuation Leon Festinger; Philip Zimbardo Anonymity and arousal in a crowd → loss of self-awareness and personal restraint (Stanford prison study). High-yield The first experiment. Norman Triplett (1898) noticed cyclists rode faster racing others than alone, arguably social psychology's first experiment. Robert Zajonc explained it: an audience raises arousal, and arousal strengthens whatever response is dominant , the right one on an easy task (better) but the wrong one on a hard task (worse). Cottrell refined it: the arousal comes from evaluation apprehension , fear of being judged, not bare presence. Group decision-making, conflict & leadership Term Who What it is Group polarisation Moscovici & Zavalloni Group discussion pushes members toward a more extreme version of their initial average leaning. Risky shift James Stoner The earlier-discovered special case: groups often reach riskier decisions than individuals would alone. Groupthink Irving Janis A highly cohesive group suppresses dissent to preserve consensus → defective decisions (Bay of Pigs). Symptoms: illusion of invulnerability, collective rationalisation, belief in the group's morality, stereotyping out-groups, self-censorship, illusion of unanimity, direct pressure on dissenters, mindguards . Remedies: devil's advocate, outside experts, leader withholds opinion, second-chance meetings. Tragedy of the commons / social dilemma Garrett Hardin Individually rational self-interest collectively depletes a shared resource (prisoner's dilemma + commons; cooperation needs trust, communication, sanctions). GRIT Charles Osgood Graduated and Reciprocated Initiatives in Tension-reduction: small, announced, unilateral concessions invite reciprocation and de-escalate conflict. Distributive vs procedural vs transactional justice Adams; John Thibaut & Walker; Tyler Distributive = fairness of outcomes ; procedural = fairness of the process (people accept bad outcomes if the process felt fair, voice, neutrality); transactional = fairness of interpersonal treatment. Great-person / trait theory — Leaders are born with distinguishing traits; weakly supported on its own. Transactional vs transformational leadership Bass; Burns Transactional leaders exchange rewards for performance; transformational leaders inspire and remake followers' values and vision (charisma, intellectual stimulation). Fred Fiedler's contingency model Fred Fiedler Effective leadership depends on the match between leader style (task- vs relationship-oriented, the LPC scale) and situational favourableness. Trap Facilitation vs loafing: social facilitation = others present make you try harder (you are watched and evaluated individually ); social loafing = others present make you try less (your effort is pooled, your individual output hidden ). The deciding variable is whether your individual output is identifiable. Bonus: risky shift is the special case, group polarisation the general rule. Watch the deindividuation attribution: Leon Festinger coined the term, but Philip Zimbardo gave the famous demonstration (Stanford prison). 23. Landmark studies, walked through Social psychology is taught through its classic experiments, and NIMHANS/MET stems often describe a study and ask you to name it, its author or its conclusion. Each landmark below follows the same shape: the question, what they did, what they found, why it matters, and the trap. Learn the design, not just the headline number, because examiners test the procedure ("judged the length of lines" vs "a dot of light that appeared to move") as the giveaway. Triplett (1898) — the first social-psychology experiment Q: does the presence of others change performance? What: Norman Triplett noticed cyclists posted faster times racing others than the clock, then had children wind fishing reels alone vs alongside a co-actor. Found: children wound faster with a co-actor. Matters: widely cited as the first published social-psychology experiment, the seed of social facilitation . Trap: Triplett observed facilitation; Robert Zajonc later explained it (dominant response); Cottrell refined the cause to evaluation apprehension. Sherif (1936) — autokinetic norm formation Q: how do group norms form when reality is ambiguous? What: in a dark room a stationary pinpoint of light appears to move (the autokinetic effect ). Alone, people gave wildly different estimates; in groups they converged on a shared figure, and each kept using it even when later tested alone. Found: a private, internalised norm forms and persists. Matters: the model case of informational social influence . Trap: Muzafer Sherif = ambiguous stimulus, real internal conversion (informational); Solomon Asch = unambiguous, public compliance (normative). The "dot of light" is the tell for Sherif. Asch (1951) — conformity on the line task Q: will people conform to a group that is clearly wrong? What: a single real participant judged which comparison line matched a standard, seated among confederates giving the same wrong answer on critical trials. Found: about 75% conformed on at least one trial; the rate per critical trial was about 33–37% . Conformity rose with group size (up to 3–4, then plateaued) and unanimity , and collapsed the moment a single ally also dissented. Matters: normative pressure can override the plain evidence of one's senses. Trap: lock the two numbers separately and remember one dissenting ally frees the participant, not the size of the majority. Milgram (1963) — obedience to authority Q: how far will ordinary people go in harming another when ordered? What: the "teacher" delivered escalating shocks (15V to 450V , labelled "XXX") to a "learner" (a confederate, never actually shocked) while a calm experimenter issued four scripted prods ("the experiment requires that you continue"). Found: 65% went all the way to 450V. Matters: situational pressure, not sadism, produced obedience. Factors that REDUCED obedience: authority physically absent / by phone; legitimacy undercut (ordinary office vs Yale); victim more present (same room, touch-proximity); and crucially peers who rebelled . Obedience rose when responsibility could be diffused. Trap: headline ~65%; know at least two reducing factors; the agentic state (seeing oneself as the authority's instrument) is the explanatory mechanism. Zimbardo (1971) — the Stanford Prison Experiment Q: do situations and roles, not dispositions, drive cruelty? What: college men were randomly assigned "guards" or "prisoners" in a mock basement prison, meant to run two weeks. Found: guards rapidly became abusive, prisoners passive/distressed; halted after six days . Matters: headline demonstration of deindividuation and the power of assigned roles . Trap: Leon Festinger coined "deindividuation"; Philip Zimbardo demonstrated it. Modern critique (demand characteristics, coached guards, low replicability) is now part of the discussion, a stem may ask what it is criticised for. Festinger & Carlsmith (1959) — $1 vs $20 Q: when does doing something for too little reward change your attitude? What: participants did an excruciatingly boring task, then were paid $1 or $20 to tell a waiting participant it was enjoyable, then privately rated their actual enjoyment. Found: the $1 group rated it more enjoyable. Matters: classic cognitive dissonance via insufficient justification . Trap: the counter-intuitive direction ( less reward → more attitude change) is the whole point; $20 gave an external justification, so no dissonance. Latané & Darley (1968–70) — the bystander effect Q: why do witnesses fail to help? What: two famous variants. In the smoke-filled room study, participants saw smoke seep in; alone, most reported it quickly, but among passive confederates most sat in the haze ( pluralistic ignorance ). In the seizure study, the more bystanders a participant believed were on an intercom, the slower and less likely they were to help ( diffusion of responsibility ). Found: more witnesses → less helping. Matters: formalised as the five-step model . Trap: match the failure to the step; the Kitty Genovese case was the journalistic spark, though its "38 witnesses" detail was later shown to be exaggerated. Darley & Batson (1973) — the Good Samaritan study Q: does being in a hurry suppress helping? What: seminary students walked to give a talk (some on the parable of the Good Samaritan) and passed a man slumped, coughing, in a doorway; the experimenters varied how rushed the student was. Found: being in a hurry was the strongest predictor of not helping; the talk topic barely mattered. Matters: the power of the situation over personal values even in prosocially primed people. Trap: "hurry > piety," situational time pressure beats disposition. Bandura (1961–63) — the Bobo doll Q: is aggression learned by imitation? What: children watched an adult model either attack or ignore an inflatable Bobo doll, then were mildly frustrated and left alone with it. Found: children who saw aggression imitated it (including novel acts and verbal aggression); seeing the model rewarded increased imitation, seeing it punished decreased performance but not learning . Matters: founded social learning theory and the learning/performance distinction. Trap: children learned the aggression regardless of the model's consequences; consequences only changed whether they performed it. Tajfel (1971) — the minimal group paradigm Q: how little does it take to produce in-group bias? What: strangers were split on a trivial basis (Klee vs Kandinsky paintings, or a coin toss), then allocated points to anonymous in-group and out-group members. Found: people favoured their own group though groups were arbitrary, with no prior contact, self-interest or conflict, and would even sacrifice absolute in-group gain to maximise the difference . Matters: the empirical bedrock of social identity theory . Trap: minimal group = bias with no real competition; contrast with Muzafer Sherif's realistic conflict. Sherif (1954) — the Robbers Cave study Q: what creates and cures intergroup hostility? What: at a boys' summer camp, two groups (Eagles, Rattlers) were put into competition for prizes, breeding hostility, then given superordinate goals requiring cooperation (a broken water supply, a stuck truck). Found: competition manufactured prejudice; shared goals dissolved it; mere contact alone did not . Matters: the field demonstration of realistic conflict theory and why the contact hypothesis requires cooperation toward common goals. Trap: it was the superordinate goal , not contact by itself, that reduced hostility. Dutton & Aron (1974) — the shaky-bridge study Q: can arousal from one source be mislabelled as attraction? What: men crossed either a high, swaying suspension bridge (fear arousal) or a low stable bridge, where an attractive female interviewer gave them her number. Found: men from the scary bridge were far more likely to call and rated her more attractive. Matters: misattribution of arousal , an application of Stanley Schachter & Jerome Singer's two-factor theory of emotion to attraction. Trap: the arousal was really fear; participants relabelled it. LaPiere (1934) — attitudes vs behaviour Q: do stated attitudes predict actual behaviour? What: LaPiere toured the US with a young Chinese couple and recorded their treatment at ~250 hotels/restaurants; they were refused only once. Months later he wrote asking whether the same establishments would serve Chinese guests; over 90% said no . Found: a glaring gap between expressed prejudice and real behaviour. Matters: set off decades of work resolved by Martin Fishbein & Icek Ajzen (attitudes predict behaviour through intentions). Trap: LaPiere = the attitude–behaviour gap ; the resolution (intentions, specificity) is the theory-of-reasoned-action line. Other landmark experiments Study Method & finding Harry Harlow (1958) monkeys Infant monkeys preferred a soft cloth "mother" over a wire one with food. Contact comfort drives attachment. Martin Seligman (1967) helplessness Dogs exposed to inescapable shock later failed to escape when they could. Learned helplessness (model of depression). David Rosenhan (1973) "being sane in insane places" Healthy pseudopatients admitted to psychiatric hospitals; diagnoses stuck. Critique of psychiatric labelling. 24. Schools & history of psychology School Core idea & figures Structuralism Break consciousness into elements via introspection. Wilhelm Wundt (first lab, 1879), Edward Titchener. Functionalism What is the mind for ? Adaptive function of behaviour. William James, influenced by Charles Darwin. Psychoanalysis Unconscious drives and early experience. Sigmund Freud. Behaviourism Only observable behaviour; learning by conditioning. John B. Watson, Ivan Pavlov, B. F. Skinner. Gestalt The whole differs from the sum of parts. Max Wertheimer, Kurt Koffka, Wolfgang Köhler. Humanistic ("third force") Free will, growth, self-actualisation. Abraham Maslow, Carl Rogers. Cognitive Mental processes as information processing; the "cognitive revolution" (1950s–60s). Ulric Neisser, Miller. Biological / evolutionary Behaviour rooted in the brain, genes, and adaptation. 25. The MCQ traps, collected Method core: experiment = the only design proving causation (manipulate IV, measure DV, random assignment). Correlation ≠ causation (third-variable + directionality). Mediator = the why ; moderator = the when/for whom . Attention selection: Donald Broadbent = early/physical; Anne Treisman = attenuation; Deutsch-Norman = late/meaning; Lavie = depends on load. Cocktail-party effect supports late/attenuation, not Broadbent. Feature search pops out (parallel); conjunction search is serial. Memory: serial position = primacy (LTM) + recency (STM); a delay wipes recency. Anterograde (no new memories, H.M.) vs retrograde (no old). Encoding specificity = Endel Tulving. Conditioning: variable-ratio = highest, most extinction-resistant. Rescorla-Wagner = prediction error, explains blocking. Bobo doll = learning ≠ performance. Emotion order: James-Lange (body first) · Cannon-Bard (simultaneous) · Schachter-Singer (body + label). Availability = ease of recall · representativeness = fit to a prototype (neglects base rates) · anchoring = stuck on a first value. All = Amos Tversky & Daniel Kahneman. The attribution swap: FAE (Ross) = over-blame others' character · actor–observer (Edward E. Jones & Richard Nisbett) = my acts = situation, your acts = character · self-serving = my success = me, my failure = the situation. Models in order: Fritz Heider → Jones & Keith Davis → Harold Kelley (consensus, consistency, distinctiveness). Self-discrepancy (Higgins): ideal-self gap → dejection (sad); ought-self gap → agitation (anxious). Self cluster: social comparison = Leon Festinger · self-perception = Bem · self-monitoring = Snyder · self-efficacy = Albert Bandura · self-handicapping = Berglas & Jones · self-verification = Swann · self-affirmation = Steele · spotlight = Gilovich · BIRGing = Robert Cialdini · TMT = Greenberg, Pyszczynski & Solomon. Dissonance vs self-perception: Festinger = arousal/discomfort, strong prior attitude; Bem = no arousal, mere inference, weak attitude. $1 > $20 (insufficient justification, Festinger & J. Merrill Carlsmith): less reward = more attitude change. Effort justification = Aronson & Mills. Balance theory = Heider. Persuasion routes: central/systematic vs peripheral/heuristic. ELM = Richard Petty & John Cacioppo; HSM = Chaiken; Yale "who-what-whom" = Carl Hovland; inoculation = McGuire; reactance = Brehm; attitude–behaviour gap = LaPiere; intention model = Martin Fishbein & Icek Ajzen; sleeper effect & functions of attitudes = Hovland / Katz. Prejudice sources: social identity / minimal group = Henri Tajfel (& Turner) · realistic conflict / Robbers Cave = Muzafer Sherif · authoritarian personality (F-scale) = Adorno. Reduction: contact hypothesis (four conditions) = Allport; jigsaw classroom = Aronson; recategorisation = Gaertner & Dovidio. Stereotype cognition: illusory correlation = Hamilton & Gifford · out-group homogeneity · stereotype threat = Steele & Aronson · stereotype content model (warmth × competence) = Fiske. Stereotype threat ≠ self-fulfilling prophecy (target's own fear vs perceiver's expectation). Hostile vs benevolent sexism = Glick & Fiske (benevolent = the "nice"-sounding one). The "who studied liking" cluster: Byrne = similarity · Robert Zajonc = mere exposure · Festinger = propinquity · Robert Sternberg = triangular love · Caryl Rusbult = investment model · Dutton & Aron = misattributed arousal (bridge). Evolutionary mate preferences = Buss (vs Eagly & Wood); dissolution phases = Duck. Conformity: Solomon Asch = unambiguous line task (normative) · Sherif = autokinetic, ambiguous (informational) · Deutsch & Gerard named the two motives · Stanley Milgram = obedience (~65%, agentic state) · Serge Moscovici = minority influence via consistency. Foot-in-the-door vs door-in-the-face: FITD = small→big (Jonathan Freedman & Scott Fraser, consistency); DITF = big→small (Cialdini, reciprocal concession); lowballing = change the deal after the yes; that's-not-all = sweeten before the yes; reciprocity norm = Gouldner. Helping: bystander effect & 5-step model = Bibb Latané & John Darley; crowd failures = pluralistic ignorance (interpret) + diffusion of responsibility (take responsibility). C. Daniel Batson = true altruism (empathy); Cialdini (negative-state relief) and Piliavin (arousal:cost-reward) = egoistic. Kin selection = Hamilton, reciprocal altruism = Trivers. Aggression: frustration–aggression = John Dollard et al.; reformulation + weapons effect = Leonard Berkowitz (& LePage); social learning/Bobo = Bandura; GAM = Anderson & Bushman; excitation-transfer = Zillmann; cognitive-neoassociation = Berkowitz; threatened egotism = Baumeister & Bushman; hostile attribution bias = Dodge; culture of honour = Nisbett & Cohen; catharsis is a myth . Groups: facilitation (Triplett/Zajonc, dominant-response) vs loafing (Latané/Ringelmann, hidden effort); evaluation apprehension = Cottrell; deindividuation = Festinger coined / Zimbardo demonstrated; group polarisation (Moscovici & Marisa Zavalloni) generalises risky shift (Stoner); groupthink = Irving Janis; tragedy of the commons = Hardin; GRIT = Osgood; distributive (outcome) vs procedural (process) justice; transactional vs transformational leadership = Bass. 26. Fast glossary (A–Z) Last-mile recall: every nameable social-psychology term reduced to a single line and its author, alphabetical so you can self-test by covering the right column. If a name fires but the definition doesn't, that is the gap to drill. Term One-line definition (and who) Actor–observer effect My acts → situation, your acts → your character (Edward E. Jones & Richard Nisbett). Agentic state Seeing oneself as an authority's instrument, not the author of the act (Stanley Milgram). Anchoring & adjustment Cling to a first value, adjust too little (Amos Tversky & Daniel Kahneman). Authoritarian personality Rigid, submissive-to-authority, prejudice-prone; F-scale (Adorno). Availability heuristic Judge likelihood by ease of recall (Tversky & Kahneman). Balance theory We seek consistency in liking-relationships, P-O-X triads (Fritz Heider). Base-rate fallacy Ignore underlying frequencies for vivid cases (Kahneman & Tversky). BIRGing Basking in reflected glory, "we won" (Robert Cialdini). Bystander effect More witnesses → less help; 5-step model (Bibb Latané & John Darley). Catharsis (myth) Venting drains aggression, largely unsupported; it raises it. Cognitive dissonance Tension from clashing cognitions drives attitude change (Leon Festinger). Companionate love Deep affection, trust, care that lasts (Hatfield & Berscheid). Conjunction fallacy Specific conjunction judged likelier than its component, "Linda" (Tversky & Kahneman). Contact hypothesis Contact cuts prejudice if equal status, common goals, cooperation, institutional support (Allport). Correspondent inference Infer a trait from freely chosen, unexpected, low-desirability acts (Jones & Keith Davis). Counterfactual thinking Imagining "what might have been"; near-misses sting most (Kahneman & Tversky). Covariation model Attribution via consensus, consistency, distinctiveness (Harold Kelley). Deindividuation Anonymity + arousal → loss of restraint (Festinger coined; Philip Zimbardo demonstrated). Descriptive vs injunctive norms What people do vs what they approve (Cialdini). Diffusion of responsibility "Someone else will help" in a crowd (Darley & Latané). Discounting / augmenting Downweight a cause if rivals present / upweight a cause acting despite obstacles (Kelley). Door-in-the-face Big refused request → smaller real one, reciprocal concession (Cialdini). Effort justification Harsher initiation → value the group more (Aronson & Mills). Elaboration Likelihood Model Central (argument) vs peripheral (cue) route to persuasion (Richard Petty & John Cacioppo). Empathy–altruism Empathy yields genuinely selfless helping (C. Daniel Batson). Equity theory Happiest when input:outcome ratios match the partner's (Walster/Adams). Evaluation apprehension Fear of being judged, not bare presence, drives facilitation arousal (Cottrell). Excitation-transfer Left-over arousal intensifies later unrelated aggression (Zillmann). False consensus effect Overestimate how many share our views (Ross). Foot-in-the-door Small request first → bigger one later, via consistency (Jonathan Freedman & Scott Fraser). Framing effect Choice flips with gain vs loss wording (Tversky & Kahneman). Frustration–aggression Blocked goals breed aggression; original strong form (John Dollard et al.). Functions of attitudes Knowledge, utilitarian, ego-defensive, value-expressive (Katz). Fundamental attribution error Over-blame others' character, ignore their situation (coined by Ross). Gain–loss theory We like rising liking, dislike falling liking, more than steady (Aronson & Linder). General Aggression Model Person + situation → internal state → appraisal → act (Anderson & Bushman). Group polarisation Discussion amplifies the group's initial leaning (Serge Moscovici & Marisa Zavalloni). Groupthink Cohesion suppresses dissent → bad decisions (Irving Janis). GRIT Announced unilateral concessions de-escalate conflict (Osgood). Halo effect One global positive impression bleeds into specific traits (Edward Thorndike). Hindsight bias "I knew it all along" once the outcome is known (Fischhoff). Hostile attribution bias Read ambiguous acts as hostile, then retaliate (Dodge). Hostile vs benevolent sexism Antagonistic vs patronising-protective; both subordinate women (Glick & Fiske). Idiosyncrasy credits Early conformity buys later licence to dissent (Hollander). Illusory correlation See a link between a minority and rare behaviour that isn't there (Hamilton & Gifford). Implicit attitudes / IAT Automatic evaluations measured by reaction time. Inoculation theory A weak counter-argument vaccinates an attitude (McGuire). Insufficient justification $1 > $20: less reward → more attitude change (Festinger & J. Merrill Carlsmith). Investment model Commitment = satisfaction + investment − alternatives (Caryl Rusbult). Jigsaw classroom Cooperative interdependence cuts prejudice (Aronson). Just-world hypothesis People get what they deserve → victim-blaming (Lerner). Kin selection / reciprocal altruism Help relatives / likely reciprocators (Hamilton; Trivers). LaPiere study The attitude–behaviour gap (LaPiere). Looking-glass self Self built from imagined views of others (Cooley). Lowballing Get the yes, then raise the cost (Cialdini). Matching hypothesis We pair with similar attractiveness levels (Walster & Berscheid). Mere-exposure effect Repeated exposure increases liking (Robert Zajonc). Minimal group paradigm Arbitrary splits produce in-group bias (Henri Tajfel). Minority influence A consistent minority converts the majority privately (Moscovici). Misattribution of arousal Arousal relabelled as attraction, the bridge study (Dutton & Aron). Need to belong Fundamental motive for lasting bonds (Baumeister & Leary). Negative-state relief We help to fix our own bad mood (Cialdini). Obedience to authority ~65% to 450V under orders (Milgram). Out-group homogeneity "They're all alike." Passionate love Intense arousal and longing (Hatfield & Berscheid). Perseverance effect Beliefs survive after the evidence is discredited. Pluralistic ignorance All stay calm because no one else looks worried. Possible selves Hoped-for/feared future selves that motivate (Markus & Nurius). Procedural vs distributive justice Fair process vs fair outcome; process can matter more (Tyler; Adams). Propinquity effect Proximity breeds friendship, Westgate study (Festinger, Stanley Schachter & Back). Reactance Threaten a freedom → want the forbidden more (Brehm). Realistic conflict theory Competition over resources breeds hostility, Robbers Cave (Muzafer Sherif). Representativeness heuristic Judge by resemblance to a prototype, neglect base rates (Tversky & Kahneman). Ringelmann effect Per-person effort falls as group grows (Max Ringelmann). Risky shift Groups decide riskier than individuals; special case of polarisation (Stoner). Schema Mental framework steering attention, encoding, retrieval (Frederic Bartlett; Fiske & Taylor). Self-affirmation Affirm a valued domain to buffer a threat elsewhere (Steele). Self-discrepancy theory Ideal-gap → dejection; ought-gap → agitation (Higgins). Self-efficacy Belief in one's capacity for a task (Albert Bandura). Self-fulfilling prophecy Expectation makes itself come true (Merton). Self-handicapping Pre-set an excuse to protect esteem (Berglas & Jones). Self-monitoring High monitors tailor to the situation, low act on inner attitudes (Snyder). Self-perception theory Infer weak attitudes from your own behaviour (Bem). Self-serving bias Success = me, failure = the situation. Self-verification Seek feedback confirming the existing self-view (Swann). Sleeper effect Low-credibility message gains force as the source is forgotten (Carl Hovland). Social comparison theory We evaluate ourselves against others (Festinger). Social dominance orientation Preference for group hierarchy (Sidanius & Pratto). Social exchange theory Relationships = rewards − costs vs CL and CL-alt (John Thibaut & Kelley). Social facilitation Audience helps easy tasks, hurts hard ones (Norman Triplett; Zajonc). Social identity theory Self-esteem from group → in-group favouritism (Tajfel & John Turner). Social impact theory Influence = strength × immediacy × number (Latané). Social loafing Less effort when individual output is hidden (Latané, Williams & Harkins). Social penetration Relationships deepen via breadth + depth of disclosure (Altman & Taylor). Sociometer theory Self-esteem gauges social acceptance (Leary). Spotlight effect Overestimate how much others notice us (Gilovich). Stereotype content model Warmth × competence → 4 emotions (Fiske). Stereotype threat Fear of confirming a stereotype hurts performance (Steele & Aronson). System justification Motive to defend the existing social order (Jost). Terror management theory Mortality awareness defends worldview & esteem (Greenberg, Pyszczynski & Solomon). That's-not-all technique Sweeten the offer before the decision (Burger). Theory of planned behaviour Intention = attitude + norm + perceived control → behaviour (Martin Fishbein & Icek Ajzen). Thin slices Accurate judgements from seconds of behaviour (Ambady & Robert Rosenthal). Thought-suppression rebound Suppressed thoughts intrude more, the white bear (Wegner). Transactive memory Shared who-knows-what system in groups (Wegner). Transformational leadership Inspire and remake followers' values vs transactional reward-exchange (Bass; Burns). Triangular theory of love Intimacy + passion + commitment → 7 types (Robert Sternberg). Two-step attribution Automatic dispositional inference, then effortful situational correction (Gilbert). Ultimate attribution error FAE applied to out-groups (Thomas Pettigrew). Weapons effect A weapon's mere presence raises aggression (Leonard Berkowitz & LePage). "What is beautiful is good" Attractiveness stereotype (Dion, Berscheid & Walster). Yale attitude-change approach Who says what to whom (Hovland). Mnemonic Last-mile routine: recall → trap discrimination → glossary sweep . Cover the right column above and recover the definition + author for every row; then re-read the §25 trap boxes; then drill the rows that don't fire instantly. That pairing (term recall + lookalike discrimination) is exactly the two skills NIMHANS and MET grade hardest. Quick name-hooks for the most-swapped clusters: Amos Tversky & Kahneman own every heuristic; Leon Festinger = dissonance + social comparison + propinquity (three different things, read the stem); Robert Cialdini = influence principles + door-in-the-face + lowballing + BIRGing + negative-state relief; Steele = self-affirmation AND stereotype threat; Albert Bandura = Bobo doll + self-efficacy + observational learning.

title: Psychological Assessment & Testing
text: Psychological Assessment & Testing A psychological test is a measuring instrument, and like any instrument it must be (a) consistent and (b) accurate. Consistent = reliability . Accurate = validity . Everything in this chapter is either a way to estimate reliability, a way to estimate validity, a way to interpret scores against norms, or a real-world test built on those foundations. We measure things we cannot see directly (anxiety, intelligence, personality) by building instruments out of items, like a thermometer made of questions, then deciding things with them: special education, army fitness, diagnosis. This chapter locks the psychometric theory first, then the major intelligence, personality, projective, and clinical instruments, with every author, year, item count, scale, score range, and exam trap in one place. In this book Item analysis & test construction Reliability (the consistency story) Validity (the accuracy story) Norms & standard scores Intelligence theories & IQ mechanics Stanford-Binet family Wechsler family Raven’s Progressive Matrices Kaufman, Cattell CFIT & special-purpose scales Group & infant/developmental scales Indian intelligence tests IQ classification & intellectual disability Objective (self-report) personality tests Projective tests Adjustment, clinical & Indian inventories Aptitude, attitude & interest scales Psychiatric & cognitive rating scales Educational measurement basics Master reference tables & trap list 1. Item analysis & test construction Each test item is a single sensor reading. If a sensor is too easy (everyone passes) it tells us nothing; too hard (no one passes) it tells us nothing; and if it disagrees with the rest of the test, something is wrong with it. That is why every well-built test goes through item analysis. Difficulty index, p The difficulty index is the proportion who got an item right. p = (number correct) / (total attempting) , range 0 to 1. p = 0.50 is the sweet spot for a free-response item because it discriminates the most. For a 4-option MCQ the optimal p is ~0.625 , halfway between chance guessing (0.25) and ceiling (1.00). p above 0.80 = too easy; p below 0.20 = too hard. Both are revision candidates because they cannot separate strong from weak students. Discrimination index, D Do high-scorers on the whole test do better on this item than low-scorers? D = p_upper − p_lower , where p_upper = proportion correct in the top 27% of scorers and p_lower = proportion in the bottom 27%. Range −1 to +1. D above 0.40 = item agrees with the test, a good signal. D near zero = random noise; both groups perform alike. Negative D = the bottom group out-performed the top group: the item is mis-keyed, ambiguous, or has a trick strong test-takers over-think. Trap Read negative discrimination as a mis-keyed / flawed item to discard immediately , NOT as a merely “hard” item. This is asked every cycle. 2. Reliability (the consistency story) Reliability is not about whether a test is correct; it is about whether it is consistent . A bathroom scale that reads 75 kg every time is reliable even if your true weight is 70 (that is a validity problem). A scale bouncing between 60, 90, 80 is unreliable, full stop. If a test is unreliable you cannot trust any single score: the same person retested gives a different answer for reasons unrelated to the trait. You are measuring noise. Definition Classical Test Theory: Observed Score = True Score + Error . Reliability is the proportion of observed-score variance that is true variance, not error. A reliability of 0.80 says 80% signal, 20% noise. There are several reliability methods because there are several ways to think about “consistency”: Across time: test the same person twice (test-retest). Across forms: give two equivalent versions (parallel/alternate forms). Within one administration, across items: check items hang together (split-half, Cronbach alpha, KR-20). Across raters: check two judges agree (Cohen kappa for categorical, ICC for continuous). Test-retest (time stability) Give the test, give it again later, correlate the two scores. High correlation = stable over time. The standard window is two to four weeks . Too long and the trait itself can change (correlation drops, but the test is not at fault); too short and memory carryover inflates the correlation. Split-half + Spearman-Brown Give the test once, split into two halves (often odd vs even items), correlate the halves. By splitting you have halved the test length, and shorter tests are less reliable, so the raw split-half correlation under estimates full-test reliability. Spearman-Brown corrects this: r_full = 2 × r_half / (1 + r_half) . Example: r_half = 0.60 → r_full = 1.20 / 1.60 = 0.75 . Always apply Spearman-Brown after any split. Cronbach alpha Imagine doing every possible split-half and averaging the result: that mean is Cronbach alpha. It is the most common internal-consistency measure for tests with multi-point (e.g. Likert) items. Alpha rises with item count, item homogeneity, and trait variance. Trap Alpha is NOT a measure of unidimensionality. A test can have high alpha and still measure two distinct constructs. The MET loves this. KR-20 (Kuder-Richardson 20) When items are right-or-wrong (dichotomous, 1/0), Cronbach alpha simplifies to KR-20: same idea, adapted for 0/1 items. So “30-item right-wrong vocabulary test, one administration, which reliability?” → KR-20 . Inter-rater: kappa and ICC When humans do the scoring (Rorschach protocols, clinical interviews, essay grades), reliability is about rater agreement. Cohen kappa for categorical decisions (OCD: yes/no), corrects for chance agreement. Kappa ≥ 0.81 = almost-perfect; 0.61–0.80 = substantial. Intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) for continuous ratings (a 0–100 severity score); different ICC forms exist depending on whether raters are random or fixed. Trap Kappa is NOT an internal-consistency measure. If a question describes a one-administration internal-structure test, kappa is the wrong answer. Standard Error of Measurement (SEM) SEM is the practical payoff of reliability: the band of error around any single observed score. SEM = SD × √(1 − r_xx) , where SD is the test SD and r_xx its reliability. Example: SD = 20, reliability 0.81 → SEM = 20 × √0.19 = 20 × 0.436 = 8.72 . A score of 100 has a 68% confidence band of roughly 91–109 (±1 SEM). Higher reliability shrinks SEM. SEM is what lets you say two scores differ meaningfully versus fall within the noise band. 3. Validity (the accuracy story) A test can be perfectly reliable yet measure the wrong thing. Validity asks whether the test measures the construct it claims to. The classical model has three broad evidence types; modern theorists (especially Samuel Messick ) fold them all into “construct validity,” but the MET still uses the classical breakdown, so know both. Content validity Does the test cover the domain it claims to? An anxiety scale that asks only about racing heart but ignores worry, restlessness, and sleep is content-deficient. Established by expert panels who rate item-domain coverage; Lawshe’s CVR is the technical formula, but expert judgment is the core. Trap Do not confuse with face validity = whether the test merely looks valid to a layperson taking it. Face validity is the weakest form. A test can have high face validity and poor content validity, or low face validity and rigorous content validity. Criterion validity Does the test correlate with a real-world outcome (the criterion)? Two flavors: Concurrent: criterion measured at the same time. E.g. a new depression scale vs an established gold standard (HAM-D) today. Used when a gold standard already exists. Predictive: criterion measured later. E.g. GRE today predicts graduate GPA two years on. Used to forecast future behaviour. Mnemonic Predictive = Postponed. Concurrent = Current. Construct validity The most abstract form. If the test truly measures Construct X, it should correlate strongly with other measures of X ( convergent ), weakly with unrelated constructs ( discriminant ), and behave as theory predicts study after study ( nomological network ). The classic technique is Campbell & Fiske’s 1959 multitrait-multimethod matrix (MTMM) , which tests convergent and discriminant validity simultaneously by measuring multiple traits with multiple methods. Validity ceiling High-yield Validity cannot exceed the square root of reliability. Max validity coefficient between Test A and B = √(r_xx_A × r_xx_B) . If A is 0.64 reliable and B is 0.81 reliable, max correlation = √(0.64 × 0.81) = 0.72 . Reliability is necessary but not sufficient for validity; unreliable tests cannot be strongly valid. 4. Norms & standard scores A raw score means nothing alone: “scored 47 on a vocabulary test” tells you nothing until you know what others score. Norms convert raw scores into a frame of reference. The two most useful conversions are percentile ranks and standard scores. Percentile ranks The percentage of the norm group scoring at or below the person’s score. A 75th percentile means 75% scored at or below this person. Easy to interpret but ordinal : the gap between the 50th and 60th percentile is far smaller than between the 90th and 99th. Standard scores These put raw scores on an interval scale with fixed mean and SD: Standard Score = M + (SD × z) , where z is the person’s z-score from the norm group. Memorize these systems cold: Score Mean SD Range / use z 0 1 ~−3 to +3, universal/research T-score 50 10 ~20–80; MMPI family, NEO-PI, Big Five, neuropsych Wechsler IQ (FSIQ/index) 100 15 ~40–160; WAIS, WISC, WPPSI, SB-5 Old Stanford-Binet IQ (1960–1986) 100 16 ~36–164 Stanine 5 2 1–9; achievement/educational tests Sten (Standard Ten) 5.5 2 1–10; 16PF Wechsler subtest scaled 10 3 1–19; subtests inside WAIS/WISC Trap Most-tested swaps: Wechsler IQ SD = 15 vs old Binet SD = 16 . Stanine SD = 2, not 1 . T-score is 50/10, not 100/10 . Sten (16PF) mean 5.5; Stanine (education) mean 5. Normal-curve landmarks: 68% within 1 SD, 95% within 2 SD, 99.7% within 3 SD. z = +1 → 84th percentile; z = +2 → 98th percentile. 5. Intelligence theories & IQ mechanics The IQ formula history (memorize the sequence) Mental Age (MA) introduced by Alfred Binet, 1908 revision: the average chronological age that performs at the child’s level. Ratio IQ = (MA / CA) × 100 : William Stern, 1912 ; applied by Terman in the Stanford-Binet 1916. Deviation IQ : Wechsler, 1939 (Wechsler-Bellevue I), comparing the examinee to age-mates via a standardized score with fixed mean & SD. Solved the problem that ratio IQ breaks down past 16 because MA stops climbing linearly. Stanford-Binet switches to deviation IQ in 1960 (Pinneau’s tables), SD = 16. SB-5 (2003) drops SD to 15 to match Wechsler. Trap Do not credit Binet with the IQ formula: Alfred Binet rejected a single global score and wanted a clinical descriptive profile. Stern wrote the ratio formula (1912); Lewis Terman put it into the Stanford-Binet (1916). Theories behind the tests Theorist Year Model One-liner Charles Spearman 1904 Two-factor: g + s All cognitive tests share a general factor g plus task-specific s . Spearman invented factor analysis for this (theory → method, not the reverse). L.L. Thurstone 1938 Primary Mental Abilities (7 PMAs) Verbal Comprehension, Word Fluency, Number, Spatial, Memory, Perceptual Speed, Reasoning. Rejected a single g . Raymond Cattell & John Horn 1966 Gf-Gc Fluid intelligence (Gf, novel reasoning) vs Crystallized (Gc, accumulated knowledge). Gf peaks early adulthood, Gc rises lifelong. Philip E. Vernon 1950 Hierarchical g → v:ed (verbal-educational) + k:m (spatial-mechanical) → minor group factors → specific. J.P. Guilford 1967 Structure of Intellect (SOI) 5 operations × 6 products × 5 contents = 150 abilities ; later expanded to 180 . Introduced divergent vs convergent thinking. Howard Gardner 1983 ( Frames of Mind ) Multiple Intelligences Linguistic, Logical-Mathematical, Musical, Bodily-Kinesthetic, Spatial, Interpersonal, Intrapersonal (7). Naturalist added 1995 → 8. Existential proposed, not confirmed. Robert Sternberg 1985 Triarchic (later Successful Intelligence, 1996) Analytical (componential), Creative (experiential), Practical (contextual). PASS / WICS extensions later. McGrew / Schneider / Carroll 1993 / 1997 / 2018 Cattell-Horn-Carroll (CHC) Integrative hierarchical model: stratum III general factor → 16+ broad abilities (stratum II) → 80+ narrow (stratum I). Underlies WJ-IV, KABC-II, DAS-II. Peter Salovey & John Mayer 1990 / 1997 Four-Branch EI Perceiving, Using, Understanding, Managing emotions. Coined “EI” academically first. Measured by MSCEIT (2002). Daniel Goleman 1995 Emotional Intelligence (popular) 5 domains: self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy, social skills. Trap Howard Gardner = 8 on Indian exams (7 original + Naturalist 1995); “9” (with Existential) is usually wrong. Charles Spearman invented factor analysis (1904). Guilford SOI = 150 then 180. Cattell appears thrice: 16PF (1949), CFIT (1949), and Gf-Gc with Horn (1966). 6. Stanford-Binet family Origin: Binet-Simon (1905, France) Authors: Alfred Binet & Théodore Simon, commissioned by the French Ministry of Public Instruction to identify children needing special schooling. Year: 1905 (original 30-item graded-difficulty scale, “follow a light” up to “abstract definitions”), revised 1908 (introduced mental age) and 1911 . Did NOT yield IQ. Binet wanted a clinical descriptive profile, not a single number. Stanford revisions (the IQ-formula era) 1916 — Stanford-Binet 1st edition. Lewis M. Terman, Stanford. First English adaptation; ~90 items. Adopted Stern’s ratio IQ = (MA/CA) × 100, mean ≈ 100. Age 2–adult. 1937 — SB-LM (2nd ed.). Terman & Maud Merrill. Two equivalent forms L and M. Still ratio IQ. 1960 — SB-LM revised (3rd ed.). Terman & Merrill. Switched to deviation IQ (Pinneau tables), M = 100, SD = 16 . 1986 — SB-IV (4th ed.). Thorndike, Hagen & Sattler. Hierarchical structure, 4 area scores (Verbal Reasoning, Abstract/Visual Reasoning, Quantitative Reasoning, Short-Term Memory), 15 subtests. Age 2–adult. 2003 — SB-5 (current). Gale H. Roid, Riverside. SD changed to 15 to align with Wechsler. Age range 2–85+. SB-5 structure (the version exam-writers mean today) 10 subtests, 5 factors × 2 domains. 5 factors: Fluid Reasoning (FR), Knowledge (KN), Quantitative Reasoning (QR), Visual-Spatial Processing (VS), Working Memory (WM) — same names across both domains. 2 domains: Verbal (5 subtests) and Nonverbal (5 subtests); each factor has one verbal + one nonverbal subtest. 3 IQ scores: Full-Scale IQ (FSIQ), Verbal IQ (VIQ), Nonverbal IQ (NVIQ). All M = 100, SD = 15. Routing subtests: Object Series/Matrices (nonverbal) and Vocabulary (verbal) set entry difficulty. Admin time: ~45–75 min full; 15–20 min abbreviated. 7. Wechsler family David Wechsler (Bellevue Hospital, NY) built his scales to fix two SB problems: it was age-stratified and clunky for adults, and ratio IQ broke down past 16. His fixes were the deviation IQ (1939) and a point-scale structure where every adult takes the same subtests. Three age bands: WPPSI (Preschool & Primary), ages 2:6–7:7, current WPPSI-IV. Lineage: 1967 → WPPSI-R 1989 → WPPSI-III 2002 → WPPSI-IV 2012 . WISC (Children), ages 6:0–16:11, current WISC-V. Lineage: 1949 → WISC-R 1974 → WISC-III 1991 → WISC-IV 2003 → WISC-V 2014 US (2016 UK, 2019 India). WAIS (Adult), ages 16:0–90:11, current WAIS-IV. Lineage: Wechsler-Bellevue I 1939 (11 subtests, first deviation IQ) → W-B II 1946 → WAIS 1955 → WAIS-R 1981 → WAIS-III 1997 (added Processing Speed, 4-index structure) → WAIS-IV 2008 → WAIS-5 2024 (rolling out; exams still default to WAIS-IV). High-yield All Wechsler FSIQ & index scores: M = 100, SD = 15. All subtest scaled scores: M = 10, SD = 3, range 1–19 . WAIS-IV (the canonical adult answer) Age range: 16:0–90:11. Total subtests: 15 (10 core + 5 supplemental). FSIQ derived from the 10 core subtests. Admin ~60–90 min. 4 index scores: Verbal Comprehension (VCI), Perceptual Reasoning (PRI), Working Memory (WMI), Processing Speed (PSI). Index Subtests (core bold, supplemental italic) VCI Similarities, Vocabulary, Information , Comprehension PRI Block Design, Matrix Reasoning, Visual Puzzles , Figure Weights, Picture Completion WMI Digit Span, Arithmetic , Letter-Number Sequencing PSI Symbol Search, Coding , Cancellation WISC-V (the children’s scale) Age range: 6:0–16:11. Total subtests: 21 (10 primary + 11 secondary, including 5 complementary scored separately). 5 primary indices: Verbal Comprehension (VCI), Visual Spatial (VSI), Fluid Reasoning (FRI), Working Memory (WMI), Processing Speed (PSI). 5 ancillary indices: Quantitative Reasoning (QRI), Auditory Working Memory (AWMI), Nonverbal (NVI), General Ability (GAI), Cognitive Proficiency (CPI). 5 complementary subtests (CHC narrow abilities): Naming Speed Literacy, Naming Speed Quantity, Immediate Symbol Translation, Delayed Symbol Translation, Recognition Symbol Translation. Index Primary subtests VCI Similarities, Vocabulary VSI Block Design, Visual Puzzles FRI Matrix Reasoning, Figure Weights WMI Digit Span, Picture Span PSI Coding, Symbol Search Secondary subtests: Information, Comprehension, Picture Concepts, Arithmetic, Letter-Number Sequencing, Cancellation. Trap WAIS-IV has 4 indices (VCI/PRI/WMI/PSI); WISC-V has 5 (VCI/VSI/FRI/WMI/PSI). The WISC-IV → WISC-V change was splitting old PRI into VSI + FRI . WPPSI-IV (the preschool scale) Age range: 2:6–7:7, split into two batteries. Ages 2:6–3:11: 7 subtests, 3 primary indices (VCI, VSI, WMI) — no FRI/PSI yet (abilities not differentiated). Ages 4:0–7:7: 15 subtests, 5 primary indices (VCI, VSI, FRI, WMI, PSI) — same structure as WISC-V. Primary subtests: Information, Similarities, Block Design, Object Assembly, Matrix Reasoning, Picture Concepts, Picture Memory, Zoo Locations, Bug Search, Cancellation. 8. Raven’s Progressive Matrices Author: John C. Raven. Years: SPM published 1938 (developed 1936), CPM 1947, APM 1943. Nature: nonverbal, multiple-choice, pattern-completion; targets Charles Spearman’s g via eductive (meaning-extracting) reasoning . “Culture-fair”: commonly so described because items are abstract shapes, but cultural loading persists (paper-pencil familiarity, formal schooling). “Culture-reduced” is the more honest phrasing. Used widely in cross-cultural research and India. Version Items Sets Age / use Standard (SPM) 60 5 sets (A, B, C, D, E) × 12 Ages 6–80+, general population Coloured (CPM) 36 3 sets (A, A b , B) × 12 Ages 5–11, elderly, intellectually disabled Advanced (APM) 36 scored + 12 practice (Set I) Set I (12 practice) + Set II (36 scored) Above-average adolescents/adults; SPM ceiling effect Trap SPM = 60, CPM = 36, APM scored = 36 (do not count the 12 practice). The shared 36 on CPM and APM is the classic swap on Indian PG papers. 9. Kaufman, Cattell CFIT & special-purpose scales Kaufman family Authors: Alan S. & Nadeen L. Kaufman. K-ABC (1983) → KABC-II (2004) , ages 3:0–18:11. Built on Alexander Luria’s neuropsychological model (simultaneous + sequential processing); KABC-II added CHC interpretation . Yields two global scores: Mental Processing Index (MPI) for Luria-style use and Fluid-Crystallized Index (FCI) for CHC-style use. 5 scales: Sequential, Simultaneous, Planning, Learning, Knowledge. Designed to reduce verbal/cultural loading and assess minority/ESL children fairly. KAIT (1993): ages 11–85, 10 subtests, separates Fluid vs Crystallized IQ explicitly. KBIT-2 (2004): 2 subtests (Verbal Knowledge + Matrices), ~20 min screen. Trap The original K-ABC (1983) was pure Luria; KABC-II (2004) yields two indices (MPI + FCI) because it supports both Luria and CHC. Cattell’s Culture Fair Intelligence Test (CFIT) Author: Raymond B. Cattell. Year: first 1949, revised 1973. Purpose: measure fluid intelligence (Gf) per Gf-Gc theory with reduced cultural/language loading. 3 scales: Scale 1 (ages 4–8 and ID adults, 8 subtests), Scale 2 (ages 8–13 and average adults, 4 subtests), Scale 3 (ages 14+ and above-average adults, 4 subtests). Scales 2 & 3 subtests (same 4): Series, Classifications, Matrices, Conditions (Topology). Forms A + B for retest. Original M = 100, SD = 24; renormed editions use SD 15 or 16. Special-purpose & nonverbal scales Leiter International Performance Scale — Russell G. Leiter, 1936 → Leiter-R 1997 → Leiter-3 2013 . Fully nonverbal, no language; for deaf, ASD, non-English speakers. Ages 3–75+. Goodenough Draw-A-Man (Florence Goodenough, 1926) → Goodenough-Harris Drawing Test (Harris, 1963) . Children draw a man (and woman + self in Harris); scored on 64–73 body-detail criteria. Ages 3–15. Drawing-based IQ estimate. Slosson Intelligence Test (SIT, 1963; SIT-R3, 2002) — brief individual screen. Differential Ability Scales (DAS-II, Elliott, 2007) — ages 2:6–17:11, CHC-aligned, popular for LD identification. Woodcock-Johnson Cognitive (WJ-IV, 2014) — explicitly CHC; ages 2–90+; GIA + 9 CHC broad abilities. CTONI-2 (Hammill et al., 2009), UNIT-2 (Bracken & McCallum, 2016), WRIT (Glutting et al., 2000), RIAS-2 (Reynolds & Kamphaus, 2015). 10. Group & infant/developmental scales Army tests (WWI) Army Alpha (1917): chaired by Robert M. Yerkes (APA president) with Otis, Lewis Terman, Edward Thorndike, Henry Goddard, Bingham, Whipple. 212 items across 8 subtests (Oral Directions, Arithmetic Problems, Practical Judgment, Synonym-Antonym, Disarranged Sentences, Number Series Completion, Analogies, Information). For literate, English-speaking recruits. Army Beta (1917): same Yerkes committee. 7 subtests (Maze, Cube Analysis, X-O Series, Digit Symbol, Number Checking, Pictorial Completion, Geometrical Construction). For illiterate / non-English recruits; administered via pantomime. Trap Army Alpha = 8 subtests, Army Beta = 7 , Bhatia = 5 . Yerkes was the chair (not Lewis Terman, who was a member but is tied to Stanford-Binet 1916). Other group tests Otis Self-Administering Tests of Mental Ability (Arthur S. Otis, 1922) — civilian descendant of Army Alpha. → OLSAT (current K–12 screen). Wonderlic Personnel Test (1937) — 50 items, 12 minutes , employment screen (famous for NFL combine use). MAB-II (Jackson, 1998) — group-administrable Wechsler-style. Plus CTMM, Henmon-Nelson, CogAT. Infant & developmental scales Bayley Scales of Infant Development (BSID) — Nancy Bayley: BSID-I 1969, BSID-II 1993, Bayley-III 2006 , Bayley-4 2019. Ages 1–42 months . Bayley-III has 5 scales: Cognitive, Language (Receptive + Expressive), Motor (Fine + Gross), Social-Emotional, Adaptive Behavior. Gesell Developmental Schedules — Arnold Gesell, 1940s. Ages 4 weeks–6 years. 5 fields: Adaptive, Gross Motor, Fine Motor, Language, Personal-Social. Yields Developmental Quotient (DQ) = (DA / CA) × 100 . Cattell Infant Intelligence Scale (Psyche Cattell, 1940) — downward extension of Stanford-Binet, ages 2–30 months. Brunet-Lézine (1951) French infant scale; Mullen Scales of Early Learning (1995) birth–68 months; Denver Developmental Screening Test (DDST 1967, Denver-II 1992) screening, ages 0–6. Trap Bayley-III = 1–42 months (not just infants). Gesell to 6 years. Cattell Infant Scale 2–30 months. Stanford-Binet starts at 2. 11. Indian intelligence tests High-yield High-yield for both MET and NIMHANS. Memorize the author-year-count quadruple for each. Bhatia’s Battery of Performance Tests of Intelligence Author: Chandra Mohan Bhatia. Year: 1955. Age: originally 11–16, extended to early adulthood. 5 subtests: (1) Koh’s Block Design (10 designs), (2) Alexander’s Pass-Along (8 problems), (3) Pattern Drawing (8 designs), (4) Immediate Memory (digits forward + backward + sentence repetition), (5) Picture Construction (5 pictures). Use: built for the Indian context; performance (nonverbal) orientation suits illiterate and rural populations. Trap Bhatia having 5 subtests is a chronic MCQ trap. The Pass-Along is Alexander’s (1932) , incorporated into Bhatia’s battery — do not say “Bhatia Pass-Along.” Bhatia is 1955 , not 1949 (1949 = WISC and CFIT; 1955 = WAIS and Bhatia). Seguin Form Board — Edouard Seguin (1907 origin), used in India ages 3–7. Nonverbal performance, 10 cut-outs; measures speed of visual-motor coordination. Often misattributed to Indian authors. Mohsin General Intelligence Test (S.M. Mohsin, 1959) — verbal group test, Hindi. Jalota’s Group Test of General Mental Ability (S. Jalota, 1972) — verbal, ages 13+, 100 items. Developmental Screening Test (DST) — Bharath Raj, 1977, ages 0–15. Vineland Social Maturity Scale, Indian adaptation — A.J. Malin, 1965 (Indian Social Quotient). 12.
