Objective (self-report) personality tests Definition Objective tests use structured items (true/false, Likert, forced-choice) with fixed scoring keys. MCQ-writers attack this area four ways: (1) swap the item count between two tests, (2) swap author/year, (3) ask which scale belongs to which test, (4) ask projective vs objective. Lock the quadruple test → items → scales → author/year cold. MMPI family (Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory) MMPI (original, 1943): Starke R. Hathaway (psychologist) & J. Charnley McKinley (psychiatrist), Univ. of Minnesota. 566 true/false items (550 unique + 16 repeats). Method = empirical criterion-keying : items retained only if they discriminated a diagnostic group from normals, not by face validity — the breakthrough versus older content-based inventories. Norms = “Minnesota normals” (724 hospital visitors), later criticised as a narrow white rural Midwest base, driving the MMPI-2 restandardisation. Clinical cutoff originally T ≥ 70. MMPI-2 (1989 restandardisation; the default version exam-writers mean): 567 true/false items. Age 18+, 6th-grade reading level, 60–90 min. Scored as T-scores (M 50, SD 10) ; clinically significant elevation T ≥ 65 . MMPI-2-RF (2008, Ben-Porath & Tellegen): 338 items; 9 Restructured Clinical (RC) scales + demoralization (RCd) + higher-order scales; common variance of demoralization pulled out so each RC scale is more specific. MMPI-3 (2020, Ben-Porath & Tellegen): 335 items, new norms, 52 scales (H-O, RC, Specific Problem, PSY-5). MMPI-A (adolescent, 1992, Butcher et al.): 478 items, ages 14–18; MMPI-A-RF (2016, 241 items). 10 clinical scales (memorize order; 5 and 0 are the supplementary ones): # Code Name Picks up 1 Hs Hypochondriasis Bodily preoccupation, somatic complaints 2 D Depression Sadness, hopelessness, low morale 3 Hy Hysteria Conversion features, somatic + denial 4 Pd Psychopathic Deviate Authority conflict, antisocial features 5 Mf Masculinity-Femininity Gender-role interest pattern 6 Pa Paranoia Suspiciousness, ideas of reference 7 Pt Psychasthenia Anxiety, obsessional rumination, doubt 8 Sc Schizophrenia Bizarre thought, alienation 9 Ma Hypomania Elevated mood, overactivity, grandiosity 0 Si Social Introversion Social withdrawal vs sociability Validity scales (the L/F/K triad is the high-yield bit): ? (Cannot Say): count of unanswered items; > 30 omissions invalidates the profile. L (Lie): 15 items detecting naive “faking good” (impossibly virtuous claims). High L = unsophisticated impression management. F (Infrequency): 60 items rarely endorsed by normals. High F = random responding, malingering, OR genuine severe pathology (cannot distinguish without more evidence). K (Correction): 30 items measuring subtle defensiveness; added as a correction to 5 clinical scales (1, 4, 7, 8, 9). VRIN (variable inconsistency → random responding), TRIN (all-true/all-false bias), F B (back F — fatigue on later items), F p (F-psychopathology — separates malingering from genuine pathology among inpatients). Interpretation: all scales plotted on one graph in T-units; clinicians read code types (e.g. 2-7/7-2 = anxious-depressed; 4-9 = antisocial acting-out). Single-scale interpretation is discouraged. Trap MMPI-2 = 567 items, 10 clinical scales (Hs D Hy Pd Mf Pa Pt Sc Ma Si), L/F/K validity, T-scores M50/SD10, cutoff T ≥ 65. Don’t confuse with 16PF’s 16 factors or its Sten scores. L = naive faking-good, F = exaggeration/random/severe, K = subtle defensiveness — don’t swap. 16PF (Sixteen Personality Factor Questionnaire) Author: Raymond B. Cattell (with Tatsuoka & Eber later). Year: 1st ed. 1949; current 5th Edition 1993 . Items: 185 (5th ed.); each 3-choice (agree / ? / disagree), except the reasoning subtest (forced-choice). Age 16+, 35–50 min. Construction: factor analysis of the lexicon — Cattell took Gordon Allport & Henry Odbert’s ~4500 trait words, reduced to ~160 surface traits, factor-analysed to 16 source traits . Scoring: raw → Sten scores (M 5.5, SD 2, range 1–10): 1–3 low pole, 4–7 average, 8–10 high pole. 5 global factors (second-order, close to Big Five): Extraversion, Anxiety, Tough-Mindedness, Independence, Self-Control. Validity indices: Impression Management (IM), Acquiescence (ACQ), Infrequency (INF). Use: normal-population assessment for selection (I/O), career, couples/family counselling. Not a clinical screen. Code Low pole ↔ High pole Code Low pole ↔ High pole A Reserved ↔ Warm M Grounded ↔ Abstracted B Concrete ↔ Abstract reasoning N Forthright ↔ Private C Reactive ↔ Emotionally stable O Self-assured ↔ Apprehensive E Deferential ↔ Dominant Q1 Traditional ↔ Open to change F Serious ↔ Lively Q2 Group-oriented ↔ Self-reliant G Expedient ↔ Rule-conscious Q3 Tolerates disorder ↔ Perfectionistic H Shy ↔ Socially bold Q4 Relaxed ↔ Tense I Utilitarian ↔ Sensitive L Trusting ↔ Vigilant Trap 16PF is NOT the Big Five. 16PF = Raymond Cattell, 185 items, 16 primary + 5 globals, Sten scores. Big Five (OCEAN) = Paul Costa & Robert McCrae (NEO). Gordon Allport & Henry Odbert’s ~4500 trait words is the lexical starting point Cattell factor-analysed — a common stem. NEO Personality Inventory (Five-Factor Model) Authors: Paul T. Costa Jr. & Robert R. McCrae (NIH/National Institute on Aging). Lineage: NEO-PI 1985 → NEO-PI-R 1992 → NEO-PI-3 2010 . Items: 240 (NEO-PI-R / NEO-PI-3), 5-point Likert, 8 items × 30 facets. Short form NEO-FFI / NEO-FFI-3 = 60 items (5 domains only, no facets). Age: 17+ (NEO-PI-3 extended to 12). Forms S (self) and R (observer). Scoring: raw → T-scores; no classic validity scales (assumes honest responding). Dominant trait model in academic psychology since the 1990s. Use: research, occupational selection, therapy planning. Domain 6 facets O — Openness Fantasy, Aesthetics, Feelings, Actions, Ideas, Values C — Conscientiousness Competence, Order, Dutifulness, Achievement Striving, Self-Discipline, Deliberation E — Extraversion Warmth, Gregariousness, Assertiveness, Activity, Excitement-Seeking, Positive Emotions A — Agreeableness Trust, Straightforwardness, Altruism, Compliance, Modesty, Tender-Mindedness N — Neuroticism Anxiety, Angry Hostility, Depression, Self-Consciousness, Impulsiveness, Vulnerability Mnemonic Big Five = OCEAN . NEO has 5 domains × 6 facets = 30 facets . NEO-PI-R/3 = 240 items; NEO-FFI = 60 — don’t confuse long and short forms. EPQ / EPQ-R (Eysenck Personality Questionnaire) Authors: Hans J. & Sybil B.G. Eysenck. Lineage: Maudsley Medical Q (1952) → Maudsley Personality Inventory (MPI, 1959) → Eysenck Personality Inventory (EPI, 1964) → EPQ (1975) → EPQ-R (1985) → EPQ-R Short (1992). Items: EPQ 90; EPQ-R 100 ; Short 48. Yes/No. Age adult; Junior EPQ ages 7–15. PEN dimensions: P — Psychoticism (tough-mindedness, aggression, low empathy; added 1975, the EPI→EPQ move), E — Extraversion (sociability, impulsivity), N — Neuroticism (emotional reactivity), plus L — Lie (social desirability). Biological anchor: Extraversion ↔ cortical arousal (introverts higher baseline), Neuroticism ↔ limbic/ANS reactivity, Psychoticism ↔ dopaminergic function. Eysenck = biology of personality (common MCQ pairing). MBTI (Myers-Briggs Type Indicator) Authors: Katharine Cook Briggs & daughter Isabel Briggs Myers, built on Carl Jung’s Psychological Types (1921). Year: first 1944, commercial 1962 (ETS); current Form M (1998) . Items: Form M = 93 forced-choice ; Form Q = 144 (adds 20 facets); Form G (older) 126. Age 14+. 4 dichotomies → 16 types: E/I (energy direction), S/N (information style), T/F (decision style), J/P (lifestyle/outer-world orientation), e.g. INTJ. Critical: scores are categorical (discrete types), NOT dimensional — the main psychometric criticism. Traits are normally distributed; dichotomisation throws away information; ~50% of takers get a different type on retest within weeks. Use: career counselling, team building, coaching. NOT for clinical diagnosis or selection. MET contrast: “Which test claims discrete types instead of continuous traits?” → MBTI. CPI (California Psychological Inventory) Author: Harrison Gough. Year: 1957 → CPI-434 (1996) → CPI-260 short. Items: 434 / 260, true-false. Scales: 20 “folk-concept” scales (Dominance, Sociability, Empathy, Independence…) under 4 themes (Interpersonal, Self-management, Achievement, Personal Style) + 3 vector scales. Use: explicitly normal populations — the non-clinical complement to MMPI (selection, counselling, leadership). Trap CPI = normal populations (Gough’s “folk concepts”); MMPI = clinical populations. Easy to swap. Other objective inventories on the MET radar Test Items Author / Year What it does PAI (Personality Assessment Inventory) 344, 4-point Leslie Morey, 1991 22 non-overlapping scales (4 validity, 11 clinical, 5 treatment, 2 interpersonal). MMPI’s main rival. HPI (Hogan Personality Inventory) 206 Robert Hogan, 1986 7 primary scales mapped to Big Five for workplace use. MCMI-IV (Millon Clinical Multiaxial) 195, T/F Theodore Millon, 2015 (orig. 1977) 14 personality-disorder + 10 clinical-syndrome scales, DSM-aligned. HEXACO-PI-R 200 (60 brief) Ashton & Lee, 2004 6 factors: Honesty-Humility, Emotionality, eXtraversion, Agreeableness, Conscientiousness, Openness. 14. Projective tests Definition Projective tests present ambiguous stimuli on the hypothesis that the subject projects unconscious needs, conflicts, and defenses onto them. Less structured scoring, weaker psychometrics, richer clinical material than objective tests. Rorschach Inkblot Test Author: Hermann Rorschach (Swiss psychiatrist). Year: Psychodiagnostik , 1921 (died 1922 at 37, before refining the system). Stimuli: 10 inkblot cards. 5 achromatic (black/grey: I, IV, V, VI, VII), 2 black + red (II, III), 3 fully chromatic (VIII, IX, X). Shorthand: “5 chromatic + 5 achromatic.” Administration: (1) Free Association / Response phase (“What might this be?”); (2) Inquiry phase (where on the blot, and what features — form, colour, shading, movement — made it look that way). Exner Comprehensive System (1974), dominant until 2011: Location: W (whole), D (common detail), Dd (unusual detail), S (white space). Determinants: F (form), M (human movement), FM (animal movement), m (inanimate movement); C (pure colour), FC (form-dominated colour), CF (colour-dominated form); C′ (achromatic colour), T (texture), V (vista), Y (diffuse shading); FD (form-dimension), (2) (pair), r (reflection). Content: H, Hd, A, Ad, An, Bl, Sx, Xy… Popularity: P (common response, e.g. bat/butterfly on card V). Form quality: +, o, u, −. Indices: Erlebnistypus (EB) = M : sum-C (Introversive vs Extratensive vs Ambitent); Lambda (L) = pure-form ratio (high = constricted/defensive); Egocentricity Index = (reflections + pairs)/R; SCZI, DEPI, CDI, S-CON. R-PAS (2011): Meyer, Viglione, Mihura, Erard & Erdberg. Updates Exner norms, drops weak indices, standardises response count (R-Optimised). Increasingly the research standard, but MET still tests Exner. Trap Rorschach = 10 inkblots (not 12, 15, or 20). Determinant trick: FC = form-dominated colour vs CF = colour-dominated. TAT (Thematic Apperception Test) Authors: Henry A. Murray & Christiana D. Morgan, Harvard Psychological Clinic. Year: 1935 (manual 1943). Stimuli: 31 picture cards total — 30 black-and-white ambiguous scenes + 1 blank. 20 cards administered per subject , selected by age (adult/child) and sex (M/F); cards coded e.g. 3BM = card 3 for Boys + Men. Procedure: subject makes up a story for each picture — what led up, what is happening, what characters think/feel, how it ends. Recorded verbatim. Theory: projective hypothesis — subject projects dominant needs (achievement, affiliation, power) and perceived environmental press . Built on Murray’s needs-press theory (Explorations in Personality, 1938). Scoring systems: Murray’s original (code needs + press); SCORS (Westen, 1985, 8 object-relations dimensions); Defense Mechanism Manual (Cramer); David McClelland’s nAch scoring. Indian adaptation: Indian TAT by Uma Choudhury (1960) , culture-adapted scenes. Trap TAT = 31 cards total, 20 administered (not 10, not 20 total). Theory = needs-press . Indian TAT = Uma Choudhury 1960. SAT (Senior Apperception Test) 16 cards Bellak & Bellak, 1973 TAT for older adults — loneliness, dependency, illness. Rosenzweig Picture-Frustration (P-F) 24 cartoon frustration scenes Saul Rosenzweig, 1944 Direction of aggression (extra-/intro-/im-punitive) × type (obstacle-dominance, ego-defense, need-persistence). Holtzman Inkblot Technique (HIT) 45 inkblot cards, 1 response each Wayne Holtzman, 1961 Psychometrically tighter Rorschach alternative (better reliability, parallel forms A & B). Rotter Incomplete Sentences Blank (RISB) 40 sentence stems Julian Rotter, 1950 “I wish…,” “My mother…”; scored for adjustment on a 0–6 scale. House-Tree-Person (HTP) Draw house, tree, person John Buck, 1948 Combined personality + cognitive screen; symbolic interpretation. Kinetic Family Drawing (KFD) “Draw your family doing something” Burns & Kaufman, 1970 Family dynamics, interaction style. Trap Rosenzweig P-F scores aggression direction × type, NOT needs-press (that’s TAT). HIT = 45 cards, 1 response each, built to fix Rorschach’s reliability. CAT = Bellak 1949, 10 cards. 15. Adjustment, clinical & Indian inventories Beck inventories (all by Aaron T. Beck, Univ. of Pennsylvania; share the 0–3 Likert skeleton) BDI / BDI-II: BDI 1961 (Aaron Beck, Ward, Mendelson, Mock, Erbaugh); BDI-II 1996, 21 items, 0–3 each, total 0–63 , past 2 weeks. Revised to match DSM-IV (added agitation, worthlessness, concentration; removed body image, work difficulty, weight loss, somatic preoccupation). Cutoffs: 0–13 minimal, 14–19 mild, 20–28 moderate, 29–63 severe. 5th–6th-grade reading. Screening/severity, not diagnostic alone. BAI (Beck Anxiety Inventory, 1988): 21 items, 0–3, total 0–63 , past week. Cutoffs: 0–7 minimal, 8–15 mild, 16–25 moderate, 26–63 severe. Loads on somatic anxiety (sweating, dizziness, racing heart) to minimise overlap with depression. BHS (Beck Hopelessness Scale, 1974): 20 true/false items. Measures pessimism about the future; more predictive of eventual suicide than depression severity alone . Cutoff ≥ 9 = elevated risk. BSS / BSI (Beck Scale for Suicide Ideation, 1979 clinician / 1991 self-report): 21 items, 0–2 each. First 5 screen desire to live/die and active/passive ideation; if positive, complete remaining 14. BYI (Beck Youth Inventories, 2001/2005): ages 7–18; 5 scales × 20 items = 100 (Depression, Anxiety, Anger, Disruptive Behavior, Self-Concept). Also CBOCI (Clark-Beck OCD Inventory, 25 items) and Beck Self-Concept Test. Trap BDI-II = 21 items, 0–3, 0–63, past 2 weeks. BAI = 21 items, past week. BHS = 20 T/F. BSS = 21 items, 0–2. BHS (hopelessness) predicts suicide better than BDI severity. Bell’s Adjustment Inventory Author: Hugh M. Bell. Student form 1934, Adult form 1938; Indian adaptations by R.K. Ojha (Hindi) and others. Items: Student form 140 ; Adult form 160 . Yes/No/? format. Areas: Home, Health, Social, Emotional (Student form = 4); Adult form adds Occupational (5). Higher score = poorer adjustment; brackets labelled excellent / good / average / unsatisfactory / very unsatisfactory. Use: screening in school/college counselling, common in Indian masters dissertations (why it persists on MET). Educational measurement basics Achievement = what you have learned, past (WIAT, school finals). Aptitude = what you can learn, future (DAT, SAT). Intelligence = general cognitive capacity (WAIS, SB). Norm-referenced: compare student to a peer group (ranking, selection). Criterion-referenced: compare to an absolute standard (mastery, licensing). Formative: during learning, low-stakes feedback. Summative: end of unit, high-stakes outcome. 19. CPI = normal populations; MMPI = clinical. Rorschach = 10 inkblots (Exner → R-PAS 2011). TAT = 31 total, 20 admin, needs-press. CAT = Bellak 1949, 10 cards. HIT = 45 cards. Bell’s: Student 140 / 4 areas; Adult 160 / adds Occupational. Beck: BDI-II 21 (0–3, 0–63, 2 weeks); BAI 21 (1 week); BHS 20 T/F (best suicide predictor); BSS 21 (0–2). Indian: TAT = Uma Choudhury 1960; WISC adaptation = MISIC (Malin 1969); Bhatia Battery = C.M. Bhatia 1955 (5 subtests); Binet-Kamat = Kamat 1934. SPM = 60, CPM = 36, APM scored = 36. Bhatia = 5, Army Beta = 7, Army Alpha = 8 subtests. WAIS-IV = 4 indices; WISC-V = 5 (old PRI split into VSI + FRI). Ratio IQ = Stern 1912, applied by Lewis Terman 1916 (not Binet). Howard Gardner = 8 intelligences (Naturalist added 1995). Cattell appears thrice: 16PF, CFIT, Gf-Gc (with Horn). Y-BOCS = OCD; PANSS = schizophrenia; MMSE = 30 points, cutoff 23–24; MoCA more sensitive.

title: Therapy, Counselling & Ethics
text: Therapy, Counselling & Ethics One consolidated chapter for everything the MET / NIMHANS paper tests on treatment: the learning principles that behaviour therapy is built on, the major schools of psychotherapy & counselling (Sharf's frame, school by school, with the third-wave and integrative models folded in), the common therapeutic factors that cut across schools, and professional ethics . Each concept lives in exactly one place. The exam tests four moves: name the theory from its claim; pin the theory to its founder; pin the named technique to its theory; and tell rival theories apart, because that is where the distractor always hides. Learn every technique in its contrast pair . In this book Learning & conditioning: the foundation How to read any theory (the master frame) Psychodynamic approaches Humanistic & existential approaches Behavioural & cognitive approaches Constructivist, feminist & systemic approaches Third-wave, integrative & specialised models Group therapy (Yalom) Common factors & the therapeutic frame Indications quick-map (what to recommend) Professional ethics Master trap list, rosters & glossary High-yield The single most-tested skill is telling near-identical pairs apart: REBT (Ellis) vs Cognitive Therapy (Aaron Beck) , systematic desensitisation (Wolpe) vs flooding , ERP (OCD) vs EMDR (trauma) , cognitive triad (Beck) vs ABC (Albert Ellis) , DBT modules (4) vs ACT hexaflex (6) , and the four family-therapy founders (Bowen / Minuchin / Haley / Satir). And in learning: shaping vs chaining , fading vs extinction , VR vs VI , latent vs insight learning . Master these pairs and most of the section answers itself. 1. Learning & conditioning: the foundation of behaviour therapy Behaviour therapy is applied learning theory, so the vocabulary below is tested both as 1-mark definition traps and as the mechanism behind clinical techniques. Read this orientation once: classical (Pavlovian) conditioning is about stimulus pairings ; operant (Skinnerian) conditioning is about consequences shaping voluntary behaviour ; priming is about one stimulus making a later one easier to process ; and habituation / sensitization are non-associative (a single stimulus, no pairing). When a question mixes the families, the answer is almost always the term whose family matches the stem. Family Terms inside Classical (Pavlovian) phenomena Extinction, spontaneous recovery, generalization, discrimination, habituation, sensitization Operant (Skinnerian) shaping tools Shaping, chaining, fading, prompting Operant reinforcement schedules FR, VR, FI, VI Cognitive / social learning Latent learning (Edward Tolman), insight learning (Wolfgang Köhler), observational learning (Albert Bandura) Implicit / cognitive priming Priming (semantic, perceptual, affective) 1.1 Operant shaping tools — shaping, chaining, fading, prompting Shaping (B. F. Skinner): reinforcing successive approximations of a target behaviour the organism does not yet emit . Train a rat to press a lever by reinforcing facing it, then approaching, then touching, then pressing. The defining feature is that the reinforcement criterion changes across trials . Clinically: skill acquisition, autism intervention. Chaining : linking a sequence of already-learned behaviours into a longer chain, where each behaviour is the discriminative stimulus (S D ) for the next and only the final link is reinforced (brushing teeth: pick up brush → wet → paste → brush → rinse → put away). Forward chaining teaches step 1 first; backward chaining teaches the last step first, so the learner always reaches the reinforcer at the natural endpoint (often preferred clinically). Used heavily in ABA / ADL skills training. Prompting : an added antecedent stimulus (verbal, gestural, physical, modelled, visual) that helps the learner emit the right response in the presence of the natural cue. Prompt hierarchy, most → least intrusive: physical → modelling → gestural → verbal → visual/positional . "Least-to-most" vs "most-to-least" prompting are classic vignette distractors. Fading : gradually removing the prompt while transferring stimulus control to the natural cue (teach "ball": full model "say ball" → partial "say buh…" → just holding up the ball). Trap Shaping vs chaining: shaping builds a new behaviour ; chaining links existing behaviours . Fading vs extinction: fading removes the prompt (an antecedent) and transfers stimulus control; extinction removes the reinforcer / UCS and eliminates the behaviour. Prompts are antecedents; reinforcement is a consequence — that distinction has been tested directly. 1.2 Classical conditioning phenomena Extinction : reduction and disappearance of a conditioned response when reinforcement (operant) or the UCS (classical) is no longer presented — Ivan Pavlov's dog stops salivating to the unpaired bell; the ignored tantrum fades. Watch for the extinction burst : a temporary increase in frequency/intensity right after reinforcement is withdrawn, before decline. Extinction does not erase learning. Spontaneous recovery : reappearance of a previously extinguished response after a rest period, with no new conditioning trials — proving extinction is suppression, not unlearning . The recovered response is typically weaker , and re-extinction is faster the second time (savings effect). Distinguish from reinstatement (re-emergence after UCS-alone presentation) and renewal (re-emergence in a new context). Generalization vs discrimination. Generalization = responding similarly to stimuli that resemble the CS / S D (Little Albert, conditioned by John B. Watson & Rosalie Rayner to fear a white rat, also feared a white rabbit, cotton wool, a Santa beard). The generalization gradient : response strength drops with distance from the original CS. Discrimination = responding only to the specific stimulus, taught by differential reinforcement (reinforce in presence of S D , withhold for S Δ ). One-liner: generalization is the default; discrimination is trained. Failure to discriminate underlies many phobias. Note: stimulus generalization (similar CS) ≠ response generalization (different responses to the same CS). 1.3 The four reinforcement schedules Schedule Definition Response pattern Classic example Trap Fixed Ratio (FR) Reinforcement after a fixed number of responses High rate, brief post-reinforcement pause , then burst; step-like record Factory piece-work, paid per 10 units (FR-10) Pause comes after the reinforcer; higher ratios = longer pauses; ratio strain if raised too fast Variable Ratio (VR) Reinforcement after an average number of responses (unpredictable) Highest, steadiest rate; almost no pause Slot machines, fishing, cold-calls — the gambling schedule Most resistant to extinction; "addictive / extremely hard to stop" → VR Fixed Interval (FI) Reinforcement for the first response after a fixed time Scallop — slow after reinforcement, accelerating as the interval ends Checking mail you know arrives at 11am; cramming before a weekly quiz Lowest overall rate of the four; time -based, not response-count (don't confuse with FR) Variable Interval (VI) Reinforcement for the first response after a variable time Steady, moderate rate; no scallop; resistant to extinction Checking phone for a text; pop quizzes Most steady rate. VR is most vigorous . Distinguish by "steady vs vigorous" Mnemonic Ratio = paid per response → high rates. Interval = paid per time → moderate rates. Variable = unpredictable → most resistant to extinction. Fixed = predictable → pause/scallop after reinforcement. Resistance to extinction: VR > VI > FR > FI > continuous (CRF). Continuous reinforcement learns fastest but extinguishes fastest (partial-reinforcement extinction effect). 1.4 Cognitive & social learning Latent learning (Edward Tolman): learning that occurs without reinforcement and without immediate behavioural expression , showing up later once reinforcement appears — proving learning ≠ performance. Tolman & Honzik (1930) rats: a group unreinforced for 10 days, then reinforced from day 11, immediately outperformed the always-reinforced group on day 12. Buzzword: cognitive map (Tolman, 1948, "Cognitive Maps in Rats and Men"); the first big challenge to strict behaviourism. Insight learning (Wolfgang Köhler, Gestalt): sudden understanding of a solution without trial-and-error. Köhler's chimp Sultan (1925) joined two short sticks to reach a banana after a pause — the "aha!" moment. Cognitive, not behaviourist; contrast with Edward Thorndike's trial-and-error / law of effect (puzzle-box cats). Stem says "aha / sudden / no gradual improvement" → insight. Observational learning (Albert Bandura): learning by watching a model ; vicarious reinforcement of the model is enough, no direct reinforcement of the learner required. Bobo doll (1961) : children who watched an adult beat the doll did the same. Four processes (tested): Attention → Retention → Reproduction → Motivation (ARRM) . Vicarious reinforcement/punishment modulate motivation. Bandura's framework = Social Learning Theory (1977) , renamed Social Cognitive Theory (1986) ; home of self-efficacy and reciprocal determinism . 1.5 Priming, habituation & sensitization Priming : exposure to one stimulus (the prime ) unconsciously speeds the response to a later one (the target ) by activating related memory representations — a form of implicit memory. Read NURSE → identify DOCTOR faster than BREAD. Subtypes: semantic (NURSE→DOCTOR), perceptual (briefly flashed word → faster identification), affective (smiling face → positive judgement). It is not classical conditioning (no UCS, reflex or pairing) and not recall (no conscious memory of the prime). Habituation vs sensitization — the simplest, non-associative learning (Kandel's Nobel work on Aplysia). Habituation = a decrease in response to a repeated harmless stimulus (you stop hearing the wall clock; Aplysia's gill-withdrawal weakens with repeated mild touch); mechanism = reduced neurotransmitter release at the sensory-motor synapse. Sensitization = an increase in response after an intense/noxious stimulus (after a loud bang you flinch at every creak); mechanism = heterosynaptic facilitation via serotonergic interneurons → increased NT release. Habituation is stimulus-specific (a new stimulus restores the response → dishabituation ). Mnemonic Habituation says "this is safe, ignore it"; sensitization says "the world is dangerous, react more." Trap Habituation vs sensory adaptation: habituation is in the CNS (learning); sensory adaptation is receptor fatigue (peripheral). Habituation vs extinction: habituation needs only one stimulus with no learning history; extinction requires a previously conditioned association. Latent vs insight: latent = hidden until reinforced (Edward Tolman, rats); insight = sudden "aha" (Wolfgang Köhler, chimps). Observational learning ≠ imitation: imitation is one component; observational learning is the whole 4-stage ARRM process. 2. How to read any theory — the master frame Sharf describes every theory on the same recurring template, and you can predict almost any "which approach" answer from where the theory sits on five axes. The book's chapter frame: (1) history of the originator · (2) theory of personality / view of human nature (how problems develop) · (3) goals of therapy · (4) techniques · (5) the therapeutic relationship · (6) uses / evidence · (7) criticisms. Definition A theory of psychotherapy = a coherent set of assumptions giving the clinician a map of personality, a set of goals , and a set of techniques that follow from the goals. A good theory (Sharf) is precise/clear, comprehensive, parsimonious, useful/applicable, and verifiable/testable. The five predictive axes: View of human nature — determined/pessimistic (psychoanalysis) vs free/optimistic/growth-oriented (person-centred, existential, Adlerian). Behavioural = neutral (a product of learning). Role of the past — past-focused (psychoanalysis, Jungian) vs present/future-focused (behavioural, cognitive, REBT, reality, Gestalt, solution-focused, narrative). Directiveness — highly directive (behaviour therapy, REBT, reality, strategic family) vs non-directive (person-centred, the extreme), with collaborative in between (Aaron Beck, Adlerian, solution-focused). The relationship — the cure itself (person-centred) vs the site of the work via transference (psychoanalysis) vs a collaboration (cognitive, Adlerian, postmodern) vs a means/working alliance (behaviour therapy, REBT). Insight vs action — insight-based (psychoanalysis, Jungian) vs action/doing-based (behavioural, reality, solution-focused, strategic); REBT and Beck use insight into thinking then behavioural action. High-yield The four "forces" / waves (NIMHANS): 1st = psychodynamic ; 2nd = behavioural / cognitive-behavioural ; 3rd = humanistic-existential ; 4th (sometimes-cited) = multicultural / social-justice (and/or transpersonal). Useful for "which wave / force" stems. 3. Psychodynamic approaches 3.1 Psychoanalysis — Sigmund Freud Originator. Sigmund Freud (1856–1939), Viennese neurologist. Working with hysteria (and Breuer's Anna O., source of the "talking cure") he concluded symptoms have hidden unconscious causes. The first systematic theory of psychotherapy, the tradition every later theory reacts to. Personality / how problems develop. Behaviour is driven by instincts (life/Eros, energy = libido ; death/Thanatos) and by an unconscious . The mind has a topographic layout (conscious / preconscious / unconscious) and a structural one: id (pleasure principle, primary process), ego (reality principle, secondary process, mediator), superego (conscience + ego ideal). Personality forms through five psychosexual stages — oral (0–1.5), anal (1.5–3), phallic (3–6: Oedipus/Electra), latency (6–puberty), genital (puberty–adulthood); over/under-gratification → fixation → adult character traits. Problems arise from unconscious conflict and unresolved early childhood; the ego manages anxiety with defence mechanisms (repression the master defence, plus projection, displacement, reaction formation, sublimation, denial, regression, rationalisation — catalogued by Anna Freud). Definition George Vaillant's defence hierarchy: psychotic (denial, distortion) → immature (projection, acting out, regression, somatization) → neurotic (intellectualisation, displacement, reaction formation, repression, isolation of affect) → mature (humour, sublimation, suppression, altruism, anticipation). Goals. Make the unconscious conscious; bring repressed material into awareness so the ego can deal with it; strengthen the ego; resolve childhood conflicts re-enacted in the present. Insight is the engine of change. Techniques. Free association (the fundamental rule, censorship off); dream analysis (the "royal road to the unconscious"; separate manifest from latent content); analysis and interpretation of resistance and transference ; attention to parapraxes (Freudian slips); and working through — repeated re-examination of a conflict across shifting contexts until insight is integrated and behaviour changes (this distinguishes intellectual from emotional/behavioural insight). Relationship. Centres on transference : the client transfers feelings about early figures onto the analyst, and analysing that is the work. The analyst stays relatively neutral (blank-screen); countertransference (the analyst's own reactions) must be monitored. Frequency. Classical psychoanalysis: 3–5×/week, couch, years. Psychoanalytic / psychodynamic therapy: 1–2×/week, face-to-face, months–years. Uses / evidence. Originally neurosis/hysteria; now personality and relational problems. Built on rich but unrepeatable case studies ; modern brief psychodynamic therapy gives more empirical footing. Criticisms. Long, expensive, largely unfalsifiable ; overweighted on sex and the deterministic past; biased sample; little support for the psychosexual stages. Trap Free association + dream analysis + transference = Sigmund Freud. The defining technique is free association; the defining relationship mechanism is the transference. Working through is NOT free association and NOT a single interpretation — it is the repeated re-encounter with the same conflict in shifting contexts until consolidated. Classic MET/NIMHANS distractor. 3.2 The post-Freudian canon Sharf and the cheatsheet both expect you to pin each neo-/post-Freudian to their one signature contribution. Theorist Core contribution Anna Freud Ego psychology; defense mechanisms systematised; child analysis through play Carl Jung Analytical psychology (see 3.3) Alfred Adler Individual psychology (see 3.4) Melanie Klein Object relations; paranoid-schizoid → depressive position; splitting, projective identification; internal objects; play therapy Donald Winnicott Object relations; "good-enough mother," holding environment, true vs false self, transitional object Heinz Kohut Self psychology; narcissistic injury; mirroring/idealising/twinship selfobjects; empathic immersion Karen Horney Basic anxiety; neurotic needs; "tyranny of the should"; feminine-psychology critique of Freud Erik Erikson 8 psychosocial stages (Trust v Mistrust → Integrity v Despair); identity crisis; ego-psychology bridge to lifespan development Harry Stack Sullivan Interpersonal psychiatry; "self-system"; anxiety as interpersonal; influenced IPT Otto Kernberg Transference-Focused Psychotherapy (TFP) for BPD; borderline personality organisation; splitting + identity diffusion 3.3 Jungian analysis — analytical psychology Originator. Carl Gustav Jung (1875–1961), Swiss psychiatrist, Freud's "crown prince" until their 1913 break over the sexual nature of libido. Personality. Jung kept the unconscious but enlarged it and de-sexualised libido into general psychic energy. The psyche = ego (consciousness) + personal unconscious (your own forgotten/repressed material, organised into emotionally charged complexes ) + collective unconscious (an inherited layer shared by all humanity, holding the archetypes : persona, shadow, anima/animus, the self ). Coined introversion / extraversion , added four functions (thinking, feeling, sensing, intuiting) → psychological types . Problems reflect one-sided development and failure of individuation , especially at midlife. Goals. Individuation : integrate conscious and unconscious, persona and shadow, into a balanced self . Techniques. Dream analysis in series with amplification (linking symbols to myth and culture) rather than free association; active imagination (dialoguing with inner images); the word-association test (reveals complexes). Four therapy stages: confession, elucidation, education, transformation. Relationship. A collaborative mutual encounter; both parties are changed by the work. Criticisms. Mystical, obscure, hard to test; collective unconscious and archetypes resist verification (the MBTI descends from his types but has weak psychometrics). Trap Collective unconscious + archetypes + individuation + amplification = Carl Jung, NOT Freud (Freud = personal unconscious only). Dreams: amplification (Jung) vs free association (Freud). 3.4 Adlerian therapy — individual psychology Originator. Alfred Adler (1870–1937), Viennese; broke from Sigmund Freud in 1911 over the sexual emphasis. A major forerunner of humanistic and cognitive therapy. Personality. The one dynamic force is striving for superiority (really, striving for competence/completion). Everyone starts with inferiority ; healthy growth compensates , derailment yields an inferiority complex or over-compensating superiority complex . Each person builds a unique style of life by about age 5; we are pulled by future fictional goals ( fictional finalism ); we are not passive ( creative power of the self ); the mark of health is social interest ( Gemeinschaftsgefühl ). Birth order shapes the style of life. Problems = a mistaken style of life + discouragement / low social interest. Goals. Foster social interest, correct the mistaken style of life and faulty basic mistakes , replace discouragement with encouragement . Techniques. Lifestyle assessment , early recollections (earliest memory reveals the style of life), birth-order analysis, family constellation , encouragement , "the question" ("how would your life be different if you were well?"), acting as if , catching oneself , spitting in the client's soup , and paradoxical intention . Relationship. Egalitarian , collaborative, encouraging. Trap Inferiority/superiority complex · style of life · social interest (Gemeinschaftsgefühl) · birth order · early recollections · encouragement = Alfred Adler. Match the three "wills": will to pleasure = Sigmund Freud, will to power/superiority = Adler, will to meaning = Viktor Frankl. 4. Humanistic & existential approaches 4.1 Existential therapy — May, Yalom, Frankl Originators. A movement, not one founder: Rollo May (brought existentialism to US psychology; existential vs neurotic anxiety, the daimonic, freedom and destiny), Irvin Yalom (the ultimate concerns), Viktor Frankl (logotherapy, forged in the camps). Roots in Kierkegaard, Nietzsche, Heidegger, Sartre, Binswanger, Boss. Human nature. No fixed human nature; we are free, responsible, and create ourselves through choices (existence precedes essence). Distress comes from facing, or fleeing, the ultimate concerns / givens of existence . Yalom's four givens: death, freedom (and its responsibility), isolation, meaninglessness. Avoiding these through inauthenticity ("bad faith") produces existential anxiety/guilt. Three modes of being-in-the-world: Umwelt (physical), Mitwelt (social), Eigenwelt (self). Goals. Live authentically , accept freedom and responsibility, confront the givens, find or create meaning . Not symptom removal. Techniques. Deliberately light on technique; the relationship is the method. Frankl's logotherapy is the named exception: paradoxical intention (deliberately wish for the feared thing to break anticipatory anxiety), dereflection (shift attention away from the self/symptom), Socratic dialogue toward meaning. Frankl's three sources of meaning : creative (work/contribution), experiential (love/beauty), attitudinal (stance toward unavoidable suffering). Relationship. A real, authentic I–Thou (Buber) encounter; presence over technique. Uses / criticisms. Grief, terminal illness, life transitions, "existential vacuum." Vague, hard to operationalise; demands an articulate client. Trap Logotherapy · will to meaning · existential vacuum · paradoxical intention · dereflection = Viktor Frankl. The four givens = Irvin Yalom. Rollo May brought existentialism to American therapy. Note: paradoxical intention appears in Frankl AND in Adlerian/strategic work — as a named logotherapy technique it's Frankl; in family work the context decides. 4.2 Person-centred therapy — Carl Rogers Originator. Carl Rogers (1902–1987), American; created client-centred (later person-centred) therapy and pioneered recorded-session research. Human nature. Deeply optimistic : every organism has an innate actualising tendency toward growth. Trouble starts when the child, needing love, takes on conditions of worth ("I'm valued only if…") and distorts/denies experience that doesn't fit the self-concept. The gap between organismic experience and self-concept is incongruence , the source of anxiety. Goals. Reduce incongruence; drop conditions of worth; reconnect with organismic valuing; become a fully functioning person (open to experience, present-living, self-trusting, free, creative). Techniques. Famously non-directive — no diagnosis, no advice, no interpretation. Change comes from the relationship itself . The core triad the therapist provides: congruence/genuineness , unconditional positive regard (UPR) , and empathic understanding . These sit within six necessary and sufficient conditions (1957): two persons in psychological contact ; the client is incongruent/anxious ; the therapist is congruent ; the therapist feels UPR ; the therapist feels empathy ; and the client perceives the empathy and regard. Skills: reflection of feeling, active listening. Outcome marker: self vs ideal-self congruence (the Q-sort ). Mnemonic "EUC" — E mpathy, U PR, C ongruence. Lock the count: six conditions total, of which the therapist supplies three (the core triad), and they are necessary AND sufficient . Trap The core triad (congruence, UPR, empathy) is Carl Rogers ; so are "six necessary and sufficient conditions," "fully functioning person," and "actualising tendency." There is no "interpretation" in Rogers (that's Freud). And note the stem flip: "the relationship is necessary and sufficient" = Rogers; "necessary but not sufficient" = Beck / CBT. 4.3 Gestalt therapy — Fritz Perls Originator. Fritz (Frederick) Perls (1893–1970), with Laura Perls and Paul Goodman. Roots in Gestalt perceptual psychology (figure/ground), psychoanalysis, existentialism. Human nature. A whole person in constant contact with the environment, organising experience into figure (salient now) and ground . Health = staying aware in the here-and-now and completing the cycle of need → contact → satisfaction → withdrawal. Trouble = unfinished business (unexpressed past feelings intruding now) and contact-boundary disturbances : introjection (swallowing others' values whole), projection , retroflection (turning back on the self what you'd do to others), confluence (no boundary), deflection . Perls described five layers of neurosis (phony, phobic, impasse, implosive, explosive). Goals. Restore present awareness ; re-own disowned parts; finish unfinished business; move from environmental support to self-support and integration of polarities. Techniques / experiments. The empty-chair technique (dialogue with an absent person or a part of the self); the two-chair / top-dog vs under-dog dialogue (the moralising "shoulds" tyrant vs the evasive resister within); staying with feeling; exaggeration; the "I take responsibility" exercise; dream work (every dream element = a projected part of the self, acted out rather than interpreted); attention to body language and language ("it" → "I"). Relationship. Active, present-centred, I–Thou dialogic; the therapist may confront and frustrate avoidance. Trap Empty chair · top-dog vs under-dog · here-and-now awareness · unfinished business · figure/ground · layers of neurosis = Gestalt / Perls. Don't assume "chair → couch → Freud"; the empty chair is Gestalt, not psychoanalysis, and not the "miracle question" (SFBT). 5. Behavioural & cognitive approaches 5.1 Behaviour therapy Originators. No single founder. Roots in classical conditioning ( Ivan Pavlov ; John B. Watson & Rosalie Rayner 's Little Albert), operant conditioning ( B. F. Skinner ), social learning ( Albert Bandura ), and clinical pioneers Joseph Wolpe (systematic desensitisation), Hans Eysenck , Arnold Lazarus (later, multimodal therapy). Personality / how problems develop. No deep "personality" structure; behaviour (including symptoms) is learned and maintained by antecedents and consequences. A phobia is a conditioned fear; a habit is a reinforced operant. Strong focus on observable behaviour , the present, and measurement. Begins with a behavioural assessment / functional analysis (A–B–C: antecedent, behaviour, consequence). Goals. Concrete, specific, measurable behavioural change agreed with the client. Technique Mechanism Indication Systematic desensitisation (Wolpe) Reciprocal inhibition : relaxation paired with graded imagined exposure up a fear hierarchy Phobias (classic) In-vivo exposure Real-world graded exposure without relaxation; habituation + extinction Specific phobia, agoraphobia, OCD, PTSD Flooding / implosion Full-intensity exposure with no hierarchy, no relaxation, no escape, until anxiety extinguishes Phobias (less used — dropout) Exposure & Response Prevention (ERP) (Foa, Kozak) Exposure to the obsessional trigger + prevention of the compulsive response OCD — first-line behavioural Tx Aversion therapy Pair the unwanted behaviour with an aversive UCS (covert sensitisation = imaginal version) Paraphilias, substance use (limited evidence + ethical issues) Token economy Operant: secondary reinforcers (tokens) exchanged for primary reinforcers Inpatient/institutional, ID, ADHD classrooms Contingency management Operant: rewards contingent on target behaviour SUDs (esp. stimulant) Behavioural activation (Lewinsohn, Jacobson) Scheduled rewarding/mastery activity; reverses the depressive withdrawal-rumination cycle Depression — comparable to CBT Modeling (Bandura) Observational learning, vicarious reinforcement; participant modeling Phobias, social skills Shaping / chaining Reinforce successive approximations / link existing behaviours (see §1.1) Skill acquisition, autism, ADLs Biofeedback Real-time physiological readouts (EMG, HRV, GSR, EEG) shape autonomic/muscle control Tension headache, migraine, anxiety, incontinence Also: contingency contracting , extinction , relaxation training , assertiveness / social-skills training . Relationship. Important but not curative; the therapist is an active teacher / trainer / consultant who forms a working alliance and reinforces progress. Uses / evidence. Phobias, anxiety, OCD, habit disorders, skills deficits, institutional/developmental settings. The strongest empirical evidence base of the classical theories. Criticisms. Can ignore feelings, insight, the relationship and the underlying cause; risk of symptom focus. Trap Systematic desensitisation (Wolpe) vs flooding: desensitisation = graded hierarchy + relaxation (reciprocal inhibition), gentle. Flooding = maximal exposure, no hierarchy, no relaxation. Same idea (exposure), opposite intensity. ERP is the first-line behavioural treatment for OCD (SSRIs = first-line pharmacotherapy); systematic desensitisation is for phobias , not OCD. Token economy = operant/Skinnerian; modeling = Albert Bandura; aversion = pairing with an unpleasant stimulus. 5.2 Rational Emotive Behavior Therapy (REBT) — Albert Ellis Originator. Albert Ellis (1913–2007), American; created REBT in the mid-1950s — the first of the cognitive-behavioural therapies (predates Aaron Beck). Personality / how problems develop. It is not events that disturb us but our beliefs about them. Disturbance comes from irrational beliefs — rigid absolutist demands phrased as musts, shoulds, oughts ( musturbation ) — plus their derivatives: awfulising/catastrophising , low frustration tolerance ("I-can't-stand-it-itis") , and global self/other-rating / damnation . The three core irrational demands: "I must do well; others must treat me well; the world must be easy/fair." Definition The A-B-C-D-E model. A = activating event; B = belief (rational or irrational); C = emotional/behavioural consequence. The insight: it is B, not A, that causes C. Therapy adds D = disputing the irrational belief (logical, empirical, pragmatic), leading to E = a new effective philosophy (sometimes A-B-C-D-E-F, F = new feeling). Goals. Identify and dispute irrational beliefs, replace them with flexible preferences, reach deep philosophical change and unconditional self-acceptance . Techniques. Active-directive disputing ; cognitive (cost-benefit analysis); emotive (rational-emotive imagery, shame-attacking exercises , humour, forceful self-statements); behavioural (homework, risk-taking, in-vivo desensitisation, reinforcement). Heavy homework and psychoeducation. Relationship. Warm but secondary; not "necessary" in the Rogerian sense. The therapist is a forceful, active, sometimes blunt teacher/debater who models unconditional acceptance while attacking the beliefs. Criticisms. Confrontational style can clash with some clients/cultures; "rational vs irrational" can be a value judgement. 5.3 Cognitive therapy — Aaron Beck Originator. Aaron T. Beck (1921–2021), American psychiatrist; developed cognitive therapy in the 1960s out of his research on depression (daughter Judith Beck carried it forward). Personality / how problems develop. Emotion and behaviour are shaped by how we interpret events. Early experience lays down schemas (core beliefs) → which generate, in the moment, automatic thoughts (rapid, plausible appraisals just below awareness) → filtered through cognitive distortions : all-or-nothing/dichotomous thinking, overgeneralisation, magnification/minimisation (catastrophising), selective abstraction/mental filter, disqualifying the positive, arbitrary inference, personalisation, labelling, "should" statements, mind-reading/fortune-telling (jumping to conclusions), emotional reasoning. Depression is marked by the cognitive triad : negative view of the self , the world , and the future . Goals. Identify, test and correct distorted thinking; change automatic thoughts and underlying schemas; teach the client to become their own therapist (cognitive restructuring). Techniques. Socratic questioning / guided discovery ; identifying and testing automatic thoughts ( thought records , dysfunctional-thought log); collaborative empiricism (client + therapist treat beliefs as hypotheses and gather evidence); behavioural experiments ; activity scheduling and mastery-and-pleasure ratings; graded task assignment; decatastrophising; downward-arrow to reach core schemas; homework. Relationship. Genuine, warm, collaborative (Carl Rogers' conditions are necessary but not sufficient ); the hallmark is collaborative empiricism — not arguing, but jointly investigating. Uses / evidence. The strongest evidence base of any single approach for depression and anxiety ; foundation of modern CBT ; extended to OCD, PTSD, eating disorders, psychosis (CBTp). Trap REBT (Ellis) vs Cognitive Therapy (Aaron Beck) — the most-tested pair. Albert Ellis = A-B-C(DE) , irrational beliefs , musturbation , disputing ; directive, confrontational, philosophical — the therapist argues the belief is illogical. Beck = automatic thoughts , cognitive distortions , schemas , cognitive triad , collaborative empiricism ; Socratic, gentler — the client tests the thought as a hypothesis against evidence. "Dispute the irrational belief" = Ellis; "test the automatic thought against the evidence" = Beck. The cognitive triad is Beck; the ABC is Ellis — examiners swap these constantly. REBT predates Beck. 5.4 Reality therapy / Choice theory — William Glasser Originator. William Glasser (1925–2013), American psychiatrist; reality therapy in the 1960s, later grounded in choice theory (originally "control theory"). Personality / how problems develop. Behaviour is our best attempt to meet five innate basic needs: survival, love/belonging, power/achievement, freedom, fun. We act to close the gap between what we want (our "quality world") and what we perceive we're getting. Choice theory: we choose nearly all our behaviour and are responsible for it. Total behavior has four inseparable components — acting, thinking, feeling, physiology — and we have the most direct control over acting and thinking (Glasser uses verbs like "depressing," "anxietying"). Problems = irresponsible choices and unsatisfying relationships, not "mental illness." Definition The WDEP system (formalised by Robert Wubbolding): W = explore Wants (needs / quality world); D = examine Doing / current behaviour; E = Evaluation (the client self-evaluates: "is what you're doing getting you what you want?"); P = make a Plan . Plans should be SAMIC (simple, attainable, measurable, immediate, controlled by the client). No excuses, no punishment, no giving up. Relationship. Warm and involved first (build involvement ), then focus on present behaviour and choices; firm but caring, refuses excuses. Trap WDEP · choice theory · total behavior · the five needs = William Glasser (WDEP formalised by Wubbolding). Don't confuse Glasser's five needs with Abraham Maslow's hierarchy, or WDEP with MI's PACE/OARS. Reality therapy is present-focused, NOT past-focused. 6. Constructivist, feminist & systemic approaches 6.1 Solution-Focused Brief Therapy & Narrative therapy These constructivist / postmodern approaches share a premise: reality is socially constructed through language and story, so therapy works on meaning, not a fixed pathology. Both are brief, collaborative, resolutely non-pathologising , and treat the client as the expert . Solution-Focused Brief Therapy (SFBT) — Steve de Shazer & Insoo Kim Berg (Brief Family Therapy Center, Milwaukee; building on MRI brief therapy and Milton Erickson). Core idea: don't analyse the problem, build the solution ; focus on what the client wants and on times the problem is already absent. Signature techniques: the miracle question ("suppose a miracle solved the problem overnight — what would you notice tomorrow?"), exception questions ("when is the problem not happening?"), scaling questions ("on 0–10, where are you, and what is +1?"), the formula first-session task , coping questions , compliments . Rule of thumb: if it works, do more; if not, do something different. 4–8 sessions typical. Narrative therapy — Michael White (Australia) & David Epston (New Zealand) . We live by stories we tell about ourselves; a problem-saturated "dominant story" traps a person. "The problem is the problem; the person is not the problem." Techniques: externalising the problem (talk about "the Anger" or "the OCD" as separate, often by naming it), mapping its influence , finding unique outcomes / sparkling moments (times the person resisted the problem), re-authoring , therapeutic documents/letters , recruiting outsider witnesses / a definitional ceremony. Trap Miracle / exception / scaling questions = SFBT (de Shazer & Berg). Externalising · re-authoring · unique outcomes = Narrative (White & Epston). Both are postmodern and "client-as-expert," but SFBT builds the solution/future while narrative re-writes the story . The "miracle question" is the most-tested single item — it's de Shazer, NOT Gestalt's empty chair. 6.2 Feminist therapy Originators. A movement from the 1960s–70s women's movement (Jean Baker Miller, Carolyn Enns, Laura Brown); often integrated with other approaches. How problems develop. Distress cannot be separated from the social/political context , especially gender-role socialisation and the unequal distribution of power . Much "pathology" in women is a reasonable response to oppression, sexism and trauma. Slogan: "the personal is political." Goals. Symptom relief plus empowerment, self-definition, awareness of how gender-role/power dynamics shaped the problem, and (often) social action. Techniques. Gender-role analysis and intervention; power analysis ; assertiveness training ; reframing/relabelling (move blame from the individual to the social cause); bibliotherapy; therapist self-disclosure; demystifying therapy. Relationship. Deliberately egalitarian — minimise the power differential, treat the client as an equal collaborator. Trap "The personal is political" · gender-role analysis · power analysis · egalitarian relationship = feminist therapy. 6.3 Family systems therapies The unit of treatment shifts from the individual to the system . Drawing on general systems theory and cybernetics , a symptom in one member (the " identified patient ") expresses a dysfunction in the whole family's patterns. Shared concepts: homeostasis (the system resists change), circular causality (a mutual loop, not A→B), feedback loops , boundaries , subsystems . School Founder(s) Signature concepts / techniques Bowenian (multigenerational) Murray Bowen Differentiation of self (separate intellect from emotion, self from family fusion — the central goal); triangulation ; nuclear family emotional system; family projection process; multigenerational transmission; emotional cutoff ; sibling position; the genogram (multigenerational map). Goal: raise differentiation, detriangulate; therapist = calm non-anxious presence. Insight-leaning, slower. Structural Salvador Minuchin Family structure : boundaries (rigid → disengaged ; diffuse → enmeshed ; clear in between), subsystems (spousal/parental/sibling), hierarchy, alignments/coalitions. Joining , mapping, enactment (family plays out the problem in session), boundary-making, unbalancing, reframing. Active, present-focused. Strategic Jay Haley, Cloé Madanes; MRI (Watzlawick, Weakland); Milton Erickson Solve the presenting problem via planned interventions; the symptom serves a function and is maintained by failed "solutions." Directives , paradoxical interventions ( prescribing the symptom ), reframing, ordeals , pretend techniques. Brief, directive, little insight. Experiential / communications (human validation) Virginia Satir (also Carl Whitaker, symbolic) Warm, growth- and communication -focused; self-esteem and congruent communication. The four stress communication stances: placater, blamer, super-reasonable (computer), irrelevant (distractor) , plus the healthy congruent / leveller . Family sculpting , family reconstruction, role play, warmth. Milan systemic Selvini Palazzoli, Boscolo, Cecchin, Prata Circular questioning , hypothesising, neutrality, reflecting team Trap Family-theorist swaps (a top NIMHANS trap): "genogram + differentiation + triangulation" → Bowen ; "boundaries (enmeshed/disengaged) + enactment + joining + subsystems" → Minuchin (structural) ; "directives + paradox / prescribe the symptom" → Jay Haley (strategic) ; "family sculpting + placater/blamer/computer/distractor" → Virginia Satir (experiential) . "Identified patient · homeostasis · circular causality" = family systems generally. 7. Third-wave, integrative & specialised models These are recognition-item favourites ("which of these is a component of ___?"). The trap is always a real concept from a different therapy, so learn the named parts of each. 7.1 Transactional Analysis (TA) — Eric Berne Originator. Eric Berne (1910–1970); popularised in Games People Play . Personality has three ego states : Parent (taught — nurturing or critical), Adult (rational here-and-now processor), Child (felt — spontaneous or adapted). Transactions can be complementary (smooth), crossed (conflict), or ulterior (hidden agenda). Early decisions form a life script ; we exchange strokes (units of recognition); we play repetitive games ("Why Don't You — Yes But") paying off in bad feelings. Four life positions , healthy = "I'm OK–You're OK." Goals: autonomy (awareness, spontaneity, intimacy), strengthen the Adult , rewrite the script via structural / game / script analysis; often contract-based and in groups. 7.2 DBT — Dialectical Behaviour Therapy (Linehan, 1993) Synthesis of behavioural change + Zen acceptance ("dialectics"). Primary target: BPD with chronic suicidality . Four skill modules: mindfulness · distress tolerance · emotion regulation · interpersonal effectiveness. Four treatment modes: individual therapy + group skills training + phone/between-session coaching + therapist consultation team (~1 year). Target hierarchy: life-threatening → therapy-interfering → quality-of-life-interfering behaviours. Mnemonic DBT modules — "My Dog Eats Iguanas": M indfulness, D istress tolerance, E motion regulation, I nterpersonal effectiveness. 7.3 ACT — Acceptance & Commitment Therapy (Hayes) Goal = psychological flexibility , not symptom reduction. The Hexaflex (6 processes): Acceptance · Cognitive Defusion · Self-as-Context · Present-Moment Contact · Values · Committed Action. Each opposed by an inflexibility process (experiential avoidance, fusion, attachment to the conceptualised self, etc.). Underpinned by Relational Frame Theory (RFT) . Techniques: defusion ("I'm having the thought that…"), values clarification, metaphors (passengers on the bus, tug-of-war with a monster). 7.4 Mindfulness-based programmes MBSR — Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (Kabat-Zinn, 1979): 8-week group; body scan, sitting meditation, mindful movement (yoga); chronic pain, stress, anxiety. MBCT — Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy (Segal, Williams, Teasdale): 8-week group combining MBSR + cognitive therapy; indication = relapse prevention in recurrent depression (≥3 episodes). Trap MBCT is for preventing relapse , not treating an acute episode. MBSR came first (1979); MBCT added the cognitive layer. 7.5 IPT — Interpersonal Therapy (Klerman & Weissman, 1984) Time-limited (12–16 sessions), originally for MDD; evidence extends to bulimia, postpartum and adolescent depression. Four problem areas (pick one focus): grief · role disputes · role transitions · interpersonal deficits. Deliberately stays in the here-and-now of relationships, not the past. Trap IPT's four areas are NOT "thoughts / feelings / behaviours / body" and NOT "transference." If you see "role dispute / role transition" → IPT. 7.6 Motivational Interviewing (Miller & Rollnick, 1991) A client-centred but directive method to resolve ambivalence and elicit change talk . Spirit — PACE: Partnership, Acceptance, Compassion, Evocation. Processes: Engaging → Focusing → Evoking → Planning. Core skills — OARS: Open questions, Affirmations, Reflections, Summaries. Change talk — DARN-CAT: Desire, Ability, Reason, Need → Commitment, Activation, Taking steps. "Roll with resistance," develop discrepancy, support self-efficacy. Indication: ambivalence, especially SUDs; also weight loss, medication adherence. Pairs naturally with the stages of change. 7.7 Trauma-focused therapies EMDR (Francine Shapiro, 1987): 8-phase protocol pairing brief recall of the trauma memory with bilateral stimulation (eye movements / taps / tones). PTSD (APA, NICE, WHO endorsed). Mechanism debated (working-memory taxation, REM-like processing, dual attention); comparable to trauma-focused CBT. CPT — Cognitive Processing Therapy (Resick & Schnicke): 12-session manualised TF-CBT for PTSD; stuck points → impact statement → Socratic dialogue + worksheets. Prolonged Exposure (Foa): imaginal + in-vivo exposure to trauma memories and avoided stimuli; manualised; equally evidence-based for PTSD. Trap ERP vs EMDR: ERP (exposure + response prevention) = OCD; EMDR (8 phases + bilateral eye movements) = trauma. Different conditions, easily confused. Definition Trauma therapist lineage (high-yield): Pierre Janet (dissociation, traumatic memory, predates Sigmund Freud) · Judith Herman (Complex PTSD; 3-stage recovery: safety → remembrance/mourning → reconnection) · Bessel van der Kolk ("the body keeps the score," somatics, polyvagal) · Edna Foa (Prolonged Exposure; ERP for OCD; emotional processing theory) · Patricia Resick (CPT) · Francine Shapiro (EMDR) · Peter Levine (Somatic Experiencing) · Marsha Linehan (DBT). 7.8 Specialised models for BPD & integration TFP — Transference-Focused Psychotherapy (Otto Kernberg): twice-weekly psychodynamic, here-and-now transference interpretation, "object relations dyads." MBT — Mentalization-Based Treatment (Bateman & Fonagy): builds the capacity to understand one's own and others' mental states; day-hospital and outpatient versions. Integrative / eclectic routes (Sharf): technical eclecticism (pick whatever techniques work, regardless of theory — Lazarus's multimodal therapy , the BASIC ID : Behaviour, Affect, Sensation, Imagery, Cognition, Interpersonal, Drugs/biology); theoretical integration (blend theories into a new whole — Wachtel's cyclical psychodynamics); the common-factors route; and assimilative integration (work from one home theory, importing techniques). Fit the therapy to the client. Trap Ego states (Parent–Adult–Child) · games · scripts · strokes · life positions = TA / Berne. Multimodal therapy / BASIC ID / technical eclecticism = Arnold Lazarus. Don't decide DBT vs ACT on the word "mindfulness" alone — both use it; DBT has 4 modules , ACT has 6 hexaflex processes . 8. Group therapy — Yalom The group is a social microcosm : relationship patterns from outside life replay in the group, and the therapist's job is to surface the here-and-now process. Format: 6–10 members + therapist(s). Bion's basic-assumption groups (dependency, fight-flight, pairing) are influential background. Definition Yalom's 11 therapeutic factors: (1) instillation of hope · (2) universality ("I'm not the only one") · (3) imparting information · (4) altruism · (5) corrective recapitulation of the primary family group · (6) development of socialising techniques · (7) imitative behaviour · (8) interpersonal learning (the engine, paired with here-and-now) · (9) group cohesiveness (the group analogue of the therapeutic alliance) · (10) catharsis · (11) existential factors (responsibility, isolation, meaning, mortality). Trap Tag words social microcosm + here-and-now + interpersonal learning → Irvin Yalom. NOT a Yalom factor: "transference interpretation," "free association," "the miracle question." 9. Common factors & the therapeutic frame Beyond Sharf's schools, NIMHANS leans on the research finding that the schools share more than they differ. High-yield Common factors & the Dodo-bird verdict. Across bona-fide therapies, much outcome is explained by common factors — the therapeutic alliance , empathy, expectancy/hope, a believable rationale + ritual, goal consensus — rather than specific techniques. The " Dodo-bird verdict " (Rosenzweig; championed by Luborsky and Bruce Wampold 's contextual model): "everyone has won and all must have prizes," i.e. all therapies achieve broadly comparable outcomes. The working alliance ( Bordin: bond + goals + tasks ) is the most robust predictor of outcome. Outcome variance (Lambert, Wampold) roughly splits: ~40% client + extra-therapeutic factors · ~30% relationship (alliance) · ~15% expectancy/placebo · ~15% specific technique. Implication: most schools work, mostly via common factors. Specific techniques matter most for specific disorders with strong protocols ( ERP for OCD, exposure for PTSD, behavioural activation for depression ). Definition Stages of change — the Transtheoretical Model (Prochaska & DiClemente): precontemplation → contemplation → preparation → action → maintenance (relapse possible). Match the intervention to the stage — "the client isn't resistant, they're precontemplative." Definition Multicultural counselling competencies (Sue & Sue, the "fourth force"): a competent counsellor has awareness (of own biases/worldview), knowledge (of the client's culture), and skills (culturally appropriate interventions). Watch for cultural encapsulation and etic vs emic . 10. Professional ethics Tested two ways: straight definition ("non-maleficence means ___") or a vignette ("a clinician does X — which principle is violated?"). The four big ones are Beauchamp & Childress's principles ; the rest are the day-to-day rules that fall out of them. Mnemonic The four core principles — "A-B-N-J" / "Auto Brings No Justice": A utonomy · B eneficence · N on-maleficence · J ustice. Principle One line In practice Autonomy Respect the client's right to decide for themselves Informed consent · right to refuse · no coercion Beneficence Act for the client's good Choosing the treatment most likely to help; promoting wellbeing Non-maleficence "First, do no harm" ( primum non nocere ) Not using unproven/harmful methods; staying within competence Justice Fairness — treat like cases alike, distribute resources fairly No discrimination; fair access; equitable waitlists 11.1 Autonomy cluster Informed consent: the client understands the nature, risks, benefits and alternatives, and agrees voluntarily and with capacity . Three pillars: disclosure · capacity · voluntariness. Assent: agreement from someone who can't legally consent (a minor) — you get their assent alongside the parent's consent . Right to refuse / withdraw at any time without penalty. Trap Paternalism = overriding a competent person's choice "for their own good" — the violation of autonomy. Only justified when the person genuinely lacks capacity. Consent vs assent: adults with capacity give consent ; minors give assent (parent consents). 11.2 Confidentiality and its limits Privacy = the client's right; confidentiality = your duty to protect it; privileged communication = the legal protection in court. Limits / when you must break it: risk of serious harm to self or others · suspected child/elder abuse ( mandatory reporting ) · court order. High-yield Duty to warn / protect (Tarasoff): if a client makes a credible threat against an identifiable person, the therapist must act to protect that person — non-maleficence/beneficence to a third party overrides confidentiality. Very common vignette. Confidentiality is not absolute. 11.3 The other named terms Term Means Fidelity Loyalty, keeping promises, being trustworthy and reliable Veracity Truth-telling — honesty about diagnosis/prognosis Competence Practising only within the limits of your training; refer out otherwise Dual / multiple relationship A second role with a client (friend, business, romantic) — a boundary violation Duty of care The legal/ethical obligation to act in the client's best interest Negligence Falling below the accepted standard of care, causing harm (basis of malpractice) Capacity / competence to consent Whether the person can understand and reason about the decision Vulnerability Extra protection owed to those who can't fully protect their own interests (children, severe MI) Termination Planned, gradual; address relapse prevention; leave the door open 11.4 Indian & international context RCI (Rehabilitation Council of India) licenses clinical psychologists and has its own code of ethics . The Mental Healthcare Act 2017 codifies advance directives, nominated representative, right to confidentiality, and consent for persons with mental illness, and decriminalises suicide attempt. The APA Ethics Code is the international reference; its five general principles: beneficence/non-maleficence, fidelity/responsibility, integrity, justice, respect for rights & dignity. Multicultural competence (Sue & Sue): awareness, knowledge, skills. 11.5 Match the scenario to the principle Scenario Principle Therapist uses an untrained technique and the client worsens Non-maleficence (+ competence) Clinician forces medication on a competent, refusing adult Autonomy violated (paternalism) Psychologist dates a current client Fidelity / dual relationship — boundary violation Therapist warns a client's named target of a credible threat Upholds duty to warn (Tarasoff); breaks confidentiality lawfully Same waitlist priority regardless of caste/income Justice Choosing the most evidence-based treatment Beneficence Hiding a poor prognosis from the client Veracity violated Sharing case details at a party Confidentiality violated Getting a 14-year-old's agreement alongside the parent's consent Assent (+ consent) Trap Beneficence vs non-maleficence: do good vs avoid harm. "Withholding a harmful drug" = non-maleficence; "giving a helpful one" = beneficence. Privacy vs confidentiality vs privilege: the right · your duty · court protection. 12. Cognitive triad = Aaron Beck; ABC = Albert Ellis. Both CBT-family, easy to swap. REBT (Ellis) vs CT (Beck). Ellis disputes irrational beliefs (directive, confrontational); Beck tests automatic thoughts as hypotheses (collaborative, Socratic). REBT predates Beck. Systematic desensitisation vs flooding. Graded + relaxation (Wolpe) vs intense, no hierarchy, no relaxation. ERP vs EMDR. ERP = OCD; EMDR (8 phases + eye movements) = trauma. DBT (4 modules) vs ACT (6 hexaflex processes). Both use "mindfulness" — don't decide on that word alone. Working through = repeated re-encounter with a conflict until integrated, NOT free association and NOT one interpretation. Empty chair = Gestalt, not psychoanalysis ("chair → couch → Freud" is wrong). Carl Rogers' three core conditions = empathy, UPR, congruence — no "interpretation." Relationship "necessary AND sufficient" = Rogers; "necessary but not sufficient" = Beck/CBT. IPT four areas = grief, role disputes, role transitions, interpersonal deficits (not "thoughts/feelings/behaviours/body"). MI spirit = PACE; skills = OARS. MI is the opposite of confronting/arguing the client out of it. Paradoxical intention appears in BOTH Frankl (logotherapy) and strategic family therapy — read the stem for context. The three wills: pleasure = Sigmund Freud, power/superiority = Alfred Adler, meaning = Frankl. Skinner). Social interest (Gemeinschaftsgefühl) Feeling of kinship with humanity; mark of health (Adler).
