Differential The examined one is Social (Pragmatic) Communication Disorder versus Autism Spectrum Disorder . Both have the social communication deficit. Autism additionally requires restricted, repetitive patterns of behaviour, interests or activities , and if those are present now or were ever present in the past, the diagnosis is autism, not SPCD. So SPCD is autism's Criterion A without autism's Criterion B, and you must ask about childhood history before settling on it. Also rule out intellectual disability, hearing loss, selective mutism (the child can speak, but does not in specific settings), and normal variation. Autism Spectrum Disorder F84.0 In plain language. Two things together, both from early childhood: the person does not do the ordinary back-and-forth of relating to other people, and the person's behaviour and interests are narrow, repetitive, and sensitive to change. DSM-5 collapsed autistic disorder, Asperger's disorder, childhood disintegrative disorder and PDD-NOS into one spectrum, and cut the old triad to a dyad by merging social and communication deficits into one criterion. A. Persistent deficits in social communication and social interaction across contexts, and all three must be present: (1) deficits in social-emotional reciprocity, from abnormal back-and-forth conversation and failure to share interests or affect through to failure to initiate or respond to social interaction; (2) deficits in non-verbal communicative behaviours, from poorly integrated verbal and non-verbal communication through abnormal eye contact and body language to a total lack of facial expression and gesture; (3) deficits in developing, maintaining and understanding relationships, from difficulty adjusting behaviour to context through difficulty making friends to an absence of interest in peers. B. Restricted, repetitive patterns of behaviour, interests or activities , at least two of four : (1) stereotyped or repetitive motor movements, use of objects or speech (lining up toys, echolalia, idiosyncratic phrases); (2) insistence on sameness, inflexible routines, ritualised patterns, extreme distress at small change; (3) highly restricted, fixated interests abnormal in intensity or focus; (4) hyper- or hypo-reactivity to sensory input or unusual interest in sensory aspects of the environment (indifference to pain or temperature, adverse response to sounds or textures, excessive smelling or touching, visual fascination with lights or movement). Criterion B4, the sensory criterion, is new in DSM-5. C. Symptoms present in the early developmental period, though they may not fully show until social demands exceed capacity, and may be masked by learned strategies later. D. Clinically significant impairment. E. Not better explained by intellectual disability or global developmental delay; to diagnose both, social communication must be below that expected for general developmental level. Specifiers Severity is coded separately for social communication and for restricted repetitive behaviours, as Level 1 requiring support , Level 2 requiring substantial support , Level 3 requiring very substantial support . Also specify: with or without accompanying intellectual impairment; with or without accompanying language impairment; associated with a known medical, genetic or environmental factor; associated with another neurodevelopmental, mental or behavioural disorder; with catatonia. Numbers Prevalence now reported around 1 in 100 worldwide and higher in US surveillance data (about 1 in 36 in recent CDC estimates). Male to female about 4:1, and girls are under-identified because of camouflaging. Concordance in monozygotic twins is high (roughly 60 to 90 percent for the broader phenotype); heritability is among the highest in psychiatry. Comorbidity Around 70 percent have at least one comorbid mental disorder and about 40 percent have two or more. Commonest: intellectual disability, ADHD (DSM-5 for the first time allowed the two to be diagnosed together, DSM-IV forbade it), anxiety disorders (especially specific phobia and social anxiety), depression, OCD, tic disorders, specific learning disorder, developmental coordination disorder, avoidant restrictive food intake disorder, sleep disorders, epilepsy (about 20 to 30 percent), gastrointestinal problems, and known genetic syndromes such as fragile X, tuberous sclerosis and Rett syndrome. Differential Social (pragmatic) communication disorder : no Criterion B, ever. Intellectual disability without autism : social skills are at the level of the mental age, not below it. Rett syndrome : in DSM-5-TR this is no longer a separate diagnosis but is coded as an associated medical condition; the pattern of regression with hand-wringing between 5 and 48 months is the clue. Selective mutism : normal social reciprocity outside the feared setting. ADHD : inattention and social intrusiveness without the qualitative social-reciprocity deficit or the repetitive behaviours. Schizophrenia with childhood onset : delusions and hallucinations appear after a period of normal development. Stereotypic movement disorder : stereotypies without the social criterion. Reactive attachment disorder : severe social neglect history, and the social deficit improves once care improves. ICD-11 Also uses a single "Autism spectrum disorder" with qualifiers for intellectual and language impairment, so the two systems agree here. ICD-11 kept Rett syndrome out of the mental disorders chapter as well. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder F90.x In plain language. Either the child cannot hold attention, or cannot stay still and cannot wait, or both, to a degree that is out of step with their age and is spoiling their life in more than one place. A. A persistent pattern of inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity , with at least six of nine symptoms in the relevant list, present for at least six months , at a level inconsistent with developmental level. From age 17 and older, five of nine is enough. Inattention list (9): careless mistakes and inattention to detail; difficulty sustaining attention; does not seem to listen when spoken to directly; does not follow through on instructions and fails to finish; difficulty organising tasks; avoids tasks requiring sustained mental effort; loses things; easily distracted by extraneous stimuli; forgetful in daily activities. Hyperactivity-impulsivity list (9): fidgets or squirms; leaves seat when remaining seated is expected; runs or climbs inappropriately (in adults, restlessness); unable to play quietly; "on the go" as if driven by a motor; talks excessively; blurts out answers; difficulty waiting turn; interrupts or intrudes. B. Several symptoms present before age 12 . C. Symptoms present in two or more settings (home, school, work, with friends). D. Clear interference with functioning. E. Not occurring exclusively during schizophrenia or another psychotic disorder, and not better explained by another mental disorder. Specifiers Predominantly inattentive presentation , predominantly hyperactive/impulsive presentation , combined presentation . Note the word: DSM-5 says presentation , not subtype, because people move between them over time. Also in partial remission , and severity mild / moderate / severe. Numbers The age-of-onset criterion was raised from 7 in DSM-IV to 12 in DSM-5 , which is the single most examined ADHD fact. Symptom count drops from 6 to 5 at age 17. Prevalence about 5 percent of children and about 2.5 percent of adults. Male to female about 2:1 in children, closer to 1.6:1 in adults; girls present more often with the inattentive picture. Comorbidity Oppositional defiant disorder (about half of combined presentation), conduct disorder (about a quarter), specific learning disorder, anxiety disorders, depressive disorders, disruptive mood dysregulation disorder, autism spectrum disorder, tic disorders including Tourette's, substance use disorders in adolescence and adulthood, and antisocial personality disorder in adults. Differential Oppositional defiant disorder : the child refuses because they resist demands, not because they cannot sustain attention. Specific learning disorder : inattention appears only in the academic domain that is hard. Intellectual disability : symptoms must exceed what the mental age predicts. Bipolar disorder : ADHD is chronic and continuous, mania is episodic with a clear change from baseline, and mania brings elevated mood and reduced need for sleep, which ADHD does not. Anxiety : inattention there is driven by worry and rumination. Reactive attachment disorder and medication effects (bronchodilators, thyroid). Also normal high activity in a young child, and an unstimulating classroom. Specific Learning Disorder F81.x In plain language. A child of ordinary intelligence, taught properly, still cannot read, write or do arithmetic at anything like age level. A. Difficulties learning and using academic skills, with at least one of six symptoms persisting for at least six months despite intervention : inaccurate or slow effortful word reading; difficulty understanding what is read; difficulties with spelling; difficulties with written expression; difficulties mastering number sense, number facts or calculation; difficulties with mathematical reasoning. B. The affected academic skills are substantially and quantifiably below those expected for chronological age and cause significant interference, confirmed by individually administered standardised achievement measures (or, over age 17, a documented history). C. Begin during school-age years, though they may not fully appear until demands exceed capacity. D. Not better accounted for by intellectual disability, uncorrected visual or auditory acuity, other mental or neurological disorders, psychosocial adversity, lack of proficiency in the language of instruction, or inadequate educational instruction. Specifiers With impairment in reading (word reading accuracy, reading rate or fluency, reading comprehension; the alternative term dyslexia is retained in the text), in written expression (spelling accuracy, grammar and punctuation, clarity or organisation; dysgraphia ), or in mathematics (number sense, memorisation of arithmetic facts, accurate or fluent calculation, accurate mathematical reasoning; dyscalculia ). Severity mild / moderate / severe. Numbers Prevalence 5 to 15 percent of school-age children across languages and cultures; about 4 percent in adults. Reading is the commonest domain. DSM-5 abolished the old IQ-achievement discrepancy requirement, which is a favourite question: you no longer need a gap between IQ and achievement, you need low achievement plus failure to respond to intervention. Comorbidity ADHD (very high overlap), communication disorders, developmental coordination disorder, autism, anxiety and depressive disorders (secondary to school failure), and conduct problems in adolescence. Differential Normal variation in academic attainment; lack of instruction or schooling disruption, which is common in Indian samples and is an explicit exclusion; intellectual disability (all domains low, not one); ADHD (performance varies with attention and improves with structure); neurocognitive disorder (skills were acquired and lost); psychosocial adversity ; sensory impairment. Motor Disorders and Tic Disorders F82, F98.4, F95.x In plain language. Clumsiness that is out of proportion to age, repetitive purposeless movement, and tics. Developmental Coordination Disorder. Acquisition and execution of coordinated motor skills is substantially below age expectation (clumsiness, slowness and inaccuracy in catching, using scissors, handwriting, cycling, sports). It interferes with daily living and academics, begins in the early developmental period, and is not explained by intellectual disability, visual impairment, or a neurological condition affecting movement (cerebral palsy, muscular dystrophy). Stereotypic Movement Disorder. Repetitive, seemingly driven and purposeless motor behaviour (hand shaking or waving, body rocking, head banging, self-biting, hitting own body). Onset in the early developmental period, interferes with activities or results in self-injury. Specify with or without self-injurious behaviour , and whether it is associated with a known medical or genetic condition or environmental factor (for example Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, intellectual disability, intrauterine alcohol exposure). Tic disorders. A tic is a sudden, rapid, recurrent, non-rhythmic motor movement or vocalisation. Tourette's Disorder : multiple motor tics and one or more vocal tics , both present at some time during the illness though not necessarily concurrently, persisting for more than 1 year since first tic onset, with onset before age 18 . Persistent (Chronic) Motor or Vocal Tic Disorder : motor or vocal tics but not both, more than 1 year, onset before 18. Provisional Tic Disorder : single or multiple motor and/or vocal tics present for less than 1 year since first onset. Numbers Tics typically begin between ages 4 and 6, peak in severity between 10 and 12, and decline through adolescence. Tourette's prevalence 3 to 8 per 1000 school-age children; male to female 2:1 to 4:1. Coprolalia occurs in only about 10 percent, which is the standard trap because popular culture treats it as the defining feature. Comorbidity Tourette's with ADHD (about half) and OCD (roughly a third to a half) is the classic triad. Also anxiety, depression, disruptive behaviour, and learning problems. Developmental coordination disorder co-occurs with ADHD (the old "DAMP" concept), specific learning disorder and autism. Stereotypic movement disorder co-occurs with intellectual disability and autism. Differential Tics versus stereotypies : tics are faster, non-rhythmic, preceded by a premonitory urge and can be briefly suppressed; stereotypies are rhythmic, prolonged, fixed, start earlier (before 3) and are not preceded by an urge. Tics versus compulsions : compulsions are performed in response to an obsession or a rule and aim to prevent something; complex tics can look identical, and the two coexist. Chorea (random, flowing, not suppressible), dystonia (sustained), myoclonus , seizures . Also substance-induced (stimulants) and other medical conditions (Huntington's, post-viral). 3. Schizophrenia spectrum and other psychotic disorders This chapter is arranged along a gradient of psychopathology , from least to most: schizotypal personality disorder, delusional disorder, brief psychotic disorder, schizophreniform disorder, schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder. Everything in it is defined by five domains: delusions, hallucinations, disorganised thinking (speech), grossly disorganised or abnormal motor behaviour including catatonia, and negative symptoms . Learn the five, then learn the durations, because duration is what separates almost every member of this chapter from its neighbour. The duration ladder, the single most examined thing in the chapter Brief psychotic disorder: at least 1 day, less than 1 month, with full return to premorbid functioning. Schizophreniform disorder: at least 1 month, less than 6 months. Schizophrenia: at least 6 months of total disturbance, including at least 1 month of active-phase symptoms. Delusional disorder: at least 1 month of delusions. So: one day, one month, six months. If a stem gives you three months of psychosis, the answer is schizophreniform, and the word "provisional" belongs in the answer if the person has not yet recovered. Delusional Disorder F22 In plain language. One or more fixed false beliefs, for a month or more, and apart from what follows directly from the belief, the person is otherwise entirely normal. The person is not obviously odd, their speech is coherent, they hold down a job. A. One or more delusions of 1 month or longer . B. Criterion A for schizophrenia has never been met. If hallucinations occur they are not prominent and are related to the delusional theme (for example the sensation of insects in delusional parasitosis). C. Apart from the impact of the delusion, functioning is not markedly impaired and behaviour is not obviously bizarre or odd. D. If manic or major depressive episodes have occurred, they have been brief relative to the duration of the delusional periods. E. Not attributable to a substance, another medical condition, or better explained by another disorder such as body dysmorphic disorder or OCD. Subtypes Erotomanic (another person, usually of higher status, is in love with the person), grandiose , jealous (the "Othello syndrome"), persecutory (the commonest), somatic , mixed , unspecified . Also specify with bizarre content . Course specifiers after 1 year: first episode currently in acute episode / in partial remission / in full remission; multiple episodes; continuous. Numbers Lifetime prevalence about 0.2 percent, so it is rare. Onset later than schizophrenia, typically middle to late adult life. The DSM-5 change worth naming: the requirement that delusions be non-bizarre was removed , and "with bizarre content" became a specifier instead. Shared delusional disorder (folie a deux) was also removed as a separate diagnosis; it is now coded as delusional disorder or under other specified schizophrenia spectrum disorder. Comorbidity Obsessive-compulsive disorder and body dysmorphic disorder (especially where insight is absent), depressive disorders (often secondary to the delusion), and paranoid, schizoid and avoidant personality disorders, which often precede the onset. Differential Schizophrenia (Criterion A met, functioning declines, negative symptoms). OCD with absent insight (the belief grew out of an obsession, and the person has compulsions). Body dysmorphic disorder with absent insight . Paranoid personality disorder (suspiciousness that never reaches delusional conviction, and is lifelong and trait-like). Substance or medication induced , and psychotic disorder due to another medical condition . Major depressive or bipolar disorder with mood-congruent psychotic features (the delusion only exists inside the mood episode). Brief Psychotic Disorder F23 In plain language. Psychosis that arrives suddenly, lasts days or a few weeks, and then goes completely, leaving the person as they were. A. Presence of one or more of: delusions, hallucinations, disorganised speech, grossly disorganised or catatonic behaviour. At least one must be from the first three (delusions, hallucinations, disorganised speech), so catatonia alone does not qualify. B. Duration at least 1 day but less than 1 month , with eventual full return to premorbid level of functioning . C. Not better explained by a depressive or bipolar disorder with psychotic features or another psychotic disorder, and not attributable to a substance or another medical condition. Specifiers With marked stressor(s) (this is the old brief reactive psychosis ), without marked stressor(s), with peripartum onset (during pregnancy or within 4 weeks postpartum), and with catatonia . Severity rated on the 5 psychotic dimensions, 0 to 4. Numbers Accounts for roughly 9 percent of first-onset psychosis in some series. Twice as common in females. Average age of onset in the mid thirties. Suicide risk is elevated, particularly in the acute phase and in younger patients. Comorbidity Personality disorders, especially borderline, schizotypal, paranoid and histrionic, are frequent precursors. Differential Schizophreniform disorder (a month or more). Substance-induced psychotic disorder , which is the leading practical mimic in a young patient, so ask about cannabis and stimulants and take a urine screen. Psychotic disorder due to another medical condition (delirium, epilepsy, thyrotoxicosis, autoimmune encephalitis). Malingering and factitious disorder . Culturally sanctioned response , such as trance or a possession state that is a normal part of a religious practice, which is explicitly excluded. Bipolar or depressive disorder with psychotic features . Personality disorder with transient stress-related paranoia, especially borderline, where the psychotic-like symptoms are brief, stress-triggered, and recur across a long history. Schizophreniform Disorder F20.81 In plain language. Schizophrenia's symptom picture, but the clock has not run long enough yet. It is a provisional label you use while waiting. A. Same as schizophrenia Criterion A: two or more of delusions, hallucinations, disorganised speech, grossly disorganised or catatonic behaviour, negative symptoms, each present for a significant portion of a 1-month period, with at least one being delusions, hallucinations or disorganised speech. B. An episode lasting at least 1 month but less than 6 months . If you are diagnosing while the person is still ill, qualify as "provisional" . C. Schizoaffective and depressive or bipolar disorder with psychotic features ruled out. D. Not substance or medical. Note that unlike schizophrenia, impaired functioning is not required . Specifiers With good prognostic features requires at least two of: onset of prominent psychotic symptoms within 4 weeks of the first noticeable change in usual behaviour; confusion or perplexity; good premorbid social and occupational functioning; absence of blunted or flat affect. Otherwise, without good prognostic features . Also with catatonia. Numbers Roughly a third recover within the 6 months and keep the diagnosis; about two-thirds progress to schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder. Incidence in developed countries is about a fifth that of schizophrenia. Comorbidity As for schizophrenia: substance use, depression, anxiety. Differential Brief psychotic disorder (under 1 month). Schizophrenia (6 months or more, including prodrome and residual). Schizoaffective (a full mood episode runs for the majority of the illness). Substance-induced and medical causes. Schizophrenia F20.9 In plain language. For at least six months the person has been drifting away from ordinary reality and ordinary functioning, and for at least one of those months they have actively had psychotic symptoms. A. Two or more of the following, each present for a significant portion of time during a 1-month period (or less if successfully treated), and at least one must be (1), (2) or (3) : (1) delusions; (2) hallucinations; (3) disorganised speech (frequent derailment or incoherence); (4) grossly disorganised or catatonic behaviour; (5) negative symptoms (diminished emotional expression or avolition). B. Level of functioning in work, interpersonal relations or self-care is markedly below the level achieved before onset (or, with childhood or adolescent onset, failure to achieve the expected level). C. Continuous signs of the disturbance persist for at least 6 months , which must include at least 1 month of Criterion A (active-phase) symptoms , and may include periods of prodromal or residual symptoms, during which the disturbance may show only negative symptoms or two or more Criterion A symptoms in attenuated form. D. Schizoaffective disorder and depressive or bipolar disorder with psychotic features have been ruled out because either no major mood episodes have occurred concurrently with the active phase, or, if they have, they have been present for a minority of the total duration of the active and residual periods. E. Not attributable to a substance or another medical condition. F. If there is a history of autism spectrum disorder or a childhood-onset communication disorder, schizophrenia is diagnosed only if prominent delusions or hallucinations , plus the other required symptoms, are also present for at least 1 month. Specifiers Course, only after 1 year of symptoms: first episode currently in acute episode / in partial remission / in full remission; multiple episodes (same three); continuous; unspecified. Also with catatonia . Severity is rated dimensionally 0 to 4 on each of the five psychotic domains. The classical subtypes (paranoid, disorganised or hebephrenic, catatonic, undifferentiated, residual) were deleted in DSM-5 because they had poor reliability, low diagnostic stability and no validity for treatment response. Naming that deletion, and why, is a stock question. Numbers Lifetime prevalence about 0.3 to 0.7 percent. Onset typically early to mid twenties in men, late twenties in women , with a second smaller peak in women after 40. About 5 to 6 percent die by suicide, about 20 percent attempt it. Heritability roughly 80 percent; monozygotic concordance about 45 to 50 percent, dizygotic about 15 percent, one affected parent about 13 percent, both parents about 45 percent. Life expectancy is reduced by roughly 15 to 20 years, mostly cardiovascular. The DSM-5 change to name: DSM-IV allowed a single symptom if the delusion was bizarre or the hallucination was a running commentary or two voices conversing (the Schneiderian first-rank concession); DSM-5 removed that special treatment , so two symptoms are always required. Comorbidity Substance use disorders are the big one, over half, and tobacco use is very high. Also obsessive-compulsive disorder and panic disorder at rates above the general population, schizotypal and paranoid personality disorders (often premorbid), depression, and medical comorbidity: metabolic syndrome, diabetes and cardiovascular disease, driven partly by antipsychotics. Differential Schizoaffective disorder and mood disorder with psychotic features , both settled by the mood-episode arithmetic in Criterion D. Schizophreniform and brief psychotic , settled by duration. Delusional disorder (Criterion A never met, no functional decline). Schizotypal personality disorder (attenuated symptoms, no frank psychosis, lifelong pattern). Obsessive-compulsive disorder with absent insight and body dysmorphic disorder . PTSD (flashbacks and hypervigilance can be mistaken for hallucinations and paranoia, but they are trauma-cued). Autism (Criterion F). Substance-induced psychotic disorder and psychotic disorder due to another medical condition , including temporal lobe epilepsy, delirium, Wilson's disease, SLE, and NMDA-receptor encephalitis. ICD-11 Requires 1 month of symptoms, not six, and does not require functional decline. So the same patient at week five can be schizophrenia under ICD-11 and schizophreniform under DSM-5-TR. That is a favourite comparison question. Schizoaffective Disorder F25.x In plain language. Psychosis and a full mood episode run alongside each other, but the psychosis has also stood alone, without the mood episode, for at least two weeks. That standalone stretch is the whole diagnosis. A. An uninterrupted period of illness during which there is a major mood episode (major depressive or manic) concurrent with Criterion A of schizophrenia . If it is a major depressive episode, depressed mood must be one of the symptoms. B. Delusions or hallucinations for 2 or more weeks in the absence of a major mood episode during the lifetime duration of the illness. This is the criterion that defines the disorder. C. Symptoms that meet criteria for a major mood episode are present for the majority of the total duration of the active and residual portions of the illness. D. Not attributable to a substance or another medical condition. Specifiers Bipolar type (a manic episode is part of the presentation; major depressive episodes may also occur) or depressive type (only major depressive episodes). Also with catatonia, course specifiers after 1 year, and dimensional severity ratings. Numbers Lifetime prevalence about 0.3 percent, roughly a third that of schizophrenia. More common in women, driven by the depressive type. Prognosis sits between schizophrenia and mood disorder, better than schizophrenia and worse than bipolar disorder. Criterion C, the "majority of the total duration" rule, was changed in DSM-5 from a cross-sectional judgment to a lifetime one, so the diagnosis became longitudinal rather than a snapshot. Comorbidity Substance use disorders, anxiety disorders, and general medical conditions at rates similar to schizophrenia. Differential Two-sided, and this is a guaranteed question. Against schizophrenia : in schizophrenia mood episodes are present for a minority of the illness, in schizoaffective they are present for the majority. Against major depressive or bipolar disorder with psychotic features : there, the psychosis occurs only during mood episodes, so if you can find two weeks of delusions or hallucinations with no mood episode, it is schizoaffective. Also substance-induced psychotic disorder and psychotic disorder due to another medical condition. Substance/Medication-Induced Psychotic Disorder, and Psychotic Disorder Due to Another Medical Condition Substance-induced: delusions and/or hallucinations that developed during or soon after substance intoxication or withdrawal or exposure to a medication capable of producing them, and are not better explained by an independent psychotic disorder. Evidence for independence would be: symptoms preceded the substance use, or persisted for a substantial period, about 1 month, after acute withdrawal ended. Does not occur exclusively during delirium. Specify onset during intoxication or during withdrawal. Common agents: alcohol, cannabis, amphetamine and other stimulants, cocaine, hallucinogens, inhalants, sedatives; medications: corticosteroids, anticholinergics, L-dopa, isoniazid, interferon. Due to another medical condition: prominent hallucinations or delusions, with evidence from history, examination or labs that the disturbance is the direct pathophysiological consequence of a medical condition, not better explained by another mental disorder, not exclusively during delirium, and causing significant impairment. Specify with delusions or with hallucinations. Classic causes: temporal lobe epilepsy, stroke, brain tumour, traumatic brain injury, Huntington's, Parkinson's, multiple sclerosis, thyroid and parathyroid disease, Cushing's, SLE, B12 deficiency, autoimmune encephalitis, HIV, neurosyphilis. Comorbidity Substance use disorders by definition, and very often a primary psychotic disorder as well, since cannabis and stimulant use are markedly elevated in people with schizophrenia. For the medical form, the comorbidity is the underlying disease itself plus the depression and anxiety that follow it. Differential Delirium is the first thing to exclude, because if consciousness and attention fluctuate, the diagnosis is delirium and not a psychotic disorder. Then a primary psychotic disorder in someone who also happens to use substances, which is settled by timing and by the one-month post-withdrawal rule. Catatonia F06.1, F20.81 etc. In plain language. A syndrome of marked psychomotor disturbance, which in DSM-5 stopped being a type of schizophrenia and became something you can attach to many disorders. Requires 3 or more of 12 : stupor (no psychomotor activity, not actively relating to environment), catalepsy (passive induction of a posture held against gravity), waxy flexibility (slight even resistance to positioning by the examiner), mutism , negativism (opposition or no response to instructions or external stimuli), posturing (spontaneous and active maintenance of a posture against gravity), mannerism (odd caricature of normal actions), stereotypy (repetitive, abnormally frequent, non-goal-directed movements), agitation not influenced by external stimuli, grimacing , echolalia , echopraxia . DSM-5 gives three ways to record it: catatonia associated with another mental disorder (used as a specifier for schizophrenia, schizoaffective, brief psychotic, schizophreniform, bipolar and depressive disorders, neurodevelopmental disorders), catatonic disorder due to another medical condition , and unspecified catatonia . Numbers Historically framed as a schizophrenia subtype, but the majority of catatonia in practice occurs in mood disorders , particularly bipolar. Responds to benzodiazepines (lorazepam challenge) and to ECT. Comorbidity Most commonly a mood disorder, particularly bipolar disorder, then schizophrenia spectrum disorders, autism spectrum disorder and intellectual disability. Medically: encephalitis, autoimmune disease, metabolic derangement and drug toxicity. Differential Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (fever, rigidity, autonomic instability, raised CK, following antipsychotic exposure) and malignant catatonia , which overlap dangerously. Non-convulsive status epilepticus , akinetic mutism , locked-in syndrome , severe Parkinsonism , and stupor from a medical or toxic cause. 4. Bipolar and related disorders DSM-5 pulled the bipolar disorders out of the old "Mood Disorders" chapter and placed them between the psychotic disorders and the depressive disorders, to signal that they bridge the two in symptoms, family history and genetics. Everything here is built from three blocks: the manic episode, the hypomanic episode, and the major depressive episode. The three episode definitions, learn these once Manic Episode A. A distinct period of abnormally and persistently elevated, expansive or irritable mood AND abnormally and persistently increased goal-directed activity or energy , lasting at least 1 week and present most of the day, nearly every day (or any duration if hospitalisation is necessary). The addition of "increased activity or energy" to Criterion A is a DSM-5 change from DSM-IV, which required mood alone. B. During the mood disturbance, 3 or more of the following ( 4 if the mood is only irritable ), to a significant degree and representing a noticeable change from usual behaviour: inflated self-esteem or grandiosity; decreased need for sleep (feels rested after 3 hours, which is not the same as insomnia); more talkative than usual or pressure to keep talking; flight of ideas or subjective racing thoughts; distractibility; increase in goal-directed activity (social, occupational, sexual) or psychomotor agitation; excessive involvement in activities with a high potential for painful consequences (buying sprees, sexual indiscretion, foolish business investments). The mnemonic is DIG FAST : Distractibility, Indiscretion, Grandiosity, Flight of ideas, Activity increase, Sleep deficit, Talkativeness. C. The disturbance is severe enough to cause marked impairment in social or occupational functioning, or to necessitate hospitalisation , or there are psychotic features . Any one of these three makes it mania rather than hypomania. D. Not attributable to a substance or another medical condition. Note the DSM-5 rule: a full manic episode that emerges during antidepressant treatment or ECT and persists at a fully syndromal level beyond the physiological effect of that treatment counts as a manic episode, and therefore as bipolar I. DSM-IV excluded it. Hypomanic Episode Same Criterion A mood plus energy change, but lasting at least 4 consecutive days . Same list of 7 symptoms, same 3 or 4 threshold. The episode is associated with an unequivocal change in functioning that is uncharacteristic of the person when not symptomatic, and the change is observable by others . The episode is not severe enough to cause marked impairment, does not require hospitalisation, and there are no psychotic features . If any of those three appear, it is by definition mania. Major Depressive Episode 5 or more of 9 symptoms during the same 2-week period, representing a change from previous functioning, and at least one must be (1) depressed mood or (2) loss of interest or pleasure. The nine: (1) depressed mood most of the day nearly every day (in children and adolescents, can be irritable mood ); (2) markedly diminished interest or pleasure in all or almost all activities; (3) significant weight loss or gain (more than 5 percent of body weight in a month) or change in appetite (in children, failure to make expected weight gain); (4) insomnia or hypersomnia; (5) psychomotor agitation or retardation, observable by others , not merely subjective; (6) fatigue or loss of energy; (7) feelings of worthlessness or excessive or inappropriate guilt, which may be delusional; (8) diminished ability to think or concentrate, or indecisiveness; (9) recurrent thoughts of death, recurrent suicidal ideation without a specific plan, a suicide attempt, or a specific plan. Mnemonic SIG E CAPS plus mood: Sleep, Interest, Guilt, Energy, Concentration, Appetite, Psychomotor, Suicide. Bipolar I Disorder F31.x In plain language. One manic episode, ever, in a lifetime. That is the entire requirement. Depression is common but is not needed for the diagnosis. Criteria have been met for at least one manic episode . The manic episode may have been preceded by and may be followed by hypomanic or major depressive episodes. The occurrence of the manic and major depressive episode(s) is not better explained by schizoaffective disorder, schizophrenia, schizophreniform disorder, delusional disorder, or other specified or unspecified schizophrenia spectrum disorder. Specifiers (these apply across bipolar and depressive disorders): with anxious distress (mild to severe, based on 2 to 5 symptoms); with mixed features (DSM-5 replaced the DSM-IV "mixed episode", which needed full criteria for both mania and depression simultaneously, with a much more usable specifier requiring 3 symptoms of the opposite pole); with rapid cycling (4 or more mood episodes in 12 months); with melancholic features ; with atypical features (mood reactivity, hypersomnia, hyperphagia, leaden paralysis, interpersonal rejection sensitivity); with mood-congruent or mood-incongruent psychotic features ; with catatonia ; with peripartum onset (during pregnancy or within 4 weeks postpartum, which is a much narrower window than the popular usage of "postpartum depression"); with seasonal pattern . Also specify current or most recent episode (manic, hypomanic, depressed, unspecified), severity, psychotic features, and remission status. Numbers 12-month prevalence about 0.6 percent; roughly equal in men and women, though rapid cycling is commoner in women. Mean age of onset about 18. Lifetime suicide risk is roughly 15 times the general population, and bipolar disorder may account for a quarter of all completed suicides. Mania lasting 1 week, hypomania 4 days: those two numbers are asked constantly. Comorbidity Extremely high. Around three-quarters have a comorbid anxiety disorder (panic disorder, social anxiety, specific phobia); more than half have an alcohol use disorder; ADHD, oppositional defiant and conduct disorder in younger patients; borderline and antisocial personality disorders; migraine; metabolic syndrome. Differential Bipolar II (never a full manic episode). Major depressive disorder (the trap: a person presenting depressed whose past hypomania has never been asked about; always screen). Generalised anxiety, panic, substance use . ADHD (chronic, not episodic, and no decreased need for sleep, and onset before 12). Borderline personality disorder , where mood shifts last hours and are reactive to interpersonal events, versus bipolar where episodes last days to weeks and are autonomous. Schizoaffective and schizophrenia . Substance-induced bipolar and related disorder (stimulants, steroids). Bipolar due to another medical condition (hyperthyroidism, Cushing's, multiple sclerosis, stroke, traumatic brain injury). Bipolar II Disorder F31.81 In plain language. At least one hypomanic episode and at least one major depressive episode, and never a full manic episode. It is not a milder illness, and DSM-5-TR says so explicitly, because the depressive burden is heavier and lasts longer. A. Criteria met for at least one hypomanic episode and at least one major depressive episode. B. There has never been a manic episode. C. Not better explained by a schizophrenia spectrum disorder. D. The symptoms of depression, or the unpredictability caused by frequent alternation between periods of depression and hypomania, cause clinically significant distress or impairment. Note that the impairment must come from the depression or the alternation, because if the hypomania itself caused marked impairment it would be mania. Numbers 12-month prevalence about 0.8 percent. Mean age at onset in the mid twenties, slightly later than bipolar I. People with bipolar II spend roughly three times as long depressed as people with bipolar I. About 5 to 15 percent go on to have a manic episode, at which point the diagnosis changes to bipolar I permanently. Comorbidity About 60 percent have three or more co-occurring disorders. Anxiety disorders (about 38 percent), substance use disorders (about 37 percent), eating disorders, especially binge-eating disorder, and personality disorders. Differential Major depressive disorder , the commonest misdiagnosis, because patients present in the depressed phase and do not report hypomania as a problem. Cyclothymic disorder (never a full major depressive episode and never a full hypomanic episode meeting all criteria). Borderline personality disorder . ADHD . Substance-induced states. Cyclothymic Disorder F34.0 In plain language. Two years of bobbing up and down, never quite reaching a full hypomanic or a full depressive episode, and never getting a clear two-month stretch of feeling normal. A. For at least 2 years ( 1 year in children and adolescents ), numerous periods with hypomanic symptoms that do not meet criteria for a hypomanic episode and numerous periods with depressive symptoms that do not meet criteria for a major depressive episode . B. During that 2-year period, the hypomanic and depressive periods have been present for at least half the time , and the person has not been without the symptoms for more than 2 months at a time . C. Criteria for a major depressive, manic or hypomanic episode have never been met. D. Not better explained by a schizophrenia spectrum disorder. E. Not substance or medical. F. Clinically significant distress or impairment. Specify with anxious distress . Numbers Lifetime prevalence 0.4 to 1 percent, equal in men and women, though women present for treatment more. Usual onset in adolescence or early adult life. Risk of progressing to bipolar I or II is roughly 15 to 50 percent. Comorbidity Substance use disorders and sleep disorders. In children, ADHD is a frequent comorbidity. Differential Bipolar II (full episodes have been met). Persistent depressive disorder (only depressive symptoms, no hypomanic periods). Borderline personality disorder , again, where the instability is interpersonally triggered. Rapid cycling bipolar . Substance-induced mood lability. Substance/Medication-Induced Bipolar and Related Disorder, and Bipolar Due to Another Medical Condition A prominent and persistent disturbance in mood, elevated or irritable with or without depressed mood, that developed during or soon after substance intoxication or withdrawal or exposure to a medication capable of producing it, or that is the direct pathophysiological consequence of a medical condition. Common substances: amphetamines and other stimulants, cocaine, phencyclidine, steroids. Common medical causes: Cushing's syndrome, hyperthyroidism, multiple sclerosis, stroke, traumatic brain injury . Remember the DSM-5 rule again: if a fully syndromal manic episode persists beyond the physiological effect of the antidepressant or ECT that triggered it, it is counted as a manic episode and the person has bipolar I, not a substance-induced disorder. Comorbidity Substance use disorders themselves, plus a primary bipolar disorder in a substantial proportion, since stimulant use is elevated in bipolar disorder. For the medical form, the endocrine or neurological disease and the depression that commonly follows it. Differential Primary bipolar I or II disorder in someone who also uses substances, settled by whether mood symptoms predate use and whether they persist about a month beyond acute intoxication or withdrawal. Delirium . Substance-induced psychotic disorder where psychosis rather than mood predominates. Personality disorders with affective instability. 5. Depressive disorders DSM-5 added two disorders to this chapter that carry a disproportionate share of exam questions because they are new: Disruptive Mood Dysregulation Disorder and Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder . It also merged dysthymia and chronic major depression into Persistent Depressive Disorder , and removed the bereavement exclusion. Know those four changes and you have most of the chapter's marks. Disruptive Mood Dysregulation Disorder F34.81 In plain language. A child who is angry or irritable almost all of the time, in between frequent explosive outbursts that are far out of proportion to whatever set them off. It was created deliberately to stop children with chronic irritability being diagnosed as paediatric bipolar disorder, which was over-diagnosed in the 2000s in the United States. A. Severe recurrent temper outbursts , verbal or behavioural, grossly out of proportion in intensity or duration to the situation or provocation. B. The outbursts are inconsistent with developmental level . C. Outbursts occur on average 3 or more times per week . D. The mood between outbursts is persistently irritable or angry most of the day, nearly every day, and is observable by others . This inter-episode criterion is what separates it from an ordinary tantrum problem. E. Criteria A to D have been present for 12 or more months , without a period of 3 or more consecutive months free of all of them. F. Present in at least 2 of 3 settings (home, school, with peers) and severe in at least one. G. Diagnosis should not be made for the first time before age 6 or after age 18 . H. By history or observation, the age at onset of criteria A to E is before 10 years . I. There has never been a distinct period lasting more than 1 day during which the full symptom criteria, except duration, for a manic or hypomanic episode have been met. J. The behaviours do not occur exclusively during a major depressive episode and are not better explained by another mental disorder such as autism, PTSD, separation anxiety, or persistent depressive disorder. K. Not attributable to a substance or another medical or neurological condition. Numbers The four numbers to hold: outbursts 3 or more times a week , duration 12 months , diagnose only between ages 6 and 18 , onset before 10 . 6-month to 1-year prevalence roughly 2 to 5 percent, commoner in males and in school-age children. Comorbidity Very high. ADHD, oppositional defiant disorder, anxiety disorders and major depressive disorder. Longitudinally, these children tend to develop unipolar depressive and anxiety disorders in adulthood, not bipolar disorder, which is the evidence base the diagnosis was built on. Differential Bipolar disorder is the point of the whole diagnosis: bipolar is episodic with a distinct period of elevated mood and decreased need for sleep, DMDD is persistent and non-episodic . Oppositional defiant disorder shares the irritability, but DMDD requires the severe outbursts and the persistent between-outburst mood; DSM-5 rules that if a child meets criteria for both, only DMDD is diagnosed . Intermittent explosive disorder requires only 3 months and has no persistent inter-episode irritability. ADHD, autism, PTSD, separation anxiety , where the irritability is explained by the other condition. ICD-11 Has no DMDD. The same child is coded as oppositional defiant disorder with chronic irritability-anger . Major Depressive Disorder F32.x single, F33.x recurrent In plain language. At least two weeks in which the person is down or has lost all interest, plus enough of the other classic symptoms, and this is a change from how they were. A. Five or more of the nine symptoms of a major depressive episode over the same 2-week period, one of which is depressed mood or anhedonia (list given in the bipolar chapter above). B. Clinically significant distress or impairment. C. Not attributable to a substance or another medical condition. D. Not better explained by a schizophrenia spectrum or other psychotic disorder. E. There has never been a manic or hypomanic episode . Specifiers Single or recurrent episode; mild, moderate, severe; with psychotic features; in partial or full remission. Plus the cross-cutting set: with anxious distress, with mixed features, with melancholic features (loss of pleasure in all activities, lack of reactivity, distinct quality of mood, early morning awakening, marked psychomotor change, excessive guilt, worse in the morning), with atypical features, with mood-congruent or mood-incongruent psychotic features, with catatonia, with peripartum onset, with seasonal pattern. Numbers 12-month prevalence about 7 percent in the United States; lifetime around 15 to 20 percent. Female to male about 2:1 , a ratio that appears at puberty. Peak onset in the twenties. About two-thirds of episodes remit with treatment; recurrence risk after one episode about 50 percent, after two about 70 percent, after three about 90 percent. Comorbidity Anxiety disorders (panic and generalised anxiety are commonest), substance use disorders, borderline personality disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder, eating disorders, and medical illness (post-stroke, post-MI, diabetes, hypothyroidism, cancer, Parkinson's). Differential Bipolar disorders , always screen for past hypomania. Persistent depressive disorder (2 years, milder). Adjustment disorder with depressed mood (identifiable stressor, does not meet full MDE criteria). Bereavement and prolonged grief disorder . Substance-induced depressive disorder (alcohol, sedatives, withdrawal from stimulants; medications: interferon, isotretinoin, some antihypertensives, corticosteroids). Depressive disorder due to another medical condition (hypothyroidism, anaemia, Cushing's, Parkinson's, stroke). Major neurocognitive disorder versus pseudodementia in an older adult. ADHD (distractibility without mood change). Demoralisation and normal sadness . DSM-5 change The bereavement exclusion was removed . In DSM-IV you could not diagnose MDD within 2 months of a death unless there were specific features. DSM-5 dropped that, on the reasoning that grief and depression can coexist and that withholding a diagnosis withheld treatment; a long footnote in the criteria set explains how to distinguish grief (waves of emptiness and yearning, self-esteem preserved, thoughts of joining the deceased) from a major depressive episode (persistent depressed mood, worthlessness, self-critical rumination, suicidal ideation about ending one's own life because of worthlessness). That footnote, and the removal itself, are heavily examined. Persistent Depressive Disorder F34.1 In plain language. Depression that has been there for at least two years, most days, at whatever intensity. DSM-5 merged DSM-IV's dysthymic disorder and chronic major depressive disorder into this one label; DSM-5-TR restored the name "dysthymia" as an alternative in the title text. A. Depressed mood for most of the day, for more days than not, for at least 2 years ( 1 year in children and adolescents , where mood may be irritable ). B. While depressed, 2 or more of six: poor appetite or overeating; insomnia or hypersomnia; low energy or fatigue; low self-esteem; poor concentration or difficulty making decisions; feelings of hopelessness. C. During the 2 years, the person has never been without the symptoms in Criteria A and B for more than 2 months at a time . D. Criteria for a major depressive disorder may be continuously present for 2 years. E. There has never been a manic or hypomanic episode, and criteria for cyclothymic disorder have never been met. F. Not better explained by a persistent schizophrenia spectrum disorder. G. Not substance or medical. H. Clinically significant distress or impairment. Specifiers The distinctive ones: with pure dysthymic syndrome (full MDE criteria not met in the preceding 2 years), with persistent major depressive episode (full criteria met throughout the preceding 2 years), with intermittent major depressive episodes, with current episode , and with intermittent major depressive episodes, without current episode . Also early onset ( before 21 ) or late onset (at 21 or after), plus anxious distress, atypical features, remission and severity. Numbers 12-month prevalence about 0.5 percent for persistent depressive disorder and about 1.5 percent for chronic major depressive disorder. Early onset before 21 predicts a worse course and more personality-disorder comorbidity. Comorbidity Compared with MDD, higher rates of anxiety disorders, substance use disorders, and personality disorders , especially cluster B and cluster C. "Double depression", a major depressive episode superimposed on dysthymia, is the classic pattern and is now captured by the intermittent-episodes specifier. Differential Major depressive disorder (episodic rather than 2 years continuous). Cyclothymia (hypomanic periods present). Bipolar II . Psychotic disorders with residual depression. Personality disorders , which may be diagnosed alongside. Depressive disorder due to another medical condition . Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder F32.81 In plain language. In the week before the period, mood collapses in a specific patterned way, it lifts within a few days of bleeding starting, and it is gone in the week after. Moved from the DSM-IV appendix into the main text in DSM-5, which is exactly what gets asked. A. In the majority of menstrual cycles, at least 5 symptoms present in the final week before the onset of menses , starting to improve within a few days after the onset of menses , and becoming minimal or absent in the week post-menses . B. One or more of these four must be present: marked affective lability; marked irritability or anger or increased interpersonal conflicts; marked depressed mood, hopelessness or self-deprecating thoughts; marked anxiety, tension, or feelings of being keyed up or on edge. C. One or more of these seven must additionally be present, to reach a total of five: decreased interest in usual activities; subjective difficulty concentrating; lethargy, easy fatigability, marked lack of energy; marked change in appetite, overeating, or specific food cravings; hypersomnia or insomnia; a sense of being overwhelmed or out of control; physical symptoms such as breast tenderness or swelling, joint or muscle pain, bloating or weight gain. D. Significant distress or interference with work, school, usual social activities or relationships. E. Not merely an exacerbation of another disorder. F. Criterion A should be confirmed by prospective daily ratings during at least 2 symptomatic cycles (a provisional diagnosis may be made before that). G. Not attributable to a substance or another medical condition. Numbers 12-month prevalence between 1.8 and 5.8 percent of menstruating women when strict prospective ratings are used, which is far below the rate of self-reported premenstrual complaints. Symptoms cease after menopause. Comorbidity Major depressive disorder is the commonest, plus anxiety disorders and bipolar disorder. Differential Premenstrual syndrome , which is far more common, needs no affective symptom, and is not as impairing. Premenstrual exacerbation of an existing depressive, bipolar or anxiety disorder, which is Criterion E, and is distinguished by symptoms being present throughout the cycle and simply worsening premenstrually. Dysmenorrhoea (pain starting with menses, not before). Hormonal treatment effects, and thyroid disease. Substance/Medication-Induced Depressive Disorder, and Depressive Disorder Due to Another Medical Condition A prominent and persistent disturbance in mood, predominantly depressed mood or markedly diminished interest or pleasure, that developed during or soon after substance intoxication or withdrawal or medication exposure, or that is the direct pathophysiological consequence of a medical condition. Common substances: alcohol, sedative-hypnotics and anxiolytics (during use), stimulants and cocaine (during withdrawal), opioids. Medications: corticosteroids, interferon-alpha, isotretinoin, reserpine and older antihypertensives, some hormonal contraceptives, varenicline. Common medical causes: hypothyroidism , Cushing's disease, Parkinson's disease, stroke (particularly left frontal), traumatic brain injury, multiple sclerosis, Huntington's, pancreatic carcinoma, vitamin B12 deficiency, obstructive sleep apnoea. Comorbidity The substance use disorder itself, and, for the medical form, the physical illness plus the anxiety, insomnia and pain conditions that travel with it. A primary depressive disorder frequently coexists, and having one raises the risk of the other. Differential Primary major depressive disorder in someone who also has a medical illness or uses substances. The tests are temporal (did it start with the exposure), dose-related, and whether it resolves when the exposure ends, plus whether the symptom picture is atypical for primary depression. The two other-specified categories worth naming Other Specified Depressive Disorder covers, among others: recurrent brief depression (depressed mood plus 4 other symptoms for 2 to 13 days, at least once a month for 12 months, never meeting criteria for another disorder), short-duration depressive episode (4 to 13 days), and depressive episode with insufficient symptoms . Examiners like recurrent brief depression because the duration is so distinctive. 6. Anxiety disorders DSM-5 broke the old anxiety chapter into three: anxiety disorders proper, obsessive-compulsive and related disorders, and trauma and stressor-related disorders. Inside the anxiety chapter, the big structural changes were that panic disorder and agoraphobia were unlinked into two separate diagnoses (DSM-IV had "panic disorder with agoraphobia" and "agoraphobia without history of panic"), that separation anxiety disorder and selective mutism moved in from the childhood chapter and are no longer restricted to children, and that panic attack became a specifier usable across the whole manual. The chapter is ordered developmentally, by typical age of onset. The 6-month rule Specific phobia, social anxiety disorder, agoraphobia and generalised anxiety disorder all require 6 months or more . In DSM-IV that 6-month requirement applied only to people under 18; DSM-5 extended it to all ages , to stop transient fears being diagnosed. Panic disorder is the exception: it needs 1 month of worry or behaviour change after an attack. Separation anxiety needs 4 weeks in children and adolescents, 6 months or more in adults . Selective mutism needs 1 month , not counting the first month of school. Separation Anxiety Disorder F93.0 In plain language. Fear of being away from the people you are attached to, that is far beyond what is normal for your age, and that shapes what you will and will not do. A. Developmentally inappropriate and excessive fear or anxiety concerning separation from attachment figures, with at least 3 of 8 : recurrent excessive distress when separation is anticipated or occurs; persistent excessive worry about losing attachment figures or about harm befalling them; persistent excessive worry about an untoward event causing separation (getting lost, being kidnapped, having an accident, becoming ill); persistent reluctance or refusal to go out, away from home, to school, to work, because of fear of separation; persistent and excessive fear of or reluctance about being alone or without attachment figures; persistent reluctance or refusal to sleep away from home or to sleep without being near a major attachment figure; repeated nightmares involving the theme of separation; repeated complaints of physical symptoms (headaches, stomach aches, nausea, vomiting) when separation from attachment figures occurs or is anticipated. B. Duration: at least 4 weeks in children and adolescents , typically 6 months or more in adults . C. Clinically significant distress or impairment. D. Not better explained by another disorder such as autism (refusal to leave home because of resistance to change), psychotic disorders (delusions about separation), agoraphobia (refusal to go out without a trusted companion), generalised anxiety disorder (worry about ill health befalling others), or illness anxiety disorder. Numbers The most prevalent anxiety disorder in children under 12, about 4 percent in children, about 1.6 percent in adolescents, and 0.9 to 1.9 percent in adults. DSM-5's change: onset before age 18 is no longer required , so adults can be diagnosed for the first time. Comorbidity In children: generalised anxiety disorder and specific phobia. In adults: specific phobia, PTSD, panic disorder, generalised anxiety disorder, social anxiety, agoraphobia, obsessive-compulsive disorder, and personality disorders. Differential Agoraphobia (fear of being unable to escape or get help, not fear of losing the attachment figure). Generalised anxiety disorder (worry is broad, not focused on separation). Autism . Conduct disorder (truancy without fear of separation, so the child leaves home rather than refusing to). School refusal is a behaviour, not a diagnosis, and may arise from separation anxiety, social anxiety, depression, or bullying, which examiners like to test. Selective Mutism F94.0 In plain language. A child who talks normally at home says nothing at school. It is not that they cannot speak, it is that in specific social settings they do not. A. Consistent failure to speak in specific social situations where there is an expectation for speaking (for example school), despite speaking in other situations. B. Interferes with educational or occupational achievement or with social communication. C. Duration at least 1 month, not limited to the first month of school . D. The failure is not attributable to a lack of knowledge of, or comfort with, the spoken language required (which matters in multilingual Indian classrooms). E. Not better explained by a communication disorder, and does not occur exclusively during autism spectrum disorder, schizophrenia or another psychotic disorder. Numbers Rare, prevalence 0.03 to 1 percent, and does not vary much by sex or ethnicity. Onset usually before age 5 , though it often comes to attention only on entering school. Comorbidity Social anxiety disorder is by far the commonest and many researchers regard selective mutism as a variant of it. Also separation anxiety disorder, specific phobia, oppositional behaviour confined to the mute settings, and communication delays. Differential Communication disorders (the difficulty is not situation-specific). Autism . Intellectual disability . Social anxiety disorder (the child may speak, with distress). Normal shyness and the silent period of a child newly immersed in a second language, which is explicitly excluded by Criterion D. Specific Phobia F40.2xx In plain language. One thing, reliably terrifying, avoided or endured with dread, for at least six months, out of proportion to the real danger. A. Marked fear or anxiety about a specific object or situation. In children this may be expressed by crying, tantrums, freezing or clinging. B. The phobic object or situation almost always provokes immediate fear or anxiety. C. It is actively avoided or endured with intense fear or anxiety. D. The fear is out of proportion to the actual danger posed, and to the sociocultural context. E. Persistent, typically lasting 6 months or more . F. Clinically significant distress or impairment. G. Not better explained by another disorder. DSM-5 removed the requirement that the person recognise the fear as excessive or unreasonable; the clinician now judges proportionality. That change also appears in social anxiety disorder and agoraphobia. Specifiers Code by stimulus: animal ; natural environment (heights, storms, water); blood-injection-injury (needles, other medical procedures); situational (aeroplanes, lifts, enclosed places); other (choking, vomiting, in children loud sounds or costumed characters). Numbers 12-month prevalence about 7 to 9 percent, the commonest anxiety disorder. Female to male about 2:1. Median onset between ages 7 and 11. The blood-injection-injury type is the exception you must be able to name: it produces a diphasic vasovagal response , with an initial rise then a sharp fall in heart rate and blood pressure and frequent fainting, whereas every other phobia produces sympathetic arousal only. It also has the strongest family loading, roughly two-thirds of sufferers have an affected relative, and it is treated with applied tension rather than pure relaxation. Comorbidity Most people with one specific phobia have several (the average is three). Comorbid with other anxiety disorders, depression, substance use, and somatic symptom disorder. Specific phobia commonly comes first and predicts later depression. Differential Agoraphobia (fear of two or more of the five agoraphobic situations, and the fear is of not escaping or not getting help). Social anxiety disorder (fear of scrutiny). Separation anxiety . Panic disorder (attacks are unexpected, not cued). OCD (avoidance is driven by an obsession, for example contamination). PTSD (avoidance follows a traumatic event). Illness anxiety disorder . Normal fear, which is proportionate and non-impairing. Social Anxiety Disorder (Social Phobia) F40.10 In plain language. Fear of being watched and judged, and of doing something humiliating in front of others, that lasts six months and shrinks the person's life. A. Marked fear or anxiety about one or more social situations in which the person is exposed to possible scrutiny by others : social interactions (conversation, meeting unfamiliar people), being observed (eating, drinking), and performing in front of others. In children, the anxiety must occur in peer settings and not just during interactions with adults. B. The person fears they will act in a way, or show anxiety symptoms, that will be negatively evaluated , that is, will be humiliating or embarrassing, will lead to rejection, or will offend others. C. The social situations almost always provoke fear or anxiety. In children this may appear as crying, tantrums, freezing, clinging, shrinking or failing to speak. D. Avoided or endured with intense fear. E. Out of proportion to the actual threat and to the sociocultural context. F. Persistent, typically 6 months or more . G. Significant distress or impairment. H, I, J. Not due to a substance or medical condition, not better explained by another mental disorder, and if another medical condition is present (Parkinson's, obesity, disfigurement from burns or injury) the fear is clearly unrelated or excessive. Specifier Performance only , where the fear is restricted to speaking or performing in public. DSM-5 replaced the DSM-IV "generalized" specifier with this narrower "performance only" one, because the generalised subtype could not be reliably drawn. Numbers 12-month prevalence about 7 percent in the United States, lower in much of Asia (0.5 to 2 percent). Slightly more common in females in community samples, roughly equal in clinical samples. Median onset age 13; about 75 percent onset between 8 and 15. Comorbidity Other anxiety disorders, major depressive disorder (usually later, and social anxiety typically precedes it), substance use disorder, especially alcohol, used as self-medication, body dysmorphic disorder, and avoidant personality disorder , which overlaps so heavily that many argue they are the same construct at different severities. Differential Normal shyness , which is a common trait and only becomes a disorder with impairment. Agoraphobia (the person is comforted by a companion, in social anxiety a companion often makes it worse). Panic disorder (unexpected attacks). Body dysmorphic disorder (fear centres on a perceived physical defect). Autism (social communication skills are deficient, not merely inhibited by anxiety). Major depressive disorder (social withdrawal from anhedonia). Avoidant personality disorder (broader, earlier, more pervasive; often diagnosed together). Taijin kyofusho , the Japanese variant where the fear is of offending or embarrassing others with one's gaze, body odour or blushing, is the standard culture question. Panic Disorder F41.0 In plain language. Repeated attacks of terror that come out of nowhere and peak within minutes, followed by at least a month of dreading the next one or rearranging life to avoid it. A. Recurrent unexpected panic attacks. A panic attack is an abrupt surge of intense fear or discomfort that reaches a peak within minutes , during which 4 or more of 13 symptoms occur: palpitations or accelerated heart rate; sweating; trembling or shaking; sensations of shortness of breath or smothering; feelings of choking; chest pain or discomfort; nausea or abdominal distress; feeling dizzy, unsteady, light-headed or faint; chills or heat sensations; paraesthesias; derealisation or depersonalisation ; fear of losing control or going crazy; fear of dying . Culture-specific symptoms such as tinnitus, neck soreness, headache or uncontrollable screaming or crying may be seen but do not count toward the four. B. At least one attack has been followed by 1 month or more of one or both: persistent concern or worry about additional attacks or their consequences (losing control, having a heart attack, going crazy); and/or a significant maladaptive change in behaviour related to the attacks (avoiding exercise or unfamiliar situations). C. Not attributable to a substance or another medical condition (hyperthyroidism, cardiopulmonary disorders). D. Not better explained by another mental disorder, where the attacks would be expected and cued: social anxiety (social situations), specific phobia (the phobic object), OCD (obsessions), PTSD (trauma reminders), separation anxiety (separation). Numbers 12-month prevalence about 2 to 3 percent in adults and adolescents. Female to male about 2:1. Median onset about age 20 to 24, uncommon before 14 and after 45. A limited-symptom attack has fewer than 4 symptoms. Nocturnal panic attacks, waking from sleep in a panic, occur in a substantial minority and are a favourite MCQ. Panic attack is not a disorder : it is a specifier that can be attached to any DSM-5 diagnosis, which was the key DSM-5 change alongside the unlinking from agoraphobia. Comorbidity Agoraphobia (very high, and now coded as two diagnoses), other anxiety disorders, major depressive disorder, bipolar disorder, alcohol use disorder, and medical conditions: mitral valve prolapse, thyroid disease, asthma, COPD, irritable bowel syndrome. Suicidal ideation and attempts are elevated. Differential Anxiety disorder due to another medical condition : hyperthyroidism, hyperparathyroidism, phaeochromocytoma, vestibular dysfunction, seizure disorders, cardiopulmonary conditions. Substance-induced : caffeine, cannabis, stimulants, alcohol withdrawal. Other anxiety disorders with cued attacks , which is Criterion D. Illness anxiety disorder . PTSD . The clinical rule to state in a written answer: unexpectedness is the defining feature, so ask "was there a trigger?". Agoraphobia F40.00 In plain language. Fear of situations you might not be able to get out of, or get help in, if something goes wrong. Not just fear of open spaces, which is the common misreading. A. Marked fear or anxiety about 2 or more of 5 situations: using public transportation; being in open spaces (car parks, marketplaces, bridges); being in enclosed places (shops, theatres, cinemas); standing in line or being in a crowd; being outside of the home alone. The requirement of two or more is a DSM-5 change and is heavily examined. B. The person fears or avoids these situations because of thoughts that escape might be difficult or help might not be available in the event of developing panic-like symptoms or other incapacitating or embarrassing symptoms (falling in the elderly, incontinence). C. The situations almost always provoke fear or anxiety. D. Actively avoided, require the presence of a companion, or are endured with intense fear. E. Out of proportion to the actual danger and the sociocultural context. F. Persistent, typically 6 months or more . G. Significant distress or impairment. H. If another medical condition is present, the fear is clearly excessive. I. Not better explained by another mental disorder. DSM-5 makes it explicit: agoraphobia is diagnosed irrespective of the presence of panic disorder , and if the person meets criteria for both, both diagnoses are given . Numbers 12-month prevalence about 1.7 percent in adolescents and adults. Female to male about 2:1. Mean onset about 17 years, with a second peak after 40. About 30 to 50 percent have panic disorder first. Comorbidity Other anxiety disorders (specific phobia, panic disorder, social anxiety, generalised anxiety), depressive disorders, PTSD, and alcohol use disorder. Differential Specific phobia, situational type : if only one of the five situations is feared, and the fear is not about escape or help, it is specific phobia. Social anxiety disorder (fear of scrutiny, and a companion does not help). Separation anxiety (fear of being away from the attachment figure, and the person is fine outside the home if the figure is present). Major depressive disorder with apathy and withdrawal. Psychotic disorders with persecutory avoidance. Realistic avoidance due to a medical condition such as inflammatory bowel disease or Parkinson's, where the concern is proportionate. Generalised Anxiety Disorder F41.1 In plain language. Six months of worrying about many everyday things, that the person cannot switch off, plus the physical toll of that worrying. A. Excessive anxiety and worry (apprehensive expectation), occurring more days than not for at least 6 months , about a number of events or activities such as work or school performance. B. The person finds it difficult to control the worry . C. The anxiety and worry are associated with 3 or more of 6 symptoms, with at least some present more days than not for the past 6 months ( only 1 item is required in children ): restlessness or feeling keyed up or on edge; being easily fatigued; difficulty concentrating or mind going blank; irritability; muscle tension; sleep disturbance. The mnemonic is WATCHERS or, more simply, remember that muscle tension is the item that best discriminates GAD from other anxiety disorders. D. Significant distress or impairment. E. Not substance or medical (hyperthyroidism). F. Not better explained by another mental disorder. Numbers 12-month prevalence about 2.9 percent in adults, 0.9 percent in adolescents. Female to male about 2:1. Median onset age 30, later than the other anxiety disorders, and onset in childhood or adolescence is unusual. Course is chronic and fluctuating with low full-remission rates. Comorbidity Major depressive disorder is the commonest and the overlap is so large that some argue for a combined "distress" construct. Also other anxiety disorders, persistent depressive disorder, substance use, somatic symptom disorder, and the physical conditions worry drives, including irritable bowel syndrome, headaches and insomnia. Differential Non-pathological anxiety , distinguished by controllability, breadth, impairment and physical symptoms. Anxiety disorder due to another medical condition , above all hyperthyroidism . Substance-induced , especially caffeine and stimulant use, and withdrawal states. Social anxiety, OCD, separation anxiety, illness anxiety, anorexia nervosa, PTSD, adjustment disorder , in each of which the worry is confined to a specific theme: scrutiny, obsessions, separation, illness, weight, the trauma, the stressor. Depressive disorders , where rumination is about the past rather than apprehension about the future. Substance/Medication-Induced Anxiety Disorder, and Anxiety Disorder Due to Another Medical Condition Panic attacks or anxiety predominate, developed during or soon after substance intoxication or withdrawal or medication exposure, or are the direct pathophysiological consequence of a medical condition, and are not better explained by an independent anxiety disorder, and do not occur exclusively during delirium. Substances: caffeine (the classic), cannabis, cocaine and amphetamines, hallucinogens, and withdrawal from alcohol, sedatives and opioids. Medications: bronchodilators, thyroid hormone, corticosteroids, decongestants, some antidepressants early in treatment. Medical conditions: hyperthyroidism , phaeochromocytoma , hypoglycaemia, hyperparathyroidism, cardiac arrhythmias, congestive heart failure, pulmonary embolism, COPD and asthma, vestibular dysfunction, seizure disorders. Comorbidity The substance use disorder itself, plus primary anxiety and depressive disorders, which are common and often predate the exposure. For the medical form, the underlying disease and the depression that follows it. Differential Primary anxiety disorders in someone who also uses substances or has a medical illness, settled by whether the anxiety predates the exposure and whether it persists about a month past acute withdrawal. Delirium , which excludes the diagnosis. Panic disorder , where attacks are unexpected and not tied to an exposure. Illness anxiety disorder , where the worry is about having a disease rather than a direct physiological effect. 7. Obsessive-compulsive and related disorders A new chapter in DSM-5, created because these conditions share repetitive thoughts and behaviours, family loading, neurocircuitry (the cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical loop) and treatment response. Hoarding disorder and excoriation disorder are brand new diagnoses in DSM-5, body dysmorphic disorder moved here from somatoform disorders, and trichotillomania moved here from impulse-control disorders. Every disorder in the chapter carries an insight specifier : with good or fair insight, with poor insight, with absent insight or delusional beliefs. That specifier is the answer to "how does DSM-5 handle a patient whose obsession has become a delusion?": you do not add a psychotic diagnosis, you use the absent-insight specifier. Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder F42.2 In plain language. Thoughts that force their way in and will not leave, and acts the person feels driven to perform to make the thoughts tolerable, eating at least an hour a day. A. Presence of obsessions, compulsions, or both . Obsessions are recurrent and persistent thoughts, urges or images that are experienced, at some time during the disturbance, as intrusive and unwanted , and that in most people cause marked anxiety or distress; the person attempts to ignore or suppress them or to neutralise them with some other thought or action. Compulsions are repetitive behaviours (hand washing, ordering, checking) or mental acts (praying, counting, repeating words silently) that the person feels driven to perform in response to an obsession or according to rules that must be applied rigidly ; they are aimed at preventing or reducing anxiety or some dreaded event, but they are not connected in a realistic way to what they are meant to neutralise, or are clearly excessive. B. The obsessions or compulsions are time-consuming (more than 1 hour per day) or cause clinically significant distress or impairment. C. Not attributable to a substance or another medical condition. D. Not better explained by another mental disorder (see the differential, which DSM lists at unusual length here). Specifiers Insight: good or fair / poor / absent or delusional. Plus tic-related , that is, the individual has a current or past history of a tic disorder, which marks out a distinct subtype with earlier onset, male predominance, more symmetry and ordering symptoms, and a better response to antipsychotic augmentation.
