Numbers 12-month prevalence about 1.2 percent. Slightly more common in adult women , but males predominate in childhood onset . Mean age at onset 19.5, with about 25 percent by age 14; onset after 35 is unusual. Untreated the course is chronic. Common symptom dimensions: contamination and cleaning; harm obsessions and checking; symmetry, ordering and counting; forbidden or taboo thoughts (aggressive, sexual, religious) with mental rituals. Comorbidity Up to 76 percent have an anxiety disorder, and up to 63 percent a depressive or bipolar disorder, with major depressive disorder commonest. About 30 percent have a lifetime tic disorder. Also obsessive-compulsive personality disorder in roughly a quarter to a third, body dysmorphic disorder, trichotillomania, hoarding, and eating disorders. In children, the sudden-onset presentation after streptococcal infection ( PANDAS , now often subsumed under PANS) is a stock question. Differential Generalised anxiety disorder : worries there are about real-life concerns and are ego-syntonic, obsessions are intrusive, often senseless, and ego-dystonic. Obsessive-compulsive personality disorder : a lifelong trait pattern of perfectionism and control, no true obsessions or compulsions , and it is ego-syntonic, so the person sees nothing wrong. This pair is the most reliably examined distinction in the chapter. Body dysmorphic disorder (thoughts confined to appearance). Hoarding disorder (no true obsession; distress arises from discarding). Trichotillomania and excoriation (no obsession precedes the act). Eating disorders (thoughts confined to food and weight). Tics and stereotyped movements (no preceding obsession, and there is a premonitory sensory urge instead). Psychotic disorders (use the absent-insight specifier rather than adding schizophrenia, unless there are other psychotic features). Major depressive disorder (ruminations are mood-congruent and not linked to compulsions). Body Dysmorphic Disorder F45.22 In plain language. The person is convinced some part of how they look is ugly or wrong, other people cannot see it, and they spend hours checking, camouflaging or seeking reassurance. A. Preoccupation with one or more perceived defects or flaws in physical appearance that are not observable or appear slight to others . B. At some point during the course, the person has performed repetitive behaviours (mirror checking, excessive grooming, skin picking, reassurance seeking) or mental acts (comparing their appearance with that of others) in response to the appearance concerns. This criterion was added in DSM-5 . C. Clinically significant distress or impairment. D. The appearance preoccupation is not better explained by concerns with body fat or weight in a person whose symptoms meet criteria for an eating disorder . Specifiers With muscle dysmorphia (the belief that one's build is too small or insufficiently muscular; occurs mostly in males and is the specifier most often asked about), plus the insight specifier. Around a third have absent insight or delusional beliefs. Numbers Point prevalence about 2.4 percent in the United States, 9 to 15 percent in dermatology patients and 7 to 8 percent in cosmetic-surgery patients. Mean age at onset 16 to 17, median 15, with two-thirds onset before 18. Roughly equal in men and women. Suicidal ideation is reported in about 80 percent and attempts in about a quarter, far higher than in OCD, which is a discriminating fact. Comorbidity Major depressive disorder is commonest and usually starts after BDD. Also social anxiety disorder, OCD, substance use disorders (particularly in muscle dysmorphia, with anabolic steroid use), and avoidant personality disorder. Differential Normal appearance concerns and clearly visible defects (which do not qualify). Eating disorders , which is Criterion D. Obsessive-compulsive disorder (the preoccupation is not restricted to appearance). Social anxiety disorder (fear of scrutiny in general, not because of a specific perceived defect). Major depressive disorder (poor self-image without the specific preoccupation and repetitive behaviours). Excoriation disorder (picking without the appearance-defect belief; if picking is to fix a perceived flaw, it is BDD). Gender dysphoria , olfactory reference syndrome (in DSM-5-TR handled under other specified obsessive-compulsive and related disorder; ICD-11 has it as a full diagnosis). Hoarding Disorder F42.3 In plain language. Getting rid of things feels intolerable, so possessions build up until the rooms cannot be used for what rooms are for. New in DSM-5. A. Persistent difficulty discarding or parting with possessions, regardless of their actual value . B. The difficulty is due to a perceived need to save the items and to distress associated with discarding them . C. The difficulty results in the accumulation of possessions that congest and clutter active living areas and substantially compromise their intended use . If living areas are uncluttered, it is only because of the interventions of third parties such as family members, cleaners or authorities. D. Clinically significant distress or impairment, including maintaining a safe environment for self and others . E. Not attributable to another medical condition (brain injury, cerebrovascular disease, Prader-Willi syndrome). F. Not better explained by another mental disorder (obsessions in OCD, decreased energy in major depressive disorder, delusions in schizophrenia, cognitive deficits in major neurocognitive disorder, restricted interests in autism). Specifiers With excessive acquisition (present in about 80 to 90 percent, either buying or acquiring free items), plus the insight specifier. Insight is characteristically poor, and many present only under pressure from family or housing authorities. Numbers Prevalence roughly 2 to 6 percent. Symptoms typically begin between ages 11 and 15, become interfering by the mid twenties and clinically impairing by the mid thirties, and severity increases with each decade of life . Prevalence is roughly three times as high in adults aged 55 to 94 as in those aged 34 to 44. Roughly equal by sex in epidemiological samples, though clinical samples are mostly female. Comorbidity About 75 percent have a comorbid mood or anxiety disorder, with major depressive disorder in around half. OCD in about 20 percent. ADHD, inattentive presentation, in about 30 percent. Differential OCD , the key one: hoarding in OCD is driven by a classic obsession (contamination fear, fear of harm from discarding, incompleteness), is usually unwanted and distressing rather than pleasurable, and there is no excessive acquisition driven by desire. Major depressive disorder (clutter accumulates from psychomotor retardation and low energy, with no attachment to the objects). Major neurocognitive disorder (accumulation begins after cognitive decline, and is self-neglect rather than saving). Autism . Schizophrenia (delusional reasons). Normal collecting , which is organised, selective and non-impairing. Trichotillomania (Hair-Pulling Disorder) F63.3 A. Recurrent pulling out of one's hair, resulting in hair loss . B. Repeated attempts to decrease or stop hair pulling. C. Clinically significant distress or impairment. D. Not attributable to another medical condition (a dermatological condition). E. Not better explained by the symptoms of another mental disorder (for example attempts to improve a perceived defect in body dysmorphic disorder). Note what DSM-5 removed from the DSM-IV criteria: the requirements for mounting tension before pulling and pleasure, gratification or relief when pulling , because many patients, particularly those pulling automatically while reading or watching television, do not report them. Numbers 12-month prevalence 1 to 2 percent. Female to male about 10:1 in adults, roughly equal in children. Onset usually coincides with, or follows, puberty. Sites: scalp commonest, then eyebrows and eyelashes; some pull from pubic, axillary and facial regions. Trichophagia , eating the hair, occurs in a minority and can cause a trichobezoar requiring surgery, which is a favourite MCQ. Comorbidity Major depressive disorder and excoriation disorder , which co-occurs in roughly a fifth to a third. Also OCD, anxiety disorders, and other body-focused repetitive behaviours (nail biting, lip chewing) coded under other specified obsessive-compulsive and related disorder. Differential Normal hair removal or grooming for cosmetic reasons. Alopecia areata and other dermatological causes, which are distinguished by the pattern; in trichotillomania hairs of varying lengths remain in the affected patch. OCD (pulling in response to an obsession, for example to achieve symmetry). Body dysmorphic disorder (pulling to remove a perceived defect). Stereotypic movement disorder . Psychotic disorder (pulling in response to a delusion or hallucination). Excoriation (Skin-Picking) Disorder F42.4 A. Recurrent skin picking resulting in skin lesions . B. Repeated attempts to decrease or stop. C. Clinically significant distress or impairment. D. Not attributable to a substance (cocaine) or another medical condition (scabies). E. Not better explained by another mental disorder (delusions or tactile hallucinations in a psychotic disorder, appearance concerns in body dysmorphic disorder, stereotypies, or intent to self-harm in non-suicidal self-injury). New in DSM-5. Numbers Lifetime prevalence about 1.4 percent or slightly higher; three-quarters or more are female . Most commonly picked sites are the face, arms and hands. Onset most often in adolescence, frequently coinciding with the onset of puberty or with acne. Course is chronic with waxing and waning. Comorbidity OCD, trichotillomania, major depressive disorder, and other body-focused repetitive behaviour disorders. Differential Non-suicidal self-injury , where the intent is to relieve emotional pain through harm; in excoriation the intent is to remove an irregularity. Body dysmorphic disorder . Psychotic disorder with delusional parasitosis or formication. Substance-induced , above all methamphetamine and cocaine. Scabies , eczema and other dermatological conditions. Substance-Induced and Medical Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders, and Other Specified Substance/medication-induced , for example the obsessions and compulsions that appear with cocaine or amphetamine use. Due to another medical condition , for example after streptococcal infection, or with basal ganglia lesions, Sydenham's chorea, Huntington's or traumatic brain injury. Other specified obsessive-compulsive and related disorder is where DSM-5-TR parks several named syndromes examiners like: body-focused repetitive behaviour disorder (nail biting, lip chewing, cheek chewing), obsessional jealousy , olfactory reference syndrome (jikoshu-kyofu, the belief that one emits a foul body odour), koro (an episode of sudden intense anxiety that the penis, or in women the vulva and nipples, will recede into the body and cause death), and shubo-kyofu (excessive fear of having a bodily deformity). Comorbidity Primary obsessive-compulsive disorder, tic disorders and, for the post-streptococcal and basal-ganglia presentations, the neurological condition itself. The named cultural syndromes co-occur with anxiety and depressive disorders. Differential Primary OCD in someone who also uses stimulants, settled by timing and by persistence past withdrawal. Psychotic disorders , where the belief is delusional and unaccompanied by rituals. Body dysmorphic disorder for shubo-kyofu, and delusional disorder, somatic type for olfactory reference syndrome with absent insight. Panic disorder for a koro episode, where the acute anxiety is the presenting feature. 8. Trauma and stressor-related disorders The one chapter in DSM where an identifiable external event is part of the criteria . It contains the two attachment disorders, acute stress disorder, PTSD, the adjustment disorders, and, new in DSM-5-TR, prolonged grief disorder . Reactive Attachment Disorder F94.1 In plain language. A severely neglected young child who has given up on adults: they do not seek comfort when distressed and do not accept it when it is offered. The internalising half of what DSM-IV called reactive attachment disorder. A. A consistent pattern of inhibited, emotionally withdrawn behaviour toward adult caregivers, shown by both: the child rarely or minimally seeks comfort when distressed, and rarely or minimally responds to comfort when distressed. B. A persistent social and emotional disturbance with at least 2 of 3 : minimal social and emotional responsiveness to others; limited positive affect; episodes of unexplained irritability, sadness or fearfulness that are evident even during non-threatening interactions with adult caregivers. C. The child has experienced a pattern of extremes of insufficient care , shown by at least one of: social neglect or deprivation (persistent lack of having basic emotional needs for comfort, stimulation and affection met); repeated changes of primary caregivers that limit opportunities to form stable attachments (frequent foster placements); rearing in unusual settings that severely limit opportunities to form selective attachments (institutions with high child-to-caregiver ratios). D. The care in Criterion C is presumed to be responsible for the disturbed behaviour in Criterion A. E. Criteria are not met for autism spectrum disorder . F. The disturbance is evident before age 5 . G. The child has a developmental age of at least 9 months . Specifiers Persistent (present for more than 12 months), and severe (all symptoms present at relatively high levels). Numbers Rare, under 10 percent even among severely neglected children, which is an important point: neglect is common, this disorder is not. Developmental age floor of 9 months matters because selective attachments have not formed before then. Comorbidity Cognitive and language delays, stereotypies, medical conditions of malnutrition, and depressive symptoms. Differential Autism spectrum disorder , which is Criterion E and is the examined pair: both show social deficits, but autism shows restricted repetitive behaviours, unusual sensory reactivity and language delay in its own pattern and does not require a history of pathogenic care; also, children with RAD improve markedly once caregiving improves, while autism does not remit. Intellectual disability (social behaviour matches mental age, and attachment behaviours are present). Depressive disorders . Disinhibited social engagement disorder , its opposite number. Disinhibited Social Engagement Disorder F94.2 In plain language. The same neglect history, the opposite behaviour: the child is over-friendly with total strangers and will wander off with anyone. DSM-5 split this out from reactive attachment disorder, because unlike RAD it does not require an absence of attachment and does not resolve simply by improving caregiving. A. A pattern of behaviour in which a child actively approaches and interacts with unfamiliar adults , with at least 2 of 4 : reduced or absent reticence in approaching and interacting with unfamiliar adults; overly familiar verbal or physical behaviour that is inconsistent with culturally sanctioned and age-appropriate social boundaries; diminished or absent checking back with the adult caregiver after venturing away, even in unfamiliar settings; willingness to go off with an unfamiliar adult with minimal or no hesitation . B. The behaviours are not limited to impulsivity, as in ADHD, but include socially disinhibited behaviour. C. Same pattern of extremes of insufficient care as in RAD. D. That care is presumed responsible. E. Developmental age of at least 9 months . Specify persistent and severe as above. Numbers Around 20 percent of children in high-risk institutional populations. Unlike RAD, it can persist even after the caregiving environment is corrected and after a secure attachment has formed, which is the fact that justifies the split. Comorbidity Cognitive and language delay, stereotypies, ADHD, and other signs of severe neglect. Differential ADHD , which is Criterion B: ADHD children are impulsive and intrusive but do not typically show the indiscriminate willingness to go off with a stranger and do not require a neglect history. Williams syndrome , which produces indiscriminate friendliness on a genetic basis. Autism . Normal extraversion , distinguished by the absence of a neglect history and by the intact checking-back behaviour. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder F43.10 In plain language. After a real, severe trauma, the event keeps coming back uninvited, the person avoids everything connected to it, their view of the world and themselves has turned dark, and their nervous system is stuck in alarm, for more than a month. A. Exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury or sexual violence, in one or more of four ways : directly experiencing the event; witnessing it in person as it occurred to others; learning that it occurred to a close family member or close friend (in cases of actual or threatened death, the event must have been violent or accidental ); or experiencing repeated or extreme exposure to aversive details of traumatic events, as with first responders collecting human remains or police repeatedly exposed to details of child abuse. That fourth route does not apply to exposure through electronic media, television, movies or pictures unless the exposure is work-related , which is the single most examined line in the criteria set. DSM-5 deleted the DSM-IV Criterion A2 , which had required the person's response to involve intense fear, helplessness or horror. B. Intrusion , 1 or more of 5 : recurrent, involuntary and intrusive distressing memories (in children over 6, repetitive play expressing themes of the trauma); recurrent distressing dreams (in children, frightening dreams without recognisable content); dissociative reactions such as flashbacks in which the person feels or acts as if the event were recurring (in children, trauma-specific re-enactment in play); intense or prolonged psychological distress at exposure to internal or external cues that symbolise or resemble an aspect of the event; marked physiological reactions to such cues. C. Avoidance , 1 or both : avoidance of, or efforts to avoid, distressing memories, thoughts or feelings about the event; avoidance of, or efforts to avoid, external reminders (people, places, conversations, activities, objects, situations). D. Negative alterations in cognitions and mood , 2 or more of 7 : inability to remember an important aspect of the event, typically due to dissociative amnesia rather than head injury or substances; persistent and exaggerated negative beliefs or expectations about oneself, others or the world ("I am bad", "no one can be trusted", "the world is completely dangerous"); persistent distorted cognitions about the cause or consequences of the event leading the person to blame themselves or others; persistent negative emotional state (fear, horror, anger, guilt, shame); markedly diminished interest or participation in significant activities; feelings of detachment or estrangement from others; persistent inability to experience positive emotions. This whole cluster is new in DSM-5 ; DSM-IV had three clusters, DSM-5 has four. E. Alterations in arousal and reactivity , 2 or more of 6 : irritable behaviour and angry outbursts with little or no provocation, typically expressed as verbal or physical aggression toward people or objects; reckless or self-destructive behaviour (new in DSM-5); hypervigilance; exaggerated startle response; problems with concentration; sleep disturbance. F. Duration of Criteria B, C, D and E is more than 1 month . G. Clinically significant distress or impairment. H. Not attributable to a substance or another medical condition. Specifiers With dissociative symptoms , which is new in DSM-5 and requires persistent or recurrent depersonalisation (feeling detached from, and as if an outside observer of, one's own mental processes or body) or derealisation (experiencing the surroundings as unreal, dreamlike, distant or distorted). With delayed expression , where full criteria are not met until at least 6 months after the event, though some symptoms may begin immediately. There is also a separate PTSD for children 6 years and younger criteria set, the "preschool subtype", the first developmental subtype in DSM, which needs only one symptom from a combined avoidance-and-negative-cognitions cluster and drops the more verbally demanding items. Numbers Lifetime risk in the United States about 8.7 percent by age 75; 12-month prevalence about 3.5 percent. Rates are much lower in most of Asia, Africa and Latin America, roughly 0.5 to 1 percent. Females are at roughly twice the risk and experience longer duration, partly because of higher exposure to sexual violence. Highest conditional rates follow rape, torture and captivity. Duration threshold 1 month : under a month, consider acute stress disorder. Comorbidity About 80 percent have at least one comorbid disorder. Commonest: major depressive disorder, substance use disorders, other anxiety disorders, bipolar disorder, and in military and veteran samples traumatic brain injury with overlapping symptoms. In children, oppositional defiant and separation anxiety disorders. Differential Acute stress disorder (3 days to 1 month). Adjustment disorder , where either the stressor does not meet Criterion A (divorce, job loss) or it does but the symptom pattern does not meet PTSD criteria. Other specified trauma and stressor-related disorder . Anxiety and obsessive-compulsive disorders (intrusions in OCD are not related to a traumatic event). Major depressive disorder (no Criterion B intrusions or Criterion E arousal). Personality disorders , especially borderline, which shares affective instability and interpersonal difficulty. Dissociative disorders . Conversion disorder . Psychotic disorders (flashbacks and reliving versus hallucinations, and this misdiagnosis is common). Traumatic brain injury . Malingering , which must be considered explicitly where compensation or legal proceedings are involved. ICD-11 Takes a completely different approach: PTSD is narrowed to three core clusters (re-experiencing in the here and now, avoidance, and a persistent sense of current threat), and a separate diagnosis of Complex PTSD adds three disturbances of self-organisation: affect dysregulation, negative self-concept, and disturbances in relationships . DSM-5-TR has no Complex PTSD; the nearest DSM approximation is PTSD with the dissociative subtype, sometimes alongside a personality-disorder diagnosis. Naming ICD-11 CPTSD and its three extra clusters is one of the highest-yield contrasts in the whole syllabus. Acute Stress Disorder F43.0 In plain language. The same kind of aftermath as PTSD, in the first month, and diagnosed by counting symptoms across all categories rather than requiring a set from each. A. The same exposure criterion as PTSD, with the same four routes and the same media exclusion. B. 9 or more of 14 symptoms from any of five categories, beginning or worsening after the event: intrusion (intrusive memories, distressing dreams, dissociative reactions or flashbacks, intense or prolonged distress or marked physiological reactions to reminders); negative mood (persistent inability to experience positive emotions); dissociative (altered sense of the reality of one's surroundings or oneself, inability to remember an important aspect of the event); avoidance (of internal reminders, of external reminders); arousal (sleep disturbance, irritable behaviour and angry outbursts, hypervigilance, problems with concentration, exaggerated startle response). The key DSM-5 change: DSM-IV required at least three dissociative symptoms; DSM-5 dropped that requirement, because many people develop PTSD without ever dissociating. C. Duration is 3 days to 1 month after trauma exposure . Symptoms typically begin immediately but must persist at least 3 days. D. Clinically significant distress or impairment. E. Not attributable to a substance or another medical condition (mild traumatic brain injury) and not better explained by brief psychotic disorder. Numbers The two numbers are 9 of 14 and 3 days to 1 month . Prevalence after trauma varies widely, under 20 percent after events not involving interpersonal assault, higher after assault, rape and mass shootings. Roughly half of those who go on to develop PTSD initially present with acute stress disorder, so it is a poor screening test taken alone. Comorbidity Prior mental disorders raise risk; depression and pain conditions commonly co-occur; head injury frequently coexists in road traffic and combat contexts. Differential PTSD after a month. Adjustment disorder (stressor does not meet Criterion A, or symptom threshold not met). Panic disorder (unexpected attacks). Dissociative disorders . Traumatic brain injury and postconcussive syndrome . Normal, adaptive acute stress reactions , which is the most important one clinically: transient distress after trauma is expected, and it becomes a disorder only at this symptom count with impairment. Adjustment Disorders F43.2x In plain language. A response to an ordinary life stressor that is bigger than you would expect or is clearly wrecking function, but does not amount to any other disorder. A. Development of emotional or behavioural symptoms in response to an identifiable stressor(s) occurring within 3 months of the onset of the stressor. B. These symptoms are clinically significant, shown by one or both of: marked distress that is out of proportion to the severity or intensity of the stressor , taking into account external context and cultural factors; and/or significant impairment in social, occupational or other important areas of functioning. C. The disturbance does not meet criteria for another mental disorder and is not merely an exacerbation of a pre-existing one. D. The symptoms do not represent normal bereavement and are not better explained by prolonged grief disorder. E. Once the stressor or its consequences have terminated, the symptoms do not persist for more than an additional 6 months . Subtypes With depressed mood; with anxiety; with mixed anxiety and depressed mood; with disturbance of conduct; with mixed disturbance of emotions and conduct; unspecified. Also specify acute (under 6 months) or persistent/chronic (6 months or longer, which happens when the stressor itself is enduring). Numbers Very common: 5 to 20 percent of outpatient mental-health caseloads, and up to about 50 percent in hospital psychiatric consultation samples, which makes it the commonest diagnosis in consultation-liaison work. The two numbers to hold: symptoms begin within 3 months of the stressor and resolve within 6 months of the stressor ending. Comorbidity Can accompany most medical illnesses, and is associated with increased suicide risk, notably in adolescents and in the medically ill. Differential Major depressive disorder (full criteria met, in which case MDD is diagnosed, not adjustment disorder). PTSD and acute stress disorder (Criterion A trauma and the specific symptom pattern). Personality disorders (long-standing pattern, though a personality disorder can be exacerbated by stress). Normal stress reactions , which is the judgment call: proportionality and impairment. Prolonged grief disorder and uncomplicated bereavement , which is now Criterion D. Prolonged Grief Disorder F43.8 NEW IN DSM-5-TR In plain language. A year or more after a death, the person is still gripped by yearning and preoccupation with the person who died, and their life has not restarted. This is the only new disorder in the 2022 Text Revision, so treat it as a guaranteed question. A. The death, at least 12 months ago , of a person who was close to the bereaved ( at least 6 months ago for children and adolescents ). B. Since the death, a persistent grief response characterised by one or both of: intense yearning or longing for the deceased; and/or preoccupation with thoughts or memories of the deceased (in children and adolescents, preoccupation may focus on the circumstances of the death). This has been present to a clinically significant degree nearly every day for at least the last month . C. Since the death, 3 or more of 8 symptoms present to a clinically significant degree nearly every day for at least the last month: identity disruption (feeling as though part of oneself has died); a marked sense of disbelief about the death; avoidance of reminders that the person is dead; intense emotional pain (anger, bitterness, sorrow) related to the death; difficulty reintegrating into relationships and activities (problems engaging with friends, pursuing interests, planning for the future); emotional numbness , that is, an absence of or marked reduction in emotional experience; feeling that life is meaningless ; intense loneliness , feeling alone or detached from others. D. Clinically significant distress or impairment. E. The duration and severity of the bereavement reaction clearly exceed expected social, cultural or religious norms for the individual's culture and context. This cultural clause is deliberate and is examinable, because mourning periods differ widely across Indian communities. F. Not better explained by another mental disorder such as major depressive disorder or PTSD, and not attributable to a substance or another medical condition. Numbers The three that matter: 12 months in adults, 6 months in children and adolescents, and symptoms present nearly every day for at least the last month . Prevalence in bereaved adults is roughly 4 to 10 percent, higher after the death of a child, after violent or unexpected death, and after suicide. Comorbidity Major depressive disorder, PTSD (especially after violent death), separation anxiety disorder, and substance use disorders. Suicide risk is elevated. Differential Normal grief , distinguished by time course and by whether the person's life has resumed. Major depressive disorder : in PGD the emotional pain is focused on the deceased and yearning is the core, while in depression the low mood is generalised and self-worth is attacked; note that yearning and preoccupation are not criteria for MDD. PTSD : intrusions there are about the traumatic event and carry a sense of current threat, whereas PGD intrusions are about the person and carry longing. Separation anxiety disorder : fear of future separation from living attachment figures, not longing for a dead one. Adjustment disorder , now excluded by Criterion D of that disorder. ICD-11 Also has Prolonged Grief Disorder, with a threshold of at least 6 months rather than 12. If a question gives a bereavement of 8 months and asks which system allows the diagnosis, the answer is ICD-11 only. 9. Dissociative disorders Disruption of, or discontinuity in, the normal integration of consciousness, memory, identity, emotion, perception, body representation, motor control and behaviour. DSM-5 placed this chapter immediately after the trauma chapter, without folding it in, to mark the close relationship without asserting that dissociation is always post-traumatic. Dissociative Identity Disorder F44.81 In plain language. Two or more distinct ways of being a self take turns running the person, and there are memory gaps that ordinary forgetting does not explain. A. Disruption of identity characterised by two or more distinct personality states , which in some cultures may be described as an experience of possession . The disruption involves marked discontinuity in sense of self and sense of agency, accompanied by related alterations in affect, behaviour, consciousness, memory, perception, cognition and sensory-motor functioning. These signs and symptoms may be observed by others or reported by the individual , which is a DSM-5 change: DSM-IV required that a state actually take control, DSM-5 permits self-report. B. Recurrent gaps in the recall of everyday events, important personal information, and/or traumatic events that are inconsistent with ordinary forgetting. DSM-5 added everyday events, since DSM-IV limited the amnesia to important personal information. C. Clinically significant distress or impairment. D. The disturbance is not a normal part of a broadly accepted cultural or religious practice . In children, the symptoms are not better explained by imaginary playmates or other fantasy play. E. Not attributable to the physiological effects of a substance (blackouts during alcohol intoxication) or another medical condition (complex partial seizures). Numbers 12-month prevalence about 1.5 percent in one US community sample, with a near-equal sex ratio in that sample though clinical samples are heavily female. Reported rates of childhood abuse and neglect in clinical samples in North America, Europe and Turkey run around 90 percent. Suicide attempts occur in over 70 percent of outpatients with the diagnosis. Comorbidity PTSD is nearly universal. Also depressive disorders, substance use disorders, somatic symptom disorder, conversion disorder, eating disorders, sleep disorders, and personality disorders, especially borderline and avoidant. Differential Other specified dissociative disorder , where identity disturbance is less than fully distinct. Major depressive disorder . Bipolar disorder (the rapid shifts here are within-day and identity-linked, not episodic mood). PTSD . Psychotic disorders : voices in DID are typically experienced as coming from inside the head and as belonging to identities, and reality testing is otherwise intact. Borderline personality disorder , which shares identity disturbance and dissociation under stress but lacks the distinct amnesia between states. Seizure disorders , particularly complex partial seizures. Factitious disorder and malingering , which DSM-5-TR discusses at length because of the forensic history around this diagnosis. Dissociative Amnesia F44.0, with fugue F44.1 A. An inability to recall important autobiographical information, usually of a traumatic or stressful nature, that is inconsistent with ordinary forgetting . Note that dissociative amnesia most often consists of localised or selective amnesia for a specific event or events, or generalised amnesia for identity and life history. B. Clinically significant distress or impairment. C. Not attributable to a substance or a neurological or other medical condition. D. Not better explained by DID, PTSD, acute stress disorder, somatic symptom disorder, or major or mild neurocognitive disorder. Specify: with dissociative fugue , that is, apparently purposeful travel or bewildered wandering associated with amnesia for identity or other important autobiographical information. Dissociative fugue is no longer a separate disorder in DSM-5, it is a specifier here. That change is asked frequently. Numbers 12-month prevalence about 1.8 percent (1.0 percent in men, 2.6 percent in women) in one US community study. Types to be able to list: localised (no recall of events during a circumscribed period, the commonest), selective (some but not all of the events in a period), generalised (whole life and identity, rare and abrupt), systematised (a specific category of information, for example all memories of one person), and continuous (each new event as it occurs). Comorbidity Depressive disorders, PTSD, conversion disorder, somatic symptom disorder, and personality disorders. Suicide risk is elevated, particularly when memory returns suddenly. Differential Neurocognitive disorders (anterograde deficits predominate, and personal identity is retained until very late). Transient global amnesia (abrupt, anterograde, resolves within 24 hours, older patients, retained identity). Post-ictal and post-traumatic amnesia . Substance-related blackouts . Malingering and factitious disorder , where secondary gain is evident. Normal and age-related forgetting . Depersonalisation/Derealisation Disorder F48.1 A. Persistent or recurrent experiences of depersonalisation, derealisation, or both . Depersonalisation : experiences of unreality, detachment, or being an outside observer with respect to one's thoughts, feelings, sensations, body or actions (perceptual alterations, distorted sense of time, unreal or absent self, emotional and/or physical numbing). Derealisation : experiences of unreality or detachment with respect to surroundings (individuals or objects experienced as unreal, dreamlike, foggy, lifeless or visually distorted). B. During these experiences, reality testing remains intact . This is the criterion that separates the disorder from psychosis and is the one examiners test. C. Clinically significant distress or impairment. D. Not attributable to a substance or another medical condition (seizures). E. Not better explained by another mental disorder such as schizophrenia, panic disorder, major depressive disorder, acute stress disorder, PTSD, or another dissociative disorder. Numbers Lifetime prevalence about 2 percent; sex ratio roughly 1:1. Mean age at onset 16, with about 20 percent onset after 20 and only 5 percent after 25; onset after 40 is unusual and should prompt a search for a medical cause. Transient depersonalisation experiences are extremely common in the general population (roughly half of adults report at least one), so the disorder requires persistence and impairment. Comorbidity Unipolar depressive disorder and anxiety disorders are the commonest; also avoidant, borderline and obsessive-compulsive personality disorders. Differential Panic disorder (depersonalisation only during attacks). Psychotic disorders (reality testing lost). Substance-induced , especially cannabis, ketamine, hallucinogens. Medical causes : temporal lobe epilepsy, migraine, vestibular disease, head injury. PTSD with the dissociative subtype . Major depressive disorder with numbing. 10. Somatic symptom and related disorders The chapter DSM-5 rewrote most radically. DSM-IV's somatisation disorder, hypochondriasis, pain disorder and undifferentiated somatoform disorder were all deleted and replaced. The organising change: DSM-IV defined these disorders by the absence of a medical explanation , which was unreliable and, worse, reinforced mind-body dualism and made patients feel disbelieved. DSM-5 defines them instead by the presence of positive psychological features , namely disproportionate thoughts, feelings and behaviours about the symptoms. Say that sentence in any long-answer question on this chapter. Somatic Symptom Disorder F45.1 A. One or more somatic symptoms that are distressing or result in significant disruption of daily life. Note it is one, not the eight-symptom count DSM-IV demanded across four body systems, and the symptom may or may not be medically explained . B. Excessive thoughts, feelings or behaviours related to the somatic symptoms or associated health concerns, shown by at least 1 of 3 : disproportionate and persistent thoughts about the seriousness of one's symptoms; persistently high level of anxiety about health or symptoms; excessive time and energy devoted to these symptoms or health concerns. C. Although any one somatic symptom may not be continuously present, the state of being symptomatic is persistent, typically more than 6 months . Specifiers With predominant pain , which is the replacement for DSM-IV's pain disorder. Persistent (severe symptoms, marked impairment, duration more than 6 months). Severity mild (one Criterion B symptom), moderate (two or more), severe (two or more plus multiple somatic complaints or one very severe symptom). Numbers Prevalence estimated 5 to 7 percent in the general adult population, higher in women. Compare DSM-IV somatisation disorder at under 1 percent: the criteria were loosened deliberately, and the standard criticism to reproduce in an essay is that this risks pathologising normal illness worry in the medically ill. Comorbidity Depressive and anxiety disorders, PTSD, and genuine medical illness, which frequently coexists. That coexistence is the point: DSM-5 explicitly permits the diagnosis alongside a diagnosed medical condition. Differential Illness anxiety disorder (few or no somatic symptoms, the fear is of having or acquiring an illness). Panic disorder (symptoms are episodic and attack-bound). Generalised anxiety disorder (worry is broader than health). Major depressive disorder . Conversion disorder (loss of function, not distress about a symptom). Delusional disorder, somatic type (fixed, unshakeable belief). Body dysmorphic disorder . OCD with health obsessions. Illness Anxiety Disorder F45.21 A. Preoccupation with having or acquiring a serious illness . B. Somatic symptoms are not present or, if present, are only mild in intensity . If another medical condition is present or there is a high risk of developing one, the preoccupation is clearly excessive or disproportionate. C. There is a high level of anxiety about health , and the person is easily alarmed about personal health status. D. The person performs excessive health-related behaviours (repeatedly checking the body for signs of illness) or exhibits maladaptive avoidance (avoids doctor appointments and hospitals). E. Illness preoccupation has been present for at least 6 months , although the specific illness feared may change. F. Not better explained by another mental disorder. Specify: care-seeking type or care-avoidant type . Numbers Prevalence 1.3 to 10 percent, roughly equal in men and women. About 75 percent of those who would have been diagnosed with DSM-IV hypochondriasis now fall under somatic symptom disorder because they do have somatic symptoms; the remaining quarter, who have few or no symptoms, become illness anxiety disorder. That reallocation is a stock question. Comorbidity Anxiety disorders, especially generalised anxiety and panic, obsessive-compulsive disorder, and depressive disorders. Personality disorders in about a fifth. Differential Somatic symptom disorder (prominent somatic symptoms). Generalised anxiety disorder . OCD (obsessions about contracting disease in the future, with compulsions; illness anxiety is about currently having it). Specific phobia of illness . Delusional disorder, somatic type . Major depressive disorder . Adjustment disorder after a genuine diagnosis. Conversion Disorder (Functional Neurological Symptom Disorder) F44.x A. One or more symptoms of altered voluntary motor or sensory function . B. Clinical findings provide evidence of incompatibility between the symptom and recognised neurological or medical conditions . This is positive evidence , for example Hoover's sign (hip extension weakness resolves on contralateral hip flexion against resistance), a tremor that entrains to a tapped rhythm, or tubular visual fields. DSM-5's key change was requiring this positive incompatibility rather than requiring a preceding psychological stressor. C. Not better explained by another medical or mental disorder. D. Causes clinically significant distress or impairment or warrants medical evaluation. Specify symptom type: with weakness or paralysis; with abnormal movement (tremor, dystonic movement, myoclonus, gait disorder); with swallowing symptoms; with speech symptom (dysphonia, slurred speech); with attacks or seizures (psychogenic non-epileptic seizures); with anaesthesia or sensory loss; with special sensory symptom (visual, olfactory or hearing disturbance); with mixed symptoms. Also acute (under 6 months) or persistent (6 months or more), and with or without psychological stressor . Numbers Incidence of persistent conversion symptoms about 2 to 5 per 100,000 per year; symptoms are seen in roughly 5 percent of referrals to neurology clinics. Two to three times more common in women . La belle indifference , a bland lack of concern about the deficit, is described classically but is not a criterion and has poor diagnostic value , which is exactly why it is asked. A history of a preceding stressor is also no longer required. Comorbidity Depressive and anxiety disorders, PTSD, dissociative disorders (which co-occur frequently), personality disorders, and genuine neurological disease, which co-occurs often, so the presence of epilepsy does not exclude psychogenic non-epileptic seizures. Differential Neurological disease , which requires proper examination, and the historically high misdiagnosis rate has fallen to around 4 percent in modern series. Factitious disorder (deliberate falsification, motive is the sick role). Malingering (deliberate, motive is external gain: compensation, avoiding duty). The distinction from both is that conversion symptoms are not intentionally produced . Somatic symptom disorder (distress about a symptom versus loss of function). Body dysmorphic disorder . Depersonalisation/derealisation . Dissociative disorders . Psychological Factors Affecting Other Medical Conditions F54 A. A medical symptom or condition (other than a mental disorder) is present. B. Psychological or behavioural factors adversely affect the medical condition in one of four ways: they have influenced the course of the condition, as shown by a close temporal association; they interfere with treatment (poor adherence); they constitute additional well-established health risks; or they influence the underlying pathophysiology, precipitating or exacerbating symptoms or necessitating medical attention. C. Not better explained by another mental disorder. Severity mild to extreme. This diagnosis replaced the old psychosomatic and DSM-IV Axis I "psychological factors affecting medical condition" framing, and it is the correct label for, say, denial of chest pain delaying treatment, or anxiety worsening asthma. Comorbidity Depressive and anxiety disorders, adjustment disorder, and the personality traits (hostility, denial, avoidance) that drive the non-adherence. The medical condition itself is the other half of the diagnosis, so cardiovascular disease, asthma, diabetes and cancer are the usual settings. Differential Somatic symptom disorder (there the psychological features attach to symptoms, here they attach to a diagnosed medical condition and worsen it). Adjustment disorder (the medical illness is the stressor causing a psychiatric response, rather than psychological factors worsening the illness). Illness anxiety disorder . Factitious Disorder F68.1x Factitious disorder imposed on self. (A) Falsification of physical or psychological signs or symptoms, or induction of injury or disease, associated with identified deception . (B) The person presents themselves to others as ill, impaired or injured. (C) The deceptive behaviour is evident even in the absence of obvious external rewards . (D) Not better explained by another mental disorder such as delusional disorder or another psychotic disorder. Specify single episode or recurrent episodes. Factitious disorder imposed on another (previously factitious disorder by proxy, and the older lay term Munchausen syndrome by proxy). Falsification or induction in another person , associated with identified deception. Note the critical coding rule: the perpetrator, not the victim, receives the diagnosis . The victim is given an abuse diagnosis code. Numbers Prevalence unknown, estimated about 1 percent of hospital inpatients. Commonest in women in the imposed-on-self form and in mothers in the imposed-on-another form; healthcare workers are over-represented. Comorbidity Depressive disorders, substance use disorders, and personality disorders, especially borderline , which is the commonest comorbid personality diagnosis in the imposed-on-self form. In the imposed-on-another form, personality pathology in the perpetrator and genuine iatrogenic harm in the victim. Differential Malingering , which is not a mental disorder in DSM-5 but a V code, "malingering", listed among other conditions that may be a focus of clinical attention. The line is motive: factitious disorder is driven by the internal need to occupy the sick role, malingering is driven by an obvious external incentive (money, drugs, avoiding work, military duty or prosecution). Somatic symptom disorder and conversion disorder , where symptoms are not intentionally produced . Borderline personality disorder , where self-injury is present but is not accompanied by deception about its origin. 11. Feeding and eating disorders DSM-5 merged the childhood feeding disorders with the adult eating disorders into one chapter, added binge-eating disorder as a full diagnosis (it was in the DSM-IV appendix), created avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder to replace "feeding disorder of infancy or early childhood", and loosened anorexia and bulimia in specific ways that are examined constantly. Pica F98.3 children, F50.89 adults A. Persistent eating of non-nutritive, non-food substances over a period of at least 1 month (paper, soap, cloth, hair, string, wool, soil, chalk, talcum powder, paint, gum, metal, pebbles, charcoal, ash, clay, starch, ice). B. The eating is inappropriate to the developmental level of the individual (so it is not diagnosed under a developmental age of about 2 years, when mouthing is normal). C. The eating behaviour is not part of a culturally supported or socially normative practice , which matters because geophagia is normative in some communities. D. If it occurs in the context of another mental disorder (intellectual disability, autism, schizophrenia) or medical condition (pregnancy), it is sufficiently severe to warrant additional clinical attention. Note that unlike the other eating disorders, pica can be diagnosed alongside anorexia and bulimia. Comorbidity Intellectual disability, autism spectrum disorder, schizophrenia, trichotillomania (with trichophagia), excoriation disorder. Medically, iron-deficiency anaemia and zinc deficiency, and in pregnancy. Differential Anorexia nervosa (eating non-food to control appetite). Factitious disorder (swallowing objects for the sick role). Non-suicidal self-injury . Normative cultural practice , which is Criterion C. Rumination Disorder F98.21 A. Repeated regurgitation of food over a period of at least 1 month . Regurgitated food may be re-chewed, re-swallowed or spat out. B. The repeated regurgitation is not attributable to an associated gastrointestinal or other medical condition such as gastro-oesophageal reflux or pyloric stenosis. C. The eating disturbance does not occur exclusively during anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, binge-eating disorder or ARFID. D. If it occurs in the context of another mental disorder such as intellectual disability, it is severe enough to warrant additional clinical attention. Comorbidity Intellectual disability, other neurodevelopmental disorders, and, in infants, neglect and understimulation. In older children and adults it co-occurs with anxiety and with the other feeding and eating disorders. Differential Gastrointestinal conditions (reflux, gastroparesis, pyloric stenosis), which are Criterion B. Bulimia nervosa (regurgitation there is part of purging after a binge, in the service of weight control). Avoidant/Restrictive Food Intake Disorder (ARFID) F50.82 In plain language. The person does not eat enough, but not because of any concern about weight or shape. That last clause is the whole diagnosis. New in DSM-5, replacing DSM-IV's feeding disorder of infancy or early childhood, and applicable at any age. A. An eating or feeding disturbance, for example apparent lack of interest in eating or food, avoidance based on the sensory characteristics of food, or concern about aversive consequences of eating (fear of choking or vomiting after a choking episode), that persistently fails to meet appropriate nutritional and/or energy needs, associated with 1 or more of 4 : significant weight loss or failure to achieve expected weight gain or faltering growth in children; significant nutritional deficiency ; dependence on enteral feeding or oral nutritional supplements ; marked interference with psychosocial functioning . B. Not better explained by lack of available food or by an associated culturally sanctioned practice (so famine, poverty and religious fasting are excluded). C. The disturbance does not occur exclusively during anorexia or bulimia , and there is no evidence of a disturbance in the way one's body weight or shape is experienced . D. Not attributable to a concurrent medical condition or better explained by another mental disorder; where it occurs alongside one, it exceeds what is routinely associated and warrants additional clinical attention. Comorbidity Anxiety disorders, obsessive-compulsive disorder, autism spectrum disorder (the sensory-based subtype in particular), ADHD, and intellectual disability. Differential Anorexia nervosa , settled by Criterion C: no body-image disturbance and no fear of fatness in ARFID. Specific phobia of choking or vomiting, which can be an alternative label when the food restriction is not the focus. Depression and psychotic disorders with reduced appetite. Normal picky eating , which is common and does not cause nutritional or psychosocial harm. Medical causes: coeliac disease, food allergy, oesophageal disorders, inflammatory bowel disease. Anorexia Nervosa F50.01 restricting, F50.02 binge-eating/purging A. Restriction of energy intake relative to requirements, leading to a significantly low body weight in the context of age, sex, developmental trajectory and physical health. Significantly low weight is defined as less than minimally normal, or, for children and adolescents, less than that minimally expected. B. Intense fear of gaining weight or of becoming fat, or persistent behaviour that interferes with weight gain , even though at a significantly low weight. That second clause is a DSM-5 addition, added because many patients, particularly in Asian samples, deny the fear but act on it. C. Disturbance in the way one's body weight or shape is experienced, undue influence of body weight or shape on self-evaluation, or persistent lack of recognition of the seriousness of the current low body weight. DSM-5 removed the amenorrhoea criterion that DSM-IV required (three consecutive missed cycles), because it excluded males, premenarchal girls, postmenopausal women and women on hormonal contraceptives, and because those who met all criteria except amenorrhoea did not differ clinically. This deletion is the most examined single fact about anorexia. Subtypes and severity Restricting type : during the last 3 months, no recurrent episodes of binge eating or purging; weight loss is accomplished by dieting, fasting and/or excessive exercise. Binge-eating/purging type : during the last 3 months, recurrent episodes of binge eating or purging (self-induced vomiting, misuse of laxatives, diuretics or enemas). Severity for adults is by BMI : mild BMI at or above 17 , moderate 16 to 16.99 , severe 15 to 15.99 , extreme below 15 . Also in partial or full remission. Numbers 12-month prevalence about 0.4 percent among young females; female to male about 10:1. Peak onset in adolescence and young adulthood; onset before puberty or after 40 is unusual. It has one of the highest mortality rates of any mental disorder , with a crude mortality rate around 5 percent per decade, from medical complications and from suicide. Physical signs to be able to list: amenorrhoea, bradycardia, hypotension, hypothermia, lanugo hair, dry skin, hypercarotenaemia, osteopenia, leukopenia, raised cortisol, low T3, and in purging patients hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis, dental enamel erosion, parotid enlargement and Russell's sign (calluses on the dorsum of the hand). Watch for refeeding syndrome , above all hypophosphataemia, on rapid nutritional restoration. Comorbidity Major depressive disorder (very high), obsessive-compulsive disorder (especially the restricting type), social anxiety disorder, alcohol and substance use disorders (especially binge-purge type), and personality disorders (obsessive-compulsive with restricting, borderline with binge-purge). Differential Bulimia nervosa , and the rule to state is simple: if criteria for anorexia are met, anorexia takes precedence , so a person who binges and purges but is significantly underweight has anorexia, binge-eating/purging type, not bulimia. ARFID (no body-image disturbance). Avoidant, depressive or psychotic causes of weight loss . Body dysmorphic disorder . Medical causes of weight loss: coeliac disease, inflammatory bowel disease, hyperthyroidism, malignancy, tuberculosis, HIV, superior mesenteric artery syndrome. Bulimia Nervosa F50.2 A. Recurrent episodes of binge eating , defined by both: eating, in a discrete period (for example within any 2-hour period), an amount of food that is definitely larger than what most individuals would eat in a similar period under similar circumstances; and a sense of lack of control over eating during the episode. B. Recurrent inappropriate compensatory behaviours to prevent weight gain: self-induced vomiting, misuse of laxatives, diuretics or other medications, fasting, or excessive exercise. C. Both the binge eating and the compensatory behaviours occur, on average, at least once a week for 3 months . DSM-IV required twice a week for 3 months, so the frequency threshold was halved in DSM-5. That halving is examined. D. Self-evaluation is unduly influenced by body shape and weight. E. The disturbance does not occur exclusively during episodes of anorexia nervosa. Severity By average number of episodes of inappropriate compensatory behaviour per week: mild 1 to 3, moderate 4 to 7, severe 8 to 13, extreme 14 or more . DSM-5 also deleted the purging and non-purging subtypes . Numbers 12-month prevalence 1 to 1.5 percent among young females; female to male about 10:1. Peak onset in late adolescence and young adulthood, slightly later than anorexia. Weight is typically normal or overweight , which is why it goes undetected for years. Crude mortality about 2 percent per decade. Comorbidity Depressive and bipolar disorders, anxiety disorders, substance use disorders in about 30 percent (alcohol and stimulants), and borderline personality disorder in a substantial minority. Self-harm and suicide risk are elevated. Differential Anorexia nervosa, binge-eating/purging type , distinguished by significantly low body weight, and anorexia takes precedence. Binge-eating disorder (binges without compensatory behaviour). Kleine-Levin syndrome and other neurological causes of hyperphagia. Major depressive disorder with atypical features (overeating without the loss-of-control quality and without compensation). Borderline personality disorder , where binge eating may be one of several impulsive behaviours. Binge-Eating Disorder F50.81 In plain language. Binges without the compensating. Promoted from the DSM-IV research appendix to a full DSM-5 diagnosis, which is the fact examiners want. A. Recurrent episodes of binge eating, defined exactly as in bulimia (large amount, discrete period, loss of control). B. The binge-eating episodes are associated with 3 or more of 5 : eating much more rapidly than normal; eating until feeling uncomfortably full; eating large amounts of food when not feeling physically hungry; eating alone because of feeling embarrassed by how much one is eating; feeling disgusted with oneself, depressed, or very guilty afterward. C. Marked distress regarding binge eating is present. D. The binge eating occurs, on average, at least once a week for 3 months . E. The binge eating is not associated with recurrent inappropriate compensatory behaviour and does not occur exclusively during bulimia nervosa or anorexia nervosa. Severity By binge episodes per week: mild 1 to 3, moderate 4 to 7, severe 8 to 13, extreme 14 or more . Numbers 12-month prevalence about 1.6 percent in adult females and 0.8 percent in adult males, so it is the commonest eating disorder and has the least skewed sex ratio (roughly 2:1 rather than 10:1). It occurs across normal-weight, overweight and obese individuals. Obesity is not a mental disorder in DSM-5 and is not the same as binge-eating disorder, a distinction that gets tested. Comorbidity Bipolar disorders, depressive disorders, anxiety disorders and, to a lesser degree, substance use disorders. Medically: obesity, metabolic syndrome, type 2 diabetes. Differential Bulimia nervosa (compensatory behaviour present). Obesity without binge eating , where overeating is not in discrete episodes and lacks the loss-of-control quality and the distress. Major depressive disorder with atypical features . Bipolar disorder in an episode with increased appetite. Prader-Willi syndrome and other medical hyperphagia. 12. Elimination disorders Enuresis F98.0 A. Repeated voiding of urine into bed or clothes, whether involuntary or intentional. B. The behaviour is clinically significant, shown by a frequency of at least twice a week for at least 3 consecutive months , or by clinically significant distress or impairment. C. Chronological age is at least 5 (or the equivalent developmental level). D. Not attributable to a substance (a diuretic, an antipsychotic) or another medical condition (diabetes, spina bifida, a seizure disorder). Specify: nocturnal only (the commonest, "monosymptomatic enuresis"), diurnal only (also called urinary incontinence), or nocturnal and diurnal . Also primary (continence never achieved) or secondary (relapse after at least 6 months of continence). Numbers Prevalence about 5 to 10 percent at age 5, 3 to 5 percent at age 10, and about 1 percent at 15 and above. Spontaneous remission is roughly 5 to 10 percent per year. Commoner in boys for the nocturnal form. Treatment of choice is the bell-and-pad urine alarm (classical conditioning), with desmopressin as pharmacological backup. Comorbidity Encopresis, sleepwalking and sleep terrors, ADHD, and developmental delays. Secondary enuresis frequently follows a psychosocial stressor such as the birth of a sibling, school entry, or family disruption. Differential Urinary tract infection, diabetes mellitus and insipidus, seizure disorder, neurogenic bladder, structural urological abnormalities, and obstructive sleep apnoea, all Criterion D. Encopresis F98.1 A. Repeated passage of faeces into inappropriate places (clothing, floor), whether involuntary or intentional. B. At least one such event per month for at least 3 months . C. Chronological age is at least 4 (or the equivalent developmental level). D. Not attributable to a substance (laxatives) or another medical condition except through a mechanism involving constipation. Specify: with constipation and overflow incontinence (the commoner form, with a palpable faecal mass and loose overflow soiling), or without constipation and overflow incontinence (more often associated with oppositional defiant disorder or conduct disorder). Numbers About 1 percent of 5-year-olds; more common in males . Note the two age floors: enuresis 5, encopresis 4. Comorbidity Enuresis, which co-occurs frequently, plus oppositional defiant disorder and conduct disorder in the without-constipation form, and ADHD. Chronic constipation with painful defecation is the usual physical driver, and shame and social withdrawal follow. Differential Hirschsprung's disease, hypothyroidism, anal fissure with retention, spinal cord lesions, and dietary causes of chronic constipation. 13. Sleep-wake disorders DSM-5 abandoned DSM-IV's split into primary sleep disorders, sleep disorders related to another mental disorder, and those due to a general medical condition, because that split forced a causal judgment clinicians could not reliably make. The DSM-5 approach is to diagnose the sleep disorder in its own right alongside any coexisting condition, on the reasoning that insomnia and depression have a bidirectional relationship and that the sleep problem needs treating either way. Say that in an essay. Insomnia Disorder F51.01 A. A predominant complaint of dissatisfaction with sleep quantity or quality, associated with 1 or more of 3 : difficulty initiating sleep; difficulty maintaining sleep, with frequent awakenings or problems returning to sleep; early-morning awakening with inability to return to sleep. B. Clinically significant distress or impairment. C. The sleep difficulty occurs at least 3 nights per week . D. Present for at least 3 months . E. Occurs despite adequate opportunity for sleep. F. Not better explained by, and does not occur exclusively during, another sleep-wake disorder. G. Not attributable to a substance. H. Coexisting mental disorders and medical conditions do not adequately explain the predominant complaint. Specify: with non-sleep disorder mental comorbidity, with other medical comorbidity, with other sleep disorder; and episodic (1 to 3 months), persistent (3 months or more), recurrent (two or more episodes within a year). Numbers The exam numbers are 3 nights a week for 3 months . About one third of adults report insomnia symptoms, 10 to 15 percent have daytime impairment, and 6 to 10 percent meet full criteria. Commoner in women (about 1.44:1) and increases with age. First-line treatment is CBT-I (stimulus control, sleep restriction, sleep hygiene, cognitive restructuring, relaxation), not hypnotics. Comorbidity Depressive, bipolar and anxiety disorders (insomnia is both a risk factor for and a residual symptom of depression), substance use disorders, and medical conditions with pain. Differential Normal sleep variation and short sleepers . Situational or acute insomnia (under 3 months). Circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorders , particularly delayed sleep phase type, where the person sleeps well if allowed their own schedule. Restless legs syndrome and breathing-related sleep disorders . Substance-induced sleep disorder (caffeine, alcohol rebound, stimulants). Narcolepsy . Hypersomnolence Disorder and Narcolepsy F51.11, G47.4xx Hypersomnolence disorder. Self-reported excessive sleepiness despite a main sleep period of at least 7 hours, with at least one of: recurrent periods of sleep or lapses into sleep within the same day; a prolonged main sleep episode of more than 9 hours per day that is non-restorative; difficulty being fully awake after abrupt awakening ( sleep inertia or sleep drunkenness). Occurs at least 3 times per week for at least 3 months , with distress or impairment. Narcolepsy. Recurrent periods of an irrepressible need to sleep, lapsing into sleep, or napping occurring within the same day, at least 3 times per week over the past 3 months , plus at least 1 of 3 : (1) episodes of cataplexy , meaning, in long-standing disease, brief episodes of sudden bilateral loss of muscle tone with retained consciousness precipitated by laughter or joking, or, in children or within 6 months of onset, spontaneous grimaces or jaw-opening episodes with tongue thrusting or global hypotonia without an emotional trigger; (2) hypocretin-1 (orexin) deficiency in CSF, at or below one third of control values; (3) nocturnal polysomnography showing REM sleep latency of 15 minutes or less, or a multiple sleep latency test with mean sleep latency of 8 minutes or less and two or more sleep-onset REM periods. Numbers Narcolepsy prevalence about 0.02 to 0.04 percent. Typical onset in adolescence or the early twenties. Strong association with HLA-DQB1*06:02 and with loss of hypothalamic hypocretin-producing neurons. The classic tetrad to name: excessive daytime sleepiness, cataplexy, sleep paralysis, hypnagogic (or hypnopompic) hallucinations . Note that only sleepiness plus one of the three objective or cataplexy criteria is required; sleep paralysis and hallucinations are not criteria in DSM-5. Comorbidity Depressive disorders (which frequently precede or follow hypersomnolence), bipolar disorder, substance use disorders, and, in narcolepsy specifically, obesity, obstructive sleep apnoea, REM sleep behaviour disorder, depression and anxiety, plus the social impairment that comes from cataplexy in public. Differential Sleep deprivation and insufficient sleep syndrome , the commonest cause of daytime sleepiness. Obstructive sleep apnoea hypopnoea . Major depressive disorder with hypersomnia . Substance effects . Kleine-Levin syndrome (recurrent hypersomnia with hyperphagia and hypersexuality in young males). Cataplexy specifically must be distinguished from syncope, atonic seizures and conversion . Breathing-Related Sleep Disorders, Circadian Rhythm Disorders, and Parasomnias Obstructive Sleep Apnoea Hypopnoea. Either polysomnographic evidence of at least 5 obstructive apnoeas or hypopnoeas per hour of sleep plus nocturnal breathing symptoms (snoring, snorting, gasping, breathing pauses) or daytime sleepiness and fatigue; or polysomnographic evidence of 15 or more events per hour regardless of symptoms. Severity by apnoea-hypopnoea index: mild under 15, moderate 15 to 30, severe over 30. Also Central Sleep Apnoea and Sleep-Related Hypoventilation . Circadian Rhythm Sleep-Wake Disorders. A persistent pattern of sleep disruption due to an alteration of the circadian system or a misalignment between the endogenous rhythm and the required schedule. Types: delayed sleep phase (the commonest in adolescents; a familial form exists), advanced sleep phase (older adults), irregular sleep-wake type , non-24-hour sleep-wake type (common in blind individuals), and shift work type . Jet lag type was removed in DSM-5. Non-REM Sleep Arousal Disorders. Recurrent episodes of incomplete awakening from sleep, usually during the first third of the major sleep episode (that is, from slow-wave, N3 sleep), accompanied by either sleepwalking or sleep terrors . The person has no or little dream imagery recalled, is relatively unresponsive during the episode, and has amnesia for it . Sleep terrors involve abrupt terror arousals with a panicky scream, intense fear and autonomic arousal. Nightmare Disorder. Repeated occurrences of extended, extremely dysphoric and well-remembered dreams, usually involving threats to survival, security or physical integrity, generally occurring during the second half of the major sleep episode (that is, from REM sleep). On awakening the person rapidly becomes oriented and alert . REM Sleep Behaviour Disorder. Repeated episodes of arousal during sleep associated with vocalisation and/or complex motor behaviours, arising during REM sleep and therefore usually more than 90 minutes after sleep onset, more frequent in the later portions of the sleep period. Upon awakening the person is completely awake, alert and not confused . Requires either REM sleep without atonia on polysomnography, or a history suggestive of the disorder plus an established synucleinopathy diagnosis. Highly examinable point: RBD is a prodrome of the alpha-synucleinopathies , so a large majority of cases eventually convert to Parkinson's disease, dementia with Lewy bodies or multiple system atrophy. Restless Legs Syndrome. An urge to move the legs, usually accompanied by or in response to uncomfortable sensations, with all three features: the urge begins or worsens during periods of rest or inactivity; is partially or totally relieved by movement; is worse in the evening or at night. Occurs at least 3 times per week for at least 3 months. Associated with iron deficiency , pregnancy and renal failure. Substance/Medication-Induced Sleep Disorder , with insomnia, daytime sleepiness, parasomnia or mixed types. Comorbidity Obstructive sleep apnoea with obesity, hypertension, type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease and depression. Circadian disorders with depressive disorders and, in the delayed phase type, adolescence itself. Non-REM arousal disorders with other parasomnias, enuresis and, in adults, obstructive sleep apnoea acting as the arousal trigger. REM sleep behaviour disorder with the alpha-synucleinopathies and with antidepressant use, which can unmask it. Restless legs syndrome with iron deficiency, pregnancy, renal failure, depression and ADHD. The differential that gets asked Sleep terrors versus nightmares. Sleep terrors: first third of the night, non-REM slow-wave sleep, marked autonomic arousal, the person is inconsolable and unresponsive, there is amnesia for the episode, and dream recall is minimal. Nightmares: second half of the night, REM sleep, the person wakes fully and can describe the dream vividly, and there is no amnesia and no confusion. Sleep terrors versus RBD. RBD occurs in REM, later in the night, the behaviour enacts a recalled dream, the person is instantly alert afterwards, and it is a disorder of older men that predicts Parkinson's. Nocturnal panic attacks also wake the person from non-REM sleep, but they are fully alert and there is no amnesia. Nocturnal seizures are stereotyped and brief. 14. Sexual dysfunctions, gender dysphoria, paraphilic disorders Sexual Dysfunctions F52.x In plain language. A problem in the ability to respond sexually or to experience sexual pleasure, that has lasted at least six months and causes distress. DSM-5 made three structural changes: it became gender-specific where the evidence supported that, it added a minimum duration of about 6 months and a frequency requirement of 75 to 100 percent of occasions to almost every dysfunction, and it merged several DSM-IV categories. Delayed Ejaculation. Marked delay in, infrequency of, or absence of ejaculation on almost all or all (75 to 100 percent) partnered sexual occasions, without the person desiring the delay. Erectile Disorder. At least one of three on almost all or all occasions: marked difficulty obtaining an erection, marked difficulty maintaining one until completion, or a marked decrease in erectile rigidity. Female Orgasmic Disorder. Marked delay in, infrequency of, or absence of orgasm, and/or markedly reduced intensity of orgasmic sensations, on almost all or all occasions. Female Sexual Interest/Arousal Disorder. Lack of, or significantly reduced, sexual interest or arousal, shown by at least 3 of 6 : absent or reduced interest in sexual activity; absent or reduced sexual or erotic thoughts or fantasies; no or reduced initiation of sexual activity and typically unreceptive to a partner's attempts to initiate; absent or reduced sexual excitement or pleasure during sexual activity in almost all encounters; absent or reduced sexual interest or arousal in response to any internal or external sexual or erotic cues; absent or reduced genital or non-genital sensations during sexual activity in almost all encounters. This diagnosis merged DSM-IV's female hypoactive sexual desire disorder and female sexual arousal disorder, on the evidence that desire and arousal are not separable in women. Male Hypoactive Sexual Desire Disorder. Persistently or recurrently deficient or absent sexual or erotic thoughts or fantasies and desire for sexual activity, judged by the clinician taking into account age and context. Genito-Pelvic Pain/Penetration Disorder. Persistent or recurrent difficulties with 1 or more of 4 : vaginal penetration during intercourse; marked vulvovaginal or pelvic pain during vaginal intercourse or penetration attempts; marked fear or anxiety about vulvovaginal or pelvic pain in anticipation of, during, or as a result of vaginal penetration; marked tensing or tightening of the pelvic floor muscles during attempted vaginal penetration. This merged DSM-IV's vaginismus and dyspareunia , because the two could not be reliably distinguished. That merger is the most-asked fact in this section. Substance/Medication-Induced Sexual Dysfunction , and Other Specified / Unspecified Sexual Dysfunction . All require duration of approximately 6 months , clinically significant distress, and that the dysfunction is not better explained by a non-sexual mental disorder, severe relationship distress (partner violence) or other significant stressors, and is not attributable to a substance or another medical condition. Specify: lifelong or acquired; generalised or situational; and severity mild, moderate or severe. DSM-5 deleted the DSM-IV subtypes "due to psychological factors" versus "due to combined factors". Numbers The two to remember across the whole group: 6 months minimum duration and 75 to 100 percent of occasions . Sexual aversion disorder was deleted in DSM-5 for lack of evidence and rare use. Comorbidity Depressive and anxiety disorders, relationship distress, and, medically, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, prostate surgery, and pelvic floor pathology. Antidepressants, particularly SSRIs, are a leading iatrogenic cause and should always be asked about. Differential Substance and medication effects (SSRIs, antipsychotics, antihypertensives, alcohol, opioids). Another medical condition (diabetic neuropathy, vascular disease, endometriosis, pelvic inflammatory disease, hypogonadism, hyperprolactinaemia). Another mental disorder , especially depression. Relationship distress and interpersonal factors , including partner violence, which are explicit exclusions. Inadequate sexual stimulation and lack of knowledge, which is common and is not a disorder. Gender Dysphoria F64.x In plain language. Distress arising from a marked incongruence between the gender a person experiences themselves to be and the one they were assigned at birth. DSM-5 renamed DSM-IV's Gender Identity Disorder to Gender Dysphoria to shift the diagnostic focus from identity itself to the distress , precisely so that being transgender is not framed as a disorder. That renaming and its rationale is the whole examinable point. In adolescents and adults. A marked incongruence between one's experienced or expressed gender and assigned gender, of at least 6 months duration, with at least 2 of 6 : a marked incongruence between experienced gender and primary and/or secondary sex characteristics; a strong desire to be rid of one's primary and/or secondary sex characteristics; a strong desire for the primary and/or secondary sex characteristics of the other gender; a strong desire to be of the other gender; a strong desire to be treated as the other gender; a strong conviction that one has the typical feelings and reactions of the other gender. Plus clinically significant distress or impairment. In children. Duration at least 6 months, with at least 6 of 8 , and Criterion A1 is mandatory : a strong desire to be of the other gender or an insistence that one is the other gender. The remaining seven cover cross-dressing preference, cross-gender roles in make-believe play, preference for the toys and activities stereotypically used by the other gender, preference for playmates of the other gender, rejection of the toys and activities typical of one's assigned gender, dislike of one's sexual anatomy, and a desire for the primary or secondary sex characteristics matching one's experienced gender. Specify: with a disorder of sex development ; and, for adolescents and adults, posttransition , meaning the person has transitioned to full-time living in the desired gender and has undergone or is preparing for at least one gender-affirming medical procedure. DSM-5-TR updated the language here: "desired gender" became "experienced gender", "cross-sex medical procedure" became "gender-affirming medical procedure", "natal male/female" became "individual assigned male/female at birth". Numbers Prevalence estimates in adults range roughly 0.005 to 0.014 percent for individuals assigned male at birth and 0.002 to 0.003 percent for those assigned female, though these come from clinic attendance and undercount.
