In children referred to clinics, rates of persistence into adolescence and adulthood have historically been reported as low for those assigned male and higher for those assigned female, but the figures are contested and the DSM-5-TR text is careful about them. Comorbidity Anxiety and depressive disorders, notably high rates of suicidality, driven substantially by stigma, family rejection and discrimination (the minority stress framework, which DSM-5-TR names). Autism spectrum disorder co-occurs at rates above the population base rate. Differential Non-conformity to gender roles , which is explicitly not a disorder. Transvestic disorder (cross-dressing for sexual arousal, with no incongruence of gender identity). Body dysmorphic disorder . Schizophrenia with delusions of belonging to another gender, which is rare. Other clinical presentations such as the desire for castration without a desire for the other gender's characteristics, which ICD-11 codes as body integrity dysphoria. ICD-11 Went further: it removed gender incongruence from the mental disorders chapter altogether and placed it in a new chapter on conditions related to sexual health, in order to retain access to care while removing the mental-illness framing. That contrast between DSM-5-TR and ICD-11 is high-yield. Paraphilic Disorders F65.x In plain language. A paraphilia is an intense and persistent sexual interest in something other than genital stimulation or preparatory fondling with phenotypically normal, physically mature, consenting human partners. A paraphilic disorder is a paraphilia that is currently causing distress or impairment to the individual, or whose satisfaction has entailed personal harm or risk of harm to others . DSM-5's central move was to separate the two: a paraphilia by itself is not a mental disorder . Say that sentence in any answer on this chapter. The eight named disorders: Voyeuristic Disorder (observing an unsuspecting person who is naked, disrobing or engaging in sexual activity; the individual must be at least 18 ); Exhibitionistic Disorder (exposure of one's genitals to an unsuspecting person; specify whether sexually aroused by exposing to prepubertal children, physically mature individuals, or both); Frotteuristic Disorder (touching or rubbing against a non-consenting person); Sexual Masochism Disorder (being humiliated, beaten, bound or otherwise made to suffer; specify with asphyxiophilia); Sexual Sadism Disorder (the physical or psychological suffering of another person); Pedophilic Disorder ; Fetishistic Disorder (use of non-living objects or a highly specific focus on non-genital body parts; the criteria explicitly exclude articles of clothing used in cross-dressing, which would be transvestic disorder, and devices designed for genital stimulation); Transvestic Disorder (cross-dressing; specify with fetishism or with autogynephilia). All require the arousal pattern over a period of at least 6 months , plus either the person having acted on the urges with a non-consenting person, or the urges causing clinically significant distress or impairment. Pedophilic Disorder specifically: over at least 6 months, recurrent, intense sexually arousing fantasies, sexual urges or behaviours involving sexual activity with a prepubescent child or children (generally age 13 or younger) ; the person has acted on these urges, or they cause marked distress or interpersonal difficulty; and the person is at least 16 years old and at least 5 years older than the child. The criteria exclude an individual in late adolescence involved in an ongoing sexual relationship with a 12 or 13 year old. Specify exclusive or non-exclusive type; sexually attracted to males, females, or both; and whether limited to incest. Every paraphilic disorder can be specified in a controlled environment (where opportunity is restricted, for example institutional settings) and in full remission (no distress, impairment or acting out for at least 5 years while in an uncontrolled environment). Numbers The three that get asked: pedophilic disorder requires the person to be at least 16 and at least 5 years older than the child, and the child to be generally 13 or younger ; voyeuristic disorder requires the person to be at least 18 ; all require 6 months . Paraphilic disorders are far more common in males; the male to female ratio for most is very high. Comorbidity Multiple paraphilias frequently coexist in the same individual. Also substance use disorders, depressive and anxiety disorders, ADHD, and antisocial personality disorder, particularly with the coercive paraphilias. Differential A paraphilia without distress, impairment or harm , which is not a disorder. Conduct disorder and antisocial personality disorder , where the offending is part of a broader antisocial pattern rather than paraphilic arousal. Substance intoxication and major neurocognitive disorder , particularly frontotemporal, where disinhibited sexual behaviour appears late in life without a lifelong pattern. Manic episode . Intellectual disability . Fetishistic versus transvestic disorder is the classic pair: if the clothing is used in cross-dressing, it is transvestic. 15. Disruptive, impulse-control and conduct disorders Conditions involving problems in the self-control of emotions and behaviour that violate the rights of others or bring the individual into significant conflict with societal norms or authority figures. DSM-5 placed antisocial personality disorder in this chapter as well as in the personality disorders chapter, dual-listing it, because it belongs conceptually to both. Oppositional Defiant Disorder F91.3 A. A pattern of angry/irritable mood, argumentative/defiant behaviour, or vindictiveness lasting at least 6 months , with at least 4 symptoms from any of these three categories, exhibited during interaction with at least one individual who is not a sibling. DSM-5 grouped the eight symptoms into these three types, which is a change from DSM-IV's flat list, and it added the sibling exclusion. Angry/irritable mood: often loses temper; is often touchy or easily annoyed; is often angry and resentful. Argumentative/defiant behaviour: often argues with authority figures or, for children and adolescents, with adults; often actively defies or refuses to comply with requests from authority figures or with rules; often deliberately annoys others; often blames others for their mistakes or misbehaviour. Vindictiveness: has been spiteful or vindictive at least twice within the past 6 months. Frequency rule, which is a DSM-5 addition and is examinable: for children under 5 , the behaviour should occur on most days for at least 6 months; for those 5 and older , at least once per week for at least 6 months (except the vindictiveness item). B. Associated with distress in the individual or others in their immediate social context, or it impacts negatively on social, educational, occupational or other areas of functioning. C. Not occurring exclusively during the course of a psychotic, substance use, depressive or bipolar disorder, and criteria for disruptive mood dysregulation disorder are not met . DSM-5 removed the DSM-IV exclusion that prohibited diagnosing ODD alongside conduct disorder, so the two can now be diagnosed together. Severity: mild (symptoms confined to one setting), moderate (two settings), severe (three or more settings). Numbers Prevalence about 1 to 11 percent, averaging around 3.3 percent. Commoner in males before adolescence (about 1.4:1); the sex difference is not consistently found in adolescents and adults. First symptoms usually appear in the preschool years, and rarely later than early adolescence. Comorbidity ADHD is the most frequent, and conduct disorder. Also anxiety disorders, major depressive disorder, and substance use disorders in adolescence. ODD is a well-established risk factor for later anxiety and depression, not only for conduct disorder. Differential Conduct disorder : ODD's defiance is directed at authority and involves no serious violation of others' basic rights or major societal norms, while conduct disorder involves aggression to people and animals, destruction of property, deceitfulness or theft, and serious rule violations. Disruptive mood dysregulation disorder : if criteria for both are met, only DMDD is diagnosed . ADHD : non-compliance driven by inattention and impulsivity, and children with ADHD alone are not typically spiteful or vindictive. Intermittent explosive disorder (high rates of anger but with serious aggression toward others, and no persistent defiance). Depressive and bipolar disorders with irritability. Normal developmental oppositionality in toddlers and adolescents, which is why the frequency and duration rules exist. Intermittent Explosive Disorder F63.81 A. Recurrent behavioural outbursts representing a failure to control aggressive impulses, shown by either : (1) verbal aggression (temper tantrums, tirades, verbal arguments or fights) or physical aggression toward property, animals or other individuals , occurring twice weekly, on average, for 3 months , where the physical aggression does not result in damage or destruction of property and does not result in physical injury to animals or other individuals; or (2) three behavioural outbursts involving damage or destruction of property and/or physical assault involving physical injury against animals or other individuals occurring within a 12-month period . B. The magnitude of aggressiveness expressed is grossly out of proportion to the provocation or to any precipitating psychosocial stressors. C. The outbursts are not premeditated and are not committed to achieve some tangible objective such as money, power or intimidation. That impulsivity criterion is what separates it from instrumental aggression in conduct disorder or antisocial personality disorder. D. Cause marked distress or impairment, or are associated with financial or legal consequences. E. Chronological age is at least 6 (or the equivalent developmental level). F. Not better explained by another mental disorder, and not attributable to another medical condition or a substance. In children aged 6 to 18, aggressive behaviour occurring as part of an adjustment disorder should not be given this diagnosis. Numbers The two pathways are the exam point: twice weekly for 3 months of non-destructive aggression, or 3 destructive or injurious outbursts in 12 months . Minimum age 6 . 12-month prevalence about 2.7 percent in the United States, commoner in those under 35 to 40 and in males. Onset is most commonly in late childhood or adolescence, rarely after 40. Comorbidity Depressive, anxiety and substance use disorders. Also ADHD, conduct disorder, oppositional defiant disorder, and antisocial and borderline personality disorders. Differential Disruptive mood dysregulation disorder : DMDD requires persistent negative mood between outbursts, and IED does not, and DMDD needs 12 months and an onset before 10. Antisocial and borderline personality disorders , where aggression occurs but is part of a wider pattern; DSM-5 permits IED alongside them if the outbursts exceed what those disorders usually produce. Conduct disorder (aggression is often premeditated and instrumental). Delirium, major neurocognitive disorder, personality change due to another medical condition . Substance intoxication or withdrawal . Adjustment disorder in children, an explicit exclusion. Conduct Disorder F91.x A. A repetitive and persistent pattern of behaviour in which the basic rights of others or major age-appropriate societal norms or rules are violated, with at least 3 of 15 criteria in the past 12 months from any of the four categories below, with at least 1 criterion present in the past 6 months . Aggression to people and animals: often bullies, threatens or intimidates; often initiates physical fights; has used a weapon that can cause serious physical harm (a bat, brick, broken bottle, knife, gun); has been physically cruel to people; has been physically cruel to animals; has stolen while confronting a victim (mugging, purse snatching, extortion, armed robbery); has forced someone into sexual activity. Destruction of property: has deliberately engaged in fire setting with the intention of causing serious damage; has deliberately destroyed others' property other than by fire setting. Deceitfulness or theft: has broken into someone else's house, building or car; often lies to obtain goods or favours or to avoid obligations (cons others); has stolen items of nontrivial value without confronting a victim (shoplifting, forgery). Serious violations of rules: often stays out at night despite parental prohibitions, beginning before age 13; has run away from home overnight at least twice while living in the parental or surrogate home, or once without returning for a lengthy period; is often truant from school, beginning before age 13. B. Clinically significant impairment in social, academic or occupational functioning. C. If the individual is 18 or older, criteria are not met for antisocial personality disorder . Specifiers Childhood-onset type (at least one symptom before age 10), adolescent-onset type (no symptoms before age 10), unspecified onset . Severity mild, moderate, severe. And the DSM-5 addition that is asked most: with limited prosocial emotions , requiring at least 2 of 4 characteristics persistently over at least 12 months in more than one relationship or setting: lack of remorse or guilt ; callous, lack of empathy ; unconcerned about performance at school or work; shallow or deficient affect . This specifier operationalises the callous-unemotional trait and marks a more severe, more stable and more heritable variant with a worse treatment response. Numbers The arithmetic to hold: 3 of 15 in 12 months, 1 in the past 6 months , and the childhood-onset cut at age 10 . 12-month prevalence 2 to 10 percent, median about 4 percent. Substantially commoner in males. Childhood-onset type is male-predominant, more aggressive, and has a worse prognosis, with a higher likelihood of progressing to antisocial personality disorder; adolescent-onset type is more equally distributed by sex and often desists. Comorbidity ADHD and oppositional defiant disorder, both very common. Also specific learning disorder, anxiety disorders, depressive and bipolar disorders, and substance use disorders. Differential Oppositional defiant disorder (defiance without rights violations). ADHD (impulsive disruptive behaviour without rule violations). Intermittent explosive disorder (aggression only, and impulsive, without the deceit, theft and rule-breaking). Depressive and bipolar disorders with irritability and aggression confined to mood episodes. Adjustment disorder with disturbance of conduct . Antisocial personality disorder in those 18 and over, which is Criterion C. Pyromania and Kleptomania F63.1, F63.2 Pyromania. Deliberate and purposeful fire setting on more than one occasion ; tension or affective arousal before the act; fascination with, interest in, curiosity about, or attraction to fire and its situational contexts (paraphernalia, uses, consequences); pleasure, gratification or relief when setting fires, witnessing them, or participating in their aftermath. The fire setting is not done for monetary gain, as an expression of sociopolitical ideology, to conceal criminal activity, to express anger or vengeance, to improve one's living circumstances, in response to a delusion or hallucination, or as a result of impaired judgment (as in major neurocognitive disorder, intellectual disability or substance intoxication). Not better explained by conduct disorder, a manic episode, or antisocial personality disorder. Kleptomania. Recurrent failure to resist impulses to steal objects that are not needed for personal use or for their monetary value ; increasing sense of tension immediately before the theft; pleasure, gratification or relief at the time of committing the theft; the stealing is not committed to express anger or vengeance and is not in response to a delusion or a hallucination ; and it is not better explained by conduct disorder, a manic episode or antisocial personality disorder. Numbers Both are rare. Kleptomania prevalence roughly 0.3 to 0.6 percent, and about 4 to 24 percent of people arrested for shoplifting; female to male about 3:1 . Pyromania is rarer still, and is male-predominant . The critical exam point for both: the great majority of shoplifters and fire setters do not have these disorders, because ordinary theft is for gain and ordinary arson is for revenge, insurance or concealment. Comorbidity Kleptomania: obsessive-compulsive disorder, bipolar and depressive disorders, anxiety disorders, eating disorders (particularly bulimia nervosa), substance use disorders, and other impulse-control disorders. Pyromania: substance use disorders, gambling disorder, depressive and bipolar disorders, and other impulse-control disorders. Differential Ordinary theft or arson (motive is gain, revenge or concealment). Malingering , feigning kleptomania to avoid prosecution. Manic episode , psychotic disorders , antisocial personality disorder , conduct disorder , major neurocognitive disorder and intellectual disability , all explicit exclusions. 16. Substance-related and addictive disorders The two DSM-5 changes to lead with: substance abuse and substance dependence were merged into a single Substance Use Disorder rated mild, moderate or severe, and Gambling Disorder was moved into this chapter , making it the first and only behavioural addiction recognised as a full DSM diagnosis. Alongside those, the criterion of recurrent legal problems was deleted and craving was added as a new criterion. Substance Use Disorder, the general criteria set F1x.x0 In plain language. The same eleven criteria apply to every substance class. They fall into four groups: impaired control, social impairment, risky use, and pharmacological criteria. Impaired control (4): (1) the substance is taken in larger amounts or over a longer period than was intended; (2) there is a persistent desire or unsuccessful efforts to cut down or control use; (3) a great deal of time is spent in activities necessary to obtain, use, or recover from the substance; (4) craving , or a strong desire or urge to use. Social impairment (3): (5) recurrent use resulting in a failure to fulfil major role obligations at work, school or home; (6) continued use despite persistent or recurrent social or interpersonal problems caused or exacerbated by the effects of the substance; (7) important social, occupational or recreational activities are given up or reduced because of use. Risky use (2): (8) recurrent use in situations in which it is physically hazardous; (9) use is continued despite knowledge of having a persistent or recurrent physical or psychological problem that is likely to have been caused or exacerbated by it. Pharmacological (2): (10) tolerance , defined by either a need for markedly increased amounts to achieve intoxication or the desired effect, or a markedly diminished effect with continued use of the same amount; (11) withdrawal , shown by the characteristic withdrawal syndrome for that substance, or by taking the substance (or a closely related one) to relieve or avoid withdrawal symptoms. Important qualification: tolerance and withdrawal occurring during appropriate medical treatment with prescribed medications such as opioid analgesics, sedatives or stimulants do not count as criteria. Severity: mild 2 to 3 symptoms, moderate 4 to 5 , severe 6 or more , within a 12-month period. That grading replaces the DSM-IV abuse/dependence dichotomy. Specify: in early remission (none of the criteria, except craving, met for at least 3 months but less than 12 months), in sustained remission (at least 12 months), on maintenance therapy , in a controlled environment . Numbers Two symptoms is the diagnostic threshold , and the severity bands 2 to 3, 4 to 5, 6 or more, all within 12 months. Early remission is 3 to 12 months, sustained remission 12 months or more. The 10 substance classes DSM-5 recognises: alcohol; caffeine; cannabis; hallucinogens (phencyclidine and other hallucinogens); inhalants; opioids; sedatives, hypnotics and anxiolytics; stimulants (amphetamine-type substances, cocaine, other); tobacco; and other or unknown substances. Note that caffeine has no use disorder in DSM-5, only intoxication, withdrawal, and caffeine-related conditions, with caffeine use disorder placed in Section III for further study. That asymmetry is examined. Comorbidity Extremely high with depressive, bipolar, anxiety and psychotic disorders, PTSD, ADHD, conduct disorder and antisocial and borderline personality disorders. Multiple substance use disorders commonly co-occur. Differential Non-pathological substance use , including heavy use that produces no criteria. Substance-induced mental disorders , which are separate diagnoses (substance-induced psychotic, bipolar, depressive, anxiety, obsessive-compulsive, sleep, sexual dysfunction, delirium and neurocognitive disorders). Independent primary mental disorders , distinguished by symptoms preceding substance use or persisting about a month beyond acute withdrawal. Intoxication and withdrawal syndromes worth knowing cold Alcohol intoxication: slurred speech, incoordination, unsteady gait, nystagmus, impairment in attention or memory, stupor or coma. Alcohol withdrawal: within hours to a few days of cessation, with 2 or more of autonomic hyperactivity, increased hand tremor, insomnia, nausea or vomiting, transient hallucinations or illusions, psychomotor agitation, anxiety, generalised tonic-clonic seizures. Specify with perceptual disturbances . Delirium tremens typically appears 48 to 96 hours after the last drink and is a medical emergency. Related conditions to name: Wernicke's encephalopathy (thiamine deficiency: confusion, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia) and Korsakoff's syndrome (anterograde and retrograde amnesia with confabulation), coded in DSM-5 as alcohol-induced major neurocognitive disorder, amnestic-confabulatory type . Opioid intoxication: pupillary constriction plus drowsiness or coma, slurred speech, impairment in attention or memory; severe overdose produces respiratory depression. Opioid withdrawal: dysphoric mood, nausea or vomiting, muscle aches, lacrimation or rhinorrhoea, pupillary dilation , piloerection, sweating, diarrhoea, yawning, fever, insomnia. It is intensely unpleasant but not usually life-threatening, which is the standard contrast with alcohol and sedative withdrawal, both of which can kill. Stimulant (cocaine, amphetamine) intoxication: tachycardia or bradycardia, pupillary dilation , elevated or lowered blood pressure, perspiration or chills, nausea or vomiting, weight loss, psychomotor agitation or retardation, muscular weakness, respiratory depression, chest pain, cardiac arrhythmias, confusion, seizures, dyskinesias, dystonias or coma. Withdrawal: dysphoric mood plus fatigue, vivid unpleasant dreams, insomnia or hypersomnia, increased appetite, psychomotor retardation or agitation, that is, the "crash". Cannabis intoxication: conjunctival injection, increased appetite, dry mouth, tachycardia. Cannabis withdrawal is new in DSM-5: irritability or anger, nervousness or anxiety, sleep difficulty, decreased appetite or weight loss, restlessness, depressed mood, plus at least one physical symptom such as abdominal pain, tremor, sweating, fever, chills or headache. Caffeine intoxication: recent consumption usually in excess of 250 mg, with 5 or more of restlessness, nervousness, excitement, insomnia, flushed face, diuresis, gastrointestinal disturbance, muscle twitching, rambling flow of thought and speech, tachycardia or cardiac arrhythmia, periods of inexhaustibility, psychomotor agitation. Caffeine withdrawal, new in DSM-5: headache, marked fatigue or drowsiness, dysphoric mood or irritability, difficulty concentrating, flu-like symptoms. Tobacco withdrawal: irritability, anxiety, difficulty concentrating, increased appetite, restlessness, depressed mood, insomnia, following at least several weeks of daily use. Hallucinogen Persisting Perception Disorder: re-experiencing, following cessation of hallucinogen use, of one or more of the perceptual symptoms experienced while intoxicated, for example geometric hallucinations, false perceptions of movement in the peripheral visual fields, flashes of colour, intensified colours, trails of images of moving objects, positive afterimages, halos around objects, macropsia and micropsia. Comorbidity Every intoxication and withdrawal syndrome sits on top of a substance use disorder, and multiple substance use disorders usually travel together (alcohol with tobacco, opioids with sedatives). Add depressive, anxiety, psychotic and neurocognitive disorders, PTSD, ADHD and antisocial and borderline personality disorders, plus the medical load: liver disease, pancreatitis, cardiomyopathy, hepatitis C and HIV. Differential The first question in every case is delirium , which changes the management. Then, for each picture: opioid versus stimulant intoxication is settled at the pupil (constricted versus dilated). Alcohol or sedative withdrawal versus opioid withdrawal is settled by danger (seizures and delirium tremens can kill, opioid withdrawal is miserable but rarely lethal). Withdrawal versus a primary anxiety or depressive disorder is settled by timing and by whether it clears within about a month of abstinence. Wernicke-Korsakoff versus dissociative amnesia is settled by the ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and confabulation. Gambling Disorder F63.0 In plain language. The only behavioural addiction in DSM-5. It was moved out of the impulse-control disorders (where DSM-IV called it "pathological gambling") into the substance-related and addictive disorders chapter, on evidence of shared reward circuitry, tolerance-like escalation, withdrawal-like states and comparable comorbidity. A. Persistent and recurrent problematic gambling behaviour leading to clinically significant impairment or distress, shown by 4 or more of 9 in a 12-month period: needs to gamble with increasing amounts of money to achieve the desired excitement (a tolerance analogue); is restless or irritable when attempting to cut down or stop (a withdrawal analogue); has made repeated unsuccessful efforts to control, cut back or stop; is often preoccupied with gambling; often gambles when feeling distressed (helpless, guilty, anxious, depressed); after losing money, often returns another day to get even ( chasing losses ); lies to conceal the extent of involvement; has jeopardised or lost a significant relationship, job, or educational or career opportunity; relies on others to provide money to relieve desperate financial situations (a bailout). B. The gambling behaviour is not better explained by a manic episode . Specify: episodic or persistent; in early remission (3 to 12 months with no criteria met) or in sustained remission (12 months or more); severity mild 4 to 5 , moderate 6 to 7 , severe 8 to 9 criteria. Note the DSM-5 change: the DSM-IV criterion of having committed illegal acts such as forgery, fraud, theft or embezzlement to finance gambling was deleted , and the threshold was lowered from 5 of 10 to 4 of 9 . Numbers Past-year prevalence about 0.2 to 0.3 percent; lifetime about 0.4 to 1.0 percent, and higher in men (about 0.6 percent) than women (about 0.2 percent). Men tend to start earlier and to have problems with strategic forms such as sports betting and card games; women start later, progress faster (the "telescoping" effect) and more often use non-strategic forms such as slot machines and bingo. Comorbidity Substance use disorders, particularly alcohol and tobacco, depressive and bipolar disorders, anxiety disorders, ADHD, and antisocial personality disorder. Suicide risk is markedly elevated. Differential Non-disordered social or professional gambling . Manic episode , which is Criterion B: a person who gambles heavily only while manic has bipolar disorder, and if the gambling predates and outlasts the mood episodes, both diagnoses are given. Antisocial personality disorder . Other medical conditions : dopamine agonists used for Parkinson's disease produce impulse-control behaviours including gambling, and that iatrogenic cause is a favourite MCQ. ICD-11 Recognises Gaming Disorder , online and offline, as a full diagnosis. DSM-5-TR does not: Internet Gaming Disorder sits in Section III as a condition for further study. Do not confuse the two systems here. 17. Neurocognitive disorders The chapter that used to be "Delirium, Dementia, Amnestic and Other Cognitive Disorders". DSM-5 replaced the word dementia with Major Neurocognitive Disorder , partly because "dementia" carries stigma and partly because it was not used for younger adults with acquired impairment from HIV or head injury. It also created Mild Neurocognitive Disorder as a new diagnosis, to capture the pre-dementia stage that the literature calls mild cognitive impairment, so that early intervention becomes possible. Amnestic disorder was absorbed into these categories. Every NCD is then given an aetiological subtype , so you diagnose twice: the syndrome, then the cause. The six cognitive domains DSM-5 works from Complex attention (sustained, divided, selective, processing speed); executive function (planning, decision making, working memory, responding to feedback, inhibition, mental flexibility); learning and memory (immediate memory, recent memory including free recall, cued recall and recognition memory, very-long-term memory, implicit learning); language (expressive, including naming, word finding, fluency, grammar and syntax, and receptive); perceptual-motor (visual perception, visuoconstructional, perceptual-motor, praxis, gnosis); social cognition (recognition of emotions, theory of mind). Social cognition is new in DSM-5 and its inclusion is what allows the behavioural-variant frontotemporal presentation to be captured. Learn all six by name. Delirium F05 In plain language. Attention and awareness break down over hours or days, they wax and wane through the day, and there is a medical cause behind it. A. A disturbance in attention (reduced ability to direct, focus, sustain and shift attention) and awareness (reduced orientation to the environment). B. The disturbance develops over a short period of time, usually hours to a few days , represents an acute change from baseline , and tends to fluctuate in severity during the course of a day . C. An additional disturbance in cognition (memory deficit, disorientation, language, visuospatial ability or perception). D. The disturbances in A and C are not better explained by another pre-existing, established or evolving neurocognitive disorder, and do not occur in the context of a severely reduced level of arousal such as coma. E. Evidence from history, physical examination or laboratory findings that the disturbance is a direct physiological consequence of another medical condition, substance intoxication or withdrawal, exposure to a toxin, or multiple aetiologies. Specify: substance intoxication delirium, substance withdrawal delirium, medication-induced delirium, delirium due to another medical condition, delirium due to multiple aetiologies. Also acute (hours to days) or persistent (weeks to months), and hyperactive , hypoactive or mixed level of activity. Numbers Prevalence in the general community about 1 to 2 percent, rising to 14 percent in those over 85. On admission to hospital 14 to 24 percent; incidence during hospitalisation 6 to 56 percent; up to 80 percent of patients in intensive care and up to 60 percent in nursing homes at some point. The hypoactive subtype is the commonest in older adults and is routinely missed, being mistaken for depression, which is a classic exam and clinical trap. Comorbidity Pre-existing major or mild neurocognitive disorder is the single largest risk factor, and delirium superimposed on dementia is extremely common. Also polypharmacy, sensory impairment, infection, dehydration, hip fracture and post-operative states. Differential Major neurocognitive disorder , and this is the pair to be able to draw as a table: delirium is acute onset with a fluctuating course, impaired attention and consciousness , disturbed sleep-wake cycle, frequent visual hallucinations , and is usually reversible ; dementia is insidious in onset with a progressive course, attention and consciousness are preserved until late , hallucinations are less common early, and it is usually irreversible . Psychotic disorders and bipolar or depressive disorders with psychotic features , in which delusions and hallucinations occur without the acute attentional disturbance and fluctuation. Acute stress disorder . Malingering and factitious disorder . Major and Mild Neurocognitive Disorder, the syndrome criteria Major NCD, Criterion A: evidence of significant cognitive decline from a previous level of performance in one or more of the six cognitive domains, based on both (1) concern of the individual, a knowledgeable informant, or the clinician that there has been a significant decline, and (2) a substantial impairment in cognitive performance , preferably documented by standardised neuropsychological testing or, in its absence, another quantified clinical assessment. The conventional benchmark is performance 2 or more standard deviations below appropriate norms, that is, at or below the 3rd percentile. Major NCD, Criterion B: the cognitive deficits interfere with independence in everyday activities , that is, at a minimum the person requires assistance with complex instrumental activities of daily living such as paying bills or managing medications. Mild NCD, Criterion A: evidence of modest cognitive decline , conventionally 1 to 2 standard deviations below norms, that is, between the 3rd and 16th percentiles. Mild NCD, Criterion B: the cognitive deficits do not interfere with independence in everyday activities, though greater effort, compensatory strategies or accommodation may be required. That independence line is the entire major-versus-mild distinction, and it is asked constantly. C. The deficits do not occur exclusively in the context of a delirium. D. The deficits are not better explained by another mental disorder such as major depressive disorder or schizophrenia. Specify: the aetiological subtype, and for major NCD, without behavioural disturbance or with behavioural disturbance (psychotic symptoms, mood disturbance, agitation, apathy or other behavioural symptoms), plus severity mild (difficulties with instrumental activities of daily living such as housework and managing money), moderate (difficulties with basic activities such as feeding and dressing), severe (fully dependent). Comorbidity Depression and anxiety are extremely common at the mild stage, when insight is retained, and apathy, agitation and psychosis appear as the disorder progresses; DSM-5 captures these with the with behavioural disturbance specifier. Delirium is superimposed frequently. Add the vascular risk load (hypertension, diabetes, atrial fibrillation), sensory impairment, falls and malnutrition. Differential Delirium , which must be excluded first (Criterion C). Major depressive disorder , that is, depressive pseudodementia. Normal ageing , which is why Criterion A2 asks for standardised testing. Intellectual disability , where the ability was never acquired rather than lost. Schizophrenia with cognitive impairment, distinguished by the lifelong history. Malingering and factitious disorder where compensation or litigation is in play. The aetiological subtypes, with what distinguishes each Alzheimer's disease. Insidious onset and gradual progression , with early and prominent impairment in learning and recent memory . Probable Alzheimer's requires evidence of a causative genetic mutation from family history or genetic testing, or all three of: clear evidence of decline in memory and learning plus at least one other domain; steadily progressive gradual decline without extended plateaus; and no evidence of mixed aetiology. Otherwise possible . It is the commonest cause of major NCD, accounting for roughly 60 to 80 percent of cases. Pathology: extracellular beta-amyloid plaques and intracellular neurofibrillary tangles of hyperphosphorylated tau , with early atrophy in the medial temporal lobe and hippocampus and a cholinergic deficit arising from the nucleus basalis of Meynert. Genetics: APOE e4 raises risk for late onset; mutations in APP (chromosome 21), presenilin 1 (chromosome 14) and presenilin 2 (chromosome 1) cause early-onset autosomal dominant disease, and people with Down syndrome almost all develop Alzheimer pathology by their forties because of the extra copy of APP on chromosome 21. Frontotemporal NCD. Insidious onset and gradual progression with either a behavioural variant (3 or more of: behavioural disinhibition, apathy or inertia, loss of sympathy or empathy, perseverative, stereotyped or compulsive/ritualistic behaviour, hyperorality and dietary changes, plus prominent decline in social cognition and/or executive ability) or a language variant (primary progressive aphasia, with prominent decline in speech production, word finding, object naming, grammar or word comprehension). Learning, memory and perceptual-motor function are relatively spared , which is the discriminator against Alzheimer's. Onset is typically earlier, in the fifties and sixties. Pathology: tau or TDP-43 inclusions; Pick bodies in the classic Pick's disease form. NCD with Lewy Bodies. Core diagnostic features: fluctuating cognition with pronounced variations in attention and alertness ; recurrent well-formed and detailed visual hallucinations ; and spontaneous features of parkinsonism, with onset subsequent to the development of cognitive decline . Suggestive features: meeting criteria for REM sleep behaviour disorder, and severe neuroleptic sensitivity , which is a safety point as well as an exam point. The conventional one-year rule : if cognitive decline begins at least a year before parkinsonism, it is NCD with Lewy bodies; if motor signs clearly precede cognition by more than a year, it is major NCD due to Parkinson's disease. Vascular NCD. The clinical features are consistent with a vascular aetiology, shown by either onset of the deficits temporally related to one or more cerebrovascular events , or evidence of decline that is prominent in complex attention, including processing speed, and in frontal-executive function . There is evidence of cerebrovascular disease from history, physical examination and/or neuroimaging sufficient to account for the deficits. Course is classically stepwise rather than smoothly progressive, with focal neurological signs. The second commonest cause of major NCD, and it frequently coexists with Alzheimer pathology as a mixed dementia. NCD due to Traumatic Brain Injury. There is evidence of a TBI with one or more of: loss of consciousness, post-traumatic amnesia, disorientation and confusion, or neurological signs. The NCD presents immediately after the injury or immediately after recovery of consciousness and persists past the acute post-injury period. Substance/Medication-Induced NCD. The impairments do not occur exclusively during delirium and persist beyond the usual duration of intoxication and acute withdrawal. Alcohol is the leading cause; specify persistent where deficits continue after an extended period of abstinence. NCD due to HIV Infection. Documented HIV infection, with a pattern that is not better explained by secondary brain disease such as progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy or cryptococcal meningitis. Typically subcortical, with slowed processing and executive difficulty. NCD due to Prion Disease. Insidious onset with rapid progression, plus motor features such as myoclonus or ataxia, or biomarker evidence. Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease is the archetype, and rapid progression over months is the discriminator. NCD due to Parkinson's Disease. Insidious onset and gradual progression in an individual with established Parkinson's disease , where the disturbance is not attributable to another condition. Probable requires no evidence of mixed aetiology and clearly preceding Parkinson's motor disease. NCD due to Huntington's Disease. Insidious onset and gradual progression, with either clinically established Huntington's or risk based on family history or genetic testing. Autosomal dominant, caused by a CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion on chromosome 4 ; presents with chorea , and cognitive change is early and executive. NCD due to Another Medical Condition and due to Multiple Aetiologies , plus Unspecified NCD . Comorbidity Each subtype carries its own load. Alzheimer's with depression and later psychosis and agitation. Vascular with stroke, hypertension, diabetes and post-stroke depression. Lewy body with REM sleep behaviour disorder, depression, orthostatic hypotension and severe antipsychotic sensitivity. Frontotemporal with motor neurone disease in a subset, and with the highest rate of being misdiagnosed as a primary psychiatric disorder. Traumatic brain injury with PTSD, substance use and chronic pain. Substance-induced with the substance use disorder itself and with Wernicke-Korsakoff. The differential that decides marks Alzheimer's versus frontotemporal: memory first versus behaviour or language first, later onset versus earlier onset, insight lost early in FTD. Alzheimer's versus Lewy body: steady decline versus fluctuating attention, visual hallucinations early in Lewy body, parkinsonism, neuroleptic sensitivity, REM sleep behaviour disorder. Alzheimer's versus vascular: smooth progression versus stepwise, memory-first versus executive-and-speed-first, focal signs and imaging. Any dementia versus delirium: onset, course, and attention. Any dementia versus depressive pseudodementia: in depression the onset is more abrupt and datable, the person complains loudly of memory loss rather than concealing it, answers "I don't know" rather than confabulating, effort is poor but performance improves with encouragement, and there is a mood history. Any dementia versus normal ageing , which is Criterion A2 and the reason for standardised testing. 18. Personality disorders An enduring pattern of inner experience and behaviour that deviates markedly from the expectations of the individual's culture , is pervasive and inflexible , has an onset in adolescence or early adulthood , is stable over time , and leads to distress or impairment. The pattern must be manifest in 2 or more of four areas: cognition (ways of perceiving and interpreting self, other people and events), affectivity (the range, intensity, lability and appropriateness of emotional response), interpersonal functioning , and impulse control . Learn that general criteria set, because a question that asks "what are the general diagnostic criteria for a personality disorder" is asking for exactly those four areas plus the pervasiveness, stability, onset and exclusion clauses. DSM-5 kept the ten categorical disorders in three clusters unchanged from DSM-IV; the alternative dimensional model sits in Section III. The three clusters Cluster A, the odd or eccentric: paranoid, schizoid, schizotypal. Cluster B, the dramatic, emotional or erratic: antisocial, borderline, histrionic, narcissistic. Cluster C, the anxious or fearful: avoidant, dependent, obsessive-compulsive. The clusters have limited validity and high co-occurrence, and DSM-5 says so; that criticism is worth stating when you list them. Cluster A: Paranoid, Schizoid, Schizotypal F60.0, F60.1, F21 Paranoid Personality Disorder. A pervasive distrust and suspiciousness of others such that their motives are interpreted as malevolent, beginning by early adulthood, with 4 or more of 7 : suspects without sufficient basis that others are exploiting, harming or deceiving them; is preoccupied with unjustified doubts about the loyalty or trustworthiness of friends or associates; is reluctant to confide in others because of unwarranted fear that the information will be used maliciously against them; reads hidden demeaning or threatening meanings into benign remarks or events; persistently bears grudges; perceives attacks on their character or reputation that are not apparent to others and is quick to react angrily or to counterattack; has recurrent suspicions, without justification, regarding the fidelity of a spouse or sexual partner. Schizoid Personality Disorder. A pervasive pattern of detachment from social relationships and a restricted range of expression of emotions , with 4 or more of 7 : neither desires nor enjoys close relationships, including being part of a family; almost always chooses solitary activities; has little if any interest in having sexual experiences with another person; takes pleasure in few if any activities; lacks close friends or confidants other than first-degree relatives; appears indifferent to the praise or criticism of others; shows emotional coldness, detachment or flattened affectivity. Schizotypal Personality Disorder. A pervasive pattern of social and interpersonal deficits marked by acute discomfort with, and reduced capacity for, close relationships, plus cognitive or perceptual distortions and eccentricities of behaviour , with 5 or more of 9 : ideas of reference (excluding delusions of reference); odd beliefs or magical thinking that influences behaviour and is inconsistent with subcultural norms (superstitiousness, belief in clairvoyance, telepathy or a sixth sense; in children and adolescents, bizarre fantasies or preoccupations); unusual perceptual experiences including bodily illusions; odd thinking and speech (vague, circumstantial, metaphorical, overelaborate or stereotyped); suspiciousness or paranoid ideation; inappropriate or constricted affect; behaviour or appearance that is odd, eccentric or peculiar; lack of close friends or confidants other than first-degree relatives; excessive social anxiety that does not diminish with familiarity and tends to be associated with paranoid fears rather than negative judgments about self. Note that schizotypal is dual-listed , appearing in both the personality disorders chapter and the schizophrenia spectrum chapter, because it is genetically related to schizophrenia. Comorbidity Cluster A disorders co-occur with each other, with depressive disorders, and with schizophrenia spectrum disorders in relatives. Schizotypal carries the highest risk of transition to a psychotic disorder. Differential Schizoid versus schizotypal: both are socially isolated, but schizotypal adds the cognitive and perceptual oddness, which schizoid lacks. Schizoid versus avoidant: the avoidant person wants relationships but fears rejection, the schizoid person does not want them. That pair is asked more often than any other in the personality chapter. Paranoid personality versus delusional disorder: suspiciousness that never reaches delusional conviction. Autism spectrum disorder , which can look schizoid but includes restricted repetitive behaviours and has a developmental onset. Schizophrenia in prodrome or residual phase . Personality change due to another medical condition and substance effects. Cluster B: Antisocial, Borderline, Histrionic, Narcissistic F60.2, F60.3, F60.4, F60.81 Antisocial Personality Disorder. A pervasive pattern of disregard for and violation of the rights of others , occurring since age 15, with 3 or more of 7 : failure to conform to social norms with respect to lawful behaviours, as shown by repeatedly performing acts that are grounds for arrest; deceitfulness, as shown by repeated lying, use of aliases or conning others for personal profit or pleasure; impulsivity or failure to plan ahead; irritability and aggressiveness, as shown by repeated physical fights or assaults; reckless disregard for the safety of self or others; consistent irresponsibility, as shown by repeated failure to sustain consistent work behaviour or honour financial obligations; lack of remorse, as shown by being indifferent to or rationalising having hurt, mistreated or stolen from another. B. The individual is at least 18 . C. There is evidence of conduct disorder with onset before age 15 . D. The antisocial behaviour does not occur exclusively during schizophrenia or bipolar disorder. Those three age-related clauses (since 15, at least 18, conduct disorder before 15) are the most examined arithmetic in the chapter. Borderline Personality Disorder. A pervasive pattern of instability of interpersonal relationships, self-image and affects, and marked impulsivity , with 5 or more of 9 : frantic efforts to avoid real or imagined abandonment (not including the self-harm in criterion 5); a pattern of unstable and intense interpersonal relationships characterised by alternating between extremes of idealisation and devaluation ( splitting ); identity disturbance, that is, a markedly and persistently unstable self-image or sense of self; impulsivity in at least two areas that are potentially self-damaging (spending, sex, substance abuse, reckless driving, binge eating), not including the self-harm in criterion 5; recurrent suicidal behaviour, gestures or threats, or self-mutilating behaviour; affective instability due to a marked reactivity of mood, with episodic dysphoria, irritability or anxiety usually lasting a few hours and only rarely more than a few days ; chronic feelings of emptiness; inappropriate intense anger or difficulty controlling anger; transient, stress-related paranoid ideation or severe dissociative symptoms . Histrionic Personality Disorder. A pervasive pattern of excessive emotionality and attention seeking , with 5 or more of 8 : is uncomfortable in situations in which they are not the centre of attention; interaction with others is often characterised by inappropriate sexually seductive or provocative behaviour; displays rapidly shifting and shallow expression of emotions; consistently uses physical appearance to draw attention to self; has a style of speech that is excessively impressionistic and lacking in detail; shows self-dramatisation, theatricality and exaggerated expression of emotion; is suggestible, that is, easily influenced by others or circumstances; considers relationships to be more intimate than they actually are. Narcissistic Personality Disorder. A pervasive pattern of grandiosity in fantasy or behaviour, need for admiration and lack of empathy , with 5 or more of 9 : has a grandiose sense of self-importance; is preoccupied with fantasies of unlimited success, power, brilliance, beauty or ideal love; believes they are special and unique and can only be understood by, or should associate with, other special or high-status people or institutions; requires excessive admiration; has a sense of entitlement; is interpersonally exploitative; lacks empathy; is often envious of others or believes that others are envious of them; shows arrogant, haughty behaviours or attitudes. Numbers Borderline prevalence about 1.6 percent in the community, rising to about 6 percent in primary care, 10 percent in psychiatric outpatients and 20 percent in inpatients; roughly 75 percent of clinical cases are female, though community samples are closer to even. About 8 to 10 percent die by suicide , which is roughly 50 times the general population rate. Antisocial personality disorder prevalence about 0.2 to 3.3 percent, strongly male-predominant, and much higher in prison populations. Narcissistic 0 to 6.2 percent, with 50 to 75 percent male. Histrionic about 1.84 percent. Comorbidity Borderline: depressive and bipolar disorders, substance use disorders, eating disorders (especially bulimia), PTSD, ADHD, and other personality disorders. Antisocial: substance use disorders, anxiety and depressive disorders, gambling disorder, somatic symptom disorder, and other Cluster B disorders. Narcissistic: depressive disorders, anorexia nervosa, substance use disorders (particularly cocaine), and other personality disorders. Differential Borderline versus bipolar II , the one that decides marks: borderline mood shifts last hours and are reactive to interpersonal events , especially perceived abandonment, while bipolar episodes last days to weeks , are relatively autonomous, and bring changes in sleep need and goal-directed activity; borderline also has chronic emptiness, identity disturbance and self-harm as the stable trait background. Borderline versus histrionic : both seek attention, but borderline adds self-destructiveness, angry disruptions of relationships and chronic emptiness. Narcissistic versus antisocial : both are exploitative, but antisocial adds impulsivity, aggression, deceit for material gain and a conduct-disorder history, while narcissistic exploitation serves admiration and status. Antisocial versus adult antisocial behaviour (a V code, where the behaviour is not part of a personality disorder, for example professional criminality without the broader pattern). Personality change due to another medical condition and substance use disorders , in which the behaviour appears only in the context of use. Cluster C: Avoidant, Dependent, Obsessive-Compulsive F60.6, F60.7, F60.5 Avoidant Personality Disorder. A pervasive pattern of social inhibition, feelings of inadequacy and hypersensitivity to negative evaluation , with 4 or more of 7 : avoids occupational activities that involve significant interpersonal contact because of fears of criticism, disapproval or rejection; is unwilling to get involved with people unless certain of being liked; shows restraint within intimate relationships because of the fear of being shamed or ridiculed; is preoccupied with being criticised or rejected in social situations; is inhibited in new interpersonal situations because of feelings of inadequacy; views self as socially inept, personally unappealing or inferior to others; is unusually reluctant to take personal risks or to engage in any new activities because they may prove embarrassing. Dependent Personality Disorder. A pervasive and excessive need to be taken care of that leads to submissive and clinging behaviour and fears of separation, with 5 or more of 8 : has difficulty making everyday decisions without an excessive amount of advice and reassurance from others; needs others to assume responsibility for most major areas of their life; has difficulty expressing disagreement with others because of fear of loss of support or approval; has difficulty initiating projects or doing things on their own because of a lack of self-confidence in judgment or abilities rather than a lack of motivation or energy; goes to excessive lengths to obtain nurturance and support from others, to the point of volunteering to do things that are unpleasant; feels uncomfortable or helpless when alone because of exaggerated fears of being unable to care for themselves; urgently seeks another relationship as a source of care and support when a close relationship ends; is unrealistically preoccupied with fears of being left to take care of themselves. Obsessive-Compulsive Personality Disorder. A pervasive pattern of preoccupation with orderliness, perfectionism and mental and interpersonal control, at the expense of flexibility, openness and efficiency , with 4 or more of 8 : is preoccupied with details, rules, lists, order, organisation or schedules to the extent that the major point of the activity is lost; shows perfectionism that interferes with task completion, for example being unable to complete a project because their own overly strict standards are not met; is excessively devoted to work and productivity to the exclusion of leisure activities and friendships, not accounted for by obvious economic necessity; is overconscientious, scrupulous and inflexible about matters of morality, ethics or values, not accounted for by cultural or religious identification; is unable to discard worn-out or worthless objects even when they have no sentimental value; is reluctant to delegate tasks or to work with others unless they submit to exactly their way of doing things; adopts a miserly spending style toward both self and others, money being viewed as something to be hoarded for future catastrophes; shows rigidity and stubbornness. Numbers Obsessive-compulsive personality disorder is the most prevalent personality disorder in the general population, roughly 2.1 to 7.9 percent, and is about twice as common in males. Avoidant about 2.4 percent, roughly equal by sex. Dependent about 0.5 to 0.6 percent, and it is diagnosed more often in females, which DSM-5-TR flags as possibly reflecting sex bias in diagnosis rather than true prevalence. Comorbidity Avoidant with social anxiety disorder (very high), depressive and bipolar disorders, and dependent and borderline personality disorders. Dependent with depressive, anxiety and adjustment disorders. Obsessive-compulsive personality disorder with obsessive-compulsive disorder in a minority, hoarding disorder, eating disorders and depressive disorders. Differential Avoidant versus social anxiety disorder : overlapping to the point that many argue they are the same dimension, with avoidant being earlier, more pervasive and involving a more global sense of inadequacy; DSM-5 permits both diagnoses together. Avoidant versus schizoid , as above, decided by whether the person desires relationships. Avoidant versus dependent : both are clinging and fear rejection, but the avoidant person avoids relationships until certain of acceptance, while the dependent person rushes into them and clings. OCPD versus OCD : OCPD has no true obsessions or compulsions and is ego-syntonic , OCD has intrusive ego-dystonic obsessions with ritualised compulsions; they can coexist, and only about a quarter to a third of OCD patients have OCPD. OCPD versus hoarding disorder : the miserly and object-retention criteria overlap, and if hoarding is prominent, hoarding disorder should be diagnosed as well. The other three personality diagnoses Personality Change Due to Another Medical Condition. A persistent personality disturbance that represents a change from the individual's previous characteristic pattern , with direct pathophysiological evidence of a medical cause, not better explained by another mental disorder, and not occurring exclusively during delirium. Specify labile, disinhibited, aggressive, apathetic, paranoid, other, combined or unspecified type. Classic causes: frontal lobe lesions, epilepsy, traumatic brain injury, tumour, Huntington's, multiple sclerosis, endocrine disease. The Phineas Gage case is the standard illustration. Other Specified Personality Disorder and Unspecified Personality Disorder , used for presentations with mixed features or where criteria for no single disorder are fully met. This category is heavily used in practice, which is itself one of the standard criticisms of the categorical system. Comorbidity Personality change due to another medical condition sits alongside the causative disease and, very often, depression, apathy and the family distress the change produces. The other specified and unspecified categories carry the same comorbid load as the specific disorders they resemble: mood, anxiety and substance use disorders above all. Two rules that answer many questions Age. Personality disorders may be diagnosed in individuals under 18 only if the features have been present for at least 1 year , with the single exception that antisocial personality disorder cannot be diagnosed before age 18 under any circumstances. Culture. The pattern must deviate from the expectations of the individual's own culture , so a habit of deference or of family interdependence that is normative in an Indian joint family is not evidence of dependent personality disorder. Both rules are examinable and both are commonly missed. 19. Section III: the alternative model, culture, and conditions for further study DSM-5 is organised in three sections. Section I is the introduction, the definition of a mental disorder, and the use of the manual. Section II is the diagnostic criteria and codes, the operational manual you actually diagnose from. Section III is "Emerging Measures and Models": assessment measures, the cultural formulation, the alternative model for personality disorders, and conditions for further study. Knowing that three-part structure, and knowing which things live in Section III rather than Section II, is worth easy marks. The Alternative DSM-5 Model for Personality Disorders (AMPD) A hybrid dimensional-categorical model, proposed for research and placed in Section III because the field could not agree to replace the categories outright. It has two criteria: Criterion A: level of personality functioning , rated on the Level of Personality Functioning Scale across four elements grouped in two domains. Self : identity and self-direction . Interpersonal : empathy and intimacy . Rated 0 (little or no impairment) to 4 (extreme impairment); moderate impairment or greater, that is a rating of 2 or more, is required for a personality disorder. Criterion B: pathological personality traits , in 5 broad domains subdivided into 25 facets : negative affectivity (versus emotional stability), detachment (versus extraversion), antagonism (versus agreeableness), disinhibition (versus conscientiousness), and psychoticism (versus lucidity). Notice that four of the five are maladaptive variants of the Big Five , with openness replaced by psychoticism, and this mapping is exactly what examiners ask for. The trait measure is the PID-5 , the Personality Inventory for DSM-5. The model retains only six specific personality disorders: antisocial, avoidant, borderline, narcissistic, obsessive-compulsive and schizotypal , plus personality disorder, trait specified for everything else. The four dropped from the alternative model are paranoid, schizoid, histrionic and dependent. The Cultural Formulation and the DSM-5-TR treatment of culture The Outline for Cultural Formulation asks for: cultural identity of the individual; cultural conceptualisations of distress; psychosocial stressors and cultural features of vulnerability and resilience; cultural features of the relationship between the individual and the clinician; and overall cultural assessment. The Cultural Formulation Interview (CFI) is a 16-question semi-structured interview, with an informant version and 12 supplementary modules, new in DSM-5. DSM-5 replaced the DSM-IV term culture-bound syndromes with three more precise concepts: cultural syndromes (clusters of symptoms that co-occur in a specific cultural group), cultural idioms of distress (ways of expressing distress that may not refer to specific symptoms, for example "thinking too much"), and cultural explanations or perceived causes (explanatory models, for example nervios , maladi moun ). That three-way replacement is a stock question. The named cultural concepts to be able to list: ataque de nervios (Latino, uncontrollable shouting, crying, trembling, heat in the chest rising to the head, often after a family stressor), dhat syndrome (South Asian, anxiety and somatic complaints attributed to semen loss in urine), khyal cap or wind attacks (Cambodian), kufungisisa ("thinking too much", Zimbabwe), maladi moun (Haitian, sent sickness), nervios , shenjing shuairuo (Chinese neurasthenia), susto (fright-induced illness, Latin America), taijin kyofusho (Japanese, fear of offending others through one's appearance or behaviour). Dhat, koro and possession states are the ones most likely to appear in an Indian entrance paper. Conditions for Further Study, the Section III list Not official diagnoses. If a question offers one of these as an answer for "which is a DSM-5 diagnosis", it is a distractor. They are: attenuated psychosis syndrome ; depressive episodes with short-duration hypomania ; persistent complex bereavement disorder (superseded in DSM-5-TR by prolonged grief disorder in Section II, so this one has effectively been promoted and renamed); caffeine use disorder ; internet gaming disorder ; neurobehavioural disorder associated with prenatal alcohol exposure ; suicidal behaviour disorder and non-suicidal self-injury (both of which DSM-5-TR converted into coded conditions that can be recorded alongside any diagnosis, so they too moved forward). Other conditions that may be a focus of clinical attention These are the Z codes , and they are not mental disorders . They include relational problems, abuse and neglect, educational and occupational problems, housing and economic problems, problems related to the social environment, problems related to crime or interaction with the legal system, and other health service encounters. Three that are examined specifically: malingering , adult antisocial behaviour and child or adolescent antisocial behaviour , borderline intellectual functioning , bereavement (uncomplicated) , age-related cognitive decline , and non-adherence to medical treatment . If a question asks "is malingering a mental disorder in DSM-5?", the answer is no, it is a condition that may be a focus of clinical attention. 20. The number sheet: every duration, age and cut-off in one place Revise from this table alone in the last hour before a paper. Almost every differential question in the syllabus is decided by one of these numbers. The differential pairs examiners keep reusing If you have twenty minutes left before a paper, read only this. Each row is a pair that has appeared repeatedly across NIMHANS, IHBAS, RML, CIP, SGT and Amity papers, with the single discriminator that settles it.
