both may be diagnosed GAD vs OCD Real-life worries that are ego-syntonic, versus intrusive ego-dystonic obsessions with compulsions OCD vs OCPD OCPD has no true obsessions or compulsions and is ego-syntonic OCD vs delusional disorder Use the absent insight specifier rather than adding a psychotic diagnosis Hoarding disorder vs OCD Distress on discarding and desire to save, versus hoarding driven by a classic obsession Trichotillomania vs OCD No obsession precedes the pulling; DSM-5 dropped the tension and relief requirements BDD vs eating disorder If the concern is body fat or weight and eating disorder criteria are met, it is the eating disorder Excoriation vs non-suicidal self-injury Removing an irregularity, versus relieving emotional pain through harm PTSD vs acute stress disorder More than 1 month versus 3 days to 1 month PTSD vs adjustment disorder Criterion A trauma and the four-cluster symptom pattern DSM PTSD vs ICD-11 complex PTSD CPTSD adds affect dysregulation, negative self-concept, relationship disturbance RAD vs autism RAD requires pathogenic care and improves when care improves; autism has restricted repetitive behaviours DSED vs ADHD Indiscriminate approach to strangers and no checking back, versus impulsivity alone Autism vs social pragmatic communication disorder Any current or past restricted repetitive behaviour makes it autism Intellectual disability vs specific learning disorder All domains low versus one academic domain low with normal intelligence Tics vs stereotypies vs compulsions Premonitory urge and suppressibility; rhythmic and earlier onset; performed in response to an obsession DID vs borderline PD Distinct identities with inter-state amnesia, versus identity disturbance without amnesia Dissociative amnesia vs neurocognitive disorder Retrograde autobiographical and identity loss with intact new learning, versus anterograde deficits Depersonalisation disorder vs psychosis Reality testing remains intact Somatic symptom disorder vs illness anxiety disorder Prominent somatic symptoms, versus few or none with fear of having an illness Conversion vs factitious vs malingering Not intentional; intentional for the sick role; intentional for external gain Anorexia vs bulimia Significantly low body weight, and anorexia takes precedence Anorexia vs ARFID ARFID has no body image disturbance and no fear of fatness Bulimia vs binge-eating disorder Presence of compensatory behaviour Sleep terrors vs nightmares First third of night, non-REM, amnesia and unresponsiveness, versus second half, REM, full recall and alertness Sleep terrors vs REM sleep behaviour disorder RBD is REM, later in the night, enacts a recalled dream, instant alertness, predicts Parkinson's ODD vs conduct disorder Defiance toward authority, versus violation of others' rights and major norms Conduct disorder vs antisocial PD Age 18 and a conduct disorder onset before 15 Kleptomania vs ordinary theft Objects not needed and not for monetary value; tension then relief Gambling disorder vs manic episode Gambling confined to mood episodes is bipolar disorder Delirium vs major NCD Acute and fluctuating with impaired attention and consciousness, versus insidious and progressive with attention preserved Major vs mild NCD Independence in everyday activities lost, versus retained with extra effort Alzheimer's vs frontotemporal NCD Memory first and later onset, versus behaviour or language first and earlier onset with memory relatively spared Alzheimer's vs Lewy body NCD Fluctuating attention, early well-formed visual hallucinations, parkinsonism, neuroleptic sensitivity, RBD Alzheimer's vs vascular NCD Gradual versus stepwise; memory-first versus processing-speed and executive-first with imaging evidence Dementia vs pseudodementia Complains of memory loss, "I don't know" answers, datable onset, mood history, improves with encouragement Schizoid vs avoidant PD Does not want relationships, versus wants them but fears rejection Schizoid vs schizotypal PD Schizotypal adds cognitive and perceptual oddness Borderline vs histrionic PD Self-destructiveness, chronic emptiness and angry ruptures in borderline Narcissistic vs antisocial PD Exploitation for admiration and status, versus for material gain with a conduct disorder history Avoidant vs dependent PD Avoids relationships until certain of acceptance, versus rushes in and clings The DSM-5 and DSM-5-TR change list, in one paragraph Multiaxial system abolished, GAF replaced by WHODAS 2.0. Schizophrenia subtypes deleted and the Schneiderian single-symptom concession removed. Autism's four disorders collapsed into one spectrum, triad reduced to a dyad, sensory criterion added. ADHD onset age raised from 7 to 12 and the symptom count reduced to 5 at age 17. Specific learning disorder's IQ-achievement discrepancy requirement abolished. Bereavement exclusion removed from major depressive disorder. DMDD and PMDD added; dysthymia and chronic MDD merged into persistent depressive disorder. Panic disorder and agoraphobia unlinked, agoraphobia now needs 2 of 5 situations, panic attack becomes a universal specifier, and the 6-month rule extended to all ages. A new obsessive-compulsive and related disorders chapter with hoarding and excoriation added and insight specifiers throughout. A new trauma and stressor-related chapter, with PTSD gaining a fourth cluster, losing Criterion A2, gaining a dissociative subtype and a preschool subtype. Dissociative fugue demoted to a specifier. Somatoform disorders rebuilt around positive psychological criteria, with somatisation disorder, hypochondriasis and pain disorder deleted and vaginismus and dyspareunia merged. Anorexia's amenorrhoea criterion deleted, bulimia's frequency halved, binge-eating disorder and ARFID added. Substance abuse and dependence merged into a graded substance use disorder, legal problems deleted, craving added, gambling disorder moved in as the first behavioural addiction. Dementia renamed major neurocognitive disorder, mild NCD created, social cognition added as a sixth domain. Personality disorders unchanged in Section II, with the alternative dimensional model in Section III. Then, in DSM-5-TR 2022: prolonged grief disorder added, unspecified mood disorder restored, suicidal behaviour and non-suicidal self-injury given codes, and the whole text revised for cultural and ethnoracial accuracy. Built for Sihan · DSM-5-TR (American Psychiatric Association, 2022), exam cut for the MET, NIMHANS, IHBAS, RML, CIP, SGT and Amity clinical psychology entrances · criteria are paraphrased in plain language for study, not reproduced verbatim, so check the manual itself for the exact wording before any clinical use.

title: Psychological Tests: Authors, Versions, Items and Subtests
text: Psychological Tests: Authors, Versions, Items and Subtests Every psychological test the Indian clinical psychology entrances (RCI MA, NIMHANS, IHBAS, RML, JSS, CIP, Amity) keep asking about, one table per test: full name, who built it and when, the current edition and the ones before it, publisher, age range, number of items, every subtest, scale or index, how it is scored and normed, what it measures, its Indian adaptation, and the trap examiners set on it. Each family opens with a from-scratch explanation of how that kind of test works and closes with a comparison table. Where a count or a year genuinely differs between sources, the table says so instead of guessing: an honest "uncertain" is worth more in the hall than a confident wrong number. In this book Intelligence tests (international) Performance tests and Indian intelligence tests Developmental, adaptive behaviour and social maturity scales Objective personality inventories Aptitude, interest, creativity and attitude measures Projective techniques Neuropsychological tests and batteries Clinical rating scales and symptom inventories Structured diagnostic interviews and the mental status examination Index of every test in this book 1. Intelligence tests (international) An intelligence test is a standardised set of tasks, given in exactly the same way to everyone, whose scores are compared with a large reference group (the norm sample ) of people of the same age. The test does not measure "intelligence" directly; it samples behaviour (defining words, copying block patterns, repeating digits) that theory and data say depends on general reasoning ability. The score tells you where a person stands relative to age-mates, which is why the same raw score means something very different at age 7 and at age 70. The modern story starts in Paris. The French government wanted a way to identify children who would not profit from ordinary schooling, and Alfred Binet and Theodore Simon (1905) produced the first practical intelligence scale: 30 tasks arranged in rough order of difficulty. In the 1908 revision Binet and Simon grouped tasks by the age at which typical children pass them, which gave the idea of a mental age (MA) : a child who passes the tasks typical of 8-year-olds has an MA of 8, whatever their actual age. A third revision followed in 1911. Mental age alone is awkward, because being 2 years behind means far more at age 4 than at age 14. The German psychologist William Stern (1912) proposed dividing mental age by chronological age (CA), giving a "mental quotient". Lewis Terman (1916) , in the Stanford revision of the Binet scale at Stanford University, multiplied this by 100 and called it the intelligence quotient : ratio IQ = (MA / CA) x 100 . A 10-year-old with an MA of 12 has a ratio IQ of 120. The ratio IQ breaks down in adolescence and adulthood, because mental age stops growing in the late teens while chronological age keeps rising, so an ordinary 40-year-old would get an absurdly low "IQ". David Wechsler (1939) , working at Bellevue Hospital in New York, solved this with the deviation IQ . Instead of a ratio, the person's score is converted to a standard score that shows how far they sit from the mean of their own age group, on a scale with mean 100 and standard deviation (SD) 15 . An IQ of 115 now means "1 SD above the age mean" (about the 84th percentile) at any age. Every major modern test uses deviation scores. Within Wechsler batteries, individual subtests are reported as scaled scores with mean 10 and SD 3 . Theoretical frameworks evolved alongside: Charles Spearman's (1904) general factor g , Raymond Cattell's (1941, 1963) fluid (Gf) versus crystallised (Gc) intelligence, John Horn's extensions, and John Carroll's (1993) three-stratum model, which merged into the Cattell-Horn-Carroll (CHC) model that now organises the indices of the Wechsler, Stanford-Binet and KABC-II. Definition Ratio IQ = (mental age / chronological age) x 100 (Stern 1912 idea, Lewis Terman 1916 formula and name). Deviation IQ = a standard score locating the person relative to same-age peers, mean 100, SD 15 on Wechsler tests (Wechsler 1939). Scaled score = subtest standard score, mean 10, SD 3. T score = mean 50, SD 10. z score = mean 0, SD 1. Exam trap "Who coined IQ?" Stern proposed the quotient (MA/CA) in 1912; Terman added the x 100 and popularised the term "IQ" in the 1916 Stanford-Binet. Wechsler introduced the deviation IQ for adults. The 1960 Stanford-Binet Form L-M also switched to a deviation IQ, but with SD 16 , not 15. Alfred Binet himself never used the IQ. How to read age ranges in this book: Wechsler-style notation "16:0 to 90:11" means 16 years 0 months up to 90 years 11 months. WAIS-IV: Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale, Fourth Edition The WAIS-IV is the standard individually administered adult intelligence test worldwide and the one most often named in Indian entrance papers. The examiner gives a series of subtests (verbal questions, block puzzles, digit repetition, symbol copying), converts each raw score to an age-scaled score, and combines these into four index scores and a Full Scale IQ. Interpretation moves from the global score (FSIQ) to the indices to individual subtests, looking for statistically significant strengths and weaknesses. The fourth edition is the one that dropped the old Verbal IQ and Performance IQ in favour of four indices. Field Detail Full name Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale, Fourth Edition Author(s), year David Wechsler (original Wechsler-Bellevue Intelligence Scale, 1939). WAIS-IV (2008) was developed by the publisher's research team after Wechsler's death (1981), still under his name. Versions Wechsler-Bellevue Form I (1939), Wechsler-Bellevue Form II (1946), WAIS (1955), WAIS-R (1981), WAIS-III (1997), WAIS-IV (2008), WAIS-5 (2024, see next entry) Publisher Pearson (formerly The Psychological Corporation) Age range 16:0 to 90:11 Items Item counts are per subtest (they differ widely, and testing stops at discontinue rules); a single total item count is not a meaningful or standard figure. 15 subtests in all. Subtests / scales / indices 10 core subtests : Verbal Comprehension: Similarities, Vocabulary, Information. Perceptual Reasoning: Block Design, Matrix Reasoning, Visual Puzzles. Working Memory: Digit Span (forward, backward and the new sequencing task), Arithmetic. Processing Speed: Symbol Search, Coding. 5 supplemental subtests : Comprehension (VCI), Picture Completion and Figure Weights (PRI), Letter-Number Sequencing (WMI), Cancellation (PSI). Figure Weights, Letter-Number Sequencing and Cancellation are normed only for ages 16 to 69. 4 indices : Verbal Comprehension Index (VCI), Perceptual Reasoning Index (PRI), Working Memory Index (WMI), Processing Speed Index (PSI). Full Scale IQ (FSIQ) from the 10 core subtests. Optional composites : General Ability Index (GAI = VCI + PRI subtests, less affected by working memory and speed) and Cognitive Proficiency Index (CPI = WMI + PSI subtests). New in WAIS-IV: Visual Puzzles, Figure Weights, Cancellation. Dropped from WAIS-III: Object Assembly and Picture Arrangement. Scoring and norms FSIQ and indices mean 100, SD 15; subtest scaled scores mean 10, SD 3. US standardisation sample 2,200. FSIQ 130 and above: very superior; 69 and below: extremely low (WAIS-IV classification labels). Measures General intellectual ability (g) and four broad abilities: verbal reasoning and knowledge, nonverbal and fluid reasoning, working memory, processing speed Indian adaptation Pearson has marketed an India edition with Indian norms (reported as WAIS-IV INDIA); year and sample details uncertain. In routine Indian practice, especially for certification, the older Indian performance scale WAPIS (Ramalingaswamy, 1974) and Indian norms of other tests are still widely used. Exam trap WAIS-IV has no VIQ or PIQ (those ended with WAIS-III). It has 4 indices, not 5 (5 primary indices belong to WISC-V and WAIS-5). The core-versus-supplemental split is 10 + 5 = 15 . Comprehension and Picture Completion are supplemental in WAIS-IV, while Visual Puzzles is core. GAI is built from VCI and PRI; CPI from WMI and PSI: examiners swap these. WAIS-5: Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale, Fifth Edition The WAIS-5 is the 2024 revision of the adult Wechsler. Its main structural change is to bring the adult test into line with WISC-V: the old Perceptual Reasoning Index is split into a Visual Spatial Index and a Fluid Reasoning Index , giving five primary indices. It was designed for both paper and digital (Q-interactive tablet) administration and shortened the subtests needed for an FSIQ. Because it is very new, Indian clinics and most Indian textbooks still teach WAIS-IV; treat WAIS-5 details below as current but verify against the manual. It was the first Wechsler to split perceptual reasoning into separate visual-spatial and fluid reasoning indices, producing five primary indices. Subtests are organised in three tiers (primary, secondary, complementary), and the FSIQ comes from just 7 primary subtests, which shortens testing. Testing starts with two routing subtests that estimate the person's level so that later subtests begin at the right difficulty. It is valued for its very wide age range and good floor and ceiling, useful in assessing both intellectual disability and high giftedness. Because no reading, speaking or culture-specific knowledge is needed, the test is used across languages and with people who have hearing or language problems. John Raven designed it to measure Charles Spearman's g , specifically eductive ability (making meaning out of confusion, seeing relations), as distinct from reproductive ability (recalling learned information), which he measured with the companion Mill Hill Vocabulary Scale. Items get "progressively" harder within each set, hence the name. Field Detail Full name Raven's Progressive Matrices: Standard (SPM), Coloured (CPM), Advanced (APM) Author(s), year John C. Performance tests and Indian intelligence tests A performance test is an intelligence test in which the person responds by doing something with materials (arranging blocks, fitting shapes into a board, sliding pieces, drawing) rather than by answering in words. Performance tests developed for three reasons. First, the US Army testing programme of World War I (the Army Alpha for literate recruits and the Army Beta for illiterate and non-English-speaking recruits, Robert Yerkes and colleagues, 1917) showed that verbal tests unfairly penalise people without schooling or language. Second, clinicians needed tests for deaf, speech-impaired and non-English-speaking children. Third, verbal and performance tasks seemed to tap partly different abilities: W. P. Alexander (1935) argued for a "practical" factor (F) beyond g, and Wechsler built both Verbal and Performance scales into his tests. India needed performance tests for the same reasons, even more acutely: at independence most of the population was not literate, the country has dozens of languages, and verbal Western tests are culturally loaded. Indian psychologists therefore did two things: they adapted Western tests (Binet-Kamat from the Stanford-Binet; MISIC from the WISC; WAPIS from the WAIS; Indian norms for Raven's and the Draw-a-Man), and they assembled batteries of existing performance tests with Indian norms (the Bhatia Battery). Many of these instruments date from the 1930s to 1970s and use old norms, a limitation examiners like to ask about, yet they remain in daily use in Indian clinics and are named in the government guidelines for certifying intellectual disability. High yield Indian adaptation pairs to memorise: Binet-Kamat (V. V. Kamat) from Stanford-Binet; MISIC (A. J. Malin, Nagpur) from WISC; WAPIS (P. Ramalingaswamy) from WAIS performance scale; Malin's VSMS (A. J. Malin, Nagpur) from Doll's Vineland; DASII (Pramila Phatak, Baroda) from Bayley; Bhatia Battery (C. M. Bhatia) is an Indian battery of mostly Western performance tests. Bhatia Battery of Performance Tests of Intelligence C. M. Bhatia assembled five tests, four performance tests and one memory test, and standardised them on Indian school children so that intelligence could be assessed without depending on literacy or a particular language. The tests are given individually with materials, and the scores are converted into an overall index. It remains one of the most-asked Indian tests in entrance MCQs, usually as "name the five subtests" or "who developed it". Kohs Block Design Test The person is given coloured cubes and a printed design card and must arrange the blocks so that their top faces reproduce the design. Success requires analysing the whole design into parts (analysis) and putting the blocks together again (synthesis), so it measures visuospatial reasoning and nonverbal abstract ability. Wechsler borrowed it as the Block Design subtest, which is still one of the best single measures of g in the Wechsler batteries and is sensitive to right parietal brain damage. Alexander Pass-Along Test The person is given a shallow tray containing coloured (red and blue) wooden blocks and must reach a target pattern shown on a card by sliding blocks along the tray, without lifting any piece out. It requires planning several moves ahead, so it measures practical problem solving and foresight. Alexander believed tests like this tap a practical ability (his "F" factor) that matters for technical and vocational success. Field Detail Full name Alexander Pass-Along Test Author(s), year W. P. Seguin Form Board Test The child is shown a wooden board with 10 recesses of different shapes; the shapes are removed and stacked, and the child must put them back as quickly as possible. It is repeated over three trials. It is one of the oldest psychological instruments, originally a training device in Edouard Seguin's physiological method of educating children with intellectual disability, later turned into a timed test. In Indian clinics it is used as a quick nonverbal measure for young children and people with intellectual disability, with results expressed as a mental age. Gesell Drawing Test The child copies a series of simple geometric figures (circle, cross, square, triangle, diamond and similar) from cards. Arnold Gesell observed that the ability to copy each shape appears at a typical age (for example a circle around 3 years, a cross around 4, a square around 4 to 5, a triangle around 5, a diamond around 7), so the most complex figure copied correctly gives a developmental level. It is used in Indian clinics as a quick visuomotor and developmental screen. Developmental, adaptive behaviour and social maturity scales An IQ test asks "how well can this person reason when tested?". A developmental scale asks "has this infant or young child reached the milestones expected for their age?", and an adaptive behaviour scale asks "how well does this person actually manage everyday life: dressing, eating, communicating, getting along with others, handling money?". These questions matter because intellectual disability is defined by two criteria, deficits in intellectual functioning and deficits in adaptive functioning, both beginning in the developmental period. A child can score 65 on an IQ test yet function independently at home and school; under DSM-5 that child may not meet criteria. Most developmental and adaptive scales are completed by observation and informant interview (usually a parent or caregiver) rather than by testing the person directly, which makes them usable with infants and with severely disabled people who cannot be tested. Scores are typically expressed as an age equivalent (developmental age, social age) and a quotient: Developmental Quotient (DQ) = developmental age / chronological age x 100 , and Social Quotient (SQ) = social age / chronological age x 100 . Modern scales (Vineland-3, Bayley-4) use deviation standard scores with mean 100, SD 15 instead. A further distinction is screening versus diagnostic assessment . Screening tests (Denver II, TDSC) are short, used on many children (for example in paediatric clinics), and only flag children who need further evaluation; they do not give a diagnosis or a reliable quotient. Diagnostic scales (Bayley, Gesell schedules, DASII) take longer and give a quantified developmental level. Definition Adaptive behaviour : the conceptual, social and practical skills people learn and perform in their everyday lives (AAIDD definition). Social age (SA) : the age level of a person's social competence on the VSMS. SQ = SA / CA x 100. DQ = developmental age / CA x 100. VSMS: Vineland Social Maturity Scale (Doll) Edgar Doll, at the Vineland Training School in New Jersey, wanted to measure what intelligence tests missed: how far a person can look after themselves and take part in social life. The VSMS is a list of everyday competencies arranged in order of the age at which they are typically achieved (from "crows, laughs" in infancy to managing others' affairs in adulthood). An informant who knows the person well is interviewed, each item is marked as habitually performed or not, and the total gives a social age and a social quotient. It was the first standardised adaptive behaviour scale. Field Detail Full name Vineland Social Maturity Scale Author(s), year Edgar A. Vineland-3: Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales, Third Edition The Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales replaced Doll's VSMS with a modern, multidimensional instrument. Adaptive behaviour is divided into domains (communication, daily living skills, socialization, motor), each with subdomains, and scored with deviation standard scores. It can be given as a semi-structured interview with a caregiver, or as parent or teacher rating forms. It is the most widely used adaptive behaviour measure in the world and central to intellectual disability and autism diagnosis. Gesell Developmental Schedules Arnold Gesell, at the Yale Clinic of Child Development, filmed and observed thousands of infants and young children and described the typical sequence and timing of developmental behaviours. His schedules turn these norms into an assessment: the child is observed with standard toys and situations, and behaviour in each of four fields is matched to an age level. Gesell's maturational theory (development unfolds according to an inner biological timetable) shaped the whole field, and the Bayley, Denver and Indian DST all borrow from his items. Bayley-4: Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development, Fourth Edition The Bayley is the most widely used individually administered infant test. The examiner presents standard toys and tasks (finding a hidden object, stacking blocks, responding to words) to the infant, and the caregiver completes questionnaires for social-emotional and adaptive behaviour. Its main use is identifying developmental delay and following up high-risk infants (for example preterm babies). Infant test scores predict later IQ only weakly, especially before about 18 months, which examiners like to ask. Classifying intellectual disability: IQ ranges, adaptive criteria and Indian certification Older systems classified intellectual disability (formerly "mental retardation") mainly by IQ ranges, roughly 2, 3, 4 and 5 SD below the mean of 100. DSM-IV-TR (2000) used overlapping bands (for example "50 to 55 up to about 70") to allow for measurement error. DSM-5 (2013) made a major change: the diagnosis still requires IQ about 2 SD below the mean (approximately 65 to 75, that is 70 plus or minus 5 for measurement error), but severity (mild, moderate, severe, profound) is now defined by adaptive functioning in three domains (conceptual, social, practical), not by IQ. ICD-11 (2019, in force 2022) uses "disorders of intellectual development" with mild, moderate, severe, profound and provisional categories, based on standardised tests where available (mild about 2 to 3 SD below the mean; moderate 3 to 4 SD; severe and profound more than 4 SD, separated from each other only by adaptive behaviour). In India, intellectual disability is one of the 21 disabilities under the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (RPwD) Act, 2016 ; "benchmark disability" is 40 percent or more, which gives access to reservations and benefits. The government guidelines for assessment (Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment; a 2018 gazette notification under the RPwD Act replaced earlier guidelines) use standardised Indian tests to obtain an IQ and a social quotient (SQ, from VSMS) for children and adults, and a DQ for young children (with "global developmental delay" for children under 5). Certification is by a medical board that includes a clinical psychologist. Objective personality inventories An objective personality inventory is a self-report questionnaire. The person reads a fixed set of statements ("I often feel tense", "I like going to parties") and answers in a fixed format (true/false, yes/no, a 3, 4 or 5 point agreement scale, or a forced choice between two statements). It is called "objective" not because the person is being objective about themselves, but because the scoring is objective: two scorers with the same answer sheet always get the same score, unlike a projective test where interpretation depends on the clinician. The weakness is the mirror image of the strength: the person can see what is being asked, so they can fake good, fake bad, answer carelessly, or simply agree with everything (acquiescence). This is why the serious clinical inventories carry validity scales that check how the test was taken before any clinical scale is read. There are three classic ways to build an inventory, and examiners love to ask which test used which. Rational (logical or content) keying: the author writes items that obviously reflect the trait, based on theory or clinical judgement. Example: Woodworth Personal Data Sheet, Bell Adjustment Inventory, the MMPI-2 content scales, the Taylor Manifest Anxiety Scale (items chosen by clinicians' judgement). Empirical criterion keying: the author does not care what an item seems to mean; an item is kept only if it statistically separates a criterion group (say, diagnosed depressed patients) from normals. The item "I prefer a shower to a bath" could land on a scale purely because the groups answered it differently. Examples: MMPI (1943), CPI, Strong Vocational Interest Blank. Factor-analytic construction: the author gives a large item pool to many people and lets factor analysis reveal which items cluster into dimensions. Examples: Raymond B. Cattell's 16PF, Hans Eysenck's EPI/EPQ, J. P. Guilford's inventories, and the Big Five tradition (NEO-PI-R). Many modern tests mix methods; the MMPI-2 Restructured Clinical scales, for instance, were built by factor analysis inside an empirically keyed instrument, and Theodore Millon's MCMI combined theory, internal consistency and external validation (a "sequential" approach). The first personality inventory was the Woodworth Personal Data Sheet (Robert S. Woodworth, 1917, published 1919), built during World War I to screen US army recruits for "shell shock" proneness (emotional instability). It had about 116 yes/no questions (sources give 116; treat the exact count as uncertain) drawn from psychiatric symptom lists, so it was rationally keyed. Every later inventory is a descendant of this idea of a "paper psychiatric interview". High yield First personality inventory: Woodworth Personal Data Sheet (1917). Classic empirically keyed test: MMPI (Hathaway and McKinley, 1943). Classic factor-analytic tests: 16PF (Raymond Cattell), EPQ (Hans Eysenck), NEO-PI-R (Paul Costa and Robert McCrae). "Sane man's MMPI" or the test for normal people built the empirical way: CPI (Gough). MMPI: Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory The MMPI was built at the University of Minnesota hospitals to give psychiatrists a quick, standardised aid to diagnosis. Starke R. Hathaway (a psychologist) and J. Charnley McKinley (a neuropsychiatrist) wrote about 1,000 statements, administered them to diagnosed patient groups and to normal visitors to the hospital (the "Minnesota normals"), and kept items that separated each patient group from normals: this is pure empirical criterion keying . The person answers True or False (or Cannot Say). Scores are converted to T scores and interpreted mainly as code types , the two or three highest elevated clinical scales (for example a "2-7" code: depressed and anxious), because the scales turned out to be poor at pure diagnosis but rich in correlates. Q-sort: Q-technique and the California Q-set In a Q-sort the person sorts a deck of cards, each carrying a descriptive statement ("I am a submissive person"), into piles from "most like me" to "least like me", with a fixed number of cards per pile so the result forms a quasi-normal distribution (commonly 9 piles). William Stephenson (1953) introduced this Q-technique : instead of correlating tests across people (R-technique), it correlates people (or the same person under different instructions) across items. Carl Rogers and his colleagues (John Butler and Gerard Haigh, 1954) used it to measure the gap between the real self and the ideal self : the correlation between the two sorts rose during successful client-centred therapy. Jack Block's California Q-set is a standard 100-item deck sorted by an observer (clinician) to describe someone's personality. Aptitude, interest, creativity and attitude measures This family covers tests that are not about psychopathology or global intelligence. An aptitude test estimates a person's potential to learn or succeed in a specific area in future (mechanical work, clerical work, numerical tasks); an achievement test , by contrast, measures what has already been learned. Because general intelligence tests give one broad score, guidance psychologists wanted multiple aptitude batteries that give a profile of separate abilities, which grew out of factor analysis (L. L. Thurstone's Primary Mental Abilities, 1938). The DAT and GATB are the two classic batteries. Interest inventories ask what a person likes or dislikes (activities, school subjects, occupations), on the logic that people are happier and stay longer in work that matches their interests. Two construction routes matter: the empirical route (Edward K. Strong Jr.: compare the answers of people successfully employed in an occupation with "people in general") and the homogeneous or rational route (G. Frederic Kuder's broad interest areas; John L. Holland's six RIASEC types). Creativity tests rest on J. P. Guilford's distinction (presidential address to the APA, 1950; Structure of Intellect model, 1956/1967) between convergent thinking , finding the single correct answer, and divergent thinking , producing many varied answers to an open problem. Divergent production is scored for fluency (number of responses), flexibility (number of different categories), originality (statistical rarity) and elaboration (amount of detail). Attitude scales measure an evaluative disposition towards an object (a group, the church, an institution). The classic scaling methods differ in how statements are chosen and how a score is formed: Thurstone uses judges to place statements on an interval scale, Likert sums agreement ratings, Guttman builds a cumulative ladder, Emory Bogardus measures social distance, and Osgood maps connotative meaning. Implicit measures (the IAT) try to bypass self-report altogether. High yield Aptitude = future potential; achievement = past learning. Strong = empirical occupational keying; Kuder = forced-choice triads, ipsative; Holland = RIASEC hexagon (used inside the Strong as General Occupational Themes). Divergent thinking scoring: fluency, flexibility, originality, elaboration (FFOE). DAT: Differential Aptitude Tests The DAT was built for educational and vocational guidance of secondary school students: rather than one IQ, it gives a profile of eight abilities so that a counsellor can say, for example, "strong mechanical and spatial, weak verbal". Each subtest is a timed multiple-choice test. The sum of Verbal Reasoning and Numerical Ability works as an index of scholastic aptitude (general academic ability). Attitude scaling methods The next entries are scaling methods rather than single published tests, but they are examined in the same way: who, when, how many points, and what the key index is. Thurstone scale: method of equal-appearing intervals Louis L. Thurstone and Ernest J. Chave (1929, The Measurement of Attitude , on attitude toward the church) first wrote a large pool of opinion statements. Many judges (around 300 in the original work) sorted each statement into 11 piles from most unfavourable to most favourable, without giving their own opinion. Each statement's scale value is the median pile it was placed in; its ambiguity is the spread of judges' placements (the interquartile range, Q). Statements with low ambiguity and evenly spaced scale values (commonly about 20 to 22) form the final scale. A respondent simply ticks the statements they agree with, and their score is the median (or mean) scale value of those statements. Items are selected by item analysis: keep items that discriminate between high and low total scorers (or correlate with the total). Projective techniques Every test in the earlier sections of this book works the same way: the item is clear, the possible answers are fixed, and the score is a count of how many answers fall in a keyed direction. A projective technique turns that logic upside down. The stimulus is deliberately ambiguous (an inkblot, a vague picture, half a sentence, a blank sheet of paper), the instructions are minimal ("What might this be?", "Tell me a story", "Finish the sentence"), and there is no right answer. Because the stimulus itself contains so little structure, whatever structure appears in the response is assumed to come from the person: their needs, fears, conflicts, defences, ways of perceiving and ways of organising experience. That assumption is called the projective hypothesis . Definition The projective hypothesis states that when a person is asked to impose meaning or organisation on an ambiguous, relatively unstructured stimulus, the response reflects the person's own enduring personality: their perceptual style, needs, motives, conflicts and defences. The less structured the stimulus, the more the response is determined by the person rather than by the stimulus. 6.0.1 Where the idea came from The word "projection" comes from Sigmund Freud, who described it in the 1890s (in his papers on paranoia, 1894 to 1896, and most fully in the Schreber case, 1911) as a defence mechanism : an unacceptable impulse or feeling of one's own is attributed to someone else ("I hate him" becomes "he hates me"). Freud also allowed a broader, non-defensive sense in which people generally read their inner world into the outer world. Projective testing borrowed the broader sense. A person who tells a story about a boy sadly staring at a violin is not necessarily defending against anything; they are simply organising an ambiguous picture using their own concerns. The phrase "projective methods" was coined by Lawrence K. Frank (1939) in his paper "Projective methods for the study of personality" in the Journal of Psychology . Frank argued that personality is a dynamic process of organising experience, and that the best way to see it is to give a person a "field" with little cultural structure and watch how they structure it, the way an X-ray reveals an inner structure without opening the body. Frank grouped together techniques that already existed: Hermann Rorschach's inkblots (1921), Carl Jung's word association (1910), and Christiana Morgan and Henry Murray's Thematic Apperception Test (1935). Henry Murray (1938, Explorations in Personality ) supplied the motivational theory (needs and press) that most storytelling techniques still use. 6.0.2 Why ambiguity matters, and what the techniques share Projective techniques share five features: (1) an ambiguous or unstructured stimulus; (2) a task that allows an almost unlimited variety of responses; (3) a disguised purpose, so the person usually does not know how the answer will be interpreted, which makes faking harder; (4) a global, holistic interpretation aiming at the whole personality rather than a single trait; and (5) heavy reliance on the trained clinician's judgement. They grew out of the psychodynamic tradition, which explains why so many of them talk about unconscious conflict, psychosexual stages and defence. In modern language many authors prefer the term performance-based personality tests (or "free-response measures") because the person performs a task in front of you and you observe how they do it, which is less theory-laden than "projection". 6.0.3 Gardner Lindzey's five-way classification (1959) Gardner Lindzey (1959) , in "On the classification of projective techniques" ( Psychological Bulletin ), sorted projective tests by the kind of response they require. This is the classification Indian MCQs ask about most often, and it appears in Anne Anastasi's and Frank Freeman's textbooks. Association : the person responds to a stimulus with the first word, image or percept that comes to mind. Examples: Rorschach Inkblot Test, Holtzman Inkblot Technique, Somatic Inkblot Series, Word Association Test (Francis Galton, Jung, Kent-Rosanoff), Hand Test. Construction : the person must create or construct a product, typically a story, from a picture. Examples: Thematic Apperception Test, Children's Apperception Test, Senior Apperception Technique, Roberts Apperception Test, Blacky Pictures, Make-A-Picture-Story. Completion : the person completes an unfinished stimulus. Examples: Rotter Incomplete Sentences Blank, Sacks Sentence Completion Test, Rosenzweig Picture-Frustration Study (completing a cartoon speech balloon), story completion methods. Choice or ordering : the person chooses among, or arranges in order, a set of alternatives according to some criterion (liking, appropriateness, attractiveness). Examples: Szondi Test (choose liked and disliked photographs), Tomkins-Horn Picture Arrangement Test, and picture-arrangement variants of the TAT. Expression : the person freely expresses themselves through a medium, and the manner (style) of production matters as much as the product. Examples: Draw-A-Person, House-Tree-Person, Kinetic Family Drawing, finger painting, play techniques, psychodrama, Bender Gestalt used projectively. Lowenfeld's World and Mosaic techniques are placed by different authors under expression or construction. Memory hook "A Clever Child Can Express" : Association, Construction, Completion, Choice/ordering, Expression. Then attach one anchor test to each: Rorschach (A), TAT (Construction), Sentence completion (Completion), Szondi (Choice), Draw-A-Person (Expression). 6.0.4 The reliability and validity problem Projective tests have been criticised since the 1950s, and you must be able to explain both sides. Standardisation : many techniques have several competing administration and scoring systems (the Rorschach had five major American systems before 1974; the TAT still has no single official system), so two clinicians may not be giving the same test. Reliability : interscorer reliability is acceptable only when a structured coding system is used (Exner's Comprehensive System, R-PAS, the Rotter ISB). Test-retest reliability is hard to estimate because stories and percepts change from occasion to occasion. Split-half reliability is usually not meaningful because cards are not equivalent items. Validity : global, intuitive interpretation has poor validity. Classic studies by Loren and Jean Chapman (1967, 1969) showed illusory correlation : clinicians "saw" relationships (for example big eyes in a drawing and paranoia) that did not exist in the data, because the signs matched their expectations. Specific, empirically keyed variables fare better: Joni Mihura and colleagues' 2013 meta-analysis in Psychological Bulletin found good validity for some Rorschach variables (especially those indexing thought disorder and perceptual accuracy) and poor validity for others, which shaped R-PAS. Norms : norms are often small, old, or American; cultural influence on content (what is "popular" or "normal") is large, which matters directly in India. Examiner effects : the examiner's behaviour, sex, rapport and even seating position influence responses (Exner seated the examiner side by side to reduce cueing). In their favour : they are hard to fake in a socially desirable direction, they bypass reading ability, they give rich idiographic material for case formulation, and they can reveal thought disorder and perceptual distortion that a self-report questionnaire, which depends on insight, cannot. High yield Frank 1939 coined the term; Sigmund Freud supplied the concept of projection; Murray supplied needs and press; Lindzey 1959 supplied the five categories. Projective = unstructured stimulus, unlimited response, disguised purpose, global interpretation. Main weakness: reliability and validity; main strength: resistance to faking and access to unconscious or unreportable material. Rorschach: Rorschach Inkblot Test The Rorschach is the best-known projective technique and the prototype of the "association" category. Hermann Rorschach, a Swiss psychiatrist working at Herisau, published it in his 1921 monograph Psychodiagnostik , based on about 400 subjects; he died in 1922, aged 37, before he could develop it further. The person is shown 10 symmetrical inkblots one at a time and asked "What might this be?" (the response or free association phase ); the examiner records every response verbatim, then goes back through each response in the inquiry phase to find out where on the blot the person saw it (location) and what about the blot made it look that way (determinants). Rorschach's own insight was that how a person sees (whole versus detail, form versus colour, movement) is more informative than what they see, so the test is fundamentally a test of perception and problem-solving under ambiguity, not just a content test. The 10 cards Colour group Cards Notes Achromatic (black, white and grey only) I, IV, V, VI, VII 5 cards. Card V (bat or butterfly) is the "easiest" popular; Card IV is often called the "father card" and Card VII the "mother card" in older lore (folk interpretation, not validated). Black and red (achromatic plus red) II, III 2 cards. The red was thought to provoke "colour shock". Fully chromatic (multi-coloured pastels) VIII, IX, X 3 cards. Card VIII has the most popular animal response (the side pink animals). Scoring (coding) categories, built up from scratch Location (where on the blot): W = whole blot; D = common detail (a frequently used area); Dd = unusual detail (a rarely used area); S = white space (always coded together with W, D or Dd, for example WS). Developmental quality (DQ) adds how well the parts are integrated: + (synthesised), o (ordinary), v/+ and v (vague). Determinants (what feature of the blot produced the percept): F = form (shape) alone; M = human movement; FM = animal movement; m = inanimate movement; chromatic colour : FC (form dominant, colour secondary), CF (colour dominant), C (pure colour, no form), Cn (colour naming); C' = achromatic colour (black, white, grey used as colour); T = texture (shading felt as touch, fur); V = vista (shading felt as depth); Y = diffuse shading (light-dark without texture or depth); FD = form dimension (depth from size or perspective, not shading); Fr / rF = reflection; (2) = pair. Shading and achromatic codes also take FT/TF, FV/VF, FY/YF, FC'/C'F forms depending on whether form dominates. Form quality (how well the percept fits the blot): in the Comprehensive System + (superior, elaborated), o (ordinary, common and accurate), u (unusual but acceptable), - (minus, distorted). Poor form quality (high X-%) indexes perceptual distortion and reality-testing problems. Content : H (whole human), (H) (fictional human), Hd (human detail), A, Ad, An (anatomy), Bl (blood), Sx (sex), Xy (X-ray), Na (nature), Bt (botany), Cg (clothing), Fd (food), Fi (fire), Ex (explosion), Art, Ay (anthropology), Cl (clouds), Ge (geography), Hh (household), Ls (landscape), Sc (science), Id (idiographic) and so on. Populars (P) : responses given very frequently in the normative sample. The Comprehensive System lists 13 populars (for example a bat or butterfly on Card V, two humans on Card III, the animals on the sides of Card VIII). Z (organisational activity) : a weighted score given when a person organises parts of the blot into a meaningful relationship; ZSum and Zd (ZSum minus the expected ZSum) index the efficiency of information scanning (overincorporation versus underincorporation). Special scores (Comprehensive System): cognitive slippage codes DV, INCOM, DR, FABCOM, ALOG, CONTAM (Level 1 and Level 2) summed as WSum6; plus AB, AG, COP, MOR, PER, CP, PSV and the later GHR/PHR (good and poor human representation). Five classical American scoring systems (before Exner) Rorschach's early death left the method without an owner, and five American schools developed in parallel: Samuel J. Beck (from his 1937 monograph onward; strongly empirical and normative), Bruno Klopfer ( The Rorschach Technique , with Douglas Kelley, 1942; phenomenological, introduced "testing the limits"), Zygmunt Piotrowski ( Perceptanalysis , 1957; known for his organic signs), Marguerite Hertz (Cleveland; frequency tables of form level), and David Rapaport and Roy Schafer (with Merton Gill, Diagnostic Psychological Testing , 1945 to 1946; psychoanalytic ego psychology; Schafer 1954 on psychoanalytic interpretation). John Exner's survey of these systems in the late 1960s found that they used different administration, codes and interpretations, so research results could not be compared. That problem is why the Comprehensive System was built. C' (C prime) is achromatic colour, not chromatic. S (white space) is never coded alone. Rorschach published in 1921, not 1911 (1911 is Eugen Bleuler's schizophrenia and Freud's Schreber case). Exner CS: Rorschach Comprehensive System John E. Exner Jr. combined the empirically best-supported elements of the five American systems into one standardised method, published in 1974 as The Rorschach: A Comprehensive System (Volume 1). Administration was fixed: examiner seated side by side with the client, the single standard question "What might this be?", a response phase followed by an inquiry phase, and verbatim recording. Responses are coded, and the codes are tallied into a Structural Summary , a page of frequencies, ratios, percentages and derived indices that is interpreted against normative data. Exner (who died in 2006) set a minimum of 14 responses : protocols with R under 14 were considered unreliable and the person was asked to give more. EA = M + WSumC (resources); es = FM + m + all shading and achromatic (demands); D = EA minus es (scaled). Lambda involves pure F. The minimum R is 14 in the Comprehensive System; in R-PAS the target is 18 to 28. SCZI was renamed and revised as PTI; an MCQ may describe PTI as a "schizophrenia index" in older terms. R-PAS: Rorschach Performance Assessment System R-PAS was developed after Exner's death by members of his research council, who wanted to keep only variables with solid empirical support (drawing on the Mihura et al. 2013 meta-analysis) and to fix the biggest practical problem of the CS: the huge variation in the number of responses, which distorts almost every other score. Its key administrative change is R-Optimised administration : the person is asked to give two, maybe three responses per card; if they give only one, the examiner prompts for another, and if they give four, the examiner pulls the card back ("prompt and pull"). This keeps most protocols in the target range of about 18 to 28 responses . Results are reported as standard scores (mean 100, SD 15) against an international normative sample, on two pages of variables. Holtzman (one response per card) is a third, separate approach. HIT: Holtzman Inkblot Technique Wayne H. Holtzman (with Joseph Thorpe, Jon Swartz and E. Wayne Herron) built the HIT in 1961 specifically to answer the psychometric criticisms of the Rorschach. Instead of 10 cards with a variable number of responses, it has many more cards and allows only one response per card , so every person contributes the same number of responses and each card can be treated like a test item. It has two parallel forms (A and B) of 45 cards each, which makes test-retest and alternate-form reliability possible, something the Rorschach cannot offer. Responses are scored on 22 standardised variables with norms. Field Detail Full name Holtzman Inkblot Technique (HIT) Author(s), year Wayne H. Holtzman, with Joseph S. Thorpe, Jon D. Swartz and E. Do not confuse with the 10-card Rorschach or with the 45 cards being "one form". Its whole selling point is parallel forms and fixed R, i.e. better reliability. SIS: Somatic Inkblot Series The Somatic Inkblot Series is a set of inkblots deliberately drawn to suggest body parts, internal organs and anatomical images , so that the person's responses reveal body image, somatic preoccupation and the emotional meaning attached to the body. It was developed by Wilfred A. Cassell, an American psychiatrist, starting around 1980, and is used in psychosomatic medicine and with patients who express distress through bodily symptoms. Like the Rorschach, it is an association technique, but the stimuli are not neutral: they are built to "pull" bodily content. TAT: Thematic Apperception Test The TAT is the prototype of the "construction" category. The person is shown pictures of people in ambiguous situations and asked to tell a dramatic story for each: what led up to the scene, what is happening now, what the characters are thinking and feeling, and how it ends. The theory (Henry Murray's personology, 1938) is that the storyteller identifies with a central character, the hero , and attributes to the hero their own needs (internal motives, for example need for achievement, affiliation, aggression, autonomy) while describing press (forces in the environment acting on the hero, for example rejection, danger, nurturance). The combination of a need and a press, with its outcome, is a thema . "Apperception" (a term from Johann Friedrich Herbart) means perceiving something in the light of past experience and existing mental contents, which is exactly what the test exploits. Field Detail Full name Thematic Apperception Test (TAT) Author(s), year Christiana D. Morgan and Henry A. Murray, 1935 ("A method for investigating fantasies", Harvard Psychological Clinic); manual by Murray, 1943 Versions 1935 original set; third and final revision of cards published with the 1943 Harvard manual (this is the set still used) Publisher Harvard University Press Age range Mainly adolescents and adults (commonly from about 14 years); children are better tested with the CAT; sources differ on the lower limit Items 31 cards : 30 pictures plus 1 blank card (card 16) . Cards are coded by number and letters: B (boys), G (girls), M (adult males), F (adult females), e.g. 3BM, 6GF, 12M. 11 cards are universal (no letter), for example 1 (boy with violin), 2, 4, 5, 10, 11, 14, 15, 16, 19, 20. Classically 20 cards per person in 2 sessions of 10 (cards 1 to 10, then the more unusual 11 to 20, at least a day apart); in practice clinicians use 8 to 12 selected cards Subtests / scales / indices No subtests. Murray's need-press analysis (needs, press, thema, outcome, hero). Later scoring systems: Leopold Bellak's (1947 onward), David McClelland and John Atkinson's need for achievement scoring (1953), Phebe Cramer's Defense Mechanism Manual, Drew Westen's SCORS (Social Cognition and Object Relations Scale) Scoring and norms No single official norm system; mostly qualitative or content-coded. Story features: hero, needs, press, outcome, levels (fantasy versus action), defences, object relations Measures Motives, interpersonal themes, conflicts, defences, object relations, mood and outlook Indian adaptation Uma Chowdhury (1960) , Indian adaptation of the TAT (Indian TAT, published by Manasayan, Delhi), with Indian figures, dress and settings; number of cards in the Indian set uncertain Exam trap 31 cards, not 30 and not 20: 30 pictures plus blank card 16 (on which the person imagines a picture and then tells a story). "20" is the number classically given to one person, in two sessions. Card 1 is the boy with the violin. Authors are Morgan AND Murray (1935); the 1943 manual is Murray's. Murray's theory term is press (environment), not "pressure". The Indian TAT is by Uma Chowdhury, not by Udai Pareek (Pareek adapted the Rosenzweig P-F). CAT: Children's Apperception Test Leopold Bellak and Sonya Sorel Bellak created the CAT in 1949 because young children found the TAT's adult human scenes hard to identify with. Following a suggestion attributed to Ernst Kris, they used animals in human-like situations (for example chicks eating at a table with a large hen in the background; a lion with a pipe and cane), on the idea that children identify more readily with animals and that animal pictures are less threatening. The pictures target feeding, sibling rivalry, parental relations, aggression, toilet training and fears of being alone at night. RISB: Rotter Incomplete Sentences Blank Sentence completion is the prototype of the "completion" category. The person is given sentence stems ("I like...", "My father...", "I regret...") and asked to complete each with their real feelings. Julian B. Rotter and Janet E. Rafferty (1950) made it one of the most psychometrically respectable projectives by providing an objective scoring manual that rates each completion for conflict versus positive adjustment, giving a total overall adjustment score. Because the stems are semi-structured, it is the least ambiguous projective, and its purpose is fairly transparent. P-F Study: Rosenzweig Picture-Frustration Study Saul Rosenzweig built the P-F Study from his own frustration-aggression theory. Each item is a cartoon of two people in a mildly frustrating everyday situation: one person says something frustrating, and the other person's speech balloon is empty. The respondent writes the first reply that comes to mind, which is assumed to show how they typically react to frustration. It is a "completion" technique, semi-projective and fairly structured, and is scored objectively on two dimensions: direction of aggression and type of reaction. WAT: Word Association Test (Galton, Jung, Kent-Rosanoff) The word association method is the oldest projective technique. A list of stimulus words is read aloud one at a time, and the person replies with the first word that comes to mind while the examiner times the reaction. Francis Galton (1879) first tried it on himself with 75 words to study the contents of the mind. Carl Gustav Jung (Studies in Word Association, 1904 to 1910; his 1909 to 1910 Clark University lectures) turned it into a clinical tool with a list of 100 stimulus words , using disturbances in responding, called complex indicators , to detect emotionally charged "complexes": prolonged reaction time, failure to respond, repeating the stimulus word, misunderstanding the word, perseveration, very personal or odd responses, clang associations, and failure to reproduce the original answer on a second run (the reproduction test). Jung also combined it with the psychogalvanic (skin conductance) response. Grace H. Kent and Aaron J. Rosanoff (1910) took the opposite, normative route: 100 neutral common words with frequency tables of responses from 1,000 normal adults, so that a response could be scored as common or idiosyncratic, used originally to distinguish psychotic from normal subjects. Field Detail Full name Word Association Test (Jung's association method; Kent-Rosanoff Free Association Test) Author(s), year Francis Galton, 1879; Carl Jung, 1904 to 1910 (100-word list); Grace Kent and Aaron Rosanoff, 1910; David Rapaport's 60-word list (1946) used diagnostically Versions Jung list, Kent-Rosanoff list, Rapaport list; many local translations Publisher Kent-Rosanoff published in American Journal of Insanity (1910); no single commercial publisher Age range Older children to adults Items Galton 75 words; Jung 100; Kent-Rosanoff 100; Rapaport 60 Subtests / scales / indices Jung: complex indicators, reaction time. Kent-Rosanoff: common versus individual (idiosyncratic) responses using frequency tables Scoring and norms Reaction time (in seconds), response content, frequency norms (Kent-Rosanoff from 1,000 normal adults) Measures Emotional complexes (Jung); commonality of thought, thought disorder (Kent-Rosanoff) Indian adaptation Hindi and other Indian language word lists have been constructed by individual researchers; standard adaptation uncertain Exam trap Carl Jung's list (complex indicators, reaction time, emotional complexes) versus Kent-Rosanoff (frequency tables, normality versus psychosis, 1,000 normals). Both have 100 words and both date from around 1910, so examiners ask which one had norms (Kent-Rosanoff) and which one detected complexes (Jung). The originator of word association is Francis Galton (1879), not Jung. Wundt used association in the laboratory too, but the clinical method is Jung's. Neuropsychological tests and batteries A neuropsychological test is a standardised task that samples one cognitive function (attention, memory, language, visuospatial skill, executive control, motor speed) so that the clinician can infer how well the brain systems underlying that function are working. The logic is borrowed from neurology: a lesion in a particular brain region produces a particular pattern of failures, so a carefully chosen set of tasks can reveal whether the brain is affected, which functions are impaired and spared, and how the person fails. Clinically, these tests are used in dementia, head injury, stroke, epilepsy, tumours, schizophrenia and other psychiatric disorders with cognitive deficits, ADHD and learning disorders, and for rehabilitation planning and capacity decisions. Historical "organicity" testing. From the 1930s to the 1960s, clinical psychologists were mostly asked one crude question: "Is this patient organic (brain damaged) or functional (psychiatric)?" Single tests were used as general screens for "organicity": the Bender Visual Motor Gestalt Test (Lauretta Bender, 1938), the Benton Visual Retention Test (Arthur Benton, 1946) and the Memory-for-Designs Test (Frances Graham and Barbara Kendall, 1946; manual 1960). The assumption was that brain damage is a single, unitary thing that any sensitive test will detect. That assumption is now known to be wrong: brain damage varies by location, size, speed of onset and age, and a right parietal stroke and a left frontal tumour produce very different profiles. Modern neuropsychology therefore asks about specific functions, not "organicity" in general, although the old screening tests remain popular in Indian clinics and in MCQs. Three approaches to assessment. (1) The fixed battery approach gives every patient the same, fixed set of tests, scored against norms, with summary indices. Examples are the Halstead-Reitan Neuropsychological Battery (Ward Halstead, 1947; Ralph Reitan) and the Luria-Nebraska Neuropsychological Battery (Charles Golden and colleagues, 1980). Strengths: comprehensive, good for research and for comparing patients; weaknesses: long (often 6 to 8 hours for the Halstead-Reitan) and not tailored to the referral question. (2) The flexible battery approach chooses a core set of tests and then adds tests depending on the referral question and on what the first results show (most clinicians work this way today; the NIMHANS Neuropsychological Battery is usually used as a flexible, domain-based set). (3) The process approach , developed by Edith Kaplan and colleagues at the Boston Veterans Administration Hospital (the "Boston Process Approach", from the 1970s and 1980s), argues that how a person reaches a score matters more than the score itself. Two patients may both score 20 on a copying task, one because of poor planning (piecemeal, fragmented copy, typical of right hemisphere or frontal damage) and the other because of missing details within an intact outline (typical of left hemisphere damage). The process approach records strategies, errors, time per item and the order of drawing. Products of this approach include the WAIS-R as a Neuropsychological Instrument (WAIS-R NI , Kaplan, Fein, Morris and Delis, 1991), the California Verbal Learning Test and the Delis-Kaplan Executive Function System (D-KEFS , Dean Delis, Edith Kaplan and Joel Kramer, 2001). Luria's qualitative approach. The Russian neuropsychologist Alexander Romanovich Luria (1902 to 1977) did not use norms or total scores. He saw every complex behaviour as a functional system built from several links located in different brain areas, and he organised the brain into three functional units : (1) the unit for regulating tone and waking (brainstem and reticular formation), (2) the unit for receiving, analysing and storing information (posterior cortex: occipital, temporal, parietal), and (3) the unit for programming, regulating and verifying activity (frontal lobes). By watching exactly where a function broke down (syndrome analysis), Luria inferred which link was damaged. His methods were collected and published in English by the Danish psychologist Anne-Lise Christensen (1975) as Luria's Neuropsychological Investigation ; Golden and colleagues later standardised Christensen's items into the Luria-Nebraska battery. Domains to know. Orientation and general cognition (MMSE, MoCA, ACE-III); attention and speed (Digit Span, Trail Making A, Stroop word and colour pages, digit vigilance, cancellation); memory (WMS, PGI Memory Scale, Rey AVLT, CVLT, Rey complex figure recall, Benton Visual Retention Test); language (Boston Naming Test, Token Test, verbal fluency, BDAE, WAB); visuospatial and constructional skill (Bender-Gestalt, Rey figure copy, clock drawing, block design); executive function (WCST, Trail Making B, Stroop interference, Tower of London, verbal fluency); motor (finger tapping, grip strength, grooved pegboard); and severity or staging scales (GCS, CDR, GDS, Hachinski). Definition Executive functions are the higher-order control processes, mainly supported by the prefrontal cortex and its circuits, that let a person plan, start, shift, inhibit, monitor and adjust goal-directed behaviour. Classic tests: WCST (set shifting), Stroop (inhibition), Trail Making B (switching), Tower of London (planning), verbal fluency (generation and strategic retrieval). Bender-Gestalt: Bender Visual Motor Gestalt Test The person copies simple geometric designs (dots, lines, curves, overlapping shapes) printed one per card, on a blank sheet, with no time limit and no eraser restrictions in most versions. The idea, drawn from Gestalt psychology, is that perceiving a design as an organised whole and reproducing it requires integrating visual perception with motor output (visual-motor integration); children's copies mature with age, and brain damage, intellectual disability or emotional disturbance distort the copies in characteristic ways (rotation, fragmentation, perseveration, overlapping difficulty, closure problems). Scoring systems count these errors (Pascal and Suttell for adults, Koppitz for children) or rate each drawing globally (Bender-Gestalt II). It is quick (about 10 minutes), non-verbal and culture-light, which is why it became one of the most used tests in the world and is part of the Indian PGI Battery of Brain Dysfunction. BVRT: Benton Visual Retention Test The BVRT is a test of visual memory and visual perception in which the person looks at a card showing one to three geometric figures and then draws them from memory (or copies them). Each design typically has two large main figures and one small peripheral figure, so the test is sensitive both to memory loss and to unilateral spatial neglect (consistently missing the peripheral figure on one side). Because three equivalent forms exist, the test can be repeated (for example before and after treatment) with less practice effect. Two scores are obtained: the number correct (0 to 10) and the error score , with errors classified into six types; the expected score is adjusted for the person's estimated premorbid IQ and age. HRB: Halstead-Reitan Neuropsychological Battery The Halstead-Reitan is the classic fixed battery : a set of tests given to everyone in the same way, designed to detect brain damage and to suggest its lateralisation (left vs right) and whether it is focal or diffuse. Ward Halstead, working at the University of Chicago, studied patients with frontal lobe lesions and developed a set of tests of what he called "biological intelligence" (as distinct from psychometric IQ). His student Ralph Reitan, at Indiana University, selected the tests that best separated brain-damaged from control patients, added several, and validated the battery over decades. Interpretation uses four methods together: level of performance (cut-offs), pattern of performance across tests, pathognomonic signs (for example aphasia), and comparison of the right and left sides of the body. LNNB: Luria-Nebraska Neuropsychological Battery The Luria-Nebraska is an attempt to combine Alexander Luria's rich qualitative items with American psychometric standardisation. Charles Golden and his colleagues at the University of Nebraska took the items in Anne-Lise Christensen's (1975) compilation of A. R. Luria's bedside methods, fixed the administration, and scored each item 0 (normal), 1 (borderline) or 2 (clearly abnormal). Items are grouped into clinical scales, and scale totals are converted to T scores where higher means more impairment . A "critical level", adjusted for age and education, marks the T score above which a scale is considered impaired. It takes about 2 to 3 hours, much shorter than the Halstead-Reitan, but it was criticised (for example by Spiers, 1981, and Adams, 1980) for being heavily verbal and for straying from Luria's qualitative spirit. NNB: NIMHANS Neuropsychological Battery (adults and children) The NIMHANS Neuropsychological Battery is the main Indian, domain-based set of neuropsychological tests, developed at the Department of Clinical Psychology, National Institute of Mental Health and Neuro Sciences (NIMHANS), Bangalore (Bengaluru). Rather than a fixed battery with one summary index, it is a collection of individually normed tests, each tied to a specific cognitive function and, where possible, to a brain region (for example WCST and Tower of London for prefrontal functions, Rey figure for right hemisphere visual memory, AVLT for left temporal verbal memory). Norms are given by age, sex and education, which matters greatly in India where education varies widely. The clinician picks the tests relevant to the case, so in practice it functions as a flexible battery. PGI-BBD: PGI Battery of Brain Dysfunction The PGI Battery of Brain Dysfunction is the classic Indian composite battery from the Postgraduate Institute of Medical Education and Research (PGIMER), Chandigarh. Instead of new tests, it combines five existing Indian or adapted tests (memory, verbal intelligence, performance intelligence, perceptual acuity and visual-motor copying), so that the overall pattern can show whether there is brain dysfunction and how severe it is. Each component yields a "dysfunction" or impairment rating, and these are combined into a total dysfunction score. It is widely used in Indian hospitals, especially in North India, and is a favourite MCQ item. Field Detail Full name PGI Battery of Brain Dysfunction (PGI-BBD) Author(s), year S. K. PGIMS: PGI Memory Scale The PGI Memory Scale is an Indian memory battery modelled loosely on the Wechsler Memory Scale but built for Indian adults, including those with limited education. Its ten subtests sample remote and recent memory, attention, immediate and delayed verbal recall, paired-associate learning, visual retention and recognition. Each subtest raw score is compared with norms, and the number and severity of low scores is summarised as a dysfunction rating rather than a single memory quotient. It is quick (about 30 to 40 minutes) and is one of the most commonly used memory tests in Indian clinical practice. "Mental balance" is an attention and mental control task, not an emotional measure. WMS: Wechsler Memory Scale The Wechsler Memory Scale is the most widely used memory battery in the world. It assesses memory the way the Wechsler intelligence scales assess intelligence: several subtests, each converted to scaled scores (mean 10, SD 3), combined into index scores (mean 100, SD 15). Modern editions deliberately separate auditory (verbal) from visual memory, and immediate from delayed recall, because different brain lesions affect these differently (left temporal damage tends to hit verbal memory, right temporal damage visual memory). Because it is co-normed with the WAIS, the clinician can directly compare a person's memory with their general ability, which is how a disproportionate memory deficit (as in amnesia or early Alzheimer's disease) is detected. Year sequence: 1945, 1987, 1997, 2009. RAVLT: Rey Auditory Verbal Learning Test The AVLT measures how well a person learns and remembers a list of unrelated words over repeated trials. The examiner reads 15 common nouns (List A) and the person recalls as many as possible, five times in a row; this produces a learning curve . Then an interference list (List B) is read once and recalled, after which the person tries List A again without hearing it (sensitive to interference and forgetting). After a 20 to 30 minute delay there is another free recall and usually a recognition trial. Patterns are informative: poor learning with poor recognition suggests a storage (hippocampal) problem, while poor free recall with good recognition suggests a retrieval (frontal-subcortical) problem. CVLT: California Verbal Learning Test The CVLT is a list-learning test built on the process approach. Its list looks like a shopping list: 16 words from 4 semantic categories (for example fruits, tools, clothing, spices), presented in mixed order. The examiner can therefore see whether the person spontaneously groups words by category ( semantic clustering , an active, frontal-dependent strategy) or just recalls them in the order heard ( serial clustering , a more passive strategy). It also measures cued recall (giving the category name), recognition, intrusions and repetitions, so it gives a detailed picture of why memory fails. ROCF: Rey-Osterrieth Complex Figure Test The person first copies a complex, abstract line drawing (a large rectangle with diagonals, a cross, triangles, circles and other details), then draws it from memory, without warning, after a short delay and again after about 30 minutes. The copy shows visuoconstructional ability and planning or organisation (does the person start with the big rectangle and fit details in, or build the figure piece by piece?), while the recall trials measure visual memory. Because it is hard to verbalise, it is often treated as a test of right hemisphere (non-verbal) memory, and the organisation of the copy is sensitive to executive dysfunction. Rey created it (1941), Osterrieth standardised it (1944). It tests both copy (construction, planning) and memory ; a poor copy makes poor recall uninterpretable as a pure memory deficit. WCST: Wisconsin Card Sorting Test The WCST is the classic test of set shifting and abstract reasoning. Four stimulus cards are placed in front of the person (one red triangle, two green stars, three yellow crosses, four blue circles), and the person must match each response card to one of them. The examiner does not say what the rule is, only "right" or "wrong" after each card. The hidden rule is colour first, then form, then number, and after 10 consecutive correct matches the examiner silently changes the rule. A healthy person notices the "wrong" feedback and shifts; a patient with dorsolateral prefrontal dysfunction tends to keep sorting by the old rule ( perseveration ). Brenda Milner (1963) showed this deficit in patients with frontal lobe excisions, which made the WCST the iconic "frontal lobe" test, although damage elsewhere can also impair it. TMT: Trail Making Test The Trail Making Test is a paper-and-pencil task in which the person draws lines to connect circles in order as fast as possible. Part A uses numbers only (1 to 25), so it mainly measures visual scanning, attention and psychomotor speed. Part B alternates numbers and letters (1, A, 2, B, 3, C and so on), so the person must keep two sequences in mind and switch between them, which adds working memory and set shifting (an executive demand). Errors are pointed out immediately and the time keeps running, so the score is completion time in seconds. Comparing B with A (B minus A, or B/A ratio) removes the effect of simple speed and isolates the switching cost. Stroop: Stroop Colour and Word Test In the Stroop effect, people are slower and make more errors when naming the ink colour of a colour word printed in a conflicting colour (the word RED printed in blue ink; correct answer "blue"). Reading is so automatic that the word meaning intrudes, and the person must actively suppress it, so the test measures response inhibition and selective attention (interference control). Clinical versions have a word-reading page, a colour-naming page and the incongruent colour-word page; the interference score shows how much slower the person is on the conflict condition than expected from their basic speed. The anterior cingulate and lateral prefrontal cortex are the brain regions most associated with the task. TOL: Tower of London The Tower of London is a planning task: the person must rearrange coloured balls on pegs to match a goal picture in the minimum number of moves, thinking the moves through before acting. The standard apparatus has three pegs of unequal length that hold 1, 2 and 3 balls respectively, and three balls (red, green, blue). Problems need from 2 to 5 moves, and the harder ones require the person to make a move that seems to go away from the goal (a subgoal), which is what taxes planning. Tim Shallice designed it to study patients with frontal lobe lesions, who make more moves, break rules and plan less before starting. Tower of Hanoi : equal pegs, discs of graded sizes , a bigger disc may never go on a smaller one. Both measure planning, but the Tower of Hanoi is also used to show preserved procedural learning in amnesia . TOH: Tower of Hanoi The Tower of Hanoi is a mathematical puzzle turned into a neuropsychological test. Discs of decreasing size are stacked on the first of three equal pegs, and the person must move the whole stack to another peg, moving one disc at a time and never placing a larger disc on a smaller one. The minimum number of moves for n discs is 2 n minus 1 (7 moves for 3 discs, 15 for 4). It measures planning and problem solving, and because amnesic patients improve across sessions without remembering having done it, it is also a classic demonstration of intact procedural (implicit) memory. The Tower of Hanoi is a puzzle (Lucas, 1883) , not a test authored by Shallice. Amnesic patients (e.g. H.M.-type cases) learn it without conscious recollection: procedural memory spared . COWA / FAS: Controlled Oral Word Association (verbal fluency) Verbal fluency tests ask the person to say as many words as possible in 60 seconds that begin with a given letter ( phonemic or letter fluency , e.g. F, A, S), excluding proper nouns, numbers and the same word with different endings, or that belong to a category ( semantic or category fluency , e.g. animals). Letter fluency demands a strategic, self-generated search and is especially sensitive to left frontal damage; category fluency leans more on the semantic store in the temporal lobes and drops early in Alzheimer's disease. The score is the number of correct words, and perseverations and rule breaks are noted.
