COWA belongs to Benton (Multilingual Aphasia Examination), not to the Boston group. Digit Span The examiner reads strings of digits at a rate of one per second, and the person repeats them; the strings grow by one digit until the person fails both trials of a length. In Digits Forward the person repeats in the same order (simple auditory attention and short-term span; normal adult span about 7, plus or minus 2, after George Miller, 1956). In Digits Backward the person reverses the order, which requires holding and manipulating information (working memory; normal adult span about 5). WAIS-IV added Digit Span Sequencing (repeat in ascending numerical order). It appears in the WAIS, WISC, original WMS, PGI Memory Scale and many screening tools. Digit span is typically preserved in pure amnesia (short-term store intact) even when long-term memory is severely impaired. BNT: Boston Naming Test The Boston Naming Test is a confrontation naming test: the person sees black-and-white line drawings, from very common objects (bed, tree) to rare ones (abacus, trellis), and must name each one. If the person misperceives the picture, a semantic (stimulus) cue is given; if they still cannot name it, a phonemic cue (the first sound) is given. Naming difficulty (anomia) is present in almost all aphasias and in Alzheimer's disease, and whether the phonemic cue helps can separate retrieval failure from loss of the word's meaning. It is a naming test, not a comprehension test (comprehension = Token Test). Token Test The Token Test measures auditory comprehension of spoken commands that grow in length and grammatical complexity, using plastic tokens that differ in shape (circles and squares), colour (five colours) and size (large and small). Commands range from "Touch the red circle" to "Put the red circle on the green square" and "Before touching the yellow circle, pick up the red square". Because the vocabulary is tiny and concrete, failure reflects difficulty processing language structure and verbal working memory, not vocabulary, so it is very sensitive to mild receptive language problems in aphasia. BDAE and WAB: Boston Diagnostic Aphasia Examination and Western Aphasia Battery These are comprehensive aphasia batteries used by speech-language pathologists and neuropsychologists to describe a patient's language profile and classify the aphasia syndrome. Both assess spontaneous speech (fluency, grammar, paraphasias), auditory comprehension, repetition, naming, reading and writing. The combination of fluency, comprehension and repetition maps onto classic syndromes: Broca's (non-fluent, comprehension relatively spared, repetition poor), Wernicke's (fluent, comprehension poor, repetition poor), conduction (fluent, comprehension good, repetition poor), transcortical types (repetition preserved), global and anomic aphasia. The WAB produces the Aphasia Quotient ; the BDAE has a 0 to 5 severity rating . Repetition is the feature that separates transcortical aphasias (preserved) from Broca's, Wernicke's and conduction aphasias (impaired). MMSE: Mini-Mental State Examination The MMSE is a 5 to 10 minute bedside screening test of global cognition, the most widely used cognitive screen in the world. It covers orientation, registration and recall of three words, attention (serial sevens or spelling WORLD backwards), naming, repetition, a three-stage command, reading, writing a sentence and copying intersecting pentagons. It was designed to be quick and to cover "only the cognitive aspects of mental functions", hence "mini". It is strongly affected by education and language and has a ceiling effect, so it misses mild cognitive impairment and is insensitive to executive deficits. It has no clock drawing (that is MoCA) and only one visuospatial item ( intersecting pentagons ). It is less sensitive to MCI than the MoCA. HMSE = Ganguli 1995 , for illiterate rural Indians. MoCA: Montreal Cognitive Assessment The MoCA is a 10-minute, one-page, 30-point screening test designed specifically to detect mild cognitive impairment (MCI) , which the MMSE often misses. It adds harder memory demands (5 words, delayed recall) and executive and visuospatial tasks (a mini trail-making task, cube copy, clock drawing, verbal fluency, abstraction). In the original validation, the MoCA detected about 90% of MCI cases compared with about 18% for the MMSE at standard cut-offs. ACE-III: Addenbrooke's Cognitive Examination The ACE is a longer (about 15 to 20 minutes) cognitive screen from Addenbrooke's Hospital, Cambridge, developed to detect dementia and to help separate Alzheimer's disease from frontotemporal dementia. It gives a 100-point total plus five domain scores, so the profile matters as well as the total (for example, low fluency and language relative to memory suggests frontotemporal dementia). The original ACE and ACE-R contained the MMSE items, so an MMSE score could be extracted; ACE-III replaced them because of MMSE copyright. CDT: Clock Drawing Test The person is asked to draw a clock face with all the numbers and set the hands to a specified time, classically "ten past eleven" (which forces the person to inhibit the pull of the "10" towards the number 10 and place the minute hand at 2). Drawing a clock requires comprehension, planning, visuospatial organisation, number knowledge, abstract representation of time and inhibition, so it is a fast, education-light screen for both visuospatial and executive dysfunction. Hemineglect shows as numbers crowded on one side. It is used alone, inside MoCA, and in the Mini-Cog (Soo Borson and colleagues, 2000: 3-word recall plus clock). GCS: Glasgow Coma Scale The Glasgow Coma Scale is a quick bedside rating of level of consciousness, used in head injury and any acute brain insult. The clinician scores the best response in three areas: eye opening, verbal response and motor response, and adds them. It is not a cognitive test but appears in neuropsychology because severity of traumatic brain injury (TBI), and therefore expected cognitive outcome, is classified using the GCS together with duration of post-traumatic amnesia. CDR: Clinical Dementia Rating The CDR is a clinician-rated staging scale for dementia severity, based on a semi-structured interview with the patient and an informant. The clinician rates six domains of cognitive and functional performance, each on a 5-point scale. A global CDR is derived by an algorithm that gives memory the primary weight, and the CDR Sum of Boxes (adding the six domain scores) gives a finer-grained measure used in research and trials. For GCS think " 4 eyes, 5 words (jive), 6 moves ": E4 V5 M6. 8. Clinical rating scales and symptom inventories A rating scale gives a number to how much of a symptom a person has. A diagnostic interview answers a yes/no question (does this person meet criteria for disorder X?). A rating scale answers "how much?" (how severe is the depression today, and has it come down since last month?). This is why rating scales are the workhorses of drug trials, outcome monitoring and audit, while diagnosis rests on interviews and clinical judgement. Most of the scales below were built in a burst between about 1959 and 1990, when psychopharmacology needed a way to show that a drug reduced symptoms more than a placebo did. The first split to learn is who does the rating . In a clinician-rated (observer-rated) scale, a trained interviewer asks questions, observes the patient and assigns the score: HAM-D, HAM-A, MADRS, BPRS, PANSS, SANS, SAPS, YMRS, Y-BOCS, CARS, ISAA, CIWA-Ar and CGI all work this way. In a self-report inventory, the person reads the items and marks the answers: BDI, BAI, PHQ-9, GAD-7, Zung SDS, GHQ, SCL-90-R, AUDIT and EPDS. Clinician ratings can capture things the patient cannot report (blunted affect, poverty of speech, lack of insight) and work with patients who cannot read; self-reports are cheap, fast and capture inner states (guilt, hopelessness) without interviewer bias, but depend on literacy, honesty and insight. A third group is informant-rated (parent or teacher): CBCL, Conners scales, M-CHAT-R/F, and the ADI-R interview of a parent. The second split is purpose . A screening tool is short and sensitive, meant to pick out possible cases in a population (GHQ-12, PHQ-9, GAD-7, AUDIT, CAGE, M-CHAT-R/F, EPDS): a positive screen means "assess further", never "diagnosis made". A severity or outcome measure tracks how bad symptoms are and how they change with treatment (HAM-D, MADRS, PANSS, Y-BOCS, YMRS, CIWA-Ar, CGI). A diagnostic instrument maps symptoms onto criteria (SCID, MINI, ADOS-2 together with ADI-R; see section 9). A disability measure rates functioning rather than symptoms (IDEAS, WHODAS 2.0, GAF, DAQ). Examiners love asking "which of these is a screening instrument?" and "which is clinician-rated?", so file every scale on both axes. Definition Anchor points are the written descriptions attached to each score on an item (for example, on HAM-D item 1, "0 = absent ... 4 = patient reports virtually only these feeling states in spontaneous verbal and non-verbal communication"). Well-defined anchors are what make two raters agree (inter-rater reliability). Sensitivity to change is the ability of a scale to move when the patient improves; MADRS was built specifically to be more sensitive to change than HAM-D. 8.1 Psychosis and schizophrenia BPRS: Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale The BPRS is the grandparent of modern psychosis ratings. John Overall and Donald Gorham (1962) wanted a short scale that could quickly measure change in hospitalised patients on the new antipsychotic drugs. After a semi-structured interview of about 20 minutes, the clinician rates each symptom on a 7-point severity scale. Some items are rated from what the patient says (anxiety, guilt), others from observation (blunted affect, motor retardation, mannerisms). It covers positive symptoms, negative symptoms, mood and anxiety, so it is a broad "general psychopathology" measure rather than a schizophrenia-only scale. Structured diagnostic interviews and the mental status examination In the 1960s and 1970s studies such as the US-UK Diagnostic Project (1972) showed that psychiatrists in New York and London gave different diagnoses to the same patients, mostly because they asked different questions and used different definitions ( information variance and criterion variance ). Two fixes followed. Operational criteria (Feighner criteria 1972, Research Diagnostic Criteria 1978, then DSM-III 1980) fixed the definitions. Structured interviews fixed the questions, so that every patient is asked the same things in the same order, and the answers are scored against the criteria. Interviews sit on a continuum. A fully structured interview (DIS, CIDI, DISC) has fixed wording and fixed coding, so it can be given by trained lay interviewers in large epidemiological surveys, but it cannot use clinical judgement. A semi-structured interview (SCID, SCAN, K-SADS, IPDE) gives required questions but lets the clinician probe, rephrase and judge whether a symptom is really present, so it needs clinically trained interviewers. A brief structured interview (MINI) trades depth for speed. The mental status examination , at the end of this section, is not a test at all: it is the clinician's systematic, here-and-now observation of the patient, and every clinical psychology viva expects you to know its headings cold. SCID-5: Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-5 The SCID is a semi-structured interview, administered by a clinician, that walks through the DSM criteria module by module (mood episodes, psychotic symptoms, substance use, anxiety, OCD, trauma, and so on), with suggested questions on the left and the DSM criterion beside them. The interviewer rates each criterion as absent, subthreshold or present, using judgement. The SCID-5 comes in several versions for different purposes, which is a favourite exam question. History tells you what has happened over months and years; the MSE records what the clinician observes and elicits now, during the interview . It is cross-sectional (one point in time), and it is written descriptively, in the patient's own words where possible, rather than with labels alone ("he said, 'my neighbours are poisoning my food'" is better than "persecutory delusions" by itself). Indian teaching (following Fish's Clinical Psychopathology and Indian textbooks such as Niraj Ahuja's) usually uses the order below. Learn the headings, then what goes under each. Memory hook " A ll P atients R eally S hould M ake T heir P sychiatrist C arefully I nquire": Appearance and behaviour, Psychomotor activity, Rapport, Speech, Mood and affect, Thought, Perception, Cognition, Insight (with judgement under cognition). 1. General appearance and behaviour What a stranger would notice: apparent age versus stated age, build, grooming and hygiene, dress (appropriate to weather and setting, or bizarre, or provocative), facial expression, eye contact, posture, gait, any physical abnormalities, tics, tremors or mannerisms. Behaviour includes attitude towards the examiner (cooperative, guarded, hostile, seductive, evasive, apathetic) and any abnormal behaviour during the interview (hallucinatory behaviour such as muttering or looking at empty corners, social withdrawal, disinhibition). Examples: unkempt and dishevelled in severe depression, schizophrenia or dementia; flamboyant, colourful, over-decorated in mania. 2. Psychomotor activity The amount and speed of movement. Increased : restlessness, pacing, hand-wringing (agitation, typical of agitated depression or anxiety), overactivity (mania), akathisia (drug-induced restlessness). Decreased : psychomotor retardation (slow movements, long pauses; depression), stupor (no movement or speech despite clear consciousness). Catatonic signs belong here: waxy flexibility (limbs stay where the examiner places them), posturing , negativism , echopraxia (copying movements), automatic obedience , mannerisms (purposeful-looking but odd movements) and stereotypies (repetitive, non-goal-directed movements). 3. Rapport Whether a working emotional connection can be established: "rapport established with ease", "established with difficulty", or "could not be established". Rapport is often hard with paranoid, negativistic or severely withdrawn patients; a strikingly "glass wall" or "praecox feeling" (the examiner's sense of being unable to reach the patient, described in schizophrenia by H. C. Rümke, 1941) was classically noted. Eye contact (maintained, avoided, staring) is usually recorded here or under appearance. 4. Speech Speech is described as an act, separately from the thought it carries. Record: rate (rapid, slow), volume (loud, soft), tone and prosody (monotonous or modulated), quantity (talkative, or poverty of speech with brief answers), reaction time (latency before answering, prolonged in depression), spontaneity (speaks spontaneously or only in reply), pressure (rapid, hard to interrupt: mania), relevance and coherence (answers to the point or not; understandable or not), and abnormalities such as stuttering, dysarthria (articulation problem, often neurological), aphasia, mutism, neologisms, echolalia (repeating the examiner's words) and clang associations (words linked by sound). 5. Mood and affect This is the most tested distinction in the MSE. Mood is the patient's pervasive and sustained emotional state, reported by the patient (subjective): "How have you been feeling in your spirits?" "Low, doctor, very low." It is recorded in the patient's own words, often alongside the clinician's description (Indian case formats write "subjective" and "objective" mood). Affect is the observable, moment-to-moment expression of emotion, seen by the examiner in face, voice and gesture. The classic analogy: mood is the climate , affect is the weather . Affect is described along several dimensions: Quality : what emotion is shown (sad, anxious, irritable, euphoric, perplexed). Range : how many different emotions are shown during the interview. Full (normal), restricted or constricted (reduced range), blunted (severe reduction in intensity), flat (virtually no expression). Reactivity : whether affect shifts appropriately with the topic or with the examiner's humour (reduced in melancholic depression). Appropriateness (congruence): whether affect matches the content of thought. Inappropriate or incongruent affect, for example laughing while describing a parent's death, is classically seen in schizophrenia. A second, separate question is whether mood is congruent with the delusions (mood-congruent versus mood-incongruent psychotic features). Stability : stable versus labile (rapid, unprovoked shifts, as in mania, organic states, pseudobulbar affect). Intensity and communicability (whether the examiner can empathise with it). Definition Other mood terms: euthymia (normal mood), dysphoria (unpleasant mood), euphoria (exaggerated well-being), elation (euphoria with increased motor activity), exaltation (intense elation with grandiosity), ecstasy (intense rapture), alexithymia (difficulty identifying and describing one's emotions, Peter Sifneos 1973), anhedonia (loss of pleasure). 6. Thought Indian MSE formats divide thought into four parts: Stream (tempo and continuity) : how fast and how smoothly thoughts flow. Flight of ideas (rapid thoughts with abrupt shifts, but connections understandable: mania), pressure of thought , retardation or slowing (depression), thought block (sudden stopping of thought mid-sentence, the patient cannot explain why: schizophrenia), perseveration (persistent repetition of the same response; organic conditions), circumstantiality (delay in reaching the goal through excessive irrelevant detail, but the goal is reached) and tangentiality (the goal is never reached) are sometimes placed here and sometimes under form. Form : the organisation and logical connection of thoughts, i.e. formal thought disorder. Loosening of associations (Eugen Bleuler, 1911: ideas shift between unrelated topics), derailment , knight's move thinking , word salad (incoherent mixture of words), neologisms (new words), overinclusion (Norman Cameron, 1938: inability to keep conceptual boundaries), concrete thinking , illogicality , and Schneider's descriptions (derailment, substitution, omission, fusion, drivelling). Content : what the patient thinks about. Delusions (fixed, false, unshakeable beliefs out of keeping with sociocultural background: persecutory, reference, grandiose, guilt, nihilistic, jealousy, erotomanic, somatic, infidelity), overvalued ideas (Carl Wernicke, 1900: strongly held but understandable beliefs that dominate life, e.g. in anorexia), obsessions , preoccupations , phobias , hypochondriacal ideas , and always suicidal and homicidal ideation , which must be asked about directly. Possession : whether the patient experiences thoughts as their own. In obsessions , thoughts are recognised as one's own though unwanted (ego-dystonic). In passivity of thought , a Schneiderian first-rank symptom, ownership is lost: thought insertion (thoughts put in by an outside agency), thought withdrawal (thoughts taken out), thought broadcasting (thoughts spread so others know them). 7. Perception Abnormal perceptual experiences, with the modality always specified. Hallucinations are perceptions without an external stimulus, experienced as real and in external space: auditory (most common in schizophrenia; second-person commenting/commanding, or third-person voices discussing the patient, a first-rank symptom, and audible thoughts, Gedankenlautwerden), visual (common in organic and delirious states), olfactory and gustatory (temporal lobe lesions, also depression), tactile (formication in cocaine and alcohol withdrawal), somatic and kinaesthetic. Illusions are misperceptions of a real stimulus. Pseudohallucinations are perceived in inner subjective space and recognised as not real (definitions differ between Karl Jaspers' and later usage). Hypnagogic (falling asleep) and hypnopompic (waking) hallucinations can be normal. Also record depersonalisation (feeling oneself unreal or detached) and derealisation (the surroundings feel unreal). 8. Cognitive functions (higher mental functions) Cognition is tested by direct bedside tasks. Formal tests such as the MMSE (Folstein, Folstein and McHugh, 1975) or the Hindi Mental State Examination (HMSE, Ganguli et al., 1995) can supplement it. Consciousness : alert, drowsy, clouded, stuporose or comatose (often recorded first). Orientation : to time (day, date, month, year, time of day), place and person . Orientation to time is lost first in organic states and orientation to person last; disorientation strongly suggests an organic condition such as delirium or dementia. Attention and concentration : attention is the ability to focus on a task; concentration is the ability to sustain that focus. Tests: serial 7s (subtract 7 from 100 repeatedly: 93, 86, 79, 72, 65; record errors and time taken), serial 3s from 20 if 7s are too hard, months of the year or days of the week backwards, and digit span (forward digit span of about 7 plus or minus 2 in normal adults; backward span is usually one or two fewer, with sources giving slightly different normal values). Digit span is strictly a test of attention and immediate registration rather than memory. Memory : immediate (registration and recall within seconds, e.g. repeating digits or three words straight away), recent (events of the past hours or days: what did you eat this morning, how did you come here; plus recall of the three words after about 5 minutes, which tests recent memory/new learning), recent past (past few months: news events) and remote (years ago: date of marriage, schooling, verified with relatives). Remote memory is typically preserved longest in dementia (Ribot's law, Théodule Ribot, 1881: recent memories are lost before older ones). General information and intelligence : fund of knowledge appropriate to education and culture (name of the Prime Minister, capital cities, recent major events), simple arithmetic, and a clinical estimate of whether intelligence is average, above or below. The questions must be adjusted for the patient's education and background. Abstraction (abstract thinking) : the ability to move from concrete instances to general concepts. Proverb interpretation ("What does 'a rolling stone gathers no moss' mean?") and similarities ("How are an apple and a banana alike?" Abstract answer: both are fruits; concrete answer: both are round, or "you can eat them"). Concrete thinking appears in schizophrenia, organic disorders and intellectual disability; proverb responses are strongly influenced by culture and education, so interpret with caution. Judgement : the ability to assess a situation and act appropriately. Personal judgement (realistic plans for one's own future, e.g. what will you do after discharge), social judgement (behaviour in social situations, observed during the interview and from history) and test judgement (responses to hypothetical situations: "What would you do if you found a stamped, addressed envelope on the road?" or "if you saw a fire in a cinema hall?"). 9. Insight Insight is the patient's awareness and understanding of their own illness: whether they recognise that they are ill, that the illness is psychological, and that they need treatment. A widely taught six-point grading appears in Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry and is reproduced in many Indian textbooks and case formats. It is a textbook teaching convention rather than a validated scale, and wording varies slightly between editions and sources: Complete denial of illness. Slight awareness of being sick and needing help, but denying it at the same time. Awareness of being sick but blaming it on others, on external factors or on organic (physical) factors. Awareness that illness is caused by something unknown in oneself. Intellectual insight : admission that one is ill and that symptoms or failures in adjustment are due to one's own irrational feelings or disturbances, but without applying this knowledge to future experiences. True emotional insight : emotional awareness of one's own motives and feelings and those of important people in one's life, which can lead to basic changes in behaviour. Structured measures of insight also exist, for example the Schedule for Assessment of Insight (Anthony David, 1990), which rates three components: recognition of illness, relabelling of unusual experiences as pathological, and treatment adherence; and the Scale to Assess Unawareness of Mental Disorder (SUMD; Xavier Amador et al., 1993). Exam trap Intellectual insight is grade 5, not the highest : the patient "knows" but does not change behaviour. Only true emotional insight (grade 6) produces change. Grade 3 (aware but blames external or organic causes) is a common choice for patients with somatisation or alcohol use. If a question cites the six grades, it is following Kaplan and Sadock; do not attribute the grading to Karl Jaspers or Fish. 9.2 MSE summary and traps MSE heading What is recorded Key examples / tests Appearance and behaviour Grooming, dress, attitude, eye contact, abnormal behaviour Unkempt in depression; colourful dress in mania; hallucinatory behaviour Psychomotor activity Amount and speed of movement Agitation, retardation, catatonic signs (waxy flexibility, posturing) Rapport Ease of establishing contact Difficult in paranoid, withdrawn patients Speech Rate, volume, tone, quantity, reaction time, coherence Pressure of speech (mania), poverty of speech, mutism Mood Subjective, sustained emotional state Recorded in patient's own words Affect Observed, moment-to-moment expression Range, reactivity, appropriateness, stability (labile), intensity Thought Stream, form, content, possession Flight of ideas, thought block, loosening, delusions, thought insertion Perception Hallucinations, illusions, depersonalisation Third-person auditory hallucinations (first-rank) Cognition Consciousness, orientation, attention, memory, information, abstraction, judgement Serial 7s, digit span, 3-word recall, proverbs, similarities, envelope test Insight Awareness of illness and need for treatment Six grades (Kaplan and Sadock convention) Exam trap Mood is subjective and sustained; affect is objective and momentary. "Patient says he feels fine but looks tearful" = euthymic reported mood with a sad (incongruent) affect. Blunted and flat affect describe range and intensity ; inappropriate affect describes congruence ; labile affect describes stability . Thought block is a disorder of stream , thought insertion a disorder of possession , a delusion a disorder of content , loosening of associations a disorder of form . Serial 7s test attention and concentration , not memory; proverbs and similarities test abstraction ; the envelope question tests test judgement . High yield Section 8 and 9 quick recall: HAM-D is clinician-rated, BDI is self-report. PANSS 30, BPRS 18, Y-BOCS 10 core, YMRS 11, CARS 15 with cut-off 30, ISAA 40 with cut-off 70. GHQ-12 is the screening default. SCL-90-R has 9 dimensions and 3 global indices. GAF was removed in DSM-5 in favour of WHODAS 2.0. Fully structured lay interviews: DIS, CIDI, DISC. title: Requested Topics
text: Requested Topics Five topics you asked for by name, each written to be learned cold from this page alone: the diathesis-stress model and its descendants, Eugen Bleuler's four A's and how the idea of schizophrenia was built, the theory of planned behaviour, every kind of brain scan an examiner can ask about, and the nine concepts you asked about after the NIMHANS paper on 31 May (dissociation, desensitization, habit reversal, flashbulb memory, paradoxical intention, ICD-11 gender incongruence, the gunas, dharana and Kegels). Theorists and years sit inside the explanations where they belong, the exam traps are flagged as you go, and each chapter closes with a self-check written the way the entrance papers write their questions. In this book The diathesis-stress model Bleuler's four A's and the history of the schizophrenia concept The theory of planned behaviour Types of brain scanning and imaging tests NIMHANS 31 May: the nine you asked about (Qs 36-41, gunas, dharana, Kegels) 1. The diathesis-stress model Why do two people who go through the same divorce, the same job loss or the same childhood poverty end up so differently, one with a major depressive episode and the other with a bad few months? And why do identical twins, who share all their genes, so often differ on whether they develop schizophrenia? The diathesis-stress model is psychology's oldest and most widely used answer to both questions. It is less a single theory than a template for explaining how a disorder comes about, and almost every modern theory of depression, anxiety and psychosis is built on it. Definition A diathesis is a predisposition or vulnerability to a disorder that a person carries before the disorder appears. The word comes from the Greek diathesis , meaning "disposition" or "arrangement" (from diatithenai , to arrange or dispose), and was used in older medicine for a constitutional tendency to a disease (for example the "gouty diathesis"). The diathesis-stress model states that a disorder develops when a diathesis is combined with sufficient stress (an adverse environmental event or condition), and that neither the diathesis alone nor the stress alone is usually sufficient. 1.1 The core idea, built from scratch Think of three ingredients: The diathesis : something relatively enduring that the person brings to the situation. It can be biological (genes, neurodevelopmental damage, a reactive stress hormone system), psychological (a negative thinking style, dysfunctional schemas, a personality trait such as neuroticism) or social and developmental (early loss, insecure attachment). It is usually latent : you cannot see it in daily behaviour until something activates it. The stress : an environmental challenge, usually after the diathesis is in place. Classic examples are negative life events (bereavement, failure, migration), chronic strain (poverty, caregiving, a hostile family) and biological insults (cannabis use, infection, sleep loss). The interaction : the outcome depends on the combination . A high-diathesis person may break down after a modest stressor; a low-diathesis person may need an extreme stressor, or may never break down at all. The statistical word for this is interaction : the effect of stress on outcome is not the same for everyone, it depends on (is "moderated by") the level of diathesis. In plain words, stress hurts the vulnerable much more than the non-vulnerable. This is why the model is often written as vulnerability x stress rather than vulnerability + stress. Exam trap The diathesis is the predisposition , never the stressor. If an option says "diathesis refers to the precipitating life event", it is wrong. The stressor is the precipitant (trigger); the diathesis is the predisposing factor. In the familiar "4 P" case formulation, diathesis maps onto predisposing factors and stress onto precipitating (and sometimes perpetuating) factors. 1.2 History: from Meehl to Zubin and Spring Paul E. Meehl (1962): schizotaxia, schizotypy, schizophrenia The modern model is usually traced to Paul E. Meehl (1962) , whose presidential address to the American Psychological Association was published in the American Psychologist as "Schizotaxia, schizotypy, schizophrenia". Meehl proposed a chain of three levels: Schizogene : Meehl hypothesised a single dominant gene (the "schizogene") as the inherited starting point. This specific single-gene claim has not been supported; schizophrenia is now understood as highly polygenic. Schizotaxia : the gene produces a subtle neural integrative defect , a fault in how the nervous system integrates information (Meehl spoke of a defect he called "hypokrisia" at the level of neuronal functioning). Schizotaxia is purely the inherited neurological vulnerability. Schizotypy : almost any schizotaxic person, growing up in any ordinary social learning environment, develops a characteristic personality organisation called schizotypy: cognitive slippage (mild thought disorder), anhedonia, interpersonal aversiveness and ambivalence. Schizotypy is learned on top of schizotaxia. Schizophrenia : only a minority of schizotypes decompensate into clinical schizophrenia, and this happens when they meet adverse environmental conditions (Meehl, writing in 1962, gave the much-criticised example of a "schizophrenogenic" mother). Most schizotypes remain compensated for life. In his later reformulation (Meehl, 1990) he gave rough figures, often quoted as about 10 percent of the population being schizotypal in his sense and about 10 percent of those developing clinical schizophrenia. Treat these as Meehl's speculative estimates, not epidemiological facts. Exam trap Schizotaxia = inherited neural integrative defect (biology). Schizotypy = the personality organisation that develops from it through social learning (psychology). Schizotypal personality disorder = a DSM diagnostic category (DSM-III, 1980, onward), partly inspired by the schizotypy concept and by the Danish adoption studies of relatives of people with schizophrenia, but not the same thing as Paul Meehl's schizotypy. Also note: in ICD-10 schizotypal disorder sits in the schizophrenia chapter (F21), whereas DSM places schizotypal personality disorder among personality disorders and also lists it in the schizophrenia spectrum chapter. David Rosenthal (1970): popularising the term The exact phrase "diathesis-stress" is often credited to David Rosenthal (1970) , in his book Genetic Theory and Abnormal Behavior , which used it to summarise the genetic and environmental evidence on schizophrenia, including the Danish adoption studies he ran with Seymour Kety and others. Who used the phrase first is uncertain; sources differ, so the safe statement is that Rosenthal popularised it. Joseph Zubin and Bonnie Spring (1977): the vulnerability-stress model Joseph Zubin and Bonnie Spring (1977) , in "Vulnerability: a new view of schizophrenia" ( Journal of Abnormal Psychology ), restated the idea in a form that is still the standard textbook diagram. Their key claims: Vulnerability is the enduring trait ; schizophrenia itself is not permanent. What a person carries for life is the vulnerability, not the illness. Episodes are time-limited . An episode occurs when stress pushes the person above their personal vulnerability threshold ; when the stress subsides the person tends to return to their premorbid level. This was a deliberate challenge to the Kraepelinian assumption of inevitable deterioration. Inborn vs acquired vulnerability . Inborn vulnerability lies in the genes and internal environment (neurophysiology). Acquired vulnerability comes from traumas, specific diseases, perinatal complications, family experiences, adolescent peer interactions and other life events. Moderators . Whether stress tips someone over also depends on their social network, ecological niche and premorbid personality. Graphically, Zubin and Spring plotted vulnerability against challenging events: a curved threshold line divides a "well" zone from an "episode" zone. A highly vulnerable person crosses the line with little stress; a person with low vulnerability needs a great deal. Memory hook Zubin and Spring = 1977 , the same year as George Engel's biopsychosocial model (1977) and one year before Kety. Remember "seven-seven: vulnerability and biopsychosocial were born together". But they are different ideas: Engel's model is a general philosophy of medicine (biology, psychology and social context all matter for every illness); the diathesis-stress model is a specific causal claim that a pre-existing vulnerability interacts with later stress. 1.3 Refinements: what form does the interaction take? Scott Monroe and Anne Simons (1991) Scott M. Monroe and Anne D. Simons (1991) , "Diathesis-stress theories in the context of life stress research: implications for the depressive disorders" ( Psychological Bulletin ), is the classic critical review. Their main points: Most theories had been vague about how diathesis and stress combine. Researchers needed to specify the form of the relationship rather than just say "both matter". Stress must be measured carefully . Self-report checklists confound the stressor with the person's reaction to it. They favoured interview-based, contextual ratings of life events (in the tradition of George Brown and Tirril Harris's Life Events and Difficulties Schedule) and the distinction between independent events (outside the person's control, such as an earthquake) and dependent events (partly produced by the person, such as a breakup after repeated arguments). Diathesis and stress are not always independent . The diathesis may shape which stressors the person meets, and stress may change the diathesis over time (a dynamic rather than fixed diathesis). Forms of the model (Ingram and Luxton, 2005) Rick Ingram and David Luxton (2005), in a widely cited chapter on vulnerability-stress models, organised the possible forms. The terms below are the ones exam setters lift: Form What it claims Dichotomous diathesis The diathesis is either present or absent (as in Paul Meehl's single gene). Without it, no amount of stress produces the disorder. Quasi-continuous diathesis The diathesis varies in degree (as with polygenic risk or a graded cognitive style). The more diathesis, the less stress needed. Ipsative (additive) model Diathesis and stress are inversely related: they add up, and disorder appears once the sum crosses a threshold. A very strong diathesis may need almost no stress, and an extreme stressor may produce disorder even in someone with little diathesis. Zubin and Spring's diagram is of this kind. Threshold (interactive) model Stress has an effect only once the diathesis (or stress) passes a certain level; below it, stress makes little difference. The exact labels vary between textbooks, so in an MCQ go by the description rather than the label alone. Stress generation (Constance Hammen, 1991) Constance Hammen (1991) , studying women with depression, showed that depressed people experience more dependent stressful events (especially interpersonal conflicts) than controls, but not more independent ones. In other words, people with a depressive diathesis partly generate their own stress. This breaks the simple assumption that stress just "happens to" the vulnerable person and is a key reason Monroe and Simons called for a dynamic model. Kindling (Robert Post, 1992) Robert M. Post (1992) , in the American Journal of Psychiatry , borrowed the term "kindling" from epilepsy research. In mood disorders the first episodes are usually triggered by major life stress, but later episodes need less and less stress, and eventually may occur almost spontaneously. The diathesis itself is being changed (sensitised) by earlier episodes. Monroe and Kate Harkness (2005) later distinguished two readings: stress sensitisation (smaller stressors become enough) and stress autonomy (episodes occur without stress). Kindling is a related idea, not a version of the original diathesis-stress model: it describes a diathesis that grows over time. 1.4 Examples of diatheses Cognitive diatheses in depression Aaron T. Beck (cognitive theory, 1967 onward): early experience lays down dysfunctional schemas (for example "I am worthless unless I am loved"). They stay latent until a congruent stressor (a rejection) activates them, producing the negative cognitive triad (self, world, future). Beck (1983) added the personality diatheses sociotropy (dependence on relationships) and autonomy (dependence on achievement and independence), with the congruency hypothesis : sociotropic people are vulnerable to interpersonal loss, autonomous people to failure. Hopelessness theory , Lyn Abramson, Gerald Metalsky and Lauren Alloy (1989) , Psychological Review : the diathesis is a negative inferential style , a tendency to explain negative events with stable and global causes, to infer negative consequences, and to infer negative things about oneself. When such a person meets negative events, they are likely to become hopeless, and hopelessness is the proximal sufficient cause of a subtype, "hopelessness depression". This is an explicit diathesis-stress theory, and it revised the earlier learned helplessness reformulation (Abramson, Martin Seligman and Teasdale, 1978). A genetic example: Caspi et al. (2003) and what happened next Avshalom Caspi, Terrie Moffitt and colleagues (2003) , in Science , used the Dunedin (New Zealand) birth cohort and reported that people carrying one or two short alleles of the serotonin transporter promoter polymorphism ( 5-HTTLPR ) were more likely to become depressed after stressful life events than people with two long alleles. It became the textbook example of a gene x environment (G x E) interaction, that is, a molecular diathesis-stress effect. The story did not hold up well. Neil Risch and colleagues (2009) , a meta-analysis in JAMA , found no evidence that 5-HTTLPR moderated the stress-depression link (stress itself strongly predicted depression). A 2011 meta-analysis by Karg and colleagues, using broader inclusion, did report support, so the literature was contested for a while. Then Richard Border and colleagues (2019) , in the American Journal of Psychiatry , tested historical depression candidate genes, including 5-HTTLPR and its interaction with stress, in very large samples and found no support. The lesson for exams: Caspi et al. is the classic G x E example, but it is now regarded as a failed replication story, and polygenic approaches have replaced single candidate genes. Schizophrenia examples Copenhagen high-risk study : begun in 1962 by Sarnoff Mednick and Fini Schulsinger . Children of mothers with schizophrenia (high genetic risk) and matched controls were followed from childhood. Among the high-risk children, those who later developed schizophrenia were more likely to have had obstetric complications and disruptive early rearing (for example separation from the mother), a diathesis-stress pattern where acquired insults act on a genetic predisposition. Finnish Adoptive Family Study of Schizophrenia , led by Pekka Tienari : adopted-away children of mothers with schizophrenia spectrum disorders were compared with adoptees of mothers without them, and the adoptive families' functioning was rated independently. High genetic risk raised the rate of schizophrenia spectrum disorders mainly when the adoptive family was rated as disturbed (dysfunctional communication); in healthy adoptive families the high-risk adoptees did about as well as controls (Tienari et al., 2004, British Journal of Psychiatry ). This is one of the cleanest human demonstrations of genotype x rearing environment interaction. A cousin: Barlow's triple vulnerability theory David H. Barlow (2000, 2002) explained anxiety and related emotional disorders through three vulnerabilities: a generalised biological vulnerability (heritable negative affect, neuroticism), a generalised psychological vulnerability (an early sense that events are uncontrollable and unpredictable) and a specific psychological vulnerability (learning that particular objects or bodily sensations are dangerous, which explains why one person develops panic disorder and another social anxiety). Stress activates these vulnerabilities. It is a diathesis-stress model with the diathesis split into three layers. 1.5 Differential susceptibility: the challenge to diathesis-stress The diathesis-stress model assumes that "vulnerable" people only ever do worse: in a good environment they are at best equal to everyone else. Jay Belsky (1997) proposed, on evolutionary grounds, that some children are simply more plastic (more responsive to rearing) than others. Because parents cannot know which rearing strategy will pay off in an unpredictable future, natural selection would favour having some offspring who are highly shaped by the environment and others who are not. Belsky and Michael Pluess (2009) , in "Beyond diathesis stress: differential susceptibility to environmental influences" ( Psychological Bulletin ), reviewed evidence that the same traits once called vulnerabilities (difficult or negatively emotional infant temperament, certain dopamine and serotonin gene variants, high physiological reactivity) make people do worse in adverse environments but better in supportive ones. The slogan is "for better and for worse" , in contrast to diathesis-stress, which is only "for worse". Biological sensitivity to context : W. Thomas Boyce and Bruce J. Ellis (2005) , Development and Psychopathology , argued that high stress reactivity (autonomic and adrenocortical) reflects heightened sensitivity to context, both harmful and protective. They proposed a U-shaped relation: highly reactive children are over-represented in both very stressful and very protective early environments. Orchid vs dandelion children : a metaphor drawn from the Swedish expression maskrosbarn ("dandelion child", one who thrives anywhere). Dandelion children do reasonably well in almost any environment; orchid children wilt under neglect but flourish spectacularly with good care. Boyce popularised it in his book The Orchid and the Dandelion (2019). Vantage sensitivity : Pluess and Belsky (2013) , Psychological Bulletin , described the positive half on its own: some individuals benefit more than others from positive experiences and interventions (for example psychotherapy or school programmes). Vantage resistance is the failure to benefit. Diathesis-stress describes the negative pole, vantage sensitivity the positive pole, and differential susceptibility combines both. Seeing the difference: the crossover interaction Plot environment quality on the x axis (adverse on the left, supportive on the right) and outcome (well-being, higher is better) on the y axis. Draw one line for the "vulnerable" or "susceptible" group and one for the comparison group. A. Diathesis-stress B. Differential susceptibility Adverse Supportive Adverse Supportive Environment quality Environment quality Well-being Well-being gap only at adverse end lines cross Vulnerable / susceptible Non-vulnerable / less susceptible Panel A (diathesis-stress) : the lines fan out toward the adverse end and converge at the supportive end. In a good environment the vulnerable do as well as everyone else; the diathesis only shows under stress. This is an ordinal (non-crossing) interaction. Panel B (differential susceptibility) : the susceptible line is steeper and crosses the other line. Susceptible people do worst in bad environments and best in good ones. This is a disordinal (crossover) interaction. To claim differential susceptibility, researchers must show the crossover point lies within the realistic range of environments, and that the "better" side is real, not just noise (Glenn Roisman and colleagues, 2012, proposed formal statistical tests for this). Feature Diathesis-stress Differential susceptibility What the trait is A vulnerability (risk factor) A plasticity or sensitivity factor Effect in adverse environment Worse outcome Worse outcome Effect in supportive environment Same as others (no advantage) Better than others Shape of interaction Ordinal, fan-shaped Crossover Key names Paul Meehl 1962, Rosenthal 1970, Zubin and Spring 1977, Monroe and Simons 1991 Belsky 1997, Boyce and Ellis 2005, Belsky and Pluess 2009, Pluess and Belsky 2013 (vantage sensitivity) 1.6 Clinical implications Prevention : if the diathesis can be identified early (family history, high-risk mental states, a negative cognitive style), stress exposure can be reduced or coping strengthened before a first episode. Clinical high-risk (prodromal) services for psychosis rest on this logic. Relapse prevention : in schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, medication is understood as lowering biological vulnerability, while psychosocial work reduces stress. Relapse signature plans teach patients and families to spot early warning signs after a stressor. Stress management and coping : problem-solving training, sleep regularity, avoiding cannabis and other drugs, and building social support all aim at the stress side or at the moderators that Zubin and Spring listed. Cognitive therapy : Aaron Beck's therapy tries to modify the diathesis itself (the schemas) so that future stressors do less damage; mindfulness-based cognitive therapy targets the kindling-like reactivation of depressive thinking in recurrent depression. Family expressed emotion (EE) : George W. Brown, J. L. T. Birley and John Wing (1972) , building on Brown's earlier work in the 1950s and 1960s, showed that people with schizophrenia discharged to families high in criticism, hostility or emotional over-involvement relapsed more often. Christine Vaughn and Julian Leff (1976) replicated this using the Camberwell Family Interview and found the risk was greatest when high-EE contact was long (more than about 35 hours a week face to face) and medication was not taken. High EE is an environmental stressor acting on a biological vulnerability. Family psychoeducation and behavioural family therapy (for example Ian Falloon's work) lower EE and reduce relapse. Indian relevance: EE studies in north India (Chandigarh, by N. N. Wig, Leff and colleagues in the 1980s, linked to the WHO Determinants of Outcome study) found that high EE was less common in Indian families than in London samples, one proposed reason for the better course of schizophrenia observed in developing-country WHO centres. High yield Paul Meehl 1962 (schizotaxia, schizotypy, schizophrenia; schizogene). Rosenthal 1970 (popularised "diathesis-stress"). Zubin and Spring 1977 (vulnerability model; episodes time-limited; inborn vs acquired vulnerability). Monroe and Simons 1991 ( Psychological Bulletin review of diathesis-stress and life stress). Hammen 1991 (stress generation). Post 1992 (kindling). Abramson, Metalsky and Alloy 1989 (hopelessness theory). Caspi 2003 (5-HTTLPR x stress), Risch 2009 and Border 2019 (failed). Belsky 1997, Belsky and Pluess 2009 (differential susceptibility). Boyce and Ellis 2005 (biological sensitivity to context). Pluess and Belsky 2013 (vantage sensitivity). Brown, Birley and Wing 1972; Vaughn and Leff 1976 (expressed emotion). Exam trap (1) Diathesis = predisposition, not trigger. (2) Schizotaxia (neural defect) vs schizotypy (personality organisation) vs schizotypal personality disorder (DSM category). (3) Zubin and Spring is 1977 , not 1962 (Meehl) or 1970 (Rosenthal). (4) In Zubin and Spring, the vulnerability is permanent, the episode is time-limited. (5) Engel's biopsychosocial model (1977) is not the diathesis-stress model. (6) Differential susceptibility is "for better and for worse"; diathesis-stress is "for worse only". (7) Stress generation (Hammen) means dependent events increase, not independent ones. (8) Kindling is Post (1992), borrowed from epilepsy research. Self-check The term "diathesis" in the diathesis-stress model refers to: (a) the precipitating life event (b) a pre-existing predisposition or vulnerability (c) the coping response to stress (d) the residual symptoms after an episode Answer: (b). Diathesis is the predisposition; the stressor is the precipitant. In Meehl's (1962) model, the inherited neural integrative defect is called: (a) schizotypy (b) schizotaxia (c) schizoid personality (d) schizophreniform state Answer: (b). Schizotaxia is the neural defect; schizotypy is the personality organisation built on it. "Vulnerability: a new view of schizophrenia", which proposed that episodes are time-limited while vulnerability is enduring, was written by: (a) Paul Meehl, 1962 (b) David Rosenthal, 1970 (c) Joseph Zubin and Bonnie Spring, 1977 (d) Scott Monroe and Anne Simons, 1991 Answer: (c). Zubin and Spring (1977), Journal of Abnormal Psychology . Hammen's (1991) finding that depressed women experience more dependent, interpersonal stressful events is known as: (a) kindling (b) stress generation (c) vantage sensitivity (d) expressed emotion Answer: (b). People with a depressive diathesis partly generate their own (dependent) stress. In the hopelessness theory of Abramson, Metalsky and Alloy (1989), the diathesis is: (a) the short allele of 5-HTTLPR (b) a negative inferential style attributing negative events to stable, global causes (c) high expressed emotion in the family (d) sociotropy Answer: (b). The cognitive diathesis is the negative inferential (attributional) style. The large 2019 study by Border and colleagues concluded that 5-HTTLPR x stress effects on depression: (a) were strongly confirmed (b) were confirmed only in women (c) were not supported (d) were larger than the main effect of stress Answer: (c). Border et al. (2019) found no support for historical candidate gene or candidate G x E hypotheses. A trait that predicts worse outcomes in adverse environments and better outcomes in supportive environments, compared with others, best fits: (a) the diathesis-stress model (b) differential susceptibility (c) the kindling hypothesis (d) the biopsychosocial model Answer: (b). "For better and for worse" with a crossover interaction is differential susceptibility. "Biological sensitivity to context" was proposed by: (a) Belsky and Pluess (2009) (b) Boyce and Ellis (2005) (c) Caspi and Moffitt (2003) (d) Ingram and Luxton (2005) Answer: (b). Boyce and Ellis (2005), Development and Psychopathology . Which component is NOT one of the classic dimensions of expressed emotion rated on the Camberwell Family Interview that predict relapse? (a) critical comments (b) hostility (c) emotional over-involvement (d) thought broadcasting Answer: (d). Thought broadcasting is a Schneiderian first-rank symptom, not an EE dimension. Robert Post's (1992) kindling hypothesis proposes that in recurrent mood disorder: (a) each later episode needs more stress than the first (b) later episodes need less stress and may become autonomous (c) stress plays no role at any stage (d) episodes are caused only by independent life events Answer: (b). Earlier episodes sensitise the system, so the threshold for later episodes falls. 2. Bleuler's four A's and the history of the schizophrenia concept "Schizophrenia" is a little over a century old as a word, and the concept has been reshaped three or four times since. Entrance examiners love this history because it is full of near-identical names, years one apart and symptom lists that sound alike. The way to keep it straight is to see each figure as answering a different question: Emil Kraepelin asked "what is the course?", Eugen Bleuler asked "what is the underlying psychological disturbance?", and Schneider asked "which symptoms can be reliably recognised and used for diagnosis?" 2.1 Before Kraepelin: the pieces Bénédict Augustin Morel (France) used the term démence précoce ("early dementia") for young people who showed early mental deterioration. The usual dates given are 1852 (Études cliniques) and 1860 (Traité des maladies mentales); sources differ on which is the "first" use. Morel worked within his theory of hereditary degeneration . Ewald Hecker (1871) described hebephrenia , an illness beginning in adolescence with silly, incongruous behaviour and rapid deterioration (the name had been suggested earlier by his teacher Karl Ludwig Kahlbaum). Karl Ludwig Kahlbaum (1874) described catatonia ("tension insanity"), with motor symptoms such as stupor, posturing and waxy flexibility. Paranoid states (with delusions as the main feature) were described by several authors as separate conditions. 2.2 Emil Kraepelin: dementia praecox Emil Kraepelin , working in Heidelberg and later Munich, revised his textbook ( Psychiatrie ) repeatedly. He used the Latin term dementia praecox in the 4th edition (1893) , at first for a narrower group among the "degenerative" processes. In the 6th edition (1899) he consolidated hebephrenia, catatonia and paranoid dementia into one disease, dementia praecox, on the grounds that, despite different symptoms, they shared: early onset (praecox = early, typically adolescence or young adulthood), and a deteriorating course ending in a characteristic weakening of mind (the "dementia"). In the same edition he set this against manic-depressive insanity , which ran an episodic course with good recovery between episodes. This Kraepelinian dichotomy (dementia praecox vs manic-depressive insanity, separated by course and outcome) still underlies the split between schizophrenia spectrum and mood disorder chapters in DSM and ICD. Kraepelin's method was longitudinal: he grouped patients by how the illness unfolded over years, recorded on his famous index cards (Zählkarten), rather than by any single symptom. Later editions (the 8th, 1909 to 1915) added further subforms such as simple dementia praecox. Exam trap Emil Kraepelin did not coin the French "démence précoce" (that is Morel). He did not coin "schizophrenia" (that is Bleuler). What Kraepelin did was unify hebephrenia, catatonia and paranoid forms under "dementia praecox" (consolidated in the 6th edition, 1899) and separate it from manic-depressive insanity. If a question asks who first described catatonia, the answer is Kahlbaum (1874); hebephrenia, Hecker (1871). 2.3 Eugen Bleuler: from dementia praecox to "the group of schizophrenias" Eugen Bleuler (1857 to 1939) was director of the Burghölzli , the psychiatric hospital of the University of Zurich, from 1898; Carl Gustav Jung worked there under him. Bleuler lived alongside his patients and was influenced by the associationist psychology of the day and by Sigmund Freud's ideas, which he applied to the content of psychotic symptoms. He introduced the word "schizophrenia" in a lecture in 1908 (to the German Psychiatric Association, Berlin). His great monograph, Dementia Praecox oder Gruppe der Schizophrenien ("Dementia praecox, or the group of schizophrenias"), appeared in 1911 as part of Gustav Aschaffenburg's handbook of psychiatry. It was translated into English only in 1950 , by Joseph Zinkin . Why rename it? "Schizophrenia" comes from Greek schizein (to split) and phren (mind). Bleuler meant the splitting (loosening) of the psychic functions from one another: thought, emotion and will no longer work together as a coherent whole, so a patient might describe a tragedy while smiling. He did not mean a "split personality" in the sense of multiple identities (that is dissociative identity disorder, a completely different condition). He also rejected Emil Kraepelin's name because his own patients showed that the illness was: not always a dementia : many did not deteriorate to a final weakened state, and some recovered, and not always praecox : onset could be later in life. The phrase "group of schizophrenias" shows that he already saw it as a heterogeneous group of conditions, not a single disease. 2.4 The four A's, one by one Eugen Bleuler did not use the phrase "four A's" himself; it is a teaching mnemonic added later by textbook writers to summarise his fundamental symptoms . Each is explained below with a clinical picture. 1. Associations (loosening of associations) For Bleuler this was the central disturbance. In normal thinking, ideas follow one another guided by a goal (the "determining tendency"). In schizophrenia the threads that link ideas are broken, so thoughts follow chance, sound or private links. Example: asked "How are you sleeping?", a patient replies, "Sleep is a bed of roses, roses are red, the Red Army marches at night, I keep watch." Modern terms that descend from this include derailment, tangentiality, incoherence and, in its mildest form, Meehl's "cognitive slippage". Bleuler also included thought blocking (sudden stopping of the train of thought). 2. Affect (affective disturbance) Emotional expression becomes flattened (blunted) or incongruous (inappropriate) to the content of thought. Example: a young man reports, without visible emotion, that his mother died last week, or laughs while describing being persecuted. Bleuler stressed that the inner emotional life might be less impoverished than it looks; what is lost is the integration between feeling and the rest of the mind. 3. Ambivalence Bleuler coined this word too. It means the simultaneous presence of contradictory feelings, wishes or thoughts toward the same object, both held at full strength without resolution. He described three forms: affective ambivalence : loving and hating the same person at the same moment; ambitendency (volitional ambivalence): wanting and not wanting to do something at once, so the patient starts to shake hands, withdraws, extends the hand again; intellectual ambivalence : thinking "I am a man" and "I am not a man" at the same time. Ordinary mixed feelings are not what he meant: in schizophrenia the opposites coexist without the normal pressure to reconcile them. 4. Autism Bleuler coined "autism" (Greek autos , self), around 1910 to 1911 (sources differ on the very first use), for the withdrawal from external reality into an inner world of fantasy , with "autistic thinking" governed by wishes and private logic rather than by reality. Example: a patient sits for hours absorbed in an inner drama, treating reality as less important than the inner world. The word was later borrowed by Leo Kanner (1943) , "Autistic disturbances of affective contact", and Hans Asperger (1944) , "autistic psychopathy", for a developmental condition of childhood. That borrowing is why the same word now names a completely different disorder. Memory hook A ssociations, A ffect, A mbivalence, A utism. None of the four is a hallucination or a delusion. Eugen Bleuler thought the dramatic "positive" symptoms were the surface; the real illness was the loosening underneath. 2.5 Two different axes: fundamental vs accessory, primary vs secondary This is the single most confused point in Bleuler questions, so build it slowly. Eugen Bleuler classified symptoms in two separate ways . Axis 1: fundamental (basic) vs accessory symptoms (a diagnostic axis) Fundamental symptoms are present, at least to some degree, in every case and at every stage, and are characteristic of schizophrenia. They are therefore what the diagnosis rests on. They include the four A's, and Bleuler also listed further fundamental disturbances (of attention, will, the "person" or sense of self, and schizophrenic "dementia" in his special sense). Accessory symptoms may or may not be present, come and go, and also occur in other illnesses. They include hallucinations, delusions , catatonic symptoms, certain disturbances of memory, speech and writing, and acute syndromes. They are often what brings the patient to hospital, yet for Bleuler they were not essential to the diagnosis. Axis 2: primary vs secondary symptoms (a theoretical, causal axis) Primary symptoms are the direct product of the underlying disease process , which Bleuler presumed to be organic. The chief primary symptom in his account was the loosening of associations (along with some others he thought organic, such as certain disturbances of consciousness and physical signs). Secondary symptoms are the person's psychological reactions to the primary disturbance and to their life situation, shaped by complexes and wishes. Much of the clinical picture, including autism, much of the affective change, hallucinations and delusions, was secondary in this sense. Because these are different axes, a symptom can be fundamental but secondary : autism is present in every case (fundamental) yet Bleuler regarded it as a psychological consequence (secondary). Hallucinations are accessory and secondary . Loosening of associations is fundamental and primary . Symptom Fundamental or accessory? Primary or secondary? Loosening of associations Fundamental Primary (the core) Autism Fundamental Largely secondary Hallucinations Accessory Secondary Delusions Accessory Secondary Catatonic symptoms Accessory Mostly secondary in his account Exam trap "Primary" is not a synonym for "fundamental", and "secondary" is not a synonym for "accessory". Many guidebooks blur them; when an MCQ asks specifically about Eugen Bleuler's primary symptom, the safest answer is loosening (disturbance) of associations. When it asks which are accessory , choose hallucinations and delusions. A fifth and sixth A? Some textbooks add Attention (Bleuler did discuss attentional disturbance among fundamental symptoms) and Avolition (or abulia, loss of will) as a fifth and sixth A. These are later teaching extensions, not part of the classic four. Do not confuse them with Nancy Andreasen's negative symptom domains on the SANS (1982): affective flattening, alogia, avolition-apathy, anhedonia-asociality and attention, sometimes called "the five A's of negative symptoms". If a question says "Bleuler's four A's", stick to associations, affect, ambivalence and autism. 2.6 Bleuler's influence: a broad concept and the US-UK gap Because Eugen Bleuler's fundamental symptoms were subtle and not tied to deterioration, his concept was broad : mild, latent and "simple" cases with no hallucinations or delusions could qualify. This broad view became dominant in the United States (helped by psychoanalytic psychiatry and by Harry Stack Sullivan and others), whereas British and European psychiatry stayed closer to Emil Kraepelin and Schneider. US-UK Diagnostic Project (John E. Cooper, Robert Kendell, Barry Gurland and colleagues, 1972, Psychiatric Diagnosis in New York and London ): New York hospital psychiatrists diagnosed schizophrenia far more often than London psychiatrists, including many patients London would have called manic-depressive or personality disordered. When the project team rated the same patients with a standardised interview (the Present State Examination), most of the difference disappeared. The gap was in diagnostic habits , not in the patients. International Pilot Study of Schizophrenia (IPSS) , WHO (1973): nine centres, including Agra in India . Seven centres shared a broadly similar core concept; Washington and Moscow used much broader concepts. The IPSS and its successor, the WHO Determinants of Outcome study (with Chandigarh as an Indian centre), also suggested a better course in developing-country centres. These findings pushed psychiatry toward operational criteria (Feighner criteria 1972, Research Diagnostic Criteria 1978, DSM-III 1980) that narrowed the American concept and leaned on Schneider's symptoms. 2.7 Kurt Schneider: first-rank symptoms Kurt Schneider (Heidelberg) took a pragmatic route. Whatever the underlying process, which symptoms are both easy to recognise and highly characteristic ? He set these out in Klinische Psychopathologie (first edition 1950, developed from earlier work in the late 1930s), translated into English by M. W. Hamilton in 1959 . In the absence of organic brain disease, the presence of a first-rank symptom (FRS) was to be taken as strongly suggestive of schizophrenia. Christopher S. Mellor (1970) later gave the standard operational definitions. The commonly cited list of 11 : Audible thoughts ( Gedankenlautwerden , also "thought echo" or écho de la pensée ): hearing one's own thoughts spoken aloud. Voices arguing or discussing the patient in the third person. Voices commenting on the patient's actions ("now she is picking up the cup"). Somatic passivity : bodily sensations experienced as imposed by an outside agency. Thought withdrawal : thoughts are taken out of the mind by an outside force. Thought insertion : thoughts that are not one's own are put into the mind. Thought broadcasting (diffusion): one's thoughts escape and are known to others. Made feelings : emotions imposed from outside. Made impulses (drives) : urges imposed from outside. Made volitional acts : actions controlled by an outside agency. Delusional perception : a normal perception is given a sudden, delusional, self-referent meaning (for example, "the traffic light turned red, so I knew I had been chosen to save the world"). This is a two-stage process: normal percept, then unconnected delusional meaning. Items 4 and 8 to 10 together are often grouped as passivity experiences (delusions of control); items 5 to 7 as thought alienation ; items 1 to 3 as third-person auditory hallucinations . Second-rank symptoms were other features that could support the diagnosis but were less specific: other kinds of hallucination, sudden delusional ideas (delusional notions), perplexity, depressive or euphoric mood changes and emotional blunting. These occur in many disorders. High yield FRS are not pathognomonic. Later studies found them in a proportion of patients with mania and other psychoses, and a substantial minority of people with schizophrenia never show any. ICD-10 gave FRS heavy weight. DSM-IV allowed a single Criterion A symptom to suffice if delusions were bizarre or hallucinations were a running commentary or two voices conversing. DSM-5 (2013) dropped this special weighting (and the classic subtypes), so these symptoms now count like any other Criterion A symptom. 2.8 After Schneider: positive and negative symptoms, Crow, Langfeldt Gabriel Langfeldt (Norway, 1939) separated "true" process schizophrenia (insidious, poor prognosis) from schizophreniform states (acute onset, clear precipitant, good prognosis). The term survives as DSM's schizophreniform disorder, though now defined by duration (1 to 6 months), not prognosis. Timothy Crow (1980) proposed two syndromes. Type I : positive symptoms, acute, good response to neuroleptics, presumed dopamine (D2) excess, reversible, no intellectual impairment. Type II : negative symptoms, chronic, poor drug response, structural brain change (ventricular enlargement), intellectual impairment, poorer outcome. Nancy Andreasen built rating scales for negative (SANS, 1982) and positive (SAPS, 1984) symptoms and, with Olsen (1982), positive, negative and mixed subtypes. The negative symptom concept looks back to Eugen Bleuler's fundamental symptoms, and the positive concept to Schneider's FRS. The terms "positive" and "negative" symptoms themselves go back to the neurologist John Hughlings Jackson in the 19th century. 2.9 Kraepelin vs Bleuler vs Schneider Feature Emil Kraepelin Eugen Bleuler Kurt Schneider Key term Dementia praecox Schizophrenia ("group of schizophrenias") First-rank symptoms Key dates 4th ed 1893 (term); 6th ed 1899 (consolidated) 1908 lecture (word coined); 1911 monograph; English 1950 (Zinkin) Klinische Psychopathologie 1950; English 1959 Basis for diagnosis Course and outcome (early onset, deterioration) Underlying psychological disturbance (fundamental symptoms) Specific, easily recognised symptoms Core features Hebephrenic, catatonic and paranoid forms with deterioration Four A's: associations, affect, ambivalence, autism 11 FRS (thought alienation, passivity, third-person voices, delusional perception) Status of hallucinations and delusions Common features Accessory (not essential) Certain specific forms are first rank Prognosis view Pessimistic (deterioration) Variable; recovery possible Not the basis for diagnosis Width of concept Moderate Broad Narrow Main legacy Dichotomy with manic-depressive illness Name; negative and cognitive symptom tradition; broad US concept ICD-10 and DSM-III to DSM-IV criteria; Present State Examination 2.10 Manfred Bleuler and long-term outcome Eugen Bleuler's son Manfred Bleuler , also director of the Burghölzli, personally followed a cohort of patients for more than two decades (the usually quoted figure is 208 patients), published in German in 1972 and in English in 1978. He found that the course was far less uniformly bad than Emil Kraepelin had held: a substantial minority recovered (often quoted as about a quarter), many reached a stable outcome after the first years, and steady progression to severe "end states" was uncommon. The exact percentages vary between secondary sources, so learn the direction of the finding rather than a single number. Do not confuse father and son: Eugen coined schizophrenia and autism; Manfred did the long-term outcome study. Exam trap (1) Bleuler coined both schizophrenia and autism ; Kanner (1943) and Asperger (1944) borrowed autism. (2) 1908 = the word introduced in a lecture; 1911 = the monograph; 1950 = English translation. Read which event the question names. (3) The four A's do not include hallucinations or delusions; those are accessory. (4) Ambivalence is the umbrella; ambitendency is its volitional form (and is listed among catatonic motor signs in modern texts). (5) Schizophrenia does not mean split personality. (6) Fundamental/accessory and primary/secondary are different axes. (7) Morel = démence précoce; Emil Kraepelin = dementia praecox; Hecker = hebephrenia (1871); Kahlbaum = catatonia (1874). (8) Schneider's FRS number 11 in the usual list; delusional perception is the only delusion among them. (9) Manfred Bleuler, not Eugen, ran the long-term outcome study. Self-check The term "schizophrenia" was first introduced by Eugen Bleuler in: (a) 1899 (b) 1908 (c) 1911 (d) 1950 Answer: (b). He used it in a 1908 lecture; the monograph followed in 1911 and the English translation in 1950. Which of the following is NOT one of Bleuler's four A's? (a) Ambivalence (b) Autism (c) Auditory hallucinations (d) Associations Answer: (c). Hallucinations were accessory symptoms for Bleuler. Emil Kraepelin consolidated hebephrenia, catatonia and paranoid dementia into dementia praecox in his: (a) 4th edition, 1893 (b) 6th edition, 1899 (c) 8th edition, 1913 (d) 1911 monograph Answer: (b). The term appears in the 4th edition, but the unified concept and the dichotomy with manic-depressive insanity date from the 6th (1899). A patient reaches out to shake the doctor's hand, withdraws it, then extends it again, repeatedly. This is best described as: (a) echopraxia (b) ambitendency (c) waxy flexibility (d) thought blocking Answer: (b). Ambitendency is the volitional form of Bleuler's ambivalence. According to Bleuler, the primary symptom, a direct product of the disease process, was: (a) delusions (b) autism (c) loosening of associations (d) hallucinations Answer: (c). Autism was fundamental but largely secondary; delusions and hallucinations were accessory and secondary. Which of these is a Schneiderian first-rank symptom? (a) Perplexity (b) Delusional perception (c) Emotional blunting (d) Second-person command hallucinations Answer: (b). Perplexity and blunting are second rank; command hallucinations in the second person are not first rank. The term "autism" was coined by: (a) Leo Kanner (b) Hans Asperger (c) Eugen Bleuler (d) Emil Kraepelin Answer: (c). Bleuler coined it for withdrawal into fantasy in schizophrenia; Kanner (1943) and Asperger (1944) borrowed it. The US-UK Diagnostic Project (Cooper et al., 1972) showed that: (a) schizophrenia was genuinely more common in New York (b) differences in diagnosis rates largely reflected psychiatrists' diagnostic habits (c) London psychiatrists used a broader concept of schizophrenia (d) first-rank symptoms were absent in American patients Answer: (b). With standardised assessment (PSE), most of the difference disappeared. In Timothy Crow's (1980) classification, Type II schizophrenia is characterised by: (a) positive symptoms and good neuroleptic response (b) negative symptoms, poor drug response and structural brain changes (c) acute onset and full recovery (d) dopamine excess without intellectual impairment Answer: (b). Options (a) and (d) describe Type I. The long-term follow-up study at the Burghölzli showing that schizophrenia frequently does not run a uniformly deteriorating course was carried out by: (a) Eugen Bleuler (b) Manfred Bleuler (c) Gabriel Langfeldt (d) Kurt Schneider Answer: (b). Manfred Bleuler, Eugen's son (published 1972). 3. The theory of planned behaviour The theory of planned behaviour (TPB) is the most widely used model in social and health psychology for predicting what people will actually do. To understand why it exists you have to start with an embarrassing problem that social psychology faced in the middle of the twentieth century: attitudes, the field's favourite concept, did not seem to predict behaviour. 3.1 The attitude-behaviour problem Gordon Allport (1935) had called attitude "the most distinctive and indispensable concept" in social psychology, on the assumption that if you know how a person feels about something you can predict how they will act toward it. Two pieces of evidence shook that assumption. Richard LaPiere (1934), "Attitudes vs. actions". Between 1930 and 1932 LaPiere travelled across the United States with a young Chinese couple at a time of strong anti-Chinese prejudice. They visited hotels, auto camps and restaurants (the commonly cited total is 251 establishments) and were refused service only once. About six months later LaPiere mailed a questionnaire to the same establishments asking "Will you accept members of the Chinese race as guests?" Of those who replied, roughly 92% said no. The stated attitude (rejection) and the actual behaviour (acceptance) were almost opposite. The study has methodological problems (the person answering the letter was probably not the person at the front desk, the couple were well dressed and accompanied by a white professor, and a letter about "the Chinese race" is a far more abstract target than a particular polite couple), but it became the classic demonstration of the gap. Allan Wicker (1969). Wicker reviewed several dozen studies that had measured both attitudes and overt behaviour and concluded that the relationship was weak: correlations rarely exceeded about .30 and the typical value was around .15. He even suggested that the attitude concept might be abandoned. A correlation of .15 means attitudes explain only about 2% of the variance in behaviour. 3.2 The rescue: the principle of compatibility Icek Ajzen and Martin Fishbein (1977, Psychological Bulletin ) argued that attitudes do predict behaviour, but only when both are measured at the same level of specificity. They originally called this the principle of correspondence ; Ajzen later relabelled it compatibility . Any behaviour has four elements, remembered as TACT : Target (toward what), Action (what is done), Context (where), and Time (when). LaPiere measured a general attitude ("the Chinese race") and tried to predict a highly specific act (serving this couple, in this hotel, on this evening). A general attitude toward religion will not predict whether you attend a particular temple next Sunday, but it will predict a broad aggregate of religious behaviours across many occasions. Conversely, a specific attitude ("my attending the temple this Sunday") predicts that specific act well. When attitude and behaviour measures are compatible, correlations rise substantially. Definition Principle of compatibility (Icek Ajzen and Martin Fishbein, 1977): an attitude predicts a behaviour well only when both are defined at the same level of generality on Target, Action, Context and Time. General attitudes predict aggregated behaviour; specific attitudes predict specific acts. 3.3 The Theory of Reasoned Action (TRA) Martin Fishbein and Icek Ajzen set out the Theory of Reasoned Action in Belief, Attitude, Intention, and Behavior: An Introduction to Theory and Research (1975), building on Fishbein's earlier expectancy-value work on attitudes in the 1960s. Ajzen and Fishbein then presented it for applied readers in Understanding Attitudes and Predicting Social Behavior (1980).
