The word "reasoned" does not mean people are perfectly logical; it means behaviour follows reasonably from the information and beliefs a person holds. The TRA has a simple chain: Behavioural intention is the immediate antecedent of behaviour. Intention is the person's readiness or plan to perform the act ("I intend to exercise three times this week"). Intention is determined by two things: the attitude toward the behaviour and the subjective norm . Attitude toward the behaviour is the person's overall positive or negative evaluation of performing the behaviour. It is built by an expectancy-value rule: for each salient outcome, multiply the strength of the belief that the behaviour leads to that outcome (behavioural belief, b ) by the evaluation of that outcome ( e ), and sum: A B = Σ b i e i . Example: "Exercising will reduce my weight" (very likely, +3) × "reducing my weight is" (very good, +3) = +9; add up across outcomes like "exercising will tire me" and "exercising will take time from study". Subjective norm is the perceived social pressure to perform or not perform the behaviour. It is built from normative beliefs (what I think specific important others, called referents, want me to do: parents, spouse, doctor) multiplied by motivation to comply with each referent, then summed: SN = Σ n j m j . The relative weight of attitude and subjective norm varies across behaviours and people. For some acts (choosing a career in a joint family) the norm dominates; for others (choosing a flavour of ice cream) attitude dominates. Everything else (personality, demographics, general attitudes toward objects) is treated as an external variable : it influences behaviour only indirectly by shaping these beliefs. The limit of the TRA: volitional control. The TRA works for behaviours fully under volitional control, where intending is enough to act. Many important behaviours are not like that. You may fully intend to quit smoking, lose weight or attend therapy but lack the skill, money, time, transport or cooperation of others. For such behaviours intention alone predicts poorly. This is the gap the TPB was built to fill. 3.4 The Theory of Planned Behaviour (TPB) Icek Ajzen extended the TRA in a book chapter, "From intentions to actions: A theory of planned behavior", in Julius Kuhl and Jürgen Beckmann (Eds.), Action Control: From Cognition to Behavior (Springer, 1985). The fully developed and most cited statement is Ajzen (1991), "The theory of planned behavior", Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes , 50, 179 to 211. Note that the TPB is Ajzen's theory alone; Martin Fishbein was co-author of the TRA, not of the TPB papers. The single addition is perceived behavioural control (PBC) : the person's perception of how easy or difficult it will be to perform the behaviour. Like the other constructs it rests on beliefs. Control beliefs ( c ) are beliefs about the presence of factors that can help or hinder (time, money, skill, a nearby gym, a supportive partner), and each is weighted by its perceived power ( p ) to facilitate or inhibit the behaviour: PBC = Σ c k p k . The two routes of PBC. PBC works in two ways, and examiners love this point: Indirect route, via intention. People form stronger intentions to do things they believe they can do. If I think quitting is impossible for me, I will hardly intend to quit. Direct route, to behaviour. PBC also predicts behaviour directly, but only to the extent that PBC is an accurate reflection of actual behavioural control . Here PBC acts as a proxy for actual control (real skills, resources, opportunities). Two people with equally strong intentions to exercise will differ in success if one actually has a gym and free time; PBC captures part of that difference. When perceptions are unrealistic (little information, a new behaviour, changed circumstances) the direct path weakens. Ajzen (1991) also suggested that PBC moderates the intention-behaviour link (intentions translate into behaviour more strongly when control is high), though in practice most studies test only additive paths. Link to self-efficacy. Ajzen explicitly noted that PBC is most compatible with Albert Bandura's (1977) concept of self-efficacy , "beliefs in one's capability to organise and execute the courses of action required" (from Bandura's 1977 Psychological Review paper, "Self-efficacy: Toward a unifying theory of behavioral change"). Later research showed PBC items split into two factors: self-efficacy / perceived capacity (ease or difficulty, confidence) and perceived controllability / autonomy (whether it is up to me). Self-efficacy items usually predict intention better. High yield TPB = TRA + perceived behavioural control. Three belief bases feed three constructs: behavioural beliefs → attitude toward the behaviour; normative beliefs → subjective norm; control beliefs → PBC. These three → intention → behaviour, plus a direct PBC → behaviour path that works only insofar as PBC mirrors actual control. Theory of planned behaviour (Ajzen, 1985, 1991) Behavioural beliefs × outcome evaluations Normative beliefs × motivation to comply Control beliefs × perceived power Attitude toward the behaviour Subjective norm Perceived behavioural control (PBC) Intention Behaviour Actual control (skills, resources) direct path (proxy) Figure: the TPB. Solid arrows are the main causal paths; the dashed arrow is the direct PBC → behaviour path, which holds only to the extent PBC reflects actual control. Delete the bottom row (control beliefs, PBC, actual control) and you have the TRA. 3.5 Later extensions Descriptive vs injunctive norms. The subjective norm in the TRA and TPB is essentially injunctive : what others think I ought to do. Robert Cialdini and colleagues (Cialdini, Reno and Kallgren, 1990, the "focus theory of normative conduct", tested with littering studies) distinguished this from the descriptive norm : what others actually do. Seeing a littered car park makes people litter more (descriptive), even if they know littering is disapproved (injunctive). TPB researchers later added descriptive norms and found they add predictive power. The Reasoned Action Approach (RAA). Martin Fishbein and Icek Ajzen (2010), Predicting and Changing Behavior: The Reasoned Action Approach , unified the TRA and TPB. The RAA keeps attitude, perceived norm and PBC, but splits each into two subcomponents: attitude into instrumental (useful/useless) and experiential (pleasant/unpleasant); perceived norm into injunctive and descriptive ; PBC into capacity and autonomy . Fishbein died in 2009, before the book appeared. 3.6 How good is the evidence? Two meta-analyses are quoted in almost every textbook. Treat the exact numbers as the commonly cited figures: Christopher Armitage and Mark Conner (2001) , British Journal of Social Psychology , about 185 independent studies: the TPB explained about 39% of the variance in intention and about 27% of the variance in behaviour . PBC added significantly to the prediction of intention over attitude and subjective norm. Subjective norm was the weakest predictor. Prediction of self-reported behaviour was better than prediction of objectively measured behaviour. Paschal Sheeran (2002) , European Review of Social Psychology , a meta-analysis of meta-analyses: the average intention-behaviour correlation was about .53, meaning intentions explain about 28% of the variance in behaviour . This leaves a large intention-behaviour gap : Sheeran showed most of the gap comes from "inclined abstainers", people who intend to act but do not. 3.7 Applications in health psychology The TPB has been applied to condom use, smoking initiation and cessation, exercise, diet, alcohol use, breast and cervical screening, medication adherence and help-seeking. In India it is a natural fit for public health behaviours such as handwashing with soap, vaccination uptake (including COVID-19 and childhood immunisation), toilet use under sanitation campaigns, tobacco and gutka cessation, and mental health help-seeking. A clinical psychologist might use it to understand why a patient with depression does not attend follow-up: is it attitude ("therapy will not help"), norm ("my family thinks seeing a psychiatrist is shameful"), or PBC ("the hospital is two buses away and I cannot take leave")? Each points to a different intervention. How a TPB questionnaire is built (Icek Ajzen's recommended procedure): Define the behaviour in TACT terms ("washing hands with soap before every meal at home over the next two weeks"). Elicitation study. In a small sample from the target population, ask open-ended questions: What are the advantages/disadvantages of doing this? Who would approve/disapprove? What would make it easier/harder? The most frequently mentioned answers become the modal salient beliefs . Main questionnaire. Build items for each belief and each direct construct, typically on 7-point scales. Direct attitude uses semantic differential pairs ("For me, washing hands before meals is: bad 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 good; unpleasant ... pleasant; harmful ... beneficial"). Belief strength items are often scored from 1 to 7 or from -3 to +3; evaluations and motivation to comply are usually bipolar. Measure behaviour later (prospective design), ideally objectively. Analyse with hierarchical regression or structural equation modelling. 3.8 Criticisms "Time to retire". Falko Sniehotta, Justin Presseau and Vera Araújo-Soares (2014), in Health Psychology Review , argued that the TPB has limited predictive validity, that its constructs often do not change behaviour when targeted in interventions, and that it is too static. Icek Ajzen published a reply defending it. Rationality bias. The model assumes deliberate, conscious processing. It neglects emotion, impulse, and automatic processes. Past behaviour and habit. Past behaviour often predicts future behaviour better than TPB variables and adds variance beyond them, which suggests habit (automatic responding cued by context) is missing from the model. Self-report and common method variance inflate correlations; objective behaviour is predicted less well. Intention-behaviour gap. Even strong intentions often fail. Sufficiency assumption. Ajzen allowed extra predictors in principle, and many have been added (moral norm, anticipated regret, self-identity), which weakens the claim that three constructs are enough. Bridging the gap: implementation intentions. Peter Gollwitzer (1999, American Psychologist ) distinguished goal intentions ("I intend to do X") from implementation intentions , "if-then" plans that link a situation to a response: "If it is 7 am on a weekday, then I will walk for 20 minutes around the park." Such plans delegate control to situational cues and help close the intention-behaviour gap. Gollwitzer and Sheeran's (2006) meta-analysis is often cited for a medium-to-large effect. 3.9 Comparison with other health behaviour models Model Origin Core constructs Proximal predictor Key point for exams Theory of Reasoned Action Martin Fishbein and Icek Ajzen, 1975; 1980 Attitude toward the behaviour, subjective norm Intention Only for volitional behaviours Theory of Planned Behaviour Icek Ajzen, 1985; 1991 Attitude, subjective norm, perceived behavioural control Intention (plus PBC directly) Adds PBC to TRA Health Belief Model Godfrey Hochbaum, Irwin Rosenstock and colleagues, US Public Health Service, 1950s (built to explain poor uptake of free tuberculosis X-ray screening) Perceived susceptibility, perceived severity, perceived benefits, perceived barriers, cues to action; self-efficacy added later (Rosenstock, Strecher and Becker, 1988) No intention construct; beliefs predict action directly "Cues to action" is unique to the HBM Protection Motivation Theory Ronald Rogers, 1975 (revised 1983) Threat appraisal (severity, vulnerability, rewards of maladaptive response) and coping appraisal (response efficacy, self-efficacy, response cost) Protection motivation (functions like intention) Built to explain fear appeals 3.10 Exam traps Exam trap TPB = TRA + PBC. Options that say TPB added "subjective norm" or "intention" are wrong; those were already in the TRA. The TRA is Fishbein and Icek Ajzen (1975); the TPB is Ajzen alone. Exam trap Years: TPB first proposed 1985 (book chapter in Kuhl and Beckmann), fully developed 1991 (OBHDP journal). Both answers can appear; "proposed" points to 1985, "the classic paper" to 1991. TRA: 1975 (and 1980). Reasoned Action Approach: 2010. Exam trap Subjective norm is perceived social pressure , not the actual opinions of others and not the actual behaviour of others (that is the descriptive norm). Attitude is toward the behaviour ("my quitting smoking"), not toward the object ("cigarettes"). PBC is perceived, not actual control ; it predicts behaviour directly only as a proxy for actual control. Memory hook "A-S-P before I-B": Attitude, Subjective norm, PBC come before Intention, then Behaviour. Beliefs underneath: Behavioural, Normative, Control ("BNC"). 3.11 Self-check The construct added by the theory of planned behaviour to the theory of reasoned action is: (a) Subjective norm (b) Behavioural intention (c) Perceived behavioural control (d) Attitude toward the object Answer: (c). Icek Ajzen added PBC to handle behaviours not under full volitional control. In TPB, the immediate antecedent of behaviour is: (a) Attitude (b) Intention (c) Normative belief (d) Self-efficacy Answer: (b). Intention is the proximal determinant (PBC may also act directly). Normative beliefs are weighted by: (a) Outcome evaluation (b) Perceived power (c) Motivation to comply (d) Response efficacy Answer: (c). Subjective norm = Σ normative belief × motivation to comply. LaPiere's (1934) study is famous for showing: (a) Cognitive dissonance after forced compliance (b) A discrepancy between stated attitudes and actual behaviour (c) Conformity to group pressure (d) The mere exposure effect Answer: (b). Establishments that served the Chinese couple later said they would refuse Chinese guests. The principle of compatibility requires attitude and behaviour to match on: (a) Target, action, context and time (b) Valence, intensity, centrality and accessibility (c) Cognition, affect and conation (d) Severity, susceptibility, benefits and barriers Answer: (a). TACT, from Ajzen and Martin Fishbein (1977). PBC is expected to predict behaviour directly when: (a) Subjective norm is weak (b) PBC accurately reflects actual control (c) The behaviour is fully volitional (d) Attitudes are negative Answer: (b). The direct path works because PBC serves as a proxy for actual control. Ajzen considered PBC most similar to: (a) Rotter's locus of control (b) Bandura's self-efficacy (c) Seligman's learned helplessness (d) Festinger's dissonance Answer: (b). Ajzen explicitly linked PBC to Bandura's (1977) self-efficacy and distinguished it from generalised locus of control. According to the commonly cited meta-analysis by Armitage and Conner (2001), TPB explains approximately what percentage of variance in behaviour? (a) 10% (b) 27% (c) 39% (d) 60% Answer: (b). About 27% for behaviour; 39% is the figure for intention. "If I finish dinner, then I will take my tablet immediately" is an example of: (a) A descriptive norm (b) A cue to action (c) An implementation intention (d) A control belief Answer: (c). Gollwitzer's (1999) if-then plans bridge the intention-behaviour gap. Which model includes "cues to action"? (a) Theory of reasoned action (b) Theory of planned behaviour (c) Health belief model (d) Protection motivation theory Answer: (c). Cues to action are a Health Belief Model construct. 4. Types of brain scanning and imaging tests Clinical psychology entrance papers ask about brain imaging in two ways: "which technique measures what" and "who invented it, when". To answer both you need a small set of organising ideas first. 4.1 The organising ideas Structural vs functional imaging. Structural (anatomical) methods show what the brain looks like: size and shape of regions, tumours, strokes, atrophy, enlarged ventricles. CT, structural MRI and DTI are structural. Functional methods show what the brain is doing: electrical activity, blood flow, oxygenation, glucose metabolism, receptor binding. EEG, MEG, fMRI, PET, SPECT and fNIRS are functional. The question to ask is: does the image change when the person changes what they are thinking? If yes, it is functional. Spatial vs temporal resolution. Spatial resolution is how precisely you can say where something is (millimetres). Temporal resolution is how precisely you can say when it happened (milliseconds to minutes). Methods that measure electrical or magnetic signals directly (EEG, MEG) are fast (milliseconds) but poor at localisation. Methods that measure blood flow or metabolism (fMRI, PET, SPECT, fNIRS) are slow, because blood responds over seconds, but fMRI and PET localise better. This is the spatial-temporal trade-off , and it is the most examined idea in this topic. Invasive vs non-invasive. Invasive methods break the skin or enter the body: injecting a radioactive tracer (PET, SPECT), injecting contrast through an arterial catheter (angiography), or placing electrodes on or in the brain (intracranial recording). EEG, MEG, MRI, fMRI and fNIRS are non-invasive. Ionising radiation. X-rays and gamma rays carry enough energy to knock electrons off atoms and can damage DNA, so exposure is limited, especially in children and pregnancy. CT and angiography use X-rays; PET and SPECT use gamma-emitting radioactive tracers. MRI uses magnetic fields and radio waves, and EEG, MEG and fNIRS use no ionising radiation at all. 4.2 Historical precursors: pneumoencephalography and cerebral angiography Feature Pneumoencephalography (PEG) Cerebral angiography Full name Pneumoencephalography (air encephalography); ventriculography when air is put directly into the ventricles Cerebral angiography; modern form is digital subtraction angiography (DSA) Inventor / key people and year Walter Dandy, Johns Hopkins: ventriculography 1918, pneumoencephalography 1919 Egas Moniz (António Egas Moniz), Lisbon, 1927; DSA developed in the late 1970s to early 1980s What it measures, physical principle CSF is drained (usually by lumbar puncture) and replaced with air; air is radiolucent, so the ventricles and subarachnoid spaces stand out on plain X-ray Radio-opaque contrast dye is injected into the arteries (now via a catheter from the femoral artery) and X-rays are taken as it flows, showing the vessels. DSA subtracts a pre-contrast image so only the vessels remain Structural or functional Structural (indirect: shape of ventricles) Structural (vascular anatomy), with some flow information Spatial resolution Poor by modern standards Very high for vessels (sub-millimetre) Temporal resolution Not applicable Seconds (can follow contrast flow) Radiation / invasive X-rays; highly invasive and very painful (severe headache, vomiting) X-rays; invasive (arterial catheter); small risk of stroke Clinical and research uses Historically, localising tumours and showing ventricular enlargement; early schizophrenia studies (W. Jacobi and H. Winkler, 1927, reported ventricular enlargement) Aneurysms, arteriovenous malformations, vessel stenosis; DSA is still the gold standard and is used for interventional treatment (coiling, thrombectomy) Limits Obsolete since CT and MRI Invasive; shows vessels, not brain tissue; increasingly replaced for diagnosis by CT and MR angiography Exam trap Egas Moniz won the 1949 Nobel Prize for prefrontal leucotomy (psychosurgery), not for angiography, although angiography is arguably his more lasting contribution. Angiography always needs contrast dye ; plain X-ray cannot see blood vessels. 4.3 Computed tomography (CT / CAT) Feature CT Full name Computed tomography; older name computerised axial tomography (CAT scan) Inventor / key people and year Allan Cormack developed the mathematics in papers of 1963 and 1964; Godfrey Hounsfield built the scanner at EMI, and the first clinical brain scan was performed on 1 October 1971 at Atkinson Morley's Hospital, London (with radiologist James Ambrose). Hounsfield and Cormack shared the 1979 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine What it measures, physical principle An X-ray tube rotates around the head; detectors measure how much the beam is attenuated along many angles; a computer reconstructs cross-sectional slices from these projections. Brightness reflects tissue density (X-ray attenuation) Structural or functional Structural (perfusion CT adds limited functional information) Spatial resolution Good, roughly 0.5 to 1 mm in modern scanners; poorer soft-tissue contrast than MRI Temporal resolution Not used for brain activity; a head scan takes seconds Radiation / invasive Ionising radiation (X-rays); non-invasive unless iodinated contrast is injected Clinical and research uses First-line in acute stroke (to exclude haemorrhage before thrombolysis), head injury, acute haemorrhage, skull fractures, calcification, hydrocephalus; useful when MRI is contraindicated Limits Radiation; poor for posterior fossa (bone artefact), small lesions, early ischaemic stroke and white matter disease; poorer grey/white matter contrast than MRI Hounsfield units (HU) put attenuation on a fixed scale: water = 0 , air = -1000 , dense bone roughly +1000 (values for bone vary, roughly +400 to above +1000). Fat is negative (around -100), CSF near 0, brain around +20 to +40. Acute blood is hyperdense (bright, roughly +50 to +80 HU, values approximate) because clotted blood is concentrated; over days to weeks it becomes isodense and then hypodense. An acute ischaemic infarct may be invisible on CT in the first hours, then appears hypodense (dark). This is why CT in stroke is used mainly to rule out bleeding. Memory hook On CT, "white is dense": bone and fresh blood bright, air and CSF dark. CT = X-rays; "CAT" is just the old name for the same scan. 4.4 Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) Feature MRI Full name Magnetic resonance imaging (originally nuclear magnetic resonance imaging; "nuclear" was dropped to avoid confusion with radioactivity) Inventor / key people and year NMR physics: Felix Bloch and Edward Purcell (1946). Raymond Damadian reported in 1971 ( Science ) that tumour tissue has different relaxation times and claimed priority for the idea of MR scanning. Paul Lauterbur published the first MR image using magnetic field gradients in 1973 ( Nature ); Peter Mansfield developed the mathematics for fast imaging and echo-planar imaging (1977). Lauterbur and Mansfield shared the 2003 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine; Damadian's exclusion was publicly contested What it measures, physical principle Hydrogen nuclei (protons, mostly in water and fat) align in a strong magnetic field (typically 1.5 or 3 tesla). A radiofrequency pulse tips them; as they relax back they emit a radio signal. Different tissues relax at different rates (T1, T2), and gradients encode position Structural or functional Structural (fMRI, DTI and MRS are special MRI techniques) Spatial resolution Very good, about 1 mm routinely, sub-millimetre at high field Temporal resolution Not applicable for structural scans (a sequence takes minutes) Radiation / invasive No ionising radiation; non-invasive (gadolinium contrast optional) Clinical and research uses Tumours, multiple sclerosis, epilepsy foci (e.g. hippocampal sclerosis), posterior fossa, dementia (hippocampal atrophy), early stroke (diffusion-weighted imaging), volumetric research in psychiatry Limits Contraindicated with pacemakers (unless MR-conditional), cochlear implants, ferromagnetic aneurysm clips, metallic foreign bodies (e.g. in the eye); noisy, claustrophobic, slow, expensive; patient must stay still T1 vs T2. On T1-weighted images CSF is dark , fat is bright and white matter is brighter than grey matter: T1 looks like the anatomy textbook and is used for anatomy and volumetric measurement. On T2-weighted images CSF is bright and most pathology (oedema, inflammation, demyelination, tumour) is bright because it contains extra water: T2 is used to find lesions. FLAIR (fluid-attenuated inversion recovery) is a T2-type image with the CSF signal suppressed, so CSF is dark while lesions stay bright; this makes periventricular multiple sclerosis plaques easy to see. Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) shows an acute ischaemic infarct within minutes, far earlier than CT. Memory hook "T2 = H 2 O bright": water (CSF) is white on T2. "World War 2": water white on T2. 4.5 Functional MRI (fMRI) Feature fMRI Full name Functional magnetic resonance imaging, usually BOLD fMRI Inventor / key people and year Seiji Ogawa described blood oxygenation level dependent (BOLD) contrast in 1990 (rat studies, PNAS ). John Belliveau published a human functional MRI study using injected contrast in 1991; the first human BOLD studies appeared in 1992 (groups including Kenneth Kwong, Ogawa and Peter Bandettini) What it measures, physical principle Deoxyhaemoglobin is paramagnetic and distorts the local magnetic field, lowering the MR signal; oxyhaemoglobin is diamagnetic and does not. When neurons become active, blood flow increases more than oxygen use, so the local concentration of deoxyhaemoglobin falls and the signal rises Structural or functional Functional Spatial resolution Good, about 1 to 3 mm Temporal resolution Moderate, seconds; the haemodynamic response peaks about 4 to 6 s after neural activity and lasts 10 to 20 s Radiation / invasive No radiation, no injection; non-invasive Clinical and research uses Cognitive neuroscience; pre-surgical mapping of language and motor areas; resting-state connectivity in psychiatric disorders Limits Indirect measure (blood, not neurons); slow; sensitive to head motion; noisy scanner; same contraindications as MRI; results are relative (task vs baseline), not absolute Why "indirect"? fMRI does not record neurons firing. It records a vascular response that follows neural activity. Nikos Logothetis and colleagues (2001) found the BOLD signal tracks local field potentials (synaptic input and local processing) better than spiking output. The haemodynamic response function may show a small initial dip, a peak at about 4 to 6 s, and a post-stimulus undershoot. Designs. In a block design the participant alternates long blocks (e.g. 20 to 30 s) of task and rest; it gives strong signal. In an event-related design brief single trials are presented and the response to each is modelled; this allows randomised trials and sorting by behaviour (e.g. remembered vs forgotten items). Resting-state fMRI measures spontaneous slow fluctuations while the person lies quietly: Bharat Biswal (1995) showed that left and right motor cortices fluctuate together at rest. Marcus Raichle and colleagues (2001, PNAS , "A default mode of brain function") named the default mode network (medial prefrontal cortex, posterior cingulate/precuneus, inferior parietal lobule), which is more active at rest and during self-referential thought and deactivates during external tasks. DMN abnormalities are reported in depression, schizophrenia, autism and Alzheimer's disease. Exam trap fMRI measures blood oxygenation (the ratio of oxygenated to deoxygenated haemoglobin), not neuronal firing, glucose use or electrical activity. And it is deoxy haemoglobin that is paramagnetic. 4.6 Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) Feature DTI Full name Diffusion tensor imaging (a form of diffusion MRI) Inventor / key people and year Peter Basser, James Mattiello and Denis Le Bihan, 1994; Le Bihan had introduced diffusion MRI in the mid 1980s What it measures, physical principle Water molecules diffuse more easily along axons than across them, because myelin and membranes restrict movement. DTI measures the direction and degree of this diffusion in each voxel Structural or functional Structural (white matter microstructure and connectivity) Spatial resolution About 2 mm Temporal resolution Not applicable Radiation / invasive None; non-invasive Clinical and research uses White matter integrity in traumatic brain injury, multiple sclerosis, schizophrenia, ageing; surgical planning to avoid major tracts Limits Crossing fibres confuse the tensor model; tractography can produce false tracts; cannot show direction of signal flow Fractional anisotropy (FA) ranges from 0 (diffusion equal in all directions, isotropic, as in CSF) to 1 (diffusion in a single direction). High FA indicates organised, intact white matter (e.g. corpus callosum); reduced FA is reported in many disorders. Tractography follows the principal diffusion direction from voxel to voxel to reconstruct fibre pathways such as the arcuate fasciculus. 4.7 Magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) MRS uses the same scanner but, instead of an image, produces a spectrum showing the concentration of chemicals in a chosen region (a "voxel"). Common peaks: N-acetylaspartate (NAA) , a marker of neuronal integrity that falls with neuronal loss; choline (membrane turnover, raised in tumours); creatine (energy metabolism, used as a reference); myo-inositol (glial marker); lactate (anaerobic metabolism); and glutamate/glutamine (often reported together as Glx) and GABA with special sequences. It is non-invasive, has no radiation, and is used in psychiatry research (e.g. glutamate in schizophrenia, GABA in depression). Its limits are low spatial resolution (voxels of a few cubic centimetres) and low signal. 4.8 Positron emission tomography (PET) Feature PET Full name Positron emission tomography Inventor / key people and year Earlier positron imaging by Gordon Brownell and William Sweet (1950s, Boston). The modern tomographic PET scanner was developed at Washington University, St Louis, by Michael Phelps, Edward Hoffman and Michel Ter-Pogossian, 1973 to 1975. 18 F-FDG was synthesised at Brookhaven by Tatsuo Ido and Alfred (Al) Wolf with colleagues, about 1976 to 1978 (sources differ on the exact year); the first human FDG brain images were made at the University of Pennsylvania (Abass Alavi, Martin Reivich) in 1976. FDG built on Louis Sokoloff's deoxyglucose method (published 1977) What it measures, physical principle A tracer labelled with a positron-emitting isotope is injected. Each positron travels a millimetre or so, meets an electron and annihilates , producing two 511 keV gamma photons travelling in opposite directions. Detectors in a ring register both photons simultaneously (coincidence detection) and the computer locates the source along that line Structural or functional Functional (metabolism, blood flow, receptor binding, protein deposits) Spatial resolution Moderate, about 4 to 5 mm clinically (better in research scanners) Temporal resolution Poor, tens of seconds (water) to many minutes (FDG uptake takes about 30 to 45 minutes) Radiation / invasive Ionising radiation; invasive (intravenous injection of a radioactive tracer) Clinical and research uses Dementia (temporoparietal hypometabolism in Alzheimer's disease), epilepsy focus (interictal hypometabolism), tumours; receptor studies, e.g. 11 C-raclopride for dopamine D2/D3 receptors and dopamine release, and amyloid PET (Pittsburgh compound B, reported in 2004) and tau PET Limits Radiation limits repeat scans; short-lived isotopes ( 15 O about 2 min, 11 C about 20 min, 18 F about 110 min) often need an on-site cyclotron; expensive; poor temporal resolution FDG (fluorodeoxyglucose) is a glucose analogue: it is taken up by active cells and phosphorylated but cannot be metabolised further, so it becomes trapped, and its concentration reflects regional glucose metabolism. With 15 O-labelled water, PET measures regional cerebral blood flow and was the main tool for cognitive activation studies in the 1980s and early 1990s before fMRI. 4.9 Single photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) Feature SPECT Full name Single photon emission computed tomography (also SPET) Inventor / key people and year David Kuhl and Roy Edwards, University of Pennsylvania, early 1960s (emission tomography reported around 1963) What it measures, physical principle A tracer emitting single gamma photons is injected; a gamma camera rotating around the head records them, and tomographic slices are reconstructed. No positrons, no annihilation, no coincidence detection Structural or functional Functional (mainly regional cerebral blood flow; also dopamine transporter) Spatial resolution Lower than PET, roughly 8 to 10 mm Temporal resolution Poor (minutes); but because HMPAO is fixed in the brain within minutes of injection, it gives a "snapshot" of flow at the moment of injection, useful for injecting during a seizure Radiation / invasive Ionising radiation; invasive (injection) Clinical and research uses Regional cerebral blood flow with 99m Tc-HMPAO or 99m Tc-ECD; ictal SPECT in epilepsy; dementia differential; DaTscan ( 123 I-ioflupane) images the dopamine transporter to distinguish Parkinsonian syndromes and dementia with Lewy bodies from essential tremor or Alzheimer's disease Limits Lower resolution and less quantitative than PET SPECT is cheaper and more widely available than PET because its isotopes (technetium-99m, half-life about 6 hours, from a generator) last longer and do not need an on-site cyclotron. That is why it is common in hospitals that cannot afford PET. Exam trap PET = positrons , which annihilate into two photons (511 keV each). SPECT = single photons . PET has better resolution; SPECT is cheaper. Both use radioactive tracers. 4.10 Electroencephalography (EEG) and event-related potentials (ERPs) Feature EEG Full name Electroencephalography Inventor / key people and year Richard Caton recorded electrical activity from animal brains in 1875. Hans Berger, Jena, made the first human recording in 1924 and published in 1929 ("Über das Elektrenkephalogramm des Menschen"); alpha is still called the "Berger rhythm". The 10-20 electrode system was introduced by Herbert Jasper in 1958 What it measures, physical principle Scalp electrodes record voltage differences produced by the summed postsynaptic potentials of large populations of synchronously active, parallel-oriented cortical pyramidal neurons Structural or functional Functional Spatial resolution Poor (centimetres); the skull smears the signal and the "inverse problem" means many source configurations fit the same scalp pattern Temporal resolution Excellent, milliseconds Radiation / invasive None; non-invasive; cheap and portable Clinical and research uses Epilepsy diagnosis, sleep staging (polysomnography), encephalopathy and delirium (diffuse slowing), brain death assessment, monitoring anaesthesia; ERP research on attention, memory and language Limits Poor localisation; mainly sees superficial cortex; artefacts from eye movements and muscle Rhythms (boundaries vary slightly between sources): Delta , about 0.5 to 4 Hz: deep (slow-wave) sleep, infants; in an awake adult suggests pathology. Theta , about 4 to 8 Hz: drowsiness, light sleep, children; frontal midline theta during concentration. Alpha , about 8 to 13 Hz: relaxed wakefulness with eyes closed, maximal over occipital regions; blocked by eye opening (alpha blocking). Beta , about 13 to 30 Hz: alert, active thinking; increased by benzodiazepines. Gamma , above about 30 Hz: feature binding, perception. In the 10-20 system electrodes are placed at 10% or 20% of the distance between skull landmarks (nasion, inion, preauricular points); letters denote region (Fp, F, C, T, P, O), odd numbers the left hemisphere, even numbers the right, and "z" the midline (Fz, Cz, Pz). ERPs are small voltage changes time-locked to a stimulus, extracted by averaging many trials. Key components: Contingent negative variation (CNV) : W. Grey Walter and colleagues (1964), a slow negative shift between a warning signal and an imperative stimulus, reflecting expectancy and preparation. P300 (P3) : Samuel Sutton, Margery Braren, Joseph Zubin and E. Roy John (1965), a positive wave about 300 ms after a rare, task-relevant stimulus in an oddball paradigm; reflects context updating; reduced amplitude in schizophrenia. Mismatch negativity (MMN) : Risto Näätänen, Anthony Gaillard and Sirkka Mäntysalo (1978), an automatic response to a deviant sound in a repetitive sequence, even without attention; reduced in schizophrenia. N400 : Marta Kutas and Steven Hillyard (1980), a negativity about 400 ms after a semantically unexpected word ("He spread the warm bread with socks"). 4.11 Magnetoencephalography (MEG) Feature MEG Full name Magnetoencephalography Inventor / key people and year David Cohen, 1968 (first recording of the alpha rhythm's magnetic field, with an induction coil); in 1972 Cohen recorded with a SQUID (superconducting quantum interference device, developed by James Zimmerman and colleagues) What it measures, physical principle The same neuronal currents that produce EEG also produce tiny magnetic fields (femtotesla range, billions of times weaker than the Earth's field). SQUID sensors cooled in liquid helium detect them inside a magnetically shielded room Structural or functional Functional Spatial resolution Better than EEG (a few millimetres for favourable sources), because magnetic fields pass through skull and scalp without being smeared Temporal resolution Excellent, milliseconds Radiation / invasive None; non-invasive Clinical and research uses Localising epileptic foci and eloquent cortex before surgery; language and auditory research Limits Very expensive; few centres; best for tangential sources (in sulcal walls) and nearly blind to radial sources (on gyral crowns) and deep sources; head must stay still Because EEG sees both radial and tangential sources but MEG mainly tangential ones, the two are complementary. Newer optically pumped magnetometers (OPMs) work without liquid helium and may make wearable MEG possible. 4.12 Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) Feature fNIRS Full name Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (also optical imaging, NIRS) Inventor / key people and year Frans Jöbsis, 1977 ( Science ), showed near-infrared light could monitor tissue oxygenation through the intact skull; functional brain studies developed in the early 1990s What it measures, physical principle Near-infrared light (about 650 to 950 nm) passes through scalp and skull; oxyhaemoglobin and deoxyhaemoglobin absorb it differently, so detectors a few centimetres from the source estimate changes in both Structural or functional Functional (haemodynamic, like fMRI) Spatial resolution Poor to moderate (about 1 to 3 cm) Temporal resolution Sampling is fast, but the haemodynamic signal itself is slow (seconds) Radiation / invasive None; non-invasive Clinical and research uses Infants and children, people who cannot lie in a scanner, naturalistic tasks (walking, conversation), bedside monitoring; it is cheap and portable and tolerant of movement Limits Reaches only the outer cortex (about 1 to 2 cm depth); no deep structures; scalp blood flow and hair interfere 4.13 Not imaging: TMS, the lesion method and intracranial recording Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) was introduced by Anthony Barker and colleagues in Sheffield in 1985. A coil held over the scalp produces a brief, strong magnetic pulse that induces an electrical current in the cortex underneath, depolarising neurons. Single pulses over motor cortex cause a muscle twitch (motor evoked potential); repetitive TMS (rTMS) can raise or lower cortical excitability for a while. It stimulates the brain; it does not image it. Its research value is causal: a temporary "virtual lesion" tests whether a region is necessary for a task. Clinically, rTMS over the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex is approved for treatment-resistant depression (US FDA clearance 2008), and it is used in Indian centres including NIMHANS (details of individual services not verified here). The lesion method infers function from what is lost after brain damage (Paul Broca's patient "Tan", 1861; Phineas Gage, 1848; H.M., 1953). It is causal but depends on accidents of nature, and lesions rarely respect functional boundaries. Intracranial recording (electrocorticography from grids on the cortex, or depth electrodes, in epilepsy surgery patients) gives both excellent temporal and excellent spatial resolution but is highly invasive and done only for clinical reasons. Exam trap TMS uses a magnet, like MRI and MEG, but it is a stimulation technique, not an imaging technique. If asked which option is "not a neuroimaging method", TMS (or ECT, or tDCS) is the answer. 4.14 Master comparison table Method Structural / functional What is measured Spatial resolution Temporal resolution Ionising radiation Pneumoencephalography Structural Air-filled ventricles on X-ray Poor Not applicable Yes Angiography / DSA Structural (vascular) Contrast-filled vessels on X-ray Very high (vessels) Seconds Yes CT Structural X-ray attenuation (density) About 0.5 to 1 mm Not applicable Yes MRI Structural Proton relaxation (T1, T2) About 1 mm Not applicable No DTI Structural Water diffusion along axons About 2 mm Not applicable No MRS Neurochemical Metabolite concentrations Low (cm voxels) Minutes No fMRI Functional Blood oxygenation (BOLD) About 1 to 3 mm Seconds No PET Functional Positron tracer: glucose, flow, receptors, amyloid About 4 to 5 mm Minutes Yes SPECT Functional Single-photon tracer: blood flow, dopamine transporter About 8 to 10 mm Minutes Yes EEG / ERP Functional Scalp electrical potentials Poor (cm) Milliseconds No MEG Functional Magnetic fields of neuronal currents Better than EEG (mm to cm) Milliseconds No fNIRS Functional Oxy/deoxyhaemoglobin by light absorption About 1 to 3 cm, surface only Seconds No TMS Neither (stimulation) Induces cortical current About 1 cm Milliseconds No High yield Best temporal resolution: EEG and MEG (milliseconds). Best spatial resolution among non-invasive functional methods: fMRI. Only invasive methods (intracranial recording) give both. Radiation: CT, angiography, PET, SPECT. No radiation: MRI family, EEG, MEG, fNIRS. 4.15 Imaging in psychiatry Schizophrenia: enlarged lateral ventricles. Eve Johnstone, Timothy Crow, Christopher Frith and colleagues (1976, The Lancet ) showed on CT that chronic schizophrenia patients had larger lateral ventricles than controls. This was the first CT demonstration and revived interest in brain structure in schizophrenia (pneumoencephalography studies from 1927 had hinted at it). Later MRI work added reduced hippocampal, temporal and grey matter volume. Hypofrontality. Reduced frontal activity in schizophrenia was first described by David Ingvar and Göran Franzén (1974) using xenon-133 regional cerebral blood flow, before PET; it was later reported in PET studies (e.g. Monte Buchsbaum and colleagues, early 1980s) and in fMRI during working memory tasks, though findings are inconsistent. Dopamine. PET with raclopride showed increased amphetamine-induced dopamine release in schizophrenia (mid-1990s studies) and is used to estimate antipsychotic D2 occupancy (therapeutic window about 65% to 80%, commonly cited). OCD. PET studies (Lewis Baxter and colleagues, 1987) reported hypermetabolism in the orbitofrontal cortex and caudate nucleus, which decreased after successful treatment with medication or behaviour therapy; this supports the cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical circuit model. Depression. Reduced activity in dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and altered subgenual cingulate activity (target of deep brain stimulation by Helen Mayberg, 2005). Dementia. MRI hippocampal atrophy and FDG-PET temporoparietal hypometabolism in Alzheimer's disease; amyloid PET to detect plaques. Indian context. NIMHANS, Bengaluru, has a dedicated neuroimaging and interventional radiology department with MRI and is a major centre for psychiatric neuroimaging research (for example, MRI studies in schizophrenia and OCD), and it offers clinical neuromodulation (rTMS, tDCS, ECT). Exact current scanner types and whether PET is available on campus were not verified, so do not rely on this paragraph for a specific factual MCQ. 4.16 Exam traps Exam trap CT uses X-rays, not magnets. CAT = computerised axial tomography = CT (same scan). MRI uses no ionising radiation (magnetic field plus radio waves). Its danger is metal, not radiation. fMRI measures blood oxygenation , not neuronal firing directly. PET-FDG measures glucose metabolism. PET uses positrons (two 511 keV photons); SPECT uses single photons . EEG: best temporal, poor spatial. fMRI: better spatial, poor temporal. MEG vs EEG: both milliseconds; MEG localises better and is less distorted by the skull, but sees mainly tangential sources and is far costlier. TMS is not an imaging technique. Angiography needs contrast dye. Egas Moniz: angiography 1927, Nobel 1949 for leucotomy. Nobel pairings: CT = Hounsfield and Cormack (1979); MRI = Lauterbur and Mansfield (2003), not Damadian. Berger: first human EEG 1924, published 1929. Do not confuse the two years. T1: CSF dark. T2: CSF bright. FLAIR: T2 with CSF made dark. 4.17 Self-check Which technique has the best temporal resolution? (a) PET (b) fMRI (c) EEG (d) SPECT Answer: (c). EEG records electrical activity in milliseconds; the others depend on slow haemodynamic or metabolic changes. The BOLD signal in fMRI depends mainly on the magnetic properties of: (a) Oxyhaemoglobin (b) Deoxyhaemoglobin (c) Glucose (d) Gadolinium Answer: (b). Deoxyhaemoglobin is paramagnetic; its local decrease raises the signal. The first clinical CT scan was performed by: (a) Paul Lauterbur, 1973 (b) Godfrey Hounsfield, 1971 (c) Egas Moniz, 1927 (d) Michael Phelps, 1975 Answer: (b). At Atkinson Morley's Hospital, London, in 1971. On a T2-weighted MRI, cerebrospinal fluid appears: (a) Dark (b) Bright (c) Invisible (d) Same as bone Answer: (b). Water is bright on T2; dark on T1 and on FLAIR. Which of the following involves no ionising radiation? (a) CT (b) PET (c) SPECT (d) MRI Answer: (d). MRI uses a magnetic field and radiofrequency pulses. Coincidence detection of two 511 keV photons is the basis of: (a) SPECT (b) PET (c) MEG (d) CT Answer: (b). Positron annihilation yields two photons travelling in opposite directions. Fractional anisotropy is a measure derived from: (a) MRS (b) DTI (c) fNIRS (d) ERP Answer: (b). FA indexes directional water diffusion, mostly reflecting white matter organisation. Which of these is NOT a neuroimaging technique? (a) MEG (b) fNIRS (c) TMS (d) SPECT Answer: (c). TMS (Barker, 1985) stimulates cortex rather than recording or imaging it. The P300 component was first described by: (a) Kutas and Hillyard, 1980 (b) Sutton and colleagues, 1965 (c) Näätänen and colleagues, 1978 (d) Grey Walter and colleagues, 1964 Answer: (b). Kutas and Hillyard described the N400, Näätänen the MMN, Grey Walter the CNV. Enlarged lateral ventricles in schizophrenia were first demonstrated on CT by: (a) Johnstone and colleagues, 1976 (b) Ingvar and Franzén, 1974 (c) Baxter and colleagues, 1987 (d) Raichle and colleagues, 2001 Answer: (a). Ingvar and Franzén described hypofrontality, Baxter the OCD PET findings, Raichle the default mode network. 5. NIMHANS 31 May: the nine you asked about Right after the NIMHANS MClinPsy paper on 31 May 2026 you sent the questions you could recall. Nine of them were asked here by name: questions 36 to 41 (George Vaillant's level for dissociation, systematic desensitization, awareness training in habit reversal, confidence in flashbulb memories, paradoxical intention, where ICD-11 puts gender incongruence), the Bavisha question on the gunas, the dharana questions and the Kegel question. Each section below is the concept with its neighbours, the ones a paper can swap in next time. The full why page with 27 questions, the trap under every wrong option, is at missed-concepts , and the same 27 are a mock in the Tests app. 5.1 Vaillant's ladder of defences (Q36: dissociation) George Vaillant ( Adaptation to Life , 1977), working from the Harvard Grant Study, ranked the defences Sigmund and Anna Freud (1936) described into four levels by maturity. Your Q36 asked where dissociation sits: neurotic . Level Defences What it means I. Psychotic Delusional projection, psychotic denial (of external reality), distortion Reality testing lost; psychosis, dreams, early childhood II. Immature Projection, schizoid fantasy, hypochondriasis, passive aggression, acting out Normal in adolescence; in adults, personality disorders and substance misuse III. Neurotic Repression, displacement, reaction formation, intellectualization (isolation, undoing), dissociation (neurotic denial) Private distress, reality testing intact, the person functions IV. Mature Altruism, humour, sublimation, suppression , anticipation Healthy adults; predicted better health, work and marriage in the Grant Study The DSM-IV Defensive Functioning Scale (1994) uses seven levels instead; dissociation is at the mental inhibitions (compromise formation) level, with repression, displacement, intellectualization, isolation of affect, reaction formation and undoing. Same neighbours, same verdict. Exam trap Suppression is conscious and mature; repression is unconscious and neurotic. Projection is immature, but delusional projection is psychotic. Dissociation is not immature, however dramatic dissociative disorders look. 5.2 Systematic desensitization and its neighbours (Q37) Joseph Wolpe, Psychotherapy by Reciprocal Inhibition (1958). Principle: reciprocal inhibition (a term from Charles Sherrington): a response incompatible with anxiety, made in the presence of the feared stimulus, weakens the stimulus-anxiety bond. That is counterconditioning. Steps: (1) relaxation training (Edmund Jacobson's progressive relaxation, 1938); (2) anxiety hierarchy rated on SUDS, 0 to 100 (Wolpe, 1969); (3) imagine each scene while relaxed, moving up only when calm. Forerunner: Mary Cover Jones (1924), little Peter and the rabbit. Technique What is done Mechanism Systematic desensitization Relaxation paired with a graded hierarchy, usually imagined Counterconditioning In vivo desensitization Same, with the real stimulus Counterconditioning Flooding Most feared stimulus at full strength, no escape, until anxiety falls Extinction Implosive therapy (Stampfl and Levis, 1967) Flooding in imagination, exaggerated scenes with psychodynamic themes Extinction Aversion therapy Unwanted behaviour paired with an emetic or a shock Classical conditioning of an aversion Exposure and response prevention (Meyer, 1966) Face the obsession's trigger, block the compulsion (OCD) Extinction plus blocking negative reinforcement Exam trap Reciprocal inhibition is the principle; systematic desensitization is the technique. 'Gradual' and 'relaxation' mean desensitization; 'full intensity' and 'no escape' mean flooding. 5.3 Habit reversal training (Q38: awareness training) Nathan Azrin and Gregory Nunn (1973). For tics, Tourette's and body-focused repetitive behaviours: trichotillomania, skin picking, nail biting, also stuttering. Original package, four phases: Awareness training : response description, response detection, early warning (the urge or first movement), situation awareness. Your Q38. Competing response training : a physically incompatible, inconspicuous action (clench fists for hair pulling) held about a minute, or three minutes in the original, or until the urge passes. Habit control motivation : inconvenience review, social support, public display. Generalization training : rehearsing the routine across situations, often in imagination. Simplified HRT (Raymond Miltenberger, Wayne Fuqua and Douglas Woods, 1998): awareness training, competing response training, social support. CBIT (John Piacentini and colleagues, 2010) is HRT plus function-based work, first-line for tics. Exam trap HRT is not the treatment for OCD (that is ERP), even though trichotillomania and excoriation sit in DSM-5's obsessive-compulsive and related chapter. Negative practice (Knight Dunlap, 1932), performing the habit on purpose until fatigue, is the opposite idea. 5.4 Flashbulb memory (Q39: confidence) Vivid, detailed memories of the circumstances in which you heard shocking news. Canonical details: place, ongoing activity, informant, own feeling, others' feeling, aftermath. Study Event Finding Roger Brown and James Kulik (1977) Kennedy assassination, 1963 Coined the term; proposed a special 'Now Print!' mechanism (Livingston, 1967) Ulric Neisser and Nicole Harsch (1992) Challenger explosion, 1986 Re-tested about 2.5 years later: accuracy poor, about a quarter wrong on every major detail, confidence still high Jennifer Talarico and David Rubin (2003) 9/11, against an everyday memory Both lost consistency at the same rate; only flashbulb memories kept vividness and belief in accuracy. 'Confidence, not consistency' Kathy Pezdek (2003) 9/11 Most students 'remembered' seeing the first plane hit live on TV; that footage aired only the next day William Hirst and colleagues (2009, 2015) 9/11, national sample Consistency dropped in year one, then levelled off; confidence stayed high Why vivid: emotional arousal at encoding (amygdala boosting hippocampal consolidation, James McGaugh) plus heavy rehearsal through media and retelling. No special mechanism needed. Exam trap Subjective confidence is very high and stays high; accuracy (consistency) falls like any memory. 'Confidence falls in step with accuracy' is wrong. 5.5 Paradoxical intention and Frankl's toolkit (Q40) Viktor Frankl, logotherapy, the 'third Viennese school' after Sigmund Freud and Alfred Adler. Primary motive: the will to meaning. Lack of meaning: existential vacuum, noogenic neurosis. Technique Targets Instruction Paradoxical intention (first described 1939) Anticipatory anxiety, fear of a symptom Intend or wish for the feared thing, with humour: 'try to stay awake', 'show them how much you can sweat' Dereflection Hyper-reflection, excessive self-watching Turn attention away from yourself, to the partner, a task, a meaning Socratic dialogue Loss of meaning Questioning that helps the client find meaning Neighbours: negative practice (Knight Dunlap, 1932: perform the habit on purpose until fatigue); symptom prescription in family therapy (Milton Erickson, Jay Haley, Paul Watzlawick, 1974); for insomnia, stimulus control (Richard Bootzin, 1972: get up if not asleep in about 20 minutes) and sleep restriction (Arthur Spielman, 1987: limit time in bed). Exam trap 'Doing the opposite of the goal to reach the goal' is paradoxical intention. 'Stop watching yourself' is dereflection. Sensate focus is William Masters and Virginia Johnson (1970), not Viktor Frankl. 5.6 Gender incongruence: where it sits now (Q41) System Name Where Key point ICD-10 Gender identity disorders, F64 (transsexualism F64.0, dual-role transvestism F64.1, GID of childhood F64.2) Chapter V, mental and behavioural Framed as a mental disorder ICD-11 (adopted 2019, in force 1 Jan 2022) Gender incongruence: HA60 adolescence or adulthood, HA61 childhood Chapter 17, Conditions related to sexual health No distress needed; code kept for access to care DSM-III (1980) Transsexualism; GID of childhood Mental disorder DSM-IV (1994) Gender identity disorder Mental disorder Identity itself labelled DSM-5 (2013), DSM-5-TR (2022) Gender dysphoria Own chapter Distress or impairment; 6 months; 2 of 6 (adults), 6 of 8 (children) Also moved to ICD-11 Chapter 17: sexual dysfunctions (HA00 to HA03) and sexual pain-penetration disorder (HA20). Stayed in Chapter 6: paraphilic disorders (6D30 to 6D3Z). Sleep-wake disorders moved out of the mental chapter to Chapter 7. Exam trap Gender incongruence was relocated, not deleted. ICD-11 says gender incongruence; DSM-5 says gender dysphoria. 5.7 The three gunas (the Bavisha question) From Samkhya (Kapila; Ishvarakrishna's Samkhya Karika ) and the Bhagavad Gita (chapters 14, 17, 18). Prakriti, matter including the mind, is made of three gunas, always present together; the dominant one shapes the person. Purusha is pure consciousness, the witness. Guna Quality In a person Clinical mapping Sattva Light, clarity, balance Calm, truthful, content, wise Mental health Rajas Activity, passion Restless, ambitious, craving, angry, greedy Anxiety, agitation, mania Tamas Darkness, heaviness, inertia Dull, lethargic, withdrawn, deluded, oversleeping Depression, apathy Bavisha, jobless, stressed, not eating, unable to act: shutdown, so tamas alone . Research measure: the Vedic Personality Inventory (David Wolf, 1998). Exam trap Yama is a limb of yoga (ethical restraints), not a guna or a state, so 'yama' and 'both yama and tamas' are wrong. Stressed and racing would be rajas; stuck and inert is tamas. 5.8 Patanjali's eight limbs (dharana) Yoga Sutras: yoga is 'chitta vritti nirodhah', stilling the mind's fluctuations (1.2). The eight limbs, ashtanga (2.29). Mnemonic: Yogis Never Argue, Peaceful People Don't Disturb Silence. # Limb Meaning 1 Yama Restraints: ahimsa, satya, asteya, brahmacharya, aparigraha 2 Niyama Observances: shaucha, santosha, tapas, svadhyaya, ishvara pranidhana 3 Asana Posture, steady and comfortable (2.46) 4 Pranayama Breath regulation 5 Pratyahara Withdrawal of the senses (2.54) 6 Dharana Concentration: binding the mind to one point (3.1) 7 Dhyana Meditation: unbroken flow of that focus (3.2) 8 Samadhi Absorption, only the object remains (3.3) Dharana + dhyana + samadhi on one object = samyama (3.4). Limbs 1 to 5 are bahiranga (outer), 6 to 8 antaranga (inner). Jnana yoga is a path in the Gita (with karma and bhakti), not a limb. Exam trap Senses in is pratyahara; mind fixed on one point is dharana; focus flowing on its own is dhyana. Pranayama before pratyahara, dharana before dhyana. 5.9 Kegels and the pelvic floor Arnold Kegel, American gynaecologist, 1948: exercises for urinary incontinence after childbirth. Target: the pelvic floor , mainly the levator ani and its pubococcygeus (PC) part, running from the pubic bone to the tailbone and supporting the bladder, bowel and uterus. Method: squeeze and lift for a few seconds, relax, repeat in sets. Uses : stress urinary incontinence, postpartum recovery, pelvic organ prolapse, incontinence after prostate surgery, faecal incontinence. Early biofeedback : Kegel's perineometer, a pressure gauge the patient watched. Biofeedback types: EMG (tension headache, pelvic floor), thermal (migraine, Raynaud's), GSR (arousal), heart rate variability, EEG or neurofeedback (ADHD, epilepsy). Sex therapy : part of directed masturbation for female orgasmic disorder (Joseph LoPiccolo and W. Charles Lobitz, 1972); an add-on for premature ejaculation; pelvic floor relaxation with graded dilators for vaginismus. Exam trap Bed-wetting in a child is not a Kegel problem. First-line is the enuresis alarm, the bell-and-pad (O. Hobart Mowrer and Willie Mae Mowrer, 1938), or desmopressin. Squeezing the buttocks or abdomen is not a Kegel. 5.10 Self-check: your nine Which type of defence mechanism is dissociation? (a) Mature (b) Immature (c) Neurotic (d) Conscious Answer: (c). Neurotic. A technique in which a response that inhibits anxiety is paired with an anxiety-provoking stimulus, step by step, to break the conditioned link between that stimulus and anxiety is: (a) Systematic desensitization (b) Flooding (c) Aversion therapy (d) Exposure and response prevention Answer: (a). Systematic desensitization. In habit reversal training (HRT), the technique used to make the person aware of the habit is: (a) Competing response training (b) Social support (c) Generalization training (d) Awareness training Answer: (d). Awareness training. The subjective confidence people have in their flashbulb memories is: (a) Low, because the event was emotionally shocking (b) Very high, and it stays high even as accuracy falls (c) Moderate, and in line with how accurate the memory is (d) High at first, then falls in step with accuracy Answer: (b). Very high, and it stays high even as accuracy falls. An intervention in which the person deliberately does, or wishes for, the very opposite of the therapeutic goal in order to reach that goal is: (a) Paradoxical intention (b) Dereflection (c) Negative practice (d) Reciprocal inhibition Answer: (a). Paradoxical intention. In ICD-11, gender incongruence is placed in: (a) Chapter 6, Mental, behavioural or neurodevelopmental disorders (b) Chapter 5, Endocrine, nutritional or metabolic diseases (c) Chapter 17, Conditions related to sexual health (d) Nowhere: it was removed from ICD-11 altogether Answer: (c). Chapter 17, Conditions related to sexual health. Bavisha lost her job. Since then she is stressed, has stopped eating properly and cannot get herself to do anything. According to yogic philosophy, the main issue she is dealing with is: (a) Yama alone (b) Tamas alone (c) Both yama and tamas (d) Rajas alone Answer: (b). Tamas alone. Which of the eight limbs of yoga is concentration, directing the mind's energy to a single point? (a) Pratyahara (b) Jnana (c) Dhyana (d) Dharana Answer: (d). Dharana. Kegel exercises strengthen which part of the body? (a) The abdominal (core) muscles (b) The pelvic floor muscles (c) The lower back (lumbar) muscles (d) The gluteal (buttock) muscles Answer: (b). The pelvic floor muscles.

title: Unit 3 – Psychometrics & Test Construction
text: Unit 3 – Psychometrics & Test Construction The science of measuring the mind: how a psychological test is built, scored and judged. This book teaches the four scales of measurement, the anatomy of a good item and how to analyse one, the full reliability and validity families with their formulae, the meaning of norms and standard scores, and the major families of real tests – intelligence, neuropsychological, personality, interest and aptitude – together with where and why each is applied (education, occupation, military, clinic). It closes with the M.Phil-style exam questions folded in. Sourced from Rodrick Prashanth's Unit 3 decks (Areas of testing, Applications of testing, Interest & aptitude tests, Item writing & item analysis, Reliability/Validity/Norms, Scales) and the M.Phil question bank, deepened to NIMHANS clinical depth. In this book Scales of measurement & attitude scaling Item writing & item analysis Reliability Validity Norms & standard scores Areas of testing: intelligence & creativity Areas of testing: neuropsychological assessment Areas of testing: personality assessment Interest & aptitude tests Applications of testing Structured personality-test construction M.Phil exam questions 1. Scales of measurement & attitude scaling The one idea. Before you can measure a psychological attribute you must decide what kind of number you are assigning. S. S. Stevens' four levels of measurement – nominal, ordinal, interval, ratio – form a ladder: each rung adds one mathematical property and therefore unlocks one more legitimate statistic. Choosing the wrong scale is the commonest hidden error in test interpretation: you cannot average ranks, and you cannot say one IQ is "twice" another. The four levels Level Allows categorising Allows ranking (order) Equal intervals True (absolute) zero Example Nominal Yes – – – Diagnosis codes, gender, jersey numbers Ordinal Yes Yes – – Rank in class, Likert agree/disagree, race finishing order Interval Yes Yes Yes – Temperature in °C, IQ scores, calendar years Ratio Yes Yes Yes Yes Reaction time, weight, number of errors, age Why each property matters. A nominal scale only labels – the numbers are names, so the only legitimate operations are counting frequencies and the mode. An ordinal scale adds order, so you can take a median and percentiles, but the gaps between ranks are unequal (the difference between 1st and 2nd is not the same "amount" as between 2nd and 3rd). An interval scale adds equal spacing, so you can finally add, subtract and compute a mean and standard deviation; but its zero is arbitrary (0°C is not "no temperature"). A ratio scale adds a true zero meaning total absence of the attribute, so ratios become meaningful: 40 errors is genuinely twice 20 errors. High-yield Memorise the ladder of properties: N ominal = categorise; O rdinal = + order; I nterval = + equal intervals; R atio = + true zero. Each level permits everything the levels below it permit, plus one more. Mnemonic NOIR (French for "black") gives the order of increasing power: N ominal → O rdinal → I nterval → R atio. Trap Interval vs ratio. Both have equal intervals; only ratio has a true zero. IQ and Celsius temperature are interval – an IQ of 0 does not mean "no intelligence," so you cannot say IQ 140 is "twice as smart" as IQ 70. Kelvin temperature and reaction time are ratio. Attitude scales Attitude measurement applies these principles to subjective opinion. The deck names four classic formats: Scale Structure Key feature Likert scale Five ordered responses on an agree/disagree or approve/disapprove continuum (e.g. Strongly Agree → Strongly Disagree) Summative; the most widely used attitude format. Strictly ordinal, though usually treated as interval in practice. Guttman scale Items ordered by intensity; a respondent who endorses one statement also endorses all milder statements on the same continuum Cumulative / unidimensional. "Check the statement from each group that is most true of you." Semantic differential (Osgood) A set of bipolar adjective scales (Healthy – Unhealthy, Pleasant – Unpleasant) anchoring a 7-point line Measures the subjective meaning and affective reaction to a concept; classic dimensions are Evaluation, Potency, Activity. Stapel scale A single ( unipolar ) adjective with 10 categories from −5 to +5, no neutral zero A one-adjective alternative to the semantic differential; forces a direction. Trap Semantic differential vs Stapel. Semantic differential uses bipolar adjective pairs with a neutral midpoint; the Stapel scale uses a single (unipolar) adjective on a −5 to +5 line with no neutral point . Guttman is cumulative (endorsing a strong item implies endorsing the weaker ones); Likert is summative. 2. Item writing & item analysis The one idea. A test is only as good as its items. Item construction is part craft (writing clear, unambiguous questions) and part statistics (keeping the items that actually discriminate among people and dropping those that do not). Item analysis is the set of empirical methods for that pruning. Guidelines for item writing (DeVellis, 2012) Define clearly what you want to measure before writing anything. Generate an item pool larger than the final test, so weak items can be discarded. Avoid exceptionally long items – length adds reading load, not information. Keep reading difficulty appropriate to the intended respondents. Avoid "double-barrelled" items that pack two ideas into one statement ("I feel anxious and depressed") – the respondent cannot answer cleanly. Mix positively and negatively worded items to counter acquiescence (yea-saying) response bias. Item formats & correction for guessing The dichotomous format scores an item 0 or 1 (true/false, right/wrong). The polytomous format gives each item more than two alternatives. In a multiple-choice item, the incorrect alternatives are called distractors ; it is usually best to write three or four good distractors per item, and three distractors are about as effective as five in most cases. Because a low-ability test-taker can score by guessing, scores are sometimes adjusted by a correction for guessing : Definition Corrected score = R − W/(n − 1) , where R = number of right responses, W = number of wrong responses, and n = number of choices per item. The formula subtracts an estimate of how many "right" answers were really lucky guesses. Mathematical treatments summarise the mean, the reliability from the binomial distribution, and a guessing threshold – the chance that a low-ability test-taker will reach each score. Personality and attitude measures, by contrast, do not score responses right or wrong; they quantify a characteristic of the response using formats such as Likert, the category scale, and the Q-sort. Item difficulty (p) Item difficulty is defined by the proportion of people who get the item correct – confusingly, a higher p means an easier item. The optimal difficulty level lies roughly halfway between 100% correct and the chance level. Worked example for a four-choice item (chance = .25): Half the difference between 1.00 and chance: (1.00 − 0.25)/2 = 0.75/2 = 0.375 Add chance back: 0.375 + 0.25 = 0.625 Shortcut: (chance + 1.00)/2 = (0.25 + 1.00)/2 = 0.625 A good test, however, needs items at many difficulty levels, because it must discriminate across the whole range of ability. For most tests, items in the range .30 to .70 maximise the information they give about differences between individuals. Some achievement tests deliberately load on harder items to identify high-ability candidates. Trap High p = EASY item, not hard. p = .90 means 90% passed it (easy); p = .20 means only 20% passed (hard). The "optimum" .625 for a 4-choice item already builds in the chance correction – for a true/false item (chance .50) the optimum is (.50 + 1.00)/2 = .75. Item discrimination Item discriminability asks whether the people who did well on a particular item also did well on the test as a whole. There are two classic approaches: The extreme-group (discrimination index) method. Compare a high-scoring group (e.g. top third of the class) with a low-scoring group (bottom third). Find the proportion in each group who got the item correct; the difference between these proportions is the discrimination index (D) . The closer D is to 1.0, the better the item. A negative D (the weak students passed it more often than the strong ones) is a red flag. The point-biserial method. The correlation between a dichotomous variable (passed/failed the item) and a continuous variable (total test score) is the point-biserial correlation , used here as an index of discriminability. On a short test, correlating an item with the total score is problematic because the item itself inflates the total, so an item-remainder (item-total minus that item) score is used – e.g. on a six-item test, correlate passing item 1 with the score from items 2–6. If the value is negative or low, drop the item. Item characteristic curves & Item Response Theory An item characteristic curve (ICC) graphs total test score on the X-axis against the proportion of examinees passing that item on the Y-axis. A good item's curve rises steeply across the ability range. Newer approaches, collectively Item Response Theory (IRT) , give each item its own ICC describing the probability of a correct response given the ability level of the test-taker . IRT models use one, two, or three parameters: difficulty, discriminability, and a guessing parameter (the probability that the lowest-ability test-takers answer correctly). Because a computer can identify exactly which items pin down a given ability level, IRT enables computer-adaptive testing : the test-taker is not forced through items far above or below their level, sparing time and embarrassment. High-yield Two pillars of item analysis: difficulty (p) = proportion correct (high = easy, optimum ~.625 for 4-choice); discrimination = does the item separate strong from weak test-takers (discrimination index D = difference in pass rates between high and low groups; point-biserial = item–total correlation). IRT generalises this to per-item curves and powers adaptive testing. Criterion-referenced tests A criterion-referenced test compares performance against a defined standard of learning rather than against other people. You first specify objectives precisely (what the programme should achieve), then evaluate items by giving the test to two groups – one that has had the learning unit and one that has not. The resulting frequency polygon looks like a V : low scorers (left) are the un-taught group, high scorers (right) the taught group. The bottom of the V is the antimode (least frequent score), which is taken as the cutting score – the point of decision separating those who have mastered the unit from those who have not. Trap Norm-referenced vs criterion-referenced. Norm-referenced compares you to others (percentile rank). Criterion-referenced compares you to a fixed standard ("80% correct = pass"); item variability is deliberately minimal, which is why traditional reliability formulae are inappropriate for them. 3. Reliability The one idea. Reliability is consistency of measurement. A reliable test gives much the same result on repeated, equivalent measurement. Reliability is never all-or-none; it is a matter of degree, expressed as a coefficient between 0.0 and 1.0. Classical (true-score) theory Classical test theory says any observed score is the sum of a true score and error: X = T + e , where T comes from factors that contribute to consistency and e from factors that contribute to inconsistency . Sources of measurement error: item selection, test administration, and test scoring. There is also systematic measurement error , where (unknown to the developer) the test consistently measures something other than the intended trait; the model becomes X = T + e s + e u (systematic + unsystematic error). Assumptions of the classical model: measurement errors are random; the mean error of measurement = 0; true scores and errors are uncorrelated (r Te = 0); errors on different tests are uncorrelated (r 12 = 0). It follows that the variance of obtained scores is the variance of true scores plus the variance of error: σ 2 X = σ 2 T + σ 2 e . Definition The reliability coefficient (r XX ) is the ratio of true-score variance to total score variance: r XX = σ 2 T / σ 2 X = σ 2 T / (σ 2 T + σ 2 e ) . It ranges from 0.0 (all error) to 1.0 (all true score). The families of reliability Reliability splits into temporal stability (test–retest, alternate-forms) and internal consistency (split-half, coefficient alpha), plus interscorer reliability for subjectively scored tests. Test–retest reliability The most straightforward method: administer the identical test twice to the same heterogeneous, representative sample and correlate the scores. Practice, maturation or schooling may raise the second score, but as long as the two sets of scores are strongly correlated, such effects do not threaten test–retest reliability. Psychometricians treat test–retest as the gold-standard approach. Its error source is changes over time . Alternate-forms (parallel-forms) reliability Two forms of a test are independently built to the same specifications (often item-by-item), so they share statistical and normative properties. Administer both to the same group and correlate. This shares features with test–retest (two administrations with a gap) but adds item-sampling differences as an extra source of error variance; alternate forms are also expensive to construct. Immediate alternate-forms isolates item sampling; delayed alternate-forms adds change over time. Split-half reliability Administer the test once , split it into two equivalent halves, and correlate the half-scores. The challenge is splitting the test into truly equivalent halves; since items are often ordered by difficulty (first half easier), the standard solution is to compare odd items vs even items . Because a half-test is shorter (and shorter tests are less reliable), the half-test correlation must be stepped up to a full-test estimate with the Spearman-Brown formula : Definition r SB = 2r hh / (1 + r hh ) , where r hh is the half-test reliability and r SB the estimated full-test reliability. Example: a half-test reliability of .70 corrects to a full-test reliability of about .82 . Split-half estimates are generally similar to, but often a little higher than, test–retest estimates. Its error sources are item sampling and the particular nature of the split. Coefficient alpha (Cronbach, 1951) Rather than rely on one arbitrary split, Lee Cronbach proposed averaging across all possible splits. Coefficient alpha can be thought of as the mean of all possible split-half coefficients, each corrected by Spearman-Brown. Definition r α = [N/(N−1)] × (1 − Σσ 2 j / σ 2 ) , where N = number of items, σ 2 j = variance of one item, Σσ 2 j = sum of item variances, and σ 2 = variance of total scores. Like all reliability estimates, α ranges 0.00–1.00. Alpha is traditionally read as an index of unidimensionality – how far the scale measures a single factor. But beware: alpha rises with the number of items, so a high alpha can occur even with several dimensions if there are many items. This is exactly why psychometricians still treat test–retest as essential. Kuder-Richardson (KR-20) Coefficient alpha is the general case of an earlier formula by G. Frederic Kuder and Marion Richardson (1937): KR-20 . KR-20 applies to the special case where each item is scored 0 or 1 (dichotomous). Coefficient alpha extends the Kuder-Richardson method to items that are not scored 0/1 – for example an attitude scale where examinees choose strongly agree / agree / disagree / strongly disagree. Interscorer (inter-rater) reliability Some tests leave much to the examiner's judgment in assigning scores – projective tests, and tests of moral development and creativity fall here. A sample of tests is scored independently by two or more examiners and the pairs of scores are correlated. Interscorer reliability supplements the other estimates but does not replace them; you would still assess test–retest or another type in a subjectively scored test. (In behavioural observation, a common convention is that two observers should agree at r ≥ 0.80, or 80% inter-rater agreement for interval recording.) Synopsis of reliability methods Method No. of forms No. of sessions Main source(s) of error Test–retest 1 2 Changes over time Alternate-forms (immediate) 2 1 Item sampling Alternate-forms (delayed) 2 2 Item sampling + changes over time Split-half 1 1 Item sampling + nature of the split Coefficient alpha 1 1 Item sampling + test heterogeneity Interscorer 1 1 Scorer differences Special circumstances Unstable characteristics. When the trait itself changes fast (e.g. an electrodermal measure of emotional reactivity), test and retest must be nearly instantaneous to give an accurate reliability index. Speed vs power tests. A speed test has uniform, easy items where the score depends on how many you finish in the time – its reliability must come from test–retest or from two separately timed half-tests (with Spearman-Brown), not from an ordinary single-session split-half. A power test gives ample time but is hard enough that no one gets a perfect score. Restriction of range. Reliability is spuriously low if estimated on a homogeneous sample (e.g. estimating an IQ test's reliability by retesting only college students). Criterion-referenced tests. Their score variability is minimal by design, so traditional reliability approaches are simply inappropriate. High-yield Match the method to the error it isolates: test–retest = stability over time; alternate-forms = item sampling (+ time if delayed); split-half / alpha / KR-20 = internal consistency; interscorer = scorer disagreement. KR-20 = dichotomous items; alpha = its general (any-scoring) form. Speed tests must NOT use single-session split-half. 4. Validity The one idea. Validity is whether the inferences drawn from a test are appropriate, meaningful and useful – classically, whether the test measures what it purports to measure. Modern theory treats validity as a unitary concept, with the traditional "types" being different lines of evidence rather than separate validities. The three traditional categories are content, criterion-related, and construct validity. Trap Reliability is necessary but not sufficient for validity.
