A bathroom scale that reads 5 kg too heavy every time is perfectly reliable yet invalid. A test can be reliable and still measure the wrong thing; but a test that is not reliable cannot be valid. The validity coefficient is in fact capped by reliability (see below). Content validity Content validity is the degree to which the items are representative of the universe of behaviour the test was meant to sample – fundamentally a sampling question. The test's items are a sample from a larger population of possible items; if the sample is representative, the test has content validity. Developers must also specify the relevant universe of responses . Content validity is hardest to ensure for ill-defined traits, where it rests on the considered opinion of expert judges. Quantifying content validity. Two expert judges rate each item on a 4-point relevance scale; ratings are dichotomised into weak (1–2) vs strong (3–4) relevance and entered in a 2×2 agreement table. The coefficient of content validity = D / (A + B + C + D) , where D is the cell where both judges rated the item strongly relevant. Example: on a 100-item test both judges agreed 87 items were strongly relevant, giving 87/(4+4+5+87) = .87. Definition Face validity is whether a test merely looks valid to users, examiners and especially examinees. It is a matter of social acceptability, not a technical form of validity . Criterion-related validity Demonstrated when a test effectively estimates performance on an outcome measure (the criterion ). The test score is useful only insofar as it predicts the criterion accurately (e.g. a college entrance exam that predicts later GPA). Two sub-types differ by timing : Concurrent validity – criterion measures obtained at about the same time as the test scores. Correlations between a new test and an established test are typical evidence; the instrument must measure the same construct as the criterion test. Predictive validity – criterion measures obtained in the future (months or years later, like college grades predicted from an entrance exam). When a test is used for prediction, a regression equation is developed. A criterion must be reliable, appropriate, and free of criterion contamination (the criterion must not be influenced by the test itself). Crucially, the validity coefficient is bounded by reliability: Definition The theoretical upper limit of the validity coefficient is the square root of (test reliability × criterion reliability): r xy ≤ √(r xx · r yy ) . The standard error of estimate (SE est ) is the margin of error expected in the predicted criterion score. Trap Concurrent vs predictive. The only difference is timing of the criterion. "Same time" = concurrent; "later" = predictive. Both are species of criterion-related validity. Construct validity A construct is a theoretical, intangible trait on which people differ (leadership ability, overcontrolled hostility, depression, intelligence, psychopathy). Construct validity is the appropriateness of inferences about the underlying construct. All constructs share two features: there is no single external referent that can validate them (they cannot be fully operationalised), yet a network of interlocking suppositions can be derived from theory. Many theorists regard construct validity as the unifying concept for all validity evidence. Construct-validity studies fall into several categories: (1) test homogeneity – whether items/subtests are homogeneous and measure a single construct (select items correlating highly with the total score); (2) developmental changes – whether scores change with age as theory predicts (older children should know more vocabulary); (3) theory-consistent group differences – high-construct people score high; (4) theory-consistent intervention effects – scores move correctly after an intervention; (5) convergent and discriminant validation ; (6) factor analysis ; (7) classification accuracy . Convergent validity – the test correlates highly with other tests sharing the same construct. Discriminant validity – the test does not correlate with measures from which it should differ. When several traits are each measured by several methods and all pairs are correlated, the result is a multitrait-multimethod (MTMM) matrix (Campbell & Fiske) – the classic design for showing convergent and discriminant validity simultaneously. Factor analysis identifies the minimum number of factors needed to account for the intercorrelations among a battery of tests; you administer the battery to several hundred subjects and analyse the correlation matrix. Classification accuracy matters for screening tests – e.g. the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE), whose validity hinges on correctly classifying people as cases or non-cases. High-yield Three validity families: content (representative sampling of the item universe; quantified by expert-judge agreement), criterion-related (predicts an outcome – concurrent = now, predictive = later), and construct (measures the theoretical trait; the unifying concept; convergent = correlates with similar, discriminant = doesn't correlate with different; MTMM matrix; factor analysis). Face validity is "looks valid" and is NOT real validity. 5. Norms & standard scores The one idea. A raw score (e.g. "32 correct") is meaningless on its own. Norms give a frame of reference by describing how a representative standardisation (normative) sample performed, so an individual's score can be located relative to others. The deck title for the reliability material was "Reliability, Validity and Norms"; this section teaches the norm concepts at the depth NIMHANS expects. The normative sample Norms are only as good as the sample they come from. A good standardisation sample is large, representative of the population for whom the test is intended, and current (norms go stale – the Flynn effect means IQ norms drift over decades). Norms can be national, local, or subgroup-specific (by age, grade, sex). A test like the Henmon-Nelson provides two sets of norms – one by age, one by grade. Percentile ranks A percentile rank is the percentage of the norm group scoring at or below a given raw score (a percentile rank of 70 means you did as well as or better than 70% of the sample). Percentiles are intuitive and require only an ordinal scale, but they are not equal-interval : near the middle of a normal distribution, scores pile up, so a few raw-score points span many percentile points; at the extremes, large raw differences move the percentile little. A percentile band (used by the Kuhlmann-Anderson) reports a range, like a confidence interval, to remind the user that any single score has measurement error. Trap Percentile rank is not a percentage-correct score. 70th percentile means "better than 70% of people," not "70% of items correct." And percentiles are ordinal, so do not average them – the gap between the 50th and 55th percentile is much smaller in raw terms than the gap between the 90th and 95th. Standard scores Standard scores re-express a raw score in standard-deviation units, putting different tests on a common, equal-interval metric. Standard score Mean SD Notes / where used z-score 0 1 The basic standard score: z = (X − M) / SD . Can be negative; carries decimals. T-score 50 10 z rescaled (T = 50 + 10z) to avoid negatives/decimals. Used by the MMPI and many personality scales. Deviation IQ 100 15 (Wechsler) Wechsler's solution; replaced the old ratio IQ (MA/CA × 100). Stanford-Binet historically used SD 16. Stanine 5 ~2 "STAndard NINE": a single-digit 1–9 scale dividing the distribution into nine bands. Coarse but compact. Sten 5.5 2 "Standard TEN": a 1–10 scale used by Cattell's 16PF. Why standard scores beat percentiles for arithmetic: because they are equal-interval (built on the underlying normal curve), you can legitimately average them and compare across tests. In a normal distribution, about 68% of scores fall within ±1 SD, 95% within ±2 SD, and 99.7% within ±3 SD – the rule that lets you convert any z to a percentile and back. Mnemonic Means and SDs to memorise: z = 0, 1 · T = 50, 10 · IQ = 100, 15 · stanine = 5, 2 (1–9) · sten = 5.5, 2 (1–10). T-score → "Ten" SD; IQ → "fifteen". Definition The deviation IQ (Wechsler) expresses intelligence as a standard score with mean 100, SD 15: it locates a person relative to their own age group , fixing the flaw of the old ratio IQ (mental age ÷ chronological age × 100), which broke down in adulthood because mental age plateaus. High-yield Raw scores are uninterpretable; norms supply meaning. Percentile rank = % scoring at or below (intuitive but ordinal, not equal-interval). Standard scores (z, T, deviation IQ, stanine, sten) are equal-interval and comparable across tests. 68–95–99.7 within ±1/2/3 SD. Wechsler IQ: mean 100, SD 15. 6. Areas of testing: intelligence & creativity The one idea. Intelligence has never had one agreed definition – each theorist measured what they conceived. The major individual tests (Wechsler, Stanford-Binet) operationalise these ideas, and creativity tests extend the toolkit to divergent thinking. Definitions of intelligence (who said what) Theorist Intelligence is… Spearman (1904, 1923) A general ability involving the eduction of relations and correlates (the basis of his "g"). Binet & Simon (1905) The ability to judge well, understand well, reason well. Lewis Terman (1916) The capacity to form concepts and grasp their significance. Pintner (1921) The ability to adapt adequately to relatively new situations in life. Thorndike (1921) The power of good responses from the point of view of truth or fact. Thurstone (1921) The capacity to inhibit instinctive adjustments, imagine alternatives, and realise modified adjustments in behaviour. Wechsler (1939) The aggregate or global capacity to act purposefully, think rationally, and deal effectively with the environment. Humphreys (1971) The entire repertoire of acquired skills, knowledge, learning sets and generalisation tendencies available at one time. Jean Piaget (1972) The superior forms of organisation/equilibrium of cognitive structuring used for adaptation. Robert Sternberg (1985/86) The capacity to automatise information processing and emit contextually appropriate behaviour in response to novelty (meta-, performance, and knowledge-acquisition components). Hans Eysenck (1986) Error-free transmission of information through the cortex. Howard Gardner (1986) The ability to solve problems or fashion products valued within one or more cultural settings. Ceci (1994) Multiple innate abilities that develop or atrophy depending on motivation and exposure. Sattler (2001) Intelligent behaviour reflects the survival skills of the species. The Wechsler tests From the 1930s, David Wechsler at Bellevue Hospital built instruments that defined adult intelligence testing. The first, the Wechsler-Bellevue Intelligence Scale (1939), drew on the Binet scales and the Army Alpha and Beta tests. It was designed to fix flaws of earlier tests: items had no appeal for adults; too many emphasised mere word manipulation; instructions stressed speed over accuracy; and reliance on mental age was irrelevant to adults. Wechsler's corrections: a test designed specifically for adults; performance items added to balance verbal questions; reduced emphasis on speed; and a new deviation IQ method (score relative to one's own age group) rather than the ratio IQ. He split the scale into Verbal and Performance sections, hoping large V–P differences would aid psychiatric diagnosis. The three modern Wechsler tests are WAIS-IV (adults), WISC-IV (children), and WPPSI-IV (preschool). Common features: 13–15 subtests and an empirically based breakdown into composite/index scores plus a Full Scale IQ. Where the originals gave only Verbal IQ and Performance IQ, the WISC-IV and WAIS-IV now yield four index scores: Verbal Comprehension, Perceptual Reasoning, Working Memory, and Processing Speed . The WPPSI-IV (ages 4:0–7:7) adds a fifth, Fluid Reasoning . Other intelligence tests Stanford-Binet, Fifth Edition (SB5) – lineage to the Binet-Simon 1905 scale; the oldest, most prestigious pedigree. Built so each of five factors is assessed in two domains (nonverbal and verbal). The five factors (from Carroll, 1993; Alan Baddeley, 1986) are fluid reasoning, knowledge, quantitative reasoning, visual-spatial processing, and working memory ; crossing 5 factors × 2 domains gives 10 subtests. Detroit Tests of Learning Aptitude-4 (DTLA-4) – revision of a 1935 instrument; individually administered, ages 6–17; 10 subtests forming 16 composites (general intelligence, optimal level, and 14 ability areas). Cognitive Assessment System-II (CAS-II) – ages 5–17; explicitly built on the PASS theory (Planning, Attention, Simultaneous, Successive) of intelligence. Kaufman Brief Intelligence Test-2 (KBIT-2) – a brief screening test with a Verbal/Crystallised scale (Verbal Knowledge, Riddles) and a Nonverbal/Fluid scale (Matrices). Its brevity suits research and signalling the need for fuller assessment. Creativity Most definitions stress novelty and usefulness of the product, and treat creativity as a kind of process. Kaufman (2012) factor-analysed 94 items into five factors – Self/Everyday, Scholarly, Performance, Mechanical/Scientific, and Artistic creativity – producing the Kaufman Domains of Creativity Scale (K-DOCS) . Classic creativity tests: Remote Associates Test (RAT) (Mednick, 1962) – a timed 40-minute paper-and-pencil test indexing the remoteness of verbal associations (find a word linking three cues, e.g. rat–blue–cottage → "cheese"). Critics (Osche, 1990) say it is more a measure of verbal intelligence than of general creativity. Composite Creative Personality Scale (Harrington, 1975) – 42 self-checked adjectives. Guilford's Structure of Intellect (SOI) model parcelled intelligence into 150 factors; from the operations dimension came divergent thinking . J. P. Guilford's experimental divergent-thinking measures (Alternate Uses, Consequences, Ideational Fluency) were standardised as the Christensen-Guilford Fluency Tests . Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking (TTCT) – loosely based on Guilford; two parallel forms (A, B) and two parts (Verbal, Figural). Verbal scoring uses Fluency (number of relevant ideas), Originality (inventiveness), and Flexibility (range of categories). Figural scoring adds Abstractness of Titles, Elaboration, and Resistance to Premature Closure. High-yield Wechsler = deviation IQ + V/P split → four indices (VC, PR, WM, PS). SB5 = 5 factors × 2 domains = 10 subtests. CAS-II = PASS theory. Creativity's signature construct is J. P. Guilford's divergent thinking ; the TTCT scores Fluency, Originality, Flexibility (+ Elaboration on the figural part). 7. Areas of testing: neuropsychological assessment The one idea. Neuropsychological tests map cognition onto brain function across discrete domains – orientation, attention, memory, language, spatial ability, and executive function. The Mental Status Examination (MSE) is the loosely structured interview that usually precedes other assessment; it describes the patient's orientation, memory, thought, feeling and judgment and is the psychological equivalent of the general physical exam. By domain Sensory input. Reitan-Klove Sensory-Perceptual Examination (unilateral/bilateral stimulation in touch, hearing, vision – especially diagnostic if errors cluster on one side of the body); Finger Localization Test (identify touched fingers without sight). Attention & concentration. Test of Everyday Attention (TEA) (Robertson et al., 1994/96) measures sustained, selective, divided attention and attentional switching, with three parallel versions. The Continuous Performance Test (CPT) (Rosvold et al., 1956) measures sustained attention/vigilance – errors of omission (failing to respond to a target) and errors of commission (responding to a non-target). Digit Span and Serial Subtractions also index attention. Learning & memory. Wechsler Memory Scale-IV (WMS-IV) – nine subtests (seven for the Standard Battery) yielding five indices (Immediate Memory, Delayed Memory, Auditory Memory, Visual Memory, Visual Working Memory). Rey Auditory Verbal Learning Test (RAVLT) – descended from Claparede's free-recall of a 15-word list; five learning trials, an interference list, immediate recall, then a recognition trial. Wide Range Assessment of Memory and Learning-2 (WRAML-2) – first comprehensive memory scale for children (5–17, norms now to 90); three indices (Verbal Memory, Visual Memory, Attention/Concentration). Language. Standardised aphasia screening tests resemble the brief clinical exam but add objective, precise scoring; their weakness is missing subtle aphasia. Spatial & manipulatory ability. Bender Visual-Motor Gestalt Test (BGT) – design copying; the original nine cards, BGT-II adds seven; assembly tests (Benton 3-D Block Construction, forms A and B). Executive functions (logical analysis, conceptualisation, reasoning, planning, flexibility). Porteus Mazes ; Wisconsin Card Sorting Test (WCST) – sort 64 cards (1–4 symbols: triangle, star, cross, circle; in red, green, yellow, blue) by an unknown principle, told only "right"/"wrong" as you go (sensitive to perseveration and set-shifting); Lezak's Tinkertoy Test – build anything from 50 pieces, scored 21–112 (pieces used, mobility, symmetry, naming); promising for Alzheimer's assessment. Screening for alcohol use disorders CAGE – four questions: C utting down, A nnoyed by criticism, G uilty about drinking, E ye-opener in the morning. More effective for screening men than women. TWEAK – developed specifically for women: T olerance, W orried friends/relatives, E ye-opener, A mnesia, feeling the need to K ut down. Mnemonic Alcohol screens: CAGE (Cut down, Annoyed, Guilty, Eye-opener) for general/men; TWEAK for women. WCST → executive/set-shifting; CPT → sustained attention (omission vs commission errors); RAVLT → verbal learning over 5 trials. 8. Areas of testing: personality assessment The deck groups personality inventories by their method of construction (the next section unpacks the four strategies in full). Key instruments named: Theory-guided inventories Personality Research Form (PRF) (Jackson) – expands Murray's needs; short forms A/B and long forms AA/BB (440 true–false items); the long form gives 20 personality scores plus two validity scores (Infrequency, Desirability). State-Trait Anxiety Inventory (STAI) – current Form Y; distinguishes transient state anxiety from stable trait anxiety. Factor-analytically derived inventories Eysenck Personality Questionnaire (EPQ) – measures three dimensions: Psychoticism (P), Extraversion (E), Neuroticism (N) , plus a Lie (L) validity scale; 90 yes/no items (age 16+); Junior EPQ has 81 items (ages 7–15). Comrey Personality Scales (CPS) – 180 items, 8 trait scales (Trust, Orderliness, Social Conformity, Activity, Emotional Stability, Extraversion, Mental Toughness, Empathy) plus Validity Check (V) and Response Bias (R). Also factor-derived: 16PF and the NEO-FFI (Big Five). Criterion-keyed inventories: the MMPI The MMPI (1943) was a 566-item true–false inventory built for psychiatric diagnosis; the MMPI-2 (1989) restandardised it. Its four classic validity scales: Cannot Say (?) – total items omitted or double-marked. L (Lie) – 15 items scored "false"; endorsing personal virtue rarely seen in the culture flags faking-good. F (Infrequency) – 60 items endorsed by normals ≤10% of the time; reflects serious maladjustment, but very high F can also mean poor reading, random responding, faking-bad, or a "cry for help". K – a subtle defensiveness scale (30 items) detecting normal-looking profiles from defensive patients. High-yield MMPI validity scales = ? (Cannot Say), L (Lie), F (Infrequency), K (defensiveness) . EPQ measures P-E-N + Lie. STAI separates state (now) from trait (enduring) anxiety. 9. Interest & aptitude tests The one idea. Interest inventories measure what a person likes (vocational preferences), distinct from aptitude tests which measure what a person can learn to do . Both feed career counselling and personnel selection. History of interest inventories The first item pool of interest activities was assembled in a 1919 seminar by Clarence S. Yoakum at Carnegie Institute of Technology – a 1,000-item pool built by rational sampling to represent the whole domain of interests. Many later inventories grew from it: the Occupational Interest Inventory (Freyd, 1922–23), Interest Report Blank (Cowdery, 1926), General Interest Survey (Kornhauser, 1927), Vocational Interest Blank (Strong, 1927) , Purdue Interest Report (Remmers, 1929), Interest Analysis Blank (Hubbard, 1930), and the Minnesota Interest Inventory (Paterson et al., 1930). The earliest inventories used the atheoretical, empirical method of contrast groups : people with similar interests cluster together and can be differentiated from dissimilar groups. This logic underlies the Strong Interest Inventory (Harmon, Hansen, Borgen & Hammer, 1994), the Career Assessment Inventory (Johansson, 1975/1986), and the Campbell Interest and Skill Survey (CISS) (Campbell, Hyne & Nilsen, 1992). Theories of vocational interest Anne Roe (1956) and John Holland (1959) drew on J. P. Guilford's factor analysis, which found seven interest factors : (a) mechanical, (b) scientific, (c) social welfare, (d) aesthetic expression, (e) clerical, (f) business, and (g) outdoor work. Holland's theory of vocational personality (RIASEC). From data with the Vocational Preference Inventory (VPI) and other inventories, Holland proposed that people can be classed into six types (or combinations): R ealistic, I nvestigative, A rtistic, S ocial, E nterprising, C onventional. The types arrange on a hexagon in R-I-A-S-E-C order: adjacent types (e.g. Realistic–Investigative, Enterprising–Conventional) are more related than opposite types (e.g. Realistic–Social, Artistic–Conventional). His theory spawned the Self-Directed Search (SDS) , the ACT Interest Inventory, the Career Decision-Making System-Revised (CDM-R; Harrington & O'Shea, 1993), and the General Occupational Themes of the Strong Interest Inventory. Mnemonic Holland's hexagon: RIASEC – " R ealistic I nvestigators A nd S ocial E nterprising C onventionals." Adjacent = similar; opposite = dissimilar. Current inventories Major current interest inventories include the Vocational Preference Inventory (Holland, 1985), the Self-Directed Search, various forms of the Kuder , the Strong Interest Inventory, the Career Assessment Inventory, the Jackson Vocational Interest Survey (JVIS) (Jackson, 1977), the unisex ACT Interest Inventory (UNIACT; Lamb & Prediger, 1981), and the Vocational Interest Inventory. Campbell Interest and Skill Survey (CISS) profile has three scale types: 7 Orientation Scales (the major interest factors from statistical clustering), 29 Basic Scales (homogeneous content clusters such as Sales, Supervision, Adult Development, International Activities, Science, Woodworking, Military/Law Enforcement), and 60 Occupational Scales (built by E. K. Strong's empirical method of contrast groups, surveying successful, satisfied workers in 60 occupations). A distinctive CISS feature is reporting both interest and self-reported skill . Aptitude test batteries Aptitude tests predict future learning/performance and rely heavily on criterion-related validity (contrast with achievement tests, which look backward at what has been learned and rest on content validity). Major multiple-aptitude batteries (also covered in the applications deck) include the General Aptitude Test Battery (GATB) , the Armed Services Vocational Aptitude Battery (ASVAB) , the Differential Aptitude Test (DAT) , and the Employee Aptitude Survey. Specialised aptitude tests include the Bennett Mechanical Comprehension Test (mechanical aptitude via pictures of belts and flywheels; forms S and T), the Minnesota Spatial Relations Test and Revised Minnesota Paper Form Board (spatial), the Crawford Small Parts Dexterity Test and Purdue Pegboard (motor/dexterity), and the Minnesota Clerical Test (Number and Name Comparison, scored for speed with errors penalised). High-yield Interest inventories built by the empirical method of contrast groups (Strong, CISS, CAI). Holland's RIASEC hexagon is the most-tested vocational theory. CISS scales = 7 Orientation + 29 Basic + 60 Occupational. Aptitude predicts future ability (criterion-related validity); achievement measures past learning (content validity). 10. Applications of testing The one idea. The same psychometric machinery serves very different settings – schools, employers, the military, and the clinic. Each setting privileges a different kind of validity evidence. Testing in education Achievement tests measure the effects of a specific programme of instruction and represent a terminal evaluation of training; their validity is mostly content-related . Aptitude tests reflect the cumulative influence of everyday experience and predict subsequent performance, relying on criterion-oriented evidence. Group achievement tests: Stanford Achievement Test (10th ed., K–12); Metropolitan Achievement Test (MAT-8, renormed 2000, with Braille/large-print/audio versions). Group mental ability tests: Kuhlmann-Anderson (KAT, 8th ed., 8 levels, nonverbal at lower levels, scores as deviation IQs or percentile bands); Henmon-Nelson (single g score, norms by age and by grade, low ceiling, caution below 80 or above 130); Cognitive Abilities Test (CogAT, verbal/quantitative/nonverbal, good for poor readers and ESL, sensitive to giftedness). Graduate/professional entrance: GRE (verbal GRE-V, quantitative GRE-Q, analytical GRE-A – essay since 2002; overpredicts younger, underpredicts older students; prone to grade inflation); Miller Analogies Test (strictly verbal, 120 analogies in 60 minutes, has an age bias); LSAT (reading comprehension, logical reasoning, analytical reasoning). Early childhood / readiness: Metropolitan Readiness Tests (6th ed.); Boehm Test of Basic Concepts (relational concepts). School readiness = prerequisite skills enabling the learner to profit from instruction. Occupational / personnel selection I/O psychology emphasises criterion-related validity for selection – tests should correlate strongly with the criterion of job performance. Guion noted the difficulty of predicting complex behaviour (partly situation-dependent) from simple tests. Autobiographical data via a Biographical Information Blank, scored by empirical keying : contrast a successful and an unsuccessful group, find which biodata items discriminate, and weight them. Employment interview: reliability assessed by correlating different interviewers; prone to halo bias (rating high/low on all dimensions from a global impression); panel interviews raise reliability. Cognitive ability tests: general (Wonderlic Personnel Test – 50 items in 12 minutes, a speeded test, points added for those 30+; Shipley, Wesman); mechanical (Bennett); clerical (Minnesota Clerical Test); the multiple-aptitude GATB (12 tests, 9 factors, 3 composites). Personality in selection: most personality–proficiency correlations are negligible, but specific criteria predict better, and the Big Five (especially Conscientiousness) show useful operational validity (corrected for sampling error, range restriction, criterion unreliability). The CPI predicts managerial potential; the Inwald Personality Inventory and MMPI screen law enforcement; the Hogan Personality Inventory (built on the Big Five) predicts performance across settings. The added unique information a test gives is its incremental validity . Integrity tests: attitudes toward theft + overt admissions; overt vs personality-based types. Work samples (a miniature replica of the job) and situational exercises (the white-collar equivalent, for managerial selection). Military The ASVAB is used across the U.S. armed services – a multiple-aptitude battery for grades 11–12 with 10 subtests (general science, arithmetic reasoning, word knowledge, paragraph comprehension, numerical operations, coding speed, auto/shop, mathematics knowledge, mechanical comprehension, electronics information) grouped into academic, occupational, and overall composites. Clinical & counselling The WAIS and Stanford-Binet are staples; clinicians also do profile analysis – examining the pattern of subtest scores via three procedures: evaluating scatter (V–P differences, subtest variation), interpreting features against base-rate data , and matching score patterns to clinical syndromes (Alzheimer's, learning disability, anxiety). Later research found little significance in scatter and favoured combining objective scores with qualitative clinical interpretation. Specific learning disability is diagnosed when there is a severe discrepancy between intellectual ability and achievement, and the child is not achieving commensurate with age and ability despite appropriate education. Tools: Kaufman Test of Educational Achievement; Woodcock-Johnson; Stanford-Binet, K-ABC, Wechsler scales (for global index + qualitative deficits). Dynamic assessment deliberately departs from standardised administration – " testing the limits " and learning-potential assessment using a test–teach–test format. Behavioural assessment From the behavioural movement (1960s–70s), many clinicians shifted to directly assessing the target behaviour (motor responses, physiological responses like heart rate, and verbal reports). Lang & Lazovik's (1963) classic desensitisation paper introduced three still-used strategies: the Fear Survey Schedule (FSS) (50 fears rated 1–7), the Behavioural Avoidance Test (BAT) (motor approach to a phobic object), and the Fear Thermometer (rate discomfort 1–10). Behavioural assessment is integrated with treatment and formalised as the single-case experimental design . Four basic measurement approaches for ongoing behaviour: Method What it records Note Permanent products A lasting trace/result of behaviour (blood alcohol level, weight loss, a wet bed) Behaviour is inferred from the product; minimal observer time, high inter-rater agreement, but no guarantee the behaviour was performed appropriately. Event recording Tally the rate of the target behaviour Only for behaviours with clear beginning and end points; low-frequency behaviours need longer periods. Duration recording How long the behaviour lasts (per occurrence, cumulative, or % of total time) Requires discrete limits. Interval recording (time sampling) Whether the behaviour occurs in chosen time intervals For behaviours with unclear limits/rate; high inter-rater reliability; cannot distinguish frequency from duration within an interval. For inter-rater reliability, behavioural assessors use two observers; a primary observer and an independent checker who rates one-third to one-half of periods. By convention, a Pearson correlation ≥ 0.80, or 80% inter-rater agreement (interval recording), is acceptable. High-yield Setting → favoured validity: achievement/education = content; aptitude & personnel = criterion-related. Personnel: empirical keying, halo bias, incremental and operational validity. Behavioural assessment's four recording methods: permanent products, event, duration, interval (time sampling). 11. Structured personality-test construction The one idea. There are four strategies for building a structured (objective) personality test, grouped into deductive (logical-content, theoretical) and empirical (criterion-group, factor-analytic). Knowing which test was built by which strategy is a perennial exam target. Deductive strategies Logical-content strategy Items are written whose content logically taps the trait. Examples: Woodworth Personal Data Sheet – the first personality inventory; a "paper-and-pencil psychiatric interview" giving a single global score. Items endorsed by ≥25% of normals were excluded (to cut false positives); only symptoms occurring twice as often in a neurotic group as in normals were kept. Bell Adjustment Inventory – multidimensional: Home, Health, Social, Vocational/Occupational, Economic, Emotional functioning. Bernreuter Personality Inventory – ages 13+, six traits (introversion, confidence, sociability…). Mooney Problem Checklist (1950) – a list of problems recurring in case histories and students' written statements. Theoretical strategy Items are derived from a personality theory. Edwards Personal Preference Schedule (EPPS) – based on Murray's (1938) need system (achievement, deference, exhibition…); Edwards selected 15 needs and, to combat social-desirability response bias, paired items of comparable desirability in a forced-choice format. Choosing between two needs yields an ipsative score (relative, not absolute). A consistency scale repeats 15 item pairs. Personality Research Form (PRF-III) and Jackson Personality Inventory-Revised (JPI-R) – also based on Murray's needs, with strict definitional standards; include an F-like infrequency scale and a K-like social-desirability scale. The JPI-R has 300 true–false items, 15 scales, five higher-order dimensions (analytical, extroverted, emotional, opportunistic, dependable). The PRF is mainly for research. Definition An ipsative score (from forced-choice formats like the EPPS) expresses the strength of one trait relative to the person's own other traits , not relative to other people – so you cannot compare ipsative scores across individuals the way you can normative scores. Empirical strategies Criterion-group strategy Items are kept only if they empirically distinguish a criterion group from controls – content is irrelevant. MMPI – the archetype. Eight original clinical scales were built from eight criterion groups of 50 patients each, compared with ~700 controls. Plus the masculinity-femininity (Mf) and social-introversion (Si) scales. Validity scales: L (rationally derived lie scale), K (empirically identified defensiveness), F (infrequency/deviant responding), and ? (Cannot Say / omissions). The original MMPI had 550 items + 16 repeated = 566 ; the MMPI-2 has 567 items and adds validity scales F B (Back F), VRIN (Variable Response Inconsistency – random responding) and TRIN (True Response Inconsistency – acquiescence), plus 15 content scales (e.g. HEA health concerns, TPA Type A, FAM family problems, WRK work interference). California Psychological Inventory (CPI) – criterion-group method applied to normally adjusted people (counselling settings). 20 scales in four classes (I: poise/self-assurance; II: socialisation/maturity/responsibility; III: achievement potential/intellectual efficiency; IV: interest modes), plus 13 special-purpose scales (managerial potential, tough-mindedness, creativity). Factor-analytic strategy Statistical factor analysis reduces many items to a few underlying dimensions. Cattell's 16PF – from a catalogue reduced to 4,504 "real" traits → 171 terms → 36 surface traits → finally 16 source traits (basic dimensions of personality). The 16 factors themselves were factor-analysed into four second-order factors . Six forms (parallel forms at three vocabulary levels); parallel versions exist for younger ages (Junior-Senior High School PQ; Children's PQ). Clinical Analysis Questionnaire (CAQ) – extends the 16PF with 12 additional factors for clinical (psychopathology) assessment. Mnemonic Four construction strategies: Deductive = Logical-content + Theoretical (write items from logic/theory); Empirical = Criterion-group + Factor-analytic (let data decide). Robert Woodworth = logical-content; EPPS/PRF = theoretical (Murray's needs); MMPI/CPI = criterion-group; 16PF = factor-analytic. Trap MMPI item counts: original MMPI = 566 (550 + 16 repeated); MMPI-2 = 567 . Don't confuse the validity scales' origins: L was rationally derived, K was empirically identified. 12. M.Phil exam questions The M.Phil question bank ranges across clinical psychology; the psychometrics-relevant items are folded into the sections above. The remaining high-yield items (history, ethics, classification, assessment-data concepts) are distilled here with their keyed answers. History & the profession Who coined the term "mental tests"? – James McKeen Cattell (not Binet, Lewis Terman, or Wechsler). Clinical psychology was shaped by the psychometric and dynamic traditions. The U.S. armed forces began working with clinical psychologists due to a sudden dramatic expansion in World War I (psychologists began working with adults in WWI). Before World War II clinical psychology was not a recognised profession; WWII drove its rise. The Shakow Report recommended high academic and personal standards for selecting graduate students; its recommendations were adopted at the Boulder conference (the scientist-practitioner / "Boulder model"). Basic criticism: training students as both scientists and professionals is desirable in theory but hard in practice. Gordon Derner introduced the term scholar-professional ; the Vail report proposed the Doctor of Psychology (Psy.D.) degree. Recommended curriculum focus areas: Assessment, Research, and Treatment . Indian legal/regulatory framework Eligibility for M.Phil Clinical Psychology: a Master's degree in Psychology . The Rehabilitation Council of India (RCI) is under the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment ; its mandate (all of the above): regulate/monitor disability services, standardise rehabilitation/special-education syllabi, and maintain the Central Rehabilitation Register. Under the Mental Health Care Act, 2017 , registration with the RCI is mandatory to practise in India; the Act mandates rehabilitation professionals to register. Recognised clinical-psychology qualification (RPWD Act, 2016): a PG diploma in (Clinical/Applied) Psychology + M.Phil in Clinical Psychology or Medical and Social Psychology . Ethical standards in India are set by the RCI and the Indian Association of Clinical Psychologists (IACP) ; ethical guidelines also come from the IACP and the National Academy of Psychology (NAOP) . Assessment-data concepts The most standardised and consistent assessment tool is tests ; the most valid form of assessment is observation . A life record example is a medical history . Clinicians conceive assessment information as samples, correlates, or signs . The approach not tied to any theoretical orientation is the correlate-oriented / psychometric approach . Cognitive-function tools: Folstein's MMSE (systematic exam of higher mental functions; Memory category assesses all sub-types; Intelligence category assesses general knowledge and abstract thinking; Insight = awareness of one's illness); Glasgow Coma Scale = consciousness; Digit Span = attention; Serial Subtractions = attention. A significant disturbance of cognitive function commonly indicates an organic psychiatric disorder . Ethics The APA's Ethical Principles has five General Principles; Equity is NOT one of them. Integrity emphasises accuracy/honesty/truthfulness; Respect for People's Rights and Dignity emphasises privacy, confidentiality and self-determination. Deontological ethics judges the intrinsic nature of actions (moral duties/obligations); the utilitarian view judges by consequences (cost-benefit). The four pillars of principle-based ethics : beneficence, non-maleficence, justice, and respect for autonomy . Beneficence = acting in the person's best interests; when principles conflict, non-maleficence ("do no harm") is often the primary obligation. Confidentiality may be broken (IACP) given sufficient evidence of abuse in the family; in couple/family therapy the therapist is a relationship advocate (Margolin, 1982). Classification & psychopathology (high-yield keyed answers) The syndromal approach classifies disorders by clinical signs and symptoms (vs the historical approach by known etiology); a syndrome is a group of symptoms/signs occurring together. The two aspects judging DSM/ICD usefulness are reliability (agreement on diagnosis) and validity (distinguishing one diagnosis from another). The nomothetic framework (pre-established categories) is the mainstream "psychiatric model"; the idiographic framework (singularity of each case) suits psychoanalytic/psychodynamic approaches. Models of normality: Medical = absence of disorder; Utopian = optimal functioning; Subjective = absence of distress/disability/help-seeking; Social = socially acceptable behaviour; Continuum = normal and disorder at two ends of a continuum (severity above a cutoff = symptom); Process = a dynamic changing process; Statistical = within two SDs of the population's normal curve. DSM-IV-TR multiaxial system: Axis I clinical diagnosis; Axis II personality disorders + mental retardation; Axis III general medical conditions; Axis IV psychosocial/environmental problems; Axis V Global Assessment of Functioning. The DSM-5 dropped the multiaxial system and added a dimensional component. High-yield Memorise: "mental tests" = Cattell ; scientist-practitioner = Boulder model (from the Shakow Report); Psy.D = Vail ; RCI under Min. of Social Justice & Empowerment ; registration mandatory under MHCA 2017 ; four ethics pillars = beneficence, non-maleficence, justice, autonomy; DSM/ICD judged on reliability & validity .

title: Unit 4 — Biological Basis of Behaviour
text: Unit 4 — Biological Basis of Behaviour The full biological machinery of behaviour, built from the ground up: how a single neuron is wired and how it fires, the chemical languages it speaks, how those neurons are assembled into the brain and the rest of the nervous system, and the circuits that drive movement, every sense, hunger and thirst, emotion, the hormones and glands, sleep, heredity, and the methods scientists use to take the whole system apart. Anchored to Carlson & Pinel-level neuroscience and prioritised for MET 2026 and NIMHANS clinical psychology. In this book Neurons: structure, types & the neural impulse Neurotransmitters Structure & functions of the nervous system Divisions of the nervous system (CNS, PNS, ANS) Divisions of the human brain & their functions The motor (sensorimotor) system Sensory systems — vision Auditory & somatosensory systems Chemical & vestibular senses Hunger & thirst Emotions Hormonal regulation of behaviour The glandular (endocrine) system Sleep & biological clocks Genetics & behaviour Invasive & non-invasive research methods 1. Neurons: structure, types & the neural impulse The neuron is the information-processing and information-transmitting element of the nervous system. Everything else in this unit is about how neurons are built, how they fire, how they talk to each other, and how billions of them are wired into the brain. Master the neuron first and the rest of the unit becomes mechanism rather than memorisation. The four regions of a neuron Part What it is Function Cell body (soma) Contains the nucleus and most of the cell's life-support machinery; shape varies widely between neuron types. Keeps the cell alive; integrates incoming signals. Dendrites Branching projections; the major receivers of messages. Receive neural messages transmitted across the synapse (the small gap between a terminal button and the dendrite). Axon A long slender tube, often myelinated; works like an electrical cord. Carries the action potential away from the soma toward the terminal buttons. Terminal buttons Little knobs at the ends of axon branches. When an action potential arrives, they secrete a chemical messenger, the neurotransmitter . Definition Action potential — a brief electrical event that starts at the axon end nearest the cell body (the axon initial segment) and travels toward the terminal buttons. It is the basic message the axon carries. Axoplasmic transport Terminal buttons need molecules that can only be made in the soma, so substances are moved along the axon along microtubule "tracks". This is an active process, separate from the action potential. Anterograde transport (soma → terminal): accomplished by the motor protein kinesin , which "walks" along microtubules carrying cargo. Remarkably fast, up to 500 mm/day. Retrograde transport (terminal → soma): accomplished by the protein dynein ; about half as fast as anterograde transport. Types (classes) of neurons Multipolar neuron — more than two processes extending from the cell body (the most common type). Unipolar neuron — one process extending from the cell body (e.g. sensory dorsal-root neurons). Bipolar neuron — two processes (e.g. in the retina). Interneurons — neurons with a short axon or no axon at all; they integrate neural activity within a single brain structure . Neuroanatomical gross structures Composed of In the CNS In the PNS Mostly cell bodies Nuclei Ganglia Mostly axons Tracts Nerves Trap Cell-body clusters are nuclei in the CNS but ganglia in the PNS; axon bundles are tracts in the CNS but nerves in the PNS. The paper loves to swap these. Glial cells There are roughly equal numbers of neurons and glia in the human brain. Four kinds matter: Oligodendrocytes — paddle-shaped processes that wrap myelin around axons in the CNS . A single oligodendrocyte produces up to 50 segments of myelin. Myelin is 80% lipid, 20% protein and speeds axonal conduction. Schwann cells — perform myelination in the PNS ; one Schwann cell wraps one axon entirely. After PNS injury they digest dead axons and form cylinders that guide axonal regrowth, which is why PNS axons regenerate and CNS axons largely do not (the difference is in the supporting cells, not the axons). Microglia — the brain's immune cells; multiply after injury, engulf debris and dead cells, and trigger inflammation. Astrocytes — the largest glia, star-shaped; provide physical support, clean up debris, supply chemicals neurons need, gate substances between blood and CNS neurons, and contract/relax blood vessels to match local blood-flow demand. The resting membrane potential Recorded with intracellular microelectrodes, the inside of a resting neuron sits at about −70 mV relative to the outside. The neuron is then said to be polarized . Four ions matter: organic anions (A−), chloride (Cl−), sodium (Na+) and potassium (K+). At rest there is more Na+ outside the cell and more K+ inside; organic anions are trapped inside (too big to cross the membrane). Na+ feels strong pressure to enter from both the concentration gradient and electrostatic (electrical) pressure, but Na+ channels are mostly closed at rest. Balance is held by: The sodium–potassium pump — actively pushes 3 Na+ out for every 2 K+ in . More open K+ channels than Na+ channels, but few K+ actually leave because the negative interior holds them in. Mnemonic Resting potential = "bow and arrow." The membrane has done its work in advance (taut bowstring) so the neuron can fire strongly and rapidly the instant it is stimulated. The action potential, step by step Depolarization to threshold: a stimulus reduces polarization toward zero. If it crosses the threshold of excitation (about −65 mV), voltage-dependent Na+ channels open wide. Rising phase: Na+ rushes in explosively (driven by diffusion + electrostatic pressure). Membrane potential shoots from −70 mV to about +40 mV , overshooting zero to a reversed polarity. Peak (~1 ms): Na+ channels become refractory (blocked) and cannot reopen until the resting potential is restored. The slower voltage-dependent K+ channels (which need more depolarization to open) are now open. Falling phase: K+ flows out (driven by diffusion + electrostatic pressure since inside is now positive), returning the membrane toward −70 mV. It briefly overshoots (hyperpolarizes) until K+ channels close. Restoration: the Na+/K+ pump removes the Na+ that leaked in and retrieves the K+ that leaked out. High-yield All-or-none law: a neuron either fires fully or not at all. The amplitude and velocity of the action potential are independent of stimulus intensity. To encode stronger stimuli the axon changes the rate/timing of firing (rate code), not the size of each spike. The refractory period Absolute refractory period — the membrane cannot produce another action potential, regardless of stimulation (Na+ channels closed). Relative refractory period — a stronger-than-usual stimulus is needed (K+ is still flowing out faster than usual). The refractory period is why action potentials normally travel one way. Conduction in the natural direction (soma → terminal) is orthodromic ; an experimentally forced backward wave is antidromic . Conduction & the myelin sheath In the thinnest unmyelinated axons conduction is <1 m/s; increasing diameter raises it to about 10 m/s. Myelin (fats 80% / proteins 20%, found only on vertebrate axons) raises speed up to 100 m/s . The sheath is interrupted at nodes of Ranvier (~1 µm wide). Between nodes the signal travels passively and decrementally; at each node it regenerates. This jumping from node to node is saltatory conduction — faster and more energy-efficient than continuous conduction. Postsynaptic potentials & integration Neurotransmitters typically do one of two things to the receptive membrane: EPSP (excitatory postsynaptic potential) — depolarizes (e.g. −70 → −67 mV), making firing more likely. IPSP (inhibitory postsynaptic potential) — hyperpolarizes (e.g. −70 → −72 mV), making firing less likely. EPSPs and IPSPs are graded (size matches stimulus strength), generated at the dendrites, travel passively, and are decremental (shrink with distance). They are summed ( integration ) two ways: spatial summation (many synapses at once) and temporal summation (one synapse firing repeatedly). If the sum reaches threshold at the axon initial segment, an action potential fires. The synapse & synaptic transmission A synapse is the junction where messages pass from one neuron to another. Classified by location: axodendritic, axosomatic, dendrodendritic, axoaxonic . By distance to target: directed (release site near the receptor) vs nondirected (released from varicosities at a distance). Small neurotransmitters are synthesized in the terminal-button cytoplasm and packaged into vesicles by the button's Golgi complex; released in a pulse. Large neurotransmitters (neuropeptides) are assembled in the soma on ribosomes, packaged by the soma's Golgi complex, and transported down microtubules (~40 cm/day); released gradually and continuously. Coexistence: a neuron can contain two neurotransmitters. Release = exocytosis. Three vesicle pools: release-ready (docked, <1%), recycling (10–15%), and reserve (85–90%). Low firing uses release-ready; faster firing recruits the recycling then reserve pools. Receptors A receptor is a protein with binding sites for particular neurotransmitters; a neurotransmitter that binds is its ligand . Two main types: Ionotropic Metabotropic Mechanism Ligand directly opens an ion channel Coupled to G proteins (GTP-sensitive) Speed Immediate PSP (Na+ in → EPSP; K+ or Cl− → IPSP) Slower onset, longer-lasting, diffuse, varied Second messenger None Yes (the first discovered was cyclic AMP, made from ATP); can travel to the nucleus and switch genes on/off Autoreceptors respond to the neuron's own transmitter, usually on the terminal button, and are metabotropic. They do not change membrane potential; instead they regulate synthesis and release of the transmitter via G proteins. Terminating the signal Reuptake — transporters draw the transmitter back into the button for recycling. Enzymatic degradation — e.g. acetylcholinesterase (AChE) in the postsynaptic membrane breaks ACh into choline and acetate. Other forms of communication: electrical synapses (gap junctions, where membranes nearly touch and ions diffuse directly between cells, mostly dendrodendritic) and neuromodulators (mostly peptides, secreted in larger amounts, diffusing widely to modulate many neurons). 2. Neurotransmitters Neurotransmitters fall into large-molecule (neuropeptides) and small-molecule classes. The small molecules are the workhorses of fast, directed synaptic transmission. The families Neuropeptides (large): pituitary peptides, hypothalamic peptides, brain-gut peptides, opioid peptides, and miscellaneous peptides. Amino acids (small): glutamate, aspartate, glycine, GABA. Monoamines (small): catecholamines (dopamine, epinephrine, norepinephrine) and indolamines (serotonin). Acetylcholine — in a class of its own. Unconventional: soluble gases (nitric oxide, carbon monoxide) and endocannabinoids (e.g. anandamide). Amino acid neurotransmitters These mediate the vast majority of fast, directed synapses in the CNS. Glutamate is the most prevalent excitatory transmitter in the mammalian CNS. GABA (gamma-aminobutyric acid), synthesized by a simple modification of glutamate, is the most prevalent inhibitory transmitter (though excitatory at a few synapses). High-yield Glutamate = main excitatory ; GABA = main inhibitory . GABA is literally made from glutamate. Monoamine neurotransmitters Each is synthesized from a single amino acid, is slightly larger than the amino acid transmitters, and has more diffuse effects. The cell bodies sit in small clusters mostly in the brain stem , with highly branched axons studded with varicosities that release transmitter diffusely. Catecholamines — dopamine, epinephrine, norepinephrine; all synthesized from the amino acid tyrosine . Indolamines — serotonin; synthesized from the amino acid tryptophan . Acetylcholine (ACh) Created by adding an acetyl group to a choline molecule. It is the transmitter at neuromuscular junctions , at many autonomic synapses, and at several CNS synapses. Neurons that release ACh are cholinergic . ACh is unusual in being deactivated mainly by enzymatic degradation (by AChE) rather than reuptake. Unconventional neurotransmitters Soluble gases (nitric oxide, carbon monoxide): produced in the cytoplasm and immediately diffuse through membranes (they are lipid-soluble) into nearby cells, where they trigger a second messenger and are quickly deactivated. Involved in retrograde transmission . Endocannabinoids: similar to THC (the psychoactive compound of marijuana); the commonest is anandamide (from Sanskrit ananda , "eternal bliss"). Synthesized on demand from membrane fats, released from dendrites and soma, and act mostly on presynaptic neurons to inhibit subsequent transmission. 3. Structure & functions of the nervous system The nervous system divides into the central nervous system (CNS) — brain and spinal cord — and the peripheral nervous system (PNS) — the nerves and ganglia outside it. Gray matter is mostly cell bodies and unmyelinated interneurons; white matter is mostly myelinated axons. The spinal cord A long conical structure whose principal jobs are to distribute motor fibres to effector organs (glands and muscles) and to collect somatosensory information for the brain. It also has its own reflexive control circuits (a degree of autonomy from the brain). Protected by the vertebral column (24 vertebrae across cervical, thoracic, lumbar regions plus the fused sacral and coccygeal portions). The cord passes through the spinal foramen of each vertebra. Early in development cord and column are the same length; the column then grows faster, displacing the spinal roots downward. The most caudal roots travel farthest and form the cauda equina . 31 paired dorsal and ventral roots fuse to become spinal nerves. Dorsal root axons are sensory (afferent) unipolar neurons with cell bodies in the dorsal root ganglia . Ventral root neurons are motor (efferent) multipolar neurons with cell bodies in the ventral horns. Cross-section: an inner H-shaped core of gray matter surrounded by white matter . The meninges Three protective membranes cover the CNS: the tough outer dura mater , the web-like arachnoid mater , and the delicate pia mater hugging the cortex. The subarachnoid space (between arachnoid and pia) is filled with cerebrospinal fluid. High-yield Afferent = inward, toward the CNS (sensory). Efferent = outward, away from the CNS to muscles/glands (motor). Dorsal root = sensory; ventral root = motor. 4. Divisions of the nervous system (CNS, PNS & the autonomic nervous system) The peripheral nervous system Cranial nerves: 12 pairs attached to the ventral surface of the brain, mostly serving sensory and motor functions of the head and neck. The exception is the vagus nerve (X) ("wandering"), which regulates organs throughout the thoracic and abdominal cavities. Olfactory information enters via the olfactory bulbs, not a typical cranial nerve route. Spinal nerves: begin at the junction of dorsal and ventral roots, then travel out to muscles and sensory receptors. The autonomic nervous system (ANS) "Autonomic" = self-governing. It regulates smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, and glands — the body's "vegetative processes." It has two divisions, sympathetic and parasympathetic. Sympathetic division (thoracolumbar) Involved in expenditure of energy (fight-or-flight). Cell bodies of its motor neurons lie in the gray matter of the thoracic and lumbar cord — hence thoracolumbar . Preganglionic axons exit via ventral roots and synapse on postganglionic neurons in the sympathetic ganglion chain ; postganglionic neurons project to target organs (intestines, stomach, kidneys, sweat glands). Controls the adrenal medulla (which resembles a sympathetic ganglion), driving release of epinephrine and norepinephrine . Neurotransmitters: preganglionic terminals release acetylcholine ; postganglionic terminals on target organs release norepinephrine . Parasympathetic division (craniosacral) Supports conservation/storage of energy — salivation, gastric and intestinal motility, secretion of digestive juices, increased GI blood flow. Preganglionic cell bodies sit in the nuclei of some cranial nerves (especially the vagus) and the sacral cord — hence craniosacral . Ganglia lie near the target organs, so postganglionic fibres are short. Neurotransmitter: both pre- and postganglionic terminals release acetylcholine . Sympathetic vs parasympathetic effects Organ Sympathetic effect Parasympathetic effect Heart Increases heart rate Decreases heart rate Blood vessels Constricts in most organs Dilates in a few organs Iris radial muscles Dilates pupils No effect Iris sphincter muscles No effect Constricts pupils Tear gland No effect Stimulates secretion Sweat gland Stimulates secretion No effect Stomach & intestine No effect Stimulates secretion Lungs Dilates bronchioles; inhibits mucous Constricts bronchioles; stimulates mucous Arrector pili muscles Erects hair (gooseflesh) No effect Mnemonic Sympathetic = S pend energy, S ympathetic ganglion chain, releases n orepinephrine at the target. Parasympathetic = re p lenish/rest, cranio s acral, releases acetyl c holine everywhere. 5. Divisions of the human brain & their functions The brain develops from the neural tube: the rostral end becomes the forebrain , with the midbrain and hindbrain behind it. In adult mammals the forebrain neocortex surrounds the mid- and hindbrain. Forebrain — telencephalon: the cerebral cortex The cerebral cortex surrounds the hemispheres like bark on a tree and is heavily convoluted, with sulci (small grooves), fissures (large grooves) and gyri (bulges). These convolutions triple the cortical surface area (~2360 cm²). Because cell bodies dominate the surface it looks grayish — gray matter ; the myelinated axons beneath give white matter . Four lobes: frontal, parietal, temporal, occipital . Three primary sensory areas receive input: the visual cortex , auditory cortex and somatosensory cortex . The association cortex (the bulk of the cortex) does everything between sensation and action — perceiving, learning, remembering, planning, acting. The rostral region handles movement/planning; the caudal region handles perceiving and learning. Sensory association cortex near a primary area handles one modality; far from it, it integrates several. Forebrain — telencephalon: limbic system & basal ganglia Neocortex = the cortex covering most of the hemispheres ("new" cortex, recent in evolution). The limbic cortex lies around the medial edge ("limbus" = border). Limbic system: Papez (1937) proposed an interconnected circuit for motivation and emotion; Paul MacLean (1949) expanded it and coined "limbic system," noting its evolution coincided with emotional responses. Key members: the amygdala (emotion) and the hippocampus (learning and memory). Basal ganglia: a collection of nuclei beneath the cortex (under the anterior lateral ventricles), involved in the control of movement . Parkinson's disease results from degeneration of midbrain neurons that project to the caudate nucleus and putamen ; symptoms include weakness, tremor, limb rigidity, poor balance and difficulty initiating movement. Forebrain — diencephalon Sits between the telencephalon and midbrain; made of the thalamus and hypothalamus. Thalamus: two lobes joined by the massa intermedia . Most input to the cortex is relayed through it. Key relay nuclei: the lateral geniculate nucleus (from the eye), the medial geniculate nucleus (from the inner ear), and the ventrolateral nucleus (from the cerebellum to primary motor cortex). Hypothalamus: lies under the thalamus at the base of the brain. Controls the autonomic and endocrine systems and organizes survival behaviours. The pituitary gland attaches via the pituitary stalk; a portal blood system connects the hypothalamus to the anterior pituitary. Neurosecretory cells release hypothalamic hormones that drive the anterior pituitary, and the hypothalamus produces the posterior-pituitary hormones oxytocin and vasopressin (made by hypothalamic neurons whose axons end in the posterior pituitary). Midbrain (mesencephalon) Surrounds the cerebral aqueduct; two parts: Tectum (dorsal): the superior colliculi (visual-motor; orient the body toward/away from visual stimuli) and inferior colliculi (auditory). Tegmentum (beneath the tectum): contains the rostral reticular formation , eye-movement nuclei, the periaqueductal gray (mediates the analgesic effects of opioids), the red nucleus and substantia nigra (both sensorimotor), and the ventral tegmental area . The substantia nigra projects to the caudate and putamen. Hindbrain Surrounds the fourth ventricle; two divisions: Metencephalon — the cerebellum and pons. Cerebellum: receives visual, auditory, vestibular and somatosensory information plus data on individual muscle movements; integrates these and smooths/coordinates motor output. Attached to the pons by the superior, middle and inferior cerebellar peduncles . Damage impairs standing, walking and coordinated movement. Pons ("bridge"): contains part of the reticular formation (important in sleep and arousal) and a large nucleus relaying cortex-to-cerebellum information. Myelencephalon — the medulla oblongata , containing reticular-formation nuclei that control vital functions: the cardiovascular system, respiration and skeletal muscle tone. 6. The motor (sensorimotor) system Three organising principles Hierarchical organisation: association cortex → secondary motor cortex → primary motor cortex → brain stem/spinal circuits. Motor output is guided by sensory input. The only movements normally not guided by sensory feedback are ballistic movements — brief, all-or-none, high-speed (e.g. swatting a fly). Learning changes the nature and locus of control — practiced sequences become automatic and shift to lower levels. Sensorimotor association cortex Posterior parietal association cortex: integrates information about the location of body parts and external objects, directs behaviour with spatial information, and directs attention. It receives from the visual, auditory and somatosensory systems and outputs to dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, secondary motor areas and the frontal eye field. Damage produces deficits in spatial perception/memory, reaching and grasping, eye-movement control and attention — the most striking being apraxia and contralateral neglect . Dorsolateral prefrontal association cortex: receives from posterior parietal cortex and projects to secondary and primary motor cortex and the frontal eye field. The decision to initiate voluntary movement may be made here. Secondary motor cortex Receives mostly from association cortex and outputs to primary motor cortex. Areas: the supplementary motor area , the premotor cortex , and the later-identified cingulate motor areas . Mirror neurons (in the ventral premotor area) fire both when performing a goal-directed hand movement and when observing the same movement in another. Primary motor cortex Located in the precentral gyrus of the frontal lobe; the major point of convergence and departure of cortical sensorimotor signals. Modern evidence suggests neurons encode the target/goal of a movement rather than just its direction. Large lesions may disrupt independent movement of a body part, produce astereognosia , and reduce speed, accuracy and force — but do not eliminate voluntary movement, thanks to parallel descending pathways. Cerebellum & basal ganglia in motor control Cerebellum: compares three inputs — descending motor signals, brain-stem motor nuclei, and somatosensory/vestibular feedback — and corrects movements that drift off course. Important in motor learning , especially timing-critical sequences. Diffuse damage costs control of direction, force, velocity and amplitude, causes tremor on attempted movement, and disturbs balance, gait, speech and eye movement. Basal ganglia: a heterogeneous collection of nuclei in cortical loops (cortex → basal ganglia → thalamus → cortex), modulating movement. Important in habit learning — gradual, trial-by-trial motor learning. Descending motor pathways Two descend in the dorsolateral region of the cord and two in the ventromedial region. Betz cells are the extremely large pyramidal neurons of primary motor cortex. Dorsolateral tracts: terminate in the contralateral half of one cord segment, often directly on motor neurons; activate distal muscles (e.g. fingers). Ventromedial tracts: more diffuse, innervate interneurons on both sides across several segments; activate proximal trunk and limb muscles (e.g. shoulders). Skeletal muscles & the neuromuscular junction Flexors move a limb toward the body; extensors ("antigravity muscles") move it away. Extrafusal fibres — served by alpha motor neurons ; provide the muscle's motive force. An alpha motor neuron + its axon + its extrafusal fibres = a motor unit . Intrafusal fibres (muscle spindles) — specialised stretch-sensitive sensory organs served by sensory and gamma motor neuron axons; their contraction tunes the sensitivity of the spindle's afferent to stretch. They are muscle-length detectors . Golgi tendon organs — stretch receptors in tendons that encode how hard the muscle is pulling ( tension , not length). A muscle fibre is a bundle of myofibrils of overlapping actin and myosin ; the overlap produces the striations of striated muscle . At the neuromuscular junction , ACh from the terminal button depolarizes the motor endplate , producing an endplate potential (much larger than a neuronal EPSP) that always fires the fibre. Depolarization opens voltage-dependent Ca²⁺ channels; calcium acts as a cofactor letting myofibrils extract energy from ATP , triggering a twitch. Contraction strength depends on the average firing rate of the motor units. 7. Sensory systems — vision Sensory receptors are specialised neurons that detect physical events and, through sensory transduction , convert them into receptor potentials (changes in membrane potential). Most sensory receptors lack axons; their receptor potential modulates neurotransmitter release onto the dendrites of the next neuron. Anatomy of the eye The eye sits in the bony orbit , moved by six extraocular muscles . Light enters through the transparent cornea , with the opaque white sclera forming the outer coat elsewhere. The amount of light is set by the pupil (an opening in the pigmented iris ). The lens (onion-like transparent layers) changes shape via the ciliary muscles to focus near or far objects — accommodation . Light passes through the vitreous humor to the retina , which is part of the brain (CNS), as is the optic nerve. The retina & photoreceptors Three cellular layers: photoreceptive, bipolar-cell, and ganglion-cell. Light must pass through the (transparent) overlying layers to reach the photoreceptors at the back. ~ 120 million rods and ~ 6 million cones . Cones: daytime vision, fine detail (highest acuity ), and colour . The fovea (central retina, most acute vision) contains only cones. Rods: do not detect colour and give poor acuity, but are far more sensitive to light. In very dim light we use rod vision, so we are effectively colour-blind and lack foveal vision. The optic disk (where ganglion-cell axons leave via the optic nerve) is the blind spot — no receptors there. Signal flow: photoreceptors → bipolar cells → ganglion cells (whose axons form the optic nerve). Horizontal and amacrine cells combine messages laterally. Transduction Transduction begins with a photopigment embedded in the lamellae of the outer segment. The rod photopigment rhodopsin = an opsin protein ( rod opsin ) + retinal . When light hits rhodopsin it splits into rod opsin and retinal, triggering a cascade that hyperpolarizes the photoreceptor. Photoreceptors are therefore "darkness detectors": they depolarize in darkness (releasing more glutamate) and hyperpolarize in light. Bipolar cells respond to glutamate two ways: ON-center cells are hyperpolarized by glutamate, OFF-center cells are depolarized. Photoreceptors and bipolar cells do not fire action potentials; they signal by graded changes in transmitter release. From retina to cortex Ganglion-cell axons form the optic nerve , which meets at the optic chiasm . Axons from the nasal (inner) halves of each retina cross; axons from the temporal (outer) halves stay on the same side. They reach the dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) of the thalamus, which has six layers : layers 1, 4, 6 from the contralateral eye; layers 2, 3, 5 from the ipsilateral eye. The inner two layers (large cells) are magnocellular ; the outer four (small cells) are parvocellular . LGN axons travel via optic radiations to primary visual cortex (V1) in the occipital lobe, also called striate cortex for its dark-staining striation. V1 maps the contralateral visual field, devoting ~25% of itself to the fovea, and is organised into layers, cytochrome-oxidase (CO) blobs and modules. CO blobs (layers 2/3, faintly 5/6) handle colour ; interblob regions handle orientation, movement and binocular disparity. Magnocellular input arrives at sublayer 4Cα, parvocellular at 4Cβ, koniocellular at sublayers 2/3. Beyond V1 lies the extrastriate cortex (V2–V5), arranged hierarchically. Visual processing then splits into two streams: the ventral stream (V2 pale/thin stripes → V4 → inferior temporal cortex; the "what" pathway) and the dorsal stream (V2 thick stripes → posterior parietal cortex; the "where"/movement pathway). V5/MT (medial temporal) specialises in movement and can receive magnocellular input directly from V1. High-yield LGN layers: 1-4-6 contralateral, 2-3-5 ipsilateral ; inner two = magnocellular, outer four = parvocellular. Ventral stream = "what" (temporal), dorsal stream = "where" (parietal). 8. Auditory & somatosensory systems The auditory system The three physical dimensions of sound map onto perception: amplitude → loudness , frequency → pitch , complexity → timbre . Path of sound: outer ear → auditory canal → vibrates the tympanic membrane (eardrum) → the three middle-ear ossicles ( malleus /hammer, incus /anvil, stapes /stirrup) → the oval window → fluid in the snail-shaped cochlea → the organ of Corti (the auditory receptor organ). The auditory system is organised tonotopically (by frequency). Ear to auditory cortex Auditory-nerve axons synapse in the ipsilateral cochlear nuclei → superior olives on both sides → (via the lateral lemniscus ) the inferior colliculi → medial geniculate nucleus of the thalamus → primary auditory cortex . Unlike the single major visual pathway, audition uses a network of pathways. Sound localisation Medial superior olives — respond to slight differences in the time of arrival of signals at the two ears. Lateral superior olives — respond to slight differences in amplitude between the ears. Both project to the superior and inferior colliculi . The deep layers of the superior colliculus (auditory input) form a map of auditory space; the superficial layers (visual input) are organised retinotopically. Auditory cortex & coding Primary auditory cortex = three adjacent areas (the core ), ringed by the belt (secondary) and then parabelt areas. It is organised in functional columns and tonotopically . Two streams: the anterior pathway → prefrontal cortex identifies sounds ( what ); the posterior pathway → posterior parietal cortex locates sounds ( where ). Pitch coding uses both place coding (different frequencies flex different parts of the basilar membrane) and rate coding (pitch proportional to firing frequency). Bilateral lesions cause temporary deafness then permanent loss of sound localisation and frequency discrimination; unilateral lesions disrupt localisation only in contralateral space. The somatosensory system Body sensations are somatosensations , served by three interacting systems: Exteroceptive — external stimuli on the skin, with divisions for mechanical (touch), thermal and nociceptive (pain) stimuli. Proprioceptive — body position, from receptors in muscles, joints and organs of balance. Interoceptive — internal conditions (e.g. temperature, blood pressure). Mechanoreceptors (encapsulated receptors and free nerve endings) detect touch and pressure. Thermoreceptors are free nerve endings of two types: cold sensors just beneath the epidermis, warmth sensors deeper; sensation is relative except at extremes. Pain (nociception) uses networks of free nerve endings; at least three nociceptor types: high-threshold mechanoreceptors (intense pressure), receptors for extreme heat/acids/ capsaicin , and TRPA1 receptors (pungent irritants — mustard oil, horseradish, tear gas). The brain can reduce pain via endogenous opioids . Somatosensory pathways & cortex Axons enter the CNS via spinal nerves; the body area served by one segment's dorsal roots is a dermatome . Face/head input enters via the trigeminal nerve (V) . Two major ascending pathways: the dorsal-column medial-lemniscus system (touch and proprioception) and the anterolateral system (pain and temperature). Wilder Penfield (1937) mapped primary somatosensory cortex ( SI , in the postcentral gyrus) and found it is somatotopic — organised as a map of the body surface, the somatosensory homunculus . SII lies just ventral to SI, receives most input from SI and (unlike SI) substantial bilateral input. SI/SII are organised in columns; their output goes to posterior parietal association cortex. A dorsal stream → posterior parietal cortex (multisensory integration, attention); a ventral stream → SII (object-shape perception). Somatosensory deficits Damage to SI is often mild (parallel pathways). Unilateral SI lesions cause minor contralateral deficits — reduced light-touch detection and reduced stereognosis (recognising objects by touch). Agnosias: Astereognosia — inability to recognise objects by touch. Asomatognosia — failure to recognise parts of one's own body (usually left side; damage to right temporal/posterior parietal lobe), often with anosognosia (failure to recognise one's own symptoms) and a component of contralateral neglect . 9. Chemical & vestibular senses Olfaction (smell) and gustation (taste) are the chemical senses — they monitor the chemical content of the environment. The vestibular sense (in the inner ear) monitors balance and head position and feeds the cerebellum and sound-localisation circuits. Olfaction Olfactory receptor cells sit in the olfactory mucosa in the upper nose. Their dendrites lie in the nasal passages; their axons pass through the cribriform plate into the olfactory bulbs , where they synapse on neurons in clusters called olfactory glomeruli (these project via the olfactory tracts). There is mirror symmetry between the two bulbs, and the layout of glomeruli is consistent across members of a species — a poorly understood chemotopic map . Each bulb projects to the medial temporal lobe — the amygdala and the piriform cortex (the primary olfactory cortex ). Two pathways leave the amygdala-piriform area: one to the limbic system (the emotional response to odours), one via the medial dorsal thalamus to the orbitofrontal cortex (conscious perception of odours). High-yield Olfaction is the only sensory system whose major pathway reaches the cortex without first passing through the thalamus . Gustation Taste receptor cells occur in clusters of 50–100 called taste buds , often on raised papillae (only the larger papillae carry buds). One presynaptic cell per bud synapses onto the carrying neuron; the other cells communicate via gap junctions. There appears to be one receptor protein per taste receptor cell , and taste receptor proteins also occur in the throat, oesophagus and lungs. Pathway: gustatory afferents leave via the facial (VII) , glossopharyngeal (IX) and vagus (X) nerves (front of tongue, back of tongue, back of oral cavity respectively) → solitary nucleus of the medulla → ventral posterior nucleus of the thalamus → primary gustatory cortex in the insula → secondary gustatory cortex in the orbitofrontal cortex . Projections are mainly ipsilateral . Damage to the chemical senses Anosmia — inability to smell. Commonest neurological cause: a blow to the head displacing the brain and shearing the olfactory nerves at the cribriform plate. Ageusia — inability to taste; rare because taste travels via three separate nerves. Partial ageusia of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue on one side can follow middle-ear damage (the facial nerve's gustatory branch passes through the middle ear). The vestibular sense Housed in the inner ear alongside the cochlea, the vestibular apparatus detects head position and movement and contributes to balance. Vestibular information is one of the inputs the cerebellum integrates to coordinate movement, and the vestibular and somatosensory systems feed motor feedback. The auditory nerve (VIII) carries both a vestibular branch and an acoustic branch . 10. Hunger & thirst Regulatory mechanisms A regulatory mechanism has four features: a system variable (the quantity regulated), a set point (its optimal value), a detector that monitors it, and a correctional mechanism that restores it. The system runs on negative feedback . Because there is a delay between eating/drinking and replenishment, behaviour is also controlled by satiety mechanisms — brain mechanisms that monitor the correctional behaviour (e.g. drinking) rather than the system variable itself. Thirst Body fluid is intracellular and extracellular (the extracellular includes intravascular blood plasma and interstitial fluid). Two kinds of thirst: Osmometric thirst — when the solute concentration of interstitial fluid rises, drawing water out of cells by osmosis. Osmoreceptors (neurons whose firing depends on their hydration) detect cell shrinkage. They lie in the lamina terminalis , in two circumventricular organs — the OVLT (organum vasculosum of the lamina terminalis) and the SFO (subfornical organ), both outside the blood–brain barrier so blood-borne substances reach them. Most osmoreceptors are in the OVLT, connected to the anterior cingulate cortex (whose activity tracks felt thirst). Volumetric thirst — when blood plasma volume falls (hypovolemia from blood loss, vomiting, diarrhoea). It produces a salt appetite .
