The kidneys detect reduced blood flow and trigger the hormone angiotensin , which initiates drinking and salt appetite, conserves water and salt, and raises blood pressure. Atrial baroreceptors (stretch-sensitive cells in the heart's atria) also detect low blood volume. Integration: the SFO is where blood angiotensin acts; SFO neurons project to the median preoptic nucleus , which integrates OVLT and baroreceptor (via the solitary tract) information and controls drinking. Damage here can cause adipsia (lack of drinking). Hunger: the metabolic background Two nutrient reservoirs: Short-term reservoir — glycogen stored in liver and muscle cells. Long-term reservoir — adipose tissue (fat), storing triglycerides (glycerol + three fatty acids). Phase Hormone What happens Absorptive (digestive tract full) Insulin (from pancreas) Glucose rises; cells use it; liver converts glucose to glycogen; excess amino acids stored as fat. Parasympathetic activity up. Fasting (tract empty) Glucagon (from pancreas) Glucose reserved for the CNS; liver converts glycogen back to glucose; fat broken into glycerol + fatty acids (used by all cells except brain). Sympathetic activity up. Signals to start a meal Ghrelin — a peptide hormone released by the GI tract (mainly the stomach) during the fasting phase; binds hypothalamic receptors to stimulate eating. It also activates dopaminergic neurons in the ventral tegmental area (reward). Hypoglycemia (low blood glucose) is a potent hunger stimulus; liver receptors trigger glucoprivic hunger , relayed to the brain via the vagus nerve . The brain monitors glucose inside the blood–brain barrier; the liver monitors glucose and fatty acids outside it. Signals to stop a meal (satiety) Sensory and gastric: tasting/swallowing plus stomach distension; falling ghrelin after a meal is a gastric satiety factor. Intestinal: the duodenum secretes cholecystokinin (CCK) in response to fats — it contracts the gallbladder, constricts the pylorus and inhibits gastric contractions. Peptide YY₃₋₃₆ (PYY) is released by the small intestine after a meal in proportion to calories consumed. Liver: nutrients arriving from the intestines signal satiety; insulin also tells the hypothalamus to stop eating. Adipose: leptin is secreted by well-nourished fat cells and acts as an anti-obesity hormone with long-term effects on metabolism and eating. Brain mechanisms of eating Brain stem: the dorsal medulla (area postrema + nucleus of the solitary tract) receives taste from the tongue and visceral signals from stomach, duodenum and liver, relaying to the forebrain. Lateral hypothalamus triggers eating via orexigenic signals: melanin-concentrating hormone (MCH), orexin, and Neuropeptide Y (NPY) (NPY injections cause ravenous eating; NPY neurons sit in the arcuate nucleus and co-release AGRP , a long-lasting orexigen). Endocannabinoids (and THC) are also orexigenic. Ventromedial hypothalamus suppresses eating. Leptin binds receptors on the NPY/AGRP neurons; the arcuate nucleus also has anorexigenic neurons secreting CART and α-MSH (α-MSH binds MC4 receptors to inhibit eating). High-yield Lateral hypothalamus = "go eat" (orexigenic: NPY, AGRP, orexin). Ventromedial hypothalamus = "stop eating" (anorexigenic: leptin, CART, α-MSH). 11. Emotions The amygdala , hypothalamus and ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) are central to processing emotion. Three components of an emotional response (fear) Behavioural — muscular movements appropriate to the situation. Autonomic — facilitate the behaviour and mobilise energy quickly. Hormonal — reinforce autonomic responses; the adrenal medulla secretes epinephrine and norepinephrine , and the adrenal cortex secretes steroid hormones that make glucose available to muscles. These components are controlled by separate neural systems, but their integration is controlled by the amygdala . Amygdala & vmPFC The amygdala organises behavioural, autonomic and hormonal responses to situations producing fear, anger or disgust, and is involved in the effects of odours/pheromones on sexual and maternal behaviour. It receives inputs from the olfactory system, temporal-lobe association cortex, frontal cortex and the rest of the limbic system; it outputs to frontal cortex, hypothalamus, hippocampal formation and brain-stem nuclei controlling autonomic and species-typical behaviours. Extinction of conditioned emotional responses involves inhibitory control of the amygdala by the vmPFC . Aggression Aggression can be an actual attack or just threat behaviours (warning postures); threatened animals show defensive or submissive behaviours. These are modulated by the hypothalamus and amygdala; the periaqueductal gray is involved in defence and predation. Serotonin inhibits risk-taking and aggression. Low CSF 5-HIAA (a serotonin metabolite) correlates with more aggression in monkeys; destroying forebrain serotonergic axons enhances aggression, and drugs that boost serotonin reduce it. Hormonal control: androgens mainly affect offensive attack (not defensive, which females also show), with organisational and activational effects mediated by the medial preoptic area . In humans androgens may primarily increase motivation for dominance, with aggression secondary. vmPFC, impulse control & moral judgement The vmPFC governs emotional reactions and impulse control; lesions cause impulsive behaviour and outbursts. The amygdala (anger/violence) matures before the prefrontal cortex (which suppresses violence). Decreased prefrontal and increased subcortical activity accompany impulsive violence; antisocial personality disorder shows reduced prefrontal gray-matter volume. The vmPFC is activated in moral judgements involving conflict between utilitarian and personal moral choices; people with vmPFC damage make more utilitarian judgements. Communication & recognition of emotion Charles Darwin proposed emotional expressions are innate; Paul Ekman 's cross-cultural work (isolated New Guinea tribe) and the similar expressions of blind and sighted children support this. Recognising others' expressions relies more on the right hemisphere ; recognising particular faces uses different circuits than recognising expressions. The amygdala is needed to recognise fearful faces and receives visual input from a subcortical route (superior colliculus + pulvinar) and a cortical route — hence affective blindsight (recognising emotional expressions without conscious sight after visual-cortex damage). The fusiform face area (fed by the parvocellular system) recognises faces; basal ganglia/insular damage disrupts recognition of disgust ; right somatosensory damage impairs facial-emotion recognition (impaired imitation). Laterality & laughter: the anterior cingulate gyrus handles the motor aspects of laughter; humour appreciation involves the right vmPFC. Emotional vs volitional facial paresis are complementary syndromes (one can smile to an emotion but not on command, or vice versa). The left half of the face tends to be more expressive. 12. Hormonal regulation of behaviour Definition Hormones (Greek horman , "to excite") are chemicals secreted by one group of cells and carried in the bloodstream to act on specific target tissues. Many are made by endocrine glands (Greek endon "within" + krinein "to secrete"). The first endocrine experiment was carried out in 1849 by Arnold Adolph Berthold (likely replicating John Hunter's earlier work). Types of chemical communication Endocrine — hormone released into the bloodstream to affect distant targets. Synaptic (neurocrine) — transmitter diffuses across the synaptic cleft; highly localised. Autocrine — released chemical acts on the releasing cell itself (e.g. autoreceptors). Paracrine — diffuses to nearby target cells; strongest effect on the nearest. Pheromone — released into the environment to affect other individuals of the same species. Allomone — affects individuals of another species. Organising principles of hormones Hormones act gradually (hours to weeks) and change the intensity or probability of behaviours rather than switching them on/off. One hormone has multiple effects; one behaviour can be affected by many hormones; hormones interact. Secreted in small amounts, often in pulses (pulsatile secretion); levels vary rhythmically over the day under circadian clocks. A hormone affects only cells with receptor proteins that recognise it. Its chemical structure is similar across vertebrates, though its function can vary by species. Neural vs hormonal communication Both are secretory; both often act via second messengers on receptor binding. The hypothalamic neurosecretory (neuroendocrine) cells are neurons in every way except that their terminals release hormones into the bloodstream rather than transmitter into a synapse — blurring the line between neurons and endocrine cells. Some peptide hormones occur even in single-celled organisms, suggesting a shared evolutionary origin. Three classes of hormone Class Made from Receptor location Protein/peptide hormones Strings of amino acids Cell-surface receptors → second messenger Amine (monoamine) hormones A modified single amino acid Cell-surface receptors → second messenger Steroid hormones Cholesterol (four carbon rings) Pass through the membrane; bind inside the cell; the steroid-receptor complex binds DNA and acts as a transcription factor Hormones influence cell growth and activity (e.g. without thyroid hormones, fewer brain cells form and mental development is stunted). Secretion is regulated by negative feedback : the hormone's output feeds back to inhibit further release. Specific hormone systems Adrenal cortex: mineralocorticoids (chiefly aldosterone , which makes kidneys retain sodium and conserve water) and sex steroids (notably androstenedione , contributing to adult body hair; excess in females causes a more masculine appearance). Thyroid gland (below the larynx): thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3) = the thyroid hormones; calcitonin promotes calcium deposition in bone. Disorders: goiter (swelling from iodine deficiency) and cretinism / congenital hypothyroidism (reduced stature and intellectual disability from early thyroid deficiency). Gonads: the hypothalamus releases GnRH , driving the anterior pituitary to release the gonadotropins FSH and LH , which drive steroid production in testes and ovaries. Kisspeptin stimulates GnRH neurons and helps govern the onset of puberty ; gonadotropin-inhibiting hormone opposes it. Social behaviour: oxytocin is released during orgasm in both sexes and (with vasopressin ) modulates social bonding/contact in rodents. Endocrine pathology: parathyroid deficiency → calcium deposition in the basal ganglia and schizophrenia-like symptoms; chronic glucocorticoid excess → Cushing's syndrome (fatigue, depression, hirsutism, autonomic changes). 13. The glandular (endocrine) system Two types of glands: Exocrine glands (e.g. sweat glands) release chemicals into ducts that carry them to body surfaces. Endocrine (ductless) glands release hormones directly into the circulatory system. Three classes of vertebrate hormone (gland view) Amino acid derivatives — e.g. epinephrine from the adrenal medulla, synthesized from tyrosine. Peptides and proteins — chains of amino acids (peptide = short, protein = long). Steroids — synthesized from cholesterol; all the sex hormones are steroids. Sex steroid hormones Two main gonadal classes: androgens (commonest = testosterone ) and estrogens (commonest = estradiol ). A third class, progestins (commonest = progesterone ), prepares the uterus and breasts for pregnancy in females; its male function is unclear (possibly sperm metabolism). The pituitary — the "master gland" Called the master gland because most of its hormones are tropic hormones that control the release of hormones from other glands (e.g. gonadotropin drives the gonads). It is really two glands fused in development: Anterior pituitary — releases the tropic hormones. Controlled by the hypothalamus through the hypothalamo-pituitary portal system (a vascular network). Posterior pituitary — releases vasopressin (antidiuretic hormone) and oxytocin . These peptide hormones are made in the paraventricular and supraoptic nuclei of the hypothalamus, transported down axons to the posterior pituitary, and released when action potentials arrive (the cells are neurosecretory cells ). Oxytocin drives uterine contraction in labour and milk ejection during suckling; vasopressin promotes water reabsorption by the kidneys; both influence stress-coping and social responses. How hormone release is regulated Neural signals — all endocrine glands except the anterior pituitary are directly regulated by the nervous system. Pituitary and pineal glands are regulated by cerebral neurons; glands outside the CNS are innervated by the ANS (often both sympathetic and parasympathetic with opposite effects). Hormonal signals — the anterior pituitary's tropic hormones drive their target glands; circulating hormones feed back to the pituitary, hypothalamus and brain (negative feedback maintaining stable blood levels). Non-hormonal chemicals — glucose, calcium and sodium levels influence release (e.g. rising blood glucose increases insulin, which lowers glucose). Pulsatile release — hormones are released in pulses, giving large minute-to-minute fluctuations in circulating levels. 14. Sleep & biological clocks Measuring & staging sleep Three standard measures define sleep stages: the EEG (electroencephalogram), the EOG (electrooculogram, eye movements) and the neck EMG (electromyogram, muscle tone). Slow-wave sleep shows large slow EEG waves; REM sleep shows fast desynchronised activity, rapid eye movements and near-total muscle relaxation. During REM, cerebral blood flow is high in the extrastriate (visual association) cortex but low in the striate cortex and prefrontal cortex; dorsolateral prefrontal cortex is implicated in remembering dreams. Dreaming External stimuli can be incorporated into dreams. Most people report dreams when woken from REM, less so from slow-wave sleep. Sleeptalking can occur in any stage (often at the transition to wakefulness); sleepwalking occurs in slow-wave sleep and never in REM (when muscles are relaxed). The activation-synthesis hypothesis holds that REM supplies the cortex with largely random information and the dream is the cortex's attempt to make sense of it. Theories & effects of deprivation Recuperation theories: being awake disrupts homeostasis and sleep restores it. Adaptation theories: sleep results from an internal 24-hour timing mechanism — we are programmed to sleep at night. Slow-wave deprivation harms cognition more than physical activity. REM sleep facilitates non-declarative learning; slow-wave sleep facilitates declarative learning. After REM deprivation there is a rebound (extra REM on recovery nights). Fatal familial insomnia (inherited) damages the thalamus, causing attention/memory deficits, autonomic and endocrine loss of control, raised body temperature and insomnia. Sleep-promoting substance: adenosine Prolonged wakefulness lowers brain glycogen , raising extracellular adenosine (a nucleoside neuromodulator with an inhibitory effect). Accumulating adenosine acts as a sleep-promoting substance — inhibiting wakefulness-promoting regions and producing the cognitive/emotional effects of sleep deprivation. Neural control of arousal At least five transmitter systems regulate arousal: Acetylcholine — pontine and basal-forebrain groups produce cortical activation/desynchrony; a medial-septum group controls the hippocampus. ACh release is highest during wakefulness and REM. Norepinephrine — from the locus coeruleus (dorsal pons), projecting widely; catecholamine agonists like amphetamine cause arousal and sleeplessness. Serotonin — from the raphe nuclei (reticular formation); stimulation causes locomotion and cortical arousal. Histamine — from the tuberomammillary nucleus (TMN) of the hypothalamus; directly increases cortical activation (which is why antihistamines cause drowsiness). Orexin (hypocretin) — from the lateral hypothalamus , projecting to nearly every arousal region. Its loss causes narcolepsy. Flip-flop circuits Sleep/wake flip-flop: slow-wave sleep begins when neurons in the ventrolateral preoptic area (vlPOA) become active and inhibit the wakefulness systems; those systems inhibit the vlPOA in return, creating a bistable switch. Adenosine tips it toward sleep; orexin holds it in the "waking" state. REM flip-flop: the sublaterodorsal nucleus (SLD) in the dorsal pons is the REM-ON region; the ventrolateral periaqueductal gray (vlPAG) is the REM-OFF region. The REM flip-flop can only switch to REM when the sleep/wake flip-flop is in the "sleeping" state. SLD neurons excite spinal inhibitory interneurons to produce the muscular paralysis that stops us acting out dreams. Disorders of sleep Insomnia: primary (difficulty falling/staying asleep) and secondary (due to pain, substances, or another condition). Treated with CBT, relaxation, sleep hygiene, and hypnotic/benzodiazepine/antihistamine drugs. Can be caused by sleep apnea (treated with surgery or a device to keep the airway open). Narcolepsy: sleep (or its components) at inappropriate times. Symptoms: sleep attacks, cataplexy , sleep paralysis, hypnagogic hallucinations. Linked to orexin loss / a chromosome-6 orexin-receptor gene mutation, sometimes after autoimmune attack of orexin neurons. Treated with stimulants, antidepressants or modafinil . REM sleep behaviour disorder: a neurodegenerative disease damages REM paralysis mechanisms so the patient acts out dreams; treated with a benzodiazepine. Slow-wave parasomnias: bedwetting (nocturnal enuresis), sleepwalking (somnambulism), night terrors (pavor nocturnus), and sleep-related eating — most common in children, usually outgrown. Biological clocks Circadian rhythms (Latin circa "about" + dies "day") cycle about every 24 hours (sleep/wake, activity, body temperature). Zeitgebers ("time-givers") are external cues such as light or clocks that entrain them. The suprachiasmatic nuclei (SCN) of the hypothalamus drive circadian (not homeostatic) regulation: they receive light via the photopigment melanopsin and relay through the subparaventricular zone and dorsomedial hypothalamus. The "ticking" lies in individual neurons — interlocking feedback loops of protein production/breakdown (~24 h). Mutations cause shifts: a per2 mutation (chromosome 2) → advanced sleep phase syndrome (4-h advance); a per3 mutation (chromosome 1) → delayed sleep phase syndrome (4-h delay). Seasonal rhythms: at night the SCN signals the pineal gland to secrete melatonin . Prolonged winter melatonin drives the winter phase of annual cycles; melatonin also helps synchronise circadian rhythms (useful for shift work, jet lag and blind people for whom light is no zeitgeber). 15. Genetics & behaviour Chromosomes & sex-linked traits Genes lie on chromosomes — threadlike DNA structures in the nucleus; an allele controlling a trait sits at the same location. Humans have 22 pairs of autosomes and 1 pair of sex chromosomes (XX or XY). Sex-linked traits are influenced by genes on the sex chromosomes; virtually all are on the X chromosome (the Y is small and carries few genes). X-linked dominant traits occur more often in females; X-linked recessive traits occur more often in males (males have only one X, so a single recessive gene is expressed; females need two). Example: colour-blindness . Sex-limited traits are visible only in one sex (e.g. X-linked hereditary prostate cancer). Chromosomal abnormality: the commonest autosomal one is Down syndrome , caused by trisomy 21 . Behavioural genetics research methods Family studies: assume blood relatives share more genes, so the more shared genetics, the more similar the traits. Use a genogram (a pictorial display of family relationships and medical history) to map hereditary patterns. Twin studies: compare similarity/concordance of traits between monozygotic (identical) twins (share 100% of genes) and dizygotic (fraternal) twins (share ~50%). If a trait is genetic, MZ twins show higher concordance. Drawback: MZ twins often share the same environment. Adoption studies: study twins reared apart to separate genes from environment — e.g. the Minnesota Study of Twins Reared Apart (Bouchard et al.) , with 59 MZ and 47 DZ pairs reared apart (plus matched pairs reared together), ages 19–68. Result: adult identical twins were substantially more alike on all psychological dimensions than fraternal twins, regardless of rearing environment. Bouchard estimated the heritability of IQ at .70 . Definition Heritability estimate — not a statement about an individual's development, but a numerical estimate of the proportion of variability in a trait, in a particular study, attributable to genetic variation in that study. Genes and experience Genetic differences can promote psychological differences by influencing experience . When a gene leads an individual to seek experiences that amplify the gene's effects, it has a multiplier effect . Turkheimer (2000) concluded that nearly all human behavioural traits are highly heritable (typically .40–.70), that the particular family environment contributes little to behavioural diversity, while other experiences contribute significantly. In a sample of 7-year-old twins, IQ heritability was low among very poor families but high among affluent families . Genomic methods Linkage studies compare known DNA markers with a trait across family members (e.g. the Huntington's disease gene was found near a known marker on chromosome 4). Genome-wide association studies compare whole or partial genomes across individuals to correlate genetic differences with diseases/traits. Targeted mutations are lab-made mutated genes inserted into mice: knockout genes (defective, no functional protein), knock-in genes (new/replacement protein), and conditional knockouts (gene switched off when the animal is given a drug, so it develops normally first). Antisense oligonucleotides are modified RNA/DNA strands that bind specific mRNA and block protein production (the trapped mRNA is then destroyed). Example: antisense oligonucleotides destroying sex-hormone receptors in the VMH of female rats inhibited female sexual behaviour. 16. Invasive & non-invasive research methods in biopsychology Neuroanatomy & histology (invasive) Histological methods ( histo = body tissue) study the structure of brain tissue by fixing, slicing and staining it: Fixation: tissue is preserved (against autolytic enzymes and microbes) in a fixative , usually formalin (an aqueous solution of formaldehyde), which cross-links proteins to strengthen the fragile tissue. Perfusion first removes blood and replaces it with saline. Sectioning: the fixed brain is sliced with a microtome (knife + mounting platform + advancing mechanism) or a cryostat (a microtome inside a freezer for very cold cutting). Staining: slices are placed in chemical solutions, then covered with mounting medium and a coverslip. Key stains: the Golgi stain (silver chromate; Camillo Golgi found it stains whole neurons black, showing individual neurons in silhouette for the first time — used to study neuron shape ); the Nissl stain (Franz Nissl, 1880s; commonest dye cresyl violet , also methylene blue; binds cell bodies to count neurons ). Tracing methods Anterograde (forward) tracing: chemicals taken up by cell bodies and transported forward to terminal buttons — traces axons projecting away from an area. Retrograde (backward) tracing: chemicals taken up by terminal buttons and transported back to cell bodies — traces axons projecting into an area. Lesion methods Aspiration lesions — accessible cortical tissue drawn off by suction through a fine glass pipette. Radio-frequency lesions — heat from a high-frequency current passed through a stereotaxically positioned electrode destroys tissue. Knife cuts — a precise cut eliminates conduction in a nerve or tract without extensive damage. Reversible lesions — temporarily eliminate activity by cooling the structure or injecting an anaesthetic (e.g. lidocaine); a non-destructive alternative. High-yield General principle: the behavioural effects of unilateral lesions are usually much milder than bilateral lesions (with notable exceptions). Recording & neurochemical methods Microelectrode (single-unit) recording: very fine-tipped wires record the activity of individual neurons; implanted via stereotaxic surgery. Signals are tiny and must be amplified. Localising receptors: autoradiography (a radioactive ligand binds receptors; a photographic emulsion localises them) vs immunocytochemistry (dye-tagged antibodies to a receptor protein — no radioactivity, and individual labelled cells can be seen under a microscope). Microdialysis: measures neurotransmitter amounts released in a brain region using a probe with a dialysis membrane permeable to some molecules. Electron microscopy: a transmission electron microscope reveals tiny structures (synaptic vesicles, organelles); a scanning electron microscope shows 3-D at lower magnification; a confocal laser scanning microscope images inside thick or living tissue (cells stained with fluorescent dye). Imaging methods Neuroimaging is either anatomical (structure/size) or functional (activation during a task). The three main techniques are CT, PET and MRI. Method Basis Notes CT (computerized tomography) X-rays; measures attenuation per voxel Widely available; poor gray/white contrast (iodine improves it); uses radiation; temporal lobe and subcortical gray are hard to image. PET (positron emission tomography) A radioactive tracer (e.g. FDG glucose, or a drug for receptor binding) emits positrons; decay produces two gamma photons detected around the head Quantifies neurotransmitter receptors, drug action and cerebral glucose metabolism/blood flow; uses radioactivity; low spatial and temporal resolution vs MRI. MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) A powerful magnet aligns hydrogen protons; an RF pulse makes them rotate; as they realign they emit detectable radio waves; the RF frequency can target a single slice High resolution (down to ~1 mm slices); no radiation. fMRI (functional MRI) Images increased oxygenated-blood flow to active regions — the BOLD signal (blood-oxygen-level-dependent) Active areas take up more oxygenated blood than needed; the deoxy/oxy-haemoglobin ratio changes the MR signal as an indirect marker of activity. DTI (diffusion tensor imaging) Tracks rapid water diffusion along axon tracts Images major tracts; helps map the connectome . Electrical & magnetic recording (non-invasive) EEG (electroencephalogram): scalp electrodes record electrical activity, first demonstrated by Berger in the 1920s; a standard tool for epilepsy. The signal is the summation of dendritic (postsynaptic) inputs. Electrodes are placed by the International 10–20 System : each site has a letter for the lobe ( F rontal, T emporal, C entral, P arietal, O ccipital) and a number for the hemisphere (even = right, odd = left; Z = midline). MEG (magnetoencephalogram): measures magnetic fields produced by electrical brain activity, using superconducting coils (in liquid helium at −269°C) and SQUID detectors. Like EEG it has excellent temporal resolution , but it can produce a functional map of activation; useful when a disorder is suspected but no anatomical abnormality is visible. EEG frequencies (brain waves) Wave Frequency Associated state Delta 0.5–3.5 Hz Sleep; predominant in newborns (first two years) Theta 4–7.5 Hz REM sleep, problem solving, hypnosis; absence of pleasure Alpha 8–12 Hz Awake and relaxed Beta (slow 13–19, fast 20–30 Hz) 13–30 Hz Tactile, auditory and emotional activation Gamma 30–50 Hz High arousal and alertness Sleep spindles 12–14 Hz Stage 2 sleep (with K-complexes) Mnemonic Slowest to fastest: D elta → T heta → A lpha → B eta → G amma. As the brain wakes and activates, waves get faster and smaller. "Deep To Awake, Busy, Going-flat-out."

title: Unit 5 — Attention, Perception & Memory
text: Unit 5 — Attention, Perception & Memory The cognitive core of the syllabus, built from Solso-style cognitive psychology and the classic learning systems: how attention selects a trickle from the flood of sensation (Donald Broadbent, Treisman, Deutsch-Norman, Daniel Kahneman), how organisms learn by association and consequence (Ivan Pavlov, B. F. Skinner, Edward Thorndike, Edwin Guthrie, Clark Hull, Spence, Edward Tolman, Albert Bandura), how memory encodes, stores and retrieves (Atkinson-Shiffrin, Alan Baddeley, Endel Tulving, Fergus Craik & Robert Lockhart), why we forget (decay, interference, retrieval failure, repression, motivated forgetting), and how the visual system builds a stable percept of form, depth and pattern (Gestalt, template/feature/prototype, Irving Biederman, Oliver Selfridge) under uncertainty (signal detection theory). Each model is taught for its mechanism and its exam relevance, with theorists, dates and the traps that examiners love. In this book Attention: forms & models Classical & instrumental conditioning Fundamental learning theories Hull, discrimination, latent & observational learning Memory processes & systems Theories of forgetting Perception: approaches, illusions & pattern recognition Distance & depth perception Form perception Signal detection theory 1. Attention: forms & models Solso defines attention as "the concentration of mental effort on sensory or mental events." More fully (Duncan 1999; Motter 1999; Posner & Fernandez-Duque 1999), attention is the means by which we actively process a limited amount of information from the enormous amount available through our senses, stored memories and other cognitive processes. It is a concentration of mental activity that includes both conscious and unconscious processes. Definition Attention = selective concentration of finite mental resources on some stimuli at the expense of others. The central problem it solves is that the sensory world delivers far more information than the system can fully process. Forms of attention Divided attention — attending to several messages simultaneously, responding to each as needed. Performance typically suffers unless the tasks are well practised; practice alters the limits of attentional capacity. Selective attention — focusing on one task/stimulus while disregarding the others. It simplifies our lives because attentional capacity is limited. The Stroop effect is the classic demonstration of the cost of selecting against a dominant response. Sustained attention (vigilance) — the maintenance of selective attention to infrequent events over long periods. There is a reliable vigilance decrement : performance declines as time-on-task wears on, affected by the neurological and physiological state of the person. Filter / bottleneck models — early selection Everyday phenomena like the cocktail-party effect (you can follow one conversation in a noisy room, yet your own name spoken across the room captures you) are explained by filter theories . Early-selection means attention operates early in the information-processing sequence: only one source (the attended one) reaches meaningful processing; unattended information is actively filtered/blocked before it can compete for scarce higher-order resources. Broadbent's switch (filter) model (1958) Donald Broadbent proposed a simple on-off switch : attention directs processing to one input channel, which is fully analysed for meaning and made available to consciousness. Because the switch is all-or-none, additional messages are completely blocked. Attention is attracted and maintained by sensory/physical attributes of messages (e.g., the voice qualities at a party). The switch does not allow unconscious processing: unattended signals left in sensory memory rapidly decay and never receive the extra processing needed for longer-term retention. A subject should therefore be able to report only the physical features of the unattended message, not its meaning. Cherry's dichotic listening & shadowing (1953) Colin Cherry created a paradigm to test early selection: dichotic listening (different messages to each ear at once) combined with shadowing (repeating one message aloud as it occurs). Shadowing forces the subject onto one message so they cannot switch. Findings that strain the strict switch: when the meaning of the shadowed sentence switches to the non-shadowed ear, shadowing is disrupted (Anne Treisman 1960) — the subject follows the meaning rather than the physical cue of ear location, allowing determination of when attention shifts. Treisman's attenuator model (1964) Anne Treisman proposed a more flexible early-selection theory using a different mechanical metaphor: instead of an off/on switch, attention works like an attenuator (regulator) that allows gradations of energy through. Most of the attended message passes through; some unattended information may also reach the level of pattern recognition. Attention thus becomes a matter of degree . Physical cues tune the attenuator, but it can also be influenced by the meaning of previously analysed material, so control is exerted by both sensory and semantic information. It remains an early-selection theory because filtering still occurs prior to full meaningful analysis; partial analysis of all signals occurs. Late-selection models — Deutsch & Deutsch (1963), Norman (1968) Late-selection models propose that all information is recognised: every sensory input activates its corresponding meaning in long-term memory, but attention then selects among the activated meanings , allowing only a limited amount to reach consciousness. Selective attention operates on response output , not input. The non-shadowed information, requiring no overt response, may be rapidly forgotten before testing. The activation of meaning is unconscious; awareness itself is treated as a response . The activity decays quickly unless the activated meaning is selected for conscious processing. High-yield Order the bottleneck: Donald Broadbent (early, all-or-none switch, physical cues) → Anne Treisman (early, attenuator, partial/graded analysis, sensory + semantic) → Deutsch-Deutsch / Norman (late selection, full recognition, filter at response) . "Where is the filter?" is the single most-tested question in this topic. Capacity models — Kahneman (1973) Daniel Kahneman recast attention not as a filter but as mental effort — a pool of cognitive resources to be allocated. Different tasks demand different amounts of capacity; the number of activities done simultaneously is set by how much capacity each requires. Attention is the process of allocating capacity to inputs (input side) and activities (output side). The figure's central element is the allocation policy , controlled by: Enduring dispositions — involuntary attention (e.g., capacity automatically allocated to the mention of your name). Momentary intentions — voluntary goals (e.g., "listen to the right ear"). Evaluation of demands — if two activities need more capacity than is available, perform one and delay the other. Arousal — total available capacity varies with arousal state (links to Yerkes-Dodson). Automatic vs controlled processing — Schneider & Shiffrin Walter Schneider and Richard Shiffrin proposed two levels of processing relevant to attention: Automatic Controlled Used for Easy tasks, highly familiar items Difficult tasks, unfamiliar items Mode Parallel (two or more items at once) Serial (one item at a time) In their study, participants saw a rapid series of 20 frames; each of four locations could hold a number, letter or dots. Exposure time was 40 or 800 ms. In the consistent-mapping condition (targets never become distractors) the task became so easy that people used automatic processing: only frame-exposure time affected accuracy — neither target-set size nor frame size mattered. In the varied-mapping condition (a target on one trial could be an irrelevant item on the next), accuracy depended on exposure time and people were more accurate searching for one target than four, and with one item per frame than four. Feature integration theory — Anne Treisman (1986, 1998) FIT explains how separately-coded features become a single perceived object, in two stages: Pre-attentive stage — an object is automatically analysed into separate features (e.g., a rolling red ball → colour red , shape round , movement to the right ). Each feature is processed in a separate brain area and they exist independently at this stage; no attention required. Focused-attention stage — attention binds the features together so we perceive the whole object. The observer's attention plays the crucial role in combining features. Trap FIT's "pre-attentive" stage is parallel and effortless ; the binding stage requires focused attention . Without attention, features can be wrongly recombined — the classic illusory conjunction . Do not confuse Anne Treisman's FIT (perception/binding) with her earlier attenuator model (auditory attention) — same author, two distinct contributions. 2. Classical & instrumental conditioning Classical (Pavlovian) conditioning Ivan Pavlov discovered the conditioned reflex. His Nobel-winning digestive work ( The Work of the Digestive Glands , 1897; Nobel Prize 1904) led him to investigate "psychical secretion" : dogs salivated to artificial/neutral stimuli, not just to food. This conditioned reflex is the simplest form of learning (an acquired behaviour). The process begins with a natural unconditioned reflex (innate): food ( UCS ) → salivation ( UCR ), a pre-programmed survival measure. When a neutral stimulus (a sound, e.g., a metronome) coincides with or immediately precedes the UCS over a few pairings, it becomes an active conditioned stimulus (CS) capable of eliciting salivation on its own (the CR ). Pavlov first called this newly acquired habit psychic secretion . Time relationships between CS and UCS Arrangement Form Note CS & UCS overlap temporally Simultaneous CS begins a fraction of a second to 5 s before UCS and continues until it occurs; CR follows the onset of CS almost immediately. CS & UCS overlap temporally Delayed CS begins 5 s to several minutes before UCS and continues until it occurs; hard to form unless a simultaneous CR is already established. CS & UCS do not overlap Short-trace CS removed for a few seconds before UCS begins. CS & UCS do not overlap Long-trace Gap between end of CS and start of UCS is 1 minute or more; formed with greater difficulty than delayed CRs. Time interval as CS Temporal UCS presented at regular intervals; if omitted, a CR appears at approximately the usual interval. CS after UCS ends Backward CS does not begin to act until after the UCS ceases (weakest arrangement). Other Pavlovian phenomena Conditioned alpha blocking — any arousing stimulus paired with a neutral stimulus can produce a CR; any form of activation acts as a UCS capable of generating a conditioned reflex. Law of summation of conditioned stimuli — a stimulus's strength is limited; beyond a level, more intensity is less effective. But two weak CSs combined within the limit produce roughly double the effect (arithmetical summation). Inhibition (extinction) — Pavlov called extinction inhibition : presenting the CS in the absence of the UCS. Four types of internal inhibition : (1) extinction/experimental extinction (CS without reinforcement); (2) retardation/inhibition of delay (withholding reinforcement beyond the bonding time destroys the CR); (3) conditioned inhibition (combining the CS with other stimuli makes it lose effect); (4) differential inhibition (extinguish peripheral CRs by reinforcing only the original stimulus, preventing spread). Irradiation (generalization) — responding to stimuli similar to the CS; Pavlov called it irradiation, believing neuronic action spreads to neighbouring brain areas. Concentration (discrimination) is the careful elimination of unwanted responses, using extinction. Reciprocal induction — combining excitatory and inhibitory conditioning to produce contrasting effects; a method of strengthening/establishing what is learned. First & second signal systems — the first signal system = sensations from the outside world (shared with animals); the second signal system (uniquely human) = stimuli that reach us as speech . Verbal conditioning and language acquisition belong here; Pavlov called the second signal system the "signal of signals." Orienting reflex — Pavlov's investigatory reflex; an innate response to investigate novel surroundings, adaptive by preparing for emergencies and conserving energy. Habituation = decreasing sensitivity with repeated stimulation ("pseudolearning"). Sensitization (dishabituation) = increased response, the disruption of established habituation. Instrumental / operant conditioning — Skinner B. F. Skinner distinguished respondent behaviour (elicited by a known stimulus) from operant behaviour (not elicited but simply emitted ). Correspondingly: Type S (respondent) conditioning = identical to classical conditioning; strength measured by the magnitude of the CR. Type R (operant) conditioning = named for the emphasis on the response ; strength measured by response rate . Core principles of Type R: any response followed by a reinforcing stimulus tends to be repeated; a reinforcing stimulus is anything that increases the rate of an operant response. Skinner even defined culture as a set of reinforcement contingencies. Apparatus & techniques Skinner box — a small test chamber (direct descendant of Edward Thorndike's puzzle box) with grid floor, light, lever and food cup; lever press fires the feeder, releasing a pellet. Cumulative recording — time on the x-axis, total responses on the y-axis; the trace rises when behaviour occurs and runs parallel to the x-axis when it does not. Lever-press conditioning — steps: (1) deprivation (place animal on a deprivation schedule); (2) magazine training (the feeder makes a loud click before delivering a pellet, away from the cup, so the click becomes a secondary reinforcer via association with food); (3) the animal eventually presses the lever, firing the magazine, whose click reinforces the press and signals the animal to the cup. Shaping — a faster route using two components: differential reinforcement (some responses reinforced, others not) and successive approximation (only responses increasingly similar to the target are reinforced). Extinction & spontaneous recovery — removing the reinforcer flattens the cumulative record to the x-axis (extinction); the response rate returns to the operant level (its rate before reinforcement). After a rest in the home cage, the animal will press again briefly without retraining — spontaneous recovery . Stimulus control, reinforcement & chaining Discriminative operant — if reinforcement is given only when a light is on, the light becomes S D (discriminative stimulus signalling reinforcement); light-off = S Δ . A discriminative operant is a response given to one set of circumstances but not another. Secondary reinforcement — a neutral stimulus paired with a primary reinforcer (food/water) acquires reinforcing properties of its own. It is independent and non-specific: it will condition new, unrelated responses. A generalized reinforcer is a secondary reinforcer paired with more than one primary reinforcer (e.g., money ). Chaining — one response brings the organism into contact with stimuli that act as S D for the next response, and so on; in the Skinner box the chain is held together by the food pellet (a primary positive reinforcer). Reinforcers vs punishment — a positive reinforcer (primary or secondary) increases response probability when added ; a negative reinforcer increases it when removed . Punishment removes something positive or adds something negative; it merely suppresses behaviour — when the threat is removed, the behaviour returns to its original level. Trap Negative reinforcement is NOT punishment. Negative reinforcement increases a behaviour by removing an aversive stimulus; punishment decreases behaviour. Examiners exploit this constantly. Schedules of reinforcement An organism reinforced on every correct response (continuous) extinguishes faster than one reinforced for only a percentage of responses — the partial reinforcement effect (PRE) : partial reinforcement leads to greater resistance to extinction. Skinner and Ferster wrote Schedules of Reinforcement . Schedule Rule Continuous (CRF) Every correct response during acquisition is reinforced. Fixed interval (FI) Reinforced for a response made only after a set interval of time. Fixed ratio (FR) Reinforced when every n th response is made. Variable interval (VI) Reinforced for responses at the end of time intervals of variable duration. Variable ratio (VR) Reinforced on the average of every n responses (e.g., VR5 ≈ one in five on average); may get two in a row or none for ten to fifteen. Verbal behaviour & related findings Verbal behaviour — Skinner argued language is explained within reinforcement theory, classifying verbal responses by their relation to reinforcement: mand (a demand; reinforced when the need is met), tact (naming objects/events appropriately; reinforced by others' confirmation of the match), echoic behaviour (reinforced when someone's response is repeated verbatim), autoclitic behaviour (verbal behaviour based on/depending upon other verbal behaviour; qualifies responses, expresses relations, provides grammatical framework). Premack principle — David Premack: any response of high frequency can reinforce a response of lower frequency; all responses are potential reinforcers. Instinctive drift — the Brelands (1961) found innate behaviour patterns gradually displace learned behaviour; learned behaviour drifts toward instinctive behaviour. Autoshaping — with non-contingent reinforcement (a pigeon reinforced at intervals regardless of behaviour) plus a disc illuminated just before food, the pigeon learns to peck the disc even though pecking is never reinforced — the animal shapes its own behaviour. 3. Fundamental learning theories Connectionism — Edward L. Thorndike (1874–1949) Edward Thorndike called the association between sense impressions and impulses to action a bond or connection — the neural connection between stimuli (S) and responses (R). His connectionism combines associationism, Darwinism and the methods of science. Selecting and connecting — the most basic learning is trial-and-error (originally "selecting and connecting"). Using puzzle boxes , he plotted time-to-escape against trials; the time fell gradually with successive trials, so he concluded learning is incremental, not insightful . Learning is not mediated by ideas — learning is direct, not mediated by thinking/reasoning (parsimony: reject reason in favour of direct S-R connection). All mammals learn alike — including humans, by the same laws. Laws of connectionism Law Statement Readiness When a conduction unit is ready to conduct, conducting is satisfying; not conducting is annoying. When not ready but forced to conduct, conducting is annoying. Exercise Connections strengthen with use ( law of use ) and weaken with disuse ( law of disuse ). Effect A response followed by a satisfying state strengthens the connection; one followed by an annoying state weakens it. He posited a neurophysiological confirming reaction (the organism is not conscious of it) to explain how effect acts after the response. Secondary concepts Multiple response (varied reaction) — the first step in learning: if the first response fails, try others. Set or attitude — dispositions/pre-adjustments the learner brings (cultural/genetic heritage; temporary states like deprivation, fatigue, emotion). Satisfiers and annoyers differ among individuals. Pre-potency of elements — "the partial or piecemeal activity of a situation"; we respond to some elements and not others. How we respond depends on what we attend to and the responses attached to it. Response by analogy — we respond to a novel situation as to a related familiar one; transfer is set by the number of identical elements the two situations share (identical-elements theory of transfer of training). He urged school curricula to resemble real-life tasks. Associative shifting — begin with an S-R connection, then gradually drop original stimulus elements and add new ones; as long as enough original elements remain, the same response is given. Revised laws (post-1930) In September 1929, before the International Congress of Psychology (New Haven), Thorndike opened his address with "I was wrong." Revised law of exercise — mere repetition (use) does not strengthen, and disuse does not weaken much; he discarded the entire law of exercise after 1930. Revised law of effect — only half true: reinforcement increases connection strength, but punishment does nothing to it. Belongingness — associations form more readily when elements "belong" together (subject & verb > the last word of one sentence and the first of the next). Spread of effect — a satisfying state increases the probability not only of the reinforced response but also of surrounding responses; neutral responses close (in similarity or time) to the reinforced one increase in frequency. Guthrie — contiguity / one-trial learning Law of contiguity — "A combination of stimuli which has accompanied a movement will on its recurrence tend to be followed by that movement" — explicitly without confirmatory waves, reinforcement or pleasant effects. One-trial learning — "A stimulus pattern gains its full associative strength on the occasion of its first pairing with a response." Recency principle — whatever we did last in a given set of circumstances is what we tend to do again when those circumstances recur. Movement-produced stimuli — movements of the body (muscles, tendons, joints) produce stimuli distinct from external stimulation; responses can be conditioned to them. Movements vs acts vs skills — movements are simple muscle contractions; acts are made of many movements (defined by what they accomplish/change in the environment); a skill is made of many acts. Practice does not improve movements but improves their coordination into acts and skills. Reinforcement — merely a mechanical arrangement explained by his one law: reinforcement changes the stimulating conditions and thereby prevents unlearning . Forgetting — like learning, occurs in one trial: all forgetting involves new learning — an alternative response occurs in the presence of a stimulus pattern. High-yield Contrast the founders by their core mechanism: Edward Thorndike = law of effect (consequences) ; Edwin Guthrie = contiguity / one-trial (no reinforcement needed) ; Ivan Pavlov = stimulus substitution (CS–UCS) ; B. F. Skinner = operant contingency (response–reinforcer) ; Clark Hull = drive reduction (need-based). 4. Hull, discrimination, latent & observational learning Clark Hull — systematic behaviour theory Hull's last book, A Behavior System , has a logical structure of postulates and theorems "much like Euclid's geometry." Postulate 1 — sensing the external environment & the stimulus trace : a stimulus trace (S) continues for a few seconds after the stimulus event ends. Postulate 2 — interaction of sensory impulses : behaviour is seldom a function of only one stimulus. Postulate 3 — unlearned behaviour : the organism is born with a hierarchy of responses (unlearned behaviour) triggered when a need arises; if one fails to satisfy the need, more than one reaction may occur. Postulate 4 — contiguity + drive reduction as necessary conditions : if a stimulus leads to a response and that response satisfies a biological need , the S-R association is strengthened — the habit grows, i.e., habit strength ( S H R ) . Primary reinforcement = need satisfaction (drive reduction); a secondary reinforcer is a stimulus closely and consistently associated with need diminution. Postulate 5 — stimulus generalization : a stimulus similar to the training stimulus can elicit a conditioned response, by similarity; Hull called this generalized habit strength ( S H̄ R ) . Postulate 6 — drives : a biological deficiency produces a drive (D) , each associated with specific drive stimuli (e.g., hunger → stomach pangs; thirst → dry mouth, lips, throat). Postulate 7 — reaction potential ( S E R ) : the likelihood of a learned response at any moment = S E R = S H R × D . Postulate 8 — reactive inhibition (I R ) : responding causes fatigue ; I R (related to the muscular work of responding) operates against eliciting the CR and dissipates when the organism rests. It explains the reminiscence effect (improved performance after a rest). Postulate 9 — conditioned inhibition ( S I R ) : because I R is a negative drive state, not responding is reinforcing (it lets I R dissipate, reducing the negative drive of fatigue); the learned response of not responding becomes conditioned inhibition ( S I R ) . Subtracting I R + S I R from S E R gives effective reaction potential ( S Ē R ) = S H R × D − (I R + S I R ) . Postulate 10 — oscillation effect ( S O R ) : an "inhibitory potentiality" varying moment to moment, subtracted to give momentary effective reaction potential ( S Ė R ) = [ S H R × D − (I R + S I R )] − S O R . Postulates 11–16 : S Ė R must exceed a reaction threshold ( S L R ) before a response can occur (11–12); the higher S E R , the shorter the latency ( S t R ) (13); S E R determines resistance to extinction (14); response amplitude (A) varies directly with S E R (15); when incompatible responses compete, the one with the greatest S E R occurs (16). 1952 revisions Incentive motivation (K) — in 1943 Hull treated magnitude of reinforcement as a learning variable; research disagreed. Crespi (1942, 1944) and Zeaman (1949) showed performance changed radically when reinforcement magnitude changed after learning was complete — the Crespi effect . Organisms learn as fast for small as for large incentives but perform differently as incentive (K) varies. Stimulus-intensity dynamism (V) — an intervening variable that varies with the intensity of the external stimulus; greater intensity → greater probability the learned response is elicited. Drive-stimulus reduction — Hull shifted from drive reduction to drive-stimulus (S D ) reduction : learning follows the reduction of drive stimuli (e.g., water quickly reduces dry-mouth stimulation). Sheffield and Roby (1950) found hungry rats reinforced by non-nutritive saccharine, challenging pure drive reduction. Revised formula : S Ė R = [ S H R × D × V × K − (I R + S I R )] − S O R . Fractional antedating goal response (r G ) — stimuli experienced just before primary reinforcement become secondary reinforcers (via classical conditioning). They reinforce the responses that bring the organism to them and elicit r G s. The r G is some fraction of the goal response (R G ) — e.g., minute chewing/salivation — and produces proprioceptive stimulation symbolised s G ; the r G –s G mechanism is the "mental" component of chaining. Habit family hierarchy — for any s G there are many possible overt responses; the most likely is the one reaching reinforcement most rapidly and with least effort (the goal-gradient hypothesis , a 1952 corollary, with delay of reinforcement J). Discrimination learning — K. W. Spence Spence's continuity theory (1936) describes discrimination learning as a cumulative process: the excitatory tendency of the positive cue is built up by successive reinforcements, while the negative cue's tendency is lowered by an active negative process ( inhibition/frustration ) that adds algebraically to the positive tendencies. Reinforced responses raise the correct cue's excitatory tendency; unrewarded responses lower the negative cue's. It accounts for transposition — selecting between two new stimuli on the basis of a previously reinforced relationship . (Gestalt theorists explain transposition by saying one learns relations among stimuli, not absolute elements.) Latent learning — Tolman Latent learning is learning not translated into performance; it can stay dormant before being shown in behaviour. Edward Tolman and Honzik (1930) ran three groups of rats in a maze: never reinforced; always reinforced; not reinforced until day 11. The third group was key — once reinforcement began on day 11, they soon performed as well as the continuously reinforced group, showing they had been learning all along. For Tolman, learning occurs through observation, independent of reinforcement ; what the animal learns is to expect reinforcement if a response is made, an expectation confirmed during acquisition. Latent extinction : a rat placed directly into an empty goal box stops traversing the maze on later trials — extinction without non-reinforced performance of the learned response. (S-R theorists like Spence explain latent extinction motivationally.) Observational learning Edward Thorndike & John B. Watson — concluded learning results only from direct, not vicarious, experience. Miller & John Dollard (1941) — accepted observational learning but explained it within Hullian theory: if imitative behaviour is reinforced it strengthens like any behaviour; imitative learning is a special case of instrumental conditioning. Three categories: same behaviour (two or more individuals respond to the same situation the same way), copying behaviour (one person's behaviour guided by another, e.g., an art instructor's corrective feedback), matched-dependent behaviour (an observer reinforced for blindly repeating a model's actions; characteristic of adults in unfamiliar situations). Imitation itself can become a habit — generalized imitation . For them, imitative learning = observation + overt responding + reinforcement. Skinnerian analysis — observe model's behaviour → match the response → matching response is reinforced; maintained by a natural schedule. The model's behaviour acts as a discriminative stimulus indicating which actions will be reinforced; imitation is "nothing more than a discriminative operant." Albert Bandura — what one learns by observing is information , processed cognitively and acted on advantageously. Both Edward Tolman's and Bandura's theories are cognitive , not reinforcement theories. The learning-performance distinction is central. Bandura (1965) : children watched a film of a model hitting/kicking a large doll; one group saw the model reinforced , one saw it punished , one saw neutral consequences. Children who saw reinforcement were most aggressive (vicarious reinforcement facilitated), those who saw punishment least (vicarious punishment inhibited). Contrary to Miller & Dollard, observational learning occurred without the observer's own overt response being reinforced. In phase two, all children offered an incentive reproduced the behaviour — all had learned it; they differed only in performance . Reciprocal determinism — Bandura (1986): a three-way interaction of person (P), environment (E), behaviour (B); behaviour influences person and environment as much as they influence behaviour. "Though the potential environment is identical for all animals, the actual environment depends upon their behaviour" (1977). 5. Memory processes & systems Cognitive psychologists describe three common operations of memory: encoding (transforming a physical/sensory input into a representation that can enter memory), storage (retaining encoded information), and retrieval (gaining access to stored information). Encoding Encoding can be acoustic, visual, semantic or another modality, and the principle differs for STM and LTM. Short-term storage — Conrad (1964) showed the importance of an acoustic code in STM. Baddeley (1966) argued STM relies primarily on an acoustic (not semantic) code: performance was much worse for visually-presented acoustically similar words, with little effect of semantic similarity. STM encoding is primarily acoustic, with some secondary semantic encoding; visual encoding occurs but is even more fleeting. Long-term storage — primarily semantic . Levels of processing also influences LTM encoding: more information moves into LTM with a semantic strategy than a non-semantic one. LTM is not exclusively semantic — there is evidence for visual and acoustic encoding too; storage is flexible. Transfer to LTM, consolidation & rehearsal Entry into long-term declarative memory occurs via deliberately attending to comprehend, and making associations between new and known information — integration called consolidation . Metamemory strategies (reflecting on one's own memory to improve it) can preserve memories during consolidation. Rehearsal — repeated recitation (overt/covert). Elaborative rehearsal elaborates items so they are meaningfully integrated or connected (more memorable, transfers to LTM); maintenance rehearsal simply repeats items, holding them in STM without transferring to LTM. Spacing effect — distributed practice (sessions spaced over time) yields better memory than massed practice; the greater the distribution, the more is remembered over long periods (ideally spaced over months). It may occur because each session's encoding context varies, enriching schemas. Sleep & consolidation — REM sleep matters; more REM after learning improves it. Insomniacs have trouble with consolidation. Neuroscience — the hippocampus is important for memory; it shows low levels of acetylcholine during the activation associated with consolidation. Reconsolidation — once a memory is recalled it may return to an unstable state, again vulnerable to interference/decay; reconsolidation re-fixes the previously-encoded information. Organizing information Stored memories are organized: participants show consistent word-order patterns in recall even when words are unrelated. Mnemonic devices organize lists to aid memorization; even music can serve as a mnemonic and a retrieval cue. Retrieval Sternberg's memory-scanning task suggested we retrieve serially and exhaustively . Categorization dramatically affects retrieval (cued recall > free recall). Material processed in certain cortical areas during perception activates those same areas again during LTM recall (recall of spatial positions activates parietal/precentral cortex; recall of faces activates the left prefrontal/temporal cortex and posterior cingulate). Recall tests test for accessibility (whether we can gain access) not availability (whether the information is stored). Initial recall is mediated by processing speed; longer-term retention is mediated by other cognitive processes (e.g., rehearsal strategies) — initial recall and actual long-term learning differ. Stages of memory — modal model (Atkinson & Shiffrin, 1968) Based on the information-processing approach ; information is processed serially through stages: sensory memory → short-term store → long-term store . Sensory memory Closely tied to perception — "a record of our percepts." It is modality-specific (visual store holds visual info, auditory store auditory info, etc.). Capacity is relatively large but duration is very short (much less than a second); the information is relatively unprocessed (physical, not meaningful). The two best-studied stores are the icon (visual) and the echo (auditory). Icon — Ulric Neisser (1967) named the brief visual store the icon , holding unprocessed (uncategorized) visual information for up to ~1 second. It can be masked/"erased" by a later stimulus (circles after letters erase the letter trace). Partial reports can be cued by colour/brightness but not by category or phonological sound — the icon's information is purely visual . Modern views see the icon lasting only ~150–200 ms before recoding into a more meaningful code (Neath & Surprenant 2003 found some category cueing was possible). Echo — Neisser (1967) named the auditory store the echo . Recall can be cued by category to some degree (it works somewhat differently from the icon); the echo has a larger capacity than the icon. The suffix effect : an auditory recall cue (a spoken word) after a list seriously hinders recall of the last few items; a mere beep/tone or visual stimulus has little effect; the more auditory similarity between suffix and list, the greater the effect. Short-term memory (STM) A system holding a limited amount of information for brief periods ; viewed as a "workbench for consciousness" — hence the alternative term working memory . Capacity ≈ 7 ± 2 independent units (Miller's magic number). If unrehearsed, information is lost in as little as 20 seconds (its retention duration). Evidence for STM as a distinct store: Serial position curve — greater recall accuracy for words early (primacy) and late (recency) in a list than in the middle. Word-length effect — memory span is greater for short than long words. Word-similarity effect — span is greater for words that do not sound alike than for those that do. Working memory — Baddeley & Hitch (1974) Richard Atkinson & Richard Shiffrin's short-term store (STS) does more than hold ~7 items: it activates relevant information from LTS into STS, was equated with consciousness, and houses control processes (rehearsal, coding, integration, decision making). Alan Baddeley & Graham Hitch (1974) argued for a working memory = a limited-capacity workspace divided between storage and control processing. Baddeley (1981, 1986, 1990) proposed three components: Central executive — directs the flow of information, choosing what is operated on, when, and how. Visuospatial sketchpad — maintains visual material through visualization. Phonological loop — carries out subvocal rehearsal to maintain verbal material. Baddeley (1992) regarded WM as an evolution of the STM idea (moving away from a passive, temporary, limited-capacity storehouse), not a competitor. Trap The word-length and word-similarity (phonological-similarity) effects are the signature evidence for the phonological loop : short words rehearse faster, and acoustically distinct words resist confusion in the loop. Long-term memory (LTM) By the memory-systems view (Endel Tulving, 1983) , LTM is not unitary but made of subsystems. Squire (2004) draws the major distinction: Declarative memory — retention of factual information and personally-experienced episodes; two types: Episodic — memory for personally-experienced events, including contextual elements (time and place). Semantic — knowledge about the world without contextual elements (where/when it was learned). Procedural memory — "knowing how" to do something; unlike declarative memory, difficult to verbalize. Retrieval in LTM Retrieval depends on cues — stimuli associated with stored information that aid its retrieval. Context-dependent memory — information entered in a particular context is easier to recall in that (or a similar) context. State-dependent retrieval — easier retrieval when the internal state at retrieval matches the state at encoding. Mood-dependent memory — what we remember in a mood is partly determined by what we learned in that same mood; the mood-congruence effect is the tendency to notice/remember information congruent with the current mood. Levels-of-processing — Craik & Lockhart (1972) Deep, meaningful processing yields more permanent retention than shallow, sensory processing. People analyse stimuli at various levels: shallow levels analyse physical/sensory characteristics (brightness, pitch); deep levels analyse meaning . A by-product of analysis is a memory trace: shallow analysis → fragile, quickly forgotten trace; deep analysis → durable, well-remembered trace. They distinguished maintenance vs elaborative rehearsal . Fergus Craik & Endel Tulving (1975) — people were ~3× more likely to recall a word if they had answered questions about its meaning than about its physical appearance. Parkin (1984) — semantic judgments (category/synonym) yielded better surprise-recall than non-semantic ones. Face recognition reviews — deep processing generally produces higher recall than shallow. Compatibility (transfer-appropriate processing) — Moscovitch & Craik (1975) and Bransford et al. (1979) noted retrieval conditions should duplicate encoding conditions for deep processing to be highly effective; deep semantic processing may not be ideal unless retrieval conditions match encoding. When tested on rhyming patterns, people did better if they had done a rhyming encoding task and worse if they had done a sentence (semantic) task. Why deep processing works — Craik & Robert Lockhart (1986) credited distinctiveness and elaboration . Hunt & Elliot (1980): distinctive short/tall letter sequences ( lymph, khaki, afghan ) are recalled better than common orthographic sequences ( leaky, kennel, airway ). 6. Theories of forgetting Logarithmic function of forgetting Hermann Ebbinghaus studied memory/forgetting and plotted forgetting as a function of time, finding the forgetting curve is approximately logarithmic (rapid initial loss, then a slow tail). Rubin and Wenzel (1996) confirmed this with their logarithmic-loss law . Interference theory Our ability to remember current learning can be disrupted by earlier or future learning. Proactive interference — earlier learning interferes with memory of later learning. Retroactive interference — later learning disrupts memory for earlier learning. Both are maximal when two different responses are associated with the same stimulus, intermediate when two similar responses share a stimulus, and minimal when two different stimuli are involved. Evidence for retroactive interference: eyewitness-testimony studies (post-event questioning interferes with the memory) and paired-associate lists; it is assumed to occur because two different responses become associated to the same stimulus. Bower, Thompson-Schill & Endel Tulving (1994) found similarity of response categories is crucial. Underwood (1957) showed proactive interference's importance: ~80% forgotten in a day if participants had previously learned 15+ lists, vs ~20% if none — though proactive interference may account for less forgetting than Underwood assumed. Interference theory also explains the serial position effect (primacy and recency) and the fan effect (Anderson 1974): the more facts learned about a concept, the longer it takes to retrieve any one of them. Decay theory Earliest theorists held forgetting occurs by decay — "forgetting due to a gradual loss of the substrate of memory." Hardt et al. (2013) argued we form numerous trivial memories daily, requiring a decay process to remove them, especially active in the hippocampus . Evidence exists for both interference and decay (at least in STM), but the evidence for decay is "not airtight." Cue-dependent forgetting / retrieval failure Endel Tulving (1974) distinguished two reasons for forgetting: Trace-dependent forgetting — the information is no longer present in memory. Cue-dependent forgetting — the information is present but not accessible (a retrieval failure ). Tulving & Psotka (1971) compared cue-dependent forgetting with interference using three recall conditions: original learning, total free recall, and total free cued recall. Retroactive interference appeared in total free recall (interference theory would say earlier lists were "unlearned"), but there was essentially no interference when category names were available (total free cued recall) — so the forgetting was basically cue-dependent retrieval failure. The encoding specificity principle states: "the probability of successful retrieval of the target item is a monotonically increasing function of informational overlap between the information present at retrieval and the information stored in memory." Prediction: when retrieval context differs from the encoded context, memory performance is worse. Kenealy (1997) manipulated context with happy/sad music at learning and retrieval (route-learning to >80% criterion), tested next day with free and cued recall. Consolidation theory Consolidation fixes information in LTM over hours (sometimes years), in two phases: the first phase (hours) focused on the hippocampus ; the second phase (days to years) involving interactions among the hippocampal region, adjacent entorhinal cortex and the neocortex . Memory traces are most vulnerable shortly after learning, so people should be more susceptible to retroactive interference early in the retention interval. Evidence: retrograde amnesia patients show impaired memory for events before onset; because the hippocampus is central to the first phase, the most recently formed memories should be most impaired. Haist, Gore & Mao (2001): selective hippocampal activation for famous faces appeared only for those famous in the 1990s, while greater entorhinal-cortex activation (connected to widespread neocortex) appeared for faces famous in the 1980s than the 1990s. Repression — Freud Sigmund Freud emphasised emotional factors in forgetting: very threatening/anxiety-provoking material is often unable to reach conscious awareness — repression . "The essence of repression lies simply in the function of rejecting and keeping something out of consciousness." Material can be repressed even when available to consciousness if it produces no emotional reaction. Evidence comes from normal "repressors": Weinberger, Schwartz & Davidson (1979) classified people as truly low-anxious, high-anxious, defensive-anxious, or repressors. Myers & Brewin (1994) found repressors were much slower to recall negative childhood memories and reported the most indifference/hostility from their fathers. Motivated / directed forgetting Directed forgetting = impaired LTM triggered by instructions to forget. Studied with the item method : each word is followed by a remember/forget instruction; recall/recognition is worse for to-be-forgotten words. Causes: the forget instruction probably causes selective rehearsal of remember items, plus inhibitory processes (successful forgetting is associated with activation in the right frontal cortex, linked to inhibition). Motivated forgetting (inhibition) — Anderson & Green (2001) developed the think/no-think paradigm : participants learn cue–target pairs, then for each cue are told to think the target (respond) or prevent it coming to mind (suppress); some cues are not shown (baseline). Anderson & Huddleston (2012) meta-analysed 47 experiments: recall is lower in the suppress than the respond condition, and lower in suppress than baseline. Strategies of inhibition: thought substitution (associating a different word with the cue) and direct suppression (focusing on the cue while blocking the target). People with the greatest activation in bilateral dorsolateral and ventrolateral prefrontal cortex (executive-control areas) were most successful at memory inhibition. High-yield Five families of forgetting: decay (trace fades), interference (proactive vs retroactive), cue-dependent retrieval failure (Endel Tulving; encoding specificity), repression (Sigmund Freud; unconscious, emotional), and motivated/directed forgetting (deliberate inhibition; think/no-think). Tulving & Psotka is the classic study showing cue-dependent forgetting can masquerade as interference. 7. Perception: approaches, illusions & pattern recognition Frameworks & approaches James Gibson (1966, 1979) framed perception via: distal (external) object → informational medium → proximal stimulation → perceptual object . Physiological approach The first step in perception is the stimulation of receptors by environmental stimuli; light reflected from an object stimulates visual receptors, triggering electrical signals toward the brain. Cortical neurons that respond best to simple shapes (lines/bars of specific orientation) are feature detectors ; perceiving a whole object depends on activity beyond the visual cortex, but feature-detector response is the first step. Sensory adaptation — receptor cells adapt to constant stimulation by ceasing to fire until stimulation changes. Because of retinal adaptation, the eyes make tiny rapid movements ( saccades ) to keep changing the image's location; constant stimulation makes a stabilized image appear to disappear. Perceptual constancies — recognizing that physical objects are consistent even though our sensory input changes; the system adjusts perception of the proximal stimulus to perceive the constant distal object. Size constancy — an object keeps the same perceived size despite changes in the proximal image size. The retinal image size depends on distance; two factors account for constancy: the size–distance invariance principle (we consider both the retinal image and apparent distance) and relative size (comparison to objects of known size). Shape constancy — perceived shape does not change as the retinal image changes (e.g., through rotation), even though parts seem to change differentially in distance; localized to the extra-striate cortex (around primary visual cortex). Brightness/colour constancy — objects and surroundings are usually lit by the same source, so lighting changes affect both simultaneously and the neural message stays unchanged. Constancy breaks down when lighting changes are unequal for object and surround. Information-processing approach Dominant in the 1960s–70s, it draws an analogy between human cognition and computerized processing: information is received, stored, recoded, transformed, retrieved and transmitted in stages , stored in specific places. People are "general-purpose symbol manipulators" achieving feats with a few mental operations; coding/storage greatly affects later use. Detection/recognition occur early; recoding/retrieval concern storage; reasoning/concept formation put information together in new ways. The tradition is rooted in structuralism . Ecological perspective & Gibson's direct perception The central tenet: cognition does not occur in isolation from cultural context; all cognition is shaped by culture and context (Lave, Murtaugh & de la Rocha 1984 found calculation methods varied with context). Gibson's direct perception is an ecological theory: in the real world, sufficient contextual information over time exists to make perceptual judgments without higher-level intelligent processes. We observe depth cues such as texture gradients to perceive proximity/distance directly. Optic array — the structural pattern of light reaching the eye; it contains all the visual information from the environment. Invariant information — the optic array provides unambiguous information via texture gradients, optic-flow patterns (changes in light pattern when the observer or environment moves) and affordances . Affordances — "opportunities for action that exist in the environment and do not depend on the animal's mind … they do not cause behaviour but simply make it possible." Gibson (1979) claimed potential uses of objects are directly perceivable . Gestalt organization Max Wertheimer developed an influential approach to form perception. Gestalt means "form"/"whole form"; the aim is to explain how the visual system combines elements in the visual field — perceiving is more than the summation of sensations . Two aspects of organizing elemental sensations: the figure–ground relationship and the grouping of elements (Gestalt laws). Figure–ground — the figure is the dominant object; the contour belongs to the figure; the figure has shape and meaning. The ground is the background, relatively disorganized. Factors favouring figure perception: orientation (vertical/horizontal > diagonal), relative size (smaller/thinner > larger), symmetry , and inclusion/surroundedness (an image inside another). Gestalt grouping laws — proximity, similarity, good continuation, closure, Prägnanz (good form/simplicity), and common fate (common motion).
