Three grades: cardinal traits (the most pervasive, powerful, dominating traits), central traits (the handful of outstanding traits describing a person), and secondary traits (least important, displayed inconspicuously and inconsistently). Functional autonomy — the motives of mature, healthy adults are no longer functionally connected to the prior experiences in which they first appeared. Perseverative functional autonomy governs low-level routine behaviours; propriate functional autonomy governs values, self-image and lifestyle (the proprium = the ego/self). Propriate functioning follows three principles: organising the energy level, mastery and competence, and propriate patterning (striving for consistency and integration). Allport described seven stages of development of the proprium from infancy to adolescence. Raymond Cattell — 16PF Defined traits as relatively permanent reaction tendencies, the basic structural units of personality. Distinguished common traits (in everyone to some degree) from unique traits (in one or a few). Used source traits (the underlying factors, obtained by factor analysis) to derive 16 basic personality factors , assessed by the Sixteen Personality Factor Questionnaire (16PF) . Three data sources: Q-data (self-report questionnaires), T-data (objective test/observational data from controlled test situations), and L-data (life-record data, e.g. school records). Hans Eysenck — the PEN model Using factor analysis Eysenck identified three dimensions: E — Extraversion vs introversion; N — Neuroticism vs emotional stability; P — Psychoticism vs impulse control (superego functioning). Biologically, extraverts have a lower base level of cortical arousal than introverts, so they actively seek excitement and stimulation; introverts shy away because their cortical arousal is already high. Trap Hans Eysenck's arousal logic is counter-intuitive: extraverts are under -aroused and seek stimulation; introverts are over -aroused and avoid it. Raymond Cattell = 16 factors; Eysenck = 3 (PEN); the Big Five = 5 . McCrae & Costa — the Five-Factor Model (Big Five / OCEAN) Emerged from extensive factor analyses of personality-describing adjectives and of personality tests/scales: O — Openness (to experience/culture/intellect): imaginative, witty, original, artistic vs shallow, plain, simple. C — Conscientiousness (lack of impulsivity; early research called it "Will"): cautious, dependable, persevering, organised vs careless, disorderly, undependable. E — Extroversion (surgency): energetic, enthusiastic, dominant, sociable, talkative vs shy, retiring, submissive, quiet. A — Agreeableness : friendly, cooperative, trusting, warm vs cold, quarrelsome, unkind. N — Neuroticism (emotional instability): nervous, high-strung, tense, volatile, moody, worrying vs calm, contented. Mnemonic OCEAN = Openness, Conscientiousness, Extroversion, Agreeableness, Neuroticism. Extensions of the trait model Ashton & Lee — HEXACO : a six-factor model adding Honesty-Humility (H) to Emotionality, eXtraversion, Agreeableness, Conscientiousness and Openness. Paulhus & Williams — the Dark Triad (2002): Narcissism (extreme selfishness, inflated sense of one's abilities, constant need for admiration), Machiavellianism (the need to manipulate others through cunning, deceit and unscrupulous behaviour), and Psychopathy (callous, insensitive, egocentric, antisocial, takes advantage of others using charm and often violence). Type approaches The idea of types is that there are discrete classes of people. Types are usually just the first step toward a fuller understanding of traits. The classic application is the assessment of people prone to heart disease — Type A versus Type B (see Stress). The motivational approach to traits — Henry Murray Henry Murray proposed needs related to personality, including the need for Achievement (n Ach), Affiliation (n Aff), Power (n Power) and Exhibition (n Exh). 5. Humanistic approach: Maslow & Rogers Abraham Maslow — the hierarchy of needs Maslow proposed a hierarchy of five innate needs that activate and direct behaviour, described as instinctoid (having a hereditary component). From strongest/lowest to weakest/highest: physiological → safety → belongingness and love → esteem → self-actualization . Lower needs must be at least partially satisfied before higher needs become influential. Outside the hierarchy sit the cognitive needs : the need to know and the need to understand. Self-actualization — the highest need: the maximum realisation and fulfilment of one's potentials, talents and abilities. Lower needs are deficit (deficiency, D) needs — failing to satisfy them produces a deficit/crisis; higher needs are growth (being, B) needs — their satisfaction improves health, happiness, contentment, fulfilment and longevity, but failing them produces no crisis. Physiological/safety needs arise in infancy; belongingness/esteem in adolescence; self-actualization not until midlife. The study of self-actualizers Self-actualizers run on metamotivation (B-motivation / Being-motivation) — concerned with fulfilling potential; others run on D-motivation (Deficiency) — striving to make up for something lacking. Metaneeds are states of being (goodness, uniqueness, perfection) rather than specific goal objects; failing to satisfy them produces metapathology . Conditions for self-actualization: freedom from social/self constraints, not distracted by lower needs, security in self-image and relationships (able to love and be loved), and realistic self-knowledge. Barriers: lower needs unmet; inadequate education or improper child-rearing (the ideal is a balance of permissiveness and regulation); and the Jonah complex — fear that maximising our potential will lead to a situation we cannot cope with. Self-actualization requires courage, discipline and self-control. Carl Rogers — self / actualization theory The goal of life is self-actualization , an innate tendency toward growth, part of a larger actualizing tendency spanning all physiological and psychological needs. The organismic valuing process evaluates experiences by how well they serve the actualizing tendency: growth-promoting experiences are sought, hindering ones avoided. Positive regard — the need for acceptance, love and approval, especially from the mother in infancy. Unconditional positive regard is granted freely; conditional positive regard ties love to behaviour. Internalised, regard becomes positive self-regard . Conditions of worth (akin to the Freudian superego) — seeing ourselves as worthy only under conditions acceptable to our parents; we avoid perceptions opposing them. Incongruence develops between the self-concept and threatening behaviours; we defend against anxiety by denying threatening parts of the experiential field. The fully functioning person (peak of development): awareness of all experiences with no conditions to defend against, the ability to live fully in each moment, trust in oneself, a sense of freedom and personal power, and creativity and spontaneity. Self-Determination Theory (Deci & Ryan) A contemporary outgrowth of Abraham Maslow's self-actualization. People have an innate tendency to express their interests and develop their capabilities, facilitated by focusing on intrinsic motivation (doing an activity for the interest and challenge of the activity itself). SDT specifies three basic needs whose satisfaction yields well-being: competence (mastering difficult tasks), autonomy (basing one's actions on one's own interests, needs and values) and relatedness (a close connection with others). 6. Existential approach: Rollo May Being-in-the-world (Dasein) — existentialists take a phenomenological approach: we exist in a world best understood from our own perspective. Dasein (German, "to exist there") expresses the basic unity of person and environment. Alienation — the illness of our time, in three areas: separation from nature, lack of meaningful interpersonal relations, and alienation from one's authentic self. We experience three simultaneous modes: Umwelt (the environment, biological drives, natural law), Mitwelt (relations with other people), and Eigenwelt (our relationship with our self). Nonbeing — awareness of self as a living, emerging being leads to dread of not being (nonbeing/nothingness). Death is the most obvious avenue, but nonbeing also appears as blind conformity or generalized hostility. Anxiety — arises when one's existence or a value identified with it might be destroyed. Freedom cannot exist without anxiety. Normal anxiety is proportionate to the threat and can be confronted consciously; neurotic anxiety is disproportionate, involves repression and is managed by blocking off awareness. Guilt — arises when we deny our potentialities, fail to perceive others' needs, or ignore our dependence on nature. Both anxiety and guilt are ontological (about the nature of being). Three forms of ontological guilt correspond to the three modes: separation guilt (Umwelt — separation from nature), guilt of Mitwelt (inadequacy with others), guilt of Eigenwelt (denial/failure of one's own potentialities). Intentionality — the structure that gives meaning to experience and lets people make decisions about the future. Care is an active state in which something matters, the opposite of apathy; without care there is no love, and care is also the source of will ("the capacity to organize one's self so that movement toward a goal may take place"). Four forms of love (Western tradition): Sex (biological release of sexual tension), Eros (psychological desire for procreation/creation through enduring union, built on care and tenderness — the salvation of sex), Philia (intimate non-sexual friendship that takes time to grow), and Agape (altruistic, disinterested esteem for the other's welfare). Eros is built on philia; philia needs agape. Freedom and destiny — healthy people both assume their freedom and face their destiny. Freedom of doing (existential freedom) = acting on one's choices; freedom of being (essential freedom) = the inner possibility of changing. Destiny = "the design of the universe speaking through the design of each one of us"; within its boundaries we have the power to choose, but it does not permit any change we wish. The power of myth — myths are the stories that unify a society; for May they are archetypal patterns comparable to Carl Jung's collective unconscious. Psychopathology — for May, apathy and emptiness (not anxiety and guilt) are the malaise of modern times; disturbed people deny their destiny, lose their freedom, and erect neurotic symptoms to renounce freedom. He saw psychopathology as a lack of communication . 7. Behavioural & social-cognitive: Bandura, Rotter, Mischel B. F. Skinner — the behavioural baseline The strict behavioural view treats personality as a set of learned response tendencies shaped by reinforcement and punishment, with no need to invoke inner traits — the backdrop against which Albert Bandura, Julian Rotter and Walter Mischel added cognition. Albert Bandura — social/observational learning Observational learning (modelling). Rather than reinforcing ourselves for each action, we learn through vicarious reinforcement — observing others' behaviour and its consequences. Learning can occur through observation/example, not only direct reinforcement. The Bobo doll experiment. Preschool children watched an adult hit and kick an inflatable Bobo doll while shouting "Sock him in the nose!"; left alone with the doll they imitated the aggression. The experimental group was about twice as aggressive as a control group not exposed to the model. Watching a model perform usually-suppressed behaviour is disinhibition (an online form is trolling ). Three factors influencing modelling: characteristics of the models (those similar in appearance/sex/age and of high status are more effective; simple behaviours are imitated more readily than complex ones); characteristics of the observers (people low in self-confidence/self-esteem imitate more); and the reward consequences (seeing a model rewarded or punished affects imitation). Four processes of observational learning: attentional → retention → production → incentive/motivational processes. Self-reinforcement — administering rewards/punishments to oneself for meeting one's own standards. Self-efficacy — our feeling of adequacy, efficiency and competence in coping with life. Low self-efficacy → feeling helpless and unable to control events; high → believing one can deal effectively with situations. Four sources of self-efficacy : performance attainment (mastery experiences), vicarious experiences, verbal persuasion, and physiological/emotional arousal — each suggesting a way to raise efficacy (reachable goals, good models, encouragement, and managing arousal through diet/stress reduction/exercise). Walter Mischel — the person-situation debate Mischel challenged the consistency of broad traits across situations (the person–situation debate ), arguing behaviour is highly situation-specific. His later Cognitive-Affective Personality System (CAPS) reframes personality as stable if…then behavioural signatures — a person behaves consistently within similar situations even if they look inconsistent across different ones. Julian Rotter — social learning & locus of control Behaviour depends on both outcome expectancy (how strongly we expect performance to bring a positive result) and reinforcement value (how much we value the expected reinforcement). The set of relevant behaviours available is the behaviour potential . Generalized vs specific expectancies. Specific expectancies attach a reward to a behaviour in a particular situation; generalized expectancies span a group of situations and give the stable, situationally consistent characteristics we call personality. Out-of-character behaviour can arise from specific expectancies. Rotter described six psychological needs developing out of biological needs: recognition-status, dominance, independence, protection-dependency, love and affection, and physical comfort. Reinforcement value is judged relative to other available reinforcers; behaviour potential, outcome expectancy and reinforcement value combine into the psychological situation . Locus of control (LOC). An internal LOC is the generalized expectancy that one's own actions lead to desired outcomes; an external LOC attributes outcomes to chance or powerful others. Later work found three orthogonal dimensions: internality , luck/chance and powerful others . Internals are more achievement-oriented and higher achievers; externals are less independent and more likely to be depressed and stressed. 8. Cognitive approaches: Kelly, Lewin, Seligman, Kohlberg Roots: Gestalt and Kurt Lewin Gestalt psychology (influential in 1920s Germany): humans seek meaning, organise sensations into meaningful perceptions, and complex stimuli are not reducible to the sum of their parts. Kurt Lewin — came out of the Gestalt tradition but focused on personality and social psychology. His field theory (1935) centres on the life space — all internal and external forces acting on an individual — and on contemporaneous causation (behaviour is caused at the moment of its occurrence by all influences present then). Cognitive styles — field dependence/independence (Witkin, Solomon Asch). Field-dependent people are heavily influenced by salient but irrelevant context, are more holistic/intuitive, and are more sensitive to social/interpersonal contexts; field-independent people are more analytical, restructure problems more, and are guided more by internalised aspects. George Kelly — personal construct theory Each person has a unique system of constructs used to understand and predict behaviour (their own and others'). Constructive alternativism — we are not controlled by our constructs; we are free to revise or replace them with alternatives. The theory is presented in scientific form, organised into a fundamental postulate and 11 corollaries . (Kelly is associated with the person-as-scientist metaphor and the Role Construct Repertory / "Rep" Test.) Martin Seligman — explanatory styles, learned helplessness & learned optimism Explanatory style — cognitive personality variables capturing one's habitual way of interpreting events. The optimistic style perceives even neutral events positively and finds eventual positives in negatives; the pessimistic style focuses on the negative potential. Optimism is associated with better outcomes, especially under challenge. Defensive pessimism (Julie Norem) — in risky situations a person reduces anxiety and improves performance by anticipating a poorer outcome; excessive optimism can be maladaptive when failure chances are high. Learned helplessness (Seligman, 1975) — repeated exposure to unavoidable punishment leads an organism to accept later punishment even when it becomes avoidable. In the classic study, dogs given inescapable shocks later failed to escape when escape was possible. Learned optimism — training people to think differently about themselves and their situations, developing the healthier responses of the optimistic style. Lawrence Kohlberg — moral development Kohlberg (1969) described three levels of moral reasoning, each with two stages: Level Stages Reasoning I. Preconventional (typical ages 4–10; external controls) 1. Orientation toward punishment & obedience; 2. Instrumental purpose & exchange Obey rules to avoid punishment (ignoring motive, focusing on physical form/consequences) or to serve self-interest ("you scratch my back"), following the golden rule instrumentally II. Conventional (usually after age 10; internalised authority standards) 3. Maintaining mutual relations, approval of others ("Am I a good boy/girl?"); 4. Social concern & conscience ("What if everybody did it?") Want to please and help others, judge intentions and develop ideas of a "good person"; later value duty, respect for authority and maintaining the social order III. Postconventional (morality of autonomous moral principles) 5. Morality of contract, individual rights & democratically accepted law; 6. Universal ethical principles Think in rational terms valuing the majority's will and society's welfare; recognise that human need can conflict with law; ultimately act on internalised principles of right, fairness and justice regardless of others' opinions, condemning themselves if they fail 9. Assessment of personality Freudian assessment techniques Free association — the patient says whatever comes to mind ("daydreaming out loud"). Catharsis = the expression of emotions expected to reduce disturbing symptoms; resistance = a blockage or refusal to disclose painful memories. Dream analysis — dreams symbolically represent repressed desires, fears and conflicts. The manifest content = the actual events of the dream; the latent content = the hidden symbolic meaning. Across the theories — how each measures personality Carl Jung — the word-association test (response delay, respiration, GSR, retest memory) to detect complexes; the MBTI derived from his types. Raymond Cattell — the 16PF , with Q-data, T-data and L-data. Hans Eysenck — questionnaires measuring the PEN dimensions. Robert McCrae & Paul Costa — the Big Five via factor-analysed self-report scales. Zuckerman — the Sensation Seeking Scale (SSS) , a 40-item paper-and-pencil questionnaire (see §15). Murray — needs (n Ach etc.) classically assessed with projective methods (the Thematic Apperception Test). High-yield Type A vs Type B is the canonical type assessment (heart-disease proneness). 16PF = Raymond Cattell, PEN = Hans Eysenck, OCEAN = Robert McCrae & Paul Costa, MBTI = Jung-derived, SSS = Zuckerman, word-association = Carl Jung. 10. Emotion & its physiology; theories of emotion Emotion is the "feeling" aspect of consciousness, with three elements: a certain physical arousal , a certain behaviour that reveals the feeling outwardly, and an inner awareness of the feeling. The physiology of emotion Arousal is created by the sympathetic nervous system : heart rate increases, breathing quickens, pupils dilate, the mouth dries. Different emotions show different physiological signatures: sadness, anger and fear raise heart rate more than disgust; disgust raises skin conductance more than happiness; anger shows vascular signs such as higher diastolic blood pressure compared with fear. The amygdala (in the limbic system, on each side of the brain) is associated with emotions such as fear and pleasure in humans and animals. Other subcortical and cortical areas — notably the frontal lobes — also process emotion: positive emotions are associated with the left frontal lobe, negative feelings (sadness, anxiety, depression) with the right frontal lobe. The endocrine response (hormonal secretions) and autonomic arousal can be triggered by a fast "low road" (thalamus → amygdala) and a slower "high road" (thalamus → cortex → amygdala). Theories of emotion Theory Sequence (snarling dog → ?) Key claim Common-sense Stimulus → conscious fear → ANS arousal "I'm shaking because I'm afraid." Feeling comes first, then the body. James-Lange Stimulus → ANS arousal & body changes → conscious fear "I'm afraid because I'm shaking." The bodily response comes first and is the emotion. Cannon-Bard Stimulus → subcortical (thalamic) activity → arousal AND fear simultaneously "I'm shaking and feeling afraid at the same time." Physiological arousal and the felt emotion occur together, independently. Schachter-Singer (two-factor / cognitive arousal) Stimulus → ANS arousal + cognitive label → fear Emotion = physiological arousal plus a cognitive interpretation/label of that arousal. Lazarus (cognitive-mediational) Stimulus → cognitive appraisal → arousal + emotion "This dog is dangerous and that makes me afraid." A cognitive appraisal must come first. Facial-feedback Stimulus → facial expression → bodily response/emotion Facial muscle movements feed back to produce or intensify the felt emotion. Trap James-Lange = body first , then feeling; Cannon-Bard = body and feeling together (thalamic); Schachter-Singer = arousal + label ; Lazarus = appraisal first. Don't confuse Schachter-Singer (label after arousal) with Lazarus (appraisal before arousal). 11. Stress, the GAS & conflict Hans Selye — the General Adaptation Syndrome (GAS) Selye, the founder of stress research, studied the sequence of physiological reactions the body uses to adapt to a stressor — the general adaptation syndrome (GAS) , in three stages: Alarm. The sympathetic nervous system is activated; the adrenal glands release hormones that increase heart rate, blood pressure and blood-sugar supply, producing a burst of energy. Reactions such as fever, nausea and headache are common. Resistance. As stress continues, the body settles into sympathetic activity, continuing to release stress hormones to fight off or resist the stressor; early alarm symptoms lessen and the person may actually feel better. One stress hormone, noradrenaline (norepinephrine) , affects the brain's processing of pain, producing a kind of analgesia (so a person under stress may not feel hitting an arm or shin). Exhaustion. When the body's resources are gone, exhaustion occurs, which can lead to stress-related diseases (high blood pressure, weakened immune system) or, without outside help, the death of the organism. Personality differences in stress (the Type theory of cardiac risk) Type Profile Health link Type A Workaholic, competitive, ambitious, hates wasting time, easily annoyed More likely to have health issues (e.g. heart disease), especially the more hostile the person Type B More easygoing, slower to anger, less competitive or driven Less likely to have health issues Type C Pleasant and at peace but finds it difficult to express emotions, especially negative ones Associated with cancer Type H ("hardy") Looks like Type A but thrives on stress via three factors: commitment, control, and seeing stressors as a challenge Less prone to heart disease Mnemonic The three C's of hardiness (Type H): Commitment, Control, Challenge. Conflict: sources and types Whenever you are torn between competing, incompatible desires, goals or actions, you are in conflict : Approach–approach — attraction to two or more desirable goals; least stressful. Avoidance–avoidance — a choice between two or more undesirable situations; more stressful. Approach–avoidance — a single goal/event has both positive and negative aspects; can be most stressful . Multiple approach–avoidance (e.g. double approach–avoidance ) — common in daily life when decisions affect two or more goals each with pros and cons. 12. Theories of motivation Motivation is the process by which activities are started, directed and continued so that physical or psychological needs/wants are met. Intrinsic vs extrinsic. Intrinsic = actions rewarding or satisfying in and of themselves; extrinsic = actions performed because they lead to an external outcome. Instinct approach. Instincts are biologically determined, innate patterns of behaviour. The older view is criticised because instincts are mainly descriptions , not explanations ; but the idea that some behaviour is hereditary remains important. Drive-reduction (Clark Hull). A need is a requirement for something essential to survival; a need creates psychological tension (a drive ) and physical arousal, and satisfying the need reduces the drive/tension (toward homeostasis ). Primary drives involve survival needs (hunger, thirst) and maintain homeostasis; secondary (acquired) drives are learned through experience or conditioning (money, social approval). Psychological-needs / McClelland. Some theories highlight learned psychological needs: need for achievement (nAch) , need for affiliation (nAff) , and need for power (nPow) . Dweck suggests need for achievement is linked to a person's view of self (fixed vs changeable mindset) and locus of control. Arousal theory. People have an optimal level of tension/arousal they work to maintain (the Yerkes-Dodson law — an inverted-U where performance peaks at moderate arousal). The need for stimulation usually settles at a moderate level but ranges low to high ( sensation seeking ). Incentive approach. Based partly on principles of learning: incentives are things that attract or lure people into action, most often through their rewarding properties (motivation pulled from outside, not just pushed by internal drives). Humanistic. Based primarily on Abraham Maslow's hierarchy — basic needs must be met before higher levels can be reached (other versions differ in number of levels and focus). Self-determination theory. Similar to Maslow's hierarchy: three universal needs — autonomy, competence and relatedness — must be met for well-being. High-yield Match the theorist: drive-reduction = Clark Hull; arousal/optimal-arousal = Yerkes-Dodson (inverted-U); nAch/nAff/nPow = David McClelland; hierarchy = Abraham Maslow; autonomy/competence/relatedness = Self-Determination (Edward Deci & Richard Ryan). Drives push from inside; incentives pull from outside. 13. Emotional & social development Emotional expression & self-conscious emotions Self-conscious emotions — embarrassment, shame, guilt, envy and pride — each involves some damage to, or enhancement of, the sense of self. Self-evaluative emotions (shame, guilt, pride) require both self-recognition (recognising oneself in a mirror/photo) and an understanding of rules or standards for evaluating one's conduct. Parents socialize emotions by modelling positive emotions, attending to infants' pleasant feelings, and being less responsive to negative displays. Emotional self-regulation Begins by the end of the first year and develops slowly: toddlers move from depending on others to regulating emotions on their own; grade-schoolers comply with culturally defined emotional display rules (suppressing unacceptable emotions and outwardly replacing them with the called-for feeling). Social referencing — by 8–10 months, infants use others' emotional expressions to infer the meaning of ambiguous situations. Emotional competence has three components: competent emotional expressivity (frequent positive, infrequent negative displays), emotional knowledge (correctly identifying others' feelings and their causes), and emotional regulation (adjusting one's arousal to an appropriate intensity to achieve goals). Each component is related to children's social competence . Temperament & development (Thomas & Chess; Rothbart) Temperament is a person's tendency to respond in predictable ways to environmental events, influenced by genetic and environmental factors; negatively-toned attributes are shaped more by nonshared environmental influences (aspects siblings do not share). Mary Rothbart & John Bates' dimensions: fearful distress, irritable distress (frustration/anger), positive affect (sociability), activity level, attention span/persistence, and rhythmicity (regularity of bodily functions). Temperamental attributes (activity level, irritability, sociability, fearfulness) are moderately stable over time, including behavioral inhibition (withdrawal from unfamiliar people/situations). Alexander Thomas & Stella Chess grouped these into profiles: Easy — even-tempered, typically positive mood, open and adaptable; regular, predictable habits. Difficult — active, irritable, irregular in habits. Slow-to-warm-up — inactive, somewhat moody, slow to adapt; responds to novelty in mildly (not intensely) negative ways. Difficult and slow-to-warm-up children are at greater risk of adjustment problems, depending on the goodness-of-fit between parenting and the child's temperament. Social development & person perception Age trends in how children perceive others: Children younger than 7–8 describe others in the same concrete, observable terms they use for the self. Behavioral comparisons phase — grade-schoolers form impressions by comparing/contrasting overt behaviours. Psychological constructs phase — later, they rely on stable traits to describe patterns. Psychological comparisons phase — young adolescents compare/contrast people on abstract psychological dimensions; by 14–16 they know situational influences can make a person act "out of character." Theories of social-cognitive development — Selman Robert Selman's role-taking theory (1980): the growth of role-taking skills underlies a mature understanding of self and others, tested with the Holly dilemma (an 8-year-old who promised her father not to climb trees, but is the only one who can rescue a kitten stuck in a tree). Social influences — equal-status contacts with friends and peers are crucial: they contribute indirectly by fostering role-taking (children must compromise to keep play going) and directly by providing experiences of what others are like. Jean Piaget assumed equal-status peer contact is an important contributor to social perspective-taking. 14. Attachment Attachment (John Bowlby, 1969) is the strong affectional tie we feel with the special people in our lives. Infants form reciprocal affectional ties to caregivers during the first year; parents' bonding strengthens as they gear behaviour to the infant's social signals and establish synchronized routines. The phases of attachment Asocial phase (0–6 weeks). Phase of indiscriminate attachment (6 weeks–7 months). Phase of specific attachments (7–9 months) — the first true attachments; the attachment object becomes a secure base for exploration . Phase of multiple attachments (9–18 months). Theories of attachment Psychoanalytic and learning theories were discredited because feeding plays less of a role in human attachment than they expected. Cognitive-developmental — attachments depend on cognitive development: infants must recognise that familiar companions have permanence (object permanence), since a stable relationship is hard to form with someone who seems to cease to exist when out of view. Harry Harlow & Zimmerman — infant monkeys separated at birth and raised with a wire surrogate or a cloth surrogate spent time with the wire mother only while feeding but ran to the cloth mother when upset or afraid — showing contact comfort is a more powerful contributor to attachment than feeding/hunger reduction. Ethological theory — Konrad Lorenz : young goslings followed almost any moving object (their mother, a duck, even a human), a behaviour he called imprinting . Imprinting is automatic (no teaching needed), occurs only within a narrowly delimited critical period after hatching, and is irreversible. In humans, infants inherit attributes that maintain contact and elicit caregiving — Lorenz's "kewpie doll" appearance (large forehead, chubby cheeks, soft rounded features) makes infants seem cute/lovable, and smiling/babbling reinforces caregiving. Attachment-related fears Stranger anxiety and separation anxiety stem from infants' wariness of strange situations and their inability to explain who strangers are or where absent companions have gone. Both usually decline in the second year as toddlers mature and venture from their secure bases to explore. Attachment quality — Ainsworth's Strange Situation The Strange Situation (Mary Ainsworth, 1978) assesses attachment quality in 1- to 2-year-olds. Four classifications: Classification Behaviour Secure Actively explores while alone with mother; may be upset by separation but greets her warmly on return and seeks contact that alleviates distress; outgoing with strangers when mother is present. Resistant (ambivalent) Stays close, explores little; very distressed at departure; ambivalent on return — angry, resists physical contact; very wary of strangers even when mother is present. Avoidant Little distress on separation; turns away from / ignores mother even when she tries to gain attention; often sociable with strangers but may avoid them too. Disorganized / disoriented (Main & Solomon, 1990) A confusing combination of resistant and avoidant patterns; on reunion may seem dazed, freeze, or approach then abruptly move away — confusion about whether to approach or avoid the caregiver. Cultural variation. The distribution of classifications varies across cultures and reflects child-rearing differences — for example Japanese mothers emphasize social routines more and exploration less than American mothers, and seek to promote the infant's amae (a state of total dependence on the mother and a presumption of her love and indulgence). Factors influencing attachment security & later development Caregiving hypothesis — sensitive, responsive caregiving → secure attachments; inconsistent, neglectful, over-intrusive or abusive caregiving → insecure attachments. Environmental stressors (poverty, a stormy marriage) also contribute. Caregiving may determine whether attachment is secure or insecure. Temperament hypothesis — infant characteristics and temperament may influence attachment by shaping caregiver–infant interactions; child temperament may determine the kind of insecurity shown when caregiving is insensitive. Internal working models — cognitive representations of self, others and relationships, constructed from interactions with caregivers; often stable over time and shaping reactions to people and challenges for years. Secure attachment predicts later intellectual curiosity and social competence. Parents' working models correspond closely to their children's. Working models can change : a secure history is no guarantee of positive adjustment, nor insecurity a certain indicator of poor outcomes. 15. Exploratory behaviour, curiosity & sensation seeking Zuckerman's sensation seeking Sensation seeking is the need for varied, novel, complex and intense sensations and experiences, and the willingness to take physical, social, legal and financial risks for the sake of such experience. Measured by the Sensation Seeking Scale (SSS) , a 40-item paper-and-pencil questionnaire. Four components Thrill and adventure seeking — desire for physical activities involving speed, danger, novelty and defiance of gravity (parachuting, scuba diving, bungee jumping). Experience seeking — novel experiences through travel, music, art or a nonconformist lifestyle with similar people. Disinhibition — release through uninhibited social activities (risky sex, impulsiveness, aggressiveness, antisocial behaviour). Boredom susceptibility — aversion to repetition, routine work and predictable people; restless discontent when exposed to them. Good vs bad sensation seeking Good sensation seeking — non-impulsive, socialized; chiefly the thrill-and-adventure-seeking component. Bad sensation seeking — impulsive, unsocialized; high scores on disinhibition, experience seeking and boredom susceptibility, plus high scores on Hans Eysenck's psychoticism scale. Characteristics of sensation seekers Age — younger people seek adventure, risk and novelty more than older people. Gender — men score higher on thrill-and-adventure seeking, disinhibition and boredom susceptibility (and higher overall sensation seeking with lower impulse control); women score higher on experience seeking. Racial/cultural — Asians scored lower on the SSS than people in Western countries; white subjects scored higher than non-whites. Risk-taking groups — three types of risk takers were identified: antisocial , adventurous , and prosocial risk takers. Antisocial (drug addicts, criminals) and adventurous (mountain climbers, sky divers) scored significantly higher on the SSS than prosocial risk takers (police, firefighters). Skydivers, firefighters, riot-control police, bungee jumpers and race-car drivers all score high. Behavioural differences — high sensation seekers are more likely than low to use and sell illicit drugs (and earlier), drink alcohol, shoplift and commit delinquent behaviour; more had tattoos and body piercings; at work they scored lower on job performance, were less likely to form social relationships at work, and less likely to try to obtain information from co-workers or supervisors. Personality correlates SSS scores (especially disinhibition) relate to Hans Eysenck's extraversion and to the asocial tendencies of psychoticism . High scores correlate with extraversion as described by Carl Jung and measured by the MBTI . No correlation was found between sensation seeking and neuroticism . High SSS scorers show high autonomy : they openly express emotions, are assertive, nonconforming and confirmed risk takers, acting independently of social conventions and others' needs. Self-regulation (Bandura, applied to exploration) When people have high self-efficacy , are confident in their reliance on proxies , and possess solid collective efficacy , they have considerable capacity to regulate their own behaviour. Albert Bandura (1994) held that people use both reactive and proactive strategies. External factors provide a standard for evaluating our behaviour and the means for reinforcement. Internal factors : self-observation (monitoring our own performance, even if attention is not complete or accurate); judgmental processes (regulating behaviour through cognitive mediation, comparing performance against personal standards rather than others' conduct, weighing the value of the activity and the performance attribution of causes); and self-reaction (responding positively or negatively to our own behaviour depending on how it measures up to personal standards). 16. Fast glossary (A–Z) Term Meaning Agape May's altruistic, disinterested love; esteem for the other's welfare. Amae Japanese state of total dependence on the mother and presumption of her indulgence. Archetype Carl Jung's inherited emotional symbol in the collective unconscious (persona, shadow, anima/animus, self, mother, hero). Basic anxiety Karen Horney: a child's feeling of being alone, helpless and insecure. Behaviour potential Julian Rotter: the likelihood of a behaviour given expectancy and reinforcement value. Cannon-Bard Arousal and emotion occur simultaneously via thalamic activity. Cardinal/central/secondary Gordon Allport's three grades of trait dominance. Cathexis Sigmund Freud: investment of libido in an object. Conditions of worth Carl Rogers: seeing oneself as worthy only under parent-acceptable conditions. Constructive alternativism Kelly: freedom to revise/replace one's constructs. Dark Triad Paulhus & Williams: narcissism, Machiavellianism, psychopathy. Dasein "To exist there"; being-in-the-world (existentialism). Drive-reduction Clark Hull: need → drive/tension → behaviour → reduction (homeostasis). Eros/Philia/Sex/Agape May's four forms of love. Explanatory style Martin Seligman: optimistic vs pessimistic habitual interpretation of events. Field dependence Witkin: reliance on salient context vs analytical field independence. Fictional finalism Alfred Adler: striving toward an imagined future goal. Functional autonomy Allport: adult motives detached from their original source. GAS Hans Selye: alarm → resistance → exhaustion. Goodness-of-fit Match between a child's temperament and parenting demands. HEXACO Ashton & Lee's six factors (adds Honesty-Humility). Id/Ego/Superego Pleasure / reality / morality principle. Imprinting Konrad Lorenz: automatic, critical-period, irreversible following response. Individuation Jung: integration of conscious and unconscious into wholeness. Inferiority complex Adler's term for pervasive feelings of helplessness. Internal working model John Bowlby: cognitive representation of self/others/relationships. James-Lange Emotion follows the bodily response ("afraid because shaking"). Jonah complex Abraham Maslow: fear of one's own potential/greatness. Lazarus Cognitive appraisal precedes emotion and arousal. Learned helplessness Seligman: accepting avoidable punishment after inescapable punishment. Libido Freud: sexual psychic energy; Jung: general (not necessarily sexual) life energy. Locus of control Rotter: internal (own actions) vs external (chance/powerful others). MBTI Jung-derived type inventory (E/I, S/N, T/F, J/P). Metamotivation Maslow's B-motivation of self-actualizers (vs D-motivation). nAch / nAff / nPow David McClelland's needs for achievement, affiliation, power. OCEAN Big Five: Openness, Conscientiousness, Extroversion, Agreeableness, Neuroticism. Object relations Mental representations of significant others (Margaret Mahler, Melanie Klein, Heinz Kohut). Organismic valuing process Rogers: judging experiences by how well they serve actualization. Parapraxis Freudian slip revealing the unconscious. PEN Hans Eysenck: Psychoticism, Extraversion, Neuroticism. Penis envy / womb envy Freud's concept; Horney's male-counterpart rebuttal. Positive regard Rogers: need for acceptance/love; unconditional vs conditional. Proprium Allport's term for the ego/self. Psychosexual stages Freud: oral, anal, phallic, latency, genital. Reinforcement value Rotter: how much one values an expected reinforcement. Schachter-Singer Two-factor emotion: arousal + cognitive label. Self-determination Edward Deci & Richard Ryan: autonomy, competence, relatedness. Self-efficacy Albert Bandura: belief in one's competence to cope; four sources. Sensation Seeking Scale Zuckerman's 40-item SSS; four components. Social interest Adler: innate potential to cooperate toward shared goals. Social referencing Using others' expressions to interpret ambiguous situations (8–10 months). Source traits Raymond Cattell's underlying factors behind the 16PF. Strange Situation Mary Ainsworth: secure, resistant, avoidant, disorganized. Style of life Adler: dominant, getting, avoiding, socially useful. Temperament types Alexander Thomas & Stella Chess: easy, difficult, slow-to-warm-up. Type A/B/C/H Cardiac-risk personality types (H = hardy: commitment, control, challenge). Yerkes-Dodson Inverted-U arousal–performance law; optimal arousal level. Word-association test Jung's method for detecting complexes.

title: Unit 8 — Social Psychology
text: Unit 8 — Social Psychology How the presence, behaviour and existence of other people shape what we think, feel and do: the field's history and grand theories, how we read other people, how groups push us into conformity, obedience and compliance, what happens inside groups, how leaders lead, why we help and why we harm, the roots of prejudice and intergroup conflict, and how all of it is applied to health, the law and the environment. Built file-by-file from the Rodrick Prashanth source decks and deepened to NIMHANS / MET clinical-psychology depth, preserving every named theorist, study, term and proposition. In this book History of social psychology Theories of social psychology Social perception Group & social influence Group dynamics Leadership styles Prosocial behaviour Aggression Theories of intergroup relationship Applying social psychology 1. History of social psychology The one idea. Social psychology is the scientific study of how the actual, imagined or implied presence of others influences an individual's thoughts, feelings and behaviour. Its history is a chain of named "firsts" and named "founders", and the paper loves to test who did what, in what year. The foundation (late 19th to early 20th century) Figure Year Contribution Norman Triplett 1897–1898 Credited with the first research article in social psychology . He noticed cyclists raced faster against others than against a clock, and designed a careful controlled experiment to study it. This is the origin of social facilitation . Max Ringelmann 1880s (published 1913) Found individuals performed worse on simple tasks such as rope-pulling when working with others. This is the origin of social loafing (the "Ringelmann effect"). William McDougall 1908 Published an early social psychology textbook; helps establish the field. Edward Ross 1908 American who published a founding social psychology text the same year. Floyd Allport 1924 His textbook is taken as establishing social psychology as a distinct experimental field. Trap Norman Triplett = social facilitation (first article, 1897–98). Max Ringelmann = social loafing (1880s, published 1913). Don't swap them. Establishing the field as a discipline is attributed to McDougall (1908), Ross (1908) and Floyd Allport (1924). 1930s–1950s: the field finds its problems 1936: Gordon Allport (younger brother of Floyd, the 1924 textbook author) and others formed the Society for the Psychological Study of Social Issues (SPSSI) . Muzafer Sherif published groundbreaking experimental research on social influence (the autokinetic-effect norm-formation studies). Kurt Lewin fled the Nazis and emigrated to the US in the early 1930s. His central contribution: behaviour is a function of the interaction between the person and the environment (the interactionist perspective ), often written B = f(P, E) . 1950s: Gordon Allport (1954) published The Nature of Prejudice . Solomon Asch (1951) demonstrated how willing people are to conform to an obviously wrong majority. Leon Festinger introduced two landmark theories: social comparison (1954, how people learn about themselves by comparing to others) and cognitive dissonance (1957, how attitudes change through one's own behaviour). 1960s–1990s: crisis and pluralism Stanley Milgram's obedience research (early/mid 1960s) linked the post-WWII era to the coming era of social revolution, showing individuals' vulnerability to the destructive commands of authority. Strong disagreements of the period (the "crisis of social psychology") were largely a reaction against the dominant method of the day, the laboratory experiment . Mid-1970s onward = an era of pluralism: laboratory and field experiments used side by side; a "hot" perspective (emotion and motivation) alongside a "cold" perspective (cognition); and the rise of international, cross-cultural and multicultural perspectives. Social psychology in a new century Social cognition dominated the final quarter of the field's first century: the study of how people perceive, remember and interpret information about themselves and others. Social neuroscience emerged as a subfield studying the relationship between neural and social processes. Behavioural genetics (the study of how genes affect behaviour) triggered research on, e.g., whether aggression is heritable and the role of genes in sexual orientation. Evolutionary psychology uses evolutionary principles to understand behaviour (e.g., asking how the psychological mechanisms underlying jealousy may have evolved from natural-selection pressures). Increasing emphasis on testing the universal generality vs cultural specificity of theories via cross-cultural and multicultural research. High-yield Norman Triplett (facilitation, first article) · Max Ringelmann (loafing) · McDougall/Ross 1908 + Floyd Allport 1924 (founding) · Lewin B = f(P,E) · Muzafer Sherif (norm formation) · Solomon Asch 1951 (conformity) · Leon Festinger 1954 social comparison / 1957 dissonance · Milgram 1960s (obedience) · Gordon Allport 1954 Nature of Prejudice . New century: social cognition, social neuroscience, behavioural genetics, evolutionary psychology, cross-cultural work. 2. Theories of social psychology The grand frameworks the field uses to explain social behaviour. Learn each by its core construct and its named author. Field theory (Kurt Lewin) Lewin, whose name is most associated with field theory , was a student of the founders of the Gestalt movement. Others (Edward Tolman 1932, Wheeler 1940, Karl Lashley 1929, Brunswik 1949) have been called field theorists, but none dealt specifically with social behaviour, so Lewin is taken as the best representative. Six principal attributes of field theory: (1) use of a constructive method ; (2) a dynamic approach; (3) emphasis on psychological processes; (4) analysis based on the situation as a whole ; (5) a distinction between systematic and historical issues; (6) a mathematical representation of the psychological situation (Lewin favoured topology ). Definition Life space = the person plus the psychological environment as it exists for him: the totality of all psychological factors influencing the individual at any given moment. A thing "exists" in the life space if it has demonstrable effects . Kurt Lewin held that the properties of the field at the present time are the only determinants of behaviour (an ahistorical orientation). Regions / life spheres: major parts of the life space (needs, profession, family, friendships), further differentiated into smaller units. Differentiation depends on age, intelligence and experience. Two added dimensions: fluidity (how distinguishable and how permeable regions are) and the reality–irreality dimension (reality = objective aspects; irreality = imagery, fantasy, hopes and fears; the psychological future has both a level of reality, "what is expected", and irreality, "hopes and fears"). Behaviour = locomotion: behaviour is any change in the life space, conceived as a locomotion of the person within it (bodily or psychological). The space of free movement is limited by barriers (boundaries that resist locomotion). Force: "that which causes change" (Lewin, 1936), with direction, strength and point of application (vector + arrow). The combination of all forces on a point is the resultant force . Valence describes whether a goal region is attractive (positive) or repulsive (negative); the strength of force is a function of valence and psychological distance. The change of force strength with distance is the goal gradient (it rises faster as one nears a negative goal than a positive one). Types of force: driving, restraining, induced (from another's wishes), own-need, and impersonal (situational requirements). Tension systems: tension is aroused when a person accepts task completion as a goal; it is discharged by completing the task and seeks equilibrium with neighbouring regions. This explains why incompleted tasks are recalled and resumed more than completed ones (the Zeigarnik effect ). Substitute satisfaction can discharge tension; its effectiveness depends on similarity, difficulty, and permeability of boundaries. Cognitive dissonance (Leon Festinger, 1957) Follows Heider's balance theory and the consistency tradition: the core principle is the tendency toward cognitive consistency . Two cognitions are dissonant if, considered alone, the obverse of one would follow from the other; consonant if one follows from the other. Four sources of dissonance: logical inconsistency; cultural mores; opinion generality (a specific opinion clashing with a more general one); past experience. Magnitude depends on the importance of the elements and the weighted proportion of relevant cognitions that are dissonant; the maximum possible dissonance equals the total resistance to change of the least resistant element. Consequences: dissonance is uncomfortable and motivates reduction; the person also actively avoids dissonance-increasing information. Decisions: dissonance is an inevitable consequence of decision; post-decision dissonance grows with the importance of the decision, the attractiveness of the unchosen option, and the cognitive overlap of the options. Forced compliance: public compliance without private change. The smaller the reward/punishment (just sufficient to elicit compliance), the greater the dissonance, hence the greater the attitude change. Selective exposure is curvilinearly related to dissonance: moderate dissonance maximises information seeking/avoidance. Social support: dissonance from disagreement varies with the number of agreeing others, importance of elements, relevance and attractiveness of the disagreer, and extent of disagreement. Trap Less-leads-to-more. In forced compliance, a smaller incentive produces more attitude change (you can't blame the small reward, so you change your attitude instead). This is the opposite of a reinforcement prediction, and is the classic dissonance exam item. Psychodynamic approach: Freud's group psychology Sigmund Freud viewed society as the product of the individual personalities within it. Four major works: Group Psychology and the Analysis of the Ego (1922), Civilization and its Discontents (1930), Totem and Taboo (1913), and The Future of an Illusion . Core ideas: society inhibits and represses instinctual impulses; the family is the fundamental agent of socialisation and the prototype for all later social relationships; groups form as a re-enactment of the individual's libidinal ties to parents ; social justice arises from envy and hostility among members; law and religion protect society against man's aggressive and sexual impulses. Rapaport's (1959) metapsychological points of view on Freud's system: the empirical (subject matter is behaviour), the Gestalt (all behaviour is the total expression of all structures and forces), the genetic (mental phenomena have historical antecedents; earlier behaviour can be reactivated), the dynamic (all behaviour is ultimately drive-determined, primarily a broad sexual/libidinal drive), the economic (behaviour regulated by distribution and flow of psychic energy), the structural (id/ego/superego intervene between arousal and investment), and the adaptive (behaviour is shaped by, and shapes, external and bodily reality). Sociobiological theory (Edward O. Wilson, 1975) In Sociobiology: The New Synthesis , Wilson outlined a framework for the biological basis of social behaviour. As a branch of evolutionary biology, it uses demographic parameters and population genetics to predict social organisation across species. Its key contribution is ultimate causation (the selective forces operating over generations) as distinct from proximate causation (mechanisms within an individual's lifetime). Sociobiology differs from evolutionary psychology : both use ultimate causal explanations, but evolutionary psychology models the underlying information-processing circuitry (cognitive programs) , whereas sociobiology steps straight from selective forces to behaviour without specifying the cognitive programs. Social cognitive theory (Albert Bandura) Began as Social Learning Theory (SLT) in the 1960s; became Social Cognitive Theory (SCT) in 1986. Learning occurs in a social context through the dynamic, reciprocal interaction of person, environment and behaviour . Constructs: reciprocal determinism , behavioural capability (knowledge + skill to perform), observational learning (modelling), reinforcements , expectations (and expectancies , the subjective value of outcomes), and self-efficacy (added when SLT became SCT; confidence in one's ability to perform a behaviour). High-yield Self-efficacy is the construct added when Social Learning Theory became Social Cognitive Theory (1986). The first five constructs (reciprocal determinism, behavioural capability, observational learning, reinforcements, expectations) were already in SLT. 3. Social perception Social perception = the process through which we seek to know and understand other people: how we learn about others, communicate without words, attribute causes, and form impressions. Nonverbal communication To understand others' emotional states we rely on nonverbal communication ("an unspoken language of facial expressions, eye contact, and body movements and postures"). The basic channels are: Facial expressions — the primary channel of emotion. Eye contact — high contact signals liking/interest; staring = continued steady gaze regardless of the recipient's response (often a sign of hostility). Body language — cues from posture, position and movement of the body. Touching — can induce positive reactions when appropriate, negative when not. Paralanguage / paralinguistic cues — tone and inflection of voice (not the words themselves). Body chemistry — even subtle olfactory cues (e.g., menstrual-cycle chemical changes) can be transmitted to others. Definition Facial feedback hypothesis: the facial expressions we show not only reflect our internal feelings but feed back to influence our subjective emotional experience. Evidence: participants given Botox (which paralyses facial muscles) reported less negative reaction to negative film clips and less positive reaction to mildly positive clips than those given Restylane (a non-paralysing control). Recognising deception Microexpressions: fleeting facial expressions lasting only a few tenths of a second. Interchannel discrepancies: inconsistencies between cues from different channels (liars struggle to control all channels at once). Eye contact: liars often blink more and show more dilated pupils. Exaggerated facial expressions: e.g., smiling more broadly than usual. Linguistic style: when lying, the pitch of the voice often rises, response latency increases, and speakers start–stop–restart sentences more. Attribution: understanding causes of behaviour Attribution = our efforts to understand the causes behind others' (and sometimes our own) behaviour. Jones & Davis (1965): correspondent inference theory We are most likely to conclude that behaviour reflects stable traits (reach a correspondent inference ) when the behaviour: is freely chosen ; yields distinctive, non-common effects (effects caused by one specific factor but not others); and is low in social desirability . Kelley's theory of causal attribution (covariation model) To answer "why?" we focus on three kinds of information: Dimension Meaning Consensus Extent to which other people react to the same stimulus in the same way (higher = more people react alike). Consistency Extent to which this person reacts the same way to the stimulus on other occasions / over time. Distinctiveness Extent to which this person reacts differently to other, different stimuli. Other dimensions of causal attribution concern whether causes are stable over time and controllable . People who believe strongly in God, or whose culture accepts complex causality, more often attribute improbable but important events to "what was meant to be" (fate). The level of interpretation we use is action identification : low-level interpretations focus on the action itself, higher-level on its ultimate goals. Sources of attributional bias Correspondence bias / Fundamental Attribution Error (FAE): the tendency to explain others' actions as stemming from dispositions even when situational causes are present. Reasons: dispositional causes are more salient ; we give situational causes insufficient weight; we begin by assuming behaviour reflects character, then under-correct for the situation. Actor–observer effect: we attribute our own behaviour to external/situational causes but others' behaviour to internal causes. Self-serving bias: we attribute positive outcomes to internal causes and negative ones to external causes (especially strong for negative events). Trap FAE = bias about others (over-attribute to disposition). Actor–observer = the self–other split (own behaviour situational, others' dispositional). Self-serving = the good–bad split for one's own outcomes (success internal, failure external). Distinguish all three. 4. Group & social influence Social influence = efforts by one or more persons to change the behaviour, attitudes or feelings of others. It can even be symbolic (occurring when others are not present and make no direct attempt). The three main forms are conformity , compliance and obedience . Social facilitation and social loafing Social facilitation: the tendency to perform simple/well-learned tasks better when others are present; more precisely, the strengthening of dominant (most likely) responses in the presence of others (on some tasks the presence of others hinders performance). Robert Zajonc: increased arousal enhances performance on easy tasks (dominant response correct) but promotes incorrect responding on complex tasks (dominant response wrong) — e.g., people do worse on hard anagrams when anxious. Why? Nickolas Cottrell → evaluation apprehension (we wonder how observers are judging us). Sanders, Baron & Moore → distraction–conflict ("driven by distraction": attention conflict overloads cognition, causing arousal). Zajonc → mere presence produces arousal even without evaluation or distraction. Social loafing: the tendency to exert less effort when pooling efforts toward a common goal than when individually accountable. Free riders benefit from the group but give little in return. High-yield The reconciling rule: when being observed increases evaluation concern, social facilitation occurs; when being lost in a crowd decreases evaluation concern, social loafing occurs. Loafing is reduced when the task is challenging/appealing/involving, when members see others as unable to contribute, when high effort is seen to bring rewards, and when members are friends or feel indispensable. Conformity Definition Conformity = changing attitudes/behaviour to adhere to existing social norms (rules indicating how we should behave). Acceptance = conformity that involves both acting and believing in accord with social pressure. Solomon Asch first systematically studied conformity: participants judged which of three comparison lines matched a standard. When confederates gave identical wrong answers, real participants tended to give the same wrong answer; three-quarters conformed at least once . Philip Zimbardo's Stanford Prison study showed the powerful impact of norms attached to social roles : participants came to behave like real guards and prisoners. Two motives for conformity: normative social influence (the desire to be liked) and informational social influence (the desire to be right/accurate). Factors: cohesiveness , group size , and the type of norm operating ( descriptive = what most people do; injunctive = what is approved/expected). Emotional contagion: we catch others' emotions; if they are dissimilar to us in important ways, we may show counter-contagion (opposite emotions). Nonconformity is encouraged by the desire to attract a mate, by power (powerful people depend less on others and take others' perspectives less), and by the desire to be unique. Minority influence: minorities can sway majorities by being consistent , avoiding appearing rigid/dogmatic, and arguing a position consistent with current social trends. Compliance (Robert Cialdini) Cialdini studied "compliance professionals" and identified six basic principles of compliance : friendship/liking, commitment/consistency, scarcity, reciprocity, authority, social validation (consensus) . Tactic Underlying principle How it works Ingratiation Friendship/liking Get others to like us (flattery, self-promotion, improved appearance, positive nonverbal cues, small favours, incidental similarity ) so they agree more readily. Foot-in-the-door Commitment/consistency Begin with a small request, then escalate to a larger one. Lowball Commitment/consistency An offer is changed to make it less attractive after the person has accepted. Door-in-the-face Reciprocity Begin with a large request; when refused, retreat to the smaller one actually desired all along. That's-not-all Reciprocity Offer additional benefits before the person decides. Playing hard to get Scarcity Suggest a person/object is scarce and hard to obtain. Deadline technique Scarcity Tell targets they have only limited time to take advantage of an offer. Trap Foot-in-the-door (small → large) is based on consistency ; door-in-the-face (large → small) is based on reciprocity . Lowball and foot-in-the-door both start small but lowball involves changing the deal after acceptance . Obedience (Stanley Milgram, 1963, 1965, 1974) The clearest, most dramatic evidence for obedience. Teacher-participants were told to increase shock strength each time the "learner" erred (the learner never actually received shocks). When teachers hesitated, the experimenter used graded prods : "Please continue"; "The experiment requires that you continue"; "It is absolutely essential that you continue"; "You have no other choice; you must go on." Reasons for destructive obedience: Transfer of responsibility onto the experimenter (the authority figure, not the participant, would be responsible). Badges/signs of authority that remind people of the norm "obey the people in charge". Immediacy of the victim: when the victim was unseen/unheard, obedience was higher. Gradual escalation of orders yields more obedience than sudden escalation; situations move quickly. Social power (French & Raven, 1959) Power = the capacity to influence others while resisting their attempts to influence you. John French and Bert Raven (1959) identified five bases of social power (reward, coercive, legitimate, referent, expert); Raven (1965, 1993) later added a sixth (informational power). Persuasion Persuasion = changing attitudes through messages. Most persuasive communicators are credible, physically attractive , and seem not to be trying to persuade. Fear appeals that are too frightening tend not to work; positively framed messages are often more effective. Definition Elaboration-Likelihood Model (ELM): persuasion occurs by two routes. The central route (systematic processing) involves careful attention to message content (argument strength matters), used when motivation and capacity are high. The peripheral route (heuristic processing) uses mental shortcuts and peripheral cues (communicator attractiveness/expertise), used when ability, capacity or motivation is low. Electronic word-of-mouth (eWoM) persuasion depends on communicator credibility, consistency among reviewers, and consistency with prior beliefs. Resistance to persuasion is increased by: reactance (negative reaction to threats to personal freedom, which can boomerang into greater opposition), forewarning (knowing someone will try to change us), selective avoidance , active counterarguing , and attitude inoculation (exposure to weak attacks so refutations are ready for stronger ones). Ego-depletion from prior self-regulation undermines our ability to resist persuasion (and makes us less honest). 5. Group dynamics A group = a collection of people perceived to be bonded together in a coherent unit to some degree. Types and structure of groups Common-bond groups: face-to-face interaction; members bonded to each other . Common-identity groups: face-to-face interaction often absent; members linked via the category rather than each other. Entitativity: the extent to which a group is perceived as a coherent whole. Entitative groups interact often, are important to members, share goals, and are similar in important ways. Key components of groups: Component Meaning Status Gained for many reasons (physical characteristics to conformity to norms); higher for prototypical or senior members; high-status members are more idiosyncratic/variable and report conforming less . Roles Sets of behaviours expected of those in particular positions; powerful when internalised as part of identity; enacting a role well can feel authentic. Norms Rules/expectations about how members should behave. Feeling rules govern emotions (in collectivist groups: maintain harmony even at personal cost; in individualist groups: value standing out). Cohesiveness All forces causing members to remain. Cohesive groups have solidarity, see themselves as homogeneous, support and cooperate with ingroup members, pursue group over individual goals, have high morale, and perform better. An outgroup/competitive threat increases cohesion. Group development and socialisation Bruce Tuckman (1965) five-stage developmental sequence: forming (orientation), storming (conflict over goals/practices), norming (consensus, cohesion, common identity), performing (smooth functioning, shared norms), adjourning (the group dissolves). Moreland & Levine's group socialisation model: three basic processes ( evaluation, commitment, role transition ) leading to five phases. Transition criteria often become formalised as rites of passage / initiation rites serving three functions: symbolic, apprenticeship, loyalty elicitation . Costs and benefits of joining: benefits include self-knowledge, progress toward goals, enhanced status, and a means of social change (when a politicised collective identity forms). Costs include loss of personal freedom and demands on time/energy/resources. After painful initiations people justify their effort and show increased positive attitudes toward the group. A schism (splintering into factions) causes emotional distress and loss of identification. Coordination, cooperation and fairness Cooperation = working together for shared goals; often fails because of social dilemmas (individuals gain by defection, but if all defect everyone loses). Negative interdependence (one's gain = another's loss) lowers cooperation. Conflict = perceiving that others have taken or will take actions incompatible with one's interests; faulty attribution can drive it. Bargaining and superordinate goals (goals both sides seek that tie their interests together) reduce conflict. Perceived fairness has three forms: distributive justice (fairness of outcomes/share of rewards), procedural justice (fairness of the procedures used to distribute), and transactional justice (how the treatment is delivered — whether distributors explain/justify decisions and show respect). Group decision-making Group polarization: groups make more extreme decisions than individuals. Two reasons: members want views more prototypical (hence more extreme) than average; and persuasive arguments in discussion shift members further in the dominant direction. Groupthink (Irving Janis): a tendency for highly cohesive groups to assume they can do no wrong and to reject information contrary to the group's view. Groups also reject criticism more from outgroup than ingroup members. Hidden-profile / shared-information bias: members fail to share unique information; discussion focuses on what everyone already knows. A remedy is to keep members unaware of others' views before discussion. Brainstorming does not produce more creativity than individuals working alone; but debate about ideas does stimulate more creative idea production. Deindividuation Definition Deindividuation = a psychological state of reduced self-awareness brought on by external conditions such as being an anonymous member of a large crowd, encouraging unrestrained, antisocial action. It is especially likely when people are in a large group, physically anonymous, and aroused/distracted. The diminished self-awareness and self-restraint increase responsiveness to the immediate situation (negative or positive). Deindividuation is less likely when self-awareness is high. High-yield Polarization = more extreme. Groupthink = cohesive groups suppress dissent (Irving Janis). Deindividuation = anonymity/arousal → reduced self-awareness → unrestrained behaviour. Brainstorming in groups is not more creative than individuals alone. 6. Leadership styles Leadership = getting group members to achieve the group's goals. Trait and situational perspectives Great person theory: attributes effective leadership to innate or acquired individual characteristics. The best Big Five predictors of effective leadership are being extraverted, open to experience, and conscientious . Situational perspective: different styles are effective in different situations; the interaction of leader behaviour and situational factors matters. Lewin's classic leadership styles Style Behaviour Autocratic Organised activities, gave orders, was aloof, focused exclusively on the task. Democratic Called for suggestions, discussed plans, behaved like an ordinary member. Laissez-faire Left the group to its own devices, intervened minimally. The two leadership dimensions (Ohio State, LBDQ) The Leader Behaviour Description Questionnaire (LBDQ) drew a distinction between two dimensions: initiating structure (define objectives and organise members' work toward them — task-oriented ) and consideration (concern for subordinates' welfare and harmonious relationships — relationship-oriented ). A single person can be high on both , and such a person is a particularly effective leader. Contingency theories Fred Fiedler's contingency theory: measures leadership style with the Least Preferred Coworker (LPC) scale (rate the person you least like working with on dimensions like pleasant–unpleasant, friendly–unfriendly). Effectiveness is contingent on three situational dimensions, in descending importance: (1) leader–member relations , (2) task structure , (3) position power (intrinsic authority of the leader's position). Normative decision theory (NDT): focused on leadership in group decision-making; identifies three strategies — autocratic (no subordinate input), consultative (input sought, leader decides), group decision-making (leader and subordinates as equal partners). Effectiveness is contingent on leader–subordinate relations and task clarity/structure. Path–goal theory: a leader's main function is to motivate followers by clarifying the paths to their goals; also classifiable as a transactional leadership theory. It distinguishes two LBDQ behaviours: structuring (most effective when followers are unclear about goals/how to reach them — new, difficult, ambiguous tasks; backfires as "meddling" when tasks are well understood) and consideration (most effective when the task is boring/uncomfortable, but not when followers are already engaged and motivated, where it can seem distracting). High-yield Fred Fiedler = LPC scale + three situational dimensions (leader–member relations > task structure > position power). Ohio State LBDQ = initiating structure (task) vs consideration (relationship). Path–goal = a transactional theory; structuring helps unclear tasks, consideration helps boring tasks. 7. Prosocial behaviour Definition Prosocial behaviour = actions by individuals that help others with no immediate benefit to the helper. Motives for helping Empathy–altruism hypothesis: because of empathy, we help those in need out of empathic concern. Empathy = the capacity to experience others' emotional states, feel sympathy, and take their perspective, with three components: emotional empathy (sharing feelings), a cognitive component ( empathic accuracy , perceiving thoughts/feelings accurately), and empathic concern (concern for another's well-being). Negative-state relief model: we help to relieve and reduce our own negative emotional discomfort. Empathic joy hypothesis: helping stems from the positive reactions recipients show, and the positive feelings this induces in helpers. Competitive altruism: we help to increase our own status and reputation. Kinship selection theory: we help relatives because it increases the chance our genes are passed on. Reciprocal altruism theory: we help non-relatives because helping is usually reciprocated, indirectly aiding our own survival. Defensive helping: helping to reduce the threat an outgroup poses to one's ingroup. Responding to emergencies: the bystander effect A bystander's response can range from apathy to heroism. Because of diffusion of responsibility , the more bystanders present, the less likely each is to help and the greater the delay (the bystander effect ). Pluralistic ignorance is the tendency to do nothing because, not knowing what is happening, each bystander relies on others' (inactive) cues. The bystander effect is weaker among people who belong to the same group. Definition John Darley & Latané (1968) five-step decision model: whether a bystander helps depends on five sequential decisions — (1) notice the event, (2) interpret it as an emergency, (3) assume responsibility , (4) know how to help , and (5) decide to implement the help. Failing any step means no help is given. Factors and emotions in helping We help those similar to us more (similarity mostly affects the emotional , not the cognitive, component of empathy); we help those we like and those not responsible for their need. Helping is increased by exposure to prosocial models and by playing prosocial video games (which prime prosocial thoughts). Gratitude increases helping by enhancing helpers' self-worth and self-efficacy. Positive feelings increase helping; negative feelings tend to reduce it (though both can enhance or inhibit depending on the situation). Feelings of elevation (being inspired by others' kind acts) increase helping. Empathy is weaker across group boundaries. Three types of perspective taking : "imagine other", "imagine self", and fantasy (empathy for a fictional character). Factors that reduce helping: social exclusion (reduces capacity for empathy), darkness /anonymity, and putting an economic value on one's time . Reactions to being helped: positive when help seems to stem from the helper's positive feelings ( autonomous motivation ); far less positive when help seems forced ( controlled motivation ). Low-status group members are reluctant to receive help from high-status groups, especially when seeking equality. 8. Aggression Definition Aggression = behaviour directed toward the goal of harming another living being who is motivated to avoid such treatment. Theoretical perspectives Drive theories (Leonard Berkowitz 1989; Feshbach 1984): aggression stems from externally elicited drives to harm. The most famous is the frustration–aggression hypothesis (John Dollard, Doob, Miller, O. Hobart Mowrer & Sears, 1939), which made two sweeping claims: (1) frustration always leads to some form of aggression, and (2) aggression always stems from frustration. Both are now considered false: frustration is a strong elicitor only under limited conditions. Social learning perspective (Albert Bandura, 1997): we are not born with aggressive responses; we acquire them through direct experience or observation of others .
