General Aggression Model (GAM) (Anderson & Bushman, 2002): two input classes — situational factors (frustration, provocation, aggressive models, discomfort) and person factors (irritability, pro-violence attitudes, hostile attribution tendency, aggression-related skills). These act through three processes: arousal , affective states (hostile feelings), and cognitions (hostile thoughts). Depending on appraisals and restraining factors, the person then engages in thoughtful or impulsive action. Causes of aggression Provocations: actions perceived as stemming from malicious intent — condescension (a very powerful source), harsh/unjustified criticism (especially personal criticism), and teasing . Excitation-transfer theory: heightened arousal can increase aggression if it persists beyond its original situation and is misattributed as anger in a new context. Social exclusion: rejection initiates a hostile cognitive mind-set, making us perceive ambiguous actions as hostile. Media violence increases aggression via priming of aggressive thoughts, weakening of restraints, and desensitization . Violent video games increase aggressive cognition, affect and behaviour, and reduce empathy/prosocial behaviour (people play them for competence and mastery, not the violent content). Cultural, personality and situational factors Cultures of honor: cultures with strong norms that aggression is appropriate in response to insults to one's honor; impact especially apparent for sexual jealousy. Evolutionary view: men feel jealousy over sexual infidelity (paternal uncertainty), women over emotional infidelity (need for mate's assistance in child rearing); manhood is "precarious" and threats to it may trigger aggression to restore it. TASS model (Traits As Situational Sensitivities): personality traits interact with situational factors; personal traits enhance aggression only when situational factors (e.g., provocation) are above threshold , and individual differences are eliminated when the situation is strong (high provocation). Type A behaviour pattern: more irritable and aggressive than Type B; more likely to engage in hostile aggression (prime objective = harming the victim) but not more instrumental aggression (aggression to attain other goals such as resources or praise). Narcissism: overinflated self-worth; react with exceptionally high aggression to ego-threatening feedback; view themselves as victims of others' transgressions. Gender: males are more aggressive overall, but the difference is highly situation-dependent and eliminated under strong provocation. Males use more direct aggression, females more indirect ; gender differences are smaller and more complex than once thought. Situational determinants: high temperatures increase aggression up to a point (then decline); alcohol increases aggression in both sexes (reduces information-processing capacity). Bullying and reducing aggression Bullying = repeated assault on others with little/no power to retaliate. Motives: holding power, being part of a "tough" high-status group, and feeling better about oneself. Among boys, power and group motives predict bullying (not feeling depressed); for girls, all three motives do. Few children are solely bullies or victims; many switch roles. Bullies make hostile/dispositional attributions ; bullies and bully-victims favour responding with aggression and have lower self-esteem . Cyberbullying = repeated online assaults (insults, exclusion, blackmail). Reducing aggression: Punishment works only when it is prompt, certain, strong, and perceived as justified . Catharsis hypothesis (venting reduces aggression) is mainly false — venting tends to increase subsequent aggression. Self-affirmation (bolstering self-esteem) can reduce aggression in high-narcissism people by preventing ego threats from triggering aggression. Trap The frustration–aggression hypothesis (John Dollard et al., 1939) and the catharsis hypothesis are both classic "this is now considered FALSE" exam items. Hostile aggression (harm is the goal) vs instrumental aggression (harm is a means to another goal) is a frequent distinction. 9. Theories of intergroup relationship How relations between groups produce prejudice, conflict and collective action. Minimal group experiments & Social Identity Theory (Tajfel) Henri Tajfel and associates set out to define an intergroup situation where social categorisation occurs on a trivial criterion but none of the usual conditions of intergroup conflict are present. The conditions were: no face-to-face interaction, complete anonymity of group membership, no instrumental/rational link between criteria and rewards, no utilitarian value of the rewards to the subject, and a number of allocation options. The first minimal group experiment (Tajfel, 1970): 64 British schoolboys (14–15) did a dot-estimation task and were assigned (actually randomly) to "overestimator/underestimator" or "more/less accurate" groups. They allocated real money to anonymous in-group and out-group members (identified only by code numbers) via a matrix offering strategies: Fairness (F) , Maximum Joint Profit (MJP) , Maximum In-group Profit (MIP) , and Maximum Difference in favour of the in-group (MD) . Result: subjects favoured the in-group, endorsing a combination of MD and MIP most often — even at the expense of absolute in-group profit. Tajfel concluded that mere social categorisation produces discriminatory intergroup behaviour without any of the normal conditions of conflict. Definition Social Identity Theory (Henri Tajfel & John Turner): people are motivated to maintain or achieve a positive self-identity . Three central processes: social categorisation (segmenting the world to impose order and provide a locus of self-identification), social identity (the part of the self-concept derived from group membership, with its value and emotional significance), and social comparison (comparing in-group to out-group, drawing on Festinger's 1954 theory). The goal is positive psychological group distinctiveness : an identity perceived as distinct and positive vis-à-vis relevant comparison groups. Negative social identity → dissatisfaction → (if cognitive alternatives are perceived) attempts to change the situation. Social change and social mobility A strategy for social change is embarked upon only when cognitive alternatives to the existing situation are perceived, which depends on two factors: stability–instability (can the hierarchy be changed?) and legitimacy–illegitimacy (is the situation just?). A disadvantaged group perceiving cognitive alternatives may: be absorbed into the dominant group, redefine the negatively evaluated characteristic, create new dimensions of comparison, or directly compete. Social mobility assumes the system is flexible and permeable, permitting free movement of individuals. Relative deprivation theory Definition Relative deprivation = a perceived discrepancy between attainments ("what is") and expectations/entitlements ("what ought to be"). It is always relative to other conditions; deprivation is not absolute. James Davies (1969) J-curve model: when attainments suddenly fall short of rising expectations, relative deprivation is acute, producing collective unrest — "revolutions of rising expectations". Gary Runciman (1966) distinguished egoistic relative deprivation (deprivation relative to similar individuals) from fraternalistic relative deprivation (comparison with dissimilar others / other groups). They are independent. Walker & Mann (1987) : fraternalistic deprivation predicts willingness for militant protest; egoistic deprivation predicts personal stress symptoms (headaches, indigestion, sleeplessness). Fraternalistic deprivation translates into protest only with: strong ingroup identification, belief that action is feasible, perceptions of injustice (procedural injustice especially potent), and a particular ingroup–outgroup comparison. Social protest and collective action Response to deprivation often involves sustained social protest. Sympathisers hold supportive attitudes that don't automatically become behaviour; they can be mobilised into activists . Klandermans views protest as intergroup behaviour occurring in "multiorganisational fields" , with four steps to participation: becoming part of the mobilisation potential, becoming a target of mobilisation attempts, developing motivation to participate, and overcoming barriers to participation. Realistic conflict theory (Muzafer Sherif) A key feature of intergroup behaviour is ethnocentrism , whose origins (Sherif 1962) lie in the nature of intergroup relations: where groups compete over scarce resources , relations become conflictual and ethnocentric. Tested in the famous Robber's Cave experiments (field experiments at summer camps, 1949/1953/1954): Phase 1: boys arrived and formed friendships in camp-wide activities. Phase 2: camp split into two groups (breaking friendships); isolated groups developed their own norms and status differences. Phase 3: intergroup competitions generated fierce hostility that generalised beyond the contests. Phase 4: introducing superordinate goals (desired by both but unachievable alone) gradually improved relations through cooperation. Cooperation, competition and social dilemmas Dilemma Structure Prisoner's dilemma Two guilty suspects questioned separately; each can confess for immunity. If both confess = moderate sentence; if neither = light sentence. A "two-person, mixed-motive, non-zero-sum game" (a zero-sum game = one's gain is always the other's loss). Trucking game Two players run trucking companies; a short shared one-lane route causes repeated head-on conflict and wasted time arguing. Commons dilemma An n-person prisoner's dilemma: cooperation by all benefits all, competition by all harms all. The classic example (100 farmers, 100-cow common) yields the tragedy of the commons when each adds an extra cow. Equity theory Equity theory specifies conditions for intergroup conflict and its resolution. Justice = a socially defined standard for evaluating resource distribution. People define justice from inputs (contributions: attributes, abilities, efforts) and outcomes (tangible/intangible rewards or punishments). For justice, outcomes need not be equal; the ratio of outcomes to inputs must be equal (Ox/Ix = Oy/Iy). Walster, Berscheid & Walster (1973) revised the formula to permit negative inputs/outcomes (using absolute values). Perceived inequity causes psychological distress; equity can be restored by actual restoration (changing real inputs/outcomes) or psychological restoration (cognitively distorting the perceived inputs/outcomes). Balance theory (Fritz Heider, 1946) The p-o-x (balance) theory : originally about the sentiments of a person (p) toward another (o) and an impersonal object (x) belonging to o; later expanded to general interpersonal relations. Heider proposed two relation types: unit relations (U / not-U: elements seen as belonging together or not, governed by Gestalt factors of similarity, proximity, common fate, good continuation, set, past experience) and sentiment relations (L / DL: liking, admiring vs disliking, rejecting). Balance in dyads: balanced when both relations are positive or both negative; imbalanced when one is positive and one negative. Balance in triads: balanced when all three relations are positive, or when two are negative and one positive; imbalanced when one is negative and two positive; ambiguous when all three are negative. (Always judged from p's viewpoint .) Consequences of the balance tendency: preference for balanced states, induction of new relations to produce balance, and pressure to change imbalanced states (by altering either sentiment or unit relations). Mnemonic Triad balance = "multiply the signs to +." A triad is balanced when the product of the three signs is positive (+++ or +−−). One negative + two positives gives a product of −, which is imbalanced and feels uncomfortable. Social exchange theory (George Homans, 1961) Homans explained elementary face-to-face interaction as the psychological exchange of rewards (positive reinforcements) and costs (negative reinforcements) between two persons. He limited the theory to behaviour that is social, directly reacted to by the other party (not a third party), and actual (not a mere norm). His unit of analysis was the elementary face-to-face social interchange ; the dyad and small group are the building blocks of larger social units. Three descriptive terms : activity , sentiment , interaction ; two key variables : quantity (frequency) and value (degree of reinforcement). Homans' propositions of human exchange: Success: the more often an action is rewarded, the more likely it is performed (a derivative of Thorndike's law of effect). Stimulus: the more similar present stimuli are to past rewarded ones, the more likely the action (stimulus generalisation / secondary reinforcement). Value: the more valuable the result, the more likely the action. Deprivation–satiation: the more often a reward has recently been received, the less valuable further units become. Aggression–approval (5a/5b): unexpected non-reward/punishment → anger and aggression; expected (or greater-than-expected) reward → pleasure and approving behaviour. Rationality: a person chooses the action whose value × probability of success is greatest. Rule of distributive justice: a person in exchange expects rewards proportional to costs, and net profits proportional to investments; evaluations of "just return" are based on past exchange experience, which sets up an expected "exchange rate". High-yield Henri Tajfel = social identity / minimal groups (MD & MIP). Muzafer Sherif = realistic conflict / Robber's Cave / superordinate goals. Fritz Heider = balance (p-o-x). George Homans = social exchange (rewards/costs, six propositions). Davies = J-curve; Runciman = egoistic vs fraternalistic relative deprivation; Walster et al. = equity ratio. The contact hypothesis & reducing prejudice Prejudice (a negative attitude toward an outgroup) is reduced by intergroup contact under favourable conditions (the contact hypothesis , traced to Gordon Allport's 1954 Nature of Prejudice ): equal status, common goals, cooperation, and institutional support. Robber's Cave demonstrated that contact alone was insufficient — superordinate goals requiring cooperation were what reduced hostility. 10. Applying social psychology How social-psychological principles are applied to clinical/health work, the law, and the environment. Social psychology in clinical / health settings Illusory correlations: the tendency to see correlations where none exist. Clinicians may perceive illusory correlations during diagnosis; hindsight explanations breed overconfidence; erroneous diagnoses can be self-confirming because interviewers seek and recall confirming information. This underscores the need for rigorous testing of intuitive conclusions and statistical prediction. Depressive realism: mildly depressed people make more accurate (rather than self-serving) judgments. Depressed people have a negative, pessimistic attributional/explanatory style , attributing failure to stable, global, internal causes. Depression is a vicious circle in which negative thoughts elicit self-defeating behaviours. Loneliness (common in individualistic societies) and shyness (a form of social anxiety marked by self-consciousness) are similar vicious circles in which negative feelings elicit off-putting behaviour. Loneliness can prompt nostalgia, which reminds people of social connections. Health psychology studies how people decide they are ill, explain symptoms, and seek/follow treatment, and the links among illness, stress and a pessimistic explanatory style. Therapy and social relations Consistent with the attitudes-follow-behaviour principle, several therapies prescribe action: we can influence feelings indirectly through behaviour. The vicious circle of depression/loneliness/anxiety can be broken at any point — by changing the environment, training constructive behaviour, or reversing negative thinking ( social skills training and explanatory-style therapy ). Improvements are best maintained when people attribute them to internal factors under their continued control rather than to the treatment program. Changing clients' attitudes requires persuasion ; therapists act as expert, trustworthy communicators. Social relations and health: close, supportive relationships lower risk of illness and premature death and foster happiness (e.g., married adults report being happier and are at less risk for depression), partly by helping people confide intimate emotions. Social psychology in law Eyewitness testimony accuracy is impaired by many factors. Assertive witnesses are more likely to be believed, although assertiveness does not reflect actual certainty. The human eye is not a video camera. Misinformation effect: incorporating misleading post-event information into one's memory so the false information is believed true. Repeated retelling lets errors creep in. To reduce errors, let witnesses recount without interruption and encourage them to visualise the scene and their emotional state. Juror judgments: with ambiguous evidence, jurors interpret it through preconceived biases and sympathise with attractive/similar defendants. Pretrial publicity and inadmissible evidence often influence jurors despite judicial instruction (especially when the admonition comes after an impression is formed). Lawyers use jury consultants ; disqualifying death-penalty opponents itself produces a biased jury. Group deliberation can entrench and polarise views, though it may make jurors more lenient when evidence is weakly incriminating. Social psychology and the environment Humanity can prepare for a sustainable future by increasing technological efficiency, creating incentives, and changing actions and attitudes to control population and moderate consumption. People in rich nations report greater happiness than those in poor nations, yet materialism fails to satisfy , explained by two principles: the adaptation-level phenomenon (adapting to a level of stimulation and reacting only to changes from it) and social comparison (evaluating oneself against others). To build a satisfying, sustainable future, individuals and societies can promote close relationships, belief-based social networks, positive thinking habits, and engaging activity ( flow ). High-yield Applied themes: illusory correlation + self-confirming diagnosis (clinical judgment); depressive realism + pessimistic explanatory style (stable/global/internal); attitudes-follow-behaviour therapy + internal attribution of improvement; misinformation effect + eyewitness fallibility (law); adaptation-level + social comparison + flow (environment/well-being).

title: Unit 9 — Human Development & Intervention
text: Unit 9 — Human Development & Intervention The arc of a human life and the clinical work built on top of it: how development proceeds from conception to old age across every domain and theory (Sigmund Freud, Erik Erikson, Jean Piaget, Lev Vygotsky, the learning and information-processing views), how language and motor skills unfold, what it means for behaviour to become abnormal and how disorders are described and classified, the full landscape of psychotherapies (psychoanalytic, person-centred, Gestalt, existential, behavioural, REBT/CBT, transactional, family/systems), and the biological and socioemotional theories of successful aging. Built from Rodrick Prashanth's MET source decks and taught to NIMHANS clinical depth, losing no named theorist, term, or stage. In this book Developmental processes, domains & periods Theories of development Piaget's cognitive stages Vygotsky & information-processing Sensorimotor & motor development Language: components, theories, periods The concept of abnormality Describing & assessing disorders Classification (DSM & ICD) & causes Psychoanalytic therapy Person-centred, Gestalt & existential Behaviour therapy REBT & Beck's cognitive therapy Transactional analysis Family & systems therapy Successful aging: biological theories Socioemotional aging & late-life disorders 1. Developmental processes, domains & periods The one idea. Developmental science studies change and stability across the lifespan. Scientists care not only about how people change but about the underlying stability or constancy of personality and behaviour over time. Two kinds of change Quantitative change — a change in number or amount : growth in height, weight, vocabulary, aggressive behaviour, or frequency of communication. Qualitative change — a change in kind, structure, or organisation . Not "more of the same" but a different form altogether. Three domains of development Change and stability occur in various domains (dimensions) of the self. Scientists discuss them separately but treat development as a single unified process . Domain What changes Physical development Growth of body and brain; change or stability in sensory capacities, motor skills, and health. Cognitive development Change or stability in mental abilities: learning, attention, memory, language, thinking, reasoning, and creativity. Psychosocial development Change and stability in emotions, personality, and social relationships. Periods of the lifespan The division of the lifespan into periods (infancy, childhood, adolescence, adulthood, old age) is a social construction : a concept about the nature of reality based on societally shared perceptions or assumptions, not a fixed biological fact. High-yield Quantitative = change in amount (height, vocabulary). Qualitative = change in kind/structure . Three domains: physical, cognitive, psychosocial. Lifespan periods are a social construction . 2. Theories of development The psychoanalytic viewpoint — Freud Sigmund Freud concluded that human development is a conflictual process : as biological creatures we have basic sexual and aggressive instincts that must be served, yet society dictates that many of these drives be restrained. The ways parents manage these urges in the first few years play a major role in shaping personality. Freud held personality was fixed in childhood — essentially formed by age 5 or 6. Psychosexual stages of development Stage Age Characteristics Fixation outcomes Oral 0–1 Mouth is the primary erogenous zone; pleasure from sucking; id is dominant . Oral incorporative (taking in) — optimism, dependency. Oral aggressive/sadistic (during teething) — pessimism, hostility, aggressiveness. Anal 1–3 Toilet training (external reality) interferes with gratification from defecation. Anal aggressive — defecates to defy parents; basis for hostile/sadistic adult behaviour. Anal retentive — stubborn, stingy, hoarding; rigid, compulsively neat, obstinate, overly conscientious. Phallic 4–5 Incestuous fantasies; Oedipus and Electra complex ; castration anxiety; superego development. Phallic character shows strong narcissism . Latency 5–puberty Period of sublimation of the sex instinct. — Genital Adolescence–adulthood Development of sex-role identity and adult social relationships. Genital type finds satisfaction in love and work , work being an acceptable outlet for sublimation of id impulses. Erikson's theory of psychosocial development Erik Erikson renounced Sigmund Freud's idea of fixity, arguing that identity formation is a lifelong process . Personality (Erikson focused on identity ) develops through eight stages as life unfolds. The outcome of each stage depends on the outcome of the previous one, and successful negotiation of each ego crisis is essential for optimal growth. He used Freud's psychosexual stages as his basis; his first five stages reflect ego crises tied to Freud's stages. Trap Sigmund Freud: personality fixed by age 5–6 , five psychosexual stages. Erik Erikson: identity is lifelong , eight psychosocial stages built on Freud's first five. Don't merge the two. The learning viewpoint — Watson & the operant view John B. Watson believed that well-learned associations between external stimuli and observable responses (called habits ) are the building blocks of development. From this perspective children do not progress through distinct biologically dictated stages; development is a continuous process of behavioural change shaped by each person's unique environment, and may differ dramatically from person to person. Operant learning theory claims development depends on external stimuli (reinforcers and punishers) rather than internal forces such as instincts, drives, or maturation. Modern developmentalists agree habits can emerge and disappear over a lifetime depending on their positive or negative consequences. The cognitive viewpoint — Jean Piaget Piaget (1950) defined intelligence as a basic life process that helps an organism adapt to its environment . As children mature they acquire ever more complex cognitive structures. A cognitive structure — what Piaget called a scheme (or schema ) — is an organised pattern of thought or action used to cope with or explain some aspect of experience. Cognitive development occurs neither solely through maturation nor solely through learning : through interaction with the environment, psychological structures become reorganised. Infants are born with simple schemata such as sucking and grasping . Definition Assimilation = actively organising new information so it fits with what is already perceived and thought. Accommodation = changing what is already perceived or thought so it fits new information. Learning occurs through these two basic mental operations. 3. Piaget's cognitive stages Jean Piaget described four stages through which all of us pass. Each new experience requires cognitive organisation or reorganisation in a mental structure (schema). Sensorimotor stage (0–2 years) Infants know the world through senses and motor action, building from inborn reflexes (sucking, grasping) toward intentional behaviour and, eventually, object permanence and mental representation. Preoperational stage (2–7 years) Marked by the appearance of the symbolic function — the ability to make one thing (a word or object) stand for or represent something else. The knowledge that an entity can stand for something other than itself is representational insight . Language is the most obvious symbolism; pretend (symbolic) play blossoms in the early preoperational period. 2½-year-olds lack dual representation — the ability to think about an object in two different ways at the same time. Deficits in preoperational reasoning Animism — attributing life and lifelike qualities to inanimate objects. Egocentrism — viewing the world from one's own perspective; difficulty recognising another's point of view. Centration — attending to one aspect of a situation to the exclusion of others (contrast with decentration). Lack of conservation — failure to recognise that properties of an object/substance do not change when its appearance is altered superficially. Lack of reversibility — inability to reverse or negate an action by mentally performing the opposite (negation). Theory of Mind (ToM) ToM develops during the preoperational period: children's developing concepts of mental activity — an understanding that humans are cognitive beings whose mental states are not always shared with or accessible to others. The most frequently used tool is the false-belief task , where the child must infer that another person does not possess knowledge that the child possesses (holds a false belief). Children usually make an egocentric response . Concrete-operational stage (7–11 years) Can solve conservation problems. Mental seriation — mentally arranging items along a quantifiable dimension (height, weight). Transitivity — recognising necessary relations among elements in a series (if A > B and B > C, then A > C). Horizontal décalage — Jean Piaget's term for uneven cognitive performance: inability to solve certain problems even though one can solve similar problems requiring the same operations (e.g., solving some conservation tasks but not others). Formal-operational stage (11–12 years and beyond) Formal operations are mental actions performed on ideas and propositions . The benchmark is hypothetico-deductive reasoning . Such thinkers are not restricted to previously acquired facts but can generate hypotheses , and can think inductively (from specific observations to broad generalisations). For them, what is possible is more important than what is real . Mnemonic Some People Can Fly — Sensorimotor, Preoperational, Concrete-operational, Formal-operational. Conservation arrives at concrete ; abstract hypotheticals arrive at formal . 4. Vygotsky & the information-processing viewpoint Vygotsky's sociocultural theory Lev Vygotsky focused on how culture — the beliefs, values, traditions, and skills of a social group — is transmitted across generations. Cognitive growth is a socially mediated activity : children acquire new ways of thinking through cooperative dialogues with more knowledgeable members of society . He rejected the notion that all children progress through the same universal stages, arguing the new skills children master are often specific to their culture rather than universal structures. Four interrelated levels of analysis Microgenetic — changes over very brief periods (seconds, minutes, days). Ontogenetic — development of the individual over their lifetime. Phylogenetic — development over evolutionary time. Sociohistorical — changes that have occurred in one's culture and the values, norms, and technologies its history generated. Core constructs Tools of intellectual adaptation — each culture provides children tools that let them use basic mental functions more adaptively. Zone of proximal development (ZPD) — the range of tasks too complex to be mastered alone but accomplishable with guidance and encouragement from a more skilful partner . Scaffolding — the process by which an expert, instructing a novice, responds contingently to the novice's behaviour so the novice gradually increases understanding. Less able children elicit more support than more capable children. Guided participation — adult–child interactions in which children's cognitions are shaped as they participate with or observe adults in culturally relevant activities (e.g., learning weaving or hunting without formal schooling). Contrast with context-independent learning ("knowledge for knowledge's sake") that prepares children for formal schooling. Trap Jean Piaget = child as a lone scientist discovering through self-directed interaction; universal stages. Lev Vygotsky = child as a social apprentice ; learning is mediated by culture and more skilful partners (ZPD, scaffolding); skills are culture-specific. The information-processing viewpoint The human mind is likened to a computer into which information flows, is operated on, and is converted to output (answers, inferences, solutions). Theorists view cognitive development as age-related changes in the mind's hardware (brain and peripheral nervous system) and software (mental processes such as attention, perception, memory, and problem-solving strategies). Crucially, development is a continuous process that is not stage-like — involving small quantitative rather than large qualitative changes. 5. Sensorimotor & motor development Basic trends of locomotor development Cephalocaudal — development proceeds head downward (head, neck, upper extremities precede legs and lower extremities). Proximodistal — development proceeds centre outward (trunk and shoulders before hands and fingers). Three views of motor sequencing/timing Viewpoint Claim Maturational Motor development is the unfolding of a genetically programmed sequence in which nerves and muscles mature in a downward and outward direction. Experiential (practice) Maturation is necessary but not sufficient ; infants physically capable of sitting/crawling/walking won't be proficient without opportunities to practise. Dynamical systems Each new skill is a construction that emerges as infants actively reorganise existing motor capabilities into new, more complex action systems; a real world of interesting objects and events gives infants reasons (purposes, motives) to reach, sit, crawl, walk, and run. New patterns are at first tentative, inefficient, uncoordinated, then become smooth and coordinated. Fine motor development — voluntary reaching & manipulatory skills Newborns come equipped with a grasping reflex and make uncoordinated prereaches (primitive thrusts) at objects in the visual field. By 2 months, reaching/grasping may seem to deteriorate as the reflexive palmar grasp disappears and prereaching occurs less often. From 3 months, voluntary reaching is a learned motor skill that does not simply "unfold"; infants make in-flight corrections, improving in accuracy. By ~4–5 months, an infant able to sit and reach inward across the body can grasp interesting objects with both hands. The palmar grasp (clumsy, claw-like grip allowing little tactile exploration) is replaced near the end of the first year by the ulnar grasp . The pincer grasp (thumb + forefinger) transforms the child from a fumbler into a skilful manipulator; by 16 months they use thumbs and forefingers to lift and explore. By the end of the second year they scribble with a crayon, copy a simple line, and build towers of five or more blocks. Fingering activity may be the primary method by which 4- to 6-month-olds gain information about objects, since unimanual grasping is still poor. 6. Language: components, theories & periods Definition Language = a small number of individually meaningless symbols (sounds, letters, gestures) combined by agreed-on rules to produce an infinite number of messages. Communication = the process by which one organism transmits information to and influences another. Vocables = unique patterns of sound a prelinguistic infant uses to represent objects, actions, or events. Five components of language Component What it covers Phonology The sound system of a language and rules for combining sounds to produce meaningful units. Phonemes = the basic units of sound used in a spoken language. Morphology The basic units of meaning. Morphemes = smallest meaningful language units. Free morphemes stand alone (e.g., "dog"); bound morphemes cannot stand alone but change meaning when attached to a free morpheme. Semantics The expressed meaning of words and sentences. Syntax The structure of a language; rules specifying how words and grammatical markers combine into meaningful sentences. Pragmatics Principles underlying effective, appropriate use of language in social contexts; involves sociolinguistic knowledge (culturally specific rules for how language should be structured and used). Theories of language development Learning theorists (empiricist) — language is obviously learned. Emphasise imitation and reinforcement . B. F. Skinner : adults shape a child's speech by selectively reinforcing babbling that resembles words, then withhold reinforcement until the child combines words into longer grammatical utterances. Social-learning theorists add that children acquire much linguistic knowledge by listening to and imitating older companions. Nativists — language acquisition is a biologically programmed activity, possibly involving specialised processing that operates most efficiently early in childhood. Evidence: linguistic universals . Noam Chomsky proposed a language acquisition device (LAD) — an inborn linguistic processor activated by verbal input, containing a universal grammar (rules common to all languages). Dan Slobin proposed an inborn language-making capacity (LMC) — cognitive/perceptual abilities specialised for language learning. The sensitive-period hypothesis was prompted by observations that child aphasics often recover lost language without therapy, whereas adult aphasics usually require extensive therapy. Interactionists — language acquisition reflects a complex interplay among biological predispositions, cognitive development, and the unique linguistic environment ( not a dedicated LAD or LMC). Like nativists they believe children are biologically prepared, but the preparation is a powerful, slowly maturing human brain. Elizabeth Bates (1999) argued grammatical speech arises out of social necessity as vocabularies grow beyond 100–200 words. Adults give children repeated opportunities to learn that conversing involves turn-taking, that things have names, and proper ways to ask and answer. Definition Child-directed speech (motherese) = the short, simple, high-pitched, often repetitive sentences adults use with young children. Adults provide negative evidence — responding to ungrammatical speech in ways that subtly signal an error: expansions (responding with a grammatically improved form) and recasts (responding with a nonrepetitive, grammatically correct statement). Periods of language development Prelinguistic period. Infants are well prepared: sensitive to intonational cues from birth, able to discriminate a wider variety of phonemes than adults. They begin cooing at ~2 months, babbling at 4–6 months, and by 7–10 months are already segmenting others' speech into phrases and wordlike units. They learn turn-taking and that gestures communicate. Receptive language is ahead of productive language. Holophrase (one-word) period. Infants speak in holophrases (one-word utterances that carry a whole sentence's meaning) and expand vocabulary one word at a time, mostly about moving/manipulable objects. A vocabulary spurt (naming explosion) occurs between 18 and 24 months. Western children mostly develop a referential style; a smaller number, and many from social-harmony cultures, adopt an expressive style. Toddlers use social/contextual cues to fast map words, aided by processing constraints (object scope constraint, mutual exclusivity, lexical context, syntactic bootstrapping), and make semantic errors of overextension and underextension . Telegraphic period. At 18–24 months toddlers produce two- and three-word sentences called telegraphic speech (omitting grammatical markers and smaller words). These follow word-order rules and express consistent semantic relations ; toddlers grow sensitive to pragmatic constraints and sociolinguistic prescriptions (e.g., politeness in requests). Preschool period (ages 2–5). Language becomes much more adult-like. Children add grammatical morphemes (-s plural, -ed past, -ing progressive, articles, prepositions, auxiliaries), may overregularise , and learn transformational grammar (turning declaratives into questions, negations, imperatives, relative clauses, compound sentences). Middle childhood & adolescence. A period of refinement: subtle exceptions to grammatical rules, complex syntax, rapid vocabulary growth, growing metalinguistic awareness , and much better referential communication skills. 7. The concept of abnormality (psychopathology) No single indicator is sufficient in and of itself to define abnormality. The more a person has difficulties across the following areas, the more likely they have a mental disorder. Seven indicators of abnormality Suffering — psychological pain or distress. Maladaptiveness — behaviour that interferes with well-being and functioning. Statistical deviancy — being statistically rare or atypical. Violation of the standards of society — breaking social/moral norms. Social discomfort — making others uneasy. Irrationality and unpredictability . Dangerousness — to self or others. Definition DSM-5 mental disorder = a syndrome present in an individual that involves clinically significant disturbance in behaviour, emotion regulation, or cognitive functioning, reflecting a dysfunction in biological, psychological, or developmental processes necessary for mental functioning. 8. Describing & assessing disorders Epidemiology & prevalence terms Mental health epidemiology studies the distribution of mental disorders across settings or population groups (epidemiology more broadly studies the distribution of diseases, disorders, and health-related behaviours). Term Meaning Point prevalence Estimated proportion of actual, active cases of a disorder at a given point in time. 1-year prevalence Everyone who experienced the disorder at any point throughout the entire year. Lifetime prevalence Number of people who have had a disorder at any time in their lives (even if now recovered). Incidence Number of new cases over a given period (typically 1 year). Lower than prevalence because it excludes preexisting cases. Comorbidity Presence of two or more disorders in the same person. Especially high in people with severe forms; in the NCS-R study, half of those with a disorder rated as serious had two or more additional disorders. Other descriptions of disorders Sex ratio — percentage of males vs females with the disorder; and age of onset , which differs across disorders. Course — most disorders follow an individual pattern: chronic (lasting a long time, sometimes a lifetime, e.g., schizophrenia); episodic (recovery within months then recurrence, e.g., mood disorders); time-limited (improves without treatment in a short period). Onset — acute (sudden) vs insidious (gradual, over an extended period). Prognosis — the anticipated course of a disorder. The mental status examination (MSE) Systematic observation of an individual's behaviour across five categories : Appearance and behaviour — general appearance, gait, grooming, posture, facial expression. Thought processes — rate/flow of speech (continuity of speech), delusions, hallucinations, obsessions. Mood and affect — mood is the predominant feeling state; affect is the feeling state accompanying what we say at a given point, judged "appropriate" or "inappropriate". Intellectual functioning — attention, concentration, memory. Sensorium — general awareness of surroundings; orientation to place, time, and person. Trap Mood vs affect: mood is the sustained, predominant feeling state (the "climate"); affect is the moment-to-moment expressed feeling (the "weather"), rated as appropriate or inappropriate. Prevalence vs incidence: prevalence counts all active cases; incidence counts only new cases. Culture-specific disorders (culture-bound syndromes) are recognised patterns of distress tied to particular cultural contexts, reminding clinicians that the expression of abnormality is shaped by culture. 9. Classification (DSM & ICD) & causes of disorders History & the two major systems The 19th-century German physician Emil Kraepelin was the first modern theorist to develop a comprehensive classification model on the basis of distinctive features (symptoms) of abnormal behaviour patterns. DSM — Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, published by the American Psychiatric Association; an outgrowth of Kraepelin's work. Introduced in 1952 ; the latest, DSM-5 , was published in 2013 . Used widely in the United States. ICD — International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, published by the WHO; now in its 11th revision (ICD-11) . A compendium of both mental and physical disorders and the most widely used diagnostic manual worldwide. DSM-5 vs DSM-IV — major changes Dispensed with the multiaxial framework. The old five axes comprised: Axis I & II — inventory of mental disorders; Axis III — medical conditions and diseases; Axis IV — psychosocial and environmental problems/sources of stress affecting functioning; Axis V — a rating scale (GAF) of overall level of functioning. Adopted a dimensional component. DSM-5 did not abandon the categorical model but expanded it to include a dimensional component for many disorders. New, reclassified, and consolidated disorders: Asperger's disorder and autistic disorder reclassified under autism spectrum disorder . Trichotillomania (hair-pulling) moved from impulse-control disorders to Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders . Pathological (compulsive) gambling moved from impulse-control to Substance Use and Addictive Behaviors . PTSD moved from anxiety disorders to a new category, Trauma- and Stressor-Related Disorders . Causes of disorders — the diathesis-stress model Definition Diathesis = a predisposition toward developing a disorder, deriving from biological, psychological, or sociocultural causal factors. Stress = the response/experience to demands perceived as taxing or exceeding one's personal resources. Many disorders develop when a stressor operates on a person who has a diathesis (vulnerability) . The model accounting for both is the diathesis-stress (stress-diathesis) model . Protective factors such as intelligence and inoculation to stress reduce the chances of disorder. Two kinds exist: the integrative stress-diathesis model and the additive stress-diathesis model. 10. Psychoanalytic therapy Goals & process The two goals of Freudian psychoanalytic therapy are to make the unconscious conscious and to strengthen the ego so behaviour is based more on reality and less on instinctual cravings or irrational guilt. Analysts assume an anonymous, nonjudgmental "blank-screen" stance , avoiding self-disclosure and maintaining neutrality to foster a transference relationship in which clients make projections onto them. Analysis of transference is the very essence of therapeutic work. Counter-transference — the therapist projecting feelings onto the client — is detrimental and to be avoided. Six basic techniques Technique What it is Maintaining the analytic framework The range of procedural/stylistic factors: analyst's relative anonymity, neutrality and objectivity, regularity and consistency of meetings, starting/ending on time, clarity on fees, basic boundary issues. Free association Clients say whatever comes to mind, however painful, silly, trivial, illogical, or irrelevant. Gives access to the unconscious. Interpretation The analyst points out, explains, and even teaches the meanings of behaviour in dreams, free association, resistances, defences, and the therapeutic relationship. Functions: enable the ego to assimilate new material and speed up uncovering further unconscious material. Dream analysis Key procedure for uncovering unconscious material and giving insight into unresolved problems. During sleep defences are lowered and repressed feelings surface. Analysis of resistance Resistance is anything that works against the progress of therapy — the client's reluctance to bring repressed unconscious material to awareness. Analysis of transference The transference situation is valuable because its manifestations let clients re-experience feelings that would otherwise be inaccessible. 11. Person-centred, Gestalt & existential therapy Person-centred therapy (Carl Rogers) Rogers held that three therapist attributes create a growth-promoting climate: Congruence — genuineness, realness. Unconditional positive regard — acceptance and caring. Accurate empathic understanding — deeply grasping the subjective world of another. The actualizing tendency is a directional process of striving toward realization, fulfilment, autonomy, and self-determination. Goals: help clients achieve greater independence and integration, and increase congruence. It is the therapist's attitude , not knowledge/theories/techniques, that facilitates change; the therapist is a catalyst . Immediacy (addressing what is going on between client and therapist) is highly valued. Offshoots: Motivational Interviewing (MI) by William R. Miller and Stephen Rollnick (early 1980s), a humanistic, client-centred, modestly directive approach matched to the stages of change (precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action, maintenance); and Person-Centred Expressive Arts Therapy (Natalie Rogers). Gestalt therapy (Fritz Perls) Arnie Beisser (1970) proposed the paradoxical theory of change : authentic change occurs more from being who we are than from trying to be who we are not. Key concepts: Holism — "Gestalt" is German for a whole/completion, a form that cannot be separated into parts without losing its essence. Field theory — the organism must be seen in its environment/context as part of a constantly changing field; emphasis on the figure (most salient experience) vs the ground (out of awareness). Therapists practise "attending to the obvious" via gestures, tone, demeanour. Figure-formation process — how the individual organises experience moment to moment as something emerges from the background into focal attention. Organismic self-regulation — equilibrium is "disturbed" by the emergence of a need, sensation, or interest. Contact & resistances to contact — contact is made by seeing, hearing, smelling, touching, moving; boundaries both connect and separate. Resistances ("contact boundary phenomena"): introjection (uncritically accepting others' beliefs), projection (disowning aspects of self by assigning them to the environment), retroflection (turning back on ourselves what we'd do to others, or doing to ourselves what we'd want others to do), deflection (distraction/veering off), confluence (blurring the self–environment differentiation). The NOW — phenomenological inquiry attends to what is occurring now; therapists ask " what " and " how " questions, rarely "why". Unfinished business — uncompleted figures leave unexpressed feelings (resentment, rage, pain, anxiety, grief, guilt). The impasse (stuck point) occurs when external support is unavailable; the therapist accompanies clients through it without rescuing or frustrating them. Energy and blocks to energy — blocked energy manifests as bodily tension, restricted voice, shallow breathing, avoiding contact. Goal: greater awareness and with it greater choice (increased awareness is itself curative). Therapists work within I/Thou dialogue in a here-and-now framework, attending to body language and speech habits ("It" talk, "You" talk, questions, language that denies power, metaphors). Miriam Polster (1987) described a three-stage integration sequence: discovery, accommodation, assimilation . Gestalt techniques Experiments vs exercises — exercises are ready-made techniques; experiments grow out of the client–therapist interaction (the cornerstone of experiential learning). Confrontation — inviting clients to examine incongruities, especially verbal–nonverbal gaps. Internal dialogue exercise — the top dog (righteous, authoritarian, "shoulds"/"oughts", the critical parent) vs the underdog (victim: defensive, apologetic, helpless, feigning powerlessness). Empty-chair technique — given by Jacob Moreno (founder of psychodrama); a vehicle for role reversal . Future projection , making the rounds , the reversal exercise , the rehearsal exercise , the exaggeration exercise , staying with the feeling , and Gestalt dream work (acting out the dream in the present; each part is a projection of the self). Existential therapy The existential tradition balances the limits and tragic dimensions of human existence against its possibilities. Schneider and Krug (2010) name three values: the freedom to become within limits; the capacity to reflect on the meaning of our choices; the capacity to act on those choices. Sartre (1971) called the failure to accept personal responsibility inauthenticity . Existential guilt grows from a sense of incompleteness — awareness of having evaded a commitment or chosen not to choose. Authenticity is living true to one's own evaluation of a valuable existence — the courage to be who we are. Four ways of being (Dasein) Umwelt — the biological world / environment. Mitwelt — "with-world"; the area of human relationships. Eigenwelt — "own-world"; the relationship individuals have with themselves. Überwelt — relationship with spiritual/religious values (added by van Deurzen; the first three were introduced by Binswanger). Irvin Yalom (1980) distinguished three types of isolation : interpersonal (distance from others), intrapersonal (separating parts of oneself via defences), and existential (being separated from the world — a profound aloneness). Other themes: meaning and meaninglessness (Viktor Frankl emphasised the search for meaning) and self-transcendence (rising above immediate situation and self-interest). Authenticity is the basic goal ; for May, "the aim of therapy is that the patient experiences his existence as real" — May (1958) asked not "How are you?" but " Where are you?" Phases: initial (clarifying assumptions about the world), middle (examining the source/authority of one's value system), and final (putting self-knowledge into action). 12. Behaviour therapy Foundations — four major areas of development Area Key ideas Classical conditioning UCS → UCR; UCS + NS → UCR; CS → CR. Learning by association. Operant conditioning Positive & negative reinforcement ; positive & negative punishment ; schedules of reinforcement (intermittent vs fixed; ratio vs interval). Social learning theory Triadic reciprocal interaction (environmental factors, personal factors, individual behaviour); self-efficacy . Cognitive behaviour therapy Emphasises the interaction among affective, behavioural, and cognitive dimensions. Basic characteristics & assumptions Focus on observable behaviour, current determinants, learning experiences that promote change , tailoring strategies to the individual, and rigorous assessment/evaluation. Based on the principles and procedures of the scientific method ; uses functional assessment (behavioural analysis) . Clients assume an active role ; BT is action-oriented and educational. Insight may not be necessary for behaviour change. The focus is on assessing overt and covert behaviour directly, identifying the problem, and evaluating change; treatment is individually tailored. Definition Functional assessment / behavioural analysis uses the ABC model — A ntecedents, B ehaviours, C onsequences — to identify the events that influence or are functionally related to a behaviour. Techniques & procedures Applied behaviour analysis (ABA) — operant techniques applied across settings: positive reinforcement, negative reinforcement, extinction (withholding reinforcement from a previously reinforced response), positive punishment, negative punishment. Relaxation training — Jacobson (1938) developed progressive muscle relaxation ; used for stress, anxiety, asthma, headache, hypertension, insomnia, irritable bowel syndrome, panic disorder. Exposure therapies — systematic confrontation with a feared stimulus (imaginal or in vivo/live). Variants of systematic desensitization: in vivo exposure (exposure to actual events), self-managed in vivo exposure (clients expose themselves when a therapist can't be present), and flooding — intense, prolonged exposure ( in vivo flooding to actual stimuli; imaginal flooding in the client's imagination). Systematic desensitization — based on classical conditioning, developed by Joseph Wolpe . Clients imagine successively more anxiety-arousing situations while engaging in a behaviour (relaxation) that competes with anxiety, becoming gradually desensitized . Steps (McNeil & Kyle, 2009): relaxation training → development of the anxiety hierarchy → systematic desensitization proper . Also used for anger, asthmatic attacks, insomnia, motion sickness, nightmares, sleepwalking. Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing (EMDR) — a form of exposure therapy combining imaginal flooding, cognitive restructuring, and rapid rhythmic eye movements / bilateral stimulation for traumatic stress; developed by Francine Shapiro (2001) . Social skills training — psychoeducation, modeling, reinforcement, behavioural rehearsal, role playing, feedback; includes anger management and assertion training . Self-modification (self-management) programs — basic steps (Watson & Tharp, 2007): selecting goals → translating goals into target behaviours → self-monitoring (behavioural diary) → working out a plan for change → evaluating the action plan. Strategies include self-monitoring, self-reward, self-contracting, stimulus control, and self-as-model. Advantage: treatment can be extended to the public. Multimodal therapy (Arnold Lazarus) — an open system encouraging technical eclecticism , grounded in social learning and cognitive theory. Personality is divided into seven areas — BASIC I.D. : B ehaviour, A ffective responses, S ensations, I mages, C ognitions, I nterpersonal relationships, D rugs (biological functions, nutrition, exercise). Premise: breadth is often more important than depth . 13. REBT & Beck's cognitive therapy Albert Ellis's Rational Emotive Behaviour Therapy (REBT) The basic assumption is that people contribute to their own psychological problems by the way they interpret events. Cognitions, emotions, and behaviours interact significantly with a reciprocal cause-and-effect relationship. REBT's basic hypothesis: our emotions stem mainly from our beliefs, evaluations, interpretations, and reactions . CBT (combining cognitive and behavioural principles in a short-term approach) has generated more empirical research than any other psychotherapy model. The focus is on working with thinking and acting rather than primarily expressing feelings; therapy is an educational process . View of emotional disturbance & the three basic musts It is our own repetition of early-indoctrinated irrational thoughts that keeps dysfunctional attitudes alive. Blame is at the core of most emotional disturbance. We escalate desires and preferences into dogmatic shoulds , musts , and oughts . The three basic irrational "musts" : "I must do well and win the approval of others for my performances." "Other people must treat me considerately, fairly, kindly, and exactly the way I want." "I must get what I want, when I want it; and I must not get what I don't want." High-yield ABCDEF framework: A (activating event) → B (belief about A) → C (emotional/behavioural consequence) → D (disputing intervention) → E (effective new philosophy) → F (new feeling). The disputing process has three components: detecting, debating, discriminating . Cognitive restructuring = replacing faulty cognitions with constructive beliefs (monitor self-talk, identify maladaptive self-talk, substitute adaptive self-talk). Goals (Ellis, 2001b): help clients achieve unconditional self-acceptance (USA) and unconditional other-acceptance (UOA) . Techniques span three classes: cognitive (disputing irrational beliefs, cognitive homework, changing one's language, psychoeducation, coping self-statements, cost-benefit analysis); emotive (rational emotive imagery, humour, role playing, shame-attacking exercises, forceful self-statements/self-dialogue); and behavioural (operant conditioning, self-management, systematic desensitization, relaxation, modeling, real-life behavioural homework). Aaron Beck's Cognitive Therapy (CT) Beck developed CT from his research on depression , observing that depressed clients had a negative bias in interpreting life events, producing cognitive distortions. CT sees problems as stemming from commonplace processes: faulty thinking, incorrect inferences from inadequate information, and failing to distinguish fantasy from reality. Assumptions: internal communication is accessible to introspection; clients' beliefs have highly personal meanings; these meanings can be discovered by the client. Cognitive distortions (logical errors) Arbitrary inferences — conclusions without supporting evidence; includes catastrophizing . Selective abstraction — conclusions based on an isolated detail. Overgeneralization — extreme beliefs from a single incident applied to dissimilar settings. Magnification and minimization — perceiving a situation as greater or lesser than it deserves. Personalization — relating external events to oneself without basis. Labeling and mislabeling — defining identity by past imperfections/mistakes. Dichotomous thinking — either-or, all-or-nothing extremes. The frequent question is " Where is the evidence for ___? " The Socratic (inductive) questioning method leads the client through questions to become aware of thoughts, identify distortions, and find adaptive replacements. Automatic thoughts are personalised notions triggered by particular stimuli that lead to emotional responses. In depression, Beck described the cognitive triad : a negative view of (1) themselves, (2) experience (interpreting in a negative manner — selective abstraction), and (3) the future (gloomy projections). Beck (1967) designed the Beck Depression Inventory (BDI) . In family work, CT emphasises schema (core beliefs) and "family schemata". Trap Albert Ellis (REBT) centres on irrational beliefs / the three musts and disputing (the D in ABCDEF), with a directive, even confrontational style. Aaron Beck (CT) centres on cognitive distortions and the cognitive triad , using collaborative Socratic questioning ("where is the evidence?"). Both restructure cognition; the flavour differs. 14. Transactional Analysis (Eric Berne) TA is a psychological theory developed by Eric Berne in the 1960s explaining why we think, act, and feel as we do. Philosophical assumptions: People are OK; everyone has the capacity to think; people decide their own destiny, and these decisions can be changed. Ego-state model (PAC) & transactions An ego-state is a set of related behaviours, thoughts, and feelings. We all have three: Parent, Adult, Child . Adult — thinking, feeling, behaving in response to the here-and-now, using all available resources. Parent — behaving, thinking, feeling as one's parents did. Child — returning to ways of behaving/thinking/feeling as one did as a child. Capital letters P, A, C indicate ego-states; small letters p, a, c indicate real-life parents, adults, children. Structural analysis uses the PAC model to understand personality. A transaction is the exchange of communications between the ego-states of two people; transactional analysis proper analyses sequences of transactions. Complementary transactions (ego-states sympathetic to one another) are effective; crossed transactions occur when a response comes from a different ego-state than expected. Any signal of recognition is a stroke . Decisional model, life-script & games TA holds that self-defeating behaviour follows strategies decided in childhood — the best way of surviving then. Because the person is responsible for these early decisions, she can redecide . Each of us writes a life-story ; the unaware version is the life-script . Parents give script-messages (how to be / not to be); negative messages are injunctions . Script analysis shows how people unawarely set up or solve problems. Distorting one's perception so it fits the script is redefining ; selectively ignoring information is discounting . Permitted childhood feelings used to cover authentic feelings are racket feelings ; storing one instead of expressing it is saving a stamp ; a game is a repetitive sequence where both parties end up with racket feelings. Symbiosis is where a person and partner together display only three ego-states (one supplies Parent and Adult, the other Child). Therapy & autonomy Eric Berne urged that the proper goal is not insight but cure , progressing through four stages: social control → symptomatic relief → transference cure → script cure . The goal of personal change is autonomy , whose components are awareness, spontaneity, and the capacity for intimacy . Client and therapist enter a contract (mutual consent, valid consideration, competency, lawful object). Therapy involves closing escape hatches (an unconditional decision never to kill/harm self or others or go crazy). The therapist's crucial function is to give permission, protection, and potency . Three schools: Classical (strengthen Adult), Redecision (do so from a Child ego-state), Cathexis (emphasis on Child as well as Adult; the client also assumes a Parent role). 15. Family & systems therapy General systems theory Feedback — the communication pattern within the units of a system, in two basic patterns: linear and circular . Two types: negative feedback (equilibrium is achieved) and positive feedback (change occurs in the system). Homeostasis — systems tend to seek stability and equilibrium; a family regulates itself to maintain stability, achieved through feedback from its units. Equifinality — many different ways to reach the same destination (related to complexity). Pathological communication patterns (schizophrenia research) Double bind — Gregory Bateson, Jackson, Jay Haley & Weakland (1956): a person receives two related but contradictory messages, one often clear and the other unclear (nonverbal), creating a "no-win" paradox. Marital schism & skew — Lidz and colleagues: marital schism = undermining the worth of the other parent by competing for the children's sympathy; marital skew = one parent's psychological disturbance dominates the home while the other accepts it, distorting reality for the children. Bowen's intergenerational (family systems) theory Based on the individual's ability to differentiate intellectual functioning from feelings . Eight core concepts: Differentiation of self — being able to separate one's intellectual processes from one's feeling processes. Triangulation — when two people are under stress they bring in a third member to dilute the anxiety/tension. Nuclear family emotional systems — when partners have relatively low differentiation, they may project their stress onto a child (the family projection process ). Family projection process — projecting parental stress onto one child. Emotional cutoff — managing unresolved attachment by emotional distance. Multigenerational transmission process — after six or seven generations of increasingly fused couples, an observer could find highly dysfunctional families vulnerable to stress and lacking differentiation. Sibling position — Bowen believed birth order affects functioning within the family. Societal regression — the broader lack of differentiation between thoughts and feelings at a societal level. Techniques: evaluation interview (any combination of members; a single member can suffice if willing to work on differentiating their own feelings rather than blaming others), genograms , interpretation (information from genograms interpreted so members understand dynamics; the therapist maintains objectivity to see patterns reflecting the family of origin), and detriangulation (Bowen worked with the healthiest, most differentiated member to make changes; he tried to separate parts of a triangle directly). Structural family therapy (Salvador Minuchin) Traces to the early 1960s with delinquent boys from poor families at the Wiltwyck School in New York. Central idea: an individual's symptoms are best understood from interactional patterns within a family. Goals: (1) reduce symptoms of dysfunction; (2) bring about structural change by modifying transactional rules and establishing more appropriate boundaries. Structural-strategic approaches were the most-used models; interventions became synonymous with the systems approach — joining, boundary setting, unbalancing, reframing, ordeals, paradoxical interventions, and enactments . Concepts Family structure — rules developed over years determining who interacts with whom (temporary or long-standing). Family subsystems — husband–wife, parents–children, siblings. Boundary permeability — rules about who participates in interactions and how. Alignments and coalitions — alignments = ways members join with or oppose each other; coalitions = alliances against another member. Minuchin uses triangle more specifically than Bowen: a coalition where "each parent demands that the child side with him against the other parent". Techniques Family mapping — diagrams of current ways families relate. Enactment — instructing the family to act out a conflict so the therapist works with it in the present. Intensity — repeating the message or changing interaction length to facilitate change. Changing boundaries — rearranging seating, changing distance, unbalancing the structure (e.g., siding with a parent in an enmeshed family to restore parental power). Reframing — offering a different explanation so a constructive change can occur. Trap Bowen vs Salvador Minuchin: Bowen is intergenerational (differentiation of self, eight concepts, genograms, detriangulation across generations). Minuchin is structural and present-focused (family structure, subsystems, boundaries, enactment, unbalancing). Both use "triangle", but Minuchin means it more narrowly (a parent–parent–child coalition). 16. Successful aging: biological theories Definition Life span = the upper boundary of life, the maximum number of years an individual can live (for humans ~120–125 years). Life expectancy = the number of years that will probably be lived by the average person born in a particular year. Genes matter for reaching extreme old age, but other factors do too; what usually contributes to surviving into the 100s is the ability to cope successfully with stress . Genetic-programming theories Theory Claim Cellular clock theory (Leonard Hayflick, 1977) Cells can divide a maximum of ~75–80 times (the Hayflick limit ); ability to divide decreases with age. The answer to why cells stop may lie at the tips of chromosomes — telomeres (DNA sequences that cap chromosomes) shorten with each division; after ~70–80 replications they are dramatically reduced and the cell can no longer reproduce. Injecting the enzyme telomerase can substantially extend cell life. Programmed senescence theory Aging results from the sequential switching on and off of certain genes. Senescence is the time when age-associated deficits become evident. Immunological theory A programmed decline in immune-system function leads to increased vulnerability to infectious disease and thus to aging and death. Hormonal stress theory Aging in the body's hormonal system can lower resilience to stress and increase disease likelihood. The hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis is a main regulatory system for responding to stress; with aging, stress hormones remain elevated longer than in youth. Prolonged elevations are linked to cardiovascular disease, cancer, diabetes, and hypertension. Variable-rate theories Free-radical theory — normal metabolism produces unstable oxygen molecules ( free radicals ) that ricochet around cells, damaging DNA and other structures, leading to disorders including cancer and arthritis. Wear-and-tear theory — cells and tissues have vital parts that simply wear out. Rate-of-living theory — the greater an organism's rate of metabolism, the shorter its life span. Autoimmune theory — the immune system becomes confused and attacks the body's own cells. 17. Socioemotional aging & late-life disorders Theories of socioemotional development in aging Theory Core idea Disengagement theory To cope effectively, older adults should gradually withdraw from society. Older adults develop increasing self-preoccupation, decrease emotional ties, and show less interest in society's affairs; by disengaging they were believed to enjoy enhanced life satisfaction. (Largely discredited but examinable.) Activity theory The more active and involved older adults are, the more likely they are to be satisfied with their lives; many achieve greater satisfaction by continuing their middle-adulthood roles into late adulthood. Socioemotional selectivity theory (Laura Carstensen) Older adults become more selective about social networks: placing high value on emotional satisfaction, they spend more time with familiar, rewarding individuals and consciously decrease total social contacts. Two classes of goals: (1) knowledge-related and (2) emotional. Selective Optimization with Compensation (SOC) (Paul Baltes & colleagues) Successful aging is linked with three factors: Selection (reduced capacity requires reducing performance in most life domains), Optimization (maintaining performance in some areas through continued practice and new technologies), and Compensation (when tasks demand a level beyond current potential — e.g., memorising fast, reacting quickly when driving — older adults compensate, especially under high mental/physical demand). High-yield Disengagement = withdraw. Activity = stay engaged. Socioemotional selectivity (Carstensen) = prune to emotionally rewarding relationships. SOC (Paul Baltes) = Select, Optimize, Compensate. Mental problems in old age Definition Dementia = the general term for physiologically caused cognitive and behavioural decline sufficient to affect daily life. Alzheimer's disease (AD) — a progressive, degenerative brain disorder. The brain shows excessive neurofibrillary tangles (twisted masses of collapsed protein fibres) and large waxy chunks of amyloid plaque (nonfunctioning tissue formed in the spaces between neurons by an abnormal variant of the protein beta amyloid ). Parkinson's disease — the second most common disorder involving progressive neurological degeneration, characterised by tremor, stiffness, slowed movement, and unstable posture .

title: Unit 10 — Emerging Areas
text: Unit 10 — Emerging Areas The newer frontiers of applied psychology, built directly from the Unit 10 source: the psychology of gender and the schools of feminism , feminist psychology and feminist therapy with their critique of traditional treatment, the workplace barriers women face, the psychology of poverty , the positive-psychology science of wellbeing and self-growth (eudaimonia vs hedonia, the major wellbeing models, character strengths and post-traumatic growth), and cyberpsychology (online disinhibition and internet addiction). Every named area, model and theorist in the file is reproduced and taught to NIMHANS depth. In this book Issues of gender Types of feminism Feminist psychology Workplace barriers: glass ceiling & relatives Feminist therapy Issues in traditional therapies Empowerment & feminist techniques The psychology of poverty Wellbeing & self-growth Models of wellbeing Character strengths & virtues Post-traumatic growth Cyberpsychology 1. Issues of gender The one distinction to never blur. The whole topic rests on separating two words the public uses interchangeably. Sex is the biological distinction between male and female, fixed at conception by the chromosomes: the male karyotype is XY and the female karyotype is XX . Gender is the culturally constructed categorisation of maleness and femaleness, that is, the social meanings of masculinity and femininity . Sex is given by biology; gender is built by culture. Definition Gender = the culturally constructed categorisation of maleness and femaleness (masculinity / femininity). Sex = the biological distinction of male (XY chromosome) and female (XX chromosome). Gender stereotypes A gender stereotype is a widely held belief about the abilities, personality traits, and social behaviour of females and males (the source attributes this definition to Weiten, 2001 ). Stereotypes are not the same as differences that actually exist; they are beliefs about the sexes, which may be exaggerated, inaccurate, or self-fulfilling. They feed the discrimination patterns described later in this book (glass ceiling, maternal wall, etc.). Minimalist vs maximalist views of gender differences How big are the psychological differences between men and women? The field splits into two camps: Maximalists believe in huge, fundamental differences between men and women. On this view the sexes are deeply, qualitatively distinct. Minimalists believe there are few fundamental differences between them. On this view the apparent gaps are small, situational, or socially produced rather than essential. Trap Maximalist = MAXimum difference; minimalist = MINimum difference. Maximalists emphasise large, fundamental sex differences; minimalists emphasise that the genuine fundamental differences are few. Do not confuse the camps because the names sound technical. High-yield Sex = biological (XY male, XX female). Gender = cultural construction of masculinity/femininity. Gender stereotype = widely held belief about males'/females' abilities, traits and social behaviour (Weiten, 2001). Maximalists = big differences; minimalists = few fundamental differences. 2. Types of feminism The source lists five branches of feminism . Each answers the same question, "what is the root of women's oppression and how do we end it?", in a different way. Learn them by their diagnosis and their strategy , because that is what is tested. Branch Core idea / diagnosis Strategy Liberal feminism Works within the structure of mainstream society. Its roots reach back to social-contract theory of government, the idea instituted by the American Revolution. Integrate women into the existing structure (equal access, equal rights) rather than overthrow it. Radical feminism Seen by many as the "undesirable" element of feminism, yet it is actually the breeding ground for many of the ideas that other branches shape and pound out. Holds that women's oppression is the deepest, original oppression. Tackle the root system of male domination (patriarchy) directly; the source ties consciousness raising to this branch. Socialist feminism The result of Marxism meeting radical feminism . Marxism recognises that women are oppressed and attributes the oppression to the capitalist / private-property system . The only way to end women's oppression is to overthrow the capitalist system . Cultural feminism Retreated to vanguardism , working instead to build a women's culture . Some of this effort has had real social benefit. Create and value a distinct women's culture rather than fight for integration. Eco-feminism Much more spiritual than political or theoretical in nature. May or may not be wrapped up with Goddess worship and vegetarianism . Its basic tenet: a patriarchal/hierarchical society will exploit its resources without regard to long-term consequences, as a direct result of the attitudes fostered in such a society. Link the domination of women to the domination of nature; resist both. Mnemonic " L iberals L obby (work within), R adicals R oot out patriarchy, S ocialists S mash capitalism, C ultural C reates a women's culture, E co links women & E arth." — L-R-S-C-E. High-yield Socialist feminism = Marxism + radical feminism , blames the capitalist/private-property system. Radical feminism is the "breeding ground" of feminist ideas and is the home of consciousness raising . Liberal feminism = integration within the system. Eco-feminism = spiritual, links patriarchy to environmental exploitation. 3. Feminist psychology Feminist psychology aims to understand the individual within the larger social and political aspects of society . Its defining move is to refuse to study a person in isolation: a woman's distress is read against the background of her social and political situation, not just her internal makeup. Key figures named in the source Karen Horney — Feminine Psychoanalysis. Horney challenged Freud from within psychoanalysis, replacing his "penis envy" account of female development with a social and cultural reading of women's psychology. She is the named author of a feminine psychoanalysis , foregrounding women's experience rather than treating it as a deviation from a male standard. Edward Strecker — "Mom-ism". Strecker is associated with the concept of Mom-ism , a (controversial, mother-blaming) idea critiqued within feminist psychology for pathologising motherhood and women's roles. Consciousness raising Consciousness raising is closely tied with radical feminism . It aims to weed out discrimination and segregation based on sex , and it maintains a key radical-feminist claim: women's oppression is not a by-product of capitalist oppression but a "primary cause" in its own right.
