In other words, against socialist feminism (which traces oppression back to capitalism), consciousness raising treats the oppression of women as primary, not derivative. Trap Both socialist feminism and consciousness raising mention capitalism, but they take opposite sides. Socialist feminism says women's oppression comes from capitalism. Consciousness raising (radical) insists it is not a by-product of capitalism but a primary cause . High-yield Feminist psychology = understand the individual within the larger social and political context. Karen Horney = feminine psychoanalysis ; Edward Strecker = "Mom-ism" ; consciousness raising = radical feminism, oppression of women as a primary cause . 4. Workplace barriers: the glass-ceiling family The source gives four named "invisible barrier" effects that describe how discrimination keeps women out of, or trapped in, particular places in the labour market. They are routinely tested as a matching set, so learn each by its precise location and mechanism. Effect What it describes Glass ceiling effect When women can't reach higher ranks, pay or positions because of discrimination, limiting beliefs, etc. The barrier is at the top , invisible but real. Maternal wall The stereotypes and forms of discrimination encountered by working mothers and by mothers seeking employment . Bias triggered specifically by motherhood. Sticky floor effect A discriminatory employment pattern that keeps workers, mainly women, in the lower ranks of the job scale . The barrier is at the bottom ; they cannot rise off the floor. Glass-cliff effect When a woman is promoted to a leadership role of an organisation that is about to collapse , set up to be a scapegoat for the failure. A precarious, high-risk promotion. Trap Ceiling vs floor vs cliff. Glass ceiling = blocked at the top . Sticky floor = stuck at the bottom . Glass cliff = promoted, but onto a failing organisation so she takes the blame. Maternal wall = bias specifically against mothers . Mnemonic Top blocked = ceiling ; bottom stuck = floor ; promoted-to-fall = cliff ; mother-penalty = wall . 5. Feminist therapy Feminist therapy is a type of therapy based on viewing individuals within their sociocultural context . It carries the central commitment of feminist psychology into the consulting room: the client's problems are understood against her social and cultural situation, not treated as purely intrapsychic faults. Two features that define the approach Not just for women. Feminist therapy is not confined to women ; it addresses gender-role conformities for clients of any gender, that is, the costs of rigidly conforming to prescribed gender roles. An egalitarian relationship. The client–therapist relationship is meant to be as egalitarian as possible , with both sides communicating on equal ground and sharing experiences . The therapist deliberately flattens the usual power hierarchy of treatment, which is itself a therapeutic statement about power. High-yield Feminist therapy = individuals understood within their sociocultural context ; not confined to women (it addresses gender-role conformity in general); the therapeutic relationship is deliberately egalitarian , with shared, equal-ground communication. 6. Issues in traditional therapies Feminist therapy arose as a critique of biases built into traditional therapy. The source names three problems. Gender bias Many traditional therapies assume that women should follow sex-roles in order to be mentally healthy . They treat gender differences as entirely biologically based and therefore encourage female clients to be submissive, expressive, and nurturant in order to achieve fulfillment . Mental health is thus equated with conformity to a feminine role. Androcentrism Androcentrism means treating being male as the norm . Feminine traits are then viewed as a deviation from the norm and as a deficiency on the part of women . The male is the yardstick; the female is measured as a falling-short of it. Definition Androcentrism = taking the male as the standard/norm, so that feminine traits appear as a deviation from, and a deficiency relative to, that norm. Intrapsychic assumptions Traditional therapy locates the trouble inside the client. As a result, therapists tend to blame clients for their symptoms, even when the client may in fact be coping admirably in a difficult and oppressive situation , and they may pathologise normal responses to oppressive environments . A reasonable reaction to an unjust situation gets relabelled as the client's disorder. Trap The intrapsychic assumption is the engine of victim-blaming: it treats a healthy reaction to an oppressive environment as a personal pathology. Feminist therapy's correction is the slogan "the personal is political" — relocate the problem from inside the person to the social situation. 7. Principles of empowerment & feminist techniques Principles of empowerment Feminist therapy works from three empowerment principles: Personal is political. A client's private distress is connected to wider social and political conditions; her problems are not purely individual failings. Egalitarian relationships. Therapy models equal power between client and therapist rather than expert-over-patient. Value the female perspective. Women's experiences and ways of knowing are treated as valid and valuable, not as deviations to be corrected. Techniques Sex-role analysis — a critique of cultural conditioning : examining how the client has been shaped by the gender roles society imposed on her, and what those roles cost her. Power analysis — examining power differentials : making visible the unequal power between the client and others (partners, employers, institutions) and how it bears on her difficulties. Assertiveness training — teaching the client to express needs and set boundaries, countering the trained submissiveness that gender bias rewards. The source also flags poverty alongside these techniques, signalling that material deprivation is part of the social context feminist therapy must address, which leads to the next major area. High-yield Empowerment principles: personal is political , egalitarian relationships , value the female perspective . Techniques: sex-role analysis (critique of cultural conditioning), power analysis (examining power differentials), assertiveness training . 8. The psychology of poverty Poverty is a condition in which a person or community is deprived of, or lacks, the essentials for a minimum standard of wellbeing and life . It is an emerging area for psychology because deprivation shapes development, stress, health and mental disorder, and because the intrapsychic-assumption trap above (blaming individuals for circumstance) bites hardest here. Types of poverty Type Meaning Absolute poverty The scarcity of basic food, clean water, health, shelter, education and information . People in absolute poverty struggle to survive and suffer many child deaths from preventable diseases like malaria, cholera and water-contamination-related diseases . Relative poverty Defined from a social perspective : living standard compared to the economic standard of the surrounding population . It is therefore a measure of income inequality , often measured as the percentage of the population with income below some fixed proportion of median income . Situational poverty A temporary poverty caused by an adverse event such as an environmental disaster, job loss, or severe health problem. Generational poverty Poverty handed down from one generation to the next . It is more complicated because there is no easy escape : people are trapped and cannot access the tools needed to get out. The source quotes Jensen (2009) : it "occurs in families where at least two generations have been born into poverty… not equipped with the tools to move out of their situation." Rural poverty Occurs in rural areas with population below 50,000 , where there are fewer job opportunities, less access to services, less support for disabilities, and fewer quality education opportunities. Urban poverty Occurs in metropolitan areas with population over 50,000 . Marked by limited access to health and education, inadequate housing and services, a violent and unhealthy environment due to overcrowding, and little or no social-protection mechanism. Trap Absolute vs relative poverty. Absolute = lacking the basics for survival (food, water, shelter), an objective threshold. Relative = below the standard of those around you, a measure of inequality tied to median income. And note the population line: rural < 50,000 , urban > 50,000 . High-yield Six types: absolute (no basics), relative (below surrounding standard = inequality, vs median income), situational (temporary, from an adverse event), generational (handed down, ≥2 generations born into it — Arthur Jensen 2009), rural (pop < 50,000), urban (pop > 50,000). 9. Wellbeing & self-growth This is the positive-psychology heart of the unit: instead of asking what makes people ill, it asks what makes life good and what helps people flourish. It opens with the two great traditions of what "wellbeing" even means. Two conceptions of wellbeing Eudaimonic wellbeing Hedonistic wellbeing Equates wellbeing with The cultivation of personal strengths and contribution to the greater good , acting in accordance with one's deeper nature and values. Pleasure and happiness . Key features Acting in accordance with one's inner nature and deeply held values ; the realization of one's true potential ; the experience of purpose or meaning in life . Maximising positive feeling and enjoyment, minimising pain. Definition Eudaimonic wellbeing = wellbeing as living in line with one's true nature and values, realising one's potential, and finding meaning. Hedonistic wellbeing = wellbeing as pleasure and happiness. Mnemonic " Hedon ist chases the feeling (pleasure/happiness); eudaimon chases the fulfilment (meaning/potential/values)." The two F's tell them apart. 10. Models of wellbeing The source lists four wellbeing models. Learn the named author and the component list of each. The holistic view of wellbeing A holistic model treats wellbeing as multi-domain. The source names the domains as emotional, intellectual, spiritual, occupational, social, and physical wellness . Health is not just absence of illness but balance across all these domains. Subjective wellbeing — Diener's tripartite model Subjective wellbeing (SWB) consists of three components (Ed Diener's tripartite model): Cognitive evaluation of life satisfaction (a judgement of how one's life is going); Presence of positive affect ; Relative absence of negative affect . SWB is the standard operationalisation of the hedonic tradition: a satisfied judgement plus lots of good feeling and little bad feeling. Carol Ryff's Six-Factor Model of Psychological Well-Being The Six-Factor Model of Psychological Well-Being was developed by Carol Ryff . It identifies six factors that contribute to an individual's psychological wellbeing, contentment and happiness. This is the leading eudaimonic model. The six factors are: Autonomy Environmental Mastery Personal Growth Positive Relations with Others Purpose in Life Self-Acceptance Mnemonic Ryff's six: " A utonomy, E nvironmental mastery, P ersonal growth, P ositive relations, P urpose, S elf-acceptance" → A-E-P-P-P-S ("A-E and three P's and S"). PERMA model — Seligman The PERMA model was given by Martin Seligman and has five measurable elements : P ositive emotions E ngagement R elationships M eaning and purpose A ccomplishment Trap Don't cross the authors: Ed Diener = the tripartite subjective wellbeing model (life satisfaction + positive affect + low negative affect). Ryff = the six-factor psychological wellbeing model. Martin Seligman = PERMA (five elements). Ryff has SIX factors; PERMA has FIVE. High-yield Ed Diener → SWB, 3 parts (life-satisfaction cognition + positive affect + relative absence of negative affect). Ryff → 6 factors (Autonomy, Environmental Mastery, Personal Growth, Positive Relations, Purpose in Life, Self-Acceptance). Martin Seligman → PERMA (Positive emotion, Engagement, Relationships, Meaning, Accomplishment). Holistic view = 6 wellness domains. 11. Character strengths & virtues Character Strengths and Virtues (CSV) is described as a groundbreaking handbook that compiles the work of researchers to create a classification system for widely valued positive traits . It is, in effect, positive psychology's answer to the diagnostic manual: instead of cataloguing disorders, it catalogues what is best in people. (CSV was authored by Christopher Peterson and Martin Seligman; it is often called the "un-DSM".) The system contains 6 classes of virtues that are made up of 24 character strengths . The six virtue classes are universally valued across cultures, and the 24 strengths are the measurable routes to expressing them. High-yield Character Strengths and Virtues = a classification of widely valued positive traits, structured as 6 virtues built from 24 character strengths . Think of it as the positive-psychology counterpart to the DSM. 12. Post-traumatic growth Post-traumatic growth (PTG) is the counterpart to PTSD: the same struggle that can break a person can, far more often, change them for the better. The source stresses the asymmetry: most trauma survivors report growth after their experience , while only a few develop PTSD . Definition Post-traumatic growth (a term coined by Tedeschi and Calhoun ) = the positive psychological change experienced as a result of the struggle with highly challenging life circumstances . The five areas of post-traumatic growth Appreciation of life — a renewed sense of the value of being alive. Relating to others — deeper, closer relationships. Personal strength — a sense of "if I survived that, I am stronger than I knew." New possibilities — new paths, goals and opportunities open up. Spiritual, existential or philosophical change — a transformed worldview or faith. Trap PTG is not simply the absence of PTSD, and it does not mean the trauma was good. It is genuine positive change that grows out of the struggle with adversity. Note the key statistic the source emphasises: growth is the common outcome; PTSD is the rare one. High-yield PTG coined by Tedeschi & Calhoun = positive psychological change from struggling with highly challenging circumstances. Five areas: appreciation of life, relating to others, personal strength, new possibilities, spiritual/existential/philosophical change . Most survivors grow; only a few develop PTSD. 13. Cyberpsychology Cyberpsychology studies the psychological effects of the internet and digital technology on human behaviour. The source focuses on two phenomena: why people behave badly online (online disinhibition) and how internet use becomes a disorder (internet addiction). Online disinhibition Cyberbullying occurs due to a phenomenon called online disinhibition : people say and do things online that they would not say or do face-to-face, because the usual social brakes are loosened. The anonymity, invisibility and distance of the screen lower the inhibitions that normally restrain hostile behaviour. The source credits Suler with identifying the areas (components) of online disinhibition. Definition Online disinhibition (Suler) = the loosening or abandonment of the social restrictions and inhibitions that would normally be present in face-to-face interaction, occurring when people are online. It is the mechanism behind cyberbullying . Internet addiction disorder (IAD) The source states that the APA has included internet addiction as a disorder in DSM-5 , and lists four components essential for a diagnosis of IAD : Excessive internet use — using the internet far more than intended, losing track of time. Withdrawal — feelings of tension, anger or depression when access is denied. Tolerance — needing more and more (better equipment, more hours, more content) to get the same satisfaction. Adverse consequences — negative effects on work, relationships, health and functioning. Mnemonic The four IAD components map onto the classic addiction tetrad: E-W-T-A — E xcessive use, W ithdrawal, T olerance, A dverse consequences. Trap The source follows the deck's claim that internet addiction was "included as a disorder in DSM-5." In the actual DSM-5, only Internet Gaming Disorder appears, and only in Section III as a condition for further study , not as a fully recognised diagnosis. For this paper, answer per the source (four components: excessive use, withdrawal, tolerance, adverse consequences) but know the real DSM-5 nuance. High-yield Cyberbullying is driven by online disinhibition (areas identified by Suler ). Internet addiction disorder has four diagnostic components: excessive internet use, withdrawal, tolerance, adverse consequences .

title: Research Methods & Statistics
text: Research Methods & Statistics How psychological knowledge is made and judged: the philosophical paradigms beneath every study, the quantitative, qualitative and mixed methods that grow from them, the experimental and non-experimental designs that license (or block) causal claims, and the statistical tests that decide whether a result is real. This book moves from epistemology to inference, builds every parametric test (t, F) from the logic of sampling distributions, extends them to MANOVA and ANCOVA, and closes with the distribution-free family. It is prioritised for MET 2026 and NIMHANS clinical psychology, with assumptions, degrees of freedom and a "which test when" decision table you can recite under pressure. In this book Paradigms & methods of research Research designs & sampling Hypothesis testing & inference Parametric test: the t-test ANOVA & experimental designs MANOVA & ANCOVA Non-parametric tests "Which test when" decision guide 1. Paradigms & methods of research The one idea behind the section. Before any method is chosen, a researcher already holds a paradigm : a way of thinking about and conducting research, a philosophy that guides how the research might be done. Method is downstream of philosophy. Two scientists can study the same phenomenon and reach different designs because they answer two prior questions differently: what is real ( ontology ) and how can we know it ( epistemology ). Definition Ontology = the nature of reality (is there one objective reality, or many constructed realities?). Epistemology = the nature of knowledge and the relationship between the knower and what is known (can the researcher stand apart from what is studied, or are they entangled with it?). Together they shape both the data-collection process and the analysis. The four research paradigms Learn each by its stance on reality, on the researcher, and on the kind of knowledge it produces. Paradigm Ontology / epistemology Typical methods Goal Positivism One objective reality exists and can be measured directly; researcher is detached and value-free Experiments, structured measurement, statistics Discover universal laws; explain and predict Post-positivism Objective reality exists but can only be known imperfectly and probabilistically ; all observation is theory-laden Quantitative methods with a plan fixed before the study; falsification Approximate truth through repeated, fallible testing Constructivism / interpretivism Reality is socially and personally constructed ; multiple realities; knower and known are inseparable Open-ended interviews, observation, narrative documents kept in text form Understand meaning from the participant's perspective Critical / transformative Reality is shaped by power, history, economics; knowledge is political Critical ethnography, participatory and emancipatory designs Expose and change unjust structures; empower Trap Positivism vs post-positivism. Both are "objective-reality" paradigms and both drive quantitative work. The shift is that positivism claims we can know reality directly and with certainty, while post-positivism (the modern stance behind most quantitative social science) says we can only know it imperfectly : every measurement is fallible, theory-laden, and provisional, so we falsify rather than prove. In exam phrasing, "quantitative research = post-positivist approach" and "qualitative research = constructivist approach". Quantitative vs qualitative vs mixed methods The paradigm choice cascades into a whole research stance. The table is high-yield because the paper tests the cascade directly. Feature Quantitative (post-positivist) Qualitative (constructivist) Plan A specific plan is developed prior to the study; tight structure Less structure on specific guidelines; general guidelines only; emergent design Data "Objective": easily classified or quantified (age, gender, test scores, recovery time) "Subjective": interpreted differently by different people (perceptions of pain, feelings about work) Collection Structured interviews / questionnaires, observations, records; scored reliably with little training Open-ended interviews, observation, narrative documents (diaries); data kept in text form Analysis Inferential statistics to generalise from sample to population Coding of themes , assigning meaning to words or images Strength Results across many studies can be combined into a large body of evidence Depth; tools for data, analysis and interpretation that quantitative work lacks Mixed methods. When the two paradigms are blended so that one sets the stage for or leads to the other , the approach is mixed methods. It rests on the pragmatic approach, which focuses on methodological rather than philosophical concerns and combines qualitative and quantitative methods, using exploratory and confirmatory methods. This widens the options for data collection, analysis tools and interpretation. Trap Using two methods in the same study but discussing them separately is not mixed methods, it is just "two methods being used". Mixed methods requires genuine integration where one paradigm feeds the other. Qualitative methods of research, in depth NIMHANS expects you to name each qualitative tradition and its signature. Observation. Being present in a situation and recording one's impressions. The primary research instrument is the self , consciously gathering sensory data. Problems: the enormous complexity of human behaviour, the impossibility of a complete record, and the subjectivity of the researcher. Types: structured (schedules predetermine the categories of behaviour/talk to be observed, e.g. Flanders' Interaction Analysis Categories, FIAC), unstructured (broad decisions made in advance, seen through the researcher's own socio-culturally constructed values), shadow studies (tracking one participant), and participant observation (the researcher joins and participates, gaining unique insight but risking distraction from the research purpose). Survey method. Studies large and small populations (universes) by selecting and studying samples to discover relative incidence, distribution and interrelations of variables. Variables = sociological facts (sex, income, religious/political affiliation, SES), opinions and attitudes. Factual "face-sheet information" is recorded on a face sheet. Uses interviews, schedules and questionnaires; other types include the panel technique (same respondents re-interviewed over time), telephone surveys (high speed, low cost) and mail questionnaires (cheap but poor response rate, cannot check answers). Researchers use a flow plan : objectives → statement of problem → sample and sampling plan → construction of the schedule/instrument → data collection → coding and tabulation → analysis and interpretation → report. Advantages : wide scope, accurate. Disadvantages : does not penetrate below the surface, demanding of time and money, can lift the respondent out of his social context and invalidate results. Phenomenology. The study of lived human phenomena within everyday social contexts, from the perspective of those who experience them. Direct approach : the detached researcher shines a light on the foreground, studying participants' mental representations (rooted in Husserl , whose starting point is a conscious actor separated from a world of objects). Indirect approach : the involved, connected observer immerses in the everyday world and lights up the background (rooted in Heidegger , who saw us as first and foremost immersed in the world, aiming to deepen understanding of "what it is to be"). Grounded theory. A theory- generating methodology; the end product is an integrated theoretical formulation. The researcher does not enter with a predefined theory. Coding sequence: open coding (concept identification, text broken apart line-by-line) → axial coding (weaving data back together, grouping concepts into categories) → selective coding (constructing the single most representative core category ). Key constructs: theoretical sampling (data gathering directed by emerging concepts), saturation (no new concepts/properties emerge; data become repetitive), and memo writing (records of the analyst's evolving thoughts). The theory is a co-construction between researcher and participants. Field studies. Ex post facto scientific inquiries into relations among variables in real social structures; the researcher does not manipulate any independent variable. Two types: exploratory (seeks "what is", discovers significant variables and relations, lays groundwork for later hypothesis testing) and hypothesis-testing . Strong in realism, social significance, strength of variables, theory orientation and heuristic quality; weakest in its ex-post-facto character (weaker statements of relation than experiments), plethora of variables, lack of precision, and practical problems (feasibility, cost, sampling, time). Focus group. A small but demographically diverse group whose reactions are studied in guided/open discussion (market research, political analysis); peer groups and professional teams work better than strangers. Problems: pecking orders, histories and animosities, confusion about purpose, and convenience/purposive sampling (not representative). Not an effective way of measuring attitudes; it is a social process in which participants co-produce an account specific to that time and place. Ethnography. Literally "writing about people"; treats people as meaning-makers and aims to describe how a culture "ticks". Tends to focus on a limited range of cases (often one setting), with strong links to anthropology (proper ethnography = participant observer in everyday life). Critical ethnographers link the "micro" (participants' meanings) to the "macro" (structural and political dimensions). Demands reflexivity (a research diary) and openness to reformulating the problem. Narrative inquiry / life history. Concerned with the production, interpretation and representation of storied accounts of lived experience. A life story becomes a life history when the researcher adds analysis of the social, historical, political and economic context. The life-history inquiry is a dialogic event co-constructed over time. Research ethics Whatever the paradigm, ethical conduct is non-negotiable. Core principles tested at NIMHANS level: Informed consent — voluntary participation with full disclosure of purpose, procedures and risks; a code of practice has to be established in advance. Confidentiality and anonymity — protecting identity and data; especially hard in focus groups. Beneficence and non-maleficence — maximise benefit, minimise harm; this is why withdrawing a successful treatment in a reversal (ABAB) design can be considered unethical in clinical settings, motivating multiple-baseline designs. Right to withdraw without penalty at any time. Debriefing — explaining the study afterwards, especially when deception was used. Justice — fair selection of participants; no exploitation of vulnerable groups. High-yield Paradigm cascade: positivism/post-positivism → quantitative → objective data → inferential statistics ; constructivism → qualitative → subjective data → thematic coding ; pragmatism → mixed methods . Ontology = nature of reality; epistemology = nature of knowledge. Husserl = direct phenomenology; Heidegger = indirect. Grounded theory codes open → axial → selective and stops at saturation. 2. Research designs & sampling A design is the structure that decides what you can conclude. The single most important question is whether the design supports a causal claim, and that turns on two features: an active (manipulated) independent variable and random assignment . The family of designs Design Active IV? Random assignment? Causal claim? True (randomised) experiment Yes Yes Yes — the gold standard Quasi-experiment Yes No (intact groups) Weak; confounds not fully ruled out Correlational No (measured, not manipulated) No No — association only Descriptive No No No — "what is", no comparison True (randomised) experimental approach Has random assignment of participants to intervention and comparison groups and an active, manipulated independent variable; the groups' scores on the dependent variable are compared. Criteria: (1) the IV must be active, i.e. manipulatable, with the experimenter able to set several levels; (2) participants are randomly assigned, so each has an equal chance of any group, and after assignment but before intervention the groups are assumed equivalent in all other respects including demographics. A study can have a weak sampling procedure and still be a true experiment (random assignment, not random sampling, is what makes it experimental). The researcher controls extraneous variables to maximise the IV's effect. Types of true-experimental designs: Posttest-only control-group design — randomise to two groups, treat one, measure both after. Pretest–posttest control-group design — measure before and after in both groups. Solomon four-group design — combines the two above to detect and control for pretest sensitisation (whether being pretested changes the effect). Randomised experimental design with matching — match participants on a relevant variable, then randomly assign within pairs. Within-subjects (crossover) design — each participant receives every condition. Quasi-experimental approach Has an active IV but no random assignment ; participants are already in intact groups, so the researcher has less control. The design's strength depends on how much control the investigator actually has over manipulating the IV. Categories: Pre-experimental designs (quasi-experiments with major limitations, no feasible comparison group or pretest): one-group posttest-only, one-group pretest–posttest, posttest-only non-equivalent groups. Pretest–posttest designs with a non-equivalent comparison group. Time-series designs — repeated measures before and after intervention, no random assignment; single-group and multiple-group time-series. Single-subject (small-n) designs (see ANOVA section). Variables and validity Independent variable (IV) = the presumed cause; dependent variable (DV) = the measured effect. Extraneous variable = any variable other than the IV that could affect the DV; a confound is an extraneous variable that systematically varies with the IV. Internal validity = the degree to which the design supports a causal claim (threatened by history, maturation, testing, instrumentation, regression to the mean, selection, attrition). External validity = generalisability to other people, settings and times. Sampling Sampling decides external validity (generalisation), whereas random assignment decides internal validity (causation). Do not confuse the two. Probability (random) sampling Non-probability sampling Simple random — every member has equal, independent chance Convenience — whoever is available Systematic — every k-th member from a list Purposive — chosen for a characteristic the researcher wants Stratified — split into strata, sample within each (proportionate or disproportionate) Quota — fill preset category counts non-randomly Cluster / multistage — sample naturally occurring groups, then within them Snowball — participants recruit further participants Trap Random sampling ≠ random assignment . Random sampling (drawing the sample from the population) supports generalisation ; random assignment (allocating participants to conditions) supports causal inference . A true experiment requires random assignment but can survive a weak (non-random) sample. Focus groups and field studies use convenience/purposive sampling, so they cannot claim a representative sample. 3. Hypothesis testing & inference All parametric tests share one engine: compare an observed result against the sampling distribution of the statistic expected if nothing were going on. Master this once and the t, F and z tests all become the same move. The logic of significance testing The four steps of hypothesis testing: Formulate a null hypothesis (H 0 ) about a population parameter (e.g. about the population mean), along with an alternative hypothesis (H 1 ) . Draw a random sample and compute the sample statistic (e.g. the sample mean). Examine the sampling distribution of the statistic under H 0 to learn which outcomes would occur, and with what relative frequency, if H 0 were true. Retain H 0 if the sample outcome is in line with what H 0 predicts; otherwise reject it and accept H 1 . The regions of rejection are the two extreme tails of the sampling distribution that lead to rejecting H 0 ; the central portion (e.g. the middle 95%) is the region of retention . For a two-tailed test at α = .05, we reject only if the outcome falls in the upper 2.5% or lower 2.5% (.025 + .025 = .05). Significance level, confidence and critical values Level of significance (α) — symbolised by the Greek letter alpha; indicates the stringency of the test. The usual level is 0.05 (95% confidence). Other levels: 0.10 (90%), 0.01 (99%), 0.001 (99.9%). Critical values separate the rejection regions from the retention region. For a normal distribution, the two-tailed z critical values are ±1.96 at .05 and ±2.58 at .01 . If the obtained z exceeds ±1.96, the sample mean differs significantly from the population mean at the .05 level. Definition Type I error = rejecting a true H 0 (a false positive); its probability is α. Type II error = retaining a false H 0 (a false negative); its probability is β. Power = 1 − β, the probability of correctly detecting a real effect. Lowering α reduces Type I error but raises Type II error. Parametric vs non-parametric Parametric tests assume the data come from a population with a specific distribution (usually normal), require interval/ratio data, and test population parameters (means, variances). Non-parametric (distribution-free) tests make few or no distributional assumptions and work on nominal or ordinal data. Parametric tests are more powerful when their assumptions hold ; non-parametric tests are the fallback when assumptions are violated. 4. Parametric test: the t-test The t-test compares means . It is the workhorse parametric test for one or two groups. There are three forms, all built on the same sampling-distribution logic. Type What it compares One-sample t-test The mean of one group against a known norm or population average (e.g. "is this group's IQ significantly above 100?") Independent-samples t-test The means of two different groups drawn independently of each other (not matched) Dependent / paired (related) samples t-test The means of two matched groups, or the same group measured twice (pre-test vs post-test) From z to t For hypothesis testing, the z of a sample mean is z = (sample mean − population mean) / standard deviation of the population . When the population standard deviation is unknown , an unbiased estimate is calculated from the sample's SD. If the actual SD of the sample is used instead of the unbiased SD, we get a t score rather than a z score. The t distribution : is more leptokurtic than the normal distribution (taller peak, heavier tails); has a larger standard deviation than the normal curve; depends on the degrees of freedom , and approaches the normal curve as df increases. The critical t value is found from a table using the degrees of freedom and the level of significance. If the obtained t statistic exceeds the critical value, H 0 is rejected. Definition Degrees of freedom (df) = the number of values free to vary when computing a statistic. For the one-sample and paired t-test, df = n − 1 . For the independent-samples t-test, df = n 1 + n 2 − 2 . One-sample t-test Tests a hypothesis about a single group, e.g. whether a group's IQ is significantly above the average of 100. Assumptions: A random sample has been drawn from the population (with-replacement sampling plan in the classical derivation). The sampling distribution of the mean follows the normal curve. (In the z version) the population standard deviation is known; when it is unknown, estimate it from the sample and use t. Formula in words: t = (sample mean − population mean) / standard error of the mean , where the standard error = s / √n. When SD or standard error is not given, t is computed from raw scores using the sum of squares (SS): the unbiased sample SD is s x = √(SS x / (n − 1)). Independent-samples t-test Instead of comparing a sample mean to a population, it considers the difference between two samples independently drawn from two populations . If the two population means are equal, then across repeated sampling sometimes (X − Y) is positive and sometimes negative, and over all possible differences the mean is zero . So the mean of the sampling distribution of differences (X − Y) is zero when the two population means are equal — that is the null hypothesis. The sampling distribution of (X − Y) is normal when both populations are normal, and tends toward normal even when they are not (central limit theorem). Testing the difference: With large samples , use z: significant if z exceeds ±1.96 (.05) or ±2.58 (.01). With smaller samples , use t, assuming the variances of X and Y are equal — the assumption of homogeneity of variance . If the variances are not equal, a pooled estimate of variance is calculated (and a correction such as Welch's can be applied). Assumptions of the independent-samples t-test: (1) independence of observations, (2) normality of the DV in each population, (3) homogeneity of variance, (4) interval/ratio measurement. Dependent / paired-samples t-test For related or paired samples (the same subjects measured twice, or matched pairs), the standard deviation differs from that of independent samples : the test works on the difference scores , so it removes between-subject variability and is generally more powerful. The statistic is t = mean of difference scores / standard error of the difference scores , with df = n − 1 (n = number of pairs). The key assumption is that the difference scores are normally distributed. Mnemonic " One norm, two free, paired diff ": One -sample compares to a norm ; independent uses df = n 1 +n 2 −2 (each group loses one, "two free"); paired works on difference scores with df = n−1. High-yield t replaces z when the population SD is unknown; t is leptokurtic and df-dependent (df = n−1 for one-sample/paired, n 1 +n 2 −2 for independent). Independent t assumes homogeneity of variance; if violated, pool the variance (or use Welch). Paired t uses difference scores and is more powerful by removing between-subject variance. For two groups, F = t² . 5. ANOVA & experimental designs Analysis of variance (ANOVA) tests mean differences across two or more groups simultaneously. It was developed by Ronald A. Fisher ; the name "F test" was given by Snedecor in Fisher's honour, and Snedecor (1946) tabulated the variance ratios (F ratios). Despite testing means, ANOVA works on variance rather than standard deviation and standard errors. Why ANOVA instead of many t-tests For k groups, running t-tests on every pair means k(k−1)/2 comparisons. Each comparison carries its own Type I error risk, so Type I error inflates as the number of comparisons grows. ANOVA tests all means at once with a single test, holding α fixed. (For exactly two groups, ANOVA and the t-test agree: F = t² .) Partitioning variance The total variability of a set of scores composed of several groups can be partitioned: Definition Total SS = SS between + SS within . Mean square (MS) = variance = SS / df . Within-group variance reflects error (innate group differences); between-group variance reflects treatment effects. If between-group variability is much greater than the error (within) variability, that indicates a treatment effect. Error (unsystematic) variance is reduced by random assignment and by controlling extraneous variables. One-way ANOVA One categorical IV (factor) with two or more levels, one DV. Degrees of freedom for k groups of n each: Source SS df MS Between groups SS between k − 1 SS between / (k−1) Within groups (error) SS within k(n − 1) SS within / k(n−1) Total SS total kn − 1 The F ratio = MS between / MS within . F should be greater than 1 to suggest a treatment effect, and must exceed the critical F (at the chosen confidence level, found from a table using df = k−1 and k(n−1)) to be significant. If the obtained F exceeds the critical F, reject H 0 . Strength of association. Significance does not measure effect size. Omega squared (ω²) gives the proportion of total variability in the scores accounted for by the treatments (eta squared, η², is the related but more biased index). Assumptions of ANOVA Assumption How tested / notes Normality of the criterion (dependent) variable Shapiro–Wilk, Jarque–Bera, Kolmogorov–Smirnov. Not essential: only extreme deviations matter because F is insensitive to smaller ones; symmetric non-normality causes only slight inflation of Type I error Homogeneity of variance (homoscedasticity) Bartlett's test, Levene's test. With normal populations and equal Ns, alpha inflation is slight; F is robust to departures Independence of the dependent scores (additivity) Each subject's score is independent of all others. This is the most important assumption, followed by homogeneity of variance If assumptions are violated, either use a suitable non-parametric test or apply a transformation of the measurement scale. Monotonic transformations leave the ordinal relationship unchanged: square-root (Poisson data, where mean = variance; e.g. √(X+0.5)), logarithmic (when SD varies with the mean, transform X to log X), reciprocal (when treatment SDs are proportional to the square of the means, transform to 1/X), and arcsine (for binomial data, i.e. proportions/percentages, transform to the angle whose sine is the square root of the proportion: sin⁻¹√p). Two-way (factorial) ANOVA Used when there are two categorical IVs and one DV. Its great advantage is that it finds interaction effects of the two variables alongside each variable's individual (main) effect. The between-groups SS now includes the interaction A×B in addition to A and B separately: Definition Total SS = SS A + SS B + SS AB + SS within . Degrees of freedom (r rows of factor A, c columns of factor B): A df = r−1 ; B df = c−1 ; interaction A×B df = (r−1)(c−1) ; within df = k(n−1) ; total df = kn−1 . Each effect gets its own F ratio (its MS ÷ MS within ). Trap An interaction effect means the effect of one IV depends on the level of the other (the lines on a plot are non-parallel). A significant interaction qualifies the main effects: do not interpret main effects in isolation when the interaction is significant. A main effect is the overall effect of one IV averaged across the levels of the other. Post-hoc tests If the ANOVA F is significant, the need arises to find where the difference lies. Ordinary t-tests between pairs would again inflate Type I error, so post-hoc tests are used that resemble t-tests but control the error rate: Fisher's Least Significant Difference (LSD) , also called Fisher's protected t-test — useful when the number of groups/treatments is small. Tukey's HSD (honestly significant difference) — yields the smallest number of significant differences and applies to a broad class of situations; the most recommended for post-hoc comparisons. Newman–Keuls test. Duncan's multiple range test. Experimental designs that control error variance Randomised block design. Random assignment equalises groups in theory but fails at low N, so blocking groups subjects on an initial measure (taken before the experiment with the same or a closely resembling instrument) to minimise within-group variance. The number of subjects per block is usually kept equal to the number of treatments; it can be run with one subject per block or n subjects per block. Repeated-measures design. Error variance is minimised by using the same subject across treatments ; the same sample is exposed to all treatment conditions (with one treatment, this becomes a pre-test/post-test on the same group). SS is partitioned into between-subjects SS, within-subjects SS and between-treatments SS, with the residual from within-subjects SS treated as the error term. Latin square design. Tries to eliminate row and column effects (e.g. order of presentation of treatments). Each treatment appears only once in each row and each column. For a p×p square: total df = p²−1 , row df = p−1 , column df = p−1 , residual (error) df = (p−1)(p−2) ; F is the ratio of treatment MS to residual MS. The number of Latin squares that can be generated for n treatments is (n!)×[(n−1)!]. Single-case (small-n) designs Single-subject research studies in detail the behaviour of each of a small number of participants (typically 2–10, hence "small-n"), focusing on the individual rather than group means, because group research can hide individual differences and produce results that represent no actual individual. It still seeks causal relationships through manipulation of an IV, careful measurement of a DV, and control of extraneous variables. AB / ABAB (reversal) design. The original and most common single-subject design. First A = baseline (observed until stable/flat); first B = intervention; then withdraw treatment for a second A ; then a second B . AB alone cannot rule out other causes; the reversal (ABAB) strengthens the inference, and more A/B phases make it more convincing. Multiple-baseline designs. Used when removing a successful treatment would be unethical. Up to three baselines are recorded simultaneously (across subjects , across behaviours , or across settings ); the intervention is introduced to one baseline at a randomly selected time while the others stay unchanged, ruling out external events as the cause. Alternating-treatment (multielement) design. Compares two treatments within the single-subject framework: establish a baseline, introduce the first treatment, then alternate the two treatments until distinct, stable response patterns to each can be discerned. High-yield ANOVA: Fisher developed it, Snedecor named F. F = MS between /MS within ; one-way df = (k−1) and k(n−1). Two-way splits SS into A + B + A×B + error and finds interactions . The most important assumption is independence/additivity , then homogeneity of variance; normality matters least. Significant F → Tukey's HSD (most recommended) post-hoc. Effect size = ω² . For two groups, F = t². 6. MANOVA & ANCOVA These extend ANOVA in two different directions: ANCOVA adds a covariate to remove nuisance variance from a single DV; MANOVA adds multiple dependent variables tested together. ANCOVA (Analysis of Covariance) ANCOVA is a method of controlling variance statistically by holding another related variable (the covariate X ) constant. The covariate is an extraneous variable whose effect we are trying to remove from the DV, increasing precision and power. It is the statistical alternative to physical control or matching. Assumptions of ANCOVA (in addition to the usual ANOVA assumptions): The covariate (X) is unaffected by the treatment (ideally measured before the intervention). The regression coefficient of Y on X is the same for all groups and is linear — the homogeneity-of-regression-slopes assumption. The correlations between X and Y are the same for all groups . How ANCOVA works. It uses ANOVA on an adjusted SS: first the DV's (Y) SS is computed for total, between and within groups; then the same is done for the covariate's (X) SS; and the adjusted SS on Y is calculated as SS adj = SS Y − (SP)² / SS X , where SP is the sum of products (of X and Y) rather than the sum of squares, computed for total, between and within groups. Degrees of freedom: ANCOVA loses one extra df (for estimating the regression on the covariate): Source ANOVA df ANCOVA df Total kn − 1 kn − 2 Treatment (between) k − 1 k − 1 Within (error) k(n − 1) k(n − 1) − 1 MANOVA (Multivariate Analysis of Variance) MANOVA is a multivariate procedure used to assess group differences across multiple metric dependent variables simultaneously : each treatment group is observed on two or more DVs. Rather than test each DV separately (which would inflate Type I error and ignore the correlations among DVs), MANOVA combines the dependent measures into a variate (a linear combination, via discriminant functions) and tests that composite for equality across groups. The dependent-variable weights are devised to produce a variate score for each respondent that is maximally different across all groups . MANOVA assesses the impact of multiple IVs on the individual DVs and on the DVs collectively. Multivariate test statistics (each can be approximated by an F statistic): Statistic What it does Wilks' lambda (U statistic) Often called the "multivariate F"; most commonly used for overall between-group significance; considers all discriminant functions, asking whether groups differ at all without focusing on a single linear combination Pillai's criterion Similar to Wilks' lambda; considers all the characteristic roots; the most robust to assumption violations Hotelling's trace (Hotelling's T²) Similar to Wilks' lambda; considers all characteristic roots Roy's greatest characteristic root (gcr) Measures differences on only the first discriminant function; gives power and specificity when the DVs are strongly interrelated on a single dimension, but is the most affected by violations of assumptions Assumptions of MANOVA: independence of observations; multivariate normality of the DVs; homogeneity of the variance–covariance matrices (tested by Box's M test, the multivariate analogue of homogeneity of variance); linearity among DVs; and adequate sample size relative to the number of DVs. Trap Distinguish the three extensions. ANOVA = one+ IV, one DV. ANCOVA = ANOVA plus a continuous covariate that is statistically removed (still one DV). MANOVA = two or more dependent variables tested together. "Covariate" ≠ "multiple DVs": a covariate is a nuisance variable you control; the DVs are the outcomes you care about. Mnemonic The "C" in AN C OVA = C ovariate (Controlled). The "M" in M ANOVA = M ultiple (dependent variables). Pick the statistic: P illai = most robu s t; R oy's = most r isky under violations but most powerful on one dimension. High-yield ANCOVA controls a covariate statistically (covariate must be unaffected by treatment, with equal/linear Y-on-X slopes across groups); it loses one extra df (total = kn−2). MANOVA tests multiple DVs via a variate; Wilks' lambda is the standard test ("multivariate F"), Pillai's is most robust, Roy's gcr is most sensitive to violations. Homogeneity of variance–covariance matrices is checked by Box's M . 7. Non-parametric tests Non-parametric (distribution-free) tests are used when the data are nominal or ordinal, when sample sizes are small, or when parametric assumptions (normality, homogeneity of variance, interval measurement) are violated. They make few assumptions about the shape of the population distribution. Learn each by its design (one sample, two related, two independent, k related, k independent) and its parametric counterpart. Chi-square (χ²) tests — for nominal/categorical data The chi-square statistic compares observed frequencies (O) with the expected frequencies (E) predicted under H 0 : χ² = ∑[(O − E)² / E] . Two main uses: Chi-square goodness of fit — tests whether the observed distribution of one categorical variable matches an expected distribution; df = k − 1 (k = number of categories). Chi-square test of independence (association) — tests whether two categorical variables are related in a contingency table; df = (r − 1)(c − 1) (r rows, c columns). Expected cell frequency = (row total × column total) / grand total. Assumptions: independent observations; categories mutually exclusive; expected frequency in each cell should be at least 5 (otherwise combine categories or use Fisher's exact test, or apply Yates' continuity correction for a 2×2 table). Sign test — two related samples (direction only) The sign test gets its name because it uses plus and minus signs rather than quantitative measures. Useful when quantitative measurement is impossible or infeasible but the two members of each pair can be ranked relative to each other. The only assumption is that the variable has a continuous distribution ; it makes no assumption about the form of the distribution of differences and does not assume all subjects come from the same population — the only requirement is matching within each pair on relevant extraneous variables. Null hypothesis: the median difference is zero, i.e. p(X a > X b ) = p(X a < X b ) = 0.5. We focus only on the direction (sign) of each pair's difference. Under H 0 , the number of "+" pairs should equal the number of "−" pairs; H 0 is rejected if too few of one sign occur. Ties: a pair showing no difference (d = 0) is dropped and N is reduced. Small samples: x = the difference in the number of each sign is found, and N and x give the probability p from the binomial distribution. Large samples (N > 25): use the normal approximation to the binomial. Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed-ranks test — two related samples (direction + magnitude) Like the sign test it uses the direction of differences, but it also uses their relative magnitude , making it a more powerful test. Procedure: For each matched pair, find the signed difference d i (each pair has one d i ). Rank all the d's without regard to sign ; assign tied d's the average of the ranks they would occupy. Affix to each rank the sign (+ or −) of the difference it represents. Compute T = the smaller of the sums of the like-signed ranks (the smaller of the sum of positive ranks and the sum of negative ranks). Determine N = the number of d's that have a sign (pairs with d = 0 are dropped). For N ≤ 25 , compare T with the critical value: reject H 0 if observed T is ≤ the table value. For N > 25 , T is practically normally distributed, so compute z and refer to the normal table (double p for a two-tailed test). The parametric counterpart is the paired-samples t-test. Mann–Whitney U test — two independent samples The non-parametric counterpart of the independent-samples t-test, for two independent groups on ordinal data. Procedure: Determine n 1 (cases in the smaller group) and n 2 (cases in the larger group). Rank together the scores of both groups, assigning rank 1 to the algebraically lowest score; ranks run 1 to N = n 1 + n 2 ; tied observations get the average of the tied ranks. Compute U by counting or by formula. Significance depends on n 2 : if n 2 ≤ 8, use the exact-probability table; if n 2 is 9–20, use the critical-value table; if n 2 > 20, compute z and use the normal table (double p for two-tailed). If the observed U's associated probability is ≤ α, reject H 0 . Kruskal–Wallis one-way ANOVA by ranks — k independent samples The non-parametric counterpart of the one-way (independent-groups) ANOVA, for independent samples . It uses the H statistic and does not require equal Ns. When the number of cases is not too small (more than 5 per group), H is distributed as χ² with k − 1 degrees of freedom , so the calculated H is checked against the chi-square table for significance. Friedman ANOVA by ranks — k related samples The non-parametric counterpart of the repeated-measures ANOVA, used for repeated measures (related samples); both one-way and two-way versions can be performed. It uses the χ² r statistic . When the number of rows/columns is not too small, χ² r is distributed as χ² with k − 1 degrees of freedom , and is checked against the chi-square table. Spearman's rank correlation (rho, ρ) — ordinal association The non-parametric counterpart of Pearson's r, used to measure the strength and direction of a monotonic relationship between two ordinal (ranked) variables. It is Pearson's correlation computed on the ranks. Formula: ρ = 1 − [6∑d² / (n(n² − 1))] , where d = the difference between the two ranks of each observation and n = the number of pairs. Spearman's ρ ranges from −1 to +1; tied ranks receive the average rank. (Kendall's tau, τ, is an alternative rank-correlation coefficient.) Trap Sign test vs Wilcoxon signed-ranks. Both handle two related samples, but the sign test uses only the direction of differences (less powerful), while Wilcoxon uses direction and magnitude (more powerful). Mann–Whitney U vs Wilcoxon signed-ranks: Mann–Whitney is for independent groups; Wilcoxon signed-ranks is for related pairs. (Confusingly, there is also a "Wilcoxon rank-sum" test that is equivalent to Mann–Whitney for independent samples.) Kruskal–Wallis vs Friedman: Kruskal–Wallis = k independent groups (H statistic); Friedman = k related measures (χ² r ). Both are distributed as χ² with k−1 df. High-yield Non-parametric ↔ parametric pairs: Mann–Whitney U ↔ independent t ; Wilcoxon signed-ranks ↔ paired t ; Kruskal–Wallis (H) ↔ one-way ANOVA ; Friedman (χ² r ) ↔ repeated-measures ANOVA ; Spearman's ρ ↔ Pearson's r ; chi-square for categorical frequencies. Kruskal–Wallis H and Friedman χ² r are both approximated by χ² with k−1 df. Chi-square independence df = (r−1)(c−1). 8. "Which test when" decision guide This is the most examinable table in the whole book. Pick the test from three features: the level of measurement , the number of groups/conditions , and whether the groups are independent or related . Research question Parametric test Non-parametric counterpart Key df One group vs a known norm One-sample t-test One-sample sign / Wilcoxon n − 1 Two independent groups Independent-samples t-test Mann–Whitney U n 1 + n 2 − 2 Two related measures (pre/post, matched) Paired-samples t-test Wilcoxon signed-ranks (or sign test) n − 1 Three+ independent groups, one IV One-way ANOVA (F) Kruskal–Wallis (H) k−1, k(n−1) Three+ related measures Repeated-measures ANOVA Friedman (χ² r ) k − 1 Two IVs, one DV (+ interaction) Two-way / factorial ANOVA — (r−1), (c−1), (r−1)(c−1) One+ IV, one DV, controlling a covariate ANCOVA — total kn − 2 One+ IV, multiple DVs together MANOVA (Wilks' Λ) — — Association between two interval variables Pearson's r Spearman's ρ / Kendall's τ n − 2 Association between two categorical variables — Chi-square (χ²) (r−1)(c−1) Mnemonic Read the question in three beats: "What scale? How many groups? Linked or not?" Interval + 2 groups + independent → independent t (or its rank cousin Mann–Whitney). Interval + 3+ groups → ANOVA (or Kruskal–Wallis). Add a covariate → ANCOVA; add DVs → MANOVA; add a second IV → factorial ANOVA with an interaction . High-yield The whole inferential toolkit is one logic applied at different scales: compare an observed statistic to its sampling distribution under H 0 , reject if it falls in the rejection region. t compares 1–2 means; F (ANOVA) compares 2+ means via variance ratio and avoids the Type I inflation of multiple t-tests; ANCOVA removes a covariate; MANOVA adds multiple DVs; the non-parametric family rank-orders the data when assumptions fail. Match measurement level, group number, and independence, and the right test names itself.

title: UGC NET Psychology — Past Papers & Syllabus
text: UGC NET Psychology — Past Papers & Syllabus A faithful reference pack for the UGC NET (subject code 04) Psychology paper: the complete official 10-unit syllabus reproduced as a clean outline, a plain-language guide to how the exam works distilled from the NTA FAQ, and three full past papers transcribed question-by-question. The December 2019 paper is reproduced with its official answer key; the June 2019 paper and the 2020 paper are reproduced verbatim from the source documents, and because no official answer key was supplied for them, every question there is marked "Answer: not in key" rather than guessed. Use this to learn the real shape, weight and wording of the exam. In this book The official syllabus (all 10 units) How the exam works December 2019 NET paper (with answer key) June 2019 NET paper 2020 NET paper 1. The official syllabus (all 10 units) This is the University Grants Commission (UGC) NET Bureau syllabus for Psychology, Code No. 04 , reproduced in full. The paper draws its questions from these ten units. Topics are listed exactly as in the official syllabus. High-yield Every NET Psychology question maps to one of these ten units. Knowing the unit a question belongs to is half the battle: it tells you which body of theory the examiner is testing. Units 1 (Emergence/systems), 2 (Methodology & Statistics) and 3 (Testing) are disproportionately heavy in the papers in this book. Unit 1. Emergence of Psychology Eastern systems: Psychological thought in major Eastern systems — Bhagavad Gita, Buddhism, Sufism and Integral Yoga. Academic psychology in India: Pre-independence era; post-independence era; 1970s (the move to addressing social issues); 1980s (Indigenization); 1990s (paradigmatic concerns, disciplinary identity crisis); 2000s (emergence of Indian psychology in academia). Issues: the colonial encounter; post-colonialism and psychology; lack of distinct disciplinary identity. Western: Greek heritage, medieval period and modern period. Structuralism, Functionalism, Psychoanalytical, Gestalt, Behaviorism, Humanistic-Existential, Transpersonal, Cognitive revolution, Multiculturalism. Four founding paths of academic psychology — Wundt, Freud, James, Dilthey. Issues: crisis in psychology due to strict adherence to the experimental-analytical paradigm (logical empiricism); Indic influences on modern psychology. Knowledge paradigms: Essential aspects — ontology, epistemology, and methodology. Paradigms of Western Psychology: Positivism, Post-Positivism, Critical perspective, Social Constructionism, Existential Phenomenology, and Co-operative Enquiry. Paradigmatic controversies. Significant Indian paradigms on psychological knowledge: Yoga, Bhagavad Gita, Buddhism, Sufism, and Integral Yoga. Science and spirituality (avidya and vidya). The primacy of self-knowledge in Indian psychology. Unit 2. Research Methodology and Statistics Research: Meaning, purpose, and dimensions. Research problems, variables and operational definitions, hypothesis, sampling. Ethics in conducting and reporting research. Paradigms of research: Quantitative, Qualitative, Mixed methods approach. Methods of research: Observation, Survey (interview, questionnaires), Experimental, Quasi-experimental, Field studies, Cross-cultural studies, Phenomenology, Grounded theory, Focus groups, Narratives, Case studies, Ethnography. Statistics: Measures of central tendency and dispersion. Normal probability curve. Parametric (t-test) and non-parametric tests (Sign test, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, Mann-Whitney test, Kruskal-Wallis test, Friedman). Power analysis. Effect size. Correlational analysis: Correlation (Product Moment, Rank Order), partial correlation, multiple correlation. Special correlation methods: Biserial, Point-biserial, tetrachoric, phi coefficient. Regression: simple linear regression, multiple regression. Factor analysis: assumptions, methods, rotation and interpretation. Experimental designs: ANOVA (one-way, factorial), Randomized Block Designs, Repeated Measures Design, Latin Square, Cohort studies, Time series, MANOVA, ANCOVA. Single-subject designs. Unit 3. Psychological Testing Types of tests. Test construction: Item writing, item analysis. Test standardization: Reliability, validity and norms. Areas of testing: Intelligence, creativity, neuropsychological tests, aptitude, personality assessment, interest inventories. Attitude scales — Semantic differential, Stapel, Likert scale. Computer-based psychological testing. Applications of psychological testing across settings: Clinical, Organizational and business, Education, Counseling, Military, Career guidance. Unit 4. Biological Basis of Behavior Sensory systems: general and specific sensations, receptors and processes. Neurons: structure, functions, types, neural impulse, synaptic transmission. Neurotransmitters. The Central and Peripheral Nervous Systems — structure and functions. Neuroplasticity. Methods of Physiological Psychology: Invasive methods (anatomical methods, degeneration techniques, lesion techniques, chemical methods, microelectrode studies); Non-invasive methods (EEG, scanning methods). Muscular and glandular system: types and functions. Biological basis of motivation: hunger, thirst, sleep and sex. Biological basis of emotion: the limbic system, hormonal regulation of behavior. Genetics and behavior: chromosomal anomalies; nature-nurture controversy (twin studies and adoption studies). Unit 5. Attention, Perception, Learning, Memory and Forgetting Attention: Forms of attention, models of attention. Perception: Approaches to the study of perception (Gestalt and physiological). Perceptual organization (Gestalt, figure and ground, laws of organization). Perceptual constancy (size, shape, colour); illusions. Perception of form, depth and movement. Role of motivation and learning in perception. Signal detection theory: assumptions and applications. Subliminal perception and related factors, information processing approach, culture and perception, perceptual styles, pattern recognition, ecological perspective on perception. Learning process: Fundamental theories (Thorndike, Guthrie, Hull). Classical conditioning: procedure, phenomena, related issues. Instrumental learning: phenomena, paradigms, theoretical issues. Reinforcement: basic variables and schedules; behaviour modification and its applications. Cognitive approaches in learning: latent learning, observational learning. Verbal learning and discrimination learning. Recent trends: neurophysiology of learning. Memory and forgetting: Memory processes (encoding, storage, retrieval). Stages of memory (sensory, short-term/working, long-term — declarative: episodic and semantic; procedural). Theories of forgetting (interference, retrieval failure, decay, motivated forgetting). Unit 6. Thinking, Intelligence and Creativity Theoretical perspectives on thought processes: Associationism, Gestalt, Information processing, Feature integration model. Concept formation: rules, types, strategies; role of concepts in thinking. Types of reasoning. Language and thought. Problem solving: types, strategies, obstacles. Decision-making: types and models. Metacognition: metacognitive knowledge and metacognitive regulation. Intelligence: Spearman; Thurstone; Jensen; Cattell; Gardner; Sternberg; Goleman; Das, Kar & Parrila. Creativity: Torrance, Getzels & Jackson, Guilford, Wallach & Kogan. Relationship between intelligence and creativity. Unit 7. Personality, Motivation, Emotion, Stress and Coping Determinants of personality: biological and socio-cultural. Approaches to personality: Psychoanalytical, Neo-Freudian, Social learning, Trait and Type, Cognitive, Humanistic, Existential, Transpersonal. Other theories: Rotter's Locus of Control, Seligman's explanatory styles, Kohlberg's theory of moral development. Basic motivational concepts: instincts, needs, drives, arousal, incentives, motivational cycle. Approaches to motivation: Psychoanalytical, Ethological, S-R, Cognitive, Humanistic. Exploratory behavior and curiosity. Zuckerman's sensation seeking. Achievement, affiliation and power. Motivational competence. Self-regulation. Flow. Emotions: physiological correlates. Theories of emotion: James-Lange, Cannon-Bard, Schachter and Singer, Lazarus, Lindsley. Emotion regulation. Conflicts: sources and types. Stress and coping: concept, models, Type A/B/C/D behaviors, stress-management strategies (Biofeedback, Music therapy, Breathing exercises, Progressive Muscular Relaxation, Guided Imagery, Mindfulness, Meditation, Yogasana, Stress Inoculation Training). Unit 8. Social Psychology Nature, scope and history of social psychology. Traditional theoretical perspectives: Field theory, Cognitive Dissonance, Sociobiology, Psychodynamic approaches, Social Cognition. Social perception (communication, attributions); attitude and its change within cultural context; prosocial behavior. Group and social influence (Social Facilitation; Social Loafing). Social influence (Conformity, Peer Pressure, Persuasion, Compliance, Obedience, Social Power, Reactance). Aggression. Group dynamics, leadership style and effectiveness. Theories of intergroup relations (Minimal Group Experiment and Social Identity Theory, Relative Deprivation Theory, Realistic Conflict Theory, Balance Theories, Equity Theory, Social Exchange Theory). Applied social psychology: Health, Environment and Law; personal space, crowding, and territoriality. Unit 9. Human Development and Interventions Developmental processes: nature, principles, factors, stages of development. Successful aging. Theories of development: Psychoanalytical, Behavioristic, Cognitive. Various aspects of development: sensory-motor, cognitive, language, emotional, social and moral. Psychopathology: concept, Mental Status Examination, classification, causes. Psychotherapies: Psychoanalysis, Person-centered, Gestalt, Existential, Acceptance Commitment Therapy, Behavior therapy, REBT, CBT, MBCT, Play therapy, Positive psychotherapy, Transactional Analysis, Dialectical Behavior Therapy, Art therapy, Performing Art Therapy, Family therapy. Applications of theories of motivation and learning in school. Factors in educational achievement. Teacher effectiveness. Guidance in schools: needs, organizational set-up and techniques. Counselling: process, skills, and techniques. Unit 10. Emerging Areas Issues of gender, poverty, disability, and migration: cultural bias and discrimination. Stigma, marginalization, and social suffering; child abuse and domestic violence. Peace psychology: violence, non-violence, conflict resolution at the macro level, role of media in conflict resolution. Wellbeing and self-growth: types of wellbeing (Hedonic and Eudemonic), character strengths, resilience and post-traumatic growth. Health: health-promoting and health-compromising behaviors, lifestyle and chronic diseases (Diabetes, Hypertension, Coronary Heart Disease), psychoneuroimmunology (Cancer, HIV/AIDS). Psychology and technology interface: digital learning; digital etiquette; cyber bullying; cyber pornography (consumption, implications); parental mediation of digital usage. 2. How the exam works UGC-NET (the National Eligibility Test) is conducted by the National Testing Agency (NTA) on behalf of the University Grants Commission. It determines eligibility for Assistant Professor only, or for Assistant Professor and Junior Research Fellowship (JRF) both, in colleges and universities. Below is the practical guidance distilled from the official NTA FAQ document. Format and mode Mode: Computer Based Test (CBT) only. Sittings: Two shifts on exam day — roughly 09:00–12:00 and 15:00–18:00. The date and slot are allotted randomly by computer (needed for the normalization process); a candidate cannot choose them. Two papers in one session: Paper 1 (general teaching/research aptitude, common to all subjects) and Paper 2 (the Psychology subject paper based on the 10-unit syllabus above). Both are attempted in the same sitting. Subjects: NET is conducted in roughly 80+ subjects; Psychology is subject code 04. High-yield There is NO negative marking in UGC-NET. The official FAQ states plainly: "No. There is no negative marking for wrong answers." So you should attempt every question — leaving a question blank can only cost you, never protect you. (This is the opposite of many other entrance tests, so do not carry a "skip if unsure" habit into NET.) Marking and result Negative marking: None. Every question carries positive marks only; wrong answers are not penalised. Qualifying criterion: Per UGC policy, the top 6% of candidates who appear in both papers and obtain the minimum qualifying marks (in aggregate of both papers) are declared NET-qualified. No all-India rank: The FAQ states "Rank is not assigned in UGC-NET." Results are pass/qualify based, with JRF allocated subject-wise and category-wise. Challenging the key: After the test, the question paper, recorded responses and the provisional answer key are released. Candidates may challenge an answer by paying a non-refundable fee (Rs 200 per question challenged) within the given window. The final result uses the answer key vetted by subject experts. No re-evaluation or re-checking is done after results. Eligibility and age Subject: Candidates should appear in the subject of their post-graduation. If their PG subject is not in the NET list, they may appear in a related subject. JRF age limit: Not more than 31 years (as on the first day of the month in which the exam concludes), with relaxations for reserved categories. There is no upper age limit for the Assistant Professor eligibility. Category concessions: Candidates in the non-creamy layer whose category is in the central OBC list, and SC/ST/PwD candidates, get fee and (where applicable) qualifying-mark concessions. Fees (as per the cited cycle) Category Fee General / Unreserved Rs. 1100 Gen-EWS / OBC-NCL Rs. 550 SC / ST / PwD / Third gender Rs. 275 Payment is online only (debit/credit card or net banking). Fees are non-refundable and applications cannot be withdrawn. Documents and most details can be edited later through the correction window. Mnemonic Remember the three numbers that define NET: 0 (zero negative marking), 6 (top 6% qualify), 2 (two papers in one session). Attempt everything, aim for the top slice, and budget time across both papers. Trap NET does not give you a "rank" or a "score out of 100" that ranks you nationally for admission the way a CET does. Qualifying is a percentile-style cut-off (top 6%). Do not confuse a NET qualification with an entrance-exam merit rank. 3. December 2019 NET paper (with answer key) This is the UGC NET Psychology December 2019 question paper, reproduced from the source document with its official answer key applied to every question. After each question the correct option is given in bold; a short explanation is added only where it is solidly established. Two questions in the official key were withdrawn (marked WQ) and are shown as "Answer: not in key (question withdrawn/dropped)." The source document's question body ran from Q1 to Q100 with one numbering gap in the original, so 99 distinct questions are reproduced here, each matched to the official key. Trap The bold "Answer: N" under each question is the official key value , not a guess. Where a question was officially withdrawn (WQ), no option is correct — do not try to pick one. In what sequence are the Social Combination rules followed for group success? (1) Additive, disjunctive, compensatory, conjunctive (2) Additive, compensatory, disjunctive, conjunctive (3) Disjunctive, compensatory, conjunctive, additive (4) Compensatory, conjunctive, disjunctive, additive Answer: 2 Which mnemonic device is used for the expression of different letters of a word? (1) Acoustics (2) Acronyms (3) Key word system (4) Clustering Answer: 3 Which of the following was described by R.B. Cattell using P-Technique of Factor Analysis? (1) Differential effects of stimulus situations on personality (2) Group formation (3) Social interactions (4) Individual differences among people Answer: 2 Which of the following would be the best method for studying the relative contribution of heredity and environment? (1) Comparing identical and fraternal twins reared together (2) Comparing identical and fraternal twins reared apart (3) Comparing siblings reared together and reared apart (4) Comparing identical and fraternal twins, half of whom have been reared apart Answer: 2 Which one of the following statements is true regarding the relationship of test length with reliability and validity? (1) As test length increases, only reliability improves. (2) As test length increases, only validity improves. (3) As test length increases, neither reliability nor validity improves. (4) As test length increases, both reliability and validity improve. Answer: 3 Match the given concepts in List I with the description given in List II. Read the following paragraph and answer questions 91 to 95. The experimental psychologist wanted to explore whether noise adversely affects reaction time (RT). She also wanted to explore whether the stress level would moderate the effect of noise. She varied noise at three levels: low (30 decibels), moderate (60 decibels) and high (90 decibels). She varied stress at two levels: low and high. From the initial pool of college students, subjects were randomly assigned to different groups. However, a few subjects could not turn up to the laboratory due to vacation. In all, two hundred and ninety-seven subjects participated in the experiment. Each subject, in each group, was tested for simple RT, disjunctive RT, and choice RT. The theory and preliminary analyses indicated the three types of RT were moderately correlated. The covariance matrices, showing the covariances among the three types of RT, were found to be quite similar for all the groups. The multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA) results were computed to explore the group differences in means. As the most common practice is, four test criteria (Pillai's criterion, Wilks' criterion, Hotelling's criterion, and Roy's criterion) were obtained. Among the different results obtained in this work, one interesting finding was that stress moderated the effect of noise level on reaction time. Q.91 Which of the following test criteria is more appropriate than the others? (1) Roy's criterion (2) Wilks' criterion (3) Hotelling's criterion (4) Pillai's criterion Answer: 2 The design employed in the above study can best be labelled as: (1) Randomized six group design with a single factor (2) Balanced factorial design (3) Unbalanced factorial design (4) Unbalanced factorial design with a covariate Answer: 2 — despite some dropouts noted, the key designates this a balanced factorial design (3 noise levels × 2 stress levels). Which one of the following conclusions can be confidently drawn from the above study? (1) Main effect of noise is significant (2) Main effect of stress is significant (3) Noise × Stress interaction is significant (4) The main effects of noise, stress and interaction effect are significant Answer: 3 — the stated finding is that stress moderated the effect of noise, i.e., a significant interaction. The above information suggests that: (1) the assumption of homogeneity of covariance matrices is not satisfied (2) the assumption of homogeneity of covariance matrices is satisfied (3) covariances among Dependent Variables (DV) are zero (4) the assumption of homogeneity of variances is not tenable Answer: 1 — the key designates option 1.
