(1) There are several groups and more than one Independent Variable (IV) (2) More than one Dependent Variable (DV) has been employed (3) More than one Dependent Variable with moderate intercorrelations has been employed (4) The moderating effect of stress on the effect of noise on RT can be demonstrated only through MANOVA Answer: 4 — the key designates option 4. Read the following paragraph and answer questions 96 to 100. A leading business school in the city had a view that its students must attain total proficiency in English language usage. As an initial step, the school authorities decided to develop a brief language usage test. The project incharge wrote 30 items. Each item had five alternative answers, one of which was correct. He administered these 30 items to a sample of 250 students. For item analysis, item-remainder correlations were computed. The item analysis retained 25 items. The twenty-five item version was administered to a fresh sample of 300 students. Three reliability coefficients were computed: split-half reliability coefficient, Kuder-Richardson (K-R) reliability coefficient, and Cronbach alpha. The Cronbach alpha was found to be 0.7. The test-retest reliability was also computed with a time-interval of eight weeks in two administrations, using the same sample. The test-retest correlation was found to be 0.26, significant at the .001 level. The school authorities, pleased with the efforts of the project incharge, asked him to add similar items and develop a 75-item version. Factors were retained on the basis of the scree plot and rotated using the varimax criterion. Three items showed cross-loadings, eighteen items loaded on only one factor, and the remaining items did not load on any factor. The Bartlett's test results in the above study suggested that: (1) The population correlation matrix is not an identity matrix (2) The population correlation matrix is an identity matrix (3) The sample correlation matrix is not an identity matrix (4) The sample correlation matrix is an identity matrix Answer: not in key. Candidate chose option 2. Which of the following is correct for the Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin test? (A) It is a test of sampling adequacy (B) Chi-square test is used to test the significance (C) Values smaller than 0.5 are desirable (D) Smaller partial correlation leads to high KMO (1) A only (2) A and B only (3) A and D only (4) B, C and D only Answer: not in key. Candidate chose option 3. Which of the following is correct in case of the three items having cross-loading? (1) They have excellent validity (2) They are conceptually sound items (3) The scale has poor reliability (4) They should not be retained in the final scale Answer: not in key. Candidate chose option 4. In the above example, what percentage of the variance would be explained by the first unrotated factor? (1) 9.9 (2) 39.6 (3) 65.6 (4) 72.0 Answer: not in key. Candidate chose option 4. Using the Kaiser-Guttman criterion, how many factors would be retained in the above study? (1) 4 (2) 8 (3) 2 (4) 3 Answer: not in key. Candidate chose option 3.

title: Statistics and Research Methods for Clinical Psychology Entrances
text: Statistics and Research Methods for Clinical Psychology Entrances Everything from scales of measurement (Stanley Smith Stevens, 1946) to MANCOVA, factor analysis and item response theory, then the whole of research methods (designs, validity, single-case, qualitative, trials, ethics), built from scratch, with a diagram on every idea that has a shape. This is a book, not a cheat sheet. Every concept is built from the ground up: what the thing is, why it exists, the formula with every symbol named, a worked example with real numbers, the assumptions it stands on, what breaks it, and who invented it. Read it cold and you will understand statistics and research design, not just recognise the words. Part I (sections 1 to 17) is statistics; Part II (sections 18 to 27) is research methods. The 64 diagrams are drawn from the actual functions or from real numbers, so the normal curve really is a normal curve, the F distribution really is an F distribution, and every single-case graph, time series and forest plot is computed. 27 sections 64 diagrams 60+ named statisticians 100+ research-methods names Every test with its assumptions Built for IHBAS · CIP · RML · JSS · DIMHANS · Amity · SGT · NIMHANS 1 · Variables and scales of measurement 2 · Frequency distributions and graphs 3 · Central tendency 4 · Dispersion 5 · Skewness and kurtosis 6 · The normal curve and standard scores 7 · Probability, sampling and the sampling distribution 8 · Hypothesis testing, errors, power, effect size 9 · The t tests 10 · ANOVA 11 · ANCOVA, MANOVA, MANCOVA 12 · Correlation 13 · Regression 14 · Non-parametric tests 15 · Psychometrics 16 · Which test to use 17 · Formula sheet and who-did-what index Part II: Research methods 18 · The research process: science, problems, hypotheses and variables 19 · Validity of a study and the control of extraneous variables 20 · Experimental and quasi-experimental designs 21 · Non-experimental designs: correlational, developmental and epidemiological 22 · Single-subject (small-N) designs 23 · Collecting the data: observation, interviews, questionnaires and scaling 24 · Qualitative and mixed-methods research 25 · Clinical trials, evidence and meta-analysis 26 · Research ethics 27 · Which design to use, the research-methods name index, and the traps How to use this book. First pass: read sections 1 to 8 straight through, because everything later is built on them. Second pass: sections 9 to 14 are the test family; do not memorise formulas, memorise the question each test answers and the assumptions it needs , because that is what entrance papers ask. Third pass: section 15 (psychometrics) is worth as many marks as ANOVA in most of these papers and is usually the least prepared. Section 16 is the decision tree; if you can walk it without looking, you can answer any "which test would you apply" item. Section 17 is the night-before page. Part II (sections 18 to 27) is research methods: read 18 to 20 in order, because validity and the threats in 19 are the language every design in 20 to 22 is judged in; 23 to 26 can be read in any order; 27 is the which-design tree, the name index and the traps. 1 Variables and scales of measurement Statistics is a set of tools for one job: getting from what you observed in a handful of people to a defensible statement about people in general. Everything in this book is either describing what you have (descriptive statistics) or generalising beyond what you have (inferential statistics). Keep that split in your head; it is the first line of a hundred exam answers. 1.1 The vocabulary you cannot skip Term Meaning Symbol Population The entire set of people or observations you actually want to talk about. Usually hypothetical and never fully measured. N Sample The subset you actually measured. Statistics exists because samples are all you ever get. n Parameter A number describing the population . Fixed, unknown, written with Greek letters. μ, σ, ρ, π Statistic A number describing the sample . Known, varies from sample to sample, written with Roman letters. M or X̄, s, r, p Variable Any characteristic that takes more than one value. X, Y Constant A characteristic that takes only one value in your study. – Datum / data A single recorded observation / the set of them. Xᵢ The rule that generates half the notation questions: Greek letters are for populations, Roman letters are for samples. μ is the population mean, M (or X̄) is the sample mean. σ is the population SD, s is the sample SD. ρ (rho) is the population correlation, r is the sample correlation. β is the population regression weight, b is the sample one. Types of variable Independent variable (IV): the one the experimenter manipulates or selects. The presumed cause. Also called the predictor (in regression) or the factor (in ANOVA). Its values are called levels . Dependent variable (DV): the one you measure. The presumed effect. Also called the criterion or the outcome. Extraneous variable: anything else that could affect the DV. Controlled by randomisation, matching, holding constant, or statistically (ANCOVA). Confounding variable: an extraneous variable that actually varies systematically with the IV , so its effect is inseparable from the IV's. A confound is an extraneous variable that got away. Mediator: the variable through which the IV acts (X → M → Y). Explains how or why . Tested by Baron and Kenny's (1986) steps or by Sobel / bootstrapped indirect effects. Moderator: a variable that changes the strength or direction of the X–Y relation. Explains when or for whom . Statistically, a moderator is an interaction . Discrete variable: takes only separate whole values (number of children, number of hospital admissions). Continuous variable: can take any value in a range; between any two values another is possible (reaction time, IQ). Measured to a limit of precision, with real limits of ±half the smallest unit: a reported weight of 62 kg means 61.5 to 62.5. Trap: mediator and moderator are the single most confused pair in research-methods sections. Mediator = the mechanism, sits between IV and DV in the causal chain. Moderator = the condition, sits outside and changes the size of the effect. "Stress causes depression through rumination" is mediation. "Stress causes depression more strongly in people with low social support" is moderation. 1.2 The four scales of measurement (S. S. Stevens, 1946) Stanley Smith Stevens , Harvard psychophysicist, published "On the theory of scales of measurement" in Science in 1946. The four-scale taxonomy is his, and it is the single most examined single fact in the statistics section of every one of these papers. Learn it perfectly. Scale What it does Properties Examples Permissible central tendency Permissible statistics Nominal (categorical) Names / labels only. Numbers are arbitrary tags. Identity / difference only. No order, no equal intervals, no true zero. Gender, diagnosis, blood group, jersey numbers, marital status, religion Mode only Frequencies, percentages, mode, χ², phi, contingency coefficient, Cramér's V Ordinal (ranks) Orders cases, but the gaps between ranks are unequal and unknown. Identity + order. No equal intervals, no true zero. Socio-economic status, ranks in a class, Likert-type agreement, Mohs hardness, stage of illness, birth order Mode and median Median, percentiles, quartile deviation, Spearman ρ, Kendall τ, Mann–Whitney U, Kruskal–Wallis Interval Equal units, but the zero point is arbitrary. Identity + order + equal intervals. No absolute zero. Temperature in °C or °F, calendar years, IQ scores, most psychological test scores, z scores Mode, median and mean Mean, SD, Pearson r, t test, ANOVA, regression, factor analysis Ratio Equal units and a true zero meaning "none of it". All four properties. Ratios are meaningful. Height, weight, reaction time, number of errors, income, age, kelvin temperature Mode, median, mean, geometric and harmonic mean Everything, plus coefficient of variation and ratio statements Mnemonic: NOIR (French for black), in order of increasing information: N ominal, O rdinal, I nterval, R atio. Each scale keeps all the properties of the ones before it and adds one. Any statistic legal at a lower scale stays legal at a higher one; the reverse is never true. The two traps that are asked every year. (1) Temperature in Celsius is interval, not ratio , because 0°C is the freezing point of water, not the absence of heat; 40°C is not "twice as hot" as 20°C. Temperature in kelvin is ratio. (2) IQ is interval, not ratio. There is no IQ of zero meaning "no intelligence", so a person with IQ 140 is not twice as intelligent as one with 70. Strictly, IQ is arguably only ordinal, but for exam purposes it is treated as interval. Why the scale decides everything downstream. The scale of your DV is the first branch of the which-test decision tree. Nominal DV means frequencies means chi-square. Ordinal DV means ranks means the non-parametric family. Interval or ratio DV means the mean and the SD are meaningful, which means the parametric family (t, ANOVA, Pearson, regression) becomes available. If you can name the scale you have already narrowed the answer to about four tests. Two more scales worth knowing Absolute scale: a counting scale where the unit is one and cannot be changed (number of children). Some texts treat it as a fifth, strongest scale. Interval-like ordinal (quasi-interval): Likert items are ordinal per item, but a summed Likert scale of many items is conventionally treated as interval. Say this explicitly if asked; examiners like the nuance. 2 Frequency distributions and graphs Raw data is unreadable. The first act of every analysis is to impose order on it, and the tool for that is the frequency distribution. 2.1 Building a grouped frequency distribution Find the range: R = highest score − lowest score (some texts add 1 for the "inclusive range"). Choose the number of class intervals: conventionally 10 to 20. Too few hides the shape, too many defeats the purpose. Find the class interval width (i): i = R / (number of intervals), rounded to a convenient number (2, 3, 5, 10). Set the intervals so they are mutually exclusive and exhaustive, and start the lowest interval at a multiple of i. Tally and count. Term Definition Example (interval 50–59) Apparent (written) limits The limits as printed. 50 and 59 Exact / real limits The true boundaries, extending half a unit each way. Used in all computation. 49.5 and 59.5 Class interval (i) Upper real limit − lower real limit. 59.5 − 49.5 = 10 Midpoint (lower limit + upper limit) / 2. Assumed to represent every score in the interval. 54.5 Cumulative frequency (cf) Running total of frequencies up to the top of that interval. – Relative frequency f / N, usually expressed as a proportion or percentage. – 2.2 The graphs Histogram bars touch: the variable is continuous Frequency polygon midpoints joined, anchored to the baseline 50% → median Ogive (cumulative frequency) always S-shaped; read percentiles off it Same grouped frequency distribution, three standard graphs. A bar diagram differs from a histogram in one way: its bars have gaps, because the variable is categorical. The three graphs of a frequency distribution. Graph Built from Used for Distinguishing feature Bar diagram Categories on X, frequency on Y Nominal or ordinal data Bars have gaps between them, because the categories are discrete Histogram Class intervals on X, frequency on Y Continuous, grouped data Bars touch , because the variable is continuous. Area is proportional to frequency Frequency polygon Midpoints joined by straight lines Comparing two or more distributions on one axis Anchored to the baseline at both ends; area under it equals the histogram's area Frequency curve A smoothed frequency polygon Showing the underlying shape Smooth, no corners; the theoretical limit as N → ∞ and i → 0 Ogive (cumulative frequency curve) Cumulative frequency plotted at the upper real limit Reading percentiles and the median straight off the graph Always S-shaped and never decreasing. The score at 50% cumulative frequency is the median Pie chart Proportions as sectors of a circle Parts of a single whole, nominal data Each 1% = 3.6° Stem-and-leaf plot (Tukey) Leading digits as stems, trailing as leaves Small datasets Shows the shape and preserves every original value Box plot (Tukey) Five-number summary Comparing groups, spotting outliers and skew Built entirely from ranks, so extreme scores cannot distort it Scatterplot / scattergram Paired X and Y values as points Correlation and regression The only honest way to see a relationship before computing r Lower whisker Q1 − 1.5×IQR Q1 (25th %ile) Median (Q2) Q3 (75th %ile) Upper whisker Q3 + 1.5×IQR Outliers Interquartile range, IQR = Q3 − Q1 (semi-interquartile range or quartile deviation Q = IQR/2) Tukey's box-and-whisker plot. Everything in it is a rank statistic, so it is unaffected by extreme scores , that is why it is paired with the median, not the mean. Box plot (John Tukey, 1977): the five-number summary drawn. Reading a box plot for skew: if the median line sits nearer the bottom of the box and the upper whisker is longer, the distribution is positively skewed. Nearer the top with a longer lower whisker means negative skew. A centred median with equal whiskers means symmetry. 3 Central tendency A measure of central tendency is a single value that best represents the whole distribution: the point around which the scores cluster. There are three you must know cold, and two more worth naming. 3.1 The mean (arithmetic average) Definition: the sum of all scores divided by the number of scores. The balance point of the distribution. Formulas. Ungrouped sample mean: M = ΣX / n . Population mean: μ = ΣX / N . Grouped data: M = ΣfXᵐ / N , where Xᵐ is the midpoint of each interval and f its frequency. Assumed-mean (short) method: M = A + (Σfd / N) × i , where A is any assumed mean, d = (Xᵐ − A)/i, and i is the class interval. Worked example Scores: 4, 7, 7, 9, 13. ΣX = 40, n = 5, so M = 40 / 5 = 8 . The six mathematical properties of the mean (each one is an exam item) The sum of deviations about the mean is exactly zero: Σ(X − M) = 0. This is what "balance point" means, and it is why you must square deviations to get a usable measure of spread. The sum of squared deviations about the mean is a minimum: Σ(X − M)² is smaller than Σ(X − any other value)². This is the least squares property , and it is the reason regression, ANOVA and the variance are all built on the mean. Adding a constant c to every score adds c to the mean. Multiplying every score by c multiplies the mean by c. The mean is affected by every single score , so one extreme score moves it. It is not resistant. The mean of a combined group is the weighted mean: Mᵗ = (n₁M₁ + n₂M₂) / (n₁ + n₂). The mean is the most reliable measure across repeated samples , that is, it has the smallest standard error, which is why inferential statistics is built on it. Trap: the mean cannot be computed from an open-ended distribution ("60 and above"), because the top interval has no midpoint. In that situation you must use the median. 3.2 The median Definition: the value that divides the ordered distribution into two equal halves. The 50th percentile, the 2nd quartile, the 5th decile. Formulas. Ungrouped, n odd: the ((n+1)/2)th score. Ungrouped, n even: the mean of the (n/2)th and (n/2 + 1)th scores. Grouped: Md = L + [(N/2 − cf) / f] × i , where L is the exact lower limit of the median class, cf the cumulative frequency below it, f the frequency of the median class and i the interval width. Worked example Scores 4, 7, 7, 9, 13 (n = 5, odd): the (5+1)/2 = 3rd score, so Md = 7 . Add a sixth score of 40: ordered 4, 7, 7, 9, 13, 40; median = (7 + 9)/2 = 8 , while the mean jumps from 8 to 13.3. That single comparison is the whole argument for the median. Properties The sum of absolute deviations from the median is a minimum: Σ|X − Md| is smaller than about any other point. (The mean minimises squared deviations; the median minimises absolute ones.) It is a positional average, so it is unaffected by extreme scores : it is robust or resistant. It can be computed for open-ended distributions and for ordinal data. It cannot be manipulated algebraically the way the mean can, so it is not used in inferential statistics. 3.3 The mode Definition: the most frequently occurring score. The point of maximum density. Grouped formula (crude vs. exact). Crude mode = midpoint of the interval with the highest frequency. Exact (King's) formula: Mo = L + [(f₁ − f₀) / (2f₁ − f₀ − f₂)] × i . Empirical relation for a moderately skewed distribution (Karl Pearson): Mo = 3Md − 2M , equivalently M − Mo = 3(M − Md) . A distribution can have no mode, one mode ( unimodal ), two ( bimodal ), or many ( multimodal ). A bimodal distribution usually means two different populations have been pooled, and that is a substantive finding, not a nuisance. It is the only measure of central tendency usable with nominal data. It is the least stable across samples and the least used inferentially. A rectangular or uniform distribution has no mode at all. 3.4 Choosing between them Use the... When Because Mean Data are interval or ratio, distribution roughly symmetrical, and you intend to do further statistics on it Most reliable, uses all the data, algebraically tractable, required by t, ANOVA and regression Median Distribution is skewed, there are outliers, the distribution is open-ended, or the data are ordinal Resistant to extreme scores; still meaningful when the mean is misleading Mode Data are nominal, or you specifically want the most typical or most common case The only legal option at nominal level; identifies the actual peak Classic applied example: income. Income distributions are strongly positively skewed, so the mean income of a country is dragged up by a few very rich people, and the median income is the honest description of the typical person. Same logic for hospital length of stay, reaction times, and number of therapy sessions attended. Two extra means worth naming Geometric mean: the nth root of the product of n scores. Used for rates of change, growth rates and ratio data. GM ≤ AM always. Harmonic mean: n divided by the sum of the reciprocals. Used for averaging rates and, in statistics, for computing the effective sample size in unequal-n ANOVA and post hoc tests. HM ≤ GM ≤ AM always. 4 Dispersion Two distributions can have the same mean and be completely different. Central tendency without dispersion is half a description. Measures of dispersion (variability, scatter, spread) tell you how far the scores stray from the centre. 4.1 Range R = highest score − lowest score. Simplest, crudest, and completely determined by the two most extreme scores, which are also the two least reliable ones. Unstable across samples. Useful only as a quick indication. 4.2 Quartile deviation (semi-interquartile range) Q = (Q₃ − Q₁) / 2 , where Q₁ is the 25th percentile and Q₃ the 75th. The interquartile range (IQR) is Q₃ − Q₁; the quartile deviation is half of it. It covers the middle 50% of scores, so it is unaffected by extreme values. It is the partner of the median : report Md and Q together, always. 4.3 Average deviation (mean deviation) AD = Σ|X − M| / N. The average distance of scores from the mean, ignoring sign. Uses all scores, which is a step up from the range, but the absolute-value operator makes it algebraically useless, so it disappeared from inferential statistics. It is minimised when taken about the median , not the mean. 4.4 Variance and standard deviation Definition: the standard deviation is the root-mean-square deviation from the mean. It is, quite literally, the typical distance a score sits from the mean, in the original units. The variance is its square. Formulas. Population variance: σ² = Σ(X − μ)² / N · population SD: σ = √[Σ(X − μ)² / N] Sample variance (unbiased estimate): s² = Σ(X − M)² / (n − 1) · sample SD: s = √[Σ(X − M)² / (n − 1)] Computational (raw-score) form: s² = [ΣX² − (ΣX)²/n] / (n − 1) The numerator Σ(X − M)² has its own name: the sum of squares (SS) . Remember that, because the whole of ANOVA is bookkeeping about sums of squares. Worked example Scores 4, 7, 7, 9, 13; M = 8. Deviations: −4, −1, −1, +1, +5. (They sum to 0, as they must.) Squared: 16, 1, 1, 1, 25. SS = 44. s² = 44 / (5 − 1) = 11.0 · s = √11 = 3.32 . If these five were the whole population: σ² = 44/5 = 8.8, σ = 2.97. Note that dividing by n gives a smaller , biased-downward answer. 4.5 Degrees of freedom: why n − 1 The idea. Degrees of freedom is the number of values in a calculation that are free to vary once the constraints are imposed. To compute the sample variance you must first compute M from the same data. That fixes one thing: the deviations must sum to zero. So if n = 5 and you know four of the deviations, the fifth is forced. Only 4 of the 5 are free. Hence df = n − 1. The consequence. Dividing SS by n gives a variance estimate that is systematically too small, because the sample mean is always closer to the sample's own scores than the population mean is. Dividing by n − 1 corrects the downward bias, and is called Bessel's correction . It makes s² an unbiased estimator of σ². Degrees of freedom for every test you will meet One-sample t: df = n − 1 · Independent t: df = n₁ + n₂ − 2 · Paired t: df = n(pairs) − 1 One-way ANOVA: df between = k − 1, df within = N − k, df total = N − 1 Two-way ANOVA: df A = a − 1, df B = b − 1, df A×B = (a−1)(b−1), df within = N − ab Repeated measures: df treatment = k − 1, df subjects = n − 1, df error = (k−1)(n−1) Pearson r significance: df = n − 2 · Simple regression: df = n − 2 · Multiple regression: df = n − k − 1 χ² goodness of fit: df = k − 1 · χ² independence: df = (r − 1)(c − 1) A general principle: df = number of observations − number of parameters you had to estimate from the data. 4.6 Coefficient of variation CV = (s / M) × 100. A relative, unit-free measure of dispersion, so it lets you compare the variability of two things measured in different units (heights in cm vs. weights in kg), or two groups with very different means. It requires a ratio scale with a meaningful zero, so it must not be used on IQ or on Celsius temperature. 4.7 Properties of the standard deviation Adding a constant to every score leaves the SD unchanged (the whole distribution shifts, the spread does not). Multiplying every score by c multiplies the SD by |c| and the variance by c². The SD is in the same units as the original scores; the variance is in squared units. That is why you report SD and analyse variance. Variances add; standard deviations do not. This is the reason ANOVA partitions variance . The SD is the most reliable measure of dispersion across repeated samples, and it is the one used in every inferential formula. It is affected by every score, including extreme ones. On badly skewed data, report the quartile deviation with the median instead. Recap of sections 1 to 4: Stevens's four scales (nominal, ordinal, interval, ratio) determine which statistics are legal. A frequency distribution and its graphs (histogram, polygon, ogive, box plot) show you the shape. Central tendency locates it: the mean is the balance point and minimises squared deviations, the median is the 50th percentile and resists outliers, the mode is the peak and the only option at nominal level. Dispersion measures how wide it is: range, quartile deviation (partner of the median), average deviation, and the standard deviation (partner of the mean), whose squared numerator SS and denominator n − 1 are the foundation of everything that follows. 5 Skewness and kurtosis Central tendency gives the location, dispersion gives the width. The third and fourth properties of a distribution are its shape : how lopsided it is (skewness) and how peaked it is (kurtosis). Formally these are the third and fourth moments about the mean; the first moment is zero by definition and the second is the variance. 5.1 Skewness Mo Md M Negative skew Mean < Median < Mode long tail to the LEFT Sk < 0 Mo = Md = M Normal (symmetrical) Mean = Median = Mode no tail Sk = 0 Mo Md M Positive skew Mode < Median < Mean long tail to the RIGHT Sk > 0 Skewness. Mo = mode, Md = median, M = mean. The name of the skew follows the tail, not the hump. The mean is dragged furthest because it is the only one of the three that uses every score's value. Definition: the degree of asymmetry of a distribution. A distribution is skewed when one tail is longer than the other. Positive (right) skew Symmetrical Negative (left) skew Tail Long tail to the right, towards high scores Both tails equal Long tail to the left, towards low scores Order Mode < Median < Mean Mode = Median = Mean Mean < Median < Mode Sk > 0 = 0 < 0 Bulk of scores Low; a few very high scores stretch it out Centred High; a few very low scores stretch it out Test example A very difficult test: most people score low A well-constructed test of average difficulty A very easy test: most people score high (a ceiling effect) Real examples Income, reaction time, number of psychiatric admissions, symptom counts in a normal population Height, IQ in the general population Age at death, scores on a mastery test, life satisfaction in a healthy sample The rule that unlocks every skew item: the skew is named for the tail , not the hump, and the mean is always dragged furthest into the tail , because the mean is the only one of the three that uses each score's actual value. So the mean is always on the tail side of the median, and the mode is always at the hump. Get the mean's position and the whole ordering falls out. Formulas. Pearson's first coefficient of skewness: Sk = (M − Mo) / s Pearson's second coefficient (used when the mode is unstable): Sk = 3(M − Md) / s Bowley's quartile coefficient: Sk = (Q₃ + Q₁ − 2Md) / (Q₃ − Q₁) , bounded between −1 and +1 Moment coefficient: g₁ = m₃ / s³ , where m₃ is the third moment about the mean = Σ(X − M)³/N Interpretation rule of thumb: |Sk| under 0.5 is approximately symmetrical, 0.5 to 1.0 is moderately skewed, over 1.0 is substantially skewed. Another common working rule: skew is a problem if it exceeds twice its own standard error. What causes skew, and what to do about it Floor effect: the measure cannot go below a limit and most people are at it. Produces positive skew. Common with symptom counts and error counts in healthy samples. Ceiling effect: the measure cannot go above a limit and most people are at it. Produces negative skew. Common with easy tests. Selection: studying only the extreme end of a population. Transformations to fix positive skew: square root (mild), logarithm (moderate), reciprocal (severe). For negative skew, reflect the variable first (subtract each score from the maximum + 1), then apply the same transformation. Or switch to a non-parametric test , which does not care about the shape. 5.2 Kurtosis Leptokurtic (Ku > 3, excess > 0) Mesokurtic (normal, Ku = 3, excess = 0) Platykurtic (Ku < 3, excess < 0) All three have the same mean and the same total area. They differ in peakedness and tail weight. Excess kurtosis = Ku − 3. Leptokurtic = tall and thin with fat tails; platykurtic = flat and broad. Kurtosis: the peakedness of the distribution. Definition: the degree of peakedness of a distribution relative to the normal curve, and equivalently the heaviness of its tails. Type Shape Ku (moment) Excess kurtosis (Ku − 3) Tails Leptokurtic Tall, thin, sharply peaked ("lepto" = slender, think a leaping narrow peak) > 3 Positive Fat: more extreme scores than a normal curve Mesokurtic The normal curve itself ("meso" = middle) = 3 0 Normal Platykurtic Flat, broad, blunt ("platy" = flat, think a plateau or a platypus) < 3 Negative Thin: fewer extreme scores; in the limit, a rectangular distribution Formula. Moment coefficient of kurtosis g₂ = m₄ / s⁴ , where m₄ = Σ(X − M)⁴/N. Percentile-based: Ku = Q / (P₉₀ − P₁₀) , which equals 0.263 for a normal curve. Most software reports excess kurtosis, so a printed value of 0 means normal, not flat. Trap: SPSS and most statistical software report excess kurtosis (already minus 3). So a reported kurtosis of 0.00 means mesokurtic (normal), while a reported 3.00 means strongly leptokurtic. Exam questions almost always use the raw moment version where normal = 3. Read the question for which convention it wants. Testing normality formally Test Who Use Read it as Shapiro–Wilk Samuel Shapiro and Martin Wilk, 1965 The most powerful normality test for small to moderate n (under about 50, usable to 2000) Non-significant (p > .05) = normal. You want it to fail Kolmogorov–Smirnov Andrey Kolmogorov and Nikolai Smirnov Compares the sample cumulative distribution to the normal one; better for larger n (with the Lilliefors correction) Non-significant = normal Skewness / kurtosis z tests – Divide the coefficient by its standard error |z| > 1.96 means significant departure at .05 Q–Q plot / P–P plot – Visual check Points on the straight diagonal = normal The large-n paradox. Shapiro–Wilk and K–S become so powerful with large n that they flag trivial, harmless departures from normality as significant. With n over about 300, trust the histogram, the Q–Q plot and the skew and kurtosis values instead of the p value, and remember that the central limit theorem has already protected you. 6 The normal curve and standard scores The normal curve was derived by Abraham de Moivre in 1733 as the limit of the binomial, developed by Pierre-Simon Laplace , and applied to measurement error by Carl Friedrich Gauss (hence "Gaussian"). The percentages are fixed properties of the curve, which is why one z score converts into every other standard score. 6.1 Properties of the normal probability curve Bell-shaped and perfectly symmetrical about the mean. Skewness = 0. Mean = median = mode , all at the centre. Asymptotic: the tails approach the X axis but never touch it, so the curve extends from −∞ to +∞. Any score has a non-zero probability. Unimodal , with a single maximum ordinate at the mean. The maximum ordinate is 0.3989 (that is, 1/√2π) when expressed in z units. Mesokurtic: kurtosis = 3, excess kurtosis = 0. Total area under the curve = 1.00 (or 100%), which is why areas can be read as probabilities. Points of inflection (where the curve changes from concave-down to concave-up) lie exactly at ±1σ. It is completely defined by two parameters: μ and σ . Change μ and the curve slides; change σ and it widens or narrows. The standard normal curve is the special case with μ = 0 and σ = 1. The quartile deviation Q = 0.6745σ, and the average deviation AD = 0.7979σ. 6.2 The area percentages (memorise these exactly) Band Area inside Area in each tail μ ± 1σ 68.26% (34.13% each side) 15.87% μ ± 2σ 95.44% (adds 13.59% each side) 2.28% μ ± 3σ 99.74% (adds 2.14% each side) 0.13% μ ± 1.96 σ 95.00% exactly 2.5% (this is where α = .05 two-tailed comes from) μ ± 2.58 σ 99.00% exactly 0.5% (this is where α = .01 two-tailed comes from) μ ± 1.645 σ 90.00% 5% (the one-tailed .05 critical value) The three numbers that carry the most marks: 68 – 95 – 99.7 for 1, 2 and 3 SD, and 1.96 and 2.58 as the exact 95% and 99% cut-offs. Every confidence interval and every z test in the paper comes out of these. 6.3 z scores Definition: a z score expresses a raw score as the number of standard deviations it lies above or below the mean. z = (X − M) / s (sample) · z = (X − μ) / σ (population) · to go back: X = M + z·s Worked example A student scores 85 on a test with M = 70 and s = 10. z = (85 − 70)/10 = +1.5 . From the table, the area below z = 1.5 is .9332, so the student is at the 93rd percentile and beat 93% of the group. A second student scores 60: z = −1.0, area below = .1587, so the 16th percentile . Properties of a z distribution The mean of a set of z scores is always 0 and the SD always 1 . Converting to z is a linear transformation. Standardising does not change the shape of the distribution. A skewed distribution converted to z scores is still exactly as skewed. This is the most frequently missed point about z scores. z scores make scores from different tests comparable, which is the whole reason they exist. Roughly 99.7% of z scores fall between −3 and +3. Trap: "z transformation normalises a distribution." False. It standardises it (fixes M = 0, s = 1) but leaves the shape untouched. To actually change the shape into a normal one you need a normalised standard score , which is computed from percentile ranks via the area table, not from the linear z formula. Normalised T scores and stanines are of this second kind. 6.4 The derived standard scores Score Mean SD Formula from z Where you meet it z 0 1 – The base currency of all standard scores T score (McCall) 50 10 T = 50 + 10z MMPI, MCMI, most clinical inventories. Any standard score converts to any other by going through z. Example: a T score of 70 means z = (70 − 50)/10 = +2.0, so the Wechsler IQ equivalent is 100 + 15(2) = 130 , the percentile is 97.7 , and the stanine is 5 + 2(2) = 9 . That single chain answers a whole family of exam items. Percentile rank is not a standard score Percentiles are ordinal, not interval. A percentile rank says what proportion of the group scored below you. Because scores pile up in the middle of a normal distribution, percentiles are squeezed together at the centre and stretched at the extremes : the difference between the 50th and 55th percentile is a tiny difference in raw score, while the difference between the 94th and 99th is large. So you must not average percentiles or do arithmetic on them. Convert to z first. This is one of the most reliably examined points in the psychometrics section. 7 Probability, sampling and the sampling distribution 7.1 Probability basics Probability p(A) = number of favourable outcomes / total number of equally likely outcomes. Ranges from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). Addition rule (for "or"): mutually exclusive events, p(A or B) = p(A) + p(B). Non-exclusive, p(A or B) = p(A) + p(B) − p(A and B). Multiplication rule (for "and"): independent events, p(A and B) = p(A) × p(B). Dependent, p(A and B) = p(A) × p(B|A). Conditional probability p(A|B): the probability of A given that B has occurred. The basis of Bayes's theorem , and of sensitivity, specificity and predictive value in diagnostic testing. Binomial distribution: the probability distribution of the number of successes in n independent trials each with probability p. Mean = np, variance = npq. As n grows it approaches the normal curve, which is exactly de Moivre's 1733 result. 7.2 Sampling Simple random every case an equal chance Stratified random sample within each stratum Cluster whole intact groups sampled Systematic every kth case from a list Filled = sampled. All four are PROBABILITY methods, so sampling error is calculable. Purposive, quota, snowball, convenience and incidental sampling are NON-probability: cheaper, but no sampling error can be estimated and generalisation is unsafe. The four probability sampling designs. Method How Strength Weakness PROBABILITY sampling: every unit has a known, non-zero chance of selection, so sampling error is calculable and generalisation is defensible Simple random Lottery or random-number table; every case has an equal chance Unbiased, the theoretical ideal, the assumption behind every inferential formula Needs a complete sampling frame; may miss small subgroups by chance Stratified random Divide the population into strata (gender, diagnosis, SES), then sample randomly within each. Proportionate or disproportionate More precise than simple random , guarantees representation of every stratum, reduces sampling error You must know the strata in advance Cluster Divide into naturally occurring groups (schools, wards, villages), randomly select whole clusters, study everyone inside Cheap and practical when the population is geographically spread; no full frame needed Largest sampling error of the probability methods, because people within a cluster are alike Systematic Choose a random start, then take every kth case (k = N/n) Simple, spreads the sample evenly through the list Fails badly if the list has a periodicity matching k Multi-stage Cluster sampling applied repeatedly (state → district → school → class) The only feasible design for national surveys Error accumulates at each stage NON-PROBABILITY sampling: selection chance unknown, so sampling error cannot be estimated and inferential statistics are strictly not justified Purposive / judgemental The researcher picks cases judged typical or informative Efficient for expert or rare populations Wide open to researcher bias Quota Fill preset quotas per subgroup, but choose within them non-randomly Gets the demographic profile right cheaply; the non-probability cousin of stratified Selection within quota is biased Snowball / chain referral Participants recruit further participants The standard method for hidden populations: substance users, sex workers, undocumented migrants Heavily networked people are over-represented Convenience / accidental / incidental Whoever is available (the classic undergraduate subject pool) Cheapest and fastest Weakest external validity of all Definitions to be exact about: sampling error is the natural, unavoidable discrepancy between a sample statistic and its population parameter, caused by chance alone; it shrinks as n grows. Sampling bias is a systematic tilt caused by a faulty method; it does not shrink with n, and a bigger biased sample is simply a bigger wrong answer. 7.3 The sampling distribution of the mean This is the pivot of the whole book. Everything inferential rests on one imaginary object. The idea. Take a sample of size n and compute its mean. Put it back, take another sample of size n, compute its mean. Do this endlessly. You now have a distribution, not of raw scores, but of sample means . That is the sampling distribution of the mean . It is theoretical; you never actually build it. But you know its three properties exactly, and that is enough to say how surprising your one real sample is. Its mean equals the population mean: μ M = μ. The sample mean is an unbiased estimator. Its standard deviation is the standard error of the mean: SE M = σ / √n , estimated in practice by s / √n . Its shape approaches normal as n grows, whatever the shape of the parent population. That is the central limit theorem. μ Population (skewed, μ = 2.0, σ = 1.2) → μ n = 2 SE = σ/√2 = 0.85 → μ n = 10 SE = σ/√10 = 0.38 → μ n = 30 SE = σ/√30 = 0.22 Central limit theorem: whatever the shape of the population, the sampling distribution of the mean approaches normal as n grows, centres on μ, and narrows by a factor of √n. n ≥ 30 is the working rule of thumb. The central limit theorem, the single result that lets you use z and t on non-normal data. The central limit theorem, stated properly Central limit theorem (CLT). As sample size n increases, the sampling distribution of the mean approaches a normal distribution with mean μ and standard deviation σ/√n, regardless of the shape of the population distribution . If the population is already normal, the sampling distribution is normal for any n. If it is not, n ≥ 30 is the conventional threshold at which the approximation is good enough. Why the CLT is the most important theorem you will be asked about. It is the licence to use z, t, F and every parametric test on real psychological data, which is almost never normally distributed. It says that the non-normality of the raw scores stops mattering once n is reasonable, because the tests are built on the sampling distribution of the mean, not on the raw scores. Standard error: the two things to get right SE is a standard deviation , specifically the SD of a sampling distribution. Every statistic has one: SE of the mean = s/√n; SE of a proportion = √(pq/n); SE of the difference between means = √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂); SE of r ≈ (1 − r²)/√(n − 1); SE of measurement (in psychometrics) = s√(1 − r xx ). SE shrinks with √n, not with n. To halve the standard error you must quadruple the sample. This is the law of diminishing returns in sample-size planning, and it is a favourite exam item. SD vs SE. The standard deviation describes how spread out the individual scores are; it is a fact about your data and it does not shrink as you collect more. The standard error describes how much a sample statistic bounces around from sample to sample; it is a fact about your estimate and it does shrink as n grows. Report SD to describe the sample; report SE (or a confidence interval) to describe the precision of your estimate. 7.4 Estimation and confidence intervals Point estimate: a single value offered as the estimate of a parameter (the sample mean estimates μ). Simple, but certainly wrong by some amount, and it carries no information about precision. Interval estimate: a range of values, with a stated confidence level, likely to contain the parameter. Always preferable. A good estimator is unbiased (its expected value is the parameter), consistent (converges on the parameter as n grows), efficient (smallest standard error among unbiased estimators) and sufficient (uses all the information in the sample). Confidence interval for a mean. σ known: CI = M ± z crit (σ/√n) · σ unknown: CI = M ± t crit (s/√n) 95% CI uses z = 1.96 · 99% CI uses z = 2.58 · 90% CI uses z = 1.645 The quantity added and subtracted is the margin of error . Worked example M = 52, s = 12, n = 36. SE = 12/√36 = 2.0. 95% CI = 52 ± 1.96(2.0) = 52 ± 3.92 = 48.08 to 55.92 . Because this interval does not contain 60, a null hypothesis that μ = 60 would be rejected at .05. That equivalence between confidence intervals and significance tests is worth stating in any answer. true population mean μ = 50 Twenty 95% confidence intervals from twenty samples. On average 19 of 20 capture μ; one misses. The interval is random, μ is fixed. "95% confident" describes the procedure over repeated sampling, not the probability that this one interval is right. What a 95% confidence interval actually means. The interpretation trap. A 95% confidence interval does not mean "there is a 95% probability that μ lies in this interval". μ is a fixed constant; it is either in the interval or it is not. The correct statement is: if we repeated this sampling procedure many times, 95% of the intervals so constructed would contain μ. The confidence is in the procedure, not in this one interval. The three things that widen a confidence interval: a higher confidence level (99% is wider than 95%), a larger standard deviation, and a smaller sample. There is a permanent trade-off between confidence and precision: you can be more certain, or you can be more specific, but not both at once with fixed n. Recap of sections 5 to 7: skew is asymmetry (named for the tail; mean drags furthest into it; Mo < Md < M for positive) and kurtosis is peakedness (lepto tall, meso normal, platy flat). The normal curve is defined by μ and σ, holds 68 / 95 / 99.7 percent within 1, 2 and 3 SD, and exactly 95% within ±1.96 SD. z scores standardise without normalising, and every derived score (T, IQ, stanine, sten) is a linear rescaling of z. Probability sampling makes sampling error calculable; stratified is the most precise, cluster the least. The sampling distribution of the mean has mean μ, SD equal to σ/√n (the standard error) and, by the central limit theorem, a normal shape once n is about 30, whatever the population looked like. Confidence intervals wrap that standard error around the sample mean. 8 Hypothesis testing, errors, power and effect size The framework you are about to learn is a hybrid of two feuding traditions. Sir Ronald Aylmer Fisher gave us the null hypothesis, the p value, significance testing, the F distribution, ANOVA, randomisation, degrees of freedom and the .05 convention. Jerzy Neyman and Egon Pearson (son of Karl) gave us the alternative hypothesis, Type I and Type II error, α and β, power, and the decision-theoretic frame. Textbooks teach them fused; historically the two camps despised each other. Naming both in an answer is an easy extra mark. 8.1 The hypotheses Null hypothesis (H₀) Alternative hypothesis (H₁ or Hₑ) States No difference, no relationship, no effect. Any observed difference is due to sampling error alone There is a difference, relationship or effect Written H₀: μ₁ = μ₂ or H₀: ρ = 0 H₁: μ₁ ≠ μ₂ (non-directional) or μ₁ > μ₂ (directional) Role The hypothesis actually tested . Always a statement of equality, so it can generate an exact sampling distribution The researcher's actual prediction; accepted only by elimination Outcome language Reject or fail to reject / retain Supported or not supported The single biggest language trap in the whole subject. You never accept the null hypothesis and you never prove anything. A non-significant result means only that you failed to find sufficient evidence against H₀; it does not establish that H₀ is true, because the failure could equally be low power, a small sample, or a poor measure. Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence. Write "failed to reject H₀" or "retained H₀", never "accepted H₀" or "proved there is no difference". Why test the null at all? Because you cannot compute a sampling distribution for "there is some difference of unspecified size", but you can compute one exactly for "the difference is zero". Falsification is logically clean: one contrary result can refute a universal claim, while no number of confirming results can prove it. Fisher borrowed the logic; Karl Popper made it a philosophy of science. 8.2 The steps of a significance test State H₀ and H₁, and decide whether the test is one-tailed or two-tailed. Set the significance level α (conventionally .05, or .01 when a false positive is costly). Choose the test statistic appropriate to the data (see section 16) and compute its degrees of freedom. Find the critical value from the table, or equivalently define the region of rejection. Compute the obtained value of the statistic from the data. Decide: if |obtained| ≥ critical (equivalently p ≤ α), reject H₀. Otherwise retain it. State the conclusion in the language of the research question, and report the effect size and a confidence interval alongside the p value. 8.3 One-tailed vs two-tailed −1.96 +1.96 α/2 = .025 α/2 = .025 Retain H₀ Two-tailed (non-directional) H₁: μ₁ ≠ μ₂ +1.645 α = .05 Retain H₀ One-tailed, right H₁: μ₁ > μ₂ −1.645 α = .05 Retain H₀ One-tailed, left H₁: μ₁ < μ₂ Same α = .05 in all three. Putting all of it in one tail lowers the critical value from 1.96 to 1.645, so a one-tailed test has more power , but only if you predicted the direction in advance. One-tailed vs two-tailed rejection regions at α = .05. Two-tailed (non-directional) One-tailed (directional) H₁ μ₁ ≠ μ₂: a difference in either direction μ₁ > μ₂ (or <): a difference in a stated direction only Rejection region Split: α/2 in each tail All of α in one tail z critical at .05 ±1.96 1.645 z critical at .01 ±2.58 2.33 Power Lower Higher , for the same α and n Risk None special A large effect in the unpredicted direction must be called non-significant When a one-tailed test is legitimate: only when the direction was predicted in advance on strong theoretical or empirical grounds, and when a result in the opposite direction would be of no interest whatsoever. Choosing the tail after seeing the data is a form of cheating with a name: p-hacking . Journals and examiners default to two-tailed. Note: F tests (ANOVA) and χ² tests are always evaluated in one tail, even when the hypothesis is non-directional. That is because both statistics are squared quantities, so only large values are inconsistent with H₀; a very small F or χ² simply means the groups are unusually alike. 8.4 Type I and Type II error critical value if H₀ is TRUE (no real effect) if H₁ is TRUE (a real effect of this size) α β 1 − β α = Type I error Reject a TRUE H₀. A false positive. You claim an effect that is not there. Set by you, usually .05 or .01. β = Type II error Retain a FALSE H₀. A false negative. You miss a real effect. Usually targeted at .20. 1 − β = Power Correctly reject a false H₀. Detect the effect that is really there. Convention: ≥ .80. Power goes UP when: • n increases (SE shrinks) • the effect size is larger • α is made less strict (.05 → .10) • the test is one-tailed • error variance is reduced • a parametric test is used Type I error, Type II error and power. Holding n fixed, α and β trade off against each other: sliding the critical value left shrinks β but grows α. Only increasing n shrinks both. H₀ is actually TRUE H₀ is actually FALSE You REJECT H₀ Type I error (α) False positive. You claim an effect that does not exist Correct decision (1 − β) Power . You detected a real effect You RETAIN H₀ Correct decision (1 − α) Confidence level Type II error (β) False negative. You missed a real effect Fix them in memory with a clinical analogy. A screening test for a disorder: a Type I error is telling a healthy person they have the disorder (false positive, over-diagnosis). A Type II error is telling a genuinely ill person they are fine (false negative, missed case). Which is worse depends entirely on the consequences, which is exactly why α is a decision, not a law of nature. α is set by the researcher before the study and equals the probability of a Type I error. Setting α = .05 means you accept a 5% chance of a false positive. β is not set directly ; it follows from α, n, the effect size and the variability. Convention targets β ≤ .20. α and β trade off at fixed n: making α stricter (.05 → .01) reduces false positives but raises β and lowers power. The only way to reduce both at once is to increase n . Some texts add Type III error (getting the right answer to the wrong question, or correctly rejecting H₀ but misidentifying the direction of the effect). 8.5 Power Power = 1 − β , the probability of correctly rejecting a false null hypothesis. In plain terms: the probability that your study will find the effect if the effect is really there. Convention: power of at least .80 . The six determinants of power (an exam favourite; learn all six) 1. Sample size (n) : the biggest lever, and the only one fully under your control. Larger n shrinks the standard error, which separates the two distributions. 2. Effect size : bigger real effects are easier to detect. 3. Significance level α : a more lenient α (.05 rather than .01) increases power, at the cost of more Type I errors. 4. One-tailed vs two-tailed : one-tailed tests are more powerful when the direction is correctly predicted. 5. Error variance : reducing it through better measurement, standardised procedure, homogeneous samples, or a repeated-measures design increases power sharply. 6. Choice of test : parametric tests are more powerful than their non-parametric equivalents when their assumptions hold . Power analysis is done a priori to determine the n needed to detect an effect of a given size, and this is what ethics committees and journals now expect. Done post hoc on an obtained effect it is largely uninformative (observed power is a direct function of the p value). Jacob Cohen wrote the standard reference ( Statistical Power Analysis for the Behavioral Sciences , 1969/1988), and G*Power is the standard free software. 8.6 The p value, and what it is not Definition. The p value is the probability of obtaining a result at least as extreme as the one observed, assuming the null hypothesis is true . Formally, p = P(data | H₀). Four things p is NOT , each of which appears as a distractor. 1. It is not the probability that H₀ is true. That would be P(H₀ | data), which is the reverse conditional and needs Bayes's theorem. 2. It is not the probability that the result is due to chance. 3. It is not a measure of the size or importance of the effect. With n = 10,000 a correlation of .03 is significant at .01 and means nothing. 4. It is not the probability that the finding will replicate. Statistical significance vs practical significance. Significance is a statement about how surprising the data would be under H₀; it is heavily driven by sample size. Practical or clinical significance is a statement about whether the effect is big enough to matter, and that is what effect size measures. A drug that lowers depression scores by 0.4 points can be highly significant in a trial of 5,000 and clinically worthless. Always report both. This is the core of the American Statistical Association's 2016 statement on p values and of the replication-crisis literature. 8.7 Effect size d = 0.20 small 85% overlap d = 0.50 medium 67% overlap d = 0.80 large 53% overlap d = 1.50 very large 26% overlap Cohen's d = (M₁ − M₂) / sᵥₒₒₓᵉᵈ · .20 small, .50 medium, .80 large Hedges' g: same idea, corrected for small n · Glass's Δ: uses the CONTROL group SD only r as effect size: .10 small, .30 medium, .50 large · r² / R² = proportion of variance explained ANOVA: η² = SSᵇᵉₜᵦᵉᵉₙ/SSᵗₔᵗₑₗ (.01 / .06 / .14) · partial η² · ω² is the less biased estimate Why it matters: p tells you IF there is an effect, effect size tells you HOW BIG. Where effect size becomes indispensable: meta-analysis. Because d and r are unit-free, results from studies using different measures can be pooled onto one scale, weighted by sample size, and combined into a single overall estimate. Gene Glass coined the term "meta-analysis" in 1976; his study with Mary Lee Smith on psychotherapy outcome (1977), finding an average d of about 0.85 for therapy versus no treatment, is the most cited example in clinical psychology and is worth naming. 9 The t tests William Sealy Gosset derived the t distribution in 1908 while working as a chemist at the Guinness brewery in Dublin, dealing with the very small samples of barley the brewery could afford. Guinness forbade employees from publishing, so he wrote under the pen name "Student" , and the test is called Student's t to this day. Fisher later gave it its modern form and the letter t. 9.1 Why t and not z z (normal) t, df = 30 t, df = 5 t, df = 1 t is flatter with fatter tails than z, so the critical value is always bigger. t₋ᵣᵢₜ at df = 1 is 12.71; at df = 30 it is 2.04; at df = ∞ it IS 1.96 = z. That is the whole difference. Use t when σ is unknown and estimated by s (which is nearly always). W. S. Gosset published it as "Student", 1908. The t distribution family against the standard normal. A z test requires you to know the population standard deviation σ. You essentially never do. When you estimate it with the sample s, you introduce a second source of error (s itself varies from sample to sample), so the resulting statistic no longer follows the normal distribution. It follows a slightly flatter, fatter-tailed distribution: the t distribution, one for every value of df. z test t test Requires σ known σ unknown, estimated by s Distribution One standard normal curve A family of curves, one per df Shape Fixed Flatter with fatter tails; approaches z as df → ∞ Critical value at .05, two-tailed 1.96 always 12.71 at df=1, 2.78 at df=4, 2.23 at df=10, 2.04 at df=30, 1.96 at df=∞ Used when Large samples with known σ, or proportions Essentially always in psychology 9.2 One-sample t test Question: does my sample mean differ from a known or hypothesised population mean? t = (M − μ) / (s / √n) · df = n − 1 In words: (what I got minus what I expected) divided by the standard error. Worked example A clinic's 25 patients score M = 108 on a wellbeing scale with s = 15. The published population mean is 100. SE = 15/√25 = 3.0. t = (108 − 100)/3.0 = 2.67 , df = 24. Critical t at .05 two-tailed, df 24 = 2.064. Since 2.67 > 2.064, reject H₀ . Effect size: d = (108 − 100)/15 = 0.53 , a medium effect. 9.3 Independent-samples t test Question: do two separate, unrelated groups differ on the DV? (Also called unpaired, uncorrelated, or between-subjects t.) t = (M₁ − M₂) / SE diff · df = n₁ + n₂ − 2 where SE diff = √[s² p (1/n₁ + 1/n₂)], and the pooled variance is s² p = (SS₁ + SS₂) / (n₁ + n₂ − 2), a weighted average of the two group variances. Worked example Therapy group: n₁ = 12, M₁ = 22, s₁ = 5. Control: n₂ = 12, M₂ = 17, s₂ = 6. s² p = (11×25 + 11×36)/22 = (275 + 396)/22 = 30.5. SE diff = √[30.5(1/12 + 1/12)] = √5.083 = 2.25. t = (22 − 17)/2.25 = 2.22 , df = 22. Critical t = 2.074, so reject H₀ . d = (22 − 17)/√30.5 = 5/5.52 = 0.91 , a large effect. Welch's t (the unequal-variances t). When Levene's test shows the variances differ, or the group sizes are very unequal, use Welch–Satterthwaite: the standard error is computed without pooling and the df are adjusted downwards (and become fractional). SPSS prints it as the "equal variances not assumed" row. Naming Welch when asked about a violation of homogeneity is a strong answer. 9.4 Paired-samples t test Question: do the same people (or matched pairs) differ across two conditions or two time points? (Also called dependent, correlated, related, matched-pairs, repeated-measures or within-subjects t.) t = M D / (s D / √n) · df = n − 1 , where n is the number of pairs The trick: compute the difference score D for each pair, then run a one-sample t test on those difference scores against μ = 0. That is all the paired t test is. Worked example Six patients, BDI before and after therapy. Differences (before − after): 8, 5, 11, 3, 7, 8. ΣD = 42, so M D = 7.0, n = 6. Deviations from 7: +1, −2, +4, −4, 0, +1. Squared: 1, 4, 16, 16, 0, 1. SS = 38, so s² D = 38/5 = 7.6 and s D = 2.76. SE = 2.76/√6 = 1.126. t = 7.0/1.126 = 6.22 , df = 5. Critical t at .05 two-tailed = 2.571, so reject H₀ : therapy produced a significant reduction. Effect size d = M D /s D = 7.0/2.76 = 2.54 , very large. Why the paired test is more powerful. Individual differences (some people are simply more depressed than others) are a large source of error variance in a between-subjects design. In a within-subjects design each person acts as their own control, so that variance is subtracted out entirely and only the change matters. The error term shrinks, t grows, and power rises. The price is the order effects (practice, fatigue, carryover, sensitisation) that within-subjects designs create, which is why you counterbalance, ideally with a Latin square. 9.5 Assumptions of the t tests Assumption What it means How you check it What to do if it fails Independence of observations Each score is unrelated to every other (within a group) By design, not by test Nothing rescues it. Its predecessor, Bartlett's test , is more powerful but very sensitive to non-normality, so Levene is preferred in practice. For the multivariate case the equivalent is Box's M test of equality of covariance matrices. Read assumption tests backwards. For Levene's, Shapiro–Wilk, Box's M, Mauchly's and the Hosmer–Lemeshow test, a non-significant result (p > .05) is the good news: it means the assumption holds. Students routinely reverse this. In every one of these tests, the null hypothesis is the assumption itself. 9.6 Why not run many t tests instead of an ANOVA The inflation of familywise error. Each t test carries a Type I error risk of α = .05. Run several and the probability that at least one is a false positive rises fast: for c independent comparisons, familywise α = 1 − (1 − .05) c . With three groups you would run three t tests, giving 1 − .95³ = .143 . With five groups that is ten comparisons and a familywise error rate of .40 : a two-in-five chance of a false claim. ANOVA tests all group differences in a single test at a single α, which is exactly the problem it was invented to solve. This is the standard answer to "why do we need ANOVA when we have the t test?" and it is asked constantly. The relationship between t and F. For exactly two groups, one-way ANOVA and the independent t test give an identical decision, and F = t² . Check it: t = 2.22 gives F = 4.93; the critical t of 2.074 squared is 4.30, which is the critical F for df 1, 22. They are the same test written two ways. Recap of sections 8 and 9: hypothesis testing sets up a null of no effect, computes how surprising the data would be if it were true, and rejects when that probability falls below α. Type I error is a false positive (rate α, set by you), Type II is a false negative (rate β), and power = 1 − β is driven mainly by sample size and effect size. The p value is P(data | H₀) and says nothing about effect magnitude, so always report Cohen's d, η² or r alongside it. The t tests compare means when σ is unknown: one-sample against a known μ, independent-samples between two unrelated groups (pooled variance, df = n₁+n₂−2), and paired-samples on difference scores (df = pairs − 1). They assume independence, normality, homogeneity of variance (test with Levene, repair with Welch) and an interval DV. Running many t tests inflates familywise error, which is why ANOVA exists. 10 Analysis of variance (ANOVA) Sir Ronald Aylmer Fisher developed ANOVA at Rothamsted Experimental Station in the 1920s, working on agricultural field trials, and published it in Statistical Methods for Research Workers (1925) and The Design of Experiments (1935). The same book gave psychology randomisation, replication, the factorial design, the null hypothesis and the .05 convention. George Snedecor named the ratio F in Fisher's honour. 10.1 The logic: partitioning variance ANOVA is misnamed. It compares means , but it does so by analysing variances . Here is the whole idea in three sentences. Take all the scores together and measure how much they vary in total. Some of that variation exists because the groups were treated differently (between-groups), and the rest exists because people differ from each other within the same treatment (within-groups, which is error). If the between-groups part is much bigger than the within-groups part, the treatment must be doing something. The within-subjects extension of the paired t test. Source df Note Between subjects n − 1 Individual differences, pulled out and discarded Within subjects: treatment k − 1 The effect of interest Within subjects: error (treatment × subjects) (k − 1)(n − 1) The denominator of F Total nk − 1 F = MS treatment / MS error , where the error term is the treatment × subjects interaction. Because between-subject variability has been removed from the error term, repeated-measures ANOVA is substantially more powerful than the equivalent between-subjects design and needs far fewer participants. Sphericity: the assumption unique to repeated measures Sphericity means the variances of the differences between every pair of conditions are equal. (Its stricter cousin, compound symmetry , requires equal variances and equal covariances.) It only becomes an issue with three or more conditions, since with two there is only one difference score. Test: Mauchly's test of sphericity . Non-significant (p > .05) means the assumption holds. If violated, correct the degrees of freedom by multiplying them by an epsilon (ε) estimate: • Greenhouse–Geisser : conservative, use when the estimated ε is below .75; • Huynh–Feldt : less conservative, use when ε is above .75; • Lower-bound : the most extreme correction; • or abandon the univariate approach and use MANOVA on the difference scores, which does not require sphericity at all. Violating sphericity inflates F and therefore the Type I error rate. Order effects and how to control them Practice effect: performance improves with repetition. Fatigue effect: it declines. Carryover: the effect of one condition persists into the next. Sensitisation: exposure to several conditions makes the purpose obvious. Counterbalancing is the fix: complete counterbalancing uses all k! orders (feasible only for small k); incomplete counterbalancing uses a Latin square , where each condition appears once in each ordinal position; randomised order per participant is the simplest option. Where carryover cannot be undone (learning a skill, a drug with a long half-life), a between-subjects design is the only honest choice. Mixed (split-plot) ANOVA Combines at least one between-subjects factor and at least one within-subjects factor. The commonest design in clinical outcome research: group (treatment vs control, between) × time (pre, post, follow-up, within). It generates two different error terms, one for the between part and one for the within part, and the effect people usually care about is the group × time interaction , because that is what "the treatment worked better than the control over time" actually means. 10.6 Assumptions of ANOVA Assumption Test Robustness / remedy Independence of observations Design Not robust. ANCOVA 1 or more categorical 1 1 or more continuous Do the group means differ after statistically equating the groups on the covariate? M at the front = M ultivariate = more than one dependent variable. C before OVA = C ovariance = at least one covariate has been partialled out. So MANCOVA = multiple DVs and covariates. Every one of these names is transparent once you know that, and papers exploit the confusion relentlessly. 11.2 ANCOVA (analysis of covariance) What it is: ANOVA with a regression built into it. Before comparing group means, ANCOVA uses the covariate to predict the DV, removes that predicted portion from both the DV and the error term, and compares the resulting adjusted means . The two things ANCOVA buys you. 1. Increased power. Variance in the DV explained by the covariate is moved out of the error term. A smaller MS error means a larger F and a better chance of detecting the treatment effect. This is the statistically respectable reason to use it. 2. Statistical control. Groups that were not equivalent at the start on some measured variable (pre-test score, age, IQ, symptom severity) can be compared as if they had been equal on it. This is the reason it is used in quasi-experiments, and it is the one that gets abused. The Lord's paradox warning. ANCOVA is not a substitute for random assignment. When intact groups differ on the covariate for reasons connected to the grouping itself, adjusting for the covariate can remove part of the real treatment effect or manufacture a spurious one. Frederic Lord (1967) showed that two defensible analyses of the same non-randomised data can give opposite answers. Say "ANCOVA is a statistical control, not a design control" if you are asked whether it fixes non-equivalent groups. Assumptions of ANCOVA (all the ANOVA ones, plus three) Linearity of the relationship between the covariate and the DV, within each group. If it is curvilinear, the adjustment is wrong. Homogeneity of regression slopes: the covariate must relate to the DV in the same way in every group . Tested by checking the covariate × IV interaction : it must be non-significant . If it is significant, ANCOVA is invalid and you should examine simple slopes or use moderated regression instead. This is the assumption unique to ANCOVA and the one most often asked about. The covariate must be measured reliably (unreliability biases the adjustment) and, ideally, measured before the treatment so that it cannot itself have been affected by the IV. A covariate influenced by the treatment removes part of the effect you are trying to measure. The covariate should be correlated with the DV (otherwise it buys no power) but uncorrelated with the IV (otherwise you are removing the treatment effect). Worked logic A trial compares CBT and waitlist on post-treatment BDI. The CBT group happened to start more depressed (pre-test M = 30 vs 24). Comparing raw post-test means is unfair. ANCOVA uses pre-test BDI as the covariate, adjusts each group's post-test mean to what it would have been had both groups started at the grand mean pre-test score, and compares those adjusted means. It also removes the (large) share of post-test variance predicted by pre-test score from the error term, which typically increases F substantially. 11.3 MANOVA (multivariate analysis of variance) What it is: ANOVA with two or more dependent variables analysed simultaneously. MANOVA forms an optimally weighted linear combination of the DVs (a variate or discriminant function) that maximally separates the groups, and tests whether the groups differ on that combination. Why not just run several ANOVAs? Three reasons. 1. Type I error control. Five separate ANOVAs at α = .05 give a familywise error rate near .23. MANOVA tests them all under one omnibus test at one α. 2. It uses the correlations among the DVs. Separate ANOVAs throw that information away. MANOVA can detect a group difference on the combination of DVs that no single DV shows on its own, which happens whenever the effect is spread thinly across correlated outcomes. 3. It protects against capitalising on chance in a set of conceptually related outcomes (for example, the several subscales of one symptom inventory). Homogeneity of variance-covariance matrices: tested by Box's M . Non-significant is what you want. Box's M is highly sensitive, so it is conventionally evaluated at α = .001; if it fails, switch to Pillai's trace. Linearity among all pairs of DVs. Absence of multicollinearity and singularity: the DVs should be correlated (about .30 to .70 is the sweet spot), but not so highly correlated that they are measuring the same thing. If two DVs correlate above about .80 or .90, combine them or drop one. Adequate sample size: the n in the smallest cell must exceed the number of DVs. More is much better; MANOVA is sensitive to outliers and small cells. 11.4 MANCOVA Multiple DVs plus one or more covariates: MANOVA's power advantages combined with ANCOVA's adjustment. It carries the union of both sets of assumptions, including homogeneity of regression slopes across groups for every DV, so it is the most demanding member of the family and needs the largest n. Use it when you have several correlated outcomes and a pre-existing difference or a strong nuisance variable to control. Two relatives to name if the question invites them. Discriminant function analysis (DFA) is the mirror image of MANOVA: MANOVA asks whether known groups differ on a set of variables, DFA asks whether a set of variables can predict group membership. Same mathematics, IV and DV swapped. Logistic regression answers the same prediction question as DFA but without requiring multivariate normality, which is why it has largely replaced DFA in clinical research. Recap of sections 10 and 11: ANOVA partitions total variance into between-groups (treatment plus error) and within-groups (error alone) and forms F = MS b /MS w , expected to be 1.00 under the null. A significant omnibus F means only that some pair differs, so it is followed by post hoc tests (Tukey HSD as default, Scheffé most conservative, Dunnett against a control, Games–Howell for unequal variances). Factorial ANOVA adds main effects and the interaction; parallel lines mean no interaction, crossing lines mean a disordinal one, and a significant interaction is interpreted before the main effects. Repeated-measures ANOVA removes individual differences from error, which raises power, but adds the sphericity assumption tested by Mauchly and corrected by Greenhouse–Geisser or Huynh–Feldt. ANCOVA adds a covariate to raise power and equate groups, and requires homogeneity of regression slopes. MANOVA handles multiple DVs through Wilks' lambda (small = large effect), Pillai's trace (most robust), Hotelling's trace and Roy's largest root, with Box's M testing the covariance matrices. MANCOVA is both at once. 12 Correlation Sir Francis Galton invented the concept while studying heredity in the 1880s and gave us the words correlation , regression and percentile . His student Karl Pearson turned it into the product-moment formula in 1896, which is why r is Pearson's r and is sometimes written r to honour Galton's "reversion". Charles Spearman produced the rank-order version in 1904, in the same paper that launched factor analysis and the g factor. 12.1 What a correlation is A correlation coefficient is a single number describing the direction and strength of the linear relationship between two variables. It runs from −1.00 through 0 to +1.00 . Sign = direction. Positive means both variables move the same way; negative means one rises as the other falls; zero means no linear relation. Absolute value = strength. The sign and the strength are completely independent: r = −.80 is exactly as strong as r = +.80, and much stronger than r = +.30. That is the most commonly missed point in the correlation section. Rough conventions (Cohen): .10 small, .30 medium, .50 large. In test-retest reliability the same number would be poor, so interpret against the context. r = +1.00 perfect positive · r² = 1.00 (100% shared variance) r = +0.70 strong positive · r² = 0.49 (49% shared variance) r = +0.30 weak positive · r² = 0.09 (9% shared variance) r = 0.00 no linear relation · r² = 0.00 (0% shared variance) r = −0.60 moderate negative · r² = 0.36 (36% shared variance) r = −1.00 perfect negative · r² = 1.00 (100% shared variance) The dashed line is the line of best fit. r measures how tightly the dots hug it; r² is the proportion of variance in Y explained by X. The same 46 cases at six different correlation strengths. 12.2 Pearson's product-moment correlation (r) Formulas. Definitional: r = Σ(z X z Y ) / n , the average product of the paired z scores. (This is where "product-moment" comes from: a moment is a deviation from the mean.) Covariance form: r = cov(X,Y) / (s X s Y ) , where cov = Σ(X−M X )(Y−M Y )/(n−1). Raw score: r = [nΣXY − ΣXΣY] / √{[nΣX² − (ΣX)²][nΣY² − (ΣY)²]} Significance: t = r√(n − 2) / √(1 − r²) , with df = n − 2 . Why covariance alone is not enough. Covariance already captures whether X and Y move together, but its size depends on the units the variables are measured in, so it cannot be compared across studies. Dividing by the two standard deviations standardises it onto a fixed −1 to +1 scale. A correlation is a standardised covariance. That one sentence answers a whole family of questions. Coefficient of determination r² is the proportion of variance in one variable that is shared with (accounted for by) the other. 1 − r² is the coefficient of non-determination or the coefficient of alienation is √(1 − r²). So r = .60 means 36% shared variance, not 60%. This non-linearity matters: doubling r from .30 to .60 multiplies the shared variance by four (from 9% to 36%).
