It shows how a new strategy is discovered and spreads, which widely spaced longitudinal tests miss. 21.5 Epidemiological designs Epidemiology studies the distribution and determinants of disorders in populations. Its designs are the same logic in a medical vocabulary: the IV is called the exposure and the DV the outcome . Prevalence and incidence Measure Definition Example Point prevalence Existing cases at one point in time ÷ population at that time Proportion of adults with a current depressive episode on the survey day Period prevalence People who were cases at any time during a period (e.g. the past 12 months) ÷ population 12-month prevalence of alcohol use disorder Lifetime prevalence People who have ever been cases, including recovered ones ÷ population Has ever met criteria for panic disorder Incidence (cumulative incidence, risk) New cases during a period ÷ people at risk (free of the disorder) at the start New cases of postpartum depression within a year of delivery Incidence rate (incidence density) New cases ÷ total person-time at risk 12 new cases per 1,000 person-years Prevalence ≈ incidence × average duration (for a fairly rare, stable condition). Schizophrenia has a low incidence but lasts long, so its prevalence is high relative to incidence; a brief adjustment disorder can have high incidence and low point prevalence. Incidence is what you need for causes (who becomes ill); prevalence is what you need for service planning (how many are ill now). India's National Mental Health Survey 2015–16 (NIMHANS), a cross-sectional prevalence study of adults in 12 states, reported a lifetime prevalence of any mental morbidity of 13.7% and a current prevalence of 10.6% (excluding tobacco use disorder). The four core designs A cross-sectional (prevalence) study measures exposure and outcome in a population sample at the same time. It gives prevalence and associations quickly, but cannot show which came first, and it over-represents long-lasting cases (people who recover or die quickly are less likely to be caught on survey day). A cohort study starts with people who are free of the outcome, classifies them by exposure, and follows them to see who develops the outcome. It gives incidence directly and so the relative risk , establishes temporal order, and can study several outcomes of one exposure. In a prospective cohort the researcher starts now and follows people into the future (the Framingham Heart Study, from 1948; Richard Doll and Austin Bradford Hill's British Doctors Study of smoking, from 1951). In a retrospective (historical) cohort both exposure and outcome have already happened, but the analysis still runs forward, from exposure recorded in old files to outcome recorded later: school records from 2005 that noted bullying, linked to clinic records in 2025. Cohort studies are slow and expensive, need very large samples for rare outcomes, and lose people to attrition. A case-control study runs the other way. It starts from the outcome : cases who have the disorder and controls who do not, as similar as possible otherwise (often matched on age and sex). It then looks back for differences in past exposure. Doll and Hill's 1950 comparison of lung cancer patients with controls, which found far more smokers among the cases, is the landmark. It is fast, cheap and the most efficient design for rare disorders (autism, early-onset psychosis, suicide), since you begin with the few cases instead of waiting for them, and it can examine many exposures at once. Its weaknesses: it cannot give incidence or relative risk, only the odds ratio ; choosing proper controls is hard (hospital controls bring Berkson's bias , Joseph Berkson, 1946); and it is vulnerable to recall bias : mothers of children with a developmental disorder search their memories of pregnancy far harder than mothers of typical children. A nested case-control study is carried out inside an existing cohort: every case that arises is compared with a sample of cohort members who were still free of the outcome at that time. Exposure data (stored blood, early questionnaires) were collected before the outcome, which removes recall bias, and only a fraction of the stored material has to be analysed. PAST FUTURE NOW: the researcher starts here Prospective cohort start with exposure, wait for the outcome: incidence, RR Exposed vs unexposed e.g. trauma yes / no, now Who develops depression? follow-up over years Retrospective (historical) cohort both already happened; still read forward Outcome measured now e.g. 2025 clinic records Exposure in old records e.g. 2005 school files Case-control start with the outcome, look back: odds ratio, recall bias Cases (depressed) and controls (not depressed) Who was exposed? interviews, records Cross-sectional both measured at one moment: prevalence only Both measured at once no time order Direction of inquiry. Cohort studies run from exposure to outcome, either forwards from now (prospective) or through old records (retrospective); case-control studies run backwards from outcome to exposure; a cross-sectional study takes both at one moment. Retrospective is not the same as case-control. A retrospective cohort uses past data but reasons from exposure to outcome; a case-control study reasons from outcome to exposure. The question "the British Doctors were questioned about smoking in 1951 and followed for decades: what design?" is a prospective cohort (observational, not experimental). "Rare outcome plus past exposure" signals case-control. Ecological studies and the ecological fallacy An ecological study uses groups (districts, states, countries) as the units: suicide rates against unemployment rates across Indian states, for example, using National Crime Records Bureau data. The ecological fallacy is drawing conclusions about individuals from a correlation between group averages. William S. Robinson (1950) gave the classic demonstration with 1930 US census data: across the 48 states, the percentage of foreign-born residents correlated +.53 with the literacy rate, yet at the individual level being foreign-born correlated −.11 with literacy. Immigrants had settled in states whose native-born populations were highly literate. A state-level correlation, even a strong one, says nothing certain about the people inside the states. (The reverse error, generalising from individuals to groups, is the atomistic fallacy.) 21.6 Measuring association: relative risk, odds ratio and attributable risk Arrange any exposure-outcome study as a 2 × 2 table with cells a (exposed, ill), b (exposed, well), c (unexposed, ill), d (unexposed, well). Risk in a group = ill ÷ everyone in that group: a/(a+b) for exposed, c/(c+d) for unexposed. Relative risk (risk ratio), RR = risk in exposed ÷ risk in unexposed. Needs incidence, so it comes from cohort studies and trials. Odds = ill ÷ well within a group: a/b and c/d. Odds ratio, OR = (a/b)/(c/d) = ad/bc . The only measure available from a case-control study, and the one logistic regression produces (section 13.5). Reading them: RR or OR = 1 means no association ; above 1, the exposure is associated with more of the outcome (a risk factor); below 1, with less (protective). A 95% confidence interval that includes 1 means the association is not significant. Risk difference (attributable risk) = risk in exposed − risk in unexposed: the excess cases due to the exposure, on an absolute scale. Attributable risk percent in the exposed = risk difference ÷ risk in exposed. Population attributable risk percent = (overall risk − risk in unexposed) ÷ overall risk: the share of all cases in the population that would disappear if the exposure did. Worked example. A cohort of 1,000 adults whose childhood records noted trauma (200 exposed) or not (800 unexposed) is assessed for depression. 60 of the 200 exposed and 80 of the 800 unexposed are depressed. Risk in exposed = 60/200 = 0.30; risk in unexposed = 80/800 = 0.10. RR = 0.30/0.10 = 3.0 : those exposed to childhood trauma were three times as likely to be depressed. Odds in exposed = 60/140 = 0.429; odds in unexposed = 80/720 = 0.111. OR = (60 × 720)/(140 × 80) = 43,200/11,200 = 3.86 . Risk difference = 0.30 − 0.10 = 0.20 : 20 extra cases per 100 exposed people (number needed to harm = 1/0.20 = 5). Attributable risk percent in the exposed = 0.20/0.30 = 67% : two-thirds of the depression among the exposed is attributable to the exposure, if the association is causal. Overall risk = 140/1,000 = 0.14, so PAR% = (0.14 − 0.10)/0.14 = 29% . Cohort of 1,000 adults followed from childhood records Depressed Not depressed Total Trauma (exposed) 60 a 140 b 200 No trauma (unexposed) 80 c 720 d 800 Total 140 860 1,000 Case-control version of the same population: take all 140 cases and half the 860 non-cases as controls (70 exposed, 360 not). OR = (60 × 360) / (80 × 70) = 3.86: the same OR. A 'risk' from that table (60/130) would be meaningless, because the researcher chose how many controls to take. Risk exposed = a/(a+b) = 60/200 = 0.30 unexposed = c/(c+d) = 80/800 = 0.10 Relative risk RR = 0.30/0.10 = 3.0 Odds exposed = a/b = 60/140 = 0.429 unexposed = c/d = 80/720 = 0.111 Odds ratio OR = ad/bc = 3.86 Impact risk difference = 0.30 − 0.10 = 0.20 AR% in exposed = 0.20/0.30 = 67% PAR% = (0.14 − 0.10)/0.14 = 29% OR (3.86) is larger than RR (3.0) because depression is common here (30% vs 10%). Worked 2 × 2 table: childhood trauma and adult depression. Risk ratio 3.0, odds ratio 3.86, risk difference 0.20 (20 extra cases per 100 exposed); the case-control sample recovers the same odds ratio. Why the OR is bigger than the RR here, and why case-control studies use it. The OR exaggerates the RR whenever the outcome is common; when the outcome is rare (roughly under 10% in both groups), b ≈ a + b and d ≈ c + d, so OR ≈ RR. That is the rare disease assumption , and it is why case-control studies of rare disorders report ORs as estimates of relative risk. The OR survives case-control sampling because it is symmetrical: the odds of exposure among cases divided by the odds of exposure among controls equals the odds of illness among the exposed divided by the odds among the unexposed, so sampling all cases and only some controls leaves it unchanged (3.86 in the figure), whereas any "risk" from that table depends on how many controls the researcher decided to take. From association to causation: the Bradford Hill criteria Austin Bradford Hill , in "The environment and disease: association or causation?" (1965), listed nine "viewpoints" for judging whether an observed association is causal. He insisted they were aids to judgement, not a checklist, and that none except temporality is indispensable. Viewpoint Question Applied to childhood trauma and adult depression Strength Is the association large? RR = 3 is stronger than most confounders could produce Consistency Is it repeated in different places, samples and designs? Found in cohort and case-control studies across countries Specificity Does the exposure lead to one particular outcome? Weak here: trauma predicts many disorders (Hill himself said this one is often absent) Temporality Does the exposure come first? The trauma was recorded in childhood: the only essential criterion Biological gradient Is there a dose-response relation? More types or longer duration of trauma, higher risk Plausibility Is there a plausible mechanism? Stress-system (HPA axis) sensitisation, negative schemas Coherence Does it fit what else is known? Consistent with stress-diathesis models Experiment Does removing or reducing the exposure reduce the outcome? Prevention and early-intervention evidence Analogy Do similar exposures have similar effects? Early adversity in animal studies 21.7 Descriptive designs: observation, case study and archival research Naturalistic observation records behaviour in its natural setting without intervening: children's play in an anganwadi, interaction on a psychiatric ward. It gives high ecological validity and is often the first step in a new area, but it is open to reactivity (people behave differently when watched) and observer bias, and it cannot explain what it records. Sampling, coding and observer reliability are covered in section 23. A case study is an intensive, usually long-term study of one person, family, group or institution, using interviews, observation, tests and records. It is idiographic (aimed at understanding the particular), in the sense Wilhelm Windelband (1894) distinguished from the nomothetic search for general laws, a distinction Gordon W. Allport (1937) brought into psychology. It is the right design for rare phenomena, for generating hypotheses, for disconfirming a universal claim with one counter-example, and for illustrating a treatment. Its limits: no control, no generalisation to others, and heavy reliance on the investigator's interpretation and on retrospective reports. (Small-N designs that add experimental control to the single case are section 22.) Case Who reported it What it is remembered for Anna O. In the worked table RR = 3.0, OR = 3.86, risk difference = 0.20, AR% = 67%, PAR% = 29%; OR approximates RR only for rare outcomes; OR or RR = 1 means no association. William S. Robinson (1950) showed the ecological fallacy; Austin Bradford Hill (1965) gave nine viewpoints for causation, of which only temporality is essential. Descriptive designs are naturalistic observation, the case study (Anna O., Little Hans, Phineas Gage, H.M., Genie) and archival research. 22 Single-subject (small-N) designs Every design in sections 20 and 21 answers its question by comparing groups: the average of the treated group against the average of the control group. That works when you want to know what happens on average to people like these. It works badly when the question is about this child, this client, this behaviour, which is the question an ABA therapist, a special educator or a rehab counsellor faces every morning. A group mean can improve while half the individuals in the group get worse; a treatment that helps the "average autistic child" may describe no real child at all. Single-subject designs (also called single-case, single-system, N = 1, intrasubject or small-N designs) answer the causal question inside one individual, by measuring that person again and again and switching the treatment on and off in a planned way. They are true experiments: the independent variable is manipulated, the dependent variable is measured repeatedly, and the rival explanations are ruled out by the pattern of the data rather than by a control group. 22.1 Why single-case research exists Section 18 introduced the two aims a science of persons can have. The nomothetic aim looks for general laws that hold across people (most of experimental psychology); the idiographic aim tries to understand the particular individual in depth. The terms come from the philosopher Wilhelm Windelband (1894) and were brought into personality psychology by Gordon Allport (1937) . Single-case designs are a bridge between the two: they study one person intensively (idiographic in method) but in order to establish lawful cause-and-effect relationships that can then be replicated across people (nomothetic in aim). Psychology actually began with single subjects: Hermann Ebbinghaus (1885) studied memory with himself as the only participant, and Ivan Pavlov's conditioning work used a handful of dogs studied for years. Group comparison with significance testing became dominant only after Ronald A. Fisher 's statistics ( The Design of Experiments , 1935) reached psychology in the 1930s and 1940s (section 20). Who built the method. B. F. Skinner (Burrhus Frederic Skinner) studied the moment-to-moment behaviour of individual rats and pigeons in The Behavior of Organisms (1938), recording each animal's responding continuously on a cumulative recorder and showing control by turning contingencies on and off. His approach is the experimental analysis of behaviour , with its own journal, the Journal of the Experimental Analysis of Behavior (1958). Murray Sidman 's Tactics of Scientific Research (1960) is the methodological bible: it argued that reliability and generality are shown by replication , not by significance tests, and defined direct and systematic replication. Michel Hersen and David H. Barlow , Single Case Experimental Designs: Strategies for Studying Behavior Change (1976), carried the logic into clinical psychology and psychiatry (third edition, 2009, with Matthew Nock). Alan E. Kazdin , Single-Case Research Designs: Methods for Clinical and Applied Settings (1982), is the other standard text, and Kazdin also wrote the classic papers on social validation (section 22.9). Applied behaviour analysis and its seven dimensions When these methods moved from the laboratory to classrooms, hospitals and homes, the field became applied behaviour analysis (ABA) , launched with the Journal of Applied Behavior Analysis in 1968. In its first volume Donald M. Baer, Montrose M. Wolf and Todd R. Risley (1968) defined ABA by seven dimensions, still memorised by every behaviour analyst: applied (the behaviour matters to the person and society), behavioural (it is observable behaviour that is measured, not a report of it), analytic (the researcher demonstrates experimental control, which is exactly what the designs in this section do), technological (procedures are described so completely that someone else could replicate them), conceptually systematic (procedures are tied to basic principles such as reinforcement), effective (the change is large enough to matter practically) and generality (the change lasts over time, appears in other settings, or spreads to other behaviours). The same paper described the two core demonstrations of control: the reversal and the multiple baseline . Case study is not a single-case experiment. A case study (section 21) is an uncontrolled, usually narrative and often retrospective account of one person: Freud's Little Hans, Breuer's Anna O., the amnesic patient H.M. It can generate hypotheses but cannot establish causation, because nothing is manipulated and there is no baseline against which change can be judged. A single-case experimental design has one participant but all the machinery of an experiment: an operationally defined target behaviour, repeated objective measurement, a stable baseline, deliberate manipulation of the independent variable in planned phases, and a demonstration that behaviour changes when, and only when, the treatment changes. "N = 1" describes the sample size, not the level of control. Kazdin also showed that a case study strengthened with objective, repeated measurement and several cases sits between the two: better than an anecdote, still short of an experiment. 22.2 The logic: repeated measurement, baseline, prediction, verification, replication A group experiment rules out history, maturation and the other threats of section 19 by having a control group experience them too. A single-case design has no control group, so the participant serves as their own control across time. That only works if the behaviour is measured repeatedly (every session, every day) under consistent conditions, so that you can see its natural level, trend and variability before anything is changed. Baseline (phase A). The target behaviour is measured under ordinary conditions, before treatment, until it is stable : no strong trend and variability small enough that an effect would be visible. The baseline has a descriptive function (how bad is the problem now) and, more importantly, a predictive function: it tells you what the behaviour would probably have looked like in future if nothing were done. Prediction. Extend the baseline line forward in your mind. That projected path is the counterfactual, the single-case equivalent of a control group. Affirmation of the consequent. Introduce the treatment (phase B). If behaviour departs from the predicted path, the treatment may be responsible, but so might a coincidental event (history) or growth (maturation). An AB comparison alone stops here. Verification. Show that the baseline prediction was correct: withdraw the treatment and see behaviour return towards the baseline level (ABA), or show that untreated baselines continue on their predicted path while another tier is treated (multiple baseline). Replication. Reintroduce the treatment and see the effect again (ABAB), or reproduce it in a second and third tier, participant or setting. Each replication makes coincidence less believable. Baseline logic (prediction, verification, replication) is the standard name for this reasoning in the applied behaviour analysis text of John Cooper, Timothy Heron and William Heward (1987; later editions). Causal inference in single-case research rests on repeated demonstrations of an effect at different points in time . The single-case standards written for the US What Works Clearinghouse by Thomas Kratochwill and colleagues (2010) require at least three demonstrations of the effect at three different points in time, and phases of at least three data points (five to meet the standard without reservation). How long a baseline, and what if it is trending? A single baseline point tells you nothing about trend or variability; two points define a line but cannot show whether it is a fluke. Three data points is the conventional minimum because it is the smallest number that can reveal a trend and a sense of variability, and more is better when the data bounce. The rule is "stability, not a fixed number": keep measuring until the pattern is predictable. Baseline trending in the therapeutic direction (the child's tantrums are already falling): do not start treatment yet. Any later improvement would be indistinguishable from the existing trend. Extend the baseline until it levels, look for what is causing the improvement, or choose a design and analysis that model the trend. Baseline trending in the counter-therapeutic direction (getting worse): you may introduce treatment, and a reversal of the trend is actually a stronger demonstration of effect. Highly variable baseline: extend it, tighten the operational definition and observation conditions, or look for the variable driving the variation (it is often the functional variable you need). Dangerous behaviour (severe self-injury, head-banging, suicide risk): ethics overrides methodology. A short baseline, or none (see the B-A-B design), is acceptable. 22.3 The A-B family: AB, ABA, ABAB, BAB and ABCB The letters are a notation. A always means baseline (no treatment). B means the first treatment, C a second, different treatment, and BC written together means B and C given at the same time. A1 and A2 number repeated phases. AB design Baseline, then treatment. It is the minimum structure and what most clinicians informally do: measure the problem for a week, then start therapy. Its weakness is that there is only one phase change, so only one demonstration of effect. If a 9-year-old's tantrums fall after a token system starts, you cannot tell whether the tokens did it or whether the child's mother returned from hospital that same week (history), the child grew out of it (maturation), or the extreme first week drifted back (regression to the mean). AB is a quasi-experimental design , the single-case analogue of the one-group pretest–posttest design, and Kratochwill's standards do not accept it as evidence of a causal effect. It is still useful as a clinical evaluation tool and when replicated across several clients. ABA (withdrawal) design Add a second baseline: treatment is withdrawn and behaviour should return towards its baseline level. Two phase changes now both point the same way, which makes a coincidental external event much less plausible. Its clinical defect is obvious: the study ends in the baseline phase , leaving the client without the treatment that worked. ABAB (reversal or withdrawal) design Baseline, treatment, withdrawal, treatment reinstated. This is the strongest single demonstration of experimental control in the single-case family: three phase changes, so three opportunities for the behaviour to change in the predicted direction, satisfying the three-demonstration standard by itself, and it ends with the client on treatment. R. Vance Hall, Diane Lund and Deloris Jackson (1968) , in the first article of the first issue of JABA , used reversal designs to show that teacher attention controlled pupils' study behaviour in ordinary classrooms. The figure below shows the same logic with a child with ADHD whose out-of-seat behaviour is treated with a token-and-praise system. 0 5 10 15 20 1 5 10 15 20 25 Sessions (school days) Out-of-seat episodes per class A1 Baseline M = 15.0 B1 Tokens + praise M = 6.1 A2 Withdrawal M = 11.8 B2 Reinstated M = 3.6 An ABAB withdrawal design computed from one child's daily counts: behaviour falls each time the token system starts and climbs back when it is withdrawn, so the treatment, not time or chance, is controlling it. Baseline (A1) is stable around 15.0 episodes per class (range 13 to 17). With tokens and praise (B1) the mean falls to 6.1; on withdrawal (A2) it climbs back to 11.8; on reinstatement (B2) it falls again, faster, to 3.6. Note the graphing conventions: vertical dashed phase-change lines, data points never joined across a phase line , each phase labelled, behaviour on the y axis and sessions on the x axis. The problems with withdrawal. (1) Ethics. Deliberately removing an effective treatment, especially for dangerous behaviour such as self-injury or aggression, may be unacceptable to parents, staff and ethics committees, and an ABA design that stops in A is worse still. Keep the withdrawal phase brief and end on treatment. (2) Irreversible behaviour. Many targets will not, and should not, return to baseline: once a child has learned to read, to use a picture-exchange card or to tie shoelaces, withdrawing the teaching does not erase the skill, and social behaviours become maintained by the natural reinforcers of peers (a "behavioural trap"). If behaviour does not reverse, the design cannot demonstrate control. (3) Sequence and carryover effects: the second B phase is not a fresh first exposure. For irreversible or dangerous targets use a multiple-baseline or changing-criterion design instead. Withdrawal versus reversal, strictly. In a true reversal design the second A phase does not just remove the treatment; it reverses the contingency (for example, attention is now given for being out of seat instead of in seat). A withdrawal design simply removes the treatment. Most textbooks and most exam papers use "reversal design" loosely for any ABAB, so accept either name unless the question insists on the distinction. BAB design Treatment, withdrawal, treatment. It is used when the behaviour is too serious to leave untreated while a baseline is collected, or when a client arrives already on treatment. It ends on treatment and has two phase changes, but it has no initial baseline , so the natural level of the problem before any intervention is never known. ABCB and A-B-A-C: comparing treatments or isolating the active ingredient In an ABCB design the C phase replaces B with a control condition that keeps everything except the hypothesised active ingredient. The classic use: B is attention contingent on appropriate behaviour; C is the same amount of attention given non-contingently (on a timer, regardless of behaviour). If behaviour worsens in C and improves again in B, it was the contingency, not the attention itself, that mattered. This avoids a full return to baseline. A-B-A-C (often extended to A-B-A-C-A) compares two different treatments, each against a baseline. The weakness is multiple-treatment interference : C always follows B, so its effect may be coloured by the earlier treatment (an order effect that cannot be counterbalanced within one person, although it can be counterbalanced across participants, A-B-A-C for one and A-C-A-B for another). 22.4 Multiple-baseline designs The multiple-baseline design solves the withdrawal problem: it never removes an effective treatment. Instead of verifying the baseline prediction by withdrawal, it verifies it with other baselines that are still running . Baselines are recorded simultaneously on three or more "tiers", and the treatment is introduced to one tier at a time, at staggered points. If each tier changes only when, and not before, the treatment reaches it, coincidence becomes implausible: an outside event (a new teacher, a festival holiday, a medication change) would have hit all tiers at the same calendar time. Across behaviours: one person, several different behaviours (a child's hand-raising, completing worksheets and staying in seat), treated one after another. Across settings: one person, one behaviour, several settings (tantrums at home, in class, in the therapy room), treatment extended to one setting at a time. Across participants (subjects): one behaviour, several people with the same problem, treatment started for each person at a different time. The most common form, and the one drawn below. 0 6 12 Aarav 1.2 → 8.2 Baseline Intervention 0 6 12 Meera 1.8 → 8.1 0 6 12 1 5 10 15 20 Sessions Kabir 0.8 → 6.4 Spontaneous requests per session A multiple-baseline design across three children: each child's requests rise only when the intervention reaches that child, and the stair-step phase line shows the staggered starts; the numbers give each child's baseline and intervention means. Aarav's requests rise from a baseline mean of 1.2 to 8.2 once teaching starts at session 6. On those same days Meera and Kabir, still in baseline, show no change; that is the verification. Meera's requests then rise from session 10 (1.8 to 8.1) and Kabir's from session 14 (0.8 to 6.4): two replications. Three tiers give the three demonstrations the standards ask for. The two assumptions of a multiple baseline. (1) Independence of baselines: treating one tier must not change the others. If teaching Aarav to request also changes Meera because they share a classroom and she imitates him, or if reducing a child's hitting also reduces kicking (response generalisation), the untreated baselines move early and the design loses its control. (2) Functional similarity: yet the tiers must be similar enough that the same treatment would be expected to work on each. The design walks a line between these. When a baseline changes before its treatment begins, the evidence for that tier is lost. The concurrent multiple baseline (the original form described by Baer, Wolf and Risley) records all tiers over the same calendar period, which is what lets it rule out history. In a non-concurrent multiple baseline, described by P. J. Watson and E. A. Workman (1981) , participants are studied at different times (one client in January, the next in March) and each is randomly assigned a baseline length in advance. It is far more practical in clinics where clients arrive one at a time, but because the tiers do not share calendar time it is weaker against history. A variant for skills that cannot be measured every day without teaching them, the multiple-probe design (Robert Horner and Donald Baer, 1978), replaces continuous baseline measurement with occasional probes. Weaknesses of all multiple baselines: some tiers wait a long time untreated, you need three or more comparable behaviours, settings or people, and the effect is shown only by its timing, not by its removal. 22.5 Changing-criterion design Some behaviours should not be switched on or off but shifted gradually : cigarettes, caffeine, minutes of exercise, pages read, minutes of on-task work, steps on a fear hierarchy. The changing-criterion design described by Donald P. Hartmann and R. Vance Hall (1976) handles these. After a baseline, the treatment (usually a reinforcement contingency) is applied in a series of phases, each with a stepwise criterion: the client earns the reward only if behaviour meets the current criterion. When behaviour is stable at that level, the criterion is changed again. Hartmann and Hall presented it as a variant of the multiple-baseline logic, in which each phase acts as the baseline for the next. 0 7 14 21 28 1 5 10 15 20 25 30 Days in the de-addiction programme Cigarettes per day Baseline M = 22.9 ≤ 18 ≤ 14 ≤ 10 ≤ 6 ≤ 3 Criterion phases (orange bar = cigarettes allowed per day) A changing-criterion design for a client in a de-addiction programme: smoking steps down each time the allowed number of cigarettes is lowered and settles at or just under each new criterion, which is the evidence of control. Experimental control is shown when behaviour tracks the criterion : it changes when, and only when, the criterion changes, and settles close to each new level. In the figure, baseline smoking averages 22.9 cigarettes a day; each criterion phase settles at or just below its limit (17.4, 13.3, 9.8, 5.8 and 3.0 a day against limits of 18, 14, 10, 6 and 3). On the first day of the ≤ 10 and ≤ 3 phases the client overshoots by one cigarette, which is typical of real data. To make the case strong: use at least three criterion changes (each change is a demonstration), vary the length of the phases (5, 4, 6, 4 and 5 days here) so that change cannot simply be following a calendar rhythm, vary the size of the steps , and, if possible, add a brief reversal to an earlier criterion (a "mini-reversal") to show that behaviour follows the criterion in both directions. Strengths: no withdrawal, one behaviour in one person is enough, and the shaping logic fits clinical goals. Weaknesses: the behaviour must already be in the person's repertoire; if behaviour runs ahead of the criterion (the client simply quits smoking at day 9), control cannot be shown; and it is hard to separate the treatment from the client's own goal-setting. 22.6 Alternating-treatments (multi-element) design and combined designs The alternating-treatments design (ATD) , named and systematised by David H. Barlow and Steven C. Hayes (1979) , compares two or more treatments in one person by alternating them rapidly : across sessions, days or parts of a day, in a random or counterbalanced order, each condition usually signalled by a distinct cue (a different therapist, room or colour card) so the person can discriminate them. Barlow and Hayes noted that it had gone by several names before; you will also see it called the multi-element (multielement) design . Each condition is plotted as its own line. If the lines separate clearly and consistently, the conditions have different effects; if they overlap, they do not differ. 0 25 50 75 100 1 5 10 15 20 Sessions % of intervals on-task Baseline Alternating treatments random order, one condition per session Best only tokens Praise Tokens An alternating-treatments design: after baseline, praise and token sessions are interleaved in random order, the token line separates clearly above the praise line, and the final phase keeps only the better treatment. In the figure a boy's on-task behaviour averages 34.8% of intervals at baseline. During alternation, praise sessions average 49.0% and token sessions 72.7%, and the two lines never cross, so tokens are the more effective treatment; the last phase uses tokens alone (84.8%). The ATD is the design behind the functional analysis of problem behaviour by Brian Iwata and colleagues (1982) , in which a child's self-injury is measured under rapidly alternated attention, demand (escape), alone and play conditions; the condition with the highest line reveals what is maintaining the behaviour. Strengths: fast (a comparison in days rather than weeks), no withdrawal, can begin without a long baseline, and handles somewhat unstable behaviour because both conditions are equally affected by any drift. Weaknesses: multiple-treatment interference (carryover or contrast between conditions alternated so closely), the conditions must be discriminable, the behaviour must respond quickly, and the rapid switching may be artificial compared with how the treatment would be used in real life. Combined designs mix these elements to answer more than one question or to shore up a weakness: a multiple baseline in which one tier also gets a brief withdrawal; an ABAB whose B phases contain an alternating-treatments comparison; a changing criterion run inside a multiple baseline across clients. In medicine the same logic appears as the randomised N-of-1 trial (Gordon Guyatt and colleagues, 1986), in which one patient receives drug and placebo in randomised, blinded, repeated periods (section 25).
