Cognitive Psychology If behaviorism had banished the mind from psychology, the cognitive revolution of the 1950s and 1960s brought it back. Behaviorists had refused to study internal mental events on the grounds that they could not be directly observed. Cognitivists countered that the mind could be studied scientifically and indirectly , by inferring internal processes from carefully measured behavior, just as physicists infer unseen particles from their effects. Drivers of the Cognitive Revolution Several developments converged to reinstate the mind as a legitimate object of study: Chomsky's 1959 critique of Skinner's Verbal Behavior : Noam Chomsky argued that language is generative (we produce sentences never heard before), that children acquire it too fast and too well to be explained by reinforcement, and that humans possess an innate Language Acquisition Device (LAD) and a transformational grammar . This devastating review is often taken as the symbolic launch of the revolution. The computer / information-processing metaphor : the mind came to be seen as an information processor that takes input, encodes, stores, retrieves, and outputs, mirroring a computer. Shannon's information theory , which gave psychology a formal vocabulary for measuring information. The 1956 "annus mirabilis" : George Miller's paper "The Magical Number Seven, Plus or Minus Two" ; Allen Newell and Herbert Simon's Logic Theorist (an early AI program); and the Dartmouth conference that christened "artificial intelligence." Earlier groundwork by Frederic Bartlett , whose 1932 work on schemas showed that memory is reconstructive, not photographic. Definition Information-processing model: the view that the mind operates like a computer, handling information through a sequence of stages: input, encoding, storage, retrieval, and output. Ulric Neisser and the Naming of the Field Ulric Neisser's 1967 textbook Cognitive Psychology named and consolidated the discipline, earning him the title "father of cognitive psychology." The Information-Processing Model of Memory The dominant framework was a set of stage models , debating whether processing is serial (one step at a time) or parallel . The landmark Atkinson-Shiffrin multi-store model (1968) proposed three stores: Store Capacity Duration Sensory register Very large Fraction of a second Short-term / working memory 7 ± 2 items ~15-30 seconds Long-term memory Essentially unlimited Potentially permanent Refinements followed. Alan Baddeley and Graham Hitch (1974) replaced the passive short-term store with an active working memory comprising a central executive directing two subsystems, the phonological loop (verbal/acoustic information) and the visuospatial sketchpad (visual and spatial information), with an episodic buffer added later (2000) to integrate them. Fergus Craik and Robert Lockhart (1972) offered an alternative levels of processing framework: memory depends not on which store but on how deeply material is encoded (shallow surface processing versus deep semantic processing). In attention, Donald Broadbent proposed the influential filter (bottleneck) model , in which a filter selects one channel of incoming information for further processing. Key Figures and Allied Lines George Miller quantified short-term capacity at seven plus or minus two "chunks." Herbert Simon and Allen Newell pioneered the study of problem-solving , building the General Problem Solver (GPS) and introducing bounded rationality (the idea that human reasoning is rational but limited by information and capacity). Jerome Bruner , also a founder of the field, advanced discovery learning and three modes of representation : enactive (action-based), iconic (image-based), and symbolic (language-based). Jean Piaget is often placed here as the great cognitive-developmental theorist. Later, Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky showed that judgment relies on heuristics (mental shortcuts) such as availability, representativeness, and anchoring , extending Simon's bounded rationality into the study of cognitive bias. Cognitive psychology also yielded clinical fruit: Aaron Beck's cognitive therapy, built on the cognitive triad (negative views of self, world, and future) and systematic cognitive distortions , and Albert Ellis's Rational Emotive Behavior Therapy (REBT) with its ABC model (Activating event, Beliefs, Consequences). Definition Schema: a mental framework or organized knowledge structure that guides how we perceive, interpret, and remember information. Connectionism and the Cognitive Science Turn From the 1980s, connectionism / parallel distributed processing (PDP) modeled cognition through networks of simple interconnected units, inspired by the brain rather than the serial computer. The field broadened into cognitive science (uniting psychology, linguistics, computer science, and philosophy) and then into cognitive neuroscience , which uses brain imaging to ground mental processes in neural activity. Legacy Cognitive psychology is the dominant paradigm in psychology today and the theoretical foundation of CBT , the most empirically supported family of psychotherapies. High-yield Cognitive revolution drivers: Chomsky's 1959 critique of B. F. Skinner, the computer/information-processing metaphor, Shannon's information theory, and the 1956 events (Miller, Allen Newell & Herbert Simon, Dartmouth AI). Ulric Neisser, 1967 named the field. Miller: 7 ± 2. Atkinson-Shiffrin: three stores, sensory register, short-term, long-term. Trap Distinguish cognitive psychology (the experimental science of mental processes, founded by Ulric Neisser, Miller, Jerome Bruner, etc.) from cognitive therapy (the clinical treatment founded by Aaron Beck). And remember it was Noam Chomsky's critique of B. F. Skinner , not Skinner himself, that helped launch the revolution. Memory hook Three stores in a row, "Sensory, Short, Long" , like a relay: information sprints through the sensory register, pauses in short -term (hold only 7 ± 2), then settles into long -term storage. 9. Indian Psychology & Eastern Systems 9.1 Orientation: What "Indian Psychology" Means Western academic psychology grew out of physiology and philosophy in 19th-century Europe and defined itself as the empirical study of behaviour and mental processes, with health understood largely as the absence of pathology. Indian psychology is a different enterprise altogether. It is indigenous , rooted in philosophy and spiritual practice (the Vedas, Upanishads, and the great darshanas), and its goal is not the removal of symptoms but self-realization and liberation ( moksha ) and the deliberate transformation of consciousness . Where Western psychology asks "how does the mind work?", Indian psychology asks "who is the knower behind the mind, and how is one freed?" The "self" here is not the ego or personality but a deeper witnessing consciousness. Indian thought is traditionally divided into nine systems ( darshanas , literally "ways of seeing"). The six orthodox systems are called āstika because they accept the authority of the Vedas; the heterodox ( nāstika ) systems reject Vedic authority. The six orthodox darshanas are conventionally studied in three allied pairs. Pair Systems Core emphasis Logic + Atomism Nyaya & Vaisheshika Valid knowledge (pramanas) and logic; atomistic metaphysics of substance Cosmology + Practice Samkhya & Yoga Dualism of consciousness and matter; the disciplined path to liberation Ritual + Knowledge Mimamsa & Vedanta Vedic ritual action (karma-kanda); ultimate reality and the self (jnana-kanda) The three heterodox (nāstika) systems are Buddhism , Jainism , and Charvaka (a materialist, empiricist school that denied the soul and afterlife). For psychology, the most heavily examined systems are Samkhya, Yoga, Vedanta, and Buddhism. 9.2 Samkhya: Purusha, Prakriti, and the Three Gunas Samkhya , attributed to the sage Kapila , is the oldest of the systems and supplies the conceptual backbone for much of Indian psychology. It is a dualism of two ultimate, eternal realities. Purusha is pure consciousness, the passive witness (sakshi); it is many (each being has its own Purusha), changeless, and does nothing. Prakriti is primordial matter or nature, the active, unconscious source of everything mental and physical. Bondage arises when Purusha mistakenly identifies with the activities of Prakriti; liberation ( kaivalya , "aloneness") comes from discriminating the two. Prakriti is composed of three gunas (strands or qualities) held in equilibrium until evolution begins. From their disturbance unfolds a fixed sequence of evolutes : first mahat / buddhi (cosmic intellect, the faculty of discrimination), then ahamkara (the ego, the "I-maker"), then manas (mind, the coordinating sense), and from these the five sense-organs, five action-organs, five subtle elements (tanmatras), and five gross elements. Note that buddhi, ahamkara, and manas together form the inner instrument (antahkarana); they are all material, not consciousness itself. Definition Guna = a constituent quality or "strand" of Prakriti (nature). The three gunas (sattva, rajas, tamas) are present in everything; what differs is their proportion. A person's temperament, mood, food, and even thoughts are classified by which guna dominates. The three gunas are the single most-tested idea in Indian psychology, so learn them cold. Guna Quality Mental state / personality Example Sattva Purity, light, harmony, balance, clarity Calm, wise, content, disciplined, compassionate A serene, clear-thinking meditator Rajas Activity, passion, restlessness, energy Driven, anxious, craving, agitated, ambitious A restless, competitive striver Tamas Inertia, darkness, dullness, heaviness Lethargic, confused, dull, depressed, negligent A sluggish, apathetic person High-yield The three gunas : Sattva = purity/light/balance, Rajas = activity/passion/restlessness, Tamas = inertia/darkness/dullness. All of nature is a mixture of the three; personality is governed by which dominates. This item appears on virtually every Indian entrance. Memory hook Gunas in descending "energy quality": S-R-T = Saint, Restless, Tired . The Saint is sattvic (calm/pure), the Restless one is rajasic (driven), the Tired one is tamasic (dull/inert). 9.3 Yoga: Patanjali and the Eight Limbs The Yoga system, set out in Patanjali's Yoga Sutras , shares Samkhya's metaphysics but adds Ishvara (a special Purusha, a focus for devotion) and supplies the practical method for stilling the mind. Its central object is the chitta (mind-stuff), whose constant fluctuations are the chitta vrittis (mental modifications). The defining aphorism is "Yogah chitta vritti nirodhah" : yoga is the cessation (restraint) of the modifications of the mind. When the vrittis are stilled, the witness (Purusha) rests in its own nature. Definition Chitta vritti = a modification or wave in the mind-stuff (thoughts, perceptions, memories, emotions). Moksha / kaivalya = liberation, the final goal: the witnessing self freed from identification with mind and matter, ending the cycle of suffering and rebirth. The path is Ashtanga Yoga , the eight limbs: Yama — ethical restraints (non-violence, truth, non-stealing, continence, non-greed) Niyama — personal observances (purity, contentment, discipline, study, surrender) Asana — steady, comfortable posture Pranayama — regulation of breath / vital energy Pratyahara — withdrawal of the senses from their objects Dharana — concentration (fixing attention on one point) Dhyana — meditation (sustained, uninterrupted flow of attention) Samadhi — absorption / union, the goal High-yield "Yogah chitta vritti nirodhah" (yoga = stilling the mind's modifications) and the eight limbs in order: Yama, Niyama, Asana, Pranayama, Pratyahara, Dharana, Dhyana, Samadhi . Examiners love asking for the sequence or for which limb is "sense-withdrawal" (Pratyahara) versus "concentration" (Dharana). Memory hook Eight limbs: "Young Novices Are Pretty Punctual During Daily Sadhana." Y-N-A-P-P-D-D-S. The last three (Dharana-Dhyana-Samadhi) practised together are called samyama . Patanjali names five kleshas (afflictions) that bind the mind: avidya (ignorance, the root of the rest), asmita (egoism / I-am-ness), raga (attachment to pleasure), dvesha (aversion to pain), and abhinivesha (clinging to life, fear of death). Yoga also describes four states of consciousness : jagrat (waking), swapna (dream), sushupti (deep dreamless sleep), and turiya ("the fourth", pure witnessing consciousness underlying the other three). Samadhi itself has grades, broadly samprajnata (with an object / seed) maturing into asamprajnata (objectless / seedless, nirbija) absorption. 9.4 Vedanta: Brahman, Atman, and the Five Sheaths Vedanta ("the end of the Vedas", based on the Upanishads) culminates in the Advaita (non-dual) teaching of Adi Shankara . Its claim is radical: there is only one reality, Brahman , and the individual self, Atman , is identical with it. The appearance of a separate world and separate selves is maya (illusion / superimposition). Liberation is not attaining something new but realizing what was always true, summed up in the great saying (mahavakya) "Tat Tvam Asi" , "Thou art That." Vedanta analyses the person as five concentric koshas (sheaths) covering the Atman, from grossest to subtlest: Kosha Sheath of Level Annamaya Food (the physical body) Gross Pranamaya Vital energy / breath Subtle Manomaya Mind (sensory-emotional) Subtle Vijnanamaya Intellect / discernment Subtle Anandamaya Bliss Causal (innermost) Trap Do not confuse Samkhya with Advaita Vedanta . Samkhya is dualist (two realities: Purusha + Prakriti) and is atheistic / non-theistic (no creator God needed). Advaita Vedanta is non-dualist (only Brahman is real; the world is maya). And while Samkhya is non-theistic, Yoga takes the same metaphysics but adds Ishvara , so Yoga is theistic. "Dualism = Samkhya, non-dualism = Advaita" is the line examiners test. 9.5 Buddhist Psychology Buddhism is a nāstika system but one of the most psychologically sophisticated. Its core is the Four Noble Truths : Dukkha — life involves suffering / unsatisfactoriness Samudaya — the cause of suffering is craving / attachment (tanha) Nirodha — suffering can cease (nirvana) Magga — the way to cessation is the Eightfold Path The Noble Eightfold Path covers right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration (grouped as wisdom, ethical conduct, and mental discipline). Three "marks of existence" frame Buddhist psychology: anicca (impermanence, nothing is fixed), dukkha (unsatisfactoriness), and anatta (no-self, there is no permanent, unchanging soul, directly opposing the Hindu Atman). The person is only a bundle of five skandhas (aggregates): form (rupa), sensation (vedana), perception (samjna), mental formations (samskara), and consciousness (vijnana). Experience arises through dependent origination (pratitya-samutpada): every state conditions the next in a chain, so there is no independent self at the centre. Trap Anatta (Buddhism) vs Atman (Vedanta). Vedanta affirms an eternal self (Atman = Brahman); Buddhism denies any permanent self (anatta / anatman). This direct opposition is a favourite MCQ. Buddhist practice of mindfulness ( sati ) and insight meditation ( vipassana ) has had an enormous modern clinical impact: it is the root of MBSR (Kabat-Zinn's Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction), MBCT (Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy for relapse prevention in depression), and the mindfulness/acceptance components of DBT and ACT. This is the clearest bridge between Eastern systems and contemporary evidence-based therapy. 9.6 Clinical Relevance and the Modern Indian Psychology Movement Several Indian constructs map directly onto clinical and personality psychology: Triguna model in assessment. The sattva-rajas-tamas scheme is used as an indigenous personality framework; Indian inventories such as the Vedic Personality Inventory and various Triguna scales measure a person's guna profile, an alternative to Western trait models. The self. Indian thought distinguishes the ego/personality from a deeper witnessing self, and tends toward a collectivistic, relational, embedded self, contrasting with the bounded, individualistic Western self. The Purusharthas , the four legitimate aims of life: dharma (duty / righteousness), artha (wealth / livelihood), kama (pleasure / desire), and moksha (liberation). A balanced, integrated life pursues all four, with moksha as the highest. The Bhagavad Gita's psychology. The Gita offers three complementary paths (yogas): Karma yoga (the path of action), Bhakti yoga (the path of devotion), and Jnana yoga (the path of knowledge). Its central teaching, nishkama karma (desireless / non-attached action, acting fully but renouncing attachment to the fruits), is widely cited for stress regulation and resilience. The modern Indian psychology movement seeks to recover these ideas as a scientific psychology. An early landmark is Jadunath Sinha's multi-volume Indian Psychology (cognition, emotion, will), which systematically extracted psychological content from the classical texts. Contemporary scholars (for example those associated with the Pondicherry / Sri Aurobindo tradition and the broader "indigenous psychology" movement) continue to develop Indian frameworks of consciousness, well-being, and self-realization as a complement to, not merely a translation of, Western psychology. High-yield Lock in the founder-text-system links: Samkhya = Kapila (Purusha/Prakriti, gunas); Yoga = Patanjali (Yoga Sutras, eight limbs, kleshas); Advaita Vedanta = Shankara (Brahman/Atman, maya, koshas); Buddhism = Four Noble Truths (anatta, anicca, skandhas). Plus the four Purusharthas (dharma-artha-kama-moksha) and the Gita's nishkama karma . 10. The Schools Side by Side: Timeline, Comparison, and Traps Everything above is one argument: each school is a reply to the one before it. Use the three tools in this section to lock the whole map down before the exam. First the timeline (who came when), then the comparison grid (what each school took as the object of study, its method, and its view of the person), then the trap recap (the swaps examiners set most often). 10.1 Timeline of the schools Era School Founder / key date Core move 1879 Structuralism Wilhelm Wundt (Leipzig lab); Edward Titchener systematised Analyse the contents of consciousness into elements via introspection 1890s-1900s Functionalism James (1890); Dewey's Reflex Arc (1896) Ask what consciousness is for : adaptation, applied psychology 1900s Psychoanalysis Sigmund Freud (Interpretation of Dreams, 1900) The dynamic unconscious drives behaviour 1912 Gestalt Max Wertheimer (phi phenomenon) Perception grasps organised wholes , not elements 1913 Behaviorism John B. Watson (manifesto); Pavlov, B. F. Skinner Study only observable behaviour ; learning by conditioning 1950s-60s Humanistic (Third Force) Maslow, Carl Rogers The whole, free, growth-seeking person 1956-67 Cognitive Miller (1956), Ulric Neisser (1967), Noam Chomsky The mind as an information processor ; mind back in science Ancient, ongoing Indian psychology Kapila, Patanjali, Shankara, Buddha Transform / transcend the mind toward liberation (moksha) 10.2 The comparison grid School Object of study Method View of the person Structuralism Structure/contents of conscious experience Analytic introspection (trained observers) A mind built of sensory elements Functionalism Functions of mind; what it does Varied; objective + applied, animal studies An organism adapting to its environment Gestalt Perceptual organisation, wholes Phenomenological experiment An active organiser of experience Behaviorism Observable behaviour (S-R) Controlled experiment; conditioning A blank slate shaped by environment Psychoanalysis The unconscious; drives and conflict Free association, dream analysis, case study Driven by unconscious instincts and early childhood Humanistic The whole person, subjective experience Phenomenology; the therapeutic relationship Free, dignified, striving toward self-actualization Cognitive Mental processes (memory, attention, thought) Controlled experiment; inference from behaviour; modelling An active information processor Indian psychology Consciousness and the self behind the mind Introspection, meditation, disciplined practice (sadhana) A witnessing consciousness seeking liberation High-yield The one-line spine of the whole unit: Structuralism = structure of consciousness; Functionalism = function of consciousness; Gestalt = organised wholes; Behaviorism = observable behaviour; Psychoanalysis = the unconscious; Humanism = the whole free person; Cognitive = information processing; Indian = liberation of consciousness. If you can say which "object of study" each school claimed, you can place any theorist or term. 10.3 The "forces" of psychology A common exam shorthand calls the major clinical traditions "forces": the first force is psychoanalysis, the second force is behaviorism, the third force is humanistic/existential psychology, and the fourth force is usually given as transpersonal (or, in some texts, multicultural) psychology. The cognitive revolution is sometimes folded in as part of a "cognitive-behavioural" mainstream rather than counted as a separate force. 10.4 Trap recap: the swaps examiners set They bait you with The correct answer "Who founded structuralism?" Edward Titchener coined and built it; Wilhelm Wundt founded experimental psychology (voluntarism) Structuralism vs functionalism Structuralism = what/structure ; functionalism = why/function Insight learning vs trial-and-error Insight = Wolfgang Köhler (sudden reorganisation); trial-and-error = Edward Thorndike (gradual) Gestalt psychology vs Gestalt therapy Wertheimer/Köhler/Koffka (perception) vs Fritz Perls (psychotherapy), unrelated Classical vs operant conditioning Classical = involuntary, antecedent elicits (Ivan Pavlov); operant = voluntary, consequence controls (B. F. Skinner) Negative reinforcement = punishment? No. Negative reinforcement increases behaviour by removing an aversive Personal vs collective unconscious Personal/dynamic = Sigmund Freud ; collective + archetypes = Carl Jung Inferiority complex; basic anxiety Inferiority/superiority = Alfred Adler ; basic anxiety = Karen Horney Psychosexual vs psychosocial stages Psychosexual = Freud ; psychosocial (8 stages, lifelong) = Erik Erikson Self-actualization vs individuation Self-actualization = Abraham Maslow ; individuation/self-realization = Jung Cognitive psychology vs cognitive therapy Science of mind = Neisser/Miller ; therapy = Aaron Beck (and Ellis's REBT) Samkhya vs Advaita Vedanta Samkhya = dualist (Purusha + Prakriti); Advaita = non-dualist (only Brahman) Atman vs anatta Eternal self (Atman) = Vedanta ; no-self (anatta) = Buddhism Memory hook If you remember nothing else, remember the chain of rebellions and one signature name per school: Wilhelm Wundt (structure), James/Dewey (function), Max Wertheimer (wholes), Watson/Skinner (behaviour), Sigmund Freud (unconscious), Maslow/Rogers (the person), Ulric Neisser (information), Patanjali (liberation). Eight names, eight schools, one century of argument, plus the timeless Indian thread.

title: Systems & Theories — Answer Explanations
text: Systems & Theories — Answer Explanations Every one of the 119 questions from the Systems & Theories mock, written out the way the test screen shows them: the correct answer and the theorist it belongs to up top, the concept built from scratch below, then each wrong option nailed to whose idea it actually is. Read it straight through to lock in who owns what, or jump to a school and skim the answer lines. Companion to the Systems & Theories teaching book and the mock itself. In this book History & Schools (19) Psychodynamic (36) Behavioural / Learning (13) Humanistic / Gestalt (21) Cognitive / Consciousness (12) Indian Psychology (18) History & Schools Q1 What do Herman Ebbinghaus, Francis Galton and Sigmund Freud share in common? ✓ Answer: D · (a) and (c) The answer is option (d) because the question rewards seeing that two separate claims are each fully true of all three men, and stopping at one undersells what they share. To place this historically, all three belong to the late nineteenth-century emergence of psychology as a science, the era when the study of mind broke away from pure philosophy and physiology and began to use real methods. Hermann Ebbinghaus (Germany, memory research), Francis Galton (England, differential psychology), and Sigmund Freud (Austria, psychoanalysis) worked in different countries and traditions and never collaborated, yet each launched a brand-new line of inquiry on his own initiative, which is exactly what option (a) means by independent pioneers. None of them merely speculated; each invented a fresh observational method to make some part of the mind studyable, which is what option (c) adds. Ebbinghaus created the nonsense-syllable technique and used himself as sole subject to chart the forgetting curve , bringing the experimental rigour of Wilhelm Wundt 's new science to the higher process of memory. Galton pioneered the measurement of individual differences , devising questionnaires, twin studies, mental tests, and the statistical idea of correlation , seeding psychometrics and behaviour genetics. Freud developed clinical tools like free association and dream interpretation to probe the unconscious, opening the dynamic/clinical tradition that ran parallel to the academic labs. Because both the pioneer claim and the novel-method claim hold for every one of the three, the combined option is correct. Lock in: when two single options are each independently true and a 'both' choice exists, the 'both' choice usually wins, so never stop at the first correct-looking answer. Panwar key: Herman Ebbinghaus, Francis Galton and Sigmund Freud, all 3 of them worked independently and were pioneers in the field of psychology. And they developed novel observational methods to study how the mind works. Why the other options are traps A. Each of them worked independently and were pioneers in the field of psychology Option (a) names their independent, pioneering originality, which is genuinely true of Ebbinghaus, Francis Galton and Sigmund Freud, so it tempts you to stop early. But it captures only half of what they share and ignores option (c)'s equally true point that each invented a new observational method. Because (c) is also correct, the combined choice (d) is the complete answer, making (a) true but incomplete. B. Each of them founded a formal psychology laboratory Founding a formal psychology laboratory belongs to Wilhelm Wundt , who opened the first lab at Leipzig in 1879 ; it is the standard distractor in any history item about early figures. None of these three founded such a lab: Hermann Ebbinghaus did self-experiments, Galton ran an anthropometric measurement station, and Sigmund Freud worked clinically. So this statement is simply false of all three and cannot be what they share. C. Each of them developed novel observational methods to study how the mind works Option (c), the invention of novel observational methods, is fully true of all three (nonsense syllables, correlation, free association), so it is tempting in its own right. The catch is that it describes only their methodological side and leaves out option (a)'s equally true point about independent pioneering. Since both single claims hold, the combined option (d) is the better and more complete answer. Q2 In which year the first mental hospital in the USA was opened? ✓ Answer: B · 1753 The answer is 1753 because that is when the Pennsylvania Hospital in Philadelphia, the first hospital in the United States, opened its doors and, crucially, admitted patients with mental illness from the very start. To see why this date matters in the history of psychology, separate a general hospital from a dedicated asylum, and place the event on the historical arc of how society moved from neglect toward treatment of the mentally ill. In the colonial era, before any organised system of care, people with mental illness were typically confined at home, jailed, or left to wander; there was no public institution to receive them, and explanations of madness were still heavily moral and supernatural rather than medical. The 1753 opening sits at the very beginning of the institutional and moral-treatment story that would later run through Philippe Pinel 'unchaining' patients in France, William Tuke 's York Retreat in England, and Dorothea Dix 's mid-nineteenth-century reform crusade across America. The Pennsylvania Hospital, championed by Benjamin Franklin and physician Thomas Bond , was founded to care for the sick poor of all kinds, and among its earliest patients were several suffering from mental illness. That detail is the whole point: organised institutional care for the mentally ill in America began not inside a separate asylum but within this general hospital in 1753. Purpose-built facilities such as the Williamsburg asylum (1773), often called the first American hospital devoted solely to the mentally ill, came later, but the recognised starting line for organised treatment is the 1753 opening. Lock in the pairing: first U.S. hospital equals 1753, Philadelphia, with mental patients among its first admissions, so the answer is this general hospital and not the later dedicated asylums. Panwar key: The first hospital in the U.S. opened its doors in 1753 in Philadelphia. While it treated a variety of patients, six of its first patients suffered from mental illness. Why the other options are traps A. 1693 1693 is far too early; the American colonies had no public hospital of any kind at that point, and the care of the mentally ill was still entirely informal (home confinement or jail). The number is a near-miss decoy designed to tempt anyone who only half-remembers a late-seventeenth-century date, but no American mental hospital existed then. C. 1793 1793 is a real and memorable Philadelphia date, but it marks the catastrophic yellow-fever epidemic that devastated the city, not the founding of any hospital. The question pairs the right city with the wrong event to bait you. The Pennsylvania Hospital had already been open for forty years by 1793, so this cannot be the founding year. D. 1547 1547 is the year London's Bethlem Hospital (the infamous 'Bedlam') was granted to the City and became a dedicated asylum, in England , not the USA. It is a tempting distractor because Bethlem is the most famous early institution for the insane. But the question asks specifically about the first American mental hospital, so an English date is wrong by country. Q3 Who established the first laboratory for experimental study of psychology? ✓ Answer: C · Wundt The answer is Wundt because Wilhelm Wundt opened the first laboratory devoted to the experimental study of psychology, and that single act is conventionally treated as the founding moment of psychology as an independent science. To grasp why this is such a landmark, place it on the historical arc. Before 1879 the study of the mind belonged to two parent disciplines: philosophy , which reasoned about mind from the armchair, and physiology , which studied the body's sensory and nervous machinery (figures like Weber, Fechner and Helmholtz). There was no separate discipline that examined mental processes through controlled experiment. Wundt fused the two when he founded his laboratory at the University of Leipzig in 1879 , Germany, deliberately creating a space where conscious experience could be measured under controlled conditions, for instance by timing reactions to stimuli (mental chronometry) and training observers to report their sensations through introspection . Because he founded both the lab and a formal research programme with students (Edward Titchener, Hall, Cattell and others) who then carried the method across Europe and America, Wundt is called the father of experimental psychology , and the school he launched is structuralism (later systematised by his pupil Titchener). He thus sits at the precise hinge between the pre-scientific philosophy of mind that came before and the procession of modern schools that followed: structuralism, then functionalism, then behaviourism, Gestalt, psychoanalysis and the cognitive era. Every later force in the history of psychology defines itself in part by how it agrees with or revolts against the experimental, consciousness-studying programme Wundt began in that room in Leipzig. The fact to lock in is the trio of name, year and place: Wundt, 1879, Leipzig. If a question asks who founded the first psychology laboratory or who made psychology an experimental science, the answer is Wundt, not the physiologists or differential-psychology figures who preceded or accompanied him. Panwar key: Wilhelm Wundt opened the first laboratory of psychology in 1879, in Leipzig, Germany. Why the other options are traps A. Galton Francis Galton belongs to the same founding era and did pioneer mental testing, individual differences, and his 'anthropometric laboratory' for measuring people, which makes 'laboratory' a tempting word-match. But Galton's was a measurement station for collecting data on the public, not a research laboratory for the controlled experimental study of consciousness, and it came after Leipzig. He did not found experimental psychology. B. Weber Ernst Weber was a physiologist whose work on sensory thresholds (Weber's law, the just-noticeable difference) directly fed into the new experimental psychology, so he is a plausible-sounding 'early scientist of the mind'. However, Weber studied sensation as physiology and founded no psychology laboratory; he is a precursor to Wilhelm Wundt, not the founder of the discipline's first lab. D. Jung Carl Jung is a famous name in psychology, which makes him an easy lure, but he was a psychoanalyst who founded analytical psychology in the early twentieth century. He was born in 1875, only four years before the Leipzig lab opened, worked in the clinical/depth tradition rather than the experimental one, and founded no early experimental laboratory. Q4 American Psychological Association (APA) was founded in: ✓ Answer: A · 1892 The answer is 1892 because the American Psychological Association was founded in July of that year, and the place and people are worth fixing alongside the date. The APA was organised at Clark University in Worcester, Massachusetts, when a small group of psychologists met to create a national society to advance psychology as a science and profession. Its driving force and first president was G. Stanley Hall , himself a giant of early American psychology: he studied in Wundt's Leipzig tradition, is credited with opening one of the first U.S. psychology laboratories (at Johns Hopkins), founded the first American psychology journal, and trained many of the country's earliest psychologists, which is why he was the natural figure to convene the new body. To place this historically, the 1890s were the moment American psychology came of age and detached itself from philosophy and physiology. The discipline born in Wundt's Leipzig laboratory in 1879 had crossed the Atlantic; William James had just published his landmark Principles of Psychology (1890); structuralism and the emerging functionalism were competing for direction; laboratories were multiplying on American campuses; and practitioners needed a shared organisation for standards, communication and annual meetings. The APA filled exactly that role and has since grown into the largest professional psychology body in the world, marking the professional, institutional phase of psychology's becoming a science. The cluster to lock in is: APA, 1892, Clark University, G. Stanley Hall as first president. Watch the year carefully, because the 1892 founding is easy to blur with the dates of subsequent annual meetings, the first formal convention, or later expansions; the foundational year this question tests is 1892. Panwar key: The American Psychological Association was formed in July 1892 at Clark University, Worcester, Massachusetts, United States. Why the other options are traps B. 1893 1893 is a deliberate off-by-one decoy. It sits right next to the true founding year and is exactly the kind of near-miss that catches a candidate who recalls 'early 1890s' but not the precise digit. It is not the APA's founding year, which was 1892; treat the one-year gap as the whole trap. C. 1896 1896 is a genuinely important date in American psychology, which is what makes it dangerous: it is the year Lightner Witmer opened the first psychological clinic (at the University of Pennsylvania), launching clinical psychology. The question is counting on you to confuse two different 'firsts'. It is not when the APA was founded, so it is wrong here. D. 1897 1897 postdates the APA's 1892 founding by five years and is simply a later year offered to muddy the timeline. There is no major APA-founding event in 1897, so it functions purely as a distractor for anyone unsure whether the association formed in the early or late 1890s. Q5 What is true about Structuralism? ✓ Answer: A · Aim was to create a "periodic table" of the "elements of sensations" The answer is option (a) because the defining, signature ambition of structuralism was to build the mental equivalent of chemistry's periodic table, cataloguing the basic elements of sensation . To understand this, place the school on the historical arc. Structuralism, founded by Wilhelm Wundt in his 1879 Leipzig laboratory and systematised by his English-born American student Edward Titchener , was the very first formal school of psychology after the discipline became a science. Its core assumption was openly borrowed from the chemistry of the day: just as complex substances reduce to a finite set of chemical elements, complex conscious experience should reduce to a finite set of irreducible mental elements, namely sensations, images and affective feelings. The method for isolating these elements was trained introspection , in which disciplined observers reported the raw contents of their awareness (the quality, intensity and duration of an experience) under controlled conditions. The aim was thus both analytic and descriptive: dissect consciousness into its atoms and arrange them into an orderly table of sensory elements. Historically, structuralism was soon challenged by functionalism (which asked what the mind is for, not what it is made of) and then largely swept aside by behaviourism , which rejected the study of consciousness altogether. Historically this was the discipline's first attempt to look like a hard science, modelling itself on chemistry's success in reducing matter to elements; its eventual failure (introspective reports proved unreliable and irreproducible between laboratories) helped trigger both functionalism and the behaviourist revolt. While structuralists did also care about consciousness in a general sense, the answer the question rewards is the unique, signature goal: the periodic table of sensations. Lock this in: structuralism equals reducing consciousness to elemental sensations, which is why option (a) beats the vaguer option (b) and why the behaviourist-flavoured option (c) is simply wrong. Panwar key: Structuralism was the first approach to understanding psychology after the field was born. The aim was to understand and be able to well describe the structures of which the human mind is formed. It also aimed at creating a table of elements of sensations like the periodic table in chemistry. Why the other options are traps B. Aim was to understand the nature of consciousness Option (b), understanding the nature of consciousness, is loosely true of structuralism and so is a tempting 'safe' choice, but it is too broad and vague: it describes the general territory rather than structuralism's distinctive aim. The signature goal the key prefers is the 'periodic table of sensations' in option (a). And option (d) 'all the above' is impossible because option (c) is false, so (b) cannot be folded into a correct 'all' answer. C. Aim was to study the behaviour and not mind Studying behaviour and not the mind describes behaviourism (John B. Watson, B. F. Skinner), the school that explicitly rejected introspection and consciousness, which is the direct opposite of structuralism. It is placed here precisely to bait a student who has not separated the schools. Structuralism studied the mind via introspection, so this statement is false of it, and its falsity is also what sinks option (d). D. all the above 'All the above' is a tempting catch-all, but it can only be correct if every component statement is true, and option (c) (behaviour not mind) flatly contradicts structuralism. Because one of the bundled claims is false, the whole 'all the above' option collapses; this is the classic rule that a single false member kills an 'all of the above' choice. Q6 According to John Dewey, ____ is the connection between sensory stimuli and motor responses. ✓ Answer: B · Reflex arc The answer is the reflex arc because in his famous 1896 paper The Reflex Arc Concept in Psychology , John Dewey took the reflex arc, the supposed connection between sensory stimulus and motor response, as his explicit subject and target of criticism. To understand the concept, start with what a reflex arc means in physiology: a stimulus excites a sensory (afferent) pathway, which connects through the nervous system to a motor (efferent) pathway, producing a response, usually diagrammed as a one-way stimulus-then-response chain. To place this historically, Dewey's paper is a founding statement of American functionalism (the Chicago school) and an early shot against the emerging stimulus-response (S-R) psychology that would harden into behaviourism under John B. Watson. The S-R view treated 'stimulus' and 'response' as two separate, basic building blocks of behaviour stitched together. Dewey argued that this carving is artificial: sensation and movement are not two detachable units but phases of one continuous, coordinated act of adaptation, in which the response loops back and reshapes how the next stimulus is even perceived (the child reaching for the candle flame is one organised act, not stimulus then separate response). Physiology, he said, implies a unity of coordinated action, whereas the old psychology wrongly treated stimulus and response as separable. This emphasis on the whole adaptive act, and on function over fixed elements, is exactly what makes the paper functionalist and a bridge toward later organism-centred and Gestalt-flavoured thinking. The fact to lock in: the term Dewey defined and then criticised is the reflex arc (the sensory-stimulus-to-motor-response connection), and his contribution was to reject its fragmentation in favour of a unified, functional act. Panwar key: John Dewey's Education theory based on his concept of functional psychology, focused on action and application. It went against the traditional concept of stimulus-response. Dewey through his theory argued that the neural circuitry of the reflex arc was being misinterpreted by behaviourist psychology which was using stimulus and response as basic units. Physiology implied a unity of coordinated action, but psychology was treating 'stimulus' and 'response' as separable. Why the other options are traps A. Efferent arc The 'efferent arc' names only the outgoing motor limb of the pathway (efferent meaning carrying signals away from the centre toward the muscles), which is genuinely part of the picture and so sounds technical and plausible. But it is just one half of the connection; the reflex arc is the whole afferent-to-efferent loop John Dewey discussed. Picking the half-term misses the unified concept he was actually targeting. C. Association arc 'Association arc' is not a term John Dewey used, and it borrows the respectable-sounding word 'association' (from associationist psychology) to seem like a real technical concept. There is no such named structure in Dewey's reflex-arc paper, so it is a pure fabrication distractor designed to tempt anyone who does not recall the exact phrase 'reflex arc'. D. Dynamic arc 'Dynamic arc' likewise is not a recognised Dewey concept; it sounds appealing because John Dewey's whole point was that the act is dynamic and continuous rather than static. The examiner is weaponising the spirit of his argument to invent a plausible-but-false label. The concept he actually named and critiqued was the reflex arc, not any 'dynamic arc'. Q7 According to Titchener, Introspection is a highly specialised form of ______ in which the psychologist attempts to study his own consciousness scientifically. ✓ Answer: D · Self observation The answer is self observation because that is precisely how Edward Titchener framed his trained method: introspection is a highly specialised form of self-observation in which the psychologist studies his own consciousness scientifically. To understand this, place Titchener and his project on the historical map. Titchener was Wundt's English-born student who carried the new German laboratory psychology to America and founded structuralism at Cornell in the 1890s, the school whose aim, inherited from Wundt's 1879 Leipzig programme, was to reduce mental life to its elemental sensations, images and affective states. Reaching those elements cannot be done by watching behaviour from outside; it requires a disciplined inward look, and Titchener characterised that look as a comparatively neutral, systematic act of observing the self , sharply distinct from casual everyday reflection. His trained observers (often called 'reagents') learned to report the raw qualities of an experience, its quality, intensity, duration and clearness, while avoiding the stimulus error , the mistake of naming the object instead of describing the bare sensation it produced (saying 'an apple' rather than 'a round red patch with these brightness and hue qualities'). So introspection for Titchener was self-observation made rigorous and scientific, a controlled report of conscious contents rather than ordinary thinking, perceiving or merely attending. Historically this very method became structuralism's fatal vulnerability: trained introspection proved unreliable and irreproducible between laboratories, with different labs reporting different 'elements', which is exactly what let behaviourism (John B. Watson, 1913) dismiss the whole enterprise as unscientific and shift psychology to observable behaviour. The distinction to lock in: Titchener's introspection is defined as a specialised form of self-observation, the neutral scientific watching of one's own conscious contents, which is why the answer is self observation and not attention, self-perception or self-thinking. Panwar key: According to Titchener, Introspection is a highly specialised form of self observation in which the psychologist attempts to study his own consciousness scientifically. Self-observation is the relatively neutral approach to study the self and was used by Edward Tichener. Why the other options are traps A. Self perception 'Self-perception' is the term from Daryl Bem's 1960s self-perception theory, the idea that we infer our own attitudes by observing our behaviour, a social-psychology concept from a completely different era and tradition. It is a tempting near-synonym because both involve the self, but Edward Titchener's structuralist method was about directly reporting the contents of consciousness, not inferring attitudes from behaviour. B. Self thinking 'Self thinking' is not a recognised technical term anywhere in structuralism's account of introspection; it is offered because it loosely echoes the idea of an inward mental act. Edward Titchener's method was deliberately distinguished from ordinary thinking, since thinking is itself one of the conscious contents to be observed, not the act of observation. The fabricated phrase is there to catch a loose match. C. Attention 'Attention' is a real and central topic in early experimental psychology (the focusing of consciousness on a stimulus), which makes it a credible decoy. But attention is an object of study, a process the introspecting observer might report on, not the act of observing one's own consciousness. Edward Titchener defined introspection as self-observation, so naming the studied process instead of the method is the trap here. Q8 The aim of Functionalism was to study ______ as it functions in adapting the ______ to its environment. ✓ Answer: B · Mind, Organism The answer is option (b), mind then organism , because the classic aim of functionalism was to study the mind as it functions in adapting the organism to its environment. To understand this, place functionalism on the historical arc and contrast it with the school it reacted against. Structuralism (Wundt's Leipzig lab and Titchener at Cornell) was the first force, asking what the mind is made of and breaking consciousness into elemental sensations through introspection. Functionalism , the distinctively American second force, was led in spirit by William James at Harvard and developed by John Dewey and James Angell at the University of Chicago around the turn of the twentieth century; it asked instead what the mind is for . This shift was driven by Charles Darwin's theory of evolution: if every biological feature exists because it aids survival, then mental processes (perceiving, remembering, feeling, willing) must also serve an adaptive purpose. The guiding question therefore became practical and biological: how do mental processes help a living creature meet the demands of its surroundings and survive? In that formula the mind is the thing studied, and the organism is what the mind serves by adapting it to its environment. This adaptive emphasis is why functionalism is often described as importing Darwinian thinking into psychology, and why it later seeded evolutionary psychology downstream and the whole tradition of applied psychology (education, industry, mental testing). The order of the blanks is exactly what the question tests: study the mind as it adapts the organism, not the reverse. Lock in the phrasing precisely: functionalism studies the mind functioning to adapt the organism to its environment. Panwar key: Functionalism was an early approach after the idea of Cartesian duality was popular. The aim was to study the mind as it functions in adapting the organism to its environment. Why the other options are traps A. Organism, Mind Option (a) uses the right two words, 'organism' and 'mind', but in the reversed order, which is exactly the trap, since careless readers grab the familiar terms without checking the slots. Functionalism studies the mind as the thing that functions to adapt the organism; making the organism adapt the mind inverts the entire logic and contradicts the Darwinian, survival-serving role functionalism assigned to mental processes. C. Thinking, Organism Option (c) narrows the first blank to 'thinking', which is tempting because thinking is an obvious mental activity. But functionalism's declared object of study was the mind in its broad sense, the whole sweep of mental processes serving adaptation, not the single faculty of thinking. Substituting one narrow process for the general subject matter makes this both too narrow and historically inaccurate. D. Attention, Individual Option (d) offers 'attention' and 'individual', both real psychology terms, which lends it a plausible feel. Attention, however, is just one specific mental process, not the overarching subject matter functionalism set out to study, and 'individual' does not match the biological framing of 'organism' adapting to its environment. The mismatch on both blanks rules it out. Q9 ______ of the American Psychological Association represents Health Psychology. ✓ Answer: B · Division 38 The answer is Division 38 because that is the APA division designated for Health Psychology , now formally called the Society for Health Psychology. To understand the answer, you need to know how the American Psychological Association is organised. Rather than being one undifferentiated body, the APA (founded 1892, the institutional milestone in psychology's becoming a profession) is split into numbered divisions, each representing a distinct specialty or interest area; the numbers roughly track the order in which divisions were chartered, not any ranking of importance, so they function as essentially arbitrary labels. Division 38 is devoted to the psychological dimensions of physical health and illness: how behaviour, stress, beliefs and emotions influence the onset and course of disease; how to promote healthy behaviour; and how psychologists work inside the healthcare system to prevent, treat and manage illness and disability. As a field, health psychology emerged as a recognised force in the 1970s, alongside the rise of behavioural medicine, and rests on the biopsychosocial model articulated by George Engel (1977), which holds that health and illness arise from the interplay of biological, psychological and social factors rather than biology alone, a direct challenge to the older purely biomedical model that the discipline helped overturn. The APA recognises clinical health psychology as a professional specialty, and Division 38 is its organisational home. The fact to lock in is the simple pairing: Division 38 equals Health Psychology. Because division numbers are arbitrary chartering labels rather than meaningful codes, this is purely a memory item, so anchor it firmly as 38 for health and do not let it slide into the neighbouring numbered divisions. Panwar key: Division 38 of the American Psychological Association represents Health Psychology. Under APA (American Psychological Association) clinical health psychology is a professionally recognized specialty that investigates and implements clinical services across diverse populations and settings to promote health and well-being and to prevent, treat and manage illness and disability. Why the other options are traps A. Division 16 Division 16 is the Division of School Psychology , the specialty serving children and education systems. It is a real, well-known division, which is what makes it a strong decoy, but it has nothing to do with physical health and illness. Health psychology is Division 38, so 16 is simply the wrong number attached to a different (and easily confused) applied specialty. C. Division 47 Division 47 is the Society for Sport, Exercise and Performance Psychology . It is a tempting trap because exercise and physical wellness sit close to the idea of 'health', and a hurried reader may equate sport/fitness with health psychology. But sport and exercise psychology is its own distinct division focused on athletic performance, not the biopsychosocial study of illness, which belongs to Division 38. D. Division 98 There is no Division 98 representing health psychology, or indeed any APA division numbered that high in this context; it is a pure fabrication distractor. The large, round-feeling number is offered to catch anyone with no firm recall who might gamble on a high number. The correct, real designation for health psychology is Division 38. Q10 Which of the following historical perspectives gave rise to the evolutionary perspective? ✓ Answer: D · Functionalism The answer is functionalism because the evolutionary perspective grew directly out of functionalism's central question, which was what mental processes are for . To understand the lineage, start with functionalism itself and its place on the historical arc. Founded in spirit by William James and developed by the Chicago school (John Dewey, Angell), functionalism arose in late-nineteenth-century America as a reaction against structuralism. Where structuralism dissected the contents of consciousness, functionalism, deeply shaped by Charles Darwin's theory of evolution, asked how consciousness helps an organism adapt to and survive in its environment. That made adaptation , purpose and survival value the heart of psychological explanation. Evolutionary psychology , a modern perspective that crystallised in the late twentieth century (associated with figures like Tooby, Cosmides and Buss), takes exactly this adaptive logic and pushes it further: it explains behaviours and mental traits as products of natural selection , asking how a given tendency would have improved survival and reproduction in ancestral environments. So the conceptual bridge between the two is the shared focus on function and adaptive value; functionalism interpreted thought and behaviour through their usefulness to the organism, and evolutionary psychology reframes that usefulness in terms of inherited, gene-based adaptations. The other schools, by contrast, centred quite different things and so could not have produced the adaptive logic: structuralism (Wilhelm Wundt, Edward Titchener) catalogued what consciousness contains ; psychoanalysis (Freud) explained behaviour through unconscious drives and childhood conflict; and behaviourism (John B. Watson, B. F. Skinner) reduced it to learned stimulus-response links forged by the environment in a single lifetime. None of these placed inherited adaptive function at the centre. Functionalism alone made 'what is this mental process for, and how does it aid survival' the organising question, and evolutionary psychology simply re-rooted that question in genes and natural selection. The distinction to lock in: it is functionalism, with its Darwinian adaptive emphasis, that seeded the modern evolutionary perspective. Panwar key: Functionalism paved the way for the understanding and interpreting human evolution and behaviour from a perspective that focused on the functionality aspect of thought and behaviour, the choices and the fears that people make and have. Why the other options are traps A. behaviourism Behaviourism (John B. Watson, B. F. Skinner) studied observable conditioned responses and explicitly banned talk of inner mental states or adaptive 'purpose', leaning on learning rather than inherited function. It is a tempting distractor because it is biological-sounding and scientific, but its whole stance, environment-driven learning over inherited adaptation, is conceptually opposed to the evolutionary emphasis on naturally selected traits, so it did not give rise to it. B. Structuralism Structuralism (Wilhelm Wundt, Edward Titchener) analysed consciousness into its elemental sensations and deliberately ignored questions of purpose, function or survival value. It is offered because it is an early foundational school, but its static, element-cataloguing aim is the exact opposite of the adaptive, functional thinking that fed evolutionary psychology. Structuralism actually provoked functionalism as a reaction, rather than seeding the evolutionary view. C. Psychoanalysis Psychoanalysis (Freud) explored unconscious drives, childhood conflict and instinctual energy. The word 'instinct' can make it feel biological and therefore evolutionary, which is the bait. But psychoanalysis explained behaviour through intrapsychic conflict and developmental history, not through the adaptive function of mental processes shaped by natural selection, so it is not the parent of the evolutionary perspective. Q11 Who is the most associated with the techniques of introspection? ✓ Answer: A · Wundt The answer is Wundt because Wilhelm Wundt is the figure most identified with the technique of introspection , having made it the signature method of the first scientific psychology. To understand this, recall what introspection meant in his hands and where it sits on the historical arc. It was not casual self-reflection but a trained, controlled, almost experimental procedure (sometimes called experimental self-observation ): observers were given a precise, repeatable stimulus and asked to report the immediate contents of their own consciousness, such as the quality, intensity and duration of a sensation, under standardised laboratory conditions, with trials repeated to check reliability. Wundt founded the first psychology laboratory at the University of Leipzig in 1879 , Germany, the act conventionally treated as psychology's birth as a science, and built his school, structuralism , around this method, using it to break conscious experience into its elemental components on analogy with chemistry. His student Edward Titchener later carried introspection to America and refined it (including the concept of the stimulus error ), but the technique is most associated with Wundt as its originator within experimental psychology. The historical contrast worth holding is the cast of other founders, each tied to a different force: William James founded functionalism and was sceptical of rigid introspection; John Watson founded behaviourism (1913) and rejected introspection outright as unscientific, demanding the study of observable behaviour instead; and Max Wertheimer founded Gestalt psychology, which studied whole perceptual forms. Indeed, introspection's eventual unreliability between laboratories is exactly what gave behaviourism its opening to dismiss the method. The fact to lock in: Wundt plus introspection plus the Leipzig 1879 lab plus structuralism form one tight cluster, so when introspection is named, the default answer is Wundt. Panwar key: Wilhelm Wundt, the founder of modern psychology, a proponent of the structuralist perspective, used the technique of introspection to understand and interpret the human mind. He started the first psychology laboratory in Leipzig, Germany. Why the other options are traps B. James William James is from the same founding generation and certainly used and discussed introspection, which makes him a credible choice. But James founded functionalism and was openly critical of the rigid, element-hunting introspection that Wilhelm Wundt and Edward Titchener practised, favouring a more naturalistic study of the 'stream of consciousness'. He is not the figure most associated with the introspective technique ; that is Wundt. C. Watson John Watson is a strong trap precisely because his name is tightly linked to introspection, but for the opposite reason: in his 1913 behaviourist manifesto he explicitly rejected introspection as unscientific and unverifiable, insisting psychology study only observable behaviour. Choosing him reverses the relationship. He is the great opponent of introspection, not its proponent, so he is wrong here. D. Wertheimer Max Wertheimer founded Gestalt psychology , which studied whole perceptual organisations ('the whole is greater than the sum of its parts') and reacted against the atomistic, element-by-element approach that introspection served. He is offered as a famous early-school founder to tempt the unsure, but his method and aims were about perceptual wholes, not the introspective reporting of elemental conscious contents. Q12 Which among the following branches of Psychology specifically studies behaviour in relation to genetic inheritance? ✓ Answer: A · Evolutionary Psychology The answer is evolutionary psychology because it is the branch that specifically explains behaviour in relation to genetic inheritance and the action of natural selection. To understand it, start with its founding logic and its place on the historical arc. Evolutionary psychology applies Charles Darwin's nineteenth-century theory of evolution to the mind, treating psychological traits, like any other biological feature, as products of the selection pressures faced by our ancestors. Conceptually it is the modern descendant of functionalism (William James, Chicago school), the early force that first asked what mental processes are for in adapting an organism to its environment; evolutionary psychology took that adaptive question and grounded it in genetics, crystallising as a named perspective in the late twentieth century through figures such as Leda Cosmides , John Tooby and David Buss . The core idea is that tendencies which improved survival and reproduction were passed down through the genes , so present-day behaviour carries the imprint of inherited adaptations shaped in the ancestral 'environment of evolutionary adaptedness'. It therefore deliberately fuses psychology with biology, asking why a given emotion, mate preference, or fear exists by reconstructing the adaptive problem it once solved. That is exactly what binds it to genetic inheritance: the explanatory chain runs from ancestral environment, to naturally selected genes, to an inherited behavioural tendency in the modern organism. By contrast, developmental psychology studies change across the lifespan, health psychology studies behaviour and illness, and experimental psychology names a method, not a content area. The distinction to lock in: when a question ties behaviour specifically to genes, heredity or natural selection, the answer is evolutionary psychology, because heredity and adaptation are its defining lens. Panwar key: Evolutionary psychology is a scientific discipline that approaches human behaviour through a lens that incorporates the effects of evolution. It combines the science of psychology with the study of biology. It specifically studies behaviour in relation to genetic inheritance. Why the other options are traps B. Development Psychology Developmental psychology studies how behaviour and abilities change across the lifespan, from infancy to old age, and it does engage genes through the nature-nurture debate, which is the tempting overlap. But it weighs nature and nurture together over time rather than focusing specifically on genetic inheritance and natural selection. The question's exact phrase 'in relation to genetic inheritance' points to evolutionary psychology, not the broader developmental field. C. Health Psychology Health psychology studies how psychological factors (stress, behaviour, beliefs) affect physical health and illness, working from the biopsychosocial model. The word 'biology' in its territory can make it feel gene-related, which is the bait. But its focus is health behaviour and the course of illness, not the inheritance of behavioural traits through genes, so it does not match a question about genetic inheritance. D. Experimental Psychology Experimental psychology is defined by its method , the use of controlled laboratory experiments, rather than by any particular subject matter, and it can be applied to memory, perception, learning and more. It is offered because it sounds rigorous and scientific. But it is not a content branch organised around genetic inheritance; choosing it confuses a methodology with a subject focus, so it is wrong here. Q13 Which among the following Schools of Thought used Introspection as a method of analysis? ✓ Answer: C · Structuralism The answer is structuralism because it is the school of thought built on introspection as its method of analysis. To understand why, recall structuralism's purpose and its place on the historical arc. Founded by Wilhelm Wundt in his 1879 Leipzig laboratory, the moment psychology became an independent science, and systematised by his English-born student Edward Titchener at Cornell, structuralism was the very first formal school of the new discipline. Its aim, borrowed from chemistry, was to reduce mental life to its most basic elements, such as sensations, images and affective feelings, and to assemble them into something like a periodic table of the mind. To reach those elements you cannot simply watch behaviour from outside; you must look inward in a disciplined way, which is exactly what introspection provided: a trained, systematic report of the raw contents of one's own consciousness under controlled laboratory conditions, with observers describing the bare qualities of an experience (intensity, duration, quality) rather than naming the object that caused it, thereby avoiding the stimulus error . So introspection and structuralism are tightly bound, the method serving the school's analytic goal of dissecting consciousness into parts. The contrast that makes this an easy lock is the other forces: behaviourism (John B. Watson, around 1913) explicitly rejected introspection as unscientific and insisted on studying only observable behaviour; functionalism (James, John Dewey) leaned on broader observation and applied work; and psychoanalysis (Freud) used clinical methods like free association and dream analysis to reach the unconscious. Indeed, introspection's unreliability between laboratories is precisely what discredited structuralism and opened the door to behaviourism's takeover. The distinction to fix: introspection is the structuralist tool, so when a question pairs a school with introspection, choose structuralism. Panwar key: It has often been claimed that Wilhelm Wundt, the father of experimental psychology and founder of structuralism, was the first to adopt introspection to experimental psychology. The focus of structuralism was on reducing mental processes down into their most basic elements. The structuralists used techniques such as introspection to analyse the inner processes of the human mind. Why the other options are traps A. Functionalism Functionalism (James, John Dewey) is a tempting near-neighbour because it too studied consciousness and is from the same early era. But functionalism asked what consciousness is for in adaptation and drew on more varied methods, including naturalistic observation, mental testing and applied work, rather than relying on strict laboratory introspection. The signature introspective method belongs to structuralism, so functionalism is the wrong pairing. B. behaviourism Behaviourism (John B. Watson, B. F. Skinner) is the strongest trap by association, because it is famous precisely for its stance on introspection, but that stance was outright rejection : Watson dismissed introspection as unscientific and demanded the study of observable behaviour alone. Choosing it reverses the relationship the question asks about. Behaviourism is introspection's chief opponent, not a school that used it. D. Psychoanalysis Psychoanalysis (Freud) did probe the mind through inward-looking clinical techniques, which superficially resembles introspection and so tempts the unwary. But its methods were free association and dream analysis aimed at uncovering the unconscious, a clinical depth approach quite different from the structuralists' controlled laboratory introspection on conscious sensory elements. So it is not the school defined by introspection as a method of analysis. Q14 Who among the following is credited with the book titled Principles of Psychology? ✓ Answer: B · William James The answer is William James because he authored the landmark two-volume work The Principles of Psychology , published in 1890. To appreciate its importance, place James on the historical arc of psychology becoming a science. The discipline had been formally born in 1879 in Wundt's Leipzig laboratory; within a decade it crossed the Atlantic, and James, working at Harvard , became its leading American voice. Trained originally as a physician before turning to physiology, psychology and philosophy, he set up an early psychology demonstration laboratory in the United States and became the inspiration for functionalism , the approach concerned with what the mind is for and how it helps the organism adapt, a Darwinian counterweight to the structuralism of Wilhelm Wundt and Titchener that asked only what the mind is made of. The Principles of Psychology was the synthesis of more than a decade of his thinking and quickly became the foundational textbook of the discipline in America, shaping generations of students (it was so vast that James later issued a condensed version, nicknamed 'Jimmy'). In it he introduced enduring ideas: the stream of consciousness , the notion that conscious experience is a continuous, flowing whole rather than a chain of discrete elements, which directly challenged the structuralists' attempt to chop the mind into sensory atoms; the importance of habit as the 'flywheel of society'; the James-Lange theory of emotion (we feel afraid because we tremble, not the reverse); and a pioneering treatment of the self . These themes positioned James as the bridge between the new laboratory science and a broader, more practical, biologically minded psychology. The fact to lock in is the author-title-year link: James wrote The Principles of Psychology in 1890. Take particular care not to attribute it to Wundt, whose own foundational text was the confusingly similar Principles of Physiological Psychology (1873-74); the English Principles of Psychology tested here belongs to William James, not Wundt. Panwar key: The Principles of Psychology is an 1890 book about psychology by William James, an American philosopher and psychologist who trained to be a physician before going into psychology. Why the other options are traps A. Wilhelm Wundt Wilhelm Wundt is the most dangerous distractor because his foundational text is titled Principles of Physiological Psychology , which is almost identical to the title in the question. The examiner is exploiting that near-collision. But Wundt's work carries the extra word 'Physiological' and belongs to the structuralist/experimental tradition, whereas the plain Principles of Psychology (1890) was written by William James. C. B.F. Skinner B.F. Skinner is a famous name in psychology, which is the lure, but he belongs to a later era and to behaviourism , and his major works were on operant conditioning, such as The Behavior of Organisms (1938) and Science and Human Behavior . He did not write a book called Principles of Psychology , so he is wrong by both period and content. D. None of the above 'None of the above' is offered to tempt anyone uncertain about all three named figures, but it is wrong because William James clearly and famously wrote The Principles of Psychology in 1890. Since a correct named author is present in the options, the catch-all 'none' choice cannot be right. Q15 Who among the following was the first female president of the American Psychological Association (APA)? ✓ Answer: D · Mary Calkins The answer is Mary Whiton Calkins because she became the first woman to serve as president of the American Psychological Association , taking office as its 14th president in 1905.
