Q17 Herman von Helmholtz (1821-94): ✓ Answer: B · He gave the trichromatic theory of colour vision The answer is option (b) because Hermann von Helmholtz (1821 to 1894) is credited with developing the trichromatic theory of colour vision. To understand the contribution, start with the puzzle it solved. The human eye must somehow encode a vast range of colours from light, and the trichromatic theory, building on the earlier proposal of Thomas Young and therefore now called the Young-Helmholtz theory , holds that colour vision rests on three types of receptors (cones), each most sensitive to a different band of wavelengths, roughly short, medium and long, corresponding to blue, green and red. Any perceived colour arises from the relative activation of these three receptor types, which is why mixing three primaries can reproduce the visible spectrum; this account was later complemented by Ewald Hering's opponent-process theory at a different stage of the visual system. To place Helmholtz historically, he was a towering nineteenth-century physician-physicist of the physiological tradition, the parent discipline that, alongside philosophy, gave birth to scientific psychology in 1879. He belongs to the crucial pre-Wundt precursors (with Weber, Fechner and Muller) whose precise sensory measurement showed that mental and neural processes could be quantified at all, making an experimental psychology conceivable. Beyond colour, he was the first to measure the speed of nerve conduction , showing that neural signals travel at a finite, measurable rate rather than instantaneously, and that single result opened the study of reaction time and mental chronometry, a tool that runs from Wilhelm Wundt's lab straight through to modern cognitive psychology. The fact to lock in: Helmholtz equals the trichromatic (Young-Helmholtz) theory of colour vision, three cone types. Do not attach to him the just-noticeable difference (Weber and Fechner) or the law of effect (Edward Thorndike). Panwar key: Herman von Helmholtz boasts a wide range of achievements. Indeed, you will still find his color theory of vision in psychology textbooks. His work paved the way for others to investigate the psychological significance of the time taken to react to a stimulus (reaction time or response latency). This approach remains important in modern psychology. Why the other options are traps A. He was a proponent of the just noticeable difference The just-noticeable difference (jnd) and the closely related Weber's law belong to Ernst Weber and Gustav Fechner , the founders of psychophysics , not to Helmholtz. The trap works because all three men are nineteenth-century German sensory scientists from the same physiological milieu, so their contributions are easily swapped. But the jnd is a psychophysics concept, while Helmholtz's signature is colour vision and nerve speed. C. He proposed the concept of the unconscious The unconscious as a psychological construct is most associated with Sigmund Freud (with roots in earlier philosophers like Schopenhauer and Hartmann), not with Helmholtz's sensory work. The decoy has a sliver of plausibility because Helmholtz did write about 'unconscious inference' in perception, but that narrow perceptual idea is not 'the concept of the unconscious' meant here, which is the Freudian dynamic unconscious. D. He gave the law of effect The law of effect , that responses followed by satisfying consequences are strengthened, was formulated by Edward Thorndike from his puzzle-box experiments and became a cornerstone of learning theory and behaviourism. It is a famous, examinable law placed here to tempt, but it belongs to a different era and a different tradition (American connectionism/behaviourism), and has nothing to do with Helmholtz's colour vision. Q18 Which one of the following branches of philosophy of science deals with the question of existence? ✓ Answer: C · Ontology The answer is ontology because, among the branches of the philosophy of science, ontology is the one that deals with the question of existence. To understand it, define the term precisely: ontology is the branch of metaphysics concerned with what exists, the nature of being , and the kinds and structures of the entities that make up reality. The word comes from the Greek ontos (being) and logos (study), and the field asks questions such as what sorts of things exist, how they are categorised, and what it means for something to be real. This contrasts with its sister branch epistemology (from episteme , knowledge), which asks not what exists but how we can know it and what counts as valid knowledge. In research methodology the two routinely appear together as the foundation of any paradigm and directly shape method choice: your ontological stance concerns the nature of the reality you study (for example, whether a single objective reality exists, the realist view, or reality is socially constructed, the relativist view), while your epistemological stance concerns how you can come to know that reality. This pairing underlies the great historical split in the human sciences between positivist research (objective reality, measured experimentally) and interpretivist research (constructed meaning, understood qualitatively), a divide that runs right through psychology's own century-long debate about whether it should imitate the natural sciences. The other listed terms are not branches about existence: post-positivism and scientific realism are positions or paradigms within the philosophy of science (largely epistemological or metaphysical stances), and 'structuralism' here names a school of thought, not a branch dealing with being. The distinction to lock in: existence and the nature of being equals ontology, while knowing equals epistemology. Panwar key: Ontology, as a branch of philosophy, is the science of what is, of the kinds and structures of objects. In simple terms, ontology seeks the classification and explanation of entities. Ontology concerns claims about the nature of being and existence. Why the other options are traps A. Post-positivism Post-positivism is a real and important position in the philosophy of science, the successor to positivism that accepts an external reality but holds our knowledge of it is always fallible and theory-laden. That is precisely an epistemological stance about how we can know reality, not a branch studying existence itself. It is a tempting, sophisticated-sounding option, but it answers the 'how do we know' question, not the 'what exists' question. B. Structuralism Structuralism appears in this options set to exploit confusion: in psychology it is Wilhelm Wundt and Edward Titchener's school analysing the structure of consciousness, and in linguistics/anthropology it is a separate movement. Either way it is a school or method, not a branch of the philosophy of science dealing with the nature of being. It is offered to catch a psychology student who pattern-matches the familiar word, but it does not concern existence. D. Scientific realism Scientific realism is the philosophical position that successful scientific theories truly describe a mind-independent world, including its unobservable entities. It does touch on existence, which makes it a clever trap, but it is a stance or claim about whether theories track reality, an epistemological/metaphysical position, rather than the branch whose defining business is the study of being. The branch dealing with existence as such is ontology. Q19 Who is often referred to as the "Founder of Modern Psychology in India"? ✓ Answer: B · Narendra Nath Sen Gupta The answer is Narendra Nath Sen Gupta because he is regarded as the founder of modern psychology in India, having established the country's first independent psychology department. Before him, the mind in India was treated largely within philosophy and the classical speculative traditions (Vedanta, Samkhya, Yoga), with no Western-style experimental discipline on Indian soil. Sen Gupta was trained at Harvard (under figures such as Hugo Munsterberg), where he absorbed the experimental, laboratory approach to the mind that had grown directly out of the Leipzig revolution. On returning, he founded the first independent department of psychology and the first psychology laboratory in India at the University of Calcutta in 1916 , the same Calcutta milieu that would soon host India's psychoanalytic movement. This shifted Indian psychology away from a purely philosophical, armchair treatment toward systematic, laboratory-based, experimental study along Western scientific lines, which is precisely the move (philosophy to experimental science) that defines the word 'modern' in his title. He also co-authored an early Indian textbook of psychology with Radhakamal Mukerjee and helped train and work alongside the next generation, including the psychoanalyst Girindra Shekhar Bose. The cluster to lock in is: Sen Gupta, first psychology department and laboratory, University of Calcutta, 1916. Take care not to credit M.V. Gopalswamy , who founded the Mysore psychology department and did important applied and experimental work, but later than Calcutta; the recognised founder tested here is Narendra Nath Sen Gupta. Panwar key: Narendra Nath Sen Gupta is regarded as the founder of modern psychology in India. He established the first independent department of psychology in India at the University of Calcutta in 1916. Why the other options are traps A. Girindra Shekhar Bose Girindra Shekhar Bose is a strong distractor because he is a genuinely foundational figure in Indian psychology, but in a different stream: he is regarded as the father of psychoanalysis in India , founder of the Indian Psychoanalytic Society and a noted correspondent of Sigmund Freud. The question asks about modern, experimental psychology and its first department, which is Sen Gupta's distinction, not the psychoanalytic tradition Bose represents. C. Amitosh Mukherjee 'Amitosh Mukherjee' is not a recognised founder of modern psychology in India; the name is offered as a plausible-sounding Bengali academic to tempt a student who knows the discipline began in Calcutta and gambles on a Bengali-sounding name. Gopalswamy is a real and important pioneer who founded the psychology department at the University of Mysore and advanced applied and experimental psychology in India, which makes him the most credible decoy. Psychodynamic Q20 Select the incorrect pair: ✓ Answer: B · Kohlberg: Formal operations The answer is the Kohlberg pair because formal operations belongs to Jean Piaget , not to Lawrence Kohlberg , whose name is tied to moral development . To see why, you must separate two figures from the cognitive-developmental tradition , a stream that sits outside the psychodynamic schools yet is constantly tested beside them. Piaget, the Swiss genetic epistemologist , mapped how children build knowledge through four invariant cognitive stages: sensorimotor (0-2), preoperational (2-7), concrete operational (7-11), and formal operational (roughly 11+), where abstract, hypothetical, and propositional reasoning emerges. Kohlberg, working at Harvard in the 1950s-70s, took Piaget's stage logic and applied it to a different domain, moral reasoning , producing three levels (each split into two stages): preconventional (obedience, self-interest), conventional (approval, law-and-order), and postconventional (social contract, universal ethical principles). But the labels do not transfer. Formal operations describes how we think abstractly; Kohlberg's stages describe how we judge right and wrong . Historically this whole question is a distractor set: none of these belong to one school. Carl Jung (analytical psychology) and Alfred Adler (individual psychology) come from the psychodynamic split off Sigmund Freud, while Albert Ellis founded a cognitive-behavioural therapy in the 1950s. Only the Kohlberg-Piaget mismatch is factually broken. Lock in: cognitive stages, including formal operations, are Piaget's; moral-reasoning stages are Kohlberg's. Any pairing that hands Kohlberg a Piagetian term is the incorrect pair every time. It is tempting because the question hopes you forget who owns the term, but the pairing is factually correct, so it cannot be the incorrect pair being asked for. C. Q21 Who published the mechanism of hysteria in 1893? ✓ Answer: B · Freud and Breuer The answer is Sigmund Freud and Breuer because the 1893 paper on the mechanism of hysteria was the joint work of Sigmund Freud and the senior Viennese physician Josef Breuer , issued as their Preliminary Communication and expanded in 1895 into Studies on Hysteria . To place this historically, it marks the literal prehistory of psychoanalysis, the moment before Freud's mature system existed, when he was still a neurologist collaborating with an older mentor. Hysteria meant physical symptoms (paralysis, blindness, mutism, fits) with no organic cause; Breuer and Freud argued these were the bodily conversion of repressed emotional trauma . Their famous case was Breuer's patient Anna O. (Bertha Pappenheim), who discovered that her symptoms eased when she traced each one back to the forgotten memory that triggered it, a process she nicknamed the talking cure or chimney-sweeping, and which Breuer labelled catharsis . From this came the seed claim, 'hysterics suffer mainly from reminiscences', meaning blocked affect, denied normal discharge, converts into symptoms. This collaboration supplied the raw ideas, the unconscious, repression, and cure through verbal recall, that Freud would soon build into psychoanalysis proper before Breuer, uneasy with the sexual emphasis, fell away. In the historical arc, Charcot comes before (Freud's 1885-86 Paris training in hypnosis), Breuer is the 1890s co-founder, and the great defectors Alfred Adler and Jung come over a decade after , breaking from a theory that did not yet exist in 1893. Lock in the chain: the 1893 hysteria work and the Anna O. case belong to Breuer, the bridge figure between hypnosis-era medicine and psychoanalysis. Panwar key: In 1893, Sigmund Freud, along with Viennese physician Joseph Breuer, published their studies on hysteria. Why the other options are traps A. Freud and Charcot Jean-Martin Charcot , the great Parisian neurologist at the Salpetriere, taught Freud about hysteria and hypnotic suggestion in 1885-86 and powerfully shaped his thinking. He is tempting because he is the other big hysteria name from that era, but he came before the Vienna work and did not co-author the 1893 paper; that was Josef Breuer. C. Freud and Adler Alfred Adler joined Freud's Wednesday circle only around 1902 and broke away in 1911 to found Individual Psychology. He tempts because he is a famous Freud associate, but he had no involvement in the 1890s hysteria studies, which predate his arrival by roughly a decade. D. Freud and Jung Carl Jung began corresponding with Freud only in 1906 and broke from him by 1913. He is a natural decoy as the most celebrated collaborator-turned-defector, but he was a teenager in 1893 and played no part in the hysteria research with Josef Breuer. Q22 Reports on sexual behaviour of men was published by ✓ Answer: B · Alfred Kinsey The answer is Alfred Kinsey because the landmark reports on human sexual behaviour, empirical survey works rather than theory, were produced by Kinsey and his team at Indiana University. To grasp their significance, note where they sit historically: not inside the psychodynamic tradition at all, but in mid-twentieth-century empirical sexology , a deliberate break from the armchair, moralistic, and psychoanalytic treatment of sex that preceded them. Kinsey was a zoologist (originally a gall-wasp taxonomist) who imported large-scale, quantitative biological data-collection into a taboo subject. The two volumes are Sexual Behaviour in the Human Male (1948) and Sexual Behaviour in the Human Female (1953), built on thousands of confidential face-to-face interviews and co-authored with Wardell Pomeroy , Clyde Martin , and (for the female volume) Paul Gebhard , published by W.B. Saunders. Their signature contribution is the Kinsey scale , a 0-to-6 continuum running from exclusively heterosexual to exclusively homosexual, which reframed orientation as a spectrum rather than two fixed boxes. The data showed that behaviours assumed rare were widespread, making the reports both scandalous and foundational, and helping launch modern sex research that later figures like William Masters and Virginia Johnson continued. The key contrast to lock in, and the trap the question is built on, is theory versus measurement: Sigmund Freud theorized about sexuality from the clinic (libido, psychosexual stages), but Kinsey measured it through surveys. When a question asks who reported on (counted, surveyed) sexual behaviour rather than who theorized about it, the answer is Kinsey, the empiricist, not any psychoanalyst. Panwar key: The Kinsey Reports are two scholarly books on human sexual behaviour, Sexual Behaviour in the Human Male (1948) and Sexual Behaviour in the Human Female (1953), written by Alfred Kinsey, Wardell Pomeroy, Clyde Martin, and (for Sexual Behaviour in the Human Female) Paul Gebhard and published by W.B. Saunders. Why the other options are traps A. Sigmund Freud Sigmund Freud made sexuality central to personality through libido and the psychosexual stages, so he is the instinctive pick. But he theorized from individual clinical cases; he never produced the statistical, interview-based survey reports the question names. The word 'reports' signals empirical data, which is Alfred Kinsey's domain, not Freud's. C. Anna Freud Anna Freud , Sigmund's daughter, pioneered child psychoanalysis and systematized the ego defence mechanisms . She tempts via the famous surname, but her work concerned defences and child analysis, not large-scale sexual-behaviour surveys. D. Karen Horney Karen Horney was a neo-Freudian known for basic anxiety and for challenging Freud on feminine psychology (penis envy versus womb envy). Q23 Who is the father of Psychoanalysis? ✓ Answer: B · Sigmund Freud The answer is Sigmund Freud because he is universally credited as the founder of psychoanalysis , the very theory and treatment method that defines the first force of depth psychology. To teach the concept, psychoanalysis is simultaneously a model of the mind and a therapy . As a model, Freud held that the mind is largely unconscious , that behaviour is driven by instinctual urges (sexual and aggressive), and that personality is structured into the id , ego , and superego . As a therapy, it works to bring repressed unconscious conflicts into awareness through free association , dream interpretation (dreams as the 'royal road to the unconscious'), and the analysis of resistance and transference. Freud, an Austrian neurologist working in Vienna, built these ideas from his 1890s clinical work on hysteria and crystallized the dream theory in The Interpretation of Dreams (1900). Historically he is the trunk of the entire psychodynamic tree: from him branch the early loyalists and then the great defectors, Alfred Adler (Individual Psychology, broke away 1911) and Carl Jung (Analytical Psychology, broke away ~1913), followed by the neo-Freudians (Karen Horney, Erich Fromm, Harry Stack Sullivan) and the ego psychologists and object-relations theorists. Every one of those schools is a reaction to Freud, which is exactly why he, not his successors, is 'the father'. The contrast to lock in: Bernheim was a hypnosis-and-suggestion figure who influenced Freud but founded nothing of the sort, while Adler and Jung each founded a rival school under a different name. The single originator of psychoanalysis itself, the parent theory they all defined themselves against, is Freud. Panwar key: Sigmund Freud is best known as the creator of the therapeutic technique known as psychoanalysis. The Austrian-born psychiatrist greatly contributed to the understanding of human psychology in areas such as the unconscious mind, sexuality, and dream interpretation. He is regarded as the father of psychoanalysis. Why the other options are traps A. Bernheim Hippolyte Bernheim , of the Nancy school, championed hypnotic suggestion and influenced the young Sigmund Freud's early thinking about the mind. He tempts as a real historical influence, but he worked in the hypnosis tradition and never created psychoanalysis; he is upstream of it, not its author. C. Adler Alfred Adler was an early member of Sigmund Freud's circle who broke away in 1911 to found Individual Psychology , emphasizing social urges and inferiority. He tempts because he is a foundational psychodynamic name, but founding a rival school is not the same as founding psychoanalysis, which was Freud's. D. Jung Carl Jung , once Sigmund Freud's anointed heir, split off around 1913 to found Analytical Psychology with its collective unconscious and archetypes. He is a strong decoy as the most famous successor, but his system is a distinct school; the parent theory of psychoanalysis belongs to Freud alone. Q24 Freud published The Interpretation of Dreams in: ✓ Answer: A · 1900 The answer is 1900 because that is the official publication date on Freud's The Interpretation of Dreams ( Die Traumdeutung ). The historical wrinkle that makes this a favourite exam item: the book physically appeared in early November 1899 , but the Leipzig-Vienna publisher Franz Deuticke post-dated it to 1900 so it would read as a work heralding the new century. The canonical exam answer is therefore 1900, even though Panwar notes the 4 November 1899 printing. To place the work historically, it is the founding text of the mature psychoanalytic theory of the unconscious, the book where Sigmund Freud moved from the early hysteria collaboration with Breuer into a system entirely his own. Its core claim is that dreams are wish-fulfilments and the 'royal road to the unconscious'. Freud distinguished the manifest content (the dream as consciously remembered) from the latent content (the hidden, often forbidden unconscious wish behind it), connected by the dream-work , the disguising machinery of condensation , displacement , and symbolization that converts the unacceptable latent wish into an acceptable manifest image. This gave Freud a route to study the unconscious in healthy people, not only patients, and made dream analysis a central pillar of psychoanalytic technique. Within the psychodynamic arc this is the early-Freud, pre-structural-model phase (the id-ego-superego scheme came later, in 1923). Lock in two linked facts: The Interpretation of Dreams is dated 1900, and its thesis is that dreams are disguised wish-fulfilments. Remembering the dawn-of-the-century post-dating immunizes you against the 1898 and even 1899 distractors. Panwar key: Sigmund Freud published The Interpretation of Dreams on November 4th, 1899. The publication date is dated 1900. Why the other options are traps B. 1898 1898 predates the book entirely; in that year Sigmund Freud was still doing the self-analysis and dream-collection that fed the work but had not published it. It tempts students who half-remember that the writing began in the late 1890s, but the published, dated work is 1900. C. 1902 1902 is two years too late. It tempts because 1902 is when Sigmund Freud gained his professorship and the Wednesday Psychological Society began forming, real milestones, but neither is the dream book's date. D. 1904 1904 is four years too late and closer to the date of The Psychopathology of Everyday Life (1901) or later works. It is a pure distance distractor, plausible only if you have no anchor for the turn-of-the-century date. Q25 Children with organic defects and those born into minority groups are likely to develop ____. ✓ Answer: B · Inferiority complex The answer is inferiority complex because in Alfred Adler's Individual Psychology, real disadvantages such as organic defects (bodily weakness or 'organ inferiority') or minority-group marginalization can intensify ordinary inferiority feelings into a chronic, disabling complex. To teach this, start from Adler's place in the psychodynamic arc: he was the first major defector from Sigmund Freud, breaking away in 1911 to replace Freud's sexual drive with a social, goal-directed psychology. His foundational claim is that every human begins life small, weak, and dependent, producing a universal baseline feeling of inferiority . In the healthy case this feeling is a motor: it drives striving for superiority (or perfection), the forward push toward mastery and competence. The trouble arises when the feeling becomes overwhelming and the person cannot move past it; it then hardens into an inferiority complex , a deep, fixed sense of inadequacy that blocks functioning instead of fuelling it. Adler singled out three childhood roots that put a person at risk: organ inferiority / physical defect , pampering , and neglect , and marginalized or minority children fall under that neglected, disadvantaged category because their handicap can feel insurmountable. The closely linked idea is compensation and overcompensation , the attempt to offset the weakness, which can sometimes mask itself as a superiority complex. Lock in Adler's crucial distinction: a normal inferiority feeling is universal and motivating, whereas an inferiority complex is the pathological, stuck version. The question's stress on defect and minority disadvantage points precisely at that pathological complex, not at the healthy striving or its overcompensated superiority mask. Panwar key: Adler in his school of Individual Psychology explains the concept of overcompensation that can lead to the development of an inferiority complex. This is a lack of self-esteem where the person is unable to rectify his feelings of inferiority. According to Adler, the hallmark of an inferiority complex is that persons are always striving to find a situation in which they excel. This drive is due to their overwhelming feelings of inferiority. There are two components of these feelings of inferiority: primary and secondary. Why the other options are traps A. Superiority complex A superiority complex , in Alfred Adler, is the overcompensated mask a person erects to cover deep inferiority, not the direct outcome of disadvantage. It tempts because it is Adler's vocabulary and is causally downstream, but the question asks what such children 'develop' as a result of their handicap, which is the inferiority complex; the superiority complex is a secondary defence layered on top. C. Compensation Compensation is Alfred Adler's healthy striving mechanism , the effort to offset a weakness through growth or skill, not a deficit state one 'develops'. It tempts as a genuine Adlerian term sitting right next to inferiority, but it names the corrective response, not the disabling condition the disadvantage produces. D. Fictional goals Fictional goals (fictional finalism) is Alfred Adler's idea that people are pulled forward by an imagined future ideal that guides the style of life. It is real Adlerian theory, which makes it tempting, but it concerns teleological motivation, not the way organic defect or minority status breeds a felt sense of inadequacy. Q26 Jung disagreed with Freud on the nature of the unconscious, arguing that it exists on two levels ____ and ____. ✓ Answer: A · Collective and individual The answer is collective and individual because Carl Jung split the unconscious into a personal (individual) unconscious and a deeper collective unconscious , and that second layer is the very point on which he broke from Sigmund Freud. To understand the dispute, contrast the two men within the psychodynamic arc. Freud's unconscious is wholly personal : a reservoir of repressed memories and forbidden wishes each individual acquires in their own lifetime. Jung, Freud's designated heir until their 1913 split that birthed Analytical Psychology , accepted that layer and named it the personal unconscious , holding forgotten and suppressed experiences unique to the person. But he insisted there is a stratum beneath it, the collective unconscious , which is inherited and shared by all of humanity, a psychic deposit of the species' evolutionary and ancestral history. Its contents are the archetypes , universal predisposing patterns and images, the shadow, the anima/animus, the wise old man, the great mother, that recur across the world's myths, religions, and dreams. Jung's deep reading of comparative religion and Eastern philosophy (Buddhism, Hinduism) and of alchemy shaped this view, which is exactly why Freud, the rationalist, rejected it as mystical. The mechanism that makes the distractors tempting is that all four options are genuine Jungian terms, so a student must know which ones name the levels versus the contents or dimensions . Lock in the single distinction: the personal/individual unconscious is yours alone and acquired in your lifetime, while the collective unconscious is universal and inherited. When a question says Jung divided the unconscious into two levels, the pair is personal/individual and collective. Panwar key: Jung, like Freud, also divided the human psyche into three parts. But in Jung's view the unconscious was divided into the personal unconscious and the collective unconscious. The personal unconscious includes memories (both recalled and suppressed) and the collective unconscious holds our experiences as a species or knowledge that we are born with. Jung's take on the human psyche was inspired by his studies into Eastern philosophy and religion such as Buddhism and Hinduism. Why the other options are traps B. Anima and animus Anima and animus are archetypes , the inner feminine within a man and the inner masculine within a woman, that reside inside the collective unconscious. They tempt because they are a famous Jungian pair, but they are contents of the deep layer, not the two structural levels of the unconscious the question asks for. C. Extroversion and introversion Extroversion and introversion are Carl Jung's two attitude types from Psychological Types (1921), describing the direction of psychic energy. They are a real, famous Jungian dichotomy, which is the lure, but they are a conscious personality dimension, not divisions of the unconscious. D. Intuitive and perceptive Intuitive and perceptive echo Carl Jung's psychological functions (he named thinking, feeling, sensation, intuition) and the later MBTI-style preferences built on him. They tempt by sounding Jungian, but they describe modes of orienting to the world, not the layered structure of the unconscious. Q27 In a psychoanalytic practice, where the patient relaxes on a couch and freely tells whatever comes into his/her mind is called ✓ Answer: C · Free association The answer is free association because that is Freud's defining technique in which the patient reclines and reports whatever enters the mind, uncensored. To teach it, recall the goal of psychoanalysis : to surface repressed material from the unconscious into conscious awareness. Direct questioning fails, because the patient's defences keep guarding the painful content. Free association sidesteps those defences by instructing the patient to voice every thought, image, and feeling exactly as it arises, however trivial, embarrassing, illogical, or irrelevant it seems. The technique rests on Freud's principle of psychic determinism : mental life is never random, so a chain of seemingly stray associations is in fact steered by underlying unconscious conflicts, and following it leads back to the repressed root. Historically this matters for placing the method in the psychodynamic arc: Freud developed free association as a replacement for hypnosis , the cathartic-hypnotic method he had absorbed from Charcot in Paris and from his colleague Josef Breuer in Vienna. He found hypnosis unreliable and, crucially, found that it made patients parrot the analyst's suggestions; free association let patients 'speak for themselves'. The technique also generates diagnostic gold: points where the patient hesitates, blanks, blushes, or abruptly changes subject signal resistance , flagging the very material the mind is defending, and the associations frequently expose transference . Lock in the picture: couch plus an uncensored stream of thought equals free association, the core royal route (alongside dream interpretation) into the unconscious in classical psychoanalysis. Panwar key: Free association is the expression of the content of consciousness without censorship as an aid in gaining access to unconscious processes. This technique is used in psychoanalysis (and also in psychodynamic theory) which was originally devised by Sigmund Freud out of the hypnotic method of his mentor and colleague, Josef Breuer. Freud described it as a phenomenon in which the patients spoke for themselves, rather than repeating the ideas of the analyst. Why the other options are traps A. Dreaming Dreaming connects to dream interpretation , the other great psychoanalytic route to the unconscious, which makes it tempting. But dreaming is a sleeping mental event that gets analysed afterward; it is not the waking, on-the-couch technique of speaking every thought aloud that the question describes. B. Narration Narration is not a defined psychoanalytic technique at all; it is an everyday word for telling an account. It tempts as a near-synonym for 'telling what comes to mind', but free association is precisely un structured and uncensored, the opposite of a coherent narrative. D. Story telling Story telling is likewise not the technical term, and it misrepresents the method: a story is organized, sequenced, and edited, whereas free association demands a deliberately disorganized, unedited flow. The deliberate absence of structure is exactly what lets repressed links surface, so 'story telling' is wrong here. Q28 Karen Horney's conception of feelings of pervasive loneliness and helplessness that are the foundation of neurosis is called ✓ Answer: C · Basic anxiety The answer is basic anxiety because Karen Horney used that exact phrase for the pervasive feeling of loneliness and helplessness she placed at the foundation of neurosis. To place her, Horney was a leading neo-Freudian : trained in the psychoanalytic tradition but rejecting Sigmund Freud's biological, libido-and-instinct account in favour of social and relational causes, and she is also famous for challenging Freud's view of feminine psychology (replacing 'penis envy' with the notion of male 'womb envy'). Her central developmental claim is that basic anxiety arises in childhood when the parent-child environment goes wrong, through domination, indifference, erratic or hostile behaviour, lack of respect for the child's individual needs, or absence of genuine warmth and guidance. The child comes to feel small, isolated, and helpless in a world perceived as potentially hostile, and this insecure foundation is what later breeds neurosis . To cope, the person adopts rigid interpersonal strategies Horney organized into three neurotic trends : moving toward people (compliance, self-effacement, seeking approval), moving against people (aggression, control, the need to dominate), and moving away from people (detachment, withdrawal). The healthy person uses all three flexibly; the neurotic clings compulsively to one. The distinction to lock in, and the one the trap options probe, is authorship and origin: 'basic anxiety' is Horney's specific named concept , learned from disturbed early relationships, distinct from Freud's drive-based 'neurotic anxiety' and from the philosophers' 'existential anxiety'. If a question ties pervasive childhood helplessness to the origin of neurosis and names Horney, the term is basic anxiety. Panwar key: Psychoanalytic theorist Karen Horney developed one of the best-known theories of neurosis. She believed that neurosis resulted from basic anxiety caused by interpersonal relationships. According to Horney, basic anxiety (and therefore neurosis) could result from a variety of situations including direct or indirect domination, indifference, erratic behaviour, lack of respect for the child's individual needs, and lack of real guidance. Why the other options are traps A. Innate anxiety Innate anxiety is not a Horney term and contradicts her central thesis. It tempts because 'innate' sounds foundational, but Karen Horney insisted basic anxiety is learned from interpersonal experience in childhood, not biologically inborn; the word 'innate' is precisely what she argued against. B. Existential anxiety Existential anxiety is a concept from existential and humanistic psychology (Rollo May, Irvin Yalom, drawing on Kierkegaard and Heidegger), denoting dread of meaninglessness, freedom, and death. It tempts as a real type of anxiety, but it belongs to a different school entirely and is not Karen Horney's foundation-of-neurosis term. D. Neurotic anxiety Neurotic anxiety is Sigmund Freud's term, the ego's fear that the id's impulses will break through and overwhelm it. It is the strongest decoy because it contains the word 'neurotic' and is genuinely about anxiety, but it is drive-based and intrapsychic, not Karen Horney's relationally-caused basic anxiety. Q29 The Ego is sometimes described as the ____ because it directs energies supplied by the Id. ✓ Answer: A · Executive The answer is executive because Freud described the ego as the executive of personality, the agency that directs and manages the psychic energy supplied by the id. To teach this, recall Freud's structural model of 1923, the mature phase of his theory that succeeded the earlier topographical (conscious/unconscious) scheme. The id is the primitive reservoir of instinctual energy demanding immediate gratification on the pleasure principle . The superego is the internalized moral code, the conscience plus the ego-ideal. The ego sits between them and faces outward toward reality, operating on the reality principle through secondary process thinking: it tries to satisfy the id's urges, but only in ways that are realistic, safe, and socially acceptable, while also honouring the superego's demands. Because it weighs costs and benefits, delays gratification, tests reality, and decides when and how desires get discharged, the ego performs an executive function , like a manager allocating resources it does not itself generate. The mechanism the question hinges on is energetic: the ego has no libido of its own ; it borrows energy from the id and channels it. Directing energy it did not produce is exactly what earns the 'executive' label. Historically, this mediator-ego became the springboard for the entire ego psychology school (Anna Freud, Heinz Hartmann, Erik Erikson), which expanded the ego's autonomous, adaptive functions. Lock in the mediator role: the id supplies the drive, the superego supplies the rules, and the ego executes , balancing both against the constraints of reality. Panwar key: The ego, according to Freud, operates based on the reality principle, which strives to satisfy the id's desires in realistic and socially appropriate ways. The reality principle weighs the costs and benefits of an action before deciding to act upon or abandon impulses, so as it tries to balance the actions of Id and superego, it performs the executive function. Why the other options are traps B. Superordinate Superordinate implies the ego ranks above the id and superego. It tempts because the ego is the decision-maker, but Sigmund Freud's ego does not dominate; it serves and balances three masters (id, superego, reality), often anxiously. 'Executive' captures managing, not outranking, so superordinate overstates its authority. C. Subordinate Subordinate wrongly demotes the ego to a servile role. It can tempt students who note the ego borrows its energy from the id and seems beholden to it, but functionally the ego is the managing, directing structure, not a subservient one, so this inverts its actual status. D. Congruence Congruence is a Rogerian / humanistic term for the match between one's self-concept and lived experience, from a completely different theoretical school. It is a pure cross-school distractor with no Freudian meaning for the ego, tempting only if you do not recognize whose vocabulary it is. Q30 According to Sigmund Freud, the id operates on ✓ Answer: A · Pleasure principle The answer is the pleasure principle because Freud held that the id operates entirely on it. To teach this, the id is the oldest and most primitive of the three structures in Freud's structural model, present from birth and wholly unconscious . It houses the instinctual drives (Eros and, later, Thanatos) and is the source of all psychic energy, the libido . The pleasure principle is its single governing rule: every wishful impulse must be satisfied immediately , regardless of consequence, logic, morality, or external reality. When the id gets what it wants we feel pleasure; when it is blocked we feel rising tension or 'unpleasure', which the id is driven to discharge at once. It pursues this through primary process thinking , a mode that is primitive, illogical, irrational, timeless, and fantasy-oriented; it can even hallucinate a mental image of the desired object (wish-fulfilment) to relieve tension temporarily. The textbook illustration is the newborn who cries the instant it is hungry, pure id on the pleasure principle, with no capacity to wait. Placing this in the psychodynamic arc, the id-ego-superego triad belongs to Freud's 1923 structural revision and seeds the later ego-psychology tradition. The distinction to lock in, and the one every distractor here tests, is that the id runs on the pleasure principle and primary process, whereas the ego runs on the reality principle and secondary process, delaying gratification to fit the real world. If the question names the id, the answer is the pleasure principle. Panwar key: The id operates on the pleasure principle (Freud, 1920) which is the idea that every wishful impulse should be satisfied immediately regardless of the consequences. When the id achieves its demands, we experience pleasure; when it is denied we experience 'unpleasure' or tension. The id engages in primary process thinking, which is primitive, illogical, irrational, and fantasy oriented. Why the other options are traps B. Reality principle The reality principle governs the ego , not the id. It is the strongest decoy because it is the matched opposite term in the same theory, but it describes the realistic, delaying, consequence-weighing agency, which is precisely not the impulsive id. Assigning it to the id reverses Sigmund Freud's scheme. C. Unconscious mind The unconscious mind is a region or level of the psyche in the topographical model, not a 'principle' on which anything operates. It tempts because the id genuinely is entirely unconscious, but the question asks what principle the id runs on, and a location is not a principle. D. Conscious mind The conscious mind is likewise a level of awareness, not an operating principle, and it is doubly wrong because the id has no conscious component at all. It is a distractor only for someone who confuses 'where the id lives' with 'how the id works'. Q31 According to Sigmund Freud, wars and violence are evidence of ✓ Answer: C · Death instinct The answer is the death instinct because Freud interpreted wars and violence as expressions of it. To teach this, you need Freud's dual-instinct theory, a doctrine that belongs to his late, post-First-World-War thought and marks a darkening of psychoanalysis after he witnessed mass slaughter. Against the earlier sex-centred picture, Freud set two great classes of drive. Eros , the life instinct , gathers the sexual and self-preservative urges and is fuelled by libido ; it binds, builds, and sustains life. Opposed to it stands Thanatos , the death instinct , introduced in Beyond the Pleasure Principle (1920), where Freud argued that 'the goal of all life is death', a pull back toward an earlier, inorganic, tensionless state. Because the organism cannot simply annihilate itself, the death instinct is typically turned outward against others, and that externalized destructiveness is what Freud saw expressed in aggression , cruelty, war, and violence. When instead it is turned inward , it can surface as self-harm, depression, masochism, or suicide. This pessimistic view, deepened in Civilization and Its Discontents (1930) and his exchange with Einstein on 'Why War?', was controversial and largely rejected by the neo-Freudians and even by Freud's own daughter's ego-psychology successors. The distinction to lock in: libido and the life instinct concern preservation, bonding, and pleasure, whereas aggression, destruction, and war trace to the death instinct (Thanatos). The question's explicit pairing of 'wars and violence' is the textbook signal for the death instinct, not Eros or libido. Panwar key: The concept of the death instinct was initially described in Beyond the Pleasure Principle, in which Freud proposed that 'the goal of all life is death.' Freud believed that people typically channel their death instincts outwards. Aggression, for example, arises from the death instinct. Sometimes these instincts towards destruction can be directed inwards, however, which can result in self-harm or suicide. Why the other options are traps A. Life instinct The life instinct (Eros) drives survival, sexuality, bonding, and creation, the constructive opposite of the destructive forces behind war. It tempts as the natural counterpart term in the dual-instinct pair, but it is causally the wrong pole: Eros builds and unites, whereas war expresses the destructive Thanatos. B. Libido Libido is the energy of Eros , the sexual/life-instinct drive, not the source of aggression. It tempts because it is Sigmund Freud's most famous energetic term, but libido fuels the life instinct; channeling destructiveness is the work of the death instinct, so attributing war to libido misroutes the energy. D. None of these 'None of these' is wrong because Freud explicitly attributed aggression and war to the death instinct in Beyond the Pleasure Principle and later works. It only tempts a student who doubts that Sigmund Freud committed to a clear answer here, but he plainly did. Q32 Errors in speech that reflect unconscious thoughts or impulses is ✓ Answer: B · Freudian slips The answer is Freudian slips because the question describes errors of speech that betray unconscious thoughts, which is exactly what a Freudian slip is. To teach this, Sigmund Freud's own technical term is parapraxis (German Fehlleistung ): a slip of the tongue, pen, or memory that, in his view, is never random but always meaningful. The mechanism rests on psychic determinism , Freud's principle that mental life is fully caused, so even a trivial verbal mistake is produced by a repressed wish, impulse, or thought leaking past the ego's censorship into everyday behaviour. A person who intends one word but substitutes another connected to what they secretly feel, or who 'forgets' a name tied to an uncomfortable association, has, on this account, exposed unconscious content. Freud laid this out in The Psychopathology of Everyday Life (1901), where he treated slips, lapses, bungled actions, and forgetting as windows into the unconscious, sitting alongside dreams and jokes as the everyday counterparts of the clinical symptom. Placing it historically, this is early-Freud material, part of the same turn-of-the-century project as the dream book, demonstrating that the unconscious operates in normal people, not only in patients. The distinction to lock in, which the distractors probe, is specificity: a defence mechanism is an unconscious anxiety-management strategy, and a cognitive distortion is a faulty thinking pattern from a rival (cognitive) school, but neither is specifically a speech error revealing the unconscious. When a question says 'errors in speech reflecting unconscious impulses', the precise answer is the Freudian slip. Panwar key: Freudian slips are the slipping of unconscious thoughts and impulses in regular speech. Defense mechanism is unconscious, cognitive distortion is asynchronicity in thoughts and behaviour. Why the other options are traps A. Defense Mechanism A defence mechanism (repression, projection, denial, and so on) is an unconscious ego strategy that wards off anxiety, and it is unconscious, which is the lure. But defences are general protective manoeuvres, not specifically slips of the tongue ; the question's defining feature is a speech error, which points to the parapraxis, not to defences broadly. C. Cognitive Distortion Cognitive distortions (catastrophizing, all-or-nothing thinking, overgeneralization) are biased thinking patterns studied in cognitive therapy by Aaron Beck and Albert Ellis, a completely different theoretical tradition. They tempt as another 'faulty mental process', but they are conscious-level reasoning errors, not unconscious verbal leaks. D. Speech disorder A speech disorder (stuttering, articulation or fluency impairment) is an organic, neurological, or developmental condition. It is a literal-minded decoy because the question also mentions 'errors in speech', but such errors have a physical or developmental cause, not an unconscious psychological one, so it misses the meaning-laden core of the Freudian slip. Q33 According to Jung, the archetype representing the feminine side of males is called: ✓ Answer: D · Anima The answer is the anima because in Carl Jung's analytical psychology the anima is the unconscious feminine archetype carried within a man. To teach this, archetypes are the universal, inherited patterns Jung located in the collective unconscious , the deep stratum shared across humanity that was his great divergence from Sigmund Freud. Among these archetypes is a contrasexual pair: every man holds an inner feminine image, the anima , and every woman holds an inner masculine image, the animus . The anima represents a man's unconscious feminine qualities, feeling, relatedness, receptivity, mood, eros, and it powerfully shapes how he relates to women (often through projection onto a partner) and to his own emotional life. Jung saw integrating the anima as essential to individuation , the lifelong process of uniting the conscious and unconscious into a balanced, whole Self; a man who denies his anima stays one-sided and is prey to moods he cannot own. To hold the related cast alongside it: the shadow is the repressed, instinctual dark side of the psyche (loosely comparable to Freud's id), and the persona is the social mask one presents to meet external demands. Placing Jung historically, he was Freud's heir until their 1913 break founded Analytical Psychology, which traded Freud's sexual drive for a symbolic, spiritual, lifelong model of growth. The distinction to lock in: anima is the feminine-within-the-male and animus is the masculine-within-the-female. The question asks for the feminine side of a male , so the answer is the anima, not the animus. Panwar key: Anima is the female side of the male. Animus is the male side of the female, shadow is nearly analogous to Freud's Id and Persona is the facade that a person assumes to balance between the internal needs and the external demands. Why the other options are traps A. Animus The animus is the exact reverse archetype, the unconscious masculine image within a woman . It is the single strongest decoy because anima and animus are near-twins differing only by direction; here the target is the feminine side of a male, which is the anima, so the animus is the inverted answer. B. Shadow The shadow is the repressed, instinctual, often darker side of the psyche, roughly analogous to Sigmund Freud's id. It tempts as another core Jungian archetype, but it is about disowned instinct and 'darkness', not gender; it is not the feminine aspect. C. Persona The persona is the social mask a person wears to satisfy external demands and present an acceptable face to the world. It is a famous Jungian term, which is the lure, but it concerns the public self, not an inner gendered archetype, so it is unrelated to the feminine-within-the-male. Q34 According to psychoanalytic perspective, the terms gratification, irrational and impulsive are related to: ✓ Answer: A · Id The answer is the id because gratification, irrationality, and impulsiveness are its defining qualities. To teach this, the id is the most primitive of Sigmund Freud's three personality structures in the 1923 structural model, wholly unconscious and present from birth. It is the storehouse of the instinctual drives and the source of all psychic energy, the libido , and it runs entirely on the pleasure principle , demanding immediate gratification of every urge without regard for logic, morality, reality, or consequence. Its characteristic mode of operation is primary process thinking : irrational, illogical, timeless, impulsive, and fantasy-driven, even capable of hallucinating the wished-for object to discharge tension. The id has no contact with the external world and cannot tolerate delay, so it pushes for instant discharge of need, which is why the trio 'gratification, irrational, impulsive' maps onto it so cleanly. Contrast it with the other agencies, which is exactly what the distractors test: the ego is partly conscious, runs on the reality principle and secondary process, and rationally delays gratification to fit the world; the superego is the internalized moral conscience and ego-ideal that judges right and wrong. A defence mechanism is a tactic the ego deploys against anxiety, not a personality structure at all. Lock in the keyword-to-structure mapping: any cluster like 'immediate gratification, irrational, impulsive, instinctual, pleasure' points straight at the id; words like 'realistic, planning, delay, mediating' point at the ego; and 'moral, ideal, conscience' point at the superego. Panwar key: According to psychoanalytic perspective, the Id is the seat of the unconscious where the irrational desires and drives are stored, it works on the pleasure principle and demands immediate gratification of needs. Why the other options are traps B. Ego The ego operates on the reality principle, mediating realistically among the id, the superego, and the external world, the very opposite of impulsive gratification. It tempts as the central decision-making structure, but its hallmark is delay and realism, not the impulsiveness the question lists. C. Superego The superego is the moral conscience and ego-ideal that restrains the id and punishes transgressions with guilt. It tempts as the third structure, but it is moralistic and inhibiting, the antithesis of irrational immediate gratification, so the descriptors do not fit it. D. Defense Mechanism Defence mechanisms are ego strategies (repression, projection, etc.) that manage anxiety; they are processes, not the impulsive drive structure itself. They tempt because they are unconscious like the id, but the question describes the instinctual seat of impulses, which is the id, not the ego's protective tactics. Q35 According to Jung, the archetype representing the masculine side of females is called: ✓ Answer: A · Animus The answer is the animus because in Carl Jung's analytical psychology the animus is the unconscious masculine archetype present within a woman. To teach this, Jung held that the collective unconscious , the inherited, species-wide stratum that was his decisive break from Sigmund Freud, contains universal archetypes , among them a contrasexual pair: each woman carries an inner masculine image, the animus , just as each man carries an inner feminine image, the anima . The animus embodies a woman's unconscious masculine qualities, assertiveness, logic, the drive toward opinion, judgment, and action, and it colours how she relates to men (often via projection) and to her own initiative and authority. Becoming aware of and integrating the animus is part of individuation , Jung's lifelong process of balancing and unifying the conscious and unconscious into a whole Self; left unexamined, the animus can manifest as rigid, dogmatic, argumentative opinionatedness. It sits among other archetypes, notably the shadow (the repressed, instinctual dark side, loosely like Freud's id) and the persona (the outward social mask). Placing Jung historically, he founded Analytical Psychology after his 1913 split from Freud, substituting a symbolic, spiritual, growth-oriented model for Freud's sexual-drive theory. The distinction to lock in is the direction of the contrasexual pair: animus is the masculine-within-the-female and anima is the feminine-within-the-male. Because the question asks for the masculine side of a female , the answer is the animus, not the anima. This is the exact mirror of the anima question, so keep the direction straight. Panwar key: Animus is the male side of the female, shadow is nearly analogous to Freud's Id and Persona is the facade that a person assumes to balance between the internal needs and the external demands. Anima is the female side of the male. Why the other options are traps B. Shadow The shadow is the repressed, instinctual dark side of the psyche, roughly analogous to Sigmund Freud's id. It tempts as a core Jungian archetype, but it concerns disowned instinct and 'darkness', not gender, so it is not the masculine aspect within a woman. C. Persona The persona is the public mask one wears to satisfy social demands and present an acceptable face. It is a famous Jungian term and therefore a lure, but it is about the outward social self, not an inner gendered archetype. D. Anima The anima is the exact reverse archetype, the unconscious feminine image within a man . It is the strongest decoy because anima and animus differ only in direction; the question targets the masculine side of a female, which is the animus, making the anima the inverted, wrong answer. Q36 Alfred Adler proposed that humans are motivated by ✓ Answer: D · Social urges The answer is social urges because Alfred Adler broke from Sigmund Freud and argued that humans are motivated fundamentally by social, not sexual, forces. To teach this, recall the split that defines Adler's place in the psychodynamic arc: he was an early member of Freud's Vienna circle who left in 1911, founding Individual Psychology precisely because he rejected Freud's grounding of motivation in libido and instinctual sexual and aggressive drives. Adler recast the person as an inherently social being whose strivings unfold within, and are oriented toward, a community. His central motivational concept is striving for superiority (or striving for perfection/completion), the forward push from a felt sense of inferiority toward competence and mastery, always pursued in a social context. Crucially, healthy striving is governed by social interest ( Gemeinschaftsgefuhl ), an innate but cultivable sense of belonging and concern for the welfare of others; the well-adjusted person channels superiority-striving into socially useful goals, whereas the maladjusted chase personal superiority at others' expense. Adler also emphasized birth order , the unique goal-directed style of life , and the creative self . Together these make him the forerunner of the more socially and culturally oriented neo-Freudians (Karen Horney, Erich Fromm, Harry Stack Sullivan) who followed. The distinction to lock in: Freud says sex and instinct drive us, but Adler says social urges , belonging, and the striving for superiority within community drive us. When the named motivator is Adler's, the answer points to social urges. Panwar key: Adler deviated from the Freudian theory where he focused on the social aspect of an individual's life. He established that individuals are motivated by social urges and not sexual impulses as Freud stated. Why the other options are traps A. Conscious drives Conscious drives is too vague and does not name Alfred Adler's specific claim. It can tempt because Adler did stress more conscious, goal-directed striving than Sigmund Freud's deep unconscious, but the question asks what motivates us, and Adler's distinctive answer is the social dimension, not merely 'conscious' versus unconscious. B. Neurotic needs Neurotic needs is Karen Horney's concept, her ten compulsive interpersonal strategies condensed into the three neurotic trends. It tempts because Horney was a fellow social-minded neo-Freudian, but the term belongs to her account of pathology, not to Alfred Adler's core theory of normal human motivation. C. Empathic understanding Empathic understanding is a therapeutic stance from Carl Rogers' humanistic, person-centred approach, a different force of psychology entirely. It is a cross-school distractor: it concerns how a therapist relates to a client, not Alfred Adler's account of what drives human behaviour. Q37 'Many mental disorders can be traced to unconscious urges or impulses and to the struggle over their expression that takes place in the hidden depths of human personality'. The above statement is related to which one of the following perspectives? ✓ Answer: D · Psychodynamic The answer is the psychodynamic perspective because the statement locates mental disorder in unconscious urges and the inner struggle over expressing them, which is the signature claim of that approach. To teach this, the psychodynamic perspective grows directly from Sigmund Freud and his successors and holds that much of mental life is unconscious and that personality runs on perpetual conflict between instinctual drives (the id), morality (the superego), and reality (the ego). Socially unacceptable wishes and impulses are pushed out of awareness by repression and other defence mechanisms , but the buried drives keep pressing for discharge. On this view, symptoms and disorders are compromise formations , the visible result of the hidden tug-of-war between forbidden impulses and the forces holding them down. The very phrasing, 'hidden depths of human personality' and 'struggle over their expression', is pure psychodynamic language. Now contrast the rival perspectives the distractors offer, which is the whole point of the question. The humanistic view (Carl Rogers, Abraham Maslow) blames distress on blocked self-actualization and incongruence, stressing growth, choice, and the present, not buried conflict. The social learning view (Bandura) explains behaviour through observation, modeling, and reinforcement, not the dynamic unconscious or the past. The Gestalt view centres on perceptual organization, present awareness, and the structuring of wholes, again not unconscious drives. Each rival explicitly downplays exactly what this statement foregrounds. Lock in the rule: any statement that traces disorder to unconscious impulses and intrapsychic conflict over their expression is psychodynamic, the only one of the four that makes the buried, conflicted unconscious the cause of pathology. Panwar key: The psychodynamic approach to human personality states that the undesirable thoughts and socially unacceptable impulses and desires are pushed to the unconscious. The struggle of expression of these is looked at as the causing factor of mental disorders and issues. The Humanistic and Social learning approaches do not consider the influence of the past. Gestalt does not consider the influence of unconscious urges. Why the other options are traps A. Gestalt Gestalt psychology concerns perceptual organization and the apprehension of wholes ('the whole is other than the sum of its parts'), and the Gestalt therapy offshoot stresses present-moment awareness. It tempts as another classic 'school', but it does not posit unconscious drives causing disorder, so it cannot own a statement built around buried impulses. B. Humanistic The humanistic perspective attributes problems to blocked self-actualization, conditions of worth, and incongruence between self and experience. It tempts because it is a major personality school, but it deliberately rejects the dark, conflict-ridden unconscious in favour of growth and choice, the opposite emphasis from this statement. C. Social Learning Social learning theory explains behaviour through observation, imitation, modeling, and reinforcement, with no appeal to a dynamic unconscious or repressed impulses. It tempts as a respectable causal account of behaviour, but it locates causes in the observable environment and learning history, not in 'the hidden depths of personality'. Q38 The defence mechanism involving an intellectual reason to justify a certain action connected only in the mind of the person after the behaviour is completed is: ✓ Answer: C · Rationalisation The answer is Rationalisation because it is the only listed defence that supplies an after-the-fact intellectual justification: a reason the person constructs in their own mind only once the behaviour is already complete . Begin with the foundation. A defence mechanism is an unconscious strategy the ego uses to reduce the anxiety that erupts when a forbidden id-impulse, or an ugly truth about oneself, threatens to reach awareness. The concept belongs squarely to classical psychoanalysis , the first force of depth psychology founded by Sigmund Freud in fin-de-siecle Vienna in the 1890s and 1900s. Freud sketched the defences across his career, but they were catalogued and systematised by his daughter Anna Freud in her 1936 work The Ego and the Mechanisms of Defence , the book that pivoted the movement from Freud's drive-focus toward the ego psychology school (later carried on by Heinz Hartmann). Rationalisation itself was named by Freud's English follower Ernest Jones in 1908. It works by manufacturing a plausible, logical, socially acceptable explanation that masks the real, often unconscious, motive. A student who failed an exam declares 'the questions were unfair' rather than admitting they did not study; a person who overpays calls it 'an investment'. The emotional verdict comes first, and reasoning is then recruited to defend it, much as a lawyer argues a case already decided. Because it requires constructing a coherent argument, rationalisation is regarded as a relatively mature, secondary defence that demands a fair degree of intelligence, unlike cruder, primitive defences such as denial or projection that simply block or expel reality. The signature mechanism is sequence : the action happens for hidden reasons, then the mind invents an acceptable cause and the person genuinely believes it, so self-esteem is protected. Historically this sits in the same defence family that later ego psychologists refined, sharpening the line between self-deceiving justification and honest reasoning. Lock in: rationalisation gives logical, self-serving reasons that justify behaviour after it is completed, swapping the true motive for a respectable one. Panwar key: Denial is denying the reality altogether, repression is involved in almost all defense mechanisms, projection is projecting the negative aspect of self onto others. Rationalisation is a secondary and much more mature defence mechanism and requires a decent amount of intelligence by explaining the reasons to justify one's actions. Why the other options are traps A. Denial Denial is a primitive, early defence (also catalogued by Anna Freud) in which the person flatly refuses to acknowledge a painful external reality, e.g. insisting a terminal diagnosis is wrong. It tempts here because both distort truth, but denial blocks reality wholesale rather than inventing an intellectual justification for a completed act, so it cannot be the after-the-fact reasoning described. B. Repression Repression is the master defence Sigmund Freud called the cornerstone of psychoanalysis: it pushes threatening thoughts, memories, or impulses out of consciousness and keeps them there. It is tempting because it underlies almost every other defence, but repression buries material; it is not the act of constructing a logical, socially acceptable excuse for behaviour that has already occurred. D. Projection Projection attributes one's own unacceptable impulses or feelings onto other people ('I'm not angry, you are'). It belongs to the same Freudian defence roster and is tempting because it too hides a true motive, but it externalises a feeling onto someone else rather than supplying a self-serving justification for one's own finished action, which is what this item demands. Q39 An investment of psychic energy in an object or person is ✓ Answer: B · Cathexis The answer is Cathexis because that is Sigmund Freud's precise term for the investment of psychic energy (libido) into an object, person, or mental image. This concept belongs to the economic point of view within classical psychoanalysis , the energy-accounting side of Sigmund Freud 's metapsychology developed in Vienna across the 1890s to 1920s. Freud's metapsychology had three angles: the topographic (conscious, preconscious, unconscious), the structural (id, ego, superego), and the economic , which treats the mind as a system that distributes a quantity of energy, and it is to this third, energy-based view that cathexis belongs. Begin with the economic premise: the psyche runs on a finite pool of mental energy that can be attached to mental representations. When the id desires something, it binds energy to the image of that thing; the stronger the cathexis, the more powerfully the person is drawn to it, so cathexis effectively measures how much an object 'matters' to the psyche. The German word Freud used was Besetzung ('occupation' or 'filling'), which his English translator James Strachey rendered with the Greek-derived 'cathexis' (from kathexis , a holding or retaining). Freud observed that when the actual object of desire is unavailable, the individual invests energy in a mental representation of it, which is exactly what cathexis names. The opposing process, anticathexis (counter-cathexis), is the ego's expenditure of energy to dam up or restrain an id impulse from reaching consciousness, the energetic basis of repression ; the more energy spent holding an impulse down, the less is free for living. Picture a grieving person whose libido stays bound to the lost loved one (Freud analysed this in Mourning and Melancholia , 1917), or the infant who first cathects the mother's breast. This drive-economic, almost hydraulic vocabulary was later de-emphasised by the neo-Freudians and the object-relations theorists, who put real relationships in place of abstract energy, yet it remains a foundational layer of Freudian theory. Lock in: cathexis is the investment of psychic/libidinal energy in an object or person, the basic currency of Freud's energy theory of mind. Panwar key: According to Freud, when the object of desire is not available, individuals tend to invest psychic energy in creating a mental image of that object. This is termed as cathexis. Why the other options are traps A. Displacement Displacement is a defence mechanism that redirects an impulse from a threatening target onto a safer substitute (the kicked-dog example). It is tempting because it too 'moves' energy, but displacement is about which target receives a feeling, not the basic act of investing energy in an object. The question asks for the energy-attachment itself, which is cathexis, not its redirection. C. Instinct An instinct or drive (Freud's Trieb ) is the bodily source of psychic energy, the demand made on the mind for work; Eros and Thanatos are the major drives. It tempts because drives and cathexis are intimately linked, but the instinct supplies the energy whereas cathexis is the act of binding that energy to a specific object, so they are not the same thing. D. Repression Repression is the ego's defence of pushing unacceptable material out of awareness, maintained energetically by anticathexis. It is tempting because it is a core Freudian term, but it describes blocking and forgetting, not the positive attachment of energy to an object or person, which is precisely what cathexis denotes. Q40 A woman reflecting her anger from her husband onto her child is an example of ✓ Answer: D · Displacement The answer is Displacement because the woman redirects an emotion away from its true, threatening target onto a safer substitute. This is a classic ego-defence from classical psychoanalysis , the first force of depth psychology. It was first described by Sigmund Freud in Vienna and formally listed among the defences by his daughter Anna Freud in The Ego and the Mechanisms of Defence (1936), the work that helped found the ego psychology school which shifted attention from the id's drives to the ego's coping machinery. Recall the general logic: defence mechanisms are the ego's unconscious tactics for managing the anxiety stirred by feelings the ego cannot safely express. In displacement the impulse itself is not denied, reversed, or transformed; only its target is swapped. The original object is too dangerous, too powerful, or unavailable, so the affect is steered toward a less threatening person or thing where it can be discharged with less risk. Here the wife is angry at her husband, but venting at him feels risky to the marriage, so she discharges that anger onto her child, who poses no threat and cannot retaliate, exactly the wrong-address pattern the question is testing. The textbook illustration is the worker scolded by the boss who goes home and kicks the dog: the affect travels down a chain from the powerful to the powerless. The same mechanism, on Freud's account, also fuels dream symbolism (emotional weight shifts from a significant image to a trivial one) and the formation of phobias , where dread attaches to a substitute object. Distinguish it sharply from projection , where you attribute your own feeling to someone else, and from sublimation , where the impulse is rechanneled into something socially valuable; both change more than the address. In displacement the feeling stays intact and fully recognisable; only the object on the receiving end changes. Lock in: displacement keeps the emotion the same but moves it from a threatening target onto a safer, substitute target. Panwar key: Displacement is the defense mechanism in which an emotion/feeling, usually the ones which are anxiety provoking or stressful about a stressor, is directed towards or onto other objects or persons which is less threatening. In this case, the woman displaces her anger for her husband towards her child, thus indulging in displacement. Why the other options are traps A. Projection Projection attributes one's own unacceptable feelings to another person, so projection here would mean the wife claiming her child or husband is the angry one, not that she herself feels anger. It tempts because it also involves another person, but it externalises the emotion's ownership rather than relocating its target , which is what displacement does in this scenario. B. Reaction Formation Reaction formation converts an unacceptable impulse into its conscious opposite, e.g. behaving with exaggerated tenderness toward someone you actually resent. It is tempting because it also disguises true anger, but it flips the feeling into love rather than shifting genuine anger onto a different person; the wife is still openly angry, just at the wrong target. C. Sublimation Sublimation rechannels a sexual or aggressive impulse into a socially valued activity such as sport, surgery, or art, and is considered the most mature defence. It tempts because aggression is involved, but here the anger is simply dumped on a substitute person, not transformed into anything constructive or admired, so it is displacement, not sublimation. Q41 The neo-Freudian include: ✓ Answer: C · Carl Jung, Karen Horney, Alfred Adler The answer is Carl Jung, Karen Horney, Alfred Adler because all three are classic neo-Freudians : theorists who accepted Sigmund Freud's foundational insight of an unconscious mind but substantially revised his system. To place them historically, picture the arc of psychodynamic thought. Sigmund Freud built psychoanalysis in Vienna from the 1890s and gathered a circle of followers; his most gifted early disciples then broke away over doctrine. Adler left in 1911 and Jung in 1913, the two great 'defectors' who each founded a rival school, and they were followed by a second wave of neo-Freudians in the 1930s and 1940s, many of them emigres shaped by social and cultural concerns. What the neo-Freudians kept : the existence of the unconscious, the formative power of early childhood, intrapsychic conflict, and defence-like processes. What they downplayed or rejected: Freud's heavy emphasis on the sexual drive (libido) as the single engine of personality. In its place they elevated social, cultural, and interpersonal forces. Adler stressed striving for superiority and compensation for feelings of inferiority (his school, Individual Psychology); Jung introduced the collective unconscious and archetypes (Analytical Psychology); and Horney , writing from a culturally minded, proto-feminist standpoint, emphasised basic anxiety arising from disturbed early relationships and famously rejected Freud's penis-envy, countering it with her own notion of 'womb envy'. By contrast, figures like Albert Bandura (social-learning theory), Hans Eysenck (trait and biological psychology), and Carl Rogers (humanistic, the 'third force') sit outside the psychodynamic lineage entirely, which is exactly why every other combination fails: each smuggles in at least one non-neo-Freudian or, in option b, Freud himself. Other commonly listed neo-Freudians include Erik Erikson (psychosocial stages) and Harry Stack Sullivan (interpersonal theory), so the group is broader than three, but Jung, Horney, and Adler are the textbook trio. Lock in: neo-Freudians kept the unconscious but traded Freud's sexual emphasis for social and cultural determinants. Panwar key: Four notable neo-Freudians include Alfred Adler, Erik Erikson, Carl Jung and Karen Horney. Why the other options are traps A. Hans Eysenck, Karen Horney, Albert Bandura Hans Eysenck was a trait and biological personality theorist (extraversion, neuroticism, psychoticism), and Albert Bandura founded social-learning/social-cognitive theory (observational learning, self-efficacy). Karen Horney is genuinely neo-Freudian, which makes the set tempting, but two of the three named belong to entirely different schools, so the option is wrong. B. Carl Roger, Sigmund Freud, Alfred Adler Carl Rogers is a humanistic (third-force) psychologist, not a neo-Freudian, and Sigmund Freud is the original whom the neo-Freudians revised, so he cannot be counted among his own successors. Alfred Adler is correctly neo-Freudian, which baits the choice, but the presence of Rogers and Freud himself disqualifies it. D. Alfred Adler, Albert Bandura Alfred Adler is indeed a neo-Freudian, so the option looks half-right, but Albert Bandura belongs to social-learning theory, a learning-based rather than psychodynamic tradition. A single non-neo-Freudian name spoils the set, and the list is also incomplete compared with the fuller correct trio. Q42 Research has begun to show some support for which of Freud's concepts? ✓ Answer: C · The concepts of an unconscious mind The answer is the concept of an unconscious mind because that is the part of Sigmund Freud 's theory that modern empirical research has actually begun to support. To see why, place Freud historically and then sort his claims into the testable and the untestable.
