Freud built classical psychoanalysis in Vienna around the late-19th-century insight that conscious awareness is only 'the tip of the iceberg'; his early topographic model divided the mind into conscious, preconscious, and unconscious, and the unconscious was the engine of everything. This is the founding premise of the entire psychodynamic tradition, the one idea that even the defectors Alfred Adler and Carl Jung and the later neo-Freudians all retained. Freud's later grand structural ideas, however, the id, ego, superego agencies, the fixed sequence of psychosexual stages, and the Oedipus complex, are difficult to operationalise and have found little scientific backing precisely because they resist falsification; a critic such as Karl Popper attacked psychoanalysis on exactly this ground. But the broad claim that much mental activity occurs outside awareness has been independently vindicated by cognitive science , the very tradition that arose in the mid-20th century partly in reaction against psychoanalysis. Research on implicit memory , automatic processing, priming, subliminal perception, and selective attention shows that perception, judgement, emotion, and behaviour are routinely shaped by information we never consciously register. An important nuance the student must keep: this cognitive 'adaptive unconscious' is not identical to Freud's seething reservoir of repressed sexual and aggressive wishes held down by active censorship; it is better described as a set of efficient, automatic information-processing routines that exist for speed, not for defence. So research supports the broad existence of unconscious processing, not Freud's specific dynamic, motivated account of it. Still, the core principle holds: the conscious mind is only a sliver of mental life. Lock in: of Freud's ideas, the existence of unconscious mental processing is the one with growing empirical support, while his structural and stage-based claims remain largely unsupported. Panwar key: Research on attention, consciousness and memory points out that there are many things in the human mental system that are out of our conscious awareness. These provide support to Freud's idea of the unconscious mind. Why the other options are traps A. The existence of an id, ego and superego The id, ego and superego form Sigmund Freud's structural model (introduced in The Ego and the Id , 1923) and are powerful as a metaphor, but they are hypothetical agencies that cannot be directly measured or falsified. It tempts because the model is iconic, yet 'some support from research' is precisely what it lacks, so it is not the answer. B. The order of the psychosexual stages The fixed order of the psychosexual stages (oral, anal, phallic, latency, genital) is a developmental sequence Sigmund Freud tied to libido. It tempts because it sounds like a testable prediction, but developmental research has not confirmed the stages or their adult-personality consequences, so this is among the unsupported claims rather than the one gaining backing. D. The existence of the Oedipus Complex The Oedipus complex is Sigmund Freud's claim of universal childhood desire for the opposite-sex parent and rivalry with the same-sex parent. It is among his most disputed ideas, criticised cross-culturally (e.g. by Malinowski) and empirically unverified. It tempts as a famous Freudian concept, but it is a textbook example of an un supported claim, so it cannot be correct. Q43 Which structure of the personality, according to Freud, works on the reality principle? ✓ Answer: B · Ego The answer is the Ego because it is the structure Sigmund Freud said operates on the reality principle . This belongs to Freud's structural model of the mind, introduced in The Ego and the Id (1923), a later, mature phase of classical psychoanalysis that revised his earlier topographic (conscious/unconscious) map and that went on to give rise to the ego psychology school of Anna Freud and Heinz Hartmann. Picture the three-part model as a permanent, three-way negotiation. The id is the primitive drive system, present from birth and wholly unconscious, running on the pleasure principle : it demands immediate, total gratification with no regard for consequences, logic, or morality. The superego is the internalised moral authority, comprising the conscience (which punishes) and the ego-ideal (which sets aspirations); it forms around ages 3 to 6 through identification with the same-sex parent at the close of the Oedipal phase, and runs on a moral, idealistic principle, pushing for perfection and inflicting guilt on transgression. Between these two opposing pressures, and pressed also by external reality, sits the ego , the executive manager, which works on the reality principle : it still seeks to satisfy the id's urges, but only in ways that are realistic, safe, and socially acceptable given the constraints of the outside world. The ego therefore delays gratification, postpones discharge, weighs consequences through secondary-process (logical, planful) thinking, and engineers practical compromises, balancing the id's hunger against the superego's prohibitions and reality's limits. It spans the conscious, preconscious, and unconscious levels and deploys defence mechanisms when the three-way conflict threatens to overwhelm it. Later ego psychologists enlarged the ego's role from mere referee to an autonomous, adaptive agency with its own 'conflict-free' functions. Lock in: id = pleasure principle, superego = morality and ideals, and the ego = reality principle, the rational mediator that adapts impulses to the real world. Panwar key: According to Freudian theory of personality, the ego works on the reality principle, balancing between the id that works on the pleasure principle and the superego that works on the moral principle. Why the other options are traps A. Id The id works on the pleasure principle , demanding immediate gratification regardless of reality, logic, or morality. It tempts because it is the most famous Freudian structure, but it is the opposite of reality-orientation: the id is the impulse the ego must restrain, so it cannot be the structure that performs reality testing. C. Superego The superego works on a moral (idealistic) principle, enforcing conscience and the ego-ideal and generating guilt. It tempts because it, like the ego, opposes the raw id, but the superego pursues moral perfection rather than realistic adaptation, so it is not the reality-principle structure described in the question. D. Libido Libido is the psychic/sexual energy of the drives, not a structure of personality at all. It tempts because it is core Freudian vocabulary, but the question asks specifically for a structure (id, ego, or superego); libido is the energy those structures invest, so it cannot be the answer. Q44 Sigmund Freud began his career as a ✓ Answer: A · Neurologist The answer is Neurologist because Sigmund Freud 's medical training and earliest career were in neurology and neuroanatomy, long before psychoanalysis existed. To trace the arc, start with his education in Vienna. Freud qualified in medicine in 1881 and worked under the physiologist Ernst Brucke in the great German physicalist tradition, studying the anatomy and physiology of the nervous system, examining the nerve cells of fish and humans, and even researching cocaine as a possible anaesthetic. He then practised as a clinical neurologist treating 'nervous' disorders and wrote technical medical monographs on aphasia and on cerebral palsy in children, work entirely within organic medicine. The decisive turn came in 1885-86 when he won a travelling grant to study in Paris under Jean-Martin Charcot , the leading neurologist of the age, who was using hypnosis to investigate and treat hysteria , patients with dramatic physical symptoms (paralyses, blindness, contractures) that had no detectable organic cause. Watching symptoms appear and dissolve under suggestion shook Freud's purely physical outlook and shifted his attention from the nervous system toward psychological causation. Back in Vienna, working with his older colleague Josef Breuer on cases such as Anna O. (Bertha Pappenheim), who herself coined the phrase 'talking cure', Freud developed the cathartic method, then free association, and from this clinical foundation gradually built the theory and technique of psychoanalysis , the founding act of the entire psychodynamic tradition. So 'psychiatrist' and 'psychoanalyst' describe what Freud eventually became , not where he began ; the whole psychodynamic arc that follows (Freud first, then the defectors Alfred Adler in 1911 and Carl Jung in 1913, then the neo-Freudians) springs from this neurological starting point. This trajectory also explains why his earliest theory, the abandoned Project for a Scientific Psychology (1895), tried to ground the mind in neurons before he gave up and turned to a purely psychological model. Lock in: Freud started as a neurologist and neuroanatomist, was trained in hysteria under Charcot in Paris, and only afterward invented psychoanalysis. Panwar key: Sigmund Freud began his medical career as a neuroanatomist and neurologist before he established the theory and techniques of Psychoanalysis. He was trained in neurology under Jean Charcot. Why the other options are traps B. Psychiatrist Psychiatrist tempts because Sigmund Freud famously treated mental disorders, but psychiatry is the medical specialty of diagnosing and treating mental illness, and Freud was not trained or board-certified in it; his formal training and first career were in neurology and neuroanatomy. He approached the mind from the nervous system, not from psychiatry, so this is where he ended up working, not how he began. C. Psychoanalyst Psychoanalyst is the role Sigmund Freud himself created ; psychoanalysis did not exist as a discipline until he built it in the late 1890s and after. It tempts because it is what he is best known for, but you cannot begin a career in a field you have not yet invented, so it describes his later identity, not his starting point. D. Philosopher Philosopher tempts because Sigmund Freud engaged sweeping ideas about civilisation, religion, and the mind, and was read like a philosopher. But he began as a working medical scientist, a neurologist and neuroanatomist; his philosophical-style theorising came much later and was always framed as science, so 'philosopher' misstates his professional origin. Q45 ________ was the proponent of Individual Psychology. ✓ Answer: C · Adler The answer is Adler because Alfred Adler founded the school known as Individual Psychology . Place him historically. Adler was an Austrian physician and one of the earliest, most prominent members of Freud's Vienna Psychoanalytic Society, even its president for a time, who broke away in 1911 after his emphasis on aggression and inferiority clashed with Sigmund Freud's emphasis on sexuality. He thereby became the first major 'defector' from classical psychoanalysis and a founding figure of the broader, more socially minded branch of depth psychology that the neo-Freudians later extended. The name itself encodes the theory: the Latin root individuum means 'undivided', so Individual Psychology treats the person as an indivisible, unified, goal-directed whole, in deliberate contrast to Freud's model of the psyche as a battleground of warring parts (id, ego, superego). Adler rejected Freud's primacy of the sexual drive and his backward-looking, deterministic stress on early fixation. In its place he proposed that the central human motive is the striving for superiority , a forward-pulling, teleological drive toward growth, mastery, competence, and completeness, which he framed as striving from a felt 'minus' situation to a felt 'plus'. This striving arises partly as compensation for the universal feelings of inferiority everyone first experiences in childhood through smallness, weakness, and dependence on adults. Adler also stressed the style of life (the unique, self-created pattern each person builds toward a private, fictional final goal) and social interest ( Gemeinschaftsgefuhl ), the sense of community and concern for the welfare of others, which he made the very yardstick of mental health. Karen Horney developed her own basic-anxiety theory, Carl Jung founded Analytical Psychology, and Erik Erikson formulated psychosocial stages, so all three are tied to other movements and do not fit. Lock in: Adler = Individual Psychology, a holistic, future-oriented theory centred on striving for superiority and compensation for inferiority. Panwar key: Alfred Adler was an Austrian psychiatrist and the proponent of Individual Psychology. He held that human thought and behaviour are individual man's striving for superiority and power, partly in compensation for his feeling of inferiority. Why the other options are traps A. Horney Karen Horney is a neo-Freudian, but her own system centred on basic anxiety arising from disturbed early relationships and on the three neurotic interpersonal trends (moving toward, against, and away from people); she did not found Individual Psychology. She tempts because she shares the neo-Freudian, socially oriented outlook with Alfred Adler, but the specific school named here is his. B. Jung Carl Jung founded Analytical Psychology , defined by the collective unconscious, archetypes, and concepts like introversion/extraversion and individuation. He tempts as the other great Freud defector of the same era, but his school's name and content are distinct from Adler's Individual Psychology, so he is wrong here. D. Erikson Erik Erikson is an ego psychologist best known for the eight psychosocial stages spanning the whole lifespan. He tempts because his work, like Adler's, broadens psychoanalysis toward social factors, but he founded no school called Individual Psychology and belongs to a later generation, so he is not the proponent in question. Q46 Inferiority complex was suggested by : ✓ Answer: D · Alfred Adler The answer is Alfred Adler because he introduced the concept of the inferiority complex , the cornerstone of his Individual Psychology . Place it historically. Adler, an Austrian physician, was an early and senior member of Freud's Vienna circle who broke with classical psychoanalysis in 1911 over Sigmund Freud's insistence on the sexual drive, becoming the first great defector of the psychodynamic movement. Across the 1910s and 1920s he built his own neo-Freudian system in which inferiority and compensation, not libido, are the motor of personality. Begin with Adler's premise that feelings of inferiority are universal : every human child starts out small, weak, and wholly dependent on more capable adults, so a baseline sense of inadequacy is a normal and even motivating part of development. In his earliest medical formulation he spoke of organ inferiority , a weak organ the body compensates for; he then generalised this into a psychological law. Healthy people compensate for inferiority feelings by striving toward competence, mastery, and superiority, turning weakness into a spur. An inferiority complex , by contrast, is the pathological outcome that develops when those feelings become exaggerated, fixed, and overwhelming, producing a deep, disabling sense of inadequacy and insecurity the person cannot move past or convert into useful effort. Adler held this could stem from actual or imagined physical or psychological deficiency, so perception mattered as much as fact. The complex can drive maladaptive overcompensation , an aggressive grab for power and dominance, or a brittle, defensive superiority complex that masks the underlying doubt with boasting and contempt. The concept flows directly from his twin ideas of compensation and striving for superiority, and it has since entered everyday language as one of psychology's most borrowed terms. Lock in: the inferiority complex, a basic feeling of inadequacy from real or imagined deficiency, was Adler's contribution, not Jung's, Sullivan's, or Erikson's. Panwar key: The term 'inferiority complex' was coined in the 1920s by French psychologist Alfred Adler. It is "a basic feeling of inadequacy and insecurity, deriving from actual or imagined physical or psychological deficiency." Why the other options are traps A. Carl Jung Carl Jung founded Analytical Psychology and is known for the collective unconscious, archetypes, and the word-association test. He tempts because he is a contemporaneous Freud defector who also worked with the idea of complexes (he coined 'complex' in the association-test context), but the specific inferiority complex is Alfred Adler's term, not Jung's. B. Harry Stack Sullivan Harry Stack Sullivan was an American neo-Freudian whose interpersonal theory made relationships and anxiety central, with concepts like the 'self-system' and the role of significant others. He tempts because his focus on insecurity overlaps thematically with inferiority feelings, but he did not originate the inferiority complex, which predates and belongs to Alfred Adler. C. Erik Erikson Erik Erikson used 'inferiority' as the negative pole of his fourth psychosocial stage, industry vs. inferiority (school age). That overlap in wording is exactly why this option tempts, but Erikson borrowed the everyday term within his stage scheme; the clinical concept of the inferiority complex itself was coined by Alfred Adler. Q47 In Freud's theory which portion of personality is concerned with the immediate gratification of primitive needs : ✓ Answer: A · Only Id The answer is Only Id because in Sigmund Freud 's structural model the id is the single agency devoted to the immediate gratification of primitive needs. Place it in the system. This is Freud's structural model , set out in The Ego and the Id (1923), the mature stage of classical psychoanalysis that superseded his earlier conscious/unconscious topographic map and on which the later ego psychology school of Anna Freud and Heinz Hartmann was built. Take the three structures in turn. The id is present from birth, entirely unconscious , and is the original reservoir from which the other structures later differentiate; it holds the basic biological drives, hunger, thirst, sex (Eros), and aggression (Thanatos). It runs purely on the pleasure principle : it demands that needs be satisfied instantly and completely, with zero tolerance for tension or delay and no concern for reality, logic, time, or morality. When immediate satisfaction is impossible, the id resorts to primary process thinking , conjuring a wish-fulfilling mental image of the desired object, the model case being the hungry infant who hallucinates the breast. The ego develops later, growing out of the id under the pressure of reality, precisely to restrain and channel it; it operates on the reality principle through secondary process (logical, planful) thinking, so it negotiates, postpones, and finds safe outlets rather than demanding instant gratification. The superego , forming around ages 3 to 6 through identification at the close of the Oedipal stage, represents internalised morality and the ego-ideal and actively opposes raw gratification, punishing it with guilt. That is exactly why every option that adds the ego or the superego is wrong: those two agencies restrain rather than seek immediate gratification, so only one structure fits. Lock in: only the id seeks immediate gratification of primitive needs, because only it operates on the pleasure principle. Panwar key: Id refers to unconscious psychic energy that works to satisfy basic urges, needs, and desires. The Id operates based on the pleasure principle, which demands immediate gratification of needs. Why the other options are traps B. Only Ego ' Only Ego ' is wrong because the ego operates on the reality principle , using secondary-process thinking to delay gratification and fit urges to real-world constraints. It tempts because the ego is the active 'doer' that gets needs met, but it does so by negotiating and postponing, the opposite of the immediate, consequence-blind gratification the question describes. C. Both id and ego ' Both id and ego ' is wrong because adding the ego spoils the answer: the ego restrains immediate gratification rather than demanding it. It tempts because id and ego work closely together and the ego serves the id's ultimate aims, but their methods are opposite, so they cannot both be the structure that seeks instant gratification. D. Both Id and Superego ' Both Id and Superego ' is wrong because the superego is the internalised conscience and ego-ideal, which opposes primitive gratification and punishes it with guilt. It tempts because both are partly unconscious and both pressure the ego, but the superego pulls toward moral restraint, the very reverse of the id's pleasure-seeking, so it does not belong with the id here. Q48 The concept of 'Collective Unconscious' has been introduced by which of the following Psychologists? ✓ Answer: C · Carl Jung The answer is Carl Jung because the collective unconscious is his signature contribution and the centrepiece of his school, Analytical Psychology . Place him historically. Jung was Sigmund Freud's close associate and once his anointed heir, the first president of the International Psychoanalytic Association, until their painful 1913 break made him, alongside Alfred Adler (who had left in 1911), one of the two great defectors from classical psychoanalysis . He then built a distinct depth psychology of his own. To grasp the concept you must separate Jung's map of the unconscious from Freud's, because both used the word 'unconscious' but meant different things. Freud's unconscious is personal : a reservoir of the individual's own repressed wishes, conflicts, and forgotten experiences, all acquired during one lifetime. Jung agreed this personal layer exists and sits just below consciousness, but he argued there is a deeper stratum beneath it that is not built from personal history at all. The collective unconscious is inherited and shared by all members of the species, an inborn psychic substrate common to humanity, the precipitate of ancestral experience laid down over evolutionary time. Its contents are the archetypes : universal, primordial images and organising patterns such as the Mother , the Shadow (the disowned dark self), the Anima and Animus (the contra-sexual inner figure), the Wise Old Man , and the unifying Self , which recur across the myths, religions, fairy tales, art, and dreams of cultures with no historical contact. Jung took the striking cross-cultural similarity of these symbols, and their appearance in the fantasies of psychotic patients who could not have learned them, as his evidence. This idea sharply distinguishes Analytical Psychology both from Freudian psychoanalysis and from the more socially focused neo-Freudians like Karen Horney and Adler. Lock in: the personal unconscious is yours alone, but the collective unconscious is inherited, shared by all humans, and populated by archetypes, and it was Jung's idea. Panwar key: Collective unconscious refers to structures of the unconscious mind which are shared among beings of the same species. It was a term coined by Carl Jung. Why the other options are traps A. Karen Horney Karen Horney was a neo-Freudian who focused on basic anxiety and the social and cultural roots of neurosis, not on inherited psychic structures. She tempts because she too revised Sigmund Freud, but her work is interpersonal and culture-oriented and contains nothing like an inherited, species-wide unconscious, so she is wrong. B. Alfred Adler Alfred Adler founded Individual Psychology and emphasised inferiority feelings and striving for superiority. He tempts as Carl Jung's fellow Freud-defector of the same period, but Adler's system is goal-directed and social, with no concept of a collective, archetype-filled unconscious, which is uniquely Jung's. D. Sigmund Freud Sigmund Freud originated the idea of the unconscious, but specifically the personal unconscious of repressed individual material. He is the strongest distractor because the question is about an 'unconscious', but he never proposed an inherited, collective layer; that extension was exactly the kind of departure that led Jung to break from him. Q49 According to Freud's stages of psychosexual development, the oedipus complex corresponds to ________. ✓ Answer: B · Phallic The answer is the Phallic stage because that is where Sigmund Freud located the Oedipus complex . This belongs to Freud's theory of psychosexual development , a core pillar of classical psychoanalysis in which personality forms through a fixed, universal sequence of stages, each defined by the bodily zone (the erogenous zone ) on which libido , the pleasure-seeking energy, is focused; too little or too much gratification at a stage produces lifelong fixation . Walk the sequence. The oral stage (0-1) centres on the mouth, sucking and biting; the anal stage (1-3) on the control and release of the bowels during toilet training; then comes the phallic stage, roughly ages 3 to 6 , when libidinal focus shifts to the genitals and the child becomes aware of sexual difference. During the phallic stage the child unconsciously develops desire for the opposite-sex parent and rivalry, even hostility, toward the same-sex parent: the Oedipus complex in boys (named for the Greek myth, and accompanied by castration anxiety , the boy's fear of paternal retaliation), and what is sometimes labelled the Electra complex in girls (a term Carl Jung, not Freud, popularised; Freud spoke of penis envy here). The conflict is resolved through identification with the same-sex parent: the child renounces the impossible desire, takes the rival 'inside' by absorbing that parent's standards, prohibitions, and values, and in doing so the superego crystallises, which is why this stage is pivotal for moral and gender-role development. After the phallic stage come latency (about age 6 to puberty, when sexual urges go dormant and energy is poured into schooling, skills, and same-sex friendships) and finally the genital stage at puberty (mature, reciprocal sexuality). So the complex belongs squarely to the phallic stage, before latency and well before the genital stage. Lock in: Oedipus complex = phallic stage (ages 3-6), resolved by identification, which builds the superego. Panwar key: Oedipus complex is the complex of emotions aroused in a young child, typically around the age of four, by an unconscious sexual desire for the parent of the opposite sex and wish to exclude the parent of the same sex. It corresponds to the phallic stage. Why the other options are traps A. Anal The anal stage (ages 1-3) centres on toilet training and the control of elimination, and fixation here yields the 'anal-retentive' or 'anal-expulsive' traits. It tempts because it sits just before the phallic stage, but the Oedipal conflict requires the genital focus and parental rivalry that only emerge later, so the anal stage is too early. C. Genital The genital stage begins at puberty and concerns mature, reciprocal sexual relationships outside the family. It tempts because its name sounds genital/sexual and so seems linked to the Oedipus complex, but by puberty the complex has long since been resolved through identification; the genital stage comes after , not during, the Oedipal period. D. Latency The latency stage (about age 6 to puberty) is precisely when sexual urges go dormant and the child sublimates energy into learning and same-sex friendships. It tempts as adjacent to the phallic stage, but latency follows the resolution of the Oedipus complex, so by definition the complex has already passed and cannot correspond to latency. Q50 The defence mechanism that involves 'evolving logical and socially acceptable explanations after the occurrence to behaviour that were actually driven by internal unconscious motives' is called as ________. ✓ Answer: C · Rationalisation The answer is Rationalisation because it is the defence that constructs logical, socially acceptable explanations after the fact for behaviour actually driven by hidden unconscious motives. Place it in the system. Rationalisation is an ego-defence from classical psychoanalysis , the founding force of depth psychology; it was first sketched within Sigmund Freud 's circle (the term itself was introduced by his English follower Ernest Jones in 1908) and later catalogued among the defences by Anna Freud in The Ego and the Mechanisms of Defence (1936), the text that anchored the ego psychology school. Recall the shared logic: defence mechanisms are the ego's unconscious tactics for managing the anxiety thrown up by forbidden id-impulses, superego guilt, or unflattering truths about the self. Rationalisation works by the substitution of motive : the real, embarrassing, or unacceptable reason for an action, which would wound self-esteem if admitted, is concealed behind a respectable-sounding justification that the person genuinely comes to believe rather than cynically invents. Crucially, the reasoning is retroactive : the act is performed for unconscious reasons, and only then does the mind supply a tidy, plausible account, so the logic follows the behaviour instead of guiding it. Classic illustrations are the 'sour grapes' pattern (dismissing the unattainable as undesirable, straight from Aesop's fable) and its mirror, the 'sweet lemons' pattern (insisting a poor outcome was exactly what you wanted all along); a person who overpays for a luxury calls it 'an investment', and a parent who shouts at a child calls it 'discipline for their own good'. Because it requires building a coherent, plausible narrative, rationalisation is considered a relatively mature and intellectual defence, demanding real cognitive effort, in contrast to primitive, reality-denying defences like denial or projection. Lock in: rationalisation hides the true unconscious motive behind a logical, socially acceptable justification produced after the behaviour has occurred. Panwar key: Rationalisation is a defence mechanism which permits an individual to deal with emotional conflicts, or internal or external stressors, by devising reassuring or self-serving logical and socially acceptable but incorrect explanations for his or her own, or others' thoughts, actions, or feelings, which cover up other motives. Why the other options are traps A. Sublimation Sublimation channels unacceptable sexual or aggressive impulses into socially valued activities such as art, sport, or surgery, and is reckoned the most mature defence. It tempts because it too is 'mature' and 'socially acceptable', but it transforms the impulse into action , whereas the question asks about producing after-the-fact explanations , which is rationalisation, not sublimation. B. Projection Projection attributes one's own unacceptable feelings or motives to other people ('she's the one who's hostile'). It tempts because it also disguises an unconscious motive, but it relocates the feeling onto someone else rather than dressing one's own behaviour in a logical justification, so it does not match the after-the-fact explaining described here. D. Displacement Displacement redirects an impulse from a threatening target onto a safer substitute (anger at the boss vented on the family). It tempts as another anxiety-managing defence, but it changes the target of a feeling rather than inventing an acceptable reason for behaviour, so it cannot be the mechanism that supplies logical post-hoc justifications. Q51 Which of the following is not associated with the 'inferiority complex'? ✓ Answer: A · Certainty in decision making The answer is Certainty in decision making because it is the one quality that does NOT belong to the inferiority complex . Place the concept first. The inferiority complex is the signature idea of Alfred Adler 's Individual Psychology , the system this Austrian physician built after becoming the first major defector from Sigmund Freud's classical psychoanalysis in 1911, when he put inferiority and compensation, rather than libido, at the centre of personality. Adler held that feelings of inferiority are universal and even motivating, the normal childhood experience of being small and dependent, but an inferiority complex develops when those feelings become exaggerated, fixed, and disabling: a deep, persistent sense of inadequacy and insecurity, a felt 'not good enough', arising from real or imagined physical or psychological deficiency. Its hallmark features all cluster around self-doubt and its fallout. Lack of self-worth is the emotional core of the complex, the conviction of being lesser. Hopelessness follows when the person feels permanently unable to measure up and stops believing effort will help. And overcompensation is the characteristic behavioural response, an exaggerated, sometimes aggressive drive to mask the inadequacy, which Adler noted can flip into a brittle, boastful superiority complex . By contrast, certainty and confidence in making decisions reflect a secure, self-assured person who trusts their own judgement, the very opposite of someone hobbled by inferiority feelings. People burdened by an inferiority complex typically show indecisiveness , hesitation, dependence on others' approval, and avoidance, not crisp decisiveness. So three of the four options genuinely describe the complex while one describes its absence, making this a 'find the odd one out' item. (The Panwar key's aside about Carl Jung and the word-association test is incidental and slightly garbled; the inferiority complex itself is firmly Adler's.) Lock in: inferiority complex means inadequacy, low self-worth, hopelessness, and overcompensation, never the confident certainty of secure decision making. Panwar key: Carl Jung created the word association test in the middle of the 20th century to unravel the subconscious. The inferiority complex involves feelings of inadequacy, lack of self-worth, overcompensation and hopelessness, not certainty in decision making. Why the other options are traps B. Lack of self-worth Lack of self-worth is the emotional heart of the inferiority complex, the felt conviction of being inadequate or 'less than'. It is listed as a distractor precisely because it does belong to the complex; in a 'which is NOT' item, picking a genuine feature is the trap, so this is a true characteristic and therefore the wrong choice. C. Overcompensation Overcompensation is the classic Adlerian behavioural response to inferiority: an exaggerated striving (for power, status, or perfection) that can harden into a superiority complex masking the underlying doubt. It tempts as the 'odd one out' because it sounds confident, but it is firmly associated with the complex, so it is not the exception the question seeks. D. Hopelessness Hopelessness commonly accompanies the deep, unresolved inadequacy of an inferiority complex, the sense that one can never close the gap. It is a real correlate of the complex, included to bait a wrong pick in this negatively framed question, so choosing it would be an error: it is a feature, not the absent quality. Q52 Which of the following does NOT characterise the Ego-defence mechanisms? ✓ Answer: D · Rational unconscious protective measures The answer is Rational unconscious protective measures because the word rational is what makes this option false: ego-defence mechanisms are precisely NOT rational. Place them in the system. Defence mechanisms are a core concept of classical psychoanalysis , the founding force of depth psychology; they were sketched by Sigmund Freud across his career and then systematically catalogued by his daughter Anna Freud in The Ego and the Mechanisms of Defence (1936), the work that launched the ego psychology tradition by turning the spotlight from the id's drives onto the ego's coping apparatus. Their purpose is fixed by the structural model: they are the ego's automatic, unconscious strategies for coping with the anxiety thrown up by conflict among the id, the superego, and external reality. Three of the four option statements name genuine features, and recognising them is how you isolate the false one. First, defences have a degree of adaptive value : used in moderation they protect us and let us keep functioning under acute stress, which is why both Freud and Anna Freud regarded them as normal rather than purely pathological. Second, many work by pushing painful experiences out of awareness , the basic logic of repression , which Freud called the cornerstone on which the whole structure of psychoanalysis rests and the parent of the other defences. Third, they characteristically distort reality , because they shield the ego by editing, denying, reversing, or rearranging uncomfortable truths rather than confronting them honestly. Above all, they operate unconsciously , outside deliberate control or awareness. That is exactly why calling them 'rational' is false: 'rational' implies conscious, reasoned, deliberate problem-solving (closer to a healthy coping strategy), whereas defences are automatic, reality-bending, and hidden from the self. Lock in: ego-defence mechanisms are unconscious, reality-distorting, somewhat adaptive coping devices, but they are not rational, deliberate measures. Panwar key: The ego-defence mechanisms operate to cope from overwhelming situations. It provides a distorted view of reality, are unconscious and push painful experiences into the unconscious. These are not necessarily rational. Why the other options are traps A. Having certain adaptive value ' Having certain adaptive value ' is a true feature of defence mechanisms: in moderation they shield the ego and preserve functioning under stress, which is why Anna Freud and later ego psychologists treated them as normal, not merely pathological. In a 'which does NOT characterise' item, this genuine trait is a trap, so selecting it would be wrong. B. Pushing painful experiences out of consciousness ' Pushing painful experiences out of consciousness ' describes the core action of repression , the foundational defence on which many others rest. It is a defining function, not an exception, and is included to bait an incorrect choice in this negatively framed question, so it is a real characteristic and therefore not the answer. C. Result in distorted view of reality ' Result in distorted view of reality ' is exactly what defences do, since they protect the ego by denying or reshaping uncomfortable truth rather than facing it. This is a true, defining property; it tempts as the odd one out only if misread, but it genuinely characterises defence mechanisms, so it is not the false statement. Q53 The re-channeling of sexual or aggressive impulses in a socially acceptable direction is known as : ✓ Answer: D · Sublimation The answer is Sublimation because it is the defence that re-channels unacceptable sexual or aggressive impulses into socially acceptable, constructive outlets. Place it historically. Sublimation is an ego-defence from classical psychoanalysis , the founding force of depth psychology; it was introduced by Sigmund Freud , who treated it not merely as a personal coping device but as the very wellspring of art, science, and civilisation itself (a theme of Civilization and Its Discontents , 1930, where culture is bought by renouncing and redirecting instinct). It was later included among the defences formally catalogued by his daughter Anna Freud in 1936 within the ego psychology tradition. Recall the shared logic of all defences: the ego must manage id-impulses that society forbids. Sublimation is unique in that it does not bury, deny, reverse, or merely relocate these urges; it transforms them, redirecting the underlying drive-energy (the libido or aggression) into activities that are valued or admired. The aggressive drive becomes competitive sport, debate, or a surgeon's incisive precision; the sexual drive becomes artistic creation or scientific curiosity; raw impulse becomes genuine achievement. Freud regarded sublimation as the healthiest, most mature and adaptive defence precisely because it permits real instinctual satisfaction while serving the social good, a true win-win rather than a mere disguise or distortion of reality, which is why it is often the only defence judged unequivocally healthy. Distinguish it carefully from displacement , which merely shifts an emotion onto a safer target without rendering it socially valuable, and from projection , which expels one's own impulses onto others; both leave the impulse essentially untransformed. Sublimation alone converts the impulse into something productive and culturally prized, which is why it is the textbook example of channeling 'rechanneling' rather than blocking. Lock in: sublimation re-channels sexual or aggressive impulses into socially acceptable, constructive activity, the most mature of the defences. Panwar key: Sublimation is the channeling of unacceptable feelings, desires, and impulses, often of a sexual or aggressive nature, into positive, socially approved activity. Sublimation is one of Anna Freud's original defense mechanisms. Why the other options are traps A. Displacement Displacement shifts an impulse from a threatening target onto a safer, substitute one (anger at the boss taken out on the family). It is the closest distractor because it, too, redirects an impulse, but it merely changes the target without making the discharge socially constructive; sublimation goes further and transforms the impulse into valued activity, which is what the question requires. B. Overcompensation Overcompensation is an Adlerian concept, not a Freudian defence: it is the exaggerated effort to overcome felt inferiority, sometimes producing a superiority complex. It tempts because it sounds like channeling drive into achievement, but it belongs to Adler's Individual Psychology and concerns inferiority, not the re-channeling of sexual or aggressive impulses into approved outlets. C. Projection Projection attributes one's own unacceptable sexual or aggressive impulses to other people ('he's the aggressive one'). It tempts because it also deals with forbidden impulses, but it externalises the impulse onto someone else rather than converting it into constructive activity, so it cannot be the mechanism described. Q54 A socially acceptable reason for actions that are really based on motives believed to be socially unacceptable is known as ________. ✓ Answer: A · rationalisation The answer is Rationalisation because it supplies a socially acceptable reason for actions whose real motives are socially unacceptable. Place it in the system. Rationalisation is an ego-defence of classical psychoanalysis , the founding force of depth psychology; it is rooted in Sigmund Freud 's account of the mind (the term itself was coined by his English follower Ernest Jones in 1908) and was later listed among the defences by his daughter Anna Freud in The Ego and the Mechanisms of Defence (1936), the founding work of the ego psychology school. Recall the shared logic: defence mechanisms are the ego's unconscious devices for warding off the anxiety raised by forbidden id-impulses, superego guilt, or unflattering truths about the self. Rationalisation operates by the substitution of motive : the genuine, embarrassing, or unacceptable reason for an action is replaced in the mind by a plausible, logical, respectable one. Because the person sincerely believes the acceptable account rather than knowingly lying, self-esteem is preserved and the true driver stays hidden from the self; the justification is engineered to be 'consciously tolerable', even admirable or superior. A manager who fires an employee out of personal dislike calls it 'a budget decision'; a person who lashes out insists they were 'only being honest'; a student who cheats argues 'everyone does it'. Contrast it carefully with reaction formation , which converts an impulse into its conscious opposite, with sublimation , which channels the impulse into valued activity, and with displacement , which shifts the feeling onto a safer target. Only rationalisation invents an acceptable cover story for unacceptable motives. Because it requires building a coherent, plausible narrative, it is reckoned a relatively mature, intellectual defence rather than a primitive one, and it is among the most common defences in everyday life precisely because it feels so reasonable from the inside. Lock in: rationalisation justifies socially unacceptable motives with a socially acceptable, logical-sounding reason. Panwar key: Rationalisation is a defense mechanism in which controversial behaviours or feelings are justified and explained in a seemingly rational or logical manner to avoid the true explanation, and are made consciously tolerable, or even admirable and superior, by plausible means. Why the other options are traps B. reaction formation Reaction formation expresses the conscious opposite of one's true unacceptable feeling, e.g. lavishing exaggerated kindness on someone you secretly hate, or moral crusading against an impulse you harbour. It tempts because it too masks an unacceptable motive, but it flips the feeling into its reverse rather than supplying a logical justification for the original behaviour, so it is not the answer. C. sublimation Sublimation channels unacceptable sexual or aggressive impulses into socially valued activity such as art or sport, and is the most mature defence. It tempts because it shares the phrase 'socially acceptable', but it transforms the impulse into action , whereas the question asks for an acceptable reason or explanation for an action, which is rationalisation. D. displacement Displacement redirects an impulse from a dangerous target onto a safer one (kicking the dog after a bad day at work). It tempts as another anxiety-managing defence, but it changes the target of a feeling rather than fabricating an acceptable justification for a motive, so it does not fit the definition given here. Q55 Who among the following is considered as the proponent of Word Association Test to understand the unconscious conflicts in an individual? ✓ Answer: B · Carl Jung The answer is Carl Jung because he developed the Word Association Test as a tool for uncovering unconscious conflicts. Place it historically. Jung devised the test in the early 1900s while working at the Burgholzli psychiatric clinic in Zurich under Eugen Bleuler, during the very period of his close collaboration with Sigmund Freud and well before their 1913 break; it later became foundational to Jung's own school, Analytical Psychology , the depth psychology he built after leaving Freud. Picture the procedure. The examiner reads out a standard list of stimulus words one at a time, and the respondent must reply with the very first word that comes to mind. Jung measured not only the content of the response but, crucially, the reaction time and any objective signs of emotional disturbance: hesitation, an unusually long pause, a bizarre or absent answer, misunderstanding or repetition of the stimulus word, even physiological arousal recorded with a galvanometer (an early lie-detector-style measure of skin response). Where these disturbances clustered around particular themes, Jung inferred the presence of an emotionally charged complex , a cluster of repressed, conflict-laden ideas and feelings snagging the otherwise smooth flow of association. This is, in fact, where the now-everyday word 'complex' originates, and this rigorous, measurable work is what first won Freud's admiration and drew the two men together. The test thus offered an early, semi-objective, partly quantitative route into the unconscious, anticipating later projective and reaction-time methods. By contrast, Henry Murray devised the story-based TAT, Donald Winnicott worked in object relations with children's play, and Freud himself relied on free association , an open-ended flow rather than this structured stimulus-word method, so none of them is the proponent here. The test remains historically important as one of the first attempts to bring measurement to the study of the unconscious. Lock in: the Word Association Test, using reaction times to stimulus words to expose unconscious complexes, was Jung's creation. Panwar key: Carl Jung created the word association test at the beginning of the 20th century to unravel the subconscious. Jung wanted to understand its manifestations and find appropriate channels to analyze it. Why the other options are traps A. Henry Murray Henry Murray developed the Thematic Apperception Test (TAT), where respondents tell stories about ambiguous pictures, and the theory of needs/press (personology). He tempts because the TAT is also a projective probe of unconscious motives, but it is a story-telling picture test, not the structured stimulus-word/reaction-time method, which is Jung's. C. Sigmund Freud Sigmund Freud accessed the unconscious through free association (the patient says whatever comes to mind, without a fixed word list) and dream analysis. He is the strongest distractor because the goal, uncovering unconscious conflict, is shared, but the specific formal, timed Word Association Test was created by Carl Jung, not Freud; their methods differ. D. Donald Winicott Donald Winnicott was a British object-relations theorist known for the 'good-enough mother', the holding environment, and transitional objects, and clinically for the Squiggle Game with children. He tempts as another depth-psychology figure, but he is associated with object relations and child play techniques, not with any word-association test. Behavioural / Learning Q56 Which ONE of the following theorists developed the concept of self-efficacy that has been used as a cognitive-behavioural theoretical explanation for how people change? ✓ Answer: C · Albert Bandura The answer is Albert Bandura because he coined and developed the construct of self-efficacy . Self-efficacy is a person's belief in their own capacity to organize and execute the actions needed to manage a situation or accomplish a specific task. Crucially it is not a measure of actual skill but of confidence in deploying skill, and it is task-specific rather than global. Bandura embedded this idea in his social-cognitive theory , which holds that behaviour emerges from a three-way interplay of personal factors (beliefs, expectations), behaviour, and environment, a loop he called reciprocal determinism . To place this in Systems & Theories: behaviourism was founded by John B. Watson (1913) as a revolt against introspection, then split into Ivan Pavlov's classical conditioning, Edward Thorndike's connectionism, and B. F. Skinner's radical operant behaviourism, all of which ignored inner mental events. Bandura, working from the 1960s, is the great bridge figure: he kept the behaviourist commitment to learning and observable behaviour but reintroduced cognition (expectations, beliefs, self-reflection), so his work sits at the hinge between strict behaviourism and the cognitive revolution. He argued efficacy beliefs grow from four sources: mastery experiences (past successes, the strongest source), vicarious experiences (watching similar others succeed, tied to his observational-learning research), verbal persuasion (encouragement), and one's physiological and affective state (arousal read as either nerves or readiness). High self-efficacy makes people set harder goals, persist through setbacks, and rebound from failure; low self-efficacy breeds avoidance and early surrender. This is exactly why self-efficacy became a leading cognitive-behavioural explanation for change: shifting a belief about one's own capability can shift action even before skill improves. Lock in: self-efficacy is a task-specific belief about one's ability to perform (Bandura), distinct from self-esteem, which is a global judgement of self-worth. Panwar key: Psychologist Albert Bandura has defined self-efficacy as one's belief in one's ability to succeed in specific situations or accomplish a task. One's sense of self-efficacy can play a major role in how one approaches goals, tasks, and challenges. Why the other options are traps A. Aaron Beck Aaron Beck is the father of cognitive therapy , known for the cognitive triad (negative views of self, world, future), schemas, and automatic thoughts. He is tempting because his work is also a cognitive-behavioural account of change, but he never developed self-efficacy; his target was distorted thinking, not belief in one's own task capability. B. Albert Ellis Albert Ellis created REBT and the ABC model , in which an Activating event plus irrational Beliefs produce emotional Consequences. The shared first name 'Albert' and the cognitive-behavioural change theme make him a trap, but Ellis targeted irrational beliefs and disputing them, not the construct of self-efficacy, which is Bandura's. D. B.F. Skinner B.F. Skinner developed operant conditioning , reinforcement schedules, and the Skinner box. He is a classic distractor because he is the archetypal learning theorist, but his radical behaviourism deliberately excluded internal beliefs. Self-efficacy is an internal cognitive construct, the very thing Skinner refused to invoke, so it cannot be his. Q57 ____ proposed that animals have the capacity to develop a mental representation, a cognitive map, of the place. ✓ Answer: A · Tolman The answer is Tolman because Edward C. Tolman proposed that animals form an internal mental representation, a cognitive map , of their environment. To place him in Systems & Theories: he worked in the 1930s-1940s, deep inside the era of strict behaviourism that John B. Watson founded in 1913 and that Clark Hull and others formalized as pure stimulus-response (S-R) learning driven only by reinforcement. Tolman was a behaviourist who broke ranks from the inside: he accepted that we study observable behaviour but insisted that between stimulus and response sit intervening variables like purposes, expectancies, and cognitive maps. His brand is therefore called purposive behaviourism (or molar behaviourism), and he is rightly seen as a forerunner of the cognitive revolution that overturned behaviourism in the 1950s-60s. The mechanism comes from his maze studies. He let hungry rats explore a maze with no food reward; strict reinforcement theory predicted they would learn nothing without reinforcement. Yet when food was finally introduced, these previously unrewarded rats solved the maze almost immediately, matching rats rewarded from the start. Tolman concluded they had silently built a cognitive map, an internal picture of the maze's spatial layout, during their reward-free wandering. The learning had occurred but stayed hidden until a motive (hunger plus reward) gave reason to display it, a phenomenon he named latent learning . This was a direct refutation of the claim that learning requires reinforcement, and it showed that behaviour can be guided by internal representations rather than mechanical S-R chains. Lock in: Tolman = cognitive map + latent learning + purposive behaviourism; he proved learning can occur without reinforcement and be stored mentally, planting the seed of the cognitive turn against pure S-R psychology. Panwar key: Tolman's experiments with rats demonstrated that organisms can learn even if they do not receive immediate reinforcement. Tolman placed hungry rats in a maze with no reward; as the unreinforced rats explored, they developed a cognitive map, a mental picture of the layout of the maze. When food was later placed in the maze, they navigated it as quickly as the rewarded group. This is known as latent learning. Why the other options are traps B. Harlow Harry Harlow is famous for his rhesus-monkey studies on attachment and contact comfort (the wire vs cloth surrogate mothers), showing comfort, not feeding, drives attachment. He is a tempting animal-learning name, but his work concerned the emotional basis of attachment, not spatial cognitive maps in mazes, which are Tolman's. C. Kohler Wolfgang Kohler , a Gestalt psychologist, demonstrated insight learning in chimpanzees (Sultan stacking boxes to reach a banana, the sudden 'aha'). He is a strong distractor because, like Edward Tolman, he opposed trial-and-error S-R accounts. But Kohler's idea is sudden perceptual restructuring, not a stored spatial map built during exploration. D. Gould Gould is linked in some texts to animal navigation and honeybee research, which superficially resembles spatial mapping, making him a plausible lure. However, the cognitive-map construct and the latent-learning maze paradigm are credited to Edward Tolman, not Gould, so he is not the theorist the key names. Q58 ____ is defined by Rotter as "the potentiality of any behaviour occurring in any given situation as calculated in relation to any single reinforcement or set of reinforcements". ✓ Answer: A · Behaviour potential The answer is behaviour potential because Julian Rotter defined this exact term as the potentiality of any behaviour occurring in a given situation, calculated in relation to a single reinforcement or set of reinforcements. To place Rotter in Systems & Theories: he is a major social-learning theorist of the 1950s who sits, like Albert Bandura, at the bridge between strict behaviourism and cognitive psychology. Pure behaviourists ( John B. Watson , B. F. Skinner ) predicted behaviour from external reinforcement alone. Rotter kept reinforcement central but added cognition : he argued behaviour is predicted from the meeting of the person's expectations and the perceived situation, not from drives or reinforcement history alone. This cognitive-behavioural emphasis is why he, Bandura, and later cognitive theorists are seen as moving psychology past pure S-R determinism. Rotter proposed four interlocking variables. Behaviour potential is the likelihood that a particular response will occur in a specific situation, judged relative to the reinforcement it is expected to bring. Expectancy is the person's subjective probability that the behaviour will actually produce that reinforcement. Reinforcement value is how much the person prefers that outcome over alternatives. The psychological situation is the context as the person perceives it. His core prediction formula links them: behaviour potential is a function of expectancy and reinforcement value. So a behaviour with high potential is one the person both expects to pay off and strongly values the payoff from. Rotter is equally famous for locus of control , the belief about whether outcomes flow from one's own actions (internal) or from luck and powerful others (external), itself a kind of generalized expectancy. Lock in: behaviour potential is the predicted likelihood of acting ; expectancy is the belief the act will be rewarded , and reinforcement value is how much that reward is wanted . Panwar key: Behaviour potential, one of the four principles given by Rotter, is the likelihood of the occurrence of a behaviour. It is calculated in relation to any single reinforcement or set of reinforcements. Why the other options are traps B. Expectancy Expectancy is genuinely one of Julian Rotter's four variables, which makes it the strongest trap. But expectancy is the subjective probability that a behaviour will lead to a given reinforcement, an input to the formula, whereas behaviour potential is the predicted likelihood of the behaviour itself, the output. The quoted definition describes the output, so expectancy is wrong here. C. Reinforcement value Reinforcement value is also a real Rotter variable, tempting for the same reason. It refers to how much the person prefers a particular reinforcer over others, the desirability of the outcome. The quoted definition is about the potential for the behaviour to occur , not how desired the reinforcer is, so this confuses value with potential. D. Punishment value ' Punishment value ' is not one of Julian Rotter's four named constructs at all; it is a manufactured term inserted to mirror 'reinforcement value'. Rotter's framework is built on reinforcement (expectancy, reinforcement value, behaviour potential, psychological situation), so an option naming punishment can be ruled out as a non-existent construct. Q59 In ____ a stimulus which is originally neutral may become reinforcing by being associated with a reinforcing stimulus. ✓ Answer: B · Secondary reinforcement The answer is secondary reinforcement because that is the process in which an originally neutral stimulus becomes reinforcing by being paired with a stimulus that already reinforces. To place this in Systems & Theories: reinforcement is the engine of operant conditioning , the framework built by B.F. Skinner in the 1930s-50s, which itself extends Thorndike's Law of Effect. This whole tradition is the heart of behaviourism , founded by John B. Watson in 1913, and it stands opposite Ivan Pavlov's classical conditioning (which pairs stimuli to elicit reflexes); secondary reinforcement is one mechanism by which neutral stimuli gain motivational power within the operant line. First separate the two basic kinds of reinforcer. A primary reinforcer satisfies a biological need on its own and requires no learning, such as food, water, warmth, or relief from pain; its reinforcing power is innate. A secondary reinforcer , also called a conditioned reinforcer , starts out neutral and carries no inherent reward value; it acquires its power only by repeated association with a primary (or already-established) reinforcer. The classic example is money , which cannot be eaten or drunk yet becomes a potent reinforcer because it reliably buys primary rewards. Praise, grades, tokens, and the clicker in animal training all work the same way. The mechanism depends on contiguity : the closer in time the once-neutral stimulus is paired with the primary reinforcer, the more effectively it absorbs reinforcing value, and the chain can extend so a secondary reinforcer conditions further neutral stimuli. This principle underlies token-economy programmes in clinical and educational settings, where tokens (secondary) are later exchanged for primary rewards. Lock in: a primary reinforcer is rewarding innately ; a secondary (conditioned) reinforcer is rewarding only through learned association with a primary one. Panwar key: The secondary reinforcement is the process in which a neutral stimulus acquires the ability to influence the future probability of a particular response by virtue of being paired with another stimulus that naturally enhances such probability. The proximity in time with the primary reinforcer makes the secondary reinforcer effective. Why the other options are traps A. Primary reinforcement A primary reinforcer (food, water, warmth, relief from pain) is innately reinforcing and needs no learning. It is the natural opposite to test against here, but the question specifies a stimulus that 'originally neutral... becomes reinforcing by being associated', which is precisely a learned, conditioned process, the definition of secondary, not primary, reinforcement. C. Discrimination Discrimination in conditioning is learning to respond to one stimulus but not to a similar one (responding differently to different stimuli). It is a tempting operant term, but it concerns which stimuli trigger a response, not how a neutral stimulus acquires reinforcing power, so it does not match the definition. D. Generalization Generalization is responding similarly to stimuli that resemble the original conditioned stimulus, the mirror process to discrimination. It is a real learning concept and so is a plausible lure, but it describes the spread of a response across similar cues, not the conversion of a neutral stimulus into a reinforcer. Q60 The aim of ____ is characteristically forthright and objective: "given the stimulus, to be able to predict the response, and given the response to be able to predict the antecedent stimulus". ✓ Answer: B · Behaviourism The answer is behaviourism because the forthright, objective aim of predicting the response from the stimulus and the stimulus from the response is the defining goal of the behaviourist school. To place it in Systems & Theories: John B. Watson launched behaviourism in 1913 with his article 'Psychology as the Behaviorist Views It' (the behaviourist manifesto), as a sharp revolt against introspection . The schools before it looked inward: structuralism ( Wilhelm Wundt , Edward Titchener ) analysed conscious experience, functionalism ( William James ) studied the purpose of mind, and psychoanalysis probed the unconscious. Watson rejected all appeals to consciousness, mind, and soul as private and unscientific, insisting psychology become a purely objective natural science studying only what can be observed and measured, namely outwardly visible behaviour. The unit of analysis became the stimulus-response (S-R) bond , the lawful link between an environmental input and a measurable behavioural output. Behaviourism rests on strict determinism , the assumption that behaviour is fully caused by external stimuli, so that knowing the stimulus lets you predict the response and knowing the response lets you infer the antecedent stimulus. That two-way predictability is exactly the aim quoted, and its ultimate purpose was prediction and control of behaviour. The school was later extended by Ivan Pavlov's classical conditioning, Thorndike's Law of Effect, and especially B. F. Skinner's operant conditioning, before the cognitive revolution of the 1950s-60s reintroduced internal mental processes. Lock in: behaviourism studies observable S-R relations and aims at prediction and control, deliberately excluding the inner conscious states that structuralism and functionalism examined. Panwar key: Behaviourism is the school that came in response to the internally-oriented psychoanalytic school and propounded the idea that behaviour is caused by external stimuli. It believes in strict determinism where, 'given the stimulus, to be able to predict the response, and given the response to be able to predict the antecedent stimulus'. Why the other options are traps A. Structuralism Structuralism (Wilhelm Wundt, Edward Titchener) aimed to break conscious experience down into its basic elements (sensations, feelings) using trained introspection . It is the very inward-looking school behaviourism rebelled against, so its goal is the opposite of predicting observable S-R links; it cannot be the objective, behaviour-predicting aim quoted. C. Functionalism Functionalism (William James) studied the purpose of mental processes in helping organisms adapt to their environment. It is a tempting distractor because it too was scientific and American, but it still concerned mind and consciousness in service of adaptation, not the deterministic stimulus-response prediction defining behaviourism. D. Gestalt School The Gestalt school (Max Wertheimer, Wolfgang Kohler, Kurt Koffka) emphasised holistic perception, summed up as 'the whole is greater than the sum of its parts'. It explicitly opposed the reductionism of S-R psychology, so it is a natural contrast option, but its concern is organized perception, not two-way S-R predictability. Q61 Bandura noted that most behaviour occurs in the absence of external rewards and punishment so that most behaviour stems from ✓ Answer: B · self-regulation The answer is self-regulation because Albert Bandura held that most behaviour occurs without external reward or punishment and therefore must stem from internal, self-generated control. To place this in Systems & Theories: behaviourism, founded by John B. Watson in 1913 and radicalized by B. F. Skinner , explained behaviour purely by external reinforcement and punishment. Bandura's social-cognitive theory (1960s onward) is the great bridge to the cognitive turn : it accepts learning and observable behaviour but argues people are not mere reactors to outside reinforcement, they are active agents who guide their own conduct. This is precisely why Bandura noticed that everyday behaviour persists even when no external reinforcer is present, a fact pure operant theory struggles to explain. Self-regulation is the capacity to govern one's behaviour through internally set standards and self-administered consequences. Bandura described it in three steps: self-observation (monitoring one's own actions), judgement (comparing those actions against a personal standard or goal), and self-response (rewarding or sanctioning oneself with pride, satisfaction, or self-criticism). Because these consequences are self-produced rather than delivered by the environment, behaviour can be sustained without any external reward, explaining the bulk of human action. Self-regulation works alongside self-efficacy , the belief in one's ability to achieve goals, and both are cognitive elements that separate Bandura from strict behaviourists. His whole model rests on reciprocal determinism , the mutual, three-way influence of person, behaviour, and environment, which replaces the one-way environmental control assumed by classic behaviourism. Lock in: self-regulation is internal control through self-set standards and self-reward, whereas external reinforcement (the thing Bandura said is usually absent) comes from outside the person. Panwar key: Self-regulation and self-efficacy are two elements of Bandura's theory that rely heavily on cognitive processes. They represent an individual's ability to control their behaviour through internal reward or punishment, in the case of self-regulation, and their beliefs in their ability to achieve desired goals as a result of their own actions, in the case of self-efficacy. Why the other options are traps A. negative reinforcement Negative reinforcement is a Skinnerian operant process: removing an aversive stimulus to strengthen a behaviour (e.g. taking a painkiller to end pain). It is a real reinforcement concept and so tempting, but it is an external consequence, exactly the kind Albert Bandura said is usually absent, so it cannot be what most behaviour stems from in his view. C. reciprocal dualism ' Reciprocal dualism ' is a fabricated term designed to sound like Albert Bandura's real concept. His actual term is reciprocal determinism (the mutual influence of person, behaviour, environment). Because the genuine construct exists with a different name, the misnamed version can be ruled out, and in any case it is not the source of behaviour the question asks for. D. behavioural determinism Behavioural determinism describes one-way control of behaviour by the environment, the classic behaviourist stance Bandura explicitly moved beyond. It is a plausible-sounding distractor, but Albert Bandura's point is precisely that behaviour comes from internal self-direction, not external determinism, so this contradicts his answer. Q62 Behaviour, emitted spontaneously or voluntarily, that operate on the environment to change is called: ✓ Answer: C · Operant behaviour The answer is operant behaviour because that is B.F. Skinner's name for behaviour that is emitted spontaneously or voluntarily and operates on the environment to produce change. To place it in Systems & Theories: Skinner was a radical behaviourist working from the 1930s, extending Thorndike's Law of Effect within the behaviourist movement that John B. Watson founded in 1913. His operant conditioning stands in deliberate contrast to Ivan Pavlov's classical conditioning, which deals with reflexes elicited by stimuli. Skinner distinguished two categories of behaviour. Respondent behaviour is reflexive and elicited automatically by a preceding stimulus, as in Pavlov's salivation to a tone; it is the basis of classical conditioning . Operant behaviour , by contrast, is not pulled out by a known stimulus but is emitted by the organism freely; the animal acts on its surroundings, and the consequences of that action determine whether it recurs. This is the basis of operant conditioning . The governing principle is that behaviour is shaped by its consequences: reinforcement (positive or negative) raises the future probability of the response, while punishment lowers it. Skinner studied this in the operant chamber (Skinner box), where a rat presses a lever to obtain food, the lever-press being the textbook operant; he also developed shaping (reinforcing successive approximations) and schedules of reinforcement . Because the response operates on the environment to change it, Skinner called it operant, and this voluntary, consequence-driven view became the core of modern behaviour therapy. Lock in: respondent behaviour is elicited by a stimulus and is involuntary; operant behaviour is emitted voluntarily and is controlled by its consequences. Panwar key: Operant behaviour is voluntary rather than elicited and is contingent upon the environment change. Why the other options are traps A. Opposition principle ' Opposition principle ' is not a recognised behaviourist term for emitted, environment-operating behaviour; it is an invented label. With no real referent in B. F. Skinner's or any standard learning framework, it can be eliminated immediately as a distractor that merely sounds technical. B. Behaviour potential Behaviour potential is Julian Rotter's social-learning concept, the likelihood of a behaviour occurring given a particular reinforcement. It is tempting because it also concerns behaviour and reinforcement, but it names a predicted probability , not a class of voluntary, environment-operating behaviour , which is B. F. Skinner's operant. D. Personal disposition Personal disposition is Gordon Allport's trait concept, a unique trait that characterizes an individual's personality structure. It belongs to trait/personality theory, an entirely different system from learning theory, so although it is a real term, it has nothing to do with conditioned or emitted behaviour. Q63 J.B. Watson, the founder and father of behaviouristic school of psychology defined 'Psychology' as the science of ______. ✓ Answer: D · behaviour The answer is behaviour because John B. Watson , the founder and father of the behaviourist school, defined psychology as the science of behaviour rather than of soul, mind, or consciousness. To place this in Systems & Theories, trace how the definition of psychology evolved. Ancient and philosophical thinkers treated psychology as the study of the soul (from psyche ). With the founding of scientific psychology, Wilhelm Wundt (first laboratory, 1879) and Edward Titchener made it the study of the conscious mind , using introspection to analyse experience, the structuralist programme. Functionalism ( William James ) shifted focus to the purpose of mind. Watson rejected all of these in 1913 with his behaviourist manifesto, the founding revolt against introspection, arguing that soul, mind, and consciousness are private and cannot be objectively observed or measured by an outsider, so they have no place in a true natural science. He insisted psychology restrict itself to publicly observable behaviour , and that its data be stimulus-response (S-R) pairs: humans and animals understood entirely through the links between environmental stimuli and measurable responses. Watson was radical in spirit, dismissing all reference to inner mental life, and he stressed the power of environment and conditioning over heredity (his famous 'give me a dozen healthy infants' claim). His programme was later extended by Ivan Pavlov , Edward Thorndike , and especially B. F. Skinner , before the cognitive revolution reintroduced mind. Lock in: Watson defined psychology as the science of observable behaviour , deliberately excluding the unobservable soul, mind, and consciousness of earlier definitions. Panwar key: Watson was a radical behaviourist and rejected the ideas of soul, mind and consciousness. He was of the opinion that humans can be understood in terms of stimulus-response pairs. Why the other options are traps A. Soul Defining psychology as the science of the soul is the oldest, philosophical conception (from the Greek psyche ). It is a tempting 'origins' answer, but Watson explicitly rejected the soul as unobservable and unscientific, so it is the antithesis of his behaviourist definition. B. Consciousness The science of consciousness is the structuralist definition (Wilhelm Wundt, Edward Titchener), studied through introspection. It is the most plausible trap because it was the leading scientific definition just before John B. Watson, but it is precisely the school Watson revolted against, making it the wrong attribution for him. C. Mind The science of the mind reflects the mentalistic definitions John B. Watson dismissed. It is tempting because 'mind' feels like the natural subject of psychology, but Watson argued the mind is private and unmeasurable, replacing it with observable behaviour as the proper subject matter. Q64 John B. Watson is best known as the founder of ✓ Answer: A · Behaviourism The answer is behaviourism because John B. Watson is universally regarded as the founder and father of the behaviourist school of psychology. To place him in Systems & Theories: the dominant approaches of the early 1900s all looked inward. Structuralism ( Wilhelm Wundt , Edward Titchener ) analysed the contents of conscious experience through introspection ; functionalism ( William James ) studied the purpose of mental processes in adaptation; and Freudian psychoanalysis probed the unconscious. Watson, an American psychologist, broke from all of them. In 1913 he published 'Psychology as the Behaviorist Views It', often called the behaviourist manifesto , proposing that psychology abandon consciousness and introspection and become the objective science of observable behaviour , studied as stimulus-response relations. He framed this partly in reaction to psychoanalysis, which he judged speculative and unscientific, and partly against the introspective structuralists. Watson emphasized conditioning and the formative power of the environment over heredity , famously claiming he could shape any healthy infant into any kind of specialist (doctor, lawyer, beggar, thief) given control of its upbringing; his Little Albert study demonstrated conditioned fear in a child. His programme was the founding act of the behaviourist revolution and was later extended by Ivan Pavlov's classical conditioning, Edward Thorndike's connectionism, and especially B. F. Skinner's operant conditioning, before the cognitive turn of the 1950s-60s. Lock in: Watson founded behaviourism , the science of observable behaviour, not structuralism or functionalism, both of which still studied inner conscious experience. Panwar key: John Watson, an American psychologist is regarded as the founder of behaviourism. He proposed this approach to psychology in response to Freudian Psychoanalysis. He regarded that behaviourism is the science of observable behaviour. Why the other options are traps B. Functionalism Functionalism was led by William James (with John Dewey and Angell), studying the function of mind in adaptation. It is a strong trap because it is, like behaviourism, an American and practically oriented school, but it predates and differs from behaviourism by still treating consciousness as its subject, and John B. Watson did not found it. C. Rationalism Rationalism is a philosophical epistemology holding that knowledge derives primarily from reason rather than the senses (René Descartes, Spinoza, Leibniz). It is not a psychological school at all, so although it sounds academic, it can be ruled out as belonging to philosophy, not to anything John B. Watson founded. D.
