Structuralism Structuralism was founded by Wilhelm Wundt and Edward Titchener and analysed conscious experience via introspection. It is the most tempting distractor because it is the school Watson directly opposed, but for that very reason it is wrong: John B. Watson rejected and replaced structuralism, he did not found it. Q65 If you express an attitude to a friend who then provides positive reinforcement, your attitude is likely to be ________. ✓ Answer: B · Strengthened The answer is strengthened because positive reinforcement , by definition, increases the future likelihood of the behaviour it follows, so an attitude that earns approval becomes stronger. To place this in Systems & Theories: reinforcement is the central mechanism of operant conditioning , developed by B.F. Skinner within the behaviourist tradition that John B. Watson founded in 1913 and that built on Thorndike's Law of Effect. The behaviourist insight applied here is that attitudes, like other learned responses, can be shaped by their consequences. A reinforcer is any consequence that raises the probability the preceding behaviour will recur. Positive reinforcement works by adding something pleasant or desirable after the behaviour, such as praise, approval, money, or attention. Two terms must be read precisely: positive means a stimulus is added (not that the outcome is morally good), and reinforcement always means the behaviour increases . So when you express an attitude and a friend responds with approval, that approval is a positive reinforcer; expressing and holding that attitude is rewarded and therefore strengthened, and you are more likely to express it again. This must be distinguished from negative reinforcement , which also increases behaviour but by removing an unpleasant stimulus, and from punishment (positive or negative), which decreases behaviour. The shared confusion students make is treating 'negative' and 'positive' as bad and good rather than as subtraction and addition. Lock in: reinforcement of either kind always strengthens behaviour, while only punishment or extinction weakens it; 'positive' simply means a pleasant stimulus was added. Panwar key: Positive reinforcement would lead to an increase in the occurrence of the behaviour preceding it. Hence, the attitude expressed in the above case are likely to be strengthened. Why the other options are traps A. Weakened Weakened is the effect of punishment (adding an aversive or removing a pleasant consequence) or of extinction (withholding reinforcement), not of reinforcement. It is tempting if one wrongly reads any conditioning as discouraging, but positive reinforcement by definition increases the behaviour, so weakening is the wrong direction. C. Both a and b ' Both a and b ' is wrong because a single positive reinforcer cannot both strengthen and weaken the same response; reinforcement reliably strengthens . This option tempts students who are unsure of the direction and hedge, but the effect of positive reinforcement is unambiguous, so 'both' is not possible. D. None of the above ' None of the above ' is wrong because strengthening is exactly what positive reinforcement produces, so a definite, correct option (strengthened) is present. This choice only appeals if one doubts that any listed effect applies, but here option b is precisely right. Q66 The law of effect was formulated by ________. ✓ Answer: A · Thorndike The answer is Thorndike because Edward L. Thorndike formulated the Law of Effect , the foundational principle linking behaviour to its consequences. To place him in Systems & Theories: Thorndike worked around 1898-1911, just as functionalism was giving way to the behaviourist era; his connectionism (learning as the strengthening of stimulus-response bonds or 'connections') is a crucial bridge that fed directly into John B. Watson's behaviourism (1913) and especially B. F. Skinner's operant conditioning. His method came from the famous puzzle box : he placed a hungry cat in a latched box with food visible outside, and the cat had to perform an action (press a lever, pull a loop) to escape and reach the food. At first the cat struggled randomly, but over repeated trials the time to escape steadily fell as the successful action was selected and useless ones dropped out, a pattern he called trial-and-error learning (or learning by selecting and connecting). From this he derived the Law of Effect : responses followed by a satisfying consequence are 'stamped in' and become more likely to recur, while responses followed by discomfort are 'stamped out' and become less likely. He also proposed the Law of Exercise (connections strengthen with practice/use and weaken with disuse) and the Law of Readiness . This consequence-driven account of learning directly anticipated Skinner's later operant conditioning, where reinforcement and punishment shape voluntary behaviour, and it stands beside Ivan Pavlov's classical conditioning as one of the twin pillars of learning theory. Lock in: the Law of Effect (and trial-and-error puzzle-box learning) belongs to Thorndike; Skinner later built on it but did not formulate it. Panwar key: Edward Thorndike initially proposed that humans and animals acquire behaviours through the association of stimuli and responses. He gave the Law of Effect, which specifies that any time a behaviour is followed by a positive consequence, that behaviour is likely to recur. Why the other options are traps B. Skinner B.F. Skinner is the most tempting trap because his operant conditioning is the direct heir of the Law of Effect and uses reinforcement to shape behaviour. But Skinner extended and renamed the idea (reinforcement, schedules); the original Law of Effect, from the puzzle-box cat studies, was stated by Thorndike before Skinner's work. C. Pavlov Ivan Pavlov discovered classical conditioning , the reflexive pairing of a neutral stimulus with an unconditioned stimulus (the salivating dogs). He is a leading learning-theory name and so a natural distractor, but his work concerns involuntary respondent learning, not the consequence-based Law of Effect, which is Thorndike's. D. Watson John B. Watson founded behaviourism in 1913 and championed conditioning, making him a plausible learning-theory choice. However, Watson's contribution was the behaviourist programme and S-R methodology; he did not formulate the Law of Effect, which Edward Thorndike had already stated from his puzzle-box experiments. Q67 Who was the first to propose and establish Psychology as the scientific study of behaviour? ✓ Answer: D · N.L. Munn The answer is N.L. Munn because the book credits N.L. Munn , author of widely used introductory psychology textbooks, with defining psychology as the scientific study of behaviour. To place this in Systems & Theories, follow the lineage of how the discipline has been defined: from the study of the soul , to the study of the conscious mind under Wilhelm Wundt (who founded the first psychology laboratory in 1879 and is called the father of experimental psychology), and finally to the study of observable behaviour . The strict scientific definition of psychology as the science of behaviour is historically the achievement of the behaviourist school, founded by John B. Watson , who in 1913 insisted psychology study only observable, measurable behaviour and abandon introspection; it was later carried forward by Edward Thorndike , Ivan Pavlov , and B. F. Skinner . Munn's textbooks popularized this behaviour-centred definition for generations of students, which is why the key attributes it to him. We retain the official answer as printed while noting the genuine nuance: conceptually it is Watson who originated the strict science-of-behaviour stance, and Munn is credited here for the definitional statement in textbook form. This is a place where the book's attribution and the deeper historical origin should both be held in mind for the exam. Lock in: Wundt made psychology the science of conscious mind ; the science-of- behaviour definition belongs to the behaviourist line credited in this key to Munn and conceptually originated by Watson in 1913. Panwar key: According to the book's key, N.L. Munn is credited here. (Note: It is John B. Watson who first defined psychology strictly as the science of behaviour in 1913; the official answer is kept as printed.) Why the other options are traps A. R.S. Woodworth R.S. Woodworth is known for dynamic psychology and the S-O-R model (adding the Organism between stimulus and response), plus a famous textbook. He is a strong trap as a textbook author of the same era, but he is not the figure credited with first defining psychology as the science of behaviour. B. J.B. William ' J.B. William ' is a garbled/non-existent name, likely a scrambling of 'J.B. Watson' and 'William James'. Because it does not correspond to any real founder of this definition, it can be eliminated outright; it is a typographic lure rather than a genuine candidate. C. Wilhelm Wundt Wilhelm Wundt founded experimental psychology in 1879 and defined it as the study of consciousness via introspection, making him the most tempting 'first/founder' answer. But his subject was the conscious mind, not behaviour, so he defined a different psychology; the science-of-behaviour definition is not his. Q68 The 'instinct theory' of motivation was developed by whom? ✓ Answer: C · William McDougall The answer is William McDougall because he developed and systematized the instinct theory of motivation . To place this in Systems & Theories: William McDougall (1871-1938) was a British-American psychologist and a key figure in social psychology and purposive (hormic) psychology , working in the early 1900s alongside the rise of behaviourism, against which he argued that behaviour is fundamentally goal-directed rather than mechanical. His instinct theory is one of the earliest formal motivation theories, predating the drive-reduction theories of Clark Hull and the humanistic theories of Abraham Maslow . Begin with the key term: an instinct , in his framework, is an inborn, inherited disposition that energizes and directs behaviour toward a particular goal without needing to be learned. McDougall argued that the engine driving all purposive conduct is a set of such innate instincts, and that each instinct has three parts: a cognitive component (perceiving the relevant object), an affective or emotional core (a feeling tied to that instinct, such as fear tied to the instinct of flight), and a conative component (the impulse to act toward the goal). He catalogued instincts such as flight (fear), curiosity, pugnacity (anger), reproduction, and the parental/protective instinct, each paired with an emotion. Because instincts supply both the energy and the direction of behaviour, he treated them as the prime movers of human action. His view was later heavily criticized when psychologists noted that naming a separate instinct for every behaviour explained nothing (circular reasoning), which helped push the field toward drive and incentive theories of motivation. Lock in: the formal instinct theory of motivation is McDougall's, not James's, Freud's, or Maslow's. Panwar key: William McDougall developed the instinct theory of motivation by emphasizing that human behavior is largely goal-directed and rooted in inherited instincts. He proposed that instincts provide both the energy and direction for behavior, making them fundamental motivators of human action. Why the other options are traps A. Sigmund Freud Sigmund Freud built a psychoanalytic instinct/drive theory around Eros (life/sexual, libido) and Thanatos (death) instincts. This shared use of the word 'instinct' makes him tempting, but Freud's was a depth-psychology account of unconscious drives, not the systematic catalogue of inherited motivational instincts the question credits to McDougall. B. William James William James did write extensively on human instincts in his Principles of Psychology and shares the first name 'William', a double lure. However, the formal, systematic instinct theory of motivation (with its cognitive-affective-conative structure) is credited to McDougall, who developed it far more fully than James's descriptive list. D. Abraham Maslow Abraham Maslow proposed the hierarchy of needs , a humanistic theory of motivation built on ascending needs (physiological to self-actualization). It is a motivation theory, which is why it tempts, but it is not an instinct theory and comes from a different, later school, so it cannot be the answer. Humanistic / Gestalt Q69 Which of the following perspectives of psychology is most concerned with the individuals reaching their maximum potential? ✓ Answer: C · Humanistic The answer is Humanistic because of the four major systems of psychology, only humanism makes the drive to reach one's maximum potential the organising centre of its whole model of the person. To place this in Systems & Theories , trace the historical arc. The first force , psychoanalysis (Sigmund Freud), explained people through unconscious drives, repressed conflict, and early childhood, casting human nature as essentially conflicted. The second force , behaviourism (John B. Watson, B. F. Skinner), reduced the person to learned stimulus-response links and reinforcement histories, refusing to study inner life at all. The cognitive view, a later development, studies how the mind encodes, stores, and retrieves information. Against the pessimism and determinism of the first two forces, Abraham Maslow and Carl Rogers launched humanistic psychology in the 1950s as the third force , joined by figures like Rollo May . Its founding premise is that human nature is fundamentally positive and growth-oriented: every person carries an innate push to become the fullest version of themselves. Maslow named this self-actualization and placed it at the apex of his hierarchy of needs; Rogers described the same end-state as the fully functioning person , guided by an actualizing tendency . Rather than reducing people to conditioning or buried conflict, humanism studies the whole individual, conscious experience, and free will , valuing subjective striving over external control. An artist who keeps creating not for reward but to express their deepest capacities is, on this view, self-actualizing. This is why neither the cognitive school (information processing) nor the behavioural school (conditioning) fits the question; only humanism is defined by maximising human potential. Lock in: humanistic psychology, the third force, is the perspective built around self-actualization and reaching one's full potential. Panwar key: Humanistic psychology believes in the positivity of human nature and is based on the ideas of self-actualization (realising and reaching one's full potential) and a fully functioning individual. Why the other options are traps A. behavioural Behaviourism, the second force founded by John B. Watson and B. F. Skinner, explains action purely through observable stimulus-response learning and reinforcement and deliberately ignores inner mental life. It is tempting because it is a major perspective, but it has no concept of inner growth or potential, treating the person as shaped from outside rather than striving from within, so it cannot be the school centred on maximum potential. B. Cognitive Cognitive psychology studies how the mind processes information: attention, memory, perception, language, and thinking. It is a plausible distractor because it does concern the inner mind, unlike behaviourism. But its focus is the mechanics of mental processing, not personal fulfilment or self-actualization, so it does not centre on a person reaching their maximum potential the way humanism does. D. Psychoanalysis Psychoanalysis, Sigmund Freud's first force , traces behaviour to unconscious conflict, repressed drives, and early experience, taking a markedly less optimistic view of human nature. It tempts because it deeply concerns the inner person, but its aim is resolving buried conflict, not realising positive potential, which is exactly the optimistic growth emphasis that distinguishes humanism from it. Q70 Who is the founder of Positive Psychology? ✓ Answer: D · Seligman The answer is Seligman because Martin Seligman is recognised as the founder of modern positive psychology as a scientific discipline. The crucial distinction is between coining a phrase and launching a field. The actual term 'positive psychology' first appeared in Abraham Maslow's 1954 book Motivation and Personality , but it stayed a passing label within the humanistic tradition. To place this in Systems & Theories : humanistic psychology (the third force, Maslow and Carl Rogers) was the first movement to insist psychology study human strengths rather than pathology, but it was often criticised as lacking scientific rigour and hard data. Positive psychology can be seen as the empirical heir to that humanistic impulse. Seligman transformed the idea into an organised research movement: during his 1998 term as president of the American Psychological Association , he made human strengths and well-being the theme of his presidency, arguing that psychology had spent decades fixated on disorder while neglecting what makes life worth living. With Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi (originator of the concept of flow , the state of absorbed engagement), he defined positive psychology as the scientific study of positive human functioning and flourishing across individual, relational, and institutional levels. What set Seligman apart from the earlier humanists was his insistence on the scientific method : measuring happiness, optimism, character strengths, and engagement empirically rather than only theorising. His work on learned optimism (a reversal of his earlier 'learned helplessness' research) and the PERMA model of well-being are concrete products. Lock in: Maslow coined the term within humanism, but Seligman is the founder who built positive psychology into a rigorous empirical science. Panwar key: Martin Seligman and Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi define positive psychology as "the scientific study of positive human functioning and flourishing on multiple levels." Martin Seligman is a pioneer of Positive Psychology (the term itself was coined by Abraham Maslow), not simply because he has a systematic theory about why happy people are happy, but because he uses the scientific method to explore it. Why the other options are traps A. Howard Gardner Howard Gardner is famous for the theory of multiple intelligences (linguistic, logical-mathematical, spatial, musical, and others), which challenged the single-IQ view of intelligence. He is a tempting name because he is a major modern psychologist working on positive human capacities, but his domain is intelligence and cognition, not the founding of positive psychology. B. Q75 Humanistic and Phenomenological approaches have been criticised for: ✓ Answer: B · Missing the wider social and cultural contexts that influence experiences and its identities The answer is that they miss the wider social and cultural contexts , because humanistic and phenomenological approaches concentrate so heavily on the individual's inner world that they can overlook the surrounding forces that shape it. Q78 The striving for fulfilment of one's potential is called ✓ Answer: C · Self-Actualization The answer is Self-Actualization because that is precisely the term for striving to fulfil one's full potential.
