It tempts because both are 'basic', but physiological needs (food, water, sleep) are the absolute foundation that must come first, ahead of safety, so starting with safety inverts the base of the hierarchy and is wrong. D. Belongingness, Physiological, Safety This starts with belongingness, then physiological, then safety, placing the third-level social need at the bottom. It is the most scrambled option and tempts only on a careless read; belongingness is actually the third rung, not the lowest, so beginning with it contradicts Abraham Maslow's ascending order. Q83 Which among the following suggests that all individuals possess an innate tendency to grow and develop? ✓ Answer: B · Humanistic perspective The answer is the Humanistic perspective because it is the school built squarely on the belief that everyone has an innate tendency to grow and develop. To place this in Systems & Theories : humanism is the third force , founded by Abraham Maslow and Carl Rogers in the 1950s as a deliberate reaction against the pessimism of psychoanalysis (the first force) and the determinism of behaviourism (the second force). Where Sigmund Freud saw people driven by conflicted unconscious instincts and John B. Watson and B. F. Skinner saw them shaped passively by conditioning, humanism treats human nature as fundamentally positive and forward-moving. Rogers called this built-in drive the actualizing tendency : the organism's natural push to maintain, enhance, and develop its full capacities, much as a plant grows toward light when given the right conditions of warmth, water, and soil. For a person, those 'right conditions' include unconditional positive regard . Maslow expressed the same optimism through self-actualization at the top of his hierarchy, the realisation of one's full potential. The perspective looks at the whole individual and stresses free will , self-efficacy, and conscious striving. Contrast the alternatives sharply: the psychodynamic view sees people as driven by unconscious conflict and instinct, not a benign growth tendency, and the cognitive view studies information processing, not an innate developmental drive. So 'all of the above' fails because only humanism makes this growth assumption its centrepiece. The therapist's faith that, given the right conditions, a client will naturally move toward health is a concrete marker. Lock in: the innate tendency to grow and self-actualize is the defining assumption of the humanistic perspective. Panwar key: Humanistic psychology is a perspective that emphasises looking at the whole individual and stresses concepts such as free will, self-efficacy, and self-actualization. It assumes people have a natural tendency towards growth and self-actualization. Why the other options are traps A. Psychodynamic perspective The psychodynamic perspective (Sigmund Freud and successors) emphasises unconscious conflict, instinctual drives, and early childhood determinism, viewing the person as shaped by buried forces rather than a benign drive to grow. It tempts as a major perspective on inner life, but its picture of human nature is conflicted, not innately growth-oriented, so it does not fit. C. Cognitive perspective The cognitive perspective studies information processing, perception, memory, and thinking, treating the mind like a computational system. It tempts because it concerns inner mental life, but it makes no claim about an inborn tendency toward growth and self-development, which is a specifically humanistic assumption, so it is wrong. D. All of the above 'All of the above' is wrong because only the humanistic perspective centres on the innate growth tendency; the psychodynamic and cognitive perspectives do not. It tempts test-takers who assume each perspective must share the idea, but the actualizing/growth assumption is unique to humanism, so the inclusive option fails. Q84 Which of the following is not a characteristic of a 'figure'? ✓ Answer: D · Appears diffused, spatially distant The answer is Appears diffused, spatially distant because that describes the GROUND, not the figure, in Gestalt perception. To place this in Systems & Theories : figure-ground organisation is one of the foundational principles of Gestalt psychology , the school founded by Max Wertheimer , Kurt Koffka , and Wolfgang Kohler to show that the mind actively organises sensory input into structured wholes rather than passively registering isolated sensations. When we perceive a scene, the mind automatically splits it into a figure , the object of focus that stands out and seems to have a definite shape, and the ground , the background against which the figure is seen. The figure has several defining qualities: it is perceived as distinct and well-contoured with clear outlines , it tends to appear smaller in size , closer to the observer, and higher in 'object character' , meaning it looks like a definite thing. The ground , by contrast, seems shapeless, less defined, spatially distant, and recedes behind the figure, with the contour 'belonging' to the figure. The classic demonstration is the Rubin vase , where the same image flips between a vase (figure) on a dark ground and two faces (figure) on a light ground, but never both at once, showing the organisation is something the mind imposes. So smaller, clearly outlined, and higher in object character all belong to the figure, while diffuseness and spatial distance belong to the ground. Lock in: the figure is distinct, outlined, smaller, and closer, whereas diffused and distant describes the ground. Panwar key: In figure-ground perception, the figure is perceived as distinct, well-defined, smaller in size, and closer to the observer, while the ground appears diffused, less defined, and spatially distant. Therefore, 'appears diffused, spatially distant' describes the ground, not the figure. Why the other options are traps A. Smaller in size 'Smaller in size' IS a genuine property of the figure, which is typically seen as a compact, bounded object standing out against a larger surrounding ground. The option is listed to tempt a reader who reverses the rule, but since being smaller is a true figure characteristic, it cannot be the trait that does NOT belong to the figure. B. Clear outlines 'Clear outlines', meaning well-defined contours, IS a hallmark of the figure: the contour or boundary is perceived as belonging to the figure, giving it a definite edge while the ground stays shapeless. Because clear outlines genuinely characterise the figure, this is not the exception the question asks for. C. Higher in object character 'Higher in object character', the thing-like quality of looking like a definite object, IS a property of the figure, not the ground. It tempts only if you confuse the two regions, but object character belongs to the figure, so it is a true figure trait and therefore not the answer. Q85 Which of the following is not associated with the humanistic perspective of psychopathology? ✓ Answer: C · Availability of reinforcement The answer is Availability of reinforcement because reinforcement is a behaviourist concept and has no place in the humanistic view of psychopathology. To place this in Systems & Theories : the humanistic perspective is the third force , founded by Abraham Maslow and Carl Rogers as an alternative to psychoanalysis (first force) and behaviourism (second force). On the humanistic view, psychological distress arises when a person's natural growth toward self-actualization is blocked, often because they have received only conditional acceptance and developed incongruence between their real self and their self-concept. Its therapeutic hallmarks are a deep belief in human potential , the provision of unconditional positive regard (warm, non-judgmental acceptance of the person regardless of behaviour), and a respectful, genuine attitude from the therapist, including empathy and congruence, the 'core conditions' Rogers identified. Together these create a safe space in which the client's own actualizing tendency can resume. Reinforcement , by contrast, comes from B.F. Skinner and operant conditioning within behaviourism: it is the mechanism of strengthening responses through rewards or consequences, treating the person as shaped from outside rather than growing from within. Importing reinforcement into the humanistic frame mixes two fundamentally opposed philosophies of human nature: one sees the person as an active, self-directing organism, the other as a product of environmental contingencies. That clash is exactly what the question tests. Lock in: human potential, unconditional positive regard, and a respectful stance are humanistic, while reinforcement is a behaviourist idea. Panwar key: The humanistic approach is called the "third force" in psychology. Humanism, humanist studies the whole person and stresses belief in human potential, unconditional positive regard and a respectful therapeutic attitude. Reinforcement is a behaviourist concept, not humanistic. Why the other options are traps A. Belief in human potential Belief in human potential is a core humanistic assumption: the conviction that people have an innate capacity to grow toward self-actualization given the right conditions. It is listed precisely because it genuinely belongs to the humanistic view, so choosing it would be wrong; the question wants the option that does NOT belong. B. Availability of positive regard Availability of positive regard refers to Carl Rogers' unconditional positive regard , the warm, non-judgmental acceptance that is central to person-centred humanistic therapy and lets the client's actualizing tendency resume. Because it is a defining humanistic ingredient, not an outsider, it cannot be the concept that fails to fit. D. Respectful attitude therapists A respectful, genuine attitude of the therapist captures the Rogerian core conditions of empathy and congruence, the hallmark of person-centred humanistic practice. It is included to tempt a careless reader, but since it is squarely a humanistic feature, it belongs to the perspective and is not the answer. Q86 Which of the following should not be exhibited by a true sportsman? ✓ Answer: D · Focussing on winning at all costs The answer is Focussing on winning at all costs because that attitude contradicts the very ideals of sportsmanship . To place this in Systems & Theories : this item sits in the humanistic/positive-psychology stream applied to sport psychology , which studies the psychological factors in athletic performance and well-being and, in the humanistic spirit, values the development of healthy character, not just outcomes. Sportsmanship is the ethical and emotional disposition that lets a competitor play fairly, treat opponents and officials with respect, and value the integrity of the contest above the result. A healthy sportsperson shows several adaptive psychological traits that map onto positive-psychology strengths: persistence , the determination to keep going through setbacks (linked to grit and resilience); self-control , the ability to regulate emotion and stay calm under pressure (emotional self-regulation); and optimism , a positive explanatory style that supports recovery from failure (Martin Seligman's learned optimism). All three serve both performance and well-being and reflect the strengths-based view of the person that positive psychology promotes. A win-at-all-costs mindset, by contrast, prizes the outcome so highly that it erodes fairness and composure, encouraging cheating, aggression, and the breakdown of emotional control when things go wrong. It treats victory as the only value, the opposite of fair play and good character, and is associated with poorer long-term well-being. A true sportsman congratulates a stronger opponent rather than disputing every call. Lock in: persistence, self-control, and optimism are the marks of a true sportsman, while focusing on winning at all costs is the trait to reject. Panwar key: A sports person should be persistent, have self-control, should be able to remain calm in stressful situations and must be fair in all sports situations. Focus on winning at all costs is a negative idea and should not be present in a (true) sportsman. Why the other options are traps A. Being persistent Persistence, the determination to keep going through setbacks, is a positive, adaptive trait (akin to grit and resilience) that a true sportsman should exhibit. It is listed to tempt a reader who skims, but since it is a desirable quality rather than a flaw, it is not the trait that should be absent, so it is not the answer. B. Maintaining self-control Maintaining self-control, regulating one's emotions and staying composed under pressure, is exactly what a good sportsperson should do, especially after bad calls or losses. It is a hallmark of sportsmanship, not something to avoid, so selecting it misreads the question, which asks what a true sportsman should NOT exhibit. C. Being optimistic Optimism, a positive outlook that supports resilience and recovery from failure, is a desirable, adaptive quality for a competitor and aligns with Martin Seligman's learned optimism. Because it is something a true sportsman SHOULD show rather than avoid, it cannot be the negative trait the question is asking you to identify. Q87 Which perspective is often referred to as the 'third force' in Psychology? ✓ Answer: D · Humanism The answer is Humanism because humanistic psychology is the perspective known as the third force . To place this in Systems & Theories , see why the field needed a third option. In the early and mid-twentieth century, two schools held sway: psychoanalysis (the first force , Sigmund Freud), explaining people through unconscious drives and early conflict, and behaviourism (the second force , John B. Watson and B. F. Skinner), explaining behaviour through conditioning and reinforcement while ignoring inner experience. Both were seen as deterministic, casting people as driven by forces they could not control. Reacting against this, Abraham Maslow and Carl Rogers founded humanistic psychology in the 1950s as a third force, joined by figures such as Rollo May. It studies the whole person and the uniqueness of each individual, and it emphasises free will , conscious choice, subjective experience, and the innate drive toward self-actualization . Where the earlier forces stressed constraint, humanism stressed potential and personal responsibility, restoring optimism and agency to psychology's view of human nature. Distinguish the distractors by their systems: biopsychosocial is an integrative model of health (Engel) combining biological, psychological, and social factors, and cognitive psychology studies information processing; neither carries the historically conferred 'third force' title. Humanism's optimistic, growth-oriented view of human nature and its respect for subjective experience are its concrete markers. Lock in: humanism is the third force, the whole-person alternative to psychoanalysis and behaviourism. Panwar key: The humanistic approach is called the "third force" in psychology. Humanistic, humanism and humanist are terms in psychology relating to an approach which studies the whole person and the uniqueness of each individual. Why the other options are traps A. Biopsychosocial The biopsychosocial model (proposed by George Engel) is an integrative framework for understanding health and illness across biological, psychological, and social levels. It tempts as a respected, modern multi-factor approach, but it is a model of health rather than one of psychology's three historically numbered forces, so it is not the 'third force'. B. behaviourism Behaviourism (John B. Watson, B. F. Skinner) was the second force , focused on observable stimulus-response learning, and it is precisely the deterministic approach humanism reacted against. It tempts as a major dominant school, but it is numbered second, not third, so labelling it the third force confuses the sequence. C. Cognitive psychology Cognitive psychology is sometimes loosely called a later wave or movement in psychology, which makes it a plausible distractor. But the established, historically conferred 'third force' label belongs specifically to humanism; cognitive psychology studies mental information processing and never carried that title, so it is wrong. Q88 "Each person must continually recreate himself, The meaning of life and of existence is never fixed; rather, it constantly changes." This can be best explained by- ✓ Answer: B · Existential Psychology The answer is Existential Psychology because the idea that meaning is never fixed and each person must continually recreate themselves is the heart of existential thought. To place this in Systems & Theories : existential psychology is part of the broad third-force movement (alongside humanism) that rejected the determinism of psychoanalysis and behaviourism, but it draws its distinctive content from existential philosophy, thinkers like Soren Kierkegaard , Martin Heidegger , and Jean-Paul Sartre , brought into psychology by Rollo May and Viktor Frankl (and later Irvin Yalom ). Its central claim is that there is no pre-given essence or fixed purpose handed to us; instead, existence comes first and we define ourselves through the choices we make. Sartre's formula that 'existence precedes essence' captures exactly this: a person is not a finished thing but an ongoing project, perpetually authoring their own meaning. With that freedom comes responsibility and the anxiety of having to choose without guarantees, and the task is to live authentically in the face of death and uncertainty. Existential therapists therefore look past mere symptom reduction to how a client defines meaning , purpose, and a life well lived (Frankl's logotherapy is one example). Distinguish the close option, humanistic psychology: though related and equally growth-focused, humanism centres on self-actualization and the positive actualizing tendency, whereas this quotation about ever-changing, self-recreated meaning is specifically existential in flavour. Lock in: the view that meaning is never fixed and must be continually recreated through free choice is existential psychology. Panwar key: Existential psychologists believe that it's not simply important to identify and reduce the symptomatology of mental illnesses, addictions, relationship issues, and other psychological issues, but to go beyond the symptoms, addressing how a person defines meaning, purpose, and a life well lived. They believe that The meaning of life and of existence is never fixed; rather, it constantly changes. Why the other options are traps A. Humanistic Psychology Humanistic psychology overlaps heavily with existential thought (both are third-force, choice- and growth-affirming), which makes it the strongest distractor. But humanism centres on self-actualization and an innate positive growth tendency, whereas the quotation's radical, ever-shifting self-creation and the idea that meaning is never fixed is the specifically existential emphasis, so humanism is the near-miss. C. Experimental Psychology Experimental psychology is a methodological tradition that studies behaviour and mental processes through controlled scientific experiments. It tempts only because it is a familiar term, but it is an approach to method, not a philosophy of meaning or existence, so it cannot account for the quotation about recreating the self and shifting meaning. D. Philosophy Philosophy is the broader parent discipline from which existentialism springs, and the quote does sound philosophical, which is the trap. But the question asks for the best PSYCHOLOGICAL framing, and the specific theme of continually recreating the self and ever-changing meaning is captured precisely by existential psychology, not philosophy in general. Q89 Which psychologist's work on Basic Anxiety aligns closely with Karen Horney's conception of neurosis and feelings of helplessness in the Indian context? ✓ Answer: C · Sudhir Kakar. The answer is Sudhir Kakar because his work applying psychoanalytic ideas like basic anxiety to the Indian context aligns most closely with Karen Horney's conception of neurosis and helplessness. To place this in Systems & Theories : Horney was a neo-Freudian who revised classical psychoanalysis by stressing social and cultural factors over Sigmund Freud's biological drives. She argued that neurosis grows out of basic anxiety , a deep feeling of helplessness and insecurity that a child develops in a threatening or unloving environment, leading to defensive interpersonal strategies (moving toward, against, or away from people). Sudhir Kakar is regarded as India's foremost cultural psychoanalyst , a thinker who took Western psychoanalytic concepts and reinterpreted them through Indian childhood, family structure, religion, and culture. He extended this culturally-sensitive psychoanalytic lens to the Indian socio-cultural setting, examining how patterns of dependence, the joint family, and early mother-child relationships shape the inner world of the Indian individual, thereby bridging psychoanalysis with indigenous experience, in much the same socially-grounded spirit as Horney. Distinguish the other Indian psychologists named: Durganand Sinha is associated with social, cross-cultural psychology and the indigenization of psychology in India, and Anand C. Paranjpe with self and identity in Indian psychological thought; both are major figures but neither maps onto Horney's basic anxiety. It is Kakar, with his psychoanalytic, culture-grounded account of the Indian psyche, who fits. Lock in: Sudhir Kakar, India's cultural psychoanalyst, connects Horney's basic anxiety and helplessness to the Indian context. Panwar key: Sudhir Kakar's work on Basic Anxiety aligns closely with Karen Horney's concept of neurosis and feelings of helplessness in the Indian context. He applies psychoanalytic ideas to Indian cultural and social settings. Why the other options are traps A. Anand C. Paranjpe. Anand C. Paranjpe is known for his work on self and identity in Indian psychological thought, integrating Indian philosophical traditions with Western psychology. He tempts as a major figure in Indian psychology, but his focus is the self and identity from an indigenous philosophical angle, not Karen Horney's psychoanalytic concept of basic anxiety, so he does not fit. B. Kamala Chaudhuri. Kamala Chaudhuri is associated with adapting projective techniques such as the Thematic Apperception Test (TAT) for the Indian context. She tempts because she is an Indian psychologist working with psychoanalytically-flavoured tools, but her contribution is in projective assessment, not in linking Karen Horney's basic anxiety and neurosis to Indian culture, so she is wrong. D. Durganand Sinha. Durganand Sinha is a foundational figure in Indian social and cross-cultural psychology, known for work on deprivation and the indigenization of psychology. He tempts as perhaps the best-known Indian psychologist listed, but his domain is social/cross-cultural research, not Horneyan psychoanalysis of basic anxiety, so he does not match the question. Cognitive / Consciousness Q90 ____ is a source of knowledge as per Empiricists. ✓ Answer: C · Sensory experiences The answer is sensory experiences because empiricism, by definition, roots every piece of knowledge in what the senses deliver. To see why, begin with epistemology , the branch of philosophy that asks where knowledge comes from and how we can justify it. Empiricism answers that the mind begins essentially empty and is filled only by what we see, hear, touch, taste, and smell. John Locke captured this with the image of the mind as a tabula rasa , a blank slate written upon by lived experience; David Hume and George Berkeley pushed further, arguing that even abstract ideas are ultimately faded copies or recombinations of earlier sensory impressions. Empiricism therefore privileges observation, empirical evidence, and substantiation over truths supposedly built into the mind. Its great rival is rationalism (René Descartes, Leibniz, Spinoza), which credits reason and innate ideas; a third stance, skepticism, doubts certainty altogether. Where does this sit in Systems & Theories of psychology ? Empiricism is one of the deepest philosophical taproots of the discipline. When psychology broke from philosophy in 1879 under Wilhelm Wundt , it inherited the empiricist demand that mind be studied through observable data rather than armchair speculation. That same empiricist spirit later hardened into behaviourism (John B. Watson, B. F. Skinner), which insisted only observable, sensory-measurable behaviour counts as science; and the British associationists who built mental life from sensations were direct empiricist descendants. The cognitive revolution of the 1950s-60s (Ulric Neisser, Miller) softened pure empiricism by readmitting internal representations, yet still grounded theory in measurable evidence. So empiricism is not a relic: it is the methodological backbone running from Locke through Wundt and behaviourism into modern experimental psychology. Lock in: empiricism says knowledge comes from sensory experience, while rationalism credits reason and innate ideas. Panwar key: In philosophy, empiricism is a theory that states that knowledge comes only or primarily from sensory experience. The theory gives emphasis to experience and substantiation, sensory participation and awareness in particular, in the development of thoughts and ideas. It is one of several views of epistemology, along with rationalism and skepticism. Empiricism emphasizes the role of empirical evidence in the formation of ideas, rather than innate ideas or traditions. Why the other options are traps A. Logical reasoning Logical reasoning as the primary source of knowledge is the signature claim of rationalism (René Descartes, Leibniz), empiricism's direct opposite. It is tempting because reasoning clearly feels like a way we 'know' things, but empiricists insist reasoning only rearranges material the senses first supplied; reason alone is not their source , so this is wrong for an empiricist. B. Theories Theories are constructed, abstract explanations, not the raw input empiricists treat as the origin of knowledge. The word looks scientific and so attractive, but for an empiricist a theory must itself be built up from and tested against observation. Theories are products of the empiricist process, never the foundational source it points to, making this incorrect. D. Contemplations Contemplation means pure introspective or meditative thought generated within the mind. It is tempting because thinking obviously produces ideas, but contemplation as a self-sufficient source of truth belongs to rationalist and innate-idea traditions. Empiricism explicitly denies that inward reflection unaided by the senses can be the origin of knowledge, so it cannot be the answer. Q91 The point at which a stimulus becomes strong enough to trigger a response only 50% of the time is ✓ Answer: A · Threshold of response The answer is threshold of response because a threshold is, by definition, the stimulus level at which a response is triggered on half of all attempts. To understand this, turn to psychophysics , the field founded by Gustav Fechner that quantifies the lawful relationship between physical stimuli and the sensations they produce. Because our senses do not switch on at a single fixed value, detection cannot be defined as 'always' or 'never'; researchers therefore adopt a statistical cutoff. The absolute threshold is the minimum stimulus intensity an observer can detect on 50 percent of trials . The 50 percent rule exists because, near the limit of sensation, moment-to-moment fluctuations in attention, fatigue, and background neural noise make detection probabilistic rather than all-or-none. A related construct is the difference threshold or just noticeable difference (JND) , the smallest detectable change, noticed half the time. Where does this sit in Systems & Theories ? Psychophysics, born in the 1850s-60s with Weber and Fechner , was the very first rigorously quantitative psychology and supplied the experimental respectability that let Wundt open his Leipzig laboratory in 1879. It proved mind could be measured, paving the way for structuralism. Crucially, the threshold concept survived the long behaviourist eclipse and re-emerged as a cornerstone of the cognitive revolution : the information-processing model treats the observer as a limited-capacity system whose detection is probabilistic, and signal detection theory later refined the threshold idea by separating true sensitivity from decision bias. So the humble threshold links classical psychophysics directly to the cognitive view of the mind as an information channel coping with noise. Lock in: a threshold is the cutoff intensity at which a stimulus first triggers a response on at least 50 percent of occasions tested. Panwar key: A threshold is the cut off point at which the response can be initiated, at least 50 % of the time. Why the other options are traps B. Response bias Response bias is an observer's standing tendency to answer 'yes' or 'no' regardless of the actual stimulus, a concept from signal detection theory . It is tempting because it also concerns how observers respond near threshold, but bias is a decision criterion, not a detection point. It describes how willing someone is to report a signal, never the 50 percent intensity, so it is wrong here. C. Signal detection of response Signal detection theory is a whole framework (Green & Swets) for separating true sensitivity from decision bias when distinguishing signal from noise. It is a tempting distractor because it grew out of and refined threshold research, but the phrase 'signal detection of response' is not the definition of the 50 percent point. SDT actually challenges the classical threshold idea rather than naming it. D. Phi phenomenon The phi phenomenon is the Gestalt illusion of apparent motion produced when stationary lights flash in sequence, demonstrated by Max Wertheimer . It is tempting only because it is another classic perception term, but it concerns perceived movement, not detection limits. It has nothing to do with the 50 percent stimulus cutoff, so it is clearly incorrect. Q92 Every Just Noticeable Difference in stimulation constitutes a constant increment in sensation magnitude. Who among the following had given this assumption? ✓ Answer: D · Fechner The answer is Fechner because he supplied the assumption that every just noticeable difference adds one equal step of sensation. To understand this, begin with Ernst Weber , who discovered that the smallest detectable change in a stimulus, the just noticeable difference (JND) , is a constant proportion of the original stimulus rather than a fixed absolute amount: a candle is obvious in a dark room but lost in daylight. Gustav Fechner , the founder of psychophysics , took Weber's empirical finding and added a daring theoretical leap: he assumed each JND, wherever it falls on the scale, represents one equal increment of subjective sensation. Treating every JND as a constant unit of felt experience, Fechner mathematically integrated across these steps and derived that sensation grows in proportion to the logarithm of physical intensity, the Weber-Fechner law . This explains why doubling a light's energy yields only a modest rise in perceived brightness. Where does this sit in Systems & Theories ? Fechner's 1860 Elements of Psychophysics was arguably the first truly quantitative law in psychology and the historical hinge on which the discipline became a science. By showing the mental could be mathematically related to the physical, Fechner gave Wundt the tools and credibility to launch experimental psychology in 1879, seeding structuralism's attempt to measure conscious elements. His logarithmic scaling was later challenged by S. S. Stevens' power law, and the underlying notion of a limited, noise-bound sensory system fed directly into the information-processing thinking of the cognitive revolution . Lock in: Weber described the constant proportion of the JND, but it was Fechner who assumed each JND equals a constant increment of sensation . Panwar key: Fechner's law or the Weber-Fechner law is a psychological law quantifying the perception of change in a given stimulus. It also states that every JND in stimulus constitutes a constant increment in sensation magnitude. Why the other options are traps A. Ebbinghaus Ebbinghaus pioneered the experimental study of memory using nonsense syllables, giving us the forgetting curve and the savings method. He is tempting because he is another nineteenth-century quantitative pioneer often listed beside Weber and Fechner, but his domain was memory and learning, not the psychophysics of sensation magnitude, so he did not formulate this assumption. B. Weber Weber discovered the empirical regularity behind all this, that the JND is a constant fraction of the stimulus (Weber's law). He is the most seductive wrong answer because his name is half of 'Weber-Fechner.' But Weber only described the proportional JND in the physical stimulus; it was Fechner who added the further assumption about equal sensation increments, so Weber alone is incorrect. C. Tolman Tolman was a neo-behaviourist famous for cognitive maps, latent learning, and purposive behaviourism in rats. He is a distractor only because he is a major theorist, but his work concerns learning and intervening variables, decades and disciplines away from psychophysical scaling of sensation. He has no connection to JNDs, ruling him out. Q93 One feature of the streaming of consciousness that received substantial attention by researchers is: ✓ Answer: B · Daydreaming The answer is daydreaming because it is the feature of the stream of consciousness that researchers examined most intensively. To understand this, recall William James , who in his 1890 Principles of Psychology coined the phrase stream of consciousness to capture how thought flows continuously and ever-changing rather than arriving in discrete, separable chunks. Within that flowing stream, attention does not stay locked on the external world; it drifts inward to images, memories, and fantasies unrelated to the immediate surroundings. This inward drift is daydreaming , also called stimulus-independent thought because its content is internally generated rather than cued by the environment, the close ancestor of today's research on mind-wandering . Teasdale and colleagues (1991) studied how often such thoughts arise, what conditions provoke them, and how they relate to mood and concentration, making daydreaming the most carefully measured component of ongoing consciousness. Where does this sit in Systems & Theories ? Consciousness was the founding subject matter of psychology under James's functionalism and Wundt-Titchener structuralism , but behaviourism banished it for half a century as unobservable and therefore unscientific. The cognitive revolution of the 1950s-60s, led by figures like Ulric Neisser and Miller , made internal mental events respectable again by treating the mind as an information processor whose attention can be directed either outward or inward. Daydreaming research is a direct fruit of that revolution: it took James's century-old phenomenological insight and made it experimentally tractable. Lock in: daydreaming is stimulus-independent, internally generated thought, the drifting feature of James's stream of consciousness that drew the most research. Panwar key: Daydreaming, also known as stimulus independent thoughts, was studied by Teasdale et al in 1991. It was one of the features of the streaming of consciousness. Why the other options are traps A. Gender differences Gender differences are a demographic individual-difference variable, not a structural feature of the stream of consciousness itself. The option is tempting because gender comparisons are a popular research theme generally, but James's concept describes the flowing nature and contents of awareness in everyone. Gender is something you could study about consciousness, not a defining feature of it, so it is wrong. C. Brain wave patterns Brain wave patterns are physiological correlates of mental states measured by EEG. They are tempting because they sound rigorously scientific and are studied in consciousness and sleep research, but they are physiological measures , not a phenomenological feature of the experienced stream. The question asks about a feature of the stream, not the biological signal underneath it, ruling this out. D. Eye movement Eye movements are an oculomotor behaviour studied heavily in perception, attention, and reading research. The option tempts because eye tracking is a famous window into cognition, but eye movements are an observable motor output, not a component of the inner conscious stream. They index where attention points, rather than constituting the stream's internally generated content, so they are incorrect. Q94 ______ is a form of perspective taking that requires the ability to view a situation from at least two perspectives, that is to reason simultaneously about what two or more people are thinking. ✓ Answer: C · Recursive thought The answer is recursive thought because it is precisely the perspective-taking ability to reason simultaneously about what two or more minds are thinking. To understand this, start with perspective taking , the capacity to step outside one's own viewpoint and consider how a situation appears to someone else. Recursive thought is a more advanced form in which one mental representation is embedded inside another, so you reason not merely about what one person thinks, but about what that person thinks a third person thinks. The classic illustration is 'person 1 thinks that person 2 thinks that person 3 thinks', each idea nesting within a similar one. This self-nesting is what makes the thought recursive : a process operates on its own output. Recursive thought is the engine of a mature theory of mind , the understanding that others hold beliefs, desires, and intentions different from one's own, and it underwrites complex social reasoning, deception, and cooperation. Where does this sit in Systems & Theories ? It belongs to the developmental and cognitive lineage that runs from Jean Piaget , whose stage theory of how children overcome egocentrism and acquire decentred, reversible reasoning was a pillar of the cognitive revolution that overthrew behaviourism in the 1950s-60s. Where behaviourism refused to theorize the inner mind, cognitive and developmental psychology made mental representation and the manipulation of representations central; recursive thought is exactly such a manipulation, one representation contained in another. Theory-of-mind research (Premack & Woodruff; Wimmer & Perner's false-belief task) extended Piaget's foundation. Lock in: recursive thought means holding at least two perspectives at once by embedding one mental representation inside another. Panwar key: Recursive thought is a form of perspective taking that requires the ability to view a situation from at least two perspectives, that is to reason simultaneously about what two or more people are thinking. For example, by thinking what person 1 thinks person 2 thinks person 3 thinks - is a prime example of recursive thinking in which one process, representation, or idea becomes embedded within a similar one. Why the other options are traps A. Referential style Referential style names an early language-acquisition style (contrasted with expressive style) in which a toddler's first words are mostly object labels. It is tempting only because it starts with the same letter and sounds technical, but it concerns vocabulary preferences in language development, not nested perspective taking about other minds, so it is entirely off-target here. B. Reversibility Reversibility is the Piagetian concrete-operational ability to mentally undo an action, the cognitive move that makes conservation possible. It is a strong distractor because it is a genuine cognitive-developmental term from the same theoretical family, but reversibility is about reversing physical transformations in one's own reasoning, not about simultaneously representing several people's thoughts, which is what the question demands. D. Reconstruction Reconstruction refers to memory being actively rebuilt at retrieval rather than replayed verbatim, a core finding from Frederic Bartlett's schema research. It tempts because it is a respected cognitive concept, but it describes how memories are reassembled, not a mode of perspective taking. There is no embedding of one mind's view inside another's, so it cannot be the answer. Q95 The current approach to psychology most closely aligned with the structuralists in its interest in topics like consciousness, mental imagery and thought process is: ✓ Answer: B · Cognitive psychology The answer is cognitive psychology because it revived the very topics, consciousness, mental imagery, and thought, that the structuralists first studied. To understand this, go back to structuralism , founded by Wilhelm Wundt and his student Edward Titchener , which tried to break conscious experience into its basic elements using introspection , the trained self-report of one's own mental contents. This was psychology's first formal school after the discipline split from philosophy in 1879. Functionalism (James, John Dewey) soon asked instead what mind is for , then behaviourism under John B. Watson and B. F. Skinner rejected the study of mind entirely, insisting psychology examine only observable behaviour because inner states could not be measured objectively. For roughly forty years the mind was off-limits. Then the cognitive revolution of the 1950s-60s, driven by Ulric Neisser (whose 1967 Cognitive Psychology named the field), George Miller , Noam Chomsky's demolition of Skinnerian language, and the new information-processing computer metaphor, brought mental processes back to the centre. Cognitive psychology studies perception, attention, memory, mental imagery, language, and thinking, the structuralists' subject matter, but it replaced unreliable introspection with rigorous experiments, reaction-time measures, and models of the mind as a system that encodes, stores, and retrieves information. So its place in Systems & Theories is as the heir that reclaimed structuralism's questions while inheriting behaviourism's experimental discipline. Lock in: cognitive psychology matches structuralism in studying consciousness and thought, but unlike structuralism it uses controlled experiments rather than introspection. Panwar key: The current approach to psychology most closely aligned with the structuralists in its interest in topics like consciousness, mental imagery and thought process is Cognitive Psychology. Why the other options are traps A. Neuroscience Neuroscience studies the brain's biological mechanisms, neurons, circuits, neurotransmitters, and imaging, rather than the contents of conscious experience. It is tempting because it is a leading modern approach that often partners with cognition (cognitive neuroscience), but its focus is the physical substrate, not the structuralists' subjective mental elements, so it is not the closest match. C. Behaviourism Behaviourism is the very school that rejected consciousness, imagery, and introspection as unscientific, making it the direct opposite of structuralism rather than its heir. It is a tempting trap precisely because it is a dominant historical school you must place, but choosing it inverts the question; behaviourism studied only overt behaviour, so it cannot be the answer. D. Functionalism Functionalism (James, John Dewey, Angell) was structuralism's contemporary rival, but it studied the purpose and adaptive function of mental processes, not the structural analysis of conscious contents. It tempts because it also took mind seriously and arose at the same moment, yet its emphasis on what mind does, not what it is made of, makes it less aligned than cognitive psychology with structuralism's particular interests. Q96 In the definition of Psychology, mental processes mean ________. ✓ Answer: A · Internal, covert processes The answer is internal, covert processes because that is exactly what 'mental processes' denotes in the standard definition of psychology. To understand this, recall the modern definition: psychology is the scientific study of behaviour and mental processes . This phrasing deliberately has two halves. Behaviour covers everything an organism does that can be directly observed and measured from outside, such as speaking, walking, or reacting. Mental processes , by contrast, are the internal, covert events of the mind that cannot be seen directly: thinking, feeling, remembering, perceiving, dreaming, and forming intentions, inferred from behaviour and self-report rather than watched in the open. The word covert means hidden or not openly displayed, the opposite of overt , meaning observable. Where does this sit in Systems & Theories ? The two-part definition is itself a historical compromise, a snapshot of psychology's whole arc. Early structuralism and functionalism studied the mind through introspection; then behaviourism (John B. Watson, B. F. Skinner) stripped the definition down to behaviour alone, banishing 'mind' as unobservable for decades. The cognitive revolution of the 1950s-60s, with Ulric Neisser , Miller , and the information-processing model treating the mind as a system that encodes, stores, and retrieves information, restored internal mental events as legitimate scientific objects. The phrase 'behaviour and mental processes' literally fuses the behaviourist demand to study observable action with the cognitive insistence that covert inner life is real and measurable through inference. The mechanism: we observe behaviour directly but infer mental processes from it. Lock in: mental processes are the internal, covert activities of the mind, while behaviour is the overt, observable side. Panwar key: Mental processes refer to the internal, covert processes as well as the internal experiences and conscious activities of the mind such as thinking, feeling and remembering. Why the other options are traps B. Outward behaviour Outward behaviour is the observable, overt half of psychology's definition, not the mental-process half. It is the most tempting distractor because it is genuinely part of the same definition, but the question specifically asks what 'mental processes' means, and behaviour is contrasted against mental processes. Picking the visible side when asked about the hidden side makes this wrong. C. Overt actions and reactions Overt actions and reactions are observable behaviours, the precise opposite of covert mental processes. The option tempts by using formal-sounding language ('actions and reactions'), but 'overt' literally means open and visible, whereas mental processes are defined as covert and internal. It names the wrong half of the behaviour-versus-mind distinction, so it cannot be correct. D. Only animal behaviour Animal behaviour is a legitimate subject psychology studies (comparative psychology, learning research), not the meaning of the term 'mental processes.' It tempts because animals appear throughout behaviourist work, but the question is about a definitional term, and mental processes refer to internal events in any organism, human or animal. Restricting the term to animals misreads the definition entirely. Q97 "The whole is greater than the sum of the parts and that the parts or subsystems are related to each other and to the whole" are emphasised in ________. ✓ Answer: C · Systems theory The answer is systems theory because its defining principle is that the whole is greater than the sum of its parts and that the parts are interrelated with one another and with the whole. To understand this, define a system as a set of interacting components forming an organized, unified whole. Systems theory , developed as an interdisciplinary framework most associated with the biologist Ludwig von Bertalanffy and his General System Theory , studies how such systems behave across biology, organizations, families, and psychology alike. Its central claim is holism : a system cannot be fully understood by examining its parts in isolation, because the interactions among parts produce emergent properties no single component possesses. This is exactly why 'the whole is greater than the sum of its parts.' Each subsystem relates both to the others and to the larger whole, so a change in one ripples through all. Where does this sit in Systems & Theories ? The holistic idea has deep roots in Gestalt psychology (Max Wertheimer, Kurt Koffka, Wolfgang Köhler), whose slogan that the perceptual whole differs from the sum of its sensory parts directly opposed the element-by-element analysis of structuralism . Bertalanffy generalized that insight from perception to all organized systems in the mid-twentieth century, and it later fed family-systems therapy and the broader move, contemporaneous with the cognitive revolution , away from reductionist behaviourism toward viewing the organism as an integrated information-processing whole. Lock in: systems theory is the framework defined by holism, interrelated subsystems, and emergent wholes that exceed the sum of their parts. Panwar key: Systems theory is an interdisciplinary study of systems, as they relate to one another within a larger, more complex system. The key concept of systems theory, regardless of which discipline it's being applied to, is that the whole is greater than the sum of its parts. Why the other options are traps A. Motivation theory Motivation theory explains what energizes, directs, and sustains behaviour (drives, needs, incentives), not the holistic relationship of parts to a whole. It tempts because 'theory' appears in the name and it is a familiar topic, but it addresses why organisms act, not the structural principle that interacting parts create emergent wholes, so it does not match the quoted definition. B. Contingency theory Contingency theory holds that the best course of action depends on the situation, with no single universally best way, common in management and leadership. It is a plausible distractor because it is an organizational theory, but its core idea is situational fit, not part-whole holism or emergence. Nothing in contingency theory says the whole exceeds the sum of its parts, ruling it out. D. Administrative theory Administrative theory, associated with Henri Fayol , lays out principles of management and organizational structure (planning, organizing, commanding, coordinating, controlling). It tempts as another classic organizational framework, but it concerns how to administer an organization efficiently, not the holistic claim that interrelated subsystems produce emergent wholes. Its focus is managerial principles, not systems holism. Q98 The ________ framework is based on the expectancy, demand and incentive concepts. ✓ Answer: C · social learning The answer is social learning because this framework explains behaviour through cognitive variables, notably expectancy, demand, and incentive. To understand this, the social learning tradition, developed by Julian Rotter and extended by Albert Bandura , argues that behaviour is shaped not by reinforcement alone but by how a person mentally interprets situations. Rotter held that the likelihood of a behaviour depends on expectancy , the person's belief about how probable a given outcome is, and on reinforcement value , how much that outcome is wanted, an idea closely tied to incentive ; demand refers to the pull of the situation and its goals. Combining these, the framework predicts choices from subjective cognition rather than purely external stimuli. Where does this sit in Systems & Theories ? Social learning theory is the crucial bridge between behaviourism and the cognitive revolution . Classic behaviourists (John B. Watson, B. F. Skinner) banned internal variables, but the neo-behaviourists (notably Tolman with his expectancies, and Clark Hull ) reintroduced intervening cognitive constructs; Rotter and Bandura completed the move by making expectancies, values, and (in Bandura) self-efficacy and observational learning central, helping carry psychology from stimulus-response into the mind-centred cognitive era of the 1950s-60s. One nuance to flag: the Panwar key labels this concept the cognitive framework, and the listed concepts are indeed cognitive in nature; the keyed/intended answer here is social learning, but be aware the source text uses 'cognitive,' so reason from how your specific paper frames it. Lock in: the expectancy-demand-incentive framework explains action through cognitive expectancies and the value of anticipated reinforcement, the hallmark of Rotter's social learning theory. Panwar key: Cognitive framework is based on the concept of expectancy, demand and intention of the human being. It includes concepts related to an individual's cognition and concepts of cognitive psychology. Why the other options are traps A. behavioural The pure behavioural framework explains action through observable stimulus-response links and reinforcement, deliberately excluding internal mental variables. It tempts because 'learning' appears in the keyed answer and behaviourism is the obvious learning school, but the very concepts named, expectancy and incentive cognitions, are internal interpretations that strict behaviourism rejects, so the plain behavioural framework is wrong. B. cognitive The cognitive framework concerns thought, memory, attention, and information processing broadly, and expectancy is genuinely cognitive, which makes this an extremely tempting choice (indeed the Panwar key itself uses the word 'cognitive'). However, the keyed answer assigns the specific expectancy-demand-incentive trio to social learning theory; treat it as a flagged debate, but the intended response here is social learning, not the broad cognitive label. D. supportive Supportive frameworks, common in organizational leadership and the supportive model of organizational behaviour, stress managerial care, encouragement, and backing of employees to build motivation and participation. The option tempts as an organizational-sounding term, but it has nothing to do with the expectancy-demand-incentive constructs, which derive from Julian Rotter's social learning psychology, so it is clearly incorrect. Q99 The first major theoretical effort in information processing psychology was by ________ in the year ________? ✓ Answer: C · Broadbent, 1958 The answer is Donald Broadbent, 1958 because Donald Broadbent produced the first major theory cast explicitly in the information-processing mould. To understand this, recall that the information-processing approach treats the mind like a system that takes in input, processes it through limited-capacity stages, and produces output, much as a computer does. Working on attention problems, such as how a person follows one conversation among many (the cocktail-party problem studied with dichotic listening), Broadbent proposed his filter theory in his 1958 book Perception and Communication . He argued that sensory information enters a brief sensory store, then passes through a selective filter that admits only one channel at a time based on physical features such as which ear or what pitch. Because this filter operates before meaning is analysed, the model is the early-selection view: a limited-capacity system must select early. Where does this sit in Systems & Theories ? Broadbent's 1958 model is often treated as a founding landmark of the cognitive revolution that overthrew behaviourism. Drawing on wartime engineering, Shannon's information theory, and the new computer metaphor, it gave psychologists a precise, mechanistic way to model the unobservable inner stages behaviourism had forbidden, alongside Miller's 1956 'magical number seven' and Chomsky's 1957 critique of behaviourist language. It directly seeded the flow-diagram models of mind later popularized by Ulric Neisser . The mechanism: selective filtering at an early stage protects a limited-capacity channel. Lock in: Broadbent (1958) gave information-processing psychology its first major theory, the early-selection filter model of attention. Panwar key: Broadbent was the first to describe the human attentional processing system using an information processing metaphor. In this view, Broadbent proposed a so-called "early selection" view of attention, such that humans process information with limited capacity and select information to be processed early. Why the other options are traps A. Treisman, 1960 Anne Treisman is hugely important to attention, but her attenuation theory came in 1960/1964 and revised Broadbent rather than founding the approach, arguing the filter turns unattended channels down rather than fully off. The date '1960' tempts as close and her name is central to attention, but the question asks for the first major effort, which predates her, so this is wrong. B. Chomsky, 1957 Noam Chomsky's 1957 Syntactic Structures was a landmark in linguistics that powerfully fuelled the cognitive revolution, and the 1957 date sits temptingly just before 1958. But Chomsky's work was a theory of grammar and a critique of behaviourist language, not an information-processing model of the human attentional system, so it is not the first major information-processing theory the question names. D. Watson, 1920 John Watson (1920) was the founder of behaviourism , the very movement that rejected the internal-processing modelling this question describes. He is a distractor because he is a famous theorist with a date, but his approach explicitly denied the study of unobservable mental stages. He could not have produced an information-processing theory, which postdates and opposes his behaviourism, so he is clearly incorrect. Q100 Which approach of psychology, the main premise is that 'basically the behaviour of an individual is governed by the brain and nervous system'? ✓ Answer: C · Neurobiological The answer is neurobiological because that approach holds behaviour is fundamentally governed by the brain and nervous system. To understand this, recognize that psychology has several broad perspectives, each explaining behaviour from a different angle. The neurobiological approach , also called the biological perspective, locates the causes of behaviour and mental processes in the body's physical machinery: the brain , the nervous system , neurons , neurotransmitters , hormones, and genes. Its core premise is that every thought, feeling, and action ultimately reflects underlying biological activity, so to explain behaviour you study how nerve cells are organized into functional circuits that process information and mediate action. A mood change might be traced to altered serotonin signalling, a memory deficit to hippocampal damage. The approach relies on brain imaging, lesion studies, and physiological recording. Where does this sit in Systems & Theories ? The biological perspective is one of psychology's oldest taproots, reaching back to René Descartes' mind-body problem and to nineteenth-century physiology, the same lab tradition (Helmholtz, Wilhelm Wundt's mentors) from which experimental psychology itself emerged in 1879. It ran in parallel through the behaviourist and cognitive eras, and when the cognitive revolution reintroduced the mind as an information processor, the biological approach fused with it to create modern cognitive neuroscience , which maps information-processing operations onto brain mechanisms. So neurobiology is both a founding root and a current partner of the cognitive paradigm. The mechanism: neural and physiological events produce psychological outcomes. Lock in: when a perspective says behaviour is fundamentally controlled by the brain and nervous system and explains it through neurons and circuits, it is the neurobiological approach. Panwar key: The study of cells of the nervous system and the organization of these cells into functional circuits that process information and mediate behaviour. The approach of psychology where the main premise is that basically the behaviour of an individual is governed by the brain and nervous system is Neurobiological. Why the other options are traps A. Psychophysical The psychophysical approach studies the lawful relationship between physical stimuli and the sensations they produce (Weber, Fechner), not the brain as the governor of behaviour. It tempts because 'physical' and 'physiological' sound similar and both feel biological, but psychophysics measures sensation-stimulus relationships at the perceptual level, not neural circuitry controlling behaviour, so it does not match the premise. B. Cognitive The cognitive approach focuses on internal information processing, thinking, attention, memory, and language, treating the mind like a computer. It is tempting because it too deals with internal causes of behaviour, but its premise centres on mental representations and processes, not on the brain and nervous system as the governing substrate. Cognition explains behaviour through information, not neurons, so it is wrong here. D. Neo-Behaviouristic Neo-behaviourism (Edward Tolman, Clark Hull) still centres on stimulus-response learning, now with intervening variables like drive or expectancy added between input and output. It tempts as a major theoretical school, but its explanatory premise is learning and conditioning, not brain-based control of behaviour. It deliberately stays at the behavioural level rather than appealing to the nervous system, making it incorrect. Q101 Who proposed the 'Bottom-up process' theory of perception? ✓ Answer: C · James Gibson The answer is James Gibson because he proposed the bottom-up, or direct, theory of perception. To understand this, perception can be explained in two opposite directions. A bottom-up process starts with the raw sensory data and builds upward, analysing information in one direction from simple features toward ever more complex representations, without relying on prior knowledge. A top-down process instead uses stored knowledge, context, and expectation to interpret what the senses deliver. James Gibson (1972) argued for the bottom-up view, which he called direct perception . He claimed the environment itself supplies all the information a perceiver needs through the rich, structured pattern of light reaching the eye, the optic array , complete with affordances and invariant cues, so perception requires no inference or guesswork; we simply pick the information up directly. This contrasts sharply with Richard Gregory's top-down constructivist account, in which perception is an active hypothesis built from past experience. Where does this sit in Systems & Theories ? The bottom-up versus top-down debate is a central theme of the cognitive revolution , which modelled the mind as an information-processing system and asked exactly how sensory input becomes meaningful perception. Gibson's ecological approach pushed back against the heavy computational, inference-laden models that dominated cognitive psychology, insisting the information is already in the world rather than constructed in the head, a stance with roots reaching back to the Gestalt emphasis on directly perceived structure. Gregory, by contrast, extended Helmholtz's nineteenth-century 'unconscious inference.' The mechanism for Gibson: direct detection of information already present in the optic array. Lock in: Gibson's bottom-up direct perception builds from raw sensory data, whereas Gregory's top-down theory relies on stored knowledge and inference. Panwar key: James Gibson (1972) argued that perception is a bottom-up process, which means that sensory information is analyzed in one direction: from simple analysis of raw sensory data to ever increasing complexity of analysis through the visual system. Why the other options are traps A. Max Wertheimer Max Wertheimer founded Gestalt psychology and demonstrated the phi phenomenon of apparent motion. He is tempting because Gestalt theory is genuinely about perception and even shares Gibson's anti-elementarist flavour, but Wertheimer did not formulate the bottom-up direct-perception theory. His contribution was Gestalt grouping principles, not Gibson's ecological account, so he is the wrong attribution. B. Herman Von Helmholtz Hermann von Helmholtz proposed unconscious inference , the idea that perception is built from rapid, automatic inferences using prior experience, which is an early top-down view. He tempts because he is a towering figure in the science of perception, but his theory is the historical ancestor of Gregory's constructivism, the very opposite of Gibson's bottom-up direct perception, so attributing the bottom-up theory to him is incorrect. D. Richard Gregory Richard Gregory is the strongest distractor because he is Gibson's direct rival and is always discussed alongside him. But Gregory championed the top-down , constructivist theory, arguing perception is an active hypothesis built from stored knowledge and inference (extending Helmholtz). He represents the exact opposite pole from the bottom-up direct perception the question asks about, so he is wrong. Indian Psychology Q102 Who among the following studies how psychological processes may differ among people of different cultures? ✓ Answer: C · Social psychologists The answer is (c) social psychologists in the official key, although the description given in the stem (studying how psychological processes differ across cultures) is textbook cross-cultural psychology ; the question preserves this debatable key. To place this on the Systems & Theories map, you must see how psychology partitions the study of culture, a partition that matters because Indian psychology itself grew out of a reaction against culture-blind Western universalism. Cross-cultural psychology takes one process (conformity, perception, memory, attribution) and compares it across two or more cultural groups to expose how culture shapes it; its working assumption is that mind is largely universal but culture produces real, measurable variation, an assumption operationalised by Geert Hofstede 's dimensions (individualism-collectivism, power distance). Cultural psychology rejects that split, holding that mind and culture are mutually constitutive and inseparable, so it interprets meaning inside a single culture rather than comparing across them. Social psychology , the keyed answer, studies how the real or imagined presence of others shapes an individual's thoughts and behaviour, usually within one society. This trio sits inside the larger indigenization debate that defines Indian psychology: scholars like Durganand Sinha argued that simply importing Western tests across cultures (the cross-cultural move) was not enough, and that India needed concepts grown from its own soil (Samkhya's gunas, the kosha model, yoga). Cross-cultural work compares; cultural and indigenous work build from within. Knowing which of these three a question is describing is the recurring trap. Lock in: comparing one psychological process between cultures to reveal cultural influence defines cross-cultural psychology , even where a particular key labels it social psychology. Panwar key: Cross-cultural psychology looks at how cultural factors influence human behaviour. While many aspects of human thought and behaviour are universal, cultural differences can lead to often surprising differences in how people think, feel, and act. Why the other options are traps A. Cultural psychologists Cultural psychologists hold that mind and culture are mutually constitutive and so study meaning within one culture, never comparing across cultures. The stem explicitly says "among people of different cultures," which is comparison, so this within-culture, anti-comparative stance is precisely the wrong description for what the question asks. B. Cross-cultural psychologists Cross-cultural psychologists are the textbook fit for the stem (they compare the same process across cultures), which is exactly why it is tempting. It is marked wrong only because this item's official key assigns the answer to social psychology; the explanatory text itself concedes the cross-cultural definition, so treat the key as the debatable one here. D. None of the above "None of the above" fails because the named subfields (cultural, cross-cultural, social) genuinely do study cultural variation in behaviour. At least one option correctly describes work on cultural differences, so a blanket rejection of all of them cannot be right. Q103 In Indian psychology, which of the following is NOT a component of Purusha and Prakriti according to Samkhya philosophy? ✓ Answer: D · Purusha is described as dynamic and ever-changing. The answer is (d) because describing Purusha as dynamic and ever-changing reverses the single most basic teaching of Samkhya. To build this from the ground up: Samkhya is one of the six classical darshanas (orthodox schools) of Indian philosophy, traditionally credited to the sage Kapila , and it is rigorously dualistic, positing two ultimate, independent, eternal principles. Purusha is pure consciousness, the eternal witness ( sakshi ): passive, attributeless, inactive, never changing, doing nothing but observing. Prakriti is unconscious primordial matter, the cosmic substance from which everything material and even mental evolves. Prakriti is woven of the three gunas , sattva, rajas and tamas, which rest in equilibrium until the mere proximity of Purusha disturbs them; Prakriti then evolves outward, unfolding intellect ( buddhi ), ego ( ahamkara ), mind ( manas ), the senses, and finally the Pancha Maha Bhutas (earth, water, fire, air, ether). So Prakriti is the dynamic, evolving pole and Purusha the still one; liberation ( kaivalya ) is the discriminative knowledge that separates the unchanging witness from active matter. On the Systems & Theories map, this Purusha-Prakriti split is the metaphysical backbone of Indian psychology: it grounds the gunas used to classify temperament, underlies the kosha (sheath) model of the self, and anchors Patanjali 's Yoga, which is essentially Samkhya plus a method (the stilling of the mind so Purusha rests in its own nature). Where Western dualism (Descartes) pits mind against body, Samkhya's deeper cut is consciousness (Purusha) against everything else including mind (which is Prakriti). Lock in: Purusha is the still, passive witness-consciousness; Prakriti is the dynamic, evolving matter, and any statement flipping the two is the false one. Panwar key: Purusha, in Samkhya philosophy, refers to unchanging pure consciousness, while Prakriti is the dynamic, changing cosmic material. Hence, the idea of Purusha being dynamic is incorrect. Why the other options are traps A. Prakriti refers to the cosmic material from which all beings emerge. This is a true statement, not the exception. Prakriti genuinely is the primordial cosmic matter ( mula-prakriti ) from which all beings and the material-mental world evolve, so it accurately describes Samkhya and cannot be the NOT answer the question demands. The question asks for the false claim; this one is correct. B. Purusha refers to the essence of pure consciousness. Also true, hence not the exception. Purusha is precisely defined as pure consciousness, the eternal witness, so this statement faithfully reports core Samkhya doctrine. A NOT question rewards the single reversed claim, and this one is not reversed, so it must be left in. C. Prakriti evolves into the Five Great Elements (Pancha Maha Bhutas). True as well, so not the exception. Among Prakriti's evolutes are indeed the Pancha Maha Bhutas, the five gross elements, produced as the gunas unfold. Because this correctly describes Prakriti's evolution, it is not the false statement the stem is hunting for. Q104 Which Indian psychologist is known for contributing significantly to organizational behavior through the concept of nurturant task leadership? ✓ Answer: B · JBP Sinha. The answer is (b) JBP Sinha because he formulated the Nurturant Task leadership model. To understand why this is an Indian-psychology landmark, start with the problem it solves. Western leadership theory (Ohio State's consideration-versus-initiating-structure, Likert's participative systems, Blake and Mouton's grid) assumed workforces that prize autonomy, equality and self-direction. Jai B. P. Sinha , a leading Indian organizational psychologist, argued that the typical Indian work culture is instead dependence-prone, status-conscious, personalised and familial, so imported participative models simply misfired. His indigenous answer is the Nurturant Task (NT) leadership model: the effective leader fuses a firm task orientation (clear goals, monitoring, demanding performance) with genuine nurturance (warmth, paternal care, concern for the subordinate's growth and wellbeing). Crucially the nurturance is conditional , extended in proportion to the subordinate's effort, so affection and productivity reinforce each other. Sinha positioned NT between the authoritarian and the participative styles and called it a transitional optimum, the realistic best fit now that can gradually move Indian workplaces toward participative management. This is exactly the indigenization project on the Systems & Theories map: rather than apply Western theory wholesale, build a model from the lived cultural psychology of the people studied, the same spirit that drives Durganand Sinha's ecology-of-cognition work and the wider Indian psychology movement. NT leadership is the organizational-behaviour flagship of that program. Lock in: nurturant task leadership = JBP Sinha , conditional warmth plus firm task focus, engineered for the Indian workplace, distinct from his namesake Durganand Sinha's deprivation research. Panwar key: JBP Sinha introduced the concept of nurturant task leadership, which emphasizes that leaders should show nurturing attitudes towards their employees to achieve the best outcomes, particularly in the Indian organizational context. Why the other options are traps A. Girishwar Misra. Girishwar Misra is a major Indian psychologist of culture, self and the indigenization of psychology, and he co-edited important volumes on Indian psychology, which makes his name plausible here. But the Nurturant Task leadership model is not his; attributing this specific organizational-behaviour concept to Misra confuses a culture-and-self theorist with an OB theorist. C. Durganand Sinha. Durganand Sinha is tempting because he shares the surname and is the most famous indigenizer of Indian psychology, but his work is on deprivation, the ecology of cognition and indigenization, not leadership. He is a different scholar from J.B.P. Sinha; the NT model belongs to JBP, so the shared name is the trap. D. Syed Mohammad Mohsin. Syed Mohammad Mohsin was an experimental and perception psychologist at Patna, in the same milieu as JBP Sinha, which is why he appears credible. However he is associated with experimental and perceptual work, not with the Nurturant Task leadership concept, so he is wrong for this specifically OB-leadership question. Q105 In 1968, which of the following events significantly contributed to the development of Clinical Psychology in India? ✓ Answer: B · The formation of the Indian Association of Clinical Psychologists (IACP). The answer is (b) because the Indian Association of Clinical Psychologists was founded in 1968, and that founding is what ties the year 1968 to the discipline's growth. To understand the significance, recognise what a professional association does for an emerging field. Clinical psychology in India had to carve out an identity separate from both general academic psychology (born at Calcutta in 1916) and from psychiatry (medical, hospital-based). The Indian Association of Clinical Psychologists (IACP) , established in 1968 , gave the field its national professional home: it convenes practitioners, sets training and ethical standards, holds annual conferences, and publishes a scholarly outlet, the Indian Journal of Clinical Psychology . This institutionalisation is what converts a scattered set of practitioners into a recognised profession with collective voice before regulators and the public. On the Systems & Theories timeline of Indian psychology, the IACP's founding belongs to the applied, professional strand, distinct from the academic-experimental strand (Sengupta, Calcutta) and from the later indigenous Indian Psychology movement (Cornelissen, the 2002 Pondicherry Manifesto, the 2008 Handbook). Statutory regulation of clinical training came still later through the Rehabilitation Council of India (RCI) , founded in 1992 and made a statutory body in 1993, but the 1968 IACP founding is the milestone keyed to the year in the question. Lock in: IACP, founded 1968 , is the event that institutionalised clinical psychology as a distinct profession in India. Panwar key: The IACP was formed in 1968 to advance the profession of clinical psychology in India. Its creation marked a pivotal moment in the institutionalization and recognition of clinical psychology in the country. Why the other options are traps A. Q106 Which of the following Indian psychologists played a key role in establishing the first psychology laboratory in India? ✓ Answer: B · Uma Chaudhuri The answer is (b) Uma Chaudhuri per the official key, which credits her with rooting early Indian psychological assessment at Calcutta and indigenizing a major projective test; note that the literal phrase "first psychology laboratory" is more commonly tied to N. N. Sengupta . The original TAT cards showed Western faces, dress and settings, which confused Indian respondents and distorted their stories, so she redrew the cards with India-specific figures and scenes to elicit valid, culturally meaningful narratives. Sengupta, which is the nuance to remember. Paranjpe Anand C. Paranjpe is a respected theorist of the self, identity and the dialogue between Indian thought and Western psychology (author of work on self and identity in Indian psychology).
