It is the statistical backbone of test construction (deriving the subscales of a personality inventory) and of construct validation, so the paper tests it through three decisions: the extraction method, the number of factors to keep, and the rotation type. PCA vs Principal Axis Factoring Definition Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is a data reduction technique: it analyses total variance (common, unique, and error variance together) to produce components that summarise the variables as efficiently as possible. Principal Axis Factoring (PAF) is true factor analysis : it analyses only the shared (common) variance to uncover the latent constructs presumed to cause the correlations. Use PCA when the goal is pure dimension reduction or computing composite scores; use PAF (or maximum-likelihood factoring) when the goal is to model latent constructs, which is the usual clinical aim. The mechanical difference sits on the diagonal of the correlation matrix being analysed: PCA places 1.0 on the diagonal (all of each variable's variance), whereas PAF places the communalities there (the shared variance only). That single change is why PCA can look like it explains more variance: it is counting the unique and error variance that PAF deliberately excludes. Factor extraction criteria (how many factors to keep) Kaiser criterion: retain factors with eigenvalues greater than 1.0 (an eigenvalue is the amount of variance a factor explains in units of single variables; an eigenvalue below 1 means the factor explains less than a single original variable, so it is not worth retaining). Simple, but it tends to over-extract factors. Scree plot: plot the eigenvalues in descending order and find the "elbow" where the curve flattens; keep the factors above the bend (Raymond Cattell's scree test). Subjective but widely used. Horn's parallel analysis: the most accurate modern method: generate eigenvalues from many sets of random data of the same size as yours, and retain only those real factors whose eigenvalues exceed the corresponding eigenvalues from the random data. It corrects the over-extraction of the Kaiser rule. Exam trap The Kaiser criterion (eigenvalue > 1) tends to OVER-extract factors , and the scree test is subjective; Horn's parallel analysis is the recommended, most accurate criterion . A question asking "the most accurate method to determine the number of factors" wants parallel analysis, not Kaiser. Do not confuse the eigenvalue (variance per factor) with the communality (variance per variable). Rotation: orthogonal vs oblique Rotation does not change how much variance is explained; it redistributes the loadings to make the solution interpretable, maximising high loadings and minimising low ones (Thurstone's "simple structure"). The fundamental choice is whether the factors are permitted to correlate: Orthogonal rotation forces the factors to remain uncorrelated (a 90-degree, independent reference frame). Methods: Varimax (the most common; it simplifies the columns, that is, the factors) and Quartimax (it simplifies the rows, that is, the variables). Use when factors are assumed independent. Oblique rotation allows the factors to correlate, reflecting reality, because psychological constructs usually overlap (anxiety and depression intercorrelate). Methods: Promax and Direct Oblimin . Oblique rotations additionally yield a factor-correlation matrix and separate pattern and structure matrices (the pattern matrix giving unique loadings, the structure matrix giving raw correlations). High-yield Orthogonal (Varimax, Quartimax) = uncorrelated factors, 90 degrees; Oblique (Promax, Direct Oblimin) = correlated factors. For real clinical constructs, which almost always intercorrelate, oblique rotation is usually more appropriate and is the defensible default. Varimax is the single most-named rotation in MCQs. Loadings, cross-loadings, and communality A factor loading is the correlation between a variable and a factor; a loading above .32 is the conventional minimum for an item to be considered meaningfully related to a factor (.32 squared is about 0.10, so roughly 10% shared variance). A cross-loading occurs when a variable loads above the cut-off on two or more factors, making it ambiguous about which construct it measures; such items are usually dropped or revised. The communality (h 2 ) of a variable is the proportion of its variance explained by all the retained factors combined, computed as the sum of its squared loadings across the factors; a low communality (say below 0.30) means the retained factors capture little of that variable, marking it a candidate for removal. Worked example: an item loads 0.6 on Factor 1 and 0.3 on Factor 2; its communality is 0.6 2 + 0.3 2 = 0.36 + 0.09 = 0.45, so the factors explain 45% of that item's variance. Memory aid Loading > .32 to keep an item; communality h 2 = shared variance an item gives to the factors; cross-loading = an item that cheats on two factors (drop it). Eigenvalue is per-factor variance (keep the factor if > 1); communality is per-variable variance. High-yield The "when assumptions fail, what do you switch to" logic is the backbone of this whole section, and the exam tests it constantly. Lock in the chain: variances unequal → Welch's t; normality fails → non-parametric (Mann-Whitney, Wilcoxon, Kruskal-Wallis, Friedman); sphericity fails → Greenhouse-Geisser / Huynh-Feldt; small expected cell counts in 2 × 2 → Fisher's exact (or Yates' correction); paired nominal → McNemar; slopes not homogeneous → ANCOVA invalid; high VIF → multicollinearity, drop or combine predictors. 3 · Psychopathology & Clinical Syndromes This is the highest-yield section in the entire entrance, because clinical psychology papers test it the way an anatomy paper tests bones: by the exact number. A disorder is not a vague mood but an operationalised object with a symptom count, a duration gate, and a near-neighbour it must be told apart from. The single most-tested fact type here is the duration threshold , the precise window of time a presentation must occupy to earn its name, because two disorders can share every symptom and differ only in how long they last. Brief psychotic disorder and schizophrenia look identical in a snapshot; only the clock separates them. The second most-tested fact type is the symptom-count gate (five of nine for depression, three of twelve for catatonia, two of five for schizophrenia Criterion A), and the third is the obligatory symptom , the one item that must be present whatever else is (depressed mood or anhedonia for depression; a delusion, hallucination, or disorganised speech for schizophrenia). Master these three machines (the clock, the count, the obligatory item) and you can reconstruct most criteria sets under exam pressure. This section teaches each disorder from its mechanism up, gives you the exact criteria and durations verbatim in tables you can memorise, and for every entry states the differential, the trick of telling it from the condition it is most often confused with, because that confusion is exactly what the distractor options are built from. We begin with how the two classification systems are architected and what causal models underpin them, then march through the full spectrum disorder by disorder. A. Diagnostic Frameworks & Comparative Systems Before any single disorder can be learned, you must grasp the scaffolding that holds all of them, because a recurring class of exam item asks not "what are the criteria for X" but "how do the two great manuals differ in the way they file X." A nosology is a system of classification of disease; psychiatry runs on two, and they embody two different philosophies of what a mental disorder even is. The two nosologies that dominate are the American Psychiatric Association's Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition, Text Revision (DSM-5-TR, 2022) and the World Health Organization's International Classification of Diseases, Eleventh Revision (ICD-11) , whose mental-and-behavioural-disorders chapter came into force in January 2022. Both are descriptive : they group disorders by observable clinical features rather than by presumed cause, a deliberately atheoretical stance inherited from DSM-III (1980), which broke from the earlier psychoanalytic, aetiology-driven framework in which disorders were defined by their supposed unconscious origin. That 1980 rupture is itself a tested fact: DSM-III is the edition credited with introducing operational criteria, the multiaxial system (later abolished in DSM-5, 2013, which collapsed the five axes into a single non-axial listing), and the atheoretical descriptive stance. DSM is built for a primarily American clinical and research audience and is famously operationalised : it specifies explicit symptom counts and time frames so that two clinicians applying it to the same patient should reach the same label (the goal of high inter-rater reliability ). ICD is a global public-health instrument used for mortality and morbidity statistics across all member states; its Clinical Descriptions and Diagnostic Requirements (CDDR) read as flexible prototypes rather than rigid checklists, because they must function across radically different health systems, from tertiary hospitals to community health workers with no laboratory access. Definition A categorical classification treats a disorder as a discrete kind: a person either meets criteria or does not (DSM's dominant logic). A dimensional classification rates a problem along a continuum of severity or trait level, accepting that pathology shades gradually into normality. The standing critique of pure categorical systems is that they draw artificial boundaries, generate excessive comorbidity (a patient piling up four labels for one underlying problem), produce diagnostic heterogeneity (two people with the same label sharing almost no symptoms), and dump residual cases into vague "not otherwise specified" or "other specified" bins. Definition Reliability is the consistency of a diagnosis (do different clinicians, or the same clinician at two times, assign the same label?). Validity is whether the diagnostic category corresponds to a real, distinct entity with a characteristic cause, course, and treatment response. The historic complaint against DSM is that its operationalised criteria bought reliability at the possible expense of validity: categories that are reproducible but may not carve nature at its joints. This reliability-versus-validity tension is itself examinable. The structural differences you must know The exam loves the points where the two systems diverge in architecture , not just in wording. Several divergences are tested repeatedly, and you should be able to state each as a one-line contrast. 1. Categorical versus dimensional spine. DSM-5-TR remains predominantly categorical, bolting dimensional elements on (severity specifiers, the cross-cutting symptom measures, the Section III alternative model for personality). ICD-11 keeps categories for most disorders but turns strongly dimensional precisely where DSM does not: personality. 2. Acute stress disorder moved out of anxiety. In older frameworks acute and post-traumatic stress reactions sat near the anxiety disorders. ICD-11 carved out a dedicated grouping, Disorders specifically associated with stress , and relocated the trauma reactions there, alongside its new prolonged grief disorder and a reworked adjustment disorder. DSM-5 had already created a separate Trauma- and Stressor-Related Disorders chapter, so both systems now treat trauma reactions as their own block rather than as a subtype of anxiety. The high-yield phrasing is that ICD-11 deleted acute stress disorder from the anxiety grouping and placed it in a trauma-specific block ; ICD-11 also classifies acute stress reaction itself as a normal reaction (a factor influencing health status rather than a mental disorder), which is a favourite trick. 3. Abolition of categorical personality disorders. This is the headline difference. The traditional model in both systems was a fixed list of named personality types. DSM-5 kept its ten categorical personality disorders in the main text but parked an Alternative Model for Personality Disorders (AMPD) in Section III, rating level of personality functioning plus five pathological trait domains. ICD-11 went all the way and abolished the categorical types entirely . It first assigns a global severity (personality difficulty below threshold, then mild, moderate, or severe) and then optionally adds up to five trait domain qualifiers : negative affectivity, detachment, dissociality, disinhibition, and anankastia, plus an optional borderline pattern qualifier retained for treatment continuity. 4. Gender and other relocations. ICD-11 moved gender incongruence out of the mental disorders chapter altogether (into a new chapter on conditions related to sexual health), explicitly de-pathologising it; DSM-5-TR retains gender dysphoria within its mental-disorders text, framing the distress (not the identity) as the clinical focus. ICD-11 also introduced complex PTSD , prolonged grief disorder (a diagnosis DSM-5-TR added too, in its 2022 revision), and gaming disorder as a recognised behavioural addiction, none of which mirror DSM exactly. Feature DSM-5-TR ICD-11 Publisher American Psychiatric Association World Health Organization Primary purpose Clinical and research diagnosis Global health statistics plus clinical use Criteria style Operationalised: explicit symptom counts and durations Prototype-based flexible descriptions (CDDR) Overall spine Predominantly categorical, dimensional add-ons Categorical for most disorders, dimensional for personality Personality disorders Ten categorical types retained; dimensional AMPD in Section III Categorical types abolished: global severity plus trait qualifiers Acute stress reaction Acute stress disorder is a diagnosable disorder in the trauma chapter Acute stress reaction reframed as a normal reaction (not a mental disorder); trauma block separate from anxiety Gender concept Gender dysphoria (within mental disorders) Gender incongruence (moved out of mental disorders entirely) High-yield ICD-11 is the system that scrapped the ten categorical personality disorders for a global severity plus trait-qualifier dimensional model. DSM-5 still lists all ten categorically and offers its dimensional model only in Section III as an emerging measure. If an item asks "which system uses a dimensional model of personality," the answer is ICD-11. If it asks "which edition introduced operational criteria and the atheoretical stance," the answer is DSM-III (1980). Exam trap Do not say DSM-5 "removed" the categorical personality disorders. It kept all ten in the main text and merely added the alternative model in Section III. Only ICD-11 abolished the categories outright. The trap option flips the two systems. A second trap reverses the gender entries: ICD-11 de-pathologised gender (incongruence, out of mental disorders); DSM-5-TR keeps gender dysphoria inside. Worked example: reading a comparison stem Consider a typical item: "A clinician using a manual rates a patient's personality not by assigning one of ten named types but by setting a global severity and then noting prominent traits such as detachment and disinhibition. Which manual is in use?" Decode it by the architecture: naming traits plus a severity grade, with no categorical type, is the ICD-11 personality model. The five trait qualifiers (negative affectivity, detachment, dissociality, disinhibition, anankastia) are the give-away vocabulary. The answer is ICD-11. This is exactly the reasoning the comparison items demand: spot the architectural fingerprint, not the disorder name. Etiological paradigms Beyond classification, the paper tests the major causal frameworks, because every therapy chapter and every formulation question rests on them. Learn the five paradigms below as a set, because comparison items ("which model explains symptoms by conditional assumptions") are common. Molecular genetics and behaviour genetics. Heritability is estimated chiefly from twin studies : comparing concordance in monozygotic (identical, sharing ~100% of genes) versus dizygotic (fraternal, ~50%) twins. The heritability coefficient , written as h squared (h 2 ), is the proportion of phenotypic variance in a population attributable to genetic variance; for schizophrenia twin-based heritability is roughly 0.8, for bipolar disorder roughly 0.7 to 0.8, both among the most heritable disorders. Linkage analysis tracks whether a disorder co-segregates within families with known genetic markers of identified chromosomal location, while genome-wide association studies (GWAS) scan the whole genome for common variants of small effect. Adoption studies separate genes from rearing environment by following children adopted away from affected biological parents. The takeaway tested most is that severe disorders (schizophrenia, bipolar, autism) are highly heritable and polygenic : many genes of small effect, not one gene; and that heritability is a population statistic, not a statement about how "genetic" any one person's illness is. Neurofunctional circuitry. This paradigm locates pathology in altered brain circuits and neurotransmitter systems: the dopamine hypothesis of psychosis (mesolimbic hyperdopaminergia driving positive symptoms, mesocortical hypodopaminergia driving negative symptoms), serotonergic and noradrenergic dysregulation in mood and anxiety, the monoamine hypothesis of depression, and structural or functional changes such as enlarged lateral ventricles in schizophrenia or amygdala hyper-reactivity in anxiety and PTSD. Psychodynamic structural and object-relational models. The structural model (Freud) explains symptoms as the surface compromise of intrapsychic conflict among id, ego, and superego, managed by defence mechanisms; signal anxiety warns the ego of a threatened breakthrough of forbidden impulses. Object-relations theory (Melanie Klein, Fairbairn, Donald Winnicott, Otto Kernberg) shifts the unit of analysis from drives to internalised relationships : pathology reflects deficient or distorted internal representations of self and others laid down in early caregiving, so a borderline patient is understood through unintegrated "all-good" and "all-bad" object images (the root of splitting). Cognitive-behavioural vulnerabilities. Behaviourism explains pathology through learning: classical conditioning (a neutral cue paired with fear), operant conditioning (avoidance negatively reinforced because it relieves anxiety, the engine that maintains phobias and OCD), and modelling/observational learning. The cognitive layer (Aaron Beck, Albert Ellis) adds enduring schemas , deep core beliefs about self, world, and future (Beck's negative cognitive triad in depression), and the conditional (operational) assumptions built on them ("if I am not perfect, I am worthless"), which, when activated by a stressor, generate the automatic negative thoughts that drive symptoms. Diathesis-stress integration. The unifying model. A diathesis is a pre-existing vulnerability (genetic, neurobiological, or cognitive) that lies dormant until a sufficient environmental stress triggers it. Neither alone suffices: a high diathesis needs only mild stress to decompensate, a low diathesis needs severe stress. The closely related biopsychosocial model (Engel) generalises this to the routine interplay of biological, psychological, and social contributors to any presentation. Memory aid Map each paradigm to its signature noun: genetics = heritability , neuro = circuit , psychodynamic = conflict / object , cognitive = schema / assumption , integrative = diathesis + stress . Match the noun in the stem to the paradigm. If a stem mentions "conditional assumptions" or "core beliefs," it is cognitive; if "object representations" or "id-ego-superego," it is psychodynamic. B. Schizophrenia Spectrum & Psychotic Disorders Psychosis is a loss of contact with reality, expressed through delusions, hallucinations, disorganised thinking and speech, grossly disorganised or catatonic behaviour, and negative symptoms. Schizophrenia is the prototype, and the whole spectrum is organised as a ladder of duration : the same psychotic picture earns a different name depending only on how long it has lasted and how completely the person recovers. DSM-5 requires at least two of five Criterion A symptoms present for a significant portion of one month (the active phase), at least one of those two being delusions, hallucinations, or disorganised speech (these three are the obligatory "core positive" trio); continuous signs of disturbance must persist for at least six months total , a window that may include prodromal and residual phases of attenuated symptoms. The five Criterion A symptoms are delusions, hallucinations, disorganised speech, grossly disorganised or catatonic behaviour, and negative symptoms. Criterion B demands marked socio-occupational dysfunction , and criteria for substance use, medical illness, and the autism/communication-disorder overlap must be excluded. The whole spectrum is gated by duration, and that ladder is the most-tested fact in the section. Disorder Duration gate (verbatim) Key feature / differential Brief psychotic disorder At least 1 day, less than 1 month, with eventual full return to premorbid functioning Shortest rung; often stress-precipitated; recovers completely Schizophreniform disorder Between 1 and 6 months (total duration) Same symptoms as schizophrenia but caught before 6 months; impaired function not required Schizophrenia At least 6 months continuous disturbance, including at least 1 month of active-phase symptoms The full disorder; marked socio-occupational decline required Schizoaffective disorder Delusions or hallucinations for at least 2 weeks in the absence of a prominent mood episode , with a major mood episode for the majority of total illness Bridges psychosis and mood; see differential below Delusional disorder At least 1 delusion for at least 1 month ; no prominent hallucinations; function otherwise largely intact Non-bizarre delusion, otherwise normal behaviour Memory aid Chant the psychotic ladder by length: brief is shortest (under one month), schizophreniform sits in the middle (one to six months), schizophrenia is longest (six months and beyond). The cut points 1 month and 6 months are simply the boundaries between the rungs. "One day to one month to six months" is the whole gate sequence. Epidemiology and course (where tested) A small cluster of epidemiological facts recurs. Schizophrenia has a lifetime prevalence of roughly 1% (about 0.3 to 0.7%) worldwide, broadly similar across cultures, with men tending to onset earlier (late teens to mid-twenties) than women (late twenties, with a smaller second peak after midlife). Twin and family data give the high heritability quoted above (around 0.8). The dopamine hypothesis (mesolimbic overactivity for positive symptoms) and the structural finding of enlarged ventricles anchor the biological story. Course modifiers worth knowing: acute onset, prominent mood symptoms, a clear precipitant, good premorbid functioning, and being married predict better outcome; insidious onset, prominent negative symptoms, and early age of onset predict worse outcome. These prognostic markers are reliably tested as "which feature predicts a good outcome" items. Brief psychotic disorder and schizophreniform disorder Brief psychotic disorder is the abrupt onset of one or more positive psychotic symptoms (delusions, hallucinations, disorganised speech, or grossly disorganised/catatonic behaviour) lasting at least one day but less than one month , after which the person returns fully to premorbid functioning. It is frequently precipitated by a marked stressor (the "with marked stressor" specifier, historically brief reactive psychosis) and may occur with peripartum onset. Schizophreniform disorder is, symptomatically, schizophrenia caught early: the identical Criterion A picture but with a total duration of one to six months . Crucially, it does not require the decline in social or occupational functioning that schizophrenia mandates. If symptoms persist past six months the diagnosis converts to schizophrenia; if they remit before one month the label was brief psychotic disorder. A provisional specifier is used while waiting to see whether the person will recover before six months. Worked vignette: a previously well 22-year-old develops persecutory delusions and auditory hallucinations three weeks after a bereavement. At week three he is floridly psychotic. If he recovers fully by week four (under one month), the retrospective label is brief psychotic disorder, with marked stressor . If he is still symptomatic at week ten (between one and six months) but his job and relationships are intact, it is schizophreniform disorder . If at month seven he remains psychotic with clear occupational collapse, it is schizophrenia . One patient, three labels, decided entirely by the clock and the functional decline. Exam trap The schizophreniform window is reckoned on total duration including prodrome and residual, not just the one-month active phase. And it is the one psychotic-spectrum diagnosis that does not require functional decline. Distractors swap these in. A further trap: brief psychotic disorder demands eventual full return to baseline; incomplete recovery pushes the case up the ladder. Schneiderian first-rank symptoms Kurt Schneider (1959) listed symptoms he thought, when present without organic cause, strongly suggested schizophrenia. They are heavily tested by name. The classic eleven, grouped: (1) audible thoughts (thought echo, hearing one's thoughts aloud); (2) voices arguing or discussing the patient in the third person; (3) voices commenting on one's actions (running commentary); (4) thought withdrawal (thoughts removed by an outside force); (5) thought insertion (alien thoughts placed in the mind); (6) thought broadcasting (thoughts diffuse out to others); (7) made (passivity) feelings; (8) made impulses; (9) made volitional acts; (10) somatic passivity (bodily sensations imposed by others); and (11) delusional perception (a normal percept given a private delusional meaning). Note that DSM-5 dropped the old special weighting that a single bizarre delusion or first-rank hallucination alone sufficed for diagnosis; two Criterion A symptoms are now always required, because research showed first-rank symptoms are neither specific to schizophrenia (they occur in mania and organic states) nor prognostically decisive. High-yield The "made" phenomena (made feelings, made impulses, made acts) plus somatic passivity are delusions of control / passivity : the sense that an external agent is driving one's body or mind. Thought insertion, withdrawal, and broadcasting are the thought-alienation triad. These are the most-asked Schneiderian items. The newer high-yield fact: DSM-5 removed their special diagnostic weighting, so a lone bizarre delusion no longer suffices. Positive versus negative symptoms: the five A's Positive symptoms are pathological additions to normal experience: delusions (fixed false beliefs held despite contrary evidence, e.g. persecutory, grandiose, referential, nihilistic), hallucinations (percepts without an external stimulus, auditory being most common in schizophrenia), disorganised speech (formal thought disorder: derailment/loosening of associations, tangentiality, word salad, neologisms), and grossly disorganised or bizarre behaviour. Negative symptoms are deficits, the loss of normal function, and they predict poorer prognosis and respond least to antipsychotics (especially the older typical agents). Memorise them as the five A's : avolition (loss of goal-directed drive), alogia (poverty of speech), anhedonia (inability to feel pleasure), asociality (withdrawal from social contact), and affective flattening (blunted/diminished emotional expression). The mesolimbic-mesocortical split from the biopsychology section maps onto this divide: limbic overactivity drives the positive symptoms, cortical underactivity drives the negative and cognitive ones. Memory aid The five negative symptoms are the 5 A's : Avolition, Alogia, Anhedonia, Asociality, Affective flattening. Positive symptoms ADD to experience; negative symptoms SUBTRACT from it. Positive symptoms respond to D2 blockade; negative symptoms barely respond, which is why they dominate the long-term disability. Catatonia: 3 of 12 signs Catatonia is a syndrome of marked psychomotor disturbance that can accompany schizophrenia, mood disorders (it is in fact commonest in mood disorders), or medical conditions; in DSM-5 it is a specifier and a stand-alone "catatonia associated with another mental disorder," not only a schizophrenia subtype. DSM-5 requires at least 3 of 12 signs. Learn all twelve, because the paper asks both the threshold number and the full list: (1) stupor (no psychomotor activity, not actively relating to environment); (2) catalepsy (passive induction of a posture held against gravity); (3) waxy flexibility (slight, even resistance to repositioning, like bending a candle); (4) mutism (no, or almost no, verbal response); (5) negativism (opposition to or no response to instructions); (6) posturing (spontaneous maintenance of a posture against gravity); (7) mannerisms (odd caricatures of normal actions); (8) stereotypies (repetitive, non-goal-directed movements); (9) psychomotor agitation (excessive, purposeless motor activity); (10) grimacing ; (11) echolalia (mimicking another's speech); and (12) echopraxia (mimicking another's movements). High-yield Catatonia = 3 of 12 signs. Distinguish catalepsy (posture passively induced and held) from waxy flexibility (the even, candle-like resistance felt while repositioning) and from cataplexy (sudden loss of muscle tone triggered by emotion, which belongs to narcolepsy, not catatonia). The catalepsy / cataplexy swap is a classic distractor. Treatment fact sometimes tested: catatonia responds to benzodiazepines (lorazepam) and to ECT, not primarily to antipsychotics, which can worsen it. Schizoaffective disorder and delusional disorder Schizoaffective disorder requires an uninterrupted period during which a major mood episode (depressive or manic) is concurrent with Criterion A schizophrenia symptoms, PLUS delusions or hallucinations for at least two weeks in the absence of a prominent mood episode at some point in the lifetime, AND mood-episode symptoms present for the majority of the total active and residual illness duration. The two-week psychosis-without-mood window is the linchpin that separates it from a mood disorder with psychotic features. It is the bridge diagnosis: more mood than schizophrenia, more psychosis than a pure mood disorder. Delusional disorder requires one or more delusions for at least one month , with Criterion A schizophrenia otherwise never met, no prominent hallucinations, and functioning not markedly impaired apart from the delusion's direct impact; behaviour is not obviously bizarre. The delusions may be non-bizarre (plausible scenarios such as being followed or deceived) or bizarre. Subtypes name the delusion's theme: erotomanic (a famous or higher-status person is in love with the patient), grandiose, jealous (the Othello syndrome of infidelity belief), persecutory (the commonest), somatic, mixed. Exam trap Schizoaffective vs. mood disorder with psychotic features: if psychosis occurs only during mood episodes, it is a mood disorder with psychotic features; if there is a period of at least two weeks of psychosis with the mood episode absent , it is schizoaffective. That two-week window is the entire differential. Delusional disorder vs. schizophrenia: delusional disorder spares function and lacks the other Criterion A symptoms; if hallucinations are prominent or function collapses, it is no longer delusional disorder. The ICD-11 contrast for psychosis ICD-11 keeps schizophrenia but, like the other clusters, softens the rigid time-and-count gates into prototypes. Two contrasts are worth carrying. First, ICD-11 requires a duration of symptoms of at least one month for schizophrenia (it does not impose DSM's full six-month total), so the same patient can meet ICD schizophrenia earlier than DSM schizophrenia, which is a tested discrepancy. Second, ICD-11 abolished the classical clinical subtypes (paranoid, hebephrenic/disorganised, catatonic, simple) that ICD-10 still listed, replacing them with cross-cutting symptom-domain specifiers; DSM-5 had already dropped the same subtypes. So the headline is: both modern systems deleted the named subtypes, but they differ on the duration gate (DSM six months total, ICD-11 one month). C. Bipolar & Related Disorders The bipolar disorders are defined by the presence of elevated-mood episodes (manic or hypomanic) on a background that usually also includes depression. The decisive distinctions are the duration and severity of the high. The conceptual key is that bipolarity is diagnosed off the highest mood state a person has ever reached: a single lifetime manic episode permanently defines Bipolar I, however much depression dominates the rest of the course. This is why the elevated pole, not the depressive one, is the diagnostic hinge. Definition A manic episode is a distinct period of abnormally elevated, expansive, or irritable mood with increased energy or goal-directed activity, lasting at least 7 consecutive days (or any duration if hospitalisation is required) , present most of the day nearly every day, with at least 3 of the DIG FAST symptoms (4 if mood is only irritable) and causing marked impairment, psychosis, or the need for hospitalisation . A hypomanic episode has the same symptom set and the same count (3, or 4 if only irritable) but lasts at least 4 consecutive days , is an unequivocal change in functioning observable by others, and does not cause marked impairment, psychosis, or hospitalisation. If psychosis or hospitalisation is present, the episode is manic by definition regardless of length. Disorder Defining requirement (verbatim) Bipolar I disorder At least 1 manic episode (at least 7 days, or any duration if hospitalised); severe socio-occupational impairment. Depressive episodes usual but not required for diagnosis. Bipolar II disorder At least 1 hypomanic episode (at least 4 days, clear functional change, no gross impairment or hospitalisation) AND at least 1 major depressive episode . Never a full manic episode. Cyclothymic disorder At least 2 years in adults (1 year in children/adolescents) of numerous hypomanic and depressive symptoms that never meet full episode criteria; symptom-free intervals cannot exceed 2 months . Rapid cycling (specifier) At least 4 distinct major mood episodes within a 12-month period . Bipolar I is the only one requiring a full manic episode; a single lifetime manic episode suffices for the diagnosis even with no depression ever. Bipolar II requires both a hypomanic episode and a major depressive episode, and the presence of any full manic episode immediately reclassifies it as Bipolar I. It is a common error to treat Bipolar II as "milder"; its depressive burden is often heavier and more chronic, and its suicide risk is high. Cyclothymia is the persistent, sub-threshold chatter of highs and lows, never reaching full episode intensity, over the required two-year span (with no symptom-free gap longer than two months). Rapid cycling is a specifier, not a separate disorder, applied when four or more episodes occur in twelve months; it is associated with poorer treatment response and, in some patients, with antidepressant exposure. Worked vignette: a 30-year-old has had two clear-cut major depressive episodes and, separately, a five-day period of decreased need for sleep, pressured speech, and overspending that her family noticed but that did not stop her working or require admission. The high is four days or more, observable, without gross impairment or hospitalisation: a hypomanic episode. Hypomania plus major depression equals Bipolar II . Now suppose that high had instead lasted eight days and ended in a psychiatric admission for grandiose, reckless behaviour: that is a manic episode, and the diagnosis jumps to Bipolar I , retrospectively reclassifying the whole illness. Memory aid Mania symptoms = DIG FAST : Distractibility, Insomnia (decreased need for sleep), Grandiosity, Flight of ideas, Activity increase, Speech (pressured), Thoughtlessness (risk-taking, e.g. spending, sex, reckless driving). Mania needs 3 of these (4 if mood is only irritable). "Decreased need for sleep" (feels rested on little sleep) is the bipolar marker, distinct from the insomnia of depression (wants sleep, cannot get it). Exam trap The mania duration is 7 days ; hypomania is 4 days . The decisive line between them is not just length but impairment : hospitalisation, psychosis, or marked dysfunction automatically makes it mania regardless of duration. A 3-day high that lands the patient in hospital is a manic episode. A second trap: cyclothymia and persistent depressive disorder share the two-year-in-adults / one-year-in-youth gate, but cyclothymia has both poles (sub-threshold highs and lows) whereas persistent depressive disorder is depressive only. Mixed features, differentials and the antidepressant caution Two further points are reliably examined. First, the "with mixed features" specifier replaced the old DSM-IV "mixed episode": a manic or hypomanic episode can carry several depressive symptoms simultaneously (or a depressive episode can carry several manic symptoms), capturing the agitated, dysphoric high that does not fit a clean pole. Second, the central management caution: giving an antidepressant alone to a bipolar patient can precipitate a switch into mania or hypomania (a manic switch) or accelerate cycling, which is why a confirmed manic history reroutes treatment to mood stabilisers (lithium, valproate, lamotrigine) or atypical antipsychotics rather than antidepressant monotherapy. Lithium is the classic mood stabiliser, with the additional tested fact that it reduces suicide risk. The most consequential clinical differential is therefore bipolar depression versus unipolar depression : a person presenting in a depressive episode may actually be bipolar, and the give-aways of hidden bipolarity are early age of onset, recurrent brief depressions, a family history of bipolar disorder, psychotic or atypical features, and any past hypomania the patient under-reports because the high felt good. Missing this is the commonest real-world and exam error in the mood chapter. High-yield A single lifetime manic episode equals Bipolar I forever, regardless of how much depression dominates. Bipolar II = hypomania + major depression, never a full mania. The "mood plus increased energy/activity" gateway is a DSM-5 addition to Criterion A. Antidepressant monotherapy in bipolar disorder risks a manic switch ; mood stabilisers are first-line, and lithium lowers suicide risk. The ICD-11 contrast for bipolar ICD-11 retains Bipolar type I and type II and cyclothymic disorder, and broadly mirrors the DSM durations (seven days for mania, four for hypomania). The notable DSM-5 change that ICD-11 also reflects is the addition of increased energy or activity to elevated/irritable mood as a required Criterion A feature for mania and hypomania (mood alone is no longer enough; there must be the energy/activity change too). This "mood plus energy" gateway is a modern, examinable update introduced to reduce over-diagnosis from mood elevation alone. D. Depressive Disorders The depressive disorders share a common feature of sad, empty, or irritable mood with somatic and cognitive changes that impair functioning; they differ in duration, timing, and developmental presentation. The depressive disorders chapter in DSM-5 was split off from the bipolar chapter (in DSM-IV they sat together as "mood disorders"), a structural change worth noting because it underlines that unipolar depression and bipolar disorder are now treated as distinct families. Definition Major depressive disorder (MDD) requires at least 5 of 9 symptoms during the same 2-week period , representing a change from previous functioning, and at least one of the five must be either depressed mood or loss of interest/pleasure (anhedonia) . The nine: depressed mood; anhedonia; significant weight/appetite change; insomnia or hypersomnia; psychomotor agitation or retardation; fatigue/loss of energy; worthlessness or excessive guilt; impaired concentration/indecisiveness; recurrent thoughts of death or suicidality. Symptoms must cause distress or impairment and not be attributable to a substance or medical condition. Disorder Criteria and duration (verbatim) Major depressive disorder At least 5 of 9 symptoms in the same 2-week block, including depressed mood or anhedonia. Persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia) Depressed mood for at least 2 years in adults (1 year in children/adolescents) ; sub-threshold; no symptom-free gap longer than 2 months . Disruptive mood dysregulation disorder (DMDD) Severe recurrent temper outbursts (verbal/behavioural) out of proportion, at least 3 times per week , across at least 12 months , with onset before age 10 (diagnosed ages 6 to 18). Premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD) Mood and physical symptoms in the final week before menses , improving within days of onset and minimal post-menses, across most cycles of the past year. Persistent depressive disorder (the DSM-5 merger of chronic MDD and the older dysthymia) is the long, low-grade depression: at least two years (one in youth) of depressed mood plus two of six features (poor appetite or overeating, insomnia or hypersomnia, low energy, low self-esteem, poor concentration, hopelessness), with no break exceeding two months. A patient can carry both diagnoses simultaneously (so-called double depression : a major depressive episode superimposed on dysthymia). DMDD was introduced to curb the over-diagnosis of paediatric bipolar disorder; its core is a persistently irritable or angry mood between the outbursts, distinguishing it from the episodic mood elevation of bipolar disorder, and it can only be first diagnosed between ages 6 and 18 with onset before age 10. PMDD ties depressive symptoms to the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle, remitting after menses, and is the depressive-chapter entry most easily forgotten. Epidemiology (where tested) MDD is among the commonest mental disorders, with a lifetime prevalence around 15 to 20% and a consistent finding that it is roughly twice as common in women as in men from adolescence onward (the 2:1 female-to-male ratio is a near-certain item). Mean age of onset is the mid-to-late twenties. The monoamine hypothesis (deficiency of serotonin and noradrenaline) underpins the first-line pharmacology (SSRIs), and the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis hyperactivity (raised cortisol, dexamethasone non-suppression) is the classic biological correlate. The 2:1 sex ratio for unipolar depression contrasts with the roughly equal sex ratio for Bipolar I, a comparison the paper sometimes tests directly. Specifier mechanics Specifiers refine an episode and are reliably tested. Melancholic features: profound despondency with loss of pleasure in nearly everything, mood non-reactive (does not lift even briefly to good news), distinct quality of depressed mood, worse in the morning (diurnal variation), terminal/early-morning insomnia (waking hours before the alarm), marked psychomotor change, anorexia/weight loss, and excessive guilt. Atypical features: the mirror image, mood reactivity preserved (brightens to positives), plus at least two of hyperphagia (increased appetite/weight), hypersomnia , leaden paralysis (heavy, leaden limbs), and a long-standing pattern of interpersonal rejection sensitivity . Peripartum onset: onset of the episode during pregnancy or within 4 weeks postpartum . Other specifiers include with psychotic features , with anxious distress , with mixed features , with catatonia , and with seasonal pattern (the basis of the lay term "seasonal affective disorder," now a seasonal-pattern specifier rather than a separate diagnosis). Exam trap The single cleanest melancholic-versus-atypical discriminator is mood reactivity . Melancholic mood is non-reactive (nothing lifts it) with early-morning waking and weight loss; atypical mood is reactive with oversleeping and overeating. The "leaden paralysis" and rejection sensitivity belong to atypical . A separate trap: the bereavement exclusion was removed in DSM-5, so a major depressive episode can be diagnosed during grief if full criteria are met (a much-debated change). Key differentials within the depressive chapter The chapter's internal differentials are tested as cleanly as its durations. MDD versus persistent depressive disorder turns on duration and intensity: MDD is the acute, full-threshold two-week (or longer) episode, whereas persistent depressive disorder is the chronic, often sub-threshold two-year floor; a patient meeting both at once is the classic double depression . MDD versus normal grief : ordinary bereavement waxes and wanes in waves tied to reminders, self-esteem is usually preserved, and thoughts of death centre on joining the deceased rather than on worthlessness, whereas a major depressive episode brings pervasive low mood, self-loathing, and global anhedonia; since DSM-5 removed the bereavement exclusion, the two can coexist. DMDD versus paediatric bipolar disorder : DMDD shows a persistently irritable baseline punctuated by outbursts, with no discrete episodes of elevated mood, while bipolar disorder shows episodic mood elevation against a normal baseline; DMDD exists precisely to stop chronically irritable children being mislabelled bipolar. DMDD versus oppositional defiant disorder : the severe temper outbursts and the threshold (three or more per week, twelve months) push toward DMDD, and where both could apply DMDD takes precedence over ODD. Memory aid Anchor the duration ladder of low mood: a major depressive episode needs 2 weeks , persistent depressive disorder needs 2 years (1 year in youth), and DMDD needs 12 months of outbursts with onset before age 10. The obligatory MDD symptom is always depressed mood or anhedonia ; without one of those two you cannot reach five-of-nine in a valid way. The ICD-11 contrast for depression ICD-11 groups depressive disorders separately from bipolar, as DSM does, and uses a similar two-week duration and symptom-cluster logic, but its CDDR phrase the symptoms as affective, cognitive-behavioural, and neurovegetative clusters rather than a strict five-of-nine count. ICD-11 introduced mixed depressive and anxiety disorder as a recognised category (sub-threshold depression and anxiety together), which DSM handles only through an "with anxious distress" specifier, not a stand-alone diagnosis. ICD-11 also classifies dysthymic disorder and recognises premenstrual dysphoric disorder. The examinable contrast: ICD-11 has a free-standing mixed anxiety-depression diagnosis; DSM-5 does not. E. Anxiety Disorders Anxiety disorders share excessive fear (an emotional response to real or perceived imminent threat, with sympathetic surge and fight-or-flight) and anxiety (anticipation of future threat, with vigilance and muscle tension), together with associated behavioural disturbance, chiefly avoidance. They are separated largely by the object of the fear and the duration over which it must persist. DSM-5 reorganised this chapter: obsessive-compulsive disorder and the trauma disorders were moved out into their own chapters, leaving the anxiety chapter to the disorders below, a structural fact worth carrying because older texts and ICD-10 still grouped them together. Disorder Criteria and duration (verbatim) Panic disorder Recurrent unexpected panic attacks followed by at least 1 month of persistent worry about future attacks or maladaptive behavioural change. Generalised anxiety disorder (GAD) Excessive, uncontrollable worry about multiple domains for at least 6 months , with at least 3 of 6 somatic/arousal signs in adults (1 in children). Specific phobia Marked fear of a specific object/situation, lasting at least 6 months , driving avoidance. Social anxiety disorder Marked fear of social/performance scrutiny, lasting at least 6 months . Agoraphobia Marked fear of at least 2 of 5 situations (public transport, open spaces, enclosed places, queues/crowds, being outside the home alone), lasting at least 6 months . Separation anxiety disorder Developmentally inappropriate fear of separation: at least 4 weeks in children/adolescents , at least 6 months in adults . Selective mutism Consistent failure to speak in specific social situations (e.g. school) despite speaking elsewhere, for at least 1 month (not limited to the first month of school). A panic attack is an abrupt surge of intense fear or discomfort peaking within minutes, with at least 4 of 13 somatic/cognitive symptoms (palpitations, sweating, trembling, shortness of breath, choking, chest pain, nausea, dizziness, chills/heat, paraesthesias, derealisation/depersonalisation, fear of losing control or "going mad," fear of dying). The attack itself is not a disorder and can occur as a specifier across many conditions; panic disorder needs the recurrent unexpected attacks plus the one-month anticipatory worry or maladaptive change (the second-arrow, the fear of the fear). GAD 's six somatic signs are restlessness/feeling keyed-up, easy fatigue, difficulty concentrating, irritability, muscle tension, and sleep disturbance; three of six are needed in adults (only one in children). Agoraphobia 's "2 of 5 situations" and GAD 's "3 somatic signs over 6 months" are favourite number facts. Most anxiety disorders show the familiar female preponderance (roughly 2:1), and onset clusters in childhood (separation anxiety, specific phobia, social anxiety) earlier than GAD and panic, which typically begin in adolescence to adulthood. Worked vignette: a 28-year-old has had several out-of-the-blue episodes of pounding heart, breathlessness, and a conviction she is about to die, each peaking in minutes; for the past six weeks she has avoided the gym and stopped driving alone for fear of another. The attacks are unexpected and recurrent; the one-month-plus worry and avoidance follow. That is panic disorder . If she instead feared the gym and car specifically because escape would be hard if an attack struck, and feared at least two such situations, the avoidance would also earn an agoraphobia diagnosis layered on top. Exam trap Specific phobia vs. agoraphobia vs. social anxiety: all three run at least 6 months. Specific phobia fears a discrete object; social anxiety fears scrutiny/embarrassment ; agoraphobia fears situations from which escape is difficult or help unavailable if panic strikes (needs 2 of 5 listed). Match the feared cue, not just the avoidance. A second trap: in DSM-5, agoraphobia and panic disorder are now separate, independently coded diagnoses (no longer "panic disorder with agoraphobia" as one label). Memory aid Separation anxiety durations: think "children are quick, adults are slow," 4 weeks for children, 6 months for adults . The longer adult requirement guards against over-diagnosing normal adult attachment worry. For GAD remember the six somatic signs with "WASTED" -style recall: Worry plus restlessness, fatigue, concentration loss, irritability, muscle tension, sleep loss; three of these six in adults. Maintenance mechanism and the panic-specific differentials The behavioural account of why anxiety disorders persist is itself examinable. O. Hobart Mowrer's two-factor theory explains a phobia in two steps: the fear is first acquired by classical conditioning (a neutral cue paired with a frightening experience), then maintained by operant conditioning , because avoidance is negatively reinforced (escaping the cue relieves anxiety, and that relief rewards the avoidance, so it strengthens and the fear never extinguishes). This is the rationale for exposure therapy : blocking avoidance lets extinction occur. In panic disorder, Clark's cognitive model adds the catastrophic misinterpretation of benign bodily sensations (reading a racing heart as an imminent heart attack), which fuels the next attack. The differentials to lock down: panic attacks in panic disorder are unexpected (out of the blue), whereas panic attacks that are reliably cued by a feared object or situation point instead to a phobia or to agoraphobia; and a panic attack is never itself a diagnosis but a transdiagnostic specifier. A crucial medical differential: the somatic storm of a panic attack can mimic, and must be distinguished from, cardiac, respiratory, endocrine (thyroid, phaeochromocytoma), and substance-related causes, so anxiety disorders are diagnoses that also require organic mimics to be excluded. High-yield The duration spine: panic disorder needs 1 month of post-attack worry; GAD, specific phobia, social anxiety, and agoraphobia all need 6 months ; separation anxiety needs 4 weeks in children, 6 months in adults ; selective mutism needs 1 month . The count facts: panic attack = 4 of 13 symptoms; GAD = 3 of 6 somatic signs (1 in children); agoraphobia = fear of 2 of 5 situations. Maintenance is by negative reinforcement of avoidance ; exposure is the corrective. The ICD-11 contrast for anxiety ICD-11 keeps a broadly parallel anxiety-and-fear-related-disorders grouping, but with two examinable differences. First, ICD-11 places separation anxiety disorder and selective mutism inside the anxiety grouping at all ages (DSM-5 also moved these into the anxiety chapter from the childhood chapter, so the systems now agree, a change from ICD-10/DSM-IV). Second, as noted under frameworks, ICD-11 keeps the trauma disorders entirely out of the anxiety block, and it does not require DSM's precise numeric counts, instead asking for a characteristic pattern over a comparable time frame. The single cleanest contrast to memorise: both modern systems now file separation anxiety and selective mutism as anxiety disorders, abandoning the old "disorders of childhood" placement. F. Obsessive-Compulsive & Related Disorders DSM-5 grouped these as a chapter separate from anxiety because they share repetitive, ritualised, body-focused or thought-focused behaviour and overlapping circuitry, specifically the cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical (CSTC) loops running through the orbitofrontal cortex, anterior cingulate, and caudate. This shared circuitry, and the shared partial response to serotonergic agents (SSRIs at higher doses) and to exposure-and-response-prevention, is the rationale for the chapter. ICD-11 likewise created an obsessive-compulsive-and-related-disorders grouping, so the two systems agree on carving OCD out of anxiety. Definition Obsessions are recurrent, intrusive, unwanted, ego-dystonic thoughts, urges, or images that cause marked anxiety, which the person attempts to ignore, suppress, or neutralise. Compulsions are repetitive behaviours (washing, checking, ordering) or mental acts (counting, praying, repeating words) the person feels driven to perform in response to an obsession or according to rigid rules, aimed at reducing anxiety or preventing a dreaded event, but not realistically connected to what they aim to prevent, or clearly excessive. OCD requires obsessions and/or compulsions that are time-consuming (more than 1 hour per day) or cause clinically significant distress or impairment. OCD carries insight specifiers : good or fair insight (recognises beliefs are probably or possibly untrue), poor insight (thinks they are probably true), and absent insight / delusional beliefs (completely convinced they are true, which does not reclassify it as a psychotic disorder), plus a tic-related specifier (a current or past tic disorder, commoner in early-onset male cases). The mechanism that maintains OCD is the negative-reinforcement loop from the behavioural paradigm: the compulsion transiently relieves obsessional anxiety, and that relief reinforces the compulsion, so the ritual strengthens over time even as it fails to address the feared outcome. The other disorders in the chapter: Body dysmorphic disorder (BDD): preoccupation with one or more perceived defects in appearance that are unnoticeable or slight to others, with repetitive behaviours (mirror checking, excessive grooming, skin picking, reassurance seeking) or mental acts (comparing one's appearance with others). The muscle dysmorphia specifier covers the belief that one's build is too small or insufficiently muscular (seen more in men). BDD carries a high suicide risk and a high rate of futile cosmetic procedures. Hoarding disorder: persistent difficulty discarding possessions regardless of value, driven by a perceived need to save and by distress at discarding, producing accumulation that congests and clutters active living spaces and compromises their intended use (a kitchen too cluttered to cook in). It was a new, free-standing DSM-5 diagnosis, previously folded into OCD or OCPD. Trichotillomania (hair-pulling disorder): recurrent pulling out of one's own hair causing hair loss, with repeated attempts to decrease or stop. Classed among the body-focused repetitive behaviours. Excoriation (skin-picking) disorder: recurrent skin picking causing skin lesions, with repeated attempts to stop. The other body-focused repetitive behaviour. PANDAS (Paediatric Autoimmune Neuropsychiatric Disorders Associated with Streptococcal infections) and the broader PITAND /PANS spectrum describe an abrupt, dramatic onset of OCD symptoms and/or tics in children following streptococcal (PANDAS) or other infectious or immune triggers, hypothesised to arise from autoantibodies cross-reacting with basal-ganglia neurons (the same CSTC circuitry). They are the autoimmune etiological network of the OCD chapter, and the clue in a stem is the sudden, overnight onset of OCD or tics in a child after a sore throat or infection. Worked vignette: a 26-year-old spends three hours a day washing his hands because intrusive, distressing images of contamination flood his mind; he knows the fear is excessive but cannot resist, and washing briefly relieves the dread before it returns. Time-consuming (over one hour), ego-dystonic intrusive thoughts (obsessions) driving a ritual (compulsion) that he recognises as excessive (good insight): this is OCD . Contrast a 26-year-old who insists colleagues follow his rigid filing system, never delegates because no one meets his standards, and feels his perfectionism is entirely correct: no intrusive thoughts, no rituals, the traits feel right to him (ego-syntonic). That is obsessive-compulsive personality disorder, not OCD. Exam trap Obsessions are ego-dystonic (experienced as alien, intrusive, distressing, resisted). This contrasts with the ego-syntonic traits of obsessive-compulsive personality disorder (OCPD), where the perfectionism and rigidity feel right and correct to the person. OCD is anxiety-driven ritual with true obsessions and compulsions; OCPD is a pervasive rigid personality style with neither. Do not confuse them; the ego-dystonic versus ego-syntonic distinction is the whole discriminator. Epidemiology, treatment and the OCD-versus-related differentials OCD has a lifetime prevalence of roughly 2 to 3% , a roughly equal sex ratio in adults (with male preponderance in early-onset childhood cases), and a characteristic bimodal onset (a childhood/adolescent peak and an early-adult peak). The most common symptom dimensions are contamination/washing, harm/checking, symmetry/ordering, and forbidden (aggressive, sexual, religious) intrusive thoughts with covert mental rituals; the last group is easily missed because the compulsions are internal. First-line treatments are exposure and response prevention (ERP) , the behavioural gold standard, and serotonergic medication (SSRIs, often at higher doses and longer trials than for depression, plus clomipramine), which is the pharmacological hint that the chapter sits on serotonergic CSTC circuitry. The internal differentials are heavily tested. OCD versus generalised anxiety disorder : GAD worries are about real-life concerns (work, health, finances) and lack the ritualised neutralising compulsions of OCD. OCD versus body dysmorphic disorder : both involve intrusive preoccupation and checking, but BDD's content is fixed on perceived ugliness of appearance. OCD versus hoarding : classic OCD discarding difficulty is driven by an obsession (contamination fear), whereas hoarding disorder reflects a perceived need to save and distress at parting, without a triggering obsession. Trichotillomania and excoriation versus OCD : the body-focused repetitive behaviours are not preceded by intrusive obsessional thoughts; the pulling or picking is its own habit-driven act, which is why they sit as a distinct sub-grouping. Memory aid Separate the four "related" disorders by their target: BDD targets appearance , hoarding targets possessions , trichotillomania targets hair , excoriation targets skin . Hair plus skin are the two body-focused repetitive behaviours. Treatment hook: "ERP plus SSRI" is the OCD answer, and the SSRI dose runs higher than in depression. High-yield OCD time gate = more than 1 hour per day (or marked distress/impairment). Insight specifiers run good/fair, poor, and absent/delusional, and even the delusional level stays in the OCD chapter (it does not become schizophrenia). The shared neurocircuitry of the whole chapter is the cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical (CSTC) loop . Trichotillomania and excoriation are the two body-focused repetitive behaviours ; hoarding is the free-standing DSM-5 newcomer. G. Trauma- & Stressor-Related Disorders This chapter is set apart from every other in the manual by a single structural feature: a defined external stressor is written into the diagnostic criteria as the necessary precipitant. In the anxiety and mood chapters the cause is left open; here the disorder cannot be diagnosed at all unless an identifiable event preceded it. DSM-5 created this chapter de novo (the reactions previously sat among the anxiety disorders), and ICD-11 made the parallel move with its Disorders specifically associated with stress grouping. The whole chapter is then organised by a single axis the examiners exploit relentlessly: the clock . Acute stress disorder, PTSD, and adjustment disorder share much of their symptom universe and are separated chiefly by onset and duration gates . Learn those gates verbatim, because the distractor options are simply the same disorder with the wrong number of days attached. Definition Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) follows exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence, sustained in one of four qualifying ways: directly experiencing it, witnessing it in person, learning that it happened to a close family member or friend (the event being violent or accidental), or experiencing repeated or extreme exposure to aversive details (the occupational route, e.g. first responders, abuse investigators). The symptoms fall into 4 clusters and must persist for more than 1 month with clinically significant distress or impairment. The Criterion A stressor and the four symptom clusters The qualifying stressor (Criterion A) is deliberately narrow: it must involve death, serious injury, or sexual violence . Ordinary severe stressors that do not cross this threshold (divorce, job loss, a non-violent bereavement, a serious but non-life-threatening illness) do not qualify for PTSD; they route to adjustment disorder instead. Importantly, learning of an event qualifies only if it happened to a close other and was violent or accidental ; reading about a disaster in the news, or routine media exposure for non-work reasons, is explicitly excluded. The four symptom clusters, each with its minimum count, are: Cluster Minimum symptoms Content B. Intrusion (re-experiencing) 1 of 5 Intrusive involuntary memories, recurrent distressing dreams, dissociative flashbacks (acting/feeling as if the event were recurring), intense psychological distress at internal or external cues, marked physiological reactivity to cues. C. Avoidance 1 of 2 Persistent effortful avoidance of trauma-related thoughts/feelings, or of external reminders (people, places, conversations, objects, situations). D. Negative alterations in cognition and mood 2 of 7 Dissociative amnesia for the event, persistent exaggerated negative beliefs about self/world, distorted blame of self or others, persistent negative emotional state, markedly diminished interest (anhedonia), detachment/estrangement, persistent inability to feel positive emotions. E. Alterations in arousal and reactivity 2 of 6 Irritable behaviour/angry outbursts, reckless or self-destructive behaviour, hypervigilance, exaggerated startle response, concentration problems, sleep disturbance. The full diagnosis therefore requires the qualifying stressor (A) plus at least one intrusion symptom (B), at least one avoidance symptom (C), at least two negative-cognition/mood symptoms (D), and at least two arousal symptoms (E), all lasting more than one month (Criterion F) with distress/impairment (G) not attributable to a substance or medical condition (H). DSM-5 also defines two specifiers: with dissociative symptoms (depersonalisation or derealisation), and with delayed expression , applied when the full criteria are not met until at least six months after the event. A separate algorithm exists for PTSD in children 6 years and younger , with developmentally adjusted, lower thresholds. The duration ladder: acute stress disorder, PTSD, adjustment disorder Disorder Onset / duration (verbatim) Stressor required Acute stress disorder Symptoms lasting from 3 days to 1 month after trauma exposure (if they persist beyond 1 month, re-diagnose as PTSD) Criterion-A trauma (death, serious injury, sexual violence) PTSD Symptoms (4 clusters) persisting for more than 1 month Criterion-A trauma Adjustment disorder Symptoms emerge within 3 months of the stressor and resolve within 6 months once the stressor or its consequences end Any identifiable stressor (need not be traumatic) Acute stress disorder (ASD) and PTSD share the symptom universe; the distinction is purely temporal. Within the first month after exposure the diagnosis is acute stress disorder (it cannot be made before day 3, which carves out the immediate normal shock reaction); from one month onward it becomes PTSD. ASD's criteria require 9 or more symptoms of 14 drawn across five categories (intrusion, negative mood, dissociation, avoidance, arousal), pooled rather than split into the four PTSD clusters, which is itself a tested contrast. Adjustment disorder is the residual stressor-linked diagnosis: clinically significant emotional or behavioural symptoms, out of proportion to an identifiable but ordinary stressor (a stressor that need not meet the Criterion-A bar), beginning within three months of onset and remitting within six months of the stressor or its consequences ending. If the reaction meets criteria for another specific disorder (a full depressive episode, say), that disorder is diagnosed instead; adjustment disorder is what remains when the reaction is real, impairing, but sub-threshold for anything more specific. Reactive attachment disorder versus disinhibited social engagement disorder Two childhood disorders in this chapter share an identical aetiology , a pattern of grossly insufficient care (social neglect, repeated changes of primary caregiver that prevent stable attachment, or rearing in settings such as institutions that severely limit selective attachment), yet present as behavioural opposites. Reactive attachment disorder (RAD) is the internalising pathway: a consistently inhibited, emotionally withdrawn child who rarely seeks comfort when distressed and rarely responds to it, with minimal social and emotional responsiveness, limited positive affect, and unexplained irritability or fearfulness. Disinhibited social engagement disorder (DSED) is the externalising pathway: a child who is overly familiar with relative strangers, reduced or absent reticence in approaching unfamiliar adults, willingness to wander off with a near-stranger, showing no normal stranger wariness. Both require a developmental age of at least 9 months (so an attachment can be expected to have formed). ICD-11 contrast: complex PTSD and prolonged grief ICD-11 reshaped this domain in three high-yield ways. First, it formally added Complex PTSD (CPTSD) as a separate sibling of PTSD. CPTSD requires the three core PTSD elements (re-experiencing in the here-and-now, avoidance, persistent sense of current threat) plus three additional disturbances in self-organisation (DSO) : affect dysregulation, persistent negative self-concept (worthlessness, shame, guilt), and disturbances in relationships (difficulty feeling close to others). It typically follows prolonged, repeated, inescapable trauma (childhood abuse, captivity, torture, domestic violence). DSM-5 has no separate complex-PTSD category; it folds such cases into PTSD, optionally with the dissociative specifier. Second, ICD-11 added prolonged grief disorder (persistent, pervasive longing or preoccupation with the deceased beyond the expected social or cultural norm, at least six months after the loss); DSM-5-TR later added its own parallel prolonged grief disorder . Third, ICD-11 reframes the immediate stress reaction itself, acute stress reaction , as a normal reaction coded among factors influencing health (a Z-code), not as a mental disorder at all, which is a favourite trap. High-yield Memorise the clock: acute stress disorder = 3 days to 1 month; PTSD = more than 1 month; adjustment disorder = onset within 3 months, resolves within 6 months . PTSD has 4 symptom clusters (intrusion, avoidance, negative cognition/mood, arousal); the Criterion-A stressor must involve death, serious injury, or sexual violence . ICD-11 alone adds Complex PTSD (PTSD triad plus the three disturbances in self-organisation). Exam trap RAD vs. DSED: same pathogenic care, opposite behaviour. RAD = withdrawn, inhibited, does not seek or respond to comfort (internalising); DSED = disinhibited, over-friendly, approaches and wanders off with strangers (externalising). The "child who wanders off with a stranger without checking back" is DSED. Second trap: a severe but non-Criterion-A stressor (divorce, redundancy) producing impairing symptoms is adjustment disorder , never PTSD, because the trauma gate is not crossed. Memory aid The PTSD clusters spell a rough "I Am Nervous And Reactive" : I ntrusion, A voidance, N egative cognition/mood, A rousal/ R eactivity. For the clock, ASD is the short fuse (under a month, starting day 3) and PTSD is the long burn (over a month). H. Dissociative & Somatic Symptom Disorders Two families are taught together here because the examiners pair them and because both turn on a deceptively simple discriminator. Dissociative disorders involve a disruption of the normal integration of consciousness, memory, identity, emotion, perception, body representation, or behaviour. Somatic symptom and related disorders involve prominent physical symptoms or health concerns producing distress and impairment. The pivotal DSM-5 reform across the somatic group was the abandonment of "medically unexplained symptoms" as the organising idea: a clinician can no longer diagnose simply because a cause was not found. The new criteria are positive psychological ones (disproportionate thoughts, feelings, and behaviours about the symptom), so a patient with a genuine medical illness can still carry the diagnosis if the psychological response is excessive. Disorder Core criterion (verbatim where dated) Key discriminator Dissociative identity disorder (DID) Disruption of identity with at least 2 distinct personality states plus recurrent gaps in recall (amnesia) for everyday events, personal information, or trauma Two-or-more identity states plus amnesia; rooted in severe early trauma Dissociative amnesia Inability to recall important autobiographical (usually traumatic/stressful) information; localised, selective, or generalised; specifier with dissociative fugue Memory loss too extensive for ordinary forgetting; no alternate identities Depersonalisation / derealisation disorder Persistent or recurrent unreality/detachment from one's own mind/body (depersonalisation) or surroundings (derealisation), with intact reality testing Preserved insight keeps it out of the psychotic spectrum Somatic symptom disorder At least 1 distressing somatic symptom PLUS disproportionate, persistent thoughts/feelings/behaviours about it, lasting at least 6 months Symptom is present ; response is excessive Illness anxiety disorder Preoccupation with having/acquiring a serious illness; somatic symptoms absent or mild; high health anxiety for at least 6 months Worry without the symptom (formerly hypochondriasis) Conversion disorder (FND) Neurological symptom (motor/sensory) showing clinical incompatibility with recognised neurological/medical disease Positive incompatibility signs, not mere absence of cause The dissociative disorders Dissociative identity disorder (DID) , historically multiple personality disorder, hinges on the coexistence of two or more distinct personality states (in some cultures described as an experience of possession), bringing marked discontinuity in sense of self and agency together with alterations in affect, behaviour, consciousness, memory, perception, and cognition. The recurrent amnesia (gaps in recall for everyday events, important personal information, or traumatic events) is a required, not optional, feature; it is strongly associated with severe, repeated childhood trauma. Dissociative amnesia is an inability to recall important autobiographical information, typically of a traumatic or stressful nature, that is too extensive to be ordinary forgetfulness; it may be localised (a circumscribed period), selective (parts of a period), or generalised (whole identity and life history, a rare and dramatic presentation). Its dissociative fugue specifier adds apparently purposeful travel or bewildered wandering associated with the amnesia. Depersonalisation/derealisation disorder is defined by what it does not abolish: insight. The person feels detached from, or an outside observer of, their own thoughts and body (depersonalisation) or experiences the world as unreal, dreamlike, or visually distorted (derealisation), yet knows these are subjective experiences. That preserved reality testing is precisely what separates it from psychosis. The somatic symptom disorders Somatic symptom disorder requires one or more genuinely distressing somatic symptoms plus excessive thoughts, feelings, or behaviours about them (disproportionate persistent thoughts about seriousness, high health anxiety, or excessive time and energy devoted to the symptoms) for at least six months; whether the symptom is medically explained is irrelevant. Illness anxiety disorder is the worry stripped of the symptom: preoccupation with having or acquiring a serious illness, with somatic symptoms absent or only mild, and a high level of health anxiety for at least six months (this absorbed most of the old hypochondriasis diagnosis). Conversion disorder / functional neurological symptom disorder presents with altered voluntary motor or sensory function (weakness, paralysis, abnormal movements, non-epileptic seizures, sensory loss, blindness) where examination demonstrates positive incompatibility with recognised neurology, for example Hoover's sign (hip-extension weakness that resolves on contralateral hip flexion) or tremor entrainment. The diagnosis rests on that demonstrated internal inconsistency, not on the mere failure to find a lesion. Factitious disorder versus malingering Factitious disorder is the deliberate falsification or induction of physical or psychological signs of illness in oneself (or, in factitious disorder imposed on another, formerly Munchausen syndrome by proxy, in a victim) with deceptive intent, but in the absence of obvious external rewards ; the motive is the internal psychological gain of occupying the sick role. Malingering is the conscious fabrication or exaggeration of symptoms for explicit external (secondary) gain : avoiding work or military duty, evading criminal prosecution, obtaining money, drugs, or disability benefits. Malingering is not a mental disorder at all but a V/Z-code condition that may be a focus of clinical attention. Worked vignette A 34-year-old man is brought to A&E unable to move his right leg after a minor car accident in which a passenger died; neurological examination shows give-way weakness, a positive Hoover's sign, and intact reflexes, with normal imaging. He is bewildered and frightened by the deficit and seeks no compensation. Reason it through: the symptom is genuinely not under voluntary control (no conscious production), the examination shows positive incompatibility with neurology (Hoover's sign), and there is no external reward sought. This is conversion disorder (FND) , not malingering (no secondary gain, not consciously produced) and not factitious disorder (not deliberately induced). Had the same man been deliberately faking the paralysis to win an injury claim, it would be malingering; had he induced it for the role of patient with no external payoff, factitious disorder. Definition Dissociation is a partial or complete disruption of the normal integration of memory, identity, consciousness, perception, or behaviour. Somatisation is the expression of psychological distress through bodily symptoms and health concerns. The first fragments the mind's integration; the second routes distress into the body. High-yield The single discriminator between factitious disorder and malingering is the presence of external (secondary) gain : malingering is conscious deception for an external reward; factitious disorder is conscious deception with no external reward, only the internal need to be sick. Conversion disorder differs from both : the symptom is not consciously produced. Depersonalisation/derealisation disorder is the dissociative disorder defined by intact reality testing . Exam trap DID vs. dissociative amnesia: both feature amnesia, but only DID has the two-or-more distinct identity states. Amnesia plus alternate identities is DID; amnesia alone (even with a fugue) is dissociative amnesia. Second trap: somatic symptom disorder requires a real, present somatic symptom with an excessive response; illness anxiety disorder is the one with somatic symptoms absent or minimal . Do not pick illness anxiety disorder for a patient who has a distressing symptom. I. Feeding, Eating & Sleep-Wake Disorders Two short but number-dense chapters are taught together. The eating disorders are separated almost entirely by weight and by the frequency-and-duration of the binge-or-compensation cycle; the sleep-wake disorders the examiners favour are gated by the 3-times-per-week-for-3-months rule that recurs across the group. Memorise the numbers first, because the prose merely explains what the numbers already decide.
