Disorder Criteria and duration (verbatim) Differential anchor Anorexia nervosa Restriction of energy intake leading to significantly low body weight; intense fear of gaining weight or becoming fat; disturbance in body-image / denial of seriousness of low weight. Subtypes: restricting vs. binge-eating/purging (last 3 months) Defined by low weight Bulimia nervosa Recurrent binge eating PLUS recurrent inappropriate compensatory behaviours (self-induced vomiting, laxatives, diuretics, fasting, excessive exercise), both at least once a week for 3 months ; self-evaluation unduly influenced by shape and weight Normal or above-normal weight Binge-eating disorder Recurrent binges (eating an objectively large amount with loss of control) with marked distress, at least once a week for 3 months , in the absence of compensatory behaviours Binge without purge Insomnia disorder Dissatisfaction with sleep quantity/quality (difficulty initiating, maintaining, or early-morning waking) at least 3 nights per week for 3 months , despite adequate opportunity to sleep Difficulty getting sleep Hypersomnolence disorder Excessive sleepiness despite a main sleep period of at least 7 hours, at least 3 times per week for 3 months Too much sleep, no orexin loss Narcolepsy Recurrent irrepressible need to sleep / lapses into sleep within the same day, at least 3 times per week over the past 3 months , with cataplexy and/or hypocretin (orexin) deficiency on CSF assay or characteristic REM findings Sleep attacks plus cataplexy / orexin loss The eating disorders Anorexia nervosa is defined by three things together: persistent restriction of energy intake leading to a significantly low body weight (in the context of age, sex, developmental trajectory, and physical health), an intense fear of gaining weight or persistent behaviour that interferes with weight gain even though already underweight, and a disturbance in the way body weight or shape is experienced (or denial of the seriousness of the low weight). Its two subtypes are reckoned over the last three months: the restricting type achieves weight loss through dieting, fasting, or excessive exercise without regular bingeing or purging, while the binge-eating/purging type involves recurrent bingeing or purging episodes. Bulimia nervosa is the cycle of recurrent binge eating (a discrete period of eating an objectively large amount with a sense of loss of control) followed by recurrent inappropriate compensatory behaviour to prevent weight gain, both occurring at least once a week for three months , with self-evaluation unduly tied to shape and weight; sufferers are characteristically at normal or above-normal weight. Binge-eating disorder shares the recurrent binges and the once-a-week-for-three-months frequency but has no compensatory behaviour, and the binges are marked by associated features (eating rapidly, until uncomfortably full, when not hungry, alone from embarrassment, with subsequent guilt). The sleep-wake disorders Insomnia disorder is dissatisfaction with sleep quantity or quality marked by difficulty initiating sleep, maintaining sleep, or early-morning awakening, present at least three nights per week for at least three months despite adequate opportunity. Hypersomnolence disorder is its mirror, excessive sleepiness despite a main sleep period of at least seven hours, with recurrent lapses, prolonged unrefreshing sleep, or difficulty being fully awake, again at least three times a week for three months. Narcolepsy couples recurrent irrepressible sleep attacks (at least three times a week over three months) with cataplexy (sudden, brief, bilateral loss of muscle tone with retained consciousness, classically triggered by strong emotion such as laughter) and/or a demonstrated deficiency of the hypothalamic neuropeptide hypocretin (orexin) in cerebrospinal fluid; sleep-onset REM periods and hypnagogic/hypnopompic hallucinations with sleep paralysis are associated features. ICD-11 classifies the sleep-wake disorders in a separate chapter of their own (not within the mental-and-behavioural-disorders block), reflecting their straddling of neurology and psychiatry, a point worth knowing for system-comparison items. Worked vignette An 18-year-old woman, BMI 15.5, is terrified of gaining weight and insists she looks fat despite obvious emaciation; she binges roughly twice a week and then vomits. Resist the reflex to call this bulimia just because she binges and purges. The decisive fact is her significantly low weight : she is at an anorexic weight, so the diagnosis is anorexia nervosa, binge-eating/purging subtype , not bulimia nervosa. Had her weight been normal or above, with the same binge-purge cycle at least weekly for three months, it would be bulimia. Weight, not the behaviour, makes the call. Definition A binge is eating, within a discrete period (e.g. two hours), an amount of food definitely larger than most people would eat in similar circumstances, accompanied by a sense of loss of control over the eating. The loss-of-control element, not the quantity alone, is what makes it a binge. High-yield Both bulimia nervosa and binge-eating disorder require binges at least once a week for 3 months ; the difference is that bulimia has compensatory behaviour and binge-eating disorder does not . The sleep trio (insomnia, hypersomnolence, narcolepsy) all use 3 times/nights per week for 3 months . Narcolepsy is anchored by cataplexy and hypocretin/orexin deficiency . Exam trap Cataplexy vs. catalepsy vs. cataptlexy confusions: cataplexy (sudden emotion-triggered loss of muscle tone) belongs to narcolepsy , whereas catalepsy (passively induced, held posture) and waxy flexibility belong to catatonia . The narcolepsy item is the one that hangs on cataplexy and orexin loss. Second trap: anorexia binge-purge subtype and bulimia both binge and purge; the discriminator is body weight (low = anorexia, normal/high = bulimia), never the behaviour itself. J. Personality Disorders (by Cluster) A personality disorder is not a symptom that comes and goes but an enduring architecture of the self that warps experience and behaviour across situations. The chapter is examined in two layers: the general criteria that any personality disorder must satisfy, and the ten specific types sorted into three clusters, each type paired with the near-neighbour it is most often confused with. Master both layers, because the paper tests the general definition as readily as the individual labels. Definition The general DSM-5 criteria for a personality disorder require an enduring pattern of inner experience and behaviour that deviates markedly from cultural expectation, manifest in at least two of four areas (cognition, affectivity, interpersonal functioning, impulse control). The pattern must be pervasive and inflexible across a broad range of situations, stable and of long duration with onset traceable to adolescence or early adulthood , not better explained by another mental disorder, and not due to a substance or medical condition. It causes clinically significant distress or impairment. The traits are characteristically ego-syntonic (felt as part of the self, not as alien intrusions), which is why insight and help-seeking are often poor. The internal differential is clean: paranoid is suspicion with social engagement; schizoid is genuine indifference to relationships without the cognitive distortions; schizotypal adds the magical thinking, ideas of reference, and perceptual aberrations that schizoid lacks. Cluster B (dramatic/erratic) is the emotionally dysregulated group. Antisocial personality disorder carries hard age gates: it is diagnosed only from age 18 , and there must be documented conduct disorder with onset before age 15 ; under 18 the diagnosis is conduct disorder, which ties this chapter back to the neurodevelopmental one. Borderline 's signature defence is splitting , the inability to hold the good and bad qualities of self or others together, so people are idealised then abruptly devalued; its mood instability is rapid and reactive to interpersonal triggers, which is the key separator from the sustained episodes of bipolar disorder. Cluster C (anxious/fearful) is governed by fear: the crucial contrast is avoidant (craves closeness but is paralysed by fear of rejection) against schizoid from Cluster A (does not want closeness at all). Worked vignette A 26-year-old woman has stormy, intense relationships that swing from idealising a new partner as perfect to condemning them as worthless within days; she dreads being left, cuts herself when a friend cancels plans, and describes a chronic sense of emptiness and an unstable sense of who she is. The rapid idealise-then-devalue pattern is splitting ; combined with abandonment fear, identity disturbance, affective instability, self-harm, and emptiness, this is borderline personality disorder . Note why it is not bipolar disorder: her mood swings are reactive to interpersonal events and last hours to days, not the sustained, autonomous week-long episodes of mania or the two-week blocks of depression. ICD-11 contrast: the dimensional model This is the headline system difference and a near-certain exam item. ICD-11 abolished the ten categorical types entirely . In their place a clinician first assigns a global severity (a sub-threshold "personality difficulty", then mild, moderate, or severe personality disorder, graded by harm to self and others and by pervasiveness), then optionally adds up to five trait domain qualifiers : negative affectivity, detachment, dissociality, disinhibition, and anankastia . A single borderline pattern qualifier was retained, largely to preserve treatment continuity and the evidence base for borderline-specific therapies. DSM-5 went only halfway: it kept all ten categorical types in the main text and parked an Alternative Model for Personality Disorders (AMPD) in Section III, which rates level of personality functioning plus five pathological trait domains (negative affectivity, detachment, antagonism, disinhibition, psychoticism). So both systems describe a dimensional model, but only ICD-11 made it the official, sole system. High-yield Antisocial personality disorder : conduct disorder before age 15 , pattern since age 15, diagnosed only at age 18 or older . Splitting is the hallmark defence of borderline personality disorder. ICD-11 abolished the categorical types for a severity-plus-five-trait-qualifier model (negative affectivity, detachment, dissociality, disinhibition, anankastia, with an optional borderline pattern). The general criteria require deviation in at least 2 of 4 areas, onset by adolescence/early adulthood. Exam trap Avoidant vs. schizoid: both are socially withdrawn, but the avoidant person desires relationships and avoids them from fear of rejection (Cluster C), while the schizoid person is genuinely indifferent to them (Cluster A). Desire-but-afraid = avoidant; doesn't-care = schizoid. Second trap: OCPD is ego-syntonic and has no true obsessions or compulsions , unlike OCD, which is ego-dystonic and ritual-driven. Third: do not say DSM-5 "removed" the ten types; it kept them and added the alternative model. Only ICD-11 abolished the categories. Neurodevelopmental & Childhood Disorders The final chapter covers disorders that onset in the developmental period and are defined by deviation from expected developmental milestones rather than by a decline from a previously normal baseline. The examiners drill the exact thresholds: the symptom counts and age gates of ADHD, the dual-domain logic of autism and intellectual disability, and the ODD-to-conduct-disorder gradient that ultimately feeds antisocial personality disorder. Learn the numbers as a block; they are the spine of the chapter. Intellectual disability and specific learning disorder Intellectual disability (intellectual developmental disorder) requires both of two deficits, with onset in the developmental period: (a) deficits in intellectual functions (reasoning, problem-solving, planning, abstract thinking, judgement, academic and experiential learning) confirmed by both clinical assessment and individualised, standardised intelligence testing; and (b) deficits in adaptive functioning that result in failure to meet developmental and socio-cultural standards for personal independence and social responsibility, across the three domains: conceptual (language, reading, money, time), social (empathy, interpersonal skills, judgement), and practical (self-care, job, money management). The decisive DSM-5 reform is that severity (mild, moderate, severe, profound) is set by adaptive functioning, not by IQ band alone , because adaptive functioning determines the level of support actually needed. Specific learning disorder is the circumscribed cousin: persistent difficulty (at least six months despite intervention) in a specific academic skill, with the skill substantially below that expected for age, specified as with impairment in reading (dyslexia), in written expression , or in mathematics (dyscalculia), and not explained by intellectual disability or sensory deficit. Autism spectrum disorder Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) also requires both of two domains, present from early development: (a) persistent deficits in social communication and social interaction across multiple contexts, demonstrated by deficits in all three of social-emotional reciprocity, nonverbal communicative behaviours, and developing/maintaining/understanding relationships; and (b) restricted, repetitive patterns of behaviour, interests, or activities , shown by at least two of four : stereotyped/repetitive movements or speech, insistence on sameness and inflexible routines, highly fixated intense interests, and hyper- or hypo-reactivity to sensory input. Symptoms must be present in the early developmental period (though they may not fully manifest until social demands exceed capacity), and severity is rated 1 to 3 by the level of support required. DSM-5 collapsed the older separate labels (autistic disorder, Asperger's disorder, childhood disintegrative disorder, PDD-NOS) into the single spectrum. ICD-11 likewise uses a unified autism spectrum disorder with qualifiers for intellectual and language impairment, a point of convergence between the systems. ADHD: the exact symptom counts and age gates Definition Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) requires a persistent pattern of inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity that interferes with functioning or development. The symptom threshold is at least 6 symptoms from a domain (inattention, or hyperactivity-impulsivity), reduced to at least 5 symptoms for those aged 17 or older , persisting for at least 6 months , with several symptoms present before age 12 , and present in at least 2 settings (e.g. home and school). Presentations: predominantly inattentive, predominantly hyperactive-impulsive, or combined. Disorder Criteria and duration (verbatim) ADHD At least 6 symptoms (5 if age 17 or older) of inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity, for at least 6 months , with several symptoms present before age 12 , across at least 2 settings Oppositional defiant disorder (ODD) Angry/irritable mood, argumentative/defiant behaviour, or vindictiveness (at least 4 symptoms across the categories), lasting at least 6 months , with at least one person who is not a sibling Conduct disorder (CD) Repetitive, persistent violation of others' rights or major age-appropriate norms across 4 clusters , with at least 3 symptoms in the past 12 months (and at least 1 in the past 6 months); childhood-onset (before age 10) vs. adolescent-onset specifier The disruptive-behaviour gradient: ODD, conduct disorder, antisocial personality The disruptive disorders form a developmental escalation that the examiners love to test as a sequence. Oppositional defiant disorder (ODD) is the milder, earlier pattern: a recurrent pattern of angry/irritable mood, argumentative/defiant behaviour, or vindictiveness lasting at least six months, directed mainly at authority figures, without the serious rights-violations of conduct disorder. Conduct disorder (CD) is graver: a repetitive and persistent pattern that violates the basic rights of others or major societal norms, across four symptom clusters , namely (1) aggression to people and animals , (2) destruction of property , (3) deceitfulness or theft , and (4) serious violations of rules (truancy, running away), with at least three symptoms in the past twelve months. Its childhood-onset subtype (at least one symptom before age 10) carries a worse prognosis. Conduct disorder before age 15 is the documented precursor required for the later diagnosis of antisocial personality disorder at age 18 or over, which is exactly how the neurodevelopmental and personality chapters interlock. The depressive chapter's disruptive mood dysregulation disorder (DMDD) also sits at this junction: chronic, persistent irritability with severe outbursts at least three times a week for at least twelve months, onset before age 10, introduced to curb the over-diagnosis of paediatric bipolar disorder. Worked vignette A 9-year-old boy is described by his teacher as unable to stay seated, blurting answers, losing his pencils and worksheets, and unable to follow multi-step instructions; the same pattern is reported at home and has been present for over a year. Apply the gates: at least six symptoms across inattention and hyperactivity-impulsivity, lasting more than six months, onset before age 12, present in at least two settings (home and school). This is ADHD, combined presentation . Now contrast a different 9-year-old who is not merely restless but deliberately cruel to the family cat, has set a fire, shoplifts, and stays out all night: that crosses into violating others' rights and major norms across the four clusters, so it is conduct disorder , not ADHD, although the two frequently co-occur. High-yield Pin the numbers: ADHD = at least 6 symptoms (5 if 17 or older), at least 6 months, several symptoms before age 12, at least 2 settings. Conduct disorder = 4 clusters, at least 3 symptoms in 12 months. ODD = at least 6 months. Intellectual disability = three adaptive domains (conceptual, social, practical), severity set by adaptive function not IQ band. ASD = social-communication deficits (all 3) and restricted/repetitive behaviours (at least 2 of 4), early-developmental onset. DMDD = outbursts at least 3 times/week for at least 12 months, onset before age 10. Exam trap ODD vs. conduct disorder: ODD is defiance, anger, and argumentativeness without serious aggression, property destruction, theft, or rule violations; conduct disorder crosses into violating others' rights across its four clusters. The "child who is argumentative and loses his temper at his parents" is ODD; the "child who is cruel to animals, sets fires, and steals" is conduct disorder. Second trap: ADHD's age gate is symptoms before age 12 (not before age 7, the old DSM-IV figure, which is the classic distractor), and the symptom count drops from 6 to 5 only at age 17 and over. For ADHD remember " 6, 6, 12, 2 ": 6 symptoms, 6 months, before 12, in 2 settings. 4 · Psychological Assessment & Psychodiagnostics Psychological testing is the operational backbone of clinical psychology: it converts vague referral questions ("is this child gifted?", "is this an organic dementia or a depressive pseudodementia?", "is this patient psychotic or malingering?") into reproducible numbers and structured behaviour samples. This section teaches the instruments that dominate the M.Phil paper, beginning with the family that quantifies general mental ability and then localises deficits to brain systems. For every test you must hold four things in your head at once: what it measures , how it is structured (the exact subtests, indices and norms), how it is scored and interpreted , and the named author and year behind it . The examiner's favourite distractors live precisely where two of these slip out of alignment: an index mistaken for the full-scale score, a subtest filed under the wrong index, a ratio IQ confused with a deviation IQ, a fixed battery confused with a flexible one, or the wrong theorist attached to the wrong battery. The whole craft of the assessment paper is telling a test apart from its near-neighbour, so each instrument below is taught from the floor up and then explicitly contrasted with the one it is most often confused with. Read each until you can reproduce its architecture, its numbers and its trap from memory. A. The Wechsler Intelligence Matrix (WAIS-IV / WISC-V) David Wechsler built the dominant family of individually administered intelligence tests, defining intelligence as "the global capacity of the individual to act purposefully, to think rationally and to deal effectively with his environment." That definition matters because it is global and aggregative : Wechsler treated intelligence as a single overall capacity expressed through many specific abilities, which is why his tests yield one summary IQ resting on top of several narrower scores. His central departure from the original Stanford-Binet was to abandon the mental-age ratio IQ and adopt the deviation IQ : a person's score is expressed as a standard score with a population mean of 100 and a standard deviation of 15, so an IQ simply states how many standard deviations the examinee sits above or below same-age peers. The adult form is the Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale, fourth edition (WAIS-IV, 2008) , for ages 16 to 90; the child form is the Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children, fifth edition (WISC-V, 2014) , for ages 6 to 16; the preschool form is the WPPSI (ages 2 years 6 months to 7 years 7 months), a third member of the family that the paper sometimes drops in as a date-or-age distractor. Earlier Wechsler scales reported a Verbal IQ and a Performance IQ; the modern editions have abandoned that two-IQ split in favour of a single Full Scale IQ (FSIQ) sitting on top of four (WAIS-IV) or five (WISC-V) index scores. Definition The Full Scale IQ (FSIQ) is the single best estimate of general intellectual ability (Charles Spearman's g ), derived from the core subtests across all index domains. Each subtest yields a scaled score (mean 10, standard deviation 3) ; the index scores and the FSIQ are composites rescaled to mean 100, standard deviation 15 . The two metrics are different scales: a "12" is a subtest scaled score (above average), while a "112" is a composite/IQ. Confusing the two metrics is a standard slip. Definition A deviation IQ expresses ability as a standard score relative to the same-age peer group (mean 100, standard deviation 15), so it stays meaningful across the lifespan. The older ratio IQ (mental age divided by chronological age, times 100) breaks down in adulthood because mental age plateaus while chronological age keeps rising, artificially deflating adult scores. Wechsler's adoption of the deviation IQ was the decisive methodological reform of the field. Classification bands The deviation metric maps onto standard descriptive bands, and the examiner expects you to attach the right label to the right range. Because the standard deviation is 15, each band is roughly one standard deviation wide. FSIQ range Classification (WAIS-IV terminology) Approx. percentile / population 130 and above Very Superior Top 2.2% (about +2 SD) 120 to 129 Superior About 6.7% 110 to 119 High Average About 16.1% 90 to 109 Average The middle 50% (mean 100) 80 to 89 Low Average About 16.1% 70 to 79 Borderline About 6.7% 69 and below Extremely Low (formerly "Intellectually Deficient") Bottom 2.2% (about −2 SD); the IQ criterion for intellectual disability The four core structural indices and their subtests The architecture of the WAIS-IV is a four-index structure. Memorise both the index names and exactly which subtests load on each, because the paper loves to mis-sort a subtest (for example, planting Arithmetic under the verbal index when it actually loads on working memory, or planting Block Design under processing speed when it loads on perceptual reasoning). Index What it measures Core subtests Supplemental subtests Verbal Comprehension Index (VCI) Acquired verbal knowledge, verbal concept formation, crystallised intelligence Similarities, Vocabulary, Information Comprehension Perceptual Reasoning Index (PRI) Fluid reasoning, non-verbal problem solving, visual-spatial processing Block Design, Matrix Reasoning, Visual Puzzles Figure Weights, Picture Completion Working Memory Index (WMI) Attention, concentration, mental manipulation of information held in mind Digit Span, Arithmetic Letter-Number Sequencing Processing Speed Index (PSI) Speed of visual scanning, graphomotor speed, mental quickness on simple tasks Symbol Search, Coding Cancellation Take each in turn. In the Verbal Comprehension Index , Similarities asks how two concepts are alike (in what way are a dog and a lion alike?) and taps abstract verbal reasoning; Vocabulary asks for word definitions and is the single best correlate of overall FSIQ and the most resistant to decline (a classic "hold" test, used to estimate premorbid ability); Information samples general fund of acquired knowledge; the supplemental Comprehension probes practical reasoning and understanding of social conventions. In the Perceptual Reasoning Index , Block Design requires the examinee to reproduce a printed geometric pattern using red-and-white blocks under time pressure (it is exquisitely sensitive to right-parietal and constructional dysfunction); Matrix Reasoning presents an incomplete visual pattern matrix to be completed from options (a near-pure fluid-reasoning, g -loaded task); Visual Puzzles asks which three pieces combine to make a target shape (mental rotation and spatial analysis); supplemental Figure Weights uses balance-scale problems for quantitative-analogical reasoning, and Picture Completion asks what important part is missing from a picture. In the Working Memory Index , Digit Span has three parts (forwards, which is simple attention span; backwards, which adds mental manipulation; and sequencing, which requires reordering), Arithmetic presents mentally solved word problems under time pressure, and supplemental Letter-Number Sequencing requires reordering an intermixed string of letters and numbers. In the Processing Speed Index , Symbol Search requires scanning to decide whether target symbols appear in a search group, Coding requires writing the symbol paired with each digit using a key (sensitive to attention, motor speed and incidental learning), and supplemental Cancellation requires marking target shapes among distractors. For PRI core trio: " BMV " (Block Design, Matrix Reasoning, Visual Puzzles). For PSI: Symbol Search and Coding are the two pencil-speed tasks. Arithmetic sounds verbal but lives in W orking memory; Digit Span is its partner there. Administration and scoring logic The Wechsler scales are individually administered (one examiner, one examinee, roughly 60 to 90 minutes), not group paper-and-pencil tests, which is part of their clinical value: the examiner observes how the person solves problems, not only the final score. Most subtests use basal and ceiling rules to keep testing efficient. The basal is a run of consecutive correct items establishing that easier items below would also be passed (so they are credited without administration); the ceiling is a run of consecutive failures establishing that harder items above would also be failed (so testing stops). Raw scores within each subtest are first converted to age-scaled scaled scores (mean 10, SD 3) using the norms table for the examinee's age band; the relevant scaled scores are then summed and converted to each index composite and to the FSIQ (mean 100, SD 15). The clinical reading then proceeds from the top down: first the FSIQ as a global estimate, then the four indices, then, crucially, the scatter between them. Clinical interpretation: index discrepancies and profile analysis The single most clinically useful output is not the FSIQ but the pattern of index discrepancies , because a meaningful gap between indices localises where the difficulty lies. When the four indices differ widely the FSIQ becomes an average of unlike things and is itself less interpretable; the clinician then interprets at the index level. A large VCI greater than PRI split suggests verbal-crystallised strengths over fluid-perceptual ability (and is sometimes seen with right-hemisphere or visuo-spatial difficulty), while PRI greater than VCI suggests the reverse (and can accompany language-based learning difficulty). A selectively depressed WMI or PSI against intact VCI and PRI is the classic signature of attentional disorders, anxiety, depression and ADHD, because working memory and processing speed are the functions most vulnerable to these states. Profile (ipsative) analysis then compares each subtest scaled score against the person's own mean to find genuine strengths and weaknesses; the examiner expects you to know that this is interpreted cautiously, since subtest scores are less reliable than composites and chance scatter is common. General Ability Index versus Cognitive Proficiency Index This is the highest-yield conceptual point in the whole Wechsler topic. Beyond the FSIQ, the WAIS-IV provides two ancillary composites that repartition the same subtests in a clinically meaningful way. Definition The General Ability Index (GAI) is computed from VCI + PRI only . It deliberately extracts the higher-order reasoning component (verbal and perceptual reasoning) while removing the contributions of working memory and processing speed. The Cognitive Proficiency Index (CPI) is computed from WMI + PSI only : it isolates the efficiency machinery (how quickly and reliably the brain manipulates and processes information). The clinical logic: working memory and processing speed are the cognitive functions most vulnerable to attentional disorders, anxiety, depression, traumatic brain injury and ADHD. When a clinician suspects that low FSIQ is being dragged down by these efficiency deficits rather than by a true reasoning limitation, the GAI gives a "purer" estimate of intellectual capacity, while a low CPI relative to a high GAI flags exactly where the efficiency bottleneck lies. A large GAI-greater-than-CPI gap is a hallmark of conditions that spare reasoning but impair processing. Worked example. A 24-year-old with a history of head injury obtains VCI 112, PRI 108, WMI 79, PSI 76, giving an FSIQ of about 94 (Average). Read naively, the FSIQ of 94 says "average intelligence," which badly misrepresents him. Computing the ancillary composites: the GAI (from VCI 112 and PRI 108) lands near 111 (High Average), whereas the CPI (from WMI 79 and PSI 76) lands near 76 (Borderline). The 35-point GAI-over-CPI gap tells the real story: his underlying reasoning capacity is High Average and intact, but an efficiency bottleneck in working memory and processing speed (exactly the post-concussive pattern) is dragging the composite down. The FSIQ of 94 is the misleading average of two very different abilities, and the GAI/CPI split is what makes that visible. This is precisely the reasoning the paper expects you to reproduce. Exam trap Do not confuse GAI with FSIQ . The FSIQ includes all four indices (VCI + PRI + WMI + PSI). The GAI deliberately drops WMI and PSI and equals VCI + PRI only. A distractor item will say "GAI = the full-scale score" or "GAI includes working memory": both are false. Also note GAI = VCI + PRI (reasoning) while CPI = WMI + PSI (efficiency); swapping which composite contains which pair is the second favourite trap. And the Wechsler uses a deviation IQ (mean 100, SD 15), not a ratio IQ; the ratio IQ belongs to the early Stanford-Binet. High-yield WAIS-IV (2008, ages 16 to 90) and WISC-V (2014, ages 6 to 16): deviation IQ, mean 100, SD 15; subtest scaled scores mean 10, SD 3. Four core indices = VCI, PRI, WMI, PSI. GAI = VCI + PRI (capacity, minus efficiency constraints); CPI = WMI + PSI (efficiency). WISC-V splits PRI into Visual Spatial + Fluid Reasoning, giving five indices. Author: David Wechsler. Definition to quote: "the global capacity to act purposefully, think rationally and deal effectively with the environment." WISC-V's five-factor structure The WISC-V split the old Perceptual Reasoning Index into two separate indices, giving a five-factor model: Verbal Comprehension, Visual Spatial, Fluid Reasoning, Working Memory and Processing Speed . The Visual Spatial Index is anchored by Block Design and Visual Puzzles; the Fluid Reasoning Index is anchored by Matrix Reasoning and Figure Weights. This reflects modern Cattell-Horn-Carroll (CHC) theory , which treats visual processing (Gv) and fluid reasoning (Gf) as distinct broad abilities rather than one "perceptual" lump. The practical upshot is that the WISC-V can separate a child who is poor at spatial construction (Gv) from a child who is poor at abstract reasoning (Gf), a distinction the old single PRI blurred. Feature WAIS-IV (adult) WISC-V (child) Age range 16 to 90 6 to 16 Number of primary indices Four Five Index list VCI, PRI, WMI, PSI VCI, Visual Spatial, Fluid Reasoning, WMI, PSI Handling of "perceptual" One PRI lump Split into Visual Spatial (Gv) + Fluid Reasoning (Gf) Exam trap The number of indices is age-specific: WAIS-IV has four primary indices, WISC-V has five . A distractor will say the adult test has five or the child test has four. The fifth index appears because the WISC-V splits PRI into Visual Spatial and Fluid Reasoning under CHC theory; it does not add a wholly new ability out of nowhere. B. Kaufman Assessment Systems Alan and Nadeen Kaufman built a family of tests explicitly grounded in a neuropsychological and information-processing theory rather than in Wechsler's atheoretical clinical tradition. Where Wechsler asked "how much general ability?", the Kaufmans asked "by what kind of processing does this person solve problems?", and they built the answer into the test's very architecture. The flagship is the Kaufman Assessment Battery for Children (K-ABC, 1983; now KABC-II, 2004) , for ages 3 to 18. Its theoretical spine is the Luria-Das distinction between sequential and simultaneous processing , drawn from the Russian neuropsychologist Alexander Luria by way of the PASS model of Das and Naglieri. Definition Sequential processing solves problems by arranging stimuli in serial, temporal, step-by-step order (for example, repeating a string of digits or hand movements in sequence); it corresponds to Luria's "successive" processing and is anchored in frontotemporal systems. Simultaneous processing integrates many stimuli at once into a single spatial or gestalt whole (for example, assembling triangles into a design, or recognising a partly drawn picture); it corresponds to Luria's "simultaneous" processing and is anchored in occipital-parietal systems. The two are dissociable processing styles, not levels of ability. The dual-model scoring system The genuinely distinctive feature of the KABC-II is that the examiner chooses, before testing, between two interpretive models, and the choice changes the global score that results. Under the Luria model the battery deliberately excludes acquired verbal knowledge , yielding the Mental Processing Index (MPI) ; this model is preferred for children from diverse language backgrounds, bilingual children, or any case where crystallised knowledge would unfairly depress the estimate of underlying processing ability. Under the Cattell-Horn-Carroll (CHC) model the battery adds a crystallised-knowledge scale, yielding the Fluid-Crystallized Index (FCI) ; this is preferred when acquired knowledge is a fair and relevant part of the construct (for example, a mainstream English-speaking child where school learning should count). The deliberate separation of processing ability from acquired knowledge was the Kaufmans' signature contribution, designed expressly to reduce cultural and educational bias : a child is not penalised on the MPI for vocabulary they never had the chance to learn. Scoring model Global index Includes acquired knowledge? Best used when Luria model Mental Processing Index (MPI) No (processing only) Bilingual, diverse-language or disadvantaged backgrounds, where crystallised knowledge would bias the estimate CHC model Fluid-Crystallized Index (FCI) Yes (adds crystallised knowledge) Mainstream cases where acquired knowledge is a fair part of the ability being measured The KABC-II also reports CHC-aligned broad-ability scales (sequential/short-term memory Gsm, simultaneous/visual processing Gv, learning ability Glr, planning/fluid reasoning Gf, and, in the CHC model only, crystallised knowledge Gc), so the same performance can be read either as Lurian processing types or as CHC broad abilities. Representative subtests anchor each style: Number Recall and Word Order load the sequential scale, while Triangles (assembling foam shapes into a model) and Rover (a route-planning task) load the simultaneous scale. The adult counterpart in the family is the Kaufman Adolescent and Adult Intelligence Test (KAIT) , which formalises the fluid/crystallised split directly, giving separate Fluid and Crystallised IQs alongside a Composite. The Kaufmans also produced the Kaufman Brief Intelligence Test (KBIT) , a short screening measure, which the paper occasionally lists as a fourth family member. Worked example: why the model choice changes the score Consider a seven-year-old who recently arrived from a non-English-speaking home and is being assessed for a possible learning disability. On the processing scales (sequential and simultaneous, both language-light) she performs solidly, but on the crystallised Knowledge scale, which depends on English vocabulary and acquired facts she has had little chance to learn, she scores poorly. Under the CHC model the Knowledge scale is included, so her Fluid-Crystallized Index (FCI) is pulled down to, say, 84, suggesting below-average ability. Under the Luria model the crystallised scale is dropped entirely, so her Mental Processing Index (MPI) reflects only her (intact) processing and lands near 98, in the Average range. The two scores describe the same child; the 14-point gap is created purely by whether acquired knowledge is counted. The correct clinical choice here is the Luria model and the MPI, because counting English vocabulary would confound limited opportunity with limited ability. This deliberate choice is exactly what the Kaufmans built the dual model to allow, and it is the reasoning the paper expects. Kaufman versus Wechsler The cleanest way to hold the Kaufman batteries in memory is by contrast with the Wechsler. Wechsler's scales are atheoretical and clinically derived : subtests were assembled because they worked in practice, and only later organised into indices. The Kaufman batteries are theory-first : the test architecture was deduced from Luria's neuropsychology and CHC theory before a single item was written. The Wechsler gives one fixed scoring route to a single FSIQ; the Kaufman gives a choice of scoring route (Luria/MPI versus CHC/FCI) selected to fit the examinee's background. And the Kaufman's explicit aim is fairness : by being able to strip out acquired knowledge it reduces the cultural and educational bias that a knowledge-laden test carries. That trio (theory-first, dual-model, bias-reducing) is the Kaufman signature and the most likely stem. Memory aid Kaufman = " processing, not just knowledge ." Sequential = one-at-a-time-in-order (Luria successive); Simultaneous = all-at-once-as-a-whole (Luria simultaneous). Two models, two indices: " Luria leaves out learning " gives the MPI (processing only); CHC C ounts C rystallised knowledge, giving the FCI. The dual-model scoring is the Kaufman signature. High-yield KABC-II (Alan and Nadeen Kaufman; ages 3 to 18) is built on Alexander Luria's sequential versus simultaneous processing distinction. Dual scoring: Luria model gives the Mental Processing Index (MPI, no acquired knowledge); CHC model gives the Fluid-Crystallized Index (FCI, adds crystallised knowledge) . Its design purpose is to reduce cultural and educational bias. The adult sibling is the KAIT (fluid/crystallised split). Exam trap The Kaufman batteries are theory-driven (Luria/CHC), in deliberate contrast to the Wechsler's atheoretical, clinically derived tradition: that contrast is the favourite stem. Do not swap the indices: the Luria model yields the MPI (knowledge excluded) and the CHC model yields the FCI (knowledge included). Sequential is Luria's "successive," not "simultaneous"; reversing sequential and simultaneous, or attaching the MPI to the CHC model, are the standard distractors. C. Stanford-Binet Intelligence Scales, Fifth Edition (SB5) The Stanford-Binet is the oldest standardised intelligence test in continuous use, and its lineage is itself examinable. It descends from Alfred Binet and Theodore Simon's 1905 Paris scale , the first practical intelligence test, devised to identify French schoolchildren needing remedial help and built around the concept of mental age (the age level at which a child is performing). It was imported to the United States and renormed at Stanford by Lewis Terman (1916) , who popularised William Stern's ratio IQ (mental age divided by chronological age, times 100) as the test's summary score; the Stanford-Binet is therefore the original home of the ratio IQ. The modern fifth edition ( SB5, Gale Roid, 2003 ) covers ages 2 to 85+ and, like the Wechsler, has long since abandoned the ratio IQ in favour of a deviation IQ (mean 100, SD 15) . Its defining architecture is a five-factor model crossed with two domains , giving a 5 x 2 matrix of ten subtests. The five factors Fluid Reasoning : novel problem solving, inductive and deductive reasoning not dependent on prior knowledge. Knowledge : accumulated general information and crystallised learning (the SB5's analogue of verbal comprehension). Quantitative Reasoning : facility with numbers, numerical concepts and quantitative problem solving. Visual-Spatial Processing : ability to see patterns, relationships and spatial orientation among figures. Working Memory : capacity to hold and transform information in immediate awareness. The 5 x 2 architecture and the three IQs The genuinely distinctive feature is that each of these five factors is measured in both a verbal domain and a non-verbal domain . So Fluid Reasoning is tested both with verbal analogies and with non-verbal matrices; Knowledge is tested both verbally and through picture absurdities; Quantitative Reasoning both verbally and with figural number problems; and so on across all five factors. Crossing five factors with two domains gives the ten subtests of the 5 x 2 grid. This crossing yields three summary IQs plus the five factor indices: a Verbal IQ (the five verbal-domain subtests), a Non-verbal IQ (the five non-verbal-domain subtests), and a Full Scale IQ (all ten). The non-verbal pathway is what makes the SB5 unusually suitable for examinees with limited language, hearing impairment, deafness, autism, or English as a second language, because a meaningful estimate can be obtained without relying on spoken or written verbal responses. Factor Verbal domain example Non-verbal domain example Fluid Reasoning Verbal analogies / early reasoning Object-series matrices Knowledge Vocabulary Picture absurdities Quantitative Reasoning Verbal quantitative problems Figural quantitative problems Visual-Spatial Processing Position and direction (verbal spatial) Form board / form patterns Working Memory Memory for sentences / last word Block-tapping / delayed response Routing, floor and ceiling Administration begins with two routing subtests (one verbal: Object-Series/Matrices for non-verbal fluid reasoning, and the Vocabulary routing subtest for the verbal side) that estimate the examinee's ability level and direct the examiner to the correct starting point in the remaining subtests, so the test is tailored to the person's level and is efficient. Each subtest is organised into testlets graded by difficulty, with basal and ceiling rules. The SB5's excellent floor and ceiling (it discriminates well at the very bottom and very top of the ability range) makes it the preferred instrument at the extremes: for diagnosing severe and profound intellectual disability, and for identifying profound giftedness, where the Wechsler scales run out of easy or hard enough items. High-yield SB5 (Roid, 2003; ages 2 to 85+) five factors: Fluid Reasoning, Knowledge, Quantitative Reasoning, Visual-Spatial Processing, Working Memory , each crossed with verbal and non-verbal domains (5 x 2 = 10 subtests), yielding Verbal IQ, Non-verbal IQ and Full Scale IQ. Lineage: Binet-Simon (1905, mental age) to Terman at Stanford (1916, ratio IQ); the SB5 is the historical home of the ratio IQ (MA/CA x 100) but the modern edition uses the deviation IQ (mean 100, SD 15). Strong floor and ceiling: the instrument of choice at the extremes of ability. Memory aid SB5 factors: " F-K-Q-V-W " = Fluid reasoning, Knowledge, Quantitative reasoning, Visual-spatial, Working memory. Remember the 5 factors x 2 domains grid: that crossing of verbal and non-verbal is what distinguishes SB5 from the Wechsler, and it is why SB5 alone yields a clean Non-verbal IQ. Exam trap The Stanford-Binet is the home of the ratio IQ (mental age over chronological age, times 100) and of the concept of mental age ; the deviation IQ is Wechsler's innovation, although the modern SB5 has adopted it too. Do not credit Wechsler with mental age, and do not say the current SB5 still uses the ratio IQ. The defining SB5 structure is 5 factors x 2 domains = 10 subtests ; a distractor will quote four factors (that is the Wechsler) or omit the verbal/non-verbal crossing. D. Indian Adaptations of Performance Tests Western verbal IQ tests are heavily culture-loaded and language-bound, so Indian clinical practice relies on performance (non-verbal, motor) batteries that were standardised on Indian populations. A "performance" test is one in which the examinee does something (arranges blocks, draws, assembles) rather than answering verbal questions, so formal schooling and language fluency play a minimal role; this is exactly what makes such tests fair for the illiterate and the educationally disadvantaged who make up much of Indian clinical caseload. Several are examined constantly, and the paper expects the author of each and the exact list of sub-tests. Bhatia's Battery of Performance Tests C. M. Bhatia (1955) assembled a battery of five performance sub-tests standardised on the Indian population, designed for the illiterate and the educationally disadvantaged because it minimises the role of formal schooling and language. It was the first Indian intelligence battery of its kind and remains a clinical workhorse for estimating IQ where verbal testing is inappropriate. The five sub-tests are: Kohs' Block Design Test : reproduce printed coloured designs with cubes whose faces are coloured; taps non-verbal abstract reasoning and visuo-constructional ability (the same task lineage that became Wechsler's Block Design). Alexander's Pass-Along Test : slide coloured blocks along channels in a frame to reproduce a pattern in the fewest moves; taps spatial planning and problem solving. Pattern Drawing Test : copy increasingly complex patterns in a single continuous line without lifting the pencil or retracing; taps visuo-motor planning. Immediate Memory Test : digits forward and digits backward (a digit-span analogue) measuring immediate auditory attention span. Picture Construction Test : assemble cut-up pieces into a meaningful picture; taps perceptual organisation and synthesis. Raw scores on the sub-tests are summed and converted to an IQ via age-based Indian norms (Bhatia also provided a method for estimating IQ from test age against chronological age). Bhatia's battery is the standard non-verbal IQ estimate for Indian adolescents and adults and is widely used clinically when verbal testing is inappropriate. Memory aid Bhatia's five: " Kohs, Pass-along, Pattern, Memory, Picture " = K-P-P-M-P . Two are eponymous ( Kohs' Block Design, Alexander's Pass-Along): the examiner loves to ask who authored which sub-test, and to mis-attribute Pass-Along to Kohs or vice versa. Malin's Intelligence Scale for Indian Children (MISIC) For children, the most-examined Indian instrument is the Malin's Intelligence Scale for Indian Children (MISIC, Arthur J. Malin, 1969) , which is an Indian adaptation of the Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children (WISC) , for ages 6 to 15. It preserves the Wechsler architecture of a Verbal scale and a Performance scale yielding a Verbal IQ, a Performance IQ and a Full Scale IQ, but with items, vocabulary and norms adapted to the Indian context. The verbal subtests include Information, Comprehension, Arithmetic, Similarities, Vocabulary and Digit Span; the performance subtests include Picture Completion, Block Design, Object Assembly, Coding and Mazes. Because it is the indigenised WISC, the MISIC is the default individual child IQ test in Indian clinical and educational settings. Test Author / year Population Structure Bhatia's Battery C. M. Malin, 1969 Indian children, ages 6 to 15 Indian adaptation of WISC: Verbal + Performance scales, three IQs Seguin Form Board Edouard Seguin (19th C.) Children / low-language adults Single form-board task, speed-based Exam trap Keep the Indian tests apart by author and target. Bhatia's Battery (Bhatia, 1955) is a five-subtest performance battery for (mainly illiterate) adolescents and adults . MISIC (Malin, 1969) is an Indian adaptation of the WISC for children , retaining the Verbal/Performance split. A distractor will swap the authors, call MISIC an adaptation of the WAIS (it is the WISC), or list Bhatia's five sub-tests under MISIC. Seguin Form Board Test The Seguin Form Board (Edouard Seguin) is a wooden board with ten recessed cut-outs of common geometric shapes; the examinee must place the matching blocks into their slots as fast as possible. It is primarily a test of eye-hand coordination, visuo-motor speed and form perception , used as a quick non-verbal screen for intellectual ability in children and in adults with limited language, and historically as a teaching device for children with intellectual disability (Seguin was a pioneer of education for the "feeble-minded"). Three variables are recorded across repeated trials: Speed (time) : typically the shortest of three trials is taken as the score; faster placement indicates better visuo-motor efficiency. Accuracy : errors in placement and the smoothness of insertion. Learning curve across trials : because the board is administered three times, the drop in completion time from trial 1 to trial 3 indexes the rate of motor learning and the benefit of practice; a flat or erratic curve (no improvement) can itself be clinically informative, suggesting poor learning or attentional fluctuation. Exam trap The Seguin Form Board is not a memory test and not a verbal test: its core variable is speed (best of three trials), with accuracy and the across-trial learning curve as the secondary measures. A distractor will frame it as measuring "vocabulary" or "auditory memory": wrong. It measures visuo-motor speed and form perception. Do not confuse it with the larger Bhatia battery; Seguin is a single form-board task, not a five-subtest battery. E. Halstead-Reitan Neuropsychological Battery (HRNB) We now move from "how much general ability?" to "which brain systems are intact or damaged?" This is the domain of fixed neuropsychological batteries , and the first key distinction the paper tests is fixed versus flexible. Definition A fixed (standardised) battery administers the same complete set of tests to every examinee regardless of the referral question, maximising comparability, norms and actuarial interpretation, at the cost of time and flexibility. A flexible (hypothesis-testing) battery , by contrast, selects tests adaptively to pursue the specific clinical question (the approach Alexander Luria himself used). The HRNB is the archetypal fixed battery; Luria's original method was the archetypal flexible one. The Halstead-Reitan Neuropsychological Battery (HRNB) was built by Ward Halstead (who developed the original tests from the 1930s) and extended and standardised by his student Ralph Reitan . Every examinee receives the same comprehensive set of tests, which yields an overall Halstead Impairment Index : the proportion of the index tests that fall in the brain-damaged range, expressed from 0 to 1. An Impairment Index of 0.5 or more suggests cerebral impairment (the higher the index, the more tests are in the impaired range). Its core diagnostic subtests are: Subtest What it measures Localising value Category Test Abstract reasoning, concept formation, hypothesis testing and learning from feedback The most sensitive single index of general cerebral (especially frontal) dysfunction Tactual Performance Test (TPT) Blindfolded placement of blocks into a form board by touch; then a memory drawing. Measures tactile form perception, spatial memory and incidental learning Localisation, manual dexterity, somatosensory and spatial memory; compares the two hands Seashore Rhythm Test Judging whether pairs of rhythmic beats are same or different Sustained auditory attention and non-verbal auditory perception (right temporal) Speech Sounds Perception Test Matching a spoken nonsense syllable to one of four printed alternatives Auditory-verbal perception and attention (left temporal) Finger Tapping Test (Finger Oscillation) Maximum tapping speed of the index finger over timed trials, each hand Pure motor speed; comparing the two hands localises lateralised motor-strip damage Two further components are routinely administered alongside the core five and often appear as distractor options: the Trail Making Test (Parts A and B) , sensitive to processing speed, visual scanning and set-shifting (Part B), and the Reitan-Indiana Aphasia Screening Test plus a sensory-perceptual examination, which screen for language and lateralised sensory deficits. The HRNB is typically paired with a Wechsler scale and the MMPI for a full picture. There are also age-banded versions (the Reitan-Indiana battery for young children and an intermediate battery for older children), a fact the paper occasionally uses to test whether you know the HRNB is not a single adult-only instrument. How it is tested in the paper The examiner mines the HRNB in three reliable ways. First, the fixed-versus-flexible distinction: a stem will describe "the same comprehensive set of tests given to every patient" and ask you to name the battery type (fixed) or the battery (Halstead-Reitan). Second, subtest-to-function matching : which subtest measures abstract concept formation (Category Test), which compares the two hands (TPT and Finger Tapping), which screens left versus right temporal auditory function (Speech Sounds Perception versus Seashore Rhythm). Third, the summary score : the name (Halstead Impairment Index) and its meaning (proportion of tests in the impaired range, cut-off about 0.5). Holding those three angles covers almost every HRNB item. Administration, scoring and interpretation logic The battery is long (often 4 to 6 hours) precisely because it is fixed and comprehensive. Each subtest produces a score that is compared against cut-offs to decide whether it falls in the "normal" or "brain-damaged" range; the proportion in the impaired range becomes the Impairment Index. The genuine interpretive power, however, comes not from any single subtest but from the pattern across the battery. Four levels of inference are used: (1) the level of performance (how far below the cut-offs), (2) pathognomonic signs (specific deficits rarely seen without brain damage), (3) patterns and relationships among scores, and (4) right-versus-left comparisons of the two body sides. Worked example of the lateralisation logic. On the Finger Tapping Test the dominant hand normally taps about 10% faster than the non-dominant hand. Suppose a right-handed patient taps 50 per ten seconds with the right hand but 30 with the left: the left hand is markedly slower than expected (it should be the faster-of-the-two-adjusted value), pointing to right-hemisphere (contralateral) motor-strip damage. The same right-greater-than-left disproportion on the TPT (the left hand taking far longer to place the blocks by touch) corroborates a right-hemisphere lesion. One battery, read across the two hands, localises the side; the Category Test then tells you whether there is additional global or frontal abstraction failure. This cross-comparison of the two sides is exactly the reasoning the paper rewards. High-yield HRNB (Halstead, then Reitan) is a fixed battery yielding the Halstead Impairment Index (cut-off about 0.5 for impairment). Know the five core subtests and what each taps: Category Test (abstract reasoning, the most sensitive single sign of brain damage), Tactual Performance Test (tactile spatial memory and localisation, hand comparison), Seashore Rhythm (auditory attention, right temporal), Speech Sounds Perception (auditory-verbal perception, left temporal), Finger Tapping (motor speed, hand comparison for lateralisation). Lateralised deficits are read by comparing the two hands. Exam trap The Category Test , not the Finger Tapping Test, is the most sensitive single measure of general (especially frontal) cerebral dysfunction; Finger Tapping is the pure motor-speed and lateralisation task. The Halstead Impairment Index is a proportion of tests in the impaired range (about 0.5 cut-off), not an IQ. Do not call the HRNB "Lurian": it is empirical/actuarial and atheoretical, the opposite pole from the Luria-Nebraska battery. F. Luria-Nebraska Neuropsychological Battery (LNNB) The Luria-Nebraska Neuropsychological Battery (LNNB) was assembled by Charles Golden and colleagues (1980), who standardised and quantified the qualitative clinical methods of the Russian neuropsychologist Alexander Luria (drawing on the items Anne-Lise Christensen had organised from Luria's work). This is the central paradox the paper exploits: Luria himself worked flexibly , testing one hypothesis at a time and adapting the examination to the individual patient, whereas Golden converted his procedures into a fixed battery with a standard sequence and quantitative scoring. The LNNB therefore has Luria's theory and content but the Halstead-Reitan's fixed, actuarial form. The battery comprises roughly 269 items grouped into 11 clinical scales . Each item is scored 0 (normal), 1 (borderline) or 2 (impaired) , so qualitative neurological deficits that Luria would have judged by clinical eye are captured on a standardised quantitative scale. The 11 clinical scales are: Scale Name What it samples C1 Motor Functions Speed, coordination, construction and imitation of movements; the largest scale C2 Rhythm Acoustico-motor organisation; perceiving and reproducing rhythmic and pitch patterns C3 Tactile Functions Cutaneous, kinaesthetic and stereognostic (touch-based) perception C4 Visual Functions Visual and spatial perception, object recognition C5 Receptive Speech Comprehension of phonemes, words and grammatical structures C6 Expressive Speech Articulation, repetition and production of speech C7 Writing Spelling and the motor act of writing C8 Reading Letter, word and passage reading C9 Arithmetic Number recognition and calculation C10 Memory Verbal and non-verbal immediate memory and learning C11 Intellectual Processes Reasoning, concept formation and problem solving Beyond the 11 clinical scales the LNNB also yields summary scales (such as Pathognomonic, Left Hemisphere and Right Hemisphere), localisation scales (estimating the lobe and side of dysfunction), and factor scales . The Pathognomonic scale is worth knowing by name: it is made of items so rarely failed by intact people that elevation strongly signals genuine brain damage, and it is the closest LNNB analogue to a single "is there impairment?" index. Raw scores on each scale are converted to T-scores (mean 50, SD 10) and interpreted against a critical level cut-off that is corrected for the examinee's age and education ; scores above the critical level on a given scale (and the configuration of the localisation scales) point to the affected functional system and its likely cerebral region. The LNNB takes far less time than the HRNB (about 2 to 3 hours) and is more explicitly theory-driven, but critics argue that its rigid quantification loses some of Luria's flexible, hypothesis-testing genius (the very flexibility that made Luria's own method powerful). Luria's theory of functional systems To interpret the LNNB you need the idea it rests on. Luria argued that no single brain region "contains" a complex behaviour such as writing or reading; instead each behaviour is produced by a functional system , a chain of cooperating brain regions, each contributing one elementary component. Because of this, the same surface deficit (say, an inability to write) can arise from damage at several different links in the chain (a motor link, a spatial link, a phonemic link), and the clinician's job is to find which link has broken by comparing performance across tasks that share or differ in their components. This is why the LNNB scales are organised by function (Motor, Receptive Speech, Writing) rather than by anatomy, and why the qualitative pattern across scales, not any single score, carries the localising information. Luria called this systematic comparison "syndrome analysis," and Golden's battery is an attempt to standardise it. Exam trap Both Halstead-Reitan and Luria-Nebraska are fixed batteries , but the count and structure differ: LNNB has 11 clinical scales with 0/1/2 item scoring and is built on Alexander Luria's theory; HRNB has its five core subtests plus the Impairment Index and is atheoretical/empirical. Do not attribute the 11 scales to Halstead-Reitan, and do not call the HRNB "Lurian." Luria's own approach was a flexible qualitative method; the Nebraska version (Golden's) is what made it fixed and quantified. The builder of the LNNB is Golden , not Luria himself. G. The NIMHANS Neuropsychological Battery This is the most heavily examined neuropsychology topic for Indian entrances because it is the indigenous battery, standardised on the Indian population at the National Institute of Mental Health and Neurosciences (NIMHANS), Bangalore, and published in its modern form by Rao, Subbakrishna and Gopukumar (2004) . Conceptually it sits between the two great Western traditions you met just above: it is neither a wholly fixed battery in the Halstead-Reitan sense (the same rigid sequence for everyone) nor a wholly flexible Lurian hypothesis-testing exercise. Instead it is a flexible, domain-sampling profile battery : it surveys each major cognitive domain (attention, executive function, learning and memory, comprehension, visuoconstruction, and so on) using named, internationally recognised tests, and the clinician selects depth according to the referral question. Its purpose is to localise deficits to brain systems and to provide Indian norms stratified by age and education, so that a deficit is judged against what a comparable Indian examinee would achieve rather than against a Western standardisation sample. There is also a separate NIMHANS Neuropsychological Battery for Children (Kar and colleagues) for paediatric work. Work through the adult battery domain by domain; the examiner builds questions by asking which test sits in which domain and what its signature score means. Definition A neuropsychological battery is a structured set of tests designed to map the integrity of distinct cognitive functions (attention, memory, language, executive control, praxis) onto the brain systems that subserve them, so that a pattern of spared and impaired scores localises dysfunction. The NIMHANS battery is the indigenous, Indian-normed exemplar; its strength is culturally fair norms and domain coverage rather than a single global impairment number. 1. Mental Status Examination and Focal Signs The battery opens with a Mental Status Examination (orientation in time, place and person; level of consciousness; a gross cognitive screen) and a survey of focal signs : lateralised motor or sensory abnormalities, aphasias, apraxias, agnosias and other hard neurological signs that flag a specific lesion site before formal testing begins. This screening tier is a gate: it decides whether the detailed battery can be validly administered at all (a delirious or grossly aphasic patient cannot give interpretable scores) and it directs which domains deserve the closest scrutiny. A right-handed patient with a word-finding difficulty, for instance, steers the examiner toward the left-hemisphere language and verbal-memory tests. 2. Attention Attention is profiled with cancellation and vigilance tasks. The Colour Cancellation Test requires the examinee to strike out target coloured stimuli scattered among distractors across a page, indexing focused and sustained visual attention and visual scanning, and revealing unilateral spatial neglect if one side of the page is consistently missed (a localising sign of contralateral, usually right-parietal, damage). Digit vigilance tasks require cancelling a target digit embedded in rows of random digits within a time limit, scored for both time taken and errors, measuring sustained attention and psychomotor speed. The Triads Test and digit-span procedures add an auditory-verbal attention measure. The logic across the tier is that attention is the substrate on which all higher functions rest: a patient who fails attention tasks cannot have their memory or executive scores taken at face value, because an attentional bottleneck masquerades as a memory or reasoning deficit. 3. Executive functions This is the richest tier and the one most often tested, because executive (frontal) function is where Indian entrance papers concentrate their neuropsychology items. It uses a cluster of classic instruments, each tapping a dissociable component of frontal control: N-Back test : a continuous working-memory task in which the examinee indicates when the current stimulus matches the one presented N steps earlier (1-back, 2-back, and so on). It loads the central executive of working memory and is a relatively pure measure of updating (continuously refreshing the contents of mind); difficulty scales with N, and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex is the principal substrate. Wisconsin Card Sorting Test (WCST) : the gold-standard test of set-shifting and frontal flexibility, detailed below. Tower of London : a planning task in which coloured beads on pegs must be rearranged to match a goal configuration in the minimum number of moves; it measures forward planning, look-ahead and the inhibition of impulsive first moves, and is sensitive to dorsolateral prefrontal dysfunction. Scores include moves taken above the minimum and planning/initiation time. Stroop Colour-Word Test : detailed below; measures response inhibition, the suppression of a prepotent over-learned response. Verbal fluency (Controlled Oral Word Association and animal naming) : generating as many words as possible to a letter (phonemic fluency) or a category (semantic/category fluency) in one minute; phonemic fluency leans on left frontal systems, category fluency additionally taps temporal/semantic stores, and the dissociation between them is itself localising. The Wisconsin Card Sorting Test in detail In the WCST (Grant and Berg, 1948) the examinee sorts response cards under four stimulus cards. They must sort by an unstated rule (colour, form or number), are told only "right" or "wrong" after each placement, and must infer the rule from the feedback. After ten consecutive correct sorts the examiner silently switches the rule, and the examinee must detect the change and shift. The diagnostic scores are: Perseverative errors : continuing to sort by the old rule after it has changed (the signature frontal-lobe failure of cognitive flexibility). A high perseverative-error count is the hallmark sign of dorsolateral prefrontal dysfunction. Categories achieved : the number of rules (out of six) the examinee successfully completed; fewer categories indicates worse abstraction and set-shifting. Failure to maintain set : breaking off a correct run before completing a category (five or more correct then an error), indicating attentional lapse or distractibility. Worked example: a patient with a frontal-lobe tumour identifies the colour rule quickly, achieves the first category, but when the rule silently switches to form, they keep sorting by colour for fifteen further trials despite every card being marked "wrong." That string of old-rule responses is a run of perseverative errors; combined with only two categories achieved, the profile localises to dorsolateral prefrontal cortex even though the patient's IQ and memory may be normal. Definition A perseverative error on the WCST is a response that persists with a previously correct sorting principle after the rule has changed. It is the cardinal index of frontal (dorsolateral prefrontal) lobe dysfunction and of impaired cognitive set-shifting. The Stroop Colour-Word Test in detail The Stroop effect (J. R. Stroop, 1935) exploits the conflict between reading, an automatic over-learned process, and colour-naming, a more effortful one. The examinee is shown colour words printed in incongruent ink (the word "RED" printed in blue ink) and must name the ink colour while suppressing the urge to read the word. The slowing on the incongruent condition relative to the baseline colour-naming condition is the interference (Stroop) score , and it measures response inhibition and the ability to override a prepotent response, mediated by the anterior cingulate and prefrontal cortex. Contrast it sharply with its near-neighbour the WCST: the Stroop tests inhibition of a competing automatic response in the moment, whereas the WCST tests flexibility, the shifting of a whole mental set after feedback. Both are "frontal," but they are not interchangeable. 4. Memory Memory is the domain with the most named instruments, so learn each one and what dissociation it buys you. The Rey Auditory Verbal Learning Test (RAVLT) presents a 15-word list (List A) read aloud over five learning trials; then a distractor 15-word list (List B) is presented once; then immediate recall of List A is tested again, a delayed recall follows after 20 to 30 minutes, and finally a recognition trial requires picking List A words out of a longer list. The components index distinct processes: Immediate recall and the learning curve (trials 1 to 5) : the rise across trials shows the rate and capacity of verbal learning; a flat curve indicates poor acquisition. Proactive interference : the degree to which already-learned List A intrudes on the learning of List B (old learning disrupting new). Retroactive interference : the drop in List A recall after List B has been interposed (new learning disrupting old); measured as the post-interference List A trial against trial 5. Delayed recall : words retained after the 20 to 30 minute delay, indexing consolidation and storage. Recognition : identifying List A words among distractors. The crucial differential: if delayed recall is poor but recognition is preserved, the deficit is one of retrieval (a sub-cortical or frontal pattern, as in Parkinson's disease or depression); if recognition is also poor, the deficit is one of encoding or storage (an amnestic, medial-temporal pattern, as in Alzheimer's disease). Memory aid Proactive interference = P ast learning P ushes forward onto new material (List A hurts List B). Retroactive interference = new material R eaches back to hurt old (List B hurts List A recall). "Recall poor but recognition spared = retrieval problem; both poor = storage problem." Other memory instruments in the NIMHANS battery: Visual Retention tests (such as the Benton Visual Retention Test): a design is shown briefly then reproduced from memory, indexing visual (non-verbal) immediate memory and visuo-constructional ability, the visual analogue of the RAVLT. The Complex Figure Test (Rey-Osterrieth) serves a similar role: the examinee first copies a complex figure (testing visuoconstruction and planning) and then reproduces it from memory after a delay (testing non-verbal memory), so a single figure dissociates construction from recall. Wechsler Memory Scale (WMS) : the standard omnibus memory battery, indexing immediate and delayed memory across auditory and visual modalities (logical memory paragraphs, paired associates, visual reproduction, and so on); Indian adaptations are incorporated into the NIMHANS battery. PGI Memory Scale (Postgraduate Institute Memory Scale, Pershad and Wig, 1977) : the indigenous Indian memory battery, comprising ten subtests that sample the major dissociable memory functions: remote memory, recent memory, mental balance, attention and concentration, delayed recall, immediate recall, verbal retention for similar pairs, verbal retention for dissimilar pairs, visual retention, and recognition . Its strength is that it dissociates remote from recent memory and separates attention-concentration from pure recall, so the profile localises which memory system has failed. 5. Comprehension, fluency and frontal-executive language; visuospatial and construction Beyond the headline tiers, the battery samples verbal comprehension and category formation (for example, similarities and proverb interpretation, which probe abstraction and concept formation), visuospatial and constructional ability (block design analogues and figure copying, sensitive to right-parietal function), and motor and praxis functions. The integrative principle is the same throughout: no single score diagnoses; the clinician reads the pattern across domains, comparing each score against age-and-education-matched Indian norms, and asks which constellation of spared and impaired functions points to which brain system. High-yield The NIMHANS battery (Rao, Subbakrishna & Gopukumar, 2004) is the Indian-normed, flexible domain-sampling battery. Domains and signature tests: Attention (Colour Cancellation, digit vigilance); Executive (N-Back, WCST with perseverative errors / categories achieved / failure to maintain set , Tower of London, Stroop interference, verbal fluency); Memory (RAVLT with immediate / interference / delayed / recognition; Visual Retention; Complex Figure; WMS; PGI Memory Scale). The RAVLT recall-versus-recognition dissociation (retrieval vs storage deficit) is a perennial item. Exam trap Match the test to its domain: WCST and Tower of London are executive (frontal) tests, not memory tests ; RAVLT is a verbal memory test, not an attention test ; the Stroop measures inhibition, not memory . The PGI Memory Scale is the Indian memory scale (Pershad and Wig); do not confuse it with the Wechsler Memory Scale. Perseverative errors belong to the WCST, not the Stroop. And do not call the NIMHANS battery a "fixed" battery like Halstead-Reitan: it is a flexible, domain-sampling battery with Indian norms. H. Objective Personality: MMPI-2 (and MMPI-2-RF) We now cross into personality assessment. The objective tradition uses fixed-item, fixed-scored self-report inventories (true/false or Likert), so that scoring is independent of the clinician's interpretation; this is the methodological opposite of the projective tradition (Rorschach, TAT) you will meet next, where an ambiguous stimulus is interpreted qualitatively. The dominant objective instrument is the Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory, second edition (MMPI-2) , with 567 true/false items , restandardised in 1989 from the 1943 original. Its founding genius ( Starke Hathaway and J. Charnley McKinley, 1943 ) was empirical criterion keying : an item was retained on a scale not because it sounded relevant but because it statistically discriminated a known clinical criterion group (say, diagnosed depressives at the University of Minnesota Hospitals) from the normal "Minnesota normals." This empirical, contrasted-groups method is what makes the MMPI relatively resistant to faking by content alone, and it is why some scale items look unrelated to the construct they measure. Definition Empirical criterion keying is a test-construction method in which items are selected for a scale solely on the basis that they empirically distinguish a criterion (diagnosed) group from a normal comparison group, irrespective of the items' face content. Its opposite is the rational/content method, where items are written to look relevant to the construct. Criterion keying is the MMPI's signature and the reason its scales are labelled by number rather than by their (often counter-intuitive) item content. Administration, scoring and the T-score metric The MMPI-2 is for adults (18 and over; the adolescent form is the MMPI-A); a sixth-grade reading level is required. Raw scores on each scale are converted to uniform T-scores with a mean of 50 and a standard deviation of 10, derived from the restandardisation sample, so that a person's elevation is read directly against the normal population. The conventional clinical cut-off is a T-score of 65 or above (this replaced the older MMPI-1 cut-off of 70); a score at or above 65 places the examinee beyond roughly the 92nd percentile and is treated as clinically significant. Profiles are interpreted only after the validity scales have shown the protocol is interpretable. Validity indicators (the lie-detectors) The MMPI-2's most distinctive feature is its battery of validity scales, which detect how the person approached the test before any clinical scale is interpreted. Learn each, because the examiner tests "which scale catches which response style." Scale Name What it detects L Lie scale Naive, unsophisticated attempts to present oneself in an unrealistically favourable, virtuous light (denying common human faults) F Infrequency scale Endorsement of rare, atypical items (items answered in the keyed direction by fewer than 10% of normals); elevated by random responding, malingering ("faking bad"), or genuine severe pathology K Defensiveness (Correction) scale Subtle, sophisticated profile distortion / guardedness; also added as a statistical correction (the "K-correction") to certain clinical scales Fb Back F (Back-page Infrequency) Infrequent responding in the second half of the booklet; catches fatigue or a shift in response set partway through VRIN Variable Response Inconsistency Inconsistent answering to item pairs of similar content (random or careless responding) TRIN True Response Inconsistency A fixed bias toward answering "true" (acquiescence) or "false" (nay-saying) regardless of content Fp Psychiatric Infrequency Items rarely endorsed even by genuine psychiatric inpatients; isolates feigned/exaggerated pathology from real severe illness S Superlative Self-Presentation Claiming superlative adjustment and virtue; another "fake good" / positive-impression-management indicator Interpretive logic: the validity scales are read first, and certain configurations are themselves diagnostic. The classic "F minus K" (Gough dissimulation) index compares the raw F and K scores: a high F with a low K (F much greater than K) suggests faking bad or a cry for help, whereas a low F with a high K (K much greater than F) suggests faking good or defensiveness.
