The intellectual roots lie in general systems theory and cybernetics (circular causality, feedback loops, homeostasis), which replace the linear "A causes B" of individual models with circular, mutually maintaining patterns. Minuchin: Structural Family Therapy Salvador Minuchin developed Structural Family Therapy (out of his work with disadvantaged families and psychosomatic conditions), which maps the family's invisible structure : its subsystems (spousal, parental, sibling), its hierarchy (who holds executive authority), and above all its boundaries , the rules governing who participates and how. Boundaries lie on a continuum: Rigid boundaries produce a disengaged family: members are isolated, autonomous to a fault, and offer little support or warmth. Diffuse boundaries produce an enmeshed family: members are over-involved, over-reactive, and lack individual autonomy; one member's upset instantly engulfs the rest. Clear boundaries (the healthy middle) allow both belonging and autonomy. Techniques restructure these patterns in the room: joining (the therapist accommodates to the family's style to gain entry), enactment (having the family play out a problematic interaction live so the therapist can observe and alter it on the spot), boundary making (strengthening or loosening boundaries, for example seating to block an over-involved parent from a child), unbalancing (temporarily siding with one member to shift a stuck hierarchy), and reframing (giving a behaviour a new, often more benign or systemic meaning so the family can respond differently). Worked example. A family presents with a defiant teenage daughter. Minuchin observes that the mother and daughter form an over-close, enmeshed dyad (diffuse boundary), while the father is peripheral and disengaged (rigid boundary), so there is no functioning parental subsystem with shared authority. Through enactment the therapist has the parents jointly set a rule in the session, physically seats the father into the discussion, and makes a boundary between the parental and sibling subsystems, restructuring the hierarchy so the parents lead together and the daughter is released from her over-involved alliance with the mother. Memory aid Pair them: rigid boundaries to disengaged (a wall between members, everyone too far apart); diffuse boundaries to enmeshed (no walls, everyone tangled together). Salvador Minuchin's flag words are boundaries, subsystems, and enactment. Bowen: Family Systems Theory Murray Bowen built a multigenerational systems theory. Its keystone is differentiation of self : the capacity to separate one's intellectual from one's emotional functioning, and to maintain a clear sense of self ("I-position") while staying connected to the family emotional system. Poorly differentiated people fuse with others and are swept along by group emotion; well-differentiated people can stay calm and think clearly under relational pressure. Multigenerational transmission describes how levels of differentiation are passed down the generations, so chronic anxiety and dysfunction accumulate across a family tree (charted on a genogram ). Triangulation is the move by which a tense two-person relationship pulls in a third party (often a child) to dilute the anxiety, the basic building block of family emotional process. Other Bowen concepts include the nuclear family emotional process , emotional cut-off , and the family projection process . Worked example. An adolescent presents with school refusal. The Bowenian therapist notices that whenever the parents' marital tension rises, the mother becomes intensely focused on the child's symptoms and the father withdraws: a classic triangle in which the child's symptom stabilises the marriage by deflecting the couple's anxiety. Therapy works to detriangulate the child and raise the parents' differentiation so they can address their conflict directly rather than routing it through the symptom-bearer. A genogram across three generations reveals the same anxious over-focus passed from the maternal grandmother, the multigenerational transmission at work. Exam trap Minuchin versus Bowen. Minuchin = structural , boundaries (rigid/disengaged vs diffuse/enmeshed), subsystems, enactment. Bowen = differentiation of self , multigenerational transmission, triangulation, genogram. The signature phrase "differentiation of self" is always Bowen; "enmeshed/disengaged boundaries" is always Minuchin. Other strategic and systemic schools The syllabus's broader systemic field also names schools the paper can quote. Jay Haley's strategic therapy (with roots in Milton Erickson) uses directives and paradoxical prescription , including prescribing the symptom (instructing the family to perform the very behaviour they want gone, exposing its function). The Milan systemic school (Selvini Palazzoli and colleagues) introduced circular questioning (asking each member about the relationship between two others to reveal the system's logic), hypothesising , neutrality , and positive connotation (reframing the symptom as serving the family's cohesion). These are worth a line because items occasionally ask "which school uses circular questioning?" (Milan) or "prescribing the symptom?" (strategic/Haley). Yalom: group psychotherapy Irvin Yalom identified eleven therapeutic factors that produce change in group therapy: instillation of hope, universality (realising one is not alone in one's problems), imparting of information, altruism (gaining from helping others), the corrective recapitulation of the primary family group, development of socialising techniques, imitative behaviour, interpersonal learning, group cohesiveness, catharsis, and existential factors. Cohesiveness is to group therapy what the therapeutic relationship is to individual therapy, the precondition for the rest. The group also moves through developmental stages as cohesion builds (an initial orientation/dependency stage, a conflict/storming stage, and a mature cohesive working stage), echoing Tuckman's forming-storming-norming-performing sequence. High-yield Irvin Yalom's eleven group therapeutic factors are commonly tested by example: "realising other members share your problem" = universality ; "benefiting by helping others" = altruism ; emotional release = catharsis ; the group re-enacting one's original family = corrective recapitulation of the primary family group . Cohesiveness is the group analogue of the therapeutic alliance. G. Clinical Ethics and Legislative Frameworks This final block is largely recall of statute and code, and it is reliably tested because the answers are unambiguous: a section number, a percentage, a case name. Master the three Indian Acts (MHCA 2017, RPwD 2016, and the RCI Act that licenses you to practise), the core professional principles, and the landmark duty-to-warn case. Frame the professional principles around the four classical biomedical ethics: autonomy (respecting the client's self-determination), beneficence (acting for their good), non-maleficence (above all, do no harm), and justice (fairness of access and treatment). The Mental Healthcare Act (MHCA), 2017 The Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 (in force from 2018) replaced the Mental Health Act of 1987 and reframed mental healthcare around the rights and autonomy of the person with mental illness, in line with India's ratification of the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. It also guarantees a right to access mental healthcare from services run or funded by the government. Its tested provisions: Advance Directive : a person may make a written directive, in advance, stating how they wish to be treated or not treated for a mental illness and who their representative will be, to take effect during a future crisis when they may lack capacity. Nominated Representative (NR) : every person has the right to appoint a representative to take decisions on their behalf and safeguard their interests during treatment. Authorities and Boards : the Act establishes a Central Mental Health Authority and State Mental Health Authorities (to register and regulate establishments and professionals), and Mental Health Review Boards (MHRBs) to review admissions, advance directives, and complaints, protecting patient rights. Capacity-based framework : treatment decisions turn on the person's capacity to make mental-healthcare decisions, and admission categories distinguish independent (voluntary) admission from supported admission with safeguards. Section 115: presumption of severe stress. Any person who attempts suicide is presumed, unless proved otherwise, to be under severe stress , and is not to be tried or punished. This effectively decriminalises attempted suicide (overriding Section 309 of the Indian Penal Code) and obliges the appropriate government to provide care, treatment, and rehabilitation to reduce the risk of recurrence. Prohibitions : the Act bans unmodified ECT (electroconvulsive therapy without muscle relaxants and anaesthesia), bans ECT for minors except with Board permission, prohibits sterilisation of persons with mental illness as a treatment, and bans chaining and seclusion as routine practice. High-yield MHCA 2017, Section 115 : presumption of severe stress in attempted suicide, decriminalising the act and mandating state-sponsored rehabilitation. This single section is the most heavily tested fact in the entire ethics block. Also remember: advance directive, nominated representative, Mental Health Review Boards, the capacity-based framework, and the ban on unmodified ECT and on sterilisation. It replaced the 1987 Act. The Rights of Persons with Disabilities (RPwD) Act, 2016 The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 (in force 2017) replaced the Persons with Disabilities Act of 1995 and expanded the list of recognised disabilities from 7 to 21 . Crucially for clinical psychology, it brought mental illness , autism spectrum disorder , specific learning disabilities , intellectual disability , and chronic neurological conditions under statutory disability classification. It defines a "person with benchmark disability" as someone with not less than 40% of a specified disability as certified by a competent (medical) authority; benchmark-disability status unlocks reservations in higher education and government employment, and other statutory benefits and protections. Exam trap The 40% threshold and the term "benchmark disability" belong to the RPwD Act 2016 , not the MHCA. The MHCA 2017 deals with treatment rights and capacity (advance directives, NR, Section 115); the RPwD Act deals with disability status, the expanded list of 21 conditions, and the 40% benchmark. Items deliberately attach the 40% figure to the wrong Act, or quote "7 disabilities" (the old 1995 Act) instead of 21. The Rehabilitation Council of India (RCI) Act, 1992 The Rehabilitation Council of India Act, 1992 created the statutory body that regulates the training and registration of rehabilitation professionals , including clinical psychologists, and maintains the Central Rehabilitation Register . This is the Act under which the entrance you are sitting is regulated: it is an offence to practise as a clinical psychologist or to use the title without RCI registration, and the RCI prescribes the recognised qualifications (the M.Phil and the newer RCI-recognised M.A. routes). Knowing that the RCI licenses clinical psychologists (whereas the MHCA governs care and the RPwD governs disability status ) is the discriminating point. Professional ethical guidelines The RCI code and the APA ethical principles converge on a common core, organised under the four classical principles named above: Informed consent : the client must be given, in understandable terms, the nature, purpose, risks, benefits, alternatives, and limits of the intervention and must agree voluntarily, with special care for children, persons lacking capacity, and diverse populations (assent is sought from those who cannot legally consent). Confidentiality and its exceptions : information is private, but confidentiality is limited and must be broken when there is an immediate risk of serious harm to self or others, in cases of child abuse, or under a valid court order. Knowing these three exceptions verbatim is the tested point. The Duty to Warn / Duty to Protect : established by Tarasoff v. Regents of the University of California (California Supreme Court, 1976). When a client makes a credible threat against an identifiable victim, the therapist's duty of confidentiality yields to a duty to protect the third party (by warning the victim, notifying police, or other reasonable steps). The court's famous formulation: "the protective privilege ends where the public peril begins." Dual (multiple) relationships : a therapist must avoid simultaneous or sequential roles (social, business, sexual, familial) that could impair objectivity or exploit the client; boundaries must be maintained, and sexual relationships with current clients are absolutely prohibited. Cultural competence : the duty to understand and adapt to the client's cultural, linguistic, and social context rather than imposing the therapist's norms. Tele-therapy ethics : digital provision adds duties around data security and privacy, verifying client identity and location, managing emergencies at a distance, obtaining consent specific to the remote modality, and confirming licensure across jurisdictions. High-yield The Duty to Warn derives from the Tarasoff case (1976). If a stem describes a client threatening an identifiable third party and asks what overrides confidentiality, the answer is the Tarasoff duty to warn/protect. Pair it with the three standard confidentiality exceptions: risk of harm to self or others, child abuse, and a valid court order . The four guiding principles are autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, and justice. Definition Dual relationship : any additional relationship with a client (social, financial, sexual, familial) beyond the professional one, prohibited where it risks impaired judgement or exploitation. Benchmark disability : not less than 40% impairment, certified under the RPwD Act 2016. Informed consent : voluntary agreement to treatment after disclosure of its nature, purpose, risks, benefits, alternatives, and limits, in terms the client understands. 6 · Foundational Psychology, Lifespan Development & Social Dynamics This section teaches the engine room of general psychology: how the mind takes in information (memory and perception), how it changes through experience (learning), how it matures across a lifetime (development), how people behave in groups (social psychology), and how stable individual differences are described (personality). For an RCI clinical-psychology entrance, this is the densest single source of factual one-mark questions: examiners love named theorists, exact stage labels and ages, the four reinforcement schedules, attachment phenotypes, and the classic social-psychology studies. The papers reliably do three things with this material: they ask you to attach a phenomenon to its theorist and year, they ask you to recall an exact number or stage label verbatim, and they set a near-neighbour as the distractor (proactive versus retroactive interference, sensitivity versus bias, assimilation versus accommodation, conformity versus obedience, self-efficacy versus locus of control). We build each concept from the floor up, name the theorist and date, give the mechanism and a worked example, state how it surfaces in the paper, then flag the exact distractor the examiner will use against you. Read each subsection once for the story and again for the numbers and names, because the numbers and names are what is actually marked. A. Memory: Structural Architectures and Forgetting Memory is the set of processes by which the nervous system encodes information (turns experience into a storable code), stores it (retains it over time), and retrieves it (brings it back into awareness). The dominant teaching model of the twentieth century treated memory not as one thing but as a sequence of separate stores, each with its own capacity, code, and duration; later models replaced the passive stores with active processing systems. You must hold both pictures, because the paper tests the contrast between them. Definition Encoding is converting a stimulus into a memory code (acoustic, visual, or semantic); storage is the maintenance of that code over time; retrieval is bringing it back into consciousness. Forgetting can be a failure at any of the three, and distinguishing an encoding failure from a retrieval failure is itself a tested distinction. The Atkinson-Shiffrin Multi-Store Model (1968) Richard Atkinson and Richard Shiffrin proposed that information flows through three structurally distinct stores in series. This is also called the modal model because it became the standard (modal) account. Information enters the sensory register, is transferred by attention to the short-term store, and is transferred by rehearsal to the long-term store; each transfer is a potential point of loss. Sensory memory (sensory register): a very brief, high-capacity, modality-specific buffer that holds a raw, literal copy of incoming sensory input for a fraction of a second. It is pre-attentive: everything that hits the senses is registered, but it decays almost instantly unless attention selects it. Sensory memory is modality-specific, so it has separate sub-stores. Iconic memory is the visual store (the word comes from icon , image); George Sperling's partial-report experiments (1960) showed iconic memory holds roughly nine to twelve items but decays within about 0.25 to 0.5 seconds. Echoic memory is the auditory store (the word comes from echo ); it lasts longer, around 2 to 4 seconds, which is why you can still "hear" the end of a sentence you were not attending to. Short-term store (STS): the contents of current awareness. Capacity is famously about seven plus or minus two items (George Miller's "magical number seven", 1956), better described in chunks than raw items. Duration without rehearsal is roughly 15 to 30 seconds. The code is largely acoustic (we tend to confuse similar-sounding items). Maintenance rehearsal (repeating) keeps items in the STS; elaborative rehearsal transfers them onward. Long-term store (LTS): effectively unlimited in capacity and potentially permanent in duration. The code is predominantly semantic (by meaning). Information must pass through the STS to reach the LTS in this model. Sperling's partial-report procedure is the worked example you should be able to reproduce. He flashed a 3-by-4 grid of letters for 50 milliseconds. In whole report , participants could name only about four or five letters (the rest had faded before they could be read out). In partial report , a tone after the display told the participant which row to report; they could report almost any cued row in full, proving that nearly all twelve letters had been briefly available in iconic memory and had decayed during the readout. The delay between display and tone, plotted against accuracy, traces the decay of iconic memory directly. Store Capacity Duration Dominant code Sensory (iconic) 9 to 12 items 0.25 to 0.5 s Visual, literal Sensory (echoic) Large 2 to 4 s Auditory, literal Short-term store 7 plus or minus 2 15 to 30 s Acoustic Long-term store Unlimited Lifelong (potentially) Semantic High-yield Iconic = visual and very brief (about a quarter second); echoic = auditory and longer (a few seconds). The short-term store holds seven plus or minus two items for 15 to 30 seconds. The serial-position curve (better recall of the first items, the primacy effect, reflecting LTS, and of the last items, the recency effect, reflecting STS) is the standard supporting evidence for the multi-store model. These exact numbers are tested verbatim. Exam trap Do not swap iconic and echoic. Iconic sounds like "icon = picture" (visual); echoic sounds like "echo = sound" (auditory). Examiners reverse the durations too: iconic is the shorter store, echoic the longer one. A second trap: a delayed distractor task abolishes the recency effect (it empties the STS) while leaving primacy intact, which is the killer evidence that the last and first items come from different stores. The Baddeley and Hitch Working Memory Model (1974) Alan Baddeley and Graham Hitch argued the unitary "short-term store" was too simple to explain how we can hold something in mind while manipulating it. They replaced the passive STS with an active, multi-component working memory system: a workspace for temporarily holding and processing information. The clinching evidence is the dual-task logic: two tasks that draw on the same subsystem interfere with each other, while two tasks that draw on different subsystems can be done together without cost, proving the subsystems are separate. Central executive: the attentional control system. It is not a store; it allocates attention, switches between tasks, suppresses irrelevant information, and coordinates the subsystems. It is modality-free and has limited capacity. Phonological loop: handles speech-based (acoustic) information. It has two parts: a phonological store (the "inner ear", holding sound traces for about 2 seconds) and an articulatory rehearsal process (the "inner voice", refreshing the trace by sub-vocal repetition). This is the component you use to hold a phone number by saying it to yourself. Its existence is shown by the word-length effect (lists of short words are recalled better than lists of long words, because long words take longer to rehearse) and by articulatory suppression (repeating "the the the" out loud blocks rehearsal and wipes out the word-length effect). Visuospatial sketchpad: the "inner eye", handling visual and spatial information (the appearance of objects and their locations). You use it to picture a route or rotate a shape mentally. Baddeley split it into a visual cache (form and colour) and an inner scribe (spatial and movement). Episodic buffer: added by Baddeley in 2000 to fix a gap in the original model. It is a limited-capacity, temporary store that integrates information from the phonological loop, the visuospatial sketchpad, and long-term memory into a single multimodal, coherent episode (a "scene"). It binds what something looks like, sounds like, and means into one representation and provides an interface between working memory and long-term memory. Definition Working memory is the active system that simultaneously holds and manipulates information in the service of a current task. The phrase "while manipulating" is what separates it from Atkinson-Shiffrin's passive short-term store: a mental-arithmetic problem (hold the numbers and operate on them) cannot be explained by a single passive buffer. High-yield The four components: central executive (boss, attention), phonological loop (sound, inner voice), visuospatial sketchpad (vision and space, inner eye), and episodic buffer (the multimodal integrator, added in 2000). The episodic buffer is the most-tested "new" piece: it binds the other stores plus long-term memory into one episode. Memory aid "Central Executive Posts Visuals and Episodes": Central executive, Phonological loop, Visuospatial sketchpad, Episodic buffer. Phonological = phone (you rehearse a phone number aloud). Craik and Lockhart's Levels of Processing (1972) Fergus Craik and Robert Lockhart offered a rival to the structural stores: instead of asking which box a memory sits in, they argued that retention depends on how deeply the item is processed at encoding. Shallow (structural) processing attends to physical form (is the word in capitals?); intermediate (phonemic) processing attends to sound (does it rhyme with "cat"?); deep (semantic) processing attends to meaning (does it fit the sentence "the ___ ran away"?). Deeper, more semantic, more elaborate processing yields stronger, longer-lasting memories, regardless of how long the item was "held". This is a process account, not a store account, and the paper contrasts the two directly. Exam trap Levels of processing (Fergus Craik and Robert Lockhart) says depth of encoding determines retention; the multi-store model (Atkinson-Shiffrin) says transfer between stores determines retention. If a stem stresses "semantic versus shallow" or "depth of processing", the answer is Craik and Lockhart, not Atkinson-Shiffrin. Do not attribute the levels-of-processing idea to Alan Baddeley. Tulving's Classification of Long-Term Memory Endel Tulving subdivided long-term memory by what kind of content is stored and what kind of awareness accompanies retrieval. The top split is declarative versus non-declarative. Declarative (explicit) memory can be consciously brought to mind and "declared" in words. It divides into: Episodic memory: memory for personally experienced events tied to a specific time and place ("what I ate at my last birthday"). Tulving linked it to autonoetic awareness (self-knowing): you mentally travel back and re-experience the event as having happened to you. Semantic memory: general world knowledge and facts, detached from when you learnt them ("Delhi is the capital of India"). It involves noetic awareness (knowing): you know the fact without re-living its acquisition. Non-declarative (implicit) memory cannot be verbalised and is expressed through performance rather than recollection. The core example is procedural memory : motor and cognitive skills (riding a bicycle, typing). Tulving linked it to anoetic awareness (non-knowing): the skill runs off without any conscious recollection of having learnt it. Other non-declarative forms include priming, classical conditioning, and habituation. How it is tested: the paper anchors this taxonomy to amnesic patient H.M. (Henry Molaison), whose bilateral medial-temporal-lobe resection (including the hippocampus) left him with a dense anterograde amnesia for new declarative facts and events, yet he could still learn new motor skills (mirror-drawing improved across days) while denying he had ever practised. This double dissociation, declarative impaired and procedural spared, is the classic evidence that these are separate memory systems. Exam trap Match the three awarenesses to the three memory types: autonoetic to episodic (re-experiencing the self in an event), noetic to semantic (knowing a fact), anoetic to procedural (no conscious knowing, just doing). The paper loves to pair "semantic" with "autonoetic" as a wrong option. Autonoetic belongs to episodic . A second trap: H.M.'s spared learning is procedural (non-declarative), so "H.M. could not learn anything new" is false. Forgetting Mechanics Forgetting is the failure to retrieve information that was once available. Several mechanisms are distinguished, and the paper sets them against one another. The Ebbinghaus forgetting curve: Hermann Ebbinghaus (1885), using himself as the only participant and learning lists of nonsense syllables, plotted retention over time and found memory drops sharply at first and then levels off . Most forgetting happens within the first hour to day; the residue decays slowly. He also discovered savings (relearning is faster than first learning) and the value of spaced over massed practice (the spacing effect). Proactive interference: old learning disrupts the retention of new material. Pro- means forward: previously stored information moves forward in time to block what comes next. Example: after years of an old phone number, you keep retrieving it instead of your new one. Retroactive interference: new learning disrupts the retention of old material. Retro- means backward: new information reaches back and overwrites the earlier code. Example: learning a new password makes you forget the previous one. The Zeigarnik effect: Bluma Zeigarnik (1927, a student of Kurt Lewin) found that interrupted or incomplete tasks are remembered better than completed ones , because an unfinished task maintains a state of tension (a "quasi-need") that keeps it active in memory. This is why a waiter remembers unpaid orders but forgets them once settled. Cue-dependent and decay accounts: Tulving's encoding specificity principle holds that retrieval succeeds when retrieval cues match the cues present at encoding, which is why context-dependent forgetting occurs (you forget in a different room or mood from the one in which you learnt). Decay theory, by contrast, attributes forgetting to the passive fading of a trace over time. Memory aid For interference, anchor on the direction of the prefix. Pro active = the p ast (old) interferes; retro active = the r ecent (new) interferes by reaching back. Old-blocks-new is proactive; new-blocks-old is retroactive. Exam trap The single most-reversed pair in the whole memory unit is proactive versus retroactive interference. If the question stem says "old learning hampers new learning" the answer is proactive ; if "new learning hampers old learning" the answer is retroactive . Zeigarnik is incomplete tasks remembered better , not worse. Do not confuse interference (competition from other material) with decay (passive fading over time). B. Learning: Conditioning and Cognitive Models Learning is a relatively permanent change in behaviour or knowledge that results from experience, distinguished from temporary changes (fatigue, drugs) and from maturation. Two associative paradigms (classical and operant) plus a cognitive tradition dominate the syllabus, and the paper tests both the vocabulary and the contrast between them. Definition Classical conditioning teaches an association between two stimuli and acts on a reflexive, involuntary response (salivation, fear). Operant conditioning teaches an association between a behaviour and its consequence and acts on voluntary, emitted behaviour. The cleanest discriminator: in classical conditioning the response is elicited before the outcome; in operant conditioning the behaviour is emitted to produce the outcome. Classical Conditioning: Pavlov and Watson Ivan Pavlov , a Russian physiologist studying digestion, discovered that a neutral stimulus, repeatedly paired with one that automatically triggers a reflex, comes itself to trigger that reflex. The vocabulary is fixed and tested: Unconditioned stimulus (UCS): automatically elicits a response (food). Unconditioned response (UCR): the automatic, unlearned reaction (salivation to food). Conditioned stimulus (CS): an originally neutral stimulus (a bell) that, after pairing with the UCS, comes to elicit a response. Conditioned response (CR): the learnt reaction to the CS (salivation to the bell). John B. Watson , the founder of American behaviourism, extended classical conditioning to emotion. In the "Little Albert" study (1920, with Rosalie Rayner), an infant was conditioned to fear a white rat (CS) by pairing it with a loud noise (UCS). The fear (CR) then generalised to other furry white objects, showing emotional responses are learnt. The clinical bridge is direct: this is the prototype for the conditioning model of phobias, and systematic desensitisation is its therapeutic reversal (extinction plus counter-conditioning). Key classical-conditioning phenomena: Acquisition: the build-up of the CR as CS and UCS are paired; strongest when the CS slightly precedes the UCS (forward conditioning). Extinction: presenting the CS repeatedly without the UCS weakens and eventually eliminates the CR. Spontaneous recovery: after extinction and a rest period, the CR reappears when the CS is presented again, showing extinction suppresses rather than erases the association. Stimulus generalisation: stimuli similar to the CS also evoke the CR (Albert fearing a rabbit). Stimulus discrimination: learning to respond only to the specific CS and not to similar stimuli. Higher-order (second-order) conditioning: a well-established CS is used to condition a new neutral stimulus, even though that new stimulus is never paired with the original UCS. Exam trap Spontaneous recovery is the favourite distractor: after extinction the CR is suppressed, not erased , so it returns after a rest. If the stem says the response "came back after a pause with no further training", the answer is spontaneous recovery, not re-acquisition. Watson, not Ivan Pavlov, did Little Albert; Pavlov is the dogs. The Rescorla-Wagner Model Robert Rescorla and Allan Wagner (1972) formalised classical conditioning mathematically. The crucial insight: conditioning depends not on simple pairing but on surprise . A UCS only drives learning to the extent it is unpredicted . The change in associative strength of a cue on a given trial is: Delta V A = alpha A × beta × (lambda − V Total ) Reading the terms: Delta V A is the change in associative strength of cue A on this trial. alpha (the salience of the CS) and beta (the learning rate set by the UCS) are learning-rate parameters between 0 and 1. lambda (the asymptote) is the maximum associative strength the UCS can support: how much learning is "possible" given this outcome. V Total is the summed associative strength already held by all cues present on the trial: how much is "already predicted". The bracket (lambda − V Total ) is the prediction error or surprise. When the outcome is fully predicted, lambda equals V Total , the bracket is zero, and no learning occurs. Large surprise drives large learning. This single equation explains several phenomena that simple-pairing accounts cannot: Blocking (Leon Kamin): if cue A already fully predicts the UCS (V Total near lambda), then adding a new cue B in compound (AB) leaves nothing to learn (bracket near zero), so B acquires little or no associative strength. The prior learning "blocks" learning about B. This is the model's flagship prediction. Overshadowing: when two cues of unequal salience are conditioned together, the more salient cue (higher alpha) grabs most of the limited associative strength, "overshadowing" the weaker cue. Uncorrelated contingencies: if a CS does not reliably predict the UCS (the UCS is just as likely without it), no net associative strength accrues, because gains on paired trials are cancelled by losses (extinction) on unpaired trials. High-yield Rescorla-Wagner says learning is driven by prediction error / surprise , captured by the term (lambda minus V Total ). Its signature explanation is blocking : a stimulus that adds no new predictive information is not learnt about. When the bracket is zero (outcome fully predicted), Delta V is zero (no learning). The Garcia Effect (Conditioned Taste Aversion) John Garcia showed that rats which became nauseous hours after drinking a flavoured solution developed a strong aversion to that taste , even though the illness was delayed by hours and was caused independently (by radiation or a drug). This broke two classical assumptions: Equipotentiality (the behaviourist claim that any CS can be associated equally easily with any UCS) is false: taste readily associates with nausea, but a light or tone does not . The pairing is biologically "prepared", reflecting evolutionary readiness to link food cues with sickness. Garcia's "bright-noisy-water" finding is the worked example: a taste cue paired with sickness produces aversion, but the same sickness paired with an audiovisual cue does not; the reverse holds for shock (audiovisual cues condition readily, taste does not). The contiguity requirement (CS and UCS must be close in time) is violated: taste aversions form across delays of hours, in a single trial . Exam trap The Garcia effect is the textbook counter-example to equipotentiality and to the need for temporal contiguity . It demonstrates "biological preparedness" and one-trial, long-delay learning. If the stem mentions taste, nausea, or "preparedness", the answer is Garcia. Operant Conditioning: Thorndike and Skinner Operant (instrumental) conditioning concerns learning from the consequences of voluntary behaviour, in contrast to classical conditioning's reflexive responses. Edward Thorndike placed cats in puzzle boxes and timed how long they took to escape. Escape time fell gradually over trials (trial-and-error learning), leading to the Law of Effect (1898) : responses followed by a satisfying consequence are "stamped in" (more likely to recur), while responses followed by discomfort are "stamped out". This is the foundation of all reinforcement theory. B. F. Skinner systematised this with the operant chamber ("Skinner box") and a precise vocabulary of consequences. The two axes are positive (add a stimulus) versus negative (remove a stimulus), crossed with reinforcement (increase behaviour) versus punishment (decrease behaviour), giving four cells: Reinforcement (behaviour increases) Punishment (behaviour decreases) Positive (add a stimulus) Positive reinforcement: add a pleasant stimulus (a treat for a lever press) Positive punishment: add an aversive stimulus (a slap) Negative (remove a stimulus) Negative reinforcement: remove an aversive stimulus (press a lever to switch off a shock) Negative punishment / omission: remove a pleasant stimulus (take away a toy) Worked example of negative reinforcement that students get wrong: a person with obsessive-compulsive disorder washes their hands and the anxiety drops. The anxiety reduction removes an aversive state , which strengthens the washing, so washing is negatively reinforced (not punished). This is exactly why compulsions persist, and it is a favourite clinical application of the concept. Two further operant tools are tested: shaping (reinforcing successive approximations to a target behaviour, used to build complex acts the animal would never emit spontaneously) and the Premack principle (a more probable, preferred behaviour can reinforce a less probable one: "you may play after you finish homework"). Exam trap "Positive" and "negative" mean add and remove, not good and bad. Negative reinforcement strengthens behaviour (by removing something aversive) and is constantly confused with punishment. Reinforcement always increases behaviour; punishment always decreases it. Escape and avoidance learning are both forms of negative reinforcement , not punishment. Schedules of Reinforcement A schedule specifies the rule by which responses are reinforced. The two dimensions are ratio (reinforce after a number of responses) versus interval (reinforce the first response after a period of time), each either fixed (constant) or variable (averaged). Continuous reinforcement (every response rewarded) produces fast acquisition but fast extinction; partial (intermittent) reinforcement produces slower acquisition but far greater resistance to extinction, the partial-reinforcement extinction effect . Schedule Rule Response pattern Fixed ratio (FR) Reinforce after a set number of responses (e.g. every 10th) High rate with a short post-reinforcement pause Variable ratio (VR) Reinforce after an unpredictable, averaged number of responses Highest, steadiest rate; most resistant to extinction Fixed interval (FI) Reinforce first response after a fixed time Scalloped : slow after reward, accelerating before the deadline Variable interval (VI) Reinforce first response after an averaged, unpredictable time Moderate, very steady rate Worked examples: a factory paying per piece is FR; a slot machine is VR (you never know which pull pays, so you keep pulling); a weekly pay cheque or a scheduled exam produces FI scalloping (effort spikes just before the deadline); checking for new email is VI (rewards arrive unpredictably over time). High-yield Variable ratio produces the highest, steadiest response rate and is the most resistant to extinction . This is the gambling schedule and is the single most-tested fact about reinforcement schedules. Fixed interval produces the characteristic scalloped curve. Ratio schedules (paid by output) always produce higher rates than interval schedules (paid by clock). Cognitive Learning The cognitive tradition argued that learning involves internal representations, not just stimulus-response bonds. Edward Tolman: latent learning and cognitive maps. Rats allowed to explore a maze without reward showed no improvement until a reward was introduced, after which they immediately performed as well as rats rewarded all along. The learning had been latent (present but not expressed) and was revealed only when motivated. Tolman argued the rats had built an internal cognitive map of the maze, demonstrating that learning (acquiring knowledge) is separable from performance (showing it). Wolfgang Kohler: insight learning. Studying chimpanzees (notably Sultan), Kohler observed that they solved problems (stacking boxes or joining sticks to reach a banana) suddenly, after a pause, rather than by gradual trial and error. This sudden reorganisation of the problem field is insight (the "aha" experience), a Gestalt phenomenon contrasting with Thorndike's incremental curve. Albert Bandura: social (observational) learning. Bandura's Bobo doll studies (1961) showed children imitate aggression they merely watch , without direct reinforcement. Observational learning runs through four subprocesses : Attention: you must notice and attend to the model's behaviour. Retention: you must store a memory representation of it. Production (motor reproduction): you must be able to reproduce the action. Motivation: you must have a reason to perform it (often via vicarious reinforcement : seeing the model rewarded). Exam trap Edward Tolman = latent learning and cognitive maps (learning without reward, performance separable from learning); Wolfgang Kohler = insight (sudden, Gestalt); Albert Bandura = observational learning (Bobo doll, learning by watching). The Bobo doll experiment is Bandura, not B. F. Skinner; the sudden "aha" is Kohler, not Tolman. Memory aid Albert Bandura's four steps in order spell "A R P M": Attention, Retention, Production, Motivation. You can only motivate (perform) what you can produce, and only produce what you retained, and only retain what you attended to. C. Perception and Attention Perception is the organisation and interpretation of sensory input into a meaningful experience. Attention is the selective allocation of limited processing resources. The syllabus targets signal detection, the Gestalt grouping laws, depth cues, the perceptual constancies and illusions, the bottom-up versus top-down debate, and the classic filter models of attention. Definition Sensation is the raw transduction of physical energy by the receptors; perception is the brain's organisation and interpretation of that input into a meaningful percept. Bottom-up (data-driven) processing builds the percept from the sensory features upward; top-down (concept-driven) processing uses prior knowledge, context, and expectation to shape what is perceived. The constancies and illusions show top-down processing at work. Signal Detection Theory (SDT) SDT models how an observer decides whether a faint signal is present against a background of noise. On every trial the signal is either present or absent, and the observer responds "yes" or "no", giving a 2-by-2 matrix: Observer says "Yes" Observer says "No" Signal present Hit Miss Signal absent False alarm Correct rejection SDT separates two independent things that older "threshold" theories confused: Sensitivity (d-prime, written d′): how well the observer can actually tell signal from noise, a measure of perceptual or discriminative ability. It is the standardised distance between the noise and signal-plus-noise distributions. Higher d-prime means the two are more separable: more hits with fewer false alarms. Sensitivity reflects the observer's capacity and is unaffected by their willingness to say yes. Response bias (beta or C): where the observer sets their decision criterion : how much evidence they demand before saying "yes". A liberal criterion (says yes readily) yields many hits but also many false alarms; a conservative criterion yields few false alarms but more misses. Bias reflects motivation, expectation, and the payoff structure, not perceptual ability. Worked example: a radiologist who is told that missing a tumour is far worse than a false alarm will shift to a liberal criterion: more hits, but also more false alarms, with no change whatever in their underlying ability to see tumours (d-prime is unchanged). This is the classic exam scenario, and it isolates a pure change in bias . Exam trap The central distinction is sensitivity (d-prime) versus response bias (beta or C) . d-prime = how good your senses are at discriminating; beta = how cautious or liberal your decision rule is. If a question says payoffs or expectations shifted the responses without changing perceptual ability, that is a change in bias , not sensitivity. SDT's whole contribution is replacing the single "absolute threshold" with these two separable measures. Gestalt Principles of Perceptual Grouping The Gestalt school (Max Wertheimer, Kurt Koffka, Wolfgang Kohler) held that "the whole is different from the sum of its parts": we perceive organised wholes, not isolated elements. The grouping laws describe how we bundle elements into objects: Proximity: elements close together are grouped (dots near each other seen as a cluster). Similarity: elements that look alike (colour, shape) are grouped. Continuity (good continuation): we perceive smooth, continuous lines rather than abrupt changes. Closure: we mentally fill gaps to perceive a complete figure (seeing a full circle from a broken outline). Common fate: elements moving together in the same direction are grouped (a flock of birds). Figure-ground: we segregate a scene into a figure (the object of attention) and a ground (the background); reversible figures such as the Rubin vase show the assignment is unstable and top-down. Pragnanz (the law of good form / simplicity): the overarching principle that we perceive the simplest, most stable, most regular organisation possible. Pragnanz is German for "conciseness" and is the master Gestalt law. High-yield Pragnanz (the law of good form / simplicity) is the umbrella Gestalt principle: the mind organises stimuli into the simplest possible form. Common fate is the one based on shared motion. Closure is filling in the gaps. Figure-ground segregation (the Rubin vase) is the most basic organisation of all. Perceptual Constancies and Illusions A perceptual constancy is the tendency to perceive an object as stable in size, shape, colour, or brightness despite changes in the retinal image. Size constancy : a person walking away projects a shrinking retinal image, yet you perceive them as a constant size because the brain scales by perceived distance. Shape constancy : a door swinging open projects a trapezoid, yet you still see a rectangular door. Colour and brightness constancy : a white shirt looks white in sunlight and in shadow despite vastly different light reaching the eye. Illusions are systematic misperceptions, often the price of these otherwise-useful constancy mechanisms. In the Muller-Lyer illusion , two equal lines appear unequal because of inward versus outward arrowheads; the standard explanation (Gregory) is misapplied size constancy : the fins are read as the near and far corners of a room, and the brain "corrects" for an inferred distance that is not really there. The Ponzo illusion (two equal bars on converging railway lines, the upper looking longer) works by the same depth-cue logic. The moon illusion (the moon looks larger near the horizon) is again a constancy effect driven by apparent-distance cues. Exam trap Constancies keep perception stable against changing input; illusions are where that machinery misfires . The Muller-Lyer is explained by misapplied size constancy (depth misreading), not by anything in the eye. Do not confuse a constancy (helpful stability) with an illusion (systematic error), and do not attribute illusions to retinal-level processes when the cause is top-down interpretation. Depth Perception: Monocular versus Binocular Cues To perceive a three-dimensional world from two-dimensional retinal images, the brain uses depth cues. Monocular cues require only one eye and convey depth in flat pictures: relative size, interposition (overlap), linear perspective (converging lines), texture gradient, aerial perspective (distant objects hazy), light and shadow, relative height, and motion parallax (nearer objects sweep past faster). These are the "pictorial" cues an artist uses. Binocular cues require both eyes: retinal (binocular) disparity (the two eyes get slightly different images; the brain reads the difference as depth, the basis of stereopsis) and convergence (the inward turning of the eyes for near objects, with the muscular feedback signalling distance). Exam trap Retinal disparity and convergence are binocular (two eyes). Everything pictorial (interposition, linear perspective, texture gradient, motion parallax) is monocular . The favourite distractor is calling motion parallax binocular: it is monocular. Attentional Gating: Filter Models Three classic models debate where in processing unattended information is filtered out. The evidence comes from dichotic listening (different messages to the two ears, with one to be shadowed) and the cocktail-party effect (you notice your own name in an unattended conversation). Donald Broadbent's early-selection filter (1958): a single filter selects one input channel early , on the basis of physical features (such as which ear), before meaning is analysed. The unattended channel is blocked entirely, so its meaning is never processed. This is the strict "bottleneck" model. Anne Treisman's attenuation model (1964): the unattended channel is not blocked but attenuated (turned down, not off). Its meaning is still weakly analysed, so highly salient items (your own name, the "cocktail-party" effect) can break through because they have low recognition thresholds. The filter weakens rather than eliminates. Deutsch and Norman late-selection model: all inputs are fully processed for meaning, and selection happens late , at the stage of response or memory, on the basis of relevance. The bottleneck is near the output, not the input. Exam trap Order them by where the filter sits. Donald Broadbent = early (filter before meaning, all-or-none). Anne Treisman = attenuation (turns the volume down, meaning still leaks; explains hearing your name). Deutsch-Norman = late (everything processed, selection at the end). The cocktail-party / own-name finding is the killer evidence against Broadbent and for Treisman. D. Lifespan Development I: Cognitive and Sociocultural Developmental psychology asks how thinking, knowledge, and reasoning change with age. The two giants are Jean Piaget (the child as a solitary constructor of knowledge through stages) and Lev Vygotsky (the child as a social apprentice whose mind is built through culture and interaction). The paper tests their concepts and, above all, the contrast between them. Piaget's Theory of Cognitive Development Jean Piaget viewed the child as a "little scientist" who actively constructs knowledge. The building blocks are schemas (organised mental frameworks for understanding the world). Development proceeds through three functional processes: Assimilation: fitting new information into an existing schema (a child who knows "dog" calls a cat "dog"). Accommodation: altering an existing schema, or creating a new one, to fit new information that will not assimilate (learning that the cat is a separate category). Equilibration: the drive to balance assimilation and accommodation. When new experience cannot be assimilated, the child feels disequilibrium and adjusts schemas to restore equilibrium ; this tension is the engine of cognitive growth. Definition A schema is an organised mental structure (a unit of knowledge) used to represent and act on the world. Cognitive growth is the progressive revision of schemas through assimilation (using the existing schema) and accommodation (changing it), kept in motion by equilibration (the search for cognitive balance). Exam trap Assimilation = fit the world into your head (no schema change). Accommodation = change your head to fit the world (schema change). Calling a cat a "dog" is assimilation; learning cat is a new category is accommodation. Equilibration is the balancing motivation, not a stage. Piaget proposed four invariant, universal stages: Stage Age Key achievements and limits Sensorimotor 0 to 2 years Knowing through senses and action; reflex modification; primary, secondary, and tertiary circular reactions; attainment of object permanence (objects exist when out of sight) Preoperational 2 to 7 years Symbolic function (language, pretend play); egocentrism , animism, centration; cannot conserve Concrete operational 7 to 11 years Conservation , decentering, reversibility, transitivity, seriation; logic limited to concrete objects Formal operational 11+ years Abstract, hypothetical-deductive reasoning; systematic problem-solving The key concepts within these stages: Object permanence: the sensorimotor milestone that things continue to exist when not perceived. Before it, "out of sight is out of mind"; its absence is tested by hiding a toy. (The classic A-not-B error, where an infant keeps reaching to the old hiding place, is the transitional sign.) Egocentrism: the preoperational inability to take another's viewpoint, demonstrated by the Three Mountains Task , where the child cannot say what a doll on the opposite side of a model sees and reports their own view. Animism: attributing life and feelings to inanimate objects ("the sun is sleeping"). Centration: focusing on one salient dimension while ignoring others, which is why preoperational children fail conservation. Conservation: understanding that quantity stays constant despite changes in appearance (the same water poured into a taller, thinner glass is the same amount). Mastered in the concrete operational stage. The worked example to know: pour water from a short wide glass into a tall thin one; the preoperational child, centring on height alone, says there is "more" water, then the concrete-operational child, decentring and using reversibility, says it is the same. Decentering: attending to multiple dimensions at once (height and width), which enables conservation. Reversibility: mentally undoing an operation (the water could be poured back). Transitivity: inferring relations (if A > B and B > C then A > C). Seriation: ordering items along a dimension (arranging sticks by length). Hypothetico-deductive reasoning: the formal-operational ability to generate hypotheses and test them systematically (the pendulum problem). High-yield Lock the stage-to-feature pairs: sensorimotor → object permanence ; preoperational → egocentrism (Three Mountains) and failure of conservation ; concrete operational → conservation, reversibility, seriation ; formal operational → abstract hypothetico-deductive reasoning . The ages (0 to 2, 2 to 7, 7 to 11, 11+) are tested verbatim. Vygotsky's Sociocultural Theory Lev Vygotsky stressed that cognition is built through social interaction and culture, in contrast to Piaget's solitary little scientist. For Vygotsky, every higher mental function appears first between people (interpsychological) and only later within the child (intrapsychological): development is the internalisation of social and cultural tools, language above all. Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD): the gap between what a child can do independently and what they can do with guidance from a more knowledgeable other. Learning happens in this zone. Scaffolding: the temporary, tailored support an adult or peer provides within the ZPD, gradually withdrawn as competence grows (like a building scaffold removed once the structure stands). The term is Wood, Jerome Bruner, and Ross's, but it operationalises Vygotsky's ZPD. Private speech to inner speech: young children talk aloud to themselves to guide action ( private speech ); this is not egocentric (Piaget's reading) but a tool for self-regulation that is gradually internalised into silent inner speech (verbal thought). Exam trap On self-talk, Piaget and Lev Vygotsky disagree: Piaget called children's talking-to-themselves egocentric speech (immature, fading away), whereas Vygotsky called it private speech (a functional self-guidance tool that becomes inner speech). The ZPD and scaffolding are Vygotsky; conservation, object permanence, and the four stages are Piaget. Piaget emphasised the solitary child and biological maturation; Vygotsky emphasised culture and the more-knowledgeable other. E. Lifespan Development II: Psychosocial, Moral, and Attachment This subsection covers three lifespan frameworks the paper draws from almost every year: Erik Erikson's eight psychosocial crises (and how they recast Sigmund Freud), Lawrence Kohlberg's three levels of moral reasoning (with Carol Gilligan's critique), and the attachment work of John Bowlby and Mary Ainsworth. Each is heavily table-tested. Erikson's Eight Psychosocial Stages Erik Erikson recast Freud's psychosexual stages as a lifelong sequence of eight psychosocial "crises", each a tension between two outcomes; resolving each yields a basic virtue (ego strength). The crucial departures from Freud: the stages run across the whole lifespan (not stopping at adolescence), the driver is social and relational (not libidinal), and the ego is given a constructive, identity-building role. Stage Conflict Age Virtue 1 Trust vs. Mistrust Infancy (0 to 1) Hope 2 Autonomy vs. Shame/Doubt Early childhood (1 to 3) Will 3 Initiative vs. Guilt Preschool (3 to 6) Purpose 4 Industry vs. Inferiority School age (6 to 12) Competence 5 Identity vs. Role Confusion Adolescence (12 to 18) Fidelity 6 Intimacy vs. Isolation Young adulthood Love 7 Generativity vs. Stagnation Middle adulthood Care 8 Ego Integrity vs. Despair Late adulthood Wisdom High-yield The virtues in order: Hope, Will, Purpose, Competence, Fidelity, Love, Care, Wisdom. Identity vs. Role Confusion (virtue: Fidelity) is the adolescent stage and the most-tested one. Generativity vs. Stagnation (Care) is middle adulthood; Integrity vs. Despair (Wisdom) is old age. Exam trap The favourite errors are mismatching the virtue to its stage (Fidelity belongs to Identity vs. Role Confusion , Care to Generativity vs. Stagnation , Wisdom to Integrity vs. Despair ) and confusing Erik Erikson's psychosocial stages with Sigmund Freud's psychosexual ones. Erikson's are eight, lifelong, and social; Freud's are five (oral, anal, phallic, latency, genital), childhood-bounded, and libidinal. Memory aid Virtues mnemonic "Hope Will Purpose Competence Fidelity, Love Care Wisdom": think of a person hoping , then willing , with a purpose and competence , staying faithful , finding love , giving care , ending in wisdom . Kohlberg's Theory of Moral Development Lawrence Kohlberg studied moral reasoning (the justification, not the verdict) using moral dilemmas, most famously the Heinz dilemma : should a man steal an unaffordable drug to save his dying wife? He identified three levels, each with two stages. Pre-conventional level (morality is external, based on consequences to the self): Stage 1: Punishment and obedience orientation: right is avoiding punishment ("Heinz should not steal, he will be jailed"). Stage 2: Instrumental hedonism (naive egoism): right is what serves one's own needs, with simple exchange ("steal it because he needs his wife", a "you scratch my back" morality). Conventional level (morality is conformity to social roles and rules): Stage 3: Good-boy / nice-girl orientation: right is gaining approval and being seen as nice ("a good husband would steal"). Stage 4: Law-and-order orientation: right is upholding laws and social duty ("stealing is against the law"). Post-conventional level (morality is based on abstract principles transcending laws): Stage 5: Social contract orientation: laws are social agreements that can be changed for the greater good; rights matter. Stage 6: Universal ethical principles: self-chosen, universal principles of justice and human dignity override unjust laws ("life is worth more than property"). Carol Gilligan's critique: Kohlberg's stages were derived from male samples and rank an abstract ethics of justice (rules, rights) as the highest morality. Gilligan argued women more often reason from an ethics of care (responsibility, relationships, avoiding harm to others), which Kohlberg's scheme wrongly scores as less mature. The difference is one of orientation, not inferiority: a gender bias in the theory, not in women. Exam trap Kohlberg scores the reasoning , not the answer: two people who both say "steal" can be at very different stages. Pre-conventional = self (punishment, reward); conventional = others (approval, law); post-conventional = principles. Carol Gilligan's contribution is the ethics of care versus ethics of justice gender critique. Do not confuse Stage 4 (law-and-order, obey the law because it is the law) with Stage 5 (social contract, laws can be changed for the greater good). Attachment Theory John Bowlby argued attachment is an innate, evolved behavioural system: infants are biologically predisposed to form a bond with a primary caregiver because proximity to a protector enhanced survival. From early interactions the infant builds internal working models : mental representations of the self (am I worthy of care?), of others (are they reliable?), and of relationships, which guide expectations for life. Harry Harlow's rhesus-monkey studies supplied the experimental backbone: infant monkeys preferred a soft cloth "mother" that provided contact comfort over a wire mother that provided milk, refuting the idea that attachment is just learnt feeding (the "cupboard-love" theory). Mary Ainsworth operationalised attachment quality with the Strange Situation , a standardised laboratory procedure of eight episodes involving separations from and reunions with the caregiver, plus a stranger. The infant's behaviour, especially at reunion , classifies the attachment: Pattern On separation On reunion Secure Distressed (caregiver is a secure base for exploration) Seeks contact and is easily comforted, then resumes play Insecure-anxious/ambivalent (resistant) Highly distressed Seeks contact but resists it: clings and pushes away, angry, hard to soothe Insecure-avoidant Little or no distress Avoids and ignores the caregiver; treats stranger and caregiver similarly Disorganised/disoriented No coherent strategy Confused, contradictory, freezing or apprehensive behaviour The first three were Ainsworth's; the disorganised/disoriented category was added later by Mary Main and Judith Solomon for infants who showed no consistent strategy (approaching then freezing, or appearing fearful of the caregiver). It is most associated with frightening caregiving, maltreatment, or unresolved parental trauma. Definition The secure base is Mary Ainsworth's term for the caregiver as a platform from which the infant confidently explores and to which it returns for comfort. The two diagnostic markers in the Strange Situation are the infant's use of the caregiver as a secure base for exploration and its behaviour at reunion ; reunion is where the pattern is read. Exam trap The reunion behaviour is the key. The avoidant infant shows little distress and ignores/avoids the caregiver at reunion. The ambivalent/resistant infant is very distressed and seeks but angrily resists comfort. Do not swap them. Disorganised is the Main and Solomon addition, linked to trauma. Harry Harlow shows contact comfort beats feeding; do not credit the Strange Situation to John Bowlby (it is Ainsworth's). F. Social Psychology: Attribution, Influence, and Groups Social psychology studies how people think about, influence, and relate to one another. The paper concentrates on attribution and its biases, cognitive dissonance, the conformity and obedience classics, compliance techniques, group-performance effects, and the bystander effect. These are almost all anchored to named experiments, so learn the study with the concept. Attribution Theory and Biases Attribution is how people explain the causes of behaviour, assigning it to internal/dispositional causes (the person's traits) or external/situational causes (the circumstances). Fritz Heider , the founder, described the "naive psychologist" who routinely sorts causes into internal versus external locus. Harold Kelley's covariation model: to attribute a behaviour, people assess whether it covaries with the person, the stimulus, or the occasion across three kinds of information: Consensus: do other people behave this way toward the same stimulus? (high = others do too). Distinctiveness: does the person behave this way only toward this stimulus or toward many? (high = only this one). Consistency: does the person behave this way toward this stimulus across time and situations ? (high = always). Low consensus, low distinctiveness, high consistency → internal (dispositional) attribution. High consensus, high distinctiveness, high consistency → external (situational) attribution. Worked example of Kelley's model: Priya laughs at a particular comedian. If no one else laughs at him (low consensus), she laughs at no other comedian (high distinctiveness), and she always laughs at him (high consistency), you attribute it externally to something about the comedian. If everyone laughs at him, she does not laugh at most things, but laughs at him every time, that pattern (high consensus, high distinctiveness, high consistency) again points external; reverse consensus and distinctiveness and the attribution swings to Priya's disposition. The systematic biases: Fundamental Attribution Error (FAE): the tendency, when explaining others' behaviour, to overweight dispositional causes and underweight situational ones (assuming a late colleague is lazy, not stuck in traffic). Actor-observer bias: we attribute our own behaviour to the situation but others' identical behaviour to their disposition (I'm late because of traffic; you're late because you're disorganised). Self-serving bias: we take credit for successes (internal: "I'm skilled") but blame failures on external factors ("the exam was unfair"), protecting self-esteem. Just-world hypothesis: the belief that the world is fair and people get what they deserve, which leads to blaming the victim (assuming a misfortune was earned). Exam trap FAE is about explaining others (over-blame disposition). The actor-observer bias adds the self/other asymmetry (situational for self, dispositional for others). Self-serving bias is the success/failure asymmetry (credit me, blame the world). These three are constantly cross-substituted as distractors. Festinger's Cognitive Dissonance Theory Leon Festinger (1957) proposed that holding two inconsistent cognitions (beliefs, attitudes, or a belief and a behaviour) produces an uncomfortable state of cognitive dissonance , a drive-like tension people are motivated to reduce. They reduce it by changing one cognition (attitude change), changing the behaviour , or adding consonant cognitions (rationalisation). The classic demonstration is Festinger and J. Merrill Carlsmith's forced-compliance / one-dollar versus twenty-dollar study (1959) . Participants did a boring task, then were paid either 1 dollar or 20 dollars to tell the next participant it was enjoyable. Counter-intuitively, the 1-dollar group later rated the task as more enjoyable. With 20 dollars, the large payment is sufficient external justification for lying, so no dissonance arises. With only 1 dollar, there is insufficient justification, so the dissonance between "I said it was fun" and "it was boring" is resolved by genuinely changing the attitude ("it actually was a bit fun"). Definition Cognitive dissonance is the aversive tension arising from holding two psychologically inconsistent cognitions. The drive to reduce it can change attitudes to match behaviour, which is why dissonance theory predicts attitude change follows behaviour (the opposite of the common-sense direction). High-yield In the forced-compliance study, the smaller reward (1 dollar) produced the greater attitude change, because insufficient external justification forces internal (attitude) change to reduce dissonance. This counter-intuitive direction is the whole point and is heavily tested. Social Influence: Conformity and Obedience Solomon Asch's conformity studies (1951): participants judged which of three comparison lines matched a standard, an easy perceptual task. When confederates unanimously gave an obviously wrong answer, about a third (roughly 33 to 37 percent) of responses conformed to the wrong majority. Asch showed conformity to group pressure even against clear perceptual evidence. Two mechanisms drive conformity: Informational social influence: conforming because you believe the group is right (you use others as a source of information), leading to genuine private acceptance; strongest in ambiguous situations. Normative social influence: conforming to be liked / accepted and to avoid rejection, leading to public compliance without private change; this drove most of Asch's effect (the task was unambiguous). Stanley Milgram's obedience studies (1963): participants ("teachers") were ordered by an experimenter to deliver escalating "shocks" to a learner for wrong answers, up to a labelled 450 volts. About 65 percent obeyed to the maximum, demonstrating that ordinary people obey a legitimate authority even against their conscience. Key modifiers reduced obedience: Proximity of the victim (obedience fell as the learner became more present) and of the authority (obedience fell when the experimenter gave orders by phone). Prestige / legitimacy of the setting and authority (obedience fell when moved from prestigious Yale to a run-down office, or when the experimenter wore ordinary clothes). Milgram explained obedience by the agentic state : the person stops seeing themselves as an autonomous agent and becomes an instrument carrying out another's wishes, shifting responsibility to the authority. Exam trap Solomon Asch = conformity to a peer group (no one orders you); about a third conform. Stanley Milgram = obedience to an authority figure (a direct command); about 65 percent fully obey. For Asch's two motives: informational = "they must be right" (ambiguity, private acceptance); normative = "I want to fit in" (public compliance). Do not confuse the two influence types, and do not swap the 33 percent (Asch conformity) with the 65 percent (Milgram obedience). Compliance Techniques Foot-in-the-door: get agreement to a small request first, then the larger target request is more likely accepted (consistency with the prior small commitment). Door-in-the-face: make a large request expected to be refused, then the smaller real request looks reasonable by contrast (reciprocal concession). Low-balling: get a commitment to an attractive offer, then reveal a higher cost; people often stay committed despite the worsened terms. Memory aid Foot-in-the-door goes small then big (you let the foot in, then the whole person). Door-in-the-face goes big then small (the big request gets the door slammed, the small one then gets in). Low-balling = bait with a low price, then raise it. Group Performance and Decision Traps Social facilitation: the presence of others improves performance on simple or well-learned tasks (Norman Triplett's cyclists rode faster with others). Social inhibition: the presence of others impairs performance on complex or novel tasks. Robert Zajonc explained both: others raise arousal, which strengthens the dominant response, which is correct on easy tasks and wrong on hard ones. Social loafing: people exert less effort when their contribution is pooled and not individually identifiable (Max Ringelmann's rope-pulling), through diffusion of responsibility . Groupthink (Irving Janis): in a cohesive group, the desire for harmony and consensus suppresses dissent and critical evaluation, producing poor decisions (symptoms include illusions of invulnerability, self-censorship, and pressure on dissenters). Group polarisation: group discussion shifts members toward a more extreme version of their initial leaning (a cautious group gets more cautious; a risky group takes the "risky shift"). Exam trap Social facilitation helps on easy/well-learned tasks; the same audience hurts on hard/novel tasks (social inhibition). Social loafing is reduced effort when pooled; groupthink is suppressed dissent for harmony; group polarisation is the shift to extremes. Polarisation makes groups more extreme , not more moderate. Robert Zajonc's mechanism is "arousal strengthens the dominant response", which is why the same crowd can help or hurt depending on task difficulty. The Bystander Effect John Darley and Bibb Latane (1968), prompted by the Kitty Genovese case, found that the more bystanders present at an emergency, the less likely any one of them is to help, and the slower the help. Two processes drive it: Diffusion of responsibility: with others present, each person feels less personal obligation to act ("someone else will"). Pluralistic ignorance: people look to others to define the situation; if everyone stays calm (each thinking the others know it is not an emergency), the group collectively misreads the event as a non-emergency. High-yield The bystander effect: helping decreases as the number of bystanders increases . Mechanisms: diffusion of responsibility (no one feels obliged) and pluralistic ignorance (everyone's calm cues read as "no emergency"). Bibb Latane and John Darley's five-step decision model (notice, interpret as emergency, take responsibility, decide how to help, act) is the supporting framework. G. Personality: Trait, Type, and Social-Cognitive Theories Personality is the characteristic, relatively enduring pattern of thinking, feeling, and behaving that distinguishes one person from another. Trait theories describe its stable dimensions; type and biological theories root them in temperament; social-cognitive theories stress the interaction of person and situation. The paper tests theorist-to-construct pairings above all, so keep each name welded to its idea. Definition A trait is a relatively stable, enduring disposition to behave in a consistent way across situations and time (the nomothetic , dimensional approach). A type is a discrete category a person belongs to (the older, typological approach). Modern personality psychology favours continuous traits over discrete types. Trait Theories Gordon Allport distinguished three levels of traits by how pervasively they shape a person: Cardinal traits: a single dominant trait that organises a whole life (rare; "Machiavellian", "narcissistic"). Most people have none. Central traits: the handful of core characteristics that describe a person (honest, kind, anxious): the basic units of personality. Secondary traits: situation-specific preferences and attitudes that appear only in particular contexts (gets impatient in queues). Raymond Cattell used factor analysis to reduce surface descriptions to underlying dimensions: Surface traits: clusters of observable behaviours that go together. Source traits: the deeper, underlying factors (the "source" of surface traits) isolated by factor analysis. Cattell identified 16 source traits , operationalised in the 16PF (Sixteen Personality Factor) Questionnaire . Hans Eysenck's PEN model proposed a small set of biologically based super-factors: Psychoticism (toughminded, aggressive, antisocial), Extraversion (sociable, outgoing), and Neuroticism (emotionally unstable, anxious). Eysenck rooted Extraversion in cortical arousal : introverts have higher baseline arousal via the Reticular Activating System (RAS) , so they are already over-stimulated and seek quiet; extraverts are chronically under-aroused and seek stimulation. Neuroticism he linked to a labile autonomic (limbic) nervous system. Paul Costa and McCrae's Five-Factor Model , measured by the NEO-PI-R , is the modern consensus: five broad dimensions, the OCEAN traits: O penness to experience (imaginative, curious), C onscientiousness (organised, dependable), E xtraversion (sociable, energetic), A greeableness (cooperative, warm), N euroticism (anxious, emotionally reactive). How it is tested: the paper asks you to count and name (Eysenck = 3, Cattell = 16, Costa and Robert McCrae = 5), to attach the instrument to the theorist (16PF = Cattell, NEO-PI-R = Costa and McCrae, EPQ = Eysenck), and to recall Eysenck's counter-intuitive arousal claim. Memory aid The Big Five spell OCEAN (Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, Neuroticism). Hans Eysenck's three spell PEN (Psychoticism, Extraversion, Neuroticism). Raymond Cattell's number is 16 (the 16PF). Gordon Allport's three are Cardinal, Central, Secondary. Exam trap Counter-intuitively, Hans Eysenck held that introverts have higher baseline cortical arousal (via the RAS), so they avoid extra stimulation, while extraverts are under-aroused and seek it. Do not say extraverts are the highly aroused ones. Raymond Cattell = 16PF and the surface/source trait distinction; Paul Costa and Robert McCrae = the Big Five (NEO-PI-R, OCEAN); Eysenck = PEN. Do not confuse Cattell's 16 source traits with the Big Five's 5 factors. Psychodynamic and Humanistic Glances Two further families round out the personality menu and supply distractors. The psychodynamic tradition (Freud) explains personality through unconscious conflict among the id (pleasure principle, instinctual drives), ego (reality principle, the executive mediator), and superego (the internalised moral standard), with defence mechanisms managing anxiety. The humanistic tradition rejects both psychodynamic determinism and behaviourism: Carl Rogers centres the drive toward self-actualisation , the gap between the real self and the ideal self (incongruence), and the therapeutic value of unconditional positive regard ; Abraham Maslow arranges motives in a hierarchy of needs (physiological, safety, love and belonging, esteem, self-actualisation), the lower needs being prepotent. These are the optimistic, growth-oriented "third force" against the deterministic first two forces. Exam trap Keep the structural model straight: the ego runs on the reality principle (mediator), the id on the pleasure principle, the superego is conscience. Self-actualisation appears in both Abraham Maslow (top of the hierarchy) and Carl Rogers (the actualising tendency), but unconditional positive regard and real-versus-ideal-self incongruence are specifically Rogers . Social-Cognitive Theories Albert Bandura's reciprocal determinism: behaviour is not caused by the person or the situation alone; instead three factors continuously influence each other in interlocking loops: behaviour , personal/cognitive factors (beliefs, expectations), and the environment . Each shapes and is shaped by the others (a triadic, two-way causation). Self-efficacy: Bandura's term for a person's belief in their own capacity to execute the actions needed to achieve a goal. High self-efficacy predicts greater effort, persistence, and resilience; it is built through mastery experiences, vicarious experience (modelling), social persuasion, and managing physiological arousal. Julian Rotter's locus of control: a generalised expectancy about the source of reinforcement. People with an internal locus believe outcomes follow from their own actions and effort; those with an external locus believe outcomes are governed by luck, fate, or powerful others. Internals tend to take more responsibility and cope more actively.
