High-yield Reciprocal determinism = the triadic, mutual causation of behaviour, person (cognition), and environment (Albert Bandura). Self-efficacy = belief in one's capability to succeed (Bandura). Locus of control = internal (I control outcomes) versus external (luck/fate controls them) (Julian Rotter). Keep self-efficacy (Bandura) and locus of control (Rotter) attributed to the right theorist. Exam trap Self-efficacy and locus of control sound similar but differ: self-efficacy is task-specific belief in your ability to perform (Albert Bandura); locus of control is a global expectancy about where reinforcement comes from , internal versus external (Julian Rotter). The paper tested these as single-fact and trap-pair items. Kurt Lewin carries two "father of" titles. Kurt Lewin (1890 to 1947) was a German-American psychologist who is named father of modern social psychology and father of action research . His central idea was that behaviour cannot be predicted from the person alone or the situation alone, but from their interaction, which he compressed into the formula B = f(P, E) : behaviour is a function of the person and the environment, considered together as one psychological field. This is field theory , borrowed deliberately from physics: a person sits in a "life space" of forces (driving forces pushing toward a goal, restraining forces holding back), and you analyse any situation by mapping those forces, a method he called force-field analysis . From the same field thinking he derived his model of planned organisational change, unfreeze (loosen the old equilibrium) then change (move) then refreeze (lock the new state in) ; the action research cycle of Plan then Act then Observe then Reflect; and his classic studies on leadership climate, which isolated three styles, autocratic, democratic, and laissez-faire , with the democratic climate producing the best morale and sustained output. Trap: they offer Gordon Allport or Floyd Allport for "father of social psychology." On this paper Lewin is the one tagged, and he owns action research outright; do not surrender the action-research label to anyone else. Norman Triplett (1898), the fishing-reel experiment. This is the first social-psychology experiment ever conducted, and both the date and the apparatus are testable. Triplett, an American psychologist, had noticed that racing cyclists rode faster when paced by or competing against others than when riding alone against the clock. To test this in the laboratory he had children wind line onto a fishing reel , sometimes alone and sometimes alongside another child doing the same task, and found they wound faster in company. This is the founding demonstration of social facilitation , the improvement of performance in the presence of others, though Triplett himself framed it as "dynamogenesis," a competitive instinct releasing latent energy. Trap: the date (1898) and the apparatus (fishing reel) are both directly examined. Do not confuse it with Max Ringelmann's rope-pulling study (1913), which demonstrated social loafing , the opposite effect, and was actually conducted earlier in data but published as the loafing phenomenon. Social facilitation vs social inhibition, Robert Zajonc's drive theory. Why does an audience sometimes help performance and sometimes wreck it? Robert Zajonc (1965) resolved the apparent contradiction with a drive theory built on three steps. First, the mere presence of others raises general physiological arousal (drive). Second, heightened arousal strengthens the dominant response , the response most likely to be emitted in that situation. Third, whether that helps depends entirely on the task. On an easy or well-learned task the dominant response is the correct one, so arousal pushes performance up: this is social facilitation . On a hard, novel, or not-yet-mastered task the dominant response is usually wrong, so arousal pushes performance down: this is social inhibition (sometimes called social interference). The single insight to carry into the exam is that the audience never simply "helps" or "hurts"; it amplifies whatever response is already dominant. Trap: "the presence of others improves performance" stated baldly is wrong, because it only boosts the dominant response, which fails on hard tasks. The rival explanation the examiners may name is Cottrell's evaluation-apprehension theory, which argues it is not mere presence but the learned expectation of being judged that drives the arousal. Definition The dominant response is the response that is most probable for a person in a given situation, given their habits and skill level. Robert Zajonc's whole account rests on it: arousal does not improve or impair performance directly, it strengthens the dominant response, which is correct on easy tasks (so performance rises) and wrong on hard tasks (so performance falls). Social loafing vs social striving. Social loafing is the tendency for individuals to exert less effort when working in a group than when working alone, because individual contribution is pooled and unidentifiable, so responsibility diffuses and motivation slackens. Its founding evidence is the Ringelmann effect : in rope-pulling, the total force of a group was less than the sum of the members' individual maximum pulls, and the per-person force fell as group size rose. Loafing was long treated as universal, but the cross-cultural work is the advanced half they test. In some collectivist cultures the effect can reverse into social striving (social compensation) , where effort rises in the group because the group's success is internalised as a personal and social value, especially when the task matters and individual slacking would let the team down. Loafing is shrunk wherever contribution is made identifiable, the task feels meaningful, or members value the group's goal. Trap: assuming loafing is universal and human-nature-fixed. The collectivist reversal into striving is precisely the nuance the paper rewards; Ringelmann is an individualist-culture finding, not a law. Tuckman's stages of group development. Bruce Tuckman (1965) proposed that small groups pass through a fixed developmental sequence: Forming, Storming, Norming, Performing , to which he and Mary Ann Jensen added a fifth stage, Adjourning , in 1977. In Forming members are polite, dependent on the leader, and orienting to the task. In Storming , stage 2 , conflict erupts: members jostle for status, resist the structure, and challenge each other and the leader; this is the stage your list flagged specifically, and it is the one most often blanked out in an exam item. In Norming the group settles, agrees roles and rules (norms), and cohesion grows. In Performing the group works productively and autonomously on the task. In Adjourning the group disbands and members disengage. Trap: "Adjourning" was added later (1977), so older textbooks stop at four stages; and Storming is stage 2 , not stage 1. A favourite distractor places conflict at the very start, but Forming (the polite orientation) comes first. Conformity, obedience, and the bystander effect (the named studies). Social-dynamics items on this paper cluster around three classic experiments whose author, finding, and apparatus are each examinable. Solomon Asch (1951) studied conformity using a line-judgement task: a single naive participant gave answers after a group of confederates who deliberately called an obviously shorter line "equal," and about a third of responses conformed to the wrong majority, showing normative social influence (going along to be accepted) even against the plain evidence of the eyes. Stanley Milgram (1963) studied obedience to authority : participants instructed by an experimenter to deliver escalating "shocks" to a confederate continued to the maximum 450 volts at strikingly high rates, demonstrating how ordinary people defer to legitimate authority (Milgram explained it as a shift into an "agentic state"). Bibb Latane and John Darley (1968) studied the bystander effect , in which the presence of others reduces the likelihood any individual helps in an emergency, through diffusion of responsibility and pluralistic ignorance; it was framed around the Kitty Genovese case. Trap: match the name to the phenomenon and do not let them slide: Asch = conformity (lines), Milgram = obedience (shocks), Latane & Darley = bystander/diffusion. Asch is normative influence; Muzafer Sherif's autokinetic study is the informational conformity classic offered as the distractor. Memory aid Tuckman in order: " Form a band, Storm off in a row, agree the Norms , Perform the gig, then Adjourn to the pub." Five stages, the fifth bolted on in 1977. For Lewin, " B = f(P,E) " and " un freeze, change , re freeze" are the two formulas worth holding verbatim. For the named studies: " A sch sees lines, M ilgram makes shocks, the B ystanders do nothing." B · Motivation & Organisational (off your paper) Full teaching in Section 6 . Frederick Herzberg, two-factor theory. Frederick Herzberg (1959) interviewed accountants and engineers about times they felt exceptionally good or bad at work, and found that the causes of satisfaction and the causes of dissatisfaction were different sets of factors , not opposite ends of one scale. Hygiene factors (also called maintenance factors) are extrinsic conditions: pay, company policy, working conditions, job security, supervision, and interpersonal relations. When these are poor they cause dissatisfaction; when they are good they merely remove dissatisfaction, returning the worker to a neutral, un-dissatisfied state, but they do not motivate. Motivators are intrinsic to the work itself: achievement, recognition, responsibility, advancement, growth, and the nature of the work. These are what produce genuine satisfaction and drive effort. The decisive structural claim is that the opposite of dissatisfaction is not satisfaction but no dissatisfaction , and the opposite of satisfaction is no satisfaction ; the two run on separate continua. The practical prescription is job enrichment , loading the work with more motivators rather than merely improving hygiene. Trap: treating "remove dissatisfaction equals create satisfaction." It does not, and that error is the entire point the theory was built to correct. Pay and conditions are hygiene, not motivators. David McClelland, need for achievement (nAch). David McClelland's acquired needs theory (also called the three needs theory or learned needs theory) holds that three motives are learned through life experience and culture rather than innate, and that one tends to dominate in any given person: the need for achievement (nAch) , the need for affiliation (nAff) , and the need for power (nPow) . People high in nAch prefer tasks of moderate difficulty (where success reflects skill, not luck or impossibility), seek personal responsibility for outcomes, and want concrete, frequent feedback on how they are doing. Because these motives are largely unconscious, McClelland measured them with the Thematic Apperception Test (TAT) , a projective test in which the respondent invents stories about ambiguous pictures and the achievement, affiliation, or power imagery in those stories is scored. Trap: confusing it with Abraham Maslow's hierarchy (a fixed innate ladder of needs, a different model entirely) or with Henry Murray , who originated both the broad list of psychogenic needs that McClelland drew his three from and co-created the TAT itself. McClelland built on Murray; do not credit the whole framework to either name alone. Maslow's hierarchy and the Maslow vs Herzberg link. Abraham Maslow's hierarchy of needs arranges human motives in an ascending order in which lower needs must be substantially met before higher ones become active: physiological (food, water, sleep), then safety (security, stability), then love and belonging (affiliation), then esteem (recognition, status), and at the apex self-actualisation (realising one's full potential), with self-transcendence added in his later writing. The first four are deficiency needs (D-needs) , motivating by their absence; self-actualisation is a growth or being need (B-need) that is never fully satiated. The examined connection is the mapping onto Herzberg: Maslow's lower deficiency needs correspond broadly to Herzberg's hygiene factors, and the upper esteem and self-actualisation needs correspond to Herzberg's motivators . Trap: Maslow's pyramid is a single ascending scale of innate needs; Herzberg's is two separate dimensions; McClelland's three needs are learned . The paper sets these three theorists against each other, so keep "Maslow = ladder, Herzberg = two factors, McClelland = three learned needs" cleanly separated. High-yield Frederick Herzberg: hygiene factors (pay, conditions, security, supervision) prevent dissatisfaction but never motivate; motivators (achievement, recognition, the work, growth) create satisfaction. They are separate dimensions . David McClelland: three learned needs (achievement, affiliation, power), high-nAch seeks moderate risk plus feedback , measured by the TAT , which traces back to Murray. Maslow: a five-level innate hierarchy, physiological to self-actualisation, deficiency needs below and growth need at the top. C · Developmental & Attachment (off your paper) Full teaching in Section 6 . John Bowlby & Mary Ainsworth, attachment. The division of labour between these two names is the testable point. John Bowlby built the theory : attachment is an innate, evolved behavioural system whose biological function is to keep the infant close to a caregiver for protection, selected because proximity raised survival in ancestral environments. From repeated interactions the infant forms an internal working model , a mental template of whether the self is worthy of care and whether others are reliable, which then guides relationships across the lifespan. Bowlby also described attachment as developing through phases and emphasised that prolonged separation or loss in early childhood (maternal deprivation) had lasting effects. Mary Ainsworth supplied the method that operationalised and measured Bowlby's theory: the Strange Situation , a structured laboratory procedure of eight episodes involving separations from and reunions with the caregiver and the entry of a stranger, scored chiefly on the infant's reunion behaviour . Trap: crediting the Strange Situation to Bowlby. The theory is Bowlby's; the Strange Situation procedure is Ainsworth's method. A clean way to hold it: Bowlby theorised, Ainsworth experimentally classified. The four attachment styles. Ainsworth's Strange Situation originally yielded three infant classifications. Secure (Type B) : the infant explores using the caregiver as a base, is distressed at separation, and is readily comforted on reunion (the marker of healthy attachment). Insecure-avoidant (Type A) : the infant shows little distress at separation and actively avoids or ignores the caregiver on reunion, having learned that bids for comfort are rebuffed. Insecure-ambivalent or resistant (Type C) : the infant is intensely distressed at separation and on reunion seeks contact yet simultaneously resists and cannot be soothed (clingy and angry at once). A fourth category, disorganised or disoriented (Type D) , was added later by Mary Main and Judith Solomon for infants showing contradictory, fearful, or freezing behaviours that fit none of the original three, often linked to frightening or maltreating care. Trap: the original Strange Situation classified three ; disorganised is the add-on (Main & Solomon). Do not confuse these infant types with the adult attachment relabels (secure, dismissing, preoccupied, fearful-avoidant), which come from a separate framework (the Adult Attachment Interview and Bartholomew's model). High-yield Attachment owners: Bowlby theory, Ainsworth Strange Situation, Harlow contact comfort (cloth monkey), Lorenz imprinting, Main & Solomon the disorganised fourth type. Original Strange Situation = three types (secure, avoidant, ambivalent); the fourth (disorganised) was added later. Harry Harlow proved attachment runs on comfort, not feeding. Harry Harlow's monkeys and contact comfort. Harry Harlow's surrogate-mother experiments (1958) are the most-cited attachment evidence on these papers, because they refuted the older "cupboard love" view that infants bond to whoever feeds them. Infant rhesus monkeys were raised with two artificial mothers: a bare wire mother fitted with a feeding bottle, and a soft cloth -covered mother with no food. The infants clung to the cloth mother almost all the time and went to the wire mother only briefly to feed, returning at once to the cloth. When frightened they ran to the cloth mother, and used her as a secure base from which to explore. The conclusion, contact comfort , is that attachment is driven by tactile, comforting contact rather than by feeding, which is exactly the evidence Bowlby drew on. Trap: the answer is contact comfort, not nourishment; the wire mother provides the food but the infant bonds to the soft cloth one. Do not credit this to Bowlby or Ainsworth (it is Harlow), and do not confuse it with Konrad Lorenz's imprinting in geese, the other ethological attachment classic offered alongside. Definition An internal working model is the mental representation of self and others that an infant builds from early attachment experiences (am I worthy of care; are others reliable), and which then shapes expectations and behaviour in later relationships. It is the mechanism by which John Bowlby's early bond is carried forward into adult life. D · Memory & Cognition (off your paper) Full teaching in Section 6 . Proactive vs retroactive interference. Interference theory explains forgetting not as decay over time but as competition between memories, and the two directions are routinely flipped in distractors. Proactive interference is when OLD learning blocks the retrieval of NEW learning: your long-memorised old phone number keeps intruding when you try to recall the new one. The old material "proacts" forward in time onto the new. Retroactive interference is the reverse, when NEW learning blocks the retrieval of OLD : after drilling the new number, you can no longer dredge up the old one, because the new material "reaches back" onto the old. The key to keeping them straight is the direction of the arrow in time: in proactive interference the disruption travels forward (earlier disrupts later); in retroactive interference it travels backward (later disrupts earlier). Trap: they simply swap the two definitions and hope you pick the wrong one. Mnemonic to lock it: PRO = forward in time (the old pushes forward onto the new); RETRO = backward in time (the new reaches back onto the old). "Retro" means going back, so the new harms the old. Johari window. A model of self-awareness and interpersonal disclosure devised by Joseph Luft and Harrington Ingham (1955); the name is simply "Jo" plus "Hari." It maps what is known and unknown about a person across two axes (known to self versus not known to self; known to others versus not known to others) into four quadrants . The Open (arena) quadrant is known to self and known to others. The Blind (blind spot) quadrant is known to others but not to the self (your unconscious mannerisms). The Hidden (facade) quadrant is known to the self but kept from others (private feelings). The Unknown quadrant is known to neither (latent potential, repressed material). The model is dynamic: feedback from others shrinks the Blind area (they tell you what you could not see), and self-disclosure shrinks the Hidden area (you reveal what you were holding back), both enlarging the Open arena and improving communication. Trap: matching the quadrant to who-knows-what is the whole trick. Open = known to self and others; Blind = others know, you do not; Hidden = you know, others do not; Unknown = nobody knows. Feedback reduces the Blind spot; disclosure reduces the Hidden. The Atkinson-Shiffrin model and the memory stores. The multi-store (modal) model of Richard Atkinson and Richard Shiffrin (1968) is the spine most memory questions hang from, so its three stores and their parameters are examinable. Sensory memory holds an unprocessed sensory trace very briefly: the visual register ( iconic memory , demonstrated by George Sperling) lasts well under a second, and the auditory register ( echoic memory ) a few seconds. Attended material passes to short-term memory (STM) , of limited capacity ( Miller's "magical number seven, plus or minus two" chunks, 1956) and a duration of roughly 15 to 30 seconds unless rehearsed, with loss by decay and displacement. Rehearsal transfers material to long-term memory (LTM) , of effectively unlimited capacity and duration. Alan Baddeley and Graham Hitch (1974) later replaced the passive STM with a working memory model of an active central executive directing a phonological loop and a visuospatial sketchpad (the episodic buffer added in 2000). Trap: capacity belongs to STM (seven plus or minus two chunks, Miller); the very brief unlimited-capacity store is sensory memory, not STM. Iconic = visual, echoic = auditory; do not swap them. Working memory (Baddeley) is the active update of STM, not a synonym for LTM. Memory aid Johari quadrants by who knows: Open = both know; Blind = only others know (it is your blind spot); Hidden = only you know (your facade); Unknown = neither knows. " F eedback fights the B lind spot; disclosure dissolves the hidden." For interference: PRO = old pro jects forward; RETRO = new retro spects backward. Memory stores: " I conic eyes, E choic ears; 7 in the short term; forever in the long." E · Indian Psychology (off your paper) Full teaching in Appendix B . This is the cluster that has cost you across every mock, and Amity weights it heavier than NIMHANS does, so over-prepare it. Trigunas. In the Sāṁkhya philosophical system the three gunas are the fundamental qualities or strands out of which all of nature (Prakriti) is woven, and every mind and object is a shifting mixture of them. Sattva is the quality of purity, clarity, harmony, knowledge, and balance (the calm, lucid mind). Rajas is the quality of activity, passion, restlessness, desire, and movement (the agitated, driven mind). Tamas is the quality of inertia, dullness, heaviness, ignorance, and darkness (the lethargic, clouded mind). The three are always present together in differing proportions, and their changing balance accounts for the variety of temperaments and states; the spiritual aim in this tradition is to raise sattva and reduce rajas and tamas. Formal psychometric guna scales exist and are studied in the Indian-approaches paper, which is why the exact qualities matter. Trap: the examiners test which guna equals which quality. Tamas is the inert, dull, dark one, and it is the distractor they pair with "laziness, sleep, and ignorance." Do not let Tamas drift toward "activity" (that is Rajas) or "purity" (that is Sattva). Pancha kosha. The five sheaths (koshas) , from the Taittiriya Upanishad, are concentric layers wrapping the true Self, running from the grossest and outermost to the subtlest and innermost. Annamaya kosha is the food sheath, the physical body sustained by food (anna). Pranamaya kosha is the vital-energy or breath sheath (prana). Manomaya kosha is the mental or sensory-mind sheath (manas), the seat of ordinary thought and emotion. Vijnanamaya kosha is the intellect or wisdom sheath (vijnana, buddhi), the faculty of discrimination and judgement. Anandamaya kosha is the bliss sheath (ananda), the subtlest layer, closest to the Self. The ordering is the load-bearing fact: it runs body to bliss, gross to subtle (Annamaya, Pranamaya, Manomaya, Vijnanamaya, Anandamaya). Trap: getting the order wrong, or swapping Manomaya (mind) with Vijnanamaya (intellect) . Mind (manas, the sensory processor) sits below intellect (vijnana, the discriminating faculty) on the path inward. Purusha vs Prakriti. This is the central dualism of Sāṁkhya , and the contrast is exactly what the paper probes. Purusha is pure consciousness, the eternal, passive, unchanging witness (sakshi) ; it is aware but does nothing and has no qualities. Prakriti is primordial matter or nature, the active, unconscious creative principle out of which the entire material and mental world (including the mind and intellect) evolves; crucially, Prakriti is what carries the three gunas . Suffering arises from the mistaken identification of the witnessing Purusha with the activities of Prakriti; liberation (kaivalya) is the discriminative knowledge that separates the two, so that consciousness recognises it was only ever the witness, never the doer. Trap: assigning the gunas to Purusha. The gunas belong to Prakriti (matter/nature), never to the pure consciousness of Purusha. Purusha is qualityless and inactive; everything that has qualities or acts is Prakriti. The four avasthas. The four states of consciousness , set out in the Mandukya Upanishad alongside the syllable Aum. Jagrat is the waking state, awareness turned outward to the gross external world. Swapna is the dream state, awareness turned inward to a subtle world of its own making. Sushupti is deep, dreamless sleep, a state of undifferentiated bliss with no objects and no duality, but still touched by ignorance. Turiya , literally "the fourth," is not a fourth experience alongside the others but the pure consciousness that underlies and transcends all three , the witness present in waking, dreaming, and deep sleep alike; it is the goal, the Self itself. Trap: forgetting that Turiya is the fourth, transcendent state , not merely another, deeper stage of sleep. Sushupti is dreamless sleep; Turiya is the pure awareness beyond even that, and treating Turiya as "very deep sleep" is the classic error. Antahkarana. The antahkarana is the "inner instrument" or inner organ, the subtle psychological apparatus through which consciousness operates, classically analysed into four functions . Manas is the sensory or processing mind, which receives and coordinates the input of the senses and generates doubt and deliberation. Buddhi is the intellect, the faculty of discrimination, decision, and judgement that resolves doubt into determination. Ahamkara is the ego or "I-maker," the function that appropriates experience to a sense of self ("I am doing this"). Chitta is the storehouse of memory and accumulated impressions (samskaras). Together they form the instrument of mind, but they are emphatically not the Self; they are the apparatus that the Self (Atman) illumines and operates through. Trap: confusing Ahamkara (the ego, the I-maker) with Atman (the true Self) . The antahkarana, ego included, is the instrument; the Atman is the consciousness behind it. The ego is a function of the apparatus, not the witness. RCI 1986 vs 1993. The Rehabilitation Council of India (RCI) matters to you personally, because it is the statutory authority that regulates and licenses clinical psychologists in India, and the date pair is the examined fact. The RCI was first set up as a registered society in 1986 , an administrative body without statutory teeth. It was then given statutory status under the Rehabilitation Council of India Act, 1992 (which came into force in 1993 ), and a 2000 amendment widened its remit. As a statutory body it maintains the Central Rehabilitation Register, prescribes minimum standards for rehabilitation professionals (including clinical psychologists via the M.Phil and equivalent qualifications), and can take action against unqualified practitioners. Trap: the 1986 (registered society) versus 1992/1993 (statutory body under the RCI Act) distinction. The society predates the Act by six years; the examiners offer 1986 and 1992 side by side to see whether you know which event each year names. Exam trap The Indian-psychology cluster is built almost entirely from one-to-one matching traps: Tamas equals inertia (not activity); the gunas belong to Prakriti (not Purusha); Turiya is transcendent consciousness (not deep sleep, which is Sushupti); Ahamkara is the ego-function (not the Atman); and RCI was a society in 1986 but a statutory body in 1992/1993 . Learn each pairing in both directions, because the distractor is always the adjacent term in the same list. Appendix B · Indian Psychology (off your own paper) High-yield Read this whole part twice. On every Amity mock so far this has been your single weakest cluster, and Amity weights indigenous/Indian psychology more heavily than any other entrance you are sitting. That combination, hardest for you and worth the most marks, means you cannot afford to merely recognise the terms. You must over-learn them: know what each concept is , which text or darshana it comes from, its internal structure, an example, and the exact trap the paper sets. Treat the tables in this part as things to reproduce from memory, not just to read. 7.1 Orientation: the six darshanas and where psychology lives Before any single concept, fix the map. "Indian psychology" in this paper is not a modern empirical discipline with a laboratory; it is the body of doctrine about the self, the mind, consciousness, and personality that lies embedded inside classical Indian philosophy. To find that doctrine and to answer questions about its source (the examiners love "which darshana/which text does this come from?"), you must know the architecture of the six systems first. Everything later in this part hangs off this scaffold, so build it carefully. Classical Indian thought is organised into six orthodox philosophical systems, the shad darshanas ("six visions"; darshana literally means "a way of seeing", from the root drish , to see). They are āstika ("orthodox", literally "it-exists-ist") schools because they accept the authority ( pramana ) of the Vedas, as opposed to the nāstika ("heterodox") systems such as Buddhism, Jainism, and the materialist Charvaka, which reject Vedic authority. The single dividing criterion between āstika and nāstika is not belief in God; it is acceptance of the Veda as a valid source of knowledge. This is itself a tested point, because candidates assume "orthodox" means "theistic", which is wrong (Samkhya, for instance, is orthodox yet classically non-theistic). Definition A darshana is a systematic philosophical viewpoint or "vision" of reality. The shad darshanas are the six orthodox (āstika) systems that accept the Vedas. The line between āstika and nāstika is drawn by acceptance versus rejection of Vedic authority , not by belief in a personal God. The six are traditionally studied in three allied pairs, each pair sharing a method or subject: Pair The two darshanas Shared concern Logic and atomism Nyaya and Vaisheshika Epistemology, valid reasoning (Nyaya); the atomic constitution of matter and its categories (Vaisheshika) Enumeration and discipline Samkhya and Yoga The metaphysics of Purusha, Prakriti, and the gunas (Samkhya); the practical method of stilling the mind (Yoga) Ritual and the end of the Veda Mimamsa and Vedanta Interpretation of Vedic ritual action (Purva Mimamsa); the philosophy of the Upanishads, the self, and Brahman (Uttara Mimamsa, i.e. Vedanta) You do not need to master all six to the same depth. What you need is to know which schools carry the psychological content, the material about the self, mind, consciousness, and personality. That content sits in three of them, and you should be able to attribute any concept in this part to the right one at a glance. Samkhya (traditionally attributed to the sage Kapila , its classical text being the Samkhya-karika of Ishvara Krishna) gives the metaphysical scaffolding: the two ultimate categories Purusha and Prakriti , and the three gunas that make up everything in nature, including the mind. The word samkhya means "enumeration", because the system counts out the twenty-five evolutes of reality. Yoga (the system of Patanjali , whose text is the Yoga Sutras ) turns Samkhya's map into an applied psychology: a practical, eight-limbed method for controlling and stilling the mind. Samkhya is the theory; Yoga is the technique. They share a metaphysics, which is why they are paired. Vedanta (the philosophy distilled from the Upanishads , the closing portion of the Veda, hence "Vedanta" = "end of the Veda") gives the model of the self in layers (the koshas , from the Taittiriya Upanishad), the four states of consciousness (the avasthas , from the Mandukya Upanishad), the inner instrument ( antahkarana ), and the identity of Atman and Brahman . A concrete way to use this map: when a question quotes a concept and asks for its origin, run the three-way sort. Is it about the gunas or the two ultimate principles? Samkhya. Is it about a practical discipline, the eight limbs, breath control, or "stilling the mind"? Yoga. Is it about sheaths, states of consciousness, the inner instrument, or Self-and-absolute identity? Vedanta/Upanishads. That single reflex answers a large share of the source-attribution items. One more relationship is worth fixing now, because the paper tests it directly: Samkhya and Yoga are a matched pair that share one metaphysics. Samkhya supplies the worldview (Purusha, Prakriti, the gunas, the twenty-five tattvas) but is essentially atheistic and theoretical ; Yoga adopts that very worldview and adds two things, a practical method (the eight limbs) and the acceptance of Ishvara (a special, untainted Purusha, a focus for devotion), which makes Yoga theistic . So a clean way to remember the difference is: same map, but Yoga adds the method and adds Ishvara. Vedanta, by contrast, stands apart from both: it is non-dualist (one consciousness) where Samkhya-Yoga are dualist (consciousness separate from matter), a divergence taken up fully in 7.7. Holding these relations now means you will rarely misattribute a concept later. Exam trap Three snares cluster here. (1) Āstika does not mean theistic. It means Veda-accepting; Samkhya is āstika yet classically atheistic. (2) Vedanta is the same darshana as Uttara Mimamsa ; do not treat "the Upanishadic philosophy" and "Vedanta" as two different schools. (3) Buddhism, Jainism, and Charvaka are nāstika (heterodox), so any psychological doctrine the paper draws from the orthodox six is NOT Buddhist; a question may dangle "Buddhism" as the source of the koshas or gunas, which is wrong (they are Vedantic and Samkhya respectively). Memory aid The three pairs: " N yaya- V aisheshika, S amkhya- Y oga, M imamsa- V edanta." For the psychology, remember S-Y-V : S amkhya (the map), Y oga (the method), V edanta (the Self). Theory, technique, transcendence. 7.2 The Trigunas (from Sāṁkhya): the three strands of nature The trigunas are the most heavily tested single topic in this whole part, because they double as a metaphysics and as a personality model, and because the matching format ("which guna is which quality?") is so easy for the examiners to set. Learn them to the point of reflex. Samkhya holds that all of manifest nature, Prakriti (primordial matter; see 7.3), is woven from three fundamental qualities or constituents called the gunas . The word guna literally means "strand" or "rope", and the image is exactly that: three strands twisted together into the single rope of experienced reality. They are not parts you can separate out; they are co-present constituents whose changing proportions give every object and every mind its character. The three are Sattva , Rajas , and Tamas . They are described in the Samkhya-karika and are given an extended psychological and ethical treatment in the Bhagavad Gita (especially chapters 14, 17, and 18), which classifies food, action, knowledge, charity, and even faith by their dominant guna; that Gita material is itself examinable. The three qualities, in full Sattva is the quality of purity, clarity, harmony, balance, and knowledge. When sattva dominates, the mind is calm, luminous, and discerning; it is associated with wisdom, contentment, equanimity, and lightness. Its characteristic colour in the tradition is white, and its experiential signature is illumination (it is the guna that reveals ). Rajas is the quality of activity, passion, movement, and restlessness. When rajas dominates, there is drive, ambition, desire, agitation, and emotional turbulence; it is the principle of motion, craving, and effort, the engine that sets things going. Its colour is red, and its signature is activity (the guna that moves ). Tamas is the quality of inertia, dullness, heaviness, and darkness. When tamas dominates, there is laziness, sleep, lethargy, confusion, ignorance, and resistance to change; it is the principle that obscures and weighs down. Its colour is black, and its signature is restraint and concealment (the guna that veils ). The neat triad is therefore: sattva reveals, rajas activates, tamas restrains. The doctrine the paper tests The crucial doctrinal point, which the paper loves to test, is that everyone has all three gunas in varying proportion . The gunas are not three rigid types of people; they are three ingredients present in every mind and every object, and a person's temperament reflects which one currently predominates. They are also in constant flux and in mutual opposition: when one rises, the others are suppressed, so a single person is more sattvic in calm, clear moments, more rajasic when driven or angry, more tamasic when dull or sleepy. In Prakriti's unmanifest state the three are in perfect equilibrium; manifestation begins only when that equilibrium is disturbed. Because the gunas belong to Prakriti, they characterise the body and mind, never the pure witnessing consciousness (this is the load-bearing link to 7.3 below: gunas are of Prakriti, not Purusha). A worked example Take one student across a single day. At dawn, after rest, she reads with a quiet, focused, contented mind: sattva predominates. By midday a deadline grips her; she is driven, anxious, irritable, unable to sit still: rajas has risen and suppressed sattva. After a heavy lunch she is foggy, sleepy, and cannot be bothered to start: tamas now dominates. Same person, same day, three guna-states. That is precisely how the tradition (and the Gita) wants you to see temperament: not a fixed label but a shifting balance. The modern-psychology bridge Indian-approaches research has operationalised this into formal psychometrics. The Guna scales (for example, instruments developed in the Indian psychology literature to measure sattva, rajas, and tamas as personality dimensions) attempt to assess a person's guna profile much as Western inventories assess traits. You should recognise that the trigunas are not only a philosophical idea but a measured personality model in the formal study of Indian approaches to personality, the indigenous counterpart to a Western trait inventory. If a question asks "the Indian/indigenous model of personality based on three innate qualities", the answer is the triguna model. Guna Core quality Psychological expression Typical distractor it is confused with Sattva Purity, clarity, harmony, knowledge, balance Calm, wise, content, luminous, discerning Mislabelled as the "active" one (that is Rajas) Rajas Activity, passion, restlessness, movement Driven, ambitious, craving, agitated, emotional Mislabelled as the "pure" one (that is Sattva) Tamas Inertia, dullness, darkness, heaviness Lazy, sleepy, confused, ignorant, resistant Mislabelled as "active" or "passionate" (it is the opposite) Definition The trigunas are the three constituent qualities of Prakriti (manifest nature): Sattva (clarity, that which reveals), Rajas (activity, that which moves), and Tamas (inertia, that which veils). They are co-present in everything in varying, ever-shifting proportions; temperament is the ratio currently dominant. Exam trap The matching item, "which guna corresponds to which quality", is the most common form. Tamas is the inert, dull, dark, sleepy one. The paper plants laziness/sleep/heaviness as distractors and tries to attach them to the wrong guna, or asks you to identify "the quality of inertia" and offers Rajas as a tempting decoy because Rajas also sounds negative. Lock it down: Sattva = clarity, Rajas = activity, Tamas = inertia. Sattva and Rajas are NOT interchangeable; Sattva is the calm/pure one, Rajas is the restless/active one. A further snare: "the gunas are types of people" is false; they are ingredients present in everyone in varying proportion. Memory aid Alphabetical S-R-T runs clarity → activity → inertia, i.e. best → middle → heaviest. " S attva = S erene, R ajas = R estless, T amas = T ired." Three Ts for Tamas: Tired, Torpid, dark (Tamas itself literally means darkness). Colours: white, red, black, top to bottom. 7.3 Purusha vs Prakriti: Sāṁkhya dualism This is the metaphysical core of Samkhya and the hinge on which the guna doctrine and much of Yoga turn. The whole system is a dualism of two ultimate, irreducible categories, and almost every Samkhya trap is a swap of one principle's attributes onto the other. Teach yourself the two columns until the swap is instantly visible. Purusha: the inactive witness Purusha (literally "person" or "spirit") is pure consciousness, the witness ( sakshi ). It is inactive, attributeless ( nirguna , "without gunas"), changeless, and merely observes. It does nothing; it simply illuminates, the way a lamp lights a room without itself acting on the furniture. Importantly, in classical Samkhya Purusha is plural : there are many purushas, one for each conscious being, which sharply distinguishes Samkhya from Vedanta's single universal consciousness (a contrast the paper exploits, see 7.7). Purusha is conscious but does nothing; it is the seer that never becomes the seen. Prakriti: the active matrix Prakriti (literally "nature", "the primary matter") is primordial matter or nature, the active, creative principle. Prakriti is unconscious but dynamic : a paradox worth stating clearly, because it is the exact inverse of Purusha (which is conscious but static). Prakriti carries the three gunas described above. In its unmanifest state ( mula-prakriti , "root-nature") the three gunas are in perfect equilibrium and nothing is manifest; when that balance is disturbed (in the presence of Purusha), Prakriti begins to evolve and unfolds, in a fixed order, into the whole manifest world: first mahat/buddhi (the cosmic intellect), then ahamkara (ego), then manas (mind) together with the senses and the subtle and gross elements, twenty-three evolutes in all. Everything you can perceive, including your own mind, intellect, ego, and personality, is a product of Prakriti. Counting Purusha and Prakriti themselves with the twenty-three evolutes gives Samkhya's famous twenty-five tattvas (principles). How bondage and liberation work The manifest world arises from the interaction of these two. Purusha's mere presence, like a magnet near iron filings (or, in the classical simile, like a lame man of clear sight riding a blind man of strong legs), disturbs Prakriti's equilibrium and sets evolution in motion; consciousness gets "reflected" in the evolving intellect (buddhi), producing the illusion that the witness is the doer. Bondage is precisely this confusion: pure consciousness mistaking itself for the activities of Prakriti, identifying "I am acting, I am suffering" when in truth only Prakriti acts and only Purusha witnesses. Liberation (kaivalya, "aloneness/isolation") is achieved through discriminative knowledge (viveka) , the clear discernment that separates Purusha from Prakriti, so that consciousness recognises it was never the doer, the gunas cease to bind, and Purusha rests, isolated, in its own nature. Note the word: liberation in Samkhya is kaivalya (isolation of the witness), not the union/merger implied by Vedantic moksha. That precise term is examinable. Purusha Prakriti What it is Pure consciousness, the witness Primordial matter / nature Active or inactive? Inactive, only observes Active, creative, evolves Conscious? Conscious (pure awareness) Unconscious but dynamic Carries the gunas? No (nirguna, attributeless) Yes, the three gunas belong here Number Plural (many) One Liberation Kaivalya: viveka separating it from Prakriti Ceases to bind once discrimination dawns A worked illustration of the confusion Picture a clear mirror (Purusha) set before a moving film (Prakriti). The mirror does nothing; it only reflects. But the reflection of the moving film in the mirror makes it look as though the stillness itself is moving, as though the witness is the actor. That false transfer (movement and agency mistakenly attributed to the motionless reflector) is bondage. When discrimination (viveka) dawns and you see that the mirror was always still and only the film moved, the misidentification dissolves: that is kaivalya. The film keeps running; you simply stop calling it "I". This is the exact reasoning a question expects when it asks "what, in Samkhya, is the cause of bondage?" (answer: non-discrimination, the confusion of Purusha with Prakriti) and "what removes it?" (answer: viveka, discriminative knowledge). The modern-psychology bridge The Samkhya split maps loosely onto the distinction between pure awareness and the contents of mind . Where Western psychology generally treats consciousness as a product of the mental apparatus (a function of the brain/mind), Samkhya inverts the relation: the mental apparatus (buddhi, ahamkara, manas) is unconscious machinery, and consciousness (Purusha) is a separate, prior witness merely reflected in it. This "consciousness as witness, not as content" stance is what makes Indian psychology distinctive in a comparative question, and it is the conceptual seed of the meditative observer stance that Yoga then operationalises. Exam trap The headline trap: the three gunas belong to PRAKRITI, not Purusha. A question will say "the gunas are qualities of ___" and offer Purusha as the wrong answer. Purusha is pure, attributeless (nirguna) witnessing consciousness; it has no gunas, no activity, and no change. A second trap pairs the wrong adjective with the wrong principle: Purusha is the inactive conscious witness; Prakriti is the active unconscious matter. If you ever read "active consciousness" or "inactive matter", a swap has been performed. A third trap: Purusha is plural in Samkhya (many witnesses) and liberation is kaivalya (isolation), not merger; the single-consciousness, merger picture belongs to Advaita Vedanta, not Samkhya. Memory aid " Pur usha is pur e and passive ; Pra kriti is pra ctical and productive ." Two P-words each. The witness is conscious-but-still; matter is active-but-blind. Gunas live with the active one (Prakriti). 7.4 The Pancha Kosha: the five sheaths of the self The doctrine of the five sheaths comes from the Taittiriya Upanishad (in its Brahmananda Valli section) and is a central Vedantic model of the self. The idea is that the true Self ( Atman ) is wrapped in five concentric coverings or koshas ("sheaths"; the word means a scabbard or husk), arranged from the grossest and most external to the subtlest and most internal, like the layers of an onion or the husks around a kernel. The Sanskrit suffix -maya means "made of" or "consisting of", so each name reads "the sheath consisting of ___". Spiritual realisation involves seeing through each sheath in turn (the method of neti neti , "not this, not this", negating identification with each layer) until the Atman, which is none of them, is realised beyond and through them. The five sheaths, gross to subtle The five, in order from gross to subtle, are: Annamaya kosha , the food sheath, the physical body built from and sustained by food ( anna = food); it is the densest covering, born of food, growing by food, returning to food. Pranamaya kosha , the vital-energy sheath, the layer of breath and life-force ( prana ) that animates the body and drives respiration, circulation, and the physiological functions; it is what makes the food-body a living body. Manomaya kosha , the mental sheath, the layer of mind and emotions ( manas = mind), of sensory processing, feeling, desire, doubt, and ordinary discursive thought; it is the seat of the wavering, perceiving, emoting mind. Vijnanamaya kosha , the wisdom/intellect sheath, the layer of vijnana : intellect, discrimination, judgement, the higher knowing and deciding faculty (it corresponds to buddhi ); it is the layer that discerns and resolves rather than merely processes. Anandamaya kosha , the bliss sheath, the subtlest and innermost layer, associated with deep peace and bliss ( ananda ), the causal-body covering closest to the Self, experienced most directly in deep dreamless sleep. The trajectory, and a Western anchor Note the trajectory carefully: it runs body → bliss, gross → subtle, outer → inner. The physical body is outermost because it is the densest; bliss is innermost because it is the subtlest and nearest to Atman. A useful (loose) mapping for revision: the five sheaths roughly track physical body, physiology/vitality, mind-and-emotion, intellect/cognition, and a deep affective ground, a layered model of the person not unlike a tiered biopsychosocial picture, except that the Vedantic point is the opposite of a hierarchy of needs : it is a hierarchy of identifications to be transcended . The Atman itself is not a sixth sheath; it is the consciousness that the sheaths cover, realised when one no longer identifies with any of them. The koshas are also grouped into the three bodies ( sharira ): Annamaya is the gross body ( sthula sharira ); Pranamaya, Manomaya, and Vijnanamaya make up the subtle body ( sukshma sharira ); and Anandamaya is the causal body ( karana sharira ). That three-body grouping is a step-up fact the harder papers reach for. # Kosha Sheath of Meaning / root 1 (grossest) Annamaya Food / physical body anna = food; the body made of and fed by food 2 Pranamaya Vital breath / energy prana = life-force; breath and vitality 3 Manomaya Mind / emotions manas = mind; sensory processing, feeling, thought 4 Vijnanamaya Intellect / wisdom / discrimination vijnana = higher knowing, judgement (buddhi) 5 (subtlest) Anandamaya Bliss ananda = bliss; nearest to Atman Definition The pancha kosha (five sheaths), from the Taittiriya Upanishad , are five concentric coverings of the Atman, from gross to subtle: Annamaya (food/body), Pranamaya (vital energy), Manomaya (mind/emotion), Vijnanamaya (intellect/discrimination), Anandamaya (bliss). The suffix -maya means "made of". The Atman is not a sheath; it is what the sheaths cover. Exam trap Two traps live here. First, ordering : the paper scrambles the five and asks for the gross-to-subtle sequence. Memorise Anna → Prana → Mano → Vijnana → Ananda (food, breath, mind, intellect, bliss). Second, the Manomaya/Vijnanamaya swap : Manomaya is the mind/emotion sheath (lower, processing, feeling); Vijnanamaya is the intellect/discrimination/wisdom sheath (higher, judging). The paper will define "the sheath of discriminative intellect" and offer Manomaya as the decoy, or define "the sheath of mind and emotion" and offer Vijnanamaya. Mind is below intellect, just as Manomaya (3rd) is below Vijnanamaya (4th). A third trap: the source is the Taittiriya Upanishad, not the Mandukya (the Mandukya gives the four states, 7.5); and Atman is not a sixth kosha. Memory aid " A P erson M ay V iew A tman", Anna, Prana, Mano, Vijnana, Ananda. The order also climbs a person: body, breath, mind, intellect, bliss, from the physical you can touch up to the bliss nearest the Self. 7.5 The Four Avasthas: states of consciousness The Mandukya Upanishad , the shortest of the principal Upanishads (just twelve verses, yet traditionally said to suffice for liberation on its own), sets out four states ( avasthas ) of consciousness and maps them onto the sacred syllable AUM (OM) . This is one of the most elegant testable structures in Indian psychology, because it links a phenomenology of consciousness (waking, dreaming, sleeping, and the ground beyond) to the three phonemes of OM plus the silence that follows. The first three are familiar experiential states; the fourth is the transcendent ground in which the other three appear and disappear. The four states, in full Jagrat is the waking state, in which consciousness is turned outward to the gross physical world through the senses; the knower here is called vaishvanara or vishva , the experiencer of gross objects, and it corresponds to the Annamaya/gross body. Swapna is the dream state, in which consciousness is turned inward and experiences a subtle world of mental impressions and images, with no external sensory input; the knower is taijasa ("the luminous one"), the experiencer of subtle objects, corresponding to the subtle body. Sushupti is deep dreamless sleep, a state of undifferentiated rest in which there are no dreams and no duality of subject and object, experienced as peace but without articulated awareness or content; the knower is prajna ("the knower"), associated with the causal body and the bliss sheath (this is why Anandamaya is linked to deep sleep). And Turiya , literally "the fourth" (from turiya = fourth), is pure consciousness itself, the substratum that underlies and transcends the other three. Turiya is not a fourth experience alongside waking, dreaming, and sleeping; it is the silent, changeless awareness that is present in and beyond all of them, the witness that knows the waker, the dreamer, and the sleeper alike. It is described apophatically: not outward-knowing, not inward-knowing, not a mass of cognition, ungraspable, the cessation of phenomena, peace, the Self. The AUM mapping and a worked illustration In the AUM mapping, the three sounds A-U-M correspond to waking, dream, and deep sleep respectively: A (the open sound made at the back, the first and grossest) is Jagrat; U (the sound that rolls forward, intermediate and subtle) is Swapna; M (the closing hum with the lips shut, the resolution) is Sushupti. Turiya is the silence after the sound of OM: the soundless awareness in which the whole syllable arises, sounds, and subsides. A way to feel the logic: chant a single OM. The voice opens (A), rolls (U), closes to a hum (M), and then there is a pause of pure attentive silence before the next breath. That silence is not a fourth noise ; it is the stillness that held all three. Turiya stands to the three states exactly as that silence stands to the three sounds. The modern-psychology bridge The first three avasthas line up neatly with constructs Western sleep science also recognises: Jagrat with the waking EEG, Swapna with REM/dreaming sleep, and Sushupti with deep slow-wave (NREM stage 3) dreamless sleep. The decisive difference is Turiya, which has no Western sleep-stage analogue at all, because it is not a physiological state of the brain but a claim about a witnessing consciousness that persists across states. That is precisely why it is the favourite trap: the examiner offers Turiya as if it were a deeper kind of sleep, when the doctrine insists it is wakeful awareness underlying sleep itself. State What it is Consciousness directed Knower AUM correspondence Jagrat Waking Outward, to the gross world Vaishvanara / Vishva A Swapna Dream Inward, to subtle impressions Taijasa U Sushupti Deep dreamless sleep Undifferentiated rest, no objects Prajna M Turiya "The fourth": pure consciousness Transcends all three; the witness The Self / Atman The silence after OM Definition The four avasthas , from the Mandukya Upanishad , are states of consciousness mapped onto OM: Jagrat (waking, A), Swapna (dream, U), Sushupti (deep dreamless sleep, M), and Turiya ("the fourth", the silence after OM): pure witnessing consciousness underlying and transcending the other three. Exam trap Turiya is the fourth, transcendent state, not a stage of sleep. The paper exploits the fact that three of the four are ordinary daily states and tries to make you treat Turiya as just "very deep sleep" or another sleep phase. It is the opposite: it is pure wakeful awareness underlying everything, the witness of waking, dreaming, and sleeping alike. Also do not confuse Sushupti (deep dreamless sleep) with Swapna (the dream state). And keep the AUM mapping the right way round: A = waking, U = dream, M = deep sleep, silence = Turiya; reversing A and M (waking versus deep sleep) is a standard distractor. If a question says "the state associated with the silence after OM" or "pure consciousness beyond the other three", the answer is Turiya. Memory aid " A wake, d U ream, slee M ", then silence. A-U-M reads top to bottom as waking → dream → deep sleep, gross → subtle → causal, exactly the kosha order of bodies; Turiya is the quiet that holds the whole syllable. Swapna has a "p" like sleeP-dream; Sushupti is the deepest "shhh". 7.6 Antahkarana: the inner instrument of mind Antahkarana (from antah = inner, and karana = instrument or organ) means the "inner instrument", the internal apparatus of mind in Vedantic and Samkhya-derived psychology. It is the mental machinery through which consciousness operates: the tool that perceives, thinks, decides, claims, and remembers. The single most important conceptual point, the one the whole doctrine is built around, is that the antahkarana is an instrument , a product and evolute of Prakriti (primordial nature), and therefore not the conscious Self that wields it. Pure consciousness (Purusha, or in Vedanta the Atman) is the user; the antahkarana is the used. When the Upanishads speak of mind as a chariot's reins and the senses as horses, the reins are antahkarana, and the rider beyond them is the Self. This builds directly on the Purusha-versus-Prakriti split: everything you can observe about your own inner life, the very fact that you can watch a thought arise, decide, or recall a memory, is the activity of an instrument, watched by a witness that is not itself an instrument. The antahkarana is classically analysed into four functions or aspects. They are not four separate organs sitting in different places; they are four modes or operations of one inner instrument, distinguished by what each does to a piece of experience as it passes through. The four are Manas, Buddhi, Ahamkara, and Chitta. Manas (from manas = mind) is the sensory and processing mind. It is the faculty that receives raw sense impressions from the five sense organs, coordinates and synthesises them into a coherent percept, and runs the back-and-forth of ordinary thinking: doubt, deliberation, desire, wishing, and wavering. Manas is characteristically indecisive ; it presents options and oscillates ("shall I, shall I not"), but it does not settle them. Buddhi (from budh = to know, to awaken) is the intellect, the higher faculty of discrimination ( viveka ), judgement, determination, and decision. Where Manas wavers, Buddhi concludes: it is the function that resolves doubt, discriminates true from false and right from wrong, and issues the final determination. It is the closest of the four to pure consciousness and the one most capable of reflecting the light of the Self clearly. Ahamkara (from aham = I, and kara = maker) is the ego or "I-maker", the function that appropriates experience to a self. It takes the impersonal stream of perception and decision and stamps it with "I" and "mine": "I am seeing this", "this is my thought", "I am the doer". It is Ahamkara that generates the felt sense of being a separate individual agent and that mistakenly identifies the witnessing Self with the body and mind. Chitta (from cit = to be conscious, here in the sense of the mind-field) is the memory store or "mind-stuff", the reservoir in which impressions ( samskaras ) left by past experience are deposited and from which they later resurface as memory, habit, and disposition. Chitta is the substrate on which the other three operate; in Patanjali's Yoga the entire mind-field that yoga sets out to still is called chitta, which is why you will meet the word again in the next subsection but one. Definition The antahkarana ("inner instrument") is the fourfold inner apparatus of mind: Manas (sensory/processing mind, doubt and desire), Buddhi (intellect, discrimination and decision), Ahamkara (ego, the "I-maker"), and Chitta (memory store of impressions). It is an evolute of Prakriti, an instrument used by consciousness, never consciousness itself. Function Role Sanskrit root One-word handle Manas Sensory/processing mind; receives impressions, coordinates senses, doubts, desires, wavers manas = mind Mind Buddhi Intellect; discrimination (viveka), judgement, determination, decision; resolves the doubt Manas raised budh = to know Decide Ahamkara Ego, the "I-maker"; appropriates experience, generates the sense of I and mine, identifies Self with body-mind aham = I Ego Chitta Memory store, mind-stuff; reservoir of impressions (samskaras) from which memory and habit resurface cit = consciousness/mind-field Memory A concrete worked example makes the division clear. Suppose you are walking at dusk and see a coiled shape on the path. Manas takes in the visual impression and presents the raw, unresolved data, registering "something coiled, long, on the path", and immediately wavers ("snake? rope?"). Buddhi then discriminates and decides: after a second look it concludes "that is a rope, not a snake". Ahamkara personalises the whole episode: "I was frightened", "I saw it", "my heart is pounding". And Chitta stores the impression, so that next time you pass that spot at dusk a faint memory-trace of fear stirs before you even look. One event, four operations, one instrument. High-yield Manas doubts/processes , Buddhi decides/discriminates , Ahamkara claims (ego, "I") , Chitta remembers (stores samskaras) . The Manas-versus-Buddhi split (wavering mind below, deciding intellect above) is the same mind-versus-intellect distinction you met in the koshas (Manomaya below Vijnanamaya). Ahamkara is the ego-function, NOT the true Self. Modern-psychology mapping. The antahkarana is, in effect, a faculty model of the mind that predates and parallels Western componential accounts. Manas, as the receiver and integrator of sense data that then hesitates, maps loosely onto sensory registration and the deliberative, conflict-laden side of decision-making. Buddhi, as the executive that discriminates and commits to a choice, maps onto executive function and judgement (the prefrontal "decider"). Ahamkara, the I-maker, anticipates modern constructs of the self-concept, ego, and the narrative sense of agency (compare the psychoanalytic ego that mediates and identifies, and contemporary work on the "self as object"). Chitta, the reservoir of impressions that shapes later behaviour without being consciously retrieved, maps onto long-term and implicit memory and onto the way stored dispositions (samskaras) function like learned habits or schemas. You can present the four-function model in the paper as an indigenous faculty psychology that distinguishes perception, executive judgement, self-reference, and memory, the same broad divisions a modern cognitive account would draw, but framed around an instrument used by a witnessing consciousness. How it is tested. The commonest item is a one-to-one match: "which component of the antahkarana is the intellect/decision faculty?" (Buddhi), "which is the ego/I-maker?" (Ahamkara), "which is the memory store?" (Chitta), "which receives sense impressions and doubts?" (Manas). A second form asks you to list the four components of the antahkarana, where the trap is to slip in Atman or Purusha as a supposed fifth. A third form gives a behavioural vignette (like the rope-snake above) and asks which faculty performs the discrimination. Exam trap Do not confuse Ahamkara (ego) with Atman (the true Self). Ahamkara is the false "I", the ego-function that mistakes itself for the Self; Atman is the real Self that the ego obscures. The whole point of the antahkarana doctrine is that this fourfold inner instrument is the apparatus of mind, a product of Prakriti, and the Self merely witnesses it. A question may ask "which is the I-maker / ego function?" (answer: Ahamkara) and dangle Atman as a trap, or ask "which is NOT a function of the antahkarana?" with Atman (or Purusha) as the correct exclusion. Also keep Manas (the wavering, processing mind) distinct from Buddhi (the deciding intellect): the paper defines "the faculty of discrimination and decision" and offers Manas as the decoy, exactly the same mind-versus-intellect swap it plays with Manomaya and Vijnanamaya in the koshas. Memory aid " M ind B uys A C ar": Manas, Buddhi, Ahamkara, Chitta. Manas senses and wavers, Buddhi decides, Ahamkara claims it as "mine", Chitta remembers it. Read in that order it is also a tiny story: you perceive, you judge, you own, you store. 7.7 Atman and Brahman: the Vedantic identity Vedanta (literally "the end/culmination of the Vedas", the body of teaching distilled from the Upanishads) turns on two terms and the claim that they are one. Atman (from an / at , breath/self) is the individual true Self, the innermost, unchanging consciousness, what you really are beneath the five koshas and behind the fourfold antahkarana. It is not the body, not the breath, not the mind, not the intellect, and not the ego; it is the pure awareness that illuminates all of these and is the constant witness of them. Brahman (from brh = to grow great, to expand) is the ultimate, infinite, attributeless reality, the absolute ground and source of everything that exists. Brahman is classically described as Sat-Chit-Ananda : sat (pure being/existence), chit (pure consciousness), and ananda (pure bliss). The decisive teaching of the Upanishads is that Atman and Brahman are, at the deepest level, identical: the consciousness at the core of the individual is numerically the same as the consciousness that is the ground of the cosmos. The wave is not a separate thing from the ocean; it is the ocean in a particular form. This identity is crystallised in the mahavakyas , the "great sayings", short Upanishadic declarations each drawn from one of the four Vedas, which the tradition treats as the most condensed statements of the truth. The four standardly cited are: Mahavakya Translation Source (Veda / Upanishad) What it asserts Tat Tvam Asi "That thou art" / "You are That" Sama Veda (Chandogya Upanishad) The individual Self is the universal reality Aham Brahmasmi "I am Brahman" Yajur Veda (Brihadaranyaka Upanishad) The Self, from the first person, is the absolute Prajnanam Brahma "Consciousness is Brahman" Rig Veda (Aitareya Upanishad) Pure consciousness is the ultimate reality Ayam Atma Brahma "This Self is Brahman" Atharva Veda (Mandukya Upanishad) The very Self here is Brahman Of these, "Tat Tvam Asi" ("That thou art") is by far the most tested. It comes from the dialogue in the Chandogya Upanishad in which the sage Uddalaka repeatedly tells his son Shvetaketu, "tat tvam asi", that subtle essence which is the Self of all this, that thou art. The phrase compresses the entire non-dualist position into three words: the "That" (Brahman, the universal) and the "thou" (Atman, the individual) are joined by "art" (are identical). Definition Atman = the individual true Self, the innermost witnessing consciousness. Brahman = the ultimate, infinite, attributeless reality (Sat-Chit-Ananda: being, consciousness, bliss). Vedanta's core claim is their identity, expressed in the mahavakya "Tat Tvam Asi" ("That thou art"). The school that takes this identity most strictly is Advaita Vedanta ("non-dualism", literally "not-two"), systematised by Shankara (Adi Shankaracharya, c. 8th century CE). Advaita holds that there is only one reality without a second: Atman is Brahman, fully and without remainder, and the apparent multiplicity of the world, the many separate selves and objects, is maya , an appearance produced by avidya (ignorance) superimposed on the one reality. The stock analogy is the rope mistaken for a snake (the same image used for Buddhi above): the snake was never really there, only the rope; likewise the manifold world is a misperception of the one Brahman. Bondage is this ignorance; liberation (moksha) is not the production of anything new but the direct realisation (not merely the belief) that the Self always already was Brahman. This is sometimes glossed as the difference between knowing the fact intellectually and awakening to it. Modern-psychology mapping. Atman as the constant witnessing awareness behind all changing mental contents anticipates the distinction between the "I" (the self-as-knower, the pure subject) and the "Me" (the self-as-known, the empirical self-concept) drawn by William James, with Atman corresponding to the witnessing "I" and the koshas/antahkarana corresponding to the constructed "Me". The Advaitic claim that suffering is rooted in mistaken self-identification (taking oneself to be the body-mind) and that relief comes through dis-identifying the witness from its contents resonates strongly with the stance-shift cultivated in mindfulness-based and acceptance-based therapies (observing thoughts as passing events rather than as the self). Transpersonal psychology has drawn on Atman-Brahman identity directly as a model of self-transcendence. High-yield Atman = individual Self; Brahman = universal absolute; they are identical . The headline mahavakya is "Tat Tvam Asi" ("That thou art") from the Chandogya Upanishad. Advaita Vedanta (non-dualism) was systematised by Shankara ; the world's multiplicity is maya ; liberation is realising Atman = Brahman. Exam trap Note the contrast with Samkhya, which the paper deliberately blurs. Samkhya is dualist (many separate purushas, eternally distinct from prakriti; liberation is kaivalya , isolation). Advaita Vedanta is strictly non-dualist (one consciousness only, Atman = Brahman; liberation is moksha , realising non-difference). A question may attribute "Atman = Brahman / non-dualism" to Samkhya, or attribute "plural selves / dualism" to Advaita; both are reversed. Second trap: do not confuse Atman with Ahamkara , the ego-function of the antahkarana. Ahamkara is the false "I" that obscures Atman; Atman is the real Self. Third: "Tat Tvam Asi" is the famous mahavakya, but the paper may offer "Aham Brahmasmi" or "Prajnanam Brahma" and ask for the source Upanishad, so learn at least that Tat Tvam Asi comes from the Chandogya. 7.8 Yoga and Patanjali: the applied psychology of mind-control The Yoga Sutras of Patanjali (a text of roughly 196 terse aphorisms, the sutras , compiled around the 2nd century BCE to 4th century CE) are the foundational text of the Yoga darshana. Yoga is the practical twin of Samkhya: it accepts Samkhya's whole metaphysics (Purusha as pure consciousness, Prakriti as nature, the three gunas, the goal of separating consciousness from its entanglement in nature) but adds two things Samkhya lacks: the acceptance of Ishvara (a special Purusha, a focus for devotion) and, above all, a systematic method . This is why Yoga functions as an applied Indian psychology: it is not merely a theory of mind but a step-by-step technology for transforming and stilling it. Patanjali's definition of yoga, given in the second sutra, is the single most quoted line in the whole of Indian psychology: "yogaḥ citta-vṛtti-nirodhaḥ" . Parsed term by term: yogah = yoga (union, or the disciplined stilling that leads to it); chitta = the mind-stuff, the whole mental field (the same chitta you met as the memory-reservoir of the antahkarana, here standing for the entire mind); vritti = a modification, fluctuation, or wave of that mind-field (a thought, perception, memory, or imagining); nirodha = restraint, cessation, stilling. So yoga is the stilling (nirodha) of the modifications (vrittis) of the mind-stuff (chitta) . The mind is normally a restless stream of these vrittis; yoga is the systematic quieting of them. The very next sutra states the payoff: tada drashtuh svarupe avasthanam , "then the seer (Purusha) abides in its own true nature". When the waves of the mind subside, the witnessing consciousness, no longer identified with the mental turbulence, rests as itself. (Patanjali classifies the vrittis into five kinds: pramana right knowledge, viparyaya error, vikalpa imagination/verbal construction, nidra sleep, and smriti memory.) Definition Patanjali defines yoga as citta-vritti-nirodha : the stilling (nirodha) of the modifications/fluctuations (vrittis) of the mind-stuff (chitta). When the mind's waves are stilled, the seer (Purusha) rests in its own nature. This is the most-tested single line in Indian psychology. Before the limbs, Patanjali names the obstacles the method must overcome: the five kleshas (afflictions), the root causes of suffering and bondage that colour and disturb the mind. They are: Avidya (ignorance, specifically mistaking the impermanent for the permanent and the non-Self for the Self; this is the root klesha from which the other four grow), Asmita (egoism, the false identification of consciousness with the instrument of mind, essentially the ahamkara error), Raga (attachment, craving for pleasure), Dvesha (aversion, the recoil from pain), and Abhinivesha (clinging to life, the deep-seated fear of death that grips even the wise). Yoga's practices are designed to thin and finally uproot these kleshas, with avidya as the master root: remove ignorance and the rest lose their soil. Klesha Translation What it is Avidya Ignorance Mistaking the impermanent for permanent, non-Self for Self; the root affliction Asmita Egoism Identifying pure consciousness with the mind/instrument (the ahamkara error) Raga Attachment Craving and clinging to pleasure Dvesha Aversion Recoiling from and resisting pain Abhinivesha Clinging to life The instinctive fear of death; will-to-live The method itself is the eight limbs (ashtanga , from ashta = eight and anga = limb ) , also called raja yoga ("royal yoga") or ashtanga yoga . The eight progress from outer ethical and physical discipline toward inner mental absorption, each limb preparing the ground for the next: # Limb Meaning What it involves 1 Yama Ethical restraints (toward others) Non-violence (ahimsa), truthfulness (satya), non-stealing (asteya), continence (brahmacharya), non-possessiveness (aparigraha) 2 Niyama Personal observances (toward oneself) Purity (saucha), contentment (santosha), austerity (tapas), self-study (svadhyaya), surrender to Ishvara (ishvara-pranidhana) 3 Asana Posture A steady, comfortable seated posture for prolonged stillness 4 Pranayama Breath regulation Control and extension of the breath (prana = vital force) 5 Pratyahara Sense-withdrawal Withdrawing the senses inward, detaching attention from external objects 6 Dharana Concentration Fixing attention on a single point or object 7 Dhyana Meditation Sustained, unbroken flow of attention on that object 8 Samadhi Absorption Complete absorption; meditator and object merge, the mind is fully stilled A structural point the paper rewards: the first five limbs (Yama to Pratyahara) are the "outer" or external limbs ( bahiranga ) , preparing the body, conduct, and senses; the last three (Dharana, Dhyana, Samadhi) are the "inner" limbs ( antaranga ) , and together this concentrative trio is given a special name, samyama . The three differ only in degree of continuity : Dharana is attention repeatedly returned to one point (it keeps slipping and being brought back); Dhyana is attention flowing unbroken to that point (a steady stream); Samadhi is attention so total that the sense of a separate meditator dissolves and only the object shines. Worked example: a student told to concentrate on a candle flame who keeps catching the mind wandering and dragging it back is in Dharana; when the attention finally settles into a continuous, effortless rest on the flame, that is Dhyana; if self-awareness drops away and "only flame" remains, with no felt watcher, that is Samadhi. High-yield Yoga = citta-vritti-nirodha (stilling the mind's modifications). The eight limbs in order : Yama, Niyama, Asana, Pranayama, Pratyahara, Dharana, Dhyana, Samadhi. First five = outer/external limbs; last three (Dharana-Dhyana-Samadhi) = inner limbs, collectively samyama . The five kleshas : Avidya (root), Asmita, Raga, Dvesha, Abhinivesha. Modern-psychology mapping. Patanjali's system is, in contemporary terms, an attention-training and emotion-regulation technology, and it is the explicit ancestor of clinical mindfulness and meditation research. Pratyahara (disengaging the senses from external pulls) and Dharana-Dhyana (focused, then sustained, attention) correspond closely to the focused-attention and open-monitoring practices studied in mindfulness, and the progression Dharana to Dhyana to Samadhi maps onto deepening concentrative absorption. The kleshas read as an indigenous cognitive model of suffering: avidya (a core cognitive distortion about self and permanence) generating attachment and aversion (the approach-avoidance drivers of much clinical distress), with abhinivesha as existential/death anxiety. The yamas and niyamas function as a values-and-conduct framework comparable to the values work in acceptance and commitment therapy. You can legitimately present ashtanga yoga in the exam as a structured, staged programme of behavioural discipline, attentional training, and cognitive insight aimed at regulating the mind. How it is tested. The most frequent items are: complete or order the eight limbs (often with one or two blanked or scrambled); identify a named limb from its description ("withdrawal of the senses" = Pratyahara; "steady posture" = Asana; "breath control" = Pranayama); recall the definition of yoga (citta-vritti-nirodha) and who gave it (Patanjali); and list the five kleshas or name the root one (Avidya). A subtler item asks for the difference between Dharana, Dhyana, and Samadhi, or for the collective name of the inner three (samyama). Exam trap Order and identity traps dominate. The classic snare is swapping Dharana (concentration, attention fixed on a point) with Dhyana (meditation, the unbroken flow), or placing Pratyahara (sense-withdrawal, limb 5) after the concentrative limbs instead of before them. Lock the sequence: senses are withdrawn (Pratyahara) before concentration begins (Dharana). A second trap attributes the definition citta-vritti-nirodha to the wrong school or sage; it is Patanjali's Yoga Sutra , not Vedanta or Samkhya proper. A third confuses the kleshas (five afflictions: avidya, asmita, raga, dvesha, abhinivesha) with the yamas/niyamas (the ethical restraints and observances of the first two limbs); the kleshas are the afflictions to be removed, the yama-niyama are practices to be cultivated. Memory aid Eight limbs in order: " Y oung N injas A lways P ractise P recise D eep D edicated S tunts", Yama, Niyama, Asana, Pranayama, Pratyahara, Dharana, Dhyana, Samadhi. The last three (Dharana to Dhyana to Samadhi) are the inner concentrative trio (samyama). Five kleshas: think " A n A ngry R aging D og A ttacks", Avidya, Asmita, Raga, Dvesha, Abhinivesha, with Avidya (ignorance) as the root of the rest. And the one-line definition you must never lose: yoga = chitta vritti nirodha , stilling the modifications of the mind. 7.9 The Purusharthas: the indigenous model of motivation and well-being Indian thought frames human motivation and a well-lived life through the four purusharthas (from purusha = a person/human, and artha = aim/object/purpose), the four legitimate aims or goals of human life.
