They are set out across the Dharmashastra literature (the treatises on righteous living, such as the Manusmriti) and woven through the epics and the Bhagavad Gita ; the Gita in particular develops the idea that one may pursue worldly aims while remaining inwardly oriented toward liberation. The four are not a ranking in which only the last matters; they are a balanced scheme in which each aim is legitimate in its place, governed and harmonised by the first. The four aims are Dharma , Artha , Kama , and Moksha . Dharma (from dhr = to hold, support, uphold) is duty, righteousness, moral and social order, ethical living in accordance with what is right for one's role and stage of life. It is the foundational aim because it is the framework within which the other worldly aims are to be pursued: wealth and pleasure are legitimate only when sought dharmically , without harm or transgression. Artha (here, wealth/means) is material prosperity, economic security, success, and the resources, possessions, status, and means necessary to live and to discharge one's duties; it is the recognition that a human being needs a material base. Kama (desire/pleasure) is the enjoyment of the senses, emotions, aesthetic and sexual pleasure, love, and the legitimate satisfaction of desire; far from being denied, it is honoured as a proper aim of life when pursued within dharma. Moksha (from much = to release, to free) is liberation, the release from samsara (the cycle of birth, death, and rebirth) and from all bondage; it is the ultimate, transcendent spiritual goal that orients and crowns the whole scheme. Purushartha Translation Domain Role in the scheme Dharma Duty / righteousness Moral and social order; ethical living The foundation and frame; governs the pursuit of the other two worldly aims Artha Wealth / means Prosperity, security, possessions, status The material base of life, sought within dharma Kama Pleasure / desire Sensory, emotional, aesthetic enjoyment, love Legitimate enjoyment, sought within dharma Moksha Liberation Release from the cycle of birth and death The ultimate, transcendent aim; crowns and orients the rest Together the four form an indigenous model of motivation and well-being . A balanced life pursues prosperity (artha) and pleasure (kama) within the bounds of righteousness (dharma), while orienting ultimately toward liberation (moksha). The traditional ashrama scheme of life-stages mirrors this trajectory: the student stage emphasises dharma (learning duty), the householder stage legitimately pursues artha and kama (raising a family, earning, enjoying), and the later forest-dweller and renunciant stages turn progressively toward moksha. A concrete example: a householder running a business is fully within the scheme when he earns honestly (artha within dharma), enjoys family and aesthetic life (kama within dharma), discharges his social and ethical duties (dharma), and keeps the ultimate horizon of liberation (moksha) in view, rather than treating wealth or pleasure as ends in themselves. Definition The four purusharthas are the legitimate aims of human life: Dharma (duty/righteousness, the governing frame), Artha (wealth/material means), Kama (pleasure/desire), and Moksha (liberation, the ultimate aim). Worldly aims (artha, kama) are pursued within dharma and oriented toward moksha. Modern-psychology mapping. The purusharthas are routinely compared with Western models of motivation and well-being, and the comparison is itself a likely exam discussion point. Like Abraham Maslow's hierarchy of needs, the scheme runs from material and security needs (artha) and the satisfaction of desire (kama) toward a higher, self-transcending aim, but the contrast is sharp and worth stating: the apex of the purusharthas is explicitly spiritual liberation (moksha) , not the secular self-actualisation that crowns Maslow's pyramid; and the whole structure is held together by an ethical-duty dimension (dharma) that has no clean Maslovian equivalent. The model also maps onto the modern distinction between hedonic well-being (kama, pleasure and enjoyment) and eudaimonic well-being (dharma and moksha, meaning, virtue, and self-transcendence), with artha supplying the material preconditions. Presented this way, the purusharthas are an integrative, indigenous account of human motivation that combines material, hedonic, ethical, and spiritual aims in one balanced framework. How it is tested. Common items: name the four purusharthas, or supply the missing one; match each term to its meaning (dharma = duty/righteousness; artha = wealth; kama = pleasure; moksha = liberation); identify the ultimate/highest aim (Moksha); identify the aim that governs or frames the others (Dharma); and compare the scheme with Maslow (the apex is liberation, not self-actualisation). Exam trap Kama means pleasure/desire in general, not merely sexual desire , and Artha means wealth/material means, not "art". The paper exploits the false friend "Artha"/"art" and the narrowed reading of "Kama". A second trap reverses the hierarchy: the ultimate aim is Moksha (liberation), and the foundational governing aim is Dharma (righteousness); a question asking for "the highest goal of life" wants Moksha, while one asking which aim "regulates the pursuit of the others" wants Dharma, and the paper swaps these. A third trap matches the wrong term to "duty": Dharma is duty/righteousness; do not pair duty with Artha or Kama. Memory aid Four aims, in their standard order: D harma (duty), A rtha (wealth), K ama (pleasure), M oksha (liberation), " DAKM " or " D uty A nd K indling, then M oksha". Dharma frames the lot (it comes first and governs); Moksha crowns it (it comes last and transcends). The two in the middle (Artha, Kama) are the worldly pair held inside dharma. 7.10 RCI history: the tested date pair and the professional frame The Rehabilitation Council of India (RCI) is the statutory body that regulates and monitors the training of rehabilitation professionals and personnel (clinical psychologists among them), prescribes minimum standards of education, and maintains the Central Rehabilitation Register of qualified professionals. For Indian clinical psychology this is not a peripheral administrative fact but the central professional frame of the discipline you are entering: RCI is the body that licenses and registers clinical psychologists in India , and lawfully practising or designating oneself as a clinical psychologist requires RCI registration. The M.Phil in Clinical Psychology (and, increasingly, RCI-approved M.A./M.Sc. programmes) is RCI-recognised training precisely because RCI prescribes and accredits the curriculum. The Council also has the authority to act against unqualified or fraudulent practitioners. This is why a "history of the profession" question on the entrance paper is fair game, and why the examiners fix on a specific, easily-confused date pair. The chronology runs as follows. The RCI began as a registered society in 1986 . At that stage it was a voluntary, non-statutory body: it could promote and coordinate training, but it had no legal teeth, no power to compel standards or to register practitioners with legal effect. Recognising that a voluntary society could not effectively regulate a profession, Parliament gave the body statutory backing through the Rehabilitation Council of India Act, 1992 . That Act was enforced (brought into force) in 1993 . The Act transformed RCI from a voluntary society into a statutory regulator with the legal authority to prescribe and recognise training programmes, lay down minimum standards of education, maintain the Central Rehabilitation Register, register qualified professionals, and prosecute unqualified practitioners. The Act was subsequently amended in 2000 to widen its scope (broadening the categories of disability and professionals covered). Year Event Status of RCI 1986 RCI established as a registered society Voluntary, non-statutory (no legal regulatory power) 1992 RCI Act passed by Parliament Granted statutory status 1993 RCI Act enforced / brought into force Statutory regulator operational 2000 RCI Act amended Scope widened Why it matters in the paper, and the worked distinction. The single fact the examiners want you to hold cleanly is the difference between RCI as a registered society and RCI as a statutory body . A registered society is formed by people voluntarily associating and registering under the Societies Registration Act; it is private and has no power to bind anyone outside its membership. A statutory body, by contrast, is created or empowered by an Act of Parliament and exercises legal authority over an entire profession. RCI was the former in 1986 and became the latter through the 1992 Act (enforced 1993). Worked example of the trap in action: the question "In which year did RCI become a statutory body?" has the answer 1992 (Act passed, status granted), or 1993 if the question specifies "brought into force", and emphatically not 1986; whereas "In which year was RCI first established/founded?" has the answer 1986 (the society), not 1992. Read which event the stem is asking about. Definition The Rehabilitation Council of India (RCI) is the statutory regulator of rehabilitation professionals in India. It prescribes and recognises training, maintains the Central Rehabilitation Register , and registers clinical psychologists; RCI registration is required to practise lawfully as a clinical psychologist. Exam trap The trap is the 1986 vs 1992/1993 distinction . In 1986 RCI was only a registered society (non-statutory); it became a statutory body with the RCI Act of 1992 (enforced 1993 ). The paper offers "1986" as the answer to "when did RCI become a statutory body?" (wrong: that is the year it was merely registered as a society) and offers "1992" for "when was RCI first established?" (wrong: that is the year of the statutory Act). Read whether the stem asks about the society (1986) or the statutory Act (1992, enforced 1993). Do not invent "1986 Act"; the society was not an Act, and there was no RCI Act until 1992. High-yield To recap the trap map for this whole part, the reliable Amity snares: (1) Tamas is inertia/dullness, not activity. (2) The gunas belong to Prakriti, never to Purusha. (3) The koshas run Anna to Prana to Mano to Vijnana to Ananda, and Manomaya (mind) is below Vijnanamaya (intellect). (4) Turiya is the transcendent fourth state, not a sleep stage. (5) In the antahkarana, Ahamkara (ego) is not Atman (Self); Manas (processing) is not Buddhi (deciding). (6) Atman = Brahman is Advaita non-dualism (Shankara, "Tat Tvam Asi"); Samkhya by contrast is dualist. (7) Yoga = citta-vritti-nirodha (Patanjali); the eight limbs run Yama to Samadhi, with Pratyahara (sense-withdrawal) before Dharana (concentration). (8) The purusharthas are Dharma-Artha-Kama-Moksha, with Moksha the highest aim and Dharma the governing frame. (9) RCI = society 1986, statutory Act 1992 (enforced 1993). If you can reproduce every table in this part from memory and recite those lines, you have neutralised your weakest, most heavily weighted cluster.

title: RML Clinical Psychology, CET-166 · Study Material from Scratch
text: RML Clinical Psychology, CET-166 · Study Material from Scratch ABVIMS & Dr. Ram Manohar Lohia Hospital · MA Clinical Psychology (RCI) via GGSIPU · the whole entrance syllabus taught from zero, tuned to how the RML paper actually behaves. Built for Sihan, 2026-07-02. You flagged RML as the emergency, so this is the first RML drop: a complete, from-scratch study text that covers every concept the CET-166 clinical paper tests, built off the syllabus in your RML Task brief and off how past RML / IPU clinical papers actually behave. Read it top to bottom and you have covered the subject core. Every theorist is given by full name (not just a surname), every test names its author, and every therapy names who developed it, because that is exactly what this paper rewards. Now expanded to the full syllabus neighborhood (2026-07-03): not just the PYQ hot topics, but the foundational build-up, the related theories, and the adjacent subtopics the examiner can swing into, so the high-yield material still gets the most room while nothing is left as a blind spot. Every one of the 12 sections gained new ground: the surrounding reasoning types and the full mental-health-law stack, sensation and cognition and language, brain-imaging methods and behaviour genetics, prenatal-to-ageing-to-death development, the self and social cognition and attraction, biological and cognitive and Indian personality models, the history of abnormality plus culture-bound syndromes, the mental status examination and rehabilitation psychology, group and play and specific behavioural therapies, Indian test adaptations and clinical rating scales, qualitative methods and ANOVA and non-parametric statistics, and the six darshanas with Yoga and Buddhist psychology in depth. Entrance CET-166 (GGSIPU) Split 70% test + 30% interview Format large MCQ block, no negative marking 12 sections · from scratch Full-syllabus expanded 2026-07-03 6-year PYQ map 2020–2025 Companion mocks 2020 2021 2022 2023 2024 2025 How to use this. This is a teaching text, not a cheatsheet: each section builds a topic from the ground up, then flags the exact traps and matching-items RML fishes for. The green Key boxes are the must-knows, the red Trap boxes are the confusions the paper exploits, the teal Who → what boxes are the theorist / founder pairings, and the purple RML tilt boxes tell you how this specific paper phrases the question. Read the 6-year PYQ map first to set your priorities, then after each section sit the matching part of any of the six live PYQ mocks ( 2020 , 2021 , 2022 , 2023 , 2024 , 2025 ) and the weak spots map straight back here. What makes the RML paper different, baked into every section below: (1) lean harder on Indian Psychology , tested past AND present; (2) treat abnormal as ICD-deep and factual , including the older signs and eponyms DSM has dropped; (3) drill who developed which therapy and the acronyms (REBT, DBT, ACT, EMDR, MI) until reflexive; (4) by the six-year PYQ count the paper is actually carried by General/basic psychology, Assessment & tests, Statistics/Research methods, Abnormal, and Biopsychology (the top five = 65% of marks; see the PYQ map ); (5) no negative marking, so attempt everything . The syllabus, 13 sections: ★ The 6-year PYQ map (read first) 1 · Reasoning, Research Aptitude & General Awareness 2 · General & Basic Psychology 3 · Biopsychology 4 · Developmental 5 · Social 6 · Personality 7 · Abnormal (ICD-deep) 8 · Clinical Psychology 9 · Counselling & Psychotherapy 10 · Assessment & Tests 11 · Research Methods & Statistics 12 · Indian Psychology 13 · Social Work (the RML 2020 strand) ★ What actually repeats: the 6-year PYQ map (2020–2025) Everything below this heading is built from the real RML papers, all six of them : 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025, which is 570 actual questions (100 each year except 2023, which had 70). Every one of those questions was tagged to a topic, the topics were counted across the six years, and the concepts that keep coming back were pulled out. So this is not a guess about what the examiner likes; it is the paper's own track record. Read this section first, let it set your priorities, then go into the twelve teaching sections knowing exactly where the marks actually live. How the marks distribute. The single table below is the whole weighting in one view: how many questions each topic drew in each of the six years, the six-year total, its share of the 570 marks, and which teaching section covers it. The bottom four rows of the ranking (cognitive, social, schools, and the rest) are still worth marks, but the top five topics, basic/general, assessment, statistics, abnormal, and biopsychology, are 65% of the entire paper on their own. That is the order to study in. Topic 2020 2021 2022 2023 2024 2025 6-yr Share Taught in General & basic psychology 3 4 10 17 38 20 92 16.1% §1–2, sensation, perception, memory, motivation, emotion, intelligence, learning Psychological assessment & tests 9 15 19 3 6 22 74 13.0% §10 Research methods & statistics 8 19 6 21 6 12 72 12.6% §11 Abnormal / psychopathology 19 13 15 1 14 8 70 12.3% §7 Biopsychology 9 6 7 7 18 18 65 11.4% §3 Developmental & child 9 18 14 2 3 8 54 9.5% §4 Counselling & psychotherapy 8 11 15 0 13 1 48 8.4% §9 Cognitive psychology 9 3 6 9 0 10 37 6.5% §2 Social psychology 16 8 8 2 2 1 37 6.5% §5 Schools & systems / applied 10 3 0 8 0 0 21 3.7% §8, §2 Every paper 100 100 100 70 100 100 570 100% the whole book Attack order, straight off the six-year data: (1) General & basic psychology and (2) Assessment & tests and (3) Research methods & statistics are the three biggest buckets, about 42% of the paper between them, and they are the most learnable (definitions, who-built-which-test, stats vocabulary), so bank them first. (4) Abnormal and (5) Biopsychology are the next tier and together add another 24%. Only after those five are solid should you spend heavily on (6) developmental, (7) therapy, (8) cognitive, (9) social, and (10) schools/systems. Personality looks like a zero in the table only because RML rarely labels a question "personality"; its content (Sigmund Freud's structure, Raymond Cattell's 16PF, Hans Eysenck's dimensions, the Big Five) is tested inside the general, abnormal and assessment buckets, so section 6 is not optional, it is spread across the others. RML tilt, confirmed by the data: two things carry across almost every year, so make them reflexive. First, "who developed what" : the paper repeatedly names a test, therapy, or theory and asks for its author (Hermann Rorschach, Henry Murray, Lee Cronbach, Albert Ellis, Aaron Beck, Jean Piaget, Erik Erikson). Second, the projective tests and the defense mechanisms , which appear in four of the six years each. If you drill only two things, drill those. The rest of this section is the concept-by-concept breakdown, topic by topic, ordered biggest bucket first. Each callout names the concept, the years it actually appeared, and the exact fact or distinction the paper fishes for. Every recurring item here has a fuller treatment in the numbered teaching sections below. Schools & Systems of Psychology, 21 questions over six years This is a small but revealing bucket. It is not "systems of psychology" in the textbook sense (structuralism, functionalism, and so on live in the General bucket). Here the recurring core is organisational / industrial behaviour, systems & family therapy, and, from 2023 onward, research software (Excel and SPSS). Learn the named theories and the named theorists, because RML asks them by name. Repeats (2020, 2023): Organisational & industrial psychology is the steadiest thread here. 2020 probed dysfunctional organisational cultures and case management premises; 2023 asked about a decentralised, empowerment-focused structure (the flat / organic structure) and about Herzberg's Two-Factor Theory. Know the two families of motivators at work. Who → what: Frederick Herzberg → Two-Factor (Motivation-Hygiene) Theory. Motivators (achievement, recognition, the work itself, responsibility, advancement) drive genuine job satisfaction; hygiene factors (salary, supervision, working conditions, company policy) only prevent dissatisfaction and never satisfy. The 2023 question keys on "motivators that lead to job satisfaction," so pick the growth-of-the-job factors, not pay. Repeats (2020): Group development ran across several 2020 items. Bruce Tuckman's stages are the must-know: forming → storming → norming → performing → adjourning . The 2020 stem "struggle with each other over leadership and group definition" = storming ; "clarified its purpose and strategy for achieving its goals" = norming . Also seen: common group properties, formed-group characteristics, and William Shulman's group-role language. Who → what: Gregory Bateson → the double-bind theory of schizophrenia. The 2021 mother-and-son vignette (she stiffens at his embrace, then blames him for withdrawing, with no escape from the contradiction) is the classic double-bind illustration: conflicting messages on different logical levels with no way to comment on or leave the situation. The 2021 "individuals, families, and cultures given different power as creators of their realities" stem points to constructivist / narrative family therapy. Repeats (2023): Research software is a 2023 cluster worth easy marks. SPSS = the standard statistical-analysis package (tabulation, graphing, statistical tests) in psychology research; MS-Excel uses PivotTables for tabulating data and the AVERAGE function for a mean of a range. Expect one or two verbatim "which software / which function" items. General & Basic Psychology, 92 questions over six years (the biggest bucket) This is the single largest slice of the RML paper and the most scatter-shot: research methodology, motivation, memory, perception, learning, the schools of psychology, stress and health, cognitive biases, and Indian psychology all live here. The good news is that it is theorist-heavy and fact-checkable, so a map of the repeats converts directly into marks. Each year has a centre of gravity: 2022-2023 lean research methods, 2024 is a memory-perception-learning avalanche, and 2025 is almost entirely motivation, schools, and Indian psychology. Repeats (2020, 2022, 2023): Research methodology and design is the largest recurring theme in this bucket. Recurring hooks: the double-blind design (controls both participant and experimenter expectancy), confounding variables (the barbecue-vs-plain-chips flavour and the radio-on/off items both test uncontrolled confounds), sampling methods ( stratified = divide into subgroups then sample each; cluster = sample whole groups), field vs lab experiments, the literature review, hypothesis formulation, plagiarism, and referencing / citation ethics. Trap: Deductive vs inductive reasoning is asked repeatedly (2023, 2024) and students flip them. Deductive = theory first, then test with observations, general → specific; its conclusion's validity depends on the truth of its premises . Inductive = gather data, find patterns, then build a theory, specific observations → broad generalisation (qualitative research leans inductive). If the stem says "starts with a theory," it is deductive. Repeats (2021, 2024, 2025): Motivation theory is a top-three repeat and dominates 2025. Know each by its one-line signature. Abraham Maslow 's hierarchy (self-actualisation = realising full potential; belonging / love must be met before esteem) appears in both 2021 and 2025. Theory & theorist Core claim (RML one-liner) Hierarchy of Needs (Abraham Maslow) Lower needs first; self-actualisation = full potential at the top Self-Determination Theory (Edward Deci & Richard Ryan) Three needs: autonomy, competence, relatedness; intrinsic motivation = internal reward & growth Expectancy Theory (Victor Vroom) Effort → performance → outcome, and the outcome must be valued (valent) Goal-Setting Theory (Edwin Locke) Specific and difficult (challenging) goals motivate best Drive-Reduction Theory (Clark Hull) Motivation reduces internal tension to restore homeostasis Incentive Theory Behaviour pulled by external rewards / incentives Social Cognitive Theory (Albert Bandura) Self-efficacy and observational learning drive motivation Trap: Self-Determination Theory's three needs are autonomy, competence, relatedness . The 2025 "which is NOT one of the three needs" item plants a decoy (often "achievement" or "esteem"). Achievement belongs to David McClelland, not to SDT. Repeats (2020, 2024): Memory is the 2024 heavyweight and links back to 2020. The founders are the answers, so memorise the name-to-concept map below. The 2024 paper alone tests the magic number, the serial-position effect, decay theory, filter / attenuation theories, tip-of-the-tongue (Roger Brown and David McNeill, 1966), the PQRST study method, and the method of reconstruction. Concept Theorist (the answer) "Magic number" 7 ± 2 (span of short-term memory) George A. Miller Primacy-recency / serial-position effect Hermann Ebbinghaus Filter theory of attention Donald Broadbent Filter-attenuation theory Anne Treisman Self-reference effect T. B. Rogers (Rogers, Kuiper & Kirker) Decay theory of forgetting Edward Thorndike (law of disuse) RML tilt: "Tip of the tongue" is a retrieval failure (the trace is stored but momentarily inaccessible), not encoding or storage. In the PQRST study method (Preview, Question, Read, Self-recitation, Test), S = Self-recitation (actively recalling in your own words). And the 2020 "what do Hermann Ebbinghaus, Francis Galton and Sigmund Freud share" item keys on their common contribution to the early study of memory / association . Repeats (2024): Perception and Gestalt organisation form a dense 2024 block. Dark adaptation = the eyes growing more sensitive to light (dim light) over time; closure = the Gestalt tendency to complete an incomplete figure; the Stroop effect = interference / selective-attention breakdown (colour word vs ink colour). Depth cues recur as a mini-family (below). 2024 depth-cue stem Monocular cue Rail tracks appear to converge Linear perspective Density of stones increases with distance Texture gradient Painted stripes on a freeway off-ramp Relative size / texture gradient Repeats (2024, 2025): Learning and conditioning span both years. Insight learning (sudden "aha" grasp of a solution) is Wolfgang Kohler's Gestalt work; shaping = reinforcing successive approximations; extinction = weakening a habit by removing all reward; stimulus generalisation vs discrimination (the furry-black-cat vs short-haired-tabby item = discrimination); a token that must be traded (five stickers) is a secondary / conditioned reinforcer . 2025 names the parent school directly: stimulus-response conditioning = behaviourism (John B. Watson, 1913). Repeats (2020, 2024, 2025): The schools of psychology and their history recur across three years. 2020 asked who first used "clinical psychology" in print ( Lightner Witmer , 1896-1907, who also opened the first psychology clinic). 2024 asked who gave "folk psychology" / Volkerpsychologie ( Wilhelm Wundt ). 2025 asked you to name whole approaches from a description. Approach (2025 stems) Signature & key figures Behaviourism Learning via stimulus-response conditioning; John B. Watson, B. F. Skinner Psychodynamic / psychoanalytic Unconscious forces & early childhood; inner drives beyond control; Sigmund Freud Humanistic Free will, growth, self-actualisation; Abraham Maslow, Carl Rogers Comparative psychology Study of animal behaviour Structuralism / founder of the field Wilhelm Wundt (first lab, 1879); "folk psychology" Repeats (2024): Stress and health cluster in 2024. Hans Selye 's General Adaptation Syndrome runs in strict order: alarm → resistance → exhaustion . Type A behaviour is the pattern most directly linked to higher coronary-heart-disease risk. Distinguish an acute stressor (short, sharp, time-limited) from a chronic one. Trap: 2024 mixes several cognitive-bias / problem-solving terms that look alike. Functional fixedness (Karl Duncker, 1945) = seeing an object only in its usual use; hindsight bias (Baruch Fischhoff, 1975) = the "I knew it all along" overestimate of past predictability; a heuristic = a rule-of-thumb shortcut for efficient search. Do not swap functional fixedness for mental set. RML tilt: Indian psychology is a live 2025 theme (five questions) and is easy to underprepare. Core points: it is rooted in Vedanta and the Indian philosophical traditions and centres on consciousness and the self ; Atman = the true self / soul (distinct from ego); it treats mental health holistically (mind-body-spirit, practices such as yoga and meditation) rather than through a purely Western symptom-and-diagnosis lens. Assessment & Tests, 74 questions over six years This topic is dominated by a handful of named tests and the reliability-validity vocabulary: the Rorschach, the MMPI (Starke Hathaway and J. Charnley McKinley, 1943), the TAT and projective logic, the reliability and validity families, and the IQ line reappear in year after year, so the recurring names below carry most of the marks. Repeats (2020, 2021, 2022, 2025): The Rorschach inkblot test is the single most-repeated item. Built by Hermann Rorschach (Swiss psychiatrist, 1921), it has 10 cards total : 5 achromatic (black and grey), 2 black-and-red, and 3 fully multicoloured, so 5 cards are coloured . It is a projective test of personality and unconscious process. RML also asks its procedure: the Enquiry (Inquiry) Phase is the second stage where the examiner returns to each blot to ask what was seen and what made it look that way (location, determinants). Who → what: Hermann Rorschach → inkblot test; Henry Murray & Christiana Morgan → Thematic Apperception Test (TAT), 1930s (1935), Harvard; Starke Hathaway & J. Charnley McKinley → MMPI; John Buck → House-Tree-Person test; Edgar Doll → Vineland Social Maturity Scale; Lee Cronbach → coefficient alpha; Alfred Binet & Theodore Simon → first intelligence test (1905); David Wechsler → WAIS/WISC. Repeats (2020, 2021, 2022): The MMPI (Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory) is asked almost every early year. It is an objective, self-report inventory that measures psychopathology and personality (clinical scales plus validity scales), NOT a projective test and NOT an intelligence test. That objective-self-report identity is the fact RML fishes for. Repeats (2020, 2021, 2022, 2025): Projective tests and their techniques. A projective test uses ambiguous stimuli to draw out unconscious thoughts, motives and personality. Learn the technique labels the paper uses: the Rorschach is an association technique ; the TAT is a construction technique (the participant constructs a story); word-association is also association-based. The TAT's stories are analysed to infer needs, motives and inner conflicts (Murray's need-press theory). Trap: TAT vs Rorschach. Both are projective, but the Rorschach uses inkblots (perception/association) while the TAT uses picture cards of people in scenes and asks for a story (apperception/construction). RML asks directly for the "key difference" and for how many TAT cards are used: the full set is 31, and roughly 20 are shown in a typical session. Who → what: the reliability family. Test-retest = same test, same people, two occasions (stability over time). Inter-rater = agreement between two scorers/observers. Split-half = correlate two halves of one test, best split by the odd-even method and corrected by Spearman-Brown. Cronbach's alpha ( Lee Cronbach ) = internal consistency across all items. RML has asked each of these by definition in 2021, 2022 and 2025. Repeats (2021, 2024, 2025): Validity types. Face validity = looks like it measures the trait, on the surface. Content validity = covers the whole domain. Criterion-related validity splits into concurrent (against a criterion measured now) and predictive (against a future criterion). Construct validity = the test truly captures the theoretical construct. Trap: the 2024 and 2025 items ask which type is NOT criterion-based. Only concurrent and predictive are criterion-based; construct and content validity are separate categories, so they are the correct "NOT criterion" answers. Repeats (2020, 2021, 2022, 2025): Intelligence and IQ. Memorise the ratio-IQ formula IQ = (Mental Age ÷ Chronological Age) × 100 (MA 8, CA 10 → IQ 80). Know the test-to-author map: WAIS/WISC are Wechsler individual intelligence scales; Raven's Standard Progressive Matrices measure nonverbal fluid intelligence; the first intelligence test was built by Alfred Binet (with Theodore Simon, 1905). RML tilt: RML likes attitude-scale and rating-scale wording. A Likert scale ( Rensis Likert ) is a summated rating scale : agree-to-disagree items are summed into one score. It appears in 2020, 2022 and 2023 phrased as "summated rating scale," "attitude measurement scale," or "a Likert scale is best described as." Research Methods & Statistics, 72 questions over six years Stats repeats cluster tightly on five spines: sampling methods, scales of measurement, the ANOVA/F machinery, central tendency, and the correlation-is-not-causation logic, with hypothesis testing errors and research ethics close behind. Repeats (2020, 2021, 2023, 2025): Sampling methods, the top stats repeat. Split probability from non-probability. Convenience/accidental (whoever is easy to recruit), snowball (participants refer others), and quota/purposive are non-probability . Systematic sampling = selecting every nth person from a list. Random sampling matters because it gives every member an equal chance and makes the sample representative, which is what licenses generalisation. Repeats (2023, 2024, 2025): Scales of measurement (S.S. Stevens). Nominal = unordered categories (car colours). Ordinal = ranked. Interval = equal intervals but an arbitrary/no true zero (temperature). Ratio = equal intervals plus a true zero and counting (number of books). Trap: zero is the discriminator. The 2024 "arbitrary zero" item is the interval scale; the 2023 "equal intervals AND a true zero point" item is the ratio scale. Do not answer ratio when it says arbitrary zero. Repeats (2020, 2022, 2025): Measures of central tendency are mean, median and mode ; standard deviation is a measure of dispersion, NOT central tendency (a common "which is NOT" answer). In a negatively skewed distribution the order is mean < median < mode , so the mean sits to the left of (below) the median. For skewed data such as anxiety scores, the median is the preferred summary because it resists outliers. Who → what: the ANOVA family (2021, 2022). Ronald Fisher → ANOVA and the F-ratio , where F = between-groups variance ÷ within-groups (pooled/error) variance, so the denominator is the pooled within-group variance . As chance (error) variance falls, F rises . Post-hoc tests (Tukey's HSD, Scheffe, Duncan's multiple range, Newman-Keuls) are run only after a significant ANOVA . ANCOVA adds one assumption ANOVA lacks: a covariate statistically controlled for. Repeats (2021, 2025): Correlation is not causation. A correlational or observational study (regularly exercising adults being less depressed, meditators being less stressed) cannot establish cause because there is no manipulation and no random assignment , so third variables and reverse causation stay open. This exact reasoning is RML's favourite "why is this conclusion not appropriate" item. Who → what: matching a test to the data. Pearson's r → two continuous variables (stress vs sleep). Biserial/point-biserial → one continuous and one dichotomous variable. Non-parametric equivalents (2023): Mann-Whitney U → independent-samples t-test; Kruskal-Wallis → one-way ANOVA (3+ independent groups); Friedman → repeated-measures design. Repeats (2022, 2023): Hypothesis-testing errors. A Type I error = rejecting a true null (false positive, controlled by alpha). A Type II error = failing to reject a null that is actually false (false negative). The 2023 stem "fails to reject the null when it is actually false" is by definition Type II . RML tilt: two smaller but reliable repeats. Informed consent (2021, 2025) = telling participants the study's purpose and procedures so they can freely decide to take part. And the normal-distribution line (2021, 2022): the z-table is derived from the standard normal curve, and the bell curve was first described by Abraham de Moivre and popularised by Carl Friedrich Gauss (hence "Gaussian"). Abnormal & Psychopathology, 70 questions over six years This is the single heaviest cluster on the CET-166 paper, and it rewards flat memorisation over reasoning. RML sits close to the ICD text, loves the older eponyms and signs (Eugen Bleuler, Schneider, Janet), and returns to the same handful of anchors every year: Sigmund Freud's defense mechanisms, schizophrenia signs, the anorexia-versus-bulimia contrast, mood disorders, and dissociation. Learn these as fact lists, not as concepts to derive under time pressure. Repeats (2020, 2022, 2024, 2025): Defense mechanisms are the number-one recurring item, almost always as a clinical vignette ("name the mechanism"). Sigmund Freud's ego defenses you must recognise on sight: sublimation (channeling an unacceptable urge into an acceptable outlet, e.g. anger into kickboxing), projection (attributing your own unacceptable thoughts or impulses to others, asked twice in 2025), displacement (redirecting a feeling from a threatening target to a safer one, e.g. yelling at the dog when angry at your partner), repression (involuntary blocking of painful material from awareness), and rationalisation (excusing failure by blaming an external cause, e.g. Clare blaming a co-worker for being fired). Mechanism Core move Paper cue Sublimation Urge → socially valued outlet Anger → kickboxing class Projection Own impulse attributed to others "attributing unacceptable thoughts to others" Displacement Feeling shifted to a safer target Yells at dog / argues with husband Repression Involuntary blocking from awareness Cannot bring anxiety-provoking material to consciousness Rationalisation Self-serving excuse for a failure Blames co-worker for being fired Splitting All-good / all-bad, no middle Seen in borderline personality disorder Projective identification Melanie Klein, paranoid-schizoid Ego defense "in paranoia" Who → what: Sigmund Freud → structural model ( id runs on the pleasure principle, ego on the reality principle, superego is morality) and the topographic model (the preconscious holds accessible memories recalled at will). Asked in 2020, 2022 (Freud on alcohol dependence = oral-stage fixation) and 2025 ("component that operates on the reality principle" = the ego). Repeats (2020, 2021, 2022, 2024): Schizophrenia recurs every one of those years. Know the positive versus negative symptom split (positive = added experiences: delusions, hallucinations; negative = lost function: flat affect, avolition, alogia, anhedonia), identical-twin concordance of roughly 50 percent , and expressed emotion (EE) = a family climate of criticism, hostility and emotional over-involvement that predicts relapse. RML also asks the ICD inclusion/exclusion criteria directly. Who → what: Kurt Schneider → First-Rank Symptoms of schizophrenia (2022 "who gave the concept", 2024 "which is NOT a first-rank symptom"). The list: audible thoughts / voices commenting or arguing, thought withdrawal-insertion-broadcasting, made (passivity) feelings, impulses and acts, and delusional perception. Anything negative-symptom (e.g. flat affect) is the classic "NOT first-rank" trap answer. Repeats (2020, 2021, 2022, 2024): Eating disorders, always framed as anorexia-versus-bulimia. Shared feature = intense fear of weight gain plus disturbed body image; the discriminator = anorexia nervosa carries markedly low body weight (and, in older criteria, amenorrhea = absence of menstrual periods), whereas bulimia nervosa runs at near-normal weight with binge eating plus compensatory behaviour (self-induced vomiting, laxatives, fasting, over-exercise). Repeats (2020, 2021, 2022, 2024): Mood / affective disorders. Bipolar is the disorder where mood "swings from one extreme to another"; a manic episode's core pair = elevated/expansive mood plus increased energy or activity. Major depressive disorder is cued by loss of interest or pleasure (anhedonia) and appetite change, NOT euphoria or specific phobias. Dysthymia (persistent depressive disorder) = milder but longer-lasting than MDD. Depression is the one the paper nicknames the " common cold of psychiatry " and the usual cause of pseudodementia . Repeats (2022, 2024, 2025): Dissociative disorders. Multiple distinct personalities within one person = dissociative identity disorder (DID). Psychodynamic theory reads dissociative symptoms as defense against trauma; dissociative amnesia is usually localised or selective, whereas generalised amnesia wipes the entire life history. RML pairs this with hysteria/conversion signs (see eponyms below). Repeats (2023, 2025): The diathesis-stress model asks the same thing twice: mental disorders arise from the interaction of a predisposing vulnerability (the diathesis, genetic or biological) with environmental stress, not from either alone. Repeats (2021, 2022, 2025): Personality disorders. They are stable, long-term, pervasive patterns. Antisocial PD = manipulation, lack of remorse, irresponsibility; obsessive-compulsive PD = driven by a need for order and control (not the same as OCD). RML tilt: The 2024 paper in particular is dense with eponyms and older signs , so bank them cold: "ambivalence" (one of Eugen Bleuler's four A's) was coined by Eugen Bleuler ; "la belle indifférence" in hysteria is attributed to Pierre Janet ; delusion of infidelity = Othello syndrome (delusional jealousy); First-Rank Symptoms = Kurt Schneider ; kleptomania is a classic French-alienist eponym. RML rewards knowing the name attached to the term, not just the term. Counselling & Psychotherapy, 48 questions over six years The therapy section is built around two obsessions RML returns to every year: who developed which therapy (founder attribution) and the mechanics of behaviour therapy and CBT . Learn the acronym-to-founder map below cold; it converts several guaranteed marks. Note that ego defense mechanisms reappear inside this section too, so the Freud grid above is doing double duty. Who → what: This is the paper's favourite therapy question type (2021, 2022, 2024 all ask it). Memorise the founder map: Therapy / concept Developer (full name) Cognitive therapy / CBT, Socratic questioning Aaron Beck REBT and the ABC model Albert Ellis DBT (distress tolerance) Marsha Linehan ACT (acceptance & commitment) Steven Hayes EMDR Francine Shapiro Motivational Interviewing (MI) William Miller & Stephen Rollnick Interpersonal Psychotherapy (IPT) Gerald Klerman & Myrna Weissman Client-centred therapy Carl Rogers Self-efficacy Albert Bandura Systematic desensitisation Joseph Wolpe Progressive deep muscle relaxation Edmund Jacobson Individual psychology, inferiority complex Alfred Adler Collective unconscious Carl Jung Repeats (2021, 2022, 2024, 2025): The cognitive family. Aaron Beck's cognitive therapy is drilled through its methods (Socratic questioning, collaborative identification of cognitive errors such as overgeneralisation and arbitrary inference, thought records for depression). Albert Ellis's REBT is drilled through the ABC model : Activating event → Beliefs → Consequences. Keep Beck (errors/distortions) and Ellis (irrational beliefs, ABC) separate in your head; the paper baits you to swap them. Repeats (2020, 2021, 2022): Behaviour therapy built on relaxation. The technique where a patient relaxes while visualising a graded hierarchy of anxiety-provoking scenes (the public-speaking vignette in 2021) is systematic desensitisation , developed by Joseph Wolpe on the principle of reciprocal inhibition / counterconditioning; the relaxation half is Edmund Jacobson's progressive deep relaxation. Repeats (2021, 2022): Operant-based methods. "Behaviour analysis" and "functional analysis" (asked verbatim, twice each) rest on the principles of operant conditioning (B.F. Skinner): behaviour is shaped by its consequences. Shaping = reinforcing successive approximations; the "Lovaas programme" = applied behaviour analysis for autism. Who → what: EMDR (2021, 2022) → Francine Shapiro, and it was developed specifically for PTSD / trauma ; the technique pairs recall of the distressing memory with bilateral eye movements. DBT and its distress tolerance module (2024) → Marsha Linehan. Trap: Defense mechanisms show up inside the therapy section, not just abnormal (2024 asked four in a row). Match them precisely: displacement (harassed at work → argues at home), projective identification in paranoia (Melanie Klein), isolation / undoing / reaction formation in OCD, and splitting in borderline personality disorder. Also do not confuse OCD's exposure treatment ERP (exposure and response prevention) with EMDR. Biopsychology, 65 questions over six years Biopsychology is the single biggest physiological load in the RML paper, and it repeats along a small set of predictable axes: which neurotransmitter goes with which disease, which lobe or structure does which job, and how the classic theories of emotion order the events. Learn the tables below cold and you clear most of the section on recognition alone. Repeats (2022, 2023, 2024, 2025): Neurotransmitter → function/disease is asked almost every year. Memorise the pairings: acetylcholine loss → Alzheimer's dementia (2022), dopamine degeneration in the substantia nigra → Parkinson's disease (2023), endorphins are the "feel-good" neurotransmitters (2024), and alcohol acts as an agonist at GABA receptors (2022). Neurotransmitter Signature link RML tests Acetylcholine Deficiency → Alzheimer's disease; muscle activation Dopamine Degeneration → Parkinson's; blocked by neuroleptics GABA Main inhibitory NT; alcohol is an agonist Endorphins "Feel-good" NT, pain relief and pleasure Serotonin / Dopamine Mood; targets of antidepressants and antipsychotics Repeats (2020, 2024): Lobe → function is a perennial. The frontal lobe handles cognitive/intellectual functioning and voluntary movement (2020, 2024), the parietal lobe interprets sensory information (2024), the occipital lobe processes vision, and the temporal lobe processes hearing and language. Lobe Main domain Frontal Voluntary movement, planning, intellect, personality Parietal Somatosensory, interpreting sensory input, spatial sense Occipital Vision Temporal Hearing, language comprehension, memory Repeats (2020, 2023, 2024, 2025): Subcortical structure → job is tested constantly. Fix these: hippocampus → consolidation of long-term memory and the site damaged in anterograde amnesia (2023, 2024); amygdala → emotion, fear and aggression, the "seat of emotion" (2023, 2025); hypothalamus → hunger/satiety centre and homeostasis (2021, 2024); medulla (brainstem) → breathing and heart rate (2023); pineal gland → melatonin and the circadian sleep-wake clock (2022, 2023). Structure Function RML fishes for Hippocampus Long-term memory consolidation; damaged in anterograde amnesia Amygdala Fear, aggression, emotional modulation of memory ("seat of emotion") Hypothalamus Satiety/hunger centre, homeostasis, links to pituitary Medulla oblongata Vital autonomic functions: breathing, heart rate Pineal gland Melatonin; circadian rhythm and sleep-wake cycle Trap: The "satiety centre" is the ventromedial hypothalamus (destroy it and the rat overeats), while the lateral hypothalamus is the hunger/feeding centre (destroy it and the rat stops eating). RML has flipped these both ways (2021, 2024). Who → what: Theories of emotion recur every cycle (2020, 2025). William James and Carl Lange (James-Lange theory): stimulus → bodily/physiological arousal → then the felt emotion ("we are afraid because we tremble"). Walter Cannon and Philip Bard (Cannon-Bard theory): arousal and emotion occur simultaneously. Stanley Schachter and Jerome Singer (two-factor theory): arousal plus a cognitive label, which explains misattribution of arousal, feeling attraction when actually just aroused by fear (2020, 2025). Who → what: Paul Ekman is tied to the six universally recognised basic emotions: happiness, sadness, fear, anger, surprise, and disgust (2025 asks which one is NOT on the list, so anything like "contempt", "pride", or "love" is the answer). Repeats (2021, 2022, 2024): Alcohol-related amnesia recurs. Chronic alcoholism → Korsakoff's syndrome (thiamine/B1 deficiency), classically involving profound retrograde amnesia and confabulation (2021, 2024). Distinguish anterograde amnesia (cannot form NEW memories, hippocampal damage) from retrograde amnesia (loss of OLD memories). Who → what: Hans Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome (GAS) describes stress in three stages: alarm, resistance, exhaustion (2020). Pair this with the fight-or-flight (Walter Cannon, 1915) response, run by the sympathetic branch of the autonomic nervous system with the adrenal glands (2024). Repeats (2022, 2024): Sleep architecture appears repeatedly. A normal night runs in roughly 90-minute cycles, giving about 4 to 6 NREM-REM cycles per major sleep period (2022, 2024). Know the NREM to REM progression and that REM is when vivid dreaming occurs. Who → what: Aphasia (loss of language) is the umbrella term (2020), and RML repeatedly probes Broca's aphasia: slow, laboured, non-fluent, telegraphic speech using only keywords, from damage to Broca's area in the left frontal lobe (2022, 2025). Contrast Wernicke's aphasia (fluent but meaningless speech, comprehension lost). Prosopagnosia is the specific inability to recognise faces (2024). Repeats (2024, 2025): Sensory systems and thresholds recur. The vestibular system (semicircular canals of the inner ear) senses spin and balance (2024); rods are the receptors for scotopic (dim-light) vision (2024); the human ear responds to roughly 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz (2024); and the absolute threshold is the minimum stimulus intensity detectable 50% of the time (2025). RML tilt: The 2024 and 2025 papers lean on split-brain and imaging facts. Cutting the corpus callosum severs communication between the two hemispheres (Roger Sperry's split-brain work); the left hemisphere is typically dominant for language and analytic processing. For imaging, EEG gives the highest temporal resolution, while CT/MRI are used to view brain structure after a head injury (2025). RML tilt: The pituitary is repeatedly framed as the "master gland" that controls the other endocrine glands and regulates growth (2024). Neuroleptic (antipsychotic) drugs treat psychosis/schizophrenia and can cause tardive dyskinesia as a long-term side effect (2022, 2025). Cognitive Psychology, 37 questions over six years Cognitive Psychology in RML clusters tightly around three areas: the architecture of memory (stores, working memory, memory types), how and why we forget, and perception with its named theorists and biases. Almost every named-psychologist question in the section comes from perception or decision-making, so bind each name to its one idea. Who → what: The stage/multi-store model (Richard Atkinson and Richard Shiffrin) runs sensory memory → short-term/working memory → long-term memory. Sensory memory holds information for the shortest duration (2020), and RML asks which store is NOT part of this model (2025). Encoding is the process that moves new information into memory (2025). Store Duration / capacity Sensory memory Shortest, under ~1 second; large raw capacity Short-term / working ~15-30 sec; ~7 items (George Miller) Long-term memory Potentially unlimited and long-lasting Who → what: Working memory (Alan Baddeley and Graham Hitch) is a repeat favourite. Know its four components: the central executive (attention controller, disrupted by a demanding secondary task, 2022), the phonological loop (verbal/auditory), the visuospatial sketchpad (visual/spatial), and the episodic buffer (2025 lists all four and asks for the model's name). Repeats (2020, 2022, 2023, 2025): Memory phenomena and types are asked every year. Lock in: the tip-of-the-tongue state is temporary retrieval failure of a known word (2020); retrieval-induced forgetting is when recalling some items suppresses related ones (2020); flashbulb memory (Roger Brown and James Kulik, 1977) is a vivid recollection of an emotionally important event (2025); semantic memory produces scripts of familiar routines (2025); the engram is the physical memory trace (Karl Lashley / Richard Semon, 2025); and dual-coding theory (Allan Paivio) says information coded both verbally and visually is best remembered (2023). Trap: Explicit (declarative) memory is conscious, includes episodic and semantic; implicit (non-declarative) memory is unconscious, includes procedural skills and priming. RML asks which statement does NOT fit one of these terms (2020, 2025), so watch for a description that swaps the two. Who → what: Classical conditioning (Ivan Pavlov) recurs across sections. In the dog experiment the bell/metronome starts as a neutral stimulus and becomes the conditioned stimulus after pairing (2020); a conditioned response eliminated by withdrawing reinforcement is called extinction (2020). Taste aversion (John Garcia effect) is single-trial learning with a long delay, an exception to normal conditioning rules (2022). Who → what: Perception theory questions are all name-driven (2020, 2022, 2023). Bind these: Gestalt psychology (Max Wertheimer, Kurt Koffka and Wolfgang Köhler) → perceiving a whole organised form rather than parts (2020); Hermann von Helmholtz → unconscious inference in perception (2023); James Gibson → affordances, the action opportunities the environment offers, and direct perception (2023); the Bayesian/probabilistic approach → perception as prior knowledge combined with sensory evidence (2023). The Muller-Lyer illusion is weaker in people from non-"carpentered" (non-Western) environments (2022). Who → what: Judgment and decision-making repeats through named biases (2023). Herbert Simon → bounded rationality, decisions limited by information and cognitive resources (2023). Confirmation bias (Peter Wason, 1960) is linked to the availability heuristic; the representativeness heuristic causes errors by ignoring base rates (Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman, 2023). Repeats (2021, 2023, 2025): Attention and recall effects surface regularly. The recency effect is better recall of the last items in a list (part of the serial position curve, 2021); change blindness is failing to notice obvious changes in a scene (2023); the misinformation effect is post-event information distorting a memory (Elizabeth Loftus, 2023); and the Stroop effect demonstrates automatic processing interfering with controlled attention (2025). Who → what: Intelligence models appear in this section too. Joy Paul Guilford's Structure of Intellect model proposes 120+ (up to 150/180) dimensions from operations x contents x products (2021). Raymond Cattell distinguished crystallised intelligence (learned knowledge and skills, an "acquired" ability) from fluid intelligence (2021). Developmental & Child Psychology, 54 questions over six years Development is the single heaviest topic on this paper, and it is dominated by the four great stage theorists. Roughly one question in three across the six years is just "match the theorist to the stage or the age," so the fastest marks here come from having Jean Piaget, Erik Erikson, Sigmund Freud, and Lev Vygotsky memorised cold. The paper then layers on a steady supply of research-design items (longitudinal vs cross-sectional), temperament, moral reasoning, and, in 2025, a fresh cluster on learning difficulties. Repeats (2020, 2021, 2022, 2025): Jean Piaget's four cognitive-development stages are the most-tested single idea in the whole fragment. 2020 asked for object permanence (the marker of the sensorimotor stage) and quizzed the conservation task; 2021 asked the age band for the preoperational child; 2022 and 2025 both went after formal operational reasoning (the stage that adds abstract, hypothetical thought). Know the order and the one-line signature of each stage. Who → what: Jean Piaget → four cognitive stages: Sensorimotor (0 to 2, object permanence), Preoperational (2 to 7, egocentrism, no conservation), Concrete operational (7 to 11, conservation and reversibility), Formal operational (11+, abstract and hypothetical reasoning). Stage (Piaget) Age Must-know marker Sensorimotor 0 to 2 Object permanence develops Preoperational 2 to 7 Egocentrism, cannot conserve Concrete operational 7 to 11 Conservation, reversibility Formal operational 11+ Abstract, hypothetical thought Repeats (2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024): Erik Erikson's eight psychosocial stages appear in five of the six years, making them tied as the paper's most reliable theme. 2020 fished for the mid-life crisis of stagnation (the feeling of "having achieved nothing for the next generation," i.e. Generativity vs Stagnation); 2021 asked when Industry vs Inferiority occurs (school-age, ~6 to 12); 2022 and 2023 both asked the adolescent crisis (Identity vs Role Confusion); 2024 asked who coined "identity crisis" (Erikson himself). Who → what: Erik Erikson → eight psychosocial crises across the lifespan. The three the paper repeatedly targets: Industry vs Inferiority (school age), Identity vs Role Confusion (adolescence, source of the "identity crisis"), and Generativity vs Stagnation (middle adulthood). Repeats (2021, 2022, 2025): Lev Vygotsky recurs three years running, always contrasted with Piaget. 2021 asked the core difference between Piaget and Vygotsky on language development (Vygotsky sees language and social interaction as driving thought, not merely reflecting it); 2022 tested his link between conceptual thinking and language; 2025 asked directly for the Zone of Proximal Development, the gap between what a child can do alone and what they can do with guidance. Who → what: Lev Vygotsky → sociocultural theory: the Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD), scaffolding, and the primacy of language and social interaction in cognitive growth. Repeats (2021, 2022): Lawrence Kohlberg's stages of moral reasoning show up two years in a row. 2021 asked which option is NOT one of his stages and tested the preconventional level (right and wrong judged by reward and punishment, the consequences of an act). 2022 tested Carol Gilligan's critique that Kohlberg's model was built on males and neglects a female "ethic of care." Who → what: Lawrence Kohlberg → three levels of moral development: Preconventional (reward and punishment), Conventional (social approval and law), Postconventional (universal ethical principles). Carol Gilligan → the "ethic of care" critique. Trap: On the Kohlberg items the paper offers plausible-sounding stage names that are not his. Preconventional morality is about consequences to the self (reward or punishment), NOT about following the law; that legal orientation belongs to the Conventional level. Repeats (2020, 2024): Sigmund Freud's psychosexual stages and complexes surface at both ends of the window. 2020 tied adult sarcasm, overeating, and nail-biting to oral-stage fixation, and asked the girl-boy complex pairing (Electra complex to girls as Oedipus complex to boys). 2024 asked the clinical term for lack of bowel control in children (encopresis), an anal-stage adjacent item. Who → what: Sigmund Freud → five psychosexual stages (Oral, Anal, Phallic, Latency, Genital); fixation at a stage leaves adult traits. Oral fixation → nail-biting, overeating, sarcasm; the Phallic stage carries the Oedipus complex (boys) and Electra complex (girls). Repeats (2020, 2025): Research-design items reward an easy point. Both 2020 ("studying people across time repeatedly") and 2025 ("the same group of individuals over a 10-year period") are simply asking you to name the longitudinal design. Do not overthink these. Trap: Longitudinal follows ONE group over time; cross-sectional compares DIFFERENT age groups at ONE time. The paper words the longitudinal stem as "same group over X years" to see if you confuse it with cross-sectional. Repeats (2021, 2022): Temperament research is asked by named authors. 2021 credited Alexander Thomas and Stella Chess with the nine dimensions of temperament (and their easy, difficult, slow-to-warm-up types); 2022 asked what is NOT in Mary Rothbart and John Bates's structure of temperament. Attach the names to the models. Repeats (2021, 2024): The critical/sensitive period appears twice. 2021 framed it as irreversible limits when infants get no early language exposure; 2024 asked where the strongest evidence for the critical-period hypothesis is found (again, language acquisition). Language is the paper's go-to example for critical periods. RML tilt: Attachment loaded almost entirely into 2021, which ran a mini-cluster: the child who seeks yet rejects the parent (resistant/ambivalent, Type C), the "internal working model" (John Bowlby) as the schema-theory prototype for later attachments, and Type D (disorganised) infants. Attribute the classification system to Mary Ainsworth's Strange Situation and the underlying theory to John Bowlby. 2025 also opened a new learning-difficulties strand (dyslexia, dyscalculia); expect it to recur. Social Psychology, 37 questions over six years Social psychology on this paper splits into two personalities. The 2020 paper is dominated by a large social-work cluster (case work, group work, and their pioneers), while 2021 onward shifts to mainstream social psychology: group processes, attitudes, conformity, and "name the theorist." Cross-year repeats are fewer here than in development, so the reliable earners are social identity theory (Henri Tajfel and John Turner, 1979), the attitude family, and conformity/influence. Repeats (2020, 2023): Social identity theory is the one social concept the paper returns to in different years. 2020 asked where we derive a large part of our identity and self-feelings from (our group memberships); 2023 asked what determines self-concept and behaviour within a group (again, the group we belong to). Same answer, same theory. Who → what: Henri Tajfel and John Turner → Social Identity Theory: part of the self-concept comes from group membership, producing in-group favouritism and out-group bias. Repeats (2021, 2023): Attitudes and their link to behaviour form a mini-family. 2021 gave the classic cognitive-dissonance scenario (a student who hates smoking then smokes at a party, feeling the tension of dissonance) and asked when attitudes least predict behaviour. 2023 asked, under the Theory of Planned Behavior (Icek Ajzen), what drives the intention to act on a health behaviour (attitude, subjective norms, and perceived behavioural control). Who → what: Leon Festinger → Cognitive Dissonance Theory (tension from holding conflicting attitudes and behaviours drives attitude change). Icek Ajzen → Theory of Planned Behavior (intention is set by attitude, subjective norms, and perceived behavioural control). Repeats (2021, 2024): Conformity and social influence recur. 2024 defined conformity outright ("changing your behaviour to match that of others in a group") and asked what Solomon Asch's classic line-judgement experiment tested (the limits of conformity to group pressure). 2021's groupthink (Irving Janis, 1972) item sits in the same influence family. Who → what: Solomon Asch → line-judgement conformity experiments (people yield to a unanimous wrong majority). Pair with Stanley Milgram → obedience to authority, the influence experiment most likely to appear alongside Asch. RML tilt: 2021 ran an unusually dense group-processes cluster that is worth pre-loading as a set. Watch for: social facilitation (an audience improves easy tasks but impairs hard or unpractised ones, so it hurts the novice dancer), social loafing (people slack in groups; fix it by making individual contributions identifiable), groupthink (reduce it by encouraging dissent and appointing a devil's advocate), deindividuation (loss of self-awareness in anonymous online or crowd settings, as with cyberbullies), and bystander apathy / diffusion of responsibility (the crowd that films but does not help). Who → what: 2022 was a pure "name the theorist" year, so bank these. Alice Eagly → Social Role Theory of gender; Leonard Berkowitz → reformulated frustration-aggression hypothesis (John Dollard and colleagues, 1939); Serge Moscovici → Social Representation Theory; Robert Cialdini → six principles of compliance (reciprocity, commitment, social proof, authority, liking, scarcity); John French and Bertram Raven → bases of social power. Trap: The 2022 compliance and power items are framed as "which is NOT included." You must know Robert Cialdini's six principles and the French and Raven power bases well enough to spot the invented seventh option, not just recognise the real ones. RML tilt: The 2020 paper carries a heavy social-work block found on no other year: schools of social work, the social case-work process and its techniques, group work as a method, and H. B. Trecker's principles of social group work. It reflects RML's applied, service-oriented framing of "social." Treat these as pure factual recall (pioneers, process steps, and the odd-one-out principle) rather than theory to reason through. Recap of the map: 570 real questions, six years. Top five topics (general, assessment, statistics, abnormal, biopsychology) = 65% of the paper, study them first. The two evergreen question shapes are "who developed what" and the projective-tests / defense-mechanisms pair. Everything flagged above is taught in full in the twelve sections that follow. 1 Section A, Reasoning, Research Aptitude & General Awareness This ~20-mark block is scored, not skimmed. It rewards speed on reasoning , precision on research methods vocabulary, and rote accuracy on the Indian mental-health system . Treat it as free marks: the answers are unambiguous once you know the definition. 1. Logical & Analytical Reasoning The CET-166 paper (and the older GGSIPU CET = Guru Gobind Singh Indraprastha University Common Entrance Test pattern it inherits) uses a fixed menu of item types. Learn the trick behind each. Series Find the rule linking consecutive terms, then extend it. Rules are arithmetic (+/−), geometric (×/÷), squares/cubes, or alternating (two interleaved series). 2, 6, 12, 20, 30, ?, differences are 4, 6, 8, 10, so next gap is 12 → 42. Analogies "A is to B as C is to D." Name the exact relationship in A:B, then force the same relationship on C:D. Doctor : Hospital :: Teacher : School (worker : workplace). Syllogisms From scratch: A syllogism gives you premises ("All A are B", "Some B are C") and asks which conclusion necessarily follows. Draw overlapping circles (Venn diagrams). A conclusion is valid ONLY if it is true in every possible diagram, not just one. "Some" means at least one and possibly all; "All A are B" does NOT let you say "All B are A". All cats are animals; all animals are mortal → All cats are mortal (valid). Trap: "Some A are B" never guarantees "Some A are not B". Existence of an overlap does not prove a non-overlap. The paper plants this "illicit converse" repeatedly. Odd-one-out (classification) Four items share a property; one breaks it. Rose, Lotus, Lily, Mango, Mango is the odd one (it is a fruit/tree, the rest are flowers). Coding-Decoding A word is enciphered by a rule (shift letters, reverse, number-for-letter). Discover the rule from the given pair, apply it to the target. If CAT = DBU (each letter +1), then DOG = EPH. Basic Data Interpretation A table/bar/pie gives numbers; questions ask totals, differences, percentages, or ratios. If a pie shows 90° for "Clinical", that slice is 90/360 = 25% of the total. Read the axis and units first, compute second. RML tilt: Reasoning items are non-verbal-friendly and answerable in under a minute; do not burn exam time deriving elegant formulas. Spot the pattern, mark, move. 2. Research Aptitude Types of research Basic (pure) vs Applied , theory-building vs solving a real problem. Descriptive (describes "what is") vs Experimental (manipulates to test cause). Qualitative (meaning, themes) vs Quantitative (numbers, statistics). Exploratory, correlational, longitudinal, cross-sectional designs. Hypotheses The null hypothesis (H₀) states "no effect / no difference / no relationship." The alternative hypothesis (H₁) states there IS one. A directional (one-tailed) hypothesis predicts the direction ( Group A scores higher ); a non-directional (two-tailed) hypothesis predicts only that a difference exists. Key. You never "prove" H₁, you reject or fail to reject H₀. A Type I error is rejecting a true H₀ (false positive, α); a Type II error is failing to reject a false H₀ (false negative, β). Variables Variable Role Independent (IV) Manipulated / presumed cause Dependent (DV) Measured / the effect Confound Unwanted variable that co-varies with the IV and offers a rival explanation Moderator Changes the strength/direction of the IV→DV link (a "for whom / when") Mediator The mechanism through which IV affects DV (a "how / why") Trap: Moderator vs mediator. A moderator sits alongside and interacts; a mediator sits in the causal chain (IV → mediator → DV). Stress is a mediator if IV causes stress which then lowers DV. Sampling Probability sampling (every unit has a known, non-zero chance; allows generalisation): Simple random , pure lottery. Systematic , every k-th unit from a random start. Stratified , divide into strata, sample within each proportionally. Cluster , sample whole groups (e.g. clinics), study all within. Non-probability sampling (chance not known; cheaper, weaker generalisation): Convenience , whoever is available. Purposive (judgmental) , chosen for a trait. Quota , fill fixed counts per category. Snowball , participants refer others (hidden populations). Reliability & Validity Reliability = consistency. Types: test-retest (same test, two times), inter-rater (two scorers agree), internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha), parallel/alternate forms , split-half . Validity = measures what it claims. Types: content (covers the domain), construct (measures the trait; includes convergent and discriminant ), criterion ( concurrent and predictive ), plus face validity (looks right). Key. A test can be reliable but NOT valid (a scale consistently 2 kg heavy). It cannot be valid without being reliable. Reliability is necessary but not sufficient for validity. Basic designs Between-subjects (different people per condition) vs within-subjects/repeated-measures (same people, all conditions). Randomised control trial (RCT) is the gold-standard experiment. Quasi-experiment (Donald Campbell and Julian Stanley, 1963) lacks random assignment; case study is single-unit depth. 3. General Awareness, Indian Mental-Health System Rehabilitation Council of India (RCI) The Rehabilitation Council of India (RCI) is a statutory body created by the RCI Act, 1992 . It regulates training of rehabilitation professionals (including clinical psychologists) and maintains the Central Rehabilitation Register . Key. To practise as a Clinical Psychologist in India you must hold RCI registration. RML's CET-166 admits to an RCI-recognised MA Clinical Psychology , which is why this is the "RCI-licensing route." Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 (MHCA 2017) Replaced the Mental Health Act, 1987. Rights-based. Key provisions: Advance directive , a person may state in advance how they wish (or do not wish) to be treated. Nominated representative , a person appointed to take decisions on their behalf. Decriminalised suicide attempt , a person attempting suicide is presumed to be under severe stress and shall not be punished under the IPC. Right to community living , protection from cruel/degrading treatment, and free treatment for the poor/homeless. Trap: The advance directive belongs to MHCA 2017 , NOT to the RCI Act or the RPwD Act. Do not confuse MHCA 2017 with the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (RPwD) Act, 2016 . National & District programmes The National Mental Health Programme (NMHP) was launched in 1982 to make mental-health care accessible and integrate it into general health services. Its field arm, the District Mental Health Programme (DMHP) , began in 1996 (Bellary model) to deliver care at the district level. Major institutes Institute Location NIMHANS (National Institute of Mental Health and Neurosciences) Bengaluru IHBAS (Institute of Human Behaviour and Allied Sciences) Delhi CIP (Central Institute of Psychiatry) Ranchi Dr. Ram Manohar Lohia Hospital (RML) New Delhi AIIMS (All India Institute of Medical Sciences) New Delhi Landmark figures (brief) India's first psychology laboratory and department were established at the University of Calcutta ; Girindrasekhar Bose founded the Indian Psychoanalytical Society (1922) . (Fuller treatment is in the Indian-psychology section.) Recap: Reasoning = spot the rule, then apply it; watch the syllogism "some/all" trap. Research aptitude = H₀/H₁, IV/DV plus moderator-vs-mediator, probability vs non-probability sampling, reliable≠valid. General awareness = RCI Act 1992 (your licence), MHCA 2017 (advance directive, nominated representative, decriminalised suicide, community living), NMHP 1982 / DMHP 1996 , and the big institutes. 4. More Reasoning Item Types The paper can rotate across many logical-reasoning families. Below are the ones most likely to appear beyond the basics already covered, each with the quick method that cracks it. 4.1 Blood Relations Decode a family chain by replacing each link with a symbol as you read it. Draw a small tree: put males and females on rows and connect with lines. From scratch: "Pointing to a man, Ravi said, 'His mother is the only daughter of my mother.'" Only daughter of Ravi's mother = Ravi's sister (or Ravi's own generation female). So the man's mother is Ravi's sister, making the man Ravi's nephew. Tip: "only daughter of my mother" often resolves to the speaker's sister or the speaker herself; test both. 4.2 Direction Sense Track movement on a compass grid (North up). Sum the net East–West and North–South displacement; final distance from start uses the Pythagorean shortcut when the two legs are perpendicular. Walk 3 km North, then 4 km East: straight-line distance = √(3²+4²) = 5 km, and you are North-East of start. Trap: Left/right turns depend on the facing direction, not on the page. Turning "right" while facing South sends you West, not East. 4.3 Seating Arrangement (Linear & Circular) Linear: everyone faces the same way; "left" and "right" are the observer's, unless stated otherwise. Circular, facing centre: a person's right hand points anticlockwise; facing outward reverses this. Key. Fix one definite clue first (an absolute position), then place relative clues around it. Keep a light pencil diagram; do not solve circular puzzles purely in your head. 4.4 Calendar & Clock Calendar: use odd days (remainder after dividing total days by 7). An ordinary year has 1 odd day, a leap year 2. A century leap-year rule: divisible by 400 is a leap year (2000 yes), a plain century (1900) is not. Clock: the minute hand gains 5.5° per minute over the hour hand. Hands overlap 11 times in 12 hours, and form a right angle 22 times in 12 hours. 4.5 Series Depth & Venn Set-Counting Number/alphabet series may mix two interleaved patterns (alternate terms) or use differences of differences. For letters, convert to position numbers (A=1 … Z=26) and read the gaps. Venn set-counting: for two sets, |A∪B| = |A| + |B| − |A∩B|. For three, add the three singles, subtract the three pair-overlaps, add back the triple overlap. In a class of 40, 25 play cricket, 20 play hockey, 10 play both: at least one sport = 25 + 20 − 10 = 35; neither = 5. 4.6 Statement-Based & Other Visual Types Type What you decide Statement & Assumption Is the unstated thing taken for granted necessarily implied? Statement & Conclusion Does the conclusion definitely follow from the given facts alone? Statement & Course of Action Is the proposed action a sensible, practical response to the problem? Cause & Effect Which event is the cause, which the effect, or are they independent? Cubes & Dice Opposite faces of a standard die sum to 7; painted-cube corner pieces show 3 faces. Input-Output Find the step rule (shift, sort, swap) applied once per step, then extend it. Ranking / Ordering Total = (rank from top) + (rank from bottom) − 1. Trap: In assumptions, an option that merely restates the statement, or is too strong ("all", "never"), is usually not a valid assumption. Stick to what is strictly necessary. 5. Research Aptitude: Going Deeper 5.1 Purpose-Based Types of Research Fundamental (basic/pure): builds theory and general knowledge, no immediate application (testing a memory model). Applied: solves a specific practical problem (does a coping programme cut relapse?). Action research (Kurt Lewin, 1946): a practitioner studies and improves their own practice in cycles of act → observe → reflect. By objective, research is also exploratory (map an unfamiliar area, generate hypotheses), descriptive (describe what exists, the "what"), or explanatory (test cause, the "why"). 5.2 Steps of the Research Process Identify and define the problem. Review the existing literature. Formulate hypotheses. Choose the research design and sample. Collect the data. Analyse and interpret the data. Draw conclusions and report. 5.3 A Good Hypothesis and Research Ethics Key. A good hypothesis is clear and specific, testable (falsifiable), states a relationship between variables, is grounded in theory, and is stated before data collection. Informed consent: participants agree freely after understanding the purpose, procedure, and risks; they may withdraw anytime. Confidentiality & anonymity: protect identities and keep data secure. Plagiarism: presenting others' work as one's own; avoid by citing every borrowed idea. Referencing awareness: psychology uses APA style (author, year, in-text; full list at the end). Institutional Ethics Committee approval is required for research on humans. 6. Indian Mental-Health System: High-Yield GK 6.1 Programmes and Committees Who → what: Joseph Bhore → Bhore Committee (1946), blueprint for India's public-health system; A. L. Mudaliar → Mudaliar Committee (1959, Health Survey and Planning Committee), reviewed progress since Bhore. National Mental Health Programme (NMHP), 1982: aims to ensure minimum mental-health care for all, integrate it into general health services, and promote community participation. District Mental Health Programme (DMHP), 1996: the NMHP's district-level arm; began from the Bellary (Karnataka) model, delivering care through district hospitals and primary health centres. National Mental Health Policy, 2014: India's first, rights-based, stresses universal access and reducing stigma. Tele-MANAS, 2022: the national tele-mental-health helpline (14416) under Ayushman Bharat; Ayushman Bharat also adds mental-health services at Health and Wellness Centres. 6.2 Key Legislation Law Core point Mental Health Act, 1987 Replaced the Indian Lunacy Act 1912; now superseded. Mental Healthcare Act (MHCA), 2017 Rights-based; decriminalises suicide attempts, allows an Advance Directive and a Nominated Representative, sets up Mental Health Review Boards. National Trust Act, 1999 For autism, cerebral palsy, intellectual disability, and multiple disabilities; enables guardianship. Rights of Persons with Disabilities (RPWD) Act, 2016 Lists 21 specified disabilities; replaced the 1995 Act; aligns with the UN Convention (UNCRPD). RML tilt: Expect a one-liner such as "Which Act decriminalised the attempt to suicide?" (answer: MHCA 2017) or "Number of disabilities under RPWD 2016?" (answer: 21). The RPWD list includes mental illness, intellectual disability, specific learning disabilities, and autism spectrum disorder. 6.3 Institutes, Cities, and Global Anchors Institute City NIMHANS Bengaluru Central Institute of Psychiatry (CIP) Ranchi RINPAS Ranchi IHBAS Delhi LGBRIMH Tezpur (Assam) WHO mhGAP (Mental Health Gap Action Programme, 2008) scales up care for mental, neurological, and substance-use disorders in low-resource settings using non-specialist health workers.
