Recap: Reasoning now spans blood relations, directions, seating, calendar/clock, series, Venn counting, and statement/visual types; research aptitude adds the basic/applied/action split, the seven-step process, hypothesis quality, and ethics; and the GK core is NMHP 1982 → DMHP 1996, MHA 1987 → MHCA 2017, RPWD 2016 (21 disabilities), National Trust 1999, Bhore and Mudaliar committees, Tele-MANAS, mhGAP, and the institute-to-city map. 7. Cause-and-Effect Reasoning From scratch: A cause-and-effect item gives you two statements and asks how they are related. Your job is to decide whether one statement is the reason and the other is the result , whether both spring from a common third cause, or whether they are simply two unrelated facts. This tests whether you can separate correlation from causation, a skill that is also core to research methodology, so RML likes it. The five standard options in this family are: (a) statement I is the cause and II is its effect; (b) statement II is the cause and I is its effect; (c) both are effects of independent causes; (d) both are effects of a common cause; (e) both are independent. The trick is that the order in which the statements are printed is not the order of causation. You must reason about what could physically or logically come first in time. 7.1 The method that cracks it Ask three questions in sequence. First, could one event have produced the other? If yes, the earlier-in-time event is the cause. Second, if neither can produce the other, is there an obvious background factor that produced both? If yes, choose "common cause". Third, if no link survives, choose "independent". Always test the time arrow: an effect cannot precede its cause. Example: (I) The government raised the price of petrol sharply. (II) The transport unions announced a strike. Here I is a plausible trigger for II, and I comes first in time, so I is the cause and II is the effect. Trap: When both statements describe consequences of a monsoon, an election, or an economic slump that is not stated, the answer is usually "common cause", not "I causes II". Do not force a direct link just because the two statements sit next to each other. 8. The Three "Statement" Families: Assumption, Argument, Conclusion From scratch: These three item types all begin with a statement, but each asks a different question, and mixing them up is the single most common way candidates lose marks in this block. Learn the one-line definition of each and the specific test each one demands. 8.1 Statement and Assumption An assumption is something the speaker takes for granted, an unstated belief without which the statement would make no sense. The test is the negation test : negate the assumption; if the statement then collapses, the assumption is implicit (valid). If the statement still stands, it is not an assumption. Example: Statement, "Please switch off the lights when you leave the room." Assumption, "The lights can be switched off." Negate it (the lights cannot be switched off) and the request becomes meaningless, so the assumption holds. 8.2 Statement and Argument Here you are given a proposal and one or more arguments for or against it, and you judge whether each argument is strong (directly relevant and weighty) or weak (irrelevant, trivial, or merely an opinion). A strong argument addresses the core issue with a real consequence; a weak one appeals to emotion, restates the question, or raises a side point. Rule: An argument that begins "Yes, because it will save money and lives" is usually strong; one that begins "No, because we have never done it before" or "Yes, because every other country does it" is usually weak. 8.3 Statement and Conclusion A conclusion is something that must follow from the given statement alone, using no outside knowledge. Treat the statement as the only truth in the universe and ask whether the conclusion is guaranteed. If the conclusion adds any information not derivable from the statement, it does not follow. Trap: Do not bring in real-world knowledge. A conclusion can be factually true in the real world yet still "not follow" because the given statement does not support it. Judge only against the printed statement. Type Question asked Winning test Assumption What is taken for granted? Negation test Argument Is this reason strong or weak? Relevance + real consequence Conclusion What must follow? Derivable from statement alone 9. Data Sufficiency From scratch: A data-sufficiency question gives a problem and two numbered statements, then asks not for the answer but whether the statements give enough information to answer it. You are testing sufficiency, not computing the final number. This saves time once you master it because you often stop before doing any arithmetic. 9.1 The five-option ladder The standard options are: (a) statement I alone is sufficient; (b) statement II alone is sufficient; (c) both together are sufficient but neither alone; (d) either alone is sufficient; (e) both together are still insufficient. Evaluate each statement separately first , covering the other with your hand, then only combine them if neither alone works. Example: What is the two-digit number? (I) The sum of its digits is 9. (II) The digit in the tens place is twice the units digit. Statement I alone gives many numbers; II alone gives many numbers; together, tens = 2 times units and digits sum to 9 gives 63 uniquely, so the answer is "both together". Trap: Never actually solve for the value once you know a single unique answer exists. Deciding "this yields exactly one value" is enough, and computing it wastes the seconds this format is designed to save. 10. Data Interpretation in Depth: Tables, Bars, Pies, and Percentage Change From scratch: Data interpretation gives you a table or chart and a cluster of questions. The chart never changes; only the questions do. The examiner is testing whether you can read the axis, pick the right cell, and run three arithmetic operations quickly: percentage, ratio, and percentage change. 10.1 Reading each chart type A table is the most information-dense and needs careful row-column matching. A bar chart compares magnitudes across categories; read the height against the axis. A pie chart shows parts of a whole, where the whole is 360 degrees or 100 percent, so a 90-degree slice is one quarter of the total. A line graph shows a trend over time; its slope, not its height, signals growth. 10.2 The percentage-change formula Rule: Percentage change = (new value minus old value) divided by old value, times 100. The denominator is always the original value, never the new one. A rise from 200 to 250 is a 25 percent increase (50/200), but a fall from 250 back to 200 is only a 20 percent decrease (50/250). Example: A pie chart shows a family spends 25 percent of a 40,000 rupee budget on rent. Rent = 0.25 times 40,000 = 10,000 rupees. If a bar chart then shows rent rose to 12,000 next year, the increase is (12,000 minus 10,000)/10,000 times 100 = 20 percent. Trap: Percentage points and percentages are not the same. A share that moves from 20 percent to 25 percent has risen by 5 percentage points but by 25 percent in relative terms. DI questions exploit this difference constantly. 10.3 Two more habits that save time First, before touching any question, read the units and the footnote : a bar labelled "in thousands" or a table with a "figures in lakh" note quietly rescales every answer. Second, when a question asks for an average across categories , do not average the percentages; convert each to an absolute value first, add them, then divide. Averaging percentages of different bases is one of the most reliable ways the paper manufactures a wrong option that looks clean. Example: two shops sell at 20 percent and 40 percent profit, but on different cost bases of 100 and 400 rupees. The combined profit is not 30 percent; it is (20 + 160)/(100 + 400) times 100 = 36 percent. 11. Approaches to Research: Qualitative, Quantitative, and by Aim From scratch: Beyond the basic-versus-applied split, RML aptitude items ask you to classify a study by its aim and by its type of data . Knowing the vocabulary lets you answer these in seconds. 11.1 By aim Exploratory research probes a poorly understood problem to generate ideas and hypotheses, often using open interviews. Descriptive research paints an accurate picture of a group or situation (surveys, case studies) but does not manipulate anything. Explanatory or experimental research tests cause and effect by manipulating an independent variable and controlling others. 11.2 By type of data Quantitative research collects numbers and uses statistics, prizing objectivity, large samples, and generalisability. Qualitative research collects words, meanings, and observations, prizing depth and context; it uses methods such as thematic analysis (Virginia Braun and Victoria Clarke, 2006) and grounded theory (Barney Glaser and Anselm Strauss, 1967). Mixed-methods research combines both. Dimension Quantitative Qualitative Data Numbers Words, meanings Logic Deductive, tests theory Inductive, builds theory Sample Large, random Small, purposive Goal Generalise Understand in depth RML tilt: Expect a one-line vignette ("a researcher interviews 8 survivors to understand their lived experience") and a demand to name the approach. Depth-plus-small-sample-plus-meaning equals qualitative; that stem is a giveaway. 12. The Research Report and APA Referencing 12.1 Standard structure of a report A research report or thesis follows a fixed skeleton, and aptitude items ask you to order or identify its parts. The core body runs: Introduction (states the problem and objectives), Review of Literature (what is already known and the gap), Method (participants, tools, procedure, design), Results (findings and statistics, no interpretation), Discussion (interpretation, limitations, implications), and References . The abstract sits at the front but is written last. Rule: Results state what was found ; Discussion states what it means . Any interpretation placed in the Results section is a structural error, and examiners test exactly this boundary. 12.2 APA referencing basics The American Psychological Association (APA) style is the standard in psychology. In-text citations use the author-and-year form, for example (Sharma, 2019). A journal reference lists author, year in parentheses, article title, italicised journal name, volume, and pages. APA is now in its 7th edition (2019/2020), a fact worth remembering for a factual GK item. Example: A book reference reads, Author, A. A. (Year). Title of the book . Publisher. Note the year comes right after the author, a hallmark that distinguishes APA from MLA. 13. Thesis, Dissertation, and Academic Terms Tested in Aptitude 13.1 Thesis versus dissertation In the Indian and British convention, a dissertation is the shorter research document submitted for a Master's degree (as in an MA or M.Sc.), while a thesis is the longer, original-contribution document submitted for an M.Phil. or PhD. (The American convention reverses the two words, which is why examiners sometimes flag the ambiguity, but for RML use the Indian sense.) 13.2 Sampling and design terms as tested Aptitude items reuse research vocabulary as pure recognition questions. Know that a population is the whole group of interest and a sample is the studied subset; a parameter describes a population while a statistic describes a sample. Probability sampling (simple random, systematic, stratified, cluster) allows generalisation; non-probability sampling (convenience, purposive, snowball, quota) does not. A pilot study is a small trial run to test the tools before the main study. Trap: Stratified sampling divides the population into groups and samples within each group; cluster sampling divides into groups and samples whole groups . Candidates swap these two constantly. 14. Teaching Aptitude Essentials From scratch: Some RML and allied entrance papers slip in a few teaching-aptitude items borrowed from the UGC-NET pattern. You do not need pedagogy training, only the standard vocabulary of levels, objectives, and evaluation. 14.1 Levels and objectives Teaching is often described at three levels : the memory level (recall of facts), the understanding level (grasp of relationships), and the reflective level (problem-solving and critical thought). Learning objectives are commonly framed with Bloom's taxonomy , which ranks cognitive skills from remembering, understanding, applying, analysing, and evaluating, up to creating. 14.2 Formative versus summative evaluation Rule: Formative evaluation happens during learning to give feedback and improve teaching (class quizzes, assignments). Summative evaluation happens at the end to certify achievement (the final exam). A quick memory hook: formative "forms" the learner along the way; summative "sums up" at the finish. RML tilt: A one-line stem like "a teacher gives weekly ungraded quizzes to adjust her lessons" points straight at formative evaluation. Watch the word "during" versus "at the end". 15. Global and National Bodies Beyond RCI and NIMHANS From scratch: The GK block rewards a clean map of who does what. RCI and NIMHANS are covered elsewhere; here are the other bodies that recur. 15.1 The core acronyms Body What it is Role WHO World Health Organization (UN, Geneva) Global health standards; publishes the ICD classification DGHS Directorate General of Health Services Technical health advice to the Union health ministry ICMR Indian Council of Medical Research Apex body for biomedical research and ethics guidelines NHRC National Human Rights Commission Protects rights, including of persons in mental-health institutions NMHC National Mental Health Commission / Authority context Oversight linked to MHCA 2017 (Central Mental Health Authority) Who → what: WHO publishes the ICD (currently ICD-11), while the APA publishes the DSM (currently DSM-5-TR). India officially uses the ICD system, a fact examiners love to check. 15.2 Diagnostic manuals in one line The ICD (International Classification of Diseases) is the WHO system used officially in India; the DSM (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders) is the APA system used widely in research and the United States. Knowing "WHO to ICD, APA to DSM" answers a whole family of questions. 16. Rights Guaranteed under the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 From scratch: The MHCA 2017 replaced the Mental Health Act of 1987 and shifted the frame from control to rights . The Act came into force in 2018 and treats access to mental healthcare as a right. RML tests the specific rights it grants. 16.1 The headline rights Right to access mental healthcare run or funded by the government, of affordable and good quality. Decriminalisation of suicide: a person who attempts suicide is presumed to be under severe stress and is not to be punished under the penal code. Advance Directive: a person may state in advance how they wish to be treated, and whom they nominate as their representative. Nominated Representative: the right to appoint a person to take decisions on one's behalf. Right to confidentiality, dignity, and protection from cruel or degrading treatment. Restrictions on procedures: electro-convulsive therapy without muscle relaxants and anaesthesia is banned, ECT is banned for minors, and sterilisation and chaining are prohibited. Rule: The MHCA 2017 defines "mental illness" but pointedly excludes mental retardation / intellectual disability from that definition, since disability is covered by the RPWD Act. This exclusion is a favourite one-mark trap. Trap: Do not confuse the Advance Directive (patient states future wishes) with the Nominated Representative (a named person who decides). Both are new to the 2017 Act, and stems deliberately blur them. 17. The RPWD Act 2016 and the National Institutes 17.1 Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 The RPWD Act 2016 replaced the older Persons with Disabilities Act of 1995 and expanded the recognised disabilities from 7 to 21 , now including mental illness, autism spectrum disorder, intellectual disability, and specific learning disabilities. It mandates reservation in higher education (5 percent) and government jobs (4 percent) and defines "benchmark disability" as 40 percent or more. Who → what: The RPWD Act is administered by the Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities (DEPwD) under the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment, the same ministry under which the RCI sits. 17.2 National institutes worth naming Several National Institutes serve specific disabilities and often appear as "match the institute to the city" items. Key ones include NIMHANS (Bengaluru, mental health and neurosciences), the Central Institute of Psychiatry or CIP (Ranchi), IHBAS (Delhi), NIEPID (Secunderabad, intellectual disabilities), NIEPMD (Chennai, multiple disabilities), Ali Yavar Jung National Institute (Mumbai, hearing), and the National Institute for the Visually Handicapped (Dehradun). RML tilt: CIP Ranchi and IHBAS Delhi appear repeatedly because both run their own clinical-psychology entrances, so an RML aspirant is expected to know them cold. 18. Important Days and Landmark Reports 18.1 The calendar of health days Day Date World Mental Health Day 10 October World Health Day 7 April World Suicide Prevention Day 10 September World Autism Awareness Day 2 April International Day of Persons with Disabilities 3 December World Alzheimer's Day 21 September 18.2 Programmes and the policy trail The National Mental Health Programme (NMHP) was launched in 1982 to make mental-health care available at the community level; its field arm, the District Mental Health Programme (DMHP) , began in 1996 under the Bellary model in Karnataka. The National Mental Health Policy was adopted in 2014, and the MHCA followed in 2017. Reading these as a timeline (1982 to 1996 to 2014 to 2017) turns a memory task into a story. Recap: cause-and-effect turns on the time arrow and the hidden common cause; the three "statement" families each demand their own test (negation, strength, must-follow); data sufficiency asks only "is it enough", never the final number; percentage change always divides by the original value. On the GK side, WHO owns the ICD and APA owns the DSM; the MHCA 2017 grants access, decriminalises suicide, and adds the Advance Directive and Nominated Representative, while excluding intellectual disability, which the RPWD 2016 (21 disabilities, 40 percent benchmark) covers instead. Anchor the policy timeline at 1982 to 2017 and the day at 10 October. 2 General & Basic Psychology From scratch: Psychology is the scientific study of behaviour and mental processes. This section builds the "core" academic base the RML CET-166 paper draws on: the schools, then the big four content areas (learning, memory, attention/perception, motivation/emotion) and intelligence. Learn each theorist as a who → what pair; the exam almost always tests matching. 1. Schools & History of Psychology Modern psychology begins in 1879 , when Wilhelm Wundt opened the first psychology laboratory at Leipzig, Germany. Each school below is a reaction to the one before it. Who → what: Wilhelm Wundt & Edward Titchener → Structuralism : break conscious experience into basic elements (sensations, feelings) using introspection . Titchener coined the term. William James → Functionalism : don't ask what the mind is , ask what it is for , how consciousness helps us adapt. Wrote Principles of Psychology (1890). Max Wertheimer , Wolfgang Köhler , Kurt Koffka → Gestalt : "the whole is different from the sum of its parts." Wertheimer's phi phenomenon (apparent motion) launched it; Köhler showed insight learning in chimpanzees. John B. Watson & B.F. Skinner → Behaviourism : study only observable behaviour, not the mind. Watson's 1913 "behaviourist manifesto" is the founding statement. Sigmund Freud → Psychoanalysis : behaviour driven by the unconscious and early childhood conflict. Carl Rogers & Abraham Maslow → Humanistic ("third force"): free will, growth, self-actualization . Ulric Neisser & George A. Miller → Cognitive revolution (1950s–60s): the mind is back, studied as information processing. Neisser's 1967 book Cognitive Psychology named the field; Miller's "magical number seven, plus or minus two" set short-term memory span. Trap: Edward Titchener (not Wilhelm Wundt) coined "structuralism," and Titchener was American-based; Wundt is the founder of experimental psychology. Also, Gestalt is perception-focused, behaviourism is learning-focused, don't swap. 2. Learning Learning = a relatively permanent change in behaviour due to experience. Classical conditioning, Ivan Pavlov Ivan Pavlov (Russian physiologist) discovered that a neutral stimulus, paired with one that already triggers a reflex, comes to trigger that reflex itself. Term Meaning Pavlov's dog US (unconditioned stimulus) triggers a reflex naturally food UR (unconditioned response) the natural reflex salivation to food CS (conditioned stimulus) was neutral, now triggers response bell CR (conditioned response) learned response to CS salivation to bell Acquisition : learning the CS–US link. Extinction : CS repeatedly without US → CR fades. Spontaneous recovery : after a rest, the extinguished CR briefly reappears. Generalization : similar stimuli also trigger the CR (a different bell). Discrimination : responding only to the specific CS, not similar ones. Higher-order conditioning : a well-learned CS acts as a US to condition a new CS. Operant conditioning, Thorndike & Skinner Edward L. Thorndike 's Law of Effect : responses followed by satisfaction are strengthened; those followed by discomfort are weakened (from his puzzle box cats). B.F. Skinner extended this: behaviour is shaped by its consequences, studied in the Skinner box . Key. Reinforcement always increases a behaviour; punishment always decreases it. "Positive" = add a stimulus, "negative" = remove one. Positive reinforcement : add something pleasant ( give a treat ). Negative reinforcement : remove something unpleasant ( seatbelt beep stops ). Positive punishment : add something aversive ( a scolding ). Negative punishment : remove something pleasant ( take away the phone ). Primary reinforcer : satisfies a biological need (food, water). Secondary reinforcer : learned value (money, praise). Shaping : reinforcing successive approximations toward a target behaviour. Schedules of reinforcement: Schedule Rule Feature Fixed Ratio (FR) after a set number of responses high rate, post-reward pause Variable Ratio (VR) after an unpredictable number highest, steadiest rate Fixed Interval (FI) first response after a set time scalloped pattern Variable Interval (VI) first response after variable time slow, steady Key. Variable Ratio (VR) produces the highest response rate and is most resistant to extinction (why gambling is so persistent). Observational learning, Albert Bandura Albert Bandura 's Bobo doll experiment showed children imitate aggression they merely watch , learning by modelling , no direct reinforcement needed. His broader social learning theory adds thought between stimulus and response. 3. Memory Who → what: Richard Atkinson & Richard Shiffrin → multi-store model : sensory memory → short-term memory (STM) → long-term memory (LTM) , with rehearsal moving info along. Alan Baddeley & Graham Hitch → working memory : replaces passive STM with an active system, central executive , phonological loop , visuospatial sketchpad (later, the episodic buffer ). Fergus Craik & Robert Lockhart → levels of processing : deeper semantic (meaning) processing is remembered better than shallow (looks, sound). Endel Tulving → memory types: episodic (personal events), semantic (facts), both declarative ; plus procedural (skills, non-declarative). Hermann Ebbinghaus → the forgetting curve : memory drops sharply then levels off; also the spacing effect . Forgetting theories: decay (unused traces fade), interference , proactive (old learning blocks new) vs retroactive (new learning blocks old), and retrieval failure . Key. Serial position effect : we best recall the first items ( primacy , rehearsed into LTM) and last items ( recency , still in STM); the middle is worst. Trap: Proactive = pro/forward , old interferes forward onto new; retroactive = new acts backward on old. Easy to reverse under time pressure. 4. Attention & Perception Who → what: Donald Broadbent → filter (bottleneck) model : an early filter selects one channel by physical features; unattended info is blocked. Anne Treisman → attenuation model : the filter turns unattended input down rather than off, so a salient word (your name) can still break through. Gestalt laws of perceptual organization: proximity , similarity , closure , continuity (good continuation) , figure–ground , common fate . Depth cues : monocular (one eye, relative size, interposition, linear perspective, texture gradient) and binocular (two eyes, retinal disparity , convergence). Perceptual constancies keep size, shape, and colour stable despite changing retinal images. 5. Motivation & Emotion Drive-reduction theory (Clark Hull): a need creates a drive that we act to reduce, restoring homeostasis . Abraham Maslow 's hierarchy of needs stacks motives: physiological → safety → love/belonging → esteem → self-actualization ; lower needs dominate until met. Theories of emotion (a classic RML matching item): Theory Core claim James–Lange body first: we feel afraid because we tremble Cannon–Bard simultaneous: arousal and emotion occur at once Schachter–Singer two-factor arousal + a cognitive label for it Richard Lazarus appraisal a cognitive appraisal comes first and causes emotion Trap: James–Lange = bodily response precedes emotion; Cannon–Bard = they are simultaneous. Reversing these two is the most common error. 6. Intelligence Who → what: Charles Spearman → two-factor theory : a general factor g underlies all abilities plus task-specific s factors (from factor analysis ). Louis Thurstone → seven primary mental abilities (verbal, numerical, spatial, memory, reasoning, word fluency, perceptual speed), no single g. Raymond B. Cattell → fluid intelligence (reasoning with novel problems, declines with age) vs crystallized intelligence (learned knowledge, holds up). Howard Gardner → multiple intelligences (linguistic, logical-mathematical, spatial, musical, bodily-kinesthetic, interpersonal, intrapersonal, naturalistic). Robert Sternberg → triarchic theory : analytical , creative , practical . J.P. Guilford → Structure of Intellect : up to 150+ abilities from operations × contents × products ; source of divergent thinking . RML tilt: The paper leans on who-said-what matching , theorist to concept, school to founder, emotion theory to claim. Memorize the Pavlov four-letter set (US/UR/CS/CR), the VR = most extinction-resistant fact, proactive vs retroactive interference, and the intelligence theorists cold; these recur almost every year. Recap: Schools: Wundt/Titchener structuralism, James functionalism, Wertheimer/Köhler/Koffka Gestalt, Watson/Skinner behaviourism, Freud psychoanalysis, Rogers/Maslow humanistic, Neisser/Miller cognitive. Learning: Pavlov classical (US/UR/CS/CR), Thorndike law of effect, Skinner reinforcement/punishment & schedules ( VR resists extinction), Bandura observational. Memory: Atkinson–Shiffrin multi-store, Baddeley–Hitch working memory, Craik–Lockhart levels, Tulving episodic/semantic/procedural, Ebbinghaus forgetting curve, serial position. Attention: Broadbent filter, Treisman attenuation. Emotion: James–Lange, Cannon–Bard, Schachter–Singer, Lazarus. Intelligence: Spearman g , Thurstone , Cattell fluid/crystallized, Gardner , Sternberg , Guilford . 7. Sensation & Psychophysics Everything you know about the world arrives first as raw energy hitting a receptor. Sensation is the pickup of that physical energy (light, sound, pressure, chemicals) by specialised receptor cells; perception is the brain's organisation and interpretation of those signals into meaningful objects and events. Sensation asks "is something there?"; perception asks "what is it?". From scratch: a receptor cannot pass physical energy directly into the nervous system. It must convert light or sound or pressure into nerve impulses (action potentials). That conversion is called transduction , and it is the single most important idea in sensation: every sense is a transducer. 7.1 Thresholds Not every stimulus is strong enough to notice. Psychophysics (founded by Gustav Fechner) measures the relationship between physical stimuli and the sensations they produce. Absolute threshold: the smallest amount of stimulus energy detectable 50% of the time (e.g. a candle flame seen on a dark clear night from about 30 miles). Difference threshold (just-noticeable-difference, JND): the smallest change in a stimulus that can be detected 50% of the time. Also called the difference limen . Subliminal stimulus: one below the absolute threshold, not consciously detected. 7.2 The three classic laws Law Theorist Core statement Weber's law Ernst Weber The JND is a constant proportion of the original stimulus, not a fixed amount. A heavier weight needs a bigger change to feel different. Fechner's law Gustav Fechner Sensation grows as the logarithm of stimulus intensity (built on Weber's constant). Big physical increases yield smaller sensory increases. Stevens' power law Stanley Smith Stevens Sensation is a power function of intensity; the exponent varies by sense (electric shock grows faster than brightness). Often considered more accurate than Fechner's. Who → what: Weber → constant fraction (JND/stimulus = k); Fechner → logarithmic sensation; Stevens → power-function sensation. Weber fraction for weight is about 1/50: you can just detect a 2g change on a 100g load, but need a 20g change on a 1000g load. 7.3 Signal detection theory Detection is not just about the stimulus; it also depends on the observer's expectations, motivation and the background "noise". Signal detection theory (SDT; David Green and John Swets, 1966) replaces the fixed threshold with two independent factors: sensitivity (how well signal is told from noise) and response criterion / bias (how willing the person is to say "yes"). Outcomes fall into hits, misses, false alarms and correct rejections. RML tilt: expect a one-liner match item: "detection depends on both stimulus intensity and decision criterion" → signal detection theory. Know that SDT explains why a tired radiologist reports more false alarms. 7.4 Sensory adaptation and the senses Sensory adaptation is the reduced sensitivity to an unchanging stimulus (you stop smelling a room, stop feeling your clothes). It keeps us tuned to change . Vision: rods and cones in the retina transduce light (photoreception). Audition: hair cells on the basilar membrane (cochlea) transduce sound vibration. Gustation and olfaction: chemoreceptors on the tongue and in the nose transduce dissolved and airborne chemicals. Somatosensation: mechanoreceptors, thermoreceptors and nociceptors handle touch, temperature and pain; the vestibular and kinaesthetic senses handle balance and body position. 8. Thinking, Cognition & Problem Solving 8.1 Concepts and categories A concept is a mental grouping of similar objects, events or ideas; it lets us handle the world without treating every item as brand new. We organise concepts around a prototype : the best, most typical example of a category (a robin is a more prototypical "bird" than a penguin). Faster categorisation of items close to the prototype is a classic exam fact (Eleanor Rosch's work). 8.2 Reasoning Deductive reasoning: from general premises to a specific, logically certain conclusion (top-down). If the premises are true, the conclusion must be true. Inductive reasoning: from specific observations to a probable general rule (bottom-up). Conclusions are likely, not guaranteed. 8.3 Problem-solving strategies Strategy What it is Algorithm Step-by-step procedure that guarantees a solution but can be slow. Heuristic Mental shortcut / rule of thumb: fast, but can fail. Means-end analysis (Allen Newell and Herbert Simon, 1972) Reduce the gap between current state and goal by breaking it into subgoals. Insight Sudden "aha" grasp of the solution (Wolfgang Kohler's ape Sultan; Gestalt view). Two classic blocks to problem solving: Mental set: the tendency to keep using a strategy that worked before, even when a simpler one exists. Functional fixedness: inability to see a novel use for an object (Karl Duncker's candle problem: not seeing the matchbox as a shelf). From scratch: the Gestalt school treated problem solving as restructuring the whole problem, so insight was a perceptual reorganisation, not trial and error. This is why insight and functional fixedness sit together in the syllabus. 8.4 Judgement and decision-making heuristics Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky showed that everyday judgement leans on heuristics that produce predictable errors (biases). Availability heuristic: judging likelihood by how easily examples come to mind (plane crashes feel common because they are vivid). Representativeness heuristic: judging by how well something matches a stereotype, ignoring base rates. Anchoring and adjustment: starting from an initial value and adjusting insufficiently. Framing effect: the same choice pulls different decisions depending on wording ("90% survive" vs "10% die"). Confirmation bias: seeking evidence that fits an existing belief and ignoring the rest. Trap: availability = ease of recall ; representativeness = resemblance to a stereotype . Exams swap the two. Kahneman won the 2002 Nobel in Economics for this work (Amos Tversky had died). 8.5 Creativity J.P. Guilford distinguished convergent thinking (narrowing to one correct answer, what IQ tests measure) from divergent thinking (generating many possible answers, the engine of creativity). Divergent thinking is judged on fluency, flexibility, originality and elaboration. 9. Language & Psycholinguistics Language is a rule-governed system for combining symbols to communicate meaning. Psycholinguists break it into levels: Phonology: the sound system; phonemes are the smallest distinctive sound units. Morphology: word structure; morphemes are the smallest meaning units. Syntax: rules for combining words into grammatical sentences. Semantics: meaning of words and sentences. Pragmatics: use of language in social context (tone, turn-taking, implied meaning). 9.1 How is language acquired? The great debate Who → what: Noam Chomsky → nativist / innate view; B.F. Skinner → learning / behaviourist view. B.F. Skinner (in Verbal Behavior , 1957) argued that language is learned like any behaviour, through imitation, reinforcement and shaping. Noam Chomsky attacked this, arguing that children produce novel sentences they were never taught and learn grammar too fast for reinforcement alone. He proposed: Language acquisition device (LAD): an innate brain mechanism for grasping grammar. Universal grammar: a common grammatical blueprint underlying all human languages. Transformational grammar: deep structure (meaning) transformed into surface structure (spoken form). 9.2 Linguistic relativity Benjamin Lee Whorf and Edward Sapir proposed the linguistic relativity hypothesis (the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis): the language we speak shapes how we think and perceive the world. The strong form (language determines thought) is largely rejected; the weak form (language influences thought) has some support. 9.3 Stages of language acquisition Cooing (around 2 months): vowel-like sounds. Babbling (around 4 to 6 months): consonant-vowel repetitions, initially universal. One-word / holophrastic (around 12 months): single words carry whole meanings. Two-word / telegraphic (around 18 to 24 months): "want milk", grammar words dropped. Sentences (from about 2.5 years): rapid grammar growth, including overregularisation ("goed"). 10. Consciousness & Cognitive Psychology as a Field Consciousness is our awareness of ourselves and our environment. Psychologists describe varied states of consciousness : normal waking awareness, sleep and dreaming, hypnosis, meditation, and drug-altered states. 10.1 The cognitive revolution From roughly the 1950s, psychology turned away from strict behaviourism and back to the study of internal mental processes. This cognitive revolution borrowed the computer as a metaphor and gave rise to the information-processing model : the mind takes in information (input), encodes and transforms it (processing / storage), and produces behaviour (output), much like a computer. 10.2 Cognitive psychology as a school Who → what: Ulric Neisser → "father of cognitive psychology"; his 1967 book Cognitive Psychology named and organised the field. Cognitive psychology studies how people perceive, attend, remember, think, reason and use language, treating these as information-processing operations that can be modelled and tested experimentally. Key. Sensation transduces energy; perception interprets it. Weber = constant fraction, Fechner = log, Stevens = power. Kahneman and Tversky = heuristics and biases. Chomsky (innate LAD, universal grammar) vs Skinner (learned verbal behaviour). Neisser = father of cognitive psychology; the information-processing model is its master metaphor. Recap: This block bridged the raw senses (psychophysics, thresholds, three laws, signal detection) to higher cognition (concepts and prototypes, reasoning, problem-solving blocks, judgement heuristics, creativity), then to language (five levels, the Chomsky-Skinner debate, Sapir-Whorf, acquisition stages) and finally to consciousness and the cognitive revolution that made cognitive psychology a school. 11. Memory Architecture: How Information Is Stored Memory is not a single box in the head; it is a set of interacting systems that differ in capacity, duration, and coding. The modern account grew out of a stage model and was later refined into a workspace model. Learn both, because RML has repeatedly asked candidates to name the store, its capacity, and the psychologist who proposed it. From scratch: Three verbs organise all of memory. Encoding is turning an experience into a memory trace. Storage is holding that trace over time. Retrieval is pulling it back out. A memory failure can happen at any of the three, and good exam answers say which stage failed. 11.1 The Atkinson–Shiffrin multi-store model Richard Atkinson and Richard Shiffrin (1968) proposed that information flows through three separate stores in sequence. First is the sensory register , which holds a near-exact copy of sensory input for a fraction of a second (iconic memory for vision, about 250 milliseconds, demonstrated by George Sperling; echoic memory for sound, about 2 to 4 seconds). If attention is paid, information passes to short-term memory (STM) , which holds roughly 7 plus or minus 2 items (George Miller's magic number) for about 15 to 30 seconds unless rehearsed. Maintenance rehearsal keeps items in STM; elaborative rehearsal transfers them to long-term memory (LTM) , which is effectively unlimited in capacity and duration. Who → what: Richard Atkinson & Shiffrin → the "modal" multi-store model (sensory register, STM, LTM as separate stores linked by attention and rehearsal). Trap: The magic number "7 plus or minus 2" is George Miller (1956), not Atkinson or Shiffrin. Later work by Nelson Cowan revised the true capacity of the focus of attention down to about 4 chunks. Do not attribute the number to Miller's students. 11.2 Baddeley and Hitch: the working memory model Alan Baddeley and Graham Hitch (1974) argued that STM is not a single passive store but an active working memory with separate components. The central executive is an attention-directing controller that has no storage of its own; it allocates resources to two slave systems. The phonological loop holds speech-based information and has two parts: a phonological store (the "inner ear") and an articulatory rehearsal process (the "inner voice"). The visuospatial sketchpad (the "inner eye") holds visual and spatial information. In 2000 Baddeley added a fourth component, the episodic buffer , a limited store that binds information from the loop, the sketchpad, and LTM into single coherent episodes. Component Handles Everyday sign Central executive Attention control, coordination Deciding what to focus on Phonological loop Verbal / acoustic material Repeating a phone number under your breath Visuospatial sketchpad Images, layout, location Picturing the route to a shop Episodic buffer Binding, linking to LTM Combining a face and a name into one memory RML tilt: A favourite item asks which component was added later. Answer: the episodic buffer (Baddeley, 2000). Another asks which component has no storage capacity: the central executive. 11.3 Levels of processing Fergus Craik and Robert Lockhart (1972) rejected the store metaphor. They argued that memory strength depends not on where information sits but on how deeply it is processed . Shallow, structural processing (how a word looks) produces weak traces; phonemic processing (how it sounds) is intermediate; deep, semantic processing (what it means) produces the strongest, most durable traces. This is why relating new material to your own life (self-reference effect) aids recall. Example: asked "Is DOG in capitals?" you barely remember the word later; asked "Does DOG fit the sentence 'The ___ chased the cat?'" you remember it well, because you processed its meaning. 11.4 Types of long-term memory Endel Tulving (1972) split LTM into episodic memory (personally experienced events tied to a time and place, "what I ate yesterday") and semantic memory (general facts and concepts detached from any learning episode, "Paris is the capital of France"). Both are declarative (explicit, consciously recalled and stated). Against these stands procedural memory , a non-declarative (implicit) store of skills and habits such as cycling or typing, which is expressed through performance rather than conscious recall. Rule: Declarative = "knowing that" (episodic + semantic), can be verbalised. Procedural = "knowing how", shown by doing. Amnesic patients often lose declarative memory while procedural learning stays intact. 11.5 The serial position effect When people recall a list, they remember the first items well (the primacy effect , because early items got the most rehearsal and reached LTM) and the last items well (the recency effect , because they are still in STM). Middle items are recalled worst. Delaying recall wipes out recency but leaves primacy, which is strong evidence for separate short-term and long-term stores. 11.6 Why we forget Forgetting is not one process. Several mechanisms have been proposed and each has a named champion. Decay theory: traces fade with the mere passage of time if unused (a very old idea, strongest for sensory and short-term memory). Interference theory: other memories block the target. Proactive interference is old learning disrupting new (your old phone number intrudes on the new one). Retroactive interference is new learning disrupting old (a new number makes you forget the old one). Cue-dependent forgetting: Endel Tulving argued the trace is intact but the retrieval cue is missing (the encoding specificity principle : recall is best when retrieval cues match encoding conditions). This covers context-dependent and state-dependent memory. Motivated forgetting: Sigmund Freud's repression , the active pushing of threatening memories out of awareness. Trap: Proactive = old harms new (moving forward in time it interferes); retroactive = new harms old (acting backward ). Students routinely swap these. Anchor on "pro = prior". 11.7 Ebbinghaus and the forgetting curve Hermann Ebbinghaus (1885), using himself and nonsense syllables, plotted the first forgetting curve : retention drops sharply within the first hour and the first day, then levels off. He also described the spacing effect (distributed practice beats massed cramming) and savings (relearning is faster than first learning). 11.8 Reconstructive memory and schemas Frederic Bartlett (1932), using his story "The War of the Ghosts", showed that memory is not a photocopy but an active reconstruction . Participants distorted the unfamiliar story to fit their own cultural expectations, a process he explained through schemas (organised packets of prior knowledge). We remember the gist and rebuild the details, often wrongly. 11.9 Loftus and the misinformation effect Elizabeth Loftus demonstrated that memory is malleable and vulnerable to post-event information. In the classic study, the verb used to describe a filmed car crash changed speed estimates: cars that "smashed" were rated faster than cars that "hit", and a week later "smashed" witnesses falsely recalled broken glass. This misinformation effect is the empirical backbone of doubts about eyewitness testimony. RML tilt: Link Loftus to the courtroom: misleading questions can implant false details, so eyewitness confidence is a poor guide to accuracy. Contrast this with a flashbulb memory , a vivid, confidently held snapshot of the moment one heard shocking news (Roger Brown & James Kulik, 1977); such memories feel accurate but are also prone to error. 11.10 Amnesia Anterograde amnesia is the inability to form new long-term memories after brain injury (the famous patient H.M. (studied by William Scoville and Brenda Milner, 1957), after hippocampal removal, could not lay down new declarative memories yet still learned new motor skills). Retrograde amnesia is the loss of memories formed before the injury. The dissociation in H.M. is the strongest single case for separating declarative and procedural memory. Memory recap: sensory register → STM (Miller's 7±2) → LTM, via attention and rehearsal (Atkinson & Shiffrin). STM is really working memory with four parts (Baddeley & Graham Hitch). Depth beats duration for durability (Craik & Lockhart). LTM splits into episodic/semantic/procedural (Tulving). Forgetting = decay, interference, missing cues, or repression. Memory is reconstructive (Bartlett) and suggestible (Loftus). 12. Models of Attention Attention is the cognitive process of selecting some inputs for deeper processing while filtering others. The history of attention research is essentially a debate over where in the processing stream the filter sits: early (before meaning) or late (after meaning). 12.1 Early-selection: Broadbent's filter Donald Broadbent (1958) proposed the first information-processing model of attention. Inputs enter a sensory buffer, then a selective filter passes only one channel (selected by physical features such as which ear or which voice) to a limited-capacity system; the rest are blocked early , before meaning is extracted. This explains the cocktail-party finding that people notice little from an unattended channel. 12.2 Attenuation: Treisman Anne Treisman (1964) softened the filter. Instead of blocking the unattended channel completely, the filter attenuates it (turns its volume down). Important words with low thresholds, such as your own name, can still break through. This explains why we hear our name spoken across a noisy room. 12.3 Late-selection: Deutsch and Norman J. Anthony Deutsch and Diana Deutsch (1963), later refined by Donald Norman, argued that all inputs are processed for meaning and the selection happens late , at the point of response or memory, based on importance. On this view nothing is filtered out early; the bottleneck is at the exit, not the entrance. 12.4 Capacity model: Kahneman Daniel Kahneman (1973) reframed attention as a pool of limited mental effort or capacity that can be flexibly allocated across tasks rather than a fixed structural filter. Arousal raises available capacity; task difficulty and enduring dispositions govern how it is spent. This model handles divided attention (two easy tasks can share the pool, two hard ones cannot). Type Meaning Selective attention Focusing on one source, ignoring others Divided attention Splitting resources across tasks (multitasking) Sustained attention Maintaining focus over long periods (vigilance) Rule: Automatic processing is fast, effortless, parallel, and needs no attention (reading a familiar word). Controlled processing is slow, effortful, serial, and capacity-limited (reading in a new language). The classic evidence is the Stroop effect: automatic word reading interferes with controlled colour naming. 13. Perception: Organising the Sensory World From scratch: Sensation is the raw detection of a stimulus by a sense organ. Perception is the brain's interpretation of that raw data into a meaningful experience. The same light can be sensed identically yet perceived differently, which is why illusions exist. 13.1 Gestalt laws of grouping The Gestalt psychologists (Max Wertheimer, Kurt Koffka, Wolfgang Köhler) argued that "the whole is different from the sum of its parts" and that the mind organises sensory elements by innate laws. Key laws: proximity (near items group together), similarity (alike items group), closure (we complete incomplete figures), continuity or good continuation (we follow smooth paths), and figure–ground (we split a scene into an object and its background). 13.2 Depth perception We build a three-dimensional world from a two-dimensional retinal image using depth cues. Binocular cues need two eyes: retinal disparity (the two eyes get slightly different images, and the brain reads the difference as depth) and convergence (the inward turn of the eyes for near objects). Monocular cues work with one eye: relative size, interposition (overlap), linear perspective, texture gradient, aerial perspective, light and shadow, and motion parallax. 13.3 Perceptual constancies Constancy is perceiving an object as stable despite changing sensory input. Size constancy (a car looks the same size as it drives away, though its retinal image shrinks), shape constancy (a door stays rectangular as it swings open), and colour constancy (a red apple looks red under different lighting). 13.4 Illusions Illusions reveal the rules the brain uses. In the Müller-Lyer illusion , a line with outward "arrowhead" fins looks shorter than an equal line with inward "feather" fins, often explained by misapplied size constancy learned from carpentered rooms. In the Ponzo illusion , two equal lines placed over converging railway tracks look unequal because the "farther" line is scaled up by linear-perspective depth cues. 13.5 Bottom-up versus top-down, and the two great theorists Bottom-up processing builds perception directly from the sensory data upward. Top-down processing uses prior knowledge, context, and expectations to interpret data. James Gibson championed direct (ecological) perception : the optic array is so rich that perception is bottom-up and needs no inference; we directly pick up affordances (what an object offers for action). Richard Gregory championed the constructivist view: perception is top-down, an active hypothesis or "best guess" that the brain constructs from incomplete data, which is why illusions fool us. RML tilt: Pair the names cleanly. Gibson = direct, data-rich, bottom-up, affordances. Gregory = constructivist, inference, top-down, perception as hypothesis. Items often give a one-line definition and ask for the theorist. 14. Theories of Emotion From scratch: An emotion has three ingredients: a physiological arousal (racing heart), a behavioural expression (running), and a subjective feeling (fear). The theories differ on the order in which these occur and which one causes which. 14.1 The classic sequence debate William James and Carl Lange (independently, the James–Lange theory ) held that the bodily reaction comes first and the emotion is our perception of it: we are afraid because we tremble, we do not tremble because we are afraid. Walter Cannon and Philip Bard (the Cannon–Bard theory ) objected that the body's responses are too slow and too similar across emotions; they proposed that the arousal and the felt emotion occur simultaneously and independently, both triggered by the thalamus. 14.2 Two-factor theory Stanley Schachter and Jerome Singer (1962) proposed the two-factor theory : emotion equals physiological arousal plus a cognitive label. Arousal is general and undifferentiated; we scan the situation to decide what to call it. Their adrenaline study showed that identically aroused participants reported euphoria or anger depending on the confederate's behaviour. This is the origin of misattribution of arousal . 14.3 Appraisal and the cognition-versus-affect debate Richard Lazarus argued that cognitive appraisal of an event (is this a threat or a challenge?) is necessary and comes before emotion; no appraisal, no emotion. Robert Zajonc disagreed, arguing that affect can precede cognition ("preferences need no inferences"), shown by the mere-exposure effect where liking rises for stimuli seen too briefly to recognise. Joseph LeDoux supplied the neuroscience: a fast, subcortical "low road" from thalamus to amygdala can trigger fear before the slower cortical "high road" identifies the stimulus. 14.4 Basic emotions and facial feedback Paul Ekman's cross-cultural studies identified a small set of basic emotions with universal facial expressions: happiness, sadness, anger, fear, disgust, and surprise. The facial-feedback hypothesis holds that our facial muscles feed back to intensify or even generate emotion, so forcing a smile can lift mood. Theory Core claim (order of events) James–Lange Body reacts first, feeling follows Cannon–Bard Arousal and feeling occur at once Schachter–Singer Arousal plus cognitive label Lazarus Appraisal (cognition) comes first Zajonc Affect can precede cognition 15. Theories of Motivation 15.1 Drive-reduction and arousal Clark Hull's drive-reduction theory says a physiological need creates an aroused drive state that motivates behaviour to restore homeostasis (balance); reducing the drive is reinforcing. But drive reduction cannot explain why we seek stimulation (roller coasters, curiosity). Arousal theory fills the gap: we act to keep arousal at an optimal level. The Yerkes–Dodson law (Robert Yerkes & John Dodson) states that performance is best at a moderate level of arousal and falls off when arousal is too low or too high, and that the optimal level is lower for difficult tasks than for easy ones. 15.2 Maslow's hierarchy of needs Abraham Maslow arranged needs in a pyramid that must be climbed from the bottom up: physiological (food, water) → safety → love and belonging → esteem → self-actualisation (realising one's full potential). The lower four are deficiency needs ; self-actualisation is a growth need . Maslow later added transcendence at the top. 15.3 McClelland's needs David McClelland proposed three learned social motives measured by the Thematic Apperception Test (Christiana Morgan and Henry Murray, 1935): the need for achievement (nAch) , the drive to master challenging goals; the need for affiliation (nAff) , the drive for warm relationships; and the need for power (nPow) , the drive to influence others. High-nAch people prefer moderately difficult, feedback-rich tasks. 15.4 Self-determination theory Edward Deci and Richard Ryan's self-determination theory holds that humans have three innate psychological needs: autonomy (feeling in control of one's actions), competence (feeling effective), and relatedness (feeling connected). It distinguishes intrinsic motivation (doing something for its own reward) from extrinsic motivation (doing it for an outside reward). A key finding is the overjustification effect : paying people for an already-enjoyed activity can undermine intrinsic interest. Rule: Incentive theory says behaviour is pulled by external goals (a "carrot"), whereas drive theory says it is pushed by internal needs. Expectancy-value approaches add that effort depends on how likely success seems multiplied by how much the outcome is valued. 16. Theories of Intelligence 16.1 Factor theories Charles Spearman, using factor analysis, found that all mental tests correlate positively and proposed a general intelligence factor, "g" , plus test-specific factors ("s"); this is his two-factor theory . Louis Thurstone disagreed with a single g and identified seven relatively independent primary mental abilities (verbal comprehension, word fluency, number, spatial, memory, perceptual speed, reasoning). Raymond Cattell split g into fluid intelligence (Gf) , the ability to reason with novel problems (peaks early, declines with age), and crystallised intelligence (Gc) , accumulated knowledge and skills (holds or rises with age). 16.2 Structure and multiple models J.P. Guilford's Structure of Intellect model rejected g entirely and proposed up to 150 distinct abilities arranged on three dimensions: operations (what you do), contents (what you do it to), and products (the result). He is also known for distinguishing convergent from divergent thinking. Howard Gardner's theory of multiple intelligences proposed several relatively independent intelligences (linguistic, logical-mathematical, spatial, musical, bodily-kinaesthetic, interpersonal, intrapersonal, naturalistic). Robert Sternberg's triarchic theory named three: analytical (problem-solving), creative (novel ideas), and practical ("street smarts", adapting to real contexts). 16.3 The PASS model and emotional intelligence The PASS model of J.P. Das and Jack Naglieri, built on Alexander Luria's brain theory, describes intelligence as four cognitive processes: Planning , Attention , and Simultaneous and Successive processing. Emotional intelligence was formally defined by Peter Salovey and John Mayer as the ability to perceive, understand, use, and regulate emotions, and popularised by Daniel Goleman. RML tilt: The PASS model (Das & Naglieri) and its Luria roots are a favourite of Indian entrance papers. Also remember the Flynn effect (James Flynn): average IQ scores have risen steadily across the twentieth century, roughly 3 points per decade, forcing periodic re-standardisation of tests. Learning: Deeper Mechanisms The core paradigms (classical conditioning, operant conditioning, observational learning) already appear earlier in this book. This section adds the finer mechanisms that exam papers test but the introduction skips. 17.1 Schedules of reinforcement B.F. Skinner showed that when reinforcement is delivered shapes behaviour as much as whether it is. Continuous reinforcement (reward every response) produces fast learning but fast extinction. Partial (intermittent) schedules produce slower extinction. There are four: Schedule Reward after Response pattern Fixed ratio (FR) A set number of responses High rate, brief post-reward pause Variable ratio (VR) An unpredictable number of responses Very high, steady, extinction-resistant (gambling) Fixed interval (FI) First response after a set time Scalloped: speeds up near the deadline Variable interval (VI) First response after an unpredictable time Slow, steady, stable Trap: Ratio schedules (based on number of responses) always produce higher response rates than interval schedules (based on time ). Variable ratio is the most resistant to extinction, which is why slot machines use it. 17.2 Shaping, generalisation, and discrimination Shaping is reinforcing successive approximations toward a target behaviour, used to build complex acts that would never occur spontaneously. Stimulus generalisation is responding to stimuli similar to the trained one (Little Albert (John B. Watson and Rosalie Rayner, 1920) feared many furry things). Discrimination is learning to respond only to a specific stimulus and not to similar ones, trained by reinforcing one and not the other. 17.3 Cognitive challenges to strict behaviourism Several findings showed that learning involves internal representation, not just stimulus-response bonds. Edward Tolman demonstrated latent learning : rats that explored a maze without reward still learned its layout (a cognitive map ) and used it the moment reward appeared, proving learning can occur without reinforcement and stay hidden until needed. Wolfgang Köhler, studying chimpanzees, described insight learning : a sudden reorganisation of the problem (the "aha" moment) rather than gradual trial and error. 17.4 Biological constraints on learning John Garcia discovered taste aversion (the "Garcia effect"): rats learned to avoid a flavour paired with nausea even when the illness came hours later, and only with taste, not with lights or sounds. This violated two rules of classical conditioning (contiguity and equipotentiality) and proved that organisms are biologically prepared to associate certain stimuli. Martin Seligman named this preparedness and also demonstrated learned helplessness : dogs given inescapable shocks later failed to escape even when they could, a model that became foundational for understanding depression. RML tilt: Learned helplessness (Seligman) and its reformulation into attributional style is a bridge item between the learning and clinical sections; expect it to reappear under depression. Taste aversion (Garcia) is the standard example that biology limits what can be conditioned. Learning recap: reinforcement timing matters (four schedules; VR is stickiest). Complex behaviour is built by shaping. Learning generalises and can be discriminated. Tolman (latent learning, cognitive maps) and Köhler (insight) show learning is cognitive, not just S-R. Garcia (taste aversion) and Seligman (preparedness, learned helplessness) show biology constrains it. 3 Biopsychology & Physiological Psychology From scratch: Biopsychology asks how the brain and body produce behaviour and mental life . Every thought, mood, and symptom you will study in clinical work has a physical substrate: cells that fire, chemicals that cross gaps, and structures that specialise. This section builds that substrate from the single cell upward. 3.1 The Neuron & the Synapse The neuron is the basic signalling cell of the nervous system. Santiago Ramón y Cajal established the neuron doctrine : the nervous system is made of discrete individual cells (not a continuous net), for which he shared the 1906 Nobel Prize with Camillo Golgi. Parts of a neuron. Dendrites are branching fibres that receive incoming signals. The soma (cell body) contains the nucleus and integrates inputs. The axon carries the signal away toward other cells. The myelin sheath is a fatty insulating layer (made by Schwann cells in the periphery, oligodendrocytes centrally) with gaps called nodes of Ranvier ; it speeds conduction via saltatory conduction . The axon terminals (terminal buttons) release chemical messengers. Resting potential. At rest the inside of the axon is about −70 mV relative to outside, kept negative by the sodium-potassium pump and selective permeability. This is polarisation . Action potential. When input pushes the membrane past its threshold (about −55 mV), voltage-gated sodium (Na + ) channels open and Na + floods in: depolarisation . Then K + exits, causing repolarisation and a brief hyperpolarisation . Key properties: it is all-or-none (a spike either fires fully or not at all, so intensity is coded by rate , not size); during the absolute refractory period no new spike can fire, and during the relative refractory period only a stronger-than-usual stimulus can. Synaptic transmission. The spike reaches the terminal, triggering calcium influx, which makes vesicles fuse and release neurotransmitter into the synaptic cleft . The transmitter binds receptors on the next (postsynaptic) neuron. It is then cleared by reuptake , enzymatic breakdown, or diffusion. An EPSP (excitatory postsynaptic potential) depolarises and makes firing more likely; an IPSP (inhibitory postsynaptic potential) hyperpolarises and makes it less likely. The neuron sums all EPSPs and IPSPs ( spatial and temporal summation ). Key. Resting −70 mV → threshold −55 mV → Na + in (depolarise) → K + out (repolarise). All-or-none; strength is coded by frequency . 3.2 Neurotransmitters Transmitter Function Clinical link Acetylcholine (ACh) Muscle movement, learning, memory Depleted in Alzheimer's disease Dopamine Reward, motivation, movement Excess/overactivity in schizophrenia ; loss in Parkinson's disease Serotonin (5-HT) Mood, sleep, appetite Low levels linked to depression and anxiety Norepinephrine Arousal, alertness, fight/flight Implicated in depression and stress GABA Main inhibitory transmitter Low activity in anxiety and seizures Glutamate Main excitatory transmitter; learning Excess causes excitotoxicity ; NMDA role in schizophrenia Endorphins Pain relief, pleasure Involved in addiction and analgesia GABA = gamma-aminobutyric acid. The dopamine hypothesis of schizophrenia holds that overactivity of dopamine (especially at D 2 receptors in mesolimbic pathways) produces the positive symptoms : hallucinations, delusions, disordered thought. Evidence: antipsychotics block dopamine and reduce these symptoms, while amphetamines (which raise dopamine) can induce psychosis. Trap: The dopamine hypothesis explains positive symptoms best. Negative symptoms (flat affect, avolition) are less well accounted for and are linked to glutamate and prefrontal underactivity. 3.3 Brain Anatomy Hindbrain. The medulla controls vital autonomic functions (heartbeat, breathing). The pons bridges the halves and relays signals, and helps regulate sleep. The cerebellum governs balance, coordination, and motor timing. Midbrain. Contains relay centres for vision and hearing and dopamine pathways; with parts of the hindbrain it forms the reticular activating system (Giuseppe Moruzzi and Horace Magoun, 1949) for arousal and attention. Forebrain. The largest region, housing the thalamus, hypothalamus, limbic system, and the cerebral cortex . The cortex is divided into four lobes : Frontal lobe , voluntary movement, planning, and personality. The prefrontal cortex handles executive function, judgment, and impulse control. Broca's area (usually left frontal) controls speech production ; damage causes non-fluent Broca's aphasia . Parietal lobe , the somatosensory cortex processes touch, temperature, and body position. Temporal lobe , hearing and language comprehension. Wernicke's area (usually left) handles language understanding ; damage gives fluent-but-meaningless Wernicke's aphasia . The hippocampus (deep temporal) forms new long-term memories. Occipital lobe , visual processing. Limbic system , the emotion-and-memory network: the amygdala (fear, aggression, emotional salience), the hippocampus (memory formation), the hypothalamus (drives, hormones, homeostasis), and the thalamus (the sensory relay station, routing all senses except smell to the cortex). Lateralization. The left hemisphere is typically dominant for language, logic, and analysis; the right hemisphere for spatial ability, faces, and holistic processing. The hemispheres communicate through the corpus callosum (studied via Roger Sperry's split-brain work). RML tilt: The Phineas Gage (case reported by John Martyn Harlow, 1848) case (1848) is a near-certain factual item. A railroad tamping iron destroyed his frontal lobe ; his intellect survived but his personality and impulse control changed drastically ("no longer Gage"). It became early evidence that the frontal lobe governs personality and social judgment. 3.4 Neuroendocrine System Hormones are chemical messengers released by glands into the blood. The pituitary ("master gland") is directed by the hypothalamus; the adrenal glands release stress hormones; the thyroid sets metabolism; the pancreas regulates blood sugar; the gonads produce sex hormones. The HPA axis (HPA = hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal) is the core stress system. Under stress the hypothalamus releases CRH → the pituitary releases ACTH → the adrenal cortex releases cortisol . Cortisol mobilises energy and suppresses non-essential functions. It also gives negative feedback to shut the axis off. Chronic HPA activation and high cortisol are linked to depression, anxiety, and PTSD (post-traumatic stress disorder). 3.5 Autonomic Nervous System The autonomic nervous system (ANS) controls involuntary organs and has two opposing branches. Sympathetic Parasympathetic Fight or flight Rest and digest Heart rate up, pupils dilate, digestion halts, adrenaline released Heart rate down, pupils constrict, digestion resumes Key. Sympathetic = arousal/expend energy; parasympathetic = calming/conserve energy. They restore homeostasis between them. 3.6 Sleep Sleep cycles through stages roughly every 90 minutes, tracked by the EEG (electroencephalogram). Stage EEG wave Feature Awake, alert Beta Fast, low amplitude Relaxed, eyes closed Alpha Calm wakefulness N1 (light) Theta Drifting off; hypnic jerks N2 Theta + sleep spindles , K-complexes True sleep onset N3 (deep/slow-wave) Delta Restorative; hardest to wake REM Beta-like (paradoxical) Dreaming; rapid eye movement; muscle atonia REM = rapid eye movement. It is called paradoxical sleep because the brain looks awake while the body is paralysed. The circadian rhythm is the ~24-hour body clock set by the suprachiasmatic nucleus of the hypothalamus and cued by light, driving melatonin (from the pineal gland) release. Trap: Delta waves mark deep (N3) sleep , not dreaming. Vivid dreaming happens in REM , whose EEG looks fast like waking. 3.7 Psychopharmacology Basics Antipsychotics , dopamine antagonists (block D 2 receptors), reducing positive symptoms of schizophrenia. Typicals like haloperidol; atypicals like risperidone (also block serotonin). Antidepressants , SSRIs (SSRI = selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor) block serotonin reuptake to raise its level (fluoxetine) ; TCAs (tricyclic antidepressants) raise serotonin and norepinephrine but have more side effects; MAOIs (monoamine oxidase inhibitors) block the enzyme that breaks these transmitters down (need dietary tyramine caution). Anxiolytics , benzodiazepines enhance GABA (the main inhibitory transmitter), calming the nervous system (diazepam, lorazepam) . Mood stabilisers , lithium is first-line for bipolar disorder , needing blood-level monitoring for a narrow therapeutic window. RML tilt: Match drug to mechanism to transmitter: antipsychotic→dopamine block, SSRI→serotonin, benzodiazepine→GABA, lithium→bipolar. These one-line pairings are frequent MCQ fodder. Recap: Neurons fire all-or-none action potentials (−70→−55 mV, Na + in) and talk chemically across synapses via EPSPs/IPSPs. Cajal gave the neuron doctrine. Key transmitters: dopamine (schizophrenia positive symptoms), serotonin/norepinephrine (mood), GABA (inhibitory/anxiety), glutamate (excitatory), ACh (memory), endorphins (pain). Brain builds from hindbrain (medulla, pons, cerebellum) to forebrain and four lobes (frontal/Broca's, parietal/somatosensory, temporal/Wernicke's + hippocampus, occipital); limbic system runs emotion and memory; Gage showed the frontal lobe shapes personality. The HPA axis pumps cortisol under stress; the ANS balances sympathetic fight-or-flight (Walter Cannon) against parasympathetic rest-and-digest. Sleep runs N1–N3 (theta→delta) plus REM, on a circadian clock. Drugs map to transmitters: antipsychotics→dopamine, SSRIs→serotonin, benzodiazepines→GABA, lithium→bipolar. 3.8 Methods of Studying the Brain How do we know what a brain region does when we cannot open a living person's skull and watch? Physiological psychology answers this by pairing older lesion logic with modern imaging. The methods split into two families: those that measure activity (recording) and those that disrupt or destroy tissue to see what is lost. From scratch: Two opposite questions drive brain science. "What happens if this part stops working?" is answered by lesions and stimulation. "What lights up while a person does a task?" is answered by EEG, PET and fMRI. Structure questions ("what does it look like?") are answered by CT and MRI. Lesion and ablation studies A lesion is damaged tissue; ablation is the deliberate surgical removal or destruction of a region (in animals, or observed in human injury). The reasoning: if removing area X abolishes behaviour Y, area X is implicated in Y. This is the oldest tool (recall Paul Broca's patient "Tan" and speech production). Limits: damage is rarely clean, and loss of a function does not prove the region alone produced it. Electrical recording and stimulation Electroencephalography (EEG): scalp electrodes record summed electrical activity of large neuron populations. Excellent time resolution (milliseconds), poor spatial resolution (cannot localise deep sources). Reads sleep stages, seizures, wakefulness rhythms (alpha, beta, delta, theta). Event-related potentials (ERP): EEG signals averaged across many repeats of a stimulus, cancelling background noise to reveal the response locked to that event (for example the P300 wave to a surprising target). Single-cell / microelectrode recording: a fine electrode records firing of one neuron. Highest precision, but invasive (mostly animals). Gave us David Hubel and Torsten Wiesel's feature-detector cells in the visual cortex. Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS): a magnetic coil over the scalp induces current that briefly excites or silences a cortical patch, creating a temporary "virtual lesion" in a healthy person. Establishes that a region is causally necessary, not just correlated. Structural and functional imaging Method What it shows Trade-off CT (computed tomography) X-ray slices → brain structure, gross damage, bleeds Structure only, uses radiation, low detail MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) Detailed structural images via magnetic fields, no radiation Structure only; expensive, loud, no metal fMRI (functional MRI) BOLD signal → blood-oxygen changes = activity, good spatial detail Slow (seconds); measures blood flow, not firing directly PET (positron emission) Radioactive tracer → metabolism, blood flow, neurotransmitter maps Injects radiation, poor time resolution, costly Key. EEG and ERP win on time (milliseconds); fMRI and PET win on space (localisation). No single method is best at both. Trap: fMRI does not measure neural firing directly; it measures the haemodynamic (blood-oxygen, BOLD) response that lags activity by a few seconds. CT shows structure, not function. 3.9 Behaviour Genetics Behaviour genetics asks how much of a trait's variation is inherited. Start with the physical units. DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) is the double-helix molecule coiled into chromosomes (humans have 23 pairs, 46 total). A gene is a segment of DNA coding for a protein. The 23rd pair are the sex chromosomes: XX female, XY male. Genotype: the actual genetic code a person carries. Phenotype: the observable trait that results (genotype plus environment). Dominant allele: expressed even with one copy. Recessive: expressed only with two copies. Heritability: the proportion of variation in a trait, within a population , attributable to genetic differences. It is a group statistic, not a personal percentage. Twin and adoption studies Monozygotic (identical) twins share ~100% of genes; dizygotic (fraternal) twins share ~50%. If identical twins resemble each other more than fraternal twins on a trait, genes are implicated. Adoption studies separate nature from nurture: an adopted child resembling biological parents points to genes, resembling adoptive parents points to environment. Trap: High heritability does not mean "unchangeable." Height is highly heritable yet responds to nutrition. Heritability describes variation in a population, never the fate of one individual. Clinically important genetic and chromosomal conditions Condition Cause Feature Down syndrome Trisomy 21 (extra chromosome 21) Intellectual disability, characteristic features Fragile X Mutation on X chromosome (FMR1) Commonest inherited intellectual disability Phenylketonuria (PKU) Recessive; cannot metabolise phenylalanine Preventable retardation via diet; screened at birth Turner syndrome Single X (45, X0) in females Short stature, no ovarian development Klinefelter syndrome Extra X in males (47, XXY) Reduced fertility, tall stature Huntington's disease Dominant gene on chromosome 4 Late-onset motor and cognitive decline RML tilt: PKU is a favourite because it proves a genetic disorder can be environmentally managed (a phenylalanine-free diet prevents the disability). Note Down syndrome = trisomy 21 and Huntington's = dominant. 3.10 Hemispheric Lateralization and the Split Brain The two cerebral hemispheres are joined by the corpus callosum , a thick band of fibres carrying information between them. Each hemisphere controls the opposite side of the body: this is contralateral control (the left hemisphere moves the right hand, and vice versa). Who → what: Roger Sperry (Nobel Prize, 1981) and his student Michael Gazzaniga studied "split-brain" patients whose corpus callosum was surgically cut to control severe epilepsy. With the bridge severed, the two hemispheres could no longer share information, revealing what each does alone. Findings: an object shown only to the left visual field (right hemisphere) could be picked out by the left hand but could not be named , because speech is usually a left-hemisphere function. This demonstrated lateralization : functions are not evenly spread across both sides. Left hemisphere (typical) Right hemisphere (typical) Language, speech, reading Spatial ability, faces Logic, analysis, calculation Music, emotion, holistic patterns Trap: The "left-brained vs right-brained personality" idea is pop-psych myth. Lateralization means relative specialisation, not that a person uses only one hemisphere. 3.11 Physiology of Motivation and Biological Rhythms Hypothalamic control of hunger The hypothalamus regulates eating through two centres: Lateral hypothalamus (LH): the "start eating" centre. Stimulation induces eating; damage causes an animal to stop eating (aphagia). Ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH): the "stop eating" (satiety) centre. Damage causes overeating and obesity (hyperphagia). Key. LH = Lights on (start). VMH = Very much full (stop). Lesioning them produces the opposite of their normal job. Thirst and sexual behaviour The hypothalamus also monitors thirst , triggered by cellular dehydration (osmotic) and by drops in blood volume. Sexual behaviour is driven by hormones: androgens such as testosterone and oestrogens, released under hypothalamic and pituitary control. Motivation here is both hormonal (internal drive) and neural (brain circuits). Pain: gate-control theory Who → what: Ronald Melzack and Patrick Wall (1965) proposed the gate-control theory : a neural "gate" in the spinal cord can open or close to let pain signals reach the brain. Rubbing an injury or psychological factors can "close the gate," explaining why pain is not a simple one-to-one readout of tissue damage. Biological rhythms and the circadian clock Circadian rhythms are roughly 24-hour cycles (sleep, temperature, hormones). The master clock is the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) in the hypothalamus, which reads light through the eyes. The SCN signals the pineal gland to release melatonin in darkness, promoting sleep. RML tilt: Remember the chain: light → SCN → pineal gland → melatonin. The SCN is the pacemaker; the pineal gland only secretes the hormone. 3.12 Stress Physiology When a stressor is perceived, the body mounts a coordinated response. Two systems fire. The fast one is the sympathetic nervous system (adrenaline, "fight or flight"). The slower, sustained one is the HPA axis . The HPA axis H ypothalamus releases CRH (corticotropin-releasing hormone).
