It means about half of the differences between people in that population are associated with genetic differences. Heritability also depends on the environment studied and can change if conditions change. Twin and adoption studies Because we cannot ethically control people's genes or upbringing, behavioural geneticists use natural experiments. The two main designs are twin studies and adoption studies. Monozygotic twins (identical twins) develop from a single fertilised egg that splits, so they share essentially 100 percent of their genes. Dizygotic twins (fraternal twins) develop from two separate eggs fertilised at the same time, so they share on average 50 percent of their genes, like ordinary siblings. If monozygotic twins are more alike on a trait than dizygotic twins raised in similar conditions, that greater similarity points to a genetic contribution. Adoption studies compare adopted children with both their biological and their adoptive parents: resemblance to the biological parents suggests a genetic influence, while resemblance to the adoptive family suggests an environmental one. Studies of monozygotic twins reared apart are especially powerful because they combine shared genes with different environments. Trap. Monozygotic = MONO = one egg = identical = 100 percent shared genes. Dizygotic = DI = two eggs = fraternal = about 50 percent shared genes. Do not swap these. "Identical" always means monozygotic. The diathesis-stress idea Genes rarely act alone. The diathesis-stress model proposes that a person may inherit a diathesis , a predisposition or vulnerability to a disorder, which only develops into the actual disorder when combined with enough environmental stress . A vulnerability to depression, for example, might stay dormant in a supportive life but emerge under severe adversity. This model neatly captures how nature and nurture work together rather than in opposition. Evolutionary psychology Evolutionary psychology explains behaviour and mental processes as products of evolution, shaped over countless generations because they helped ancestors survive and reproduce. Its foundation is the theory of natural selection . Who → what. Charles Darwin (1809 to 1882) set out the theory of evolution by natural selection in his 1859 book On the Origin of Species . The core idea: individuals vary; some variations improve survival and reproduction in a given environment; those individuals leave more offspring, so the helpful traits become more common over generations. An adaptation is any inherited feature, physical or behavioural, that arose through natural selection because it improved survival or reproduction. Traits such as fear of dangerous animals or the human infant's readiness to bond with caregivers can be viewed as adaptations. A refinement of the theory is inclusive fitness , the idea that an organism can pass on its genes not only by reproducing itself but also by helping close relatives, who share many of the same genes, to survive and reproduce. Inclusive fitness helps explain altruism toward kin, which pure individual survival cannot easily account for. 2.12 Psychophysics and perceptual organisation Psychophysics is the scientific study of the relationship between physical stimuli (such as the intensity of a light or the loudness of a tone) and the psychological sensations they produce. It was one of the very first areas of experimental psychology and gave the young science a rigorous, measurable subject matter. Thresholds and the just noticeable difference The absolute threshold is the smallest amount of a stimulus that a person can detect at least half the time. A classic example is the faint glow of a single candle seen from a great distance on a dark clear night. The difference threshold , also called the just noticeable difference (JND), is the smallest change in a stimulus that a person can reliably notice as different from the original. Who → what. Ernst Weber (1795 to 1878), a German physiologist, discovered that the just noticeable difference is a constant proportion of the original stimulus, not a fixed amount. This is Weber's law . If you can just tell 100 grams apart from 110 grams (a 10 percent increase), then to notice a change from 200 grams you need about 220 grams, again a 10 percent increase. Who → what. Gustav Fechner (1801 to 1887), also German, built on Weber's finding to relate the strength of the physical stimulus to the intensity of the resulting sensation, proposing that sensation grows with the logarithm of stimulus intensity ( Fechner's law ). His 1860 book Elements of Psychophysics effectively founded psychophysics as a discipline and coined the term. Trap. Weber's law is about the just noticeable difference between two stimuli and states it is a constant ratio of the starting stimulus. Fechner's law goes further and links physical intensity to the felt magnitude of the sensation using a logarithm. Weber = the JND is a constant proportion; Fechner = sensation is a log function of intensity. Do not merge the two names. Signal detection theory Classical threshold thinking assumed a fixed cut-off below which a stimulus is simply not sensed. Signal detection theory (David Green and John Swets, 1966) challenged this by arguing that detecting a faint stimulus depends not only on the stimulus but also on the observer's decision-making, including their expectations, motivation, and willingness to say "yes". Detection is treated as a judgement made against a background of noise, and two people with identical senses may report differently because they set their decision criterion in different places. This introduced the idea that perception involves an element of decision, not just raw sensitivity. Gestalt principles of perceptual organisation Once sensations reach the brain they are organised into meaningful wholes. The Gestalt school of psychology (Gestalt is German for form or whole ) held that the mind naturally organises parts into structured wholes, summed up in the phrase that the whole is more than the sum of its parts. Who → what. Max Wertheimer (1880 to 1943) is regarded as a founder of Gestalt psychology. His study of apparent motion (the illusion of movement created by lights flashed in sequence, the phi phenomenon) helped launch the school, which set out the principles by which we group visual elements. Figure and ground: we automatically separate a scene into a figure (the object of attention) that stands out against a background (the ground). Proximity: elements that are close together are perceived as belonging to the same group. Similarity: elements that look alike (in colour, shape, or size) are grouped together. Closure: we mentally fill in gaps to perceive a complete, whole figure even when parts are missing. Continuity (good continuation): we tend to perceive smooth, continuous lines and patterns rather than abrupt, broken ones. Common fate: elements that move together in the same direction are seen as a single group. Depth perception Depth perception is the ability to see the world in three dimensions and to judge distance, even though the image on each retina is flat and two-dimensional. The brain uses cues, some needing both eyes and some available to a single eye. Binocular cues depend on having two eyes: Retinal disparity: because the two eyes are set a little apart, each receives a slightly different image; the brain compares the difference to judge distance. The nearer the object, the larger the disparity. Convergence: as an object comes closer, the eyes turn inward; the brain reads the degree of inward turning as a signal of nearness. Monocular cues (also called pictorial cues, because artists use them to suggest depth on a flat canvas) need only one eye. They include relative size (nearer objects appear larger), interposition or overlap (a nearer object partly blocks a farther one), linear perspective (parallel lines seem to converge in the distance), texture gradient (detail becomes finer with distance), and aerial perspective (distant objects look hazier). Perceptual constancies Perceptual constancy is the tendency to perceive an object as unchanging even when the image it casts on the retina changes. This stability is what lets the world seem coherent rather than chaotic. Size constancy: a person walking away is seen as the same size, though their retinal image shrinks. Shape constancy: a door is seen as rectangular whether shut or swung open, though its retinal image becomes a trapezoid. Colour constancy: a familiar object keeps its perceived colour under changing lighting. Visual illusions An illusion is a consistent misperception of a real stimulus, and illusions are valuable because they expose the rules the brain normally uses to build perception. Muller-Lyer illusion: two lines of equal length appear different because of the arrowheads at their ends. The line with outward-pointing fins (like a corner going away) looks longer than the one with inward-pointing fins. Ponzo illusion: two identical horizontal lines placed across converging lines (like receding railway tracks) look unequal, the upper one appearing longer because depth cues make the brain judge it as farther away and therefore larger. Why. Illusions such as Muller-Lyer and Ponzo are thought to arise because the brain applies depth and size cues that usually serve us well in the real three-dimensional world, but which misfire when applied to flat drawings. They show that perception is an active construction, not a passive copy of the retinal image. Recap. Sleep is an active circadian process run by the suprachiasmatic nucleus, pineal gland and melatonin, cycling through NREM stages N1 to N3 (theta then delta waves) and paradoxical REM, with restorative and evolutionary theories explaining its purpose. Behavioural genetics uses genes, chromosomes and DNA, the genotype-phenotype distinction, dominant and recessive alleles, heritability (variation in a population, not a single person), and monozygotic-versus-dizygotic twin and adoption studies, alongside the diathesis-stress model and Charles Darwin's evolutionary account of adaptation and inclusive fitness. Psychophysics, founded by Weber and Fechner, measures absolute and difference thresholds and the JND (Weber = constant ratio; Fechner = logarithmic sensation), extended by signal detection theory; and perception is organised by Wertheimer's Gestalt principles, binocular and monocular depth cues, perceptual constancies, and revealing illusions like Muller-Lyer and Ponzo. 2.13 The complete map: brain, body & behaviour, and the people who mapped them This is the full roster of the landmark discoveries, systems, and models in biopsychology that an aptitude paper can name and expect you to place with the right person. It runs across three families: the neuron and how signals cross it, how the brain is organised and localised, and the physiology of emotion, stress, sleep, and motivation. Learn the pairing (finding → person → one-line idea) and no named result can ambush you. Key. The "#" runs continuously across all three families so every entry has a unique number. "Who" gives the full name the first time; a discovery is filed under the person(s) an exam most often credits. Read each core-idea line as the single sentence you would write if asked "what is this?" Trap. Do not swap the aphasia pair: Broca is broken speech production (frontal), Wernicke is broken comprehension (temporal). Likewise, Cajal won on the neuron doctrine while Camillo Golgi championed the wrong reticular theory even though his stain made the work possible. And keep the emotion theories straight: James-Lange says body first (arousal → emotion), Cannon-Bard says both at once. Recap. Three families cover the biopsychology map: Family A builds the signal (Cajal's neuron, Sherrington's synapse, Hodgkin-Huxley's spike, Loewi's chemical transmission, Hebb's plasticity, and the transmitter-to-disorder links); Family B localises function (Broca, Wernicke, Penfield, Lashley, Sperry, Hubel-Wiesel, Olds-Milner); Family C runs emotion, stress, sleep, and the senses (Papez, LeDoux, Cannon, Selye, Aserinsky-Kleitman, and the James-Lange versus Cannon-Bard debate). Fix the finding-to-person pairing and the whole "who discovered this?" column of the paper is safe. 3 Developmental Psychology Developmental psychology studies how humans change and stay the same across the entire lifespan, from conception to death. It asks three linked questions: what changes (body, thinking, emotion, personality, social ties), when it changes (the timing and order of milestones), and why it changes (the mechanisms behind growth). This section builds every major theory from zero, then flags the exact contrasts and confusions that entrance papers love to test. 3.1 The Big Debates & Research Designs Before any single theory, developmental science is organised around a handful of recurring arguments. Every theorist you meet later takes a side (often implicitly) on each of these, so learn the debate first and the theorists become easy to sort. Nature vs nurture This is the oldest question in the field: does development come mainly from nature (genes, biological maturation, inherited temperament) or from nurture (environment, learning, culture, parenting)? The modern answer is both, interacting . Genes set a range of possibilities (a reaction range ); environment decides where in that range a person lands. Related ideas: epigenetics (experience switches genes on or off without changing the DNA code) and gene–environment correlation (a child's genes shape the environments they are exposed to, e.g. a musically gifted child seeks out instruments). Key. Almost no serious theory is purely nature or purely nurture. The exam-correct framing is interactionism : genes and environment continuously shape each other. Continuity vs discontinuity Is development a smooth, gradual, quantitative build-up ( continuity , like a ramp), or a series of distinct qualitative jumps into new stages ( discontinuity , like a staircase)? Learning theorists (Skinner) lean continuity; stage theorists (Jean Piaget, Erik Erikson, Sigmund Freud, Lawrence Kohlberg) lean discontinuity. Trap. "Stage theory" is a strong marker of the discontinuity side. If a question names Jean Piaget, Erik Erikson, Sigmund Freud, or Lawrence Kohlberg and asks about the nature of change, the answer is discontinuous / qualitative / stage-like, not gradual. Critical vs sensitive periods A critical period is a rigid, narrow window during which a specific experience must occur for normal development, or the ability is lost for good (Konrad Lorenz's imprinting in geese; some aspects of vision). A sensitive period is softer: a window when the organism is especially receptive and learning is easiest, but development can still happen (harder, less complete) outside it (first-language and accent acquisition). Key. Critical = rigid, all-or-none, permanent loss. Sensitive = optimal-but-flexible. Human language is usually called a sensitive period, not a strict critical one. Stability vs change Do early traits (temperament, attachment style, intelligence) persist across life ( stability ), or can people fundamentally transform ( change )? Most evidence shows moderate stability with real room for change, especially with new relationships and environments. Research designs in developmental psychology Because the subject is change over time, the study design is itself an exam favourite. Design How it works Strength Weakness Cross-sectional Different age groups tested at the same time (e.g. 5-, 10-, 15-year-olds today) Fast, cheap, no dropout Cohort effects : age differences may reflect the era each group grew up in, not development Longitudinal The same people followed and re-tested across years Shows true individual change & development Slow, costly, attrition (dropout), practice effects Sequential (cross-sequential) Several age cohorts each followed over time (a blend of the two) Separates age effects from cohort effects Complex, expensive to run Trap. Cohort effect is the signature weakness of cross-sectional designs; attrition (participant dropout) is the signature weakness of longitudinal designs. Papers swap these to test you. 3.2 Prenatal Development & Teratogens Development begins at conception. The roughly 38-40 weeks of pregnancy are divided into three stages, and knowing their order and hallmark events is standard exam content. Stage Time span Hallmark events Germinal Conception → ~2 weeks Rapid cell division of the zygote ; the ball of cells ( blastocyst ) travels down and implants in the uterine wall Embryonic ~2 – 8 weeks The embryo forms all major organs and body systems ( organogenesis ); heart begins to beat; most vulnerable stage to damage Fetal ~9 weeks → birth The fetus grows in size; organs mature and become functional; movement, sleep–wake cycles; age of viability (~22–24 weeks) when survival outside the womb becomes possible Teratogens A teratogen is any environmental agent (drug, virus, chemical, radiation) that causes harm to the developing embryo or fetus. Key principles: harm depends on timing (the embryonic period is most sensitive because organs are forming), dose , and the genetic vulnerability of mother and child. Common teratogens: alcohol (causes Fetal Alcohol Syndrome , marked by facial abnormalities and intellectual disability), nicotine, cocaine and other drugs, the rubella virus, and high-dose radiation. Key. The embryonic stage is the period of maximum teratogen vulnerability because that is when organs are being built. Same insult in the fetal stage usually does less structural damage. 3.3 Jean Piaget: Cognitive Development Who → what. Jean Piaget , a Swiss psychologist, proposed that children are active "little scientists" who construct knowledge by acting on the world, passing through four fixed, universal, qualitatively distinct stages of thinking ( cognitive constructivism ). The engine: how thinking grows Schema (plural schemas / schemata): a mental framework or "file" for organising information (a child's "dog" schema = four legs, fur, barks). Assimilation : fitting new information into an existing schema (seeing a cat and calling it "dog"). Accommodation : changing the schema to fit new information (learning cats are a separate category and updating the schema). Equilibration : the drive to balance assimilation and accommodation; disequilibrium (when old schemas fail) pushes the child to a higher level of understanding. Trap. Do not swap these two. Assimilation = the world bends to fit your existing schema (schema stays the same). Accommodation = your schema bends to fit the world (schema changes). The four stages Stage Age range Key features & the achievement Sensorimotor Birth – ~2 yrs Knows the world through senses and movement. Key gain: object permanence (objects still exist when out of sight; before this, "out of sight, out of mind"). Beginnings of symbolic thought at the end. Preoperational ~2 – 7 yrs Symbolic thinking, language, pretend play. But thinking is limited by egocentrism (cannot take another's viewpoint), centration (focusing on one feature), and lack of conservation . No true logical operations yet. The "three-mountains task" shows egocentrism. Concrete operational ~7 – 11 yrs Logical thinking about concrete objects. Masters conservation (quantity stays the same despite a change in shape), reversibility (mentally undoing an action), classification, and seriation (ordering). Still struggles with abstract, hypothetical ideas. Formal operational ~11 yrs → adulthood Abstract reasoning , hypothetical-deductive logic, systematic problem solving, thinking about "what if" and ideals. Adolescent egocentrism (David Elkind, 1967) may reappear ( imaginary audience , personal fable ). Why. The classic conservation test: pour water from a short wide glass into a tall thin glass. A preoperational child says the tall glass "has more" (fooled by height, i.e. centration). A concrete-operational child knows the amount is unchanged, because they grasp reversibility. This single demonstration is the boundary between the two stages and is heavily tested. Critiques of Piaget He underestimated young children; with simpler methods, object permanence and some abilities appear earlier than he claimed. Development is more continuous and domain-specific than his neat universal stages suggest; not everyone reaches formal operations in every area. He neglected culture and social interaction as engines of cognitive growth (the gap that Lev Vygotsky fills). 3.4 Lev Vygotsky: Sociocultural Theory Who → what. Lev Vygotsky , a Russian psychologist, argued that cognitive development is driven by social interaction and culture . Children learn through guided participation with more skilled partners; thinking is first social ("between people") and then becomes internal ("within the person"). Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD) : the gap between what a child can do alone and what they can do with help from a skilled partner. Learning happens best inside this zone. Scaffolding : the temporary, adjustable support a teacher or peer gives, gradually withdrawn as the child becomes competent (like scaffolding removed once a building stands). Note: the term "scaffolding" was coined by Jerome Bruner and colleagues, building on Vygotsky's ZPD. More Knowledgeable Other (MKO) : anyone with more skill or knowledge on the task (a parent, teacher, older peer, even a tool). Private speech : children talk out loud to themselves to guide their own behaviour; this later goes underground as silent inner speech that regulates thought. Vygotsky saw this as helpful self-guidance; Jean Piaget dismissed similar talk as merely "egocentric" and non-social. Piaget vs Vygotsky (a classic exam pairing) Dimension Jean Piaget Lev Vygotsky Engine of growth Individual exploration; the "lone scientist" Social interaction & culture; the "apprentice" Role of language Reflects thought that already developed Drives and shapes thought (inner speech) Learning & development Development leads / limits learning (must be ready) Learning leads development (within the ZPD) Stages Universal, fixed stages No fixed universal stages; culturally variable Private speech Egocentric, immature, fades Adaptive self-guidance, becomes inner speech Trap. "Learning leads development," "ZPD," "scaffolding," and "MKO" are all Vygotsky . "Object permanence," "conservation," "assimilation/accommodation," and the four stages are all Piaget . Do not attribute one's concept to the other. 3.5 Erik Erikson: Psychosocial Development Who → what. Erik Erikson , a German-born ego psychologist, proposed eight psychosocial stages spanning the whole lifespan. Each stage centres on a crisis (a tension between two poles); resolving it well yields a lasting virtue (basic strength). Development is lifelong and social, not just childhood and sexual. Stage Approx. age Crisis Virtue gained 1 0 – 1 yr (infancy) Trust vs Mistrust Hope 2 1 – 3 yrs (toddler) Autonomy vs Shame & Doubt Will 3 3 – 6 yrs (preschool) Initiative vs Guilt Purpose 4 6 – 12 yrs (school age) Industry vs Inferiority Competence 5 12 – 18 yrs (adolescence) Identity vs Role Confusion Fidelity 6 18 – 40 yrs (young adult) Intimacy vs Isolation Love 7 40 – 65 yrs (middle adult) Generativity vs Stagnation Care 8 65+ yrs (late adult) Integrity vs Despair Wisdom Key. Memorise stage 5 above all: Identity vs Role Confusion in adolescence, virtue Fidelity . It is Erikson's most cited stage and the launch point for James Marcia's identity statuses (below). 3.6 Sigmund Freud: Psychosexual Development Who → what. Sigmund Freud , founder of psychoanalysis, proposed five psychosexual stages . At each stage libidinal (sexual) energy centres on a different erogenous zone ; how conflicts there are handled shapes adult personality. Stage Age Focus & conflict Oral 0 – 1 yr Mouth (sucking, biting); weaning Anal 1 – 3 yrs Bowel/bladder control; toilet training Phallic 3 – 6 yrs Genitals; Oedipus / Electra complex (Carl Jung, 1913), identification with same-sex parent, superego forms Latency 6 yrs – puberty Sexual urges dormant; energy into school, friendships, skills Genital Puberty onward Mature adult sexuality; capacity for love and work Fixation occurs when a conflict at a stage is unresolved (through too little or too much gratification), leaving libido "stuck" there and shaping adult traits. Oral fixation → smoking, overeating, dependency; anal-retentive → stubborn, orderly, stingy. Erikson vs Freud (contrast) Motivation : Freud = sexual/biological drives; Erik Erikson = social relationships and identity. Span : Freud stops at puberty (5 stages, ending in the genital stage); Erikson covers the whole lifespan (8 stages). Focus : Freud on the id and unconscious conflict; Erikson on the ego and healthy adaptation. Tone : Freud emphasises pathology from early fixation; Erikson emphasises growth and strengths (virtues). Trap. Erik Erikson was a neo-Freudian who expanded Sigmund Freud, keeping stages but making them psycho social and lifelong. Their childhood stages roughly align in age; the giveaway is that only Erikson has stages for adulthood and old age. 3.7 Lawrence Kohlberg: Moral Development Who → what. Lawrence Kohlberg extended Jean Piaget's ideas to moral reasoning . Using dilemmas (famously the Heinz dilemma : should a man steal an over-priced drug to save his dying wife?), he judged not the yes/no answer but the reasoning behind it, yielding three levels of two stages each. Level Stage Reasoning basis I. Preconventional (self-interest; typical of children) 1. Obedience & punishment "Avoid punishment." Right = not getting caught 2. Instrumental / self-interest "What's in it for me?" Right = fair exchange, rewards II. Conventional (social approval & law) 3. Good boy / good girl Right = pleasing others, being seen as nice 4. Law & order Right = obeying rules, laws, duty, authority III. Postconventional (abstract principles) 5. Social contract Laws are social agreements that can be changed for the greater good 6. Universal ethical principles Self-chosen ethical principles (justice, human rights) override unjust laws Key. Kohlberg scores the reasoning , not the choice. Two people who both say "Heinz should steal the drug" can be at completely different stages depending on why . Carol Gilligan's critique Carol Gilligan , once Kohlberg's collaborator, argued his theory was gender-biased : it was built on male samples and treated abstract justice as the highest morality, thereby scoring women as "lower." She proposed that women tend to reason from an ethic of care (relationships, compassion, responsibility to others), which is different, not inferior, to the male-typical ethic of justice . Trap. Carol Gilligan = ethic of care and the charge of gender bias against Kohlberg. Kohlberg = ethic of justice . Do not credit "care ethics" to Kohlberg. 3.8 Attachment Attachment is the deep, enduring emotional bond between a child and caregiver. Three names dominate: Harry Harlow (that it is not about food), John Bowlby (the theory), and Mary Ainsworth (how to measure the types). Who → what. Harry Harlow raised infant rhesus monkeys with two wire "mothers": one made of bare wire that dispensed milk, and one covered in soft cloth with no milk. The babies clung to the cloth mother and ran to her when frightened, going to the wire mother only to feed. This proved attachment is built on contact comfort , not just food, demolishing the earlier "cupboard love" idea. Who → what. John Bowlby founded attachment theory : attachment is an evolved, biological system that keeps the infant close to a caregiver for survival. The infant builds an internal working model , a mental template of relationships ("Am I worthy of care? Are others reliable?") that guides later relationships. He also emphasised a sensitive period for forming attachments and the damage of maternal deprivation . Who → what. Mary Ainsworth devised the Strange Situation , a lab procedure of separations and reunions between an infant, caregiver, and stranger. How the infant behaves, especially at reunion , reveals the attachment style. Attachment style Behaviour in the Strange Situation Caregiving linked to it Secure Explores using caregiver as a base; distressed at separation; easily comforted at reunion Sensitive, responsive Insecure–avoidant Little distress at separation; ignores/avoids caregiver at reunion Unresponsive, rejecting Insecure–ambivalent / resistant Very distressed at separation; at reunion seeks yet resists comfort (clingy and angry), hard to soothe Inconsistent Disorganised Confused, contradictory, fearful behaviour; no coherent strategy Frightening / abusive / traumatic Key. Ainsworth identified the first three styles. The fourth, disorganised attachment, was added later by Mary Main . If a paper asks who added disorganised attachment, the answer is Mary Main, not Ainsworth. 3.9 Language Development Language emerges in a strikingly universal order across cultures, which is itself evidence in the nature–nurture debate. Milestone Approx. age What it is Cooing ~2 – 3 months Vowel-like sounds ("ooo", "aaa") Babbling ~6 months Repeated consonant–vowel strings ("bababa"); starts universal, then narrows to the native language's sounds Holophrases (one-word) ~12 months Single words carry a whole sentence's meaning ("milk!" = "I want milk") Telegraphic speech (Roger Brown and Colin Fraser, 1963) ~18 – 24 months Two-word combos with only key content words, function words dropped ("want cookie", "mummy go") A common error here is overregularisation (applying a grammar rule too widely, e.g. "goed," "foots"), which actually shows the child has learned the rule rather than merely imitating. Chomsky vs Skinner (the nativist–behaviourist debate) B.F. Skinner (behaviourist): language is learned like any behaviour, through imitation, reinforcement, and shaping by parents. Noam Chomsky (nativist): children learn language far too fast and too creatively for pure reinforcement to explain, and produce sentences they have never heard (the "poverty of the stimulus"). He proposed an innate Language Acquisition Device (LAD) , a built-in biological readiness for grammar, and a universal grammar common to all languages. Trap. LAD and universal grammar = Noam Chomsky (innate/nativist). Reinforcement/imitation = B. F. Skinner (learned/behaviourist). Overregularisation errors ("goed") are strong evidence against pure imitation and thus favour Chomsky. 3.10 Lifespan, Adolescence & Aging Urie Bronfenbrenner: ecological systems theory Who → what. Urie Bronfenbrenner pictured the developing child at the centre of nested environmental "systems," like a set of Russian dolls, each layer influencing development. System What it includes Microsystem Immediate, direct settings: family, school, peers, the child's actual daily contacts Mesosystem Connections between microsystems (e.g. parent–teacher relationship) Exosystem Settings that affect the child indirectly (e.g. a parent's workplace, local government) Macrosystem The broad culture, values, laws, customs, and economy Chronosystem The dimension of time: life transitions and historical events over the lifespan Trap. Meso = links between the child's own settings; exo = a setting the child is not directly in but which still affects them. Chronosystem is the time layer, added later. James Marcia: identity statuses (adolescence) James Marcia operationalised Erik Erikson's stage 5 using two dimensions: exploration (actively trying out options) and commitment (settling on a choice). Their combinations give four identity statuses : Status Exploration Commitment Identity diffusion No No Foreclosure No Yes (commitment without exploring, e.g. adopting parents' plan) Moratorium Yes (in crisis, exploring now) No (not yet) Identity achievement Yes (explored) Yes (then committed) Key. The maturity order is diffusion → foreclosure → moratorium → achievement. Foreclosure = commitment without exploration; moratorium = exploration without commitment yet. These two are the most confused pair. Paul Baltes: lifespan development principles Paul Baltes argued development is a lifelong process best summarised by a few principles: Lifelong : development continues from birth to death; no age dominates. Multidimensional & multidirectional : it involves many domains, and abilities can rise and fall at the same time (some grow, some decline). Gain–loss balance : every stage brings both gains and losses together. Plasticity : capacities remain modifiable across life. Contextual : shaped by history, culture, and non-normative life events. Baltes also described healthy aging as Selective Optimisation with Compensation (SOC) : selecting fewer goals, optimising effort on them, and compensating for losses. In cognition he distinguished fluid intelligence (raw processing speed, declines with age) from crystallised intelligence (accumulated knowledge, stable or rising). Elisabeth Kubler-Ross: stages of grief Who → what. Elisabeth Kubler-Ross , studying the terminally ill, described five stages of coping with dying and grief: Denial → Anger → Bargaining → Depression → Acceptance (mnemonic DABDA). Trap. The stages are not a rigid, universal sequence; people skip stages, repeat them, or reorder them. Modern view treats them as common reactions, not a fixed ladder. The ordered five for recall: Denial, Anger, Bargaining, Depression, Acceptance. Recap. The big debates (nature/nurture, continuity/discontinuity, critical/sensitive periods) and designs (cross-sectional cohort effect vs longitudinal attrition) frame everything. Prenatal = germinal, embryonic (peak teratogen risk), fetal. Jean Piaget = 4 cognitive stages (object permanence → egocentrism → conservation/reversibility → abstract) driven by assimilation/accommodation; Vygotsky counters with ZPD, scaffolding, MKO, and "learning leads development." Erikson = 8 lifelong psychosocial crises with virtues (identity vs role confusion in adolescence); Sigmund Freud = 5 psychosexual stages plus fixation. Lawrence Kohlberg = pre/conventional/postconventional (6 stages, judges reasoning); Carol Gilligan adds the ethic of care. Attachment: Harry Harlow (contact comfort), John Bowlby (internal working model), Ainsworth's Strange Situation (secure/avoidant/ambivalent) plus Main's disorganised. Language runs cooing → babbling → holophrases → telegraphic, with Chomsky's LAD against B. F. Skinner's reinforcement. Lifespan: Bronfenbrenner's nested systems, Marcia's four identity statuses, Baltes's lifespan principles, and Kubler-Ross's DABDA grief stages. 3.11 Urie Bronfenbrenner's Ecological Systems Theory Most developmental theories look inside the child: at stages of thought, at drives, at attachment bonds. Urie Bronfenbrenner (1917–2005), a Russian-born American psychologist, argued that this was only half the picture. A child never develops in a vacuum. Development happens inside a set of nested environments, layered like the rings of an onion, each one influencing the child and being influenced in turn. His ecological systems theory (later renamed the bioecological model to stress the child's own biology) maps these layers from the ones closest to the child outward to the broadest cultural forces. Who → what. Urie Bronfenbrenner → ecological (bioecological) systems theory: the developing child sits at the centre of five nested environmental systems, from the immediate microsystem out to the time-based chronosystem. The five systems, moving outward from the child, are these. Microsystem. The innermost ring: the immediate settings the child directly experiences and acts within. Family, classroom, peer group, the local playground. Here influence is a two-way street. The child shapes these settings just as they shape the child; a cheerful, easy baby draws warm responses, while an irritable one may draw tension. Mesosystem. Not a new place, but the web of connections between microsystems . What happens between home and school, between family and peers. A child whose parents attend school meetings and know the teacher tends to do better than one whose home and school never connect. Exosystem. Settings the child is not part of but which still affect them through the microsystem. A parent's workplace: a stressful job or a supportive one, night shifts, a layoff, or a generous parental-leave policy all reach the child indirectly. Macrosystem. The broad cultural blanket: the values, laws, customs, religion, and economic patterns of the wider society. Whether a culture prizes individual achievement or family duty; whether education is free; caste, class, and gender expectations. Chronosystem. The dimension of time : how the child and every other layer change across the lifespan and across historical eras. A parent's divorce (its impact differs one year later versus five), or growing up with smartphones versus growing up without them. Why. The model is a favourite in exams because it makes influence concrete at every distance from the child. If asked which system a parent's job belongs to, the answer is the exosystem, because the child does not live in that setting yet is shaped by it. Trap. Do not confuse the mesosystem with the exosystem . The mesosystem is the link between two settings the child does take part in (home–school). The exosystem is a setting the child does not take part in (the parent's office). Also, the chronosystem is about time , not a physical place at all. 3.12 Temperament and Parenting Thomas and Chess: temperamental types and goodness of fit Long before a child can think in Piagetian stages or form Eriksonian identity, they already have a characteristic style of responding to the world. Temperament is the early-appearing, biologically rooted pattern of emotional reactivity and self-regulation, the raw material on which later personality is built. Two American child psychiatrists, Alexander Thomas (1914–2003) and Stella Chess (1914–2007), launched the landmark New York Longitudinal Study , following children from infancy and rating them on dimensions such as activity level, rhythmicity (regularity of sleep and hunger), approach or withdrawal to new things, adaptability, mood, and intensity of reaction. From these they identified three broad temperamental types. Easy child (about 40% of their sample): regular in habits, cheerful in mood, adapts readily to new situations and people. Difficult child (about 10%): irregular in habits, slow to accept change, intense and often negative in mood, prone to crying and tantrums. Slow-to-warm-up child (about 15%): mild and low in activity, initially withdraws from novelty but adapts slowly with gentle, repeated exposure. (The remainder did not fit neatly into one type.) Who → what. Alexander Thomas & Stella Chess → three temperament types (easy, difficult, slow-to-warm-up) and the principle of goodness of fit : healthy development depends on the match between the child's temperament and the demands of their environment. Their most important idea is goodness of fit . No temperament is doomed or destined; what matters is the match between the child's style and the expectations and handling of the caregivers. A difficult child with patient, flexible parents who do not take the intensity personally may thrive. The same child with harsh or overwhelmed parents may spiral into conflict. A slow-to-warm-up child pushed to perform in front of strangers fits poorly with that demand and grows anxious, but the same child given time to observe fits well. Why. Goodness of fit dissolves the false question "is it the child or the parenting?" The answer is the fit between the two . This is a frequently tested phrase, so tie it firmly to Alexander Thomas and Stella Chess. Baumrind's parenting styles, extended by Maccoby and Martin The American developmental psychologist Diana Baumrind (1927–2018) studied preschoolers and their parents and identified distinct styles of parenting that predicted how children turned out. She originally described three. Authoritative. High warmth and high control together. Parents set clear, firm rules but explain them, listen to the child, and adjust. Consistently linked to the best outcomes: confident, socially competent, self-reliant children. Authoritarian. High control but low warmth. Rules are strict and unexplained ("because I said so"), obedience is demanded, and there is little give-and-take. Children tend to be obedient but anxious, withdrawn, or lacking in initiative. Permissive (indulgent). High warmth but low control. Parents are affectionate and lenient, making few demands and setting few limits. Children may be impulsive, self-centred, and poor at self-regulation. Later, Eleanor Maccoby (1917–2018) and John Martin reorganised Baumrind's scheme along two clean dimensions, demandingness (control, expectations) and responsiveness (warmth, acceptance), which produces a two-by-two grid. That grid revealed a fourth cell Baumrind had not named as a distinct style: low in both dimensions. Neglectful (uninvolved). Low warmth and low control. Parents are detached, meeting basic physical needs but otherwise disengaged from the child's life. Linked to the poorest outcomes across social, emotional, and academic measures. Who → what. Diana Baumrind → three parenting styles (authoritative, authoritarian, permissive). Eleanor Maccoby & John Martin → recast them on demandingness × responsiveness and added the fourth, neglectful/uninvolved , style. Style Demandingness (control) Responsiveness (warmth) Typical child outcome Authoritative High High Confident, socially competent, self-reliant Authoritarian High Low Obedient but anxious, low initiative Permissive (indulgent) Low High Impulsive, poor self-control Neglectful (uninvolved) Low Low Poorest outcomes overall Trap. The two easily confused pairs are authoritative (high warmth + high control, the good one) versus authoritarian (low warmth + high control, the harsh one). The words look alike; the outcomes do not. Remember: authoritati ve = v alued and warm. Also do not credit the fourth style to Diana Baumrind; the neglectful style came from Maccoby and Martin. 3.13 Gender and Moral Development Critiques Gender identity and gender constancy Gender identity is a child's private sense of being a boy or a girl, usually established by about age three. But young children do not yet grasp that gender is permanent. The understanding that one's gender stays the same across time and situations, regardless of hairstyle, clothing, or activity, is called gender constancy , a concept drawn from Lawrence Kohlberg's cognitive account of gender. It arrives in steps: first the child can label gender, then grasps its stability over time (a boy will become a man), and finally its consistency across appearances (a boy in a dress is still a boy). Full constancy typically appears around age six or seven, in step with the concrete-operational gains in conservation. Sandra Bem: gender schema theory and androgyny The American psychologist Sandra Bem (1944–2014) proposed gender schema theory : children build a mental framework, a schema , of what counts as masculine or feminine in their culture, and then filter new information through it, paying attention to and remembering what fits and shaping their own behaviour to match. Bem also challenged the old assumption that masculine and feminine were opposite ends of a single line. She argued they are two separate dimensions, so a person can score high on both. She called this combination androgyny (from Greek andro , male, and gyne , female): possessing both instrumental "masculine" traits (assertiveness, independence) and expressive "feminine" traits (warmth, nurturance). She built the Bem Sex-Role Inventory to measure it and argued that androgynous people are more flexible and better adjusted across varied situations. Who → what. Sandra Bem → gender schema theory (children process the world through a learned gender framework) and androgyny as a healthy blend of masculine and feminine traits, measured by the Bem Sex-Role Inventory. Carol Gilligan: the ethic of care Carol Gilligan (born 1936), an American psychologist and once a colleague of Lawrence Kohlberg, mounted the best-known feminist critique of his stage theory of moral development. Kohlberg had built his stages from studies of boys and treated the highest morality as abstract justice and universal principles. Gilligan argued this yardstick was biased: it made women look morally "lower" simply because they often reasoned differently. In her book In a Different Voice (1982) she proposed that women more often speak in an ethic of care , grounded in relationships, responsibility, and not wanting to hurt others, rather than an ethic of justice based on rules and rights. Neither voice is superior; Kohlberg's scale had simply mistaken one voice for the whole of morality. Trap. Match the pair correctly: Lawrence Kohlberg = ethic of justice (rules, rights, abstract principles); Carol Gilligan = ethic of care (relationships, responsibility, compassion). Gilligan's charge was gender bias in Kohlberg's method, not that women lack morality. Harry Harlow: contact comfort in rhesus monkeys Why does a baby cling to its mother? The behaviourist answer of the mid-twentieth century was simple: the mother is associated with food, so the infant learns to love the source of feeding. The American psychologist Harry Harlow (1905–1981) overturned this "cupboard love" view with his famous studies of infant rhesus monkeys . He raised babies with two artificial surrogate "mothers": one made of bare wire that dispensed milk, and one made of soft terrycloth that gave no food. The behaviourist prediction was that the infants would bond with the feeding wire mother. Instead, they clung to the soft cloth mother almost all day, running to her when frightened and visiting the wire mother only briefly to feed. Harlow called the comfort of soft touch contact comfort and showed it, not food, was the basis of the bond. Who → what. Harry Harlow → rhesus-monkey surrogate-mother studies proving contact comfort (soft touch), not feeding, drives attachment; this undercut the drive-reduction (Clark Hull, 1943) "cupboard love" theory and supported later attachment theory. Why. Harry Harlow's work is the empirical bridge to John Bowlby and Mary Ainsworth: it demonstrated that the need for a comforting, secure body to cling to is primary, not a by-product of hunger. Frightened infants used the cloth mother as a base from which to explore, foreshadowing the "secure base" idea. 3.14 Lifespan and Later-Life Models Paul Baltes: the lifespan perspective and SOC The German psychologist Paul Baltes (1939–2006) insisted that development does not stop at adolescence and is not simply decline thereafter. His lifespan developmental perspective holds that development is lifelong , multidimensional (many domains at once), multidirectional (some capacities grow while others shrink), plastic (changeable), and always embedded in history and culture. At every age there is a shifting balance of gains and losses . To explain how people adapt to loss, especially in old age, Baltes and his collaborator Margret Baltes described selective optimization with compensation (SOC). Ageing people cope by three coordinated strategies. Selection. Narrowing goals to the few that matter most, given shrinking resources. An older musician keeps only a small repertoire. Optimization. Investing effort and practice into those chosen goals to keep performance high. Compensation. Using new means or aids to offset losses. The pianist Arthur Rubinstein, Baltes's own example, played fewer pieces (selection), practised them more (optimization), and slowed before fast passages so the contrast made them seem faster (compensation). Who → what. Paul Baltes → the lifespan perspective (development is lifelong, multidirectional, plastic, gain-and-loss) and selective optimization with compensation (SOC) as the strategy for adapting to age-related decline. Ainsworth's Strange Situation classifications, with Main's fourth pattern Building on John Bowlby's attachment theory, the American-Canadian psychologist Mary Ainsworth (1913–1999) devised a laboratory procedure, the Strange Situation , to measure the quality of an infant's attachment. In a series of episodes a one-year-old is observed exploring a room, meeting a stranger, being briefly separated from the mother, and, crucially, reunited with her. The reunion behaviour reveals the attachment pattern. Ainsworth described three, and later Mary Main (1943–2023), with Judith Solomon, added a fourth. Classification On separation On reunion Caregiving linked to it Secure May be distressed; uses mother as a base to explore Seeks her, is soothed, returns to play Sensitive, responsive Insecure-avoidant Little distress Ignores or avoids mother Rejecting, unresponsive Insecure-ambivalent (resistant) Very distressed Seeks contact yet resists it, hard to soothe, angry Inconsistent Disorganized (Main) Confused, no clear strategy Contradictory, dazed, or fearful behaviour Frightening, often linked to abuse or trauma Who → what. Mary Ainsworth → the Strange Situation and three attachment types (secure, avoidant, ambivalent/resistant). Mary Main & Judith Solomon → the fourth, disorganized , type, marked by contradictory, fearful reunion behaviour. Trap. Distinguish the two insecure "organised" types by the reunion. Avoidant infants seem indifferent and turn away; ambivalent/resistant infants are intensely distressed and cannot be comforted, clinging and pushing away at once. The disorganized type has no consistent strategy at all, and it is credited to Main, not Mary Ainsworth. Self-concept across childhood Self-concept is the set of beliefs a person holds about who they are. It is not fixed at birth but grows and reorganises across childhood. The famous rouge test (also called the mirror or mark test), studied by Michael Lewis and Jeanne Brooks-Gunn, shows that self-recognition emerges around 18 to 24 months: a toddler with a spot of rouge secretly dabbed on the nose will touch their own nose when shown a mirror, proving they recognise the reflection as themselves. From there the self-concept matures in a clear direction. Early childhood. The self is described in concrete, observable, physical terms ("I have brown hair, I have a dog, I can run fast") and is often unrealistically positive. Middle childhood. Descriptions become psychological and comparative ("I am kind, I am better at maths than my brother"), as social comparison sharpens. Adolescence. The self becomes abstract, integrated, and reflective , weaving traits, values, beliefs, and future goals into a coherent identity, linking directly to Erik Erikson's identity task. Why. Notice the same trajectory that runs through cognitive development: from concrete and outer to abstract and inner. The child who first knows the self by hair colour later knows it by values, mirroring the move from concrete to formal operations. Recap. Bronfenbrenner nested the child in five systems from the immediate microsystem out to the time-based chronosystem, with the mesosystem linking settings the child inhabits and the exosystem touching them from settings they do not. Alexander Thomas and Stella Chess named three temperaments (easy, difficult, slow-to-warm-up) and made goodness of fit the key. Diana Baumrind gave three parenting styles, and Maccoby and Martin added the neglectful fourth on demandingness × responsiveness, with authoritative (warm + firm) the healthiest. Bem offered gender schema theory and androgyny; Carol Gilligan answered Lawrence Kohlberg's justice ethic with an ethic of care; Harry Harlow proved contact comfort, not food, drives attachment. Baltes made development lifelong and gave SOC for adapting to loss; Ainsworth's Strange Situation classified attachment into secure, avoidant, and ambivalent, with Main adding disorganized; and self-concept matures from concrete outer traits toward abstract inner identity. 3.15 The complete map: every theory of development and its theorist Developmental psychology asks how thought, personality, morality, and relationships change from infancy to old age. This map gathers the whole landscape in five families: cognitive & language, psychosocial & personality, moral, attachment & social, and ecological & lifespan. Learn the name, the theorist, and the one-line hook so any paper cue is instantly placed. Key. Each row pairs a theory or model with the theorist who is the standard exam answer and a single-line core idea. Rows are numbered continuously across all five families; a theory is filed under the family that best fits its central question.
