F. Skinner (learned language). Recap. Twenty-eight theories across five families: cognitive & language (Piaget, Vygotsky, Bruner, Siegler, Chomsky vs Skinner, theory of mind), psychosocial & personality (Freud, Erikson, Marcia, Elkind, Mahler, Gesell, Havighurst), moral (Kohlberg, Gilligan, Piaget), attachment & social (Bowlby, Ainsworth, Harlow, Lorenz, Bandura, Baumrind, Alexander Thomas & Stella Chess), and ecological & lifespan (Bronfenbrenner, Baltes, Sameroff, Rutter). Fix each name to its theorist and one-line idea and no developmental cue can catch you out. 4 Abnormal & Clinical Psychology Abnormal psychology studies patterns of thought, feeling and behaviour that fall outside the ordinary range and cause problems for the person or those around them. Clinical psychology takes that knowledge and applies it: assessment, diagnosis, formulation and treatment of psychological distress. This section builds from the ground up – what "abnormal" even means, how disorders are classified, why they arise, and the main families of disorder you must recognise for the entrance. 4.1 What counts as "abnormal"? The 4 Ds There is no single line that separates the normal from the abnormal. Instead, clinicians weigh several overlapping criteria, remembered as the 4 Ds . The more of them that apply, and the more strongly, the more confidently we call a pattern disordered. Deviance – the behaviour departs from what a society considers acceptable or statistically usual. Hearing voices no one else hears deviates from shared norms of perception. Distress – the person suffers. Someone with severe anxiety feels genuine anguish. (Note: distress is not always present; a person in a manic episode may feel wonderful.) Dysfunction – the pattern interferes with daily life: work, study, relationships, self-care. This is the most clinically weighted of the four. Danger – the behaviour poses risk of harm to self or others. This is the least common criterion and is over-emphasised in popular thinking. Key. No single D is necessary or sufficient. A skydiver deviates and courts danger yet has no disorder; a grieving widow feels intense distress that is not pathological. Diagnosis rests on the pattern across the Ds, its persistence, and its context. Trap. "Abnormal = statistically rare" is only one narrow model. Very high intelligence is statistically rare but not a disorder; depression is common yet clearly pathological. Rarity alone never defines abnormality. 4.2 Models of abnormality Before modern classification, different lenses competed to define what "abnormal" was. Each still shapes how we think today. Statistical model – abnormality as deviation from the average (e.g. an IQ two standard deviations below the mean). Clean but blind to whether the deviation is harmful. Sociocultural model – abnormality is defined by violation of a culture's norms and roles; what is disordered in one society may be accepted in another. Highlights labelling and cultural relativity. Biological (medical) model – disorders are illnesses with organic causes (genes, neurotransmitters, brain structure) treated like physical disease. Psychological model – abnormality arises from mental processes: unconscious conflict, faulty learning, distorted cognition, or blocked growth, depending on the school. A short history Who → what. Philippe Pinel (France, late 1700s) pioneered moral treatment – he unchained inmates at the Bicêtre and Salpêtrière asylums and insisted the mentally ill be treated humanely rather than as prisoners or the possessed. He shifted madness from a moral or demonic problem to a medical one. Who → what. Emil Kraepelin (Germany, late 1800s) is the father of modern psychiatric classification . He grouped disorders by observed symptom clusters and course, distinguishing dementia praecox (later renamed schizophrenia) from manic-depressive insanity (mood disorder). His descriptive method is the direct ancestor of the DSM and ICD. 4.3 Classification systems: DSM-5-TR vs ICD-11 Two manuals dominate. Knowing who publishes each, how they are built, and how they differ is a common exam target. Feature DSM-5-TR ICD-11 Publisher American Psychiatric Association (APA) World Health Organization (WHO) Full name Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 5th ed., Text Revision (2022) International Classification of Diseases, 11th revision (in force 2022) Scope Mental disorders only All diseases and health conditions; mental disorders are one chapter Primary use Detailed clinical/research diagnosis, dominant in the USA Global health statistics, morbidity/mortality coding, used worldwide Structure Explicit diagnostic criteria sets with symptom counts and durations Prototype/clinical descriptions with diagnostic guidelines, more flexible Access Purchased (copyright revenue for APA) Freely available Approach Largely categorical (present/absent), with growing dimensional elements Categorical but more openly dimensional (e.g. personality disorder severity) Key. Categorical classification asks "does the person have the disorder, yes or no?" and sorts people into discrete boxes. Dimensional classification rates traits or severity along a continuum (mild → severe). Real distress is continuous, so both manuals are drifting toward dimensional thinking, most visibly in how ICD-11 rates personality disorder by severity rather than by named type. Trap. The DSM is not a global standard. Outside North America, and for all official health statistics, the WHO's ICD is the reference. Do not assume "DSM" means "the world's manual". 4.4 Etiological models: why disorders arise "Etiology" means cause. Several theoretical models each explain psychopathology through a different mechanism. Biological – genetics, neurotransmitter imbalance (e.g. serotonin in depression, dopamine in psychosis), hormones, brain structure and injury. Psychodynamic – symptoms express unconscious conflict, usually rooted in early childhood, as defended-against impulses break through (Sigmund Freud's legacy). Behavioural – disorders are learned : maladaptive responses acquired through classical conditioning (Ivan Pavlov), operant reinforcement or modelling. A phobia is a conditioned fear. Cognitive – distorted, irrational or negative thinking drives the disorder; change the thought and the emotion follows (Aaron Beck, Albert Ellis). Humanistic – distress arises when growth toward one's potential is blocked, often by conditions of worth imposed by others (Carl Rogers, Abraham Maslow). Sociocultural – family systems, poverty, discrimination, culture and social stress shape and label disorder. Integrative models Modern clinical psychology rarely picks just one lens. Biopsychosocial model (George Engel) – every disorder reflects an interaction of biological, psychological and social factors; assessment and treatment must address all three. Diathesis-stress model – a person carries a predisposition or vulnerability (the diathesis , e.g. genetic risk) that only becomes a disorder when enough environmental stress is applied. Neither alone is sufficient; disorder emerges from their interaction. Why. The diathesis-stress idea explains why two people facing the same trauma diverge: one develops PTSD, the other does not. Their thresholds differ because their underlying vulnerabilities differ. It is the single most examined integrative concept in this topic. 4.5 Anxiety disorders Anxiety disorders share excessive, persistent fear or worry that is out of proportion to real threat and impairs functioning. In DSM-5-TR the anxiety chapter was slimmed down: OCD and PTSD were moved out into their own chapters (see below). Disorder Core feature Generalised anxiety disorder (GAD) Chronic, free-floating, uncontrollable worry about many everyday things for ≥6 months, with restlessness, fatigue, tension, poor sleep. Panic disorder Recurrent unexpected panic attacks (surges of terror with palpitations, breathlessness, chest pain, fear of dying) plus persistent worry about further attacks. Specific phobia Marked, irrational fear of a specific object or situation (heights, spiders, blood, flying), with avoidance. Agoraphobia Fear of places from which escape is hard or help unavailable (crowds, open spaces, public transport); may lead to being housebound. Social anxiety disorder Intense fear of scrutiny and negative evaluation in social or performance situations, driving avoidance. A 24-year-old avoids buses and shopping malls; last month, boxed in a crowd, her heart raced, she felt she was suffocating and about to die, and she fled. She now maps her day around escape routes. → Panic attacks with agoraphobic avoidance. OCD and related disorders (now a separate DSM-5 chapter) Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) combines obsessions (intrusive, unwanted thoughts, images or urges that cause anxiety, e.g. contamination fears) with compulsions (repetitive acts or mental rituals performed to reduce that anxiety, e.g. washing, checking, counting). The compulsion briefly relieves distress, which reinforces it. Related disorders in this chapter include body dysmorphic disorder, hoarding disorder and trichotillomania (hair-pulling). Trauma- and stressor-related disorders (also a separate DSM-5 chapter) Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) follows exposure to a life-threatening or horrifying event and is defined by four symptom clusters: intrusion (flashbacks, nightmares), avoidance of reminders, negative changes in mood and cognition , and hyperarousal (startle, hypervigilance), lasting more than one month. Acute stress disorder is the same picture within the first month. Trap. In DSM-5-TR, OCD and PTSD are not anxiety disorders – each has its own chapter. In the older DSM-IV they were housed under anxiety, and ICD keeps them nearby. Many exam items hinge on this reclassification. 4.6 Mood (affective) disorders Mood disorders centre on disturbance of emotional state – either depressed, elevated, or swinging between the two. Disorder Core feature Major depressive disorder (MDD) ≥2 weeks of depressed mood and/or loss of interest (anhedonia) plus symptoms such as weight/appetite change, sleep disturbance, fatigue, worthlessness, poor concentration, thoughts of death. Episodic. Persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia) Chronic low-grade depression lasting ≥2 years; less intense than MDD but grinding and long-lasting. Bipolar I disorder At least one full manic episode (elevated/irritable mood, grandiosity, reduced sleep, pressured speech, risky behaviour) ≥1 week; depressive episodes usually occur too but are not required. Bipolar II disorder At least one hypomanic episode (milder, shorter elevation, no marked impairment or psychosis) plus at least one major depressive episode. Never a full mania. Cyclothymic disorder ≥2 years of fluctuating hypomanic and depressive symptoms that never reach full episode criteria; the "milder chronic" cousin of bipolar. Key. The line between Bipolar I and II is the presence of full mania (I) versus only hypomania (II). Mania causes marked impairment or psychosis or hospitalisation; hypomania does not. Dysthymia is to MDD what cyclothymia is to bipolar – the chronic, milder shadow. Who → what. Aaron Beck proposed the cognitive triad of depression: the depressed person holds automatic negative views of the (1) self ("I am worthless"), (2) world/experience ("everything is against me"), and (3) future ("it will never get better"). These distortions, not external reality, sustain the low mood, and correcting them is the target of cognitive therapy (CBT). A 30-year-old man reports two weeks of not being able to enjoy anything, sleeping twelve hours yet exhausted, feeling he has "ruined everything" and that his family would be better off without him. → Major depressive episode with the cognitive triad clearly active. 4.7 Schizophrenia spectrum Schizophrenia is a severe disorder of thought, perception and behaviour in which contact with reality is impaired (psychosis). Symptoms are grouped as positive and negative. Positive symptoms (added to normal experience): delusions (fixed false beliefs), hallucinations (usually auditory), disorganised speech, grossly disorganised or catatonic behaviour. Negative symptoms (normal functions lost): flat affect, alogia (poverty of speech), avolition (lack of drive), anhedonia, social withdrawal. These respond poorly to medication and predict worse outcome. Who → what. Eugen Bleuler coined the term "schizophrenia" (splitting of psychic functions, not "split personality") and defined its core fundamental symptoms as the 4 A's : A ssociation disturbance (loosened, illogical thought), A ffect disturbance (blunted or inappropriate emotion), A mbivalence (contradictory feelings/impulses at once), and A utism (withdrawal into an inner private world). Hallucinations and delusions he regarded as secondary. Who → what. Kurt Schneider listed first-rank symptoms he considered strongly suggestive of schizophrenia: audible thoughts, voices arguing or commenting on one's actions, thought insertion, thought withdrawal, thought broadcasting, made (externally controlled) feelings, impulses and acts, and delusional perception. Useful clinically, though not disorder-specific. Subtypes: a historical note DSM-IV and ICD-10 named subtypes – paranoid, disorganised (hebephrenic), catatonic, undifferentiated and residual. DSM-5 abolished these subtypes because they were unstable and had poor predictive value, replacing them with a dimensional rating of symptom severity. Cause and course The dopamine hypothesis proposes that positive symptoms arise from overactivity of dopamine transmission (especially D2 receptors) in mesolimbic pathways; antipsychotics block D2 receptors, and dopamine agonists like amphetamine can trigger psychosis. It is an incomplete picture (glutamate and serotonin also matter) but a heavily tested one. Prognosis is better with acute/sudden onset, clear precipitating stress, good pre-morbid functioning, prominent mood/positive symptoms and late onset; it is worse with insidious onset, prominent negative symptoms and early onset. Trap. "Schizophrenia" does not mean "split/multiple personality" – that is dissociative identity disorder. Bleuler's "splitting" referred to the fragmentation of thought, emotion and will within one mind, not several personalities. 4.8 Personality disorders A personality disorder is an enduring, inflexible, pervasive pattern of inner experience and behaviour that deviates markedly from cultural expectation, is stable from adolescence/early adulthood, and causes distress or impairment. DSM-5 groups the ten into three clusters. Cluster Theme Disorders A Odd / eccentric Paranoid (pervasive distrust), Schizoid (detachment, indifference to relationships), Schizotypal (odd beliefs, magical thinking, eccentric behaviour) B Dramatic / emotional / erratic Antisocial (disregard for others' rights, deceit, no remorse), Borderline (unstable relationships, self-image and affect, impulsivity, fear of abandonment), Histrionic (excessive emotionality and attention-seeking), Narcissistic (grandiosity, need for admiration, lack of empathy) C Anxious / fearful Avoidant (social inhibition, hypersensitivity to rejection), Dependent (excessive need to be cared for, clinging), Obsessive-compulsive personality (rigid perfectionism, orderliness, control) Trap. Obsessive-compulsive personality disorder (OCPD) is a Cluster C personality style of rigid perfectionism and is ego-syntonic (the person sees nothing wrong). OCD is the anxiety-related disorder of obsessions and compulsions and is ego-dystonic (the person is tormented by it). Different diagnoses, easy to confuse. 4.9 Other major categories (briefly) Dissociative disorders – disruption of memory, identity or awareness: dissociative identity disorder (two or more distinct personality states, formerly "multiple personality"), dissociative amnesia (inability to recall important, often traumatic personal information), depersonalisation/derealisation disorder (feeling detached from oneself or that the world is unreal). Somatic symptom & related disorders – distressing bodily symptoms with disproportionate thoughts and behaviour: somatic symptom disorder , illness anxiety disorder (health anxiety), and conversion disorder (functional neurological symptoms such as paralysis or blindness with no organic cause). Feeding & eating disorders – anorexia nervosa (restriction, very low weight, intense fear of gaining, distorted body image), bulimia nervosa (binge–purge cycles at normal or above weight), binge-eating disorder (recurrent binges without compensatory purging). Neurodevelopmental disorders – onset in the developmental period: intellectual disability (deficits in intellectual and adaptive functioning), autism spectrum disorder (social-communication deficits plus restricted, repetitive behaviours), attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) (inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity). Substance-related and addictive disorders – problematic patterns of substance use (tolerance, withdrawal, craving, loss of control, use despite harm) plus behavioural addictions such as gambling disorder. 4.10 Clinical process basics Diagnosis is only part of clinical work. Two foundational tools: The Mental Status Examination (MSE) The MSE is a structured snapshot of the patient's current mental functioning at the time of interview – the psychological equivalent of a physical exam. Its components: Appearance and behaviour – grooming, dress, eye contact, psychomotor activity, cooperativeness. Speech – rate, volume, tone, fluency. Mood and affect – mood is the patient's reported emotional state; affect is the observed, moment-to-moment expression (its range, appropriateness, congruence). Thought process – the form/flow of thinking (logical, tangential, loosened, flight of ideas). Thought content – delusions, obsessions, suicidal or homicidal ideation. Perception – hallucinations, illusions. Cognition – orientation (time, place, person), attention, memory. Insight and judgement – awareness of illness and quality of decision-making. Key. Distinguish mood (subjective, reported, the "climate") from affect (objective, observed, the "weather"). And distinguish thought process (how thoughts flow) from thought content (what the thoughts are about). Both pairs are classic viva and MCQ traps. Formulation and regulation Case formulation goes beyond the diagnostic label to build a working explanation of this person's problems – often organised as predisposing, precipitating, perpetuating and protective factors (the "4 Ps") – and it directly guides the treatment plan. Where diagnosis says "what", formulation says "why, for this person, now". Key. In India, the practice of clinical psychology is regulated by the Rehabilitation Council of India (RCI) under the RCI Act, 1992. Only professionals with an RCI-recognised qualification (such as the M.Phil in Clinical Psychology, now transitioning to an RCI-approved MA route) registered on the Central Rehabilitation Register may practise as clinical psychologists. This is why entrance exams like SGT's feed into RCI-recognised programmes. Recap. Abnormality is judged by the 4 Ds (deviance, distress, dysfunction, danger), read through statistical, sociocultural, biological and psychological models, on a road paved by Philippe Pinel's moral treatment and Emil Kraepelin's classification. Two manuals classify disorders – the APA's DSM-5-TR (detailed, criteria-based, categorical drifting dimensional) and the WHO's ICD-11 (global, guideline-based, more dimensional). Causes are framed biologically, psychodynamically, behaviourally, cognitively, humanistically and socioculturally, integrated by the biopsychosocial and diathesis-stress models. The major families: anxiety (GAD, panic, phobias, agoraphobia, social anxiety) with OCD and PTSD now split off; mood disorders (MDD, dysthymia, bipolar I vs II, cyclothymia, with Aaron Beck's cognitive triad); the schizophrenia spectrum (positive vs negative symptoms, Bleuler's 4 A's, Schneider's first-rank symptoms, the dopamine hypothesis); ten personality disorders in Clusters A, B and C; and dissociative, somatic, eating, neurodevelopmental and substance-related disorders. Clinical work rests on the MSE and case formulation, and in India is governed by the RCI. 4.11 Neurodevelopmental and childhood disorders Neurodevelopmental disorders are a group of conditions with onset in the developmental period, typically before a child enters grade school. Their defining feature is that they produce impairments of personal, social, academic, or occupational functioning that arise from disturbances in the growth and maturation of the brain and nervous system. Because the deficits appear early and shape the course of later development, they are placed at the very front of the DSM-5-TR (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition, Text Revision) classification. This subsection covers the five clusters most likely to be tested: intellectual developmental disorder, autism spectrum disorder, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, specific learning disorder, and the disruptive behaviour disorders of childhood. Intellectual developmental disorder Intellectual developmental disorder (the term used in ICD-11, the Eleventh Revision of the International Classification of Diseases; DSM-5-TR names it intellectual developmental disorder or intellectual disability) is defined by deficits in two domains that both begin during the developmental period. The first is intellectual functioning : reasoning, problem solving, planning, abstract thinking, judgement, and learning, confirmed both by clinical assessment and by standardized, individually administered intelligence testing. The second is adaptive functioning : how well the person meets everyday standards of personal independence and social responsibility across the conceptual (language, reading, money, time), social (empathy, friendship, social judgement), and practical (self-care, job, money management) domains. Key. A modern diagnosis of intellectual developmental disorder does not rest on an IQ number alone. Severity is graded by adaptive functioning , not by the intelligence quotient (William Stern, 1912), because it is adaptive skill that determines the level of support a person needs. This is a deliberate shift away from the older practice of defining the categories purely by IQ bands. DSM-5-TR recognizes four severity levels, defined by how much support the person requires across the conceptual, social, and practical domains. Mild: the largest group; academic difficulties emerge in school years, but many adults live and work with intermittent support. May hold a job and manage a household with help on complex tasks such as banking or legal decisions. Moderate: markedly limited conceptual skills; language and academic progress are slow; ongoing support for daily living is needed. Severe: very limited conceptual skills; little understanding of written language or number; the person needs support for all activities of daily living. Profound: conceptual skills largely involve the physical world; the person depends on others for all aspects of daily physical care, health, and safety, though may take part in some routine activities. Trap. Do not confuse intellectual developmental disorder with global developmental delay . Global developmental delay is a provisional label reserved for children under age five who cannot yet be reliably assessed by standardized testing. It is a placeholder, not a lifelong diagnosis, and must be re-evaluated as the child grows. Autism spectrum disorder Autism spectrum disorder is a neurodevelopmental condition built on two core symptom clusters that must both be present. The DSM-5-TR merged several earlier separate labels (autistic disorder, Asperger's disorder, and pervasive developmental disorder) into a single spectrum precisely because they shared this dyad and differed mainly in severity. Persistent deficits in social communication and social interaction across multiple contexts: problems in social-emotional reciprocity (back-and-forth conversation, sharing of interests and emotions); deficits in nonverbal communicative behaviours (eye contact, gesture, facial expression); and difficulties developing, maintaining, and understanding relationships. Restricted, repetitive patterns of behaviour, interests, or activities , shown by at least two of: stereotyped or repetitive motor movements, speech, or use of objects; insistence on sameness and inflexible routines; highly restricted, fixated interests of abnormal intensity; and hyper- or hypo-reactivity to sensory input (for example, indifference to pain or adverse reaction to specific sounds or textures). Symptoms must be present in the early developmental period, though they may not fully manifest until social demands exceed capacities. Severity is rated by the level of support required (Level 1 requiring support, Level 2 requiring substantial support, Level 3 requiring very substantial support), and clinicians specify whether it occurs with or without accompanying intellectual or language impairment. Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a persistent pattern of inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity that interferes with functioning or development. Several symptoms must be present before age 12, in two or more settings (for example, home and school), a criterion designed to rule out situational misbehaviour. DSM-5-TR describes three presentations, and knowing the difference is a common exam point. Predominantly inattentive presentation: difficulty sustaining attention, careless mistakes, not seeming to listen, disorganization, forgetfulness, and losing things, without enough hyperactive symptoms. Predominantly hyperactive-impulsive presentation: fidgeting, leaving one's seat, restlessness, talking excessively, blurting out answers, difficulty waiting turns, and interrupting. Combined presentation: criteria for both inattention and hyperactivity-impulsivity are met; this is the most common presentation in clinical samples. Trap. ADHD uses the word presentation , not subtype , because the picture can change over a person's life: a child who is combined may look predominantly inattentive as a teenager. Also, the onset criterion is before age 12 in DSM-5-TR, raised from the "before age 7" used in the earlier DSM-IV. Examiners often test this specific number. Specific learning disorder Specific learning disorder is a difficulty learning and using academic skills that is well below what is expected for the person's age and not explained by intellectual disability, poor schooling, or sensory problems. DSM-5-TR folds the older separate reading, writing, and mathematics disorders into one diagnosis with specifiers. With impairment in reading (dyslexia): problems with word reading accuracy, reading rate or fluency, and reading comprehension. With impairment in written expression (dysgraphia): difficulties with spelling accuracy, grammar and punctuation, and clarity or organization of written expression. With impairment in mathematics (dyscalculia): difficulties with number sense, memorization of arithmetic facts, accurate or fluent calculation, and mathematical reasoning. Disruptive behaviour disorders Two childhood disorders are marked by problems in self-control of emotions and behaviour that bring the child into conflict with authority and social norms. Oppositional defiant disorder is a recurrent pattern of angry or irritable mood, argumentative or defiant behaviour, and vindictiveness lasting at least six months, directed especially at authority figures. The child loses their temper, argues with adults, defies rules, and blames others, but generally does not seriously violate the basic rights of others or major societal rules. Conduct disorder is more severe: a repetitive pattern in which the basic rights of others or major age-appropriate norms are violated, grouped into aggression to people and animals, destruction of property, deceitfulness or theft, and serious rule violations (for example, truancy or running away). Conduct disorder in childhood is a recognized precursor to antisocial personality disorder in adulthood, which cannot be diagnosed before age 18. Childhood disorder Core defining feature Intellectual developmental disorder Deficits in intellectual AND adaptive functioning, onset in developmental period Autism spectrum disorder Social-communication deficits PLUS restricted, repetitive behaviours Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder Inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity, onset before age 12, two or more settings Specific learning disorder Academic skill (reading, writing, or maths) far below expected, not due to low IQ Oppositional defiant disorder Angry, argumentative, defiant pattern toward authority, without violating others' rights Conduct disorder Repeated violation of others' rights and major social norms 4.12 Trauma-, stressor-, dissociative, and somatic disorders These three families share a common thread: psychological distress that follows overwhelming experience or is expressed through disruptions of consciousness, memory, identity, or bodily function. DSM-5-TR groups the trauma- and stressor-related disorders together, treating exposure to a stressful or traumatic event as an explicit diagnostic requirement, a rare instance in the manual where cause is written into the definition. Trauma- and stressor-related disorders Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) follows exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence, whether experienced directly, witnessed, learned about happening to a close other, or through repeated exposure to aversive details (as with first responders). Its symptoms fall into four clusters: Intrusion: recurrent involuntary memories, distressing dreams, flashbacks in which the event feels as if it is recurring, and marked distress at reminders. Avoidance: effortful avoidance of memories, thoughts, feelings, or external reminders of the event. Negative alterations in cognition and mood: inability to recall key features, persistent negative beliefs, distorted blame, persistent negative emotional states, detachment, and inability to feel positive emotion. Alterations in arousal and reactivity: irritability, reckless behaviour, hypervigilance, exaggerated startle, concentration problems, and sleep disturbance. Key. The single most tested distinction here is duration. Acute stress disorder describes a similar reaction lasting from three days up to one month after the trauma. If the disturbance persists beyond one month , the diagnosis becomes post-traumatic stress disorder . Acute stress disorder is not simply "mild PTSD"; it is defined by its short window. Adjustment disorder is a broader, milder category: emotional or behavioural symptoms (depressed mood, anxiety, or conduct disturbance) that develop within three months of an identifiable stressor and are out of proportion to it or cause significant impairment. The stressor need not be traumatic; it can be an ordinary life event such as a divorce, job loss, or relocation. Symptoms resolve within six months once the stressor or its consequences end. Trap. Adjustment disorder is often called a residual or "wastebasket" category, but it has strict boundaries: it applies only when the reaction does not meet criteria for another specific disorder and does not represent normal bereavement. If the full PTSD or major depressive picture is present, that specific diagnosis takes priority. Dissociative disorders Dissociation is a disruption of the normally integrated functions of consciousness, memory, identity, emotion, perception, and behaviour. The dissociative disorders are frequently, though not always, linked to trauma. Dissociative identity disorder: the presence of two or more distinct personality states (in some cultures described as an experience of possession), accompanied by recurrent gaps in the recall of everyday events, personal information, or traumatic events that go beyond ordinary forgetting. It was formerly called multiple personality disorder. Dissociative amnesia: an inability to recall important autobiographical information, usually of a traumatic or stressful nature, that is too extensive to be ordinary forgetfulness. It may occur with dissociative fugue , apparently purposeful travel or bewildered wandering with amnesia for identity. Depersonalization/derealization disorder: persistent or recurrent experiences of unreality or detachment from one's own self (depersonalization: feeling like an outside observer of one's thoughts or body) or from surroundings (derealization: the world feeling dreamlike, foggy, or visually distorted), while reality testing remains intact. Trap. Dissociative identity disorder is heavily mythologized. Two corrections matter for exams. First, it is not the same as schizophrenia; "split personality" is a popular misnomer for schizophrenia, which involves psychosis, not separate identities. Second, in depersonalization/derealization the person knows the experience is not real; intact reality testing is what separates it from a psychotic disorder. Somatic symptom and related disorders These disorders feature distressing bodily symptoms together with abnormal thoughts, feelings, and behaviours in response to them. DSM-5-TR deliberately shifted the emphasis away from whether a symptom is "medically unexplained" and toward the person's excessive reaction, because unexplained-symptom judgements proved unreliable. Somatic symptom disorder: one or more distressing somatic symptoms plus disproportionate and persistent thoughts, high anxiety about health, or excessive time and energy devoted to the symptoms. The bodily symptom is real and present; the problem lies in the excessive response. Illness anxiety disorder: preoccupation with having or acquiring a serious illness when somatic symptoms are absent or only mild. Anxiety centres on the meaning and implication of health, not on a present symptom. This category absorbed much of what was formerly called hypochondriasis. Functional neurological symptom disorder (conversion disorder): symptoms of altered voluntary motor or sensory function (for example, weakness, paralysis, non-epileptic seizures, or blindness) that are incompatible with recognized neurological disease. The classic finding is la belle indifférence , a striking lack of concern about the deficit, though it is not required for diagnosis. Key. Distinguish these from factitious disorder and malingering . In somatic symptom, illness anxiety, and conversion disorders the symptoms are not consciously produced; the suffering is genuine. In factitious disorder the person deliberately falsifies symptoms to assume the sick role (an internal motive). In malingering symptoms are faked for an external reward (money, avoiding work), and malingering is not a mental disorder at all. 4.13 Feeding/eating, substance-related, and neurocognitive disorders Feeding and eating disorders The eating disorders are disturbances of eating or eating-related behaviour that harm physical health and psychosocial functioning. Three are central to the syllabus. Anorexia nervosa: restriction of energy intake leading to significantly low body weight, an intense fear of gaining weight or persistent behaviour that prevents weight gain, and a disturbance in the way body weight or shape is experienced. Specified as restricting type or binge-eating/purging type. The hallmark is the low body weight . Bulimia nervosa: recurrent episodes of binge eating (eating an unusually large amount with a sense of loss of control) followed by recurrent inappropriate compensatory behaviour to prevent weight gain (self-induced vomiting, laxatives, fasting, or excessive exercise), occurring on average at least once a week for three months. Body weight is typically normal or above. Binge-eating disorder: recurrent binge eating with marked distress but without the regular compensatory behaviours seen in bulimia. It is the most common eating disorder and was added as a formal diagnosis in DSM-5. Feature Anorexia nervosa Bulimia nervosa Binge-eating disorder Body weight Significantly low Usually normal or above Often overweight Binge eating Only in one subtype Yes, defining Yes, defining Compensatory behaviour Possible (purging subtype) Yes, defining No Core fear/feature Fear of weight gain, low weight Binge-purge cycle, loss of control Distress over bingeing Trap. The presence or absence of a single feature separates these. If body weight is significantly low, think anorexia nervosa even when bingeing and purging occur. Bulimia nervosa versus binge-eating disorder turns on compensatory behaviour : both binge, but only bulimia regularly purges, fasts, or over-exercises to undo it. Substance-related and addictive disorders DSM-5-TR made a major structural change here. The earlier DSM-IV split problem use into two separate diagnoses, substance abuse (a milder pattern) and substance dependence (the more severe, physiological pattern). DSM-5-TR abolished that split and combined them into a single substance use disorder measured on a severity continuum. Who → what. The American Psychiatric Association, in publishing DSM-5 (2013), collapsed the abuse-versus-dependence dichotomy into one substance use disorder rated as mild (2 to 3 symptoms), moderate (4 to 5), or severe (6 or more) out of eleven criteria spanning impaired control, social impairment, risky use, and pharmacological features. Two pharmacological criteria deserve careful definition because they are routinely confused. Tolerance: needing markedly increased amounts of the substance to achieve the desired effect, or a markedly diminished effect from the same amount. It reflects the body adapting so that more is required. Withdrawal: a substance-specific syndrome of unpleasant physical and psychological symptoms that appears when a heavy, prolonged user cuts down or stops, and which is often relieved by taking the substance again. Trap. Tolerance and withdrawal are not the same thing and neither alone equals addiction. Tolerance is "I need more to feel it"; withdrawal is "I feel sick when I stop." A patient on prescribed opioids for pain can develop both physiological tolerance and withdrawal without meeting the behavioural criteria for a substance use disorder, so DSM-5-TR notes that tolerance and withdrawal from appropriately prescribed medication do not count toward the diagnosis. Neurocognitive disorders Neurocognitive disorders are conditions in which the primary deficit is an acquired decline in cognition (attention, memory, language, executive function, perception, or social cognition) from a previously higher level. The word "acquired" separates them from the neurodevelopmental disorders, where the deficit was present from early life. Two forms anchor this topic. Delirium is an acute disturbance of attention and awareness that develops over hours to days, tends to fluctuate through the day, and is accompanied by additional cognitive disturbance. It is a direct physiological consequence of a medical condition, substance intoxication or withdrawal, medication, or a combination. Critically, delirium is usually reversible when the underlying cause is treated. Major neurocognitive disorder (the DSM-5-TR term that replaced dementia ) is a significant decline in one or more cognitive domains that interferes with independence in everyday activities. When the decline is present but does not yet compromise independence, it is labelled mild neurocognitive disorder . The most common cause is Alzheimer's disease, a progressive neurodegenerative condition marked pathologically by amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles, with insidious onset and gradual worsening, memory being the earliest and most prominent loss. Who → what. Alois Alzheimer, the German psychiatrist and neuropathologist, described the disease that bears his name in 1906 after examining a patient, Auguste Deter, and identifying the characteristic plaques and tangles in her brain at autopsy. His work gave the most common form of dementia its name. Trap. Delirium versus dementia (major neurocognitive disorder) is a favourite examination contrast. Delirium has acute onset (hours to days), a fluctuating course, impaired attention and consciousness , and is usually reversible . Dementia has gradual onset (months to years), a stable or progressive course, relatively preserved consciousness until late, prominent memory loss, and is usually irreversible . The two can coexist, and a person with dementia is at higher risk of developing a superimposed delirium. Recap. Neurodevelopmental disorders (intellectual developmental disorder graded by adaptive functioning, autism spectrum disorder's social-communication-plus-repetitive dyad, ADHD's three presentations with onset before age 12, specific learning disorder, and the oppositional defiant/conduct disorder pair) begin in early life. The trauma-related disorders hinge on duration (acute stress disorder within one month, PTSD beyond it, adjustment disorder for milder stressors), while dissociative disorders disrupt identity, memory, and perception with intact reality testing, and somatic disorders express distress through excessive reactions to bodily symptoms. Finally, eating disorders separate on weight and compensatory behaviour, substance use disorder now runs on a single severity continuum (with tolerance and withdrawal kept distinct), and neurocognitive disorders contrast reversible, fluctuating delirium against progressive, memory-led major neurocognitive disorder, the commonest form named after Alois Alzheimer. 4.14 The complete map: models of abnormality & the people behind them Abnormal psychology asks two linked questions: what causes disorder, and how do we name it. This is the full roster of explanatory models, the disorder-specific theories examiners quote, the classification landmarks, and the critical voices who pushed back. Learn the pairing of model to person to one-line idea; single-best-answer items live exactly here. Key. A model is a lens that decides what "abnormal" means, where it comes from, and how you treat it. Two big jobs: explain (why does it happen) and classify (what do we call it). Most modern practice is integrative (biopsychosocial), but exams still test each pure model and its author. Six explanatory models (biological, psychodynamic, behavioural, cognitive, humanistic-existential, sociocultural) plus the integrators (diathesis-stress, biopsychosocial). Disorder-specific theories: helplessness and hopelessness for depression, dopamine and expressed emotion for schizophrenia, monoamines for mood. Classification runs Kraepelin to Bleuler to DSM-5-TR and ICD-11, with Pinel, Dix, and Charcot in the history. The critics (Szasz, Scheff, Rosenhan) question whether the labels are real at all. 5 Psychological Assessment & Testing A psychological test is a standardized sample of behaviour. Two words in that sentence do all the work. Sample means we never measure the whole of a person; we measure a slice and infer the rest. Standardized means the slice is taken the same way every time: same items, same instructions, same scoring, same comparison group. If either word fails, the number the test spits out is meaningless. This chapter builds the machinery that lets us trust a test score, then walks through the actual instruments a clinical psychologist in India uses, and closes on who is legally allowed to use them. 5.1 Psychometric foundations: reliability Reliability asks one question: if I measured again, would I get the same answer? A bathroom scale that reads 60 kg, then 64 kg, then 58 kg for the same person in one minute is unreliable. It is not that the readings are wrong in any deep sense; they are simply inconsistent , and inconsistency alone makes a test useless. Reliability is quantified as a correlation coefficient running from 0 to 1; for a clinical test we usually want it above 0.80, and for high-stakes decisions above 0.90. There are several kinds of reliability because there are several sources of inconsistency, and each method isolates one source. Test–retest reliability. Give the same test to the same people twice, some weeks apart, and correlate the two sets of scores. This isolates instability over time . Its enemy is the carry-over effect : people remember their earlier answers, or genuinely change between sittings. Best suited to stable traits (intelligence), poorly suited to fluctuating states (mood). Split-half reliability. Split the test into two halves (usually odd items versus even items), score each half, and correlate them. This isolates internal consistency : do the items hang together? Because a half-test is shorter and shorter tests are less reliable, the raw correlation is corrected upward with the Spearman–Brown formula. Cronbach's alpha. Devised by Lee Cronbach, alpha is the average of all possible split-halves at once. It is the standard modern index of internal consistency for a scale with many items scored on a range (like a Likert questionnaire). High alpha means the items are measuring one common thing. Inter-rater (inter-scorer) reliability. Do two independent examiners, watching the same performance, give the same score? This isolates examiner subjectivity . It matters enormously for tests where scoring involves judgement, such as the Rorschach or a projective drawing, and much less for a machine-scored multiple-choice test. Cohen's kappa is the usual index. Parallel (alternate) forms reliability. Build two equivalent versions of the test and correlate them; this isolates the accident of which particular items were chosen, and sidesteps memory effects that plague test–retest. Who → what. Lee Cronbach gave us coefficient alpha (1951), the single most-cited index of internal consistency in all of psychology. 5.2 Validity Validity asks a completely different question: does the test measure what it claims to measure? A scale can be perfectly reliable and still invalid. My bathroom scale might read exactly 60 kg every single time (perfectly reliable) while I actually weigh 70 kg, because it is miscalibrated (invalid). Reliability is about consistency; validity is about truth. Content validity. Do the items cover the whole domain they claim to? A depression scale that asks only about sadness but ignores sleep, appetite, and suicidal thought has poor content validity. Judged by expert review of the item pool, not by a statistic. Criterion validity. Does the test agree with an external, real-world benchmark (the "criterion")? Two flavours by timing: Concurrent validity – test and criterion measured at the same time . A new short depression screener is given alongside a full clinical interview today; do they agree today? Predictive validity – test now predicts a criterion in the future . An entrance exam taken in June predicts first-year marks the following March. Construct validity (Lee Cronbach and Paul Meehl, 1955). The deepest and most abstract kind. A "construct" is an unobservable theoretical entity (intelligence, anxiety, extraversion). Construct validity asks whether the test truly taps that entity, established by a web of evidence: convergent validity (it correlates with other measures of the same construct) and discriminant validity (it does not correlate with measures of unrelated constructs). An anxiety scale should correlate with other anxiety measures and should not correlate with, say, shoe size. Trap. Reliability and validity are constantly confused. Memorise the two arrows. Reliability = consistency (same answer on repetition). Validity = accuracy (the right answer). A test must be reliable to be valid (an erratic instrument can't be measuring anything real), but it can be reliable without being valid (a consistently miscalibrated scale). So reliability is necessary but not sufficient for validity. Reliability sets the ceiling: a test's validity can never exceed the square root of its reliability. 5.3 Standardization, norms, and error Standardization is the process of fixing the administration and scoring, and of building the yardstick against which any individual is compared. Norms are that yardstick: the distribution of scores obtained by a large, representative standardization sample . A raw score of 34 on a test means nothing by itself; it becomes meaningful only when we say "34 is at the 70th percentile for 25-year-old Indian graduates". This is why Indian norms matter so much (Section 5.5): a test normed on American children mislabels Indian children. Key. A raw score is mute. It speaks only after being placed against a norm group . Always ask: normed on whom? No measurement is perfect, so every observed score is the true score plus error: Observed = True + Error . The standard error of measurement (SEM) quantifies that error band. It lets us build a confidence interval around a score: an IQ of 100 with an SEM of 3 really means "true IQ is very likely between roughly 94 and 106". The SEM shrinks as reliability rises, tying the two foundations together: reliability tells us how much to trust the number, and the SEM turns that trust into a range. 5.4 Levels of measurement and types of scores Before scoring, we must know what kind of number we hold. Stanley Smith Stevens' four levels, from least to most information, govern which statistics are even legal. Level What it captures Example Legal statistics Nominal Names / categories only; no order Diagnosis code, gender, blood group Mode, frequency, chi-square Ordinal Rank order, but unequal gaps Rank in a merit list, Likert "agree/disagree" Median, percentile, rank correlation Interval Equal gaps, but arbitrary zero Temperature in °C, IQ score, calendar year Mean, SD, Pearson r Ratio Equal gaps and a true zero Reaction time, weight, number of errors All, including ratios ("twice as fast") Trap. IQ and most psychological test scores are interval, not ratio . There is no true zero of intelligence, so you cannot say an IQ of 140 is "twice as smart" as 70. That ratio statement requires a true zero, which only ratio scales have. Once we have a raw score we convert it into a derived score that locates the person in the norm group. Percentile rank. The percentage of the norm group scoring at or below you. Intuitive but ordinal : the gap between the 50th and 55th percentile is tiny, while the gap between the 90th and 95th is large, because scores bunch in the middle. z-score. How many standard deviations you are above or below the mean. Mean = 0, SD = 1. A z of +1.5 is one and a half SDs above average. The parent of all standard scores. T-score. A rescaled z with mean = 50 and SD = 10, chosen to avoid negatives and decimals. Used on the MMPI (Starke Hathaway and J. Charnley McKinley, 1943) and many clinical scales; a T of 70 (two SDs up) is the usual clinical cut-off. Stanine. "Standard nine": a 1–9 scale with mean = 5 and SD = 2. Coarse but simple. Deviation IQ. A standard score with mean = 100 and SD = 15 (Wechsler) or 16 (Stanford–Binet). It has replaced the old ratio IQ (see 5.5). 5.5 Intelligence testing: the historical spine Who → what. Alfred Binet and his collaborator Theodore Simon , commissioned by the French government in 1905 to identify schoolchildren needing special help, built the first practical intelligence scale . Their genius idea was mental age : a child who solves the tasks that an average 8-year-old solves has a mental age of 8, whatever the birthday says. The story moves in four leaps: Binet & Simon (1905, Paris) introduce mental age and an age-graded task ladder. Purely practical, atheoretical, aimed at placement. Lewis Terman (1916, Stanford University) imports and re-standardizes the scale on American children as the Stanford–Binet , and popularises the ratio IQ (William Stern, 1912): IQ = (Mental Age ÷ Chronological Age) × 100. A 10-year-old with a mental age of 12 gets an IQ of 120. David Wechsler (from 1939, New York) attacks the ratio IQ's fatal flaw (see trap) and replaces it with the deviation IQ , which simply asks how far you deviate from your own age group . He also splits intelligence into verbal and performance scales, so a non-English-speaker can still show ability. His family of tests dominates clinical practice today. John Raven (1938, London) builds the Progressive Matrices , a pattern-completion test with no words at all, designed to be culture-fair and to tap Charles Spearman's g directly. Trap. The ratio IQ breaks down in adulthood. Mental age plateaus in the late teens while chronological age keeps climbing, so the ratio MA÷CA falls with every birthday and would make everyone look like they are losing intelligence. This is exactly why Wechsler's deviation IQ (comparison within one's own age band) replaced it, and why modern Stanford–Binet editions also use deviation IQ. Fluid ( Gf ) is on-the-spot reasoning in novel situations and declines with age; crystallized ( Gc ) is accumulated knowledge and holds or grows with age. 5.6 Indian intelligence adaptations A Western test dropped unchanged into India fails twice: its items assume unfamiliar objects and its norms describe the wrong population. India's answer was two-pronged: build performance tests that lean on doing rather than on English, and re-standardize verbal scales on Indian samples. Who → what. Chandra Mohan Bhatia built Bhatia's Battery of Performance Tests (1955), the classic Indian performance battery, precisely so that illiterate and rural testees could be assessed without any reading. Bhatia's Battery of Performance Tests (Chandra Mohan Bhatia, 1955). Five sub-tests: Koh's Block Design, Alexander's Pass-along, Pattern Drawing, Immediate Memory, and Picture Construction. Non-verbal, timed, suited to the illiterate; a workhorse in Indian clinics for age 11+. Malin's Intelligence Scale for Indian Children (MISIC) – Lalitha Malin 's Indian adaptation of the WISC, with Verbal and Performance sub-tests and Indian norms; the most widely used individual child IQ test in India. Binet–Kamat Test of Intelligence – V. V. Kamat's Indian adaptation of the Stanford–Binet (into Kannada and Marathi), yielding mental age and IQ for Indian children. Seguin Form Board Test – Edouard Seguin's shape-fitting board, used in India as a quick non-verbal test of speed and eye-hand coordination and a rough screen for intellectual disability in young children. Draw-A-Man Test – Florence Goodenough's drawing test, adapted for Indian children by Pramila Pathak ; the child draws a person and the score reflects cognitive maturity through the detail of the drawing. Why. Culture-fair and performance tests matter in India because a large share of testees are non-literate or speak a language the test was never written in. A verbal, English-normed test would confound lack of schooling with lack of intelligence , systematically mislabelling the poor and rural as impaired. Performance batteries (Bhatia, Seguin) and re-normed scales (MISIC, Binet–Kamat) remove that confound. 5.7 Personality assessment Personality tests split into two philosophies. Objective tests use fixed items with fixed scoring (true/false, Likert); they are reliable and easy to score but transparent, so they can be faked. Projective tests present ambiguous stimuli on the theory that the person will "project" unconscious material onto them; they are rich and hard to fake but weak on reliability and validity. Objective personality tests MMPI (Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory) – Starke Hathaway & John McKinley . The giant of clinical personality assessment: hundreds of true/false items yielding clinical scales (depression, paranoia, schizophrenia, etc.) plus built-in validity scales (L, F, K) that detect lying and faking. Empirically keyed: items were kept if they statistically separated patient groups, not on theory. 16PF (Sixteen Personality Factor Questionnaire) – Raymond Cattell , derived by factor analysis into sixteen source traits. A normal-range trait test. NEO-PI / Big Five – Paul Costa & Robert McCrae . Measures the five-factor model: Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, Neuroticism (OCEAN). The dominant modern trait framework. Eysenck Personality Questionnaire (EPQ) – Hans Eysenck . Three broad dimensions: Extraversion–Introversion, Neuroticism–Stability, and Psychoticism, grounded in biological theory. Projective personality tests Rorschach Inkblot Test – Hermann Rorschach (1921). Ten symmetrical inkblots; the person says what each might be, and responses are coded for location, determinants (form, colour, movement), and content. Exner's Comprehensive System later standardized scoring. Thematic Apperception Test (TAT) – Henry Murray & Christiana Morgan . The person tells a story about ambiguous pictures of people; the stories reveal needs, drives, and conflicts (Murray's theory of needs). Sentence Completion Test – the person finishes stems like "My greatest fear is…"; semi-structured, easier to score than the Rorschach (e.g. Rotter's Incomplete Sentences Blank). Draw-A-Person Test – the person draws a human figure; features are interpreted for self-image and conflict (Machover). Also used as a rough cognitive screen in children. Indian TAT adaptation – Uma Chowdhury 's Indian adaptation of the TAT, redrawing the cards with Indian figures, dress, and settings so the pictures actually resemble the testee's world. Do not muddle the two great objective inventories. The MMPI is a clinical instrument built to detect psychopathology by empirical keying; the 16PF is a normal-range trait test built by factor analysis . Different purpose, different method. And the MMPI is objective despite its clinical use, while the Rorschach is projective : objective/projective is about item format, not about whether the test is clinical. 5.8 Neuropsychological and clinical rating scales Neuropsychological tests infer the integrity of the brain from behaviour, most classically through visuo-motor tasks where organic damage shows up as distortion. Bender Visual-Motor Gestalt Test (Lauretta Bender) – the person copies nine geometric designs; rotations, distortions, and integration errors screen for organic brain dysfunction and are also read developmentally in children. Luria–Nebraska Neuropsychological Battery – a standardized battery based on Alexander Luria's clinical methods, surveying motor, tactile, visual, language, memory, and intellectual functions to localise deficits.
