The Beck scales are self-report (the patient rates themselves); the Hamilton scales are clinician-rated (the interviewer scores from observation). Papers love to swap these. Remember: Beck → patient's pen, Hamilton → clinician's pen. 5.9 Ethics of testing A test is an act of power over a person's life, so its use is bound by ethics. Informed consent. The testee (or guardian) must understand the purpose, procedure, and use of results and agree freely before testing. Competence. A tester must use only tests they are trained and qualified to administer and interpret; using a test beyond one's training is malpractice. Test security. Test items and manuals must be kept confidential. If items leak into the public domain, the test is compromised and its norms invalidated. Confidentiality. Results are private and shared only with proper consent and on a need-to-know basis. Cultural fairness. The test and its norms must fit the testee's language and culture; using an inappropriate norm group is itself an ethical failure (this is the ethical face of Section 5.6). Key. In India the Rehabilitation Council of India (RCI) regulates who may use clinical psychological tests. Only professionals holding an RCI-recognised qualification (the M.Phil in Clinical Psychology and RCI registration as a Clinical Psychologist) are legally entitled to independently administer and interpret clinical assessments. This is why the qualification matters so much: it is not a formality but a legal licence to test. Recap. Every test is a standardized sample of behaviour that is only trustworthy if it is reliable (consistent: test–retest, split-half, Cronbach's alpha, inter-rater) and valid (accurate: content, criterion [concurrent/predictive], construct) – reliability being necessary but not sufficient for validity. Raw scores mean nothing until placed against norms and expressed as derived scores (percentile, z, T, stanine, deviation IQ), with the SEM giving the error band; and the score's kind is fixed by its level of measurement (nominal → ordinal → interval → ratio, with IQ being interval). Intelligence testing runs Binet & Simon → Terman's Stanford–Binet (ratio IQ) → Wechsler (deviation IQ) → Raven (culture-fair) , theorised by Charles Spearman, Thurstone, Howard Gardner, Robert Sternberg, and Raymond Cattell, and Indianised by Bhatia, Malin (MISIC), Binet–Kamat, Seguin, and Pathak's Draw-A-Man . Personality splits into objective (MMPI, 16PF, NEO-PI, EPQ) and projective (Rorschach, TAT with Chowdhury's Indian cards, Sentence Completion, Draw-A-Person); neuropsychology adds Bender-Gestalt, Luria–Nebraska, and the Indian PGI Battery; and severity is tracked with Beck (self-report) versus Hamilton (clinician-rated) scales, Y-BOCS, and the MMSE. All of it is bound by ethics – consent, competence, security, fairness – and, in India, by RCI regulation of who may test at all. 5.10 Test Construction and Item Analysis A psychological test does not appear ready-made. It is engineered, piece by piece, through a disciplined sequence of steps that turn a fuzzy idea (“let us measure test anxiety”) into a finished instrument with a fixed set of items, a scoring key, and evidence that it works. This subsection opens the workshop and looks at how items are actually written, tried out, and kept or discarded. The stages of building a test Test construction is usually described as an ordered pipeline. Each stage feeds the next, and a weak early stage cannot be rescued by a strong later one. Define the construct and purpose. State exactly what the test measures (for example, mathematical reasoning) and what decisions it will inform (selection, diagnosis, research). Write a test blueprint (test specification). A plan, often laid out as a table, that fixes how many items will cover each content area and each level of thinking, so the finished test samples the domain in the intended proportions. Write the item pool. Produce far more items than the final test needs, because many will be discarded during analysis. Expert and sensitivity review. Subject-matter experts judge whether each item is accurate and on-target; a bias or sensitivity panel checks that items are fair across groups and free of offensive or culturally loaded content. Pilot testing (try-out). Administer the draft items to a sample resembling the intended test takers, purely to gather data on how the items behave. Item analysis. Compute statistics for every item and use them to keep, revise, or drop items. Assemble the final form, then standardize. Select surviving items following the blueprint, then collect norms and reliability and validity evidence on a fresh sample. Key. Item analysis is the quality-control stage. It is done on pilot data, before the final form is fixed, and its whole job is to identify which items earn a place in the finished test. Writing and reviewing items Good items follow craft rules: one idea per item, plain unambiguous language, no unintended clues, distractors (the wrong options in a multiple-choice item) that are plausible to someone who does not know the answer, and no “all of the above” crutches. After drafting, items pass through expert review for content accuracy and through a sensitivity review for fairness before any statistics are gathered. Item difficulty index (p) The item difficulty index , written p , is simply the proportion of test takers who answer an item correctly. If 70 of 100 examinees get an item right, p = 0.70. Note the counter-intuitive naming: a high p means an easy item, and a low p means a hard item. For most purposes items around p = 0.50 are prized because they spread people out most; very easy (p near 1.0) and very hard (p near 0.0) items separate almost nobody. Trap. Do not read the difficulty index as “how difficult.” A large p value marks an EASY item, not a hard one. High p, easy; low p, hard. Item discrimination index (D) The item discrimination index , written D , asks a different question: does this item separate the people who did well on the whole test from those who did poorly? A common method compares an upper group (say the top 27 percent of total scores) with a lower group (the bottom 27 percent). D is the proportion correct in the upper group minus the proportion correct in the lower group. D ranges from −1 to +1. A high positive D means the strong examinees pass it and the weak ones fail it, which is exactly what a good item should do. A D near zero means the item does not distinguish, and a negative D is a warning sign: weaker examinees are passing an item that stronger ones miss, often signalling a mis-keyed or misleading item. Index What it answers Formula in words Good value Difficulty (p) How many got it right? Proportion correct Around 0.50 (spreads people) Discrimination (D) Does it separate strong from weak? Upper-group p minus lower-group p High positive (0.30 or above) Item-total correlation Does it agree with the whole test? Correlation of item with total score Positive and sizeable Trap. Difficulty and discrimination are different things. An item can be easy yet still discriminate, or moderate in difficulty yet discriminate poorly. Never treat p and D as the same number. Item-total correlation The item-total correlation is the correlation between how examinees score on a single item and their total score on the test. It is a continuous cousin of the discrimination index and is often reported as the point-biserial correlation for right-or-wrong items. A positive, healthy item-total correlation means the item pulls in the same direction as the test as a whole, which supports internal consistency. Items with near-zero or negative item-total correlations are candidates for removal. Distractor analysis For multiple-choice items, distractor analysis inspects each wrong option separately. A good distractor is chosen by some lower-group examinees but by few upper-group examinees. A distractor that nobody picks is dead weight and could be replaced; a distractor that the upper group picks more than the lower group may be misleading or the key may be wrong. Example: if the top scorers keep choosing option (c) while (b) is keyed correct, the writer re-examines whether (c) is defensibly also correct. Item response theory: a plain-language introduction Item response theory (IRT) is a modern framework that models the relationship between a person’s underlying ability (called theta ) and the probability of answering a particular item correctly. The classical indices above (p and D) depend on the sample used, whereas IRT tries to describe item properties in a way that is more independent of the particular group tested. The centrepiece is the item characteristic curve (ICC) , an S-shaped (ogive) curve. The horizontal axis is ability; the vertical axis is the probability of a correct response. As ability rises, the probability of getting the item right climbs from low to high. Two features of the curve carry meaning: the point along the ability axis where the curve is steepest reflects the item’s difficulty (harder items sit further to the right), and the steepness of the curve reflects the item’s discrimination (steeper curves separate ability levels more sharply). More elaborate IRT models also add a guessing parameter, the small floor probability that a low-ability examinee gets a multiple-choice item right by chance. Why. IRT underlies computer-adaptive testing, where the computer picks the next item to match the ability estimate it has formed so far, delivering a precise score with fewer items than a fixed-length paper test. The test blueprint (revisited) and cross-validation The test blueprint deserves a second mention because it governs which surviving items are chosen for the final form. It is a two-way table crossing content areas with cognitive levels, with a target number of items in each cell, ensuring the finished test represents the domain in the right proportions rather than over-sampling whatever was easiest to write. Finally, statistics computed on the very sample used to build a test tend to look flatteringly good because the selection has capitalized on chance features of that sample. Cross-validation checks the test on a fresh, independent sample. The usual finding is shrinkage : the validity coefficient drops when the test meets new data, because the sample-specific luck does not repeat. A test that holds up under cross-validation, with little shrinkage, is trustworthy; one whose numbers collapse was partly an illusion of the original sample. Key. Always cross-validate. Expect some shrinkage. A validity that survives a new sample is real; one that vanishes was overfitting to the build sample. 5.11 Projective Techniques in Depth The projective hypothesis The projective hypothesis is the founding idea behind an entire family of tests: when a person is shown an ambiguous, unstructured stimulus and asked to make sense of it, the structure they impose comes from within, revealing their own needs, conflicts, feelings, and ways of organizing experience. Because the stimulus is vague, there is no obviously correct answer, so the person “projects” personal material onto it. Projective techniques deliberately hide their purpose, which makes them harder to fake than a straightforward questionnaire. Who → what. The distinction between objective and projective techniques, and the very term projective methods , was popularized by Lawrence Frank in 1939. The Rorschach Inkblot Test The Rorschach Inkblot Test presents ten cards, each bearing a symmetrical inkblot, some black-and-grey, some with colour. The examinee says what each blot might be, and the examiner records the response along with where on the blot it was seen (location), what features prompted it (determinants such as form, colour, movement, shading), and how conventional the content is. Scoring rests on these codes rather than on the storyline alone. Who → what. The Rorschach was created by Hermann Rorschach , a Swiss psychiatrist, published in 1921 in his work Psychodiagnostik . Because rival scoring systems multiplied over the decades, John Exner integrated the best-supported elements into the Exner Comprehensive System , which became the most widely taught scoring approach and gave the instrument far more standardization than it previously had. The Thematic Apperception Test The Thematic Apperception Test (TAT) uses cards showing people in ambiguous situations. The examinee tells a story for each: what led up to the scene, what is happening, what the characters are thinking and feeling, and how it turns out. The stories are read for recurring needs (the drives of the hero) and press (the forces of the environment), following the personality theory of its author. Who → what. The TAT was developed at Harvard by Henry Murray and Christiana Morgan in the 1930s, tied to Murray’s theory of needs. The Children’s Apperception Test Who → what. The Children’s Apperception Test (CAT) was created by Leopold Bellak (with Sonya Sorel Bellak). Its cards show animals in human-like situations, on the assumption that young children relate more readily to animal figures. Figure-drawing techniques Figure-drawing tests ask the examinee to draw, then interpret features of the drawing as expressions of personality or, sometimes, developmental maturity. They are quick, need only paper and pencil, and are popular with children. Who → what. The Draw-A-Person test as a projective personality measure is associated with Karen Machover . (An earlier drawing test by Florence Goodenough used the human figure as an intelligence measure, a different purpose.) Who → what. The House-Tree-Person test (HTP) , in which the examinee draws a house, a tree, and a person, was devised by John Buck . The Rosenzweig Picture-Frustration Study Who → what. The Rosenzweig Picture-Frustration Study (P-F Study) , created by Saul Rosenzweig , presents cartoon scenes in which one figure frustrates another; the examinee supplies the frustrated figure’s reply, which is scored for the direction of aggression (turned outward, inward, or avoided). Sentence completion and word association Sentence Completion Tests give the examinee incomplete stems (for example, “My greatest fear ...”) to finish in their own words; the completions are read for attitudes and conflicts. A well-known version is the Rotter Incomplete Sentences Blank by Julian Rotter . These sit at the more structured, easier-to-score end of the projective family. Who → what. The word-association method , in which the examinee replies with the first word each stimulus word brings to mind and reaction time and unusual replies are noted, was developed as a clinical tool by Carl Jung , who used it to detect emotionally charged “complexes.” Projective test Author(s) Stimulus / task Chiefly taps Rorschach Inkblot Test Hermann Rorschach Ten inkblots to interpret Perception, thought organization Thematic Apperception Test Henry Murray & Christiana Morgan Tell a story to picture cards Needs, motives, conflicts Children’s Apperception Test Leopold Bellak Stories to animal-scene cards Children’s conflicts, relationships Draw-A-Person Karen Machover Draw a human figure Body image, personality signs House-Tree-Person John Buck Draw house, tree, person Self, environment, relationships Picture-Frustration Study Saul Rosenzweig Reply for a frustrated figure Direction of aggression Rotter Incomplete Sentences Blank Julian Rotter Finish sentence stems Attitudes, adjustment Word Association Carl Jung First word to a stimulus word Emotional complexes Strengths and criticisms Strengths: projective techniques are hard to fake, can bypass a person’s defences, open rich clinical material, and let the examinee respond freely rather than choose from fixed options. Criticisms: their scoring is often subjective, so inter-scorer and retest reliability tend to be low ; validity evidence is uneven; interpretation leans heavily on the examiner’s skill; administration and scoring are time-consuming; and the stimuli and norms can be culturally loaded , so a response deemed unusual in one culture may be ordinary in another. Trap. Objective versus projective is about item structure and scoring , not about honesty. Objective tests (like the MMPI) have fixed response options and mechanical scoring; projective tests use ambiguous stimuli and interpretive scoring. “Objective” does not mean “more truthful,” only more standardized in format. 5.12 Aptitude, Interest, Achievement and Neuropsychological Batteries Aptitude tests An aptitude test measures the potential to acquire a skill or succeed in some future training or job, that is, what a person could learn given the chance. This is the forward-looking cousin of the achievement test. Who → what. The Differential Aptitude Tests (DAT) , by George Bennett, Harold Seashore, and Alexander Wesman , yield separate scores for several aptitudes (verbal reasoning, numerical ability, abstract reasoning, mechanical reasoning, space relations, and more) and are widely used for educational and vocational guidance. Who → what. The General Aptitude Test Battery (GATB) was developed by the United States Employment Service for occupational counselling and selection, measuring a spread of aptitudes (such as general learning, verbal, numerical, spatial, and psychomotor abilities) in one battery. Interest inventories An interest inventory does not measure ability at all; it measures preferences , what a person likes and dislikes, and matches those patterns to occupations. It is a staple of career counselling. Who → what. The Strong Interest Inventory , originating with Edward Strong , compares a person’s likes to those typical of people happily employed in various occupations. Who → what. The Kuder Preference Record , by Frederic Kuder , groups interests into broad areas (such as outdoor, mechanical, scientific, artistic, literary, social service, and clerical) and reports the relative strength of each. Achievement tests An achievement test measures what a person has already learned , the present level of knowledge or skill in a defined content area, typically after instruction. A school examination is the everyday example; standardized achievement batteries do the same with norms. Trap. Aptitude versus achievement is a matter of time direction, not test format. Achievement looks backward at what has been learned; aptitude looks forward at capacity to learn. The very same arithmetic item can serve either purpose depending on whether it is used to certify past learning or to predict future performance. Neuropsychological batteries A neuropsychological battery is a set of tests used to detect and describe cognitive impairment linked to brain dysfunction, mapping strengths and deficits across attention, memory, language, visuospatial skill, and executive function. Who → what. The Halstead-Reitan Neuropsychological Battery , built by Ward Halstead and extended by Ralph Reitan , is a fixed battery of tests (such as the Category Test and the Tactual Performance Test) used to detect and localize brain damage. Who → what. The Luria-Nebraska Neuropsychological Battery , developed by Charles Golden and colleagues from the clinical procedures of Alexander Luria , is a standardized battery organized around Luria’s qualitative approach to brain function. Who → what. The Bender Visual-Motor Gestalt Test , by Lauretta Bender , asks the examinee to copy a set of geometric designs; distortions in the reproductions are read as signs of visuo-motor and perceptual difficulty, and it is used as a screen for neurological and developmental problems. In the Indian context, two instruments matter especially. The PGI Memory Scale , developed at the Postgraduate Institute of Medical Education and Research, Chandigarh (associated with Dwarka Prasad and Nandini Wig), is an Indian-standardized battery assessing several facets of memory. The NIMHANS neuropsychological battery , developed at the National Institute of Mental Health and Neurosciences, Bengaluru, is the widely used Indian-standardized battery that provides norms suited to the Indian population across attention, executive function, memory, and related domains. Why. Norms built abroad can mislabel a healthy Indian examinee as impaired because of language, schooling, and cultural differences. Indian-standardized tools like the PGI Memory Scale and the NIMHANS battery exist precisely to give a fair local yardstick. Trap. The Bender-Gestalt is a visuo-motor and screening test, not a full neuropsychological battery on its own, and not a projective personality test, although it is sometimes borrowed for emotional-indicator interpretation. Keep its primary purpose (visuo-motor screening) clear. Recap. Tests are built through a pipeline (construct, blueprint, item pool, review, pilot, item analysis, standardization). Item analysis keeps good items using difficulty (p, proportion correct, high means easy), discrimination (D, upper minus lower group), item-total correlation, and distractor analysis; item response theory models ability against the probability of a correct answer via the item characteristic curve; cross-validation guards against shrinkage. Projective techniques rest on the projective hypothesis: Rorschach (Hermann Rorschach, scored via the Exner Comprehensive System), TAT (Henry Murray and Christiana Morgan), CAT (Leopold Bellak), Draw-A-Person (Karen Machover), House-Tree-Person (John Buck), the Rosenzweig Picture-Frustration Study, sentence completion (Julian Rotter), and word association (Carl Jung), all rich but weak on reliability and culturally loaded. Aptitude measures future potential (DAT; GATB), achievement measures past learning, interest inventories measure preferences (Strong; Kuder), and neuropsychological batteries (Halstead-Reitan, Luria-Nebraska, Bender-Gestalt, plus the Indian PGI Memory Scale and NIMHANS battery) map brain-related cognition. 5.13 The complete map: every major test and its author This is the safety-net roster: the major psychological tests, scales, and batteries an aptitude paper may name, each tied to its author and a one-line note on what it measures. Learn the pairing (test, author, what it measures) and most "who devised this test" items answer themselves. Indian tests and adaptations are grouped last because entrance papers love them. Key. Read every row as three linked facts: the test , its author(s) , and the construct it measures . Full names are given first so you recognise the person however the question phrases it. It is sometimes called "the talking cure," a phrase that goes back to one of Sigmund Freud's early patients. Counselling is a close cousin: it also uses a helping relationship, but tends to focus on specific problems, decisions and adjustment rather than deep personality change. This whole section builds each major approach from the ground up, always naming who developed what, because "match the therapy to its founder" is a favourite question type in this paper. 6.1 What psychotherapy is, and what all therapies share There are hundreds of named therapies, yet research repeatedly shows they work partly through the same underlying ingredients. These shared ingredients are called the common factors . Saul Rosenzweig first argued in 1936 that different therapies succeed for reasons they hold in common, and he jokingly used the Dodo bird from Alice in Wonderland ("Everybody has won, and all must have prizes") to name the finding that most bona fide therapies produce roughly similar outcomes. This is called the Dodo bird verdict . The therapeutic alliance (working alliance). The bond of trust between client and therapist, plus their agreement on the goals and tasks of therapy. Edward Bordin described its three parts as bond, goals and tasks . The alliance is one of the strongest predictors of good outcome, regardless of the school of therapy. An emotionally charged, confiding relationship with a helping person. A healing setting that raises the client's expectation of being helped. A rationale or "myth" – a believable explanation of the problem. A ritual or procedure that both parties believe in and carry out. Hope, catharsis (emotional release) and new learning. Key. Common factors (especially the therapeutic alliance) explain a large share of why therapy works. The specific techniques matter too, but no technique works well without the relationship carrying it. Therapies also differ on two practical dimensions you should be able to name: Directive vs non-directive. A directive therapist actively guides, teaches, assigns homework and challenges thoughts (behaviour therapy, Aaron Beck's and Albert Ellis's cognitive work). A non-directive therapist mainly follows the client, reflecting and clarifying rather than steering (Carl Rogers's person-centred therapy is the classic example). Individual vs group. Individual therapy is one client with one therapist. Group therapy treats several clients together, adding unique healing forces such as universality and peer feedback (see Irvin Yalom below). Related formats include couples and family therapy. Why. Examiners love the directive/non-directive split because it cleanly separates the humanistic camp (non-directive) from the behavioural and cognitive camps (directive). Anchor Carl Rogers at the non-directive pole and you can place everyone else relative to him. 6.2 Psychodynamic therapy: Sigmund Freud and after Who → what. Sigmund Freud developed psychoanalysis , the first formal system of psychotherapy, in Vienna around the 1890s–1900s. Freud held that much of mental life is unconscious and that current symptoms grow from unresolved childhood conflicts, especially around sexual and aggressive urges. The aim of psychoanalysis is to make the unconscious conscious, so that buried conflict can be understood and worked through. The mind, in his structural model , has three parts: Id – the primitive, unconscious reservoir of drives, ruled by the pleasure principle (wants satisfaction now). Ego – the reality-based executive that mediates between id, superego and the outer world, ruled by the reality principle . Superego – the internalised moral conscience and ideals, largely from the parents. Core techniques of psychoanalysis: Free association. The client says whatever comes to mind, without censoring, so hidden material surfaces. Dream analysis. Freud called dreams "the royal road to the unconscious." The remembered dream ( manifest content ) is interpreted for its disguised meaning ( latent content ). Transference. The client unconsciously transfers feelings about important early figures (often parents) onto the therapist. Analysing it is central to the cure. Resistance. Anything that blocks the work – falling silent, missing sessions, changing the subject – signals a defended conflict worth exploring. Interpretation. The analyst offers tentative explanations that link present feelings to unconscious past conflict, timed for when the client can accept them. Working through. Repeatedly re-examining the same conflict across many situations until insight becomes lasting change. Defense mechanisms are the ego's unconscious strategies for keeping anxiety-provoking material out of awareness. Freud named them and his daughter Anna Freud catalogued them systematically: Repression – pushing threatening thoughts out of consciousness (the master defense). Denial – refusing to accept an external reality. Projection – attributing one's own unacceptable impulses to someone else. Displacement – redirecting an impulse onto a safer target (shouting at the dog after a bad day at work) . Sublimation – channelling an impulse into a socially valued activity (the healthiest defense). Reaction formation – turning an impulse into its opposite. Rationalisation – inventing acceptable reasons for unacceptable behaviour. Regression – retreating to an earlier, more childish stage. Intellectualisation – dealing with a threat through abstract thought, stripped of feeling. The neo-Freudians kept the idea of the unconscious but broke from Freud's heavy emphasis on sexuality: Who → what. Carl Jung founded analytical psychology , adding the collective unconscious and its archetypes , plus the ideas of introversion/extraversion and individuation. Who → what. Alfred Adler founded individual psychology , stressing the inferiority complex , striving for superiority, birth order and social interest. Who → what. Melanie Klein pioneered object relations and child play therapy, focusing on the infant's inner world of internalised "objects" (people). Later object-relations and attachment thinkers include Donald Winnicott and John Bowlby. Trap. Do not confuse the founders. Sigmund Freud = psychoanalysis; Carl Jung = analytical psychology; Alfred Adler = individual psychology. "Individual psychology" is Adler's label and has nothing to do with individual (one-to-one) therapy format. 6.3 Behaviour therapy Behaviour therapy applies learning theory to change behaviour directly, holding that maladaptive behaviour is learned and can therefore be unlearned. It is present-focused, directive and measurable. It has two engines: classical conditioning (Ivan Pavlov) and operant conditioning (B. F. Skinner). Who → what. Mary Cover Jones is called the "mother of behaviour therapy." Working with the boy "Peter," she reduced a child's fear of a rabbit by gradually pairing the feared object with pleasant eating – an early demonstration of counter-conditioning that inspired later desensitization. Classical-conditioning based methods: Who → what. Joseph Wolpe developed systematic desensitization , built on reciprocal inhibition (you cannot be relaxed and anxious at the same time). Teach deep relaxation (often progressive muscle relaxation). Build an anxiety hierarchy , ranking feared situations from mild to terrifying. While relaxed, the client imagines each step, moving up the ladder only when the lower step no longer triggers anxiety. Relaxation replaces fear at every rung. Exposure therapy. Facing the feared stimulus (in imagination, in vivo , or via virtual reality) until anxiety fades through habituation and extinction . Flooding. Intense, prolonged exposure to the most feared situation at full strength (no gentle ladder), continued until the fear burns out. Aversion therapy. Pairing an unwanted behaviour (drinking, smoking) with an unpleasant stimulus so the behaviour loses its appeal (a drug that causes nausea with alcohol) . Operant-conditioning based methods rest on B.F. Skinner's principle that behaviour is shaped by its consequences (reinforcement increases behaviour, punishment decreases it): Who → what. B.F. Skinner established operant conditioning , the basis for token economies (Teodoro Ayllon and Nathan Azrin, 1968), shaping and contingency management. Token economy. Desired behaviours earn tokens that are later exchanged for rewards; widely used on wards and in classrooms. Shaping. Reinforcing successive approximations that get closer and closer to a target behaviour. Contingency management. Systematically arranging rewards and consequences so they follow (are contingent on) specific behaviours; a contingency contract writes this down. Why. Classical-conditioning methods change reflexive, emotional responses like fear; operant methods change voluntary behaviour through its consequences. Sort any technique by asking: is it treating an automatic fear (classical) or a chosen action being rewarded/punished (operant)? 6.4 Cognitive therapy and CBT Cognitive approaches say it is not events themselves but our interpretations of events that drive our feelings. Change the thinking and the emotion changes. Two founders dominate. Who → what. Aaron Beck developed cognitive therapy , originally for depression, later expanded into Cognitive Behaviour Therapy (CBT). Beck argued that depressed people are trapped in the cognitive triad : negative views of the self , the world , and the future . These are fed by automatic thoughts (quick, involuntary negative appraisals) and sustained by cognitive distortions , systematic errors in thinking such as: All-or-nothing (black-and-white) thinking. Overgeneralisation – one setback means "always." Catastrophising – expecting the worst. Mental filter – focusing only on the negative. Personalisation – blaming oneself for things outside one's control. "Should" statements and mind-reading . Beck's therapist uses Socratic questioning (guided discovery through gentle questions), collaborative empiricism (client and therapist test beliefs together like scientists), thought records and behavioural experiments to examine and revise these thoughts. Who → what. Albert Ellis developed Rational Emotive Behaviour Therapy (REBT) , built on the ABC model . A – Activating event. Something happens. B – Belief. An irrational belief about the event ("I must be approved by everyone") . C – Consequence. The emotional and behavioural result. Ellis added D – Disputing the irrational belief and E – the new Effect . His signature target is "musturbation" – rigid demands phrased as musts and shoulds. His style is far more forceful and confrontational than Beck's gentle questioning. Trap. Aaron Beck vs Albert Ellis is a classic exam contrast. Both are cognitive and both use the idea that beliefs cause distress, but: Aaron Beck uses gentle Socratic questioning / collaborative empiricism and speaks of automatic thoughts and the cognitive triad (therapy: cognitive therapy / CBT). Albert Ellis is directive and confrontational , uses the ABC(DE) model and attacks irrational beliefs / "musts" (therapy: REBT). Remember Ellis came first (1950s) and Beck a little later (1960s). 6.5 Humanistic and existential therapies These approaches reject both the determinism of psychoanalysis and the mechanism of behaviourism (John B. Watson, 1913). They see people as basically good, free and driven toward growth. The therapist's job is to create conditions for that growth rather than to fix or condition the client. Who → what. Carl Rogers developed person-centred (client-centred) therapy , the model non-directive humanistic therapy. Rogers believed every person has an actualizing tendency , an inbuilt drive to grow toward their full potential, which unfolds when the relationship offers three core conditions : Unconditional positive regard – warm, non-judgemental acceptance of the client as a person. Empathy – accurately sensing and reflecting the client's inner world. Congruence (genuineness) – the therapist is real and transparent, not hiding behind a professional mask. Key. Rogers's three core conditions – unconditional positive regard, empathy, congruence – are among the most tested facts in this whole topic. Memorise all three by name. Who → what. Fritz Perls (with Laura Perls) developed Gestalt therapy , focused on the here-and-now and taking responsibility for present experience. Gestalt therapy aims for awareness of what one is feeling and doing right now, completing "unfinished business." Its best-known technique is the empty chair , where the client speaks to an imagined person (or part of the self) seated in an empty chair, then switches seats to reply. Who → what. Victor Frankl developed logotherapy , the "third Viennese school," centred on the will to meaning – the idea that finding meaning, even in suffering, is the primary human drive. Frankl drew on his own survival in Nazi concentration camps. Existential therapy (associated with Rollo May and, in the group/existential blend, Irvin Yalom) confronts the "givens" of existence – death, freedom, isolation and meaninglessness – and helps the client live authentically in the face of them. Logotherapy is one existential branch. 6.6 Third-wave and newer approaches The "third wave" of behaviour therapy keeps CBT's rigor but adds acceptance, mindfulness and values rather than only trying to change thoughts. Who → what. Marsha Linehan developed Dialectical Behaviour Therapy (DBT) , first for chronically suicidal clients and borderline personality disorder. It balances (the "dialectic" of) acceptance and change , and teaches four skill modules: mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation and interpersonal effectiveness . Who → what. Steven Hayes developed Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) , which teaches psychological flexibility : accept inner experiences, defuse from thoughts, and commit to action guided by personal values . Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy (MBCT). Developed by Zindel Segal, Mark Williams and John Teasdale to prevent relapse in recurrent depression; it blends CBT with the mindfulness training of Jon Kabat-Zinn's MBSR. Who → what. William Miller and Stephen Rollnick developed Motivational Interviewing (MI) , a collaborative, client-centred style for strengthening a person's own motivation to change, especially in addictions. It works with ambivalence and "rolls with resistance" rather than arguing. Who → what. James Prochaska and Carlo DiClemente developed the Transtheoretical Model / Stages of Change , often paired with Motivational Interviewing. Precontemplation – not yet considering change. Contemplation – weighing it up. Preparation – getting ready to act. Action – actively changing. Maintenance – sustaining the change (with possible relapse and recycling). 6.7 Family and group therapy Systemic and family therapies treat the family as the unit , not the individual. The idea is that a symptom in one member (the "identified patient") often expresses a problem in the whole family system. Who → what. Salvador Minuchin developed structural family therapy , mapping the family's structure – its subsystems, boundaries (too rigid or too enmeshed ) and hierarchies – and actively restructuring them. Who → what. Murray Bowen developed Bowenian (intergenerational) family systems therapy , with key ideas of differentiation of self , triangulation , and the multigenerational transmission of patterns (mapped on a genogram ). Who → what. Irvin Yalom is the key name for group therapy , cataloguing the therapeutic factors that make groups heal. Yalom's therapeutic factors include universality ("I am not the only one"), instillation of hope , imparting information , altruism (helping others helps you), group cohesiveness , interpersonal learning , catharsis , and the corrective recapitulation of the primary family group (the group re-plays and repairs old family dynamics). Trap. Match the family-therapy founders precisely: Salvador Minuchin = structural (boundaries, enmeshment); Bowen = intergenerational (differentiation, triangles, genogram). For group work, the name to give is Irvin Yalom and his therapeutic factors (universality is the most-quoted one). 6.8 The counselling process, and counselling vs psychotherapy Counselling typically unfolds in identifiable stages . A common way to remember them: Rapport / relationship building. Establish trust, warmth and the working alliance. Assessment / exploration. Understand the problem, history and context; clarify what the client wants. Goal-setting. Agree clear, realistic goals together. Intervention / working phase. Apply the chosen techniques and support change. Termination and follow-up. Consolidate gains, prepare for ending, and plan for maintenance and relapse prevention. Effective counselling rests on micro-skills (systematised by Allen Ivey and echoing Carl Rogers). Learn these named skills: Attending – posture, eye contact and presence (often taught with the SOLER acronym). Active listening. Open and closed questions. Reflection of feeling – naming the emotion the client expresses. Paraphrasing – restating content in your own words. Summarising. Clarifying, confronting (gently), and silence. How counselling differs from psychotherapy. The two overlap heavily and use many of the same skills, but examiners expect you to state the classic distinctions: Dimension Counselling Psychotherapy Focus Specific problems, decisions, adjustment, "here and now" Deeper, long-standing personality and emotional patterns Depth More surface / present-oriented More depth, often exploring the past Duration Usually shorter Often longer Typical clients Broadly well people facing situational stress May include more serious or entrenched disorders Settings Schools, careers, workplaces, community Clinics, hospitals, private practice Key. Say the distinction as a spectrum, not a wall: counselling leans toward specific, shorter, present-focused help for adjustment; psychotherapy leans toward deeper, longer work on entrenched patterns. In practice the same professional may do both. 6.9 Master summary table: therapy → founder → core technique → best-suited-for Therapy Founder Core technique / idea Best suited for Psychoanalysis Sigmund Freud Free association, dream analysis, transference, interpretation Deep-seated unconscious conflict, personality issues Analytical psychology Carl Jung Collective unconscious, archetypes, individuation Meaning, mid-life and identity concerns Individual psychology Alfred Adler Inferiority complex, social interest, lifestyle analysis Self-esteem, family and social functioning Systematic desensitization Joseph Wolpe Relaxation + anxiety hierarchy (reciprocal inhibition) Phobias, specific anxieties Operant methods (token economy, shaping) B.F. If you can attach each technique to its founder and say who it best helps, this section is exam-ready. 6.10 Cognitive and behavioural techniques in depth The earlier subsections introduced cognitive therapy and behaviour therapy as broad families. This subsection goes inside them, to the actual techniques a therapist uses in the room. Two names dominate the cognitive side: Aaron Temkin Beck , an American psychiatrist who built Cognitive Therapy, and Albert Ellis , an American clinical psychologist who built Rational Emotive Behaviour Therapy. On the behavioural side the central name is Joseph Wolpe , a South African psychiatrist who created systematic desensitization. Learn to tell these approaches apart, because entrance papers love to swap them. Aaron Beck's cognitive model Who → what. Aaron Temkin Beck (1921–2021) developed Cognitive Therapy in the 1960s, originally for depression. He proposed that emotional disorders are maintained not by events themselves but by the biased thoughts a person has about those events. Beck's model rests on three linked ideas. First, the cognitive triad : in depression a person holds negative views of the self ("I am worthless"), the world or current experience ("everything is against me"), and the future ("nothing will ever improve"). These three negative streams feed one another. Second, automatic thoughts : rapid, involuntary appraisals that pop into the mind without deliberate reasoning. They feel true and go unquestioned, which is exactly why they are powerful. Third, deeper schemas or core beliefs : stable underlying assumptions ("I am unlovable") laid down early in life that generate the automatic thoughts. Beck catalogued recurring errors of reasoning, called cognitive distortions . A working list every candidate should recognise: All-or-nothing thinking (also called black-and-white or dichotomous thinking): seeing things in only two categories, with no middle ground. "If I am not perfect I am a total failure." Overgeneralization : treating one negative event as a never-ending pattern. "I failed this test, so I fail at everything." Catastrophizing (magnification): expecting the worst possible outcome and treating it as certain. "If I stumble in the interview my whole career is over." Personalization : taking responsibility for events that were not one's fault. "My friend is quiet today; it must be because of me." Mental filter (selective abstraction): focusing on a single negative detail while ignoring the whole picture. Dwelling on one critical remark inside a page of praise. Mind reading and fortune telling : assuming you know others' thoughts, or predicting the future negatively, without evidence. Emotional reasoning : treating a feeling as proof of fact. "I feel guilty, so I must have done something wrong." "Should" statements : rigid rules about how oneself and others must behave, producing guilt or anger when broken. Labelling : attaching a fixed global label to oneself. "I am a loser," rather than "I made a mistake." Beck's therapy trains the client to catch automatic thoughts, test them against evidence, and generate more balanced alternatives, often recorded on a thought record (a worksheet with columns for the situation, the emotion, the automatic thought, evidence for and against, and a balanced response). Albert Ellis and Rational Emotive Behaviour Therapy Who → what. Albert Ellis (1913–2007) founded Rational Emotive Therapy in 1955, later renamed Rational Emotive Behaviour Therapy (REBT) . It is usually considered the earliest form of cognitive behaviour therapy, predating Beck's clinical work. Ellis's central tool is the ABC framework : A – Activating event : the situation that seems to trigger distress. B – Belief : the thought or, more precisely, the irrational belief the person holds about the event. C – Consequence : the emotional and behavioural result. Ellis's key claim is that A does not cause C. Instead B causes C . The same event (failing an exam) produces despair in one person and mild disappointment in another, because their beliefs differ. Ellis argued that distress flows from rigid, absolute demands he summed up as "musts" (which he playfully called musturbation ): "I must succeed," "others must treat me well," "the world must be fair." From these grow secondary irrational beliefs such as awfulizing ("it is awful and unbearable"), low frustration tolerance , and global self-rating ("I am worthless"). To ABC he added D and E . D – Disputing : actively challenging the irrational belief. The therapist asks whether the belief is logical, whether there is evidence for it, and whether it is helpful. E – Effective new belief (and new emotion): a flexible preference ("I would strongly prefer to succeed, but I can stand it if I do not") replacing the rigid demand. REBT disputing is comparatively direct and confrontational, in keeping with Ellis's style. Trap. Beck vs Albert Ellis. Beck → Cognitive Therapy , cognitive triad, automatic thoughts and distortions, a gentle collaborative-empirical style using guided discovery. Ellis → REBT , the ABC(DE) model, irrational "must" beliefs, a more direct disputing style. Both attack thinking, but the labels and vocabulary are distinct. Do not credit the ABC model to Beck or the cognitive triad to Ellis. Socratic questioning and guided discovery Socratic questioning is the signature conversational method of Beckian cognitive therapy. Rather than telling the client that a thought is wrong, the therapist asks a series of open questions that lead the client to examine the thought and reach a new conclusion themselves: "What is the evidence for that? Is there another way to see this? What would you say to a friend who thought this?" This process of leading someone to their own insight through questioning is called guided discovery . It is collaborative, not lecturing, and it builds the client's own reasoning skill. Behavioural experiments A behavioural experiment is a planned real-world test of a belief. If a socially anxious client believes "if I speak up people will laugh at me," the therapist and client design a small experiment (asking a question in a group) and observe what actually happens. Experience, not argument, updates the belief. Behavioural experiments bridge the cognitive and behavioural halves of CBT: the thought is cognitive, but the test is behavioural. The behaviour-therapy toolkit Who → what. Joseph Wolpe (1915–1997) developed systematic desensitization in the 1950s, applying reciprocal inhibition to human fears. It is the classic behavioural treatment for phobias. Reciprocal inhibition is the principle that two opposing responses cannot occur strongly at the same time: a person cannot be deeply relaxed and intensely anxious simultaneously. Wolpe used relaxation to inhibit anxiety. Systematic desensitization combines three steps: Train the client in deep relaxation (usually progressive muscle relaxation). Build an exposure hierarchy (also called an anxiety or fear hierarchy): a ranked ladder of feared situations from least to most frightening, each rated on a subjective scale. Pair relaxation with the feared images or situations, starting at the bottom of the ladder and climbing only when each step is comfortable, so relaxation replaces anxiety at every rung. Because desensitization is graded (gradual) and paired with relaxation, it is gentle. Contrast this with the intense exposure methods: Flooding : exposing the client directly to the most feared real situation at full intensity, with no gradual ladder, until anxiety naturally subsides through extinction and habituation . There is no relaxation pairing. Implosion (implosive therapy): like flooding but conducted in imagination rather than real life, often with vividly exaggerated feared scenes. Trap. Systematic desensitization vs flooding. Desensitization → gradual , uses a hierarchy, pairs exposure with relaxation (reciprocal inhibition), starts at the easy end. Flooding → maximum intensity at once , no hierarchy, no relaxation, relies on habituation. Implosion is flooding done in imagination . The remaining tools rest on operant conditioning (consequences shape behaviour) or classical conditioning (associations shape responses): Aversion therapy : pairing an unwanted behaviour with an unpleasant stimulus so the behaviour becomes distasteful. A drug that induces nausea when alcohol is drunk. This uses classical conditioning to attach a negative response. Token economy : a structured programme, common on inpatient wards, in which desired behaviours earn tokens (secondary reinforcers) that can later be exchanged for privileges or goods. It is an application of operant reinforcement, associated with Burrhus Frederic Skinner 's principles and developed clinically by Teodoro Ayllon and Nathan Azrin. Contingency management : arranging clear consequences (rewards, or loss of rewards) so they follow specific behaviours, making the link between action and outcome explicit. A token economy is one form of it. Relaxation training : teaching bodily calm, most often through progressive muscle relaxation (tensing and releasing muscle groups in sequence), described by Edmund Jacobson , plus controlled breathing. It underpins desensitization and is a treatment for anxiety in its own right. Key. Cognitive techniques change thoughts (distortions, irrational beliefs) through questioning and testing. Behavioural techniques change behaviour through conditioning (exposure, reinforcement, association). CBT deliberately uses both, because thoughts and actions maintain each other. 6.11 Specialised and process-focused approaches Beyond the main schools sit several targeted methods and, cutting across every therapy, a set of process constructs that describe what actually happens in the relationship. Both are heavily examined. Motivational interviewing Who → what. William Richard Miller and Stephen Rollnick developed Motivational Interviewing (MI) , first for addictions. It is a collaborative, client-centred style for strengthening a person's own motivation to change. MI assumes that lecturing a reluctant person increases resistance. Instead the therapist works with the client's ambivalence (the coexisting wish to change and wish to stay the same), guiding them to voice their own reasons for change, called change talk . Its spirit is often summarised as partnership, acceptance, compassion, and evocation (drawing motivation out of the client rather than imposing it). A well-known principle is rolling with resistance rather than arguing against it. Crisis intervention Crisis intervention is brief, immediate, active help for a person overwhelmed by an acute crisis (a suicidal state, disaster, sudden loss). Its goals are short-term: ensure safety, reduce immediate distress, mobilise coping and support, and restore the person to at least their pre-crisis level of functioning. It is time-limited and problem-focused, not deep personality change. Grief and bereavement work Grief counselling helps a person mourn a loss and adapt to life without the person or thing lost. Elisabeth Kübler-Ross described commonly cited stages of dying and grief (denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance), though these are now understood as possible reactions rather than a fixed sequence everyone must pass through. Modern approaches also speak of the tasks of mourning (accepting the reality of the loss, working through the pain, adjusting, and finding an enduring connection while moving on), associated with J. William Worden. A key clinical distinction is between normal grief and complicated or prolonged grief that does not ease over time. Dialectical Behaviour Therapy in depth Who → what. Marsha M. Linehan developed Dialectical Behaviour Therapy (DBT) , originally for chronically suicidal clients and borderline personality disorder. Its "dialectic" is the balance between acceptance of the client as they are and the push for change . Standard DBT combines individual therapy with a skills group teaching four skill modules : Mindfulness : observing and describing present experience without judgement; the core skill underlying the others. Distress tolerance : surviving crises without making them worse (self-soothing, distraction, radical acceptance). Emotion regulation : understanding, reducing vulnerability to, and changing painful emotions. Interpersonal effectiveness : asking for what one needs and saying no while keeping relationships and self-respect. DBT is usually classed as a "third-wave" cognitive behavioural therapy because of its heavy use of mindfulness and acceptance. Eye-Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing Who → what. Francine Shapiro developed Eye-Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing (EMDR) in the late 1980s, primarily for trauma and post-traumatic stress disorder. In EMDR the client holds a distressing memory in mind while following a repeated bilateral stimulation (typically the therapist's finger moving side to side, producing back-and-forth eye movements, or alternating taps or tones). Over sets, the memory is meant to lose its intensity and be reprocessed into a less disturbing, more adaptive form. EMDR is a recognised trauma treatment; note that its distinctive ingredient is the bilateral eye-movement component paired with structured recall. Interpersonal Psychotherapy Interpersonal Psychotherapy (IPT) , developed by Gerald Klerman and Myrna Weissman , is a brief, structured, evidence-based treatment for depression. It links mood symptoms to current relationship problems and focuses on a small number of problem areas: grief (complicated bereavement), role disputes (conflict with a significant person), role transitions (a major life change such as divorce or retirement), and interpersonal deficits (loneliness and difficulty forming relationships). It works on the present social world, not childhood. Technique / approach Originator What it does Cognitive Therapy (triad, automatic thoughts) Aaron Temkin Beck Identifies and tests distorted thoughts through guided discovery REBT (ABC model, disputing) Albert Ellis Disputes rigid irrational "must" beliefs that cause distress Systematic desensitization Joseph Wolpe Graded exposure paired with relaxation (reciprocal inhibition) Progressive muscle relaxation Edmund Jacobson Tense-and-release calming used within many therapies Motivational Interviewing William R. Miller & Stephen Rollnick Evokes the client's own change talk, rolls with resistance Dialectical Behaviour Therapy Marsha M. Linehan Balances acceptance and change; four skill modules EMDR Francine Shapiro Bilateral eye movements plus recall to reprocess trauma Interpersonal Psychotherapy Gerald Klerman & Myrna Weissman Treats depression through current relationship problems Process constructs that cut across all therapies Whatever the school, certain relationship processes appear in every therapy, and questions often test the definitions. Therapeutic alliance (working alliance): the collaborative bond between client and therapist, made of an emotional bond plus agreement on the goals and tasks of therapy. Its strength is one of the most reliable predictors of good outcome, described in this three-part form by Edward Bordin . Transference : the client unconsciously redirects feelings from important past figures (often a parent) onto the therapist . A concept from Sigmund Freud 's psychoanalysis. Countertransference : the therapist's own emotional reactions to the client, whether stirred up by the client or arising from the therapist's own history. It must be recognised so it does not distort the work. Resistance : anything in the client that works against the progress of therapy (missing sessions, changing the subject, falling silent). Psychodynamic therapy treats resistance as meaningful material to be understood, not merely an obstacle. Cultural competence : the therapist's awareness of, respect for, and skill in working across the client's culture, language, values, and identity, so that therapy fits the client rather than imposing the therapist's assumptions. Ethical boundaries and confidentiality : keeping the relationship professional (no exploitation, no dual relationships), and protecting the privacy of what the client discloses. Confidentiality has recognised limits: risk of serious harm to self or others, abuse of a child, or a legal order can require disclosure. Beyond these limits, privacy is a foundation of trust. Trap. Transference vs countertransference. Transference → the client's feelings displaced onto the therapist. Countertransference → the therapist's feelings toward the client. Match the direction to the correct person. The common-factors view Who → what. Saul Rosenzweig in 1936 argued that different therapies work about equally well and that their shared ingredients matter more than their unique techniques. He borrowed the Dodo Bird 's line from Alice in Wonderland : "Everybody has won, and all must have prizes," giving the idea its nickname, the Dodo Bird Verdict . Decades later Bruce E. Wampold gathered the modern evidence for this position in his "contextual model," arguing that factors common to all effective therapies (a strong alliance, the therapist's empathy and belief in the treatment, a shared rationale that makes sense to the client, and the client's own expectation of change) account for much of therapy's benefit, alongside specific techniques. The common-factors view does not say technique is worthless; it says the relationship and shared ingredients carry a great deal of the weight. Recap. Beck built Cognitive Therapy (cognitive triad, automatic thoughts, distortions, guided discovery via Socratic questioning); Ellis built REBT (the ABC, then D disputing and E, targeting irrational "must" beliefs). Wolpe's systematic desensitization pairs a graded exposure hierarchy with relaxation through reciprocal inhibition, unlike full-intensity flooding or imaginal implosion; the behavioural toolkit also holds aversion therapy, token economies, contingency management, and relaxation training. Specialised methods include Miller and Rollnick's motivational interviewing, crisis intervention, grief work, Linehan's DBT with its four skill modules, Shapiro's EMDR, and Klerman and Weissman's interpersonal psychotherapy. Cutting across all of them are the alliance, transference and countertransference, resistance, cultural competence, ethical boundaries and confidentiality, and the common-factors "Dodo Bird" view from Rosenzweig to Wampold. 6.12 The complete map: every therapy and its founder This is the safety net for the therapy question you did not see coming. An aptitude paper can name any approach and ask only for its founder or its one central idea. Read this roster from top to bottom once, then again by family, until every name binds to a single line you can recall on sight. Key. "Core idea" is the one clause an examiner would accept as the essence, not the whole theory.
