Likewise, Carl Rogers is person-centred (not Fritz Perls, who is Gestalt), and Viktor Frankl is logotherapy (not Irvin Yalom, who is existential). Solution-focused therapy is de Shazer and Berg together; narrative therapy is White and Epston together, so never pair the wrong two names. Recap. Thirty-eight approaches sit in six families: psychodynamic (Freud, Jung, Adler and the object-relations line), humanistic and existential (Rogers, Perls, Frankl, Yalom), behavioural and cognitive (Wolpe, Skinner, Beck, Ellis), third-wave mindfulness (Linehan, Hayes, Kabat-Zinn), systemic and brief (Bowen, Minuchin, Satir, Berne, Glasser), and a cluster of standalone methods (Shapiro's EMDR, Axline's play, Moreno's psychodrama). Bind each name to its one line and any founder question is a gift. 7 Statistics & Research Methodology Clinical psychology is an empirical science. Every claim it makes – that a therapy works, that a scale measures anxiety, that two symptoms co-occur – rests on data. Statistics is the toolkit for turning messy numbers into defensible conclusions, and research methodology is the discipline of designing studies so those numbers mean what we think they mean. This section builds both from zero, then flags the traps that entrance papers love. 7.1 Why psychology needs statistics Human behaviour is variable: no two people, and no one person on two days, respond identically. Because of this variability we can never study everyone we care about, and we can never read a result off a single case with certainty. Statistics does two jobs. Descriptive statistics summarize the data we actually collected (averages, spread, shape). Inferential statistics let us reason from a small studied group to the larger group we care about, while honestly quantifying how uncertain that leap is. Why. Without statistics a therapist could not tell whether clients improved because of the treatment or just by chance (regression to the mean, natural recovery, placebo). Statistics is how psychology separates real effects from noise. Population vs sample; parameter vs statistic A population is the entire set of people (or observations) we want to draw conclusions about, for example "all adults with generalized anxiety disorder in India". A sample is the subset we actually measure. A numerical fact about a population is a parameter (usually unknown, written with Greek letters: the population mean is mu, the population standard deviation is sigma). The matching numerical fact computed from a sample is a statistic (the sample mean is x-bar, the sample standard deviation is s). Inferential statistics is essentially using statistics to estimate parameters. Key. Parameter → population (mu, sigma, rho). Statistic → sample (x-bar, s, r). We compute statistics because parameters are almost always unknowable in full. Types of variables A variable is any characteristic that can take different values. How we may analyse a variable depends first on its scale of measurement , a scheme owed to the psychophysicist Stanley Smith Stevens. Scale What it does Legal operations Example Nominal Names / categories only, no order = or not-equal; count frequencies, mode Diagnosis, gender, blood group Ordinal Ordered categories, unequal/unknown gaps Rank; median, percentiles Likert agreement, socioeconomic class, tumour stage Interval Equal intervals, arbitrary zero (zero not "none") Add / subtract; mean, standard deviation Temperature in Celsius, IQ score, calendar year Ratio Equal intervals, true zero (zero means none) All, including ratios / multiplication Reaction time, weight, number of errors Trap. A true zero means "you can say twice as much". 40 kg is twice 20 kg (ratio), but 40 °C is NOT twice as hot as 20 °C because 0 °C is arbitrary (interval). IQ and most psychological test scores are treated as interval, not ratio: an IQ of 0 does not mean "no intelligence", so "twice as intelligent" is meaningless. By role in a study : the independent variable (IV) is the presumed cause, the one the experimenter manipulates or selects (therapy type). The dependent variable (DV) is the presumed effect, the outcome measured (symptom score). A confounding variable is a third variable that rides along with the IV and offers a rival explanation for changes in the DV (if the therapy group is also younger, age confounds the result). By values a variable can take : a discrete variable takes separated, usually countable values (number of panic attacks); a continuous variable can take any value within a range, limited only by measurement precision (reaction time, height). Who → what. Stanley Smith Stevens → the nominal / ordinal / interval / ratio taxonomy of measurement scales (1946), the backbone of choosing a statistical test. 7.2 Descriptive statistics: centre and spread Two questions describe almost any batch of scores: where is the middle, and how spread out are they? Measures of central tendency Mean (arithmetic average): add all scores, divide by the number of scores. Uses every value, so it is the most informative for symmetric data, but it is pulled toward extreme scores . Median : the middle value when scores are ordered (average of the two middle values if the count is even). It ignores the size of extreme scores, so it is robust to outliers and skew . Mode : the most frequent value. The only centre usable for nominal data; a distribution can have two modes (bimodal) or none unique. Situation Best centre Reason Symmetric, interval/ratio, no outliers Mean Uses all information, feeds later tests Skewed data or outliers (income, reaction time) Median Not dragged by the tail Nominal / categorical data Mode Only "average" that is meaningful for categories Effect of skew. In a symmetric distribution mean = median = mode. In a positively (right) skewed distribution (a long tail of high scores), the order is mode < median < mean: the mean is dragged rightward by the tail. In a negatively (left) skewed distribution the order reverses: mean < median < mode. A useful memory hook is that the mean chases the tail. Measures of dispersion Range : highest minus lowest score. Trivial to compute but decided entirely by the two most extreme scores, so it is unstable. Interquartile range (IQR) : the spread of the middle 50% of the data (third quartile minus first quartile, Q3 – Q1). Robust to outliers; it is the "box" in a box plot and the natural partner of the median. Variance : the mean of the squared deviations from the mean. Squaring removes the sign so deviations do not cancel, but it leaves the units squared (points-squared), which is hard to interpret. Standard deviation (SD) : the square root of the variance, so it returns to the original units. It is the single most used index of spread: roughly, the typical distance of a score from the mean. Why. We square deviations rather than just averaging them because raw deviations from the mean always sum to zero (the positives and negatives cancel exactly). Squaring, then taking the root at the end, gives a spread measure in the original units. Trap. Mean vs median under skew. Report the median , not the mean, for skewed variables such as income, hospital length-of-stay, or reaction time. Newspapers quoting "average income" as the mean overstate the typical person because a few very high earners inflate the mean; the median (the person in the middle) is the honest "typical" value. Same logic in clinical data: one client with a 900-day illness duration can make the "average" duration meaningless. 7.3 The normal distribution The normal (Gaussian) distribution is the bell-shaped curve that approximates many natural and psychological variables (height, IQ, measurement error). Its properties: Symmetric about the mean; mean, median, and mode coincide at the centre. Bell-shaped and asymptotic: the tails approach the horizontal axis but never touch it, so extreme scores are rare but never strictly impossible. Fully defined by just two parameters: the mean (location) and the standard deviation (width). Total area under the curve equals 1 (100% of cases). The 68–95–99.7 rule (the empirical rule) In any normal distribution, about 68% of scores fall within 1 SD of the mean, about 95% within 2 SD (more precisely 1.96 SD), and about 99.7% within 3 SD. On an IQ test with mean 100 and SD 15, roughly 95% of people score between 70 and 130, and a score above 145 is beyond 3 SD, seen in well under 1% of people. z-scores and standardization A z-score restates a raw score as the number of standard deviations it lies above or below the mean: z = (score – mean) / standard deviation. Converting a whole distribution to z-scores is standardization ; the result is the standard normal distribution , which has mean 0 and SD 1. Standardizing lets us compare scores from different scales (a z of +1.5 on a depression scale and +1.5 on an anxiety scale are equally extreme) and lets us look up the exact proportion of the curve beyond any point. Key. A z-score is a location on the curve, not a probability. Its sign gives direction (above / below the mean) and its magnitude gives how unusual the score is. z = 0 is exactly average; |z| > 2 is unusual (top / bottom ~2.5% each tail). Skewness and kurtosis Skewness measures asymmetry: positive skew has a long right tail, negative skew a long left tail, zero skew is symmetric. Kurtosis measures tail-heaviness / peakedness: a leptokurtic curve is tall and thin with heavy tails (more extreme scores than normal), a platykurtic curve is flat with thin tails, and a mesokurtic curve matches the normal. These shape indices tell us whether it is safe to assume normality before running parametric tests. Other distributions in brief The binomial distribution models the number of successes in a fixed number of yes/no trials (correct vs incorrect items). The Poisson distribution models counts of rare events in a fixed interval (relapses per year). The t distribution is bell-shaped but with fatter tails than the normal and is used for small samples; as sample size grows it converges to the normal. The chi-square and F distributions are skewed and underlie tests of frequencies and of variances, respectively. 7.4 Correlation Correlation quantifies how strongly two variables move together, on a scale from –1 through 0 to +1. The sign gives direction : positive means they rise together, negative means one rises as the other falls. The magnitude gives strength : 0 means no linear relationship, and ±1 means a perfect straight-line relationship. A scatterplot (each case a dot with its two scores as coordinates) is the first thing to inspect: it shows direction, strength, linearity, and outliers at a glance. Karl Pearson's product-moment correlation (r) Pearson's r measures the strength of the linear association between two interval or ratio variables that are roughly normally distributed. Rough interpretation of magnitude (after Jacob Cohen's conventions): about 0.1 is small / weak, about 0.3 is medium / moderate, about 0.5 and above is large / strong. Squaring it gives the coefficient of determination (r-squared), the proportion of variance in one variable explained by the other; r = 0.4 means only 16% shared variance. Who → what. Karl Pearson → the product-moment correlation coefficient r, the standard index of linear association for continuous data. Charles Spearman's rank-order correlation (rho) Spearman's rho is the correlation computed on the ranks of the scores rather than the raw values. Use it when the data are ordinal , when the relationship is monotonic but not straight-line, or when outliers or non-normality make Pearson's r untrustworthy. Because it works on ranks, it is a non-parametric cousin of Pearson's r. Who → what. Charles Spearman → rank-order correlation (rho) for ordinal / non-normal data (and, separately, the two-factor theory of intelligence, the "g" factor). Trap. Correlation is not causation. A strong r tells you two variables travel together, not that one causes the other. Three rival explanations always remain: reverse causation (B causes A), a lurking third variable causing both (ice-cream sales and drownings both rise with summer heat), and pure coincidence. Only a controlled experiment can establish causation. Also beware: r near 0 rules out a linear relationship only; a strong U-shaped (curvilinear) relationship can have r near 0. 7.5 Inferential logic: from sample to population Inference is the reasoned leap from the sample we measured to the population we care about. The machinery has a few core ideas. Sampling distribution and standard error Imagine drawing many samples of the same size and computing the mean of each. Those means themselves form a distribution, the sampling distribution of the mean . The Central Limit Theorem states that, as sample size grows, this sampling distribution becomes approximately normal regardless of the shape of the original population, which is why so many tests can assume normality. The standard deviation of that sampling distribution is the standard error (SE) : it measures how much a sample mean typically bounces around the true population mean. Crucially, SE shrinks as sample size grows (SE = SD divided by the square root of n), which is the mathematical reason larger studies give more precise estimates. Null and alternative hypotheses We frame a testable question as two rival statements. The null hypothesis (H0) says there is no effect / no difference / no relationship (the therapy does nothing; the two group means are equal). The alternative hypothesis (H1) says there is an effect. Significance testing is a proof-by-contradiction: we assume H0 is true and ask how surprising our data would be under that assumption. Alpha, the p-value, and confidence intervals The significance level (alpha) is the threshold of surprise we set in advance for rejecting H0, conventionally 0.05 (5%). It is the risk of a false alarm we are willing to tolerate. The p-value is the probability of obtaining data at least as extreme as ours if H0 were true . If p is less than alpha, we reject H0 and call the result "statistically significant". A confidence interval (CI) is a range of plausible values for the parameter. A 95% CI means that if we repeated the study endlessly, about 95% of such intervals would contain the true value. A 95% CI for a difference that excludes 0 corresponds to a significant result at alpha 0.05. Trap. The p-value is NOT the probability that H0 is true, and it is NOT the probability the result was due to chance. It is the probability of the data given H0. A result can be statistically significant (small p) yet trivially small in real-world terms if the sample is huge, which is exactly why we also report effect size . Conversely, "p > 0.05" means "failed to reject H0", NOT "H0 is proven true": absence of evidence is not evidence of absence. Type I and Type II error H0 is really TRUE H0 is really FALSE We reject H0 Type I error (false positive), probability = alpha Correct: true detection (power = 1 – beta) We keep H0 Correct: true negative (1 – alpha) Type II error (false negative), probability = beta A Type I error is a false alarm: claiming an effect that is not real (convicting an innocent H0). A Type II error is a miss: failing to detect an effect that is real. Lowering alpha to guard against Type I error raises the risk of Type II error, so the two trade off. In drug trials a Type I error approves a useless drug; a Type II error shelves a working one. Statistical power and effect size Statistical power is the probability of correctly rejecting a false H0, that is, of detecting a real effect (power = 1 – beta). Convention aims for power of at least 0.80. Power rises with a larger sample, a larger true effect, a higher alpha, and lower measurement noise. Effect size is a scale-free measure of how big an effect actually is, independent of sample size. Jacob Cohen formalized this; Cohen's d expresses the difference between two means in standard-deviation units, with rough benchmarks of 0.2 (small), 0.5 (medium), and 0.8 (large). Correlation r is itself an effect size, and eta-squared serves the same role for ANOVA. Who → what. Jacob Cohen → effect size and power analysis in psychology; Cohen's d, and the small / medium / large conventions that let us judge practical (not just statistical) importance. Key. Significance answers "is there likely an effect?"; effect size answers "how big is it?"; power answers "was my study large enough to find it?". A complete result reports all three, plus a confidence interval. 7.6 Common statistical tests Choosing a test depends on the number and type of variables, the number of groups, and whether the groups are independent or the same people measured repeatedly. Test When to use What it compares z-test One mean vs a known value, population SD known, large n Sample mean against a population mean One-sample t-test One mean vs a known value, population SD unknown Sample mean against a fixed benchmark Independent-samples t-test Two separate groups, one continuous DV Two group means (therapy vs control) Paired-samples t-test Same people twice, or matched pairs Two means within the same subjects (pre vs post) One-way ANOVA Three or more groups, one continuous DV Several means simultaneously (via the F ratio) Post-hoc test (Tukey, Bonferroni, Scheffe) After a significant ANOVA Which specific pairs of means differ Chi-square goodness of fit One categorical variable Observed vs expected frequencies Chi-square test of independence Two categorical variables Whether two categories are associated The t-test family (William Gosset) The t-test compares means when the population standard deviation is unknown and the sample is small; it uses the fatter-tailed t distribution to stay honest under that extra uncertainty. Its three forms are the one-sample (one mean vs a fixed value), the independent-samples (two unrelated groups), and the paired-samples (two measurements on the same or matched subjects). Who → what. William Gosset (Student) → the t distribution and t-test, developed while doing quality control at the Guinness brewery; he published under the pen name "Student" because his employer forbade staff from publishing. Analysis of variance (Ronald Fisher) ANOVA extends the logic of the t-test to three or more groups in one test, avoiding the inflated Type I error you would get from running many t-tests. It works by partitioning total variability into between-groups variance (differences among group means) and within-groups variance (noise inside each group); the F ratio is between-groups over within-groups. A large F says the group means differ by more than chance noise predicts. A significant ANOVA says "at least one group differs" but not which, so a post-hoc test (Tukey's HSD, Bonferroni, Scheffe) then pinpoints the specific pairs. Who → what. Ronald Fisher → analysis of variance (ANOVA), the F distribution, the null-hypothesis testing framework, and the principle of randomization in experimental design. Chi-square The chi-square test works on frequencies / counts of categorical data. Goodness of fit checks whether one variable's observed frequencies match an expected pattern (are diagnoses evenly distributed across seasons?). The test of independence checks whether two categorical variables are associated (is treatment response related to gender?). Both compare observed counts to the counts expected if H0 were true. Parametric vs non-parametric Parametric tests (z, t, ANOVA, Pearson's r) assume the data are interval/ratio, roughly normally distributed, and (for group comparisons) have similar variances (homogeneity of variance) and independent observations. When those assumptions fail – ordinal data, small samples, heavy skew, outliers – we switch to non-parametric tests, which work on ranks or counts and assume much less. Parametric test Non-parametric equivalent Design Independent-samples t-test Mann-Whitney U Two independent groups Paired-samples t-test Wilcoxon signed-rank Two related measures One-way ANOVA Kruskal-Wallis Three or more independent groups Pearson's r Spearman's rho Association of two variables Key. Parametric tests are more powerful when their assumptions hold; non-parametric tests are the safe fallback when data are ordinal, badly skewed, or small. Match the test to the scale of measurement and the design (independent vs related groups) first. 7.7 Research methodology: the scientific method and designs The scientific method and steps of research Identify the problem and review existing literature. Formulate a clear, testable hypothesis and define concepts operationally (state exactly how each variable will be measured). Choose a research design and sampling method. Collect data using reliable, valid instruments. Analyse the data with appropriate statistics. Interpret results, draw conclusions, and relate them back to the hypothesis and theory. Report and disseminate; replication and peer review test the finding's durability. Why. An operational definition (for example, "depression = score above 13 on the Beck Depression Inventory") is what makes a study repeatable and testable. Without it, two researchers studying "depression" might measure completely different things. Research designs True experiment : the researcher manipulates the IV and uses random assignment to conditions. This is the only design that supports strong causal claims, because randomization equalizes confounders across groups on average. Quasi-experiment (Donald Campbell and Julian Stanley, 1963): has an IV manipulation or group comparison but lacks random assignment (comparing existing intact groups such as two schools). Causal inference is weaker because groups may differ at the start. Correlational : measures variables as they naturally occur and assesses association without manipulation. Good for prediction and for variables that cannot ethically be manipulated, but cannot establish cause. Case study : intensive, in-depth study of a single person, group, or event. Rich and hypothesis-generating (Sigmund Freud's cases, patient H.M.), but not generalizable and open to observer bias. Survey : self-report from a sample via questionnaire or interview; efficient for attitudes and prevalence, but vulnerable to response biases (social desirability, acquiescence). Observational : watching and recording behaviour, either naturalistic (in the field, no interference) or controlled (in a set-up like a lab playroom); high realism but limited control. Longitudinal : the same people followed over time (tracks true within-person change and development, but slow and prone to participant drop-out / attrition). Cross-sectional : different age or cohort groups compared at one time point (fast and cheap, but age differences can be confounded with cohort / generation effects). Internal vs external validity Internal validity is the degree to which we can be sure the IV, and not something else, caused the change in the DV. External validity is the degree to which the findings generalize beyond the study to other people, settings, and times. The two often trade off: tight laboratory control boosts internal validity but the artificial setting can hurt external validity. Common threats to internal validity include history (an outside event during the study), maturation (natural change over time), testing (practice effects from being measured before), instrumentation (the measuring tool drifting), regression to the mean (extreme scorers drifting toward average on retest), selection (pre-existing group differences), and attrition / mortality (non-random drop-out). Threats to external validity include unrepresentative samples (over-reliance on WEIRD or undergraduate samples) and artificial settings. Control techniques Randomization (random assignment): allocating participants to conditions by chance so that confounders are spread evenly across groups; the single most powerful control. Blinding : keeping participants ( single-blind ), or both participants and the researchers who interact with them ( double-blind ), unaware of condition, to block placebo and experimenter-expectancy effects. Counterbalancing : in within-subjects designs, varying the order of conditions across participants so that practice and fatigue (order effects) do not systematically favour one condition. Standardization : giving every participant the same instructions, environment, and procedure to hold extraneous variables constant. 7.8 Sampling How we pick the sample decides whether it fairly represents the population. Methods split into two families. Probability sampling (every member has a known, non-zero chance of selection; supports generalization and error estimation): Simple random sampling : every individual has an equal chance (names from a hat, random number generator). The gold standard for representativeness. Systematic sampling : pick every k-th person from a list after a random start. Easy, but risky if the list has a hidden periodic pattern. Stratified sampling : divide the population into meaningful subgroups (strata) such as age or gender, then sample randomly within each, guaranteeing each stratum is represented in proportion. Cluster sampling : divide the population into naturally occurring clusters (schools, clinics), randomly select whole clusters, and study everyone (or a sample) inside. Cheaper for geographically spread populations, but less precise. Non-probability sampling (selection chances unknown; convenient but hard to generalize from): Convenience sampling : whoever is easiest to reach (psychology undergraduates). Fast but biased. Purposive (judgmental) sampling : the researcher hand-picks cases fitting a criterion (experts, a specific diagnosis). Snowball sampling : existing participants recruit others they know; used for hidden or hard-to-reach populations (people who use illicit drugs). Quota sampling : fill preset quotas for subgroups (50 men, 50 women) but choose within each non-randomly. Trap. Do not confuse the two errors. Sampling error is the ordinary, random gap between a sample statistic and the true parameter simply because a sample is not the whole population; it shrinks as sample size grows. Sampling bias is a systematic tilt from a flawed selection method (a convenience sample, or non-response); it does NOT shrink with a larger sample – a bigger biased sample is just a bigger biased sample. Only better sampling design, not more people, fixes bias. 7.9 Reliability, validity, qualitative methods, and ethics Reliability and validity of research and measures Reliability is consistency: does the measure give the same result under the same conditions? Its forms are test-retest (stable across time), inter-rater (different observers agree), internal consistency (items hang together, indexed by Cronbach's alpha), and parallel-forms (two versions agree). Validity is accuracy: does the measure actually assess what it claims? Its forms include content validity (items cover the whole construct), criterion validity (correlates with an external benchmark, split into concurrent and predictive ), and construct validity (fits the theoretical network, with convergent and discriminant evidence). Key. A measure can be reliable without being valid, but not valid without being reliable. A miscalibrated scale that always reads 5 kg heavy is perfectly reliable (consistent) yet invalid (wrong). Reliability is necessary but not sufficient for validity. Qualitative methods in brief Where quantitative research counts and measures, qualitative research seeks meaning in words and experience. Thematic analysis (Virginia Braun and Victoria Clarke, 2006) codes textual data and groups the codes into recurring themes. Grounded theory (Barney Glaser and Anselm Strauss, 1967) builds a theory upward from the data through iterative coding, letting categories emerge rather than testing a pre-set hypothesis. Phenomenology aims to describe the essence of participants' lived experience of a phenomenon from their own point of view. These methods prize depth, context, and the participant's voice over generalizable numbers. Research ethics Informed consent : participants agree to take part after being told the study's purpose, procedures, risks, and their right to withdraw at any time without penalty. Special provisions cover minors and those unable to consent. Confidentiality and anonymity : personal data are protected, and identities are kept private or removed from records. Protection from harm : physical and psychological risk is minimized and justified by the study's value. Debriefing : after participation (especially if deception was used and justified), participants are fully informed of the true purpose and any deception is explained. Institutional review : an Institutional Review Board (IRB) or ethics committee must approve the study before data collection, weighing risks against benefits. Professional guidelines : the American Psychological Association (APA) Ethics Code (and in India the Rehabilitation Council of India norms) set standards for integrity, avoiding harm, and honest reporting of results. Trap. Deception is permitted only when a study cannot be done otherwise, the risk is low, and it is followed by a full debrief; it never overrides the duty to protect participants. Consent obtained by hiding real risks is not informed consent. And confidentiality has limits: a clinician-researcher who learns of imminent danger to self or others may have a duty to breach it. Recap. Statistics turns variable behaviour into defensible conclusions. Describe data with the right centre (mean for symmetric, median for skewed, mode for categories) and spread (SD, IQR). The normal curve plus z-scores let us locate and compare scores (68–95–99.7). Correlation (Karl Pearson's r for continuous, Charles Spearman's rho for ranks) measures association but never proves causation. Inference rests on sampling distributions and the standard error; we test a null hypothesis against an alpha, read a p-value and confidence interval, and weigh Type I against Type II error, always reporting effect size (Jacob Cohen's d) and power alongside significance. Pick the test by scale and design: William Gosset's t-tests for one or two means, Ronald Fisher's ANOVA for three or more, chi-square for frequencies, and non-parametric equivalents when assumptions fail. Sound methodology (true experiments with randomization, blinding, and counterbalancing), representative probability sampling, reliable and valid measures, and firm ethics (informed consent, confidentiality, debriefing, IRB approval) are what make the numbers trustworthy in the first place. 7.10 Comparing groups and modelling relationships Once a psychologist has collected data and summarised it, the central task is usually to ask a comparative or predictive question. Do two groups differ? Does one variable predict another? The family of procedures below answers such questions. Each one produces a test statistic (a single number computed from the data) which is then converted into a probability so the researcher can decide whether an observed difference is likely to be real or merely the product of sampling noise. The t-tests A t-test compares means when the sample is small and the population standard deviation is unknown. The test was devised by William Sealy Gosset , a chemist and statistician working at the Guinness brewery in Dublin, who published under the pen name "Student" in 1908 because his employer forbade staff from publishing. For this reason the distribution he derived is still called Student's t-distribution . There are three common forms. One-sample t-test. Compares the mean of one sample against a known or hypothesised population value. A clinic's mean depression score is compared against the published national average of 10. Independent-samples t-test. Compares the means of two separate, unrelated groups. Mean anxiety scores of a therapy group versus a waitlist group. Paired-samples (dependent) t-test. Compares two scores from the same people (or matched pairs), such as before and after an intervention. Each client's stress score at week 1 versus the same client's score at week 8. Who → what. William Sealy Gosset ("Student") → the t-test and t-distribution, born of quality control at a brewery, for making inferences from small samples. Analysis of variance (ANOVA) When there are more than two groups, running many t-tests inflates the chance of a false positive. Analysis of variance , developed by Sir Ronald Aylmer Fisher in the 1920s while working on agricultural experiments at Rothamsted, solves this by comparing all group means in a single test. ANOVA works by partitioning the total variability in the data into between-groups variance (differences among the group means) and within-groups variance (random variability inside each group). Their ratio is the F-ratio , named by later authors in Fisher's honour. A large F means the group means differ more than would be expected from chance alone. One-way ANOVA. One independent variable (factor) with three or more levels. Comparing three drug doses on reaction time. Factorial ANOVA. Two or more factors examined at once (for example a 2×2 design). It yields a main effect for each factor plus one or more interaction effects . Repeated-measures ANOVA. The same participants are measured under every condition or at several time points, the many-condition extension of the paired t-test. It removes stable individual differences, increasing sensitivity. Analysis of covariance (ANCOVA). An ANOVA that first statistically removes the influence of a continuous nuisance variable, the covariate . Comparing therapies for depression while adjusting for each client's baseline severity. MANOVA. Multivariate analysis of variance handles two or more dependent variables simultaneously in one analysis. Key. An interaction effect means the effect of one factor depends on the level of another . A drug may help young patients but not older ones. The effect of "drug" changes across the levels of "age", so drug and age interact. When an interaction is present, main effects must be interpreted cautiously. Post-hoc tests A significant ANOVA tells the researcher that at least one group differs, but not which ones. Post-hoc ("after this") tests then compare pairs of groups while controlling the overall false-positive rate. The most widely taught is Tukey's Honestly Significant Difference (HSD) , devised by John Wilder Tukey . Others include the Bonferroni correction (which divides the alpha level by the number of comparisons) and the Scheffe test. Linear regression Where correlation only measures the strength of a relationship, regression uses one or more variables to predict another. In simple linear regression a single predictor (independent variable) forecasts an outcome (dependent variable) through the equation of a straight line, conventionally written Y = a + bX, where a is the intercept (the predicted value of Y when X is zero) and b is the slope (how much Y changes for each one-unit rise in X). Multiple linear regression extends this with several predictors, each with its own slope, so the model becomes Y = a + b1X1 + b2X2 + and so on. The coefficient of determination, R-squared , states the proportion of variance in the outcome explained by the predictors: an R-squared of 0.40 means the model accounts for 40 per cent of the variability in Y. Trap. Correlation and regression are related but not identical. Correlation is symmetric and unitless: it merely describes how strongly two variables move together, with no direction of prediction. Regression is directional: it names one variable the predictor and one the outcome and produces an equation to estimate actual values. Reporting a regression slope as if it proved causation is a further, separate error. The chi-square test All the tests above need at least one continuous, roughly normal variable. When the data are frequencies of categories (counts, not measurements) the appropriate procedure is the chi-square (χ-squared) test , developed by Karl Pearson . It compares the counts actually observed against the counts expected under a hypothesis. There are two common uses. Goodness-of-fit. Tests whether one categorical variable follows an expected distribution. Are the four blood types present in the sample in the proportions the population predicts? Test of independence. Tests whether two categorical variables are associated. Is diagnosis (depression / anxiety / neither) independent of gender? Non-parametric tests Parametric tests assume the data are measured on an interval or ratio scale and are drawn from a roughly normal population. When these assumptions fail (small samples, ordinal data such as ranks, or badly skewed distributions), non-parametric alternatives are used. They work on ranks rather than raw scores and therefore make fewer assumptions about the shape of the distribution. Question Parametric test Non-parametric counterpart Two independent groups Independent-samples t-test Mann-Whitney U test Two related scores (before / after) Paired-samples t-test Wilcoxon signed-rank test Three or more independent groups One-way ANOVA Kruskal-Wallis test Three or more related conditions Repeated-measures ANOVA Friedman test Association between two variables Pearson's r Spearman's rank-order correlation (rho) Spearman's rank-order correlation , developed by the psychologist Charles Edward Spearman (also famous for the "g" factor of general intelligence), is simply Pearson's correlation computed on ranks; it captures any consistent monotonic relationship, even a curved one, and resists outliers. Trap. Non-parametric does not mean "no assumptions" or "always safer". These tests have less statistical power than their parametric cousins when the parametric assumptions actually hold, so defaulting to them needlessly can hide a real effect. Choose them because the assumptions are violated, not out of caution alone. 7.11 Decision errors, power and effect size Every significance test is a decision made under uncertainty, and any decision can be wrong. This subsection sets out the logic of that decision and the tools that describe how good it is. The two hypotheses Inference begins with two rival statements. The null hypothesis (H-nought) states that there is no effect, no difference, or no relationship in the population. The alternative hypothesis (H-one) states that there is one. The test never proves the null; it only decides whether there is enough evidence to reject it. If the evidence is weak, the researcher fails to reject the null, which is not the same as proving it true. The two error types Reality Test rejects H-nought Test keeps H-nought No true effect exists Type I error (alpha): false alarm Correct decision A true effect exists Correct decision (power) Type II error (beta): miss A Type I error is rejecting a true null: declaring an effect that is not really there. Its probability is alpha , conventionally set at 0.05. A Type II error is failing to reject a false null: missing an effect that is genuinely present. Its probability is beta . Trap. Students routinely swap the two. A memory aid: a Type I error is like convicting an I nnocent person (a false positive); a Type II error is letting a guilty one go free (a false negative). Lowering alpha to avoid false positives tends to raise beta, so the two errors trade off against each other. Statistical power Power is the probability of correctly detecting a real effect, defined as 1 minus beta. A study with power of 0.80 has an 80 per cent chance of finding an effect that truly exists. Power rises with a larger sample size, a bigger true effect, a larger alpha, and lower measurement error. Under-powered studies are a major cause of failed replications because they miss real effects and, when they do reach significance, tend to over-estimate the effect's size. Effect size A p-value tells you whether an effect is likely to be real, but not how large or important it is. With a huge sample, a trivial difference can be "statistically significant". Effect size measures the magnitude of an effect independently of sample size. Cohen's d. Devised by Jacob Cohen , it expresses the difference between two means in standard-deviation units. Rough conventions: 0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large. Pearson's r. As an effect size it indexes the strength of a relationship, from 0 to 1 in absolute value. Eta-squared (η-squared). Used with ANOVA, it gives the proportion of variance in the outcome explained by a factor, similar in spirit to R-squared. Confidence intervals A confidence interval is a range of plausible values for a population parameter, computed from the sample. A 95 per cent confidence interval means that if the study were repeated endlessly, about 95 per cent of such intervals would contain the true value. A narrow interval signals a precise estimate; a wide one signals uncertainty. If a 95 per cent interval for a difference excludes zero, the result is significant at the 0.05 level, so intervals and tests carry consistent information while the interval also shows magnitude and precision. The meaning of a p-value Key. A p-value is the probability of obtaining data at least as extreme as those observed if the null hypothesis were true . It is NOT the probability that the null is true, NOT the probability the result happened "by chance", and NOT a measure of effect size. A small p (for example less than 0.05) means the data would be surprising under the null, so the null is rejected. One-tailed versus two-tailed, degrees of freedom, and assumptions A two-tailed test checks for a difference in either direction and is the default. A one-tailed test checks only one direction and is justified only when a directional prediction is made in advance; it has more power in that direction but is blind to an effect the other way. Degrees of freedom are the number of values in a calculation that are free to vary; for a one-sample t-test with n cases the degrees of freedom are n minus 1. They determine the exact shape of the reference distribution. Parametric tests rest on assumptions that should be checked: normality of the outcome (or of residuals), homogeneity of variance (roughly equal spread across groups, also called homoscedasticity), independence of observations, and an interval or ratio level of measurement . When these are seriously violated, the non-parametric tests of 7.10 are the safer choice. 7.12 Designs and validity threats The finest statistics cannot rescue a poorly designed study. Design determines what conclusions the numbers can bear, above all whether a cause can be claimed. Three broad design families True experimental designs. The researcher manipulates the independent variable and uses random assignment of participants to conditions. Only this combination licenses strong causal claims, because randomisation balances out unknown differences between groups. Quasi-experimental designs. There is manipulation or a comparison but no random assignment , often because groups are pre-existing (for example two schools). Causal inference is weaker because the groups may differ at the outset. Non-experimental designs. No manipulation at all; the researcher observes and measures (for example correlational and survey studies). These describe relationships but cannot establish cause. Further design distinctions Factorial designs. Two or more independent variables crossed together, allowing main effects and interactions to be studied at once, as in 7.10. Single-subject designs. One participant (or very few) is studied intensively across baseline and treatment phases, common in behaviour therapy. The classic form is the A-B-A-B reversal design , where A is baseline and B is treatment. Longitudinal designs. The same people are followed over time; they reveal genuine change but are slow and suffer participant drop-out (attrition). Cross-sectional designs. Different age or cohort groups are measured once at the same time; they are quick but confound age with cohort (generational) effects. Sequential designs. A hybrid that follows several cohorts longitudinally, separating true developmental change from cohort effects. Confounding and control A confounding variable is an extraneous factor that varies alongside the independent variable and offers a rival explanation for the result. If a new therapy is given only in the morning and the comparison therapy only in the evening, time of day confounds the comparison. Researchers reduce confounds through control : random assignment, holding conditions constant, counterbalancing the order of conditions, and using control or placebo groups. The four types of validity Validity here refers to the soundness of the inferences drawn from a study, a framework crystallised by Donald Thomas Campbell and Julian Stanley in their influential 1963 monograph on experimental design. Internal validity. The degree to which the study can claim that the independent variable, and nothing else, caused the change in the dependent variable. Threatened by confounds. External validity. The degree to which findings generalise to other people, settings, and times. Construct validity. Whether the operations used truly capture the intended theoretical concept (for example whether a questionnaire really measures "anxiety"). Statistical-conclusion validity. Whether the statistical inferences about the relationship are correct, threatened by low power, violated assumptions, or unreliable measures. Campbell and Stanley threats to internal validity Threat What it means History An outside event occurs during the study and affects the outcome. A news crisis raises everyone's anxiety mid-study. Maturation Participants naturally change over time (grow older, more tired, recover) regardless of treatment. Testing Taking a test the first time changes performance on a later administration (practice effect). Instrumentation The measuring tool or the raters change over the course of the study. Regression to the mean (Francis Galton, 1886) Extreme scorers tend to score nearer the average on retesting simply through statistical chance, mimicking a treatment effect. Selection Groups differ systematically before the study begins because they were not randomly assigned. Attrition (mortality) Participants drop out unevenly across groups, distorting the comparison. Who → what. Donald Thomas Campbell & Julian Stanley → the systematic catalogue of threats to internal and external validity, the backbone of experimental design teaching ever since. Trap. Regression to the mean (Francis Galton) is one of the most common causes of false "treatment works" claims. If you select the most distressed clients (the extreme scorers) and re-test them, their average will drift toward the mean even with no treatment at all. Without a control group, this natural drift is easily mistaken for a real effect. Recap. Choose the analysis to match the question and the data: t-tests (Gosset) for one or two means, ANOVA (Fisher) for several with interactions revealed in factorial designs, regression for prediction and R-squared, chi-square for category counts, and rank-based non-parametric tests when parametric assumptions fail. Every test can err: a Type I error is a false alarm (alpha), a Type II error is a miss (beta), power is 1 minus beta, and effect size plus confidence intervals describe magnitude that a p-value alone cannot. Finally, only a true experiment with random assignment supports strong causal claims; Campbell and Stanley's threats (history, maturation, testing, regression to the mean, selection, attrition) are the rival explanations that good design and adequate validity are built to rule out. 7.13 The complete map: statistics, designs & the people behind them This roster gathers, in one place, every statistical test, research design, and measurement technique that an aptitude paper is likely to name, each pinned to the person who invented it and boiled down to one exam line. The rest cluster naturally around these. 8 General Awareness: History, Schools & Core Psychology This section is the backbone of the SGT University MA Clinical Psychology paper. The examiners lean heavily on "general psychology" one-liners: who founded which school, which theorist is tied to which experiment, and which term names which effect. If you can attach a name to an idea and an idea to a date , you will clear most of these questions in seconds. We build every topic from zero, then flag the traps that catch tired candidates. Key. The examiner is testing associations: founder → school , experiment → theorist , effect → discoverer . Learn psychology as a set of linked pairs and the general-awareness block becomes free marks. 8.1 History & Schools of Psychology Psychology as a formal science is usually dated to 1879 , when Wilhelm Wundt opened the first psychology laboratory at the University of Leipzig, Germany. Before that, questions about the mind belonged to philosophy and physiology. Wundt made the mind a subject for controlled experiment, which is why he is called the "father of experimental psychology". After Wundt, psychology split into competing schools of thought , each with a founder and one core idea. The table below is the single most examined item in this whole section. School Founder(s) Core idea / method Structuralism Wilhelm Wundt; Edward Titchener Break conscious experience into its basic elements (sensations, feelings) using introspection . First lab, 1879. Functionalism William James Study what the mind is for – how mental processes help us adapt. His book "The Principles of Psychology" (1890) launched it. Gestalt Max Wertheimer, Wolfgang Kohler, Kurt Koffka Perception is organised into wholes: "the whole is other than the sum of its parts". Studied insight and perceptual grouping. Behaviourism John B. Watson; B.F. Skinner Study only observable behaviour, not the mind. Learning through conditioning. Watson's 1913 manifesto; Skinner's operant work. Psychoanalysis Sigmund Freud Behaviour driven by the unconscious , early childhood, and conflict between id, ego and superego. Humanistic ("third force") Abraham Maslow; Carl Rogers Focus on growth, free will, self-actualization and the whole person. A reaction against both behaviourism and psychoanalysis. Cognitive Ulric Neisser; George Miller The mind as an information processor . Neisser's "Cognitive Psychology" (1967) named the field; the "cognitive revolution" of the 1950s–60s. Evolutionary (rooted in Charles Darwin) Behaviour and mental traits shaped by natural selection for survival and reproduction. Positive psychology Martin Seligman Scientific study of strengths, wellbeing and flourishing, not just disorder. Founded around 1998. Who → what. Wundt → first lab (1879) + structuralism. James → functionalism. Wertheimer → Gestalt. Watson → behaviourism. Freud → psychoanalysis. Maslow/Rogers → humanistic. Neisser → cognitive. Seligman → positive psychology. Trap. Wilhelm Wundt is the founder of the lab, but the word "structuralism" and the word "introspection" as a formal method are most tightly associated with his student Edward Titchener . If a question asks who named structuralism, the answer is Titchener, not Wundt. Trap. The Gestalt slogan is "the whole is other than the sum of its parts" (Kurt Koffka's careful wording), often loosely quoted as "greater than". Either phrasing points to Gestalt, never to structuralism, which does the opposite by breaking wholes into elements. Why. These schools are not just history. Modern clinical practice inherits directly from them: behaviourism → behaviour therapy; cognitive → cognitive therapy; psychoanalysis → psychodynamic therapy; humanistic → person-centred therapy. Knowing the parent school helps you place any therapy question. 8.2 Learning: Classical Conditioning Learning is a relatively permanent change in behaviour due to experience. The oldest experimental model is classical conditioning , discovered by the Russian physiologist Ivan Pavlov while studying dog digestion. A neutral stimulus that is repeatedly paired with a biologically important one comes to trigger the same response. Unconditioned stimulus (US): food, which naturally causes salivation. Unconditioned response (UR): salivation to food (unlearned). Conditioned stimulus (CS): the bell, after pairing with food. Conditioned response (CR): salivation to the bell alone (learned). Four processes are examined constantly: Acquisition: the CS and US are paired and the CR is built up. Extinction: the CS is presented without the US, and the CR fades. Spontaneous recovery: after a rest, an extinguished CR briefly reappears. Generalization: stimuli similar to the CS also trigger the CR (a bell of a slightly different pitch). Discrimination: the organism learns to respond only to the exact CS, not to similar ones. John B. Watson extended classical conditioning to humans in the famous "Little Albert" experiment (1920). He paired a white rat (neutral) with a loud, frightening noise (US) until the infant Albert became afraid of the rat (CR), and the fear generalized to other furry objects. This showed emotions themselves can be conditioned. Trap. Ivan Pavlov → dogs, salivation, classical conditioning (involuntary reflex). B. F. Skinner → rats/pigeons, levers, operant conditioning (voluntary behaviour + consequences). Do not swap them. John B. Watson used classical conditioning on Little Albert. 8.3 Learning: Operant Conditioning Operant conditioning explains how consequences shape voluntary behaviour. Its groundwork was laid by Edward Thorndike , whose law of effect states that behaviours followed by satisfying consequences are strengthened, and those followed by unpleasant ones are weakened (from his puzzle-box experiments with cats). B.F. Skinner formalised this using the "Skinner box", coining the terms reinforcement and punishment. Consequence Add a stimulus (positive) Remove a stimulus (negative) Reinforcement (behaviour increases) Positive reinforcement: give a reward praise, food pellet Negative reinforcement: remove something unpleasant seatbelt beep stops Punishment (behaviour decreases) Positive punishment: add something unpleasant a scolding Negative punishment: take away something pleasant lose phone privileges Trap. "Negative" does not mean bad, and "positive" does not mean good. Positive = add a stimulus; negative = remove a stimulus. Negative reinforcement increases behaviour (it is still reinforcement); only punishment decreases behaviour. Schedules of reinforcement (Charles Ferster and B. F. Skinner, 1957) govern how often a response is rewarded: Fixed ratio: reward after a set number of responses pay per 10 items made . Variable ratio: reward after an unpredictable number of responses; produces the highest, most persistent responding slot machines, gambling . Fixed interval: reward for the first response after a set time a weekly paycheck . Variable interval: reward for the first response after an unpredictable time checking for a text reply . Key. Variable-ratio schedules give the highest and most extinction-resistant response rate. This is the classic MCQ answer for "which schedule is hardest to extinguish". 8.4 Learning: Observational Learning Not all learning needs direct reinforcement. Albert Bandura showed we learn by watching others, in his Bobo doll experiment: children who watched an adult act aggressively toward an inflatable Bobo doll later imitated that aggression. This is the basis of his social learning theory (later "social cognitive theory"), which adds thinking and expectation to behaviourism. Bandura identified four steps for observational learning: attention (notice the model), retention (remember it), reproduction (be able to perform it), and motivation (a reason to do it, often via vicarious reinforcement – seeing the model rewarded). Who → what. Ivan Pavlov → classical conditioning. Edward Thorndike → law of effect (puzzle box). B. F. Skinner → operant conditioning + schedules. Bandura → observational learning + Bobo doll. 8.5 Memory Memory is examined through its models and its failures. The dominant framework is the multi-store model of Richard Atkinson and Richard Shiffrin (1968), which proposes three stores information flows through. Sensory memory: very brief, large capacity; holds raw sensory input for under a second (iconic for vision, echoic for sound). Short-term memory (STM): holds about 7 ± 2 items (George Miller's "magical number seven") for ~15–30 seconds; kept alive by rehearsal. Long-term memory (LTM): effectively unlimited capacity and duration. Alan Baddeley and Graham Hitch (1974) replaced the passive STM idea with working memory , an active system with a central executive directing two slave systems: the phonological loop (verbal/acoustic material) and the visuospatial sketchpad (visual/spatial material); Baddeley later added the episodic buffer . Fergus Craik and Robert Lockhart (1972) proposed the levels of processing theory: memory strength depends on depth of processing, not on stores. Shallow processing (how a word looks) gives weak memory; deep semantic processing (what a word means) gives strong memory. For types of LTM, Endel Tulving distinguished: Episodic memory: personal events, tied to time and place your last birthday . Semantic memory: general facts and meanings the capital of France . Procedural memory: skills and how-to knowledge riding a bicycle ; part of implicit (non-declarative) memory. Forgetting was first measured by Hermann Ebbinghaus , whose forgetting curve showed memory drops sharply soon after learning, then levels off. Explanations include decay (traces fade with time), interference (proactive: old learning blocks new; retroactive: new learning blocks old), and retrieval failure (cues missing). Trap. STM capacity (7±2) is George Miller ; the multi-store model is Richard Atkinson & Richard Shiffrin ; working memory is Alan Baddeley & Graham Hitch ; levels of processing is Fergus Craik & Robert Lockhart ; episodic/semantic memory is Endel Tulving ; the forgetting curve is Ebbinghaus . These five pairs are a favourite matching question. 8.6 Motivation & Emotion Motivation is what energizes and directs behaviour. Key theories: Abraham Maslow's hierarchy of needs ( Abraham Maslow ): needs are arranged in a pyramid – physiological, safety, love/belonging, esteem, and self-actualization at the top. Lower needs must be reasonably met before higher ones drive behaviour. Drive-reduction theory ( Clark Hull ): a physiological need creates a drive (tension); behaviour aims to reduce the drive and restore homeostasis . Henry Murray's needs: a list of psychological needs (achievement, affiliation, power, autonomy). Murray also created the Thematic Apperception Test (TAT) to measure them. Intrinsic vs extrinsic motivation: intrinsic = doing something for its own satisfaction; extrinsic = doing it for an external reward or to avoid punishment. Emotion theories are a guaranteed table question. They differ on the order of the physical arousal, the felt emotion, and the thinking. Theory Theorist(s) Core claim (order of events) James-Lange William James & Carl Lange Stimulus → bodily arousal first → we then feel the emotion. "We are afraid because we tremble." Cannon-Bard Walter Cannon & Philip Bard Arousal and emotion happen at the same time and independently. Two-factor Stanley Schachter & Jerome Singer Emotion = physiological arousal + a cognitive label for that arousal. Cognitive appraisal Richard Lazarus A cognitive appraisal of the situation must come first; thought precedes emotion. Basic emotions Paul Ekman A small set of universal, cross-cultural emotions with distinct facial expressions (happiness, sadness, fear, anger, surprise, disgust). Trap. James-Lange = "body first, then emotion". Cannon-Bard = "both at once". Schachter-Singer = "arousal + label". Do not confuse Schachter-Singer's two factors with Lazarus's appraisal; the two-factor theory needs bodily arousal plus a label, while Lazarus makes thought alone the trigger. 8.7 Intelligence & Cognition (capstone) Assessment is covered in its own section, so here we only need the concepts. Intelligence is broadly the capacity to learn, reason, and adapt to the environment. Charles Spearman proposed a general factor, "g" , underlying all mental abilities, plus specific factors ("s"). The g debate pits this single-factor view against multiple-intelligence views (Howard Gardner's multiple intelligences, Robert Sternberg's triarchic theory). The nature–nurture debate asks how much intelligence is inherited versus shaped by environment; the modern answer is that both interact. Thinking and problem-solving use mental shortcuts called heuristics . Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky showed these shortcuts produce systematic biases : Availability heuristic: judging likelihood by how easily examples come to mind. Representativeness heuristic: judging by how well something matches a stereotype, ignoring base rates. Anchoring: relying too heavily on the first piece of information. Confirmation bias (Peter Wason, 1960): seeking evidence that supports what we already believe. Key. Heuristics and biases → Kahneman & Tversky . Kahneman's "System 1" (fast, automatic) versus "System 2" (slow, effortful) thinking is a common one-liner. 8.8 Social Psychology Core Social psychology studies how people influence one another. It contributes several of the most famous experiments in the discipline, each welded to one name. Attitudes & persuasion: an attitude has cognitive, affective and behavioural components. Persuasion is analysed via the elaboration likelihood model (central route = arguments; peripheral route = cues like attractiveness). Cognitive dissonance ( Leon Festinger ): the discomfort of holding two conflicting beliefs, or acting against a belief, drives us to change an attitude to restore consistency. Conformity ( Solomon Asch ): in the line-judgment study, people gave obviously wrong answers to match a unanimous group – normative social influence. Obedience ( Stanley Milgram ): participants delivered what they believed were dangerous shocks because an authority figure told them to; showed obedience to authority. Bystander effect ( John Darley & Bibb Latane ): the more bystanders present, the less likely any one person helps, due to diffusion of responsibility . Attribution theory ( Fritz Heider ): we explain behaviour by internal (dispositional) or external (situational) causes. The fundamental attribution error (Lee Ross, 1977) is overusing internal causes for others' behaviour while excusing our own as situational. Prejudice: a negative attitude toward a group; linked to stereotyping and discrimination. Groupthink ( Irving Janis ): the drive for group harmony overrides realistic appraisal of alternatives, leading to poor decisions. Trap. Solomon Asch = conformity (lines, peer group). Stanley Milgram = obedience (shocks, authority). Do not swap them: conformity is yielding to peers, obedience is following an authority's command. Who → what. Festinger → cognitive dissonance. Asch → conformity. Milgram → obedience. Darley & Latane → bystander effect. Heider → attribution. Janis → groupthink. 8.9 Indian Psychology & Context SGT is an Indian university, so a few Indian-context items appear. Modern scientific psychology in India began with the first laboratory and department at Calcutta University (1916). The figure most examined is Durganand Sinha , a pioneer who charted the growth of psychology in India, pushed for indigenization (psychology rooted in Indian realities rather than borrowed wholesale from the West), and wrote on the psychology of poverty and rural life. Papers also test survey-level familiarity with concepts drawn from Indian thought : The three gunas (from Samkhya philosophy and the Bhagavad Gita): sattva (purity, balance, clarity), rajas (activity, passion, restlessness), and tamas (inertia, dullness, darkness). Personality and mental states are seen as a mix of these qualities. Yoga psychology: Patanjali's Yoga Sutras describe the mind (chitta) and its modifications (vrittis), and a path of mental discipline and self-regulation toward samadhi ; a forerunner of ideas about attention and consciousness. The self in Indian philosophy: the distinction between the empirical self (ego, ahamkara) and the deeper true self (atman), and the goal of self-realization – a more spiritual, holistic view of the person than Western trait models. Finally, the regulation of the profession. The Rehabilitation Council of India (RCI) , a statutory body under the Ministry of Social Justice & Empowerment, regulates the training and practice of clinical psychologists in India. It maintains the Central Rehabilitation Register, and a clinical psychologist must hold an RCI-recognised qualification (such as the M.Phil in Clinical Psychology, now transitioning to RCI-approved MA/PsyD routes) and register with the RCI to practise legally. Key. For the Indian block, lock in three answers: Durganand Sinha → indigenization / growth of Indian psychology; three gunas → sattva, rajas, tamas; RCI → the statutory body that licenses clinical psychologists in India. Recap. Psychology became a science with Wilhelm Wundt's 1879 lab, then split into schools – structuralism, functionalism, Gestalt, behaviourism, psychoanalysis, humanistic, cognitive – each pinned to a founder. Learning runs from Ivan Pavlov's classical conditioning through B. F. Skinner's operant conditioning (positive/negative reinforcement and punishment, variable-ratio being hardest to extinguish) to Albert Bandura's observational learning. Memory is the Atkinson-Shiffrin stores, Baddeley-Hitch working memory, Craik-Lockhart levels of processing, Endel Tulving's episodic/semantic/procedural, and Hermann Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve. Motivation spans Abraham Maslow's hierarchy, Clark Hull's drive reduction and Murray's needs; emotion is the James-Lange / Cannon-Bard / Schachter-Singer / Lazarus / Ekman table. Cognition adds the g debate and Kahneman-Tversky heuristics. Social psychology is a set of name-experiment pairs: Festinger dissonance, Asch conformity, Milgram obedience, Darley-Latane bystander, Heider attribution. For India, remember Durganand Sinha , the three gunas , and the RCI . Learn every idea as a name-attached pair and this section becomes your strongest scoring block. 8.10 The complete map: every school of psychology and its founders This is the safety-net roster. If an aptitude paper names a school, system, or founding milestone, it is almost certainly on this list. Read it as a checklist: for each row, be able to pair the school with the right person and recall the one-line core idea . Full names are given first so a distractor using only a surname cannot trip you. Key. Families group the schools by era and outlook: (A) the early schools that founded the discipline, (B) the behaviourist tradition, (C) depth psychology and the humanistic reaction against it, (D) cognitive and modern movements, and (E) founding milestones (firsts, labs, clinics). Rows are numbered continuously across all families. Family A: The early schools # School / system / milestone Founder(s) Core idea in one line 1 Structuralism Wilhelm Wundt; Edward Bradford Titchener Analyse conscious experience into its basic elements (sensations, images, feelings). 2 Introspection Wilhelm Wundt Trained self-observation and report of one's own conscious contents as the core method. 3 Act psychology Franz Brentano Study mental acts (the act of seeing, judging) rather than static contents; mind is intentional, always directed at an object. 4 Functionalism William James; John Dewey; James Rowland Angell; Harvey Carr Study what the mind is for: how consciousness helps the organism adapt to its environment. 5 Gestalt psychology Max Wertheimer; Wolfgang Kohler; Kurt Koffka The whole is different from the sum of its parts; we perceive organised wholes, not isolated bits. 6 Field theory Kurt Lewin Behaviour is a function of the person and the environment together (the total life space or field). Family B: The behaviourist tradition # School / system / milestone Founder(s) Core idea in one line 7 Behaviourism John Broadus Watson Psychology should study only observable behaviour, not the unobservable mind. 8 Classical conditioning Ivan Pavlov A neutral stimulus paired with a natural one comes to trigger the same reflex response. 9 Connectionism (law of effect) Edward Lee Thorndike Responses followed by satisfaction are stamped in; learning is trial and error strengthening stimulus–response bonds. 10 Operant behaviourism Burrhus Frederic Skinner Behaviour is shaped by its consequences; reinforcement raises and punishment lowers its future rate. 11 Drive-reduction (hypothetico-deductive) Clark Leonard Hull Learning is driven by reducing biological needs, worked out through formal, testable equations. 12 Purposive behaviourism Edward Chace Tolman Behaviour is goal-directed and guided by cognitive maps; learning can be latent, shown only when useful.
