Watson founded behaviourism, but Ivan Pavlov (a physiologist) did the dog experiments; Lightner Witmer opened the first clinic (1896), while Hall opened the first American lab ; Abraham Maslow gave the hierarchy of needs, Carl Rogers gave person-centred therapy (both humanistic, different people); and do not confuse Carl Jung (analytical, collective unconscious) with Alfred Adler (individual, inferiority). Recap. Five families, thirty-five rows: the early schools (structuralism, functionalism, Gestalt), the behaviourist line (Watson to Skinner, Tolman, Hull), depth psychology and its humanistic reply (Freud, Jung, Adler, the neo-Freudians, Maslow, Rogers), the cognitive and modern movements (the cognitive revolution, evolutionary, positive psychology), and the founding firsts (1879 lab, 1896 clinic, 1915 Calcutta department). If you can name the school, the person, and the one-line idea for each, no history-of-psychology item on the aptitude paper should surprise you. 9 Learning & Conditioning Almost everything a person does, from fearing a dentist's drill to typing without looking at the keys, was learned. Psychology treats learning not as a vague idea but as a precise process that can be measured in the laboratory. This chapter builds the topic from the ground up: what learning is (and is not), the two great forms of conditioning that dominate the exam, the observational and cognitive kinds of learning that go beyond simple stimulus and response, and the clinical applications that flow from all of them. The material is dense with names, so each theorist, test, and study is given in full at first mention; the test loves to ask you to match a person to an idea, and the surest way to lose marks is to confuse two similar-sounding mechanisms. 9.1 What learning is (and is not) Learning is defined as a relatively permanent change in behaviour or in behavioural potential that results from experience. Each clause of that definition matters. Relatively permanent excludes brief changes caused by fatigue, illness, hunger, or drugs, which fade once the state passes. Change in behaviour or behavioural potential allows for learning that has occurred but is not yet shown (a person may have learned a route without walking it). Results from experience is the decisive clause: it distinguishes learning from changes that are wired into the body by biology. Two such biological changes must be told apart from learning. Maturation is a change in behaviour due to physical growth and the unfolding of the genetic programme, not experience: an infant walks when the nervous system and muscles are ready, whether or not anyone teaches it. A reflex is an automatic, unlearned response to a stimulus, such as the knee-jerk or the eye-blink to a puff of air; reflexes are present from birth and do not require practice. Learning, by contrast, always traces back to what the organism has experienced. Trap. A change caused by fatigue, drugs, or maturation is not learning, even though behaviour changes. The exam sets traps by describing a behaviour change and asking whether it counts as learning; check whether the cause was experience . 9.2 Classical conditioning: Ivan Pavlov Classical conditioning (also called Pavlovian or respondent conditioning) is learning in which a neutral stimulus, by being paired with a stimulus that already produces a response, comes to produce that response by itself. It was discovered by the Russian physiologist Ivan Petrovich Pavlov while he studied salivation in dogs. Pavlov noticed that the dogs salivated not only when food touched the mouth but also at the sight of the attendant who fed them, and he set out to study this systematically. Who → what. Ivan Petrovich Pavlov → classical (respondent) conditioning; the salivating-dog experiments; the terms unconditioned and conditioned stimulus and response. The four core terms follow directly from his procedure. The unconditioned stimulus (UCS) is a stimulus that naturally and automatically triggers a response without any learning; for Pavlov this was the food (meat powder). The unconditioned response (UCR) is the natural, automatic reaction to the UCS; here, salivation to food. The conditioned stimulus (CS) is an originally neutral stimulus (a bell or metronome) that, after being paired repeatedly with the UCS, comes to trigger a response. The conditioned response (CR) is the learned reaction to the CS; salivation to the bell alone. Note that the CR and UCR are often the same behaviour (salivation) but are named by what triggers them. Why. Conditioning works because the CS comes to signal or predict the UCS. The dog salivates to the bell because the bell has become a reliable forecaster of food; learning is essentially the picking up of predictive relationships between events. Acquisition, extinction, and recovery Acquisition is the initial stage in which the CS and UCS are paired and the CR is established and strengthened. It works best when the CS appears just before the UCS (forward pairing) rather than at the same time or afterward. Extinction is the weakening and eventual disappearance of the CR when the CS is presented repeatedly without the UCS; the bell keeps ringing but no food comes, and salivation to the bell fades. Spontaneous recovery is the reappearance of a weakened CR after a rest period, showing that extinction does not erase the original learning but suppresses it. Generalization, discrimination, higher-order conditioning Stimulus generalization is the tendency for stimuli similar to the CS to also trigger the CR: a dog conditioned to a bell of one pitch will salivate somewhat to bells of nearby pitches. Stimulus discrimination is the learned ability to respond to the CS but not to other, similar stimuli, achieved when only the true CS is paired with the UCS. Higher-order conditioning (second-order conditioning) occurs when an established CS is used to condition a new neutral stimulus: once a bell reliably produces salivation, pairing a light with the bell can make the light produce salivation too, even though the light was never paired directly with food. Trap. Do not confuse generalization with discrimination. Generalization is responding to similar stimuli (widening); discrimination is responding only to the exact CS (narrowing). They are opposite processes. 9.3 Watson, Little Albert, and Garcia's taste aversion John Broadus Watson , the American founder of the school of behaviourism , argued that psychology should study only observable behaviour and that emotions could be conditioned. With his assistant Rosalie Rayner, Watson conducted the famous Little Albert experiment in 1920. An eleven-month-old infant, "Albert," was shown a white rat (originally neutral, the CS), and each time he reached for it a loud clanging noise (UCS) was made behind him, producing fear and crying (UCR). After several pairings Albert cried and withdrew at the sight of the rat alone (CR), and this fear generalized to other furry white objects such as a rabbit and a fur coat. The study showed that an emotional reaction, a phobia, could be classically conditioned. Who → what. John Broadus Watson (with Rosalie Rayner) → behaviourism; the Little Albert study proving fear can be conditioned in humans. John Garcia demonstrated a striking exception to the rule that any CS can be paired with any UCS. In his studies of taste aversion , rats that consumed a flavoured solution and later felt nauseated (even hours afterward) developed a strong avoidance of that taste after a single pairing. Crucially, the aversion attached readily to tastes but not to sights or sounds. This is now called the Garcia effect , and it illustrates biological preparedness (Martin Seligman, 1970): organisms are evolutionarily prepared to associate certain stimuli (taste with illness) far more easily than arbitrary ones, because such associations aided survival. Who → what. John Garcia → conditioned taste aversion (the Garcia effect) and biological preparedness; learning with a long CS–UCS delay and in a single trial. Why. Taste aversion breaks two "rules" of ordinary conditioning: it forms after one trial and across a delay of hours. This is adaptive; an animal that got sick after eating something must avoid that food to survive, so evolution biased the learning system toward taste–illness links. 9.4 Operant conditioning: Thorndike and Skinner Operant conditioning (also called instrumental conditioning) is learning in which the consequences of a behaviour determine how likely that behaviour is to be repeated. Where classical conditioning concerns involuntary, reflexive responses elicited by stimuli, operant conditioning concerns voluntary behaviours emitted by the organism and shaped by their outcomes. The groundwork was laid by Edward Lee Thorndike , who studied how cats escaped from a puzzle box he built. A hungry cat placed inside had to operate a latch to get out and reach food. Over successive trials the cat escaped faster, and Thorndike concluded that behaviours followed by satisfying consequences are "stamped in." He named this the law of effect : responses that produce a satisfying outcome become more likely, and responses that produce discomfort become less likely, in a given situation. He described the improvement as gradual trial-and-error learning , not sudden insight. Who → what. Edward Lee Thorndike → the puzzle box, trial-and-error learning, and the law of effect (satisfying consequences strengthen a response). Burrhus Frederic Skinner extended this into a full experimental system. He invented the operant chamber , universally known as the Skinner box , in which an animal such as a rat or pigeon presses a lever or pecks a key to receive food, with responses recorded automatically. Skinner replaced Thorndike's mentalistic word "satisfying" with the observable concept of reinforcement : any consequence that increases the frequency of the behaviour it follows. Who → what. Burrhus Frederic Skinner → the operant chamber (Skinner box), the language of reinforcement and punishment, and schedules of reinforcement. Reinforcement and punishment Two dimensions define the four consequences. "Positive" means a stimulus is added ; "negative" means a stimulus is removed . "Reinforcement" always increases behaviour; "punishment" always decreases it. Combining them gives four cases. Positive reinforcement: adding a pleasant stimulus to increase behaviour. A rat gets a food pellet for pressing the lever, so it presses more. Negative reinforcement: removing an unpleasant stimulus to increase behaviour. A rat presses the lever to switch off a loud noise, so it presses more. Positive punishment: adding an unpleasant stimulus to decrease behaviour. A child touches a hot stove, feels pain, and stops touching it. Negative punishment: removing a pleasant stimulus to decrease behaviour. A teenager loses phone privileges for coming home late, so lateness drops. Trap. Negative reinforcement is NOT punishment. Both involve something unpleasant, but negative reinforcement increases a behaviour by removing the unpleasant thing, whereas punishment decreases behaviour. This is one of the most heavily tested confusions on the paper. Reinforcers themselves come in two kinds. A primary reinforcer satisfies a biological need and is reinforcing on its own, such as food, water, or warmth. A secondary reinforcer (also called a conditioned reinforcer) gains its power by being associated with a primary reinforcer; money, praise, and tokens are secondary reinforcers because they can be exchanged for or have been paired with primary rewards. Schedules of reinforcement A schedule of reinforcement is the rule determining which responses get reinforced. Under continuous reinforcement every correct response is reinforced; this produces fast learning but also fast extinction once reinforcement stops. Under partial (intermittent) reinforcement only some responses are reinforced, which produces slower learning but far greater resistance to extinction. There are four classic partial schedules, defined by whether reinforcement depends on the number of responses (ratio) or the passage of time (interval), and on whether the requirement is fixed or variable . Schedule Rule Response pattern Example Fixed-ratio (FR) Reinforce after a set number of responses High rate; brief pause after each reinforcer Pay per 10 items assembled Variable-ratio (VR) Reinforce after an unpredictable number of responses Very high, steady rate; most resistant to extinction Slot machine, gambling Fixed-interval (FI) Reinforce first response after a set time Scalloped; responding speeds up as the time nears Checking mail near delivery time Variable-interval (VI) Reinforce first response after an unpredictable time Slow, steady, consistent rate Checking for a text that may arrive any time Key. Variable-ratio schedules produce the highest response rate and the greatest resistance to extinction, which is exactly why gambling is so persistent. Ratio schedules generally yield higher rates than interval schedules. Partial reinforcement also explains a robust finding: the partial-reinforcement extinction effect , which states that behaviours learned under partial reinforcement resist extinction longer than those learned under continuous reinforcement. When reinforcement has always been intermittent, its absence is harder to detect, so the behaviour persists. Building complex behaviour New behaviours are rarely produced whole, so they are built up. Shaping is the reinforcement of successive approximations , that is, steps that come progressively closer to the target behaviour; to teach a rat to press a lever, one first reinforces facing the lever, then approaching it, then touching it, then pressing. Chaining links a sequence of separate behaviours into one continuous performance, with each step serving as the cue for the next. A related tool is the Premack principle , named after David Premack , which states that a more probable (preferred) behaviour can reinforce a less probable one: "eat your vegetables and then you may have dessert" uses the preferred dessert to reinforce the less-preferred vegetables. Who → what. David Premack → the Premack principle (a high-frequency, preferred activity can reinforce a low-frequency one). Escape and avoidance Two forms of negative-reinforcement learning are distinguished by timing. Escape learning is learning a response that terminates an aversive stimulus already present, such as opening an umbrella once the rain has started. Avoidance learning is learning a response that prevents an aversive stimulus from occurring at all, cued by a warning signal, such as taking an umbrella when clouds gather. Avoidance is important clinically because it maintains phobias: the person who flees before anxiety peaks never learns that the feared outcome would not have happened. 9.5 Observational learning: Albert Bandura Observational learning (also called social learning or modeling) is learning by watching the behaviour of others, called models , and its consequences, without direct reinforcement of one's own behaviour. Its leading figure is Albert Bandura , whose Bobo doll experiment demonstrated it. Children watched an adult behave aggressively toward an inflatable "Bobo" doll, hitting and kicking it; when later left alone with the doll, these children imitated the aggression far more than children who had not seen the model, and they even copied novel actions they had never performed before. Who → what. Albert Bandura → observational (social) learning, the Bobo doll experiment, and the concept of vicarious reinforcement. Bandura identified four processes required for observational learning to occur. In order they are: attention (the observer must notice the model's behaviour), retention (the behaviour must be remembered, usually stored as a mental representation), reproduction (the observer must be physically able to reproduce the action), and motivation (the observer must have a reason to perform it). Motivation is often supplied by vicarious reinforcement , which is the increase in a behaviour after seeing a model rewarded for it (and the corresponding vicarious punishment when the model is penalized). In the Bobo studies, children who saw the aggressive model rewarded imitated more than those who saw the model punished. Key. Bandura's four processes in order: A ttention → R etention → R eproduction → M otivation. Learning can occur through observation alone, without the observer ever being directly reinforced. 9.6 Cognitive learning: Tolman, Kohler, Seligman Strict behaviourism treated the mind as a "black box," but several findings forced the recognition that internal mental processes matter in learning. Edward Chace Tolman studied rats in mazes and found evidence of latent learning , learning that occurs without reinforcement and remains hidden until there is a reason to show it. Rats allowed to wander a maze with no reward later learned the rewarded route far faster than rats with no prior exposure, proving they had learned the layout all along. Tolman argued they had formed a cognitive map , an internal mental representation of the spatial environment. Who → what. Edward Chace Tolman → latent learning and cognitive maps; evidence that learning can occur without reinforcement and be stored mentally. Wolfgang Kohler , a founder of Gestalt psychology, studied problem solving in chimpanzees and described insight learning : the sudden grasp of a solution, experienced as an "aha" moment, rather than gradual trial and error. His chimpanzee Sultan , faced with a banana out of reach, suddenly fitted two sticks together to rake it in, or stacked boxes to climb to a hanging fruit, having apparently solved the problem mentally before acting. Insight contrasts sharply with Edward Thorndike's trial-and-error curve. Who → what. Wolfgang Kohler → insight learning; the chimpanzee Sultan solving problems suddenly by mental restructuring, not trial and error. Martin Seligman described learned helplessness , a state in which an organism exposed to unavoidable, uncontrollable aversive events stops trying to escape even when escape later becomes possible. Dogs given inescapable shocks failed to jump a low barrier to safety in a later situation where escape was easy, having "learned" that their actions did not matter. Seligman linked this to human depression, seeing a parallel between the passive giving-up of the animals and the hopelessness of a depressed person. Who → what. Martin Seligman → learned helplessness (giving up after uncontrollable aversive events) and its link to depression. 9.7 Classical versus operant conditioning Because the two forms of conditioning are constantly contrasted on the exam, the differences are worth setting side by side. Feature Classical conditioning Operant conditioning Chief figures Pavlov, John B. Watson Thorndike, B. F. Skinner Type of behaviour Involuntary, reflexive, elicited Voluntary, emitted Basis of learning Association of two stimuli (CS with UCS) Association of behaviour with its consequence Role of the organism Passive; response is drawn out Active; organism operates on the environment Order of events Stimulus comes before the response Consequence comes after the response Example Salivating to a bell Pressing a lever for food Trap. Classical conditioning shapes involuntary responses (salivation, fear, reflexes); operant conditioning shapes voluntary behaviour (lever-pressing, studying). If a question describes an automatic bodily reaction, think classical; if it describes a chosen action followed by a reward or penalty, think operant. 9.8 Applications The principles above underlie a family of practical techniques. Behaviour modification is the systematic use of operant principles (reinforcement, extinction, shaping) to change maladaptive behaviour and build adaptive behaviour, widely used with children, in classrooms, and in institutions. A prominent example is the token economy , in which desired behaviours earn tokens (secondary reinforcers) that can later be exchanged for privileges or goods; token economies have been used in psychiatric wards and special-education settings to encourage self-care and cooperation. Biofeedback applies conditioning to normally involuntary bodily processes. Instruments give the person moment-to-moment information about a physiological function such as muscle tension, heart rate, or skin temperature, and by using that feedback as a reinforcing signal the person gradually learns some voluntary control, which helps with tension headaches, hypertension, and anxiety. Key. A token economy is an application of operant conditioning: tokens are secondary (conditioned) reinforcers. Biofeedback teaches control over involuntary functions by turning a bodily signal into feedback the person can respond to. Recap. Learning is a relatively permanent change in behaviour due to experience, distinct from maturation and reflex. Classical conditioning (Ivan Pavlov; UCS, UCR, CS, CR; acquisition, extinction, spontaneous recovery, generalization, discrimination, higher-order conditioning; Watson's Little Albert; John Garcia's prepared taste aversion) links stimuli and governs involuntary responses. Operant conditioning (Thorndike's law of effect; B. F. Skinner's chamber; the four consequences; primary and secondary reinforcers; the four reinforcement schedules with variable-ratio strongest; shaping, chaining, Premack; escape versus avoidance) links behaviour to its consequences and governs voluntary action. Albert Bandura's observational learning adds modeling, four processes, and vicarious reinforcement; Edward Tolman (latent learning, cognitive maps), Wolfgang Kohler (insight, Sultan), and Martin Seligman (learned helplessness) add the cognitive dimension. Applications include behaviour modification, token economies, and biofeedback. Remember the two headline traps: negative reinforcement is not punishment, and classical is involuntary while operant is voluntary. 9.9 The complete map: every theory of learning and its theorist This is the safety-net roster: the full set of learning theories an aptitude paper can name, each pinned to its theorist and a one-line core idea. If a name shows up in a question stem, it should be recognisable from this table. Read it as three families: behavioural and associative, cognitive, and social and applied. Key. Match the theorist to the mechanism, not just the label. Ivan Pavlov, Edward Thorndike, Skinner and Guthrie all study association, but the unit differs: reflex pairing, stimulus and response bond, response and consequence, and stimulus and movement contiguity. Aptitude items reward that precision. Behavioural theories explain learning through association and consequence (Pavlov, Thorndike, Skinner, Guthrie, Hull, Mowrer, plus the biological and formal refinements of Seligman, Garcia, Rescorla and Wagner, Premack, Ebbinghaus and Hebb). Cognitive theories add internal representation and meaning (Tolman, Kohler, Bruner, Ausubel, Piaget, Vygotsky, Gagne). Social and applied theories put it to work in the classroom and clinic (Bandura, Kolb, Bloom, Skinner's programmed instruction, Terrace's errorless learning). Know the theorist, the unit of learning, and the one-line mechanism for each. 10 Memory, Attention & Cognition Every waking moment floods the mind with more information than it can possibly process, so the first task of the cognitive system is to decide what to let in. From that filtered stream, some material is held for a few seconds, some is rehearsed and stored for a lifetime, and much is simply lost. On top of these memory operations sit the higher activities of thinking: forming concepts, solving problems, reasoning, judging, deciding, and using language. This chapter builds the whole picture from the ground up, defining each term as it appears and naming each theorist in full. The organising theme is that the human being is an information processor : information enters through the senses, is transformed (encoded), kept (stored), and later brought back (retrieved), and every stage can succeed or fail. 10.1 Attention: the gateway to processing Attention is the process of selectively concentrating on one aspect of the environment while ignoring others. Because processing capacity is limited, attention acts as a gate that admits some inputs and blocks the rest. The classic demonstration is the cocktail-party effect (Colin Cherry, 1953): at a noisy party you can follow one conversation and screen out the others, yet if someone across the room says your name, your attention snaps to it. This shows that unattended information is not fully discarded; at least some of it is monitored for personal relevance. Selective attention and filter (bottleneck) models Selective attention means focusing on one source of information among many. Researchers described this with bottleneck models , so called because information must squeeze through a narrow channel where only one message passes at a time. They disagreed about where along the processing stream the bottleneck sits. Who → what. Donald Broadbent proposed the first filter model (early selection, 1958). Incoming messages are held briefly in a sensory buffer, then a filter selects one message on the basis of its physical features (which ear, pitch, loudness) and passes only that one on for meaning to be extracted. The unattended channel is blocked before its meaning is analysed. Trap. Donald Broadbent's filter is early selection: it screens by physical properties before meaning. The cocktail-party name-detection finding is a problem for a strict early filter, because if the other channel were fully blocked you could never notice your own name in it. Who → what. Anne Treisman answered that criticism with the attenuation model (1964). The unattended channel is not blocked outright but attenuated (turned down, like lowering a volume dial). Weakened signals still reach meaning analysis, and words with a low "threshold" for activation, such as your own name or a highly expected word, can still get through even when turned down. Who → what. J. Anthony Deutsch and Diana Deutsch (1963), later developed by Donald Norman , proposed late-selection theory. Here all incoming messages are processed for meaning, and the bottleneck comes only at the end, at the point of response or conscious awareness, where the most relevant item is selected. Selection is late, after semantic analysis, not before it. Model Theorist Where selection happens Filter (early) Donald Broadbent Before meaning; blocks by physical features Attenuation Anne Treisman Unattended channel turned down, not blocked Late selection Deutsch, Deutsch & Norman After meaning; at response/awareness Divided attention; automatic vs controlled processing Divided attention is the attempt to attend to two or more things at once, as in driving while talking. Whether this succeeds depends on how much mental effort each task needs. Controlled processing is slow, effortful, conscious, and demands attention (a learner driver managing the clutch). Automatic processing is fast, effortless, and runs with little conscious control (an experienced driver changing gear without thinking). Practice converts controlled processing into automatic processing, which frees capacity for other tasks. The Stroop effect , in which naming the ink colour of a colour word (the word "red" printed in blue ink) is slowed because reading is automatic, shows how hard automatic processes are to switch off. Why. Automaticity is the reason skilled activity feels easy: by offloading routine steps to automatic processing, the limited pool of controlled attention is spared for novelty and problem solving. 10.2 Memory as information processing: the multi-store model The dominant framework treats memory as a flow through stores. Encoding is converting information into a form the system can hold; storage is keeping it over time; retrieval is getting it back out. A failure at any of these three produces what we loosely call "forgetting". Who → what. Richard Atkinson and Richard Shiffrin proposed the multi-store model (also called the modal model, 1968): information passes through a sensory register , then a short-term store , then, if rehearsed, a long-term store . The sensory register The sensory register (sensory memory) holds an exact but very brief copy of raw sensory input. Iconic memory is the visual sensory store, lasting about a quarter to half a second. Echoic memory (named by Ulric Neisser, 1967) is the auditory sensory store, lasting a few seconds, which is what lets you "replay" the end of a sentence you barely heard. Who → what. George Sperling (1960) demonstrated iconic memory with the partial-report technique . Shown a grid of letters for a fraction of a second, people could report only about four in a "whole report", but if a tone cued them which row to report immediately after the display vanished, they could report almost any row. This proved that nearly all the letters were briefly available in a rapidly fading icon. Short-term store and working capacity The short-term store (short-term memory, STM) holds a small amount of information for roughly 15 to 30 seconds unless it is refreshed by rehearsal (mental repetition). Information is lost through decay or displacement by new items. Who → what. George Miller (1956), in "The Magical Number Seven, Plus or Minus Two", argued that short-term capacity is about seven items (range five to nine). The limit is not the amount of raw data but the number of chunks . Chunking is grouping items into meaningful units, so that "1 9 4 7 1 9 9 1" (eight digits) becomes two dates (two chunks), vastly expanding what fits. Long-term store The long-term store (long-term memory, LTM) has effectively unlimited capacity and can hold information for years or a lifetime. In the multi-store model, material moves from STM to LTM through elaborative rehearsal (linking it to existing knowledge), not mere repetition. Store Capacity Duration Coding Sensory register Very large (all input) Iconic ~0.5 s; echoic ~2–4 s Raw sensory (visual, auditory) Short-term store 7 ± 2 chunks ~15–30 s without rehearsal Mainly acoustic (sound-based) Long-term store Effectively unlimited Minutes to a lifetime Mainly semantic (meaning-based) Key. The three stores differ on three dimensions: capacity, duration, and coding. STM codes mostly by sound (people confuse "B" and "V", which sound alike), LTM codes mostly by meaning (people confuse "big" and "large", which mean alike). 10.3 Working memory: an active workbench Who → what. Alan Baddeley and Graham Hitch (1974) replaced the single passive short-term store with a working memory model, an active system that both holds and manipulates information. It has four parts. Central executive: the attentional controller that directs the other components, allocates effort, and switches between tasks. It has limited capacity and no storage of its own. Phonological loop: handles sound-based and verbal information. It has a store (the "inner ear") and an articulatory rehearsal process (the "inner voice") that keeps words alive by silent repetition. Visuospatial sketchpad: the "inner eye", which holds and manipulates visual and spatial information, such as picturing a route or rotating a shape. Episodic buffer: added by Baddeley in 2000, a limited store that integrates information from the loop, the sketchpad, and long-term memory into a single coherent episode. Why. Working memory explains why you can do two tasks at once only if they use different components: repeating digits (phonological loop) while tracking a moving dot (visuospatial sketchpad) is easy, but two verbal tasks compete and interfere. 10.4 Levels of processing and the serial position effect Who → what. Fergus Craik and Robert Lockhart (1972) offered the levels-of-processing account, arguing that memory strength depends not on which store an item sits in but on how deeply it is processed. Shallow processing attends to surface features (is the word in capitals?); deep (semantic) processing attends to meaning (does the word fit this sentence?). Deeper, more meaningful processing yields stronger, longer-lasting memories. The serial position effect describes the finding that, when people recall a list, memory is best for items at the start and end and worst for the middle. The primacy effect is superior recall of early items, thought to reflect extra rehearsal that moved them into long-term memory. The recency effect is superior recall of the last items, thought to reflect their still being in short-term memory at the moment of recall. Trap. Do not swap them. Primacy = first items (long-term memory); recency = recent, i.e. last items (short-term memory). A filled delay before recall wipes out the recency effect but leaves primacy intact, strong evidence for two separate stores. 10.5 Types of long-term memory Long-term memory is not one thing. The broadest split is between explicit (declarative) memory , which is conscious and can be "declared" or stated, and implicit (non-declarative) memory , which shows up in behaviour without conscious recollection. Who → what. Endel Tulving (1972) divided explicit memory into episodic memory , the record of personally experienced events tied to a time and place (your last birthday), and semantic memory , general knowledge of facts and meanings with no personal time-stamp (the capital of France). Episodic memory: events, autobiographical, "remembering" a specific occasion. Semantic memory: facts, concepts, vocabulary, "knowing" without reliving. Procedural memory: implicit memory (Peter Graf and Daniel Schacter, 1985) for skills and how to do things (cycling, typing), expressed through performance. Priming: implicit facilitation in which recent exposure to a stimulus speeds later processing of it or a related one, without any conscious memory of the exposure. Trap. Episodic vs semantic: both are explicit, but episodic is where/when it happened to me and semantic is context-free knowledge . "I remember eating mango yesterday" is episodic; "mangoes are fruit" is semantic. 10.6 Retrieval, context, and vivid memories Who → what. Endel Tulving and Donald Thomson stated the encoding specificity principle : retrieval is best when the cues present at recall match those present at encoding. Memory is not a pure copy; it depends on the fit between learning and testing conditions. Two consequences follow. Context-dependent memory (Duncan Godden and Alan Baddeley, 1975) means recall improves when the external environment at retrieval matches that at encoding; divers who learned words underwater recalled them better underwater. State-dependent memory means recall improves when the internal state (mood, arousal, or the effect of a substance) matches. A flashbulb memory (Roger Brown and James Kulik, 1977) is a vivid, detailed, and confidently held memory of the moment one learned of a shocking event; such memories feel photographic but research shows they can be inaccurate despite the confidence. 10.7 Schemas and reconstructive memory Who → what. Frederic Bartlett (1932) argued that remembering is reconstructive , not reproductive: we rebuild the past using schemas , organised packets of prior knowledge and expectations. In his "War of the Ghosts" study, British participants read an unfamiliar Native American folk tale and, on repeated recall, unconsciously distorted it to fit their own cultural schemas, dropping strange details and rationalising odd events. Key. Memory is an active reconstruction shaped by schemas, not a video replay. This makes memory efficient and meaningful but also systematically prone to distortion. Eyewitness memory and the misinformation effect Who → what. Elizabeth Loftus demonstrated the misinformation effect , in which information encountered after an event alters the memory of the event itself. In the classic study, participants who saw a car accident and were asked how fast the cars were going when they "smashed" gave higher speed estimates, and a week later were more likely to falsely report broken glass, than those asked about cars that "hit". Leading questions reshape memory, which is why eyewitness testimony can be confidently wrong. 10.8 Forgetting and amnesia Who → what. Hermann Ebbinghaus (1885), studying his own memory for nonsense syllables, plotted the forgetting curve : forgetting is rapid at first and then levels off. He measured memory with the savings method , comparing how much less effort it took to relearn material than to learn it originally; the "saving" reveals memory that recognition alone would miss. Several theories explain why forgetting occurs. Decay theory: memory traces fade with the passage of time if not used. Interference theory: other memories compete and block the target. Proactive interference is when old learning disrupts new (your old phone number intrudes on the new one). Retroactive interference is when new learning disrupts old (a new password makes the old one hard to recall). Retrieval failure / cue-dependent forgetting: the memory is stored but the right cue is missing, as in the "tip of the tongue" (Roger Brown and David McNeill, 1966) state; the word returns once a cue appears. Motivated forgetting: in the Freudian tradition, threatening or painful memories are pushed out of awareness (repression). Trap. Proactive vs retroactive: think of the direction in time. Pro active acts forward , old harming new. Retro active acts backward , new harming old. Amnesia Amnesia is memory loss from brain injury or disease. Anterograde amnesia is the inability to form new long-term memories after the injury; the past is intact but new events do not stick. Retrograde amnesia is the loss of memories formed before the injury. Who → what. The patient H.M. (Henry Molaison), whose hippocampus was surgically removed to treat epilepsy, developed profound anterograde amnesia: he could not form new explicit memories, yet he could learn new motor skills (procedural memory) while having no memory of practising them. His case proved that explicit and implicit memory rely on different brain systems and that the hippocampus is critical for forming new declarative memories. 10.9 Cognition: concepts, imagery, and problem solving Cognition refers to all mental activities involved in acquiring, storing, and using knowledge. Its building blocks are concepts , mental categories that group objects or ideas by shared features (the concept "bird"). Many concepts are organised around a prototype , the most typical or representative example; a robin is a better prototype of "bird" than a penguin, so we judge category membership faster for typical members. Mental imagery is the representation of information in a picture-like form, allowing operations such as mentally rotating an object; the time to rotate an image increases with the angle of rotation, suggesting imagery preserves spatial structure. Problem solving A problem exists when there is a gap between a current state and a goal state with no obvious route between them. Strategies vary in reliability. Algorithm: a step-by-step procedure that guarantees a correct solution if followed (working through every possible move), but can be slow. Heuristic: a mental shortcut or rule of thumb that is fast and usually works but does not guarantee success. Insight: a sudden realisation of a solution, the "aha" experience, in which the answer appears whole rather than through gradual steps. Two obstacles frequently block solutions. Functional fixedness (Karl Duncker, 1945) is the tendency to see an object as usable only in its customary way (failing to see a coin could serve as a screwdriver). Mental set is the tendency to persist with a strategy that worked before even when a simpler one is now available. 10.10 Reasoning, judgment, and decision making Reasoning is drawing conclusions from information. Deductive reasoning moves from general premises to a specific, logically certain conclusion (all men are mortal; Socrates is a man; therefore Socrates is mortal). Inductive reasoning moves from specific observations to a probable general conclusion (every crow I have seen is black, so crows are probably black); its conclusions are likely but never guaranteed. Who → what. Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman showed that everyday judgment relies on heuristics that, while efficient, produce systematic errors (biases). Availability heuristic: judging how likely or frequent something is by how easily examples come to mind. Vivid, recent events (plane crashes) seem more common than they are. Representativeness heuristic: judging probability by how well something matches a typical example (a prototype), while ignoring base rates. A quiet man who likes poetry is judged more likely to be a librarian than a farmer, even though farmers vastly outnumber librarians. Anchoring and adjustment: starting from an initial value (the anchor) and adjusting insufficiently, so the final estimate stays biased toward the anchor. The framing effect (Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman, 1981) shows that decisions shift with how options are worded even when the facts are identical: a treatment described as having a "90% survival rate" is chosen more often than the same treatment described as having a "10% mortality rate". Why. These heuristics are not signs of stupidity; they are efficient adaptations to a world of limited time and information. They mislead only in specific, predictable situations, which is exactly what makes the biases scientifically interesting. 10.11 Language Language is a system of symbols combined by rules to communicate meaning. It is studied at several levels. Phonemes: the smallest units of sound that distinguish meaning (the /b/ and /p/ that separate "bat" from "pat"). Morphemes: the smallest units of meaning (the word "cats" has two: "cat" and the plural "-s"). Syntax: the rules of grammar governing how words combine into sentences. Semantics: the rules that assign meaning to words and sentences. Who → what. Noam Chomsky argued that children acquire language too fast and from too little input to be explained by imitation alone, so the brain must contain an innate language acquisition device (LAD) . He proposed a universal grammar , a set of grammatical principles common to all human languages, which the child applies to whatever specific language surrounds them. Who → what. Benjamin Lee Whorf , with Edward Sapir, proposed linguistic relativity (the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis): the language one speaks shapes how one thinks and perceives the world, for example by the categories its vocabulary provides. The strong "language determines thought" version is now rejected, but a weaker "language influences thought" version has empirical support. Children pass through broadly universal stages of language acquisition : cooing (vowel-like sounds, from about two months), babbling (repeated consonant-vowel sounds such as "ba-ba", from about six months), the one-word (holophrastic) stage (single words standing for whole ideas, around one year), the two-word (telegraphic) stage (two-word combinations stripped of grammatical extras, "want milk", around two years), and then rapid expansion into full grammatical sentences. Recap. Attention gates a flood of input; filter theories differ on whether selection is early (Donald Broadbent), attenuated (Anne Treisman), or late (Deutsch and Norman), and practice turns controlled processing automatic. Memory is information processing across stores (Richard Atkinson and Richard Shiffrin): a fleeting sensory register (iconic, George Sperling; echoic), a limited short-term store of seven plus or minus two chunks (George Miller), and an unlimited long-term store, with the stores differing in capacity, duration, and coding. Working memory (Alan Baddeley and Graham Hitch) makes short-term memory an active workbench of central executive, phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad, and episodic buffer, while depth of processing (Fergus Craik and Robert Lockhart) and the serial position effect (primacy = first, recency = last) shape what endures. Long-term memory splits into explicit episodic and semantic (Endel Tulving) and implicit procedural and priming; retrieval follows encoding specificity, and memory is reconstructive and schema-driven (Frederic Bartlett), hence the misinformation effect (Elizabeth Loftus). Forgetting follows the Ebbinghaus curve through decay, proactive and retroactive interference, cue-dependent failure, and motivated forgetting, with amnesia (patient H.M.) dissociating explicit from implicit memory. Higher cognition works through concepts and prototypes, imagery, algorithms, heuristics, insight, and reasoning, with the judgment heuristics of Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman (availability, representativeness, anchoring) and the framing effect, and language builds from phonemes and morphemes through syntax and semantics, guided by Noam Chomsky's language acquisition device and universal grammar and questioned by Benjamin Lee Whorf's linguistic relativity. 10.12 The complete map: models of memory, attention & cognition and their authors This is the safety-net roster for the cognitive block: every named model, effect, or theory of memory, attention, language, and thought that an aptitude paper could pin to an author. Learn the pairing (name plus person) and the one-line idea; that is usually all a single mark asks. Rows are numbered continuously across families. Key. A model is a proposed structure or process; an effect is an observed regularity in the data. In an exam, the safest anchor is the author's surname plus one distinguishing word (store, loop, level, schema, filter, chunk). Full names are given first, then the tag you will actually recall. The first is why an organism does anything at all: why it eats now rather than later, why one student grinds for a first-class degree while another drifts, why a frightened animal freezes and another one flees. That is the study of motivation . The second is what it feels like from the inside and how the body registers it: the pounding heart before an exam, the flush of anger, the warmth of relief. That is the study of emotion . The two are tightly braided (a strong feeling pushes us to act, and acting changes what we feel), so psychology treats them together. This chapter builds both from the ground up: first the vocabulary and the major theories of motivation, then the biological motives, then emotion and its competing theories, and finally stress, where motivation and emotion meet the body most sharply. 11.1 The vocabulary of motivation Motivation is the internal process that initiates, directs, and sustains behaviour toward a goal. It explains not just that behaviour happens but its energy (how vigorous), its direction (toward what), and its persistence (for how long). Because motivation cannot be seen directly, it is an intervening variable : we infer it from what an organism does. Four closely related terms must be kept apart. Need. A state of deprivation or requirement, either biological (food, water, warmth) or psychological (achievement, belonging). A need is the underlying lack. Drive. The aroused, tense internal state that a need produces and that pushes the organism to act. Hunger the need produces the hunger drive; the drive is the felt push. Example: not having eaten for a day is a need; the gnawing restlessness that makes you seek food is the drive. Motive. A more general term for any specific internal reason for behaving, often used for learned or social motivations (a motive to achieve, to affiliate, to dominate). Incentive. An external goal object that pulls behaviour. Where a drive pushes from inside, an incentive pulls from outside. Example: the smell of fresh bread can make you hungry even when you have just eaten; the bread is an incentive. Key. Drives push from within (internal states of tension); incentives pull from without (external goal objects). Most real behaviour is a mix of both. 11.2 Instinct theory: William McDougall The earliest scientific account of motivation was instinct theory . An instinct is a complex, unlearned, fixed pattern of behaviour that is characteristic of an entire species (birds building nests, salmon swimming upstream). The psychologist William McDougall argued that human behaviour too is driven by a set of inborn instincts (he listed motives such as curiosity, pugnacity, and parental care), and that these instincts supply the energy behind all conduct. Who → what. William McDougall proposed the first influential instinct theory of human motivation, holding that inborn, species-wide instincts energize behaviour. Instinct theory faded because it explained too much and predicted too little. Psychologists kept adding instincts (one survey counted thousands proposed by various writers) until naming an instinct became merely relabelling the behaviour it was supposed to explain. Saying a person fights because of a fighting instinct is circular. Instinct theory does survive, in refined form, in ethology (the biological study of animal behaviour) and in evolutionary psychology , which treats many motives as adaptations shaped by natural selection. Trap. Instinct theory was not disproved by evidence so much as abandoned for being circular and unfalsifiable . Do not say it was refuted by an experiment. 11.3 Drive-reduction theory: Clark Hull and homeostasis Drive-reduction theory , associated most with Clark Leonard Hull , rests on the idea of homeostasis : the body's tendency to maintain a stable, balanced internal state (constant temperature, blood sugar, fluid levels). When the body strays from its balance point (a physiological need arises), a drive is created; behaviour that reduces the need and restores balance reduces the drive, and that reduction is reinforcing. So we act to return to equilibrium, the way a thermostat switches the heating off once the set temperature is reached. Who → what. Clark L. Hull built drive-reduction theory : needs create drives, behaviour that reduces the drive restores homeostasis and is reinforced. Hull distinguished two kinds of drive: Primary drives. Unlearned, tied directly to biological survival (hunger, thirst, warmth, sleep, sex). Secondary drives. Learned through association with the satisfaction of primary drives. Example: money satisfies no biological need directly, but because it buys food and shelter it becomes a powerful learned drive. Trap. Drive reduction cannot explain behaviour that raises tension: riding roller coasters, solving puzzles, exploring for its own sake. We do not always seek to reduce arousal; sometimes we seek to increase it. That gap is exactly what arousal theory fills. 11.4 Arousal theory and the Yerkes-Dodson law Arousal theory holds that organisms are motivated to maintain an optimal level of arousal (alertness and activation), not a minimum. When arousal is too low we seek stimulation (we get bored and go looking for something to do); when it is too high we seek calm. Curiosity and play, which drive-reduction theory struggled with, fall out naturally: they raise arousal toward the optimum. The classic principle here is the Yerkes-Dodson law (Robert Yerkes and John Dillingham Dodson): performance improves with arousal up to a point and then declines, producing an inverted-U curve. Some arousal helps; too much hurts. The law adds a refinement: the optimal level depends on task difficulty. For easy or well-learned tasks a higher level of arousal is best; for hard or complex tasks a lower level is best, because high arousal disrupts fine control. Who → what. Robert M. Yerkes and John D. Dodson gave the Yerkes-Dodson law : an inverted-U between arousal and performance, with the optimum lower for difficult tasks. Key. A little pre-exam nerves sharpens performance; being paralysed with panic ruins it. Same person, same exam, different points on the same inverted-U. 11.5 Incentive theory and expectancy-value Where drive theory looks inward, incentive theory looks outward: behaviour is pulled by the anticipated value of external rewards and the wish to avoid punishments. The strength of the pull depends on how attractive the incentive is and how likely it seems that acting will secure it. Expectancy-value theory (John William Atkinson, 1957) formalizes this: the motivation to pursue a goal is roughly the product of expectancy (how likely am I to succeed?) and value (how much do I want it?). If either is near zero, motivation is near zero: a huge prize you are certain you cannot win does not motivate, and neither does a trivial prize you are certain you can win. 11.6 Maslow's hierarchy of needs Abraham Harold Maslow , a founder of humanistic psychology , arranged human needs into a hierarchy , usually drawn as a pyramid. Lower needs are said to be more basic and to demand satisfaction first; only as they are reasonably met does the person become concerned with the needs above. From the bottom up the five classic levels are: Physiological needs : food, water, air, sleep, warmth. The survival floor. Safety needs : security, shelter, stability, freedom from threat. Belongingness and love needs : friendship, intimacy, acceptance, being part of a group. Esteem needs : achievement, competence, respect from others and self-respect. Self-actualization : realizing one's full potential, becoming all one is capable of becoming. Maslow later added, above esteem, cognitive needs (to know and understand), aesthetic needs (for order and beauty), and, at the very top, self-transcendence (connection to something beyond the self). He drew a crucial distinction between the lower four, which he called deficiency needs (D-needs, arising from lack, and quieted once filled), and growth needs or being-needs (B-needs, such as self-actualization, which are never fully satisfied and grow stronger the more they are engaged). Who → what. Abraham Maslow proposed the hierarchy of needs and the concept of self-actualization , and split deficiency needs from growth needs . Trap. The strict "lower before higher" ordering is an idealization, not an iron law. People starve for a cause, artists neglect comfort for their work, and belonging can override safety. Exam answers should present the levels as Abraham Maslow ordered them but note the hierarchy is not rigidly fixed. 11.7 Murray's manifest needs and the Thematic Apperception Test Henry Alexander Murray catalogued a long list of psychological (rather than biological) needs, which he called manifest needs , among them the need for achievement, affiliation, dominance, order, and autonomy. He argued these needs vary in strength from person to person and are often not consciously acknowledged. To measure them indirectly he co-developed (with Christiana Morgan) the Thematic Apperception Test (TAT) , a projective test in which a person makes up stories about ambiguous pictures; the themes that recur in the stories are read as clues to the person's dominant needs. Who → what. Henry Murray catalogued manifest needs and co-created the Thematic Apperception Test (TAT) to measure them by the stories people project onto ambiguous pictures. 11.8 McClelland: achievement, affiliation, and power David Clarence McClelland took three of Murray's needs and studied them intensively, often measuring them from TAT-style stories. His theory is sometimes called the acquired-needs or three-needs theory, because he held these motives are largely learned through culture and experience. Need for achievement (nAch) : the drive to meet standards of excellence, to master tasks, to do things well. High-nAch people prefer moderately difficult goals (challenging but attainable) and want clear feedback on results. Need for affiliation (nAff) : the drive for warm, friendly relationships and social acceptance. Need for power (nPow) : the drive to influence, control, or have impact on others. Who → what. David McClelland developed the study of the need for achievement, affiliation, and power as acquired social motives. Trap. Do not confuse the need for achievement (a drive to do a task well against a standard of excellence) with the need for power (a drive to influence or control other people ). One is about personal mastery; the other is about impact on others. A common multiple-choice trap swaps them. 11.9 Self-determination theory: intrinsic vs extrinsic motivation Self-determination theory (SDT) , developed by Edward Deci and Richard Ryan , distinguishes two broad sources of motivation. Intrinsic motivation is doing something for its own sake, because it is interesting or satisfying in itself (reading for pleasure, playing music for the joy of it). Extrinsic motivation is doing something for a separable outcome (a reward, a grade, avoiding punishment). SDT holds that intrinsic motivation flourishes when three basic psychological needs are met: autonomy (a sense of choice), competence (a sense of effectiveness), and relatedness (a sense of connection). A striking prediction of SDT is the overjustification effect : paying people to do something they already enjoy can reduce their intrinsic interest, because they come to see the activity as done for the reward rather than for itself. When the reward stops, the behaviour drops off more than it would have if no reward had ever been given. Who → what. Edward Deci and Richard Ryan built self-determination theory , distinguishing intrinsic from extrinsic motivation and naming the overjustification effect . Why. The overjustification effect matters practically: rewarding children for reading, or bonuses for already-loved work, can quietly kill the very interest they were meant to boost. Extrinsic rewards work best where intrinsic interest is low to begin with. 11.10 Biological motives Hunger Hunger is regulated in large part by the hypothalamus , a small brain structure just below the thalamus. Two regions were classically identified as opposing centres. The lateral hypothalamus (LH) acts as a hunger centre : stimulating it makes an animal eat, damaging it makes the animal stop eating. The ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH) acts as a satiety centre : stimulating it stops eating, damaging it leads to overeating and obesity. A simple mnemonic: L ateral = L et's eat; V entro M edial = V ery M uch full. Chemical signals also regulate appetite over the longer term. Leptin is a hormone released by fat cells ; higher fat stores mean more leptin, which signals fullness and suppresses appetite. Ghrelin is a hormone released mainly by the stomach when it is empty; it stimulates hunger. Roughly, leptin says "stop" and ghrelin says "go." Key. Lateral hypothalamus = ON switch for eating (hunger centre). Ventromedial hypothalamus = OFF switch (satiety centre). Leptin (from fat) suppresses hunger; ghrelin (from the stomach) triggers it. Thirst Thirst arises from two kinds of signal: a drop in the volume of fluid in the body (for instance after bleeding or heavy sweating) and a rise in the concentration of salts in the blood (which pulls water out of cells). Both are monitored by the hypothalamus, which triggers the drive to drink and the release of hormones that make the kidneys conserve water. Sexual motivation Sexual motivation is unusual among biological motives: it is essential to the species but not to the survival of the individual, and in humans it is shaped as much by learning, culture, and relationships as by hormones such as testosterone and oestrogen. Unlike hunger and thirst, it is not a homeostatic drive that builds from deprivation and switches off when a deficit is repaired. 11.11 Emotion: the three components An emotion is a complex reaction pattern with three components that psychologists agree on, even while they argue about their order: Physiological arousal : bodily changes driven largely by the autonomic nervous system (racing heart, sweating, adrenaline). Cognitive appraisal : the mental interpretation of the situation and of one's own state (labelling something as a threat, an insult, or good news). Behavioural / expressive component: outward expression and action tendency (a facial expression, a raised voice, the urge to approach or flee). The great theories of emotion differ mainly on which component comes first and causes the others: does the body react and then we feel, do we feel and the body reacts together, or must we interpret our arousal before an emotion exists at all? 11.12 Theories of emotion Who → what. William James and (independently) Carl Lange gave the James-Lange theory : the bodily response comes first, and the emotion is our perception of that bodily response. James-Lange theory. The counter-intuitive claim is that we do not tremble because we are afraid; we are afraid because we tremble. A stimulus triggers a specific pattern of bodily arousal, and the emotion is our awareness of that pattern. Order: stimulus → arousal → emotion. A strength is that it takes the body seriously; a weakness is that different emotions can share very similar arousal (fear and excitement both race the heart), so bodily feedback alone may not tell them apart. Who → what. Walter Cannon and Philip Bard gave the Cannon-Bard theory : arousal and the felt emotion occur at the same time , both triggered together (via the thalamus) rather than one causing the other. Cannon-Bard theory. Walter Cannon objected that bodily changes are too slow and too similar across emotions to be the source of feeling. He and Philip Bard proposed that a stimulus is routed to the brain, which fires off the bodily arousal and the conscious emotion simultaneously and independently . Order: stimulus → arousal AND emotion together. Who → what. Stanley Schachter and Jerome Singer gave the two-factor (cognitive-arousal) theory : emotion requires both physiological arousal and a cognitive label for that arousal. Schachter-Singer two-factor theory. Here emotion is arousal plus interpretation. We notice we are aroused, look to the situation for an explanation, and label the arousal accordingly; the same racing heart might be labelled fear on a cliff edge or love on a date. Order: stimulus → arousal → cognitive label → emotion. This theory explains why context matters so much to what we feel. Who → what. Richard Lazarus argued that cognitive appraisal comes first : even a rapid, unconscious appraisal of the situation must precede and shape the emotion. Lazarus appraisal theory. For Richard Lazarus, appraisal is primary; there is no emotion without some evaluation of the event's meaning for one's wellbeing, even if that appraisal is fast and outside awareness. Who → what. Robert Zajonc argued the opposite of Lazarus: affect can precede cognition , so we can feel (like or fear something) before we have consciously thought about it. Zajonc and Lazarus held a famous debate. Zajonc pointed to instant preferences and fears that arise before any conscious analysis (the mere-exposure effect , in which we come to like things simply because they are familiar, is his). The modern view is that both are right: some emotional responses are fast and pre-cognitive, others depend on deliberate appraisal. Facial-feedback hypothesis. Facial expressions do not just show emotion; they can feed back and intensify or even produce it. Holding the face in a smile can make a situation feel a little more pleasant; frowning can make it feel worse. This is the expressive component acting as a cause, a cousin of the James-Lange idea. Theory What comes first Core claim James-Lange Arousal, then emotion Emotion is the perception of bodily changes Cannon-Bard Arousal and emotion together Brain triggers both at once, independently Schachter-Singer Arousal, then cognitive label Emotion = arousal + interpretation of it Lazarus Cognitive appraisal Appraisal is necessary and primary Zajonc Affect (can precede cognition) We can feel before we think Trap. The three most-confused theories differ only in ordering . James-Lange: arousal then emotion (sequential). Cannon-Bard: arousal and emotion together (simultaneous). Schachter-Singer: arousal then a cognitive label then emotion. Memorize which word (then, together, label) goes with which name. 11.13 Basic emotions: Ekman and Plutchik Paul Ekman argued that a small set of basic emotions are universal : recognized and expressed through the same facial expressions across all human cultures, which suggests they are biologically built in rather than learned. His classic list is happiness, sadness, fear, anger, surprise, and disgust (he later added contempt). His cross-cultural studies, including with people who had little contact with the outside world, found the same expressions read the same way everywhere. Who → what. Paul Ekman established a set of basic, universal emotions with cross-culturally recognized facial expressions. Robert Plutchik proposed a wheel of emotions : eight primary emotions arranged in four opposing pairs (joy vs sadness, trust vs disgust, fear vs anger, surprise vs anticipation). On his model, emotions vary in intensity (annoyance shading into rage) and combine like colours to form more complex feelings (for example, joy plus trust yields love). Who → what. Robert Plutchik created the wheel of emotions : eight primary emotions in opposing pairs that vary in intensity and blend into complex emotions. 11.14 Stress and coping Stress is the process by which we perceive and respond to events (called stressors ) that we appraise as threatening or challenging. Its study sits at the junction of motivation, emotion, and the body. Who → what. Walter Cannon described the fight-or-flight response : an acute stressor triggers the sympathetic nervous system and adrenaline, preparing the body to confront or escape the threat. Fight-or-flight is the immediate emergency reaction: heart rate and breathing speed up, blood is diverted to the muscles, and the body is primed for vigorous action. It is adaptive for short, physical threats but costly if switched on chronically. Who → what. Hans Selye described the General Adaptation Syndrome (GAS) , the body's three-stage response to prolonged stress. Hans Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome (GAS) traces how the body responds to sustained stress in three stages: Alarm reaction. The body's first mobilization, essentially fight-or-flight: resources are marshalled and resistance briefly dips then rises. Resistance. The body adapts and copes at a high but sustainable level; stress hormones stay elevated as it holds the line. Exhaustion. If the stressor persists too long, reserves are depleted; vulnerability to illness, breakdown, and burnout rises. Trap. Walter Cannon's fight-or-flight is the acute, immediate emergency response; Selye's GAS is the longer, three-stage course of prolonged stress. The alarm stage of GAS contains fight-or-flight; do not treat the two theories as rivals. Richard Lazarus and Susan Folkman stressed that what makes an event stressful is appraisal . In primary appraisal we ask "is this a threat?"; in secondary appraisal we ask "can I cope with it?" They distinguished two broad styles of coping : Problem-focused coping : acting on the stressor itself to change or remove it (making a study plan for a hard exam). Best when the situation is controllable. Emotion-focused coping : managing one's emotional reaction rather than the stressor (relaxation, reframing, seeking comfort). Best when the situation cannot be changed. Who → what. Richard Lazarus and Susan Folkman built the appraisal-and-coping model, distinguishing problem-focused from emotion-focused coping. Finally, Thomas Holmes and Richard Rahe tried to quantify life stress with the Social Readjustment Rating Scale (SRRS) . They assigned life change units to major life events (death of a spouse scored highest, followed by divorce, and so on down to minor events); a person's total over a year was meant to predict the risk of stress-related illness. The scale is important historically for treating stress as measurable, though it has been criticized for ignoring how differently individuals appraise the same event. Who → what. Thomas Holmes and Richard Rahe created the Social Readjustment Rating Scale , scoring life events in life change units to estimate stress-related illness risk. Recap. Motivation initiates, directs, and sustains behaviour; keep need (lack), drive (internal push), motive (reason), and incentive (external pull) apart. The theories run from McDougall's instincts through Clark Hull's drive reduction (homeostasis, primary vs secondary drives) to arousal theory with the inverted-U Yerkes-Dodson law , then incentive and expectancy-value. Content theories add Abraham Maslow's hierarchy (deficiency vs growth needs), Murray's manifest needs (measured by the TAT), David McClelland's achievement/affiliation/power, and Edward Deci and Richard Ryan's self-determination theory with the overjustification effect. Biological motives centre on the hypothalamus (lateral = hunger, ventromedial = satiety) and hormones (leptin suppresses, ghrelin stimulates). Emotion has three components (arousal, cognition, expression); the theories differ on order: James-Lange (arousal then emotion), Cannon-Bard (both at once), Schachter-Singer (arousal plus label), Lazarus (appraisal first), Robert Zajonc (affect can precede cognition), plus facial feedback, Paul Ekman's universal basic emotions, and Robert Plutchik's wheel. Stress runs from Cannon's fight-or-flight through Selye's three-stage GAS to Richard Lazarus and Folkman's appraisal-and-coping (problem- vs emotion-focused) and the Holmes-Rahe scale. 11.15 The complete map: theories of motivation & emotion and their theorists Aptitude papers love to pair a named theory of motivation or emotion with the wrong theorist. This is the safety-net roster: every model likely to be named, tied to its author, with a one-line core idea. Learn the person and the one-line hook for each, then no matching item can surprise you. Key. Motivation asks why we act (what energises and directs behaviour); emotion asks what we feel and in what order body, thought and feeling arrive. Families A and B cover motivation (biological then cognitive/work); Families C and D cover emotion (physiological then cognitive/appraisal).
