Anchor each to its theorist and its one-line hook. 12 Social Psychology Human beings are profoundly social animals. Almost nothing we do, from the opinions we hold to the shirts we buy to the way we behave in an emergency, is untouched by the presence, real or imagined, of other people. Social psychology is the scientific study of how the thoughts, feelings, and behaviours of individuals are influenced by the actual, imagined, or implied presence of others. This definition, given by the American psychologist Gordon Allport, deliberately includes imagined and implied presence: you slow your car on an empty highway because a police officer might be watching, and you behave more politely because you imagine how others would judge you. This chapter builds the field from zero: how we form and change attitudes, how we explain behaviour, how groups and authorities sway us, why prejudice arises, when we help strangers, and what draws us to one another. 12.1 Attitudes and the ABC Model An attitude is a relatively enduring evaluation, favourable or unfavourable, of a person, object, idea, or situation. Attitudes are not the same as facts; they are judgements coloured by feeling. Psychologists analyse an attitude into three components, called the ABC model . Affective component: the emotions and feelings the object evokes. Feeling anxious at the sight of a snake. Behavioural component: the way the attitude disposes you to act. Crossing the road to avoid the snake. Cognitive component: the thoughts and beliefs you hold about the object. Believing that snakes are dangerous. Attitudes are learned, not innate. They form through classical conditioning (an object repeatedly paired with pleasant or unpleasant feelings acquires that emotional tone), through operant conditioning (attitudes that earn approval are strengthened), through observational learning (children absorb the attitudes of parents and peers), and through direct experience with the object itself, which tends to produce stronger and more stable attitudes. 12.2 The Attitude-Behaviour Gap Common sense says attitudes drive behaviour. Often they do, but the link is looser than expected. The classic demonstration came from the American sociologist Richard LaPiere . In the early 1930s he travelled across the United States with a young Chinese couple, stopping at over 250 hotels and restaurants. They were refused service only once. Months later he wrote to the same establishments asking whether they would serve Chinese guests; over 90 percent of those who replied said they would not . Their stated attitude (prejudice) flatly contradicted their actual behaviour (courteous service). Who → what. Richard LaPiere (1934) exposed the attitude-behaviour gap : what people say their attitude is often fails to predict what they actually do. Later research clarified when attitudes do predict behaviour: when the attitude is strong, specific to the behaviour in question, formed through direct experience, and when situational pressures are weak. Weak or general attitudes are easily overridden by the demands of the moment. 12.3 Persuasion: Changing Attitudes Persuasion is the deliberate effort to change attitudes through communication. Systematic study of it began during the Second World War with the American psychologist Carl Hovland and his colleagues at Yale University, whose work is called the Yale approach (or Yale communication model). They asked, in effect, who says what to whom , and identified the factors that make a message persuasive. The source: credible, expert, trustworthy, and likeable communicators persuade more. The message: two-sided arguments, moderate fear appeals, and clear conclusions work better in many settings. The audience: intelligence, self-esteem, age, and prior commitment all affect how a message lands. Who → what. Carl Hovland led the Yale attitude-change programme, framing persuasion as source, message, channel, and audience factors. The Elaboration Likelihood Model The most influential modern theory of persuasion is the elaboration likelihood model of the American psychologists Richard Petty and John Cacioppo . Elaboration means the amount of careful, effortful thinking a person devotes to a message. The model proposes two routes to persuasion. Central route: when the listener is motivated and able to think, they scrutinise the actual quality of the arguments. Attitude change through this route is deep, lasting, and resistant to counter-persuasion. Peripheral route: when the listener is unmotivated or distracted, they rely on superficial cues (an attractive spokesperson, a catchy jingle, the sheer number of arguments). Change through this route is shallow and short-lived. Why. Advertisers exploit both routes: a technical product aimed at experts uses central-route evidence, while an impulse product uses peripheral cues like celebrity and music. 12.4 Cognitive Dissonance and Self-Perception Sometimes changing our behaviour changes our attitudes, rather than the reverse. The landmark theory here is cognitive dissonance theory , proposed in 1957 by the American psychologist Leon Festinger . Dissonance is the uncomfortable psychological tension that arises when we hold two inconsistent thoughts, or when our behaviour clashes with our attitude. Because the tension is unpleasant, we are motivated to reduce it, usually by changing the attitude to fit the behaviour. In the famous 1959 experiment by Leon Festinger and James Carlsmith, participants performed an extremely boring task and were then paid either one dollar or twenty dollars to tell the next person it was enjoyable. Those paid only one dollar later rated the task as more enjoyable than those paid twenty dollars. Why? The twenty-dollar group had ample external justification for lying (the money), so felt no dissonance. The one-dollar group had insufficient justification, so to reduce the tension of having lied for almost nothing, they convinced themselves the task really was interesting. Who → what. Leon Festinger (1957) proposed cognitive dissonance theory: inconsistency between attitude and behaviour creates tension that pushes the attitude to shift. A rival explanation is self-perception theory , offered by the American psychologist Daryl Bem . Bem argued that we often do not have strong pre-existing attitudes at all; instead we infer our attitudes by observing our own behaviour, just as an outside observer would. "I keep eating salad, so I must like salad." Where dissonance theory relies on inner tension, self-perception relies on cool self-observation. Both survive; dissonance better explains cases involving clear conflict, self-perception better explains cases where the attitude was weak or unclear to begin with. 12.5 Social Cognition and Attribution Attribution is the process of explaining the causes of behaviour, our own and others'. The founder of attribution theory was the Austrian-American psychologist Fritz Heider , who described ordinary people as naive psychologists or naive scientists constantly trying to work out why others act as they do. Heider drew the central distinction of the whole field: we attribute behaviour either to internal (dispositional) causes, such as personality, effort, or attitude, or to external (situational) causes, such as luck, task difficulty, or social pressure. Who → what. Fritz Heider (1958) founded attribution theory and the internal-versus-external distinction that organises it. Kelley's Covariation Model The American psychologist Harold Kelley systematised how people decide between internal and external causes. His covariation model says we act like statisticians, watching how behaviour "covaries" with possible causes across three dimensions. Consensus: do other people behave the same way toward this stimulus? If everyone laughs at the comedian, consensus is high. Consistency: does this person behave the same way across time and situations? If she always laughs at him, consistency is high. Distinctiveness: does the person behave this way only toward this stimulus? If she laughs only at this comedian, distinctiveness is high. High consensus, high consistency, and high distinctiveness together point to an external attribution (it is the comedian). Low consensus, high consistency, and low distinctiveness point to an internal attribution (she laughs at everything). Attributional Biases People are not the cool statisticians Kelley described; attribution is riddled with systematic errors. Fundamental attribution error (Lee Ross, 1977): the tendency, when explaining other people's behaviour, to overestimate internal dispositions and underestimate the situation. Assuming the driver who cut you off is a rude person, not someone rushing to hospital. Actor-observer bias (Edward Jones and Richard Nisbett, 1971): we attribute our own behaviour to the situation but others' behaviour to their disposition. "I failed because the exam was unfair; he failed because he is lazy." Self-serving bias: we credit our successes to internal factors (ability) but blame our failures on external factors (bad luck), protecting self-esteem. Just-world hypothesis (Melvin Lerner): the belief that the world is fundamentally fair, so people get what they deserve. This can lead to blaming the victim of misfortune, reasoning that they must somehow have brought it on themselves. Trap. Do not confuse the fundamental attribution error with the actor-observer bias. The fundamental attribution error is about over-attributing other people's behaviour to disposition. The actor-observer bias is the contrast between how we explain ourselves (situation) versus others (disposition). The actor-observer bias includes the self side; the fundamental attribution error is only about judging others. 12.6 Social Influence: Conformity Conformity is changing one's behaviour or belief to match that of a group. Two early experiments are essential. The Turkish-American psychologist Muzafer Sherif used the autokinetic effect , an optical illusion in which a stationary pinpoint of light in a dark room appears to move. Alone, participants gave widely varying estimates of how far it "moved". Placed in groups, their estimates converged on a shared group norm, and they kept using that norm even when tested alone again. Because the situation was genuinely ambiguous, this showed conformity born of uncertainty. The American psychologist Solomon Asch then asked whether people would conform even when the correct answer was obvious. In his line-judgment study (1951), a participant sat with several confederates and judged which of three comparison lines matched a standard line. The answer was clear, yet the confederates unanimously gave a wrong answer on certain trials. About 75 percent of real participants conformed to the obviously wrong majority at least once, and roughly a third of all critical responses went along with the group. Who → what. Solomon Asch (1951) showed with unambiguous line judgments that people conform to a unanimous majority even against the clear evidence of their own eyes. Why do we conform? Deutsch and Gerard distinguished two motives. Normative social influence: conforming to be liked and accepted , to avoid rejection or ridicule. This typically produces public compliance without private belief. Asch's participants privately knew the answer but went along to fit in. Informational social influence: conforming because we believe others have accurate information , especially in ambiguous situations. This produces genuine private acceptance. Sherif's participants truly did not know the answer, so they used the group as information. Trap. Match the study to the motive. Solomon Asch's clear lines produced mainly normative influence (fear of standing out). Muzafer Sherif's ambiguous light produced mainly informational influence (genuine uncertainty). Normative changes public behaviour; informational changes private belief. 12.7 Obedience to Authority Conformity is yielding to peers; obedience is yielding to a figure of authority who issues a direct command. The definitive research was conducted by the American psychologist Stanley Milgram at Yale University in the early 1960s, partly to understand how ordinary Germans had participated in the Holocaust. Participants were told they were in a "learning" experiment and were instructed by an experimenter in a lab coat to deliver electric shocks of increasing voltage to a "learner" (actually a confederate who received no real shocks) each time he made an error. The shock generator was labelled up to 450 volts and "Danger: Severe Shock". Despite the learner's scripted screams and eventual silence, a startling 65 percent of participants continued all the way to the maximum 450 volts when prodded by the experimenter's calm insistence that "the experiment requires that you continue". Milgram concluded that ordinary people will inflict serious harm on an innocent person when instructed by a legitimate authority. Obedience rose when the authority was close and prestigious, and fell when the victim was close, the authority was distant, or other "participants" rebelled. Who → what. Stanley Milgram (1963) demonstrated that about two-thirds of ordinary people would deliver apparently lethal shocks under orders from an authority figure. 12.8 Compliance Techniques Compliance is agreeing to a direct request. Researchers have catalogued reliable techniques that increase it. Foot-in-the-door (Jonathan Freedman and Scott Fraser, 1966): secure agreement to a small request first, then a larger one. Having complied once, people wish to appear consistent. Agreeing to display a small sign, then a large billboard. Door-in-the-face (Robert Cialdini and colleagues, 1975): make a large, unreasonable request that is refused, then follow with the smaller request you actually wanted. The concession triggers reciprocity. "Volunteer for two years?" No. "Then just one afternoon?" Yes. Low-balling: get commitment to an attractive offer, then reveal added costs. Because people have already committed, many stay in. Agreeing to a car price, then being told fees were "forgotten". 12.9 The Stanford Prison Experiment The American psychologist Philip Zimbardo extended the study of situational power in his 1971 Stanford prison experiment . Volunteer students were randomly assigned to be "guards" or "prisoners" in a simulated basement prison. Within days the guards became cruel and abusive and the prisoners became passive and distressed. The study, planned for two weeks, was halted after six days. Zimbardo argued that the situation and the assigned roles, not the personalities of the students, produced the brutality. The study is now also famous for its serious ethical and methodological criticisms, including the possibility that guards were coached toward harshness. Trap. Keep the three great social-influence studies distinct. Solomon Asch studied conformity to peers (line judgments). Stanley Milgram studied obedience to an authority (electric shocks). Philip Zimbardo studied the power of assigned roles and situations (prison simulation). Peers, authority, roles. 12.10 Group Processes Mere membership of a group changes how we perform and decide. Social Facilitation The very first social psychology experiment, by the American psychologist Norman Triplett in 1898, found that cyclists rode faster when racing against others than against the clock. Social facilitation is the tendency for the presence of others to improve performance. The American psychologist Robert Zajonc later resolved an apparent contradiction: the presence of others improves performance on simple or well-learned tasks but impairs it on complex or novel ones, because arousal strengthens the dominant response, which is correct for easy tasks and wrong for hard ones. Who → what. Norman Triplett (1898) ran arguably the first social psychology experiment; Robert Zajonc explained facilitation and impairment through arousal and the dominant response. Social Loafing The opposite can also happen. The French engineer Max Ringelmann found in the 1910s that people pulling together on a rope exerted less individual effort than when pulling alone. Social loafing is the reduction in individual effort when working in a group where personal contributions cannot be identified, because responsibility feels shared. Deindividuation and Group Polarization Deindividuation (Leon Festinger, Albert Pepitone and Theodore Newcomb, 1952) is the loss of individual self-awareness and self-restraint that can occur in a crowd, especially under anonymity, leading to impulsive and sometimes antisocial behaviour, as in riots or online mobs. Group polarization (Serge Moscovici and Marisa Zavalloni, 1969) is the tendency for group discussion to strengthen the members' initial leanings, so that a group of mildly cautious people becomes very cautious, and a group of mildly risky people becomes very risky, after debating. Groupthink The American psychologist Irving Janis coined groupthink to describe the faulty decision-making that occurs in highly cohesive groups when the desire for harmony and unanimity overrides realistic appraisal of alternatives. Symptoms include an illusion of invulnerability, self-censorship of doubts, pressure on dissenters, and the emergence of self-appointed "mindguards" who shield the group from disturbing information. Janis analysed foreign-policy fiascos such as the 1961 Bay of Pigs invasion as products of groupthink. Who → what. Irving Janis (1972) named groupthink: cohesive groups suppress dissent and reach poor decisions in pursuit of consensus. Minority Influence Influence is not only top-down. The French psychologist Serge Moscovici showed that a consistent, confident minority can, over time, convert the majority to its view. Minority influence tends to produce genuine, private, and lasting attitude change rather than mere public compliance, and is a key engine of social innovation. 12.11 Intergroup Relations: Prejudice and Its Reduction Three linked concepts describe negative intergroup responses. A stereotype is a cognitive belief that generalises characteristics to all members of a group. Prejudice is an affective negative attitude toward a group and its members. Discrimination is the behavioural expression, unfair treatment based on group membership. They map neatly onto the ABC model: stereotype (cognitive), prejudice (affective), discrimination (behavioural). Realistic Conflict Theory and Robbers Cave The Turkish-American psychologist Muzafer Sherif tested where intergroup hostility comes from in his 1954 Robbers Cave study . At a summer camp, boys were split into two groups (the "Eagles" and the "Rattlers"). Competition for scarce prizes rapidly bred hostility, name-calling, and raids. This supports realistic conflict theory : intergroup prejudice arises from real or perceived competition over limited resources. Crucially, Sherif then reduced the hostility not by mere contact but by introducing superordinate goals , shared aims (such as fixing the camp water supply) that neither group could achieve alone, forcing cooperation. Who → what. Muzafer Sherif (1954) showed with the Robbers Cave study that competition breeds prejudice (realistic conflict theory) and that superordinate goals dissolve it. Social Identity Theory The British social psychologist Henri Tajfel argued that competition is not even necessary. In his "minimal group" studies, merely categorising people into arbitrary groups was enough to make them favour their own. His social identity theory holds that part of our self-concept comes from group memberships, so we boost self-esteem by favouring the in-group and derogating the out-group . Prejudice can thus arise from the sheer act of dividing people into "us" and "them". Who → what. Henri Tajfel developed social identity theory: in-group favouritism can arise from mere categorisation, without any competition for resources. The Contact Hypothesis The American psychologist Gordon Allport proposed the contact hypothesis in 1954: prejudice can be reduced by contact between groups, but only under favourable conditions, namely equal status between the groups, common goals, intergroup cooperation, and the support of authorities or social norms. Mere contact without these conditions can even worsen hostility. 12.12 Prosocial Behaviour and the Bystander Effect Prosocial behaviour is any act intended to benefit another. Research was galvanised by the 1964 murder of Kitty Genovese in New York, which early reports claimed was witnessed by many neighbours who did nothing (later journalism corrected several details, but the psychological question endured). The American psychologists Bibb Latane and John Darley asked why. They demonstrated the bystander effect : the more people present at an emergency, the less likely any one of them is to help. The key mechanism is diffusion of responsibility : when many are present, each person feels that responsibility to act is shared and diluted, so no one acts. Additional factors are pluralistic ignorance (each bystander looks to others' inaction and concludes there is no emergency) and evaluation apprehension (fear of embarrassment if one intervenes wrongly). Latane and Darley modelled helping as a five-step decision: notice the event, interpret it as an emergency, assume responsibility, decide how to help, and then act. Who → what. Bibb Latane and John Darley (1968) identified the bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility: help becomes less likely as the number of witnesses grows. What motivates the helping that does occur? The American psychologist Daniel Batson proposed the empathy-altruism hypothesis : when we feel genuine empathy for a person in need, we are moved to help for their sake alone, a truly altruistic motive, rather than merely to relieve our own discomfort. Without empathy, helping is more likely to be egoistic, aimed at reducing our own distress or gaining reward. 12.13 Aggression Aggression is behaviour intended to harm another who is motivated to avoid the harm. One classic account is the frustration-aggression hypothesis , put forward in 1939 by the American psychologist John Dollard and colleagues, which held that frustration (the blocking of a goal) always leads to aggression, and aggression always stems from frustration. Later theorists softened this: frustration produces a readiness for aggression that may be displaced onto a substitute target or inhibited, rather than an inevitability. A second major account is the social learning of aggression, associated with the Canadian-American psychologist Albert Bandura. His "Bobo doll" studies showed that children who watched an adult beat an inflatable doll later imitated that aggression, demonstrating that aggression can be learned by observation and modelling, not only driven by frustration. 12.14 Interpersonal Attraction Finally, social psychology studies what draws people together. Several robust factors emerge. Proximity: physical or functional nearness is the strongest predictor of who becomes friends; we like those we encounter often. Mere-exposure effect: demonstrated by Robert Zajonc, repeated exposure to a stimulus, including a person, tends to increase liking for it, even without conscious recognition. Similarity: we are attracted to those who share our attitudes, values, and background; the folk idea that "opposites attract" is largely unsupported. Physical attractiveness: attractive people are liked more and, through the "halo effect" (Edward Thorndike, 1920), are assumed to possess other good qualities. Matching hypothesis (Elaine Walster and colleagues, 1966): in choosing long-term partners, people tend to pair with others of roughly similar physical attractiveness rather than always pursuing the most attractive available person. 12.15 A Table of Landmark Studies The following studies recur on entrance examinations; memorise the pairing of researcher, study, and core finding. Researcher Study Core finding Norman Triplett (1898) Cyclists racing Presence of others speeds performance (social facilitation). Max Ringelmann (1913) Rope-pulling Individual effort drops in groups (social loafing). Richard LaPiere (1934) Travelling with a Chinese couple Stated attitudes fail to predict behaviour (attitude-behaviour gap). Muzafer Sherif (1935) Autokinetic effect Groups form norms in ambiguity (informational conformity). Solomon Asch (1951) Line judgment People conform to a wrong unanimous majority (normative conformity). Muzafer Sherif (1954) Robbers Cave Competition breeds prejudice; superordinate goals reduce it. Leon Festinger & James Carlsmith (1959) Boring-task, one dollar vs twenty Insufficient justification shifts attitudes (cognitive dissonance). Stanley Milgram (1963) Obedience shock study 65 percent obeyed to maximum voltage under authority. Albert Bandura (1961) Bobo doll Aggression learned by observation and imitation. Bibb Latane & John Darley (1968) Bystander emergencies More witnesses, less helping (diffusion of responsibility). Philip Zimbardo (1971) Stanford prison Assigned roles and situation drive cruelty. Irving Janis (1972) Analysis of policy fiascos Cohesive groups suppress dissent (groupthink). Key. Social psychology's master lesson is the power of the situation : ordinary people, placed in the right circumstances, will conform against the evidence of their own eyes (Asch), obey to the point of apparent lethal harm (Milgram), adopt brutal roles (Zimbardo), and walk past emergencies (Latane and Darley). Explaining behaviour by disposition alone is the fundamental attribution error itself. Recap. Attitudes have affective, behavioural, and cognitive components; they predict behaviour only weakly (LaPiere), and can be changed by persuasion through central or peripheral routes (Richard Petty and John Cacioppo) or shifted by our own behaviour through cognitive dissonance (Festinger) or self-perception (Bem). We explain behaviour as internal or external (Fritz Heider), using consensus, consistency, and distinctiveness (Harold Kelley), but fall into the fundamental attribution error, actor-observer, self-serving, and just-world biases. Social influence spans conformity (Sherif's informational, Asch's normative), obedience (Milgram), compliance tricks, and the power of roles (Zimbardo). Groups show facilitation (Triplett, Robert Zajonc), loafing (Ringelmann), deindividuation, polarization, groupthink (Janis), and minority influence. Prejudice arises from competition (Sherif's Robbers Cave, realistic conflict) and mere categorisation (Henri Tajfel's social identity), and is reduced by superordinate goals and favourable contact (Allport). We help less in crowds (bystander effect) but more when we feel empathy (C. Daniel Batson), aggress from frustration (Dollard) and imitation (Bandura), and are attracted by proximity, mere exposure, similarity, and matching. 12.16 The complete map: every social-psychology theory and its theorist Social psychology is the general-psychology area an aptitude paper most loves to test through name-matching: a theory in one column, a theorist in the other. Why does a friend behave with such maddening consistency that you can predict, weeks in advance, exactly how they will react to bad news? The answer psychologists reach for is personality : the enduring, organised pattern of thinking, feeling, and behaving that makes a person recognisably themselves across time and across situations. This chapter walks from the oldest attempts to sort people into types, through the trait movement that counted and measured them, into the depth psychologies that looked for hidden engines, and out to the humanistic, behavioural, and Indian views that each redraw the picture. Each family answers three questions differently: what is a human being basically like, where does personality come from, and how can it be measured. Keep those three questions in mind as the theorists file past. 13.1 What personality means Gordon Allport (Gordon Willard Allport), one of the first psychologists to make personality a respectable scientific field, defined it in 1937 as "the dynamic organization within the individual of those psychophysical systems that determine his characteristic behavior and thought." Unpack that sentence slowly. Dynamic organization means personality is not a heap of separate habits but an active, changing structure. Psychophysical means it is neither purely mental nor purely bodily but both at once, rooted in the nervous system yet expressed in thought. Determine means personality is causal: it actually produces behaviour, it is not just a label pasted on afterwards. Characteristic means it captures what is typical and distinctive about this one person. Who → what. Gordon Allport → gave psychology its working definition of personality (1937) and launched the modern trait approach; insisted each person is finally unique. Two research strategies flow from this. The nomothetic approach (from the Greek nomos , law) looks for general laws that apply to everyone, placing each person on the same set of dimensions so people can be compared, ranked, and correlated. The idiographic approach (from idios , one's own) studies the single individual in depth, seeking the pattern that is true of this person and perhaps no other. A questionnaire that scores you on five universal traits is nomothetic; a long case study of one life is idiographic. Allport valued both and warned against letting the search for averages erase the individual. Key. Nomothetic = universal laws, comparison across people (traits, tests). Idiographic = the unique whole person, studied in depth (case study). Good personality science needs both. The determinants of personality are usually grouped as biological (genes, temperament, hormones, brain), environmental and cultural (family, upbringing, society, language), and situational (the demands of the moment). The great debates in this chapter are largely arguments about which determinant matters most and how they combine. 13.2 Type theories: sorting people into kinds The oldest idea is that people come in a small number of types , discrete categories you either belong to or do not. It is intuitive but crude, because real people shade into one another rather than falling into neat boxes. The four-humour theory descends from the Greek physician Hippocrates (Hippocrates of Kos, around 400 BCE) and was systematised by the Roman physician Galen (Aelius Galenus, second century CE). They held that the body contains four fluids or humours, and that the one in excess sets the temperament: too much blood makes a sanguine person (cheerful, sociable), yellow bile a choleric person (irritable, driven), black bile a melancholic person (sad, thoughtful), and phlegm a phlegmatic person (calm, sluggish). The physiology is long dead, but the four labels survive because they name recognisable moods. Who → what. Hippocrates → proposed the four humours; Galen → turned them into the four temperaments (sanguine, choleric, melancholic, phlegmatic), the ancestor of all type theory. Two twentieth-century theories tied personality to body build. The German psychiatrist Ernst Kretschmer proposed that slender asthenic (or leptosomic) builds tend toward a withdrawn, schizoid temperament, while short round pyknic builds tend toward the sociable, mood-swinging cyclothymic temperament, with a muscular athletic type in between. The American psychologist William Sheldon (William Herbert Sheldon) rebuilt this into somatotype theory, rating each body on three dimensions: Endomorphy → soft, round build; the temperament he called viscerotonia , relaxed, sociable, food-loving. Mesomorphy → hard, muscular build; somatotonia , energetic, assertive, adventurous. Ectomorphy → thin, fragile build; cerebrotonia , restrained, private, intellectual. Trap. William Sheldon's and Ernst Kretschmer's body-type claims sound scientific but are largely discredited; the correlations were weak and the method biased. Know them as historically important type theories, not as established facts. Carl Jung (Carl Gustav Jung) contributed the single most durable type distinction: introversion versus extraversion . The introvert's psychic energy flows inward toward thoughts and feelings; the extravert's flows outward toward people and things. Jung meant these as tendencies, not rigid boxes, and this pair later became a cornerstone of the trait theories in section 13.3. Finally, the American cardiologists Meyer Friedman and Ray Rosenman described the Type A and Type B behaviour patterns. Type A people are competitive, impatient, time-pressured, and easily angered; Type B people are relaxed and easy-going. Their notable finding, from observing heart patients, was that Type A behaviour is linked to higher risk of coronary heart disease, making this a rare type theory with real medical weight (the hostility component especially). Who → what. Meyer Friedman & Ray Rosenman → the Type A / Type B behaviour patterns; Type A (hurried, hostile, competitive) linked to heart disease. 13.3 Trait theories: measuring the dimensions Trait theorists abandoned discrete boxes for continuous dimensions . A trait is a relatively stable disposition to behave in a certain way across situations; everyone has some amount of every trait, so we differ in degree, not in kind. The question became: how many traits are there, and which are basic? Gordon Allport's traits Allport distinguished three levels. A cardinal trait is a single ruling passion so dominant it organises a whole life, so strong the person's name becomes an adjective (a "scrooge," a "narcissist"); most people have none. Central traits are the five to ten characteristic qualities you would list to describe a friend (honest, anxious, generous). Secondary traits are narrow preferences that surface only in particular contexts (nervous in exams, fond of spicy food). Key. Allport's three levels: cardinal (one all-dominating trait, rare) > central (the handful that define you) > secondary (situation-specific quirks). Raymond Cattell and factor analysis The British-American psychologist Raymond Cattell (Raymond Bernard Cattell) brought statistics to the problem. He used factor analysis , a technique that scans a large table of correlations and finds the smaller number of underlying dimensions that account for how the measured variables cluster together. Cattell distinguished surface traits , clusters of behaviour that visibly go together, from source traits , the deeper underlying factors that cause those clusters. Factor-analysing thousands of trait words, he arrived at 16 source traits and built the 16 Personality Factor Questionnaire (16PF) to measure them (for example, reserved vs outgoing, trusting vs suspicious, relaxed vs tense). Who → what. Raymond Cattell → used factor analysis to reduce personality to 16 source traits; built the 16PF; distinguished surface traits (visible clusters) from source traits (underlying causes). Hans Eysenck and the PEN model The German-British psychologist Hans Eysenck (Hans Jurgen Eysenck) argued Cattell's sixteen factors were too many and themselves correlated; a smaller set of broad, biologically grounded super-factors would do. His PEN model has three: Extraversion vs Introversion (E) → sociable and stimulation-seeking vs quiet and reserved. Eysenck rooted this in cortical arousal : introverts have naturally higher baseline brain arousal, so they seek less external stimulation to feel comfortable, while extraverts are chronically under-aroused and hunt for excitement. Neuroticism vs Stability (N) → anxious, moody, and reactive vs calm and even. He tied this to reactivity of the autonomic nervous system. Psychoticism (P) → a later-added dimension of tough-mindedness, aggression, and cold non-conformity, linked tentatively to testosterone. Eysenck's insistence on a biological basis and on a very few broad dimensions is his signature. His E and N dimensions have held up extremely well in later research. Who → what. Hans Eysenck → the PEN model (Psychoticism, Extraversion, Neuroticism); argued personality has a biological, inherited basis (introverts = higher cortical arousal). The Big Five (Five Factor Model) Decades of factor-analytic work by many researchers, brought to prominence by Paul Costa (Paul T. Costa Jr.) and Robert McCrae (Robert R. McCrae), converged on five broad factors, remembered by the acronym OCEAN : O penness to experience → imaginative, curious, unconventional vs practical and conventional. C onscientiousness → organised, disciplined, dependable vs careless and impulsive. E xtraversion → sociable, energetic, assertive vs reserved. A greeableness → kind, trusting, cooperative vs hostile and suspicious. N euroticism → anxious, emotionally unstable vs calm (its opposite pole is emotional stability). The model rests on the lexical hypothesis : the idea that the most important individual differences have, over history, become encoded as single words in ordinary language, so that analysing the trait-adjectives of a language will reveal the true structure of personality. The Big Five is today the most widely accepted framework, measured by the NEO-PI (NEO Personality Inventory). It sits neatly between Cattell's sixteen and Eysenck's three: Eysenck's E and N reappear, while his single P roughly splits into low Conscientiousness and low Agreeableness, and Openness is added. Trap. Do not confuse the counts. Raymond Cattell = 16 factors, Hans Eysenck (PEN) = 3, Big Five / Costa & Robert McCrae = 5. All three used factor analysis; they disagree only on how many factors best summarise the data. Why. The numbers differ because factor analysis lets the researcher choose how broadly to group. Slice finely and you get Cattell's 16; group into the broadest possible super-factors and you get Eysenck's 3; the Big Five is the middle level most researchers find replicates best across cultures and languages. 13.4 Psychodynamic theories: the hidden engine Where trait theory describes the surface, psychodynamic theory hunts for the hidden forces beneath. It begins with Sigmund Freud (Sigmund Freud, Austrian neurologist, founder of psychoanalysis). Freud's structure of the mind Freud pictured the mind at two angles. The topographic model divides awareness into the conscious (what you are aware of right now), the preconscious (what you could easily call to mind, like your phone number), and the unconscious (wishes, fears, and memories kept out of awareness by force, yet still driving behaviour). The structural model divides the personality into three agencies: Id → present from birth, entirely unconscious, the reservoir of instinctual drives; it runs on the pleasure principle , demanding immediate gratification. Ego → the executive that develops to deal with reality; it runs on the reality principle , delaying gratification until it is safe and appropriate, mediating between id, superego, and world. Superego → the internalised moral authority, the conscience and the ego-ideal, absorbed from parents and society; it judges and punishes with guilt. When the ego is overwhelmed by conflict between these agencies it feels anxiety , and it protects itself with defence mechanisms , unconscious strategies that distort reality to reduce distress: repression (pushing threats out of awareness), projection (attributing one's own unacceptable impulses to others), denial , displacement (redirecting an impulse to a safer target), rationalisation (inventing acceptable reasons), reaction formation (acting the opposite of a forbidden urge), regression , and sublimation (channelling impulses into socially valued work). Freud's psychosexual stages (oral, anal, phallic, latency, genital) are treated in the developmental chapter and only noted here. Who → what. Sigmund Freud → founded psychoanalysis; id / ego / superego; conscious / preconscious / unconscious; defence mechanisms; personality driven mostly by unconscious sexual and aggressive instincts. Carl Jung's analytical psychology Carl Jung broke from Freud and founded analytical psychology . He accepted a personal unconscious but added a deeper collective unconscious , a layer inherited by all humans containing archetypes , universal images and themes that recur across myths and cultures. Key archetypes include the persona (the social mask we present), the shadow (the dark, denied side of the self), the anima (the feminine element in a man) and the animus (the masculine element in a woman), and the self (the archetype of wholeness and integration). Jung saw motivation as more than sexual; he described a general life energy and the lifelong process of individuation , becoming a whole, integrated person. Who → what. Carl Jung → analytical psychology; the collective unconscious and its archetypes (persona, shadow, anima, animus, self); introversion/extraversion; broke with Freud over the sexual emphasis. Alfred Adler's individual psychology Alfred Adler (Austrian physician) founded individual psychology . For him the master motive is not sex but the drive to overcome a universal childhood inferiority . Every child begins small and helpless; this inferiority feeling spurs a lifelong striving for superiority , meaning striving for competence, mastery, and completion. When this goes wrong it hardens into an inferiority complex (paralysing self-doubt) or a compensating superiority complex (arrogant over-striving). Each person develops a unique style of life , an overall strategy for pursuing their goals, shaped early on. Adler stressed birth order (first-borns dethroned by a sibling, pampered youngest children, and so on) as one influence on that style, and made social interest ( Gemeinschaftsgefuhl ), a feeling of connection with and concern for humanity, his mark of psychological health. Who → what. Alfred Adler → individual psychology; inferiority and the striving for superiority; style of life; birth order; social interest as the sign of health. Trap. The favourite exam question contrasts the three depth theorists on motivation. Sigmund Freud → unconscious sexual/aggressive drives (pleasure); Carl Jung → the collective unconscious and individuation (broader spiritual energy); Alfred Adler → overcoming inferiority and striving for superiority (conscious goals and social interest, NOT sex). Freud's unconscious is a seething cauldron; Adler barely uses the unconscious at all. Karen Horney and the neo-Freudians Karen Horney (German-American psychoanalyst, pronounced HORN-eye) argued personality is shaped less by instinct than by the child's social relationships. Her central concept is basic anxiety : the feeling of being isolated and helpless in a potentially hostile world, arising when parents fail to meet a child's need for safety. To cope, people develop ten neurotic needs (for affection, for a partner, for power, for prestige, and so on), which she grouped into three broad interpersonal styles: Moving toward people → the compliant, self-effacing solution: winning safety through love and approval. Moving against people → the aggressive, expansive solution: winning safety through power and control. Moving away from people → the detached solution: winning safety through withdrawal and self-sufficiency. The healthy person uses all three flexibly; the neurotic is locked rigidly into one. Horney also delivered a famous feminist critique of Freud : she rejected his idea of penis envy as the core of feminine psychology, arguing that women's frustrations come from real social and cultural disadvantage, not anatomy, and she countered with the notion of male "womb envy" of women's power to bear children. Who → what. Karen Horney → basic anxiety; ten neurotic needs grouped as moving toward / against / away from people; challenged Freud's penis-envy account of women, blaming culture not anatomy. Erich Fromm (German social psychologist) extended this social emphasis, arguing that modern freedom brings isolation, so people often "escape from freedom" into conformity, submission, or destructiveness rather than face the burden of choosing for themselves. Alongside these thinkers, the object-relations school (associated with Melanie Klein, W.R.D. Fairbairn, and Donald Winnicott) shifted the focus from drives to the infant's earliest relationships with caregivers, the internalised "objects" that become templates for all later relationships. These are noted briefly; the thread they share is the move away from Freud's biology toward the social and relational. 13.5 Humanistic theories: growth and the self Humanistic psychology, the "third force" after psychoanalysis and behaviourism (John B. Watson, 1913), rejected the view of humans as either bundles of dark instincts or passive products of conditioning. It sees people as basically good, free, and driven toward growth. Carl Rogers (Carl Ransom Rogers) built his theory around the self-concept , the organised set of beliefs a person holds about who they are. He distinguished the real self (who you actually are) from the ideal self (who you wish to be); a wide gap between them, called incongruence , breeds distress, while a close match, congruence , marks health. Children develop conditions of worth when love is made conditional on behaving as others demand ("I will love you only if..."), and they then distort their experience to keep that approval. The antidote is unconditional positive regard , being accepted and valued without conditions, which frees a person to grow into the fully functioning person : open to experience, living in the present, trusting themselves, and free. Who → what. Carl Rogers → the self-concept; real vs ideal self; conditions of worth; unconditional positive regard; the fully functioning person; founder of client-centred therapy. Abraham Maslow (Abraham Harold Maslow) is best known for his hierarchy of needs (treated in the motivation chapter) topped by self-actualization , the drive to fulfil one's unique potential and become all one is capable of becoming. He studied psychologically healthy, high-achieving people and found they shared traits like realism, acceptance, autonomy, and creativity, and that they reported peak experiences , moments of intense joy, wonder, and self-transcendence in which they felt whole and at one with the world. Who → what. Abraham Maslow → self-actualization at the top of the needs hierarchy; studied healthy people; peak experiences. 13.6 Behavioural and social-cognitive theories This family locates personality not inside the person but in learning and situations. For B.F. Skinner (Burrhus Frederic Skinner) and radical behaviourism , "personality" is not a real inner thing at all; it is simply the collection of learned behaviour patterns a person's reinforcement history has shaped. There is no need to postulate an inner self, traits, or unconscious: change the reinforcement contingencies and you change the person. What we call a "trait" is just a habit that has been rewarded consistently. Who → what. B.F. Skinner → radical behaviourism; personality = learned behaviour shaped by reinforcement history; no inner self needed. Later theorists softened this by putting thought back in. Albert Bandura (Canadian-American psychologist) proposed reciprocal determinism : the person (their thoughts and beliefs), their behaviour, and the environment all influence one another in a continuous three-way loop, rather than the environment simply stamping the person. His most influential concept is self-efficacy , a person's belief in their own capability to succeed at a specific task; high self-efficacy leads people to attempt more, persist longer, and recover from failure faster. Who → what. Albert Bandura → social-cognitive theory; reciprocal determinism (person, behaviour, environment loop); self-efficacy (belief in one's own capability). Julian Rotter (Julian Bernard Rotter) added locus of control , a person's generalised belief about what controls the outcomes in their life. Those with an internal locus believe outcomes flow from their own effort and choices; those with an external locus believe outcomes are ruled by luck, fate, or powerful others. Rotter also stressed expectancy : whether we perform a behaviour depends on how much we expect it to bring a reward we value. Walter Mischel (Austrian-American psychologist) lit the fuse of the person-situation debate by showing, in 1968, that broad traits often predict behaviour poorly because behaviour varies so much across situations; a person "honest" on a test may cheat at cards. He argued we must weigh the situation, not just the trait. Mischel is also famous for the delay of gratification studies, the marshmallow test , in which young children who could resist eating one marshmallow now to earn two later tended to show better outcomes years afterward, a demonstration of self-regulation as a stable and consequential personal quality. Who → what. Julian Rotter → locus of control (internal vs external) and expectancy. Walter Mischel → the person-situation debate; the marshmallow test of delayed gratification. 13.7 Indian perspectives on personality Indian thought approaches personality through the triguna , the theory of three fundamental qualities ( gunas ) that constitute all of nature ( prakriti ) and combine in different proportions in every person: Sattva → the quality of purity, clarity, balance, calm, wisdom, and goodness. Rajas → the quality of activity, passion, restlessness, ambition, and desire. Tamas → the quality of inertia, dullness, ignorance, and lethargy. Every personality is a shifting blend of the three, and the balance can be cultivated, for example toward greater sattva, through disciplined living. Unlike Western trait models, the triguna is embedded in a moral and spiritual framework aimed at growth. The Indian concept of self also differs sharply from the Western: where much Western theory centres a bounded individual ego, Indian thought distinguishes the everyday, socially embedded, changeable self ( ahankara , the "I-maker") from a deeper, unchanging true self ( atman ), and treats the good life as gradually loosening identification with the surface ego. This gives Indian personality psychology an idiographic, developmental, and transcendent flavour that complements the nomothetic Western tests. Key. Triguna: Sattva (calm clarity) · Rajas (restless activity) · Tamas (dull inertia). Everyone is a blend; the aim is to cultivate sattva. 13.8 The four paradigms compared Step back and the whole chapter sorts into four great paradigms. This table answers the three opening questions for each. Paradigm View of human nature Source of personality Key figures How assessed Psychodynamic Driven by hidden, often irrational unconscious forces; conflict-ridden Early childhood; unconscious drives and conflicts Sigmund Freud, Carl Jung, Alfred Adler, Horney, Erich Fromm Projective tests (Rorschach, TAT), free association, dream analysis Trait Describable by stable, measurable dimensions; consistent across situations Largely inherited biology plus environment; enduring dispositions Gordon Allport, Raymond Cattell, Hans Eysenck, Costa & Robert McCrae Self-report questionnaires (16PF, EPQ, NEO-PI); factor analysis Humanistic Basically good, free, and growth-seeking; conscious and self-aware The self-concept and the drive toward self-actualization Rogers, Abraham Maslow Q-sort, self-concept scales, interviews, personal experience Behavioural / social-cognitive Shaped by learning and situations; malleable, not fixed Reinforcement history; learning; beliefs and the environment B. F. Skinner, Albert Bandura, Rotter, Walter Mischel Direct behavioural observation; situation-specific measures; self-efficacy scales Why. No single paradigm is simply right. Each captures something real: the trait view predicts and compares well, the psychodynamic view illuminates inner conflict, the humanistic view honours growth and freedom, and the behavioural view explains change. A complete picture of a person borrows from all four. 13.9 How personality is measured Two broad testing traditions match the paradigms. Objective (self-report) tests present clear statements the person rates about themselves; they are easy to score and standardised. Examples include Cattell's 16PF , Eysenck's EPQ (Eysenck Personality Questionnaire), the Big Five NEO-PI , and the widely used clinical inventory the MMPI (Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory). Projective tests , favoured by the psychodynamic school, present ambiguous stimuli on the assumption that people "project" their hidden inner world onto them: the Rorschach inkblot test (Hermann Rorschach) and the Thematic Apperception Test (TAT) (Henry Murray and Christiana Morgan), in which the person makes up stories about pictures. Objective tests are reliable but can be faked; projective tests are rich but hard to score reliably. Trap. Match the test to the school. Projective tests (Rorschach, TAT) = psychodynamic. Self-report inventories (16PF, EPQ, NEO-PI, MMPI) = trait/objective. Mixing these up is a classic exam slip. Recap. Personality is the enduring pattern that makes a person recognisably themselves (Gordon Allport), studied nomothetically (universal dimensions) or idiographically (the unique individual). Type theories sort people into kinds (four humours of Hippocrates and Galen; Ernst Kretschmer's and William Sheldon's body types; Carl Jung's introvert/extravert; Friedman and Rosenman's Type A/B). Trait theories place everyone on continuous dimensions and disagree only on the count: Allport's cardinal/central/secondary, Cattell's 16 source traits, Eysenck's 3 (PEN, biologically based), and the Big Five/OCEAN of Paul Costa and Robert McCrae built on the lexical hypothesis. Psychodynamic theories seek hidden engines: Sigmund Freud's id/ego/superego and unconscious drives, Jung's collective unconscious and archetypes, Alfred Adler's striving to overcome inferiority, Karen Horney's basic anxiety and moving toward/against/away. Humanistic theories stress growth: Carl Rogers's self-concept, conditions of worth, and unconditional positive regard, and Abraham Maslow's self-actualization and peak experiences. Behavioural and social-cognitive theories stress learning and situation: B. F. Skinner's reinforcement, Albert Bandura's reciprocal determinism and self-efficacy, Julian Rotter's locus of control, Walter Mischel's person-situation debate and marshmallow test. Indian thought adds the triguna (sattva, rajas, tamas) and a layered self. Four paradigms, four answers, one person. 13.10 The complete map: every theory of personality and its theorist Personality items in an aptitude paper are almost always match-the-theory-to-the-theorist. This roster gathers, in one place, the full set of personality theories you could be asked to name, grouped into four families and numbered continuously. Skim the core-idea column until each name and its one-line signature stick. Key. Read every row as theorist plus signature idea, not as a definition to memorise word for word. Names in bold are the label examiners use; the person in bold beside it is who to write on the line. Full names are given first so a first-initial-only option cannot trip you.
