Watch the near-neighbours: Sigmund Freud is psychosexual while Erik Erikson is psychosocial; Carl Jung's collective unconscious is not Alfred Adler's inferiority; Cattell's 16 factors, Eysenck's 3 and the Big Five are three different counts, so match the number to the name. William Sheldon gives somatotypes but Ernst Kretschmer gives constitutional types, and Julian Rotter's locus of control is often mis-tagged to Albert Bandura. Recap. Four families cover the field: psychodynamic (Freud, Jung, Adler, Horney, Sullivan, Fromm, Erikson, object relations, self psychology); trait and type (Allport, Cattell, Eysenck, Big Five, HEXACO, Sheldon, Kretschmer, Gray, Cloninger); humanistic (Maslow, Rogers, Kelly, Murray, May); and social-cognitive and behavioural (Bandura, Mischel, Rotter, Skinner, McAdams). Fix the theorist to the one-line signature and the match items answer themselves. 14 Intelligence Intelligence is one of the oldest and most argued-over ideas in psychology. Everyone recognises it in daily life: the friend who grasps a new game in minutes, the child who reasons her way out of a problem no one taught her, the elder whose store of knowledge seems bottomless. Yet turning that everyday recognition into a precise scientific definition, and then into a number, has kept psychologists busy for more than a century. This chapter builds the concept from the ground up. It asks what intelligence is , surveys the major theories that describe its structure, explains where the familiar IQ score comes from, looks at the two extremes of the distribution, weighs the heredity-versus-environment debate, and closes with newer ideas such as emotional intelligence (Peter Salovey and John Mayer, 1990) and creativity. The actual test batteries used to measure intelligence (the Wechsler scales, the Binet-Kamat, the Bhatia battery, and so on) are treated in the assessment chapter; here the focus stays on theory and concept . 14.1 What is intelligence? There is no single agreed definition. Different psychologists have emphasised different things, which is itself a clue that intelligence is not one simple property but a bundle of related capacities. Who → what. Alfred Binet (French psychologist, 1857–1911) treated intelligence practically, as good judgement, comprehension and reasoning, the ability to adapt one's thinking to a goal and to criticise one's own conclusions. Who → what. David Wechsler (Romanian-American psychologist, 1896–1981) gave the most quoted textbook definition: intelligence is "the global capacity of the individual to act purposefully, to think rationally, and to deal effectively with his environment." The word global matters: he saw intelligence as an overall capacity built from many specific abilities plus non-intellectual factors such as drive and persistence. A famous half-joke, often attributed to Edwin Boring , defines intelligence as "whatever intelligence tests measure." It sounds circular, but it flags a real point: for a long time the concept was pinned to the tests rather than the other way round. Most modern definitions converge on a few recurring elements: the ability to learn from experience, to reason and solve problems, to think abstractly, and to adapt to new situations. Key. Definitions of intelligence cluster around four themes: learning from experience, abstract reasoning, problem solving, and adaptation to the environment. No one definition is "correct"; each theory below picks which of these to foreground. 14.2 Psychometric and factor theories The psychometric approach studies intelligence by measuring people on many tasks and then using factor analysis (a statistical method that finds clusters of test items which rise and fall together) to infer the underlying abilities. This is where the debate over "one intelligence versus many" was first fought with numbers. 14.2.1 Spearman's two-factor theory Who → what. Charles Spearman (English psychologist, 1863–1945) noticed that people who do well on one mental test tend to do well on others. This tendency for all cognitive tests to correlate positively he called the positive manifold . To explain it, Spearman proposed that every test performance draws on two factors. The first is g , a general factor of mental energy or power that runs through all intellectual tasks. The second is s , a specific factor unique to each particular task (verbal, numerical, spatial and so on). Doing well on an arithmetic test, for example, uses your general g plus the s specific to arithmetic. Spearman is remembered as the founder of the idea of general intelligence , and g remains one of the most robust findings in the field. Key. In Spearman's model, every ability = g (shared across all tasks) + s (unique to that one task). The positive manifold is the evidence for g . 14.2.2 Thurstone's primary mental abilities Who → what. Louis Leon Thurstone (American psychologist, 1887–1955) challenged Spearman. Using a different factor-analytic method, he argued intelligence is not one general factor but a set of independent primary mental abilities (PMAs). Thurstone described seven such abilities: verbal comprehension , word fluency , number (arithmetic), spatial visualisation , associative memory , perceptual speed , and inductive reasoning . In his view, describing a person by a single IQ number wastes information; a profile across the seven PMAs is more faithful. Later analyses showed the PMAs themselves correlate, which actually points back towards a higher-order g , and Thurstone eventually accepted a place for it. The Spearman–Thurstone disagreement (one factor versus several) set the template for a debate that still runs. 14.2.3 Cattell's fluid and crystallized intelligence Who → what. Raymond Bernard Cattell (British-American psychologist, 1905–1998), a student of Spearman, split g into two broad factors. Fluid intelligence (Gf) is the capacity to reason, see patterns and solve novel problems independent of learned knowledge . It is what you use on a puzzle you have never seen. It peaks in early adulthood and gradually declines with age, and is sensitive to biological factors. Crystallized intelligence (Gc) is the store of knowledge, vocabulary and skills acquired through education and experience . It is culture-loaded and, importantly, it holds steady or even grows into old age. The distinction elegantly explains why an older adult can be slower on an unfamiliar reasoning puzzle (declining Gf) yet richer in general knowledge and judgement (intact Gc). Cattell's collaborator John Leonard Horn extended the model to many more broad factors. Trap. Fluid versus crystallized is easy to reverse. Fluid = on-the-spot reasoning with novel material, declines with age. Crystallized = accumulated knowledge , stays or grows with age. A memory hook: crystals build up slowly over time, like your knowledge. 14.2.4 Vernon's hierarchical model Who → what. Philip Ewart Vernon (English psychologist, 1905–1987) reconciled Spearman and Thurstone with a hierarchy . At the top sits g . Below it, g splits into two major group factors: v:ed (verbal-educational) and k:m (spatial-mechanical-practical). Each of these divides into minor group factors, and those into specific factors at the bottom. This arrangement showed that "one g " and "many abilities" are not rivals; abilities can be layered, general at the top and increasingly specific toward the base. 14.2.5 Guilford's Structure of Intellect Who → what. Joy Paul Guilford (American psychologist, 1897–1987) rejected g entirely and proposed a three-dimensional model, the Structure of Intellect (SOI) . Guilford argued that any intellectual act can be classified along three axes: Operations (what the mind does): cognition, memory, divergent production, convergent production, and evaluation. Contents (the kind of material): figural, symbolic, semantic, and behavioural. Products (the form of the result): units, classes, relations, systems, transformations, and implications. Multiplying the categories (originally 5 × 4 × 6) yielded 120 distinct abilities , later expanded by Guilford to 150 and beyond. Critics found the model unwieldy and hard to validate, but it was hugely influential in one respect: its divergent production operation put creativity firmly on the map (see 14.9). 14.2.6 The Cattell-Horn-Carroll synthesis Modern psychometrics has largely converged on the Cattell-Horn-Carroll (CHC) theory, which merges Cattell and Horn's Gf-Gc work with John Bissell Carroll 's three-stratum model. CHC pictures intelligence in three layers: a general g at the top (stratum III), around ten broad abilities in the middle (stratum II, such as Gf, Gc, memory, processing speed), and many narrow abilities at the base (stratum I). CHC now underlies the design of most contemporary intelligence tests. 14.3 Systems and modern theories Dissatisfied with a single number, several theorists in the late twentieth century argued intelligence is broader than what school-style tests capture. 14.3.1 Gardner's multiple intelligences Who → what. Howard Earl Gardner (American psychologist, born 1943) proposed the theory of multiple intelligences in 1983, arguing there are several relatively independent intelligences, each with its own brain basis, rather than one general ability. His original list contained seven, later expanded: Linguistic (words and language) Logical-mathematical (reasoning, numbers, logic) Spatial (visualising, navigating) Musical (rhythm, pitch, tone) Bodily-kinesthetic (body control, athletics, dance) Interpersonal (understanding others) Intrapersonal (understanding oneself) Naturalistic (recognising patterns in nature), added later Gardner also floated a possible existential intelligence. The theory is popular among educators because it validates non-academic talents, but critics note it lacks strong psychometric support and that Gardner's "intelligences" may be better described as talents or aptitudes. 14.3.2 Sternberg's triarchic theory Who → what. Robert Jeffrey Sternberg (American psychologist, born 1949) proposed the triarchic theory , dividing intelligence into three interacting aspects. Analytical (componential) intelligence: the reasoning and evaluating abilities that IQ tests already measure. Creative (experiential) intelligence: dealing with novelty and automatising familiar tasks; insight and invention. Practical (contextual) intelligence: "street smarts", the ability to adapt to, shape or select real-world environments, drawing on tacit knowledge that is rarely taught explicitly. Sternberg later folded these into the idea of successful intelligence : the ability to set and reach personally meaningful goals in one's cultural context by capitalising on strengths and correcting weaknesses, balancing analytical, creative and practical skills. 14.3.3 The PASS theory Who → what. Jagannath Prasad Das (Indian-Canadian psychologist), with J.A. Naglieri and J.R. Kirby, built the PASS theory of intelligence on the neuropsychology of Alexander Romanovich Luria (Russian neuropsychologist, 1902–1977). PASS names four cognitive processes rooted in Luria's functional units of the brain: Planning : setting goals, choosing and monitoring strategies (frontal lobes). Attention : arousal and focused, selective attention (brainstem and lower structures). Simultaneous processing: integrating separate pieces into a whole, as in spatial reasoning (occipital-parietal region). Successive processing: handling information in serial order, as in language and sequencing (frontotemporal region). PASS is notable for grounding intelligence in brain function and for underlying the CAS (Cognitive Assessment System). It carries special weight in Indian syllabi because of Das's central role. 14.4 Comparison of the major theories Theorist Structure proposed One-line idea Charles Spearman g + specific factors (s) One general factor runs through all mental tasks. Louis Thurstone Seven primary mental abilities Intelligence is several independent abilities, not one. Raymond Cattell Fluid (Gf) and crystallized (Gc) Split g into on-the-spot reasoning versus learned knowledge. Philip Vernon Hierarchy: g → v:ed & k:m → specifics General and specific abilities are layered, not rivals. J.P. Guilford Structure of Intellect (120+ cells) Operations × contents × products; no g. Cattell-Horn-Carroll Three strata: g / broad / narrow Modern synthesis behind most current tests. Howard Gardner Eight (or more) multiple intelligences Many independent, domain-specific intelligences. Robert Sternberg Triarchic: analytical, creative, practical Successful intelligence balances three real-world aspects. J.P. Das (after Alexander Luria) PASS: planning, attention, simultaneous, successive Intelligence as four brain-based cognitive processes. Trap. g versus multiple intelligences is a classic exam contrast. Spearman (and later CHC) keep a unifying g ; Thurstone, J. P. Guilford and Howard Gardner emphasise many distinct abilities and downplay or reject a single general factor. Don't attribute "multiple intelligences" to Robert Sternberg (his is the triarchic theory) or to Thurstone (his are "primary mental abilities"); the phrase belongs to Gardner. 14.5 The IQ concept The intelligence quotient (IQ) is a score that expresses how a person's test performance compares with others. Its history explains why the modern number no longer literally involves a "quotient". 14.5.1 Mental age Who → what. Alfred Binet and Theodore Simon (French physician, 1873–1961) built the first practical intelligence scale in 1905 to identify Parisian schoolchildren who needed extra help. They introduced mental age (MA) : a child who solves the items that an average eight-year-old solves has a mental age of 8, whatever their actual age. 14.5.2 The ratio IQ Who → what. William Stern (German psychologist, 1871–1938) turned mental age into a single ratio, later multiplied by 100 by Lewis Terman : the ratio IQ . The formula is: IQ = (mental age ÷ chronological age) × 100 . A ten-year-old (chronological age 10) with a mental age of 12 has an IQ of (12 ÷ 10) × 100 = 120 . If mental age equals chronological age, IQ is exactly 100, the average by definition. Why. The ratio IQ works well for children but breaks down for adults. Mental growth flattens after adolescence while chronological age keeps rising, so the ratio would make every adult look as though their IQ is falling year on year. That flaw is exactly what the deviation IQ was invented to fix. 14.5.3 The deviation IQ Who → what. David Wechsler replaced the ratio with the deviation IQ : a score based on how far a person deviates from the average of their own age group, expressed in standard-deviation units. The deviation IQ is set so the mean is 100 and (on the Wechsler scales) the standard deviation is 15 . Your IQ now says where you stand relative to same-age peers, not a ratio of mental to chronological age. Nearly all modern tests use deviation IQs. Trap. Ratio IQ (Stern/Terman, MA ÷ CA × 100) is not the same as deviation IQ (Wechsler, standard scores against an age group). If a question gives you mental age and chronological age and asks you to compute, it wants the ratio formula. If it talks about mean 100 and SD 15, it means the deviation IQ. 14.5.4 The normal distribution and classification IQ scores in the population follow, closely, the normal distribution (the symmetric bell curve). With a mean of 100 and SD of 15, about 68% of people score between 85 and 115, and about 95% between 70 and 130. Scores are grouped into descriptive bands. Approximate IQ range Classification 130 and above Very superior / gifted 120–129 Superior 110–119 High average 90–109 Average 80–89 Low average 70–79 Borderline Below 70 Intellectual disability range Key. Modern IQ: mean 100, SD 15, normally distributed. About two-thirds of people fall between 85 and 115. The exact band labels vary a little across manuals, so learn the structure rather than memorising every boundary. 14.6 The two extremes 14.6.1 Intellectual disability Intellectual disability (formerly "mental retardation") is diagnosed when there are significant limitations in both intellectual functioning (reasoning, problem solving, roughly IQ below 70) and adaptive behaviour (everyday conceptual, social and practical skills), with onset during the developmental period. Both criteria must be met; a low IQ alone is not enough. Traditional severity levels, keyed to IQ, are: Level Approx. IQ range Mild 50–69 Moderate 35–49 Severe 20–34 Profound Below 20 Current diagnostic systems (DSM-5, ICD-11) now define severity mainly by the level of adaptive functioning support the person needs rather than by IQ alone, but the IQ-based levels are still widely taught. 14.6.2 Giftedness At the upper extreme, giftedness refers to markedly above-average ability, conventionally an IQ around 130 or higher, though modern conceptions (for example that of Joseph Renzulli ) add creativity and task commitment. Who → what. Lewis Madison Terman (American psychologist, 1877–1956), who created the Stanford-Binet, launched in 1921 a famous longitudinal study of over 1,500 highly gifted Californian children (nicknamed the "Termites"). Followed for decades, they generally grew into healthy, successful, well-adjusted adults, puncturing the myth that gifted children are frail or socially awkward. The study also showed that very high IQ alone does not guarantee eminence; motivation and opportunity matter. 14.7 Heredity versus environment How much of the variation in intelligence is due to genes and how much to environment is one of psychology's most sensitive debates. The evidence comes chiefly from kinship studies. Twin studies compare identical (monozygotic) twins, who share all their genes, with fraternal (dizygotic) twins, who share about half. Identical twins, even those reared apart, show markedly more similar IQs, pointing to a substantial genetic contribution. Adoption studies compare adopted children with both their biological and their adoptive parents. Correlations with biological parents support heredity; the rise in adopted children's scores when raised in enriched homes supports environment. The consensus is that both matter and that they interact: heritability of IQ is often estimated around 0.5 in adults, meaning roughly half the variation within a studied population is associated with genetic differences. Crucially, heritability is a population statistic and does not say how much of any one person's intelligence is "fixed", nor does it explain differences between groups. Who → what. James Robert Flynn (1934–2020) documented the Flynn effect : average IQ scores rose steadily across the twentieth century, roughly three points per decade in many countries. Because genes cannot change that fast, the rise must be largely environmental (better nutrition, education, health, and familiarity with abstract, test-like thinking). The effect is powerful evidence that environment shapes measured intelligence. Trap. High heritability does not mean "unchangeable" or "genetic and therefore fixed". The Flynn effect proves scores can climb rapidly through environment even if IQ is highly heritable within a generation. Heritability and malleability are separate ideas. 14.8 Emotional intelligence Intelligence about emotions became a major topic in the 1990s. Two versions must be kept apart. Who → what. Peter Salovey (American psychologist) and John D. Mayer (American psychologist) coined emotional intelligence (EI) in 1990 and defined the scientific ability model : EI is a set of mental abilities to perceive , use (facilitate thinking with), understand , and manage emotions in oneself and others. Being an ability, it can in principle be tested with right-and-wrong performance items. Who → what. Daniel Goleman (American psychologist and journalist) popularised EI in his 1995 bestseller, using a broader mixed model that blends emotional abilities with personality traits and competencies such as self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy and social skill, and argued EI can matter more than IQ for life success. Trap. Do not credit Goleman with coining emotional intelligence. Peter Salovey and John Mayer defined it (the ability model); Daniel Goleman popularised it (the broader mixed model). Exam items love this distinction. 14.9 Creativity Creativity, the ability to produce work that is both novel and useful/appropriate , overlaps with but is not identical to intelligence. Beyond a modest IQ threshold (around 120), the two show little further correlation, the threshold hypothesis . Who → what. J.P. Guilford distinguished convergent thinking (narrowing many possibilities to one correct answer, what IQ tests reward) from divergent thinking (generating many varied answers to an open problem, the engine of creativity). Divergent thinking is judged by fluency , flexibility , originality and elaboration . Who → what. Ellis Paul Torrance (American psychologist, 1915–2003), often called the "father of creativity", built on Guilford's ideas to create the widely used Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking (TTCT) , scoring verbal and figural tasks on fluency, flexibility, originality and elaboration. 14.10 Culture fairness and Indian adaptations Intelligence tests can be unfair when items assume a particular language, schooling or cultural knowledge, which mainly taps crystallized ability. Culture-fair or culture-reduced tests try to minimise this, usually by relying on non-verbal, figural reasoning (for example Raven's Progressive Matrices and Cattell's Culture Fair Intelligence Test ), which lean on fluid ability. In India, Western tests have been adapted and re-standardised for local languages and norms (for instance the Binet-Kamat Test by C.H. Rice , the Malin's Intelligence Scale for Indian Children , and the non-verbal Bhatia Battery of Performance Tests by Chandra Mohan Bhatia ). The construction, administration and scoring of these batteries are covered in the assessment chapter; the point here is conceptual: no test is entirely culture-free, and fair measurement requires appropriate norms for the population being tested. Why. A test standardised on urban English-speaking children will underestimate a rural child who is equally able but unfamiliar with the material. This is why fluid, non-verbal, locally normed tests exist and why cross-cultural comparison of raw IQ scores is treated with caution. 14.11 The complete map: all 30 theories of intelligence Sections 14.2 to 14.10 gave the deep treatment to the theories a general paper hits most often. This map is the full set : every theory or model of intelligence you might see named in an aptitude paper, each tied to the person who proposed it, in one place. If a question drops a name you did not deep-read above, find it here. The theories fall into four families: factor / structural (how many abilities are there and how do they stack?), systems & cognitive-process (what does the mind actually do?), definitional & developmental (what is intelligence?), and emotional / social (intelligence beyond IQ). Key. The single most examined fact about any theory is who proposed it and its one headline idea . Learn every row of these four tables as a "name → idea" pair and you own the whole topic, not one tenth of it. Family A: Factor-analytic / structural theories (how many abilities, and how do they stack?) # Theory / model Theorist(s) Core idea in one line 1 Two-factor theory ( g + s ) Charles Spearman Every task draws on one general factor g plus a task- specific factor s ; positive manifold is the evidence for g. 2 Sampling / "bonds" theory Godfrey Thomson There is no single g; each test samples many overlapping neural bonds , and the overlap only looks like g. 3 Primary Mental Abilities (7 PMAs) Louis L. Thurstone Intelligence is several independent group factors (verbal, number, space, memory, word fluency, perceptual speed, reasoning), not one g. 4 Group-factor hierarchy Cyril Burt An early hierarchy : g at the top, broad group factors beneath, specific factors at the bottom. 5 Hierarchical model Philip E. Vernon g → two major group factors v:ed (verbal-educational) and k:m (spatial-mechanical) → minor factors → specifics. 6 Fluid & Crystallized (Gf-Gc) Raymond B. Cattell g splits into fluid (Gf, on-the-spot reasoning, declines with age) and crystallized (Gc, stored knowledge, holds with age). 7 Investment theory Raymond B. Cattell Crystallized ability grows by investing fluid ability into learning over a lifetime. 8 Extended Gf-Gc John L. Horn Expanded Cattell's two factors into 9–10 broad abilities (adding visual, auditory, short-term memory, processing speed, and more). 9 Three-Stratum theory John B. Carroll From re-analysing 460+ datasets: g (stratum III) over 8 broad (II) over ~70 narrow abilities (I). 10 Cattell-Horn-Carroll (CHC) Cattell, Horn & Carroll (integrated by Kevin McGrew) The merged, dominant modern taxonomy of cognitive abilities; underlies the Woodcock-Johnson and KABC batteries. 11 Structure of Intellect (SOI) J.P. Guilford No g; ability = operations × contents × products , yielding up to 180 distinct abilities ; introduced divergent thinking. 12 Radex model Louis Guttman Abilities arranged geometrically by complexity (simplex) and content (circumplex), with g-loaded tests at the centre. Family B: Systems & cognitive-process theories (what does the mind actually do?) # Theory / model Theorist(s) Core idea in one line 13 Multiple Intelligences Howard Gardner Eight (+1) autonomous intelligences (linguistic, logical-mathematical, spatial, musical, bodily-kinaesthetic, interpersonal, intrapersonal, naturalistic, ?existential), each with its own neural base. 14 Triarchic theory Robert J. Sternberg Three parts: analytical (componential), creative (experiential), practical (contextual) intelligence. 15 Successful Intelligence / WICS Robert J. Sternberg Later reframing: balance analytical, creative and practical abilities (plus wisdom ) to reach your own goals in your own culture. 16 PASS theory J.P. Das, Jack Naglieri & J.R. Kirby Intelligence = four processes: P lanning, A ttention, S imultaneous, S uccessive; operationalised by the CAS. 17 Three functional units (neuropsychological) Alexander R. Luria The brain works in three blocks ( arousal , coding , planning ); the foundation PASS was built on. 18 Bioecological model Stephen J. Ceci Multiple cognitive potentials are realised only through context and knowledge; there is no single context-free g. 19 Minimal cognitive architecture Mike Anderson Intelligence = a basic processing-speed mechanism plus two specific processors and dedicated modules. 20 Two-level theory Arthur R. Jensen Level I (associative: rote memory) versus Level II (conceptual: abstract reasoning) abilities. Family C: Definitional & developmental theories (what is intelligence?) # Theory / model Theorist(s) Core idea in one line 21 Cognitive-correlates / information-processing Earl Hunt Links elementary cognitive tasks (reaction time, working-memory speed) to measured verbal ability. 22 Practical-judgement definition Alfred Binet Intelligence = judgement, comprehension, reasoning and the ability to criticise one's own conclusions. 23 Global-capacity definition David Wechsler The global/aggregate capacity to act purposefully, think rationally and deal effectively with the environment. 24 Adaptation / developmental view Jean Piaget Intelligence is biological adaptation to the environment through assimilation and accommodation, maturing in stages. 25 Intelligence A / B (/ C) Donald O. Hebb (C added by Philip Vernon ) A = innate genetic potential, B = intelligence actually shown in behaviour, C = the sample a test score captures. 26 Social intelligence Edward L. Thorndike Split intelligence into abstract , mechanical and social (understanding and managing people). Family D: Emotional & social intelligence (beyond IQ) # Theory / model Theorist(s) Core idea in one line 27 Ability model of EI Peter Salovey & John D. Mayer EI is a real ability to perceive, use, understand and manage emotions; testable with right/wrong items (MSCEIT). 28 Mixed / competency model of EI Daniel Goleman EI blends emotional abilities with personality competencies : self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy, social skill. 29 Emotional-Social Intelligence (EQ-i) Reuven Bar-On Coined "EQ" ; a mixed model of intrapersonal, interpersonal, adaptability, stress-management and general-mood competencies. 30 Trait EI (emotional self-efficacy) K.V. Petrides EI treated as a cluster of personality traits measured by self-report, distinct from the ability model. Trap. Do not merge people who share a lineage. Raymond Cattell made the fluid/crystallized split, Horn broadened it, Carroll stacked it into three strata, and only the three together make the CHC model. Likewise Salovey and John Mayer built the scientific ability model of EI while Daniel Goleman popularised the looser mixed model and Bar-On coined "EQ": the name in the question tells you which model is meant. Recap. Intelligence has no single agreed definition; Wechsler's "global capacity to act purposefully, think rationally and deal effectively with the environment" is the standard textbook line. Psychometric theories range from Spearman's single g , through Thurstone's seven primary mental abilities, Cattell's fluid/crystallized split, Vernon's hierarchy and Guilford's Structure of Intellect, to the modern CHC synthesis. Systems theories broaden the idea: Gardner's multiple intelligences, Sternberg's triarchic (analytical, creative, practical) successful intelligence, and Das's brain-based PASS theory after Luria. IQ evolved from Binet and Simon's mental age, through Stern and Lewis Terman's ratio IQ (MA ÷ CA × 100), to Wechsler's deviation IQ (mean 100, SD 15) on a normal curve. The extremes are intellectual disability (defined by intellectual and adaptive deficits) and giftedness (Terman's Termites). Heredity and environment both matter and interact, with twin and adoption studies showing substantial heritability while the Flynn effect proves environmental power. Emotional intelligence splits into Salovey and John Mayer's ability model and Goleman's popular mixed model, and creativity rests on Guilford's divergent thinking and Torrance's tests. Remember the three classic traps: g versus multiple intelligences, fluid versus crystallized, and ratio versus deviation IQ. And 14.11 is the safety net: all 30 theories of intelligence , each tied to the person who proposed it, in four families, so no named theory in the paper can catch you out. 15 The attack plan & the interview You have now been through the seven core areas. This closer is how you turn the reading into marks, plus the second stage most candidates under-prepare: the interview. The written-test attack order A general aptitude paper is won on breadth and speed of recognition, not on any single deep topic. Spend your remaining prep like this: Lock the founder pairings. Across Sections 5, 6 and 8 there are perhaps sixty "who made this" facts (Wilhelm Wundt / the first lab, Alfred Binet / the first intelligence scale, Hermann Rorschach / the inkblot, Joseph Wolpe / systematic desensitization, Carl Rogers / person-centred therapy, Aaron Beck / cognitive therapy, Ivan Pavlov / classical conditioning). These are the cheapest, most frequent marks in a general paper. Own the classification landmarks. DSM-5-TR vs ICD-11, Jean Piaget's four stages with ages, Erik Erikson's eight stages, Abraham Maslow's hierarchy, the neurotransmitter-to-disorder links. High-frequency, high-certainty. Keep stats shallow but correct. Mean vs median under skew, reliability vs validity, Type I vs Type II error, when to use a t-test vs ANOVA vs chi-square. A general paper rarely asks you to compute; it asks you to pick the right tool. Answer everything. No SGT negative-marking rule is published, so a blank is a guaranteed zero while a considered guess is not. Never leave one. Key. If you only had one evening, you would re-read every teal Who → what box in this book and nothing else, and you would still clear most of a general aptitude paper. That is where this format concentrates the marks on purpose. The interview: the second gate SGT's entrance is written test then personal interview. The interview is not a formality; it is a selection stage, and it is the part you can most reliably control because it rewards clarity, not recall. Panels for an RCI MA Clinical Psychology seat tend to probe the same things. What they probe What a strong answer sounds like Why clinical psychology A specific, honest reason grounded in your own experience, not "I want to help people." Name what pulled you toward the clinical, assessment-and-therapy side over counselling or research. Why an RCI course Show you know that RCI licensure is what lets you practise clinical psychology in India, and that SGT's MA is the RCI-recognised route. Core concept checks Be able to define, in one clean sentence each: what a clinical psychologist does vs a psychiatrist vs a counsellor; what CBT is; what reliability and validity mean; one ethical principle. A named model or therapist Have one therapy you can talk about with some depth (pick from Section 6, e.g. Aaron Beck's cognitive therapy or Carl Rogers's person-centred approach) so a follow-up does not catch you flat. Ethics & self-awareness Confidentiality and its limits, informed consent, knowing your scope. Panels like a candidate who knows what they do not yet know. Why this matters. Two candidates can score the same on the written test; the interview is where the seat is actually decided. Ten minutes of rehearsing your "why clinical psychology" answer out loud is worth more per mark than another pass over stats. Who → what, the interview version. If they ask you to name people, the safe, high-value names to have ready are: Sigmund Freud (psychoanalysis), Carl Rogers (person-centred / unconditional positive regard), Aaron Beck (cognitive therapy), Albert Ellis (REBT), Ivan Pavlov (classical conditioning), B.F. Skinner (operant conditioning), Jean Piaget (cognitive development), and for India, the Rehabilitation Council of India as the licensing body. Recap. SGT is a two-stage, breadth-first general-psychology entrance with no published syllabus, so this book prepped the seven areas it samples rather than a topic list. Win the written test on the founder pairings and the classification landmarks, keep stats shallow but correct, answer every question because no negative marking is published, and treat the interview as a real selection gate you can rehearse. You are already prepped for the content; this book just gathered it in one place. Good luck.

title: History of Psychology
text: History of Psychology — Study with Psycho Didi (MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF) History of Psychology Study with Psycho Didi · MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF notes Source pp. 3–7 Founding lab Wilhelm Wundt, Leipzig, 1879 Themes Western timeline · Greek & 17th-c. philosophers · schools & founders · Indian psychology India Sen Gupta, Calcutta 1916 · NIMHANS What this covers. The full history of psychology as a discipline: the Western chronology from the first psychology course (1875) through positive psychology (1998), the Greek theorists (Hippocrates' humoral theory, Socrates, Plato, Aristotle) and the 17th-century philosophers who framed the mind, the major schools of psychology with their founders and "forces," the parallel history of psychology and clinical psychology in India, and the Indian systems (Yoga, Buddhism, Hinduism, Jainism, Sufism) that form Indian psychology. Original diagrams. 8 diagrams from the Psycho Didi PDF (pages 4 to 7) sit under the section they belong to, exactly as drawn. Tap one to open it full size and zoom in. Contents: 1 · Western Timeline 2 · Greek Theorists 3 · 17th-Century Philosophers 4 · Major Schools of Psychology 5 · Psychology in India 6 · Clinical Psychology in India 7 · Yoga Psychology 8 · Indian Psychology 1 · Western Timeline Timeline of psychology. A winding road timeline marking psychology milestones from the first psychology course in 1875 to positive psychology in 1998. Psycho Didi notes · p. 4 The chronology below tracks how psychology developed as a formal discipline, from its first course and laboratory to the emergence of each major school. Year Milestone 1875 First psychology course, by William James on Physiological Psychology at Harvard 1879 Wilhelm Wundt established the first psychological laboratory at the University of Leipzig, Germany 1892 American Psychological Association (APA) established 1896 Structuralism 1896 Functionalism 1900 Psychoanalysis (Sigmund Freud) 1912 Gestalt psychology (Max Wertheimer, Kurt Koffka and Wolfgang Köhler) 1913 Behaviourism (John B. Watson, 1913) 1940s Existentialism 1954 Humanistic psychology 1956 Cognitive psychology 1998 Positive psychology Key: Wundt (1879, Leipzig) founded the first psychology lab — the conventional birth of psychology as a science. James taught the first psychology course (1875) and later founded functionalism. 2 · Greek Theorists Greek theorists. The mind-body argument followed by the key ideas of Socrates, Plato and Aristotle, next to an illustrated head. Psycho Didi notes · p. 4 The Mind–Body Argument Monists: mind and body are a single entity. Dualists: mind and body are separate entities. Hippocrates — Humoral Theory Hippocrates: humoral theory. Hippocrates' four humors (black bile, yellow bile, blood and phlegm) with the temperament linked to each. Psycho Didi notes · p. 4 Hippocrates was a dualist . His humoral theory linked four bodily humors to four temperaments. Humor Temperament Character Black bile Melancholic Sad, depressed, poetic and artistic Yellow bile Choleric Fiery, energetic, and passionate Blood Sanguine Warm-hearted, cheerful, optimistic, and confident Phlegm Phlegmatic Slow, quiet, rational, and consistent Socrates Dualist. Focused on morality . Explained eudemonia : long-lasting contentment, peace and happiness comes from building virtues like honesty, generosity, kindness, altruism, etc. Plato Dualist. Allegory of the cave and allegory of the chariot . Tripartite theory of the soul: rational (mind), emotional (spirited), and appetites (pleasures). Theory of forms: forms are universals and are the purest representation of things that actually exist. Aristotle Monist. Gave the first theory of cognitive sciences ; described sensation and perception — special sensible and common sensible . Theory of associationism : law of contiguity, law of frequency, law of similarity, law of contrast. Trap: Hippocrates, Socrates and Plato were dualists ; Aristotle was a monist . The four laws of association (contiguity, frequency, similarity, contrast) belong to Aristotle. 3 · 17th-Century Philosophers 17th century philosophers. The main ideas of Descartes, Locke, Kant and Dilthey set side by side in four columns. Psycho Didi notes · p. 4 René Descartes Famously stated "cogito, ergo sum" ("I think, therefore I am"). Innatism: the mind is born with ideas and knowledge. Dualist. Believed the pineal gland to be the seat of the soul. John Locke Empiricism: all knowledge comes from the senses. Tabula Rasa: individuals are born as a blank slate and all knowledge is acquired from the external world. Rejected innatism . Immanuel Kant Rejected the soul as the subject matter of psychology. Types of knowledge: A priori knowledge: innate knowledge — rationalism. A posteriori knowledge: empiricism. William Dilthey Best known for the way he distinguished between the natural and human sciences . Wrote Ideas for a Descriptive and Analytic Psychology (1894). Who → what: René Descartes → innatism + "cogito, ergo sum" + pineal gland; Locke → empiricism + tabula rasa; Kant → a priori / a posteriori knowledge; Dilthey → natural vs. human sciences. 4 · Major Schools of Psychology Major schools of psychology. A table of nine schools of psychology, from structuralism (1896) to transpersonal (1960s), with each founder and a short description. Psycho Didi notes · p. 5 Each school is defined by its founder(s), method of study, and central focus. Several are tagged as a "force" in psychology. School (year) Founder(s) Description Structuralism (1896) Edward Bradford Titchener Aimed to discover the structural elements of the mind. Method: introspection . Emphasized basic conscious elements. Functionalism (1896) William James Assumed that thinking, like the senses, developed because it was adaptive — it contributed to our ancestors' survival. The role of consciousness is adaptation . Psychoanalysis (1900) Sigmund Freud Two levels of reality: conscious and unconscious. Unconscious instincts: eros (life instincts) and thanatos (death instincts). Parts of personality: id, ego, superego. 1st force in psychology. Gestalt (1912) Max Wertheimer, Kurt Koffka, Wolfgang Köhler Method: phenomenology . Studied conscious experience and mental processes. Focus on holism . Behaviourism (1913) John Watson; most famous behaviourist: B. F. Skinner Focus on behaviour only and discredited mental processes. 2nd force in psychology. Existential (1940s) Rollo May Method: phenomenology . Focus on freedom, meaning, and death. Martin Heidegger's Dasein: Umwelt (nature), Mitwelt (people), Eigenwelt (oneself), Uberwelt (spirituality). Humanistic (1954) Carl Rogers and Abraham Maslow Method: phenomenology . Focused on the potential of individuals and highlighted each person's subjectivity, consciousness, free will and other special human qualities. 3rd force in psychology. Cognitive (1956) Ulric Neisser Focused on cognition and mental process. Analogy of the brain as a computer . Transpersonal (1960s) Abraham Maslow and Victor Frankl Concerned with the study of humanity's highest potential, and the recognition, understanding, and realization of unitive, spiritual, and transcendental states of human consciousness. 4th force in psychology. Key — the four forces: 1st = Psychoanalysis, 2nd = Behaviourism, 3rd = Humanistic, 4th = Transpersonal. Trap: Behaviourism was founded by John Watson ; B. F. Skinner is named as the most famous behaviourist, not the founder. 5 · Psychology in India History of psychology in India. A two-column timeline of Indian psychology milestones from 1905 to 1964, a tree with three institutions at the roots of clinical psychology in India, and notes on yoga psychology. Psycho Didi notes · p. 6 The growth of psychology as a subject and its spread across Indian universities. Year Milestone 1905 Introduction of experimental psychology as an independent subject 1916 First department of psychology in India at the University of Calcutta, under Dr. Narendra Nath Sen Gupta (father of modern psychology in India) 1922 First doctorate in the subject given to Girendra Shekhar Bose at Calcutta for his work on repression; Bose started the Indian Psychoanalytical Society at Calcutta 1923 Establishment of the section of psychology and educational sciences division of the Indian Science Congress Association 1924 Second psychology dept. at the University of Mysore under M. V. Gopalswamy 1925 Sen Gupta founded the Indian Psychological Association 1926 Indian Journal of Psychology started 1929 Dept of psychology at the University of Lucknow 1932 Dept of psychology at Aligarh Muslim University 1943 Dept of psychology at the University of Madras 1946 Dept of psychology at the University of Patna, headed by H. P. Maiti 1947 Bose published Samiksha 1949 Dept of psychology at Banaras Hindu University 1950 Dept of psychology at the University of Pune, headed by V. K. Kothukar 1964 Dept of psychology at Delhi University Who → what: Sen Gupta → first psychology dept (Calcutta, 1916) + Indian Psychological Association (1925); Bose → first doctorate (repression, 1922) + Indian Psychoanalytical Society + Samiksha (1947). 6 · Clinical Psychology in India Three key institutions (roots of clinical psychology in India) All India Institute of Mental Health (now NIMHANS ), Bangalore Ranchi Hospital for Mental Disease Calcutta Mental Hospital Timeline Clinical psychology in India timeline. Eight shield-shaped markers listing clinical psychology milestones in India from 1954 to 2016.
