title: Research & Statistics
text: Research & Statistics — Study with Psycho Didi (MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF) Research & Statistics Study with Psycho Didi · MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF notes Type I vs Type II error Parametric vs non-parametric Reliability & validity t-test / ANOVA / factor analysis Research designs What this covers. Core research methodology and statistics for the exam: key terms, the research process, variables and designs, descriptive and inferential statistics (central tendency, dispersion, t-tests, ANOVA family), factor analysis and regression, reliability and validity (with threats), standard scores, and research ethics. Original diagrams. 14 diagrams from the Psycho Didi PDF (pages 9 to 13) sit under the section they belong to, exactly as drawn. Tap one to open it full size and zoom in. Contents: 1 · Terms to Know · 2 · What is Research (Steps & Types) · 3 · Variables · 4 · Research Designs · 5 · Descriptive Statistics · 6 · Inferential Statistics: t-test & ANOVA · 7 · Factor Analysis & PCA · 8 · Regression & Correlation · 9 · Reliability · 10 · Validity & Threats · 11 · Standard Scores · 12 · Research Ethics 1 · Terms to Know Research and statistics terms to know. Colour-coded cards defining core research and statistics terms, arranged around a central Type I and Type II error table. Psycho Didi notes · p. 9 Type I and Type II errors. A decision table that crosses the conclusion drawn with the true state of nature and marks the two correct conclusions (one labelled power), the Type I error and the Type II error. Psycho Didi notes · p. 9 Random assignment: giving every participant an equal chance of being in an experimental or control group. Internal validity: extent to which an experiment investigates what it is supposed to. External validity: generalisability. Demand characteristics: factors that influence a participant's behaviour based on what they think the purpose of the experiment is. Observer expectancy effect: experimenter communicates expectations unintentionally (Pygmalion / Rosenthal effect). Descriptive statistics: the branch of statistics which deals with descriptions of obtained data. Inferential statistics: deals with drawing conclusions about a large group of individuals on the basis of observations of a few participants. Parameter: a measurable characteristic of a population. Confidence interval: the mean of your estimate plus and minus the variation in that estimate. Null hypothesis: the claim that the effect being studied does not exist. Alternate hypothesis: statement that suggests there is a relationship between the variables being studied. Significance level: the probability of rejecting the null hypothesis when it is true, i.e., the probability of making a Type I error. Effect size: a quantitative measure of the magnitude of the experimental effect. The larger the effect size, the stronger the relationship between the two variables. Skewness: a lopsided and asymmetrical curve because of extreme data. Kurtosis: the term used to identify the degree of steepness or shallowness of a distribution. Post hoc test: "like a post mortem." Requires two conditions: a directional hypothesis and a significant F ratio. Trap: Type I error = null hypothesis is true but we reject it (alternate is false but we accept it) → "false alarm." Type II error = null hypothesis is false but we accept it (alternate is true but we reject it) → "miss." The significance level is the probability of making a Type I error. Key: Test power is the probability that the test will reject the null hypothesis when the alternate hypothesis is true, i.e., it will not make a Type II error. Feature Parametric test Non-parametric test Assumptions Generalizable; normal probability curve; uses mean; homogeneity of variance; probability sample; large sample size Assumption-free test Test power Higher Low test power Data type Interval / ratio Nominal data only Example t-test, ANOVA Chi square 2 · What is Research (Steps & Types) Research is a systematic, controlled, empirical, critical investigation. Steps Steps of research. The eight steps of research, from identifying a research problem to reporting findings. Psycho Didi notes · p. 10 Identify a research problem Review of literature Formulate a hypothesis Research design Collect data Analyse data Interpret data Report findings 3 · Variables Variables. The definition of a variable and its types: independent, dependent, extraneous (controlled and confounding), stimulus, organismic and behavioural. Psycho Didi notes · p. 10 A variable in research is a characteristic, number, or quantity that can be measured or counted and can take on different values. Type Description Independent variable (IV) Manipulated. Dependent variable (DV) Not manipulated; changes with change in IV. Extraneous variables Controlled. Confounding variables Uncontrolled extraneous variables that affect results. Stimulus variable e.g. light (always IV). Organismic variable e.g. age. Behavioural / response variable e.g. response rate (always DV). 4 · Research Designs Research: steps, variables and types of research. A flowchart branching from types of research into experiment, observation, correlation and special designs, alongside boxes on research steps, the definition of research and variables. Psycho Didi notes · p. 10 Experiment Experiment (lab): complete control on secondary (error) variance, e.g. lab experiment. Field experiment: secondary variance just greater than lab experiment; happens in a real setting; difficult to control extraneous variables. Quasi experiment: secondary variance greatest; no random assignment; non-equivalent groups, e.g. ex post facto studies. Correlation Not causation established; only helps us understand association. Gives us the direction of the relationship. Can't control extraneous variables. Generalization is possible. Types: positive, negative, zero. Trap: Correlation is not causation. It shows association and direction but cannot control extraneous variables. Observation Can be naturalistic or controlled . Can be participant or non-participant . Special Designs Longitudinal design Involves taking a single group and studying it for a long period; the group is called a cohort . Founder note: Lewis Terman — eugenics (Francis Galton, 1883). Prospective study: looking at the future. Retrospective study: looking at the past. Cross-sectional design Various age groups are compared at the same time. Cohort-sequential (cross-sequential) Cross-sectional + longitudinal; also known as cross-sequential. Survey Uses questionnaires and observation; usually used to check attitude towards something. Tools used: survey, interviews; can be participant or non-participant. Who → what: Lewis Terman — associated with eugenics and long-term longitudinal cohort study. 5 · Descriptive Statistics Statistics: descriptive and inferential. A flowchart splitting descriptive statistics into central tendency and variance, and inferential statistics into t-test and ANOVA tables with degrees of freedom and non-parametric equivalents. Psycho Didi notes · p. 11 Measures of Central Tendency Measure Definition Scale Mean Average; sensitive to extreme data; parametric. Interval / ratio Median Mid point. Ordinal Mode Most frequent data point. Nominal Key: Empirical relationship: Mode = 3 Median − 2 Mean . Frequency is measured by: Ogive curve, Histogram, Bar graph. Variance / Dispersion How the scores are spread around the mean. Range = highest frequency − lowest frequency. Standard deviation: spread of scores around the mean. Variance: standard deviation squared. Average deviation: mean of absolute deviations. Quartile deviation (for median values): QD = (Q3 − Q1) / 2. 6 · Inferential Statistics: t-test & ANOVA t-test Type Description Degrees of freedom Non-parametric equivalent Single sample To verify whether the sample belongs to the population. N − 1 Wilcoxon signed rank test, Kolmogorov–Smirnov test Paired sample Studying a sample 2 times (pre-test and post-test). N − 1 Wilcoxon signed rank test Matched samples Meant to be a repeated-measures test, but due to participant attrition, their characteristics are matched with new participants. N − 1 Wilcoxon signed rank test Independent samples Between-groups test. N − 2 Mann-Whitney U test ANOVA ANOVA is used to compare two or more factors, i.e., the effect of two independent variables on a single dependent variable. Type Description Degrees of freedom Non-parametric equivalent One way Compares levels of a single independent variable over the dependent variable. Main: K − 1; Error: N − K; Total: N − 1 Kruskal Wallis H test Repeated measures Single group of participants measured at multiple levels. K − 1; Interaction: (K − 1)(N − 1); Total: N − 1 Friedman's ANOVA Two way Effect of two independent variables. K − 1; (K1 − 1) × (K2 − 1); N − K; N − 1 Friedman's ANOVA MANOVA Assessing multiple dependent variables simultaneously. K − 1; (K1 − 1) × (K2 − 1); N − 1 — ANCOVA Adjusts for the influence of a covariate in testing. K − 1; (K1 − 1) × (K2 − 1); N − K − 1; N − 1 — 7 · Factor Analysis & PCA Factor analysis, PCA and regression. An overview of factor analysis, its confirmatory and exploratory types, PCA with a scree plot, factor rotation, regression and research ethics. Psycho Didi notes · p. 12 Who → what: Factor analysis was given by Charles Spearman while creating his theory of intelligence. It uses a correlational design. Types Type Purpose Details / Methods Exploratory For creating a new theory. Unique variance: one factor is enough to explain variance; method = principal component method (unrotated factors given). Common variance: gives factors that explain variance together but not individually; methods = principal axis method, maximum likelihood estimation, generalized least squares. Confirmatory For verifying another theory. Changes cannot be made. PCA (Principal Component Analysis) Scree plot. A scree plot of eigenvalues against component number for 18 components, with arrows pointing to the 5th and 8th factors. Psycho Didi notes · p. 12 Uses Cattell's scree plot (for a large number of factors) and the Kaiser–Guttman criterion (for a small number of factors, < 20). Eigenvalues indicate how much variance we expect each factor to explain; an eigenvalue of 1 is the minimum expectation from each factor. In a scree plot: x-axis = order of factors; y-axis = unreduced eigenvalues. Identity matrix: all the factors have 0 correlation with each other except with themselves. Factor Rotation Allows us to decide if a second round of FA is required. Rotation Result Angle Types Oblique rotation Gives correlated factors; makes factors suitable for further FA. Non-90° angles oblimin, geomin, promax Orthogonal rotation Gives uncorrelated factors. 90° equimax, quartimax, varimax 8 · Regression & Correlation Regression and partial correlation. Boxes giving the simple and multiple regression equations and the definition of partial correlation. Psycho Didi notes · p. 12 Simple (bivariate) regression: Y = a + bx + E. Multiple regression: Y = a + b1x1 + b2x2 + b3x3 + E, where b = partial slope. The regression coefficient is indicated by β . R = geometric mean of partial correlation (range 0–1). Variance = R × R × 100%. Partial correlation Studying a single correlation in a multiple correlation matrix by removing the impact of other correlations. 9 · Reliability Reliability and validity. A reliability diagram linking test-retest, parallel forms, inter-rater, split half and internal consistency (with its three methods), above a validity wheel and a list of threats to validity. Psycho Didi notes · p. 13 Reliability checks if our test is consistent. It can be external and internal. Method Description Notes / Formula Test–retest Give the test to the same group after some time gap, and correlate the two tests (2 administrations). Source of error: practice effect, time sampling error, carryover effects. Parallel / equivalent forms Correlate the new test with a previous version of the test or a similar test. Can be done with or without a time gap. Split half Comparing the first half of the score with the 2nd half; odd-even method may be used. Formula: r = 2r / (1 + r). Similar to Cronbach's alpha but can only be used for dichotomous items. Internal consistency Correlating performance on each item with overall performance across participants. — Kuder–Richardson method Internal consistency for dichotomous items. — Inter-rater Agreement of raters with regards to performance of participants. Cohen's kappa is used (r should be > .8). Key — Spearman–Brown correction: used to correct for the effect of the length of the test. Formula: Kr / (1 + (K − 1)r), where K = test length; r = correlation. Key — Cronbach's alpha: average of all possible split halves; applicable to dichotomous and polytomous items. 10 · Validity & Threats Types of validity. A four-part validity wheel (face, content, criterion and construct) with definitions and the concurrent, predictive, convergent and divergent sub-types. Psycho Didi notes · p. 13 Validity Meaning Face validity What a judge or expert thinks about the test; how much a test appears to be accurate (MMPI (Starke Hathaway and J. Charnley McKinley, 1943) has poor face validity). Content validity Items are relevant and representative of the target construct. Construct validity Used to validate a theory. Comparing a new test with another test that correlates to the same construct. Refers to the accuracy of the test. Criterion validity The extent to which the test fulfills the criteria made by another source. Sub-types Concurrent validity (criterion): the extent that a measure simultaneously relates to another measure that it is supposed to relate to, e.g. comparing a new personality questionnaire with the 16PF (Raymond Cattell). Predictive validity (criterion): the extent that a measure predicts another measure, e.g. predicting a real exam through mocks. Convergent validity (construct): the extent that different measures of the same construct converge or strongly correlate with one another. Divergent validity (construct): the extent that measures of different constructs diverge or minimally correlate with one another. Threats to Validity Threats to validity. Two lists of internal and external threats to validity. Psycho Didi notes · p. 13 Internal threats External threats Confounding variables; selection bias; test-taker history; maturation; repeated testing; mortality; diffusion; compensatory rivalry; experimenter bias Generalizability; aptitude-treatment interaction; situations; pre-test effect; post-test effect; Rosenthal effect 11 · Standard Scores Standard scores. A card showing when Z and T scores are used, with the mean and SD of sten and stanine scores. Psycho Didi notes · p. 9 Score Use Mean SD Z score Normal data (always preferred) 0 1 T score Clinical setting (non-normal) 50 10 Sten Standard ten 5.5 2 Stanine Standard nine 5 2 12 · Research Ethics Research ethics. A list of research ethics principles: risk-benefit ratio, informed consent, privacy, confidentiality, minimizing deception and debriefing. Psycho Didi notes · p. 12 Research ethics involve a subjective evaluation of the risk-benefit ratio. Informed consent: a person's explicitly expressed willingness to participate in a research project based on a clear understanding of the nature of the research. Privacy: the rights of individuals to decide how information about them is to be communicated to others. Confidentiality: information obtained from a research participant will be kept secret and private. Minimizing deception. Debriefing: explaining to participants the need for deception, addressing misconceptions, and removing harmful effects resulting from deception.

title: Biological Basis of Behaviour
text: Biological Basis of Behaviour — Study with Psycho Didi (MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF) Biological Basis of Behaviour Study with Psycho Didi · MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF notes 4 lobes · limbic system · basal ganglia 7 neurotransmitters 12 cranial nerves Endocrine glands & hormones Sympathetic vs Parasympathetic What this covers. Development and organization of the nervous system; the forebrain and its four lobes; the limbic system and basal ganglia; diencephalon, midbrain and hindbrain; meninges and ventricles; important Broadmann's areas; techniques to study the brain; dysfunctions of the brain by region; neurotransmitters, hormones and the endocrine glands; glial cells; the peripheral nervous system (cranial and spinal nerves); and the autonomic nervous system. Original diagrams. 16 diagrams from the Psycho Didi PDF (pages 15 to 24) sit under the section they belong to, exactly as drawn. Tap one to open it full size and zoom in. Contents: 1 · Development & Organization of the Nervous System · 2 · The Forebrain & the Four Lobes · 3 · The Limbic System · 4 · The Basal Ganglia · 5 · Diencephalon: Thalamus, Hypothalamus, Epithalamus · 6 · Midbrain (Mesencephalon) · 7 · Hindbrain: Cerebellum, Pons, Medulla, ARAS · 8 · Meninges & Ventricles · 9 · Important Broadmann's Areas · 10 · Techniques to Study the Brain · 11 · Dysfunctions of the Brain · 12 · Neurotransmitters · 13 · Hormones & the Endocrine Glands · 14 · Glial Cells · 15 · Peripheral Nervous System & Cranial Nerves · 16 · The Autonomic Nervous System 1 · Development & Organization of the Nervous System Development of the brain. A flowchart that splits the nervous system into its divisions and traces each neural tube subdivision to the brain structures, ventricles and functions that develop from it. Psycho Didi notes · p. 15 The Nervous System is divided into the Central Nervous System (CNS) and the Peripheral Nervous System (PNS) . Central Nervous System (CNS) — the Brain and the Spinal Cord . Peripheral Nervous System (PNS) — includes the Autonomic Nervous System (with its Sympathetic and Parasympathetic divisions) and the Somatic Nervous System (with its Afferent and Efferent nervous systems). Enteric Nervous System — controls the smooth muscle and glandular tissue in the digestive system. Development from the neural tube The brain develops from the neural tube , forming the following divisions: Primary vesicle Sub-division Becomes Forebrain (Prosencephalon) Telencephalon Cerebral hemispheres / four lobes Diencephalon Thalamus, hypothalamus, epithalamus Midbrain Mesencephalon Midbrain Hindbrain (Rhombencephalon) Metencephalon Pons and cerebellum Myelencephalon Medulla Don't confuse. Afferent nerves carry sensory information toward the CNS; Efferent nerves carry motor commands away from the CNS. Similarly, the Sympathetic system drives "fight or flight" (Walter Cannon, 1915) while the Parasympathetic system drives "rest and digest." 2 · The Forebrain & the Four Lobes The forebrain contains the neocortex , which contains the primary and association cortexes . Key. In the cerebral cortex, grey matter is outside and white matter is inside . Lobe Functions Frontal Lobe Executive functioning; association; motor cortex; Broca's area (left hemisphere); metacognition Parietal Lobe Sensation; haptic memory; proprioception; the " where " pathway Occipital Lobe Awareness of visual stimuli Temporal Lobe Auditory cortex; Wernicke's area (left hemisphere); part of the hippocampus; stores declarative memories; olfactory bulb 3 · The Limbic System The limbic system. A table giving the function and dysfunction of each limbic system and basal ganglia structure, with a small brain illustration beside each name. Psycho Didi notes · p. 16 Key structures of the limbic system, their functions, and dysfunctions: Name Function Dysfunction Amygdala Fear and rage; emotional and flashbulb memory (Roger Brown and James Kulik, 1977); sense fear and aggression in others; recognize learning, memory consolidation of emotional memories Kluver-Bucy syndrome; Hyperorality; Hypersexuality Hippocampus Encoding new memory; shaped like a seahorse; located in temporal lobe Anterograde amnesia; PTSD Septum Pleasure; inhibits aggression Sham rage / Septal rage Thalamus Relay (contralateral); contains LGN, MGN, VLN, Pulvinar Extreme pain in opposite side of the body Hypothalamus Homeostasis; controls endocrine glands; eating (Lateral, Anterior, Ventromedial); sleep (Suprachiasmatic nucleus) Aphagia; Adipsia Cingulate gyrus Memories; regulate aggression — Who → what. Papez (1937) — the Papez circuit: pain information transmission; recollecting pleasant memories. Dysfunction: aggressive behaviour, shyness. Amygdala (detail) Fear and rage center Encodes emotional memories Sense fear in others Hippocampus (detail) Encode declarative memories Role in PTSD Damaged by long exposure to glucocorticoids Cingulate gyrus (detail) Transmission Important in decision making Pain Social interaction Sex Largest part 4 · The Basal Ganglia The Basal Ganglia handle motor coordination and inhibition; they prevent unnecessary motor movements and activity in the white matter of the frontal lobe. Dysfunction: tremors, involuntary muscle movements, abnormal increase in tone, difficulty initiating movements, and abnormal posture. Components of the basal ganglia: caudate , putamen , globus pallidus , substantia nigra , nucleus accumbens , and subthalamic nuclei . Structure Function Dysfunction Caudate Planning; learning; memory; romantic interaction Overactivity Putamen Speech articulation; addiction; motor learning Overactivity Nucleus Accumbens Motivation and action; drug self administration Depression, addiction, anxiety, difficulty experiencing positive emotions Subthalamic Nucleus Regulate voluntary movement Hemiballismus: sudden, large, flailing movements on one side of the body Globus Pallidus Proprioceptive movement Parkinson's disease, dystonia, and gait abnormalities Substantia Nigra Motor movement; reward functioning Motor control issues, most notably seen in Parkinson's disease 5 · Diencephalon: Thalamus, Hypothalamus, Epithalamus Thalamus The largest part of the diencephalon . Nuclei include: Medial Geniculate nucleus Lateral Geniculate Nucleus Ventrolateral preoptic nucleus Pulvinar Hypothalamus Controls homeostasis and the endocrine glands (see the Limbic System section for detail). Epithalamus Penial (pineal) gland 3rd ventricle 6 · Midbrain (Mesencephalon) Tectum — Posterior (roof) Superior colliculi (vision) and inferior colliculi (audition) Orientation Tegmentum — Anterior (floor) Substantia nigra : black substance, reward learning Red nucleus : limb movements Periaqueductal gray : fear, pain response The Cerebral Aqueduct runs through the midbrain. 7 · Hindbrain: Cerebellum, Pons, Medulla, ARAS Cerebellum Classical conditioning (Ivan Pavlov) Motor coordination and proprioception Involuntary and voluntary movement Walking, gait, posture Pons Consciousness General arousal Sleep and wakefulness ARAS (Ascending Reticular Activating System) General arousal Consciousness 4As : alertness, attentiveness, arousal, awakeness Damage = unconsciousness Activates higher cortex Medulla Breathing Maintaining organ systems Heart circulation Respiratory control Houses the 4th ventricle 8 · Meninges & Ventricles Meninges of the Brain Meninges of the brain. A box listing the three meninges, dura mater, arachnoid mater and pia mater, with what the arachnoid and pia mater contain. Psycho Didi notes · p. 15 Dura mater Arachnoid mater — contains the subarachnoid space that holds CSF Pia mater — contains blood vessels Ventricles Ventricles. A cross diagram placing ventricles V1 and V2 on an intraventricular formation axis and V3 and V4 on a cerebral aqueduct axis with the choroid plexus at V4, beside a labelled drawing of the ventricular system. Psycho Didi notes · p. 17 Lateral Ventricles (V1, V2 — the two lateral ventricles) Third ventricle (V3) Fourth ventricle (V4) Connected via the cerebral aqueduct and intraventricular (interventricular) foramen Choroid plexus — produces CSF 9 · Important Broadmann's Areas Other important brain areas. The page header with the ventricles diagram, the visual system flow from V1 and V2 to V3, V4, V5 and V3A toward the temporal and parietal lobes, and the heading of the Broadman's areas table. Psycho Didi notes · p. 17 Important Broadman's areas: areas 1 to 5. A table giving the name, function and lesion effect of areas 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5, with a brain image marking each area. Psycho Didi notes · p. 17 Important Broadman's areas: areas 6 to 45. A table giving the name, function and lesion causes for areas 6, 9, 10, 17, 22 and 37, Wernicke's area (22, 39, 40) and Broca's area (44, 45), with brain images marking most areas. Psycho Didi notes · p. 18 Alongside the Broadmann's areas, the note maps the visual system stream: areas V1, V2, V3, V3A, V4, V5 , running from the occipital lobe toward the parietal lobe (dynamic form, motion) and the temporal lobe (recognition, shape). Area no. Name Function Lesion's effect 1, 2, 3 Primary somatosensory cortex Localization of touch, temperature, vibration, pain; sensory perception; orofacial movement Agraphesthesia, astereognosia, loss of vibration, proprioception and fine touch, potentially hemineglect if the non-dominant hemisphere is affected 4 Primary motor cortex Contralateral finger/hand/wrist or orofacial movements, learned motor sequences, breathing control, and voluntary blinking Paralysis of the contralateral side of the body 5 Somatosensory association cortex Stereopsis, line bisection judgments, processing chaotic patterns, using spatial imagery in deductive reasoning, motor execution, bimanual manipulation, working memory, language processing, visuomotor attention, pain perception, tactile localization, saccadic eye movement Ideomotor apraxia: loss of ability to produce purposeful, skilled movements. Astereognosis: tactile agnosia 6 Premotor and Supplementary Motor Cortex Motor sequencing/planning, laughter/smiling, interlimb coordination, movement learning and initiation, motor imagery, speech motor programming, language processing and switching, speech perception, object naming, lip-reading, word retrieval, lexical decision on words and pseudo-words, syntactical processing, working memory, mnemonic rehearsal, episodic long-term memory, topographic memory, visuospatial and visuomotor attention, attention to human voices Affect sensory guidance of movement and control of proximal and trunk muscles. Kinetic apraxia 9 Dorsolateral / anterior prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) Integrating sensory and mnemonic information, regulation of intellectual function and action, the act of deception and lying Dysexecution syndrome: problems with affect, social judgement, executive memory, abstract thinking, and intentionality 10 Anterior prefrontal cortex Reasoning, task flexibility, problem solving, planning, execution, working memory, processing emotional stimuli, inferential reasoning, decision making, calculation of numerical processes Similar to what would be seen in Area 9, since the two areas are associated 17 Primary visual cortex (V1) Contains a well-defined map of the spatial information required for vision Cortical blindness 22 Primary auditory cortex Involves complex language and auditory processing Difficulty finding words, semantic paraphasias, prosopagnosia, disturbances in drawing 37 Fusiform Gyrus Processing of color information, face and body recognition, word and number recognition Difficulties in visual recognition 22, 39, 40 Wernicke's area Helps people understand spoken and written language Language disorders 44, 45 Broca's area Production of speech Broca's aphasia: a deficit in the ability to speak and produce the proper words/sounds 10 · Techniques to Study the Brain Techniques to study the brain. A mind map branching from the title to history, ablation, neurosurgery, gene knockout, stereotaxic surgery, optogenetic stimulation, lesion types and imaging techniques, each with short notes and icons. Psycho Didi notes · p. 19 History Trephination : creating a hole in the skull or nail to relieve pressure or treat a health condition. Autopsy : a medical examination of a body after death. Ablation : complete removal of a part of the brain (mostly for treatment). Gene knockout : use of genetic engineering to inactivate or remove one or more specific genes from an organism. Imaging techniques Computed Axial Tomography (CAT) : introduced in 1960; 360-degree X-ray; 3D/2D structural image. EEG : electrical activity. EMG : magnetic activity. MEG : muscle tension. EOG : sleep studies, eye movement. PET : introduced in 1973; functional image of the brain (2D); fluorodeoxyglucose injected in carotid artery. MRI : traces radioactive field of hydrogen present in brain; 3D image of structure; high spatial resolution. fMRI : traces BOLD (Blood Oxygen Level Dependent) signal; gives structural as well as functional image. BOLD contrast: checks difference between active and inactive areas. Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS) : non-invasive; uses magnetic pulses to stimulate the brain and treat conditions like depression and obsessive-compulsive disorder. Single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) : 2D structural, 3D functional image; location of seizures can be checked. Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) : optical imaging technique; light measures blood flow changes; good temporal resolution. Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) : better spatial resolution than MRI. Note the labels as given. This source lists EMG as "magnetic activity," MEG as "muscle tension," and MRI as tracing a "radioactive field of hydrogen." These are the definitions exactly as printed in the source. Surgical & stimulation techniques Stereotaxic surgery : uses an atlas and an instrument; useful for lesion and surgery; invasive. Optogenetic stimulation : a genetic technique that enables scientists to activate or inhibit the activity of specific neuron populations using light. Neurosurgery : done for treatment. Lesions (controlled destruction) Aspiration lesion : for suction action; only for shallow areas and cerebral cortex. Knife cut lesion : severing, tissue sectioning (for biopsy). Reversible lesion : functional lesion; cryogenic (put freezing agents); uses a cryoprobe (cryogenic blockade). Chemical lesion : excitotoxic lesions performed through stereotaxis — kainic acid (glutamate neuron), ibotenic acid, 6-hydroxy-dopamine (monoamine). Radiofrequency lesion : bilateral lesions show better effect than unilateral. 11 · Dysfunctions of the Brain Dysfunctions of the brain. A mind map of the deficits linked to each brain region, from lateralization and split brain to the hindbrain, lobes, midbrain and limbic system, with a Words to Know box of deficit terms. Psycho Didi notes · p. 20 Lateralization and Localization Specific parts of the brain control specific functions. Who → what. Franz Gall and Johann Casper — studies of localization. Roger Sperry and Michael Gazzaniga — the Split Brain Experiment : severing the corpus callosum leads to the binding problem . Karl Lashley — controlled lesioning; concept of equipotentiality : each area of the brain has an equal role in each function. Lateralization = functional dominance of one hemisphere over the other. Lobes Occipital Cortical blindness — people confabulate because they can't see. Anton syndrome : lack of insight Scotoma Nystagmus Agnosia Colour agnosia Frontal Recent memory impairments Reduced concentration Behaviour disorder Reduction in new information learning Lack of inhibition Flat affect Contralateral plegia Paresis Dysfunctional executive functioning Decreased fluency of speech Apathy Parietal Tactile agnosia Loss of haptic memory Hemineglect / Contralateral / Unilateral (in extreme cases, person forgets half of his/her body) Anosognia : not aware of deficit (hemineglect) Apraxia : unable to remember motor sequence Decreased proprioception Balint's syndrome : simultagnosia, ocular apraxia, optic ataxia Visual ataxia Temporal Decreased auditory processing Amnesia Korsakoff syndrome : due to thiamine deficiency (irreversible) Association agnosia (inferior temporal pathway) Prosopagnosia (damage to fusiform gyrus – right) Broca's area : expressive aphasia Wernicke's area : fluent aphasia Hindbrain Cerebellum Tremors Nystagmus (involuntary eye movement) Balint's syndrome — can't adjust to sharpen movement accuracy skills. Tone silent: improper tone estimation Detection: finger rhythm tapping with metronome ARAS / Pons / Medulla ARAS : unconsciousness; altered consciousness (delirium) Pons : coma Medulla : death Midbrain and Limbic System Basal Ganglia Parkinson's Chorea (resembles dancing) Hypokinetic Tics, Tourette's (1 vocal tic, 2 motor tics) Caudate and putamen damage: chorea and hyperkinesia Limbic System Lateral Hypothalamus : aphagia (lack hunger) Ventromedial hypothalamus : Hyperphagia (very hungry) Amygdala : Kluver-Bucy syndrome; Hypersexuality; Hyperorality Thalamus Altered states of consciousness Loss of perception Thalamus syndrome : pain in opposite side of the body Hypothalamus Anterior Hypothalamus : issues with parasympathetic nervous system; asexual behaviour; issues with temperature regulation Posterior Hypothalamus : problems with sympathetic nervous system; Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH) Corpus Callosum Split brain syndrome Words to Know Term Meaning Agnosia Not knowing Ageusia Can't taste Anosmia Can't smell Aphasia Language loss Apraxia Loss of motor memory Ataxia Loss of motor coordination Paralysis Complete loss of function Paresis Reduction in muscle strength Adipsia Lack of thirst Aphagia Lack of hunger Paraphegia Loss of function below stomach Agrammatism Not being able to use grammar 12 · Neurotransmitters Neurotransmitters. A table of six neurotransmitters giving their synthesis site or receptors, functions, agonists, antagonists, disorders and a historical note. Psycho Didi notes · p. 23 Name Synthesis / Receptors Functions Agonist Antagonist Disorders Misc. Acetylcholine Cholinergic pathways. Receptors: neuromuscular junction Stimulating muscles; communication between sensory and motor neurons; attention, arousal, sleep, memory Muscarine; Nicotine (low); Sarin Nicotine (high); Scopolamine; Bungarotoxin; Curare; Botulinum toxin; Hemicholinium Alzheimer's dementia Otto Loewi, 1921: discovered the role of acetylcholine as an endogenous neurotransmitter Norepinephrine Locus coeruleus (pons) Fight or flight (Walter Cannon); sympathetic activation; learning, memory, sleep, emotion Stimulants Clonidine (Catapres); Prazosin (Minipress); Terazosin Excess: anxiety. Low: depression — Dopamine Substantia Nigra (Tegmentum) (D2 receptors) Pleasure; motor movement Heroine; Alcohol; Opium; Nicotine; Amphetamine Chlorpromazine Excess: positive symptoms of schizophrenia. Low: Parkinson's — Serotonin Raphe Nuclei (pons) Controls aggression; mood stability; memory, learning, sleep; present in enteric nervous system SSRIs MAOIs; Ondansetron; Granisetron; Dolasetron; Palonosetron Low: depression — GABA Throughout CNS (enzyme: glutamate-decarboxylase) Inhibitory functions Benzodiazepines; Barbiturates Bicuculline; Picrotoxin Low: anxiety, tics, Tourette's — Glutamate NMDA; AMPA; Kainate LTP, memory Ibotenic, Kainic acid Memantine; Riluzole Excess: excitotoxicity, Huntington's. Low: Alzheimer's — Who → what. Otto Loewi (1921) discovered the role of acetylcholine as an endogenous neurotransmitter. 13 · Hormones & the Endocrine Glands Site → Hormone → Function Hormones: site, hormone and function. A table listing each hormone-producing site with its hormones and their functions, each site shown with a small organ icon. Psycho Didi notes · p. 21 Site Hormone Function Hypothalamus Releasing Hormone Promote release from pituitary Anterior Pituitary TSH; LH; FSH; ACTH; Prolactin; Growth Hormone (GH) Thyroid; ovulation; ovum maturation; steroid; milk production; body growth Posterior Pituitary Vasopressin; Oxytocin Increases BP, reduces urine volume; cervical contraction, milk production, sexual experience Penial (pineal) gland Melatonin Regulate sleep, circadian rhythm, etc. Testis Testosterone Development and maintenance of male sex characteristics Ovaries Oestrogen; Progesterone Reproductive and sexual development of women; supports menstruation and maintaining a pregnancy Pancreas Insulin; Glucagon Moving glucose from the blood into cells; breaks glycogen Kidney Renin Regulate blood pressure and sodium and potassium levels Adrenal Medulla Epinephrine; Norepinephrine Helps the body respond to stressful situations; increases alertness, arousal and attention Adrenal Cortex Aldosterone; Cortisol Reduces salt in urine; increases blood sugar Fat cells Leptin Fat set point Types of Hormones Types of hormones. Hormones grouped by structure into steroid and peptide types and by function into homeostatic, gonadal and glucocorticoid hormones, with examples of each. Psycho Didi notes · p. 21 Based on structure: Steroid : synthesized from fat — e.g. testosterone, cortisol Peptide hormone : synthesized by DNA like protein — e.g. insulin, endorphin, growth hormone Based on function: Homeostatic hormones — Aldosterone, renin, ADH Gonadal hormones Glucocorticoids — immunosuppression (dementia, PTSD) Endocrine Glands: Gland → Hormone → Disease → Function Endocrine glands. A table of six endocrine glands giving each gland's hormones, related diseases and functions, with an organ illustration beside each gland. Psycho Didi notes · p. 22 Gland Hormone Disease Function Adrenal Cortex Aldosterone; Glucocorticoids Low: Addison's; High: Cushing's disease Regulates sodium and water balance in the body; mediates the body's response to stress Adrenal Medulla Epinephrine; Norepinephrine (catecholamines) Anxiety, depression, headaches, sleeping problems; low blood sugar (hypoglycemia); changes in blood pressure, heart rate Flight or Fight Thyroid Tetraiodothyronine T4; Triiodothyronine T3; Thyroxine PCOD; Hyperthyroidism; Hypothyroidism; Cretinism; Grave's disease; Goitre Metabolism, heart rate, and body temperature Pancreas Insulin (Beta cells); Glucagon (Alpha cells) Diabetes mellitus; glucagonoma Distributes glucose; turns glycogen to glucose Hypothalamus Releasing hormones Hypothalamic obesity; Diabetes insipidus; Cushing's disease; Prolactinoma; Hypothalamic hypothyroidism; Non-24-hour sleep-wake syndrome; Hypopituitarism; Oxytocin deficiency Controlling body temperature, hunger, and sleep Pituitary Anterior: TSH, LH, FSH, ACTH, Prolactin, Growth Hormone (GH). Posterior: vasopressin, oxytocin Acromegaly; Cushing's Syndrome; Diabetes Insipidus; Empty Sella Syndrome; Hypopituitarism Produces and releases hormones that control many bodily functions, including growth, metabolism, reproduction, and more 14 · Glial Cells Glial cells. A panel listing the CNS glial cells (astrocytes, ependymal cells, oligodendrocytes, microglia) and the PNS glial cells (satellite and Schwann cells) with what each one does. Psycho Didi notes · p. 24 CNS glial cells Astrocytes : maintain the structure of the cell; control concentration of neurotransmitters; maintain blood brain barrier Ependymal cells : produce CSF Oligodendrocytes : myelinate neurons of the CNS Microglia : brain's immune cell; soldiers of the nervous system PNS glial cells Satellite cells : similar function to astrocytes, but in the PNS Schwann cells : myelinate neurons of the PNS Don't confuse. Oligodendrocytes myelinate CNS neurons; Schwann cells myelinate PNS neurons. Stress axes HPA axis and SAM pathway. Two arrow chains showing the HPA axis from CRF to insulin resistance and the SAM pathway from the hypothalamus to epinephrine and norepinephrine. Psycho Didi notes · p. 24 HPA Axis CRF → Anterior Pituitary ACTH → Adrenal cortex Cortisol → metabolism increase; insulin resistance SAM pathway Hypothalamus → SNS → Adrenal Medulla → Epinephrine and Norepinephrine 15 · Peripheral Nervous System & Cranial Nerves Peripheral nervous system. A page map covering glial cells, the 12 cranial nerves, spinal nerve counts, key PNS facts, the HPA axis and SAM pathway, and the sympathetic versus parasympathetic nervous systems. Psycho Didi notes · p. 24 The Peripheral Nervous System is anything apart from the brain and spinal cord. Who → what. Charles Sherrington — if the spinal cord detaches from the brain, it will still function. Bell-Magendie Law — all dorsal connections are sensory and ventral connections are motor. PNS nerves can reform after damage. Cranial Nerves (12) # Nerve Function 1 Olfactory Smell 2 Optic Vision 3 Oculomotor Eye movement 4 Trochlear Eye movement 5 Trigeminal Masticatory movement 6 Abducens Eye movement 7 Facial Facial movement 8 Auditory vestibular Hearing 9 Glossopharyngeal Tongue and pharynx 10 Vagus Heart 11 Accessory Neck muscles 12 Hypoglossal Tongue Spinal Nerves Region Number Cervical 8 Thoracic 12 Lumbar 5 Sacral 5 Coccygeal 1 16 · The Autonomic Nervous System Feature Sympathetic NS Parasympathetic NS Nerves Thoracic and Lumbar nerves Cranial and Sacral nerves System "Flight or Fight" system "Rest and Digest" system Blood vessels Constrict blood vessels — Heart Increased heart rate Slows heartbeat Respiration Increased respiration Constricts bronchi Digestion Inhibits digestion Metabolic activity decreases Brain / metabolism — Brain activity decreases; metabolic activity decreases Pupils Pupils dilate — Saliva — Stimulates flow of saliva Tear ducts Tear ducts inhibited — Bladder Constricts bladder Contracts bladder Glucose Stimulates glucose release — GSR (Galvanic Skin Response) GSR increases (decreased skin resistance) GSR decreases (skin resistance increases) Don't confuse. Sympathetic = Thoracic and Lumbar nerves, "fight or flight (Walter Cannon)," pupils dilate, heart rate up, digestion inhibited, GSR increases. Parasympathetic = Cranial and Sacral nerves, "rest and digest," slows heartbeat, stimulates saliva, GSR decreases. Mechanism. In sympathetic arousal, galvanic skin response increases because sweat gland activity rises, which decreases skin resistance . Under parasympathetic dominance, GSR decreases as skin resistance increases.

title: Psychopathology
text: Psychopathology — Study with Psycho Didi (MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF) Psychopathology Study with Psycho Didi · MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF notes Biggest chapter (PDF pp. 25–55) DSM-5-TR (2022) & ICD-11 (2022) based Full disorder coverage, every duration cutoff MSE + all diagnostic groups + named syndromes Psychopharmacology appendix What this covers. The complete psychopathology core: the 4 D's of abnormality and the history of clinical psychology; the six approaches to treatment; case history and the full Mental Status Examination (MSE); the DSM and ICD classification systems and how they differ; then every major diagnostic group in DSM-5 order — neurodevelopmental, anxiety, OCD-related, depressive (mood), bipolar/mania, schizophrenia spectrum, trauma/stressor-related, dissociative, somatic, feeding/eating, sleep-wake, sexual/gender/paraphilic, personality, substance-related, and neurocognitive disorders — plus named eponymous syndromes, culture-specific syndromes, and a psychopharmacology reference. Original diagrams. 55 diagrams from the Psycho Didi PDF (pages 26 to 55) sit under the section they belong to, exactly as drawn. Tap one to open it full size and zoom in. Contents: 1 · Foundations & Approaches · 2 · Case History & MSE · 3 · DSM & ICD Classification · 4 · Neurodevelopmental Disorders · 5 · Anxiety Disorders · 6 · OCD & Related Disorders · 7 · Depressive (Mood) Disorders · 8 · Bipolar & Related Disorders · 9 · Schizophrenia Spectrum & Psychotic Disorders · 10 · Trauma & Stressor-Related Disorders · 11 · Dissociative Disorders · 12 · Somatic Symptom & Related Disorders · 13 · Feeding & Eating Disorders · 14 · Sleep-Wake Disorders · 15 · Sexual Dysfunctions, Gender Dysphoria & Paraphilias · 16 · Personality Disorders · 17 · Substance-Related & Addictive Disorders · 18 · Neurocognitive Disorders · 19 · Named / Eponymous Syndromes · 20 · Culture-Specific Syndromes · 21 · Psychopharmacology Reference 1 · Foundations & Approaches to Psychopathology Different Terms Introduction to psychopathology. Boxes listing the 4 D's of abnormality, early history of humane treatment, and definitions of abnormal, psychopathology and clinical psychology. Psycho Didi notes · p. 26 Abnormal: outlining atypicality. Abnormality depends on the intensity and frequency of behaviour. Psychopathology: part of abnormality — the medical angle of the abnormal (involves neuroimaging, aetiology, diagnosis, prognosis). Clinical Psychology: application of psychological principles in the treatment of mental disorders. The 4 D's of Abnormality: Deviance (social and statistical), Distress (causing unhappiness), Dysfunction (unable to show adaptive behaviour), Danger (to oneself and others). History of Clinical Psychology History of clinical psychology. A box noting the founding of the APA, Lightner Witmer's role, and the 1952 start of the DSM and ICD-6. Psycho Didi notes · p. 26 Historically the mentally ill were tied, chained and kept in inhumane conditions. 1826 — Philippe Pinel introduced moral therapy . 1802–1887 — Dorothea Dix advocated for humane treatment. APA founded 1892 ; first president G. Stanley Hall . Lightner Witmer — founder of clinical psychology; opened the first clinic. DSM introduced in 1952 ; ICD-6 in 1952 . Current diagnosis is more spectrum-oriented. Named figures. Pinel (moral therapy), Dorothea Dix (humane treatment advocacy), G. Stanley Hall (first APA president), Lightner Witmer (founder of clinical psychology, first clinic). The Six Approaches (with pros & cons) Approaches to psychopathology. A chart linking each approach's view of abnormality to its therapies and to its pros and cons. Psycho Didi notes · p. 26 Approach View of abnormality Methods Pros Cons Biological Organic problems, biochemical imbalances Drugs, ECT, surgery Effective for those who don't respond to other treatments Side effects; neglects non-biological problems Humanistic Failure to strive towards one's potential / being out of touch with feelings Client-centred, Gestalt, Existential Recognizes positive human goals, values and needs Unsupportive; limited research Behavioural Reinforcement history, environment Desensitization, aversion, operant conditioning (B. F. Skinner), token economy, modelling, social skills training Research supports effectiveness Not long-lasting; neglects cognitive processes Psychodynamic Internal / unconscious conflicts Free association, catharsis, analysis of resistance / transference / dreams First major alternative to biological treatment; abnormal function rooted in same processes as normal function Depends on therapist's subjective interpretation Cognitive Irrational / dysfunctional thoughts REBT, CBT Considerable research support Dysfunctional thinking may not cause abnormal functioning Sociocultural Dysfunctional society — — — 2 · Case History & Mental Status Examination Case History Case history and mental status examination. A one-page overview of case history taking, from personal information and history of present illness to past, family, personal and treatment history and physical examination. Psycho Didi notes · p. 27 Four assessment techniques are used: Observation, Conversation, Exploration, Testing . Personal information: name, father's/husband's name; sociodemographic profile (age, sex, education, occupation, socio-economic status, marital status, religion, residence, mother tongue, address); source of referral; type of admission; identification marks. Informant reliability — the 5 C's (SIMS): Contact (between patient and informant), Closeness of relationship, Continuity of the account, Consistency of the verbatim, Corroborativeness between sources. History of Present Illness — the factors Factor Definition Predisposing Factors operating from early life that determine vulnerability to develop a disorder Precipitating Events that occur shortly before the onset of a disorder Perpetuating Factors due to which the disorder is maintained or aggravated Limiting Factors which limit the illness from extensive progress Modifying Factors which modify the natural or expected course of the illness Mode of onset: abrupt, acute, insidious. Course of illness: continuous, episodic, fluctuating. Progress of illness: improving, deteriorating, static. Compliance: the extent to which the patient's behaviour (taking medications, following diets, other lifestyle changes) coincides with medical recommendations. Also covered: treatment history, past history (medical & psychiatric), family history (genogram, consanguinity), personal history (birth & early development, childhood disorders, home atmosphere, scholastic/extracurricular, occupational, menstrual, sexual & marital, forensic), premorbid personality (individualized styles of dealing with the environment characteristic of a person prior to onset), and physical examination (by physician). Mental Status Examination (MSE) General appearance and behaviour. A panel of MSE parameters covering general appearance, dress, posture, eye contact, estimate of age, body build, facial expression and touch with surroundings, with the disorders each finding suggests. Psycho Didi notes · p. 28 Attitude towards the examiner. Definitions of frank, defensive, cooperative, seductive, hostile, guarded, attentive and evasive attitudes, with the disorders linked to each. Psycho Didi notes · p. 28 Rapport and motor behaviour. Six strategies and three types of rapport, followed by a grid of motor behaviour signs with their definitions and associated disorders. Psycho Didi notes · p. 29 Speech. A panel of speech parameters such as intensity, pitch, quality, reaction time, speed, ease, productivity, deviation and manner of relating, with example disorders. Psycho Didi notes · p. 30 Cognitive functions. Definitions of orientation, attention, abstract ability, intelligence, concentration and memory, with the conditions in which each is disturbed. Psycho Didi notes · p. 31 Mood and affect. Definitions of mood and affect and the dimensions of affect: quality, mobility, intensity, reactivity, communicability, appropriateness and diurnal variation. Psycho Didi notes · p. 31 Thought. A panel describing disturbances of thought under stream, form, possession and content, with definitions and linked conditions. Psycho Didi notes · p. 32 Perception. Sensory distortions (changes in intensity, quality and spatial form) and sensory deception (hallucinations in each sense). Psycho Didi notes · p. 33 Other psychotic phenomena. Definitions of somatic passivity and the made phenomena: made act, made affect and made impulse. Psycho Didi notes · p. 33 Judgement. A definition of judgement and its three types: social, personal and test judgement. Psycho Didi notes · p. 33 Insight. Intellectual versus true emotional insight and the six grades of the insight rating scale. Psycho Didi notes · p. 33 The part of clinical assessment describing the sum total of the examiner's observations and impressions of a psychiatric patient at the time of interview. General Appearance & Behaviour Parameter Finding & associations Eye contact Assesses rapport, truthfulness, insight, concentration. Partial (fleeting); Absent — complete loss (Paranoid Schizophrenia, Acute delusional disorder). Depression → lowered eyes; Anxiety → shifting gaze. Dress Appropriate (normal); Shabby (Dementia, Substance abuse); Inappropriate , e.g. rain hood on a dry day (Mania, Histrionic PD). Facial expression Depression → corners of mouth turned down, vertical furrows on brow. Anxiety → horizontal forehead creases, widened palpebral fissures, dilated pupils. May be fixed/wooden (parkinsonian drug side effects) or reflect thyrotoxicosis. Posture Depression → hunched shoulders, gaze downward. Anxiety → edge of chair, gripping sides. Agitated depression → tremulous, picking at fingernails. Mania → restlessness. Catatonia → odd postures. Estimate of age Younger than stated → Histrionic PD; Older than stated → Depression or Chronic Schizophrenia. General appearance Kempt (normal, OCPD); Overtly made up (mania/hypomania, histrionic/narcissistic PD, some schizophrenia); Unkempt/untidy (organic psychosis, dementia, substance abuse, severe depression, schizophrenia); Sickly ; Perplexed . Body-build typologies. Ernst Kretschmer: Pyknics (stocky/rounded), Leptosomes (long/linear), Athletics (broad-shouldered/muscular). William Sheldon's somatotypes: Endomorph (round, fat abdomen), Mesomorph (cubical head, muscular), Ectomorph (thin, receding chin, spindly limbs). Attitude towards the examiner Frank and Cooperative / Attentive (normal). Defensive & Guarded (Paranoid Schizophrenia, Delusional disorder). Evasive (Organic psychoses, Substance abuse). Hostile (Paranoid Schizophrenia, Antisocial PD). Seductive . Rapport A bidirectional empathetic relationship. Easily established — normal persons, Mania; Established with difficulty — Schizophrenia, Dementia, Depression; Not possible — Paranoid Schizophrenia, Dementia, Depression. Motor Behaviour (selected signs) Sign Description / association Retardation Slowness of initiation/execution — Depression Hyperactivity Increased motor activity, often with over-talkativeness Mannerisms Unusual repeated goal-directed action (e.g. odd hand movements when shaking hands) Stereotypy Repetitive, non-goal-directed action carried out uniformly Grimace Non-goal-directed facial expression; e.g. Schnauzkrampf (snout spasm) — Schizophrenia Tics Sudden involuntary twitchings — Gilles de la Tourette syndrome (SIMS) Waxy flexibility Person maintains the body position into which they are placed Negativism Verbal/non-verbal opposition to suggestion — catatonic schizophrenia Echolalia Repeating another's words — catatonic schizophrenia Echopraxia Repetition by imitation of another's movements Ambivalence Co-existence of two opposing impulses toward the same thing — Schizophrenia, borderline state, OCD Automatic obedience Undue compliance with instructions — catatonia Waxy flexibility, odd posturing, rigidity, self-injury Catatonia; self-injurious behaviour → Borderline PD Also noted: preoccupied, restless, awkward (apraxia, MR), destructive (catatonic/manic excitement), silly smiling (Mania, Hebephrenia), aggressive, perseveration, dyskinesia, dystonia, chorea, athetosis, hallucinatory behaviour, gestures, touching the examiner. Speech Intensity: excessively loud (Mania, Hypomania), abnormally soft (vocal cord palsy, Depression, Paranoid Schizophrenia). Pitch: monotonous (parietal lobe damage, chronic schizophrenia, depression). Reaction time: increased (hypothyroidism, depression, schizophrenia), decreased (Mania). Speed: very slow (depression, dementia, hypothyroidism); rapid with prolixity/flight of ideas (mania, hypomania, hyperthyroidism). Pressure of speech — increased, accelerated, hard to interrupt (Mania, Schizophrenia, cognitive disorders). Ease: hesitant (head injury, anxiety), mutism (stupor, dementia), slurring (cerebellar damage), stuttering/stammering (severe anxiety, schizophrenia), whispering (pseudobulbar palsy), muttering (schizophrenia, dementia). Deviations: rhyming/punning (mania), talking past the point ( Ganser's syndrome , schizophrenia), clang association (schizophrenia, mania), stereotypy (catatonic schizophrenia), perseveration. Cognitive Functions Orientation (time, place, person), attention, concentration, memory (immediate / recent / remote), abstract ability, intelligence (comprehension, general information, vocabulary, calculation). Thinking style Definition & association Concrete thinking Thinking bound to actual things/events & immediate experience — Schizophrenia, young children Functional thinking Abstraction relating only to functional aspects — Schizophrenia, MR Over-abstraction Excessive manifestation of a concept beyond relevance — Schizophrenia, philosophical preoccupations Mood & Affect Mood = persistent, sustained emotion colouring perception of the world. Affect = present emotional responsiveness inferred from expression. Quality: dysphoric, anxious, irritable, depressed, elevated, euphoric, elated, exalted, ecstatic, euthymic. Intensity: shallow (lack of depth), blunted (greatly diminished, uniform voice), flat (no affect displayed). Appropriateness: Paramimia — lack of unity between modes of emotional expression; Parathymia — expression opposite to what is expected (e.g. laughing at tragic news). Diurnal variation: worse in morning (endogenous depression, headache), worse in evening (anxiety, delirium/ sundowning ), worse at night (uremia). Thought Aspect Key terms Stream Acceleration, pressured speech, flight of ideas (rapid, chance connections still understandable), prolixity (ordered flight, returns to task), retardation/bradyphrenia, poverty of speech (laconic), circumstantiality (reaches point via trivia), tangentiality (oblique, never reaches point), thought blocking (sudden arrest → blank) Form Negative type (loses ability to form concept) vs positive type (false concept by blending incongruous elements): loosening of associations, derailment, neologism, over-inclusion Possession Obsession , rumination , compulsion , thought alienation — insertion, withdrawal, broadcasting, thought echo Content Worry, phobias, impulse, somatic symptoms, religious preoccupations (OCD), magical thinking, depressive cognition (worthlessness/helplessness/hopelessness), suicidal/homicidal ideas, inflated self-esteem, delusion (a false firm belief) Perception Sensory distortion — intensity: hyperaesthesia, hyperacusis, hypoacusis. Quality: Xanthopsia (yellow), Chloropsia (green), Erythropsia (red/pink). Spatial form: Micropsia (smaller), Macropsia/megalopsia (larger), Porropsia (retreat into distance without size change). Sensory deception — Hallucination: perception without an adequate external stimulus (auditory, visual, olfactory, gustatory, tactile). Delusion vs Hallucination. A delusion is a false firm belief (a disorder of thought content ). A hallucination is a perception without an adequate external stimulus (a disorder of perception ). An illusion is a misperception of a real stimulus. Don't conflate them. Other psychotic phenomena. Somatic passivity — belief that outside influences play on the body. Made phenomenon — made act (actions under external control), made affect (feelings not one's own), made impulse (impulse admitted as one's own action but not one's own drive). Judgement & Insight Judgement: social, personal, test. Insight — degree of awareness/understanding of being ill (intellectual vs true emotional insight), rated on a 6-point scale: Insight — 6-point scale: Grade 1 complete denial → Grade 2 slight awareness but denying → Grade 3 attributed to external/physical factors → Grade 4 due to something unknown in self → Grade 5 intellectual insight → Grade 6 true emotional insight. 3 · Classification — DSM & ICD The DSM The DSM. DSM editions from DSM-I to DSM-5 arranged around a history box, with the five axes, DSM-5 categories, new and eliminated disorders, and criticism. Psycho Didi notes · p. 34 Emil Kraepelin differentiated dementia praecox (a biological illness from anatomical/toxic processes) from manic depression (an episodic disorder not leading to permanently impaired brain function) as the two forms of psychosis. Edition Year Key features DSM-I 1952 Developed by the American Psychiatric Association; 100 conditions; division into psychosis & neurosis DSM-II 1962 Written in paragraphs as explanations DSM-III 1980 Multiaxial system introduced; symptomatic criteria; started aligning with ICD DSM-IV & IV-TR 1994 Five-axis system fully articulated DSM-5 2013 Multiaxial system dropped; spectrum approach; Roman numerals replaced by Arabic DSM-5-TR 2022 Latest; added prolonged grief disorder The five axes (DSM-III to IV-TR): Axis I clinical syndromes (V codes); Axis II personality disorders & intellectual disability; Axis III general medical condition; Axis IV psychosocial & environmental problems; Axis V global assessment of functioning (GAF). DSM-5 disorder categories Neurodevelopmental; Schizophrenia-spectrum & other psychotic; Bipolar & related; Depressive; Anxiety; Obsessive-compulsive & related; Trauma & stressor-related; Dissociative; Somatic symptom & related; Feeding & eating; Sexual dysfunctions; Gender dysphoria; Paraphilic disorders; Sleep-wake; Disruptive, impulse-control & conduct; Neurocognitive; Substance-related & addictive; Personality disorders. New in DSM-5: social (pragmatic) communication disorder; disruptive mood dysregulation disorder; premenstrual dysphoric disorder; hoarding disorder; excoriation (skin-picking) disorder; disinhibited social engagement disorder; binge eating disorder; central sleep apnea; sleep-related hypoventilation; REM sleep behaviour disorder; restless legs syndrome; caffeine withdrawal; cannabis withdrawal; major NCD with Lewy Body Disease; mild neurocognitive disorder. Eliminated: sexual aversion; polysubstance-related disorder. Criticism of DSM: medicalization (over-diagnosis), pharmaceutical influence, cultural and ethical concerns, comorbidity. The ICD The ICD. ICD editions arranged around a box of its uses, with the F-code categories, ICD-11 changes, an ICD-10 versus ICD-11 comparison and a Venn diagram of ICD versus DSM. Psycho Didi notes · p. 35 International Classification of Diseases. ICD-6: 1948/49. Essential for standardization, research & epidemiology, healthcare management, resource allocation, global consistency. Block ICD grouping F00–09 Organic mental disorders (neurocognitive) F10–19 Substance use disorders F20–29 Schizophrenia and related F30–39 Mood disorders F40–49 Neurotic, stress-related, somatoform disorders F50–59 Behavioural syndromes associated with physiological disturbances F60–69 Personality disorders F70–79 Intellectual disability (neurodevelopmental) F80–89 Psychological development disorders F90–98 Emotional development disorders F99 Unspecified ICD editions: ICD-9 (1977), ICD-10 (1993), ICD-11 (2022). ICD-11 eliminated acute stress disorder and gender incongruence as a personality disorder (dimensional approach instead of categorization) and added prolonged grief disorder, compulsive sexual behaviour, gaming disorder. ICD vs DSM ICD DSM Origin 1949 1952 Authoring body WHO APA Scope Broader Narrower Outlook Global American Editions 11 5 Similarities: symptoms overlap; both are authoritative guidebooks. Other differences: cultural considerations, billing/insurance, acceptance and use. General anxiety features, the features of neurosis, trait versus state anxiety, and motor, autonomic, cognitive, affective and other symptoms. Psycho Didi notes · p. 38 Anxiety disorders according to DSM 5. Notes on each DSM-5 anxiety disorder, from generalized anxiety disorder and phobias to selective mutism and unspecified anxiety disorder. Psycho Didi notes · p. 38 Neurosis — subjective distress; ego-dystonic; insight present; personality & behaviour preserved; absence of organicity; reaction to stress & adjustment; somatoform. Anxiety symptoms. Motor (tremors, restlessness, muscle twitch, fearful face); autonomic/visceral (palpitation, tachycardia, sweating, flushes, hyperventilation, chest constriction, mouth dryness, reduced micturition, mydriasis); cognitive (poor concentration, distractibility, hyperarousal, vigilance); affective (apprehension, fearfulness, inability to relax, irritability, feelings of doom); other (noise sensitivity, insomnia, increased startle response). Trait anxiety ("I often feel anxious") vs state anxiety ("I feel anxious now") — those with trait anxiety also have state anxiety. Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) Most diagnosed anxiety disorder; free-floating anxiety; for 6 months or more ; constant low arousal of the sympathetic nervous system. DDx: OCD, PTSD, mood disorder, physical causes, realistic anxiety. Treatment: benzodiazepine, SSRI, barbiturates (old), CBT, relaxation, psychodynamic therapy. Social Anxiety Disorder Severe irrational fear of evaluation; dysfunction at work and relationships; ≥ 6 months ; sometimes only due to evaluation of performance. Specific Phobia Defence mechanism: displacement . Irrational, disproportional fear of certain animals, natural environment, situations, blood/injection, others. Fear out of proportion; insight present; inability to control fear; avoidance of the object. Agoraphobia Fear of being in a place where they can't get up and leave; fear of crowded/enclosed places. Treatment: clomipramine, venlafaxine, buspirone. Panic Disorder Feelings of impending doom; hippocampus and amygdala involved; periodic, discrete bouts of panic/terror in the absence of any real threat; feels like a heart attack; should be present for more than a month . Separation Anxiety Disorder Fear that something will happen to the attachment figure if away; can happen in adults; may have vomiting; ≥ 6 months in adults, ≥ 4 weeks in children . Selective Mutism Children remain silent except before close people; normal intelligence; family history of SAD; may develop SAD in adulthood; duration > 1 month ; treatment: social skills training. Psycho Didi notes · p. 39 Young-adulthood onset; most common in males; family history. Obsessions: ego-dystonic, irrational, absurd, distressing, recognised as one's own idea. Compulsions: to neutralize the obsession; not realistic; irrational; insight present; subjective; may diminish the anxiety associated with the obsession. Major patterns: contamination, pathological doubt, intrusive thought, symmetry (tics). Aetiology. Dysfunction in fronto-striatal brain circuitry ( caudate ). Defence mechanisms: reaction formation, isolation of affect, undoing . DSM specifier: with good/fair insight; with poor insight; with absent insight/delusional beliefs; tic-related.
