Boxes on aetiology, physical signs, prognosis, treatment and features, with a flowchart branching to MDD, persistent depressive disorder, DMDD and PMDD. Psycho Didi notes · p. 40 Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) Duration ≥ 2 weeks. Mnemonic SIGECAPS: S leep disturbance (REM latency, early-morning awakening); low I nterest; G uilt; E nergy deficit; reduced C oncentration; reduced A ppetite; P sychomotor agitation/retardation; S uicidal ideation. Specifiers/features: with psychotic features (schizoaffective); atypical features (hypersomnia, overeating); melancholic features (in old age); catatonic features. Persistent Depressive Disorder (Dysthymia) Symptoms persist for 2 years ; no suicidal ideation; no hospitalization; symptoms never absent for longer than 2 months. MDD vs Persistent Depressive Disorder. MDD = ≥ 2 weeks, may include suicidal ideation and hospitalization. Persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia) = ≥ 2 years, no suicidal ideation, no hospitalization, symptoms never absent > 2 months. Double depression = MDD superimposed on dysthymia (a poor-prognosis feature). Disruptive Mood Dysregulation Disorder (DMDD) For children and adolescents; a precursor to bipolar ; sudden anger, throwing fits, tantrums; persistent negative moods; sadness translated into complete outbursts. DDx: oppositional defiant disorder. Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder (PMDD) Mood shifts or other dysphoria in the week or two before the menstrual period. Prognosis, subtypes & aetiology Good prognosis Poor prognosis Acute onset; typical clinical features; severe depression; well-adjusted premorbid personality; good treatment response Comorbidity with personality disorder/alcohol abuse; double depression; chronic stress; unfavourable early environment; hypochondriacal features; poor drug compliance Endogenous Exogenous Absence of any precipitating life event Due to a precipitating life event; less likelihood of psychosis; more somatic complaints; less likelihood of suicide Physical signs. Veraguth's fold — triangular fold in the nasal corner of the upper eyelid. Omega sign on the forehead. Aaron Beck's cognitive triad — negative view of self, world, future. Also: learned helplessness (Martin Seligman). Aetiology: unipolar depression concordance rate 46%; abnormality in monoamine, acetylcholine and GABA neurotransmitters; hormonal disturbances; neuroanatomical — reduced dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and increased HPA axis. Treatment: pharmacotherapy takes 3–4 weeks; maintained for 6 months (prophylactic). Tricyclic antidepressants (block reuptake of serotonin & norepinephrine, the "-pramines"; anticholinergic side effects — constipation, urinary retention, blurred vision, dry mouth). SSRIs / NaSSA / SNRI (side effects: nausea, anxiety, diarrhoea). MAOIs. Antipsychotics. Therapies: CBT, mindfulness, IPT, ECT, TMS, vagus nerve stimulation, deep brain stimulation, sleep deprivation therapy, phototherapy (1500–10,000 lux). 8 · Bipolar & Related Disorders (Mania) Mood Disorders: Mania. A one-page summary of mania with boxes for aetiology and prevalence, mania versus hypomania, treatment, the DIG FAST criteria and specifiers, plus a flowchart branching into Bipolar I, Bipolar II and cyclothymic disorder. Psycho Didi notes · p. 41 Manic episode criteria — mnemonic DIG FAST: D istractibility; I mpulsivity; G randiosity; F light of ideas; A ctivity (goal-directed) increase; S leep deficit; T alkativeness. Bipolar I Requires a manic episode . Major depressive episodes common but not required for diagnosis. Bipolar II A hypomanic episode and at least one major depressive episode ; there has never been a full manic episode. Bipolar I vs Bipolar II — and Mania vs Hypomania. Mania (Bipolar I): lasts 1 week , accompanied by less intense depression, may have psychotic features, requires hospitalization. Hypomania (Bipolar II): lasts 4 days , accompanied by major depressive episodes, may not require hospitalization, never a full manic episode. Bipolar I needs a manic episode; Bipolar II needs hypomania + ≥ 1 MDE and no full mania. Cyclothymic Disorder Periods with hypomanic symptoms (not meeting full criteria) and depressive symptoms (not meeting full criteria) for at least 2 years , during which symptoms have not been absent for more than 2 months. Specifiers Mood-congruent psychotic features; mood-incongruent psychotic features; catatonia; peripartum onset; seasonal pattern; hypomania; mixed episodes (cycle in 7 days); anxious distress; rapid cycling; melancholic features; atypical features. Aetiology & prevalence. Bipolar disorder is the most genetically influenced disorder (74% if both parents affected). Neurotransmitters: increased dopamine activity. Genetic factors: chromosomes 18q, 22q, 21q. Mania more common in men; depression more common in women; onset 30 years and above; more in divorced/single persons. Treatment: Lithium (side effects: postural tremors [treated with beta-blockers], memory disturbance, intracranial tension, peripheral neuropathy, hypothyroidism, polyuria, diabetes; lithium toxicity — tremors, renal impairment, ataxia, delirium, increased reflexes, convulsions, vomiting, kidney issues), Valproate (acute mania), Lamotrigine (depressive), Carbamazepine, Oxcarbazepine, antipsychotics, benzodiazepines, antidepressants; ECT; therapy. Treatment continued for 2 years. 9 · Schizophrenia Spectrum & Other Psychotic Disorders Schizophrenia and Other Psychotic Disorders. A grid of boxes covering positive and negative symptoms, history, types, epidemiology, prognosis, speech and catatonia, etiology, the duration rules for other psychotic disorders, and treatment. Psycho Didi notes · p. 49 History. Emil Kraepelin gave the term dementia praecox (1896); his classification: simple dementia, paranoia, catatonia, hebephrenia. Eugen Bleuler coined the term schizophrenia and gave the 4 A's : Ambivalence, Autism, Association (disturbance), Affect disturbance . Karl Kahlbaum — catatonia. Symptoms Negative symptoms: affective flattening, avolition, apathy, anhedonia, asociality, alogia. Schneider's First-Rank Symptoms (positive). Audible thoughts (1st person); voices heard arguing (3rd person); voices commenting on one's actions; thought withdrawal; thought diffusion/broadcasting; made feeling; made impulse; made actions; somatic passivity. Also: hallucinations; delusions (erotomania, grandeur, guilt, jealousy, passivity, persecution, poverty, reference, somatic, thought control). Speech disturbances: poverty of speech, echolalia, verbigeration (continual repetition of stereotyped phrases), perseveration. Catatonia (Karl Kahlbaum): agitation, cataplexy (sudden muscle weakness/paralysis), echolalia/echopraxia, exaggerated compliance, grimace, mannerism, mutism, stereotypy, posturing, waxy flexibility. Types (subtypes) Paranoid; Catatonic; Disorganized/Hebephrenic; Undifferentiated; Residual; Simple ( worst prognosis ). Also pfropfschizophrenie — schizophrenia and mental retardation coexisting. Type 1 Type 2 Ventricles Normal ventricles Dilated ventricles Damage No organic damage; no comorbidity — Medication response Good prognosis Low response to medication Duration & the psychotic-disorder family Disorder Duration Symptoms to be met Schizophrenia 6+ months All Schizophreniform disorder 1–6 months All Schizoaffective disorder 2 weeks Schizophrenia + mood disorder Delusional disorder 1 month Delusion Brief psychotic disorder 1 day and 1 night All Schizophreniform vs Schizophrenia (the classic duration trap). Schizophreniform = 1–6 months ; Schizophrenia = 6+ months — same full symptom set, only the duration cutoff differs. Brief psychotic disorder is even shorter (1 day–1 month), and schizoaffective requires both schizophrenia and a mood disorder. Etiology, epidemiology & prognosis Positive symptoms — excess dopamine in the mesolimbic tract (VTA → limbic region). Negative symptoms — dopamine dysregulation in the mesocortical pathway (VTA → prefrontal lobe). Genetic loci: 1q, 5q, 6p, 6q, 8p, 10p, 13q, 15q, 22q. Biochemical: dopamine, serotonin, glutamate, GABA. Epidemiology: 1% lifetime; 0.15–0.25% per 1000; good prognosis in females; bad prognosis with low SES. Good prognosis Poor prognosis Abrupt/sudden onset; late onset; catatonic; in females; positive symptoms present; history of mood disorders Insidious onset; early onset; simple/disorganized schizophrenia; in males; negative symptoms present; history of schizophrenia Treatment. Typical antipsychotics (dopamine receptor antagonists; side effect: Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome, NMS) — Chlorpromazine (1950), Haloperidol, Phenothiazines, Thioxanthene, Butyrophenones. Atypical antipsychotics (target 5-HT receptors, partially block D2) — Clozapine (treatment-resistant schizophrenia), Olanzapine, Quetiapine; do not cause tardive dyskinesia. 10 · Trauma & Stressor-Related Disorders Trauma and Stress Related Disorders. An illustrated page summarising PTSD, complex PTSD, prolonged grief disorder, acute stress disorder, adjustment disorder, reactive attachment disorder and disinhibited social engagement disorder. Psycho Didi notes · p. 43 Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) Occurs after rape, floods, abduction, plane crash, soldiers of war; symptoms don't develop immediately. Was classified under anxiety disorders until DSM-IV-TR. Symptoms: avoidance of situations/places/memories; intrusive flashbacks, re-experiencing, nightmares; arousal (hypervigilance, exaggerated startle); depersonalization & derealization. Diagnosed if symptoms appear within 6 months after trauma; symptoms present for more than a month. Brain regions: hippocampus, amygdala. Acute Stress Disorder All PTSD symptoms for less than 1 month ; also experience dissociation; 9/14 symptoms of PTSD must be present. Acute Stress Disorder vs PTSD. ASD = PTSD symptoms lasting < 1 month (with prominent dissociation). PTSD = symptoms > 1 month, appearing within 6 months of trauma. Note ICD-11 eliminated acute stress disorder as a diagnosis. Complex PTSD (ICD-11) Prolonged exposure to trauma. Disturbances in self-organization — the person must experience 2/3 of: (1) emotional dysregulation, (2) interpersonal disturbances, (3) [disturbed self-perception]. Clinical features: re-experiencing, avoidance, hyperarousal, impaired self-perception, difficulty maintaining relationships. Treatment: prevention/disaster management, practical help, SSRIs, benzodiazepines, EMDR (Francine Shapiro). Prolonged Grief Disorder (DSM-5-TR & ICD-11) Intense, persistent grief; difficulty accepting loss; intrusive thoughts/memories; avoidance; emotional numbness; identity disturbance (feeling like we have died with the other person); unable to function for more than 6 months . Treatment: grief counselling, group therapy, SSRIs. Adjustment Disorder Not being able to adjust to a new situation; psychological and physical symptoms (depression, anxiety) for a span of 3–6 months . Specifiers: anxiety, depression, behaviour, conduct. Reactive Attachment Disorder Unable to form reciprocal relationships; faced rejection in childhood; periods of irritable sadness; issues develop before age 5 ; persistent if symptoms last longer than a year . DDx: ASD, depression. Disinhibited Social Engagement Disorder Outcome of abuse, insufficient caregiving, neglect, frequent change; shyness; don't check in with regular caregiver; may become excessively familiar with strangers. 11 · Dissociative Disorders Dissociative & Somatic Disorders. A two-column page with dissociative disorders on the left (clinical features, types of gain, amnesia, fugue, depersonalization/derealization, DID and ICD-10 types) and somatic symptom, conversion, illness anxiety and factitious disorders on the right. Psycho Didi notes · p. 44 A group of normally integrated mental processes become separated from the rest. Clinical features: disturbance in integrated consciousness; sudden onset, temporary course; precipitatory stress; secondary gain; no physical abnormality; affects memory, identity, perception; produced unconsciously by the psyche. Types of gain. Primary — internal psychological motivation to reduce guilt. Secondary — external psychological motivation for assurance/social support. Tertiary — parent's/close person's benefit. Dissociative Amnesia (Psychogenic Amnesia) Types: circumscribed (personal event-specific), selective (forgetting some things), generalized (forgetting everything), continuous (from a stressful event till present), systematized (everything about an event). Dissociative Fugue Wandering/running off; losing old identity and picking up a new one; termination is abrupt. Depersonalization/Derealization Disorder Depersonalization — cutting off/detachment from oneself. Derealization — experience of what is real and not real may be lost. Occurs without overlap with other disorders. Dissociative Identity Disorder (DID) At least 2 distinct identities; personality states called alter egos . Other dissociative presentations (ICD-10) Dissociative trance or possession disorder; dissociative stupor; dissociative disorder of movement and sensation ( la belle indifférence ) — physical symptoms due to psychological causes. 12 · Somatic Symptom & Related Disorders Somatic Symptom (Somatoform) Disorder Chronic pain without any physical cause; conviction persists despite negative test results; duration 6+ months ; onset may be due to stress. Clinical features: 4 pain symptoms, 2 GI symptoms, 1 sexual symptom, 1 pseudo-neurological symptom. Treatment: psychotherapy. Illness Anxiety Disorder (Hypochondriasis) Over-concern with normal body function; terribly worried about having a serious illness; symptoms don't remain constant; unconsciously start mimicking symptoms (not psychotic); addicted to internet searches. Subtypes: care-seeking , care-avoidant . Duration 6+ months. Conversion Disorder (Hysteria / Functional Neurological Symptom Disorder) Body function is lost due to a psychological issue; primary and secondary gain; psychogenic non-epileptic seizures (PNES) ; disturbance of consciousness; la belle indifférence ; duration 6+ months . Factitious Disorder Person wants to stay sick for attention; maintains the sick role; simulates symptoms. Types: for self ; by proxy (Munchausen syndrome) — keeping a child sick. Pseudologia fantastica — telling stories, pathological lying. Person pretends to have non-measurable diseases; "professionals as patients". 13 · Feeding & Eating Disorders Feeding & Eating Disorders. An illustrated page with the features, types, severity levels and treatment of anorexia, bulimia, binge eating disorder, rumination disorder, pica and avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder. Psycho Didi notes · p. 51 Anorexia Nervosa Restricted food intake to markedly reduced body weight; obsessing about obesity/weight gain; distorted self-perception of being overweight. Characteristic symptoms: disturbance of body image; fear of fatness & excessive emphasis on thinness; restriction of energy intake (significantly less weight than normal); amenorrhea (compulsory until DSM-IV), hypothermia, edema, bradycardia, reduced sexual activity; cuts food into small pieces and rearranges it; cooks for other people. Types: restricting type, purging type. Treatment: hospitalization, reinforcement for healthy eating, CBT, SSRIs. Bulimia Nervosa Normal body weight; binge eating followed by purging; gobbles food in large quantities; no distorted view of being overweight ; morbid fear of weight gain; normal sexual functioning; not secretive. Duration 3+ months. Severity (episodes/week): Mild 1–3; Moderate 4–7; Severe 8–13; Extreme 14 or more. Anorexia vs Bulimia. Anorexia → markedly reduced body weight and a distorted body image . Bulimia → normal body weight , binge-purge cycles, and no distorted view of being overweight; not secretive. Binge Eating Disorder Heavy episodes of eating; episodes often occur in private; craving for calorie-dense food with high speed of consumption; duration 3+ months ; severity measured like bulimia. Rumination Disorder Repeated regurgitation of food — chewed, swallowed, brought back to the mouth and chewed again; may lead to nutritional deficiency; may happen in infants and intellectually disabled children (usually males); malnutrition and vulnerability to disease; may increase gastro-oesophageal reflux; duration 1+ months . Pica Consuming non-nutritive, non-food substances; duration 1+ months ; not eating normal food; nutritional deficiency; behaviour often recognized only when bowel-obstruction surgery becomes necessary; may be found in children with ID and ASD; usually low socioeconomic status. Avoidant/Restrictive Food Intake Disorder (Food Fad Disorder) Child becomes addicted to one kind of food and refuses anything else; may commence due to parent-child conflict. 3 categories: don't care about eating; restrict diet due to sensory issues; don't eat because of an unpleasant experience. DDx: anxiety. 14 · Sleep-Wake Disorders Why we sleep & sleep stages Sleep Disorders: Introduction and Stages. Psycho Didi notes · p. 42 Features. A box listing five features of personality disorders: disharmonious attitude or behaviour, enduring pattern, clearly maladaptive, appearing during adolescence, and personal or social distress. Psycho Didi notes · p. 42 General features: ego-syntonic ; don't seek psychiatric help unless other symptoms co-occur; deviate from social norm — unhappy and impaired; abnormal behaviour and subjective experience causing significant impairment; disharmonious attitude; enduring, maladaptive pattern; appear during adolescence; personal/social distress. A column of bullet lists for paranoid, schizoid and schizotypal personality disorders with their features, differential diagnosis and treatment. Psycho Didi notes · p. 42 Paranoid Personality Disorder Obsessive rumination; excessive suspiciousness; heightened self-importance; persistently bears grudges; conspiracy theories; suspicious of partner's fidelity. Treatment: supportive psychotherapy, benzodiazepines, antipsychotics. DDx: delusional disorder. Schizoid Personality Disorder Emotional bluntness; lack of pleasure from activities; limited capacity to express feelings; indifference to praise/criticism; little interest in sexual experience; prefers solitary activities; preoccupation with fantasy and introspection. Schizotypal Personality Disorder Ideas of reference; odd beliefs/magical thinking; eccentric behaviour; odd thinking; suspiciousness/paranoid ideas; inappropriate/constricted affect; poor rapport; lack of close friends; unusual perceptual experience; stereotypical thinking; quasi-psychotic episodes; belief in telepathy and thought broadcast; inner world like a child; may experience psychosis under severe stress; 3/9 symptoms needed . ICD-10 puts it under schizophrenia. Treatment: antidepressants, antipsychotics, benzodiazepines; psychoanalysis, individual therapy. Cluster B — Dramatic & Emotional Cluster B: Dramatic & Emotional. A column of bullet lists for antisocial, histrionic, borderline and narcissistic personality disorders with their features, defence mechanisms and treatment. Psycho Didi notes · p. 42 Antisocial Personality Disorder Callous unconcern for others' feelings; disregard for social norms; can't maintain relationships; low frustration tolerance; can't experience guilt; proneness to blame others; history of conduct disorder; EEG abnormality; ADHD comorbidity; genetic predisposition; comes to psychiatry from legal authorities; 3/6 symptoms to be met . DSM-5 also includes impulse-control disorder. Treatment: carbamazepine, beta-blockers. Histrionic Personality Disorder Extreme attention-seeking; emotionalism seeps into all areas; self-dramatization; suggestibility; shallow and labile affect; continual attention-seeking; inappropriately seductive; over-concern with physical attractiveness; flamboyant. Defence mechanisms: acting out, dissociation. Treatment: antidepressants, psychotherapy. Borderline Personality Disorder Impulsive; labile; self-harm clearly visible to others; unstable relationships; fragile self-esteem; unclear preferences; devaluation or idealisation; fear of abandonment; chronic feelings of emptiness; accident proneness. Primary defence: splitting ; comorbidity with depression; also called emotionally unstable personality disorder . Treatment: Dialectical Behaviour Therapy (DBT; Marsha Linehan, 1993) . Narcissistic Personality Disorder Sense of grandiosity; fantasy of unlimited success; attention/praise-seeking; lack of empathy; shaky self-esteem; thirst for admiration; unable to face criticism; tries to impress new people; believes they are special/talented; develops depression if faced with rejection. Cluster C — Anxious & Fearful Cluster C: Anxious & Fearful. A column of bullet lists for avoidant, dependent and obsessive-compulsive personality disorders with their features and treatment. Psycho Didi notes · p. 42 Avoidant Personality Disorder Feelings of inadequacy; belief that they are socially inept, inferior, unappealing; preoccupation with being rejected; unwillingness to involve socially; restricted lifestyle; 3/6 traits should be present; depression may develop. Treatment: beta-blockers, SSRI, CBT, social skills training. Dependent Personality Disorder Need for others to take care of them and make decisions; subordination of one's own needs; unwillingness to make demands; fear of being abandoned; can't make decisions without excessive reassurance; may develop passive-aggressive personality. Obsessive-Compulsive Personality Disorder (OCPD) Excessive doubt; need to exert interpersonal control; preoccupation with details; excessive conscientiousness; adherence to social convention; others should submit to their ways; unwelcome thoughts. Psychodynamic view: fixation in the anal stage (Sigmund Freud, 1905). ICD calls it anankastic personality disorder. Treatment: psychotherapy. OCD vs OCPD. OCD (an anxiety-related disorder) involves ego- dystonic obsessions and compulsions with insight. OCPD (a personality disorder) is an ego- syntonic , pervasive pattern of perfectionism, control and orderliness — the person sees nothing wrong with it. ICD calls OCPD "anankastic." 17 · Substance-Related & Addictive Disorders Substance Related Disorders. An overview of clinical symptoms, etiology, other symptoms, dependence and harmful use, ending with the five classes of substances and examples of each. Psycho Didi notes · p. 46 ICD-10: "mental and behavioural disorders due to psychoactive substance use" — more focus on consequence. Initial denial, then tolerance and withdrawal. Etiology. Brain areas: striatum, nucleus accumbens (addiction behaviour). Neurotransmitter systems: dopamine, opioid, catecholamines, GABA. Hereditary factors involved. Clinical syndromes (ICD) (1) Acute intoxication; (2) withdrawal state; (3) dependence syndrome ; (4) harmful use — causing harm to the individual but dependence criteria not met; damage to physical/mental health; issues in daily functioning. Dependence: behavioural, physical & psychological craving; difficulty controlling use; withdrawal symptoms; tolerance; neglect of alternative pleasures; persistence with substance use. Classes of substances CNS stimulants: cocaine, amphetamine, caffeine, nicotine. Depressants: alcohol, barbiturates, benzodiazepines, inhalants. Opioids: narcotics, heroin, morphine. Cannabis. Hallucinogen & phencyclidine. Cocaine CNS Stimulants: Cocaine and Amphetamine. A table giving the effects, withdrawal symptoms and miscellaneous notes for cocaine and amphetamine. Psycho Didi notes · p. 46 Blocks D1, D2 dopamine receptors; increases dopamine & norepinephrine in the synapse; sympathomimetic; vasoconstriction; once used as an anaesthetic; crack = freebase of cocaine (high craving). Intoxication: euphoria, pupil dilation, tachycardia, sweating. Miscellaneous: nasal perforation, tongue turns black. Withdrawal: low energy/exhaustion, hunger, suicidal ideation. Formication (Magnan's phenomenon / cocaine bugs) — sensation of insects crawling on/under the skin (tactile hallucination). Cocaine-induced psychotic disorder — similar to paranoid schizophrenia. Amphetamine Euphoria; potential for psychotic disorder; used for performance enhancement. Substances: methamphetamines, dextroamphetamines, methylphenidate. Acute intoxication: paranoid ideation, auditory hallucination, visual illusion. Withdrawal: fatigue; vivid/unpleasant dreams; insomnia or hypersomnia; increased appetite; psychomotor agitation or retardation. Nicotine Substances: Nicotine to Inhalants. A table giving the effects, withdrawal symptoms and miscellaneous notes for nicotine, caffeine, opioids, hallucinogens and phencyclidine, cannabis, and inhalants. Psycho Didi notes · p. 47 Enhances attention, learning, reaction time, problem-solving. Most common in India as beedi; nicotine and carbon monoxide responsible for cardiovascular disorder. Withdrawal: craving, irritability, anxiety, difficulty concentrating, bradycardia, drowsiness, decreased REM sleep, increased appetite. Treatment: nicotine replacement therapy; Bupropion; Clonidine; Nortriptyline; Varenicline (new); behaviour therapy, CBT. Caffeine Effects: anxiety, jittery, restless, insomnia, flushed face. Withdrawal: headaches, fatigue, irritability, difficulty concentrating. Opioids Opiates (natural) — poppy; opioids (synthetic) — heroin (quick absorption). Effects: euphoria, warmth, high dependence potential, facial flushing, sedation. Overdose: respiratory depression, coma, pupil constriction, cyanosis. Withdrawal: muscle cramps, body aches, insomnia, anxiety, hypertension, tachycardia, nausea, vomiting, anorexia. Treatment: long-acting opioid — methadone, buprenorphine for 2–3 weeks, slowly tapered. Withdrawal duration: 6–8 hrs; peak 2nd–3rd day, reduces by 8–10 days. Hallucinogens & Phencyclidine LSD, psilocybin mushroom, MDMA (ecstasy), angel dust (PCP). Effects: depersonalization, derealization, synesthesia, hallucinations, illusions, autonomic hyperactivity, altered perception; may cause a "bad trip" (benzodiazepines given to reduce). No physical dependence; tolerance; withdrawal rarely seen; LSD associated with flashback phenomena . Treatment: psychotherapy. PCP: behavioural changes, dizziness, nystagmus, slurred speech, unsteady gait, lethargy, tremors, muscle weakness, blurred vision, stupor, euphoria; rapid reach to lungs/brain/bloodstream. Overdose: lesions in the brain, cognitive deficits. Cannabis Bhang, charas, ganja, weed, hash. Effects: behavioural changes, impaired motor coordination, anxiety, slowed time, red eyes, increased appetite, dry mouth, rapid heartbeat, impaired judgement. Withdrawal: irritability, anger, aggression, nervousness, sleep difficulties, decreased appetite, restlessness, depressed mood. Treatment: rehabilitation, behaviour therapy, psychotherapy. Inhalants (Depressants) Gasoline, spray paint, thinner. Effects like a depressant: lethargy, depressed reflexes, psychomotor retardation, tremors, generalized muscle weakness, blurred vision, stupor, euphoria. Withdrawal: agitation/irritability, powerful headaches, nausea, excessive sweating, tremors and convulsions, abdominal cramping, intense cravings. Alcohol Alcohol. A table row for alcohol listing its effects, reverse tolerance, the withdrawal seizure timeline, Jellinek's and Cloninger's typologies, treatment and evaluation tools. Psycho Didi notes · p. 48 Jellinek's typology of alcoholism: (1) Alpha — psychological dependence, early stage, relieving emotional issues, can leave alcohol if desired; (2) Beta — physical consequences (liver sclerosis) started, no psychological/physical dependence, no addiction; (3) Gamma — addiction with loss of control, tolerance, physical dependence; (4) Delta — maintenance drinking, can't abstain, loss of control; (5) Epsilon — dipsomania, periodic/binge drinking, most advanced. Robert Cloninger's typology: Type 1 — later onset, more psychological dependence, guilt, no sense of control. Type 2 — starts early, socially disruptive, more physical dependence, sensation seeking, better sense of control. Legal limit: 30 mg/dl. 10% discarded, 90% absorbed; peak absorption 30–90 minutes. Reverse tolerance: body degraded so much that even a lesser amount has effects. Withdrawal timeline (seizures): 6–8 hrs — coarse tremors; 12–24 hrs — alcoholic hallucinosis; 24–48 hrs — alcohol withdrawal seizures (tonic-clonic); 48–72 hrs — delirium tremens . Evaluation: CAGE questionnaire (John Ewing, 1984) — Cut down, Annoyed, Guilty, Eye-opener; AUDIT; SADQ. Treatment: benzodiazepines, thiamine, carbamazepine, disulfiram, anti-craving agents; CBT, Alcoholics Anonymous, family/group therapy. 18 · Neurocognitive Disorders Neurocognitive Disorders. A mind map of neurocognitive disorders covering the 4 As, delirium, cortical, subcortical and pseudo dementia, and the features of Alzheimer's, TBI, vascular, Huntington's, Lewy body, Parkinson's, Korsakoff's, frontotemporal and mild neurocognitive disorder. Psycho Didi notes · p. 45 ICD-11: organic mental disorder. Episodic memory (Endel Tulving, 1972) is first to go; semantic memory is last to go. Defies Occam's razor: no single explanation. Marked by anxiety, sleep problems, psychosis. Cognitive impairment — the 4 A's: Aphasia, Agnosia, Amnesia, Apraxia. Plus disturbance of consciousness (delirium), visual hallucinations, transient delusions. Dementia (Major Neurocognitive Disorder) Amnesia, aphasia, apraxia, agnosia; personality changes (frontotemporal lobe); hallucinations, delusions, mood symptoms; progressive; reduced intellectual functioning; impaired memory & self-care; perseveration; disorientation in time/place/person. Type Examples & features Cortical dementia (fronto-, temporo-, parieto-) Hallucination, delusion; cognitive functioning more compromised. E.g. Alzheimer's, Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (mad cow disease) Subcortical dementia Motor issues, depressive. E.g. Huntington's chorea, Parkinson's disease, progressive supranuclear palsy, Wilson's disease Alzheimer's Disease Most common dementia; 5% of people by age 65 (pre-senile); 2–30% by age 85 (senile) ; females outnumber males 3:1 ; linked with chromosomes 1, 14, 21 (autosomal). Marked by neurofibrillary tangles (barrier in the cholinergic pathway) and beta-amyloid plaques ; hippocampal degeneration. Symptoms: confusion with time/location, difficulty completing familiar tasks, misplacing items, memory loss, difficulty problem-solving, social withdrawal, poor judgement, unfounded emotions, difficulty with words, trouble with images; anterograde then retrograde amnesia. Delirium Metabolic encephalopathy; disturbance of consciousness; impaired attention; impaired time/place/person orientation; impaired immediate memory; perceptual disturbances (hallucinations); hypo/hyperactivity; disturbed sleep-wake cycle; autonomic disturbances. Sundowning — increased problems in the evening. Floccillation — patient picks at bedclothes. Occupational delirium. Acetylcholine and ARAS implicated. Predisposing factors: pre-existing dementia, extreme old age, history of delirium, drug dependence, cerebral lesions, surgery, severe psychological symptoms, psychotropic medicines. Treatment: treat underlying cause, antipsychotics, benzodiazepines. Delirium vs Dementia (and Pseudodementia). Delirium = acute, fluctuating disturbance of consciousness/attention with visual hallucinations; reversible. Dementia = chronic, progressive decline in cognition with clear consciousness. Pseudodementia (depressive) — complains about memory impairment, emphasizes disability/distress, says "don't know," recent-memory impairment, variable test performance, past history of mood episodes. Dementia due to Traumatic Brain Injury Loss of consciousness/delirium; male-predominant (bike accidents), elderly (falls); consciousness (4 A's) affected; diagnosable through scans; amnesia seen first; hemiparesis. Heavy instance of repeated head trauma; hyper- and hypokinesia; procedural memory affected. Vascular Dementia Multi-infarction; small vascular strokes (heart issue); insufficient oxygen supplied to the brain. Huntington's 100% genetic — caused by the HTT gene (dominant) on the 12th chromosome ; chorea; hyperkinesia; cognitive + motor deficit; glutamate excitotoxicity. Lewy Body Disease New in DSM-5. Lewy bodies = bits of alpha-synuclein protein (in cytoplasm) of brain cells, located in brainstem, substantia nigra, locus coeruleus. Cognitive symptoms start first, followed by motor symptoms; fluctuating attention; hallucinations ( can't prescribe antipsychotics ); late onset of Parkinson-like symptoms. Duration: chronic. Parkinson's Pill-rolling tremors, bradykinesia, rigidity, slow movements, stooped posture, postural instability, akinesia, freezing of gait, micrographia. Korsakoff's Thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency caused by chronic alcoholism and lack of nutrition. Less severe — Wernicke's encephalopathy: global amnesia, confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia; acute symptoms; sudden onset; reversible. Korsakoff's: irreversible, confabulation observed, chronic onset; found in older adults. Wernicke's vs Korsakoff's. Both from thiamine (B1) deficiency. Wernicke's encephalopathy = acute, sudden onset, reversible (confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia). Korsakoff's = chronic, irreversible, with confabulation. Frontotemporal Dementia Accounts for 5% of all dementia; cortical dementia (hallucination and delusion); executive functions impacted. Behavioural variant — socially inappropriate, apathy, fixed mindset. Language variant — inappropriate words, grammar. Types: frontal variant; semantic dementia (temporal); progressive non-fluent aphasia. Mild Neurocognitive Disorder Doesn't meet criteria for major dementia but marked dysfunction; person scores below 1 standard deviation on tests; minor loss of cognitive functioning. 19 · Named / Eponymous Syndromes Miscellaneous Disorders. A grid of labelled boxes, each giving a short description of a named syndrome such as Capgras, Cotard's, Fregoli, Ganser, Kleine-Levin and Othello syndrome. Psycho Didi notes · p. 52 Delusional misidentification syndromes. Capgras syndrome — belief that a loved one or pet has been replaced by an identical imposter. Fregoli syndrome — belief that familiar people are in disguise or have changed their appearance. Syndrome of intermetamorphosis — delusion that people have swapped identities while maintaining the same appearance (total psychological + physical transformation, not just disguise). Syndrome of subjective doubles — delusion that others have swapped identities while keeping the same appearance. Reduplicative paramnesia — delusional belief that identical places and events exist. Other classic named syndromes. Cotard's syndrome (Dr Jules Cotard, 1882) — delusions that one is dead or does not exist; a nihilistic delusion ; treatment: ECT. Othello syndrome — delusional belief/overvalued idea that one's spouse/partner is unfaithful. De Clérambault's syndrome (erotomania) — the patient, often a single woman, believes an exalted person is in love with her. Charles-Bonnet syndrome — visual hallucinations without any other psychotic features or psychiatric disorder. Couvade syndrome — a spouse complains of obstetric symptoms during his partner's pregnancy and parturition. Diogenes syndrome — gross self-neglect, especially among elderly reclusive persons; often wealthy and intelligent; ~50% have no psychiatric illness (may have paranoid PD). Ganser syndrome — giving approximate answers to simple questions; a dissociative disorder; can understand but can't give pointed answers; happens in prisoners; clouding of consciousness, hallucinations, delusions. Kleine-Levin syndrome (KLS, "sleeping beauty disorder") — hypersomnolence, hypersexuality, hyperorality; early description by Alexandre Jacques François Brière de Boismont (1862) ; mostly adolescent males; spontaneous disappearance of symptoms. Blocq's disease (astasia-abasia) — inability to walk/stand in a normal manner; bizarre gait not suggestive of an organic lesion; a conversion symptom (dissociative motor disorder in ICD-10 / conversion disorder in DSM-5). Briquet's syndrome (St Louis hysteria) — multiple physical complaints in several systems with no physical cause; begins before age 30; chronic; frequent medical contact. Ekbom's syndrome — unpleasant sensations predominantly in the legs (rarely arms); occur only at rest; worse in the evening/night. Chronic fatigue (Myalgic encephalomyelitis) — fatigue, malaise, headache, pharyngitis, low-grade fever, cognitive complaints. Restless legs syndrome — uncomfortable leg sensation (like insects crawling under skin); urge to move/walk; difficulty initiating sleep; medication: Ropinirole. 20 · Culture-Specific (Culture-Bound) Syndromes Culture Specific Disorders. A table naming culture-bound syndromes from Ataque de Nervios to Ode-ori with the culture where each is seen and a short description. Psycho Didi notes · p. 53 Culture Specific Disorders (continued). The second part of the culture-bound syndrome table, adding more syndromes (many from regions of India) with their cultures and descriptions. Psycho Didi notes · p. 54 Disorder Culture Description Ataque de Nervios Hispanics Attacks of crying, trembling, uncontrollable shouting, physical/verbal aggression, intense heat in the chest moving to the head Amok, Mal de Pelea Malaysians, Laotians, Filipinos, Polynesians, Papua New Guineans, Puerto Ricans Dissociative disorder — outburst of violence, aggression or homicidal behaviour at people and objects Brain fag African Americans Problems with concentration/thinking among high-school and university students facing schooling challenges Bouffée Délirante Haitians Sudden outburst of aggression, agitation with confusion, psychomotor excitement; resembles brief psychotic disorder Colera Hispanics Anger and rage disturbing body balance → headache, screaming, stomach pain, loss of consciousness, fatigue Dhat East Indians, Chinese, Sri Lankans Extreme anxiety with sense of weakness, exhaustion and discharge of semen Koro Asians Desire to grasp the penis (in women, vulva/nipples) from fear it will retract into the body and cause death Falling Out African Americans Seizure-like symptoms from traumatic events such as robberies Ghost Sickness American Indians Weakness, dizziness, fainting, anxiety, hallucinations, confusion, loss of appetite from witches/evil forces Hwa-byung Asians Pain in the upper abdomen, fear of death, tiredness from imbalance between reality and anger Latah Asians Sudden fright → imitative behaviours beyond control (echopraxia/echolalia); follows commands, verbal repetition of obscenities Mal de ojo Hispanics Vomiting, fever, diarrhea and mental problems attributed to the "evil eye" Mal puesto, hex, root work, voodoo death African Americans, Hispanics Unnatural diseases/death from the power of people using evil spirits Ode-ori Nigerians Sensation of parasites crawling in the head, heat in the head, paranoid fears of attack by evil spirits Piblokto Arctic/subarctic Inuit Excitement, coma, convulsive seizures resembling abrupt dissociation; amnesia, withdrawal, irritability, irrational behaviour (breaking furniture, eating feces, obscenities) Susto, Miedo, Espanto, Pasmo Hispanics Tiredness and weakness from frightening/startling experiences Taijin kyofusho Asians Guilt about embarrassing others, timidity from feeling one's appearance/odor/expressions offend others Wacinko American Indians Anger, withdrawal, mutism, suicide as a reaction to disappointment and interpersonal problems Wind or Cold Illness Asians and Hispanics Fear of cold/wind; weakness and susceptibility to illness from belief that natural/supernatural elements are unbalanced Possession syndrome Rural India Possession by the soul/spirit of a dead relative or local deity; changed tone, even gender change if the possessing soul is of the opposite sex Dhat syndrome East India Nighttime discharges with severe anxiety, uneasiness, hypochondriasis; related to sexual ineptitude Koro Northeast India Fear of genital retraction and death; seen in both sexes Bhanmati sorcery South India Attributed to psychiatric illness — somatization, conversion, dysthymia, anxiety, schizophrenia, etc. Gilhari syndrome West Rajasthan Small blood-filled swelling that changes position (as if a squirrel/lizard moves in the body toward the neck, obstructing airways → death if not destroyed); medically explained as strong muscle contraction from severe tension/stress Jhinjhinia West Bengal Sudden sensation of tingling and numbness in the legs spreading upward through the body Suudu South India (Tamil culture) Extreme abdominal pain, dark-yellow urine, painful/burning micturition, headaches, fatigue, constipation, dry mouth Mass Hysteria India Short-lived epidemics of hysteria where hundreds to thousands behave in a way they normally would not Suchi-bai syndrome Bengal A condition like obsessional neurosis 21 · Psychopharmacology Reference Psychopharmacology. Drug lists grouped into typical and atypical antipsychotics, antidepressant classes, mood stabilizers, benzodiazepines, anti-epileptics, and drugs used for substance detoxification and abstinence. Psycho Didi notes · p. 55 Antipsychotics Typical (1st generation, D2 antagonism) Atypical (2nd generation, 5-HT2 + D2 antagonism) Effective for positive symptoms Effective for both positive and negative symptoms Phenothiazines: Chlorpromazine, Thioridazine, Triflupromazine, Fluphenazine, Perphenazine. Thioxanthenes: Thiothixene, Flupenthixol. Butyrophenones: Haloperidol, Droperidol, Penfluridol. Miscellaneous: Pimozide, Loxapine, Molindone. Clozapine (1st atypical antipsychotic), Olanzapine, Risperidone, Paliperidone, Iloperidone, Quetiapine, Ziprasidone, Aripiprazole, Sertindole, Zotepine, Lurasidone, Asenapine, Amisulpride. Antidepressants Class (mechanism) Agents TCAs & tetracyclics (block serotonin & norepinephrine transporters) Imipramine, Desipramine, Trimipramine, Amitriptyline, Nortriptyline, Protriptyline, Amoxapine, Doxepin, Maprotiline, Clomipramine SSRIs (block reuptake of 5-HT) Fluoxetine, Fluvoxamine, Citalopram, Escitalopram, Sertraline, Paroxetine, Vilazodone SNRIs (dual reuptake inhibitors) Venlafaxine, Desvenlafaxine, Duloxetine, Milnacipran, Levomilnacipran MAOIs (inhibit metabolism of monoamines) Tranylcypromine, Phenelzine, Isocarboxazid Atypical antidepressants Trazodone, Nefazodone, Mirtazapine, Bupropion, Tianeptine, Amineptine Mood stabilizers, benzodiazepines & anti-epileptics Mood stabilizers: Lithium, Valproate, Carbamazepine, Oxcarbazepine, Lamotrigine. Benzodiazepines: Alprazolam, Chlordiazepoxide, Clorazepate, Diazepam, Halazepam, Lorazepam, Oxazepam, Prazepam, Quazepam, Clonazepam. Anti-epileptics: Carbamazepine, Lamotrigine, Levetiracetam, Sodium valproate, Pregabalin, Clobazam, Oxcarbazepine, Phenytoin. Substance detoxification, abstinence & overdose Substance Detoxification / management Alcohol Detox: Benzodiazepines (esp. chlordiazepoxide), Carbamazepine; antipsychotics for delirium tremens & alcoholic hallucinosis. Abstinence: deterrent agent Disulfiram ; anti-craving agents Naltrexone, Acamprosate, Topiramate, Fluoxetine, Baclofen Opioids Substitution: Methadone, Buprenorphine, Clonidine; antagonist Naltrexone; overdose Naloxone Nicotine Substitution: nicotine gums, lozenges, patches, inhalers & spray; Bupropion, Clonidine, Nortriptyline, Varenicline; antipsychotics

title: Psychological Testing
text: Psychological Testing — Study with Psycho Didi (MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF) Psychological Testing Study with Psycho Didi · MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF notes Neuropsychological batteries Intelligence & Indian tests Projective & objective personality tests MMPI · 16PF · NEO-PI · EPQ Test → author → what it measures What this covers. A complete tour of psychological tests for the clinical/NET syllabus: neuropsychology foundations and batteries (Halstead-Reitan, Luria-Nebraska, AIIMS, NIMHANS) plus individual neuro tests (WCST, Bender-Gestalt, Stroop, Tower tests, ROCF, CANTAB, MMSE, PGIBBD, WMS); intelligence tests (Stanford-Binet 5, Raven's, CFIT, Kaufman family, Leiter) and Indian adaptations (Bhatia's Battery, Binet-Kamat, Kulshreshtha, WAPIS, MISIC); and personality tests split into projective (Rorschach, TAT, Rosenzweig, Szondi, sentence-completion and drawing tests) and non-projective objective inventories (MMPI family, MCMI, MBTI, EPPS, Holland, MPQ, 16PF (Raymond Cattell), NEO-PI (Paul Costa and Robert McCrae), EPQ). Every test name, author, age range, subtest and cutoff is preserved. Original diagrams. 16 diagrams from the Psycho Didi PDF (pages 57 to 68) sit under the section they belong to, exactly as drawn. Tap one to open it full size and zoom in. Contents: 1 · Introduction to Neuropsychology · 2 · Neuropsychological Tests: goals, categories, approaches · 3 · Halstead-Reitan Battery · 4 · Other Neuropsychological Tests · 5 · Intelligence Tests · 6 · Indian Intelligence Tests · 7 · Personality Tests: overview · 8 · Projective Tests · 9 · Non-Projective Tests (Non Factor Analytic) · 10 · Non-Projective Tests (Factor Analytic) 1 · Introduction to Neuropsychology Intro to Neuropsychology. Mind map linking neuropsychology (the study of brain function and behaviour) to its history, neuroplasticity research findings and the two types of neuroplasticity. Psycho Didi notes · p. 57 Neuropsychology is the study of brain function and behaviour. Neuroplasticity Experience expectant — development according to expected growth pattern. Experience dependent — plasticity dependent on new learning, based on new experiences. History of the mind–brain question Mentalism (Aristotle) — a non-material psyche is responsible for behaviour. Dualism (René Descartes) — the body is like a machine (only controls reflex); the mind controls the machine. Materialism (Charles Darwin) — the mind is just our brain; neuroplasticity is based on evolution, the capacity to change. Research findings Florenz and Galls challenged localization: removed the cortex of 3 dogs. Young children can recover fast from brain damage (stem cells migrate). In adults, new neurons (2%) are formed in the hippocampus and striatum. Functioning improves with physiotherapy. 2 · Neuropsychological Tests: goals, categories, approaches Neuropsychological tests. Mind map of neuropsychological testing that branches into its introduction, goals, commonly named tests, categories assessed, sensitivity and specificity, and fixed versus flexible battery approaches. Psycho Didi notes · p. 57 Neuropsychological testing allows for an in-depth analysis of functional limitation associated with brain dysfunction, and is required for diagnosis by some diagnostic criteria for neurological disorders. Goals (Schaefer et al., 2023) Establish a baseline. Gauge an individual's cognitive strengths and weaknesses and aid in treatment planning. Assist in establishing diagnoses. Establish lateralization and possible etiology of brain lesions. Track progress in rehab. Determination of disability, return to work/school, driving ability or legal purposes. Categories assessed Abstract · Attention · Daily activities · Emotional Distress · Language · Memory · Motor skills · Orientation · Sensation · Perception · Visuospatial reasoning. Sensitivity and Specificity Key. Sensitivity = a test's ability to correctly identify people who have a disease. Specificity = a test's ability to correctly identify people who do not have a disease. Approaches to Neuropsychological tests Approach Description Example Fixed battery Uses the same battery of tests for every client; maintains a constant testing condition; comprehensive normative data; better psychometric properties; broader empirical base for interpretations. Halstead-Reitan Battery Flexible battery Only those measures directly related to the patient's presenting symptoms should be administered. The administered battery inherently changes with a patient's referral question. Uses a core battery of tests and techniques for clients with various syndromes; tests implemented vary based on the practitioner as well as context. Meyers Neuropsychological Battery Commonly named neuropsychological tests Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale (WAIS) Raven's Progressive Matrices Shipley Institute of Living Scale The Wisconsin Card Sorting Test (WCST; David Grant and Esta Berg, 1948) Proverbs The Wechsler Memory Scale (WMS) The Rey-Osterrieth Complex Figure (ROCF) test The Benton Visual Retention Test (BVRT) Consonant trigrams Stroop test 3 · Halstead–Reitan Neuropsychological Test Battery Halstead-Reitan Neuropsychological Test Battery. Overview of the Halstead-Reitan battery with its introduction, extra information, five scales and other measures, illustrated with photos of the Booklet Category Test, Tactual Performance Test boards and a finger tapping device. Psycho Didi notes · p. 58 Founder note. The Halstead-Reitan battery arose from one of the first neuropsychology labs in America; it proposed the theory of "biological intelligence" . Introduction Created one of the first neuropsychology labs in America. First neuropsychological test to have a factor-analytic process. Was made to test head trauma. Created: 1935. Time taken: 6–8 hours. 1956: The Halstead-Reitan Test Battery begins to emerge as the premiere test battery in neuropsychology. Now it can detect tremors, cerebrovascular accidents, infections, degenerative diseases, learning disabilities, neurological disorders. Proposed theory of "biological intelligence". Extra information Total 7 scores. Removed: critical flicker fusion test, time sense test. For ages: 15+. Based on T-score value. 6-point score. Scales / Measures Category test — measures abstract reasoning and concept formation; requires the examinee to find the rule for categorizing pictures of geometric shapes. Tactual performance test (Seguin) — measures kinesthetic and sensorimotor ability; requires a blindfolded examinee to place blocks in the appropriate cutout on an upright board with the dominant hand, then non-dominant hand, then both hands; also tests for incidental memory of blocks (score: total time, memory, location). Seashore Rhythm Test — measures attention and auditory perception; requires the examinee to indicate whether paired musical rhythms are same or different. Speech sound perception test — measures attention and auditory-visual synthesis; requires the examinee to pick from four choices the written version of taped nonsense words. Finger tapping test — measures motor speed; requires the examinee to tap a telegraph-key-like lever as quickly as possible for 10 seconds. Other measures Grip strength — requires the examinee to squeeze as hard as possible; separate trials with each hand. Trail making, parts A, B — requires the examinee to connect numbers (part A) or numbers and letters in alternating order (part B) with a pencil line under pressure of time. Tactile form recognition — requires the examinee to recognize simple shapes (e.g., triangle) placed in the palm of the hand. Sensory-Perceptual Exam — requires the examinee to respond to simple bilateral sensory tasks, e.g., detecting which finger has been touched. Aphasia Screening test — tasks include naming a pictured item (e.g., fork), repeating short phrases. Supplementary: WAIS-III, WRAT-3, MMPI-2, memory tests such as Wechsler Memory Scale-III or Rey Auditory Verbal Learning Test. 4 · Other Neuropsychological Tests Other Neuropsychological Tests: Luria-Nebraska, Vineland, Bender-Gestalt, WCST. Mind map of the Luria-Nebraska battery, the Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales, the Bender-Gestalt Test and the Wisconsin Card Sorting Test, with a clock-drawing sample, Bender-Gestalt design cards, Vineland-3 materials and WCST cards. Psycho Didi notes · p. 59 Luria-Nebraska Test Battery Founder note. Luria-Nebraska — started in 1978, standardized by Golden in 1980. The AIIMS and NIMHANS batteries are based on this. 269 items (0, 1, 2 scale); T scores are used. In some areas 2 scores are assigned to the same task: speed and accuracy. Can check any organic damage. Total 14 scales: motor, rhythm, tactile, visual, receptive speech, expressive speech, writing, reading, arithmetic, memory, intellectual scales, pathognomonic — left and right hemisphere. The Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales (VABS) / Vineland Social Maturity Scale (VSMS) Founder note. Developed by American psychologist Edgar Arnold Doll (1935). Most widely used test to measure adaptive behaviour in existence; can be used from birth until death. For younger children, there is a semi-structured interview with parents. Domains: communication, daily living skills, socialization, motor skills, maladaptive behaviour (optional). Can check for Autism Spectrum Disorder, deficits in adaptation, genetic disorders, traumatic brain injury. Age 7–90: given only 3 subtests (not the motor skills subtest). Age 0–7: given all 4 subtests. The Wisconsin Card Sorting Test (WCST) Founder note. Given by E.A. Berg in 1948 (60 cards); Heaton modified it in 1981 to a total of 64 cards. Order: Colour → Form → Number. Can break rapport if the client is unable to answer correctly. Bilateral prefrontal dysfunction patients are excited to give the test even if they give wrong answers. Checks for perseveration. Scored using Milner's criteria. The Bender-Gestalt Test (BGT) Founder note. Developed in 1938 by Lauretta Bender . Tests: hand-eye coordination, perseveration, prefrontal damage. Involves 13 designs for children less than 8 years and 12 designs for age 8 years and above. Memory recall process; global scoring system. Clients are given a lot of sheets, but asked to draw on only one. Visuospatial difficulties identified (lesions in right parietal lobe). Seguin Form Board Test Other Neuropsychological Tests: Seguin, BVRT, Seashore, Stroop, ROCF, CANTAB, Tower tests. Mind map of the Seguin Form Board, Benton Visual Retention, Seashore, Stroop, Rey-Osterrieth Complex Figure, CANTAB and Tower tests, with a form board photo, a Stroop colour-word chart, a sample complex figure drawing and a Tower of London diagram. Psycho Didi notes · p. 60 Founder note. Indian adaptation by J. Bharatraj ; norms by S. K. Goel . Part of the Halstead-Reitan test battery (1947). Client is asked to draw the board from memory. Earlier it was used to test eye-hand / visuomotor coordination. Earlier given as 10 blocks of Gesell figures. The Benton Visual Retention Test (BVRT) Founder note. Developed by Arthur Benton . Currently: 5th edition; includes 10 designs. Clients are required to see and copy 10 designs immediately out of memory. Time taken: 5 minutes. The Seashore Test Founder note. The tests were developed by Carl E. Seashore . Used in the Halstead-Reitan Battery. 3–5 errors considered normal. Measures musical ability and cerebral function. Seashore Rhythm Test — a subtest of the Seashore Measures of Musical Talent that measures generalized cerebral function; age-related problems occur. Stroop Test Test of selective attention, response conflict and inhibition; errors indicate dysfunction. Because of conceptual primacy, colour takes longer to recognize. No age bias. For checking smaller lesions, more items need to be added. Indicative of frontal functioning; biggest test is 4 block/trial. Tower Tests Tests for frontal, planning and executive dysfunction. A measure of means-end analysis (Allen Newell and Herbert Simon, 1972). Requires the client to reach the final goal in the least number of moves possible. Test Apparatus Least number of moves possible Tower of London Utilizes balls 5 Tower of Hanoi Utilizes rings 6 Dependent on working backwards; one has to visualize; repeat-state avoidance. Checks for inhibition of conflicting responses and working memory. Prepotent: goal-subgoal conflict. The Rey-Osterrieth Complex Figure Test (ROCF) Founder note. Developed by Rey in 1941; standardized by Osterrieth in 1944. Measures visuospatial construction ability, visual memory, and executive functioning by the prefrontal lobe. 3 stages: copy, immediate recall, delayed recall. Uses one-for-one diagram. Checks for: fine motor coordination, visuospatial memory, planning and organization, attention and coordination. Age-related bias may be present. Cambridge Neuropsychological Test Automated Battery (CANTAB) Computerized test. Time taken: 40–45 mins. Checks for dementia; frontal, temporal, hippocampal dysfunction. Checks for organic as well as non-organic damage. Independent of language and not sensitive to gender. Subtests: psychomotor coordination and motor speed; reasoning and planning abilities; spatial memory; attention and vigilance. Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) Other Neuropsychological Tests: MMSE, PGIBBD, AIIMS, NIMHANS, WMS. Mind map of the Mini-Mental State Examination, the PGI Battery of Brain Dysfunction, the AIIMS and NIMHANS neuropsychological batteries and the Wechsler Memory Scale. Psycho Didi notes · p. 61 Basic exam of cognitive screening; 11 items. A score of 23/30 and lesser is considered pathological. Domains: orientation, repetition, verbal recall, attention, calculation, language and visual construction. Made in 1975, standardized in 1995. Time taken: 5–10 mins. Used for people with neurocognitive disorder. Drawbacks: heavily verbal; the test has a "floor effect" (can't tell high deterioration). The Postgraduate Institute of Brain Dysfunction (PGIBBD) Founder note. Given by Prashad and Verma , 1990; 2007. Language: Hindi; available for all. For ages: 20–59 years. 19 domains. 5 subtests: PGI Memory scale: immediate, recent, very short term, long term, verbal, non-verbal. Bhatia short scale: Koh's block design, Alexander Pass Along. VAIS: 1. info, 2. digit span, 3. arithmetic, 4. verbal comprehension. Nahor Benson test: organic brain pathology. Bender Gestalt Test. The Wechsler Memory Scale (WMS) Given for the first time in 1945. 4th edition: 2009. Working memory deficits indicate frontal lobe damage; long-term memory deficits indicate temporal lobe damage. Checks for auditory, visual, visual working, immediate, and delayed memory. Does not check much of: verbal memory or verbal working memory and remote memory. Time taken: 80 minutes. Checks for neurocognitive disorders (Korsakoff). The AIIMS Neuropsychological Battery Founder note. Given by Surya Gupta , 2000 — a Hindi adaptation of the Luria-Nebraska test. Training only given by the author; very expensive. 160 items; ages 15–80 years. Used to assess cognitive function; has versions for younger individuals. Scales: motor, tactile, visual, receptive speech, expressive speech, reading, writing, arithmetic, memory, intellectual processes, left hemisphere, right hemisphere, pathognomonic. The NIMHANS Neuropsychological Battery Founder note. Version used: 2004 by Dr. Rao . Inspired by Luria-Nebraska. The test is available but the manual is not. Developed on the principles of localization and lateralization. Checks for attention, visual search, mental search, psychomotor deficit, working memory (frontal lobe damage). Also checks for temporal (BVRT) and parietal lobe (BGT) damage. Includes 19 tests. Popular tests: tower test, Stroop task, complex figure, finger tapping, WCST. 5 · Intelligence Tests Intelligence Tests: history and timeline. Scroll tracing intelligence testing from anthropometry to psychometric testing, next to a timeline of milestones from 1890 to 2014. Psycho Didi notes · p. 62 History Anthropometry (Francis Galton) Chronometry — RT test (Fechner) Mental Test (Cattell) Psychometric testing (Binet) Dates and timeline Year Milestone 1890 Cattell — Mental test. 1905 1st psychometric test by Binet to identify children with special needs. 1912 Stern gave the term IQ. 1916 IQ formula; Stanford-Binet test. 1917 Army Alpha (Robert Yerkes, 1917) and Army Beta test. 1939 Wechsler Bellevue scale introduced deviation IQ. 2003 Stanford-Binet Test-5. 2004 The Kaufman Assessment Battery for Children (KABC II). 2008 WAIS. 2012 WPPSI. 2014 WISC. Key. Basal age = the last level where we get all answers correct. Ceiling age = the lowest level where we get all answers correct. Stanford-Binet Test-5 Stanford-Binet Test-5. Tree diagram of the Stanford-Binet 5 showing its key facts, basal and ceiling age, and the five factor scores with the tasks under each. Psycho Didi notes · p. 62 Follows Cattell-Horn-Carroll theory; given in 2003. 10 subtests; deviation IQ used; uses factor analysis. Age: 2–85 years. 5 factor scores Fluid reasoning — matrices, absurdities, inductive reasoning. Knowledge — procedural, general knowledge, missing details, vocabulary, difficult words. Quantitative reasoning — arithmetic problem, word problem, counting. Visuospatial reasoning — puzzles, direction problems. Working memory — words, sentences, short visual info. Raven's Progressive Matrices Intelligence Tests: CAS-II, Kaufman tests and culture fair tests. Panel covering the Cognitive Assessment System-II, the three Kaufman tests (KABC, KAIT, KBIT), culture fair tests (Draw A Person, Leiter), the Culture Fair Intelligence Test and Raven's Progressive Matrices, with sample KBIT pictures and a Raven's matrix item. Psycho Didi notes · p. 63 Coloured Progressive Matrices (36 cards). Advanced Progressive Matrices (48 cards). Standard Progressive Matrices (60 cards). Power and speed test; measures Fluid Intelligence. Mean = 100; SD = 15. Culture Fair Intelligence Test (CFIT) Founder note. By Raymond Cattell . Group test; speed and power test; 3 forms; only non-verbal test. Different from other tests in reading, experience, language, speed/tempo, environmental experiences. Can be given in groups. The Kaufman Adolescent and Adult Intelligence Test (KAIT) Founder note. Kaufman tests by Alan Kaufman . Age: 11–85+. Based on Cattell-Horn-Carroll theory (fluid and crystallized intelligence) and some part of Jean Piaget's theory. Culture biased. Cognitive Assessment System-II (CAS-II) Based on PASS theory (Das, Naglieri). Only for adolescents; used for scholarship tests. Contains the Naglieri Nonverbal Aptitude test. Mean: 100, S.D.: 3. The Kaufman Assessment Battery for Children (KABC) Based on PASS theory. 4 global scales: Simultaneous, Successive, Mental Processing, Achievement. Culture biased. The Kaufman Brief Intelligence Test (KBIT) Age: 4–90 years; both verbal and nonverbal. Time taken: 20 minutes. Mean: 100, SD: 15. Culture Fair Tests Draw A Person Test (DAPT) 1926; performance test to measure observation and conceptual thinking. Leiter International Performance Scale Performance test; made for African groups; elimination of verbal instruction; no time limit. Tests: reasoning, visualisation, attention, memory. 6 · Indian Intelligence Tests Indian Intelligence Tests. Tree diagram grouping Indian intelligence tests into a performance test (Bhatia's Battery), tests based on Binet's test (Binet Kamat, Kulshreshtha) and tests based on Wechsler's test (WAPIS, MISIC), with a photo of the MISIC kit. Psycho Didi notes · p. 63 Bhatia's Battery of Performance Tests of Intelligence Given in 1940; normed for ages 11–16 years. Performance test. Includes: Koh's block design — speed and power. Alexander Pass along — speed and power. Pattern drawing — speed and power. Immediate memory: digit span — verbal and power. Picture construction. Different norms for rural and urban population. Can be only administered individually. Not completely culture fair. Binet Kamat Test Bombay Karnataka version of the Binet Simon Scale; based on the 1916 Simon Binet test. Used ratio IQ. Ages: 3–22 years, separate norms. Measures: language, reasoning, conceptual thinking, social intelligence, memory, visuomotor performance. Heavily verbal — can't check subnormal intelligence. Items are not appropriate to current times; easy to administer. Severe and profound mental retardation. Kulshreshtha Intelligence Test 1960; Hindi adaptation of the Stanford-Binet (Lewis Terman, 1916) test. Ages: 2–22 years; each age level = 6 items. Verbal and performance tests; uses ratio IQ. Tests based on Wechsler's test Wechsler Adult Performance Intelligence Scale (WAPIS) Founder note. Made by Prabha Ramalingaswami (1974). 11 subtests (from WAIS): 6 verbal, 5 non-verbal. Picture completion and picture arrangement have been modified. Malin's Intelligence Scale for Indian Children (MISIC) Founder note. Arthur J. Malin of Nagpur reformed Wechsler's scales. Ages: 6–15 years; 2–2.5 years. 11 subtests: 6 verbal: i. information, ii. general comprehension, iii. arithmetic, iv. analogy and similarity, v. vocabulary, vi. digit span. 5 non-verbal: i. block design, ii. picture completion, iii. object assembly, iv. symbol coding, v. maze. 7 · Personality Tests: overview Personality Tests. Tree diagram of personality assessment showing an introduction timeline and four types (personality inventories, non projective tests, projective tests, observation), with the California Personality Inventory, Bell's Adjustment Inventory and observational tests in boxes below. Psycho Didi notes · p. 64 Projective tests began in 1800. 1st test: Word Association test — Francis Galton, Emil Kraepelin, Carl Jung . 1916: Carl Jung's first standardized word association test. 1917: 1st objective test — Woodworth's Personal Data Sheet. Types / categories of personality assessment Observational tests — rating scales and interview technique. Rating scales: judgement about personality in some categories. Interviews: structured and unstructured. Personality inventories (self-report: forced choice). Non-projective tests , Observation . Bell's Adjustment Inventory 1934; to diagnose adjustment problems. Home: satisfaction/dissatisfaction; health: shyness, introversion. Student form and occupation form; 140 Qs. Adapted in Indian languages. California Personality Inventory 1957, 1987; work-related inventory. Measures behaviour in the organizational setting. 8 · Projective Tests Projective Tests: association techniques and construction tests. Page splitting projective tests into association techniques and construction tests, covering the Word Association Test, Rorschach Inkblot Test, Blacky's Picture Test, Thematic Apperception Test and Rosenzweig Picture Frustration Study. Psycho Didi notes · p. 65 Association techniques Rorschach Inkblot Test Founder note. 1921, by Herman Rorschach ; he created it while playing klexography. Projective vs objective. The Rorschach is a projective association technique studying unconscious thoughts, unlike objective self-report inventories (MMPI, 16PF). Scoring is subjective and system-dependent (Exner etc.), not criterion-keyed. Administration: 10 cards, 7×10 inches, shown one at a time in sequence. Card Theme i Paranoia ii Violence, communication, dominance iii Sexual preference iv Father card v Hostility, castration complex, schizophrenia vi Intimate relationships vii Mother card viii Emotions / complex situations ix Uncertainty / ambiguity x Life situation / oral fixation Phases: Performance proper. Enquiry: ask what, why, where it was seen. Testing the limits: done to give participants with weird responses another chance. Studies unconscious thoughts. Average number of responses: 20–25; per card: 3–5. Focus on: content of the story, feeling or tone, subject's behaviour apart from the responses. Scoring system: Levey, Beck S., Hertz, Klopfer, Exner (1974). Latest scoring system by Exner : 1993. Scoring based on: location, determinant, form quality, content, popular responses. Blacky's Picture Test Based on Sigmund Freud's psychosexual stages; for children ages 5 and older; 11 cartoon stimuli. In addition to requesting a story for each card, the examiner also presents multiple-choice questions based on stages of psychosexual development. Word Association Test Founder note. Also known as free association technique. First systematically described by Francis Galton (1879); introduced into the psychological laboratory by Wilhelm Wundt ; first applied to the study of abnormality by Emil Kraepelin ; adapted for use as a projective technique by Carl Jung . Construction tests Thematic Apperception Test (TAT) Founder note. Given by Henry Murray and Christina Morgan (1935, 43); based on Murray's theory of personology. Can be both idiographic and nomothetic. 19 cards, for male, female, boys, girls; total cards that can be given: 20. Blank card: Card no. 16. Bellack's scoring system is used. Analysis: Hero · Needs of the hero · Thema · Outcome. Needs of the hero: Needs motivated by desire for power, property, prestige, knowledge, creativity: achievement, acquisition, aggression, construction, counteraction, dominance, exposition, recognition, understanding. Needs motivated by affection, admiration, sympathy, love, dependence: affiliation, deference, nurturance, sex, succorance. Needs motivated by desire for freedom, change, excitement, play: autonomy, change/travel adventure, excitation/dissipation, play. Miscellaneous needs: abasement, blame avoidance, cognizance, harm avoidance, passivity, rejection, retention, sentience. Presses: Press of deprivation: acquisition, retention. Press descriptive of an empty, alien, or rejecting environment: lack of things/opportunities/friends, human support; loss; rejection; uncongenial environment. Press of coercion and restraint: dominance; imposed task, duty or training. Press descriptive of a hostile aggressive environment: aggression. Press of danger, injury, death: affliction, death of hero, physical danger, physical injury. Press of friendliness, sympathy, respect, dependent, love: affiliation, deference, nurturance, sex, succorance. Miscellaneous press: birth of offspring, claustrum, cognizance, example, exposition, luck. 3 levels of interpretation: descriptive level, interpretive level, diagnostic level. Rosenzweig Picture Frustration Study Consists of 24 cartoon pictures each portraying two persons in a frustrating situation. Responses are scored as to whether, and to what degree, they indicate that the subject exhibits aggression towards the source of the frustration; assumes blame or guilt as the cause of frustration; or justifies, minimizes or denies the frustration. The score is based on a total of nine factors derived from combinations of three types of aggression and three directions of aggression. Three types of aggression: obstacle dominance, ego defense, need persistence. Three directions of aggression: extragression, imagression, intragression. What to ask: current situation; thoughts and feelings of the character; preceding events; outcome. Choice or ordering tests: Szondi Projective Tests: choice or ordering, completion and expressive tests. Page linking projective tests to choice or ordering tests (Szondi), completion tests (Sentence Completion, Sack's Sentence Completion) and expressive tests (House Tree Person, Draw A Man, Kinetic Family Drawing). Psycho Didi notes · p. 66 Founder note. Developed by Leopold Szondi in 1935. Intended to reveal a person's innermost suppressed traits, the parts of yourself you have pushed down into your subconscious. Number of photos: 48. The test involves looking at a series of 48 photos of people with distinct expressions on their faces. The patient picks the friendliest faces and the unfriendliest, the idea being that a person identifies with like people and that their choices from the pictures would represent traits of themselves. Completion tests Sentence Completion Test Semi-projective. 1940: first given by Rohde and Hidreth . Sack's Sentence Completion Test Founder note. By Joseph M. Sacks . Developed to explore specific clusters of attitudes or significant areas of an individual's life. Number of items: 60. 4 subscales: family, sex, relationships, self concepts — each measured on 15 different attitudes such as fears, guilt, and goals. A rating sheet with the four appropriate stems rearranged under the 15 attitude headings allows a clinician to rate the examinee's responses on a continuum that ranges from no significant disturbance to severely disturbed. Expressive tests House Tree Person Test (HTP) Asks for the drawing of a house, a tree, and a person, in order to evaluate them together and globally. Person: who is the person; how old he is; what does he do best; what does he like least. Tree: what kind of tree it is; how old it is; what season it is; has someone tried to cut it down; who waters it; does it have enough light to grow. Usually administered on children. Draw A Man Test Founder note. Goodenough , 1926. Scoring: Chen-Sea (2000). Patients are given a blank piece of paper (8.5×11) entitled "Draw an Entire Man" and a pencil, and are asked to draw an entire man from memory. Kinetic Family Drawing Founder note. Burns and Kaufman , 1970. Helps assess a child's self-concept and family dynamics. The child is asked to draw a picture of their family, including themselves, "doing something". 9 · Non-Projective Tests (Non Factor Analytic) Non-Projective Tests (Non Factor Analytic): MMPI family, MCMI, MBTI. Boxed fact cards for the MMPI, MMPI-2, MMPI-II-RF, MMPI-A, MMPI-3, the Millon Clinical Multiaxial Inventory and the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator. Psycho Didi notes · p. 67 Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory (MMPI) Founder note. Given by Hathaway & McKinley (1989); ages 18 and above. 567 items. 1943: 1st test of validity scales. 1989: Revision. MMPI-A published in 1992. Uses the criterion keyed method (criterion validity). T scores. Time taken: 40–45 minutes. Validity Scales CNS — cannot say. L — Lie scale. F — Infrequency scale, faking bad (1st half). K — Defensiveness / Evasiveness. Fb — Faking bad (last half). VRIN — Variable Response Inconsistency. TRIN — True Response Inconsistency. F-K — Honesty of test. S — Superlative self presentation. Fp — Faking psychopathology in a clinical setting. Fs — Overreporting somatic symptoms. Why it matters. People scoring high on the K scale show high adjustment, insight, higher socioeconomic status, education. People scoring low on the K scale: masochistic tendencies. Clinical Scales Hs — Hypochondriasis D — Depression Hy — Hysteria Pd — Psychopathic deviate Mf — Masculinity Femininity Pa — Paranoia Pt — Psychasthenia Sc — Schizophrenia Ma — Hypomania Si — Social Introversion Other Scales 28 Harris-Lingoes subscales. Content scales: Butcher, Graham, Williams & Ben-Porath (1990). Content component scales (Ben-Porath & Sherwood, 1993). Personality Psychopathology Five scales (PSY-5; Harkness et al., 2002). Restructured clinical scales (Tellegen et al., 2003). Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory 2 (MMPI-2) Validity scales and clinical scales: same as MMPI. Version Author / Year Age Items Scales MMPI Hathaway & McKinley 18+ 567 Validity + Clinical MMPI-2-RF (restructured form) 2008 18+ 338 50 (an alternative to MMPI-II, not a total replacement) MMPI-A Adolescents 14–18 478 Validity and clinical same as MMPI-2; additionally F1 & F2 scales and other subscales MMPI-3 Yossef Ben-Porath & Auke Tellegen (2020) — 335 52 Millon Clinical Multiaxial Inventory (MCMI) Founder note. Given by Theodore Millon . 4th edition based on DSM-5. 5th grade reading level; made for age 18+. 195 true or false questions. Time taken: 25–30 mins. Scales 15 personality pattern scales. 10 clinical syndrome scales. 5 validity scales: 3 modifying indices, 2 random response indicators. 45 Grossman personality facet scales. Clinical scales — severe SS — thought disorder CC — major depression PP — delusional disorder A — generalized anxiety H — somatic symptom N — Bipolar D — Persistent depression B — Alcohol use T — Drug Use R — PTS Validity Scales X — disclosure Y — desirability Z — debasement V — invalidity W — inconsistency Myers-Briggs Type Indicator (MBTI) Founder note. By Isabel Myers and Katherine Briggs ; made by the theoretical method (Carl Jung). Highly used by organizations. Interest inventory: Ipsative (every single option has the same value). Types: extroversion vs introversion; sensing vs intuiting; thinking vs feeling; judging vs perceiving. Criticism: little scientific evidence; weak validity; incomprehensive and vague. Allport, Vernon & Lindzey — Study of Values Scale Non-Projective Tests (Non Factor Analytic): Study of Values, EPPS, Holland, MPQ. Boxed fact cards for the Allport, Vernon and Lindzey Study of Values scale, the Edwards Personal Preference Schedule, Holland's Interest Inventory with a RIASEC hexagon, and the Multiphasic Personality Questionnaire. Psycho Didi notes · p. 68 Ipsative; given in 1931. Based on six value orientations: theoretical, economic, aesthetic, social, political, religious. 240 points; interest inventory. Edwards Personal Preference Schedule (EPPS) Founder note. By Ellen Edwards ; derived from Murray's theory. Interest inventory: ipsative. Validity scales: social desirability, consistency. 225 items; used in vocational training. Based on Murray's needs: Achievement, Deference, Order, Exhibition, Autonomy, Affiliation, Intraception, Succourance, Dominance, Abasement, Nurturance, Change, Endurance, Heterosexuality, Aggression. Holland's Interest Inventory Based on Holland's Theory of Vocational Types or the RIASEC model. Vocational Types: Realistic (R), Investigative (I), Artistic (A), Social (S), Enterprising (E), Conventional (C). Multiphasic Personality Questionnaire (MPQ) Founder note. Developed by Murthy (1964); the Indian version of MMPI-2. Age: 18 and above. 100 statements, forced choice type. 2 validity scales: K scale, Repressor Sensitiser. 7 clinical scales: Anxiety, Manic, Psychopathic deviation, Depression, Paranoid, Schizophrenia, Hysteria. 10 · Non-Projective Tests (Factor Analytic) Non-Projective Tests (Factor Analytic): 16 PF, EPQ, NEO-PI. Fact cards for Cattell's 16 PF (traits, 16 source traits, types of data), the Eysenck Personality Questionnaire and the NEO-PI. Psycho Didi notes · p. 68 16 PF Founder note. By Raymond Cattell ; made using factor analysis. Type of traits: temperamental, ability, dynamic (bipolar). Surface traits are a combination of source traits. Oblique design used for factor analysis. Gave the specification equation R = f(S,P). Identified 11 second-order factors. Used multiple abstract variance analysis to measure heritability of traits. 16 source traits Warmth · Reasoning · Emotional stability · Dominance · Liveliness · Rule conscious · Social boldness · Sensitivity · Vigilance · Abstractness · Privateness · Apprehension · Open to change · Self reliance · Perfection · Tension. Types of data Key. Objective measurement: the participant should not know what is being measured. L data — D, J, K, P factors are a part of L data. Q data T data Global 5 scale — created out of second-order factors. Response style scales: acquiescence; impression management (narcissists will show a lot of social desirability); infrequency. NEO-PI Founder note. By Paul Costa and Robert McCrae ; based on the five factor model / big five model. Year: 1978. No lie scale, no validity scales. Number of items: 240; orthogonal rotation used. Three versions: NEO-PI (1985), NEO-PI-R (1992), NEO-PI-3 (2005). Domains measured by NEO-PI: Extraversion, Agreeableness, Neuroticism, Openness, Conscientiousness. Each domain has 6 facets. The psychoticism scale of EPI correlates negatively with agreeableness and conscientiousness scales. Eysenck Personality Questionnaire (EPQ) Founder note. By Hans Eysenck . Theory: Type → Trait → Habit → S-R (smallest). Focuses on nature (biological disposition) only. 108 items; current version: EPQ-R (1985). Can measure 22 personality disorders. Three dimensions (PEN): Psychoticism – Impulse control (gave this dimension after working at Maudsley hospital). Extroversion – Introversion.
