Neuroticism – Emotional Stability. 4th dimension: Lie scale. Reliability vs validity check. Note the distinct validity-scale families across objective tests: MMPI (Starke Hathaway and J. Charnley McKinley, 1943) uses criterion-keyed validity scales (L, F, K, VRIN, TRIN…); MCMI uses X/Y/Z/V/W; EPPS uses social desirability + consistency; MPQ uses K + Repressor-Sensitiser; the 16PF uses response-style scales (acquiescence, impression management, infrequency); NEO-PI has no validity/lie scales, whereas the EPQ (Hans Eysenck and Sybil Eysenck, 1975) adds a Lie scale as its 4th dimension. Don't confuse a validity scale (detects faking) with a clinical/content scale (measures the trait).

title: Psychological Interventions
text: Psychological Interventions — Study with Psycho Didi (MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF) Psychological Interventions Study with Psycho Didi · MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF notes Psychodynamic → Sigmund Freud Behaviour therapy: 3 wings CBT waves 1–3 Humanistic & existential Stress, coping & counselling What this covers. The full sweep of psychological interventions: psychodynamic psychotherapy (Freud, defence mechanisms, transference) and transactional analysis (Eric Berne); behaviour therapy across its classical-conditioning, operant and modelling wings; the three waves of cognitive-behaviour therapy (Beck's CT and Ellis's REBT, then DBT, MBCT, MBSR (Jon Kabat-Zinn, 1979) and ACT with other third-wave therapies); EMDR (Francine Shapiro); gestalt therapy (Fritz Perls) and its many techniques; humanistic and existential therapy (Carl Rogers, Karl Jaspers, Sartre, Viktor Frankl, Irvin Yalom); stress and coping models; and the principles of counselling and guidance. Original diagrams. 25 diagrams from the Psycho Didi PDF (pages 70 to 80) sit under the section they belong to, exactly as drawn. Tap one to open it full size and zoom in. Contents: 1 · Psychodynamic Psychotherapy · 2 · Transactional Analysis · 3 · Behaviour Therapy · 4 · Cognitive-Behaviour Therapy (Waves 1–3) · 5 · EMDR · 6 · Gestalt Therapy · 7 · Humanistic & Existential Therapy · 8 · Stress and Coping · 9 · Counselling and Guidance 1 · Psychodynamic Psychotherapy Psychodynamic psychotherapy: Freud. Infographic page on Freud with his photo, early life, career, important therapy processes, defence mechanisms, dreams and dream work, and an illustration of a client on a couch with a therapist. Psycho Didi notes · p. 70 Psychodynamic psychotherapy → Sigmund Freud. Worked with Joseph Breuer (the case of Anna 'O' ); influenced by Jean-Martin Charcot (hypnosis) and Breuer (catharsis). Freud — early life & career Was his mother's favourite child; observed his own life; was attracted to his mother and scared of his father. Started teaching at the University of Vienna in 1873. Died in Britain from jaw cancer. Career milestones: cocaine exploration; influence of Jean-Martin Charcot (hypnosis) and Josef Breuer (catharsis); movement from resistance to suggestion → concentration technique → free association; publication of Studies on Hysteria . Defence mechanisms Defence Core idea Repression Keeping unpleasant memories or thoughts buried in the unconscious. Primal : innately part of the Id. Proper : unacceptable derivatives of original id impulses. Denial Refusing to recognise an unpleasant reality. Rationalization Creating a socially acceptable excuse to justify unacceptable behaviour. Reaction formation Not acknowledging unacceptable impulses and over-emphasising their opposite. Projection Transferring one's unacceptable qualities or impulses to others. Important processes Process Meaning Resistance Reluctance to discuss certain topics; conscious defence mechanisms. Transference The patient projects feelings meant for others onto the therapist. Counter-transference The therapist develops emotional reactions towards the patient. Working through Discussing emotionally charged material over many therapy sessions. Trap — transference vs counter-transference. Transference = patient → therapist (patient projects feelings for others onto the therapist). Counter-transference = therapist → patient (therapist develops emotional reactions towards the patient). Dreams Manifest content: the clearly identifiable stories, characters, events and actions. Latent content: the unconscious thoughts, desires, fears and conflicts. Dream work Mechanism Function Condensation Condensing multiple thoughts into a single dream element or symbol. Displacement Shifting emotional significance from one object to another. Symbolization Representing an action or idea through symbols. Secondary revision Rationalizing latent content. 2 · Transactional Analysis Transactional analysis: Eric Berne. Introduction and four types of analysis beside three circles showing the Parent ego (nurturing and critical), Adult ego and Child ego (free and adapted). Psycho Didi notes · p. 71 Transactional Analysis → Eric Berne. Transactional Analysis is a psychotherapeutic method characterised by a creative combination of cognitive and psychodynamically oriented psychotherapy, enriched by aspects of communication therapy and gestalt therapy (Fritz Perls) processes. Types of analysis Structural analysis: individual personality analysis. Transactional analysis: dialogue analysis. Game analysis: saying something and meaning something else (analysis of ulterior transactions). Script analysis: compulsive, rigid transactions that people act out compulsively. Ego states Parent ego — Nurturing parent and Critical parent. Adult ego. Child ego — Free child and Adapted child. Transactions Transactions. Three Parent-Adult-Child diagrams with arrows showing complementary, crossed and ulterior transactions between two people. Psycho Didi notes · p. 71 Complementary transactions. Crossed transactions. Ulterior transactions — e.g. saying "You don't love me" while meaning "You love my brother so much!" 3 · Behaviour Therapy Behaviour therapy: introduction, applications and features. Introduction and assumptions of behaviour therapy, its applications and fields of use, and its key features, with a small illustration of three people. Psycho Didi notes · p. 72 Behaviour therapy is the application of experimentally derived principles of learning to the treatment of psychological disorders. Assumptions An empirical approach. Most behaviour is learned and therefore can be unlearned. Maladaptive behaviours are learned in the same manner as adaptive ones. The historical account of the development of a problem behaviour is less relevant than the present factors. It rejects the assumptions of traditional trait theory. Features Focus on present factors. Functional assessment and behavioural analysis. Recognition of individual–environment interaction. Active client participation. Two core features: extinction and counter-conditioning . Goal is to reduce maladaptive behaviours. Applications Used in treating anxiety, depression, PTSD, substance abuse, eating and sexual disorders, and hypertension. Applied across diverse fields: developmental disability, mental illness, education and special education, and community psychology. Techniques based on classical conditioning Techniques based on classical conditioning. Notes on systematic desensitization with its steps, aversion therapy, and flooding and implosion, with small illustrations. Psycho Didi notes · p. 72 Systematic desensitization Systematic desensitization → Joseph Wolpe (1958). Based on reciprocal inhibition : the process in which maladaptive responses learned due to prior conditioning with aversive events are eliminated by developing antagonistic responses. Steps: Jacobson's Progressive Muscle Relaxation (JPMR). Development of an anxiety hierarchy and exposure in vitro . Desensitization (Subjective Unit of Distress < 25). Flooding Involves therapist-controlled, prolonged exposure to anxiety-provoking conditioned stimuli (CS), simultaneously blocking the individual's chance of escape and avoidance. Implosion Implosion → Thomas Stampfl (1966). A variant of flooding, but it takes place at the imaginary level. Trap — systematic desensitization vs flooding. Systematic desensitization (Wolpe) is graded : it climbs an anxiety hierarchy with relaxation, keeping distress low (reciprocal inhibition). Flooding is maximal : prolonged full-intensity exposure with escape/avoidance blocked, no gradual hierarchy. Implosion (Stampfl) = flooding done in imagination. Aversion therapy An avoidance-learning method in which the individual is required to perform a response to avoid punishment. Example: alcohol + disulfiram causes vomiting, so the person learns to avoid alcohol. Used for treating OCD, paraphilia and substance-use disorders; also applied in clinical psychology, rehabilitation, business, self-management and sports-psychology interventions. Techniques based on operant conditioning (1st wave) Techniques based on operant conditioning (1st wave). Differential reinforcement and its four types, token economy, response cost, time out, shaping and chaining. Psycho Didi notes · p. 72 Differential reinforcement Refers to the implementation of two clearly different degrees of reinforcement for two behaviours, one of which is to be replaced by the other. Type Purpose DRO — of other behaviour (or zero-rate behaviour) Reinforcing the non-occurrence of the target behaviour. DRL — of low-rate behaviour Designed to decrease a behaviour to an acceptable level. DRI — of incompatible behaviour Reinforcing responses that are topographically incompatible with the possibility of the target behaviour. DRA — of alternate behaviour The reinforced behaviour need not be topographically incompatible; it may be any desirable alternate behaviour. Other operant techniques Technique Core idea Token economy (Teodoro Ayllon and Nathan Azrin, 1968) A reinforcement system based on the delivery of tokens. Tokens earned for specific target behaviour can be spent on different things within a defined therapeutic environment, or saved for future purchases. Response cost Withdrawal of acquired positive reinforcers following undesirable or problematic behaviour. Time out Temporarily separating a person from an environment where an unacceptable behaviour has occurred. Example: a player getting a red card in a football match. Shaping Reinforcing behaviours that are successively closer approximations of the desired or targeted behaviour. Chaining Teaching a behaviour using behaviour chains — sequences of individual behaviours that, when linked together, form a terminal behaviour. Techniques based on modelling Techniques based on modelling. Introduction, functions and variants of modelling, with a nesting doll illustration. Psycho Didi notes · p. 72 Modelling → Albert Bandura (S-O-R theory). Process of learning: attention → retention → motor reproduction → motivation. Functions: teaching through demonstration, promoting behaviour, motivating behaviour, anxiety reduction, and discouraging behaviours. Variants: Covert — live modelling, symbolic modelling, participant modelling, self-modelling. Overt — imaginative. 4 · Cognitive-Behaviour Therapy (Waves 1–3) Key — the three waves. 1st wave = behaviour therapy (operant/classical conditioning). 2nd wave = cognitive therapy — Beck's CT and Ellis's REBT. 3rd wave = acceptance/mindfulness-based therapies (DBT, MBCT, MBSR (Jon Kabat-Zinn), ACT, and others). Beck's Cognitive Therapy (2nd wave) Beck’s cognitive therapy (2nd wave). Introduction to Beck’s cognitive therapy, a cognitive triad triangle of self, world and future around negative feelings, and a list of twelve cognitive distortions. Psycho Didi notes · p. 73 Cognitive therapy → Aaron Beck. Based on the concept that our thoughts, feelings, physical sensations and actions are interconnected, and that negative thoughts and feelings can trap us in a vicious cycle. Cognitive triad Self — "I am a failure." World — "Everybody is unfair." Future — "I will never succeed." Cognitive distortions Distortion Meaning All or nothing Dichotomous, extremes of language such as "always". Mental filter Only paying attention to certain evidence, skewing it as meaning more than it does. Mind reading Assuming you know what someone else is thinking or feeling. Overgeneralizing Seeing a pattern based on a single event, or being overly broad in your conclusions. Disqualifying the positive A type of mental filter discounting the good things that have happened or that you have done. Fortune telling Assuming you know what will happen in the future. Magnification Blowing things out of proportion. Emotional reasoning "Because I'm thinking or feeling it, it must be true." Labelling Assigning labels to ourselves or others, putting people in a box so they can't and won't change. Minimization Inappropriately shrinking something to make it seem less important; rationalization, justification, blaming. Shoulds and musts Unrealistic expectations. Personalization Taking responsibility for something that is not yours to own. Self-instruction training Self instruction training. Steps of Meichenbaum’s self instruction training, with an illustration of a hand pointing at an open book. Psycho Didi notes · p. 73 Self-instruction training → Donald Meichenbaum. Modelling: demonstrating assertive behaviour. Practice: role playing. Self-instruction: overt, then covert. Practice in real life. Rational Emotive Behaviour Therapy (REBT) Rational Emotive Behaviour Therapy. Notes on Ellis’s REBT with an A-B-C-D-E flow diagram, the three major irrational clusters and REBT techniques. Psycho Didi notes · p. 73 REBT → Albert Ellis (a directive therapy). Ellis coined the term musterbation to indicate that irrational beliefs are usually expressed as musts, shoulds, ought-tos, have-tos and got-tos. Three major irrational clusters: "I must do well and win approval for my performances." "Others must treat me kindly and considerately." "Conditions under which I live must be arranged so that I get practically everything I want comfortably, quickly and easily." Techniques: Socratic questioning, confrontation, role playing, and shame-attacking exercises (homework outside of therapy). Trap — Beck vs Albert Ellis. Beck (Cognitive Therapy) targets cognitive distortions and the cognitive triad (self–world–future) through collaborative empiricism and Socratic guided discovery. Ellis (REBT) targets irrational beliefs ("musterbation": musts/shoulds) and is more directive/confrontational, using the ABC framework and shame-attacking exercises. Third-wave therapies (3rd wave) Cognitive-behaviour therapy: 3rd wave. Four boxes on MBCT, ACT with its six-process triangle, MBSR, and DBT with its four skill modules, plus a list of other third-wave therapies. Psycho Didi notes · p. 74 Dialectical Behaviour Therapy (DBT) DBT → Marsha M. Linehan. Emerged as a treatment for chronically parasuicidal women with Borderline Personality Disorder. Three main principles: Everything is interconnected or interrelated. Reality is not static. The truth (which is always evolving) can be found by integrating or synthesizing differing (and possibly opposite) views. Four core skill modules: core mindfulness skills, interpersonal effectiveness skills, emotion regulation skills, and distress tolerance skills. Steps / stages: Identifying safety and life-threatening behaviours. Addressing therapy-interfering behaviours. Enhancing quality of life. Adaptation and growth. Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy (MBCT) MBCT → Zindel Segal, Mark Williams & John Teasdale. Features: thought-process focused; promotes a new way of being with painful affect and challenging circumstances; distinguishing thoughts as thoughts (vs statements of fact); noticing and allowing thoughts and feelings without fixing, changing or avoiding; behavioural interventions focused on developing present-moment awareness; and the therapist also embodies the approach. Structure: 8 consecutive weekly sessions of about 2 hours each — Phase 1 (teaching), Phase 2 (application). Used for: anxiety disorders, bipolar disorder, depression associated with medical illness, low mood, unhappiness, depression-relapse prevention, and treatment-resistant depression. Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR) Structure: 8 consecutive weekly sessions, 5 hours per week — Phase 1 (teaching), Phase 2 (application). Features: focuses on cultivating mindfulness, contemplation, listening and speaking; a briefer integrative practice. Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) ACT → Steven Hayes. The ACT acronym: A: Accept your thoughts and feelings, and be present. C: Choose a valued direction. T: Take action. Six core processes (grouped as Open up / Be present / Do what matters): Contact with the present moment (be here now). Defusion (watch your thinking). Acceptance (open up). Self as context (pure awareness). Values (know what matters). Committed action (doing what it takes). Other third-wave therapies Functional Analytic Psychotherapy (FAP). Metacognitive Therapy (MCT). Compassion Focused Therapy (CFT). 5 · Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing (EMDR) Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing (EMDR). Key facts about EMDR and its five-step procedure, with an illustration of a person hugging her knees beside two shadow figures. Psycho Didi notes · p. 75 EMDR → Francine Shapiro (1987). Considered a behaviour therapy by some authors. Used in PTSD. Not falsifiable. Book: Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing: Basic Principles, Protocols . Procedure History taking. Desensitization: focus on emotion and bodily sensation. Bilateral stimulation: eye movement, tactile, auditory stimulation. Reprocessing: the trauma that occurred in the past. Installation: of positive beliefs. 6 · Gestalt Therapy Gestalt therapy. One box covering the introduction to gestalt therapy, the integration sequence, boundaries, contact and its levels, types of awareness, and contact disturbances. Psycho Didi notes · p. 75 Gestalt therapy → Fritz Perls and Laura Perls (1940s). Influenced by the existential school, phenomenology and field theory. Focuses on re-owning disowned parts of the self. Self: internal and external (one dominates or is dominated). Real change comes when we try to be our true self rather than being someone else. Increasing awareness enables informed choices and leads to a more meaningful life. Insight comes through the help of therapy. A directional, confrontational therapy Emphasizes that one must understand the field-theory diagram in order to understand oneself. Clients should take responsibility for their life problems. Movement from environmental support to self-support. A confrontational therapy style — Perls intentionally frustrated clients (skilful frustration) . Focuses on restoring awareness. Types of awareness (Polster & Polster, 1973) Sensation and action. Feeling. Wants. Values and assessment. Focus on current experience: the here and now; the what and how. Contact and levels Contact: interacting meaningfully with others. Fusion: fusing with others. Level of contact Description Phony layer People complimenting when they want something from you. Phobic layer Avoidance of pain, grief. Impasse layer Unable to change and unable to solve. Implosive layer Becoming aware of self but keeping feelings inside. Explosive layer Taking action and expression. When contact is not genuine and authentic (Polster & Polster) Disturbance Meaning Introjection Swallowing whole, or accepting others' views without questioning. Retroflection Doing to ourselves what we would like to do to other people. Projection Assigning aspects of ourselves onto others. Deflection Avoidance. Confluence The boundary between oneself and others becomes muted. Integration sequence Discovery: self-realization prompting newfound awareness. Accommodation: skills to navigate challenging situations. Assimilation: learning to influence the environment. Boundaries Boundaries are rigid and must be challenged and crossed; language must be used as a method to challenge boundaries. Types of boundaries: body boundaries, value boundaries, familiarity boundaries, expressive boundaries. Gestalt therapy techniques Gestalt therapy techniques. Ten gestalt therapy techniques, each with a short description and an illustration. Psycho Didi notes · p. 76 Technique Description The Internal Dialogue Exercise (top dog vs underdog) The topdog is the voice of what the person should do; the underdog is the rebellious part that resists the topdog's demands. The client converses as both. The Empty-Chair Technique (by Joseph Moreno) A role-playing technique in which all the parts are played by the client, so introjects can surface and the client can experience the conflict more fully. Future Projection Technique An anticipated event is brought into the present moment and acted out. Making the Rounds Asking a person in a group to go up to others and either speak to or do something with each person — to confront, to risk, to disclose the self, to experiment with new behaviour, and to grow and change. The Reversal Exercise Clients take the plunge into the very thing fraught with anxiety and make contact with submerged, denied parts of themselves. The Rehearsal Exercise Rehearsing aloud in a group so that others can experience the internal thinking process. The Exaggeration Exercise Repeating and exaggerating a movement or gesture to help clients become more aware of their emotions. Staying With the Feeling At key moments when clients wish to flee an unpleasant feeling, the therapist urges them to stay with and go deeper into the feeling or behaviour they wish to avoid. Dream Work The Gestalt approach does not interpret and analyze dreams; instead, it brings dreams back to life and relives them as though happening now. "I" statements Clients are encouraged to use the phrase "I" to take responsibility for their own feelings and actions. 7 · Humanistic & Existential Therapy Humanistic and existential therapy. Notes on Carl Rogers, Karl Jaspers, Jean Paul Sartre, Viktor Frankl with the meaning triangle, and Irvin Yalom, with photos of the theorists. Psycho Didi notes · p. 77 Carl Rogers — Client-Centred Therapy Client-centred therapy → Carl Rogers. Rogers believed that people can consciously and rationally change their thoughts and behaviour from undesirable to desirable. Conditions of therapy: A congruent therapist. Unconditional positive regard for the client. Accurate empathy. After therapy, the person gets closer to becoming a congruent and fully functioning person. Karl Jaspers — Boundary Situations Boundary situations are conditions of human life that are difficult to overcome. They are basic facts about human life, such as death, suffering, guilt and struggle. They are unchanging and unalterable, although the way they appear to humans may change; they are experienced at the limit of one's existence. Significance of boundary situations: Reveal being as such. Reveal the potential for self-realization. Remove the cover of a private world view. Expose people to the reality of opposites, contradictions and death. Jean-Paul Sartre — Existential Psychoanalysis Believed there is no inherent meaning to life; any meaning you find is your own. People are "condemned to be free". In existential psychoanalysis , the therapist's role is to confront excuses for misery. Viktor Frankl — Logotherapy Logotherapy → Viktor Frankl. Emphasis on existential and spiritual questions. Meaning is found through the "meaning triangle" of Attitude , Experience and Creativity . Books: Man's Search for Meaning ; Recollections: An Autobiography . Techniques for transcending problems: Attitude modulation: changing negative to positive. Dereflection: redirecting focus from our issue to other, greater issues. Paradoxical intention: cracking jokes about difficult situations. Socratic dialogue (by Guttman): guided questioning — the approach questions beliefs, the guidance busts misunderstanding, and the outcome is reduced self-absorption. Irvin Yalom Focus: death, freedom, isolation and meaninglessness. Themes: Death and existence — live authentically. Freedom and responsibility. Existential isolation. Meaning and purpose. Authenticity and self-awareness. 8 · Stress and Coping Stress and coping: stress and the Social Readjustment Rating Scale. Definition of stress, types of stressors and stress, and notes on Holmes and Rahe’s Social Readjustment Rating Scale. Psycho Didi notes · p. 78 Stress and coping illustration. Illustration of a woman with leaves and flowers growing from her head. Psycho Didi notes · p. 78 Stress is a state brought on by any situation that threatens, or appears to threaten, a person's sense of well-being, thus challenging the person's ability to cope. Types of stressors and stress Acute: a short-term stressor that has a definite endpoint. Chronic: a long-term stressor that often lacks a definite endpoint. Eustress: an optimal amount of stress required to motivate you. Distress: stress that occurs when we are unable to meet the demands of our environment with our limited resources. Personality & stress Personality and stress. Type A, B, C and D personalities with their traits and the illness each is prone to. Psycho Didi notes · p. 78 Type A / Type B personality → Meyer Friedman & Raymond Rosenman (cardiologists, late 1950s). Type Traits Prone to Type A Self-driven, competitive, achievers, risk-takers, show hostility. Coronary heart disease. Type B Charismatic, easy-going, not easily stressed, lacking a sense of urgency. — Type C Introverts, lone workers, sticklers for details, perfectionists, unassertive. Cancer. Type D Negative affectivity (worry, gloominess) and social inhibition; distressed. Depression. The Social Readjustment Rating Scale Social Readjustment Rating Scale → Thomas Holmes & Richard Rahe (1967). They compiled a list of 43 events likely to change a person's life and therefore cause stress. Based on participant ratings, each event was assigned a point value from 1 to 100; these units were called life change units . Types of stressors (Thomas Holmes & Rahe): catastrophic/cataclysmic events, and daily hassles. Physiological responses to stress Physiological responses to stress. Two flowcharts for the HPA axis and the SAM pathway, with notes on allostasis and cortisol. Psycho Didi notes · p. 78 HPA axis: CRF → anterior pituitary → ACTH → adrenal cortex → cortisol → metabolism increase and insulin resistance. SAM pathway: hypothalamus → SNS → adrenal medulla → epinephrine and norepinephrine. Allostasis is a process of adaptation to acute stress by releasing stress hormones in the event of a challenge, with the goal of restoring homeostasis; it occurs because the HPA axis is activated during stress. Constant cortisol release causes immunosuppression. Cognitive appraisal / mediation theory Cognitive appraisal / mediation theory. Lazarus’s primary and secondary appraisal of a stressor. Psycho Didi notes · p. 78 Cognitive appraisal (mediation) theory → Richard Lazarus. Primary appraisal: we examine the stressor and assess how severe it is — identifying it as a threat (a future danger), a challenge (a current situation to be confronted and overcome), or a harm or loss . Secondary appraisal: we evaluate our own resources and ability to cope with the threat, challenge or loss. General Adaptation Syndrome (GAS) General Adaptation Syndrome. The three GAS stages listed above a graph of resistance to stress over time across the alarm, resistance and exhaustion stages. Psycho Didi notes · p. 78 General Adaptation Syndrome → Hans Selye. Stage 1: alarm. Stage 2: resistance. Stage 3: exhaustion. Response to stress & coping Response to stress. Tree diagram splitting response to stress into defending and coping, coping into adaptive and maladaptive, and adaptive coping into problem focused and emotion focused. Psycho Didi notes · p. 79 Defending vs Coping ; Adaptive vs Maladaptive . Problem-focused coping (source: external) vs Emotion-focused coping (source: internal). Explanatory styles Explanatory styles. Optimistic and pessimistic styles compared for a negative event and a positive event by duration, scope and source, with an illustration of a woman with flowers in her hair. Psycho Didi notes · p. 79 Explanatory styles → Martin Seligman. The characteristic manner in which we explain events; explanatory styles make a difference in how we appraise and respond to stressors. Dimension Optimistic style Pessimistic style Duration Temporary Permanent Scope Specific Global Source External Internal Interventions Interventions for stress. Stress interventions split into a physiological level and a psychological level, with two small illustrations. Psycho Didi notes · p. 79 Physiological level: Simple breathing exercises — pranayam, box breathing. Guided imagery: a method of treating stress and anxiety in which one replaces disturbing memories with positive mental energy. Biofeedback: a self-regulation technique through which patients learn to voluntarily control what were once thought to be involuntary body processes. Progressive Muscle Relaxation — introduced by Edmund Jacobson (1920) , also called JPMR; types of relaxation: top-down and bottom-up. Psychological level: Mindfulness meditation: slows racing thoughts, living in the present, letting go of negativity to calm body and mind — attitude, attention and intention. Stress inoculation (by Donald Meichenbaum, 1985 ): stages of education/conceptualization → rehearsal/skill acquisition → implementation/skill application and follow-through. Social support: an effective, active, problem-focused network of friends; ask for help. 9 · Counselling and Guidance Counselling and guidance. One page covering the dimensions, need, goals, process, stages, steps and important steps of counselling, plus the relationship, termination, influencing factors and qualities of counsellor and client, with an illustration of a woman. Psycho Didi notes · p. 80 Dimensions A good counselling relationship, therapeutic intervention, and psychological process. Essential features Theorist Essential features for counselling Carl Rogers Unconditional positive regard, empathy, congruence. Carkhuff Respect, confrontation, immediacy, concreteness, self-disclosure. Need & goals Need: when stress-related symptoms are out of proportion, loneliness, job issues, career problems. Goals: Healthy development of personality. Providing support. Emotional release. Awareness. Value clarification and change. Process & steps Process: pre-counselling (see if the client is suitable) → identify the need for counselling → prepare for counselling → conduct counselling → follow-up. Steps of counselling: Identify → Prepare → Conduct → Termination → Follow-up. Important steps: background information → identifying core issues → case formulation → goal setting → intervention implementation → evaluation → closure. Length and intensity of counselling depend on the severity of the problem, motivation of the client, type of problems, and age of the client. Stages of counselling: Beginning → Middle → Ending Developing a relationship / beginning: establish a safe environment, help people express, active listening, paraphrasing, focus on feelings. Middle: transform the problem into a goal, explore approaches to the goal, help the person choose a way towards the goal, make a contract to fulfil the plan, summarize and get verification, get feedback and confirmation. Analysing fears: abandonment, rejection, not being enough. It is important that clients gain recognition for their skills and experience; being confronted from a caring position; re-experiencing past events in the present. Analysis of transference and countertransference — the reaction to the counsellor–client relationship. Termination of a relationship The client no longer requires help. The counsellor cannot provide any more benefit to the client. Premature termination: termination before it is due. Referral: when the client needs to be referred to another professional. Follow-up. Factors affecting counselling Structure: the psychological and physical atmosphere. Initiative: whether the client himself wants to change or not (difficult if the client is reluctant). Settings. Qualities of counsellor and client Qualities of a counsellor: self-aware, honest, congruent, good communication skills, knowledgeable. Trap — YAVIS vs HOUND clients. YAVIS = Young, Attractive, Verbal, Intelligent, Successful → tend to get better help. HOUND = Homely, Old, Unattractive, Nonverbal, Dumb → less likely to be helped. Working in a relationship Leading: redirecting the conversation towards change. Accurate empathy — components: empathic rapport, communication attunement. Types: primary ; advanced (making implicit explicit, identifying themes, connecting islands). Self-disclosure: the counsellor's problems, facts about the counsellor's role, and reaction to the client. Analysis of transference and countertransference.

title: Health Psychology, Ethics & Laws
text: Health Psychology, Ethics & Laws — Study with Psycho Didi (MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF) Health Psychology, Ethics & Laws Study with Psycho Didi · MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF notes Health-behaviour models (HBM, TPB, TTM) Levels of prevention APA Ethics Code (Principles A–E) Mental Healthcare Act 2017 RCI & RPWD Acts What this covers. Two linked areas. First, Health Psychology : epidemiology basics, the levels of prevention (primordial, primary, secondary, tertiary), and the major health-behaviour and illness models (Health Belief Model, Theory of Planned Behaviour, Transtheoretical Model, biopsychosocial model (George Engel, 1977)). Second, Psychology in Practice — Ethics & Laws : the APA General Principles and Ethical Standards, and the history of Indian mental-health legislation from the colonial Lunacy Acts through the RCI Act, the disability acts, and the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 and its 2022 amendment. Original diagrams. 8 diagrams from the Psycho Didi PDF (pages 82 to 85) sit under the section they belong to, exactly as drawn. Tap one to open it full size and zoom in. Contents: Health Psychology · Ethics & Laws Health Psychology Epidemiology and disease measures Epidemiology. Definition of epidemiology with morbidity, incidence, prevalence and mortality, under an illustration of two researchers with a magnifying glass. Psycho Didi notes · p. 82 Epidemiology is the study of the frequency, distribution and causes of infectious and non-infectious disease in a population. Its core measures are: Term Meaning Morbidity The number of cases of a disease that exist at some given point in time. Incidence The number of new cases at some given point of time. Prevalence The total number of existing cases at some given point of time. Mortality The number of deaths due to particular causes. Don't confuse. Incidence counts only new cases; prevalence counts all existing cases (new + old). Morbidity is about illness; mortality is about death. Levels of prevention Types of prevention. Diagram branching from types of prevention to primordial, primary, secondary and tertiary prevention, each with examples and an icon. Psycho Didi notes · p. 82 Level Focus Primordial prevention Inhibit the emergence of risk factors in the form of environmental, economic, social, and behavioral conditions and cultural patterns of living, etc. Primary prevention Awareness programs, psychoeducation, vaccination, wearing a helmet. Secondary prevention Early detection and treatment; reversal of problems/damage. Tertiary prevention Only management, since reversal is not possible; stopping further progression of problems. Key. Order by when they act: Primordial (before risk factors even appear) → Primary (before disease) → Secondary (early disease, still reversible) → Tertiary (established disease, manage and limit progression). Health-behaviour models Biopsychosocial model of health. Venn diagram of biological, psychological and social or environmental factors that overlap around mental health. Psycho Didi notes · p. 82 Health belief model, TTM and theory of planned behaviour. Notes on the six constructs of the health belief model, the six stages of the transtheoretical model, and the three components of the theory of planned behaviour. Psycho Didi notes · p. 82 The Health Belief Model (HBM) Given by Rosenstock . It explains health behaviour through six constructs : Perceived susceptibility — a person's subjective perception of the risk of acquiring an illness or disease. Perceived severity — a person's feelings on the seriousness of contracting an illness or disease. Perceived benefits — a person's perception of the effectiveness of various actions available to reduce the threat of illness or disease. Perceived barriers — a person's feelings on the obstacles to performing a recommended health action. Cue to action — the stimulus needed to trigger the decision-making process to accept a recommended health action. Self-efficacy (Albert Bandura, 1977) — the level of a person's confidence in his or her ability to successfully perform a behaviour. Theory of Planned Behaviour (TPB) Given by Icek Ajzen ; earlier called the Theory of Reasoned Action . According to this theory, a health behaviour is the direct result of a behavioural intention . Behavioural intentions are themselves made up of three components: Attitudes toward the specific action — beliefs about the outcomes of the behaviour (e.g. "if I change my diet, I will lose weight, improve my health, and be more attractive") and evaluations of those outcomes (e.g. "being healthy and looking good are desirable"). Subjective norms regarding the action — normative beliefs (e.g. "my family and friends think I should change my diet") and motivation to comply (e.g. "I want to do what they want me to do"). Perceived behavioural control — e.g. "I will be able to change my diet". Transtheoretical Model of behaviour change (TTM) Given by James Prochaska . It posits that health behaviour change involves progress through six stages of change : Precontemplation Contemplation Preparation Action Maintenance Termination Biopsychosocial model of health Health and illness are understood as the product of interacting biological, psychological, and social factors, rather than biology alone. Model → author. Health Belief Model → Rosenstock Theory of Planned Behaviour (formerly Theory of Reasoned Action) → Ajzen Transtheoretical Model (TTM) → James Prochaska Don't confuse. HBM's self-efficacy vs TPB's perceived behavioural control — both are about confidence to perform the behaviour but belong to different models. TPB's older name is the Theory of Reasoned Action (which lacked perceived behavioural control). Ethics & Laws APA Ethical Principles and Code of Conduct APA code of conduct: introduction. Banner title and introduction describing the parts of the APA Ethical Principles of Psychologists and Code of Conduct. Psycho Didi notes · p. 84 APA preamble and five general principles. The preamble and goal of the APA ethics code, followed by general principles A to E. Psycho Didi notes · p. 84 APA ten ethical standards. The ten sections of the APA ethical standards with a one-line summary of each. Psycho Didi notes · p. 84 The American Psychological Association's (APA) Ethical Principles of Psychologists and Code of Conduct consists of an Introduction, a Preamble, five General Principles (A–E) , and specific Ethical Standards . The Ethics Code applies only to psychologists' activities that are part of their scientific, educational, or professional roles as psychologists. Preamble and goal In the Preamble, psychologists are committed to increasing scientific and professional knowledge of behavior, respect and protect civil and human rights, and strive to help the public in developing informed judgments and choices concerning human behavior. Goal of the Ethics Code: the welfare and protection of the individuals and groups with whom psychologists work, and the education of members, students, and the public regarding the ethical standards of the discipline. General Principles (A–E) Key. The General Principles are aspirational in nature; they cannot form the basis for sanctions. The Ethical Standards (below) are the enforceable rules. Principle Content A: Beneficence and Non-maleficence Psychologists strive to benefit those with whom they work and take care to do no harm. B: Fidelity and Responsibility Psychologists establish relationships of trust; they are aware of their professional and scientific responsibilities to society and to the specific communities in which they work. C: Integrity Psychologists seek to promote accuracy, honesty, and truthfulness in the science, teaching, and practice of psychology; they strive to keep their promises and to avoid unwise or unclear commitments. D: Justice Psychologists recognize that fairness and justice entitle all persons to access to and benefit from the contributions of psychology, and to equal quality in the processes, procedures, and services conducted by psychologists. E: Respect for People's Rights and Dignity Psychologists respect the dignity and worth of all people, and the rights of individuals to privacy, confidentiality, and self-determination. Ethical Standards (Sections 1–10) Section Standard 1. Resolving Ethical Issues Address ethical conflicts, report serious violations, and avoid retaliation against whistleblowers. 2. Competence Work within areas of expertise, seek ongoing training, and refer cases beyond one's competence. 3. Human Relations Avoid discrimination, exploitation, and conflicts of interest; obtain informed consent and minimize harm. 4. Privacy and Confidentiality Maintain confidentiality, inform clients of its limits, and securely handle records. 5. Advertising and Public Statements Ensure honesty in self-promotion, avoid misleading claims, and do not use client testimonials. 6. Record Keeping and Fees Keep accurate records, maintain transparency in billing, and handle financial matters ethically. 7. Education and Training Provide fair, accurate instruction and ensure students meet competency standards. 8. Research and Publication Obtain informed consent, protect participants, avoid plagiarism, and credit contributions properly. 9. Assessment Use valid tests, ensure fairness in administration and interpretation, and explain results clearly. 10. Therapy Obtain informed consent, clarify roles in multi-client settings, avoid dual relationships, and ethically terminate treatment. Why it matters. Informed consent and confidentiality recur across multiple standards (Human Relations, Privacy & Confidentiality, Research, Assessment, Therapy). They are not single rules but threads that run through the whole code. Mental Health Laws in India Mental health laws in India. Road timeline of Indian mental health laws from the colonial Lunacy Acts to the Mental Healthcare (Amendment) Bill 2022, with notes on each law. Psycho Didi notes · p. 85 Colonial laws 1851 — The Lunatic Removal Act 1858 — The Lunacy (Supreme Courts) Act 1858 — The Lunacy (District Courts) Act of 1858 The Mental Health Act, 1987 Implemented in 1993 . It is organized into 10 sections : Section Subject I Wordings II Establishment process III Establishment and maintenance IV Admission and Detention V Inspection, discharge, leaves VI Property of Mentally Ill VII Maintenance of mentally ill VIII Protection of human rights IX Penalty and Procedure X Miscellaneous Advantages: better than the Lunacy Act; OPD for outpatient cases; prohibition on research without consent; separate spaces for children and adults. Disadvantages: treatment like criminals; isolation from society; exclusion of dementia and mental retardation; government men don't need a license; suicide considered an offence; excessive focus on hospitalization; no provision for rehabilitation. Other key statutes and milestones 1982 — NMHP (National Mental Health Programme) launched: treatment of disorder within the community using PHC (Primary Health Centres), providing training. 1985 — Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act. 1992 — RCI Act (Rehabilitation Council of India Act). 1995 — Persons with Disabilities Act: mental illness was considered a disability for the first time. 2013 — New Mental Health Bill: no solitary confinement; community living; confidentiality; right to contact family; legal aid. 2016 — Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act (RPWD). 1995 Persons with Disabilities Act — recognized disabilities Physical: cerebral palsy, leprosy, dwarfism, muscular dystrophy, acid attack Visual impairment Hearing impairment Speech and language Intellectual disability (ID): autism, specific learning disabilities 2016 Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act (RPWD) — added disabilities and benefits Additional recognized conditions: Neurological: multiple sclerosis, Parkinson's disease Blood diseases: thalassemia, sickle cell anaemia Mental illness (vague) Multiple disabilities Benefits: 5% reservation in education; 4% reservation in jobs; punishment for violation; special courts. Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 Government support. Key characteristics: A person can't be held for more than 90 days . Appeal to Magistrate for discharge. Monthly checks. Licensing and supervision. Legal aid. Advantages: Decriminalizes suicide. Everybody has the right to mental health care. Central and State Mental Health Authority to advise government. Client's role in admission, treatment and discharge. Prohibits ECT (in specified circumstances). Establish hospitals nearby. Insurance. Financial punishment (₹50k–₹500k) and jail. No sterilization. Disadvantages: Not made by mental health professionals. Does not talk about awareness and prevention. Western-standard based. Expenditure allocation not clear. Key. The advance directive is a signature feature of the 2017 Act: a person can state in advance how they wish to be treated (or not treated) for mental illness and nominate a representative. Mental Healthcare (Amendment) Bill, 2022 Decriminalizes suicide. Strengthens community mental health. Ensures patient rights and care quality. Mandates insurance for mental illnesses. Reduces stigma through awareness. Don't confuse the three big acts. Mental Health Act 1987 (implemented 1993, 10 sections, hospitalization-heavy, suicide an offence) → Mental Healthcare Act 2017 (decriminalizes suicide, advance directive, right to care, 90-day cap) → Mental Healthcare (Amendment) Bill 2022 (reinforces decriminalized suicide, community care, mandatory insurance). Watch the years. Lunatic Removal Act 1851 ; Lunacy Acts 1858 ; NMHP 1982 ; NDPS Act 1985 ; MHA 1987 (implemented 1993); RCI Act 1992 ; Persons with Disabilities Act 1995 ; New Mental Health Bill 2013 ; RPWD Act 2016 ; Mental Healthcare Act 2017 ; Amendment Bill 2022 .

title: Cognitive Psychology
text: Cognitive Psychology — Study with Psycho Didi (MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF) Cognitive Psychology Study with Psycho Didi · MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF notes Sensation & perception Attention & SDT Learning & conditioning Memory models & forgetting Intelligence & creativity Thinking · problem solving · language What this covers. The whole cognitive block: how a stimulus becomes a perception (Gestalt organization, constancies, motion and depth cues, colour and sound theories, top-down vs bottom-up perception), theories of attention and signal detection, classical and operant conditioning (B. F. Skinner) plus cognitive/social learning, the multi-store, working-memory and levels-of-processing (Fergus Craik and Robert Lockhart, 1972) models, forgetting and memory distortion, the major theories of intelligence and creativity, thinking and concept formation, problem-solving heuristics and cognitive biases, and theories of language development. Original diagrams. 107 diagrams from the Psycho Didi PDF (pages 87 to 107) sit under the section they belong to, exactly as drawn. Tap one to open it full size and zoom in. Contents: 1 · Sensation & Perception · 2 · Colour & Sound Perception · 3 · Attention · 4 · Classical & Operant Conditioning · 5 · Cognitive & Social Learning · 6 · Memory Models · 7 · Forgetting & Memory Distortion · 8 · Intelligence · 9 · Creativity · 10 · Thinking & Concepts · 11 · Problem Solving, Reasoning & Decision-Making · 12 · Language Development 1 · Sensation & Perception Process and types of perception. Flow from stimulation to transduction, sensation, attention and perception, with arrows splitting perception into top-down and bottom-up types. Psycho Didi notes · p. 87 The perceptual sequence runs stimulation → transduction → sensation → attention → perception . Perception can be driven two ways: Top-down — expectation driven (knowledge and context shape what we perceive). Bottom-up — stimulus / data driven (the raw sensory input drives perception). Top-down vs bottom-up. Top-down = expectation/knowledge driven (constructivist, e.g. Gregory). Bottom-up = stimulus/data driven (direct/ecological, e.g. Gibson). Endogenous attention is top-down; exogenous attention is bottom-up. Gestalt psychology Gestalt psychology. Notes on the phi phenomenon, the six laws of organization and Pragnanz, with an overlapping rings drawing for Pragnanz. Psycho Didi notes · p. 87 Core dictum: the whole is greater than the sum of its parts. Key ideas include the Phi phenomenon and the law of Prägnanz — every stimulus pattern is seen so that the resulting structure is as simple as possible. Max Wertheimer — founder of Gestalt perception; described the Phi phenomenon , a type of stroboscopic motion , best seen at a time interval of 30 to 200 milliseconds . Laws of Perceptual Organization Law Principle Proximity Objects physically close together are grouped together. Continuity Stimuli falling along the same plane tend to be grouped together. Closure We fill in small gaps so objects are still perceived as whole. Similarity Stimuli resembling one another tend to be grouped together. Common region Stimuli in a common area or ground are grouped together. Common fate Objects moving in a similar direction are grouped together. Perceptual Constancy Perceptual constancy. Definitions of colour or brightness constancy, size constancy and shape constancy. Psycho Didi notes · p. 87 Colour / brightness constancy — perceiving colour or brightness as constant despite changes in lighting. Size constancy — perceiving an object as the same size regardless of its distance from the observer. Shape constancy — perceiving an object as maintaining its shape despite changes in orientation. Apparent (Illusory) Motion Apparent motion and the autokinetic effect. Definition of apparent motion and the autokinetic effect found by Muzafer Sherif (1935). Psycho Didi notes · p. 87 Induced motion. Definition of induced motion with a photo of the moon behind drifting clouds as the example. Psycho Didi notes · p. 87 Phi phenomenon, motion parallax and stroboscopic effect. Three panels on the phi and beta phenomena with critical flicker fusion, motion parallax with a train passenger drawing, and the stroboscopic effect with a multi-exposure dancer photo. Psycho Didi notes · p. 87 Perception of motion when there actually is none. Autokinetic effect — a stationary point of light appears to move in a dark room. Found by Muzafer Sherif (1935) . Induced motion — motion of one object causes a nearby stationary object to appear to move (e.g. clouds moving past the moon make the moon appear to race through the clouds). Phi phenomenon — an optical illusion in which stationary objects shown in rapid succession, past the threshold at which they can be perceived separately, appear to move. Temporal threshold: 30–200 ms . Beta phenomenon — similar to the phi phenomenon but usually circular motion. Critical Flicker Fusion Frequency — the frequency at which a flickering light appears steady; the threshold where separate/discontinuous images seem to fuse. Motion parallax — as we move, nearby objects appear to glide rapidly past us while more distant objects move more slowly (extremely far objects such as the moon seem to move away from you). Stroboscopic effect — a rapid succession of still images or lights creates the illusion of motion. Depth & Distance Cues Depth perception and the visual cliff. Visual cliff apparatus drawing next to notes on binocular cues (convergence, retinal, vertical and horizontal disparity, horopter) and monocular cues. Psycho Didi notes · p. 88 Monocular cues Cue Description Accommodation Change in the lens shape as the eye focuses. Interposition (overlap / partial occlusion) A closer object cuts off the view of part or all of a more distant one. Relative size The closer of two same-size objects casts a larger image on the retina. Texture gradient Closer objects have a coarser, more distinct texture; far objects appear more densely packed / smooth. Aerial / atmospheric perspective Closer objects appear sharper than more distant, hazy objects. Relative height / elevation Objects closest to the horizon appear farthest; the lowest objects in the field of vision seem closest. Linear perspective Parallel lines (e.g. edges of sidewalks) seem to converge in the distance. Relative brightness The closer of two identical objects reflects more light to your eyes. Binocular cues Binocular convergence — depth cue based on the inward movement of the eyes as they focus on nearby objects. Retinal disparity — the slight difference in the images seen by each eye, used by the brain to perceive depth. Vertical disparity — due to the image falling on a different place in the retina. Horizontal disparity — due to the difference in angles at which the eyes are placed. Horopter — the imaginary line at which an object placed there produces no disparity. Eleanor Gibson & Richard Walk — the Visual Cliff depth-perception experiment on 3–6 month-old babies; concluded that depth perception is innate . Perceptual Set Perceptual set. Bruner and Goodman (1947) coin study notes, with a coin and a same-size cardboard disc showing that the coin loomed larger. Psycho Didi notes · p. 88 Refers to the influence of values on perception. Jerome Bruner & Goodman (1947) — coins were perceived as larger than same-size cardboard discs, and more so by poor children than rich children. Because coin size correlates with value, valuable coins "loomed larger" in perception even when the cardboard was the same size. Top-Down Theories of Perception Top-down theories of perception. Three columns on Gregory's processing theory, template matching theory and prototype theory. Psycho Didi notes · p. 88 Constructivist theory (Processing theory) — proponent Richard Gregory (1970) . Perception is a hypothesis based on prior knowledge; we actively construct our perception of reality from the environment and stored information. Higher-order thinking is involved. Template Matching theory — a template is an internal construct that, when matched by sensory stimuli, leads to recognition of an object. "Lock and key" idea of pattern recognition; the object must match the template exactly . Prototype theory (Eleanor Rosch, 1975) — an alternative to template matching. A prototype for each object is stored in memory; a pattern is checked against the prototype and recognised if resemblance is found. Not as rigid as templates. Shortcoming: does not account for exceptions. Bottom-Up Theories of Perception Bottom-up theories of perception. Notes on Gibson's direct perception, feature detection theory, Biederman's geon theory and Selfridge's pandemonium model with its four demons. Psycho Didi notes · p. 88 J. J. Gibson — Direct (Ecological) Perception : the information in the stimulus itself is the important element; learning and cognition are unnecessary because there is enough information in the environment to make an interpretation. Constraints — a barrier in the environment that helps perception. Affordance — a mediator in the environment that helps perception. Light feedback — from the reflection of light we decide whether to move forward or backward. Feature Detection theory — object recognition is high-order processing preceded by a step in which complex incoming stimuli are identified according to simpler features. Irving Biederman (1987) — Geon theory (aka recognition by components ): the human information-processing system has a limited number of simple geometric shapes ( geons , "geometric ions") that combine to form meaningful objects. Identifying an object from its geons = the principle of componential recovery ; each geon's unique set of Non-Accidental Properties gives geons the property of discriminability . Oliver Selfridge — Pandemonium Model ("pandemonium" = a very noisy, chaotic place). Four kinds of demons: image demons (sensation) → feature demons (feature separation) → cognitive demons (compare with memory) → decision demons (perception). 2 · Theories of Colour & Sound Perception Vision — photoreceptor cells Vision. Labelled human eye anatomy diagram with notes on rods and cones, properties of colour, opponent process and trichromatic theories, dark vs light adaptation and the visual pathway. Psycho Didi notes · p. 89 Rods Cones Vision Achromatic, night vision (scotopic) Chromatic vision (photopic) Number ~120 million ~6–8 million Photopigment Rhodopsin (from vitamin A) Photopsin Activated Only in low-light / scotopic vision Bright light; types L, M, S cones Visual pathway: Photoreceptors → Horizontal cells → Bipolar cells → Amacrine cells → Ganglion cells → Optic nerve → Optic chiasm → Optic tract → Lateral geniculate nucleus → Primary visual cortex. Properties of colour Visible spectrum of light: 380 to 760 nm . Hue — the actual colour seen. Saturation — concentration of colour. Brightness — intensity of light. Young–Helmholtz — Trichromatic theory of colour : the retina has three types of colour receptor, each especially sensitive to red, green or blue ; stimulating combinations produces all other colours. Ewald Hering — Opponent-Process theory : three sets of opponent retinal processes enable colour vision — red–green, yellow–blue, white–black . If one colour of a pair is perceived, the other cannot be. Explains afterimages . Dark vs Light adaptation Light adaptation Dark adaptation Transition Rod → cone dominance Cone → rod dominance Mechanism Photopigment bleaching; pupil constriction Chemical changes in photoreceptors; pupil dilation Photosensitivity Low High Time Takes less time Takes more time (rods must be regenerated) Audition Audition. Labelled ear anatomy diagram with notes on properties of sound, the auditory pathway, place theory, frequency theory and the volley principle. Psycho Didi notes · p. 89 Properties of sound Audible frequency: 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz . Amplitude — height of the sound wave; determines loudness. Frequency — waves per second; determines pitch. Timbre — quality of sound. Hermann von Helmholtz — Place theory : we hear different pitches because different sound waves trigger activity at different places along the cochlea's basilar membrane. Best explains high pitches . Rinne & Rutherford (1880) — Frequency theory : the brain reads pitch by monitoring the frequency of neural impulses travelling up the auditory nerve. Does not explain sound sensing above 1000 Hz. Best explains low pitches . Key — Volley principle (Ernest Wever and Charles Bray, 1930). Supports frequency theory: neurons fire in alternating rapid succession so that, combined, they achieve a frequency above 1000 waves per second. Auditory pathway: Pinna → Auditory canal → Tympanic membrane → Hammer (Malleus) → Anvil (Incus) → Stirrup (Stapes) → Cochlea → Auditory nerve → Cochlear nerve → Superior olivary complex → Lateral lemniscus → Inferior colliculus → Medial geniculate body → Auditory cortex. Other senses Proprioception. Proprioception branching into kinesthetic and vestibular senses, each with a stick-figure illustration. Psycho Didi notes · p. 89 Kinesthetic / Proprioception — sense of body position and movements. Vestibular — sense of head positioning (parietal lobe); semi-circular canals and cerebellum involved. 3 · Theories of Attention Attention is the concentration of mental activity that lets you take in a limited portion of the vast stream of information available from both your sensory world and your memory. Sequence: sensation → attention → perception . Types of attention (source) Introduction to attention. Definition of attention, the sensation to attention to perception sequence, and exogenous (bottom-up) vs endogenous (top-down) attention. Psycho Didi notes · p. 90 Hierarchical model of attention. Sohlberg and Mateer pyramid of attention levels from focused at the base through sustained, selective and alternating to divided at the top, with definitions and the determinants of vigilance. Psycho Didi notes · p. 90 Exogenous — controlled by the stimulus; bottom-up. Endogenous — the brain internally decides what is important; top-down. Sohlberg & Mateer (1987, 1989) — Hierarchical model of attention : focused → sustained → selective → alternating → divided. Focused attention — ability to focus attention on a stimulus. Sustained attention (vigilance) — ability to attend to a stimulus/activity over a long period. Determinants: sensory factor, temporal certainty, spatial certainty, clarity of stimuli. Selective attention — ability to attend to a specific stimulus in the presence of distracting stimuli. Alternating attention — ability to shift focus between two or more stimuli. Divided attention (multitasking) — ability to attend to different stimuli at the same time. Signal Detection Theory (SDT) Signal detection theory. SDT notes with a two by two table of hit, correct rejection, false alarm and miss for liberal and conservative responders. Psycho Didi notes · p. 90 Wesley W. Peterson & Theodore G. Birdsall — Signal Detection Theory : detection of a signal depends on sensitivity and response bias . Sensitivity (d′) = number of hits − number of false alarms. Signal present Signal absent Responds "yes" Hit (correct) False alarm (incorrect) Responds "no" Miss (incorrect) Correct rejection (correct) For a liberal participant the receiver-operating (ROC) curve peaks towards the right; for a conservative participant it peaks towards the left. Theories of Selective Attention Theories of selective attention. Notes on Cherry, Broadbent's filter model and Treisman's attenuation model, with flow diagrams of the selection filter and the attenuator. Psycho Didi notes · p. 90 Late selection model. Deutsch and Deutsch notes with a flow diagram where messages pass physical analysis and semantic analysis before the attended message reaches awareness and response. Psycho Didi notes · p. 91 Multimode attention theory and perceptual load. Notes on Johnston and Heinz's three-stage multimode theory and Lavie and Tsal's perceptual load theory. Psycho Didi notes · p. 91 Feature integration theory. Treisman and Gelade notes with a diagram of colour and orientation feature maps feeding a map of locations, plus example displays of a colour singleton search and a conjunction search. Psycho Didi notes · p. 91 Spotlight theory of attention. Spotlight theory notes with a circular blurred-text illustration marking the focus, fringe and margin. Psycho Didi notes · p. 91 Shortcomings of selective attention. Definitions of inattentional blindness and change blindness. Psycho Didi notes · p. 91 Selective attention is tested with a shadowing / dichotic listening task. Colin Cherry (1953) — early selection model : no overlap in dichotic listening; we do not understand a stimulus before we perceive it. Donald Broadbent (1958) — Filter model (a bottleneck model): we filter information right after we notice it, at the sensory level. Anne Treisman (1980) — Attenuation model : explains the cocktail-party phenomenon . Instead of blocking stimuli out, the filter merely weakens the strength of stimuli other than the target. Deutsch & Deutsch (1963) — Late Selection model : stimuli are filtered out only after being analysed for both their physical properties and their meaning. Johnston & Heinz (1978) — Multimode attention theory : attention is a flexible system that selects a stimulus at three stages — (1) sensory representations created, (2) semantic representations created, (3) both sensory and semantic representations enter consciousness. More processing requires more mental effort. Lavie & Tsal (1994) — Perceptual Load theory : perception is a limited-capacity process that proceeds automatically until that capacity is filled. Anne Treisman & Garry Gelade (1980) — Feature Integration Theory (FIT) : explains how an individual combines pieces of observable information about an object to form a complete perception. Two kinds of visual search: feature search (fast, pre-attentive, primitive features) and conjunction search (slower, effortful; targets defined by a conjunction of features). Eriksen & St James (1986); Michael Posner et al. — Spotlight theory of attention : people can attend to only one region of space at a time. Inspired by William James , attention has a focus (central area extracting high-resolution information where attention is directed), a fringe (extracts information more crudely, extending over a specified area), and a margin (the cut-off between them). Shortcomings of selective attention Inattentional blindness (Arien Mack and Irvin Rock, 1998) — people fail to see things that are actually there. Change blindness — inability to detect changes in objects or scenes being viewed. 4 · Classical & Operant Conditioning Key — definition. Learning is a relatively permanent change in behaviour as a result of experience. Two basic kinds of learning Introduction to learning. Definition of learning and the split into non-associative learning (habituation, sensitization) and associative learning (classical and instrumental conditioning). Psycho Didi notes · p. 92 Non-associative learning (short term) — learning about a single stimulus: Habituation — a decreased behavioural response to an innocuous stimulus. Sensitization — an increase in a behavioural response to an intense stimulus. Associative learning (long term) — learning relationships among events: classical conditioning and instrumental (operant) conditioning . Classical Conditioning Strength of conditioning. Delayed, trace, simultaneous and backward conditioning, each drawn as CS and UCS arrows showing their timing. Psycho Didi notes · p. 92 Classical conditioning and principles of conditioning. Pavlov notes with a before, during and after conditioning dog illustration, the five principles with dog examples, and a first-order vs second-order conditioning table. Psycho Didi notes · p. 92 Contiguity and contingency. Rescorla's view that the CS must predict the US, with positive, negative and zero contingency. Psycho Didi notes · p. 92 Major points to be remembered. Summary list of classical conditioning features: reflex based, respondent, passive, S-S type, and the amygdala's role. Psycho Didi notes · p. 93 Classical conditioning and biological preparedness. Notes on biological preparedness with the Garcia and Koelling rat diagram and a cues by consequences table for sweet and click cues. Psycho Didi notes · p. 93 Ivan Pavlov (1897) — first researched classical conditioning: a previously neutral stimulus becomes associated with another stimulus through repeated pairing. Based on three broad principles: Contiguity — nearness in space and time. Contingency — prediction power. Blocking — a CS blocks conditioning with another neutral stimulus. Principles of conditioning Principle Meaning Example (Pavlov's dog) Acquisition CS & US repeatedly paired so CS acquires US properties. Dog learns to salivate to the bell. Extinction CS presented without US; CR fades and disappears. Dog stops salivating to the bell. Spontaneous recovery After extinction & rest, CS again produces a faint CR. Dog salivates again on hearing the bell. Generalization CR shown to stimuli similar to the CS. Dog salivates to other bell-like noises. Discrimination CR shown only to the CS, not to similar stimuli. Dog salivates only to the specific bell. Second-order (higher-order) conditioning — once a CS elicits a CR, that CS can briefly be used as a US to condition a response to a new stimulus. Strength / timing of conditioning Type Timing (CS vs US) Note Delayed Bell rings and, while still ringing, food is presented. Conditioning occurs the fastest . Trace CS, then a short break, then the US. — Simultaneous CS and US presented at the same time. — Backward US presented first, followed by the CS. E.g. taste aversions in pregnancy / chemotherapy. Contiguity and Contingency Robert Rescorla — conditioning involves cognitive components. The CS must be a reliable predictor of the US (contingency); mere temporal contiguity is not enough. Positive contingency — CS predicts the presence of the UCS → excitatory conditioning . Zero contingency — no pattern, so no learning takes place. Negative contingency — CS predicts the absence of the UCS → inhibitory conditioning . Classical conditioning & biological preparedness Animals and humans are biologically prepared to make certain connections more easily (e.g. learned taste aversions can be learnt in a single trial). John Garcia & Robert Koelling (1966) — rats more readily learned certain associations: food more likely to become CS for nausea ; noise more likely to become CS for shock . Key — classical conditioning at a glance. Totally based on reflexes ; response is elicited by the stimulus (also called respondent conditioning ); passive learning; reflexes can be conditioned or unconditioned; magnitude of response matters; it is an S–S type of conditioning. The amygdala (lateral nucleus) organizes emotional responses provoked by aversive stimuli. Operant Conditioning Operant conditioning introduction. Thorndike and Skinner notes with a drawing of Thorndike's cat puzzle box and a labelled Skinner box. Psycho Didi notes · p. 93 Reinforcement and punishment. Two by two table of positive and negative reinforcement and punishment, defined as adding or removing pleasant or unpleasant stimuli. Psycho Didi notes · p. 93 Principles of operant conditioning. Acquisition, extinction, spontaneous recovery, generalization and discrimination, each with a rat and bar example. Psycho Didi notes · p. 93 Shaping and chaining. Definitions of shaping and chaining with a chain-link icon. Psycho Didi notes · p. 93 Reinforcement schedules. The two basic schedule types, continuous and partial, and when each works better. Psycho Didi notes · p. 93 Schedules of reinforcement. Tree of the four partial schedules (fixed ratio, variable ratio, fixed interval, variable interval) with a learning over time graph showing a separate line for each schedule. Psycho Didi notes · p. 94 Learning and maintaining fear. Two-stage account of fear: classical conditioning or escape learning first, then instrumental avoidance learning. Psycho Didi notes · p. 94 Edward Thorndike — learning theory leading to operant conditioning (B. F. Skinner); used a cat in a puzzle box ( trial-and-error learning ). His theory is called associationism / connectionism . Three laws: law of readiness , law of practice/exercise , and the law of effect (behaviour followed by pleasant consequences is repeated; behaviour followed by unpleasant consequences is stopped). B. F. Skinner (1937) — coined the term operant conditioning . The Skinner box delivers food via a lever/disk; the food is a reinforcer and giving it is reinforcement . Operant/instrumental conditioning = learning the relationship between responses and outcomes (an S–R association). Principles of operant conditioning Acquisition — the rat learns to press the bar for food. Extinction — the rat unlearns the bar–food connection and stops pressing. Spontaneous recovery — after extinction and rest, the rat presses the bar again. Generalization — the rat presses other objects that look like the bar. Discrimination — the rat learns to press only a particular bar. Reinforcement & Punishment Positive (add) Negative (remove) Reinforcement (increases behaviour) Deliver a pleasant stimulus after the response (add pleasant). Remove an unpleasant/aversive stimulus after the response (remove unpleasant). Punishment (reduces behaviour) Deliver an unpleasant/aversive stimulus after the response (add unpleasant). Remove a pleasant stimulus after the response (remove pleasant). Negative reinforcement ≠ punishment. Negative reinforcement removes something unpleasant to increase a behaviour; punishment reduces a behaviour. Don't confuse "negative" (remove) with "punishment" (weaken). Shaping and Chaining Shaping — reinforces the steps used to reach the desired behaviour. Chaining — animals are taught to perform a number of responses successively to get a reward. Reinforcement schedules Two basic types: Continuous (rewarded every time; better for learning new behaviour) and Partial (better once behaviour is learnt; more resistant to extinction ). Schedule Reinforcement provided... Fixed ratio After a fixed number of responses. Variable ratio After a number of responses that varies unpredictably. Fixed interval After a fixed amount of time since the last reinforcement. Variable interval After an amount of time that varies unpredictably since the last reinforcement. Learning and maintaining fear (two-factor) Stage 1 — classical conditioning / escape learning: through repeated pairing of the warning light (CS) and shock (UCS), the animal learns the light predicts the shock and shows a conditioned fear response (CR) to the light alone. Stage 2 — instrumental conditioning / avoidance learning: successful reduction of the aversive stimulus reinforces and strengthens the avoidance behaviour. It gives temporary relief, but the long-run consequences of avoidance are detrimental. 5 · Cognitive & Social Learning Learned Helplessness Learned helplessness. Maier and Seligman two-stage experiment notes with a drawing of the shuttle box, its warning light, electrified grid floor and barrier. Psycho Didi notes · p. 94 Cognitive approach to learning. Notes on Woodworth's S-O-R approach and Kohler's insight learning with chimpanzees. Psycho Didi notes · p. 94 Martin Seligman — cognitive approach to learning: control over the outcome of behaviour is as important for learning as contiguity and contingency. Experiment — Maier & Seligman (1976): Stage 1: some dogs learn that whether they receive a shock depends on their own behaviour; other dogs learn they have no control over the shock. Stage 2: both groups placed in a shuttle box; a tone signals an imminent shock, and the dog must jump the barrier to avoid it. Found: control dogs learn the response rapidly; yoked dogs do not. They had learned that shocks were uncontrollable, and this non-control made avoidance learning impossible → learned helplessness . Robert Woodworth — S–O–R approach : to predict the response we must know not only the stimulus but also the organism stimulated; human motivations and conscious decisions play an important part in behaviour. Wolfgang Köhler (1925) — Insight learning , studied on chimpanzees: insight occurs when one suddenly realises how to solve a problem. Learning happens in a sudden way due to insight, not gradual strengthening of the S–R connection. Social Learning Theory Social learning theory. Bandura notes with the attention, retention, motor reproduction and motivation sequence and three Bobo doll conditions: reinforced, not reinforced and punished model. Psycho Didi notes · p. 94 Albert Bandura — Social Learning Theory (aka observational learning ): learning is achieved by mentally rehearsing and then imitating the observed actions of models. An S–O–R theory. Process of learning (sequence): attention → retention → motor reproduction → motivation. Bobo doll experiment — conditions: model hits doll and is reinforced (vicarious reinforcement), model hits doll and is not reinforced , model hits doll and is punished (vicarious punishment). Key. Learning occurs in all three conditions irrespective of reinforcement; however, reproduction of behaviour was dependent on reinforcement. Tolman's Purposive Behaviourism Tolman's purposive behaviourism. Tolman and Honzik latent learning notes with a graph of maze errors over 17 daily trials for rewarded, never-rewarded and delayed-reward rat groups. Psycho Didi notes · p. 95 Edward Tolman — Purposive behaviourism (aka latent learning, expectancy, place learning, sign-stimulus theory). Experiment: Tolman & Honzik (1930) . Group A — reinforced on each trial; Group B — never reinforced; Group C — reinforced only on day 11. Found: Group C had actually learnt the maze without reinforcement ( latent learning ) but showed it once reinforcement appeared. The rats developed a cognitive map — a mental representation of the maze. Components of learning: the significate (desired outcome/goal), the sign (stimulus prompting action), and means–end relations (the learner's internal thought process). Field Theory Field theory. Lewin's field theory notes with a life space diagram (person, driving and restraining vectors, barrier, goal) and the four types of conflict. Psycho Didi notes · p. 95 Kurt Lewin (1930) — Field Theory , based on Gestalt psychology, an S–O–R approach: a person's psychological state affects their social field and vice versa. "Field" = the totality of a person's experiences, needs and topography; field forces (intrinsic or extrinsic) drive behaviour. Types of conflict Conflict Description Vacillation / equilibrium Approach–approach Two goals, both valued. Low vacillation, low equilibrium. Avoidance–avoidance Two goals, both undesirable; running away is more likely. More vacillation and equilibrium. Approach–avoidance One goal has both positive and negative vectors. Highest vacillation; equilibrium stage very long. Double approach–avoidance Multiple goals each with positive and negative vectors. Conflict resolved more easily when equilibrium is less. 6 · Theories of Memory Introduction to memory. Definition of memory as the capacity to register, store and recover information, with a brain and clock icon. Psycho Didi notes · p. 96 Key — definition. Memory is our capacity to register, store and recover information over time — the persistence of learning over time. It is a complex mental system involving multiple stages of information processing. Early models Models of memory: early models. Primary memory (William James) and secondary memory (Waugh and Norman, 1965) with what each holds. Psycho Didi notes · p. 96 In the mid-1960s researchers proposed two structures of memory: Primary memory — proposed by William James ; holds temporary information currently in use. Secondary memory — proposed by Waugh & Norman (1965) ; holds information permanently or for a very long time. Sperling & iconic memory George Sperling and iconic memory. Iconic memory notes with the Sperling (1960) letter grid figure comparing whole report and partial report. Psycho Didi notes · p. 96 George Sperling — iconic memory : a type of visual memory lasting only a fraction of a second. Sensory memory capacity is much larger than believed.
