Trial and error, heuristics and algorithms defined, with heuristics branching into formal and informal, the informal ones marked as obstacles to problem solving. Psycho Didi notes · p. 105 Heuristics listed under formal. The left-hand heuristic list from satisficing to hill climbing, each with a one-line definition. Psycho Didi notes · p. 105 Formal methods: Trial and error — try a number of different solutions until the correct one is reached. Algorithm — sequences of operations that, in theory, guarantee a solution. Heuristics — general rules of thumb that help achieve a solution while decreasing effort by letting us examine fewer cues. Informal heuristics: Heuristic Description Satisficing (Herbert Simon, 1956) Consider options one by one and select the first that is satisfactory / good enough to meet a minimum level of acceptability. Elimination by aspects Eliminate alternatives by focusing on aspects of each, one at a time. Selection by aspects Select from alternatives by focusing on aspects of each, one at a time. Lexicographic heuristic Choose the option best on a single criterion, ignoring other factors. Analogy Use an old solution to solve a new problem. Means–end analysis Compare current position with the goal and take steps to reduce the difference. Example: Tower of Hanoi . Repeated state avoidance A formal heuristic: avoiding repetition leads to solution in the minimum number of steps. Hill climbing A formal heuristic: combine two or more steps into a single step to reach the goal. Judgment & decision-making heuristics Heuristics listed under informal. The right-hand heuristic list from availability to framing, including the halo and horn effects under anchoring. Psycho Didi notes · p. 105 Heuristic Description Availability Judge frequency/likelihood by the ease with which relevant instances come to mind. Representativeness Judge frequency/likelihood by how much the event resembles the typical case. Anchoring & adjustment Judge by starting from an anchor and adjusting up or down. Simulation Judge by the ease with which you can imagine or mentally simulate an event. Peak–end Judge past experiences almost entirely on their peak and their end. Base rate Decide based on probability (base rates). Contagion Decide based on the idea that things once in contact continue to influence each other. Scarcity Place more value on objects that are scarce. Framing Decide based on how information is presented rather than the information itself. Halo effect (Edward Thorndike, 1920) — being influenced by a person's initial impression or external features (favourable). Horn effect — allowing an unfavourable first impression to influence overall judgment. Obstacles to problem solving Obstacles to problem solving. Mind map of five obstacles: fixed mindset, mental set, functional fixedness, fallacies (gambler's, hot hand, sunk cost, conjunction) and cognitive biases. Psycho Didi notes · p. 106 Fallacies — a failure in reasoning that renders an argument invalid. Fixed mindset — belief that you have a fixed amount of intelligence/skill and no effort can improve performance. Mental set — tendency to keep trying a previously used solution even when an easier method exists; represents overactive top-down processing. Functional fixedness (Karl Duncker, 1945) — the uses we assign to an object tend to remain fixed/stable. Metacognition in problem solving Metacognition in problem solving. Tree splitting metacognition into knowledge (declarative, conditional, procedural) and regulation (planning, checking outcomes, monitoring). Psycho Didi notes · p. 106 Metacognition (John Flavell, 1976) — cognition about cognitive phenomena; thinking about thinking. Components: Metacognitive knowledge — declarative knowledge, procedural knowledge, conditional knowledge. Metacognitive regulation — planning (prior to a problem), monitoring (during learning), and checking outcomes. Cognitive biases Cognitive biases. Definitions of confirmation bias with the Barnum effect, hindsight bias, overconfidence and illusory correlation. Psycho Didi notes · p. 106 All cognitive biases can lead to cognitive distortions. Bias / fallacy Description Confirmation bias (Peter Wason, 1960) Attending to information that confirms one's beliefs while ignoring the rest. (Related: Barnum effect — accepting vague, general personality descriptions as uniquely applicable to oneself, e.g. astrology.) Hindsight bias (Baruch Fischhoff, 1975) Believing, in retrospect, that we easily saw all the signs leading to an outcome. Illusory correlation (Loren Chapman, 1967) Seeing events/attributes as going together even when they do not. Overconfidence Over-evaluating one's skills, knowledge or judgement. Gambler's fallacy Belief that if an event occurred more than normal in the past, it is less likely in the future. Hot-hand fallacy Belief that a person with past successes has a greater chance of success in future attempts. Sunk-cost fallacy (Hal Arkes and Catherine Blumer, 1985) Continuing to invest in something simply because one already has, hoping to recover the investment. Conjunction fallacy (Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman, 1983) Giving a higher estimate for a subset of events than for the larger set containing it. 12 · Theories of Language Development Key. Psycho Didi notes · p. 107 Age Milestone 2–4 months Pre-vocal learning; cooing . 6 months Babbling ; phonemes — meaningless units of speech. 1 year Learns morphemes — the smallest unit of speech that carries meaning (content morphemes; function morphemes = tense / singular–plural). Uses a holophrase — one word conveying a full sentence. 2 years Learns syntax — the rules of grammar. 3 years Telegraphic speech (Roger Brown and Colin Fraser, 1963) — 2–3 word phrases; makes errors of growth from overuse of syntax. 4–5 years Learns pragmatics (not necessary for language development). Holophrase errors: over-extension (child calls every dog "Timmy") and under-extension (mummy is only my mummy). Errors of growth: overregularization and over-generalisation . Semantics — meaning of words and sentences. Pragmatics — appropriate use of language in different contexts. Serial order of learning: Phonemes → Morphemes → Semantics (Holophrase) → Syntax → Pragmatics. Sapir–Whorf Hypothesis The Sapir Whorf hypothesis. The linguistic relativity hypothesis (1956) that the language people speak shapes how they think. Psycho Didi notes · p. 107 Sapir–Whorf Hypothesis (1956) — linguistic relativity : speakers of different languages have differing cognitive systems that influence how they think about the world; we cannot think about things not experienced in our culture. Behaviorist approach Behaviorist approach. Skinner's six elementary verbal operants laid out as a grid of definitions, plus the secondary autoclitic operant. Psycho Didi notes · p. 107 B. F. Skinner — identified six elementary verbal operants plus one secondary operant. Verbal operant Description Mand A demand. Tact Speaker names things/actions in the environment; the "naming explosion". Echoic Repeating what has been heard. Intraverbal Speaker responds to another speaker's verbal behaviour. Textual Reading without any implication that the reader understands what is read. Transcription Writing/spelling words that are spoken to the individual (Skinner also called this "taking dictation"). Autoclitic (secondary) Softens or modifies the effect of subsequent statements (e.g. "I don't mean to criticize, but..."). Vygotsky's theory of language Vygotsky's theory of language. Vygotsky's primitive, naive, external (egocentric) and ingrowth stages of language with short descriptions. Psycho Didi notes · p. 107 Lev Vygotsky — stages of language development. Primitive stage — infant experimenting with sound production; cooing / "ga-ga". Naive stage — baby speaks words without grasping their purpose and meaning. External (egocentric) stage — child uses objects to signify meaning and words; rhyming is used in this phase. Ingrowth stage — inner speech shortens (called predication ). Nativist theory — Chomsky Nativist theories: Noam Chomsky. Chomsky's language acquisition device, modularity, deep vs surface structure, transformational grammar and ambiguous sentences. Psycho Didi notes · p. 107 Noam Chomsky — nativist theory: children have an innate Language Acquisition Device (LAD) . Language is modular — a set of specific linguistic abilities that do not follow the principles of other cognitive processes. Deep structure — the underlying syntactic structure linking phrase structures through transformation rules. Surface structure — the phrase structures resulting from applying transformational rules. Transformational grammar — two sentences may have very different surface structures but similar deep structures. Ambiguous sentences — two sentences may have identical surface structures but very different deep structures. Bruner — LASS Jerome Bruner. Bruner's language acquisition support system of parents, teachers and elders. Psycho Didi notes · p. 107 Jerome Bruner — Language Acquisition Support System (LASS) : parents, teachers and elders act as a support system that helps in the acquisition of language.

title: Personality & Motivation
text: Personality & Motivation — Study with Psycho Didi (MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF) Personality & Motivation Study with Psycho Didi · MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF notes Sigmund Freud · Carl Jung · Karen Horney · Alfred Adler · Erich Fromm Humanistic & Existential Murray's Personology Motivation: drive, arousal, need theories nAch · ERG · Self-Determination What this covers. The major approaches to personality — psychoanalytic/psychodynamic (Freud), the neo-Freudians and analytical psychology (Jung, Horney, Adler, Fromm), humanistic (Carl Rogers), existential and transpersonal approaches (Heidegger, Rollo May, Wilber), and Murray & Morgan's personology — followed by the theories of motivation (instinct, arousal, drive-reduction, and the need theories of Abraham Maslow, Alderfer, David McClelland, Edward Deci & Richard Ryan, and Zuckerman). Original diagrams. 18 diagrams from the Psycho Didi PDF (pages 109 to 115) sit under the section they belong to, exactly as drawn. Tap one to open it full size and zoom in. Contents: 1 · Psychoanalytic & Psychodynamic (Freud) · 2 · Neo-Freudian & Analytical Psychology · 3 · Humanistic Approach (Rogers) · 4 · Existential & Transpersonal Approaches · 5 · Personology (Murray & Morgan) · 6 · Theories of Motivation & Emotion 1 · Psychoanalytic & Psychodynamic (Freud) Approaches to personality: psychodynamic (Freud). Freud's topographical model drawn as an iceberg, beside notes on life and death instincts, the id, ego and superego, three types of anxiety and the defence mechanisms. Psycho Didi notes · p. 109 Theory → Theorist. Psychosexual / psychodynamic personality theory → Sigmund Freud . Freud — the psychodynamic model Sigmund Freud used a topographical model of the mind and held that behaviour springs from innate instincts and unconscious conflict. Life and death instincts — both are innate: Life instinct (eros) — libidinal energy that pushes us to function; survival-related instincts. Death instinct (thanatos) — instincts to hurt; destructive energy. The Id, Ego and Superego Structure Principle Develops in Id Pleasure principle — seeks immediate gratification Oral phase Ego Reality principle Anal phase Superego Morality principle Phallic stage The superego consists of two parts: Ego ideal — rewards ideal behaviour. Conscience — punishes with guilt. Three types of anxiety (Freud) Anxiety Nature Description Realistic anxiety Realistic fear The fear of an actual item. Moral anxiety Social fear Fear of punishment; represented by shame and guilt. Neurotic anxiety Nervous fear The fear of being overwhelmed; feeling that you are about to lose it; fear of the id taking over. Defence mechanisms Repression — keeping unpleasant memories or thoughts buried in the unconscious. Primal: innately part of the id. Proper: unacceptable derivatives of original id impulses. Denial — refusing to recognize an unpleasant reality. Rationalization — creating a socially acceptable excuse to justify unacceptable behaviour. Reaction formation — not acknowledging unacceptable impulses and over-emphasizing their opposite. Projection — transferring one's unacceptable qualities or impulses to others. Displacement — diverting one's impulses to a more acceptable target. Sublimation — channelling socially unacceptable impulses into acceptable activities. Regression — reverting to immature ways of responding. Identification — enhancing self-esteem by imagining or forming alliances with others. Intellectualization — ignoring troubling emotional aspects by focusing on abstract ideas or thoughts. Suppression — actively choosing to ignore something to do what is better and more important at the moment. Key. Id = pleasure principle (oral); Ego = reality principle (anal); Superego = morality principle (phallic), made of the ego ideal (rewards) and conscience (guilt). Repression is the "primal" defence; suppression is conscious, repression is unconscious. 2 · Neo-Freudian & Analytical Psychology Jung — Analytical Psychology Jung: analytical psychology. A comparison of Freud and Jung on the role of libido, the forces that influence personality and the unconscious. Psycho Didi notes · p. 109 Jung's structure of the psyche, energy principles and archetypes. A circle split into ego, personal unconscious and collective unconscious with arrows to their features, plus Jung's energy principles, psychological types and major archetypes. Psycho Didi notes · p. 110 Theory → Theorist. Analytical psychology → Carl Jung . Point of difference Sigmund Freud Jung Role of libido Sexual energy Broad psychic energy Forces that influence personality Present in the past only Present in the past as well as the future The unconscious Personal unconscious Personal and collective unconscious Structures of the psyche: Ego — is in control of itself; the conscious mind. Personal unconscious — accessible once in a while; personal memories that have lost their intensity. Collective unconscious — shared memories (patterns of behaviour), motifs, primordial patterns. Contains complexes , formed if a collective unconscious element completely takes over our personality. Energy principles: The principle of opposites — every wish or feeling has its opposite. The principle of equivalence — there is a constant amount of energy in our psyche. The principle of entropy — redistribution of energy within our psyche. Four functions: thinking, feeling, sensing, intuiting. Psychological types — attitudes: introversion / extraversion; rational / irrational. Archetypes and the anima/animus: Anima — the female archetype in the male psyche. Animus — the male archetype in the female psyche. Syzygy — anima and animus (Carl Jung) together. Self — finding a balance between the different aspects of ourselves. Persona — a mask, a facade to meet society's demands; a compromise between your needs and society's demands. Shadow — deepest, darkest instincts; comparable to the id. Other major archetypes: Joker , Wise Old Man , Hero , Witch , Villain . Horney Horney: neurotic needs. Notes on Karen Horney with a diagram of the three neurotic orientations, towards, against and away from people, and the needs under each. Psycho Didi notes · p. 110 Karen Horney gave the concept of womb envy . When children are born they have basic anxiety ; if they are met with love and care this anxiety subsides and a healthy personality develops. In the neurotic personality there is a huge difference between the ideal and the real self, because of a rigid ideal self. Neurotic needs — three orientations: Orientation Normal Neurotic Needs Towards people Friendly Compliant Seeks acceptance and help all the time; need for affection and approval; need for a partner who will control their life. Against people Competitive Aggressive Need for power, prestige, personal achievement; need to exploit other people; need to compete all the time. Away from people Autonomous Detached Need to move away from people; independence; self-reliance; perfection; narrow limits. Adler — Individual Psychology Adler: individual psychology. Key ideas of Adler with the types of inferiority, his birth order traits, three types of problems and four styles of life. Psycho Didi notes · p. 111 Theory → Theorist. Individual psychology → Alfred Adler . Adler's approach is future-oriented , non-deterministic and idiographic . Fictional finalism — dreams that may not come true and are fictional, but motivate the child to do well in life. Masculine protest — when female children feel male children within the family are being treated better, they behave more like boys as a protest. Organ inferiority — experienced by each child when they are young. Types of inferiority: Type Description Primary inferiority The "original and normal feeling" of inferiority maintained by an infant. This feeling is productive, as it provides motivation for the child to develop. Secondary inferiority The inferiority feeling in the adult that results when the child develops an exaggerated feeling of inferiority. These feelings in the adult are what are harmful, and they comprise the inferiority complex . Adler's interpretation of birth order: Position Typical characteristics First born Perfectionist, achiever, leader, bossy, responsible, motivated, conscientious, controlling, cautious, reliable. Middle born Adaptable, independent, go-between, people pleaser, can be rebellious, feels left out, peacemaker, social. Last born Social, charming, outgoing, uncomplicated, manipulative, seeks attention, self-centred, fun, confident. The only child Conscientious, responsible, perfectionist, centre of attention, mature for their age, seek approval, sensitive, leader. Three types of problems: problems of occupation; problems of love; problems involving our behaviour towards others. Four styles of life: the dominant type; the getting type; the avoiding type; the socially useful type. Erich Fromm Erich Fromm: needs and character types. Fromm's needs listed beside a branching diagram of five character types with a short description of each. Psycho Didi notes · p. 111 Erich Fromm was a Neo-Freudian . He identified two fundamental needs: freedom and belonging . Character orientations: Type Description Productive Nurturing, loving, meaningful; a good spouse and friend; the only healthy approach. Exploitative Deceives; manipulative; disregard for others' well-being. Marketing Relationship is considered a transactional exchange; shallow; opportunistic. Receptive Compliant; dependent. Hoarding Possession. Needs: Relatedness — connection. Transcendence — meaning. Rootedness — belonging to a safe space; if too much, causes inflexibility. Don't confuse — Freud vs Carl Jung vs Alfred Adler. Freud: libido = sexual energy, personality shaped by the past , only a personal unconscious. Jung: libido = broad psychic energy, past and future , personal and collective unconscious (archetypes). Adler: future-oriented, striving from inferiority, birth order and social interest, non-deterministic and idiographic. Karen Horney = womb envy + three interpersonal orientations; Erich Fromm = freedom vs belonging + five character types. 3 · Humanistic Approach (Rogers) Theory → Theorist. Person-centred / self theory → Carl Rogers . Humanists hold that humans want to reach their highest potential. Actualization is the process of becoming a fully functioning individual. Rogers Humanistic: Rogers. Notes on Rogers with a table of conditional versus unconditional positive regard, circles showing congruence and incongruence of self concept and experience, and a star of the fully functioning person's traits. Psycho Didi notes · p. 112 Phenomenology argues that the only reality of which we can be sure is our own subjective world of experience — our inner perception of reality. The phenomenal field is the accumulation of a person's experiences. Research technique — Q-sort (mixed method): Qualitative: ideal self, through preference arrangement. Quantitative: factor analysis. The Fully Functioning Person: open to experience; existential living; trusts feelings; creativity and spontaneity; a fulfilled life; freedom of choice; a continual need to grow. Congruence vs incongruence — the degree of overlap between the self-concept and experience : congruence = they match; incongruence = a gap between them. Conditional vs unconditional positive regard: Conditional Unconditional Having conditions that need to be met in order to receive love. Love without any condition. An effort to manipulate the actions of individuals. No effort to manipulate or control an individual. Child develops conditions of worth . Congruent personality; child develops the organismic valuing process ; does not need therapy. Key. Unconditional positive regard → organismic valuing process → congruent, healthy personality. Conditional regard → conditions of worth → incongruence. 4 · Existential & Transpersonal Approaches Existential approach Existential: Heidegger and Rollo May. Heidegger's existential anxiety and four modes of Dasein, and Rollo May's types of anxiety and four stages of development shown as a cycle of arrows. Psycho Didi notes · p. 112 Proponents: Rollo May , Viktor Frankl , Martin Heidegger . Meaning in life is what keeps you grounded. Dasein = "to be in the world". Heidegger Martin Heidegger's modes of being-in-the-world: Mode Meaning Umwelt One's relationship with the natural world or environment. Mitwelt Our relationship with other people and the meanings given to those relationships. Eigenwelt One's relationship with oneself and how we interpret things based on self. Uberwelt Spirituality. Existential anxiety — the fear that we won't be alive. It can motivate us to achieve our best potential (proportionate), or demotivate us so that we wish to give up, thinking nothing really matters (neurotic). Rollo May Types of anxiety: Normal ; Neurotic (disproportionate to the situation). Four stages of development: Innocence — physical and psychological dependence. Rebellion — people define themselves in opposition to or defiance of another. Ordinary — the normal adult ego; a healthy, mature personality. Creative — transcending our usual limited viewpoint and catching a glimpse of ultimate reality. Transpersonal psychology Transpersonal psychology. Notes on the origins, methods and altered states of transpersonal psychology, Ken Wilber's stages, and a diagram of the pre-personal, personal and transpersonal groups. Psycho Didi notes · p. 113 Founded by Abraham Maslow and Stanislav Grof ; it also has roots in earlier work by psychologists such as William James and Carl Jung . Methods: psychedelic; transpersonal therapy; dreamwork; mindfulness. Altered state of consciousness: connectedness beyond ego boundaries; altruism, creativity, intuitive wisdom; a journey into self-exploration. Groups: Personal (concerns of the ego); Transpersonal (concerns beyond the ego). Division — Ego: the central organizer of behaviour. Ken Wilber's transpersonal stages of development: Pre-personal — when you don't understand self fully. Vision logic — integration of mind and body. Psychic — empathetic understanding. Subtle — across archetypal forms. Causal — non-dual awareness. Final — freely transverse between all stages. 5 · Personology (Murray & Morgan) Personology: Henry Murray and Christina Morgan. Murray and Morgan's principles, needs, divisions of id, ego and superego, press, thema and complexes. Psycho Didi notes · p. 113 Theory → Theorist. Personology → Henry Murray & Christina Morgan . Principles Personality is rooted in the brain. The process of tension reduction is satisfying, but a tension-free state is a source of distress. An individual's personality develops over time. Personality is not fixed or static. Each person is unique. Structures: Id — innate impulses that society considers unacceptable; Superego — internalization of cultural values. Needs Category Description Primary Survival-related. Secondary Emotional or psychological. Proactive Spontaneous; achievement-related. Reactive Response to object; harm-avoidance. Types of needs: materialistic, affiliation, information, power, achievement, sensual. Press, thema and complexes Press — the influence of environment and past events on the current activation of a need. Thema — need × press + how they affect personality = unity thema. Subsidation: one need will activate another, and the second need will fulfil the first need. Complexes: Complex Description Claustral (womb) The desire to reinstate the conditions experienced in the mother's womb. Oral Same as Freud's. Anal Same as Freud's. Urethral Characterized by excessive ambition and a distorted, enlarged sense of self-esteem. Genital Castration complex. 6 · Theories of Motivation & Emotion Instinct theory Instinct theory. Notes on instinct theory and Freud's object relations theory, including the four characteristics of an instinct. Psycho Didi notes · p. 114 Behaviour is motivated by instincts that are inborn and that are activated by environmental stimuli. Sigmund Freud's object relations theory — basic instincts from eros motivate us; explains motivation in terms of primary needs. Homeostatic approach — disturbance of homeostasis creates drive. Instincts have four basic characteristics (S-A-I-O): Source — source of deficit (internal). Aim — what we want to do. Impetus — the drive that propels us to act. Object — that through which the instinct achieves its aim. Arousal theory Theories of motivation: arousal theory. Notes on arousal theory and the Yerkes-Dodson law beside an inverted U graph of performance quality against arousal level for difficult and easy tasks. Psycho Didi notes · p. 114 Behaviour is motivated by the need to achieve optimum levels of arousal. Yerkes-Dodson law — arousal increases performance up to a point, after which additional arousal impedes performance. Alderfer's ERG theory Alderfer's ERG theory. Notes on ERG theory above a pyramid that lines up Maslow's five levels with Alderfer's growth, relatedness and existence needs. Psycho Didi notes · p. 114 One does not necessarily start from the lowest level. Moving from a lower level to an upper level of the hierarchy is called succession progression . Moving from a higher level to a lower level is called frustration regression . Maslow's need hierarchy Maslow's need hierarchy. Notes on Maslow's theory above an eight level pyramid with deficiency needs at the base and growth needs at the top. Psycho Didi notes · p. 114 Theory → Theorist. Hierarchy of needs → Abraham Maslow . Lower needs come from deficiencies; higher needs come from satisfaction. Measured with the Personal Orientation Inventory . Progression is only upward, but not automatic. Jonah complex — fear of your own best potential. Self-determination theory Self determination theory. The three basic needs of self determination theory and the three causality orientations with the needs and motivation linked to each. Psycho Didi notes · p. 114 Three basic needs: Autonomy — the need to control the course of our lives. Competence — the need to be effective in dealing with the environment. Relatedness — the need to have close, affectionate relationships with others. Causality orientations: Orientation Needs satisfied Motivation Autonomous Autonomy, competence, relatedness Intrinsic motivation Controlled Competence, relatedness Extrinsic motivation Impersonal None Amotivation Drive-reduction theory (Clark Hull) Drive reduction theory. A cycle from bodily need to drive, motivated behaviour and homeostasis, labelled with the terms of Hull's equation, next to the equation and a key to each term. Psycho Didi notes · p. 115 Theory → Theorist. Drive-reduction theory → Clark Hull . A homeostatic approach. A bodily need (e.g. hydration) creates a drive ; the organism is motivated to satisfy the drive through goal-directed behaviour, restoring homeostasis (drive reduced, need satisfied). Equation: SER = V × D × J × K × SHR − SIR − IR − SOR − SLR Term Meaning SER Excitatory / reaction potential V Need D Drive J Delay K Size of incentive SHR Habit strength SIR Conditioned inhibition IR Fatigue (reactive inhibition) SOR Random error SLR Minimum reinforcement required for learning to occur McClelland's theory of needs McClelland's theory of needs. Three overlapping circles for power, achievement and affiliation, next to lists of the qualities of high and low achievers. Psycho Didi notes · p. 115 Theory → Theorist. Need for achievement / acquired-needs theory → David McClelland . All three needs are learned : Power (nPow) , Achievement (nAch) , Affiliation (nAff) . Qualities of the high achiever (high nAch) Qualities of the low achiever (low nAch) High motivation to achieve success Low motivation to achieve success Low motivation to avoid failure High motivation to avoid failure Focuses on the pride of success Focuses on shame and worry that may result from failure Ascribes success to stable and internal factors Ascribes success to unstable and external factors Ascribes failure to unstable and external factors Ascribes failure to stable and internal factors within one's control Internal locus of control (Julian Rotter, 1966) for success External locus of control for success High perceived competence; believes achievement is within own control Low perceived competence; believes achievement is outside own control Seeks out challenges and able competitors and tasks Usually adopts outcome goals; avoids challenge, seeks out very difficult or very easy tasks and competitors Performs well in evaluative conditions; likes feedback Performs badly in evaluative situations; dislikes feedback Zuckerman's sensation-seeking theory Zuckerman's sensation seeking theory. A branching diagram of the four types of sensation seeking above a drawing of hikers climbing a hill. Psycho Didi notes · p. 115 Theory → Theorist. Sensation-seeking theory → Marvin Zuckerman . Four types: Thrill and adventure seeking Experience seeking Disinhibition Boredom susceptibility Key. Need theories to keep straight: Abraham Maslow (hierarchy, deficiency vs growth needs), Alderfer (ERG — succession progression vs frustration regression), David McClelland (learned nAch/nPow/nAff), Edward Deci & Richard Ryan (self-determination — autonomy, competence, relatedness). Clark Hull's drive-reduction is the homeostatic model; Yerkes-Dodson governs the optimum-arousal model. Don't confuse — the need theorists. Abraham Maslow = a fixed upward hierarchy driven by deficiency then growth; Alderfer's ERG = flexible, allows frustration regression; David McClelland = three learned needs measured by projective tests, no hierarchy. And in McClelland's model, high-nAch people take internal credit for success while low-nAch people show an external locus for success and an internal one for failure.

title: Developmental Psychology
text: Developmental Psychology — Study with Psycho Didi (MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF) Developmental Psychology Study with Psycho Didi · MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF notes Prenatal stages & teratogens Jean Piaget · Erik Erikson · Lawrence Kohlberg · Sigmund Freud Attachment: Mary Ainsworth · John Bowlby · Harry Harlow Jerome Bruner · James Marcia · Urie Bronfenbrenner · Elkind Lifespan & reflexes What this covers. The full arc of human development: prenatal screening and prenatal stages, teratogens and genetic/chromosomal disorders, the lifespan phases and infant reflexes, then the major stage theories: Freud's psychosexual stages, Erikson's eight psychosocial stages, Piaget's cognitive and moral stages, Kohlberg's moral levels, plus Bruner , Marcia , Elkind and Bronfenbrenner , and finally theories of attachment ( Ainsworth , Bowlby , Harlow ). Original diagrams. 18 diagrams from the Psycho Didi PDF (pages 117 to 120) sit under the section they belong to, exactly as drawn. Tap one to open it full size and zoom in. Contents: 1 · Prenatal screening & development · 2 · Genetic, chromosomal & congenital disorders · 3 · Lifespan development & reflexes · 4 · Freud's psychosexual stages · 5 · Erikson's psychosocial stages · 6 · Piaget's cognitive stages · 7 · Piaget's moral development · 8 · Kohlberg's moral development · 9 · Bruner, Marcia, Elkind & Bronfenbrenner · 10 · Theories of attachment 1 · Prenatal screening & development Ways to sample for abnormalities Ways to sample for abnormalities. A box listing prenatal screening methods with when each is done and what it checks for. Psycho Didi notes · p. 117 Method Timing What it checks / does Amniocentesis 14th week Checks for genetic abnormalities; done through amniotic fluid Fetoscopy 5 weeks Checks for haemophilia, sickle cell anaemia, limb defects Ultrasound — Tells about the size, shape, and placement of the foetus Maternal Blood Analysis 2nd month Can check for neural tube defect Chorionic villus sampling 8th week Chorionic biopsy is performed; detects all genetic problems Prenatal development stages Stages. A box listing the germinal, embryonic and foetal stages of prenatal development with small foetus drawings. Psycho Didi notes · p. 117 Stage Period Germinal stage Ovulation and implantation Embryonic stage Up to 8 weeks Foetal stage 8+ weeks Teratogens Drugs / Alcohol Alcohol: heart defects Cocaine: vascular disruption Valproate: ear problems Vitamin A deficiency: Spina bifida Infections Rubella: microcephaly Toxoplasma: hydrocephalus Varicella: limb defects Conditions Diabetes: neural tube defects Key. Match the screening method to its window: Fetoscopy (5 wk) → CVS (8 wk) → Amniocentesis (14 wk); Maternal Blood Analysis in the 2nd month checks for neural tube defect. 2 · Genetic, chromosomal & congenital disorders Prenatal deformities. A flowchart that branches prenatal deformities into teratogenic, genetic (recessive, dominant and X linked), genetic mutation and congenital causes, with example disorders and their features under each. Psycho Didi notes · p. 117 Genetic disorders Inheritance patterns include Recessive , Dominant , and X-linked . Disorder Key features Tay Sachs CNS degeneration; usually die at 3-4 y/o Cystic Fibrosis Lungs secrete mucus PKU (Phenylketonuria) Intellectual disability; phenylalanine hydroxylase is absent; damage to CNS when exposed to proteins Sickle Cell Anaemia Sickle-shaped RBC; pain; swelling; short life span Huntington's disease Neurocognitive; death after 10-20 years of symptoms; excitotoxicity; mental deterioration Marfan syndrome Tall, elongated arms and limbs; heart defects; eye abnormalities; skeletal deformity; death in young adulthood Fragile X syndrome Mutation in FMR1 gene (Fragile X messenger ribonucleoprotein is not made); developmental delays; learning disability, intellectual disability, Autism Spectrum Disorder; elongated face Haemophilia Blood fails to clot; excessive internal bleeding Diabetes insipidus Insufficient production of vasopressin; excessive thirst Duchenne muscular dystrophy Muscular dystrophy; death from weakness of heart muscle; loss of ability to walk Genetic mutations (chromosomal) Numerical Disorder Features Trisomy 21 (Down's syndrome) Intellectual disability; weak muscle tone; intellectual disability Turner's syndrome (XO) In females; heart defects; abnormal secondary sexual characteristics; webbed neck Klinefelter's syndrome (47, XXY) In males; too tall; osteoporosis; sterility Triple X syndrome (47, XXX) — Structural Disorder Features Cri Du Chat (5p) Microcephaly; intellectual disability; autism/ADHD symptoms; low birth weight; respiratory impairment Pallister Killian Presence of extra material on chromosome 12; intellectual disability; mosaicism; poor muscle tone; seizures; cataracts; stiff joint Prader Willi (15a) Intellectual disability; reduced social functioning; rigid behavioural preferences Congenital Cerebral Palsy Due to head trauma to mother and other problems during development Motor deficits / epilepsy / intellectual disability Classification (based on body parts affected): mono, hemi, di, quadri Types: spastic, ataxic, mixed, athetoid Fetal Alcohol Syndrome Cause: having alcohol during pregnancy Structural: microcephaly, irregular facial features, decreased muscle tone Neurological: intellectual disability, epilepsy, poor eye-hand coordination Functional: low IQ, developmental disability, learning disorders, language development delays 3 · Lifespan development & reflexes Lifespan development phases Lifespan development. A silhouette row from crawling baby to elderly adult above a list of lifespan phases and their age ranges. Psycho Didi notes · p. 118 Phase Age range Prenatal Conception to birth Infancy and toddlerhood Birth to 2 years Early childhood 2-6 years Middle childhood 6-12 years Adolescence 12-20 years Emerging adulthood (Jeffrey Arnett, 2000) 20-25 years Young adulthood 25-45 years Middle adulthood 45-60 years Later adulthood 60 years to death Infant reflexes Reflexes. A list of infant reflexes with a short description of each. Psycho Didi notes · p. 118 Reflex Description Moro reflex Fight-or-flight reaction, sympathetic nervous system response; "monkey hanging from a tree" Rooting reflex Autonomic response to locate food and breast Palmar Grasp Reflex Autonomic flexion of the fingers to grab when the palm is stimulated Asymmetric Tonic Neck Reflex Assists with movement through birth canal at delivery; important for cross-pattern movement Spinal Galant Reflex Important during the birthing process; helps to facilitate movement of the hips during descending the birthing canal Babinski reflex Toes spread out when sole of the foot is touched Plantar / stepping reflex — 4 · Freud's psychosexual stages of development Freud's psychosexual stages of development. A list of the five psychosexual stages with the age, erogenous zone and fixation types for each. Psycho Didi notes · p. 118 Theory → theorist. Psychosexual stages of development were proposed by Sigmund Freud . Stage Age Erogenous zone Key features Oral stage 0-2 years Mouth Types of oral fixation — oral incorporative: dependent, naïve, collecting and hoarding objects; oral biting: sarcastic, mean Anal stage 2-3 years Anus Ego develops. Fixations — anal retentive: rigid, strict, excessive organization, excessive cleanliness, OCD type, hoarding, miserly, stingy; anal expulsive: spendthrift, disorganized, messy Phallic stage 3-7 years Genitals Superego develops; Oedipus complex Latency stage 7-11 years None No fixation; sexual energy is sublimated towards activities like sports, studies, same-gender friendships Genital stage 11 and above Genitals Healthy adult development occurs here; interest in opposite sex develops Trap. Don't confuse anal retentive (rigid, overly clean, hoarding, OCD-type) with anal expulsive (messy, disorganized, spendthrift) — they are opposite fixations of the same anal stage. 5 · Erikson's psychosocial development theory Erikson's psychosocial development theory. Key features of Erikson's theory, how it differs from Freud, and the maladjustment linked to each pole of every crisis. Psycho Didi notes · p. 119 Erikson's eight stages. A table of Erikson's eight stages with the age, the crisis and the basic strength for each. Psycho Didi notes · p. 119 Theory → theorist. The eight psychosocial stages were given by Erik Erikson , rooted in ego psychology and the epigenetic principle of development. Stage Age Crisis (ways of coping) Basic strength Oral-sensory 0-1 Trust vs Mistrust Hope Muscular-anal 1-3 Autonomy vs Shame and Doubt Will Locomotor-genital 3-5 Initiative vs Guilt Purpose Latency 6-11 Industry vs Inferiority Competence Adolescence 12-18 Identity vs Role confusion Fidelity Young adulthood 18-35 Intimacy vs Isolation Love Adulthood 35-55 Generativity vs Stagnation Care Old age 55+ Integrity vs Despair Wisdom Differences from Freud 8 stages of personality Greater emphasis on ego Impact on personality of cultural and historical forces Maladjustment (per pole of each crisis) Pole Maladjustment Trust Sensory maladjustment Mistrust Withdrawal Autonomy Shameless wilfulness Shame Compulsion Initiative Ruthlessness Guilt Inhibition Industry Narrow virtuosity Inferiority Inertia Identity Fanaticism Role confusion Repudiation Intimacy Promiscuity Isolation Exclusivity Generativity Overextension Stagnation Rejectivity Integrity Presumption Despair Disdain Why it matters. Erik Erikson's development is discontinuous (stages) and governed by the epigenetic principle : each stage builds on the resolution of the one before it, with a specific basic strength (virtue) as the payoff. Trap. Erikson stages are easily confused. Note the age boundaries: Latency (6-11) = Industry vs Inferiority maps onto Sigmund Freud's latency, but Erik Erikson adds three adult stages (Intimacy, Generativity, Integrity) that Freud's genital stage collapses into one. 6 · Piaget's stages of cognitive development Piaget's stages of cognitive development. Notes on the four Piagetian stages with pictures of the three mountains task and a liquid conservation task. Psycho Didi notes · p. 119 Theory → theorist. The four stages of cognitive development were given by Jean Piaget . Stage Age Key learning / task Sensorimotor stage Birth to 2 years Child learns object permanence ; tested with the A-not-B task Preoperational stage 2-7 years Learns symbolic thought , animism ; egocentrism tested with the Three Mountains task Concrete operational stage 7-11 years Learns conservation , reversibility , mathematical operations; conservation task Formal operational stage 11 and above Learns hypothetico-deductive reasoning and abstract reasoning; pendulum task Sensorimotor: sequence of events Motor reflexes Primary circular reactions — e.g. putting everything in the mouth Secondary circular reactions — manipulation of objects Synthesis of secondary circular reactions Tertiary circular reactions — object permanence achieved here; goal-directed behaviour; mental representations; concept formation Imitation involves: Deferred imitation: repeating action after some time has passed Inferred imitation: imitating only correct behaviour and not the incorrect one Horizontal décalage When a child is able to perform conservation of mass (or any other thing) but unable to do the conservation task for length or density (or anything else). Trap: assimilation vs accommodation. In Jean Piaget's framework, assimilation fits new information into an existing schema, while accommodation changes the schema to fit new information. Do not swap them. Trap: Piaget vs Lev Vygotsky. Piaget saw cognitive development as an individual, stage-based process driven from within the child. Vygotsky emphasized the social and cultural context (learning through interaction, scaffolding, the Zone of Proximal Development) driving development. Piaget = discovery within stages; Vygotsky = socially mediated learning. 7 · Piaget's theory of moral development Piaget's theory of moral development. Notes on heteronomous and autonomous morality with the age range and main idea of each. Psycho Didi notes · p. 120 Stage Age Also known as / features Heteronomous Morality 5-9 years Moral realism — morality imposed from the outside Autonomous Morality 9-10 years Moral relativism — morality based on your own rules; children recognize there is no absolute right or wrong and that morality depends on intentions, not consequences 8 · Kohlberg's theory of moral development Kohlberg's theory of moral development. Notes on Kohlberg's study and his three levels of morality with the substages under each. Psycho Didi notes · p. 120 Theory → theorist. The three levels of morality were given by Lawrence Kohlberg . He presented children, adolescents and young adults with stories that included moral dilemmas, such as the story of Heinz , in his longitudinal study. He studied a group of boys in the age group 10-16 for over 20 years. Level Substages Pre-conventional morality Punishment avoidance; instrumental or reward Conventional morality Good boy/girl, social acceptance, good interpersonal relationship; social order / avoiding censure (Law and Order orientation) Post-conventional morality Social contract and individual rights; universal ethical principles Trap. Keep Piaget's moral stages (Heteronomous / Autonomous, ages 5-10) distinct from Lawrence Kohlberg's three levels (Pre-conventional / Conventional / Post-conventional). Kohlberg used the Heinz dilemma ; Piaget did not. 9 · Bruner, Marcia, Elkind & Bronfenbrenner Jerome Bruner's theory of cognitive development — modes of representation Jerome Bruner's modes of representation. A list of Bruner's enactive, iconic and symbolic modes of representation with what each involves. Psycho Didi notes · p. 118 Mode Description Enactive Mode Learning through actions and motor responses Iconic Mode Learning through mental images and visual representations Symbolic Mode Learning through abstract symbols like language and numbers James Marcia's theory of identity development James Marcia's theory of identity development. A table rating the four identity statuses as low or high on exploration and commitment. Psycho Didi notes · p. 118 Identity status is defined by two dimensions: Exploration and Commitment . Identity status Exploration Commitment Identity diffusion Low Low Identity foreclosure Low High Identity moratorium High Low Identity achievement High High Elkind's adolescent egocentrism Elkind's adolescent egocentrism. A list of the three types of adolescent egocentrism with the typical thought behind each. Psycho Didi notes · p. 118 There are three types of adolescent egocentrism: The imaginary audience — "everyone is looking at me" The mythological fable — "that won't ever happen to me" The personal fable — "nobody knows what it's like to be me" Ecological systems theory Ecological systems theory. Nested coloured circles with arrows pointing to Bronfenbrenner's micro, meso, exo, macro and chrono systems and a definition of each. Psycho Didi notes · p. 118 Theory → theorist. Ecological systems theory was given by Urie Bronfenbrenner (1979) . System Description Microsystem Concerns relations between the developing person and the immediate environment Mesosystem Connections among immediate settings Exosystem Social settings that affect but do not contain the developing person Macrosystem The values, laws, customs, and resources of the culture that affect activities and interactions at all inner layers Chronosystem Not a specific context; refers to the dynamic, ever-changing nature of the person's environment 10 · Theories of attachment Mary Ainsworth's attachment styles Theories of attachment: Mary Ainsworth's attachment styles. A table of how infants with each attachment style react when the mother leaves and when she returns. Psycho Didi notes · p. 120 Theory → theorist. Attachment styles (measured via the Strange Situation) were given by Mary Ainsworth . Style Mother leaves Mother returns Secure Upset Happy Anxious / avoidant Indifferent Indifferent Ambivalent / resistant Cries; upset Angry Disorganized Dazed and scared Dazed and scared Trap. On reunion, secure babies are comforted (happy), avoidant babies stay indifferent, ambivalent/resistant babies are angry (seek but resist contact), and disorganized babies look dazed and scared. Watch the reunion column, not just the separation. Contact Comfort Theory Contact Comfort Theory. Notes on the Harlows' monkey study comparing a wire feeding mother with a cloth mother. Psycho Didi notes · p. 120 Theory → theorist. Contact Comfort Theory was given by Harry Harlow and Margaret Harlow . They raised monkeys with two artificial mothers — one a bare wire cylinder with a wooden head and an attached feeding bottle; the other a cylinder with no bottle but covered with foam rubber and wrapped with terry cloth. The infants much preferred contact with the comfortable cloth mother, even while feeding from the nourishing mother. John Bowlby's ecological theory of attachment (1969) John Bowlby's ecological theory of attachment. A list of Bowlby's four phases of attachment with the age range and main features of each. Psycho Didi notes · p. 120 Theory → theorist. The four phases of attachment were given by John Bowlby (1969) . Phase Age Features Pre-attachment phase Birth to 6 weeks Recognize their own mother's smell, voice and face Attachment-in-the-making phase 6 weeks to 6-8 months Infants respond differently to a familiar caregiver than to a stranger, but they still do not protest when separated from mother Clear-cut attachment phase (monotropy) 6-8 months to 18 months-2 years Clear-cut attachment with 1 primary attachment figure Formation of a reciprocal relationship 18 months to 2 years and on Rapid growth in representation and language permits toddlers to understand some of the factors that influence the parent's coming and going and to predict her return; children negotiate with the caregiver, using requests and persuasion to alter her goals Key. Bowlby's term monotropy = the child's clear-cut, single primary attachment figure, emerging in the clear-cut attachment phase (6-8 months onward).

title: Social Psychology
text: Social Psychology — Study with Psycho Didi (MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF) Social Psychology Study with Psycho Didi · MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF notes Attribution & biases Cognitive dissonance (Leon Festinger, 1957) Persuasion & social influence Conformity · Compliance · Obedience Helping · Proxemics What this covers. The core of social psychology as it appears in MPhil Clinical and UGC NET JRF papers: a timeline of landmark thinkers and studies, attribution theory and its many biases, Harold Kelley's covariation model, cognitive dissonance (Leon Festinger, 1957) and attitude change, the Elaboration Likelihood Model (Richard Petty and John Cacioppo, 1986), the three types of social influence (compliance, conformity, obedience) with their techniques and classic experiments, social norms, prosocial helping (the decision stage model), and proxemics (personal space zones). Original diagrams. 16 diagrams from the Psycho Didi PDF (pages 122 to 123) sit under the section they belong to, exactly as drawn. Tap one to open it full size and zoom in. Contents: 1 · Timeline of Social Psychology · 2 · Attribution & Attributional Biases · 3 · Kelley's Covariation Model · 4 · Cognitive Dissonance · 5 · Attitude Change (Elaboration Likelihood Model) · 6 · Social Influence: Compliance, Conformity, Obedience · 7 · Social Norms · 8 · Prosocial Behaviour & Helping · 9 · Proxemics (Personal Space) 1 · Timeline of Social Psychology Timeline of social psychology. A winding road timeline marking key social psychology figures and studies from 1917 to 1994. Psycho Didi notes · p. 122 Key figures and landmark studies that shaped the field, in chronological order. Year Figure Contribution 1917 John Dewey The need for social psychology 1935 Muzafer Sherif Conformity studies 1940s — Field theory (Kurt Lewin) 1950s Solomon Asch Conformity study 1954 Gordon Allport Nature of prejudice 1959 Erving Goffman Presentation of self 1961 Serge Moscovici Social representation 1963 Stanley Milgram Obedience study 1965 William Glasser Choice theory 1968 Robert Zajonc Mere exposure effect 1971 Philip Zimbardo Stanford Prison experiment 1971 Elliot Aronson Jigsaw classroom 1972 Spence and Helmreich Attitude towards women 1977 Brown and Kulik Flashbulb memories 1994 Ignacio Martín-Baró Liberation psychology 2 · Attribution & Attributional Biases Attribution. Notes defining attribution and its two categories, dispositional and situational. Psycho Didi notes · p. 122 Attribution refers to the way in which people assign responsibility for certain outcomes. Typically attribution falls into two categories: Dispositional (individual) — assumes that the cause of a behaviour or outcome is internal. Situational — assigns the cause to the environment or external conditions. Watch the biases. Several attributional biases are easily confused. The fundamental attribution error (Lee Ross, 1977) is about judging others , while the actor–observer bias and self-serving bias concern how we explain our own actions. Learn the direction (internal vs external) each one pulls. Types of attributional bias Flexible attribution. A list of attributional biases, each with a one-line definition. Psycho Didi notes · p. 122 Flexible attribution — a general label for the shifting, motivated way people assign causes. Fundamental attribution error — when judging the behaviour of others, people are more likely to overestimate the role of dispositional attributes and to underestimate the role of the situation. Self-serving bias — seeing the cause of actions as internal when the outcomes are positive and external when the results are negative. Actor–observer bias — we tend to attribute our own actions to the situation. Optimism bias — we like to believe that bad things happen to other people, but not to ourselves. Just-world belief ( M. J. Lerner ) — a belief that the world is essentially fair and just (leads to victim blaming). Self-fulfilling prophecy — because person A expects person B to achieve or fail, person B is likely to do just that. Positive: Rosenthal / Pygmalion effect Negative: Golem effect 3 · Kelley's Covariation Model Kelley's Covariation Model (1967). A table showing the levels of consensus, consistency and distinctiveness that lead to an internal or an external attribution. Psycho Didi notes · p. 122 Covariation model → Harold Kelley (1967). Explains whether we make an internal or external attribution based on three kinds of information: consensus, consistency, and distinctiveness. Information Internal attribution External attribution Consensus Low High Consistency High High Distinctiveness Low High 4 · Cognitive Dissonance Cognitive dissonance. Notes on Festinger's cognitive dissonance, the minimum justification effect, the types of dissonance and the ways to reduce it. Psycho Didi notes · p. 122 Cognitive dissonance → Leon Festinger. Cognitive dissonance refers to the tension that results from holding conflicting beliefs, attitudes, opinions, or values, or when our actions do not coincide with these cognitions. Key — minimum justification effect. Dissonance is experienced when external rewards are not adequate to justify behaviour. Therefore: Large reward = small attitude change Small reward = large attitude change Types of cognitive dissonance Free choice — when you liked both options. Forced choice — when you dislike both options. Methods of reducing dissonance Changing one's attitude Changing one's behaviour Trivialization 5 · Attitude Change (Elaboration Likelihood Model) Elaboration Likelihood Model. A table comparing the central and peripheral routes by audience, processing effort and how long the attitude change lasts. Psycho Didi notes · p. 123 Elaboration Likelihood Model → Richard Petty and John Cacioppo (1986). Route Audience Processing Duration of change Central route Motivated; analytical High effort Long-lasting Peripheral route Unmotivated; non-analytical Low effort Temporary 6 · Social Influence: Compliance, Conformity, Obedience Social influence. A short list of the three main types of social influence and what each behaviour change is based on. Psycho Didi notes · p. 123 There are three main types of social influence: Compliance — behaviour change based on a request. Conformity — behaviour change based on social pressure. Obedience — behaviour change based on instruction from an authority. Don't confuse the three. Compliance follows a request , conformity follows social pressure (peers/group), and obedience follows an authority's instruction . The source of the influence is the key distinction. Compliance — Principles of Persuasion Compliance. Cialdini's principles of persuasion with the compliance techniques listed under each principle. Psycho Didi notes · p. 123 Principles of persuasion → Robert Cialdini. Principle Techniques Friendship / liking Ingratiation (flattery and praise to get others to like you) Commitment / consistency Foot-in-the-door; Lowball technique Scarcity Deadline technique; Playing hard to get Reciprocity Door-in-the-face; That's-not-all Social validation — Authority — Obedience Obedience: teacher-learner experiment. An illustration of Milgram's set-up with the learner, the teacher participant and the experimenter, followed by the factors that affect obedience and a drawing of people talking. Psycho Didi notes · p. 123 Teacher–learner experiment → Stanley Milgram (1963). Factors impacting the level of obedience: Distance between experimenter and subject Distance between teacher and learner Expertise of the experimenter Signs of authority of the experimenter Conformity Conformity. A tree splitting conformity into normative and informative social influence, with the motive, type and duration of each. Psycho Didi notes · p. 123 The autokinetic effect experiment (1935). A cartoon of Sherif's study in which people give different reports about whether a single point of light in the dark moved. Psycho Didi notes · p. 123 Line judgement task (1951). A cartoon of Asch's study showing a row of stooges, one innocent participant and the card of comparison lines A, B and C. Psycho Didi notes · p. 123 Stanford Prison experiment (1971). A photo from Zimbardo's study with notes that it examined role conformity and deindividuation. Psycho Didi notes · p. 123 Line judgement task (1951) → Solomon Asch. Stanford Prison experiment (1971) → Philip Zimbardo and colleagues — studied role conformity and the effects of deindividuation. The autokinetic effect experiment (1935) → Muzafer Sherif. Type Motive Nature Duration Normative For social approval Public conformity Short term Informative For rational reasons Private conformity Long term 7 · Social Norms Norms. A tree dividing norms into descriptive and injunctive, with injunctive norms split into prescriptive and proscriptive. Psycho Didi notes · p. 123 Descriptive norms — simply tell what to do (what is actually done). Injunctive norms — tell what ought to be done. Prescriptive — what to do. Proscriptive — what not to do. 8 · Prosocial Behaviour & Helping Decision stage model of helping. A flowchart of the five steps a bystander goes through before helping, with the reason help fails at each step. Psycho Didi notes · p. 122 Decision stage model of helping → John Darley and Bibb Latané (1970). Steps involved in helping behaviour, and why a bystander may fail at each step: Step Not helped due to 1. Noticing the event Distraction 2. Interpret the event as an emergency Pluralistic ignorance; ambiguity; relationship between attacker and victim 3. Assume responsibility Diffusion of responsibility 4. Know the appropriate form of assistance Lack of knowledge; lack of competence 5. Implement the decision Audience inhibition; costs exceed rewards 9 · Proxemics (Personal Space) Theory of Proxemics. Concentric circles showing Edward Hall's four personal space zones with their distances and typical uses. Psycho Didi notes · p. 122 Theory of Proxemics → Edward Hall (1966). Zone Distance Used for Intimate space 6–18 inches Hugging, whispering or touching Personal space 1.5 to 4 feet Family members or close friends Social space 4 to 12 feet Acquaintances Public space 12 to 25 feet Public speaking situations

title: Effects, Phenomena, Theories & Originators
text: Effects, Phenomena, Theories & Originators One consolidated lookup for every named effect, phenomenon, illusion, theory, complex and the people behind them. The five old sweeps overlapped heavily (an "effect" carries an originator; a theory carries a theorist), so each item now lives in exactly one entry: the definition, who coined it, the classic study, and the confusable lookalike, together. Drill it both directions: cover the "Who" column and name the person; cover the description and name the term. High-yield NIMHANS / MET ask this two ways. (1) Name the "____ effect / theory / complex" and ask who proposed it (answer = a person). (2) Describe a scene/finding with no name and ask you to name it (answer = the effect/theory). Almost every trap is a same-family lookalike (halo↔horn, Pygmalion↔Golem, placebo↔nocebo, James-Lange↔Cannon-Bard, McCall's T↔Student's t). Always learn each item with its twin. In this reference Named effects (grouped) Phenomena, illusions, biases & clinical signs Theories & models (by domain) Named complexes & syndromes Who originated what — theorists Psychometrics, statistics & standard scores 1. Named effects Every named "____ effect," its originator, and the one-line hook. Grouped by domain so the good-twin / bad-twin pairs sit together. 1.1 Memory & learning effects Effect Who What it is Zeigarnik effect Bluma Zeigarnik Interrupted / unfinished tasks are remembered better than completed ones. Von Restorff (isolation) effect Hedwig von Restorff The odd-one-out item in a list stands out and is recalled best. Serial position effect Ebbinghaus (named by Murdock) First + last items in a list recalled best (= primacy + recency together). Primacy effect — First items recalled well (rehearsed into long-term store). Recency effect — Last items recalled well (still in short-term store). A delay/distractor kills recency, not primacy. Spacing (distributed practice) effect Ebbinghaus Spread-out study beats cramming for long-term retention. Testing effect — Retrieving (self-testing) cements memory better than re-reading. Generation effect Slamecka & Graf Info you generate yourself is remembered better than info you just read. Self-reference effect Rogers, Kuiper & Kirker Material related to yourself is encoded and recalled better. Misinformation effect Elizabeth Loftus Post-event misleading info distorts the original memory (eyewitness work). Picture superiority effect Allan Paivio (dual-coding) Pictures are remembered better than words. Encoding-specificity / context effect Tulving & Thomson Recall is best when retrieval cues match the encoding context (state/context-dependent memory). Levels-of-processing effect Craik & Robert Lockhart Deeper (semantic) processing → better memory than shallow (visual/acoustic). Trap Remove the delay/distractor and it's the recency end that vanishes (STM decays); primacy survives. Zeigarnik = unfinished remembered; von Restorff = distinctive remembered — don't merge them. 1.2 Attention & perception effects Effect Who What it is Stroop effect J. Ridley Stroop Slower to name ink colour when the word spells a different colour (automatic reading interferes). Cocktail-party effect Colin Cherry Selective attention to one voice in a crowd, yet you still catch your own name. McGurk effect McGurk & MacDonald What you see the mouth do changes what you hear (audio-visual speech fusion). Ventriloquist effect — Sound is mislocated toward a plausible visual source. Troxler effect (fading) Ignaz Troxler Fixate steadily and unchanging peripheral stimuli fade from awareness. Motion aftereffect (waterfall illusion) — After staring at motion, a static scene appears to drift the opposite way. Bouba/kiki effect Wolfgang Köhler (later Ramachandran) People map "bouba" to round shapes, "kiki" to spiky ones (sound symbolism). Tetris effect — Heavy repeated activity intrudes into imagery/dreams. Trap The phi phenomenon and autokinetic phenomenon are labelled "phenomena," not "effects" — they live in §2.1. Same content, the label decides where the examiner files it. 1.3 Social & expectancy effects Effect Who What it is Halo effect Edward Thorndike One good trait (e.g. looks) bleeds into an overall positive judgement. Horn(s) effect — The negative mirror of halo: one bad trait darkens the whole impression. Pygmalion (Rosenthal) effect Rosenthal & Jacobson High teacher/leader expectations → the person actually performs better (self-fulfilling prophecy). Golem effect — Low expectations → worse performance (the dark twin of Pygmalion). Hawthorne effect Elton Mayo (Western Electric studies) People change behaviour because they know they're being observed. John Henry effect Saretsky A control group tries extra hard because it knows it's the comparison (a research artefact). Mere-exposure effect Robert Zajonc Repeated exposure alone increases liking (also a persuasion lever: familiarity breeds liking). Bystander effect Latané & John Darley More onlookers → less likely any one helps (diffusion of responsibility). After Kitty Genovese. 5-step decision model: notice → interpret → take responsibility → know how → act. (Theory form in §3.6.) Ringelmann effect Max Ringelmann Per-person effort drops as group size grows (precursor to social loafing). Pratfall effect Elliot Aronson A competent person becomes more likeable after a small blunder. Spotlight effect Thomas Gilovich Overestimating how much others notice you. False-consensus effect Lee Ross Overestimating how many people share your views/choices. Lake Wobegon / above-average effect — Most people rate themselves above average (illusory superiority). Cheerleader effect — Faces look more attractive in a group than alone. Overjustification effect Lepper, Greene & Richard Nisbett Paying for an already-enjoyed activity kills the intrinsic motivation. Boomerang effect Hovland tradition (akin to Brehm) Persuasion backfires, shifting the attitude the opposite way (cousin of reactance, §3.6). Trap Same-study, different name: Pygmalion = Robert Rosenthal & Lenore Jacobson (high expectation lifts), Golem = low expectation drops, Hawthorne = Mayo (being watched changes behaviour). Examiners swap these three constantly. 1.4 Judgment & decision effects Effect Who What it is Barnum / Forer effect Bertram Forer Accepting vague, general descriptions as uniquely true of you (horoscopes, cold reading). Dunning–Kruger effect Dunning & Kruger Low-skill people overestimate their own competence. Anchoring effect Tversky & Daniel Kahneman First number seen drags later estimates toward it. (Bias form: §2.6.) Framing effect Tversky & Kahneman Same facts, different wording (gain vs loss) flips the choice. Endowment effect Richard Thaler You value a thing more just because you own it. IKEA effect Norton, Mochon & Ariely You over-value things you partly built yourself. Decoy (asymmetric dominance) effect Huber et al. A third inferior option nudges choice between the other two. Bandwagon effect — Adopting a belief because many others hold it. Actor–observer effect Jones & Richard Nisbett Your own acts blamed on the situation, others' on their character. Availability in judgment Tversky & Kahneman Easily recalled examples seem more frequent than they are (availability heuristic — §2.6). Pollyanna effect Matlin & Stang Positive items are processed and recalled more readily than negative. High-yield Anchoring, framing and availability are written up both as effects (here) and as cognitive biases/heuristics (§2.6). If the stem says "bias/heuristic," it's §2.6; if it says "effect," it's here. Same content, two labels — scan both. 1.5 Persuasion, media & population effects Effect Who What it is Sleeper effect Carl Hovland (Yale) A message from a low-credibility source persuades more over time once you forget the source. Werther effect David Phillips Spike in copycat suicides after a publicised one. Papageno effect Niederkrotenthaler Responsible media coverage of coping can reduce suicide (the protective opposite of Werther). Mozart effect Rauscher et al. A brief, small spatial-reasoning bump after Mozart (popularly overstated). Flynn effect James Flynn Population IQ scores have risen generation on generation (forces test re-norming). Matthew effect Robert Merton "Rich get richer": early advantage compounds (reading, science credit). Kuleshov effect Lev Kuleshov Viewers read emotion into a neutral face based on the adjacent shot (film editing). 1.6 Biological & clinical effects Effect Who What it is Placebo effect — Improvement from an inert treatment driven by expectation. Nocebo effect — Negative symptoms from an inert treatment (the dark twin of placebo). Garcia effect (taste aversion) John Garcia One-trial conditioned aversion to a taste; biological preparedness; defies classic CC timing rules. Coolidge effect Frank Beach (named it) Renewed sexual interest when a novel partner is introduced. Westermarck effect Edvard Westermarck Reverse sexual imprinting: people raised together in early childhood feel no attraction (incest avoidance). Kindling effect Goddard (seizure model) Repeated sub-threshold stimulation lowers the threshold for episodes (mood/seizure recurrence). Tolerance / sensitisation — Same drug dose gives less effect (tolerance) or more (sensitisation) with repetition. Trap Six "good twin / bad twin" pairs: placebo↔nocebo, Werther↔Papageno, Pygmalion↔Golem, halo↔horn, primacy↔recency, tolerance↔sensitisation . Learn only one of each and the distractor will be the other. 2. Phenomena, illusions, biases & clinical signs Named things the mind/brain does : illusions, attention failures, memory glitches, group phenomena, biases and neuropsych signs. The stem usually describes the experience and wants the name (or who described it). 2.1 Perceptual illusions Illusion Who What you see Müller-Lyer Franz Müller-Lyer Two equal lines look unequal depending on arrow-head direction (inward vs outward fins). Ponzo Mario Ponzo Two equal lines on converging "railway" lines look unequal (depth misread). Ebbinghaus (Titchener) circles Ebbinghaus A circle ringed by big circles looks smaller than the same circle ringed by small ones. Zöllner Johann Zöllner Parallel lines look slanted because of crossing hatch marks. Kanizsa triangle Gaetano Kanizsa You "see" a white triangle edge that isn't drawn (illusory/subjective contours). Necker cube Louis Necker A wire cube flips between two 3-D orientations (bistable perception). Rubin's vase Edgar Rubin Faces-or-vase: figure–ground reversal. Ames room Adelbert Ames A distorted room makes equal-size people look giant vs tiny. Moon illusion — The moon looks larger near the horizon than overhead. Hermann grid — Ghostly grey blobs appear at the white intersections of a black grid. Café wall Gregory & Heard Straight mortar lines look wedge-shaped between offset tiles. Phi phenomenon Max Wertheimer Lights flashing in sequence look like one moving light (the founding Gestalt demo of apparent motion). Autokinetic phenomenon used by Muzafer Sherif A still point of light in the dark seems to drift; Sherif used it to study norm formation. Trap Three "size of equal lines" illusions: Müller-Lyer = arrow fins; Ponzo = converging rails; Ebbinghaus = circle surrounded by other circles. Examiners mix these three. 2.2 Gestalt grouping principles From Max Wertheimer, Kurt Koffka & Wolfgang Köhler. "The whole is other than the sum of its parts." Master law = Prägnanz (we see the simplest, most stable form). The Gestalt theory of perception itself is in §3.11. Principle What groups together Proximity Things close together are seen as a group. Similarity Things that look alike are grouped. Continuity (good continuation) We follow smooth, continuous lines over abrupt changes. Closure We fill gaps to see a complete figure. Figure–ground We split a scene into an object and its background. Common fate Things moving together are grouped. Prägnanz (good form) The overarching law: perceive the simplest, most regular organisation. 2.3 Attention & perception phenomena Phenomenon Who What it is Inattentional blindness Mack & Rock; Simons & Chabris (gorilla) You miss an obvious unexpected object while attending elsewhere. Change blindness Simons & Levin You fail to notice a large change across a visual interruption. Attentional blink Raymond, Shapiro & Arnell Brief inability to detect a 2nd target ~200–500 ms after the 1st. Cocktail-party phenomenon Colin Cherry Tracking one voice in noise, yet still catching your own name (effect form: §1.2). Weber's law / JND Ernst Weber The just-noticeable difference is a constant proportion of the stimulus. Fechner's law Gustav Fechner Sensation grows with the log of stimulus intensity (founded psychophysics). Sensory adaptation — Constant stimulation → declining response (you stop feeling your clothes). Pareidolia — Seeing meaningful patterns (faces) in random stimuli (clouds, toast). Synaesthesia — One sense automatically triggers another (hearing colours, tasting words). Blindsight Lawrence Weiskrantz Responding to visual stimuli without conscious sight (V1 damage). Perceptual constancy — Objects seen as stable in size/shape/colour despite changing retinal image. 2.4 Memory phenomena Phenomenon Who What it is Tip-of-the-tongue (TOT) Brown & McNeill Knowing a word is there but not retrieving it (you often get its first letter/length). Flashbulb memory Brown & Kulik Vivid, confident memory of where you were during a shocking event (often inaccurate). Déjà vu / jamais vu — Novel scene feels familiar / familiar scene feels alien. Reminiscence bump — Older adults recall disproportionately many memories from ages ~10–30. Childhood (infantile) amnesia — Few/no episodic memories before ~age 3–4. Proactive interference — Old learning blocks new (old password keeps coming up). Retroactive interference — New learning blocks old (new password erases the old one). Forgetting curve Hermann Ebbinghaus Retention drops sharply then levels off; relearning is faster (savings). Misattribution / source-monitoring error Daniel Schacter Right memory, wrong source (cryptomnesia: feeling you invented something you read). 2.5 Group & social phenomena Phenomenon Who What it is Social facilitation Norman Triplett; Robert Zajonc Presence of others boosts easy tasks, harms hard ones. Social loafing Bibb Latané; Ringelmann roots Individuals slack in groups when effort isn't identifiable. Diffusion of responsibility Darley & Latané The mechanism behind the bystander effect: "someone else will." Group polarisation Serge Moscovici; Stoner (risky shift) Group discussion pushes members to a more extreme version of their leaning. Groupthink Irving Janis Cohesive group suppresses dissent for consensus → bad decisions (illusion of unanimity, self-censorship; e.g. Bay of Pigs). Deindividuation Leon Festinger; Philip Zimbardo Loss of self-awareness/restraint in a crowd or anonymity. Conformity Solomon Asch Going along with a group's wrong judgement (line task); normative conformity. Obedience Stanley Milgram Following authority's orders against your own conscience (shock study). Bystander apathy Latané & John Darley The umbrella phenomenon: less help as the crowd grows (effect form: §1.3). Risky shift Stoner Groups make riskier decisions than individuals (early name for polarisation). 2.6 Cognitive biases & heuristics Heuristics = mental shortcuts (largely Amos Tversky & Daniel Kahneman). Biases = the systematic errors they cause. Bias / heuristic Who What it is Availability heuristic Tversky & Kahneman Judge frequency by how easily examples come to mind. Representativeness heuristic Tversky & Kahneman Judge by resemblance to a prototype (ignores base rates → conjunction fallacy). Anchoring & adjustment Tversky & Kahneman Cling to an initial value when estimating (effect form: §1.4). Confirmation bias Peter Wason Seeking/weighting evidence that fits your belief. Hindsight bias Baruch Fischhoff "I knew it all along" after the outcome is known. Fundamental attribution error coined by Lee Ross Over-attributing others' behaviour to character, under-weighting situation. Self-serving bias — Credit success to self, blame failure on circumstance. Sunk-cost fallacy — Continuing because of past investment that can't be recovered. Gambler's fallacy — Believing past random outcomes change future odds. Loss aversion / framing Kahneman & Tversky (prospect theory) Losses hurt more than equivalent gains feel good. Trap Tells: "judged by ease of recall" = availability; "judged by stereotype/prototype" = representativeness; "blamed the person not the situation" = FAE (Ross). Don't swap the two heuristics. 2.7 Neuropsych & clinical phenomena/signs Phenomenon / sign Who What it is Phantom limb Mitchell; Ramachandran Sensation/pain in an amputated limb (cortical remapping). Capgras delusion Joseph Capgras Belief that a loved one has been replaced by an identical impostor. Fregoli delusion — Belief that different people are one person in disguise. Cotard delusion Jules Cotard Belief that one is dead, doesn't exist, or is rotting (nihilistic delusion). Folie à deux Lasègue & Falret A shared delusion transmitted between two close people. Anosognosia Joseph Babinski Unawareness/denial of one's own deficit (e.g. paralysis after stroke). Confabulation — Filling memory gaps with fabricated events without intent to lie (Korsakoff). Hemispatial neglect — Ignoring one side of space after (usually right) parietal damage. Sundowning — Worsening confusion/agitation in the late afternoon/evening (dementia). Pseudobulbar affect — Uncontrollable laughing/crying out of proportion to feeling. La belle indifférence — Surprising lack of concern about a disabling symptom (conversion disorder). Trap Delusional misidentification trio: Capgras = loved one is an impostor; Fregoli = strangers are one disguised person; Cotard = "I am dead." A classic NIMHANS distractor set. (More eponymous syndromes in §4.) 3. Theories & models Every named theory/model, its author and the one-line claim, grouped so rival theories (each other's distractors) sit side by side. Learn the contrast , not the theory alone. 3.1 Learning theories Theory Author Core claim Classical conditioning Ivan Pavlov Neutral stimulus paired with a reflex-evoking one comes to evoke the reflex. Connectionism / Law of Effect Edward Thorndike Responses followed by satisfaction are stamped in (trial-and-error, puzzle box). Operant conditioning B. F. Skinner Behaviour is shaped by its consequences (reinforcement/punishment). Contiguity theory Edwin Guthrie One-trial learning by sheer stimulus–response pairing in time. Insight learning Wolfgang Köhler Sudden restructuring of a problem ("aha"), shown in chimps (Sultan). Latent learning / cognitive maps Edward Tolman Learning happens without reinforcement and shows up later (maze rats). Social / observational learning Albert Bandura We learn by watching and modelling others (Bobo doll). Rescorla–Wagner model Rescorla & Wagner Conditioning depends on surprise / prediction error, not mere pairing. Premack principle David Premack A high-frequency activity can reinforce a low-frequency one ("grandma's rule"). Conditions / hierarchy of learning Robert Gagné Eight learning types from signal learning up to problem-solving; later five learned capabilities + nine instructional events. Meaningful learning / advance organizers David Ausubel New material is anchored to existing knowledge; pre-teach an advance organizer first. Reception, not discovery. Discovery learning Jerome Bruner Learn by exploring and figuring it out yourself; spiral curriculum; enactive → iconic → symbolic representation. Two-factor (avoidance) theory O. H. Mowrer Avoidance = classical conditioning of fear + operant reinforcement from escaping it. Explains why phobias persist. 3.2 Motivation theories Theory Author Core claim Hierarchy of needs Abraham Maslow Needs climb from physiological → safety → love → esteem → self-actualisation. ERG theory Clayton Alderfer Existence, Relatedness, Growth (Maslow condensed; allows regression). Two-factor (motivation-hygiene) Frederick Herzberg Hygiene factors prevent dissatisfaction; motivators create satisfaction. Drive-reduction Clark Hull Behaviour reduces physiological drives to restore homeostasis.
