Arousal theory / Yerkes–Dodson law Yerkes & Dodson Performance peaks at moderate arousal (inverted-U); optimum is lower for hard tasks. Self-determination theory Deci & Ryan Intrinsic motivation needs autonomy, competence, relatedness. Expectancy theory Victor Vroom Effort = expectancy × instrumentality × valence. Goal-setting theory Edwin Locke Specific, hard, accepted goals drive higher performance. Need for achievement (nAch) David McClelland; Atkinson Achievement/affiliation/power needs; measured via TAT. Atkinson: hope-of-success vs fear-of-failure tug-of-war. Flow Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi Total absorption when challenge matches skill. Opponent-process theory Richard Solomon Every emotional state triggers an opposing after-reaction (addiction, thrill). Theory X / Theory Y Douglas McGregor Managers assume workers dislike work and need control (X) or seek responsibility and self-direction (Y). Incentive theory (behaviourist tradition) Behaviour is pulled by external rewards/goals, not just pushed by internal drives. Attribution theory of motivation Bernard Weiner How you explain success/failure (locus × stability × controllability) shapes future emotion & expectancy. 3.3 Emotion theories (the order of events is the trap) Theory Author Sequence James–Lange James & Lange Stimulus → bodily arousal → emotion ("we're afraid because we tremble"). Emotion = reading your own physiology. Cannon–Bard Cannon & Bard Stimulus → arousal and emotion simultaneously (thalamic); body feedback not needed. Schachter–Singer two-factor Schachter & Singer Arousal + cognitive label → emotion (same racing heart becomes fear or excitement by context). Cognitive appraisal Richard Lazarus Appraisal of the event comes first; cognition precedes emotion. Affective primacy Robert Zajonc Emotion can occur before and without cognition ("preferences need no inferences"; mere-exposure is his evidence). Facial-feedback hypothesis Tomkins; Paul Ekman Facial expressions feed back to intensify/trigger the felt emotion. Basic emotions Paul Ekman Six universal, cross-cultural facial emotions. Wheel of emotions Robert Plutchik Eight primary emotions in opposing pairs, combining into others. Trap The classic swap: James-Lange = body first ; Cannon-Bard = both at once ; Schachter-Singer = arousal + label ; Lazarus = appraisal first ; Robert Zajonc = feeling before thinking . Lazarus vs Zajonc is the famous "primacy of cognition vs affect" debate. 3.4 Personality theories Theory Author Core idea Psychoanalytic Sigmund Freud Id/ego/superego; psychosexual stages; unconscious conflict & defences. Analytical psychology Carl Jung Collective unconscious, archetypes, introversion/extraversion. Individual psychology Alfred Adler Inferiority/superiority, striving for superiority, style of life, birth order. Trait (idiographic) Gordon Allport Cardinal/central/secondary traits; functional autonomy. 16PF / factor trait Raymond Cattell 16 source traits via factor analysis; fluid vs crystallised intelligence. PEN model Hans Eysenck Psychoticism, Extraversion, Neuroticism (biological arousal basis). Big Five / Five-Factor (OCEAN) Costa & Robert McCrae Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, Neuroticism. Need-press / personology Henry Murray Needs interact with environmental "press"; gave the TAT. Personal construct theory George Kelly "Man as scientist"; we build bipolar constructs to predict events. Social-cognitive Albert Bandura Reciprocal determinism; self-efficacy. Locus of control / social learning Julian Rotter Behaviour = expectancy × reinforcement value; internal vs external control. Person–situation / CAPS Walter Mischel Behaviour is situation-specific; cognitive-affective system; delay of gratification (marshmallow test). Self theory (humanistic) Carl Rogers Self-concept, congruence, unconditional positive regard, fully-functioning person. Interpersonal theory Harry Stack Sullivan Personality forms in relationships; the self-system (good/bad/not-me). Somatotype theory William Sheldon Endomorph/mesomorph/ectomorph body types map to temperament (Ernst Kretschmer was the precursor). Neurotic needs / basic anxiety Karen Horney Childhood basic anxiety drives 10 neurotic needs, grouped into moving toward / against / away from people. Critiqued Freud's penis envy with "womb envy". Humanistic psychoanalysis Erich Fromm Personality shaped by the need to escape isolation/freedom; character orientations (productive vs non-productive). Psychodynamic–learning (frustration-aggression) Dollard & Miller Recast Freud in learning terms; habit hierarchy; the frustration–aggression hypothesis. 3.5 Developmental theories Theory Author Core idea Cognitive development Jean Piaget 4 stages: sensorimotor, preoperational, concrete & formal operational. Sociocultural Lev Vygotsky Learning is social; ZPD & scaffolding; language drives thought. Psychosocial development Erik Erikson 8 lifespan stages, each a crisis (trust vs mistrust … integrity vs despair). Psychosexual development Sigmund Freud Oral, anal, phallic, latency, genital stages. Moral development Lawrence Kohlberg Pre-conventional → conventional → post-conventional reasoning. Ethic of care Carol Gilligan Critiqued Kohlberg; women reason via care/relationships, not just justice. Ecological systems Urie Bronfenbrenner Micro/meso/exo/macro/chrono systems; later PPCT model. Attachment theory John Bowlby Innate bonding system; secure base; internal working models; maternal deprivation. Strange Situation / styles Mary Ainsworth Secure, anxious-ambivalent, avoidant (Main later: disorganised). Identity statuses James Marcia Diffusion, foreclosure, moratorium, achievement (crisis × commitment). Temperament types Thomas & Chess Easy, difficult, slow-to-warm-up; goodness-of-fit. Maturation theory Arnold Gesell Development unfolds on a biological timetable (norms). Trap Jean Piaget = development drives learning, individual discovery, fixed stages. Lev Vygotsky = learning drives development, social/cultural, ZPD. Erikson's stages (psychosocial, 8 across the lifespan) ≠ Freud's (psychosexual, 5 to puberty). 3.6 Social-psychology theories Theory Author Core idea Cognitive dissonance Leon Festinger Tension from clashing cognitions drives attitude change (usually change the attitude, not the act). Social comparison Leon Festinger We evaluate ourselves by comparing to others when no objective yardstick exists. Attribution theory Fritz Heider We explain behaviour as internal (dispositional) or external (situational); people as naive scientists. Covariation model Harold Kelley Attribution uses consensus, consistency, distinctiveness. Correspondent inference Jones & Davis We infer disposition from freely chosen, unexpected, low-social-desirability acts (non-common effects). Balance theory Fritz Heider We seek consistency among our liking/relationships (P-O-X triangles). Social identity theory Tajfel & Turner Group membership shapes self-concept; in-group favouritism (minimal group paradigm). Realistic conflict theory Muzafer Sherif Competition over scarce resources breeds intergroup hostility; superordinate goals dissolve it (Robbers Cave). Elaboration Likelihood Model Petty & John Cacioppo Persuasion via central (thoughtful, lasting) vs peripheral (cues, weak) route. Yale attitude-change approach Carl Hovland Persuasion mapped by source × message × audience (also gave the sleeper effect, §1.5). Self-perception theory Daryl Bem We infer our own attitudes by observing our behaviour (rival to dissonance). Psychological reactance Jack Brehm (1966) Threatened freedom → wanting the forbidden thing more (engine of reverse psychology). Prof-flagged. Social exchange theory Thibaut & Kelley Relationships weighed by rewards minus costs (comparison level). Equity theory J. S. Adams We want a fair ratio of inputs to outcomes vs others. Bystander effect / diffusion of responsibility Latané & John Darley More witnesses → less help; 5-step decision model (notice → interpret → take responsibility → know how → act). Effect form: §1.3. Social impact theory Bibb Latané Influence of a group = strength × immediacy × number of sources. Frustration–aggression hypothesis John Dollard et al. (rev. Leonard Berkowitz) Frustration breeds aggression; Berkowitz added that aggressive cues are needed. Authoritarian personality (F-scale) Adorno et al. A rigid type that submits to authority and is hostile to out-groups; proposed to explain susceptibility to fascism. Mnemonic Compliance techniques cluster with reactance: foot-in-the-door (Jonathan Freedman & Scott Fraser, small→big), door-in-the-face and low-ball (Robert Cialdini et al.), and Cialdini's 6 principles of influence (reciprocity, commitment/consistency, social proof, authority, liking, scarcity — scarcity works because of reactance). Trap Scenario tell: "told he can't have X, so he wants it more / does it anyway" = reactance (Brehm) . "Tried, failed repeatedly, gave up even when he could win" = learned helplessness (Seligman, §3.10) . Don't swap them. 3.7 Intelligence theories Theory Author Core idea Two-factor (g + s) Charles Spearman A general factor g plus task-specific factors; factor analysis. Primary mental abilities Louis Thurstone 7 independent abilities, no single g . Fluid vs crystallised (Gf-Gc) Raymond Cattell & Horn (→ CHC) Fluid = reasoning power (peaks young); crystallised = accumulated knowledge (holds with age). Structure of intellect J. P. Guilford 180 abilities (operations × content × products); divergent thinking. Multiple intelligences Howard Gardner 8+ independent intelligences (linguistic, musical, bodily-kinesthetic…). Triarchic theory Robert Sternberg Analytical, creative, practical intelligence (also the love triangle). Hierarchical model Philip Vernon g at top → verbal-educational & spatial-mechanical → specifics. Emotional intelligence Peter Salovey & John Mayer (popularised by Daniel Goleman) Perceiving, using, understanding, managing emotion. PASS theory Das, Naglieri & Kirby Intelligence = Planning, Attention, Simultaneous & Successive processing (built on Luria). Three-stratum theory (CHC) John Carroll g at top, 8 broad abilities below, ~70 narrow ones; merged with Cattell-Horn into the CHC model behind modern IQ tests. 3.8 Memory & cognition models Model Author Core idea Multi-store model Atkinson & Richard Shiffrin Sensory → short-term → long-term, linked by attention & rehearsal. Working memory model Baddeley & Hitch Central executive + phonological loop + visuospatial sketchpad (+ episodic buffer). Levels of processing Craik & Robert Lockhart Memory depends on depth of encoding, not a fixed store (effect form: §1.1). Episodic vs semantic memory Endel Tulving Memory for events vs general knowledge (later: procedural; encoding specificity). Dual-coding theory Allan Paivio Verbal + visual codes; images are remembered better (picture superiority, §1.1). Spreading activation Collins & Elizabeth Loftus Semantic network where activating one concept primes related ones. Reconstructive memory / schema theory Frederic Bartlett Memory isn't a recording; we rebuild it to fit our schemas ("War of the Ghosts"). Basis of eyewitness error. 3.9 Language-development theories Theory Author Core idea Behaviourist (learning) B. F. Skinner Language is learned via imitation + reinforcement. Nativist / LAD / Universal Grammar Noam Chomsky Innate language-acquisition device; grammar is hard-wired (rebutted Skinner). Critical period hypothesis Eric Lenneberg Language must be acquired within an early window. Interactionist / LASS Jerome Bruner Social interaction (language acquisition support system) scaffolds language. Linguistic relativity (Sapir–Whorf) Sapir & Benjamin Lee Whorf Language shapes/constrains thought. Cognitive Jean Piaget Language follows cognitive development (thought before language). Trap The famous clash: B. F. Skinner (learned via reinforcement) vs Noam Chomsky (innate LAD/UG). Chomsky's review of Skinner's Verbal Behavior launched the cognitive revolution. 3.10 Stress & abnormal-psychology models Model Author Core idea General Adaptation Syndrome Hans Selye Alarm → resistance → exhaustion response to chronic stress. Transactional model of stress Lazarus & Susan Folkman Stress = primary + secondary appraisal; problem- vs emotion-focused coping. Diathesis–stress model — Disorder arises when a predisposition (diathesis) meets enough stress. Biopsychosocial model George Engel Illness from interacting biological, psychological & social factors. Learned helplessness Seligman & Maier Uncontrollable aversive events → giving up; model of depression. (Later: learned optimism, Martin Seligman.) Cognitive triad Aaron Beck Depression = negative views of self, world & future; schemas. ABC model Albert Ellis Activating event → Belief → Consequence; irrational beliefs drive distress (REBT). Hopelessness theory Abramson, Metalsky & Alloy Reformulated helplessness: a depressive attributional style. 3.11 Perception theories Theory Author Core idea Gestalt Max Wertheimer, Kurt Koffka, Wolfgang Köhler The whole is organised by grouping laws (Prägnanz). Principles in §2.2. Direct / ecological perception James Gibson Bottom-up: the optic array provides enough info directly (affordances). Constructivist perception Richard Gregory Top-down: perception is hypothesis-testing from prior knowledge. Feature-integration theory Anne Treisman Features detected in parallel; attention binds them into objects. Signal detection theory Green & Swets Detection = sensitivity (d′) + response criterion (bias), not a fixed threshold. 3.12 Career & counselling theories Theory Author Core idea RIASEC / vocational types John Holland Match person type to work environment (Realistic, Investigative, Artistic, Social, Enterprising, Conventional). Life-span, life-space Donald Super Career develops across life stages; self-concept implemented in work. Developmental career choice Eli Ginzberg Occupational choice as a developmental process (fantasy → tentative → realistic). Social learning / happenstance John Krumboltz Career shaped by learning experiences and planned chance. Needs theory of career Anne Roe Early parent-child climate shapes person-oriented vs non-person-oriented careers. Circumscription & compromise Linda Gottfredson Children narrow options by gender, then prestige, then interests; compromise when reality bites. 4. Named complexes & syndromes The eponym family NIMHANS loves. Same "name → who → what" format. The three at the top of the trap box were specifically flagged by Sihan's professor. Trap Prof-flagged, lock these cold. Icarus complex = Henry Murray. McCall's T score = William McCall (mean 50, SD 10; §6 — recognise it from the definition ; the trap is Student's t, a test statistic by Gosset). Psychological reactance = Jack Brehm (§3.6 — recognise it from a scenario ). Two question shapes: "who coined this named complex" AND "here's a phenomenon described in words, name it." Complex / syndrome Who What it is Icarus complex Henry Murray Soaring ambition + craving for attention/admiration ending in a fall; fascination with fire, ascent, falling, narcissism. (Same Murray who gave the TAT, needs/press, personology — §5.) Jonah complex Abraham Maslow Fear of your own greatness; running from self-actualisation (opposite flavour to Icarus). Inferiority / superiority complex Alfred Adler Core of Adlerian theory; overcompensation for felt inferiority. Oedipus / Electra complex Sigmund Freud (Oedipus); Carl Jung coined Electra Phallic-stage attachment to the opposite-sex parent. Cinderella complex Colette Dowling Unconscious wish to be taken care of / fear of independence. Peter Pan syndrome Dan Kiley Adult who refuses to grow up. (Kiley also: Wendy syndrome , the over-mothering partner.) Diogenes syndrome Clark et al. Senile self-neglect, squalor, hoarding, social withdrawal. Othello syndrome John Todd Delusional / morbid jealousy of a partner. Munchausen syndrome Richard Asher Feigning illness for the sick role (factitious disorder). Couvade syndrome — Father develops pregnancy symptoms ("sympathetic pregnancy"). Stockholm syndrome Nils Bejerot (named it) Captive bonds with the captor. Trap Complex ownership: inferiority/superiority = Alfred Adler ; womb envy = Karen Horney ; Electra = Carl Jung (named it), Oedipus = Sigmund Freud; Jonah = Abraham Maslow ; Icarus = Murray . Don't default everything to Freud. 5. Who originated what — theorists The reverse drill: name → what they own . For a person you'll meet here, the named effect, theory or complex they coined is defined in §§1–4; this section bundles each theorist so one concept pulls the whole name up. The distractor is always a same-field contemporary. 5.1 Psychoanalytic & neo-Freudian Theorist What they own Sigmund Freud Psychoanalysis; id/ego/superego; psychosexual stages; defence mechanisms; the unconscious; dream interpretation; Oedipus complex; free association & transference. Carl Jung Analytical psychology; collective unconscious; archetypes; introversion/extraversion; coined the Electra complex; word-association. Alfred Adler Individual psychology; inferiority/superiority complex; striving for superiority; style of life; birth order; social interest. Karen Horney Basic anxiety; moving toward/against/away from people; womb envy (reply to penis envy); neurotic needs. Erik Erikson 8 psychosocial stages; identity crisis; ego psychology. Erich Fromm Escape from Freedom; character orientations; humanistic psychoanalysis. Harry Stack Sullivan Interpersonal theory; the self-system; good-me / bad-me / not-me. Melanie Klein Object relations; play therapy; paranoid-schizoid & depressive positions. Anna Freud Child psychoanalysis; systematised the defence mechanisms. D. W. Winnicott Good-enough mother; transitional object; holding environment; true/false self. Heinz Kohut Self psychology; narcissism; empathic mirroring. 5.2 Humanistic, existential & trait theorists Theorist What they own Abraham Maslow Hierarchy of needs; self-actualisation; peak experiences; Jonah complex. Carl Rogers Person-centred therapy; self-concept; congruence; unconditional positive regard; fully-functioning person; real vs ideal self. Gordon Allport Cardinal/central/secondary traits; functional autonomy (a motive outliving its original cause); idiographic approach; contact hypothesis. Raymond Cattell 16PF; source vs surface traits; fluid vs crystallised intelligence; factor analysis of personality. Hans Eysenck PEN model; biological/arousal basis of personality (introverts over-aroused, extraverts under-aroused). Costa & Robert McCrae Big Five / NEO-PI (OCEAN). Henry Murray Personology; needs & press; the TAT (with Morgan); Icarus complex; nAch roots. George Kelly Personal construct theory; Rep grid; "man as scientist." Julian Rotter Locus of control (internal/external); social learning; expectancy × reinforcement value. Walter Mischel Person–situation debate; CAPS; the marshmallow test (delay of gratification). Rollo May / Viktor Frankl Existential psychology; May (anxiety/the daimonic); Frankl (logotherapy, meaning, paradoxical intention). William Sheldon Somatotypes (endo/meso/ectomorph). Ernst Kretschmer Body-build → temperament types (pyknic/asthenic/athletic); precursor to Sheldon. 5.3 Behaviourist & learning theorists Theorist What they own Ivan Pavlov Classical conditioning; the salivating dogs. John B. Watson Founded behaviourism; Little Albert; "give me a dozen healthy infants…". B. F. Skinner Operant conditioning; reinforcement schedules; Skinner box; verbal behaviour; radical behaviourism. Edward Thorndike Law of Effect; connectionism; puzzle box; the halo effect. Edward Tolman Latent learning; cognitive maps; purposive behaviourism. Wolfgang Köhler Insight learning (chimps); Gestalt; the bouba/kiki demo. Albert Bandura Social learning; Bobo doll; self-efficacy; reciprocal determinism. Edwin Guthrie Contiguity theory (one-trial learning). Clark Hull Drive-reduction theory; mathematico-deductive behaviourism. Joseph Wolpe Systematic desensitisation; reciprocal inhibition. Mnemonic The animal-study set: dogs = Ivan Pavlov ; cats/puzzle box = Edward Thorndike ; chimps/insight = Wolfgang Köhler ; monkeys/contact comfort = Harry Harlow ; rats/cognitive maps = Edward Tolman ; Bobo doll = Albert Bandura ; Little Albert = John B. Watson . 5.4 Cognitive & developmental theorists Theorist What they own Jean Piaget Cognitive-development stages; schemas; assimilation/accommodation; object permanence; conservation. Lev Vygotsky Sociocultural theory; ZPD; scaffolding; private speech. Jerome Bruner Discovery learning; spiral curriculum; enactive/iconic/symbolic; LASS. Lawrence Kohlberg Stages of moral development. Urie Bronfenbrenner Ecological systems; PPCT model. John Bowlby Attachment theory; maternal deprivation; internal working models. Mary Ainsworth Strange Situation; secure/anxious/avoidant attachment. Harry Harlow Rhesus monkeys; contact comfort over food (wire vs cloth mother). Noam Chomsky Universal grammar; LAD; rebutted B. F. Skinner; cognitive revolution. Ulric Neisser "Cognitive Psychology" (named the field); ecological memory. Endel Tulving Episodic vs semantic memory; encoding specificity. Baddeley & Hitch Working-memory model. Elizabeth Loftus Misinformation effect; eyewitness memory; false memories. 5.5 Social psychologists Theorist What they own Leon Festinger Cognitive dissonance; social comparison; deindividuation roots. Kurt Lewin Father of social psych; field theory; B = f(P,E); action research; group dynamics. Solomon Asch Conformity (line task); impression formation (central traits). Stanley Milgram Obedience to authority; small-world / six degrees. Philip Zimbardo Stanford prison experiment; deindividuation; the Lucifer effect. Muzafer Sherif Realistic conflict; Robbers Cave; autokinetic norm formation. Fritz Heider Attribution theory; balance theory. Harold Kelley Covariation model (consensus, consistency, distinctiveness); social exchange (with John Thibaut). Jones & Davis Correspondent inference theory. Lee Ross Coined the fundamental attribution error; false-consensus effect. Bernard Weiner Attribution theory of motivation (locus × stability × controllability). Tajfel & Turner Social identity theory; minimal group paradigm. Irving Janis Groupthink. Latané & John Darley Bystander effect; diffusion of responsibility; Bibb Latané's social impact theory. Carl Hovland Yale attitude-change approach; the sleeper effect. Petty & John Cacioppo Elaboration Likelihood Model. Daryl Bem Self-perception theory. Robert Cialdini Six principles of influence; door-in-the-face & low-ball. Jack Brehm Psychological reactance. Adorno et al. Authoritarian personality (F-scale). Norman Triplett First social-psych experiment → social facilitation. 5.6 Intelligence & testing Theorist What they own Alfred Binet First practical intelligence test (with Simon); mental age. Lewis Terman Stanford-Binet; longitudinal study of gifted children ("Termites"); popularised the ratio IQ. David Wechsler WAIS/WISC; deviation IQ (mean 100, SD 15). Charles Spearman Two-factor theory; g ; factor analysis (stats role in §6). Louis Thurstone Primary mental abilities; attitude scaling (equal-appearing intervals). J. P. Guilford Structure of intellect; divergent thinking. Howard Gardner Multiple intelligences. Robert Sternberg Triarchic theory; love triangle. Salovey & Mayer Emotional intelligence (Daniel Goleman popularised). Hermann Rorschach The inkblot test. William Stern Ratio IQ (MA/CA × 100). Trap CBT-family ownership (therapy founders in §5.7): cognitive triad & cognitive therapy = Beck ; REBT & ABC = Albert Ellis ; DBT = Marsha Linehan ; ACT = Hayes . Beck and Ellis are the constant distractor pair. 5.7 Therapy founders Founder Therapy Sigmund Freud Psychoanalysis (free association, transference). Aaron Beck Cognitive therapy / CBT; cognitive triad. Albert Ellis REBT; ABC model; irrational beliefs. Carl Rogers Person-centred / client-centred therapy. Fritz Perls Gestalt therapy; empty chair; here-and-now. Joseph Wolpe Systematic desensitisation; behaviour therapy. Viktor Frankl Logotherapy (meaning); paradoxical intention. William Glasser Reality therapy; choice theory. Marsha Linehan Dialectical behaviour therapy (DBT). Steven Hayes Acceptance & commitment therapy (ACT). Eric Berne Transactional analysis (Parent-Adult-Child). Salvador Minuchin Structural family therapy. Jacob Moreno Psychodrama; group psychotherapy; the term "group therapy." Irvin Yalom Existential & group therapy; 11 therapeutic factors. Francine Shapiro EMDR. 6. Psychometrics, statistics & standard scores The "who gave what" layer NIMHANS bolts onto the clinical material: measurement terms, statistical tests, and the standard-score family. Two of the three prof-flagged curveballs (McCall's T, Student's t) live here. 6.1 Psychometrics & measurement terms Term Originator What it is T score (mean 50, SD 10) William McCall A standard score rescaled to mean 50, SD 10, killing negatives and decimals. MMPI reports it. This is the McCall's T the prof asked. Factor analysis, g , two-factor theory Charles Spearman Invented factor analysis; argued intelligence is one general factor (g) plus specific factors. Spearman–Brown prophecy formula; rank correlation (rho) Spearman Predicts how reliability rises with test length; rho correlates two sets of ranks. Coefficient (Cronbach's) alpha Lee Cronbach Standard index of internal consistency (items hang together). Above ~0.7 acceptable. Construct validity (the paper) Cronbach & Paul Meehl A test is valid if it behaves the way the underlying construct theoretically should. KR-20 / KR-21 Kuder & Richardson Internal-consistency formulas for right/wrong (dichotomous) items; special case of alpha. Kappa (inter-rater); Cohen's d (effect size) Jacob Cohen Kappa = chance-corrected rater agreement; d = mean difference in SD units (0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large); statistical power. Product-moment correlation (r); chi-square Karl Pearson r = strength/direction of a linear relationship (−1 to +1); standard deviation term. Correlation concept; regression to the mean Francis Galton First conceived correlation; regression to the mean; eugenics; first mental tests. Likert (summative agree–disagree) scale Rensis Likert Strongly-agree-to-strongly-disagree; sum item scores. Treated as interval-ish. Equal-appearing intervals; law of comparative judgment; PMA Louis Thurstone Attitude scales with judged equal intervals; argued for several primary mental abilities, not one g. Guttman scalogram (cumulative scaling) Louis Guttman Agreeing with a strong item implies agreeing with all weaker ones; score pins your exact pattern. Semantic differential Charles Osgood Rate a concept between bipolar adjective pairs; dimensions = evaluation, potency, activity. Multitrait–multimethod matrix; convergent/discriminant validity Campbell & Fiske A grid checking a test correlates with same-trait measures (convergent) but not different ones (discriminant). Item Response Theory / Rasch model Georg Rasch (IRT also Lord & Novick) Models a correct answer from person ability and item difficulty on one scale (basis of adaptive testing). Critical incident technique John Flanagan Collect real examples of effective/ineffective behaviour to define what a job requires. Ratio IQ (MA/CA × 100) William Stern (popularised by Lewis Terman) Old IQ = mental age ÷ chronological age × 100; breaks down in adulthood, replaced by deviation IQ. Deviation IQ (mean 100, SD 15) David Wechsler Modern IQ: standing relative to your age group on a normal curve. 6.2 Statistical tests & who gave them High-yield Student's t = William Sealy Gosset. "Student" is a pseudonym , not a person. Gosset worked at the Guinness brewery in Dublin and published the t-test in 1908 under the pen name because Guinness barred staff from publishing. "Who was Student / who gave the t-test" → Gosset. The t-test compares means when the sample is small and the population SD is unknown . Test Who gave it What it's for Student's t-test / t-distribution W. S. Gosset ("Student", 1908) Compare means, small n, σ unknown. Flavours: one-sample (df = n−1), independent two-sample (df = n₁+n₂−2), paired (before/after, same people). ANOVA / F-test Ronald Fisher (the F named for Fisher by Snedecor) Compare 3+ group means at once. F = between-group var ÷ within-group var. Also: null hypothesis, p < .05, experimental design. Chi-square (χ²) Karl Pearson Association / goodness-of-fit for categorical data. Pearson r Karl Pearson Linear correlation, interval data. Spearman rho (ρ) Charles Spearman Rank correlation (ordinal / non-normal). Mann–Whitney U Mann & Whitney Nonparametric twin of the independent t (two unrelated groups). Wilcoxon signed-rank Frank Wilcoxon Nonparametric twin of the paired t. Kruskal–Wallis H Kruskal & Wallis Nonparametric twin of one-way ANOVA. Friedman test Milton Friedman Nonparametric repeated-measures ANOVA. McNemar test Quinn McNemar Paired nominal data (before/after yes-no). Trap "Student" is Gosset , not a real student, and McCall's T (a standard score) ≠ Student's t (a test statistic) — the shared letter is the bait. 2 groups → t-test; 3+ groups → ANOVA (don't run repeated t-tests). Parametric → nonparametric: independent t → Mann–Whitney , paired t → Wilcoxon , one-way ANOVA → Kruskal–Wallis . F-test/ANOVA = Fisher ; chi-square = Pearson . Definition t vs z: use z when the population SD is known and/or n is large; use t when SD is estimated from a small sample. As df → ∞ the t-distribution becomes the normal (z) curve. t is shorter and fatter-tailed than z. 6.3 The standard-score family (so McCall's T sits in context) Score Mean SD Note z-score 0 1 The base; everything else is a rescaled z. T score (McCall) 50 10 No negatives, no decimals needed; MMPI uses T. Stanine 5 ~2 1–9 scale ("standard nine"). Sten 5.5 2 1–10 ("standard ten"); used in 16PF. Deviation IQ 100 15 Wechsler (Stanford-Binet SD 16). Wechsler scaled (subtest) 10 3 Each subtest; sum → index/IQ. SD 3 is a common distractor. Wechsler index 100 15 VCI, PRI/WMI, PSI etc. NCE (normal-curve equiv.) 50 21.06 Looks like a percentile but is equal-interval; matches percentile at 1, 50, 99. Percentile rank — — Not equal-interval; bunches near the mean. Don't average percentiles. Definition Conversion you can be asked: T = 50 + 10z. So z = +1 → T = 60; z = −2 → T = 30. MMPI clinical-range cut is usually T ≥ 65 . Linear T = rescaled z (keeps the shape); normalised T = forced to a normal curve via percentile→z first. Both still mean 50, SD 10.

title: Lookalikes — telling two close terms apart on the options
text: Lookalikes — telling two close terms apart on the options For when plain definitions aren't enough and the trap is a near-identical distractor. Each block is one confusable pair: what's the same (why both look right), what differs (line by line), and the one tell — the single thing in the stem that splits them. Read the tell, not the whole block, on exam day. Built 2026-05-25. Effects Phenomena Theories Theorists Social Psych Cognitive Lookalikes How to use it. The examiner picks two real, correct-sounding terms and bets you can't split them. Don't re-derive both definitions. Find the tell word in the stem (added vs removed? up vs down? before vs after? thought vs act?) and the option falls out. These are the pairs that actually bleed marks on MET/NIMHANS. Jump to: 1. Learning & conditioning 2. Developmental 3. Sensation & perception 4. Memory & cognition 5. Stats & research 6. Abnormal / clinical 7. Defense mechanisms 8. Therapy 9. Social 10. Intelligence 1. Learning & conditioning Classical conditioning vs Operant conditioning Same: both are associative learning; both show acquisition, extinction, spontaneous recovery, generalisation and discrimination. Classical (Ivan Pavlov) Operant (B. F. Skinner) Behaviour Involuntary, reflexive (salivation, fear) Voluntary, emitted (lever press) Association Stimulus → stimulus (CS–US) Behaviour → consequence (response–reinforcer) Learner Passive, responds to a cue Active, operates on the environment Reinforcer timing Comes before/with the response Comes after the response The tell: Is the behaviour automatic and triggered by a cue that comes first (classical), or voluntary and shaped by what happens after (operant)? Any "reward / consequence / punishment" in the stem → operant. Negative reinforcement vs Punishment Same: both are operant procedures and both usually involve an aversive/unpleasant stimulus, so they read alike. Negative reinforcement Punishment Effect on behaviour Increases it Decreases it What happens Removes an aversive stimulus (take painkiller → pain gone) Adds aversive (positive) or removes pleasant (negative) "Negative" means Subtraction, not "bad" — The tell: Did the behaviour go up or down ? Up = reinforcement (negative = the bad thing was taken away ). Down = punishment. "Negative" is about removal, never about being unpleasant. Positive punishment vs Negative punishment Same: both decrease a behaviour. Positive punishment Negative punishment Operation Add something aversive (scolding, spanking) Remove something pleasant (take phone, time-out, fine) Other name — Response cost / omission The tell: Positive = something was added ; negative = something was taken away . Both still reduce the behaviour, so judge by add vs subtract, not by good vs bad. Primary reinforcer vs Secondary reinforcer Same: both strengthen behaviour when they follow it. Primary Secondary (conditioned) Why it reinforces Innately satisfies a biological need (food, water, sex, warmth) Learned value through association Learning needed? No Yes (money, tokens, praise, grades) The tell: Does it satisfy a body need directly (primary) or only because you learned it stands for something else (secondary)? Money is the classic secondary reinforcer. Shaping vs Chaining Same: both build complex operant behaviour using reinforcement. Shaping Chaining What's reinforced Successive approximations to one target behaviour Linking a sequence of already-learned behaviours Picture it Refining one act closer and closer Step 1 → step 2 → step 3 as a chain The tell: One behaviour polished step-by-step (shaping) vs several separate behaviours joined in order (chaining). Stimulus generalisation vs Stimulus discrimination Same: both describe how a conditioned response transfers (or doesn't) across stimuli. Generalisation Discrimination Response to similar cues Yes — spreads to stimuli like the CS No — only the exact CS triggers it Little Albert (John B. Watson and Rosalie Rayner, 1920) Feared all furry white things Would fear only the rat The tell: Response spreads to lookalikes (generalisation) vs narrows to one exact cue (discrimination). 2. Developmental Assimilation vs Accommodation (Jean Piaget) Same: the twin processes of adaptation ; both are how a schema deals with new information. Assimilation Accommodation Schema Stays the same — new info forced into it Changes / a new one is created to fit reality Example Calls a whale a "fish" Learns a whale is a mammal, makes a new category The tell: Did the existing schema stay put (assimilation) or did it have to change (accommodation)? If the child updated their mental category, it's accommodation. Piaget vs Lev Vygotsky Same: both constructivists; both say the child actively builds knowledge rather than passively absorbing it. Piaget Vygotsky Engine of development The individual child exploring; cognition leads language Social/cultural interaction; language leads cognition Signature terms Stages, schema, assimilation/accommodation, egocentrism ZPD, scaffolding, More Knowledgeable Other, private speech The tell: Is the driver the child alone (Piaget) or a guiding social other / ZPD (Vygotsky)? Any "scaffolding" or "zone of proximal development" → Vygotsky. 3. Sensation & perception Sensation vs Perception Same: both are stages of taking in stimulus information. Sensation Perception What it is Raw detection by sense organs + transduction Brain's organisation & interpretation of it Direction Bottom-up (data in) Top-down (meaning added) The tell: Detecting the raw signal at the receptor (sensation) vs making sense of / recognising it (perception). Interpretation, meaning, recognition → perception. Absolute threshold vs Difference threshold (JND) Same: both are psychophysics thresholds (Weber/Fechner). Absolute threshold Difference threshold (JND) Detects Minimum intensity to detect a stimulus 50% of the time Smallest detectable change between two stimuli Law — Weber's law: JND is a constant proportion The tell: Detecting that one stimulus is present (absolute) vs detecting a difference between two (difference / JND). "Just noticeable difference" → difference threshold. 4. Memory & cognition Proactive interference vs Retroactive interference Same: both are forgetting caused by interference between old and new learning. Proactive Retroactive Direction Old blocks new (forward) New blocks old (backward) What you forget The new material The old material Example Old password keeps coming up New password wipes the old one The tell: Which is forgotten? Forget the new → proactive (" pro = prior learning interferes forward"). Forget the old → retroactive. Recall vs Recognition Same: both are measures of retrieval from long-term memory. Recall Recognition Task Produce the info with little/no cue (essay, free recall) Identify the correct item among options (MCQ) Difficulty Harder Easier — the answer is in front of you The tell: Generate it from scratch (recall) vs pick it out of choices (recognition). A multiple-choice exam tests recognition. Anterograde amnesia vs Retrograde amnesia Same: both are memory loss, usually after brain injury, defined relative to the moment of injury. Anterograde Retrograde Lost memories Can't form new memories after the event Lost old memories from before the event Time direction Forward from injury Backward from injury The tell: " Antero = after" — no new memories form. Retrograde = the past is gone. (H.M. (studied by William Scoville and Brenda Milner, 1957) = classic anterograde.) Explicit (declarative) vs Implicit (non-declarative) memory Same: both are long-term memory systems. Explicit / declarative Implicit / non-declarative Awareness Conscious — you can state it Unconscious — shows in performance Contents Facts (semantic) + events (episodic) Skills (procedural), priming, conditioning The tell: Can you consciously declare it (explicit) or does it just show up as a skill/habit (implicit)? Riding a bike = implicit/procedural. 5. Stats & research methods Type I error vs Type II error Same: both are wrong decisions in null-hypothesis testing. Type I (α) Type II (β) Mistake Reject a true null = false positive Fail to reject a false null = false negative In words Claim an effect that isn't there Miss a real effect The tell: False alarm = Type I (α). Miss = Type II (β). "Type I = I see something that isn't there." Reliability vs Validity Same: both are desirable psychometric properties of a test or measure. Reliability Validity Question it answers Is it consistent / repeatable? Does it measure what it's supposed to? Relationship Can be reliable but not valid (consistently wrong) Validity requires reliability, not vice versa The tell: Consistency = reliability; accuracy/measures-the-right-thing = validity. Same spot every time = reliable; the bullseye = valid. Independent variable vs Dependent variable Same: both are the variables defined in an experiment. Independent (IV) Dependent (DV) Role Manipulated — the presumed cause Measured — the outcome (depends on the IV) The tell: What the experimenter changes = IV; what they measure as the result = DV. 6. Abnormal / clinical Delusion vs Hallucination Same: both are psychotic symptoms; both appear in schizophrenia. Delusion Hallucination Disturbance of Thought content — a false, fixed belief Perception — a false sensory experience Example "The FBI is tracking me" Hearing voices with no one there The tell: A wrong belief (delusion) vs a wrong perception (hallucination). If there's a sensory experience, it's a hallucination. Illusion vs Hallucination Same: both are perceptual disturbances. Illusion Hallucination External stimulus? Yes — a real stimulus is misperceived No — perception with no stimulus at all Example A shadow looks like an intruder Seeing a person who isn't there The tell: Is there a real object being misread (illusion) or nothing there to begin with (hallucination)? Obsession vs Compulsion Same: both are core to OCD; both are distressing and unwanted. Obsession Compulsion Type Intrusive thought , image or urge (mental) Repetitive act or ritual (behaviour) Function Causes the anxiety Done to relieve the anxiety The tell: The thought that intrudes (obsession) vs the act done to neutralise it (compulsion). Hand-washing = compulsion; the fear of germs = obsession. Affect vs Mood Same: both describe emotional state in a mental status exam. Affect Mood Timescale Momentary, observable expression Sustained, pervasive feeling Analogy The weather The climate The tell: Short-term, outwardly observed = affect; sustained, subjectively reported = mood. Delirium vs Dementia Same: both cause cognitive impairment and confusion, often in older patients. Delirium Dementia Onset Acute, fluctuating (hours–days) Gradual, progressive (months–years) Consciousness Clouded, attention impaired Clear early; memory leads Reversible? Usually yes Usually no The tell: Sudden onset + fluctuating + altered consciousness = delirium. Slow, progressive, alert = dementia. Neurosis vs Psychosis Same: both are older umbrella categories of mental disorder. Neurosis Psychosis Reality contact Intact — insight present Lost — no insight Examples Anxiety, phobia, OCD Schizophrenia, delusional disorder The tell: Is reality testing intact with insight (neurosis) or broken (psychosis)? Delusions/hallucinations → psychosis. Positive vs Negative symptoms (schizophrenia) Same: both are symptom clusters of schizophrenia. Positive Negative Nature Added to normal experience Loss / absence of normal function Examples Hallucinations, delusions, disorganised speech Flat affect, alogia, avolition, anhedonia The tell: Excess / something added = positive; deficit / something missing = negative. 7. Defense mechanisms Repression vs Suppression Same: both push distressing material out of awareness. Repression Suppression Awareness Unconscious, involuntary Conscious, deliberate The tell: Done unknowingly (repression) vs on purpose (suppression). "Decided not to think about it" = suppression. Displacement vs Sublimation Same: both redirect an unacceptable impulse onto a new target. Displacement Sublimation New target A safer but still similar target A socially valued, productive outlet Example Yell at the kids instead of the boss Channel aggression into sport or surgery The tell: Just a safer target (displacement) vs a constructive, socially-approved channel (sublimation). Sublimation is the mature one. Projection vs Reaction formation Same: both defend against one's own unacceptable feelings. Projection Reaction formation Strategy Attribute your impulse to someone else Act the opposite of your impulse Example "He hates me" (when you hate him) Hating someone → being overly nice to them The tell: Pin the feeling on someone else (projection) vs flip to the opposite behaviour (reaction formation). 8. Therapy Transference vs Countertransference Same: both are displaced feelings inside the psychodynamic therapeutic relationship. Transference Countertransference Whose feelings The client's , redirected onto the therapist The therapist's , redirected onto the client The tell: Client → therapist = transference. Therapist → client = countertransference. 9. Social Conformity vs Compliance vs Obedience Same: all three are behaviour change due to social influence. Conformity Compliance Obedience Source of pressure Implicit group norm A direct request An order from authority Study Solomon Asch (lines) Foot-in-the-door (Jonathan Freedman and Scott Fraser, 1966) Stanley Milgram (shocks) The tell: Group norm with no one asking (conformity) vs someone requests (compliance) vs an authority commands (obedience). Stereotype vs Prejudice vs Discrimination Same: all three are components of intergroup bias and constantly swapped in options. Stereotype Prejudice Discrimination Component (ABC) Cognition — a belief Affect — a negative attitude Behaviour — an action The tell: Thought = stereotype, feeling = prejudice, action = discrimination. Map it to A ffect / B ehaviour / C ognition. 10. Intelligence Fluid intelligence vs Crystallised intelligence (Raymond Cattell) Same: both are Cattell's components of general intelligence (Gf–Gc). Fluid (Gf) Crystallised (Gc) What it is Reasoning with novel problems, independent of knowledge Accumulated knowledge, vocabulary, learned skills With age Declines earlier Holds up / keeps rising The tell: On-the-spot novel reasoning (fluid) vs stored, learned knowledge (crystallised). If age makes it better , it's crystallised. That's the lookalikes set. If a pair you keep missing isn't here, send it and I'll add a block. Related sweeps: Phenomena , Effects , Theories , Theorists . Sihan MET 2026 + NIMHANS prep · /notes/differentiators/ · built 2026-05-25

title: The Textbook — Everything in One Page
text: The Textbook — Everything in One Page Your single self-contained source. Built 2026-05-22, the night before MET. This is the one page. Read it top to bottom and you have read everything. Every list, definition, table, trap box and concept you have ever been given is inlined here, organised by your 8 exam sections, with a ★C common-section concept pack right at the top (the high-yield general psych that section hammers, the foundations and the confusable pairs that quietly cost marks), plus a §9 rapid-recall sweep (the easily-forgotten names/durations and the general-psych foundations) at the end, so it reads like your own textbook. There are no links out to other pages, nothing to chase, all the content lives right here. Study from this page only tonight. Sections are folded so it isn't a wall of text: tap any one to open it, or hit Expand all to read straight through. Jump to ★ Your mock misses, fixed ★C. Common-section concept pack 1. Biopsychology / Neuro 2. Developmental 3. Abnormal 4. Assessment / Tests 5. Psychotherapy / Learning / Ethics 6. Research / Biostats 7. Language 8. Social / Memory / Acts / Founders 9. Rapid Recall (easily forgotten + general psych) Exam-day rules Expand all Collapse all Tap a section to open it. Everything is still here, just folded away. ★ Your mock misses, fixed here Every question you got wrong, guessed, or flagged on the real NIMHANS 2024 PYQ mock (91.25/100) maps to a block below. If you only have an hour, read these rows, then read the red trap boxes. What tripped you The fix Section WAIS scaled score of 10 = ? Exactly average, 50th percentile (subtest mean 10, SD 3) Biostats WAIS-IV core subtest NOT in WISC-V Letter-Number Sequencing (WAIS-IV WMI core; WISC-V uses Picture Span instead) Assessment IQ test = which kind of test? Ability test (maximum performance). Not power, not speed. Assessment Bystander effect explained by… Diffusion of responsibility (John Darley and Bibb Latané, 1968) + pluralistic ignorance Social Mania NOT first-line drug Fluoxetine (an SSRI; can trigger a manic switch) Neuro BPD feature NOT in NPD Pervasive instability of relationships + self-image Abnormal "Real relationship" + UPR over "alliance" Person-centred (Carl Rogers) Therapy Kohut / self-psychology / "mirroring" Failure of parental mirroring → grandiosity; mirroring + idealizing failure → fragmented self Therapy What is ataxia vs apraxia? Ataxia = loss of coordination/balance ; apraxia = can't sequence learned movements Neuro Who is Kitty Genovese? 1964 NYC murder, allegedly many witnesses, none helped → launched bystander research Social Type D personality (Johan Denollet)? Negative affectivity + social inhibition ; poor cardiac prognosis Abnormal Escape vs avoidance learning Escape terminates an aversive stimulus already on; avoidance prevents its onset Therapy Object relations meaning Internalised mental representations of self and others Therapy Memory: what/where/when of an event Episodic memory Memory Spearman → factor analysis, Wilhelm Wundt → ? Introspection (structuralism's method) Founders MHCA 2017 + minors Minor can appoint a nominated representative; views considered age-appropriately Acts OR / RR of 1 No association. >1 increased risk, <1 protective Biostats NNT 1 / ARR. Lower NNT = better drug Biostats "Data" singular or plural? Plural in formal use ("data are…"); datum is singular Language ★C. Common-Section Concept Pack high-yield general psych · the foundations · the bits that quietly cost marks This is the section that is bleeding your marks. The subject blocks above are your strong ground; the common section is general psychology, and it punishes shaky foundations and confusable pairs more than raw facts. So this pack is built differently: every block ends in the exact distinction the examiner uses to separate the two options that look identical. Read it for the contrasts, not the trivia. If you can run the cover-and-test set at the very end (C.11) clean, the common section stops costing you. C.1 The schools of psychology (the "isms"), in order Almost every general paper has one "who founded / what method / which school" item. Learn them as a story: each school is a reaction to the one before it. School Core claim Method Key names Structuralism Break consciousness into its basic elements (sensations, feelings) Introspection Wilhelm Wundt (first lab, 1879), Edward Titchener Functionalism Why does the mind do what it does; its purpose and adaptation Observation, applied focus William James, Dewey, Angell Gestalt The whole is different from the sum of its parts; perception is organised Phenomenology Max Wertheimer, Kurt Koffka, Wolfgang Köhler Psychoanalysis Behaviour is driven by the unconscious and early conflict Free association, dream analysis, case study Sigmund Freud, later Jung, Alfred Adler Behaviourism Study only observable behaviour; the mind is a black box Controlled experiment, conditioning John B. Watson, Ivan Pavlov, Skinner, Edward Thorndike Humanistic People are growth-oriented and free; the "third force" Phenomenology, client report Maslow, Carl Rogers Cognitive Mind as an information processor; mental processes are real and studiable Experiment, modelling, reaction time Ulric Neisser (coined it, 1967), Miller, Donald Broadbent Biological Behaviour reduces to brain, neurochemistry, genes Lesion, imaging, twin studies Sperry, Hebb Evolutionary Behaviour was selected because it aided survival/reproduction Cross-species, adaptationist reasoning Buss, Tooby & Cosmides Positive Study strengths, well-being and flourishing, not just pathology Empirical, intervention trials Seligman, Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi TRAP: Wilhelm Wundt = structuralism + introspection (the first lab). James = functionalism . Ulric Neisser = cognitive . John B. Watson named behaviourism but Wundt is "father of experimental psychology"; Kurt Lewin is "father of social psychology"; Wundt is NOT a functionalist. Gestalt is a perception school, not a therapy (do not confuse it with Perls' Gestalt therapy ). C.2 Sensation vs perception, and psychophysics Sensation = the raw signal a receptor sends up (bottom-up). Perception = the brain organising and interpreting it (adds top-down expectation, context, schema). Same retinal image, two perceptions = perception > sensation. Absolute threshold: the smallest intensity detectable 50% of the time. Difference threshold = JND (just noticeable difference): the smallest change you can detect 50% of the time. Sensory adaptation: constant unchanging stimulus, receptors stop responding (you stop feeling your watch). Law What it says The hook Weber's law The JND is a constant proportion of the original stimulus, not a fixed amount Add 1 candle to 1, you notice; add 1 to 100, you do not Fechner's law Sensation grows with the logarithm of stimulus intensity Built psychophysics on Weber's finding Stevens' power law Sensation is a power function of intensity (fits more senses than Fechner) The modern refinement Signal Detection Theory (David Green and John Swets, 1966): detection is not just sensitivity, it is a decision. Four outcomes: Hit (signal there, said yes), Miss (signal there, said no), False alarm (no signal, said yes), Correct rejection (no signal, said no). d′ = true sensitivity; the criterion (β) = how willing you are to say "yes". A tired or motivated observer shifts criterion, not sensitivity. TRAP: Weber = constant ratio (JND). Fechner = log . Do not say Weber gives a fixed amount. SDT separates sensitivity (d′) from response bias (criterion); a question about "willingness to report" is about the criterion, not d′. C.3 Gestalt organisation, constancies, depth cues Gestalt grouping laws: figure-ground (Edgar Rubin, 1915), proximity (near things group), similarity (alike things group), closure (fill the gap), continuity / good continuation (smooth lines), common fate (things moving together group), Prägnanz (we see the simplest possible form). The umbrella principle is Prägnanz, "the law of good figure". Perceptual constancies: size, shape, colour, brightness stay stable even as the retinal image changes. A door is still rectangular when open (shape constancy). Depth cues: binocular = retinal disparity + convergence (need both eyes, work near). Monocular = relative size, interposition/overlap, linear perspective, texture gradient, aerial perspective, motion parallax, light & shadow (work with one eye, mostly for distance). TRAP: Retinal disparity and convergence are the only two binocular cues; everything else is monocular. Motion parallax is monocular even though it sounds complex. C.4 Learning: the distinctions that quietly cost marks Classical (Ivan Pavlov) Operant (B. F. Skinner) What is learned An association between two stimuli An association between behaviour and its consequence Behaviour is Reflexive, involuntary (elicited) Voluntary (emitted) Order Stimulus comes before the response Consequence comes after the response Example Dog salivates to a bell Rat presses a lever for food Classical terms: UCS → UCR (unlearned); the NS becomes the CS when paired, producing the CR . Acquisition (learning), extinction (CS alone, CR fades), spontaneous recovery (the CR returns after a rest), generalisation (similar stimuli also trigger it), discrimination (only the exact CS does). Little Albert (John B. Watson and Rosalie Rayner, 1920) = generalised fear; Garcia effect = one-trial taste aversion (biological preparedness). The four operant contingencies (the classic trap): "Positive" = add a stimulus, "Negative" = remove one. "Reinforcement" = behaviour increases , "Punishment" = behaviour decreases . Increases behaviour (reinforcement) Decreases behaviour (punishment) Add stimulus (positive) Positive reinforcement (give a treat) Positive punishment (give a scolding) Remove stimulus (negative) Negative reinforcement (stop the alarm by buckling up) Negative punishment / omission (take away the phone) TRAP (this is the one people miss): Negative reinforcement is NOT punishment. It removes something unpleasant to increase a behaviour. Taking aspirin to end a headache is negatively reinforced. Punishment always decreases behaviour. Reinforcement schedule Pattern Response feature Fixed ratio (FR) Reward after a set number of responses High rate, short post-reward pause Variable ratio (VR) Reward after an unpredictable number Highest, steadiest rate; most resistant to extinction (gambling) Fixed interval (FI) Reward for the first response after a set time Scalloped (work speeds up near the deadline) Variable interval (VI) Reward after an unpredictable time Slow, steady (checking for a text) Other learning terms: Shaping = reinforcing successive approximations. Primary reinforcer = innately satisfying (food, water); secondary = learned value (money, tokens). Premack principle = a high-frequency behaviour reinforces a low-frequency one ("eat your veggies, then dessert"). Continuous reinforcement learns fastest; partial reinforcement resists extinction best (the partial-reinforcement effect). TRAP: "Most resistant to extinction" = variable ratio . "Fastest acquisition" = continuous . Do not swap those two questions. C.5 Motivation Theory Core idea Instinct Behaviour is innate and species-typical (early, now largely rejected as a full account) Drive-reduction (Clark Hull) A need creates a drive (tension); behaviour reduces it to restore homeostasis Arousal / optimal level We seek an optimum level of arousal, not zero (explains curiosity); see Yerkes-Dodson Incentive External rewards pull behaviour (drives push, incentives pull) Abraham Maslow's hierarchy Physiological → safety → love/belonging → esteem → self-actualisation; lower needs first Self-determination (Edward Deci & Richard Ryan) Three innate needs: autonomy, competence, relatedness David McClelland Acquired needs: achievement (nAch), affiliation, power Yerkes-Dodson law: performance is an inverted-U of arousal. The optimum is lower for difficult/complex tasks and higher for simple/well-learned ones. TRAP: Intrinsic motivation = the activity itself is the reward; extrinsic = an outside reward. The overjustification effect: paying someone for something they already enjoy can reduce the intrinsic motivation. Drives push (internal need), incentives pull (external goal). C.6 Emotion: the theories side by side Every emotion question turns on the order of three events: the stimulus, the bodily arousal, and the felt emotion. Learn the sequence each theory claims. Theory The sequence it claims James-Lange Stimulus → bodily arousal → emotion. "We are afraid because we tremble." Emotion follows the body. Cannon-Bard Stimulus → arousal AND emotion at the same time (thalamus routes to both). Body and feeling are simultaneous, not causal. Schachter-Singer two-factor Stimulus → arousal → cognitive label of that arousal → emotion. Same arousal, different label, different emotion (the adrenaline study). Lazarus appraisal Stimulus → cognitive appraisal comes first → arousal + emotion. Thinking precedes feeling. Facial feedback The face itself feeds emotion: holding a smile can lift mood. TRAP: James-Lange = body first , then emotion. Cannon-Bard = simultaneous . Schachter-Singer adds a cognitive label to arousal. Lazarus puts appraisal first . A stem about "interpreting your racing heart as either fear or excitement" is Schachter-Singer. C.7 Memory Multi-store (Atkinson-Shiffrin): sensory register (iconic ~0.5 s, echoic ~2–4 s) → short-term (~7±2 items, ~15–30 s, lost by displacement/decay) → long-term (effectively unlimited). Rehearsal moves STM → LTM. Working memory (Alan Baddeley): the central executive directs three slaves: the phonological loop (verbal), the visuospatial sketchpad (visual/spatial), and the episodic buffer (binds + links to LTM). This replaced the passive STM "box". LTM types: Explicit/declarative (conscious) splits into episodic (events, what/where/when) and semantic (facts). Implicit/non-declarative includes procedural (skills), priming, and conditioning. Levels of processing (Fergus Craik & Robert Lockhart): deeper, semantic processing yields better recall than shallow (visual/phonemic) processing. Serial position: first items recalled well ( primacy , rehearsed into LTM) and last items recalled well ( recency , still in STM). A delay before recall wipes recency but not primacy. Forgetting: decay (trace fades), interference , cue-dependent (encoding-specificity, state- and context-dependent recall), motivated forgetting (repression). Ebbinghaus = the forgetting curve (steep then levels off). Memory is reconstructive: Frederic Bartlett's schemas ("War of the Ghosts"), Elizabeth Loftus's misinformation effect (leading questions reshape eyewitness memory). TRAP: Proactive interference = old learning blocks new ("pro" = forward, old pushes ahead). Retroactive = new learning blocks old ("retro" = backward). Recall (produce it) is harder than recognition (pick it out). Episodic = tied to a time and place; semantic = a free-floating fact. C.8 Intelligence and IQ scoring Theory Claim Spearman A general factor g underlies all abilities, plus task-specific s Thurstone 7 independent primary mental abilities, no single g Cattell-Horn Fluid (reasoning on novel problems, declines with age) vs crystallised (accumulated knowledge, holds/rises) Howard Gardner 8 multiple intelligences (linguistic, logical-math, spatial, musical, bodily, interpersonal, intrapersonal, naturalist) Robert Sternberg Triarchic: analytical, creative, practical Peter Salovey & John Mayer / Goleman Emotional intelligence (the model / the popularisation) Scoring foundations: Ratio IQ = (mental age / chronological age) × 100 (old Stanford-Binet). Deviation IQ (Wechsler) = mean 100, SD 15 ; it compares you to your age peers. A WAIS subtest scaled score has mean 10, SD 3 , so a 10 is exactly average (50th percentile). The Flynn effect = average IQ scores rose across the 20th century, so norms need re-standardising. TRAP: Full-scale IQ mean 100 SD 15; scaled subtest mean 10 SD 3. A scaled score of 10 = average, NOT low. Fluid intelligence (Raymond Cattell and John Horn) falls with age; crystallised does not. C.9 Statistics & research the common section quietly tests Central tendency: mean (pulled toward the tail by skew/outliers), median (robust, best for skewed income-type data), mode (the only one usable for nominal data). In a positive (right) skew the order is mode < median < mean; in a negative skew it reverses. The mean is dragged toward the longer tail. Normal curve: symmetrical, mean = median = mode. 68 / 95 / 99.7 of cases fall within 1 / 2 / 3 SD. A z-score = how many SDs a value sits from the mean. Correlation: r ranges −1 to +1 ; the sign is direction, the absolute value is strength. r = 0 means no linear relationship. r² (coefficient of determination) = proportion of variance shared. Correlation does not equal causation (third-variable, directionality problems). Reliability (consistency) vs validity (accuracy). Reliability types: test-retest, inter-rater, internal consistency (Cronbach's α, split-half). Validity types: content, construct, criterion (concurrent + predictive). A test can be reliable but not valid (a consistent bathroom scale that reads 5 kg heavy). It cannot be valid without being reliable. Levels of measurement (NOIR; Stanley Smith Stevens, 1946): Nominal (categories), Ordinal (ranked), Interval (equal gaps, no true zero, e.g. Celsius/IQ), Ratio (true zero, e.g. weight, reaction time). Variables: the independent variable is manipulated; the dependent variable is measured. A confound varies with the IV and offers a rival explanation. Random assignment (to groups) controls confounds; random sampling gives generalisability. They are not the same thing. TRAP: Reliable ≠ valid: consistency is not accuracy. In a positively skewed distribution the mean is the highest of the three averages (pulled right). Random assignment ≠ random sampling . Interval has no true zero; ratio does. C.10 Developmental spine (compact) Piaget stage Age Hallmark Sensorimotor 0–2 Object permanence develops Preoperational 2–7 Symbols, egocentrism, no conservation Concrete operational 7–11 Conservation, reversibility, logic on concrete things Formal operational 11+ Abstract and hypothetical reasoning Erik Erikson (8 crises): trust v mistrust → autonomy v shame → initiative v guilt → industry v inferiority → identity v role confusion (adolescence) → intimacy v isolation → generativity v stagnation → integrity v despair. Lawrence Kohlberg: Preconventional (punishment/reward) → Conventional (social approval/law-and-order) → Postconventional (social contract/universal ethics). Attachment (Ainsworth Strange Situation): secure; insecure-avoidant; insecure-resistant/ambivalent; (Main & Solomon) disorganised. Harry Harlow's monkeys = contact comfort over food; John Bowlby = the attachment behavioural system + monotropy. TRAP: Jean Piaget's assimilation = fit new info into an existing schema; accommodation = change the schema to fit new info. Object permanence = sensorimotor ; conservation = concrete operational . Lev Vygotsky stresses the social/ZPD, Piaget the individual constructor. C.11 Cover-and-test: the confusable pairs that quietly cost marks This is the highest-yield drill in the pack. Cover the right column. If you can give the distinction for every row without peeking, the common section is no longer your weak point. Confusable pair The one-line distinction Sensation vs perception Sensation = raw detection (bottom-up); perception = interpretation (adds top-down) Negative reinforcement vs punishment Neg. reinforcement increases behaviour by removing something bad; punishment decreases behaviour Positive vs negative (in conditioning) Positive = add a stimulus; negative = remove one. Nothing to do with good/bad Classical vs operant Classical = involuntary, stimulus before response; operant = voluntary, consequence after response Proactive vs retroactive interference Proactive = old blocks new; retroactive = new blocks old Recall vs recognition Recall = produce it from scratch (harder); recognition = identify the right one (easier) Assimilation vs accommodation Assimilate = bend the world to the schema; accommodate = bend the schema to the world Reliability vs validity Reliability = consistent; validity = measures what it claims. Reliable need not be valid Random sampling vs random assignment Sampling = who gets in the study (generalisability); assignment = which group they go to (controls confounds) Independent vs dependent variable IV = manipulated cause; DV = measured effect Mean vs median in skew The mean chases the tail; the median resists it. Use median for skewed data Fluid vs crystallised intelligence Fluid = reason on the novel (falls with age); crystallised = stored knowledge (holds) Ratio vs deviation IQ Ratio = MA/CA×100 (old); deviation = SD-based comparison to age peers (mean 100, SD 15) James-Lange vs Cannon-Bard James-Lange = body first then emotion; Cannon-Bard = both at once Intrinsic vs extrinsic motivation Intrinsic = the act rewards itself; extrinsic = an outside reward. Beware the overjustification effect Drive vs incentive Drives push from an internal need; incentives pull from an external goal Episodic vs semantic memory (Endel Tulving, 1972) Episodic = tied to a time/place; semantic = a free-standing fact Weber vs Fechner Weber = JND is a constant ratio; Fechner = sensation grows with the log of intensity Binocular vs monocular depth cues Binocular = disparity + convergence (two eyes); everything else, incl. motion parallax, is monocular Conformity vs obedience Conformity (Solomon Asch) = matching peers; obedience (Stanley Milgram) = following an authority's order g vs s (Spearman) g = the general factor across all tasks; s = ability specific to one task Primacy vs recency Primacy = early items (into LTM via rehearsal); recency = last items (still in STM, wiped by delay) If you run C.11 clean, you have closed the gap. These pairs are exactly the "looks like two right answers" items that the common section uses to separate the 70s from the 90s. 1. Biopsychology & Neuropsychology MET 15 Q · NIMHANS 15 Q 1.1 The neuron and glia Dendrites receive input (spines multiply surface area). Soma integrates input. Axon hillock = trigger zone, decides if threshold is reached. Axon conducts the AP. Axon terminals release neurotransmitter. Neuron types: Sensory (afferent, periphery → CNS, pseudounipolar); Motor (efferent, CNS → muscle/gland, multipolar); Interneurons (local CNS processing, most common). Glial cell Location Function Oligodendrocyte CNS Myelinates many axons (one cell, many segments) Schwann cell PNS Myelinates one axon segment per cell Astrocyte CNS Blood-brain barrier, K+ buffering, NT recycling Microglia CNS Immune defence, phagocytosis Ependymal cell Ventricles Produces and circulates CSF Satellite cell PNS ganglia Supports cell bodies in PNS TRAP: CNS myelination = oligodendrocyte. PNS myelination = Schwann cell. 1.2 The action potential (the single most testable neurophysiology topic) An AP is a ~1 ms electrical pulse travelling down the axon. The whole story is " Na+ in, K+ out ": Na+ rushing in depolarises; K+ leaving repolarises. Resting membrane potential ~ −70 mV. Set by K+ leak channels (membrane ~50× more permeable to K+), NOT by the Na/K pump. Threshold ~ −55 mV. Na/K pump: 3 Na+ out, 2 K+ in per ATP. Electrogenic. Maintains the gradient but does not set RMP. Phase 1 Depolarisation: voltage-gated Na+ channels open → Na+ in → spike to ~ +30 mV. Phase 2 Repolarisation: Na+ channels inactivate, voltage-gated K+ channels open (slower) → K+ out. Phase 3 Hyperpolarisation: K+ channels stay open briefly → undershoot below −70 mV. Phase 4 Return: K+ channels close, Na/K pump restores ions. Ion concentrations: "K is in, Na is out, Cl is out, Ca is way out." Equilibrium potentials: K+ −90 mV, Na+ +60 mV, Cl− −65 mV, Ca²⁺ +120 mV. All-or-none law: once threshold is reached the AP fires at constant amplitude; stimulus intensity is coded by frequency , not amplitude. Refractory periods: Absolute = Na+ channels inactivated, no stimulus however strong can fire another AP (ensures one-way propagation). Relative = membrane hyperpolarised (K+ still open), a stronger stimulus can fire one. TRAP: Inactivated ≠ closed. The Na+ channel has 3 states: closed (resting), open (during AP), inactivated (after, "ball and chain" blocks the pore). Resets only after repolarisation. Propagation: continuous (unmyelinated C fibres, 0.5–2 m/s) vs saltatory (myelinated, AP jumps between Nodes of Ranvier, up to 120 m/s in A-alpha). Conduction velocity rises with myelination > axon diameter > temperature. Demyelination (MS, Guillain-Barré) slows/blocks conduction. Synaptic transmission: AP arrives → voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels open, Ca²⁺ enters → vesicles fuse (SNARE proteins, synaptotagmin = Ca²⁺ sensor) → NT released → binds postsynaptic receptors → EPSP (Na+/Ca²⁺ in, depolarising) or IPSP (Cl− in or K+ out, hyperpolarising) → cleared by reuptake, enzymatic breakdown, or diffusion. Summation (spatial + temporal) at the axon hillock decides if a new AP fires. TRAP: Ca²⁺ is the trigger ion for NT release at the terminal. Without Ca²⁺ entry, no transmitter is released. 1.3 Neurotransmitters (the 7 families) NT Class / made from Cleared by Clinical link Acetylcholine (ACh) Choline + acetyl-CoA Acetylcholinesterase Low in Alzheimer's; myasthenia gravis (anti-AChR); NMJ Dopamine Catecholamine (Tyrosine → DOPA → DA) Reuptake, MAO, COMT ↑ mesolimbic = +ve schizophrenia. Low nigrostriatal = Parkinson's. Reward/addiction. Norepinephrine Catecholamine (DA + β-hydroxylase) Reuptake, MAO Arousal, sympathetic. Locus coeruleus. Low in depression. Serotonin (5-HT) Indolamine (Tryptophan) Reuptake (SERT), MAO Mood, sleep, appetite. Low → depression, OCD. Raphe nuclei. Glutamate Amino acid (Glutamine) Astrocyte reuptake Main excitatory NT. NMDA/AMPA/kainate. LTP, learning. Excess = excitotoxicity. GABA Amino acid (from Glutamate via GAD) Reuptake Main inhibitory NT. GABA-A ionotropic = target of benzos, alcohol, barbiturates. Endorphins Peptide (POMC) Peptidases Pain modulation, runner's high. μ, κ, δ receptors. TRAP: Hippocampal LTP depends on the NMDA receptor (coincidence detector — needs glutamate AND postsynaptic depolarisation to displace the Mg²⁺ block; Ca²⁺ entry triggers LTP). AMPA carries the fast EPSP. Hebb: "neurons that fire together wire together." 1.3a Neurotransmitters — the deep note, one per transmitter The table above is the cheat-sheet. This is the full read: for each transmitter — what it is, where it's made, its receptors, what it does in brain and body, what too much or too little looks like, and the drugs that hit it. If a question asks "which NT" or "which drug," the answer is in one of these boxes. The two-minute frame: Glutamate is the gas (excitatory), GABA is the brake (inhibitory) — together they run ~90% of fast CNS signalling. The monoamines (dopamine, norepinephrine, serotonin, plus histamine) are the slow, mood/arousal modulators that nearly every psych drug targets. ACh straddles muscle, the parasympathetic body, and memory. Everything else (peptides, glycine, gases) fills in the edges. ① Glutamate — the main excitatory transmitter Aspect Detail What it is An amino-acid neurotransmitter. The principal excitatory NT of the CNS — most fast excitation in the brain is glutamate. Where it's made From glutamine via the glutamate–glutamine cycle (astrocytes recycle released glutamate back to glutamine); also from α-ketoglutarate (Krebs cycle). Made in the presynaptic terminal. Receptors Ionotropic: NMDA (Ca²⁺-permeable, Mg²⁺-blocked coincidence detector → LTP), AMPA (fast Na⁺ EPSP), kainate. Metabotropic: mGluR1–8 (G-protein, slow modulation). Brain & body Fast excitation, learning and memory (LTP) , cortical processing, sensory transmission. Building block of GABA and of protein. Too much Excitotoxicity — Ca²⁺ overload kills neurons: stroke, traumatic brain injury, ALS, neurodegeneration. Also seizures. Too little / blocked NMDA hypofunction → psychosis (a leading schizophrenia model); cognitive and memory impairment. Drugs that hit it NMDA antagonists: ketamine and PCP (dissociatives, model psychosis; ketamine is also a rapid antidepressant), memantine (Alzheimer's), dextromethorphan. Glutamate-lowering: riluzole (ALS), lamotrigine (reduces release). TRAP: Ketamine/PCP cause psychotic-like states by blocking NMDA, not by raising dopamine — this is the glutamate (NMDA-hypofunction) model of schizophrenia. ② GABA — the main inhibitory transmitter Aspect Detail What it is γ-aminobutyric acid, an amino-acid NT. The principal inhibitory NT of the CNS — the brain's brake. Where it's made From glutamate by the enzyme GAD (glutamic acid decarboxylase), which needs vitamin B6 (pyridoxal phosphate) as a cofactor. Receptors GABA-A (ionotropic, opens Cl⁻ channel → hyperpolarisation; has the benzodiazepine, barbiturate, alcohol and neurosteroid sites). GABA-B (metabotropic, ↑K⁺ efflux / ↓Ca²⁺; target of baclofen). Brain & body Dampens excitability, anxiolysis, sedation/sleep, regulates muscle tone, prevents runaway firing. Too much / enhanced Sedation, ataxia, respiratory depression — especially when alcohol + benzodiazepines are combined. Too little Anxiety, seizures (epilepsy), spasticity. B6 deficiency lowers GABA → seizures. Drugs that hit it Benzodiazepines (↑ frequency of Cl⁻ channel opening), barbiturates (↑ duration ), alcohol, z-drugs (zolpidem); baclofen (GABA-B, spasticity); tiagabine (reuptake block), vigabatrin (GABA-transaminase block), valproate. TRAP: Benzos increase how often the chloride channel opens; barbiturates increase how long it stays open. Barbiturates can open it without GABA at high dose → far more lethal in overdose. ③ Dopamine — reward, movement, psychosis Aspect Detail What it is A catecholamine (monoamine), made from the amino acid tyrosine. Where it's made Tyrosine → L-DOPA (by tyrosine hydroxylase , the rate-limiting step) → dopamine (by DOPA decarboxylase). Cell bodies in the substantia nigra (pars compacta) , VTA , and hypothalamus (arcuate). Four pathways Nigrostriatal (movement — lost in Parkinson's), mesolimbic (reward; excess → positive symptoms), mesocortical (cognition; low → negative symptoms), tuberoinfundibular (inhibits prolactin). Receptors D1-like (D1, D5 — Gs, excitatory) and D2-like (D2, D3, D4 — Gi, inhibitory). Antipsychotics work mainly by blocking D2. Cleared by Reuptake (DAT), then MAO and COMT. Too much Mesolimbic excess → positive symptoms of schizophrenia (delusions, hallucinations); reward/addiction; mania. Too little Nigrostriatal loss → Parkinson's (resting tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia); D2 blockade → hyperprolactinaemia (galactorrhoea) and extrapyramidal side-effects; low mesocortical DA → negative/cognitive symptoms. Drugs that hit it Raise it: L-DOPA + carbidopa, agonists (pramipexole, ropinirole, bromocriptine), stimulants (amphetamine, cocaine, methylphenidate block DAT/release DA), MAO-B inhibitors (selegiline), COMT inhibitors (entacapone). Block it: antipsychotics — typicals (haloperidol) and atypicals. TRAP: The same drug class trades one problem for another. Block dopamine to treat psychosis → you risk Parkinsonism + raised prolactin. Boost dopamine to treat Parkinson's → you risk psychosis. It is one transmitter pulling four levers. ④ Serotonin (5-HT) — mood, sleep, appetite, impulse Aspect Detail What it is An indolamine (monoamine), made from the amino acid tryptophan. Where it's made Tryptophan → 5-HTP (by tryptophan hydroxylase , rate-limiting) → 5-HT. CNS source = the raphe nuclei of the brainstem. ~90% of body serotonin is in the gut (enterochromaffin cells); also stored in platelets. Receptors Seven families (5-HT1–7), almost all GPCRs. 5-HT3 is the only ionotropic one (cation channel → nausea/vomiting). 5-HT1A (anxiety/depression autoreceptor), 5-HT2A (psychedelics; atypical-antipsychotic target). Cleared by Reuptake via SERT , then MAO → 5-HIAA (the urinary metabolite). Brain & body Mood, sleep, appetite/satiety, impulse control, temperature; in the body: gut motility, vasoconstriction, platelet aggregation. Too much Serotonin syndrome (agitation, hyperthermia, clonus, autonomic instability — often SSRI + MAOI or + tramadol); carcinoid syndrome. Too little Depression, anxiety, OCD, increased aggression/impulsivity. Drugs that hit it SSRIs (fluoxetine, sertraline), SNRIs (venlafaxine), TCAs, MAOIs; buspirone (5-HT1A partial agonist); triptans (5-HT1B/1D, migraine); ondansetron (5-HT3 block, antiemetic); LSD/psilocybin (5-HT2A agonists); atypical antipsychotics (5-HT2A antagonism). TRAP: 5-HT3 is the odd one out — it's the only ligand-gated ion channel in the serotonin family, and blocking it (ondansetron) stops vomiting. Every other 5-HT receptor is a G-protein receptor. ⑤ Acetylcholine (ACh) — muscle, parasympathetic, memory Aspect Detail What it is An ester; the first neurotransmitter ever discovered (Otto Loewi's "Vagusstoff"). Where it's made Choline + acetyl-CoA via choline acetyltransferase (ChAT). Found at the neuromuscular junction , all autonomic ganglia, all parasympathetic postganglionic neurons (+ sympathetic to sweat glands), and the basal forebrain (nucleus basalis of Meynert) for memory. Receptors Nicotinic (ionotropic, ligand-gated Na⁺/K⁺ — NMJ, ganglia, CNS) and Muscarinic (M1–M5, GPCR — parasympathetic targets and CNS). Cleared by Acetylcholinesterase → choline + acetate (choline is recycled). Brain & body Muscle contraction (NMJ), "rest and digest" parasympathetic tone, arousal, attention, and learning/memory . Too much Cholinergic crisis (SLUDGE / DUMBELS — salivation, lacrimation, urination, diarrhoea, miosis…) from organophosphate pesticides and nerve agents that block acetylcholinesterase. Too little Alzheimer's (degeneration of basal-forebrain cholinergic neurons → memory loss); myasthenia gravis (autoantibodies vs nicotinic AChR → fatigable weakness). Drugs that hit it AChE inhibitors: donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine (Alzheimer's); pyridostigmine/neostigmine (myasthenia); physostigmine. Anticholinergics: atropine, scopolamine, benztropine. Neuromuscular blockers: curare, succinylcholine. TRAP: "Dry as a bone, red as a beet, mad as a hatter" = anticholinergic (muscarinic-block) toxicity. The opposite — wet everywhere (SLUDGE) — is cholinergic excess.
