Atropine treats the wet one. ⑥ Norepinephrine (noradrenaline) — arousal & fight-or-flight Aspect Detail What it is A catecholamine (monoamine), one step beyond dopamine. Where it's made Dopamine + dopamine β-hydroxylase → norepinephrine. CNS source = the locus coeruleus (pons). Also released by sympathetic postganglionic neurons and the adrenal medulla. Receptors Adrenergic α1, α2, β1, β2, β3 (all GPCR). α2 is the presynaptic autoreceptor that shuts off its own release. Cleared by Reuptake (NET), then MAO and COMT. Brain & body Arousal, vigilance, attention, mood; sympathetic fight-or-flight (Walter Cannon, 1915) — ↑heart rate, ↑BP, bronchodilation, pupil dilation. Too much Anxiety, hypertension, PTSD hyperarousal/nightmares ; pheochromocytoma. Too little Depression, fatigue, poor concentration (a target in ADHD). Drugs that hit it SNRIs (venlafaxine, duloxetine), atomoxetine (NRI, ADHD), TCAs, stimulants. α2 agonists clonidine/guanfacine lower central NE (ADHD, anxiety, BP). β-blocker propranolol (performance anxiety, akathisia). α1-blocker prazosin (PTSD nightmares). Note — epinephrine (adrenaline): made from norepinephrine by the enzyme PNMT in the adrenal medulla. It is mostly a circulating hormone (the main adrenal output) and only a minor CNS transmitter. ⑦ Histamine — wakefulness, allergy, gastric acid Aspect Detail What it is A monoamine, made from the amino acid histidine (by histidine decarboxylase). Where it's made CNS: the tuberomammillary nucleus of the hypothalamus. Periphery: mast cells, basophils, and enterochromaffin-like cells of the stomach. Receptors H1 (allergy + wakefulness), H2 (gastric acid), H3 (presynaptic CNS autoreceptor), H4 (immune). Brain & body Promotes wakefulness/arousal , regulates appetite; drives allergy/inflammation and gastric acid secretion in the body. Clinical / drugs H1 blockers: diphenhydramine (sedating — crosses the blood-brain barrier), loratadine (non-sedating). H2 blockers: famotidine, ranitidine (acid/ulcers). H1-blocking side-effects (sedation, weight gain) explain a lot of antipsychotic and antidepressant tolerability. ⑧ Glycine — the spinal-cord brake Aspect Detail What it is The simplest amino acid; the major inhibitory NT of the spinal cord and brainstem . Where it's made From the amino acid serine. Receptors Glycine receptor (ionotropic, opens Cl⁻ → inhibition); also an obligatory co-agonist at the NMDA receptor (glutamate alone is not enough). Brain & body Inhibits motor neurons; provides reciprocal inhibition so opposing muscles relax. Clinical Strychnine blocks glycine receptors → convulsions/rigidity. Tetanus toxin blocks glycine release → spastic paralysis (lockjaw). ⑨ Endorphins & endogenous opioids — the body's painkillers Aspect Detail What they are Neuropeptides: β-endorphin (cleaved from POMC), enkephalins , and dynorphins . Receptors Opioid receptors μ (mu), δ (delta), κ (kappa) — all inhibitory (Gi) GPCRs. μ drives most analgesia and euphoria. Brain & body Pain modulation (down the PAG/descending pathway), reward, "runner's high," mood; in the body, constipation and (via μ) respiratory depression. Drugs that hit it Agonists: morphine, heroin, fentanyl (μ). Antagonist: naloxone/naltrexone (reverses overdose, blocks reward). Partial agonist: buprenorphine. ⑩ The rest — neuropeptides & unconventional transmitters Transmitter Made from / where Does what / clinical hook Substance P Peptide; sensory (pain) neurons Carries pain signals via the NK1 receptor; NK1 blockers (aprepitant) treat nausea. Oxytocin Peptide; paraventricular/supraoptic hypothalamus → posterior pituitary Bonding, trust, labour contractions, milk let-down. Vasopressin (ADH) Same hypothalamic source → posterior pituitary Water retention, blood pressure; also social/aggression behaviour. Nitric oxide (NO) Gasotransmitter; from arginine, made on demand Retrograde messenger (postsynaptic → presynaptic); vasodilation (penile erection — sildenafil works here). Endocannabinoids (anandamide, 2-AG) Lipids; made on demand from membrane Retrograde messengers at CB1 (CNS — appetite, mood; the THC target) and CB2 (immune). Two "backwards" transmitters: nitric oxide and the endocannabinoids are retrograde — they're released by the post synaptic cell and act back on the pre synaptic terminal to turn its output down. Opposite direction to every classical NT above. 1.4 Nervous system organisation Nervous System ├── CNS (brain + spinal cord) └── PNS ├── Somatic NS (voluntary, skeletal muscle) └── Autonomic NS ├── Sympathetic ("fight/flight") — thoracolumbar T1–L2, NE ├── Parasympathetic ("rest/digest") — craniosacral (CN III,VII,IX,X + S2–S4), ACh └── Enteric ("gut brain") ANS contrasts: Sympathetic ↑ heart rate, dilates pupil, ↓ GI; pre/post-ganglionic NT = ACh/NE (sweat glands are the ACh exception). Parasympathetic ↓ heart rate (vagus), constricts pupil, ↑ GI; ACh/ACh. 1.5 Brain anatomy & lobes Region Structures Function Forebrain Cortex, basal ganglia, limbic system, thalamus, hypothalamus Higher cognition, emotion, motor planning, autonomic control Midbrain Tectum (sup/inf colliculi), tegmentum, substantia nigra, red nucleus, PAG Visual/auditory reflexes, motor control, pain modulation Hindbrain Pons, medulla, cerebellum Vital functions, balance, fine motor coordination Lobe Key areas Lesion produces Frontal Motor cortex (precentral), prefrontal, Broca's (L) Paralysis, executive deficits, Broca's aphasia, personality change (Phineas Gage) Parietal Somatosensory (postcentral), association cortex Left hemispatial neglect if right lesion; Gerstmann's if left; agnosia Temporal Primary auditory, Wernicke's (L), hippocampus, amygdala Wernicke's aphasia, anterograde amnesia, Klüver-Bucy Occipital Primary visual (V1), visual association Cortical blindness, visual agnosia, prosopagnosia (fusiform) Thalamus — sensory relay for all senses except smell. LGN (vision), MGN (hearing), VPL (touch), VPM (face). Hypothalamus — homeostasis, hormones, the 4 Fs. VMH lesion = hyperphagia + obesity ; LH lesion = aphagia . SCN = circadian. Supraoptic → ADH. Paraventricular → oxytocin + CRH. Basal ganglia — caudate, putamen, globus pallidus, subthalamic nucleus, substantia nigra. Red nucleus is NOT basal ganglia (it's midbrain tegmentum). Lesions: Parkinson's (SN), Huntington's (caudate/putamen), hemiballismus (subthalamic). Limbic system — hippocampus (memory), amygdala (fear), cingulate, fornix, mammillary bodies, septum. Cerebellum — coordination, timing, motor learning. Lesion: ataxia, dysmetria, intention tremor. Hemispheres: Left = language, logic, sequential, math. Right = spatial, music, faces, emotion, holistic. Corpus callosum severance = split-brain (Roger Sperry, Michael Gazzaniga). 1.5b Limbic system: function by structure Structure Function Lesion / clinical hook Hippocampus Forms and consolidates new declarative (explicit) memories; spatial navigation (place cells) Bilateral damage = anterograde amnesia (patient H.M.) Amygdala Fear conditioning, threat detection, attaches emotional weight to memory Damage = Klüver-Bucy (placidity, hyperorality, hypersexuality), blunted fear Hypothalamus Homeostasis and the 4 Fs; the bridge from limbic system to endocrine (via pituitary) and autonomic systems VMH lesion = overeating; LH lesion = no eating Cingulate gyrus (anterior) Emotion regulation, conflict/error monitoring, attention, the affective (suffering) component of pain Cingulotomy historically used for severe OCD/chronic pain Fornix Output cable carrying hippocampal signals to the mammillary bodies and hypothalamus Section disrupts memory recall Mammillary bodies Memory relay station in the Papez circuit Degenerate in Wernicke-Korsakoff (thiamine/B1 deficiency): confabulation, anterograde amnesia Septal nuclei Reward and pleasure; dampen aggression James Olds and Peter Milner self-stimulation studies (the "pleasure centre") Olfactory bulb Smell, the only sense that reaches cortex without a thalamic relay Explains the strong smell-to-memory and smell-to-emotion link Papez circuit (emotion + memory loop): hippocampus → fornix → mammillary bodies → anterior thalamus → cingulate → back to hippocampus. 1.5c Basal ganglia: function by structure Overall job: initiate and scale voluntary movement, suppress unwanted movement, and drive procedural (habit) learning. It works as a loop: cortex → striatum → pallidum → thalamus → back to cortex. Structure Function Lesion / disorder Striatum = caudate + putamen Main input zone, receives signals from the cortex Degenerates in Huntington's (chorea) Caudate Cognition, goal-directed action, part of OCD circuitry Overactive caudate loops in OCD and Tourette's Putamen Habit learning and motor execution Loss of movement automaticity Globus pallidus (GPi / GPe) Output zone; GPi is the main inhibitory output to the thalamus Pallidotomy / deep-brain-stimulation target in Parkinson's Subthalamic nucleus Brake within the indirect pathway Lesion = hemiballismus (wild flinging of one side) Substantia nigra (pars compacta) Supplies dopamine to the striatum Degenerates in Parkinson's (resting tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia) Direct vs indirect pathway: the direct pathway (dopamine on D1, the "go" route) facilitates movement; the indirect pathway (dopamine on D2, the "no-go" route) suppresses it. Dopamine from the substantia nigra tips the balance toward movement, so losing it (Parkinson's) makes movement hard to start. TRAP: Parkinson's is hypokinetic (too little movement, dopamine loss in the substantia nigra). Huntington's and hemiballismus are hyperkinetic (too much movement, loss in the caudate/putamen and subthalamic nucleus). The red nucleus is midbrain, NOT basal ganglia. 1.6 Cranial nerves I–XII # Name Type Function I Olfactory S Smell. Only CN that does NOT relay through thalamus. II Optic S Vision. V Trigeminal B Face sensation, mastication. VI Abducens M Lateral rectus only. VII Facial B Facial expression, taste (anterior 2/3), salivation, lacrimation. Parasympathetic carriers: III, VII, IX, X. 1.7 Sensory systems Vision: rods (peripheral, low light, no colour) + cones (foveal, colour, acuity). Cones densest at the fovea centralis. Optic disc = blind spot. Pathway: retina → optic nerve → chiasm (nasal fibres cross) → optic tract → LGN → V1. Theories: trichromatic (Young-Helmholtz, retinal) + opponent-process (Ewald Hering, post-retinal). Dorsal stream "where/how" (parietal); ventral stream "what" (temporal). Audition: outer → middle (malleus, incus, stapes) → cochlea → hair cells on basilar membrane → CN VIII → cochlear nuclei → MGN → Heschl's gyrus. Place theory (Békésy): base = high frequencies, apex = low; best for high. Frequency theory (Ernest Rutherford, 1886): firing rate = frequency, works <500 Hz. Volley principle (Ernest Wever and Charles Bray, 1930) bridges mid-range. Somatosensation: dorsal column-medial lemniscus (touch, vibration, proprioception, decussates at medulla) vs spinothalamic (pain, temp, decussates at spinal level of entry). Taste: sweet, salty, sour, bitter, umami. CN VII / IX / X. Insula = primary gustatory cortex. Smell: olfactory epithelium → bulb → piriform cortex (no thalamus relay), closest to limbic system. 1.8 Motor systems Pyramidal (corticospinal): M1 (Brodmann 4) → internal capsule → peduncle → pons → medullary pyramids. Decussates at the pyramids of the medulla (~85–90% → lateral corticospinal tract). Extrapyramidal: rubrospinal (flexor bias), vestibulospinal (postural extensor), reticulospinal (locomotion), tectospinal (head/neck orienting). Meaney/McGowan epigenetics: maternal licking ↑ glucocorticoid receptors → calmer adult. 1.11 Sleep (full primer) Sleep = NREM (3 stages) + REM. One cycle ~ 90 min ; 4–6 cycles/night. N3 dominates the first half; REM dominates the second half and lengthens through the night. Stage EEG / signature Notes NREM 1 (~5%) Theta (4–8 Hz) Light, hypnic jerks, hypnagogic images NREM 2 (~45–55%) Sleep spindles + K-complexes Most of the night; spindles gate sensory input NREM 3 (~15–20%) Delta (0.5–4 Hz, high amplitude) Deep/slow-wave. Growth hormone. Parasomnias (sleepwalking, night terrors, enuresis) come OUT of N3 REM (~20–25%) Mixed, low-voltage (looks awake) Paradoxical : brain active, body in atonia . Vivid dreams, eye bursts, autonomic instability, thermoregulation fails. NOT delta-dominant. Neural control: sleep pressure from adenosine (caffeine blocks adenosine receptors); VLPO = GABAergic "sleep switch"; wake driven by the ARAS (histamine, orexin, NE, 5-HT, ACh). SCN = master circadian clock, entrained by light via the retinohypothalamic tract → pineal → melatonin in darkness. REM-ON = cholinergic (PPT/LDT); REM-OFF = aminergic (NE, 5-HT). Memory: declarative consolidated in NREM (delta replay); procedural in REM + spindles; emotional in REM. Disorders: Narcolepsy = orexin/hypocretin deficiency; cataplexy is pathognomonic. RBD = loss of atonia in REM, older men, α-synucleinopathy warning (Parkinson/Lewy body). RLS = urge to move legs at rest (dopamine/iron). Kleine-Levin = the 3 H's (hypersomnia + hyperphagia + hypersexuality), young males. Insomnia DSM-5: 3 nights/wk × 3 months. 1.12 Emotion, arousal, learning & LTP Theories of emotion: James-Lange (body first, "we feel sad because we cry"); Cannon-Bard (body + emotion simultaneously, thalamic); Schachter-Singer (two-factor: arousal + cognitive label); Lazarus (appraisal precedes emotion). Yerkes-Dodson law: inverted-U of arousal vs performance. Optimum is lower for complex tasks, higher for simple/well-learned tasks. Memory substrates: hippocampus (declarative consolidation), amygdala (emotional/fear), striatum (procedural/habit), cerebellum (motor conditioning). LTP strengthens synapses (NMDA receptor critical, Ca²⁺ entry, AMPA insertion); LTD weakens them. Papez circuit: hippocampus → fornix → mammillary → anterior thalamus → cingulate → entorhinal → hippocampus. 1.13 Mania first-line drugs & psychopharmacology First-line for acute mania: Lithium · Valproate (Divalproex) · atypical antipsychotics (Olanzapine, Risperidone, Quetiapine, Aripiprazole). Carbamazepine is second-line. NOT first-line (your mock miss): Fluoxetine and any SSRI/antidepressant — they can trigger a manic switch . Antidepressants are avoided in acute mania. Critical period = rigid biological window, lost if missed (Lorenz imprinting). Sensitive period = optimal but flexible (language acquisition). Psychological Assessment & Tests MET 15 Q · NIMHANS 10 Q The whole map: a psychological test is a measuring instrument that must be (a) consistent = reliability and (b) accurate = validity . Everything else is a way to estimate one of those, interpret scores against norms, or an example of a real test. 4.1 Item analysis Difficulty index p = proportion who got the item right (0–1). Sweet spot 0.50 for free-response, ~0.625 for a 4-option MCQ (halfway between guessing 0.25 and ceiling). p > 0.80 too easy, < 0.20 too hard. Discrimination index D = p(top 27%) − p(bottom 27%), range −1 to +1. D > 0.40 good. Negative D = mis-keyed/ambiguous item, discard immediately. 4.2 Reliability (consistency) Classical test theory: Observed = True + Error. Reliability = proportion of variance that is true. Test-retest (across time; standard window 2–4 wks). Parallel forms (across forms). Split-half + Spearman-Brown correction (r_full = 2·r_half / (1 + r_half)); Cronbach α (≥0.7 acceptable, ≥0.8 good) = mean of all possible split-halves; KR-20 for dichotomous (0/1) items. Inter-rater: Cohen κ (categorical, Landis & Koch: 0.61–0.80 substantial, 0.81+ almost perfect), ICC (continuous). SEM = SD·√(1 − r_xx). Higher reliability → smaller SEM → tighter confidence band around a score. TRAP: Cronbach α is NOT a measure of unidimensionality — a test can have high α and still measure two constructs. And κ is NOT internal consistency. 4.3 Validity (accuracy) Content: covers the domain (expert panels, Lawshe's CVR). Face validity = looks valid to a layperson, the weakest form. Criterion: Concurrent (criterion now) vs Predictive = Postponed (criterion later). Construct: convergent (correlates with similar) + discriminant (not with unrelated) + nomological network. Campbell & Fiske's multitrait-multimethod matrix (MTMM, 1959). Validity ceiling: max validity = √(reliability). Unreliable tests cannot be strongly valid. Reliability is necessary but not sufficient for validity. 4.4 Test classification Type Means Maximum performance (ability/aptitude/achievement, e.g. IQ) Do your best . There is a right answer Typical performance (personality, interest, attitude) What you usually do. No right answer Power test Hard items, generous time — measures ceiling of ability Speed test Easy items, tight time — measures how fast The exact trap you missed: an IQ test is an ability test (maximum performance), not a power or speed test. Achievement = what you learned (past, WIAT). Aptitude = what you can learn (future, DAT/SAT). Intelligence = general capacity. Norm-referenced (vs peers) vs criterion-referenced (vs absolute standard). Formative (during) vs summative (end). 4.5 Standard scores & norms Standard score = M + (SD × z). Chaining = link existing behaviours (each is the S D for the next; backward chaining preferred clinically). Fading = remove the prompt (extinction removes the reinforcer ). Prompting hierarchy: physical → modelling → gestural → verbal → visual. Extinction: watch for the extinction burst ; extinction suppresses, doesn't erase. Spontaneous recovery proves the memory is intact. Generalization is the default; discrimination is trained by differential reinforcement. Schedules: VR = highest, steadiest rate, most resistant to extinction (gambling). VI = steady moderate (checking phone). FR = post-reinforcement pause then burst (piece-work). FI = scallop (studying before a weekly quiz). Resistance: VR > VI > FR > FI > continuous. Latent learning (Tolman, cognitive map — learning without reinforcement, shown later). Insight learning (Köhler's Sultan, sudden "aha"). Observational learning (Bandura Bobo doll; 4 processes ARRM: Attention → Retention → Reproduction → Motivation; vicarious reinforcement). Escape vs avoidance (your mock guess): Escape = behaviour terminates an aversive stimulus that is already present (turn off a loud alarm). Avoidance = behaviour prevents the aversive stimulus from starting (leave before the alarm). Assent = a minor's agreement alongside a parent's consent. Paternalism = overriding a competent person's choice (violates autonomy). Language & Communication Skills MET 15 Q · NIMHANS 5 Q · highest fast-marks ratio 7.1 Subject-verb agreement The verb agrees with the subject in number, not the nearest noun. Each, every, either, neither, one, anyone, everyone, nobody → singular ("Each of the participants was given…"). Either/or, neither/nor → verb agrees with the nearer subject ("Neither the patient nor the family members were informed"). "A number of" = plural; "the number of" = singular. None defaults singular in formal writing. "Data are" — data is technically plural (datum singular); treat as plural in exam contexts. Singular-looking: news, mathematics, physics, politics, statistics. Plural-only: scissors, trousers, glasses. 7.2 Voice & conditionals Active → passive: object becomes subject; verb → "be" + past participle. "The committee will announce the results" → "The results will be announced by the committee." Conditional If-clause Main clause Zero (general truths) present present First (real future) present will + base Second (hypothetical) past would + base Third (counterfactual past) past perfect ("Had she taken") would have + past participle Mixed past perfect would + base " Had she taken the medication, she would have recovered sooner" = third conditional (inversion is formal). 7.3 Punctuation & prepositions Restrictive vs non-restrictive clauses: non-restrictive (extra info, removable) → commas + "who"; restrictive (defines which) → no commas, "that". "The patient, who was anxious, refused" (one patient) vs "The patient who was anxious refused" (picks out one of several). Semicolon joins two independent clauses; colon introduces a list/explanation. It's = it is; its = possessive. Prepositions: insist on , depend on, comply with, consist of, refer to, suffer from, object to, accuse of, married to (not with), prefer X to Y, superior/inferior to (not than), discuss (no preposition). "Between you and me ." 7.4 Modifiers, parallelism & common corrections Dangling modifier: "Walking down the street, the building looked tall" (the building isn't walking). Parallelism: "reading, writing, and swimming" (not "to swim"). Like (before a noun) vs as (before a clause). Who (subject) vs whom (object). Less (uncountable) vs fewer (countable). Between (two) vs among (3+). "The reason is that " (not "because"). Social psych first since that is where the named-experiment questions cluster. Theorist What they actually did · the trap Social psychology Solomon Asch Conformity. Line-judgement task: pick which of 3 lines matches a standard. Confederates deliberately gave a wrong answer; about 75% of real subjects conformed at least once, ~33% on average. Conformity is normative (fit in / avoid disapproval), not informational. Trap: Asch = group peer pressure; Stanley Milgram = authority . Conformity dropped sharply with one dissenting ally. Milgram Obedience. "Teacher" told by experimenter to shock a "learner" for wrong answers, up to 450V. 65% went to the maximum shock. Showed ordinary people obey a legitimate authority. Trap: obedience = following an authority's order ; conformity (Asch) = matching peers . Philip Zimbardo Stanford Prison Experiment. Students randomly assigned guard/prisoner roles; "guards" turned abusive fast, study stopped after 6 days. Power of the situation/assigned role over personality (deindividuation). Trap: situational, not dispositional. Muzafer Sherif Robbers Cave / realistic conflict theory. Two boys' camp groups; competition bred hostility, and superordinate goals (shared tasks neither group could solve alone) reduced it. Contact alone was not enough. Henri Tajfel Social identity theory + minimal group paradigm. Even arbitrary grouping (e.g. coin toss) produced in-group favouritism . Identity comes from group membership; basis of prejudice. Leon Festinger Cognitive dissonance + social comparison theory. Festinger & J. Merrill Carlsmith: people paid $1 to lie about a boring task changed their attitude more than those paid $20 (less external justification → more internal change). Trap: the smaller reward causes the bigger attitude shift. Latane & John Darley Bystander effect / diffusion of responsibility (Kitty Genovese). More bystanders → less likely any one helps. Steps: notice → interpret as emergency → assume responsibility → help. Kurt Lewin "Father of social psychology." Field theory (B = f(P,E): behaviour is a function of person and environment); leadership styles; unfreeze–change–refreeze model of change. Fritz Heider Attribution theory + balance theory. We explain behaviour by internal (dispositional) vs external (situational) causes. Related: fundamental attribution error = over-blaming the person, under-weighting the situation. Harold Kelley Covariation model of attribution: we judge cause using consensus, consistency, distinctiveness . Bem Self-perception theory: we infer our own attitudes by observing our own behaviour (the reverse of dissonance). Learning Ivan Pavlov Classical conditioning. Neutral stimulus (bell) paired with food (UCS) becomes a conditioned stimulus producing salivation (CR). Terms: acquisition, extinction, spontaneous recovery, generalisation, discrimination. John B. Watson Behaviourism founder. Little Albert: conditioned a baby to fear a white rat (paired with a loud noise); fear generalised to furry things. Edward Thorndike Law of effect (cat puzzle box): responses followed by satisfaction are stamped in. Precursor to operant conditioning. B. F. Skinner Operant conditioning. Behaviour shaped by consequences. Reinforcement schedules: variable-ratio gives the highest, most extinction-resistant response rate. Positive/negative reinforcement both increase behaviour; punishment decreases it. Albert Bandura Social learning / Bobo doll: children imitated aggression they observed , no direct reward needed. Also self-efficacy and reciprocal determinism. Edward Tolman Latent learning + cognitive maps (purposive behaviourism). Tolman & Honzik maze: the group given a reward only from day 11 suddenly matched the always-rewarded group, proving they'd learned the maze all along without reinforcement. Behaviour is goal-directed ; animals build a mental "map." Trap: learning ≠ performance. Julian Rotter Social learning theory + locus of control. Behaviour potential = expectancy × reinforcement value . Internal LOC ("I control my outcomes") vs external LOC ("luck/fate/others do"); measured by his I–E Scale . Cognitive bridge between behaviourism and personality. Memory Ebbinghaus Forgetting curve using nonsense syllables; most forgetting happens fast then levels off. Also the spacing effect. Miller "Magic number 7 ± 2" : short-term memory holds about 5–9 chunks. Alan Baddeley Working memory model (4 parts): central executive, phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad, episodic buffer. Replaced the single STM box. Endel Tulving Long-term memory split: episodic (events) vs semantic (facts) vs procedural (skills). Elizabeth Loftus Misinformation effect: leading questions distort eyewitness memory ("smashed" vs "hit" changed speed estimates). Memory is reconstructive. Frederic Bartlett Reconstructive memory + schemas ("War of the Ghosts"): recall is rebuilt to fit existing schemas, not replayed. Development Jean Piaget 4 cognitive stages: sensorimotor (object permanence), preoperational (egocentrism, no conservation), concrete operational (conservation), formal operational (abstract). Assimilation vs accommodation. Lev Vygotsky Sociocultural: learning is social. Zone of proximal development = gap between what a child can do alone vs with help; scaffolding . Erik Erikson 8 psychosocial stages , each a crisis (e.g. trust vs mistrust, identity vs role confusion in adolescence). Spans the whole lifespan. Lawrence Kohlberg Moral development: 3 levels (pre-conventional, conventional, post-conventional), 6 stages. Trap: Carol Gilligan criticised it as male-biased and added the ethic of care . Bowlby / Ainsworth Attachment. Ainsworth's Strange Situation → secure, anxious-ambivalent, avoidant (+ disorganised). Harry Harlow's monkeys: contact comfort beats food. Personality Sigmund Freud Psychoanalysis: id–ego–superego; 5 psychosexual stages (oral, anal, phallic, latency, genital); defence mechanisms; unconscious. Carl Jung Analytical psychology: collective unconscious, archetypes, introversion/extraversion. Alfred Adler Individual psychology: inferiority complex, striving for superiority, birth order. Eysenck / Cattell / Allport Trait theorists: Hans Eysenck = PEN (3 dims); Raymond Cattell = 16 PF ; Gordon Allport = cardinal/central/secondary. Big Five (OCEAN) is the dominant model now. Rogers / Maslow Humanistic: Carl Rogers = client-centred, unconditional positive regard, congruence; Abraham Maslow = hierarchy of needs → self-actualisation. Intelligence & therapy Spearman Two-factor: general g + specific s ; invented factor analysis. Gardner / Sternberg Howard Gardner = multiple intelligences (8); Robert Sternberg = triarchic (analytical, creative, practical). Binet / Terman / Wechsler Binet = first practical test (mental age); Lewis Terman = Stanford-Binet, IQ ratio; Wechsler = WAIS/WISC, deviation IQ (mean 100, SD 15). Beck / Ellis Aaron Beck = cognitive triad + CBT; Albert Ellis = REBT , the ABC model. Both target distorted thinking. Selye / Lazarus Hans Selye = General Adaptation Syndrome (alarm, resistance, exhaustion); Lazarus = cognitive appraisal of stress (primary/secondary). 9.2 Durations & numbers Item Lock this Major depressive episode at least 2 weeks Persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia) at least 2 years (1 year in children) Manic episode at least 1 week (or any length if hospitalised) Hypomanic episode at least 4 days Generalised anxiety disorder at least 6 months PTSD symptoms longer than 1 month Acute stress disorder 3 days to 1 month Schizophrenia 6 months total, at least 1 month active phase Schizophreniform 1 to 6 months Brief psychotic disorder 1 day to 1 month Insomnia disorder 3 nights per week for at least 3 months Iconic memory (visual sensory) about 0.25 to 1 second (George Sperling) Echoic memory (auditory sensory) about 2 to 4 seconds Short-term memory 15 to 30 seconds, capacity 7 plus or minus 2 (Miller) IQ standard deviation Wechsler 15, Stanford-Binet 16 (SB-5 uses 15) 9.3 Components & "how many" Model The parts DBT (4 skill modules) mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation, interpersonal effectiveness ACT hexaflex (6) acceptance, defusion, present moment, self-as-context, values, committed action Carl Rogers' core conditions (3) congruence/genuineness, unconditional positive regard, empathy Aaron Beck's cognitive triad (3) negative view of self, world, future Ellis ABC Activating event, Belief, Consequence Big Five (OCEAN) Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, Neuroticism Baddeley working memory (4) central executive, phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad, episodic buffer Kubler-Ross (5) denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance Yalom therapeutic factors 11 (e.g. universality, instillation of hope, catharsis, group cohesiveness) Piaget stages (4) sensorimotor, preoperational, concrete operational, formal operational Lawrence Kohlberg 3 levels (pre-conventional, conventional, post-conventional), 6 stages 9.4 General psychology nuggets Area Lock this Perception: psychophysics Weber's law (JND is a constant proportion of the stimulus); Fechner's law (sensation grows with the log of intensity) Perception: signal detection hit / miss / false alarm / correct rejection; d-prime = sensitivity, beta = response criterion Perception: feature integration (Treisman) preattentive feature detection, then attention binds features into objects Gestalt laws proximity, similarity, closure, continuity, common fate, figure-ground Attention models Broadbent early-selection filter; Treisman attenuation; Deutsch-Norman late selection; Stroop = automatic reading interferes Memory model Atkinson-Shiffrin: sensory then short-term then long-term; serial position = primacy + recency Emotion theories James-Lange (arousal then emotion), Cannon-Bard (simultaneous), Schachter-Singer two-factor (arousal + label), Lazarus (appraisal first) Arousal Yerkes-Dodson: performance is best at moderate arousal (inverted U) Reinforcement schedules variable ratio gives the highest steady rate and is most resistant to extinction 9.5 Landmark experiments Study Showed Stanley Milgram Obedience to authority (65 percent went to the maximum shock) Solomon Asch Conformity to a wrong majority Philip Zimbardo (Stanford Prison) Power of assigned roles / situation Darley & Bibb Latane Bystander effect, diffusion of responsibility (Kitty Genovese) Festinger & Carlsmith Cognitive dissonance (the 1 dollar group changed attitude more than the 20 dollar group) Muzafer Sherif (Robbers Cave) Realistic conflict; superordinate goals reduce it Henri Tajfel (minimal group) Social identity, in-group favouritism from arbitrary grouping Albert Bandura (Bobo doll) Observational learning / modelling of aggression Martin Seligman Learned helplessness TRAP: James-Lange = body first ("I tremble, therefore I am afraid"). Cannon-Bard = body and feeling at once. Schachter-Singer = body plus a cognitive label. Mixing these up is a classic exam trap. 9.6 Schools / perspectives of psychology Perspective Core idea · key name Structuralism Break consciousness into elements via introspection · Wundt, Edward Titchener Functionalism What is the purpose of behaviour (adaptation) · William James Behaviourism Only observable behaviour; stimulus–response · John B. Watson, Skinner, Ivan Pavlov Gestalt "The whole is more than the sum of parts" · Max Wertheimer, Koffka, Köhler Psychoanalytic Unconscious drives, early childhood · Sigmund Freud Humanistic ("3rd force") Free will, self-actualisation, growth · Rogers, Abraham Maslow Cognitive Mind as information processor; memory, thinking · Ulric Neisser Biological / Evolutionary Behaviour from brain, genes, neurochemistry / shaped by natural selection Trigger: "lab + introspection" → Wundt/structuralism. "purpose/adaptation" → James/functionalism. "whole > parts" → Gestalt. "free will/self-actualisation" → humanistic. 9.7 Motivation & drive Theory Says Abraham Maslow's hierarchy Physiological → safety → love/belonging → esteem → self-actualisation . Lower needs first Drive-reduction (Clark Hull) Need → drive → behaviour to restore homeostasis Arousal / Yerkes-Dodson Seek optimal arousal; moderate arousal = best performance (inverted-U); hard tasks need lower arousal Incentive theory Pulled by external rewards (vs pushed by internal drives) Intrinsic vs extrinsic For its own sake vs for a reward. Overjustification effect : paying for an enjoyed task kills intrinsic motivation Self-determination (Edward Deci & Richard Ryan) Three needs: autonomy, competence, relatedness David McClelland Need for achievement, affiliation, power 9.8 States of consciousness (sleep one-glance) Item Recall Sleep stages NREM 1→2→3 (deep / slow-wave / delta), then REM (dreaming, paralysis, EEG looks awake) Cycle length ~90 min; REM lengthens toward morning Circadian rhythm ~24 hr clock; suprachiasmatic nucleus + melatonin (pineal) Sleep spindles / K-complexes Hallmark of Stage 2 NREM Delta waves Stage 3 deep sleep; sleepwalking / night terrors arise here 9.9 Personality — theories & types Approach One thing to remember Big Five (OCEAN) Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, Neuroticism — the dominant trait model Hans Eysenck Three dimensions: Extraversion, Neuroticism, Psychoticism (PEN); biologically based Raymond Cattell 16 PF ; source vs surface traits; factor analysis Gordon Allport Cardinal, central, secondary traits Sigmund Freud (structural) Id (pleasure) – Ego (reality) – Superego (morality) Albert Bandura Reciprocal determinism : person ↔ behaviour ↔ environment; self-efficacy Carl Rogers Self-concept; congruence between real and ideal self; conditions of worth Locus of control (Julian Rotter) Internal ("I control outcomes") vs external ("luck/fate does") 9.10 Intelligence — theories Theorist Model Spearman Two-factor: general g + specific s ; factor analysis Thurstone 7 primary mental abilities (no single g) Cattell-Horn Fluid (novel reasoning, declines with age) vs crystallised (knowledge, stable/rises) Howard Gardner Multiple intelligences (linguistic, logical, musical, spatial, bodily, inter/intra-personal, naturalist) Robert Sternberg Triarchic : analytical, creative, practical Goleman / Salovey-Mayer Emotional intelligence (perceive, use, understand, manage emotion) Cross-link: IQ scoring, deviation IQ, WAIS/WISC subtests live in §4 Assessment ; "scaled score 10 = 50th percentile" is your mock miss. 9.11 Freudian defense mechanisms Defense Quick example Repression Push a threatening thought out of awareness (the master defense) Denial Refuse to accept reality ("I'm not sick") Projection Attribute your own impulse to someone else ("you hate me") Displacement Redirect a feeling to a safer target (yell at the dog, not the boss) Sublimation Channel an impulse into a useful act (aggression → surgery/sport) — the "mature" one Reaction formation Act the opposite of the true feeling (hate disguised as overcare) Rationalisation Logical-sounding excuse for the real motive ("I didn't want it anyway") Regression Revert to an earlier developmental stage under stress Intellectualisation / Undoing Use abstract thinking to avoid the feeling / ritually cancel an act 9.12 Heuristics & cognitive biases Bias / heuristic What it is Availability heuristic (Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman, 1973) Judge likelihood by how easily examples come to mind (plane crashes feel common) Representativeness Judge by resemblance to a prototype; ignores base rates Anchoring Over-rely on the first number/info given Confirmation bias (Peter Wason, 1960) Seek info that confirms what you already believe Framing effect (Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman, 1981) Same info, different wording → different choice (90% survive vs 10% die) Hindsight bias (Baruch Fischhoff, 1975) "I knew it all along" after the outcome is known Functional fixedness / Mental set Can't see a novel use for an object / stuck on a strategy that worked before 9.13 Learning — fast contrasts Pair Difference Classical vs operant Ivan Pavlov: involuntary, stimulus pairing. B. F. Skinner: voluntary, consequences shape behaviour Positive vs negative Positive = add a stimulus; Negative = remove one. Reinforcement ↑ behaviour, punishment ↓ it Escape vs avoidance Escape ends an aversive stimulus already on; avoidance prevents its onset (your mock miss) Shaping / spontaneous recovery Reward successive approximations / an extinguished response briefly returns after a pause Conditioning detail (escape/avoidance, alliance, object relations) is in §5 ; emotion-theory and psychophysics rows are in 9.4 above. 9.14 Biostatistics rapid recall NIMHANS's biggest gap Cue Lock this Choosing the test — 2 groups, parametric independent t-test (paired data → paired t-test) 3+ groups, parametric ANOVA (one-way); repeated measures if same subjects 2 groups, non-parametric Mann-Whitney U (paired → Wilcoxon signed-rank) 3+ groups, non-parametric Kruskal-Wallis Two categorical variables Chi-square (Fisher's exact if cells small) Strength of a linear relationship Pearson r (parametric) / Spearman rho (ranks) Odds ratio / relative risk = 1 no association ; >1 = risk, <1 = protective (your mock miss) NNT = 1 / ARR ; ARR = control event rate − treatment event rate Type I error (alpha) false positive — reject a true null Type II error (beta) false negative — keep a false null; power = 1 − beta p-value P(data this extreme if null true). NOT the probability the null is true Sensitivity vs specificity Sensitivity = true-positive rate ( SnNout , rules out); specificity = true-negative rate ( SpPin , rules in) PPV / NPV depend on prevalence ; sensitivity/specificity do not Skew Positive (right) skew: mean > median > mode ; tail points to the higher numbers Parametric assumptions normal distribution, homogeneity of variance, interval/ratio data r and r² r ranges −1 to +1; r² = proportion of variance explained ; correlation ≠ causation TRAP: "Data is plural" (one datum, many data). And p < 0.05 only means statistically significant, not clinically important or "null is false." 9.15 Assessment — reliability, validity & score conversions Item Lock this Reliability types test-retest (stability), inter-rater (between scorers), internal consistency ( Cronbach's alpha / split-half), parallel forms Validity types content, criterion ( concurrent + predictive ), construct ( convergent + discriminant ), face Reliability vs validity Reliability is necessary but not sufficient for validity; a test can be reliable but not valid, never valid without being reliable z-score mean 0 , SD 1 T-score mean 50 , SD 10 Deviation IQ (Wechsler) mean 100 , SD 15 (Stanford-Binet old = 16) Wechsler scaled subtest score mean 10 , SD 3 — so scaled score 10 = 50th percentile (your mock miss) Sten / Stanine sten mean 5.5 (SD 2); stanine mean 5 (SD 2) Normal curve 68 / 95 / 99.7 within 1 / 2 / 3 SD; percentile = % scoring at or below you 9.16 Abnormal — disorder → hallmark & first-line Disorder Hallmark · first-line Major depression 2+ weeks low mood/anhedonia · SSRI (+ CBT) Bipolar I (mania) 1+ week elevated mood · lithium / valproate (mood stabiliser); antidepressant alone can trigger mania Schizophrenia positive + negative symptoms, 6 months · antipsychotic; clozapine for treatment-resistant OCD obsessions + compulsions · SSRI (high dose) + ERP (exposure & response prevention) Panic disorder recurrent unexpected attacks · SSRI + CBT Specific phobia marked fear of object/situation · exposure therapy (systematic desensitisation) PTSD symptoms >1 month after trauma · trauma-focused CBT / EMDR; SSRI GAD 6 months excessive worry · CBT; SSRI/SNRI (buspirone) Borderline PD instability of mood/relationships/self, fear of abandonment · DBT ADHD inattention/hyperactivity · stimulants (methylphenidate) Trigger: "compulsions/rituals" → OCD & ERP. "fear of abandonment + DBT" → BPD. "treatment-resistant schizophrenia" → clozapine. 9.17 Neuro one-glance — cranial nerves, localisation, aphasia Item Recall 12 cranial nerves (order) O lfactory, O ptic, O culomotor, T rochlear, T rigeminal, A bducens, F acial, V estibulocochlear, G lossopharyngeal, V agus, A ccessory, H ypoglossal Sensory / motor / both " Some Say Marry Money But My Brother Says Big Brains Matter Most " (S/M/B per nerve) Broca's aphasia non-fluent, effortful, comprehension intact · frontal (Broca's area) Wernicke's aphasia fluent but meaningless, poor comprehension · temporal (Wernicke's area) Conduction aphasia can't repeat · arcuate fasciculus Frontal lobe executive function, planning, personality (Phineas Gage) Hippocampus forming new long-term memories (H.M. → anterograde amnesia) Amygdala fear, emotional salience Cerebellum balance, coordination, motor learning Hypothalamus homeostasis, 4 F's, drives the pituitary 9.17a Motor control — who does what classic NIMHANS swap-trap Structure Job Lock the trap Premotor cortex plans externally / sensory-cued movement (see it, reach for it); preps posture before M1 fires premotor = external / cue-driven SMA (supplementary motor area) plans internally generated, self-initiated movement; sequencing from memory + bimanual coordination SMA = internal / from within (premotor vs SMA = external vs internal) Basal ganglia initiate / select / gate movement; set vigour , scale force & amplitude "scales force / amplitude" → basal ganglia · resting tremor (Parkinson's) · chorea = Huntington's Cerebellum timing, coordination, balance, error correction; compares intended vs actual and smooths on the fly "timing / smoothing / coordination" → cerebellum · intention tremor, ataxia, dysmetria Two traps: resting tremor = basal ganglia, intention tremor = cerebellum. "Force/amplitude" = basal ganglia, "timing/smoothing" = cerebellum. Full version on the biopsych cheatsheet §8 . 9.18 The Acts, founders & "X is to Y" Pairing Lock this Mental Healthcare Act 2017 (India) — decriminalised suicide, right to treatment, advance directive RPwD Act (Rights of Persons with Disabilities) 2016 — 21 disabilities, replaced the 1995 Act RCI Act (Rehabilitation Council of India) 1992 — regulates training of psychologists/therapists POCSO 2012 — Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Wilhelm Wundt : ___ first psychology lab (1879) Binet : ___ first practical intelligence test (mental age) Aaron Beck : ___ cognitive therapy / cognitive triad Carl Rogers : ___ client-centred therapy Joseph Wolpe : ___ systematic desensitisation Beck vs Albert Ellis cognitive triad / collaborative empiricism vs REBT / ABC, more confrontational 9.19 Language — grammar traps & one-word substitutions Trap The fix Subject-verb agreement "Each / every / neither / one of" takes a singular verb; "a number of" = plural, "the number of" = singular Either/neither ... or/nor verb agrees with the nearer subject Fewer vs less fewer = countable, less = uncountable Between vs among between = two, among = three or more Lie vs lay lie (recline, no object) vs lay (put down, takes an object) One-word: fear of enclosed spaces claustrophobia (open/public spaces = agoraphobia) One-word: study of populations demography One-word: one who knows many languages polyglot One-word: incapable of being corrected incorrigible One-word: bitter attack in speech/writing diatribe (vs panegyric/eulogy = praise) Highest fast-marks section — grammar and vocab are pure recall, no reasoning. Deeper drills in §7 . Exam-day rules Longest option is often correct on these papers, but only as a tiebreaker, never over knowledge. "NOT" / "EXCEPT" questions — circle the NOT, you're hunting the odd one out. This is where tired people lose marks. Negative marking −0.25: answer if you can eliminate 2 options; skip a pure blind guess. Don't change a first instinct unless you find a concrete reason to. That's the whole syllabus on one page. Read it through once tonight, then on a second pass just the tables and the red trap boxes. Everything you flagged in the mocks is inlined here. You already scored 91.25 — tonight is about locking what you know , not learning new things. Stop early, sleep, trust yourself tomorrow. Sihan MET 2026 + NIMHANS prep · /notes/textbook/ · the one self-contained source · built 2026-05-22

title: Mock Debriefs & Weak-Spot Fixes
text: Mock Debriefs & Weak-Spot Fixes Every concept you got wrong, guessed, or flagged across all the mocks (MET Mock 1, the NIMHANS PYQ-based mock, the diagnostic-baseline drills, and the MPhil/PEP sets) consolidated into one corrective read, organised by topic, not by which mock it came from. Where a miss recurred across mocks it is marked as a persistent weak spot. This is where you fix what tripped you. Nothing is cut: every corrected answer, distractor analysis, mnemonic, and exam trap from the originals lives here, merged so each concept appears once. In this book The recurring weak spots (read first) Exam-day execution rules Biopsychology & neuroanatomy Neurochemistry, endocrine & pharmacology Famous cases & amnesias Assessment, IQ history & tests Research methods & biostatistics Psychotherapy: who founded what Abnormal psychology & classification Social psychology & the self Developmental psychology Cognitive: memory, learning, psychophysics, creativity Language & verbal reasoning MPhil layer: ethics, law, culture, MSE The recurring weak spots (read first) Across every mock the same clusters bled marks. These are your real syllabus, ranked by how often and how badly they recurred. Each links to its full fix below. Weak spot Where it recurred The fix in one line Pituitary / hypothalamus / endocrine axis NIMHANS mock (3 of 6 biopsych wrongs), diagnostic baseline FLAT PiG anterior pituitary; melatonin is pineal; cortisol is adrenal cortex , not medulla; hypothalamus integrates endocrine + autonomic Neuroanatomy: tracts, lobes, basal ganglia MET Mock 1 (6 biopsych wrongs) Corticospinal crosses at medullary pyramids; right parietal → left neglect; red nucleus is NOT basal ganglia Therapy school attribution MET Mock 1 (4 wrongs), NIMHANS (3 wrongs) Match technique → school → founder by trigger word; empty chair = Fritz Perls, musterbation = Albert Ellis, therapeutic community = Maxwell Jones Standard scores & WAIS structure Both mocks, diagnostic Subtest scaled M=10 SD=3; index M=100 SD=15; +1 SD = 84th pct; VCI + PRI = 3 core subtests each Reliability statistic ↔ concept NIMHANS, MET, diagnostic (Cohen's kappa missed twice) Kappa = inter-rater categorical; alpha/KR-20 = internal consistency; ICC = inter-rater continuous Sampling: stratified vs cluster vs non-probability MET Mock 1 + NIMHANS (quota/cluster swapped) Stratified = sample within strata; cluster = whole clusters; "can't compute sampling error" = non-probability (quota) ICD vs DSM durations NIMHANS (schizophrenia), MET (dysthymia, PTSD clusters) NIMHANS leans ICD: schizophrenia ≥1 month (ICD) vs ≥6 months (DSM); read which classification the stem names Named social-psych concepts NIMHANS (Genovese, Type D, anomie all wrong) Pure trivia: learn the named effect + its discoverer + its two-factor mechanism Sleep architecture (REM vs delta) Diagnostic (twice), MET Mock 1 (elimination) REM = atonia + wake-like EEG (paradoxical); delta/N3 = slow wave + normal tone; parasomnias (sleepwalking) are N3 "NOT / EXCEPT" negation-blindness Every mock — careless misses Underline the negation before reading options; this is your most expensive avoidable error High-yield Your self-notes are the syllabus. Every "wtf is X" / "never read this" / "don't know shit about this" you wrote on a question is a topic you had not opened. The same notes recurred across mocks, which means a gap left unfixed reappears. The NIMHANS mock sat at 71.25 vs an 80 cutoff (gap 8.75 = roughly 9 wrongs to convert); 6 of those wrongs were in biopsych alone, so fixing that one section clears the line. On MET Mock 1 your attempted-accuracy was 92% (49 right, 4 wrong) but you skipped 47 — there the gap was coverage, not accuracy. PYQ analysis of 300 NIMHANS questions (2023–25) shows Therapy + Abnormal + Biopsych together = ~49% of marks; that is where to spend time. Trap Your guessing is luck-loaded. On the NIMHANS mock you guessed ~17 times and got 14 right; that regresses toward ~50% on the real paper, so plan against a score nearer 68 than 71. A guess is only worth it on MET-style scoring (+4/−1) once you have eliminated 2+ options. Exam-day execution rules Underline NOT / EXCEPT / LEAST / ALL in the stem before reading options. Half your "knew it but got it wrong" misses are negation-blindness (the ACTH/melatonin pituitary question, the Bandura "not required" question). ~20% of NIMHANS PYQs are NOT-stems. On a NOT-question, pick the outlier , not the most familiar item. On antonym / odd-one-out items, find the outlier first. If 3 of 4 options agree in meaning, the 4th is almost always the answer (gregarious: 3 synonyms + reclusive). Read the relationship in the stem — synonym? antonym? part-whole? cause-effect? — before scanning options. Eliminate extreme-word options on RC main-idea questions: "every, always, never, all, none, only, must" are usually too strong. Pick the most general statement the passage actually supports. Hedging language ("can," "may," "in some cases," "a range of") → tone is "supportive but qualified," not absolute. If the stem names ICD, give ICD durations; if DSM, give DSM. If unspecified on NIMHANS, default to ICD (Indian exam). MET often leans DSM. Don't guess on biostats unless the RR/OR/HR/NNT table is firm. You were guessing 4–5 of 10 biostats questions — a coin flip on ~20% of NIMHANS marks. Pacing: 100 Qs / 90 min ≈ 54 sec/Q. Over 90 sec → mark and skip, return later. Don't change a first instinct unless you find a concrete reason. Last 5 minutes: never leave a blank where there is no negative marking; with −0.25, only answer if you eliminated 2 options. Length of options is not a reliable tell on the real paper — don't lean on it. NIMHANS uses heavy case-vignette stems; practise extracting the diagnostic core fast. Biopsychology & neuroanatomy This was the single biggest leak: 6 wrong on each of the two full mocks. You are not weak on biopsych in general — you are weak on where structures are , which side does what , and endocrine/neurology trivia . Lock the locations and the lesions follow. Motor & sensory tract decussations The corticospinal tract decussates at the pyramids of the medulla. You missed this twice (picked "pons" once, "spinal cord at level of entry" once). ~85–90% of fibres cross at the pyramidal decussation in the lower medulla to form the lateral corticospinal tract ; the remaining ~10–15% stay ipsilateral as the anterior corticospinal tract and cross only at the spinal segmental level (that is the trap behind the "level of entry" distractor — only the minor anterior pathway crosses there). Tract Function Decussation site Corticospinal (lateral, ~85%) Voluntary motor Pyramids of medulla Corticospinal (anterior, ~15%) Voluntary motor Spinal cord, segmental level Spinothalamic (anterolateral) Pain, temperature, crude touch Spinal cord, 1–2 levels above entry Dorsal column / medial lemniscus Fine touch, proprioception, vibration Medulla (caudal, internal arcuate fibres) Optic nerve (nasal fibres) Vision Optic chiasm (→ bitemporal hemianopia if sectioned) Trochlear (CN IV) Superior oblique Decussates before exit; only CN to do so + only one exiting dorsally Mnemonic Motor crosses in the medulla ; sensory pain/temp crosses in the cord ; touch/proprioception crosses in the medulla . So a hemisection ( Brown-Séquard syndrome ) gives ipsilateral motor + ipsilateral fine-touch loss + contralateral pain/temperature loss starting 1–2 segments below the lesion. UMN lesion = spasticity, hyperreflexia, Babinski up; LMN = flaccid, atrophy, fasciculations, areflexia. Lobe-by-lobe lesion signs You picked "prosopagnosia" for a right parietal lesion; the answer is left hemispatial neglect . Right inferior parietal (supramarginal/angular) lesions cause the patient to ignore the left side of space (eats only the right of the plate, draws only the right half of a clock). Prosopagnosia is right/bilateral fusiform (temporo-occipital), not parietal. Lobe / region Side Classic lesion sign Frontal (Broca, BA 44/45) L Broca's aphasia (non-fluent, comprehension intact) Frontal (orbitofrontal) any Phineas Gage: disinhibition, poor judgment, personality change Frontal (DLPFC) any Executive dysfunction, perseveration (WCST) Temporal (Wernicke, BA 22) L Wernicke's aphasia (fluent nonsense, poor comprehension) Temporal (medial) bilateral Anterograde amnesia (H.M., hippocampus) Temporal (fusiform) R or bilateral Prosopagnosia Parietal (inferior) R Left hemispatial neglect Parietal (Gerstmann) L Acalculia + agraphia + finger agnosia + L–R disorientation Occipital any Cortical blindness, Anton's syndrome (denial of blindness) The aphasia table (NIMHANS rotates these every paper) Broca's lesion = posterior inferior frontal gyrus (BA 44/45), dominant hemisphere → expressive aphasia: telegraphic, agrammatic, effortful speech, but comprehension relatively intact and the patient is aware their output is broken (hence frustration/depression). Type Fluency Comprehension Repetition Lesion Broca (expressive) Non-fluent Intact Impaired L inferior frontal (44/45) Wernicke (receptive) Fluent (nonsense) Impaired Impaired L superior temporal (22) Conduction Fluent Intact Impaired Arcuate fasciculus Global Non-fluent Impaired Impaired Large L MCA (Broca + Wernicke) Transcortical motor Non-fluent Intact Intact Above Broca, watershed Transcortical sensory Fluent Impaired Intact Below Wernicke, watershed Transcortical mixed Non-fluent Impaired Intact Both watersheds Anomic Fluent Intact Intact Angular gyrus / diffuse Mnemonic "Transcortical = repetition spared" because the perisylvian loop (Broca ↔ arcuate ↔ Wernicke) is intact, just disconnected from the rest of cortex. The "A" deficits (you asked "what's ataxia") Term Deficit Apraxia Can't sequence learned, purposeful movements despite intact motor/sensory function (can't mime brushing hair) Ataxia Loss of coordination and balance (cerebellar) — unsteady gait, dysmetria.
