Mechanism: waiters used cognitive strategies (look away, reframe as "cloud not food") → the hot/cool system (hot = limbic/impulsive, cool = prefrontal/regulatory). Caveat: Watts, Duncan & Quan (2018) found effects shrink when SES is controlled. Connects to executive function (Diamond), self-regulation (Mary Rothbart), delay aversion in ADHD (Sonuga-Barke). Thomas & Chess miss — and the rest of the dev canon Thomas & Chess NYLS temperament types: difficult child (the MET dev wrong, picked "difficult" correctly elsewhere but missed slow-to-warm-up — see above). Visual cliff (Gibson & Walk, 1960): depth perception by crawl age ~6–8 months (you picked "only after age 2"). Pre-crawlers perceive the cliff (HR drops) but only crawlers act on it. Erikson's 8 stages + virtues (NIMHANS Tier-1, both age range and virtue asked): Trust v Mistrust (0–1, Hope), Autonomy v Shame (1–3, Will), Initiative v Guilt (3–6, Purpose), Industry v Inferiority (6–12, Competence), Identity v Role Confusion (12–18, Fidelity), Intimacy v Isolation (18–40, Love), Generativity v Stagnation (40–65, Care), Ego Integrity v Despair (65+, Wisdom). Bandura observational learning (ARRM): Attention → Retention → Reproduction → Motivation. Reinforcement is NOT required — vicarious reinforcement is enough (Bobo Doll, 1961). You marked the "not required = reinforcement" question wrong by accident (picked Reproduction); also: reciprocal determinism, self-efficacy (4 sources: mastery, vicarious, social persuasion, physiological state), modelling (live/symbolic/verbal). Lawrence Kohlberg: pre-conventional → conventional → post-conventional (6 stages). James Marcia: diffusion, foreclosure, moratorium, achievement (exploration × commitment). Diana Baumrind: authoritative > authoritarian/permissive/neglectful (warmth × control). Urie Bronfenbrenner: micro/meso/exo/macro/chrono + PPCT. Harlow contact comfort; still-face (Tronick); Fantz preferential looking; DeCasper & Fifer (prefers mother's voice). Cognitive: memory, learning, psychophysics, creativity Baddeley working memory (you picked central executive for the binder) The component that integrates phonological loop + sketchpad + LTM is the episodic buffer (added 2000), a limited multimodal store . The central executive is the attentional controller (task-switching), NOT a store. Component Role Capacity / type Central executive Attentional control, task-switching Modality-free, limited Phonological loop Verbal + acoustic ~2 sec; phonological store + articulatory rehearsal Visuospatial sketchpad Visual + spatial Visual cache + inner scribe Episodic buffer (2000) Binds slave systems + LTM Limited multimodal store Related models: Atkinson-Shiffrin (1968, sensory → STM → LTM); Alan Baddeley & Graham Hitch (1974) replaced the single STM box; Cowan (focus of attention, ~4 chunks); Miller (1956, "magical 7±2"). Backward digit span = working memory. Memory taxonomy (Squire) + the episodic miss "What/where/when of an event" → episodic memory. Long-term — Declarative/Explicit (conscious; hippocampus + MTL): Episodic (events) + Semantic (facts). Long-term — Non-declarative/Implicit (unconscious): Procedural (skills; basal ganglia + cerebellum + motor cortex, intact in H.M.) + Priming + Classical conditioning + Non-associative (habituation, sensitisation). Sensory memory: iconic (visual, ~250 ms, George Sperling), echoic (auditory, ~2–4 s). Prospective memory = remembering to do something later. Anterograde vs retrograde amnesia; Ribot's law. Psychophysics (Weber / Fechner / Stevens + SDT) Weber's Law (1834): ΔI/I = k — JND is a constant fraction of intensity (1 candle vs adding 1 to 100). Fechner's Law (1860): Sensation = k × log(intensity). Stevens' Power Law (1957): Sensation = k × (intensity)^a (brightness ~0.33, length ~1.0, shock ~3.5). Psychophysics methods (Fechner): limits, constant stimuli, adjustment. Signal detection theory (Green & Swets): d′ = sensitivity, β/c = response criterion (bias); outcomes = hit, miss, false alarm, correct rejection; threshold is a decision under uncertainty, not a fixed value. Creativity (Wallas + theorists; "don't know this theory") Wallas (1926) 4 stages: Preparation → Incubation → Illumination ("aha") → Verification (some add "intimation" as a 5th). Theorists: J. P. Guilford (convergent vs divergent; Alternate Uses Test), E. Paul Torrance (TTCT: fluency, flexibility, originality, elaboration), Mednick (Remote Associates Test), Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi (flow; systems model = person + domain + field), Amabile (componential: domain skills + creativity processes + task motivation), Robert Sternberg (investment theory). Köhler chimps = insight learning. Other cognitive quick reference Heuristics: representativeness, availability, anchoring; algorithm vs heuristic; planning fallacy. Indian psychology (NIMHANS Tier-2): Triguna (Sattva, Rajas, Tamas); Ashtanga Yoga 8 limbs (Yama, Niyama, Asana, Pranayama, Pratyahara, Dharana, Dhyana, Samadhi — Karma is NOT a limb). Carl Jung: collective unconscious, archetypes (Shadow, Anima/Animus, Self, Persona), individuation, synchronicity (Oedipus complex is Sigmund Freud, not Jung). Gestalt principles: Prägnanz, proximity, similarity, continuity, closure, common fate. Kurt Lewin's life space / force-field. Language & verbal reasoning MET has a language section (6 wrong on Mock 1); NIMHANS does not. Mostly rule-recall — fix the rule once and stop bleeding marks. Antonyms / analogies (find the outlier) You picked a synonym (affable / verbose) for antonym items. If 3 of 4 options agree, the 4th is the answer. In analogies (GREGARIOUS:RECLUSIVE :: GARRULOUS:?), read the relationship first — it's antonyms, so garrulous → taciturn (not the synonyms loquacious/verbose). Word Synonym Antonym Gregarious sociable, affable, convivial reclusive, solitary Garrulous / loquacious / verbose talkative, wordy taciturn, laconic, reticent, terse Ephemeral fleeting, transient permanent, enduring, perennial Ubiquitous omnipresent scarce, rare Sanguine optimistic morose, pessimistic Magnanimous generous petty, vindictive Pragmatic practical idealistic, dogmatic Equivocal ambiguous unequivocal, clear Frugal sparing prodigal, profligate Capricious unpredictable steadfast, constant Obsequious servile, fawning domineering, assertive Pernicious harmful beneficial, salutary Grammar fundamentals Subject-verb agreement: Each/every/either/neither/none/anyone/everyone/somebody/nobody = singular ("Each of the participants was given…"). Either…or/Neither…nor → verb agrees with the nearer subject. Collective nouns (team, committee) = singular as a unit, plural as individuals. "A number of" = plural; "the number of" = singular. Data/criteria/phenomena/media are technically plural. Prepositions: insist on ; depend on; differ from (things)/with (people); comprise (no "of"); consist of; compare to (resemble)/with (analyse); discuss (no "about"); accuse of; congratulate on; complain about/of (a symptom). Parts of speech (suffix tells): adjectives -ive/-ous/-able/-ful/-less/-al/-ic; adverbs usually -ly; nouns -tion/-ment/-ness/-ity/-ism/-er/-ist; verbs -ate/-ify/-ise/-en. Predicate adjectives follow linking verbs (be, seem, feel, become) and describe the subject — "the data were inconclusive" → adjective , not adverb. Reading comprehension Main idea = the most general statement the passage supports; eliminate extreme-word options ("every, always, never, only") and options that are true-but-specific or that contradict the passage. Tone: hedges ("can," "may," "a range of") → "supportive but qualified," not absolute. Know: dismissive (rejects), sarcastic/ironic (means opposite), polemical (attacking), didactic (lecturing), laudatory (praising), cautionary (warning), indignant (angry at injustice), nostalgic (wistful). MPhil layer: ethics, law, culture, MSE The clinical-psych entrance layer that NET-style prep skips. Across the PEP MPhil-specific sets the weighting was: ethics/professional (~11), MSE/clinical assessment (~8), diagnosis (~6), trauma/therapy (~6), LGBTQ/culture (~5), history/legal (~4). APA ethics + ethical theory APA General Principles (5) Beauchamp & Childress (4) List Beneficence & Nonmaleficence · Fidelity & Responsibility · Integrity · Justice · Respect for People's Rights & Dignity Autonomy · Beneficence · Non-maleficence · Justice High-yield APA = 5 ("BFIJR"). Integrity = accuracy/honesty/truthfulness. "Equity" is NOT an APA principle — the relevant one is Justice (a classic distractor). Deontology (Immanuel Kant): judges by intrinsic rightness + duty (categorical imperative); consequences don't change rightness. Utilitarianism (Bentham, Mill): judges by consequences (cost-benefit, greatest good). The bait: an option that says "deontology = cost-benefit" is the reversed/wrong one. Competency, gifts, boundaries Competence: practise only within training/credentials; taking a case outside competence without supervision/referral is the violation. Ethical competency = ability to recognise and reason through dilemmas, not just know rules. Gifts: generally discouraged (boundary/dual-relationship risk); acceptable only when nominal/token value and refusing would harm the relationship or be culturally insulting. Large/quid-pro-quo = never. Dual relationships: avoid roles that impair objectivity. Boundary crossing (minor, sometimes benign) vs boundary violation (harmful/exploitative, e.g. sexual contact — always prohibited). Also: confidentiality + Tarasoff (duty to warn/protect). History & training models Name / model Owns Lightner Witmer Coined "clinical psychology"; first psychological clinic (1896, Penn) James McKeen Cattell Coined "mental tests" (1890); Wilhelm Wundt's student; US psychometrics Gordon Derner Professional/scholar-professional model; first university professional school (Adelphi) Scientist-practitioner (Boulder, 1949) Equal research + practice → Ph.D. Practitioner-scholar (Vail, 1973) Practice-first → Psy.D. Clinical scientist (McFall, 1990s) Research/empirical primacy RCI + Indian Acts Act / body The one thing tested RCI Statutory body under Ministry of Social Justice & Empowerment (NOT Health/Education); registers rehab professionals incl. clinical psychologists RCI Act, 1992 Created RCI; practising without registration is an offence; why an MPhil Clinical must be RCI-recognised Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 Rights-based; decriminalised suicide; advance directive + nominated representative; Mental Health Review Boards; capacity-based consent. Minors can appoint a nominated representative, views considered age-appropriately. Replaced Mental Health Act 1987 RPwD Act, 2016 Expanded disabilities 7 → 21; ≥40% = "benchmark disability"; replaced PwD Act 1995 National Trust Act, 1999 Welfare/guardianship for autism, CP, ID, multiple disabilities Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 2013 Age of consent → 18 (post-Nirbhaya) POCSO Act, 2012 Child = under 18; mandatory reporting of sexual offences POSH 2013 · JJ Act 2015 · UNCRC Workplace sexual-harassment of women; children in conflict with law; child = under 18 with evolving capacities + best-interests principle Minority stress + LGBTQ affirmative practice Minority stress model (Meyer, 2003): excess stress on stigmatised groups explains higher mental-health problems; it is unique (added on top of general stress), chronic , and socially based . Distal stressors = external (discrimination, violence, rejection); proximal = internal (internalised stigma, concealment, expectation of rejection). Depathologisation: homosexuality removed from DSM in 1973 (DSM-II); ICD-10 retained "ego-dystonic sexual orientation"; ICD-11 removed it entirely. Affirmative self-acceptance sequence: awareness → reducing internalised stigma → disclosure/coming out → community/connectedness → integrated positive identity. Affirmative therapy is one of the MPhil-layer modalities; ABA (autism), IPT (4 problem areas), Dodo Bird verdict (common-factors equivalence) also appear. MSE depth Consciousness: level of alertness; GCS grades it via Eye(4)+Verbal(5)+Motor(6), score 3–15 — measures consciousness, not attention/memory/IQ. Insight: patient's awareness of their own illness (distinct from orientation/consciousness/recall). Affect vs mood: affect = immediate, observable expression (quality, range, reactivity); mood = sustained internal climate (persistence). "Persistence" belongs to mood, not affect (a NOT-question trap). Thought form: flight of ideas (rapid, loose links) ≠ perseveration (repeats one idea) ≠ circumstantiality (over-detail, eventually arrives) ≠ tangentiality (never arrives). Culture-bound syndromes Syndrome Region Core feature Koro SE Asia, China Fear genitals are retracting into the body; fear of death Dhat India Anxiety over semen loss, fatigue, weakness Amok Malaysia Sudden violent outburst after brooding ("running amok") Latah SE Asia Exaggerated startle → echolalia, echopraxia, automatic obedience Pibloktoq Arctic / Inuit Sudden dissociative excitement, then amnesia Susto Latin America "Soul loss" from a frightening event Taijin kyofusho Japan Fear of offending/embarrassing others with one's body (vs Western social phobia = fear of being judged)

title: The Full Manipal Viva Sheet
text: The Full Manipal Viva Sheet 141 questions with model answers, word for word, in the order a clinical psychology panel actually walks through them. Built 6 Aug 2026 for the MAHE / MCHP M.A. Clinical Psychology department session on 7 August 2026 , App No 126202084. This is the answers page. The logistics, the slot finder and tonight's checklist are on the Manipal sheet . Questions 141 Format Q → model answer → the follow-up Answer length 20 to 40 seconds Drill mode hides every answer Every answer here is built to one shape, because that shape is what gets marked: definition, then theorist, then example . Say the definition in one clean sentence. Name who it comes from. Give one concrete instance, preferably from a real client or your own data. Then stop talking. A panel asking a viva question wants to know whether you own the concept, not whether you can talk for two minutes about it. The commonest way to lose marks in an oral is to answer correctly and then keep going until you say something wrong. Drill mode: off Reveal all Drill mode hides every answer. Read the question, say it out loud, then tap the card to check yourself. Jump to: 0 · The shape of an answer 1 · Openers 2 · Definitions Bank 3 · Core definitions 4 · MSE and assessment 5 · Psychometrics 6 · Psychopathology 7 · Therapy schools 8 · Development and psychodynamics 9 · Ethics and law 10 · Stats and methods 11 · Dissertation defence 12 · Vignettes 13 · Curveballs and the close 0 · The shape of an answer Question type Structure Length "What is X?" Definition in one sentence → theorist and year → one example → stop. 15 to 20 seconds "Difference between X and Y?" Name the dimension they differ on first, then one line each. Never list X fully then Y fully. 20 seconds "How would you manage this case?" Safety first → what you would rule out → assessment → provisional formulation → intervention → supervision. 45 to 60 seconds "Why do you think that?" Give the reasoning, then name what would change your mind. Panels mark for the second half. 20 seconds Something you do not know "I'm not certain, sir. My understanding is ___, but I'd want to check that before I state it." Then stop. 8 seconds Your three anchors. The M.Sc (you have the theory), the 250+ YourDOST clients across roughly 473 sessions (you are not theory-only), the dissertation with 214 participants analysed in SPSS by you (you can do research). Any question you have not prepared for, walk it back to one of those three. You are never empty-handed. 1 · Openers Tell us about yourself. "Good morning sir, good morning ma'am. I'm Mohammed Sihan. I did my M.Sc in Clinical Psychology at Jain Deemed-to-be University, Bangalore, 2022 to 2024. Alongside and since, I've been working as a counsellor on YourDOST, an online mental health platform, where I've carried over 250 individual clients across roughly 473 sessions, mostly anxiety, low mood, relationship distress and academic stress. My dissertation was a quantitative study on pornography consumption in relation to personality, aggression and sexual compulsivity in Indian young adults, 214 participants, Spearman correlations and logistic regression in SPSS. What I want next is structured clinical training under supervision, in a hospital setting, with real assessment and real diagnostic work. That's why I applied here." Forty-five seconds, all evidence, and it ends by handing them the next question. You control the follow-up instead of waiting for it. Why clinical psychology? "Three reasons, one personal, one academic, one professional. Personally, the work I've done on YourDOST is the only work I've done where I finish a session more awake than I started it. Academically, my M.Sc pulled me towards psychopathology and assessment specifically, the diagnostic side rather than the purely supportive side. Professionally, I keep running out of road with real clients: I can stabilise someone and do CBT work on a thought loop, but when there's an obsessive-compulsive presentation or a possible bipolar pattern underneath, my role is to refer, not to assess and formulate. I don't want to keep stopping at the referral." One personal line, one academic, one professional, and no sob story. The third reason is the one only somebody with real caseload hours can give. Why Manipal? Why this department? "Because of the setting. MAHE is one of the few places where clinical psychology training sits inside a full teaching hospital system, so it isn't classroom-only, there's actual patient contact and multidisciplinary work alongside psychiatry. Second, MCHP has a long-standing training tradition and dedicated faculty in the department, so supervision isn't an afterthought. Third, the structure of this programme specifically: a two-year MA with supervised practicum and a dissertation, on the RCI track, rather than a degree that leaves me academically qualified and professionally unlicensed. I sat the MET, I'm in the interview band, this is my first choice." Concrete without faking insider knowledge. Do not invent faculty names, centre names or accreditation claims. Vague-but-true beats specific-but-wrong when you are talking to the people who run the department. You already have an M.Sc in Clinical Psychology. Why a second master's? "The M.Sc gave me the academic base and the research training, and I've used both, I ran a full quantitative dissertation off it. What it didn't give me was supervised clinical practice inside a hospital, and that's the piece the RCI-recognised route provides. I'm not repeating a degree, I'm adding the supervised clinical training and the professional recognition my present qualification doesn't carry." Own it in the first sentence. Any hesitation here reads as "he couldn't get in anywhere else." What have you read recently? "Marsha Linehan's Building a Life Worth Living . It's her memoir, and what struck me is that DBT came out of her own experience of being on the wrong side of the treatment, being the patient nobody could hold. It changed how I think about validation. Before that I read it as a technique you apply before you get to the change work. She writes it as the thing that makes change possible at all, and I notice the difference in my own sessions when I skip it." Name one real book, one sentence on why, and make the why about your practice. Do not name a textbook, and do not name something you have not actually read, because the next question is always "what did you make of it?" What are your strengths? "Two. First, volume of contact hours, over 250 clients, which means I've built the reflex of sitting with distress without rushing to fix it. Second, I'm comfortable with data. I did my own SPSS analysis rather than handing it to someone, so when I read a paper I read the method section, not just the abstract." What is your weakness? "My clinical exposure is heavily weighted to online counselling with a relatively high-functioning population. I haven't worked on a ward, and I haven't sat with severe mental illness in an acute phase. I know the psychopathology academically, but I haven't seen most of it. That's precisely the gap this programme fills, and it's the honest answer rather than saying I work too hard." A real weakness that the programme fixes. Never give a disguised strength, panels have heard "I'm a perfectionist" a hundred times and it costs you credibility for the rest of the interview. Where do you see yourself in five years? "Working as a clinical psychologist in a hospital or an institutional setting, RCI registered, with a caseload that includes assessment and not only therapy. I'd like to still be doing research alongside it, in behavioural addiction and impulse control, which is where my dissertation sat. Longer term I'd want to supervise, but I'm aware that's a decade of clinical hours away, not five years." What if you don't get in here? "I'd reapply. I've also sat for the other RCI-track entrances this cycle, so I have parallel options, but the plan doesn't change: supervised clinical training, then registration. I've built a year of preparation around this and I'd spend another one on it if I had to." No desperation, no bluffing that you have nowhere else to go, and no implying you have a better offer. Steady is the right register. Why should we take you over the other candidates? "I won't compare myself to people I haven't met, sir. What I'd say is that I come in with three things already done: a master's in this exact subject, a completed quantitative dissertation I analysed myself, and 250-plus clients of real contact hours. Most applicants have one of those. So I need the clinical supervision from you, not the basics." 2 · Definitions Bank: the general concepts These are the ordinary psychology words, not the clinical ones. Every viva has a stretch where they stop asking about you and start asking "what is personality", "what is intelligence", "define learning". It is the cheapest section of the interview to win and the easiest to fumble, because you know all of this and will still ramble if you have not fixed the wording in advance. One shape for all twenty-nine: the definition in one line, the theorist attached, then the follow-up they always ask . Say the definition. Name the man. Stop. Let them ask the follow-up, and have it ready. The one mistake here. Answering "what is personality" with a list of theories. They asked for the definition, not the syllabus. Give the sentence, give the name, then be quiet. If you open with Sigmund Freud, Carl Jung, Alfred Adler and Gordon Allport, you have told the panel you cannot separate a definition from a topic, and they will keep pushing until you say something wrong. Define personality. "Personality is the dynamic organisation within the individual of those psychophysical systems that determine his characteristic behaviour and thought. That's Allport, and it's worth quoting because every word in it is doing work: dynamic, so it changes; organisation, so it's a system and not a list of traits; psychophysical, so it's mind and body together; and characteristic, so it's what's consistent about the person across situations." Trait versus type, or nomothetic versus idiographic. Trait approaches treat personality as continuous dimensions everyone sits somewhere on, so Gordon Allport, Raymond Cattell's sixteen factors, Hans Eysenck's three, the Big Five. Type approaches sort people into discrete categories, so William Sheldon's somatotypes, Carl Jung's introvert and extravert, Type A and Type B. Traits describe, types classify, and the modern evidence is dimensional, which is why the Big Five survived and typologies did not. Nomothetic means studying variables across large samples to find general laws, which is what a trait questionnaire does. Idiographic means studying the individual case in depth, which is what Allport himself argued for with personal dispositions and the case study. Say clinical work needs both: the psychometrics are nomothetic, the formulation is idiographic. Quoting Allport verbatim is the single highest-yield sentence in this whole section. They know the quote. Getting it word for word says trained, not read-up. Define intelligence. "Intelligence is the global capacity of the individual to act purposefully, to think rationally and to deal effectively with his environment. That's Wechsler. Global, because it's an aggregate rather than one ability, and effectively, because it's judged by how well the person handles the world, not by what's inside his head." The models, in order. Charles Spearman's two-factor theory: every task loads on general ability, g, plus a specific factor s, and g is what the positive manifold in the correlations is telling you. L. L. Thurstone rejected a single g and gave seven primary mental abilities, verbal comprehension, word fluency, number, space, memory, perceptual speed and reasoning. Raymond Cattell split g into fluid intelligence, reasoning with novel material, which peaks early and declines, and crystallised, accumulated knowledge, which holds up. Howard Gardner's multiple intelligences: eight relatively independent intelligences including musical, bodily-kinaesthetic and the two personal ones, criticised because they're closer to talents than to measured abilities. Robert Sternberg's triarchic: componential or analytic, experiential or creative, and contextual or practical, which is the one IQ tests miss. If they want the modern answer, say the Cattell-Horn-Carroll model is the one current test batteries are actually built on. Define memory. "Memory is the set of processes by which information is encoded, stored and retrieved. Three stages, and a failure at any one of them looks like forgetting from outside. The classic structural account is Richard Atkinson and Shiffrin's multi-store model, 1968: sensory register, short-term store, long-term store, with rehearsal moving material across." Alan Baddeley and Graham Hitch replaced short-term memory with working memory, because short-term store as a passive box couldn't explain how people hold and manipulate at the same time. Four components: the phonological loop for verbal and acoustic material, with a store and an articulatory rehearsal process; the visuospatial sketchpad for visual and spatial material; the central executive, an attentional controller that allocates resources and doesn't store anything itself; and the episodic buffer, added in 2000, which binds information from the subsystems and long-term memory into single episodes. On long-term memory use Endel Tulving: declarative or explicit, splitting into episodic, events with a time and place, and semantic, facts; against non-declarative or implicit, which is procedural skills, priming and conditioning. Anterograde amnesia is the clinical proof of the split, HM lost episodic learning and kept procedural learning. What is cognitive dissonance? "Cognitive dissonance is the psychological discomfort a person feels when they hold two inconsistent cognitions, and that discomfort motivates them to change an attitude or a behaviour to reduce it. Festinger, 1957. The classic demonstration is Festinger and J. Merrill Carlsmith, 1959: subjects paid one dollar to say a boring task was interesting rated it as more enjoyable than subjects paid twenty dollars, because twenty dollars is a sufficient external justification and one dollar isn't, so the only way to resolve it is to decide you actually liked the task." Where it shows up clinically. It's the engine of motivational interviewing: you deliberately develop discrepancy between the person's behaviour and their own stated values, and let the dissonance do the work rather than arguing with them. It also explains post-decisional regret, effort justification, and why insight alone doesn't change behaviour, because the cheaper route to reducing dissonance is usually to change the cognition rather than the act. Define learning. "Learning is a relatively permanent change in behaviour or behavioural potential that results from experience or practice. Kimble's definition, and the qualifiers are the whole answer: relatively permanent, so it excludes fatigue and drug effects; potential, because learning can occur without being performed; and from experience, so it excludes maturation." The distinction they want is learning versus performance, and it's Tolman's. His rats in the latent learning study formed a cognitive map of the maze with no reward, and it showed only when reward was introduced, so learning had happened without being performed. After that, name the types: classical conditioning, operant conditioning, observational learning through Bandura's Bobo doll, insight learning through Wolfgang Köhler, and verbal learning through Ebbinghaus. Define motivation. "Motivation is the internal process that initiates, directs and sustains goal-directed behaviour. It's inferred, never observed, you see the behaviour and infer the drive behind it. The classical account is Hull's drive-reduction theory: a physiological need creates a drive state, behaviour that reduces the drive is reinforced." Why drive reduction isn't enough, and what replaced it. It can't explain curiosity, exploration or play, where organisms increase arousal rather than reduce it, which is what the optimal arousal theories and the Yerkes-Dodson law handle. Then the hierarchy of needs, Abraham Maslow: physiological, safety, belongingness and love, esteem, self-actualisation, with the lower needs prepotent. Then the split that matters clinically, Edward Deci and Richard Ryan's self-determination theory: intrinsic motivation from autonomy, competence and relatedness against extrinsic motivation from external reward, and the over-justification effect, where rewarding an intrinsically motivated behaviour reduces it. David McClelland's need for achievement, affiliation and power is the one to add if they're asking in an organisational frame. Define emotion. "An emotion is a complex reaction pattern with three components: a subjective feeling, a physiological arousal response, and a behavioural or expressive response. So it's what you feel, what your body does, and what shows on your face." The four theories, and the order they came in is the answer. James-Lange: the bodily change comes first and the emotion is your perception of it, you're afraid because you run. Cannon-Bard: the thalamus sends signals to cortex and body simultaneously, so feeling and arousal are parallel, not sequential, because visceral changes are too slow and too undifferentiated to produce distinct emotions. Stanley Schachter and Jerome Singer's two-factor theory: emotion is undifferentiated arousal plus a cognitive label taken from the situation, which is the adrenaline study with the confederate. Lazarus: cognitive appraisal comes first, primary appraisal asks is this a threat to me, secondary asks can I cope with it, and the emotion follows the appraisal. Say the Lazarus line last, because appraisal is what CBT operates on. If they ask mood versus emotion, mood is longer, lower in intensity and usually without a clear object; emotion is short, intense and directed at something. Define perception. "Perception is the process of organising and interpreting sensory information so that it has meaning. Sensation is the raw registration of the stimulus by the receptor, perception is what the brain makes of it, which is why the same retinal image can be seen two ways in an ambiguous figure." Bottom-up versus top-down. Gibson's direct or bottom-up theory says the optic array contains enough information for perception without inference, and there's no need for the brain to add anything. Gregory's constructivist or top-down theory says perception is an active hypothesis built from fragmentary sensory data plus stored knowledge, which is why illusions happen, the hypothesis is wrong. The reconciliation is that Gibson works for rich viewing conditions and Gregory works for poor, degraded or ambiguous ones. Add the Gestalt organising laws, figure and ground, proximity, similarity, closure, continuity and common fate, and add perceptual constancy, size, shape, colour and brightness, which is what makes the illusions work. Define attention. "The best definition is still William James: 'It is the taking possession by the mind, in clear and vivid form, of one out of what seem several simultaneously possible objects or trains of thought.' Operationally, attention is the selective allocation of limited processing capacity to some stimuli at the expense of others." The filter models, in sequence. Donald Broadbent's early selection: a filter at the sensory stage selects on physical characteristics and blocks the unattended channel completely, which fails because people hear their own name on the unattended ear, that's the cocktail party effect and Neville Moray's demonstration. Anne Treisman's attenuation: the filter weakens rather than blocks, so unattended material still gets through if its threshold is low, and your own name has a permanently low threshold. Deutsch and Deutsch's late selection: everything is analysed for meaning and the selection happens at the response stage. Daniel Kahneman moved from filters to a capacity model, attention as a limited pool of resources allocated flexibly. Clinically, name the types: sustained, selective, divided, alternating, and say that sustained attention is what a digit vigilance test measures and divided attention is what a Trails B measures. Define consciousness. "Consciousness is awareness of oneself and of the environment, and of one's own mental processes. It's the one every definition struggles with, so give the two dimensions clinicians use: level of consciousness, meaning arousal, which runs from alert through drowsy, confused, stuporous to comatose; and content of consciousness, meaning what you're aware of. William James described it as a stream, continuous, always changing, personal and selective." Sigmund Freud's topographic model against the clinical assessment of consciousness. Freud: conscious, what's in awareness now; preconscious, what can be brought into awareness; unconscious, what's actively kept out and reaches you only through dreams, slips and symptoms. Clinically, altered states are sleep, dreaming, hypnosis, meditation and drug states, and the pathological alterations are delirium, which is a clouding with fluctuating attention, and the dissociative states, where consciousness is intact in level but split in content. Do not merge the two vocabularies, one is psychodynamic and the other is neuropsychiatric. Define attitude. "An attitude is a learned predisposition to respond in a consistently favourable or unfavourable manner towards a given object, person or situation. Allport, 1935, called it the most distinctive and indispensable concept in social psychology. Three components, the ABC model: affective, what you feel about it; behavioural or conative, how you tend to act; cognitive, what you believe about it." Do attitudes predict behaviour? Mostly weakly, which is LaPiere's classic finding, and the answer is the theory of planned behaviour, Icek Ajzen: behaviour follows intention, and intention comes from attitude, subjective norm and perceived behavioural control. For attitude change go to persuasion, the elaboration likelihood model, Richard Petty and John Cacioppo: the central route works through argument quality and produces durable change, the peripheral route works through cues like attractiveness and produces change that doesn't last. Leon Festinger's dissonance is the other route to change, and measurement is Thurstone, Likert and the semantic differential of Osgood. Define self-concept. "Self-concept is the organised, consistent set of perceptions and beliefs a person holds about himself. Rogers, and for him it has three parts: self-image, what you see yourself as; self-esteem, how much you value yourself; and the ideal self, what you wish you were." Congruence and incongruence, and it's the whole of Rogerian theory. When self-concept and experience match, the person is congruent and functioning; when experience is inconsistent with the self-concept, it's distorted or denied, and that incongruence is what produces anxiety and defensiveness. It arises from conditions of worth, positive regard given conditionally in childhood, so therapy supplies unconditional positive regard to dissolve them. If they want the wider literature: William James split it into the I, the knower, and the Me, the known, with material, social and spiritual selves; Cooley's looking-glass self and Mead's generalised other make it social; Markus calls the units self-schemas; and Higgins's self-discrepancy theory says an actual-ideal gap produces dejection and depression while an actual-ought gap produces agitation and anxiety. Define stress and coping. "Stress is a state of psychological and physiological tension that arises when the demands on a person are appraised as taxing or exceeding their resources. That's Lazarus and Folkman's transactional model, and the word appraised is the point: stress is not in the event, it's in the relationship between the person and the event. Coping is the constantly changing cognitive and behavioural effort to manage those demands." Hans Selye and the two-way split of coping. Selye's general adaptation syndrome is the physiological account, three stages, alarm with sympathetic activation and the HPA axis firing, resistance where the body sustains a high level of arousal, and exhaustion where the resources deplete and disease appears. He also separated eustress, facilitative stress, from distress. Lazarus is the cognitive account: primary appraisal asks is this harm, threat or challenge, secondary appraisal asks what can I do about it, and reappraisal updates both. Coping splits into problem-focused, changing the stressor, which works when the situation is controllable, and emotion-focused, changing the response to it, which works when it isn't, plus avoidance coping, which is the one that predicts poor outcomes. Add social support as a buffer and the Holmes and Rahe scale as the measurement. Define adjustment. "Adjustment is the continuous process by which a person alters his behaviour, or his environment, to achieve a more harmonious relationship between himself and his surroundings. It's a process and an outcome at the same time: adjustment as achieving a state of balance, and adjustment as the ongoing effort of getting there." Adjustment versus adaptation, and where maladjustment becomes a diagnosis. Adaptation is the biological term, changes in the organism that improve survival, largely species-level and evolutionary. Adjustment is the psychological term, individual and lifelong, and can be by changing the self, alloplastic versus autoplastic if they want the pair. Clinically, when the response to an identifiable stressor is out of proportion or impairs functioning within three months of onset, that's adjustment disorder, and in DSM-5-TR it now sits in the trauma- and stressor-related disorders chapter, not on its own. The healthy markers are realistic perception, ability to deal with stress, positive self-image, ability to express feelings and good interpersonal relations. Define creativity. "Creativity is the ability to produce work that is both novel and appropriate, so original and useful in its context, because novelty alone is just oddness. Guilford is the name to attach: he separated convergent thinking, which converges on the one correct answer and is what IQ tests measure, from divergent thinking, generating many possible answers, which is what creativity requires." How you measure it, and does it correlate with intelligence. Measurement is E. Paul Torrance, the Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking, scored on four dimensions: fluency, the number of ideas; flexibility, the number of different categories; originality, how statistically rare they are; and elaboration, the detail added. Process is Wallas's four stages, preparation, incubation, illumination and verification. And the relationship with intelligence is the threshold hypothesis: intelligence and creativity correlate up to roughly an IQ of 120 and are largely independent above it, so a high IQ is necessary but not sufficient. Define aptitude. "Aptitude is the potential or capacity of a person to acquire a specific skill or knowledge with training. It's predictive: it tells you what someone could learn, not what they've already learned." Aptitude versus achievement versus intelligence, and this is a three-way distinction they like because most candidates blur it. Aptitude looks forward, potential to acquire; achievement looks backward, what has already been acquired through instruction; intelligence is the general capacity underlying both, broader and less tied to a specific domain. The catch, and say it, is that the distinction is about the purpose of the test rather than the item content: the same item can serve as an aptitude item or an achievement item depending on whether you're predicting or measuring attainment. Examples are the Differential Aptitude Test, the General Aptitude Test Battery and the Minnesota Clerical Test. Define temperament. "Temperament is the biologically based, constitutional style of behaviour, the how of behaviour rather than the what or the why, present from infancy and relatively stable. It's the raw material personality is built on: temperament is what you're born with, personality is what experience makes of it." Alexander Thomas and Stella Chess, the New York Longitudinal Study. Nine dimensions, activity level, rhythmicity, approach or withdrawal, adaptability, threshold of responsiveness, intensity of reaction, quality of mood, distractibility, and attention span and persistence. Those cluster into three types: the easy child, about forty per cent; the difficult child, about ten; and the slow-to-warm-up child, about fifteen, with the rest not classifiable. The concept that matters clinically is goodness of fit, outcomes depend on the match between the child's temperament and the demands and style of the caregiver, not on temperament alone, so a difficult temperament isn't a prognosis. Add Buss and Plomin's EAS model, emotionality, activity and sociability, and Jerome Kagan's behavioural inhibition, which is the temperamental precursor of later anxiety disorder. Define conditioning. "Conditioning is the process of learning associations. Classical conditioning, Pavlov, is learning an association between two stimuli, so a neutral stimulus paired repeatedly with an unconditioned stimulus comes to elicit a conditioned response. Operant conditioning, Skinner, is learning an association between a behaviour and its consequence, so behaviour is shaped by what follows it." The difference, said properly, is respondent versus emitted behaviour: in classical conditioning the response is elicited and involuntary, and the stimulus comes before the behaviour; in operant it is emitted and voluntary, and the consequence comes after. Then give the classical processes: acquisition, extinction, spontaneous recovery, generalisation, discrimination and higher-order conditioning. And name the clinical applications, because that's the real reason they ask: systematic desensitisation and flooding are counter-conditioning, aversion therapy is classical, token economy and contingency management are operant, and Watson's Little Albert plus O. Hobart Mowrer's two-factor theory, classical acquisition of the fear and operant maintenance by avoidance, is the model behind every phobia. Define reinforcement. "A reinforcer is any consequence that increases the probability of the behaviour it follows. Skinner, and note the definition is functional, not descriptive: something is a reinforcer only if the behaviour actually goes up, which is why chocolate isn't a reinforcer for a child who dislikes chocolate." Positive versus negative reinforcement versus punishment, and it is the single commonest confusion in a viva. Positive means adding a stimulus, negative means removing one, and reinforcement always increases behaviour while punishment always decreases it. So negative reinforcement is removing something aversive to increase behaviour, taking the painkiller to remove pain, and it's not punishment. Then the schedules: continuous reinforcement gives fast acquisition and fast extinction; of the partial schedules, fixed ratio, variable ratio, fixed interval and variable interval, variable ratio produces the highest and steadiest rate and is the most resistant to extinction, which is the gambling answer. Add the Premack principle, a higher-frequency behaviour reinforces a lower-frequency one, and primary versus secondary reinforcers. What are defence mechanisms? "Defence mechanisms are unconscious strategies used by the ego to reduce the anxiety that arises from conflict between the id, the superego and reality. Sigmund Freud introduced the idea, Anna Freud systematised it in The Ego and the Mechanisms of Defence , 1936. Two features define them: they operate unconsciously, and they distort reality to some degree." Are they pathological? No, and that's the answer they're testing. George Vaillant's hierarchy is the way to say it: pathological defences, denial and delusional projection; immature, projection, acting out, passive aggression, regression and fantasy; neurotic, repression, reaction formation, displacement, intellectualisation, rationalisation and undoing; and mature, sublimation, altruism, humour, suppression and anticipation. Suppression is conscious and mature, repression is unconscious, and that pair is a favourite. Defences are pathological only by rigidity, by level, and by whether they're used where a more adaptive one was available. Repression is the primary defence, the one all the others are built on. Define insight. "Insight has two entirely separate meanings and you should say so before you answer. In learning, insight is the sudden reorganisation of the perceptual field that produces a solution, without trial and error, which is Köhler's work with Sultan the chimpanzee stacking boxes to reach the banana, and it's the Gestalt objection to Thorndike. In clinical work, insight is the patient's awareness that he is ill and that his experiences are the product of that illness." Grade the clinical one, because that's what they want. The traditional six grades run from complete denial of illness, through some awareness of being ill but blaming it on others or on physical causes, to intellectual insight, awareness of being ill and of the psychological causes, and finally true or emotional insight, where the awareness actually changes behaviour. David's 1990 model is the modern one and easier to defend: three components, recognition of illness, the ability to relabel unusual mental events as pathological, and compliance with treatment. Insight is a dimension, not a yes or no, and it's poorest in mania and in schizophrenia, better in depression and typically retained in the anxiety disorders and OCD, which is why obsessions are ego-dystonic. What is transfer of learning? "Transfer of learning is the effect of previous learning on the learning or performance of a new task. Thorndike's identical elements theory is the explanation: transfer occurs to the degree the two tasks share identical elements, which is why learning Latin doesn't improve general reasoning, against the old formal discipline view." The types. Positive transfer, prior learning helps, learning Spanish after Italian. Negative transfer, prior learning interferes, driving on the other side of the road. Zero transfer, no effect. Then direction: proactive transfer, earlier learning affecting later, and retroactive, later learning affecting the retention of earlier. Also lateral transfer, applying it to a task of similar difficulty, against vertical transfer, applying it to a higher-order task. Judd's generalisation theory is the alternative to Edward Thorndike, transfer occurs through the general principle understood rather than the shared elements, and Judd's water-jet experiment is the demonstration. Say why it matters: it's the whole rationale for homework in CBT, therapy is worthless if it doesn't transfer out of the room. Define forgetting. "Forgetting is the failure to retrieve information that was previously encoded and stored. Ebbinghaus mapped it with nonsense syllables and gave the forgetting curve: loss is very rapid in the first hour and then levels off, which is why spaced repetition works and cramming doesn't." The theories, and the honest ranking. Trace decay, the memory fades with time through disuse, weak because time alone doesn't predict loss, what you do in the interval does. Interference, which is the best-supported: proactive interference, old learning disrupting new, and retroactive, new learning disrupting old. Retrieval failure or cue-dependent forgetting, Endel Tulving, where the trace is intact but the cue is missing, and the encoding specificity principle, plus state-dependent and context-dependent recall, are the evidence for it. Motivated forgetting or repression, Sigmund Freud, where anxiety-laden material is kept out of awareness, which is clinically important and experimentally weak. And organic causes, so anterograde and retrograde amnesia. If they push on where the tip-of-the-tongue phenomenon fits, it's the proof of retrieval failure. Define thinking and problem solving. "Thinking is the mental manipulation of internal representations, images, concepts and propositions, to arrive at new information or a solution. Problem solving is directed thinking aimed at moving from a given state to a goal state when the route isn't obvious. Newell and Herbert Simon's framework is the one to name: a problem space with an initial state, a goal state, operators and constraints, and problem solving is search through that space." Algorithms versus heuristics, then the blocks. An algorithm is a systematic procedure that guarantees a solution but can be prohibitively slow; a heuristic is a shortcut that's fast and usually works but doesn't guarantee anything, so means-ends analysis, working backwards, and hill climbing. Then the obstacles: mental set or Einstellung, Luchins's water jar problem, where a previously successful strategy is applied to a problem it doesn't fit; functional fixedness, Karl Duncker's candle problem, where an object's usual function blocks you from seeing another use; and confirmation bias in hypothesis testing, Peter Wason's selection task. Add Tversky and Kahneman on the judgement heuristics, availability, representativeness and anchoring, because that's where the clinical relevance sits, in diagnostic error. Define language. "Language is a structured, rule-governed system of arbitrary symbols used to communicate meaning, and its defining feature is generativity: a finite set of elements and rules produces an infinite number of novel utterances. The levels are phonemes, morphemes, syntax, semantics and pragmatics." The nature-nurture debate, which is the only follow-up here. Skinner's Verbal Behavior , 1957, treats language acquisition as operant conditioning, imitation and reinforcement. Chomsky's 1959 review demolished it on three grounds: the poverty of the stimulus, children produce sentences they've never heard; the regularity of children's errors, "goed" and "mouses" are over-regularisations that were never reinforced; and the speed and universality of the sequence. His answer is a language acquisition device and a universal grammar, with competence separated from performance and deep structure from surface structure. The other name to have is Eric Lenneberg's critical period hypothesis, with Genie as the tragic evidence, and Vygotsky if they want the socio-cultural line, that thought and speech have separate roots and merge at about two, with egocentric speech becoming inner speech. Benjamin Lee Whorf's linguistic relativity, that language shapes thought, survives only in its weak form. What is group dynamics? "Group dynamics is the study of the forces operating within a group that determine how its members behave and how the group develops and performs. Kurt Lewin coined the term, and his field theory line is the one to give: behaviour is a function of the person and the environment, and a group is a dynamic whole in which a change in any part changes the rest." The stages and the group effects. Tuckman's stages of development: forming, storming, norming, performing, and adjourning, added later. Then the phenomena. Social facilitation, Norman Triplett and Robert Zajonc, performance improves on well-learned tasks in the presence of others and worsens on novel ones. Social loafing, Max Ringelmann and later Bibb Latané, individual effort falls as group size rises when contributions can't be identified. Groupthink, Irving Janis, where cohesion and the desire for unanimity suppress dissent and realistic appraisal, with the Bay of Pigs as the case. Group polarisation, discussion pushes the group's average position further in the direction it already leant, which subsumes the risky shift. Deindividuation, Philip Zimbardo. And the structural terms, norms, roles, status and cohesiveness. If you're asked why it matters, say it's the whole rationale of group therapy, and Irvin Yalom's therapeutic factors, universality, cohesiveness, interpersonal learning, are group dynamics used deliberately. Define leadership. "Leadership is the process of influencing a group towards the achievement of shared goals. The word is influence, not authority, which is what separates a leader from a manager: authority is given by position, influence is exercised regardless of it." The four eras of the theory, in order, and this is the whole answer. Trait theories, the great man view, leaders have inborn characteristics, which failed because no consistent trait set predicted leadership across situations. Behavioural theories, what leaders do rather than what they are, so the Ohio State studies with initiating structure and consideration, the Michigan studies with task-oriented and employee-oriented, and Kurt Lewin, Lippitt and White's three styles, autocratic, democratic and laissez-faire, where democratic produced the best morale and the best sustained work. Contingency theories, effectiveness depends on the situation, so Fred Fiedler's model with the least-preferred-coworker scale, where task-oriented leaders do best in very favourable and very unfavourable situations and relationship-oriented leaders do best in the middle, plus Hersey and Blanchard's situational leadership matched to follower maturity. And the modern pair, Burns and Bass: transactional leadership working through exchange and contingent reward, transformational working through idealised influence, inspirational motivation, intellectual stimulation and individualised consideration. Define prejudice. "Prejudice is a preconceived, usually negative attitude towards the members of a group, held on the basis of their group membership alone. Allport, The Nature of Prejudice , 1954, and his definition is 'an antipathy based on a faulty and inflexible generalisation'. Faulty and inflexible is the operative phrase: it survives contrary evidence, which is what makes it prejudice rather than a judgement." Prejudice versus stereotype versus discrimination, and they will ask it. Map them onto the ABC of attitude: the stereotype is the cognitive component, the belief about what the group is like; prejudice is the affective component, the feeling towards them; discrimination is the behavioural component, the actual unequal treatment. Then the explanations: Adorno's authoritarian personality, prejudice as a personality style arising from harsh parenting; Muzafer Sherif's realistic conflict theory, competition over scarce resources, the Robbers Cave study; Henri Tajfel's social identity theory, where mere categorisation into in-group and out-group produces bias with no competition at all, the minimal group paradigm; and scapegoating from the frustration-aggression hypothesis. For reduction, Gordon Allport's own contact hypothesis, and give his four conditions, equal status, common goals, intergroup cooperation and institutional support, plus Aronson's jigsaw classroom and superordinate goals from the Robbers Cave resolution. Define conformity. "Conformity is a change in behaviour or belief as a result of real or imagined group pressure, where the pressure is implicit and no direct request is made. Asch is the demonstration: judging line lengths, about seventy-five per cent of participants conformed to an obviously wrong unanimous majority at least once, and about a third of all critical trials were conforming responses, on a task with an unambiguous correct answer." Why people conform, and how it differs from compliance and obedience. Deutsch and Gerard: normative influence, conforming to be accepted and to avoid rejection, which produces public compliance without private acceptance; and informational influence, conforming because you believe the group is right, which is Muzafer Sherif's autokinetic effect study with an ambiguous stimulus and produces genuine internalisation. Solomon Asch's variations are the evidence base: conformity rises with group size up to about three or four and then plateaus, and collapses to under ten per cent with one dissenting ally, and falls when responses are written rather than public. Then the distinction: conformity is yielding to implicit group pressure from peers; compliance is agreeing to a direct request, Robert Cialdini's foot-in-the-door and door-in-the-face; obedience is following a direct order from an authority, Stanley Milgram, sixty-five per cent to the maximum shock. Kelman's three levels, compliance, identification and internalisation, is the neat way to close it. The one-line version of the whole section, for the last read on the way in: Concept One line The name to attach Personality Dynamic organisation within the individual of those psychophysical systems that determine his characteristic behaviour and thought Gordon Allport Intelligence Global capacity to act purposefully, think rationally and deal effectively with the environment Wechsler Memory Encoding, storage and retrieval of information Richard Atkinson & Richard Shiffrin; Alan Baddeley Cognitive dissonance Discomfort from two inconsistent cognitions, which motivates attitude change Leon Festinger, 1957 Learning Relatively permanent change in behaviour or behavioural potential resulting from experience Kimble; Tolman on learning vs performance Motivation Internal process that initiates, directs and sustains goal-directed behaviour Clark Hull; Abraham Maslow; Deci & Ryan Emotion Complex reaction pattern with a subjective, a physiological and an expressive component James-Lange, Cannon-Bard, Schachter-Singer, Lazarus Perception Organising and interpreting sensory information so that it has meaning Gibson bottom-up, Gregory top-down Attention Selective allocation of limited processing capacity James; Donald Broadbent, Treisman, Daniel Kahneman Consciousness Awareness of self, environment and one's own mental processes; level and content James; Freud's topography Attitude Learned predisposition to respond favourably or unfavourably to an object Allport, 1935; ABC model Self-concept Organised, consistent set of perceptions and beliefs about oneself Carl Rogers; James's I and Me Stress and coping Demands appraised as taxing or exceeding resources, and the effort to manage them Richard Lazarus & Susan Folkman; Selye's GAS Adjustment Continuous process of altering self or environment to achieve harmony between them Lazarus; DSM adjustment disorder Creativity Producing work that is both novel and appropriate Guilford divergent thinking; E. F. Skinner Reinforcement Any consequence that increases the probability of the behaviour it follows Skinner; variable ratio, Premack Defence mechanisms Unconscious ego strategies that reduce anxiety by distorting reality Anna Freud, 1936; George Vaillant's hierarchy Insight Sudden perceptual reorganisation (learning); awareness of being ill (clinical) Wolfgang Köhler; David, 1990 Transfer of learning Effect of prior learning on new learning or performance Edward Thorndike's identical elements; Judd Forgetting Failure to retrieve information previously encoded and stored Ebbinghaus; interference; Endel Tulving Thinking and problem solving Manipulation of internal representations; directed search through a problem space Allen Newell & Herbert Simon; Duncker, Luchins Language Rule-governed system of arbitrary symbols, defined by generativity Noam Chomsky vs Skinner; Lev Vygotsky Group dynamics Forces within a group that determine member behaviour and group performance Kurt Lewin; Tuckman; Irving Janis Leadership Process of influencing a group towards shared goals Lewin, Lippitt & White; Fred Fiedler; Bass Prejudice Antipathy based on a faulty and inflexible generalisation about a group Allport, 1954; Henri Tajfel; Muzafer Sherif Conformity Change in behaviour or belief from real or imagined group pressure Solomon Asch; Deutsch & Gerard; Milgram for obedience If they ask one you haven't got. Every one of these can be answered from the same skeleton even if the exact wording is gone: what it is in one sentence, the process or components it breaks into, one named theorist, and one example. Say that much and stop. A definition given in four clean sentences with one name attached marks higher than three minutes of everything you know about the topic. 3 · Core definitions These are the ones they actually ask. Definition, theorist, example, in that order, every time. Define clinical psychology. "Clinical psychology is the branch of psychology concerned with the assessment, diagnosis, formulation, treatment and prevention of psychological distress and mental disorder. The term was coined by Lightner Witmer in 1896, who opened the first psychological clinic at the University of Pennsylvania, and he later founded the journal The Psychological Clinic . In practice it's the discipline that takes a presenting complaint, converts it into a formulation using psychological science, and treats it, for example doing an ERP-based intervention for an obsessive-compulsive presentation rather than only offering support." Definition, theorist and year, then an example. That is the template for the whole section, and using it consistently is itself a signal you have been trained. Clinical psychology versus counselling psychology versus psychiatry. "The dimension is severity and role, not subject matter. Psychiatry is medical, an MD, so prescribing and physical treatments are theirs. Clinical psychology works with diagnosable mental disorder using psychological assessment and psychotherapy, and in India it's an RCI-registered profession. Counselling psychology traditionally works with adjustment, developmental and situational problems in a relatively better-functioning population. The overlap is large in practice and the boundary is about severity, setting and statutory scope of practice." How do you define abnormality? "There's no single criterion, so the working answer is the four Ds. Deviance, behaviour that departs markedly from cultural and statistical norms. Distress, subjective suffering. Dysfunction, interference with occupational, social or personal functioning. And danger, risk to self or others. No one of them is sufficient on its own, a religious ascetic is deviant without being disordered, and dysfunction is usually the most clinically useful of the four. Context and culture qualify all of them." Say all four, they mark for all four. The qualifier at the end, that no single D is sufficient and culture qualifies them, is what turns a memorised list into an answer. What is a case formulation? "A formulation is a working hypothesis that explains why this person has this problem now, linking predisposing, precipitating, perpetuating and protective factors to the presenting complaint. The 4 Ps. Predisposing is vulnerability, temperament, family history, early adversity. Precipitating is the trigger, the exam failure, the loss. Perpetuating is what's maintaining it now, avoidance, safety behaviours, family accommodation. Protective is what's working, intelligence, a supportive partner, insight. Unlike a diagnosis, which classifies, a formulation explains, and it's directly testable, if the formulation is right the intervention it implies should work." This is the single most useful thing you can say in a clinical viva, and it is the answer that separates people who have been supervised from people who have only read. If a vignette comes up, formulate before you diagnose. "Diagnosis or formulation, which matters more?" Then you say: "They do different jobs. Diagnosis gives you shared language, an evidence base and access to services. Formulation gives you the individual mechanism and tells you what to actually do on Tuesday. Two people with the same diagnosis can need opposite interventions, which is why the formulation is what I'd treat from." Difference between a sign and a symptom. "A symptom is subjective, what the patient reports, for example 'I feel low'. A sign is objective, what the clinician observes, for example psychomotor retardation or a flat affect. A syndrome is a cluster of signs and symptoms that run together, and a disorder is a syndrome plus distress or impairment plus a defined course." Mood versus affect. "Mood is subjective and sustained, the pervasive emotional climate the patient reports, the weather over a season. Affect is observed and momentary, what I see in the room, the weather today. So I record mood in the patient's own words and I describe affect on range, reactivity, appropriateness and intensity. A patient can report a depressed mood while showing a constricted affect, and that mismatch is itself clinical information." The season-and-day image is worth using out loud. It signals you understand the distinction rather than having memorised the sentence. Insight and how you grade it. "Insight is the patient's awareness that they are ill and that their experiences are a product of illness, plus their willingness to accept treatment. It isn't binary, it's graded: from complete denial of illness, through slight awareness with simultaneous denial, awareness but blamed on external factors, awareness that it's due to something unknown in the self, intellectual insight, up to true emotional insight where the understanding actually changes behaviour. Clinically the last step is the one that predicts adherence." Insight versus judgement. "Insight is understanding of one's own illness. Judgement is the capacity to make appropriate decisions and act on them, and it's assessed as personal, social and test judgement. A patient can have preserved judgement in ordinary situations while having no insight into a delusion, and the two are recorded separately in the MSE for that reason." Illusion, hallucination, delusion. "An illusion is a misperception of a real external stimulus, seeing a rope as a snake. A hallucination is a perception in the absence of any external stimulus, occurring in the external world, with the full force of a real perception and not under voluntary control, that's Esquirol's classic definition. A delusion isn't a perceptual disturbance at all, it's a disorder of thought content, a fixed false belief held with conviction against contrary evidence and not explained by the person's culture or religion." "What about a pseudohallucination?" Then you say: "It's experienced in inner subjective space rather than the external world, and the person usually retains some awareness of its unreal quality. Classic example is a hallucinated voice heard 'inside the head' rather than through the ears." Disorder of thought: form, content, possession. "Thought is examined on three axes. Form is how thinking is organised, so circumstantiality, tangentiality, derailment or loosening of associations, flight of ideas, thought block, neologisms. Content is what's being thought, so delusions, overvalued ideas, obsessions, phobias, suicidal ideation. Possession is whether the thoughts are experienced as the person's own and under their control, which covers thought insertion, withdrawal and broadcasting, and obsessions where ownership is retained but control is lost." Most candidates only know form and content. Naming possession as the third axis, and placing thought insertion there rather than under content, is a trained answer. Obsession versus delusion. "On insight and ownership. An obsession is ego-dystonic, the person recognises it as their own thought, finds it senseless and resists it. A delusion is ego-syntonic, held with full conviction as true, and not resisted. The boundary blurs in OCD with poor or absent insight, which DSM-5-TR now specifies with an insight qualifier." What is comorbidity, and why does it matter clinically? "The co-occurrence of two or more disorders in the same person, and it's the rule rather than the exception, depression with anxiety being the commonest pair. It matters because it worsens prognosis, complicates the treatment sequence, and often reflects a shared underlying vulnerability rather than two separate illnesses, which is the argument behind dimensional models like HiTOP and ICD-11's dimensional approach to personality disorder." 4 · MSE and assessment Take me through the mental status examination. "The MSE is a systematic cross-sectional description of the patient's mental functioning at the time of the interview. It's to psychiatry what the physical examination is to medicine, a snapshot of now, not a history. In order: appearance and behaviour, including general appearance, attitude, psychomotor activity, rapport and eye contact. Then speech, on rate, volume, tone, and relevance. Then mood and affect. Then thought, examined on form, content and possession. Then perception, hallucinations, illusions, depersonalisation and derealisation. Then cognition, which is orientation, attention and concentration, memory, intelligence and abstraction. Then judgement, and finally insight." Say it in order, without hesitation. Fumbling the order of the MSE in front of a clinical psychology panel is the single most avoidable loss in the whole viva. How do you test attention and concentration at the bedside? "Digit span forward and backward, serial sevens or serial threes if the patient's education makes sevens unfair, spelling a word backwards, and naming the days or months in reverse. I'd interpret them against the patient's education, because serial sevens fail for arithmetic reasons in someone with limited schooling and that isn't inattention." How do you assess memory in an MSE? "By time frame. Immediate retention and recall with digit span or three-word registration. Recent memory with events of the last few days and recall of those three words after five minutes. Remote memory with personal and historical information from years back. In an amnestic or dementing process recent memory goes first while remote memory is relatively preserved, and that gradient is itself diagnostic." What goes into a full psychodiagnostic assessment? "Referral question first, because it determines everything else. Then a clinical interview and history, the MSE, then psychological testing chosen to answer the referral question, usually an intelligence test, a personality measure, symptom rating scales, and neuropsychological screening where organicity is a question. Then integration into a report with a formulation and recommendations. A battery is never a fixed list, it's assembled around the question being asked." "It depends on the referral question" is the sentence that tells them you have thought about assessment as a clinical act rather than a set of tests. Which intelligence tests would you use, in India? "For adults, the WAIS-IV, and in Indian settings the Binet-Kamat Test and Bhatia's Battery of Performance Tests, which is especially useful where language or literacy is a barrier. For children, the WISC and Malin's Intelligence Scale for Indian Children, the Seguin Form Board for a quick performance estimate, the Vineland Social Maturity Scale for adaptive functioning, and the Developmental Screening Test. The WAIS gives four index scores: verbal comprehension, perceptual reasoning, working memory and processing speed." Objective versus projective tests. "Objective tests use structured stimuli and fixed response formats with standardised scoring, so the MMPI-2, 16PF, NEO-PI-R, EPQ. Projective tests use ambiguous stimuli on the projective hypothesis, that the person imposes their own needs and conflicts on the ambiguity, so the Rorschach, TAT, sentence completion, Draw-A-Person. The trade-off is that objective tests have stronger psychometrics but are open to faking and response sets, projective tests are harder to fake but have weaker reliability and validity, which is why the Rorschach needed a standardised system like Exner's." What does the Rorschach actually measure? "Perceptual-cognitive process rather than content alone, how the person organises ambiguous stimuli. Ten inkblots, five achromatic and five with colour. Scoring on location, determinants, form quality, content and popularity, and it's the structural summary that's interpreted, not any single response. Exner's Comprehensive System was the attempt to give it defensible psychometrics." Name the tests for organicity. "As a screen, the Bender Visual Motor Gestalt Test, and the MMSE as a bedside cognitive screen. For a full picture, the PGI Battery of Brain Dysfunction and the NIMHANS Neuropsychological Battery, which is the standard Indian battery and assesses attention, executive function, learning and memory, and visuospatial function. A screen tells me whether to investigate, it doesn't tell me where the lesion is." Which rating scales do you know, and what for? "Depression, BDI as a self-report and HAM-D as a clinician-rated scale. Anxiety, BAI and HAM-A. OCD, the Y-BOCS, which is the standard for severity and treatment response. Psychosis, PANSS and BPRS. Mania, the Young Mania Rating Scale. For diagnosis specifically rather than severity, the SCID as the full structured interview and the MINI as the brief one." "Rating scale or diagnosis, what's the difference?" Then you say: "A rating scale quantifies severity and tracks change, it doesn't diagnose. You can score high on the BDI in a grief reaction. Diagnosis comes from the clinical interview against criteria, the scale monitors it." What is standardisation, and what are norms? "Standardisation is administering and scoring a test under uniform, specified conditions so that scores are comparable across people. Norms are the distribution of scores from a defined reference sample, which is what makes an individual score interpretable at all. This is exactly why using an American norm set on an Indian population is a problem, and why the Indian adaptations, MISIC and Binet-Kamat, exist." How would you break bad news, or give feedback on a test result? "Feedback is part of the assessment, not an afterthought. I'd start from what they came in worried about, use plain language and no jargon, give the finding in one sentence, check what they've understood rather than assuming, name what it does and doesn't mean, and end on what happens next so they don't leave with a label and no plan. With a child I'd do it with the parents and separately in age-appropriate terms with the child." What is rapport, and how do you build it in the first five minutes? "A working relationship in which the patient feels safe enough to disclose accurately. Practically: open with their concern rather than my checklist, use their words back to them, allow silences, keep the first questions open, and be explicit about confidentiality and its limits at the start. In assessment specifically, rapport is a validity issue, not a courtesy, an unrapportful examiner gets an underestimate of ability." 5 · Psychometrics: reliability and validity What is reliability? "Reliability is the consistency of a measure, the degree to which it produces stable, repeatable scores free of random error. In classical test theory an observed score is a true score plus error, and reliability is the proportion of observed variance that is true score variance. It's estimated in four ways: test-retest for stability across time, parallel or alternate forms for equivalence, split-half where you correlate two halves and correct with the Spearman-Brown formula because halving a test shortens it, and internal consistency, where KR-20 is used for dichotomously scored items and Cronbach's alpha is the general case. Inter-rater reliability, Cohen's kappa, applies where scoring involves judgement." Naming Spearman-Brown as a correction for length, and KR-20 as the dichotomous special case of alpha, is the detail that separates a memorised list from an understood one. What is validity? "Validity is whether a test measures what it claims to measure, and whether the inferences drawn from its scores are justified. Content validity, does the item pool cover the whole construct. Criterion validity, does it relate to an external standard, which splits into concurrent, measured at the same time, and predictive, measured later. Construct validity, does it behave the way the theory says it should, which splits into convergent, correlating with measures of the same construct, and discriminant, not correlating with measures of different ones. Face validity is whether it merely looks appropriate, which is a matter of acceptability, not evidence." Relationship between reliability and validity. "A test can be reliable without being valid, but it can never be valid without being reliable. A scale that reads three kilos heavy every time is perfectly reliable and completely invalid. Reliability sets the ceiling on validity, because a test can't correlate with anything more strongly than it correlates with itself." Have the weighing-scale example ready. It is the fastest way to prove you understand rather than recall, and this exact question comes up constantly. What is Cronbach's alpha and what is an acceptable value? "A coefficient of internal consistency, the average of all possible split-half correlations, so it estimates how far the items measure a single underlying construct. Above 0.7 is generally acceptable, above 0.8 good, and for a clinical decision-making instrument you'd want above 0.9. It's inflated by test length, so a very high alpha on a long scale can mean redundant items rather than a good scale. My dissertation used the BFI-10, which has only two items per trait, so its internal consistency is inherently low, and I reported that as a limitation." Bringing your own instrument in, with its psychometric weakness named before they find it, converts a textbook answer into a research answer. Sensitivity and specificity. "Sensitivity is the proportion of true cases the test correctly identifies, so it rules disorder out when negative. Specificity is the proportion of non-cases correctly identified, so it rules disorder in when positive. They trade off against each other as you move the cut-off. For a screening instrument you want high sensitivity, because missing a case is costlier than a false alarm you can rule out later, and for a confirmatory test you want high specificity."
